docs.text: Installing Drift involves adding the core library, a database executor, and the code generation tools. Once installed and configured, Drift generates type-safe database APIs, allowing you to work with SQLite using clean, maintainable Dart code.

docs.title: Setting Up a Database
docs.text: Create a database class that manages your tables, database connection, and schema.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A Drift database is the central class that represents your application's SQLite database. It defines which tables belong to the database, manages the connection to SQLite, and provides the entry point for performing queries.

Every interaction with your database—whether inserting, updating, deleting, or querying data—starts from this class.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Instead of interacting with SQLite directly, Drift uses a database class to:

  • Group related tables into a single database.
  • Provide a type-safe API for queries.
  • Manage the database connection.
  • Track the database schema version.
  • Generate helper methods and data classes.

This gives your application a single, organized interface for working with the database.

docs.title: Define a Database Class
docs.text:
import 'package:drift/drift.dart';

part 'app_database.g.dart';

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users, Todos])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

Explanation:

  • part 'app_database.g.dart' includes the generated code.
  • @DriftDatabase marks the class as a Drift database.
  • tables lists every table managed by this database.
  • _$AppDatabase is generated by Drift.
  • super.executor provides the database connection.
  • schemaVersion identifies the current database schema version.

docs.title: Create a Database Instance
docs.text:
final database = AppDatabase(databaseConnection);

Explanation:

  • databaseConnection is a database executor that opens and communicates with SQLite.
  • Once created, the database instance can be reused throughout your application.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the database class as the application's database manager.

App
 │
 ▼
AppDatabase
 │
 ├── Users Table
 ├── Todos Table
 ├── Posts Table
 │
 ▼
SQLite Database

Instead of each table connecting to SQLite independently, the database class manages them all through a single connection.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A database with a single table.

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

Explanation:

  • The database contains only the Users table.
  • Drift generates APIs for querying and modifying users.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A task management application might have:

@DriftDatabase(
  tables: [
    Users,
    Projects,
    Tasks,
    Comments,
    Labels,
  ],
)
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 3;
}

Explanation:

  • Multiple related tables are grouped into a single database.
  • Increasing schemaVersion indicates that the database structure has changed.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Create a database class when:

  • Starting a new Drift project.
  • Managing one or more tables.
  • Organizing your application's local storage.
  • Providing a central API for database operations.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid creating multiple database classes unless your application genuinely requires separate databases.

For most applications, a single database containing multiple tables is easier to manage and maintain.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep a single database class for most applications.
  • Organize table definitions into separate files.
  • Register all tables inside the @DriftDatabase annotation.
  • Keep the database class focused on configuration.
  • Move complex queries into DAOs instead of placing them directly in the database class.

docs.title: Forgetting the generated part file
docs.text:
Wrong

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {}

Explanation:

  • Without the part directive, the generated code cannot be linked.

Correct

part 'app_database.g.dart';

Explanation:

  • Includes the generated implementation.

docs.title: Not registering a table
docs.text:
Wrong

@DriftDatabase(tables: [])

Explanation:

  • Drift won't generate APIs for tables that aren't registered.

Correct

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])

Explanation:

  • Every table used by the database should be listed here.

docs.title: Placing business logic inside the database
docs.text:
Wrong

class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  Future<void> completeProjectAndNotifyUsers() async {
    // Large amount of application logic...
  }
}

Explanation:

  • Mixing business logic with database configuration makes the class harder to maintain.

Correct

  • Keep the database responsible for persistence.
  • Place complex query logic in DAOs and business logic in repositories or services.

docs.text: The database class is the foundation of every Drift application. It brings together your tables, manages the SQLite connection, defines the schema version, and serves as the primary interface for all database operations.

docs.title: Code Generation
docs.text: Generate type-safe Dart code from your Drift database definitions.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Code generation is the process where Drift analyzes your annotated database classes, tables, DAOs, and SQL files, then generates Dart code that you use in your application.

Instead of writing repetitive boilerplate code yourself, Drift creates it automatically.

The generated code includes:

  • Database implementations
  • Data classes
  • Companion classes
  • Query APIs
  • Table metadata
  • DAO implementations

You should never edit this generated code manually.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Without code generation, you would have to manually write code for:

  • Mapping database rows to Dart objects.
  • Creating insert and update objects.
  • Building query helpers.
  • Validating table definitions.
  • Connecting tables to the database.

This is repetitive, error-prone, and difficult to maintain.

Drift generates this code for you, allowing you to focus on defining your database instead of implementing its plumbing.

docs.title: Mark Classes for Generation
docs.text:
@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

Explanation:

  • @DriftDatabase tells Drift to generate database code.
  • _$AppDatabase is created during code generation.

docs.title: Include the Generated File
docs.text:
part 'app_database.g.dart';

Explanation:

  • Connects your source file with the generated implementation.

docs.title: Generate the Code
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build

Explanation:

  • Generates all missing or updated Drift files once.

docs.title: Automatically Regenerate Code
docs.text:
dart run build_runner watch

Explanation:

  • Watches your project for changes and regenerates code automatically.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of code generation as a compiler for your database definitions.

Your Dart Code
    │
    ▼
Annotations
    │
    ▼
Drift Generator
    │
    ▼
Generated .g.dart Files
    │
    ▼
Your Application

You write the database schema.

Drift writes the implementation.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Suppose you define a table.

class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • This is all you write manually.

After running the generator, Drift creates:

  • A data class (User)
  • A companion (UsersCompanion)
  • Table information
  • Query helpers

All of this is generated automatically.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Imagine adding a new column.

TextColumn get email => text()();

After running code generation:

  • The generated data class now includes email.
  • Companion classes are updated.
  • Query APIs understand the new column.
  • Type safety is preserved automatically.

No manual updates are required.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Run code generation whenever you:

  • Add a new table.
  • Modify a table.
  • Create or update a DAO.
  • Change a database class.
  • Add SQL query files.
  • Update annotations used by Drift.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
You should not run code generation if nothing has changed in your annotated files.

Also, never attempt to replace generated files with manually written implementations.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use build_runner watch during development.
  • Commit generated files if it matches your team's workflow.
  • Never modify generated files.
  • Keep your annotations clean and organized.
  • Regenerate code after every schema change.

docs.title: Editing generated files
docs.text:
Wrong

// app_database.g.dart

class _$AppDatabase {
  // Modified manually
}

Explanation:

  • Your changes will be overwritten the next time code generation runs.

Correct

Modify the source file instead.

class Users extends Table {
  // Update the table definition here
}

Explanation:

  • Source files are the only files you should edit.

docs.title: Forgetting to regenerate
docs.text:
Wrong

Adding a new table but not running:

dart run build_runner build

Explanation:

  • The generated APIs won't include your changes.

Correct

Run the generator after every change to annotated Drift code.

docs.title: Missing the part directive
docs.text:
Wrong

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {}

Explanation:

  • The generated code cannot be linked without the part directive.

Correct

part 'app_database.g.dart';

Explanation:

  • Includes the generated implementation in your source file.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Code generation is a core part of Drift. It transforms your database definitions into strongly typed Dart code, eliminating boilerplate and providing compile-time safety. By defining your schema and letting Drift generate the implementation, you get a cleaner, safer, and more maintainable database layer.

docs.title: Your First Query
docs.text: Retrieve data from your database using Drift's type-safe query builder.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A query is a request to read, insert, update, or delete data from your database. In Drift, queries are built using Dart APIs instead of writing raw SQL strings.

Your first query is typically a simple SELECT statement that retrieves all rows from a table.

Drift converts these Dart APIs into SQL behind the scenes, while ensuring type safety and compile-time validation.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Writing SQL directly as strings has several drawbacks:

  • SQL syntax errors are only discovered at runtime.
  • Column names are manually typed and prone to mistakes.
  • Mapping rows to Dart objects requires extra code.
  • Refactoring becomes difficult.

Drift's query builder solves these problems by providing a fluent, strongly typed API that integrates naturally with Dart.

docs.title: Selecting All Rows
docs.text:
final users = await select(users).get();

Explanation:

  • select(users) creates a query for the users table.
  • get() executes the query.
  • The result is returned as a list of generated data classes.

docs.title: Selecting a Single Row
docs.text:
final user = await (select(users)
      ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1)))
    .getSingle();

Explanation:

  • where() adds a filter to the query.
  • equals() creates a SQL equality condition.
  • getSingle() expects exactly one matching row.

docs.title: Watching a Query
docs.text:
final stream = select(users).watch();

Explanation:

  • watch() returns a stream instead of executing the query immediately.
  • The stream emits new results whenever the table changes.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the query builder as constructing a SQL statement step by step.

select(users)
      │
      ▼
Add filters
      │
      ▼
Add ordering
      │
      ▼
Execute
      │
      ▼
SQLite
      │
      ▼
Generated Data Classes

You describe what data you want, and Drift generates the corresponding SQL.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Retrieve every user from the database.

final allUsers = await select(users).get();

Explanation:

  • Returns every row from the users table as a list of generated User objects.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Load all incomplete tasks.

final pendingTasks = await (select(tasks)
      ..where((t) => t.completed.equals(false)))
    .get();

Explanation:

  • Filters the tasks table to include only incomplete tasks.
  • Returns the matching rows as generated data classes.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use Drift queries when you need to:

  • Retrieve data from a table.
  • Filter specific records.
  • Load data for your UI.
  • Fetch related information.
  • Build reactive interfaces using streams.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid using the query builder when:

  • You need SQL features that Drift doesn't support directly. In such cases, use custom SQL.
  • You're performing database schema changes, which belong in migrations.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Prefer the query builder over raw SQL whenever possible.
  • Use watch() for data that should automatically update in the UI.
  • Keep complex queries inside DAOs.
  • Fetch only the data you need.
  • Reuse query logic instead of duplicating it throughout the application.

docs.title: Using getSingle() for multiple rows
docs.text:
Wrong

final user = await select(users).getSingle();

Explanation:

  • getSingle() throws an exception unless exactly one row exists.

Correct

final usersList = await select(users).get();

Explanation:

  • get() is intended for queries that return multiple rows.

docs.title: Using get() when reactive updates are needed
docs.text:
Wrong

final users = await select(users).get();

Explanation:

  • The result is fetched only once and won't update automatically.

Correct

final usersStream = select(users).watch();

Explanation:

  • watch() keeps the UI synchronized with database changes.

docs.title: Writing raw SQL unnecessarily
docs.text:
Wrong

customSelect('SELECT * FROM users');

Explanation:

  • Raw SQL bypasses Drift's type-safe APIs and compile-time checks.

Correct

select(users).get();

Explanation:

  • The query builder is safer, easier to refactor, and integrates with generated types.

docs.text:

  • Ordering
  • Limiting
  • Watching Queries
  • Insert
  • Update
  • Delete
  • Custom SQL

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Drift's query builder provides a type-safe way to retrieve data from your database. Instead of writing SQL strings, you build queries using Dart APIs, and Drift generates the SQL automatically. This approach reduces boilerplate, improves type safety, and makes database code easier to read and maintain.

docs.title: GeneratedDatabase
docs.text: GeneratedDatabase is the base class that all Drift database classes inherit from.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
GeneratedDatabase is the core database class provided by Drift. It contains the functionality needed to communicate with SQLite, manage tables, execute queries, run transactions, and handle schema migrations.

When you create your own database class, you don't extend GeneratedDatabase directly. Instead, you extend a generated class (such as _$AppDatabase), which itself extends GeneratedDatabase.

GeneratedDatabase
        ▲
        │
_$AppDatabase   (Generated)
        ▲
        │
AppDatabase     (Your Class)

Most developers never interact with GeneratedDatabase directly, but every Drift database is built upon it.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Every database needs common functionality, such as:

  • Opening connections
  • Executing SQL
  • Managing transactions
  • Registering tables
  • Running migrations
  • Watching streams

Instead of generating all of this code for every project, Drift places this shared functionality inside GeneratedDatabase.

Your generated database class inherits these capabilities automatically.

docs.title: Creating a Database
docs.text:
@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

Explanation:

  • _$AppDatabase is generated by Drift.
  • _$AppDatabase extends GeneratedDatabase.
  • Your AppDatabase inherits all database functionality through the generated class.

docs.title: Inheritance Chain
docs.text:
GeneratedDatabase
        │
        ▼
_$AppDatabase
        │
        ▼
AppDatabase

Explanation:

  • GeneratedDatabase provides the core implementation.
  • _$AppDatabase connects your tables and generated APIs.
  • AppDatabase is where you add your own database-specific methods.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of GeneratedDatabase as the engine of your database.

                GeneratedDatabase
         (Database Engine)
                     │
      ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
      │              │              │
 Transactions   Query Engine   Table Registry
      │              │              │
      └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                     │
             _$AppDatabase
                     │
              Your AppDatabase

Your database class doesn't implement these features itself—it inherits them from GeneratedDatabase.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A minimal database.

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

Explanation:

Although you never mention GeneratedDatabase, your database still gains:

  • Query APIs
  • CRUD operations
  • Transactions
  • Streams
  • Migration support

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
You can add your own methods alongside the inherited functionality.

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;

  Future<List<User>> activeUsers() {
    return (select(users)
          ..where((u) => u.isActive.equals(true)))
        .get();
  }
}

Explanation:

  • select() is available because your database ultimately inherits from GeneratedDatabase.
  • You can combine generated APIs with your own helper methods.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
You typically don't use GeneratedDatabase directly.

Instead, you'll work with your own database class, which automatically inherits from it.

Understanding GeneratedDatabase is useful when:

  • Learning how Drift is structured.
  • Reading generated code.
  • Understanding where database APIs come from.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Don't write:

class AppDatabase extends GeneratedDatabase

Drift generates an intermediate class (_$AppDatabase) that should always be used instead.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always extend the generated database class.
  • Let Drift manage the inheritance hierarchy.
  • Keep custom database methods small and focused.
  • Move larger query logic into DAOs.

docs.title: Extending the wrong class
docs.text:
Wrong

class AppDatabase extends GeneratedDatabase

Explanation:

  • This bypasses Drift's generated implementation and won't work correctly.

Correct

class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase

Explanation:

  • The generated class includes all table registrations and generated APIs.

docs.title: Modifying generated classes
docs.text:
Wrong

Editing:

app_database.g.dart

Explanation:

  • Generated files are overwritten every time code generation runs.

Correct

Modify only your own database class and regenerate the code when needed.

docs.title: Assuming GeneratedDatabase contains your tables
docs.text:
Wrong

Thinking GeneratedDatabase knows about your application's tables.

Explanation:

  • GeneratedDatabase is generic.
  • Your generated subclass (_$AppDatabase) registers the specific tables defined in your project.

Correct

Let Drift generate the subclass that connects your tables to the database engine.

docs.text:

  • Database Connection
  • Opening the Database
  • Code Generation
  • Defining Tables
  • DAOs

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: GeneratedDatabase is the foundation of every Drift database. It provides the core database functionality, while Drift generates a subclass that connects your tables and queries. Your own database class extends this generated class, giving you a clean, type-safe interface for interacting with SQLite without dealing with the underlying implementation.

docs.title: Database Connection
docs.text: A database connection is the bridge between your Drift database and the underlying SQLite database.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Before Drift can read or write data, it needs a connection to a SQLite database. This connection is provided through a database executor, which knows how to open the database file and execute SQL statements.

When you create your AppDatabase, you pass it a database connection.

final db = AppDatabase(connection);

Without a connection, your database cannot perform any operations.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Drift separates the database logic from the database connection.

This separation allows Drift to:

  • Support multiple platforms.
  • Support different SQLite implementations.
  • Make databases easier to test.
  • Allow custom connection strategies.

Instead of hardcoding how the database is opened, Drift lets you provide the connection when creating the database.

docs.title: Passing a Connection
docs.text:
final database = AppDatabase(connection);

Explanation:

  • connection is responsible for communicating with SQLite.
  • AppDatabase uses this connection for all database operations.

docs.title: Creating a Connection with drift_flutter
docs.text:
final database = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(
    name: 'app.db',
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • driftDatabase() creates a SQLite database connection for Flutter.
  • name specifies the database file name.
  • Drift automatically manages opening the database.

Note: There are multiple ways to create a database connection depending on your platform and storage requirements. This page focuses on the concept of a database connection. Specific connection methods are covered in Opening the Database.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the connection as a bridge.

Flutter App
      │
      ▼
 AppDatabase
      │
      ▼
Database Connection
      │
      ▼
 SQLite

Your application never communicates with SQLite directly.

Every query flows through the database connection.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Creating a database instance.

final db = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'todo.db'),
);

Explanation:

  • A connection is created for the todo.db database.
  • The same connection is used for every query executed through db.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A larger application might create the database once and share it throughout the app.

final database = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'company.db'),
);

The database instance is then injected into repositories, DAOs, or services, ensuring every part of the application uses the same connection.

Explanation:

  • Sharing a single database instance avoids opening multiple connections unnecessarily.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Create a database connection when:

  • Initializing your application.
  • Creating your database instance.
  • Connecting to a SQLite database.
  • Setting up an in-memory database for testing.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid creating a new connection every time you need to execute a query.

Instead, create one database instance and reuse it throughout your application.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Create a single database instance for your application.
  • Reuse the same connection whenever possible.
  • Close the database when it's no longer needed.
  • Keep connection creation separate from business logic.
  • Use different connection strategies for production and testing when appropriate.

docs.title: Creating multiple database instances
docs.text:
Wrong

Future<void> loadUsers() async {
  final db = AppDatabase(
    driftDatabase(name: 'app.db'),
  );

  await db.select(db.users).get();
}

Explanation:

  • A new connection is opened every time the method runs.
  • This wastes resources and can lead to unexpected behavior.

Correct

final db = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'app.db'),
);

Future<void> loadUsers() async {
  await db.select(db.users).get();
}

Explanation:

  • Reuse a single database instance throughout the application.

docs.title: Mixing connection logic with application logic
docs.text:
Wrong

Creating database connections in multiple widgets or services.

Explanation:

  • Connection management becomes difficult.
  • Multiple database instances may be created accidentally.

Correct

Create the database once during application startup and inject it where needed.

docs.title: Forgetting to close the database
docs.text:
Wrong

Creating a database connection without ever disposing it.

Explanation:

  • Resources remain allocated longer than necessary.

Correct

Close the database when the application or test no longer needs it.

await db.close();

Explanation:

  • Releases the underlying database resources.

docs.text:
• GeneratedDatabase
  • Opening the Database
  • Database Lifecycle
  • Multiple Databases
  • In-Memory Database

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A database connection allows Drift to communicate with SQLite. It acts as the bridge between your application and the database engine. By creating a single shared connection and passing it to your database class, you ensure efficient, reliable, and maintainable database access throughout your application.

docs.title: Database Lifecycle
docs.text: Understand how a Drift database is created, used, and closed during your application's lifetime.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
The database lifecycle refers to the different stages a Drift database goes through while your application is running.

A typical lifecycle looks like this:

Create Database
       │
       ▼
Open Connection
       │
       ▼
Execute Queries
       │
       ▼
Watch Streams
       │
       ▼
Close Database

Most applications create the database once when the app starts, use it throughout the app's lifetime, and close it when it's no longer needed.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Opening a SQLite database is relatively expensive compared to executing queries.

Continuously opening and closing the database for every operation can:

  • Reduce performance.
  • Waste system resources.
  • Create multiple unnecessary connections.
  • Make state management more difficult.

By treating the database as a long-lived object, Drift provides better performance and a more predictable architecture.

docs.title: Creating the Database
docs.text:
final db = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'app.db'),
);

Explanation:

  • Creates the database instance.
  • Opens the connection when needed.

docs.title: Using the Database
docs.text:
final users = await db.select(db.users).get();

Explanation:

  • Executes queries through the existing database instance.
  • No new connection is created.

docs.title: Closing the Database
docs.text:
await db.close();

Explanation:

  • Closes the database connection.
  • Releases any underlying resources.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the database like a file.

Open File
    │
Read / Write
    │
Read / Write
    │
Read / Write
    │
Close File

You don't repeatedly open and close the file every time you read a line.

A database works the same way.

Open it once, use it many times, and close it when you're finished.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Application startup.

final db = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'todo.db'),
);

Throughout the application:

await db.select(db.tasks).get();

await db.into(db.tasks).insert(task);

await db.delete(db.tasks).go();

Finally:

await db.close();

Explanation:

  • One database instance serves the entire application.
  • The connection remains open until it's explicitly closed.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A Flutter application might create the database during dependency injection.

App Starts
     │
     ▼
Create AppDatabase
     │
     ▼
Inject into DAOs
     │
     ▼
Repositories
     │
     ▼
UI
     │
     ▼
App Closes
     │
     ▼
Database Closed

Every layer shares the same database instance.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Follow the standard lifecycle when:

  • Building Flutter applications.
  • Using dependency injection.
  • Working with repositories or DAOs.
  • Managing a local SQLite database.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid:

  • Creating a new database instance for every query.
  • Closing the database immediately after each operation.
  • Keeping multiple unnecessary database instances alive.

These patterns waste resources and complicate your application.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Create the database once.
  • Share a single database instance.
  • Close the database only when it's no longer needed.
  • Inject the database into DAOs or repositories.
  • Let the database live as long as your application requires.

docs.title: Opening the database repeatedly
docs.text:
Wrong

Future<List<User>> loadUsers() async {
  final db = AppDatabase(
    driftDatabase(name: 'app.db'),
  );

  return db.select(db.users).get();
}

Explanation:

  • A new database is created every time the method is called.

Correct

final db = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'app.db'),
);

Future<List<User>> loadUsers() {
  return db.select(db.users).get();
}

Explanation:

  • The same database instance is reused.

docs.title: Closing the database too early
docs.text:
Wrong

await db.close();

await db.select(db.users).get();

Explanation:

  • Queries cannot execute after the database has been closed.

Correct

Close the database only when the application is shutting down or when the database is no longer needed.

docs.title: Creating multiple shared databases
docs.text:
Wrong

Widget A → AppDatabase()

Widget B → AppDatabase()

Widget C → AppDatabase()

Explanation:

  • Multiple connections to the same database are unnecessary in most applications.

Correct

AppDatabase
      │
 ┌────┼────┐
 │    │    │
DAO Repository UI

Explanation:

  • Share a single database instance across the application.

docs.title: Related APIs
docs.text:
• Database Connection
  • Opening the Database
  • Multiple Databases
  • Transactions
  • DAOs
  • In-Memory Database

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The database lifecycle describes how a Drift database is created, used, and eventually closed. In most applications, you should create a single database instance, reuse it throughout the app, and close it only when it's no longer needed. This approach improves performance, simplifies architecture, and ensures efficient resource management.

docs.title: Opening the Database
docs.text: Open a SQLite database so Drift can read and write data.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Opening the database is the process of creating a connection between your Drift database and the underlying SQLite database.

This is typically done once when your application starts. After the database is opened, all queries, inserts, updates, and deletes use the same connection.

The way you open a database depends on your platform and storage requirements.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Drift separates defining a database from opening a database.

Your database class describes:

  • Tables
  • DAOs
  • Schema version
  • Migrations

Opening the database determines:

  • Where the database is stored.
  • How SQLite is initialized.
  • Which executor is used.
  • How the connection is managed.

This separation makes Drift flexible enough to support Flutter, Dart, web, testing, and custom database implementations.

docs.title: Using drift_flutter
docs.text:
The simplest way to open a database in a Flutter application is with drift_flutter.

final database = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(
    name: 'app.db',
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • driftDatabase() creates a SQLite database connection.
  • name specifies the database file.
  • AppDatabase uses this connection for all operations.

docs.title: Using an In-Memory Database
docs.text:
final database = AppDatabase(
  NativeDatabase.memory(),
);

Explanation:

  • Creates a temporary database stored entirely in memory.
  • All data is lost when the database is closed.
  • Commonly used for testing.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Opening the database is like opening a file before editing it.

Application
      │
      ▼
Open Database
      │
      ▼
SQLite Connection
      │
      ▼
Read / Write Data

Once the connection is established, every database operation uses it.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Create a persistent local database.

final db = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'todo.db'),
);

Explanation:

  • Creates (or opens) todo.db.
  • Existing data is preserved between app launches.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A Flutter application usually creates the database once during startup.

final database = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'company.db'),
);

The database instance is then shared with repositories, DAOs, or dependency injection.

Explanation:

  • Opening the database once avoids repeatedly creating new connections.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Open the database when:

  • Your application starts.
  • Initializing dependency injection.
  • Creating the application's database instance.
  • Setting up an in-memory database for tests.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid opening the database:

  • Before every query.
  • Inside widgets that rebuild frequently.
  • Inside methods that are called repeatedly.

Instead, create one shared database instance and reuse it.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Open the database only once.
  • Reuse the same database instance.
  • Choose the appropriate executor for your platform.
  • Use an in-memory database for testing.
  • Close the database when it's no longer needed.

docs.title: Opening the database repeatedly
docs.text:
Wrong

Future<void> loadData() async {
  final db = AppDatabase(
    driftDatabase(name: 'app.db'),
  );

  await db.select(db.users).get();
}

Explanation:

  • A new connection is created every time the method runs.

Correct

final db = AppDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'app.db'),
);

Future<void> loadData() async {
  await db.select(db.users).get();
}

Explanation:

  • A single database instance is reused throughout the application.

docs.title: Opening the database inside a widget
docs.text:
Wrong

class HomePage extends StatelessWidget {
  final db = AppDatabase(
    driftDatabase(name: 'app.db'),
  );
}

Explanation:

  • Widgets shouldn't be responsible for creating database connections.
  • This makes dependency management more difficult.

Correct

Create the database during application initialization and inject it where needed.

docs.title: Using an in-memory database unintentionally
docs.text:
Wrong

AppDatabase(
  NativeDatabase.memory(),
);

Explanation:

  • All data disappears when the application exits.

Correct

Use a persistent database for production and reserve in-memory databases for testing.

• Database Connection
  • Database Lifecycle
  • GeneratedDatabase
  • Multiple Databases
  • In-Memory Database

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Opening the database establishes the connection between Drift and SQLite. This connection is typically created once during application startup and reused throughout the app. By separating database configuration from connection creation, Drift supports multiple platforms and connection strategies while keeping your database code clean and maintainable.

docs.title: Database Configuration
docs.text: Configure how your Drift database behaves, including its schema version, migrations, and lifecycle hooks.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Database configuration is the process of defining settings that control how your database is initialized and managed.

These settings determine things such as:

  • The current schema version.
  • How migrations are performed.
  • What happens when the database is first created.
  • How upgrades and downgrades are handled.

These configurations are typically defined by overriding properties or methods in your database class.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
As your application grows, your database schema will evolve. New tables, columns, and relationships may be added over time.

Database configuration allows Drift to:

  • Keep track of schema changes.
  • Upgrade existing databases safely.
  • Run initialization logic.
  • Maintain compatibility between app versions.

Without proper configuration, users could lose data or encounter database errors after updating the app.

docs.title: Setting the Schema Version
docs.text:
@override
int get schemaVersion => 1;

Explanation:

  • schemaVersion identifies the current version of your database schema.
  • Increase this value whenever the database structure changes.

docs.title: Configuring Migrations
docs.text:
@override
MigrationStrategy get migration => MigrationStrategy(
  onCreate: (m) async {
    await m.createAll();
  },
  onUpgrade: (m, from, to) async {
    // Migration logic
  },
);

Explanation:

  • MigrationStrategy defines how the database is created and upgraded.
  • onCreate runs when the database is created for the first time.
  • onUpgrade runs when moving between schema versions.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of database configuration as the blueprint for your database's lifecycle.

Database Starts
       │
       ▼
Read Configuration
       │
       ├── Schema Version
       ├── Migration Strategy
       ├── Creation Logic
       └── Upgrade Logic
       │
       ▼
Database Ready

Before Drift begins executing queries, it checks this configuration to ensure the database is in the expected state.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A basic configuration with only a schema version.

class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

Explanation:

  • Drift creates the database using schema version 1.
  • No custom migration logic is needed until the schema changes.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Suppose version 2 of your app adds a new table.

@override
int get schemaVersion => 2;

@override
MigrationStrategy get migration => MigrationStrategy(
  onUpgrade: (m, from, to) async {
    if (from < 2) {
      await m.createTable(tasks);
    }
  },
);

Explanation:

  • Existing users are upgraded from version 1 to version 2.
  • Only the new table is created, preserving existing data.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Configure your database when:

  • Creating a new Drift database.
  • Changing your schema.
  • Adding migrations.
  • Initializing database data.
  • Handling upgrades between app versions.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Database configuration should not be used for:

  • Business logic.
  • CRUD operations.
  • Complex queries.
  • Application initialization unrelated to the database.

Keep configuration focused on database behavior.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Start with schemaVersion set to 1.
  • Increment the schema version whenever the schema changes.
  • Keep migration logic small and well-tested.
  • Never modify an existing migration after release.
  • Test migrations before publishing updates.

docs.title: Forgetting to increase the schema version
docs.text:
Wrong

Adding a new column without changing:

@override
int get schemaVersion => 1;

Explanation:

  • Drift won't detect that the schema has changed.

Correct

@override
int get schemaVersion => 2;

Explanation:

  • Increasing the schema version tells Drift that a migration is required.

docs.title: Putting business logic in migrations
docs.text:
Wrong

onUpgrade: (m, from, to) async {
  await sendAnalytics();
}

Explanation:

  • Migrations should only modify the database schema or data.

Correct

Keep migrations focused on database changes only.

docs.title: Recreating tables during upgrades
docs.text:
Wrong

await m.createAll();

inside every upgrade.

Explanation:

  • Recreating existing tables can cause migration failures or data loss.

Correct

Only apply the specific schema changes needed for that version.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Database configuration defines how Drift initializes and manages your database. It includes the schema version, migration strategy, and lifecycle hooks that keep your database consistent as your application evolves. A well-configured database makes upgrades safer and ensures long-term maintainability.

docs.title: Multiple Databases
docs.text: Manage more than one database within the same application.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A Drift application can contain multiple databases, each with its own tables, schema, and connection.

While most applications only need a single database, there are situations where separating data into multiple databases makes sense.

Each database is completely independent and manages its own:

  • Tables
  • Schema version
  • Migrations
  • Queries
  • Transactions
  • Database connection

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Keeping all data in one database isn't always the best approach.

Using multiple databases can help when:

  • Different parts of an application are unrelated.
  • Data should be isolated for security or organization.
  • Separate modules evolve independently.
  • Different databases require different storage strategies.

Drift supports multiple databases by allowing you to create multiple database classes.

docs.title: Defining Multiple Databases
docs.text:
@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class UserDatabase extends _$UserDatabase {
  UserDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Products])
class ProductDatabase extends _$ProductDatabase {
  ProductDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

Explanation:

  • UserDatabase manages only the Users table.
  • ProductDatabase manages only the Products table.
  • Each database has its own generated implementation and schema.

docs.title: Creating Database Instances
docs.text:
final userDb = UserDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'users.db'),
);

final productDb = ProductDatabase(
  driftDatabase(name: 'products.db'),
);

Explanation:

  • Each database uses its own SQLite file.
  • Operations on one database do not affect the other.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of each database as its own storage system.

Application
     │
     ├──────────────┐
     ▼              ▼
UserDatabase   ProductDatabase
     │              │
 users.db      products.db

Each database has its own connection, tables, and migrations.

There is no direct relationship between them.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A chat application might separate user accounts from cached messages.

UserDatabase
├── Users
└── Profiles

CacheDatabase
├── Messages
└── Images

Each database serves a different purpose.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A large enterprise application could have:

AuthenticationDatabase
├── Users
├── Roles
└── Permissions

BusinessDatabase
├── Customers
├── Orders
└── Invoices

AnalyticsDatabase
├── Events
├── Metrics
└── Reports

Each module can evolve independently with its own schema version and migration history.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use multiple databases when:

  • Different modules have completely independent data.
  • Separate migration histories are required.
  • Different databases use different storage locations.
  • Sensitive data should be isolated.
  • You're building a modular application.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid multiple databases when:

  • The data is related.
  • Tables need joins or foreign keys.
  • Most queries involve data from multiple tables.

In these cases, a single database with multiple tables is usually a better design.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Prefer a single database unless there's a clear reason to separate data.
  • Group related tables in the same database.
  • Keep each database focused on one domain.
  • Use meaningful names for database files.
  • Manage each database's migrations independently.

docs.title: Splitting related tables across databases
docs.text:
Wrong

UserDatabase
└── Users

OrderDatabase
└── Orders

Explanation:

  • If Orders references Users, they can't use foreign keys or joins across databases.

Correct

AppDatabase
├── Users
└── Orders

Explanation:

  • Related tables belong in the same database.

docs.title: Creating unnecessary databases
docs.text:
Wrong

UsersDatabase

TasksDatabase

SettingsDatabase

ProductsDatabase

Explanation:

  • Multiple small databases increase complexity without providing benefits.

Correct

AppDatabase
├── Users
├── Tasks
├── Settings
└── Products

Explanation:

  • Most applications are easier to manage with a single database.

docs.title: Assuming databases share transactions
docs.text:
Wrong

Expecting a transaction in one database to automatically include operations in another database.

Explanation:

  • Transactions are scoped to a single database connection.

Correct

Treat each database as an independent unit with its own transaction lifecycle.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Drift supports multiple databases by allowing you to define multiple database classes, each with its own tables, schema, and connection. While this is useful for isolating unrelated data or building modular applications, most projects are better served by a single database containing multiple related tables.

docs.title: Defining Tables
docs.text: Define the structure of your database by creating tables with columns and constraints.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A table represents a collection of related data in your database. Every row in a table represents a single record, while each column stores a specific piece of information about that record.

In Drift, tables are defined as Dart classes by extending the Table class.

Instead of writing SQL like CREATE TABLE, you describe the table using Dart APIs, and Drift generates the corresponding SQLite schema.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Traditionally, database tables are created using SQL statements.

For example:

CREATE TABLE users (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL
);

While SQL is powerful, it doesn't integrate well with Dart's type system.

Drift lets you define tables in Dart, which provides:

  • Compile-time validation.
  • Strong typing.
  • Automatic code generation.
  • Better IDE support.
  • Easier refactoring.

docs.title: Creating a Table
docs.text:
class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • extends Table tells Drift this class defines a database table.
  • integer() creates an integer column.
  • text() creates a text column.
  • autoIncrement() marks the column as an auto-incrementing primary key.
  • The final () completes the column definition.

docs.title: Registering the Table
docs.text:
After defining a table, register it in your database.

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Users])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 1;
}

Explanation:

  • Only registered tables become part of the database.
  • Drift generates APIs for every registered table.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a table as a spreadsheet.

Users
+----+---------+
| ID | Name    |
+----+---------+
| 1  | Alice   |
| 2  | Bob     |
| 3  | Charlie |
+----+---------+

The table definition describes the structure, while the rows contain the actual data.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A products table.

class Products extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  RealColumn get price => real()();
}

Explanation:

  • Each getter defines one column.
  • Drift generates the SQL and corresponding Dart classes automatically.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A task management application.

class Tasks extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get title => text()();

  TextColumn get description => text().nullable()();

  BoolColumn get completed => boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();

  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();
}

Explanation:

  • nullable() allows a column to store NULL.
  • withDefault() provides a default value for new rows.
  • Drift generates a Task data class and a TasksCompanion for inserts and updates.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Define a table whenever you need to store a new type of data.

Examples include:

  • Users
  • Products
  • Orders
  • Notes
  • Messages
  • Settings

Each table should represent a single type of entity.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid creating a new table when:

  • The data naturally belongs in an existing table.
  • A simple column is sufficient.
  • You're storing temporary, in-memory data.

Also, don't create one table for every screen in your application. Tables should model your data, not your UI.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use singular concepts for each table (e.g., a Users table stores user records).
  • Give columns descriptive names.
  • Keep tables focused on a single entity.
  • Add only the columns you need.
  • Use appropriate column types.
  • Organize table definitions into separate files as your project grows.

docs.title: Forgetting to extend Table
docs.text:
Wrong

class Users {}

Explanation:

  • Drift won't recognize this as a database table.

Correct

class Users extends Table {}

Explanation:

  • Extending Table enables Drift's table generation.

docs.title: Forgetting to register the table
docs.text:
Wrong

class Users extends Table {
  // ...
}

But not adding it to the database.

Explanation:

  • Drift only generates APIs for registered tables.

Correct

@DriftDatabase(
  tables: [Users],
)

Explanation:

  • Register every table in the @DriftDatabase annotation.

docs.title: Mixing unrelated data
docs.text:
Wrong

Users Table
------------
id
name
email
productName
orderDate
invoiceNumber

Explanation:

  • A table should represent one entity, not multiple unrelated concepts.

Correct

Users
Orders
Products
Invoices

Explanation:

  • Split different entities into separate tables and relate them when necessary.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Tables define the structure of your database. In Drift, you create tables by extending the Table class and defining columns using Dart APIs. Drift then generates the SQL schema, data classes, and query helpers, giving you a type-safe and maintainable way to model your application's data.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text: Columns define the individual pieces of data stored in a table.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A column represents a single attribute of the data stored in a table. Every column has a name, a data type, and optional constraints that determine what values it can store.

For example, a Users table might contain columns such as:

  • id
  • name
  • email
  • age
  • createdAt

Each row in the table stores one value for every column.

In Drift, columns are defined using builder methods such as integer(), text(), boolean(), and dateTime().

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Columns define the structure and rules of your data.

Without columns, a table would have no way of knowing:

  • What information it stores.
  • What type of data is allowed.
  • Whether values are required.
  • Whether default values should be applied.

Drift uses column definitions to generate:

  • SQLite table definitions.
  • Data classes.
  • Companion classes.
  • Type-safe query APIs.

docs.title: Defining Columns
docs.text:
class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  IntColumn get age => integer()();

  BoolColumn get isActive => boolean()();

  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();
}

Explanation:

  • integer() creates an integer column.
  • text() creates a text column.
  • boolean() creates a boolean column.
  • dateTime() creates a DateTime column.
  • autoIncrement() makes the column the table's auto-incrementing primary key.

docs.title: Nullable Columns
docs.text:
TextColumn get bio => text().nullable()();

Explanation:

  • nullable() allows the column to contain NULL.
  • Without it, the column is required.

docs.title: Default Values
docs.text:
BoolColumn get isVerified =>
    boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();

Explanation:

  • withDefault() assigns a value when none is provided during insertion.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of columns as the fields on a form.

User

Name        ___________

Email       ___________

Age         ___________

Active      ☑

Each field corresponds to one column in the database.

Every row fills in those fields with actual values.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A products table.

class Products extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  RealColumn get price => real()();
}

Explanation:

  • Each getter defines one column in the table.
  • Drift generates the corresponding SQLite schema automatically.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A blog posts table.

class Posts extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get title => text()();

  TextColumn get content => text()();

  BoolColumn get published =>
      boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();

  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();

  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt =>
      dateTime().nullable()();
}

Explanation:

  • published defaults to false.
  • updatedAt is nullable because a new post may not have been edited yet.

docs.title: Common Column Types
docs.text: Drift Type SQLite Type Dart Type integer() INTEGER int text() TEXT String real() REAL double boolean() INTEGER bool dateTime() INTEGER DateTime blob() BLOB Uint8List

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Define a column for every piece of information that belongs to an entity.

Examples include:

  • User name
  • Product price
  • Order status
  • Creation date
  • Email address
  • Profile picture

Each column should represent a single value.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid:

  • Combining multiple values into one column.
  • Creating duplicate columns.
  • Storing unrelated data together.

For example, instead of:

address = "New York, USA, 10001"

Prefer separate columns when the values need to be queried independently.

city
country
zipCode

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Choose the correct column type.
  • Keep column names descriptive.
  • Make columns nullable only when necessary.
  • Use default values for predictable behavior.
  • Avoid storing multiple pieces of information in one column.
  • Keep columns focused on a single attribute.

docs.title: Using the wrong column type
docs.text:
Wrong

TextColumn get age => text()();

Explanation:

  • Age is numeric data and should not be stored as text.

Correct

IntColumn get age => integer()();

Explanation:

  • Numeric values should use integer columns.

docs.title: Making everything nullable
docs.text:
Wrong

TextColumn get name => text().nullable()();

Explanation:

  • If every column is nullable, your data becomes less reliable.

Correct

TextColumn get name => text()();

Explanation:

  • Only allow NULL when the value is genuinely optional.

docs.title: Using text for boolean values
docs.text:
Wrong

TextColumn get active => text()();

Explanation:

  • Storing "true" and "false" as text wastes space and complicates queries.

Correct

BoolColumn get active => boolean()();

Explanation:

  • Use the appropriate column type for the data being stored.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Columns define the individual fields within a table. Each column has a specific data type and optional constraints that determine how data is stored and validated. Choosing the right column types and keeping each column focused on a single piece of information leads to a well-structured and maintainable database schema.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Constraints define rules that control what data can be stored in a table.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Constraints are rules applied to columns or tables to ensure that only valid data is stored in the database.

For example, a constraint can require that:

  • A value must not be NULL.
  • A value must be unique.
  • A number must be positive.
  • A referenced row must exist in another table.

By enforcing these rules at the database level, SQLite helps maintain data integrity regardless of where the data comes from.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Without constraints, invalid or inconsistent data can easily enter your database.

For example:

  • Two users could have the same email.
  • An order could reference a customer that doesn't exist.
  • A product could have a negative price.
  • Required fields could be left empty.

Constraints prevent these situations automatically, reducing bugs and improving data reliability.

docs.title: NOT NULL
docs.text:
By default, Drift columns are required unless marked as nullable.

TextColumn get name => text()();

Explanation:

  • The column cannot store NULL.
  • Every row must provide a value for name.

docs.title: Nullable
docs.text:
TextColumn get bio => text().nullable()();

Explanation:

  • nullable() allows the column to contain NULL.
  • Use it only for optional data.

docs.title: UNIQUE
docs.text:
TextColumn get email => text().unique()();

Explanation:

  • Every email value must be unique.
  • Attempting to insert a duplicate value results in an error.

docs.title: CHECK
docs.text:
IntColumn get age =>
    integer().check(age.isBiggerOrEqualValue(0))();

Explanation:

  • check() enforces a custom validation rule.
  • Here, only non-negative ages are allowed.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of constraints as security guards for your database.

        Insert Row
            │
            ▼
     Constraint Checks
            │
   ┌────────┼────────┐
   │        │        │
 NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK
   │        │        │
   └────────┼────────┘
            │
     Valid Data?
       │       │
      Yes      No
       │        │
       ▼        ▼
   Store Row   Reject Row

Before SQLite stores a row, it verifies that all constraints are satisfied.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A users table with required and unique fields.

class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  TextColumn get email => text().unique()();
}

Explanation:

  • name is required.
  • email must be unique across all users.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A products table with validation.

class Products extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  RealColumn get price =>
      real().check(price.isBiggerThanValue(0))();

  IntColumn get stock =>
      integer().check(stock.isBiggerOrEqualValue(0))();
}

Explanation:

  • Product prices must be greater than zero.
  • Stock cannot be negative.
  • Invalid rows are rejected before they're stored.

docs.title: Common Constraints in Drift
docs.text: Constraint Purpose nullable() Allows NULL values unique() Prevents duplicate values check() Validates values using an expression autoIncrement() Creates an auto-incrementing primary key references() Creates a foreign key relationship withDefault() Assigns a default value

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use constraints whenever your data has rules that must always be enforced.

Examples include:

  • Email addresses must be unique.
  • Prices cannot be negative.
  • Every task must have a title.
  • Orders must reference existing customers.
  • Status values must follow specific rules.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid using constraints for business rules that change frequently.

For example:

  • User permission checks.
  • Feature flags.
  • Application-specific workflows.

These are usually better handled in your application's business logic rather than the database.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Let the database enforce data integrity.
  • Make required fields non-nullable.
  • Use unique() only when duplicates should never exist.
  • Use check() for simple validation rules.
  • Keep constraints simple and easy to understand.

docs.title: Making required fields nullable
docs.text:
Wrong

TextColumn get username => text().nullable()();

Explanation:

  • Usernames are typically required.
  • Allowing NULL may lead to incomplete records.

Correct

TextColumn get username => text()();

Explanation:

  • Required fields should remain non-nullable.

docs.title: Forgetting unique constraints
docs.text:
Wrong

TextColumn get email => text()();

Explanation:

  • Multiple users could register with the same email address.

Correct

TextColumn get email => text().unique()();

Explanation:

  • The database guarantees email uniqueness.

docs.title: Relying only on application validation
docs.text:
Wrong

Checking values only before insertion in Dart code.

Explanation:

  • Data inserted from another source or future code changes could bypass these checks.

Correct

Use database constraints alongside application validation.

Explanation:

  • The application improves the user experience.
  • The database guarantees data integrity.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Constraints enforce rules that keep your database consistent and reliable. Drift provides APIs for defining common constraints such as required fields, uniqueness, and custom validation, allowing SQLite to reject invalid data before it's stored. Proper use of constraints helps protect your data and reduces the need for repetitive validation throughout your application.

docs.title: Primary Keys
docs.text: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A primary key is a column, or a combination of columns, whose value uniquely identifies every row in a table.

Every table should have a primary key so that each record can be uniquely identified.

For example, in a Users table:

id name 1 Alice 2 Bob 3 Charlie

The id column is the primary key because each value is unique and identifies exactly one user.

In Drift, the most common way to define a primary key is by using autoIncrement().

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Without a primary key, it becomes difficult to uniquely identify a row.

For example, if two users have the same name:

id name 1 John 2 John

Updating or deleting a specific user based only on their name would be unreliable.

A primary key ensures every row has a unique identity, making queries, updates, relationships, and indexing more efficient.

docs.title: Auto-Incrementing Primary Key
docs.text:
class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • autoIncrement() creates an integer primary key.
  • SQLite automatically assigns a unique value for each new row.
  • The id column becomes the table's primary key.

docs.title: Custom Primary Key
docs.text:
If you don't use autoIncrement(), you can define the primary key manually.

class Users extends Table {
  TextColumn get email => text()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  @override
  Set<Column> get primaryKey => {email};
}

Explanation:

  • primaryKey specifies which column uniquely identifies each row.
  • Here, email acts as the primary key instead of an auto-generated ID.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a primary key as a unique ID card.

Users

ID   Name
------------
1    Alice
2    Bob
3    Charlie

Even if two people have the same name, their ID numbers are different.

The database uses the primary key to distinguish one row from another.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A products table.

class Products extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • Every product receives a unique ID automatically.
  • The ID can be used to retrieve, update, or delete a specific product.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A country table using ISO country codes.

class Countries extends Table {
  TextColumn get code => text()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  @override
  Set<Column> get primaryKey => {code};
}

Explanation:

  • Country codes such as US, IN, and JP are already unique.
  • There's no need for an additional auto-incrementing ID.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use a primary key for:

  • Every database table.
  • Identifying individual records.
  • Creating relationships between tables.
  • Updating or deleting specific rows.
  • Ensuring every record has a unique identity.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid using a column as a primary key if:

  • Its value may change over time.
  • Duplicate values are possible.
  • It doesn't uniquely identify a row.

For example, names, phone numbers, and addresses are often poor primary keys because they can change or may not be unique.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Give every table a primary key.
  • Prefer autoIncrement() for most tables.
  • Use natural keys only when they're guaranteed to be unique and stable.
  • Keep primary keys simple whenever possible.
  • Avoid changing primary key values after records are created.

docs.title: Forgetting a primary key
docs.text:
Wrong

class Users extends Table {
  TextColumn get name => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • The table has no unique way to identify its rows.

Correct

class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • Every row now has a unique identifier.

docs.title: Using non-unique values
docs.text:
Wrong

@override
Set<Column> get primaryKey => {name};

Explanation:

  • Multiple users can have the same name.

Correct

@override
Set<Column> get primaryKey => {email};

Explanation:

  • Use a column that is guaranteed to be unique.

docs.title: Using mutable data as a primary key
docs.text:
Wrong

Using a username as the primary key.

Explanation:

  • Usernames may change over time, affecting relationships and references.

Correct

Use an immutable ID or another stable unique value.

docs.text:
• Composite Keys

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A primary key uniquely identifies every row in a table. In Drift, this is commonly achieved with autoIncrement(), though any unique and stable column can be used as a custom primary key. Choosing an appropriate primary key is essential for maintaining data integrity and building relationships between tables.

docs.title: Composite Keys
docs.text: A composite key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A composite key is a primary key made up of multiple columns instead of a single column.

Individually, each column may contain duplicate values, but the combination of their values must be unique.

For example, consider a table that records which students are enrolled in which courses.

studentId courseId 1 101 1 102 2 101

Neither studentId nor courseId is unique on its own, but the combination of both uniquely identifies each enrollment.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Some data naturally requires multiple values to identify a record.

Using a single auto-incrementing ID in these situations may not accurately represent the relationship between the data.

Composite keys are commonly used for:

  • Many-to-many relationships
  • Junction tables
  • Lookup tables
  • Records identified by multiple attributes

They ensure that duplicate combinations cannot be inserted into the database.

docs.title: Defining a Composite Key
docs.text:
class Enrollments extends Table {
  IntColumn get studentId => integer()();

  IntColumn get courseId => integer()();

  @override
  Set<Column> get primaryKey => {
    studentId,
    courseId,
  };
}

Explanation:

  • primaryKey returns a set of columns that together form the primary key.
  • Each individual column can contain duplicate values.
  • The combination of both columns must be unique.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a composite key as using multiple fields to identify something.

Student ID + Course ID
        │
        ▼
Unique Enrollment

For example:

Student Course Valid? 1 101 ✅ 1 102 ✅ 2 101 ✅ 1 101 ❌ Duplicate

The database treats the pair (1, 101) as the unique identifier.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A table storing user permissions.

class UserPermissions extends Table {
  IntColumn get userId => integer()();

  TextColumn get permission => text()();

  @override
  Set<Column> get primaryKey => {
    userId,
    permission,
  };
}

Explanation:

  • A user can have multiple permissions.
  • Each permission can belong to multiple users.
  • A user cannot have the same permission twice.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A shopping application storing items in an order.

class OrderItems extends Table {
  IntColumn get orderId => integer()();

  IntColumn get productId => integer()();

  IntColumn get quantity => integer()();

  @override
  Set<Column> get primaryKey => {
    orderId,
    productId,
  };
}

Explanation:

  • An order can contain many products.
  • A product can appear in many orders.
  • The same product cannot appear twice in the same order.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use composite keys when:

  • Two or more columns together identify a record.
  • Building many-to-many relationship tables.
  • Preventing duplicate combinations of values.
  • Modeling relationships without introducing an unnecessary ID column.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid composite keys when:

  • A single column uniquely identifies the row.
  • An auto-incrementing ID is sufficient.
  • The combination of columns may change frequently.

For most tables, a single primary key is simpler and easier to work with.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep composite keys small.
  • Use only columns that naturally identify the record.
  • Avoid including mutable columns in a composite key.
  • Prefer composite keys for junction tables and relationship tables.
  • Don't add an auto-incrementing ID unless it serves a purpose.

docs.title: Using only one column
docs.text:
Wrong

@override
Set<Column> get primaryKey => {studentId};

Explanation:

  • A student can enroll in multiple courses.
  • studentId alone does not uniquely identify a row.

Correct

@override
Set<Column> get primaryKey => {
  studentId,
  courseId,
};

Explanation:

  • The combination uniquely identifies each enrollment.

docs.title: Adding an unnecessary ID column
docs.text:
Wrong

IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

IntColumn get studentId => integer()();

IntColumn get courseId => integer()();

Explanation:

  • If the combination of studentId and courseId already identifies each row, the additional ID may be unnecessary.

Correct

Use the natural composite key when it accurately represents the relationship.

docs.title: Including mutable columns
docs.text:
Wrong

@override
Set<Column> get primaryKey => {
  userId,
  username,
};

Explanation:

  • If username changes, the primary key changes as well.

Correct

Use stable values that are unlikely to change.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A composite key uses multiple columns together as a table's primary key. It is useful when no single column uniquely identifies a record, especially in junction tables and many-to-many relationships. By using the combination of values as the unique identifier, Drift helps maintain data integrity without requiring an additional ID column.

docs.title: Foreign Keys
docs.text: A foreign key creates a relationship between tables by referencing the primary key of another table.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A foreign key is a column whose value refers to a row in another table.

It establishes a relationship between two tables and ensures that the referenced row exists.

For example, consider two tables:

Users

id name 1 Alice 2 Bob

Posts

id userId title 1 1 Hello World 2 2 Drift Tutorial

The userId column in the Posts table is a foreign key because it references the id column in the Users table.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Without foreign keys, related data can become inconsistent.

For example:

  • A post could reference a user that doesn't exist.
  • An order could reference a deleted customer.
  • A comment could belong to a non-existent post.

Foreign keys help maintain referential integrity by ensuring relationships between tables remain valid.

docs.title: Defining a Foreign Key
docs.text:
class Posts extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  IntColumn get userId =>
      integer().references(Users, #id)();

  TextColumn get title => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • references() creates a foreign key relationship.
  • Users is the table being referenced.
  • #id refers to the primary key column of the Users table.
  • Every userId value must exist in the Users table.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a foreign key as a reference or link.

Users
+----+--------+
| ID | Name   |
+----+--------+
| 1  | Alice  |
| 2  | Bob    |
+----+--------+

        ▲
        │
        │ userId
        │
Posts
+----+--------+----------------+
| ID | userId | Title          |
+----+--------+----------------+
| 1  |   1    | Hello World    |
| 2  |   2    | Drift Tutorial |
+----+--------+----------------+

Instead of storing the user's entire information in every post, the post stores only the user's ID.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A comments table.

class Comments extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  IntColumn get postId =>
      integer().references(Posts, #id)();

  TextColumn get content => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • Every comment belongs to a post.
  • postId references the Posts table.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
An orders table.

class Orders extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  IntColumn get customerId =>
      integer().references(Customers, #id)();

  DateTimeColumn get orderDate => dateTime()();
}

Explanation:

  • Every order belongs to a customer.
  • SQLite prevents orders from referencing customers that don't exist.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use foreign keys when:

  • One table depends on another.
  • Modeling one-to-one relationships.
  • Modeling one-to-many relationships.
  • Modeling many-to-many relationships through junction tables.
  • Maintaining referential integrity.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid foreign keys when:

  • Tables are completely unrelated.
  • The referenced data is stored in another database.
  • There is no logical relationship between the tables.

Don't create foreign keys simply because two tables have similar columns.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Reference primary keys whenever possible.
  • Use foreign keys to model real relationships.
  • Keep related tables in the same database.
  • Choose meaningful column names such as userId or productId.
  • Avoid storing duplicate data when a relationship can be used instead.

docs.title: Storing duplicate information
docs.text:
Wrong

class Posts extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get authorName => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • The author's name is duplicated in every post.
  • Updating the user's name becomes difficult.

Correct

IntColumn get userId =>
    integer().references(Users, #id)();

Explanation:

  • Store a reference to the user instead of duplicating user data.

docs.title: Missing foreign key relationships
docs.text:
Wrong

IntColumn get userId => integer()();

Explanation:

  • SQLite doesn't know that userId should reference the Users table.

Correct

IntColumn get userId =>
    integer().references(Users, #id)();

Explanation:

  • The relationship is enforced by the database.

docs.title: Referencing unrelated tables
docs.text:
Wrong

Orders
   │
   ▼
Products

When the relationship doesn't actually exist.

Explanation:

  • Foreign keys should represent real relationships in your data model.

Correct

Create foreign keys only when one record genuinely depends on another.
