  • One-to-Many
  • Many-to-Many

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Foreign keys establish relationships between tables by referencing the primary key of another table. They help maintain referential integrity, prevent invalid references, and reduce data duplication. By using foreign keys, you can model real-world relationships while keeping your database consistent and reliable.

docs.title: Default Values
docs.text: Default values provide automatic values for columns when no value is explicitly supplied during insertion.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A default value is a value that SQLite automatically assigns to a column if an insert operation doesn't provide one.

Instead of requiring every insert to specify every column, you can define sensible defaults for commonly used values.

For example, a new task might automatically start as incomplete, or a new user account might be enabled by default.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Without default values, every insert must explicitly provide values for every required column.

For example:

  • New tasks should usually be incomplete.
  • New users might be active by default.
  • Counters often start at zero.

Rather than repeating these values in every insert statement, you can define them once in the table definition.

This reduces boilerplate and ensures consistent data.

docs.title: Defining a Default Value
docs.text:
class Tasks extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get title => text()();

  BoolColumn get completed =>
      boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();
}

Explanation:

  • withDefault() assigns a default value to the column.
  • Constant(false) tells SQLite to use false when no value is provided.
  • The default is only applied during insertion.

docs.title: Overriding the Default
docs.text:
await into(tasks).insert(
  TasksCompanion.insert(
    title: 'Write documentation',
    completed: true,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Providing a value explicitly overrides the default.
  • SQLite only uses the default when the column is omitted.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of default values as pre-filled answers on a form.

Task Form

Title        ___________

Completed    ☑ false (default)

If you leave the field unchanged, the default value is used.

If you enter your own value, it replaces the default.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A users table.

class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  BoolColumn get isActive =>
      boolean().withDefault(const Constant(true))();
}

Explanation:

  • Every new user is active unless another value is provided.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A products table.

class Products extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  IntColumn get stock =>
      integer().withDefault(const Constant(0))();

  BoolColumn get available =>
      boolean().withDefault(const Constant(true))();
}

Explanation:

  • New products start with zero stock.
  • Products are available by default.
  • Insert operations only need to provide values that differ from these defaults.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use default values when:

  • A column usually starts with the same value.
  • The value is predictable.
  • You want to reduce repetitive insert code.
  • The default makes sense for most new records.

Common examples include:

  • false
  • true
  • 0
  • Empty strings
  • Current timestamps (when appropriate)

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid default values when:

  • Every insert should explicitly provide the value.
  • The value depends on application logic.
  • Different situations require different initial values.

Don't use defaults to hide missing or incorrect application logic.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use defaults for common initial values.
  • Keep default values simple and predictable.
  • Choose defaults that make sense for most records.
  • Avoid unnecessary defaults on required business data.
  • Document defaults so they're easy to understand.

docs.title: Repeating the default during every insert
docs.text:
Wrong

await into(tasks).insert(
  TasksCompanion.insert(
    title: 'Buy milk',
    completed: false,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • completed already has a default value.
  • Providing it every time adds unnecessary repetition.

Correct

await into(tasks).insert(
  TasksCompanion.insert(
    title: 'Buy milk',
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • SQLite automatically uses the default value.

docs.title: Using the wrong default
docs.text:
Wrong

BoolColumn get isActive =>
    boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();

Explanation:

  • If new users should normally be active, this default doesn't match the application's behavior.

Correct

Choose a default that reflects the most common case.

docs.title: Assuming defaults apply to updates
docs.text:
Wrong

Expecting a default value to be applied when updating an existing row.

Explanation:

  • Default values are only used during insertion.
  • Updates only change the columns you explicitly modify.

Correct

Provide the desired value during updates.

docs.title: Related APIs
docs.text:
• Columns
  • Constraints
  • Insert
  • Companions
  • Value

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Default values allow SQLite to automatically assign values to columns during insertion when no value is provided. They reduce repetitive insert code, improve consistency, and make common initialization behavior part of the database schema rather than the application logic.

docs.title: Generated Columns
docs.text: Generated columns are columns whose values are automatically calculated from other columns.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A generated column doesn't store a value that you manually provide. Instead, SQLite computes its value using an expression based on one or more other columns.

Whenever the referenced columns change, the generated column is automatically updated.

For example, instead of manually calculating a person's full name every time, the database can generate it from the first and last name.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Sometimes a column's value is completely derived from other data.

Without generated columns, you would need to:

  • Calculate the value in your application.
  • Store the calculated value.
  • Keep it synchronized whenever the source data changes.

This can lead to duplicated logic and inconsistent data.

Generated columns let SQLite handle these calculations automatically.

docs.title: Defining a Generated Column
docs.text:
class Users extends Table {
  TextColumn get firstName => text()();

  TextColumn get lastName => text()();

  TextColumn get fullName => text().generatedAs(
    firstName + const Constant(' ') + lastName,
  )();
}

Explanation:

  • generatedAs() defines a column whose value is computed automatically.
  • The expression uses other columns from the same table.
  • fullName is generated by SQLite and should not be set manually.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a generated column as a spreadsheet formula.

First Name    Last Name
    │             │
    └──────┬──────┘
           ▼
      Full Name

You edit the input values, and the calculated value updates automatically.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A products table that calculates the total value of the stock.

class Products extends Table {
  IntColumn get quantity => integer()();

  RealColumn get price => real()();

  RealColumn get inventoryValue =>
      real().generatedAs(quantity * price)();
}

Explanation:

  • inventoryValue is calculated from quantity and price.
  • You never provide a value for inventoryValue when inserting or updating data.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A task management application.

class Tasks extends Table {
  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();

  DateTimeColumn get dueDate => dateTime()();

  IntColumn get daysRemaining => integer().generatedAs(
    dueDate.dartCast<int>() - createdAt.dartCast<int>(),
  )();
}

Explanation:

  • The generated column is computed automatically from the other date columns.
  • Changes to either date automatically affect the generated value.

Note: The exact expression depends on the calculation you're performing and SQLite's supported functions.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use generated columns when:

  • A value can always be derived from other columns.
  • You want to avoid storing duplicate data.
  • The calculation should always remain consistent.
  • The value is frequently queried.

Examples include:

  • Full names
  • Total prices
  • Discounts
  • Inventory values
  • Calculated metrics

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid generated columns when:

  • The value should be entered manually.
  • The calculation depends on application logic.
  • The value depends on external services or APIs.
  • The calculation changes frequently.

Generated columns should only depend on data available within the same row.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep generated expressions simple.
  • Use generated columns for deterministic calculations.
  • Don't duplicate calculated values in normal columns.
  • Let SQLite maintain generated values automatically.
  • Document complex generated expressions.

docs.title: Manually inserting generated values
docs.text:
Wrong

await into(users).insert(
  UsersCompanion.insert(
    firstName: 'John',
    lastName: 'Doe',
    fullName: 'John Doe',
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Generated columns are computed by SQLite.
  • Their values should not be supplied manually.

Correct

await into(users).insert(
  UsersCompanion.insert(
    firstName: 'John',
    lastName: 'Doe',
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • SQLite calculates fullName automatically.

docs.title: Storing duplicated calculated data
docs.text:
Wrong

Price
Quantity
TotalPrice

Where TotalPrice is manually updated.

Explanation:

  • The calculated value can become inconsistent if updates are missed.

Correct

Use a generated column so the value is always derived from the source columns.

docs.title: Using generated columns for unrelated logic
docs.text:
Wrong

Using a generated column to store values returned by an API.

Explanation:

  • Generated columns can only calculate values from columns in the same row.

Correct

Store external values in normal columns.

  • Custom SQL Expressions

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Generated columns automatically calculate their values from other columns in the same table. They eliminate duplicated data, reduce maintenance, and ensure derived values always remain consistent. By moving simple calculations into the database, you can keep your schema cleaner and avoid repetitive application logic.

docs.title: Custom Types
docs.text: Custom types allow you to store Dart types that SQLite doesn't support natively.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
SQLite supports only a small set of built-in data types, such as:

  • Integer
  • Text
  • Real
  • Blob
  • Null

However, applications often work with richer Dart types like:

  • Enums
  • Objects
  • JSON models
  • Custom classes

Custom types allow these Dart types to be stored in SQLite by converting them to and from supported database types.

In Drift, this is done using type converters.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
SQLite doesn't understand Dart-specific types.

For example, SQLite cannot directly store:

  • Color
  • UserRole
  • Address
  • Settings
  • Money

Without custom types, you would need to manually convert these values every time you insert or read data.

Type converters automate this conversion, allowing you to work with your custom Dart types while Drift handles the database representation.

docs.title: Using a Custom Type
docs.text:
enum UserRole {
  admin,
  user,
  guest,
}

class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get role =>
      text().map(const UserRoleConverter())();
}

Explanation:

  • map() attaches a type converter to the column.
  • Drift exposes the column as UserRole in Dart.
  • SQLite stores the converted value.

Note: Creating custom converters is covered in the TypeConverter section.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a type converter as a translator.

Dart Object
     │
     ▼
Type Converter
     │
     ▼
SQLite Value

When writing data:

UserRole.admin
        │
        ▼
    "admin"
        │
        ▼
     SQLite

When reading data:

SQLite
   │
"admin"
   │
   ▼
UserRole.admin

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Store an enum.

enum Priority {
  low,
  medium,
  high,
}

class Tasks extends Table {
  TextColumn get priority =>
      text().map(const PriorityConverter())();
}

Explanation:

  • Drift automatically converts between Priority and the stored database value.
  • Your application works directly with the enum instead of raw strings.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Store a custom settings object.

class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get settings =>
      text().map(const SettingsConverter())();
}

Explanation:

  • The converter transforms the Settings object into a storable format, such as JSON.
  • Reading the column automatically recreates the original object.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use custom types when working with:

  • Enums
  • JSON models
  • Value objects
  • Domain models
  • Custom Dart classes

They help keep your application code strongly typed while remaining compatible with SQLite.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid custom types when:

  • SQLite already provides a suitable built-in type.
  • A simple text(), integer(), or boolean() column is sufficient.
  • The conversion adds unnecessary complexity.

Don't create custom types for data that can be stored naturally.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep converters simple and predictable.
  • Use converters for reusable domain types.
  • Prefer enums over raw strings when appropriate.
  • Ensure conversions are reversible.
  • Reuse converters across multiple tables when possible.

docs.title: Storing enums as raw strings everywhere
docs.text:
Wrong

TextColumn get role => text()();

Explanation:

  • Every query must manually convert between strings and enums.
  • Invalid string values become harder to detect.

Correct

TextColumn get role =>
    text().map(const UserRoleConverter())();

Explanation:

  • Drift handles the conversion automatically.

docs.title: Writing conversion logic repeatedly
docs.text:
Wrong

if (role == UserRole.admin) {
  // Convert manually
}

Explanation:

  • Manual conversions scattered throughout the application are difficult to maintain.

Correct

Use a reusable type converter.

docs.title: Using custom types unnecessarily
docs.text:
Wrong

Creating a converter for an integer value that doesn't require special handling.

Explanation:

  • Built-in SQLite types should be used whenever possible.

Correct

Reserve custom types for values that SQLite cannot represent directly.

docs.title: Related APIs
docs.text:
• TypeConverter
  • Enum Conversion
  • JSON Conversion
  • Custom Objects
  • Reusable Converters
  • Columns

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Custom types let you work with Dart-specific types while storing compatible values in SQLite. By using type converters, Drift automatically converts data between your application's types and SQLite's supported types, resulting in cleaner, safer, and more expressive code.

docs.title: Table Inheritance
docs.text: Table inheritance lets multiple tables share common column definitions through Dart inheritance.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
As your application grows, you may have several tables that contain the same columns.

For example:

  • createdAt
  • updatedAt
  • id
  • deletedAt

Instead of defining these columns in every table, you can place them in a base table class and have other tables inherit from it.

This reduces duplication and keeps table definitions consistent.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Without inheritance, shared columns must be copied into every table.

For example:

Users
├── createdAt
├── updatedAt

Products
├── createdAt
├── updatedAt

Orders
├── createdAt
├── updatedAt

If you later decide to modify one of these shared columns, you'll need to update every table individually.

Table inheritance allows common columns to be defined once and reused across multiple tables.

docs.title: Creating a Base Table
docs.text:
abstract class BaseTable extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();

  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime()();
}

Explanation:

  • BaseTable contains columns shared by multiple tables.
  • Declaring it as abstract indicates it isn't meant to become a table on its own.

docs.title: Inheriting the Base Table
docs.text:
class Users extends BaseTable {
  TextColumn get name => text()();
}

class Products extends BaseTable {
  TextColumn get title => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • Users and Products inherit all columns from BaseTable.
  • Each table can define its own additional columns.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of table inheritance as a template.

          BaseTable
        ┌─────────────┐
        │ id          │
        │ createdAt   │
        │ updatedAt   │
        └──────┬──────┘
               │
      ┌────────┴────────┐
      ▼                 ▼
    Users           Products
      │                 │
     name             title

Each table receives the shared columns while adding its own unique fields.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A base table for timestamps.

abstract class TimestampedTable extends Table {
  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();

  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime()();
}

class Notes extends TimestampedTable {
  TextColumn get title => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • Notes automatically includes both timestamp columns.
  • Only table-specific columns need to be added.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
An e-commerce application.

abstract class EntityTable extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();

  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime()();
}

class Customers extends EntityTable {
  TextColumn get name => text()();
}

class Orders extends EntityTable {
  DateTimeColumn get orderDate => dateTime()();
}

class Products extends EntityTable {
  TextColumn get title => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • Every table shares a common structure.
  • Changes to shared columns only need to be made in one place.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use table inheritance when:

  • Multiple tables share the same columns.
  • You want to reduce duplicated code.
  • Common fields should remain consistent across tables.
  • Building large applications with many tables.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid table inheritance when:

  • Only one table uses the shared columns.
  • The shared columns are unrelated.
  • Inheritance makes the table hierarchy harder to understand.

Don't create deep inheritance hierarchies just to avoid a few repeated lines of code.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep base tables focused on genuinely shared columns.
  • Make base table classes abstract.
  • Avoid multiple levels of inheritance.
  • Use descriptive names such as BaseTable or TimestampedTable.
  • Keep table-specific columns in the derived table.

docs.title: Duplicating shared columns
docs.text:
Wrong

class Users extends Table {
  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();

  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime()();
}

class Products extends Table {
  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();

  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime()();
}

Explanation:

  • The same columns are repeated across multiple tables.

Correct

abstract class TimestampedTable extends Table {
  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();

  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime()();
}

Explanation:

  • Shared columns are defined once and inherited where needed.

docs.title: Putting unrelated columns in the base table
docs.text:
Wrong

abstract class BaseTable extends Table {
  TextColumn get productName => text()();

  TextColumn get customerName => text()();
}

Explanation:

  • Not every table needs these columns.

Correct

Only include columns that are truly common to all inheriting tables.

docs.title: Overusing inheritance
docs.text:
Wrong

BaseTable
    │
TimestampedTable
    │
AuditableTable
    │
SoftDeleteTable
    │
Users

Explanation:

  • Deep inheritance hierarchies make table definitions harder to follow.

Correct

Prefer a simple, shallow inheritance structure.

docs.title: Related APIs
docs.text:
• Defining Tables

  • Generated Data Classes
  • TypeConverter
  • Constraints

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Table inheritance allows multiple Drift tables to share common column definitions through Dart inheritance. It helps reduce duplication, improves consistency, and makes large database schemas easier to maintain by centralizing shared fields in a reusable base table.

docs.title: Generated Data Classes
docs.text: Generated data classes represent rows in your database tables as strongly typed Dart objects.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
When you define a table in Drift, it automatically generates a corresponding Dart data class.

Each instance of the generated data class represents a single row in the table.

For example, given a Users table, Drift generates a User data class.

Instead of working with raw database rows, your application works with typed Dart objects.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Without generated data classes, query results would typically be returned as maps.

For example:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Alice",
  "age": 25
}

Accessing values by string keys is error-prone and lacks type safety.

Generated data classes provide:

  • Strong typing.
  • Compile-time checking.
  • Better IDE support.
  • Easier serialization.
  • Cleaner application code.

docs.title: Defining a Table
docs.text:
class Users extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();

  TextColumn get name => text()();

  IntColumn get age => integer()();
}

Explanation:

  • Drift uses this table definition to generate a User data class automatically.

docs.title: Using the Generated Data Class
docs.text:
final users = await select(usersTable).get();

for (final user in users) {
  print(user.name);
}

Explanation:

  • select(...).get() returns a list of generated data class instances.
  • Each property corresponds to a column in the table.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a generated data class as a Dart representation of a database row.

Database Row
+----+-------+-----+
| 1  | Alice | 25  |
+----+-------+-----+
        │
        ▼
Generated User Object

User(
  id: 1,
  name: "Alice",
  age: 25,
)

Each row becomes a Dart object with typed fields.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Reading all products.

final products = await select(products).get();

for (final product in products) {
  print(product.name);
}

Explanation:

  • Each item in products is a generated Product object.
  • Columns are exposed as Dart properties.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Finding a specific task.

final task = await (select(tasks)
      ..where((t) => t.id.equals(1)))
    .getSingle();

print(task.title);
print(task.completed);

Explanation:

  • getSingle() returns one generated Task object.
  • The result can be used directly throughout your application.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Generated data classes are used whenever you:

  • Read data from the database.
  • Pass database records between layers.
  • Display query results.
  • Serialize database records.
  • Work with individual rows.

They are the standard representation of database records in Drift.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Don't use generated data classes for:

  • Partial inserts.
  • Partial updates.
  • Optional update values.

For these operations, use companion classes instead.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Treat generated data classes as immutable models.
  • Use them for reading data.
  • Pass them between repositories and UI when appropriate.
  • Prefer companions for inserts and updates.
  • Avoid modifying generated code manually.

docs.title: Using a data class for inserts
docs.text:
Wrong

final user = User(
  id: 1,
  name: 'Alice',
  age: 25,
);

await into(users).insert(user);

Explanation:

  • Data classes represent complete rows.
  • Inserts often require optional or omitted fields such as auto-incrementing IDs.

Correct

Use a companion class for insert operations.

docs.title: Editing generated files
docs.text:
Wrong

Modifying the generated .g.dart file.

Explanation:

  • Generated code is recreated every time Drift runs code generation.
  • Manual changes are lost.

Correct

Modify the table definition and regenerate the code.

docs.title: Confusing data classes with tables
docs.text:
Wrong

Assuming the generated User class defines the database schema.

Explanation:

  • The table defines the schema.
  • The generated data class represents a row of data.

Correct

Use the table for schema definitions and the generated data class for working with query results.

docs.title: Related APIs
docs.text:
• Companions
  • Insertable
  • Value
  • Defining Tables
  • Select

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Generated data classes provide a strongly typed representation of rows in your database tables. Drift automatically generates these classes from your table definitions, allowing you to work with Dart objects instead of raw database rows. They are primarily used for reading and representing data, while companion classes handle inserts and updates.

docs.title: Companions
docs.text: Companion classes provide a flexible way to insert and update rows in a Drift database.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
For every table you define, Drift automatically generates a companion class.

If you have a table named Users, Drift generates:

  • User — Represents a complete database row.
  • UsersCompanion — Represents values used for inserts and updates.

Unlike generated data classes, companion classes allow columns to be omitted, making them ideal for creating and modifying records.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
When inserting or updating data, you don't always provide every column.

For example:

  • Auto-increment IDs are generated automatically.
  • Some columns have default values.
  • Some columns are nullable.
  • Updates often modify only a few columns.

Generated data classes represent complete rows, but companions let you specify only the values you want to insert or update.

docs.title: Inserting with a Companion
docs.text:
```dart id="go0r2z" await into(users).insert( UsersCompanion.insert( name: 'Alice', age: 25, ), ); 

Explanation:

* `UsersCompanion.insert()` creates a companion for insertion.
* Required columns are passed as parameters.
* Auto-generated and default columns can be omitted.

---

## Updating with a Companion

```dart id="9m04v6"
await (update(users)
      ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1)))
    .write(
      UsersCompanion(
        age: const Value(26),
      ),
    );

Explanation:

  • Only the age column is updated.
  • Other columns remain unchanged.
  • Value() indicates that the column should be included in the update.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of companions as partial rows.

```text id="wn34yf" Generated Data Class

User ├── id ├── name └── age

    │

Companion

UsersCompanion ├── name └── age 

A data class represents an entire row.

A companion represents only the values involved in an insert or update.

---

# Examples

## Simple Example

Insert a new product.

```dart id="6rj0i8"
await into(products).insert(
  ProductsCompanion.insert(
    name: 'Laptop',
    price: 999.99,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • The database generates the product ID automatically.
  • Only the required values are supplied.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Update only a user's email address.

```dart id="4k7gm4" await (update(users) ..where((u) => u.id.equals(5))) .write( UsersCompanion( email: const Value('alice@example.com'), ), ); 

Explanation:

* Only the `email` column changes.
* Every other column keeps its current value.

---

# When to Use

Use companion classes when:

* Inserting new rows.
* Updating existing rows.
* Omitting optional columns.
* Working with default values.
* Performing partial updates.

They are the recommended way to write data in Drift.

---

# When NOT to Use

Don't use companions when:

* Reading query results.
* Passing complete database records.
* Representing an entire row.

For these cases, use the generated data class instead.

---

# Best Practices

* Use `.insert()` constructors for inserts.
* Use companion objects for updates.
* Include only the columns you want to modify.
* Let SQLite handle auto-generated values.
* Prefer companions over manually implementing `Insertable`.

---

# Common Mistakes

## Using a generated data class for inserts

**Wrong**

```dart id="h9v0u8"
await into(users).insert(
  User(
    id: 1,
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Generated data classes represent complete rows.
  • Auto-generated columns often shouldn't be provided manually.

Correct

```dart id="lygmzt" await into(users).insert( UsersCompanion.insert( name: 'Alice', age: 25, ), ); 

Explanation:

* The companion lets Drift generate missing values automatically.

---

## Forgetting `Value()` during updates

**Wrong**

```dart id="rmwqhz"
UsersCompanion(
  age: 26,
);

Explanation:

  • Companion fields expect Value<T> objects for updates.

Correct

dart id="4hhjlwm" UsersCompanion( age: const Value(26), );

Explanation:

  • Value() marks the field as intentionally included in the update.

docs.title: Using companions to represent database rows
docs.text:
Wrong

Passing a companion throughout your application as if it were a model.

Explanation:

  • Companions are designed for write operations, not as domain models.

Correct

Use generated data classes when working with retrieved records.

docs.text:
• Generated Data Classes
  • Value
  • Insertable
  • Insert

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Companion classes provide a flexible way to insert and update data in Drift. Unlike generated data classes, companions allow columns to be omitted, making them ideal for partial writes, default values, and auto-generated fields. They are the standard mechanism for write operations in Drift.

docs.title:
Value

Value<T> tells Drift whether a column should be included in an insert or update operation.

What is it?

Value<T> is a wrapper used inside companion classes to distinguish between:

  • A column that should be updated.
  • A column that should be left unchanged.

This distinction is important because null can itself be a valid value.

For example, during an update:

  • Do you want to set bio to null?
  • Or do you want to leave bio unchanged?

Without Value<T>, Drift wouldn't know the difference.
Updating a Value
docs.text:
```dart id="tb98z8" await (update(users) ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1))) .write( UsersCompanion( age: const Value(26), ), ); 

Explanation:

* `Value(26)` tells Drift to update the `age` column.
* Columns not wrapped in `Value()` are left unchanged.

---

## Setting a Nullable Column to NULL

```dart id="j4umqk"
await (update(users)
      ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1)))
    .write(
      UsersCompanion(
        bio: const Value(null),
      ),
    );

Explanation:

  • Value(null) explicitly sets the database column to NULL.
  • This is different from omitting the column entirely.

docs.title: Leaving a Column Unchanged
docs.text:
```dart id="9o8v2z" await (update(users) ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1))) .write( UsersCompanion( name: const Value('Alice'), ), ); 

Explanation:

* Only `name` is updated.
* Every other column remains unchanged.

---

# Mental Model

Think of `Value<T>` as an instruction.

```text id="5ujccw"
Value(25)
     │
     ▼
Update this column

--------------

Value(null)
     │
     ▼
Update this column to NULL

--------------

Column omitted
     │
     ▼
Don't touch this column

Value<T> doesn't just hold a value—it also tells Drift what action to take.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Update a product's price.

```dart id="tw4hpm" await (update(products) ..where((p) => p.id.equals(3))) .write( ProductsCompanion( price: const Value(499.99), ), ); 

Explanation:

* Only the `price` column changes.
* All other columns keep their existing values.

---

## Real-World Example

Update a user's profile.

```dart id="8qj2lm"
await (update(users)
      ..where((u) => u.id.equals(8)))
    .write(
      UsersCompanion(
        name: const Value('Alice'),
        bio: const Value(null),
      ),
    );

Explanation:

  • The user's name is updated.
  • The bio is explicitly cleared.
  • Other columns remain unchanged.

docs.title:
When to Use

Use Value<T> when:

  • Updating rows with companion classes.
  • Setting nullable columns to NULL.
  • Performing partial updates.
  • Explicitly controlling which columns are written.

When NOT to Use

You typically don't need Value<T> when:

  • Reading data.
  • Working with generated data classes.
  • Using the .insert() constructor of a companion, where required fields are passed directly.

Best Practices
  • Wrap update values in Value().
  • Use Value(null) to intentionally store NULL.
  • Omit fields you don't want to update.
  • Don't use null directly inside companions.
  • Think of Value() as indicating "include this column."
Forgetting Value()
docs.text:
Wrong

```dart id="ng1qje" UsersCompanion( age: 30, ); 

Explanation:

* Companion fields expect `Value<T>` objects for updates.

**Correct**

```dart id="y1hfq5"
UsersCompanion(
  age: const Value(30),
);

Explanation:

  • Value() marks the column for updating.

docs.title: Using null instead of Value(null)
docs.text:
Wrong

```dart id="b4ntwh" UsersCompanion( bio: null, ); 

Explanation:

* This means the column is omitted from the update.
* The existing database value remains unchanged.

**Correct**

```dart id="zt4lhh"
UsersCompanion(
  bio: const Value(null),
);

Explanation:

  • Value(null) explicitly updates the column to NULL.

docs.title: Wrapping every value unnecessarily
docs.text:
Wrong

Using Value() everywhere, including when constructing objects that don't require companions.

Explanation:

  • Value<T> is specifically designed for companion classes and write operations.

Correct

Use Value() only where Drift expects it.

docs.title:
Summary

Value<T> is a wrapper that tells Drift whether a column should be included in an insert or update operation. It removes the ambiguity between "leave this column unchanged" and "set this column to NULL," making partial updates safe and explicit.
Insertable
docs.text: Insertable represents any object that can be inserted into a Drift table.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Insertable is an interface used by Drift for objects that can be written to a database table.

When you call an insert method, Drift expects an Insertable.

Several Drift-generated classes already implement this interface, including:

  • Generated data classes
  • Companion classes

This means both can be passed to insert operations, although companion classes are usually the preferred choice.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Drift supports multiple ways of representing data that can be inserted into a table.

Instead of requiring insert methods to accept only one specific class, Drift uses the Insertable interface.

This provides flexibility while keeping the insert APIs consistent.

docs.title: Inserting with a Companion
docs.text:
await into(users).insert(
  UsersCompanion.insert(
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • UsersCompanion implements Insertable.
  • Drift converts it into the values needed for the insert operation.

docs.title: Inserting with a Generated Data Class
docs.text:
await into(users).insert(
  User(
    id: 1,
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Generated data classes also implement Insertable.
  • The object can be inserted directly if it contains all required values.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of Insertable as a common contract.

            Insertable
                 ▲
        ┌────────┴────────┐
        │                 │
        │                 │
Generated Data      Companion
     Class             Class
        │                 │
        └────────┬────────┘
                 ▼
         into(table).insert(...)

Anything that implements Insertable can be passed to Drift's insert APIs.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Insert a new task.

await into(tasks).insert(
  TasksCompanion.insert(
    title: 'Write documentation',
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • The companion implements Insertable.
  • Drift extracts the column values automatically.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A helper method that accepts any insertable object.

Future<void> saveUser(
  Insertable<User> user,
) async {
  await into(users).insert(user);
}

Explanation:

  • The method accepts any object implementing Insertable<User>.
  • Callers can provide either a companion or another compatible implementation.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
You'll encounter Insertable when:

  • Reading Drift API signatures.
  • Creating reusable insert methods.
  • Writing generic repository code.
  • Working with advanced Drift APIs.

In day-to-day development, you'll most commonly use companion classes instead of interacting with Insertable directly.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid implementing Insertable yourself unless you have a specific advanced use case.

For most applications:

  • Use generated data classes to read data.
  • Use companion classes to insert and update data.

Drift already generates the required implementations.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Prefer companion classes for inserts.
  • Use generated data classes for reading query results.
  • Treat Insertable as an implementation detail unless writing generic APIs.
  • Let Drift-generated classes handle the interface.
  • Avoid custom implementations unless necessary.

docs.title: Implementing Insertable unnecessarily
docs.text:
Wrong

class MyUser implements Insertable<User> {
  // Custom implementation
}

Explanation:

  • Most applications don't need custom Insertable implementations.
  • This adds unnecessary complexity.

Correct

Use the generated companion class.

docs.title: Confusing Insertable with a model
docs.text:
Wrong

Treating Insertable as a data model for your application.

Explanation:

  • Insertable is an interface for database write operations.
  • It is not intended to represent business or domain models.

Correct

Use generated data classes or your own domain models where appropriate.

docs.title: Using generated data classes for every insert
docs.text:
Wrong

await into(users).insert(
  User(
    id: 1,
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • This requires providing every necessary value, including fields that may be auto-generated.

Correct

await into(users).insert(
  UsersCompanion.insert(
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Companion classes are designed specifically for insert operations.

docs.title: Related APIs
docs.text:
• Companions
  • Generated Data Classes
  • Value
  • Insert
  • Update

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Insertable is the interface that represents objects capable of being inserted into a Drift table. Companion classes and generated data classes already implement this interface, allowing them to be passed directly to insert methods. While you'll rarely interact with Insertable directly, understanding its role helps explain how Drift's insert APIs accept different kinds of objects in a consistent way.

docs.title: Custom Data Classes
docs.text: Custom data classes let you use your own Dart classes instead of Drift's generated data classes.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
By default, Drift generates a data class for every table.

For example:

Users Table
      │
      ▼
Generated User class

However, Drift also allows you to use your own Dart class to represent rows from a table.

This gives you complete control over the structure, behavior, and APIs of your data objects.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Generated data classes are suitable for most applications, but sometimes you need more control.

For example, you might want to:

  • Use an existing domain model.
  • Add custom methods.
  • Add computed properties.
  • Integrate with another architecture.
  • Share models between different data sources.

Custom data classes let you keep your application's models independent from Drift's generated code.

docs.title: Using a Custom Data Class
docs.text:
class User {
  final int id;
  final String name;

  const User({
    required this.id,
    required this.name,
  });
}

Explanation:

  • This is your own Dart class.
  • It is not generated by Drift.
  • You decide its fields, constructors, and methods.

Note: Configuring Drift to use custom row classes requires additional annotations and mapping, which are covered in the official Drift documentation and advanced configuration guides.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the data class as the object your application works with.

Database Row
      │
      ▼
Mapping
      │
      ▼
Your User Class

Instead of using Drift's generated object, the row is represented by your own class.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
A custom product model.

class Product {
  final int id;
  final String name;
  final double price;

  const Product({
    required this.id,
    required this.name,
    required this.price,
  });
}

Explanation:

  • The class is completely independent of Drift.
  • Additional methods or properties can be added as needed.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
A richer domain model.

class User {
  final int id;
  final String firstName;
  final String lastName;

  const User({
    required this.id,
    required this.firstName,
    required this.lastName,
  });

  String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';
}

Explanation:

  • The class includes computed properties.
  • Business-related behavior can live alongside the data.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use custom data classes when:

  • Your project already has domain models.
  • You follow Clean Architecture.
  • You want additional methods or computed properties.
  • Models are shared across multiple layers.
  • You need complete control over your data objects.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid custom data classes when:

  • You're building a small application.
  • Drift's generated data classes meet your needs.
  • You don't need custom behavior.

Generated data classes are simpler and require less configuration.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Prefer generated data classes unless customization is necessary.
  • Keep custom models focused on your application's domain.
  • Avoid duplicating generated classes without a clear reason.
  • Separate persistence concerns from business logic when appropriate.
  • Use meaningful methods and computed properties instead of duplicating data.

docs.title: Creating custom classes unnecessarily
docs.text:
Wrong

Creating custom classes that contain exactly the same fields as the generated data classes without adding any new behavior.

Explanation:

  • This increases maintenance without providing additional value.

Correct

Use generated data classes unless your application benefits from custom models.

docs.title: Mixing generated and custom models inconsistently
docs.text:
Wrong

Using generated data classes in some parts of the application and custom models in others without a clear conversion strategy.

Explanation:

  • This can make the codebase harder to understand and maintain.

Correct

Choose a consistent approach and map between models when necessary.

docs.title: Putting database-specific logic in domain models
docs.text:
Wrong

Adding Drift-specific APIs or persistence logic directly to your custom data classes.

Explanation:

  • This tightly couples your models to the database implementation.

Correct

Keep custom data classes focused on representing your application's data and behavior.

docs.title: Related APIs
docs.text:
• Generated Data Classes
  • Companions
  • Insertable
  • TypeConverter
  • Repository Pattern

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Custom data classes allow you to replace Drift's generated row classes with your own Dart models. They are useful when your application requires richer domain models, shared business objects, or additional behavior. For most applications, however, the generated data classes are sufficient and provide the simplest development experience.

docs.title: Insert
docs.text: Insert adds new rows to a table.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
An insert operation creates a new record in a database table.

Whenever your application stores new information—such as a new user, task, or product—you perform an insert.

In Drift, inserts are performed using the into() API.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Databases store data as rows inside tables.

Without insert operations, your database would remain empty because there would be no way to add new records.

Insert operations are one of the four fundamental CRUD operations:

  • Create → Insert
  • Read → Select
  • Update → Update
  • Delete → Delete

docs.title: Basic Insert
docs.text:
await into(users).insert(
  UsersCompanion.insert(
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • into(users) specifies the target table.
  • insert() creates a new row.
  • UsersCompanion.insert() provides the values to insert.
  • Auto-generated and default columns can be omitted.

docs.title: Inserting All Required Values
docs.text:
await into(products).insert(
  ProductsCompanion.insert(
    name: 'Laptop',
    price: 999.99,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Required columns must be provided.
  • Columns with default values are filled automatically by SQLite.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of inserting as adding a new row to a spreadsheet.

Users

Before

+----+------+
| ID | Name |
+----+------+
| 1  | Bob  |
+----+------+

        │
        ▼
     Insert

        │
        ▼

After

+----+-------+
| ID | Name  |
+----+-------+
| 1  | Bob   |
| 2  | Alice |
+----+-------+

Every successful insert appends a new row to the table.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Insert a task.

await into(tasks).insert(
  TasksCompanion.insert(
    title: 'Learn Drift',
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • A new task is added to the database.
  • Columns with defaults or auto-generated values are handled automatically.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Registering a new user.

await into(users).insert(
  UsersCompanion.insert(
    name: 'Alice',
    email: 'alice@example.com',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • A new user record is created.
  • Drift validates the insert against the table's constraints before SQLite stores it.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use insert when you need to:

  • Register a new user.
  • Create a new task.
  • Save a new order.
  • Add a product.
  • Store application data for the first time.

Every new record begins with an insert.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Don't use insert when:

  • Modifying an existing row.
  • Replacing an existing record.
  • Removing data.

Instead, use:

  • update() for modifications.
  • replace() for replacing rows.
  • delete() for removing rows.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use companion classes for inserts.
  • Let auto-increment columns generate their own values.
  • Take advantage of default values.
  • Validate user input before inserting.
  • Handle insertion errors appropriately.

docs.title: Providing auto-generated IDs
docs.text:
Wrong

await into(users).insert(
  User(
    id: 1,
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Auto-incrementing IDs should usually be generated by SQLite.

Correct

await into(users).insert(
  UsersCompanion.insert(
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 25,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • SQLite automatically assigns the ID.

docs.title: Forgetting required columns
docs.text:
Wrong

await into(users).insert(
  UsersCompanion.insert(),
);

Explanation:

  • Required columns must be supplied.

Correct

Provide all required values when constructing the companion.

docs.title: Using insert to modify existing data
docs.text:
Wrong

Calling insert() to change an existing user's information.

Explanation:

  • Inserts always create new rows.
  • They do not modify existing records.

Correct

Use update() when changing existing rows.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Insert creates new rows in a Drift table. Using the into().insert() API along with companion classes provides a type-safe way to add data while allowing SQLite to handle auto-generated values and defaults. It is the primary operation for creating new records in your database.

docs.title: Batch Insert
docs.text: Batch insert adds multiple rows to a table in a single operation.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A batch insert allows you to insert many records at once instead of performing separate insert operations for each row.

Rather than sending multiple database operations, Drift groups them into a single batch, making inserts much faster and more efficient.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Imagine importing 1,000 contacts.

Without batching:

Insert Contact 1
Insert Contact 2
Insert Contact 3
...
Insert Contact 1000

This requires 1,000 separate database operations.

With batch inserts:

Batch
├── Contact 1
├── Contact 2
├── Contact 3
...
└── Contact 1000

The database processes them together, reducing overhead and improving performance.

docs.title: Basic Batch Insert
docs.text:
await batch((batch) {
  batch.insertAll(
    users,
    [
      UsersCompanion.insert(
        name: 'Alice',
        age: 25,
      ),
      UsersCompanion.insert(
        name: 'Bob',
        age: 30,
      ),
    ],
  );
});

Explanation:

  • batch() creates a batch operation.
  • insertAll() inserts multiple rows into the table.
  • Each item in the list is a companion object representing one row.

docs.title: Batch Insert with Multiple Tables
docs.text:
await batch((batch) {
  batch.insertAll(users, usersList);

  batch.insertAll(products, productsList);
});

Explanation:

  • A single batch can contain operations for multiple tables.
  • Drift executes them efficiently as one grouped operation.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of mailing letters.

Without batching:

Post Office

Trip 1 → One letter
Trip 2 → One letter
Trip 3 → One letter

With batching:

One Trip

📦
├── Letter 1
├── Letter 2
├── Letter 3
└── Letter 4

Instead of making many small trips, you deliver everything together.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Insert multiple tasks.

await batch((batch) {
  batch.insertAll(
    tasks,
    [
      TasksCompanion.insert(title: 'Buy milk'),
      TasksCompanion.insert(title: 'Read book'),
      TasksCompanion.insert(title: 'Exercise'),
    ],
  );
});

Explanation:

  • Three tasks are inserted in one database operation.
  • This is more efficient than three separate inserts.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Importing products from an API.

await batch((batch) {
  batch.insertAll(
    products,
    productCompanions,
  );
});

Explanation:

  • productCompanions contains many products.
  • Drift inserts them together, making bulk imports much faster.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use batch inserts when:

  • Importing large datasets.
  • Syncing data from a server.
  • Restoring backups.
  • Seeding a database.
  • Inserting many records at once.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid batch inserts when:

  • Inserting only one or two rows.
  • Each insert depends on the result of the previous insert.
  • Individual error handling is required for each insert.

For small numbers of inserts, a normal insert() is often simpler.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Batch as many related inserts as practical.
  • Use companion classes for batch inserts.
  • Group operations that belong together.
  • Use batches for imports and synchronization tasks.
  • Avoid creating unnecessarily large batches if memory usage becomes a concern.

docs.title: Repeating individual inserts
docs.text:
Wrong

for (final user in usersList) {
  await into(users).insert(user);
}

Explanation:

  • Each iteration performs a separate database operation.
  • This is slower for large collections.

Correct

await batch((batch) {
  batch.insertAll(users, usersList);
});

Explanation:

  • All rows are inserted together.

docs.title: Using batches for a single insert
docs.text:
Wrong

await batch((batch) {
  batch.insert(
    users,
    UsersCompanion.insert(
      name: 'Alice',
      age: 25,
    ),
  );
});

Explanation:

  • A batch adds unnecessary complexity for a single operation.

Correct

Use into(users).insert(...) for individual inserts.

docs.title: Mixing unrelated operations unnecessarily
docs.text:
Wrong

Adding unrelated database operations to the same batch simply because they occur close together in code.

Explanation:

  • Batches should group operations that naturally belong together.
  • Overusing batches can make code harder to understand.

Correct

Use batches for logically related bulk operations.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Batch insert allows multiple rows to be inserted efficiently in a single database operation. It reduces database overhead, improves performance, and is ideal for bulk imports, synchronization, and large datasets. For individual records, a normal insert is usually the simpler choice.

docs.title: Update
docs.text: Update modifies existing rows in a table.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
An update operation changes the values of one or more columns in existing database rows.

Unlike an insert, which creates a new row, an update modifies data that already exists.

In Drift, updates are performed using the update() API.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Data changes over time.

For example:

  • A user updates their email address.
  • A task is marked as completed.
  • A product's price changes.
  • An order's status is updated.

Without update operations, you would have to delete the old row and insert a new one, which is inefficient and can break relationships.

docs.title: Updating a Row
docs.text:
```dart id="d0rj5g" await (update(users) ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1))) .write( UsersCompanion( age: const Value(26), ), ); 

Explanation:

* `update(users)` targets the `users` table.
* `where()` selects the rows to update.
* `write()` applies the new values.
* `Value(26)` marks the `age` column for updating.

---

## Updating Multiple Columns

```dart id="8zqgqt"
await (update(users)
      ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1)))
    .write(
      UsersCompanion(
        name: const Value('Alice Smith'),
        age: const Value(26),
      ),
    );

Explanation:

  • Both name and age are updated.
  • Any omitted columns remain unchanged.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of updating as editing a row in a spreadsheet.

```text id="zjlwmm" Before

+----+-------+-----+ | ID | Name | Age | +----+-------+-----+ | 1 | Alice | 25 | +----+-------+-----+

    │
    ▼
 Update Age

    │
    ▼

After

+----+-------+-----+ | ID | Name | Age | +----+-------+-----+ | 1 | Alice | 26 | +----+-------+-----+ 

The row stays the same; only the selected columns change.

---

# Examples

## Simple Example

Mark a task as completed.

```dart id="yvc5nt"
await (update(tasks)
      ..where((t) => t.id.equals(5)))
    .write(
      TasksCompanion(
        completed: const Value(true),
      ),
    );

Explanation:

  • Only the completed column changes.
  • The rest of the task remains unchanged.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Update a customer's contact information.

```dart id="zrd7p0" await (update(customers) ..where((c) => c.id.equals(10))) .write( CustomersCompanion( email: const Value('alice@example.com'), phone: const Value('1234567890'), ), ); 

Explanation:

* Both contact fields are updated.
* Other customer information remains untouched.

---

# When to Use

Use update when you need to:

* Edit user information.
* Mark tasks as complete.
* Change product prices.
* Update order statuses.
* Modify existing records.

---

# When NOT to Use

Don't use update when:

* Creating new records.
* Replacing an entire row.
* Deleting data.

Instead, use:

* `insert()` for new rows.
* `replace()` to replace an entire record.
* `delete()` to remove rows.

---

# Best Practices

* Always use a `where()` clause unless you intentionally want to update every row.
* Update only the columns that need to change.
* Use companion classes for updates.
* Wrap updated values in `Value()`.
* Validate user input before updating the database.

---

# Common Mistakes

## Forgetting the `where()` clause

**Wrong**

```dart id="5g4v1k"
await update(users).write(
  UsersCompanion(
    age: const Value(26),
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Every row in the table is updated.
  • This is a common and potentially serious mistake.

Correct

```dart id="h2p4fd" await (update(users) ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1))) .write( UsersCompanion( age: const Value(26), ), ); 

Explanation:

* Only the intended row is modified.

---

## Forgetting `Value()`

**Wrong**

```dart id="g6x1je"
UsersCompanion(
  age: 26,
);

Explanation:

  • Companion fields require Value<T> for updates.

Correct

dart id="wn2s7x" UsersCompanion( age: const Value(26), );

Explanation:

  • Value() explicitly marks the field for updating.

docs.title: Using update to create new data
docs.text:
Wrong

Attempting to add a new user with update().

Explanation:

  • Updates only affect existing rows.
  • If no matching row exists, nothing is updated.

Correct

Use insert() to create new records.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Update modifies existing rows in a Drift table without creating new ones. By combining update(), where(), and companion classes, you can safely change specific columns while leaving the rest of the row unchanged. Always use a where() clause to ensure only the intended rows are updated.

docs.title: Replace
docs.text: Replace updates an existing row by replacing all of its column values.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
replace() updates a row using an entire data object instead of updating individual columns.

Unlike update(), which modifies only selected columns, replace() treats the provided object as the complete replacement for the existing row.

The row is identified using its primary key.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Sometimes you already have a complete object representing the latest state of a row.

For example:

  • A user edits every field in a profile.
  • A form submits all values at once.
  • You retrieve an object, modify it, and save it back.

Using replace() is simpler than creating a companion and wrapping every changed field with Value().

docs.title: Replacing a Row
docs.text:
final user = User(
  id: 1,
  name: 'Alice',
  age: 26,
);

await update(users).replace(user);

Explanation:

  • replace() uses the row's primary key (id) to find the existing record.
  • Every column in the object is written back to the database.
  • The row must already exist.

docs.title: Updating an Existing Object
docs.text:
final existingUser = await (select(users)
      ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1)))
    .getSingle();

final updatedUser = existingUser.copyWith(
  age: 27,
);

await update(users).replace(updatedUser);

Explanation:

  • The existing row is read from the database.
  • copyWith() creates an updated version.
  • replace() writes the new object back.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of replacing as swapping an entire document.

Before

User
├── id: 1
├── name: Alice
└── age: 25

        │
        ▼
     Replace

        │
        ▼

User
├── id: 1
├── name: Alice
└── age: 26

Instead of editing one field individually, the entire object becomes the new database row.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Update a product.

await update(products).replace(
  Product(
    id: 3,
    name: 'Laptop',
    price: 899.99,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • The product with ID 3 is replaced.
  • Every property in the Product object is written to the database.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Saving an edited profile.

final updatedCustomer = customer.copyWith(
  email: 'alice@example.com',
  phone: '1234567890',
);

await update(customers).replace(updatedCustomer);

Explanation:

  • The application edits the object in memory.
  • The updated object replaces the corresponding database row.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use replace() when:

  • You already have the complete object.
  • Saving data from an edit form.
  • Updating most or all columns.
  • Working with immutable models and copyWith().

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Avoid replace() when:

  • Only one or two columns need updating.
  • You don't have all column values.
  • You're performing partial updates.

In these situations, update() with a companion is usually more appropriate.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Ensure the object has a valid primary key.
  • Use copyWith() to modify immutable data classes.
  • Use replace() only when updating complete objects.
  • Prefer update() for partial changes.
  • Verify that the row exists before replacing if necessary.

docs.title: Using replace() for partial updates
docs.text:
Wrong

await update(users).replace(
  User(
    id: 1,
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 0,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • Every field in the object is written to the database.
  • Placeholder or incorrect values may overwrite existing data.

Correct

Use update() with a companion when only a few columns need to change.

docs.title: Forgetting the primary key
docs.text:
Wrong

await update(users).replace(
  User(
    id: 0,
    name: 'Alice',
    age: 26,
  ),
);

Explanation:

  • replace() uses the primary key to locate the row.
  • An incorrect or missing key may prevent the update.

Correct

Provide the correct primary key value for the row being replaced.

docs.title: Confusing replace() with SQL REPLACE
docs.text:
Wrong

Assuming replace() inserts a new row if one doesn't exist.

Explanation:

  • Drift's replace() performs an update based on the primary key.
  • It is not the same as SQLite's INSERT OR REPLACE.

Correct

Use replace() to update existing rows, and use upsert() when you need insert-or-update behavior.

docs.text:

  • Generated Data Classes

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: replace() updates an existing row by writing an entire data object back to the database. It is most useful when you already have a complete model, such as after editing a form or using copyWith(). For partial updates, update() with companion classes is generally the better choice.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text: Delete removes rows from a table.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
A delete operation permanently removes one or more rows from a database table.

Once a row is deleted, it is no longer returned by queries unless it is inserted again.

In Drift, deletions are performed using the delete() API.

docs.title: Why does it exist?
docs.text:
Applications often need to remove data.

For example:

  • A user deletes a note.
  • A completed task is removed.
  • An old log entry is cleaned up.
  • An expired session is deleted.

Without delete operations, the database would continue to grow with unwanted or outdated data.

docs.title: Deleting a Single Row
docs.text:
await (delete(users)
      ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1)))
    .go();

Explanation:

  • delete(users) targets the users table.
  • where() specifies which rows to remove.
  • go() executes the delete operation.

docs.title: Deleting Multiple Rows
docs.text:
await (delete(tasks)
      ..where((t) => t.completed.equals(true)))
    .go();

Explanation:

  • Every completed task is deleted.
  • All rows matching the condition are removed.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of deleting as removing rows from a spreadsheet.

Before

+----+-------+
| ID | Name  |
+----+-------+
| 1  | Alice |
| 2  | Bob   |
| 3  | Carol |
+----+-------+

Delete ID = 2

        │
        ▼

After

+----+-------+
| ID | Name  |
+----+-------+
| 1  | Alice |
| 3  | Carol |
+----+-------+

The deleted row no longer exists in the table.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Delete a product.

await (delete(products)
      ..where((p) => p.id.equals(5)))
    .go();

Explanation:

  • Removes the product whose ID is 5.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Delete expired notifications.

await (delete(notifications)
      ..where((n) => n.expiresAt.isSmallerThanValue(DateTime.now())))
    .go();

Explanation:

  • All expired notifications are removed.
  • Active notifications remain untouched.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use delete when you need to:

  • Remove unwanted records.
  • Delete user-created content.
  • Clean up old data.
  • Remove expired records.
  • Implement data cleanup tasks.

docs.title: When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Don't use delete when:

  • Updating existing data.
  • Temporarily hiding records.
  • Archiving data.

For these cases:

  • Use update() to modify data.
  • Consider a soft-delete flag such as isDeleted.
  • Archive important records instead of permanently removing them.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always use a where() clause unless you intentionally want to delete every row.
  • Confirm destructive actions with users when appropriate.
  • Consider soft deletes for important business data.
  • Use transactions when deleting related records.
  • Back up important data before bulk deletions.

docs.title: Forgetting the where() clause
docs.text:
Wrong

await delete(users).go();

Explanation:

  • Every row in the table is deleted.
  • This is one of the most common and dangerous database mistakes.

Correct

await (delete(users)
      ..where((u) => u.id.equals(1)))
    .go();

Explanation:

  • Only the intended row is removed.

docs.title: Deleting instead of updating
docs.text:
Wrong

Deleting a user just to change their email address.

Explanation:

  • The user's data and relationships are lost.

Correct

Use update() to modify existing records.

docs.title: Accidentally deleting related data
docs.text:
Wrong

Deleting a parent record without considering related child records.

Explanation:

  • This may violate foreign key constraints or leave orphaned data, depending on your schema.

Correct

Understand your table relationships and use transactions or cascading rules when appropriate.
