  • Value: true or false (boolean).
  • Use cases: Inline editing, WYSIWYG editors, collaborative editing.
  • Example: <div contenteditable="true">Edit me</div>

docs.title: Concept 13: spellcheck – Spell‑Checking
docs.text:
• Purpose: Enables or disables spell‑checking on text input fields and contenteditable elements.
  • Value: true or false (boolean).
  • Use cases: Form inputs, text areas, editable content.
  • Example: <textarea spellcheck="true">...</textarea>

docs.title: Concept 14: accesskey – Keyboard Shortcut
docs.text:
• Purpose: Provides a keyboard shortcut for interacting with the element.
  • Value: A single character (e.g., s, 1, ?).
  • Use cases: Accessibility and power‑user shortcuts.
  • Example: <button accesskey="s">Save</button> (Alt+S on Windows, Ctrl+Option+S on Mac).
  • Note: Conflicts with browser and OS shortcuts; use sparingly.

docs.title: Concept 15: draggable – Drag and Drop
docs.text:
• Purpose: Enables the element to be draggable via the HTML Drag and Drop API.
  • Value: true or false (boolean).
  • Use cases: Drag‑and‑drop interfaces, sorting, file upload.
  • Example: <img src="photo.jpg" draggable="true">

docs.title: Concept 16: translate – Translation Control
docs.text:
• Purpose: Indicates whether the element's content should be translated when the page is translated.
  • Value: yes (translate) or no (do not translate).
  • Use cases: Preserving brand names, code snippets, or specific phrases.
  • Example: <p translate="no">Brand Name</p>

docs.title: Concept 17: inert – Inertness
docs.text:
• Purpose: Makes the element and its descendants non‑interactive (ignores clicks, focus, and events).
  • Value: Boolean (presence = true).
  • Use cases: Disabling parts of the UI while a modal is open, improving accessibility.
  • Example: <div inert>...</div>

docs.title: Step‑by‑Step: Browser Processing of Global Attributes
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a start tag with global attributes.
    │
    ▼
2.  It parses the attribute names and values.
    │
    ▼
3.  It creates a DOM element node.
    │
    ▼
4.  It sets the attributes as properties on the node.
    │   ├── `id` → `element.id`
    │   ├── `class` → `element.className` and `element.classList`
    │   ├── `style` → `element.style` (CSSStyleDeclaration)
    │   ├── `data-*` → `element.dataset`
    │   ├── `aria-*` → `element.getAttribute('aria-*')` (no direct property)
    │   └── others → stored as attributes.
    │
    ▼
5.  The browser applies CSS based on `id`, `class`, and `style`.
    │
    ▼
6.  The accessibility tree is built using `aria-*`, `role`, `lang`, etc.
    │
    ▼
7.  The element is rendered (or hidden) based on `hidden` and other attributes.
    │
    ▼
8.  User interaction is influenced by `tabindex`, `contenteditable`, `accesskey`, and `draggable`.

docs.title: class and classList
docs.text:
The class attribute is reflected in the DOM as className and provides the classList API for easier manipulation.

const element = document.querySelector('.my-class');
element.classList.add('active');
element.classList.remove('hidden');
element.classList.toggle('open');

docs.title: data-* and dataset
docs.text:
data-* attributes are accessed via dataset:

const div = document.querySelector('[data-user-id]');
console.log(div.dataset.userId); // "42"
div.dataset.role = 'admin'; // Adds data-role="admin"

docs.title: aria-* and role
docs.text:
ARIA attributes are set via setAttribute and read via getAttribute:

element.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Close');
console.log(element.getAttribute('aria-label'));

docs.title: The Element Interface
docs.text: All HTML elements inherit from the Element interface, which provides methods for working with global attributes: - getAttribute(name) - setAttribute(name, value) - removeAttribute(name) - hasAttribute(name) - attributes – a NamedNodeMap of all attributes.

docs.title: Reflection of Global Attributes
docs.text:
• id → element.id (string)
  • class → element.className (string) and element.classList (DOMTokenList)
  • style → element.style (CSSStyleDeclaration)
  • data-* → element.dataset (DOMStringMap)
  • title → element.title
  • lang → element.lang
  • dir → element.dir
  • hidden → element.hidden (boolean)
  • tabindex → element.tabIndex (number)
  • contenteditable → element.contentEditable (string: "true", "false", "inherit")
  • draggable → element.draggable (boolean)
  • spellcheck → element.spellcheck (boolean)
  • translate → element.translate (boolean)
  • inert → element.inert (boolean)

docs.title: dataset Implementation
docs.text: dataset is a live DOMStringMap that reflects the data-* attributes. When you set a property on dataset, it updates the corresponding attribute.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of Global Attributes
docs.text:
1.  Author writes global attributes in the HTML.
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── Attributes are stored on the element nodes.
    │
    ▼
4.  CSS is applied based on `id`, `class`, and `style`.
    │
    ▼
5.  Accessibility tree is built using `aria-*`, `role`, `lang`, `dir`.
    │
    ▼
6.  JavaScript can read, modify, or remove global attributes.
    │
    ▼
7.  User interaction is influenced by `tabindex`, `contenteditable`, `accesskey`, `draggable`.
    │
    ▼
8.  Re‑rendering may occur if attributes affect layout or style.
    │
    ▼
9.  When the page is unloaded, attributes are destroyed with the DOM.

docs.title: Example 1: Using id, class, and style
docs.text:
<div id="header" class="container main" style="background: #f0f0f0; padding: 20px;">
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
</div>

Code Breakdown: - id="header" – unique identifier. - class="container main" – two classes for styling. - style="background: #f0f0f0; padding: 20px;" – inline styles.

docs.title: Example 2: Using data-* and JavaScript
docs.text:
<button id="saveBtn" data-action="save" data-target="profile">Save</button>
<script>
    const btn = document.getElementById('saveBtn');
    console.log(btn.dataset.action); // "save"
    console.log(btn.dataset.target); // "profile"
    btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
        const action = this.dataset.action;
        const target = this.dataset.target;
        console.log(`Performing ${action} on ${target}`);
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 3: Using aria-* and role for Accessibility
docs.text:
<div role="button" tabindex="0" aria-label="Close" aria-disabled="false">✕</div>
<script>
    const btn = document.querySelector('[role="button"]');
    btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
        // Simulate button click
        console.log('Closed');
    });
    // Keyboard support: Enter or Space
    btn.addEventListener('keydown', function(e) {
        if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') {
            e.preventDefault();
            this.click();
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 4: Using hidden and contenteditable
docs.text:
<div>
    <p id="editable" contenteditable="true">Edit this text</p>
    <button id="toggleEdit">Toggle Edit Mode</button>
    <button id="hideShow">Hide/Show</button>
</div>
<script>
    const p = document.getElementById('editable');
    document.getElementById('toggleEdit').addEventListener('click', function() {
        p.contentEditable = p.contentEditable === 'true' ? 'false' : 'true';
    });
    document.getElementById('hideShow').addEventListener('click', function() {
        p.hidden = !p.hidden;
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 5: Using lang, dir, and title
docs.text:
<p lang="fr" dir="ltr" title="This is a French phrase">Bonjour, comment ça va?</p>
<p lang="ar" dir="rtl" title="مرحباً بالعالم">مرحباً بالعالم</p>

docs.title: Example 6: Using tabindex for Focus Management
docs.text:
<button>Button 1</button>
<div tabindex="0">Focusable div</div>
<button>Button 2</button>
<button tabindex="-1">Not tabbable</button>

Focus order: Button 1 → Focusable div → Button 2. The last button is not reachable via Tab.

docs.title: Example 7: Using accesskey
docs.text:
<button accesskey="s">Save</button>
<button accesskey="c">Cancel</button>
Usage: Press Alt+S (Windows) or Ctrl+Option+S (Mac) to trigger the Save button.

docs.title: Example 8: Using inert to Disable a Section
docs.text:
<div inert>
    <button>Cannot click</button>
    <input type="text" placeholder="Cannot type">
</div>
Behaviour: All interactive elements inside the inert container are disabled.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text:
• CSS styling – using id and class to target elements.
  • JavaScript hooks – using id, class, and data-* for selection and data storage.
  • Accessibility – using aria-*, role, lang, dir, tabindex to make content accessible.
  • Internationalisation – using lang and dir for multilingual content.
  • Interactive editing – using contenteditable for rich text editing.
  • Hiding/showing content – using hidden for conditional display.
  • Keyboard shortcuts – using accesskey for power users.
  • Drag‑and‑drop – using draggable for drag interfaces.
  • Tooltips – using title for additional information.

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use id only when necessary – it must be unique. Prefer class for styling and data-* for data.

  2. Use class for styling groups – not id. Use meaningful, semantic names.

  3. Avoid inline style – keep styles in external CSS for maintainability and caching.

  4. Use data-* for custom data – never use non‑standard attributes.

  5. Use aria-* and role only when needed – prefer native semantic elements first.

  6. Always provide lang on the <html> element – and override on individual elements when necessary.

  7. Use dir for RTL languages – set dir="rtl" on appropriate elements.

  8. Use title sparingly – it's not accessible to all users (not readable on touch devices).

  9. Be careful with tabindex – use 0 for focusable elements, -1 for programmatic focus, and avoid positive values.

  10. Use hidden for temporary hiding – not for permanent removal (use CSS display: none or remove from DOM).

  11. Use inert for disabling sections – it's more accessible than relying on JavaScript.

  12. Test accesskey – ensure it doesn't conflict with browser or OS shortcuts.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate id Values
docs.text:
<div id="main">...</div>
<div id="main">...</div>   <!-- Duplicate -->
Why it's wrong: id must be unique. Duplicates cause JavaScript and CSS issues.

✅ Correct: Use unique IDs or class.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using style for All Styling
docs.text:
<p style="color: red; font-size: 20px;">Text</p>
Why it's wrong: Inline styles are hard to maintain and cannot be cached.

✅ Correct: Use CSS classes.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Non‑standard Attributes Instead of data-*
docs.text:
<div user-id="123">Profile</div>
Why it's wrong: Not standard; may cause validation errors.

✅ Correct: 

<div data-user-id="123">Profile</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting aria-label on Icon Buttons
docs.text:
<button>✕</button>   <!-- Screen reader: "X" or unknown -->
Why it's wrong: The button has no accessible name; screen readers won't know its purpose.

✅ Correct: 

<button aria-label="Close">✕</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Misusing tabindex with Positive Values
docs.text:
<div tabindex="5">First</div>
<div tabindex="1">Second</div>
Why it's wrong: Positive tabindex values override natural DOM order, causing confusion.

✅ Correct: Use tabindex="0" and rely on DOM order.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using hidden Instead of CSS display: none
docs.text:
<div hidden>...</div>
Why it's wrong: hidden is semantically correct for temporary hiding, but if you need to hide for layout purposes (e.g., responsive design), use CSS.

✅ Correct: Use CSS display: none or visibility: hidden for layout‑based hiding.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using accesskey Without Checking Conflicts
docs.text:
<button accesskey="a">Action</button>
Why it's wrong: Alt+A is often used by browser for "Add Bookmark" or other functions.

✅ Correct: Choose less common keys; test thoroughly.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• id and class – using them for CSS and JavaScript is fast; no performance concerns.
  • style – inline styles can be slower to parse than CSS classes, but the difference is negligible.
  • data-* – dataset is fast; no performance concerns.
  • hidden – similar to display: none; no performance benefit over CSS.
  • inert – can improve performance by preventing event propagation in disabled sections.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• data-* – may expose sensitive data; avoid storing secrets or personal information.
  • aria-* – no direct security implications, but incorrect ARIA can confuse assistive tech.
  • title – can be used in XSS if user‑controlled content is inserted unsafely.
  • style – can inject malicious CSS; sanitize user input.
  • contenteditable – beware of XSS; sanitize user input before saving.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect an element to see all its attributes.
  • Console – use document.querySelector('.class').attributes to list all attributes.
  • classList – use element.classList to inspect classes.
  • dataset – use console.log(element.dataset) to see all data attributes.
  • computedStyle – check how style and class affect rendering.
  • Accessibility Inspector – in DevTools, check ARIA attributes and roles.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• id – for unique identification (JavaScript, CSS, form labels).
  • class – for grouping and styling.
  • style – only for dynamic styles (use CSS for static).
  • title – for tooltips or additional context.
  • lang – always on <html>, override on specific parts.
  • dir – for RTL languages.
  • data-* – for custom application data.
  • aria-* and role – for accessibility enhancements.
  • tabindex – to make non‑interactive elements focusable.
  • hidden – for temporary hiding.
  • contenteditable – for editable content areas.
  • spellcheck – for text inputs.
  • accesskey – for keyboard shortcuts.
  • draggable – for drag‑and‑drop interfaces.
  • translate – to control translation.
  • inert – to disable sections.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Avoid style for static styling.
  • Avoid id for styling (use class).
  • Avoid accesskey if it conflicts with browser shortcuts.
  • Avoid title for critical information (not accessible to all users).
  • Avoid positive tabindex values (use 0 or -1).

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Element‑Specific Attributes
  • ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)
  • CSS Selectors (ID, Class, Attribute)
  • JavaScript DOM APIs (getElementById, querySelector, classList, dataset)
  • HTML Validation
  • Internationalization (i18n)
  • Accessibility (WCAG)

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The id attribute is case‑sensitive in CSS and JavaScript (but not in HTML).

  • The class attribute is named class in HTML, but in JavaScript you access it via className because class is a reserved word.

  • The data-* attributes were introduced in HTML5 to standardise custom attributes, replacing the old practice of using rel or custom attributes.

  • The hidden attribute is a boolean attribute; its presence hides the element, but it can be overridden by CSS (display: block).

  • The contenteditable attribute makes any element editable, turning it into a rich text editor.

  • The inert attribute is relatively new and is useful for disabling parts of the UI while maintaining accessibility.

  • The role attribute is part of ARIA and can be used on any element to change its semantic meaning for assistive tech.

  • The accesskey attribute is supported in all modern browsers but is often underused due to conflicts.

  • The translate attribute is respected by some browsers and translation tools, allowing you to prevent automatic translation of specific content.

  • The draggable attribute is part of the HTML Drag and Drop API and works with JavaScript events.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Global attributes are attributes that can be used on any HTML element.
  • They include id, class, style, title, lang, dir, data-*, aria-*, role, tabindex, hidden, contenteditable, spellcheck, accesskey, draggable, translate, inert, and others.
  • Purpose: Identity, grouping, styling, custom data, accessibility, internationalisation, interaction control, and more.
  • Best practices: Use class for styling, data-* for data, id for uniqueness, aria-* for accessibility, and avoid inline style for static styling.
  • Common mistakes include duplicate ids, misusing tabindex, forgetting aria-label, and using non‑standard attributes.
  • Global attributes are the universal modifiers that make HTML flexible and powerful.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Boolean attributes are a special type of HTML attribute that represent a true/false state simply by their presence or absence in the start tag. Unlike regular attributes that require a name-value pair (e.g., href="https://example.com"), boolean attributes are binary – if the attribute is present, the value is true; if it is absent, the value is false. The actual value assigned to the attribute is irrelevant; the browser only cares whether the attribute exists.

Boolean attributes are typically used for enabling or disabling features, toggling states, or controlling behavior. Common examples include disabled, required, checked, readonly, hidden, and autofocus.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Boolean attributes serve several essential purposes:

  • Enable/disable features – disabled prevents interaction; readonly prevents editing.
  • Set default states – checked pre‑selects a checkbox or radio button; selected pre‑selects an option.
  • Control behavior – required enforces form validation; autofocus sets initial focus.
  • Simplify syntax – no need for ="true" or ="false"; presence alone conveys meaning.
  • Improve readability – cleaner, more concise markup compared to explicit true/false values.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Boolean attributes are a subset of all HTML attributes. They appear in the start tag like any other attribute, but they are treated differently by the parser. They are commonly used on interactive elements like form controls, but some (like hidden) are global.

<!-- Boolean attribute present → feature enabled -->
<input type="checkbox" checked>
<button disabled>Click</button>

<!-- Boolean attribute absent → feature disabled -->
<input type="checkbox">
<button>Click</button>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: In the early web, authors needed a way to enable or disable features on elements. The natural approach was to use attributes with true/false values, like disabled="true" and disabled="false". However, this created a problem: what happens if disabled is present but set to "false"? Does that mean the element is disabled or not? There was confusion, and browsers handled it inconsistently.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text:
• Ambiguous values – disabled="false" was interpreted as true by some browsers because the attribute was present.
  • Redundant syntax – disabled="true" is longer than just disabled.
  • Inconsistent behavior – browsers handled disabled="false" differently.
  • Validation confusion – validators had to distinguish between valid and invalid boolean attribute usage.
  • XHTML complexity – XHTML required boolean attributes to have a value (e.g., disabled="disabled"), which was more verbose.

docs.title: Why Boolean Attributes Were Standardised
docs.text:
The HTML specification introduced boolean attributes to provide a clear, unambiguous syntax for binary states. The rule is simple:

  • Presence → the feature is enabled (true).
  • Absence → the feature is disabled (false).

The value (if provided) is ignored, though the convention is to use the attribute name itself or an empty string. This eliminates confusion, simplifies parsing, and makes the markup cleaner. XHTML required the attribute name as the value (e.g., disabled="disabled"), but HTML5 relaxes this to just the name.

docs.title: The Syntax of Boolean Attributes
docs.text:
<!-- Correct: attribute present → true -->
<input type="checkbox" checked>
<input type="text" required>
<button disabled>Click</button>

<!-- Also correct: attribute present with value → still true -->
<input type="checkbox" checked="checked">
<input type="text" required="required">
<button disabled="disabled">Click</button>

<!-- Also correct: attribute present with empty string → still true -->
<input type="checkbox" checked="">
<input type="text" required="">
<button disabled="">Click</button>

<!-- Incorrect: attribute absent → false -->
<input type="checkbox">
<input type="text">
<button>Click</button>

docs.title: Common Boolean Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Used On Purpose checked <input type="checkbox">, <input type="radio"> Pre‑selects the control. selected <option> Pre‑selects the option in a dropdown. disabled <button>, <input>, <select>, <textarea>, <fieldset> Disables interaction. readonly <input>, <textarea> Prevents editing (but still focusable and submittable). required <input>, <select>, <textarea> Makes the field mandatory for form submission. autofocus <button>, <input>, <select>, <textarea> Automatically focuses the element on page load. multiple <input type="file">, <select> Allows multiple selections. novalidate <form> Disables form validation. formnovalidate <button type="submit">, <input type="image"> Disables validation for a specific submit button. hidden Global Hides the element from rendering. open <details> Expands the details widget by default. async <script> Loads the script asynchronously. defer <script> Defers script execution until after parsing. download <a>, <area> Suggests downloading the linked resource instead of navigating. ismap <img> Indicates the image is a server‑side image map. reversed <ol> Reverses the numbering of an ordered list. spellcheck Global (but typically on form controls) Enables/disables spell‑checking. contenteditable Global Makes content editable by the user. draggable Global Enables drag‑and‑drop. translate Global Controls whether content should be translated. inert Global Makes the element and its descendants non‑interactive.

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Present → True Absent → False Example checked Checkbox is checked. Checkbox is unchecked. <input type="checkbox" checked> disabled Element cannot be interacted with. Element is interactive. <button disabled> required Field must be filled. Field is optional. <input required> readonly Value cannot be changed. Value can be changed. <input readonly> hidden Element is not rendered. Element is rendered. <div hidden> autofocus Element receives focus on load. Element does not autofocus. <input autofocus> multiple Multiple items can be selected. Only one item can be selected. <select multiple> open <details> is expanded. <details> is collapsed. <details open> novalidate Form validation is skipped. Form validation is performed. <form novalidate>

docs.title: The "Light Switch" Analogy
docs.text: Boolean attributes are like light switches. The presence of the switch (attribute) means the light is on (true). The absence means the light is off (false). You don't need to set the switch to "on" or "off"; its presence alone conveys the state.

docs.title: The "Key in the Lock" Analogy
docs.text: Think of boolean attributes as keys in a lock. If the key is present (attribute exists), the feature is unlocked (true). If the key is absent, it's locked (false). The shape of the key doesn't matter – just its presence.

docs.title: The "Checkbox" Analogy
docs.text: Boolean attributes work exactly like checkboxes in a form. A checked checkbox means true; an unchecked checkbox means false. The label on the checkbox (the value) is irrelevant to the state – the state is determined solely by whether the box is checked.

docs.title: Concept 1: Presence Means True
docs.text:
The most important rule: if a boolean attribute is present in the start tag, its value is true. The value assigned to it (if any) is ignored by the browser's parser. All of the following are equivalent:

<input disabled>
<input disabled="disabled">
<input disabled="">
<input disabled="true">
<input disabled="false">   <!-- Still disabled! -->
<input disabled="anything"> <!-- Still disabled! -->

docs.title: Concept 2: Absence Means False
docs.text:
If a boolean attribute is omitted, its value is false. There is no way to set a boolean attribute to false while still including it in the tag (since presence always means true).

<input>                    <!-- not disabled -->

docs.title: Concept 3: The Value Is Ignored
docs.text: When a boolean attribute is present, the value is ignored by the browser. The only thing that matters is the attribute's presence. This is why disabled="false" still disables the element.

docs.title: Concept 4: DOM Reflection as Boolean
docs.text:
In the DOM, boolean attributes are reflected as boolean properties on the element object. For example:

  • element.disabled → true or false
  • element.checked → true or false
  • element.required → true or false
  • element.readonly → true or false
  • element.hidden → true or false
  • element.autofocus → true or false

docs.title: Concept 5: XHTML Compatibility
docs.text: In XHTML, boolean attributes must have a value (typically the attribute name itself), e.g., disabled="disabled". In HTML5, this is optional, and the shorter disabled form is preferred.

docs.title: Concept 6: Setting Boolean Attributes via JavaScript
docs.text:
In JavaScript, you set boolean attributes using the property (preferred) or setAttribute:

// Using the property (preferred)
element.disabled = true;   // Disables the element
element.disabled = false;  // Enables the element

// Using setAttribute (less preferred)
element.setAttribute('disabled', '');   // Disables (presence → true)
element.removeAttribute('disabled');    // Enables (removes attribute)

Important: setAttribute('disabled', 'false') still disables the element because the attribute is present. Use the property (disabled = false) or removeAttribute.

docs.title: Concept 7: Boolean Attributes vs "True/False" Attributes
docs.text:
Not all attributes that accept true/false values are boolean attributes. Some attributes (like aria-disabled) use explicit values:

<!-- Boolean attribute (presence = true) -->
<button disabled>Click</button>

<!-- Non‑boolean attribute (explicit value) -->
<button aria-disabled="true">Click</button>
<button aria-disabled="false">Click</button>

docs.title: Concept 8: Validation and Boolean Attributes
docs.text:
Boolean attributes are often used for form validation:

  • required – field must be filled.
  • disabled – field is not submittable.
  • readonly – field is submittable but not editable.
  • novalidate – form validation is skipped.

docs.title: Step‑by‑Step: Browser Processing of Boolean Attributes
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters an attribute in the start tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It checks if the attribute name is in the list of boolean attributes.
    │
    ▼
3.  If the attribute is present:
    │   ├── If it has no value → sets the property to `true`.
    │   ├── If it has a value → sets the property to `true` (value is ignored).
    │   └── The element's behavior changes (disabled, checked, etc.).
    │
    ▼
4.  If the attribute is absent:
    │   └── The property remains `false` (default state).
    │
    ▼
5.  When the DOM is built, the property reflects the state.
    │
    ▼
6.  JavaScript can read the property (`element.disabled`) or change it.

docs.title: DOM Reflection
docs.text:
Boolean attributes are reflected as boolean properties in the DOM:

const input = document.querySelector('input[type="checkbox"]');
console.log(input.checked); // true if checked, false otherwise

input.checked = true; // checks the checkbox
input.checked = false; // unchecks it

docs.title: setAttribute vs Property
docs.text:
// Using setAttribute (less recommended)
element.setAttribute('disabled', 'disabled'); // disables
element.setAttribute('disabled', '');        // also disables
element.removeAttribute('disabled');         // enables

// Using the property (preferred)
element.disabled = true;   // disables
element.disabled = false;  // enables

docs.title: The toggleAttribute Method
docs.text:
Modern browsers support toggleAttribute for boolean attributes:

// Toggle the "disabled" attribute
element.toggleAttribute('disabled'); // toggles presence, reflects as true/false

docs.title: The Boolean Attribute List
docs.text: The HTML specification maintains a list of boolean attributes. The parser uses this list to determine how to handle each attribute.

docs.title: Reflection Pattern
docs.text:
Boolean attributes follow the reflection pattern in the DOM API. Each boolean attribute has a corresponding property on the element interface:

Attribute DOM Property Interface disabled disabled HTMLInputElement, HTMLButtonElement, etc. checked checked HTMLInputElement selected selected HTMLOptionElement required required HTMLInputElement, HTMLSelectElement, HTMLTextAreaElement readonly readOnly HTMLInputElement, HTMLTextAreaElement autofocus autofocus HTMLInputElement, HTMLButtonElement, etc. hidden hidden HTMLElement open open HTMLDetailsElement multiple multiple HTMLSelectElement, HTMLInputElement

docs.title: hidden vs aria-hidden
docs.text:
• hidden (boolean) – tells the browser to not render the element.
  • aria-hidden="true" – hides the element from assistive technologies but still renders it visually.
<!-- Hidden from everyone -->
<div hidden>Not visible</div>

<!-- Visible but hidden from screen readers -->
<div aria-hidden="true">Visible, but ignored by screen readers</div>

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Boolean Attribute
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the boolean attribute in the HTML.
    │   └── Example: <input type="checkbox" checked>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document.
    │   └── The boolean attribute is recognised as present.
    │   └── The corresponding DOM property is set to `true`.
    │
    ▼
4.  The element's behavior is affected:
    │   ├── Checkbox is checked.
    │   ├── Button is disabled.
    │   ├── Field is required.
    │   └── etc.
    │
    ▼
5.  The page is rendered with the configured state.
    │
    ▼
6.  User interaction may change the state:
    │   ├── Clicking a checkbox toggles `checked`.
    │   ├── JavaScript may change `disabled`.
    │   └── etc.
    │
    ▼
7.  The attribute may be updated in the DOM (via JavaScript).
    │   └── `element.setAttribute` or `element.removeAttribute`
    │
    ▼
8.  When the page is unloaded, the attribute is destroyed.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Boolean Attributes in a Form
docs.text:
<form>
    <label for="agree">I agree to the terms</label>
    <input type="checkbox" id="agree" name="agree" checked>

    <label for="username">Username</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" required>

    <label for="country">Country</label>
    <select id="country" name="country" required>
        <option value="">Select...</option>
        <option value="us" selected>United States</option>
        <option value="ca">Canada</option>
    </select>

    <fieldset disabled>
        <legend>Disabled Section</legend>
        <input type="text" placeholder="Cannot type here">
        <button>Cannot click</button>
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit" disabled>Submit</button>
</form>

Code Breakdown: - checked – checkbox is pre‑checked. - required – username and country fields are mandatory. - selected – "United States" is pre‑selected in the dropdown. - disabled – the entire fieldset and the submit button are disabled.

docs.title: Example 2: Working with Boolean Attributes in JavaScript
docs.text:
<div>
    <input type="checkbox" id="agreeCheckbox">
    <label for="agreeCheckbox">I agree</label>
    <button id="submitBtn">Submit</button>
</div>

<script>
    const checkbox = document.getElementById('agreeCheckbox');
    const button = document.getElementById('submitBtn');

    // Initially, the button is enabled
    button.disabled = false;

    // When checkbox changes, toggle the button
    checkbox.addEventListener('change', function() {
        button.disabled = !this.checked;
    });

    // Reading boolean attributes
    console.log(checkbox.checked); // true or false
    console.log(button.disabled); // true or false

    // Using setAttribute (less recommended)
    button.setAttribute('disabled', ''); // disables
    button.removeAttribute('disabled');  // enables

    // Using toggleAttribute
    checkbox.toggleAttribute('checked'); // toggles checked state
</script>

docs.title: Example 3: The hidden Attribute
docs.text:
<div id="message" hidden>
    <p>This message is hidden initially.</p>
</div>
<button id="toggleBtn">Toggle Message</button>

<script>
    const message = document.getElementById('message');
    const btn = document.getElementById('toggleBtn');

    btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
        message.hidden = !message.hidden;
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 4: The open Attribute on <details>
docs.text:
<details open>
    <summary>Click to expand/collapse</summary>
    <p>This content is visible by default because `open` is present.</p>
</details>

<details>
    <summary>Click to expand</summary>
    <p>This content is hidden initially because `open` is absent.</p>
</details>

<script>
    // Toggle the `open` attribute dynamically
    const details = document.querySelector('details');
    details.open = !details.open;
</script>

docs.title: Example 5: The autofocus Attribute
docs.text:
<form>
    <label for="name">Name</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" autofocus placeholder="I will be focused">

    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email">

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

Behaviour: The "Name" input will be focused when the page loads, skipping the default focus behavior.

docs.title: Example 6: The novalidate Attribute on Forms
docs.text:
<form novalidate>
    <input type="email" required placeholder="Email">
    <button type="submit">Submit (no validation)</button>
</form>

<form>
    <input type="email" required placeholder="Email">
    <button type="submit">Submit (validation enabled)</button>
</form>

Behaviour: The first form will skip validation; the second will require a valid email.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text:
• Form controls – checked, selected, disabled, readonly, required, autofocus, multiple.
  • Media elements – autoplay, controls, loop, muted, playsinline.
  • Script loading – async, defer.
  • Content visibility – hidden, open (for <details>).
  • Global behavior – hidden, inert, contenteditable, draggable, spellcheck, translate.

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use the short form – prefer disabled over disabled="disabled" in HTML5 for cleaner markup.

  2. Use DOM properties in JavaScript – use element.disabled = true/false rather than setAttribute('disabled', '...'). Properties are more reliable and intuitive.

  3. Never set boolean attributes to "false" – disabled="false" will still disable the element because the attribute is present. Use removeAttribute or set the property to false.

  4. Use toggleAttribute for toggling – element.toggleAttribute('disabled') is a clean way to toggle boolean attributes.

  5. Be aware of XHTML compatibility – if you're generating XHTML, use disabled="disabled".

  6. Use hidden for temporary hiding – hidden is semantic and accessible for temporary hiding. For permanent hiding, remove the element or use CSS.

  7. Use inert for disabling sections – inert is more accessible than manually disabling all children.

  8. Combine required with aria-required – for better accessibility, though required alone is sufficient.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Setting Boolean Attributes to "false"
docs.text:
<input type="checkbox" checked="false">   <!-- Still checked! -->
<button disabled="false">Click</button>   <!-- Still disabled! -->
Why it's wrong: Boolean attributes are true when present, regardless of the value. The "false" value is ignored.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="checkbox">          <!-- unchecked -->
<input type="checkbox" checked>  <!-- checked -->
<button>Click</button>           <!-- enabled -->
<button disabled>Click</button>  <!-- disabled -->

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using setAttribute('disabled', 'false') in JavaScript
docs.text:
element.setAttribute('disabled', 'false'); // Still disables!
Why it's wrong: setAttribute sets the attribute to present, which always means true.

✅ Correct: 

element.disabled = false;          // enables
element.removeAttribute('disabled'); // enables

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Use checked for Checkboxes
docs.text:
<input type="checkbox">   <!-- Unchecked by default -->
Why it's wrong: If you want the checkbox checked by default, you need checked.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="checkbox" checked>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using readonly on <select> (It Doesn't Work)
docs.text:
<select readonly>   <!-- Doesn't work! -->
Why it's wrong: readonly is not valid on <select>. Use disabled instead, but note that disabled also prevents submission.

✅ Correct: 

<select disabled>   <!-- Disabled, not submittable -->

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using disabled on <fieldset> Without Understanding the Effect
docs.text:
<fieldset disabled>
    <input type="text" value="Cannot edit">
    <button>Cannot click</button>
</fieldset>
Why it's wrong: Works as expected, but note that disabled on a fieldset disables all child controls.

✅ Correct: Use disabled on <fieldset> when you want to disable a group of controls.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using hidden When You Should Use CSS display: none
docs.text:
<div hidden>...</div>
Why it's wrong: hidden is semantically for temporary hiding. If you need to hide for layout purposes (e.g., responsive design), use CSS display: none or visibility: hidden.

✅ Correct: Use CSS for responsive hiding.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Boolean attributes have negligible performance impact – they are just attributes.
  • Using hidden is similar to display: none; no performance benefit.
  • Using inert can improve performance by preventing event propagation in disabled sections.
  • JavaScript property access (element.disabled) is faster than getAttribute/setAttribute.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• disabled – prevents user interaction, but does not prevent server‑side submission if the element is re‑enabled via developer tools. Always validate on the server.
  • readonly – prevents editing but still submits the value. Ensure the value is safe.
  • required – only client‑side validation; always validate on the server.
  • autofocus – can be annoying for users; use sparingly.
  • hidden – does not prevent access via developer tools; don't rely on it for security.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the element to see if the boolean attribute is present.
  • Console – use element.disabled (or the appropriate property) to check the state.
  • element.getAttribute('disabled') – returns "disabled" if present, null if absent.
  • element.hasAttribute('disabled') – returns true or false.
  • Performance panel – check for layout recalculations when boolean attributes change.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: • Always – when you need to enable or disable a feature, set a default state, or control behavior. Use the appropriate boolean attribute for the job.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Avoid – using boolean attributes for non‑binary states. Use value attributes for configuration (e.g., maxlength, min, max).
  • Avoid – using disabled="false" – it's misleading and incorrect.
  • Avoid – using readonly on elements that don't support it (e.g., <select>).

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Global Attributes
  • Element‑Specific Attributes
  • DOM Properties vs Attributes
  • Form Validation
  • Accessibility (ARIA)
  • XHTML vs HTML
  • setAttribute vs Property

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• In HTML5, you can write disabled (without a value) and it's valid. In XHTML, you must write disabled="disabled".

  • The checked attribute is a boolean attribute, but the value attribute (which sets the value submitted) is a normal attribute. They serve different purposes.

  • The selected attribute on <option> is a boolean attribute. If present, the option is pre‑selected.

  • The open attribute on <details> is a boolean attribute. If present, the details widget is expanded by default.

  • The multiple attribute on <select> allows multiple selections. It's a boolean attribute.

  • The async and defer attributes on <script> are both boolean attributes. async loads asynchronously; defer defers execution.

  • The hidden attribute is global, but it can be overridden by CSS (display: block).

  • The inert attribute is relatively new and is used to make an element and its descendants non‑interactive, which is more accessible than manually disabling all children.

  • Some boolean attributes have no corresponding CSS property (e.g., checked), but they affect rendering via the DOM.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Boolean attributes are attributes whose presence means true and absence means false.
  • They are used to enable/disable features, set default states, and control behavior.
  • Key rule: Presence = true, absence = false. The value is ignored.
  • Common examples: checked, disabled, required, readonly, hidden, autofocus, selected, multiple.
  • In JavaScript, use the property (e.g., element.disabled = true) rather than setAttribute.
  • Never set a boolean attribute to "false" – it will still be true because the attribute is present.
  • Best practices: use the short form (disabled), use DOM properties in JS, avoid setAttribute for boolean attributes.
  • Common mistakes include setting disabled="false", using setAttribute incorrectly, and forgetting checked on checkboxes.
  • Boolean attributes are essential for forms, media, scripts, and interactive components.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Custom data attributes (also known as data-* attributes) are a special class of HTML attributes that allow you to store arbitrary, application‑specific data directly on HTML elements. They are defined using the prefix data- followed by a custom name, such as data-user-id, data-role, or data-last-login. Unlike other attributes that have predefined meanings (like href or src), custom data attributes have no built‑in browser behavior – they are purely for developer use.

Custom data attributes are part of the HTML5 specification and are supported in all modern browsers. They provide a clean, standardised way to embed custom data in a document without resorting to non‑standard attributes, hidden elements, or external storage.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Custom data attributes serve several essential purposes:

  • Store application state – persist data like user IDs, roles, or configuration flags on elements.
  • Provide data for JavaScript – act as a data source for scripts without requiring server lookups.
  • Enable progressive enhancement – enhance elements with additional functionality based on data.
  • Simplify UI logic – avoid complex CSS class hacks or JSON strings in attributes.
  • Support unobtrusive JavaScript – keep data out of JavaScript code and in the DOM where it belongs.
  • Improve maintainability – centralise data on the elements they relate to.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Custom data attributes are global attributes – they can be used on any HTML element. They are placed in the start tag like any other attribute, but they are specifically reserved for custom data and are ignored by browsers (except for the DOM API that exposes them).

<!-- Syntax -->
<element data-*="value">Content</element>

<!-- Examples -->
<div data-user-id="12345" data-role="admin">Profile</div>
<button data-action="save" data-target="profile">Save</button>
<li data-category="fruit" data-price="1.99">Apple</li>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before data-* attributes were standardised, developers needed a way to associate custom data with elements. They resorted to various workarounds:

  • Using rel or class attributes – misusing standard attributes for data storage.
  • Using custom attributes – userid="12345", which were invalid and caused validation errors.
  • Storing data in JavaScript objects – disconnected from the DOM, making it hard to keep in sync.
  • Using hidden elements – <input type="hidden" value="12345"> or <span style="display:none">data</span>.
  • Using comment nodes – not accessible via standard DOM traversal.

These approaches were messy, non‑standard, and difficult to maintain.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Approach Limitation Custom attributes (foo="bar") Invalid HTML; validation errors; future compatibility issues. rel attribute Not designed for data; limited use cases. class attribute Meant for styling; abusing it for data is confusing and has length limits. Hidden elements Clutters the DOM; not semantically meaningful. JavaScript objects Disconnected from elements; hard to keep in sync with DOM changes. Comments Not accessible via standard DOM traversal methods.

docs.title: Why Custom Data Attributes Were Introduced
docs.text:
HTML5 introduced data-* attributes to provide a standardised, validated, and clean way to store custom data on elements. They offer:

  • Valid HTML – data-* attributes are valid and won't cause validation errors.
  • Semantic clarity – clearly separated from standard attributes.
  • JavaScript accessibility – exposed via the dataset API, making them easy to read and modify.
  • Maintainability – data lives on the elements it relates to, not in separate data structures.
  • Flexibility – can store any string data, including JSON strings for complex data.
  • Extensibility – new data-* attributes can be added without affecting existing code.

docs.title: The Syntax of Custom Data Attributes
docs.text:
data-* = value
  • data- is the required prefix.
  • * is a custom name chosen by the developer (must be lowercase, can contain hyphens).
  • value is the data (any string).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
<!-- Basic examples -->
<div data-user-id="12345">User Profile</div>
<button data-action="save">Save</button>
<img data-src="image.jpg" data-alt="Description">

<!-- Multiple data attributes -->
<div 
    data-user-id="12345" 
    data-role="admin" 
    data-last-login="2026-09-08" 
    data-preferences='{"theme":"dark","notifications":true}'
>
    User Dashboard
</div>

<!-- Hyphenated names (converted to camelCase in JavaScript) -->
<div data-user-id="12345">Profile</div>     <!-- dataset.userId -->
<div data-role-type="admin">Profile</div>   <!-- dataset.roleType -->
<div data-last-login-date="2026-09-08">Profile</div> <!-- dataset.lastLoginDate -->

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose JavaScript Access data-user-id Stores a user identifier. element.dataset.userId data-role Stores the user's role. element.dataset.role data-last-login Stores a date. element.dataset.lastLogin data-preferences Stores a JSON object (as a string). JSON.parse(element.dataset.preferences) data-role-type Stores a compound key (hyphenated). element.dataset.roleType

docs.title: JavaScript Access: The dataset Property
docs.text:
The dataset property provides access to all data-* attributes on an element.

const div = document.querySelector('[data-user-id]');

// Read data attributes
console.log(div.dataset.userId);        // "12345"
console.log(div.dataset.role);          // "admin"
console.log(div.dataset.lastLogin);     // "2026-09-08"

// Parse JSON data
const preferences = JSON.parse(div.dataset.preferences);
console.log(preferences.theme);         // "dark"

// Set data attributes
div.dataset.userId = "67890";           // Updates data-user-id
div.dataset.role = "editor";            // Updates data-role
div.dataset.newData = "hello";          // Adds data-new-data="hello"

// Remove data attributes
delete div.dataset.userId;              // Removes data-user-id

docs.title: The "Post‑it Note" Analogy
docs.text: Custom data attributes are like Post‑it notes you stick on objects. They carry extra information that's not part of the object's primary purpose. You can read them, write on them, remove them, and replace them without affecting the object itself. The Post‑it notes are visible to anyone who looks closely (the dataset API) but don't affect the object's main function.

docs.title: The "Luggage Tag" Analogy
docs.text: Think of data-* attributes as luggage tags on a suitcase (the element). The tag contains information about the luggage (owner, destination, flight number) that helps you identify and handle it. The tag is attached to the luggage but doesn't change its appearance or function. You can read the tag, update it, or remove it as needed.

docs.title: The "Metadata Shelf" Analogy
docs.text: Elements have a metadata shelf where you can store extra information. The data-* attributes are books on that shelf. Each book has a title (the attribute name) and content (the attribute value). The shelf is always there, and you can add, remove, or update books at any time.

docs.title: Concept 1: The data-* Prefix
docs.text:
All custom data attributes must begin with the prefix data-. This is required by the HTML specification to distinguish them from standard attributes and prevent conflicts with future additions to the language.

<!-- Correct -->
<div data-user-id="123">...</div>

<!-- Incorrect (not a custom data attribute) -->
<div user-id="123">...</div>   <!-- Invalid -->

docs.title: Concept 2: Attribute Names and Dataset Mapping
docs.text:
The names of data-* attributes are transformed when accessed via the dataset property:

  • The data- prefix is removed.
  • Hyphens (-) in the name are converted to camelCase.
Attribute dataset Property data-user-id dataset.userId data-role dataset.role data-last-login dataset.lastLogin data-role-type dataset.roleType data- dataset. (invalid, attribute must have a name after the prefix)

docs.title: Concept 3: Values Are Strings
docs.text:
data-* attribute values are always strings in the DOM. When you access them via dataset, they are returned as strings. To store complex data, you need to serialise (e.g., using JSON.stringify) and parse (using JSON.parse) the values.

// Storing complex data
const user = { id: 12345, name: "Alice", role: "admin" };
div.dataset.user = JSON.stringify(user);

// Retrieving complex data
const userData = JSON.parse(div.dataset.user);
console.log(userData.name); // "Alice"

docs.title: Concept 4: Case Sensitivity
docs.text:
In HTML, attribute names are case‑insensitive. However, data-* attributes are conventionally written in lowercase with hyphens. When accessed via dataset, they are converted to camelCase, which is case‑sensitive in JavaScript.

<!-- Both are the same in HTML, but conventional is lowercase -->
<div data-user-id="123">...</div>
<div data-USER-ID="123">...</div>   <!-- Same attribute! -->

Important: dataset converts the attribute name to camelCase. data-user-id → userId. If you use uppercase in the attribute name (data-USER-ID), it still maps to userId (because it's case‑insensitive).

docs.title: Concept 5: Dynamic Data
docs.text:
Custom data attributes are live – changes to the DOM are immediately reflected in dataset, and changes to dataset are immediately reflected in the DOM.

// Setting via dataset updates the DOM
div.dataset.userId = "67890";
// The DOM now has data-user-id="67890"

// Removing via dataset removes the attribute
delete div.dataset.userId;
// The attribute data-user-id is removed from the DOM

docs.title: Concept 6: Data Attributes and CSS
docs.text:
Custom data attributes can be used in CSS attribute selectors:

/* Select elements with a specific data attribute */
[data-user-id] {
    background-color: #f0f0f0;
}

/* Select elements with a specific value */
[data-role="admin"] {
    border: 2px solid gold;
}

/* Select elements where a data attribute exists */
[data-user-id="12345"] {
    font-weight: bold;
}

docs.title: Concept 7: Data Attributes and Pseudoclasses
docs.text: Custom data attributes can be used with CSS pseudoclasses like :not and combinators, but they cannot be used with :nth-child or other structural pseudoclasses.

docs.title: Concept 8: Invalid Attribute Names
docs.text: Attribute names after data- must be valid. They cannot contain uppercase letters (though HTML is case‑insensitive, the convention is lowercase). They cannot start with a number. They cannot contain spaces or special characters (except hyphens).

docs.title: Step‑by‑Step: Browser Processing of Custom Data Attributes
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters an attribute starting with `data-`.
    │   └── Example: <div data-user-id="12345">
    │
    ▼
2.  It parses the attribute name and value.
    │   └── name = "data-user-id", value = "12345"
    │
    ▼
3.  It creates a DOM element node.
    │
    ▼
4.  It stores the attribute in the element's attributes collection.
    │
    ▼
5.  The `dataset` property provides a live `DOMStringMap` view of all `data-*` attributes.
    │   └── The attribute name is transformed: `data-user-id` → `userId`.
    │
    ▼
6.  The attribute is accessible via:
    │   ├── `element.getAttribute('data-user-id')` → "12345"
    │   ├── `element.dataset.userId` → "12345"
    │   └── CSS selectors: `[data-user-id="12345"]`
    │
    ▼
7.  Changes to `dataset` are reflected in the DOM, and vice versa.

docs.title: dataset Implementation
docs.text:
dataset is a live DOMStringMap (a special object) that reflects the data-* attributes. When you set a property on dataset, it updates the corresponding attribute. When the attribute changes, the dataset property is updated.

// Setting dataset property updates the DOM
div.dataset.userId = "67890";
// The DOM now has data-user-id="67890"

// Removing dataset property removes the DOM attribute
delete div.dataset.userId;
// The DOM attribute is removed

docs.title: The data-* Attributes in the DOM
docs.text: In the DOM, data-* attributes are stored in the attributes collection like any other attribute. They are distinguished by the data- prefix.

docs.title: The DOMStringMap Interface
docs.text:
dataset returns a DOMStringMap object, which is a live view of the data-* attributes. It has the following behavior:

  • Setting a property element.dataset.foo = "bar" adds data-foo="bar" to the element.
  • Reading element.dataset.foo returns the value of data-foo (or undefined if not present).
  • Deleting a property delete element.dataset.foo removes the data-foo attribute.

docs.title: Memory and Performance
docs.text: data-* attributes are stored in the DOM as attributes, which means they are part of the element's memory footprint. Large amounts of data stored as data-* attributes can increase memory usage. For large datasets, consider using WeakMap or other JavaScript data structures.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of Custom Data Attributes
docs.text:
1.  Author writes `data-*` attributes in the HTML.
    │   └── <div data-user-id="12345">
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── Attributes are stored on the element nodes.
    │
    ▼
4.  The `dataset` property is available via JavaScript.
    │
    ▼
5.  JavaScript reads, modifies, or removes `data-*` attributes.
    │   ├── Reading: `element.dataset.userId`
    │   ├── Modifying: `element.dataset.userId = "67890"`
    │   └── Removing: `delete element.dataset.userId`
    │
    ▼
6.  CSS attribute selectors can target `data-*` attributes.
    │   └── `[data-user-id="12345"] { ... }`
    │
    ▼
7.  When the page is unloaded, attributes are destroyed.

docs.title: Example 1: Storing User Data in a Profile Card
docs.text:
<div 
    class="profile-card" 
    data-user-id="12345" 
    data-role="admin" 
    data-last-login="2026-09-08"
    data-preferences='{"theme":"dark","notifications":true}'
>
    <h3>User Profile</h3>
    <p>ID: <span id="userIdDisplay">12345</span></p>
    <p>Role: <span id="roleDisplay">admin</span></p>
    <p>Last Login: <span id="loginDisplay">2026-09-08</span></p>
    <button id="updateBtn">Update Profile</button>
</div>

<script>
    const card = document.querySelector('.profile-card');

    // Read data
    console.log(card.dataset.userId);     // "12345"
    console.log(card.dataset.role);       // "admin"
    console.log(card.dataset.lastLogin);  // "2026-09-08"
    const preferences = JSON.parse(card.dataset.preferences);
    console.log(preferences.theme);       // "dark"

    // Update data
    document.getElementById('updateBtn').addEventListener('click', function() {
        card.dataset.role = "editor";
        card.dataset.lastLogin = new Date().toISOString().split('T')[0];
        document.getElementById('roleDisplay').textContent = "editor";
        document.getElementById('loginDisplay').textContent = card.dataset.lastLogin;
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 2: Using Data Attributes for Dynamic Content
docs.text:
<div id="product-list">
    <div class="product" data-id="1" data-name="Laptop" data-price="999.99" data-category="electronics">
        <h3>Laptop</h3>
        <p>Price: $999.99</p>
        <button class="add-to-cart">Add to Cart</button>
    </div>
    <div class="product" data-id="2" data-name="Headphones" data-price="49.99" data-category="electronics">
        <h3>Headphones</h3>
        <p>Price: $49.99</p>
        <button class="add-to-cart">Add to Cart</button>
    </div>
</div>

<script>
    document.querySelectorAll('.add-to-cart').forEach(button => {
        button.addEventListener('click', function() {
            const product = this.closest('.product');
            const id = product.dataset.id;
            const name = product.dataset.name;
            const price = parseFloat(product.dataset.price);
            console.log(`Added ${name} (ID: ${id}) to cart for $${price}`);
        });
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 3: Using Data Attributes for UI State
docs.text:
<button data-state="collapsed" id="toggleBtn">Show More</button>
<div id="content" hidden>This content is initially hidden.</div>

<script>
    const btn = document.getElementById('toggleBtn');
    const content = document.getElementById('content');

    btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
        const state = this.dataset.state;
        if (state === 'collapsed') {
            this.dataset.state = 'expanded';
            this.textContent = 'Show Less';
            content.hidden = false;
        } else {
            this.dataset.state = 'collapsed';
            this.textContent = 'Show More';
            content.hidden = true;
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 4: Using Data Attributes with CSS
docs.text:
<div class="notification" data-type="success">Operation successful!</div>
<div class="notification" data-type="error">Something went wrong!</div>
<div class="notification" data-type="warning">Please check your input!</div>

<style>
    .notification[data-type="success"] {
        background-color: #d4edda;
        color: #155724;
        border-color: #c3e6cb;
    }
    .notification[data-type="error"] {
        background-color: #f8d7da;
        color: #721c24;
        border-color: #f5c6cb;
    }
    .notification[data-type="warning"] {
        background-color: #fff3cd;
        color: #856404;
        border-color: #ffc107;
    }
</style>

docs.title: Example 5: Storing and Retrieving Complex Data with JSON
docs.text:
<div 
    id="app"
    data-config='{"theme":"dark","language":"en","sidebar":true,"notifications":["email","push"]}'
>
    <p>App configuration loaded.</p>
</div>

<script>
    const app = document.getElementById('app');
    const config = JSON.parse(app.dataset.config);

    console.log(config.theme);          // "dark"
    console.log(config.language);       // "en"
    console.log(config.sidebar);        // true
    console.log(config.notifications);  // ["email", "push"]

    // Update the config
    config.theme = "light";
    app.dataset.config = JSON.stringify(config);
</script>

docs.title: Example 6: Using Data Attributes for Pagination
docs.text:
<button class="page-btn" data-page="1">1</button>
<button class="page-btn" data-page="2">2</button>
<button class="page-btn" data-page="3">3</button>
<div id="content">Page 1 content</div>

<script>
    document.querySelectorAll('.page-btn').forEach(btn => {
        btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
            const page = this.dataset.page;
            document.getElementById('content').textContent = `Page ${page} content`;

            // Update active state
            document.querySelectorAll('.page-btn').forEach(b => {
                b.classList.toggle('active', b.dataset.page === page);
            });
        });
    });
</script>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text:
• Storing user IDs – data-user-id, data-account-id.
  • Storing configuration – data-theme, data-language.
  • Storing state – data-state, data-active, data-visible.
  • Storing item metadata – data-price, data-category, data-sku.
  • Storing API data – data-endpoint, data-method, data-params.
  • Storing tracking data – data-track-category, data-track-action, data-track-label.
  • Storing preferences – data-preferences, data-settings.
  • Storing validation rules – data-min, data-max, data-pattern.
  • Storing UI state – data-tab, data-accordion, data-modal.
  • Storing event data – data-action, data-target, data-extra.

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use descriptive names – data-user-id is clearer than data-uid.

  2. Use lowercase and hyphens – convention for attribute names: data-user-id, not data-userId.

  3. Store only primitive data – use JSON for complex structures; parse with JSON.parse and stringify with JSON.stringify.

  4. Use dataset for JavaScript access – it's cleaner and more consistent than getAttribute/setAttribute.

  5. Avoid storing sensitive data – data-* attributes are visible in the DOM and can be read by anyone.

  6. Use data attributes for progressive enhancement – enhance functionality based on data presence.

  7. Avoid using data attributes for styling – use CSS classes for presentation; data attributes for data.

  8. Keep data small – large amounts of data increase DOM size and memory usage.

  9. Use data attributes as a last resort – for simple data, consider using id or class. For complex data, consider using a JavaScript data store.

  10. Document your data attributes – explain what they're used for, especially in larger codebases.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Non‑Standard Attributes Instead of data-*
docs.text:
<div user-id="12345">Profile</div>
Why it's wrong: Not standard; validation errors; potential conflicts with future HTML features.

✅ Correct: 

<div data-user-id="12345">Profile</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Parse JSON Data
docs.text:
const user = div.dataset.user; // Returns a string
console.log(user.name); // undefined
Why it's wrong: dataset always returns strings. You need to parse JSON.

✅ Correct: 

const user = JSON.parse(div.dataset.user);
console.log(user.name);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using dataset with Invalid Names
docs.text:
<div data-userId="12345">Profile</div>
Why it's wrong: While HTML is case‑insensitive, the convention is lowercase with hyphens. data-userId is not conventional and may cause confusion.

✅ Correct: 

<div data-user-id="12345">Profile</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Storing Sensitive Data in data-*
docs.text:
<div data-password="secret123">Profile</div>
Why it's wrong: data-* attributes are visible in the DOM and can be read by anyone. Never store sensitive data.

✅ Correct: Store sensitive data in a secure server‑side session.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using data-* Instead of id or class
docs.text:
<div data-main="true">Content</div>
Why it's wrong: Use id for uniqueness, class for grouping, data-* for data.

✅ Correct: 

<div id="main" class="container">Content</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Using dataset in JavaScript
docs.text:
const id = div.getAttribute('data-user-id'); // Less clean
Why it's wrong: dataset is cleaner and handles the transformation automatically.

✅ Correct: 

const id = div.dataset.userId;

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• DOM size – each data-* attribute adds to the element's attribute collection. For large numbers of elements, this can increase memory usage.
  • dataset access – is fast and efficient; similar to getAttribute.
  • Parsing JSON – JSON.parse is fast but adds overhead; avoid excessive parsing in loops.
  • CSS selectors – [data-*] attribute selectors are slower than id or class selectors but faster than complex combinators.
  • Updates – frequent updates to dataset cause DOM mutations, which trigger reflows and repaints.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Data visibility – data-* attributes are visible in the DOM and can be read by anyone using developer tools. Never store sensitive data (passwords, tokens, personal information) in data-* attributes.

  • XSS (Cross‑Site Scripting) – when setting dataset values from user input, ensure the data is sanitized. Avoid innerHTML for inserting data; use textContent or dataset directly.

  • Data injection – an attacker could inject data-* attributes via XSS to alter application behavior. Always sanitize user input.

  • JSON parsing – JSON.parse can throw errors if the data is malformed. Wrap in try/catch when parsing user‑supplied data.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect an element to see all data-* attributes.
  • Console – use console.log(element.dataset) to see all data attributes as an object.
  • getAttribute – use element.getAttribute('data-user-id') to verify the raw value.
  • Event listeners – ensure data attributes are set before event listeners fire.
  • MutationObserver – listen for changes to data-* attributes.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• When you need to store application data on an element – and the data is not sensitive.
  • When you need to enhance elements with additional functionality – progressive enhancement.
  • When you need to pass data from the server to the client – embed data in the HTML rather than making extra API calls.
  • When you need to maintain state in the DOM – for UI components like tabs, accordions, or modals.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For sensitive data – never store passwords, tokens, or personal information.
  • For large datasets – use a JavaScript data store or WeakMap.
  • For styling – use CSS classes instead.
  • When you need a unique identifier – use id.
  • When you need to group elements – use class.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Global Attributes
  • dataset API
  • getAttribute / setAttribute
  • JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)
  • Progressive Enhancement
  • Unobtrusive JavaScript
  • CSS Attribute Selectors
  • HTML Validation

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The data-* attributes were introduced in HTML5 to standardise custom attributes. Before that, developers used rel, class, or custom attributes like userid="123".

  • The dataset property is a live DOMStringMap – changes to it are immediately reflected in the DOM and vice versa.

  • Attribute names in dataset are converted to camelCase: data-user-id → userId, data-role-type → roleType.

  • You can use JSON in data-* attributes to store complex data, but remember to parse it with JSON.parse and stringify with JSON.stringify.

  • CSS attribute selectors can target data-* attributes: [data-user-id="12345"] { ... }.

  • The data-* attributes are ignored by browsers; they have no built‑in behavior. They are purely for developer use.

  • The data-* attributes are valid in HTML5 and will not cause validation errors.

  • You can use multiple data-* attributes on the same element.

  • There is no limit to the number of data-* attributes, but large numbers can impact performance.

  • The data-* attributes are not accessible via dataset in older browsers (IE10 and below). Use getAttribute for legacy support.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Custom data attributes (data-*) are standardised HTML attributes for storing application‑specific data on elements.
  • They are valid in HTML5 and will not cause validation errors.
  • Accessible via the dataset property in JavaScript, which converts hyphenated names to camelCase.
  • Values are always strings; use JSON.parse/JSON.stringify for complex data.
  • Best practices: use descriptive names, store only non‑sensitive data, use dataset over getAttribute, and avoid using data attributes for styling.
  • Common mistakes include using non‑standard attributes, forgetting to parse JSON, storing sensitive data, and not using dataset.
  • Use cases include storing user IDs, configuration, UI state, item metadata, and tracking data.
  • Custom data attributes are a powerful tool for progressive enhancement, unobtrusive JavaScript, and maintainable code.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
ARIA attributes (Accessible Rich Internet Applications attributes) are a set of special HTML attributes defined by the W3C that add semantic information to HTML elements for assistive technologies. ARIA does not change an element's visual appearance or behavior—it only modifies the accessibility tree, the data structure that screen readers and other assistive technologies use to interpret and present content to users.

ARIA attributes enable developers to convey roles (what an element is), states (what condition it's in), and properties (additional characteristics) to assistive technologies. This is especially important for custom interactive widgets, dynamic content, and complex applications where native HTML semantics are insufficient.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ARIA attributes serve several essential purposes:

  • Provide semantics for custom widgets – when native HTML elements can't achieve the required visual design or behavior, ARIA supplies the missing accessibility information.
  • Communicate dynamic state changes – inform assistive technologies when content updates, expands, collapses, or becomes selected.
  • Establish relationships between elements – associate labels, descriptions, and controls with their targets.
  • Enable keyboard accessibility – ensure custom interactive elements are operable via keyboard.
  • Bridge the gap between visual design and accessibility – when semantic HTML cannot be used due to design constraints.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
ARIA attributes are global attributes – they can theoretically be used on any HTML element, though some attributes are restricted based on the element's role. They are placed in the start tag alongside other attributes.

<!-- Basic ARIA attributes -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0" aria-label="Close">✕</div>
<nav role="navigation" aria-label="Main Navigation">...</nav>
<button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="panel">Toggle</button>

The ARIA specification is maintained by the W3C as part of the WAI-ARIA suite. The current stable version is WAI-ARIA 1.2, with WAI-ARIA 1.3 in development. The "ARIA in HTML" specification defines the authoring rules for using ARIA attributes on HTML elements.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTML provides a rich set of semantic elements – <button>, <nav>, <main>, <h1>–<h6>, and many more. These elements convey meaning to assistive technologies out of the box. However, modern web applications often require custom interactive widgets that go beyond native HTML:

  • Custom dropdowns that look and behave differently from native <select>.
  • Complex tree controls for file explorers or navigation.
  • Custom sliders with unique visual designs.
  • Live updating regions that change content dynamically.
  • Modal dialogs that trap focus.

These custom widgets, often built with <div> and <span> elements, have no inherent semantics for assistive technologies. A screen reader sees a <div> as a generic container – it doesn't know it's a button, a slider, or a menu. Without additional information, these widgets are inaccessible.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Generic elements for custom widgets Screen readers cannot identify the widget's purpose or behavior. Dynamic content updates Screen readers don't announce changes automatically. No relationship information Users cannot understand connections between elements (e.g., which label belongs to which input). No state information Users don't know if a toggle is on or off, if a menu is expanded or collapsed. Lack of keyboard accessibility Custom widgets often cannot be operated via keyboard. No landmark navigation Users cannot jump between page sections.

docs.title: Why ARIA Was Introduced
docs.text:
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) was developed by the W3C to address these gaps. It provides a vocabulary of roles, states, and properties that can be added to any element to convey accessibility information. ARIA allows developers to:

  • Define an element's role (role="button", role="slider", role="menu").
  • Communicate states (aria-expanded="true", aria-checked="false").
  • Provide properties (aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-controls).
  • Make dynamic content accessible (aria-live, aria-atomic).
  • Establish relationships (aria-labelledby, aria-owns).

However, ARIA comes with a crucial caveat: "First Rule of ARIA Use: If you can use a native HTML element with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible, then do so". ARIA is a complement to semantic HTML, not a replacement.

docs.title: The Syntax of ARIA Attributes
docs.text:
aria-* = "value"

ARIA attributes always start with the prefix aria-, followed by the specific attribute name.

docs.title: ARIA Attribute Categories
docs.text:
ARIA attributes fall into four main categories:

Category Purpose Examples Widget attributes Provide information about interactive elements and their states. aria-checked, aria-disabled, aria-expanded, aria-selected Live region attributes Manage dynamic content updates. aria-live, aria-atomic, aria-relevant, aria-busy Drag-and-drop attributes Support drag-and-drop interactions. aria-grabbed, aria-dropeffect Relationship attributes Define relationships between elements. aria-describedby, aria-labelledby, aria-controls, aria-owns

docs.title: Global ARIA Attributes
docs.text:
Some ARIA attributes can be used on any HTML element, regardless of its role. These are called global attributes:

Global ARIA Attribute Purpose aria-atomic Indicates whether a live region should be announced as a whole or in parts. aria-busy Indicates that an element is being modified and assistive technologies should wait. aria-controls Identifies the element(s) controlled by the current element. aria-current Indicates the current item within a container (e.g., current page in a pagination). aria-describedby Identifies the element(s) that describe the current element. aria-details Identifies the element(s) that provide additional information. aria-disabled Indicates the element is perceivable but disabled. aria-errormessage Identifies the element that provides an error message. aria-flowto Identifies the next element in an alternative reading order. aria-haspopup Indicates the element has a popup context menu or sub-menu. aria-hidden Hides the element from assistive technologies. aria-invalid Indicates the entered value is invalid. aria-label Provides an accessible name for the element. aria-labelledby Identifies the element(s) that label the current element. aria-live Indicates that an element will be updated and should be announced. aria-owns Identifies an element or elements owned by the current element. aria-relevant Indicates what types of changes should be announced in a live region. aria-roledescription Provides a human-readable description of the element's role.

Note: aria-label and aria-labelledby are not allowed on elements with role="presentation" or role="none".

docs.title: Basic Examples
docs.text:
<!-- Role: defines what the element is -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0">Click me</div>

<!-- State: communicates current condition -->
<button aria-expanded="false">Show more</button>

<!-- Property: provides additional information -->
<button aria-label="Close dialog">✕</button>

<!-- Relationship: links elements together -->
<label id="name-label">Name:</label>
<input type="text" aria-labelledby="name-label">

<!-- Live region: announces updates -->
<div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
    <p>Status: Loading...</p>
</div>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute What It Does Why It Matters role="button" Tells assistive technologies this <div> behaves like a button. Screen readers announce "button" and expect button-like interactions. tabindex="0" Makes the <div> focusable via keyboard. Buttons must be keyboard accessible. aria-expanded="false" Indicates the expandable content is currently collapsed. Users know whether to expect expanded content. aria-label="Close dialog" Provides an accessible name (since "✕" alone is not descriptive). Screen readers announce "Close dialog" instead of "X". aria-labelledby="name-label" Associates the input with the label element. Screen readers announce the label when the input is focused. aria-live="polite" Announces updates when the user is not busy. Dynamic content is announced without interrupting the user.

docs.title: The "Closed Captions" Analogy
docs.text: Think of ARIA attributes as closed captions for a movie. The movie (the visual interface) is already there. The captions (ARIA) provide additional information that makes it accessible to people who can't hear (assistive technologies). The captions don't change the movie itself – they just add a layer of understanding.

docs.title: The "Tour Guide" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a museum where you can't see the exhibits. A tour guide (ARIA) describes each exhibit: "This is a button" (role), "It is currently pressed" (state), "It controls the lighting in this room" (property). The guide doesn't change the exhibits – it just explains them.

docs.title: The "Instruction Manual" Analogy
docs.text: ARIA attributes are like an instruction manual for assistive technologies. They explain what each element is, what state it's in, how it relates to other elements, and what happens when it changes. The manual doesn't change the product itself – it just makes it understandable.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Three Pillars of ARIA: Roles, States, and Properties
docs.text:
ARIA attributes are divided into three types:

  1. Roles – define what an element is (e.g., role="button", role="navigation", role="slider").
  2. States – define current conditions that can change (e.g., aria-expanded, aria-checked, aria-selected).
  3. Properties – define characteristics that are more static (e.g., aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-controls).

docs.title: Concept 2: Roles
docs.text:
Roles define the type of an element. They are set using the role attribute.

<div role="button">Submit</div>
<nav role="navigation">...</nav>
<div role="dialog">...</div>

Common roles:
