docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
Browsers apply default styles to headings. For example (simplified):

h1 { font-size: 2em; font-weight: bold; margin: 0.67em 0; }
h2 { font-size: 1.5em; font-weight: bold; margin: 0.83em 0; }
h3 { font-size: 1.17em; font-weight: bold; margin: 1em 0; }
h4 { font-size: 1em; font-weight: bold; margin: 1.33em 0; }
h5 { font-size: 0.83em; font-weight: bold; margin: 1.67em 0; }
h6 { font-size: 0.67em; font-weight: bold; margin: 2.33em 0; }

docs.title: The hgroup Element (Obsolete)
docs.text: The <hgroup> element was introduced to group multiple headings (e.g., a title and subtitle) into a single heading in the outline. It is now obsolete and should not be used. Use <p> with appropriate styles for subtitles.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of Headings
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the heading elements in the HTML.
    │   └── Example: <h1>My Page</h1>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── Heading nodes are created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (large, bold, margin).
    │
    ▼
5.  The document outline is built.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers expose the headings for navigation.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines index the heading text.
    │
    ▼
9.  (Optional) JavaScript may modify headings dynamically.

docs.title: Example 1: A Blog Post with Proper Heading Hierarchy
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>The Future of Web Development</h1>
    <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>

    <h2>Introduction</h2>
    <p>Web development is evolving rapidly...</p>

    <h2>Key Trends</h2>
    <h3>Artificial Intelligence</h3>
    <p>AI is transforming how we build applications...</p>
    <h3>Web Components</h3>
    <p>Web Components are becoming mainstream...</p>

    <h2>Challenges</h2>
    <h3>Performance</h3>
    <p>Performance remains a critical concern...</p>
    <h3>Accessibility</h3>
    <p>Making the web accessible to all...</p>

    <h2>Conclusion</h2>
    <p>The future is bright for web development.</p>
</article>

Code Breakdown: - <h1> – the title of the blog post. - <h2> – major sections: Introduction, Key Trends, Challenges, Conclusion. - <h3> – subsections within Key Trends and Challenges. - Logical hierarchy without skipping levels.

docs.title: Example 2: A Product Page
docs.text:
<main>
    <h1>Product Name</h1>
    <p>Product description goes here.</p>

    <h2>Features</h2>
    <ul>
        <li>Feature 1</li>
        <li>Feature 2</li>
    </ul>

    <h2>Specifications</h2>
    <table>
        <tr><th>Weight</th><td>1.2 kg</td></tr>
        <tr><th>Dimensions</th><td>30 x 20 x 5 cm</td></tr>
    </table>

    <h2>Reviews</h2>
    <article>
        <h3>Great product!</h3>
        <p>I love this product...</p>
    </article>
    <article>
        <h3>Good value</h3>
        <p>This is a great value for money...</p>
    </article>
</main>

docs.title: Example 3: A Documentation Page
docs.text:
<h1>API Documentation</h1>

<h2>Authentication</h2>
<p>To use the API, you need an API key...</p>

<h2>Endpoints</h2>
<h3>GET /users</h3>
<p>Returns a list of users...</p>
<h3>POST /users</h3>
<p>Creates a new user...</p>

<h2>Error Handling</h2>
<h3>400 Bad Request</h3>
<p>The request was malformed...</p>
<h3>401 Unauthorized</h3>
<p>The API key is invalid...</p>

docs.title: Example 4: Headings with CSS Customisation
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Styled Headings</title>
    <style>
        h1 {
            font-size: 2.5rem;
            color: #2c3e50;
            border-bottom: 3px solid #3498db;
            padding-bottom: 10px;
        }
        h2 {
            font-size: 2rem;
            color: #34495e;
            margin-top: 30px;
        }
        h3 {
            font-size: 1.5rem;
            color: #7f8c8d;
            margin-top: 20px;
        }
        /* Deep nesting (rare) */
        h4 { font-size: 1.2rem; }
        h5 { font-size: 1rem; }
        h6 { font-size: 0.85rem; color: #95a5a6; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Styled Page</h1>
    <h2>Chapter 1</h2>
    <h3>Section 1.1</h3>
    <h4>Sub-section 1.1.1</h4>
    <h5>Detail A</h5>
    <h6>Lowest level detail</h6>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Example 5: Dynamically Changing Headings (JavaScript)
docs.text:
<h1 id="mainTitle">Welcome</h1>
<button onclick="changeTitle()">Change Title</button>

<script>
    function changeTitle() {
        const title = document.getElementById('mainTitle');
        title.textContent = 'New Title';
        title.style.color = 'blue';
        title.classList.add('updated');
    }
</script>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text:
• Page titles – <h1> for the main title of the page.
  • Blog posts – <h1> for the post title, <h2> for sections, <h3> for subsections.
  • Product pages – <h1> for product name, <h2> for features, specifications, reviews.
  • Documentation – <h1> for the document title, <h2> for chapters, <h3> for sections.
  • FAQs – <h2> or <h3> for questions, <p> for answers.
  • Pricing tables – <h2> for plan names, <h3> for features.

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use only one <h1> per page – it should be the main title of the page.

  2. Follow a logical hierarchy – don't skip levels. <h1> → <h2> → <h3> → etc.

  3. Use headings semantically – not for visual styling only. If you want big, bold text, use CSS, not headings.

  4. Include keywords naturally – search engines use heading text to understand content.

  5. Keep headings concise – short, descriptive phrases are best.

  6. Use headings to break up content – make the page scannable.

  7. Test with screen readers – navigate by headings to ensure the structure makes sense.

  8. Use heading elements inside sectioning elements – <section>, <article>, etc. should have headings.

  9. Avoid empty headings – a heading without content is meaningless.

  10. Use CSS to style headings – don't rely on default browser styles.

  11. Consider accessibility – screen readers rely on headings for navigation.

  12. Use heading levels appropriately – don't use <h4> when <h3> is expected, even if you prefer the visual appearance.

  13. Maintain a flat hierarchy – avoid nesting deeper than 3–4 levels.

  14. Use proper punctuation – but avoid periods at the end of headings (convention).

  15. Be consistent – use the same heading style across all pages of a site.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Multiple <h1> Elements
docs.text:
<h1>My Site</h1>
<h1>About Us</h1>   <!-- Two H1s -->
Why it's wrong: There should be only one <h1> per page. Screen readers treat <h1> as the page's main title.

✅ Correct: 

<h1>My Site</h1>
<h2>About Us</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Skipping Heading Levels
docs.text:
<h1>Title</h1>
<h3>Subsection</h3>   <!-- Skipped <h2> -->
Why it's wrong: Skipping levels breaks the document outline and confuses screen reader users.

✅ Correct: 

<h1>Title</h1>
<h2>Section</h2>
<h3>Subsection</h3>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Headings for Visual Styling
docs.text:
<h4>This text is small but I want it bold and big</h4>
Why it's wrong: Headings are for structure, not styling. Use CSS for visual appearance.

✅ Correct: 

<p class="lead">This text is styled with CSS.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Empty Headings
docs.text:
<h2></h2>
Why it's wrong: A heading without content is meaningless and clutters the document outline.

✅ Correct: Ensure every heading has meaningful content.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Over‑Nesting Headings
docs.text:
<h1>Title</h1>
<h2>Section</h2>
<h3>Subsection</h3>
<h4>Sub-subsection</h4>
<h5>Sub-sub-subsection</h5>
<h6>Too deep</h6>
Why it's wrong: Deep nesting makes the document hard to navigate. Most content doesn't need more than 3–4 levels.

✅ Correct: Flatten the structure where possible.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using hgroup
docs.text:
<hgroup>
    <h1>Title</h1>
    <h2>Subtitle</h2>
</hgroup>
Why it's wrong: <hgroup> is obsolete and should not be used.

✅ Correct: 

<h1>Title</h1>
<p class="subtitle">Subtitle</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Headings as "Click to Expand" Without Proper ARIA
docs.text:
<h2 onclick="toggleSection()">Click to expand</h2>
Why it's wrong: Headings are not interactive by default. Screen readers expect headings to be navigable, not clickable.

✅ Correct: Use a <button> inside the heading or add role="button" with proper ARIA.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Headings are lightweight – they have minimal performance impact.
  • The document outline – building the outline has negligible overhead.
  • CSS selectors – targeting headings with simple selectors (h1, h2) is fast.
  • Accessibility tree – headings add nodes to the accessibility tree, but this is minimal.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Headings have no direct security implications – they are structural elements.
  • However, user‑generated content in headings should be sanitized to prevent XSS.
  • Ensure innerHTML is not used with user input when updating headings dynamically; use textContent.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect headings to see their level and content.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the heading level in the accessibility tree.
  • Headings Map extension – visualises the document outline.
  • Lighthouse – audits for heading hierarchy and missing headings.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6') to list all headings.
  • Screen reader testing – navigate by headings to ensure the structure makes sense.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: • Always – headings are essential for document structure. Every page should have a clear heading hierarchy.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For visual styling only – use CSS instead.
  • For interactive elements – use <button> or <a> for clickable elements.
  • For subtitles – use <p> with CSS styling.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Document Outline
  • Sectioning Elements (<section>, <article>, <nav>, <aside>)
  • Accessibility (WCAG 2.4.6, 2.4.10)
  • SEO (Search Engine Optimization)
  • CSS (styling headings)
  • ARIA (role="heading", aria-level)

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <h1> element was the only heading in HTML 1.0. <h2>–<h6> were added later.

  • In the HTML5 outline algorithm, you can use <h1> multiple times if they are inside different sectioning elements. However, this is not widely supported, so it's still best practice to use one <h1> per page.

  • Heading levels can be styled differently for different devices (e.g., mobile vs desktop) using CSS media queries.

  • Screen readers like NVDA and JAWS allow users to press 1–6 to jump to the next heading of that level.

  • The heading hierarchy is one of the most important factors for SEO. Google uses headings to understand the main topics of a page.

  • Some content management systems (CMS) automatically generate a document outline from headings.

  • In HTML5, the <hgroup> element was intended to group multiple headings but was removed from the spec. Use <p> with CSS for subtitles.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Headings (<h1>–<h6>) define the hierarchical structure of a document.
  • They are essential for accessibility (screen reader navigation), SEO (search engine indexing), and readability (visual structure).
  • Best practices: use one <h1> per page, follow a logical hierarchy (no skipping levels), use headings semantically (not for styling), and keep them concise and descriptive.
  • Common mistakes include using multiple <h1>s, skipping levels, using headings for styling, and leaving headings empty.
  • Headings are the spine of your content – they hold everything together.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <p> element (short for "paragraph") is the fundamental HTML element for defining a block of text that forms a distinct unit of content. It is the most commonly used element for wrapping prose, descriptions, explanations, and any continuous text that should be treated as a single logical block. A paragraph in HTML represents a thematic grouping of text, typically consisting of one or more sentences addressing a particular point or idea.

The <p> element is a block-level element, meaning it starts on a new line, takes up the full width of its container, and stacks vertically with other block elements. It is also flow content and palpable content, and its content model is phrasing content – it can contain text and inline elements (like <strong>, <em>, <a>, <span>), but not block-level elements.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <p> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Groups related sentences – treats them as a single unit of thought.
  • Creates visual separation – browsers add margin above and below paragraphs by default.
  • Provides semantic meaning – conveys that the text is a paragraph of prose, not a heading, list, or other structure.
  • Enables styling – serves as a styling hook for CSS (e.g., font, line-height, text-indent).
  • Supports accessibility – screen readers treat paragraphs as units of text, and users can navigate between them.
  • Improves readability – visual breaks make long text easier to scan and digest.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <p> element is a flow content element that can appear anywhere flow content is accepted – inside <body>, <div>, <section>, <article>, <aside>, <main>, <header>, <footer>, and other flow containers. It cannot be nested inside another <p> element (paragraphs cannot contain paragraphs), and it cannot contain block-level elements.

<section>
    <h2>Section Title</h2>          ← Heading (block)
    <p>This is a paragraph.</p>     ← Paragraph (block, phrasing content inside)
    <p>Another paragraph.</p>       ← Another paragraph
</section>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML, documents were plain text. Without paragraph breaks, long passages of text would be a single continuous block, making them extremely difficult to read and understand. Readers had no visual or structural cues to indicate where one idea ended and another began.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No paragraph structure Text was a continuous stream with no logical grouping. Manual line breaks Authors had to insert blank lines manually, which was inconsistent. No semantic meaning Machines couldn't identify units of prose. No styling hooks Styles couldn't be applied to paragraphs as units. Poor accessibility Screen readers had no structure to navigate.

docs.title: Why the <p> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <p> element was one of the first elements in HTML (present in HTML 1.0). It was introduced to provide a standardised, semantic way to mark up paragraphs. This enables:

  • Logical grouping – sentences that belong together are wrapped in a single element.
  • Consistent rendering – browsers apply default margins, creating visual separation.
  • Semantic meaning – machines understand that the content is prose.
  • Styling flexibility – CSS can target paragraphs specifically.
  • Accessibility – screen readers can navigate between paragraphs.

The <p> element is the backbone of readable web content. Without it, the web would be an ocean of unstructured text.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of a Paragraph
docs.text:
<p>This is a paragraph of text.</p>
  • Opening tag: <p>
  • Content: Phrasing content (text and inline elements)
  • Closing tag: </p>

docs.title: A Simple Paragraph
docs.text: <p>HTML is the standard markup language for creating web pages.</p>

docs.title: Multiple Paragraphs
docs.text:
<p>This is the first paragraph. It introduces the topic.</p>
<p>This is the second paragraph. It provides more detail.</p>
<p>This is the third paragraph. It concludes the discussion.</p>

docs.title: Paragraphs with Inline Elements
docs.text:
<p>
    This paragraph contains <strong>bold text</strong>, 
    <em>italic text</em>, and a 
    <a href="https://example.com">link</a>.
</p>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <p> Opens a paragraph. Marks the beginning of a block of prose. </p> Closes the paragraph. Marks the end of the block. Text content The actual prose. The words that make up the paragraph. <strong>, <em>, <a> Inline elements. Add semantic meaning and formatting within the text.

docs.title: Paragraphs and Whitespace
docs.text:
In HTML, whitespace is collapsed. Multiple spaces, tabs, and newlines are treated as a single space. To create line breaks, use <br> or separate paragraphs.

<p>
    This     text
    has   multiple
    spaces and
    line breaks.
</p>
<!-- Renders as: "This text has multiple spaces and line breaks." -->

docs.title: Omission of Closing Tag
docs.text:
In HTML5, the closing </p> tag can be omitted if the paragraph is immediately followed by certain block-level elements (like another <p>, <div>, <h1>–<h6>, <ul>, etc.). However, including the closing tag is best practice for clarity.

<!-- Valid but not recommended -->
<p>First paragraph
<p>Second paragraph

<!-- Recommended -->
<p>First paragraph</p>
<p>Second paragraph</p>

docs.title: The "Container of Thoughts" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a paragraph as a container that holds a single, coherent unit of thought. Just as you wouldn't put two unrelated ideas in the same sentence, you shouldn't put two unrelated ideas in the same paragraph. The <p> element groups related sentences together, like a box that keeps them organised.

docs.title: The "Breath" Analogy
docs.text: A paragraph is like a breath in speech. When you speak, you pause for breath at natural breaks in your message. Each paragraph represents one "breath" of content – a chunk of information that belongs together. The pause (the margin between paragraphs) gives the reader a moment to digest what they've read.

docs.title: The "Building Block" Analogy
docs.text: Paragraphs are the bricks of a document. Headings are the floors, sections are the rooms, but paragraphs are the individual bricks that fill the rooms with content. They are the most basic and most common unit of text.

docs.title: Concept 1: Block-Level Element
docs.text:
The <p> element is a block-level element. This means:

  • It starts on a new line.
  • It takes up the full width of its container.
  • It stacks vertically with other block elements.
  • It has margins above and below (by default, 1em top and bottom).
<p>First paragraph.</p>
<p>Second paragraph.</p>
<!-- Each starts on a new line with space between them. -->

docs.title: Concept 2: Content Model: Phrasing Content
docs.text:
The <p> element can only contain phrasing content – text and inline elements. It cannot contain block-level elements like <div>, <h1>–<h6>, <ul>, <ol>, <table>, <section>, <article>, etc.

<!-- Valid -->
<p>This is <strong>bold</strong> and <em>italic</em>.</p>

<!-- Invalid: block element inside a paragraph -->
<p>
    <div>This is a div inside a paragraph.</div>
</p>

What the browser does with invalid content: It closes the <p> before the block element, resulting in:

<p></p>
<div>This is a div inside a paragraph.</div>
<p></p>

docs.title: Concept 3: Default Browser Styles
docs.text:
Browsers apply default styles to paragraphs:

p {
    display: block;
    margin-top: 1em;
    margin-bottom: 1em;
    margin-left: 0;
    margin-right: 0;
}

These can be overridden with CSS:

p {
    margin: 0 0 1rem 0;
    line-height: 1.6;
    text-indent: 2em;
}

docs.title: Concept 4: Whitespace Collapsing
docs.text:
In HTML, sequences of whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) are collapsed into a single space. To preserve whitespace, use the <pre> element or CSS white-space: pre.

<p>This     text    will    be    collapsed.</p>
<!-- Renders as: "This text will be collapsed." -->

docs.title: Concept 5: Paragraphs and Line Breaks
docs.text:
Do not use <br> to create space between paragraphs. Use separate <p> elements or CSS margins.

<!-- Bad: using <br> for spacing -->
<p>First paragraph.<br><br>Second paragraph.</p>

<!-- Good: separate paragraphs -->
<p>First paragraph.</p>
<p>Second paragraph.</p>

docs.title: Concept 6: The align Attribute (Deprecated)
docs.text:
The align attribute on <p> (e.g., <p align="center">) is deprecated and should not be used. Use CSS text-align instead.

<!-- Bad (deprecated) -->
<p align="center">Centered text</p>

<!-- Good -->
<p style="text-align: center;">Centered text</p>

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of Paragraphs
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<p>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the paragraph.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content inside the paragraph:
    │   ├── Text nodes are added as children.
    │   ├── Inline elements (strong, em, a, span) are added as children.
    │   └── If a block element is encountered, the parser closes the paragraph first.
    │
    ▼
4.  When the `</p>` tag is encountered (or inferred), the paragraph is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied (display: block, margins).
    │
    ▼
6.  The paragraph is rendered as a block, with space above and below.
    │
    ▼
7.  The paragraph is exposed in the accessibility tree as a text unit.

docs.title: The Parser's "In Body" Insertion Mode
docs.text:
When the parser is in the "in body" mode and encounters a <p> start tag:

  1. It closes any open <p> element (if the current node is a <p>).
  2. It inserts a new <p> element into the DOM.
  3. It switches to the "in paragraph" insertion mode.

When a block element (like <div>) is encountered inside a <p>:

  1. The parser implicitly closes the <p> (even without a </p> tag).
  2. It processes the block element as a sibling of the paragraph.

docs.title: The innerHTML and textContent Properties
docs.text:
In JavaScript, you can access the content of a paragraph:

const p = document.querySelector('p');
console.log(p.textContent); // The text content
console.log(p.innerHTML);   // The HTML content (including inline elements)

docs.title: The HTMLParagraphElement Interface
docs.text: In the DOM, <p> elements are represented by the HTMLParagraphElement interface, which inherits from HTMLElement.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
Browsers apply the following default styles to paragraphs:

p {
    display: block;
    margin-block-start: 1em;
    margin-block-end: 1em;
    margin-inline-start: 0;
    margin-inline-end: 0;
}

The margin-block properties are logical properties that map to margin-top/margin-bottom for horizontal writing modes.

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text: In the accessibility tree, a <p> element is exposed as a paragraph node. Screen readers announce the text content of the paragraph. Users can navigate between paragraphs using keyboard shortcuts (e.g., in some screen readers, pressing P jumps to the next paragraph).

docs.title: Paragraphs and the DOM
docs.text: Each <p> element creates a DOM node. Paragraphs can contain text nodes and inline element nodes. The childNodes property includes both text nodes and element nodes.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Paragraph
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<p>` element with content.
    │
    ▼
2.  The file is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the HTML and creates the DOM.
    │   └── Paragraph nodes are created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (block, margins).
    │
    ▼
5.  CSS may override the default styles.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers expose the paragraph as a unit of text.
    │
    ▼
8.  JavaScript may modify the paragraph dynamically.
    │   └── Changing text, adding/removing inline elements.
    │
    ▼
9.  When the page is unloaded, the paragraph is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
// Change paragraph text
const p = document.querySelector('p');
p.textContent = 'New text.';

// Add an inline element
const strong = document.createElement('strong');
strong.textContent = 'bold';
p.appendChild(strong);

// Remove a paragraph
p.remove();

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Paragraphs
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Paragraphs Example</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>My First Article</h1>

    <p>This is the first paragraph. It introduces the topic of the article.</p>

    <p>This is the second paragraph. It provides more details about the topic.</p>

    <p>This is the third paragraph. It concludes the article with final thoughts.</p>
</body>
</html>

Code Breakdown: - Three <p> elements, each representing a distinct unit of thought. - Each paragraph starts on a new line with space between them.

docs.title: Example 2: Paragraphs with Inline Elements
docs.text:
<p>
    HTML is a <strong>markup language</strong> used to create web pages. 
    It was invented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Berners-Lee">Tim Berners-Lee</a> 
    in <time datetime="1989">1989</time>. 
    The latest version, <em>HTML5</em>, includes many new features.
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <strong> – emphasizes importance. - <a> – link to external resource. - <time> – machine-readable date. - <em> – emphasis.

docs.title: Example 3: Paragraphs Inside Sectioning Elements
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>Article Title</h1>
    <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>

    <section>
        <h2>Introduction</h2>
        <p>This is the introduction to the article. It sets the stage for the content that follows.</p>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Main Content</h2>
        <p>The main content goes here. It provides the core information.</p>
        <p>More details are provided in this second paragraph.</p>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Conclusion</h2>
        <p>The conclusion summarizes the key points and offers final thoughts.</p>
    </section>
</article>

docs.title: Example 4: Styling Paragraphs with CSS
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Styled Paragraphs</title>
    <style>
        p {
            font-family: Georgia, serif;
            font-size: 1.1rem;
            line-height: 1.7;
            margin-bottom: 1.5rem;
            text-align: justify;
            hyphens: auto;
        }
        p.lead {
            font-size: 1.3rem;
            font-weight: bold;
            color: #2c3e50;
        }
        p.note {
            font-size: 0.9rem;
            color: #7f8c8d;
            border-left: 4px solid #3498db;
            padding-left: 1rem;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <p class="lead">This is a lead paragraph, styled to be larger and more prominent.</p>
    <p>This is a regular paragraph with justified text and automatic hyphenation.</p>
    <p class="note">This is a note paragraph, styled with a left border and smaller text.</p>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Example 5: Common Mistake – Block Element Inside a Paragraph
docs.text:
<!-- Invalid -->
<p>
    <div>This is a div inside a paragraph.</div>
</p>

<!-- What the browser does -->
<p></p>
<div>This is a div inside a paragraph.</div>
<p></p>

Why it's wrong: The <p> element cannot contain block-level elements. The parser closes the <p> before the <div>.

docs.title: Example 6: The text-indent Property
docs.text:
<style>
    p.indented {
        text-indent: 2em;
    }
</style>
<p class="indented">
    This paragraph has an indented first line, like a traditional book paragraph.
    This is a common stylistic choice in publishing.
</p>

docs.title: Example 7: Dynamic Paragraph Updates with JavaScript
docs.text:
<div id="content">
    <p id="message">Click the button to change this text.</p>
</div>
<button id="changeBtn">Change Text</button>

<script>
    document.getElementById('changeBtn').addEventListener('click', function() {
        const p = document.getElementById('message');
        p.textContent = 'The text has been changed!';
        p.style.color = 'blue';
        p.style.fontWeight = 'bold';
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 8: Using white-space to Preserve Formatting
docs.text:
<style>
    p.preformatted {
        white-space: pre-line; /* Preserves line breaks but collapses spaces */
    }
    p.pre-wrap {
        white-space: pre-wrap; /* Preserves line breaks and spaces */
    }
</style>
<p class="preformatted">
    This text
    has line breaks
    but spaces are collapsed.
</p>
<p class="pre-wrap">
    This   text
    has   line breaks
    and   spaces are preserved.
</p>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text:
• Body text – the primary use case: wrapping paragraphs of prose.
  • Blog posts – each paragraph represents a distinct idea.
  • Descriptions – product descriptions, about sections, etc.
  • Instructions – step-by-step text.
  • Quotes – introductory text before a blockquote.
  • Notes and warnings – styled paragraphs for important information.
  • Legal text – terms and conditions, privacy policies.

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <p> for paragraphs of text – don't use <div> or <br> for prose.

  2. Don't use <br> for spacing – use separate <p> elements or CSS margins.

  3. Keep paragraphs focused – one idea per paragraph. Long paragraphs are hard to read.

  4. Use inline elements for emphasis – <strong>, <em>, <a>, <code>, etc.

  5. Avoid using <p> for layout – use <div> or semantic elements for structure.

  6. Close your paragraphs – even though the closing tag is optional, include it for clarity.

  7. Use CSS for styling – don't use deprecated attributes like align.

  8. Don't nest paragraphs – <p> cannot contain another <p>.

  9. Use text-indent for book-style paragraphs – if desired.

  10. Ensure good contrast and readability – use appropriate font sizes and line heights.

  11. Use <p> inside sectioning elements – but not the other way around (block inside inline).

  12. Consider accessibility – paragraphs are read as units by screen readers.

  13. Avoid empty paragraphs – <p></p> adds space but has no content; use CSS margins instead.

  14. Use lang attribute on paragraphs in different languages – for screen reader pronunciation.

  15. Use class for styling – not id (unless unique).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <br> for Spacing Between Paragraphs
docs.text:
<p>First paragraph.<br><br>Second paragraph.</p>
Why it's wrong: Using <br> for spacing is not semantic. It's better to use separate <p> elements.

✅ Correct: 

<p>First paragraph.</p>
<p>Second paragraph.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting a Block Element Inside a Paragraph
docs.text:
<p>
    <div>This is a div inside a paragraph.</div>
</p>
Why it's wrong: <p> cannot contain block-level elements. The parser will close the <p> before the <div>.

✅ Correct: 

<div>
    <p>This is a paragraph inside a div.</p>
</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <p> for Layout
docs.text:
<p style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
    <span>Item 1</span>
    <span>Item 2</span>
</p>
Why it's wrong: <p> is for prose, not layout. Use <div> or a semantic container.

✅ Correct: 

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
    <span>Item 1</span>
    <span>Item 2</span>
</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Empty Paragraphs for Spacing
docs.text:
<p></p>
<p>Content</p>
<p></p>
Why it's wrong: Empty paragraphs add space but have no content. Use CSS margin instead.

✅ Correct: 

.content { margin-top: 20px; }

<p class="content">Content</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using align Attribute
docs.text:
<p align="center">Centered text</p>
Why it's wrong: The align attribute is deprecated.

✅ Correct: 

<p style="text-align: center;">Centered text</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Using <p> for Prose
docs.text:
<div>This is a paragraph of text but not marked up as a paragraph.</div>
Why it's wrong: Using <div> for prose loses semantic meaning. Screen readers won't identify it as a paragraph.

✅ Correct: 

<p>This is a paragraph of text.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Paragraphs for Headings
docs.text:
<p><strong>This is a heading</strong></p>
Why it's wrong: Headings have semantic meaning and are navigable by screen readers. Use <h1>–<h6>.

✅ Correct: 

<h2>This is a heading</h2>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Paragraphs are lightweight – each adds a DOM node, but the impact is minimal.
  • Excessive paragraphs – thousands of paragraphs can slow down rendering, but this is rare.
  • text-indent and text-align – have negligible performance impact.
  • white-space: pre – may cause longer rendering times if the content is large.
  • Dynamic updates – changing paragraph text triggers repaints; batch updates where possible.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into paragraphs, use textContent instead of innerHTML to prevent script injection.
  • innerHTML – if you must use it, sanitize the input.
  • Links in paragraphs – ensure href values are safe (no javascript: URLs).
  • target="_blank" – use rel="noopener noreferrer" to prevent tabnabbing.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect paragraphs to see their content and styles.
  • Computed styles – check the applied margin, line-height, and font-size.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('p') to list all paragraphs.
  • textContent vs innerHTML – verify which one you're using when manipulating paragraphs.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting (block elements inside <p>).

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For any block of prose – descriptions, explanations, narratives, instructions.
  • Inside sectioning elements – <section>, <article>, <aside>, <main>, <header>, <footer>.
  • For notes, warnings, and tips – styled paragraphs.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For headings – use <h1>–<h6>.
  • For lists – use <ul>, <ol>, <dl>.
  • For layout – use <div>, <section>, or CSS Grid/Flexbox.
  • For single words or phrases – use <span> if inline, or no element if just text.
  • For preformatted text – use <pre>.
  • For quotes – use <blockquote> for block quotes, <q> for inline quotes.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Text Content
  • Headings (<h1>–<h6>)
  • Block vs Inline Elements
  • Phrasing Content
  • Flow Content
  • <br> (line break)
  • <div> (generic container)
  • <span> (inline container)
  • <pre> (preformatted text)
  • CSS text-indent, text-align, line-height, margin
  • Accessibility (screen reader navigation)

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <p> element was one of the first HTML elements, present in HTML 1.0 (1991).

  • In HTML5, the closing </p> tag can be omitted if the paragraph is followed by certain block-level elements.

  • The default margin for <p> is 1em on the top and bottom. This can be changed with CSS.

  • The text-indent property is used in book publishing to indent the first line of a paragraph. It's less common on the web.

  • The <p> element cannot contain another <p> element. Paragraphs cannot be nested.

  • The <p> element is a palpable content element – it is visible and perceivable by users.

  • In the accessibility tree, paragraphs are exposed as paragraph nodes.

  • Some screen readers allow users to navigate by paragraph (e.g., pressing P in NVDA).

  • The <p> element is one of the most frequently used elements in HTML.

  • Empty paragraphs (<p></p>) are valid but not recommended; they add space but no content.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <p> element defines a paragraph of text – a block of prose that forms a distinct unit of content.
  • It is a block-level element and can only contain phrasing content (text and inline elements).
  • Default styles include a display: block and margins of 1em top and bottom.
  • Best practices: use <p> for prose, don't use <br> for spacing, don't nest block elements, use CSS for styling, and keep paragraphs focused.
  • Common mistakes include using <br> for spacing, nesting block elements inside paragraphs, using <p> for layout, and using empty paragraphs for spacing.
  • The <p> element is essential for readability, accessibility, and semantic structure.
  • It is the most common element for text content on the web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Text formatting in HTML refers to the set of inline elements used to apply semantic meaning or stylistic emphasis to portions of text within a block-level element like a paragraph. These elements allow authors to mark up specific words or phrases to convey importance, emphasis, emphasis, code, abbreviations, and other textual nuances.

HTML provides two broad categories of text formatting elements:

  • Semantic (logical) elements – convey meaning and importance (e.g., <strong>, <em>, <mark>, <code>, <abbr>, <cite>, <dfn>, <kbd>, <samp>, <var>, <time>, <del>, <ins>, <sub>, <sup>, <small>).
  • Presentational (physical) elements – convey visual styling without semantic meaning (e.g., <b>, <i>, <u>, <s>). These are discouraged in favor of CSS and semantic equivalents.

The key principle is: use semantic elements to convey meaning, and use CSS to control appearance.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Text formatting elements serve several essential purposes:

  • Convey meaning – indicate importance, emphasis, definition, citation, or code.
  • Improve accessibility – screen readers interpret semantic elements and adjust pronunciation or tone.
  • Enhance SEO – search engines use semantic markup to understand content emphasis.
  • Enable styling hooks – CSS can target semantic elements to apply visual styles.
  • Support internationalization – elements like <bdi> and <bdo> handle bidirectional text.
  • Provide machine-readable data – <time>, <data>, and <var> expose structured information.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Text formatting elements are phrasing content and inline elements. They appear inside block-level containers like <p>, <h1>–<h6>, <li>, <td>, <figcaption>, and others. They do not create new blocks; they flow within the text.

<p>
    This is a paragraph with <strong>important</strong> text,
    <em>emphasized</em> words, and a <a href="#">link</a>.
</p>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Plain text has no way to distinguish between different types of emphasis or meaning. Is a bold word simply visually bold, or is it important? Is an italicized phrase just stylized, or is it a technical term? Without semantic markup, machines (browsers, screen readers, search engines) cannot tell the difference.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic markup Machines couldn't distinguish importance from styling. Presentational elements only <b> and <i> conveyed no meaning beyond appearance. Inconsistent rendering Different browsers styled elements differently. Poor accessibility Screen readers couldn't adjust tone for emphasis. No machine-readable data Dates, times, and variables weren't identifiable.

docs.title: Why Text Formatting Elements Were Introduced
docs.text:
HTML introduced text formatting elements to provide semantic meaning alongside visual presentation. The evolution went from purely presentational (<b>, <i>) to semantic (<strong>, <em>) as the web matured and accessibility became a priority. This enables:

  • Meaningful markup – <strong> means "important", <em> means "emphasized".
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce emphasis and importance.
  • SEO – search engines understand which content is emphasized.
  • Styling flexibility – CSS can style semantic elements differently.
  • Machine readability – elements like <time> and <data> provide structured data.

docs.title: Semantic Text Formatting Elements
docs.text:
<!-- Strong importance (typically rendered bold) -->
<p>This is <strong>very important</strong> information.</p>

<!-- Emphasis (typically rendered italic) -->
<p>You <em>must</em> read this carefully.</p>

<!-- Highlighted/marked text -->
<p>Search results: <mark>HTML</mark> is the standard markup language.</p>

<!-- Code snippet -->
<p>Use the <code>console.log()</code> function to debug.</p>

<!-- Abbreviation -->
<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is the foundation of the web.</p>

<!-- Citation -->
<p>As stated in <cite>The Art of War</cite>, "Know your enemy."</p>

<!-- Definition term -->
<p><dfn>HTML</dfn> is the standard markup language for web pages.</p>

<!-- Keyboard input -->
<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>C</kbd> to copy.</p>

<!-- Sample output -->
<p>The program output: <samp>Hello, World!</samp></p>

<!-- Variable -->
<p>The equation is <var>x</var> = <var>y</var> + 2.</p>

<!-- Time -->
<p>The event is on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time>.</p>

<!-- Deleted text -->
<p>The price was <del>$99</del> now $79.</p>

<!-- Inserted text -->
<p>The price was $99 now <ins>$79</ins>.</p>

<!-- Subscript -->
<p>Water is H<sub>2</sub>O.</p>

<!-- Superscript -->
<p>E = mc<sup>2</sup>.</p>

<!-- Small print -->
<p><small>Terms and conditions apply.</small></p>

<!-- Bidirectional isolation -->
<p>Text with <bdi>مرحبا</bdi> embedded.</p>

<!-- Bidirectional override -->
<p><bdo dir="rtl">This text is reversed.</bdo></p>

docs.title: Presentational Text Formatting Elements (Discouraged)
docs.text:
<!-- Bold (stylistic, no semantic meaning) -->
<p>This is <b>bold</b> text.</p>

<!-- Italic (stylistic, no semantic meaning) -->
<p>This is <i>italic</i> text.</p>

<!-- Underline -->
<p>This is <u>underlined</u> text.</p>

<!-- Strikethrough -->
<p>This is <s>struck through</s> text.</p>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element Semantic Meaning Default Rendering <strong> Strong importance Bold <em> Stress emphasis Italic <mark> Highlighted/relevant Yellow background <code> Code fragment Monospace <abbr> Abbreviation Dotted underline (with title) <cite> Citation/title of work Italic <dfn> Definition term Italic <kbd> Keyboard input Monospace <samp> Sample output Monospace <var> Variable Italic <time> Date/time No default styling <del> Deleted text Strikethrough <ins> Inserted text Underline <sub> Subscript Lowered, smaller <sup> Superscript Raised, smaller <small> Side comment Smaller font <bdi> Bidirectional isolation No default styling <bdo> Bidirectional override No default styling

docs.title: The "Highlighter and Pen" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of text formatting elements as different writing tools:

  • <strong> – a bold marker that says "this is important".
  • <em> – an italic pen that says "stress this word".
  • <mark> – a highlighter that says "this is relevant".
  • <code> – a typewriter font that says "this is code".
  • <abbr> – a footnote that provides the full expansion.
  • <del> – a red pen that crosses out deleted text.
  • <ins> – a green pen that underlines inserted text.

Each tool conveys a specific meaning, not just a visual style.

docs.title: The "Semantic vs Presentational" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of the difference between semantic and presentational elements as the difference between:

  • Saying "This is important" (semantic) – the meaning is in the message.
  • Saying "This is bold" (presentational) – the meaning is in the appearance.

If you use <strong>, you're saying "this is important". If you use <b>, you're saying "this is bold". The first is meaningful; the second is just visual.

docs.title: The "Language of Emphasis" Analogy
docs.text:
In spoken language, you can emphasize words by:

  • Speaking louder – like <strong> (importance).
  • Speaking slower – like <em> (emphasis).
  • Pausing – like <mark> (highlighting).
  • Changing tone – like <cite> (quoting).
  • Spelling out – like <abbr> (abbreviation).

HTML provides elements to capture these nuances in written text.

docs.title: Concept 1: Semantic vs Presentational Elements
docs.text:
• Semantic elements (<strong>, <em>, <mark>, <code>, etc.) – convey meaning. They tell the browser, screen reader, and search engine what the text represents.
  • Presentational elements (<b>, <i>, <u>, <s>) – convey visual style. They don't add meaning; they just change appearance.

Rule: Use semantic elements whenever possible. Use presentational elements only when no semantic element fits.

docs.title: Concept 2: <strong> vs <b>
docs.text:
Aspect <strong> <b> Meaning Strong importance Stylistic offset (no importance) Screen readers Announces emphasis May not announce SEO Considered important Not considered Use case Warnings, critical information Keywords in a product name, stylized text

Example: <strong>Warning!</strong> vs <b>Product Name</b>.

docs.title: Concept 3: <em> vs <i>
docs.text:
Aspect <em> <i> Meaning Stress emphasis Alternative voice (technical term, foreign word, thought) Screen readers Announces emphasis May not announce SEO Considered emphasized Not considered Use case "You must read this" "The term Homo sapiens"

Example: You <em>must</em> try this vs The <i>E. coli</i> bacterium.

docs.title: Concept 4: <mark> – Highlighting
docs.text:
The <mark> element represents text that is highlighted for reference purposes, often in a context where it's relevant to the user's current activity (e.g., search results).

<p>Search results for "HTML": <mark>HTML</mark> is the standard markup language...</p>

docs.title: Concept 5: <code>, <kbd>, <samp>, <var>
docs.text:
These elements represent different types of technical content:

  • <code> – a fragment of computer code.
  • <kbd> – user keyboard input.
  • <samp> – sample output from a program.
  • <var> – a variable in a mathematical or programming context.
<p>Use <code>print()</code> to output. Press <kbd>Enter</kbd>. The result is <samp>Hello</samp>. The variable <var>x</var> holds the value.</p>

docs.title: Concept 6: <abbr> – Abbreviations
docs.text:
The <abbr> element represents an abbreviation or acronym. The title attribute provides the full expansion.

<p><abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr> was founded in 1948.</p>

docs.title: Concept 7: <time> – Machine-Readable Dates
docs.text:
The <time> element represents a specific period in time. The datetime attribute provides a machine-readable format.

<p>The concert is on <time datetime="2026-12-25">Christmas Day</time>.</p>

docs.title: Concept 8: <del> and <ins> – Document Changes
docs.text:
• <del> – represents text that has been deleted from the document.
  • <ins> – represents text that has been inserted into the document.
<p>The price was <del>$99</del> <ins>$79</ins>.</p>

docs.title: Concept 9: <sub> and <sup> – Subscript and Superscript
docs.text:
• <sub> – subscript text (lowered baseline).
  • <sup> – superscript text (raised baseline).
<p>H<sub>2</sub>O and E=mc<sup>2</sup>.</p>

docs.title: Concept 10: <small> – Side Comments
docs.text:
The <small> element represents side comments and small print (e.g., legal disclaimers, copyright notices).

<p><small>© 2026 My Company. All rights reserved.</small></p>

docs.title: Concept 11: <bdi> and <bdo> – Bidirectional Text
docs.text:
• <bdi> – isolates a span of text that might be formatted in a different direction.
  • <bdo> – overrides the current text direction.
<p>User <bdi>مرحبا</bdi> wrote a comment.</p>
<p><bdo dir="rtl">This text is reversed.</bdo></p>

docs.title: Concept 12: <u> – Unarticulated Annotation
docs.text:
The <u> element represents text with a non-textual annotation (e.g., a misspelled word). It's often rendered with an underline.

<p>This is <u>underlined</u> text.</p>

Note: In HTML5, <u> is not for underlining arbitrary text. Use CSS text-decoration: underline for that.

docs.title: Concept 13: <s> – Strikethrough
docs.text:
The <s> element represents text that is no longer accurate or relevant.

<p><s>Sold out</s> Available now!</p>

Note: <s> is for text that is no longer accurate. <del> is for text that has been deleted from the document.

docs.title: Concept 14: CSS for Text Styling
docs.text:
While HTML elements provide semantic meaning, CSS controls the visual presentation:

strong { font-weight: bold; }
em { font-style: italic; }
mark { background-color: yellow; }
code { font-family: monospace; }

You can style any element to look like any other, but the semantic meaning remains.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of Text Formatting Elements
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters an inline formatting element (e.g., `<strong>`).
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content inside (text and other inline elements).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default browser styles are applied:
    │   ├── <strong> → font-weight: bold
    │   ├── <em> → font-style: italic
    │   ├── <mark> → background-color: yellow
    │   ├── <code> → font-family: monospace
    │   └── etc.
    │
    ▼
6.  CSS can override these default styles.
    │
    ▼
7.  The element is exposed in the accessibility tree with its semantic role.
    │   └── Screen readers announce <strong> as "important" and <em> as "emphasized".
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines index the emphasized text with additional weight.

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
• <strong> – exposed as "strong" or "important".
  • <em> – exposed as "emphasis".
  • <mark> – exposed as "highlighted" or "marked".
  • <code> – exposed as "code".
  • <abbr> – exposed with the title as the expansion.
  • <del> – exposed as "deleted".
  • <ins> – exposed as "inserted".

docs.title: SEO Impact
docs.text: Search engines treat <strong> and <em> as signals of importance. Content inside these elements may be given more weight in ranking algorithms. However, overuse dilutes the effect.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
All text formatting elements inherit from HTMLElement and have specific interfaces:

  • <strong> → HTMLElement
  • <em> → HTMLElement
  • <mark> → HTMLElement
  • <code> → HTMLElement
  • <abbr> → HTMLElement
  • <time> → HTMLTimeElement
  • <del> → HTMLModElement
  • <ins> → HTMLModElement

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
Browsers apply default styles to text formatting elements. For example:

strong { font-weight: bold; }
em { font-style: italic; }
mark { background-color: yellow; color: black; }
code { font-family: monospace; }
abbr[title] { text-decoration: underline dotted; }
cite { font-style: italic; }
dfn { font-style: italic; }
kbd { font-family: monospace; }
samp { font-family: monospace; }
var { font-style: italic; }
del { text-decoration: line-through; }
ins { text-decoration: underline; }
sub { vertical-align: sub; font-size: smaller; }
sup { vertical-align: super; font-size: smaller; }
small { font-size: smaller; }
b { font-weight: bold; }
i { font-style: italic; }
u { text-decoration: underline; }
s { text-decoration: line-through; }

docs.title: The Accessibility API
docs.text:
Screen readers use the accessibility tree to determine how to announce text. For example:

  • <strong> may be announced with a change in voice or a slight pause.
  • <em> may be announced with a different tone.
  • <abbr> may announce the full expansion from the title attribute.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Text Formatting Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the text formatting element in the HTML.
    │   └── Example: <strong>Important</strong>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The element node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied.
    │
    ▼
5.  CSS may override the default styles.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered with the formatted text.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers expose the semantic meaning.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines index the emphasized text.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the element dynamically.
    │   └── Changing text content, adding/removing elements.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Example 1: Semantic Formatting in a Blog Post
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>Understanding HTML Text Formatting</h1>

    <p>
        HTML provides <strong>semantic elements</strong> for text formatting.
        These elements convey <em>meaning</em>, not just appearance.
        For example, <code><strong></code> indicates 
        <strong>strong importance</strong>, while <code><em></code> 
        indicates <em>stress emphasis</em>.
    </p>

    <p>
        The <abbr title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C</abbr> 
        defines the standards for HTML. The latest version is 
        <mark>HTML5</mark>, which is a <cite>Living Standard</cite>.
    </p>

    <p>
        <small>Note: This article was published on 
        <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time>.</small>
    </p>
</article>

docs.title: Example 2: Technical Documentation
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>API Reference</h2>

    <p>
        To make a request, use the <code>fetch()</code> function.
        Press <kbd>F12</kbd> to open the developer tools.
        The response will be logged as <samp>{"status": "ok"}</samp>.
    </p>

    <p>
        The variable <var>response</var> holds the result.
        The formula is <var>E</var> = <var>m</var><var>c</var><sup>2</sup>.
    </p>

    <p>
        <strong>Warning:</strong> This API is rate-limited.
        <em>Do not</em> exceed 100 requests per minute.
    </p>
</section>

docs.title: Example 3: Showing Document Changes
docs.text:
<p>
    The meeting has been 
    <del datetime="2026-09-07">moved to Monday</del> 
    <ins datetime="2026-09-08">rescheduled to Tuesday</ins>.
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <del> – shows deleted text (strikethrough). - <ins> – shows inserted text (underline). - datetime attributes provide machine-readable timestamps.

docs.title: Example 4: Search Results with <mark>
docs.text:
<h2>Search Results for "HTML"</h2>
<p>
    <mark>HTML</mark> is the standard markup language for creating web pages.
    Learn <mark>HTML</mark> with our comprehensive guide.
</p>

docs.title: Example 5: Abbreviations and Definitions
docs.text:
<p>
    <dfn id="html-def">HTML</dfn> stands for 
    <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>.
    It is the foundation of the web.
</p>

<p>
    <abbr title="Cascading Style Sheets">CSS</abbr> is used for styling.
    <abbr title="JavaScript">JS</abbr> is used for behavior.
</p>

docs.title: Example 6: Chemical and Mathematical Formulas
docs.text:
<p>Water: H<sub>2</sub>O</p>
<p>Carbon dioxide: CO<sub>2</sub></p>
<p>Einstein's equation: E = mc<sup>2</sup></p>
<p>Area of a circle: πr<sup>2</sup></p>

docs.title: Example 7: Styling Text Formatting Elements
docs.text:
<style>
    strong {
        color: #c0392b;
        font-weight: 700;
    }
    em {
        color: #2980b9;
        font-style: italic;
    }
    mark {
        background-color: #f1c40f;
        padding: 0 4px;
        border-radius: 3px;
    }
    code {
        background-color: #f4f4f4;
        padding: 2px 6px;
        border-radius: 3px;
        font-family: 'Courier New', monospace;
        font-size: 0.9em;
    }
    abbr[title] {
        border-bottom: 1px dotted #7f8c8d;
        cursor: help;
    }
    del {
        color: #e74c3c;
        text-decoration: line-through;
    }
    ins {
        color: #27ae60;
        text-decoration: none;
        background-color: #d5f5e3;
    }
</style>

docs.title: Example 8: Bidirectional Text
docs.text:
<p>
    The user <bdi>إيان</bdi> wrote a comment in Arabic.
    The text direction is isolated so it doesn't affect surrounding text.
</p>

<p>
    <bdo dir="rtl">This text is displayed right-to-left.</bdo>
</p>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Element Use Case <strong> Warnings, critical information, key points <em> Stress emphasis, technical terms, foreign words <mark> Search results, highlighted text <code> Code snippets, function names, file paths <abbr> Acronyms, abbreviations with expansions <cite> Titles of books, articles, films <dfn> Defining a term for the first time <kbd> Keyboard shortcuts, user input <samp> Program output, error messages <var> Variables in math or programming <time> Dates, times, durations <del> Deleted text in document revisions <ins> Inserted text in document revisions <sub> Chemical formulas, footnotes <sup> Mathematical exponents, ordinal numbers <small> Legal disclaimers, copyright, side comments <bdi> User-generated content in unknown direction <bdo> Overriding text direction

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use semantic elements over presentational – <strong> instead of <b>, <em> instead of <i>.

  2. Use <strong> for importance, <em> for emphasis – don't confuse the two.

  3. Use <mark> for highlighting relevance – not for arbitrary highlighting.

  4. Use <code> for code, <kbd> for keyboard, <samp> for output – each has a specific meaning.

  5. Provide title on <abbr> – for the full expansion.

  6. Use <time> with datetime – for machine-readable dates.

  7. Use <del> and <ins> for document changes – not just for visual strikethrough/underline.

  8. Don't use <u> for underlining arbitrary text – use CSS text-decoration: underline instead.

  9. Don't use <b> and <i> for emphasis – use <strong> and <em>.

  10. Style with CSS – use CSS to control appearance, not presentational elements.

  11. Keep formatting minimal – too much emphasis dilutes meaning.

  12. Test with screen readers – ensure semantic elements are announced correctly.

  13. Use <small> for side comments – not for making text smaller in general.

  14. Use <sub> and <sup> for typographic purposes – not for visual effects.

  15. Use <bdi> for user-generated content – to prevent bidirectional text issues.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <b> Instead of <strong>
docs.text:
<p><b>Warning!</b> This is important.</p>
Why it's wrong: <b> has no semantic meaning. Screen readers won't announce it as important.

✅ Correct: 

<p><strong>Warning!</strong> This is important.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <i> Instead of <em>
docs.text:
<p>You <i>must</i> read this.</p>
Why it's wrong: <i> is for alternative voice, not emphasis.

✅ Correct: 

<p>You <em>must</em> read this.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <u> for Underlining
docs.text:
<p>This is <u>underlined</u> text.</p>
Why it's wrong: <u> is for unarticulated annotations (e.g., misspellings), not arbitrary underlining. Underlined text can be confused with links.

✅ Correct: 

<p>This is <span style="text-decoration: underline;">underlined</span> text.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <s> for Deleted Text
docs.text:
<p><s>Old price: $99</s> New price: $79</p>
Why it's wrong: <s> is for text that is no longer accurate, not for document changes. <del> is for deletions.

✅ Correct: 

<p><del>Old price: $99</del> <ins>New price: $79</ins></p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <mark> for General Highlighting
docs.text:
<p>This is <mark>important</mark> information.</p>
Why it's wrong: <mark> is for highlighting text relevant to a specific context (like search results). For importance, use <strong>.

✅ Correct: 

<p>This is <strong>important</strong> information.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Providing title on <abbr>
docs.text:
<p><abbr>HTML</abbr> is the standard.</p>
Why it's wrong: Without title, the abbreviation has no expansion. Screen readers can't announce it.

✅ Correct: 

<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is the standard.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <time> Without datetime
docs.text:
<p>The event is on <time>next Friday</time>.</p>
Why it's wrong: Without datetime, the time isn't machine-readable.

✅ Correct: 

<p>The event is on <time datetime="2026-09-11">next Friday</time>.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <sub> and <sup> for Visual Effects
docs.text:
<p>This is <sup>superscript</sup> for no reason.</p>
Why it's wrong: <sub> and <sup> are for typographic conventions (chemical formulas, mathematical exponents).

✅ Correct: Use CSS vertical-align for visual effects.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Inline elements are lightweight – each adds a small DOM node.
  • Excessive formatting – too many inline elements can slow down rendering and increase DOM size.
  • CSS styling – applying complex styles to text formatting elements can trigger repaints.
  • Accessibility tree – semantic elements add nodes to the accessibility tree, but the impact is minimal.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into text formatting elements, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – if you must use it, sanitize the input.
  • title on <abbr> – can be used for XSS if user-controlled; sanitize.
  • datetime on <time> – should be validated to prevent injection.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect text formatting elements to see their semantic role.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check how elements are announced by screen readers.
  • Computed styles – see the applied font-weight, font-style, text-decoration.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('strong') to list all strong elements.
  • Validator – check for deprecated elements and attributes.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Element When to Use <strong> For important, serious, or urgent content. <em> For stress emphasis, technical terms, foreign words. <mark> For highlighting text relevant to the current context. <code> For code snippets, function names, file paths. <abbr> For abbreviations and acronyms. <cite> For titles of creative works. <dfn> For defining a term. <kbd> For keyboard input. <samp> For sample output. <var> For variables. <time> For dates and times. <del> For deleted text in document revisions. <ins> For inserted text in document revisions. <sub> For subscripts (chemical formulas, footnotes). <sup> For superscripts (exponents, ordinal numbers). <small> For side comments, legal text. <bdi> For user-generated content with unknown direction. <bdo> For overriding text direction.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• <b> and <i> – when semantic elements fit better.
  • <u> – for arbitrary underlining; use CSS.
  • <s> – for deleted text; use <del>.
  • <mark> – for importance; use <strong>.
  • <sub> and <sup> – for visual effects; use CSS.
  • <small> – for making all text smaller; use CSS.
  • <big> – deprecated; use CSS font-size.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Phrasing Content
  • Inline Elements
  • Block vs Inline Elements
  • CSS Text Styling (font-weight, font-style, text-decoration)
  • Accessibility (screen reader pronunciation)
  • SEO (content emphasis)
  • Internationalization (bidirectional text)
  • HTML5 Living Standard

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <b> and <i> elements were originally presentational, but HTML5 redefined them as "stylistic offsets" with no semantic meaning.

  • The <strong> element is not just "bold" – it represents importance. Similarly, <em> is not just "italic" – it represents stress emphasis.

  • The <mark> element was introduced in HTML5 to represent highlighted text, particularly in search results.

  • The <time> element can represent dates, times, durations, and time zones using the datetime attribute.

  • The <abbr> element's title attribute is announced by screen readers when the user hovers or focuses on the abbreviation.

  • The <del> and <ins> elements can carry cite and datetime attributes to reference the source of the change and the time it was made.

  • The <bdi> element is particularly useful for user-generated content (like comments) that may contain text in a different direction.

  • The <small> element is not just for making text smaller – it represents "side comments" like legal disclaimers.

  • The <var> element is for variables in mathematical expressions or programming code, not just italic text.

  • In HTML5, the <u> element is redefined to represent text with a non-textual annotation (like a misspelling), not just underlining.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Text formatting elements in HTML convey semantic meaning and/or visual style to portions of text.
  • Semantic elements (<strong>, <em>, <mark>, <code>, <abbr>, <cite>, <dfn>, <kbd>, <samp>, <var>, <time>, <del>, <ins>, <sub>, <sup>, <small>, <bdi>, <bdo>) should be used over presentational elements.
  • Presentational elements (<b>, <i>, <u>, <s>) are discouraged; use semantic equivalents or CSS.
  • Best practices: use <strong> for importance, <em> for emphasis, <mark> for highlighting, <code> for code, and CSS for visual styling.
  • Common mistakes include using <b> instead of <strong>, <i> instead of <em>, <u> for underlining, and <s> for deleted text.
  • Text formatting is essential for accessibility, SEO, and semantic clarity.
  • Use CSS to control appearance, and HTML to convey meaning.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Quotes in HTML are elements used to mark up quoted text – passages taken from another source and reproduced in a document. HTML provides two primary elements for quotations:

  • <blockquote> – for block-level quotations (longer passages that stand alone as a block).
  • <q> – for inline quotations (short quotes that flow within a sentence or paragraph).

Additionally, HTML provides the <cite> element to reference the source of a quote, and the cite attribute (on <blockquote> and <q>) to provide a machine-readable URL of the source.

Quotations are a fundamental part of written communication – academic papers, news articles, blog posts, and legal documents all rely on quoting sources. HTML's quote elements provide semantic meaning, accessibility, and styling hooks for this essential content type.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Quote elements serve several essential purposes:

  • Semantic meaning – clearly identify quoted material as distinct from the author's own words.
  • Accessibility – screen readers may announce quotations differently (e.g., "quote" and "unquote").
  • Styling – browsers apply default styles (indentation for blockquotes, quotation marks for <q>).
  • Attribution – the <cite> element links the quote to its source.
  • Legal and academic integrity – proper markup helps distinguish original content from borrowed content.
  • SEO – search engines may treat quoted content differently from original content.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Quote elements are flow content and phrasing content (for <q> and <cite>). They can appear in paragraphs, articles, sections, and other content containers. <blockquote> is a block-level element, while <q> and <cite> are inline elements.

<article>
    <h1>Article Title</h1>
    <p>The author said:</p>

    <blockquote cite="https://example.com/source">
        <p>This is a longer quotation that stands alone as a block.</p>
    </blockquote>

    <p>As someone once said, <q>short quotes flow inline</q>.</p>

    <p>Source: <cite>The Art of War</cite></p>
</article>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before HTML provided quote elements, authors had no standard way to mark up quoted text. They might use italics, quotation marks, or indentation, but these were purely visual cues. Machines (browsers, screen readers, search engines) couldn't distinguish quoted material from the author's own words. This created problems for:

  • Accessibility – screen readers couldn't indicate the beginning and end of quotes.
  • Attribution – there was no standard way to link a quote to its source.
  • Styling – quotes couldn't be styled consistently across browsers.
  • Semantics – search engines couldn't tell what was original and what was quoted.
  • Legal clarity – proper attribution was difficult to enforce.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic quote elements Machines couldn't identify quoted content. Visual-only cues Italics and indentation were inconsistent. No attribution mechanism Sources couldn't be linked programmatically. Poor accessibility Screen readers couldn't announce quotes. No styling hooks Quotes couldn't be styled consistently.

docs.title: Why Quote Elements Were Introduced
docs.text:
HTML introduced <blockquote> in HTML 1.0 and <q> in HTML 4.0 to provide semantic markup for quotations. The <cite> element was also introduced to reference sources. These elements enable:

  • Clear semantics – quoted content is distinguished from original content.
  • Accessibility – screen readers can announce the beginning and end of quotations.
  • Attribution – the <cite> element and cite attribute link quotes to sources.
  • Styling – default styles (indentation, quotation marks) can be customised with CSS.
  • Legal and academic integrity – proper markup encourages proper attribution.

docs.title: The <blockquote> Element
docs.text:
Used for block-level quotations – longer passages that stand alone as a block.

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/source">
    <p>This is a longer quotation that stands alone as a block. It can contain multiple paragraphs and other block-level content.</p>
    <p>It is typically indented to distinguish it from the surrounding text.</p>
</blockquote>

docs.title: The <q> Element
docs.text:
Used for inline quotations – short quotes that flow within a sentence or paragraph.

<p>As the author said, <q>This is a short quotation.</q></p>

docs.title: The <cite> Element
docs.text:
Used to reference the source of a quote. It is an inline element.

<p>As stated in <cite>The Art of War</cite>, "Know your enemy."</p>

docs.title: The cite Attribute
docs.text:
Both <blockquote> and <q> can have a cite attribute that provides a URL to the source of the quote.

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/source">
    <p>Quoted text here.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>As someone said, <q cite="https://example.com/source">Short quote.</q></p>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element/Attribute What It Does Why It Matters <blockquote> Marks a block-level quotation. Creates visual separation (indentation) and semantic meaning. <q> Marks an inline quotation. Browsers add quotation marks automatically. <cite> References the source of a quote. Provides attribution and context. cite attribute Provides a URL to the source. Machine-readable attribution (though not visible to users).

docs.title: The "Quotation Marks" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <q> as automatic quotation marks. Just as you would put quotation marks around a short quote in writing, <q> tells the browser to add them. For longer quotes, <blockquote> is like indenting a passage in a book – it sets the quote apart visually and semantically.

docs.title: The "Guest Speaker" Analogy
docs.text: A <blockquote> is like a guest speaker at an event. The speaker stands apart from the main presentation (indented), delivers their message (the quote), and then the main presentation resumes. The <cite> element is like the introduction – "Our next speaker is from..." – it tells you who the speaker is.

docs.title: The "Nested Conversation" Analogy
docs.text: When you quote someone, you're embedding their words in your own. <q> is like a brief aside – "She said 'hello' and left." <blockquote> is like a longer digression – "She then gave a long speech: '...' – and then she left." The quote is clearly marked as separate from your own words.

docs.title: Concept 1: <blockquote> vs <q>
docs.text: Aspect <blockquote> <q> Display Block-level (starts on new line, indented) Inline (flows within text) Use case Longer quotations (multiple sentences, paragraphs) Short quotations (a phrase or sentence) Default styling Indented (margin-left/right: 40px) Quotation marks added Content model Flow content (can contain paragraphs, lists, etc.) Phrasing content (inline elements only) cite attribute Yes Yes

docs.title: Concept 2: The cite Attribute
docs.text:
The cite attribute on <blockquote> and <q> provides a URL to the source of the quotation. It is not displayed to users by default, but it is machine-readable.

<blockquote cite="https://www.example.com/article">
    <p>The quote goes here.</p>
</blockquote>

Note: The cite attribute is not well-supported by screen readers and is often ignored. It's still valid HTML, but don't rely on it for accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 3: The <cite> Element
docs.text:
The <cite> element is used to reference the title of a creative work (book, article, film, song, etc.) or the source of a quote. It is an inline element and is typically rendered in italics.

<p>As stated in <cite>The Art of War</cite>, "Know your enemy."</p>

Important: <cite> is for the title of the source, not the author's name. For the author, use a regular <a> or <span>.

docs.title: Concept 4: Quotation Marks and Language
docs.text:
The type of quotation marks used by <q> depends on the language of the document (set by the lang attribute). For example:

  • English: "..." (double quotes)
  • French: « ... » (guillemets)
  • German: „..." (low-9 quotes)
<html lang="en">
    <p><q>English quote</q></p>  <!-- Renders as "English quote" -->
</html>

<html lang="fr">
    <p><q>Citation française</q></p>  <!-- Renders as « Citation française » -->
</html>

docs.title: Concept 5: Nested Quotes
docs.text:
Quotes can be nested. When <q> is used inside another <q>, browsers may use different quotation marks for the inner quote (e.g., single quotes inside double quotes in English).

<p>She said, <q>He told me, <q>Hello</q>.</q></p>
<!-- Renders as: She said, "He told me, 'Hello'." -->

docs.title: Concept 6: <blockquote> Content Model
docs.text:
<blockquote> can contain flow content – including paragraphs, headings, lists, and even other blockquotes. This makes it suitable for long quotations that span multiple paragraphs.

<blockquote>
    <p>First paragraph of the quote.</p>
    <p>Second paragraph of the quote.</p>
    <ul>
        <li>Point 1</li>
        <li>Point 2</li>
    </ul>
</blockquote>

docs.title: Concept 7: <q> Content Model
docs.text:
<q> can only contain phrasing content – text and inline elements. It cannot contain block-level elements.

<!-- Valid -->
<p><q>Short quote with <strong>emphasis</strong>.</q></p>

<!-- Invalid -->
<p><q><div>Block inside inline quote</div></q></p>

docs.title: Concept 8: The <blockquote> Default Styles
docs.text:
Browsers apply default styles to <blockquote>:

blockquote {
    display: block;
    margin-block-start: 1em;
    margin-block-end: 1em;
    margin-inline-start: 40px;
    margin-inline-end: 40px;
}

These can be overridden with CSS.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of Quotes
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<blockquote>` or `<q>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content inside:
    │   ├── For `<blockquote>`: flow content (paragraphs, lists, etc.)
    │   └── For `<q>`: phrasing content (text, inline elements)
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   ├── `<blockquote>` → indented (margin-left/right: 40px)
    │   └── `<q>` → quotation marks added (via CSS `quotes` property)
    │
    ▼
6.  The language (`lang` attribute) determines the type of quotation marks.
    │
    ▼
7.  CSS can override the default styles.
    │
    ▼
8.  The element is exposed in the accessibility tree.
    │   └── Screen readers may announce "quote" and "unquote".

docs.title: The quotes CSS Property
docs.text:
The quotes property in CSS defines the quotation marks used for <q> and <blockquote>:

q {
    quotes: "“" "”" "‘" "’"; /* Double, then single */
}

Browsers have default quotes values based on the lang attribute.

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
• <blockquote> is exposed as a "blockquote" or "quote" node.
  • <q> is exposed as an "inline quote" node.
  • Screen readers may announce "quote" at the beginning and "unquote" at the end.
  • <cite> is exposed as a "citation" node.

docs.title: The HTMLQuoteElement Interface
docs.text: In the DOM, both <blockquote> and <q> are represented by the HTMLQuoteElement interface, which inherits from HTMLElement. It has a cite property that reflects the cite attribute.

docs.title: The HTMLModElement Interface (for <del> and <ins>)
docs.text: Not directly related to quotes, but worth noting: <del> and <ins> also have cite attributes and are represented by HTMLModElement.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
blockquote {
    display: block;
    margin-block-start: 1em;
    margin-block-end: 1em;
    margin-inline-start: 40px;
    margin-inline-end: 40px;
}

q {
    display: inline;
}

q::before {
    content: open-quote;
}

q::after {
    content: close-quote;
}

The open-quote and close-quote values use the quotes property to determine which characters to insert.

docs.title: Language-Dependent Quotes
docs.text:
Browsers use the lang attribute to determine the correct quotation marks. The default quotes values for some languages:

Language quotes Value English (en) "“" "”" "‘" "’" French (fr) "« " " »" "‹ " " ›" German (de) "„" "“" "‚" "‘" Japanese (ja) "「" "」" "『" "』"

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Quote Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the quote element in the HTML.
    │   └── Example: <blockquote cite="...">...</blockquote>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The quote element node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (indentation for blockquote, quotes for q).
    │
    ▼
5.  The `lang` attribute determines the quotation mark style.
    │
    ▼
6.  CSS may override the default styles.
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
8.  Screen readers expose the quote semantics.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the quote dynamically.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Example 1: A Block Quote with Attribution
docs.text:
<figure>
    <blockquote cite="https://www.example.com/speech">
        <p>The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.</p>
    </blockquote>
    <figcaption>
        — Franklin D. Roosevelt, <cite>First Inaugural Address</cite>
    </figcaption>
</figure>

Code Breakdown: - <blockquote> – the quotation. - cite attribute – URL to the source (not displayed). - <figcaption> – the attribution. - <cite> – the title of the speech.

docs.title: Example 2: An Inline Quote
docs.text:
<p>
    When asked about the project, she said, 
    <q cite="https://www.example.com/interview">It was the most challenging work of my career.</q>
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <q> – the inline quotation. - Browsers add quotation marks automatically. - cite attribute – URL to the interview (not displayed).

docs.title: Example 3: Nested Quotes
docs.text:
<p>
    The professor explained, 
    <q>As Aristotle said, <q>We are what we repeatedly do.</q></q>
</p>

Rendering (in English): 

The professor explained, "As Aristotle said, 'We are what we repeatedly do.'"

Code Breakdown: - Outer <q> – double quotation marks. - Inner <q> – single quotation marks (automatically handled by the browser).

docs.title: Example 4: Block Quote with Multiple Paragraphs
docs.text:
<blockquote cite="https://www.example.com/book">
    <p>This is the first paragraph of a long quotation. It sets the context.</p>
    <p>This is the second paragraph. It provides more detail.</p>
    <p>This is the third paragraph. It concludes the quotation.</p>
</blockquote>

Code Breakdown: - <blockquote> can contain multiple <p> elements. - The entire block is indented.

docs.title: Example 5: Styling Blockquotes with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    blockquote {
        margin: 2rem 0;
        padding: 1rem 2rem;
        border-left: 4px solid #3498db;
        background-color: #f8f9fa;
        font-style: italic;
        color: #2c3e50;
        border-radius: 0 8px 8px 0;
    }
    blockquote footer {
        margin-top: 1rem;
        font-style: normal;
        font-size: 0.9rem;
