        color: #7f8c8d;
    }
    blockquote footer::before {
        content: "— ";
    }
</style>

<blockquote>
    <p>The only way to do great work is to love what you do.</p>
    <footer>Steve Jobs, <cite>Stanford Commencement Address</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

docs.title: Example 6: Quotes with Language-Specific Quotation Marks
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Quotes in Different Languages</title>
</head>
<body>
    <p lang="en">English: <q>Hello</q></p>
    <p lang="fr">French: <q>Bonjour</q></p>
    <p lang="de">German: <q>Hallo</q></p>
    <p lang="ja">Japanese: <q>こんにちは</q></p>
</body>
</html>

Rendering: - English: "Hello" - French: « Bonjour » - German: „Hallo" - Japanese: 「こんにちは」

docs.title: Example 7: Using <cite> for Source Attribution
docs.text:
<p>
    As noted in <cite>The Pragmatic Programmer</cite>, 
    <q>Good design is easier to change than bad design.</q>
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <cite> – the title of the book (italicised by default). - <q> – the quote (with automatic quotation marks).

docs.title: Example 8: Blockquote with <footer> for Attribution
docs.text:
<blockquote>
    <p>Stay hungry, stay foolish.</p>
    <footer>
        — Steve Jobs, <cite>Stanford Commencement Address, 2005</cite>
    </footer>
</blockquote>

Code Breakdown: - <footer> inside <blockquote> – a semantic way to attribute the quote. - This is a common pattern in HTML5.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Element Long quotations from books, speeches, articles <blockquote> Short quotations within a sentence <q> Attribution of a quote to its source <cite> or <footer> Testimonials <blockquote> with <footer> Pull quotes in articles <blockquote> styled with CSS Legal quotations <blockquote> Academic citations <blockquote> + <cite> Nested quotations <q> inside <q> Multilingual quotations <q> with lang attribute

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <blockquote> for longer quotes – passages that stand alone as a block.

  2. Use <q> for short quotes – phrases that flow within a sentence.

  3. Don't use <q> for quotations longer than a sentence – use <blockquote> instead.

  4. Provide attribution – use <cite> or a <footer> inside <blockquote>.

  5. Don't use <cite> for the author's name – use <cite> for the title of the work, and a regular <a> or <span> for the author.

  6. Use the cite attribute for URLs – even though it's not displayed, it provides machine-readable attribution.

  7. Don't manually add quotation marks with <q> – the browser adds them automatically.

  8. Use CSS to style blockquotes – default indentation may not match your design.

  9. Use lang for multilingual quotes – ensures correct quotation marks.

  10. Don't use <blockquote> for indentation – use CSS margin or padding instead.

  11. Test with screen readers – ensure quotes are announced correctly.

  12. Use <figure> for quotes with attributions – a common pattern that groups the quote and its attribution.

  13. Keep quotes accurate – don't alter quoted text. Use <del> and <ins> for edits.

  14. Use <blockquote> for testimonials – with <footer> for the author.

  15. Avoid nesting <blockquote> too deeply – it can be confusing.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <blockquote> for Indentation
docs.text:
<blockquote>
    <p>This paragraph is indented but it's not a quote.</p>
</blockquote>
Why it's wrong: <blockquote> is for quotations, not for visual indentation.

✅ Correct: 

<p style="margin-left: 40px;">This paragraph is indented but not a quote.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Manually Adding Quotation Marks with <q>
docs.text:
<p><q>"This is a quote."</q></p>
Why it's wrong: <q> adds quotation marks automatically. Adding them manually results in double quotes.

✅ Correct: 

<p><q>This is a quote.</q></p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <cite> for the Author's Name
docs.text:
<p>As <cite>John Doe</cite> said, <q>Hello</q>.</p>
Why it's wrong: <cite> is for the title of a work, not the author's name.

✅ Correct: 

<p>As John Doe said in <cite>His Book</cite>, <q>Hello</q>.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <q> for Long Quotations
docs.text:
<p><q>This is a very long quotation that spans multiple sentences. It should be a blockquote, not an inline quote. The q element is only for short quotes.</q></p>
Why it's wrong: <q> is for short, inline quotations. Long quotes should use <blockquote>.

✅ Correct: 

<blockquote>
    <p>This is a very long quotation...</p>
</blockquote>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <blockquote> Inside <p>
docs.text:
<p>Some text <blockquote>A quote</blockquote> more text.</p>
Why it's wrong: <blockquote> is a block-level element and cannot be inside a <p> (which only accepts phrasing content).

✅ Correct: 

<p>Some text</p>
<blockquote>A quote</blockquote>
<p>More text.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using the cite Attribute for Visible Attribution
docs.text:
<blockquote cite="John Doe">
    <p>Quote here.</p>
</blockquote>
Why it's wrong: The cite attribute is for a URL, not a name. It's also not displayed to users.

✅ Correct: 

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/source">
    <p>Quote here.</p>
</blockquote>
<footer>— John Doe</footer>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Close <q> or <blockquote>
docs.text:
<p><q>Unclosed quote</p>
Why it's wrong: Unclosed tags can cause unexpected DOM structure.

✅ Correct: 

<p><q>Closed quote</q></p>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Quote elements are lightweight – each adds a small DOM node.
  • <q> and <cite> – inline elements with minimal rendering cost.
  • <blockquote> – block-level element with default margins; no significant performance impact.
  • CSS styling – complex styles (shadows, gradients) may affect performance but are independent of the quote element itself.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated quotes, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • cite attribute – ensure URLs are safe (no javascript: URLs).
  • <blockquote> content – if user-generated, sanitize to prevent script injection.
  • Attribution links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for external links.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect quote elements to see their structure.
  • Computed styles – check the applied margin, quotes, and font-style.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('blockquote') to list all blockquotes.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check how quotes are announced.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting (blockquote inside p).

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Element When to Use <blockquote> For long quotations that stand alone as a block. <q> For short, inline quotations within a sentence. <cite> For the title of a creative work or the source of a quote. cite attribute For providing a URL to the source (machine-readable).

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• <blockquote> – for indentation or layout purposes; use CSS.
  • <q> – for long quotations; use <blockquote>.
  • <cite> – for author names; use <span> or <a>.
  • cite attribute – for visible attribution; use <footer> or <cite>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <figure> and <figcaption> (for quote attribution)
  • <footer> (for attribution inside blockquote)
  • <cite> (for source titles)
  • CSS quotes property
  • Language (lang attribute) and quotation marks
  • Phrasing Content
  • Flow Content
  • Accessibility (screen reader announcements)

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <blockquote> element was present in HTML 1.0 (1991). The <q> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997).

  • The cite attribute on <blockquote> and <q> is not displayed by browsers and is often ignored by screen readers. It's still valid but of limited practical use.

  • The <q> element adds quotation marks using CSS ::before and ::after pseudo-elements with the open-quote and close-quote values.

  • The type of quotation marks used by <q> depends on the lang attribute. For example, French uses guillemets (« »), German uses low-9 quotes („ ").

  • Nested <q> elements automatically use different quotation marks (e.g., single quotes inside double quotes in English).

  • The <cite> element is for the title of a work, not the author. This is a common misconception.

  • HTML5 allows <footer> inside <blockquote> to provide attribution – a semantic pattern for quotes with sources.

  • The <blockquote> element's default indentation (40px on each side) can be overridden with CSS.

  • Some CSS frameworks (like Bootstrap) provide .blockquote classes for styling blockquotes.

  • The <q> element is not supported in Internet Explorer 8 and earlier (they don't add quotation marks). Use CSS if you need to support legacy browsers.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Quote elements in HTML provide semantic markup for quoted text.
  • <blockquote> – for block-level quotations (longer passages).
  • <q> – for inline quotations (short phrases).
  • <cite> – for the title of a creative work or the source of a quote.
  • cite attribute – provides a machine-readable URL to the source.
  • Best practices: use <blockquote> for long quotes, <q> for short quotes, provide attribution with <cite> or <footer>, don't manually add quotation marks, and use CSS for styling.
  • Common mistakes include using <blockquote> for indentation, manually adding quotation marks, using <cite> for author names, and nesting <blockquote> inside <p>.
  • Quote elements are essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and proper attribution.
  • Use the lang attribute to ensure correct quotation marks for different languages.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Code elements in HTML are a group of inline (and one block-level) elements used to mark up computer code, technical content, and user input/output. These elements provide semantic meaning to text that represents code, commands, variables, keyboard input, and program output. They allow browsers, screen readers, and search engines to understand that the content is technical in nature and should be treated differently from ordinary prose.

The primary code-related elements are:

  • <code> – a fragment of computer code (inline).
  • <pre> – preformatted text (block-level, preserves whitespace).
  • <kbd> – user keyboard input (inline).
  • <samp> – sample output from a program (inline).
  • <var> – a variable in a mathematical or programming context (inline).

Together, these elements form a small but powerful vocabulary for technical documentation, tutorials, API references, and developer-focused content.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Code elements serve several essential purposes:

  • Semantic clarity – distinguish code from prose, so machines understand the content type.
  • Accessibility – screen readers may announce code differently or provide navigation.
  • Styling hooks – CSS can target code elements to apply monospace fonts, backgrounds, and syntax highlighting.
  • Whitespace preservation – <pre> preserves spaces, tabs, and line breaks for code blocks.
  • Readability – monospace fonts and visual cues help developers scan code quickly.
  • Copy-paste accuracy – preserving exact formatting ensures code can be copied correctly.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Code elements are phrasing content (except <pre>, which is flow content). They appear inside paragraphs, list items, table cells, and other phrasing contexts. <pre> is a block-level element used for multi-line code blocks.

<p>Use the <code>console.log()</code> function to debug.</p>

<pre><code>
function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
</code></pre>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Technical documentation, tutorials, and developer blogs frequently contain code snippets, terminal commands, keyboard shortcuts, and program output. Before dedicated code elements existed, authors had to rely on <pre> alone or use <tt> (teletype text, deprecated). There was no way to distinguish between:

  • A code snippet and a variable name.
  • A keyboard shortcut and program output.
  • A command and a filename.

This made technical content less accessible and harder to style consistently.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic code markup All technical text looked the same. <tt> was presentational No semantic meaning; deprecated. No distinction between code and output Machines couldn't differentiate. Whitespace collapsing Code blocks lost indentation and line breaks. No syntax highlighting hooks Styling was inconsistent and manual.

docs.title: Why Code Elements Were Introduced
docs.text:
HTML introduced code elements to provide semantic markup for technical content:

  • <code> – for code fragments.
  • <kbd> – for keyboard input.
  • <samp> – for sample output.
  • <var> – for variables.
  • <pre> – for preserving whitespace in code blocks.

This enables:

  • Meaningful markup – machines understand what is code, input, output, or a variable.
  • Accessibility – screen readers can announce code appropriately.
  • Styling – CSS can apply monospace fonts and syntax highlighting.
  • Formatting – <pre> preserves whitespace, critical for code readability.
  • Interoperability – tools (IDEs, documentation generators) can parse code elements.

docs.title: The <code> Element
docs.text:
Used for inline code fragments – function names, variable names, file paths, HTML tags, CSS properties.

<p>Use the <code>console.log()</code> function to print output.</p>
<p>The <code><div></code> element is a generic container.</p>
<p>Set the <code>color</code> property to <code>red</code>.</p>

docs.title: The <pre> Element
docs.text:
Used for preformatted text – preserves whitespace and line breaks. Typically combined with <code> for code blocks.

<pre>
function greet(name) {
    return "Hello, " + name + "!";
}
</pre>

docs.title: The <kbd> Element
docs.text:
Used for keyboard input – keys, shortcuts, and user input.

<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>C</kbd> to copy.</p>
<p>Type <kbd>exit</kbd> to quit.</p>

docs.title: The <samp> Element
docs.text:
Used for sample output from a program or system.

<p>The program outputs: <samp>Hello, World!</samp></p>
<p>Error: <samp>File not found</samp></p>

docs.title: The <var> Element
docs.text:
Used for variables in mathematical or programming contexts.

<p>The equation is <var>x</var> = <var>y</var> + <var>z</var>.</p>
<p>The variable <var>count</var> holds the number of items.</p>

docs.title: Combined Example
docs.text:
<p>
    Use the <code>fetch()</code> function. Press <kbd>F12</kbd> to open
    DevTools. The response will be logged as <samp>{"status": "ok"}</samp>.
    Store it in <var>response</var>.
</p>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element What It Represents Default Rendering <code> Code fragment Monospace font <pre> Preformatted text Monospace font, preserves whitespace <kbd> Keyboard input Monospace font <samp> Sample output Monospace font <var> Variable Italic, monospace in some browsers

docs.title: Common Combinations
docs.text: Combination Use Case <pre><code> Multi-line code blocks <kbd><kbd> Nested keys (e.g., Ctrl + C) <code><var> Variables inside code <samp> Terminal output

docs.title: The "Typewriter" Analogy
docs.text:
Code elements represent text that would appear in a typewriter font on a computer terminal:

  • <code> – a snippet of code you might see in a source file.
  • <kbd> – what you type on the keyboard.
  • <samp> – what the computer prints back.
  • <var> – a placeholder that changes.
  • <pre> – text with exact spacing, like a printout.

Each element tells the browser, "This text belongs to a specific technical context."

docs.title: The "Instructions Manual" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of a user manual for a device:

  • <code> – the part number or model code.
  • <kbd> – the buttons you press.
  • <samp> – the screen display.
  • <var> – the value you enter.
  • <pre> – a diagram or table with exact formatting.

The manual uses different typography for each type of content, and HTML uses different elements for the same purpose.

docs.title: The "Recipe" Analogy
docs.text:
A recipe contains:

  • Ingredients (variables, <var>).
  • Instructions (steps, <code>).
  • Utensils (tools, <kbd>).
  • Results (final dish, <samp>).
  • Diagrams (layout, <pre>).

Just as a recipe distinguishes these, HTML distinguishes code, input, output, and variables.

docs.title: Concept 1: The <code> Element
docs.text:
• Purpose: Mark up a fragment of computer code.
  • Content model: Phrasing content (text and inline elements).
  • Default rendering: Monospace font (usually Courier or similar).
  • Use cases: Function names, variable names, HTML tags, CSS properties, file paths, command names.
  • Example: <code>console.log()</code>

Note: <code> is for inline code. For multi-line code blocks, wrap <code> inside <pre>.

docs.title: Concept 2: The <pre> Element
docs.text:
• Purpose: Preserve whitespace and line breaks exactly as written.
  • Content model: Phrasing content (but often used with <code>).
  • Default rendering: Monospace font, whitespace preserved.
  • Use cases: Code blocks, ASCII art, preformatted text, poetry.
  • Example: 
    <pre>
    Line 1
        Indented Line 2
    Line 3
</pre>

Important: <pre> preserves spaces, tabs, and newlines. This makes it essential for code blocks where indentation matters.

docs.title: Concept 3: The <kbd> Element
docs.text:
• Purpose: Mark up user keyboard input.
  • Content model: Phrasing content.
  • Default rendering: Monospace font.
  • Use cases: Keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl + C), commands typed by the user (git commit), key names (Enter, Esc).
  • Example: Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save.

docs.title: Concept 4: The <samp> Element
docs.text:
• Purpose: Mark up sample output from a program or system.
  • Content model: Phrasing content.
  • Default rendering: Monospace font.
  • Use cases: Terminal output, error messages, program results.
  • Example: The command returned <samp>Success</samp>.

docs.title: Concept 5: The <var> Element
docs.text:
• Purpose: Mark up a variable in a mathematical or programming context.
  • Content model: Phrasing content.
  • Default rendering: Italic (and sometimes monospace).
  • Use cases: Mathematical variables (x, y), programming variables (count, total).
  • Example: The sum of <var>a</var> and <var>b</var>.

docs.title: Concept 6: Combining Elements
docs.text:
These elements are often combined for richer semantics:

<!-- Code block -->
<pre><code>function hello() {
    console.log("Hello");
}</code></pre>

<!-- Keyboard shortcut -->
<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>P</kbd>.</p>

<!-- Variable inside code -->
<p>The <code><var>count</var>++</code> expression increments the counter.</p>

<!-- Sample output with code -->
<p>Run <code>node app.js</code>. Output: <samp>Server running on port 3000</samp></p>

docs.title: Concept 7: <pre> and Whitespace
docs.text:
Without <pre>, HTML collapses whitespace:

<p>
    This     text
    has   multiple
    spaces.
</p>
<!-- Renders as: "This text has multiple spaces." -->

With <pre>, whitespace is preserved:

<pre>
    This     text
    has   multiple
    spaces.
</pre>
<!-- Renders exactly as written. -->

docs.title: Concept 8: Syntax Highlighting
docs.text:
Code elements provide hooks for syntax highlighting libraries (like Prism.js, Highlight.js):

<pre><code class="language-javascript">
function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
</code></pre>

The class="language-javascript" tells the highlighter which language to use.

docs.title: Concept 9: Escaping Code in HTML
docs.text:
When displaying HTML code, you must escape <, >, and &:

<p>Use the <code><div></code> element.</p>
<!-- Renders as: Use the <div> element. -->

Character entities:

Character Entity < < > > & & " "

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of Code Elements
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a code element (e.g., `<code>`).
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content inside (text and inline elements).
    │
    ▼
4.  If the element is `<pre>`, whitespace is preserved.
    │   └── Multiple spaces, tabs, and newlines are kept as-is.
    │
    ▼
5.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
6.  Default styles are applied:
    │   ├── <code> → font-family: monospace
    │   ├── <pre> → font-family: monospace; white-space: pre
    │   ├── <kbd> → font-family: monospace
    │   ├── <samp> → font-family: monospace
    │   └── <var> → font-style: italic
    │
    ▼
7.  CSS can override these default styles.
    │
    ▼
8.  The element is exposed in the accessibility tree.
    │   └── Screen readers may announce code differently.

docs.title: The white-space CSS Property
docs.text:
The <pre> element uses white-space: pre by default, which preserves whitespace. Other elements use white-space: normal, which collapses whitespace.

pre {
    white-space: pre;
}
code {
    white-space: normal;
}

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
• <code> – exposed as "code" or "monospace text".
  • <pre> – exposed as "preformatted text".
  • <kbd> – exposed as "keyboard input".
  • <samp> – exposed as "sample output".
  • <var> – exposed as "variable".

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
code {
    font-family: monospace;
}
pre {
    font-family: monospace;
    white-space: pre;
    margin: 1em 0;
}
kbd {
    font-family: monospace;
}
samp {
    font-family: monospace;
}
var {
    font-style: italic;
}

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
All code elements inherit from HTMLElement:

  • <code> → HTMLElement
  • <pre> → HTMLPreElement
  • <kbd> → HTMLElement
  • <samp> → HTMLElement
  • <var> → HTMLElement

docs.title: The HTMLPreElement Interface
docs.text: <pre> has its own interface (HTMLPreElement), which historically had a width attribute (deprecated). It has no special methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

docs.title: Whitespace Handling
docs.text:
The parser treats whitespace inside <pre> differently:

  • Spaces, tabs, and newlines are preserved.
  • This is controlled by the white-space: pre CSS property.

docs.title: Syntax Highlighting
docs.text:
Syntax highlighters parse the text content of <code> elements and wrap tokens in <span> elements with classes:

<pre><code class="language-js">
<span class="token keyword">function</span> 
<span class="token function">greet</span>
<span class="token punctuation">(</span>
<span class="token parameter">name</span>
...
</code></pre>

This is done by JavaScript libraries, not the browser.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Code Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the code element in the HTML.
    │   └── Example: <code>console.log()</code>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The code element node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  If `<pre>`, whitespace is preserved.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied (monospace font).
    │
    ▼
6.  CSS may override the default styles.
    │
    ▼
7.  Syntax highlighting may be applied by JavaScript.
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered with the styled code.
    │
    ▼
9.  Screen readers expose the semantic meaning.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Example 1: Inline Code in a Paragraph
docs.text:
<p>
    To create a new variable in JavaScript, use the 
    <code>let</code> or <code>const</code> keyword.
    For example: <code>let x = 10;</code>
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <code> marks each code fragment. - Browsers render it in a monospace font.

docs.title: Example 2: Multi-line Code Block
docs.text:
<pre><code>
function fibonacci(n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);
}
</code></pre>

Code Breakdown: - <pre> preserves whitespace and line breaks. - <code> marks the content as code. - The combination is the standard for code blocks.

docs.title: Example 3: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
<p>
    To save the file, press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd>.
    To undo, press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Z</kbd>.
    To quit, press <kbd>Esc</kbd>.
</p>

Code Breakdown: - Each <kbd> represents a single key. - The + sign is plain text between the <kbd> elements.

docs.title: Example 4: Program Output
docs.text:
<p>
    Running <code>npm install</code>...
    Output: <samp>added 150 packages in 12.5s</samp>
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <code> for the command. - <samp> for the output.

docs.title: Example 5: Variables in Mathematics
docs.text:
<p>
    The area of a circle is <var>π</var> × <var>r</var><sup>2</sup>,
    where <var>r</var> is the radius.
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <var> for variables. - <sup> for the exponent.

docs.title: Example 6: A Tutorial with Mixed Code Elements
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>Getting Started with Git</h1>

    <p>
        First, install Git. Then open your terminal and run
        <code>git init</code> to initialise a repository.
    </p>

    <p>
        To stage all files, run <code>git add .</code>.
        To commit, run <code>git commit -m "Initial commit"</code>.
    </p>

    <p>
        Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>C</kbd> to cancel any running command.
    </p>

    <p>
        The output should look like:
    </p>

    <pre><samp>
Initialized empty Git repository in /path/to/.git/
[main (root-commit) abc1234] Initial commit
 3 files changed, 100 insertions(+)
    </samp></pre>
</article>

docs.title: Example 7: Styling Code Elements with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    code {
        font-family: 'Fira Code', 'Courier New', monospace;
        background-color: #f4f4f4;
        padding: 2px 6px;
        border-radius: 4px;
        font-size: 0.9em;
        color: #c7254e;
    }

    pre {
        background-color: #2d2d2d;
        color: #f8f8f2;
        padding: 1rem;
        border-radius: 8px;
        overflow-x: auto;
        font-family: 'Fira Code', 'Courier New', monospace;
        font-size: 0.9rem;
        line-height: 1.5;
    }

    pre code {
        background: none;
        padding: 0;
        color: inherit;
        font-size: inherit;
    }

    kbd {
        background-color: #eee;
        border: 1px solid #ccc;
        border-radius: 4px;
        padding: 2px 6px;
        font-family: monospace;
        font-size: 0.9em;
        box-shadow: 0 1px 0 #bbb;
    }

    var {
        font-style: italic;
        color: #6f42c1;
    }

    samp {
        background-color: #f8f9fa;
        padding: 2px 6px;
        border-radius: 4px;
        font-family: monospace;
        color: #e83e8c;
    }
</style>

docs.title: Example 8: Escaping HTML in Code
docs.text:
<p>
    The <code><h1></code> element defines a top-level heading.
    The <code><p></code> element defines a paragraph.
</p>

Code Breakdown: - < renders as <. - > renders as >. - Without escaping, the browser would interpret <h1> and <p> as HTML tags.

docs.title: Example 9: Syntax Highlighting with Prism.js
docs.text:
<pre><code class="language-python">
def hello(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

hello("World")
</code></pre>

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/prismjs@1.29.0/prism.min.js"></script>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/prismjs@1.29.0/themes/prism.min.css">

Code Breakdown: - class="language-python" tells Prism.js which language to highlight. - Prism.js processes the code and adds <span> elements with token classes.

docs.title: Example 10: Using <pre> for ASCII Art
docs.text:
<pre>
    /\_/\
   ( o.o )
    > ^ <
</pre>

Code Breakdown: - <pre> preserves the exact spacing of the ASCII art. - Without <pre>, the art would collapse into a single line.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Element Use Case <code> Function names, variable names, file paths, HTML tags, CSS properties, command names <pre> Multi-line code blocks, ASCII art, poetry, preformatted tables <kbd> Keyboard shortcuts, command-line input, key names <samp> Terminal output, error messages, program results <var> Mathematical variables, programming variables

docs.title: Combined Use Cases
docs.text:
• Documentation – API references, tutorials, guides.
  • Blog posts – technical articles with code examples.
  • Educational content – programming courses, tutorials.
  • Forum posts – sharing code snippets.
  • Stack Overflow – Q&A with code.
  • GitHub READMEs – project documentation.
  • Technical specifications – RFCs, W3C specs.

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <code> for inline code – not for multi-line blocks.

  2. Use <pre><code> for code blocks – the standard combination.

  3. Escape HTML entities in code – use <, >, &.

  4. Use <kbd> for keyboard input – not for code or output.

  5. Use <samp> for program output – not for input.

  6. Use <var> for variables – not for code.

  7. Don't use <tt> – it's deprecated; use <code> instead.

  8. Keep code lines short – for readability, especially on mobile.

  9. Add class="language-*" for syntax highlighting – for libraries like Prism.js.

  10. Use CSS for styling – don't rely on default browser styles.

  11. Ensure sufficient contrast – code should be readable.

  12. Use white-space: pre-wrap for long lines – to wrap code on smaller screens.

  13. Consider tab-size for tabs – set tab-size: 4 for consistent indentation.

  14. Test with screen readers – ensure code is announced appropriately.

  15. Don't nest <pre> inside <p> – <pre> is block-level; <p> only accepts phrasing content.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <code> for Multi-line Code Without <pre>
docs.text:
<code>
function hello() {
    console.log("Hello");
}
</code>
Why it's wrong: Without <pre>, whitespace is collapsed, and the code loses its formatting.

✅ Correct: 

<pre><code>
function hello() {
    console.log("Hello");
}
</code></pre>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <pre> Without <code> for Code Blocks
docs.text:
<pre>
function hello() {
    console.log("Hello");
}
</pre>
Why it's wrong: <pre> preserves whitespace but doesn't semantically mark the content as code.

✅ Correct: 

<pre><code>...</code></pre>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Escaping HTML in Code
docs.text:
<p>The <code><div></code> element is a container.</p>
Why it's wrong: The <div> will be parsed as an HTML element, not displayed as text.

✅ Correct: 

<p>The <code><div></code> element is a container.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <kbd> for Code
docs.text:
<p>Run <kbd>npm install</kbd> to install dependencies.</p>
Why it's wrong: <kbd> is for keyboard input, not commands. Use <code>.

✅ Correct: 

<p>Run <code>npm install</code> to install dependencies.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <var> for Code
docs.text:
<p>The <var>console.log()</var> function logs to the console.</p>
Why it's wrong: <var> is for variables, not function names. Use <code>.

✅ Correct: 

<p>The <code>console.log()</code> function logs to the console.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <pre> Inside <p>
docs.text:
<p>Here is code: <pre><code>...</code></pre></p>
Why it's wrong: <pre> is block-level and cannot be inside <p>.

✅ Correct: 

<p>Here is code:</p>
<pre><code>...</code></pre>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <tt>
docs.text:
<p>Use the <tt>console.log()</tt> function.</p>
Why it's wrong: <tt> is deprecated and has no semantic meaning.

✅ Correct: 

<p>Use the <code>console.log()</code> function.</p>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Code elements are lightweight – each adds a small DOM node.
  • <pre> with large content – very large code blocks can increase rendering time.
  • Syntax highlighting – adds DOM nodes (spans) and JavaScript processing; may impact performance.
  • CSS styling – complex styles (shadows, gradients) on code blocks can affect performance.
  • Copy-paste – preserving whitespace in <pre> ensures accurate copy-paste.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated code, always escape HTML entities. Use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – if you must use it, sanitize the input.
  • Syntax highlighting libraries – ensure they are from trusted sources.
  • class="language-*" – validate the language class to prevent injection.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect code elements to see their structure.
  • Computed styles – check the applied font-family, white-space, and background-color.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('pre code') to list all code blocks.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting (pre inside p).
  • Test copy-paste – ensure code copies correctly.
  • Test with screen readers – ensure code is announced appropriately.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Element When to Use <code> Inline code fragments (function names, variable names, tags, properties). <pre> Multi-line code blocks, ASCII art, preformatted text. <kbd> Keyboard shortcuts, command-line input. <samp> Program output, error messages, terminal output. <var> Variables in math or programming.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• <code> – for multi-line blocks without <pre>.
  • <pre> – for non-code preformatted text without <code> (though it's valid, <code> adds semantic meaning).
  • <kbd> – for code or commands; use <code>.
  • <samp> – for user input; use <kbd>.
  • <var> – for code; use <code>.
  • <tt> – deprecated; use <code>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Phrasing Content
  • Flow Content
  • CSS font-family: monospace
  • CSS white-space
  • Syntax Highlighting (Prism.js, Highlight.js)
  • Character Entities (<, >, &)
  • Accessibility (screen reader announcements)
  • Technical Documentation

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <tt> element (teletype text) was the original way to display monospace text. It is now deprecated in favor of <code>.

  • The <pre> element preserves whitespace by applying white-space: pre in CSS.

  • The <code> element is often combined with <pre> for code blocks, but <code> can also be used inline.

  • The <kbd> element can be nested to represent complex key combinations: <kbd><kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>C</kbd></kbd>.

  • The <samp> element is for sample output, but it can also be used for system messages.

  • The <var> element is for variables, but it's also used for placeholders in code examples.

  • Syntax highlighting libraries like Prism.js and Highlight.js parse <code> elements and add <span> elements with token classes.

  • The tab-size CSS property controls the width of tab characters in <pre> blocks.

  • The white-space: pre-wrap value preserves whitespace but allows wrapping, which is useful for long code lines on mobile.

  • The <pre> element can be used for ASCII art, poetry, and any text where exact spacing matters.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Code elements in HTML provide semantic markup for technical content.
  • <code> – inline code fragments.
  • <pre> – preformatted text (preserves whitespace).
  • <kbd> – keyboard input.
  • <samp> – sample output.
  • <var> – variables.
  • Best practices: use <pre><code> for code blocks, escape HTML entities, use <kbd> for keys, <samp> for output, and <var> for variables. Style with CSS and consider syntax highlighting.
  • Common mistakes include using <code> without <pre> for multi-line code, not escaping HTML, using <kbd> for commands, and nesting <pre> inside <p>.
  • Code elements are essential for technical documentation, tutorials, and developer-focused content.
  • They provide semantic meaning, accessibility, and styling hooks for code and technical text.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Preformatted text in HTML is text that is displayed exactly as it is written in the source code, with all whitespace and line breaks preserved. This is achieved using the <pre> element (short for "preformatted"). Unlike normal HTML content, where sequences of spaces, tabs, and newlines are collapsed into a single space, the <pre> element maintains the exact spacing and line breaks, making it ideal for displaying code blocks, ASCII art, poetry, and any content where precise formatting is essential.

The <pre> element is a block-level element and flow content. It uses a monospace font by default, which ensures that each character occupies the same amount of horizontal space, preserving alignment. It is commonly combined with the <code> element to semantically mark up code blocks.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Preformatted text serves several essential purposes:

  • Preserve whitespace – maintain exact indentation, spacing, and line breaks.
  • Display code blocks – code relies on indentation and line breaks for readability.
  • Display ASCII art – art made from text characters requires precise positioning.
  • Display poetry – line breaks and spacing are meaningful in poems.
  • Display preformatted data – tables, logs, and structured text that need exact alignment.
  • Enable copy-paste accuracy – preserving formatting ensures content can be copied correctly.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <pre> element is a block-level element that can appear anywhere flow content is accepted. It is commonly used inside <body>, <div>, <section>, <article>, <figure>, and other flow containers. It is often combined with <code> for code blocks, and with <samp> for program output.

<article>
    <h2>Code Example</h2>
    <pre><code>
function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
    </code></pre>
</article>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTML is designed to be a flowing text format, not a fixed-layout format. By default, it collapses whitespace – multiple spaces become one, and line breaks are ignored. This is desirable for prose, where the exact spacing doesn't matter, but it's disastrous for content where whitespace is meaningful:

  • Code – indentation indicates nesting and structure. Without preserving whitespace, code becomes unreadable.
  • ASCII art – characters are positioned precisely to form images. Collapsing spaces destroys the art.
  • Poetry – line breaks and spacing are part of the poem's form and meaning.
  • Tabular data – alignment of columns is often achieved with spaces.
  • Log files – timestamps and levels are often aligned with spaces.

Before <pre>, authors had no reliable way to preserve this formatting. They resorted to hacks like using <br> for every line and   for every space, which was tedious, error-prone, and bloated the HTML.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Whitespace collapsing Code and ASCII art lost their formatting. No line break preservation Line breaks in code were ignored. Manual <br> and   Tedious, error-prone, and bloated markup. No monospace default Alignment was inconsistent. Poor copy-paste Copied text lost its original formatting.

docs.title: Why <pre> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <pre> element was introduced in HTML 1.0 (1991) to provide a standardised way to preserve whitespace and line breaks. It was designed for:

  • Computer code – the primary use case.
  • Preformatted text – any text where exact spacing matters.
  • Email and forum posts – where users wanted to preserve formatting.

The <pre> element uses a monospace font by default, ensuring that alignment is maintained. When combined with <code>, it provides semantic meaning alongside formatting.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <pre>
docs.text:
<pre>
This is preformatted text.
    Indentation is preserved.
        Further indentation is preserved.

Line breaks are also preserved.
</pre>

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
This is preformatted text.
    Indentation is preserved.
        Further indentation is preserved.

Line breaks are also preserved.

docs.title: Combining <pre> with <code>
docs.text:
The most common use case is wrapping code blocks:

<pre><code>
function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
</code></pre>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <pre> Preserves whitespace and line breaks. Essential for code, ASCII art, and poetry. <code> Marks the content as code. Adds semantic meaning; enables syntax highlighting. Text content The actual preformatted text. Displayed exactly as written.

docs.title: Escaping HTML in <pre>
docs.text:
When displaying HTML code, you must escape <, >, and &:

<pre><code>
<div class="container">
    <p>Hello</p>
</div>
</code></pre>

Rendering: 

<div class="container">
    <p>Hello</p>
</div>

docs.title: Whitespace Handling in <pre>
docs.text:
• Spaces – preserved exactly.
  • Tabs – preserved (rendered as 8 spaces by default, can be changed with tab-size).
  • Newlines – preserved as line breaks.
  • Leading/trailing whitespace – preserved, but the first newline after <pre> is ignored by the parser.
<pre>
    This line starts with 4 spaces.
</pre>

Note: The newline immediately after the opening <pre> tag is ignored. This allows you to write:

<pre>
Content
</pre>

Without the first line being empty.

docs.title: The tab-size CSS Property
docs.text:
You can control how tabs are rendered:

pre {
    tab-size: 4; /* Renders tabs as 4 spaces */
}

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Feature Behavior Spaces Preserved exactly as written. Tabs Preserved; width controlled by tab-size. Newlines Preserved as line breaks. First newline Ignored by the parser. Default font Monospace. Default white-space pre.

docs.title: The "Typewriter" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <pre> as a typewriter – what you type is exactly what you get. There's no automatic formatting, no collapsing of spaces, no reflowing of text. The text appears on the page exactly as it was typed, with the same spacing and line breaks.

docs.title: The "Photocopy" Analogy
docs.text: If normal HTML is like retyping a document (where spacing might change), <pre> is like photocopying it – the exact layout, spacing, and line breaks are preserved. You see the document exactly as it was.

docs.title: The "Graph Paper" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <pre> as graph paper where each character occupies one square. Because the font is monospace, every character takes up the same width, so you can align text precisely by counting spaces. This is why <pre> is perfect for tables, ASCII art, and code.

docs.title: Concept 1: Whitespace Preservation
docs.text:
The defining feature of <pre> is that it preserves whitespace. This is controlled by the CSS property white-space: pre, which is applied by default.

pre {
    white-space: pre;
}

The white-space property has several values:

Value Behavior normal Collapses whitespace, wraps text. pre Preserves whitespace, no wrapping. pre-wrap Preserves whitespace, allows wrapping. pre-line Collapses spaces but preserves line breaks. nowrap Collapses whitespace, no wrapping.

docs.title: Concept 2: Monospace Font
docs.text:
<pre> uses a monospace font by default. In a monospace font, every character occupies the same width, which is essential for alignment.

pre {
    font-family: monospace;
}

Common monospace fonts: Courier New, Consolas, Monaco, Fira Code, JetBrains Mono.

docs.title: Concept 3: Content Model
docs.text:
<pre> has a phrasing content model – it can contain text and inline elements, but not block-level elements. However, because it preserves whitespace, it can visually mimic block-level structures.

<!-- Valid -->
<pre>Text with <strong>bold</strong> and <em>italic</em>.</pre>

<!-- Invalid: block element inside pre -->
<pre>
    <div>Block inside pre</div>
</pre>

What the browser does with invalid content: The <pre> is closed before the block element, similar to <p>.

docs.title: Concept 4: <pre> and <code> Together
docs.text:
The combination <pre><code> is the standard for code blocks:

  • <pre> – preserves whitespace and line breaks.
  • <code> – marks the content as code (semantic meaning).
<pre><code>
const greeting = "Hello, World!";
console.log(greeting);
</code></pre>

docs.title: Concept 5: The First Newline
docs.text:
The HTML parser ignores the first newline immediately after the opening <pre> tag. This is a convenience feature that allows you to write:

<pre>
Content
</pre>

Without the first line being empty. The rendering starts with "Content".

docs.title: Concept 6: Tabs and tab-size
docs.text:
Tabs are preserved in <pre>, but their width is determined by the tab-size CSS property. The default is 8 spaces in most browsers.

pre {
    tab-size: 4;
}

docs.title: Concept 7: Escaping HTML Entities
docs.text:
Because <pre> can contain text that looks like HTML, you must escape <, >, and &:

<pre><code>
<h1>Heading</h1>
</code></pre>

docs.title: Concept 8: Overflow and Wrapping
docs.text:
By default, <pre> does not wrap long lines; it overflows horizontally. To enable wrapping:

pre {
    white-space: pre-wrap; /* Preserves whitespace but wraps */
    word-wrap: break-word; /* Breaks long words */
}

Or use overflow-x: auto to add a horizontal scrollbar:

pre {
    overflow-x: auto;
}

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <pre>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<pre>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the `<pre>` element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content inside:
    │   ├── The first newline immediately after `<pre>` is ignored.
    │   ├── All subsequent whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) is preserved.
    │   ├── Text nodes are created with the exact whitespace.
    │   └── Inline elements are processed normally.
    │
    ▼
4.  When the `</pre>` tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   ├── font-family: monospace
    │   ├── white-space: pre
    │   └── display: block
    │
    ▼
6.  CSS can override these default styles.
    │
    ▼
7.  The element is rendered with the exact formatting.
    │
    ▼
8.  The element is exposed in the accessibility tree as preformatted text.

docs.title: The Parser's Handling of Whitespace
docs.text:
The HTML parser has special rules for <pre>:

  • Whitespace inside <pre> is treated as significant.
  • The parser does not collapse spaces, tabs, or newlines.
  • The first newline after <pre> is ignored.

docs.title: The white-space CSS Property
docs.text:
The white-space: pre value tells the browser to:

  • Preserve sequences of whitespace.
  • Preserve line breaks.
  • Not wrap text.

This is what makes <pre> work.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
pre {
    display: block;
    font-family: monospace;
    white-space: pre;
    margin: 1em 0;
}

docs.title: The HTMLPreElement Interface
docs.text: In the DOM, <pre> is represented by the HTMLPreElement interface, which inherits from HTMLElement. It historically had a width attribute (deprecated) but now has no special properties beyond those of HTMLElement.

docs.title: Whitespace in the DOM
docs.text:
When the parser encounters <pre>, it creates text nodes that include the exact whitespace characters. These are stored in the DOM as-is.

const pre = document.querySelector('pre');
console.log(pre.textContent); // Includes spaces, tabs, and newlines

docs.title: The white-space Property in CSSOM
docs.text:
The white-space property is part of the CSSOM. You can read and modify it:

const pre = document.querySelector('pre');
console.log(getComputedStyle(pre).whiteSpace); // "pre"
pre.style.whiteSpace = 'pre-wrap'; // Allow wrapping

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text: In the accessibility tree, <pre> is exposed as "preformatted text" or "text block". Screen readers typically read the text as-is, respecting the line breaks.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <pre> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<pre>` element with content.
    │
    ▼
2.  The file is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the HTML and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<pre>` node is created.
    │   └── Whitespace is preserved in text nodes.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (monospace, white-space: pre).
    │
    ▼
5.  CSS may override the default styles.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered with the exact formatting.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers expose the preformatted text.
    │
    ▼
8.  JavaScript may modify the content dynamically.
    │   └── Changing text, adding/removing elements.
    │
    ▼
9.  When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const pre = document.querySelector('pre');
pre.textContent = 'New preformatted\ntext with line breaks.';
// The text will be rendered with the line break preserved.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Preformatted Text
docs.text:
<pre>
    This text is preformatted.
        Indentation is preserved.
    Line breaks are preserved.

    This is the end.
</pre>

Rendering: 

    This text is preformatted.
        Indentation is preserved.
    Line breaks are preserved.

    This is the end.

docs.title: Example 2: Code Block
docs.text:
<pre><code>
function fibonacci(n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);
}

console.log(fibonacci(10)); // 55
</code></pre>

Code Breakdown: - <pre> – preserves whitespace and line breaks. - <code> – marks the content as code. - The indentation and line breaks are essential for readability.

docs.title: Example 3: ASCII Art
docs.text:
<pre>
    /\_/\
   ( o.o )
    > ^ <
   /     \
  (       )
   \_____/
</pre>

Rendering: 

    /\_/\
   ( o.o )
    > ^ <
   /     \
  (       )
   \_____/

Why <pre> is essential: Without <pre>, the spacing would collapse, and the art would be destroyed.

docs.title: Example 4: Poetry
docs.text:
<pre>
    Roses are red,
    Violets are blue,
    Sugar is sweet,
    And so are you.
</pre>

Why <pre> is useful: Poetry relies on line breaks and indentation, which <pre> preserves.

docs.title: Example 5: Tabular Data with Alignment
docs.text:
<pre>
Name       Age    City
---------- -----  ------------
Alice      30     New York
Bob        25     Los Angeles
Charlie    35     Chicago
</pre>

Rendering: 

Name       Age    City
---------- -----  ------------
Alice      30     New York
Bob        25     Los Angeles
Charlie    35     Chicago

Why <pre> is useful: Columns are aligned with spaces, which <pre> preserves.

docs.title: Example 6: Escaping HTML in Code Blocks
docs.text:
<pre><code>
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello, World!</h1>
</body>
</html>
</code></pre>

Rendering: 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello, World!</h1>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Example 7: Styling <pre> with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    pre {
        background-color: #2d2d2d;
        color: #f8f8f2;
        padding: 1rem;
        border-radius: 8px;
        overflow-x: auto;
        font-family: 'Fira Code', 'Courier New', monospace;
        font-size: 0.9rem;
        line-height: 1.5;
        tab-size: 4;
    }
    pre code {
        background: none;
        padding: 0;
        color: inherit;
        font-size: inherit;
    }
</style>

<pre><code>
const greeting = "Hello, World!";
console.log(greeting);
</code></pre>

docs.title: Example 8: Wrapping Long Lines
docs.text:
<style>
    pre {
        white-space: pre-wrap;
        word-wrap: break-word;
        background-color: #f4f4f4;
        padding: 1rem;
        border-radius: 4px;
    }
</style>

<pre>
This is a very long line of preformatted text that would normally overflow the container, but with white-space: pre-wrap, it will wrap to the next line instead of causing a horizontal scrollbar.
</pre>

docs.title: Example 9: <pre> with Inline Elements
docs.text:
<pre>
This is <strong>bold</strong> and this is <em>italic</em>.
    Indentation is still preserved.
</pre>

Code Breakdown: - Inline elements work inside <pre>. - The whitespace around them is preserved.

docs.title: Example 10: <pre> for Log Output
docs.text:
<pre>
[2026-09-08 10:00:00] INFO  Server starting...
[2026-09-08 10:00:01] INFO  Listening on port 3000
[2026-09-08 10:00:02] WARN  Deprecated API used
[2026-09-08 10:00:03] ERROR Failed to connect to database
</pre>

Why <pre> is useful: Logs often have aligned columns and precise formatting.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Why <pre> Code blocks Preserves indentation and line breaks. ASCII art Requires precise character positioning. Poetry Line breaks and spacing are meaningful. Tabular data Aligns columns with spaces. Log output Aligns timestamps and levels. Configuration files Preserves formatting of config snippets. Mathematical proofs Preserves alignment of equations. Email templates Preserves formatting of plain-text emails.

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <pre><code> for code blocks – the standard combination.

  2. Escape HTML entities – use <, >, & for <, >, &.

  3. Set tab-size – for consistent tab rendering.

  4. Use overflow-x: auto – to handle long lines without breaking layout.

  5. Consider white-space: pre-wrap – for responsive design, to wrap long lines.

  6. Don't use <pre> for layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

  7. Keep lines short – for readability on smaller screens.

  8. Use syntax highlighting – for code blocks, with libraries like Prism.js or Highlight.js.

  9. Provide a caption – use <figure> and <figcaption> for context.

  10. Test copy-paste – ensure the copied text matches the displayed text.

  11. Don't nest <pre> inside <p> – <pre> is block-level; <p> only accepts phrasing content.

  12. Use <pre> semantically – only for content where whitespace is meaningful.

  13. Add aria-label if needed – for accessibility context.

  14. Avoid trailing whitespace – it's preserved but can cause layout issues.

  15. Use line-height for readability – code is easier to read with generous line spacing.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <pre> for Non-Preformatted Text
docs.text:
<pre>This is just a normal paragraph of text that doesn't need preformatting.</pre>
Why it's wrong: <pre> should only be used when whitespace is meaningful. For normal prose, use <p>.

✅ Correct: 

<p>This is just a normal paragraph of text.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Escaping HTML in Code Blocks
docs.text:
<pre><code>
<div>Hello</div>
</code></pre>
Why it's wrong: The <div> will be parsed as HTML, not displayed as text.

✅ Correct: 

<pre><code>
<div>Hello</div>
</code></pre>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <pre> Inside <p>
docs.text:
<p>Here is code: <pre><code>...</code></pre></p>
Why it's wrong: <pre> is block-level and cannot be inside <p> (which only accepts phrasing content).

✅ Correct: 

<p>Here is code:</p>
<pre><code>...</code></pre>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <pre> Without <code> for Code
docs.text:
<pre>
function hello() {
    console.log("Hello");
}
</pre>
Why it's wrong: <pre> preserves whitespace but doesn't convey that the content is code. Use <code> for semantic meaning.

✅ Correct: 

<pre><code>
function hello() {
    console.log("Hello");
}
</code></pre>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting overflow-x for Long Lines
docs.text:
<pre>
This is a very long line that will overflow the container and cause a horizontal scrollbar on the whole page.
</pre>
Why it's wrong: Without overflow-x: auto, long lines can break the layout.

✅ Correct: 

pre { overflow-x: auto; }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <pre> for Layout
docs.text:
<pre>
Header
    Content
Footer
</pre>
Why it's wrong: <pre> is not for layout. Use HTML structure and CSS.

✅ Correct: 

<header>Header</header>
<main>Content</main>
<footer>Footer</footer>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Mobile Responsiveness
docs.text:
<pre>
A very long code line that doesn't wrap and forces horizontal scrolling on mobile devices.
</pre>
Why it's wrong: Long lines on mobile cause horizontal scrolling, which is bad UX.

✅ Correct: 

pre { white-space: pre-wrap; word-wrap: break-word; }

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <pre> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • Large content – very large <pre> blocks can increase rendering time, especially with syntax highlighting.
  • white-space: pre – disables text wrapping, which can cause horizontal overflow; this is intentional.
  • Syntax highlighting – adds many <span> elements, which can impact performance on large code blocks.
  • tab-size – no significant performance impact.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <pre>, always escape HTML entities. Use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – if you must use it, sanitize the input.
  • Syntax highlighting libraries – ensure they are from trusted sources.
  • class="language-*" – validate the language class to prevent injection.
  • Copy-paste – be aware that users can copy code that may be malicious; add warnings if necessary.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <pre> to see its content and styles.
  • Computed styles – check white-space, font-family, and tab-size.
  • Console – use document.querySelector('pre').textContent to see the exact content.
  • Test copy-paste – ensure the copied text matches the displayed text.
  • Test with long lines – ensure overflow-x is working.
  • Test on mobile – ensure responsiveness with pre-wrap if needed.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Code blocks – the primary use case.
  • ASCII art – where exact character positioning matters.
  • Poetry – where line breaks and spacing are meaningful.
  • Tabular data with alignment – when using spaces for alignment.
  • Log output – for aligned timestamps and levels.
  • Configuration files – for preserving formatting.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Normal prose – use <p>.
  • Layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • Headings – use <h1>–<h6>.
  • Lists – use <ul>, <ol>, <dl>.
  • Content that should wrap – use <p> with white-space: pre-wrap if needed, or just use <pre> with pre-wrap.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <code> – for inline code fragments.
  • <kbd> – for keyboard input.
  • <samp> – for sample output.
  • <var> – for variables.
  • CSS white-space – controls whitespace handling.
  • CSS tab-size – controls tab width.
  • CSS overflow-x – handles horizontal overflow.
  • Syntax Highlighting (Prism.js, Highlight.js)
  • Character Entities (<, >, &)
  • <figure> and <figcaption> – for captions.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <pre> element was present in HTML 1.0 (1991) and is one of the oldest elements in HTML.

  • The first newline immediately after <pre> is ignored by the parser – a convenience feature for cleaner markup.

  • The default tab-size is 8 in most browsers, but you can change it with CSS.

  • <pre> uses white-space: pre by default, which preserves whitespace and prevents wrapping.

  • The white-space: pre-wrap value preserves whitespace but allows wrapping – useful for responsive design.

  • Syntax highlighting libraries like Prism.js and Highlight.js parse <pre><code> blocks and add <span> elements with token classes.

  • ASCII art is often created using <pre> because it relies on precise character positioning.

  • The <pre> element can contain inline elements like <strong>, <em>, and <a>, but not block-level elements.

  • The overflow-x: auto CSS property is commonly used with <pre> to handle long lines.

  • Some developers use <pre> for layout hacks, but this is discouraged in favor of CSS.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Preformatted text is text displayed exactly as written, with all whitespace and line breaks preserved.
  • The <pre> element is used for preformatted text.
  • It is a block-level element with a monospace font and white-space: pre by default.
  • It is commonly combined with <code> for code blocks.
  • Best practices: use <pre><code> for code, escape HTML entities, set tab-size, use overflow-x: auto, and consider white-space: pre-wrap for responsiveness.
  • Common mistakes include using <pre> for normal prose, not escaping HTML, nesting <pre> inside <p>, and ignoring mobile responsiveness.
  • <pre> is essential for code blocks, ASCII art, poetry, log output, and any content where exact formatting matters.
  • The <pre> element preserves the exact layout of text, making it a critical tool for technical content.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <abbr> element is an inline HTML element used to mark up an abbreviation or acronym within text. It provides a way to associate the abbreviated form (e.g., "HTML") with its full expansion (e.g., "HyperText Markup Language") through the title attribute. When a user hovers over the abbreviation, the browser displays the full expansion as a tooltip. Screen readers may also announce the expansion.

The <abbr> element is a phrasing content element, meaning it can be used within paragraphs, headings, list items, table cells, and other inline contexts. It is a semantic element – it tells browsers, assistive technologies, and search engines that the enclosed text is an abbreviation and provides the means to decode it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <abbr> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Clarity – provides the full expansion of an abbreviation on demand (hover or focus).
  • Accessibility – screen readers can announce the expansion, helping users who are unfamiliar with the abbreviation.
  • Semantics – marks up abbreviations as distinct from regular text, providing machine-readable meaning.
  • SEO – search engines can understand the relationship between the abbreviation and its expansion.
  • Styling – provides a hook for CSS to style abbreviations (e.g., dotted underline).
  • Consistency – encourages authors to define abbreviations once and reference them consistently.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <abbr> element is an inline element that can appear anywhere phrasing content is accepted – inside <p>, <h1>–<h6>, <li>, <td>, <figcaption>, <blockquote>, and other phrasing contexts. It is part of the text-level semantics group of elements, alongside <strong>, <em>, <code>, <time>, and others.

<p>
    <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is the standard
    markup language for creating web pages.
</p>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Abbreviations and acronyms are everywhere in technical, scientific, and professional writing. Terms like "HTML", "CSS", "API", "NASA", "WHO", "FAQ", "CPU", and "GDP" are used constantly. However, not all readers know what these abbreviations stand for. In printed documents, authors often define an abbreviation on first use and then use the short form afterward. On the web, before <abbr>, there was no standard way to provide the expansion on demand.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic markup for abbreviations Machines couldn't identify abbreviations. The <acronym> element Was non-standard, inconsistent, and eventually deprecated. No tooltip mechanism Users had to guess or look up abbreviations. No accessibility support Screen readers couldn't announce expansions. Inconsistent styling Abbreviations looked like regular text.

docs.title: Why <abbr> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <abbr> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) to provide a standardised, semantic way to mark up abbreviations and acronyms. It replaced the problematic <acronym> element, which was often misused and inconsistently supported. The <abbr> element:

  • Works for both abbreviations (e.g., "etc.") and acronyms (e.g., "HTML").
  • Uses the title attribute to provide the full expansion.
  • Is supported by all modern browsers.
  • Is accessible to screen readers.
  • Provides a styling hook for CSS.

The <acronym> element was deprecated in HTML5 and should not be used. The <abbr> element is the correct choice for all abbreviations and acronyms.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <abbr>
docs.text:
<abbr title="Full Expansion">Abbreviation</abbr>
  • <abbr> – the element that marks the abbreviation.
  • title – the full expansion of the abbreviation (required for the tooltip).
  • Content – the abbreviation itself.

docs.title: Simple Examples
docs.text:
<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is the foundation of the web.</p>

<p><abbr title="Cascading Style Sheets">CSS</abbr> is used for styling web pages.</p>

<p><abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr> was founded in 1948.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="National Aeronautics and Space Administration">NASA</abbr> was established in 1958.</p>

docs.title: Abbreviation Without title (Not Recommended)
docs.text:
<p><abbr>HTML</abbr> is the foundation of the web.</p>

Why it's not recommended: Without title, the abbreviation has no expansion, and screen readers cannot announce it. The <abbr> element is pointless without the title attribute (though it's technically valid).

docs.title: Abbreviations in Different Languages
docs.text:
The lang attribute can be used on <abbr> to specify the language of the abbreviation or its expansion:

<p>
    The French equivalent of <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is
    <abbr lang="fr" title="Langage de balisage hypertexte">HTML</abbr>.
</p>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <abbr> Marks the abbreviation. Provides semantic meaning. title Provides the full expansion. Displayed as a tooltip on hover. Content The abbreviation itself. The visible text. lang (optional) Specifies the language of the expansion. For multilingual content.

docs.title: Default Browser Behavior
docs.text:
• Tooltip: Most browsers display the title as a tooltip on hover.
  • Styling: Browsers apply a dotted underline to <abbr> elements that have a title attribute.
  • Screen readers: Some screen readers announce the expansion when the abbreviation is encountered.

docs.title: The "Footnote" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <abbr> as a footnote attached directly to the text. When you see the abbreviation, you can "hover" over it to see the full expansion, just as you would look down at a footnote to see the full term. The title attribute is like the footnote text – it's there when you need it but doesn't clutter the main text.

docs.title: The "Dictionary" Analogy
docs.text: The <abbr> element is like a mini dictionary embedded in your text. Each abbreviation is a word with a definition (the title). Readers can look up the definition by hovering, without leaving the page.

docs.title: The "Sticky Note" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine sticking a sticky note on an abbreviation with the full expansion written on it. The note is hidden until someone looks closely (hovers). This is exactly what the title attribute does – it's a hidden note that appears on hover.

docs.title: Concept 1: Abbreviation vs. Acronym
docs.text:
In common usage, both "abbreviation" and "acronym" refer to shortened forms of words:

  • Abbreviation – a shortened form of a word or phrase (e.g., "etc." for "et cetera", "Dr." for "Doctor").
  • Acronym – an abbreviation formed from the initial letters of other words and pronounced as a word (e.g., "NASA", "HTML").

In HTML5, the <abbr> element is used for both. The <acronym> element, which was intended for acronyms, is deprecated.

docs.title: Concept 2: The title Attribute
docs.text:
The title attribute is required for the <abbr> element to be meaningful. It provides the full expansion of the abbreviation:

<abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>

Behavior: The title is displayed as a tooltip when the user hovers over the abbreviation. Some screen readers also announce it.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Deprecated <acronym> Element
docs.text:
The <acronym> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 but was deprecated in HTML5. It was intended to mark up acronyms, but it was often misused and inconsistently supported. Use <abbr> instead.

<!-- Deprecated -->
<acronym title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</acronym>

<!-- Correct -->
<abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>

docs.title: Concept 4: No Visual Change Without title
docs.text: The <abbr> element without a title attribute has no visual effect. It's semantically valid but provides no benefit. Always include title.

docs.title: Concept 5: The lang Attribute on <abbr>
docs.text:
You can use the lang attribute on <abbr> to specify the language of the expansion:

<p>
    <abbr lang="fr" title="Langage de balisage hypertexte">HTML</abbr>
</p>

This is useful for multilingual content.

docs.title: Concept 6: CSS Styling of <abbr>
docs.text:
By default, browsers apply a dotted underline to <abbr> elements with a title attribute. You can customise this:

abbr[title] {
    border-bottom: 1px dotted #666;
    cursor: help;
    text-decoration: none;
}

The cursor: help property changes the cursor to a question mark, indicating a tooltip.

docs.title: Concept 7: Accessibility Considerations
docs.text:
• Screen readers may announce the title when the abbreviation is encountered.
  • The title attribute is not accessible on touch devices (no hover).
  • Best practice: Define the abbreviation in the text on first use, then use <abbr> for subsequent occurrences.
<p>
    <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> (HyperText Markup Language)
    is the foundation of the web. HTML is used to create web pages.
</p>

docs.title: Concept 8: SEO Implications
docs.text:
Search engines can use the title attribute to understand the relationship between the abbreviation and its expansion. This can help with:

  • Keyword relevance – the full expansion may contain keywords.
  • Context – search engines understand the content better.
  • Rich snippets – in some cases, abbreviations may be displayed with their expansions.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <abbr>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters an `<abbr>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It reads the `title` attribute and stores it on the node.
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes the content (the abbreviation text).
    │
    ▼
5.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
6.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── Dotted underline (if `title` is present).
    │
    ▼
7.  The tooltip behavior is enabled:
    │   └── On hover, the browser displays the `title` as a tooltip.
    │
    ▼
8.  The element is exposed in the accessibility tree:
    │   └── Some screen readers announce the expansion.
    │
    ▼
9.  CSS can override the default styles.

docs.title: The title Attribute and Tooltips
docs.text:
The title attribute is a global attribute that provides advisory information. When used on <abbr>, it becomes the expansion of the abbreviation. Browsers display it as a tooltip on hover.

Limitation: The tooltip is not accessible on touch devices (no hover state) and may not be announced by all screen readers.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text: In the accessibility tree, <abbr> may be exposed as a text node with a description (the title). Screen readers may announce the expansion or provide it on demand.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
abbr[title] {
    text-decoration: underline dotted;
}

This creates the dotted underline that signals to users that there's more information available.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <abbr> is represented by the HTMLElement interface (it doesn't have a specific interface). The title attribute is reflected as the title property.

const abbr = document.querySelector('abbr');
console.log(abbr.title); // "HyperText Markup Language"
console.log(abbr.textContent); // "HTML"

docs.title: The title Property
docs.text: The title property is available on all HTML elements (it's a global attribute). On <abbr>, it serves as the expansion.

docs.title: Deprecated <acronym>
docs.text: The <acronym> element is still supported in some browsers for backward compatibility but should not be used. It is represented by the HTMLElement interface.

docs.title: CSS text-decoration
docs.text:
The dotted underline is created with text-decoration: underline dotted. This can be overridden:

abbr {
    text-decoration: none;
    border-bottom: 1px dashed #999;
}

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an <abbr> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<abbr>` element with a `title` attribute.
    │   └── Example: <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<abbr>` node is created with the `title` attribute.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (dotted underline).
    │
    ▼
5.  The tooltip behavior is enabled (on hover).
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers expose the abbreviation and may announce the expansion.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines index the abbreviation and its expansion.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the `title` or content dynamically.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const abbr = document.querySelector('abbr');
abbr.title = 'New Expansion';
abbr.textContent = 'NEW';

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Abbreviation
docs.text:
<p>
    <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is the standard
    markup language for creating web pages.
</p>

Rendering: The abbreviation "HTML" is displayed with a dotted underline. Hovering over it shows the tooltip "HyperText Markup Language".

docs.title: Example 2: Multiple Abbreviations in a Paragraph
docs.text:
<p>
    <abbr title="Cascading Style Sheets">CSS</abbr> is used for styling, while
    <abbr title="JavaScript">JS</abbr> is used for behavior. Together with
    <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>, they form the
    core technologies of the web.
</p>

docs.title: Example 3: Abbreviation in a Heading
docs.text:
<h1>
    The <abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr> Guidelines
</h1>
<p>
    The <abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr> has published new guidelines.
</p>

docs.title: Example 4: Defining an Abbreviation on First Use
docs.text:
<p>
    <dfn id="html-def">
        <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>
    </dfn>
    is the standard markup language for web pages.
</p>
<p>
    As mentioned, <a href="#html-def">HTML</a> is used to structure content.
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <dfn> – marks the defining instance of the term. - <abbr> – marks the abbreviation. - The id allows linking back to the definition.

docs.title: Example 5: Abbreviation with Language
docs.text:
<p>
    In French, <abbr lang="fr" title="Organisation mondiale de la santé">OMS</abbr>
    stands for the World Health Organization.
</p>

docs.title: Example 6: Styling Abbreviations with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    abbr[title] {
        border-bottom: 1px dotted #3498db;
        cursor: help;
        text-decoration: none;
        color: #2980b9;
        font-weight: 500;
    }
    abbr[title]:hover {
        background-color: #ebf5fb;
        border-bottom-style: solid;
    }
</style>

<p>
    <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is the foundation of the web.
</p>

docs.title: Example 7: Abbreviation in a Table
docs.text:
<table>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Term</th>
            <th>Definition</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr></td>
            <td>Markup language for web pages.</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td><abbr title="Cascading Style Sheets">CSS</abbr></td>
            <td>Stylesheet language for presentation.</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: Example 8: Abbreviation with JavaScript Tooltip Enhancement
docs.text:
<p>
    <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language" id="html-abbr">HTML</abbr> is the foundation of the web.
</p>

<script>
    const abbr = document.getElementById('html-abbr');
    abbr.addEventListener('click', function() {
        alert(`The expansion of ${this.textContent} is: ${this.title}`);
    });
</script>

Note: This is a simple example. In production, use a proper tooltip library that works on touch devices.

docs.title: Example 9: Common Abbreviations in Technical Content
docs.text:
<p>
    The <abbr title="Application Programming Interface">API</abbr> returns
    <abbr title="JavaScript Object Notation">JSON</abbr> data over
    <abbr title="HyperText Transfer Protocol">HTTP</abbr>.
    The <abbr title="Uniform Resource Locator">URL</abbr> must be valid.
</p>

docs.title: Example 10: Abbreviation with lang for Bilingual Content
docs.text:
<p lang="en">
    The <abbr lang="fr" title="Organisation des Nations unies">ONU</abbr>
    is the French abbreviation for the United Nations.
</p>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Technical documentation API, HTTP, JSON, HTML, CSS Scientific writing DNA, RNA, NASA, WHO Business and finance GDP, CEO, IPO, ROI Legal documents LLC, NDA, IP Medical content MRI, CT, HIV, WHO Academic writing PhD, BA, MSc, GPA Everyday language etc., e.g., i.e., vs. Government and organizations FBI, CIA, UN, EU Internet slang LOL, BRB, FYI, ASAP

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always include the title attribute – it's the whole point of <abbr>.

  2. Define abbreviations on first use – write the full term, then the abbreviation in parentheses or with <abbr>.

  3. Use <abbr> for both abbreviations and acronyms – don't use the deprecated <acronym>.

  4. Don't overuse <abbr> – only use it for abbreviations that readers might not know.

  5. Use lang for foreign-language expansions – if the expansion is in a different language.

  6. Style <abbr> consistently – use CSS for a consistent look.

  7. Test on touch devices – tooltips don't work on touch; provide alternative methods if needed.

  8. Consider accessibility – some screen readers may not announce the title. Define the abbreviation in the text on first use.

  9. Don't use <abbr> for styling only – use <span> with CSS if you just want visual styling.

  10. Keep expansions concise – the title should be the full expansion, not a long definition.

  11. Use <dfn> for definitions – when defining a term for the first time, wrap it in <dfn>.

  12. Validate your HTML – the W3C validator checks for correct usage.

  13. Don't nest <abbr> inside another <abbr> – it's confusing and unnecessary.

  14. Use cursor: help – to indicate that a tooltip is available.

  15. Consider mobile users – provide alternative ways to access expansions (e.g., a glossary link).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <abbr> Without title
docs.text:
<p><abbr>HTML</abbr> is the foundation of the web.</p>
Why it's wrong: Without title, the abbreviation has no expansion. It's semantically valid but provides no benefit.

✅ Correct: 

<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is the foundation of the web.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using the Deprecated <acronym> Element
docs.text:
<acronym title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</acronym>
Why it's wrong: <acronym> is deprecated in HTML5. Use <abbr>.

✅ Correct: 

<abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <abbr> for Every Occurrence Without Definition
docs.text:
<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is used. 
<abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is great.</p>
Why it's wrong: Repeated expansions clutter the text. Define on first use and use the abbreviation without <abbr> afterward.

✅ Correct: 

<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> (HyperText Markup Language) is used. HTML is great.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <abbr> for Visual Styling Only
docs.text:
<p><abbr>Text</abbr></p>
Why it's wrong: <abbr> without title has no semantic meaning. Use <span> for styling.

✅ Correct:
