docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Page footer Site-wide contact information Article footer Author contact details Contact page Business contact information Blog post Author bio and contact E-commerce Customer service contact Corporate website Office addresses, phone numbers Personal website Email, social media links Non-profit Donation and volunteer contact Legal documents Contact for legal inquiries Resume/CV Contact details for the candidate

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <address> only for contact information – not for arbitrary postal addresses.

  2. Place <address> in a <footer> – for site-wide or article-specific contact information.

  3. Use <a href="mailto:..."> for email – makes it clickable.

  4. Use <a href="tel:..."> for phone – makes it clickable on mobile.

  5. Use <br> for line breaks – to format the address lines.

  6. Use <strong> for the organisation name – to emphasise it.

  7. Add microdata for SEO – use itemprop for structured data.

  8. Override the default italic style – if it doesn't fit your design.

  9. Keep it concise – contact information should be easy to scan.

  10. Don't nest <address> elements – it's confusing and unnecessary.

  11. Don't use <address> for headings – use <h1>–<h6>.

  12. Test with screen readers – ensure contact information is announced correctly.

  13. Validate your HTML – the W3C validator checks for correct usage.

  14. Use rel="noopener noreferrer" for external links – for security.

  15. Consider privacy – don't expose personal contact information without consent.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <address> for Non-Contact Postal Addresses
docs.text:
<address>
    1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20500
</address>
Why it's wrong: This is a postal address in a news article, not the author's contact information.

✅ Correct: 

<p>1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20500</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <address> Inside <address>
docs.text:
<address>
    <address>Nested address</address>
</address>
Why it's wrong: Nesting <address> elements is unnecessary and confusing.

✅ Correct: 

<address>
    Contact information here.
</address>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <address> for Headings
docs.text:
<address>
    <h1>Contact Us</h1>
    ...
</address>
Why it's wrong: Headings should not be inside <address>.

✅ Correct: 

<h1>Contact Us</h1>
<address>
    ...
</address>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting mailto: or tel:
docs.text:
<address>
    Email: info@example.com
</address>
Why it's wrong: The email is not clickable.

✅ Correct: 

<address>
    Email: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">info@example.com</a>
</address>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <address> for Styling Only
docs.text:
<address>This is italic text.</address>
Why it's wrong: <address> is for contact information, not for making text italic.

✅ Correct: 

<p><em>This is italic text.</em></p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Using <br> for Line Breaks
docs.text:
<address>
    123 Main Street Anytown USA
</address>
Why it's wrong: Without <br>, the address appears on a single line.

✅ Correct: 

<address>
    123 Main Street<br>
    Anytown, USA
</address>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <address> Without Contact Information
docs.text:
<address>
    Welcome to our website!
</address>
Why it's wrong: The content is not contact information.

✅ Correct: 

<p>Welcome to our website!</p>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <address> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • Microdata – adds attributes but minimal performance impact.
  • No default JavaScript – no scripts attached.
  • Rendering – the italic style has no significant performance cost.
  • CSS styling – complex styles on <address> may affect performance, but the impact is minimal.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated contact information, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • mailto: and tel: links – validate the values to prevent injection.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for links with target="_blank".
  • Privacy – don't expose personal contact information without consent.
  • Spam – email addresses in plain text can be harvested by spam bots. Consider obfuscation or a contact form.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <address> to see its content and styles.
  • Computed styles – check the font-style and display properties.
  • Console – use document.querySelector('address') to inspect the element.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting (e.g., <address> inside <address>).
  • Test with screen readers – ensure contact information is announced correctly.
  • Check microdata – use Google's Rich Results Test to verify structured data.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For contact information – email, phone, physical address, social media.
  • In page footers – for site-wide contact details.
  • In article footers – for author contact information.
  • On contact pages – for business contact details.
  • With microdata – for structured data and SEO.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For arbitrary postal addresses – use <p> instead.
  • For headings – use <h1>–<h6>.
  • For general prose – use <p>.
  • For styling only – use <p> with CSS.
  • For non-contact information – use the appropriate semantic element.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <footer> – often contains <address>.
  • <article> – can have an <address> in its footer.
  • <a href="mailto:..."> – email links.
  • <a href="tel:..."> – phone links.
  • Microdata – structured data with itemprop.
  • Schema.org – vocabulary for structured data.
  • SEO – local business listings.
  • Accessibility – screen reader announcements.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <address> element was introduced in HTML 3.2 (1997).

  • In HTML4, <address> was an inline element. In HTML5, it was redefined as a block-level element.

  • The default font-style: italic for <address> is a legacy from print, where addresses were often italicised. You can override it with CSS.

  • The <address> element is not for arbitrary postal addresses – only for contact information of the nearest <article> or the document.

  • The <address> element can be combined with microdata to provide structured contact information for search engines.

  • Screen readers may announce <address> as "contact information" or simply read the text.

  • The <address> element is commonly placed inside <footer>, but it can appear anywhere flow content is accepted.

  • Email addresses in <address> are often targeted by spam bots – consider using a contact form or obfuscation.

  • The mailto: scheme can include a subject and body: <a href="mailto:info@example.com?subject=Hello&body=Message">.

  • The tel: scheme is primarily for mobile devices and can include the country code: <a href="tel:+15551234567">.

  • The <address> element has no specific DOM interface – it uses HTMLElement.

  • Some developers use <address> for semantic SEO benefits, as search engines may use it for local business listings.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <address> element marks up contact information for the nearest <article> or the document.
  • It is a block-level element and flow content.
  • It is not for arbitrary postal addresses – only for contact information.
  • Best practices: use mailto: for email, tel: for phone, <br> for line breaks, <strong> for organisation names, and microdata for SEO.
  • Common mistakes include using <address> for non-contact postal addresses, nesting <address> elements, and forgetting mailto: or tel: links.
  • The <address> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.
  • It is commonly used in footers, contact pages, and article footers for author information.
  • The default italic style can be overridden with CSS.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that convey meaning about the content they contain, rather than merely describing how that content should look. A semantic element clearly describes its purpose to both the developer reading the code and the machine (browser, screen reader, search engine) processing it.

For example, <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, and <footer> are semantic elements—their names describe their role in the document. In contrast, <div> and <span> are non-semantic elements—they tell you nothing about what they contain. Semantics is about meaning, not appearance.

Semantic HTML is not a separate language or framework; it is a philosophy and set of best practices for using the existing HTML elements in a way that maximises clarity, accessibility, and machine-readability.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Semantic HTML serves several essential purposes:

  • Accessibility – screen readers use semantic elements to navigate and understand content structure.
  • SEO – search engines use semantic elements to determine the importance and relevance of content.
  • Maintainability – semantic markup is easier to read, understand, and maintain.
  • Consistency – semantic elements have predictable behaviour across browsers.
  • Future-proofing – semantic markup survives redesigns and technology changes.
  • Interoperability – other tools (readers, parsers, crawlers) can understand the content.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Semantic HTML is a foundational concept that applies to every element you write. It is not an add-on or a library; it is a way of thinking about HTML. It sits at the intersection of:

  • HTML structure – how content is organised.
  • Accessibility – how content is perceived by all users.
  • SEO – how content is discovered and ranked.
  • Maintainability – how content is edited and updated.
Semantic HTML
│
├── Accessibility (screen readers, keyboard users)
├── SEO (search engines, rich snippets)
├── Maintainability (developers, future editors)
├── Interoperability (parsers, crawlers, tools)
└── Future-proofing (survives redesigns)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
In the early days of the web, HTML was used purely for presentation. Elements like <font>, <center>, and <table> (for layout) were common. Authors used <div> and <span> for everything, with class names like header, nav, and footer to simulate meaning. But these class names were invisible to machines—screen readers, search engines, and other tools couldn't tell a navigation menu from a content block.

This "divitis" (overuse of <div>) created several problems:

  • Inaccessible content – screen readers had to guess the structure, often providing a confusing experience.
  • Poor SEO – search engines couldn't distinguish main content from sidebars or footers.
  • Fragile code – class names like .header could change, breaking styles and scripts.
  • No machine-readable structure – tools couldn't understand the page's organisation.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Divitis (overuse of <div>) No semantic meaning; machines couldn't understand structure. Presentational elements <font>, <center> mixed presentation with structure. Class names for structure Invisible to machines; fragile and inconsistent. No landmarks Screen reader users couldn't navigate between sections. No document outline Headings were the only structural cue, and they were often misused. Table-based layouts Semantic misuse; inaccessible and hard to maintain.

docs.title: Why Semantic HTML Was Introduced
docs.text:
HTML5 introduced a set of semantic elements that describe the purpose of content, not its appearance:

  • <header> – introductory content.
  • <nav> – navigation links.
  • <main> – primary content.
  • <article> – self-contained content.
  • <section> – thematic grouping.
  • <aside> – tangentially related content.
  • <footer> – footer content.
  • <figure> and <figcaption> – self-contained media with caption.
  • <time> – machine-readable dates.
  • <mark> – highlighted relevance.

These elements were designed to:

  • Provide meaning – machines can understand the role of each part of the page.
  • Improve accessibility – screen readers can navigate by landmarks and structure.
  • Enhance SEO – search engines can identify main content and its context.
  • Simplify styling – semantic elements have predictable default styles.
  • Encourage best practices – authors are guided toward meaningful markup.

The shift to semantic HTML is part of the broader movement toward a Semantic Web, where content is marked up with meaning that both humans and machines can understand.

docs.title: Non-Semantic vs. Semantic HTML
docs.text:
Non-Semantic (Bad):

<div class="header">
    <div class="nav">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        </ul>
    </div>
</div>
<div class="main">
    <div class="article">
        <div class="title">Article Title</div>
        <div class="content">Article content...</div>
    </div>
</div>
<div class="footer">
    <div class="copyright">© 2026</div>
</div>

Semantic (Good):

<header>
    <nav>
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>
<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Article Title</h1>
        <p>Article content...</p>
    </article>
</main>
<footer>
    <p>© 2026</p>
</footer>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Non-Semantic Semantic Why Semantic Is Better <div class="header"> <header> Machines know it's a header. <div class="nav"> <nav> Machines know it's navigation. <div class="main"> <main> Machines know it's the main content. <div class="article"> <article> Machines know it's self-contained. <div class="title"> <h1> Machines know it's a heading. <div class="content"> <p> Machines know it's a paragraph. <div class="footer"> <footer> Machines know it's a footer.

docs.title: Common Semantic Elements
docs.text: Element Meaning <header> Introductory content or navigational aids. <nav> Navigation links. <main> Primary content of the document. <article> Self-contained, distributable content. <section> Thematic grouping of content. <aside> Tangentially related content. <footer> Footer for its nearest sectioning content. <figure> Self-contained media (image, diagram, code). <figcaption> Caption for a <figure>. <time> Machine-readable date/time. <mark> Highlighted/relevant text. <details> Disclosure widget. <summary> Summary for <details>. <dialog> Dialog box.

docs.title: Semantic Elements for Text
docs.text: Element Meaning <strong> Strong importance. <em> Stress emphasis. <abbr> Abbreviation. <cite> Citation. <code> Code fragment. <var> Variable. <samp> Sample output. <kbd> Keyboard input. <time> Date/time. <address> Contact information.

docs.title: The "Labeled Boxes" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine you have a set of boxes. If you label them "Kitchen," "Bedroom," and "Bathroom," anyone can understand what's inside each box. If you label them "Box 1," "Box 2," and "Box 3," only you know what's inside. Semantic HTML is like labeling your boxes meaningfully—everyone (including machines) can understand the contents.

docs.title: The "Road Signs" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a website as a city. Non-semantic HTML is like having no road signs—you have to guess where you are and where you're going. Semantic HTML is like having clear road signs—"Main Street," "City Hall," "Park"—that tell you exactly what each area is. Screen readers and search engines are like drivers who rely on those signs to navigate.

docs.title: The "Book Structure" Analogy
docs.text: A book has a clear structure: title page, table of contents, chapters, sections, index. Semantic HTML is like using that structure on the web—<header> is the title page, <nav> is the table of contents, <article> is a chapter, <section> is a section, <footer> is the index or colophon. Machines can navigate the book just as easily as humans.

docs.title: Concept 1: Semantics vs. Presentation
docs.text:
• Semantics – the meaning of the content (what it is).
  • Presentation – the appearance of the content (how it looks).

HTML is for semantics; CSS is for presentation. Semantic HTML means choosing elements based on what the content is, not how it should look.

<!-- Bad: using <div> for a button because it looks right -->
<div class="button" onclick="submit()">Submit</div>

<!-- Good: using <button> for a button, then styling it -->
<button type="submit">Submit</button>

docs.title: Concept 2: The Document Outline
docs.text: Semantic HTML contributes to the document outline—the hierarchical structure of the page. Headings (<h1>–<h6>) and sectioning elements (<section>, <article>, <nav>, <aside>) create this outline, which screen readers and search engines use to understand the page.

docs.title: Concept 3: Landmarks
docs.text:
Semantic elements create landmarks—navigable regions of the page. Screen readers allow users to jump between landmarks (e.g., "skip to main content," "go to navigation"). The main landmark roles are:

Role Element banner <header> (when not inside a sectioning element) navigation <nav> main <main> complementary <aside> contentinfo <footer> (when not inside a sectioning element) search <form role="search"> region <section> with an accessible name

docs.title: Concept 4: Semantic Elements Have Default Behaviour
docs.text:
Semantic elements come with built-in behaviour:

  • <button> is focusable and clickable.
  • <a> is focusable and navigable.
  • <input> accepts user input.
  • <nav> is a landmark.
  • <main> is a landmark.

Non-semantic elements like <div> and <span> have no default behaviour—you have to add it with JavaScript and ARIA.

docs.title: Concept 5: The First Rule of ARIA
docs.text:
"If you can use a native HTML element with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible, then do so."

Semantic HTML is the first choice; ARIA is the fallback when no native element fits.

docs.title: Concept 6: Semantic HTML Is Not About Styling
docs.text: Semantic elements have default styles, but those can be changed with CSS. The semantic meaning remains regardless of styling. You can make an <h1> look small, and you can make a <span> look like a heading—but only <h1> conveys the meaning of a heading.

docs.title: Concept 7: The <div> and <span> Are Not Evil
docs.text: <div> and <span> are non-semantic elements, but they are not "bad." They are useful when no semantic element fits—for layout, grouping, or styling hooks. The problem is overuse (divitis). Use semantic elements where possible, and fall back to <div> or <span> when necessary.

docs.title: Concept 8: Semantic HTML and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use semantic elements to:

  • Identify the main content (<main>).
  • Understand the hierarchy (<h1>–<h6>).
  • Recognise navigation (<nav>).
  • Find publication dates (<time>).
  • Extract contact information (<address>).

This can improve rankings and enable rich snippets.

docs.title: Concept 9: Semantic HTML and Accessibility
docs.text:
Screen readers rely on semantic elements to:

  • Navigate by landmarks.
  • Jump between headings.
  • Identify lists, tables, and forms.
  • Understand the structure of the page.

Without semantic HTML, screen reader users have a much harder time understanding and navigating content.

docs.title: Concept 10: Semantic HTML and Maintainability
docs.text:
Semantic markup is self-documenting:

<!-- Non-semantic: what is this? -->
<div class="box1">
    <div class="box2">...</div>
</div>

<!-- Semantic: clear purpose -->
<article>
    <section>...</section>
</article>

The second example is easier to understand for anyone reading the code.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How Semantic HTML Is Processed
docs.text:
1.  The browser parses the HTML and builds the DOM.
    │
    ▼
2.  Semantic elements are recognised and added to the accessibility tree.
    │   ├── <header> becomes a "banner" landmark.
    │   ├── <nav> becomes a "navigation" landmark.
    │   ├── <main> becomes a "main" landmark.
    │   ├── <article> becomes an "article" role.
    │   ├── <section> becomes a "region" if it has a heading.
    │   └── <footer> becomes a "contentinfo" landmark.
    │
    ▼
3.  The document outline is built from headings and sectioning elements.
    │
    ▼
4.  Screen readers use the accessibility tree and outline to provide navigation.
    │
    ▼
5.  Search engines use the semantic structure to understand and rank content.
    │
    ▼
6.  CSS is applied based on the elements and their classes/IDs.
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered for all users.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
The accessibility tree is a simplified version of the DOM that assistive technologies use. Semantic elements create specific roles in this tree:

Element Accessibility Role <header> banner <nav> navigation <main> main <article> article <section> region (if labelled) <aside> complementary <footer> contentinfo <h1>–<h6> heading (with level) <ul> list <li> listitem <button> button <a href> link

docs.title: Screen Reader Navigation
docs.text:
Screen reader users can:

  • Jump between landmarks (e.g., D for landmarks in NVDA).
  • Navigate by headings (e.g., H for next heading, 1–6 for specific levels).
  • Navigate by lists, tables, and forms.
  • Skip to main content.

Without semantic HTML, these navigation methods are unavailable.

docs.title: Semantic Elements in the DOM
docs.text:
Semantic elements are represented by specific DOM interfaces:

  • <header> → HTMLElement
  • <nav> → HTMLElement
  • <main> → HTMLElement
  • <article> → HTMLElement
  • <section> → HTMLElement
  • <aside> → HTMLElement
  • <footer> → HTMLElement

Most semantic elements don't have unique DOM interfaces—they rely on their tag name for meaning.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text: The browser's accessibility engine builds the accessibility tree from the DOM. Semantic elements create specific nodes and roles in this tree, which screen readers consume.

docs.title: The Document Outline Algorithm
docs.text: The HTML5 outline algorithm determines the structure of the document from headings and sectioning elements. However, this algorithm is not widely implemented by browsers. In practice, the heading hierarchy (<h1>–<h6>) is the primary means of conveying document structure.

docs.title: SEO and Semantic HTML
docs.text:
Search engines like Google use semantic elements to:

  • Identify the main content (<main>).
  • Understand the heading hierarchy.
  • Recognise navigation and footer content.
  • Extract structured data (microdata, JSON-LD).

Google's algorithms reward well-structured, accessible content.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of Semantic HTML
docs.text:
1.  Author writes semantic HTML, choosing elements based on meaning.
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and builds the DOM.
    │
    ▼
4.  The accessibility tree is built with semantic roles.
    │
    ▼
5.  The document outline is derived from headings and sections.
    │
    ▼
6.  Screen readers use the accessibility tree for navigation.
    │
    ▼
7.  Search engines index the content with semantic understanding.
    │
    ▼
8.  CSS is applied for visual presentation.
    │
    ▼
9.  The page is rendered for all users.
    │
    ▼
10. JavaScript may modify the DOM dynamically.

docs.title: Example 1: A Complete Semantic Page
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Semantic HTML Example</title>
</head>
<body>
    <header>
        <h1>My Website</h1>
        <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
                <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
                <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
    </header>

    <main>
        <article>
            <header>
                <h2>Article Title</h2>
                <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>
            </header>

            <section>
                <h3>Introduction</h3>
                <p>This is the introduction...</p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h3>Main Content</h3>
                <p>This is the main content...</p>
                <figure>
                    <img src="diagram.png" alt="System architecture diagram">
                    <figcaption>Figure 1: System architecture</figcaption>
                </figure>
            </section>

            <footer>
                <p>Author: <a href="mailto:author@example.com">Jane Doe</a></p>
            </footer>
        </article>

        <aside>
            <h3>Related Articles</h3>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
                <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
            </ul>
        </aside>
    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 My Website</p>
        <address>
            Contact: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">info@example.com</a>
        </address>
    </footer>
</body>
</html>

Key Semantic Elements: - <header> – page header. - <nav> – navigation. - <main> – primary content. - <article> – self-contained content. - <section> – thematic grouping. - <aside> – related content. - <footer> – page footer. - <time> – machine-readable date. - <figure> / <figcaption> – image with caption. - <address> – contact information.

docs.title: Example 2: Non-Semantic vs. Semantic Comparison
docs.text:
Non-Semantic: 

<div id="header">
    <div id="nav">...</div>
</div>
<div id="content">
    <div class="post">
        <div class="title">Title</div>
        <div class="text">Content</div>
    </div>
</div>
<div id="footer">...</div>

Semantic: 

<header>
    <nav>...</nav>
</header>
<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Title</h1>
        <p>Content</p>
    </article>
</main>
<footer>...</footer>

docs.title: Example 3: Semantic Text Elements
docs.text:
<p>
    The <abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr> was founded in 
    <time datetime="1948">1948</time>. The <strong>most important</strong> 
    thing to remember is that <em>prevention</em> is better than cure.
    Use the <code>washHands()</code> function regularly.
</p>

Code Breakdown: - <abbr> – abbreviation with expansion. - <time> – machine-readable date. - <strong> – strong importance. - <em> – stress emphasis. - <code> – code fragment.

docs.title: Example 4: Semantic Forms
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <fieldset>
        <legend>Personal Information</legend>

        <label for="name">Name:</label>
        <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>

        <label for="email">Email:</label>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

Semantic Elements: - <fieldset> – groups related controls. - <legend> – caption for the fieldset. - <label> – labels for inputs. - <input type="email"> – semantic input type.

docs.title: Example 5: Semantic Tables
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Month</th>
            <th scope="col">Sales</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">January</th>
            <td>$10,000</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">February</th>
            <td>$12,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <td>Total</td>
            <td>$22,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>
</table>

Semantic Elements: - <caption> – table title. - <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> – row groups. - <th scope="col"> – column header. - <th scope="row"> – row header.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text:
• All websites – semantic HTML is a best practice for every project.
  • Accessibility-critical sites – government, education, healthcare.
  • SEO-focused sites – content-heavy sites, blogs, news.
  • Large codebases – semantic markup is easier to maintain.
  • Team projects – clear structure aids collaboration.
  • Long-lived projects – semantic markup survives redesigns.

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use semantic elements first – <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <footer>.

  2. Use headings for structure – <h1>–<h6> in logical order, one <h1> per page.

  3. Use <main> for primary content – only one per page.

  4. Use <nav> for navigation – not for every group of links.

  5. Use <article> for self-contained content – blog posts, news, comments.

  6. Use <section> for thematic groupings – with a heading.

  7. Use <aside> for tangential content – sidebars, pull quotes.

  8. Use <figure> and <figcaption> for media – with captions.

  9. Use <time> for dates and times – with datetime.

  10. Use <address> for contact information – not for arbitrary postal addresses.

  11. Use <button> for buttons – not <div> with onclick.

  12. Use <a> for links – not <button> for navigation.

  13. Use <label> for form inputs – associate with for.

  14. Use <table> for tabular data – not for layout.

  15. Use <ul>, <ol>, <dl> for lists – not <div> with bullets.

  16. Fall back to <div> and <span> when no semantic element fits – they are not evil, just non-semantic.

  17. Don't use ARIA if native HTML works – follow the First Rule of ARIA.

  18. Validate your HTML – use the W3C validator.

  19. Test with screen readers – ensure semantic structure is navigable.

  20. Keep the document outline logical – no skipped heading levels.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Divitis (Overuse of <div>)
docs.text:
<div class="header">
    <div class="nav">...</div>
</div>
Why it's wrong: No semantic meaning; machines can't understand structure.

✅ Correct: 

<header>
    <nav>...</nav>
</header>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div> for Buttons
docs.text:
<div class="button" onclick="submit()">Submit</div>
Why it's wrong: Not focusable, not keyboard-accessible, no semantic role.

✅ Correct: 

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <span> for Headings
docs.text:
<span class="heading">My Title</span>
Why it's wrong: No semantic meaning; screen readers don't recognise it as a heading.

✅ Correct: 

<h1>My Title</h1>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <h1> Elements
docs.text:
<h1>My Site</h1>
<h1>About Us</h1>
Why it's wrong: Only one <h1> per page; violates document outline.

✅ Correct: 

<h1>My Site</h1>
<h2>About Us</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <section> Without a Heading
docs.text:
<section>
    <p>Content</p>
</section>
Why it's wrong: <section> should have a heading to be a meaningful section.

✅ Correct: 

<section>
    <h2>Section Title</h2>
    <p>Content</p>
</section>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <article> for Everything
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>My Site</h1>
    <article>
        <h2>About</h2>
    </article>
</article>
Why it's wrong: <article> is for self-contained, distributable content. Not everything is an article.

✅ Correct: Use <section> for thematic groupings that aren't self-contained.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <nav> for Every Group of Links
docs.text:
<nav>
    <a href="#">Link 1</a>
    <a href="#">Link 2</a>
</nav>
<p>Some text with <a href="#">a link</a>.</p>
<nav>
    <a href="#">Link 3</a>
</nav>
Why it's wrong: <nav> is for major navigation blocks, not every link.

✅ Correct: Use <nav> for primary navigation; use <a> alone for inline links.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <table> for Layout
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <td>Sidebar</td>
        <td>Main Content</td>
    </tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Tables are for tabular data, not layout.

✅ Correct: Use CSS Grid or Flexbox for layout.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using ARIA Instead of Native Semantics
docs.text:
<div role="button" tabindex="0" onclick="submit()">Submit</div>
Why it's wrong: The First Rule of ARIA says use native elements first.

✅ Correct: 

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Semantic elements are lightweight – no performance penalty.
  • DOM size – fewer elements = smaller DOM = faster parsing.
  • Accessibility tree – semantic elements add nodes, but the impact is minimal.
  • SEO – semantic HTML can improve search rankings, indirectly affecting traffic.
  • No JavaScript required – semantic elements have built-in behaviour, reducing script overhead.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – semantic HTML doesn't prevent XSS; always sanitize user input.
  • innerHTML – avoid using it with user input; use textContent or a sanitizer.
  • javascript: URLs – avoid in href and src.
  • target="_blank" – use rel="noopener noreferrer".
  • No direct security implications – semantic HTML is about structure, not security.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the DOM to see the semantic structure.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the accessibility tree for landmarks and roles.
  • Lighthouse – audits for semantic HTML and accessibility.
  • W3C Validator – checks for correct usage of semantic elements.
  • Screen reader testing – navigate by landmarks and headings.
  • HeadingsMap extension – visualises the document outline.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: • Always – semantic HTML is a best practice for every project.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Never – you can't avoid semantics entirely. However, you can fail to use semantic elements when they would be appropriate.

  • Exception: When no semantic element fits, use <div> or <span>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Accessibility (WCAG)
  • ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)
  • SEO (Search Engine Optimization)
  • Document Outline
  • Landmarks
  • Screen Readers
  • Semantic Web
  • HTML5 Living Standard
  • <div> and <span> (non-semantic elements)
  • Microdata and JSON-LD

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The term "semantic HTML" became popular with the introduction of HTML5, which added many new semantic elements.

  • The <div> and <span> elements are not deprecated—they are simply non-semantic. They should be used when no semantic element fits.

  • The First Rule of ARIA is: "If you can use a native HTML element with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible, then do so."

  • Screen readers like NVDA and JAWS allow users to navigate by landmarks (e.g., pressing D in NVDA to jump to the next landmark).

  • Google's search algorithms reward well-structured, accessible content, which semantic HTML provides.

  • The HTML5 outline algorithm was intended to create a document outline from sectioning elements, but it is not widely implemented in browsers. The heading hierarchy remains the primary structural cue.

  • Semantic HTML can improve SEO by helping search engines understand the main content, navigation, and other sections.

  • The <main> element should appear only once per page and contains the primary content.

  • The <article> element is for content that could stand alone and be syndicated (e.g., a blog post, a news story).

  • The <section> element is for thematic groupings of content, typically with a heading.

  • The <aside> element is for content tangentially related to the main content (e.g., a sidebar, a pull quote).

  • The <figure> element is for self-contained media (images, diagrams, code snippets) that could be moved without affecting the flow of the document.

  • Semantic HTML is a key part of Progressive Enhancement—it ensures the page works for everyone, regardless of device or ability.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that convey meaning about the content they contain.
  • It contrasts with non-semantic HTML, which uses <div> and <span> for everything, providing no meaning to machines.
  • Key benefits: accessibility (screen readers), SEO (search engines), maintainability (developers), and future-proofing.
  • Core semantic elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <footer>, <figure>, <figcaption>, <time>, <address>.
  • Best practices: use semantic elements first, fall back to <div>/<span> when necessary, follow the First Rule of ARIA, and validate your HTML.
  • Common mistakes include divitis, using <div> for buttons, multiple <h1>s, using <section> without headings, and using ARIA when native HTML works.
  • Semantic HTML is essential for accessibility, SEO, and maintainable code.
  • It is not a separate language or framework—it's a philosophy of using HTML meaningfully.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <header> element is a semantic HTML element that represents introductory content or navigational aids for its nearest ancestor sectioning content or the document itself. It typically contains a logo, site title, navigation menu, search form, or a combination of these elements. The <header> element is not restricted to the top of the page – it can appear inside <article>, <section>, <aside>, or <main> to introduce that specific section.

The <header> element is part of the flow content and palpable content categories. It is a block-level element and creates a banner landmark when it is a direct child of the <body> (i.e., not nested inside another sectioning element). When nested inside an <article> or <section>, it does not create a banner landmark but still provides semantic structure.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <header> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Semantic clarity – identifies introductory content as distinct from the main body.
  • Accessibility – creates a banner landmark (when at the top level) that screen reader users can navigate to.
  • SEO – helps search engines understand the site's branding and navigation.
  • Organization – groups related introductory elements (logo, title, nav) into a single block.
  • Styling – provides a hook for CSS to style headers consistently.
  • Reusability – can be used at multiple levels (page, article, section).

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <header> element is flow content and can appear anywhere flow content is accepted. It is most commonly used in:

  • Top of the page – for site-wide branding and navigation.
  • Inside <article> – for article titles, author info, and publication dates.
  • Inside <section> – for section headings and introductory content.
  • Inside <aside> – for sidebar headings.
<body>
    <header>
        <h1>My Website</h1>
        <nav>...</nav>
    </header>
    <main>
        <article>
            <header>
                <h2>Article Title</h2>
                <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>
            </header>
            <p>Article content...</p>
        </article>
    </main>
    <footer>...</footer>
</body>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML5, there was no semantic element for introductory content. Developers used <div class="header"> or <div id="header"> to mark up the top section of a page. While this worked visually, it provided no semantic meaning to machines. Screen readers couldn't identify the header as a landmark, search engines couldn't distinguish it from other content, and the markup was fragile (dependent on class names).

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic header element Machines couldn't identify introductory content. <div class="header"> Class names are invisible to machines; fragile. No banner landmark Screen reader users couldn't jump to the header. No distinction from other content Search engines couldn't identify site branding. Inconsistent styling Each developer used their own class names.

docs.title: Why <header> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <header> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standardised, semantic way to mark up introductory content. It enables:

  • Clear semantics – machines understand that the content is introductory.
  • Accessibility – creates a banner landmark for screen reader navigation.
  • SEO – helps search engines identify site branding and navigation.
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.
  • Reusability – can be used at multiple levels (page, article, section).

The <header> element is part of the broader semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more understandable to both humans and machines.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <header>
docs.text:
<header>
    <!-- Introductory content -->
</header>

docs.title: Simple Page Header
docs.text:
<header>
    <h1>My Website</h1>
    <p>Welcome to my corner of the internet.</p>
</header>

docs.title: Header with Navigation
docs.text:
<header>
    <h1>My Website</h1>
    <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
            <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

docs.title: Header Inside an Article
docs.text:
<article>
    <header>
        <h2>Article Title</h2>
        <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time> by <a href="/author">Jane Doe</a></p>
    </header>
    <p>Article content...</p>
</article>

docs.title: Header Inside a Section
docs.text:
<section>
    <header>
        <h3>Section Title</h3>
        <p>This section covers...</p>
    </header>
    <p>Section content...</p>
</section>

docs.title: Multiple Headers on a Page
docs.text:
<body>
    <!-- Page header (banner landmark) -->
    <header>
        <h1>My Site</h1>
        <nav>...</nav>
    </header>

    <main>
        <article>
            <!-- Article header (no landmark) -->
            <header>
                <h2>Article Title</h2>
                <p>By Jane Doe</p>
            </header>
            <p>Content...</p>
        </article>

        <article>
            <header>
                <h2>Another Article</h2>
                <p>By John Smith</p>
            </header>
            <p>Content...</p>
        </article>
    </main>

    <footer>...</footer>
</body>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <header> Marks the introductory content. Provides semantic meaning. <h1>–<h6> Headings inside the header. Defines the title of the section/page. <nav> Navigation inside the header. Groups navigation links semantically. <p> Additional information (e.g., publication date). Provides context. <time> Machine-readable date. Enables parsing by machines.

docs.title: The "Book Cover" Analogy
docs.text: Think of the <header> element as the cover of a book (for the page header) or the chapter title page (for an article header). It introduces what follows, contains the title, author, and perhaps a table of contents (navigation). Just as a book cover is distinct from the chapters, the header is distinct from the main content.

docs.title: The "Newspaper Masthead" Analogy
docs.text: The page <header> is like a newspaper masthead – it contains the newspaper's name, logo, and main navigation (sections like "Sports," "Business"). The article <header> is like the headline and byline of an individual article – it introduces that specific story.

docs.title: The "Conference Name Badge" Analogy
docs.text: Think of the <header> as a name badge at a conference. It tells you who the person is (the title), what organisation they belong to (branding), and perhaps their role. For an article, it's like the title slide of a presentation – it introduces the content that follows.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Banner Landmark
docs.text:
When <header> is a direct child of <body> (or not nested inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section>), it creates a banner landmark in the accessibility tree. Screen reader users can navigate directly to it using landmark navigation (e.g., pressing D in NVDA).

<body>
    <header>
        <!-- This creates a banner landmark -->
    </header>
</body>

When <header> is nested inside a sectioning element, it does not create a banner landmark:

<article>
    <header>
        <!-- No banner landmark -->
    </header>
</article>

docs.title: Concept 2: <header> Is Not Restricted to the Top
docs.text:
Unlike the name suggests, <header> can appear anywhere in the document. It represents introductory content for its nearest ancestor sectioning content. This means you can have multiple <header> elements on a page.

<article>
    <header>Article Header</header>
    <section>
        <header>Section Header</header>
    </section>
</article>

docs.title: Concept 3: Content Model
docs.text:
The <header> element accepts flow content, but it cannot contain another <header> or <footer> element. It also should not contain a <main> element.

<!-- Valid -->
<header>
    <h1>Title</h1>
    <nav>...</nav>
</header>

<!-- Invalid: nested header -->
<header>
    <header>Nested header</header>
</header>

docs.title: Concept 4: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <header> element has no default visual styling in most browsers. It behaves like a <div> by default:

header {
    display: block;
}

This means you need to style it with CSS to achieve the desired appearance.

docs.title: Concept 5: <header> vs <div class="header">
docs.text: Aspect <header> <div class="header"> Semantic meaning Introductory content None Accessibility Banner landmark No landmark SEO Recognised by search engines Not recognised Styling No default styles No default styles Maintainability Self-documenting Depends on class names

docs.title: Concept 6: <header> and <h1>–<h6>
docs.text:
The <header> element typically contains a heading (<h1>–<h6>) that titles the section or page. However, a heading is not required inside <header>. The header can contain only a logo, navigation, or other introductory content.

<!-- Valid: no heading -->
<header>
    <img src="logo.png" alt="Company Logo">
    <nav>...</nav>
</header>

docs.title: Concept 7: <header> and <footer>
docs.text:
The <header> and <footer> elements are often used together:

  • <header> – introductory content.
  • <footer> – concluding content (author info, copyright, related links).
<article>
    <header>
        <h2>Article Title</h2>
    </header>
    <p>Content...</p>
    <footer>
        <p>Author: Jane Doe</p>
    </footer>
</article>

docs.title: Concept 8: <header> and ARIA
docs.text:
If you need to provide a label for a <header> that is not a banner landmark (e.g., inside an article), you can use aria-label or aria-labelledby:

<article>
    <header aria-label="Article header">
        <h2>Article Title</h2>
    </header>
</article>

However, this is rarely necessary because the heading inside the header usually provides enough context.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <header>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<header>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content (flow content, excluding nested header/footer).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── display: block
    │
    ▼
6.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   ├── If it's a direct child of <body> → banner landmark
    │   └── If nested → no landmark (but still semantic)
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
8.  Screen readers can navigate to the banner landmark (if applicable).

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, <header> is exposed as:

  • banner – when it's a direct child of <body>.
  • generic – when nested inside an article or section (no landmark).
  • The heading inside the header (<h1>–<h6>) is exposed as a heading node.

docs.title: The Document Outline
docs.text: The <header> element does not directly affect the document outline. The outline is determined by headings and sectioning elements. However, the heading inside the header contributes to the outline.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
header {
    display: block;
}

No other default styles are applied. You must use CSS for layout and appearance.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <header> is represented by the HTMLElement interface. It has no specific properties or methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

const header = document.querySelector('header');
console.log(header.textContent); // The text content
console.log(header.innerHTML); // The HTML content

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
The browser's accessibility engine determines whether a <header> creates a banner landmark based on its position in the DOM:

  • Direct child of <body> → banner landmark.
  • Inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section> → no landmark.

This is specified in the HTML-AAM (Accessibility API Mapping) specification.

docs.title: The Banner Landmark
docs.text: The banner landmark is one of the ARIA landmark roles. It is used to identify the site-wide header. Screen readers provide shortcuts to navigate to it (e.g., D in NVDA, Ctrl+Option+U in VoiceOver).

docs.title: SEO and <header>
docs.text:
Search engines use <header> to identify:

  • Site branding (logo, site name).
  • Navigation structure.
  • Article titles and author information.

This can help with ranking and rich snippets.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <header> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<header>` element with introductory content.
    │   └── Example: <header><h1>Title</h1><nav>...</nav></header>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<header>` node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── Banner landmark (if at top level).
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers can navigate to the banner landmark.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines index the content.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the header dynamically.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const header = document.querySelector('header');
header.innerHTML = '<h1>New Title</h1>';

        </ul>

</header>

docs.title: Example 3: Article Header
docs.text:
<article>

        <h2>How to Use Semantic HTML</h2>
        <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time> by <a href="/author/jane">Jane Doe</a></p>
    </header>
    <p>Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that convey meaning...</p>
</article>

docs.title: Example 4: Section Header

<section>
    <header>
        <h3>Introduction</h3>
        <p>This section provides an introduction to the topic.</p>
    </header>
    <p>Content...</p>
</section>

docs.title: Example 5: Multiple Headers on a Page
docs.text:
<body>
    <header>
        <h1>My Blog</h1>
        <nav>...</nav>
    </header>

    <main>
        <article>
            <header>
                <h2>First Post</h2>

</body>

docs.title: Example 6: Header with Logo and Search
docs.text:
<header>
    <a href="/">
        <img src="logo.png" alt="Company Logo">
    </a>
    <h1>My Company</h1>
    <form role="search" action="/search" method="GET">
        <label for="search">Search:</label>
        <input type="search" id="search" name="q">
        <button type="submit">Go</button>

docs.title: Example 7: Styling the Header with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    header {
        display: flex;
        justify-content: space-between;
        align-items: center;
        padding: 1rem 2rem;
        background-color: #2c3e50;

<header>

    }
</style>

<header>
    <h1>My Website</h1>
    <nav>...</nav>
</header>

docs.title: Example 9: Header Inside <aside>
docs.text:
<aside>
    <header>
        <h3>Related Articles</h3>
    </header>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>

docs.title: Example 10: Header with Hero Image
docs.text:
<header>
    <img src="hero.jpg" alt="A beautiful landscape" width="100%" height="300">
    <h1>Welcome to My Site</h1>
    <p>Discover amazing content</p>
</header>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Site-wide header Logo, site title, main navigation Article header Article title, author, publication date Section header Section title, introductory text Sidebar header Sidebar title Hero section Large image, headline, call to action Search header Logo, search form Sticky header Navigation that stays at the top Minimal header Just a logo or title

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <header> for introductory content – not for arbitrary containers.

  2. Place the site header as a direct child of <body> – to create a banner landmark.

  3. Use <header> inside <article> and <section> – for article/section titles.

  4. Include a heading (<h1>–<h6>) inside <header> – when appropriate.

  5. Use <nav> inside <header> – for navigation links.

  6. Don't nest <header> inside another <header> – it's invalid.

  7. Don't use <header> for layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

  8. Style <header> with CSS – it has no default styling.

  9. Use aria-label if the header's purpose is unclear – e.g., aria-label="Site header".

  10. Keep the header concise – too much content dilutes its purpose.

  11. Make navigation accessible – use <nav> with aria-label.

  12. Test with screen readers – ensure the banner landmark is announced.

  13. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting.

  14. Consider mobile responsiveness – headers often need to adapt to small screens.

  15. Use <header> for hero sections – it's appropriate for introductory content.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div class="header"> Instead of <header>
docs.text:
<div class="header">
    <h1>My Site</h1>
</div>
Why it's wrong: No semantic meaning; no banner landmark.

✅ Correct: 

<header>
    <h1>My Site</h1>
</header>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <header> Inside <header>
docs.text:
<header>
    <header>Nested header</header>
</header>
Why it's wrong: Invalid nesting; confusing for machines.

✅ Correct: 

<header>
    <h1>Title</h1>
</header>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <header> for Non-Introductory Content
docs.text:
<header>
    <p>This is just a paragraph, not introductory content.</p>
</header>
Why it's wrong: <header> should contain introductory content, not arbitrary prose.

✅ Correct: 

<p>This is just a paragraph.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <h1> Elements in Multiple Headers
docs.text:
<header><h1>Site Title</h1></header>
<article>
    <header><h1>Article Title</h1></header>
</article>
Why it's wrong: Only one <h1> per page; use <h2> for article titles.

✅ Correct: 

<header><h1>Site Title</h1></header>
<article>
    <header><h2>Article Title</h2></header>
</article>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting <nav> Inside Header
docs.text:
<header>
    <a href="/">Home</a>
    <a href="/about">About</a>
</header>
Why it's wrong: Navigation links should be inside a <nav> element.

✅ Correct: 

<header>
    <nav>
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <header> for the Entire Page Layout
docs.text:
<header>
    <h1>Title</h1>
    <p>Content</p>
    <footer>Footer</footer>
</header>
Why it's wrong: <header> is for introductory content, not the whole page.

✅ Correct: 

<header>
    <h1>Title</h1>
</header>
<main>
    <p>Content</p>
</main>
<footer>Footer</footer>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Multiple <header> Elements at the Top Level
docs.text:
<body>
    <header>Header 1</header>
    <header>Header 2</header>
</body>
Why it's wrong: Multiple top-level headers create multiple banner landmarks, which is confusing.

✅ Correct: Use one top-level <header> and nest others inside sectioning elements.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <header> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • No default styles – no rendering cost beyond the content.
  • Accessibility tree – adds a landmark node, but the impact is minimal.
  • Sticky headers – position: sticky can cause performance issues if the header is large or complex; test on low-end devices.
  • Complex layouts – using Flexbox or Grid inside <header> has no significant performance impact.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <header>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for target="_blank".
  • Search forms – validate input on the server; don't rely on client-side validation alone.
  • No direct security implications – <header> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <header> to see its content and styles.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the banner landmark.
  • Computed styles – check the display property (should be block by default).
  • Console – use document.querySelector('header') to inspect the element.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting (header inside header).
  • Screen reader testing – navigate to the banner landmark.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and semantic HTML.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For site-wide introductory content – logo, site title, main navigation.
  • For article headers – article title, author, publication date.
  • For section headers – section title, introductory text.
  • For sidebar headers – sidebar title.
  • For hero sections – large image, headline, call to action.
  • For search headers – logo, search form.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For arbitrary containers – use <div>.
  • For main content – use <main>.
  • For footers – use <footer>.
  • For navigation-only blocks – use <nav> (though <nav> inside <header> is fine).
  • For every group of elements – only for introductory content.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <footer> – concluding content.
  • <nav> – navigation.
  • <main> – primary content.
  • <article> – self-contained content.
  • <section> – thematic grouping.
  • <aside> – tangentially related content.
  • ARIA Landmarks – banner, navigation, main, contentinfo.
  • Document Outline – headings and sectioning elements.
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <header> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • A <header> element creates a banner landmark only when it is a direct child of <body>. When nested inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section>, it does not create a landmark.

  • You can have multiple <header> elements on a page – one for the site, one for each article, one for each section.

  • The <header> element does not have any default visual styling. It behaves like a <div> by default.

  • The <header> element can contain flow content, but it cannot contain another <header> or <footer>.

  • The <header> element is commonly used with <nav> for site navigation.

  • Screen readers like NVDA and JAWS allow users to jump to the banner landmark using keyboard shortcuts.

  • The <header> element is part of the semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more accessible and machine-readable.

  • Search engines use <header> to identify site branding and navigation, which can improve SEO.

  • The <header> element is often styled with position: sticky to create a sticky header that stays at the top of the viewport while scrolling.

  • The <header> element can contain a hero image and headline for a landing page.

  • The <header> element is not the same as the <head> element. <head> is for metadata; <header> is for introductory content in the body.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <header> element represents introductory content or navigational aids for its nearest ancestor sectioning content or the document.
  • It is a block-level element and flow content.
  • It creates a banner landmark when it is a direct child of <body>.
  • It can be used at multiple levels: page, article, section, aside.
  • Best practices: use <header> for introductory content, place the site header as a direct child of <body>, use <nav> inside <header> for navigation, include a heading when appropriate, and style with CSS.
  • Common mistakes include using <div class="header"> instead of <header>, nesting <header> inside <header>, using multiple <h1>s, and using <header> for non-introductory content.
  • The <header> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.
  • It is one of the most commonly used semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <footer> element is a semantic HTML element that represents a footer for its nearest ancestor sectioning content or the document itself. A footer typically contains information about the author, copyright data, links to related documents, contact information, or other concluding content. Like <header>, the <footer> element is not restricted to the bottom of the page – it can appear inside <article>, <section>, <aside>, or <main> to conclude that specific section.

The <footer> element is part of the flow content and palpable content categories. It is a block-level element and creates a contentinfo landmark when it is a direct child of the <body> (i.e., not nested inside another sectioning element). When nested inside an <article> or <section>, it does not create a landmark but still provides semantic structure.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <footer> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Semantic clarity – identifies concluding content as distinct from the main body.
  • Accessibility – creates a contentinfo landmark (when at the top level) that screen reader users can navigate to.
  • SEO – helps search engines understand the site's footer content (copyright, contact, related links).
  • Organization – groups related concluding elements (copyright, contact, links) into a single block.
  • Styling – provides a hook for CSS to style footers consistently.
  • Reusability – can be used at multiple levels (page, article, section).

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <footer> element is flow content and can appear anywhere flow content is accepted. It is most commonly used in:

  • Bottom of the page – for site-wide copyright, contact, and legal information.
  • Inside <article> – for author info, publication date, and related links.
  • Inside <section> – for section-level conclusions.
  • Inside <aside> – for sidebar footers.
<body>
    <header>...</header>
    <main>
        <article>
            <header>...</header>
            <p>Article content...</p>
            <footer>
                <p>Author: Jane Doe</p>
            </footer>
        </article>
    </main>
    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 My Website</p>
        <address>Contact: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">info@example.com</a></address>
    </footer>
</body>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML5, there was no semantic element for concluding content. Developers used <div class="footer"> or <div id="footer"> to mark up the bottom section of a page. While this worked visually, it provided no semantic meaning to machines. Screen readers couldn't identify the footer as a landmark, search engines couldn't distinguish it from other content, and the markup was fragile (dependent on class names).

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic footer element Machines couldn't identify concluding content. <div class="footer"> Class names are invisible to machines; fragile. No contentinfo landmark Screen reader users couldn't jump to the footer. No distinction from other content Search engines couldn't identify site-wide information. Inconsistent styling Each developer used their own class names.

docs.title: Why <footer> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <footer> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standardised, semantic way to mark up concluding content. It enables:

  • Clear semantics – machines understand that the content is concluding.
  • Accessibility – creates a contentinfo landmark for screen reader navigation.
  • SEO – helps search engines identify copyright, contact, and related information.
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.
  • Reusability – can be used at multiple levels (page, article, section).

The <footer> element is part of the broader semantic HTML movement, complementing <header> to provide a clear beginning and end to sections.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <footer>
docs.text:
<footer>
    <!-- Concluding content -->
</footer>

docs.title: Simple Page Footer
docs.text:
<footer>
    <p>© 2026 My Website. All rights reserved.</p>
</footer>

docs.title: Footer with Contact Information
docs.text:
<footer>
    <p>© 2026 My Company</p>
    <address>
        Contact: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">info@example.com</a><br>
        123 Main Street, Anytown, USA
    </address>
</footer>

docs.title: Footer with Navigation Links
docs.text:
<footer>
    <nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/privacy">Privacy Policy</a></li>
            <li><a href="/terms">Terms of Service</a></li>
            <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
    <p>© 2026 My Company</p>
</footer>

docs.title: Footer Inside an Article
docs.text:
<article>
    <header>
        <h2>Article Title</h2>
        <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>
    </header>
    <p>Article content...</p>
    <footer>
        <p>Author: <a href="/author/jane">Jane Doe</a></p>
        <p>Tags: <a href="/tag/html">HTML</a>, <a href="/tag/semantics">Semantics</a></p>
    </footer>
</article>

docs.text:
<section>
    <header>
        <h3>Section Title</h3>
    </header>
    <p>Section content...</p>
    <footer>
        <p>Last updated: <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>
    </footer>
</section>

docs.title: Multiple Footers on a Page
docs.text:
<body>
    <header>...</header>
    <main>
        <article>
            <header>...</header>
            <p>Content...</p>
            <footer>
                <p>Author: Jane Doe</p>
            </footer>
        </article>

        <article>
            <header>...</header>
            <p>Content...</p>
            <footer>
                <p>Author: John Smith</p>
            </footer>
        </article>
    </main>
    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 My Website</p>
    </footer>
</body>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <footer> Marks the concluding content. Provides semantic meaning. <p> Copyright notice. Common footer content. <address> Contact information. Semantic element for contact details. <nav> Footer navigation links. Groups related links. <time> Machine-readable date. Enables parsing by machines.

docs.title: The "Book Colophon" Analogy
docs.text: Think of the <footer> element as the colophon of a book – the section at the end that contains information about the publication, copyright, author, and related works. Just as a colophon concludes a book, the footer concludes a web page or section.

docs.title: The "Letter Signature" Analogy
docs.text: A <footer> is like the signature block at the end of a letter. It contains the author's name, contact information, and perhaps a postscript. It signals the end of the main content and provides additional information.

docs.title: The "Movie Credits" Analogy
docs.text: Think of the <footer> as the end credits of a movie. It contains the copyright notice, production companies, contact information, and related links. It appears at the end, after the main content, and provides context about the production.

docs.title: Concept 1: The contentinfo Landmark
docs.text:
When <footer> is a direct child of <body> (or not nested inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section>), it creates a contentinfo landmark in the accessibility tree. Screen reader users can navigate directly to it using landmark navigation.

<body>
    <footer>
        <!-- This creates a contentinfo landmark -->
    </footer>
</body>

When <footer> is nested inside a sectioning element, it does not create a contentinfo landmark:

<article>
    <footer>
        <!-- No contentinfo landmark -->
    </footer>
</article>

docs.title: Concept 2: <footer> Is Not Restricted to the Bottom
docs.text:
Unlike the name suggests, <footer> can appear anywhere in the document. It represents concluding content for its nearest ancestor sectioning content. This means you can have multiple <footer> elements on a page.

<article>
    <header>Article Header</header>
    <p>Content...</p>
    <footer>Article Footer</footer>
</article>
<section>
    <header>Section Header</header>
    <p>Content...</p>
    <footer>Section Footer</footer>
</section>

docs.title: Concept 3: Content Model
docs.text:
The <footer> element accepts flow content, but it cannot contain another <header> or <footer> element. It also should not contain a <main> element.

<!-- Valid -->
<footer>
    <p>Copyright 2026</p>
    <address>Contact: info@example.com</address>
</footer>

<!-- Invalid: nested footer -->
<footer>
    <footer>Nested footer</footer>
</footer>

docs.title: Concept 4: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <footer> element has no default visual styling in most browsers. It behaves like a <div> by default:

footer {
    display: block;
}

This means you need to style it with CSS to achieve the desired appearance.

docs.title: Concept 5: <footer> vs <div class="footer">
docs.text: Aspect <footer> <div class="footer"> Semantic meaning Concluding content None Accessibility contentinfo landmark No landmark SEO Recognised by search engines Not recognised Styling No default styles No default styles Maintainability Self-documenting Depends on class names

docs.title: Concept 6: <footer> and <address>
docs.text:
The <address> element is commonly placed inside <footer> to provide contact information:

<footer>
    <address>
        Contact: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">info@example.com</a>
    </address>
</footer>

The <address> element is for contact information of the nearest <article> or the document. When inside a <footer> that is a direct child of <body>, it represents the site-wide contact information.

docs.title: Concept 7: <footer> and <header> Symmetry
docs.text:
The <header> and <footer> elements are often used together:

  • <header> – introductory content.
  • <footer> – concluding content.
<article>
    <header>
        <h2>Article Title</h2>
        <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>
    </header>
    <p>Article content...</p>
    <footer>
        <p>Author: Jane Doe</p>
    </footer>
</article>

docs.title: Concept 8: <footer> and ARIA
docs.text:
If you need to provide a label for a <footer> that is not a contentinfo landmark (e.g., inside an article), you can use aria-label:

<article>
    <footer aria-label="Article footer">
        <p>Author: Jane Doe</p>
    </footer>
</article>

However, this is rarely necessary because the content itself usually provides enough context.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <footer>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<footer>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content (flow content, excluding nested header/footer).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── display: block
    │
    ▼
6.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   ├── If it's a direct child of <body> → contentinfo landmark
    │   └── If nested → no landmark (but still semantic)
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
8.  Screen readers can navigate to the contentinfo landmark (if applicable).

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, <footer> is exposed as:

  • contentinfo – when it's a direct child of <body>.
  • generic – when nested inside an article or section (no landmark).
  • The content inside is exposed as regular text and elements.

docs.title: The Document Outline
docs.text: The <footer> element does not directly affect the document outline. The outline is determined by headings and sectioning elements.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
footer {
    display: block;
}

No other default styles are applied. You must use CSS for layout and appearance.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <footer> is represented by the HTMLElement interface. It has no specific properties or methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

const footer = document.querySelector('footer');
console.log(footer.textContent); // The text content
console.log(footer.innerHTML); // The HTML content

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
The browser's accessibility engine determines whether a <footer> creates a contentinfo landmark based on its position in the DOM:

  • Direct child of <body> → contentinfo landmark.
  • Inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section> → no landmark.

This is specified in the HTML-AAM (Accessibility API Mapping) specification.

docs.title: The contentinfo Landmark
docs.text: The contentinfo landmark is one of the ARIA landmark roles. It is used to identify the site-wide footer. Screen readers provide shortcuts to navigate to it.

docs.title: SEO and <footer>
docs.text:
Search engines use <footer> to identify:

  • Copyright information.
  • Contact details.
  • Related links.
  • Legal information (privacy policy, terms of service).

This can help with local business listings and understanding the site's structure.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <footer> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<footer>` element with concluding content.
    │   └── Example: <footer><p>© 2026</p></footer>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<footer>` node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── contentinfo landmark (if at top level).
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers can navigate to the contentinfo landmark.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines index the content.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the footer dynamically.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const footer = document.querySelector('footer');
footer.innerHTML = '<p>Updated copyright 2026</p>';
