docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Site-wide footer Copyright, contact, legal links Article footer Author info, publication date, tags Section footer Last updated date, related links Sidebar footer Sidebar conclusion Newsletter signup Email subscription form Social media links Links to social profiles Contact information Address, phone, email Legal information Privacy policy, terms of service Sitemap links Links to all pages Back-to-top link Link to scroll to top

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <footer> for concluding content – not for arbitrary containers.

  2. Place the site footer as a direct child of <body> – to create a contentinfo landmark.

  3. Use <footer> inside <article> and <section> – for article/section conclusions.

  4. Include contact information in <address> – inside the footer.

  5. Use <nav> for footer navigation – with aria-label.

  6. Don't nest <footer> inside another <footer> – it's invalid.

  7. Don't use <footer> for layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

  8. Style <footer> with CSS – it has no default styling.

  9. Keep the footer concise – too much content dilutes its purpose.

  10. Make navigation accessible – use <nav> with aria-label.

  11. Test with screen readers – ensure the contentinfo landmark is announced.

  12. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting.

  13. Consider mobile responsiveness – footers often need to adapt to small screens.

  14. Use <footer> for sticky footers – with CSS position: sticky or flexbox.

  15. Don't use <footer> for the entire page layout – it's for concluding content.

  16. Use <time> for dates – in the footer (e.g., last updated).

  17. Provide a way to navigate back to the top – a "back to top" link is common.

  18. Include a copyright notice – it's customary and often legally required.

  19. Link to privacy policy and terms of service – important for legal compliance.

  20. Test on different devices – ensure the footer looks good everywhere.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div class="footer"> Instead of <footer>
docs.text:
<div class="footer">
    <p>© 2026</p>
</div>
Why it's wrong: No semantic meaning; no contentinfo landmark.

✅ Correct: 

<footer>
    <p>© 2026</p>
</footer>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <footer> Inside <footer>
docs.text:
<footer>
    <footer>Nested footer</footer>
</footer>
Why it's wrong: Invalid nesting; confusing for machines.

✅ Correct: 

<footer>
    <p>Content</p>
</footer>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <footer> for Non-Concluding Content
docs.text:
<footer>
    <p>This is just a paragraph, not concluding content.</p>
</footer>
Why it's wrong: <footer> should contain concluding content, not arbitrary prose.

✅ Correct: 

<p>This is just a paragraph.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Top-Level <footer> Elements
docs.text:
<body>
    <footer>Footer 1</footer>
    <footer>Footer 2</footer>
</body>
Why it's wrong: Multiple top-level footers create multiple contentinfo landmarks, which is confusing.

✅ Correct: Use one top-level <footer> and nest others inside sectioning elements.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <footer> for Navigation Only
docs.text:
<footer>
    <nav>
        <a href="/">Home</a>
        <a href="/about">About</a>
    </nav>
</footer>
Why it's wrong: <footer> should contain concluding content, not just navigation. However, navigation inside a footer is fine as long as there is other content (e.g., copyright).

✅ Correct: 

<footer>
    <nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
    <p>© 2026 My Company</p>
</footer>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <footer> Without Any Content
docs.text:
<footer></footer>
Why it's wrong: An empty footer is meaningless.

✅ Correct: Include at least a copyright notice or contact information.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting <address> for Contact Information
docs.text:
<footer>
    <p>Contact: info@example.com</p>
</footer>
Why it's wrong: Contact information should be in an <address> element for semantics.

✅ Correct: 

<footer>
    <address>Contact: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">info@example.com</a></address>
</footer>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <footer> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • No default styles – no rendering cost beyond the content.
  • Accessibility tree – adds a landmark node, but the impact is minimal.
  • Sticky footers – position: sticky can cause performance issues if the footer is large or complex; test on low-end devices.
  • Complex layouts – using Flexbox or Grid inside <footer> has no significant performance impact.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <footer>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for target="_blank".
  • Contact forms – validate input on the server; don't rely on client-side validation alone.
  • No direct security implications – <footer> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <footer> to see its content and styles.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the contentinfo landmark.
  • Computed styles – check the display property (should be block by default).
  • Console – use document.querySelector('footer') to inspect the element.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting (footer inside footer).
  • Screen reader testing – navigate to the contentinfo landmark.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and semantic HTML.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For site-wide concluding content – copyright, contact, legal links.
  • For article footers – author info, publication date, tags.
  • For section footers – last updated date, related links.
  • For sidebar footers – sidebar conclusion.
  • For newsletter signup – email subscription form.
  • For social media links – links to social profiles.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For arbitrary containers – use <div>.
  • For main content – use <main>.
  • For headers – use <header>.
  • For navigation-only blocks – use <nav> (though <nav> inside <footer> is fine).
  • For every group of elements – only for concluding content.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <header> – introductory content.
  • <nav> – navigation.
  • <main> – primary content.
  • <article> – self-contained content.
  • <section> – thematic grouping.
  • <aside> – tangentially related content.
  • <address> – contact information.
  • ARIA Landmarks – banner, navigation, main, contentinfo.
  • Document Outline – headings and sectioning elements.
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <footer> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • A <footer> element creates a contentinfo landmark only when it is a direct child of <body>. When nested inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section>, it does not create a landmark.

  • You can have multiple <footer> elements on a page – one for the site, one for each article, one for each section.

  • The <footer> element does not have any default visual styling. It behaves like a <div> by default.

  • The <footer> element can contain flow content, but it cannot contain another <header> or <footer>.

  • The <footer> element is commonly used with <address> for contact information.

  • Screen readers like NVDA and JAWS allow users to jump to the contentinfo landmark using keyboard shortcuts.

  • The <footer> element is part of the semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more accessible and machine-readable.

  • Search engines use <footer> to identify copyright, contact, and legal information, which can help with local business listings.

  • The <footer> element is often styled with a dark background and light text for contrast.

  • A sticky footer (one that stays at the bottom of the viewport) can be created with CSS position: sticky or flexbox.

  • The <footer> element is not the same as the <address> element. <address> is for contact information; <footer> is for concluding content.

  • Some websites use <footer> for sitemap links – a list of all pages on the site.

  • The <footer> element can contain a newsletter signup form – a common pattern for collecting email addresses.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <footer> element represents concluding content for its nearest ancestor sectioning content or the document.
  • It is a block-level element and flow content.
  • It creates a contentinfo landmark when it is a direct child of <body>.
  • It can be used at multiple levels: page, article, section, aside.
  • Best practices: use <footer> for concluding content, place the site footer as a direct child of <body>, use <address> for contact information, use <nav> with aria-label for footer navigation, and style with CSS.
  • Common mistakes include using <div class="footer"> instead of <footer>, nesting <footer> inside <footer>, using multiple top-level footers, and forgetting <address> for contact information.
  • The <footer> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.
  • It is one of the most commonly used semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <main> element is a semantic HTML element that represents the dominant, primary content of the <body> of a document. It contains the content that is directly related to or expands upon the central topic of the page – the reason the user came to the site. The <main> element is designed to exclude content that is repeated across multiple pages, such as site headers, navigation menus, sidebars, footers, and copyright notices.

Crucially, the <main> element must be unique per document – there can be only one visible <main> element on a page at a time. It is a block-level element and flow content, and it creates a main landmark in the accessibility tree, allowing screen reader users to jump directly to the primary content.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <main> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Semantic clarity – identifies the primary content of the page, distinguishing it from repeated site-wide content.
  • Accessibility – creates a main landmark that screen reader users can navigate to directly (often with a "skip to main content" link).
  • SEO – helps search engines identify the most important content on the page, potentially improving rankings.
  • Readability – makes the document structure clearer for developers.
  • Styling – provides a hook for CSS to style the main content area.
  • Reader mode – browsers and extensions can use <main> to extract the primary content for distraction-free reading.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <main> element is a direct child of <body> (or a descendant of <body> that is not inside <article>, <aside>, <footer>, <header>, or <nav>). It should contain the unique content of the page – everything that is not repeated across the site.

<body>
    <header>
        <nav>...</nav>
    </header>
    <main>
        <h1>Page Title</h1>
        <p>Primary content...</p>
    </main>
    <footer>...</footer>
</body>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML5, there was no semantic way to identify the primary content of a page. Developers used <div id="main"> or <div class="content">, but these were invisible to machines. Screen reader users had to wade through navigation, headers, and sidebars on every page before reaching the main content – a tedious and frustrating experience. Search engines also struggled to distinguish the unique content from repeated boilerplate.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic main content element Machines couldn't identify primary content. <div id="main"> Class/ID names are invisible to machines; fragile. No main landmark Screen reader users couldn't skip to main content. Poor SEO Search engines couldn't distinguish unique content from boilerplate. No reader mode Browsers couldn't extract the primary content for distraction-free reading.

docs.title: Why <main> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <main> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standardised, semantic way to mark up the primary content of a page. It enables:

  • Clear semantics – machines understand which content is the primary focus.
  • Accessibility – creates a main landmark that screen readers can navigate to.
  • SEO – helps search engines identify the most important content.
  • Reader mode – enables browsers to extract the main content for clean reading.
  • Skip links – provides a target for "skip to main content" links.
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.

The <main> element is a cornerstone of the semantic HTML movement, ensuring that the most important content is clearly identified for all users and machines.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <main>
docs.text:
<main>
    <!-- Primary content -->
</main>

docs.title: Simple Page with <main>
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <header>
        <h1>My Website</h1>
        <nav>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
                <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
    </header>

    <main>
        <h1>Welcome to My Website</h1>
        <p>This is the primary content of the page.</p>
    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 My Website</p>
    </footer>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: <main> with <article>
docs.text:
<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Article Title</h1>
        <p>Article content...</p>
    </article>
    <article>
        <h1>Another Article</h1>
        <p>More content...</p>
    </article>
</main>

docs.title: <main> with Multiple Sections
docs.text:
<main>
    <section>
        <h2>Introduction</h2>
        <p>Introduction content...</p>
    </section>
    <section>
        <h2>Features</h2>
        <p>Features content...</p>
    </section>
    <section>
        <h2>Pricing</h2>
        <p>Pricing content...</p>
    </section>
</main>

docs.title: The hidden Attribute on <main>
docs.text:
You can have multiple <main> elements in a document, but only one should be visible at a time. Others should be hidden with the hidden attribute:

<main>
    <!-- Primary content -->
</main>
<main hidden>
    <!-- Alternate content (e.g., for different routes in an SPA) -->
</main>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <main> Marks the primary content. Provides semantic meaning and a landmark. Content The unique content of the page. Everything that is not repeated site-wide. hidden (optional) Hides alternate main content. Allows multiple <main> elements with only one visible.

docs.title: Common Mistakes in Syntax
docs.text:
• Placing <main> inside <article>, <aside>, <header>, <footer>, or <nav> – it must be a top-level element.
  • Having multiple visible <main> elements.
  • Including repeated content (header, nav, footer) inside <main>.

docs.title: The "Main Course" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a meal: the appetizer is the header (introduces the meal), the side dishes are the navigation and sidebars (complement the meal), the dessert is the footer (concludes the meal), and the main course is the <main> element (the reason you're there). Just as the main course is the centerpiece of a meal, <main> is the centerpiece of a web page.

docs.title: The "Newspaper Article" Analogy
docs.text: In a newspaper, the masthead (header), section navigation (nav), ads and sidebars (aside), and classifieds (footer) are repeated in every issue. The article itself – the news story you bought the paper to read – is the <main> content. It's the unique, primary content of that page.

docs.title: The "Movie Screen" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a movie theater: the marquee (header), concession stand (nav), posters (aside), and exit signs (footer) are all around the screen. The movie itself – the reason you bought a ticket – is the <main> content. It's the focus of the experience.

docs.title: Concept 1: The main Landmark
docs.text:
The <main> element creates a main landmark in the accessibility tree. Screen reader users can navigate directly to it, often via keyboard shortcuts (e.g., pressing M in NVDA) or a "skip to main content" link.

<main>
    <!-- This creates a main landmark -->
</main>

docs.title: Concept 2: One Visible <main> Per Document
docs.text:
The HTML specification requires that there be no more than one visible <main> element in a document at any given time. However, you can have multiple <main> elements if all but one have the hidden attribute:

<main>
    <!-- Visible main content -->
</main>
<main hidden>
    <!-- Hidden main content (e.g., for client-side routing) -->
</main>

This is useful for Single Page Applications (SPAs) where different routes might have different main content.

docs.title: Concept 3: <main> Is Not for Repeated Content
docs.text:
The <main> element should not contain content that is repeated across multiple pages, such as:

  • Site header
  • Navigation menu
  • Sidebars
  • Footer
  • Copyright notice
  • Logo

These should be outside <main>.

docs.title: Concept 4: Content Model
docs.text:
The <main> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Headings (<h1>–<h6>)
  • Paragraphs (<p>)
  • Articles (<article>)
  • Sections (<section>)
  • Images, videos, and other media
  • Forms

It cannot contain nested <main> elements (except when using hidden for SPAs).

docs.title: Concept 5: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <main> element has no default visual styling in most browsers. It behaves like a <div> by default:

main {
    display: block;
}

This means you need to style it with CSS to achieve the desired appearance.

docs.title: Concept 6: <main> vs <div id="main">
docs.text: Aspect <main> <div id="main"> Semantic meaning Primary content None Accessibility main landmark No landmark SEO Recognised by search engines Not recognised Styling No default styles No default styles Maintainability Self-documenting Depends on ID/class Reader mode Supported Not supported

docs.title: Concept 7: <main> and "Skip to Main Content"
docs.text:
The <main> element is a common target for "skip to main content" links, which allow keyboard and screen reader users to bypass navigation:

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

<header>...</header>

<main id="main-content">
    <!-- Primary content -->
</main>

The skip link is usually visually hidden until focused, then appears at the top of the page.

docs.title: Concept 8: <main> and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use <main> to identify the primary content of a page. This can help with:

  • Ranking – content inside <main> may be given more weight.
  • Featured snippets – search engines can extract the main content for snippets.
  • Understanding – search engines can distinguish the main content from boilerplate.

docs.title: Concept 9: <main> and Reader Mode
docs.text: Browsers and extensions (like Safari's Reader Mode, Firefox's Reader View) use <main> to extract the primary content of a page for distraction-free reading. Without <main>, they have to guess.

docs.title: Concept 10: <main> and ARIA
docs.text:
The <main> element has an implicit ARIA role of main. If you need to use a different element (e.g., a <div>), you can add role="main":

<div role="main">
    <!-- Primary content -->
</div>

However, using <main> is always preferred over adding role="main" to a <div>.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <main>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<main>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content (flow content).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── display: block
    │
    ▼
6.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   └── main landmark
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
8.  Screen readers can navigate to the main landmark.
    │
    ▼
9.  Search engines identify the primary content.
    │
    ▼
10. Reader mode can extract the main content.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text: In the accessibility tree, <main> is exposed as a main landmark. Screen readers provide shortcuts to navigate to it (e.g., M in NVDA, D then M in JAWS).

docs.title: The Document Outline
docs.text: The <main> element does not directly affect the document outline. The outline is determined by headings and sectioning elements. However, the content inside <main> contributes to the outline.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
main {
    display: block;
}

No other default styles are applied. You must use CSS for layout and appearance.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <main> is represented by the HTMLElement interface. It has no specific properties or methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

const main = document.querySelector('main');
console.log(main.textContent); // The text content
console.log(main.innerHTML); // The HTML content

docs.title: The main Landmark
docs.text: The main landmark is one of the ARIA landmark roles. It is used to identify the primary content of the document. The browser's accessibility engine maps <main> to the main role.

docs.title: The "One Visible <main>" Rule
docs.text: The HTML parser enforces the rule that there should be no more than one visible <main> element. If multiple <main> elements are present without hidden, the parser may still create multiple nodes, but the accessibility tree may only expose one. It's best to follow the rule explicitly.

docs.title: SEO and <main>
docs.text:
Search engines like Google use <main> to identify the primary content. This can influence:

  • Indexing – the main content is given more weight.
  • Ranking – content inside <main> may rank higher.
  • Featured snippets – the main content is more likely to be selected.

docs.title: Reader Mode
docs.text: Browsers' reader modes (Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View) use <main> (and other heuristics) to extract the primary content. This provides a clean, distraction-free reading experience.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <main> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<main>` element with primary content.
    │   └── Example: <main><h1>Title</h1><p>Content</p></main>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<main>` node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── main landmark.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers can navigate to the main landmark.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines identify the primary content.
    │
    ▼
9.  Reader mode can extract the main content.
    │
    ▼
10. JavaScript may modify the main content dynamically.
    │
    ▼
11. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const main = document.querySelector('main');
main.innerHTML = '<h1>New Content</h1><p>Updated...</p>';

Correct approach:

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Blog post Article content with comments Product page Product details, reviews, specifications Documentation API reference, guides, tutorials Landing page Hero section, features, call to action Contact page Contact form, address, map About page Company history, team, mission Search results List of results and pagination Dashboard Widgets, charts, data tables SPA views Different views for different routes

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <main> for primary content – not for repeated content.

  2. Place <main> as a direct child of <body> – not inside <article>, <aside>, <header>, <footer>, or <nav>.

  3. Have only one visible <main> per page – use hidden for alternate main content in SPAs.

  4. Include a heading inside <main> – typically <h1> for the page title.

  5. Use a "skip to main content" link – for accessibility.

  6. Don't put repeated content inside <main> – keep header, nav, and footer outside.

  7. Use <main> with <article> and <section> – for semantic structure.

  8. Style <main> with CSS – it has no default styling beyond display: block.

  9. Don't nest <main> inside another <main> – invalid.

  10. Use id on <main> for skip links – e.g., id="main-content".

  11. Test with screen readers – ensure the main landmark is announced.

  12. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting and the one-visible-<main> rule.

  13. Use <main> for SEO – search engines use it to identify primary content.

  14. Keep <main> focused – only content that is unique to the page.

  15. Consider reader mode – <main> enables distraction-free reading.

  16. Use <main> for accessibility – the main landmark is crucial for screen reader navigation.

  17. Don't use <main> for layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox for layout.

  18. Use <main> with semantic elements – <article>, <section>, <header>, <footer>.

  19. Ensure <main> is not hidden by default – it should be visible for the primary content.

  20. Test on different devices – ensure <main> looks good everywhere.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Visible <main> Elements
docs.text:
<main>Content 1</main>
<main>Content 2</main>
Why it's wrong: There should be only one visible <main> per document.

✅ Correct: 

<main>Content 1</main>
<main hidden>Content 2</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <main> Inside <article>
docs.text:
<article>
    <main>Content</main>
</article>
Why it's wrong: <main> should be a direct child of <body>, not nested inside <article>.

✅ Correct: 

<main>
    <article>Content</article>
</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Putting Repeated Content Inside <main>
docs.text:
<main>
    <header>Site Header</header>
    <nav>...</nav>
    <p>Content</p>
    <footer>Footer</footer>
</main>
Why it's wrong: <main> should not contain repeated content like headers, navigation, or footers.

✅ Correct: 

<header>Site Header</header>
<nav>...</nav>
<main>
    <p>Content</p>
</main>
<footer>Footer</footer>

docs.text:
<div id="main">
    <p>Content</p>
</div>

✅ Correct: 

<main>
    <p>Content</p>
</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Heading Inside <main>
docs.text:
<main>
    <p>Content without a heading.</p>
</main>
Why it's wrong: <main> should typically have a heading to identify the page's main topic.

✅ Correct: 

<main>
    <h1>Page Title</h1>
    <p>Content...</p>

docs.text:

    <nav>...</nav>
</header>
<main>Content</main>

✅ Correct: 

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>
<header>...</header>
<main id="main-content">Content</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <main> Inside <aside>
docs.text:
<aside>
    <main>Content</main>
</aside>
Why it's wrong: <main> is for the primary content of the page, not for sidebar content.

✅ Correct: 

<aside>
    <p>Sidebar content</p>
</aside>
<main>
    <p>Main content</p>
</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <main> Elements Without hidden
docs.text:
<main>Home</main>
<main>About</main>
<main>Contact</main>
Why it's wrong: Only one <main> should be visible at a time.

✅ Correct: 

<main id="home">Home</main>
<main id="about" hidden>About</main>
<main id="contact" hidden>Contact</main>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <main> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • No default styles – no rendering cost beyond the content.
  • Accessibility tree – adds a landmark node, but the impact is minimal.
  • Skip links – negligible performance impact.
  • SPA routing – toggling hidden on multiple <main> elements is fast.
  • Complex layouts – using Flexbox or Grid inside <main> has no significant performance impact.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <main>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for target="_blank".
  • Forms – validate input on the server; don't rely on client-side validation alone.
  • No direct security implications – <main> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <main> to see its content and styles.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the main landmark.
  • Computed styles – check the display property (should be block by default).
  • Console – use document.querySelector('main') to inspect the element.
  • Validator – check for multiple visible <main> elements and incorrect nesting.
  • Screen reader testing – navigate to the main landmark.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and semantic HTML.
  • Reader mode – test in Safari Reader or Firefox Reader View to see if the main content is extracted correctly.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For primary content – the unique content of the page.
  • For blog posts – article content.
  • For product pages – product details.
  • For documentation – API reference, guides.
  • For contact pages – contact forms.
  • For search results – list of results.
  • For SPA views – different views for different routes.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For repeated content – headers, navigation, footers, sidebars.
  • For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For sidebar content – use <aside>.
  • For navigation – use <nav>.
  • For article-specific content – use <article> inside <main>.
  • For multiple visible instances – only one visible <main> per page.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <body> – contains <main>.
  • <header> – introductory content.
  • <footer> – concluding content.
  • <nav> – navigation.
  • <article> – self-contained content.
  • <section> – thematic grouping.
  • <aside> – tangentially related content.
  • ARIA Landmarks – banner, navigation, main, contentinfo.
  • Skip Links – "Skip to main content."
  • Reader Mode – browser feature using <main>.
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <main> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • The <main> element creates a main landmark in the accessibility tree, allowing screen reader users to jump directly to the primary content.

  • There should be only one visible <main> element per document. You can have multiple <main> elements if all but one have the hidden attribute.

  • The <main> element is a common target for "skip to main content" links, which allow keyboard users to bypass navigation.

  • Search engines like Google use <main> to identify the primary content of a page, which can influence rankings.

  • Browser reader modes (Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View) use <main> (and other heuristics) to extract the primary content for distraction-free reading.

  • The <main> element should not contain content that is repeated across pages, such as headers, navigation, sidebars, or footers.

  • The <main> element has an implicit ARIA role of main. You can add role="main" to a <div>, but using <main> is preferred.

  • In a Single Page Application (SPA), you can have multiple <main> elements (one per route) and toggle the hidden attribute to show the active view.

  • The <main> element does not have any default visual styling. It behaves like a <div> by default.

  • The <main> element is part of the semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more accessible and machine-readable.

  • The <main> element is not the same as the <body> element. <body> contains everything; <main> contains only the primary content.

  • Screen readers like NVDA and JAWS allow users to jump to the main landmark using keyboard shortcuts.

  • The <main> element is essential for accessibility, SEO, and reader mode.

  • A "skip to main content" link is a best practice for accessibility – it allows keyboard users to bypass repetitive navigation.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <main> element represents the dominant, primary content of the <body> of a document.
  • It is a block-level element and flow content.
  • It creates a main landmark in the accessibility tree.
  • There should be only one visible <main> element per document.
  • It should not contain repeated content (header, nav, footer, sidebar).
  • Best practices: place <main> as a direct child of <body>, include a heading inside <main>, use a "skip to main content" link, and don't nest <main> inside other sectioning elements.
  • Common mistakes include multiple visible <main> elements, nesting <main> inside <article>, putting repeated content inside <main>, and using <div id="main"> instead of <main>.
  • The <main> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, SEO, and reader mode.
  • It is one of the most important semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <section> element is a semantic HTML element that represents a thematic grouping of content, typically with a heading. It is used to divide a document into logical, self-contained regions – such as chapters, tabs, or parts of a page – that share a common theme or purpose. A <section> is not a generic container; it carries the semantic meaning of "this content belongs together as a distinct unit."

The <section> element is a sectioning content element, meaning it contributes to the document outline (along with <article>, <nav>, and <aside>). It is flow content and palpable content, and it is a block-level element. When it has an accessible name (typically from a heading inside it), it creates a region landmark in the accessibility tree, allowing screen reader users to navigate directly to it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <section> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Semantic grouping – groups related content into a thematic unit.
  • Document structure – contributes to the document outline, making the page easier to navigate.
  • Accessibility – creates a region landmark when it has an accessible name, enabling screen reader navigation.
  • SEO – helps search engines understand the structure and topic of the page.
  • Styling – provides a meaningful hook for CSS to style distinct sections.
  • Maintainability – self-documenting code that clearly expresses intent.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <section> element is flow content and can appear inside <body>, <main>, <article>, <aside>, <section>, <div>, and other flow containers. It is most commonly used in:

  • Long articles – to break content into chapters or parts.
  • Landing pages – to group features, pricing, testimonials, and calls to action.
  • Documentation – to organise API references, guides, and tutorials.
  • Forms – to group related fields into logical units.
<main>
    <section>
        <h2>Introduction</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
    <section>
        <h2>Features</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
    <section>
        <h2>Pricing</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
</main>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML5, there was no semantic element for grouping content into thematic sections. Developers used <div> with class names like class="section", class="chapter", or class="part". While this worked visually, it provided no semantic meaning to machines. Screen readers couldn't identify the sections, search engines couldn't understand the structure, and the document outline was flat (determined only by headings).

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic grouping element Machines couldn't identify thematic units. <div class="section"> Class names are invisible to machines; fragile. Flat document outline Only headings provided structure; sections were invisible. No region landmark Screen reader users couldn't navigate to sections. Inconsistent styling Each developer used their own class names.

docs.title: Why <section> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <section> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standardised, semantic way to group content into thematic units. It enables:

  • Clear semantics – machines understand that the content forms a distinct section.
  • Document outline – sections contribute to the outline, making the page structure explicit.
  • Accessibility – creates a region landmark when it has an accessible name.
  • SEO – helps search engines understand the page's structure and topics.
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.
  • Maintainability – self-documenting code.

The <section> element is part of the broader semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more understandable to both humans and machines. It is distinct from <article> (which is for self-contained content) and <div> (which is non-semantic).

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <section>
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>Section Title</h2>
    <!-- Section content -->
</section>

docs.title: Simple Section with Heading
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>About Us</h2>
    <p>We are a company dedicated to...</p>
</section>

docs.title: Multiple Sections in an Article
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>How to Use Semantic HTML</h1>
    <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>

    <section>
        <h2>Introduction</h2>
        <p>Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that convey meaning...</p>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Benefits</h2>
        <p>Semantic HTML improves accessibility, SEO, and maintainability...</p>
        <h3>Accessibility</h3>
        <p>Screen readers can navigate by landmarks...</p>
        <h3>SEO</h3>
        <p>Search engines can identify the main content...</p>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Conclusion</h2>
        <p>Semantic HTML is essential for modern web development...</p>
    </section>
</article>

docs.title: Section with Sub-Sections
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>Chapter 1</h2>
    <p>...</p>

    <section>
        <h3>Section 1.1</h3>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h3>Section 1.2</h3>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
</section>

docs.title: Section with an Accessible Name
docs.text:
To create a region landmark, the <section> must have an accessible name. This can be provided by:

A heading inside the section (most common): 

<section>
    <h2>Contact Information</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</section>

aria-labelledby referencing a heading: 

<section aria-labelledby="contact-heading">
    <h2 id="contact-heading">Contact Information</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</section>

aria-label providing a direct label: 

<section aria-label="Contact Information">
    <p>...</p>
</section>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <section> Marks a thematic grouping. Provides semantic meaning and structure. <h2>–<h6> Heading for the section. Provides the section's title and accessible name. <p> Content inside the section. The actual content of the grouping. aria-labelledby References the heading for the accessible name. Creates a region landmark. aria-label Provides a direct label. Alternative to aria-labelledby.

docs.title: The "Book Chapters" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a <section> as a chapter in a book. A chapter groups related content under a single heading, and multiple chapters make up the book. Just as chapters give a book structure, <section> gives a web page structure. A chapter can have sub-sections (like sub-headings), and a book can have multiple chapters.

docs.title: The "Filing Cabinet" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a filing cabinet. Each drawer is a <section> – it groups related documents (content) under a label (heading). You can have folders inside drawers (sub-sections), and the cabinet (document) is organised into logical, navigable units.

docs.title: The "Department Store" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a department store. Each department (e.g., Men's Clothing, Electronics, Home Goods) is a <section> – it groups related products under a sign (heading). The store (document) is divided into sections, each with its own theme. You can navigate to a specific department to find what you need.

docs.title: Concept 1: Sectioning Content
docs.text:
The <section> element is sectioning content. This means:

  • It contributes to the document outline.
  • It can have its own heading hierarchy.
  • It is one of four sectioning elements: <section>, <article>, <nav>, <aside>.

docs.title: Concept 2: The region Landmark
docs.text:
When a <section> has an accessible name (from a heading, aria-labelledby, or aria-label), it creates a region landmark in the accessibility tree. Screen reader users can navigate to it using landmark navigation.

<!-- Creates a region landmark -->
<section>
    <h2>Contact</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</section>

<!-- No region landmark (no accessible name) -->
<section>
    <p>Content without a heading.</p>
</section>

Best practice: Always give <section> an accessible name (usually via a heading). Otherwise, it's just a generic container, and you should use <div> instead.

docs.title: Concept 3: <section> vs <div>
docs.text:
Aspect <section> <div> Semantic meaning Thematic grouping None Document outline Contributes to outline Does not contribute Accessibility region landmark (if named) No landmark Heading Should have a heading No heading required Use case Thematic groups of content Generic containers, styling

Rule: Use <section> for thematic groupings with a heading; use <div> for generic containers and styling-only wrappers.

docs.title: Concept 4: <section> vs <article>
docs.text:
Aspect <section> <article> Semantic meaning Thematic grouping Self-contained, distributable content Standalone Not necessarily Yes (could be syndicated) Examples Chapters, tabs, parts of a page Blog posts, news stories, comments Heading Typically has a heading Typically has a heading Syndication Not suitable Suitable

Rule: Use <article> for content that could stand alone (e.g., a blog post); use <section> for thematic groupings within a page or article.

docs.title: Concept 5: Content Model
docs.text:
The <section> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Headings (<h1>–<h6>)
  • Paragraphs (<p>)
  • Articles (<article>)
  • Nested sections (<section>)
  • Images, videos, and other media
  • Forms

docs.title: Concept 6: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <section> element has no default visual styling in most browsers. It behaves like a <div> by default:

section {
    display: block;
}

This means you need to style it with CSS to achieve the desired appearance.

docs.title: Concept 7: Sectioning and the Document Outline
docs.text:
The HTML5 outline algorithm was intended to create a document outline from sectioning elements, allowing each section to have its own <h1>. However, this algorithm is not widely implemented by browsers. In practice:

  • Use headings (<h1>–<h6>) to convey hierarchy.
  • Use <section> to group content thematically.
  • Don't rely on the outline algorithm for navigation.

docs.title: Concept 8: <section> and Accessibility
docs.text: For a <section> to be useful to screen reader users, it must have an accessible name. Without a name, it's just a generic container (like a <div>). The name is typically provided by a heading inside the section.

docs.title: Concept 9: <section> and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use <section> to understand the structure of a page. Content inside sections is grouped thematically, which can help search engines:

  • Identify the main topics of the page.
  • Understand the relationship between content blocks.
  • Improve the relevance of search results.

docs.title: Concept 10: When Not to Use <section>
docs.text:
• For styling only – use <div> instead.
  • For self-contained content – use <article> instead.
  • For navigation – use <nav> instead.
  • For sidebars – use <aside> instead.
  • Without a heading – if there's no heading, it's probably not a section; use <div>.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <section>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<section>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content (flow content).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── display: block
    │
    ▼
6.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   ├── If it has an accessible name → region landmark
    │   └── If no accessible name → generic (no landmark)
    │
    ▼
7.  The document outline is updated (in theory, though not widely implemented).
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
9.  Screen readers can navigate to the region landmark (if applicable).

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, <section> is exposed as:

  • region – when it has an accessible name (from a heading, aria-labelledby, or aria-label).
  • generic – when it has no accessible name.

The accessible name is usually derived from the first heading inside the section.

docs.title: The Document Outline Algorithm
docs.text: The HTML5 outline algorithm was designed to create a document outline from sectioning elements. However, it is not widely implemented by browsers. In practice, headings provide the primary structural cues.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
section {
    display: block;
}

No other default styles are applied. You must use CSS for layout and appearance.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <section> is represented by the HTMLElement interface. It has no specific properties or methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

const section = document.querySelector('section');
console.log(section.textContent); // The text content
console.log(section.innerHTML); // The HTML content

docs.title: The region Landmark
docs.text: The region landmark is one of the ARIA landmark roles. It is used to identify a section of the page that has an accessible name. The browser's accessibility engine maps <section> to the region role when it has an accessible name.

docs.title: How the Accessible Name Is Derived
docs.text:
The accessible name of a <section> is derived from:

  1. aria-labelledby – references another element that provides the name.
  2. aria-label – provides a direct name.
  3. The first heading inside the section (e.g., <h1>–<h6>).

If none of these are present, the section has no accessible name and does not create a region landmark.

docs.title: SEO and <section>
docs.text:
Search engines use <section> to understand the structure of a page. Content inside sections is grouped thematically, which can help search engines:

  • Identify the main topics of the page.
  • Understand the relationship between content blocks.
  • Improve the relevance of search results.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <section> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<section>` element with a heading and content.
    │   └── Example: <section><h2>Title</h2><p>Content</p></section>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<section>` node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── region landmark (if it has an accessible name).
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers can navigate to the region landmark (if applicable).
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines index the content with structural understanding.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the section dynamically.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const section = document.querySelector('section');
section.innerHTML = '<h2>New Title</h2><p>Updated content...</p>';

docs.title: Example 10: Section Without a Heading (Not Recommended)
docs.text:
<!-- Bad: no heading, no accessible name -->
<section>
    <p>This content is grouped but has no heading.</p>
</section>

Why it's not recommended: Without a heading, the section has no accessible name and does not create a region landmark. It should be a <div> instead.

✅ Correct: 

<div>
    <p>This content is grouped but has no heading.</p>
</div>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Long articles Breaking content into chapters Landing pages Hero, features, pricing, testimonials Documentation API reference, guides, tutorials Forms Grouping related fields Blog posts Introduction, main content, conclusion Product pages Description, specifications, reviews Tabs Each tab panel is a section Chapters Sub-sections within a chapter Contact pages Contact form, address, map About pages History, team, mission

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <section> for thematic groupings – not for generic containers.

  2. Always include a heading – <section> should have a heading (<h2>–<h6>) to provide an accessible name.

  3. Use headings to define the hierarchy – don't rely on the HTML5 outline algorithm (not widely implemented).

  4. Don't use <section> for styling only – use <div> if there's no semantic meaning.

  5. Don't use <section> for self-contained content – use <article> instead.

  6. Don't use <section> for navigation – use <nav> instead.

  7. Don't use <section> for sidebars – use <aside> instead.

  8. Use aria-labelledby or aria-label if there's no visible heading – to create a region landmark.

  9. Keep sections focused – one theme per section.

  10. Use id on sections for linking – e.g., #features, #pricing.

  11. Style <section> with CSS – it has no default styling beyond display: block.

  12. Test with screen readers – ensure the region landmark is announced.

  13. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting and accessible names.

  14. Use <section> with <article> – sections inside articles for chapters or parts.

  15. Use <section> with <main> – sections inside main for primary content groups.

  16. Avoid over-nesting – too many nested sections can be confusing.

  17. Don't use <section> without a heading – if there's no heading, use <div>.

  18. Consider SEO – sections help search engines understand the page structure.

  19. Use semantic headings inside sections – <h2>, <h3>, etc.

  20. Test on different devices – ensure sections look good everywhere.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <section> Without a Heading
docs.text:
<section>
    <p>Content without a heading.</p>
</section>
Why it's wrong: Without a heading, the section has no accessible name and does not create a region landmark. Use <div> instead.

✅ Correct: 

<div>
    <p>Content without a heading.</p>
</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <section> for Styling Only
docs.text:
<section class="card">
    <p>This is a card.</p>
</section>
Why it's wrong: If there's no thematic meaning, use <div> with a class.

✅ Correct: 

<div class="card">
    <p>This is a card.</p>
</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <section> for Self-Contained Content
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>Blog Post Title</h2>
    <p>Blog post content...</p>
</section>
Why it's wrong: Blog posts are self-contained and should use <article>.

✅ Correct: 

<article>
    <h2>Blog Post Title</h2>
    <p>Blog post content...</p>
</article>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <section> for Navigation
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>Navigation</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</section>
Why it's wrong: Navigation should use <nav>.

✅ Correct: 

<nav>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <section> for Sidebars
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
    </ul>
</section>
Why it's wrong: Sidebars should use <aside>.

✅ Correct: 

<aside>
    <h2>Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <section> Inside <section> Without Hierarchy
docs.text:
<section>
    <section>
        <section>
            <p>Deeply nested sections.</p>
        </section>
    </section>
</section>
Why it's wrong: Deeply nested sections without headings are confusing and unnecessary.

✅ Correct: Flatten the structure; use headings to define hierarchy.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <h1> Elements in Sections
docs.text:
<section>
    <h1>Section Title</h1>
</section>
<section>
    <h1>Another Section</h1>
</section>
Why it's wrong: Only one <h1> per page. Use <h2> for sections.

✅ Correct: 

<h1>Page Title</h1>
<section>
    <h2>Section Title</h2>
</section>
<section>
    <h2>Another Section</h2>
</section>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <section> for Non-Thematic Grouping
docs.text:
<section>
    <p>Just a random paragraph.</p>
</section>
Why it's wrong: There's no thematic grouping. Use <p> alone or a <div> if grouping is needed for styling.

✅ Correct: 

<p>Just a random paragraph.</p>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <section> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • No default styles – no rendering cost beyond the content.
  • Accessibility tree – adds a region landmark when it has an accessible name, but the impact is minimal.
  • Document outline – the outline algorithm is not widely implemented, so there's no significant performance cost.
  • Nesting – deeply nested sections can increase DOM size; keep it shallow.
  • CSS styling – complex styles on <section> may affect performance, but the impact is minimal.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <section>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for target="_blank".
  • No direct security implications – <section> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <section> to see its content and structure.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the region landmark (if it has an accessible name).
  • Computed styles – check the display property (should be block by default).
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('section') to list all sections.
  • Validator – check for sections without headings and other semantic issues.
  • Screen reader testing – navigate to the region landmark.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and semantic HTML.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For thematic groupings of content – chapters, parts of a page.
  • For landing pages – hero, features, pricing, testimonials.
  • For documentation – API reference, guides, tutorials.
  • For forms – grouping related fields.
  • For articles – breaking content into logical parts.
  • For blog posts – introduction, main content, conclusion.
  • For tabs – each tab panel is a section.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For generic containers – use <div>.
  • For self-contained content – use <article>.
  • For navigation – use <nav>.
  • For sidebars – use <aside>.
  • For styling only – use <div>.
  • Without a heading – if there's no heading, use <div>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <article> – self-contained content.
  • <nav> – navigation.
  • <aside> – tangentially related content.
  • <main> – primary content.
  • <header> – introductory content.
  • <footer> – concluding content.
  • <div> – generic container (non-semantic).
  • Document Outline – headings and sectioning elements.
  • ARIA Landmarks – region, main, navigation, etc.
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <section> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • A <section> element creates a region landmark in the accessibility tree only when it has an accessible name (from a heading, aria-labelledby, or aria-label).

  • The HTML5 outline algorithm was intended to allow multiple <h1> elements in sections, but it is not widely implemented by browsers. In practice, use one <h1> per page and <h2>–<h6> for sections.

  • The <section> element is not a generic container. If there's no thematic meaning, use <div>.

  • The <section> element is often confused with <article>. The key difference: <article> is self-contained and could be syndicated; <section> is a thematic grouping within a page or article.

  • Screen readers like NVDA and JAWS allow users to navigate to region landmarks using keyboard shortcuts.

  • Search engines use <section> to understand the structure of a page, which can improve SEO.

  • The <section> element has no default visual styling beyond display: block.

  • A <section> can contain other <section> elements, creating a hierarchy of sections.

  • The <section> element is part of the sectioning content category, along with <article>, <nav>, and <aside>.

  • The <section> element is commonly used in landing pages, documentation, and long-form articles.

  • Using <section> without a heading is a common mistake. If there's no heading, use <div>.

  • The <section> element can be styled with CSS to create visually distinct blocks.

  • The <section> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.

  • The <section> element is one of the most commonly used semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <section> element represents a thematic grouping of content, typically with a heading.
  • It is a sectioning content element and flow content.
  • It creates a region landmark in the accessibility tree when it has an accessible name.
  • It contributes to the document outline (in theory, though not widely implemented).
  • Best practices: always include a heading, use <section> for thematic groupings, don't use it for styling or generic containers, and use <article> for self-contained content.
  • Common mistakes include using <section> without a heading, using it for styling only, using it for self-contained content, and using it for navigation or sidebars.
  • The <section> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.
  • It is one of the most important semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <article> element is a semantic HTML element that represents a self-contained, independent, and distributable piece of content. It is content that could stand alone, detached from the rest of the page, and still make complete sense. Examples include a blog post, a news story, a forum post, a user comment, a product review, or a social media update.

The <article> element is a sectioning content element, meaning it contributes to the document outline (along with <section>, <nav>, and <aside>). It is flow content and palpable content, and it is a block-level element. An <article> can be nested inside another <article> (e.g., a comment on a blog post), and it can contain its own <header>, <footer>, <section>, and <aside> elements.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <article> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Semantic clarity – identifies self-contained content as distinct from the surrounding page.
  • Accessibility – creates an article landmark that screen reader users can navigate to.
  • SEO – helps search engines identify the primary content of the page, which can improve rankings.
  • Syndication – content inside <article> can be extracted and syndicated (e.g., RSS feeds).
  • Reader mode – browsers and extensions use <article> to extract the primary content for distraction-free reading.
  • Styling – provides a hook for CSS to style individual content pieces.
  • Maintainability – self-documenting code that clearly expresses intent.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <article> element is flow content and can appear inside <body>, <main>, <section>, <aside>, or another <article>. It is most commonly used in:

  • Blog posts – each post is an article.
  • News articles – each story is an article.
  • Forum posts – each thread or post is an article.
  • User comments – each comment is an article.
  • Product reviews – each review is an article.
  • Social media feeds – each post is an article.
  • Widgets – self-contained widgets can be articles.
<main>
    <article>
        <header>
            <h1>Blog Post Title</h1>
            <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>
        </header>
        <p>Blog post content...</p>
        <footer>
            <p>Author: Jane Doe</p>
        </footer>
    </article>
    <article>
        <header>
            <h1>Another Post</h1>
            <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-09">September 9, 2026</time></p>
        </header>
        <p>More content...</p>
    </article>
</main>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML5, there was no semantic element for self-contained content. Developers used <div class="post"> or <div class="article"> to mark up blog posts, news stories, and comments. While this worked visually, it provided no semantic meaning to machines. Screen readers couldn't identify individual articles, search engines couldn't distinguish the main content from boilerplate, and content couldn't be easily syndicated or extracted for reader mode.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic article element Machines couldn't identify self-contained content. <div class="post"> Class names are invisible to machines; fragile. No article landmark Screen reader users couldn't navigate between articles. Poor SEO Search engines couldn't distinguish articles from boilerplate. No syndication Content couldn't be easily extracted for RSS feeds. No reader mode Browsers couldn't extract articles for distraction-free reading.

docs.title: Why <article> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <article> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standardised, semantic way to mark up self-contained content. It enables:

  • Clear semantics – machines understand that the content is a self-contained unit.
  • Accessibility – creates an article landmark for screen reader navigation.
  • SEO – helps search engines identify the primary content of the page.
  • Syndication – content can be extracted for RSS/Atom feeds.
  • Reader mode – browsers can extract articles for clean reading.
  • Nesting – articles can be nested (e.g., comments on a blog post).
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.

The <article> element is part of the broader semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more understandable to both humans and machines.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <article>
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>Article Title</h1>
    <p>Article content...</p>
</article>

docs.title: Simple Blog Post
docs.text:
<article>
    <header>
        <h1>How to Use Semantic HTML</h1>
        <p>Published on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time> by <a href="/author/jane">Jane Doe</a></p>
    </header>
    <p>Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that convey meaning...</p>
    <footer>
        <p>Tags: <a href="/tag/html">HTML</a>, <a href="/tag/semantics">Semantics</a></p>
    </footer>
</article>

docs.title: Multiple Articles on a Page
docs.text:
<main>
    <article>
        <h2>First Post</h2>
        <p>Content of the first post...</p>
    </article>
    <article>
        <h2>Second Post</h2>
        <p>Content of the second post...</p>
    </article>
    <article>
        <h2>Third Post</h2>
        <p>Content of the third post...</p>
    </article>
</main>

docs.title: Nested Articles (Comments)
docs.text:
<article>
    <header>
        <h2>Blog Post Title</h2>
        <p>By Jane Doe on <time datetime="2026-09-08">September 8, 2026</time></p>
    </header>
    <p>The blog post content...</p>

    <section>
        <h3>Comments</h3>
        <article>
            <header>
                <h4>Comment by John</h4>
                <p>Posted on <time datetime="2026-09-08T14:30">September 8, 2026 at 2:30 PM</time></p>
            </header>
            <p>Great article!</p>
        </article>
        <article>
            <header>
                <h4>Comment by Alice</h4>
                <p>Posted on <time datetime="2026-09-08T15:00">September 8, 2026 at 3:00 PM</time></p>
            </header>
            <p>Very helpful, thanks!</p>
        </article>
    </section>
</article>

docs.title: Article Inside a Section
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>Latest News</h2>
    <article>
        <h3>News Story 1</h3>
        <p>...</p>
    </article>
    <article>
        <h3>News Story 2</h3>
        <p>...</p>
    </article>
</section>

docs.title: Article with Sections
docs.text:
<article>
    <header>
        <h1>Complete Guide to HTML Semantics</h1>
    </header>

    <section>
        <h2>Introduction</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Benefits</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Conclusion</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>

    <footer>
        <p>Author: Jane Doe</p>
    </footer>
</article>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <article> Marks a self-contained piece of content. Provides semantic meaning and a landmark. <header> Introductory content for the article. Article title, author, publication date. <h1>–<h6> Article title. Defines the article's topic. <section> Thematic groupings within the article. Chapters, parts, or logical divisions. <footer> Concluding content for the article. Author info, tags, related links. <time> Machine-readable publication date. Enables parsing by machines.

docs.title: The "Newspaper Article" Analogy
docs.text: Think of an <article> as a newspaper article. It has a headline, a byline, a publication date, body content, and possibly tags or related links. It could be cut out of the newspaper and still make sense on its own. Multiple articles appear on a single page, and each is self-contained.

docs.title: The "Magazine Feature" Analogy
docs.text: A magazine has multiple features, each with its own title, author, and content. Each feature is an <article> – it could be read independently, shared with a friend, or syndicated to another publication. The magazine itself is the container (the <main> or <body>), and each feature is a self-contained unit.

docs.title: The "Social Media Post" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a social media feed. Each post is an <article> – it has an author, a timestamp, content (text, images, video), and possibly comments (nested articles). Each post is self-contained and could be shared or embedded elsewhere. The feed (the page) contains multiple articles.

docs.title: The "Forum Thread" Analogy
docs.text: In a forum, the original post is an <article>, and each reply is also an <article>. They are nested: the replies are inside the thread, which is inside the forum. Each reply is self-contained and could be quoted or linked to directly.

docs.title: Concept 1: Self-Contained Content
docs.text:
The defining characteristic of an <article> is that it is self-contained – it could be removed from the page and still make sense. Ask yourself: "Could this content be syndicated in an RSS feed?" If yes, it's an <article>.

Examples of self-contained content: - Blog posts - News stories - Forum posts - User comments - Product reviews - Social media updates

Examples of content that is not self-contained: - A navigation menu - A sidebar with related links - A site header - A footer with copyright information - A section of a larger article (unless it's also self-contained)

docs.title: Concept 2: The article Landmark
docs.text:
The <article> element creates an article landmark in the accessibility tree. Screen reader users can navigate between articles using landmark navigation.

<article>
    <!-- This creates an article landmark -->
</article>

Unlike the main landmark (which should only appear once per page), you can have multiple article landmarks on a page.

docs.title: Concept 3: Nesting Articles
docs.text:
Articles can be nested inside other articles. This is common for:

  • Comments on a blog post – the post is an article, each comment is a nested article.
  • Replies to a forum post – the original post is an article, each reply is a nested article.
  • Reviews on a product page – the product is not an article, but each review is an article.
<article>
    <h2>Blog Post</h2>
    <p>...</p>
    <article>
        <h3>Comment 1</h3>
        <p>...</p>
    </article>
    <article>
        <h3>Comment 2</h3>
        <p>...</p>
    </article>
</article>

docs.title: Concept 4: <article> vs <section>
docs.text:
Aspect <article> <section> Semantic meaning Self-contained, distributable content Thematic grouping of content Standalone Yes (could be syndicated) Not necessarily Nesting Can be nested Can be nested Examples Blog posts, news, comments Chapters, tabs, parts of a page Heading Typically has a heading Should have a heading Syndication Suitable Not suitable Landmark article region (if named)

Rule: Use <article> for content that could stand alone; use <section> for thematic groupings within a page or article.

docs.title: Concept 5: <article> vs <div>
docs.text:
Aspect <article> <div> Semantic meaning Self-contained content None Accessibility article landmark No landmark SEO Recognised by search engines Not recognised Syndication Suitable Not suitable Reader mode Supported Not supported Use case Blog posts, news, comments Generic containers, styling

Rule: Use <article> for self-contained content; use <div> for generic containers and styling.

docs.title: Concept 6: Content Model
docs.text:
The <article> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Headings (<h1>–<h6>)
  • Paragraphs (<p>)
  • Sections (<section>)
  • Nested articles (<article>)
  • Headers and footers (<header>, <footer>)
  • Asides (<aside>)
  • Images, videos, and other media
  • Forms

docs.title: Concept 7: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <article> element has no default visual styling in most browsers. It behaves like a <div> by default:

article {
    display: block;
}

This means you need to style it with CSS to achieve the desired appearance.

docs.title: Concept 8: <article> and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use <article> to identify the primary content of a page. This can help with:

  • Ranking – content inside <article> may be given more weight.
  • Featured snippets – search engines can extract the article content for snippets.
  • Rich results – articles can be marked up with structured data (e.g., Article schema).

docs.title: Concept 9: <article> and Syndication
docs.text: Content inside <article> is suitable for syndication (RSS/Atom feeds). The article's title, author, publication date, and content can be extracted and republished elsewhere.

docs.title: Concept 10: <article> and Reader Mode
docs.text: Browsers and extensions (like Safari's Reader Mode, Firefox's Reader View) use <article> (and other heuristics) to extract the primary content of a page for distraction-free reading. Without <article>, they have to guess.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <article>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters an `<article>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content (flow content).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── display: block
    │
    ▼
6.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   └── article landmark
    │
    ▼
7.  The document outline is updated (in theory, though not widely implemented).
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
9.  Screen readers can navigate to the article landmark.
    │
    ▼
10. Search engines identify the article content.
    │
    ▼
11. Reader mode can extract the article content.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text: In the accessibility tree, <article> is exposed as an article landmark. Screen readers provide shortcuts to navigate between articles (e.g., A in NVDA).

docs.title: The Document Outline Algorithm
docs.text: The HTML5 outline algorithm was designed to create a document outline from sectioning elements. Articles contribute to this outline, but the algorithm is not widely implemented by browsers. In practice, headings provide the primary structural cues.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
article {
    display: block;
}

No other default styles are applied. You must use CSS for layout and appearance.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <article> is represented by the HTMLElement interface. It has no specific properties or methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

const article = document.querySelector('article');
console.log(article.textContent); // The text content
console.log(article.innerHTML); // The HTML content

docs.title: The article Landmark
docs.text: The article landmark is one of the ARIA landmark roles. It is used to identify a self-contained piece of content. The browser's accessibility engine maps <article> to the article role.

docs.title: Multiple Article Landmarks
docs.text: Unlike the main landmark, you can have multiple article landmarks on a page. Each <article> creates its own landmark in the accessibility tree.

docs.title: SEO and <article>
docs.text:
Search engines like Google use <article> to identify the primary content of a page. This can influence:

  • Indexing – the article content is given more weight.
  • Ranking – articles may rank higher for relevant queries.
  • Featured snippets – article content is more likely to be selected.
  • Rich results – articles can be marked up with structured data.

docs.title: Reader Mode
docs.text: Browsers' reader modes (Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View) use <article> (and other heuristics) to extract the primary content. This provides a clean, distraction-free reading experience.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an <article> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<article>` element with self-contained content.
    │   └── Example: <article><h1>Title</h1><p>Content</p></article>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<article>` node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── article landmark.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers can navigate to the article landmark.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines identify the article content.
    │
    ▼
9.  Reader mode can extract the article content.
    │
    ▼
10. JavaScript may modify the article dynamically.
    │
    ▼
11. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const article = document.querySelector('article');
article.innerHTML = '<h1>New Title</h1><p>Updated content...</p>';

docs.title: Example 4: Blog Post with Comments (Nested Articles)
docs.text:
<article>

    </header>

    <section>

                <h3>John</h3>
                <p><time datetime="2026-09-08T14:30">September 8, 2026 at 2:30 PM</time></p>
            </header>
