docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Blog posts Each post is an article News stories Each story is an article Forum posts Each thread or post is an article User comments Each comment is a nested article Product reviews Each review is an article Social media posts Each post is an article Widgets Self-contained widgets RSS feeds Articles are syndicated Reader mode Articles are extracted Documentation Each guide or tutorial

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <article> for self-contained content – content that could stand alone.

  2. Ask: "Could this be syndicated?" – if yes, it's an article.

  3. Include a heading – <article> should have a heading (<h1>–<h6>).

  4. Use <header> and <footer> – for article metadata and concluding content.

  5. Use <time> for dates – with datetime for machine readability.

  6. Nest articles for comments/replies – each comment is an article.

  7. Don't use <article> for navigation – use <nav>.

  8. Don't use <article> for sidebars – use <aside>.

  9. Don't use <article> for generic containers – use <div>.

  10. Use <section> for thematic groupings within an article.

  11. Use structured data – for SEO (e.g., Article schema).

  12. Style <article> with CSS – it has no default styling beyond display: block.

  13. Test with screen readers – ensure the article landmark is announced.

  14. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting and headings.

  15. Use <main> for the primary content – articles go inside <main>.

  16. Keep articles focused – one topic per article.

  17. Use id on articles for linking – e.g., #post-1.

  18. Consider SEO – articles help search engines understand the page.

  19. Use semantic headings inside articles – <h1>, <h2>, etc.

  20. Test on different devices – ensure articles look good everywhere.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <article> for Navigation
docs.text:
<article>
    <h2>Navigation</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</article>
Why it's wrong: Navigation should use <nav>.

✅ Correct: 

<nav>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <article> for Sidebars
docs.text:
<article>
    <h2>Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
    </ul>
</article>
Why it's wrong: Sidebars should use <aside>.

✅ Correct: 

<aside>
    <h2>Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <article> for Styling Only
docs.text:
<article class="card">
    <p>This is a card.</p>
</article>
Why it's wrong: If there's no self-contained content, use <div> with a class.

✅ Correct: 

<div class="card">
    <p>This is a card.</p>
</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <article> Without a Heading
docs.text:
<article>
    <p>Content without a heading.</p>
</article>
Why it's wrong: Articles should have a heading to identify their topic.

✅ Correct: 

<article>
    <h2>Article Title</h2>
    <p>Content...</p>
</article>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Nesting Articles for Comments
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>Blog Post</h1>
    <p>Content...</p>
</article>
<div class="comment">
    <p>Great post!</p>
</div>
Why it's wrong: Comments are self-contained and should be nested articles.

✅ Correct: 

<article>
    <h1>Blog Post</h1>
    <p>Content...</p>
    <article>
        <h2>Comment</h2>
        <p>Great post!</p>
    </article>
</article>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <article> for Sections
docs.text:
<article>
    <h2>Introduction</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</article>
<article>
    <h2>Features</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</article>
Why it's wrong: If these are parts of a larger article, use <section>.

✅ Correct: 

<article>
    <h1>Main Article</h1>
    <section>
        <h2>Introduction</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
    <section>
        <h2>Features</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
</article>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <h1> Elements in Articles
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>Article 1</h1>
</article>
<article>
    <h1>Article 2</h1>
</article>
Why it's wrong: Only one <h1> per page. Use <h2> for multiple articles.

✅ Correct: 

<h1>My Blog</h1>
<article>
    <h2>Article 1</h2>
</article>
<article>
    <h2>Article 2</h2>
</article>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <article> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • No default styles – no rendering cost beyond the content.
  • Accessibility tree – adds an article landmark, but the impact is minimal.
  • Nesting – deeply nested articles can increase DOM size; keep it reasonable.
  • CSS styling – complex styles on <article> may affect performance, but the impact is minimal.
  • Reader mode – no performance cost; it's a browser feature.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <article>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for target="_blank".
  • User comments – sanitize all user-generated content to prevent XSS.
  • No direct security implications – <article> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <article> to see its content and structure.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the article landmark.
  • Computed styles – check the display property (should be block by default).
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('article') to list all articles.
  • Validator – check for articles without headings and other semantic issues.
  • Screen reader testing – navigate to the article landmark.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and semantic HTML.
  • Reader mode – test in Safari Reader or Firefox Reader View.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For self-contained content – blog posts, news stories, comments.
  • For content that could be syndicated – RSS/Atom feeds.
  • For user-generated content – comments, reviews, forum posts.
  • For widgets – self-contained widgets.
  • For social media posts – each post is an article.
  • For product reviews – each review is an article.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For navigation – use <nav>.
  • For sidebars – use <aside>.
  • For generic containers – use <div>.
  • For thematic groupings – use <section>.
  • For the primary content of a page – use <main>.
  • For introductory content – use <header>.
  • For concluding content – use <footer>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <main> – primary content of the page.
  • <section> – thematic grouping of content.
  • <nav> – navigation.
  • <aside> – tangentially related content.
  • <header> – introductory content.
  • <footer> – concluding content.
  • Document Outline – headings and sectioning elements.
  • ARIA Landmarks – article, main, navigation, etc.
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.
  • Structured Data – Article schema for SEO.
  • RSS/Atom Feeds – syndication formats.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <article> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • An <article> creates an article landmark in the accessibility tree. Unlike main, you can have multiple article landmarks on a page.

  • The key question to ask when deciding whether to use <article> is: "Could this content be syndicated in an RSS feed?" If yes, it's an article.

  • Articles can be nested – a blog post is an article, and each comment is a nested article.

  • The <article> element is often confused with <section>. The key difference: <article> is self-contained and distributable; <section> is a thematic grouping within a page or article.

  • Search engines like Google use <article> to identify the primary content of a page, which can influence rankings.

  • Browser reader modes (Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View) use <article> (and other heuristics) to extract the primary content for distraction-free reading.

  • The <article> element has no default visual styling beyond display: block.

  • A <article> can contain its own <header>, <footer>, <section>, and <aside> elements.

  • The <article> element is part of the sectioning content category, along with <section>, <nav>, and <aside>.

  • The <article> element is commonly used in blog posts, news sites, forums, and social media feeds.

  • Structured data (e.g., itemprop="articleBody") can be added to <article> for rich results in search engines.

  • The <article> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, SEO, and syndication.

  • The <article> element is one of the most commonly used semantic elements in modern web development.

  • The <article> element can be styled with CSS to create visually distinct content blocks.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <article> element represents a self-contained, independent, and distributable piece of content.
  • It is a sectioning content element and flow content.
  • It creates an article landmark in the accessibility tree.
  • Multiple <article> elements can appear on a page.
  • Articles can be nested (e.g., comments on a blog post).
  • Best practices: use <article> for self-contained content, include a heading, use <header> and <footer> for metadata, nest articles for comments, and use structured data for SEO.
  • Common mistakes include using <article> for navigation, sidebars, or generic containers; using it without a heading; and not nesting articles for comments.
  • The <article> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, SEO, and syndication.
  • It is one of the most important semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <aside> element is a semantic HTML element that represents a portion of a document whose content is tangentially related to the content around it. In other words, it contains content that is related but not essential to the main flow — information that could be removed without significantly affecting the primary message of the page.

Think of <aside> as the "by the way" content: sidebars, pull quotes, related links, advertisements, author bios, fun facts, glossary terms, or supplementary information. It is content that complements the main content but is not part of its direct narrative.

The <aside> element is a sectioning content element, meaning it contributes to the document outline (along with <section>, <article>, and <nav>). It is flow content and palpable content, and it is a block-level element. When it has an accessible name (from a heading or ARIA label), it creates a complementary landmark in the accessibility tree, allowing screen reader users to navigate directly to it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <aside> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Semantic clarity – identifies content that is related to but separate from the main content.
  • Accessibility – creates a complementary landmark when it has an accessible name.
  • Document structure – contributes to the document outline.
  • SEO – helps search engines distinguish main content from supplementary content.
  • Styling – provides a meaningful hook for CSS to style sidebars and supplementary content.
  • Maintainability – self-documenting code that clearly expresses the role of the content.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <aside> element is flow content and can appear inside <body>, <main>, <article>, <section>, or another <aside>. It is most commonly used in:

  • Sidebars – related links, advertisements, author bios.
  • Pull quotes – highlighted quotes from an article.
  • Fun facts – tangential information related to the content.
  • Glossary terms – definitions of terms used in the content.
  • Related articles – links to other content on the site.
  • Author bios – information about the author of an article.
<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Article Title</h1>
        <p>Main content...</p>

        <aside>
            <h2>Related Links</h2>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="#">Link 1</a></li>
                <li><a href="#">Link 2</a></li>
            </ul>
        </aside>
    </article>
</main>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML5, there was no semantic element for tangentially related content. Developers used <div class="sidebar"> or <div class="related"> to mark up sidebars, pull quotes, and supplementary information. While this worked visually, it provided no semantic meaning to machines. Screen readers couldn't identify the sidebar as a landmark, search engines couldn't distinguish supplementary content from main content, and the markup was fragile (dependent on class names).

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic aside element Machines couldn't identify supplementary content. <div class="sidebar"> Class names are invisible to machines; fragile. No complementary landmark Screen reader users couldn't jump to the sidebar. Poor SEO Search engines couldn't distinguish main from supplementary content. Inconsistent styling Each developer used their own class names.

docs.title: Why <aside> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <aside> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standardised, semantic way to mark up tangentially related content. It enables:

  • Clear semantics – machines understand that the content is supplementary.
  • Accessibility – creates a complementary landmark for screen reader navigation.
  • SEO – helps search engines distinguish main content from sidebars and related links.
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.
  • Document outline – contributes to the outline, making the structure explicit.
  • Styling – provides a meaningful hook for CSS.

The <aside> element is part of the broader semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more understandable to both humans and machines.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <aside>
docs.text:
<aside>
    <h2>Aside Title</h2>
    <!-- Supplementary content -->
</aside>

docs.title: Simple Sidebar
docs.text:
<aside>
    <h2>Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">How to Use Semantic HTML</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Understanding ARIA Landmarks</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">HTML5 Sectioning Elements</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>

docs.title: Pull Quote
docs.text:
<aside>
    <blockquote>
        <p>The best way to predict the future is to invent it.</p>
        <footer>— Alan Kay</footer>
    </blockquote>
</aside>

docs.title: Author Bio
docs.text:
<aside>
    <h2>About the Author</h2>
    <img src="author.jpg" alt="Jane Doe" width="100" height="100">
    <p>Jane Doe is a web developer with 10 years of experience. She writes about HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.</p>
</aside>

docs.title: Aside Inside an Article
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>How to Use Semantic HTML</h1>
    <p>Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that convey meaning...</p>

    <aside>
        <h2>Did You Know?</h2>
        <p>The `<aside>` element was introduced in HTML5 to mark up content that is tangentially related to the main content.</p>
    </aside>

    <p>More main content...</p>
</article>

docs.title: Aside with a Heading and an Accessible Name
docs.text:
<aside aria-labelledby="related-heading">
    <h2 id="related-heading">Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>

docs.title: Aside with aria-label
docs.text:
<aside aria-label="Advertisement">
    <p>Sponsored content...</p>
</aside>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <aside> Marks supplementary content. Provides semantic meaning and a landmark. <h2>–<h6> Heading for the aside. Provides the aside's title and accessible name. <ul> List of related links. Common aside content. <blockquote> Pull quote. Common aside content. <img> Author image. Common in author bios. aria-labelledby References the heading for the accessible name. Creates a complementary landmark. aria-label Provides a direct label. Alternative to aria-labelledby.

docs.title: The "Sidebar" Analogy
docs.text: Think of an <aside> as a sidebar in a newspaper or magazine. It runs alongside the main article and contains related information, quotes, or advertisements. It's not essential to the main story, but it adds context and value. If you removed the sidebar, the main article would still make sense.

docs.title: The "Margin Notes" Analogy
docs.text: In a textbook, there are often margin notes — small boxes or notes in the margins that provide additional information, definitions, or related facts. They are tangentially related to the main text but not part of the main narrative. The <aside> element serves the same purpose on the web.

docs.title: The "Conversation Aside" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a conversation where someone says, "By the way..." — they're adding a tangential point that's related but not essential to the main topic. That's an <aside>. It's a "by the way" content block.

docs.title: Concept 1: Tangentially Related Content
docs.text:
The defining characteristic of <aside> is that its content is tangentially related to the surrounding content. It's not the main point, but it's related. Ask yourself: "If I removed this content, would the main content still make sense?" If yes, it could be an <aside>.

Examples of tangentially related content:

  • Related articles or links
  • Pull quotes
  • Author bios
  • Advertisements
  • Fun facts
  • Glossary terms
  • Sidebars with supplementary information
  • Biographical information
  • Bibliography or references

docs.title: Concept 2: The complementary Landmark
docs.text:
When an <aside> has an accessible name (from a heading, aria-labelledby, or aria-label), it creates a complementary landmark in the accessibility tree. Screen reader users can navigate to it using landmark navigation.

<!-- Creates a complementary landmark -->
<aside>
    <h2>Related Links</h2>
    <ul>...</ul>
</aside>

<!-- No complementary landmark (no accessible name) -->
<aside>
    <p>Some supplementary content.</p>
</aside>

Best practice: Give <aside> an accessible name when it's a significant region of the page (e.g., a sidebar). For minor asides (e.g., a pull quote), a name may not be necessary.

docs.title: Concept 3: <aside> vs <div>
docs.text:
Aspect <aside> <div> Semantic meaning Supplementary content None Accessibility complementary landmark (if named) No landmark SEO Recognised by search engines Not recognised Use case Sidebars, pull quotes, related links Generic containers, styling

Rule: Use <aside> for supplementary content; use <div> for generic containers and styling.

docs.title: Concept 4: <aside> vs <section>
docs.text:
Aspect <aside> <section> Semantic meaning Supplementary content Thematic grouping of content Relation to main content Tangential Part of the main content Examples Sidebars, pull quotes, related links Chapters, parts of an article Landmark complementary region (if named)

Rule: Use <aside> for content that is tangential to the main content; use <section> for content that is part of the main content.

docs.title: Concept 5: Content Model
docs.text:
The <aside> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Headings (<h1>–<h6>)
  • Paragraphs (<p>)
  • Lists (<ul>, <ol>)
  • Blockquotes (<blockquote>)
  • Images, videos, and other media
  • Forms
  • Sections

docs.title: Concept 6: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <aside> element has no default visual styling in most browsers. It behaves like a <div> by default:

aside {
    display: block;
}

This means you need to style it with CSS to achieve the desired appearance.

docs.title: Concept 7: <aside> Inside vs Outside <main>
docs.text:
The <aside> element can appear:

  • Inside <main> – as a sidebar or supplementary content within the main content area.
  • Outside <main> – as a sidebar that runs alongside the main content.
<!-- Inside main -->
<main>
    <article>...</article>
    <aside>Sidebar</aside>
</main>

<!-- Outside main -->
<main>
    <article>...</article>
</main>
<aside>Sidebar</aside>

The choice depends on the layout and the relationship of the aside to the main content.

docs.title: Concept 8: <aside> and ARIA
docs.text:
If you need to provide a label for an <aside> that isn't derived from a heading, you can use aria-label or aria-labelledby:

<aside aria-label="Advertisement">
    <p>Sponsored content...</p>
</aside>

docs.title: Concept 9: <aside> and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use <aside> to identify supplementary content. This helps them:

  • Distinguish main content from sidebars and related links.
  • Understand the primary topic of the page.
  • Avoid indexing supplementary content as the main content.

docs.title: Concept 10: <aside> and Reader Mode
docs.text: Browsers and extensions (like Safari's Reader Mode, Firefox's Reader View) often ignore <aside> content when extracting the main article. This is because <aside> is supplementary and not part of the main narrative.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <aside>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters an `<aside>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content (flow content).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── display: block
    │
    ▼
6.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   ├── If it has an accessible name → complementary landmark
    │   └── If no accessible name → generic (no landmark)
    │
    ▼
7.  The document outline is updated (in theory, though not widely implemented).
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
9.  Screen readers can navigate to the complementary landmark (if applicable).
    │
    ▼
10. Search engines identify the aside as supplementary content.
    │
    ▼
11. Reader mode may ignore the aside when extracting the main article.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, <aside> is exposed as:

  • complementary – when it has an accessible name.
  • generic – when it has no accessible name.

The accessible name is usually derived from the first heading inside the aside, or from aria-labelledby or aria-label.

docs.title: The Document Outline Algorithm
docs.text: The HTML5 outline algorithm was designed to create a document outline from sectioning elements. Asides contribute to this outline, but the algorithm is not widely implemented by browsers. In practice, headings provide the primary structural cues.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
aside {
    display: block;
}

No other default styles are applied. You must use CSS for layout and appearance.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <aside> is represented by the HTMLElement interface. It has no specific properties or methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

const aside = document.querySelector('aside');
console.log(aside.textContent); // The text content
console.log(aside.innerHTML); // The HTML content

docs.title: The complementary Landmark
docs.text: The complementary landmark is one of the ARIA landmark roles. It is used to identify a section of the page that supports the main content but is not essential to it. The browser's accessibility engine maps <aside> to the complementary role when it has an accessible name.

docs.title: How the Accessible Name Is Derived
docs.text:
The accessible name of an <aside> is derived from:

  1. aria-labelledby – references another element that provides the name.
  2. aria-label – provides a direct name.
  3. The first heading inside the aside (e.g., <h1>–<h6>).

If none of these are present, the aside has no accessible name and does not create a complementary landmark.

docs.title: SEO and <aside>
docs.text:
Search engines use <aside> to distinguish supplementary content from main content. This helps them:

  • Identify the primary content of the page.
  • Avoid indexing sidebars and related links as the main content.
  • Improve the relevance of search results.

docs.title: Reader Mode
docs.text: Browsers' reader modes (Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View) often ignore <aside> content when extracting the main article. This is because <aside> is supplementary and not part of the main narrative.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an <aside> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<aside>` element with supplementary content.
    │   └── Example: <aside><h2>Related Links</h2><ul>...</ul></aside>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<aside>` node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── complementary landmark (if it has an accessible name).
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers can navigate to the complementary landmark (if applicable).
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines identify the aside as supplementary content.
    │
    ▼
9.  Reader mode may ignore the aside.
    │
    ▼
10. JavaScript may modify the aside dynamically.
    │
    ▼
11. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const aside = document.querySelector('aside');
aside.innerHTML = '<h2>New Links</h2><ul>...</ul>';

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Sidebar
docs.text:
<aside>
    <h2>Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">How to Use Semantic HTML</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Understanding ARIA Landmarks</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">HTML5 Sectioning Elements</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>

docs.title: Example 2: Pull Quote
docs.text:
<aside>
    <blockquote>
        <p>The best way to predict the future is to invent it.</p>
        <footer>— Alan Kay</footer>
    </blockquote>
</aside>

docs.title: Example 3: Author Bio
docs.text:
<aside>
    <h2>About the Author</h2>
    <img src="author.jpg" alt="Jane Doe" width="100" height="100">
    <p>Jane Doe is a web developer with 10 years of experience. She writes about HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.</p>
    <p>Follow her on <a href="https://twitter.com/janedoe">Twitter</a>.</p>
</aside>

docs.title: Example 4: Aside Inside an Article
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>How to Use Semantic HTML</h1>
    <p>Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that convey meaning...</p>

    <aside>
        <h2>Did You Know?</h2>
        <p>The `<aside>` element was introduced in HTML5 to mark up content that is tangentially related to the main content.</p>
    </aside>

    <p>More main content...</p>
</article>

docs.title: Example 5: Aside with aria-labelledby
docs.text:
<aside aria-labelledby="related-heading">
    <h2 id="related-heading">Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>

docs.title: Example 6: Aside with aria-label
docs.text:
<aside aria-label="Advertisement">
    <p>Sponsored content...</p>
</aside>

docs.title: Example 7: Sidebar in a Page Layout
docs.text:
<body>
    <header>...</header>
    <div class="layout">
        <main>
            <article>
                <h1>Article Title</h1>
                <p>Main content...</p>
            </article>
        </main>
        <aside>
            <h2>Sidebar</h2>
            <p>Related links, ads, or other supplementary content.</p>
        </aside>
    </div>
    <footer>...</footer>
</body>

docs.title: Example 8: Multiple Asides on a Page
docs.text:
<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Article Title</h1>
        <p>Main content...</p>

        <aside>
            <h2>Pull Quote</h2>
            <blockquote>
                <p>An important quote from the article.</p>
            </blockquote>
        </aside>

        <p>More content...</p>

        <aside>
            <h2>Related Links</h2>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="#">Link 1</a></li>
                <li><a href="#">Link 2</a></li>
            </ul>
        </aside>
    </article>
</main>

docs.title: Example 9: Styling Asides with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    aside {
        background-color: #f8f9fa;
        border-left: 4px solid #3498db;
        padding: 1rem;
        margin: 1rem 0;
        border-radius: 0 8px 8px 0;
    }
    aside h2 {
        color: #2c3e50;
        margin-top: 0;
        font-size: 1.2rem;
    }
    aside ul {
        list-style: none;
        padding: 0;
    }
    aside li {
        margin-bottom: 0.5rem;
    }
    aside a {
        color: #2980b9;
        text-decoration: none;
    }
    aside a:hover {
        text-decoration: underline;
    }
</style>

<aside>
    <h2>Related Articles</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#">Article 1</a></li>
        <li><a href="#">Article 2</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>

docs.text:
<aside>
    <h2>Glossary</h2>
    <dl>
        <dt>Semantic HTML</dt>
        <dd>Using HTML elements that convey meaning.</dd>
        <dt>Landmark</dt>
        <dd>A navigable region of a web page.</dd>
        <dt>ARIA</dt>
        <dd>Accessible Rich Internet Applications.</dd>
    </dl>
</aside>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Sidebar Related links, advertisements Pull quote Highlighted quote from an article Author bio Information about the author Fun fact Tangential information related to the content Glossary Definitions of terms Related articles Links to other content on the site Advertisement Sponsored content Bibliography References cited in the article Biographical info Information about a person mentioned Newsletter signup Email subscription form Social media links Links to social profiles Table of contents Navigation within a long article

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <aside> for tangentially related content – not for main content.

  2. Ask: "Is this content essential to the main message?" – if no, it could be an aside.

  3. Include a heading when appropriate – to provide an accessible name.

  4. Use aria-labelledby or aria-label if there's no visible heading – to create a complementary landmark.

  5. Don't use <aside> for main content – use <main> or <article>.

  6. Don't use <aside> for navigation – use <nav>.

  7. Don't use <aside> for generic containers – use <div>.

  8. Style <aside> with CSS – it has no default styling beyond display: block.

  9. Use <aside> inside <article> – for pull quotes, related links, and supplementary information.

  10. Use <aside> outside <main> – for sidebars that run alongside the main content.

  11. Test with screen readers – ensure the complementary landmark is announced.

  12. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting and accessible names.

  13. Keep asides focused – one topic or purpose per aside.

  14. Use semantic elements inside asides – <blockquote>, <ul>, <dl>, etc.

  15. Consider SEO – asides help search engines distinguish main from supplementary content.

  16. Use id on asides for linking – e.g., #related-links.

  17. Don't overuse asides – too many asides can clutter the page.

  18. Use asides for advertisements – with aria-label="Advertisement".

  19. Use asides for pull quotes – to highlight key points from the article.

  20. Test on different devices – ensure asides look good everywhere.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <aside> for Main Content
docs.text:
<aside>
    <h1>Main Article</h1>
    <p>This is the main content of the page.</p>
</aside>
Why it's wrong: The main content should use <main> or <article>, not <aside>.

✅ Correct: 

<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Main Article</h1>
        <p>This is the main content of the page.</p>
    </article>
</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <aside> for Navigation
docs.text:
<aside>
    <h2>Navigation</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</aside>
Why it's wrong: Navigation should use <nav>.

✅ Correct: 

<nav>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <aside> Without an Accessible Name
docs.text:
<aside>
    <p>Some supplementary content.</p>
</aside>
Why it's wrong: Without an accessible name, the aside doesn't create a complementary landmark. If it's a significant region, it should have a name.

✅ Correct: 

<aside aria-label="Supplementary content">
    <p>Some supplementary content.</p>
</aside>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <aside> for Styling Only
docs.text:
<aside class="highlight">
    <p>This is just highlighted text.</p>
</aside>
Why it's wrong: If there's no semantic meaning, use <div> with a class.

✅ Correct: 

<div class="highlight">
    <p>This is just highlighted text.</p>
</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <aside> Inside <p>
docs.text:
<p>Some text <aside>Supplementary content</aside> more text.</p>
Why it's wrong: <aside> is a block-level element and cannot be inside a <p> (which only accepts phrasing content).

✅ Correct: 

<p>Some text</p>
<aside>Supplementary content</aside>
<p>More text.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <aside> for the Entire Sidebar Column Without a Heading
docs.text:
<aside>
    <div>...</div>
    <div>...</div>
    <div>...</div>
</aside>
Why it's wrong: Without a heading or label, the aside has no accessible name and doesn't create a landmark.

✅ Correct: 

<aside aria-label="Sidebar">
    <div>...</div>
    <div>...</div>
    <div>...</div>
</aside>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <aside> Elements Without Labels
docs.text:
<aside>...</aside>
<aside>...</aside>
<aside>...</aside>
Why it's wrong: Multiple unlabelled asides create multiple complementary landmarks (if named) or none (if not named), which can be confusing.

✅ Correct: 

<aside aria-label="Related Links">...</aside>
<aside aria-label="Advertisement">...</aside>
<aside aria-label="Author Bio">...</aside>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <aside> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • No default styles – no rendering cost beyond the content.
  • Accessibility tree – adds a complementary landmark when it has an accessible name, but the impact is minimal.
  • Nesting – deeply nested asides can increase DOM size; keep it reasonable.
  • CSS styling – complex styles on <aside> may affect performance, but the impact is minimal.
  • Reader mode – no performance cost; it's a browser feature.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <aside>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for target="_blank".
  • Advertisements – be cautious with third-party ad scripts; they can introduce security risks.
  • No direct security implications – <aside> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <aside> to see its content and structure.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the complementary landmark (if it has an accessible name).
  • Computed styles – check the display property (should be block by default).
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('aside') to list all asides.
  • Validator – check for asides without accessible names and other semantic issues.
  • Screen reader testing – navigate to the complementary landmark.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and semantic HTML.
  • Reader mode – test in Safari Reader or Firefox Reader View to ensure asides are ignored.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For sidebars – related links, advertisements, author bios.
  • For pull quotes – highlighted quotes from an article.
  • For fun facts – tangential information related to the content.
  • For glossary terms – definitions of terms used in the content.
  • For related articles – links to other content on the site.
  • For author bios – information about the author of an article.
  • For advertisements – sponsored content.
  • For bibliographies – references cited in the article.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For main content – use <main> or <article>.
  • For navigation – use <nav>.
  • For generic containers – use <div>.
  • For thematic groupings – use <section>.
  • For introductory content – use <header>.
  • For concluding content – use <footer>.
  • For styling only – use <div>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <main> – primary content of the page.
  • <article> – self-contained content.
  • <section> – thematic grouping of content.
  • <nav> – navigation.
  • <header> – introductory content.
  • <footer> – concluding content.
  • <div> – generic container (non-semantic).
  • Document Outline – headings and sectioning elements.
  • ARIA Landmarks – complementary, main, navigation, etc.
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <aside> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • An <aside> creates a complementary landmark in the accessibility tree only when it has an accessible name (from a heading, aria-labelledby, or aria-label).

  • The key question to ask when deciding whether to use <aside> is: "If I removed this content, would the main content still make sense?" If yes, it's an aside.

  • <aside> is often confused with <section>. The key difference: <aside> is tangentially related to the main content; <section> is part of the main content.

  • Screen readers like NVDA and JAWS allow users to navigate to complementary landmarks using keyboard shortcuts.

  • Search engines use <aside> to distinguish supplementary content from main content, which can improve SEO.

  • Browser reader modes (Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View) often ignore <aside> content when extracting the main article.

  • The <aside> element has no default visual styling beyond display: block.

  • An <aside> can contain its own <header>, <footer>, <section>, and even nested <aside> elements.

  • The <aside> element is part of the sectioning content category, along with <section>, <article>, and <nav>.

  • The <aside> element is commonly used in sidebars, pull quotes, author bios, and advertisements.

  • Structured data can be added to <aside> for rich results in search engines.

  • The <aside> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.

  • The <aside> element is one of the most commonly used semantic elements in modern web development.

  • Using <aside> without an accessible name is a common mistake. If it's a significant region, give it a heading or an aria-label.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <aside> element represents a portion of a document whose content is tangentially related to the content around it.
  • It is a sectioning content element and flow content.
  • It creates a complementary landmark in the accessibility tree when it has an accessible name.
  • It can be used inside <article>, <main>, <section>, or <body>.
  • Best practices: use <aside> for supplementary content, include a heading or aria-label, don't use it for main content or navigation, and style with CSS.
  • Common mistakes include using <aside> for main content, navigation, or generic containers; using it without an accessible name; and nesting it inside <p>.
  • The <aside> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.
  • It is one of the most important semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <nav> element is a semantic HTML element that represents a section of a page whose purpose is to provide navigation links — either within the current document or to other documents. It is designed to mark up major navigation blocks, such as site-wide menus, table-of-contents lists, breadcrumb trails, and pagination controls.

The <nav> element is a sectioning content element, meaning it contributes to the document outline (along with <section>, <article>, and <aside>). It is flow content and palpable content, and it is a block-level element. When it has an accessible name (from a heading, aria-labelledby, or aria-label), it creates a navigation landmark in the accessibility tree, allowing screen reader users to jump directly to it.

Crucially, <nav> is not for every group of links. It is reserved for major navigation areas — not for individual links scattered throughout prose. Using it too liberally dilutes its value for assistive technology users.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <nav> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Semantic clarity – identifies navigation as a distinct type of content.
  • Accessibility – creates a navigation landmark that screen reader users can navigate to directly.
  • Document structure – contributes to the document outline.
  • SEO – helps search engines understand the site's navigation structure.
  • Styling – provides a hook for CSS to style navigation menus consistently.
  • Maintainability – self-documenting code that clearly expresses the role of the content.
  • Skip links – provides a target for "skip navigation" links (though skip links usually target <main>).

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <nav> element is flow content and can appear inside <body>, <header>, <footer>, <aside>, <article>, or <section>. It is most commonly used in:

  • Site headers – for the primary site-wide navigation menu.
  • Page footers – for secondary navigation (privacy policy, terms, sitemap).
  • Sidebars – for in-page navigation (table of contents).
  • Articles – for related links or pagination.
<header>
    <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
            <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML5, there was no semantic element for navigation blocks. Developers used <div id="nav"> or <div class="navigation"> to mark up menus. While this worked visually, it provided no semantic meaning to machines. Screen readers couldn't identify navigation as a distinct landmark, search engines couldn't distinguish navigation from main content, and users had no way to skip past navigation menus to reach the main content.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic nav element Machines couldn't identify navigation blocks. <div id="nav"> ID/class names are invisible to machines; fragile. No navigation landmark Screen reader users couldn't jump to navigation or skip it. Poor SEO Search engines couldn't distinguish navigation from content. No standard for link lists Navigation markup was inconsistent across sites. No skip-navigation Users had to tab through every link to reach main content.

docs.title: Why <nav> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <nav> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standardised, semantic way to mark up navigation blocks. It enables:

  • Clear semantics – machines understand that the content is navigation.
  • Accessibility – creates a navigation landmark for screen reader navigation.
  • Skip navigation – users can skip past navigation to reach the main content.
  • SEO – helps search engines identify and understand the site's navigation.
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.
  • Styling – provides a meaningful hook for CSS.

The <nav> element is part of the broader semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more understandable to both humans and machines.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <nav>
docs.text:
<nav>
    <!-- Navigation links -->
</nav>

docs.title: Simple Navigation Menu
docs.text:
<nav>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Navigation with aria-label
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Navigation with a Heading
docs.text:
<nav aria-labelledby="main-nav-heading">
    <h2 id="main-nav-heading">Main Navigation</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Navigation Inside a Header
docs.text:
<header>
    <h1>My Website</h1>
    <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
            <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

docs.title: Navigation Inside a Footer
docs.text:
<footer>
    <nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/privacy">Privacy Policy</a></li>
            <li><a href="/terms">Terms of Service</a></li>
            <li><a href="/sitemap">Sitemap</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
    <p>© 2026 My Website</p>
</footer>

docs.title: Breadcrumb Navigation
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
    <ol>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
        <li aria-current="page">Laptops</li>
    </ol>
</nav>

docs.title: Table of Contents Navigation
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Table of contents">
    <h2>On This Page</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#introduction">Introduction</a></li>
        <li><a href="#features">Features</a></li>
        <li><a href="#pricing">Pricing</a></li>
        <li><a href="#conclusion">Conclusion</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Pagination Navigation
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Pagination">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="?page=1" aria-label="Previous page">Previous</a></li>
        <li><a href="?page=1">1</a></li>
        <li><a href="?page=2" aria-current="page">2</a></li>
        <li><a href="?page=3">3</a></li>
        <li><a href="?page=3" aria-label="Next page">Next</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Multiple Navigations on a Page
docs.text:
<header>
    <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Article Title</h1>
        <nav aria-label="Table of contents">
            <ul>
                <li><a href="#section-1">Section 1</a></li>
                <li><a href="#section-2">Section 2</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
        <section id="section-1">...</section>
        <section id="section-2">...</section>
    </article>
</main>

<footer>
    <nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/privacy">Privacy</a></li>
            <li><a href="/terms">Terms</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</footer>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <nav> Marks a navigation block. Provides semantic meaning and a landmark. <ul> / <ol> List of links. Semantic structure for navigation links. <li> List item. Each link is a list item. <a> Navigation link. The actual link. aria-label Provides an accessible name. Creates a navigation landmark. aria-labelledby References the heading for the accessible name. Alternative to aria-label. aria-current Indicates the current page or item. Improves accessibility for current state.

docs.title: The "Table of Contents" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <nav> as a table of contents in a book. It helps readers find what they're looking for quickly. Just as a table of contents is a distinct section of the book, <nav> is a distinct section of the page — it's navigation, not content.

docs.title: The "Road Map" Analogy
docs.text: A <nav> element is like a road map — it helps you get from one place to another. It's not the destination (the main content), but it's essential for finding your way. A website might have several maps: a site-wide map (main navigation), a local map (breadcrumbs), and a detail map (table of contents).

docs.title: The "Menu at a Restaurant" Analogy
docs.text: The <nav> is like the menu at a restaurant. It lists the available options and helps you decide what to order. It's not the meal itself (the main content), but it's how you choose what you want.

docs.title: Concept 1: Not Every Link Needs <nav>
docs.text:
The <nav> element is for major navigation blocks. It should not be used for every group of links. For example:

<!-- Bad: overusing <nav> -->
<p>Read more about <nav><a href="/html">HTML</a></nav> and <nav><a href="/css">CSS</a></nav>.</p>

<!-- Good: inline links without <nav> -->
<p>Read more about <a href="/html">HTML</a> and <a href="/css">CSS</a>.</p>

Rule: Use <nav> for major navigation areas (site menus, breadcrumbs, tables of contents, pagination). Don't use it for individual links in prose.

docs.title: Concept 2: The navigation Landmark
docs.text:
The <nav> element creates a navigation landmark in the accessibility tree. Screen reader users can navigate directly to it using landmark navigation (e.g., N in NVDA, D then N in JAWS).

<nav>
    <!-- This creates a navigation landmark -->
</nav>

docs.title: Concept 3: Multiple <nav> Elements
docs.text:
You can have multiple <nav> elements on a page. Each one should have a unique accessible name to distinguish it from the others.

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Table of contents">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Footer navigation">...</nav>

Best practice: Always provide a unique label when there's more than one <nav> on a page.

docs.title: Concept 4: Accessible Names
docs.text:
The <nav> element should have an accessible name so that screen reader users can distinguish it from other navigation regions. The name can be provided by:

  • aria-label – a direct label.
  • aria-labelledby – references another element (usually a heading).
  • A heading inside <nav> – the heading provides the name.
<!-- Using aria-label -->
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">...</nav>

<!-- Using aria-labelledby -->
<nav aria-labelledby="nav-heading">
    <h2 id="nav-heading">Main Navigation</h2>
    ...
</nav>

docs.title: Concept 5: Content Model
docs.text:
The <nav> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Lists (<ul>, <ol>) – the most common structure for navigation.
  • Headings (<h1>–<h6>) – optional, but useful for labelling.
  • Paragraphs (<p>) – less common.
  • Other flow content.

The most common pattern is a <ul> with <li> items containing <a> links.

docs.title: Concept 6: <nav> vs <div id="nav">
docs.text: Aspect <nav> <div id="nav"> Semantic meaning Navigation None Accessibility navigation landmark No landmark SEO Recognised by search engines Not recognised Styling No default styles No default styles Maintainability Self-documenting Depends on ID/class Skip navigation Supported Not supported

docs.title: Concept 7: <nav> and <menu> (Not the Same)
docs.text: The <menu> element is not for navigation. It is a semantic alternative to <ul> for toolbars and context menus. Use <nav> with <ul> for navigation.

docs.title: Concept 8: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <nav> element has no default visual styling in most browsers. It behaves like a <div> by default:

nav {
    display: block;
}

You need to style it with CSS to create a horizontal or vertical menu.

docs.title: Concept 9: <nav> and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use <nav> to identify navigation links. This helps them:

  • Understand the site's structure.
  • Identify the most important pages (linked in the main navigation).
  • Distinguish navigation from content.

docs.title: Concept 10: <nav> and "Skip to Content"
docs.text:
The <nav> element is a common target for "skip navigation" links, which allow keyboard users to bypass the navigation and jump straight to the main content:

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">...</nav>

<main id="main-content">...</main>

docs.title: Concept 11: <nav> and aria-current
docs.text:
When a navigation link represents the current page or current item, use aria-current="page" to indicate this to assistive technologies:

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

Other values for aria-current include step, location, date, time, true, and false.

docs.title: Concept 12: Breadcrumb Navigation
docs.text:
Breadcrumbs are a type of navigation that shows the user's location in the site hierarchy. Use <nav> with aria-label="Breadcrumb" and an ordered list:

<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
    <ol>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
        <li aria-current="page">Laptops</li>
    </ol>
</nav>

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <nav>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<nav>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content (flow content).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── display: block
    │
    ▼
6.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   └── navigation landmark.
    │
    ▼
7.  The accessible name is derived from:
    │   ├── aria-label
    │   ├── aria-labelledby
    │   └── The first heading inside the nav (if present)
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
9.  Screen readers can navigate to the navigation landmark.
    │
    ▼
10. Search engines identify the navigation links.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, <nav> is exposed as a navigation landmark. Screen readers provide shortcuts to navigate to it (e.g., N in NVDA).

If there are multiple <nav> elements, each is exposed as a separate navigation landmark. The accessible name distinguishes them (e.g., "Main navigation", "Footer navigation").

docs.title: The Document Outline Algorithm
docs.text: The HTML5 outline algorithm was designed to create a document outline from sectioning elements. Navs contribute to this outline, but the algorithm is not widely implemented by browsers. In practice, headings provide the primary structural cues.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
nav {
    display: block;
}

No other default styles are applied. You must use CSS for layout and appearance.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <nav> is represented by the HTMLElement interface. It has no specific properties or methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

const nav = document.querySelector('nav');
console.log(nav.textContent); // The text content
console.log(nav.innerHTML); // The HTML content

docs.title: The navigation Landmark
docs.text: The navigation landmark is one of the ARIA landmark roles. It is used to identify a section of the page that contains navigation links. The browser's accessibility engine maps <nav> to the navigation role.

docs.title: Multiple Navigation Landmarks
docs.text: Unlike the main landmark, you can have multiple navigation landmarks on a page. Each <nav> creates its own landmark in the accessibility tree. The accessible name distinguishes them.

docs.title: SEO and <nav>
docs.text:
Search engines like Google use <nav> to identify navigation links. This can influence:

  • Indexing – links in navigation are more likely to be crawled.
  • Ranking – pages linked in main navigation may be considered more important.
  • Understanding – search engines can distinguish navigation from content.

docs.title: Skip Navigation
docs.text:
Screen reader and keyboard users often use "skip to main content" links to bypass navigation. These links target the <main> element (or an element inside it):

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>
<nav>...</nav>
<main id="main-content">...</main>

The skip link is usually visually hidden until focused, then appears at the top of the page.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <nav> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<nav>` element with navigation links.
    │   └── Example: <nav aria-label="Main"><ul>...</ul></nav>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<nav>` node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── navigation landmark.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers can navigate to the navigation landmark.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines identify the navigation links.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the nav dynamically.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const nav = document.querySelector('nav');
nav.innerHTML = '<ul><li><a href="/">Home</a></li><li><a href="/new">New</a></li></ul>';

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Site Navigation
docs.text:
<header>
    <h1>My Website</h1>
    <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
            <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

docs.title: Example 2: Navigation with aria-current
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Example 3: Footer Navigation
docs.text:
<footer>
    <nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/privacy">Privacy Policy</a></li>
            <li><a href="/terms">Terms of Service</a></li>
            <li><a href="/sitemap">Sitemap</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
    <p>© 2026 My Website</p>
</footer>

docs.title: Example 4: Breadcrumb Navigation
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
    <ol>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
        <li><a href="/products/laptops">Laptops</a></li>
        <li aria-current="page">MacBook Pro</li>
    </ol>
</nav>

docs.title: Example 5: Table of Contents
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Table of contents">
    <h2>On This Page</h2>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#introduction">Introduction</a></li>
        <li><a href="#features">Features</a></li>
        <li><a href="#pricing">Pricing</a></li>
        <li><a href="#conclusion">Conclusion</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

<article>
    <section id="introduction">
        <h2>Introduction</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
    <section id="features">
        <h2>Features</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
    <!-- ... -->
</article>

docs.title: Example 6: Pagination
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Pagination">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="?page=1" aria-label="Previous page">Previous</a></li>
        <li><a href="?page=1">1</a></li>
        <li><a href="?page=2" aria-current="page">2</a></li>
        <li><a href="?page=3">3</a></li>
        <li><a href="?page=3" aria-label="Next page">Next</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Example 7: Multiple Navigations
docs.text:
<header>
    <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Article Title</h1>
        <nav aria-label="Table of contents">
            <ul>
                <li><a href="#section-1">Section 1</a></li>
                <li><a href="#section-2">Section 2</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
        <section id="section-1">...</section>
        <section id="section-2">...</section>
    </article>
</main>

<footer>
    <nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/privacy">Privacy</a></li>
            <li><a href="/terms">Terms</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</footer>

docs.title: Example 8: Navigation with Dropdown Menus
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li>
            <a href="/products" aria-haspopup="true" aria-expanded="false">Products</a>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/products/laptops">Laptops</a></li>
                <li><a href="/products/phones">Phones</a></li>
                <li><a href="/products/tablets">Tablets</a></li>
            </ul>
        </li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

Note: The aria-haspopup and aria-expanded attributes should be managed with JavaScript to reflect the actual state of the dropdown.

docs.title: Example 9: Styling Navigation with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    nav[aria-label="Main navigation"] {
        background-color: #2c3e50;
        padding: 1rem;
    }
    nav[aria-label="Main navigation"] ul {
        list-style: none;
        margin: 0;
        padding: 0;
        display: flex;
        gap: 1rem;
    }
    nav[aria-label="Main navigation"] a {
        color: white;
        text-decoration: none;
        padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
        border-radius: 4px;
    }
    nav[aria-label="Main navigation"] a:hover {
        background-color: #34495e;
    }
    nav[aria-label="Main navigation"] a[aria-current="page"] {
        background-color: #3498db;
    }
</style>

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Example 10: Navigation with a Search Form
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
    <form role="search" action="/search" method="GET">
        <label for="search">Search:</label>
        <input type="search" id="search" name="q" placeholder="Search...">
        <button type="submit">Go</button>
    </form>
</nav>

Note: The role="search" on the form creates a search landmark, which is separate from the navigation landmark.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Site-wide navigation Main menu in the header Footer navigation Privacy policy, terms, sitemap Breadcrumb navigation Showing the user's location Table of contents In-page navigation for long articles Pagination Navigating between pages of results Sidebar navigation Related links, categories Dropdown menus Multi-level navigation Mobile menus Hamburger menus Search forms Search input within navigation Social media links Links to social profiles Language switchers Switching between languages Account menus Profile, settings, logout

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <nav> for major navigation blocks – not for every group of links.

  2. Include an aria-label – to distinguish multiple navs on a page.

  3. Use <ul> or <ol> for link lists – semantic structure for navigation links.

  4. Use <a> for links – not <button> or <div> with JavaScript.

  5. Use aria-current="page" – to indicate the current page or item.

  6. Don't use <nav> for inline links – use <a> alone in prose.

  7. Don't use <nav> for the main content – use <main>.

  8. Don't use <nav> for sidebars – use <aside>.

  9. Keep navigation concise – too many links can overwhelm users.

  10. Make navigation keyboard accessible – ensure all links are focusable.

  11. Use CSS for styling – <nav> has no default styling beyond display: block.

  12. Test with screen readers – ensure the navigation landmark is announced.

  13. Use skip links – allow keyboard users to skip past navigation.

  14. Use aria-haspopup and aria-expanded for dropdowns – managed with JavaScript.

  15. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting and accessible names.

  16. Use semantic headings inside <nav> – if a heading is used, it should be a real heading.

  17. Consider mobile responsiveness – navigation often needs to adapt to small screens.

  18. Use role="search" for search forms – to create a search landmark.

  19. Don't nest <nav> inside another <nav> – it's confusing.

  20. Test on different devices – ensure navigation works everywhere.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <nav> for Every Group of Links
docs.text:
<p>Read more: <nav><a href="/html">HTML</a></nav> and <nav><a href="/css">CSS</a></nav>.</p>
Why it's wrong: <nav> is for major navigation blocks, not inline links.

✅ Correct: 

<p>Read more: <a href="/html">HTML</a> and <a href="/css">CSS</a>.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div id="nav"> Instead of <nav>
docs.text:
<div id="nav">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    </ul>
</div>
Why it's wrong: No semantic meaning; no navigation landmark.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Navigations Without Labels
docs.text:
<nav>...</nav>
<nav>...</nav>
<nav>...</nav>
Why it's wrong: Multiple unlabelled navigation landmarks are confusing for screen reader users.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Footer navigation">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Pagination">...</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <nav> Without a List
docs.text:
<nav>
    <a href="/">Home</a>
    <a href="/about">About</a>
</nav>
Why it's wrong: While valid, the list structure (<ul>/<ol>) is preferred for navigation links.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <button> for Navigation Links
docs.text:
<nav>
    <button onclick="navigate('/')">Home</button>
</nav>
Why it's wrong: Navigation should use <a> elements, not <button> with JavaScript.

✅ Correct: 

<nav>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <nav> Inside <nav>
docs.text:
<nav>
    <nav>Nested navigation</nav>
</nav>
Why it's wrong: Nested navigation is confusing and unnecessary.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Sub navigation">...</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting aria-current
docs.text:
<nav>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>
Why it's wrong: The current page is not indicated to assistive technologies.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <nav> for the Table of Contents Without a Label
docs.text:
<nav>
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#section-1">Section 1</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>
Why it's wrong: Without a label, the nav's purpose is unclear.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Table of contents">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#section-1">Section 1</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <nav> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • No default styles – no rendering cost beyond the content.
  • Accessibility tree – adds a navigation landmark, but the impact is minimal.
  • Multiple navs – each adds a landmark node; the impact is minimal.
  • CSS styling – complex styles on <nav> may affect performance, but the impact is minimal.
  • Dropdown menus – JavaScript for managing dropdowns can add overhead; use CSS-only solutions where possible.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <nav>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for target="_blank".
  • javascript: URLs – avoid in href.
  • Open redirects – validate redirect URLs to prevent phishing.
  • No direct security implications – <nav> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <nav> to see its content and structure.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the navigation landmark.
  • Computed styles – check the display property (should be block by default).
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('nav') to list all navs.
  • Validator – check for navs without accessible names and other semantic issues.
  • Screen reader testing – navigate to the navigation landmark.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and semantic HTML.
  • Keyboard testing – ensure all navigation links are focusable and operable via keyboard.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For site-wide navigation – main menu in the header.
  • For footer navigation – privacy policy, terms, sitemap.
  • For breadcrumb navigation – showing the user's location.
  • For table of contents – in-page navigation for long articles.
  • For pagination – navigating between pages of results.
  • For sidebar navigation – related links, categories.
  • For dropdown menus – multi-level navigation.
  • For mobile menus – hamburger menus.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For individual links in prose – use <a> alone.
  • For the main content – use <main>.
  • For sidebars – use <aside> (though navigation can be inside an aside).
  • For generic containers – use <div>.
  • For thematic groupings – use <section>.
  • For self-contained content – use <article>.
  • For every group of links – only for major navigation blocks.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <main> – primary content of the page.
  • <article> – self-contained content.
  • <section> – thematic grouping of content.
  • <aside> – tangentially related content.
  • <header> – introductory content.
  • <footer> – concluding content.
  • <div> – generic container (non-semantic).
  • Document Outline – headings and sectioning elements.
  • ARIA Landmarks – navigation, main, complementary, etc.
  • aria-current – indicates the current item.
  • aria-label / aria-labelledby – accessible names.
  • Skip Links – "Skip to main content."
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <nav> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • A <nav> creates a navigation landmark in the accessibility tree. You can have multiple navigation landmarks on a page, but each should have a unique accessible name.

  • The <nav> element is not for every group of links. It should be reserved for major navigation blocks. Inline links in prose should just use <a>.

  • Screen readers like NVDA and JAWS allow users to jump to navigation landmarks using keyboard shortcuts (e.g., N in NVDA).

  • The aria-current="page" attribute indicates the current page in a navigation menu. Other values include step, location, date, time, true, and false.

  • Breadcrumb navigation should use <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> with an <ol> (ordered list) to reflect the hierarchy.

  • Pagination should use <nav aria-label="Pagination"> with a <ul> and aria-current="page" on the current page.

  • The <nav> element has no default visual styling beyond display: block.

  • Search forms inside navigation can use role="search" to create a search landmark.

  • The "skip to main content" link is a common accessibility feature that allows keyboard users to bypass navigation.

  • Google uses <nav> to identify navigation links, which can influence the crawling and ranking of linked pages.

  • The <nav> element is part of the sectioning content category, along with <section>, <article>, and <aside>.

  • The <nav> element is commonly used in site headers, footers, sidebars, and articles (for tables of contents).

  • Nested <nav> elements are discouraged — use multiple sibling <nav> elements with unique labels instead.

  • The <nav> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.

  • The <nav> element is one of the most commonly used semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <nav> element represents a section of a page whose purpose is to provide navigation links.
  • It is a sectioning content element and flow content.
  • It creates a navigation landmark in the accessibility tree.
  • Multiple <nav> elements can appear on a page, each with a unique accessible name.
  • Best practices: use <nav> for major navigation blocks, include an aria-label, use <ul>/<ol> for link lists, use <a> for links, and use aria-current="page" for the current page.
  • Common mistakes include using <nav> for inline links, using it without a label, using <div id="nav"> instead of <nav>, and forgetting aria-current.
  • The <nav> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.
  • It is one of the most important semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <figure> element is a semantic HTML element that represents self-contained content — typically media such as an image, diagram, illustration, code snippet, or chart — that is referenced from the main flow of the document but can be moved to another location (or removed entirely) without affecting the meaning of the surrounding content. A <figure> is often accompanied by a <figcaption> element, which provides a caption or legend for the figure.

The <figure> element is part of the flow content and palpable content categories. It is a block-level element. When used with <figcaption>, the figure becomes a self-contained unit — the media and its caption are treated as a single entity. This is significant for accessibility, as screen readers can associate the caption with the media.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <figure> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Semantic grouping – groups media with its caption into a single logical unit.
  • Accessibility – associates the caption (<figcaption>) with the media for screen readers.
  • Document flow – allows media to be moved or removed without breaking the surrounding content.
  • Styling – provides a hook for CSS to style figures and captions consistently.
  • Maintainability – self-documenting code that clearly expresses the relationship between media and caption.
  • Reusability – figures can be reused across different documents or contexts.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <figure> element is flow content and can appear anywhere flow content is accepted — inside <body>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, and even inside <li> or <dd>. It is most commonly used in:

  • Articles and blog posts – for images, diagrams, and charts.
  • Documentation – for code snippets, screenshots, and diagrams.
  • Scientific papers – for figures, graphs, and tables.
  • Product pages – for product images with captions.
  • Tutorials – for step-by-step illustrations.
<figure>
    <img src="diagram.png" alt="System architecture diagram">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: System architecture</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before HTML5, there was no standard way to associate a caption with an image, diagram, or code snippet. Developers used <div class="figure"> with a <p class="caption"> or <span class="caption">, but these were invisible to machines. Screen readers couldn't reliably associate the caption with the media, and the relationship was purely visual (based on proximity). If the media and caption were separated (e.g., by responsive design or CSS), the association was lost.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic figure element Machines couldn't identify media-caption pairs. <div class="figure"> Class names are invisible to machines; fragile. No accessible caption association Screen readers couldn't announce the caption as part of the media. Caption separation If media and caption were visually separated, the association was lost. Inconsistent styling Each developer used their own class names.

docs.title: Why <figure> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <figure> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standardised, semantic way to group media with its caption. It enables:

  • Clear semantics – machines understand that the content is a figure with a caption.
  • Accessibility – the <figcaption> is programmatically associated with the figure.
  • Self-contained content – the figure can be moved or removed without affecting the surrounding content.
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.
  • Styling – provides a meaningful hook for CSS.

The <figure> element is part of the broader semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more understandable to both humans and machines.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <figure>
docs.text:
<figure>
    <!-- Media (image, diagram, code, etc.) -->
    <figcaption>Caption text</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Simple Image with Caption
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="sunset.jpg" alt="A beautiful sunset over the ocean">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Sunset over the Pacific Ocean</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Figure with Multiple Images
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="before.jpg" alt="Before the renovation">
    <img src="after.jpg" alt="After the renovation">
    <figcaption>Figure 2: Before and after the renovation</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Figure with a Code Snippet
docs.text:
<figure>
    <pre><code>
function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
    </code></pre>
    <figcaption>Listing 1: A simple greeting function</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Figure with a Diagram
docs.text:
<figure>
    <svg width="200" height="200" viewBox="0 0 200 200">
        <circle cx="100" cy="100" r="80" fill="lightblue" />
        <text x="100" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20">Diagram</text>
    </svg>
    <figcaption>Figure 3: A simple diagram</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Figure Without a Caption
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="decorative.jpg" alt="Decorative image">
</figure>

Note: A <figure> without a <figcaption> is valid, but the caption is what gives the figure its context.

docs.title: Figure with Caption Before Media
docs.text:
<figure>
    <figcaption>Figure 4: A beautiful sunset</figcaption>
    <img src="sunset.jpg" alt="Sunset over the ocean">
</figure>

Note: The <figcaption> can appear before or after the media, but it must be the first or last child of the <figure>.

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <figure> Groups media with its caption. Provides semantic meaning and a self-contained unit. <img> The media. The main content of the figure. <figcaption> The caption. Describes the media and is programmatically associated with it. <pre><code> Code snippet. Common figure content in technical documentation. <svg> Vector graphic. Common figure content for diagrams.

docs.title: The "Magazine Figure" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a <figure> as a figure in a magazine or textbook. It's an image, diagram, or chart with a caption underneath (or above). The caption explains what the figure shows. The figure is self-contained — you can look at it in isolation and understand it. If you removed it from the page, the surrounding text would still make sense (though you might miss the illustration).

docs.title: The "Museum Exhibit" Analogy
docs.text: A <figure> is like a museum exhibit — it's a self-contained display with a placard (caption) that explains what you're looking at. The exhibit can be moved to another room (or removed) without affecting the other exhibits. The placard is essential for understanding the exhibit.

docs.title: The "Photo Album" Analogy
