docs.text: Think of a photo album where each photo has a caption written below it. Each photo and its caption form a single unit — a <figure>. You can rearrange the photos or remove one without affecting the others. The caption tells you what the photo is about.

docs.title: Concept 1: Self-Contained Content
docs.text:
The defining characteristic of a <figure> is that it is self-contained — it can be moved to another location (or removed) without affecting the meaning of the surrounding content. This is similar to <article>, but <figure> is specifically for media and illustrations, not for prose.

Examples of figure content: - Images - Diagrams - Illustrations - Charts and graphs - Code snippets - Screenshots - Videos - Audio players - Tables (in some cases)

docs.title: Concept 2: The <figcaption> Element
docs.text:
The <figcaption> element provides a caption or legend for the <figure>. It is optional (a figure can exist without a caption), but when present, it must be the first or last child of the <figure>.

<!-- Caption after media (most common) -->
<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Caption text</figcaption>
</figure>

<!-- Caption before media -->
<figure>
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Caption text</figcaption>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
</figure>

docs.title: Concept 3: Only One <figcaption> Per <figure>
docs.text: A <figure> can have at most one <figcaption>. If you need multiple captions, you can use multiple figures or put additional text outside the figure.

docs.title: Concept 4: Content Model
docs.text:
The <figure> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Images (<img>)
  • Code blocks (<pre><code>)
  • SVG (<svg>)
  • Video (<video>)
  • Audio (<audio>)
  • Tables (<table>)
  • Text (though prose is usually outside figures)
  • Multiple media elements

The <figcaption> element accepts flow content but should be concise (a caption, not a paragraph of prose).

docs.title: Concept 5: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <figure> element has default margins in most browsers:

figure {
    display: block;
    margin: 1em 40px;
}

The <figcaption> element has no default styling (it inherits from its parent). You need to style it with CSS if you want a specific look.

docs.title: Concept 6: <figure> vs <div>
docs.text:
Aspect <figure> <div> Semantic meaning Self-contained media with caption None Accessibility Caption associated with media No association Use case Images, diagrams, code, charts Generic containers, styling Self-contained Yes No

Rule: Use <figure> for media with captions; use <div> for generic containers.

docs.title: Concept 7: <figure> vs <aside>
docs.text:
Aspect <figure> <aside> Semantic meaning Self-contained media with caption Tangentially related content Content Media (images, diagrams, code) Supplementary content (links, ads, bios) Landmark No landmark complementary (if named) Caption Uses <figcaption> Uses headings or other content

Rule: Use <figure> for media with captions; use <aside> for supplementary content like sidebars.

docs.title: Concept 8: <figure> and Accessibility
docs.text:
The <figure> and <figcaption> elements work together to provide an accessible media-caption pair. Screen readers may announce the caption as part of the figure, and the <img> inside the figure should have an alt attribute for the image itself.

<figure>
    <img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart showing sales growth from 2020 to 2026">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Sales growth from 2020 to 2026</figcaption>
</figure>

Note: The alt text should describe the image, while the <figcaption> provides the figure number and context. They serve different purposes.

docs.title: Concept 9: <figure> and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use <figure> and <figcaption> to understand the relationship between images and their captions. This can help with:

  • Image search – captions provide context for images.
  • Content understanding – search engines can understand the role of the media.
  • Rich results – in some cases, figures may appear in search results.

docs.title: Concept 10: <figure> and Reader Mode
docs.text: Browsers' reader modes (Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View) typically include figures with their captions, as they are part of the primary content. This is different from <aside>, which is often excluded.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <figure>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<figure>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes the content (flow content):
    │   ├── Media (images, diagrams, code)
    │   ├── Optional <figcaption>
    │   └── Other flow content
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   └── display: block; margin: 1em 40px;
    │
    ▼
6.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   └── figure role (with caption if present)
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
8.  Screen readers can associate the caption with the figure.
    │
    ▼
9.  Search engines identify the figure and its caption.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text: In the accessibility tree, <figure> is exposed as a figure role. The <figcaption> is exposed as a caption or associated with the figure. Screen readers may announce the caption when the figure is encountered.

docs.title: The Document Outline Algorithm
docs.text: The <figure> element does not directly affect the document outline. The outline is determined by headings and sectioning elements.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
figure {
    display: block;
    margin: 1em 40px;
}

No default styles are applied to <figcaption>. You must use CSS for styling.

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <figure> and <figcaption> are represented by the HTMLElement interface. They have no specific properties or methods beyond those of HTMLElement.

const figure = document.querySelector('figure');
console.log(figure.textContent); // The text content (includes caption)
console.log(figure.innerHTML); // The HTML content

docs.title: The figure Role
docs.text: The figure role is a standard ARIA role. It is used to identify a self-contained unit of content, usually with a caption. The browser's accessibility engine maps <figure> to the figure role.

docs.title: The figcaption Association
docs.text: The <figcaption> element is programmatically associated with its parent <figure>. This association is exposed in the accessibility tree, allowing screen readers to announce the caption when the figure is encountered.

docs.title: SEO and <figure>
docs.text:
Search engines like Google use <figure> and <figcaption> to:

  • Identify images and their captions.
  • Understand the context of media.
  • Improve image search results.

docs.title: Reader Mode
docs.text: Browsers' reader modes (Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View) typically include figures with their captions, as they are part of the primary content.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <figure> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<figure>` element with media and a caption.
    │   └── Example: <figure><img src="..." alt="..."><figcaption>...</figcaption></figure>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<figure>` and `<figcaption>` nodes are created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block; margin: 1em 40px).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── figure role with associated caption.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers can announce the figure and its caption.
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines identify the figure and its caption.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the figure dynamically.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const figure = document.querySelector('figure');
figure.querySelector('img').src = 'new-image.jpg';
figure.querySelector('figcaption').textContent = 'Figure 1: New caption';

docs.title: Example 1: Image with Caption in an Article
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>Understanding Climate Change</h1>
    <p>Climate change is one of the most pressing issues of our time...</p>

    <figure>
        <img src="temperature-chart.png" alt="Line graph showing global temperature rise from 1880 to 2026">
        <figcaption>Figure 1: Global temperature rise from 1880 to 2026</figcaption>
    </figure>

    <p>As shown in Figure 1, temperatures have risen significantly...</p>
</article>

docs.title: Example 2: Code Snippet with Caption
docs.text:
<article>
    <h1>JavaScript Functions</h1>
    <p>Here's a simple function that greets a user:</p>

    <figure>
        <pre><code>
function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

console.log(greet("World")); // "Hello, World!"
        </code></pre>
        <figcaption>Listing 1: A simple greeting function</figcaption>
    </figure>

    <p>As you can see in Listing 1...</p>
</article>

docs.title: Example 3: Diagram with Caption
docs.text:
<figure>
    <svg width="400" height="200" viewBox="0 0 400 200">
        <rect x="50" y="50" width="100" height="100" fill="lightblue" stroke="black" />
        <rect x="250" y="50" width="100" height="100" fill="lightgreen" stroke="black" />
        <line x1="150" y1="100" x2="250" y2="100" stroke="black" stroke-width="2" />
        <text x="100" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">Client</text>
        <text x="300" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">Server</text>
    </svg>
    <figcaption>Figure 2: Client-server architecture</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 4: Multiple Images in a Figure
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="step1.jpg" alt="Step 1: Open the application">
    <img src="step2.jpg" alt="Step 2: Click the settings button">
    <img src="step3.jpg" alt="Step 3: Select your preferences">
    <figcaption>Figure 3: Steps to configure the application</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 5: Figure with Caption Before Media
docs.text:
<figure>
    <figcaption>Figure 4: A beautiful sunset over the ocean</figcaption>
    <img src="sunset.jpg" alt="Sunset over the ocean">
</figure>

docs.title: Example 6: Figure Without a Caption
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="decorative.jpg" alt="Decorative background pattern">
</figure>

Note: A figure without a caption is valid, but it should still be self-contained content.

docs.title: Example 7: Figure with a Blockquote
docs.text:
<figure>
    <blockquote>
        <p>The only way to do great work is to love what you do.</p>
        <footer>— Steve Jobs</footer>
    </blockquote>
    <figcaption>Quote from Steve Jobs' Stanford Commencement Address</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 8: Figure with a Table
docs.text:
<figure>
    <table>
        <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
        <thead>
            <tr><th>Month</th><th>Sales</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr><td>January</td><td>$10,000</td></tr>
            <tr><td>February</td><td>$12,000</td></tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>
    <figcaption>Table 1: Monthly sales figures for 2026</figcaption>
</figure>

Note: The <caption> inside the table is separate from the <figcaption> for the figure. The table caption provides the table's title, while the figcaption provides the figure's caption.

docs.title: Example 9: Styling Figures with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    figure {
        margin: 2rem 0;
        padding: 1rem;
        background-color: #f8f9fa;
        border-radius: 8px;
        text-align: center;
    }
    figure img {
        max-width: 100%;
        height: auto;
        border-radius: 4px;
    }
    figcaption {
        margin-top: 1rem;
        font-size: 0.9rem;
        color: #6c757d;
        font-style: italic;
    }
    figcaption::before {
        content: "— ";
    }
</style>

<figure>
    <img src="chart.png" alt="Sales chart">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Sales growth over the past year</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 10: Figure with a Video
docs.text:
<figure>
    <video controls width="640">
        <source src="tutorial.mp4" type="video/mp4">
        <track kind="subtitles" src="tutorial.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">
        <p>Your browser does not support video.</p>
    </video>
    <figcaption>Video 1: Tutorial on using the application</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 11: Responsive Figure
docs.text:
<style>
    figure {
        max-width: 100%;
        margin: 1rem 0;
    }
    figure img {
        width: 100%;
        height: auto;
    }
    figcaption {
        margin-top: 0.5rem;
        font-size: 0.9rem;
        color: #666;
    }
    @media (min-width: 768px) {
        figure {
            max-width: 600px;
            margin: 2rem auto;
        }
    }
</style>

<figure>
    <img src="hero.jpg" alt="A beautiful landscape" srcset="hero-small.jpg 400w, hero-medium.jpg 800w, hero-large.jpg 1200w" sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 600px">
    <figcaption>Figure 5: A beautiful landscape</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 12: Figure in a Documentation Page
docs.text:
<main>
    <h1>API Documentation</h1>

    <section>
        <h2>Authentication Flow</h2>
        <p>The authentication flow is as follows:</p>

        <figure>
            <img src="auth-flow.png" alt="Flowchart showing the authentication process from client to server and back">
            <figcaption>Figure 1: Authentication flow</figcaption>
        </figure>

        <p>As shown in Figure 1, the client sends credentials...</p>
    </section>
</main>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Images with captions Photos, illustrations Diagrams Flowcharts, architecture diagrams Charts and graphs Bar charts, line graphs, pie charts Code snippets Listings, examples Screenshots UI screenshots, error messages Videos Tutorials, demos Audio Podcasts, sound clips Tables Data tables with captions Quotes Pull quotes with attribution Maps Geographic maps with legends Mathematical formulas Equations with labels Chemical structures Diagrams with labels

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <figure> for self-contained media – images, diagrams, code, charts.

  2. Include a <figcaption> when the media needs explanation – captions provide context.

  3. Place <figcaption> as the first or last child – it must be first or last inside <figure>.

  4. Provide alt text on images inside figures – the alt describes the image; the caption describes the figure.

  5. Keep captions concise – a caption should be a brief description, not a paragraph.

  6. Use figure numbers – e.g., "Figure 1", "Table 2", "Listing 3" – for reference in the text.

  7. Reference figures in the text – e.g., "As shown in Figure 1..."

  8. Don't use <figure> for decorative images – if the image is purely decorative, it doesn't need a figure.

  9. Don't use <figure> for layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

  10. Style <figure> with CSS – it has default margins that you may want to override.

  11. Use <figcaption> for the caption, not <p> or <span> – it's the semantic element for captions.

  12. Don't nest <figure> inside <p> – <figure> is block-level; <p> only accepts phrasing content.

  13. Use <figure> for code listings – with <pre><code> and a <figcaption>.

  14. Use <figure> for tables when they need a caption – though tables have their own <caption> element.

  15. Test with screen readers – ensure the figure and caption are announced correctly.

  16. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting and caption placement.

  17. Consider responsive images – use srcset and sizes for images in figures.

  18. Use <figure> in documentation – for screenshots, diagrams, and code listings.

  19. Don't overuse <figure> – only for self-contained media, not for every image.

  20. Test on different devices – ensure figures look good everywhere.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div class="figure"> Instead of <figure>
docs.text:
<div class="figure">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
    <p class="caption">Figure 1: Caption</p>
</div>
Why it's wrong: No semantic meaning; caption is not programmatically associated with the media.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Caption</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <p> or <span> for Captions
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
    <p>Figure 1: Caption</p>
</figure>
Why it's wrong: The caption should use <figcaption> for semantic association.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Caption</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <figure> Inside <p>
docs.text:
<p>Some text <figure><img src="image.jpg" alt="Description"></figure> more text.</p>
Why it's wrong: <figure> is a block-level element and cannot be inside a <p> (which only accepts phrasing content).

✅ Correct: 

<p>Some text</p>
<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
</figure>
<p>More text.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <figcaption> Elements
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
    <figcaption>Caption 1</figcaption>
    <figcaption>Caption 2</figcaption>
</figure>
Why it's wrong: Only one <figcaption> is allowed per <figure>.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description">
    <figcaption>Caption 1</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing alt on Images Inside Figures
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Caption</figcaption>
</figure>
Why it's wrong: The image needs alt text for accessibility, even if there's a caption.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Description of the image">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Caption</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <figure> for Decorative Images
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="decorative-line.png" alt="">
    <figcaption>Decorative line</figcaption>
</figure>
Why it's wrong: Decorative images don't need a figure or caption.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="decorative-line.png" alt="">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placing <figcaption> in the Middle of the Figure
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="image1.jpg" alt="First image">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Caption</figcaption>
    <img src="image2.jpg" alt="Second image">
</figure>
Why it's wrong: <figcaption> must be the first or last child of <figure>.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <img src="image1.jpg" alt="First image">
    <img src="image2.jpg" alt="Second image">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Caption</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <figure> for Non-Self-Contained Content
docs.text:
<figure>
    <p>This is just a paragraph, not a figure.</p>
</figure>
Why it's wrong: <figure> is for self-contained media, not for arbitrary prose.

✅ Correct: 

<p>This is just a paragraph.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Referencing Figures in the Text
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="chart.png" alt="Sales chart">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Sales growth</figcaption>
</figure>
<p>Sales have grown significantly over the past year.</p>
Why it's wrong: The figure is not referenced in the text, so the reader may not know when to look at it.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <img src="chart.png" alt="Sales chart">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Sales growth</figcaption>
</figure>
<p>As shown in Figure 1, sales have grown significantly over the past year.</p>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <figure> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • Default margins – the default margin: 1em 40px can be overridden with CSS.
  • Images – the main performance consideration is the size and format of images inside figures. Use responsive images (srcset, sizes), lazy loading (loading="lazy"), and modern formats (WebP, AVIF).
  • Code blocks – syntax highlighting adds DOM nodes and JavaScript processing; may impact performance on large listings.
  • Accessibility tree – adds a figure role and associated caption; minimal impact.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <figure> or <figcaption>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External images – be cautious with user-supplied image URLs; they can be used for tracking or malicious purposes.
  • SVG – inline SVG can contain scripts; sanitize if user-generated.
  • No direct security implications – <figure> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <figure> to see its content and structure.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the figure role and associated caption.
  • Computed styles – check the display and margin properties.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('figure') to list all figures.
  • Validator – check for multiple <figcaption> elements and incorrect nesting.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the figure and caption are announced correctly.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and semantic HTML.
  • Test responsive images – check that srcset and sizes work correctly.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For images with captions – photos, illustrations.
  • For diagrams – flowcharts, architecture diagrams.
  • For charts and graphs – bar charts, line graphs.
  • For code snippets – listings, examples.
  • For screenshots – UI screenshots, error messages.
  • For videos – tutorials, demos.
  • For audio – podcasts, sound clips.
  • For tables with captions – when the table needs a figure caption.
  • For quotes with attribution – pull quotes.
  • For maps with legends – geographic maps.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For decorative images – use <img> alone.
  • For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For generic containers – use <div>.
  • For prose – use <p>.
  • For navigation – use <nav>.
  • For sidebars – use <aside>.
  • For self-contained prose – use <article>.
  • For thematic groupings – use <section>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <figcaption> – the caption for a <figure>.
  • <img> – images.
  • <pre> and <code> – code listings.
  • <svg> – vector graphics.
  • <video> and <audio> – media.
  • <table> – tabular data.
  • <blockquote> – quotations.
  • ARIA figure role – accessibility role.
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.
  • Structured Data – for images and media.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <figure> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • A <figure> can have at most one <figcaption>. The caption must be the first or last child of the figure.

  • The <figcaption> provides an accessible name for the figure, which is announced by screen readers.

  • The alt text on an image and the <figcaption> serve different purposes: the alt describes the image itself; the caption provides context and a figure number.

  • The <figure> element can contain multiple media elements (e.g., before/after images) with a single caption.

  • The <figure> element has default margins (1em 40px) that you may want to override with CSS.

  • Search engines use <figure> and <figcaption> to understand the relationship between images and their captions, which can improve image search.

  • The <figure> element is commonly used in scientific papers, textbooks, and technical documentation.

  • A <figure> without a <figcaption> is valid but provides less context.

  • The <figure> element is part of the flow content and palpable content categories.

  • The <figure> element can be nested inside <article>, <section>, <aside>, <main>, and <body>.

  • The <figure> element is not a landmark; it does not create a navigable region in the accessibility tree.

  • Browser reader modes typically include figures with their captions, as they are part of the primary content.

  • The <figure> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.

  • The <figure> element is one of the most commonly used semantic elements in modern web development.

  • A <figure> with a code listing uses <pre><code> for the code and <figcaption> for the listing number.

  • The <figure> element can be used for pull quotes with <blockquote> and <figcaption>.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <figure> element represents self-contained content — typically media such as an image, diagram, illustration, code snippet, or chart — that is referenced from the main flow of the document.
  • It is a block-level element and flow content.
  • It is often accompanied by a <figcaption> element, which provides a caption or legend.
  • The <figcaption> must be the first or last child of the <figure>.
  • Only one <figcaption> is allowed per <figure>.
  • Best practices: use <figure> for self-contained media, include a <figcaption> when the media needs explanation, provide alt text on images, keep captions concise, reference figures in the text, and style with CSS.
  • Common mistakes include using <div class="figure"> instead of <figure>, using <p> for captions, nesting <figure> inside <p>, multiple <figcaption> elements, missing alt on images, and using <figure> for decorative images.
  • The <figure> element is essential for semantic clarity, accessibility, and SEO.
  • It is one of the most important semantic elements in modern web development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <details> element is a semantic HTML element that creates a disclosure widget — a native, interactive component that can be toggled between two states: collapsed (content hidden) and expanded (content visible). It is typically paired with a <summary> element, which serves as the clickable label or heading for the widget. When the user clicks the summary (or presses Enter/Space while focused), the details widget opens or closes, revealing or hiding the content inside.

The <details> element is part of the flow content, interactive content, and palpable content categories. It is a block-level element. Its native behaviour is built into the browser — no JavaScript is required to toggle the content, making it a powerful tool for creating accessible, progressively enhanced disclosures.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <details> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Native disclosure – creates an expandable/collapsible widget without JavaScript.
  • Accessibility – keyboard-accessible, screen-reader-friendly, and semantically meaningful.
  • Progressive enhancement – works even when JavaScript is disabled.
  • Space efficiency – hides non-essential content until the user requests it.
  • FAQ sections – ideal for questions and answers.
  • Table of contents – collapsible navigation.
  • Spoiler content – hidden until the user chooses to reveal it.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <details> element is flow content and can appear anywhere flow content is accepted — inside <body>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <div>, and even inside <li> or <td>. It is most commonly used in:

  • FAQ pages – each question is a <summary>, each answer is the details content.
  • Documentation – collapsible sections for advanced topics.
  • Settings panels – advanced options hidden by default.
  • Table of contents – collapsible navigation.
  • Spoiler sections – hidden until clicked.
  • Long articles – collapsible sections for supplementary information.
<details>
    <summary>What is HTML?</summary>
    <p>HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language...</p>
</details>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before <details>, creating an expandable/collapsible widget required JavaScript. Developers had to:

  1. Create a button or clickable element.
  2. Add an event listener.
  3. Toggle the visibility of the content.
  4. Manage ARIA attributes (aria-expanded, aria-controls).
  5. Handle keyboard accessibility.
  6. Manage focus.

This was error-prone, inconsistent across implementations, and often inaccessible. Native HTML had no built-in disclosure widget.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No native disclosure widget Required JavaScript to implement. Inconsistent implementations Each developer had their own pattern. Accessibility issues Many custom widgets lacked keyboard support or ARIA. No progressive enhancement Widgets broke when JavaScript was disabled. Maintenance burden Custom code needed to be maintained and tested.

docs.title: Why <details> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <details> element was introduced in HTML5 to provide a native, accessible, and progressively enhanced disclosure widget. It enables:

  • Zero JavaScript – the toggle works natively.
  • Built-in accessibility – keyboard support, screen reader announcements.
  • Progressive enhancement – works even without JavaScript.
  • Consistency – a standard element with predictable behaviour.
  • Simple API – open attribute controls the state.
  • Styling – can be styled with CSS.

The <details> element is part of the broader semantic HTML movement, which aims to make the web more accessible and reduce reliance on JavaScript for basic interactions.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <details>
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Click to expand</summary>
    <p>Hidden content goes here.</p>
</details>
  • <details> – the container.
  • <summary> – the clickable label (always the first child, or the first child after the open attribute).
  • Content – any flow content, hidden until expanded.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>What is HTML?</summary>
    <p>HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the standard markup language for creating web pages.</p>
</details>

docs.title: Details with open Attribute
docs.text:
The open boolean attribute makes the details expanded by default:

<details open>
    <summary>This is expanded by default</summary>
    <p>You can see this content immediately.</p>
</details>

docs.title: Details Without <summary>
docs.text:
If you omit the <summary> element, the browser provides a default label (usually "Details" or "▶"):

<details>
    <p>This content is hidden until you click the default summary.</p>
</details>

Note: It's best practice to always provide a <summary> element.

docs.title: Multiple Details in a FAQ
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>What is HTML?</summary>
    <p>HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language...</p>
</details>

<details>
    <summary>What is CSS?</summary>
    <p>CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets...</p>
</details>

<details>
    <summary>What is JavaScript?</summary>
    <p>JavaScript is a programming language...</p>
</details>

docs.title: Nested Details
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Chapter 1: Introduction</summary>
    <p>Introduction content...</p>
    <details>
        <summary>Section 1.1: Background</summary>
        <p>Background content...</p>
    </details>
    <details>
        <summary>Section 1.2: Overview</summary>
        <p>Overview content...</p>
    </details>
</details>

docs.title: Details with Interactive Content
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Show Settings</summary>
    <form>
        <label for="name">Name:</label>
        <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
        <button type="submit">Save</button>
    </form>
</details>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <details> Container for the disclosure widget. Provides the toggle behaviour. <summary> Clickable label that toggles the widget. The user interacts with this to open/close. open Boolean attribute; makes the widget expanded by default. Controls the initial state. Content Any flow content. Hidden until expanded.

docs.title: The "Drawer" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <details> as a drawer in a cabinet. The <summary> is the drawer handle — you pull it to open the drawer and reveal what's inside. When you push it back, the drawer closes and the contents are hidden. The drawer is closed by default (unless you specify open), and it works without any special tools (JavaScript).

docs.title: The "FAQ Accordion" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a FAQ page where each question is clickable and expands to reveal the answer. Each question-answer pair is a <details> element. The question is the <summary>, and the answer is the hidden content. You can have multiple FAQs on a page, and each one opens and closes independently.

docs.title: The "Spoiler Tag" Analogy
docs.text: In forums, a spoiler tag hides content until you click to reveal it. The <details> element is the native HTML equivalent — it hides content behind a summary that the user must click to reveal. This is useful for spoilers, NSFW content, or any content that should be hidden by default.

docs.title: The "Foldable Section" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a long document with foldable sections — each section can be collapsed to hide its content or expanded to reveal it. The <details> element provides this functionality natively, without JavaScript. This is useful for documentation, table of contents, or any long content that benefits from being collapsible.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Disclosure Widget Pattern
docs.text:
The <details> element implements the disclosure widget pattern — a UI component that toggles the visibility of content. The pattern consists of:

  • A trigger (the <summary>) — what the user clicks.
  • The content — what is shown or hidden.
  • A state — expanded or collapsed.

This is a common pattern in web UIs, and <details> provides a native, accessible implementation.

docs.title: Concept 2: The <summary> Element
docs.text:
The <summary> element is the clickable label for the <details> widget. It must be the first child of <details> (unless there is no summary, in which case the browser provides a default). The <summary> is displayed as a clickable label with a disclosure triangle (▶ or ▼) that indicates the state.

<details>
    <summary>Click me</summary>  <!-- Must be first child -->
    <p>Hidden content...</p>
</details>

Key points: - Only one <summary> is allowed per <details>. - If omitted, the browser provides a default label (usually "Details"). - The <summary> can contain phrasing content or a heading (<h1>–<h6>).

docs.title: Concept 3: The open Attribute
docs.text:
The open attribute is a boolean attribute that controls whether the details widget is expanded or collapsed:

  • Present → expanded.
  • Absent → collapsed (default).
<!-- Collapsed by default -->
<details>
    <summary>Click to expand</summary>
    <p>Hidden content...</p>
</details>

<!-- Expanded by default -->
<details open>
    <summary>Already expanded</summary>
    <p>Visible content...</p>
</details>

In JavaScript, you can read and modify the open property:

const details = document.querySelector('details');
console.log(details.open); // true or false
details.open = true;       // Expands the widget
details.open = false;      // Collapses the widget

docs.title: Concept 4: The toggle Event
docs.text:
When the <details> widget is opened or closed, the browser fires a toggle event. You can listen for this event to run code when the state changes:

const details = document.querySelector('details');
details.addEventListener('toggle', function() {
    console.log('State changed. Open:', this.open);
});

Note: The toggle event does not bubble (in most browsers), so you must attach the listener to each <details> element individually.

docs.title: Concept 5: Accessibility
docs.text:
The <details> element is natively accessible:

  • Keyboard: The <summary> is focusable. Pressing Enter or Space toggles the widget.
  • Screen readers: The <summary> is announced as a "disclosure triangle" or "button" with an expanded/collapsed state.
  • ARIA: The browser automatically applies the correct ARIA roles and states (button, aria-expanded).

You don't need to add any ARIA attributes — the browser handles it.

docs.title: Concept 6: Content Model
docs.text:
The <details> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Paragraphs (<p>)
  • Lists (<ul>, <ol>)
  • Images (<img>)
  • Forms (<form>)
  • Headings (<h1>–<h6>)
  • Tables (<table>)
  • Other <details> elements (nested)

The <summary> element accepts phrasing content or a heading (<h1>–<h6>).

docs.title: Concept 7: Styling <details> with CSS
docs.text:
The <details> and <summary> elements can be styled with CSS:

details {
    border: 1px solid #ccc;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 0.5rem;
}

summary {
    font-weight: bold;
    cursor: pointer;
}

details[open] {
    background-color: #f8f9fa;
}

/* Style the disclosure triangle */
summary::marker {
    color: #3498db;
}

The disclosure triangle (▶) is a marker — you can style it with ::marker or remove it with list-style: none:

summary {
    list-style: none; /* Hides the default triangle */
}
summary::before {
    content: "▶ "; /* Custom triangle */
}
details[open] summary::before {
    content: "▼ ";
}

docs.title: Concept 8: <details> vs. JavaScript Accordions
docs.text:
Aspect <details> JavaScript Accordion JavaScript required No Yes Accessibility Built-in Requires ARIA and keyboard handling Progressive enhancement Works without JS Breaks without JS Styling Limited but sufficient Full control Animation Hard (height transitions) Easy Complexity Low High Maintenance Low High

Rule: Use <details> when you need a simple disclosure; use a JavaScript accordion when you need complex animations or custom behaviour.

docs.title: Concept 9: <details> and name Attribute (Exclusive Accordions)
docs.text:
The name attribute allows you to create exclusive accordions — where only one <details> in a group can be open at a time:

<details name="faq">
    <summary>Question 1</summary>
    <p>Answer 1</p>
</details>
<details name="faq">
    <summary>Question 2</summary>
    <p>Answer 2</p>
</details>
<details name="faq">
    <summary>Question 3</summary>
    <p>Answer 3</p>
</details>

When you open one <details> with a given name, any other <details> with the same name that is open will be automatically closed. This is useful for FAQ sections where you want only one answer visible at a time.

docs.title: Concept 10: <details> and SEO
docs.text: Search engines can index the content inside <details> even when it's collapsed. Google has confirmed that content inside <details> is indexed and can appear in search results. This makes <details> a safe choice for FAQ content — it's accessible, space-efficient, and SEO-friendly.

docs.title: Concept 11: <details> and aria-expanded (Not Needed)
docs.text:
Because <details> is natively accessible, you should not add aria-expanded to the <summary> or <details> element. The browser automatically exposes the correct state to assistive technologies.

<!-- Bad: unnecessary ARIA -->
<details aria-expanded="false">
    <summary aria-expanded="false">Click me</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>

<!-- Good: native semantics -->
<details>
    <summary>Click me</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <details>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<details>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It checks for the `open` attribute:
    │   ├── If present → the details is expanded.
    │   └── If absent → the details is collapsed (default).
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes the content:
    │   ├── The first `<summary>` becomes the clickable label.
    │   ├── If no `<summary>` → browser provides a default label.
    │   └── Other content becomes the hidden content.
    │
    ▼
5.  When the closing tag is encountered, the element is closed.
    │
    ▼
6.  Default styles are applied:
    │   ├── display: block
    │   └── The disclosure triangle (▶) is shown.
    │
    ▼
7.  The element is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   ├── role: group (or disclosure)
    │   ├── The summary is a button with aria-expanded.
    │   └── The content is hidden from screen readers when collapsed.
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
9.  When the user clicks the summary:
    │   ├── The `open` attribute is toggled.
    │   ├── The content is shown/hidden.
    │   ├── The `toggle` event is fired.
    │   └── Screen readers announce the state change.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text: In the accessibility tree, <details> is exposed as a group with a button (the summary) and the hidden content. The button has an aria-expanded state (true or false), which the browser manages automatically.

docs.title: The toggle Event
docs.text:
The toggle event is fired when the <details> is opened or closed. It does not bubble by default (though this may change in future specifications). You can listen for it on each <details> element:

document.querySelectorAll('details').forEach(details => {
    details.addEventListener('toggle', () => {
        console.log('Toggled:', details.open);
    });
});

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
details {
    display: block;
}

summary {
    display: list-item; /* or block in some browsers */
    cursor: pointer;
}

The disclosure triangle is created by the ::marker pseudo-element (or the list-style property).

docs.title: The HTMLDetailsElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <details> is represented by the HTMLDetailsElement interface, which inherits from HTMLElement. It has one specific property:

  • open – a boolean that reflects the open attribute.
const details = document.querySelector('details');
console.log(details.open); // true or false
details.open = true;       // Expands the widget

docs.title: The <summary> Element
docs.text: The <summary> element is represented by the HTMLElement interface. It has no specific properties beyond those of HTMLElement.

docs.title: The toggle Event
docs.text: The toggle event is of type Event (not a special interface). It is fired on the <details> element when the state changes.

docs.title: Browser Implementation
docs.text: The <details> element is implemented natively in the browser's rendering engine. The disclosure triangle is rendered by the browser, and the toggle behaviour is handled by the browser's event system. No JavaScript is required for the basic functionality.

docs.title: Accessibility API
docs.text:
The browser maps <details> to the appropriate accessibility roles and states:

  • The <details> element is a group (or disclosure in some implementations).
  • The <summary> is a button with aria-expanded.
  • The content is hidden from the accessibility tree when collapsed.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <details> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<details>` element with a `<summary>` and content.
    │   └── Example: <details><summary>Click</summary><p>Content</p></details>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<details>` and `<summary>` nodes are created.
    │   └── The `open` attribute is read.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (display: block, disclosure triangle).
    │
    ▼
5.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── group with a button (summary) and hidden content.
    │
    ▼
6.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  User clicks the summary (or presses Enter/Space):
    │   ├── The `open` attribute is toggled.
    │   ├── The content is shown/hidden.
    │   ├── The `toggle` event is fired.
    │   └── Screen readers announce the state change.
    │
    ▼
8.  JavaScript may listen for the `toggle` event or modify the `open` property.
    │
    ▼
9.  When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const details = document.querySelector('details');

// Expand the details
details.open = true;

// Collapse the details
details.open = false;

// Toggle the details
details.open = !details.open;

// Listen for toggle events
details.addEventListener('toggle', () => {
    console.log('State:', details.open);
});

docs.title: Example 1: Simple FAQ

</details>

Behaviour: Only one question can be open at a time.

    <p>You can see this content immediately.</p>

    <details>

    <form>
        <label for="api-key">API Key:</label>
        <input type="text" id="api-key" name="api-key">

        <label for="timeout">Timeout (seconds):</label>
        <input type="number" id="timeout" name="timeout" value="30">

        <button type="submit">Save</button>
    </form>

    <summary><h2>What is Semantic HTML?</h2></summary>
    <p>Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that convey meaning...</p>
</details>

Note: Using a heading inside <summary> is valid and can be useful for document structure.

docs.title: Example 8: Details with an Image
docs.text:

    <summary>Show diagram</summary>
    <figure>
        <img src="diagram.png" alt="System architecture diagram">
        <figcaption>Figure 1: System architecture</figcaption>

docs.title: Example 9: Styling <details> with CSS
docs.text:
<style>
    details {
        border: 1px solid #ccc;
        border-radius: 4px;
        margin-bottom: 1rem;
        padding: 0.5rem;
    }

    summary {
        font-weight: bold;
        cursor: pointer;
        padding: 0.5rem;
        list-style: none; /* Hide default triangle */
    }

    summary::before {
        content: "▶ ";
        display: inline-block;
        transition: transform 0.2s;
    }

    details[open] summary::before {
        transform: rotate(90deg);
    }

    details[open] {
        background-color: #f8f9fa;
    }

    details p {
        margin: 0.5rem 0 0 1.5rem;
    }
</style>

<details>
    <summary>What is HTML?</summary>
    <p>HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language...</p>
</details>

docs.title: Example 10: Details with JavaScript
docs.text:
<details id="myDetails">
    <summary>Click to expand</summary>
    <p>Hidden content...</p>
</details>

<button id="expandBtn">Expand</button>
<button id="collapseBtn">Collapse</button>
<button id="toggleBtn">Toggle</button>

<script>
    const details = document.getElementById('myDetails');

    document.getElementById('expandBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        details.open = true;
    });

    document.getElementById('collapseBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        details.open = false;
    });

    document.getElementById('toggleBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        details.open = !details.open;
    });

    details.addEventListener('toggle', () => {
        console.log('Details is now:', details.open ? 'open' : 'closed');
    });
</script>

            <tr><th>Property</th><th>Value</th></tr>
        </thead>

            <tr><td>Battery</td><td>5000 mAh</td></tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <summary>Show code example</summary>
    <pre><code>
function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
    </code></pre>
</details>

docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>⚠️ Spoiler Alert: Click to reveal</summary>
    <p>The butler did it.</p>
</details>

docs.title: Example 14: Details in a Documentation Page
docs.text:
<main>
    <h1>API Documentation</h1>

    <details>
        <summary>Authentication</summary>
        <p>To authenticate, include your API key in the header...</p>
    </details>

    <details>
        <summary>Endpoints</summary>
        <ul>
            <li><code>GET /users</code> — Returns a list of users</li>
            <li><code>POST /users</code> — Creates a new user</li>
            <li><code>DELETE /users/:id</code> — Deletes a user</li>
        </ul>
    </details>

    <details>
        <summary>Error Handling</summary>
        <p>Errors are returned as JSON objects...</p>
    </details>
</main>

docs.title: Example 15: Details with role="group" (Not Needed)
docs.text:
The browser automatically applies the correct roles. You don't need to add ARIA:

<!-- Bad: unnecessary ARIA -->
<details role="group">
    <summary role="button" aria-expanded="false">Click</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>

<!-- Good: native semantics -->
<details>
    <summary>Click</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example FAQ sections Each question-answer pair Table of contents Collapsible navigation Advanced settings Hidden options Spoiler content Hidden until clicked Documentation Collapsible sections Code examples Hidden code blocks Specifications Hidden tables Image galleries Collapsible images Forms Optional fields Nested navigation Hierarchical menus Product details Collapsible specifications Legal text Terms and conditions Long articles Collapsible sections Interactive tutorials Step-by-step instructions

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always include a <summary> – it's the clickable label. Without it, the browser provides a generic default.

  2. Place <summary> as the first child – it must be the first child of <details>.

  3. Use descriptive summary text – the summary should clearly indicate what will be revealed.

  4. Don't add ARIA attributes – the browser handles accessibility natively.

  5. Use the open attribute for default-expanded – if you want the content visible initially.

  6. Use the name attribute for exclusive accordions – to allow only one open at a time.

  7. Style with CSS – the default styles are minimal; use CSS for a polished look.

  8. Use ::marker for the triangle – to customise the disclosure triangle.

  9. Listen for the toggle event – to run code when the state changes.

  10. Keep content inside <details> accessible – all interactive elements inside should be keyboard-accessible.

  11. Don't nest <details> too deeply – it can be confusing.

  12. Use <details> for progressive enhancement – it works without JavaScript.

  13. Test with screen readers – ensure the state is announced correctly.

  14. Validate your HTML – check for multiple <summary> elements and incorrect nesting.

  15. Consider SEO – content inside <details> is indexed by search engines.

  16. Use <details> for FAQ sections – it's the ideal use case.

  17. Use <details> for table of contents – collapsible navigation is useful for long documents.

  18. Don't use <details> for primary navigation – use <nav>.

  19. Use open in JavaScript – to programmatically expand or collapse.

  20. Test on different devices – ensure the details widget works everywhere.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Omitting <summary>
docs.text:
<details>
    <p>Content without a summary.</p>
</details>
Why it's wrong: While valid, the browser provides a generic default label ("Details"). It's better to provide a descriptive summary.

✅ Correct: 

<details>
    <summary>Click to expand</summary>
    <p>Content...</p>
</details>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <summary> Elements
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Summary 1</summary>
    <summary>Summary 2</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>
Why it's wrong: Only one <summary> is allowed per <details>. The second summary is ignored.

✅ Correct: 

<details>
    <summary>Summary</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Adding aria-expanded Manually
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary aria-expanded="false">Click</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>
Why it's wrong: The browser manages aria-expanded natively. Adding it manually can cause conflicts.

✅ Correct: 

<details>
    <summary>Click</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placing <summary> After Other Content
docs.text:
<details>
    <p>Content</p>
    <summary>Summary</summary>
</details>
Why it's wrong: <summary> must be the first child (or the first child after the open attribute).

✅ Correct: 

<details>
    <summary>Summary</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <details> for Primary Navigation
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Menu</summary>
    <nav>
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</details>
Why it's wrong: Navigation should use <nav>. <details> is for disclosure widgets, not primary navigation.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <details> Inside <p>
docs.text:
<p>Some text <details><summary>Click</summary>Content</details> more text.</p>
Why it's wrong: <details> is a block-level element and cannot be inside a <p>.

✅ Correct: 

<p>Some text</p>
<details>
    <summary>Click</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>
<p>More text.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <details> Without Styling
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Click</summary>
    <p>Content</p>
</details>
Why it's wrong: The default styling may not match your design. Use CSS for a polished look.

✅ Correct: Add CSS to style the details and summary.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting the name Attribute for Exclusive Accordions
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Question 1</summary>
    <p>Answer 1</p>
</details>
<details>
    <summary>Question 2</summary>
    <p>Answer 2</p>
</details>
Why it's wrong: Without the name attribute, multiple details can be open at once (which may be fine for some use cases).

✅ Correct (for exclusive accordion): 

<details name="faq">
    <summary>Question 1</summary>
    <p>Answer 1</p>
</details>
<details name="faq">
    <summary>Question 2</summary>
    <p>Answer 2</p>
</details>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <details> for Large Amounts of Content
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Show entire book</summary>
    <p>Chapter 1...</p>
    <p>Chapter 2...</p>
    <!-- 100,000 words -->
</details>
Why it's wrong: Very large content inside <details> can be overwhelming and hurt performance.

✅ Correct: Break large content into multiple sections or use navigation.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <details> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • No JavaScript required – the toggle works natively, so there's no script overhead.
  • Content is hidden – when collapsed, the content is not rendered (though it's still in the DOM).
  • Images – if the content contains images, they are loaded even when the details is collapsed (unless loading="lazy" is used).
  • Large content – very large content inside <details> can increase DOM size and memory usage.
  • Animation – animating the height of <details> is difficult because the content is hidden with display: none when collapsed. Use CSS transitions on grid-template-rows or max-height for animation.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) – when inserting user-generated content into <details> or <summary>, use textContent instead of innerHTML.
  • innerHTML – avoid with user input; use a sanitizer if necessary.
  • External links – use rel="noopener noreferrer" for target="_blank".
  • Forms – validate input on the server; don't rely on client-side validation alone.
  • No direct security implications – <details> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <details> to see its content and the open attribute.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check for the group role and button (summary) with aria-expanded.
  • Computed styles – check the display property and the ::marker style.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('details') to list all details.
  • details.open – check the current state.
  • Toggle event – use addEventListener('toggle', ...) to debug state changes.
  • Validator – check for multiple <summary> elements and incorrect nesting.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the state is announced correctly.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For FAQ sections – each question-answer pair.
  • For table of contents – collapsible navigation.
  • For advanced settings – hidden options.
  • For spoiler content – hidden until clicked.
  • For documentation – collapsible sections.
  • For code examples – hidden code blocks.
  • For specifications – hidden tables.
  • For image galleries – collapsible images.
  • For forms – optional fields.
  • For nested navigation – hierarchical menus.
  • For product details – collapsible specifications.
  • For legal text – terms and conditions.
  • For long articles – collapsible sections.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For primary navigation – use <nav>.
  • For main content – use <main>.
  • For sidebars – use <aside>.
  • For generic containers – use <div>.
  • For thematic groupings – use <section>.
  • For self-contained content – use <article>.
  • For very large content – break it into sections.
  • For critical content – content that must be visible should not be hidden.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <summary> – the clickable label for <details>.
  • open attribute – controls the state.
  • toggle event – fired when the state changes.
  • name attribute – for exclusive accordions.
  • ARIA group role – accessibility role.
  • ARIA button role – for the summary.
  • aria-expanded – managed natively by the browser.
  • Semantic HTML – the broader philosophy.
  • Progressive enhancement – works without JavaScript.
  • Disclosure widget pattern – the UI pattern.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <details> element was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • The <details> element provides a native disclosure widget — no JavaScript is required to toggle the content.

  • The <summary> element is the clickable label for <details>. If omitted, the browser provides a default label (usually "Details" or "▶").

  • The open attribute is a boolean attribute — its presence means the details is expanded.

  • The toggle event is fired when the <details> is opened or closed. It does not bubble in most browsers.

  • The name attribute (introduced in 2023) allows you to create exclusive accordions — only one <details> with the same name can be open at a time.

  • The <details> element is natively accessible — keyboard support and screen reader announcements are built in. You don't need to add ARIA attributes.

  • Search engines like Google index content inside <details> even when it's collapsed. This makes it safe for FAQ content.

  • The disclosure triangle (▶) is a marker — you can style it with ::marker or remove it with list-style: none.

  • The <details> element is part of the interactive content category, meaning it's focusable and can be interacted with.

  • The <details> element is commonly used in FAQ sections, documentation, and table of contents.

  • The <details> element can be nested — a <details> inside another <details> creates a hierarchical disclosure.

  • The <summary> element can contain a heading (<h1>–<h6>) for document structure.

  • The <details> element is not a landmark — it does not create a navigable region in the accessibility tree.

  • The <details> element works in all modern browsers, including Internet Explorer 11 (though with some styling differences).

  • The <details> element is a key example of progressive enhancement — it works even when JavaScript is disabled.

  • The <details> element can be animated with CSS using grid-template-rows or max-height, though it's not straightforward.

  • The <details> element is one of the most useful HTML5 additions for creating interactive content without JavaScript.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <details> element creates a disclosure widget — a native, interactive component that can be toggled between collapsed and expanded states.
  • It is a block-level element and flow content.
  • It is typically paired with a <summary> element, which serves as the clickable label.
  • The open boolean attribute controls the initial state (expanded if present).
  • The toggle event fires when the state changes.
  • The name attribute enables exclusive accordions.
  • It is natively accessible — no ARIA or JavaScript required.
  • Best practices: always include a <summary>, place it first, don't add ARIA attributes, use open for default-expanded, use name for exclusive accordions, style with CSS, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include omitting <summary>, multiple <summary> elements, adding aria-expanded manually, placing <summary> after other content, and using <details> for primary navigation.
  • The <details> element is essential for FAQ sections, documentation, table of contents, and any content that benefits from being collapsible.
  • It is one of the most useful HTML5 elements for creating interactive content without JavaScript.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <dialog> element is a semantic HTML element that represents a dialog box — a modal or non-modal window that appears on top of the rest of the page to prompt the user for a response, display information, or confirm an action. Dialogs are commonly used for alerts, confirmations, forms, image lightboxes, and settings panels.

The <dialog> element has a native JavaScript API for opening and closing, plus a ::backdrop pseudo-element for styling the overlay behind the dialog. When opened as a modal (using showModal()), the dialog blocks interaction with the rest of the page, traps focus, and can be dismissed with the Escape key — all natively, without custom JavaScript.

The <dialog> element is part of the flow content and interactive content categories. It is a block-level element. It is a relatively modern addition to HTML (in the HTML Living Standard since around 2013, but only achieving widespread browser support around 2020–2022).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <dialog> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Native modal dialogs – no need for custom modal libraries.
  • Accessibility – focus trapping, keyboard dismissal (Escape), and screen reader announcements are built in.
  • Stacking context – modal dialogs appear on top of all other content (top layer).
  • Backdrop styling – the ::backdrop pseudo-element styles the overlay.
  • Simple API – show(), showModal(), and close() methods.
  • Progressive enhancement – falls back gracefully when JavaScript is unavailable (though dialogs typically require JS to open).
  • Form integration – a <form method="dialog"> inside a <dialog> automatically closes the dialog on submission.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <dialog> element is flow content and can appear anywhere flow content is accepted. It is typically placed near the end of the document (inside <body>), and its visibility is controlled by JavaScript. It is most commonly used in:

  • Confirmation dialogs – "Are you sure you want to delete this?"
  • Alert dialogs – "Your session has expired."
  • Form dialogs – login, signup, settings.
  • Image lightboxes – viewing images in full screen.
  • Promotional popups – newsletter signups, cookie notices.
  • Modal editors – editing content inline.
<dialog id="myDialog">
    <h2>Confirm Action</h2>
    <p>Are you sure you want to proceed?</p>
    <form method="dialog">
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Confirm</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<button id="openBtn">Open Dialog</button>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before <dialog>, creating modal dialogs required a significant amount of custom JavaScript and CSS. Developers had to:

  1. Create a <div> overlay with position: fixed and high z-index.
  2. Prevent body scrolling when the dialog was open.
  3. Trap focus inside the dialog so users couldn't Tab to content behind it.
  4. Handle the Escape key to close the dialog.
  5. Manage focus restoration to the element that opened the dialog.
  6. Add ARIA attributes (role="dialog", aria-modal="true", aria-labelledby).
  7. Ensure the dialog was announced correctly by screen readers.
  8. Deal with edge cases like nested modals, scroll locking, and mobile viewport quirks.

This was complex, error-prone, and often resulted in inaccessible modals. Even popular libraries often had subtle accessibility bugs.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No native modal element Required custom JavaScript and CSS. Focus trapping was manual Many modals were keyboard-inaccessible. No native Escape handling Required custom keydown listeners. Z-index management was fragile Modals could be hidden behind other elements. No native backdrop Required a separate overlay element. Accessibility was often broken Missing ARIA attributes, incorrect focus management. Inconsistent implementations Each library had its own behaviour.

docs.title: Why <dialog> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <dialog> element was introduced in the HTML Living Standard to provide a native, accessible, and robust implementation of modal and non-modal dialogs. It enables:

  • Zero JavaScript for toggling – show(), showModal(), and close() methods.
  • Built-in focus trapping – modal dialogs automatically trap focus.
  • Built-in Escape handling – pressing Escape closes the dialog.
  • Top layer rendering – modal dialogs render on top of everything else.
  • Native backdrop – the ::backdrop pseudo-element styles the overlay.
  • Form integration – <form method="dialog"> closes the dialog on submit.
  • Accessibility – correct roles, focus management, and screen reader support are built in.
  • Styling – can be styled with CSS like any other element.

The <dialog> element is part of the broader movement toward native, accessible web platform features that reduce reliance on JavaScript libraries.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <dialog>
docs.text:
<dialog id="myDialog">
    <p>This is a dialog.</p>
    <button id="closeBtn">Close</button>
</dialog>

<button id="openBtn">Open Dialog</button>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('myDialog');
    const openBtn = document.getElementById('openBtn');
    const closeBtn = document.getElementById('closeBtn');

    openBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        dialog.showModal(); // Opens as a modal
    });

    closeBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        dialog.close(); // Closes the dialog
    });
</script>

docs.title: Modal vs. Non-Modal
docs.text:
The <dialog> element can be opened in two ways:

  • Non-modal (show()) – the dialog appears on top of the page, but the user can still interact with the rest of the page. There is no backdrop, no focus trapping, and Escape does not close it (you must close it manually or with a close button).
  • Modal (showModal()) – the dialog appears on top of everything (in the top layer), the rest of the page is inert (not interactive), a backdrop is shown, focus is trapped inside the dialog, and Escape closes it.
<script>
    // Non-modal
    dialog.show();

    // Modal
    dialog.showModal();
</script>

docs.title: The open Attribute
docs.text:
The open boolean attribute makes the dialog visible by default (as a non-modal dialog):

<dialog open>
    <p>This dialog is open by default (non-modal).</p>
</dialog>

Note: The open attribute only creates a non-modal dialog. To open a modal dialog, you must use showModal().

docs.title: Form Integration: method="dialog"
docs.text:
A <form> with method="dialog" inside a <dialog> will close the dialog when submitted. The value of the submit button is available via the dialog's returnValue property:

<dialog id="confirmDialog">
    <form method="dialog">
        <p>Are you sure you want to delete this item?</p>
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Confirm</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('confirmDialog');
    dialog.showModal();
    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        console.log('User chose:', dialog.returnValue); // "cancel" or "confirm"
    });
</script>

docs.title: The ::backdrop Pseudo-Element
docs.text:
The ::backdrop pseudo-element styles the overlay behind a modal dialog:

dialog::backdrop {
    background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5);
    backdrop-filter: blur(4px);
}

docs.title: Basic Confirmation Dialog
docs.text:
<dialog id="confirmDialog">
    <h2>Confirm Deletion</h2>
    <p>Are you sure you want to delete this item? This action cannot be undone.</p>
    <form method="dialog">
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<button id="deleteBtn">Delete Item</button>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('confirmDialog');
    const deleteBtn = document.getElementById('deleteBtn');

    deleteBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        dialog.showModal();
    });

    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        if (dialog.returnValue === 'confirm') {
            // Perform the delete action
            console.log('Item deleted!');
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <dialog> The dialog container. Hidden by default; shown with JS. showModal() Opens the dialog as a modal. Adds backdrop, traps focus, Escape closes. show() Opens the dialog as non-modal. No backdrop, no focus trap, Escape doesn't close. close() Closes the dialog. Removes the dialog from the top layer. open attribute Opens the dialog by default (non-modal). Useful for static content. <form method="dialog"> Closes the dialog on submit. Simple way to handle user choices. returnValue The value of the clicked button. Used to determine the user's choice. ::backdrop Styles the overlay behind a modal. Customise the backdrop with CSS. close event Fires when the dialog is closed. Run code after the dialog closes.

docs.title: The "Popup Window" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a <dialog> as a popup window that appears on top of the page. When it's modal, it's like a window that blocks all interaction with the page behind it — you must deal with the dialog before you can continue. When it's non-modal, it's like a floating panel you can move away from and come back to later.

docs.title: The "Modal Hotel" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine you're checking into a hotel. The receptionist (the modal dialog) has your full attention — you can't proceed to your room (the main page) until you've completed check-in. The receptionist asks you questions (the form), and when you're done, they give you a key (the returnValue) and the interaction ends. You can't ignore the receptionist and walk past.

docs.title: The "Lightbox" Analogy
docs.text: Think of an image lightbox — you click an image, and it enlarges to fill the screen with a dark backdrop behind it. The rest of the page is dimmed and unclickable. You can close the lightbox by clicking the close button or pressing Escape. This is exactly how a modal <dialog> behaves.

docs.title: Concept 1: Modal vs. Non-Modal
docs.text:
Aspect Modal (showModal()) Non-Modal (show() or open) Backdrop Yes (::backdrop) No Focus trapping Yes No Escape closes Yes No Rest of page interactive No (inert) Yes Top layer Yes No Use case Alerts, confirmations, forms Floating panels, tooltips, notifications

Rule: Use showModal() for anything that requires the user's full attention. Use show() for non-critical, dismissible overlays.

docs.title: Concept 2: The Top Layer
docs.text:
When a dialog is opened as a modal, it is rendered in the top layer — a special rendering layer that sits above all other content on the page, regardless of z-index. This means you don't have to worry about z-index conflicts. The top layer also handles the backdrop automatically.

/* No need for z-index: 9999 */
dialog[open] {
    /* Rendered in the top layer automatically */
}

docs.title: Concept 3: The ::backdrop Pseudo-Element
docs.text:
Every modal dialog has a ::backdrop pseudo-element that covers the entire viewport behind the dialog. It is only rendered when the dialog is opened with showModal(). You can style it to add a dark overlay, blur, or any other effect.

dialog::backdrop {
    background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5);
}

docs.title: Concept 4: Focus Management
docs.text:
• Modal dialogs trap focus: When a modal dialog is open, Tab cycles through focusable elements inside the dialog only. This is done automatically by the browser.
  • Focus returns: When the dialog closes, focus returns to the element that was focused before the dialog opened. This is also automatic.
  • Autofocus: The first focusable element inside the dialog receives focus when the dialog opens, or the element with the autofocus attribute.
<dialog>
    <form method="dialog">
        <input type="text" autofocus> <!-- Gets focus when dialog opens -->
        <button>Submit</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

docs.title: Concept 5: The returnValue Property
docs.text:
When a dialog is closed via a <form method="dialog">, the returnValue property is set to the value of the button that was clicked. This is a convenient way to determine the user's choice.

<dialog id="myDialog">
    <form method="dialog">
        <button value="yes">Yes</button>
        <button value="no">No</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('myDialog');
    dialog.showModal();
    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        console.log(dialog.returnValue); // "yes" or "no"
    });
</script>

You can also set the returnValue programmatically:

dialog.close('custom value');

docs.title: Concept 6: The close Event
docs.text:
When a dialog is closed, the close event is fired. This is useful for running cleanup code, updating the UI, or processing the user's choice.

dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
    console.log('Dialog closed. Return value:', dialog.returnValue);
});

docs.title: Concept 7: The cancel Event
docs.text:
When a modal dialog is dismissed via the Escape key, the cancel event is fired before the dialog closes. You can prevent the default behaviour (closing) if needed:

dialog.addEventListener('cancel', (event) => {
    // Prevent the dialog from closing on Escape
    event.preventDefault();
    console.log('Escape pressed but dialog not closed');
});

Note: The cancel event only fires for modal dialogs. Non-modal dialogs are not affected by the Escape key.

docs.title: Concept 8: Content Model
docs.text:
The <dialog> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Headings (<h1>–<h6>)
  • Paragraphs (<p>)
  • Forms (<form>)
  • Lists (<ul>, <ol>)
  • Images (<img>)
  • Any other flow content

docs.title: Concept 9: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
The <dialog> element has default browser styling that makes it look like a centered box:

dialog {
    display: block;
    position: absolute;
    left: 0;
    right: 0;
    width: fit-content;
    height: fit-content;
    margin: auto;
    border: solid;
    padding: 1em;
    background-color: white;
    color: black;
}

dialog:not([open]) {
    display: none;
}

When opened as a modal, the dialog is centered in the viewport and rendered in the top layer.

docs.title: Concept 10: Accessibility
docs.text:
The <dialog> element is natively accessible:

  • Role: dialog (or alertdialog if role="alertdialog").
  • Modal: aria-modal="true" is applied automatically for modal dialogs.
  • Focus: Trapped inside the modal, returned when closed.
  • Escape: Closes the modal automatically.
  • Screen readers: Announce the dialog and its contents.

You should still provide an accessible name for the dialog, typically by referencing a heading with aria-labelledby:

<dialog aria-labelledby="dialogTitle">
    <h2 id="dialogTitle">Confirm Action</h2>
    <p>Are you sure?</p>
</dialog>

docs.title: Concept 11: method="dialog" vs method="post"
docs.text:
A form inside a dialog can use either method="dialog" or a regular method:

  • method="dialog": Closes the dialog on submit. The form data is not sent to the server.
  • method="post" or method="get": Submits the form to the server, which may close the dialog or not (depending on the response).
<!-- Closes the dialog, no server request -->
<form method="dialog">
    <button value="confirm">Confirm</button>
</form>

<!-- Submits to server -->
<form action="/submit" method="post">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: Concept 12: Multiple Dialogs and Stacking
docs.text:
Multiple modal dialogs can be open at the same time, and they stack in the order they were opened. The most recently opened dialog is on top and receives focus. This is useful for nested dialogs (e.g., a confirmation dialog on top of a settings dialog).

<dialog id="dialog1">...</dialog>
<dialog id="dialog2">...</dialog>
<script>
    dialog1.showModal();
    dialog2.showModal(); // On top of dialog1
</script>

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <dialog>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<dialog>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the element.
    │
    ▼
3.  It checks for the `open` attribute:
    │   ├── If present → the dialog is visible (non-modal).
    │   └── If absent → the dialog is hidden (display: none).
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes the content (flow content).
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied (centered box, display: none when closed).
    │
    ▼
6.  The dialog is added to the DOM but not rendered (if closed).
    │
    ▼
7.  JavaScript calls `showModal()` or `show()`:
    │   ├── For modal:
    │   │   ├── The dialog is rendered in the top layer.
    │   │   ├── The `::backdrop` is created.
    │   │   ├── The rest of the page becomes inert.
    │   │   ├── Focus is moved to the first focusable element.
    │   │   └── Escape closes the dialog.
    │   └── For non-modal:
    │       ├── The dialog is rendered as a regular block.
    │       ├── No backdrop.
    │       ├── No focus trapping.
    │       └── Escape does not close the dialog.
    │
    ▼
8.  When the dialog is closed (`close()` or Escape):
    │   ├── The dialog is removed from the top layer.
    │   ├── The backdrop is removed.
    │   ├── Focus returns to the previously focused element.
    │   └── The `close` event is fired.

docs.title: The Top Layer
docs.text: The top layer is a special rendering layer that sits above all other content on the page, including elements with high z-index. When a dialog is opened with showModal(), it is placed in the top layer, along with its ::backdrop. This is why modal dialogs always appear on top and don't need z-index management.

docs.title: Focus Trapping
docs.text: When a modal dialog is open, the browser traps focus inside the dialog. This means pressing Tab cycles through the focusable elements inside the dialog only, and pressing Shift+Tab cycles backwards. The user cannot tab to the rest of the page. This is handled natively by the browser.

docs.title: The ::backdrop Pseudo-Element
docs.text:
The ::backdrop pseudo-element is generated by the browser when a modal dialog is opened. It covers the entire viewport behind the dialog. You can style it with CSS:

dialog::backdrop {
    background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5);
    backdrop-filter: blur(4px);
}

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text: In the accessibility tree, <dialog> is exposed as a dialog role. When opened as a modal, it is marked as modal (aria-modal="true"). The dialog's label is derived from aria-labelledby or aria-label.

docs.title: The HTMLDialogElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <dialog> is represented by the HTMLDialogElement interface, which inherits from HTMLElement. It has the following properties and methods:

Property/Method Type Description open Boolean Reflects the open attribute. returnValue String The value returned when the dialog is closed. show() Method Opens the dialog as non-modal. showModal() Method Opens the dialog as modal. close(returnValue) Method Closes the dialog with an optional return value. 
const dialog = document.querySelector('dialog');
dialog.showModal();       // Opens as modal
console.log(dialog.open); // true
dialog.close('confirmed'); // Closes with return value
console.log(dialog.returnValue); // "confirmed"

docs.title: The cancel and close Events
docs.text:
• cancel: Fired when the user presses Escape on a modal dialog. Can be prevented.
