<img src="https://cdn.example.com/images/logo.png" alt="Logo">

<!-- External font -->
<link rel="preload" href="https://fonts.example.com/font.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: Absolute URLs for Metadata
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Canonical URL (must be absolute) -->
    <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/blog/post.html">

    <!-- Open Graph (must be absolute) -->
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/blog/post.html">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/images/og-image.jpg">

    <!-- Twitter Card (must be absolute) -->
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/images/twitter-image.jpg">

    <!-- hreflang (must be absolute) -->
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/post.html">
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="es" href="https://example.com/es/post.html">
</head>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters https:// The scheme. Tells the browser how to communicate. example.com The host. Identifies the server. :443 The port (optional). Default for HTTPS is 443. /blog/post.html The path. Identifies the resource on the server. ?page=2 The query (optional). Passes parameters to the server. #section-3 The fragment (optional). Identifies a location within the page.

docs.title: The "Street Address" Analogy
docs.text: An absolute URL is like a complete street address: "1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20500, USA." It works from anywhere in the world — you can mail a letter from Tokyo or Timbuktu, and it will arrive at the same place. A relative URL is like saying "the house next door" — it only makes sense if you know where you're standing.

docs.title: The "GPS Coordinates" Analogy
docs.text: An absolute URL is like GPS coordinates — precise, context-independent, and universally understood. A relative URL is like giving directions — "turn left at the second light" — which only work if you know where the journey started.

docs.title: The "ISBN" Analogy
docs.text: An absolute URL is like an ISBN for a book. Every book has a unique ISBN that identifies it globally, regardless of which library or bookstore you're in. A relative URL is like a shelf number in a specific library — it only makes sense within that library.

docs.title: The "Full Name vs. Nickname" Analogy
docs.text: An absolute URL is a person's full legal name — it uniquely identifies them anywhere in the world. A relative URL is a nickname — it works within a social group but is ambiguous outside it.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Components of an Absolute URL
docs.text:
An absolute URL has several components, as defined in the URL Living Standard:

scheme://user:password@host:port/path?query#fragment
  • Scheme – the protocol (http, https, mailto, tel, etc.).
  • Userinfo – optional username and password (deprecated for security).
  • Host – the domain name or IP address.
  • Port – optional port number.
  • Path – the path to the resource.
  • Query – optional query string.
  • Fragment – optional fragment identifier.

In practice, most absolute URLs look like: 

https://example.com/path/to/page.html?query=value#fragment

docs.title: Concept 2: The Scheme
docs.text:
The scheme (or protocol) tells the browser how to communicate with the server. Common schemes:

Scheme Description Use Case https HTTP Secure Modern web (recommended) http HTTP Legacy web (deprecated) mailto Email Email links tel Telephone Phone links ftp File Transfer Protocol File downloads (rare) data Inline data Small embedded resources blob Binary large object Browser-generated data file Local file system Local files (not for web) ws / wss WebSocket Real-time communication sms SMS Text messages (mobile) geo Geographic location Maps

Best practice: Use https for all web resources. Avoid http.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Host
docs.text:
The host identifies the server that holds the resource. It can be:

  • A domain name: example.com, www.example.com, blog.example.com.
  • An IP address: 192.168.1.1, [2001:db8::1] (IPv6).
  • localhost: for local development.

The host is case-insensitive: EXAMPLE.COM and example.com are the same.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Port
docs.text:
The port is optional. If omitted, the default port for the scheme is used:

Scheme Default Port http 80 https 443 ftp 21 ws 80 wss 443

In practice, ports are almost never specified for web URLs (they're implicit).

docs.title: Concept 5: The Path
docs.text:
The path identifies the resource on the server. It is case-sensitive on most servers.

https://example.com/Blog/Post.html
                     └────┬────┘
                     case-sensitive

The path can be: - A file path: /blog/post.html - A directory: /blog/ - A dynamic route: /api/users/123 - Empty: https://example.com (defaults to /)

docs.title: Concept 6: The Query String
docs.text:
The query string (or query parameters) passes data to the server. It starts with ? and consists of key-value pairs separated by &.

https://example.com/search?q=html&page=2
                            └───┬───┘
                            query string
  • Keys and values are separated by =.
  • Pairs are separated by &.
  • Values are URL-encoded (spaces become %20 or +).

docs.title: Concept 7: The Fragment
docs.text:
The fragment (or hash) identifies a location within the page. It starts with #.

https://example.com/page.html#section-3
                             └────┬────┘
                             fragment

The fragment is: - Not sent to the server — it's handled by the browser. - Used to scroll to an element with the matching id. - Used by JavaScript to manage client-side state.

docs.title: Concept 8: The Relationship Between Absolute and Relative URLs
docs.text:
Every relative URL is ultimately resolved to an absolute URL by the browser. The absolute URL is what the browser actually uses to make the request.

Relative URL: "../about.html"
Base URL:     "https://example.com/blog/post.html"
Absolute URL: "https://example.com/about.html"

docs.title: Concept 9: Absolute URLs for Canonicalization
docs.text:
A canonical URL is an absolute URL that tells search engines which version of a page is the "preferred" one. This is essential for SEO when a page can be accessed via multiple URLs.

<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/blog/post.html">

Why: Search engines treat https://example.com/blog/post.html, https://example.com/blog/post.html?ref=twitter, and https://example.com/blog/post.html#comments as potentially different pages. The canonical tag tells them which one is authoritative.

docs.title: Concept 10: Absolute URLs in Open Graph
docs.text:
The Open Graph protocol requires absolute URLs for og:url, og:image, and other properties. This is because social media platforms need to fetch these resources from outside the context of your page.

<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/blog/post.html">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/images/og-image.jpg">

docs.title: Concept 11: Absolute URLs in Sitemaps
docs.text:
Sitemaps (XML files that list a site's pages) require absolute URLs:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/</loc>
    </url>
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/about.html</loc>
    </url>
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/blog/post.html</loc>
    </url>
</urlset>

docs.title: Concept 12: Absolute URLs in JSON-LD
docs.text:
Structured data (JSON-LD, Microdata) requires absolute URLs for properties like url, image, and mainEntityOfPage:

{
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "Article",
    "url": "https://example.com/blog/post.html",
    "image": "https://example.com/images/post-image.jpg",
    "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Jane Doe",
        "url": "https://example.com/authors/jane-doe"
    }
}

docs.title: Concept 13: Absolute URLs in RSS/Atom Feeds
docs.text:
RSS and Atom feeds require absolute URLs for links and images:

<item>
    <title>My Blog Post</title>
    <link>https://example.com/blog/post.html</link>
    <guid>https://example.com/blog/post.html</guid>
</item>

docs.title: Concept 14: Absolute URLs in Emails
docs.text:
HTML emails must use absolute URLs because there is no "current document" for relative URLs to resolve against:

<a href="https://example.com/sale">
    <img src="https://example.com/images/banner.jpg" alt="Sale">
</a>

docs.title: Concept 15: Security and Absolute URLs
docs.text:
Absolute URLs can be a security risk if they point to untrusted resources. Best practices:

  • Use HTTPS – never HTTP for production.
  • Sanitize user input – never insert user-supplied URLs directly into href or src.
  • Avoid javascript: URLs – they can execute scripts.
  • Use rel="noopener noreferrer" – for external links with target="_blank".
  • Validate redirects – prevent open redirects.
  • Use Content Security Policy (CSP) – restrict allowed sources.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing an Absolute URL
docs.text:
1.  Browser encounters an absolute URL in an HTML attribute.
    │   └── Example: <a href="https://example.com/about.html">
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses the URL into components:
    │   ├── Scheme: https
    │   ├── Host: example.com
    │   ├── Path: /about.html
    │   ├── Query: (none)
    │   └── Fragment: (none)
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser does NOT need to resolve the URL (it's already absolute).
    │
    ▼
4.  When the user clicks the link:
    │   ├── Browser checks if the URL is safe (e.g., not javascript:).
    │   ├── Browser makes a DNS lookup for example.com.
    │   ├── Browser establishes a TCP connection (port 443 for HTTPS).
    │   ├── Browser performs a TLS handshake (for HTTPS).
    │   ├── Browser sends an HTTP GET request for /about.html.
    │   └── Browser receives the response and renders the page.
    │
    ▼
5.  The URL is added to the browser history.

docs.title: URL Parsing
docs.text:
The browser parses the absolute URL using the URL Living Standard algorithm. JavaScript exposes the components via the URL object:

const url = new URL('https://example.com:8443/blog/post.html?page=2#section-3');

console.log(url.protocol); // "https:"
console.log(url.hostname); // "example.com"
console.log(url.port);     // "8443"
console.log(url.pathname); // "/blog/post.html"
console.log(url.search);   // "?page=2"
console.log(url.hash);     // "#section-3"
console.log(url.origin);   // "https://example.com:8443"
console.log(url.href);     // full URL

docs.title: The Difference Between href and getAttribute('href')
docs.text:
When you read the href property, the browser returns the resolved absolute URL:

const link = document.querySelector('a');
link.getAttribute('href'); // "https://example.com/about.html" (raw)
link.href;                  // "https://example.com/about.html" (resolved)

For absolute URLs, the raw and resolved values are the same. For relative URLs, they differ.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
When the browser navigates to an absolute URL, it must resolve the hostname to an IP address:

  1. Browser cache – checks if the hostname was recently resolved.
  2. OS cache – checks the operating system's DNS cache.
  3. Hosts file – checks the local hosts file.
  4. DNS server – queries the configured DNS server.
  5. Root DNS – if not cached, the DNS server queries the root, TLD, and authoritative DNS servers.

This is why preconnect and dns-prefetch can improve performance — they resolve the DNS early.

docs.title: HTTP Request
docs.text:
Once the IP address is known, the browser:

  1. Establishes a TCP connection (3-way handshake).
  2. Performs a TLS handshake (for HTTPS).
  3. Sends an HTTP request: 
    GET /about.html HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: ...
Accept: text/html
  4. Receives the response: 
    HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 1234
...

The browser then renders the response.

docs.title: The URL Interface
docs.text:
The URL Living Standard defines the URL interface, implemented in JavaScript:

interface URL {
    constructor(url, base);
    // Properties
    href: string;
    origin: string;
    protocol: string;
    username: string;
    password: string;
    host: string;
    hostname: string;
    port: string;
    pathname: string;
    search: string;
    searchParams: URLSearchParams;
    hash: string;
    // Methods
    toString(): string;
    toJSON(): string;
}

docs.title: The URL Parsing Algorithm
docs.text:
The URL parsing algorithm is defined in the URL Living Standard. It is a state machine that processes the URL character by character, producing a URL record with the following components:

  • scheme
  • username
  • password
  • host
  • port
  • path (a list of segments)
  • query
  • fragment

The algorithm handles edge cases like: - Invalid characters. - Percent-encoding. - Special schemes (http, https, etc.). - Backslashes (treated as forward slashes for special schemes).

docs.title: The Browser's URL Implementation
docs.text:
Each browser implements its own URL parser:

  • Chrome/Edge: uses the url library from Chromium.
  • Firefox: uses nsStandardURL in Gecko.
  • Safari: uses CFURL from CoreFoundation (with WebKit additions).

Despite different implementations, they all follow the same specification, so URLs resolve consistently.

docs.title: The DNS Resolver
docs.text:
DNS resolution is handled by the operating system, not the browser. The browser calls the OS resolver (e.g., getaddrinfo on Unix), which:

  1. Checks the local cache.
  2. Checks the hosts file.
  3. Queries the configured DNS server.

Browsers may implement their own DNS cache and prefetching to improve performance.

docs.title: The Network Stack
docs.text:
Once the URL is resolved to an IP address, the browser's network stack:

  1. Opens a socket (TCP).
  2. Performs the TLS handshake (for HTTPS).
  3. Sends the HTTP request.
  4. Receives the response.
  5. Passes the response to the rendering engine.

docs.title: The Same-Origin Policy
docs.text:
The same-origin policy is a security mechanism that restricts how resources from one origin (scheme + host + port) can interact with resources from another origin. Absolute URLs are compared by their origin:

https://example.com/page1  ← same origin
https://example.com/page2  ← same origin
https://other.com          ← different origin
http://example.com         ← different origin (different scheme)
https://example.com:8443   ← different origin (different port)

The same-origin policy affects AJAX, cookies, and many other web APIs.

docs.title: SEO and Absolute URLs
docs.text:
Search engines use absolute URLs to:

  • Crawl the web (following links).
  • Canonicalize pages (via canonical tags).
  • Build the link graph (the network of links between pages).
  • Rank pages (PageRank and similar algorithms).
  • Serve the correct page to users.

The canonical URL tells search engines which absolute URL is the "preferred" one for a page.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an Absolute URL
docs.text:
1.  Author writes an absolute URL in an HTML attribute.
    │   └── Example: <a href="https://example.com/about.html">
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and encounters the absolute URL.
    │   └── The URL is parsed into components.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser validates the URL:
    │   ├── Checks the scheme (is it allowed?).
    │   ├── Checks the host (does it exist?).
    │   └── Sanitizes the URL (removes dangerous schemes).
    │
    ▼
5.  User clicks the link:
    │   ├── Browser performs DNS lookup.
    │   ├── Browser establishes a connection.
    │   ├── Browser sends the HTTP request.
    │   └── Browser receives the response.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser renders the new page.
    │
    ▼
7.  The URL is added to the browser history.
    │
    ▼
8.  The URL is stored in bookmarks (if the user bookmarks the page).
    │
    ▼
9.  The URL is shared (if the user copies and pastes it).
    │
    ▼
10. Search engines crawl the URL and index the page.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Canonical URL
docs.text:
1.  Author adds a <link rel="canonical" href="..."> tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  Search engine crawls the page.
    │
    ▼
3.  Search engine reads the canonical URL.
    │
    ▼
4.  Search engine consolidates all duplicate URLs into the canonical one.
    │
    ▼
5.  Search engine indexes the page under the canonical URL.
    │
    ▼
6.  Search engine displays the canonical URL in search results.

docs.title: Example 1: External Link
docs.text: <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML">MDN HTML Docs</a>

docs.title: Example 2: External Link with Security Attributes
docs.text:
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">
    Visit Example.com
</a>

docs.title: Example 3: Canonical URL
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/blog/post.html">
</head>

Why: Prevents duplicate content issues when a page is accessible via multiple URLs.

docs.title: Example 4: Open Graph Metadata
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta property="og:type" content="article">
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/blog/post.html">
    <meta property="og:title" content="My Blog Post">
    <meta property="og:description" content="A great article about HTML.">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/images/og-image.jpg">
</head>

Why: Social media platforms require absolute URLs for previews.

docs.title: Example 5: Twitter Card Metadata
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="My Blog Post">
    <meta name="twitter:description" content="A great article about HTML.">
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/images/twitter-image.jpg">
</head>

docs.title: Example 6: hreflang for Multilingual Sites
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/en/page.html">
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/page.html">
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="es" href="https://example.com/es/page.html">
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="https://example.com/page.html">
</head>

Why: Tells search engines about language-specific versions of the page.

docs.title: Example 7: External Stylesheet
docs.text:
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.example.com/styles/main.css">

Why: External resources must use absolute URLs.

docs.title: Example 8: External Script
docs.text: <script src="https://cdn.example.com/scripts/app.js" defer></script>

docs.title: Example 9: External Image
docs.text: <img src="https://cdn.example.com/images/logo.png" alt="Company Logo">

docs.title: Example 10: Preconnect to External Domain
docs.text:
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

Why: Establishes early connections to external domains, improving performance.

docs.title: Example 11: Preload External Resource
docs.text: <link rel="preload" href="https://cdn.example.com/fonts/roboto.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: Example 12: DNS Prefetch
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">

Why: Resolves the DNS for the external domain early, reducing latency.

docs.title: Example 13: Sitemap with Absolute URLs
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-09-08</lastmod>
        <changefreq>daily</changefreq>
        <priority>1.0</priority>
    </url>
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/about.html</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-08-15</lastmod>
        <changefreq>monthly</changefreq>
        <priority>0.8</priority>
    </url>
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/blog/post.html</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-09-01</lastmod>
        <changefreq>weekly</changefreq>
        <priority>0.6</priority>
    </url>
</urlset>

docs.title: Example 14: JSON-LD Structured Data
docs.text:
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "Article",
    "headline": "How to Use Absolute URLs",
    "url": "https://example.com/blog/absolute-urls.html",
    "image": "https://example.com/images/absolute-urls.jpg",
    "datePublished": "2026-09-08",
    "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Jane Doe",
        "url": "https://example.com/authors/jane-doe"
    },
    "publisher": {
        "@type": "Organization",
        "name": "My Blog",
        "logo": {
            "@type": "ImageObject",
            "url": "https://example.com/images/logo.png"
        }
    }
}
</script>

docs.title: Example 15: RSS Feed with Absolute URLs
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<rss version="2.0">
    <channel>
        <title>My Blog</title>
        <link>https://example.com</link>
        <description>A blog about HTML and the web.</description>
        <item>
            <title>How to Use Absolute URLs</title>
            <link>https://example.com/blog/absolute-urls.html</link>
            <guid>https://example.com/blog/absolute-urls.html</guid>
            <pubDate>Mon, 08 Sep 2026 00:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
            <description>An article about absolute URLs.</description>
        </item>
    </channel>
</rss>

docs.title: Example 16: HTML Email with Absolute URLs
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Newsletter</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Newsletter</h1>
    <p>Check out our latest article:</p>
    <a href="https://example.com/blog/absolute-urls.html">
        <img src="https://example.com/images/article-thumbnail.jpg" alt="Article Thumbnail">
        <br>
        How to Use Absolute URLs
    </a>
    <p>
        <a href="https://example.com/unsubscribe">Unsubscribe</a>
    </p>
</body>
</html>

Why: Email clients don't have a "current document" — all URLs must be absolute.

docs.title: Example 17: Absolute URL with Port
docs.text: <a href="https://example.com:8443/api/v1/users">API Endpoint</a>

docs.title: Example 18: Absolute URL with Query String
docs.text: <a href="https://example.com/search?q=html&page=2&sort=relevance">Search Results</a>

docs.title: Example 19: Absolute URL with Fragment
docs.text:
<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/a#attributes">
    Link Attributes
</a>

docs.title: Example 20: Using the URL API in JavaScript
docs.text:
const url = new URL('https://example.com/blog/post.html?page=2#section-3');

console.log(url.protocol);  // "https:"
console.log(url.hostname);  // "example.com"
console.log(url.pathname);  // "/blog/post.html"
console.log(url.search);    // "?page=2"
console.log(url.hash);      // "#section-3"
console.log(url.origin);    // "https://example.com"

// Modify components
url.pathname = '/about.html';
url.searchParams.set('page', '3');
console.log(url.href); // "https://example.com/about.html?page=3#section-3"

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example External links https://example.com Canonical URLs <link rel="canonical" href="..."> Open Graph metadata og:url, og:image Twitter Cards twitter:image hreflang Language alternates Sitemaps XML sitemap URLs JSON-LD Structured data URLs RSS/Atom feeds Feed links HTML emails All links and images CDN resources External CSS, JS, images APIs Resource endpoints Bookmarks User-shared URLs Social media shares Shared post URLs QR codes Encoded URLs Print materials URLs on business cards, posters Redirects HTTP Location headers

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use HTTPS – always use https:// for production; avoid http://.

  2. Use absolute URLs for external resources – CSS, JS, images from CDNs.

  3. Use absolute URLs for canonical tags – required by search engines.

  4. Use absolute URLs for Open Graph and Twitter Cards – required by social platforms.

  5. Use absolute URLs for sitemaps – required by the sitemap protocol.

  6. Use absolute URLs for JSON-LD – required by schema.org.

  7. Use absolute URLs for RSS/Atom feeds – required by feed readers.

  8. Use absolute URLs in HTML emails – email clients have no base URL.

  9. Use rel="noopener noreferrer" – for external links with target="_blank".

  10. Use preconnect and dns-prefetch – for external domains to improve performance.

  11. Avoid hardcoding absolute URLs for internal links – use relative URLs for portability.

  12. Use the URL API – for programmatic URL manipulation in JavaScript.

  13. Sanitize user input – never insert user-supplied URLs directly into href or src.

  14. Validate redirects – prevent open redirects.

  15. Use Content Security Policy (CSP) – restrict allowed sources.

  16. Avoid javascript: URLs – they can execute scripts.

  17. Keep URLs short – shorter URLs are easier to share and remember.

  18. Use lowercase for schemes and hosts – they're case-insensitive, but lowercase is conventional.

  19. Encode special characters – use %20 for spaces, %2F for slashes in values.

  20. Test URLs in multiple contexts – browsers, email clients, social media platforms.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using http:// Instead of https://
docs.text:
<a href="http://example.com">Example</a>
Why it's wrong: Insecure; browsers may block or warn; search engines may penalize.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="https://example.com">Example</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Relative URLs in Emails
docs.text:
<a href="/about.html">About</a>
Why it's wrong: Email clients have no "current document" — the link will break.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="https://example.com/about.html">About</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Relative URLs for Open Graph Images
docs.text:
<meta property="og:image" content="/images/og-image.jpg">
Why it's wrong: Social media platforms can't resolve relative URLs.

✅ Correct: 

<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/images/og-image.jpg">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting rel="noopener" with target="_blank"
docs.text:
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">External</a>
Why it's wrong: The new page can access window.opener and potentially redirect the original page.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">External</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using javascript: URLs
docs.text:
<a href="javascript:alert('Hello')">Click</a>
Why it's wrong: XSS risk; blocked by CSP; bad practice.

✅ Correct: 

<button onclick="alert('Hello')">Click</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Hardcoding Absolute URLs for Internal Links
docs.text:
<a href="https://example.com/about.html">About</a>
Why it's wrong: Breaks portability; site can't be moved without rewriting links.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="/about.html">About</a>  <!-- Root-relative -->

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting the Canonical Tag
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>My Page</title>
</head>
Why it's wrong: Search engines may index duplicate URLs for the same content.

✅ Correct: 

<head>
    <title>My Page</title>
    <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/page.html">
</head>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using the Wrong Scheme for mailto:
docs.text:
<a href="http://mailto:info@example.com">Email</a>
Why it's wrong: mailto: is a scheme, not a URL with a protocol.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="mailto:info@example.com">Email</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Encode Special Characters
docs.text:
<a href="https://example.com/search?q=hello world">Search</a>
Why it's wrong: Spaces are not allowed in URLs.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="https://example.com/search?q=hello%20world">Search</a>
<!-- or -->
<a href="https://example.com/search?q=hello+world">Search</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Absolute URLs for Internal Links in a Subdirectory
docs.text:
<!-- Site is at https://example.com/v2/ -->
<a href="/about.html">About</a>
<!-- Resolves to: https://example.com/about.html (wrong!) -->
Why it's wrong: Root-relative URLs resolve against the domain root, not the subdirectory.

✅ Correct: Use document-relative URLs or configure the server appropriately.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• DNS resolution – absolute URLs require DNS lookups for external domains. Use dns-prefetch and preconnect to resolve DNS early.
  • Connection setup – external resources require new TCP and TLS connections. Use preconnect to establish connections early.
  • Caching – absolute URLs are cached by the browser; relative URLs are resolved and then cached. No performance difference.
  • CDN – using absolute URLs to a CDN can improve performance by serving resources from a location closer to the user.
  • HTTP/2 – supports multiplexing, so multiple external resources from the same domain can share a connection.
  • Preload – use <link rel="preload"> with absolute URLs to load critical resources early.
  • Preconnect – use <link rel="preconnect"> to establish early connections to external domains.
  • DNS prefetch – use <link rel="dns-prefetch"> to resolve DNS for external domains early.

docs.title: Performance Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use preconnect for external domains that will be used soon.
  2. Use dns-prefetch for domains that may be used later.
  3. Use preload for critical resources (fonts, hero images, key CSS/JS).
  4. Use a CDN for static assets.
  5. Minimize the number of external domains – each requires a DNS lookup and connection.
  6. Use HTTP/2 for multiplexing.
  7. Use crossorigin for fonts and other resources that require CORS.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• HTTPS – always use HTTPS for production. Never use HTTP for sensitive data.
  • Mixed content – loading HTTP resources on an HTTPS page triggers mixed content warnings and may be blocked.
  • XSS – never use user input in href or src without sanitization.
  • Open redirects – validate redirect URLs to prevent phishing.
  • javascript: URLs – never use them; they can execute scripts.
  • data: URLs – can be used for XSS if not sanitized.
  • target="_blank" – use rel="noopener noreferrer" to prevent tabnabbing.
  • rel="nofollow" – use for untrusted links to discourage crawling.
  • rel="sponsored" – use for paid links.
  • rel="ugc" – use for user-generated content.
  • Content Security Policy (CSP) – restrict allowed sources.
  • Subresource Integrity (SRI) – verify external scripts and styles.
  • Referrer Policy – control referrer information sent to external sites.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – especially in href, src, and <base>.
  2. Use HTTPS – for all resources.
  3. Use rel="noopener noreferrer" – for external links.
  4. Use SRI – for external scripts and styles.
  5. Use CSP – to restrict allowed sources.
  6. Validate redirects – prevent open redirects.
  7. Avoid javascript: URLs – use event listeners instead.
  8. Set Referrer-Policy – to control referrer leakage.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect an element to see the raw href/src attribute.
  • DevTools Console – use element.href to see the resolved URL.
  • DevTools Network panel – see the actual URLs requested by the browser.
  • new URL(url) – parse and inspect URL components in the console.
  • document.baseURI – check the document's base URL.
  • Broken link checkers – use tools like linkchecker, Screaming Frog, or W3C Link Checker.
  • Lighthouse – audits for broken links and SEO issues.
  • curl or wget – fetch URLs from the command line.
  • dig or nslookup – check DNS resolution.
  • ping or traceroute – check network connectivity.
  • SSL Labs – check HTTPS configuration.
  • Security Headers – check security headers.
  • Google Search Console – check for indexing issues.
  • Facebook Sharing Debugger – test Open Graph metadata.
  • Twitter Card Validator – test Twitter Card metadata.
  • Google Rich Results Test – test structured data.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For external links – links to other websites.
  • For canonical URLs – required by search engines.
  • For Open Graph and Twitter Cards – required by social platforms.
  • For hreflang – language alternates.
  • For sitemaps – required by the sitemap protocol.
  • For JSON-LD – structured data.
  • For RSS/Atom feeds – feed links.
  • For HTML emails – all links and images.
  • For CDN resources – external CSS, JS, images.
  • For API endpoints – resource locations.
  • For bookmarks and sharing – user-shared URLs.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For internal links – use relative URLs for portability.
  • For site-wide resources – use root-relative URLs.
  • For links between related pages – use document-relative URLs.
  • For email links – use mailto:.
  • For phone links – use tel:.
  • For javascript: URLs – never use.
  • For data: URLs – use sparingly for small embedded resources.
  • For file: URLs – not for web content.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Relative URLs – context-dependent URLs.
  • Root-relative URLs – start with /.
  • Document-relative URLs – resolve against the current directory.
  • Protocol-relative URLs – start with // (deprecated).
  • Base URL – the URL against which relative URLs are resolved.
  • <base> element – overrides the base URL.
  • URL Living Standard – the specification for URL parsing.
  • URL API – JavaScript API for working with URLs.
  • Scheme – the protocol (http, https, etc.).
  • Host – the domain name or IP address.
  • Port – the port number.
  • Path – the path to the resource.
  • Query string – parameters passed to the server.
  • Fragment – a location within the page.
  • Canonical URL – the preferred URL for a page.
  • Open Graph – social media metadata.
  • Twitter Cards – Twitter metadata.
  • hreflang – language alternates.
  • Sitemap – XML file listing pages.
  • JSON-LD – structured data format.
  • Same-origin policy – security mechanism.
  • DNS – Domain Name System.
  • HTTP – HyperText Transfer Protocol.
  • HTTPS – HTTP Secure.
  • CDN – Content Delivery Network.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The concept of a URL (Uniform Resource Locator) was introduced by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991 and formalized in RFC 1738 (1994).

  • The first URL ever used was http://info.cern.ch/ — the first web page, still online today.

  • The term "absolute URL" was coined to distinguish it from "relative URL" when relative URLs were introduced.

  • The scheme (protocol) is the first part of an absolute URL. It tells the browser how to communicate with the server.

  • The host is case-insensitive: EXAMPLE.COM and example.com are the same.

  • The path is case-sensitive on most servers: /Blog/Post.html and /blog/post.html are different.

  • The fragment (#section) is not sent to the server — it's handled entirely by the browser.

  • The query string (?key=value) is sent to the server as part of the HTTP request.

  • The default port for HTTPS is 443, for HTTP is 80. Ports are usually omitted from URLs.

  • Open Graph requires absolute URLs for og:url and og:image because social media platforms fetch these resources from outside your site.

  • Sitemaps require absolute URLs as specified by the sitemap protocol.

  • JSON-LD requires absolute URLs for properties like url, image, and sameAs.

  • HTML emails must use absolute URLs because email clients have no base URL.

  • RSS/Atom feeds must use absolute URLs for links and GUIDs.

  • The same-origin policy compares URLs by their origin (scheme + host + port). Different origins can't access each other's resources.

  • Canonical URLs prevent duplicate content issues by telling search engines which URL is the "preferred" one.

  • hreflang links should use absolute URLs to specify language-specific versions of a page.

  • The URL API in JavaScript uses the same URL parsing algorithm as the browser, making it the recommended way to work with URLs programmatically.

  • preconnect and dns-prefetch are performance hints that resolve DNS and establish connections to external domains early.

  • rel="noopener noreferrer" is essential for external links with target="_blank" to prevent tabnabbing and referrer leakage.

  • rel="nofollow" tells search engines not to follow a link or pass authority. Use it for untrusted links.

  • rel="sponsored" identifies paid links, as required by search engine guidelines.

  • rel="ugc" identifies user-generated content (e.g., in comments), as recommended by search engines.

  • Content Security Policy (CSP) can restrict which absolute URLs are allowed to load resources.

  • Subresource Integrity (SRI) verifies that external scripts and styles haven't been tampered with.

  • HTTPS is now the standard for the web. HTTP is deprecated for most uses and can trigger browser warnings.

  • Mixed content (loading HTTP resources on an HTTPS page) is blocked by modern browsers.

  • The absolute URL is the canonical form of a web address. Relative URLs are a convenience for authors; absolute URLs are what the browser ultimately uses.

  • Search engines resolve relative URLs to absolute URLs when crawling. The absolute URL is what gets indexed.

  • QR codes encode absolute URLs, which is why they work when scanned from anywhere.

  • Business cards and print materials use absolute URLs because there's no context to resolve relative URLs.

  • The DNS system resolves hostnames to IP addresses. Without DNS, the web as we know it wouldn't exist.

  • HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support multiplexing, allowing multiple resources from the same domain to share a connection.

  • CDNs (Content Delivery Networks) use absolute URLs to serve resources from locations closer to the user.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• An absolute URL is a URL that contains all the information needed to locate a resource: scheme, host, port (optional), path, query (optional), and fragment (optional).
  • It is context-independent — it works from anywhere, regardless of the current document's location.
  • Components: scheme://host:port/path?query#fragment.
  • Common schemes: https, http, mailto, tel, ftp, data, ws/wss.
  • Absolute URLs are required for: external links, canonical tags, Open Graph, Twitter Cards, hreflang, sitemaps, JSON-LD, RSS/Atom feeds, and HTML emails.
  • Best practices: use HTTPS, use absolute URLs for external resources and metadata, use rel="noopener noreferrer" for external links, use preconnect and dns-prefetch for performance, and sanitize user input.
  • Common mistakes include using HTTP instead of HTTPS, using relative URLs in emails and metadata, forgetting rel="noopener", and hardcoding absolute URLs for internal links.
  • Absolute URLs are the canonical form of a web address — the foundation of the web's addressing system.
  • They are essential for external linking, SEO, social sharing, APIs, and data interchange.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A fragment (also called a fragment identifier or hash) is the part of a URL that begins with the # character and identifies a specific location within a resource – typically a section of an HTML document. Unlike other parts of a URL, the fragment is not sent to the server; it is processed entirely by the browser (or client). Its primary purpose is to allow linking to a specific part of a page, whether that's a section with a matching id, a piece of text (via text fragments), or a state in a single‑page application.

Example: 

https://example.com/page.html#section-3
                             └────┬────┘
                             fragment

The fragment can also be used without a full URL: 

#section-3

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Fragments serve several essential purposes:

  • Deep linking – link directly to a specific section of a long document.
  • Table of contents – navigate within a page.
  • Skip links – bypass navigation and jump to main content.
  • Footnotes and references – link to citations at the bottom of a page.
  • State management – store application state in the URL (for SPAs).
  • Text fragments – link to specific text within a page.
  • CSS targeting – style the targeted element with :target.
  • Accessibility – help screen reader users navigate to specific content.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Fragments are used in any URL context:

  • <a href="#section"> – links within a page.
  • <a href="page.html#section"> – links to a section on another page.
  • <link rel="canonical"> – canonical URLs (fragments usually omitted).
  • JavaScript location.hash – read or set the fragment.
  • CSS :target – style the targeted element.
  • Text fragments (#:~:text=) – link to specific text.
<!-- Link to a fragment on the same page -->
<a href="#introduction">Go to Introduction</a>

<!-- The target element -->
<h2 id="introduction">Introduction</h2>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before fragments, linking to a specific part of a long document was impossible. If you wanted to reference a particular section of a web page, you could only link to the top of the page and tell the reader to scroll down manually. This was impractical for long documents, academic papers, documentation, and FAQs.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No way to link to a specific section Readers had to scroll manually. No deep linking Couldn't share a link to a specific part. No table of contents navigation Long pages were hard to navigate. No state in URL Single-page apps couldn't bookmark state. No text-level linking Couldn't link to specific text.

docs.title: Why Fragments Were Introduced
docs.text:
Fragments were part of the original URL specification (RFC 1630, 1994) and were designed to allow linking to anchors within a document. In early HTML, anchors were created with the <a name="..."> element. In HTML5, the id attribute became the standard way to define a fragment target.

Fragments enable:

  • Deep linking – link to any section of a document.
  • Table of contents – in-page navigation.
  • Skip links – accessibility improvements.
  • State management – SPAs can use the fragment to store state.
  • Text fragments – modern browsers support linking to specific text.
  • CSS :target – style the targeted element.

The fragment is a simple but powerful feature that has been part of the web since its inception.

docs.title: The Fragment Identifier
docs.text:
A fragment begins with # and continues to the end of the URL (or until a ? if it's part of a query, but fragments come after queries). It can contain any characters, but certain characters should be percent-encoded.

https://example.com/page.html#section-3
                             └────┬────┘
                             fragment

docs.title: Same-Page Fragment Link
docs.text:
<!-- Link to a section on the same page -->
<a href="#section-2">Jump to Section 2</a>

<!-- The target element -->
<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>

docs.title: Cross-Page Fragment Link
docs.text:
<!-- Link to a section on another page -->
<a href="other-page.html#section-3">Go to Section 3 on Other Page</a>

docs.title: Fragment with Query String
docs.text:
<a href="search.html?q=html#results">Search for HTML and jump to results</a>

Note: The query string comes before the fragment.

docs.title: Named Anchors (Obsolete)
docs.text:
In HTML4, you could use <a name="section"> as a fragment target. In HTML5, this is obsolete – use id instead.

<!-- Obsolete (HTML4) -->
<a name="section-2"></a>
<h2>Section 2</h2>

<!-- Modern (HTML5) -->
<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>

docs.title: Text Fragments (Modern)
docs.text:
Text fragments allow linking to specific text within a page. They use the syntax #:~:text=targetText.

<a href="https://example.com/page.html#:~:text=target%20text">
    Jump to "target text"
</a>

Browser support: Chrome, Edge (since 2020). Firefox and Safari have not implemented it yet (as of 2026).

docs.title: Fragment in JavaScript
docs.text:
// Read the fragment
console.log(window.location.hash); // "#section-2"

// Set the fragment (scrolls to the element)
window.location.hash = "#section-3";

// Listen for fragment changes
window.addEventListener('hashchange', () => {
    console.log('Fragment changed to:', window.location.hash);
});

docs.title: Fragment and CSS :target
docs.text:
/* Style the element that matches the fragment */
:target {
    background-color: yellow;
    border-left: 4px solid orange;
}

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters #section-2 Fragment identifier. Identifies a specific element by id. id="section-2" Target element. The element with this id is scrolled to. #:~:text= Text fragment syntax. Links to specific text (Chrome/Edge). window.location.hash JavaScript property. Read or set the fragment. :target CSS pseudo-class. Styles the targeted element.

docs.title: The "Bookmark" Analogy
docs.text: A fragment is like a bookmark in a book. You can place a bookmark at a specific page (the URL) and a specific line (the fragment). When you open the book to that bookmark, you go directly to that line, not just the page. The bookmark is not part of the book itself — it's an external marker that helps you find your place.

docs.title: The "Table of Contents" Analogy
docs.text: A fragment is like a table of contents entry in a book. It tells you the page number (the URL) and the section (the fragment). Clicking it takes you directly to that section. The table of contents is not part of the content — it's a navigation aid.

docs.title: The "GPS Waypoint" Analogy
docs.text: A fragment is like a GPS waypoint within a city (the URL). The city is the page; the waypoint is the specific location within it. When you navigate to the waypoint, you go directly to that spot, not just the city entrance.

docs.title: The "Highlight" Analogy
docs.text: A text fragment is like a highlighter on a page. You can share a link that highlights specific text, just as you might highlight a passage in a book to share with a friend.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Fragment Identifier
docs.text:
The fragment identifier is the part of the URL after #. It is not sent to the server – it is handled by the browser. The browser uses it to:

  1. Find the element with the matching id.
  2. Scroll that element into view.
  3. Apply the :target CSS pseudo-class.
  4. Update the browser history.

docs.title: Concept 2: The id Attribute
docs.text:
The id attribute is the standard way to define a fragment target in HTML5. Each id must be unique within the document. The value can be any string, but it should be a valid identifier (no spaces, no special characters except -, _, :, .).

<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>

docs.title: Concept 3: Same-Page vs. Cross-Page Fragments
docs.text:
• Same-page fragments – #section-2 – the browser scrolls to the target on the current page.
  • Cross-page fragments – page.html#section-2 – the browser loads page.html, then scrolls to the target.

docs.title: Concept 4: Fragment and History
docs.text:
When you navigate to a fragment, the browser:

  • Does not reload the page (for same-page fragments).
  • Adds a new entry to the browser history.
  • Fires the hashchange event.
  • Updates the :target pseudo-class.

This is why fragments are useful for SPAs – they allow state changes without full page reloads.

docs.title: Concept 5: The :target Pseudo-Class
docs.text:
The :target CSS pseudo-class matches the element that is the target of the fragment. It allows you to style the targeted element differently.

:target {
    background-color: yellow;
}

docs.title: Concept 6: Text Fragments
docs.text:
Text fragments (#:~:text=) allow linking to specific text within a page, even if the text doesn't have an id. The syntax is:

#:~:text=[prefix-,]textStart[,textEnd][,-suffix]

Example: 

https://example.com/page.html#:~:text=target%20text

Browser support: Chrome and Edge (since 2020). Firefox and Safari have not implemented it as of 2026.

docs.title: Concept 7: Fragment Directives
docs.text:
Text fragments are a type of fragment directive – a way to pass instructions to the browser via the fragment. The :~: syntax separates the directive from the fragment identifier.

#:~:text=...

Other fragment directives may be added in the future.

docs.title: Concept 8: The name Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text: In HTML4, <a name="..."> was used to create fragment targets. In HTML5, this is obsolete – use id instead. However, browsers still support name for backward compatibility.

docs.title: Concept 9: Fragment and SEO
docs.text:
• Fragments are not indexed separately – search engines index the page, not the fragment.
  • Fragment links – Google may show "Jump to" links in search results for pages with a table of contents.
  • Canonical URLs – should not include fragments (they identify the page, not a section).
  • Sitemaps – should not include fragments.

docs.title: Concept 10: Fragment and Accessibility
docs.text:
• Skip links – use fragments to skip navigation and jump to main content.
  • Table of contents – helps screen reader users navigate long pages.
  • Focus management – when a fragment is navigated to, the browser moves focus to the target element (if it's focusable).
  • :target styling – can help sighted users see which section they jumped to.

docs.title: Concept 11: Fragment and Fixed Headers
docs.text:
When you navigate to a fragment, the target element may be hidden behind a fixed header. You can use CSS scroll-margin-top to offset the scroll position.

:target {
    scroll-margin-top: 80px; /* Height of fixed header */
}

docs.title: Concept 12: Fragment and Smooth Scrolling
docs.text:
You can enable smooth scrolling with CSS:

html {
    scroll-behavior: smooth;
}

Or with JavaScript:

element.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' });

docs.title: Concept 13: Fragment in Single Page Applications (SPAs)
docs.text: SPAs often use the fragment to store application state (e.g., #/dashboard, #/settings). This allows bookmarking and sharing specific views. However, modern SPAs often use the History API (pushState) with path-based routing instead.

docs.title: Concept 14: Fragment and the hashchange Event
docs.text:
The hashchange event fires when the fragment changes (without a page reload). It's useful for SPAs and for responding to fragment navigation.

window.addEventListener('hashchange', () => {
    console.log('Fragment:', window.location.hash);
});

docs.title: Concept 15: Fragment and the scroll Event
docs.text:
When the browser scrolls to a fragment, it fires a scroll event. You can listen for it to run code after the scroll.

window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
    // ...
});

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing a Fragment
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a link with a fragment (e.g., <a href="#section-2">).
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser checks if the fragment target exists on the current page:
    │   ├── If yes → the browser scrolls to the element with the matching id.
    │   └── If no → the browser does nothing (or scrolls to top).
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser updates the URL in the address bar.
    │   └── The fragment is added (or changed) without a page reload.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser adds a new entry to the history.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser fires the `hashchange` event.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser applies the `:target` CSS pseudo-class to the target element.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser scrolls the target element into view (respecting `scroll-margin-top`).
    │
    ▼
8.  If the target element is focusable, the browser moves focus to it.
    │
    ▼
9.  The page is now at the target section.

docs.title: Cross-Page Fragment Navigation
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a link to another page with a fragment (e.g., page.html#section-3).
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser loads page.html.
    │
    ▼
3.  After the page loads, the browser looks for the element with id="section-3".
    │
    ▼
4.  If found, the browser scrolls to it.
    │
    ▼
5.  If not found, the browser stays at the top.
    │
    ▼
6.  The URL in the address bar includes the fragment.

docs.title: Text Fragment Processing
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a text fragment link.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser loads the page.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the fragment directive `:~:text=...`.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser searches the page for the specified text.
    │
    ▼
5.  If found, the browser scrolls to it and highlights the text.
    │
    ▼
6.  A "copy link to highlight" option may be shown.

docs.title: The :target Pseudo-Class
docs.text:
The :target pseudo-class matches the element whose id matches the fragment. It is updated dynamically when the fragment changes.

:target {
    background-color: yellow;
}

docs.title: The hashchange Event
docs.text:
The hashchange event fires when the fragment changes. It does not fire when the page loads with a fragment (only when the fragment changes after load).

window.addEventListener('hashchange', (event) => {
    console.log('Old URL:', event.oldURL);
    console.log('New URL:', event.newURL);
});

docs.title: The URL Parser and Fragment
docs.text:
The URL parser (per the URL Living Standard) splits the URL into components, including the fragment. The fragment is stored as a string and is not sent to the server in the HTTP request.

const url = new URL('https://example.com/page.html?q=1#section-2');
console.log(url.hash); // "#section-2"
console.log(url.search); // "?q=1"

docs.title: The Browser's Fragment Handling
docs.text:
When the browser navigates to a fragment:

  1. It checks if the fragment matches an element's id.
  2. If found, it scrolls the element into view.
  3. It applies the :target pseudo-class.
  4. It updates the history and fires hashchange.
  5. It may move focus to the element (if it's focusable).

docs.title: The :target Implementation
docs.text: The :target pseudo-class is implemented in the CSS engine. It matches the element with the id equal to the fragment. The matching is case-sensitive.

docs.title: Text Fragment Implementation
docs.text:
Text fragments are implemented in the browser's rendering engine. The browser:

  1. Parses the :~:text= directive.
  2. Searches the page's text content for the specified text.
  3. Scrolls to the first match.
  4. Highlights the text.
  5. May show a "copy link to highlight" option.

docs.title: The hashchange Event
docs.text: The hashchange event is fired by the browser when the fragment changes. It is a HashChangeEvent with oldURL and newURL properties.

docs.title: The scroll-margin-top Property
docs.text:
The scroll-margin-top CSS property adds an offset when scrolling to a target element. It is useful for fixed headers.

:target {
    scroll-margin-top: 80px;
}

docs.title: The scroll-behavior Property
docs.text:
The scroll-behavior CSS property controls whether scrolling is smooth or instant.

html {
    scroll-behavior: smooth;
}

docs.title: Browser History and Fragments
docs.text: Fragment navigation adds a new entry to the browser history. This allows the user to use the Back and Forward buttons to navigate between fragments.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Fragment Link
docs.text:
1.  Author creates an element with an id (the target).
    │   └── <h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>
    │
    ▼
2.  Author creates a link with the fragment.
    │   └── <a href="#section-2">Jump to Section 2</a>
    │
    ▼
3.  User clicks the link.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser finds the target element.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser scrolls the target into view.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser updates the URL and history.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser fires the `hashchange` event.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser applies `:target` styles.
    │
    ▼
9.  If the target is focusable, focus moves to it.
    │
    ▼
10. User can bookmark or share the URL with the fragment.

docs.title: Dynamic Fragment Changes
docs.text:
// Change the fragment programmatically
window.location.hash = '#section-3';

// Listen for fragment changes
window.addEventListener('hashchange', () => {
    console.log('Fragment changed to:', window.location.hash);
});

docs.title: Example 1: Table of Contents
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Table of contents">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="#introduction">Introduction</a></li>
        <li><a href="#features">Features</a></li>
        <li><a href="#pricing">Pricing</a></li>
        <li><a href="#conclusion">Conclusion</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

<article>
    <section id="introduction">
        <h2>Introduction</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
    <section id="features">
        <h2>Features</h2>

        <p>...</p>
    </section>
    <section id="conclusion">
        <h2>Conclusion</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
</article>

docs.title: Example 2: Skip Link
docs.text:
<style>
    .skip-link {

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

docs.text:
<p>
    This is a statement.<sup><a href="#footnote-1" id="ref-1">[1]</a></sup>
</p>

<footer>

            <p>This is the footnote. <a href="#ref-1">Back to reference</a></p>
        </li>
    </ol>
</footer>

<a href="#section-2">Go to Section 2</a>

docs.text:

docs.title: Example 9: JavaScript Fragment Handling
docs.text:
<a href="#section-2" id="fragmentLink">Go to Section 2</a>
<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>

<script>
    const link = document.getElementById('fragmentLink');
    link.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
        // Prevent default if needed
        // event.preventDefault();
        console.log('Navigating to:', link.hash);
    });

    window.addEventListener('hashchange', () => {
        console.log('Fragment changed to:', window.location.hash);
        // Custom behavior
    });
</script>

</style>

<nav>

</nav>

    <h2>Tab 1 Content</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</div>
<div id="tab2" class="tab-content">

</div>
<div id="tab3" class="tab-content">
