docs.title: Example 11: Fragment and SPA Routing
docs.text:
<a href="#/dashboard">Dashboard</a>
<a href="#/settings">Settings</a>
<a href="#/profile">Profile</a>

<div id="app"></div>

<script>
    function render() {
        const route = window.location.hash.slice(1) || '/';
        const app = document.getElementById('app');
        switch (route) {
            case '/dashboard':
                app.innerHTML = '<h1>Dashboard</h1>';
                break;
            case '/settings':
                app.innerHTML = '<h1>Settings</h1>';
                break;
            case '/profile':
                app.innerHTML = '<h1>Profile</h1>';
                break;
            default:
                app.innerHTML = '<h1>Home</h1>';
        }
    }

    window.addEventListener('hashchange', render);
    render();
</script>

docs.title: Example 12: Scroll to Element Programmatically
docs.text:
// Scroll to an element with a specific id
document.getElementById('section-2').scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' });

// Or using the fragment
window.location.hash = '#section-2';

docs.title: Example 13: Multiple Fragments (Not Standard)
docs.text:
Standard URLs support only one fragment. If you need multiple targets, you can use a single fragment and handle it with JavaScript:

<a href="#section-2,section-3">Go to Sections 2 and 3</a>

<script>
    window.addEventListener('hashchange', () => {
        const ids = window.location.hash.slice(1).split(',');
        ids.forEach(id => {
            const el = document.getElementById(id);
            if (el) el.scrollIntoView();
        });
    });
</script>

Note: This is non-standard and works only with custom JavaScript.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Table of contents In-page navigation Skip links "Skip to main content" Footnotes Link to citations Cross-page links Link to a section on another page Tabs CSS-only tabs with :target SPA routing Hash-based routing Text fragments Link to specific text Styling targets Highlight the target section Back to top Link to #top Modal windows Open modal with :target Accordion Expand section with :target Deep linking Link to a specific state Documentation Link to specific API methods Legal documents Link to specific clauses

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use unique id values – each id must be unique within the document.

  2. Use descriptive id names – e.g., #introduction, not #s1.

  3. Provide a table of contents – for long pages.

  4. Use skip links – for accessibility.

  5. Style the :target – to help users see where they landed.

  6. Use scroll-margin-top – to offset fixed headers.

  7. Use scroll-behavior: smooth – for a better user experience.

  8. Test cross-page fragments – ensure the target exists on the destination page.

  9. Avoid fragments in canonical URLs – canonical URLs should identify the page, not a section.

  10. Avoid fragments in sitemaps – sitemaps should list pages, not sections.

  11. Use text fragments sparingly – they're only supported in Chrome and Edge.

  12. Provide fallbacks for text fragments – ensure the content is still accessible.

  13. Use hashchange for SPAs – but consider the History API for modern routing.

  14. Don't rely on fragments for critical state – they can be lost when sharing.

  15. Use :target for styling, not for functionality – JavaScript is more reliable for dynamic behavior.

  16. Test with screen readers – ensure fragment navigation works.

  17. Test with keyboard navigation – ensure skip links work.

  18. Validate your HTML – check for duplicate id values.

  19. Keep fragment names short – but descriptive.

  20. Document your fragment conventions – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate id Values
docs.text:
<h2 id="section">Section 1</h2>
<h2 id="section">Section 2</h2>
Why it's wrong: id must be unique. The browser will only target the first one.

✅ Correct: 

<h2 id="section-1">Section 1</h2>
<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using name Instead of id
docs.text:
<a name="section-2"></a>
<h2>Section 2</h2>
Why it's wrong: The name attribute on <a> is obsolete in HTML5. Use id.

✅ Correct: 

<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting the # in the Fragment
docs.text:
<a href="section-2">Section 2</a>
Why it's wrong: Without #, the browser treats it as a relative URL, not a fragment.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="#section-2">Section 2</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Spaces in id Values
docs.text:
<h2 id="section 2">Section 2</h2>
Why it's wrong: Spaces are not allowed in id values (and would need to be encoded in the fragment).

✅ Correct: 

<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Providing a Target for the Fragment
docs.text:
<a href="#section-2">Go to Section 2</a>
<!-- No element with id="section-2" -->
Why it's wrong: The link will not scroll anywhere. The browser may stay at the top.

✅ Correct: Ensure the target element exists: 

<a href="#section-2">Go to Section 2</a>
<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Fragments in Canonical URLs
docs.text:
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/page.html#section-2">
Why it's wrong: Canonical URLs should identify the page, not a section. Fragments in canonical URLs can cause confusion.

✅ Correct: 

<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/page.html">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Fragments in Sitemaps
docs.text:
<url>
    <loc>https://example.com/page.html#section-2</loc>
</url>
Why it's wrong: Sitemaps should list pages, not sections. Fragments in sitemaps are ignored or cause errors.

✅ Correct: 

<url>
    <loc>https://example.com/page.html</loc>
</url>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting scroll-margin-top for Fixed Headers
docs.text:
<header style="position: fixed; height: 80px;">...</header>
<a href="#section-2">Go to Section 2</a>
<h2 id="section-2">Section 2</h2>
Why it's wrong: The fixed header will cover the target element when scrolled to.

✅ Correct: 

:target {
    scroll-margin-top: 80px;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing Cross-Page Fragments
docs.text:
<!-- On page1.html -->
<a href="page2.html#section-3">Go to Section 3</a>
<!-- On page2.html, there is no id="section-3" -->
Why it's wrong: The link will load page2.html but not scroll to any section.

✅ Correct: Ensure the target exists on the destination page.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Fragments for State That Should Be in the Path
docs.text:
<a href="#/products/123">Product 123</a>
Why it's wrong: Hash-based routing is a legacy approach. Modern SPAs use the History API with path-based routing (/products/123).

✅ Correct (with History API): 

<a href="/products/123">Product 123</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using :target for Critical Functionality
docs.text:
<style>
    .modal:target {
        display: block;
    }
</style>
<a href="#modal">Open Modal</a>
<div id="modal" class="modal">...</div>
Why it's wrong: :target-based modals have limitations (e.g., no Escape key handling, no focus trapping). Use <dialog> instead.

✅ Correct: 

<dialog id="myModal">...</dialog>
<button onclick="document.getElementById('myModal').showModal()">Open Modal</button>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Scrolling – fragment navigation triggers a scroll, which is generally fast but can be janky if the page is heavy.
  • Smooth scrolling – scroll-behavior: smooth can improve perceived performance but may be slower on low-end devices.
  • Text fragments – searching for text can be slow on large pages, but the impact is minimal.
  • hashchange event – listening for hashchange is lightweight.
  • History entries – each fragment change adds a history entry, which is negligible.
  • CSS :target – applying styles to the target is fast.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use scroll-behavior: smooth – for a better experience.
  2. Use scroll-margin-top – to avoid scrolling behind fixed headers.
  3. Avoid heavy animations on :target – keep it simple.
  4. Use requestAnimationFrame – if you need custom scrolling.
  5. Test on low-end devices – ensure smooth scrolling works.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – never use user input in id or fragment values without sanitization.
  • Open redirects – fragments don't cause redirects, but they can be used to manipulate client-side routing.
  • Clickjacking – fragments can be used to scroll to a specific part of a page in an iframe, but modern browsers have protections.
  • Text fragments – can be used to highlight arbitrary text, which could be misleading. Browsers show a "copy link to highlight" option to indicate the source.
  • No server-side impact – fragments are not sent to the server, so they can't be used for server-side attacks.
  • Client-side routing – if using hash-based routing, validate the fragment to prevent injection.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – especially if used in id or fragment values.
  2. Validate fragments – in SPAs, ensure the fragment matches expected routes.
  3. Avoid javascript: URLs – they can be used in href with fragments.
  4. Use rel="noopener noreferrer" – for external links.
  5. Content Security Policy (CSP) – restrict allowed sources.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the target element to see its id.
  • DevTools Console – use window.location.hash to see the current fragment.
  • document.getElementById('section-2') – check if the target exists.
  • window.addEventListener('hashchange', ...) – log fragment changes.
  • element.scrollIntoView() – test scrolling programmatically.
  • getComputedStyle(element).scrollMarginTop – check the scroll-margin-top value.
  • Validator – check for duplicate id values.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and SEO.
  • Test cross-page fragments – navigate from another page.
  • Test with keyboard – ensure skip links work.
  • Test with screen readers – ensure fragment navigation works.
  • Test text fragments – in Chrome/Edge, ensure they work.
  • Check browser support – for text fragments and other features.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For table of contents – in-page navigation.
  • For skip links – accessibility.
  • For footnotes – link to citations.
  • For cross-page links – link to a section on another page.
  • For CSS-only tabs – with :target.
  • For SPA routing – hash-based routing (legacy).
  • For text fragments – link to specific text (Chrome/Edge).
  • For deep linking – link to a specific state.
  • For documentation – link to specific sections.
  • For legal documents – link to specific clauses.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For canonical URLs – should not include fragments.
  • For sitemaps – should not include fragments.
  • For server-side logic – fragments are not sent to the server.
  • For critical functionality – use JavaScript for dynamic behavior.
  • For modern SPA routing – use the History API instead.
  • For modals – use <dialog> instead of :target.
  • For accordions – use <details> instead of :target.
  • For state that should be in the path – use path-based routing.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• URL – Uniform Resource Locator.
  • Fragment identifier – the part after #.
  • id attribute – defines the target.
  • :target – CSS pseudo-class.
  • hashchange event – fires when the fragment changes.
  • Text fragments – #:~:text=.
  • Fragment directives – :~: syntax.
  • History API – pushState, replaceState.
  • Skip links – accessibility feature.
  • Scroll behavior – scroll-behavior, scroll-margin-top.
  • SPA routing – hash-based vs. path-based.
  • Canonical URL – should not include fragments.
  • Sitemap – should not include fragments.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The fragment identifier was part of the original URL specification (RFC 1630, 1994).

  • The term "fragment" comes from the idea that the URL points to a fragment of the resource, not the whole thing.

  • The fragment is not sent to the server – it's handled entirely by the browser.

  • In HTML4, fragments were targeted with <a name="...">. In HTML5, the id attribute is the standard.

  • The :target pseudo-class was introduced in CSS3 and is supported in all modern browsers.

  • The hashchange event was introduced in HTML5 and is supported in all modern browsers.

  • Text fragments were introduced by Google in 2020 and are supported in Chrome and Edge. They allow linking to specific text without an id.

  • Text fragments use the syntax #:~:text=. The :~: is called a fragment directive.

  • You can link to multiple text fragments using &: 

    #:~:text=first&text=second

  • The scroll-margin-top CSS property is essential for fixed headers. Without it, the target element is hidden behind the header.

  • The scroll-behavior: smooth CSS property enables smooth scrolling for fragment navigation.

  • Fragments are used in SPAs for routing, but modern SPAs use the History API for cleaner URLs.

  • Google Search may show "Jump to" links in search results for pages with a table of contents.

  • Canonical URLs should not include fragments, as they identify the page, not a section.

  • Sitemaps should not include fragments, as they list pages, not sections.

  • The id attribute must be unique within the document. Duplicate ids cause unpredictable behavior.

  • The :target pseudo-class matches the element with the id equal to the fragment. The matching is case-sensitive.

  • Fragment navigation adds a new entry to the browser history, allowing Back and Forward navigation.

  • Focus management – when a fragment is navigated to, the browser may move focus to the target element if it's focusable.

  • Skip links use fragments to bypass navigation. They are a simple but powerful accessibility feature.

  • Text fragments are not supported in Firefox or Safari as of 2026. Always provide a fallback.

  • Fragment identifiers can contain any characters, but certain characters should be percent-encoded.

  • The window.location.hash property returns the fragment including the #.

  • The window.location.hash can be set to change the fragment and scroll to the target.

  • The hashchange event fires when the fragment changes, but not when the page loads with a fragment.

  • scrollIntoView() can be used to scroll to an element programmatically, with options for smooth scrolling.

  • :target can be used for CSS-only tabs, modals, and accordions, but these have limitations. Native elements like <dialog> and <details> are preferred.

  • Fragment directives are an extensible mechanism for passing instructions to the browser via the fragment. Text fragments are the first use case.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A fragment (or fragment identifier) is the part of a URL after # that identifies a specific location within a resource.
  • It is not sent to the server – it is processed by the browser.
  • Fragments enable deep linking, table of contents, skip links, footnotes, and SPA routing.
  • The id attribute defines the target element for a fragment.
  • The :target CSS pseudo-class styles the targeted element.
  • The hashchange event fires when the fragment changes.
  • Text fragments (#:~:text=) allow linking to specific text (Chrome/Edge).
  • Best practices: use unique ids, descriptive names, scroll-margin-top for fixed headers, scroll-behavior: smooth, and test cross-page fragments.
  • Common mistakes include duplicate ids, using name instead of id, forgetting the #, and using fragments in canonical URLs or sitemaps.
  • Fragments are a simple but powerful feature that has been part of the web since its inception.
  • They are essential for navigation, accessibility, and deep linking.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A download link is a hyperlink that, when clicked, downloads a file to the user's device rather than navigating to it in the browser. In HTML, download links are created using the <a> element with the download attribute. When the download attribute is present, the browser fetches the linked resource and saves it to the user's file system instead of displaying it (e.g., showing a PDF in the browser's built-in viewer) or navigating away from the current page.

The download attribute can be used with or without a value:

  • <a href="file.pdf" download> – downloads the file with its original filename.
  • <a href="file.pdf" download="report.pdf"> – downloads the file and renames it to report.pdf.

The download attribute is a boolean attribute with an optional string value. It works only for same-origin URLs (or blob: and data: URLs) for security reasons — you cannot force a download of a file from a different domain using this attribute alone.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Download links serve several essential purposes:

  • File distribution – allow users to download PDFs, documents, images, software, and other files.
  • User control – give users the option to save files instead of viewing them inline.
  • Renaming – provide a friendly filename for the downloaded file.
  • Offline access – enable users to save content for offline use.
  • Data export – allow users to download their data (CSV, JSON, etc.).
  • Software distribution – provide installers, ZIP archives, and executables.
  • Media downloads – allow users to save images, audio, and video.
  • Reports and invoices – generate downloadable documents.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Download links are used wherever a file needs to be saved to the user's device:

  • E-commerce – downloadable invoices, receipts, product manuals.
  • Documentation – PDF guides, cheat sheets, API references.
  • Software – installers, updates, SDKs.
  • Media – images, audio, video, wallpapers.
  • Data – CSV, JSON, XML exports.
  • Education – worksheets, syllabi, course materials.
  • Government – forms, regulations, public records.
  • Marketing – brochures, whitepapers, case studies.
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Download Report</a>
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download="annual-report-2026.pdf">Download Annual Report</a>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before the download attribute, browsers would handle linked files based on their MIME type and the user's browser settings:

  • PDFs – displayed in the browser's built-in viewer (or downloaded, depending on settings).
  • Images – displayed inline in the browser.
  • Videos – played in the browser.
  • HTML files – navigated to (replacing the current page).
  • Unknown types – downloaded automatically.

This behaviour was inconsistent and unpredictable. A user clicking a link to a PDF might see it open in the browser, or it might download, depending on their settings. A user clicking a link to an image would see it displayed, not downloaded. There was no way to force a download or suggest a filename.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No way to force download Browsers decided based on MIME type. No way to rename files Downloaded files kept their server filename. Inconsistent behaviour Different browsers, different results. Required server-side headers Content-Disposition: attachment was the only way. Poor UX for file distribution Users had to right-click and "Save As." No native HTML solution Developers relied on server configuration.

docs.title: Why the download Attribute Was Introduced
docs.text:
The download attribute was introduced in HTML5 to provide a client-side, declarative way to indicate that a link should download a file rather than navigate to it. It enables:

  • Consistent behaviour – the browser downloads the file instead of displaying it.
  • Filename control – the author can suggest a filename.
  • No server configuration – works without Content-Disposition headers.
  • Better UX – users get a clear download action.
  • Progressive enhancement – works even without JavaScript.

The download attribute is part of the broader HTML5 effort to make the web platform more capable without relying on server-side configuration or JavaScript.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of download
docs.text:
<a href="file.pdf" download>Download</a>
<a href="file.pdf" download="newname.pdf">Download with new name</a>

docs.title: Simple Download Link
docs.text: <a href="/files/manual.pdf" download>Download Manual (PDF)</a>

docs.title: Download Link with Custom Filename
docs.text:
<a href="/files/report-2026.pdf" download="annual-report.pdf">
    Download Annual Report
</a>

docs.title: Download Link for an Image
docs.text:
<a href="/images/wallpaper.jpg" download="wallpaper.jpg">
    Download Wallpaper
</a>

docs.title: Download Link for a ZIP Archive
docs.text:
<a href="/downloads/project-files.zip" download>
    Download Project Files (ZIP)
</a>

docs.title: Download Link with File Type Indication
docs.text:
<a href="/files/data.csv" download="data.csv">
    Download Data (CSV, 2.4 MB)
</a>

docs.title: Download Link with an Image Thumbnail
docs.text:
<a href="/files/brochure.pdf" download="brochure.pdf">
    <img src="/images/brochure-thumb.jpg" alt="Brochure cover">
    Download Brochure (PDF)
</a>

docs.title: Download Link with Button Styling
docs.text:
<a href="/files/guide.pdf" download class="btn btn-primary">
    Download Guide
</a>

docs.title: Multiple Download Links
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li><a href="/files/guide.pdf" download>Download Guide (PDF)</a></li>
    <li><a href="/files/cheatsheet.pdf" download>Download Cheat Sheet (PDF)</a></li>
    <li><a href="/files/examples.zip" download>Download Examples (ZIP)</a></li>
</ul>

docs.title: Download Attribute with data: URLs
docs.text:
<a href="data:text/plain;charset=utf-8,Hello%20World" download="hello.txt">
    Download Hello World
</a>

docs.title: Download Attribute with blob: URLs
docs.text:
// Create a blob and download it
const blob = new Blob(['Hello, World!'], { type: 'text/plain' });
const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
const link = document.createElement('a');
link.href = url;
link.download = 'hello.txt';
link.click();
URL.revokeObjectURL(url);

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters href The URL of the file to download. Required for the link to work. download Indicates the file should be downloaded. Changes browser behaviour from navigation to download. download="name" Suggests a filename for the download. Gives the user a friendly filename. Link text Describes the file. Should indicate the file type and size. class="btn" Styles the link as a button. Makes the download action prominent.

docs.title: The "Take-away Box" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a download link as a take-away box at a restaurant. Instead of eating the meal in the restaurant (viewing the file in the browser), you ask for a box (the download attribute) to take it home (save it to your device). The box's label (the download filename) tells you what's inside.

docs.title: The "Vending Machine" Analogy
docs.text: A download link is like a vending machine. You press a button (click the link), and the item (the file) is dispensed (downloaded) into your hands. You can choose the item, and the machine gives it to you in a standard package (the file format).

docs.title: The "Library Checkout" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a download link as checking out a book from a library. Instead of reading it in the library (viewing in the browser), you take it home (download) to read at your leisure. The librarian (the browser) stamps the book with a due date (the filename), and you can keep it as long as you like (it's saved to your device).

docs.title: The "Print vs. Save" Analogy
docs.text: A regular link is like reading a document on screen. A download link is like printing or saving the document to your computer. The download attribute tells the browser: "Don't just show this — save it."

docs.title: Concept 1: The download Attribute
docs.text:
The download attribute is a boolean attribute with an optional string value:

  • download (no value) – downloads the file with its original filename.
  • download="filename.ext" – downloads the file and suggests filename.ext as the name.

The browser may or may not respect the suggested filename, depending on the user's settings and the browser's behaviour.

docs.title: Concept 2: Same-Origin Restriction
docs.text:
The download attribute only works for same-origin URLs (or blob: and data: URLs). For cross-origin URLs, the browser ignores the download attribute and navigates to the URL instead (or opens it in a new tab).

<!-- Works: same-origin -->
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Download</a>

<!-- Does NOT work: cross-origin -->
<a href="https://other-site.com/file.pdf" download>Download</a>
<!-- The browser will navigate to the URL instead -->

Why: Security. If any site could force downloads from any other site, it could be used for malicious purposes (e.g., forcing downloads of malware).

Workaround: For cross-origin files, the server must send a Content-Disposition: attachment header.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Content-Disposition Header
docs.text:
The Content-Disposition HTTP response header tells the browser whether to display the file inline or download it. It is the server-side equivalent of the download attribute.

Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="report.pdf"
  • inline – display the file in the browser (default for most types).
  • attachment – download the file.
  • filename – suggests a filename.

When to use which:

  • download attribute – for same-origin files, simple, no server configuration.
  • Content-Disposition header – for cross-origin files, or when you need consistent behaviour across all clients.

docs.title: Concept 4: Filename Suggestions
docs.text:
The download attribute's value is a suggestion, not a command. The browser may:

  • Use the suggested filename.
  • Use the server's filename (from Content-Disposition).
  • Use the URL's last path segment.
  • Ask the user where to save the file (depending on settings).

The browser may also sanitise the filename (removing path separators, special characters, etc.) for security.

docs.title: Concept 5: Supported File Types
docs.text:
The download attribute works with any file type, but the browser's behaviour depends on the MIME type:

File Type Without download With download PDF Opens in viewer Downloads Image Displays inline Downloads Video Plays in browser Downloads Audio Plays in browser Downloads HTML Navigates to page Downloads ZIP Downloads Downloads Unknown Downloads Downloads

docs.title: Concept 6: The download Attribute and MIME Types
docs.text:
The browser determines how to handle a file based on its MIME type (from the server's Content-Type header). The download attribute overrides this behaviour and forces a download.

Best practice: Configure the server to send the correct Content-Type for each file, even if you use the download attribute.

docs.title: Concept 7: Download Links and Security
docs.text:
• Same-origin restriction – prevents cross-origin downloads.
  • Filename sanitisation – the browser sanitises the suggested filename to prevent path traversal.
  • MIME sniffing – browsers may sniff the file type for security.
  • Content-Disposition – the server can override the download attribute.
  • XSS – never use user input in the download value without sanitisation.
  • Malware – downloaded files can contain malware; users should be cautious.

docs.title: Concept 8: Download Links and Accessibility
docs.text:
• Link text – should describe the file (e.g., "Download Annual Report (PDF, 2.4 MB)").
  • File type – indicate the format (PDF, ZIP, etc.).
  • File size – indicate the size (helpful for users on limited data).
  • Keyboard accessibility – links are focusable and activated with Enter.
  • Screen readers – announce the link text and the download attribute (in some browsers).
  • Visual indicators – use icons to indicate downloads.

docs.title: Concept 9: Download Links and SEO
docs.text:
• Downloads are not indexed – search engines index pages, not downloadable files (generally).
  • Link text – should be descriptive for users and search engines.
  • File types – indicate the format for users.
  • rel="nofollow" – use for untrusted downloads.
  • Sitemaps – can include downloadable files (e.g., PDFs) but not fragments.

docs.title: Concept 10: Download Links vs. Navigation Links
docs.text: Aspect Download Link Navigation Link Behaviour Downloads file Navigates to page Attribute download None Use case File distribution Page navigation Browser history Not added Added Back button Not applicable Works SEO File not indexed Page indexed

docs.title: Concept 11: Forcing Downloads with JavaScript
docs.text:
While the download attribute is the primary way to force downloads, JavaScript can also trigger downloads:

// Create a temporary link and click it
function downloadFile(url, filename) {
    const link = document.createElement('a');
    link.href = url;
    link.download = filename;
    document.body.appendChild(link);
    link.click();
    document.body.removeChild(link);
}

This is useful for: - Downloading dynamically generated content (blobs). - Downloading data from APIs. - Triggering downloads programmatically.

docs.title: Concept 12: Downloading Generated Content
docs.text:
You can generate files on the client and download them using Blob and URL.createObjectURL:

const data = 'Hello, World!';
const blob = new Blob([data], { type: 'text/plain' });
const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
const link = document.createElement('a');
link.href = url;
link.download = 'hello.txt';
link.click();
URL.revokeObjectURL(url);

This is useful for: - Exporting data as CSV, JSON, etc. - Downloading generated reports. - Saving user-created content.

docs.title: Concept 13: Downloading Data from APIs
docs.text:
You can fetch data from an API and download it:

async function downloadFromAPI(url, filename) {
    const response = await fetch(url);
    const blob = await response.blob();
    const objectUrl = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
    const link = document.createElement('a');
    link.href = objectUrl;
    link.download = filename;
    link.click();
    URL.revokeObjectURL(objectUrl);
}

docs.title: Concept 14: The Content-Type Header
docs.text:
The server's Content-Type header tells the browser the MIME type of the file. This affects how the browser handles the file:

MIME Type Browser Behaviour (without download) application/pdf Opens in viewer image/jpeg Displays inline video/mp4 Plays in browser audio/mpeg Plays in browser text/html Navigates to page application/zip Downloads application/octet-stream Downloads

docs.title: Concept 15: The Content-Disposition Header
docs.text:
The Content-Disposition header is the server-side way to control download behaviour:

Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="report.pdf"
Content-Disposition: inline; filename="report.pdf"
  • attachment – download the file.
  • inline – display the file in the browser.

The filename parameter suggests a filename.

Best practice: Use Content-Disposition: attachment for files that should always be downloaded, regardless of the client.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing a Download Link
docs.text:
1.  Author writes a download link.
    │   └── <a href="/files/report.pdf" download="annual-report.pdf">
    │
    ▼
2.  User clicks the link.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser checks the `download` attribute:
    │   ├── Is the URL same-origin?
    │   │   ├── Yes → proceed with download.
    │   │   └── No → ignore `download` and navigate to the URL.
    │   └── Is the URL a blob: or data: URL?
    │       └── Yes → proceed with download.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser fetches the file from the server.
    │   └── The server responds with the file and its headers.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser checks the `Content-Disposition` header:
    │   ├── If `attachment` → download.
    │   ├── If `inline` → display inline (but `download` attribute overrides).
    │   └── If absent → use `download` attribute.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser determines the filename:
    │   ├── From the `download` attribute (if present).
    │   ├── From the `Content-Disposition` header (if present).
    │   └── From the URL's last path segment (fallback).
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser sanitises the filename:
    │   ├── Removes path separators (`/`, `\`).
    │   ├── Removes special characters.
    │   └── Ensures the filename is safe.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser saves the file to the user's download folder.
    │   └── Or prompts the user to choose a location (depending on settings).
    │
    ▼
9.  Browser shows a download notification.
    │
    ▼
10. The page is NOT navigated away from.
    │   └── The download happens in the background.

docs.title: Cross-Origin Download
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a cross-origin download link.
    │   └── <a href="https://other-site.com/file.pdf" download>
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser checks the origin:
    │   └── Different from the current page → ignore `download`.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser navigates to the URL (or opens it in a new tab).
    │
    ▼
4.  The other site's server determines the behaviour:
    │   ├── If `Content-Disposition: attachment` → download.
    │   └── If `inline` or absent → display in browser.
    │
    ▼
5.  The user sees the file in the browser (not downloaded).

docs.title: JavaScript-Triggered Download
docs.text:
1.  JavaScript creates a Blob or fetches data.
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript creates an object URL: URL.createObjectURL(blob).
    │
    ▼
3.  JavaScript creates a temporary `<a>` element with `download`.
    │
    ▼
4.  JavaScript calls `link.click()` to trigger the download.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser downloads the file.
    │
    ▼
6.  JavaScript calls `URL.revokeObjectURL(url)` to free memory.

docs.title: The HTMLAnchorElement.download Property
docs.text:
In the DOM, the download attribute is reflected as the download property on the HTMLAnchorElement interface:

const link = document.querySelector('a');
console.log(link.download); // "annual-report.pdf" or ""
link.download = 'new-name.pdf'; // Updates the attribute

docs.title: The download Attribute and the Fetch Specification
docs.text:
When a download link is clicked, the browser initiates a fetch request (per the Fetch specification) with a special flag that indicates the response should be treated as a download. The browser then:

  1. Fetches the resource.
  2. Determines the filename.
  3. Sanitises the filename.
  4. Saves the file to the download folder.

docs.title: The Content-Disposition Header
docs.text:
The Content-Disposition header is parsed by the browser's network stack. It supports:

  • inline – display the file.
  • attachment – download the file.
  • filename – suggest a filename.
  • filename* – suggest a filename with encoding (RFC 5987).

Example: 

Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="report.pdf"; filename*=UTF-8''r%C3%A9sum%C3%A9.pdf

docs.title: The download Attribute and Blob URLs
docs.text: Blob URLs (blob:) and data URLs (data:) are considered same-origin for the purposes of the download attribute. This allows JavaScript to generate files and download them.

docs.title: The download Attribute and Sandboxed Iframes
docs.text:
In a sandboxed iframe (with sandbox attribute), the download attribute may be blocked unless the allow-downloads flag is present:

<iframe src="page.html" sandbox="allow-downloads"></iframe>

docs.title: The download Attribute and CSP
docs.text:
Content Security Policy (CSP) can restrict downloads via the sandbox directive:

Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-downloads;

docs.title: Browser Behaviour Differences
docs.text: Browser Filename Suggestion Cross-Origin Blob URLs Chrome Respects download Ignores download Works Firefox Respects download Ignores download Works Safari Respects download Ignores download Works Edge Respects download Ignores download Works

docs.title: Security: Filename Sanitisation
docs.text:
Browsers sanitise the filename to prevent:

  • Path traversal – removing / and \.
  • Special characters – removing characters that are invalid in filenames.
  • Reserved names – preventing names like CON, PRN on Windows.
  • Length limits – truncating excessively long names.

docs.title: Security: MIME Type Sniffing
docs.text:
Browsers may sniff the MIME type of a downloaded file to prevent:

  • MIME confusion attacks – e.g., a file declared as image/jpeg that is actually an HTML file.
  • XSS via downloads – e.g., an HTML file downloaded and then opened.

To prevent sniffing, servers can send: 

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Download Link
docs.text:
1.  Author writes a download link with the `download` attribute.
    │   └── <a href="/files/report.pdf" download="annual-report.pdf">
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `download` attribute is stored on the link.
    │
    ▼
4.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
5.  User clicks the link.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser checks the origin and the `download` attribute.
    │   └── If same-origin → proceed with download.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser fetches the file.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser determines the filename and sanitises it.
    │
    ▼
9.  Browser saves the file to the download folder.
    │
    ▼
10. Browser shows a download notification.
    │
    ▼
11. The page remains as it was (no navigation).
    │
    ▼
12. The user can open the downloaded file.

newLink.download = 'annual-report.pdf';

    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
    ctx.fillStyle = '#3498db';
    ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 400, 200);
    ctx.fillStyle = 'white';
    ctx.font = '30px Arial';

    document.getElementById('downloadCanvas').addEventListener('click', () => {

</script>

        try {
            const response = await fetch('/api/data');
            const blob = await response.blob();
            const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
            const link = document.createElement('a');
            link.href = url;
            link.download = 'api-data.json';
            link.click();
            URL.revokeObjectURL(url);
        } catch (error) {
            console.error('Download failed:', error);
        }

</script>

docs.title: Example 12: Download with Progress Indicator
docs.text:
<button id="downloadBtn">Download Large File</button>
<progress id="progress" value="0" max="100" hidden></progress>

<script>
    document.getElementById('downloadBtn').addEventListener('click', async () => {
        const progress = document.getElementById('progress');
        progress.hidden = false;

        const response = await fetch('/files/large-file.zip');
        const contentLength = response.headers.get('Content-Length');
        const total = parseInt(contentLength, 10);

        const reader = response.body.getReader();
        const chunks = [];
        let received = 0;

        while (true) {
            const { done, value } = await reader.read();
            if (done) break;

            chunks.push(value);
            received += value.length;
            progress.value = (received / total) * 100;
        }

        const blob = new Blob(chunks);
        const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
        const link = document.createElement('a');
        link.href = url;
        link.download = 'large-file.zip';
        link.click();
        URL.revokeObjectURL(url);

        progress.hidden = true;
    });
</script>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example PDF documents Reports, guides, manuals Images Photos, wallpapers, graphics Audio Music, podcasts, sound effects Video Movies, tutorials, demos ZIP archives Project files, backups CSV/JSON/XML Data exports Software Installers, updates E-books EPUB, MOBI Presentations PPT, Keynote Spreadsheets XLSX, CSV Invoices PDF invoices Receipts PDF receipts Forms PDF forms Legal documents Contracts, agreements Marketing materials Brochures, whitepapers

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use the download attribute for same-origin files – simple and declarative.

  2. Use Content-Disposition: attachment for cross-origin files – the only reliable way.

  3. Provide a meaningful filename – use download="report-2026.pdf" for clarity.

  4. Indicate the file type – in the link text: "Download Guide (PDF)".

  5. Indicate the file size – helpful for users on limited data: "PDF, 2.4 MB".

  6. Use descriptive link text – "Download Annual Report" not "Click here".

  7. Style download links as buttons – to make them prominent.

  8. Use icons – to indicate downloads visually.

  9. Test in multiple browsers – behaviour may vary.

  10. Test cross-origin downloads – ensure they work as expected.

  11. Configure Content-Type headers – so the browser knows the file type.

  12. Use X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff – to prevent MIME sniffing.

  13. Sanitise user input – never use user input in the download value without sanitisation.

  14. Avoid path traversal – don't allow / or \ in the filename.

  15. Provide fallbacks – for browsers that don't support the download attribute.

  16. Use JavaScript for generated content – with Blob and URL.createObjectURL.

  17. Revoke object URLs – after the download to free memory.

  18. Handle errors – in JavaScript downloads, catch and display errors.

  19. Show progress – for large downloads, use a progress indicator.

  20. Test with screen readers – ensure download links are announced correctly.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using download for Cross-Origin Files
docs.text:
<a href="https://other-site.com/file.pdf" download>Download</a>
Why it's wrong: The download attribute is ignored for cross-origin URLs. The browser will navigate to the URL instead.

✅ Correct: Use Content-Disposition: attachment on the server, or proxy the file through your server: 

<a href="/proxy/download?url=https://other-site.com/file.pdf">Download</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting the download Attribute
docs.text:
<a href="/files/report.pdf">Download Report</a>
Why it's wrong: Without the download attribute, the browser may open the PDF in its viewer instead of downloading it.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Download Report</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Path Separators in the Filename
docs.text:
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download="../../etc/passwd">Download</a>
Why it's wrong: The browser will sanitise the filename, but it's a security risk. Never allow user input in the download value.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="/files/report.pdf" download="report.pdf">Download</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Indicating the File Type
docs.text:
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Download</a>
Why it's wrong: The user doesn't know what type of file they're downloading.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Download Report (PDF)</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using "Click Here" as Link Text
docs.text:
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Click here</a>
Why it's wrong: The link text doesn't describe the file. Screen reader users hear "Click here, link" with no context.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Download Annual Report (PDF)</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Revoke Object URLs
docs.text:
const blob = new Blob(['data'], { type: 'text/plain' });
const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
link.href = url;
link.click();
// Forgot to revoke!
Why it's wrong: Object URLs persist in memory until revoked, causing memory leaks.

✅ Correct: 

const blob = new Blob(['data'], { type: 'text/plain' });
const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
link.href = url;
link.click();
URL.revokeObjectURL(url); // Free memory

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Handling Download Errors
docs.text:
fetch('/api/data').then(response => response.blob()).then(blob => {
    // Download
});
Why it's wrong: If the fetch fails, the error is unhandled.

✅ Correct: 

fetch('/api/data')
    .then(response => {
        if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Download failed');
        return response.blob();
    })
    .then(blob => { /* Download */ })
    .catch(error => console.error('Download failed:', error));

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using download on a <link> Element
docs.text:
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" download>
Why it's wrong: The download attribute is only valid on <a> and <area> elements.

✅ Correct: Use a download link: 

<a href="style.css" download>Download CSS</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming the Filename Will Be Respected
docs.text:
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download="annual-report.pdf">
Why it's wrong: The browser may ignore the suggested filename if the server sends a Content-Disposition header with a different filename, or if the user's settings override it.

✅ Correct: Configure the server to send the desired filename: 

Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="annual-report.pdf"

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing in Safari
docs.text:
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Download</a>
Why it's wrong: Safari has historically had quirks with the download attribute (e.g., opening PDFs in the browser instead of downloading). Test in all target browsers.

✅ Correct: Test and provide fallbacks if needed.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• File size – large files take time to download; indicate the size to users.
  • Network speed – users on slow connections may struggle with large downloads; provide alternatives.
  • Server bandwidth – downloads consume server bandwidth; use a CDN for large files.
  • Caching – downloaded files may be cached; use cache headers appropriately.
  • Concurrent downloads – browsers limit the number of concurrent downloads per domain.
  • Progress indicators – for large files, show progress to keep users informed.
  • Resumable downloads – support range requests for large files.
  • Compression – compress files before download (ZIP, GZIP) to reduce size.
  • Object URLs – revoke object URLs after use to free memory.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use a CDN – for large files, serve them from a CDN.
  2. Compress files – use ZIP or GZIP for text-based files.
  3. Optimize images – use modern formats (WebP, AVIF) and appropriate sizes.
  4. Use Content-Length – so browsers can show progress.
  5. Support range requests – for resumable downloads.
  6. Cache aggressively – for static files that don't change.
  7. Revoke object URLs – after JavaScript downloads.
  8. Limit concurrent downloads – to avoid overwhelming the server.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Same-origin restriction – the download attribute only works for same-origin URLs.
  • Filename sanitisation – browsers sanitise filenames to prevent path traversal.
  • MIME sniffing – use X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff to prevent MIME confusion attacks.
  • Malware – downloaded files can contain malware; users should be cautious.
  • XSS – never use user input in the download value without sanitisation.
  • Content-Disposition – the server can override the download attribute.
  • CSP – can restrict downloads via the sandbox directive.
  • Sandboxed iframes – downloads may be blocked unless allow-downloads is present.
  • HTTPS – always use HTTPS to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.
  • Integrity – use integrity attributes for downloaded scripts and styles.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitise user input – especially in download values.
  2. Use HTTPS – for all downloads.
  3. Set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff – to prevent MIME sniffing.
  4. Set Content-Disposition: attachment – for files that should always be downloaded.
  5. Validate file types – on the server, ensure uploaded files are safe.
  6. Scan for malware – if users can upload files, scan them for malware.
  7. Use CSP – to restrict downloads and other behaviours.
  8. Avoid data: URLs for large files – they can be inefficient and insecure.
  9. Use rel="noopener noreferrer" – for external links.
  10. Monitor downloads – log and monitor downloads for suspicious activity.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <a> element to see the download attribute.
  • DevTools Console – check link.download to see the attribute value.
  • DevTools Network panel – see the download request and response headers.
  • Check Content-Disposition – in the Network panel, look at the response headers.
  • Check Content-Type – ensure the MIME type is correct.
  • Test in multiple browsers – behaviour may vary.
  • Test cross-origin – ensure the download attribute is ignored (as expected).
  • Test with JavaScript disabled – ensure downloads still work.
  • Test with large files – ensure the download completes.
  • Test with slow connections – ensure progress indicators work.
  • Check for errors – in the Console for JavaScript downloads.
  • Use curl -I – to check response headers from the command line.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For same-origin files – PDFs, images, ZIPs, etc.
  • For generated content – CSV, JSON, etc.
  • For data exports – user data, reports.
  • For software distribution – installers, updates.
  • For media downloads – images, audio, video.
  • For documents – reports, guides, manuals.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For cross-origin files – use Content-Disposition instead.
  • For navigation – use a regular link.
  • For displaying content – use a regular link or embed.
  • For streaming media – use <video> or <audio>.
  • For inline viewing – use a regular link (if the browser can display it).
  • For pages – use a regular link.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <a> element – the anchor element.
  • href attribute – the file URL.
  • download attribute – forces download.
  • Content-Disposition header – server-side download control.
  • Content-Type header – the MIME type.
  • Blob – binary large object for generated content.
  • URL.createObjectURL – creates a URL for a Blob.
  • URL.revokeObjectURL – frees memory.
  • fetch API – for downloading data.
  • XMLHttpRequest – legacy API for downloads.
  • data: URLs – inline data URLs.
  • blob: URLs – Blob URLs.
  • X-Content-Type-Options – prevents MIME sniffing.
  • Content-Security-Policy – can restrict downloads.
  • sandbox attribute – can block downloads.
  • allow-downloads – sandbox flag for downloads.
  • integrity attribute – for Subresource Integrity.
  • rel="noopener noreferrer" – for external links.
  • rel="nofollow" – for untrusted downloads.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The download attribute was introduced in HTML5. It did not exist in HTML 4.01.

  • The download attribute is a boolean attribute with an optional string value.

  • The download attribute only works for same-origin URLs. For cross-origin files, the server must send Content-Disposition: attachment.

  • Content-Disposition is the server-side equivalent of the download attribute. It works for all origins.

  • Browsers sanitise the filename in the download attribute to prevent path traversal attacks.

  • The download attribute works with blob: and data: URLs, allowing JavaScript to generate and download files.

  • URL.createObjectURL creates a temporary URL for a Blob or File. You must call URL.revokeObjectURL to free memory.

  • The download attribute is supported in all modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge).

  • Safari has historically had quirks with the download attribute, sometimes opening PDFs in the browser instead of downloading.

  • The Content-Type header tells the browser the MIME type of the file. This affects how the browser handles the file.

  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff prevents browsers from MIME-sniffing, which can prevent certain attacks.

  • Content-Disposition supports filename* for encoded filenames (RFC 5987): 

    Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=UTF-8''r%C3%A9sum%C3%A9.pdf

  • Sandboxed iframes may block downloads unless the allow-downloads flag is present.

  • CSP can restrict downloads via the sandbox directive.

  • The download attribute can be used on <area> elements as well as <a> elements.

  • JavaScript-generated downloads are useful for exporting data, generating reports, and saving user-created content.

  • The Blob constructor takes an array of data and an options object: 

    new Blob(['Hello'], { type: 'text/plain' });

  • The canvas.toBlob() method generates a Blob from a canvas, which can be downloaded.

  • Progress indicators for downloads can be implemented using the fetch API and reading the response body in chunks.

  • Resumable downloads are supported via HTTP range requests (Range header).

  • Download managers (like Internet Download Manager) can intercept downloads and provide additional features.

  • The download attribute is a small but powerful feature that improves the user experience for file distribution.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A download link is a hyperlink that downloads a file to the user's device instead of navigating to it.
  • It uses the download attribute on the <a> element.
  • The download attribute can be used with or without a value:
  • download – downloads with the original filename.
  • download="name.ext" – suggests a filename.
  • It only works for same-origin URLs (or blob: and data: URLs).
  • For cross-origin files, use the Content-Disposition: attachment header on the server.
  • Best practices: use descriptive link text, indicate file type and size, style download links as buttons, test in multiple browsers, and use JavaScript for generated content.
  • Common mistakes include using download for cross-origin files, forgetting the attribute, using path separators in filenames, and not revoking object URLs.
  • Downloads can be generated with JavaScript using Blob, URL.createObjectURL, and a temporary <a> element.
  • Security considerations: sanitise user input, use HTTPS, set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and use Content-Disposition: attachment for files that should always be downloaded.
  • Download links are essential for file distribution, data export, software distribution, and media downloads.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An email link (also called a mailto link) is a hyperlink that, when clicked, opens the user's default email client with a new message pre-addressed to a specified email address. Email links are created using the <a> element with an href that uses the mailto: scheme, followed by one or more email addresses and optional parameters for the subject, body, CC, and BCC fields.

Example: 

<a href="mailto:info@example.com">Email Us</a>

Unlike regular web links that navigate to a URL, mailto: links trigger an external application (the email client) through the operating system's protocol handler. This makes them a bridge between the web and desktop/mobile email applications.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Email links serve several essential purposes:

  • Contact – provide a quick way for users to email the site owner or a specific department.
  • Feedback – enable users to send feedback, questions, or support requests.
  • Inquiries – allow potential customers to ask about products or services.
  • Reporting – let users report bugs, abuse, or issues.
  • Subscriptions – allow users to subscribe to newsletters or mailing lists.
  • Sharing – let users share content via email with pre-filled subject and body.
  • Convenience – no need to copy the email address, open the email client, and paste it manually.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Email links are used wherever a website wants to provide a direct email contact option:

  • Contact pages – general inquiries, support, sales.
  • Footers – site-wide contact email.
  • Author bios – contact the author.
  • Article pages – report an error or provide feedback.
  • Product pages – ask about a product.
  • Error pages – report a broken link.
  • Documentation – contact the documentation team.
  • Job listings – apply for a job.
<p>Contact us at <a href="mailto:info@example.com">info@example.com</a></p>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before mailto: links, if a website wanted users to email them, they had to display the email address as plain text. Users would then have to:

  1. Read the email address.
  2. Remember it (or copy it).
  3. Open their email client.
  4. Create a new message.
  5. Paste the address.
  6. Type a subject.
  7. Type a body.

This was tedious and error-prone. Users often mistyped addresses or gave up. There was no direct way to link from a web page to an email client.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No direct email link Users had to manually copy and paste. Tedious workflow Multiple steps to send an email. Error-prone Typos in email addresses. No pre-filled fields Users had to type subject and body. Poor UX High friction for contacting the site.

docs.title: Why mailto: Was Introduced
docs.text:
The mailto: scheme was defined in RFC 1738 (1994), the same specification that defined HTTP and other URL schemes. It was designed to provide a standardized way to link to an email address, leveraging the operating system's protocol handler to open the default email client.

mailto: enables:

  • Direct email links – one click to compose an email.
  • Pre-filled fields – subject, body, CC, BCC.
  • Multiple recipients – comma-separated addresses.
  • Cross-platform support – works on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android.
  • No JavaScript required – pure HTML solution.
  • Standardized – defined in RFC 6068 (2010), which updated the mailto: specification.

The mailto: scheme is part of the broader URL specification and is implemented in all major browsers and operating systems.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of mailto:
docs.text: <a href="mailto:email@example.com">Link text</a>

docs.title: Simple Email Link
docs.text: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">Email Us</a>

docs.title: Email Link with Visible Address
docs.text: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">info@example.com</a>

docs.title: Email Link with Subject
docs.text: <a href="mailto:info@example.com?subject=Inquiry">Send an Inquiry</a>

docs.title: Email Link with Subject and Body
docs.text:
<a href="mailto:info@example.com?subject=Inquiry&body=Hello%2C%20I%20have%20a%20question.">
    Send an Inquiry
</a>

docs.title: Email Link with CC and BCC
docs.text:
<a href="mailto:info@example.com?cc=manager@example.com&bcc=archive@example.com">
    Email Us
</a>

docs.title: Email Link with Multiple Recipients
docs.text: <a href="mailto:info@example.com,support@example.com">Contact Us</a>

docs.title: Email Link with All Parameters
docs.text:
<a href="mailto:info@example.com?cc=manager@example.com&bcc=archive@example.com&subject=Inquiry&body=Hello%2C%20I%20have%20a%20question.">
    Send an Inquiry
</a>

docs.title: Email Link with Encoded Characters
docs.text:
<!-- Spaces must be encoded as %20 -->
<a href="mailto:info@example.com?subject=Hello%20World&body=This%20is%20a%20test.">
    Email Us
</a>

<!-- Line breaks must be encoded as %0A or %0D%0A -->
<a href="mailto:info@example.com?body=Line%201%0ALine%202">Email Us</a>

docs.title: Email Link with mailto: and No Address (Opens Empty Compose)
docs.text: <a href="mailto:">Send an Email</a>

docs.title: Email Link with an Image
docs.text:
<a href="mailto:info@example.com">
    <img src="email-icon.png" alt="Email Us">
</a>

docs.title: Email Link with an Icon and Text
docs.text:
<a href="mailto:info@example.com" class="email-link">
    ✉ Email Us
</a>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters mailto: The scheme. Tells the browser to open the email client. info@example.com The recipient. The email address. ?subject=... Sets the subject. Pre-fills the subject line. &body=... Sets the body. Pre-fills the message body. &cc=... Sets the CC field. Carbon copy recipients. &bcc=... Sets the BCC field. Blind carbon copy recipients. %20 Encoded space. Spaces must be encoded in URLs. %0A Encoded newline. Line breaks in the body.

docs.title: The "Postage Stamp" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a mailto: link as a pre-addressed postage stamp. The envelope (the email) is already addressed to the recipient, and the subject and body are pre-written. All the user has to do is add their message and "send" it. The stamp connects the web page to the postal service (the email client).

docs.title: The "Speed Dial" Analogy
docs.text: A mailto: link is like a speed dial button on a phone. Instead of dialing the full number, you press one button and the call is initiated. The mailto: link does the same for email — one click and the email client opens with the address pre-filled.

docs.title: The "Pre-filled Form" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a mailto: link as a pre-filled form. The recipient, subject, and body are already filled in. The user just needs to review, add their message, and submit (send). This reduces friction and speeds up the process.

docs.title: The "Handoff" Analogy
docs.text: A mailto: link is a handoff from the browser to the email client. The browser says: "I've done my part — here's the email composition; you take it from here." The email client takes over and handles the actual sending.

docs.title: Concept 1: The mailto: Scheme
docs.text:
The mailto: scheme is defined in RFC 6068 (2010). It follows this syntax:

mailto:address1,address2?header1=value1&header2=value2
  • Addresses – comma-separated email addresses (recipients).
  • Headers – optional query parameters for subject, body, cc, bcc.

docs.title: Concept 2: The Recipient Address
docs.text:
The recipient address is the email address that the message will be sent to. It comes immediately after mailto:.

<a href="mailto:info@example.com">Email Us</a>

Multiple recipients are separated by commas:

<a href="mailto:info@example.com,support@example.com">Contact Us</a>

Note: Commas in email addresses must be encoded as %2C if they are part of the address itself (rare).

docs.title: Concept 3: Optional Headers
docs.text:
The mailto: scheme supports several optional headers:

Header Description Example subject The subject line. subject=Inquiry body The message body. body=Hello%2C%20World cc Carbon copy recipients. cc=manager@example.com bcc Blind carbon copy recipients. bcc=archive@example.com

Headers are separated by & and come after a ?.

<a href="mailto:info@example.com?subject=Inquiry&body=Hello">

docs.title: Concept 4: URL Encoding
docs.text:
Because mailto: URLs follow URL syntax, special characters must be percent-encoded:

Character Encoding Space %20 Newline %0A (or %0D%0A for CRLF) & %26 ? %3F = %3D # %23 + %2B , %2C

Example: 

<a href="mailto:info@example.com?subject=Hello%20World&body=Line%201%0ALine%202">

docs.title: Concept 5: Line Breaks in the Body
docs.text:
Line breaks in the body must be encoded as %0A (LF) or %0D%0A (CRLF). Different email clients may handle these differently.

<a href="mailto:info@example.com?body=Line%201%0ALine%202%0ALine%203">

Best practice: Use %0D%0A for maximum compatibility.

docs.title: Concept 6: Multiple Recipients
docs.text:
Multiple recipients can be specified in the mailto: address, separated by commas:

<a href="mailto:info@example.com,support@example.com">Contact Us</a>

Recipients in the cc and bcc fields are also comma-separated:

<a href="mailto:info@example.com?cc=manager@example.com,lead@example.com">

docs.title: Concept 7: The mailto: Link and the User's Email Client
docs.text:
When a user clicks a mailto: link, the browser hands off the email composition to the default email client set in the operating system. This could be:

  • Desktop: Outlook, Apple Mail, Thunderbird, Windows Mail.
  • Webmail: Gmail, Yahoo Mail, Outlook.com (if configured as the default handler).
  • Mobile: Apple Mail, Gmail, Samsung Email.

The browser has no control over which email client opens — it depends on the user's system settings.

docs.title: Concept 8: mailto: on Mobile Devices
docs.text: On mobile devices, mailto: links typically open the default email app. This is usually seamless, as mobile operating systems handle mailto: URLs natively.

docs.title: Concept 9: mailto: and Webmail Users
docs.text:
Users who use webmail (Gmail, Yahoo Mail, etc.) may not have a default email client configured. In this case, clicking a mailto: link may:

  • Open the webmail service (if configured).
  • Show a dialog asking which app to use.
  • Do nothing (if no handler is configured).

This is a common source of frustration for webmail users. Providing a contact form as an alternative is a good practice.

docs.title: Concept 10: mailto: and Spam
docs.text:
Displaying email addresses in mailto: links can attract spam bots that scrape websites for email addresses. To mitigate this:

  • Obfuscate the email address – use JavaScript to build the address.
  • Use a contact form – instead of displaying the email.
  • Use an image – display the email as an image (not accessible).
  • Use CSS – hide the address from scrapers (but not all).
  • Use a CAPTCHA – on the contact form.

Note: Obfuscation is not foolproof. Determined spammers can still find the address.

docs.title: Concept 11: mailto: and Accessibility
docs.text:
• Link text – should describe the action: "Email Us" or the email address itself.
  • Screen readers – announce the link and the mailto: scheme.
  • Keyboard accessible – links are focusable and activated with Enter.
  • Email as image – not accessible; avoid.
  • Obfuscated email – may not be accessible to screen readers if JavaScript is required.

docs.title: Concept 12: mailto: and Security
docs.text:
• Phishing – attackers can use mailto: links with misleading addresses. Users should verify the address.
  • Spam – scrapers harvest email addresses from mailto: links.
  • Malware – mailto: links themselves are safe, but the resulting email could contain malware.
  • No encryption – mailto: links don't encrypt the email; it's sent as plain text unless the email client uses encryption.

docs.title: Concept 13: mailto: vs. Contact Forms
docs.text:
Aspect mailto: Link Contact Form Setup Simple (HTML only) Requires server-side processing User experience Opens email client Stays on the website Spam risk High (address exposed) Lower (CAPTCHA, validation) Tracking None Can track submissions Validation None Can validate input Attachments User can attach files Limited (unless file upload) Mobile Opens email app Works in browser Webmail users May not work Always works

Best practice: Provide both — a contact form for webmail users and a mailto: link for those who prefer their email client.

docs.title: Concept 14: The mailto: Scheme and the URL Specification
docs.text:
The mailto: scheme is defined in RFC 6068, which specifies:

  • The syntax of mailto: URLs.
  • The allowed headers (subject, body, cc, bcc, etc.).
  • Encoding requirements.

Browsers implement mailto: by passing the URL to the operating system's protocol handler.

docs.title: Concept 15: mailto: with Internationalized Email Addresses
docs.text:
Internationalized email addresses (with non-ASCII characters) must be encoded using punycode or percent-encoding.

<a href="mailto:user%40example.com?subject=Hello">Email</a>

Note: Internationalized email addresses are not widely supported yet.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing a mailto: Link
docs.text:
1.  Author writes a `mailto:` link.
    │   └── <a href="mailto:info@example.com?subject=Inquiry">
    │
    ▼
2.  User clicks the link.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser recognizes the `mailto:` scheme.
    │   └── It's not a web URL (http/https), so it's not fetched.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser passes the `mailto:` URL to the operating system's protocol handler.
    │   └── The OS determines which application is registered for `mailto:`.
    │
    ▼
5.  The default email client opens.
    │
    ▼
6.  The email client parses the `mailto:` URL:
    │   ├── Sets the "To" field to info@example.com.
    │   ├── Sets the "Subject" field to "Inquiry".
    │   ├── Sets the "Body" field (if provided).
    │   ├── Sets the "CC" field (if provided).
    │   └── Sets the "BCC" field (if provided).
    │
    ▼
7.  The user composes the email.
    │
    ▼
8.  The user sends the email.
    │
    ▼
9.  The email client sends the email via SMTP.
    │
    ▼
10. The email is delivered to the recipient's inbox.

docs.title: The OS Protocol Handler
docs.text:
The operating system maintains a registry of protocol handlers:

  • Windows: Registry (HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\mailto).
  • macOS: Launch Services.
  • Linux: xdg-open and MIME handlers.
  • iOS/Android: System-level handlers.

Browsers delegate mailto: URLs to these handlers.

docs.title: Browser Behaviour
docs.text:
Different browsers handle mailto: slightly differently:

Browser Behaviour Chrome Opens the default email client. May show a dialog if no handler is set. Firefox Opens the default email client. Has a setting for mailto: handling. Safari Opens the default email client (Apple Mail by default on macOS). Edge Opens the default email client.

docs.title: Webmail Integration
docs.text:
Some browsers allow users to configure a webmail service (e.g., Gmail) as the handler for mailto: links:

  • Chrome: Settings → Privacy and security → Site settings → Additional content settings → Protocol handlers.
  • Firefox: Settings → General → Applications → mailto.

This allows users to compose emails in their webmail service instead of a desktop client.

docs.title: The mailto: URL Parsing
docs.text:
The mailto: URL is parsed per RFC 6068. The parser extracts:

  1. To – the recipient addresses (comma-separated).
  2. Headers – the query parameters (subject, body, cc, bcc).

Example: 

mailto:info@example.com,support@example.com?cc=manager@example.com&subject=Inquiry&body=Hello

Parsed: - To: info@example.com, support@example.com - CC: manager@example.com - Subject: Inquiry - Body: Hello

docs.title: The HTMLAnchorElement and mailto:
docs.text:
The mailto: URL is stored in the href attribute. JavaScript can read and modify it:

const link = document.querySelector('a[href^="mailto:"]');
console.log(link.href); // "mailto:info@example.com?subject=Inquiry"

docs.title: URL Encoding and Decoding
docs.text:
When constructing a mailto: URL, special characters must be encoded. JavaScript provides:

  • encodeURIComponent() – encodes a string for use in a URL component.
  • decodeURIComponent() – decodes an encoded string.
const subject = encodeURIComponent('Hello World');
const body = encodeURIComponent('Line 1\nLine 2');
const mailto = `mailto:info@example.com?subject=${subject}&body=${body}`;

docs.title: The Operating System Integration
docs.text:
Browsers integrate with the OS protocol handler via:

  • Windows: ShellExecute with the mailto: URL.
  • macOS: NSWorkspace.openURL.
  • Linux: xdg-open.

The OS then launches the registered application.

docs.title: Webmail Handlers
docs.text:
Webmail services register themselves as protocol handlers:

  • Gmail: https://mail.google.com/mail/?extsrc=mailto&url=%s
  • Outlook.com: https://outlook.live.com/mail/0/deeplink/compose?mailtouri=%s
  • Yahoo Mail: https://compose.mail.yahoo.com/?To=%s

When a user configures a webmail handler, the browser redirects mailto: URLs to the webmail service.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a mailto: Link
docs.text:
1.  Author writes a `mailto:` link.
    │   └── <a href="mailto:info@example.com?subject=Inquiry">
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `href` attribute is stored.
    │
    ▼
4.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
5.  User clicks the link.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser passes the `mailto:` URL to the OS protocol handler.
    │
    ▼
7.  OS launches the default email client.
    │
    ▼
8.  Email client opens with pre-filled fields.
    │
    ▼
9.  User composes and sends the email.
    │
    ▼
10. Email is delivered.

docs.title: Dynamic mailto: Links
docs.text:
// Create a mailto link dynamically
const link = document.createElement('a');
link.href = 'mailto:info@example.com?subject=Inquiry&body=Hello';
link.textContent = 'Email Us';
document.body.appendChild(link);

docs.title: Building mailto: Links with JavaScript
docs.text:
function createMailtoLink(email, subject, body) {
    const params = new URLSearchParams();
    if (subject) params.set('subject', subject);
    if (body) params.set('body', body);
    return `mailto:${email}?${params.toString()}`;
}

const link = createMailtoLink('info@example.com', 'Hello', 'This is a test.');
console.log(link);
// "mailto:info@example.com?subject=Hello&body=This+is+a+test."

Note: URLSearchParams encodes spaces as +, which is valid for query strings but may not work in all email clients. Use encodeURIComponent for better compatibility.

        subject: 'Inquiry',
        body: 'Hello, I have a question.'
    });

    link.href = `mailto:info@example.com?${params.toString()}`;
    link.textContent = 'Email Us';
    document.body.appendChild(link);
</script>

Note: URLSearchParams encodes spaces as +, which may not work in all email clients. For best compatibility, use encodeURIComponent.

docs.title: Example 15: Email Link with Manual Encoding
docs.text:
function buildMailto(email, subject, body, cc, bcc) {
    const parts = [];
    if (subject) parts.push(`subject=${encodeURIComponent(subject)}`);
    if (body) parts.push(`body=${encodeURIComponent(body)}`);
    if (cc) parts.push(`cc=${encodeURIComponent(cc)}`);
    if (bcc) parts.push(`bcc=${encodeURIComponent(bcc)}`);
    const query = parts.length ? `?${parts.join('&')}` : '';
    return `mailto:${email}${query}`;
}

const link = buildMailto(
    'info@example.com',
    'Inquiry',
    'Hello,\n\nI have a question.',
    'manager@example.com'
);
console.log(link);
