docs.text: Threat Defence Tabnabbing rel="noopener" Referrer leakage rel="noreferrer" or Referrer-Policy SEO spam rel="nofollow", rel="sponsored", rel="ugc" XSS via href URL sanitization, CSP navigate-to javascript: URLs Block with CSP, sanitize input Phishing Verify URLs, warn users, use rel="external" Malware downloads Content-Disposition, X-Content-Type-Options Tracking via ping Disable, or inform users

docs.title: Example: A Fully Hardened External Link
docs.text:
<a href="https://untrusted.com"
   target="_blank"
   rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow sponsored ugc"
   referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
   hreflang="en"
   type="text/html">
    Visit untrusted.com
    <span class="visually-hidden">(opens in a new tab, external site)</span>
</a>

Every attribute here is a security decision:

  • href — points to an external, untrusted domain.
  • target="_blank" — opens in a new tab.
  • rel="noopener" — prevents tabnabbing.
  • rel="noreferrer" — prevents referrer leakage.
  • rel="nofollow" — tells search engines not to follow.
  • rel="sponsored" — marks as a paid link.
  • rel="ugc" — marks as user-generated content.
  • referrerpolicy="no-referrer" — per-link referrer policy.
  • hreflang="en" — declares the language of the target.
  • type="text/html" — declares the MIME type of the target.
  • Visible and hidden text — warns users about the new tab and external site.

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Security Purpose href The most critical — must be validated and sanitized. target Controls the browsing context — _blank requires noopener. rel Declares the relationship — noopener, noreferrer, nofollow, sponsored, ugc. referrerpolicy Per-link control over referrer headers. hreflang Hints the language of the destination. type Hints the MIME type of the destination. Link text Must accurately describe the destination — no deception.

docs.title: The "Open Door" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of every link as a door in your house. Without security:

  • The door might lead to a thief's hideout (phishing).
  • The thief might sneak in through another door while you're distracted (tabnabbing).
  • The thief might learn your address while walking out (referrer leakage).
  • The door might be booby-trapped (malware download).
  • The door might be mislabelled ("Exit" but actually leads to the basement) — phishing.

Link security is about knowing who built the door, where it leads, and what happens when you walk through it.

docs.title: The "Handshake" Analogy
docs.text:
When you click a link, you're effectively shaking hands with an unknown party. Without security:

  • You might not know who you're shaking hands with (phishing).
  • They might hold on to your hand and not let go (tabnabbing).
  • They might learn things about you (referrer leakage).
  • They might slip you a virus (malware download).

Secure links ensure that every handshake is authenticated, non-binding, and safe.

docs.title: The "Firewall" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of each security attribute as a layer of a firewall:

  • rel="noopener" — blocks tabnabbing.
  • rel="noreferrer" — blocks referrer leakage.
  • rel="nofollow" — blocks SEO spam.
  • CSP — blocks javascript: URLs.
  • Sanitization — blocks XSS.
  • Referrer-Policy — blocks referrer leakage globally.

Each layer defends against a specific threat. Defence in depth means using multiple layers.

docs.title: Concept 1: Phishing and Social Engineering
docs.text:
Threat: An attacker crafts a link that appears to point to a trusted destination but actually points to a malicious site.

Techniques:

  • Misleading link text – https://trusted-bank.com displayed but href="https://evil.com".
  • Homograph attacks – using visually similar characters (e.g., Cyrillic а instead of Latin a).
  • Punycode – xn--80ak6aa92e.com looks like apple.com.
  • Subdomain tricks – paypal.com.evil.com appears to be paypal.com.
  • URL shorteners – bit.ly/xyz hides the real destination.
  • Open redirects – trusted.com/redirect?url=evil.com.

Defences:

  • Validate href values.
  • Warn users before navigating to external sites.
  • Use rel="external" (informational).
  • Display the full URL on hover (browser default).
  • Avoid URL shorteners for sensitive links.
  • Use Referrer-Policy and Content-Security-Policy.

docs.title: Concept 2: Tabnabbing
docs.text:
Threat: A page opened via target="_blank" can access window.opener and redirect the original page to a phishing site. When the user returns to the original tab, they see the phishing page instead of the site they trusted.

Attack:

<!-- Attacker's page, opened via target="_blank" -->
<script>
    window.opener.location = 'https://phishing-site.com';
</script>

Defences:

  • rel="noopener" — sets window.opener to null.
  • rel="noreferrer" — implies noopener and also omits the referrer.
  • Modern browsers default to noopener for target="_blank".

docs.title: Concept 3: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via href
docs.text:
Threat: If user input is inserted directly into an href attribute without sanitization, an attacker can inject a javascript: URL that executes arbitrary code.

Attack:

<!-- User input: javascript:alert(document.cookie) -->
<a href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">Click me</a>

Defences:

  • Sanitize user input — allow only http:, https:, mailto:, tel:, and other safe schemes.
  • Use a well-tested sanitization library (e.g., DOMPurify).
  • Set a Content Security Policy that blocks javascript: URLs.
  • Use rel="nofollow" for user-generated links.
  • Encode output with the correct context (HTML attribute encoding).

docs.title: Concept 4: Referrer Leakage
docs.text:
Threat: When a user clicks a link, the browser sends a Referer header containing the URL of the current page. This can leak sensitive information:

  • Session tokens in the URL.
  • Internal paths (e.g., /admin/secret-page).
  • Query parameters (e.g., ?token=abc123).
  • User IDs or other PII.

Defences:

  • rel="noreferrer" — omits the referrer for that link.
  • Referrer-Policy HTTP header — sets the policy globally.
  • referrerpolicy attribute — sets the policy per link.
  • Best practice: Set Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin (the modern default).

docs.title: Concept 5: SEO Spam and Link Manipulation
docs.text:
Threat: Attackers exploit links to manipulate search rankings:

  • Comment spam – links in comments to boost SEO.
  • Paid links – undisclosed paid links that violate search engine guidelines.
  • User-generated links – links in forums, wikis, and social media.

Defences:

  • rel="nofollow" — tells search engines not to follow the link.
  • rel="sponsored" — identifies paid links.
  • rel="ugc" — identifies user-generated content.
  • Google's guidelines: All three are respected by search engines.

docs.title: Concept 6: Malicious Downloads
docs.text:
Threat: A link with the download attribute can deliver malware disguised as a legitimate file. The filename can be misleading.

Attack:

<a href="virus.exe" download="invoice.pdf">Download Invoice</a>

Defences:

  • Validate the download filename.
  • Use Content-Disposition: attachment on the server.
  • Set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff to prevent MIME sniffing.
  • Scan uploaded files for malware.
  • Use Content-Security-Policy to restrict downloads.
  • Warn users before downloading files from untrusted sources.

docs.title: Concept 7: The ping Attribute
docs.text:
Threat: The ping attribute sends a POST request to one or more URLs when a link is clicked. This can be used for tracking without the user's knowledge.

Attack:

<a href="https://example.com" ping="https://tracker.com/log">Click me</a>

Defences:

  • Avoid using ping unless necessary.
  • Inform users if tracking is used.
  • Use Referrer-Policy to limit tracking.
  • Users can disable ping in some browsers.

docs.title: Concept 8: Open Redirects
docs.text:
Threat: A trusted site has a redirect endpoint that accepts a URL parameter. An attacker uses it to redirect users to a malicious site.

Attack:

https://trusted.com/redirect?url=https://evil.com

The user sees trusted.com in the URL bar but ends up at evil.com.

Defences:

  • Validate redirect URLs — allow only same-origin or whitelisted domains.
  • Don't expose open redirect endpoints.
  • Use a warning page for external redirects.
  • Use rel="noreferrer" for links to redirect endpoints.

docs.title: Concept 9: javascript: URLs
docs.text:
Threat: A javascript: URL in href executes JavaScript when clicked. This is a common XSS vector.

Attack:

<a href="javascript:alert('XSS')">Click me</a>

Defences:

  • Block javascript: URLs via CSP (script-src directive).
  • Sanitize all user input to remove javascript:.
  • Never insert user input directly into href.
  • Use event listeners instead of javascript: URLs.

docs.title: Concept 10: data: URLs
docs.text:
Threat: A data: URL can embed arbitrary content (including HTML, SVG, and scripts) in the URL itself. This can be used for XSS.

Attack:

<a href="data:text/html,<script>alert('XSS')</script>">Click me</a>

Defences:

  • Block data: URLs in CSP.
  • Sanitize user input to remove data: URLs.
  • Use Content-Disposition: attachment for data URLs.

docs.title: Concept 11: Homograph Attacks
docs.text:
Threat: Attackers use visually similar characters from different scripts to create deceptive domains.

Examples:

  • аpple.com (Cyrillic а) vs apple.com (Latin a).
  • rnicrosoft.com vs microsoft.com.
  • paypa1.com vs paypal.com.

Defences:

  • Browsers display punycode for mixed-script domains.
  • Verify URLs before clicking.
  • Use bookmarklets or password managers that match by domain.
  • Educate users.

docs.title: Concept 12: Link Text Deception
docs.text:
Threat: The visible text of a link may not match the href destination.

Attack:

<a href="https://evil.com">https://trusted-bank.com</a>

Defences:

  • Display the full URL on hover (browser default).
  • Use title attribute to show the URL (not reliable).
  • Warn users about external links.
  • Use a link preview tool.

docs.title: Concept 13: target="_blank" Default Behaviour
docs.text:
Threat: Historically, target="_blank" allowed the new page to access window.opener. Modern browsers default to noopener, but older browsers don't.

Defences:

  • Always add rel="noopener" explicitly.
  • Modern browsers (Chrome 88+, Firefox 79+, Safari 12.1+) default to noopener.
  • Test on older browsers if you support them.

docs.title: Concept 14: Content Security Policy (CSP)
docs.text:
Threat: Without CSP, an attacker who can inject a link can execute arbitrary JavaScript, load external resources, or exfiltrate data.

Defences:

  • default-src 'self' — restrict all resources to same-origin.
  • script-src 'self' — restrict scripts.
  • object-src 'none' — block plugins.
  • base-uri 'self' — prevent <base> injection.
  • navigate-to 'self' — restrict navigation (experimental).
  • form-action 'self' — restrict form submission.

docs.title: Concept 15: Subresource Integrity (SRI)
docs.text:
Threat: If an external script or stylesheet is compromised, the attacker can execute arbitrary code.

Defences:

  • integrity="sha384-..." — verify the hash of the resource.
  • crossorigin="anonymous" — required for SRI.
<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"
        integrity="sha384-abc123..."
        crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

docs.title: Concept 16: rel="noopener" vs rel="noreferrer"
docs.text:
Attribute Prevents tabnabbing Omits referrer noopener ✅ ❌ noreferrer ✅ ✅

Best practice: Use both — rel="noopener noreferrer".

docs.title: Concept 17: The rel Attribute Values
docs.text: Value Purpose noopener Prevents tabnabbing. noreferrer Prevents referrer leakage and tabnabbing. nofollow Tells search engines not to follow. sponsored Identifies paid links. ugc Identifies user-generated content. external Indicates an external link (informational). author Links to the author. license Links to the license. next / prev Links to next/previous in a sequence. tag Links to a tag page.

docs.title: Concept 18: Sanitization Libraries
docs.text:
Rolling your own sanitization is error-prone. Use well-tested libraries:

Library Language Purpose DOMPurify JavaScript Sanitize HTML (including links). bleach Python Sanitize HTML. OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer Java Sanitize HTML. HtmlSanitizer .NET Sanitize HTML. Sanitize Ruby Sanitize HTML.

docs.title: Concept 19: URL Validation
docs.text:
Validate URLs before using them in href:

function isSafeUrl(url) {
    try {
        const parsed = new URL(url);
        return ['http:', 'https:', 'mailto:', 'tel:'].includes(parsed.protocol);
    } catch {
        return false;
    }
}

Rules:

  • Allow only http:, https:, mailto:, tel:, and other safe schemes.
  • Block javascript:, data:, vbscript:, file:.
  • Block URLs with embedded credentials.
  • Block URLs with unusual characters.

docs.title: Concept 20: Link Auditing
docs.text:
Regularly audit links for security:

  • Check for target="_blank" without rel="noopener".
  • Check for user-generated links without rel="nofollow ugc".
  • Check for external links without rel="noopener noreferrer".
  • Check for javascript: URLs.
  • Check for data: URLs.
  • Check for open redirects.
  • Check for misleading link text.
  • Check for malware downloads.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: A Secure Link Navigation
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a link.
    │   └── <a href="https://external.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow">
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser validates the URL:
    │   ├── Checks the scheme (http, https, mailto, tel, etc.).
    │   ├── Blocks javascript:, data:, vbscript:, file:.
    │   └── Checks against CSP navigate-to (if set).
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser creates a new browsing context (due to target="_blank").
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser sets window.opener to null (due to rel="noopener").
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser omits the Referer header (due to rel="noreferrer").
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser omits the ping (if present, blocked by policy).
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser navigates to the URL.
    │
    ▼
8.  The new page loads in the new tab.
    │
    ▼
9.  The original page remains unchanged and secure.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: A Tabnabbing Attack (Without noopener)
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a link with target="_blank" (no rel="noopener").
    │   └── <a href="https://evil.com" target="_blank">Click me</a>
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser creates a new tab and navigates to evil.com.
    │
    ▼
3.  evil.com executes:
    │   └── window.opener.location = 'https://phishing-site.com';
    │
    ▼
4.  The original tab is silently redirected to phishing-site.com.
    │
    ▼
5.  User returns to the original tab and sees a fake login page.
    │
    ▼
6.  User enters credentials, which are stolen by the attacker.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: XSS via javascript: URL (Without Sanitization)
docs.text:
1.  User submits a comment with the text:
    │   └── <a href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">Click me</a>
    │
    ▼
2.  Server stores the comment without sanitization.
    │
    ▼
3.  Another user views the comment.
    │
    ▼
4.  The malicious link is rendered in the HTML.
    │
    ▼
5.  The user clicks the link.
    │
    ▼
6.  The browser executes the JavaScript in the href.
    │
    ▼
7.  The attacker's script runs in the context of the trusted site.
    │
    ▼
8.  Cookies, tokens, and data are stolen.

docs.title: How Browsers Handle noopener
docs.text:
When a browser sees rel="noopener" on a target="_blank" link:

  1. It creates the new browsing context.
  2. It sets window.opener to null in the new context.
  3. The new page cannot access window.opener or manipulate the original page.

docs.title: How Browsers Handle noreferrer
docs.text:
When a browser sees rel="noreferrer":

  1. It omits the Referer header from the HTTP request.
  2. It also sets window.opener to null (noreferrer implies noopener).

docs.title: How Browsers Handle nofollow, sponsored, ugc
docs.text: These rel values are not enforced by the browser — they are hints to search engines. The browser ignores them; search engine crawlers read them.

docs.title: How CSP Blocks javascript: URLs
docs.text:
The script-src directive in CSP blocks inline scripts and javascript: URLs:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'

With this policy, javascript: URLs are blocked.

docs.title: How CSP Blocks data: URLs
docs.text:
The default-src or script-src directive can block data: URLs:

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'

docs.title: How Referrer-Policy Works
docs.text:
The Referrer-Policy header or referrerpolicy attribute controls how much referrer information is sent:

Value Behaviour no-referrer No referrer is sent. no-referrer-when-downgrade Referrer sent for HTTPS→HTTPS, omitted for HTTPS→HTTP (default in older browsers). origin Only the origin is sent (e.g., https://example.com). origin-when-cross-origin Full referrer for same-origin, origin for cross-origin. same-origin Full referrer for same-origin, none for cross-origin. strict-origin Only the origin, and only for HTTPS→HTTPS. strict-origin-when-cross-origin Full referrer for same-origin, origin for cross-origin HTTPS→HTTPS, none for HTTPS→HTTP (modern default). unsafe-url Always sends the full referrer (not recommended).

docs.title: How Sanitization Libraries Work
docs.text:
DOMPurify, for example:

  1. Parses the HTML into a DOM.
  2. Walks the DOM tree.
  3. Removes disallowed elements and attributes.
  4. Removes disallowed URL schemes (javascript:, data:, etc.).
  5. Serializes the sanitized DOM back to HTML.

docs.title: How SRI Works
docs.text:
Subresource Integrity:

  1. The integrity attribute contains a hash of the expected resource.
  2. The browser fetches the resource.
  3. The browser computes the hash of the fetched resource.
  4. If the hashes match, the resource is used.
  5. If not, the resource is blocked.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Secure Link
docs.text:
1.  Author writes a link with security attributes.
    │   └── <a href="https://external.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow">
    │
    ▼
2.  Server sanitizes any user-generated links.
    │   └── Uses DOMPurify or similar.
    │
    ▼
3.  Server sets security headers.
    │   ├── Content-Security-Policy
    │   ├── Referrer-Policy
    │   ├── X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
    │   └── X-Frame-Options: DENY
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser parses the HTML.
    │   └── Validates the URL.
    │
    ▼
5.  User clicks the link.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser applies security policies.
    │   ├── Blocks javascript: URLs (CSP).
    │   ├── Blocks data: URLs (CSP).
    │   ├── Sets window.opener to null (noopener).
    │   └── Omits Referer (noreferrer).
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser navigates to the URL.
    │
    ▼
8.  New page loads securely.
    │
    ▼
9.  User is protected from tabnabbing, referrer leakage, and XSS.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Link Audit
docs.text:
1.  Collect all links on the site.
    │   └── Use a crawler like Screaming Frog.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check for security issues:
    │   ├── target="_blank" without rel="noopener".
    │   ├── External links without rel="noopener noreferrer".
    │   ├── User-generated links without rel="nofollow ugc".
    │   ├── javascript: URLs.
    │   ├── data: URLs.
    │   ├── Open redirects.
    │   ├── Misleading link text.
    │   └── Malware downloads.
    │
    ▼
3.  Remediate issues.
    │   └── Add missing rel attributes, sanitize URLs, etc.
    │
    ▼
4.  Re-audit to confirm.
    │
    ▼
5.  Monitor continuously.

docs.title: Example 1: Insecure External Link (Tabnabbing Risk)
docs.text:
<a href="https://external.com" target="_blank">External</a>

Problems: - No rel="noopener" — tabnabbing risk. - No rel="noreferrer" — referrer leakage. - No rel="nofollow" — SEO spam risk (if user-generated).

Secure version: 

<a href="https://external.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow">
    External
</a>

docs.title: Example 2: XSS via javascript: URL
docs.text:
<!-- User input: javascript:alert(document.cookie) -->
<a href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">Click me</a>

Problem: Executes JavaScript in the user's browser.

Secure version: 

<!-- Sanitize the URL first -->
<a href="https://safe-site.com">Click me</a>

docs.title: Example 3: Referrer Leakage
docs.text:
<!-- Current URL: https://example.com/admin/secret-page?token=abc123 -->
<a href="https://external.com">External</a>

Problem: The external site receives the full URL (including token) in the Referer header.

Secure version: 

<a href="https://external.com" rel="noreferrer">External</a>

Or set a global Referrer-Policy: 

Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

docs.title: Example 4: SEO Spam in Comments
docs.text:
<!-- User comment -->
<div class="comment">
    <p>Great article! Check out <a href="https://spammy-site.com">my site</a>.</p>
</div>

Problem: The link passes SEO authority to the spammy site.

Secure version: 

<div class="comment">
    <p>Great article! Check out <a href="https://spammy-site.com" rel="nofollow ugc">my site</a>.</p>
</div>

docs.title: Example 5: Misleading Link Text
docs.text:
<a href="https://evil.com">https://trusted-bank.com</a>

Problem: The visible text says trusted-bank.com but the link goes to evil.com.

Secure version: 

<a href="https://trusted-bank.com">https://trusted-bank.com</a>
Or, for external links: 
<a href="https://evil.com" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow">
    https://evil.com
</a>

docs.title: Example 6: Open Redirect
docs.text:
<a href="https://trusted.com/redirect?url=https://evil.com">Click me</a>

Problem: The user sees trusted.com but ends up at evil.com.

Secure version: Validate redirect URLs on the server: 

// Server-side: only allow same-origin redirects
const allowedOrigins = ['https://trusted.com'];
const url = req.query.url;
if (isAllowedOrigin(url)) {
    res.redirect(url);
} else {
    res.status(400).send('Invalid redirect URL');
}

docs.title: Example 7: Malware Download
docs.text:
<a href="virus.exe" download="invoice.pdf">Download Invoice</a>

Problem: The file is malware disguised as a PDF.

Secure version: - Scan uploaded files for malware. - Set Content-Disposition: attachment and Content-Type on the server. - Set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. - Warn users before downloading.

docs.title: Example 8: ping Tracking
docs.text:
<a href="https://example.com" ping="https://tracker.com/log">Click me</a>

Problem: The ping attribute sends a POST request to the tracker when clicked.

Secure version: Remove ping unless necessary, and inform users.

docs.title: Example 9: data: URL XSS
docs.text:
<a href="data:text/html,<script>alert('XSS')</script>">Click me</a>

Problem: Executes JavaScript in the user's browser.

Secure version: Block data: URLs via CSP: 

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'

docs.title: Example 10: Homograph Attack
docs.text:
<a href="https://аpple.com">https://apple.com</a>

Problem: The href uses a Cyrillic а instead of Latin a. The visible text looks like apple.com.

Secure version: Always verify the actual URL, not just the visible text.

docs.title: Example 11: Secure External Link Component
docs.text:
<!-- Component: SecureExternalLink -->
<a
    href="https://external.com"
    target="_blank"
    rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow"
    referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
>
    External Link
    <span class="visually-hidden">(opens in a new tab)</span>
    <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span>
</a>

docs.title: Example 12: Sanitizing User-Generated Links (Node.js)
docs.text:
const DOMPurify = require('dompurify');
const { JSDOM } = require('jsdom');
const window = new JSDOM('').window;
const purify = DOMPurify(window);

function sanitizeUserHtml(html) {
    return purify.sanitize(html, {
        ALLOWED_TAGS: ['a', 'b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'p', 'br'],
        ALLOWED_ATTR: ['href', 'title'],
        ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP: /^(?:(?:https?|mailto|tel):|[^a-z]|[a-z+.\-]+(?:[^a-z+.\-:]|$))/i
    });
}

docs.title: Example 13: Sanitizing URLs (JavaScript)
docs.text:
function sanitizeUrl(url) {
    try {
        const parsed = new URL(url, window.location.origin);
        const allowedProtocols = ['http:', 'https:', 'mailto:', 'tel:'];
        if (!allowedProtocols.includes(parsed.protocol)) {
            return '#';
        }
        return parsed.href;
    } catch {
        return '#';
    }
}

docs.title: Example 14: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    script-src 'self';
    style-src 'self';
    img-src 'self' https:;
    object-src 'none';
    base-uri 'self';
    form-action 'self';
    frame-ancestors 'none';
    navigate-to 'self';

docs.title: Example 15: Referrer-Policy Header
docs.text:
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

This sends the full URL for same-origin requests and only the origin for cross-origin requests (over HTTPS).

docs.title: Example 16: Subresource Integrity
docs.text:
<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"
        integrity="sha384-abc123..."
        crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

docs.title: Example 17: X-Content-Type-Options
docs.text:
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

Prevents MIME sniffing, which can lead to XSS if a file is misinterpreted as HTML.

docs.title: Example 18: X-Frame-Options
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options: DENY

Prevents the page from being embedded in an iframe, which can prevent clickjacking.

docs.title: Example 19: Link Auditing Script
docs.text:
// Audit all links on the page for security issues
document.querySelectorAll('a').forEach(link => {
    const issues = [];
    if (link.target === '_blank' && !link.rel.includes('noopener')) {
        issues.push('Missing rel="noopener"');
    }
    if (link.href.startsWith('javascript:')) {
        issues.push('javascript: URL');
    }
    if (link.href.startsWith('data:')) {
        issues.push('data: URL');
    }
    if (link.hostname !== window.location.hostname && !link.rel.includes('noopener')) {
        issues.push('External link without noopener');
    }
    if (issues.length > 0) {
        console.warn('Link issues:', link.href, issues);
    }
});

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Secure Link Module
docs.text:
<!-- SecureLink component -->
<template id="secure-link-template">
    <a part="link">
        <slot></slot>
        <span class="visually-hidden">(opens in a new tab)</span>
        <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span>
    </a>
</template>

<script>
class SecureLink extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        const template = document.getElementById('secure-link-template');
        const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
        const link = clone.querySelector('a');

        const href = this.getAttribute('href');
        const external = this.hasAttribute('external');

        link.href = sanitizeUrl(href);

        if (external) {
            link.target = '_blank';
            link.rel = 'noopener noreferrer nofollow';
            link.referrerPolicy = 'no-referrer';
        }

        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).appendChild(clone);
    }
}

customElements.define('secure-link', SecureLink);
</script>

<!-- Usage -->
<secure-link href="https://external.com" external>
    Visit External Site
</secure-link>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Threat Defence External links Tabnabbing, referrer leakage rel="noopener noreferrer" User-generated links XSS, SEO spam Sanitization, rel="nofollow ugc" Paid links SEO manipulation rel="sponsored" Downloads Malware Content-Disposition, nosniff Open redirects Phishing URL validation javascript: URLs XSS CSP, sanitization data: URLs XSS CSP, sanitization Referrer leakage Data exposure Referrer-Policy, rel="noreferrer" Homograph attacks Phishing Punycode, user education Misleading link text Phishing Verify URLs, warn users ping tracking Privacy Remove ping, inform users External scripts Compromise SRI Iframes Clickjacking X-Frame-Options, CSP

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use rel="noopener noreferrer" with target="_blank" – prevents tabnabbing and referrer leakage.

  2. Use rel="nofollow" for untrusted links – prevents SEO spam.

  3. Use rel="sponsored" for paid links – complies with search engine guidelines.

  4. Use rel="ugc" for user-generated content – tells search engines it's user-submitted.

  5. Sanitize all user-generated URLs – use a well-tested library like DOMPurify.

  6. Validate URL schemes – allow only http:, https:, mailto:, tel:.

  7. Block javascript: and data: URLs – via CSP and sanitization.

  8. Set a Content Security Policy – restrict scripts, styles, frames, and navigation.

  9. Set a Referrer-Policy – use strict-origin-when-cross-origin.

  10. Set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff – prevents MIME sniffing.

  11. Set X-Frame-Options: DENY – prevents clickjacking.

  12. Use SRI for external scripts and styles – verifies integrity.

  13. Warn users about external links – with an icon or text.

  14. Avoid URL shorteners for sensitive links – they hide the destination.

  15. Avoid ping unless necessary – and inform users.

  16. Regularly audit links – use automated tools.

  17. Educate users – about phishing and verifying URLs.

  18. Test with security tools – OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, etc.

  19. Keep dependencies updated – sanitization libraries, CSP, etc.

  20. Document your link security policy – for maintainability.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: target="_blank" Without rel="noopener"
docs.text:
<a href="https://external.com" target="_blank">External</a>
Why it's wrong: Tabnabbing risk — the new page can redirect the original.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="https://external.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">External</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Inserting User Input Directly into href
docs.text:
<a href="<?php echo $_GET['url']; ?>">Click me</a>
Why it's wrong: XSS via javascript: or data: URLs.

✅ Correct: Sanitize and validate the URL before output: 

<?php
$url = $_GET['url'] ?? '';
if (filter_var($url, FILTER_VALIDATE_URL) && in_array(parse_url($url, PHP_URL_SCHEME), ['http', 'https'])) {
    echo '<a href="' . htmlspecialchars($url, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') . '" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow">Click me</a>';
}
?>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting rel="noreferrer"
docs.text:
<a href="https://external.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">External</a>
Why it's wrong: The referrer header is still sent, leaking the current URL.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="https://external.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">External</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using rel="nofollow" for All External Links
docs.text:
<a href="https://trusted-partner.com" rel="nofollow">Partner</a>
Why it's wrong: nofollow should be used for untrusted or paid links, not trusted partners.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="https://trusted-partner.com">Partner</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on title for URL Display
docs.text:
<a href="https://evil.com" title="https://trusted.com">Click me</a>
Why it's wrong: The title is not displayed on mobile, and users may not hover.

✅ Correct: Ensure the visible link text matches the destination, or warn users.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Validating Redirect URLs
docs.text:
app.get('/redirect', (req, res) => {
    res.redirect(req.query.url); // Open redirect!
});
Why it's wrong: Attackers can use your site to redirect to malicious sites.

✅ Correct: 

app.get('/redirect', (req, res) => {
    const url = req.query.url;
    if (isAllowedUrl(url)) {
        res.redirect(url);
    } else {
        res.status(400).send('Invalid URL');
    }
});

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No CSP
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>My Site</title>
</head>
Why it's wrong: No protection against XSS via javascript: URLs or injected scripts.

✅ Correct: 

<head>
    <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'">
    <title>My Site</title>
</head>
Or via HTTP header: 
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Referrer-Policy
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>My Site</title>
</head>
Why it's wrong: The full URL is sent in the Referer header to external sites.

✅ Correct: 

Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using data: URLs for Downloads
docs.text:
<a href="data:application/octet-stream;base64,..." download="file.exe">Download</a>
Why it's wrong: data: URLs can be used for XSS and are blocked by CSP.

✅ Correct: Serve the file from the server with proper headers.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Warning Users About External Links
docs.text:
<a href="https://external.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">External</a>
Why it's wrong: Users may be surprised by the new tab.

✅ Correct: 

<a href="https://external.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">
    External <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span>
    <span class="visually-hidden">(opens in a new tab)</span>
</a>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• noopener – negligible performance impact.
  • noreferrer – negligible performance impact.
  • nofollow – no performance impact (search engine hint).
  • CSP – negligible performance impact; may block resources.
  • SRI – adds a small overhead for hash verification.
  • Sanitization – server-side sanitization has a cost; use efficient libraries.
  • ping – adds a POST request on click; small overhead.
  • URL validation – negligible performance impact.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use efficient sanitization libraries – DOMPurify is fast.
  2. Cache sanitized content – avoid re-sanitizing on every request.
  3. Use CSP reports – monitor violations without blocking.
  4. Use SRI only for critical resources – it adds overhead.
  5. Minimize ping usage – it adds a network request.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations (Meta)
docs.text: This entire chapter is about security, but here is a consolidated checklist:

docs.title: For Every Link
docs.text:
• [ ] Is the href validated and sanitized?
  • [ ] Is the URL scheme allowed (http, https, mailto, tel)?
  • [ ] Is target="_blank" accompanied by rel="noopener noreferrer"?
  • [ ] Is rel="nofollow" used for untrusted links?
  • [ ] Is rel="sponsored" used for paid links?
  • [ ] Is rel="ugc" used for user-generated content?
  • [ ] Is the visible link text accurate?
  • [ ] Is there a warning for external links or new tabs?
  • [ ] Is the download filename safe?
  • [ ] Is the ping attribute necessary?

docs.title: For the Page
docs.text:
• [ ] Is a Content Security Policy set?
  • [ ] Is a Referrer-Policy set?
  • [ ] Is X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff set?
  • [ ] Is X-Frame-Options: DENY set?
  • [ ] Is SRI used for external scripts and styles?
  • [ ] Is user-generated content sanitized?
  • [ ] Are open redirects prevented?
  • [ ] Is the server configured to prevent MIME sniffing?

docs.title: For the Application
docs.text:
• [ ] Are dependencies up to date?
  • [ ] Are security headers tested?
  • [ ] Are links audited regularly?
  • [ ] Are users educated about phishing?
  • [ ] Is there an incident response plan?

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect links for rel, target, and href.
  • DevTools Network panel – check the Referer header in requests.
  • DevTools Console – use document.querySelectorAll('a') to audit links.
  • Check window.opener – in the new tab, verify it's null.
  • Check CSP violations – in the Console, look for CSP errors.
  • Check Referrer-Policy – in the Network panel, verify the Referer header.
  • Use OWASP ZAP – automated security scanning.
  • Use Burp Suite – manual security testing.
  • Use Lighthouse – audits for security best practices.
  • Use Security Headers – online tool to check headers.
  • Use SRI Hash Generator – generate integrity hashes.
  • Use DOMPurify – test sanitization in the browser.
  • Use npm audit – check for vulnerable dependencies.

docs.title: 16. When to Use (Security Measures)
docs.text:
• rel="noopener noreferrer" – always with target="_blank".
  • rel="nofollow" – for untrusted or user-generated links.
  • rel="sponsored" – for paid links.
  • rel="ugc" – for user-generated content.
  • CSP – on every page.
  • Referrer-Policy – on every page.
  • SRI – for external scripts and styles.
  • Sanitization – for all user input.
  • URL validation – for all dynamic URLs.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use (Security Measures)
docs.text:
• rel="nofollow" – for trusted internal or partner links.
  • rel="noopener" – for same-tab links (not needed).
  • target="_blank" – for internal links (avoid new tabs).
  • ping – unless you have a legitimate use case and inform users.
  • data: URLs – for large files or user-generated content.
  • javascript: URLs – never.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Content Security Policy (CSP) – HTTP header for restricting resources.
  • Referrer-Policy – HTTP header for controlling referrer.
  • Subresource Integrity (SRI) – verifies external resources.
  • X-Content-Type-Options – prevents MIME sniffing.
  • X-Frame-Options – prevents clickjacking.
  • Tabnabbing – a specific attack.
  • Reverse tabnabbing – a specific form of tabnabbing.
  • Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) – a class of attacks.
  • Phishing – social engineering attack.
  • Open redirect – a vulnerability.
  • Homograph attack – a phishing technique.
  • Punycode – encoding for internationalized domains.
  • DOMPurify – a sanitization library.
  • OWASP – Open Web Application Security Project.
  • Sanitization – cleaning user input.
  • URL validation – verifying URLs.
  • rel attribute – relationship to the destination.
  • target attribute – browsing context.
  • href attribute – the URL.
  • download attribute – downloads the file.
  • ping attribute – tracking on click.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Tabnabbing was first described by Aza Raskin in 2010. It remained a widespread vulnerability for years because browsers didn't default to noopener until 2020–2021.

  • Modern browsers (Chrome 88+, Firefox 79+, Safari 12.1+, Edge 88+) default to noopener for target="_blank", even without the rel attribute.

  • rel="noreferrer" implies noopener — you don't need both, but it's common to see rel="noopener noreferrer".

  • rel="nofollow" was introduced by Google in 2005 to combat comment spam. It was later joined by rel="sponsored" and rel="ugc" in 2019.

  • CSP can block javascript: URLs with the script-src directive.

  • CSP can block data: URLs with the default-src directive.

  • Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin is the modern default in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge. It sends the full URL for same-origin requests and only the origin for cross-origin requests.

  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff prevents browsers from MIME-sniffing, which can prevent XSS if a file is misinterpreted.

  • X-Frame-Options: DENY prevents the page from being embedded in an iframe, preventing clickjacking.

  • SRI (Subresource Integrity) was introduced in 2016 to verify the integrity of external resources.

  • DOMPurify is the most widely used sanitization library for JavaScript. It's fast and well-tested.

  • Open redirects are a common vulnerability in login and logout flows. Always validate redirect URLs.

  • Homograph attacks use visually similar characters from different scripts (e.g., Cyrillic а vs Latin a). Browsers display punycode for mixed-script domains.

  • ping is supported in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, but not Safari. It sends a POST request when a link is clicked.

  • navigate-to is an experimental CSP directive that restricts navigation. It is not widely supported yet.

  • Security headers (CSP, Referrer-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options) can be set via HTTP headers or <meta> tags (though HTTP headers are preferred).

  • OWASP ZAP and Burp Suite are popular tools for security testing.

  • Lighthouse includes a "Best Practices" audit that checks for some link security issues.

  • Security Headers (securityheaders.com) is an online tool to check your HTTP security headers.

  • The rel attribute is a hint to search engines and browsers; its enforcement depends on the consumer.

  • Link auditing should be part of every security review. Automated tools can catch many issues.

  • User education is a critical defence against phishing. No amount of technical protection can prevent a user from clicking a malicious link.

  • Defence in depth is the key principle: use multiple layers of protection (validation, sanitization, CSP, rel attributes, user education).

  • Link security is everyone's responsibility — developers, designers, content authors, and users.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Link security encompasses the threats and defences related to hyperlinks in HTML.
  • Major threats: phishing, tabnabbing, XSS, referrer leakage, SEO spam, malware downloads, open redirects, javascript: URLs, data: URLs, homograph attacks, misleading link text, ping tracking.
  • Key defences:
  • rel="noopener noreferrer" with target="_blank" — prevents tabnabbing and referrer leakage.
  • rel="nofollow" / rel="sponsored" / rel="ugc" — prevents SEO spam.
  • Sanitization — prevents XSS via javascript: and data: URLs.
  • URL validation — allows only safe schemes.
  • CSP — restricts scripts, styles, frames, and navigation.
  • Referrer-Policy — controls referrer leakage.
  • SRI — verifies external resources.
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — prevents MIME sniffing.
  • X-Frame-Options: DENY — prevents clickjacking.
  • Best practices: always use rel="noopener noreferrer" with target="_blank", sanitize user input, set security headers, validate redirects, warn users about external links, and regularly audit links.
  • Common mistakes: target="_blank" without rel="noopener", inserting user input directly into href, no CSP, no Referrer-Policy, open redirects, and misleading link text.
  • Defence in depth is essential — no single measure is sufficient.
  • Link security is a continuous process — audit regularly, update dependencies, and educate users.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An ordered list is a semantic HTML structure that represents a sequence of related items in which order matters. It is created using the <ol> element, with each item in the list wrapped in an <li> (list item) element. By default, browsers display ordered lists with sequential numbering (1, 2, 3, …), but the numbering style, starting point, and direction can all be customised.

Ordered lists communicate meaning beyond mere enumeration — they imply priority, sequence, ranking, or progression. Examples include step-by-step instructions, ranked results, legal clauses, recipe directions, and priority queues.

Example: 

<ol>
    <li>Preheat the oven to 180°C.</li>
    <li>Mix the flour and sugar.</li>
    <li>Bake for 25 minutes.</li>
</ol>

Rendered: 1. Preheat the oven to 180°C. 2. Mix the flour and sugar. 3. Bake for 25 minutes.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <ol> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Sequence – conveys that the items follow a specific order.
  • Ranking – represents priority (e.g., "Top 10 movies of 2026").
  • Instructions – provides step-by-step directions.
  • Navigation – represents numbered navigation or breadcrumbs.
  • Legal and technical documents – numbered clauses and sections.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce the list and its item count.
  • SEO – search engines understand the structure and can surface list-based rich results.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <ol> element is flow content and palpable content. It is a block-level element and can appear anywhere flow content is accepted — inside <body>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <div>, <nav>, <li> (nested lists), and <figure>. It is one of the three list types in HTML, alongside <ul> (unordered) and <dl> (description).

<article>
    <h2>How to Make Tea</h2>
    <ol>
        <li>Boil water.</li>
        <li>Add tea leaves.</li>
        <li>Steep for 3 minutes.</li>
        <li>Strain and serve.</li>
    </ol>
</article>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
In plain text, lists have no inherent structure. If you write:

1. Boil water
2. Add tea leaves
3. Steep for 3 minutes

a machine cannot reliably distinguish this from any other text containing numbers. There is no semantic marker that says "these lines form a list" or "this list is ordered". This matters for:

  • Accessibility – screen readers can't announce the list or its length.
  • SEO – search engines can't understand the structure.
  • Styling – CSS can't target list items.
  • Maintainability – if items are reordered, the numbers become wrong.
  • Machine readability – APIs can't extract the list as structured data.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic list Machines can't identify lists. Manual numbering Adding/removing items breaks the numbering. Poor accessibility Screen readers can't announce item count. No styling hooks CSS can't target list items. No structure in APIs Data extraction is unreliable. Limited extensibility Can't change numbering style without manual edits.

docs.title: Why the <ol> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <ol> element was part of the original HTML specification (HTML 1.0, 1991) by Tim Berners-Lee. It was designed to represent numbered lists in technical documents, legal contracts, and scientific papers — content types where order and numbering are essential.

It enables:

  • Automatic numbering – the browser generates numbers, so adding/removing items doesn't break the list.
  • Semantic structure – machines know the content is an ordered list.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce "list of N items" and read items as "item 1 of N".
  • Styling – CSS can target the list and its items.
  • Flexibility – numbering style, starting point, and direction can be customised.
  • Nesting – lists can be nested to represent hierarchies.

The <ol> element is one of the oldest and most useful HTML elements. It is a foundational building block for structured content on the web.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <ol>
docs.text:
<ol>
    <li>First item</li>
    <li>Second item</li>
    <li>Third item</li>
</ol>

Rendered: 1. First item 2. Second item 3. Third item

docs.title: The <li> Element
docs.text:
Each item in an ordered list is wrapped in an <li> (list item) element. The <li> element is flow content but can only appear as a child of <ol>, <ul>, or <menu>.

<ol>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ol>

docs.title: Changing the Numbering Style (type)
docs.text:
The type attribute changes the numbering style:

Value Style Example 1 Decimal numbers (default) 1, 2, 3 a Lowercase letters a, b, c A Uppercase letters A, B, C i Lowercase Roman numerals i, ii, iii I Uppercase Roman numerals I, II, III 
<ol type="a">
    <li>First item</li>
    <li>Second item</li>
</ol>

Rendered: a. First item b. Second item

docs.title: Starting the List at a Different Number (start)
docs.text:
The start attribute sets the starting number:

<ol start="5">
    <li>Item 5</li>
    <li>Item 6</li>
</ol>

Rendered: 5. Item 5 6. Item 6

Note: The start attribute works with all type values. For type="a", start="5" starts at "e".

docs.title: Reversing the Order (reversed)
docs.text:
The reversed boolean attribute reverses the order of the numbering:

<ol reversed>
    <li>Third item</li>
    <li>Second item</li>
    <li>First item</li>
</ol>

Rendered: 3. Third item 2. Second item 1. First item

Use case: Countdowns, "Top 10" lists presented in ascending order.

docs.title: Setting the Value of an Individual Item (value)
docs.text:
The value attribute on <li> sets the number for that item:

<ol>
    <li>First item</li>
    <li value="5">Fifth item</li>
    <li>Sixth item</li>
</ol>

Rendered: 1. First item 5. Fifth item 6. Sixth item

Use case: Skipping numbers, restarting numbering mid-list.

docs.title: Nested Ordered Lists
docs.text:
<ol>
    <li>Step 1
        <ol>
            <li>Sub-step 1a</li>
            <li>Sub-step 1b</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
    <li>Step 2</li>
</ol>

Rendered: 1. Step 1 1. Sub-step 1a 2. Sub-step 1b 2. Step 2

Note: Nested lists should be placed inside the <li> element, not between <li> elements.

docs.title: Mixed Lists (Ordered and Unordered)
docs.text:
<ol>
    <li>Prepare the ingredients:
        <ul>
            <li>Flour</li>
            <li>Sugar</li>
            <li>Eggs</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Mix them together.</li>
</ol>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <ol> Defines the ordered list. Creates a numbered list. <li> Defines a list item. Each item is a separate entry. type Changes the numbering style. Decimal, letters, Roman numerals. start Sets the starting number. Useful for continuing lists. reversed Reverses the numbering. Countdowns and top-N lists. value Sets an item's number. Overrides the sequence.

docs.title: The "Numbered Recipe" Analogy
docs.text: Think of an ordered list as a recipe. The steps must be followed in order — you can't bake before mixing. The numbers tell you the sequence. If you add a step in the middle, the numbers automatically adjust.

docs.title: The "Ranking" Analogy
docs.text: An ordered list is like a ranking — "1st place, 2nd place, 3rd place". The order carries meaning: 1st is more important than 2nd. This is why ordered lists are used for "Top 10" lists, leaderboards, and priority queues.

docs.title: The "Numbered Outline" Analogy
docs.text: Think of an ordered list as an outline in a document. Numbered sections (1, 1.1, 1.2, 2, 2.1) create a hierarchy. HTML doesn't automatically number nested lists with dotted notation (1.1), but the structure mirrors it.

docs.title: The "Queue" Analogy
docs.text: An ordered list is like a queue — items are processed in order. First in, first out. The order is the point.

docs.title: Concept 1: <ol> vs <ul>
docs.text:
Aspect <ol> (Ordered) <ul> (Unordered) Meaning Order matters Order doesn't matter Default marker Numbers (1, 2, 3) Bullets (•) Use case Instructions, rankings Features, categories Semantic weight Sequence Enumeration

Rule: Use <ol> when the order of items matters (e.g., instructions, rankings). Use <ul> when it doesn't (e.g., lists of features, categories).

docs.title: Concept 2: The <li> Element
docs.text:
The <li> element is the only valid child of <ol> (and <ul>, <menu>). It can contain flow content — text, inline elements, other lists, images, forms, and even block-level elements.

<ol>
    <li>
        <h3>Step 1</h3>
        <p>Detailed explanation of step 1.</p>
    </li>
    <li>
        <h3>Step 2</h3>
        <p>Detailed explanation of step 2.</p>
    </li>
</ol>

docs.title: Concept 3: The type Attribute
docs.text:
The type attribute changes the numbering style. It is presentational (it changes appearance), but it's also semantic (it hints at the kind of numbering: numeric, alphabetic, or Roman).

Value Description 1 Decimal numbers (default). a Lowercase Latin alphabet. A Uppercase Latin alphabet. i Lowercase Roman numerals. I Uppercase Roman numerals.

Note: The type attribute is deprecated in HTML4 but valid in HTML5. However, for full control over numbering, use CSS list-style-type.

docs.title: Concept 4: The start Attribute
docs.text:
The start attribute specifies the starting number of the list. It accepts an integer.

<ol start="3">
    <li>Item 3</li>
    <li>Item 4</li>
</ol>

Note: The start attribute affects the numbering, not the content. The first item is always "Item 3" in the example above — but its number is 3.

docs.title: Concept 5: The reversed Attribute
docs.text:
The reversed boolean attribute reverses the numbering:

<ol reversed>
    <li>Third</li>
    <li>Second</li>
    <li>First</li>
</ol>

Rendered: 3. Third 2. Second 1. First

Use case: Countdowns, "Top 10" lists.

docs.title: Concept 6: The value Attribute
docs.text:
The value attribute on <li> sets the number for that item and all subsequent items (unless overridden).

<ol>
    <li>First</li>
    <li value="5">Fifth</li>
    <li>Sixth</li>
</ol>

Rendered: 1. First 5. Fifth 6. Sixth

docs.title: Concept 7: Nested Lists
docs.text:
Lists can be nested inside <li> elements. The nested list gets its own numbering sequence (starting from 1 by default).

<ol>
    <li>Chapter 1
        <ol>
            <li>Section 1.1</li>
            <li>Section 1.2</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
    <li>Chapter 2</li>
</ol>

Best practice: Place the nested list inside the <li> element it belongs to, not between <li> elements.

docs.title: Concept 8: Styling with CSS
docs.text:
The <ol> and <li> elements can be styled with CSS:

ol {
    list-style-type: decimal; /* Default */
    padding-left: 1.5rem;
    margin-bottom: 1rem;
}

li {
    margin-bottom: 0.5rem;
}

li::marker {
    color: #3498db;
    font-weight: bold;
}

docs.title: Concept 9: list-style-type in CSS
docs.text:
The CSS list-style-type property overrides the type attribute:

ol {
    list-style-type: upper-roman;
}
Value Description decimal 1, 2, 3 (default) decimal-leading-zero 01, 02, 03 lower-alpha a, b, c upper-alpha A, B, C lower-roman i, ii, iii upper-roman I, II, III lower-greek α, β, γ none No marker

docs.title: Concept 10: list-style-position
docs.text:
ol {
    list-style-position: inside; /* Marker inside the content box */
}
  • outside (default) – the marker is outside the content box.
  • inside – the marker is part of the content, affecting text wrapping.

docs.title: Concept 11: The ::marker Pseudo-Element
docs.text:
The ::marker pseudo-element styles the list marker (the number):

li::marker {
    color: #e74c3c;
    font-size: 1.2em;
    font-weight: bold;
}

Note: Not all CSS properties apply to ::marker. color, font-*, content, and animation are supported.

docs.title: Concept 12: Accessibility
docs.text:
Screen readers announce ordered lists as:

  • "List of N items" (the count).
  • "Item 1 of N", "Item 2 of N", etc.

This helps users understand the structure and their position in the list.

Best practice: Use <ol> only when the order matters; using it for unordered content is misleading.

docs.title: Concept 13: SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use ordered lists to understand sequence and priority:

  • "Top 10" lists may appear in featured snippets.
  • Step-by-step instructions may appear in "HowTo" rich results.
  • FAQ lists may appear in "FAQ" rich results.

Best practice: Use <ol> for instructions, rankings, and sequences; combine with structured data for richer results.

docs.title: Concept 14: The <menu> Element
docs.text: The <menu> element is a semantic alternative to <ul> for toolbars and context menus. It is not for numbered lists. Use <ol> for ordered lists.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <ol>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters an `<ol>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the ordered list.
    │   └── The `type`, `start`, and `reversed` attributes are read.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes each `<li>` child:
    │   ├── Creates a list item node.
    │   ├── Assigns a number based on `start`, `value`, and position.
    │   └── Recursively processes nested lists.
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the list is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   ├── display: block
    │   ├── padding-inline-start: 40px
    │   ├── list-style-type: decimal
    │   └── list-style-position: outside
    │
    ▼
6.  The list is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   └── role: list, items: listitem
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered with the list.

docs.title: The Numbering Algorithm
docs.text:
The browser assigns numbers to <li> elements as follows:

  1. Start with the value of start (default 1).
  2. If reversed is present, count down instead of up.
  3. For each <li>:
  4. If value is set, use it as the current number.
  5. Otherwise, use the current number.
  6. Increment (or decrement) the current number for the next item.
  7. Nested lists start their own count.

docs.title: CSS list-style-type
docs.text:
The CSS list-style-type property controls the marker style. It overrides the type attribute.

ol {
    list-style-type: upper-roman;
}

docs.title: The ::marker Pseudo-Element
docs.text:
The marker (number or bullet) is rendered as a ::marker pseudo-element. It can be styled:

li::marker {
    color: red;
}

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, <ol> is exposed as a list with a listitem for each <li>. The list items are numbered based on the type, start, reversed, and value attributes.

Screen readers may announce: - "List of 3 items" - "Item 1 of 3" - The text content of each item.

docs.title: The HTMLOListElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <ol> is represented by the HTMLOListElement interface, which inherits from HTMLElement. It has the following properties:

Property Type Description type String Reflects the type attribute. start Number Reflects the start attribute. reversed Boolean Reflects the reversed attribute. compact Boolean Obsolete (was used in HTML4). 
const ol = document.querySelector('ol');
console.log(ol.type);     // "1", "a", "A", "i", "I"
console.log(ol.start);    // 1
console.log(ol.reversed); // false

docs.text:

Property Type Description value Number Reflects the value attribute.

console.log(li.value); // 1, 2, 3, etc.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
ol {
    display: block;
    list-style-type: decimal;
    margin-block-start: 1em;

docs.title: The list-style-type Property
docs.text: The list-style-type CSS property determines the marker. It is a longhand for list-style.

docs.title: The ::marker Pseudo-Element
docs.text: The marker is rendered as a ::marker pseudo-element. It is a child of the <li> element but not part of the DOM tree — it's a generated content box.

docs.title: Accessibility Mapping
docs.text:
The browser's accessibility engine maps:

  • <ol> → role: list
  • <li> → role: listitem
  • The type, start, reversed, and value attributes affect the numbering exposed to assistive technologies.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an Ordered List
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<ol>` and `<li>` elements.
    │   └── <ol><li>Item 1</li><li>Item 2</li></ol>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<ol>` and `<li>` nodes are created.
    │
    ▼
4.  The browser assigns numbers to each `<li>`.
    │   └── Based on start, reversed, value, and position.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied.
    │   └── list-style-type: decimal, padding, margins.
    │
    ▼
6.  The list is rendered with markers.
    │
    ▼
7.  The accessibility tree is built.
    │   └── role: list, items: listitem.
    │
    ▼
8.  Screen readers announce the list.
    │   └── "List of N items", "Item 1 of N", etc.
    │
    ▼
9.  Search engines may use the list for rich results.
    │
    ▼
10. JavaScript may modify the list dynamically.
    │   └── Adding/removing items, changing attributes.
    │
    ▼
11. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
// Add a new list item
const ol = document.querySelector('ol');
const newLi = document.createElement('li');
newLi.textContent = 'New item';
ol.appendChild(newLi);

// Change the starting number
ol.start = 10;

// Reverse the list
ol.reversed = true;

// Change an item's value
const li = document.querySelector('li');
li.value = 5;
