docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Glossary Term and definition FAQ Question and answer Product specs Property and value Metadata Key and value Documentation Parameter and description Dictionary Word and meaning Contact info Label and detail Statistics Label and number Timeline Date and event Configuration Option and description Translations Word and translation Testimonials Name and quote Key–value data Key and value Event details Attribute and value

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <dl> for term–description pairs – not for general lists.

  2. Use <dt> for the term and <dd> for the description – don't reverse them.

  3. Keep <dt> and <dd> as siblings – both are direct children of <dl>.

  4. Use <dd> for flow content – it can contain paragraphs, lists, and other block elements.

  5. Use <dt> for phrasing content – it should be short (a term or question).

  6. Use <div> wrappers – for styling grids and flexbox layouts.

  7. Style with CSS – don't rely on default indentation.

  8. Use <dl> for FAQ – with structured data for rich results.

  9. Use <dl> for metadata – e.g., author, published date, category.

  10. Test with screen readers – ensure the term–description relationship is announced.

  11. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting.

  12. Don't use <dl> for layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

  13. Keep terms concise – a word or short phrase.

  14. Keep descriptions readable – one or more sentences.

  15. Use <dl> for key–value data – it's semantically appropriate.

  16. Consider <dl> for statistics – with custom CSS for big numbers.

  17. Use <dl> for configuration options – with <code> for option names.

  18. Combine with structured data – for FAQ, Product, and other rich results.

  19. Test on mobile – ensure the grid layout works on small screens.

  20. Document your conventions – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting <dd> Inside <dt>
docs.text:
<dl>
    <dt>HTML
        <dd>HyperText Markup Language</dd>
    </dt>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: <dt> and <dd> must be siblings, not nested.

✅ Correct: 

<dl>
    <dt>HTML</dt>
    <dd>HyperText Markup Language</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <ul> for Term–Description Pairs
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li><strong>HTML</strong> — HyperText Markup Language</li>
    <li><strong>CSS</strong> — Cascading Style Sheets</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: <ul> is for grouped items, not term–description pairs. Use <dl>.

✅ Correct: 

<dl>
    <dt>HTML</dt>
    <dd>HyperText Markup Language</dd>
    <dt>CSS</dt>
    <dd>Cascading Style Sheets</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <dl> for General Lists
docs.text:
<dl>
    <dt>Item 1</dt>
    <dd>Item 2</dd>
    <dd>Item 3</dd>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: <dl> is for term–description pairs, not general lists.

✅ Correct: Use <ul> for general lists.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placing Content Directly Inside <dl>
docs.text:
<dl>
    <p>Some text</p>
    <dt>Term</dt>
    <dd>Description</dd>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: Only <dt>, <dd>, and <div> are valid children of <dl>.

✅ Correct: 

<dl>
    <dt>Term</dt>
    <dd>Some text</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <dt> for Long Descriptions
docs.text:
<dl>
    <dt>This is a very long question that should really be in the dd element because it's the content, not the term</dt>
    <dd>Answer</dd>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: <dt> is for the term (short). <dd> is for the description (can be long).

✅ Correct: 

<dl>
    <dt>Question?</dt>
    <dd>This is a very long answer that explains everything in detail.</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <dl> Without <dt> or <dd>
docs.text:
<dl>
    <div>Just a div</div>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: <div> must contain <dt> and <dd> elements.

✅ Correct: 

<dl>
    <div>
        <dt>Term</dt>
        <dd>Description</dd>
    </div>
</dl>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <dl> for Layout
docs.text:
<dl>
    <dt>Left column</dt>
    <dd>Right column</dd>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: <dl> is for term–description pairs, not layout.

✅ Correct: Use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Close <dd> Elements
docs.text:
<dl>
    <dt>Term</dt>
    <dd>Description
    <dt>Another term</dt>
    <dd>Another description</dd>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: While browsers may infer closing tags, it's better practice to close them explicitly.

✅ Correct: 

<dl>
    <dt>Term</dt>
    <dd>Description</dd>
    <dt>Another term</dt>
    <dd>Another description</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <dl> for a Single Pair
docs.text:
<dl>
    <dt>The only term</dt>
    <dd>The only description</dd>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: A single-pair <dl> is rarely meaningful. Use a <p> or a <div>.

✅ Correct: Use a <p> for single pairs.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Styling <dd> to Remove Default Indentation
docs.text:
<dl>
    <dt>Term</dt>
    <dd>Description</dd>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: The default margin-inline-start: 40px may not fit your design.

✅ Correct: 

dd {
    margin-inline-start: 0;
}

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <dl> is lightweight – one DOM node per pair, plus the container.
  • Default styles – dd has a default margin-inline-start: 40px, which can be overridden.
  • Nested content – <dd> can contain block-level content, increasing DOM size.
  • CSS Grid – using display: grid on <dl> is efficient.
  • Large lists – lists with thousands of pairs can impact rendering; consider virtualization.
  • div wrappers – add extra DOM nodes but are useful for layout.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep <dd> content concise – avoid unnecessarily long descriptions.
  2. Use CSS Grid for layout – more efficient than floats or tables.
  3. Avoid inline styles – use CSS classes.
  4. Virtualize long lists – for lists with hundreds of pairs.
  5. Minify HTML – reduce file size.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if <dt> or <dd> content contains user-generated data, sanitize it before rendering.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent or a sanitizer.
  • Injection – never insert user input directly into <dt> or <dd> without escaping.
  • No direct security implications – <dl> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into terms or descriptions.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate structure – ensure <dt> and <dd> are properly nested.
  4. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <dl>, <dt>, and <dd> elements.
  • Computed styles – check margin-inline-start on <dd> and font-weight on <dt>.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the list, term, and definition roles.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('dl dt') to list all terms.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the term–description relationship is announced.
  • Test with CSS disabled – ensure the list still makes sense.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For glossaries – terms and definitions.
  • For FAQs – questions and answers.
  • For product specs – properties and values.
  • For metadata – keys and values.
  • For documentation – parameters and descriptions.
  • For dictionaries – words and meanings.
  • For contact info – labels and details.
  • For statistics – labels and numbers.
  • For timelines – dates and events.
  • For configuration – options and descriptions.
  • For translations – words and translations.
  • For key–value data – any name–value pair.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For general lists – use <ul> or <ol>.
  • For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For single pairs – use <p> or <div>.
  • For sequenced steps – use <ol>.
  • For grouped items – use <ul>.
  • For navigation menus – use <ul>.
  • For tabular data – use <table>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <ol> – ordered list.
  • <ul> – unordered list.
  • <li> – list item.
  • <dt> – description term.
  • <dd> – description details.
  • <menu> – semantic alternative to <ul>.
  • CSS Grid – for laying out <dl>.
  • Structured data – FAQPage, Product, HowTo.
  • JSON-LD – for rich results.
  • Accessibility – list, term, definition roles.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <dl> element was introduced in HTML 3.2 (1997). It was originally called a "definition list" and only supported <dt> (definition term) and <dd> (definition description).

  • In HTML5, the <dl> element was redefined as a "description list" — it can now represent any term–description or name–value pair, not just definitions.

  • The <dt> element originally stood for "definition term" and the <dd> element for "definition description".

  • In HTML5, you can use multiple <dt> elements followed by one <dd>, or one <dt> followed by multiple <dd> elements.

  • In HTML5, you can wrap <dt>–<dd> pairs in a <div> for styling purposes. This is not valid in HTML4.

  • The <dd> element has a default margin-inline-start: 40px in most browsers, creating the indentation.

  • Screen readers announce <dl> as a description list (or "definition list" in older screen readers). The relationship between <dt> and <dd> is preserved.

  • The <dl> element is used in structured data for FAQ pages, product specifications, and other rich results.

  • Google's FAQ rich results can be triggered by marking up questions and answers with <dl> and structured data.

  • The <dl> element is often used in API documentation to document parameters and their descriptions.

  • Product spec sheets are a natural fit for <dl> — each property (<dt>) is paired with its value (<dd>).

  • Metadata blocks (author, published date, category) are often marked up with <dl> for semantics and styling.

  • Statistics (users, countries, uptime) can be marked up with <dl> and styled with CSS for a dashboard look.

  • The <dl> element is not for general lists — use <ul> or <ol>.

  • The <dl> element is not for layout — use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

  • The <dt> element should contain phrasing content (short terms), while <dd> can contain flow content (long descriptions, lists, paragraphs).

  • The <dl> element is one of the three list types in HTML, alongside <ul> and <ol>.

  • Definition lists were part of the original HTML design, inspired by the need to represent glossaries and dictionaries in technical documents.

  • The <dl> element can be styled with CSS Grid to create a two-column layout: terms on the left, descriptions on the right.

  • display: grid on <dl> with grid-template-columns: auto 1fr is a common pattern for term–description layouts.

  • The <dl> element is supported in all modern browsers and has been for decades.

  • HTML5 Doctor famously debated whether <dl> should be used for things other than definitions. The consensus: it's a "description list" and can be used for any name–value pair.

  • The <dl> element is often used in recipes to list ingredients (term: ingredient, description: quantity).

  • The <dl> element is used in timelines (term: date, description: event).

  • The <dl> element is used in translation tables (term: word, description: translation).

  • Microdata and JSON-LD can be combined with <dl> for rich results.

  • The <dl> element is a small but powerful part of HTML's semantic vocabulary.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A description list (<dl>) represents a list of term–description pairs.
  • It is created with <dl>, <dt> (term), and <dd> (description) elements.
  • <dt> and <dd> must be siblings — direct children of <dl>.
  • You can have multiple terms, one description, or one term, multiple descriptions.
  • <div> wrappers can group pairs for styling.
  • The default styles are: <dt> bold, <dd> indented.
  • CSS Grid is commonly used to lay out <dl> as a two-column table.
  • Best practices: use <dl> for term–description pairs, use <dt> for short terms, use <dd> for descriptions, style with CSS, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include nesting <dd> inside <dt>, using <ul> for term–description pairs, using <dl> for general lists, and forgetting to close <dd> elements.
  • The <dl> element is essential for glossaries, FAQs, product specs, metadata, documentation, and any key–value data.
  • It is one of the three list types in HTML and a fundamental part of semantic markup.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A nested list is a list that is placed inside another list, creating a hierarchical structure of items and sub-items. Nested lists are used to represent multi-level information — outlines, site maps, multi-step procedures with sub-steps, categories with sub-categories, and any content where items belong to other items.

In HTML, nesting is achieved by placing a complete <ul>, <ol>, or <dl> inside an <li> element of a parent list. The parent list is the outer list; the list inside the <li> is the inner list (or nested list). Any combination of list types is allowed — ordered inside unordered, unordered inside ordered, ordered inside ordered, and so on.

Example: 

<ul>
    <li>Fruits
        <ul>
            <li>Apples</li>
            <li>Bananas</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Vegetables</li>
</ul>

Rendered: • Fruits ◦ Apples ◦ Bananas • Vegetables

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Nested lists serve several essential purposes:

  • Hierarchy – represent parent–child relationships between items.
  • Outlines – structure documents with chapters and sections.
  • Site maps – show the structure of a website.
  • Multi-step procedures – main steps with sub-steps.
  • Categories – categories with sub-categories.
  • Navigation menus – dropdown or multi-level menus.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce the nesting depth and item counts.
  • SEO – search engines understand the hierarchy and can surface site maps and outlines.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Nested lists appear inside an <li> element of a parent <ul>, <ol>, or <menu>. They are not siblings of the parent list — they are children of a list item. This placement is crucial: it tells the browser (and assistive technologies) that the nested list belongs to that specific item.

<ol>
    <li>Chapter 1
        <ol>
            <li>Section 1.1</li>
            <li>Section 1.2</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
    <li>Chapter 2</li>
</ol>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Many types of content are inherently hierarchical:

  • A book has chapters, which have sections, which have sub-sections.
  • A website has sections, which have pages, which have sub-pages.
  • A procedure has steps, which have sub-steps.
  • A product catalog has categories, which have sub-categories.

Without nesting, this content would have to be flattened into a single level, losing the parent–child relationships. Flattened lists are harder to read, understand, and navigate — especially for screen reader users.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Flat lists only No hierarchy; all items at the same level. Manual indentation Fragile and inconsistent. No semantic relationship Machines can't tell which items belong to which. Poor accessibility Screen readers can't announce nesting depth. No styling hooks CSS can't target nested lists easily. No structure in APIs Data extraction loses hierarchy.

docs.title: Why Nested Lists Were Introduced
docs.text:
Nested lists were part of the original HTML specification — the ability to nest lists inside list items was included from the beginning. The design was simple but powerful: any list can be placed inside an <li> element, and the browser handles the indentation and numbering automatically.

Nested lists enable:

  • Semantic hierarchy – machines know the parent–child relationships.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce the depth and item counts.
  • Automatic numbering – nested ordered lists restart their numbering.
  • Automatic indentation – browsers indent nested lists by default.
  • Flexibility – any combination of list types can be nested.
  • Styling – CSS can target nested lists to customise markers and indentation.

The ability to nest lists is one of HTML's simplest yet most powerful features.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of a Nested List
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Parent item
        <ul>
            <li>Child item 1</li>
            <li>Child item 2</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

Key rule: The nested list goes inside the <li> element, not between <li> elements.

docs.title: Nested Unordered List
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Fruits
        <ul>
            <li>Apples</li>
            <li>Bananas</li>
            <li>Cherries</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Vegetables
        <ul>
            <li>Carrots</li>
            <li>Broccoli</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

Rendered: • Fruits ◦ Apples ◦ Bananas ◦ Cherries • Vegetables ◦ Carrots ◦ Broccoli

docs.title: Nested Ordered List
docs.text:
<ol>
    <li>Chapter 1
        <ol>
            <li>Section 1.1</li>
            <li>Section 1.2</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
    <li>Chapter 2
        <ol>
            <li>Section 2.1</li>
            <li>Section 2.2</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
</ol>

Rendered: 1. Chapter 1 1. Section 1.1 2. Section 1.2 2. Chapter 2 1. Section 2.1 2. Section 2.2

Note: Nested ordered lists restart their numbering at 1 by default.

docs.title: Ordered List Inside Unordered List
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Recipe Steps
        <ol>
            <li>Preheat the oven.</li>
            <li>Mix the ingredients.</li>
            <li>Bake for 25 minutes.</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
    <li>Tips
        <ul>
            <li>Use room-temperature eggs.</li>
            <li>Don't overmix.</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

docs.title: Unordered List Inside Ordered List
docs.text:
<ol>
    <li>Gather the ingredients:
        <ul>
            <li>Flour</li>
            <li>Sugar</li>
            <li>Eggs</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Mix them together.</li>
    <li>Bake for 25 minutes.</li>
</ol>

docs.title: Deeply Nested Lists
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Level 1
        <ul>
            <li>Level 2
                <ul>
                    <li>Level 3
                        <ul>
                            <li>Level 4</li>
                        </ul>
                    </li>
                </ul>
            </li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

Rendered: • Level 1 ◦ Level 2 ▪ Level 3 • Level 4

Note: Most browsers cycle through disc → circle → square → disc for unordered list markers at each level.

docs.title: Mixed Nesting (Ordered and Unordered)
docs.text:
<ol>
    <li>Chapter 1
        <ul>
            <li>Topic A
                <ol>
                    <li>Subtopic A.1</li>
                    <li>Subtopic A.2</li>
                </ol>
            </li>
            <li>Topic B</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Chapter 2</li>
</ol>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters Outer <ul> / <ol> The parent list. Contains the top-level items. <li> A list item. Can contain text and a nested list. Inner <ul> / <ol> The nested list. Must be inside the <li>, not between items. Indentation Browser default. Nested lists are indented automatically.

docs.title: The "Outline" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of a nested list as a document outline:

1. Introduction
    1.1 Background
    1.2 Motivation
2. Methods
    2.1 Data Collection
    2.2 Analysis
3. Results

Each level represents a deeper level of detail. The numbering (1, 1.1, 1.2) shows the hierarchy. The indentation shows the nesting.

docs.title: The "Folder Tree" Analogy
docs.text:
A nested list is like a file system:

📁 Documents
    📁 Work
        📄 Report.docx
        📄 Presentation.pptx
    📁 Personal
        📄 Resume.pdf

Each folder can contain files and sub-folders. The nesting represents the hierarchy.

docs.title: The "Family Tree" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of a nested list as a family tree:

Grandparent
    Parent 1
        Child 1
        Child 2
    Parent 2
        Child 3

Each level represents a generation. The nesting shows the relationships.

docs.title: The "Menu" Analogy
docs.text:
A nested list is like a restaurant menu with categories and sub-categories:

Appetizers
    Salads
        Caesar Salad
        Greek Salad
    Soups
        Tomato Soup
        Minestrone
Main Courses
    Pasta
    Pizza

Each category can have sub-categories, which can have items.

docs.title: Concept 1: Placement Inside <li>
docs.text:
The most important rule of nested lists: the nested list must be inside an <li> element, not between <li> elements.

<!-- Correct: nested list inside <li> -->
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
        <ul>
            <li>Sub-item</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

<!-- Incorrect: nested list between <li> elements -->
<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <ul>
        <li>Sub-item</li>
    </ul>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

Why: The nested list belongs to "Item 1", so it must be inside that item's <li> element. Placing it between items breaks the semantic relationship.

docs.title: Concept 2: Automatic Indentation
docs.text:
Browsers automatically indent nested lists. Each level of nesting adds 40px of padding-inline-start by default.

ul ul {
    padding-inline-start: 40px;
}

docs.title: Concept 3: Marker Cycling
docs.text:
For unordered lists, browsers cycle through markers at each nesting level:

  • Level 1: disc (•)
  • Level 2: circle (◦)
  • Level 3: square (▪)
  • Level 4: disc (•) again

For ordered lists, the numbering style depends on the type attribute. By default, nested ordered lists restart at 1.

docs.title: Concept 4: Nested Ordered Lists Restart
docs.text:
Nested ordered lists restart their numbering at 1 by default:

<ol>
    <li>Chapter 1
        <ol>
            <li>Section 1</li>  <!-- 1 -->
            <li>Section 2</li>  <!-- 2 -->
        </ol>
    </li>
</ol>

To continue numbering, use the start attribute on the nested <ol>.

docs.title: Concept 5: Mixed Nesting
docs.text:
You can nest any combination of <ul>, <ol>, and <menu>:

  • <ul> inside <ol> – unordered list inside ordered list.
  • <ol> inside <ul> – ordered list inside unordered list.
  • <ul> inside <ul> – nested unordered list.
  • <ol> inside <ol> – nested ordered list.

This flexibility allows you to represent complex hierarchies.

docs.title: Concept 6: Content Model
docs.text:
• The nested list is a flow content element inside the <li>.
  • The <li> can contain text and a nested list.
  • The nested list can contain its own <li> elements, which can contain further nested lists.
<li>
    Item text
    <ul>
        <li>Sub-item
            <ul>
                <li>Sub-sub-item</li>
            </ul>
        </li>
    </ul>
</li>

docs.title: Concept 7: Default Browser Styles
docs.text:
ul ul, ol ol, ul ol, ol ul {
    margin-block-start: 0;
    margin-block-end: 0;
    padding-inline-start: 40px;
}

Nested lists have no extra margin above or below, but they add horizontal padding for indentation.

docs.title: Concept 8: Styling Nested Lists
docs.text:
You can target nested lists with CSS:

/* Target all nested unordered lists */
ul ul {
    list-style-type: circle;
    padding-left: 1.5rem;
}

/* Target deeply nested lists */
ul ul ul {
    list-style-type: square;
}

docs.title: Concept 9: Accessibility
docs.text:
Screen readers announce nested lists as:

  • The parent list and its items.
  • Each nested list and its items.
  • The nesting depth is conveyed through the order and structure.

Best practice: Keep nesting depth reasonable (3–4 levels). Very deep nesting is hard to navigate.

docs.title: Concept 10: Navigation Menus
docs.text:
Nested lists are the standard for multi-level navigation menus:

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li>
            <a href="/products">Products</a>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/products/laptops">Laptops</a></li>
                <li><a href="/products/phones">Phones</a></li>
            </ul>
        </li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Concept 11: Site Maps
docs.text:
Nested lists are commonly used for site maps (both as navigation and as a page structure):

<nav aria-label="Site map">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
                <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
            </ul>
        </li>
        <li><a href="/products">Products</a>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/products/laptops">Laptops</a></li>
                <li><a href="/products/phones">Phones</a></li>
            </ul>
        </li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Concept 12: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Deeply nested lists increase DOM size and rendering complexity. For very deep nesting (10+ levels), consider alternatives like:

  • Flattening the structure.
  • Using <details> for collapsible sections.
  • Lazy loading subtrees.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of a Nested List
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters the outer `<ul>` or `<ol>`.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the outer list.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes each `<li>` child:
    │   ├── Creates a list item node.
    │   ├── Processes the item's text content.
    │   └── If a nested list is present:
    │       ├── Creates a nested list node.
    │       ├── Processes the nested list's `<li>` elements.
    │       └── Attaches the nested list as a child of the `<li>`.
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered, the outer list is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied:
    │   ├── Outer list: padding-inline-start: 40px
    │   ├── Nested list: padding-inline-start: 40px
    │   ├── Nested list markers: disc → circle → square
    │   └── Nested ordered lists restart at 1.
    │
    ▼
6.  The list is added to the accessibility tree:
    │   └── role: list, with nested lists as children.
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered with indentation and markers.

docs.title: The DOM Structure
docs.text:
A nested list creates a hierarchical DOM structure:

<ul>
├── <li>
│   ├── Text: "Item 1"
│   └── <ul>          ← Nested list
│       ├── <li>Sub-item 1</li>
│       └── <li>Sub-item 2</li>
└── <li>Item 2</li>

The nested <ul> is a child of the <li>, not a sibling of the outer <ul>.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, the nested list is a child of the list item. Screen readers announce:

  • The outer list and its items.
  • When an item contains a nested list, the screen reader announces the nested list and its items.

The nesting depth is conveyed through the order and structure.

docs.title: The DOM Structure
docs.text:
The <li> element is the key to nested lists. It can contain:

  • Flow content – text, inline elements, block-level elements.
  • A nested list – <ul>, <ol>, or <menu>.

The nested list is a direct child of the <li>, not of the outer list.

docs.title: The ::marker Pseudo-Element
docs.text:
Nested lists have their own markers. The browser cycles through markers for unordered lists:

Depth Default Marker 1 disc (•) 2 circle (◦) 3 square (▪) 4 disc (•) again

docs.title: Numbering for Ordered Lists
docs.text:
Nested ordered lists restart at 1 by default. The start attribute can be used to continue numbering:

<ol>
    <li>Item
        <ol start="5">
            <li>Item 5</li>
            <li>Item 6</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
</ol>

docs.title: CSS Reset for Nested Lists
docs.text:
Browsers apply margin-block-start: 0 and margin-block-end: 0 to nested lists (to avoid extra vertical space), but they add padding-inline-start: 40px for indentation.

ul ul, ol ol, ul ol, ol ul {
    margin-block-start: 0;
    margin-block-end: 0;
    padding-inline-start: 40px;
}

docs.title: Accessibility Mapping
docs.text:
The browser's accessibility engine maps:

  • The outer list → role: list.
  • Each <li> → role: listitem.
  • The nested list → role: list (as a child of the <li>).

The nesting depth is conveyed through the structure and the number of items.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Nested List
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the nested list inside an `<li>` element.
    │   └── <ul><li>Item<ul><li>Sub-item</li></ul></li></ul>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The outer list, list item, and nested list nodes are created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied.
    │   └── Indentation, marker cycling, numbering.
    │
    ▼
5.  The list is rendered with nesting.
    │
    ▼
6.  The accessibility tree is built.
    │   └── Nested lists as children of list items.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers announce the hierarchy.
    │
    ▼
8.  JavaScript may modify the list dynamically.
    │   └── Adding/removing nested items, collapsing/expanding.
    │
    ▼
9.  When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
// Add a nested list to an existing list item
const li = document.querySelector('li');
const nestedUl = document.createElement('ul');
const subLi = document.createElement('li');
subLi.textContent = 'New sub-item';
nestedUl.appendChild(subLi);
li.appendChild(nestedUl);

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Nested Unordered List
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Fruits
        <ul>
            <li>Apples</li>
            <li>Bananas</li>
            <li>Cherries</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Vegetables
        <ul>

docs.title: Example 12: JavaScript-Generated Nested List
docs.text:
<ul id="dynamic-tree"></ul>

<script>
    const data = [
        {
            name: 'Fruits',
            children: [
                { name: 'Apples' },
                { name: 'Bananas' },
                {
                    name: 'Citrus',
                    children: [
                        { name: 'Oranges' },
                        { name: 'Lemons' }
                    ]
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            name: 'Vegetables',
            children: [
                { name: 'Carrots' },
                { name: 'Broccoli' }
            ]
        }
    ];

    function renderList(items, parent) {
        const ul = document.createElement('ul');
        items.forEach(item => {
            const li = document.createElement('li');
            li.textContent = item.name;
            if (item.children) {
                renderList(item.children, li);
            }
            ul.appendChild(li);
        });
        parent.appendChild(ul);
    }

    renderList(data, document.getElementById('dynamic-tree'));
</script>

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Place nested lists inside <li> – not between <li> elements.

  2. Use indentation consistently – 2 or 4 spaces per level for readability.

  3. Keep nesting shallow – 3–4 levels maximum for most content.

  4. Use semantic elements – <ul>, <ol>, or <dl> depending on the content.

  5. Use <nav> for navigation lists – with aria-label.

  6. Style with CSS – use CSS selectors like ul ul, ul ul ul.

  7. Use CSS counters – for custom numbering schemes (e.g., 1.1, 1.1.1).

  8. Consider <details> for collapsible lists – for large hierarchies.

  9. Use start for continuing numbering – in nested ordered lists.

  10. Test with screen readers – ensure the hierarchy is announced.

  11. Validate your HTML – check for correct nesting.

  12. Don't over-nest – deep nesting is hard to read and maintain.

  13. Use consistent marker styles – across a site.

  14. Avoid mixing too many list types – keep it simple.

  15. Use role="tree" for interactive trees – only if you need advanced ARIA.

  16. Test on mobile – ensure nested lists render well on small screens.

  17. Use padding-inline-start – for logical indentation (respects RTL).

  18. Consider the reading order – nested lists are read depth-first.

  19. Document your structure – in a style guide.

  20. Keep the hierarchy meaningful – every level should have a purpose.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placing the Nested List Between <li> Elements
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <ul>
        <li>Sub-item</li>
    </ul>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: The nested list must be inside the <li> element it belongs to.

✅ Correct: 

<ul>
    <li>Item 1
        <ul>
            <li>Sub-item</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Closing the <li> Before the Nested List
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
    <ul>
        <li>Sub-item</li>
    </ul>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Without closing the <li>, the browser may interpret the nested list incorrectly.

✅ Correct: 

<ul>
    <li>Item 1
        <ul>
            <li>Sub-item</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Over-Nesting
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Level 1
        <ul>
            <li>Level 2
                <ul>
                    <li>Level 3
                        <ul>
                            <li>Level 4
                                <ul>
                                    <li>Level 5
                                        <ul>
                                            <li>Level 6</li>
                                        </ul>
                                    </li>
                                </ul>
                            </li>
                        </ul>
                    </li>
                </ul>
            </li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Deep nesting is hard to read, navigate, and maintain. It also increases DOM size.

✅ Correct: Flatten the structure or use a different representation (e.g., <details>, a table, or separate pages).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Nested Lists for Layout
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>
        <ul>
            <li>Column 1</li>
            <li>Column 2</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Nested lists are for hierarchy, not layout. Use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

✅ Correct: 

<div style="display: flex; gap: 1rem;">
    <div>Column 1</div>
    <div>Column 2</div>
</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Style Nested Lists
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item
        <ul>
            <li>Sub-item</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Default indentation may not fit your design.

✅ Correct: 

ul ul {
    padding-left: 1.5rem;
    list-style-type: circle;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Nested Ordered Lists Without Restarting or Continuing
docs.text:
<ol>
    <li>Item 1
        <ol>
            <li>Sub-item</li>  <!-- Restarts at 1 -->
        </ol>
    </li>
</ol>
Why it's wrong: Sometimes you want the numbering to continue (e.g., 1.1, 1.2). Use start to continue.

✅ Correct: 

<ol>
    <li>Item 1
        <ol start="2">
            <li>Sub-item 2</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
</ol>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mixing Too Many List Types
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item
        <ol>
            <li>Sub-item
                <dl>
                    <dt>Term</dt>
                    <dd>Description</dd>
                </dl>
            </li>
        </ol>
    </li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: While valid, mixing too many list types can be confusing. Use the appropriate type for the content.

✅ Correct: Use the simplest structure that fits the content.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing with Screen Readers
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item
        <ul>
            <li>Sub-item</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Screen readers may announce nested lists differently. Test to ensure the hierarchy is clear.

✅ Correct: Test with NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <br> for Indentation
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item</li>
    <li>   Sub-item</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: This is not semantic. Use nested lists.

✅ Correct: 

<ul>
    <li>Item
        <ul>
            <li>Sub-item</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Nested Lists for Non-Hierarchical Data
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
        <ul>
            <li>Item 2</li>  <!-- Item 2 is not a child of Item 1 -->
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Nested lists imply a parent–child relationship. If items are peers, use a flat list.

✅ Correct: 

<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• DOM size – each nested list adds DOM nodes. Deep nesting increases DOM size.
  • Rendering – deeply nested lists increase layout complexity.
  • CSS selectors – ul ul ul selectors can be slow for very deep nesting.
  • Marker rendering – each level requires a marker. Minimal cost.
  • Large lists – lists with thousands of items (nested or not) can impact rendering; consider virtualization.
  • <details> – using <details> for collapsible lists can improve initial render performance.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep nesting shallow – 3–4 levels maximum.
  2. Use CSS Grid or Flexbox for layout – instead of nested lists.
  3. Use <details> for collapsible content – native and efficient.
  4. Virtualize very large lists – for lists with hundreds of items.
  5. Minify HTML – reduce file size.
  6. Avoid inline styles – use CSS classes.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if nested list items contain user-generated content, sanitize it before rendering.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent or a sanitizer.
  • Injection – never insert user input directly into <li> without escaping.
  • No direct security implications – <ul> and <ol> nesting itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into list items.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate structure – ensure <li> elements are properly nested.
  4. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the nested list structure.
  • Collapse/expand nodes – in the Elements panel to see the hierarchy.
  • Computed styles – check padding-inline-start and list-style-type.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the list structure and nesting.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('li') to count all list items.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the hierarchy is announced correctly.
  • Test with CSS disabled – ensure the list still makes sense.
  • Test with JavaScript disabled – ensure the list renders.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For hierarchical content – outlines, site maps, taxonomies.
  • For multi-level navigation – dropdown menus, mega menus.
  • For procedures with sub-steps – recipes, tutorials.
  • For categories and sub-categories – product catalogs.
  • For document structure – chapters, sections, sub-sections.
  • For file trees – folders and files.
  • For table of contents – navigation within a document.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For flat lists – use a single-level list.
  • For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For non-hierarchical data – use a flat list.
  • For very deep hierarchies – use a different structure (e.g., <details>, separate pages).
  • For simple menus – a flat <ul> may be sufficient.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <ul> – unordered list.
  • <ol> – ordered list.
  • <dl> – description list.
  • <li> – list item.
  • <menu> – semantic alternative to <ul>.
  • <details> – collapsible content.
  • CSS selectors – ul ul, ol ol, etc.
  • CSS counters – for custom numbering.
  • padding-inline-start – for logical indentation.
  • Accessibility – list structure and nesting.
  • ARIA – role="tree", role="treeitem", role="group".
  • Site maps – XML sitemaps vs. HTML site maps.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Nested lists have been part of HTML since HTML 1.0 (1991) — the ability to nest lists inside list items was included from the beginning.

  • The key rule of nested lists: the nested list must be inside the <li> element, not between <li> elements. This is one of the most common mistakes in HTML.

  • Browsers automatically cycle through markers for nested unordered lists: disc → circle → square → disc.

  • Nested ordered lists restart at 1 by default. Use the start attribute to continue numbering.

  • Screen readers announce nested lists with their depth and item count, making the hierarchy clear to users.

  • Site maps are commonly built with nested lists because the structure of a website is inherently hierarchical.

  • Multi-level navigation menus are almost always built with nested lists, often styled with CSS for dropdowns.

  • The padding-inline-start property is used for nested list indentation. Unlike padding-left, it respects the text direction (LTR/RTL).

  • CSS counters can create custom numbering schemes for nested lists, such as "1.1", "1.1.1", etc.

  • The counters() function in CSS is used with counter-reset and counter-increment to create hierarchical numbering.

  • <details> can be used inside <li> to create collapsible nested lists — native collapsibility without JavaScript.

  • ARIA tree roles (role="tree", role="treeitem", role="group") are for advanced interactive trees, but for simple hierarchical lists, native nesting is sufficient.

  • Deeply nested lists (10+ levels) are hard to read and navigate. Most content needs only 3–4 levels.

  • The start attribute on nested ordered lists can be used to continue numbering from a specific point.

  • Mixed nesting (e.g., <ul> inside <ol>) is valid and useful for representing complex hierarchies.

  • The <menu> element is a semantic alternative to <ul> for toolbars and context menus. It can also be nested.

  • Nested description lists (<dl> inside <dd>) are valid and can represent hierarchical key–value data.

  • The accessibility tree exposes nested lists as a tree structure, with each nested list as a child of its parent list item.

  • HTML5 allows <div> wrappers inside <dl>, but not inside <ul> or <ol> — nested lists must be inside <li>.

  • Site maps for search engines are XML files, not HTML lists. HTML site maps are for users; XML sitemaps are for crawlers.

  • The ::marker pseudo-element can style nested list markers differently at each level.

  • Nested lists are a fundamental part of document outlines, site maps, navigation menus, and taxonomies.

  • The list-style-position: inside value can affect how nested lists wrap text.

  • display: grid or display: flex on a nested list can create multi-column layouts, though this is unusual.

  • Nested lists are one of the simplest yet most powerful features of HTML — they let you represent any hierarchy.

  • The W3C HTML specification explicitly defines the rules for nested lists: only <li> elements can contain nested lists.

  • Accessibility experts recommend keeping nesting shallow and using clear, descriptive list item text.

  • Nested lists are used in documentation, navigation, site maps, taxonomies, recipes, and countless other contexts.

  • The <li> element is the only valid parent of a nested list. Placing a nested list elsewhere is invalid HTML.

  • Nested lists are read depth-first by screen readers, which is the natural reading order for hierarchical content.

  • The start attribute works with type to continue numbering in any style (e.g., type="a" start="5" starts at "e").

  • Nested lists are a key part of semantic HTML — they convey hierarchy that would otherwise be lost in flat markup.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A nested list is a list placed inside an <li> element of a parent list.
  • Key rule: The nested list must be inside the <li>, not between <li> elements.
  • Any combination of <ul>, <ol>, and <menu> can be nested.
  • Browsers automatically indent nested lists and cycle markers for unordered lists (disc → circle → square).
  • Nested ordered lists restart at 1 by default; use start to continue numbering.
  • CSS controls indentation (padding-inline-start), markers (list-style-type), and custom numbering (CSS counters).
  • Best practices: place nested lists inside <li>, keep nesting shallow (3–4 levels), use <nav> for navigation, style with CSS, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include placing the nested list between <li> elements, over-nesting, using nested lists for layout, and forgetting to close the <li>.
  • Nested lists are essential for document outlines, site maps, navigation menus, taxonomies, multi-step procedures, and any hierarchical content.
  • They are one of the simplest yet most powerful features of HTML — the foundation of hierarchical structure on the web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
List best practices are a set of guidelines, patterns, and conventions for choosing, structuring, and styling HTML lists (<ul>, <ol>, <dl>) in a way that maximises semantics, accessibility, maintainability, and performance. They synthesise the individual rules covered in the chapters on ordered, unordered, description, and nested lists into a cohesive decision-making framework.

List best practices answer questions like:

  • Which list type should I use?
  • When should I nest lists?
  • How do I style lists without breaking semantics?
  • How do I make lists accessible?
  • How do I avoid common pitfalls?

They are not rigid rules — they are heuristics that help you write list markup that works for users, search engines, and future maintainers.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
List best practices serve several essential purposes:

  • Consistency – a shared vocabulary for list decisions across teams and projects.
  • Accessibility – ensure lists are usable by screen reader users and keyboard users.
  • Semantic correctness – choose the right list type for the content.
  • Maintainability – write list markup that is easy to read, extend, and refactor.
  • Performance – avoid unnecessary nesting and DOM bloat.
  • SEO – help search engines understand the structure and surface rich results.
  • Interoperability – ensure lists work across browsers, devices, and assistive technologies.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
List best practices are a meta-layer over the technical knowledge of <ul>, <ol>, <dl>, and <li>. They guide your decision-making at every step: choosing a list type, nesting lists, adding attributes, and styling them. They apply to every project, every page, and every component.

List Best Practices
│
├── Choosing the Right List Type
├── Semantic Structure
├── Accessibility
├── Nesting Discipline
├── Styling Without Breaking Semantics
├── Navigation Lists
├── Metadata and Definition Lists
├── Performance
└── Validation and Testing

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Lists are deceptively simple. A <ul> with a few <li> elements seems trivial. But in practice, lists are used in dozens of contexts — navigation menus, feature lists, FAQs, glossaries, product specs, site maps, documentation, card grids — and each context has its own requirements and pitfalls.

Without best practices, developers make inconsistent choices:

  • Using <ul> for ordered steps.
  • Using <div> for lists (losing semantics).
  • Over-nesting lists for layout purposes.
  • Removing list markers without preserving semantics.
  • Forgetting to nest lists inside <li>.
  • Using <dl> for general lists.
  • Ignoring accessibility.

These choices accumulate into inconsistent, inaccessible, and hard-to-maintain codebases.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Problem Consequence Inconsistent list types Confusing for users and machines. Div-based "lists" Lost semantics; inaccessible. Over-nesting Bloated DOM; hard to maintain. list-style: none without role="list" Screen readers lose list semantics in Safari/VoiceOver. No aria-label on nav lists Ambiguous navigation. Deep nesting Poor performance and readability. Ignoring dl Missing semantic opportunities.

docs.title: Why Best Practices Were Established
docs.text:
List best practices emerged from:

  • WCAG – accessibility guidelines for lists.
  • ARIA Authoring Practices – guidance on roles and states.
  • Browser vendor documentation – MDN, Web.dev, etc.
  • Community experience – lessons learned from real-world projects.
  • Style guides – Google, Airbnb, and others publish HTML style guides.

Following these practices leads to better outcomes for users, developers, and businesses.

docs.title: 3. Syntax / Basic Usage (Core Principles in Action)
Principle 1: Choose the Right List Type
Principle 2: Use <li> as the Only Child of <ul> and <ol>
docs.text:
Bad: 

<ul>
    <p>Some text</p>
    <li>Item 1</li>
</ul>

Good: 

<ul>
    <li>Some text</li>
    <li>Item 1</li>
</ul>

docs.title: Principle 3: Nest Lists Inside <li>
docs.text:
Bad: 

<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <ul>
        <li>Sub-item</li>
    </ul>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

Good: 

<ul>
    <li>Item 1
        <ul>
            <li>Sub-item</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: Principle 4: Use <nav> for Navigation Lists
docs.text:
Bad: 

<ul>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
</ul>

Good: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Principle 5: Preserve Semantics When Removing Markers
docs.text:
Bad: 

ul {
    list-style: none;
    padding: 0;
}
(Safari/VoiceOver may remove list semantics.)

Good: 

<ul role="list">
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

ul {
    list-style: none;
    padding: 0;
}

Or: 

ul {
    list-style: none;
    padding: 0;
}
ul li {
    display: list-item;
}

docs.title: Principle 6: Use <dl> for Term–Description Pairs
docs.text:
Bad: 

<ul>
    <li><strong>HTML</strong> — HyperText Markup Language</li>
    <li><strong>CSS</strong> — Cascading Style Sheets</li>
</ul>

Good: 

<dl>
    <dt>HTML</dt>
    <dd>HyperText Markup Language</dd>
    <dt>CSS</dt>
    <dd>Cascading Style Sheets</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: Principle 7: Keep Nesting Shallow
docs.text:
Bad: 

<ul>
    <li>Level 1
        <ul>
            <li>Level 2
                <ul>
                    <li>Level 3
                        <ul>
                            <li>Level 4
                                <ul>
                                    <li>Level 5</li>
                                </ul>
                            </li>
                        </ul>
                    </li>
                </ul>
            </li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

Good: 3–4 levels maximum, or use a different structure (e.g., <details>, separate pages).

docs.title: Principle 8: Don't Use Lists for Layout
docs.text:
Bad: 

<ul style="display: flex;">
    <li>Column 1</li>
    <li>Column 2</li>
</ul>

Good: 

<div style="display: flex;">
    <div>Column 1</div>
    <div>Column 2</div>
</div>

Exception: Navigation menus and card grids often use <ul> with display: flex/grid because the items are semantically a list.

docs.title: The "Toolbox" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of list types as tools in a toolbox:

  • <ol> – a numbered checklist for sequences.
  • <ul> – a bullet list for grouped items.
  • <dl> – a dictionary for term–description pairs.

Using the right tool for the job is the essence of list best practices. Using a screwdriver as a hammer works, but it's inefficient and can damage the tool.

docs.title: The "Contract with Machines" Analogy
docs.text: Choosing the right list type is like signing a contract with machines. You promise to use <ol> for ordered content and <ul> for unordered content. In return, machines promise to interpret your content correctly. Breaking the contract (e.g., using <ul> for steps) confuses machines and users alike.

docs.title: The "Code Review Checklist" Analogy
docs.text:
List best practices are like a code review checklist. Before you ship list markup, you mentally review it:

  • Is the list type correct?
  • Is nesting done correctly?
  • Is the list accessible?
  • Is the styling appropriate?
  • Is the structure semantic?

If you can answer "yes" to all, you've followed best practices.

docs.title: The "Building Blocks" Analogy
docs.text: Lists are building blocks for larger structures — navigation menus, card grids, FAQs, glossaries. Best practices ensure the blocks are stacked correctly so the larger structure is stable.

docs.title: Concept 1: Semantic Choice — <ol> vs <ul> vs <dl>
docs.text:
The first and most important decision is choosing the right list type:

Question Answer List Type Does order matter? Yes <ol> Does order matter? No <ul> Is it a term–description pair? Yes <dl>

Common mistakes: - Using <ul> for instructions (should be <ol>). - Using <ol> for features (should be <ul>). - Using <ul> for glossaries (should be <dl>).

Rule: The semantics of the list type should match the semantics of the content.

docs.title: Concept 2: <li> as the Only Child
docs.text:
The <ul> and <ol> elements accept only <li> children. Any other content must be wrapped in <li>.

<!-- Valid -->
<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

<!-- Invalid -->
<ul>
    <p>Paragraph</p>
    <li>Item 1</li>
</ul>

docs.title: Concept 3: Nesting Inside <li>
docs.text:
Nested lists must be inside the <li> element they belong to, not between <li> elements.

<!-- Valid -->
<li>Item
    <ul>
        <li>Sub-item</li>
    </ul>
</li>

<!-- Invalid -->
<li>Item</li>
<ul>
    <li>Sub-item</li>
</ul>

docs.title: Concept 4: Preserving Semantics with list-style: none
docs.text:
In Safari and VoiceOver, list-style: none removes the list semantics — screen readers no longer announce the list. The fix is to add role="list" to the <ul> or <ol>.

<ul role="list">
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

Why: Safari's accessibility engine has a long-standing bug where list-style: none removes the list role. Adding role="list" restores it.

docs.title: Concept 5: Navigation Lists Need <nav> and Labels
docs.text:
A navigation menu should be wrapped in <nav> with an aria-label (especially if there are multiple navs on the page).

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

<nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/privacy">Privacy</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Concept 6: aria-current="page" for Current Items
docs.text:
In navigation menus, mark the current page with aria-current="page".

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Concept 7: Styling Without Breaking Semantics
docs.text:
Lists can be styled extensively with CSS without breaking semantics:

ul {
    list-style: none;
    padding: 0;
    margin: 0;
}
ul li {
    display: inline-block;
    margin-right: 1rem;
}

But if you remove the markers, consider the accessibility implications (see Concept 4).

docs.title: Concept 8: Lists for Card Grids
docs.text:
Card grids are often built with <ul> and <li> because the items are semantically a list.

<ul class="card-grid">
    <li class="card">
        <h3>Card 1</h3>
        <p>Description</p>
    </li>
    <li class="card">
        <h3>Card 2</h3>
        <p>Description</p>
    </li>
</ul>

.card-grid {
    list-style: none;
    padding: 0;
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
    gap: 1rem;
}

docs.title: Concept 9: Lists for Site Maps
docs.text:
Site maps are naturally hierarchical and should use nested <ul>.

<nav aria-label="Site map">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
            </ul>
        </li>
        <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: Concept 10: Lists for Glossaries and FAQs
docs.text:
Glossaries and FAQs are term–description pairs and should use <dl>.

<dl>
    <dt>HTML</dt>
    <dd>HyperText Markup Language</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: Concept 11: Lists for Documentation
docs.text:
Documentation often uses all three list types:

  • <ol> for step-by-step procedures.
  • <ul> for feature lists, options, and parameters.
  • <dl> for parameter descriptions and glossaries.

docs.title: Concept 12: Performance — Keep Lists Shallow
docs.text: Deep nesting increases DOM size and rendering complexity. Keep nesting to 3–4 levels maximum.

docs.title: Concept 13: Accessibility — Test with Screen Readers
docs.text:
Test lists with NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, or TalkBack to ensure they're announced correctly. Pay attention to:

  • Whether the list is announced.
  • Whether the item count is announced.
  • Whether nested lists are announced.
  • Whether the current item (aria-current) is announced.

docs.title: Concept 14: SEO — Use Lists for Structured Content
docs.text:
Search engines use lists to understand grouped and sequenced content. Combine lists with structured data for rich results:

  • FAQPage – <dl> with questions and answers.
  • HowTo – <ol> with steps.
  • ItemList – <ul> or <ol> with items.

docs.title: Concept 15: Validation — Ensure Correct Structure
docs.text:
Validate your HTML to catch list structure errors:

  • Only <li> as children of <ul>/<ol>.
  • Nested lists inside <li>.
  • Correct <dt>/<dd> structure in <dl>.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: A List Review Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Identify the Content
    │   └── Is it ordered, unordered, or term–description?
    │
    ▼
2.  Choose the List Type
    │   ├── Ordered → <ol>
    │   ├── Unordered → <ul>
    │   └── Term–description → <dl>
    │
    ▼
3.  Structure the List
    │   ├── Use <li> for items.
    │   ├── Nest inside <li> if needed.
    │   └── Keep nesting shallow.
    │
    ▼
4.  Add Semantics
    │   ├── <nav> for navigation lists.
    │   ├── aria-label for multiple navs.
    │   └── aria-current for the current item.
    │
    ▼
5.  Style with CSS
    │   ├── Use list-style-type, list-style-position.
    │   ├── Use ::marker for custom markers.
    │   ├── Add role="list" if removing markers.
    │   └── Avoid layout hacks with lists.
    │
    ▼
6.  Validate
    │   ├── W3C HTML Validator.
    │   └── Accessibility audit (Lighthouse, axe).
    │
    ▼
7.  Test
    │   ├── Screen reader testing.
    │   ├── Keyboard navigation.
    │   └── Responsive design.
    │
    ▼
8.  Review and Refine
    │   └── Iterate until the list is semantic, accessible, and maintainable.

docs.title: The List Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Is the list type correct for the content?
  • [ ] Are only <li> elements direct children of <ul>/<ol>?
  • [ ] Are nested lists inside <li> elements?
  • [ ] Is nesting limited to 3–4 levels?
  • [ ] Is the navigation list wrapped in <nav>?
  • [ ] Are multiple navs labelled with aria-label?
  • [ ] Is the current item marked with aria-current="page"?
  • [ ] Is role="list" added if list-style: none is used?
  • [ ] Are markers styled with CSS (not hardcoded)?
  • [ ] Is <dl> used for term–description pairs?
  • [ ] Are <dt> and <dd> siblings inside <dl>?
  • [ ] Is the list validated?
  • [ ] Is the list tested with a screen reader?
  • [ ] Is the list responsive?

docs.title: How List Type Affects the Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
Element Accessibility Role <ul> list <ol> list <li> listitem <dl> list (or definitionlist) <dt> term (or listitem) <dd> definition (or listitem)

The list-style: none bug in Safari/VoiceOver removes the list role. Adding role="list" restores it.

docs.title: How list-style: none Affects Semantics
docs.text:
ul {
    list-style: none;
}

In Safari/VoiceOver, this removes the list role from the <ul>. The fix:

<ul role="list">

ul {
    list-style: none;
}

This forces the list role to be preserved.

docs.title: How <nav> Affects the Accessibility Tree
docs.text: <nav> creates a navigation landmark in the accessibility tree. Screen reader users can jump to it. Multiple navs should have unique aria-labels.

docs.title: How aria-current Works
docs.text: aria-current="page" tells assistive technologies that the link represents the current page. Screen readers may announce "current page" or "current".

docs.title: How SEO Uses Lists
docs.text:
Search engines use lists to understand structure:

  • Ordered lists – sequence, rankings, steps.
  • Unordered lists – grouped items, features.
  • Description lists – term–description pairs, FAQs, metadata.

Structured data (JSON-LD) can be combined with lists for rich results.

docs.title: How Validation Catches Errors
docs.text:
The W3C validator checks:

  • Only <li> as children of <ul>/<ol>.
  • Nested lists inside <li>.
  • <dt>/<dd> structure in <dl>.
  • Correct attributes.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of List Best Practices
docs.text:
1.  Planning
    │   └── Choose the semantic structure before writing code.
    │
    ▼
2.  Authoring
    │   └── Write semantic list markup using the right type.
    │
    ▼
3.  Review
    │   └── Check against the list checklist.
    │
    ▼
4.  Validation
    │   └── Run the W3C validator.
    │
    ▼
5.  Testing
    │   ├── Screen reader testing.
    │   ├── Keyboard navigation.
    │   └── Responsive testing.
    │
    ▼
6.  Deployment
    │   └── Ship the semantic, accessible list.
    │
    ▼
7.  Maintenance
    │   ├── Keep the structure semantic as content changes.
    │   └── Re-validate and re-test after updates.
    │
    ▼
8.  Refactoring
    │   └── Improve list semantics over time.

docs.title: Example 1: The Right List for the Job
docs.text:
<!-- Ordered: steps -->
<ol>
    <li>Preheat the oven.</li>
    <li>Mix the ingredients.</li>
    <li>Bake for 25 minutes.</li>
</ol>

<!-- Unordered: features -->
<ul>
    <li>Fast</li>
    <li>Responsive</li>
    <li>Accessible</li>
</ul>

<!-- Description: glossary -->
<dl>
    <dt>HTML</dt>
    <dd>HyperText Markup Language</dd>
    <dt>CSS</dt>
    <dd>Cascading Style Sheets</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: Example 2: Accessible Navigation Menu
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul role="list">
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="/services">Services</a></li>
        <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

<style>
    nav ul {
        list-style: none;
        padding: 0;
        display: flex;
        gap: 1rem;
    }
</style>

docs.title: Example 3: Preserving Semantics with role="list"
docs.text:
<ul role="list" class="card-grid">
    <li class="card">Card 1</li>
    <li class="card">Card 2</li>
    <li class="card">Card 3</li>
</ul>

<style>
    .card-grid {
        list-style: none;
        padding: 0;
        display: grid;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
        gap: 1rem;
    }
</style>

docs.title: Example 4: FAQ with <dl> and Structured Data
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
    <dl itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/FAQPage">
        <div itemprop="mainEntity" itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Question">
            <dt itemprop="name">What is HTML?</dt>
            <dd itemprop="acceptedAnswer" itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Answer">
                <div itemprop="text">HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.</div>
            </dd>
        </div>
        <div itemprop="mainEntity" itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Question">
            <dt itemprop="name">What is CSS?</dt>
            <dd itemprop="acceptedAnswer" itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Answer">
                <div itemprop="text">CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.</div>
            </dd>
        </div>
    </dl>
</section>

docs.title: Example 5: Nested List Done Right
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Documentation">
    <ul>
        <li>
            <a href="/getting-started">Getting Started</a>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/getting-started/installation">Installation</a></li>
                <li><a href="/getting-started/configuration">Configuration</a></li>
            </ul>
        </li>
        <li>
