docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Best Practice Navigation menus <nav> + <ul> + aria-label Breadcrumbs <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> + <ol> Feature lists <ul> Step-by-step instructions <ol> Glossaries <dl> FAQs <dl> + structured data Product specs <dl> Metadata <dl> Site maps Nested <ul> Card grids <ul role="list"> with display: grid Tag clouds <ul> with display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap Social media links <ul> with role="list" Checklists <ul> with custom markers Tables of contents Nested <ol> Documentation Mixed lists as appropriate

docs.title: Choosing the Right List Type
docs.text:
1. Use <ol> for ordered content – steps, rankings, sequences.
  2. Use <ul> for unordered content – features, categories, navigation.
  3. Use <dl> for term–description pairs – glossaries, FAQs, metadata.
  4. Use <menu> for toolbars – semantic alternative to <ul>.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
1. Use <li> as the only child of <ul>/<ol>.
  2. Nest lists inside <li> – not between items.
  3. Keep nesting shallow – 3–4 levels maximum.
  4. Use semantic elements – <ul>, <ol>, <dl> — not <div>.
  5. Use <dl> with <dt> and <dd> as siblings.
  6. Use <div> wrappers in <dl> for styling (HTML5 only).

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
1. Use <nav> for navigation lists.
  2. Add aria-label to multiple navs.
  3. Use aria-current="page" for the current item.
  4. Add role="list" if using list-style: none (Safari/VoiceOver bug).
  5. Test with screen readers.
  6. Ensure keyboard accessibility — all links focusable.
  7. Keep list items concise — long items are hard to scan.
  8. Use descriptive link text — "About Us" not "Click here".

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
1. Use CSS list-style-type — not the obsolete type attribute.
  2. Use ::marker for custom marker styling.
  3. Use CSS counters for custom numbering (e.g., 1.1, 1.1.1).
  4. Use padding-inline-start for logical indentation.
  5. Don't use lists for layout — use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  6. Exception: Navigation menus and card grids are semantically lists.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
1. Wrap navigation in <nav>.
  2. Use <ul> for navigation menus.
  3. Use <ol> for breadcrumbs (order matters).
  4. Use aria-label on <nav> when there are multiple navs.
  5. Use aria-current="page" for the current page.
  6. Provide a mobile-friendly menu — e.g., hamburger menu.

docs.title: SEO
docs.text:
1. Use <ol> for "HowTo" content — with structured data.
  2. Use <dl> for FAQ content — with structured data.
  3. Use <ul> for "ItemList" content — with structured data.
  4. Keep list items descriptive — search engines use the text.
  5. Use structured data for rich results.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
1. Validate your HTML — W3C validator.
  2. Check for invalid nesting.
  3. Check for missing role="list" if using list-style: none.
  4. Check for aria-label on multiple navs.
  5. Check for aria-current on navigation.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
1. Keep lists shallow — avoid deep nesting.
  2. Use <details> for collapsible lists — native and efficient.
  3. Virtualize very large lists — for hundreds of items.
  4. Minify HTML — reduce file size.
  5. Avoid inline styles — use CSS classes.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
1. Use meaningful class names — not .red or .big.
  2. Comment complex list structures — for maintainability.
  3. Document your list conventions — in a style guide.
  4. Review lists regularly — as the site evolves.
  5. Stay updated — follow HTML Living Standard changes.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <ul> for Ordered Content
docs.text:
<h2>How to Make Tea</h2>
<ul>
    <li>Boil water.</li>
    <li>Add tea leaves.</li>
    <li>Steep for 3 minutes.</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: The steps have a specific order; use <ol>.

✅ Correct: 

<ol>
    <li>Boil water.</li>
    <li>Add tea leaves.</li>
    <li>Steep for 3 minutes.</li>
</ol>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <ul> for Glossaries
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li><strong>HTML</strong> — HyperText Markup Language</li>
    <li><strong>CSS</strong> — Cascading Style Sheets</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Term–description pairs should use <dl>.

✅ Correct: 

<dl>
    <dt>HTML</dt>
    <dd>HyperText Markup Language</dd>
    <dt>CSS</dt>
    <dd>Cascading Style Sheets</dd>
</dl>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div> Instead of <ul>
docs.text:
<div class="features">
    <div>Fast</div>
    <div>Responsive</div>
    <div>Accessible</div>
</div>
Why it's wrong: Loses list semantics; screen readers won't announce the list.

✅ Correct: 

<ul class="features">
    <li>Fast</li>
    <li>Responsive</li>
    <li>Accessible</li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placing Content Directly Inside <ul>
docs.text:
<ul>
    <p>Some text</p>
    <li>Item 1</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Only <li> is a valid child of <ul>.

✅ Correct: 

<ul>
    <li>Some text</li>
    <li>Item 1</li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting a List Between <li> Elements
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <ul>
        <li>Sub-item</li>
    </ul>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Nested lists must be inside an <li>.

✅ Correct: 

<ul>
    <li>Item 1
        <ul>
            <li>Sub-item</li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Removing Markers Without Preserving Semantics
docs.text:
<ul style="list-style: none;">
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Safari/VoiceOver may remove the list semantics.

✅ Correct: 

<ul role="list" style="list-style: none;">
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <ul> for Layout
docs.text:
<ul style="display: flex;">
    <li>Column 1</li>
    <li>Column 2</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Lists are for related items, not layout. Use <div>.

✅ Correct: 

<div style="display: flex;">
    <div>Column 1</div>
    <div>Column 2</div>
</div>

Exception: If the items are semantically a list (e.g., a card grid), use <ul>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Navigation Menu Without <nav>
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Screen readers can't jump to the navigation.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Navs Without Labels
docs.text:
<nav>
    <ul>...</ul>
</nav>
<nav>
    <ul>...</ul>
</nav>
Why it's wrong: Screen reader users can't distinguish between the navs.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>...</ul>
</nav>
<nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
    <ul>...</ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Using aria-current for the Current Page
docs.text:
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>
Why it's wrong: The current page is not indicated.

✅ Correct: 

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Deep Nesting
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Level 1
        <ul>
            <li>Level 2
                <ul>
                    <li>Level 3
                        <ul>
                            <li>Level 4
                                <ul>
                                    <li>Level 5</li>
                                </ul>
                            </li>
                        </ul>
                    </li>
                </ul>
            </li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: Deep nesting is hard to read, navigate, and maintain.

✅ Correct: Keep nesting to 3–4 levels; use <details> or separate pages for deeper hierarchies.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using the Obsolete type Attribute
docs.text:
<ul type="square">
Why it's wrong: The type attribute is obsolete in HTML5.

✅ Correct: 

<ul class="square">

.square { list-style-type: square; }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Hardcoding Bullets or Numbers
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>• Item 1</li>
    <li>• Item 2</li>
</ul>
Why it's wrong: The browser adds bullets automatically.

✅ Correct: 

<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <dl> for General Lists
docs.text:
<dl>
    <dt>Item 1</dt>
    <dd>Item 2</dd>
</dl>
Why it's wrong: <dl> is for term–description pairs, not general lists.

✅ Correct: Use <ul> for general lists.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• DOM size – each list adds DOM nodes. Deep nesting increases DOM size.
  • Rendering – deeply nested lists increase layout complexity.
  • CSS selectors – ul ul ul selectors can be slow for very deep nesting.
  • Marker rendering – each level requires a marker. Minimal cost.
  • Large lists – lists with thousands of items can impact rendering; consider virtualization.
  • <details> – using <details> for collapsible lists can improve initial render performance.
  • display: grid or display: flex – efficient for card grids and menus.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep lists shallow – avoid deep nesting.
  2. Use <details> for collapsible content.
  3. Virtualize very large lists.
  4. Minify HTML.
  5. Avoid inline styles.
  6. Use CSS classes.
  7. Use content-visibility: auto for large lists (with caution).

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if list items contain user-generated content, sanitize it before rendering.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent or a sanitizer.
  • Injection – never insert user input directly into <li>, <dt>, or <dd> without escaping.
  • Navigation links – validate URLs to prevent open redirects and XSS.
  • No direct security implications – list elements themselves are not security risks.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into list items.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate URLs – for navigation links.
  4. Use rel="noopener noreferrer" – for external links.
  5. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the list structure.
  • Collapse/expand nodes – to see the hierarchy.
  • Computed styles – check list-style-type, padding-inline-start.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the list and listitem roles.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('ul') to count lists.
  • getComputedStyle(ul).listStyleType – check the marker style.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting and attributes.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the list is announced correctly.
  • Test with CSS disabled – ensure the list still makes sense.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and SEO.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For grouped content – features, categories, tags.
  • For ordered content – steps, rankings, sequences.
  • For term–description pairs – glossaries, FAQs, metadata.
  • For navigation – menus, breadcrumbs, site maps.
  • For card grids – when items are semantically a list.
  • For documentation – parameters, options, procedures.
  • For structured data – FAQ, HowTo, ItemList.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For single items – use <p> or <div>.
  • For arbitrary grouping – use <div> if there's no semantic list.
  • For tabular data – use <table>.
  • For content that isn't a list – don't force it.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <ul> – unordered list.
  • <ol> – ordered list.
  • <dl> – description list.
  • <li> – list item.
  • <dt> – description term.
  • <dd> – description details.
  • <menu> – semantic alternative to <ul>.
  • <nav> – navigation landmark.
  • aria-label – for multiple navs.
  • aria-current – for the current page.
  • role="list" – preserves list semantics with list-style: none.
  • list-style-type – CSS property for marker style.
  • ::marker – CSS pseudo-element for marker styling.
  • CSS counters – for custom numbering.
  • Structured data – for rich results.
  • WCAG – accessibility guidelines.
  • ARIA Authoring Practices – guidance for ARIA.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <ul>, <ol>, and <dl> elements have been part of HTML since HTML 1.0 (1991). They are among the oldest HTML elements.

  • The Safari/VoiceOver list-style: none bug has been a known issue for years. Adding role="list" is the recommended workaround.

  • Screen readers announce lists as "list of N items" and each item as "item N of M". This helps users understand the structure.

  • Search engines use lists to understand grouped and sequenced content. Combining lists with structured data can trigger rich results.

  • Breadcrumb navigation should use <ol> because the order of pages matters (from general to specific).

  • Navigation menus should use <ul> wrapped in <nav> with aria-label.

  • The aria-current="page" attribute tells assistive technologies which link represents the current page.

  • CSS counters can create custom numbering schemes like "1.1", "1.1.1", "1.1.1.1" for nested lists.

  • The ::marker pseudo-element can style markers with color, font, and content.

  • Card grids are often built with <ul> because the cards are semantically a list.

  • The <details> element can be used inside <li> to create collapsible nested lists without JavaScript.

  • Deep nesting (10+ levels) is hard to read and navigate. Most content needs only 3–4 levels.

  • display: grid on a <ul> is a common technique for card layouts.

  • display: flex on a <ul> is a common technique for horizontal navigation menus.

  • The padding-inline-start property is used for logical indentation (respects RTL).

  • Structured data (JSON-LD, Microdata) can be combined with lists for rich results.

  • WCAG 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) requires that lists be marked up semantically.

  • WCAG 2.4.6 (Headings and Labels) applies to list headings and labels.

  • WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) requires that lists have appropriate roles.

  • The ARIA Authoring Practices recommends using native HTML lists wherever possible.

  • The HTML Living Standard defines the content models for lists: <li> is the only valid child of <ul> and <ol>.

  • Lists are read depth-first by screen readers, which is the natural reading order for hierarchical content.

  • Nested lists are a key part of document outlines, site maps, navigation menus, and taxonomies.

  • List semantics are preserved even when lists are styled as grids or flex containers.

  • List items can contain any flow content, including headings, paragraphs, images, and other lists.

  • Description lists (<dl>) are used in FAQ rich results by Google.

  • Ordered lists (<ol>) are used in HowTo rich results by Google.

  • Unordered lists (<ul>) are used in ItemList rich results by Google.

  • role="list" is the recommended fix for the Safari/VoiceOver list-style: none bug.

  • Testing with screen readers is essential for ensuring list accessibility.

  • Consistency in list usage across a site improves usability and maintainability.

  • Documentation of list conventions helps teams maintain consistency.

  • List best practices are not rigid rules — they are heuristics that guide good decisions.

  • Following list best practices leads to more accessible, maintainable, and semantic HTML.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• List best practices are guidelines for choosing, structuring, and styling HTML lists.
  • Choose the right list type: <ol> for ordered content, <ul> for unordered content, <dl> for term–description pairs.
  • Use <li> as the only child of <ul> and <ol>.
  • Nest lists inside <li> — not between items.
  • Keep nesting shallow — 3–4 levels maximum.
  • Preserve semantics with role="list" when using list-style: none.
  • Use <nav> for navigation lists with aria-label and aria-current.
  • Use <dl> for glossaries, FAQs, and metadata.
  • Use structured data for rich results (FAQ, HowTo, ItemList).
  • Style with CSS — list-style-type, ::marker, CSS counters.
  • Don't use lists for layout — use CSS Grid or Flexbox (except when items are semantically a list, like card grids).
  • Validate and test — with the W3C validator and screen readers.
  • Common mistakes: using <ul> for ordered content, using <div> instead of <ul>, placing content directly inside <ul>, nesting lists between <li> elements, and removing markers without preserving semantics.
  • List best practices lead to more accessible, maintainable, and semantic HTML — benefiting users, developers, and search engines alike.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A table structure in HTML is the hierarchical arrangement of elements that define a two-dimensional grid of data — rows and columns — where the intersection of a row and column forms a cell containing data. It is created using the <table> element as the container, with rows defined by <tr> (table row), header cells by <th> (table header), and data cells by <td> (table data).

A well-structured table separates:

  • The table itself (<table>).
  • The caption (<caption>) — a title for the table.
  • Column groups (<colgroup> and <col>) — for styling columns.
  • Row groups (<thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>) — for header, body, and footer rows.
  • Rows (<tr>).
  • Cells (<th> for headers, <td> for data).

This hierarchy mirrors how data is organised in spreadsheets and databases: rows represent records, columns represent fields, and cells hold values.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Table structure serves several essential purposes:

  • Tabular data – represents data with two or more dimensions.
  • Semantic relationship – links cells to their row and column headers.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce header-cell associations.
  • SEO – search engines understand the tabular structure.
  • Styling – CSS can target rows, columns, and cells precisely.
  • Data extraction – tools can parse tables as structured data.
  • Layout (historical) – tables were used for layout before CSS matured (now discouraged).

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <table> element is flow content and palpable content. It is a block-level element and can appear anywhere flow content is accepted — inside <body>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <div>, <figure>, and <li>. It is not related to the other list elements, but like lists, it provides structured representation of grouped information.

<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Month</th>
            <th scope="col">Sales</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">January</th>
            <td>$10,000</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">February</th>
            <td>$12,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Some data is inherently two-dimensional: a grid of values where each value is identified by its position in a row and a column. Examples include:

  • Financial reports (rows = months, columns = categories).
  • Scientific data (rows = samples, columns = measurements).
  • Timetables (rows = days, columns = hours).
  • Product comparison (rows = features, columns = products).
  • Sports standings (rows = teams, columns = statistics).

Without a dedicated structure, authors had to fake grids using monospaced text, columns of <div> elements, or nested lists. These approaches have serious problems:

  • No semantic relationship – machines can't tell which header belongs to which cell.
  • Poor accessibility – screen readers can't announce "Sales for January is $10,000".
  • No structure in APIs – data extraction is unreliable.
  • Fragile styling – columns can't be styled independently.
  • No machine readability – search engines can't extract tabular data.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic table Machines can't identify tabular data. Monospaced text Fragile, hard to maintain, inaccessible. CSS columns or floats No row/column relationship, fragile. Nested lists No 2D structure, confusing. No header–cell association Screen readers can't announce context. No styling hooks Columns can't be styled independently.

docs.title: Why the <table> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <table> element was introduced in HTML 3.2 (1997) — although earlier versions had rudimentary table support via the <pre> element and the "HTML+" proposal. The <table> element was designed to represent tabular data with rows and columns, mirroring the structure of spreadsheets.

It enables:

  • Semantic structure – machines know the content is a table.
  • Header–cell relationships – <th> cells are associated with <td> cells via scope and headers.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce the row and column headers for each cell.
  • Styling – CSS can target rows (<tr>), columns (<col>), and cells.
  • Data extraction – tools can parse the table as a two-dimensional array.
  • Structured data – search engines can use tables for rich results.

The <table> element was heavily used for layout in the 1990s and early 2000s before CSS matured. This usage is now strongly discouraged — tables should only be used for tabular data. The HTML specification includes detailed rules for table structure to ensure accessibility and interoperability.

docs.title: The "Spreadsheet" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a table as a spreadsheet. Rows are records, columns are fields, and cells are values. The row headers (like "January") and column headers (like "Sales") provide context for each cell. Just as a spreadsheet has a header row and header column, an HTML table uses <th> to mark those headers.

docs.title: The "Grid Coordinates" Analogy
docs.text:
A table is like a grid with coordinates. Each cell has an (x, y) position — its column and row. The headers provide the labels for those coordinates. For example, the cell at (column=Sales, row=January) contains $10,000.

              Month (header)    Sales (header)
              ──────────────    ──────────────
January       January           $10,000        ← Cell
(row header)
February      February          $12,000        ← Cell

docs.title: The "Excel Sheet" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine pasting a table from Excel into a web page. The structure — rows, columns, headers, footers — mirrors the spreadsheet. HTML tables bring that structure to the web, with semantics and accessibility for screen readers.

docs.title: The "Database Record" Analogy
docs.text: Each row is like a database record; each column is a field; each cell is a value. The <th> elements are the field names.

docs.title: Concept 1: The <table> Container
docs.text:
The <table> element is the container. It accepts:

  • <caption> (optional, must be first).
  • <colgroup> (optional).
  • <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> (row groups).
  • <tr> (direct rows, though row groups are preferred).

The <table> element can appear inside any flow content context.

docs.title: Concept 2: The <caption> Element
docs.text:
The <caption> element provides a title or description for the table. It must be the first child of <table>. It is announced by screen readers before the table data.

<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    ...
</table>

Why: A caption helps users understand what the table represents.

docs.title: Concept 3: The <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> Elements
docs.text:
These elements group rows into logical sections:

  • <thead> – the header rows (typically one row with <th> cells).
  • <tbody> – the main body rows (one or more <tbody> groups).
  • <tfoot> – the footer rows (typically totals or summaries).

The order in the markup can be <thead>, <tfoot>, <tbody> (in HTML4) or <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> (in HTML5). The browser always renders <tfoot> at the bottom.

docs.title: Concept 4: The <tr> Element
docs.text: The <tr> element defines a table row. It is a child of <table>, <thead>, <tbody>, or <tfoot>. It contains <th> or <td> cells.

docs.title: Concept 5: The <th> and <td> Elements
docs.text:
• <th> – a header cell. By default, it's bold and centered. It can have a scope attribute to indicate whether it's a header for a row, column, or group.
  • <td> – a data cell. By default, it's left-aligned and regular weight.

docs.title: Concept 6: The scope Attribute
docs.text:
The scope attribute on <th> indicates what the header applies to:

Value Meaning col The header applies to the entire column below it. row The header applies to the entire row to its right. colgroup The header applies to a group of columns. rowgroup The header applies to a group of rows. 
<th scope="col">Month</th>
<th scope="row">January</th>

Why: The scope attribute helps screen readers announce the correct header for each cell.

docs.title: Concept 7: The colspan and rowspan Attributes
docs.text:
• colspan – the number of columns a cell spans.
  • rowspan – the number of rows a cell spans.
<td colspan="2">Spans two columns</td>
<td rowspan="2">Spans two rows</td>

Note: Spanning should be used sparingly, as it complicates accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 8: The <colgroup> and <col> Elements
docs.text:
The <colgroup> element groups <col> elements, which define columns. The <col> element can have span and style attributes (though style is often applied via CSS classes).

<colgroup>
    <col span="1" class="label-column">
    <col span="3" class="data-columns">
</colgroup>

Use case: Styling columns without targeting each cell.

docs.title: Concept 9: The headers Attribute
docs.text:
For complex tables with irregular headers, the headers attribute on <td> references the id values of the relevant header cells.

<table>
    <tr>
        <th id="name">Name</th>
        <th id="age">Age</th>
        <th id="city">City</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td headers="name">Alice</td>
        <td headers="age">30</td>
        <td headers="city">New York</td>
    </tr>
</table>

Note: For most tables, scope is sufficient. headers is used for complex tables with irregular structures.

docs.title: Concept 10: Content Model
docs.text:
• <table> – accepts <caption>, <colgroup>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, <tr> (in that order).
  • <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> – accept <tr> elements.
  • <tr> – accepts <th> and <td> elements.
  • <th> and <td> – accept flow content.

docs.title: Concept 11: Default Browser Styling
docs.text:
Browsers apply default styles:

table {
    display: table;
    border-collapse: separate;
    border-spacing: 2px;
    border: 1px solid gray;
}

th {
    display: table-cell;
    font-weight: bold;
    text-align: center;
    vertical-align: middle;
}

td {
    display: table-cell;
    text-align: left;
    vertical-align: middle;
}

The default border and spacing can be changed with CSS.

docs.title: Concept 12: Accessibility — Header–Cell Association
docs.text:
The combination of <th>, scope, and row/column position creates the header–cell association. Screen readers use this to announce:

"January, Sales: $10,000."

Without <th> and scope, screen readers can't provide this context.

docs.title: Concept 13: Table vs. Layout
docs.text:
Tables should only be used for tabular data, not for layout. Layout should use CSS Grid or Flexbox. The HTML specification includes a warning about this.

Exception: HTML emails often use tables for layout because email clients have limited CSS support. This is a legacy practice but still common.

docs.title: Concept 14: Complex Tables
docs.text:
For tables with irregular headers (e.g., headers spanning multiple rows or columns), use:

  • colspan and rowspan on <th> and <td>.
  • id on header cells.
  • headers on data cells to reference the header IDs.
  • scope for simple cases.

docs.title: Concept 15: Table vs. Description List
docs.text:
Aspect Table Description List Structure 2D grid Term–description pairs Use case Multi-column data Glossaries, FAQs Accessibility Header–cell association Term–definition association Example Financial report Dictionary

Rule: Use tables for 2D data; use <dl> for term–description pairs.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of a Table
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<table>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the table.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes each child:
    │   ├── <caption> → creates a caption node.
    │   ├── <colgroup> → creates a column group node.
    │   ├── <thead> → creates a header row group.
    │   ├── <tbody> → creates a body row group.
    │   ├── <tfoot> → creates a footer row group.
    │   └── <tr> → creates a row (wrapped in an implicit <tbody>).
    │
    ▼
4.  For each row, it processes the cells:
    │   ├── <th> → creates a header cell node.
    │   └── <td> → creates a data cell node.
    │
    ▼
5.  The browser computes the table grid:
    │   ├── Determines the number of columns.
    │   ├── Assigns cells to grid positions.
    │   └── Handles colspan and rowspan.
    │
    ▼
6.  Default styles are applied.
    │
    ▼
7.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   ├── role: table.
    │   ├── role: row for each <tr>.
    │   ├── role: columnheader for <th scope="col">.
    │   ├── role: rowheader for <th scope="row">.
    │   └── role: cell for <td>.
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered with the table.

docs.title: The Table Grid Algorithm
docs.text:
The browser builds the table grid using an algorithm defined in the HTML specification:

  1. Determine the number of columns.
  2. For each row, assign cells to columns, accounting for colspan and rowspan.
  3. Fill in any gaps with empty cells.

This algorithm ensures consistent rendering even for complex tables.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree:

  • <table> → role: table.
  • <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> → role: rowgroup.
  • <tr> → role: row.
  • <th scope="col"> → role: columnheader.
  • <th scope="row"> → role: rowheader.
  • <td> → role: cell.

Screen readers use these roles to announce the table structure.

docs.title: Table Layout Algorithms
docs.text:
CSS provides two table layout algorithms:

  • table-layout: auto (default) – the browser adjusts column widths based on content.
  • table-layout: fixed – the browser uses fixed column widths, improving performance for large tables.

docs.title: The HTMLTableElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <table> is represented by HTMLTableElement:

Property/Method Description caption Returns the <caption> element. tHead Returns the <thead> element. tBodies Returns a collection of <tbody> elements. tFoot Returns the <tfoot> element. rows Returns all <tr> elements. insertRow(index) Inserts a new row. deleteRow(index) Deletes a row. createCaption() Creates a <caption>. deleteCaption() Deletes the caption. 
const table = document.querySelector('table');
console.log(table.rows.length); // Number of rows
console.log(table.tHead);        // <thead> element

docs.title: The HTMLTableRowElement Interface
docs.text:
<tr> is represented by HTMLTableRowElement:

Property/Method Description cells Returns all <td> and <th> cells. rowIndex The row's position in the table. sectionRowIndex The row's position in its row group. insertCell(index) Inserts a new cell. deleteCell(index) Deletes a cell.

docs.title: The HTMLTableCellElement Interface
docs.text:
<th> and <td> are represented by HTMLTableCellElement:

Property Description cellIndex The cell's position in the row. colSpan The value of the colspan attribute. rowSpan The value of the rowspan attribute. headers The value of the headers attribute. scope The value of the scope attribute (for <th>).

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
table {
    display: table;
    border-collapse: separate;
    border-spacing: 2px;
    border: 1px solid gray;
    box-sizing: border-box;
    text-indent: initial;
}

thead {
    display: table-header-group;
    vertical-align: middle;
    border-color: inherit;
}

tbody {
    display: table-row-group;
    vertical-align: middle;
    border-color: inherit;
}

tfoot {
    display: table-footer-group;
    vertical-align: middle;
    border-color: inherit;
}

tr {
    display: table-row;
    vertical-align: inherit;
    border-color: inherit;
}

th {
    display: table-cell;
    font-weight: bold;
    text-align: center;
    vertical-align: middle;
}

td {
    display: table-cell;
    vertical-align: inherit;
}

docs.title: Table Layout Algorithms
docs.text:
• Auto layout: The browser distributes column widths based on content. Slower for large tables.
  • Fixed layout: Column widths are set by the first row or by explicit widths. Faster.

docs.title: The border-collapse Property
docs.text:
• border-collapse: separate (default) – each cell has its own border, with spacing between them.
  • border-collapse: collapse – borders are merged into a single border.
table {
    border-collapse: collapse;
}

docs.title: The border-spacing Property
docs.text:
Controls the spacing between cells when border-collapse: separate.

table {
    border-spacing: 0;
}

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Table
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<table>`, `<tr>`, `<th>`, and `<td>` elements.
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── Table, row, and cell nodes are created.
    │
    ▼
4.  The browser builds the table grid.
    │   └── Determines columns, assigns cells, handles spans.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied.
    │   └── Borders, spacing, alignment.
    │
    ▼
6.  The table is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  The accessibility tree is built.
    │   └── Table, row, columnheader, rowheader, cell roles.
    │
    ▼
8.  Screen readers announce the table.
    │   └── Table with N rows, M columns.
    │
    ▼
9.  Search engines may use the table for rich results.
    │
    ▼
10. JavaScript may modify the table dynamically.
    │   └── Adding/removing rows, updating cells.
    │
    ▼
11. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
// Add a row
const table = document.querySelector('table');
const newRow = table.insertRow(-1); // Insert at the end
const cell1 = newRow.insertCell(0);
cell1.textContent = 'New Row';
const cell2 = newRow.insertCell(1);
cell2.textContent = '$5,000';

// Update a cell
const cell = table.rows[1].cells[1];
cell.textContent = '$15,000';

docs.title: Example 11: Table with Sorting via JavaScript
docs.text:
<table id="sortable">
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col" data-sort="name">Name</th>
            <th scope="col" data-sort="age">Age</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr><td>Charlie</td><td>35</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Alice</td><td>30</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Bob</td><td>25</td></tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

<script>
    document.querySelectorAll('th[data-sort]').forEach(th => {
        th.style.cursor = 'pointer';
        th.addEventListener('click', () => {
            const table = th.closest('table');
            const tbody = table.tBodies[0];
            const rows = Array.from(tbody.rows);
            const key = th.dataset.sort;
            const index = Array.from(th.parentElement.children).indexOf(th);
            rows.sort((a, b) => a.cells[index].textContent.localeCompare(b.cells[index].textContent));
            rows.forEach(row => tbody.appendChild(row));
        });
    });
</script>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Financial reports Monthly sales, budgets Scientific data Measurements, samples Timetables Schedules, calendars Product comparison Features, prices Sports standings Teams, statistics Employee directory Names, roles, contacts Inventory Items, quantities Pricing tables Tiers, features Statistics Metrics, KPIs Data exports CSV-like views Course schedules Days, times Event agendas Time, session

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <table> only for tabular data – not for layout.

  2. Include a <caption> – to describe the table's purpose.

  3. Use <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> – to group rows logically.

  4. Use <th> for header cells – with scope="col" or scope="row".

  5. Use <td> for data cells – never for headers.

  6. Use scope – for simple tables; use headers for complex tables.

  7. Use colspan and rowspan sparingly – they complicate accessibility.

  8. Use <colgroup> and <col> – for styling columns.

  9. Style with CSS – use border-collapse, border-spacing, padding.

  10. Avoid presentational attributes – border, cellpadding, cellspacing, width are obsolete.

  11. Use table-layout: fixed – for large tables with known column widths.

  12. Make tables responsive – with horizontal scroll or responsive patterns.

  13. Test with screen readers – ensure header–cell associations are announced.

  14. Validate your HTML – check for invalid nesting.

  15. Use <caption> before <colgroup> – the order matters.

  16. Don't use tables for layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

  17. Provide a summary – for complex tables (via <caption> or aria-describedby).

  18. Use aria-describedby – for additional context.

  19. Sort rows with JavaScript – while preserving accessibility.

  20. Document your table conventions – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Tables for Layout
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <td>Sidebar</td>
        <td>Main Content</td>
    </tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Tables are for data, not layout. Use CSS Grid or Flexbox.

✅ Correct: Use CSS for layout.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Omitting <th> for Headers
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <td><strong>Name</strong></td>
        <td><strong>Age</strong></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Alice</td>
        <td>30</td>
    </tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Screen readers won't announce header–cell associations.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <tr>
        <th scope="col">Name</th>
        <th scope="col">Age</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Alice</td>
        <td>30</td>
    </tr>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using scope Without Value
docs.text:
<th scope>Name</th>
Why it's wrong: The scope attribute should have a value (col, row, etc.).

✅ Correct: 

<th scope="col">Name</th>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Presentational Attributes
docs.text:
<table border="1" cellpadding="10" cellspacing="0" width="100%">
Why it's wrong: These attributes are obsolete.

✅ Correct: 

<table class="data-table">

.data-table {
    border-collapse: collapse;
    width: 100%;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Close Cells
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <td>Cell 1
        <td>Cell 2
    </tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: While browsers may infer closing tags, it's better to close them explicitly.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <tr>
        <td>Cell 1</td>
        <td>Cell 2</td>
    </tr>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <td> for Table Headers
docs.text:
<tr>
    <td><strong>Name</strong></td>
</tr>
Why it's wrong: Use <th> for headers, not <td> with bold.

✅ Correct: 

<tr>
    <th>Name</th>
</tr>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Omitting <tbody>
docs.text:
<table>
    <thead>
        <tr><th>Name</th></tr>
    </thead>
    <tr><td>Alice</td></tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Missing <tbody> is not invalid (browsers infer it), but explicit row groups improve clarity and accessibility.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <thead>
        <tr><th>Name</th></tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr><td>Alice</td></tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using colspan Without Adjusting Column Count
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <th colspan="2">Name</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Alice</td>
        <td>Bob</td>
        <td>Charlie</td> <!-- Wrong column count -->
    </tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: The columns don't match, causing layout issues.

✅ Correct: Ensure all rows have the correct number of columns.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Providing a Caption
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr><th>Name</th><th>Age</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Alice</td><td>30</td></tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Users and screen readers don't know the table's purpose.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <caption>Employee Directory</caption>
    <tr><th>Name</th><th>Age</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Alice</td><td>30</td></tr>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <caption> After <thead>
docs.text:
<table>
    <thead><tr><th>Name</th></tr></thead>
    <caption>Directory</caption>
</table>
Why it's wrong: <caption> must be the first child of <table>.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <caption>Directory</caption>
    <thead><tr><th>Name</th></tr></thead>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Overusing Tables
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr><td><h1>My Website</h1></td></tr>
    <tr><td><p>Welcome!</p></td></tr>
    <tr><td><footer>© 2026</footer></td></tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: This is not tabular data; it's a layout.

✅ Correct: Use <header>, <main>, <footer>.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Table layout – table-layout: auto (default) requires the browser to measure content; slower for large tables. table-layout: fixed is faster.
  • Table rendering – tables are more expensive to render than block-level content. Large tables can slow down page rendering.
  • DOM size – each cell adds a DOM node. Large tables can increase memory usage.
  • Repaints – changes to a table cell may trigger reflows of the entire table.
  • Virtualization – for very large tables (hundreds of rows), consider virtualization.
  • border-collapse: collapse – slightly faster than separate.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use table-layout: fixed – for known column widths.
  2. Use border-collapse: collapse – for simpler rendering.
  3. Limit table size – virtualize large tables.
  4. Avoid complex spans – they complicate layout.
  5. Minify HTML – reduce file size.
  6. Use <colgroup> – for column styling (avoids per-cell styling).

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if table cells contain user-generated content, sanitize it before rendering.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent or a sanitizer.
  • Injection – never insert user input directly into <td>, <th>, or <caption> without escaping.
  • Data leakage – tables often contain sensitive data; ensure access controls are in place.
  • No direct security implications – the <table> element itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into table cells.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate structure – ensure the table structure is well-formed.
  4. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.
  5. Protect sensitive data – with server-side access controls.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the table structure.
  • Computed styles – check display: table, border-collapse, border-spacing.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the table, row, columnheader, rowheader, cell roles.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('table') to count tables.
  • table.rows – see all rows.
  • table.rows[i].cells – see all cells in a row.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting and obsolete attributes.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure header–cell associations are announced.
  • Test with CSS disabled – ensure the table still makes sense.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility and SEO.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For tabular data – financial reports, statistics, comparisons.
  • For structured data – schedules, timetables, directories.
  • For product comparisons – features, prices.
  • For scientific data – measurements, samples.
  • For email layouts (legacy) – email clients have limited CSS support.
  • For data exports – CSV-like views.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For lists – use <ul>, <ol>, or <dl>.
  • For term–description pairs – use <dl>.
  • For single-column data – use a list.
  • For navigation – use <nav> with <ul>.
  • For card layouts – use CSS Grid.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <tr> – table row.
  • <th> – table header cell.
  • <td> – table data cell.
  • <caption> – table caption.
  • <colgroup> – column group.
  • <col> – column.
  • <thead> – header row group.
  • <tbody> – body row group.
  • <tfoot> – footer row group.
  • scope attribute – header scope.
  • headers attribute – header–cell association for complex tables.
  • colspan and rowspan – cell spanning.
  • border-collapse – CSS property for border merging.
  • border-spacing – CSS property for cell spacing.
  • table-layout – CSS property for layout algorithm.
  • Structured data – for tabular rich results.
  • ARIA – role="table", role="row", role="columnheader", etc.
  • CSS Grid – for layout (replaces tables).

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <table> element was introduced in HTML 3.2 (1997), although earlier versions had rudimentary table support.

  • Tables were widely used for layout in the 1990s and early 2000s before CSS matured. This usage is now strongly discouraged.

  • The <th> element creates a header cell that is announced by screen readers with the associated data cells.

  • The scope attribute tells screen readers whether a header applies to a row (row), column (col), row group (rowgroup), or column group (colgroup).

  • The headers attribute on <td> references the id values of header cells. It's used for complex tables with irregular header structures.

  • colspan and rowspan allow cells to span multiple columns or rows. They should be used sparingly as they complicate accessibility.

  • The <caption> element must be the first child of <table>.

  • The <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> elements group rows logically. Browsers render <tfoot> at the bottom even if it appears before <tbody> in the markup.

  • The <colgroup> and <col> elements allow styling columns without targeting each cell.

  • table-layout: fixed can significantly speed up rendering for tables with known column widths.

  • border-collapse: collapse merges cell borders into a single border, producing a cleaner look.

  • Screen readers announce tables as "table with N rows, M columns" and read the headers for each cell.

  • The HTML specification includes a warning about using tables for layout: "Tables must not be used as layout aids."

  • Email clients often require tables for layout because they have limited CSS support. This is a legacy practice.

  • The <table> element is one of the most complex elements in HTML, with a detailed content model and rendering algorithm.

  • display: table in CSS allows non-table elements to behave like tables. This is useful for some layout patterns but should be used carefully.

  • role="table", role="row", role="cell", etc. are ARIA roles that mirror the native table semantics. They should only be used when native tables can't be used.

  • The table grid algorithm in the HTML specification determines how cells are positioned when colspan and rowspan are used.

  • Sticky table headers are a popular technique for large tables. They use position: sticky on <thead> th.

  • Responsive tables can be implemented with horizontal scroll, stacking (using display: block on small screens), or data attributes.

  • The <table> element is not deprecated, but its use for layout is discouraged.

  • Structured data (JSON-LD, Microdata) can be combined with tables for rich results.

  • Accessibility experts recommend keeping tables simple and using scope for header–cell associations.

  • The aria-describedby attribute can provide additional context for a table.

  • The <caption> element is announced by screen readers before the table data.

  • table-layout: fixed requires the first row (or <col> widths) to define column widths.

  • border-spacing only applies when border-collapse: separate.

  • The <col> element can have span but not width (the width attribute is obsolete).

  • Table rows can have a rowspan that extends beyond the number of rows in the row group — the browser will handle it.

  • Table cells can contain any flow content, including paragraphs, lists, images, and even other tables (nested tables).

  • Nested tables are valid but discouraged for performance and accessibility reasons.

  • The <table> element has been part of the web since the beginning and remains essential for tabular data.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A table structure is the hierarchical arrangement of elements that define a two-dimensional grid of data.
  • It is created with <table>, <caption>, <colgroup>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, <tr>, <th>, and <td>.
  • The <caption> element provides a title and must be the first child of <table>.
  • Row groups (<thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>) organise rows logically.
  • Header cells (<th>) with scope create header–cell associations for accessibility.
  • Data cells (<td>) contain the data.
  • colspan and rowspan allow cells to span multiple columns or rows.
  • <colgroup> and <col> allow styling columns.
  • Best practices: use tables only for tabular data, include a caption, use <th> with scope, use row groups, style with CSS, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include using tables for layout, omitting <th>, using presentational attributes, and forgetting the caption.
  • The <table> element is essential for financial reports, statistics, timetables, product comparisons, and any two-dimensional data.
  • It is one of the most structured and semantically rich elements in HTML — the foundation of tabular data on the web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Header cells are table cells that contain header information — labels that describe the data in other cells. They are created using the <th> element (short for "table header"). A <th> cell can act as a column header (describing the data below it) or a row header (describing the data to its right). Header cells are essential for making tables understandable to both sighted users and assistive technologies.

By default, browsers render <th> content in bold and centered, distinguishing it visually from data cells (<td>). However, the real value of <th> lies in its semantic meaning: it tells browsers and screen readers that the cell contains header information, not data. This enables assistive technologies to announce the correct header when reading a data cell.

Example: 

<table>
    <tr>
        <th scope="col">Month</th>
        <th scope="col">Sales</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <th scope="row">January</th>
        <td>$10,000</td>
    </tr>
</table>

In this table, "Month" and "Sales" are column headers, while "January" is a row header. Screen readers can announce: "January, Sales: $10,000."

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Header cells serve several essential purposes:

  • Label data – provide context for data cells.
  • Accessibility – screen readers use headers to announce cell context.
  • Semantic structure – distinguish headers from data.
  • Visual distinction – default bold/centered styling.
  • Styling hooks – CSS can target <th> separately from <td>.
  • Data extraction – tools can identify headers and data.
  • SEO – search engines understand the table structure.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <th> element is a table cell that appears inside a <tr> (table row). It can be a child of <tr> within <thead>, <tbody>, or <tfoot>. It is one of the two cell types in HTML tables, alongside <td> (table data). It is flow content and can contain any flow content — text, inline elements, paragraphs, lists, images, and even other tables.

<table>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Product</th>
            <th scope="col">Price</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">Widget</th>
            <td>$9.99</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
In a table, data cells (<td>) contain values, but those values have no meaning without context. A cell containing "$10,000" is meaningless unless you know it's the sales figure for January in the North region. The header cells provide that context.

Before <th> was standardized, authors had to fake headers using <td> with bold text, or use <thead> without semantic header cells. This created several problems:

  • No semantic distinction – machines couldn't tell headers from data.
  • Poor accessibility – screen readers couldn't announce the correct header for a cell.
  • Fragile styling – bold text could be changed without changing the meaning.
  • No header–cell association – data cells had no programmatic link to their headers.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No semantic header cell Machines couldn't identify headers. <td> with bold text No programmatic association; fragile. No scope attribute Screen readers couldn't determine header scope. No headers attribute Complex tables lacked header–cell association. Poor accessibility Screen readers couldn't announce cell context.

docs.title: Why the <th> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <th> element was introduced in HTML 3.2 (1997) as part of the table model. It was designed to represent header cells — cells that label rows or columns of data. Combined with the scope attribute (introduced in HTML4), it enables:

  • Semantic structure – machines know the cell is a header.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce the header for each data cell.
  • Styling – CSS can target headers separately.
  • Data extraction – tools can identify headers and data.
  • Visual clarity – default bold/centered styling.

The <th> element is a small but critical part of making tables accessible and machine-readable.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <th>
docs.text: <th>Header text</th>

docs.title: Column Header
docs.text:
<tr>
    <th scope="col">Name</th>
    <th scope="col">Age</th>
</tr>

docs.title: Row Header
docs.text:
<tr>
    <th scope="row">Alice</th>
    <td>30</td>
</tr>

docs.title: Table with Both Column and Row Headers
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Employee Directory</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Name</th>
            <th scope="col">Department</th>
            <th scope="col">Salary</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">Alice</th>
            <td>Engineering</td>
            <td>$120,000</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">Bob</th>
            <td>Design</td>
            <td>$95,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: The scope Attribute
docs.text:
The scope attribute tells the browser (and screen readers) whether the header applies to a column, row, column group, or row group.

Value Description col Header applies to the column below it. row Header applies to the row to its right. colgroup Header applies to a group of columns. rowgroup Header applies to a group of rows. 
<th scope="col">Month</th>
<th scope="row">January</th>

docs.title: Header with colspan
docs.text:
<tr>
    <th colspan="2" scope="colgroup">Name</th>
    <th scope="col">Age</th>
</tr>
<tr>
    <td>First</td>
    <td>Last</td>
    <td>30</td>
</tr>

docs.title: Header with rowspan
docs.text:
<tr>
    <th rowspan="2" scope="rowgroup">Name</th>
    <td>Alice</td>
</tr>
<tr>
    <td>Bob</td>
</tr>

docs.title: The headers Attribute (Complex Tables)
docs.text:
For complex tables with irregular headers, use headers on <td> to reference the id of the relevant <th> cells.

<table>
    <tr>
        <th id="name">Name</th>
        <th id="age">Age</th>
        <th id="city">City</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td headers="name">Alice</td>
        <td headers="age">30</td>
        <td headers="city">New York</td>
    </tr>
</table>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose Values scope Defines what the header applies to. col, row, colgroup, rowgroup colspan Number of columns the header spans. Integer rowspan Number of rows the header spans. Integer headers Space-separated IDs of header cells. IDs abbr Abbreviated version of the header (for screen readers). String

docs.title: The abbr Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text:
The abbr attribute on <th> provided an abbreviated version of the header for screen readers. It is obsolete in HTML5 and not supported by modern browsers. Use aria-label or a shorter header text instead.

<!-- Obsolete -->
<th abbr="Q1">First Quarter</th>

docs.title: The "Spreadsheet Headers" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a table as a spreadsheet. The column headers (A, B, C) and row headers (1, 2, 3) provide coordinates for each cell. In HTML, <th> provides the labels — "Month", "Sales", "January" — that make the data meaningful.

docs.title: The "Map Coordinates" Analogy
docs.text: A table is like a map grid. The column headers are the x-axis labels, the row headers are the y-axis labels, and the data cells are the locations. Without the labels, you can't find anything.

docs.title: The "Menu Categories" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a restaurant menu. The categories (Appetizers, Main Courses, Desserts) are column headers, and the items (Salad, Steak, Cake) are row headers. The prices are data cells. The headers organise the data.

docs.title: The "Database Fields" Analogy
docs.text: In a database, each column has a field name (header), and each row is a record. The <th> element is the field name; the <td> elements are the field values.

docs.title: Concept 1: <th> vs <td>
docs.text:
Aspect <th> <td> Meaning Header cell Data cell Default style Bold, centered Regular, left-aligned Accessibility role columnheader or rowheader cell scope attribute Yes No headers attribute Can have an id Can have headers Use case Labels Data

Rule: Use <th> for headers, <td> for data.

docs.title: Concept 2: The scope Attribute
docs.text:
The scope attribute is the most important attribute on <th>. It tells screen readers which cells the header applies to.

  • scope="col" – the header is a column header (applies to cells below).
  • scope="row" – the header is a row header (applies to cells to the right).
  • scope="colgroup" – the header applies to a group of columns.
  • scope="rowgroup" – the header applies to a group of rows.

Best practice: Always use scope on <th> in simple tables. It's the most reliable way to ensure accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 3: Header–Cell Association
docs.text:
The association between a header and its data cells is called header–cell association. It is created by:

  1. Position – headers in <thead> apply to columns; headers in <tbody> with scope="row" apply to rows.
  2. scope attribute – explicitly declares the scope.
  3. headers attribute – references header IDs (for complex tables).

Screen readers use this association to announce: "January, Sales: $10,000."

docs.title: Concept 4: Column Headers
docs.text:
Column headers are <th> cells that label columns. They typically appear in the first row of the table, inside <thead>.

<thead>
    <tr>
        <th scope="col">Month</th>
        <th scope="col">Sales</th>
    </tr>
</thead>

docs.title: Concept 5: Row Headers
docs.text:
Row headers are <th> cells that label rows. They typically appear in the first column of the table, inside <tbody>.

<tbody>
    <tr>
        <th scope="row">January</th>
        <td>$10,000</td>
    </tr>
</tbody>

docs.title: Concept 6: Headers with colspan and rowspan
docs.text:
Headers can span multiple columns or rows:

<th colspan="2" scope="colgroup">Name</th>
<th rowspan="2" scope="rowgroup">Region</th>

Note: Spanning headers should be used carefully, as they complicate accessibility. Use headers for complex tables.

docs.title: Concept 7: The headers Attribute
docs.text:
For complex tables with irregular headers, the headers attribute on <td> references the id values of the relevant <th> cells.

<th id="name">Name</th>
<td headers="name">Alice</td>

When to use: When scope alone is insufficient — e.g., headers that span multiple columns or rows, or headers in different parts of the table.

docs.title: Concept 8: Accessibility
docs.text:
Screen readers use <th>, scope, and headers to announce the correct header for each data cell. Without these, the table is just a grid of numbers with no context.

Best practice: Always use <th> with scope for simple tables. Use headers for complex tables. Test with screen readers.

docs.title: Concept 9: Styling Header Cells
docs.text:
th {
    background: #2c3e50;
    color: white;
    font-weight: bold;
    text-align: left;
    padding: 0.75rem;
}

You can style <th> separately from <td>.

docs.title: Concept 10: The abbr Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text: The abbr attribute on <th> provided an abbreviated version of the header for screen readers. It is obsolete in HTML5. Use shorter header text or aria-label instead.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <th>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<th>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the header cell.
    │
    ▼
3.  It reads the `scope`, `colspan`, `rowspan`, and `headers` attributes.
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes the content (flow content).
    │
    ▼
5.  When the closing tag is encountered, the cell is closed.
    │
    ▼
6.  The browser computes the table grid.
    │
    ▼
7.  Default styles are applied:
    │   ├── font-weight: bold
    │   ├── text-align: center
    │   └── display: table-cell
    │
    ▼
8.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   ├── role: columnheader (for scope="col")
    │   ├── role: rowheader (for scope="row")
    │   └── role: cell (if no scope)
    │
    ▼
9.  The page is rendered.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree:

  • <th scope="col"> → role: columnheader.
  • <th scope="row"> → role: rowheader.
  • <th> without scope → role: cell (or columnheader/rowheader based on position).

Screen readers use the roles and the header–cell associations to announce the table.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
th {
    display: table-cell;
    font-weight: bold;
    text-align: center;
    vertical-align: middle;
    padding: 1px;
}

The font-weight: bold and text-align: center distinguish <th> from <td>.

docs.title: The scope Attribute's Effect
docs.text:
The scope attribute determines the role in the accessibility tree:

  • scope="col" → columnheader.
  • scope="row" → rowheader.
  • scope="colgroup" → columnheader (for a group).
  • scope="rowgroup" → rowheader (for a group).

Without scope, the browser infers the role from the position:

  • In <thead> → columnheader.
  • In <tbody> with only one <th> in the row → rowheader.

However, explicit scope is more reliable across browsers and screen readers.

docs.title: The headers Attribute's Effect
docs.text: The headers attribute on <td> creates a direct association between the data cell and the header cells, bypassing the inference from position. This is used for complex tables.

docs.title: The HTMLTableCellElement Interface
docs.text:
Both <th> and <td> are represented by the HTMLTableCellElement interface:

Property Description cellIndex The cell's position in the row. colSpan The value of the colspan attribute. rowSpan The value of the rowspan attribute. headers The value of the headers attribute. scope The value of the scope attribute (for <th>). abbr The value of the abbr attribute (obsolete). 
const th = document.querySelector('th');
console.log(th.scope);   // "col"
console.log(th.colSpan); // 1

docs.title: The Accessibility Mapping
docs.text:
The browser's accessibility engine maps <th> to:

  • columnheader if scope="col" or if it's in <thead>.
  • rowheader if scope="row" or if it's the first cell in a <tbody> row.
  • cell if no scope and position is ambiguous.

The headers attribute creates direct associations.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
th {
    display: table-cell;
    font-weight: bold;
    text-align: center;
    vertical-align: middle;
}

docs.title: The scope Attribute in the Spec
docs.text: The scope attribute is defined in the HTML specification. It is an enumerated attribute with values row, col, rowgroup, colgroup, and the empty string (default).

docs.title: The headers Attribute in the Spec
docs.text: The headers attribute is a space-separated list of IDs. Each ID must match the id of a <th> element in the same table.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Header Cell
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<th>` element with `scope` and content.
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<th>` node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  The browser computes the table grid.
    │
    ▼
5.  Default styles are applied (bold, centered).
    │
    ▼
6.  The accessibility tree is built.
    │   └── role: columnheader or rowheader.
    │
    ▼
7.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
8.  Screen readers announce the headers and their associated data cells.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the table dynamically.
    │   └── Adding/removing headers, changing scope.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
// Change a header's scope
const th = document.querySelector('th');
th.scope = 'row';

// Add a new header cell
const tr = document.querySelector('tr');
const newTh = document.createElement('th');
newTh.scope = 'col';
newTh.textContent = 'New Column';
tr.appendChild(newTh);

<table>

            <th scope="col" data-sort="age" style="cursor: pointer;">Age</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr><td>Charlie</td><td>35</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Alice</td><td>30</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Bob</td><td>25</td></tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

<script>
    document.querySelectorAll('th[data-sort]').forEach(th => {
        th.addEventListener('click', () => {
            const table = th.closest('table');
            const tbody = table.tBodies[0];
            const rows = Array.from(tbody.rows);
            const index = Array.from(th.parentElement.children).indexOf(th);
            rows.sort((a, b) => a.cells[index].textContent.localeCompare(b.cells[index].textContent));
            rows.forEach(row => tbody.appendChild(row));
        });
    });
</script>
