                <td>$10,000</td>
                <td>$11,000</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <th scope="row">East</th>
                <td>$11,000</td>
                <td>$13,000</td>
                <td>$14,000</td>
                <td>$15,000</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <th scope="row">West</th>
                <td>$9,000</td>
                <td>$10,000</td>
                <td>$12,000</td>
                <td>$13,000</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
        <tfoot>
            <tr>
                <th scope="row">Total</th>
                <td>$38,000</td>
                <td>$44,000</td>
                <td>$49,000</td>
                <td>$53,000</td>
            </tr>
        </tfoot>
    </table>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Column headers Month, Sales, Region Row headers January, North, Alice Group headers Q1, Q2 (grouped under "Sales") Sticky headers Tables with many rows Sortable headers Clickable headers for sorting Comparison tables Features vs. products Financial reports Rows = months, columns = categories Statistics Rows = teams, columns = metrics Timetables Rows = days, columns = hours Directories Rows = people, columns = details

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use <th> for headers – never <td> with bold text.

  2. Use scope on every <th> – col for column headers, row for row headers.

  3. Use <thead> for column headers – and <tbody> for row headers.

  4. Use <th> in the first column for row headers – with scope="row".

  5. Use colspan and rowspan sparingly – for grouped headers.

  6. Use headers for complex tables – when scope is insufficient.

  7. Include a <caption> – to describe the table.

  8. Style <th> with CSS – use background, color, font-weight.

  9. Don't use the obsolete abbr attribute – use aria-label or shorter text.

  10. Test with screen readers – ensure headers are announced correctly.

  11. Validate your HTML – check for correct scope values and headers references.

  12. Use aria-label for icon-only headers – e.g., aria-label="First Quarter".

  13. Don't use <th> for data – use <td>.

  14. Don't omit scope – it's essential for accessibility.

  15. Use scope="colgroup" and scope="rowgroup" – for group headers.

  16. Keep headers concise – short, descriptive labels.

  17. Avoid headers with mixed content – keep them simple.

  18. Test on mobile – ensure headers are visible.

  19. Consider sticky headers – for long tables.

  20. Document your table conventions – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <td> for Headers
docs.text:
<tr>
    <td><strong>Name</strong></td>
    <td><strong>Age</strong></td>
</tr>
Why it's wrong: Screen readers won't announce these as headers.

✅ Correct: 

<tr>
    <th scope="col">Name</th>
    <th scope="col">Age</th>
</tr>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Omitting scope
docs.text:
<th>Name</th>
Why it's wrong: Screen readers may not correctly associate the header with its cells.

✅ Correct: 

<th scope="col">Name</th>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using scope Without Value
docs.text:
<th scope>Name</th>
Why it's wrong: The scope attribute requires a value.

✅ Correct: 

<th scope="col">Name</th>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using the Obsolete abbr Attribute
docs.text:
<th abbr="Q1">First Quarter</th>
Why it's wrong: abbr is obsolete in HTML5.

✅ Correct: 

<th scope="col" aria-label="First Quarter">Q1</th>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <th> for Data Cells
docs.text:
<tr>
    <th>Alice</th>
    <td>30</td>
</tr>
Why it's wrong: "Alice" is data, not a header.

✅ Correct: 

<tr>
    <td>Alice</td>
    <td>30</td>
</tr>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting scope="row" for Row Headers
docs.text:
<tr>
    <th>January</th>
    <td>$10,000</td>
</tr>
Why it's wrong: The header's scope is not explicitly declared.

✅ Correct: 

<tr>
    <th scope="row">January</th>
    <td>$10,000</td>
</tr>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using headers Without id
docs.text:
<td headers="name">Alice</td> <!-- No th with id="name" -->
Why it's wrong: The headers attribute references IDs that must exist.

✅ Correct: 

<th id="name">Name</th>
<td headers="name">Alice</td>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Close <th>
docs.text:
<th>Name
<td>Alice</td>
Why it's wrong: The <th> is not closed, causing parsing issues.

✅ Correct: 

<th>Name</th>
<td>Alice</td>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Overusing colspan and rowspan
docs.text:
<th colspan="5" rowspan="5">All Data</th>
Why it's wrong: Complex spans confuse screen readers and users.

✅ Correct: Use spans sparingly; use headers for complex associations.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing with Screen Readers
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr><th scope="col">Name</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Alice</td></tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Without testing, you don't know if headers are announced correctly.

✅ Correct: Test with NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <th> is lightweight – one DOM node per header cell.
  • Default styles – bold and centered; minimal rendering cost.
  • Sticky headers – position: sticky on <th> can improve usability but has a small performance cost.
  • Large tables – many header cells increase DOM size; virtualize if needed.
  • Complex spans – colspan and rowspan complicate layout; use sparingly.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep headers simple – avoid unnecessary content.
  2. Use scope – no performance impact.
  3. Use headers sparingly – only for complex tables.
  4. Use table-layout: fixed – for faster rendering.
  5. Minify HTML – reduce file size.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if header content contains user-generated data, sanitize it before rendering.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent or a sanitizer.
  • Injection – never insert user input directly into <th> without escaping.
  • No direct security implications – <th> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into header cells.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate structure – ensure the table structure is well-formed.
  4. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <th> elements.
  • Computed styles – check font-weight, text-align, background.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the columnheader or rowheader role.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('th') to list all headers.
  • th.scope – check the scope value.
  • Validator – check for invalid scope values and missing id references.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure headers are announced correctly.
  • Test with CSS disabled – ensure the table still makes sense.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For column headers – labels for columns.
  • For row headers – labels for rows.
  • For group headers – labels for row or column groups.
  • For sortable headers – clickable headers for sorting.
  • For sticky headers – headers that stay visible while scrolling.
  • For comparison tables – features vs. products.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For data cells – use <td>.
  • For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For non-tabular content – use lists or paragraphs.
  • For decorative text – use <span> or <div>.
  • For single-cell tables – use a paragraph.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <table> – table container.
  • <tr> – table row.
  • <td> – table data cell.
  • <caption> – table caption.
  • <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> – row groups.
  • <colgroup>, <col> – column groups.
  • scope attribute – header scope.
  • headers attribute – header–cell association.
  • colspan, rowspan – cell spanning.
  • abbr attribute – obsolete.
  • ARIA – columnheader, rowheader, cell roles.
  • Accessibility – header–cell associations.
  • Screen readers – announce headers.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <th> element was introduced in HTML 3.2 (1997) as part of the table model.

  • The scope attribute was introduced in HTML4 to improve table accessibility.

  • The abbr attribute on <th> was introduced in HTML4 but deprecated in HTML5. It was intended to provide an abbreviated version of the header for screen readers, but it was poorly supported.

  • Screen readers use <th>, scope, and headers to announce the correct header for each data cell.

  • The default styling for <th> is bold and centered, distinguishing it from <td>.

  • You can style <th> separately from <td> using CSS.

  • The scope attribute values are: col, row, colgroup, rowgroup.

  • The headers attribute creates a direct association between a data cell and one or more header cells, bypassing the inference from position.

  • For simple tables, scope is sufficient. For complex tables, use headers.

  • Screen readers announce tables as "table with N rows, M columns" and read the headers for each cell.

  • The colspan and rowspan attributes can be used on <th> to create grouped headers.

  • Sticky table headers are a popular technique for large tables. They use position: sticky on <thead> th.

  • Sortable table headers are often implemented with JavaScript, adding aria-sort to indicate the sort direction.

  • The aria-sort attribute can be used on <th> to indicate the current sort order: ascending, descending, none, or other.

  • role="columnheader" and role="rowheader" are the ARIA roles that correspond to <th scope="col"> and <th scope="row">.

  • The HTML specification recommends using scope on <th> elements for simple tables.

  • WCAG 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) requires that header–cell associations be programmatically determinable.

  • WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) requires that table headers have appropriate roles.

  • Testing with screen readers is essential for ensuring table accessibility.

  • Table headers are one of the most important accessibility features of HTML tables.

  • The <th> element can contain flow content, including paragraphs, lists, and images.

  • Nested tables can have their own header cells, but nested tables are discouraged for performance and accessibility reasons.

  • The headers attribute is useful for tables with irregular headers, such as those with headers that span multiple rows or columns.

  • scope="colgroup" and scope="rowgroup" are used for headers that apply to a group of columns or rows.

  • The id attribute on <th> is used with the headers attribute on <td> to create associations.

  • aria-label can be used on <th> to provide a more descriptive name for screen readers when the visible text is abbreviated.

  • aria-describedby can be used on <th> to reference a description elsewhere on the page.

  • aria-sort is used on <th> to indicate the current sort order in sortable tables.

  • Sticky headers are implemented with position: sticky on the <th> elements in <thead>.

  • Responsive tables often use overflow-x: auto on a wrapper to allow horizontal scrolling.

  • table-layout: fixed can improve rendering performance for large tables.

  • border-collapse: collapse produces a cleaner look for tables.

  • The <th> element is essential for making tables accessible and machine-readable.

  • Header cells are one of the most important parts of a well-structured table.

  • Best practices for header cells include using <th>, scope, <thead>, and testing with screen readers.

  • Common mistakes include using <td> for headers, omitting scope, and using the obsolete abbr attribute.

  • Following best practices for header cells leads to more accessible, maintainable, and semantic tables.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Header cells (<th>) are table cells that contain labels for rows or columns.
  • They are essential for making tables understandable to screen readers and other assistive technologies.
  • The scope attribute tells the browser whether a header applies to a column (col), row (row), column group (colgroup), or row group (rowgroup).
  • Column headers typically appear in <thead>; row headers typically appear in the first column of <tbody>.
  • The headers attribute on <td> references header IDs for complex tables.
  • colspan and rowspan allow headers to span multiple columns or rows.
  • The abbr attribute is obsolete; use aria-label or shorter text instead.
  • Best practices: always use <th> for headers, use scope on every header, use <thead> for column headers, test with screen readers, and validate your HTML.
  • Common mistakes include using <td> for headers, omitting scope, using abbr, and overusing colspan/rowspan.
  • The <th> element is essential for accessible, semantic, and machine-readable tables.
  • It is one of the most important parts of a well-structured table.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <caption> element is a semantic HTML element that provides a title or description for a table. It is the first child of the <table> element and appears above the table by default (though its position can be changed with CSS). The caption describes the table's purpose, content, or source, giving users context before they read the data.

Unlike a heading (<h1>–<h6>) that structures the document, the <caption> element is bound to its table — it is part of the table itself. This binding is programmatic: assistive technologies announce the caption as the table's name, and the caption is included when the table is copied or exported.

Example: 

<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales (2026)</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Month</th>
            <th scope="col">Sales</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">January</th>
            <td>$10,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <caption> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Context – tells users what the table is about before they read the data.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce the caption as the table's name.
  • Semantic binding – the caption is programmatically associated with the table.
  • SEO – search engines use the caption to understand the table's topic.
  • Data export – the caption is included when the table is copied to a spreadsheet.
  • Styling – provides a hook for CSS to style the table title.
  • Print – the caption appears in printed versions of the table.
  • Accessibility compliance – WCAG requires tables to have a caption or equivalent.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <caption> element is a child of <table> and must be the first child (before <colgroup>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, and <tr>). It is flow content and can contain any flow content — text, inline elements, paragraphs, lists, and even other tables (though nesting tables in captions is unusual).

<table>
    <caption>Table 1: Employee Directory</caption>
    <thead>...</thead>
    <tbody>...</tbody>
</table>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A table without a caption is a grid of numbers with no context. A user (or a screen reader) encountering a table with rows like "January $10,000" and "February $12,000" has to infer what the numbers mean. Is it sales? Expenses? Temperatures? Without a title, the table is ambiguous.

Before <caption> was standardized, authors had to place a heading or paragraph outside the table:

<h3>Monthly Sales</h3>
<table>
    ...
</table>

This approach has several problems:

  • No programmatic association – the heading is not bound to the table.
  • Fragile – if the table is moved, the heading might not follow.
  • Poor accessibility – screen readers don't announce the heading as the table's name.
  • No data export – the heading isn't included when the table is copied.
  • No styling hook – the heading can't be styled as part of the table.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No built-in table title Users had to infer the table's purpose. Heading outside the table No programmatic association. Screen readers couldn't announce the title Poor accessibility. No data export The title was lost when copying. No styling hook The title couldn't be styled with the table.

docs.title: Why the <caption> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <caption> element was introduced in HTML 3.2 (1997) as part of the table model. It was designed to provide a title or description for a table, bound to the table itself. It enables:

  • Semantic binding – the caption is programmatically associated with the table.
  • Accessibility – screen readers announce the caption as the table's name.
  • Data export – the caption is included when the table is copied.
  • Styling – the caption is a child of the table, so it can be styled with the table.
  • Print – the caption appears in printed versions.
  • SEO – search engines use the caption to understand the table.

The <caption> element is a small but critical part of making tables understandable and accessible.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <caption>
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Table title or description</caption>
    <!-- table content -->
</table>

docs.title: Simple Caption
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Month</th>
            <th scope="col">Sales</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">January</th>
            <td>$10,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: Caption with Numbering
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Table 1: Quarterly Sales by Region</caption>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

docs.title: Caption with Description
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Employee Salaries (USD, 2026)</caption>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

docs.title: Caption with Additional Context
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>
        Monthly Sales (2026)
        <span class="caption-note">Data updated on the first of each month.</span>
    </caption>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

docs.title: Caption Positioned Below the Table (CSS)
docs.text:
caption {
    caption-side: bottom;
}

By default, captions appear above the table. Use caption-side: bottom to place them below.

docs.title: Caption with text-align
docs.text:
caption {
    text-align: left; /* Default is center */
    padding: 0.5rem 0;
    font-weight: bold;
}

docs.title: Caption with Multiple Lines
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>
        Table 2: Annual Revenue by Product Category
        <br>
        <small>All figures in USD, rounded to the nearest thousand.</small>
    </caption>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part What It Does Why It Matters <caption> Defines the table's title. Provides context and accessibility. Position Must be the first child of <table>. Ensures correct rendering and semantics. Content Any flow content. Can include text, spans, small text, etc. caption-side CSS property for position. top (default) or bottom. text-align CSS property for alignment. center (default), left, or right.

docs.title: The "Title of a Document" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a <caption> as the title of a document. Just as a document's title tells you what it's about before you read the content, a table's caption tells you what the table contains before you read the data. The title is part of the document, not separate from it.

docs.title: The "Name Badge" Analogy
docs.text: A <caption> is like a name badge on a table. It identifies the table and gives context. Without a name badge, you'd have to guess who the person is (or what the table is about).

docs.title: The "Museum Placard" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a table as a museum exhibit. The caption is the placard that describes what you're looking at. Without the placard, the exhibit is just a collection of artifacts with no context.

docs.title: The "Spreadsheet Tab Name" Analogy
docs.text: In a spreadsheet, each sheet has a tab name (e.g., "Q1 Sales", "Expenses"). The <caption> is like the tab name — it tells you what the table contains before you look at the data.

docs.title: Concept 1: Caption Must Be First Child
docs.text:
The <caption> element must be the first child of <table>. It cannot appear after <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, or <tr>.

<!-- Correct -->
<table>
    <caption>Title</caption>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

<!-- Incorrect -->
<table>
    <thead>...</thead>
    <caption>Title</caption>
</table>

Why: The HTML specification requires the caption to be first. Placing it later causes parsing errors and unexpected rendering.

docs.title: Concept 2: Only One Caption Per Table
docs.text:
A table can have at most one <caption> element. Multiple captions are invalid.

<!-- Invalid -->
<table>
    <caption>Caption 1</caption>
    <caption>Caption 2</caption>
</table>

docs.title: Concept 3: Caption Position
docs.text:
By default, the caption appears above the table. The caption-side CSS property controls the position:

  • top (default) – caption appears above the table.
  • bottom – caption appears below the table.
caption {
    caption-side: bottom;
}

Note: caption-side: left and caption-side: right are not supported in most browsers.

docs.title: Concept 4: Caption Alignment
docs.text:
The default text-align for captions is center. You can change it:

caption {
    text-align: left;
}

docs.title: Concept 5: Caption Content Model
docs.text:
The <caption> element accepts flow content. It can contain:

  • Text.
  • Inline elements (<strong>, <em>, <span>, <a>, etc.).
  • Block-level elements (<p>, <div>, etc. — though these are unusual in captions).
  • Images.
<caption>
    <strong>Table 1:</strong> Monthly Sales
    <br>
    <small>All figures in USD.</small>
</caption>

docs.title: Concept 6: Accessibility — Caption as Table Name
docs.text:
Screen readers use the <caption> as the accessible name for the table. When a screen reader encounters the table, it announces:

"Table: Monthly Sales. Table with 3 rows, 2 columns."

This gives the user context before reading the data.

Best practice: Always provide a caption (or an equivalent via aria-label or aria-labelledby).

docs.title: Concept 7: Caption vs. Heading
docs.text:
Aspect <caption> <h1>–<h6> Purpose Title for a table. Title for a document section. Position Inside <table>. Outside the table. Accessibility Table's accessible name. Section's heading. Document outline Not part of the outline. Part of the outline. Data export Included when copying the table. Not included.

Rule: Use <caption> for table titles; use headings for section titles.

docs.title: Concept 8: Caption vs. aria-label
docs.text:
You can use aria-label on <table> to provide an accessible name without a visible caption:

<table aria-label="Monthly Sales">
    ...
</table>

Difference:

  • <caption> – visible and accessible.
  • aria-label – accessible only (not visible).

Best practice: Use <caption> for visible titles; use aria-label for tables where a visible title is not appropriate.

docs.title: Concept 9: Caption and aria-describedby
docs.text:
For additional context beyond the title, use aria-describedby to reference a description elsewhere on the page:

<table aria-describedby="table-desc">
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    ...
</table>
<p id="table-desc">Data is updated on the first of each month.</p>

docs.title: Concept 10: Caption and SEO
docs.text: Search engines use the <caption> to understand the table's topic. A descriptive caption can improve the table's relevance for search queries.

docs.title: Concept 11: Caption and Printing
docs.text: When a table is printed, the caption appears above (or below) the table, giving context on the printed page.

docs.title: Concept 12: Caption and Data Export
docs.text: When a table is copied to a spreadsheet, the caption is often included as the first row or as a note, providing context in the exported data.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <caption>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<caption>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the caption.
    │
    ▼
3.  It checks if the caption is the first child of the table:
    │   ├── If yes → associates it with the table.
    │   └── If no → parsing error (may be moved or ignored).
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes the caption's content (flow content).
    │
    ▼
5.  When the closing tag is encountered, the caption is closed.
    │
    ▼
6.  Default styles are applied:
    │   ├── display: table-caption
    │   ├── caption-side: top
    │   └── text-align: center
    │
    ▼
7.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   └── role: caption (or used as the table's accessible name).
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered with the caption above the table.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, the <caption> is used as the accessible name of the <table>. Screen readers announce:

"Table: Monthly Sales. Table with 3 rows, 2 columns."

Without a caption, the table has no accessible name, and screen readers announce just "Table."

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
caption {
    display: table-caption;
    text-align: center;
    caption-side: top;
    padding: 3px;
}

The display: table-caption value makes the caption behave like a table caption.

docs.title: The caption-side Property
docs.text:
caption {
    caption-side: top;    /* default */
    caption-side: bottom; /* below the table */
}

docs.title: The text-align Property
docs.text:
caption {
    text-align: center; /* default */
    text-align: left;
    text-align: right;
}

docs.title: The HTMLTableCaptionElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <caption> is represented by the HTMLTableCaptionElement interface, which inherits from HTMLElement. It has no specific properties beyond those of HTMLElement.

const caption = document.querySelector('caption');
console.log(caption.textContent); // The caption text

docs.title: The Table's caption Property
docs.text:
The <table> element has a caption property that returns the <caption> element (if present):

const table = document.querySelector('table');
console.log(table.caption); // <caption> element or null

docs.title: The Accessibility Mapping
docs.text:
The browser's accessibility engine uses the <caption> as the accessible name of the <table>. This is exposed to assistive technologies.

If no caption is present, the table has no accessible name (unless aria-label or aria-labelledby is provided).

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
caption {
    display: table-caption;
    text-align: center;
    caption-side: top;
}

docs.title: The caption-side Property
docs.text: The caption-side property is part of CSS2.1 and is supported in all modern browsers. It accepts top and bottom.

docs.title: The display: table-caption Value
docs.text: The display: table-caption value makes the caption behave like a table caption — it's rendered outside the table's border box but is part of the table's structure.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <caption> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<caption>` element as the first child of `<table>`.
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<caption>` node is created and associated with the table.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied (centered, top).
    │
    ▼
5.  The table is rendered with the caption.
    │
    ▼
6.  The accessibility tree is built.
    │   └── The caption is the table's accessible name.
    │
    ▼
7.  Screen readers announce the caption.
    │   └── "Table: Monthly Sales. Table with 3 rows, 2 columns."
    │
    ▼
8.  Search engines may use the caption for context.
    │
    ▼
9.  JavaScript may modify the caption dynamically.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the element is destroyed.

docs.title: Example 18: Caption in a Data Export
docs.text:
// When exporting a table to CSV, include the caption as a header row
function tableToCSV(table) {
    const caption = table.querySelector('caption');
    const rows = [];
    if (caption) {
        rows.push([caption.textContent.trim()]);
    }
    table.querySelectorAll('tr').forEach(tr => {
        const cells = Array.from(tr.querySelectorAll('th, td'))
            .map(cell => `"${cell.textContent.trim().replace(/"/g, '""')}"`);
        rows.push(cells.join(','));
    });
    return rows.join('\n');
}

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Financial reports "Monthly Sales (2026)" Statistics "Population by Country" Timetables "Class Schedule — Fall 2026" Comparison tables "Product Feature Comparison" Directories "Employee Directory" Sports standings "Premier League Standings" Scientific data "Experiment Results" Data exports "CSV Export — September 2026" Pricing tables "Pricing Plans" Inventory "Warehouse Inventory" Survey results "Customer Satisfaction Survey" Course schedules "Course Offerings — Spring 2026"

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always provide a caption – for tables with data.

  2. Place the caption first – it must be the first child of <table>.

  3. Use only one caption – multiple captions are invalid.

  4. Make the caption descriptive – tell users what the table is about.

  5. Include units – e.g., "(USD, 2026)" in the caption.

  6. Add numbering – "Table 1:" for reference in the text.

  7. Use <small> for secondary info – e.g., "All figures in USD."

  8. Style the caption with CSS – use caption-side, text-align, padding.

  9. Don't use a heading instead of a caption – headings are for sections, captions are for tables.

  10. Use aria-label for non-visible titles – when a visible caption isn't appropriate.

  11. Use aria-describedby for additional context – beyond the caption.

  12. Test with screen readers – ensure the caption is announced.

  13. Validate your HTML – check that the caption is first.

  14. Consider caption-side: bottom – for tables where the caption reads better below.

  15. Use lang and dir – for multilingual captions.

  16. Don't nest tables in captions – it's unusual and unnecessary.

  17. Keep captions concise – but descriptive.

  18. Include the caption in data exports – for context.

  19. Use the caption for SEO – search engines use it for context.

  20. Document your caption conventions – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placing the Caption After <thead>
docs.text:
<table>
    <thead>...</thead>
    <caption>Title</caption>
</table>
Why it's wrong: The caption must be the first child of <table>.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <caption>Title</caption>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Captions
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Caption 1</caption>
    <caption>Caption 2</caption>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Only one caption is allowed.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <caption>Caption</caption>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using a Heading Instead of a Caption
docs.text:
<h3>Monthly Sales</h3>
<table>
    ...
</table>
Why it's wrong: The heading is not programmatically associated with the table.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    ...
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Caption at All
docs.text:
<table>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>
Why it's wrong: The table has no accessible name; screen readers announce just "Table."

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <caption> Outside <table>
docs.text:
<caption>Title</caption>
<table>...</table>
Why it's wrong: <caption> must be inside <table>.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <caption>Title</caption>
    ...
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <caption> for Layout
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Header</caption>
    <tr><td>Content</td></tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: The caption is for the table's title, not for layout.

✅ Correct: Use <caption> for the title only.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting Units in the Caption
docs.text:
<caption>Sales</caption>
Why it's wrong: The reader doesn't know the units.

✅ Correct: 

<caption>Sales (USD, 2026)</caption>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using a Very Long Caption
docs.text:
<caption>This is a very long caption that goes on and on and on and takes up multiple lines and is hard to read...</caption>
Why it's wrong: Long captions are hard to scan.

✅ Correct: Keep the caption concise; use <small> for secondary info.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing with Screen Readers
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    ...
</table>
Why it's wrong: Without testing, you don't know if the caption is announced.

✅ Correct: Test with NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <figcaption> Instead of <caption>
docs.text:
<figure>
    <table>...</table>
    <figcaption>Monthly Sales</figcaption>
</figure>
Why it's wrong: <figcaption> is for figures, not tables. Use <caption> for tables.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <table>
        <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
        ...
    </table>
    <figcaption>Data source: Company CRM.</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <caption> is lightweight – one DOM node, minimal overhead.
  • Rendering – captions have negligible rendering cost.
  • Styling – simple CSS for captions is efficient.
  • Data export – including the caption in exports adds minimal cost.
  • Accessibility tree – captions add the table's accessible name; minimal impact.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep captions concise – shorter captions render faster.
  2. Use CSS for styling – avoid inline styles.
  3. Avoid unnecessary markup – keep the caption simple.
  4. Use <small> for secondary info – not a separate element.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if the caption contains user-generated content, sanitize it before rendering.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent or a sanitizer.
  • Injection – never insert user input directly into <caption> without escaping.
  • No direct security implications – <caption> itself is not a security risk.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into captions.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate structure – ensure the caption is first.
  4. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <caption> element.
  • Computed styles – check caption-side, text-align, display.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the table's accessible name.
  • Console – use document.querySelector('caption').textContent to read the caption.
  • table.caption – returns the caption element.
  • Validator – check that the caption is first and only one.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the caption is announced.
  • Test with CSS disabled – ensure the caption still makes sense.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For data tables – any table with data.
  • For financial reports – title and units.
  • For statistics – title and source.
  • For timetables – title and period.
  • For comparison tables – title and context.
  • For directories – title and scope.
  • For data exports – title included in exports.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For section titles – use <h1>–<h6>.
  • For figure captions – use <figcaption>.
  • For multiple titles – only one caption per table.
  • For decorative text – use <span> or <div>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <table> – table container.
  • <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> – row groups.
  • <tr> – table row.
  • <th> – header cell.
  • <td> – data cell.
  • <colgroup>, <col> – column groups.
  • <figcaption> – figure caption.
  • aria-label – alternative accessible name.
  • aria-labelledby – references another element for the name.
  • aria-describedby – references a description.
  • caption-side – CSS property for position.
  • text-align – CSS property for alignment.
  • WCAG – accessibility guidelines.
  • SEO – search engine optimization.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <caption> element was introduced in HTML 3.2 (1997) as part of the table model.

  • The caption must be the first child of <table> — placing it elsewhere causes parsing errors.

  • Only one caption is allowed per table. Multiple captions are invalid.

  • By default, captions appear above the table. Use caption-side: bottom to place them below.

  • The default text-align for captions is center. Use text-align: left or right to change it.

  • Screen readers use the <caption> as the accessible name of the table.

  • Without a caption, a table has no accessible name — screen readers announce just "Table."

  • You can use aria-label on <table> as an alternative to a visible caption.

  • You can use aria-describedby on <table> to reference a longer description.

  • The caption property on the <table> element returns the caption element.

  • The <figcaption> element is for figure captions, not table captions. Both can be used together.

  • The display: table-caption value makes the caption behave like a table caption.

  • Search engines use the caption to understand the table's topic.

  • Data exports (e.g., copying a table to a spreadsheet) often include the caption.

  • Print versions of tables include the caption.

  • The caption is not part of the document outline — it doesn't appear in the table of contents.

  • The caption can contain any flow content, including links, images, and <small> elements.

  • lang and dir attributes can be used on <caption> for multilingual content.

  • Structured data (e.g., itemprop="about") can be applied to the caption.

  • WCAG 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) recommends that tables have a caption or equivalent.

  • Best practice: always provide a caption for data tables.

  • The caption is concise — usually one line, with optional secondary info in <small>.

  • The caption is not a heading — it's a title for the table.

  • The <caption> element is one of the most important accessibility features of HTML tables.

  • Testing with screen readers is essential to ensure the caption is announced correctly.

  • Common mistakes include placing the caption after <thead>, using multiple captions, and omitting the caption entirely.

  • Following best practices for captions leads to more accessible, understandable tables.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <caption> element provides a title or description for a table.
  • It must be the first child of <table>.
  • Only one caption is allowed per table.
  • By default, captions appear above the table; caption-side: bottom places them below.
  • The default text-align is center; use text-align: left or right to change it.
  • Screen readers use the caption as the table's accessible name.
  • Best practices: always provide a caption, place it first, make it descriptive, include units, use <small> for secondary info, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include placing the caption after <thead>, using multiple captions, omitting the caption, and using a heading instead.
  • The <caption> element is essential for accessible, understandable, and well-structured tables.
  • It is one of the most important parts of a well-structured table.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Column groups are a structural feature of HTML tables that allow you to define and style whole columns — or groups of columns — without targeting individual cells. They are created using two elements:

  • <colgroup> – a container for one or more column definitions.
  • <col> – a single column (or span of columns) within a <colgroup>.

Together, they let authors:

  • Define column widths.
  • Apply styling to entire columns.
  • Group columns logically for styling or scripting.
  • Provide structure before the table's rows are parsed.

Column groups are a presentational and structural feature. They do not contain data — they only describe the columns of the table. The <colgroup> element is a child of <table>, appearing after <caption> and before <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, and <tr>.

Example: 

<table>
    <caption>Quarterly Sales</caption>
    <colgroup>
        <col class="label-column">
        <col span="3" class="data-columns">
    </colgroup>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Quarter</th>
            <th scope="col">Q1</th>
            <th scope="col">Q2</th>
            <th scope="col">Q3</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">2026</th>
            <td>$15k</td>
            <td>$18k</td>
            <td>$20k</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Column groups serve several essential purposes:

  • Column styling – apply styles to entire columns without repeating them on each cell.
  • Column widths – define widths for columns, improving layout predictability.
  • Semantic grouping – group related columns (e.g., "Q1, Q2, Q3" under "Sales").
  • Performance – reduce the number of CSS rules needed.
  • Accessibility – provide structural hints to assistive technologies.
  • Maintainability – centralise column definitions in one place.
  • Table layout – with table-layout: fixed, column widths are respected.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <colgroup> element is a child of <table>, positioned after <caption> (if present) and before <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, and <tr>. It can contain:

  • <col> elements (one per column or group of columns).

The <col> element is an empty (void) element — it has no closing tag and no content.

<table>
    <caption>...</caption>     ← First
    <colgroup>                 ← Second
        <col>
        <col>
    </colgroup>
    <thead>...</thead>         ← After colgroup
    <tbody>...</tbody>
</table>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
In a table with many columns, applying styles to individual cells is repetitive and error-prone:

/* Repetitive and error-prone */
td:nth-child(1) { width: 100px; background: #f0f0f0; }
td:nth-child(2) { width: 80px; background: #f8f9fa; }
td:nth-child(3) { width: 80px; background: #f8f9fa; }
td:nth-child(4) { width: 80px; background: #f8f9fa; }

This approach has several problems:

  • Repetition – each column must be targeted individually.
  • Fragility – adding or removing a column breaks the nth-child selectors.
  • No semantic grouping – related columns (e.g., Q1, Q2, Q3) can't be styled as a unit.
  • Performance – many selectors increase CSS complexity.
  • Column widths – without <colgroup>, column widths are determined by content, which can lead to uneven layouts.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No column grouping Each column must be styled individually. nth-child fragility Adding a column breaks selectors. No group styling Related columns can't be styled as a unit. Unpredictable widths Column widths depend on content. No structural hints Assistive technologies lack column info.

docs.title: Why Column Groups Were Introduced
docs.text:
The <colgroup> and <col> elements were introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) as part of the table model. They were designed to:

  • Define column widths – with width attribute (now CSS).
  • Group columns – for styling and semantics.
  • Provide structure – before rows are parsed.
  • Improve performance – fewer CSS rules needed.

The <col> element's span attribute allows one <col> to represent multiple columns, reducing markup.

The width attribute on <col> was the original way to set column widths, but it's now obsolete. Use CSS width instead.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <colgroup>
docs.text:
<colgroup>
    <col>
    <col>
</colgroup>

docs.title: Column Group with span
docs.text:
<colgroup>
    <col span="2">
    <col>
</colgroup>

This defines 2 columns with the first <col> and 1 column with the second — 3 columns total.

docs.title: Simple Column Group Example
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    <colgroup>
        <col class="month-column">
        <col class="sales-column">
    </colgroup>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Month</th>
            <th scope="col">Sales</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">January</th>
            <td>$10,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

.month-column {
    width: 40%;
    background: #f8f9fa;
}
.sales-column {
    width: 60%;
    background: #ffffff;
}

docs.title: Column Group with Styling
docs.text:
<table>
    <colgroup>
        <col style="background: #f0f0f0;">
        <col span="3" style="background: #ffffff;">
    </colgroup>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

docs.title: Multiple Column Groups
docs.text:
A table can have multiple <colgroup> elements:

<table>
    <colgroup>
        <col style="width: 20%;">
    </colgroup>
    <colgroup>
        <col style="width: 40%;">
        <col style="width: 40%;">
    </colgroup>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

Use case: Grouping columns logically for styling.

docs.title: Column Group with span and Classes
docs.text:
<colgroup>
    <col span="1" class="label-column">
    <col span="3" class="data-columns">
</colgroup>

.label-column {
    background: #f1f3f5;
}
.data-columns {
    background: #ffffff;
}

docs.title: The span Attribute
docs.text:
The span attribute on <col> defines how many columns the <col> element applies to.

<col span="3">

This one <col> applies to three consecutive columns.

Default: span="1".

docs.title: The width Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text:
The width attribute on <col> was used to set column widths. It is obsolete in HTML5. Use CSS width instead.

<!-- Obsolete -->
<col width="100">


<!-- Correct -->
<col style="width: 100px;">
<col class="fixed-width">

.fixed-width { width: 100px; }

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element/Attribute Purpose Notes <colgroup> Container for column definitions. First child after <caption>. <col> Defines a column or span of columns. Empty (void) element. span Number of columns. Default: 1. class CSS class for styling. Preferred over style. style Inline styles. Use with caution.

docs.title: The "Column Template" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <colgroup> as a column template for the table. Just as a spreadsheet has column headers (A, B, C) with properties (width, format), <colgroup> defines those properties once, and they apply to the entire column below.

docs.title: The "CSS Grid Template" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <colgroup> as the grid template for a CSS Grid. Just as grid-template-columns: 1fr 3fr defines the width of columns, <colgroup> with <col> elements defines the columns of a table. The template is applied before the content.

docs.title: The "Skeleton" Analogy
docs.text:
A table's structure can be thought of as a skeleton:

  • <colgroup> – the spine (column structure).
  • <thead> – the top of the skeleton (header rows).
  • <tbody> – the body (data rows).
  • <tfoot> – the bottom (footer rows).

The <colgroup> is defined first, so the table "knows" its column structure before filling in the rows.

docs.title: The "Blueprint" Analogy
docs.text: The <colgroup> is like a blueprint for the table's columns. It specifies how many columns there are, how wide they are, and how they're styled. The rows fill in the blueprint with data.

docs.title: Concept 1: Position in the Table
docs.text:
The <colgroup> element must appear after <caption> and before <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, and <tr>.

<table>
    <caption>Title</caption>
    <colgroup>
        <col>
    </colgroup>
    <thead>...</thead>
    <tbody>...</tbody>
</table>

Why: The browser needs column definitions before it processes rows.

docs.title: Concept 2: <col> Is an Empty Element
docs.text:
The <col> element is empty (void) — it has no closing tag and no content.

<!-- Correct -->
<col>
<col span="2">

<!-- Incorrect -->
<col></col>
<col span="2"></col>

docs.title: Concept 3: The span Attribute
docs.text:
The span attribute on <col> defines how many columns the <col> element applies to.

<colgroup>
    <col span="2">  <!-- Applies to 2 columns -->
    <col>            <!-- Applies to 1 column -->
</colgroup>

The total span of all <col> elements should equal the number of columns in the table.

docs.title: Concept 4: Number of Columns
docs.text:
The number of columns in the table is determined by:

  1. The sum of span attributes on <col> elements.
  2. The maximum number of cells in any row (if <colgroup> is absent or incomplete).

Best practice: Ensure the <colgroup> matches the actual number of columns.

docs.title: Concept 5: Styling Columns
docs.text:
Only a limited set of CSS properties apply to <col>:

  • background (and its longhands).
  • border (in border-collapse: collapse mode).
  • width.
  • visibility.

Other properties (e.g., color, font-size, text-align) do not apply to <col> — they must be applied to cells.

col {
    background: #f0f0f0; /* Works */
    width: 100px;         /* Works */
    color: red;           /* Does NOT work on <col> */
}

Why: The <col> element has no content of its own — it's a column definition. Only properties that affect the column's box (background, border, width) apply.

docs.title: Concept 6: Column Widths
docs.text:
Column widths can be set with CSS width on <col>:

col {
    width: 150px;
}

Or inline:

<col style="width: 150px;">

Note: Column widths are respected more predictably with table-layout: fixed.

docs.title: Concept 7: table-layout: fixed
docs.text:
With table-layout: fixed, column widths are determined by:

  1. The first row's cell widths.
  2. The <col> widths.
  3. The table's width.
table {
    table-layout: fixed;
    width: 100%;
}

Benefit: Faster rendering and predictable column widths.

docs.title: Concept 8: Multiple <colgroup> Elements
docs.text:
A table can have multiple <colgroup> elements:

<colgroup>
    <col class="label">
</colgroup>
<colgroup>
    <col class="data">
    <col class="data">
</colgroup>

Use case: Grouping columns into logical sections.

docs.title: Concept 9: <colgroup> with span
docs.text:
A <colgroup> element can have its own span attribute (without <col> children):

<colgroup span="3"></colgroup>

This defines a column group spanning 3 columns, but without individual column definitions.

Rarely used — most authors use <col> children.

docs.title: Concept 10: Accessibility
docs.text:
The <colgroup> and <col> elements are not announced by screen readers — they are purely presentational. However, they contribute to the table's structure.

Best practice: Don't rely on <colgroup> for accessibility. Use <th>, scope, and headers for header–cell associations.

docs.title: Concept 11: SEO
docs.text: Search engines use the table's structure (rows, cells, headers) for indexing. <colgroup> is presentational and does not directly affect SEO.

docs.title: Concept 12: Performance
docs.text:
Column groups improve performance by:

  • Reducing the number of CSS rules needed.
  • Providing column widths upfront (with table-layout: fixed).
  • Allowing the browser to lay out columns before parsing rows.

docs.title: Concept 13: The width Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text: The width attribute on <col> was used in HTML4 but is obsolete in HTML5. Use CSS width instead.

docs.title: Concept 14: Styling Limitations
docs.text:
Only a limited set of CSS properties apply to <col>:

Property Applies? background Yes border Yes (with border-collapse: collapse) width Yes visibility Yes color No font-* No text-align No padding No (partially)

Why: The <col> element has no content — it only affects the column's box.

docs.title: Concept 15: Column Borders
docs.text:
With border-collapse: collapse, borders on <col> are applied to the cells in that column.

table {
    border-collapse: collapse;
}
col {
    border-left: 2px solid #3498db;
}

Note: Border behavior varies across browsers. Test carefully.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing of <colgroup>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<colgroup>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the column group.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes each `<col>` child:
    │   ├── Creates a `<col>` node.
    │   ├── Reads the `span` attribute (default 1).
    │   └── Applies CSS styles.
    │
    ▼
4.  When the closing tag is encountered (or the next section starts), the group is closed.
    │
    ▼
5.  The browser computes the table's column structure:
    │   ├── Determines the total number of columns.
    │   ├── Assigns widths from `<col>` elements (if `table-layout: fixed`).
    │   └── Applies backgrounds and borders.
    │
    ▼
6.  The browser processes rows and cells.
    │
    ▼
7.  The table is rendered with the column styles.

docs.title: The Table Grid Algorithm
docs.text:
The browser uses the following to determine column structure:

  1. Count the <col> elements and their span attributes.
  2. If the count is less than the actual number of columns, the remaining columns are implicit.
  3. If the count is more, the extra <col> elements are ignored.

Best practice: Make the <colgroup> match the table's columns exactly.

docs.title: CSS Application
docs.text: Only certain CSS properties apply to <col>. The browser applies them to the column's box, which affects all cells in that column.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
colgroup {
    display: table-column-group;
}

col {
    display: table-column;
}

These values make the elements behave like table columns. They have no visual rendering of their own.

docs.title: Interaction with table-layout
docs.text:
• table-layout: auto – column widths are determined by content; <col> widths are suggestions.
  • table-layout: fixed – column widths are determined by the first row and <col> widths; more predictable.

docs.title: The HTMLTableColElement Interface
docs.text:
Both <colgroup> and <col> are represented by the HTMLTableColElement interface:

Property Description span Reflects the span attribute. width Reflects the obsolete width attribute. align Obsolete. valign Obsolete. ch Obsolete. chOff Obsolete. 
const col = document.querySelector('col');
console.log(col.span);  // 1
console.log(col.width); // "" (obsolete)

docs.title: The Table's cols Property (Not Standard)
docs.text: There is no standard cols property on <table> (unlike rows). To access columns, you query <col> elements directly.

docs.title: The Accessibility Mapping
docs.text: The <colgroup> and <col> elements are not exposed in the accessibility tree. They are purely presentational.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
colgroup {
    display: table-column-group;
}

col {
    display: table-column;
}

These display values make the elements part of the table's column structure.

docs.title: CSS Properties on <col>
docs.text:
Only a subset of CSS properties apply to <col>:

  • background and its longhands.
  • border and its longhands (with border-collapse: collapse).
  • width.
  • visibility.

Other properties are ignored because <col> has no content.

docs.title: Browser Support
docs.text: <colgroup> and <col> are supported in all modern browsers. The CSS properties that apply to <col> vary slightly, so test in your target browsers.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Column Group
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<colgroup>` and `<col>` elements.
    │   └── <colgroup><col class="label"><col span="3" class="data"></colgroup>
    │
    ▼
2.  File is deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the document and creates the DOM.
    │   └── The `<colgroup>` and `<col>` nodes are created.
    │
    ▼
4.  The browser computes the column structure.
    │   └── Determines the number of columns.
    │
    ▼
5.  The browser applies CSS styles to the columns.
    │   └── Backgrounds, widths, borders.
    │
    ▼
6.  The table is rendered with the column styles.
    │
    ▼
7.  JavaScript may modify the columns dynamically.
    │   └── Adding/removing `<col>`, changing classes.
    │
    ▼
8.  When the page is unloaded, the elements are destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
// Change a column's width
const col = document.querySelector('col');
col.style.width = '200px';

// Add a new column definition
const colgroup = document.querySelector('colgroup');
const newCol = document.createElement('col');
newCol.className = 'new-column';
colgroup.appendChild(newCol);

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Column styling Highlighting a specific column Column widths Fixed-width columns Zebra striping Alternating column colors Financial tables Right-aligned amount columns Schedule tables Time column vs. day columns Comparison tables Feature column vs. product columns Data exports Structured columns for CSV Responsive tables Predictable column widths

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Place <colgroup> after <caption> – before row groups and rows.

  2. Use one <col> per column – or use span for multiple columns.

  3. Ensure the total span matches the number of columns – mismatches cause layout issues.

  4. Use classes for styling – not inline styles.

  5. Use width in CSS – not the obsolete width attribute.

  6. Use table-layout: fixed – for predictable column widths.

  7. Only use supported CSS properties – background, border, width, visibility.

  8. Don't rely on <col> for text styling – use cell-level styles.

  9. Test in multiple browsers – <col> behavior varies.

  10. Use <colgroup> for semantic grouping – not just styling.

  11. Don't use <colgroup> for accessibility – use <th> and scope.

  12. Keep the column count consistent – don't have more or fewer <col> elements than columns.

  13. Use span to reduce markup – for repeated columns.

  14. Consider visibility: collapse – for hiding columns (with caution).

  15. Test with border-collapse: collapse – for column borders.

  16. Use nth-child selectors as a fallback – if <col> styling doesn't work.

  17. Validate your HTML – check for correct structure.

  18. Document your column conventions – in a style guide.

  19. Use <colgroup> with table-layout: fixed – for performance.

  20. Keep the number of columns reasonable – too many columns are hard to read.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placing <colgroup> After <thead>
docs.text:
<table>
    <thead>...</thead>
    <colgroup><col></colgroup>
</table>
Why it's wrong: <colgroup> must come before row groups.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <colgroup><col></colgroup>
    <thead>...</thead>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <col> with a Closing Tag
docs.text:
<col></col>
Why it's wrong: <col> is a void element.

✅ Correct: 

<col>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Applying Unsupported CSS to <col>
docs.text:
col {
    color: red;
    font-weight: bold;
    text-align: center;
}
Why it's wrong: These properties don't apply to <col>.

✅ Correct: Apply to cells: 

td, th {
    color: red;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: <col> Span Mismatch
docs.text:
<table>
    <colgroup>
        <col span="2">
    </colgroup>
    <tr>
        <td>1</td>
        <td>2</td>
        <td>3</td>  <!-- Third column not covered -->
    </tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: The span doesn't match the number of columns.

✅ Correct: 

<colgroup>
    <col span="3">
</colgroup>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using the Obsolete width Attribute
docs.text:
<col width="100">
Why it's wrong: The width attribute is obsolete.

✅ Correct: 

<col style="width: 100px;">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No <colgroup> When Column Styling Is Needed
docs.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <td style="background: #f0f0f0;">...</td>
        <td style="background: #f0f0f0;">...</td>
        <td style="background: #f0f0f0;">...</td>
    </tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Repetitive and error-prone.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <colgroup>
        <col style="background: #f0f0f0;">
        <col style="background: #f0f0f0;">
        <col style="background: #f0f0f0;">
    </colgroup>
    <tr>...</tr>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <colgroup> for Accessibility
docs.text:
<colgroup>
    <col aria-label="Name">
</colgroup>
Why it's wrong: <col> is not announced by screen readers.

✅ Correct: Use <th scope="col"> for accessibility.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Adding More <col> Elements Than Columns
docs.text:
<colgroup>
    <col>
    <col>
    <col>
    <col>
    <col>
</colgroup>
<table>
    <tr><td>1</td><td>2</td><td>3</td></tr>
</table>
Why it's wrong: Extra <col> elements are ignored, causing confusion.

✅ Correct: Match the number of columns.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Close <colgroup>
docs.text:
<colgroup>
    <col>
    <thead>...</thead>
Why it's wrong: Missing </colgroup> can cause parsing issues.

✅ Correct: 

<colgroup>
    <col>
</colgroup>
<thead>...</thead>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <colgroup> Outside <table>
docs.text:
<colgroup><col></colgroup>
<table>...</table>
Why it's wrong: <colgroup> must be inside <table>.

✅ Correct: 

<table>
    <colgroup><col></colgroup>
</table>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Faster rendering – <colgroup> provides column widths upfront, especially with table-layout: fixed.
  • Fewer CSS rules – column styles are applied once instead of per-cell.
  • Reduced DOM size – <col> elements are lightweight.
  • Table layout – table-layout: fixed with <col> widths is the fastest table layout algorithm.
  • Browser support – well-supported; no performance concerns.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use table-layout: fixed – for faster rendering.
  2. Define widths in <col> – not in cells.
  3. Use span – to reduce the number of <col> elements.
  4. Use classes – instead of inline styles.
  5. Keep the number of columns reasonable – very wide tables are slow.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if column classes or styles contain user-generated data, sanitize it.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent or a sanitizer.
  • Injection – never insert user input into <col> attributes without escaping.
  • No direct security implications – <colgroup> and <col> are not security risks.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into table attributes.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate structure – ensure <col> elements match the column count.
  4. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect <colgroup> and <col> elements.
  • Computed styles – check display: table-column-group and table-column.
  • Check column widths – with table-layout: fixed, verify the widths.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll('col') to count columns.
  • Validator – check for correct structure.
  • Test in multiple browsers – column styling varies.
  • Test with CSS disabled – ensure the table still makes sense.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For column styling – highlighting, zebra striping.
  • For column widths – predictable layouts.
  • For grouping columns – logical sections.
  • For performance – faster rendering with table-layout: fixed.
  • For financial tables – right-aligned amount columns.
  • For schedule tables – time column vs. day columns.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For accessibility – use <th> and scope.
  • For content styling – use cell-level styles.
  • For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For small tables – the overhead may not be worth it.
  • For unpredictable column counts – if columns change dynamically.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <table> – table container.
  • <caption> – table title.
  • <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> – row groups.
  • <tr> – table row.
  • <th> – header cell.
  • <td> – data cell.
  • table-layout – CSS property for layout algorithm.
  • border-collapse – CSS property for border merging.
  • visibility: collapse – hides a column.
  • CSS selectors – nth-child as a fallback.
  • Accessibility – <col> is not announced.
  • Performance – table-layout: fixed for fast rendering.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <colgroup> and <col> elements were introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) as part of the table model.

  • The <col> element is a void element — it has no closing tag and no content.

  • Only a limited set of CSS properties apply to <col>: background, border, width, and visibility.

  • Other properties (e.g., color, font-size, text-align) do not apply to <col> — they must be applied to cells.

  • With table-layout: fixed, column widths are determined by the <col> elements and the first row.

  • table-layout: fixed is the fastest table layout algorithm.

  • The span attribute on <col> defines how many columns the <col> applies to.

  • A table can have multiple <colgroup> elements.

  • The width attribute on <col> is obsolete in HTML5 — use CSS width instead.

  • <colgroup> is not announced by screen readers — it's purely presentational.

  • <col> styling for background works in all modern browsers.

  • Border styling on <col> requires border-collapse: collapse.

  • visibility: collapse on <col> hides the column in most browsers, but behavior varies.

  • The HTMLTableColElement interface represents both <colgroup> and <col>.

  • The display: table-column-group and display: table-column values make the elements part of the table structure.

  • Zebra-striped columns are a common use case for <colgroup>.

  • Fixed-width columns are easier to achieve with <colgroup> and table-layout: fixed.

  • The nth-child selector can be used as a fallback for column styling.

  • Column groups improve performance by reducing the number of CSS rules needed.

  • Best practice: use <colgroup> for column styling and widths, but use <th> and scope for accessibility.

  • Common mistakes include placing <colgroup> after <thead>, using <col> with a closing tag, and applying unsupported CSS to <col>.

  • Following best practices for column groups leads to more maintainable, performant tables.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Column groups (<colgroup> and <col>) define and style whole columns in a table.
  • <colgroup> is a container for <col> elements.
  • <col> is a void element that defines a column or span of columns.
  • The span attribute on <col> defines how many columns it applies to.
  • <colgroup> must appear after <caption> and before row groups and rows.
  • Only a limited set of CSS properties apply to <col>: background, border, width, visibility.
  • Use table-layout: fixed for predictable column widths and faster rendering.
  • Best practices: place <colgroup> correctly, use classes for styling, match the column count, and use <col> for presentational purposes only.
  • Common mistakes include placing <colgroup> after <thead>, using <col> with a closing tag, applying unsupported CSS, and span mismatches.
  • Column groups are essential for column styling, column widths, and performance in tables.
  • They are a small but powerful feature of HTML tables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Row groups are structural elements in HTML tables that divide rows into logical sections: header, body, and footer. They are created using three elements:

  • <thead> – groups the header rows (typically one row of column headers).
  • <tbody> – groups the body rows (the main data).
  • <tfoot> – groups the footer rows (typically totals, summaries, or footnotes).

Together, they give tables a semantic structure that mirrors how data is organized in documents — a title/header at the top, the main content in the middle, and a summary/footer at the bottom. Row groups are children of <table>, and they contain <tr> (table row) elements.

Example: 

<table>
    <caption>Monthly Sales</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Month</th>
            <th scope="col">Sales</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">January</th>
            <td>$10,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">Total</th>
            <td>$10,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>
</table>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Row groups serve several essential purposes:

  • Semantic structure – divide the table into header, body, and footer.
  • Accessibility – screen readers use row groups to understand the table's structure and announce the sections.
  • Styling – CSS can target <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> for section-level styling.
  • Scrolling – <thead> can be made sticky; <tbody> can be scrollable.
  • Print – <thead> and <tfoot> can be repeated on each printed page.
  • Data organization – separate headers from data and summaries.
  • Multiple sections – a table can have multiple <tbody> elements for grouped data.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Row groups are children of <table>, positioned after <caption> and <colgroup>. They contain <tr> elements. If row groups are omitted, the browser wraps all rows in an implicit <tbody>.

<table>
    <caption>...</caption>     ← First
    <colgroup>...</colgroup>   ← Second
    <thead>...</thead>         ← Header rows
    <tbody>...</tbody>         ← Body rows
    <tfoot>...</tfoot>         ← Footer rows
</table>

The order in the markup can be <thead>, <tfoot>, <tbody> (HTML4) or <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> (HTML5). The browser always renders <tfoot> at the bottom.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A table without row groups is a flat list of rows. There is no way to distinguish the header row (which labels the columns) from the body rows (which contain data) or the footer row (which summarizes the data). This creates several problems:

  • No semantic distinction – machines can't tell headers from data.
  • Poor accessibility – screen readers can't announce the header separately.
  • No styling hooks – CSS can't target header, body, and footer rows differently.
  • No print repetition – headers and footers aren't repeated on each printed page.
  • No scrolling – tables can't have a fixed header with a scrollable body.
  • No logical grouping – data can't be divided into multiple sections.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Flat rows No distinction between header, body, and footer. No semantic structure Screen readers can't announce sections. No styling hooks CSS can't target sections. No print repetition Headers aren't repeated on each page. No scrolling No fixed header with scrollable body. No multiple sections Data can't be grouped logically.

docs.title: Why Row Groups Were Introduced
docs.text:
The <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> elements were introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) as part of the table model. They were designed to:

  • Provide semantic structure – separate header, body, and footer.
  • Improve accessibility – screen readers announce the sections.
  • Enable styling – CSS can target each section.
  • Support printing – headers and footers are repeated on each page.
  • Enable scrolling – tables can have a fixed header with a scrollable body.
  • Allow multiple sections – a table can have multiple <tbody> elements.

Row groups are a critical part of making tables understandable, accessible, and maintainable.

docs.title: The Basic Structure of Row Groups
docs.text:
<table>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Header 1</th>
            <th>Header 2</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>Data 1</td>
            <td>Data 2</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <td>Footer 1</td>
            <td>Footer 2</td>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>
</table>
