            border: 1px solid #dee2e6;
            border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 1rem;
            width: 100%;
            box-sizing: border-box;
        }
        input:focus, select:focus, textarea:focus {
            outline: 2px solid #3498db;
            outline-offset: 2px;
        }
        fieldset {
            border: 1px solid #dee2e6;
            border-radius: 8px;
            padding: 1rem;
        }
        legend {
            font-weight: bold;
            color: #2c3e50;
        }
        .checkbox-label,
        .radio-label {
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.5rem;
            font-weight: normal;
            margin-bottom: 0.5rem;
        }
        button {
            padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
            background: #3498db;
            color: white;
            border: none;
            border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 1rem;
            cursor: pointer;
        }
        button:hover {
            background: #2980b9;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Labels Demo</h1>

    <form action="/submit" method="POST">
        <div class="form-group">
            <label for="name">
                Name:
                <span class="required" aria-hidden="true">*</span>
            </label>
            <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required autocomplete="name">
        </div>

        <div class="form-group">
            <label for="email">
                Email:
                <span class="required" aria-hidden="true">*</span>
            </label>
            <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required autocomplete="email">
        </div>

        <div class="form-group">
            <label for="phone">Phone:</label>
            <input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" autocomplete="tel">
        </div>

        <div class="form-group">
            <label for="country">Country:</label>
            <select id="country" name="country">
                <option value="">Select...</option>
                <option value="us">United States</option>
                <option value="ca">Canada</option>
                <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
            </select>
        </div>

        <fieldset>
            <legend>Preferred contact method:</legend>
            <label class="radio-label">
                <input type="radio" name="contact" value="email" checked>
                Email
            </label>
            <label class="radio-label">
                <input type="radio" name="contact" value="phone">
                Phone
            </label>
        </fieldset>

        <fieldset>
            <legend>Interests:</legend>
            <label class="checkbox-label">
                <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="tech" checked>
                Technology
            </label>
            <label class="checkbox-label">
                <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="sports">
                Sports
            </label>
            <label class="checkbox-label">
                <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="music">
                Music
            </label>
        </fieldset>

        <div class="form-group">
            <label for="message">Message:</label>
            <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5"></textarea>
        </div>

        <label class="checkbox-label">
            <input type="checkbox" name="terms" value="yes" required>
            I agree to the terms and conditions
        </label>

        <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    </form>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Text inputs Name, email, phone Checkboxes Terms, subscribe, interests Radio buttons Gender, contact method Selects Country, category Textareas Message, comment File uploads Document, image Date inputs Birthday, appointment Range inputs Volume, rating Search inputs Site search Multi-step forms Step labels Settings forms Preferences Checkout forms Shipping, payment Login forms Username, password Survey forms Rating, feedback

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use <label> – every form control needs one.

  2. Prefer explicit association – use for/id for clarity.

  3. Use for matching the id – ensure they match exactly.

  4. Use implicit association for checkboxes/radios – wrapping is convenient.

  5. Place labels before controls – for text inputs, select, textarea.

  6. Place labels after controls – for checkboxes and radios.

  7. Keep labels concise – short, descriptive text.

  8. Avoid placeholder as label – use <label>.

  9. Use <fieldset> and <legend> – for groups.

  10. Indicate required fields – with a visual indicator.

  11. Associate error messages – with aria-describedby.

  12. Use aria-label only when necessary – prefer <label>.

  13. Don't use aria-label and <label> together – aria-label overrides.

  14. Test with screen readers – ensure labels are announced.

  15. Test click-to-focus – click the label to focus the control.

  16. Style labels consistently – with CSS.

  17. Use display: block – to place label above control.

  18. Don't use labels for non-labelable elements – e.g., <div>.

  19. Don't use multiple labels for one control – one label per control.

  20. Document your label conventions – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Label on Input
docs.text:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

Why it's wrong: Placeholder disappears on input; no accessible name.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: for Value Doesn't Match id
docs.text:
<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="user-email" name="email">

Why it's wrong: The label is not associated with the input.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="user-email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="user-email" name="email">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate id Values
docs.text:
<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email1">
<input type="email" id="email" name="email2">

Why it's wrong: id must be unique; the label associates with the first.

✅ Correct: Use unique IDs.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Labels for One Control
docs.text:
<label for="name">Name:</label>
<label for="name">(required)</label>
<input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers may concatenate or become confused.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="name">Name (required):</label>
<input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Labeling a Non-Labelable Element
docs.text:
<label for="myDiv">Click me:</label>
<div id="myDiv">Content</div>

Why it's wrong: <div> is not labelable.

✅ Correct: Labels are only for form controls.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using aria-label Instead of <label>
docs.text:
<input type="email" aria-label="Email">

Why it's wrong: No visible label; sighted users can't see what the field is for.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <label> and aria-label Together
docs.text:
<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" aria-label="E-mail address">

Why it's wrong: aria-label overrides the visible label; screen readers announce "E-mail address" but sighted users see "Email:". This violates WCAG 2.5.3 (Label in Name).

✅ Correct: Use only <label> or ensure they match.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting Labels for Checkboxes/Radios
docs.text:
<input type="checkbox" name="subscribe">

Why it's wrong: No accessible name; tiny click target.

✅ Correct: 

<label>
    <input type="checkbox" name="subscribe" value="yes">
    Subscribe to newsletter
</label>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using placeholder as the Only Label
docs.text:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

Why it's wrong: Placeholder disappears on input; low contrast; not always announced.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Label Not Visible
docs.text:
<label for="search" class="sr-only">Search:</label>
<input type="search" id="search" name="search" placeholder="Search...">

Why it's wrong: sr-only hides the label visually; sighted users see only the placeholder.

✅ Correct: Use a visible label, or aria-label if the design truly requires no visible label.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Label Text Doesn't Describe the Field
docs.text:
<label for="email">Field 1:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

Why it's wrong: "Field 1" doesn't describe the field.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Label with No Text
docs.text:
<label for="email"></label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

Why it's wrong: Empty label; no accessible name.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• <label> is lightweight – one DOM node per label.
  • Click-to-focus – native browser behavior; no performance cost.
  • Accessibility tree – labels add accessible names; minimal overhead.
  • Styling – labels can be styled without performance concerns.
  • Floating labels – CSS-only; minimal performance impact.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep labels concise – shorter text renders faster.
  2. Use CSS for styling – avoid inline styles.
  3. Avoid JavaScript for click-to-focus – it's native.
  4. Use CSS for floating labels – no JavaScript required.
  5. Minify HTML – reduce file size.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if label content contains user-generated data, sanitize it.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent.
  • Injection – never insert user input directly into <label> without escaping.
  • No direct security implications – labels themselves are not a security risk.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into labels.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate structure – ensure labels are properly associated.
  4. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the label and its for attribute.
  • Computed styles – check the label's display and styling.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the accessible name of the control.
  • Console – use input.labels to see associated labels.
  • label.control – returns the associated control.
  • Validator – check for invalid for values and duplicate IDs.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the label is announced.
  • Click testing – click the label to focus the control.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility.
  • axe DevTools – checks for missing labels.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For every form control – always use a label.
  • For text inputs – name, email, phone.
  • For checkboxes – terms, subscribe.
  • For radio buttons – gender, contact method.
  • For selects – country, category.
  • For textareas – message, comment.
  • For file uploads – document, image.
  • For date inputs – birthday, appointment.
  • For search inputs – site search.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For non-form elements – labels are only for labelable elements.
  • For hidden inputs – type="hidden" cannot be labeled.
  • For buttons with visible text – the button text is the label.
  • For decorative elements – labels are for interactive controls.
  • As a replacement for headings – use <h1>–<h6>.
  • As a replacement for <legend> – use <legend> for groups.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <input> – the input element.
  • <select> – dropdown.
  • <textarea> – multi-line text.
  • <button> – button.
  • <fieldset> – groups related controls.
  • <legend> – caption for a fieldset.
  • for attribute – explicit association.
  • id attribute – target for for.
  • aria-label – accessible name without visible label.
  • aria-labelledby – references another element for the name.
  • aria-describedby – references a description.
  • WCAG 1.3.1 – info and relationships.
  • WCAG 3.3.2 – labels or instructions.
  • WCAG 4.1.2 – name, role, value.
  • WCAG 2.5.3 – label in name.
  • Screen readers – NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <label> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) to improve form accessibility.

  • Clicking a label focuses the associated control — or toggles a checkbox/radio.

  • The for attribute must match the id of a labelable element.

  • Labelable elements include <button>, <input> (except hidden), <meter>, <output>, <progress>, <select>, and <textarea>.

  • Implicit association (wrapping) doesn't require for/id but can make styling trickier.

  • Explicit association is preferred for clarity and maintainability.

  • The accessible name of a control is computed from aria-labelledby, aria-label, <label>, placeholder, and title — in that order.

  • If both <label> and aria-label are present, aria-label overrides the visible label — a WCAG 2.5.3 violation.

  • placeholder is not a substitute for a label — it disappears on input and has poor contrast.

  • Multiple labels for one control are allowed but discouraged.

  • Empty labels provide no accessible name.

  • Screen readers announce the label when the control is focused.

  • Click-to-focus is native — no JavaScript required.

  • Floating labels are a popular design pattern — labels that move above the input when focused or filled.

  • display: block on labels places them above the control.

  • display: inline (default) places them beside the control.

  • WCAG 1.3.1 requires label–control associations to be programmatic.

  • WCAG 3.3.2 requires labels for all inputs.

  • WCAG 4.1.2 requires controls to have accessible names.

  • WCAG 2.5.3 requires the accessible name to match the visible label.

  • input.labels returns the labels associated with a control.

  • label.control returns the control associated with a label.

  • label.htmlFor reflects the for attribute.

  • Best practices include always using <label>, matching for to id, and testing with screen readers.

  • Common mistakes include missing labels, mismatched for/id, and using aria-label instead of <label>.

  • Following best practices for labels leads to more accessible, usable, and maintainable forms.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <label> element provides a visible, descriptive caption for a form control.
  • It associates text with a control via explicit (for/id) or implicit (wrapping) association.
  • Clicking a label focuses the control or toggles checkboxes/radios.
  • Screen readers announce the label as the accessible name of the control.
  • Best practices: always use <label>, prefer explicit association, place labels before controls (except checkboxes/radios), use <fieldset>/<legend> for groups, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include missing labels, mismatched for/id, duplicate IDs, multiple labels for one control, and using aria-label instead of <label>.
  • Labels are essential for accessibility, usability, and form completion.
  • They are one of the most important features of accessible HTML forms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A button is an interactive HTML element that users click, tap, or activate via keyboard to trigger an action. HTML provides two ways to create buttons:

  • <button> element — a container element that can hold text, icons, and other inline content. It is the preferred way to create buttons in modern HTML.
  • <input> element with type="submit", type="reset", or type="button" — a void element whose label is set via the value attribute.

Buttons are the primary mechanism for submitting forms, resetting forms, and triggering JavaScript actions. They are among the most interactive elements on the web.

Example: 

<!-- Preferred: <button> element -->
<button type="submit">Submit</button>

<!-- Alternative: <input> element -->
<input type="submit" value="Submit">

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Buttons serve several essential purposes:

  • Form submission – submit form data to a server.
  • Form reset – clear form fields to their default values.
  • Generic actions – trigger JavaScript (open a dialog, toggle a menu, etc.).
  • Navigation-like actions – though links (<a>) are preferred for navigation.
  • Accessibility – native buttons are keyboard-accessible and screen-reader-friendly.
  • Consistency – browsers provide default button styling and behavior.
  • Progressive enhancement – submit buttons work even without JavaScript.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Buttons are interactive content and phrasing content (for <button>) or flow content (depending on context). They can appear anywhere interactive content is accepted — inside <form>, <div>, <p>, <li>, <td>, and more.

<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

    <button type="submit">Save</button>
    <button type="reset">Clear</button>
</form>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before buttons, form submission relied on <input type="submit"> — a specialized input whose label was set via the value attribute. This worked, but had several limitations:

  • No rich content – the label was plain text only; no icons, no HTML.
  • Styling limitations – <input> elements are harder to style consistently.
  • value attribute collision – the value attribute served double duty as both the label and the submitted value.
  • No type="button" alternative – generic buttons were also <input> elements with the same limitations.

Developers wanted buttons that could contain icons, spans, and other markup; that were easier to style; and that had a cleaner separation between label and value.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence <input type="submit"> only No rich content in buttons. value as label Label and submitted value were coupled. Harder to style Inconsistent styling across browsers. No generic button <input type="button"> was limited. Accessibility issues Some custom buttons were not keyboard-accessible.

docs.title: Why the <button> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <button> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) to provide a richer, more flexible alternative to <input type="submit">. It enables:

  • Rich content – text, icons, spans, images.
  • Clear separation – label is the content; submitted value is the value attribute.
  • Easier styling – <button> is a container, easier to style consistently.
  • Three types – submit, reset, button.
  • Accessibility – native keyboard support and screen reader announcements.

The <button> element is now the preferred way to create buttons in HTML.

docs.title: The <button> Element
docs.text:
<button type="submit">Submit</button>
<button type="reset">Reset</button>
<button type="button">Click Me</button>
  • type="submit" (default) – submits the form.
  • type="reset" – resets the form.
  • type="button" – no default action; used with JavaScript.

docs.title: The <input> Element
docs.text:
<input type="submit" value="Submit">
<input type="reset" value="Reset">
<input type="button" value="Click Me">
  • The value attribute sets the label.
  • Cannot contain rich content.

docs.title: Submit Button
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: Reset Button
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
    <button type="reset">Clear</button>
</form>

docs.title: Generic Button with JavaScript
docs.text:
<button type="button" id="myBtn">Click Me</button>

<script>
    document.getElementById('myBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        alert('Button clicked!');
    });
</script>

docs.title: Button with Icon
docs.text:
<button type="submit">
    <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16" viewBox="0 0 16 16">
        <path d="M8 1v10m0 0l-4-4m4 4l4-4M2 14h12" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
    </svg>
    Save
</button>

docs.title: Button with Image
docs.text:
<button type="submit">
    <img src="save-icon.png" alt="" width="16" height="16">
    Save
</button>

docs.title: Disabled Button
docs.text: <button type="submit" disabled>Submit</button>

docs.title: Button with value
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="save">Save</button>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="delete">Delete</button>
</form>

The server receives action=save or action=delete, depending on which button was clicked.

docs.title: Button with form Attribute (Outside Form)
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST">
    <input type="text" name="name">
</form>

<button type="submit" form="myForm">Submit</button>

docs.title: Button with formaction, formmethod, etc.
docs.text:
<form action="/default" method="POST">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    <button type="submit" formaction="/special" formmethod="POST">Save Draft</button>
</form>

Override attributes: - formaction – overrides action. - formmethod – overrides method. - formenctype – overrides enctype. - formnovalidate – skips validation. - formtarget – overrides target.

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose Notes type Button type submit, reset, button name Field name Submitted with the button's value value Submitted value Distinguishes multiple buttons disabled Disables the button Not focusable, not clickable form Associates with a form Outside the <form> element formaction Overrides form action Per-button action formmethod Overrides form method Per-button method formnovalidate Skips validation Per-button

docs.title: The "Button" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a <button> as a physical button on a machine. Pressing it triggers an action — starting, stopping, resetting, saving. The label on the button tells you what it does. A disabled button is like a button that's been locked — it looks like a button but doesn't respond.

docs.title: The "Sign vs. Action" Analogy
docs.text: A link (<a>) is a sign pointing to another location. A button is an action you perform. Links navigate; buttons act. This distinction is important for both semantics and accessibility.

docs.title: The "Three Types" Mental Model
docs.text:
• submit — sends the form.
  • reset — clears the form.
  • button — does nothing on its own; needs JavaScript.

docs.title: The "Native vs. Custom" Mental Model
docs.text: Before <button>, buttons were built from <div>s with JavaScript. These custom buttons were often inaccessible (no keyboard support, no screen reader role). Native <button> elements are keyboard-accessible by default, have the correct role, and are announced correctly.

docs.title: The "Label vs. Value" Mental Model
docs.text:
For <button>:

  • Label = the button's content (text, icon).
  • Value = the value attribute (submitted with the form).

For <input type="submit">:

  • Label = the value attribute.
  • Value = also the value attribute (for submit, nothing is submitted unless name is set).

The <button> element separates these concerns cleanly.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Three Button Types
Concept 2: <button> vs <input type="submit">
docs.text:
Aspect <button> <input type="submit"> Content Rich (text, icons, HTML) Plain text only Label Content value attribute Submitted value value attribute value attribute Styling Easier Harder Default type submit (in form) submit Self-closing No (has closing tag) Yes (void) Pseudo-elements ::before, ::after work ::before, ::after limited

Rule: Prefer <button> for new code.

docs.title: Concept 3: The type Attribute
docs.text:
Always specify type. Without it, the browser default may surprise you.

<!-- Bad: defaults to submit inside a form -->
<button>Click</button>

<!-- Good: explicit type -->
<button type="button">Click</button>

docs.title: Concept 4: The value Attribute
docs.text:
For <button>, the value attribute is submitted with the form when the button is clicked. Combined with name, it lets the server know which button was clicked.

<button type="submit" name="action" value="save">Save</button>
<button type="submit" name="action" value="delete">Delete</button>

Server receives action=save or action=delete.

docs.title: Concept 5: The disabled Attribute
docs.text:
A disabled button:

  • Is not clickable.
  • Is not focusable.
  • Is not submitted with the form.
  • Is announced as "dimmed" or "unavailable" by screen readers.
<button type="submit" disabled>Submit</button>

Note: Don't use disabled for form validation — it prevents the user from fixing the error. Instead, use aria-disabled="true" and validate on submit.

docs.title: Concept 6: The form Attribute
docs.text:
A button outside a <form> can be associated with it using the form attribute:

<form id="myForm">
    <input type="text" name="name">
</form>

<button type="submit" form="myForm">Submit</button>

docs.title: Concept 7: Override Attributes
docs.text:
Buttons inside a form can override the form's attributes:

Button Attribute Overrides formaction action formmethod method formenctype enctype formnovalidate Validation formtarget target 
<form action="/save" method="POST">
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
    <button type="submit" formaction="/publish">Publish</button>
</form>

docs.title: Concept 8: Keyboard Accessibility
docs.text:
Native buttons are keyboard-accessible:

  • Tab – moves focus to the button.
  • Enter – activates the button.
  • Space – activates the button.

Important: Enter and Space both work for native buttons. Custom buttons built with <div> often only support Enter.

docs.title: Concept 9: Screen Reader Announcements
docs.text:
Screen readers announce buttons as:

  • "Submit, button" (for <button>Submit</button>).
  • "Save, button" (for <button>Save</button>).

Disabled buttons are announced as "dimmed" or "unavailable".

docs.title: Concept 10: Buttons vs. Links
docs.text:
Aspect <button> <a> Purpose Action Navigation Role button link Keyboard Enter + Space Enter Right-click Context menu (limited) Open in new tab, copy link href No Yes Use case Submit, toggle, open Navigate

Rule: Use <a> for navigation; use <button> for actions.

docs.title: Concept 11: Styling Buttons
docs.text:
Buttons can be styled with CSS:

button {
    padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
    background: #3498db;
    color: white;
    border: none;
    border-radius: 4px;
    cursor: pointer;
    font-size: 1rem;
}

button:hover {
    background: #2980b9;
}

button:focus {
    outline: 2px solid #2c3e50;
    outline-offset: 2px;
}

button:disabled {
    background: #bdc3c7;
    cursor: not-allowed;
}

docs.title: Concept 12: Button Icons
docs.text:
Icons can be added as SVG or images:

<button type="submit">
    <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16"><!-- icon --></svg>
    Save
</button>

Accessibility tip: Mark icons as aria-hidden="true" and provide visible text.

docs.title: Concept 13: Icon-Only Buttons
docs.text:
Icon-only buttons need an accessible name:

<button type="button" aria-label="Close">✕</button>

Without aria-label, the button's accessible name is just "✕" (or nothing), which is unclear.

docs.title: Concept 14: Toggle Buttons
docs.text:
Toggle buttons use aria-pressed to indicate state:

<button type="button" aria-pressed="false" id="toggleBtn">Bold</button>

<script>
    const btn = document.getElementById('toggleBtn');
    btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const pressed = btn.getAttribute('aria-pressed') === 'true';
        btn.setAttribute('aria-pressed', !pressed);
    });
</script>

docs.title: Concept 15: Buttons and Progressive Enhancement
docs.text:
A submit button works even without JavaScript — it submits the form natively. A <button type="button"> requires JavaScript to do anything.

Best practice: Use <button type="submit"> for form submission; enhance with JavaScript only when needed.

docs.title: Concept 16: The popovertarget Attribute (Modern)
docs.text:
Buttons can control popovers natively:

<button popovertarget="myPopover">Open Menu</button>
<div id="myPopover" popover>Menu content</div>

docs.title: Concept 17: The commandfor Attribute (Newer)
docs.text:
Modern browsers support declarative commands:

<button commandfor="myDialog" command="show-modal">Open Dialog</button>
<dialog id="myDialog">...</dialog>

Note: Browser support varies; check compatibility.

docs.title: Concept 18: Accessibility — The First Rule of ARIA
docs.text:
If a <button> element fits, use it — don't use <div role="button">.

<!-- Bad -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0" onclick="doSomething()">Click</div>

<!-- Good -->
<button type="button" onclick="doSomething()">Click</button>

docs.title: Concept 19: Buttons in Forms
docs.text:
• A form can have multiple submit buttons with different name/value pairs.
  • A form can have multiple reset buttons (rare).
  • A form can have generic buttons that trigger JavaScript.
  • A form's first submit button is the default when pressing Enter.
<form>
    <input type="text" name="q">
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="search">Search</button>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="lucky">I'm Feeling Lucky</button>
</form>

docs.title: Concept 20: The autofocus Attribute
docs.text:
A button can autofocus on page load:

<button type="submit" autofocus>Submit</button>

Note: Use sparingly — autofocus can be disorienting.

docs.title: Concept 21: Button Reset Behavior
docs.text:
A <button type="reset"> resets all controls in the form to their default values (specified via value, checked, selected attributes).

<form>
    <input type="text" name="name" value="Default">
    <input type="checkbox" name="agree" checked>
    <button type="reset">Reset</button>
</form>

docs.title: Concept 22: Accessibility and Focus
docs.text:
• Buttons are focusable by default.
  • The focus indicator should be visible.
  • Don't remove the focus outline without providing an alternative.
  • Custom buttons must be focusable (tabindex="0").

docs.title: Concept 23: Button Role
docs.text:
The <button> element has an implicit button role. The accessible name comes from:

  1. aria-labelledby
  2. aria-label
  3. The button's content (text)
  4. title (fallback)

docs.title: Concept 24: Button State
docs.text:
Buttons have states:

  • Default – normal.
  • Hover – mouse over.
  • Focus – keyboard-focused.
  • Active – being pressed.
  • Disabled – not interactive.

CSS pseudo-classes:

  • :hover
  • :focus
  • :focus-visible
  • :active
  • :disabled

docs.title: Concept 25: Buttons and Touch
docs.text:
On touch devices, buttons should be at least 44×44 CSS pixels for accessibility (WCAG 2.5.5).

button {
    min-width: 44px;
    min-height: 44px;
    padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
}

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing a Button
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<button>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the button.
    │
    ▼
3.  It reads the `type` attribute (default: "submit" inside a form).
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes the button's content (text, icons, etc.).
    │
    ▼
5.  When the closing tag is encountered, the button is closed.
    │
    ▼
6.  The accessibility tree node is created:
    │   └── role: button, name: button text.
    │
    ▼
7.  Default styles are applied.
    │
    ▼
8.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
9.  User clicks or presses Enter/Space:
    │   ├── submit → form submission
    │   ├── reset → form reset
    │   └── button → click event only

docs.title: Button Activation
docs.text:
• Mouse: click.
  • Keyboard: Enter or Space when focused.
  • Screen reader: virtual cursor + Enter/Space.
  • Touch: tap.

docs.title: Form Submission Flow
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a submit button.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser checks validation:
    │   ├── Invalid → show errors, prevent submission.
    │   └── Valid → proceed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser collects form data.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser submits to the action URL using method.
    │
    ▼
5.  Server responds.

docs.title: The click Event
docs.text:
All buttons fire a click event:

button.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
    console.log('Button clicked');
});

For submit buttons, the click event fires before the submit event.

docs.title: The submit Event
docs.text:
The form's submit event fires when a submit button is clicked:

form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    e.preventDefault(); // Prevent default submission
    // Custom submission logic
});

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree:

  • <button> → role: button.
  • <input type="submit"> → role: button.
  • The accessible name is the button's text or value.
  • State includes disabled if present.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
button {
    display: inline-block;
    padding: 1px 6px;
    border: 2px outset buttonborder;
    background-color: buttonface;
    color: buttontext;
    cursor: default;
    font-family: inherit;
    font-size: inherit;
}

button:disabled {
    color: graytext;
}

Browsers apply OS-specific styling. Override with CSS for consistency.

docs.title: The HTMLButtonElement Interface
docs.text:
In the DOM, <button> is represented by HTMLButtonElement:

Property Description type Button type: submit, reset, button value Submitted value name Field name disabled Whether disabled form The associated form formAction Override for action formMethod Override for method formEnctype Override for enctype formNoValidate Override for novalidate formTarget Override for target labels Associated labels validity Validity state willValidate Whether validated checkValidity() Returns validity setCustomValidity() Sets custom error 
const btn = document.querySelector('button');
console.log(btn.type);     // "submit"
console.log(btn.value);    // ""
console.log(btn.disabled); // false

docs.title: The HTMLInputElement Interface (for <input type="submit">)
docs.text: Similar properties, but with value serving double duty as the label.

docs.title: The Button Role
docs.text: The <button> element has an implicit button role in the accessibility tree. This is why you don't need to add role="button".

docs.title: Accessibility Mapping
docs.text: Element Role Accessible Name <button>Save</button> button "Save" <button aria-label="Close">✕</button> button "Close" <input type="submit" value="Save"> button "Save" <button disabled>Save</button> button (disabled) "Save" (dimmed)

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
Browsers apply OS-specific button styling. This is why buttons look different on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

To make buttons consistent, reset their styles:

button {
    all: unset;
    /* Then apply your own styles */
    padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
    background: #3498db;
    color: white;
    border-radius: 4px;
    cursor: pointer;
}

Caution: all: unset also removes the focus indicator and other important defaults. Use with care.

docs.title: The click Event
docs.text: All buttons fire a click event. Submit and reset buttons also trigger their default actions after the click event, unless prevented.

docs.title: The disabled Property
docs.text:
A disabled button:

  • Has disabled attribute.
  • Does not fire click events.
  • Is skipped in tab order.
  • Is announced as unavailable by screen readers.
  • Is not submitted with the form.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Button
docs.text:
1.  Author writes a `<button>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses the HTML and creates the DOM node.
    │
    ▼
3.  The accessibility tree node is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default styles are applied.
    │
    ▼
5.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
6.  User interacts:
    │   ├── Focus → focus styles applied.
    │   ├── Hover → hover styles applied.
    │   ├── Click/Enter/Space → click event fires.
    │   └── Default action (submit/reset/none) executes.
    │
    ▼
7.  JavaScript may modify the button dynamically:
    │   ├── Change text.
    │   ├── Change type.
    │   ├── Disable/enable.
    │   └── Change attributes.
    │
    ▼
8.  When the page is unloaded, the button is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const btn = document.querySelector('button');

// Change text
btn.textContent = 'New Label';

// Disable
btn.disabled = true;

// Change type
btn.type = 'button';

// Add event listener
btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    console.log('Clicked');
});

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Submit Button
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 2: Submit and Reset Buttons
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
    <button type="reset">Clear</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 3: Generic Button with JavaScript
docs.text:
<button type="button" id="openBtn">Open Dialog</button>

<dialog id="myDialog">
    <p>This is a dialog.</p>
    <button type="button" onclick="document.getElementById('myDialog').close()">Close</button>
</dialog>

<script>
    document.getElementById('openBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        document.getElementById('myDialog').showModal();
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 4: Multiple Submit Buttons
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="title">Title:</label>
    <input type="text" id="title" name="title">

    <button type="submit" name="action" value="draft">Save Draft</button>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="publish">Publish</button>
</form>

The server receives action=draft or action=publish.

docs.title: Example 5: Icon Button
docs.text:
<button type="button" aria-label="Close dialog">
    <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16" viewBox="0 0 16 16">
        <path d="M2 2L14 14M14 2L2 14" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
    </svg>
</button>

docs.title: Example 6: Icon and Text Button
docs.text:
<button type="submit" class="btn-save">
    <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16" viewBox="0 0 16 16">
        <path d="M2 8L6 12L14 4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
    </svg>
    Save
</button>

docs.title: Example 7: Disabled Button
docs.text:
<form id="myForm">
    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
    <button type="submit" id="submitBtn" disabled>Submit</button>
</form>

<script>
    const email = document.getElementById('email');
    const btn = document.getElementById('submitBtn');
    email.addEventListener('input', () => {
        btn.disabled = !email.validity.valid;
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 8: Toggle Button
docs.text:
<button type="button" id="themeToggle" aria-pressed="false">Dark Mode</button>

<script>
    const btn = document.getElementById('themeToggle');
    btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const pressed = btn.getAttribute('aria-pressed') === 'true';
        btn.setAttribute('aria-pressed', !pressed);
        document.body.classList.toggle('dark-mode');
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 9: Button with form Attribute
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
</form>

<button type="submit" form="myForm">Submit</button>

docs.title: Example 10: Override Attributes
docs.text:
<form action="/save" method="POST">
    <label for="title">Title:</label>
    <input type="text" id="title" name="title">

    <button type="submit">Save</button>
    <button type="submit" formaction="/publish" formmethod="POST">Publish</button>
    <button type="submit" formnovalidate>Save Draft (Skip Validation)</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 11: Buttons in a Toolbar
docs.text:
<div role="toolbar" aria-label="Text formatting">
    <button type="button" aria-label="Bold"><strong>B</strong></button>
    <button type="button" aria-label="Italic"><em>I</em></button>
    <button type="button" aria-label="Underline"><u>U</u></button>
</div>

docs.title: Example 12: Button Group
docs.text:
<div role="group" aria-label="Alignment">
    <button type="button" aria-pressed="true">Left</button>
    <button type="button" aria-pressed="false">Center</button>
    <button type="button" aria-pressed="false">Right</button>
</div>

docs.title: Example 13: Button with Loading State
docs.text:
<button type="submit" id="submitBtn">
    <span class="label">Submit</span>
    <span class="spinner" hidden>⏳</span>
</button>

<script>
    document.querySelector('form').addEventListener('submit', () => {
        const btn = document.getElementById('submitBtn');
        btn.disabled = true;
        btn.querySelector('.label').hidden = true;
        btn.querySelector('.spinner').hidden = false;
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 14: Link-Styled as Button
docs.text:
<a href="/signup" class="btn">Sign Up</a>

<style>
    .btn {
        display: inline-block;
        padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
        background: #3498db;
        color: white;
        text-decoration: none;
        border-radius: 4px;
    }
</style>

Note: Use <a> for navigation — it's semantically correct.

docs.title: Example 15: Button-Styled as Link
docs.text:
<button type="button" onclick="location.href='/signup'" class="link-btn">
    Sign Up
</button>

Note: Not recommended — use <a> for navigation.

docs.title: Example 16: formnovalidate Button
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

    <button type="submit">Submit (Validated)</button>
    <button type="submit" formnovalidate>Save Draft (No Validation)</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 17: Confirmation Button
docs.text:
<form action="/delete" method="POST" id="deleteForm">
    <input type="hidden" name="id" value="123">
    <button type="button" id="deleteBtn">Delete</button>
</form>

<script>
    document.getElementById('deleteBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        if (confirm('Are you sure you want to delete?')) {
            document.getElementById('deleteForm').submit();
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 18: Button with autofocus
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="GET">
    <label for="q">Search:</label>
    <input type="search" id="q" name="q">
    <button type="submit" autofocus>Search</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 19: Accessible Icon Button with Tooltip
docs.text:
<button type="button" aria-label="Delete item" title="Delete item">
    <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16" viewBox="0 0 16 16">
        <path d="M2 4h12M5 4V2h6v2M4 4l1 10h6l1-10" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
    </svg>
</button>

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Form with Multiple Button Types
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Buttons Demo</title>
    <style>
        body {
            font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
            max-width: 600px;
            margin: 2rem auto;
            padding: 0 1rem;
        }
        form {
            display: flex;
            flex-direction: column;
            gap: 1rem;
        }
        .form-group {
            display: flex;
            flex-direction: column;
        }
        label {
            font-weight: 500;
            margin-bottom: 0.25rem;
        }
        input, textarea {
            padding: 0.5rem;
            border: 1px solid #dee2e6;
            border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 1rem;
        }
        .button-group {
            display: flex;
            gap: 0.5rem;
            flex-wrap: wrap;
        }
        button {
            padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
            border: none;
            border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 1rem;
            cursor: pointer;
            display: inline-flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.25rem;
            min-height: 44px;
        }
        .btn-primary {
            background: #3498db;
            color: white;
        }
        .btn-primary:hover {
            background: #2980b9;
        }
        .btn-secondary {
            background: #ecf0f1;
            color: #2c3e50;
        }
        .btn-secondary:hover {
            background: #bdc3c7;
        }
        .btn-danger {
            background: #e74c3c;
            color: white;
        }
        .btn-danger:hover {
            background: #c0392b;
        }
        button:focus {
            outline: 2px solid #2c3e50;
            outline-offset: 2px;
        }
        button:disabled {
            opacity: 0.5;
            cursor: not-allowed;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Buttons Demo</h1>

    <form action="/submit" method="POST">
        <div class="form-group">
            <label for="title">Title:</label>
            <input type="text" id="title" name="title" required>
        </div>

        <div class="form-group">
            <label for="content">Content:</label>
            <textarea id="content" name="content" rows="5"></textarea>
        </div>

        <div class="button-group">
            <button type="submit" name="action" value="draft" formnovalidate class="btn-secondary">
                💾 Save Draft
            </button>
            <button type="submit" name="action" value="publish" class="btn-primary">
                🚀 Publish
            </button>
            <button type="reset" class="btn-secondary">
                🔄 Reset
            </button>
            <button type="button" id="previewBtn" class="btn-secondary">
                👁 Preview
            </button>
        </div>
    </form>

    <script>
        document.getElementById('previewBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
            alert('Preview not implemented in this demo.');
        });
    </script>
</body>
