docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Button Type Form submission type="submit" Form reset type="reset" Open dialog type="button" Toggle menu type="button" + aria-expanded Toggle state type="button" + aria-pressed Delete with confirmation type="button" + JS Save draft type="submit" + formnovalidate Publish type="submit" + name/value Close dialog type="button" Pagination <a> preferred Icon-only action type="button" + aria-label Search type="submit" File upload type="submit" Login type="submit" Signup type="submit"

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <button> over <input type="submit"> – richer content, easier styling.

  2. Always specify type – avoid accidental submissions.

  3. Use type="button" for non-submit actions – inside a form, the default is submit.

  4. Use <a> for navigation – buttons are for actions.

  5. Provide accessible names – text or aria-label for icon buttons.

  6. Don't disable submit buttons for validation – let users fix errors.

  7. Use aria-pressed for toggle buttons – indicates state.

  8. Use aria-expanded for expand/collapse buttons – indicates state.

  9. Use name and value for multiple submit buttons – to distinguish them.

  10. Use formnovalidate for draft saves – skip validation when needed.

  11. Ensure touch targets are at least 44×44px.

  12. Provide visible focus indicators – don't remove outlines.

  13. Test keyboard navigation – Tab, Enter, Space.

  14. Test with screen readers – ensure the button is announced.

  15. Style buttons consistently – reset browser defaults.

  16. Use cursor: pointer – to indicate interactivity.

  17. Provide loading states – disable and show a spinner.

  18. Avoid autofocus – unless truly needed.

  19. Group related buttons – with role="group" or role="toolbar".

  20. Document button conventions – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div> as a Button
docs.text:
<div class="button" onclick="submit()">Submit</div>

Why it's wrong: No keyboard support, no role, no accessibility.

✅ Correct: 

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting type
docs.text:
<form>
    <button>Click</button>  <!-- Submits the form! -->
</form>

Why it's wrong: Inside a form, <button> defaults to type="submit".

✅ Correct: 

<form>
    <button type="button">Click</button>
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <a> for Actions
docs.text:
<a href="#" onclick="doSomething()">Click</a>

Why it's wrong: <a> is for navigation; the # also jumps to the top.

✅ Correct: 

<button type="button" onclick="doSomething()">Click</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Icon-Only Button Without aria-label
docs.text:
<button type="button">✕</button>

Why it's wrong: Screen reader announces "✕" or nothing.

✅ Correct: 

<button type="button" aria-label="Close">✕</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Disabling Submit for Validation
docs.text:
<button type="submit" disabled>Submit</button>

Why it's wrong: Users can't submit even after fixing errors.

✅ Correct: Validate on submit, show errors, and let users fix them.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Removing Focus Outline
docs.text:
button:focus {
    outline: none;
}

Why it's wrong: Keyboard users can't see which button is focused.

✅ Correct: 

button:focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid #2c3e50;
    outline-offset: 2px;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Submit Buttons Without name/value
docs.text:
<button type="submit">Save</button>
<button type="submit">Delete</button>

Why it's wrong: The server can't tell which button was clicked.

✅ Correct: 

<button type="submit" name="action" value="save">Save</button>
<button type="submit" name="action" value="delete">Delete</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using disabled for Loading Without Announcing
docs.text:
<button type="submit" disabled>Loading...</button>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers don't know why the button is disabled.

✅ Correct: 

<button type="submit" aria-disabled="true" aria-busy="true">
    <span aria-hidden="true">⏳</span>
    <span class="sr-only">Loading</span>
</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Button Without Accessible Name
docs.text:
<button type="button"></button>

Why it's wrong: No accessible name; screen readers announce "button".

✅ Correct: 

<button type="button" aria-label="Close">✕</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using role="button" on <button>
docs.text:
<button role="button">Submit</button>

Why it's wrong: Redundant — <button> already has the button role.

✅ Correct: 

<button>Submit</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Button Inside a Link
docs.text:
<a href="/page">
    <button>Click</button>
</a>

Why it's wrong: Interactive content inside a link is invalid.

✅ Correct: Use either a link or a button, not both.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: type="button" Outside a Form for Submission
docs.text:
<button type="button" onclick="document.forms[0].submit()">Submit</button>

Why it's wrong: Unnecessary JavaScript — use type="submit".

✅ Correct: 

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Buttons are lightweight – one DOM node each.
  • Native buttons – faster than custom <div> buttons.
  • No performance cost for disabled state.
  • Event listeners – one per button is fine; event delegation for many.
  • Loading states – disable the button on submit to prevent double submission.
  • pointer-events: none – can be used to disable clicks during loading.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use event delegation – one listener on a parent for many buttons.
  2. Debounce rapid clicks – prevent double submission.
  3. Disable buttons during async operations.
  4. Minimize inline styles – use CSS classes.
  5. Use CSS for hover/focus states – no JavaScript needed.
  6. Minify HTML/CSS – reduce file size.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• CSRF protection – use tokens for form submissions.
  • Double submission – disable the button during submission.
  • XSS – never insert user input into button text or attributes without escaping.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input.
  • Rate limiting – prevent brute force attacks.
  • HTTPS – mandatory for sensitive form submissions.
  • Server‑side validation – always validate on the server, even if the button is disabled client‑side.
  • formaction override – validate on the server; don't trust the client.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use HTTPS – for all form submissions.
  2. CSRF tokens – include in all state-changing forms.
  3. Server-side validation – never trust client input.
  4. Disable buttons during submission – prevent double submission.
  5. Sanitize user input – before displaying in button text.
  6. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.
  7. Rate limiting – for sensitive actions.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the button.
  • Computed styles – check the applied styles.
  • Console – use button.type, button.disabled, button.value.
  • Event listeners – use the Event Listeners panel.
  • Network panel – see the form submission when a submit button is clicked.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the button's role and name.
  • Validator – check for invalid nesting.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the button is announced.
  • Keyboard testing – Tab, Enter, Space.
  • Test disabled state – ensure it's not focusable.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For form submission – type="submit".
  • For form reset – type="reset".
  • For actions – type="button".
  • For dialogs – open/close.
  • For toggles – with aria-pressed.
  • For expand/collapse – with aria-expanded.
  • For icon actions – with aria-label.
  • For loading states – disable + spinner.
  • For confirmations – type="button" + confirm().

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For navigation – use <a>.
  • For links – use <a>.
  • For non-interactive content – use <span> or <div>.
  • As a wrapper for other interactive content – invalid nesting.
  • Without an accessible name – always provide one.
  • Without a type – always specify.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <button> – the button element.
  • <input type="submit"> – alternative submit button.
  • <input type="reset"> – alternative reset button.
  • <input type="button"> – alternative generic button.
  • <a> – for navigation.
  • <form> – the form container.
  • type attribute – submit, reset, button.
  • name and value – for multiple submit buttons.
  • disabled – disables the button.
  • form – associates with a form.
  • formaction, formmethod, formenctype, formnovalidate, formtarget – overrides.
  • aria-pressed – toggle state.
  • aria-expanded – expand/collapse state.
  • aria-label – accessible name for icon buttons.
  • role="button" – ARIA fallback (not needed for <button>).
  • click event – fires on activation.
  • submit event – fires on form submission.
  • WCAG 2.5.5 – touch target size.
  • WCAG 2.1.1 – keyboard accessible.
  • WCAG 4.1.2 – name, role, value.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <button> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) as a richer alternative to <input type="submit">.

  • Inside a <form>, a <button> without a type defaults to type="submit".

  • Outside a form, a <button> without a type defaults to type="button" (in most browsers).

  • <button> can contain rich content — icons, spans, images — while <input type="submit"> cannot.

  • Keyboard activation: <button> responds to both Enter and Space. <a> responds only to Enter.

  • aria-pressed makes a button a toggle button — it indicates an on/off state.

  • aria-expanded indicates whether a controlled element is expanded or collapsed.

  • Icon-only buttons need an aria-label to be accessible.

  • formnovalidate on a submit button skips client-side validation for that submission.

  • formaction overrides the form's action for a specific button.

  • Multiple submit buttons with different name/value let the server know which was clicked.

  • Disabled buttons are not focusable and not submitted.

  • role="button" is unnecessary on <button> — it already has the role.

  • <div role="button"> requires tabindex="0" and keyboard event handlers.

  • The First Rule of ARIA: use native <button> instead of <div role="button">.

  • Touch target size: WCAG 2.5.5 requires at least 44×44 CSS pixels.

  • Focus indicators are essential for keyboard users. Don't remove them.

  • cursor: pointer is not the default for buttons in all browsers — add it.

  • Buttons can have autofocus — but use sparingly.

  • popovertarget allows a button to control a popover natively (modern browsers).

  • commandfor and command allow declarative commands (newer feature).

  • Loading states should disable the button and announce "busy" to screen readers.

  • Double submission can be prevented by disabling the button during async operations.

  • CSRF tokens are essential for state-changing form submissions.

  • <button> in a link is invalid — do not nest interactive elements.

  • <a> styled as a button is fine for navigation — it's semantically correct.

  • Best practices include always specifying type, providing accessible names, and testing with screen readers.

  • Common mistakes include forgetting type, using <div> as a button, and removing focus outlines.

  • Following best practices for buttons leads to more accessible, maintainable, and usable forms.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A button is an interactive element that triggers an action when clicked, tapped, or activated via keyboard.
  • HTML provides two ways to create buttons: <button> (preferred) and <input type="submit/reset/button">.
  • The type attribute determines the button's behavior: submit, reset, or button.
  • Always specify type — inside a form, the default is submit.
  • Use <button> for rich content and easier styling.
  • Use <a> for navigation; use <button> for actions.
  • Icon-only buttons need an aria-label.
  • Toggle buttons use aria-pressed.
  • Expand/collapse buttons use aria-expanded.
  • Multiple submit buttons use name and value to distinguish them.
  • Override attributes (formaction, formmethod, etc.) allow per-button behavior.
  • Disabled buttons are not focusable and not submitted — use sparingly for validation.
  • Best practices: always specify type, provide accessible names, ensure touch targets are 44×44px, provide focus indicators, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include using <div> as a button, forgetting type, and removing focus outlines.
  • Buttons are essential for form submission, form reset, dialog control, toggles, and JavaScript-driven actions.
  • They are one of the most important interactive elements on the web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <select> element is an HTML form control that presents a dropdown menu (or list box) of options from which the user can choose. Each choice is defined by an <option> element nested inside the <select>. The user's selection is submitted as a name–value pair, where the name comes from the <select> element and the value comes from the selected <option>.

A <select> can be configured to allow single selection (default) or multiple selections (with the multiple attribute), and it can be grouped into categories using <optgroup>. When styled with CSS, it can be transformed from a plain dropdown into a rich, custom UI — but native behaviour ensures keyboard accessibility and screen reader support without JavaScript.

Example: 

<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country">
    <option value="">Select a country...</option>
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca">Canada</option>
    <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
</select>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <select> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Constrained input – forces the user to choose from a predefined set of options.
  • Space efficiency – a dropdown takes less space than a list of radio buttons.
  • Semantic grouping – <optgroup> groups related options.
  • Accessibility – native keyboard navigation and screen reader support.
  • Form submission – submits the selected value(s) as part of the form.
  • Default selection – can pre-select an option with selected.
  • Placeholder – a disabled option can act as a prompt.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <select> element is phrasing content and interactive content. It is a form-associated element that can appear inside a <form> (or be associated with one via the form attribute). It can contain <option> and <optgroup> elements, and it can be styled with CSS.

<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="category">Category:</label>
    <select id="category" name="category">
        <option value="tech">Technology</option>
        <option value="sports">Sports</option>
        <option value="music">Music</option>
    </select>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Forms need a way to let users choose from a predefined set of options without typing. Radio buttons work for small sets (2–5 options), but for larger sets they consume too much space. Text inputs require validation and are error-prone. Before <select>, developers had to build custom dropdowns with JavaScript — which were often inaccessible, inconsistent, and fragile.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No native dropdown Custom JavaScript widgets required. Radio buttons for large sets Too much space; overwhelming. Text inputs for constrained data Typos, invalid values. No grouping Long lists were hard to scan. Inconsistent behaviour Each custom widget behaved differently. Accessibility issues Custom widgets often lacked keyboard support.

docs.title: Why the <select> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <select> element was introduced in HTML 2.0 (1995) as part of the original form controls. It was designed to:

  • Provide a native dropdown – no JavaScript required.
  • Support single and multiple selection – with the multiple attribute.
  • Allow grouping – with <optgroup>.
  • Ensure accessibility – native keyboard navigation.
  • Enable form submission – selected value(s) submitted as name–value pairs.
  • Conserve space – dropdowns are compact.

The <select> element is one of the oldest and most widely used form controls. It remains the standard way to present constrained choices.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <select>
docs.text:
<select name="name">
    <option value="value1">Label 1</option>
    <option value="value2">Label 2</option>
</select>

docs.title: Simple Dropdown
docs.text:
<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country">
    <option value="">Select a country...</option>
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca">Canada</option>
    <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
</select>

docs.title: With Default Selected Option
docs.text:
<select name="country">
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca" selected>Canada</option>
    <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
</select>

The selected attribute pre-selects the option.

docs.title: With Disabled Placeholder Option
docs.text:
<select name="country" required>
    <option value="" disabled selected>Choose a country</option>
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca">Canada</option>
</select>

docs.title: With Option Groups
docs.text:
<label for="car">Choose a car:</label>
<select id="car" name="car">
    <optgroup label="Swedish Cars">
        <option value="volvo">Volvo</option>
        <option value="saab">Saab</option>
    </optgroup>
    <optgroup label="German Cars">
        <option value="mercedes">Mercedes</option>
        <option value="audi">Audi</option>
    </optgroup>
</select>

docs.title: Multiple Selection
docs.text:
<label for="fruits">Choose fruits (hold Ctrl/Cmd to select multiple):</label>
<select id="fruits" name="fruits" multiple size="5">
    <option value="apple">Apple</option>
    <option value="banana">Banana</option>
    <option value="cherry">Cherry</option>
    <option value="date">Date</option>
    <option value="elderberry">Elderberry</option>
</select>
  • multiple allows multiple selections.
  • size="5" displays 5 options in a list box.

docs.title: Multiple with Pre-selected Options
docs.text:
<select name="fruits" multiple size="5">
    <option value="apple" selected>Apple</option>
    <option value="banana">Banana</option>
    <option value="cherry" selected>Cherry</option>
</select>

docs.title: With Disabled Option
docs.text:
<select name="country">
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca" disabled>Canada (not available)</option>
    <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
</select>

docs.title: With form Attribute (Outside Form)
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country" form="myForm">
    <option value="us">United States</option>
</select>

docs.title: Select with required
docs.text:
<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country" required>
    <option value="" disabled selected>Choose a country</option>
    <option value="us">United States</option>
</select>

docs.title: Select with autocomplete
docs.text:
<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country" autocomplete="country">
    <option value="us">United States</option>
</select>

docs.title: Select with size
docs.text:
<select name="fruits" size="4">
    <option value="apple">Apple</option>
    <option value="banana">Banana</option>
    <option value="cherry">Cherry</option>
    <option value="date">Date</option>
</select>

Without multiple, size shows a list box with the specified number of visible rows.

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element/Attribute Purpose <select> The dropdown/list box. <option> A single choice. <optgroup> A group of options. name Field name (submitted). multiple Allow multiple selections. size Number of visible rows. required Mandatory selection. disabled Disables the control. form Associate with a form outside. autocomplete Autofill hint. selected Pre-select an option. disabled on option Disable a specific option. value on option Submitted value.

docs.title: The "Menu" Analogy
docs.text: Think of a <select> as a restaurant menu. Each <option> is a dish. The <optgroup> elements are sections (Appetizers, Main Courses, Desserts). The multiple attribute turns the menu into a buffet where you can pick several dishes.

docs.title: The "Folder" Analogy
docs.text: A <select> is like a folder containing files (options). You open the folder to see the files and pick one. With multiple, you can pick several files. With <optgroup>, the folder has subfolders.

docs.title: The "Radio Buttons in a Box" Analogy
docs.text: A <select> is like a collapsed set of radio buttons. When closed, it shows only the selected option. When opened, it shows all options. The multiple attribute turns it into a set of checkboxes.

docs.title: The "Native vs. Custom" Mental Model
docs.text: Before <select>, custom dropdowns were built with JavaScript. These were inconsistent and often inaccessible. The native <select> provides keyboard navigation, screen reader support, and OS‑native UI for free.

docs.title: Concept 1: The <option> Element
docs.text:
Each <option> represents a choice. It can have:

  • value – the value submitted when selected. If omitted, the text content is used.
  • selected – pre-selects the option.
  • disabled – disables the option.
  • label – an alternative label (rarely used).
<option value="us">United States</option>

docs.title: Concept 2: The <optgroup> Element
docs.text:
<optgroup> groups related options. It has a label attribute (required) that displays as a group heading.

<optgroup label="North America">
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca">Canada</option>
</optgroup>

Note: Options inside an <optgroup> cannot be selected as a group — only individual options.

docs.title: Concept 3: The multiple Attribute
docs.text:
The multiple boolean attribute allows multiple selections. The user holds Ctrl (Windows/Linux) or Cmd (macOS) to select multiple options.

<select name="fruits" multiple>
    <option value="apple">Apple</option>
    <option value="banana">Banana</option>
</select>

When multiple is present, the control renders as a list box, not a dropdown.

docs.title: Concept 4: The size Attribute
docs.text:
The size attribute specifies the number of visible options:

  • Without multiple: shows a list box with size rows.
  • With multiple: shows a scrollable list box with size rows.
<select name="fruits" multiple size="5">

Default size is 1 (dropdown) without multiple, and 4 with multiple.

docs.title: Concept 5: The required Attribute
docs.text:
required makes the selection mandatory. The first option must have an empty value to act as a placeholder.

<select name="country" required>
    <option value="" disabled selected>Choose a country</option>
    <option value="us">United States</option>
</select>

Note: For multiple, required requires at least one selection.

docs.title: Concept 6: The selected Attribute
docs.text:
Pre-selects an option. If multiple options have selected, the last one wins (in single-select mode).

<option value="ca" selected>Canada</option>

docs.title: Concept 7: The disabled Attribute
docs.text:
Disables the <select> (user cannot interact) or an individual <option> (cannot be selected).

<select name="country" disabled>...</select>
<option value="ca" disabled>Canada</option>

docs.title: Concept 8: Option Values
docs.text:
• If value is present, it is submitted.
  • If value is omitted, the option's text content is submitted.
<option>United States</option>  <!-- Submits "United States" -->
<option value="us">United States</option>  <!-- Submits "us" -->

Best practice: Always provide a value for clarity.

docs.title: Concept 9: Placeholder Option
docs.text:
A common pattern is to use a disabled, selected, empty‑value option as a placeholder:

<option value="" disabled selected>Choose a country</option>

Why: Forces the user to make a conscious choice; validates with required.

docs.title: Concept 10: Keyboard Navigation
docs.text:
Native <select> supports:

  • Tab – focus the select.
  • Space / Enter – open the dropdown.
  • Arrow keys – navigate options.
  • Enter – select the highlighted option.
  • Escape – close without selecting.
  • Type‑ahead – type letters to jump to options.

docs.title: Concept 11: Screen Reader Support
docs.text:
Screen readers announce:

  • The label of the select.
  • The current selection.
  • The list of options when opened.
  • The group labels (<optgroup>) when navigating.

docs.title: Concept 12: Styling <select>
docs.text:
Native <select> has limited styling options. Common properties:

select {
    padding: 0.5rem;
    border: 1px solid #ccc;
    border-radius: 4px;
    font-size: 1rem;
    background: white;
}

Note: appearance: none removes native styling, but you must provide your own arrow icon.

docs.title: Concept 13: Custom Styling with appearance: none
docs.text:
select {
    appearance: none;
    background: url('arrow.svg') no-repeat right 0.5rem center;
    background-size: 1rem;
    padding-right: 2rem;
}

docs.title: Concept 14: The form Attribute
docs.text:
A <select> outside a form can be associated with one:

<form id="myForm">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
<select name="country" form="myForm">...</select>

docs.title: Concept 15: Accessibility
docs.text:
• Label – always use <label>.
  • Keyboard – native support.
  • Screen readers – announce options and groups.
  • Required – announced as required.
  • Disabled – announced as disabled.
  • Multiple – announced as multi‑select.

docs.title: Concept 16: Select vs. Radio Buttons
docs.text:
Aspect <select> Radio Buttons Space Compact Takes more space Options Many (5+) Few (2–5) Visibility Hidden until opened Always visible Keyboard Arrow keys Arrow keys Multiple With multiple Independent checkboxes Use case Large lists Small sets

Rule: Use radio buttons for 2–5 options; use <select> for 5+ options.

docs.title: Concept 17: Select vs. Datalist
docs.text: Aspect <select> <datalist> Input Choose from list Type or choose Validation Must be in list Free text allowed Browser support Universal Limited Use case Constrained choices Suggestions

docs.title: Concept 18: The size Attribute and List Boxes
docs.text:
A <select> with size > 1 and no multiple behaves like a list box — all options visible, only one selectable.

<select name="fruit" size="4">
    <option value="apple">Apple</option>
    <option value="banana">Banana</option>
    <option value="cherry">Cherry</option>
    <option value="date">Date</option>
</select>

docs.title: Concept 19: Select with multiple and size
docs.text:
<select name="fruits" multiple size="5">
    <option value="apple">Apple</option>
    <option value="banana">Banana</option>
    <option value="cherry">Cherry</option>
</select>

Note: Multi‑select is often a poor UX on mobile — consider checkboxes instead.

docs.title: Concept 20: Select and Form Submission
docs.text:
• Single select: submits one name–value pair.
  • Multiple select: submits multiple name–value pairs with the same name.
<select name="fruits" multiple>
    <option value="apple" selected>Apple</option>
    <option value="banana" selected>Banana</option>
</select>

Submits: fruits=apple&fruits=banana.

docs.title: Concept 21: The selectedOptions Property
docs.text:
JavaScript can access selected options:

const select = document.querySelector('select');
console.log(select.selectedOptions); // HTMLCollection of selected options

docs.title: Concept 22: The value Property
docs.text:
For single select, select.value returns the value of the selected option.

select.value = 'us'; // Set selection programmatically

For multiple select, select.value returns only the first selected value. Use selectedOptions for all.

docs.title: Concept 23: The options Property
docs.text:
select.options returns an HTMLOptionsCollection of all <option> elements.

console.log(select.options.length); // Number of options
console.log(select.options[0].text); // First option's text

docs.title: Concept 24: The selectedIndex Property
docs.text:
select.selectedIndex returns the index of the selected option (or -1 if none).

console.log(select.selectedIndex); // 0, 1, 2, ...

docs.title: Concept 25: Select Events
docs.text:
• change – fires when the selection changes.
  • input – fires on selection change (modern browsers).
select.addEventListener('change', (e) => {
    console.log(e.target.value);
});

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing a <select>
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters a `<select>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the select.
    │
    ▼
3.  It reads attributes: name, multiple, size, required, etc.
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes each `<option>` child:
    │   ├── Creates an option node.
    │   ├── Sets value (or uses text content).
    │   └── Reads `selected` and `disabled`.
    │
    ▼
5.  It processes `<optgroup>` children:
    │   ├── Creates an optgroup node.
    │   └── Processes nested options.
    │
    ▼
6.  When the closing tag is encountered, the select is closed.
    │
    ▼
7.  Default styles are applied.
    │
    ▼
8.  The accessibility tree is built:
    │   ├── role: combobox (single) or listbox (multiple).
    │   └── options as children.
    │
    ▼
9.  The page is rendered.
    │
    ▼
10. User interacts:
    │   ├── Opens dropdown.
    │   ├── Navigates with arrows.
    │   ├── Selects with Enter.
    │   └── `change` event fires.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
• <select> (single) → role: combobox.
  • <select multiple> → role: listbox.
  • <option> → role: option.
  • <optgroup> → role: group with a label.

Screen readers announce the label, current selection, and options.

docs.title: The change Event
docs.text:
Fires when the user commits a selection:

select.addEventListener('change', (e) => {
    console.log('Selected:', e.target.value);
});

docs.title: Form Submission
docs.text:
• Single select: one name–value pair.
  • Multiple select: one name–value pair per selected option.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
select {
    display: inline-block;
    padding: 1px 2px;
    border: 1px solid buttonborder;
    background: buttonface;
    color: buttontext;
    font-family: inherit;
    font-size: inherit;
}

docs.title: The HTMLSelectElement Interface
docs.text:
Property/Method Description value Value of the selected option (single) or first selected (multiple). selectedIndex Index of the selected option. selectedOptions Collection of selected options (multiple). options Collection of all <option> elements. length Number of options. multiple Whether multiple selection is allowed. size Number of visible rows. required Whether selection is required. disabled Whether disabled. form The associated form. labels Associated labels. add(option, before) Adds an option. remove(index) Removes an option. item(index) Returns the option at index. namedItem(name) Returns the option with the given id/name. 
const select = document.querySelector('select');
console.log(select.value);          // "us"
console.log(select.selectedIndex);  // 0
console.log(select.options.length); // 3
select.value = 'ca';                 // Change selection

docs.title: The HTMLOptionElement Interface
docs.text: Property Description value The value attribute. text The text content. selected Whether selected. disabled Whether disabled. defaultSelected Whether selected by default. index Position in the options collection. label The label attribute.

docs.title: The HTMLOptGroupElement Interface
docs.text: Property Description label The group label. disabled Whether disabled.

docs.title: Accessibility Mapping
docs.text: Element Role <select> (single) combobox <select multiple> listbox <option> option <optgroup> group

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text: Browsers apply OS‑specific styling. Use appearance: none to override.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <select>
docs.text:
1.  Author writes the `<select>` with options.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses and creates DOM nodes.
    │
    ▼
3.  Default styles applied.
    │
    ▼
4.  Accessibility tree built.
    │
    ▼
5.  Page rendered.
    │
    ▼
6.  User interacts:
    │   ├── Focus.
    │   ├── Open dropdown.
    │   ├── Navigate options.
    │   ├── Select option(s).
    │   └── `change` event fires.
    │
    ▼
7.  Form submission includes selected value(s).
    │
    ▼
8.  JavaScript may modify options dynamically.
    │
    ▼
9.  When the page is unloaded, the select is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
// Add a new option
const newOption = new Option('Mexico', 'mx');
select.add(newOption);

// Remove an option
select.remove(0);

// Change selection
select.value = 'ca';

// Listen for changes
select.addEventListener('change', (e) => {
    console.log(e.target.value);
});

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Country Dropdown
docs.text:
<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country">
    <option value="">Select...</option>
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca">Canada</option>
    <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
</select>

docs.title: Example 2: Required with Placeholder
docs.text:
<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country" required>
    <option value="" disabled selected>Choose a country</option>
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca">Canada</option>
</select>

docs.title: Example 3: Grouped Options
docs.text:
<label for="car">Choose a car:</label>
<select id="car" name="car">
    <optgroup label="Swedish Cars">
        <option value="volvo">Volvo</option>
        <option value="saab">Saab</option>
    </optgroup>
    <optgroup label="German Cars">
        <option value="mercedes">Mercedes</option>
        <option value="audi">Audi</option>
    </optgroup>
</select>

docs.title: Example 4: Multiple Selection
docs.text:
<label for="fruits">Choose fruits:</label>
<select id="fruits" name="fruits" multiple size="5">
    <option value="apple">Apple</option>
    <option value="banana">Banana</option>
    <option value="cherry">Cherry</option>
    <option value="date">Date</option>
    <option value="elderberry">Elderberry</option>
</select>

docs.title: Example 5: Pre-selected Options
docs.text:
<select name="fruits" multiple size="5">
    <option value="apple" selected>Apple</option>

<p id="output"></p>

docs.title: Example 11: Dynamic Options
docs.text:
<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country">
    <option value="">Loading...</option>
</select>

<script>
    const countries = [
        { value: 'us', label: 'United States' },
        { value: 'ca', label: 'Canada' },
        { value: 'uk', label: 'United Kingdom' }
    ];
    const select = document.getElementById('country');
    select.innerHTML = '<option value="">Select...</option>';
    countries.forEach(c => {
        const option = new Option(c.label, c.value);
        select.add(option);
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 12: Dependent Dropdowns
docs.text:
<label for="country">Country:</label>
<select id="country" name="country">
    <option value="">Select...</option>
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca">Canada</option>
</select>

<label for="state">State/Province:</label>
<select id="state" name="state" disabled>
    <option value="">Select a country first</option>
</select>

<script>
    const data = {
        us: ['California', 'New York', 'Texas'],
        ca: ['Ontario', 'Quebec', 'British Columbia']
    };
    const country = document.getElementById('country');
    const state = document.getElementById('state');
    country.addEventListener('change', () => {
        state.innerHTML = '<option value="">Select...</option>';
        state.disabled = !country.value;
        (data[country.value] || []).forEach(s => {
            state.add(new Option(s, s.toLowerCase()));
        });
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 13: Multi-select with "Select All"

<button type="button" id="selectAll">Select All</button>
<button type="button" id="clearAll">Clear All</button>

    document.getElementById('clearAll').addEventListener('click', () => {
        document.querySelectorAll('#fruits option').forEach(o => o.selected = false);
    });
</script>

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Select Demo</title>
    <style>
        body {
            font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
            max-width: 600px;
            margin: 2rem auto;
            padding: 0 1rem;
        }

            display: flex;
