    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
</div>

docs.title: Example 16: Fieldset and Grid Layout
docs.text:
<style>
    fieldset {
        display: grid;
        grid-template-columns: auto 1fr;
        gap: 0.5rem 1rem;
        align-items: center;
    }
    legend {
        grid-column: 1 / -1;
    }
</style>

<fieldset>
    <legend>Login</legend>
    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username">
    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password">
</fieldset>

docs.title: Example 17: Fieldset with Validation
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST">
    <fieldset id="contact">
        <legend>Contact Information</legend>
        <label for="email">Email:</label>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<script>
    document.getElementById('myForm').addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
        const fieldset = document.getElementById('contact');
        if (!fieldset.checkValidity()) {
            e.preventDefault();
            alert('Please fill out the contact information.');
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 18: Fieldset with Legend as Heading
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <legend><h2>Shipping Address</h2></legend>
    <label for="street">Street:</label>
    <input type="text" id="street" name="street">
</fieldset>

Note: Using a heading inside <legend> is valid and can help with document outline.

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Form with Fieldsets
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Fieldset Demo</title>
    <style>
        body {
            font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
            max-width: 600px;
            margin: 2rem auto;
            padding: 0 1rem;
        }
        form {
            display: flex;
            flex-direction: column;
            gap: 1rem;
        }
        fieldset {
            border: 1px solid #dee2e6;
            border-radius: 8px;
            padding: 1rem;
            background: #f8f9fa;
            display: flex;
            flex-direction: column;
            gap: 0.5rem;
        }
        legend {
            font-weight: bold;
            color: #2c3e50;
            padding: 0 0.5rem;
            background: white;
            border: 1px solid #dee2e6;
            border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 1rem;
        }
        label {
            font-weight: 500;
            margin-top: 0.5rem;
        }
        input, select, textarea {
            padding: 0.5rem;
            border: 1px solid #dee2e6;
            border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 1rem;
            width: 100%;
            box-sizing: border-box;
        }
        input:focus, select:focus, textarea:focus {
            outline: 2px solid #3498db;
            outline-offset: 2px;
        }
        .radio-group label,
        .checkbox-group label {
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.5rem;
            font-weight: normal;
            margin: 0.25rem 0;
        }
        button {
            padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
            background: #3498db;
            color: white;
            border: none;
            border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 1rem;
            cursor: pointer;
        }
        button:hover {
            background: #2980b9;
        }
        fieldset:disabled {
            opacity: 0.6;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Fieldset Demo</h1>

    <form action="/submit" method="POST">
        <fieldset>
            <legend>Personal Information</legend>
            <label for="name">Name:</label>
            <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
            <label for="email">Email:</label>
            <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
        </fieldset>

        <fieldset>
            <legend>Preferred Contact Method</legend>
            <div class="radio-group">
                <label>
                    <input type="radio" name="contact" value="email" checked>
                    Email
                </label>
                <label>
                    <input type="radio" name="contact" value="phone">
                    Phone
                </label>
                <label>
                    <input type="radio" name="contact" value="mail">
                    Mail
                </label>
            </div>
        </fieldset>

        <fieldset>
            <legend>Interests</legend>
            <div class="checkbox-group">
                <label>
                    <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="tech" checked>
                    Technology
                </label>
                <label>
                    <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="sports">
                    Sports
                </label>
                <label>
                    <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="music">
                    Music
                </label>
            </div>
        </fieldset>

        <fieldset id="shipping" disabled>
            <legend>Shipping Address</legend>
            <label for="street">Street:</label>
            <input type="text" id="street" name="street">
            <label for="city">City:</label>
            <input type="text" id="city" name="city">
            <label for="zip">ZIP:</label>
            <input type="text" id="zip" name="zip">
        </fieldset>

        <label>
            <input type="checkbox" id="enableShipping" checked>
            Enable shipping address
        </label>

        <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    </form>

    <script>
        document.getElementById('enableShipping').addEventListener('change', (e) => {
            document.getElementById('shipping').disabled = !e.target.checked;
        });
        // Initial state: enable if checked
        document.getElementById('shipping').disabled = !document.getElementById('enableShipping').checked;
    </script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Personal information Name, email, phone Address forms Shipping, billing Payment information Card details Radio groups Gender, contact method Checkbox groups Interests, preferences Multi-step forms Step-by-step wizards Conditional sections Show/hide based on selection Disabled sections Not-applicable fields Surveys Grouped questions Settings panels Grouped preferences Nested groups Contact info → email/phone Login/signup Account details

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <fieldset> for related form controls – always group related fields.
  2. Always include a <legend> – it provides the group label.
  3. Place <legend> as the first child – required by the spec.
  4. Use <fieldset> for radio and checkbox groups – essential for accessibility.
  5. Use disabled for conditional sections – one attribute disables all controls.
  6. Don't nest too deeply – 2–3 levels is usually enough.
  7. Style fieldsets consistently – reset browser defaults.
  8. Use name for JavaScript access – when needed.
  9. Use form attribute for fieldsets outside forms – for layout flexibility.
  10. Test with screen readers – ensure the legend is announced.
  11. Don't use <fieldset> for layout – use <div> or CSS Grid.
  12. Avoid empty <fieldset> – always have at least one control.
  13. Use aria-describedby for additional help – beyond the legend.
  14. Keep legends concise – short, descriptive.
  15. Use <fieldset> in multi-step forms – enables/disables steps.
  16. Test dynamic disabling – ensure controls are properly disabled.
  17. Avoid disabling entire forms – users may not understand why.
  18. Use :disabled CSS – to style disabled groups.
  19. Document fieldset conventions – in a style guide.
  20. Consider role="group" as fallback – if <fieldset> can't be used.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No <legend>
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
</fieldset>

Why it's wrong: The group has no accessible name.

✅ Correct: 

<fieldset>
    <legend>Personal Information</legend>
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
</fieldset>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <legend> Elements
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <legend>Group 1</legend>
    <legend>Group 2</legend>
</fieldset>

Why it's wrong: Only one <legend> is allowed per <fieldset>.

✅ Correct: Use one <legend>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: <legend> Not First Child
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <input type="text" name="name">
    <legend>Personal Information</legend>
</fieldset>

Why it's wrong: <legend> must be the first child.

✅ Correct: 

<fieldset>
    <legend>Personal Information</legend>
    <input type="text" name="name">
</fieldset>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div> for Radio Groups
docs.text:
<div>
    <p>Gender:</p>
    <input type="radio" name="gender" value="male"> Male
    <input type="radio" name="gender" value="female"> Female
</div>

Why it's wrong: No semantic group, no accessible group label.

✅ Correct: 

<fieldset>
    <legend>Gender</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="male"> Male</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="female"> Female</label>
</fieldset>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Disabling Individual Controls Instead of Fieldset
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="field1" disabled>
<input type="text" name="field2" disabled>
<input type="text" name="field3" disabled>

Why it's wrong: Repetitive, easy to miss one.

✅ Correct: 

<fieldset disabled>
    <legend>Disabled Section</legend>
    <input type="text" name="field1">
    <input type="text" name="field2">
    <input type="text" name="field3">
</fieldset>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Empty Fieldset
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <legend>Empty</legend>
</fieldset>

Why it's wrong: No controls to group; meaningless.

✅ Correct: Only use fieldsets with controls.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <fieldset> for Layout
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <legend>Layout</legend>
    <div>Column 1</div>
    <div>Column 2</div>
</fieldset>

Why it's wrong: Fieldset is for grouping form controls, not layout.

✅ Correct: Use CSS Grid or Flexbox for layout.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing Disabled State
docs.text:
<fieldset disabled>
    <legend>Section</legend>
    <input type="text" name="field">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</fieldset>

Why it's wrong: The submit button is disabled and won't submit the form.

✅ Correct: Place the submit button outside the disabled fieldset.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Legend Not Visible
docs.text:
<style>
    legend {
        display: none;
    }
</style>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers may still announce it, but sighted users lose context.

✅ Correct: Keep the legend visible.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Fieldsets Without Legends
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <input type="text" name="field1">
</fieldset>
<fieldset>
    <input type="text" name="field2">
</fieldset>

Why it's wrong: Neither group has a label; screen readers announce "group" without context.

✅ Correct: Always include a <legend>.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Fieldsets are lightweight – one DOM node per group.
  • Disabled inheritance – efficiently handled by the browser.
  • Rendering – fieldsets have default borders and padding; negligible cost.
  • Nested fieldsets – minor overhead; use sparingly.
  • CSS Grid/Flexbox on fieldsets – some browsers have quirks; test performance.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep nesting shallow – 2–3 levels max.
  2. Avoid unnecessary fieldsets – only group related controls.
  3. Use CSS for styling – avoid inline styles.
  4. Minify HTML – reduce file size.
  5. Test large forms – with many fieldsets.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• XSS – if fieldset content contains user-generated data, sanitize it.
  • innerHTML – avoid using innerHTML with user input; use textContent.
  • Injection – never insert user input into <legend> or fieldset attributes without escaping.
  • CSRF – use tokens for form submissions.
  • No direct security implications – fieldsets themselves are not a security risk.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user input – before inserting into forms.
  2. Use textContent – instead of innerHTML for text.
  3. Validate structure – ensure the fieldset is well-formed.
  4. Use CSP – to restrict inline scripts and styles.
  5. Use CSRF tokens – for state-changing forms.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the fieldset and legend.
  • Computed styles – check display, border, padding.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the group role and legend as name.
  • Console – use fieldset.disabled, fieldset.elements.
  • fieldset.form – returns the associated form.
  • Validator – check for missing legends, multiple legends, legend not first.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the legend is announced.
  • Test disabled state – ensure all controls are disabled.
  • Test dynamic changes – toggling disabled should work.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For related form controls – always group related fields.
  • For radio button groups – essential for accessibility.
  • For checkbox groups – essential for accessibility.
  • For address forms – shipping vs. billing.
  • For payment forms – card details.
  • For multi-step forms – step grouping.
  • For conditional sections – enabling/disabling groups.
  • For surveys – grouped questions.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For layout – use CSS Grid or Flexbox.
  • For non-form content – use <section> or <div>.
  • For single controls – no need to group one field.
  • Without a legend – always include a legend.
  • As a replacement for <div> – fieldsets are for form groups.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <legend> – the group caption.
  • <form> – the form container.
  • <label> – labels for individual controls.
  • <input> – form controls.
  • <select> – dropdown.
  • <textarea> – multi-line text.
  • <button> – form buttons.
  • disabled – disables all controls in a group.
  • name – JavaScript access.
  • form – associates with a form outside.
  • role="group" – ARIA fallback.
  • aria-describedby – additional context.
  • fieldset.elements – controls inside.
  • WCAG 1.3.1 – info and relationships.
  • WCAG 3.3.2 – labels or instructions.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <fieldset> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) to improve form accessibility.

  • It is the only element that can contain a <legend> as its first child.

  • A disabled fieldset disables all descendant form controls — including nested fieldsets and buttons.

  • Controls inside a disabled fieldset are not submitted with the form.

  • The <fieldset> element creates a group role in the accessibility tree.

  • The <legend> becomes the accessible name of the group.

  • Screen readers announce the legend when the user enters the group.

  • Radio button groups should always be wrapped in a <fieldset> with a <legend>.

  • Checkbox groups should also use <fieldset> + <legend> for the group label.

  • The <fieldset> element has a name attribute (HTML5) that lets JavaScript access it via form.elements.

  • The form attribute on a fieldset associates it with a form outside its DOM tree.

  • The default browser style for <fieldset> includes a groove border and padding.

  • The <legend> element is rendered on the border of the fieldset by default — a unique behavior.

  • Styling <legend> is notoriously tricky; float: left or display: block can help.

  • Nested fieldsets are valid and useful for hierarchical grouping.

  • Multi-step forms often use fieldsets with disabled to control progress.

  • The fieldset.elements property returns all form controls inside.

  • fieldset.checkValidity() always returns true — fieldsets themselves aren't validated.

  • A disabled fieldset skips validation for its controls.

  • The <fieldset> element is flow content and sectioning content.

  • Best practices include always using a <legend>, grouping related controls, and testing with screen readers.

  • Common mistakes include missing legends, multiple legends, and legend not first.

  • Following best practices for fieldsets leads to more accessible, structured, and maintainable forms.

  • The <fieldset> element is one of the most important accessibility features of HTML forms.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <fieldset> element groups related form controls into a single logical unit.
  • It is paired with a <legend> element that provides a caption for the group.
  • The <legend> must be the first child of the <fieldset>.
  • A disabled fieldset disables all descendant controls — and they are not submitted.
  • The <fieldset> creates a group role in the accessibility tree, with the legend as the accessible name.
  • Radio button groups and checkbox groups should always be wrapped in a <fieldset> with a <legend>.
  • Best practices: always include a <legend>, use fieldsets for related controls, use disabled for conditional sections, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include missing legends, multiple legends, legend not first, and using fieldsets for layout.
  • Fieldsets are essential for personal information, address forms, payment forms, multi-step forms, and conditional sections.
  • They are one of the most important elements for form accessibility and structure on the web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Form validation is the process of checking whether the data a user has entered into a form meets the expected requirements before it is accepted or submitted. HTML provides a native, declarative validation system — often called constraint validation — that allows developers to specify rules using attributes on form controls, without writing any JavaScript. When a form is submitted, the browser automatically checks all constraints and, if any fail, prevents submission and displays an error message.

The native validation system is complemented by:

  • JavaScript validation – for custom rules and better UX.
  • Server-side validation – the only truly reliable validation (must always be present).
  • ARIA – to announce errors to assistive technologies.

Example: 

<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

If the user enters an invalid email or leaves the field empty, the browser shows an error and blocks submission.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Form validation serves several essential purposes:

  • Data quality – ensures data is correct, complete, and in the expected format.
  • User feedback – gives users immediate feedback on errors.
  • Server protection – reduces the load of invalid submissions reaching the server.
  • Security – the first line of defence against malformed or malicious input (but never the only one).
  • Accessibility – error messages must be accessible to all users.
  • Compliance – many industries require validated data (finance, healthcare, government).
  • UX – prevents frustration of submitting invalid data and waiting for server responses.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Validation is a cross-cutting concern that touches every form control. It combines:

  • HTML attributes – required, pattern, min, max, minlength, maxlength, type, step.
  • CSS – :valid, :invalid, :required, :optional pseudo-classes.
  • JavaScript – the Constraint Validation API.
  • ARIA – aria-invalid, aria-describedby, role="alert".
  • Server-side code – always required.
Validation Layers
│
├── Client-side (HTML attributes)
├── Client-side (JavaScript)
├── Accessibility (ARIA)
└── Server-side (language-specific)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Without validation, users can submit anything — empty required fields, malformed email addresses, out-of-range numbers, mismatched passwords, invalid credit cards. The server receives garbage data, which it must handle:

  • Data corruption – invalid data enters the database.
  • Security vulnerabilities – malformed input can exploit server bugs.
  • Poor UX – users wait for a server round-trip to learn about an error.
  • Wasted resources – the server processes invalid submissions.
  • Frustration – users repeat the form after a delayed error.

Before HTML5, validation required JavaScript for even basic rules. This was:

  • Inconsistent – every site implemented its own.
  • Inaccessible – custom error messages were often not announced.
  • Fragile – JavaScript could be disabled.
  • Verbose – boilerplate code for every form.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No native validation JavaScript required for every rule. Inconsistent UI Each site had its own error display. Inaccessible Errors not announced to screen readers. Easily bypassed JavaScript could be disabled. Verbose code Boilerplate for every form. No mobile optimization Mobile keyboards not aligned with input types.

docs.title: Why Native Validation Was Introduced
docs.text:
HTML5 introduced constraint validation to provide a native, declarative, accessible validation system. It enables:

  • Declarative rules – required, pattern, min, max, type.
  • Native UI – browsers show error messages automatically.
  • Accessibility – errors are announced by screen readers.
  • Mobile optimization – correct keyboards for each type.
  • CSS integration – :valid, :invalid pseudo-classes.
  • JavaScript API – the Constraint Validation API for custom rules.

The native validation system doesn't replace server-side validation — it's an enhancement for UX. But it's a huge improvement over custom JavaScript-only validation.

docs.title: Required Fields
docs.text:
<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

Constraint: Field must not be empty.

docs.title: Type Validation
docs.text:
<input type="email" name="email">    <!-- must be a valid email -->
<input type="url" name="website">     <!-- must be a valid URL -->
<input type="number" name="age">      <!-- must be numeric -->
<input type="date" name="birthday">   <!-- must be a valid date -->

docs.title: Length Validation
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="username" minlength="3" maxlength="20">
<textarea name="message" minlength="10" maxlength="500"></textarea>

docs.title: Range Validation
docs.text:
<input type="number" name="age" min="18" max="120">
<input type="range" name="volume" min="0" max="100">
<input type="date" name="birthday" min="1900-01-01" max="2026-12-31">

docs.title: Pattern Validation
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="Five-digit ZIP code">
<input type="tel" name="phone" pattern="[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}" title="Format: 555-123-4567">

Important: Always include a title attribute with the pattern so users know what's expected.

docs.title: Step Validation
docs.text:
<input type="number" name="quantity" min="0" max="100" step="5">

Constraint: Value must be a multiple of step offset by min.

docs.title: Multiple Validation
docs.text:
<input type="email" name="emails" multiple>

Constraint: Each comma-separated value must be a valid email.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" required minlength="3" maxlength="20">

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

    <label for="age">Age:</label>
    <input type="number" id="age" name="age" min="18" max="120" required>

    <label for="zip">ZIP Code:</label>
    <input type="text" id="zip" name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="Five-digit ZIP code" required>

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: CSS Validation States
docs.text:
input:valid {
    border-color: green;
}

input:invalid {
    border-color: red;
}

input:required {
    border-left: 3px solid orange;
}

input:optional {
    border-left: 3px solid gray;
}

input:in-range {
    background: #f0fff0;
}

input:out-of-range {
    background: #fff0f0;
}

docs.title: Constraint Validation API
docs.text:
const form = document.querySelector('form');
const input = document.querySelector('input');

// Check validity
console.log(input.checkValidity()); // true or false
console.log(input.validity.valid);

// Report validity (shows error)
input.reportValidity();

// Set custom error
input.setCustomValidity('Custom error message');
input.setCustomValidity(''); // Clear

// Check all form controls
console.log(form.checkValidity());

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Constraint required Value must not be empty. type="email" Must be a valid email. type="url" Must be a valid URL. type="number" Must be numeric. minlength Minimum length. maxlength Maximum length. min Minimum value. max Maximum value. pattern Must match regex. step Must be a multiple of step. multiple Multiple values allowed.

docs.title: The "Bouncer" Analogy
docs.text: Think of validation as a bouncer at a club. The bouncer checks IDs (required), ensures people are old enough (min), and verifies they're on the guest list (pattern). Only those who pass can enter (submit). The bouncer works automatically — you don't need to ask them to check.

docs.title: The "Checklist" Analogy
docs.text: Validation is like a checklist before takeoff. Each item must be checked: required (fuel), format (correct coordinates), range (altitude within limits). If any item fails, the flight is delayed. The checklist is applied automatically every time.

docs.title: The "Contract" Analogy
docs.text: Validation is a contract between the form and the user. The form states its requirements (constraints), and the user agrees to meet them. If the user breaks the contract (invalid input), the form refuses to submit.

docs.title: The "Concentric Circles" Mental Model
docs.text:
Validation happens in concentric circles:

  1. HTML attributes – the innermost, easiest.
  2. JavaScript – additional custom rules.
  3. ARIA – accessibility announcements.
  4. Server-side – the outermost, ultimate authority.

Each circle catches what the previous one misses.

docs.title: The "Never Trust the Client" Mental Model
docs.text: The most important mental model: never trust the client. Client-side validation (HTML or JavaScript) is for user experience — it gives instant feedback. But it can be bypassed (disable JS, use curl, modify HTML). Server-side validation is the only true validation — it must always be present.

docs.title: Concept 1: Constraint Validation
docs.text:
The HTML5 constraint validation system applies constraints to form controls. Each control either satisfies or violates its constraints. If any control is invalid, the form cannot be submitted.

<input type="email" required>

Constraints: - Must not be empty (required). - Must match email format (type="email").

docs.title: Concept 2: The validity Property
docs.text:
Each form control has a validity property — a ValidityState object with boolean flags:

Property Meaning valid All constraints pass. valueMissing required and empty. typeMismatch Doesn't match type (email, url, number). patternMismatch Doesn't match pattern. tooLong Exceeds maxlength. tooShort Below minlength. rangeUnderflow Below min. rangeOverflow Above max. stepMismatch Doesn't match step. badInput Browser can't parse. customError Custom error set. 
const input = document.querySelector('input');
if (input.validity.valueMissing) {
    console.log('Field is required');
}

docs.title: Concept 3: The checkValidity() Method
docs.text:
Returns true if the control is valid, false otherwise. Fires an invalid event if invalid.

input.checkValidity(); // true/false
form.checkValidity();  // true if all controls valid

docs.title: Concept 4: The reportValidity() Method
docs.text:
Like checkValidity(), but also shows the browser's error message if invalid.

input.reportValidity();
form.reportValidity();

docs.title: Concept 5: The setCustomValidity() Method
docs.text:
Sets a custom error message. The control is considered invalid until setCustomValidity('') is called.

if (password.value !== confirm.value) {
    confirm.setCustomValidity('Passwords do not match');
} else {
    confirm.setCustomValidity('');
}

docs.title: Concept 6: The invalid Event
docs.text:
Fires on each invalid control when validity is checked.

input.addEventListener('invalid', () => {
    console.log('Invalid input');
});

Note: The invalid event does not bubble, so you must attach listeners to each control.

docs.title: Concept 7: The novalidate Attribute
docs.text:
The novalidate attribute on <form> disables native validation. Useful for custom validation.

<form novalidate>
    ...
</form>

docs.title: Concept 8: The formnovalidate Attribute
docs.text:
The formnovalidate attribute on a submit button disables validation for that submission.

<button type="submit" formnovalidate>Save Draft</button>

docs.title: Concept 9: CSS Validation Pseudo-Classes
docs.text:
Pseudo-Class Matches :valid Controls that pass validation. :invalid Controls that fail validation. :required Controls with required. :optional Controls without required. :in-range Values within min/max. :out-of-range Values outside min/max. :read-only Controls with readonly. :read-write Controls without readonly. :placeholder-shown Controls showing placeholder. :default Default-selected controls. :indeterminate Checkboxes/radios in indeterminate state.

Caution: :invalid applies on page load for empty required fields. Use :user-invalid (newer) or JavaScript to avoid premature styling.

docs.title: Concept 10: The :user-invalid Pseudo-Class
docs.text:
A newer pseudo-class that only matches after the user interacts:

input:user-invalid {
    border-color: red;
}

Browser support: Modern browsers (2023+).

docs.title: Concept 11: Accessible Error Messages
docs.text:
Screen readers must be able to announce errors. Techniques:

  • aria-invalid="true" on the control.
  • aria-describedby referencing the error message.
  • role="alert" on the error container.
  • aria-live="polite" for dynamic errors.
<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" aria-describedby="email-error" aria-invalid="true">
<span id="email-error" role="alert">Please enter a valid email.</span>

docs.title: Concept 12: Browser Validation Messages
docs.text:
Browsers show their own error messages. These vary by browser and locale. To customize:

  • Use setCustomValidity().
  • Use JavaScript validation with custom messages.
  • Use CSS for visual cues.

docs.title: Concept 13: Client vs. Server Validation
docs.text:
Aspect Client-Side Server-Side Speed Instant Delayed Security Bypassable Reliable UX Good feedback Poor feedback Cost Free (HTML) Server resources Use case UX enhancement True validation

Rule: Always validate on both sides. Client for UX, server for security.

docs.title: Concept 14: Regular Expressions in pattern
docs.text:
The pattern attribute uses JavaScript regex syntax (without slashes):

<input pattern="[0-9]{5}">           <!-- 5 digits -->
<input pattern="[A-Za-z]{3,}">        <!-- 3+ letters -->
<input pattern="\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}">   <!-- phone format -->

Note: The pattern is anchored — it must match the entire value.

docs.title: Concept 15: The title Attribute with pattern
docs.text:
Always pair pattern with title:

<input pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="Five-digit ZIP code">

The browser shows the title in the validation message.

docs.title: Concept 16: The inputmode Attribute
docs.text:
While not a validation attribute, inputmode complements validation:

<input type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]*">

Shows a numeric keyboard on mobile.

docs.title: Concept 17: The autocomplete Attribute
docs.text:
Autofill helps users avoid validation errors by providing correctly formatted data.

<input type="email" autocomplete="email" required>

docs.title: Concept 18: The type Attribute as Validation
docs.text:
The type attribute provides built-in validation:

  • email – must be a valid email.
  • url – must be a valid URL.
  • number – must be numeric.
  • date – must be a valid date.
  • time – must be a valid time.
  • color – must be a hex color.

docs.title: Concept 19: Validation and Accessibility
docs.text:
• Labels – every control must have a label.
  • Error messages – associated via aria-describedby.
  • aria-invalid – set to true on invalid controls.
  • role="alert" – announces errors immediately.
  • Focus – move focus to the first invalid field.
  • Color – don't rely on color alone.
  • Text – always provide text descriptions.

docs.title: Concept 20: The form.checkValidity() Method
docs.text:
Returns true if all controls are valid:

if (form.checkValidity()) {
    form.submit();
} else {
    // Show errors
}

docs.title: Concept 21: Focus Management
docs.text:
When validation fails, focus should move to the first invalid control:

form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    const invalid = form.querySelector(':invalid');
    if (invalid) {
        e.preventDefault();
        invalid.focus();
    }
});

docs.title: Concept 22: Validation and Progressive Enhancement
docs.text:
Native validation works without JavaScript. Enhance with:

  • Custom error messages.
  • Real-time validation.
  • Complex rules.

Best practice: Ensure the form works with JavaScript disabled.

docs.title: Concept 23: The willValidate Property
docs.text: input.willValidate is true if the control is subject to validation, false otherwise (e.g., disabled, readonly, or not a form control).

docs.title: Concept 24: Validation and Disabled Controls
docs.text:
Disabled controls are not validated and not submitted.

<input type="email" required disabled>

Note: Readonly controls are validated (if required, they must have a value).

docs.title: Concept 25: Validation and Hidden Inputs
docs.text: Hidden inputs (type="hidden") are not validated.

docs.title: Concept 26: The minlength and maxlength Attributes
docs.text:
minlength/maxlength apply to text inputs and textareas:

<input type="text" minlength="3" maxlength="20">
<textarea minlength="10" maxlength="500"></textarea>

Note: These count Unicode code points.

docs.title: Concept 27: Validation and step
docs.text:
The step attribute applies to number, range, date, time, datetime-local, month, week:

<input type="number" min="0" max="100" step="5">
<input type="time" step="900"> <!-- 15-minute increments -->

docs.title: Concept 28: Validation and multiple
docs.text:
For email and file:

<input type="email" multiple>        <!-- comma-separated -->
<input type="file" multiple>          <!-- multiple files -->

docs.title: Concept 29: Validation and accept
docs.text:
For file inputs:

<input type="file" accept="image/*">

Note: This is a hint, not a validation rule. Users can still select other files.

docs.title: Concept 30: The reportValidity() vs checkValidity()
docs.text: Method Returns Shows Error checkValidity() Boolean No reportValidity() Boolean Yes

docs.title: Concept 31: Form-Level Validation
docs.text: form.checkValidity() checks all controls. form.reportValidity() shows the first error.

docs.title: Concept 32: The submit Event and Validation
docs.text:
Native validation runs before the submit event fires. If validation fails, the event doesn't fire.

form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    // Only runs if validation passes
    e.preventDefault();
    // Custom submission logic
});

docs.title: Concept 33: The invalid Event
docs.text:
Fires on each invalid control when validity is checked:

input.addEventListener('invalid', (e) => {
    e.preventDefault(); // Suppress default message
    // Show custom message
});

Note: The default message is shown unless preventDefault() is called.

docs.title: Concept 34: Custom Validation
docs.text:
input.addEventListener('input', () => {
    if (input.value.length < 3) {
        input.setCustomValidity('Must be at least 3 characters');
    } else {
        input.setCustomValidity('');
    }
});

docs.title: Concept 35: Server-Side Validation
docs.text:
Always validate on the server:

  • Whitelist allowed values.
  • Sanitize input.
  • Escape output.
  • Validate length, format, range.
  • Use parameterized queries for SQL.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Native Validation Flow
docs.text:
1.  User fills out the form and clicks submit.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser runs constraint validation:
    │   ├── For each control, check all constraints.
    │   ├── If any fail, the control is invalid.
    │   └── Focus moves to the first invalid control.
    │
    ▼
3.  If any control is invalid:
    │   ├── The `invalid` event fires on each.
    │   ├── The browser shows its error message.
    │   ├── The form submission is prevented.
    │   └── The `submit` event does NOT fire.
    │
    ▼
4.  If all controls are valid:
    │   ├── The `submit` event fires.
    │   ├── The form is submitted.
    │   └── The server processes the data.

docs.title: Validation Order
docs.text:
Constraints are checked in this order:

  1. required – is the field filled?
  2. type – does it match the type?
  3. min/max – is it within range?
  4. minlength/maxlength – is the length correct?
  5. pattern – does it match?
  6. step – is it on a step boundary?
  7. customError – was setCustomValidity called?

docs.title: The ValidityState Object
docs.text:
const input = document.querySelector('input');
console.log(input.validity);
// ValidityState {
//   valid: true,
//   valueMissing: false,
//   typeMismatch: false,
//   patternMismatch: false,
//   tooLong: false,
//   tooShort: false,
//   rangeUnderflow: false,
//   rangeOverflow: false,
//   stepMismatch: false,
//   badInput: false,
//   customError: false
// }

docs.title: Browser Default Messages
docs.text:
Browsers show messages like:

  • "Please fill out this field."
  • "Please enter an email address."
  • "Please enter a URL."
  • "Value must be less than or equal to 100."

These are localized by the browser.

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
The accessibility tree exposes:

  • The control's validity state (aria-invalid).
  • The error message via aria-describedby.
  • The required state.

Screen readers announce: "Email, required, invalid entry, please enter an email address."

docs.title: Custom Validation Flow
docs.text:
form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    // Custom validation
    if (!customRule()) {
        showError();
        return;
    }
    // Proceed with submission
    form.submit();
});

docs.title: The Constraint Validation API
docs.text:
Defined in the HTML specification:

  • HTMLInputElement, HTMLSelectElement, HTMLTextAreaElement, HTMLButtonElement implement ValidityState.
  • Each has validity, validationMessage, willValidate, checkValidity(), reportValidity(), setCustomValidity().

docs.title: The ValidityState Interface
docs.text:
interface ValidityState {
    readonly attribute boolean valueMissing;
    readonly attribute boolean typeMismatch;
    readonly attribute boolean patternMismatch;
    readonly attribute boolean tooLong;
    readonly attribute boolean tooShort;
    readonly attribute boolean rangeUnderflow;
    readonly attribute boolean rangeOverflow;
    readonly attribute boolean stepMismatch;
    readonly attribute boolean badInput;
    readonly attribute boolean customError;
    readonly attribute boolean valid;
}

docs.title: The Validation Algorithm
docs.text:
When a control's value changes or validation is triggered:

  1. Compute valueMissing (if required and empty).
  2. Compute typeMismatch (if type-specific validation fails).
  3. Compute patternMismatch (if pattern is set and doesn't match).
  4. Compute tooLong/tooShort (if maxlength/minlength).
  5. Compute rangeUnderflow/rangeOverflow (if min/max).
  6. Compute stepMismatch (if step and value not on boundary).
  7. Compute badInput (if the browser can't parse the value).
  8. Compute customError (if setCustomValidity set a message).
  9. Set valid to true only if all others are false.

docs.title: The invalid Event
docs.text: Fired on invalid controls when checkValidity() or submission triggers validation. Does not bubble; can be captured with capture phase.

docs.title: The form.checkValidity() Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Iterate all controls.
  2. Call checkValidity() on each.
  3. Return true if all pass.

docs.title: Browser Error Messages
docs.text: Browsers generate messages from the constraint that failed. Localized strings are stored in the browser's locale files.

docs.title: Custom Validity
docs.text: setCustomValidity(msg) sets the customError flag and stores the message. The control becomes invalid until cleared.

docs.title: Accessibility Mapping
docs.text:
• :invalid → aria-invalid="true" in the accessibility tree.
  • required → aria-required="true".
  • validationMessage → exposed as the control's "description" or "error".

docs.title: Server-Side Validation
docs.text:
Server-side validation is language-specific:

  • Node.js: Joi, Yup, express-validator.
  • Python: Pydantic, WTForms, Marshmallow.
  • Ruby: ActiveModel::Validations.
  • PHP: Respect\Validation, Symfony Validator.
  • Java: Bean Validation (JSR 380).

docs.title: The Lifecycle of Validation
docs.text:
1.  Page loads with form.
    │
    ▼
2.  User focuses and types into controls.
    │
    ▼
3.  Real-time validation may run (JavaScript).
    │
    ▼
4.  User clicks submit.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser runs constraint validation.
    │   ├── If valid → submit event fires, form submits.
    │   └── If invalid → invalid events fire, error shown.
    │
    ▼
6.  Server receives data.
    │
    ▼
7.  Server validates:
    │   ├── If valid → process and respond.
    │   └── If invalid → return errors to client.
    │
    ▼
8.  Client displays server errors.
    │
    ▼
9.  User corrects and resubmits.

docs.title: Real-Time Validation
docs.text:
input.addEventListener('input', () => {
    if (input.validity.valid) {
        input.classList.remove('error');
        input.classList.add('success');
    } else {
        input.classList.add('error');
        input.classList.remove('success');
    }
});

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Required Validation
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 2: Email Validation
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 3: Password with Length Validation
docs.text:
<form action="/signup" method="POST">
    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" minlength="8" maxlength="64" required>
    <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 4: Pattern Validation for ZIP Code
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="zip">ZIP Code:</label>
    <input type="text" id="zip" name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="Five-digit ZIP code" required>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 5: Number Range Validation
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="age">Age (18–120):</label>
    <input type="number" id="age" name="age" min="18" max="120" required>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 6: Date Range Validation
docs.text:

docs.title: Example 7: Password Confirmation with Custom Validation
docs.text:
<form id="signupForm" action="/signup" method="POST">
    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" minlength="8" required>

    <label for="confirm">Confirm Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="confirm" name="confirm" required>

    <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>

<script>
    const form = document.getElementById('signupForm');
    const password = document.getElementById('password');
    const confirm = document.getElementById('confirm');

    function validatePasswords() {
        if (password.value !== confirm.value) {
            confirm.setCustomValidity('Passwords do not match');
        } else {
            confirm.setCustomValidity('');
        }
    }

    password.addEventListener('input', validatePasswords);
    confirm.addEventListener('input', validatePasswords);
</script>

docs.title: Example 8: Custom Error Messages
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST" novalidate>
    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required aria-describedby="email-error">
    <span id="email-error" role="alert" style="color: red;"></span>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<script>
    const form = document.getElementById('myForm');
    const email = document.getElementById('email');
    const error = document.getElementById('email-error');

    form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
        if (!email.validity.valid) {
            e.preventDefault();
            email.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
            if (email.validity.valueMissing) {
                error.textContent = 'Email is required.';
            } else if (email.validity.typeMismatch) {
                error.textContent = 'Please enter a valid email address.';
            }
            email.focus();
        }
    });

    email.addEventListener('input', () => {
        if (email.validity.valid) {
            email.removeAttribute('aria-invalid');
            error.textContent = '';
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 15: Server-Side Validation (Node.js + Express)
docs.text:
const express = require('express');
const { body, validationResult } = require('express-validator');

const app = express();
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true }));

app.post('/signup', [
    body('email').isEmail().normalizeEmail(),
    body('password').isLength({ min: 8 }),
    body('age').isInt({ min: 18, max: 120 })
], (req, res) => {
    const errors = validationResult(req);
    if (!errors.isEmpty()) {
        return res.status(400).json({ errors: errors.array() });
    }
    // Process valid data
    res.json({ success: true });
});

docs.title: Example 16: Server-Side Validation (Python + Flask)
docs.text:
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
from wtforms import Form, StringField, IntegerField, validators
from email_validator import validate_email, EmailNotValidError

app = Flask(__name__)

class SignupForm(Form):
    email = StringField('Email', [validators.DataRequired()])
    password = StringField('Password', [validators.Length(min=8)])
    age = IntegerField('Age', [validators.NumberRange(min=18, max=120)])

@app.route('/signup', methods=['POST'])
def signup():
    form = SignupForm(request.form)
    if not form.validate():
        return jsonify({'errors': form.errors}), 400
    try:
        validate_email(form.email.data)
    except EmailNotValidError as e:
        return jsonify({'error': str(e)}), 400
    return jsonify({'success': True})

docs.title: Example 18: Accessible Error Summary
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST" novalidate>
    <div id="error-summary" role="alert" aria-live="assertive" hidden>
        <h2>Please fix the following errors:</h2>
        <ul id="error-list"></ul>
    </div>

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required aria-describedby="email-error">
    <span id="email-error" role="alert"></span>

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<script>
    const form = document.getElementById('myForm');
    form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
        const invalidControls = form.querySelectorAll(':invalid');
        if (invalidControls.length > 0) {
            e.preventDefault();
            const summary = document.getElementById('error-summary');
            const list = document.getElementById('error-list');
            list.innerHTML = '';
            invalidControls.forEach(control => {
                const li = document.createElement('li');
                const a = document.createElement('a');
                a.href = `#${control.id}`;
                a.textContent = control.validationMessage;
                li.appendChild(a);
                list.appendChild(li);
            });
            summary.hidden = false;
            invalidControls[0].focus();
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 19: Validation with Async Check
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/signup" method="POST">
    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" required minlength="3">
    <span id="username-status" aria-live="polite"></span>
    <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>

<script>
    const username = document.getElementById('username');
    const status = document.getElementById('username-status');

    username.addEventListener('input', async () => {
        if (username.value.length < 3) return;
        const response = await fetch(`/api/check-username?q=${encodeURIComponent(username.value)}`);
        const data = await response.json();
        if (data.taken) {
            username.setCustomValidity('Username is already taken');
            status.textContent = '✗ Taken';
            status.style.color = 'red';
        } else {
            username.setCustomValidity('');
            status.textContent = '✓ Available';
            status.style.color = 'green';
        }
    });
</script>
