docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Method Enctype Search GET URL-encoded Login POST URL-encoded Signup POST URL-encoded Contact form POST URL-encoded File upload POST multipart/form-data Checkout POST URL-encoded Filters GET URL-encoded Comment posting POST URL-encoded Data export GET URL-encoded Settings update POST URL-encoded Multi-step forms POST URL-encoded AJAX forms POST URL-encoded or multipart

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use POST for state-changing operations – GET is for retrieval.
  2. Use GET for search and filters – bookmarkable and cacheable.
  3. Always validate on the server – client-side is UX only.
  4. Use enctype="multipart/form-data" for file uploads.
  5. Include CSRF tokens – for state-changing forms.
  6. Disable the submit button during submission – prevent double submission.
  7. Use novalidate only when necessary.
  8. Provide clear error messages – accessible and specific.
  9. Redirect after POST (Post/Redirect/Get) – prevent resubmission.
  10. Use requestSubmit() for validation-aware submission.
  11. Use fetch for AJAX submissions – modern and clean.
  12. Don't set Content-Type manually for FormData – the browser sets it.
  13. Use FormData for file uploads with fetch.
  14. Test without JavaScript – ensure progressive enhancement.
  15. Test with slow networks – handle timeouts.
  16. Log server-side validation failures – for security monitoring.
  17. Rate-limit submissions – prevent abuse.
  18. Use HTTPS – mandatory for sensitive data.
  19. Document form submission conventions – in a style guide.
  20. Test with screen readers – ensure submission feedback is announced.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using GET for Sensitive Data
docs.text:
<form method="GET">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>

Why it's wrong: Password appears in URL and server logs.

✅ Correct: 

<form method="POST">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting enctype for File Uploads
docs.text:
<form method="POST">
    <input type="file" name="file">
</form>

Why it's wrong: File uploads require multipart/form-data.

✅ Correct: 

<form method="POST" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    <input type="file" name="file">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No CSRF Token
docs.text:
<form method="POST">
    <input type="text" name="amount">
</form>

Why it's wrong: Vulnerable to CSRF attacks.

✅ Correct: 

<form method="POST">
    <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="...">
    <input type="text" name="amount">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Submit Button
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <input type="text" name="name">
</form>

Why it's wrong: Users can't submit (except by pressing Enter).

✅ Correct: 

<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <input type="text" name="name">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Double Submission
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

Why it's wrong: Clicking twice submits twice.

✅ Correct: Disable the button on submit.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Server-Side Validation
docs.text:
// Client-side only
if (email.validity.valid) form.submit();

Why it's wrong: Client-side validation can be bypassed.

✅ Correct: Also validate on the server.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Setting Content-Type Manually with FormData
docs.text:
fetch('/submit', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: new FormData(form),
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'multipart/form-data' } // Wrong!
});

Why it's wrong: The browser sets the boundary; manual Content-Type breaks parsing.

✅ Correct: 

fetch('/submit', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: new FormData(form)
    // No manual Content-Type
});

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Redirecting After POST
docs.text:
app.post('/submit', (req, res) => {
    saveToDatabase(req.body);
    res.send('Success!'); // Refresh resubmits
});

Why it's wrong: Refreshing resubmits the form.

✅ Correct: 

app.post('/submit', (req, res) => {
    saveToDatabase(req.body);
    res.redirect(303, '/success'); // Post/Redirect/Get
});

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using form.submit() When Validation Is Needed
docs.text:
form.submit(); // Bypasses validation

Why it's wrong: Skips constraint validation.

✅ Correct: 

form.requestSubmit(); // Includes validation

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Feedback During AJAX Submission
docs.text:
form.addEventListener('submit', async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    await fetch('/submit', { method: 'POST', body: new FormData(form) });
});

Why it's wrong: Users don't know if the submission is in progress.

✅ Correct: Disable the button, show a spinner, announce status.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Error Handling in AJAX
docs.text:
const response = await fetch('/submit', { method: 'POST', body: formData });
const data = await response.json();

Why it's wrong: Network errors and HTTP errors are ignored.

✅ Correct: Use try/catch and check response.ok.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing name Attributes
docs.text:
<input type="text" id="name">

Why it's wrong: The value is not submitted.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="text" id="name" name="name">

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Request size – minimize form data; avoid sending large files unnecessarily.
  • Encoding – URL-encoded is smaller than multipart; use multipart only for files.
  • AJAX – avoids full page reloads, improving perceived performance.
  • Progress indicators – for file uploads, use XMLHttpRequest with progress events.
  • Debouncing – prevent rapid submissions.
  • Caching – GET requests can be cached; POST cannot.
  • Compression – use gzip/brotli on the server.
  • Connection reuse – HTTP/2 multiplexes requests.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use AJAX for smoother UX – no full page reload.
  2. Show progress for file uploads – use XMLHttpRequest.
  3. Debounce submissions – prevent double submissions.
  4. Minimize payload – send only necessary fields.
  5. Compress responses – use gzip/brotli.
  6. Cache GET requests – for search and filters.
  7. Use HTTP/2 – for multiplexing.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• HTTPS – mandatory for sensitive data.
  • CSRF tokens – prevent cross-site request forgery.
  • Server-side validation – never trust client input.
  • Input sanitization – prevent XSS and injection.
  • Output escaping – prevent XSS when displaying data.
  • Rate limiting – prevent brute force and DoS.
  • Password fields – use type="password" and POST.
  • File upload validation – restrict types and sizes.
  • Logging – log validation failures for monitoring.
  • Error messages – don't leak sensitive information.
  • Session management – use secure cookies (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite).
  • CORS – restrict cross-origin requests.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use HTTPS everywhere.
  2. Include CSRF tokens.
  3. Validate on the server – always.
  4. Sanitize input – before storage or display.
  5. Escape output – prevent XSS.
  6. Use parameterized queries – prevent SQL injection.
  7. Rate-limit submissions – prevent abuse.
  8. Validate file uploads – type, size, content.
  9. Use secure cookies – HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite.
  10. Log and monitor – for security incidents.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Network panel – inspect the submission request and response.
  • Request headers – check Content-Type, Content-Length, Referer.
  • Request body – verify the encoded data.
  • Response status – check for 200, 302, 400, 500.
  • Console – log FormData contents.
  • form.checkValidity() – check if the form is valid.
  • form.elements – inspect all controls.
  • Event listeners – check submit listeners.
  • Breakpoints – pause on submit to inspect state.
  • Server logs – check for errors on the server.
  • curl – test endpoints independently.
  • Postman – test API endpoints.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure feedback is announced.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For all data submission – forms are the standard.
  • For logins, signups, contact forms – POST.
  • For search and filters – GET.
  • For file uploads – POST + multipart.
  • For AJAX applications – fetch + FormData.
  • For progressive enhancement – native submission.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For navigation – use <a>.
  • For real-time data – use WebSockets or SSE.
  • For large binary data – use chunked uploads.
  • For non-form data – use JSON APIs.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <form> – the form element.
  • <input> – form controls.
  • <button> – submit, reset, button.
  • <select> – dropdown.
  • <textarea> – multi-line text.
  • <label> – labels.
  • <fieldset> – groups.
  • action – submission URL.
  • method – GET or POST.
  • enctype – encoding type.
  • target – response target.
  • novalidate – skip validation.
  • submit event – fires before submission.
  • formdata event – modify data.
  • FormData – JS API for form data.
  • fetch – modern AJAX.
  • XMLHttpRequest – legacy AJAX.
  • CSRF – cross-site request forgery.
  • Post/Redirect/Get – pattern.
  • Idempotency – safe to repeat.
  • Content-Type – encoding header.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Form submission was introduced in HTML 2.0 (1995) — one of the earliest features.

  • The default method is GET; the default enctype is application/x-www-form-urlencoded.

  • GET appends data to the URL; POST sends it in the body.

  • POST is not idempotent — repeating it may duplicate actions.

  • File uploads require enctype="multipart/form-data" and POST.

  • CSRF tokens are hidden inputs that prevent cross-site request forgery.

  • The Post/Redirect/Get pattern prevents duplicate submissions on refresh.

  • form.submit() bypasses validation and the submit event.

  • form.requestSubmit() validates and fires the submit event.

  • FormData can be sent directly with fetch — the browser sets the Content-Type.

  • Never set Content-Type manually with FormData — the boundary must be included.

  • Successful controls are those with a name, not disabled, and checked/selected as applicable.

  • Submit buttons only submit their name/value if clicked.

  • Multiple submit buttons with different name/value let the server know which was clicked.

  • GET requests are bookmarkable and cacheable; POST are not.

  • Sensitive data should never be sent via GET — it appears in URLs and logs.

  • HTTPS is mandatory for form submissions.

  • Server-side validation is the only true validation — client-side can be bypassed.

  • Rate limiting prevents brute-force and DoS attacks.

  • Logging validation failures helps detect attacks.

  • accept-charset controls the character encoding.

  • novalidate disables native validation; formnovalidate disables it per button.

  • target="_blank" opens the response in a new tab — use rel="noopener".

  • AJAX submission avoids page reloads and enables richer UX.

  • Progress indicators for file uploads use XMLHttpRequest with upload.progress.

  • Best practices include HTTPS, CSRF tokens, server-side validation, and Post/Redirect/Get.

  • Common mistakes include GET for passwords, forgetting enctype, and no CSRF token.

  • Following best practices for form submission leads to secure, reliable, and user-friendly applications.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Form submission is the process of collecting, encoding, and sending form data to a server.
  • It is triggered by a submit button, Enter key, or JavaScript.
  • action specifies the URL; method specifies GET or POST; enctype specifies encoding.
  • GET is for retrieval (search, filters); POST is for changes (logins, signups, payments).
  • multipart/form-data is required for file uploads.
  • Successful controls (with name, not disabled) are submitted.
  • The submit event fires before submission; formdata event allows modification.
  • FormData and fetch enable AJAX submission.
  • CSRF tokens protect against cross-site request forgery.
  • Post/Redirect/Get prevents duplicate submissions.
  • Best practices: use POST for changes, validate on the server, disable during submission, use CSRF tokens, and test with screen readers.
  • Common mistakes include GET for sensitive data, forgetting enctype, and no server-side validation.
  • Form submission is the foundation of web interactivity — the bridge between client and server.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
GET and POST are the two primary HTTP methods used by HTML forms to submit data to a server. They define how the form data is transmitted and where it is placed in the HTTP request:

  • GET – sends the form data as a query string appended to the URL. It is the default method for HTML forms and is used for retrieving data.
  • POST – sends the form data in the body of the HTTP request. It is used for submitting or changing data on the server.

The choice between GET and POST is one of the most consequential decisions in form design. It affects:

  • The URL the user sees.
  • The size of the data you can send.
  • Whether the request is bookmarkable or cacheable.
  • Whether the request is idempotent (safe to retry).
  • The security of the data (GET exposes it in the URL; POST hides it in the body).
  • The server-side parsing (query string vs. body).

Example: 

<!-- GET: data appears in the URL -->
<form action="/search" method="GET">
    <input type="text" name="q">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>
<!-- Submits: /search?q=html -->

<!-- POST: data goes in the request body -->
<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <input type="text" name="username">
    <input type="password" name="password">
    <button type="submit">Log In</button>
</form>
<!-- Submits body: username=Alice&password=secret -->

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The GET vs POST distinction exists to:

  • Reflect the semantic intent of the request — retrieval vs. modification.
  • Protect the user – sensitive data should not appear in URLs.
  • Enable caching and bookmarking – for safe, idempotent requests.
  • Protect the server – unsafe operations should not be triggered by a bookmark or back button.
  • Support different data sizes – URLs have limits; POST bodies do not.
  • Enable proper browser behaviour – revalidation, reload, and history.
  • Comply with HTTP semantics – GET must be safe and idempotent; POST is not.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The method attribute is set on the <form> element. It determines the HTTP method used for the submission. It is used alongside action, enctype, and target to fully describe how the form is submitted.

<form action="/endpoint" method="GET|POST" enctype="...">
    ...
</form>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTTP is a stateless protocol — every request is independent. But web applications need to distinguish between two fundamentally different kinds of operations:

  • Reading data – searches, filters, lookups, pagination. These should be safe (no side effects) and idempotent (repeatable).
  • Writing data – logins, signups, payments, comments. These change state and should not be accidentally repeated.

If all requests were the same, the web would be unreliable:

  • A user could bookmark a payment submission and re-trigger it later.
  • The browser back button could re-submit a purchase.
  • Search results could not be cached or shared.
  • Sensitive data would appear in URLs and server logs.
  • Browsers couldn't know which requests are safe to prefetch.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Only one method No distinction between read/write All data in URL Sensitive data exposed Limited URL length Cannot send large payloads No caching semantics Browsers can't cache safely No idempotency Retrying causes duplicates No bookmarking of searches Users can't share search URLs

docs.title: Why the GET/POST Distinction Was Introduced
docs.text:
HTTP/1.0 (1996) formalised the distinction between safe methods (GET, HEAD) and unsafe methods (POST, PUT, DELETE). HTML forms adopted this distinction early:

  • GET – for retrieval. Safe, idempotent, bookmarkable, cacheable.
  • POST – for submission. Unsafe, non-idempotent, not bookmarkable, not cacheable.

This mirrors the RESTful design principle that:

  • GET should be used for reading resources.
  • POST should be used for creating or modifying resources.

The distinction is not just a convention — browsers, proxies, caches, and search engines all rely on it.

docs.title: GET Form
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="GET">
    <label for="q">Search:</label>
    <input type="search" id="q" name="q">
    <label for="category">Category:</label>
    <select id="category" name="category">
        <option value="all">All</option>
        <option value="books">Books</option>
        <option value="electronics">Electronics</option>
    </select>
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

URL after submission: 

/search?q=html&category=books

docs.title: POST Form
docs.text:
<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username">
    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password">
    <button type="submit">Log In</button>
</form>

Request body: 

username=Alice&password=secret123

docs.title: GET with File Upload (Not Possible)
docs.text:
<!-- WRONG: File uploads don't work with GET -->
<form action="/upload" method="GET" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    <input type="file" name="file">
</form>

Why: GET cannot send a request body, so files cannot be transmitted.

docs.title: POST with File Upload
docs.text:
<form action="/upload" method="POST" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    <label for="file">Choose a file:</label>
    <input type="file" id="file" name="file">
    <button type="submit">Upload</button>
</form>

docs.title: Default Method
docs.text:
If method is omitted, the browser defaults to GET:

<form action="/search">
    <input type="text" name="q">
</form>
<!-- Submits as GET: /search?q=... -->

Best practice: Always specify method explicitly.

docs.title: Overriding Per-Button
docs.text:
<form action="/default" method="POST">
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
    <button type="submit" formmethod="GET" formaction="/preview">Preview</button>
</form>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part GET POST Data location URL query string Request body action URL without query URL enctype Ignored Used for encoding Example URL /search?q=html /login Example body (none) username=Alice&password=secret Browser back May re-fetch Warns before resubmitting Refresh Safe Warns: "confirm resubmission"

docs.title: The "Postcard vs. Sealed Envelope" Analogy
docs.text:
• GET is a postcard. Everything written on it (the URL) is visible to everyone who handles it — postal workers, recipients, anyone who sees it lying around. It's lightweight, cheap, and easy to share.
  • POST is a sealed envelope. The contents (the body) are hidden from casual observers. It's used for things that should not be public — passwords, payments, personal data.

docs.title: The "Library Card Catalog" Analogy
docs.text:
• GET is like looking up a book in a card catalog. You search by title, author, or subject. The query (the search terms) is part of the record. You can bookmark the search, share it, and repeat it — the library doesn't change.
  • POST is like checking out a book. You fill out a form (name, card number, due date). The library's state changes — the book is now checked out. You can't "re-check out" by repeating the same form without consequences.

docs.title: The "Order Form" Analogy
docs.text:
• GET is like asking the waiter what's on the menu. The question is ephemeral; you can ask again, and nothing changes.
  • POST is like placing an order. The kitchen starts cooking. You can't repeat the order by asking again — that would create a duplicate order.

docs.title: The "Idempotency" Mental Model
docs.text:
The most important mental model:

  • GET must be idempotent — calling it once or ten times has the same effect (no side effects).
  • POST is not idempotent — calling it once or ten times may create ten records, ten orders, or ten charges.

This is why browsers warn before resubmitting a POST but silently re-fetch a GET.

docs.title: The "Safety" Mental Model
docs.text:
• Safe methods (GET, HEAD) do not modify server state. They are safe to prefetch, cache, and crawl.
  • Unsafe methods (POST, PUT, DELETE) modify state. They must be explicitly triggered by the user.

Search engine crawlers only follow GET links — never POST. That's why every page you want indexed must be reachable via GET.

docs.title: Concept 1: Data Location
docs.text:
Method Data Location GET URL query string POST Request body

GET: 

GET /search?q=html&category=books HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

POST: 

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 30

username=Alice&password=secret

docs.title: Concept 2: Data Size Limits
docs.text:
• GET: URLs are limited in length. Browser limits vary (2000–8000 characters). Server limits also apply.
  • POST: The body size is limited only by server configuration (often hundreds of MB).

Rule: Use POST for large data; GET for small, simple data.

docs.title: Concept 3: Bookmarkability
docs.text:
• GET – URLs are bookmarkable, shareable, and can be added to history.
  • POST – URLs do not contain the data; bookmarking loses the submission.

Use case: Search results should be bookmarkable (GET). Login credentials should not (POST).

docs.title: Concept 4: Cacheability
docs.text:
• GET – cacheable by browsers, proxies, and CDNs. Improves performance.
  • POST – not cacheable (by default). Each request is treated as unique.

Result: GET is faster for repeated requests; POST is safer for state changes.

docs.title: Concept 5: Idempotency
docs.text:
• GET – idempotent. Repeating it has no side effects.
  • POST – not idempotent. Repeating it may duplicate actions.

Consequence: Browsers warn before re-submitting a POST on refresh or back. GET can be re-fetched silently.

docs.title: Concept 6: Security
docs.text:
• GET – data appears in the URL, browser history, server logs, and referrer headers. Never use for sensitive data.
  • POST – data is in the body. Safer, but still requires HTTPS.

Rule: Use POST for passwords, tokens, payments, and personal information.

docs.title: Concept 7: Server-Side Parsing
docs.text:
Most server frameworks expose GET and POST data differently:

Framework GET Data POST Data Express (Node.js) req.query req.body Flask (Python) request.args request.form Django (Python) request.GET request.POST PHP $_GET $_POST Rails (Ruby) params (merged) params (merged) ASP.NET Request.QueryString Request.Form

docs.title: Concept 8: HTTP Semantics (RFC 7231)
docs.text:
• GET – "transfer a current representation of the target resource". Safe, idempotent.
  • POST – "perform resource-specific processing on the request payload". Unsafe, not idempotent.

Using them correctly aligns your application with HTTP semantics and enables caching, crawling, and proper browser behaviour.

docs.title: Concept 9: The Default Method
docs.text:
If method is omitted, the browser uses GET. This is a common source of accidental data exposure.

<!-- Accidentally GET — dangerous! -->
<form action="/login">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>

Best practice: Always specify method.

docs.title: Concept 10: GET for Search, POST for Changes
docs.text:
The canonical rule of thumb:

  • GET – for search, filters, pagination, and anything that is safe and idempotent.
  • POST – for logins, signups, checkout, comments, and anything that changes state.

docs.title: Concept 11: Post/Redirect/Get (PRG)
docs.text:
After a POST, always redirect to prevent resubmission:

POST /submit → 303 See Other → Location: /success → GET /success

Why: Without the redirect, refreshing the confirmation page resubmits the form.

docs.title: Concept 12: Browser Behaviour on Refresh
docs.text:
• GET – refreshing re-fetches silently.
  • POST – refreshing prompts: "Confirm form resubmission?"

This is a direct consequence of idempotency: GET is safe to repeat; POST is not.

docs.title: Concept 13: Back Button Behaviour
docs.text:
• GET – the back button re-fetches the previous URL (possibly from cache).
  • POST – the back button may prompt to resubmit or show a cached result.

docs.title: Concept 14: GET and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines only crawl GET links. If your content is only reachable via POST, it will not be indexed.

Best practice: Ensure every page you want indexed is reachable via a GET link.

docs.title: Concept 15: Security Implications of GET
docs.text:
• Data appears in the URL, browser history, and server logs.
  • Data is included in the Referer header when the user clicks a link.
  • URLs may be shared, emailed, or pasted into chat.
  • URLs may be cached by proxies and CDNs.

Consequence: Never use GET for passwords, tokens, credit card numbers, or any sensitive data.

docs.title: Concept 16: Security Implications of POST
docs.text:
• Data is in the body — not visible in the URL.
  • Still visible to anyone with network access unless HTTPS is used.
  • Vulnerable to CSRF without tokens.
  • Requires Content-Type header for correct parsing.

docs.title: Concept 17: The Size Limit Reality
docs.text:
• Browsers: Chrome ~2 MB, Firefox ~1 MB, Safari ~80 KB (for GET URLs).
  • Servers: Apache default ~8 KB, Nginx ~8 KB, IIS ~16 KB (for GET URLs).
  • POST: Server-dependent; often 1–2 MB by default, configurable.

Consequence: Use POST for large payloads.

docs.title: Concept 18: Encoding Differences
docs.text:
• GET – URL-encoded, spaces become + or %20.
  • POST – encoded based on enctype (application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain).

docs.title: Concept 19: When to Use Each
docs.text: Scenario Method Search GET Filters GET Pagination GET Login POST Signup POST Contact form POST Checkout POST File upload POST Settings update POST Comment post POST Newsletter subscribe POST

docs.title: Concept 20: The "Safe Method" Rule
docs.text:
A method is safe if it doesn't change server state. GET is safe; POST is not.

Consequence: Search engines, browsers, and proxies may prefetch GET requests, but never POST.

docs.title: Concept 21: GET with Query Parameters vs. Path Parameters
docs.text:
Sometimes GET uses path parameters instead of query strings:

/products/42           ← path parameter
/products?id=42        ← query parameter

Both are valid, but forms always use query strings.

docs.title: Concept 22: POST and CSRF
docs.text:
POST is the most common target for CSRF attacks because it changes state. Always use CSRF tokens:

<form method="POST">
    <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="...">
    ...
</form>

docs.title: Concept 23: GET and CSRF
docs.text:
GET is generally safe from CSRF because it shouldn't change state. But if a GET endpoint does change state (a design flaw), it's vulnerable.

Best practice: Never use GET for state-changing operations.

docs.title: Concept 24: RESTful Equivalents
docs.text:
While HTML forms only support GET and POST, RESTful APIs often use:

  • GET – read.
  • POST – create.
  • PUT – update (replace).
  • PATCH – update (partial).
  • DELETE – delete.

HTML forms can only use GET or POST directly; other methods require JavaScript (fetch with method: 'PUT').

docs.title: Concept 25: Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
docs.text:
• GET – no body, so no Content-Length.
  • POST – body present, Content-Length set automatically.

docs.title: Concept 26: Browsers and Form Resubmission
docs.text:
Browsers handle POST resubmission carefully:

  • Reload after POST → prompt to confirm.
  • Back button after POST → may prompt or show cached.
  • Forward button → may prompt.

This is why Post/Redirect/Get is essential.

docs.title: Concept 27: Server-Side Security
docs.text:
• GET endpoints should be safe to call repeatedly — no side effects.
  • POST endpoints should validate CSRF, input, and permissions.
  • Never trust the client — always validate on the server.

docs.title: Concept 28: The referrer Header and GET
docs.text:
When the user clicks a link on a GET page, the Referer header includes the full URL with query parameters. This leaks sensitive data if GET is misused.

Mitigation: Use POST for sensitive data, or set Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.

docs.title: Concept 29: GET and Browser History
docs.text: Every GET request is added to browser history. If GET is misused for actions, the user's history becomes cluttered with action URLs — and the back button might re-trigger them.

docs.title: Concept 30: URL Length and Practical Limits
docs.text:
• Chrome: ~2 MB.
  • Firefox: ~1 MB.
  • Safari: ~80 KB.
  • IE/Edge: ~2,083 characters (older versions).

Best practice: Keep GET URLs under 2,000 characters for compatibility.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: GET Submission
docs.text:
1.  User submits the form.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser collects successful controls.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser URL-encodes the data.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser appends it to the action URL as a query string.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser sends the GET request:
    │   GET /search?q=html&category=books HTTP/1.1
    │   Host: example.com
    │
    ▼
6.  Server parses the query string.
    │
    ▼
7.  Server responds.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser displays the response and updates the URL bar.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: POST Submission
docs.text:
1.  User submits the form.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser collects successful controls.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser encodes the data (URL-encoded or multipart).
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser sends the POST request with the data in the body:
    │   POST /login HTTP/1.1
    │   Host: example.com
    │   Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
    │   Content-Length: 30
    │
    │   username=Alice&password=secret
    │
    ▼
5.  Server parses the body.
    │
    ▼
6.  Server responds (often with a redirect).
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser follows the redirect (if any) via GET.

docs.title: HTTP Request Comparison
docs.text:
GET: 

GET /search?q=html HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Accept: text/html

POST: 

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 30

username=Alice&password=secret

docs.title: Browser Back/Refresh Behaviour
docs.text: Action GET POST Refresh Silent re-fetch Confirm resubmission Back Re-fetch from cache May prompt or show cached Forward Re-fetch May prompt Bookmark Works (URL includes data) Data lost Share URL Works Data lost Cache Yes No

docs.title: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
docs.text:
POST /submit
    ↓
303 See Other
Location: /success
    ↓
GET /success

Prevents duplicate submissions when the user refreshes.

docs.title: The HTTP Request
docs.text:
Both methods share the same request line structure, differing in:

  • Request line: method name (GET vs. POST).
  • URL: GET includes query string.
  • Body: POST includes data.
  • Headers: POST includes Content-Type and Content-Length.

docs.title: The URL Query String
docs.text:
For GET, the browser:

  1. Encodes each name and value using application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
  2. Joins pairs with &.
  3. Appends to the URL after ?.

Example: 

name=Alice&email=alice%40example.com&message=Hello+World

docs.title: The POST Body
docs.text:
For POST, the body is encoded based on enctype:

  • application/x-www-form-urlencoded – URL-encoded, same as GET but in the body.
  • multipart/form-data – boundaries and parts (for file uploads).
  • text/plain – simple key=value lines.

docs.title: Server-Side Parsing
docs.text:
Frameworks parse the query string and body into accessible data structures:

// Express
app.get('/search', (req, res) => {
    const q = req.query.q;       // GET
});

app.post('/login', (req, res) => {
    const username = req.body.username; // POST
});

docs.title: Caching Behaviour
docs.text:
• GET is cacheable per HTTP caching rules (ETag, Last-Modified, Cache-Control).
  • POST is not cacheable by default — but can be with Cache-Control headers (rare).

docs.title: Browser Revalidation
docs.text:
When the user hits Back, the browser may:

  • Show the cached page.
  • Revalidate with the server (GET).
  • Prompt the user (POST).

docs.title: Idempotency in HTTP
docs.text:
• GET is idempotent — repeating it has no side effects.
  • POST is not idempotent — repeating it may create duplicates.
  • PUT and DELETE are idempotent.
  • PATCH is not necessarily idempotent.

docs.title: The Referer Header
docs.text: For GET requests triggered by clicking a link, the Referer header contains the full URL including query parameters. For POST, the referrer is the page URL, not the body.

docs.title: Browser URL Bar
docs.text:
• GET – the URL bar updates to include the query string.
  • POST – the URL bar does not change (the body is not visible).

docs.title: The Content-Length Header
docs.text: For POST, Content-Length is set to the byte length of the encoded body. For GET, no Content-Length is sent.

docs.title: The Content-Type Header
docs.text: Method Content-Type GET (none) POST (URL-encoded) application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST (multipart) multipart/form-data; boundary=... POST (plain) text/plain

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Form Submission (GET vs. POST)
docs.text:
1.  User fills out the form.
    │
    ▼
2.  User clicks submit.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser reads the `method` attribute.
    │   ├── GET → encode data as query string
    │   └── POST → encode data as body
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser constructs the HTTP request.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser sends the request.
    │
    ▼
6.  Server parses:
    │   ├── GET → query string
    │   └── POST → body
    │
    ▼
7.  Server processes and responds.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser handles the response:
    │   ├── HTML → display
    │   ├── Redirect → navigate
    │   └── Error → show error
    │
    ▼
9.  Browser updates history (GET) or prompts on resubmit (POST).

docs.title: Dynamic Method Change
docs.text:
const form = document.querySelector('form');
form.method = 'POST'; // Switch from GET to POST

docs.title: Example 1: GET Search Form
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="GET">
    <label for="q">Search:</label>
    <input type="search" id="q" name="q" required>
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

Result: /search?q=html

docs.title: Example 2: GET Filter Form
docs.text:
<form action="/products" method="GET">
    <label for="category">Category:</label>
    <select id="category" name="category">
        <option value="all">All</option>
        <option value="books">Books</option>
        <option value="electronics">Electronics</option>
    </select>

    <label for="min-price">Min Price:</label>
    <input type="number" id="min-price" name="min_price" min="0">

    <button type="submit">Filter</button>
</form>

Result: /products?category=books&min_price=10

docs.title: Example 3: GET Pagination
docs.text:
<nav>
    <a href="?page=1">1</a>
    <a href="?page=2">2</a>
    <a href="?page=3">3</a>
</nav>

Note: Pagination links are GET requests (href links). Forms are also used.

docs.title: Example 4: POST Login Form
docs.text:
<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" required autocomplete="username">

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" required autocomplete="current-password">

    <button type="submit">Log In</button>
</form>

Result: POST body with username and password.

docs.title: Example 5: POST Contact Form
docs.text:
<form action="/contact" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

    <label for="message">Message:</label>
    <textarea id="message" name="message" required></textarea>

    <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 6: POST File Upload
docs.text:
<form action="/upload" method="POST" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    <label for="file">Choose a file:</label>
    <input type="file" id="file" name="file" required>

    <button type="submit">Upload</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 7: GET for Search with Multiple Parameters
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="GET">
    <label for="q">Query:</label>
    <input type="search" id="q" name="q">

    <label for="sort">Sort by:</label>
    <select id="sort" name="sort">
        <option value="relevance">Relevance</option>
        <option value="date">Date</option>
        <option value="price">Price</option>
    </select>

    <label for="page">Page:</label>
    <input type="number" id="page" name="page" value="1" min="1">

    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

Result: /search?q=html&sort=date&page=2

docs.title: Example 8: POST with CSRF Token
docs.text:
<form action="/transfer" method="POST">
    <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="abc123def456...">

    <label for="amount">Amount:</label>
    <input type="number" id="amount" name="amount" required>

    <button type="submit">Transfer</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 9: Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
docs.text:
// Express.js
app.post('/submit', (req, res) => {
    saveToDatabase(req.body);
    res.redirect(303, '/success');
});

app.get('/success', (req, res) => {
    res.render('success');
});

docs.title: Example 10: Conditional Method Change
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/search" method="GET">
    <label for="q">Search:</label>
    <input type="search" id="q" name="q">

    <label>
        <input type="checkbox" id="saveSearch" name="save">
        Save this search
    </label>

    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

<script>
    const form = document.getElementById('myForm');
    const saveCheckbox = document.getElementById('saveSearch');
    saveCheckbox.addEventListener('change', () => {
        // Saving requires POST; searching uses GET
        form.method = saveCheckbox.checked ? 'POST' : 'GET';
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 11: GET with Filtering and Pagination Combined
docs.text:
<form action="/articles" method="GET">
    <label for="tag">Tag:</label>
    <input type="text" id="tag" name="tag">

    <label for="author">Author:</label>
    <input type="text" id="author" name="author">

    <label for="page">Page:</label>
    <input type="number" id="page" name="page" value="1" min="1">

    <label for="per_page">Per Page:</label>
    <select id="per_page" name="per_page">
        <option value="10">10</option>
        <option value="25">25</option>
        <option value="50">50</option>
    </select>

    <button type="submit">Apply Filters</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 12: POST with Redirect After Submission
docs.text:
<form action="/comment" method="POST">
    <label for="comment">Comment:</label>
    <textarea id="comment" name="comment" rows="4" required></textarea>
    <button type="submit">Post Comment</button>
</form>

Server: 

app.post('/comment', (req, res) => {
    saveComment(req.body.comment);
    res.redirect(303, '/post/123');
});

docs.title: Example 13: Comparing GET and POST in the Same App
docs.text:
<!-- Search (GET) -->
<form action="/search" method="GET">
    <input type="search" name="q">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

<!-- Contact (POST) -->
<form action="/contact" method="POST">
    <input type="text" name="name">
    <input type="email" name="email">
    <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 14: GET with Query Parameters in Links
docs.text:
<a href="/search?q=html&category=books">Books about HTML</a>

This is a GET request even though it's a link, not a form.

docs.title: Example 15: POST with JSON Body (AJAX)
docs.text:
const data = { username: 'Alice', password: 'secret' };
fetch('/login', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(data)
});

Note: This bypasses form encoding; the server must parse JSON.

docs.title: Example 16: GET with JSON Response (AJAX)
docs.text:
fetch('/api/search?q=html')
    .then(response => response.json())
    .then(data => console.log(data));

docs.title: Example 17: Preventing Resubmission with PRG
docs.text:
// Server
app.post('/order', (req, res) => {
    createOrder(req.body);
    res.redirect(303, `/order/${orderId}`);
});

app.get('/order/:id', (req, res) => {
    res.render('order', { order: getOrder(req.params.id) });
});

docs.title: Example 18: GET and POST in a Single Form (With Button Override)
docs.text:
<form action="/preview" method="GET">
    <label for="content">Content:</label>
    <textarea id="content" name="content"></textarea>

    <button type="submit">Preview</button>
    <button type="submit" formaction="/publish" formmethod="POST">Publish</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 19: Security Audit — Finding Misused GET
docs.text:
// Audit: find forms with GET that contain password fields
document.querySelectorAll('form[method="GET" i]').forEach(form => {
    if (form.querySelector('input[type="password"]')) {
        console.warn('GET form with password field:', form);
    }
});

docs.title: Example 20: Complete GET vs POST Demo
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>GET vs POST Demo</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 700px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        form { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 2rem; padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 8px; }
        label { font-weight: 500; }
        input, textarea { padding: 0.5rem; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 4px; }
        button { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; background: #3498db; color: white; border: none; border-radius: 4px; cursor: pointer; }
        button:hover { background: #2980b9; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>GET vs POST Demo</h1>

    <h2>Search (GET)</h2>
    <p>Data appears in the URL. Bookmarkable and shareable.</p>
    <form action="/search" method="GET">
        <label for="q">Search:</label>
        <input type="search" id="q" name="q">
        <button type="submit">Search</button>
    </form>

    <h2>Login (POST)</h2>
    <p>Data is hidden in the request body. Not visible in the URL.</p>
    <form action="/login" method="POST">
        <label for="username">Username:</label>
        <input type="text" id="username" name="username">
        <label for="password">Password:</label>
        <input type="password" id="password" name="password">
        <button type="submit">Log In</button>
    </form>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Method Why Search GET Bookmarkable, shareable, cacheable Filters GET Same as search Pagination GET Bookmarkable Login POST Sensitive data, state change Signup POST Creates a user Contact form POST Sends a message Checkout POST Creates an order File upload POST Requires body Comment post POST Creates a comment Settings update POST Changes state Newsletter subscribe POST Creates a subscription Voting POST Changes state Like/favorite POST Changes state Refresh data GET Read-only Fetch page GET Read-only

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use GET for retrieval – search, filters, pagination.
  2. Use POST for state changes – logins, signups, payments.
  3. Never use GET for sensitive data – passwords, tokens, personal info.
  4. Always specify method – don't rely on the default.
  5. Use HTTPS for POST – even for non-sensitive data, to prevent tampering.
  6. Use CSRF tokens with POST – prevent cross-site attacks.
  7. Use Post/Redirect/Get – prevent resubmission on refresh.
  8. Keep GET URLs short – under 2000 characters for compatibility.
  9. Use POST for file uploads – with multipart/form-data.
  10. Validate on the server – regardless of method.
  11. Log POST requests – for audit trails.
  12. Don't use GET for actions – like "delete" or "logout".
  13. Set Cache-Control for GET – enable caching where safe.
  14. Set Cache-Control: no-store for POST – prevent caching.
  15. Use Referrer-Policy – prevent URL leakage.
  16. Test with the browser DevTools – verify the request method.
  17. Document the choice – in code comments or API docs.
  18. Audit for misused methods – passwords in GET, actions in GET.
  19. Use RESTful semantics – GET for read, POST for create.
  20. Consider PUT/PATCH/DELETE for APIs – via JavaScript.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using GET for Login
docs.text:
<form action="/login" method="GET">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>

Why it's wrong: The password appears in the URL, browser history, and server logs.

✅ Correct: 

<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using POST for Search
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="POST">
    <input type="search" name="q">
</form>

Why it's wrong: Search results can't be bookmarked, shared, or cached.

✅ Correct: 

<form action="/search" method="GET">
    <input type="search" name="q">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No method Attribute
docs.text:
<form action="/login">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>

Why it's wrong: Defaults to GET — password leaks into URL.

✅ Correct: 

<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using GET for State Changes
docs.text:
<form action="/delete" method="GET">
    <input type="hidden" name="id" value="42">
    <button type="submit">Delete</button>
</form>

Why it's wrong: GET must be safe; this changes state. A prefetch or a shared link could delete data.

✅ Correct: 

<form action="/delete" method="POST">
    <input type="hidden" name="id" value="42">
    <button type="submit">Delete</button>
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: File Upload with GET
docs.text:
<form action="/upload" method="GET" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    <input type="file" name="file">
</form>

Why it's wrong: GET cannot send a body, so files can't be uploaded.

✅ Correct: 

<form action="/upload" method="POST" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    <input type="file" name="file">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting Post/Redirect/Get
docs.text:
app.post('/submit', (req, res) => {
    saveData(req.body);
    res.send('Success!');
});

Why it's wrong: Refreshing the success page resubmits the form.

✅ Correct: 

app.post('/submit', (req, res) => {
    saveData(req.body);
    res.redirect(303, '/success');
});

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mixing Query and Body Data Confusingly
docs.text:
// POST with data in both URL and body
fetch('/submit?id=42', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: new FormData(form)
});

Why it's wrong: Mixing methods confuses the server and validation.

✅ Correct: Use query strings for identification (GET semantics) and body for data (POST semantics).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No CSRF Token in POST
docs.text:
<form method="POST">
    <input type="text" name="amount">
</form>

Why it's wrong: Vulnerable to CSRF attacks.

✅ Correct: 

<form method="POST">
    <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="...">
    <input type="text" name="amount">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using GET for Actions That Trigger Emails
docs.text:
<form action="/send-email" method="GET">
    <input type="email" name="to">
</form>

Why it's wrong: A GET request can be triggered by a prefetch, a link, or a crawler.

✅ Correct: 

<form action="/send-email" method="POST">
    <input type="email" name="to">
</form>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming POST is Secure Without HTTPS
docs.text:
<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>

Why it's wrong: POST data is in plain text unless HTTPS is used.

✅ Correct: Use HTTPS for all submissions.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Overusing POST for Everything
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="POST">

Why it's wrong: Loses bookmarking, caching, and browser history benefits.

✅ Correct: Use GET for retrieval.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• GET is cacheable – improves performance for repeated requests.
  • POST is not cacheable – every request hits the server.
  • GET URLs are smaller – but limited in length.
  • POST bodies are larger – but can be compressed.
  • HTTP/2 – both methods benefit from multiplexing.
  • CDN caching – only works for GET.
  • Browser prefetch – only for GET (safe methods).

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use GET for cacheable data – search results, product listings.
  2. Use POST for unique data – logins, comments.
  3. Enable compression – gzip/brotli for POST bodies.
  4. Use HTTP/2 – for multiplexing.
  5. Minimize POST payload – send only necessary fields.
  6. Use Cache-Control headers – to control caching.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• GET is visible – URLs appear in logs, history, referrers.
  • POST is hidden – body is not in the URL, but still requires HTTPS.
  • CSRF – POST is the primary target; use tokens.
  • Idempotency – GET must be safe; POST must not be triggered by accidents.
  • Logging – POST bodies may be logged; avoid sensitive data in URLs.
  • Referrer – GET URLs leak via the Referer header.
  • Bookmarks – GET URLs are bookmarked; never put secrets in URLs.
  • Crawlers – GET pages are crawled; POST pages are not.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use HTTPS – always.
  2. Use POST for sensitive data.
  3. Never use GET for state changes.
  4. Add CSRF tokens to POST forms.
  5. Set Referrer-Policy: no-referrer – for sensitive pages.
  6. Avoid logging sensitive POST data.
  7. Use Cache-Control: no-store – for sensitive responses.
  8. Rate-limit POST endpoints – prevent abuse.
  9. Validate on the server – regardless of method.
  10. Audit for GET misuse – passwords, tokens in URLs.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Network panel – inspect the request method.
  • Request URL – see if data is in the URL (GET) or body (POST).
  • Request headers – check Content-Type and Content-Length.
  • Request payload – verify the body.
  • Response status – check for redirects (302/303) after POST.
  • Console – log form.method to verify.
  • Server logs – confirm the method.
  • curl -v – inspect requests from the command line.
  • Postman – test GET and POST endpoints.
  • Browser history – verify GET URLs are bookmarkable.
  • Refresh behaviour – confirm POST prompts on refresh.

docs.title: 16. When to Use GET
docs.text:
• For retrieval – search, filters, pagination.
  • For safe, idempotent operations – no side effects.
  • For data you want bookmarked – search results, product pages.
  • For data you want cached – improve performance.
  • For data you want indexed – SEO-friendly URLs.
  • For small amounts of data – under 2000 characters.

docs.title: 17. When to Use POST
docs.text:
• For state changes – logins, signups, payments.
  • For sensitive data – passwords, tokens, personal info.
  • For large data – file uploads, long text.
  • For data you don't want bookmarked – credentials.
  • For data you don't want cached – real-time actions.
  • For operations with side effects – creating, updating, deleting.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• HTTP methods – GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS.
  • Idempotency – safe to repeat.
  • Safety – no side effects.
  • URL query string – GET data.
  • Request body – POST data.
  • enctype – encoding.
  • CSRF – cross-site request forgery.
  • Post/Redirect/Get – anti-resubmission pattern.
  • Cache-Control – HTTP caching.
  • Referrer-Policy – URL leakage prevention.
  • RESTful APIs – method semantics.
  • FormData – JavaScript form data.
  • fetch – modern AJAX.
  • XMLHttpRequest – legacy AJAX.
  • Content-Type – request encoding.
  • Content-Length – request size.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• GET is the default method for HTML forms — always specify explicitly.

  • GET data is limited by URL length; POST data is limited by server configuration.

  • POST cannot be bookmarked — the data is in the body, not the URL.

  • GET requests can be cached by browsers, proxies, and CDNs; POST cannot.

  • Search engines only crawl GET links — POST pages are not indexed.

  • Browser refresh after POST prompts "Confirm form resubmission"; after GET it re-fetches silently.

  • Post/Redirect/Get (PRG) prevents duplicate POST submissions.

  • CSRF attacks target state-changing endpoints, usually POST.

  • Referer headers can leak GET query parameters to third-party sites.

  • Idempotency: GET is idempotent; POST is not.

  • HTTP/1.0 (1996) formalised the GET/POST distinction.

  • HTML forms only support GET and POST — not PUT, PATCH, or DELETE (those require JavaScript).

  • Never use GET for passwords — they appear in URLs, logs, and history.

  • Never use GET for actions — crawlers, prefetchers, and bookmarks could trigger them.

  • POST with multipart/form-data is the only way to upload files via forms.

  • File inputs are ignored in GET — the browser strips them.

  • URL length limits: Chrome ~2 MB, Firefox ~1 MB, Safari ~80 KB, older IE ~2083 chars.

  • RESTful APIs use GET for reading, POST for creating, PUT for updating, DELETE for deleting.

  • Fetch with method: 'POST' can send JSON instead of form-encoded data.

  • Content-Type distinguishes form-encoded, multipart, and JSON bodies.

  • Best practices include using GET for retrieval, POST for changes, HTTPS, CSRF tokens, and Post/Redirect/Get.

  • Common mistakes include GET for passwords, missing method, and no CSRF token.

  • Following best practices for GET vs POST leads to secure, performant, and user-friendly web applications.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• GET and POST are the two HTTP methods used by HTML forms.
  • GET sends data as a URL query string; POST sends data in the request body.
  • GET is for retrieval (search, filters); POST is for changes (logins, signups, payments).
  • GET is safe, idempotent, bookmarkable, and cacheable.
  • POST is unsafe, non-idempotent, not bookmarkable, and not cacheable.
  • Sensitive data must use POST.
  • File uploads require POST with multipart/form-data.
  • Default method is GET — always specify explicitly.
  • Post/Redirect/Get prevents duplicate submissions.
  • CSRF tokens protect POST endpoints.
  • Search engines only crawl GET links.
  • Best practices: use GET for retrieval, POST for changes, HTTPS for all, CSRF tokens for POST, and server-side validation.
  • Common mistakes include GET for passwords, no method, GET for state changes, and forgetting CSRF tokens.
  • The GET vs POST distinction is fundamental to how the web works — using the right method matters for security, performance, usability, and correct browser behaviour.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The autocomplete attribute is an HTML attribute that provides a hint to the browser about what kind of data a form control expects. It enables the browser's autofill feature to suggest and automatically populate values that the user has previously entered or that are stored in the browser's password manager. The attribute can be applied to <form> and to individual <input>, <select>, and <textarea> elements.

The value of the autocomplete attribute is a space-separated token list that describes the expected data (e.g., name, email, street-address) and optionally how the field relates to others (e.g., section-payment, shipping, billing). Browsers use this information to match fields with stored data, making form filling faster, less error-prone, and more accessible.

Example: 

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">

When the user focuses this field, the browser may offer a dropdown of previously used email addresses.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The autocomplete attribute serves several essential purposes:

  • Speed – users fill forms faster with autofill.
  • Accuracy – reduces typos and mistakes.
  • Accessibility – helps users with motor or cognitive disabilities.
  • Mobile convenience – autofill from the device's keyboard suggestions.
  • Password management – enables password managers to save and fill credentials.
  • Payment autofill – browsers can autofill credit card details.
  • Semantic clarity – tells browsers exactly what each field means.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The autocomplete attribute is a global attribute for form controls. It can be set on:

  • <form> – sets the default for all controls within.
  • <input> – most types (except hidden, submit, reset, button, image).
  • <select> – for dropdowns (rarely used).
  • <textarea> – for multi-line text.

It is part of the form autofill system, which also includes:

  • The browser's built-in password manager.
  • Operating system keychains (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, etc.).
  • Third-party password managers (1Password, Bitwarden, etc.).
  • Payment autofill (credit cards).
<form autocomplete="on">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" autocomplete="name">

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">
</form>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Filling out forms is tedious. Users repeatedly type the same information — name, email, address, phone number, credit card details — on every site. On mobile, it's even worse: small keyboards, autocorrect, and typos make form filling slow and frustrating. Studies show that form abandonment increases with every additional field and that users often abandon forms that are hard to fill.

Before autocomplete, browsers had to guess what each field was for. A field named email might be recognized, but user_email, email_address, contact_email, or e-mail might not. This led to inconsistent autofill behaviour — sometimes it worked, sometimes it didn't.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No standard field names Browsers guessed; autofill often failed Inconsistent autofill Users couldn't rely on it Password managers struggled Fields not recognized as credentials Payment autofill unreliable Card details not filled Mobile autofill limited No context for keyboard suggestions Accessibility gaps Users with disabilities had to type everything

docs.title: Why the autocomplete Attribute Was Introduced
docs.text:
The autocomplete attribute was introduced in HTML5 to provide a standard vocabulary for describing form fields. It was designed to:

  • Standardize field names – so browsers and password managers can recognize them.
  • Enable reliable autofill – across sites and browsers.
  • Improve mobile experience – keyboard suggestions and autofill.
  • Support accessibility – help users with disabilities.
  • Enable payment autofill – standardized credit card fields.
  • Support password managers – recognize login and signup fields.
  • Allow fine-grained control – off, on, new-password, current-password, etc.

The attribute has evolved over time. The HTML Living Standard now defines a comprehensive list of tokens and a mechanism for grouping fields into sections.

docs.title: The autocomplete Attribute
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="name" autocomplete="name">

The value is a space-separated token list. The tokens fall into these categories:

Category Examples Field name name, email, tel, street-address Name/address type shipping, billing (prefix) Section section-payment (prefix) Contact type home, work, mobile, fax, pager Credential type username, new-password, current-password, one-time-code Payment type cc-number, cc-exp, cc-csc, cc-name, cc-type Other off, on

docs.title: Simple Examples
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="name" autocomplete="name">
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="tel" name="phone" autocomplete="tel">
<input type="text" name="address" autocomplete="street-address">
<input type="text" name="zip" autocomplete="postal-code">

docs.title: Login Form
docs.text:
<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" autocomplete="username">

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password">

    <button type="submit">Log In</button>
</form>

docs.title: Signup Form
docs.text:
<form action="/signup" method="POST">
    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" autocomplete="username">

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" autocomplete="new-password">

    <label for="confirm">Confirm Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="confirm" name="confirm" autocomplete="new-password">

    <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>

docs.title: Checkout Form (Payment Autofill)
docs.text:
<form action="/checkout" method="POST">
    <fieldset>
        <legend>Shipping Address</legend>
        <label for="ship-name">Name:</label>
        <input type="text" id="ship-name" name="ship-name" autocomplete="shipping name">
        <label for="ship-address">Address:</label>
        <input type="text" id="ship-address" name="ship-address" autocomplete="shipping street-address">
        <label for="ship-city">City:</label>
        <input type="text" id="ship-city" name="ship-city" autocomplete="shipping address-level2">
        <label for="ship-zip">ZIP:</label>
        <input type="text" id="ship-zip" name="ship-zip" autocomplete="shipping postal-code">
    </fieldset>

    <fieldset>
        <legend>Payment</legend>
        <label for="cc-name">Name on Card:</label>
        <input type="text" id="cc-name" name="cc-name" autocomplete="cc-name">
        <label for="cc-number">Card Number:</label>
        <input type="text" id="cc-number" name="cc-number" autocomplete="cc-number">
        <label for="cc-exp">Expiry:</label>
        <input type="text" id="cc-exp" name="cc-exp" autocomplete="cc-exp">
        <label for="cc-csc">CVC:</label>
        <input type="text" id="cc-csc" name="cc-csc" autocomplete="cc-csc">
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Place Order</button>
</form>

docs.title: Disabling Autocomplete
docs.text:
<form autocomplete="off">
    ...
</form>

Or per field:

<input type="text" name="code" autocomplete="off">

Note: Browsers may ignore autocomplete="off" for certain fields (e.g., passwords, emails) as a security/usability measure.

docs.title: Sectioning Fields
docs.text:
Use section-* to distinguish multiple forms of the same type on one page (e.g., two addresses):

<input type="text" name="ship-address" autocomplete="section-shipping street-address">
<input type="text" name="bill-address" autocomplete="section-billing street-address">

docs.title: Contact Type Prefixes
docs.text:
<input type="email" name="work-email" autocomplete="work email">
<input type="email" name="home-email" autocomplete="home email">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Token Meaning name Full name given-name First name family-name Last name email Email address tel Phone number street-address Street address address-level1 State/Province address-level2 City postal-code ZIP/Postal code country Country cc-number Credit card number cc-exp Expiry date cc-csc CVC/CVV username Username new-password New password current-password Existing password one-time-code OTP code

docs.title: The "Label on a Drawer" Analogy
docs.text: Think of the autocomplete attribute as a label on a drawer in a filing cabinet. The browser (the file clerk) reads the label ("Email") and knows exactly which file to pull from its storage (the user's saved data). Without the label, the clerk has to guess — and often guesses wrong.

docs.title: The "Name Tag at a Conference" Analogy
docs.text: When you attend a conference, your name tag tells others who you are and where you're from. The autocomplete attribute is a name tag for a form field — it tells the browser "this is an email field" or "this is a credit card number field," so the browser can help you fill it.

docs.title: The "Universal Translator" Analogy
docs.text: The autocomplete attribute acts like a universal translator between your form and the browser's data store. Different sites use different names (email, user_email, contact_email), but the autocomplete token (email) is universal. The browser always knows what it means.

docs.title: The "Shipping vs. Billing" Mental Model
docs.text:
When a form has both shipping and billing addresses, the autocomplete attribute can prefix the field name with shipping or billing:

  • autocomplete="shipping street-address"
  • autocomplete="billing street-address"

This tells the browser to fill the correct address in each section.

docs.title: The "Password Manager" Mental Model
docs.text:
For password managers, autocomplete tokens are crucial:

  • username – identifies the username field.
  • current-password – identifies the existing password field (login).
  • new-password – identifies the new password field (signup, password change).

Password managers use these tokens to know when to offer saving, updating, or filling credentials.

docs.title: Concept 1: Field Name Tokens
docs.text:
The most important tokens describe what the field contains:

Token Description name Full name honorific-prefix Mr., Mrs., Dr., etc. given-name First name additional-name Middle name family-name Last name honorific-suffix Jr., Sr., PhD, etc. nickname Nickname email Email address username Username new-password New password current-password Current password one-time-code One-time code organization Company name organization-title Job title street-address Full street address address-line1 Address line 1 address-line2 Address line 2 address-line3 Address line 3 address-level4 Neighborhood (some countries) address-level3 District (some countries) address-level2 City address-level1 State/Province postal-code ZIP/Postal code country Country code country-name Country name tel Phone number tel-country-code Country code tel-national Phone number without country code tel-area-code Area code tel-local Local number tel-extension Extension cc-name Name on card cc-given-name First name on card cc-additional-name Middle name on card cc-family-name Last name on card cc-number Card number cc-exp Expiry date cc-exp-month Expiry month cc-exp-year Expiry year cc-csc Security code (CVC/CVV) cc-type Card type bday Birthday bday-day Birth day bday-month Birth month bday-year Birth year sex Gender url Website URL photo Photo URL language Language impp Instant messaging URL

docs.title: Concept 2: The off and on Values
docs.text:
• off – suggests the browser should not autofill this field.
  • on – suggests the browser should autofill (default).

Important: Browsers may ignore off for sensitive fields like passwords and emails.

docs.title: Concept 3: Section Prefixes
docs.text:
Use section-* to distinguish multiple sections of the same type:

<input autocomplete="section-shipping street-address">
<input autocomplete="section-billing street-address">

The section name is arbitrary; the browser uses it to group fields.

docs.title: Concept 4: Contact Type Prefixes
docs.text:
Use home, work, mobile, fax, pager to specify the contact type:

<input autocomplete="home email">
<input autocomplete="work email">
<input autocomplete="mobile tel">

docs.title: Concept 5: Shipping and Billing Prefixes
docs.text:
Use shipping or billing to specify the address type:

<input autocomplete="shipping street-address">
<input autocomplete="billing street-address">

Note: These are field name prefixes (before the field name), not separate tokens.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Order of Tokens
docs.text:
The token list is order-sensitive in this way:

  1. Section (optional): section-*
  2. Address type (optional): shipping or billing
  3. Contact type (optional): home, work, etc.
  4. Field name (required): e.g., email

Example: 

<input autocomplete="section-primary shipping work email">

docs.title: Concept 7: WebAuthn and autocomplete
docs.text:
The autocomplete attribute interacts with the WebAuthn standard:

  • autocomplete="webauthn" – hints that a field is for a WebAuthn credential.

Note: This is a newer addition; support varies.

docs.title: Concept 8: The autocomplete Attribute on <form>
docs.text:
Setting autocomplete on <form> provides the default for all controls within:

<form autocomplete="on">
    ...
</form>

Controls can override the form's setting.

docs.title: Concept 9: Browser Behaviour
docs.text:
• Chrome – supports most tokens; uses heuristics.
  • Firefox – supports most tokens; uses heuristics.
  • Safari – supports most tokens; integrates with iCloud Keychain.
  • Edge – supports most tokens; integrates with Windows Hello.

docs.title: Concept 10: Password Managers
docs.text:
Password managers (1Password, Bitwarden, LastPass, Dashlane) rely on autocomplete tokens to:

  • Identify login fields (username, current-password).
  • Identify signup fields (new-password).
  • Detect password changes.
  • Offer to save credentials.

docs.title: Concept 11: Payment Autofill
docs.text:
Browsers can autofill credit card details using:

  • cc-name
  • cc-number
  • cc-exp
  • cc-csc

This requires the user to have saved a card in the browser.

docs.title: Concept 12: Address Autofill
docs.text:
Browsers can autofill addresses using:

  • street-address
  • address-line1
  • address-line2
  • address-level2
  • address-level1
  • postal-code
  • country

docs.title: Concept 13: Autofill vs. Autocomplete
docs.text:
• Autocomplete – the browser suggests values based on what the user has typed before (like a search box's suggestions).
  • Autofill – the browser automatically fills the entire field with a stored value.

The autocomplete attribute controls autofill, not the dropdown suggestions.

docs.title: Concept 14: The aria-autocomplete Attribute
docs.text: aria-autocomplete is an ARIA attribute for custom widgets (e.g., comboboxes), not for native form controls. For native inputs, use the autocomplete attribute.

docs.title: Concept 15: Browser Ignoring autocomplete="off"
docs.text:
Browsers may ignore off for:

  • Password fields.
  • Email fields.
  • Login forms.

Reason: Usability and security. Users expect password managers to work.

Workaround: Use autocomplete="new-password" or autocomplete="current-password" for password fields.

docs.title: Concept 16: The autocomplete Attribute and Validation
docs.text: The autocomplete attribute does not affect validation. It only affects autofill.

docs.title: Concept 17: The autocomplete Attribute and Accessibility
docs.text: Screen readers may announce the autocomplete hint. It helps users with cognitive disabilities by reducing the need to remember and type information.

docs.title: Concept 18: The autocomplete Attribute and SEO
docs.text: The autocomplete attribute does not directly affect SEO. However, better form UX can lead to more conversions.

docs.title: Concept 19: Browser Support
docs.text: All modern browsers support autocomplete. Support for specific tokens varies. Test in target browsers.

docs.title: Concept 20: The autocomplete Attribute and Mobile Keyboards
docs.text:
On mobile, autocomplete works with the keyboard's autofill suggestions. For example:

  • autocomplete="email" – suggests saved emails.
  • autocomplete="tel" – suggests saved phone numbers.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Autofill
docs.text:
1.  User loads a page with a form.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses the HTML and identifies form controls.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser reads the `autocomplete` attribute on each control.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser matches the token with stored user data:
    │   ├── Password manager: username, passwords.
    │   ├── Address book: name, address, phone.
    │   └── Payment: credit card details.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser highlights fields it can autofill.
    │
    ▼
6.  User focuses a field.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser shows a dropdown of suggestions or auto-fills.
    │
    ▼
8.  User selects a value.
    │
    ▼
9.  Browser fills the field.
    │
    ▼
10. Browser may fill related fields (e.g., address, card details).

docs.title: Heuristic Matching
docs.text:
Even without autocomplete, browsers try to guess field purpose from:

  • The name attribute.
  • The id attribute.
  • The <label> text.
  • The placeholder.
  • The type.

The autocomplete attribute overrides heuristics.

docs.title: The Token Parsing Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Split the value by spaces.
  2. The first token may be a section (section-*).
  3. The next token may be an address type (shipping/billing).
  4. The next token may be a contact type (home/work/etc.).
  5. The last token is the field name.
  6. The browser uses the field name to match stored data.

docs.title: Password Manager Integration
docs.text:
Password managers use the autocomplete attribute to:

  • Detect login forms (username + current-password).
  • Detect signup forms (username + new-password).
  • Detect password change forms (current-password + new-password).
  • Detect one-time codes (one-time-code).

docs.title: Payment Autofill
docs.text:
Browsers with payment autofill:

  1. Detect cc-number, cc-exp, cc-csc.
  2. Prompt the user to select a saved card.
  3. Fill the fields.

Note: Payment autofill requires the user to have saved a card in the browser.

docs.title: Address Autofill
docs.text:
Browsers with address autofill:

  1. Detect street-address, address-level2, postal-code, etc.
  2. Prompt the user to select a saved address.
  3. Fill the fields.

docs.title: Default Behaviour
docs.text: Without autocomplete, browsers use heuristics. With autocomplete, they use the explicit token.

docs.title: The autocomplete Attribute in the DOM
docs.text:
const input = document.querySelector('input');
console.log(input.autocomplete); // "email"
input.autocomplete = 'tel'; // Change dynamically

docs.title: The autocomplete Attribute in the Form
docs.text:
const form = document.querySelector('form');
console.log(form.autocomplete); // "on"

docs.title: The HTMLInputElement.autocomplete Property
docs.text:
Reflects the autocomplete attribute:

console.log(input.autocomplete); // "email"
input.autocomplete = 'name';

docs.title: Browser Autofill Implementation
docs.text:
Each browser has its own autofill engine:

  • Chrome: Chrome Autofill, Google Password Manager.
  • Firefox: Form Autofill, Firefox Password Manager.
  • Safari: AutoFill, iCloud Keychain.
  • Edge: Autofill, Microsoft Password Manager.

These engines:

  1. Parse the autocomplete tokens.
  2. Match them to stored data.
  3. Fill the fields.

docs.title: The Password Manager API
docs.text: Browsers expose a Credential Management API that password managers can integrate with. The autocomplete attribute is one of the signals used.

docs.title: The autocomplete Attribute and the HTML Standard
docs.text:
The HTML Living Standard defines:

  • The list of valid tokens.
  • The token syntax (section, address type, contact type, field name).
  • The off and on values.

docs.title: The autocomplete Attribute and WebAuthn
docs.text:
WebAuthn uses the autocomplete attribute to identify credential fields:

<input type="text" name="username" autocomplete="username webauthn">

Note: Support for webauthn varies.

docs.title: The autocomplete Attribute and Mobile
docs.text:
On mobile, the autocomplete attribute is used by the keyboard's autofill system:

  • iOS: QuickType suggestions, iCloud Keychain.
  • Android: Autofill Framework, Google Autofill.

docs.title: The autocomplete Attribute and Accessibility APIs
docs.text: The autocomplete token may be exposed to accessibility APIs, helping screen readers announce field purpose.

docs.title: Browser Differences
docs.text: Browser Token Support Heuristics Chrome Excellent Strong Firefox Excellent Strong Safari Good Strong (iCloud) Edge Excellent Strong (Windows)

docs.title: The autocomplete Attribute and the name Attribute
docs.text: The name attribute is still used as a fallback heuristic. The autocomplete attribute overrides it.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of Autocomplete
docs.text:
1.  Author writes form controls with `autocomplete` attributes.
    │
    ▼
2.  File deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses HTML.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser reads `autocomplete` tokens.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser matches tokens to stored data.
    │
    ▼
6.  User focuses a field.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser shows autofill suggestions.
    │
    ▼
8.  User selects a suggestion.
    │
    ▼
9.  Browser fills the field.
    │
    ▼
10. Browser may fill related fields.
    │
    ▼
11. User submits the form.
    │
    ▼
12. Browser may offer to save new data.

docs.title: Dynamic Changes
docs.text: input.autocomplete = 'new-password'; // Change dynamically

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Login Form
docs.text:
<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" autocomplete="username">

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password">

    <button type="submit">Log In</button>
</form>

Code Breakdown: - autocomplete="username" – tells the browser this is the username. - autocomplete="current-password" – tells the browser this is the existing password (login).

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" autocomplete="new-password">

    <label for="confirm">Confirm Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="confirm" name="confirm" autocomplete="new-password">

    <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>

Code Breakdown: - autocomplete="name" – full name. - autocomplete="email" – email address. - autocomplete="new-password" – new password (signup).

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Registration Form with Autocomplete
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Registration</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 600px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        form { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.75rem; }
        fieldset { border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 8px; padding: 1rem; }
        legend { font-weight: bold; color: #2c3e50; }
        label { font-weight: 500; margin-top: 0.5rem; }
        input { padding: 0.5rem; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 4px; font-size: 1rem; width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box; }
        input:focus { outline: 2px solid #3498db; outline-offset: 2px; }
        button { padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem; background: #3498db; color: white; border: none; border-radius: 4px; font-size: 1rem; cursor: pointer; }
        button:hover { background: #2980b9; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Registration</h1>
    <form action="/register" method="POST">
        <fieldset>
            <legend>Account Information</legend>
            <label for="username">Username:</label>
            <input type="text" id="username" name="username" autocomplete="username" required>

            <label for="email">Email:</label>
            <input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required>

            <label for="password">Password:</label>
