            <input type="password" id="password" name="password" autocomplete="new-password" required minlength="8">
        </fieldset>

        <fieldset>
            <legend>Personal Information</legend>
            <label for="name">Full Name:</label>
            <input type="text" id="name" name="name" autocomplete="name" required>

            <label for="phone">Phone:</label>
            <input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" autocomplete="tel" required>

            <label for="address">Address:</label>
            <input type="text" id="address" name="address" autocomplete="street-address" required>

            <label for="city">City:</label>
            <input type="text" id="city" name="city" autocomplete="address-level2" required>

            <label for="zip">ZIP:</label>
            <input type="text" id="zip" name="zip" autocomplete="postal-code" required>

            <label for="country">Country:</label>
            <input type="text" id="country" name="country" autocomplete="country-name" required>
        </fieldset>

        <button type="submit">Register</button>
    </form>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Autocomplete Token Login username, current-password Signup username, email, new-password Password change current-password, new-password Checkout cc-name, cc-number, cc-exp, cc-csc Shipping address shipping name, shipping street-address, etc. Billing address billing name, billing street-address, etc. Contact form name, email, tel Profile name, given-name, family-name, bday Search (usually off) OTP one-time-code Job application organization, organization-title Social media nickname, url, photo

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use autocomplete – even if you think the browser will guess.
  2. Use the most specific token – given-name instead of name when possible.
  3. Use new-password for signup – not current-password.
  4. Use current-password for login – helps password managers.
  5. Use shipping/billing prefixes – for address forms.
  6. Use section-* – for multiple forms of the same type on one page.
  7. Use home/work prefixes – for contact fields.
  8. Use one-time-code – for OTP fields.
  9. Use cc-* tokens – for payment fields.
  10. Don't rely on autocomplete="off" – browsers may ignore it.
  11. Use autocomplete="off" on search fields – to avoid autofill dropdowns.
  12. Pair with inputmode – for correct mobile keyboards.
  13. Test with password managers – 1Password, Bitwarden, etc.
  14. Test with browser autofill – Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge.
  15. Test on mobile – iOS and Android autofill.
  16. Keep field names consistent – helps heuristics as a fallback.
  17. Use <label> – autocomplete works better with labels.
  18. Avoid duplicate tokens – each field should have a unique token.
  19. Document your tokens – in a style guide.
  20. Review browser support – for newer tokens like webauthn.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Omitting autocomplete
docs.text:
<input type="email" name="email">

Why it's wrong: Browser has to guess; autofill may fail.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using current-password for Signup
docs.text:
<input type="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password">

Why it's wrong: Tells password managers this is an existing password.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="password" name="password" autocomplete="new-password">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using name Instead of given-name/family-name
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="first" autocomplete="name">

Why it's wrong: name is for the full name; given-name is more precise.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="text" name="first" autocomplete="given-name">
<input type="text" name="last" autocomplete="family-name">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Section Prefix for Duplicate Addresses
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="ship-address" autocomplete="street-address">
<input type="text" name="bill-address" autocomplete="street-address">

Why it's wrong: Browser can't distinguish shipping from billing.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="text" name="ship-address" autocomplete="shipping street-address">
<input type="text" name="bill-address" autocomplete="billing street-address">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using autocomplete="off" for Passwords
docs.text:
<input type="password" name="password" autocomplete="off">

Why it's wrong: Browsers ignore off for passwords; use new-password or current-password.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="password" name="new" autocomplete="new-password">
<input type="password" name="current" autocomplete="current-password">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using autocomplete="on" on Every Field
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="search" autocomplete="on">

Why it's wrong: on is the default; not a specific token.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="search" name="search" autocomplete="off">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting one-time-code
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="otp">

Why it's wrong: Mobile users don't get OTP autofill.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="text" name="otp" autocomplete="one-time-code" inputmode="numeric">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using autocomplete on Hidden Inputs
docs.text:
<input type="hidden" name="token" autocomplete="off">

Why it's wrong: Hidden inputs don't have autocomplete.

✅ Correct: Omit autocomplete on hidden inputs.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing with Password Managers
docs.text:
<input type="password" name="password">

Why it's wrong: You don't know if password managers will work.

✅ Correct: Test with 1Password, Bitwarden, etc.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Non-Standard Tokens
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="email" autocomplete="user-email">

Why it's wrong: user-email is not a standard token.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="text" name="email" autocomplete="email">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mixing Prefixes Incorrectly
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="email" autocomplete="email work">

Why it's wrong: The order is wrong; prefix comes before field name.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="text" name="email" autocomplete="work email">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting autocomplete on Checkout
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="cc-number">

Why it's wrong: Users can't autofill card details.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="text" name="cc-number" autocomplete="cc-number">

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Autofill reduces typing – faster form completion.
  • Browser overhead – negligible; autofill is handled natively.
  • No JavaScript – autocomplete is a native feature.
  • Mobile benefits – significant time savings.
  • Password managers – improve login speed.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use autocomplete on all relevant fields – speeds up form filling.
  2. Use inputmode – for correct mobile keyboards.
  3. Use autocomplete="off" for search – avoids distraction.
  4. Test on real devices – autofill behaviour varies.
  5. Minify HTML – reduce file size.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Autofill can expose data – if a user shares their device.
  • Password managers – rely on autocomplete for security.
  • Phishing – attackers can mimic fields to capture autofilled data.
  • Sensitive fields – consider autocomplete="off" for high-risk fields.
  • Payment fields – use cc-* tokens; browsers protect card data.
  • One-time codes – use one-time-code for OTP autofill.
  • HTTPS – required for autofill of sensitive data.
  • CSRF – autocomplete doesn't protect against CSRF.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use HTTPS – for all forms.
  2. Use autocomplete="off" – for sensitive fields if needed.
  3. Use new-password/current-password – helps password managers.
  4. Use one-time-code – for OTPs.
  5. Use cc-* tokens – for card fields.
  6. Test with password managers – ensure they work.
  7. Educate users – about autofill risks.
  8. Use CSRF tokens – for state-changing forms.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the autocomplete attribute.
  • Computed styles – check if autofill styles are applied.
  • Console – use input.autocomplete to read the value.
  • Password manager extensions – check if they detect the fields.
  • Browser autofill – test by focusing the field.
  • Mobile testing – test autofill on iOS/Android.
  • chrome://settings/autofill – inspect saved data.
  • Firefox about:logins – inspect saved logins.
  • Safari Preferences – inspect saved passwords.
  • Validator – check for invalid tokens.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the field purpose is announced.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For all form controls – autocomplete should be on every relevant field.
  • For login/signup – username, email, passwords.
  • For checkout – card details, addresses.
  • For contact forms – name, email, phone.
  • For profile forms – name, address, birthday.
  • For OTP fields – one-time-code.
  • For search fields – usually off.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For hidden inputs – no effect.
  • For submit/reset/button inputs – no effect.
  • For search fields – usually off to avoid autofill dropdowns.
  • For high-risk fields – consider off if autofill is a security risk.
  • For fields with no standard token – use off or omit.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <input> – form control.
  • <form> – form container.
  • <select> – dropdown.
  • <textarea> – multi-line text.
  • <label> – labels.
  • autocomplete – the attribute.
  • Autofill – browser feature.
  • Password managers – 1Password, Bitwarden, etc.
  • Credential Management API – browser API for credentials.
  • WebAuthn – passwordless authentication.
  • inputmode – mobile keyboard hint.
  • type – input type.
  • name – field name (fallback heuristic).
  • Payment autofill – credit card autofill.
  • Address autofill – address autofill.
  • One-time code – OTP autofill.
  • Sectioning – section-* prefixes.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The autocomplete attribute was introduced in HTML5 (2014).

  • The HTML Living Standard defines over 50 autocomplete tokens.

  • Browsers may ignore autocomplete="off" for passwords and emails.

  • Password managers rely heavily on autocomplete tokens.

  • new-password and current-password are critical for password managers.

  • one-time-code enables OTP autofill on mobile.

  • cc-number, cc-exp, cc-csc enable payment autofill.

  • shipping and billing prefixes distinguish addresses.

  • section-* distinguishes multiple forms of the same type on one page.

  • home, work, mobile prefixes specify contact type.

  • webauthn is a newer token for WebAuthn credentials.

  • Autofill is different from autocomplete suggestions — autofill fills the entire field, while suggestions show a dropdown of past entries.

  • Mobile autofill uses the autocomplete attribute for keyboard suggestions.

  • The name attribute is still used as a fallback heuristic.

  • Browsers use heuristics even without autocomplete, but the attribute overrides them.

  • Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge all support autocomplete tokens.

  • 1Password, Bitwarden, LastPass, and Dashlane all use the autocomplete attribute.

  • Payment autofill requires the user to have saved a card in the browser.

  • Address autofill requires the user to have saved an address.

  • Autofill can be a security risk on shared devices.

  • autocomplete="off" is often ignored for password fields due to usability.

  • Best practices include using the most specific token, using new-password for signup, and testing with password managers.

  • Common mistakes include omitting autocomplete, using current-password for signup, and not using section prefixes.

  • Following best practices for autocomplete leads to faster, more accurate, and more accessible forms.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The autocomplete attribute hints to the browser what data a form field expects.
  • It enables autofill — browser-assisted filling of form data.
  • Values are space-separated tokens describing field name, section, address type, and contact type.
  • Key tokens include name, email, tel, street-address, cc-number, username, new-password, current-password, one-time-code.
  • Prefixes (shipping, billing, home, work, section-*) provide context.
  • off suggests no autofill; on is the default.
  • Browsers may ignore off for passwords and emails.
  • Password managers rely on autocomplete for login/signup detection.
  • Payment autofill uses cc-* tokens.
  • Address autofill uses address tokens.
  • OTP autofill uses one-time-code.
  • Best practices: use the most specific token, use new-password/current-password, use prefixes, test with password managers and on mobile.
  • Common mistakes include omitting autocomplete, using current-password for signup, and not using section prefixes.
  • The autocomplete attribute is essential for fast, accurate, and accessible form filling.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Form accessibility is the practice of building HTML forms that can be perceived, understood, navigated, and operated by all users, including those using screen readers, keyboard-only navigation, voice control, switch devices, screen magnifiers, and other assistive technologies. It ensures that every form control has a programmatic label, every error is announced and recoverable, every interaction is keyboard-operable, and the overall form is logically structured so assistive technologies can present it meaningfully.

Forms are the most critical area of web accessibility. Unlike static content, forms require the user to do something — type, select, choose, submit. If a form is inaccessible, the user is completely blocked from the task — no account creation, no purchase, no contact, no access.

Example: 

<form action="/contact" method="POST">
    <fieldset>
        <legend>Contact Information</legend>

        <label for="name">Name:</label>
        <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required
               aria-describedby="name-error">
        <span id="name-error" role="alert"></span>

        <label for="email">Email:</label>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required
               autocomplete="email">
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Form accessibility serves several essential purposes:

  • Inclusion – ensures users with disabilities can complete tasks.
  • Legal compliance – WCAG, ADA, Section 508, EN 301 549 require it.
  • Usability – accessible forms are easier for everyone.
  • Error prevention – clear labels and errors reduce mistakes.
  • Screen reader support – programmatic labels and roles.
  • Keyboard support – all controls reachable and operable.
  • Cognitive support – clear structure and instructions.
  • Mobile support – larger touch targets, correct keyboards.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Form accessibility is a cross-cutting concern that touches every aspect of form design:

Form Accessibility
│
├── Labels and accessible names
├── Fieldsets and legends (grouping)
├── Keyboard navigation
├── Error handling and validation
├── Focus management
├── Screen reader announcements
├── ARIA roles and properties
├── Touch target size
├── Color and contrast
└── Testing with assistive technologies

It is not a separate feature — it is how you build forms correctly.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Forms are inherently interactive and complex. Unlike static text, they require:

  • Perceiving the labels and instructions.
  • Understanding what each field expects.
  • Navigating to each control.
  • Operating the controls (typing, selecting, checking).
  • Responding to validation errors.
  • Submitting the form.

For a sighted mouse user, this is trivial. For a blind user with a screen reader, or a motor-impaired user with only a keyboard, or a cognitive-impaired user who needs clear instructions — every step is a potential barrier.

Without accessibility:

  • Screen reader users hear "edit text" with no label — they don't know what to type.
  • Keyboard users can't reach or activate controls.
  • Voice control users can't target fields that lack accessible names.
  • Users with motor impairments struggle with small click targets.
  • Users with cognitive disabilities are confused by unclear errors.
  • Users of screen magnifiers lose context when zoomed in.

An inaccessible form is a wall — the user cannot proceed.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No <label> Screen readers hear "edit text" No fieldset for groups Radio/checkbox groups lack context Unclear errors Users don't know what to fix No keyboard support Users can't complete the form Small touch targets Motor-impaired users struggle Color-only errors Color-blind users miss errors No aria-describedby Errors not announced Placeholder as label Label disappears on input

docs.title: Why Form Accessibility Standards Were Established
docs.text:
Form accessibility standards emerged from:

  • WCAG 1.0 (1999) – required labels and keyboard access.
  • WCAG 2.0 (2008) – required programmatic label association, error identification, error suggestion.
  • ARIA (2008+) – provided roles and properties for custom widgets.
  • WCAG 2.1 (2018) – added touch target size, reflow, and other criteria.
  • WCAG 2.2 (2023) – added focus appearance and dragging movement criteria.
  • Section 508, ADA, EN 301 549 – legal requirements.

These standards ensure that forms are universally usable — not just for the majority but for everyone.

docs.title: The Accessible Form Checklist
docs.text: Requirement Implementation Every control has a label <label for="id"> or wrapping Groups have legends <fieldset> + <legend> Errors are announced aria-describedby, role="alert", aria-invalid Keyboard accessible Native controls, logical tab order Focus visible Don't remove outlines Touch targets ≥ 44×44 px CSS min-height/min-width No color-only information Text + icons + color Autocomplete hints autocomplete attribute Instructions before fields Paragraphs before the form Required fields indicated required + visual indicator

docs.title: Accessible Contact Form
docs.text:
<form action="/contact" method="POST">
    <h1>Contact Us</h1>
    <p>All fields marked with * are required.</p>

    <fieldset>
        <legend>Your Information</legend>

        <label for="name">Name <span aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
        <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required
               autocomplete="name" aria-required="true">

        <label for="email">Email <span aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required
               autocomplete="email" aria-required="true">

        <label for="phone">Phone (optional)</label>
        <input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" autocomplete="tel">
    </fieldset>

    <fieldset>
        <legend>Your Message</legend>

        <label for="subject">Subject</label>
        <select id="subject" name="subject" required>
            <option value="">Choose a subject...</option>
            <option value="general">General Inquiry</option>
            <option value="support">Support</option>
            <option value="feedback">Feedback</option>
        </select>

        <label for="message">Message <span aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
        <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5" required
                  aria-required="true"></textarea>
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Send Message</button>
</form>

docs.title: Error Handling with ARIA
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST" novalidate>
    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required
           aria-describedby="email-error" aria-invalid="false">
    <span id="email-error" role="alert"></span>

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<script>
    const form = document.getElementById('myForm');
    const email = document.getElementById('email');
    const error = document.getElementById('email-error');

    form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
        if (!email.validity.valid) {
            e.preventDefault();
            email.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
            if (email.validity.valueMissing) {
                error.textContent = 'Email is required.';
            } else if (email.validity.typeMismatch) {
                error.textContent = 'Please enter a valid email address.';
            }
            email.focus();
        }
    });

    email.addEventListener('input', () => {
        if (email.validity.valid) {
            email.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'false');
            error.textContent = '';
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Keyboard-Accessible Custom Widget
docs.text:
<!-- Bad: div-based button -->
<div class="button" onclick="submit()">Submit</div>

<!-- Good: native button -->
<button type="submit">Submit</button>

<!-- If a custom widget is truly necessary: -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0"
     onclick="submit()"
     onkeydown="if(event.key==='Enter'||event.key===' ')submit()">
    Submit
</div>

Note: The First Rule of ARIA — use native elements first.

docs.title: Grouping with Fieldset and Legend
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <legend>Preferred Contact Method</legend>

    <label>
        <input type="radio" name="contact" value="email" checked>
        Email
    </label>

    <label>
        <input type="radio" name="contact" value="phone">
        Phone
    </label>

    <label>
        <input type="radio" name="contact" value="mail">
        Mail
    </label>
</fieldset>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element/Attribute Accessibility Purpose <label for="id"> Programmatic association with control. <fieldset> + <legend> Group label for related controls. aria-describedby Associates a description or error. aria-invalid Indicates the control has an error. role="alert" Announced immediately when populated. aria-required Announces the field is required. required Native + announced by screen readers. autocomplete Improves form filling. inputmode Correct mobile keyboard. tabindex Controls focus order (use 0 or -1).

docs.title: The "Assistive Technology User" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine using a website without seeing the screen. You hear only what the screen reader announces. You navigate with the Tab key. You activate controls with Enter or Space. Every control must announce its purpose, state, and any errors. A form that relies on visual layout fails you completely.

docs.title: The "Voice Control" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine using your voice to fill a form. You say "click the Email field." If the field has no accessible name, the voice software doesn't know which field you mean. An accessible form gives every field a clear, spoken name.

docs.title: The "Cognitive Load" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a form with unclear labels, cryptic errors, and no instructions. Even without a disability, you'd struggle. Accessibility benefits everyone — clearer labels, clearer errors, and logical structure help all users.

docs.title: The "Concentric Circles" Mental Model
docs.text:
Accessibility happens in concentric circles:

  1. Semantic HTML – the innermost, most important.
  2. ARIA – only when native semantics are insufficient.
  3. Keyboard support – always required.
  4. Visual design – contrast, focus, size.
  5. Testing – with real assistive technologies.

Each circle catches what the previous misses.

docs.title: The "First Rule of ARIA" Mental Model
docs.text:
If you can use a native HTML element with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible, then do so.

For forms, this means:

  • <button> — not <div role="button">.
  • <input> — not <div contenteditable>.
  • <select> — not a custom dropdown.
  • <label> — not <span> with aria-label.

docs.title: Concept 1: Accessible Names
docs.text:
Every form control must have an accessible name — the text that assistive technologies announce. The name comes from (in order of priority):

  1. aria-labelledby
  2. aria-label
  3. <label> (associated via for or wrapping)
  4. placeholder (fallback — not recommended)
  5. title (fallback — not recommended)

Best practice: Always use <label>.

docs.title: Concept 2: Programmatic Label Association
docs.text:
The <label> must be programmatically associated with the control:

  • Explicit: <label for="email">Email:</label><input id="email">
  • Implicit: <label>Email: <input></label>

Visual proximity is not enough — the association must be in the DOM.

docs.title: Concept 3: Grouping with Fieldset and Legend
docs.text:
Radio buttons and checkboxes should be grouped with <fieldset> and <legend>:

<fieldset>
    <legend>Gender</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="male"> Male</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="female"> Female</label>
</fieldset>

Why: Screen readers announce "Gender, group" when entering the group, giving context.

docs.title: Concept 4: Keyboard Accessibility
docs.text:
All form controls must be keyboard-operable:

  • Tab – move to the next control.
  • Shift+Tab – move to the previous control.
  • Enter – activate buttons and links; submit forms.
  • Space – toggle checkboxes, activate buttons.
  • Arrow keys – navigate radio buttons, selects, sliders.
  • Escape – close dropdowns, dialogs.

Native controls support these automatically. Custom widgets must implement them.

docs.title: Concept 5: Focus Management
docs.text:
• Focus indicator – must be visible (don't remove outlines).
  • Logical tab order – follow the visual order.
  • Focus on errors – move focus to the first invalid field.
  • Focus trapping – in modals and dialogs.
  • Focus restoration – return focus after closing dialogs.

docs.title: Concept 6: Error Identification and Announcement
docs.text:
Errors must be:

  • Identified – which field is invalid (aria-invalid="true").
  • Described – why it's invalid (aria-describedby).
  • Announced – immediately (role="alert").
  • Actionable – tell the user how to fix it.
<input type="email" id="email" aria-describedby="email-error" aria-invalid="true">
<span id="email-error" role="alert">Please enter a valid email address.</span>

docs.title: Concept 7: Required Field Indication
docs.text:
• Native: required attribute.
  • ARIA: aria-required="true" (redundant but sometimes helpful).
  • Visual: Asterisk (*) or "(required)".
  • Accessible: The asterisk should be aria-hidden="true" if the required attribute is present, to avoid double announcement.
<label for="email">Email <span aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
<input type="email" id="email" required>

docs.title: Concept 8: ARIA Roles for Forms
docs.text: Role Purpose form Form landmark (with accessible name). search Search landmark. group Group of controls (fieldset equivalent). radiogroup Radio button group. listbox Custom select. combobox Autocomplete/custom dropdown. alert Error message. status Status message (polite). alertdialog Alert dialog.

docs.title: Concept 9: ARIA Properties for Forms
docs.text: Property Purpose aria-label Accessible name (no visible label). aria-labelledby References another element for the name. aria-describedby References a description. aria-required Indicates required. aria-invalid Indicates invalid. aria-disabled Indicates disabled. aria-readonly Indicates read-only. aria-errormessage References the error message (newer). aria-autocomplete Autocomplete behaviour for custom comboboxes. aria-expanded For expandable elements. aria-controls References the controlled element. aria-activedescendant For composite widgets.

docs.title: Concept 10: ARIA States for Forms
docs.text: State Purpose aria-checked Checkbox/radio state. aria-selected Option selected in a listbox. aria-pressed Toggle button state. aria-expanded Expanded/collapsed state. aria-disabled Disabled state. aria-busy Loading state.

docs.title: Concept 11: Instructions and Help Text
docs.text:
Instructions should be:

  • Before the form (general instructions).
  • Before the field (field-specific).
  • Associated with the field via aria-describedby.
<label for="password">Password:</label>
<input type="password" id="password" aria-describedby="password-help" required>
<p id="password-help">Must be at least 8 characters with a number and a symbol.</p>

docs.title: Concept 12: Autocomplete for Accessibility
docs.text:
The autocomplete attribute helps users with:

  • Motor impairments – less typing.
  • Cognitive impairments – less to remember.
  • Vision impairments – less reliance on typing.

docs.title: Concept 13: Touch Target Size
docs.text:
WCAG 2.5.5 (AAA) and WCAG 2.5.8 (AA, 2.2) require touch targets of at least 24×24 CSS pixels (AA) or 44×44 CSS pixels (AAA).

input, select, textarea, button {
    min-height: 44px;
    min-width: 44px;
    padding: 0.5rem;
}

docs.title: Concept 14: Color Contrast
docs.text:
Text and controls must have sufficient contrast:

  • Normal text: 4.5:1 (AA), 7:1 (AAA).
  • Large text: 3:1 (AA), 4.5:1 (AAA).
  • UI components: 3:1 (AA).

Don't rely on color alone to convey errors — use text and icons too.

docs.title: Concept 15: Focus Visible
docs.text:
WCAG 2.4.7 requires a visible focus indicator. Don't remove outlines:

/* Bad */
button:focus { outline: none; }

/* Good */
button:focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid #2c3e50;
    outline-offset: 2px;
}

docs.title: Concept 16: Responsive Design
docs.text: Forms must be usable at 320px width (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow). Avoid horizontal scrolling.

docs.title: Concept 17: Screen Reader Modes
docs.text:
Screen readers have two modes:

  • Browse mode – navigate by headings, landmarks, and text.
  • Forms mode – interact with form controls.

The user switches to forms mode when focusing on a control. Accessible markup ensures the switch works correctly.

docs.title: Concept 18: Voice Control
docs.text: Voice control software uses the accessible name to target controls. Users say "click Email field" — the name must match.

docs.title: Concept 19: Screen Magnifiers
docs.text: Users with screen magnifiers see only a portion of the screen. Focus management and logical structure are critical.

docs.title: Concept 20: Cognitive Accessibility
docs.text:
• Clear labels – short, descriptive.
  • Clear errors – specific, actionable.
  • Instructions – before the field.
  • Consistent layout – predictable patterns.
  • Avoid time limits – or allow extension.
  • Avoid memory requirements – use autocomplete.

docs.title: Concept 21: Accessible Custom Widgets
docs.text:
When native controls can't be used (rare), custom widgets must implement:

  • Role – role="combobox", role="listbox", etc.
  • States – aria-expanded, aria-selected, etc.
  • Properties – aria-controls, aria-activedescendant.
  • Keyboard – all interactions.
  • Focus – managed correctly.
  • Names – accessible labels.

Follow the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG).

docs.title: Concept 22: Accessible Form Validation
docs.text:
• Client-side – native HTML validation + ARIA.
  • Server-side – required for security.
  • Error summary – at the top of the form.
  • Inline errors – next to each field.
  • Focus – move to the first error.
  • Announcement – role="alert" or aria-live.

docs.title: Concept 23: Accessible Form Submission Feedback
docs.text:
• Loading state – aria-busy="true".
  • Success message – role="status".
  • Error message – role="alert".
  • Focus management – move to the message if needed.

docs.title: Concept 24: Accessible Reset/Cancel
docs.text:
• Reset button – should not be the default (avoid accidental data loss).
  • Confirmation – if destructive.
  • Keyboard accessible – native buttons.

docs.title: Concept 25: WCAG Success Criteria for Forms
docs.text: Criterion Requirement 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) Programmatic labels and groups 1.3.5 (Identify Input Purpose) autocomplete for known fields 1.4.3 (Contrast) Sufficient contrast 1.4.10 (Reflow) Usable at 320px 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast) UI components 3:1 1.4.12 (Text Spacing) Adjustable spacing 1.4.13 (Content on Hover/Focus) Dismissable, hoverable, persistent 2.1.1 (Keyboard) All functionality keyboard-accessible 2.4.3 (Focus Order) Logical focus order 2.4.6 (Headings and Labels) Descriptive 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) Visible focus indicator 2.5.5 (Target Size, AAA) 44×44 px 2.5.8 (Target Size, AA, 2.2) 24×24 px 3.3.1 (Error Identification) Errors identified 3.3.2 (Labels or Instructions) Labels/instructions provided 3.3.3 (Error Suggestion) Suggestions provided 3.3.4 (Error Prevention) Confirmations for important actions 3.3.7 (Redundant Entry, 2.2) Don't ask for the same data twice 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication, 2.2) No cognitive tests

docs.title: Concept 26: Accessible Authentication (WCAG 3.3.8)
docs.text:
Do not require users to:

  • Solve puzzles (CAPTCHA).
  • Remember passwords.
  • Perform cognitive tests.

Allow:

  • Password managers (autocomplete="current-password").
  • Paste.
  • WebAuthn.
  • Email/SMS codes.

docs.title: Concept 27: Redundant Entry (WCAG 3.3.7)
docs.text:
Don't ask for the same information twice:

  • Pre-fill known data.
  • Auto-populate from earlier steps.
  • Provide "same as shipping" checkbox.

docs.title: Concept 28: Accessible Authentication
docs.text:
• Allow paste in password fields.
  • Support password managers.
  • Provide alternative authentication.
  • Avoid CAPTCHA when possible.

docs.title: Concept 29: Accessible Form Errors
docs.text:
• Identify the field (aria-invalid="true").
  • Describe the error (aria-describedby).
  • Announce the error (role="alert").
  • Focus the first error.
  • Suggest a fix.
  • Persist until fixed.

docs.title: Concept 30: Testing with Assistive Technologies
docs.text:
Automated tools catch ~30% of issues. Manual testing with:

  • Screen readers – NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack.
  • Keyboard only – Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrows.
  • Voice control – Dragon, Voice Access.
  • Screen magnifiers – ZoomText, Windows Magnifier.
  • High contrast mode – Windows High Contrast.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Screen Reader User Filling a Form
docs.text:
1.  User navigates to the page.
    │
    ▼
2.  Screen reader announces the page structure (headings, landmarks).
    │
    ▼
3.  User navigates to the form landmark.
    │
    ▼
4.  Screen reader announces: "Contact form, form."
    │
    ▼
5.  User tabs into the first field.
    │
    ▼
6.  Screen reader announces: "Name, edit text, required."
    │
    ▼
7.  User types their name.
    │
    ▼
8.  User tabs to the next field.
    │
    ▼
9.  Screen reader announces: "Email, edit text, required."
    │
    ▼
10. User enters an invalid email.
    │
    ▼
11. User submits the form.
    │
    ▼
12. Screen reader announces: "Email, invalid entry. Please enter a valid email address."
    │
    ▼
13. Focus moves to the email field.
    │
    ▼
14. User corrects the email.
    │
    ▼
15. User resubmits and succeeds.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, a form is exposed as:

form "Contact form"
├── group "Your Information"
│   ├── textbox "Name" (required)
│   └── textbox "Email" (required)
├── group "Your Message"
│   ├── combobox "Subject" (required)
│   └── textbox "Message" (multiline, required)
└── button "Send Message"

Screen readers traverse this tree, announcing each node's role, name, state, and properties.

docs.title: Keyboard Interaction Flow
docs.text:
Tab → Name field → Tab → Email field → Tab → Subject select →
Tab → Message textarea → Tab → Send button → Enter → Submit

Each native control is focusable and operable.

docs.title: Error Announcement Flow
docs.text:
Submit → Validation fails → aria-invalid="true" set →
Error text inserted into role="alert" span →
Screen reader announces immediately →
Focus moves to invalid field →
User corrects → aria-invalid="false" → Error cleared

docs.title: Focus Management
docs.text:
form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    const invalid = form.querySelector(':invalid');
    if (invalid) {
        e.preventDefault();
        invalid.focus();
        invalid.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'center' });
    }
});

docs.title: ARIA Live Regions
docs.text:
• role="alert" – assertive; announced immediately.
  • role="status" – polite; announced when the user is idle.
  • aria-live="assertive" – same as role="alert".
  • aria-live="polite" – same as role="status".

docs.title: The aria-busy State
docs.text:
When a form is submitting, set aria-busy="true" to tell screen readers to wait:

<form aria-busy="true">...</form>

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree for Forms
docs.text:
The browser builds the accessibility tree from the DOM. Form controls are exposed with:

  • Role – textbox, checkbox, radio, combobox, button, etc.
  • Name – from <label>, aria-label, aria-labelledby.
  • Description – from aria-describedby, title.
  • State – required, invalid, disabled, checked, etc.
  • Value – the current value.

docs.title: Accessible Name Computation
docs.text:
The algorithm (simplified):

  1. If aria-labelledby is set, concatenate the referenced elements' text.
  2. Else if aria-label is set, use it.
  3. Else if the element is a <label>-associated control, use the label text.
  4. Else if the element has a title, use it.
  5. Else if the element has a placeholder, use it (fallback).
  6. Else, no accessible name (a failure).

docs.title: Role Mapping
docs.text: Element Role <input type="text"> textbox <input type="email"> textbox <input type="password"> textbox <input type="search"> searchbox <input type="number"> spinbutton <input type="range"> slider <input type="checkbox"> checkbox <input type="radio"> radio <input type="file"> button <input type="submit"> button <input type="color"> textbox (with colour semantics) <input type="date"> textbox (with date semantics) <select> (single) combobox <select multiple> listbox <textarea> textbox (multiline) <button> button <fieldset> group <legend> (name of the group) <output> status <progress> progressbar <meter> meter

docs.title: State Mapping
docs.text:
• required → aria-required="true" in the tree.
  • disabled → aria-disabled="true".
  • readonly → aria-readonly="true".
  • checked → aria-checked="true".
  • :invalid → aria-invalid="true".
  • :focus → focused state.

docs.title: The aria-errormessage Property
docs.text:
Newer than aria-describedby, aria-errormessage references an error message that is only announced when the field is invalid:

<input type="email" id="email" aria-errormessage="email-error" aria-invalid="true">
<span id="email-error">Please enter a valid email.</span>

Note: Support varies; aria-describedby is more widely supported.

docs.title: Accessibility API Integration
docs.text:
Browsers expose the accessibility tree to:

  • Windows: Microsoft UI Automation (UIA), IAccessible2.
  • macOS: NSAccessibility.
  • Linux: ATK/AT-SPI.
  • Android: AccessibilityNodeInfo.
  • iOS: UIAccessibility.

Screen readers consume these APIs.

docs.title: The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)
docs.text:
The APG provides patterns for accessible widgets:

  • Combobox – custom autocomplete.
  • Listbox – custom select.
  • Radio group – custom radio.
  • Slider – custom range.
  • Dialog – modal.
  • Disclosure – expand/collapse.

Note: Always prefer native HTML over custom ARIA widgets.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an Accessible Form
docs.text:
1.  Author writes semantic HTML with labels, fieldsets, and ARIA.
    │
    ▼
2.  File deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses HTML and builds the DOM.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser builds the accessibility tree.
    │   ├── Roles, names, states, properties.
    │   └── Label associations.
    │
    ▼
5.  User navigates with screen reader or keyboard.
    │
    ▼
6.  Screen reader announces each control's role, name, state.
    │
    ▼
7.  User fills the form.
    │
    ▼
8.  User submits.
    │
    ▼
9.  Validation runs:
    │   ├── If invalid → aria-invalid set, error announced, focus moved.
    │   └── If valid → submit.
    │
    ▼
10. Feedback announced (success or error).
    │
    ▼
11. User corrects and resubmits (if needed).

docs.title: Continuous Accessibility
docs.text:
Accessibility is not a one-time task. As content changes:

  • Re-test with screen readers.
  • Update labels and errors.
  • Ensure new fields follow the same patterns.
  • Validate with automated tools.

docs.title: Example 1: Accessible Login Form
docs.text:
<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <h1>Log In</h1>

    <label for="username">Username:</label>
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" required
           autocomplete="username" aria-required="true">

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" required
           autocomplete="current-password" aria-required="true">

    <button type="submit">Log In</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 2: Accessible Signup Form
docs.text:
<form action="/signup" method="POST">
    <h1>Sign Up</h1>

    <fieldset>
        <legend>Account Information</legend>

        <label for="username">Username:</label>
        <input type="text" id="username" name="username" required
               minlength="3" autocomplete="username">

        <label for="email">Email:</label>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required
               autocomplete="email">

        <label for="password">Password:</label>
        <input type="password" id="password" name="password" required
               minlength="8" autocomplete="new-password"
               aria-describedby="password-help">
        <p id="password-help">At least 8 characters.</p>
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 3: Accessible Radio Group
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <legend>Preferred Contact Method</legend>

    <label>
        <input type="radio" name="contact" value="email" checked>
        Email
    </label>

    <label>
        <input type="radio" name="contact" value="phone">
        Phone
    </label>

    <label>
        <input type="radio" name="contact" value="mail">
        Mail
    </label>
</fieldset>

docs.title: Example 4: Accessible Checkbox Group
docs.text:
<fieldset>
    <legend>Interests</legend>

    <label>
        <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="tech" checked>
        Technology
    </label>

    <label>
        <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="sports">
        Sports
    </label>

    <label>
        <input type="checkbox" name="interests" value="music">
        Music
    </label>
</fieldset>

docs.title: Example 5: Accessible Error Handling
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST" novalidate>
    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required
           aria-describedby="email-error" aria-invalid="false">
    <span id="email-error" role="alert"></span>

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<script>
    const form = document.getElementById('myForm');
    const email = document.getElementById('email');
    const error = document.getElementById('email-error');

    form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
        if (!email.validity.valid) {
            e.preventDefault();
            email.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
            if (email.validity.valueMissing) {
                error.textContent = 'Email is required.';
            } else if (email.validity.typeMismatch) {
                error.textContent = 'Please enter a valid email address (e.g., you@example.com).';
            }
            email.focus();
        }
    });

    email.addEventListener('input', () => {
        if (email.validity.valid) {
            email.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'false');
            error.textContent = '';
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 6: Accessible Error Summary
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST" novalidate>
    <div id="error-summary" role="alert" aria-live="assertive" hidden>
        <h2>Please fix the following errors:</h2>
        <ul id="error-list"></ul>
    </div>

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" required minlength="8">

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<script>
    document.getElementById('myForm').addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
        const invalid = e.target.querySelectorAll(':invalid');
        if (invalid.length > 0) {
            e.preventDefault();
            const summary = document.getElementById('error-summary');
            const list = document.getElementById('error-list');
            list.innerHTML = '';
            invalid.forEach(control => {
                const li = document.createElement('li');
                const a = document.createElement('a');
                a.href = `#${control.id}`;
                a.textContent = `${control.previousElementSibling.textContent} ${control.validationMessage}`;
                li.appendChild(a);
                list.appendChild(li);
            });
            summary.hidden = false;
            invalid[0].focus();
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 7: Accessible Required Field
docs.text:
<label for="email">
    Email
    <span aria-hidden="true">*</span>
</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required aria-required="true">

Note: The required attribute already announces "required"; the asterisk is for sighted users.

docs.title: Example 8: Accessible Help Text
docs.text:
<label for="password">Password:</label>
<input type="password" id="password" name="password"
       aria-describedby="password-help" required>
<p id="password-help">Must be at least 8 characters with a number and a symbol.</p>

docs.title: Example 9: Accessible Autocomplete
docs.text:
<form action="/checkout" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" autocomplete="name" required>

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required>

    <label for="address">Address:</label>
    <input type="text" id="address" name="address" autocomplete="street-address" required>

    <label for="cc-number">Card Number:</label>
    <input type="text" id="cc-number" name="cc-number"
           autocomplete="cc-number" inputmode="numeric" required>

    <button type="submit">Place Order</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 10: Accessible Search Form
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="GET" role="search">
    <label for="q">Search:</label>
    <input type="search" id="q" name="q" autocomplete="off">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 11: Accessible File Upload
docs.text:
<form action="/upload" method="POST" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    <label for="file">Choose a file:</label>
    <input type="file" id="file" name="file" accept="image/*"
           aria-describedby="file-help">
    <p id="file-help">Accepted formats: JPG, PNG. Maximum size: 5 MB.</p>
    <button type="submit">Upload</button>
</form>

docs.title: Example 12: Accessible Date Picker
docs.text:
<label for="birthday">Birthday:</label>
<input type="date" id="birthday" name="birthday"
       aria-describedby="birthday-help">
<p id="birthday-help">Format: YYYY-MM-DD.</p>

docs.title: Example 13: Accessible Conditional Fields
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label>
        <input type="radio" name="hasCompany" value="no" checked>
        I don't have a company
    </label>
    <label>
        <input type="radio" name="hasCompany" value="yes">
        I have a company
    </label>

    <fieldset id="companyFieldset" disabled aria-disabled="true">
        <legend>Company Details</legend>
        <label for="companyName">Company Name:</label>
        <input type="text" id="companyName" name="companyName">
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<script>
    const radios = document.querySelectorAll('input[name="hasCompany"]');
    const fieldset = document.getElementById('companyFieldset');
    radios.forEach(radio => {
        radio.addEventListener('change', () => {
            const disabled = radio.value === 'no';
            fieldset.disabled = disabled;
            fieldset.setAttribute('aria-disabled', disabled);
        });
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 14: Accessible Multi-Step Form
docs.text:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
    <fieldset id="step1">
        <legend>Step 1: Personal Information</legend>
        <label for="name">Name:</label>
        <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
        <button type="button" onclick="nextStep(2)">Next</button>
    </fieldset>

    <fieldset id="step2" disabled>
        <legend>Step 2: Contact</legend>
        <label for="email">Email:</label>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
        <button type="button" onclick="nextStep(1)">Back</button>
        <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    </fieldset>
</form>

<script>
    function nextStep(step) {
        document.querySelectorAll('fieldset').forEach(fs => fs.disabled = true);
        const fieldset = document.getElementById('step' + step);
        fieldset.disabled = false;
        fieldset.querySelector('input').focus();
    }
</script>

docs.title: Example 15: Accessible Loading State
docs.text:
<form id="myForm" action="/submit" method="POST">
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
    <button type="submit" id="submitBtn">
        <span class="label">Submit</span>
        <span class="spinner" hidden aria-hidden="true">⏳</span>
    </button>
</form>

<div id="status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></div>

<script>
    document.getElementById('myForm').addEventListener('submit', async (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        const btn = document.getElementById('submitBtn');
        const status = document.getElementById('status');
        btn.disabled = true;
        btn.setAttribute('aria-busy', 'true');
        btn.querySelector('.label').textContent = 'Submitting...';
        status.textContent = 'Submitting form...';
        try {
            await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1500));
            status.textContent = 'Form submitted successfully.';
        } catch (error) {
            status.textContent = 'Submission failed. Please try again.';
        } finally {
            btn.disabled = false;
            btn.removeAttribute('aria-busy');
            btn.querySelector('.label').textContent = 'Submit';
        }
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 16: Accessible Password with Visibility Toggle
docs.text:
<label for="password">Password:</label>
<input type="password" id="password" name="password" required>
<button type="button" id="togglePassword" aria-label="Show password" aria-pressed="false">
    Show
</button>

<script>
    const toggle = document.getElementById('togglePassword');
    const password = document.getElementById('password');
    toggle.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const isPassword = password.type === 'password';
        password.type = isPassword ? 'text' : 'password';
        toggle.setAttribute('aria-pressed', isPassword);
        toggle.setAttribute('aria-label', isPassword ? 'Hide password' : 'Show password');
        toggle.textContent = isPassword ? 'Hide' : 'Show';
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 17: Accessible Custom Checkbox
docs.text:
<!-- Preferred: native checkbox -->
<label>
    <input type="checkbox" name="terms" required>
    I agree to the terms
</label>

<!-- If custom styling is absolutely necessary: -->
<div role="checkbox" aria-checked="false" tabindex="0" id="customCheckbox">
    I agree to the terms
</div>

<script>
    const checkbox = document.getElementById('customCheckbox');
    checkbox.addEventListener('click', toggle);
    checkbox.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
        if (e.key === ' ' || e.key === 'Enter') {
            e.preventDefault();
            toggle();
        }
    });
    function toggle() {
        const checked = checkbox.getAttribute('aria-checked') === 'true';
        checkbox.setAttribute('aria-checked', !checked);
    }
</script>

Note: The First Rule of ARIA — prefer native <input type="checkbox">.

docs.title: Example 18: Accessible Autocomplete Combobox
docs.text:
<label for="country">Country:</label>
<input type="text" id="country" name="country"
       role="combobox"
       aria-expanded="false"
       aria-controls="country-list"
       aria-autocomplete="list"
       autocomplete="country-name">
<ul id="country-list" role="listbox" hidden>
    <li role="option" id="country-us">United States</li>
    <li role="option" id="country-ca">Canada</li>
    <li role="option" id="country-uk">United Kingdom</li>
</ul>

Note: Native <select> or <datalist> is preferred. This pattern requires full keyboard support per the APG.

docs.title: Example 19: Accessible Confirmation Dialog
docs.text:
<button type="button" id="deleteBtn">Delete Item</button>

<dialog id="confirmDialog" aria-labelledby="dialogTitle">
    <h2 id="dialogTitle">Confirm Deletion</h2>
    <p>Are you sure you want to delete this item? This action cannot be undone.</p>
    <form method="dialog">
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<script>
    document.getElementById('deleteBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        document.getElementById('confirmDialog').showModal();
    });
</script>

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Accessible Form
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Accessible Form</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 600px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        form { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 1rem; }
        fieldset { border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 8px; padding: 1rem; }
        legend { font-weight: bold; color: #2c3e50; }
        label { font-weight: 500; display: block; margin-top: 0.5rem; }
        input, select, textarea {
            padding: 0.5rem; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 1rem; width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box; min-height: 44px;
        }
        input:focus, select:focus, textarea:focus {
            outline: 2px solid #3498db; outline-offset: 2px;
        }
        input[aria-invalid="true"] { border-color: #e74c3c; }
        .error { color: #e74c3c; font-size: 0.875rem; }
        .help { color: #6c757d; font-size: 0.875rem; }
        .required { color: #e74c3c; }
        button {
            padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem; background: #3498db; color: white;
            border: none; border-radius: 4px; font-size: 1rem; cursor: pointer;
            min-height: 44px;
        }
        button:hover { background: #2980b9; }
        button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #2c3e50; outline-offset: 2px; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Contact Us</h1>
    <p>Fields marked with <span class="required" aria-hidden="true">*</span> are required.</p>

    <form action="/contact" method="POST" novalidate>
        <fieldset>
            <legend>Your Information</legend>

            <label for="name">Name <span class="required" aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
            <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required autocomplete="name"
                   aria-required="true" aria-describedby="name-error">
            <span id="name-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>

            <label for="email">Email <span class="required" aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
            <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required autocomplete="email"
                   aria-required="true" aria-describedby="email-error">
            <span id="email-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>

            <label for="phone">Phone</label>
            <input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" autocomplete="tel"
                   aria-describedby="phone-help">
            <p id="phone-help" class="help">Format: (555) 123-4567</p>
        </fieldset>

        <fieldset>
            <legend>Your Message</legend>

            <label for="subject">Subject <span class="required" aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
            <select id="subject" name="subject" required aria-required="true"
                    aria-describedby="subject-error">
                <option value="">Choose a subject...</option>
                <option value="general">General Inquiry</option>
                <option value="support">Support</option>
                <option value="feedback">Feedback</option>
            </select>
            <span id="subject-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>

            <label for="message">Message <span class="required" aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
            <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5" required
                      aria-required="true" aria-describedby="message-error"></textarea>
            <span id="message-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>
        </fieldset>

        <button type="submit">Send Message</button>
    </form>

    <script>
        const form = document.querySelector('form');
        const fields = ['name', 'email', 'subject', 'message'];

        form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
            e.preventDefault();
            let firstInvalid = null;

            fields.forEach(id => {
                const field = document.getElementById(id);
                const error = document.getElementById(id + '-error');
                if (!field.validity.valid) {
                    field.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
                    error.textContent = field.validationMessage;
                    if (!firstInvalid) firstInvalid = field;
                } else {
                    field.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'false');
                    error.textContent = '';
                }
            });

            if (firstInvalid) {
                firstInvalid.focus();
            } else {
                form.submit();
            }
        });

        fields.forEach(id => {
            const field = document.getElementById(id);
            field.addEventListener('input', () => {
                const error = document.getElementById(id + '-error');
                if (field.validity.valid) {
                    field.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'false');
                    error.textContent = '';
                }
            });
        });
    </script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Accessibility Focus Login Labels, autocomplete, password manager support Signup Password requirements, error announcements Contact form Labels, fieldset, error handling Checkout Address, payment autofill, error summary Survey Radio/checkbox groups, fieldset Search Label, role="search" Settings Grouped fieldsets, toggles File upload Label, help text, accept Multi-step Focus management, fieldset per step Feedback Rating (radio), textarea Booking Date pickers, error handling Job application File upload, text fields, error handling Donation Payment fields, autocomplete Newsletter Email, autocomplete, error handling

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use <label> – associate via for/id or wrapping.
  2. Use <fieldset> and <legend> for groups – radio and checkbox groups.
  3. Use aria-describedby for help text and errors.
  4. Use aria-invalid="true" on invalid fields.
  5. Use role="alert" for error messages.
  6. Use role="status" for success messages.
  7. Move focus to the first invalid field.
  8. Don't remove focus outlines – use :focus-visible.
  9. Ensure touch targets are ≥ 44×44 px.
  10. Use autocomplete – for faster filling.
  11. Use inputmode – for correct mobile keyboards.
  12. Indicate required fields – visually and programmatically.
  13. Provide error suggestions – tell the user how to fix it.
  14. Use aria-busy="true" – during submission.
  15. Use aria-live – for dynamic updates.
  16. Use role="search" – for search forms.
  17. Test with screen readers – NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack.
  18. Test with keyboard only – Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space.
  19. Test with high contrast mode – Windows High Contrast.
  20. Test with zoom – at 200% and 320px width.
  21. Use semantic HTML first – avoid ARIA unless necessary.
  22. Follow the ARIA Authoring Practices – for custom widgets.
  23. Validate with automated tools – Lighthouse, axe, WAVE.
  24. Document your conventions – in a style guide.
  25. Re-test after changes – accessibility is ongoing.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No <label>
docs.text:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

Why it's wrong: No accessible name; placeholder disappears.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placeholder as Label
docs.text:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

Why it's wrong: Placeholder disappears on input; low contrast.

✅ Correct: Always use <label>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Fieldset for Radio Groups
docs.text:
<p>Gender:</p>
<input type="radio" name="gender" value="male"> Male
<input type="radio" name="gender" value="female"> Female

Why it's wrong: No programmatic group label.

✅ Correct: 

<fieldset>
    <legend>Gender</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="male"> Male</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="female"> Female</label>
</fieldset>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Error Announcement
docs.text:
<input type="email" required>
<span>Invalid email</span>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers don't announce the error.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="email" required aria-describedby="email-error" aria-invalid="true">
<span id="email-error" role="alert">Invalid email</span>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Removing Focus Outline
docs.text:
input:focus { outline: none; }

Why it's wrong: Keyboard users can't see focus.

✅ Correct: 

input:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #3498db; }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div> as Button
docs.text:
<div class="btn" onclick="submit()">Submit</div>

Why it's wrong: Not keyboard-accessible, no button role.

✅ Correct: 

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Color-Only Error Indication
docs.text:
input:invalid { border-color: red; }

Why it's wrong: Color-blind users can't distinguish.

✅ Correct: Also provide text and icons.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Error Suggestion
docs.text:
<span role="alert">Error</span>

Why it's wrong: User doesn't know how to fix it.

✅ Correct: 

<span role="alert">Please enter a valid email address (e.g., you@example.com).</span>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Touch Targets Too Small
docs.text:
button { padding: 2px 4px; font-size: 10px; }

Why it's wrong: Hard to tap on mobile.

✅ Correct: Minimum 44×44 px.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No autocomplete on Login
docs.text:
<input type="password" name="password">

Why it's wrong: Password managers can't identify the field.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No inputmode on Numeric Fields
docs.text:
<input type="text" name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{5}">

Why it's wrong: Full keyboard on mobile.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="text" name="zip" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]{5}">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Required Indication
docs.text:
<input type="email" required>

Why it's wrong: Sighted users don't know it's required until error.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="email">Email <span aria-hidden="true">*</span></label>
<input type="email" id="email" required>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: aria-required Without required
docs.text:
<input type="email" aria-required="true">

Why it's wrong: aria-required alone doesn't trigger validation.

✅ Correct: 

<input type="email" required aria-required="true">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using aria-label Instead of <label>
docs.text:
<input type="email" aria-label="Email">

Why it's wrong: No visible label for sighted users.

✅ Correct: 

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No role="search" on Search Form
docs.text:
<form action="/search" method="GET">

Why it's wrong: Screen reader users can't jump to the search landmark.

✅ Correct: 

<form action="/search" method="GET" role="search">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Loading State Announced
docs.text:
<button disabled>Loading...</button>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers don't know why.

✅ Correct: 

<button aria-busy="true" aria-disabled="true">Loading...</button>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Native controls – fastest and most accessible.
  • ARIA – no rendering cost, but complex custom widgets may be slower.
  • Live regions – minimal performance impact.
  • Focus management – negligible.
  • Screen readers – performance is the browser's concern, not the page's.
  • Touch targets – larger targets may affect layout but not performance.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use native HTML – no JavaScript needed.
  2. Avoid unnecessary ARIA – keep it minimal.
  3. Use CSS for visual states – not JavaScript.
  4. Test on low-end devices – with screen readers.
  5. Minify HTML/CSS – reduce file size.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• CSRF tokens – hidden inputs, accessible and secure.
  • XSS – sanitize user input before displaying.
  • Accessible authentication – don't require cognitive tests (WCAG 3.3.8).
  • Password managers – support autocomplete for security.
  • HTTPS – mandatory for sensitive forms.
  • Autocomplete – can be a security risk on shared devices; allow off for sensitive fields.
  • No sensitive data in labels – labels are visible and announced.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use HTTPS – for all forms.
  2. Include CSRF tokens – in hidden inputs.
  3. Support password managers – via autocomplete.
  4. Allow paste – in password fields (WCAG 3.3.8).
  5. Avoid CAPTCHA – when possible; use alternative verification.
  6. Sanitize output – prevent XSS.
  7. Validate on the server – always.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the form structure.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the accessibility tree.
  • Computed styles – check contrast, focus, and size.
  • Console – use document.querySelectorAll(':invalid') to find errors.
  • Lighthouse – audits for accessibility.
  • axe DevTools – browser extension for testing.
  • WAVE – web accessibility evaluation tool.
  • NVDA – free Windows screen reader.
  • JAWS – commercial Windows screen reader.
  • VoiceOver – macOS/iOS screen reader.
  • TalkBack – Android screen reader.
  • Keyboard testing – Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space.
  • High contrast mode – Windows High Contrast.
  • Zoom – test at 200% and 320px width.
  • Validator – check for invalid ARIA attributes.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For every form – accessibility is mandatory.
  • For all form controls – labels, fieldsets, ARIA where needed.
  • For error handling – always announce errors.
  • For interactive widgets – follow the APG.
  • For login/signup – support password managers.
  • For checkout – support payment autofill.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Don't use ARIA when native HTML suffices – the First Rule of ARIA.
  • Don't use aria-label when a visible label is possible.
  • Don't use role="button" on <button> – redundant.
  • Don't remove focus outlines.
  • Don't rely on color alone.
  • Don't use custom widgets when native works.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• WCAG – Web Content Accessibility Guidelines.
  • ARIA – Accessible Rich Internet Applications.
  • ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG).
  • Screen readers – NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack.
  • Keyboard navigation – Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space.
  • Focus management – :focus, :focus-visible.
  • Accessible names – <label>, aria-label, aria-labelledby.
  • Descriptions – aria-describedby, aria-errormessage.
  • States – aria-invalid, aria-required, aria-disabled.
  • Live regions – role="alert", role="status", aria-live.
  • Fieldset and legend – grouping.
  • Autocomplete – form filling.
  • Inputmode – mobile keyboards.
  • Touch targets – WCAG 2.5.5, 2.5.8.
  • Color contrast – WCAG 1.4.3, 1.4.11.
  • Reflow – WCAG 1.4.10.
  • Accessible authentication – WCAG 3.3.8.
  • Redundant entry – WCAG 3.3.7.
  • Section 508, ADA, EN 301 549 – legal requirements.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Forms are the most critical area of web accessibility — an inaccessible form blocks the user entirely.

  • WCAG 2.0 (2008) introduced the requirement for programmatic labels and error identification.

  • WCAG 2.1 (2018) added touch target size (2.5.5) and reflow (1.4.10).

  • WCAG 2.2 (2023) added focus appearance (2.4.11), dragging movements (2.5.7), target size minimum (2.5.8), consistent help (3.2.6), redundant entry (3.3.7), and accessible authentication (3.3.8).

  • The First Rule of ARIA: use native HTML first.

  • <label> is the single most important element for form accessibility.

  • <fieldset> + <legend> is the standard for grouping radio and checkbox controls.

  • role="alert" causes immediate announcement by screen readers.

  • aria-invalid="true" tells screen readers the field has an error.

  • aria-describedby associates help text and errors with the field.

  • aria-errormessage is newer but not as widely supported as aria-describedby.

  • Focus must be visible — WCAG 2.4.7. Don't remove outlines.

  • Touch targets should be ≥ 44×44 px — WCAG 2.5.5 (AAA) and 2.5.8 (AA, 2.2).

  • WCAG 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication) — don't require cognitive tests like CAPTCHA or password memorization.

  • WCAG 3.3.7 (Redundant Entry) — don't ask for the same information twice in a multi-step process.

  • Screen readers have two modes: browse mode and forms mode. Accessible markup ensures proper switching.

  • Password managers rely on autocomplete for login and signup detection.

  • autocomplete="current-password" identifies a login password; new-password" identifies a new password.

  • role="search" creates a search landmark — WCAG 1.3.1.

  • The accessibility tree is what screen readers consume. Semantic HTML ensures accuracy.

  • Automated tools catch ~30% of accessibility issues — manual testing is essential.

  • Testing with real assistive technologies is the gold standard.

  • Accessibility benefits everyone — clearer labels, clearer errors, better structure.

  • Legal requirements exist in many jurisdictions: ADA, Section 508, EN 301 549, AODA, and more.

  • Best practices include always using labels, fieldsets, ARIA where needed, and testing with assistive technologies.

  • Common mistakes include no label, no fieldset, no error announcement, and removing focus outlines.

  • Following best practices for form accessibility leads to inclusive, usable, and legally compliant forms.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Form accessibility ensures that all users — including those with disabilities — can complete forms.
  • Every control must have an accessible name — use <label> with for/id or wrapping.
  • Radio and checkbox groups should use <fieldset> + <legend>.
  • Errors must be identified, described, announced, and actionable — use aria-invalid, aria-describedby, and role="alert".
  • Focus must move to the first invalid field on submission.
  • Focus indicators must be visible — don't remove outlines.
  • Touch targets should be ≥ 44×44 px.
  • Use autocomplete to help users fill forms faster.
  • Use inputmode for correct mobile keyboards.
  • Test with screen readers — NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack.
  • Test with keyboard only — Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space.
  • Test with high contrast and zoom — at 200% and 320px.
  • Use automated tools — Lighthouse, axe, WAVE — but don't rely on them alone.
  • Follow WCAG — 1.3.1, 1.4.3, 2.1.1, 2.4.7, 3.3.1, 3.3.2, 3.3.3, 3.3.7, 3.3.8.
  • Use semantic HTML first — the First Rule of ARIA.
  • Common mistakes include no labels, no fieldsets, no error announcements, and removing focus outlines.
  • Form accessibility is not optional — it's a legal requirement and an ethical obligation.
  • Accessible forms benefit everyone — clearer labels, clearer errors, better structure, and better UX.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <img> element is an HTML element that embeds an image into a web page. It is a void (empty) element — it has no closing tag and no content — and it references an external image file via the src attribute. The browser fetches the image and renders it inline at the point where the <img> element appears in the document flow.

Images are the most common non-text content on the web. They convey information, enhance design, illustrate concepts, and drive engagement. HTML provides a rich set of attributes to control how images are loaded, displayed, and described — including src, alt, width, height, srcset, sizes, loading, and decoding.

Example: 

<img src="sunset.jpg" alt="A golden sunset over the Pacific Ocean" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <img> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Visual content – photographs, illustrations, diagrams, charts.
  • Branding – logos, icons, favicons.
  • Navigation – image-based links, icons in menus.
  • Information – infographics, maps, charts.
  • Decoration – backgrounds, borders, separators.
  • Responsive media – multiple image sources for different devices.
  • Accessibility – alt text describes the image for screen readers.
  • Performance – lazy loading, responsive images, modern formats.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <img> element is phrasing content, embedded content, and palpable content. It is an inline element by default (though it behaves as an inline-block for sizing). It can appear anywhere phrasing content is accepted — inside <p>, <a>, <figure>, <picture>, <div>, <li>, <td>, and more.

<figure>
    <img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart showing sales growth from 2020 to 2026" width="600" height="400">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Sales growth over the past 6 years.</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before the <img> element, the web was text-only. Documents could not include visual content natively. To share images, users had to:

  • Download them separately via FTP.
  • Link to them (but they opened in a separate viewer).
  • Describe them in text (but text can't replace visual information).

This limited the web to textual communication, excluding photography, design, data visualization, and countless other forms of visual content.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No native image support Web was text-only External viewers required Poor UX No inline display Images couldn't be embedded in text No accessibility Blind users had no description No responsive images Same image for all devices No performance controls Large images loaded unconditionally

docs.title: Why the <img> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <img> element was introduced in HTML 2.0 (1995) — a pivotal moment in web history. It was proposed by Marc Andreessen of Netscape and initially met with resistance from purists who wanted HTML to remain purely structural. But the web community overwhelmingly embraced it, and images became one of the defining features of the web.

The <img> element enables:

  • Inline images – embedded directly in text flow.
  • Universal support – any browser can display images.
  • Accessibility – the alt attribute provides descriptions.
  • Interactivity – images can be links, buttons, or image maps.
  • Design – logos, backgrounds, and visual identity.
  • Data visualization – charts, graphs, and infographics.

The <img> element is one of the most important additions to HTML, and its impact on the web cannot be overstated.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <img>
docs.text:
<img src="URL" alt="Description">
  • src – the URL of the image (required).
  • alt – alternative text (required for accessibility).

docs.title: Simple Image
docs.text: <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view">

docs.title: Image with Dimensions
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view" width="800" height="600">

Why dimensions matter: Setting width and height prevents layout shift while the image loads (improves CLS — Cumulative Layout Shift).

docs.title: Image as a Link
docs.text:
<a href="/">
    <img src="logo.png" alt="Company Homepage">
</a>

docs.title: Image with Tooltip
docs.text: <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view" title="Taken in 2026">

docs.title: Responsive Image with srcset
docs.text:
<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w,
             photo-800.jpg 800w,
             photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A scenic mountain view">

docs.title: Image with Lazy Loading
docs.text: <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view" loading="lazy">

docs.title: Image with Async Decoding
docs.text: <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view" decoding="async">

docs.title: Image with fetchpriority
docs.text: <img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero image" fetchpriority="high">

docs.title: Decorative Image (Empty Alt)
docs.text:
<img src="divider.png" alt="">

Important: Empty alt (not missing alt) tells screen readers to skip the image.

docs.title: Image Inside <picture> (Art Direction)
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="hero-wide.jpg">
    <source media="(min-width: 400px)" srcset="hero-medium.jpg">
    <img src="hero-small.jpg" alt="Hero image">
</picture>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose src Image URL (required) alt Alternative text (required) width Width in pixels height Height in pixels srcset Responsive image candidates sizes Sizes for srcset loading lazy or eager decoding sync, async, or auto fetchpriority high, low, or auto crossorigin CORS setting referrerpolicy Referrer policy usemap Client-side image map ismap Server-side image map

docs.title: The "Picture Frame" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <img> as a picture frame on a wall. The src is the picture inside; the alt is a label describing it; the width and height are the frame's dimensions; the title is a plaque with additional details. Just as a frame can hang on any wall, an image can appear anywhere in the document.

docs.title: The "Window" Analogy
docs.text: An image is a window into another file. The browser looks through the window (the <img> element) and sees the image (the file at src). If the window is broken (image fails to load), the alt text tells you what was supposed to be there.

docs.title: The "Story with Captions" Analogy
docs.text: A document with images is like a story with illustrations. The text is the narrative; the images are the illustrations. The alt is the caption for readers who can't see the illustration. The <figure> and <figcaption> are the formal caption and numbering.

docs.title: The "Chameleon" Mental Model
docs.text:
A well-crafted image is a chameleon — it adapts to its context:

  • Different sizes – srcset provides multiple resolutions.
  • Different formats – <picture> provides modern formats with fallbacks.
  • Different devices – sizes adjusts the layout.
  • Different priorities – loading and fetchpriority control when it loads.

docs.title: The "Two Lives" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every image has two lives:
