  1. Visual life – what sighted users see.
  2. Accessible life – what screen readers announce.

The alt attribute is the bridge between them. A good image has both lives intact.

docs.title: Concept 1: The src Attribute
docs.text:
The src attribute specifies the URL of the image. It can be:

  • Absolute: https://example.com/image.jpg
  • Relative: images/photo.jpg
  • Data URL: data:image/png;base64,...
<img src="images/photo.jpg" alt="A photo">

Note: The src attribute is required for <img>.

docs.title: Concept 2: The alt Attribute
docs.text:
The alt attribute provides alternative text for the image. Its purpose depends on the image's role:

Image Type Alt Text Informative Describe the content and function Decorative Empty (alt="") Functional (link/button) Describe the action Complex (chart) Short description + longer description elsewhere Logo Company name Image of text The text itself

Important: alt is required — even if empty.

docs.title: Concept 3: Image Formats
docs.text:
Format Best For Transparency Animation JPEG Photographs No No PNG Graphics, transparency Yes No GIF Simple animations Yes Yes WebP Modern all-purpose Yes Yes AVIF Modern, best compression Yes Yes SVG Vector graphics Yes Yes

Best practice: Use modern formats (WebP, AVIF) with fallbacks.

docs.title: Concept 4: The width and height Attributes
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" width="800" height="600">

Why: Setting dimensions reserves space for the image, preventing layout shift (CLS). The browser maintains the aspect ratio if only one dimension is set via CSS.

docs.title: Concept 5: Responsive Images (srcset + sizes)
docs.text:
<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w,
             photo-800.jpg 800w,
             photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A photo">
  • srcset – provides multiple image sources with descriptors (400w).
  • sizes – tells the browser how much space the image occupies at each viewport.

The browser picks the best candidate based on viewport and pixel density.

docs.title: Concept 6: Art Direction with <picture>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="wide.jpg">
    <source media="(min-width: 400px)" srcset="medium.jpg">
    <img src="small.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Use case: Different images (crops, compositions) for different viewports.

docs.title: Concept 7: Modern Format Fallback
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

The browser picks the first supported format.

docs.title: Concept 8: Lazy Loading
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy">

Values:

  • lazy – load when near the viewport.
  • eager – load immediately (default).

Best practice: Use lazy for below-the-fold images; use eager for hero images.

docs.title: Concept 9: Decoding
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" decoding="async">

Values:

  • sync – decode synchronously (blocks rendering).
  • async – decode asynchronously (non-blocking).
  • auto – browser decides.

Best practice: Use async for non-critical images.

docs.title: Concept 10: Fetch Priority
docs.text:
<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high">

Values:

  • high – prioritise loading.
  • low – deprioritise.
  • auto – default.

Use case: high for LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) images.

docs.title: Concept 11: Image Maps
docs.text:
<img src="map.png" alt="Map" usemap="#map">
<map name="map">
    <area shape="rect" coords="0,0,100,100" href="/region1" alt="Region 1">
    <area shape="circle" coords="200,100,50" href="/region2" alt="Region 2">
</map>

Note: Image maps are rare in modern web development.

docs.title: Concept 12: CORS and crossorigin
docs.text:
<img src="https://cdn.example.com/photo.jpg" alt="Photo" crossorigin="anonymous">

Use case: When the image is used in a <canvas> and needs to be readable.

docs.title: Concept 13: The referrerpolicy Attribute
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" referrerpolicy="no-referrer">

Controls the Referer header for the image request.

docs.title: Concept 14: SVG Images
docs.text:
SVG can be embedded in three ways:

  1. As <img>: 
    <img src="icon.svg" alt="Icon">
  2. Inline SVG: 
    <svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>
  3. As CSS background: 
    .icon { background-image: url('icon.svg'); }

Inline SVG is best when you need to style it with CSS or animate it.

docs.title: Concept 15: Image Accessibility
docs.text:
• alt text – describes the image.
  • Decorative images – alt="".
  • Complex images – short alt + long description nearby.
  • Images of text – avoid; use real text.
  • Contrast – sufficient contrast for text on images.

docs.title: Concept 16: The figure and figcaption Elements
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart showing sales growth">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Sales growth over the past 6 years.</figcaption>
</figure>

Why: Groups the image with its caption semantically.

docs.title: Concept 17: Image Optimization
docs.text:
• Choose the right format – WebP/AVIF for photos.
  • Compress – use tools like ImageOptim, Squoosh.
  • Resize – don't serve 4000px images at 400px.
  • Use srcset – serve appropriate sizes.
  • Lazy load – below-the-fold images.
  • Use a CDN – for faster delivery.

docs.title: Concept 18: Placeholder and Blur-Up
docs.text:
<img src="placeholder.jpg"
     data-src="actual.jpg"
     alt="Photo"
     class="lazyload">

JavaScript swaps data-src into src when the image is near the viewport, often using a blurred placeholder.

docs.title: Concept 19: Background Images (CSS)
docs.text:
.hero {
    background-image: url('hero.jpg');
    background-size: cover;
    background-position: center;
}

Note: Background images are not announced by screen readers and cannot have alt text. Use <img> for meaningful content.

docs.title: Concept 20: Image Security
docs.text:
• Hotlinking – other sites linking to your images, consuming bandwidth.
  • Image injection – SVG can contain scripts; sanitize user uploads.
  • EXIF data – may contain GPS coordinates; strip before publishing.
  • Mixed content – HTTPS pages should only load HTTPS images.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing an Image
docs.text:
1.  The tokenizer encounters an `<img>` tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the image.
    │
    ▼
3.  It reads the `src` attribute and resolves it.
    │
    ▼
4.  It reads the `srcset` and `sizes` attributes (if present).
    │
    ▼
5.  It determines the best image source based on:
    │   ├── Viewport size
    │   ├── Device pixel ratio
    │   └── Network conditions
    │
    ▼
6.  It creates a placeholder box (using width/height if set).
    │
    ▼
7.  It fetches the image from the network.
    │
    ▼
8.  It decodes the image (sync or async).
    │
    ▼
9.  It paints the image in the placeholder box.
    │
    ▼
10. The `load` event fires on the image.

docs.title: Responsive Image Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Parse srcset to get candidate images and their widths (400w, 800w, etc.).
  2. Parse sizes to determine the display width at the current viewport.
  3. Multiply by the device pixel ratio to get the required pixel width.
  4. Choose the smallest candidate that is ≥ the required width.

Example: - Viewport: 800px, DPR: 2 - sizes: (max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw → 50vw = 400px - Required: 400 × 2 = 800px - Candidates: 400w, 800w, 1200w - Choice: 800w

docs.title: The load and error Events
docs.text:
img.addEventListener('load', () => console.log('Image loaded'));
img.addEventListener('error', () => console.log('Image failed to load'));

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
In the accessibility tree, <img> is exposed as:

  • role: img
  • name: the alt text
  • description: the title (if present)

Screen readers announce: "A golden sunset over the Pacific Ocean, image."

If alt="", the image is skipped — appropriate for decorative images.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
img {
    display: inline-block;
    overflow: clip;
    overflow-clip-margin: content-box;
}

docs.title: The naturalWidth and naturalHeight Properties
docs.text:
console.log(img.naturalWidth);  // Actual image width in pixels
console.log(img.naturalHeight); // Actual image height in pixels

docs.title: The complete Property
docs.text: console.log(img.complete); // true if loaded (or failed)

docs.title: The HTMLImageElement Interface
docs.text:
Property/Method Description src The image URL alt Alternative text srcset Responsive candidates sizes Sizes for srcset width Display width height Display height naturalWidth Intrinsic width naturalHeight Intrinsic height complete True if loaded or failed currentSrc The actual URL used loading Lazy or eager decoding Sync or async fetchPriority Fetch priority crossOrigin CORS setting isMap Server-side image map useMap Client-side image map decode() Promise that resolves when decoded referrerPolicy Referrer policy 
const img = document.querySelector('img');
console.log(img.src);           // Resolved URL
console.log(img.currentSrc);    // The source actually chosen
console.log(img.naturalWidth);  // e.g., 1920
console.log(img.complete);      // true or false

docs.title: Image Loading Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Fetch – the browser fetches the image bytes.
  2. Decode – the bytes are decoded into a bitmap.
  3. Paint – the bitmap is painted onto the screen.

Each step can be controlled:

  • Fetch: loading, fetchpriority, crossorigin.
  • Decode: decoding.
  • Paint: CSS object-fit, object-position.

docs.title: The decode() Method
docs.text:
await img.decode();
// Image is decoded and ready to paint

Use case: Pre-decode images before displaying them to avoid jank.

docs.title: The object-fit CSS Property
docs.text:
img {
    width: 300px;
    height: 200px;
    object-fit: cover;
}

Values:

  • fill (default) – stretch.
  • contain – fit inside.
  • cover – fill, cropping.
  • none – no scaling.
  • scale-down – smaller of none or contain.

docs.title: The object-position CSS Property
docs.text:
img {
    object-fit: cover;
    object-position: center top;
}

Positions the image within its box.

docs.title: The aspect-ratio CSS Property
docs.text:
img {
    aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
    width: 100%;
    height: auto;
}

Sets the aspect ratio without affecting the intrinsic size.

docs.title: Browser Caching
docs.text:
Images are cached based on:

  • Cache-Control headers.
  • ETag / Last-Modified.
  • Expires header.

Use long cache lifetimes for versioned image URLs.

docs.title: Image Decoding
docs.text:
• Synchronous – blocks the main thread; can cause jank.
  • Asynchronous – decodes off the main thread; smoother.
  • Progressive – displays a low-quality version first, then sharpens.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an Image
docs.text:
1.  Author writes `<img src="..." alt="...">`.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses HTML and creates the DOM node.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser reads `src`, `srcset`, `sizes`.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser creates a placeholder box (if width/height set).
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser fetches the image.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser decodes the image.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser paints the image.
    │
    ▼
8.  `load` event fires.
    │
    ▼
9.  Image is visible.
    │
    ▼
10. If image fails, `error` event fires.
    │
    ▼
11. When the page is unloaded, the image is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Image Loading
docs.text:
const img = new Image();
img.src = 'photo.jpg';
img.alt = 'A photo';
img.onload = () => document.body.appendChild(img);
img.onerror = () => console.error('Failed to load');

docs.title: Responsive Image Re-selection
docs.text: When the viewport changes, the browser may re-evaluate srcset and load a different image. This is automatic.

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Image
docs.text: <img src="sunset.jpg" alt="A golden sunset over the ocean" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Example 2: Image as Link

<a href="/">
    <img src="logo.png" alt="Company Homepage" width="200" height="60">
</a>

    <source media="(min-width: 400px)" srcset="hero-small.jpg">
    <img src="hero-fallback.jpg" alt="A panoramic mountain landscape" width="800" height="400">
</picture>

    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo" width="800" height="600">

<img src="thumbnail.jpg" alt="Video thumbnail" class="video-thumb">

    img {
        max-width: 100%;

    }
</style>

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Example 15: Lazy Loading with IntersectionObserver
docs.text:
<img data-src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo" class="lazy" width="800" height="600">
<noscript><img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo" width="800" height="600"></noscript>

<script>
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
        entries.forEach(entry => {
            if (entry.isIntersecting) {
                const img = entry.target;
                img.src = img.dataset.src;
                observer.unobserve(img);
            }
        });
    });
    document.querySelectorAll('.lazy').forEach(img => observer.observe(img));
</script>

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Image Gallery
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Image Gallery</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 1200px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(250px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; list-style: none; padding: 0; }
        figure { margin: 0; }
        figure img { width: 100%; height: 200px; object-fit: cover; border-radius: 8px; }
        figcaption { font-size: 0.875rem; color: #6c757d; margin-top: 0.5rem; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Image Gallery</h1>

    <ul class="gallery">
        <li>
            <figure>
                <img src="gallery-1-400.jpg"
                     srcset="gallery-1-400.jpg 400w, gallery-1-800.jpg 800w"
                     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 250px"
                     alt="A mountain landscape at sunrise"
                     loading="lazy"
                     width="400" height="300">
                <figcaption>Sunrise over the mountains.</figcaption>
            </figure>
        </li>
        <li>
            <figure>
                <img src="gallery-2-400.jpg"
                     srcset="gallery-2-400.jpg 400w, gallery-2-800.jpg 800w"
                     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 250px"
                     alt="A calm lake reflecting the sky"
                     loading="lazy"
                     width="400" height="300">
                <figcaption>A peaceful lake at dawn.</figcaption>
            </figure>
        </li>
        <li>
            <figure>
                <img src="gallery-3-400.jpg"
                     srcset="gallery-3-400.jpg 400w, gallery-3-800.jpg 800w"
                     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 250px"
                     alt="A forest path in autumn"
                     loading="lazy"
                     width="400" height="300">
                <figcaption>Autumn in the forest.</figcaption>
            </figure>
        </li>
    </ul>
</body>
</html>

docs.text: Use Case Example Photographs Blog post images, galleries Logos Company branding Icons Navigation, buttons Illustrations Tutorials, articles Charts/Graphs Data visualization Maps Location context Product images E-commerce Avatars User profiles Hero images Landing pages Background images Hero sections (CSS) Infographics Marketing content Diagrams Technical documentation

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use alt – even if empty (alt="").
  2. Describe function, not appearance – for functional images.
  3. Use empty alt for decorative images.
  4. Set width and height – prevent layout shift.
  5. Use srcset and sizes – for responsive images.
  6. Use modern formats – WebP, AVIF.
  7. Use <picture> for art direction.
  8. Lazy-load below-the-fold images.
  9. Use fetchpriority="high" for LCP images.
  10. Use decoding="async" for non-critical images.
  11. Compress images – use Squoosh, ImageOptim.
  12. Serve the right size – don't serve 4000px images at 400px.
  13. Use a CDN – for global delivery.
  14. Use <figure> and <figcaption> – for captioned images.
  15. Avoid images of text – use real text.
  16. Test with screen readers – ensure alt is announced.
  17. Test on slow connections – ensure lazy loading works.
  18. Test on high-DPI displays – ensure images are sharp.
  19. Monitor CLS – use width/height and aspect-ratio.
  20. Strip EXIF data – for privacy.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing alt Attribute
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg">

Why it's wrong: Screen readers may read the filename; no accessible description.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using alt for Decorative Images
docs.text:
<img src="divider.png" alt="Divider">

Why it's wrong: Decorative images should have empty alt.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="divider.png" alt="">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No width/height
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo">

Why it's wrong: Causes layout shift as the image loads.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Serving Large Images
docs.text:
<img src="photo-4000.jpg" alt="A photo" width="400" height="300">

Why it's wrong: Wastes bandwidth; slower loading.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="photo-400.jpg" alt="A photo" width="400" height="300"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w" sizes="400px">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Responsive Images
docs.text:
<img src="large.jpg" alt="A photo">

Why it's wrong: Same image for all devices.

✅ Correct: Use srcset and sizes.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Eager Loading Below-the-Fold Images
docs.text:
<img src="below-fold.jpg" alt="A photo" loading="eager">

Why it's wrong: Wastes bandwidth on images the user may never see.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="below-fold.jpg" alt="A photo" loading="lazy">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using alt for Text-Heavy Images
docs.text:
<img src="chart.png" alt="Sales grew 20% in 2024, 15% in 2025, and 10% in 2026">

Why it's wrong: Long alt text is hard to hear; use a longer description elsewhere.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart showing sales growth" aria-describedby="chart-desc">
    <figcaption id="chart-desc">Sales grew 20% in 2024, 15% in 2025, and 10% in 2026.</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Fallback for Modern Formats
docs.text:
<img src="image.avif" alt="A photo">

Why it's wrong: Older browsers can't display AVIF.

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using title as a Substitute for alt
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" title="A scenic mountain view">

Why it's wrong: title is not reliably announced; alt is required.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No loading="lazy" for Gallery
docs.text:
<img src="gallery-1.jpg" alt="Gallery image">
<img src="gallery-2.jpg" alt="Gallery image">
<!-- 50 more images -->

Why it's wrong: All images load at once; slow page.

✅ Correct: Add loading="lazy" to all.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Image size – compress to reduce transfer size.
  • Format – use WebP/AVIF for better compression.
  • Lazy loading – defer off-screen images.
  • Responsive images – serve appropriate sizes.
  • CDN – for faster delivery.
  • Caching – long cache lifetimes for versioned images.
  • Decoding – async for non-critical images.
  • Fetch priority – high for LCP images.
  • Layout shift – set width/height or aspect-ratio.
  • Sprite sheets – combine small icons into one image (older technique; often replaced by SVG).

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Compress images – Squoosh, ImageOptim.
  2. Use modern formats – WebP, AVIF.
  3. Lazy load – below the fold.
  4. Responsive images – srcset + sizes.
  5. Use a CDN.
  6. Set dimensions – prevent CLS.
  7. Use fetchpriority – for LCP images.
  8. Use decoding="async".
  9. Test with Lighthouse – measure LCP, CLS, and image savings.
  10. Monitor performance – with RUM tools.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• EXIF data – may contain GPS coordinates; strip before publishing.
  • SVG injection – SVG can contain scripts; sanitize user uploads.
  • Hotlinking – other sites linking to your images; use a CDN or referrer policy.
  • Image proxies – consider using an image proxy (Cloudinary, Imgix) for user-uploaded images.
  • Mixed content – HTTPS pages should only load HTTPS images.
  • CORS – use crossorigin when needed.
  • Content-Security-Policy – restrict image sources with img-src.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Strip EXIF – for user-uploaded images.
  2. Sanitize SVG – remove scripts.
  3. Use HTTPS – for all images.
  4. Set img-src in CSP – restrict sources.
  5. Use referrerpolicy – for sensitive images.
  6. Validate uploads – file type, size, content.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <img> element.
  • Computed styles – check display, width, height, object-fit.
  • Network panel – verify the image request and size.
  • Console – check for load errors.
  • img.currentSrc – see which source was chosen.
  • img.naturalWidth – see the intrinsic size.
  • img.complete – check if loaded.
  • Lighthouse – audits for image optimization.
  • DevTools Coverage – see unused bytes.
  • Performance panel – inspect LCP and CLS.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the img role and name.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure alt is announced.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For visual content – photographs, illustrations, diagrams.
  • For branding – logos, icons.
  • For information – charts, maps.
  • For decoration – with empty alt.
  • For links – with descriptive alt.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For backgrounds – use CSS background-image.
  • For text – use real text (accessibility, SEO).
  • For icons – use SVG or icon fonts.
  • For animations – use CSS or video.
  • For complex interactivity – use <canvas> or <svg>.

docs.text:
• <picture> – art direction and format fallback.
  • <source> – candidate sources for <picture>.
  • <figure> and <figcaption> – captioned images.
  • <map> and <area> – image maps.
  • <svg> – vector graphics.
  • <canvas> – dynamic graphics.
  • srcset and sizes – responsive images.
  • loading – lazy/eager.
  • decoding – sync/async.
  • fetchpriority – fetch priority.
  • object-fit and object-position – CSS sizing.
  • aspect-ratio – CSS aspect ratio.
  • WebP, AVIF – modern formats.
  • Image optimization – compression, resizing.
  • Accessibility – alt text.
  • SEO – image search, alt text.
  • EXIF – metadata, privacy.
  • CORS – cross-origin images.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <img> element was introduced in HTML 2.0 (1995) by Marc Andreessen — a pivotal moment in web history.

  • The alt attribute stands for "alternative text" and is required for accessibility.

  • Empty alt (alt="") tells screen readers to skip the image — correct for decorative images.

  • Missing alt is different from empty alt — missing alt may cause screen readers to read the filename.

  • Setting width and height prevents layout shift (CLS) while the image loads.

  • srcset and sizes enable responsive images — the browser picks the best source.

  • <picture> enables art direction and format fallback.

  • WebP and AVIF offer better compression than JPEG and PNG.

  • loading="lazy" defers loading of off-screen images.

  • fetchpriority="high" prioritises LCP images.

  • decoding="async" decodes off the main thread — smoother rendering.

  • The object-fit CSS property controls how an image fills its box.

  • The aspect-ratio CSS property sets the aspect ratio without intrinsic size.

  • SVG can be embedded as <img>, inline <svg>, or CSS background.

  • Inline SVG can be styled and animated with CSS and JavaScript.

  • Image maps (<map> and <area>) define clickable regions in an image.

  • EXIF data can reveal GPS coordinates — strip before publishing.

  • SVG can contain scripts — sanitize user-uploaded SVGs.

  • Hotlinking is when other sites link to your images — use a CDN or referrer policy.

  • Content-Security-Policy can restrict image sources with img-src.

  • Lighthouse audits for image optimization and reports savings.

  • The <picture> element is not a container for multiple images — it's a wrapper for sources and a fallback <img>.

  • The currentSrc property tells you which image the browser actually loaded.

  • The naturalWidth and naturalHeight properties give the intrinsic size.

  • The complete property is true when the image has loaded (or failed).

  • The decode() method returns a promise that resolves when the image is decoded.

  • Screen readers announce images as "image" with the alt text.

  • Images of text are discouraged — use real text for accessibility and SEO.

  • Alt text should be concise — usually under 125 characters.

  • Complex images should have a short alt and a longer description nearby.

  • Best practices include always using alt, setting dimensions, using responsive images, and lazy loading.

  • Common mistakes include missing alt, no width/height, and no responsive images.

  • Following best practices for images leads to faster, more accessible, and more engaging web pages.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <img> element embeds an image into a web page.
  • It is a void element with a required src and alt.
  • The alt attribute provides alternative text — required for accessibility.
  • Decorative images use alt="".
  • width and height prevent layout shift (CLS).
  • srcset and sizes enable responsive images.
  • <picture> enables art direction and format fallback.
  • Modern formats (WebP, AVIF) offer better compression.
  • loading="lazy" defers off-screen images.
  • fetchpriority="high" prioritises LCP images.
  • decoding="async" decodes off the main thread.
  • object-fit and object-position control how images fill their box.
  • aspect-ratio sets the aspect ratio.
  • SVG can be embedded as <img> or inline.
  • Image maps define clickable regions.
  • EXIF data can leak GPS coordinates.
  • SVG can contain scripts — sanitize uploads.
  • Best practices: always use alt, set dimensions, use responsive images, lazy load, and use modern formats.
  • Common mistakes include missing alt, no dimensions, and no responsive images.
  • Images are essential for visual content, branding, information, and engagement on the web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Responsive images are images that adapt to the user's device, viewport size, screen resolution, and network conditions. Instead of serving a single image to every device, responsive images allow the browser to choose the most appropriate source from a set of candidates — selecting a smaller image for a phone, a larger one for a desktop, a higher-resolution one for a Retina display, and a different crop for a narrow layout.

HTML provides two mechanisms for responsive images:

  • srcset + sizes on <img> — for resolution switching (same image, different sizes).
  • <picture> + <source> — for art direction and format fallback (different images or formats for different conditions).

Together, these features solve one of the biggest performance problems of the modern web: serving images that are too large, too small, or incorrectly cropped for the user's context.

Example: 

<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w,
             photo-800.jpg 800w,
             photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A scenic mountain view"
     width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Responsive images serve several essential purposes:

  • Performance – serve smaller images to smaller devices, reducing bandwidth and load time.
  • Visual quality – serve higher-resolution images to high-DPI displays.
  • Art direction – serve different crops or compositions for different layouts.
  • Format fallback – serve modern formats (AVIF, WebP) with fallbacks for older browsers.
  • User experience – avoid blurry images on Retina displays and oversized images on phones.
  • Bandwidth savings – reduce data usage, especially on mobile.
  • SEO – faster pages rank better; Google uses page speed as a ranking factor.
  • Core Web Vitals – reduce LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift).

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Responsive images are a cross-cutting concern that combines:

  • HTML – srcset, sizes, <picture>, <source>.
  • CSS – media queries, max-width: 100%, object-fit.
  • Server-side – image resizing, format conversion, CDN.
  • Build tools – generating multiple sizes and formats.
  • Performance monitoring – LCP, CLS, and bandwidth metrics.

They sit at the intersection of media, performance, and responsive design.

Responsive Images
│
├── Resolution Switching (srcset + sizes)
├── Art Direction (<picture> + media)
├── Format Fallback (<picture> + type)
├── Lazy Loading (loading="lazy")
├── Priority Hints (fetchpriority)
└── CSS (object-fit, aspect-ratio)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before responsive images, developers had two bad options:

  1. Serve one large image to everyone – looks great on desktops and Retina displays but wastes bandwidth on phones and slows page loads.
  2. Serve one small image to everyone – fast on phones but blurry on desktops and Retina displays.

Neither option was acceptable. A hero image might be 200 KB on a phone but 2 MB on a desktop — a 10× difference. Serving the desktop image to a phone wasted data and slowed the page. Serving the phone image to a desktop looked unprofessional.

Meanwhile, Retina displays (introduced with the iPhone 4 in 2010) doubled the pixel density. An image that looked sharp on a standard display looked blurry on Retina. Developers needed to serve 2× images — but only to devices that needed them.

And art direction was impossible: a wide landscape image that worked on desktop might crop poorly on a narrow phone. Developers had to either compromise or use CSS hacks.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence One image for all devices Wasteful or blurry No Retina support Blurry on high-DPI displays No art direction Poor crops on different viewports No format fallback Couldn't use modern formats Manual JavaScript solutions Complex, fragile, often inaccessible No browser optimization Browser couldn't choose the best image

docs.title: Why Responsive Images Were Introduced
docs.text:
Responsive images were introduced through the Responsive Images Community Group and the <picture> element specification, which became part of HTML5. The goal was to let developers provide multiple image candidates and let the browser choose the best one based on:

  • Viewport size – how wide is the screen?
  • Device pixel ratio – how dense is the display?
  • Network conditions – how fast is the connection? (optional)
  • Art direction – which crop or composition is appropriate?
  • Format support – which format can the browser display?

The result was two complementary features:

  1. srcset + sizes — for resolution switching (same image, different sizes).
  2. <picture> + <source> — for art direction and format fallback.

Responsive images enable:

  • Optimal performance – the browser loads only what it needs.
  • Optimal quality – high-DPI displays get high-resolution images.
  • Optimal composition – different crops for different layouts.
  • Optimal format – modern formats with fallbacks.
  • No JavaScript – the browser handles selection natively.

docs.title: Resolution Switching with srcset (Width Descriptors)
docs.text:
<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w,
             photo-800.jpg 800w,
             photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A scenic mountain view"
     width="800" height="600">
  • srcset – candidate images with their intrinsic widths (400w, 800w, 1200w).
  • sizes – how wide the image will be displayed at various viewports.
  • The browser picks the best candidate based on viewport and DPR.

docs.title: Resolution Switching with srcset (Pixel Density Descriptors)
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg"
     srcset="photo.jpg 1x,
             photo@2x.jpg 2x,
             photo@3x.jpg 3x"
     alt="A scenic mountain view">
  • 1x, 2x, 3x – pixel density descriptors.
  • Use when the image is displayed at a fixed size.

Note: You cannot mix w and x descriptors in the same srcset.

docs.title: The sizes Attribute
docs.text:
<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw,
            (max-width: 900px) 50vw,
            33vw"
     alt="A photo">
  • 100vw – 100% of the viewport width.
  • 50vw – 50% of the viewport width.
  • 33vw – 33% of the viewport width.
  • 600px – a fixed width.
  • calc(100vw - 2rem) – a calculated width.

The first matching media condition is used.

docs.title: Art Direction with <picture>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="hero-wide.jpg">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="hero-medium.jpg">
    <source media="(min-width: 400px)" srcset="hero-small.jpg">
    <img src="hero-fallback.jpg" alt="A panoramic mountain landscape">
</picture>
  • The browser picks the first <source> whose media condition matches.
  • The <img> is the fallback and is required.

docs.title: Format Fallback with <picture>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>
  • The browser picks the first <source> whose type it supports.
  • The <img> is the fallback for older browsers.

docs.title: Combining Art Direction, Resolution, and Format
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)"
            srcset="hero-wide.avif 1200w, hero-wide@2x.avif 2400w"
            sizes="100vw"
            type="image/avif">
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)"
            srcset="hero-wide.jpg 1200w, hero-wide@2x.jpg 2400w"
            sizes="100vw"
            type="image/jpeg">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)"
            srcset="hero-medium.avif 800w, hero-medium@2x.avif 1600w"
            sizes="100vw"
            type="image/avif">
    <img src="hero-small.jpg" alt="A panoramic mountain landscape">
</picture>

docs.title: Lazy Loading with Responsive Images
docs.text:
<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A photo"
     loading="lazy"
     width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Priority Hints
docs.text:
<img src="hero-800.jpg"
     srcset="hero-400.jpg 400w, hero-800.jpg 800w, hero-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="100vw"
     alt="Hero image"
     fetchpriority="high"
     width="1200" height="600">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose srcset Candidate images with descriptors sizes Display sizes at various viewports <picture> Wrapper for art direction and format fallback <source> Candidate source with media, srcset, type, sizes media Media query for art direction type MIME type for format fallback loading lazy or eager fetchpriority high, low, or auto

docs.title: The "Wardrobe" Analogy
docs.text: Think of responsive images as a wardrobe. You have the same outfit in different sizes (small, medium, large) and different styles (casual, formal). The browser is like a personal stylist: it looks at the occasion (viewport, device, network) and picks the best outfit (image) from your wardrobe.

docs.title: The "Menu" Analogy
docs.text:
A responsive image is like a restaurant menu with multiple options:

  • srcset – the list of dishes (images) with their portion sizes (400w, 800w).
  • sizes – the table size (how much room you have).
  • <picture> – the menu categories (appetizers, mains, desserts) — different courses for different needs.
  • The browser – the waiter who picks the best dish for your table.

docs.title: The "Tailor" Analogy
docs.text: Think of the browser as a tailor. You provide a set of measurements (srcset) and the customer's requirements (sizes, media). The tailor picks the garment that fits best. The customer doesn't have to choose — the tailor does it automatically.

docs.title: The "Two Problems, Two Solutions" Mental Model
docs.text:
There are two distinct problems in responsive images:

  1. Resolution switching – "same image, different sizes."
  2. Solution: srcset + sizes.
  3. Art direction – "different image for different contexts."
  4. Solution: <picture> + <source media="...">.

Format fallback is a third use case, solved with <picture> + <source type="...">.

docs.title: The "Browser Knows Best" Mental Model
docs.text: The most important insight: the browser chooses the image, not the developer. You provide candidates and hints; the browser combines them with its knowledge of the viewport, DPR, network, and cache to pick the best source. This is why srcset and sizes are hints, not commands.

docs.title: The "Resolution Switching vs. Art Direction" Mental Model
docs.text: Problem Solution When to Use Same image, different sizes srcset + sizes Photos that work at any size Different image for different layouts <picture> + media Crops, compositions Modern format with fallback <picture> + type AVIF/WebP with JPEG fallback

docs.title: Concept 1: Width Descriptors (w)
docs.text:
Width descriptors tell the browser the intrinsic width of each candidate:

srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
  • 400w means the image is 400 pixels wide.
  • The browser uses this to calculate which candidate is appropriate.

docs.title: Concept 2: Pixel Density Descriptors (x)
docs.text:
Pixel density descriptors tell the browser the DPR for each candidate:

srcset="photo.jpg 1x, photo@2x.jpg 2x, photo@3x.jpg 3x"
  • 1x – standard display.
  • 2x – Retina display (2× DPR).
  • 3x – high-end phones (3× DPR).

Note: Use x descriptors when the image is displayed at a fixed size (e.g., a logo).

docs.title: Concept 3: The sizes Attribute
docs.text:
The sizes attribute tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed:

sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
  • Media conditions are evaluated in order.
  • The first match wins.
  • The default (no media condition) is the fallback.

Format: (media-condition) length or just length for the default.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Browser's Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Parse srcset to get candidates with widths.
  2. Parse sizes to get the display width at the current viewport.
  3. Multiply by the DPR to get the required pixel width.
  4. Choose the smallest candidate that is ≥ the required width.
  5. If none is large enough, choose the largest.

docs.title: Concept 5: The <picture> Element
docs.text:
The <picture> element is a wrapper for <source> elements and an <img>:

<picture>
    <source ...>
    <source ...>
    <img ...>
</picture>
  • The browser evaluates each <source> in order.
  • The first matching <source> is used.
  • The <img> is the fallback.

docs.title: Concept 6: The <source> Element
docs.text:
The <source> element has:

  • media – a media query (for art direction).
  • srcset – candidate images with descriptors.
  • sizes – sizes for the candidates.
  • type – MIME type (for format fallback).

docs.title: Concept 7: media for Art Direction
docs.text:
<source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="hero-wide.jpg">

The browser uses the first <source> whose media query matches.

docs.title: Concept 8: type for Format Fallback
docs.text:
<source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">

The browser uses the first <source> whose type it supports.

Note: The browser does not check if the image is valid — it trusts the type attribute.

docs.title: Concept 9: Order of <source> Elements
docs.text:
The order matters:

  1. Format fallback – put modern formats first.
  2. Art direction – put more specific media queries first.
  3. Resolution switching – put larger images first (browser picks).

Best practice: 

<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="wide.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="wide.jpg" type="image/jpeg">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="medium.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="medium.jpg" type="image/jpeg">
    <img src="small.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: Concept 10: The currentSrc Property
docs.text:
console.log(img.currentSrc); // The URL actually used

This tells you which candidate the browser selected.

docs.title: Concept 11: Responsive Images and CSS
docs.text:
img {
    max-width: 100%;
    height: auto;
}

Why: Ensures images never overflow their container.

docs.title: Concept 12: The object-fit Property
docs.text:
img {
    width: 300px;
    height: 200px;
    object-fit: cover;
}

Values:

  • fill – stretch (default).
  • contain – fit inside.
  • cover – fill, cropping.
  • none – no scaling.
  • scale-down – smaller of none or contain.

docs.title: Concept 13: The aspect-ratio Property
docs.text:
img {
    aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
    width: 100%;
    height: auto;
}

Why: Reserves space before the image loads, preventing layout shift.

docs.title: Concept 14: Lazy Loading
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo" loading="lazy">

Values:

  • lazy – load when near the viewport.
  • eager – load immediately (default).

Best practice: Use lazy for below-the-fold images; eager for hero images.

docs.title: Concept 15: Fetch Priority
docs.text:
<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high">

Values:

  • high – prioritise loading.
  • low – deprioritise.
  • auto – default.

Use case: high for LCP images.

docs.title: Concept 16: Preloading Responsive Images
docs.text:
<link rel="preload"
      as="image"
      href="hero-1200.jpg"
      imagesrcset="hero-400.jpg 400w, hero-800.jpg 800w, hero-1200.jpg 1200w"
      imagesizes="100vw">

Use case: Preload the hero image to improve LCP.

docs.title: Concept 17: Server-Side Responsive Images
docs.text:
Many CDNs and image services (Cloudinary, Imgix, Cloudflare Images) generate responsive variants automatically:

<img src="https://cdn.example.com/image/upload/w_800/photo.jpg"
     srcset="https://cdn.example.com/image/upload/w_400/photo.jpg 400w,
             https://cdn.example.com/image/upload/w_800/photo.jpg 800w,
             https://cdn.example.com/image/upload/w_1200/photo.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A photo">

docs.title: Concept 18: Build-Time Responsive Images
docs.text:
Build tools (Webpack, Vite, Eleventy) can generate multiple sizes and formats:

// Vite example
import heroImage from './hero.jpg?responsive';

docs.title: Concept 19: The image-set() CSS Function
docs.text:
.hero {
    background-image: image-set(
        url('hero-1x.jpg') 1x,
        url('hero-2x.jpg') 2x
    );
}

Note: Limited browser support for image-set() in CSS.

docs.title: Concept 20: Responsive Images and Core Web Vitals
docs.text:
• LCP – the hero image is often the LCP element; use fetchpriority="high" and preload.
  • CLS – set width/height or aspect-ratio to prevent layout shift.
  • FID/INP – responsive images reduce main-thread work.

docs.title: Concept 21: Browser Support
docs.text:
• srcset + sizes – all modern browsers.
  • <picture> – all modern browsers.
  • AVIF – Chrome, Firefox, Safari (2022+).
  • WebP – all modern browsers.
  • loading="lazy" – all modern browsers.
  • fetchpriority – Chrome, Edge, Firefox (2023+).
  • image-set() – Chrome, Safari; partial Firefox.

docs.title: Concept 22: Responsive Images and SEO
docs.text:
• Google uses mobile-first indexing.
  • Fast pages rank better.
  • alt text is indexed for image search.
  • Structured data (ImageObject) can enhance image search.

docs.title: Concept 23: Responsive Images and Accessibility
docs.text:
• Always provide alt text.
  • Use <picture> for art direction, but keep alt on the <img>.
  • Ensure images are not the only way to convey information.

docs.title: Concept 24: Responsive Images and Bandwidth
docs.text:
• Phones on cellular connections benefit most.
  • Serving 400w instead of 1200w saves ~90% of bytes.
  • Lazy loading below-the-fold images saves even more.

docs.title: Concept 25: The "Mobile-First" Responsive Image Strategy
docs.text:
• Start with the smallest image.
  • Use srcset to provide larger images.
  • Use sizes to tell the browser how the image is displayed.
  • Let the browser choose.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
1.  Browser parses the `<img>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  It reads the `srcset` attribute.
    │   ├── Parses candidates: (URL, descriptor).
    │   └── Descriptors are widths (`400w`) or DPR (`2x`).
    │
    ▼
3.  It reads the `sizes` attribute.
    │   ├── Evaluates media conditions.
    │   └── Determines the display width at the current viewport.
    │
    ▼
4.  It calculates the required pixel width:
    │   └── display width × device pixel ratio.
    │
    ▼
5.  It selects the best candidate:
    │   ├── Smallest candidate ≥ required width.
    │   └── Or largest if none is big enough.
    │
    ▼
6.  It fetches the selected image.
    │
    ▼
7.  It decodes and paints the image.
    │
    ▼
8.  It sets `currentSrc` to the chosen URL.

docs.title: Example Selection
docs.text:
Given: 

<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw">

  • Viewport: 800px, DPR: 2
  • sizes: 50vw (since 800px > 600px) = 400px
  • Required: 400 × 2 = 800px
  • Candidates: 400w, 800w, 1200w

  • Choice: 800w

  • Viewport: 400px, DPR: 2

  • sizes: 100vw (since 400px ≤ 600px) = 400px
  • Required: 400 × 2 = 800px
  • Candidates: 400w, 800w, 1200w

  • Choice: 800w

  • Viewport: 400px, DPR: 1

  • sizes: 100vw = 400px
  • Required: 400 × 1 = 400px
  • Candidates: 400w, 800w, 1200w
  • Choice: 400w

docs.title: Art Direction Selection
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="wide.jpg">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="medium.jpg">
    <img src="small.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>
  • Viewport: 1400px → wide.jpg
  • Viewport: 900px → medium.jpg
  • Viewport: 500px → small.jpg (fallback)

docs.title: Format Fallback Selection
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>
  • Browser supports AVIF → image.avif
  • Browser supports WebP but not AVIF → image.webp
  • Browser supports neither → image.jpg

docs.title: The <picture> Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Iterate <source> elements in order.
  2. For each <source>:
  3. Check type (if present). If unsupported, skip.
  4. Check media (if present). If no match, skip.
  5. If both pass, use the <source>.
  6. If no <source> matches, use the <img>.

docs.title: The currentSrc Property
docs.text:
const img = document.querySelector('img');
console.log(img.currentSrc); // The URL actually used

Use case: Debugging which image the browser chose.

docs.title: The sizes Attribute and CSS
docs.text:
The sizes attribute should match the actual CSS width of the image:

img {
    width: 50vw;
}

<img sizes="50vw" ...>

If they don't match, the browser may choose a suboptimal image.

docs.title: The w Descriptor and Intrinsic Width
docs.text:
The w descriptor is the actual intrinsic width of the image file:

<img srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w">
  • photo-400.jpg must actually be 400 pixels wide.
  • photo-800.jpg must actually be 800 pixels wide.

If the widths are wrong, the browser chooses the wrong image.

docs.title: The srcset Parsing Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Split the value by commas.
  2. For each candidate:
  3. Trim whitespace.
  4. Split by whitespace.
  5. First part is the URL.
  6. Second part (optional) is the descriptor.
  7. If the descriptor ends in w, it's a width.
  8. If it ends in x, it's a pixel density.
  9. If no descriptor, it defaults to 1x.

docs.title: The sizes Parsing Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Split the value by commas.
  2. For each entry:
  3. If it starts with (, it's a media condition followed by a length.
  4. Otherwise, it's a length (the default).
  5. Evaluate media conditions in order.
  6. The first match wins.
  7. If no match, use the default.

docs.title: The Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
1. For each candidate with a w descriptor:
  2. Calculate density = width / displayWidth.
  3. For each candidate with an x descriptor:
  4. Use its density directly.
  5. Pick the candidate with the smallest density ≥ DPR.
  6. If none, pick the largest.

docs.title: The <picture> Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
1. For each <source> in order:
  2. If type is present and unsupported, skip.
  3. If media is present and doesn't match, skip.
  4. Otherwise, use this <source>.
  5. If no <source> matches, use the <img>.

docs.title: The HTMLImageElement Interface
docs.text: Property Description src The src attribute srcset The srcset attribute sizes The sizes attribute currentSrc The URL actually used naturalWidth Intrinsic width naturalHeight Intrinsic height complete True if loaded loading lazy or eager fetchPriority high, low, auto

docs.title: The HTMLPictureElement Interface
docs.text:
• No specific properties.
  • Acts as a wrapper for <source> and <img>.

docs.title: The HTMLSourceElement Interface
docs.text: Property Description src The src attribute srcset The srcset attribute sizes The sizes attribute media The media attribute type The type attribute

docs.title: Browser Caching
docs.text:
• The browser caches each candidate image separately.
  • If the viewport changes and a different candidate is needed, it's fetched.
  • Cached images are reused.

docs.title: The load Event
docs.text:
Fires when the selected image loads:

img.addEventListener('load', () => {
    console.log('Loaded:', img.currentSrc);
});

docs.title: The error Event
docs.text:
Fires when the image fails to load:

img.addEventListener('error', () => {
    console.error('Failed:', img.currentSrc);
});

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
• The <picture> element is not exposed.
  • The <img> is exposed with the alt text.
  • currentSrc is not exposed to assistive technologies.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Responsive Image
docs.text:
1.  Author writes `<img srcset sizes>` or `<picture>`.
    │
    ▼
2.  File deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses the HTML.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser evaluates `srcset` and `sizes`:
    │   ├── Parses candidates.
    │   ├── Evaluates media conditions.
    │   └── Determines required pixel width.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser selects the best candidate.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser fetches the image.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser decodes the image.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser paints the image.
    │
    ▼
9.  `load` event fires.
    │
    ▼
10. `currentSrc` is set.
    │
    ▼
11. If viewport changes, the browser may re-evaluate and load a different candidate.

docs.title: Responsive Re-evaluation
docs.text:
When the viewport changes (e.g., resizing, rotating), the browser may:

  • Re-evaluate sizes.
  • Choose a different candidate.
  • Fetch it if not cached.

docs.title: The resize Event
docs.text:
You can listen for viewport changes:

window.addEventListener('resize', () => {
    console.log('Current image:', img.currentSrc);
});

docs.title: Example 1: Basic srcset with w Descriptors
docs.text:
<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w,
             photo-800.jpg 800w,
             photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A scenic mountain view"
     width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Example 2: srcset with x Descriptors
docs.text:
<img src="logo.png"
     srcset="logo.png 1x,
             logo@2x.png 2x,
             logo@3x.png 3x"
     alt="Company logo"
     width="200" height="60">

docs.title: Example 3: Art Direction with <picture>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="hero-wide.jpg">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="hero-medium.jpg">
    <source media="(min-width: 400px)" srcset="hero-small.jpg">
    <img src="hero-fallback.jpg" alt="A panoramic mountain landscape" width="800" height="400">
</picture>

docs.title: Example 4: Format Fallback
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo" width="800" height="600">
</picture>

docs.title: Example 5: Art Direction + Format Fallback + Resolution
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)"
            srcset="hero-wide.avif 1200w, hero-wide@2x.avif 2400w"
            sizes="100vw"
            type="image/avif">
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)"
            srcset="hero-wide.jpg 1200w, hero-wide@2x.jpg 2400w"
            sizes="100vw"
            type="image/jpeg">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)"
            srcset="hero-medium.avif 800w, hero-medium@2x.avif 1600w"
            sizes="100vw"
            type="image/avif">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)"
            srcset="hero-medium.jpg 800w, hero-medium@2x.jpg 1600w"
            sizes="100vw"
            type="image/jpeg">
    <img src="hero-small.jpg" alt="A panoramic mountain landscape" width="800" height="400">
</picture>

docs.title: Example 6: Responsive Logo
docs.text:
<img src="logo-200.png"
     srcset="logo-100.png 100w,
             logo-200.png 200w,
             logo-400.png 400w"
     sizes="200px"
     alt="Company logo"
     width="200" height="60">

docs.title: Example 7: Responsive Hero with fetchpriority
docs.text:
<img src="hero-1200.jpg"
     srcset="hero-600.jpg 600w,
             hero-1200.jpg 1200w,
             hero-2400.jpg 2400w"
     sizes="100vw"
     alt="Hero image"
     fetchpriority="high"
     width="1200" height="600">

docs.title: Example 8: Lazy-Loaded Gallery
docs.text:
<ul class="gallery">
    <li>
        <img src="photo-1-400.jpg"
             srcset="photo-1-400.jpg 400w, photo-1-800.jpg 800w"
             sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 300px"
             alt="Gallery image 1"
             loading="lazy"

// .eleventy.js
const Image = require("@11ty/eleventy-img");

module.exports = function(eleventyConfig) {
    eleventyConfig.addShortcode("image", async function(src, alt, sizes) {
        const metadata = await Image(src, {
            widths: [400, 800, 1200],
            formats: ["avif", "webp", "jpeg"],
            outputDir: "./_site/img/"
        });
        const imageAttributes = {
            alt,
            sizes,
            loading: "lazy",
            decoding: "async"
        };
        return Image.generateHTML(metadata, imageAttributes);
    });
};

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Technique Hero images srcset + sizes + fetchpriority="high" Galleries srcset + sizes + loading="lazy" Art direction <picture> + media Format fallback <picture> + type Retina logos srcset + x descriptors Responsive cards srcset + sizes + CSS Background images image-set() (CSS) Dark mode images <picture> + prefers-color-scheme Thumbnails srcset + sizes + object-fit Avatars srcset + x descriptors Banners <picture> + media Product images srcset + sizes + loading="lazy"

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always provide width and height – prevents layout shift.
  2. Use srcset and sizes – for resolution switching.
  3. Use <picture> – for art direction and format fallback.
  4. Use modern formats – AVIF, WebP, with fallbacks.
  5. Use loading="lazy" – for below-the-fold images.
  6. Use fetchpriority="high" – for LCP images.
  7. Preload the hero image – with imagesrcset and imagesizes.
  8. Use object-fit – for consistent sizing.
  9. Use aspect-ratio – for reserving space.
  10. Match sizes to CSS – ensure the browser chooses correctly.
  11. Use x descriptors – for fixed-size images (logos).
  12. Use w descriptors – for flexible images (photos).
  13. Don't mix w and x – in the same srcset.
  14. Order <source> correctly – specific media queries first.
  15. Test on real devices – not just emulators.
  16. Test on slow networks – ensure lazy loading works.
  17. Monitor Core Web Vitals – LCP and CLS.
  18. Use a CDN – for global delivery.
  19. Use build tools – to generate responsive variants.
  20. Document your strategy – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No srcset
docs.text:
<img src="large.jpg" alt="A photo">

Why it's wrong: Same image for all devices.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A photo"
     width="800" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Wrong sizes Value
docs.text:
<img srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w" sizes="100vw">

Why it's wrong: If the image is displayed at 50vw, sizes="100vw" causes the browser to choose an image that's too large.

✅ Correct: Match sizes to the actual CSS width.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Incorrect Width Descriptors
docs.text:
<img srcset="photo-800.jpg 400w, photo-1200.jpg 800w">

Why it's wrong: The w descriptor must be the actual intrinsic width.

✅ Correct: 

<img srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mixing w and x
docs.text:
<img srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo@2x.jpg 2x">

Why it's wrong: You cannot mix width and density descriptors in the same srcset.

✅ Correct: Use one or the other.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No <img> in <picture>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: The <img> is required as a fallback.

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Wrong <source> Order
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.jpg" type="image/jpeg">
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="fallback.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: The browser always picks JPEG (first supported), never AVIF.

✅ Correct: Put AVIF first.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No alt on <img> Inside <picture>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: No accessible description.

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Lazy Loading the Hero Image
docs.text:
<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" loading="lazy">

Why it's wrong: Delays LCP; the hero should load immediately.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Dimensions
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo" srcset="..." sizes="...">

Why it's wrong: Causes layout shift (CLS).

✅ Correct: Add width and height.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using srcset Without sizes
docs.text:
<img srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w" alt="A photo">

Why it's wrong: Without sizes, the browser assumes 100vw.

✅ Correct: Add sizes.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing on Real Devices
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Emulators may not accurately reflect DPR and network.

✅ Correct: Test on real phones, tablets, and desktops.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Serving Oversized Images
docs.text:
<img src="photo-4000.jpg" alt="A photo" width="400" height="300">

Why it's wrong: Wastes bandwidth.

✅ Correct: Serve the right size.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Format Fallback
docs.text:
<img src="image.avif" alt="A photo">

Why it's wrong: Older browsers can't display AVIF.

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• LCP – the hero image is often the LCP element; use fetchpriority="high" and preload.
  • CLS – set width/height or aspect-ratio to prevent layout shift.
  • Bandwidth – serving smaller images reduces data usage.
  • Cache – each candidate is cached separately.
  • Decode – use decoding="async" for non-critical images.
  • Lazy loading – defers off-screen images.
  • CDN – global delivery, automatic resizing.
  • Build tools – generate variants at build time.
  • Image compression – reduce file size.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use responsive images – serve the right size.
  2. Use modern formats – AVIF, WebP.
  3. Lazy load – below the fold.
  4. Preload – the hero image.
  5. Use fetchpriority – for LCP.
  6. Set dimensions – prevent CLS.
  7. Use a CDN.
  8. Compress images.
  9. Monitor Core Web Vitals.
  10. Test on slow networks.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• EXIF data – strip GPS coordinates before publishing.
  • SVG injection – sanitize user-uploaded SVGs.
  • Hotlinking – use a CDN or referrer policy.
  • Mixed content – HTTPS pages should only load HTTPS images.
  • Content-Security-Policy – restrict image sources with img-src.
  • CORS – use crossorigin when needed.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Strip EXIF – for user-uploaded images.
  2. Sanitize SVG – remove scripts.
  3. Use HTTPS – for all images.
  4. Set img-src in CSP – restrict sources.
  5. Use referrerpolicy – for sensitive images.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <img> and <picture>.
  • Computed styles – check display, width, height, object-fit.
  • Network panel – verify which image was loaded.
  • Console – use img.currentSrc to see the chosen URL.
  • img.naturalWidth – intrinsic width.
  • img.complete – true if loaded.
  • Lighthouse – audits for image optimization.
  • DevTools Coverage – see unused bytes.
  • Performance panel – inspect LCP and CLS.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the img role and name.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure alt is announced.
  • Test on real devices – different DPR and network conditions.
  • Throttle network – in DevTools to simulate slow connections.
  • Test with JavaScript disabled – native responsive images work without JS.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For any image that appears at different sizes – hero, gallery, cards.
  • For Retina displays – use x descriptors.
  • For art direction – use <picture>.
  • For format fallback – use <picture>.
  • For LCP images – preload + fetchpriority="high".
  • For below-the-fold images – loading="lazy".

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For small icons – use SVG.
  • For background images – use CSS background-image with image-set().
  • For decorative images – use CSS backgrounds.
  • For images that never change size – a single src is fine.
  • For SVG – SVG is resolution-independent; no need for srcset.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <img> – the image element.
  • <picture> – wrapper for art direction and format fallback.
  • <source> – candidate source.
  • srcset – candidate images.
  • sizes – display sizes.
  • media – media query.
  • type – MIME type.
  • loading – lazy/eager.
  • decoding – sync/async.
  • fetchpriority – fetch priority.
  • object-fit – CSS sizing.
  • object-position – CSS positioning.
  • aspect-ratio – CSS aspect ratio.
  • image-set() – CSS image candidates.
  • Preload – <link rel="preload">.
  • LCP – Largest Contentful Paint.
  • CLS – Cumulative Layout Shift.
  • DPR – Device Pixel Ratio.
  • CDN – Content Delivery Network.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Responsive images were introduced through the Responsive Images Community Group and the <picture> element specification.

  • The srcset attribute was first proposed by Mat Marquis in 2012.

  • The w descriptor stands for width — the intrinsic width of the image.

  • The x descriptor stands for pixel density — the DPR of the target display.

  • You cannot mix w and x descriptors in the same srcset.

  • The sizes attribute is only used with w descriptors.

  • The browser chooses the image, not the developer — srcset and sizes are hints.

  • <picture> is not a container for multiple images — it's a wrapper for <source> elements and a fallback <img>.

  • The <img> is required inside <picture>.

  • The order of <source> elements matters — the first matching one wins.

  • Format fallback uses the type attribute.

  • Art direction uses the media attribute.

  • AVIF offers better compression than WebP and JPEG.

  • WebP offers better compression than JPEG and PNG.

  • loading="lazy" defers off-screen images.

  • fetchpriority="high" prioritises LCP images.

  • Preloading the hero image improves LCP.

  • aspect-ratio reserves space and prevents CLS.

  • object-fit: cover crops images to fill their box.

  • image-set() is a CSS function for responsive background images.

  • CDNs like Cloudinary, Imgix, and Cloudflare Images generate responsive variants automatically.

  • Build tools like Eleventy Image, Vite, and Webpack generate variants at build time.

  • Google uses mobile-first indexing — responsive images are essential for SEO.

  • Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP) are affected by image loading.

  • The currentSrc property tells you which image the browser chose.

  • The naturalWidth and naturalHeight properties give the intrinsic size.

  • Best practices include using srcset, sizes, <picture>, modern formats, lazy loading, and preloading.

  • Common mistakes include no srcset, wrong sizes, mixing w and x, and wrong <source> order.

  • Following best practices for responsive images leads to faster, sharper, and more efficient web pages.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Responsive images adapt to the user's device, viewport, and screen resolution.
  • Two mechanisms: srcset + sizes (resolution switching) and <picture> + <source> (art direction and format fallback).
  • srcset provides candidate images with w (width) or x (density) descriptors.
  • sizes tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed.
  • <picture> wraps <source> elements and a required fallback <img>.
  • media enables art direction (different images for different viewports).
  • type enables format fallback (AVIF → WebP → JPEG).
  • loading="lazy" defers off-screen images.
  • fetchpriority="high" prioritises LCP images.
  • Preload the hero image with imagesrcset and imagesizes.
  • object-fit and aspect-ratio control sizing and prevent CLS.
  • Best practices: use srcset, sizes, <picture>, modern formats, lazy loading, preloading, and test on real devices.
  • Common mistakes include no srcset, wrong sizes, mixing w and x, and wrong <source> order.
  • Responsive images are essential for performance, visual quality, bandwidth savings, and Core Web Vitals.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <picture> element is an HTML container that allows developers to provide multiple image sources for a single <img> element, enabling the browser to choose the most appropriate image based on the user's device, viewport, screen resolution, format support, and other conditions. Unlike srcset on <img> — which is for resolution switching (same image at different sizes) — <picture> is for art direction (different images or crops for different layouts) and format fallback (serving modern formats like AVIF and WebP with fallbacks for older browsers).

The <picture> element is a wrapper that contains zero or more <source> elements followed by exactly one <img> element. The <img> is required — it serves as the fallback for browsers that don't support <picture> and as the element that carries the alt text, width, height, and other attributes. The <source> elements provide alternative sources with conditions (media, type) that the browser evaluates in order.

Example: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view" width="800" height="600">
</picture>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <picture> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Art direction – serve different crops or compositions for different viewports.
  • Format fallback – serve modern formats (AVIF, WebP) with fallbacks for older browsers.
  • Resolution switching – combine with srcset for multiple resolutions.
  • Dark mode images – serve different images for light and dark color schemes.
  • Localization – serve different images for different languages or regions.
  • Responsive design – adapt images to the layout.
  • Performance – serve the smallest suitable image.
  • Accessibility – preserve alt text on the <img> element.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <picture> element is phrasing content and embedded content. It is an inline element that can appear anywhere phrasing content is accepted — inside <p>, <figure>, <a>, <div>, <li>, <td>, and more. It is part of the responsive images system, alongside srcset and sizes on <img>.

Responsive Images
│
├── srcset + sizes on <img>        → Resolution switching
└── <picture> + <source>           → Art direction + format fallback
    ├── <source media="...">       → Art direction
    ├── <source type="...">        → Format fallback
    ├── <source srcset="..." sizes="..."> → Resolution switching
    └── <img>                      → Fallback (required)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before <picture>, developers faced three impossible problems:

Problem 1: Art Direction

A wide landscape image that looks great on a desktop monitor might crop poorly on a narrow phone. A hero image with text on the left might have the text cut off on mobile. Developers needed to serve different images for different layouts — but <img> only allowed one src and srcset only allowed different sizes of the same image.

Problem 2: Format Fallback

New image formats (WebP, then AVIF) offered dramatically better compression than JPEG and PNG. But not all browsers supported them. Developers needed to serve modern formats to browsers that supported them, and fallbacks to those that didn't. srcset couldn't do this — it had no mechanism for format detection.

Problem 3: Conditional Images

Developers wanted to serve different images based on:

  • Color scheme (light vs. dark mode).
  • Language or region.
  • User preferences.
  • Media type (print vs. screen).

srcset couldn't handle these conditions — it only handled resolution and viewport.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No art direction Poor crops on different viewports No format fallback Couldn't use modern formats No conditional images Same image for all contexts Manual JavaScript solutions Complex, fragile, often inaccessible srcset alone Only resolution switching CSS background-image No alt text, no accessibility

docs.title: Why <picture> Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <picture> element was introduced through the Responsive Images Community Group (RICG) and became part of HTML5. It was designed to solve art direction and format fallback — the two problems srcset couldn't solve.

The design was inspired by the <video> and <audio> elements, which already used <source> children to provide multiple media sources with fallbacks. The <picture> element adopted the same pattern:

<picture>
    <source ...>
    <source ...>
    <img ...>  <!-- Required fallback -->
</picture>

<picture> enables:

  • Art direction – different images for different layouts via media.
  • Format fallback – modern formats with fallbacks via type.
  • Resolution switching – combined with srcset and sizes.
  • Conditional images – via media queries (prefers-color-scheme, orientation, etc.).
  • Accessibility – the <img> carries alt text.
  • No JavaScript – the browser handles selection natively.
  • Progressive enhancement – works even in older browsers.

The <picture> element is one of the most important additions to HTML for modern responsive design.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <picture>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="..." type="..." media="...">
    <img src="..." alt="...">
</picture>
  • <source> – zero or more alternative sources.
  • <img> – exactly one; the fallback and accessible element.

docs.title: Simple Format Fallback
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A scenic mountain view" width="800" height="600">
</picture>

docs.title: Simple Art Direction
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="hero-wide.jpg">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="hero-medium.jpg">
    <img src="hero-small.jpg" alt="A panoramic mountain landscape" width="800" height="400">
</picture>
