docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element/Attribute Purpose <picture> Wrapper for sources and fallback <img> <source> Candidate source with conditions srcset Candidate image(s) with descriptors sizes Display sizes for srcset media Media query for art direction type MIME type for format fallback <img> Fallback and accessible element (required) alt Alternative text (required on <img>) width/height Dimensions (prevents layout shift) loading lazy or eager fetchpriority high, low, or auto decoding sync, async, or auto

docs.title: The "Menu with Courses" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of <picture> as a restaurant menu with multiple courses:

  • The <img> is the "house special" — always available.
  • Each <source> is a different course — appetizer, main, dessert.
  • media is the "available at this time" condition.
  • type is the "available in this kitchen" condition.
  • The browser is the waiter who picks the best course for you.

docs.title: The "Travel Itinerary" Analogy
docs.text:
A <picture> element is like a travel itinerary with multiple options:

  • If it's raining, take the indoor tour.
  • If it's sunny, take the outdoor tour.
  • If you're in Paris, take the French tour.
  • Otherwise, take the default tour.

The browser picks the first option whose conditions match.

docs.title: The "Playlist" Analogy
docs.text: <source> elements are like songs on a playlist. The browser plays the first one it can (supported format, matching media query). If it can't play any, it falls back to the <img> — like a default track.

docs.title: The "If-Else" Mental Model
docs.text:
The <picture> element is essentially a conditional chain:

if (browser supports AVIF) → use AVIF
else if (browser supports WebP) → use WebP
else if (viewport ≥ 1200px) → use wide.jpg
else if (viewport ≥ 800px) → use medium.jpg
else → use fallback.jpg (the <img>)

The browser evaluates conditions in order and uses the first match.

docs.title: The "Art Direction vs. Resolution Switching" Mental Model
docs.text:
Problem Solution Element Same image, different sizes srcset + sizes <img> Different image, different contexts media <picture> + <source> Modern format with fallback type <picture> + <source>

Rule: Use srcset on <img> for resolution switching; use <picture> for art direction and format fallback.

docs.title: Concept 1: The <picture> Element
docs.text:
The <picture> element is a wrapper. It has no attributes of its own and no rendering. Its only purpose is to contain <source> elements and one <img>.

<picture>
    <!-- sources -->
    <img src="..." alt="...">
</picture>

docs.title: Concept 2: The <source> Element
docs.text:
The <source> element provides a candidate source with optional conditions:

Attribute Purpose srcset Candidate image(s) sizes Display sizes for srcset media Media query condition type MIME type condition width Intrinsic width (rarely used) height Intrinsic height (rarely used)

docs.title: Concept 3: The <img> Element (Required)
docs.text:
The <img> is required inside <picture>. It serves as:

  • The fallback for browsers that don't support <picture>.
  • The accessible element — carries the alt text.
  • The styled element — carries class, id, width, height, loading, etc.
<img src="fallback.jpg" alt="A photo" width="800" height="600" loading="lazy">

docs.title: Concept 4: The Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
The browser evaluates <source> elements in document order:

  1. For each <source>:
  2. If type is present and unsupported → skip.
  3. If media is present and doesn't match → skip.
  4. Otherwise, use this <source>.
  5. If no <source> matches → use the <img>.

Important: The first matching <source> wins, not the best one.

docs.title: Concept 5: media for Art Direction
docs.text:
The media attribute accepts any valid media query:

<source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="wide.jpg">
<source media="(orientation: landscape)" srcset="landscape.jpg">
<source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="dark.jpg">
<source media="print" srcset="print.png">

docs.title: Concept 6: type for Format Fallback
docs.text:
The type attribute specifies the MIME type:

<source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
<source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">

The browser checks if it supports the type before using the source.

docs.title: Concept 7: Order of <source> Elements
docs.text:
Order matters:

  1. Format fallback – put modern formats first (AVIF, then WebP, then JPEG).
  2. Art direction – put more specific media queries first.
  3. Resolution switching – put larger images first (browser picks).

Best practice: 

<picture>
    <!-- Most specific conditions first -->
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="wide.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="wide.jpg" type="image/jpeg">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="medium.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="medium.jpg" type="image/jpeg">
    <img src="small.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: Concept 8: <source> Cannot Be Empty
docs.text: Each <source> must have a srcset (or src) attribute. A <source> without a source is invalid.

docs.title: Concept 9: The <img> Carries the Semantics
docs.text:
The <img> inside <picture> is the actual element that:

  • Carries the alt text.
  • Carries width, height, class, id.
  • Is exposed to the accessibility tree.
  • Can be styled with CSS.

The <source> elements are invisible — they only provide candidates.

docs.title: Concept 10: <picture> Does Not Appear in the Accessibility Tree
docs.text: The <picture> element is not exposed to the accessibility tree. Only the <img> is. This is why the <img> must carry the alt text.

docs.title: Concept 11: Format Support Detection
docs.text: The browser checks type against its supported formats. It does not download the image to check — it trusts the type attribute.

docs.title: Concept 12: Combining srcset and media
docs.text:
A <source> can have both media and srcset with sizes:

<source media="(min-width: 1200px)"
        srcset="wide-1200.jpg 1200w, wide-2400.jpg 2400w"
        sizes="100vw">

docs.title: Concept 13: The <picture> Element and CSS
docs.text:
The <picture> element has no rendering — it's a transparent wrapper. CSS properties like width, height, display should be applied to the <img>, not <picture>.

/* Bad */
picture { width: 100%; }

/* Good */
picture img { width: 100%; height: auto; }

docs.title: Concept 14: <picture> and loading
docs.text:
The loading attribute goes on the <img>, not <picture> or <source>:

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo" loading="lazy">
</picture>

docs.title: Concept 15: <picture> and fetchpriority
docs.text:
The fetchpriority attribute goes on the <img>:

<picture>
    <source srcset="hero.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high">
</picture>

docs.title: Concept 16: <picture> and Preload
docs.text:
Preloading a <picture> source requires imagesrcset and imagesizes:

<link rel="preload"
      as="image"
      href="hero.jpg"
      imagesrcset="hero.avif"
      imagesizes="100vw"
      type="image/avif">

Note: Preloading <picture> sources is complex; test carefully.

docs.title: Concept 17: <picture> and Dark Mode
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="logo-dark.svg" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
    <img src="logo-light.svg" alt="Company logo" width="200" height="60">
</picture>

Use case: Different logos for light and dark themes.

docs.title: Concept 18: <picture> and Print
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="logo-print.png" media="print">
    <img src="logo-screen.png" alt="Company logo" width="200" height="60">
</picture>

Use case: High-resolution print versions.

docs.title: Concept 19: <picture> and <figure>
docs.text:
<figure>
    <picture>
        <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
        <img src="image.jpg" alt="A scenic view" width="800" height="600">
    </picture>
    <figcaption>Figure 1: A scenic view.</figcaption>
</figure>

Use case: Combining art direction with captions.

docs.title: Concept 20: Browser Support
docs.text: Feature Support <picture> All modern browsers <source> in <picture> All modern browsers media All modern browsers type All modern browsers AVIF Chrome, Firefox, Safari (2022+) WebP All modern browsers prefers-color-scheme All modern browsers

docs.title: Concept 21: Fallback for Older Browsers
docs.text:
Older browsers that don't support <picture> will:

  • Ignore the <source> elements.
  • Render the <img> inside.

This is progressive enhancement — the <img> is the fallback.

docs.title: Concept 22: The srcset Attribute in <source>
docs.text:
The srcset in <source> uses the same syntax as <img srcset>:

<source srcset="image-400.jpg 400w, image-800.jpg 800w" sizes="100vw">

docs.title: Concept 23: <picture> vs. <img srcset>
docs.text: Aspect <picture> <img srcset> Art direction Yes No Format fallback Yes No Resolution switching Yes Yes Required <img> Yes N/A Complexity Higher Lower Use case Different images Same image, different sizes

docs.title: Concept 24: <picture> and SEO
docs.text:
• Search engines index the <img> and its alt.
  • The <source> elements are not indexed.
  • Use meaningful alt text on the <img>.

docs.title: Concept 25: <picture> and Accessibility
docs.text:
• The <img> carries the alt text.
  • The <picture> element is not exposed.
  • Screen readers announce the <img> with its alt.
  • Ensure the alt text describes the image in all contexts.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing a <picture>
docs.text:
1.  The parser encounters a `<picture>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the picture.
    │
    ▼
3.  It processes each `<source>` child:
    │   ├── Creates a source node.
    │   └── Reads `srcset`, `sizes`, `media`, `type`.
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes the `<img>` child:
    │   ├── Creates an img node.
    │   └── Reads `src`, `alt`, `width`, `height`, etc.
    │
    ▼
5.  When the closing tag is encountered, the picture is closed.
    │
    ▼
6.  The browser evaluates the sources in order:
    │   ├── For each `<source>`:
    │   │   ├── If `type` is present and unsupported → skip.
    │   │   ├── If `media` is present and doesn't match → skip.
    │   │   └── Otherwise, use this source.
    │   └── If no source matches, use the `<img>`.
    │
    ▼
7.  The browser resolves the chosen source's `srcset` and `sizes`:
    │   └── Selects the best candidate based on viewport and DPR.
    │
    ▼
8.  The browser fetches the chosen image.
    │
    ▼
9.  The browser decodes and paints the image.
    │
    ▼
10. The `<img>` element exposes the chosen URL via `currentSrc`.

docs.title: The <picture> Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
For each <source> in document order:
    If source.type is present:
        If browser doesn't support source.type → skip
    If source.media is present:
        If media query doesn't match → skip
    Use this <source> (break)

If no <source> matched:
    Use the <img>

docs.title: The srcset Selection (Within a Chosen <source>)
docs.text:
1. Parse srcset candidates.
  2. Evaluate sizes to get display width.
  3. Multiply by DPR to get required width.
  4. Choose the smallest candidate ≥ required width.

docs.title: The currentSrc Property
docs.text:
const img = document.querySelector('picture img');
console.log(img.currentSrc); // The URL actually used

This tells you which source the browser chose.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
• <picture> is not exposed.
  • <source> elements are not exposed.
  • <img> is exposed with its alt, width, height.

docs.title: Default User Agent Styles
docs.text:
picture {
    display: inline;
}

No visual rendering. The <img> inside is rendered normally.

docs.title: Fallback Behaviour
docs.text:
If a browser doesn't support <picture>:

  • It ignores <source> elements.
  • It renders the <img> inside.

This is why the <img> is required and must have a valid src.

docs.title: The HTMLPictureElement Interface
docs.text:
Property Description (none) No specific properties

The <picture> element has no properties of its own. It's a transparent wrapper.

docs.title: The HTMLSourceElement Interface
docs.text: Property Description src The src attribute srcset The srcset attribute sizes The sizes attribute media The media attribute type The type attribute width The width attribute height The height attribute

docs.title: The HTMLImageElement (Inside <picture>)
docs.text:
The <img> inside <picture> behaves exactly like a normal <img>:

Property Description src Fallback URL srcset Candidates sizes Sizes currentSrc The URL actually used alt Alternative text width Display width height Display height naturalWidth Intrinsic width naturalHeight Intrinsic height loading lazy or eager fetchPriority Fetch priority

docs.title: The Selection Algorithm in Detail
docs.text:
The HTML spec defines the algorithm:

  1. Let picture be the <picture> element.
  2. Let img be the <img> child.
  3. For each child of picture in order:
  4. If the child is a <source>:
    • If type is present and unsupported → continue.
    • If media is present and doesn't match → continue.
    • Let selectedSource be this source.
    • Break.
  5. If selectedSource is set:
  6. Use its srcset and sizes.
  7. Else:
  8. Use the img's src, srcset, and sizes.

docs.title: The currentSrc Algorithm
docs.text: After selection, currentSrc is set to the chosen URL. If the <img>'s src was used, currentSrc equals src.

docs.title: The type Support Check
docs.text: The browser checks type against its list of supported MIME types. This is a synchronous check — no network request is made.

docs.title: The media Match
docs.text: The browser evaluates the media query against the current environment (viewport, orientation, color scheme, etc.). This is a synchronous check.

docs.title: Browser Differences
docs.text: Browser <picture> Support AVIF Support Chrome Yes Yes Firefox Yes Yes (2021+) Safari Yes Yes (2022+) Edge Yes Yes

docs.title: The <source> Element and <picture> vs. <video>
docs.text:
The <source> element is used in both <picture> and <video>/<audio>, but the attributes differ:

  • <picture>: srcset, sizes, media, type.
  • <video>: src, type, media.

docs.title: Fallback for <picture>-Unaware Browsers
docs.text: Older browsers (IE 11 and earlier) ignore <picture> and <source>, rendering only the <img>. This is the intended fallback.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <picture> Element
docs.text:
1.  Author writes `<picture>` with `<source>` and `<img>`.
    │
    ▼
2.  File deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses HTML.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser creates DOM nodes for picture, sources, img.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser evaluates `<source>` elements in order:
    │   ├── Checks `type` support.
    │   ├── Checks `media` match.
    │   └── Selects the first match.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser resolves `srcset` and `sizes` for the chosen source.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser fetches the chosen image.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser decodes and paints the image.
    │
    ▼
9.  `<img>` `load` event fires.
    │
    ▼
10. `currentSrc` is set to the chosen URL.
    │
    ▼
11. If the environment changes (resize, color scheme), the browser may re-evaluate.

docs.title: Re-evaluation on Environment Change
docs.text:
When the viewport resizes or the color scheme changes, the browser:

  1. Re-evaluates the <source> elements.
  2. May choose a different source.
  3. Fetches the new image if not cached.

docs.title: Dynamic Modification
docs.text:
const picture = document.querySelector('picture');
const img = picture.querySelector('img');
console.log(img.currentSrc); // The URL actually used

Note: You cannot dynamically add or remove <source> elements and expect immediate re-evaluation in all browsers. Test carefully.

<div class="card">
    <picture>
        <source media="(min-width: 800px)"
                srcset="card-wide.avif"
                type="image/avif">
        <source media="(min-width: 800px)"
                srcset="card-wide.jpg"
                type="image/jpeg">
        <source srcset="card-square.avif"
                type="image/avif">
        <img src="card-square.jpg"
             alt="A scenic mountain landscape"
             width="400" height="400"
             loading="lazy">
    </picture>
    <h3>Mountain Landscape</h3>
    <p>A beautiful view from the summit.</p>
</div>

docs.title: Example 19: Print + Screen Combination
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source media="print" srcset="hero-print.png">
    <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="hero-dark.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="hero-light.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="hero-light.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="hero-light.jpg" alt="A hero image"
         width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high">
</picture>

docs.title: Example 20: Complete <picture> Demo
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Picture Element Demo</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 1200px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        .hero { width: 100%; height: auto; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; border-radius: 8px; }
        figure { margin: 2rem 0; }
        figcaption { font-size: 0.875rem; color: #6c757d; margin-top: 0.5rem; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Picture Element Demo</h1>

    <!-- Format fallback + art direction -->
    <h2>Hero Image</h2>
    <picture>
        <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="hero-wide.avif" type="image/avif">
        <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="hero-wide.webp" type="image/webp">
        <source media="(min-width: 1200px)" srcset="hero-wide.jpg" type="image/jpeg">
        <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="hero-medium.avif" type="image/avif">
        <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="hero-medium.webp" type="image/webp">
        <source media="(min-width: 800px)" srcset="hero-medium.jpg" type="image/jpeg">
        <source srcset="hero-small.avif" type="image/avif">
        <source srcset="hero-small.webp" type="image/webp">
        <img src="hero-small.jpg" alt="A panoramic mountain landscape at sunrise"
             class="hero" width="800" height="450" fetchpriority="high">
    </picture>

    <!-- Dark mode logo -->
    <h2>Dark Mode Logo</h2>
    <picture>
        <source srcset="logo-dark.svg" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
        <img src="logo-light.svg" alt="Company logo" width="200" height="60">
    </picture>

    <!-- Figure with caption -->
    <h2>Chart</h2>
    <figure>
        <picture>
            <source srcset="chart.avif" type="image/avif">
            <source srcset="chart.webp" type="image/webp">
            <img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart showing sales growth"
                 width="800" height="500" loading="lazy">
        </picture>
        <figcaption>Figure 1: Sales growth from 2020 to 2026.</figcaption>
    </figure>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Technique Modern format fallback <source type="..."> Art direction <source media="..."> Dark mode images media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" Print-specific images media="print" Orientation-based images media="(orientation: ...)" Language-specific images hreflang (limited support) Responsive logos Density descriptors Responsive heroes Art direction + format fallback Product images Format fallback + resolution Gallery images Format fallback + lazy loading Avatars Density descriptors Banners Art direction

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always include <img> – it's required and the fallback.
  2. Put alt on the <img> – not on <source>.
  3. Put width/height on the <img> – prevent layout shift.
  4. Put loading on the <img> – not on <picture>.
  5. Put fetchpriority on the <img> – for LCP.
  6. Put class/id on the <img> – not on <picture>.
  7. Order sources by specificity – most specific first.
  8. Put modern formats first – AVIF, then WebP, then JPEG.
  9. Use type for format fallback – not media.
  10. Use media for art direction – not type.
  11. Combine type and media – for art direction + format.
  12. Combine srcset and sizes – within a <source>.
  13. Test in multiple browsers – especially Safari for AVIF.
  14. Test with JavaScript disabled – works natively.
  15. Don't use <picture> for resolution switching alone – use <img srcset>.
  16. Use <img srcset> for simpler cases – less complex.
  17. Preload hero images – with imagesrcset and imagesizes.
  18. Test on real devices – DPR and color scheme vary.
  19. Validate your HTML – check for required <img>.
  20. Document your strategy – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing <img>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: The <img> is required.

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: alt on <source>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif" alt="A photo">
    <img src="image.jpg">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: alt belongs on the <img>, not <source>.

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Wrong Source Order
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.jpg" type="image/jpeg">
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="fallback.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: The browser always picks JPEG (first supported), never AVIF.

✅ Correct: Put AVIF first.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: loading on <picture>
docs.text:
<picture loading="lazy">
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: loading belongs on the <img>.

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo" loading="lazy">
</picture>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <picture> for Resolution Switching Only
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image-400.jpg 400w, image-800.jpg 800w" sizes="100vw">
    <img src="image-800.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: This is simpler with <img srcset>.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="image-800.jpg"
     srcset="image-400.jpg 400w, image-800.jpg 800w"
     sizes="100vw"
     alt="A photo">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: media on <img>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <img src="image.jpg" media="(min-width: 800px)" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: media is not valid on <img>.

✅ Correct: Use <source media="...">.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No type for Format Fallback
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: Without type, the browser uses the first source regardless of format support.

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No width/height
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: Causes layout shift (CLS).

✅ Correct: Add width and height to the <img>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: <source> Without srcset
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: A <source> must have a srcset (or src).

✅ Correct: 

<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Styling <picture> Instead of <img>
docs.text:
picture {
    width: 100%;
    height: auto;
    border-radius: 8px;
}

Why it's wrong: <picture> has no rendering; styles should be on the <img>.

✅ Correct: 

picture img {
    width: 100%;
    height: auto;
    border-radius: 8px;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Fallback for Older Browsers
docs.text:
<picture>
    <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: Older browsers show nothing (no <img>).

✅ Correct: Always include <img>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nested <picture>
docs.text:
<picture>
    <picture>
        <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
    </picture>
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="A photo">
</picture>

Why it's wrong: <picture> cannot be nested.

✅ Correct: Use a single <picture>.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Format fallback – AVIF can reduce file size by 50% vs. JPEG.
  • Art direction – serving mobile-optimized crops reduces bytes.
  • Lazy loading – defer off-screen images.
  • Preloading – hero images can be preloaded with imagesrcset.
  • Fetch priority – fetchpriority="high" for LCP images.
  • Decoding – decoding="async" for non-critical images.
  • Caching – each candidate is cached separately.
  • CDN – use a CDN for global delivery.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use AVIF – best compression.
  2. Use WebP – fallback for AVIF.
  3. Lazy load – below the fold.
  4. Preload – hero images.
  5. Use fetchpriority – for LCP.
  6. Set dimensions – prevent CLS.
  7. Compress images – before uploading.
  8. Use a CDN – for global delivery.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• SVG injection – sanitize user-uploaded SVGs.
  • EXIF data – strip GPS coordinates.
  • Hotlinking – use a CDN or referrer policy.
  • Mixed content – HTTPS pages should load HTTPS images.
  • CSP – restrict image sources with img-src.
  • CORS – use crossorigin when needed.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Strip EXIF – for user-uploaded images.
  2. Sanitize SVG – remove scripts.
  3. Use HTTPS – for all images.
  4. Set img-src in CSP – restrict sources.
  5. Use referrerpolicy – for sensitive images.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <picture>, <source>, and <img>.
  • Computed styles – check the <img> styles.
  • Network panel – verify which image was loaded.
  • Console – use img.currentSrc to see the chosen URL.
  • img.naturalWidth – intrinsic width.
  • Lighthouse – audits for image optimization.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the img role and name.
  • Test with prefers-color-scheme – in DevTools Rendering panel.
  • Test with different viewports – to verify art direction.
  • Test in Safari – for AVIF support.
  • Test with JavaScript disabled – native behavior.
  • Validate HTML – check for required <img>.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For format fallback – AVIF/WebP with JPEG fallback.
  • For art direction – different crops for different viewports.
  • For dark mode images – via prefers-color-scheme.
  • For print-specific images – via media="print".
  • For orientation-based images – via media="(orientation: ...)".
  • For combining multiple conditions – type + media + srcset.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For simple resolution switching – use <img srcset>.
  • For SVG – resolution-independent.
  • For background images – use CSS background-image.
  • For small icons – use SVG or icon fonts.
  • For a single image – no need for <picture>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <img> – the image element.
  • <source> – candidate source.
  • srcset – candidate images.
  • sizes – display sizes.
  • media – media query.
  • type – MIME type.
  • currentSrc – the URL actually used.
  • loading – lazy/eager.
  • fetchpriority – fetch priority.
  • decoding – sync/async.
  • prefers-color-scheme – color scheme media query.
  • orientation – orientation media query.
  • image-set() – CSS image candidates.
  • Preload – <link rel="preload">.
  • AVIF, WebP – modern formats.
  • LCP – Largest Contentful Paint.
  • CLS – Cumulative Layout Shift.
  • DPR – Device Pixel Ratio.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <picture> element was introduced through the Responsive Images Community Group (RICG).

  • It was inspired by the <video> and <audio> elements, which also use <source> children.

  • The <img> inside <picture> is required — it's the fallback for browsers that don't support <picture>.

  • The <picture> element is not exposed to the accessibility tree — only the <img> is.

  • The order of <source> elements matters — the first matching one wins.

  • The type attribute is checked before the image is downloaded — the browser trusts the MIME type.

  • AVIF offers up to 50% better compression than JPEG.

  • WebP offers about 25–35% better compression than JPEG.

  • Safari added AVIF support in 2022 (Safari 16).

  • The <source> element is used in both <picture> and <video>/<audio>, but the attributes differ.

  • The media attribute accepts any valid CSS media query.

  • prefers-color-scheme is a media query for light/dark mode.

  • orientation is a media query for landscape/portrait.

  • Print-specific images can be served with media="print".

  • The <picture> element has no rendering — it's a transparent wrapper.

  • CSS should target the <img>, not the <picture>.

  • currentSrc tells you which image the browser chose.

  • srcset inside <source> uses the same syntax as <img srcset>.

  • You cannot mix w and x descriptors in the same srcset.

  • Preloading a <picture> source requires imagesrcset and imagesizes.

  • The fallback for <picture>-unaware browsers is the <img> element.

  • Best practices include always including <img>, putting alt on the <img>, and ordering sources correctly.

  • Common mistakes include missing <img>, wrong source order, and no type.

  • Following best practices for <picture> leads to faster, sharper, and more efficient web pages.

  • The <picture> element is essential for modern responsive design — it solves problems that srcset alone cannot.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <picture> element provides multiple image sources for a single <img>.
  • It is used for art direction (different images for different layouts) and format fallback (AVIF/WebP with JPEG fallback).
  • It contains zero or more <source> elements and exactly one <img> (required).
  • The <img> carries the alt, width, height, class, id, loading, and fetchpriority.
  • The <source> elements carry srcset, sizes, media, and type.
  • The browser evaluates <source> elements in order and picks the first match.
  • Order matters: put modern formats first, then more specific media queries.
  • media is for art direction; type is for format fallback.
  • srcset + sizes inside a <source> enables resolution switching.
  • Best practices: always include <img>, put alt on the <img>, order sources correctly, and test in multiple browsers.
  • Common mistakes include missing <img>, wrong source order, no type, and putting alt on <source>.
  • <picture> is essential for modern responsive design — it solves problems that srcset alone cannot.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML-based markup language for describing two-dimensional vector graphics. Unlike raster image formats (JPEG, PNG, WebP) that store images as a grid of pixels, SVG stores images as mathematical descriptions of shapes, paths, lines, curves, and text. This means SVG images can be scaled to any size without losing quality — they are resolution-independent.

SVG is not just an image format — it is a full graphics platform with support for:

  • Shapes (rectangles, circles, ellipses, lines, polygons, polylines, paths).
  • Styling (fill, stroke, gradients, patterns, filters).
  • Animation (SMIL, CSS, JavaScript).
  • Interactivity (hover, click, focus).
  • Text (with full font support).
  • Accessibility (roles, titles, descriptions).

In HTML, SVG can be used in three ways:

  1. As an image — <img src="icon.svg" alt="Icon">.
  2. Inline in HTML — <svg>...</svg> directly in the document.
  3. As a CSS background — background-image: url('icon.svg').

Example (inline SVG): 

<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100" aria-label="A blue circle">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
SVG serves several essential purposes:

  • Resolution independence – looks sharp at any size and DPI.
  • Small file size – simple graphics are much smaller than raster equivalents.
  • Scalability – perfect for logos, icons, and illustrations.
  • Animation – can be animated with CSS, SMIL, or JavaScript.
  • Interactivity – elements can respond to user events.
  • Accessibility – can be described with titles, descriptions, and ARIA.
  • Styling – can be styled with CSS (inline SVG).
  • Programmability – can be manipulated with JavaScript via the DOM.
  • Searchability – text in SVG is real text, indexed by search engines.
  • Print quality – vector graphics print perfectly at any size.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
SVG is both a standalone image format and an inline markup language embedded in HTML. It is embedded content and phrasing content when inline. It appears wherever images appear:

  • Icons – navigation, buttons, UI elements.
  • Logos – company branding.
  • Illustrations – diagrams, infographics.
  • Charts and graphs – data visualization.
  • Maps – interactive maps.
  • Animations – animated illustrations.
  • Backgrounds – decorative patterns.
<!-- As an image -->
<img src="logo.svg" alt="Company logo" width="200" height="60">

<!-- Inline in HTML -->
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M12 2L2 22h20L12 2z" fill="currentColor"/>
</svg>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before SVG, web graphics were raster-only. Raster formats (GIF, JPEG, PNG) store images as a grid of pixels. This creates several problems:

  1. Resolution dependence – a raster image has a fixed resolution. Scaling it up makes it blurry; scaling it down wastes pixels.
  2. Retina displays – high-DPI screens require 2× or 3× images, increasing file size.
  3. Large file sizes – simple graphics (logos, icons) require many pixels to look sharp, bloating file sizes.
  4. No animation – GIFs were the only animated format, and they were large and limited to 256 colors.
  5. No interactivity – raster images can't respond to clicks or hover.
  6. No programmability – you can't manipulate individual shapes in a raster image.
  7. No searchable text – text baked into an image is invisible to search engines.
  8. No accessibility – raster images need alt text, but can't describe complex structures.

For logos, icons, and illustrations, these limitations were severe. A company logo needed multiple resolutions for different devices, multiple formats for different contexts, and couldn't be animated or interacted with.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Fixed resolution Blurry when scaled up Large file sizes Slow loading No animation (except GIF) Limited motion graphics No interactivity Static images No programmability Can't manipulate shapes No searchable text Poor SEO No accessibility structure Only alt text Retina issues Multiple images needed

docs.title: Why SVG Was Introduced
docs.text:
SVG was developed by the W3C and became a W3C Recommendation in 2001 (SVG 1.0). It was designed to solve the problems of raster graphics on the web by using vector math instead of pixels.

SVG was inspired by:

  • PostScript – Adobe's page description language.
  • PGML (Precision Graphics Markup Language) – submitted by Adobe, IBM, Netscape, and Sun.
  • VML (Vector Markup Language) – submitted by Microsoft and Macromedia.

The W3C combined these into SVG, an XML-based vector graphics format.

SVG enables:

  • Resolution independence – vector math scales perfectly.
  • Small file sizes – simple graphics are compact.
  • Animation – via SMIL, CSS, or JavaScript.
  • Interactivity – elements can be interactive.
  • Programmability – DOM access to every shape.
  • Accessibility – titles, descriptions, ARIA.
  • Searchability – text is real text.
  • Styling – CSS support.

SVG was initially slow to gain adoption due to poor browser support (especially Internet Explorer). But with the rise of HTML5 and modern browsers, SVG is now universally supported and is the standard format for icons, logos, and illustrations on the web.

docs.title: Three Ways to Use SVG in HTML
docs.text:
1. As an image (external SVG file):

<img src="icon.svg" alt="Settings icon" width="24" height="24">

2. Inline SVG (inside HTML):

<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100" aria-label="A blue circle">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>

3. As a CSS background:

.icon {
    background-image: url('icon.svg');
    background-size: contain;
    background-repeat: no-repeat;
}

docs.title: The <svg> Root Element
docs.text:
The <svg> element is the root of an SVG document (or inline SVG). It defines the coordinate system and the viewport.

<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    ...
</svg>
Attribute Purpose width The rendered width of the SVG height The rendered height of the SVG viewBox The coordinate system (min-x min-y width height) preserveAspectRatio How to fit the viewBox into the viewport xmlns The XML namespace (for standalone SVG) role ARIA role (e.g., img) aria-label Accessible name

docs.title: Basic Shapes
docs.text:
SVG provides basic shapes as elements:

Element Shape <rect> Rectangle <circle> Circle <ellipse> Ellipse <line> Line <polyline> Polyline <polygon> Polygon <path> Arbitrary path

docs.title: Rectangle
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <rect x="10" y="10" width="180" height="80" fill="blue" />
</svg>

docs.title: Circle
docs.text:
<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="red" />
</svg>

docs.title: Ellipse
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <ellipse cx="100" cy="50" rx="90" ry="40" fill="green" />
</svg>

docs.title: Line
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <line x1="10" y1="10" x2="190" y2="90" stroke="black" stroke-width="2" />
</svg>

docs.title: Polygon
docs.text:
<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <polygon points="50,10 90,90 10,90" fill="purple" />
</svg>

docs.title: Polyline
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <polyline points="10,80 50,20 90,60 130,10 170,80" fill="none" stroke="blue" stroke-width="2" />
</svg>

docs.title: Path (Most Powerful)
docs.text:
The <path> element is the most versatile shape, capable of drawing any 2D shape.

<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <path d="M10 50 Q 50 10, 90 50 T 90 90 L 10 90 Z" fill="orange" />
</svg>

Path commands:

Command Purpose M Move to (absolute) m Move to (relative) L Line to (absolute) l Line to (relative) H / h Horizontal line V / v Vertical line C / c Cubic Bézier curve S / s Smooth cubic Bézier Q / q Quadratic Bézier curve T / t Smooth quadratic Bézier A / a Arc Z / z Close path

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="50" viewBox="0 0 200 50">
    <text x="10" y="30" font-family="Arial" font-size="20" fill="black">Hello, SVG!</text>
</svg>

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <g fill="blue">
        <rect x="10" y="10" width="80" height="80" />
        <circle cx="150" cy="50" r="40" />
    </g>
</svg>

docs.title: Gradients
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <defs>
        <linearGradient id="grad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
            <stop offset="0%" stop-color="blue" />
            <stop offset="100%" stop-color="red" />
        </linearGradient>
    </defs>
    <rect x="10" y="10" width="180" height="80" fill="url(#grad)" />
</svg>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element/Attribute Purpose <svg> Root container viewBox Coordinate system <rect> Rectangle <circle> Circle <ellipse> Ellipse <line> Line <polyline> Polyline <polygon> Polygon <path> Arbitrary path <text> Text <g> Group <defs> Definitions (gradients, filters) <linearGradient> Linear gradient <radialGradient> Radial gradient fill Fill color stroke Stroke color stroke-width Stroke width

docs.title: The "Blueprint" Analogy
docs.text: Think of SVG as a blueprint for a building. A blueprint doesn't contain the building itself — it contains the instructions to build it. You can build the building at any scale, and it will always be the same building. Similarly, an SVG file contains instructions (shapes and paths), not pixels. It can be rendered at any size.

docs.title: The "Vector vs. Raster" Mental Model
docs.text:
• Raster (JPEG, PNG) = Mosaic art. Thousands of tiny colored tiles. Zoom in, and you see the tiles.
  • SVG = Pencil drawing. Lines and curves described mathematically. Zoom in, and the lines stay smooth.

docs.title: The "DOM for Graphics" Mental Model
docs.text:
Inline SVG is part of the HTML DOM. Every SVG element (<circle>, <rect>, <path>) is a DOM node that can be:

  • Styled with CSS.
  • Manipulated with JavaScript.
  • Made interactive with event listeners.
  • Animated.

This makes SVG a programmable graphics platform, not just an image format.

docs.title: The "Three Lives of SVG" Mental Model
docs.text:
SVG has three lives depending on how it's used:

  1. As an image (<img src="...">) — a black box, no CSS, no JS access, no interactivity.
  2. Inline in HTML — full access to CSS, JS, and DOM. Interactive and programmable.
  3. As a CSS background — decorative, no accessibility, no interactivity.

Choosing the right use is critical.

docs.title: The "Path is Everything" Mental Model
docs.text: The <path> element can draw any shape — lines, curves, arcs, and combinations. In fact, most SVG icons are only paths. Learning path syntax (M, L, C, Z) is the key to creating and understanding SVG graphics.

docs.title: The "Coordinate System" Mental Model
docs.text:
SVG uses a coordinate system where:

  • (0, 0) is the top-left corner.
  • x increases to the right.
  • y increases downward.
  • Units are user units (not pixels, though they often correspond).

The viewBox defines this coordinate system, independent of the rendered size.

docs.title: Concept 1: The viewBox Attribute
docs.text:
The viewBox attribute defines the coordinate system of the SVG:

viewBox="min-x min-y width height"
  • min-x, min-y – the top-left corner of the viewBox.
  • width, height – the size of the viewBox.

Example: 

<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 50">

  • The viewBox is 100 × 50 units.
  • The rendered size is 200 × 100 pixels.
  • The scale factor is 2×.

Why it matters: The viewBox makes SVG resolution-independent. You can render the same SVG at any size.

docs.title: Concept 2: preserveAspectRatio
docs.text:
Controls how the viewBox fits into the viewport:

<svg viewBox="0 0 100 50" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet">
Value Behaviour xMidYMid meet (default) Center, scale to fit xMinYMin meet Top-left, scale to fit xMidYMid slice Center, scale to cover none Stretch to fill

docs.title: Concept 3: The Coordinate System
docs.text:
SVG coordinates start at (0, 0) in the top-left:

(0,0) ────────────► x
  │
  │
  │
  ▼
  y
  • x increases to the right.
  • y increases downward.

docs.title: Concept 4: Fill and Stroke
docs.text:
Shapes have two visual properties:

  • fill – the interior color (default: black).
  • stroke – the outline color (default: none).
<rect x="10" y="10" width="80" height="80" fill="blue" stroke="black" stroke-width="2" />

Values:

  • Named colors (red, blue).
  • Hex (#ff0000).
  • rgb(), rgba(), hsl().
  • none – no fill/stroke.
  • currentColor – inherits from CSS color.

docs.title: Concept 5: Groups (<g>)
docs.text:
The <g> element groups shapes. Common attributes applied to the group are inherited by children:

<g fill="blue" stroke="black" stroke-width="2">
    <rect x="10" y="10" width="80" height="80" />
    <circle cx="150" cy="50" r="40" />
</g>

docs.title: Concept 6: defs and use
docs.text:
The <defs> element defines reusable graphics. The <use> element references them:

<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <defs>
        <circle id="dot" cx="0" cy="0" r="10" fill="red" />
    </defs>
    <use href="#dot" x="30" y="50" />
    <use href="#dot" x="100" y="50" />
    <use href="#dot" x="170" y="50" />
</svg>

docs.title: Concept 7: Gradients
docs.text:
Linear gradient:

<defs>
    <linearGradient id="lg" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
        <stop offset="0%" stop-color="blue" />
        <stop offset="100%" stop-color="red" />
    </linearGradient>
</defs>
<rect width="100" height="100" fill="url(#lg)" />

Radial gradient:

<defs>
    <radialGradient id="rg" cx="50%" cy="50%" r="50%">
        <stop offset="0%" stop-color="white" />
        <stop offset="100%" stop-color="black" />
    </radialGradient>
</defs>

docs.title: Concept 8: Text
docs.text:
SVG text is real text — selectable, searchable, and accessible:

<text x="10" y="30" font-family="Arial" font-size="20" fill="black">
    Hello, SVG!
</text>

docs.title: Concept 9: Paths
docs.text:
The <path> element is the most powerful. Its d attribute contains path commands:

M10 10 L90 10 L90 90 L10 90 Z
  • M10 10 – move to (10, 10).
  • L90 10 – line to (90, 10).
  • L90 90 – line to (90, 90).
  • L10 90 – line to (10, 90).
  • Z – close path.

docs.title: Concept 10: Inline SVG vs. External SVG
docs.text: Aspect Inline SVG External SVG (<img>) CSS styling Yes No (limited) JavaScript access Yes No Interactivity Yes No Caching No (part of HTML) Yes Accessibility Full (title, desc, ARIA) alt only Use case Icons, interactive graphics Logos, illustrations

docs.title: Concept 11: SVG in <img>
docs.text:
<img src="logo.svg" alt="Company logo" width="200" height="60">

Pros: Cacheable, simple, no inline code. Cons: No CSS/JS access, no interactivity, limited accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 12: Inline SVG
docs.text:
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M12 2L2 22h20L12 2z" fill="currentColor"/>
</svg>

Pros: Full CSS/JS access, interactivity, accessibility. Cons: Not cacheable, bloats HTML.

docs.title: Concept 13: SVG Accessibility
docs.text:
Inline SVG supports:

  • <title> – accessible name.
  • <desc> – accessible description.
  • role="img" – identifies as an image.
  • aria-label / aria-labelledby – accessible name.
  • aria-hidden="true" – decorative.
<svg role="img" aria-labelledby="svg-title" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
    <title id="svg-title">A blue circle</title>
    <circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10" fill="blue" />
</svg>

docs.title: Concept 14: SVG Animation
docs.text:
SVG can be animated in three ways:

  1. SMIL (declarative):
<circle cx="50" cy="50" r="20" fill="blue">
    <animate attributeName="r" from="20" to="40" dur="1s" repeatCount="indefinite" />
</circle>
  1. CSS (for inline SVG):
circle {
    animation: pulse 1s infinite;
}
@keyframes pulse {
    0%, 100% { r: 20; }
    50% { r: 40; }
}
  1. JavaScript (full control).

docs.title: Concept 15: SVG Filters
docs.text:
SVG has powerful filters:

<defs>
    <filter id="blur">
        <feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="5" />
    </filter>
</defs>
<circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" filter="url(#blur)" />

docs.title: Concept 16: SVG Masks and Clips
docs.text:
• <clipPath> – clips content to a shape.
  • <mask> – masks content using luminance.

docs.title: Concept 17: SVG Patterns
docs.text:
<defs>
    <pattern id="stripes" width="20" height="20" patternUnits="userSpaceOnUse">
        <rect width="10" height="20" fill="blue" />
        <rect x="10" width="10" height="20" fill="white" />
    </pattern>
</defs>
<rect width="200" height="100" fill="url(#stripes)" />

docs.title: Concept 18: SVG Symbols
docs.text:
The <symbol> element defines a reusable symbol:

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="display: none;">
    <symbol id="icon-star" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
        <path d="M12 2l3 7h7l-6 4 2 7-6-4-6 4 2-7-6-4h7z" />
    </symbol>
</svg>

<svg width="24" height="24"><use href="#icon-star" /></svg>

Use case: Icon sprites.

docs.title: Concept 19: SVG and CSS
docs.text:
Inline SVG can be styled with CSS:

.icon {
    fill: currentColor;
    stroke: none;
    width: 24px;
    height: 24px;
}
.icon:hover {
    fill: blue;
}

Note: fill and stroke are CSS properties in SVG.

docs.title: Concept 20: SVG and JavaScript
docs.text:
const circle = document.querySelector('circle');
circle.addEventListener('click', () => {
    circle.setAttribute('fill', 'red');
});

docs.title: Concept 21: SVG File Structure
docs.text:
An external SVG file is an XML document:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>

docs.title: Concept 22: SVG Optimization
docs.text:
• SVGO – the standard SVG optimizer.
  • Remove metadata, comments, and unnecessary attributes.
  • Round coordinates.
  • Use <use> for repeated shapes.
  • Minify paths.

docs.title: Concept 23: SVG Browser Support
docs.text: SVG is supported in all modern browsers. IE 9+ supports basic SVG; IE 11 supports most features.

docs.title: Concept 24: SVG vs. Canvas
docs.text: Aspect SVG Canvas Type Vector Raster DOM Yes (inline) No CSS Yes No Accessibility Yes No Performance Good for few shapes Good for many shapes Use case Icons, logos, charts Games, image processing

docs.title: Concept 25: SVG vs. Icon Fonts
docs.text:
Aspect SVG Icon Fonts Resolution Any Any Color Multi-color Single color Accessibility Full Limited Performance Good Good Use case Modern icons Legacy icons

Best practice: Use SVG for icons, not icon fonts.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Rendering Inline SVG
docs.text:
1.  The parser encounters an `<svg>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the SVG.
    │
    ▼
3.  It reads the `viewBox`, `width`, `height`.
    │
    ▼
4.  It processes child elements:
    │   ├── `<rect>` → creates a rect node.
    │   ├── `<circle>` → creates a circle node.
    │   ├── `<path>` → creates a path node.
    │   └── etc.
    │
    ▼
5.  It applies CSS styles.
    │
    ▼
6.  It computes the geometry:
    │   ├── Coordinates are in user units.
    │   └── Scaled to fit the viewport.
    │
    ▼
7.  It rasterizes the SVG to pixels.
    │
    ▼
8.  It paints the SVG on the screen.
    │
    ▼
9.  The SVG is part of the DOM.
    │   ├── CSS can style it.
    │   ├── JavaScript can manipulate it.
    │   └── Events can be attached.

docs.title: The viewBox Transformation
docs.text:
viewBox: 0 0 100 50
Viewport: 200 × 100

Scale: 200/100 = 2 (x), 100/50 = 2 (y)

A point at (50, 25) in user units → (100, 50) in pixels.

docs.title: SVG Rendering Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Parse – XML is parsed into a DOM.
  2. Style – CSS is applied.
  3. Layout – geometry is computed.
  4. Paint – the SVG is rasterized.

For inline SVG, the SVG is part of the main DOM and rendering pipeline.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
Inline SVG with role="img" is exposed as:

  • role: img
  • name: from <title>, aria-label, or aria-labelledby.
  • description: from <desc>.

Screen readers announce: "A blue circle, image."

docs.title: SVG Animation
docs.text:
• SMIL – the browser's SVG animation engine.
  • CSS – the browser's CSS animation engine (for inline SVG).
  • JavaScript – the browser's JS engine (DOM manipulation).

docs.title: SVG Filters
docs.text:
Filters are applied during the paint phase. They use a filter pipeline:

Input → Filter Primitive 1 → Filter Primitive 2 → Output

Each primitive (feGaussianBlur, feColorMatrix, etc.) transforms the image.

docs.title: The SVGSVGElement Interface
docs.text: Property/Method Description viewBox The viewBox object width The width height The height currentScale The current scale factor currentTranslate The current translation createSVGPoint() Creates an SVGPoint createSVGMatrix() Creates an SVGMatrix getElementById() Finds an element by ID

docs.title: The SVGElement Interface
docs.text: All SVG elements inherit from SVGElement, which inherits from Element.

docs.title: Common SVG Interfaces
docs.text: Element Interface <svg> SVGSVGElement <g> SVGGElement <rect> SVGRectElement <circle> SVGCircleElement <ellipse> SVGEllipseElement <line> SVGLineElement <polyline> SVGPolylineElement <polygon> SVGPolygonElement <path> SVGPathElement <text> SVGTextElement <use> SVGUseElement <defs> SVGDefsElement <linearGradient> SVGLinearGradientElement <radialGradient> SVGRadialGradientElement

docs.title: SVG Attributes vs. CSS Properties
docs.text:
Many SVG attributes have CSS equivalents:

Attribute CSS Property fill fill stroke stroke stroke-width stroke-width opacity opacity transform transform

Best practice: Use CSS for styling; use attributes for geometry.

docs.title: The SVG DOM
docs.text:
Inline SVG is part of the HTML DOM. You can:

const svg = document.querySelector('svg');
const circle = svg.querySelector('circle');
circle.setAttribute('fill', 'red');

docs.title: SVG Namespaces
docs.text:
SVG uses the namespace http://www.w3.org/2000/svg. When creating SVG elements dynamically:

const svgNS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';
const circle = document.createElementNS(svgNS, 'circle');
circle.setAttribute('cx', '50');
circle.setAttribute('cy', '50');
circle.setAttribute('r', '40');

docs.title: SVG vs. HTML Parsing
docs.text:
• HTML parser – handles <svg> as foreign content.
  • XML parser – handles SVG as XML.

This means:

  • Case sensitivity: SVG elements are case-sensitive (<linearGradient>, not <lineargradient>).
  • Self-closing: <circle /> is valid in SVG.
  • Namespaces: required for standalone SVG.

docs.title: SVG Caching
docs.text:
• External SVG – cached like any other image.
  • Inline SVG – not cached (part of HTML).
  • SVG sprites – the sprite file is cached; <use> references it.

docs.title: SVG Optimization
docs.text:
SVGO removes:

  • XML declarations.
  • Comments.
  • Metadata.
  • Unnecessary attributes.
  • Unused elements.
  • Redundant paths.

It also:

  • Minifies path data.
  • Rounds coordinates.
  • Merges paths.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an SVG
docs.text:
1.  Author writes SVG (inline or external).
    │
    ▼
2.  File deployed (or embedded in HTML).
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses SVG:
    │   ├── Inline: part of HTML parsing.
    │   └── External: separate XML parsing.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser creates DOM nodes for SVG elements.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser applies CSS styles.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser computes geometry.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser rasterizes and paints.
    │
    ▼
8.  SVG is interactive (if inline).
    │   ├── CSS can style it.
    │   ├── JS can manipulate it.
    │   └── Events can be attached.
    │
    ▼
9.  SVG may be animated.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the SVG is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic SVG Creation
docs.text:
const svgNS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';
const svg = document.createElementNS(svgNS, 'svg');
svg.setAttribute('viewBox', '0 0 100 100');
svg.setAttribute('width', '100');
svg.setAttribute('height', '100');

const circle = document.createElementNS(svgNS, 'circle');
circle.setAttribute('cx', '50');
circle.setAttribute('cy', '50');
circle.setAttribute('r', '40');
circle.setAttribute('fill', 'blue');

svg.appendChild(circle);
document.body.appendChild(svg);

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Circle
docs.text:
<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 2: Rectangle with Stroke
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <rect x="10" y="10" width="180" height="80" fill="none" stroke="black" stroke-width="2" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 3: Polygon (Triangle)
docs.text:
<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <polygon points="50,10 90,90 10,90" fill="purple" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 5: Grouped Shapes
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <g fill="blue" stroke="black" stroke-width="2">
        <rect x="10" y="10" width="80" height="80" />
        <circle cx="150" cy="50" r="40" />
    </g>
</svg>

docs.title: Example 6: Linear Gradient
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <defs>
        <linearGradient id="grad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
            <stop offset="0%" stop-color="blue" />
            <stop offset="100%" stop-color="red" />
        </linearGradient>
    </defs>
    <rect x="10" y="10" width="180" height="80" fill="url(#grad)" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 7: Radial Gradient
docs.text:
<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <defs>
        <radialGradient id="rgrad" cx="50%" cy="50%" r="50%">
            <stop offset="0%" stop-color="white" />
            <stop offset="100%" stop-color="blue" />
        </radialGradient>
    </defs>
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="url(#rgrad)" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 8: Text
docs.text:
<svg width="300" height="50" viewBox="0 0 300 50">
    <text x="10" y="30" font-family="Arial" font-size="24" fill="black">Hello, SVG!</text>
</svg>

docs.title: Example 9: Reusable Symbol (<use>)
docs.text:
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="display: none;">
    <symbol id="icon-check" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
        <path d="M9 16.17L4.83 12l-1.42 1.41L9 19 21 7l-1.41-1.41z" />
    </symbol>
</svg>

<svg width="24" height="24"><use href="#icon-check" fill="green" /></svg>
<svg width="24" height="24"><use href="#icon-check" fill="red" /></svg>

docs.title: Example 10: Inline Icon with currentColor
docs.text:
<style>
    .icon {
        width: 24px;
        height: 24px;
        fill: currentColor;
    }
    .link { color: #3498db; }
    .link:hover { color: #2980b9; }
</style>

<a href="#" class="link">
    <svg class="icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">
        <path d="M12 2l3 7h7l-6 4 2 7-6-4-6 4 2-7-6-4h7z" />
    </svg>
    Click me
</a>

docs.title: Example 11: Accessible SVG
docs.text:
<svg role="img" aria-labelledby="svg-title svg-desc" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="100" height="100">
    <title id="svg-title">A blue circle</title>
    <desc id="svg-desc">A blue circle with a black outline on a white background.</desc>
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" stroke="black" stroke-width="2" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 12: Decorative SVG
docs.text:
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="100" height="100" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>

Note: focusable="false" prevents IE 11 from focusing the SVG.

docs.title: Example 13: Animated SVG (CSS)
docs.text:
<style>
    .pulse {
        animation: pulse 1s infinite;
    }
    @keyframes pulse {
        0%, 100% { r: 20; }
        50% { r: 40; }
    }
</style>

<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle class="pulse" cx="50" cy="50" r="20" fill="blue" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 14: Animated SVG (SMIL)
docs.text:
<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="20" fill="blue">
        <animate attributeName="r" from="20" to="40" dur="1s" repeatCount="indefinite" />
    </circle>
</svg>

docs.title: Example 15: SVG with Filter
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100">
    <defs>
        <filter id="blur">
            <feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="3" />
        </filter>
    </defs>
    <circle cx="100" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" filter="url(#blur)" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 16: SVG Chart (Bar Chart)
docs.text:
<svg width="300" height="200" viewBox="0 0 300 200" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart showing quarterly sales">
    <title>Quarterly Sales</title>
    <!-- Axes -->
    <line x1="40" y1="10" x2="40" y2="180" stroke="black" />
    <line x1="40" y1="180" x2="290" y2="180" stroke="black" />
    <!-- Bars -->
    <rect x="60" y="100" width="40" height="80" fill="#3498db" />
    <rect x="120" y="70" width="40" height="110" fill="#3498db" />
    <rect x="180" y="40" width="40" height="140" fill="#3498db" />
    <rect x="240" y="60" width="40" height="120" fill="#3498db" />
    <!-- Labels -->
    <text x="70" y="195" font-size="12">Q1</text>
    <text x="130" y="195" font-size="12">Q2</text>
    <text x="190" y="195" font-size="12">Q3</text>
    <text x="250" y="195" font-size="12">Q4</text>
</svg>

docs.title: Example 17: SVG Icon Sprite
docs.text:
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="display: none;">
    <symbol id="icon-home" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
        <path d="M10 20v-6h4v6h5v-8h3L12 3 2 12h3v8z" />
    </symbol>
    <symbol id="icon-user" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
        <path d="M12 12c2.21 0 4-1.79 4-4s-1.79-4-4-4-4 1.79-4 4 1.79 4 4 4zm0 2c-2.67 0-8 1.34-8 4v2h16v-2c0-2.66-5.33-4-8-4z" />
    </symbol>
</svg>

<svg width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#icon-home" /></svg>
<svg width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#icon-user" /></svg>

docs.title: Example 18: SVG Logo
docs.text:
<svg width="200" height="60" viewBox="0 0 200 60" role="img" aria-label="Acme Corp logo">
    <rect x="0" y="0" width="60" height="60" rx="8" fill="#3498db" />
    <text x="80" y="40" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" font-weight="bold" fill="#2c3e50">
        Acme Corp
    </text>
</svg>

docs.title: Example 19: Interactive SVG Map
docs.text:
<svg width="300" height="200" viewBox="0 0 300 200" role="img" aria-label="Map of regions">
    <title>Interactive Map</title>
    <path d="M10,10 L100,10 L100,100 L10,100 Z" fill="#3498db" stroke="white" stroke-width="2"
          tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="North region"
          onclick="alert('North')" />
    <path d="M110,10 L200,10 L200,100 L110,100 Z" fill="#e74c3c" stroke="white" stroke-width="2"
          tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="South region"
          onclick="alert('South')" />
    <path d="M210,10 L300,10 L300,100 L210,100 Z" fill="#27ae60" stroke="white" stroke-width="2"
          tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="East region"
          onclick="alert('East')" />
</svg>

docs.title: Example 20: Complete SVG Demo
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>SVG Demo</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 800px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        section { margin-bottom: 2rem; }
        .icon { width: 32px; height: 32px; fill: currentColor; vertical-align: middle; }
        .link { color: #3498db; text-decoration: none; display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem; }
        .link:hover { color: #2980b9; }
        .card { display: inline-block; padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 8px; margin: 0.5rem; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>SVG Demo</h1>

    <section>
        <h2>Basic Shapes</h2>
        <svg width="300" height="100" viewBox="0 0 300 100" aria-label="Shapes demo">
            <rect x="10" y="20" width="60" height="60" fill="#3498db" />
            <circle cx="120" cy="50" r="30" fill="#e74c3c" />
            <polygon points="200,20 230,80 170,80" fill="#27ae60" />
            <ellipse cx="270" cy="50" rx="25" ry="35" fill="#f39c12" />
        </svg>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Inline Icon (currentColor)</h2>
        <a href="#" class="link">
            <svg class="icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">
                <path d="M12 2l3 7h7l-6 4 2 7-6-4-6 4 2-7-6-4h7z" />
            </svg>
            Starred
        </a>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Gradient</h2>
        <svg width="200" height="100" viewBox="0 0 200 100" aria-label="Gradient demo">
            <defs>
                <linearGradient id="demo-grad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
                    <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#3498db" />
                    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#e74c3c" />
                </linearGradient>
            </defs>
            <rect x="10" y="10" width="180" height="80" rx="8" fill="url(#demo-grad)" />
        </svg>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Accessible SVG</h2>
        <svg role="img" aria-labelledby="chart-title chart-desc" width="300" height="200" viewBox="0 0 300 200">
            <title id="chart-title">Quarterly Sales</title>
            <desc id="chart-desc">Bar chart showing sales for Q1 through Q4, with Q3 highest.</desc>
            <line x1="40" y1="10" x2="40" y2="180" stroke="black" />
            <line x1="40" y1="180" x2="290" y2="180" stroke="black" />
            <rect x="60" y="100" width="40" height="80" fill="#3498db" />
            <rect x="120" y="70" width="40" height="110" fill="#3498db" />
            <rect x="180" y="40" width="40" height="140" fill="#3498db" />
            <rect x="240" y="60" width="40" height="120" fill="#3498db" />
            <text x="70" y="195" font-size="12">Q1</text>
            <text x="130" y="195" font-size="12">Q2</text>
            <text x="190" y="195" font-size="12">Q3</text>
            <text x="250" y="195" font-size="12">Q4</text>
        </svg>
    </section>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Technique Icons Inline SVG with currentColor Logos SVG <img> or inline Illustrations Inline SVG or external file Charts Inline SVG Maps Inline SVG with interactive paths Animations SMIL, CSS, or JS Background patterns SVG with <pattern> Icon sprites <symbol> + <use> Data visualization Inline SVG with JS UI elements Inline SVG for full CSS control

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use SVG for icons, logos, and illustrations.
  2. Use inline SVG for interactive/stylable graphics.
  3. Use <img> for simple logos/illustrations.
  4. Always include viewBox – for scalability.
  5. Use currentColor – for icons that inherit text color.
  6. Add <title> and <desc> – for accessibility.
  7. Use role="img" – for meaningful SVG.
  8. Use aria-hidden="true" – for decorative SVG.
  9. Add focusable="false" – to prevent IE 11 focus.
  10. Optimize with SVGO – remove unnecessary data.
  11. Use <symbol> + <use> – for icon sprites.
  12. Use fill="none" – for stroke-only icons.
  13. Set width/height – to prevent layout shift.
  14. Test with screen readers – ensure accessibility.
  15. Test on high-DPI displays – SVG scales perfectly.
  16. Use CSS for styling – not presentation attributes.
  17. Minify SVG – reduce file size.
  18. Inline critical SVG – for above-the-fold icons.
  19. Cache external SVG – for repeated use.
  20. Document your SVG strategy – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing viewBox
docs.text:
<svg width="100" height="100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>

Why it's wrong: Without viewBox, the SVG doesn't scale.

✅ Correct: 

<svg width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Accessibility
docs.text:
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24">
    <path d="M12 2l3 7h7l-6 4 2 7-6-4-6 4 2-7-6-4h7z" />
</svg>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers don't know what the SVG is.

✅ Correct: 

<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" role="img" aria-label="Star">
    <path d="M12 2l3 7h7l-6 4 2 7-6-4-6 4 2-7-6-4h7z" />
</svg>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Styling External SVG with CSS
docs.text:
<img src="icon.svg" class="icon">

.icon { fill: red; } /* Doesn't work */

Why it's wrong: External SVG is a separate document; CSS doesn't cross.

✅ Correct: Use inline SVG or mask-image.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting xmlns on Standalone SVG
docs.text:
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" />
</svg>

Why it's wrong: Standalone SVG files need xmlns.

✅ Correct: 

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" />
</svg>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using SVG for Photos
docs.text:
<img src="photo.svg" alt="A photo">

Why it's wrong: SVG is for vector graphics, not photos. Raster is better.

✅ Correct: Use JPEG/WebP for photos.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Fallback for Old Browsers
docs.text:
<svg>...</svg>

Why it's wrong: Very old browsers may not support SVG.

✅ Correct: 

<svg>...</svg>
<img src="fallback.png" alt="Fallback">

Note: Modern browsers all support SVG.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Inline SVG Bloat
docs.text:
<!-- Repeating the same SVG 100 times -->
<svg>...</svg>
<svg>...</svg>
<!-- ... -->

Why it's wrong: Bloats HTML; wastes bandwidth.

✅ Correct: Use <symbol> + <use>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing focusable="false"
docs.text:
<svg aria-hidden="true">...</svg>

Why it's wrong: IE 11 may focus the SVG.

✅ Correct: 

<svg aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">...</svg>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No width/height
docs.text:
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24">
    ...
</svg>

Why it's wrong: May cause layout shift.

✅ Correct: Add width and height.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Optimizing SVG
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Generator: Adobe Illustrator 15.0.0, SVG Export Plug-In . SVG Version: 6.00 Build 0) -->
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" ...>
    <!-- 100 lines of metadata -->
</svg>

Why it's wrong: Wastes bytes.

✅ Correct: Run through SVGO.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using SMIL for Everything
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: SMIL support varies; CSS is more consistent.

✅ Correct: Use CSS for simple animations.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing on Multiple Browsers
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: SVG rendering varies.

✅ Correct: Test on Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Small file size – SVG is often smaller than raster.
  • Gzip compression – SVG compresses very well.
  • Inline SVG – no extra HTTP request.
  • External SVG – cacheable.
  • SVG sprites – one request for many icons.
  • Rendering cost – complex SVG can be expensive.
  • Animation – SMIL/CSS is efficient; JS can be heavy.
  • Filters – expensive; use sparingly.
  • Masks – expensive; use sparingly.
  • Large paths – can be slow to render.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Optimize with SVGO.
  2. Use <symbol> + <use> for sprites.
  3. Inline critical SVG.
  4. Cache external SVG.
  5. Avoid complex filters.
  6. Simplify paths.
  7. Use CSS animations over JS.
  8. Test with Lighthouse.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• SVG injection – SVG can contain <script> and <foreignObject>.
  • Sanitize user SVG – remove scripts, event handlers, and external references.
  • Use DOMPurify – with SVG profile.
  • CSP – restrict SVG scripts.
  • External references – block external URLs.
  • Use as image – <img src="..."> is safe (scripts don't run).
  • Inline SVG – must be sanitized.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sanitize user SVG – always.
  2. Use DOMPurify – for sanitization.
  3. Block scripts – with CSP.
  4. Block external references.
  5. Prefer <img> for untrusted SVG.
  6. Validate SVG – before serving.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect SVG elements.
  • Computed styles – check fill, stroke.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check role and name.
  • Console – query SVG elements with querySelector.
  • getBBox() – get the bounding box.
  • getBoundingClientRect() – get the rendered size.
  • SVGOMG – online optimizer.
  • Lighthouse – audits for SVG.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure accessible name.
  • Test in multiple browsers.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For icons – inline SVG.
  • For logos – inline or <img>.
  • For illustrations – inline or <img>.
  • For charts – inline SVG.
  • For interactive graphics – inline SVG.
  • For animations – inline SVG.
  • For scalable graphics – SVG.
  • For print-quality graphics – SVG.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For photos – use JPEG/WebP/AVIF.
  • For complex scenes – use Canvas or WebGL.
  • For pixel-precise raster – use raster.
  • For very large graphics – raster may be smaller.
  • For video – use <video>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <img> – image element.
  • <picture> – responsive images.
  • <canvas> – raster graphics.
  • <svg> – SVG root.
  • <path> – SVG paths.
  • <symbol> – reusable symbols.
  • <use> – reuse symbols.
  • <defs> – definitions.
  • <linearGradient> – gradients.
  • <filter> – SVG filters.
  • <mask> – masking.
  • <clipPath> – clipping.
  • viewBox – coordinate system.
  • preserveAspectRatio – scaling.
  • SMIL – SVG animation.
  • CSS animations – for inline SVG.
  • DOMPurify – sanitization.
  • SVGO – optimization.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• SVG became a W3C Recommendation in 2001.

  • SVG was inspired by PostScript, PGML, and VML.

  • SVG uses XML syntax — case-sensitive, self-closing tags.

  • The viewBox attribute is what makes SVG resolution-independent.

  • SVG is part of the DOM when inline — CSS and JS work on every shape.

  • currentColor lets icons inherit the surrounding text color.

  • The <path> element can draw any 2D shape — most icons are only paths.

  • SVG files are text — they can be edited in a text editor.

  • SVG files compress extremely well with gzip.

  • SVGO is the standard SVG optimizer.

  • SVG sprites use <symbol> + <use> for efficiency.

  • SMIL is SVG's native animation language; CSS also works.

  • <foreignObject> allows HTML inside SVG.

  • SVG supports filters like blur, drop shadow, and color matrix.

  • SVG supports gradients, patterns, masks, and clips.

  • IE 9+ supports SVG; IE 11 supports most features.

  • Accessibility: use <title>, <desc>, role="img", and aria-label.

  • Decorative SVG should use aria-hidden="true" and focusable="false".

  • External SVG in <img> is sandboxed — scripts don't run.

  • Inline SVG can contain scripts — sanitize user-uploaded SVG.

  • Canvas is better for many shapes; SVG is better for few shapes.

  • SVG is better for accessibility, CSS, and interactivity.

  • Icon fonts are legacy; SVG is modern best practice.

  • Best practices include viewBox, accessibility, and optimization.

  • Common mistakes include missing viewBox, no accessibility, and no optimization.

  • Following best practices for SVG leads to sharp, accessible, and efficient graphics.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML-based format for 2D vector graphics.
  • It is resolution-independent — scales to any size without losing quality.
  • It can be used as an image (<img>), inline in HTML, or as a CSS background.
  • The <svg> root defines the viewport and coordinate system via viewBox.
  • Basic shapes: <rect>, <circle>, <ellipse>, <line>, <polyline>, <polygon>, <path>.
  • <path> is the most powerful — can draw any 2D shape.
  • Styling: fill, stroke, stroke-width; can be styled with CSS (inline).
  • Gradients: <linearGradient>, <radialGradient>.
  • Reuse: <defs>, <symbol>, <use>.
  • Animation: SMIL, CSS, JavaScript.
  • Accessibility: <title>, <desc>, role="img", aria-label, aria-hidden.
  • Best practices: viewBox, accessibility, optimization, and testing.
  • Common mistakes include missing viewBox, no accessibility, and no optimization.
  • SVG is essential for icons, logos, illustrations, charts, and interactive graphics on the modern web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <audio> element is an HTML element that embeds sound content directly into a web page. It allows developers to play audio files — music, podcasts, sound effects, voice recordings, and more — natively in the browser, without requiring third-party plugins like Adobe Flash or QuickTime. The element provides built-in playback controls, supports multiple audio formats through child <source> elements, and exposes a rich JavaScript API for programmatic control.

The <audio> element is a media element, alongside <video>. It is embedded content and phrasing content. It can appear anywhere phrasing content is accepted — inside <p>, <figure>, <div>, <li>, <td>, and more. It is one of the most important additions of HTML5, eliminating the plugin dependency that plagued the early web.

Example: 

<audio controls>
    <source src="podcast.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
    <source src="podcast.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
    <p>Your browser does not support the audio element.</p>
</audio>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <audio> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Native audio playback – no plugins required.
  • Multiple formats – fallback via <source> elements.
  • Playback controls – play, pause, volume, seek, download.
  • Programmatic control – play, pause, seek, volume via JavaScript.
  • Events – play, pause, ended, timeupdate, volumechange, etc.
  • Accessibility – keyboard-accessible controls; captions/transcripts via <track>.
  • Streaming – supports streaming audio (via HTTP range requests).
  • Background audio – for games, ambient sounds, notifications.
  • Podcasts and music – the primary delivery format for audio on the web.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <audio> element is embedded content and phrasing content. It is a block-level element when display: block is applied, but by default it is inline. It can be styled with CSS and controlled with JavaScript.

<figure>
    <audio controls preload="metadata">
        <source src="episode-1.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
        <source src="episode-1.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
        <track kind="captions" src="episode-1.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">
        <p>Your browser does not support the audio element. <a href="episode-1.mp3">Download the episode</a>.</p>
    </audio>
    <figcaption>Episode 1: The History of the Web</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before HTML5, playing audio on the web required plugins. The dominant plugin was Adobe Flash, but others included QuickTime, RealPlayer, Windows Media Player, and Silverlight. Each plugin:

  • Required a separate installation.
  • Had its own security vulnerabilities.
  • Was proprietary and platform-specific.
  • Was often buggy and resource-heavy.
  • Was inaccessible to assistive technologies.
  • Didn't work on mobile devices (notably, iOS never supported Flash).

This created a fragmented, fragile, and insecure ecosystem. Developers had to choose between multiple plugin technologies, and users had to install and maintain them.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Plugin dependency Users had to install Flash/QuickTime Security vulnerabilities Flash was a constant attack target Platform-specific Not available on all devices (iOS) Inaccessible Screen readers couldn't access plugins Battery drain Flash consumed excessive CPU No standardization Each plugin had its own API No mobile support Flash never worked on iOS No native API Developers couldn't control playback easily

docs.title: Why the <audio> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <audio> element was introduced in HTML5 (drafted in 2008, standardized in 2014) as part of the effort to eliminate plugin dependency. It was designed to:

  • Provide native audio – no plugin required.
  • Support multiple formats – with <source> fallbacks.
  • Expose a JavaScript API – play, pause, seek, volume.
  • Fire events – for synchronization with other content.
  • Be accessible – native controls are keyboard-accessible.
  • Work on mobile – iOS and Android support <audio> natively.
  • Support captions – via <track> (for video mainly, but also audio).
  • Be standardized – W3C/WHATWG specification.
