docs.title: Example 20: Complete Accessible Video Player
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Accessible Video Player</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 800px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        .player { background: #f8f9fa; padding: 1rem; border-radius: 8px; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; }
        video { width: 100%; height: auto; border-radius: 8px; background: #000; }
        .controls { display: flex; gap: 0.5rem; align-items: center; margin-top: 1rem; flex-wrap: wrap; }
        button { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; min-height: 44px; min-width: 44px; border: none; border-radius: 4px; background: #3498db; color: white; cursor: pointer; font-size: 1rem; }
        button:hover { background: #2980b9; }
        button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #2c3e50; outline-offset: 2px; }
        input[type="range"] { flex: 1; min-width: 150px; }
        .time { font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.875rem; color: #6c757d; }
        progress { width: 100%; height: 8px; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Accessible Video Player</h1>
    <div class="player">
        <video id="video" preload="metadata" poster="poster.jpg" playsinline>
            <source src="tutorial.mp4" type="video/mp4">
            <source src="tutorial.webm" type="video/webm">
            <track kind="captions" src="tutorial-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
            <track kind="captions" src="tutorial-es.vtt" srclang="es" label="Español">
            <track kind="descriptions" src="tutorial-desc.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio Description">
            <p>Your browser doesn't support video. <a href="tutorial.mp4" download>Download the video</a>.</p>
        </video>

        <progress id="progress" value="0" max="100" aria-label="Playback progress"></progress>
        <div class="time" id="timeDisplay">0:00 / 0:00</div>

        <div class="controls">
            <button id="playPauseBtn" aria-label="Play">▶ Play</button>
            <button id="backBtn" aria-label="Rewind 10 seconds">⏪ 10s</button>
            <button id="forwardBtn" aria-label="Forward 10 seconds">10s ⏩</button>
            <label for="volume">Volume:</label>
            <input type="range" id="volume" min="0" max="1" step="0.01" value="1" aria-label="Volume">
            <button id="fsBtn" aria-label="Fullscreen">⛶ Fullscreen</button>
            <button id="pipBtn" aria-label="Picture-in-Picture">⧉ PiP</button>
        </div>

        <div id="status" role="status" aria-live="polite" style="margin-top: 0.5rem; color: #6c757d;"></div>
    </div>

    <script>
        const video = document.getElementById('video');
        const playPauseBtn = document.getElementById('playPauseBtn');
        const backBtn = document.getElementById('backBtn');
        const forwardBtn = document.getElementById('forwardBtn');
        const volume = document.getElementById('volume');
        const progress = document.getElementById('progress');
        const timeDisplay = document.getElementById('timeDisplay');
        const status = document.getElementById('status');
        const fsBtn = document.getElementById('fsBtn');
        const pipBtn = document.getElementById('pipBtn');

        function formatTime(seconds) {
            if (isNaN(seconds)) return '0:00';
            const m = Math.floor(seconds / 60);
            const s = Math.floor(seconds % 60);
            return `${m}:${s.toString().padStart(2, '0')}`;
        }

        playPauseBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
            if (video.paused) {
                video.play();
            } else {
                video.pause();
            }
        });

        video.addEventListener('play', () => {
            playPauseBtn.textContent = '⏸ Pause';
            playPauseBtn.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Pause');
            status.textContent = 'Playing';
        });

        video.addEventListener('pause', () => {
            playPauseBtn.textContent = '▶ Play';
            playPauseBtn.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Play');
            status.textContent = 'Paused';
        });

        video.addEventListener('timeupdate', () => {
            progress.value = (video.currentTime / video.duration) * 100;
            timeDisplay.textContent = `${formatTime(video.currentTime)} / ${formatTime(video.duration)}`;
        });

        video.addEventListener('ended', () => {
            status.textContent = 'Finished';
            playPauseBtn.textContent = '▶ Play';
        });

        video.addEventListener('error', () => {
            status.textContent = 'Error loading video.';
        });

        backBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
            video.currentTime = Math.max(0, video.currentTime - 10);
        });

        forwardBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
            video.currentTime = Math.min(video.duration, video.currentTime + 10);
        });

        volume.addEventListener('input', () => {
            video.volume = volume.value;
        });

        progress.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
            const rect = progress.getBoundingClientRect();
            const percent = (e.clientX - rect.left) / rect.width;
            video.currentTime = percent * video.duration;
        });

        fsBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
            if (document.fullscreenElement) {
                document.exitFullscreen();
            } else {
                video.requestFullscreen();
            }
        });

        pipBtn.addEventListener('click', async () => {
            if (document.pictureInPictureElement) {
                await document.exitPictureInPicture();
            } else {
                await video.requestPictureInPicture();
            }
        });
    </script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example Tutorials Educational content with captions Marketing Product videos with autoplay (muted) Entertainment Movies, TV shows Video calls WebRTC video streams Background video Hero sections (muted autoplay) Live streaming HLS/DASH streams Video podcasts Video episodes Training Corporate training videos E-commerce Product demos Gaming Game trailers News Video reports Social media Short video clips

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always include controls – unless building custom controls.
  2. Provide multiple formats – MP4 (H.264) and WebM.
  3. Use preload="metadata" – for most cases.
  4. Never autoplay unmuted – it's hostile.
  5. Use playsinline – for iOS inline playback.
  6. Provide a poster – for visual context before playback.
  7. Set width/height – prevent layout shift.
  8. Provide captions – for accessibility (WCAG 1.2.2).
  9. Provide audio descriptions – for blind users (WCAG 1.2.5).
  10. Provide transcripts – for SEO and accessibility.
  11. Label custom controls – with aria-label.
  12. Support keyboard – Space to play/pause, arrows for seek.
  13. Show loading state – with loadstart, canplay.
  14. Handle errors – listen for error events.
  15. Use crossorigin – if using Canvas/Web Audio.
  16. Test on mobile – iOS and Android behave differently.
  17. Test with screen readers – ensure controls are announced.
  18. Compress video – use appropriate bitrate and codec.
  19. Use a CDN – for faster delivery.
  20. Consider adaptive streaming – for long videos.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Autoplay Unmuted
docs.text:
<video autoplay>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: Browsers block it; users hate it; wastes data.

✅ Correct: 

<video autoplay muted playsinline>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No controls
docs.text:
<video>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: No way for users to play/pause.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Single Format
docs.text:
<video controls src="video.webm">

Why it's wrong: Safari doesn't support WebM.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <source src="video.webm" type="video/webm">
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Poster
docs.text:
<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: Shows a blank or black box before playback.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls poster="poster.jpg">
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Captions
docs.text:
<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: Deaf and hard-of-hearing users can't access the content. WCAG violation.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No playsinline
docs.text:
<video autoplay muted>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: iOS forces fullscreen playback.

✅ Correct: 

<video autoplay muted playsinline>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No preload
docs.text:
<video controls>
    <source src="large-video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: Browser may preload the entire file, wasting bandwidth.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls preload="metadata">
    <source src="large-video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing type
docs.text:
<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: Browser must download the file to determine the format.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Fallback Content
docs.text:
<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: Users with old browsers see nothing.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support video. <a href="video.mp4">Download</a>.</p>
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Keyboard Support for Custom Controls
docs.text:
<div onclick="video.play()">Play</div>

Why it's wrong: Not keyboard-accessible.

✅ Correct: Use <button>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Error Handling
docs.text:
video.play();

Why it's wrong: If the file is missing, the promise rejects silently.

✅ Correct: 

video.play().catch(error => console.error('Playback failed:', error));

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No aria-label on Custom Controls
docs.text:
<button id="play">▶</button>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers announce "▶" with no context.

✅ Correct: 

<button id="play" aria-label="Play">▶</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing on iOS
docs.text:
<video autoplay>

Why it's wrong: iOS blocks autoplay and forces fullscreen.

✅ Correct: Test with playsinline and muted.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• File size – compress video; use appropriate bitrate and codec.
  • Format – MP4 (H.264) is universal; WebM (VP9) is smaller.
  • Preload – metadata avoids downloading the entire file.
  • Streaming – HTTP range requests enable seeking.
  • Adaptive streaming – HLS/DASH adjust quality to network.
  • CDN – for global delivery.
  • Caching – long cache lifetimes.
  • Bitrate – 2–5 Mbps for 720p, 5–10 Mbps for 1080p.
  • Resolution – 720p is often sufficient; 1080p for high-quality.
  • Frame rate – 24–30 fps for most content.
  • Lazy loading – don't load until needed.
  • Poster – reduces initial visual load.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Compress video – use FFmpeg or HandBrake.
  2. Use preload="metadata".
  3. Use a CDN.
  4. Cache aggressively.
  5. Consider adaptive streaming for long videos.
  6. Use poster for visual context.
  7. Avoid autoplay.
  8. Monitor bandwidth.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• CORS – use crossorigin when needed.
  • HTTPS – required for secure playback.
  • Content-Security-Policy – restrict media sources with media-src.
  • Autoplay abuse – avoid unexpected video.
  • User privacy – video may reveal user behavior.
  • Malicious files – validate video files.
  • DRM – use EME for protected content.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use HTTPS – for all video.
  2. Set media-src in CSP.
  3. Validate uploads – file type, size, content.
  4. Avoid autoplay.
  5. Use crossorigin – for Canvas/Web Audio.
  6. Sanitize metadata – EXIF and ID3 tags.
  7. Use DRM – for premium content.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <video> element.
  • Network panel – verify the video request and size.
  • Console – check for errors and events.
  • video.currentSrc – see the chosen source.
  • video.readyState – check readiness.
  • video.networkState – check network state.
  • video.error – inspect errors.
  • video.canPlayType() – test format support.
  • Event listeners – log events.
  • Lighthouse – audits for media.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the role and name.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure controls are announced.
  • Test on mobile – iOS and Android.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For tutorials.
  • For marketing videos.
  • For entertainment.
  • For background video (muted).
  • For live streaming.
  • For video podcasts.
  • For training.
  • For product demos.
  • For news reports.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For audio-only content – use <audio>.
  • For animated GIFs – use <video> with autoplay muted loop playsinline (better performance).
  • For static images – use <img>.
  • For animations – use CSS or SVG for simple animations.
  • For interactive graphics – use Canvas or SVG.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <audio> – audio element.
  • <source> – candidate sources.
  • <track> – captions and subtitles.
  • controls – native controls.
  • autoplay – autoplay.
  • loop – loop.
  • muted – mute.
  • preload – preload.
  • poster – thumbnail.
  • playsinline – iOS inline.
  • WebVTT – captions format.
  • MSE – Media Source Extensions.
  • EME – Encrypted Media Extensions.
  • HLS/DASH – adaptive streaming.
  • HTMLVideoElement – DOM interface.
  • HTMLMediaElement – shared interface.
  • TextTrack – captions interface.
  • Picture-in-Picture – floating video.
  • Fullscreen – expanded video.
  • Accessibility – captions, transcripts.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <video> element was introduced in HTML5 (drafted 2008, standardized 2014).

  • It replaced Adobe Flash and other plugins for video playback.

  • iOS never supported Flash — this was a major driver for native video.

  • The <video> element cannot autoplay unmuted in most browsers.

  • The preload="metadata" value loads only the duration and dimensions, not the entire file.

  • MP4 (H.264) is universally supported; WebM (VP9) is open-source.

  • Safari only supports MP4 (H.264) and HEVC.

  • WebVTT is the standard format for captions and subtitles.

  • The <track> element supports captions, subtitles, descriptions, chapters, and metadata.

  • Picture-in-Picture is natively supported in Chrome, Edge, and Safari.

  • Fullscreen is natively supported in all modern browsers.

  • The playsinline attribute is required for inline playback on iOS.

  • MSE (Media Source Extensions) enables adaptive streaming (HLS, DASH).

  • EME (Encrypted Media Extensions) enables DRM.

  • canPlayType() returns "probably", "maybe", or "".

  • The play() method returns a Promise (unlike pause()).

  • The play() Promise rejects if autoplay is blocked.

  • currentSrc tells you which source the browser chose.

  • videoWidth and videoHeight give the intrinsic dimensions.

  • readyState values: HAVE_NOTHING, HAVE_METADATA, HAVE_CURRENT_DATA, HAVE_FUTURE_DATA, HAVE_ENOUGH_DATA.

  • networkState values: NETWORK_EMPTY, NETWORK_IDLE, NETWORK_LOADING, NETWORK_NO_SOURCE.

  • Accessibility: captions are required for WCAG 1.2.2; audio descriptions for 1.2.5.

  • Best practices: controls, multiple formats, preload="metadata", playsinline, poster, captions.

  • Common mistakes: autoplay unmuted, no controls, single format, no captions, no playsinline.

  • Following best practices for video leads to accessible, performant, and pleasant experiences.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <video> element embeds video content natively in HTML.
  • It replaced Adobe Flash and other plugins for video playback.
  • Attributes: controls, autoplay, loop, muted, preload, poster, width, height, playsinline, crossorigin.
  • Child elements: <source> (candidate sources), <track> (captions).
  • JavaScript API: play(), pause(), currentTime, duration, volume, playbackRate, muted, loop, videoWidth, videoHeight, requestFullscreen(), requestPictureInPicture().
  • Events: play, pause, ended, timeupdate, loadedmetadata, canplay, volumechange, seeking, error.
  • Best practices: controls, multiple formats, preload="metadata", never autoplay unmuted, playsinline, poster, captions.
  • Common mistakes include autoplay unmuted, no controls, single format, missing playsinline, and no captions.
  • Video is essential for tutorials, marketing, entertainment, background video, live streaming, and video podcasts on the modern web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <track> element is an HTML element that provides timed text tracks for media elements (<video> and <audio>). These tracks are synchronized with the media's timeline and provide captions, subtitles, descriptions, chapters, and metadata — all essential for accessibility, internationalization, and enhanced user experience.

A <track> element is a void (empty) element that references an external WebVTT file (.vtt). The browser parses the file, aligns the cues with the media timeline, and renders them when the corresponding time range is active. Multiple <track> elements can be attached to a single media element, each serving a different purpose (e.g., English captions, Spanish subtitles, audio descriptions, chapters).

Example: 

<video controls width="640" height="360">
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
    <track kind="subtitles" src="subtitles-es.vtt" srclang="es" label="Español">
    <track kind="descriptions" src="descriptions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio Description">
</video>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <track> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Accessibility – captions for deaf and hard-of-hearing users; descriptions for blind users.
  • Internationalization – subtitles for translation into other languages.
  • Navigation – chapters for jumping to specific parts of a video.
  • Metadata – machine-readable data synchronized with the media.
  • Searchability – captions and subtitles are indexed by search engines.
  • User experience – captions help in noisy or quiet environments.
  • Compliance – WCAG 1.2.2 (Captions), 1.2.3 (Audio Description), 1.2.5 (Audio Description for prerecorded media).
  • SEO – transcripts and captions improve discoverability.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <track> element is a child of <video> or <audio>. It is not a standalone element — it must be associated with a media element. It is phrasing content and embedded content. Multiple <track> elements can be attached to a single media element.

<figure>
    <video controls width="800" height="450" poster="poster.jpg" preload="metadata">
        <source src="tutorial.mp4" type="video/mp4">
        <source src="tutorial.webm" type="video/webm">
        <track kind="captions" src="tutorial-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
        <track kind="captions" src="tutorial-es.vtt" srclang="es" label="Español">
        <track kind="descriptions" src="tutorial-desc.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio Description">
        <track kind="chapters" src="tutorial-chapters.vtt" srclang="en" label="Chapters">
        <p>Your browser doesn't support video. <a href="tutorial.mp4">Download</a>.</p>
    </video>
    <figcaption>Tutorial: Getting Started with HTML</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Video and audio content on the web is inherently inaccessible to users who:

  • Cannot hear – deaf and hard-of-hearing users miss dialogue, sound effects, and music.
  • Cannot see – blind users miss visual information (actions, text on screen, scene changes).
  • Do not understand the language – foreign-language users need subtitles.
  • Are in noisy environments – users in public places cannot hear the audio.
  • Are in quiet environments – users in libraries or at night need captions.
  • Have cognitive disabilities – captions can aid comprehension.

Before <track>, providing captions and subtitles required:

  • Burning them into the video – not accessible, not searchable, not translatable.
  • Using proprietary formats – like SAMI, RealText, or Flash captions.
  • Manual JavaScript implementations – complex, fragile, not standardized.
  • Third-party services – expensive, lock-in, not integrated.

There was no native, standardized way to provide timed text for media on the web.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No native caption support Required plugins or burned-in text No standardized format Each platform used its own No accessibility Deaf/blind users excluded No internationalization No easy translation No navigation No chapters or markers No metadata Machine-readable data unavailable No SEO benefit Text in video invisible to search engines No user control Users couldn't choose language or toggle captions

docs.title: Why the <track> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <track> element was introduced in HTML5 (drafted 2008, standardized 2014) alongside <video> and <audio>. It was designed to provide a native, standardized, accessible way to attach timed text to media.

It enables:

  • Native captions – rendered by the browser, controllable by the user.
  • Multiple languages – users choose their preferred language.
  • Accessibility – WCAG-compliant captions and descriptions.
  • Navigation – chapters for jumping within the media.
  • Metadata – machine-readable data synchronized with the media.
  • Styling – captions can be styled with CSS (::cue).
  • Programmatic control – JavaScript API (TextTrack, VTTCue).
  • Searchability – captions indexed by search engines.

The <track> element is part of the broader HTML5 media effort, alongside <video>, <audio>, MSE, and EME. It makes media on the web accessible and internationalized by default.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <track>
docs.text:
<track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  • kind – the type of track (captions, subtitles, descriptions, chapters, metadata).
  • src – the URL of the WebVTT file.
  • srclang – the language of the track (BCP 47 tag).
  • label – a user-visible label.
  • default – enable by default (boolean).

docs.title: Captions Track
docs.text:
<track kind="captions" src="captions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>

Purpose: For deaf and hard-of-hearing users. Includes dialogue and sound effects.

docs.title: Subtitles Track
docs.text:
<track kind="subtitles" src="subtitles-es.vtt" srclang="es" label="Español">

Purpose: For translation of dialogue.

docs.title: Descriptions Track
docs.text:
<track kind="descriptions" src="descriptions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio Description">

Purpose: For blind and low-vision users. Describes visual information.

docs.title: Chapters Track
docs.text:
<track kind="chapters" src="chapters.vtt" srclang="en" label="Chapters">

Purpose: Navigation markers for jumping within the media.

docs.title: Metadata Track
docs.text:
<track kind="metadata" src="metadata.vtt" srclang="en" label="Metadata">

Purpose: Machine-readable data synchronized with the media.

docs.title: Multiple Tracks
docs.text:
<video controls width="640" height="360">
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
    <track kind="captions" src="captions-es.vtt" srclang="es" label="Español">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions-fr.vtt" srclang="fr" label="Français">
    <track kind="subtitles" src="subtitles-de.vtt" srclang="de" label="Deutsch">
    <track kind="descriptions" src="descriptions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio Description">
    <track kind="chapters" src="chapters.vtt" srclang="en" label="Chapters">
</video>

docs.title: WebVTT File Format
docs.text:
The <track> element references a WebVTT file. The format is simple:

WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
Hello, world!

00:00:05.000 --> 00:00:10.000
This is a caption.

00:00:10.000 --> 00:00:15.000 align:start position:10%
<v Speaker>This is a styled caption.</v>

Components:

  • WEBVTT – the file header (required).
  • Cue timings – start --> end.
  • Cue text – the caption text.
  • Cue settings – optional (alignment, position, size, line).
  • Cue identifiers – optional (for referencing).
  • Voice tags – <v Speaker>...</v>.
  • Class tags – <c.classname>...</c>.
  • Bold/italic/underline – <b>, <i>, <u>.

docs.title: WebVTT with Cue Identifiers
docs.text:
WEBVTT

intro
00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
Welcome to the video.

chapter-1
00:00:05.000 --> 00:00:10.000
Chapter 1: Introduction.

docs.title: WebVTT with Cue Settings
docs.text:
WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000 align:start position:10%
Caption at the start, 10% from the left.

00:00:05.000 --> 00:00:10.000 align:end position:90%
Caption at the end, 90% from the left.

00:00:10.000 --> 00:00:15.000 line:0 size:50%
Caption at the top, 50% width.

Cue settings:

Setting Values align start, center, end, left, right position 0% to 100% line 0 to 100 or auto size 0% to 100% vertical rl (right-to-left), lr (left-to-right)

docs.title: WebVTT with Voice Tags
docs.text:
WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
<v Narrator>Once upon a time...</v>

00:00:05.000 --> 00:00:10.000
<v Alice>Hello, how are you?</v>

docs.title: WebVTT with Class Tags
docs.text:
WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
<c.yellow>This caption is yellow.</c>

docs.title: WebVTT with Bold, Italic, Underline
docs.text:
WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
This is <b>bold</b> and <i>italic</i> and <u>underlined</u>.

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose kind Type of track: captions, subtitles, descriptions, chapters, metadata src URL of the WebVTT file srclang Language (BCP 47) label User-visible label default Enable by default

docs.title: The "Subtitle Overlay" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <track> as a subtitle overlay on a movie. The movie (the <video>) plays on screen; the subtitles (the <track>) appear on top, synchronized with the timeline. Multiple subtitle tracks exist (English, Spanish, French), and the user chooses which one to display.

docs.title: The "Timed Text" Mental Model
docs.text:
A <track> is timed text — text that appears at specific times during the media. Each cue has:

  • A start time – when the text appears.
  • An end time – when the text disappears.
  • Text content – what is displayed.
  • Optional settings – alignment, position, size.

This is fundamentally different from static text — it's synchronized with the media.

docs.title: The "Multiple Roles" Mental Model
docs.text:
A single <track> can play many roles:

Role Purpose Audience Captions Dialogue + sound effects Deaf/hard-of-hearing Subtitles Translation of dialogue Foreign-language viewers Descriptions Visual description Blind/low-vision Chapters Navigation All users Metadata Machine-readable data Developers/machines

The kind attribute determines the role.

docs.title: The "WCAG Compliance" Mental Model
docs.text:
Providing captions and descriptions is not just a nice-to-have — it's a legal and ethical requirement:

  • WCAG 1.2.2 (Captions) – captions for prerecorded video with audio.
  • WCAG 1.2.3 (Audio Description) – audio description for prerecorded video.
  • WCAG 1.2.5 (Audio Description for prerecorded) – audio description at AAA level.

The <track> element is the primary way to comply.

docs.title: The "User Choice" Mental Model
docs.text:
The user is in control:

  • Which track to display (English, Spanish, etc.).
  • Whether to display it at all.
  • How it's styled (via browser settings or CSS ::cue).

The <track> element provides the options; the user chooses.

docs.title: The "WebVTT is Just Text" Mental Model
docs.text:
A WebVTT file is just a text file. It can be:

  • Created in any text editor.
  • Generated programmatically.
  • Served from any web server.
  • Cached like any other resource.
  • Versioned like any other file.

This simplicity is one of its strengths.

docs.title: Concept 1: The <track> Element
docs.text:
The <track> element is a void element — it has no closing tag and no content. It references an external WebVTT file via the src attribute and describes the track via kind, srclang, and label.

<track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">

docs.title: Concept 2: The kind Attribute
docs.text:
The kind attribute defines the purpose of the track:

Value Purpose subtitles (default) Translation of dialogue captions Dialogue + sound effects for deaf users descriptions Audio descriptions for blind users chapters Navigation markers metadata Machine-readable data

Note: If kind is omitted, the default is subtitles.

docs.title: Concept 3: The src Attribute
docs.text:
The src attribute specifies the URL of the WebVTT file:

<track src="captions.vtt">

The URL can be relative or absolute. CORS applies for cross-origin tracks.

docs.title: Concept 4: The srclang Attribute
docs.text:
The srclang attribute specifies the language of the track:

<track srclang="en" label="English">
  • Uses BCP 47 language tags (en, fr, es, zh-CN, etc.).
  • Required when kind="subtitles".
  • Not required for chapters or metadata.

docs.title: Concept 5: The label Attribute
docs.text:
The label attribute provides a user-visible label for the track:

<track label="English">

The label appears in the browser's caption menu. It should be descriptive and in the user's language.

docs.title: Concept 6: The default Attribute
docs.text:
The default boolean attribute enables the track by default:

<track kind="captions" src="captions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>

Note: Only one track per kind should have default.

docs.title: Concept 7: The WebVTT Format
docs.text:
WebVTT (Web Video Text Tracks) is the standard format for timed text on the web:

WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
Hello, world!
  • WEBVTT – required header.
  • Cue timings – start --> end.
  • Cue text – the caption.
  • Cue settings – optional.

docs.title: Concept 8: The TextTrack API
docs.text:
The <track> element exposes a TextTrack object via the track property:

const track = document.querySelector('track');
const textTrack = track.track;
console.log(textTrack.kind);     // "captions"
console.log(textTrack.label);    // "English"
console.log(textTrack.language); // "en"
console.log(textTrack.mode);     // "disabled", "hidden", "showing"

docs.title: Concept 9: The mode Property
docs.text:
The mode property controls whether the track is displayed:

Value Behaviour disabled Not loaded, not displayed hidden Loaded, not displayed (cues fire events) showing Loaded and displayed 
textTrack.mode = 'showing';

docs.title: Concept 10: The VTTCue Interface
docs.text:
Each cue in a WebVTT file is represented by a VTTCue object:

const cue = new VTTCue(0, 5, 'Hello, world!');
cue.align = 'start';
cue.position = 10;
textTrack.addCue(cue);

docs.title: Concept 11: The activeCues Property
docs.text:
The activeCues property returns the cues currently active:

const activeCues = textTrack.activeCues;
for (const cue of activeCues) {
    console.log(cue.text);
}

docs.title: Concept 12: The cuechange Event
docs.text:
Fires when the active cues change:

textTrack.addEventListener('cuechange', () => {
    for (const cue of textTrack.activeCues) {
        console.log(cue.text);
    }
});

docs.title: Concept 13: Captions vs. Subtitles
docs.text:
Aspect Captions Subtitles Audience Deaf/hard-of-hearing Foreign-language viewers Content Dialogue + sound effects Translation of dialogue Language Same as audio Different from audio kind captions subtitles

Rule: Use captions for accessibility; use subtitles for translation.

docs.title: Concept 14: Audio Descriptions
docs.text:
Audio descriptions are separate audio tracks (not text tracks) that describe visual information. The <track kind="descriptions"> provides text descriptions that can be read by screen readers or converted to audio.

<track kind="descriptions" src="descriptions.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio Description">

docs.title: Concept 15: Chapters
docs.text:
Chapters are navigation markers:

<track kind="chapters" src="chapters.vtt" srclang="en" label="Chapters">

chapters.vtt: 

WEBVTT

Chapter 1
00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:30.000
Introduction

Chapter 2
00:00:30.000 --> 00:01:00.000
Getting Started

docs.title: Concept 16: Metadata Tracks
docs.text:
Metadata tracks contain machine-readable data synchronized with the media. They are not displayed to the user.

<track kind="metadata" src="metadata.vtt" srclang="en" label="Metadata">

Use case: Synchronizing slides, annotations, or interactive elements.

docs.title: Concept 17: Styling Captions with ::cue
docs.text:
Captions can be styled with the ::cue pseudo-element:

video::cue {
    background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.7);
    color: white;
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
    font-size: 1.2em;
}

video::cue(.yellow) {
    color: yellow;
}

docs.title: Concept 18: WebVTT Cue Settings
docs.text:
Cue settings control position, alignment, and size:

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000 align:start position:10%
Caption at the start, 10% from the left.
Setting Values align start, center, end, left, right position 0% to 100% line 0 to 100 or auto size 0% to 100% vertical rl, lr

docs.title: Concept 19: WebVTT Tags
docs.text:
WebVTT supports inline tags for styling:

Tag Purpose <b> Bold <i> Italic <u> Underline <v Speaker> Voice <c.classname> Class <ruby> Ruby text <rt> Ruby annotation

docs.title: Concept 20: WebVTT Comments
docs.text:
Comments start with NOTE:

WEBVTT

NOTE This is a comment.

docs.title: Concept 22: CORS and Tracks
docs.text:
Cross-origin tracks require CORS headers:

<track src="https://cdn.example.com/captions.vtt" crossorigin="anonymous">

docs.title: Concept 23: Track Loading
docs.text:
Tracks are loaded:

  • disabled – not loaded until needed.
  • hidden – loaded but not displayed.
  • showing – loaded and displayed.

docs.title: Concept 24: Browser Support
docs.text: The <track> element is supported in all modern browsers. WebVTT is the standard format.

docs.title: Concept 25: Accessibility Compliance
docs.text:
WCAG requirements for media:

Criterion Requirement 1.2.1 Audio-only and video-only (prerecorded) 1.2.2 Captions (prerecorded) 1.2.3 Audio description or media alternative (prerecorded) 1.2.4 Captions (live) 1.2.5 Audio description (prerecorded) 1.2.6 Sign language (prerecorded) 1.2.7 Extended audio description (prerecorded) 1.2.8 Media alternative (prerecorded) 1.2.9 Audio-only (live)

The <track> element is essential for compliance with 1.2.2, 1.2.3, and 1.2.5.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing a <track>
docs.text:
1.  The parser encounters a `<track>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  It creates a DOM node for the track.
    │
    ▼
3.  It reads the attributes: `kind`, `src`, `srclang`, `label`, `default`.
    │
    ▼
4.  It fetches the WebVTT file from `src`.
    │
    ▼
5.  It parses the WebVTT file:
    │   ├── Reads the `WEBVTT` header.
    │   ├── Parses STYLE and REGION blocks.
    │   ├── Parses each cue (timing + text + settings).
    │   └── Creates `VTTCue` objects.
    │
    ▼
6.  It creates a `TextTrack` object:
    │   ├── `kind`
    │   ├── `label`
    │   ├── `language`
    │   ├── `mode` (default: `disabled`)
    │   └── `cues` (list of VTTCue objects)
    │
    ▼
7.  If `default` is set:
    │   └── Sets `mode` to `showing`.
    │
    ▼
8.  As the media plays:
    │   ├── The browser checks the current time.
    │   ├── It finds cues whose time range includes the current time.
    │   ├── It adds them to `activeCues`.
    │   ├── It fires the `cuechange` event.
    │   └── It renders the cue text (if `mode="showing"`).
    │
    ▼
9.  The captions appear on the video.

docs.title: The WebVTT Parsing Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Read the file as UTF-8.
  2. Verify the WEBVTT header.
  3. Parse STYLE blocks (CSS for ::cue).
  4. Parse REGION blocks (positioning regions).
  5. Parse cues:
  6. Optional cue identifier.
  7. Timing line: start --> end settings.
  8. Text lines until a blank line.
  9. Create VTTCue objects.
  10. Add them to the TextTrack.

docs.title: The Cue Matching Algorithm
docs.text:
1. On each timeupdate event:
  2. Get the current time.
  3. Find cues where startTime <= currentTime < endTime.
  4. Update activeCues.
  5. Fire cuechange if the set changed.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
The browser renders active cues as an overlay on the media:

  • Position – based on align, position, line, size.
  • Style – based on ::cue CSS and cue tags.
  • Stacking – multiple cues stack vertically.

docs.title: WebVTT File Parsing
docs.text:
The browser parses the WebVTT file using a specific algorithm:

  1. Header – check for WEBVTT.
  2. Blocks – STYLE, REGION, NOTE, cue.
  3. Cue – identifier, timings, text, settings.
  4. Validation – malformed cues are ignored.

docs.title: The Cue Rendering Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Get active cues – based on current time.
  2. Position each cue – based on cue settings.
  3. Apply styles – ::cue CSS and inline tags.
  4. Render – paint the caption on the video.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a <track>
docs.text:
1.  Author writes `<track>` inside `<video>` or `<audio>`.
    │
    ▼
2.  File deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses HTML and creates the DOM node.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser creates a `TextTrack` object.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser fetches the WebVTT file.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser parses the WebVTT file.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser creates `VTTCue` objects.
    │
    ▼
8.  If `default`, sets `mode` to `showing`.
    │
    ▼
9.  As media plays:
    │   ├── Browser checks current time.
    │   ├── Finds active cues.
    │   ├── Fires `cuechange`.
    │   └── Renders cues (if `showing`).
    │
    ▼
10. User can toggle tracks via browser controls.
    │
    ▼
11. When the media ends, cues stop.

<video id="video" controls width="640" height="360">
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

<script>
    const video = document.getElementById('video');
    const track = video.addTextTrack('captions', 'English', 'en');
    track.mode = 'showing';

    const cues = [
        { start: 0, end: 5, text: 'Hello, world!' },
        { start: 5, end: 10, text: 'This is a caption.' },
        { start: 10, end: 15, text: 'Goodbye!' }
    ];

    cues.forEach(c => {
        const cue = new VTTCue(c.start, c.end, c.text);
        track.addCue(cue);

</script>

docs.title: Example 14: Captions with Search
docs.text:
<video id="video" controls width="640" height="360">
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
</video>

<input type="search" id="search" placeholder="Search captions...">
<div id="results"></div>

<script>
    const video = document.getElementById('video');
    const track = video.textTracks[0];

    track.addEventListener('load', () => {
        document.getElementById('search').addEventListener('input', (e) => {
            const query = e.target.value.toLowerCase();
            const results = document.getElementById('results');
            results.innerHTML = '';
            if (!query) return;

            for (const cue of track.cues) {
                if (cue.text.toLowerCase().includes(query)) {
                    const div = document.createElement('div');
                    const a = document.createElement('a');
                    a.href = '#';
                    a.textContent = `${formatTime(cue.startTime)} - ${cue.text}`;
                    a.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
                        e.preventDefault();
                        video.currentTime = cue.startTime;
                        video.play();
                    });
                    div.appendChild(a);
                    results.appendChild(div);
                }
            }
        });
    });

    function formatTime(seconds) {
        const m = Math.floor(seconds / 60);
        const s = Math.floor(seconds % 60);
        return `${m}:${s.toString().padStart(2, '0')}`;
    }
</script>

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Accessible Video with Tracks
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Accessible Video with Tracks</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 800px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        video { width: 100%; height: auto; background: #000; border-radius: 8px; }
        video::cue {
            background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.8);
            color: white;
            font-family: 'Arial', sans-serif;
            font-size: 1.1em;
        }
        .controls { margin-top: 1rem; display: flex; gap: 1rem; align-items: center; flex-wrap: wrap; }
        button { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; min-height: 44px; border: none; border-radius: 4px; background: #3498db; color: white; cursor: pointer; }
        button:hover { background: #2980b9; }
        button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #2c3e50; outline-offset: 2px; }
        select { padding: 0.5rem; min-height: 44px; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 4px; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Accessible Video with Tracks</h1>

    <video id="video" controls width="800" height="450" poster="poster.jpg" preload="metadata" playsinline>
        <source src="tutorial.mp4" type="video/mp4">
        <source src="tutorial.webm" type="video/webm">
        <track kind="captions" src="captions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English Captions" default>
        <track kind="captions" src="captions-es.vtt" srclang="es" label="Subtítulos en Español">
        <track kind="descriptions" src="descriptions-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio Description">
        <track kind="chapters" src="chapters.vtt" srclang="en" label="Chapters">
        <p>Your browser doesn't support video. <a href="tutorial.mp4">Download</a>.</p>
    </video>

    <div class="controls">
        <label for="captionSelect">Captions:</label>
        <select id="captionSelect">
            <option value="off">Off</option>
            <option value="en" selected>English</option>
            <option value="es">Español</option>
        </select>

        <button id="toggleDescriptions" aria-pressed="false">Audio Descriptions: Off</button>

        <span id="currentCaption" aria-live="polite"></span>
    </div>

    <script>
        const video = document.getElementById('video');
        const captionSelect = document.getElementById('captionSelect');
        const toggleDescriptions = document.getElementById('toggleDescriptions');
        const currentCaption = document.getElementById('currentCaption');

        // Caption language selection
        captionSelect.addEventListener('change', () => {
            const lang = captionSelect.value;
            for (const track of video.textTracks) {
                if (track.kind === 'captions') {
                    if (lang === 'off') {
                        track.mode = 'disabled';
                    } else {
                        track.mode = track.language === lang ? 'showing' : 'disabled';
                    }
                }
            }
        });

        // Audio description toggle
        toggleDescriptions.addEventListener('click', () => {
            const descTrack = Array.from(video.textTracks).find(t => t.kind === 'descriptions');
            if (descTrack) {
                const showing = descTrack.mode === 'showing';
                descTrack.mode = showing ? 'hidden' : 'showing';
                toggleDescriptions.textContent = showing ? 'Audio Descriptions: Off' : 'Audio Descriptions: On';
                toggleDescriptions.setAttribute('aria-pressed', !showing);
            }
        });

        // Display current caption
        for (const track of video.textTracks) {
            track.addEventListener('cuechange', () => {
                if (track.mode === 'showing' && track.kind === 'captions') {
                    currentCaption.textContent = '';
                    for (const cue of track.activeCues) {
                        currentCaption.textContent += cue.text + ' ';
                    }
                }
            });
        }
    </script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always provide captions – for any video with audio.
  2. Use the correct kind – captions for accessibility; subtitles for translation.
  3. Include srclang – for all captions and subtitles.
  4. Provide a descriptive label – user-visible in the caption menu.
  5. Set default on one track – the primary caption track.
  6. Provide audio descriptions – for blind users.
  7. Provide chapters – for navigation.
  8. Use WebVTT – the standard format.
  9. Style captions – with ::cue for readability.
  10. Test with screen readers – ensure captions are announced.
  11. Test on mobile – caption rendering varies.
  12. Use CORS for cross-origin – with crossorigin on the media.
  13. Validate WebVTT – with a validator.
  14. Provide transcripts – for SEO and accessibility.
  15. Keep cues short – 1–2 lines, 32–42 characters per line.
  16. Sync cues precisely – avoid overlapping or gaps.
  17. Use voice tags – for multiple speakers.
  18. Use class tags – for styling.
  19. Test in multiple browsers – Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge.
  20. Document your caption workflow – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No kind
docs.text:
<track src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">

Why it's wrong: Defaults to subtitles, which is wrong for accessibility.

✅ Correct: 

<track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No srclang
docs.text:
<track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" label="English">

Why it's wrong: srclang is required for captions and subtitles.

✅ Correct: 

<track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No label
docs.text:
<track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en">

Why it's wrong: Users can't identify the track in the menu.

✅ Correct: 

<track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple default Tracks
docs.text:
<track kind="captions" src="en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
<track kind="captions" src="es.vtt" srclang="es" label="Español" default>

Why it's wrong: Only one track per kind should be default.

✅ Correct: 

<track kind="captions" src="en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
<track kind="captions" src="es.vtt" srclang="es" label="Español">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using kind="subtitles" for Captions
docs.text:
<track kind="subtitles" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">

Why it's wrong: Subtitles are for translation; captions are for accessibility.

✅ Correct: 

<track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Wrong WebVTT Header
docs.text:
00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
Hello!

Why it's wrong: The WEBVTT header is required.

✅ Correct: 

WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
Hello!

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Overlapping Cues
docs.text:
WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:05.000
First cue.

00:00:03.000 --> 00:00:08.000
Second cue.

Why it's wrong: Overlapping cues may render incorrectly.

✅ Correct: Ensure cues don't overlap unless intentional.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Captions for Speech
docs.text:
<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Why it's wrong: WCAG violation; deaf users can't access.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Captions on Mobile
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Mobile users need captions too.

✅ Correct: Test on mobile and ensure captions render.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No ::cue Styling
docs.text:
<video controls>
    <track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
</video>

Why it's wrong: Default styles may be hard to read.

✅ Correct: 

video::cue {
    background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.8);
    color: white;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: CORS Errors
docs.text:
<track src="https://cdn.example.com/captions.vtt">

Why it's wrong: Cross-origin requires crossorigin.

✅ Correct: 

<video crossorigin="anonymous">
    <track src="https://cdn.example.com/captions.vtt">
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Fallback Content
docs.text:
<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">
</video>

Why it's wrong: Users with old browsers see nothing.

✅ Correct: 

<video controls>
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support video. <a href="video.mp4">Download</a>.</p>
</video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing WebVTT Syntax
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Malformed WebVTT files may not load.

✅ Correct: Validate with a WebVTT validator.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Long Cues
docs.text:
WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:30.000
This is a very long caption that spans multiple lines and is hard to read because it stays on screen for 30 seconds and contains a lot of text that the user has to read quickly...

Why it's wrong: Long cues are hard to read.

✅ Correct: Keep cues short (1–2 lines, 2–7 seconds).

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• WebVTT file size – small (a few KB per minute).
  • Loading – tracks are loaded lazily (when enabled).
  • Parsing – fast, even for large files.
  • Rendering – minimal impact.
  • Caching – tracks are cached like any resource.
  • Multiple tracks – additional tracks add minimal overhead.
  • Styling – ::cue has negligible cost.
  • Search – JS search over cues is fast.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep WebVTT files small.
  2. Use mode="disabled" for unused tracks.
  3. Cache tracks with long cache lifetimes.
  4. Use a CDN for global delivery.
  5. Minify WebVTT – remove comments and extra whitespace.
  6. Test with Lighthouse.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• CORS – use crossorigin for cross-origin tracks.
  • HTTPS – required for secure playback.
  • Content-Security-Policy – restrict track sources with media-src.
  • XSS – WebVTT is text, not HTML; no script execution.
  • Malicious cues – validate WebVTT files.
  • Privacy – tracks may reveal viewing habits.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use HTTPS – for all tracks.
  2. Set media-src in CSP.
  3. Validate WebVTT – before serving.
  4. Use CORS – for cross-origin.
  5. Sanitize metadata – remove sensitive data.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <track> element.
  • Network panel – verify the WebVTT request.
  • Console – check for errors.
  • video.textTracks – list all tracks.
  • track.mode – check the mode.
  • track.cues – list all cues.
  • track.activeCues – list active cues.
  • cuechange event – log cue changes.
  • WebVTT validator – validate the file.
  • Lighthouse – audits for media accessibility.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the track.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure captions are announced.
  • Test in multiple browsers – Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For any video with audio – captions.
  • For any video with dialogue – subtitles.
  • For any video with visual information – audio descriptions.
  • For long videos – chapters.
  • For interactive video – metadata.
  • For searchable video – captions.
  • For WCAG compliance – captions and descriptions.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For audio-only content – use transcripts.
  • For static text – use HTML text.
  • For animations – use SVG or Canvas.
  • For non-timed text – use HTML.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <video> – video element.
  • <audio> – audio element.
  • <source> – candidate sources.
  • WebVTT – the caption format.
  • TextTrack – the DOM interface.
  • VTTCue – the cue interface.
  • ::cue – CSS pseudo-element.
  • WCAG – accessibility guidelines.
  • Captions – for deaf users.
  • Subtitles – for translation.
  • Descriptions – for blind users.
  • Chapters – for navigation.
  • Metadata – machine-readable data.
  • CORS – cross-origin resources.
  • Media accessibility – the broader field.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <track> element was introduced in HTML5 (drafted 2008, standardized 2014).

  • WebVTT stands for Web Video Text Tracks.

  • WebVTT is a W3C standard for timed text.

  • The <track> element is a void element — no closing tag, no content.

  • The kind attribute determines the track's purpose.

  • captions are for deaf users; subtitles are for translation.

  • descriptions are for blind users; chapters are for navigation.

  • metadata tracks are not displayed but fire events.

  • WCAG 1.2.2 requires captions for prerecorded video.

  • WCAG 1.2.5 requires audio descriptions for prerecorded video.

  • ::cue is the CSS pseudo-element for styling captions.

  • Voice tags (<v Speaker>) identify different speakers.

  • Class tags (<c.classname>) enable CSS styling.

  • Cue settings control alignment, position, line, and size.

  • Regions define reusable positioning areas.

  • TextTrack is the DOM interface for tracks.

  • VTTCue represents a single cue.

  • addTextTrack() creates tracks programmatically.

  • cuechange fires when active cues change.

  • activeCues returns the currently active cues.

  • Safari requires crossorigin for cross-origin tracks.

  • WebVTT supports STYLE and REGION blocks.

  • WebVTT supports comments (NOTE).

  • Thumbnails can be provided via metadata tracks.

  • Captions improve SEO — text is indexed.

  • Best practices: correct kind, srclang, label, default, ::cue styling.

  • Common mistakes: no kind, no srclang, no label, multiple default.

  • Following best practices for tracks leads to accessible, internationalized, and searchable media.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <track> element provides timed text tracks for <video> and <audio>.
  • It references an external WebVTT file with captions, subtitles, descriptions, chapters, or metadata.
  • Attributes: kind, src, srclang, label, default.
  • Track kinds: captions (accessibility), subtitles (translation), descriptions (blind users), chapters (navigation), metadata (machine-readable).
  • WebVTT is the standard format — simple, text-based, styleable.
  • Caption styling is done with ::cue.
  • TextTrack and VTTCue are the DOM interfaces.
  • Best practices: correct kind, srclang, label, default, captions for all videos with audio, audio descriptions for all videos with visual information.
  • Common mistakes include no kind, no srclang, no label, multiple default, and no ::cue styling.
  • Tracks are essential for accessibility, internationalization, navigation, and SEO.
  • They are the primary way to comply with WCAG 1.2.2 and 1.2.5 on the web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Lazy loading is a technique that defers the loading of non-critical resources until they are actually needed — typically when they are about to enter the user's viewport. Instead of loading every image, video, iframe, and script on page load, the browser waits until the user scrolls near them, reducing initial page weight, saving bandwidth, and improving performance metrics like Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Time to Interactive (TTI), and Total Blocking Time (TBT).

HTML supports lazy loading natively for <img> and <iframe> through the loading="lazy" attribute. For other resources (video, audio, background images), lazy loading is typically implemented with the Intersection Observer API in JavaScript.

Example: 

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" loading="lazy">
<iframe src="https://example.com/embed" loading="lazy"></iframe>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Lazy loading serves several essential purposes:

  • Performance – reduces initial page load size and time.
  • Bandwidth savings – only loads what the user actually sees.
  • Battery savings – less data and CPU on mobile devices.
  • Core Web Vitals – improves LCP, CLS, and INP.
  • User experience – faster perceived load time.
  • Server savings – fewer requests to the server.
  • Scalability – pages with thousands of images remain fast.
  • Mobile first – essential for users on slow connections.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Lazy loading is a performance optimization technique that applies to any resource that is:

  • Not immediately visible in the viewport.
  • Expensive to load (large images, videos, iframes).
  • Optional for the initial render (ads, analytics, social embeds).

It works alongside:

  • Responsive images (srcset, sizes, <picture>).
  • Resource hints (preload, prefetch, preconnect).
  • Caching (HTTP caching, Service Workers).
  • CDNs (global delivery).
Performance Optimization
│
├── Resource Hints (preload, prefetch, preconnect)
├── Lazy Loading (this chapter)
├── Responsive Images
├── Caching
├── Compression
└── CDN

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A typical modern web page loads dozens or hundreds of resources:

  • Images – hero, thumbnails, gallery, avatars, icons.
  • Videos – trailers, embedded players.
  • Iframes – ads, embeds, social widgets.
  • Scripts – analytics, chat widgets, third-party libraries.
  • Fonts – custom typefaces.
  • Styles – multiple CSS files.

Without lazy loading, the browser tries to fetch all of them at once on page load, even if the user never scrolls down. This causes:

  • Slow initial load – the network is saturated with unnecessary requests.
  • High bandwidth usage – especially painful on mobile data.
  • Battery drain – decoding and rendering costs.
  • Poor Core Web Vitals – high LCP, high TBT, high CLS.
  • Wasted server resources – requests for content never seen.
  • Poor user experience – users wait for content they don't need.

Studies show:

  • A 1-second delay in page load can reduce conversions by 7%.
  • 53% of mobile users abandon pages that take longer than 3 seconds to load.
  • Images account for ~50% of a typical page's weight.

Lazy loading solves the problem by loading only what the user is about to see.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Eager loading of all resources Slow initial load High bandwidth usage Wasted data Battery drain Shorter mobile battery life Poor Core Web Vitals Lower SEO ranking Server load Higher costs Poor UX on slow connections Users abandon the page No native support (pre-HTML5) Required JavaScript libraries

docs.title: Why Lazy Loading Was Introduced
docs.text:
Lazy loading has existed as a JavaScript technique for over a decade. Libraries like LazyLoad, lozad.js, and lazysizes were widely used. But JavaScript-based lazy loading had drawbacks:

  • Required additional JavaScript.
  • Slower (JS must load before images can be lazy-loaded).
  • Accessible only after JS loads.
  • More complex to implement correctly.

In HTML5, the loading attribute was introduced to provide native lazy loading for <img> and <iframe>. This enables:

  • No JavaScript – native browser support.
  • Faster – the browser can start lazy-loading immediately.
  • More reliable – no dependency on JS libraries.
  • Simpler – one attribute.
  • Better performance – browsers optimize native lazy loading.
  • Progressive enhancement – works even if JS is disabled.

Native lazy loading was first supported in Chrome 76 (2019), and is now supported in all modern browsers.

docs.title: Native Lazy Loading with loading="lazy"
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" loading="lazy">
<iframe src="https://example.com/embed" loading="lazy"></iframe>

Values:

Value Behaviour lazy Load when near the viewport eager Load immediately (default) auto Browser decides

docs.title: Native Lazy Loading for Images
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" loading="lazy" width="800" height="600">

Note: Always include width and height to prevent layout shift.

docs.title: Native Lazy Loading for Iframes
docs.text: <iframe src="https://example.com/embed" loading="lazy" width="800" height="600" title="Embedded content"></iframe>

docs.title: Native Lazy Loading for Videos (via preload)
docs.text:
<video controls preload="none" poster="poster.jpg" width="640" height="360">
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

Note: preload="none" tells the browser not to preload the video. It loads when the user plays it.

docs.title: Intersection Observer for Custom Lazy Loading
docs.text:
<img data-src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" class="lazy" width="800" height="600">
<noscript>
    <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" width="800" height="600">
</noscript>

<script>
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
        entries.forEach(entry => {
            if (entry.isIntersecting) {
                const img = entry.target;
                img.src = img.dataset.src;
                img.classList.remove('lazy');
                observer.unobserve(img);
            }
        });
    });

    document.querySelectorAll('.lazy').forEach(img => observer.observe(img));
</script>

docs.title: Responsive Lazy Loading
docs.text:
<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A scenic view"
     loading="lazy"
     width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Lazy Loading Background Images
docs.text:
<div class="lazy-bg" data-bg="hero.jpg" style="height: 400px;"></div>

<script>
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
        entries.forEach(entry => {
            if (entry.isIntersecting) {
                const el = entry.target;
                el.style.backgroundImage = `url(${el.dataset.bg})`;
                observer.unobserve(el);
            }
        });
    });

    document.querySelectorAll('.lazy-bg').forEach(el => observer.observe(el));
</script>

docs.title: Lazy Loading with srcset and sizes
docs.text:
<img data-src="photo-800.jpg"
     data-srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     data-sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
     alt="A scenic view"
     class="lazy"
     width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute/Technique Purpose loading="lazy" Native lazy loading loading="eager" Load immediately preload="none" Don't preload video IntersectionObserver Custom lazy loading data-src Deferred image URL data-srcset Deferred responsive sources noscript Fallback for JS-disabled

docs.title: The "Waiter Serving Food" Analogy
docs.text:
Think of the browser as a waiter at a restaurant:

  • Eager loading = the waiter brings every dish to the table at once, filling the table with food the customer may not want.
  • Lazy loading = the waiter brings dishes as the customer is ready for them — appetizers first, then mains, then dessert.

Lazy loading serves content just in time.

docs.title: The "Library Book Cart" Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a library with a cart of books. Eager loading pushes the entire cart to your table, even if you only want one book. Lazy loading delivers books as you request them — one at a time, just before you need them.

docs.title: The "Fog of War" Mental Model
docs.text: In strategy games, the map is covered by fog of war — you only see what's near your units. Lazy loading is like fog of war for the web: content near the viewport is loaded; content far away stays unloaded until it's needed.

docs.title: The "Conveyor Belt" Mental Model
docs.text: Think of the page as a conveyor belt moving past the user. Eager loading puts everything on the belt at once; lazy loading adds items just before they reach the user.

docs.title: The "Priorities" Mental Model
docs.text:
Not all resources are equally important:

Priority Resource Strategy Highest Above-the-fold images loading="eager", fetchpriority="high" High Critical CSS/JS Preload Medium Below-the-fold images loading="lazy" Low Ads, embeds, analytics loading="lazy", defer Lowest Footer images, third-party loading="lazy", Intersection Observer

Lazy loading is about matching resource priority to user needs.

docs.title: Concept 1: The loading Attribute
docs.text:
The loading attribute is a native HTML attribute for lazy loading <img> and <iframe>:

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy">
Value Behaviour lazy Load when near the viewport eager Load immediately auto Browser decides

docs.title: Concept 2: When "Lazy" Loads
docs.text:
Browsers use heuristics to decide when to load a lazy image:

  • Chrome: loads when the image is within a distance based on connection speed (e.g., 1250px on fast connections, 2500px on slow).
  • Firefox: similar heuristics.
  • Safari: loads when near the viewport.

The exact distance varies. The goal is to load just before the user sees the image.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Intersection Observer API
docs.text:
The Intersection Observer API observes when an element enters or exits the viewport:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach(entry => {
        if (entry.isIntersecting) {
            // Load the resource
        }
    });
});
observer.observe(element);

Options:

  • root – the element used as the viewport (default: browser viewport).
  • rootMargin – margin around the root (e.g., 200px to load early).
  • threshold – the percentage of the target visible (e.g., 0.1).

docs.title: Concept 4: rootMargin
docs.text:
The rootMargin option lets you load resources before they enter the viewport:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, {
    rootMargin: '200px 0px'
});

This loads images when they're within 200px of the viewport.

docs.title: Concept 5: threshold
docs.text:
The threshold option defines how much of the element must be visible:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, {
    threshold: 0.1
});

0.1 means 10% of the element must be visible.

docs.title: Concept 6: loading="lazy" vs. Intersection Observer
docs.text:
Aspect loading="lazy" Intersection Observer Native ✅ ❌ (JS required) Works without JS ✅ ❌ Customizable ❌ ✅ Supports images ✅ ✅ Supports iframes ✅ ✅ Supports other resources ❌ ✅

Best practice: Use loading="lazy" for images and iframes. Use Intersection Observer for other resources (backgrounds, videos, custom widgets).

docs.title: Concept 7: Lazy Loading Above-the-Fold Images
docs.text:
Do NOT lazy load above-the-fold images (hero, LCP image). Instead:

<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high">

Use fetchpriority="high" to prioritise LCP images.

docs.title: Concept 8: Lazy Loading and CLS
docs.text:
Lazy loading can cause layout shift (CLS) if dimensions aren't reserved:

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy" width="800" height="600">

Always set width and height — or use aspect-ratio in CSS.

docs.title: Concept 9: Lazy Loading and LCP
docs.text:
Lazy loading hurts LCP if applied to the LCP element. The LCP image should be loaded eagerly with high priority:

<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high">

Rule: Lazy load below-the-fold images; eager load above-the-fold images.

docs.title: Concept 10: preload="none" for Video
docs.text:
Videos have a preload attribute (not loading):

<video controls preload="none" poster="poster.jpg">

preload="none" defers video loading until the user plays it.

docs.title: Concept 11: Lazy Loading with IntersectionObserver for Videos
docs.text:
const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach(entry => {
        if (entry.isIntersecting) {
            const video = entry.target;
            video.src = video.dataset.src;
            video.load();
            observer.unobserve(video);
        }
    });
});

docs.title: Concept 12: Lazy Loading Background Images
docs.text:
Background images set via CSS background-image are not lazy loaded natively:

.hero {
    background-image: url('hero.jpg');
}

Use JavaScript with Intersection Observer to lazy load them.

docs.title: Concept 13: The noscript Fallback
docs.text:
For JavaScript-based lazy loading, always provide a <noscript> fallback:

<img data-src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" class="lazy">
<noscript>
    <img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo">
</noscript>

Why: Users with JS disabled see the images.

docs.title: Concept 14: Native Lazy Loading Is Progressive Enhancement
docs.text:
loading="lazy" degrades gracefully:

  • Browsers that support it: lazy load.
  • Browsers that don't: load eagerly (like normal).

This is progressive enhancement — no harm to older browsers.

docs.title: Concept 15: Lazy Loading and SEO
docs.text:
• Googlebot supports loading="lazy".
  • Googlebot scrolls pages to trigger lazy loading.
  • Ensure images are discoverable (in the DOM, with valid src or data-src).
  • Avoid lazy loading critical content.

docs.title: Concept 16: Lazy Loading and Accessibility
docs.text:
• alt text is required regardless of lazy loading.
  • Screen readers may not scroll, so lazy-loaded content might not load.
  • Best practice: Provide a "load more" button for critical content.

docs.title: Concept 17: The loading Attribute on <iframe>
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://example.com/embed" loading="lazy" title="Embedded content"></iframe>

Use case: Embeds (YouTube, maps, social widgets) that are below the fold.

docs.title: Concept 18: Lazy Loading and Ads
docs.text:
Ads are often the heaviest resources:

<ins class="adsbygoogle"
     data-ad-client="ca-pub-..."
     data-ad-slot="..."
     loading="lazy"></ins>

docs.title: Concept 19: Lazy Loading Third-Party Scripts
docs.text:
Third-party scripts (analytics, chat widgets) can be loaded lazily:

<script>
    window.addEventListener('load', () => {
        const script = document.createElement('script');
        script.src = 'https://example.com/chat-widget.js';
        document.body.appendChild(script);
    });
</script>

Or with Intersection Observer for on-demand loading.

docs.title: Concept 20: Lazy Loading Libraries
docs.text:
Before native support, libraries were used:

  • lazysizes – popular, feature-rich.
  • lozad.js – lightweight, uses Intersection Observer.
  • LazyLoad – vanilla JS.

Best practice: Use native loading="lazy" when possible; fall back to libraries for advanced needs.

docs.title: Concept 21: Lazy Loading and Service Workers
docs.text:
Service Workers can intercept requests and provide offline or lazy-loaded content:

// In a service worker
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
    event.respondWith(
        caches.match(event.request).then(response => response || fetch(event.request))
    );
});

docs.title: Concept 22: Content-visibility CSS
docs.text:
The content-visibility CSS property can skip rendering off-screen content:

.card {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: 300px 200px;
}

Note: content-visibility is different from lazy loading but serves a similar purpose (deferring rendering).

docs.title: Concept 23: Lazy Loading and Core Web Vitals
docs.text:
• LCP – don't lazy load LCP images.
  • CLS – set dimensions.
  • INP – lazy loading reduces main-thread work.

docs.title: Concept 24: Lazy Loading and Mobile
docs.text:
Mobile benefits most from lazy loading:

  • Slower connections.
  • Limited data plans.
  • Battery constraints.

docs.title: Concept 25: Testing Lazy Loading
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools Network panel – filter by image, scroll, see when images load.
  • Coverage panel – see unused bytes.
  • Lighthouse – audits for lazy loading.
  • WebPageTest – filmstrip view.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Lazy Loading with loading="lazy"
docs.text:
1.  Browser parses the HTML and encounters an image.
    │
    ▼
2.  It reads the `loading` attribute.
    │
    ▼
3.  If `loading="lazy"`:
    │   ├── Browser stores the image as "pending".
    │   ├── It doesn't fetch the image yet.
    │   └── It creates a placeholder box (using width/height).
    │
    ▼
4.  As the user scrolls:
    │   ├── The browser tracks the viewport.
    │   ├── When the image is near the viewport (based on heuristics):
    │   │   ├── It fetches the image.
    │   │   ├── It decodes the image.
    │   │   └── It paints the image.
    │   └── If the image never enters the viewport, it's never loaded.
    │
    ▼
5.  The `load` event fires when the image is loaded.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Intersection Observer Lazy Loading
docs.text:
1.  JavaScript creates an IntersectionObserver.
    │
    ▼
2.  It observes elements with the `lazy` class.
    │
    ▼
3.  When an element enters the viewport:
    │   ├── The callback fires with the entry.
    │   ├── `entry.isIntersecting` is `true`.
    │   ├── The script swaps `data-src` to `src`.
    │   ├── The browser fetches the image.
    │   └── The observer unobserves the element.
    │
    ▼
4.  Elements not yet intersecting remain unloaded.

docs.title: The Browser's Lazy Loading Heuristics
docs.text:
Chrome (and others) use heuristics:

  • Fast connection (4G): load when within ~1250px.
  • Slow connection (2G): load when within ~2500px.
  • Save-Data enabled: load when within ~8000px? No — actually it may be more conservative.

The goal is to anticipate the user's scroll and load just in time.

docs.title: Intersection Observer Flow
docs.text: Observe → Element enters viewport → Callback fires → Load resource → Unobserve

docs.title: Lazy Loading and the Browser Cache
docs.text:
• Lazy loaded images are cached like eager images.
  • On a second visit, they're loaded from cache.
  • loading="lazy" doesn't affect caching.

docs.title: Lazy Loading and HTTP/2
docs.text:
• HTTP/2 multiplexing reduces the benefit of reducing requests.
  • But lazy loading still saves bandwidth and reduces initial load.

docs.title: Lazy Loading and Priority Hints
docs.text:
• fetchpriority="high" – for LCP images.
  • fetchpriority="low" – for below-the-fold images.
  • fetchpriority="auto" – default.

docs.title: Native Lazy Loading vs. Eager Loading
docs.text: Aspect Lazy Eager Load timing Near viewport Immediately Bandwidth Reduced Full Initial load Faster Slower LCP impact Neutral/harmful Positive Best for Below the fold Above the fold

docs.title: The loading Attribute in the HTML Spec
docs.text: The loading attribute is an enumerated attribute with values lazy, eager, and auto (default).

docs.text:
interface IntersectionObserver {
    constructor(callback, options);
    observe(target);
    unobserve(target);

    takeRecords();
    root;

    thresholds;
}

docs.text:
Browser Images Iframes Chrome 76+ 76+ Firefox 75+ 75+ Safari 15.4+ 16.4+ Edge 79+ 79+

Note: Older Safari required JavaScript fallback.

docs.title: Browser Support for Intersection Observer
docs.text: All modern browsers support it. Older browsers need a polyfill.

docs.title: Lazy Loading in the Browser Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Parse – the <img> element is parsed.
  2. Defer – if loading="lazy", defer the fetch.
  3. Observe – the browser observes the element's position.
  4. Trigger – when near the viewport, fetch the image.
  5. Decode – decode the image.
  6. Paint – paint the image.

docs.title: Priority Hints
docs.text:
fetchpriority influences the browser's priority for the resource:

<img src="hero.jpg" fetchpriority="high">
<img src="photo.jpg" loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low">

docs.title: Lazy Loading and preload
docs.text:
• Preload – forces the browser to fetch a resource early.
  • Lazy loading – defers fetching a resource.

Use preload for LCP images; use lazy loading for the rest.

docs.title: Lazy Loading and Service Worker
docs.text: Service Workers can intercept lazy-loaded requests and serve cached responses.

docs.title: Lazy Loading and CSS content-visibility
docs.text:
.lazy-section {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: 500px;
}

Skips rendering off-screen content, similar to lazy loading.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of a Lazy-Loaded Image
docs.text:
1.  Author writes `<img src="photo.jpg" loading="lazy">`.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses HTML.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser defers the fetch.
    │
    ▼
4.  Placeholder box created (using width/height).
    │
    ▼
5.  User scrolls.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser detects image near viewport.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser fetches the image.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser decodes the image.
    │
    ▼
9.  Browser paints the image.
    │
    ▼
10. `load` event fires.
    │
    ▼
11. Image visible.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an Intersection-Observed Element
docs.text:
1.  Script creates IntersectionObserver.
    │
    ▼
2.  Script observes element.
    │
    ▼
3.  Element not intersecting → nothing.
    │
    ▼
4.  User scrolls.
    │
    ▼
5.  Element enters viewport.
    │
    ▼
6.  Callback fires with entry.
    │
    ▼
7.  Script loads resource (e.g., sets `src`).
    │
    ▼
8.  Script unobserves element.
    │
    ▼
9.  Browser fetches and renders.

docs.title: Example 6: Intersection Observer Lazy Loading
docs.text:
<img data-src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" class="lazy" width="800" height="600">
<noscript>
    <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" width="800" height="600">
</noscript>

<script>
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
        entries.forEach(entry => {
            if (entry.isIntersecting) {
                const img = entry.target;
                img.src = img.dataset.src;
                img.classList.remove('lazy');
                observer.unobserve(img);
            }
        });
    }, {
        rootMargin: '200px 0px',
        threshold: 0.01
    });

    document.querySelectorAll('.lazy').forEach(img => observer.observe(img));
</script>

<script>
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
        entries.forEach(entry => {
            if (entry.isIntersecting) {
                const el = entry.target;
                el.style.backgroundImage = `url(${el.dataset.bg})`;
                el.classList.remove('lazy-bg');
                observer.unobserve(el);
            }
        });
    }, {
        rootMargin: '200px 0px'
    });

    document.querySelectorAll('.lazy-bg').forEach(el => observer.observe(el));
</script>

</video>

<script>
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
        entries.forEach(entry => {
            if (entry.isIntersecting) {
                const video = entry.target;
                video.src = video.dataset.src;
                video.load();
                observer.unobserve(video);
            }
        });
    }, {
        rootMargin: '200px 0px'
    });

    document.querySelectorAll('.lazy-video').forEach(v => observer.observe(v));
</script>

     data-src="photo.jpg"
     alt="A scenic view"
