  5. Use allow – for feature permissions.
  6. Set referrerpolicy – for privacy.
  7. Use responsive sizing – with aspect-ratio.
  8. Avoid iframes for critical content – SEO and accessibility.
  9. Provide fallback content – for browsers without iframe support (rare).
  10. Use X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors – prevent clickjacking.
  11. Use postMessage – for cross-origin communication.
  12. Always verify event.origin – in message handlers.
  13. Test with screen readers – ensure accessibility.
  14. Avoid nesting too many iframes – performance.
  15. Consider alternatives – sometimes a link is better.
  16. Use HTTPS – for all iframe sources.
  17. Test on mobile – iframes can be slow.
  18. Monitor performance – iframes can impact LCP and CLS.
  19. Use credentialless – for untrusted embeds (experimental).
  20. Document your iframe strategy – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No title Attribute
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://example.com"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: Accessibility failure; screen readers can't describe the iframe.

✅ Correct: 

<iframe src="https://example.com" title="Example website"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: allow-scripts + allow-same-origin
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://untrusted.com" sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: The iframe can remove its own sandbox attribute, defeating the purpose.

✅ Correct: Use only one, depending on trust level: 

<iframe src="https://untrusted.com" sandbox="allow-scripts"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No sandbox for Untrusted Content
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://untrusted.com"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: Untrusted code runs with full permissions.

✅ Correct: 

<iframe src="https://untrusted.com" sandbox></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No loading="lazy"
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://youtube.com/embed/..."></iframe>

Why it's wrong: Loads heavy content upfront.

✅ Correct: 

<iframe src="..." loading="lazy"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No event.origin Check
docs.text:
window.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
    console.log(event.data); // Security risk!
});

Why it's wrong: Any origin can send messages.

✅ Correct: 

window.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
    if (event.origin !== 'https://trusted.com') return;
    console.log(event.data);
});

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: postMessage with '*'
docs.text:
iframe.contentWindow.postMessage(data, '*');

Why it's wrong: The message can be intercepted by any origin.

✅ Correct: 

iframe.contentWindow.postMessage(data, 'https://trusted.com');

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No X-Frame-Options
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Your site can be embedded by attackers (clickjacking).

✅ Correct: Set X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN or CSP: frame-ancestors 'self'.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Iframe for Navigation
docs.text:
<iframe src="page.html"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: Breaks history, bookmarking, and accessibility.

✅ Correct: Use normal page navigation.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Iframe for Critical Content
docs.text:
<iframe src="important-content.html"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: SEO and accessibility issues.

✅ Correct: Include content in the parent page.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No allowfullscreen
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://youtube.com/embed/..."></iframe>

Why it's wrong: Users can't enter fullscreen.

✅ Correct: 

<iframe src="..." allowfullscreen></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No allow for Camera/Mic
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://example.com/camera-app"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: The camera/mic won't work.

✅ Correct: 

<iframe src="..." allow="camera; microphone"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Responsive Sizing
docs.text:
<iframe src="..." width="800" height="450"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: Overflows on mobile.

✅ Correct: Use aspect-ratio and width: 100%.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Separate document – extra HTTP request.
  • Extra parse and render – the iframe is a full page.
  • Memory – each iframe is a browsing context.
  • Process isolation – cross-origin iframes use separate processes.
  • Blocking – iframes can delay load if not lazy-loaded.
  • LCP – iframes can be LCP elements (rare).
  • CLS – iframes without dimensions cause layout shift.
  • INP – iframe scripts can block if same-process.
  • Nesting – nested iframes multiply cost.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use loading="lazy" – for off-screen iframes.
  2. Set dimensions – prevent CLS.
  3. Use aspect-ratio – for responsive iframes.
  4. Limit iframes – fewer is better.
  5. Use postMessage – avoid same-origin DOM access overhead.
  6. Monitor LCP – iframes can affect it.
  7. Use a CDN – for iframe sources.
  8. Test on mobile – iframes are slower on mobile.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Sandbox – always for untrusted content.
  • allow-scripts + allow-same-origin – never together.
  • X-Frame-Options – prevent clickjacking.
  • CSP frame-ancestors – flexible clickjacking protection.
  • CSP frame-src – restrict what your page can embed.
  • postMessage – always verify origin.
  • HTTPS – required for secure iframes.
  • credentialless – cookie-less embedding.
  • referrerpolicy – control referrer leakage.
  • Payment iframes – PCI compliance.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Sandbox untrusted content.
  2. Never combine allow-scripts + allow-same-origin.
  3. Set X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors.
  4. Verify event.origin in postMessage.
  5. Specify targetOrigin in postMessage.
  6. Use HTTPS – for all iframes.
  7. Use credentialless – for third-party embeds.
  8. Set referrerpolicy – for privacy.
  9. Monitor for clickjacking.
  10. Test with security tools.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the iframe.
  • DevTools Console – select the iframe's context to run scripts in it.
  • Network panel – verify the iframe request.
  • Security panel – check for mixed content and security issues.
  • Application panel – inspect iframe cookies/storage (same-origin).
  • iframe.contentDocument – check for SecurityError.
  • iframe.contentWindow – access the Window.
  • postMessage – log messages and origins.
  • Lighthouse – audits for iframes.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check the iframe's role and name.
  • Screen reader testing – ensure the iframe is announced.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For video embeds – YouTube, Vimeo.
  • For maps – Google Maps.
  • For social embeds – tweets, posts.
  • For ads – isolated third-party ads.
  • For payment forms – Stripe, PayPal.
  • For untrusted content – sandboxed.
  • For micro-frontends – independent widgets.
  • For code playgrounds – CodePen, JSFiddle.
  • For legacy integration – older apps.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For critical content – SEO and accessibility.
  • For navigation – use normal links.
  • For simple embeds – use <img>, <video>, or <blockquote>.
  • For same-origin content – include it directly.
  • When a link is enough – don't embed unnecessarily.
  • When performance is critical – iframes are heavy.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <frame> – obsolete frameset element.
  • <frameset> – obsolete frameset container.
  • <embed> – embeds external content (plugins).
  • <object> – embeds external resources.
  • <video> – video element.
  • <audio> – audio element.
  • <canvas> – drawing surface.
  • <svg> – vector graphics.
  • Same-origin policy – security boundary.
  • postMessage – cross-origin messaging.
  • sandbox – restrictions.
  • allow – permissions policy.
  • X-Frame-Options – clickjacking protection.
  • CSP frame-ancestors – clickjacking protection.
  • CSP frame-src – embedding restrictions.
  • Clickjacking – attack.
  • Process isolation – security.
  • Micro-frontends – composition pattern.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <iframe> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) but was supported in IE 3 earlier.

  • The <frameset> and <frame> elements are obsolete in HTML5 — iframe replaced them.

  • An iframe creates a nested browsing context — a browser within a browser.

  • The sandbox attribute was introduced in HTML5.

  • Never combine allow-scripts and allow-same-origin — it nullifies the sandbox.

  • Iframes are subject to the same-origin policy.

  • Cross-origin communication uses postMessage.

  • Always verify event.origin in message handlers.

  • Clickjacking is an attack where your site is embedded in a transparent iframe.

  • X-Frame-Options and CSP frame-ancestors prevent clickjacking.

  • CSP frame-src restricts what sources your page can embed.

  • loading="lazy" defers off-screen iframes.

  • Stripe, PayPal, and Adyen use iframes for PCI compliance.

  • Ads are often served in iframes for isolation.

  • Micro-frontends are sometimes composed with iframes.

  • srcdoc embeds inline HTML without a separate file.

  • credentialless loads an iframe without credentials (experimental).

  • allowfullscreen allows fullscreen playback.

  • allow controls feature permissions (camera, mic, geolocation).

  • Process isolation in modern browsers isolates cross-origin iframes.

  • Screen readers announce the iframe's title.

  • Best practices: title, loading="lazy", sandbox, X-Frame-Options, verify origins.

  • Common mistakes: no title, no sandbox, postMessage with '*', no origin check.

  • Following best practices for iframes leads to secure, accessible, and performant web pages.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <iframe> element embeds another HTML document inside the current page.
  • It creates a nested browsing context with its own URL, DOM, JS, and CSS.
  • Attributes: src, srcdoc, title, width, height, loading, sandbox, allow, allowfullscreen, referrerpolicy, csp, name, credentialless.
  • Sandbox restricts capabilities; never combine allow-scripts + allow-same-origin.
  • postMessage enables cross-origin communication; always verify event.origin.
  • Same-origin iframes allow direct DOM access; cross-origin iframes do not.
  • Security: use sandbox, X-Frame-Options, CSP frame-ancestors, verify origins.
  • Performance: use loading="lazy", set dimensions, avoid unnecessary iframes.
  • Accessibility: always include title.
  • Common mistakes include missing title, no sandbox, postMessage with '*', and no origin check.
  • Iframes are essential for video embeds, maps, ads, payments, micro-frontends, and sandboxed content.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <embed> element is an HTML element that embeds external content — typically a resource handled by a browser plugin or a built-in handler — into the current document. It is a void (empty) element that references an external resource via the src attribute and specifies its MIME type via the type attribute. The embedded content is rendered as a replaced element inside the document flow.

Unlike <iframe>, which embeds a full HTML document in an isolated browsing context, <embed> embeds a non-HTML resource that the browser renders natively or via an external plugin. Historically, <embed> was used for Flash, QuickTime, and other plugins. Today, its practical uses are narrower: PDFs (in some browsers), SVG documents, and certain media types.

Example: 

<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <embed> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Embedding external resources – PDFs, SVG documents, and plugin-based content.
  • Legacy plugin support – Flash, QuickTime, and other plugins (mostly obsolete now).
  • Simple resource embedding – when an iframe is overkill for a non-HTML resource.
  • Fallback content – works alongside <object> for plugin-based content.
  • Void element simplicity – no closing tag, no children, minimal markup.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <embed> element is embedded content, flow content, and phrasing content. It is a replaced element that occupies space like an image. It can appear anywhere phrasing content is accepted — inside <p>, <div>, <figure>, <td>, and more.

<figure>
    <embed src="brochure.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <figcaption>Product Brochure (PDF)</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
In the 1990s and early 2000s, the web needed to embed non-HTML content — Flash animations, QuickTime videos, PDFs, Java applets, and other rich media. The original <img> element only handled raster images. The <applet> element handled Java applets. But there was no generic way to embed any external resource.

Developers needed a flexible element that could embed any external resource, letting the browser or a plugin handle the rendering. The <embed> element was that solution — a simple, void element with a src and a type that told the browser what to do.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No generic embed element Each content type needed its own element <applet> only for Java No flexibility <img> only for images Couldn't embed PDFs, Flash, etc. No plugin mechanism Browsers couldn't handle arbitrary content No standard API Each plugin used its own markup

docs.title: Why the <embed> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <embed> element was introduced by Netscape in the mid-1990s and later standardized in HTML5 (2014). It was designed as a generic, plugin-friendly embed element that could handle any MIME type the browser or a plugin could render.

Its key features:

  • Void element – no closing tag, no content.
  • Generic – any MIME type.
  • Plugin-friendly – delegates rendering to the browser or a plugin.
  • Simple – one element, a few attributes.

Over time, as plugins (especially Flash) were deprecated, <embed> became less common. Today, it's mainly used for:

  • PDFs – in browsers that render them natively.
  • SVG – for embedding SVG documents.
  • Legacy content – Flash and QuickTime fallbacks.

The <embed> element remains in the HTML Living Standard but is less frequently used than <iframe>, <video>, <audio>, <img>, or <object>.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <embed>
docs.text:
<embed src="URL" type="MIME-TYPE" width="W" height="H">
  • src – the URL of the resource.
  • type – the MIME type (helps the browser choose a handler).
  • width / height – dimensions.

docs.title: Simple Embed
docs.text: <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Embedding SVG
docs.text: <embed src="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300">

docs.title: Embedding Flash (Obsolete)
docs.text:
<embed src="animation.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash" width="400" height="300">

Note: Flash is deprecated and no longer supported in modern browsers.

docs.title: Embedding Audio/Video (Rare)
docs.text:
<embed src="audio.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" width="300" height="50">

Note: Prefer <audio> and <video> for media.

docs.title: Embed with Fallback (Inside <object>)
docs.text:
<object data="movie.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash" width="400" height="300">
    <embed src="movie.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash" width="400" height="300">
    <p>Your browser does not support this content.</p>
</object>

Note: The <embed> inside <object> acts as a fallback for browsers that don't support <object>.

docs.title: Embed with All Attributes
docs.text:
<embed src="content.pdf"
       type="application/pdf"
       width="800"
       height="600"
       title="Product Brochure">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose src The URL of the resource type The MIME type width Width in pixels height Height in pixels title Advisory title name (Obsolete) Name for scripting

docs.title: The "Plug and Play" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <embed> as a plug-and-play socket. You plug in a resource (PDF, SVG, plugin), and the browser (or a plugin) handles it. The type tells the browser which socket to use. Unlike <iframe>, which builds a whole new room, <embed> just plugs something in.

docs.title: The "Universal Adapter" Analogy
docs.text: <embed> is like a universal adapter for external content. You give it a URL and a MIME type, and it delegates to whatever the browser has available to render that type — a PDF viewer, an SVG renderer, or a plugin.

docs.title: The "Black Box" Mental Model
docs.text: An <embed> element is a black box — you provide a URL and dimensions, and the browser fills the box with the rendered resource. You don't have direct control over what's inside, and there's no DOM access (unlike inline SVG or same-origin iframes).

docs.title: The "Legacy" Mental Model
docs.text: <embed> is primarily a legacy element. Its origins are in the plugin era (Netscape, Flash, QuickTime). While it's still valid HTML5, its uses are limited. Modern alternatives — <iframe> for HTML, <img> for images, <video>/<audio> for media, <object> for generic embedding — are preferred in most cases.

docs.title: The "Void Element" Mental Model
docs.text: Unlike <object> (which can contain fallback content), <embed> is a void element — no closing tag, no children. This makes it simple but limits its flexibility.

docs.title: Concept 1: The src Attribute
docs.text:
The src attribute specifies the URL of the resource to embed:

<embed src="document.pdf">

Note: The resource is fetched asynchronously; the browser continues rendering.

docs.title: Concept 2: The type Attribute
docs.text:
The type attribute specifies the MIME type:

<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">

Why: It tells the browser which handler to use. Without it, the browser may guess (often incorrectly).

Common MIME types:

MIME Type Resource application/pdf PDF image/svg+xml SVG application/x-shockwave-flash Flash (obsolete) video/quicktime QuickTime audio/mpeg MP3 video/mp4 MP4

docs.title: Concept 3: The width and height Attributes
docs.text:
Set the dimensions in pixels:

<embed src="..." width="800" height="600">

Note: Without dimensions, <embed> may collapse to a default size or the intrinsic size of the resource.

docs.title: Concept 4: The title Attribute
docs.text:
Provides an advisory title (tooltip):

<embed src="..." title="Product Brochure">

Note: title is not the same as alt. For accessibility, wrap the embed in a <figure> with a <figcaption>.

docs.title: Concept 5: The name Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text: The name attribute was used for scripting references. It is obsolete.

docs.title: Concept 6: Void Element
docs.text:
<embed> has no closing tag and no content:

<embed src="...">  <!-- Correct -->
<embed src="..."></embed>  <!-- Incorrect -->

docs.title: Concept 7: Browser Support
docs.text:
<embed> is supported in all modern browsers. However, plugin support varies:

  • PDF – most browsers render inline or open in a viewer.
  • SVG – most browsers render inline.
  • Flash – no longer supported.
  • QuickTime – no longer supported.

docs.title: Concept 8: Embed vs. Object
docs.text:
Aspect <embed> <object> Content Void element Can contain fallback Complexity Simple More flexible Browser support Good Excellent Fallback None Yes Use case Simple embedding Complex embedding

Note: <object> is generally more reliable for complex embeddings, as it supports fallback content.

docs.title: Concept 9: Embed vs. iframe
docs.text: Aspect <embed> <iframe> Content Non-HTML resources HTML documents Browsing context No Yes DOM access No Same-origin only Use case PDFs, SVG, plugins HTML pages, widgets

docs.title: Concept 10: Embed vs. img
docs.text:
Aspect <embed> <img> Content Any resource Raster images only Rendering Delegated Native Accessibility Limited alt text Use case PDFs, SVG Photos, graphics

Best practice: Use <img> for raster images, <embed> for non-image resources.

docs.title: Concept 11: Embed vs. video/audio
docs.text:
Aspect <embed> <video>/<audio> Rendering Plugin/delegated Native Controls Depends on plugin Native controls JavaScript API None Rich API Use case Legacy media Modern media

Best practice: Use <video> and <audio> for media.

docs.title: Concept 12: Embedding PDFs
docs.text:
<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

Note: Not all browsers render PDFs inline. Some download or open externally.

docs.title: Concept 13: Embedding SVG
docs.text:
<embed src="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300">

Note: For inline SVG (with CSS/JS access), use <svg> directly instead.

docs.title: Concept 14: Embedding Flash (Obsolete)
docs.text:
<embed src="animation.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash">

Note: Flash was deprecated in 2020 and is no longer supported in modern browsers.

docs.title: Concept 15: The <param> Element (Obsolete)
docs.text:
Historically, <param> was used to pass parameters to plugins embedded via <object>:

<object>
    <param name="autoplay" value="true">
    <embed src="...">
</object>

Note: <param> is obsolete in HTML5 (still valid in <object> but rarely used).

docs.title: Concept 16: Accessibility
docs.text:
The <embed> element has limited accessibility:

  • No alt attribute.
  • No accessible name from the element itself.
  • Screen readers may not announce it well.

Best practice:

  • Wrap in <figure> with a <figcaption>.
  • Provide a link to download the resource.
  • Use <object> with fallback content for better accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 17: Fallback Content
docs.text:
<embed> has no fallback content (it's a void element). For fallback:

  • Wrap in <object> (which supports fallback).
  • Provide a link to the resource.
  • Use <noscript> if needed.

docs.title: Concept 18: CSP and Embed
docs.text:
Content Security Policy restricts embedding:

  • object-src – controls <embed>, <object>, <applet>.
  • frame-src – controls <iframe>.
Content-Security-Policy: object-src 'none';

Why: Prevents plugin-based attacks.

docs.title: Concept 19: Browser Behaviour
docs.text:
• PDFs – Chrome, Firefox, Edge render inline; Safari may download.
  • SVG – All modern browsers render inline.
  • Flash – No modern browser supports it.
  • Plugins – Generally deprecated.

docs.title: Concept 20: When to Use <embed>
docs.text:
• Embedding PDFs – when inline rendering is desired.
  • Embedding SVG – for standalone SVG files.
  • Legacy fallback – inside <object> for old browsers.
  • Simple non-HTML content – when iframe is overkill.

docs.title: Concept 21: When NOT to Use <embed>
docs.text:
• For HTML documents – use <iframe>.
  • For raster images – use <img>.
  • For video/audio – use <video>/<audio>.
  • For inline SVG – use <svg>.
  • For critical content – accessibility issues.

docs.title: Concept 22: <object> as the Modern Alternative
docs.text:
<object> is generally preferred over <embed>:

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support PDFs. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

Benefits: Fallback content, better accessibility, richer API.

docs.title: Concept 23: The <applet> Element (Obsolete)
docs.text: <applet> was used to embed Java applets. It is obsolete.

docs.title: Concept 24: SVG as an Alternative to <embed>
docs.text:
For SVG, inline <svg> is more powerful:

<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="400" height="300">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue"/>
</svg>

Benefits: CSS styling, JS access, accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 25: Security Concerns
docs.text:
• Plugins – Historically a major security risk (Flash, Java).
  • CSP – Restrict with object-src 'none'.
  • Sandboxing – Not available for <embed> (unlike <iframe>).
  • Untrusted content – Avoid embedding untrusted resources.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing <embed>
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters `<embed>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  Creates a DOM node (replaced element).
    │
    ▼
3.  Reads `src` and `type` attributes.
    │
    ▼
4.  Checks if a handler is available for `type`:
    │   ├── Native handler (PDF, SVG) → use it.
    │   ├── Plugin handler → use it (if installed).
    │   └── No handler → show placeholder or error.
    │
    ▼
5.  Fetches the resource (or uses cache).
    │
    ▼
6.  Creates a nested rendering context (not a browsing context).
    │
    ▼
7.  Renders the resource inside the element's box.
    │
    ▼
8.  The `<embed>` element becomes a replaced element in the layout.

docs.title: Rendering vs. Browsing Context
docs.text:
• <iframe> – creates a browsing context (separate document, separate JS, separate DOM).
  • <embed> – creates a rendering context (delegated rendering, no DOM access).
  • <object> – similar to <embed> but can contain fallback.

docs.title: Browser Handling of MIME Types
docs.text: MIME Type Modern Handling application/pdf Built-in PDF viewer (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) image/svg+xml Native SVG rendering application/x-shockwave-flash No support video/quicktime No support audio/mpeg May fall back to <audio> text/html May not render (use <iframe>)

docs.title: CSP object-src
docs.text:
The object-src CSP directive restricts <embed>:

Content-Security-Policy: object-src 'none';

Effect: <embed>, <object>, and <applet> are blocked.

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
<embed> is exposed as a replaced element:

  • role: document or application (varies).
  • name: from title (limited).

Note: Accessibility support is weak. Prefer <object> or <iframe> with title.

docs.title: Fallback Behaviour
docs.text:
<embed> has no fallback content. If the browser can't render it:

  • It shows a placeholder (e.g., broken plugin icon).
  • It may show a download link.
  • It may show nothing.

Solution: Wrap in <object> for fallback.

docs.title: The HTMLEmbedElement Interface
The Rendering Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Fetch – the browser downloads the resource.
  2. Handler selection – the browser chooses a handler based on type.
  3. Rendering – the handler renders the resource.
  4. Paint – the browser paints the rendered output.

docs.title: Browser Engine Integration
docs.text:
• Blink (Chrome) – uses internal PDF viewer, SVG renderer.
  • Gecko (Firefox) – uses pdf.js for PDF, native SVG.
  • WebKit (Safari) – uses native PDF and SVG rendering.

docs.title: CSP Interaction
docs.text:
The CSP object-src directive is checked before rendering:

  • If object-src 'none', <embed> is blocked.
  • If object-src 'self', <embed> must be same-origin.

docs.title: Replaced Element
docs.text:
<embed> is a replaced element — its content is not in the DOM tree; the browser's rendering engine handles it. This is why:

  • CSS cannot style the interior.
  • JavaScript cannot access the interior.
  • The element's box is defined by width/height or intrinsic size.

docs.title: SVG Rendering
docs.text:
When type="image/svg+xml":

  • The browser parses the SVG as a document.
  • Renders it into the embed box.
  • No CSS/JS access from parent.

docs.title: PDF Rendering
docs.text:
When type="application/pdf":

  • Chrome/Edge use the built-in PDF viewer.
  • Firefox uses pdf.js.
  • Safari uses its native PDF renderer.

Some browsers download the PDF instead of rendering it.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an <embed>
docs.text:
1.  Author writes `<embed src="..." type="...">`.
    │
    ▼
2.  File deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses HTML and creates the DOM node.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser reads `src` and `type`.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser fetches the resource.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser selects the appropriate handler.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser renders the resource.
    │
    ▼
8.  The replaced element is displayed.
    │
    ▼
9.  No direct JS/CSS access to the interior.
    │
    ▼
10. When the page is unloaded, the embed is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Creation
docs.text:
const embed = document.createElement('embed');
embed.src = 'document.pdf';
embed.type = 'application/pdf';
embed.width = 800;
embed.height = 600;
document.body.appendChild(embed);

docs.title: Example 1: Embedding a PDF
docs.text: <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Example 2: Embedding an SVG
docs.text: <embed src="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300">

docs.title: Example 3: Embed with Figure and Caption
docs.text:
<figure>
    <embed src="brochure.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <figcaption>Product Brochure (PDF) — <a href="brochure.pdf">Download</a></figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 4: Embed with Link Fallback
docs.text:
<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
<p>If the PDF doesn't display, <a href="document.pdf">download it here</a>.</p>

docs.title: Example 5: Embed Inside Object (Fallback)
docs.text:
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support this content. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

docs.title: Example 6: Embedding SVG with Figure
docs.text:
<figure>
    <embed src="logo.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="200" height="60">
    <figcaption>Company Logo</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 7: Responsive Embed
docs.text:
<style>
    .embed-wrapper {
        position: relative;
        padding-bottom: 75%;
        height: 0;
    }
    .embed-wrapper embed {
        position: absolute;
        top: 0;
        left: 0;
        width: 100%;
        height: 100%;
    }
</style>

<div class="embed-wrapper">
    <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">
</div>

docs.title: Example 8: Embed with title
docs.text:
<embed src="document.pdf"
       type="application/pdf"
       width="800"
       height="600"
       title="Product Brochure">

docs.title: Example 9: Legacy Flash Embed (Not Supported)
docs.text:
<embed src="animation.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash" width="400" height="300">

Note: This will not render in modern browsers.

docs.title: Example 10: Embed vs. Object Comparison
docs.text:
<!-- Embed: simple, no fallback -->
<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

<!-- Object: fallback content -->
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

docs.title: Example 11: Embed with srcdoc (Not Supported)
docs.text: Note: <embed> does not support srcdoc (unlike <iframe>).

docs.title: Example 12: Embed with JS Detection
docs.text:
<embed id="myEmbed" src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

<script>
    const embed = document.getElementById('myEmbed');
    embed.addEventListener('load', () => {
        console.log('Embed loaded');
    });
    embed.addEventListener('error', () => {
        console.log('Embed failed');
    });
</script>

Note: load and error events are not reliably supported on <embed>.

docs.title: Example 13: Embed with CSP
docs.text:
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="object-src 'self'">
<embed src="/document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Example 14: Embed in a Card
docs.text:
<div class="card">
    <h3>Document Viewer</h3>
    <embed src="report.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="100%" height="500">
</div>

docs.title: Example 15: Embed for Music Score
docs.text: <embed src="score.musicxml" type="application/vnd.recordare.musicxml+xml" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Example 16: Embed with Figure Caption and Download
docs.text:
<figure>
    <embed src="annual-report.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="100%" height="600">
    <figcaption>
        Annual Report 2026.
        <a href="annual-report.pdf" download>Download PDF</a>.
    </figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 17: Embedding an SVG with Fallback Image
docs.text:
<object data="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300">
    <embed src="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300">
    <img src="diagram.png" alt="A system diagram" width="400" height="300">
</object>

docs.title: Example 18: Dynamic Embed with JavaScript
docs.text:
function embedDocument(url, type) {
    const container = document.getElementById('viewer');
    container.innerHTML = '';
    const embed = document.createElement('embed');
    embed.src = url;
    embed.type = type;
    embed.width = '100%';
    embed.height = '600';
    container.appendChild(embed);
}
embedDocument('report.pdf', 'application/pdf');

docs.title: Example 19: Embed in a Modal
docs.text:
<dialog id="pdfDialog">
    <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <form method="dialog"><button>Close</button></form>
</dialog>

<button onclick="document.getElementById('pdfDialog').showModal()">View PDF</button>

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Embed Demo
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Embed Demo</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 900px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        section { margin-bottom: 2rem; }
        embed { width: 100%; height: 500px; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 8px; display: block; }
        figure { margin: 0; }
        figcaption { font-size: 0.875rem; color: #6c757d; margin-top: 0.5rem; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Embed Demo</h1>

    <section>
        <h2>PDF Embed</h2>
        <figure>
            <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" title="Sample PDF document">
            <figcaption>Sample PDF — <a href="document.pdf">Download</a></figcaption>
        </figure>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>SVG Embed</h2>
        <figure>
            <embed src="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300" title="System diagram">
            <figcaption>System Architecture Diagram</figcaption>
        </figure>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Embed Inside Object (with Fallback)</h2>
        <object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="100%" height="500">
            <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="100%" height="500">
            <p>Your browser doesn't support this content. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
        </object>
    </section>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example PDF viewing Inline PDF display SVG documents Standalone SVG files Legacy plugin content Flash (obsolete) Rich media MusicXML, 3D models Document previews Contracts, forms Legacy <object> fallback For old browsers

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always specify type – helps the browser choose a handler.
  2. Set width and height – prevent layout shift.
  3. Wrap in <figure> – for captions and accessibility.
  4. Provide a download link – for fallback.
  5. Prefer <object> – for complex embeddings with fallback.
  6. Prefer <iframe> – for HTML documents.
  7. Prefer <img> – for raster images.
  8. Prefer <video> / <audio> – for media.
  9. Prefer inline <svg> – for SVG with CSS/JS access.
  10. Use title – for advisory information.
  11. Avoid embedding untrusted content – no sandbox available.
  12. Set CSP object-src – restrict sources.
  13. Test in multiple browsers – behavior varies.
  14. Test on mobile – embeds can be slow.
  15. Provide fallback content – via <object> or a link.
  16. Avoid <embed> for critical content – accessibility issues.
  17. Document your embed strategy – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No type Attribute
docs.text:
<embed src="document.pdf">

Why it's wrong: The browser may not know how to handle the resource.

✅ Correct: 

<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Dimensions
docs.text:
<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">

Why it's wrong: The embed may collapse or use intrinsic size unpredictably.

✅ Correct: 

<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Closing Tag
docs.text:
<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf"></embed>

Why it's wrong: <embed> is a void element; no closing tag.

✅ Correct: 

<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <embed> for HTML Documents
docs.text:
<embed src="page.html" type="text/html">

Why it's wrong: Use <iframe> for HTML.

✅ Correct: 

<iframe src="page.html" title="Embedded page"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <embed> for Raster Images
docs.text:
<embed src="photo.jpg" type="image/jpeg">

Why it's wrong: Use <img>.

✅ Correct: 

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <embed> for Video
docs.text:
<embed src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">

Why it's wrong: Use <video>.

✅ Correct: 

<video src="video.mp4" controls></video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Fallback
docs.text:
<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">

Why it's wrong: Users with browsers that can't render PDFs see nothing.

✅ Correct: 

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support PDFs. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Embedding Untrusted Content Without Sandbox
docs.text:
<embed src="https://untrusted.com/file.pdf" type="application/pdf">

Why it's wrong: No sandbox available for <embed>.

✅ Correct: Use <iframe sandbox> for untrusted content: 

<iframe src="https://untrusted.com/file.pdf" sandbox title="Untrusted content"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Accessibility
docs.text:
<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">

Why it's wrong: Screen readers can't describe the embed.

✅ Correct: 

<figure>
    <embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <figcaption>Product Brochure (PDF) — <a href="document.pdf">Download</a></figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <embed> for Flash
docs.text:
<embed src="animation.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash">

Why it's wrong: Flash is no longer supported.

✅ Correct: Convert to HTML5, video, or SVG.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No width/height
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Causes layout shift.

✅ Correct: Always set dimensions.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Separate HTTP request – each embed fetches a resource.
  • Extra rendering cost – delegated to the handler.
  • No lazy loading – <embed> doesn't support loading="lazy".
  • No caching hints – server must send caching headers.
  • Memory – depends on the resource.
  • Blocking – can delay page load.
  • No priority hints – no fetchpriority.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Set dimensions – prevent CLS.
  2. Lazy load with JS – for off-screen embeds.
  3. Cache aggressively – with Cache-Control.
  4. Use a CDN – for global delivery.
  5. Compress resources – smaller files.
  6. Limit embeds – fewer is better.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Plugins – historically a major security risk.
  • CSP object-src – restrict embed sources.
  • No sandbox – <embed> cannot be sandboxed.
  • Untrusted content – avoid; use <iframe sandbox> instead.
  • HTTPS – required for secure embeds.
  • Download fallback – ensure downloads are from trusted sources.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Restrict object-src – CSP.
  2. Avoid untrusted embeds – no sandbox available.
  3. Use HTTPS – for all embeds.
  4. Validate resources – before serving.
  5. Prefer <iframe sandbox> – for untrusted content.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <embed> element.
  • Network panel – verify the resource request.
  • Console – check for errors.
  • Browser-specific testing – PDF and SVG rendering varies.
  • embed.src – check the URL.
  • embed.type – check the MIME type.
  • Lighthouse – audits.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check role and name.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For PDFs – inline display in supported browsers.
  • For SVG documents – standalone SVG files.
  • As fallback inside <object> – for old browsers.
  • For simple non-HTML content – when iframe is overkill.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For HTML documents – use <iframe>.
  • For raster images – use <img>.
  • For video/audio – use <video>/<audio>.
  • For inline SVG – use <svg>.
  • For untrusted content – use <iframe sandbox>.
  • For critical content – accessibility issues.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <object> – generic embedding with fallback.
  • <iframe> – HTML document embedding.
  • <img> – raster images.
  • <video> – video.
  • <audio> – audio.
  • <svg> – vector graphics.
  • <param> – parameters for plugins (obsolete).
  • <applet> – Java applets (obsolete).
  • MIME type – resource type.
  • CSP object-src – restriction.
  • Plugin – external renderer.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <embed> element was introduced by Netscape in the mid-1990s.

  • It was standardized in HTML5 (2014).

  • <embed> is a void element — no closing tag, no content.

  • It has no fallback content (unlike <object>).

  • Flash was deprecated in 2020; <embed> for Flash no longer works.

  • PDFs render inline in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge; Safari may download.

  • SVG renders inline in all modern browsers.

  • <embed> cannot be sandboxed — unlike <iframe>.

  • CSP object-src controls <embed>.

  • <object> is generally preferred over <embed> for fallback support.

  • <embed> has weak accessibility — wrap in <figure>.

  • <embed> supports title, src, type, width, height — that's about it.

  • No loading="lazy" for <embed> — lazy load with JavaScript if needed.

  • The name attribute is obsolete.

  • The <param> element was used to pass parameters to plugins via <object>.

  • <applet> was used for Java applets; it is obsolete.

  • Best practices: type, dimensions, figure caption, download link, prefer <object>.

  • Common mistakes: no type, no dimensions, closing tag, no fallback.

  • Following best practices for <embed> leads to functional, accessible, and secure embedding of non-HTML content.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <embed> element embeds non-HTML external content — PDFs, SVG, legacy plugins.
  • It is a void element with a src and type.
  • Attributes: src, type, width, height, title (and obsolete name).
  • No fallback content — wrap in <object> for fallback.
  • Weak accessibility — wrap in <figure> with a caption.
  • No sandbox — use <iframe sandbox> for untrusted content.
  • CSP object-src restricts embedding.
  • Best practices: specify type, set dimensions, wrap in <figure>, provide a download link, prefer <object> or <iframe> when appropriate.
  • Common mistakes include no type, no dimensions, closing tag, and using it for HTML/images/video.
  • <embed> is a legacy element — still valid, but with limited modern use cases.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <object> element is an HTML element that embeds external resources — HTML documents, images, PDFs, SVG, video, audio, or plugin-based content — into the current document. Unlike <embed>, which is a void element, <object> is a container element that can hold fallback content rendered when the resource cannot be displayed. It provides a generic, standardized way to embed any resource the browser can handle, with graceful degradation built in.

<object> is one of the oldest embedding mechanisms on the web, predating <iframe> in some contexts. It is the successor to the obsolete <applet> element and a more flexible alternative to <embed>. It supports nested fallbacks — you can nest <object> elements inside each other, each attempting a different resource until one succeeds.

Example: 

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support PDFs. <a href="document.pdf">Download the PDF</a>.</p>
</object>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <object> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Generic embedding – embed any resource by MIME type.
  • Fallback content – provide alternatives if the resource cannot be displayed.
  • Nested fallbacks – chain multiple attempts for maximum compatibility.
  • Accessibility – fallback content can describe the resource for screen readers.
  • Plugin delegation – historically used for plugins (Flash, QuickTime, Java).
  • PDF and SVG embedding – modern use case for document display.
  • Micro-frontends – embedding independent HTML applications.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
The <object> element is embedded content, flow content, and phrasing content. It is a replaced element that occupies space like an image. It can appear anywhere phrasing content is accepted — inside <p>, <div>, <figure>, <td>, and more.

<figure>
    <object data="brochure.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
        <p>PDF not supported. <a href="brochure.pdf">Download the brochure</a>.</p>
    </object>
    <figcaption>Product Brochure (PDF)</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before <object>, embedding external content was fragmented:

  • <img> – only raster images.
  • <applet> – only Java applets.
  • <embed> – generic but no fallback content.
  • Plugins – each used its own markup, often proprietary.

Developers needed a generic, standardized, fallback-capable embedding element. If one resource type failed, another should be tried. If all failed, a text description should be shown. The <object> element was that solution.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence <img> limited to images No PDFs, SVG, plugins <applet> limited to Java No flexibility <embed> has no fallback Users see nothing on failure Plugin markup varied Fragmented, non-standard No nesting No chained fallbacks Poor accessibility Screen readers couldn't describe

docs.title: Why the <object> Element Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <object> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997) as the modern, standardized, generic embedding element. It was designed to:

  • Embed any resource – images, PDFs, SVG, HTML, plugins.
  • Provide fallback content – rendered when the resource fails.
  • Support nesting – fallback can itself be an <object>.
  • Improve accessibility – fallback text describes the resource.
  • Delegate to plugins – Flash, QuickTime, Java.
  • Standardize embedding – one element for all cases.

The <object> element replaces both <applet> (for Java) and <embed> (in most cases). Modern browsers support it universally, and it remains the preferred generic embedding element alongside <iframe> and <embed>.

docs.title: The Basic Syntax of <object>
docs.text:
<object data="URL" type="MIME-TYPE" width="W" height="H">
    <!-- Fallback content -->
</object>
  • data – the URL of the resource (note: data, not src).
  • type – the MIME type.
  • width / height – dimensions.
  • Fallback content – shown if the resource cannot be displayed.

docs.title: Simple PDF Embed
docs.text:
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support PDFs. <a href="document.pdf">Download the PDF</a>.</p>
</object>

docs.title: SVG Embed
docs.text:
<object data="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300">
    <img src="diagram.png" alt="A system diagram" width="400" height="300">
</object>

docs.title: Image Embed (Alternative to <img>)
docs.text:
<object data="photo.jpg" type="image/jpeg" width="800" height="600">
    <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" width="800" height="600">
</object>

Note: Prefer <img> for raster images.

docs.title: HTML Embed (Alternative to <iframe>)
docs.text:
<object data="page.html" type="text/html" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support embedded HTML. <a href="page.html">Open page</a>.</p>
</object>

Note: <iframe> is preferred for HTML documents.

docs.title: Nested Fallbacks
docs.text:
<object data="movie.mp4" type="video/mp4" width="640" height="360">
    <object data="movie.webm" type="video/webm" width="640" height="360">
        <object data="movie.ogv" type="video/ogg" width="640" height="360">
            <p>Your browser doesn't support this video. <a href="movie.mp4">Download</a>.</p>
        </object>
    </object>
</object>

Note: Each <object> tries to render its resource; if it fails, the fallback (the next <object>) is attempted.

docs.title: Object with Parameters
docs.text:
<object data="animation.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash" width="400" height="300">
    <param name="autoplay" value="true">
    <param name="loop" value="false">
    <p>Flash not supported. <a href="animation.swf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

Note: <param> is obsolete but historically used with plugins.

docs.title: Object with name
docs.text:
<object data="page.html" type="text/html" name="myFrame" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Fallback content</p>
</object>

Note: The name attribute allows targeting via <a target> and <form target>. However, <iframe> is more commonly used for this purpose.

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose data The URL of the resource type The MIME type width / height Dimensions name Name for targeting (rarely used) form Associates with a form (rarely used) <param> Parameters for plugins (obsolete) Fallback content Any flow content, including nested <object>

docs.title: The "Nested Boxes" Analogy
docs.text: Think of <object> as a set of nested boxes. The outermost box tries to display a resource. If it can't, it opens to reveal a smaller box inside, which tries another resource. If that also fails, a third box, and so on — until finally a text description is shown. This is the essence of fallback chaining.

docs.title: The "Backup Plan" Mental Model
docs.text:
<object> always has a backup plan:

  • Plan A: Display the primary resource.
  • Plan B: Display a fallback resource.
  • Plan C: Display a fallback resource.
  • Plan D: Show text content.

Unlike <embed>, <object> is never left empty — there's always something to show.

docs.title: The "Universal Wrapper" Mental Model
docs.text:
<object> is a universal wrapper for external content. It can wrap:

  • Images (image/jpeg).
  • SVG (image/svg+xml).
  • PDFs (application/pdf).
  • HTML (text/html).
  • Video (video/mp4).
  • Audio (audio/mpeg).
  • Flash (application/x-shockwave-flash — obsolete).
  • Any MIME type.

The type attribute tells the browser how to interpret the wrapped content.

docs.title: The "Object vs. Embed" Mental Model
docs.text:
Aspect <object> <embed> Fallback Yes No Nesting Yes No Closing tag Yes No (void) Attributes data, type src, type Use case Preferred for reliability Legacy, simple embedding

Rule: Use <object> when you need fallback; use <embed> for simple, trusted embeds.

docs.title: The "Replace the Obsolete" Mental Model
docs.text:
<object> is designed to replace obsolete elements:

  • <applet> (Java) → <object>.
  • <embed> → <object> with fallback.
  • Plugin-specific markup → <object> with type.

docs.title: Concept 1: The data Attribute
docs.text:
The data attribute specifies the URL of the resource:

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">

Note: Unlike <embed>, which uses src, <object> uses data.

docs.title: Concept 2: The type Attribute
docs.text:
The type attribute specifies the MIME type:

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">

Why: The browser uses type to decide how to render the resource.

docs.title: Concept 3: The width and height Attributes
docs.text:
Set the dimensions in pixels:

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Concept 4: Fallback Content
docs.text:
The content between <object> and </object> is the fallback:

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">
    <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

Rendered when:

  • The resource fails to load.
  • The MIME type is unsupported.
  • The plugin is missing.

Fallback can be:

  • Text and inline elements.
  • Block elements (paragraphs, lists).
  • Images (<img>).
  • Another <object> (nested fallback).
  • Video or audio.

docs.title: Concept 5: Nested Fallbacks
docs.text:
<object data="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <object data="video.webm" type="video/webm">
        <object data="video.ogv" type="video/ogg">
            <p>No video support. <a href="video.mp4">Download</a>.</p>
        </object>
    </object>
</object>

Why: Provides multiple chances for the browser to render a resource.

docs.title: Concept 6: The <param> Element (Obsolete)
docs.text:
The <param> element passes parameters to plugins:

<object data="animation.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash">
    <param name="autoplay" value="true">
    <param name="quality" value="high">
</object>

Note: <param> is obsolete in HTML5 for most uses, but still valid in <object>.

docs.title: Concept 7: The name Attribute
docs.text:
The name attribute allows the <object> to be targeted by links and forms:

<a href="page.html" target="myFrame">Load in object</a>
<object data="page.html" type="text/html" name="myFrame" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Fallback</p>
</object>

Note: <iframe> is preferred for this use case.

docs.title: Concept 8: Object vs. iframe
docs.text:
Aspect <object> <iframe> Content Any resource HTML documents Browsing context Limited Full DOM access No Same-origin only Fallback Yes Yes (content between tags) Sandbox No Yes Accessibility Good (fallback) Good (title)

Best practice: Use <iframe> for HTML documents and sandboxing; <object> for non-HTML resources with fallback.

docs.title: Concept 9: Object vs. Embed
docs.text: Aspect <object> <embed> Fallback Yes No Nesting Yes No Attributes data src Preferred Yes Less preferred

docs.title: Concept 10: Object vs. img
docs.text:
Aspect <object> <img> Content Any resource Raster images alt No Yes Use case PDFs, SVG Photos

Best practice: Use <img> for images, <object> for other resources.

docs.title: Concept 11: PDF Embedding
docs.text:
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

Browser behaviour:

  • Chrome, Firefox, Edge: render inline.
  • Safari: may download.
  • Mobile: often downloads.

docs.title: Concept 12: SVG Embedding
docs.text:
<object data="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300">
    <img src="diagram.png" alt="System diagram" width="400" height="300">
</object>

Note: For inline SVG (with CSS/JS access), use <svg>.

docs.title: Concept 13: HTML Embedding
docs.text:
<object data="page.html" type="text/html" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Fallback</p>
</object>

Note: Some browsers restrict embedding HTML via <object> for security. Use <iframe>.

docs.title: Concept 14: Video Embedding
docs.text:
<object data="video.mp4" type="video/mp4" width="640" height="360">
    <p>Video not supported. <a href="video.mp4">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

Note: <video> is the modern, preferred element.

docs.title: Concept 15: Audio Embedding
docs.text:
<object data="audio.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" width="300" height="50">
    <p>Audio not supported. <a href="audio.mp3">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

Note: <audio> is the modern, preferred element.

docs.title: Concept 16: Accessibility
docs.text:
<object> supports fallback content — this is its accessibility advantage:

<object data="chart.png" type="image/png">
    <p>Bar chart showing sales growth from 2020 to 2026. Q1 2020: $1M, Q2 2020: $1.2M, ...</p>
</object>

Note: The fallback text describes the resource for screen readers and browsers that can't render the resource.

Best practice: Always provide meaningful fallback.

docs.title: Concept 17: The form Attribute
docs.text: The form attribute associates the <object> with a form (rarely used).

docs.title: Concept 18: Browser Support
docs.text: <object> is supported in all modern browsers. Rendering varies by MIME type and browser.

docs.title: Concept 19: CSP and Object
docs.text:
The CSP object-src directive restricts <object>:

Content-Security-Policy: object-src 'self'

Why: Prevents embedding of untrusted content.

docs.title: Concept 20: The <param> Legacy
docs.text: While <param> is obsolete in modern HTML, it still works inside <object> for legacy plugins.

docs.title: Concept 21: The classid Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text: classid was used to identify the plugin (e.g., the Java plugin). It is obsolete.

docs.title: Concept 22: The codebase Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text: codebase was used to specify the base URL for plugin downloads. It is obsolete.

docs.title: Concept 23: The archive Attribute (Obsolete)
docs.text: archive was used to list archives needed by a Java applet. It is obsolete.

docs.title: Concept 24: Modern Use Cases
docs.text:
• PDF display – inline PDF viewer.
  • SVG display – standalone SVG.
  • Fallback chaining – for maximum compatibility.
  • Legacy applets – rarely, for old content.

docs.title: Concept 25: Deprecation of Plugin Content
docs.text: Since Flash and Java applets are deprecated, <object> is now used primarily for native resources (PDFs, SVG, images).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Processing <object>
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters `<object>` element.
    │
    ▼
2.  Creates a DOM node (replaced element).
    │
    ▼
3.  Reads `data` and `type` attributes.
    │
    ▼
4.  Checks if a handler is available for `type`:
    │   ├── Native handler (PDF, SVG, image) → use it.
    │   ├── Plugin handler → use it (if installed).
    │   └── No handler → use fallback content.
    │
    ▼
5.  Fetches the resource.
    │
    ▼
6.  Renders the resource inside the element's box.
    │
    ▼
7.  If rendering fails, the fallback content is displayed.
    │   ├── Fallback may be another `<object>` (nested).
    │   ├── Fallback may be text (accessible description).
    │   └── Fallback may be a link (download).

docs.title: The Fallback Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Browser attempts to render the resource at data.
  2. If it can't (unsupported MIME type, missing plugin, failed fetch), it tries the fallback.
  3. The fallback may be:
  4. Text – displayed inline.
  5. Another <object> – recursively attempted.
  6. An <img> – displayed.
  7. A <video> or <audio> – played.
  8. A <p> – descriptive text.
  9. If the fallback also fails, continue to the next level.
  10. Eventually, text is displayed if all else fails.

docs.title: Rendering vs. Browsing Context
docs.text:
• <object> – creates a replaced element, not a browsing context.
  • <iframe> – creates a browsing context (separate document, JS, DOM).
  • <object type="text/html"> – may create a limited context in some browsers.

docs.title: CSP object-src
docs.text:
The CSP object-src directive restricts <object>:

  • If object-src 'none', <object> is blocked.
  • If object-src 'self', only same-origin <object> allowed.

docs.title: Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
<object> is exposed as:

  • role: document, img, or application (varies by resource).
  • name: from title or fallback content.

Note: Fallback content is critical for accessibility. If the resource is visual and can't be rendered, the fallback text describes it.

docs.title: Browser Differences
docs.text: Browser PDF SVG HTML Chrome ✅ inline ✅ inline Limited Firefox ✅ pdf.js ✅ inline Limited Safari ✅ / download ✅ inline Limited Edge ✅ inline ✅ inline Limited

docs.title: The contentDocument Property
docs.text:
For same-origin <object> with HTML content, contentDocument may be accessible:

const obj = document.querySelector('object');
console.log(obj.contentDocument); // Same-origin only

Note: This varies by browser and content type.

docs.title: The HTMLObjectElement Interface
docs.text: Property Description data The URL type The MIME type name The name width Width height Height contentDocument The Document (if HTML, same-origin) contentWindow The Window (if HTML, same-origin) form Associated form validity Form validity

docs.title: The Replaced Element Model
docs.text:
<object> is a replaced element — the interior is not DOM, but a rendered resource:

  • CSS cannot style the interior.
  • JavaScript cannot access the interior (unless HTML same-origin).
  • The element's box is defined by width/height or intrinsic size.

docs.title: Fallback Rendering
docs.text:
The browser decides which fallback to render based on:

  1. Support for the MIME type.
  2. Success fetching the resource.
  3. Presence of a plugin (historically).

docs.title: Content Types
docs.text:
• PDFs – rendered by the browser's built-in or pdf.js viewer.
  • SVG – rendered natively.
  • Images – rendered as replaced content.
  • HTML – rendered in a limited browsing context (varies).
  • Plugins – obsolete in modern browsers.

docs.title: CSP Interaction
docs.text:
object-src is checked before rendering:

Content-Security-Policy: object-src 'none';

Blocks all <object> elements.

docs.title: Accessibility API
docs.text:
<object> is exposed with:

  • Role – document, img, application.
  • Name – from title, fallback text.
  • Description – from fallback text.

The fallback is essential — without it, screen readers have nothing to announce.

docs.title: The Lifecycle of an <object>
docs.text:
1.  Author writes `<object>` with `data`, `type`, and fallback.
    │
    ▼
2.  File deployed.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses HTML and creates the DOM node.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser reads `data` and `type`.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser fetches the resource.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser selects the appropriate handler.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser attempts to render the resource.
    │   ├── Success → resource displayed.
    │   └── Failure → fallback content displayed.
    │
    ▼
8.  The replaced element (or fallback) is visible.
    │
    ▼
9.  When the page is unloaded, the object is destroyed.

docs.title: Dynamic Creation
docs.text:
const obj = document.createElement('object');
obj.data = 'document.pdf';
obj.type = 'application/pdf';
obj.width = 800;
obj.height = 600;
obj.innerHTML = '<p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>';
document.body.appendChild(obj);

docs.title: Example 1: PDF with Fallback
docs.text:
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Your browser doesn't support PDFs. <a href="document.pdf">Download the PDF</a>.</p>
</object>

docs.title: Example 2: SVG with Image Fallback
docs.text:
<object data="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300">
    <img src="diagram.png" alt="System diagram" width="400" height="300">
</object>

docs.title: Example 3: Nested Video Fallbacks
docs.text:
<object data="movie.mp4" type="video/mp4" width="640" height="360">
    <object data="movie.webm" type="video/webm" width="640" height="360">
        <object data="movie.ogv" type="video/ogg" width="640" height="360">
            <p>No video support. <a href="movie.mp4">Download the video</a>.</p>
        </object>
    </object>
</object>

docs.title: Example 4: Image with Text Fallback
docs.text:
<object data="chart.png" type="image/png" width="800" height="400">
    <p>Bar chart showing sales growth: 2020: $1M, 2021: $1.2M, 2022: $1.5M, 2023: $1.8M.</p>
</object>

docs.title: Example 5: Object in Figure
docs.text:
<figure>
    <object data="brochure.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
        <p>PDF not supported. <a href="brochure.pdf">Download the brochure</a>.</p>
    </object>
    <figcaption>Product Brochure (PDF)</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: Example 6: Responsive Object
docs.text:
<style>
    .object-wrapper {
        position: relative;
        padding-bottom: 75%;
        height: 0;
    }
    .object-wrapper object {
        position: absolute;
        top: 0;
        left: 0;
        width: 100%;
        height: 100%;
    }
</style>

<div class="object-wrapper">
    <object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf">
        <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
    </object>
</div>

docs.title: Example 7: Object with Parameters (Legacy)
docs.text:
<object data="animation.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash" width="400" height="300">
    <param name="autoplay" value="true">
    <param name="quality" value="high">
    <p>Flash not supported.</p>
</object>

Note: Flash is obsolete.

docs.title: Example 8: Object as Link Target
docs.text:
<a href="page1.html" target="myObject">Page 1</a>
<a href="page2.html" target="myObject">Page 2</a>

<object data="page1.html" type="text/html" name="myObject" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Fallback content</p>
</object>

Note: <iframe> is preferred for this use case.

docs.title: Example 9: Object with title
docs.text:
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600" title="Product Brochure">
    <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

docs.title: Example 10: Nested Fallbacks with Images
docs.text:
<object data="photo.avif" type="image/avif" width="800" height="600">
    <object data="photo.webp" type="image/webp" width="800" height="600">
        <object data="photo.jpg" type="image/jpeg" width="800" height="600">
            <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A scenic view" width="800" height="600">
        </object>
    </object>
</object>

docs.title: Example 11: Object with Video Fallback
docs.text:
<object data="video.mp4" type="video/mp4" width="640" height="360">
    <video controls width="640" height="360">
        <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
        <source src="video.webm" type="video/webm">
        <p>Video not supported. <a href="video.mp4">Download</a>.</p>
    </video>
</object>

docs.title: Example 12: Object with Audio Fallback
docs.text:
<object data="audio.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" width="300" height="50">
    <audio controls>
        <source src="audio.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
        <p>Audio not supported. <a href="audio.mp3">Download</a>.</p>
    </audio>
</object>

docs.title: Example 13: Object Inside Object for Multiple Formats
docs.text:
<object data="presentation.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <object data="presentation.html" type="text/html" width="800" height="600">
        <p>Neither PDF nor HTML supported. <a href="presentation.pdf">Download PDF</a>.</p>
    </object>
</object>

docs.title: Example 14: Object with JS Detection
docs.text:
<object id="myObject" data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Fallback</p>
</object>

<script>
    const obj = document.getElementById('myObject');
    console.log(obj.data); // "document.pdf"
    console.log(obj.type); // "application/pdf"
</script>

docs.title: Example 15: Object in a Modal
docs.text:
<dialog id="pdfDialog">
    <object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
        <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
    </object>
    <form method="dialog"><button>Close</button></form>
</dialog>

<button onclick="document.getElementById('pdfDialog').showModal()">View PDF</button>

docs.title: Example 16: Object with CSP
docs.text:
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="object-src 'self'">
<object data="/document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>Fallback</p>
</object>

docs.title: Example 17: Object vs. Embed Side by Side
docs.text:
<!-- Object: fallback content -->
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
</object>

<!-- Embed: no fallback -->
<embed src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Example 18: Object with Image Data URI
docs.text:
<object data="data:image/svg+xml,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='blue'/></svg>" type="image/svg+xml" width="100" height="100">
    <p>SVG not supported.</p>
</object>

docs.title: Example 19: Object for Flash (Legacy)
docs.text:
<object classid="clsid:D27CDB6E-AE6D-11cf-96B8-444553540000" width="400" height="300">
    <param name="movie" value="animation.swf">
    <param name="quality" value="high">
    <embed src="animation.swf" quality="high" width="400" height="300">
    <p>Flash not supported.</p>
</object>

Note: Flash is obsolete and no longer supported.

docs.title: Example 20: Complete Object Demo
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Object Demo</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 900px; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 0 1rem; }
        section { margin-bottom: 2rem; }
        object { width: 100%; height: 500px; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 8px; display: block; }
        figure { margin: 0; }
        figcaption { font-size: 0.875rem; color: #6c757d; margin-top: 0.5rem; }
        .object-wrapper { position: relative; padding-bottom: 75%; height: 0; }
        .object-wrapper object { position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Object Demo</h1>

    <section>
        <h2>PDF with Fallback</h2>
        <figure>
            <object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" title="Sample PDF">
                <p>Your browser doesn't support PDFs. <a href="document.pdf">Download the PDF</a>.</p>
            </object>
            <figcaption>Sample PDF document</figcaption>
        </figure>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>SVG with Image Fallback</h2>
        <figure>
            <object data="diagram.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="400" height="300" title="System diagram">
                <img src="diagram.png" alt="System architecture diagram" width="400" height="300">
            </object>
            <figcaption>System Architecture</figcaption>
        </figure>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Nested Video Fallbacks</h2>
        <object data="movie.mp4" type="video/mp4" width="640" height="360">
            <object data="movie.webm" type="video/webm" width="640" height="360">
                <object data="movie.ogv" type="video/ogg" width="640" height="360">
                    <p>No video support. <a href="movie.mp4">Download the video</a>.</p>
                </object>
            </object>
        </object>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Responsive Object</h2>
        <div class="object-wrapper">
            <object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" title="Responsive PDF">
                <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download</a>.</p>
            </object>
        </div>
    </section>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Example PDF display Inline PDF viewer with fallback SVG display Standalone SVG with image fallback Image with fallback <object> wrapping <img> Video with fallback <object> wrapping <video> Audio with fallback <object> wrapping <audio> Legacy plugin content Flash, Java applets (obsolete) Nested fallbacks Multiple format attempts Alternative to <embed> When fallback is needed Accessible rich media Text fallback for screen readers

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always provide fallback content – that's the point of <object>.
  2. Specify type – helps the browser choose a handler.
  3. Set width and height – prevent layout shift.
  4. Wrap in <figure> – for captions and context.
  5. Provide a download link – as final fallback.
  6. Use <iframe> – for HTML documents.
  7. Use <video> / <audio> – for media.
  8. Use <img> – for raster images.
  9. Use <svg> – for inline SVG.
  10. Use <object> – for PDFs, SVG, and fallback chains.
  11. Avoid plugins – obsolete.
  12. Set CSP object-src – restrict sources.
  13. Test in multiple browsers – rendering varies.
  14. Test on mobile – embeds can be slow.
  15. Use title – for advisory information.
  16. Prefer <object> over <embed> – for fallback.
  17. Avoid nesting too deeply – 2–3 levels max.
  18. Document your object strategy – in a style guide.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Fallback Content
docs.text:
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf"></object>

Why it's wrong: Users with browsers that can't render the PDF see nothing.

✅ Correct: 

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600">
    <p>PDF not supported. <a href="document.pdf">Download the PDF</a>.</p>
</object>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using src Instead of data
docs.text:
<object src="document.pdf" type="application/pdf"></object>

Why it's wrong: <object> uses data, not src.

✅ Correct: 

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf"></object>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No type Attribute
docs.text:
<object data="document.pdf"></object>

Why it's wrong: The browser may not know how to render it.

✅ Correct: 

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf"></object>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Dimensions
docs.text:
<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf"></object>

Why it's wrong: The embed may collapse or use unpredictable size.

✅ Correct: 

<object data="document.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="800" height="600"></object>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <object> for HTML Documents
docs.text:
<object data="page.html" type="text/html"></object>

Why it's wrong: <iframe> is preferred; some browsers restrict HTML in <object>.

✅ Correct: 

<iframe src="page.html" title="Embedded page"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <object> for Video
docs.text:
<object data="video.mp4" type="video/mp4"></object>

Why it's wrong: <video> is the modern element.

✅ Correct: 

<video src="video.mp4" controls></video>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Accessibility
docs.text:
<object data="chart.png" type="image/png"></object>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers can't describe the chart.

✅ Correct: 

<object data="chart.png" type="image/png" width="800" height="400">
    <p>Bar chart showing sales growth: 2020: $1M, 2021: $1.2M, 2022: $1.5M.</p>
</object>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <object> for Flash
docs.text:
<object data="animation.swf" type="application/x-shockwave-flash"></object>

Why it's wrong: Flash is no longer supported.

✅ Correct: Convert to HTML5, video, or SVG.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nesting Too Deeply
docs.text:
<object data="a" type="...">
    <object data="b" type="...">
        <object data="c" type="...">
            <object data="d" type="...">
                <p>Too deep.</p>
            </object>
        </object>
    </object>
</object>

Why it's wrong: Complex and hard to maintain.

✅ Correct: Use 2–3 levels max.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No width/height
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Causes layout shift (CLS).

✅ Correct: Always set dimensions.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Separate HTTP request – each <object> fetches a resource.
  • Rendering cost – delegated to the handler.
  • No native lazy loading – use JavaScript for off-screen objects.
  • Caching – server must send caching headers.
  • Memory – depends on the resource.
  • Blocking – can delay page load.
  • No priority hints – no fetchpriority.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Set dimensions – prevent CLS.
  2. Lazy load with JS – for off-screen objects.
  3. Cache aggressively – with Cache-Control.
  4. Use a CDN – global delivery.
  5. Compress resources – smaller files.
  6. Limit objects – fewer is better.

docs.title: 14. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Plugins – historically a major security risk.
  • CSP object-src – restrict embed sources.
  • No sandbox – <object> cannot be sandboxed.
  • Untrusted content – avoid; use <iframe sandbox>.
  • HTTPS – required for secure embeds.
  • Download fallback – ensure downloads are trusted.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Restrict object-src – CSP.
  2. Avoid untrusted objects – no sandbox.
  3. Use HTTPS – for all objects.
  4. Validate resources – before serving.
  5. Prefer <iframe sandbox> – for untrusted content.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools Elements panel – inspect the <object> element.
  • Network panel – verify the resource request.
  • Console – check for errors.
  • Browser-specific testing – PDF, SVG rendering varies.
  • obj.data – check the URL.
  • obj.type – check the MIME type.
  • obj.contentDocument – same-origin only.
  • Lighthouse – audits.
  • Accessibility Inspector – check role and name.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• For PDFs – with fallback.
  • For SVG documents – with image fallback.
  • For fallback chaining – nested <object> for multiple formats.
  • For accessible rich media – with descriptive fallback.
  • As an alternative to <embed> – when fallback is needed.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For HTML documents – use <iframe>.
  • For raster images – use <img>.
  • For video/audio – use <video>/<audio>.
  • For inline SVG – use <svg>.
  • For untrusted content – use <iframe sandbox>.
  • For simple embeds – use <embed>.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <embed> – simple embedding without fallback.
  • <iframe> – HTML document embedding.
  • <img> – raster images.
  • <video> – video.
  • <audio> – audio.
  • <svg> – vector graphics.
  • <param> – plugin parameters (obsolete).
  • <applet> – Java applets (obsolete).
  • MIME type – resource type.
  • CSP object-src – restriction.
  • Plugin – external renderer.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <object> element was introduced in HTML 4.0 (1997).

  • It uses data, not src — a common mistake.

  • <object> can contain fallback content — the key advantage over <embed>.

  • Fallback content can be nested <object> elements for multiple attempts.

  • <object> replaced the obsolete <applet> element.

  • Flash was deprecated in 2020; <object> for Flash no longer works.

  • PDFs render inline in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge; Safari may download.

  • SVG renders inline in all modern browsers.

  • <object> cannot be sandboxed — unlike <iframe>.

  • CSP object-src controls <object>.

  • <object> has good accessibility — fallback text describes the resource.

  • The name attribute allows targeting via links and forms.

  • The <param> element passes parameters to plugins.

  • classid, codebase, archive are obsolete attributes.

  • Best practices: fallback content, type, dimensions, figure caption, download link.

  • Common mistakes: no fallback, src instead of data, no type, no dimensions.

  • Following best practices for <object> leads to accessible, robust, and compatible embedding of external content.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <object> element embeds external resources — PDFs, SVG, images, video, audio, HTML, plugins.
  • It uses data (not src) and type attributes.
  • It is a container element — can contain fallback content.
  • Fallback can be text, images, video, audio, or nested <object>.
  • Nested fallbacks chain multiple attempts for maximum compatibility.
  • Best practices: always provide fallback, specify type, set dimensions, wrap in <figure>, provide download link.
  • Common mistakes include no fallback, using src instead of data, no type, no dimensions.
  • <object> is the preferred generic embedding element for non-HTML content with fallback.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <canvas> element is an HTML element that provides a bitmap drawing surface controlled entirely by JavaScript. Unlike SVG, which describes vector graphics declaratively in markup, <canvas> is a blank rectangular region — a grid of pixels — that JavaScript draws onto programmatically. It is a low-level, immediate-mode rendering API where you issue drawing commands (fill this rectangle, draw this line, render this image), and the browser rasterizes them onto the canvas.

The <canvas> element has two primary APIs:
