  • <iframe> – for isolated SVG widgets.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Inline – for very large SVGs used across many pages.
  • <img> – for interactive SVG.
  • CSS background – for accessible SVG.
  • Data URI – for large SVGs.
  • <embed> – generally.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <svg> – the SVG root element.
  • <symbol> – reusable symbol.
  • <use> – reuse symbol.
  • viewBox – coordinate system.
  • currentColor – CSS inheritance.
  • SVGO – optimiser.
  • <img> – image element.
  • <object> – object element.
  • <iframe> – iframe element.
  • <picture> – picture element.
  • CSS background-image.
  • mask-image – CSS mask.
  • CORS – cross-origin.
  • CSP – content security policy.
  • Accessibility – SVG roles, titles, descriptions.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• SVG can be embedded in seven different ways in HTML.
  • Inline SVG is the most powerful — full CSS/JS access.
  • <img> SVG is the most cacheable — but sandboxed.
  • SVG sprites combine caching with inline control.
  • currentColor only works for inline SVG (and sprites).
  • viewBox makes SVG scalable to any size.
  • SVGO can reduce SVG size by 30–70%.
  • Gzip compresses SVG extremely well (it's XML text).
  • SVG in <img> is sandboxed — scripts don't run.
  • Inline SVG runs scripts in the parent context — sanitize untrusted SVG.
  • SVG accessibility requires <title> and <desc>.
  • role="img" + aria-label is the recommended pattern.
  • aria-hidden="true" + focusable="false" for decorative SVG.
  • Cross-origin <use> requires CORS.
  • SVG as a data URI is inline in CSS/HTML — no extra request.
  • SVG sprites are the modern alternative to icon fonts.
  • Best practices include choosing the right method, viewBox, accessibility, and SVGO.
  • Common mistakes include using <img> for interactive SVG, missing viewBox, no accessibility.
  • Following best practices for SVG embedding leads to sharp, accessible, and efficient graphics.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• SVG can be embedded in HTML in seven ways: inline <svg>, <img>, <object>, <iframe>, CSS background, <embed>, <picture>, and sprites.
  • Inline <svg> – full CSS/JS access, currentColor, interactivity, accessibility. Not cacheable.
  • <img> – cacheable, simple, alt text. No CSS/JS access, no currentColor.
  • <object> – fallback content, cacheable. Inconsistent.
  • <iframe> – full isolation. Heavy.
  • CSS background – cacheable, no accessibility.
  • Sprite (<symbol> + <use>) – cacheable + styleable.
  • Best practices: choose the right method, viewBox, accessibility, SVGO.
  • Common mistakes include using <img> for interactive SVG, missing viewBox, no accessibility.
  • SVG embedding is essential for icons, logos, charts, maps, and interactive graphics on the modern web.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Security considerations for embedded content are the browser-enforced boundaries, platform policies, and developer practices that prevent untrusted content — loaded via <iframe>, <object>, <embed>, <canvas>, <img>, or inline <svg> — from compromising the host page, its users, or its data.

Embedded content is a trust problem, not a feature problem. Every embed is a decision to bring someone else's code or data into your origin's blast radius.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
These protections exist to:

  • Isolate origins — keep foreign code from reaching into your document.
  • Constrain capabilities — limit what embedded content can do (scripts, forms, popups, navigation).
  • Prevent clickjacking — stop invisible overlays stealing user clicks.
  • Prevent XSS — stop foreign content from executing scripts in your context.
  • Prevent data exfiltration — block reads of cookies, storage, and pixel data.
  • Prevent resource abuse — stop DoS via runaway SVG, canvas, or frames.
  • Preserve user privacy — control credential, referrer, and feature leakage.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Embedded Content
├── <iframe>  → sandbox, CSP frame-ancestors, X-Frame-Options, allow, credentialless
├── <object>  → CSP object-src, plugin policy
├── <embed>   → CSP object-src, legacy plugin risk
├── <canvas>  → same-origin policy, origin-clean flag, CORS
├── <img>     → SVG script execution, CORS, data URIs
├── <svg>     → inline script injection, <foreignObject>, DoS
└── Headers   → CSP, COOP, COEP, XFO, Permissions-Policy

The embedding method determines the attack surface. <img> is sandboxed by default. Inline <svg> is not. <iframe> is a blank slate you must configure.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Embedding foreign content means trusting code you did not write and cannot audit. That content may:

  • Contain <script> that runs in your origin (if inline or unsandboxed).
  • Read cookies and localStorage if it shares your origin.
  • Overlay invisible buttons over your UI (clickjacking).
  • Silently redirect the top-level page to a phishing site.
  • Exfiltrate cross-origin pixels via canvas.
  • Consume CPU/memory until the tab crashes.

Without browser-enforced boundaries, an embed is equivalent to pasting an attacker's JavaScript into your page.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Consequence 1990s No same-origin policy enforcement in embeds Any frame could read the parent 2000s No sandbox attribute Framed widgets had full power 2000s No CSP Any script from any origin could run 2008–09 No X-Frame-Options Clickjacking was trivial 2010s SVG treated as harmless images <script> in SVG executed in some contexts 2015+ Canvas used without CORS awareness Cross-origin pixels readable via timing

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Each mechanism is a response to a documented attack class:

  • X-Frame-Options (2009) — Microsoft's response to clickjacking campaigns.
  • sandbox (HTML5, ~2010) — Google's response to drive-by iframes.
  • CSP frame-ancestors (CSP2, 2014) — W3C's more granular clickjacking control.
  • Canvas origin-clean flag (2010s) — response to pixel-theft via cross-origin images.
  • COOP / COEP (2020–21) — response to Spectre-class side channels.
  • credentialless (2023) — response to cross-site cookie leakage in embeds.
  • require-trusted-types-for (2020+) — response to DOM-XSS via innerHTML.

Security was added after damage was demonstrated, not designed up front.

docs.title: Sandboxed Iframe — Most Restrictive
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://untrusted.example.com/widget"
        sandbox
        title="Untrusted widget">
</iframe>

Code Breakdown:

  • sandbox (empty string) — applies every restriction: no scripts, no forms, no same-origin, no popups, no plugins, no top navigation.
  • title — required for accessibility; screen readers announce the frame by this name.

docs.title: Sandboxed Iframe — Allowing Only Scripts
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://widget.example.com/embed"
        sandbox="allow-scripts"
        title="Widget">
</iframe>

Code Breakdown:

  • allow-scripts — enables JS in the frame.
  • Everything else remains blocked: forms, same-origin, popups, top-nav.

docs.title: Sandboxed Iframe — Trusted Third Party
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://player.vimeo.com/video/123"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-presentation"
        allow="fullscreen; picture-in-picture"
        loading="lazy"
        referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
        title="Video player">
</iframe>

Code Breakdown:

  • allow-scripts allow-same-origin — permits the player to run and access its own origin (acceptable here because the player is a known, trusted party — but never for untrusted content).
  • allow="fullscreen; picture-in-picture" — Permissions Policy grants features to the frame.
  • loading="lazy" — defers loading offscreen.
  • referrerpolicy — controls referrer leakage.

docs.title: CSP Header — Clickjacking + Embedding Policy
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    frame-src https://trusted.example.com;
    object-src 'none';
    frame-ancestors 'self';
    base-uri 'self';
    form-action 'self';
    require-trusted-types-for 'script';
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

Code Breakdown:

  • default-src 'self' — safe baseline.
  • frame-src — whitelists who can be framed.
  • object-src 'none' — kills <object> and <embed>.
  • frame-ancestors 'self' — only same-origin can frame this page.
  • base-uri 'self' — prevents <base> hijacking.
  • form-action 'self' — stops forms posting to attacker origins.
  • require-trusted-types-for 'script' — forces typed values for DOM sinks.
  • X-Frame-Options — legacy fallback for old browsers.

docs.title: Canvas with CORS
docs.text:
const img = new Image();
img.crossOrigin = 'anonymous';   // request CORS approval
img.src = 'https://cdn.example.com/photo.png';
img.onload = () => {
    ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);
    const data = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 100, 100); // allowed because clean
};

Code Breakdown:

  • crossOrigin = 'anonymous' — makes the browser send an Origin header; the server must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • If CORS is refused, the canvas becomes tainted and getImageData() throws.

docs.title: The "Guest in Your House" Model
docs.text:
• No sandbox — the guest has a key to every room. Full trust.
  • sandbox (empty) — the guest is confined to the entry hall. No access to anything.
  • sandbox="allow-scripts" — the guest can talk, but not touch.
  • Separate origin — the guest is in a different building. Even shouting can't reach you.

docs.title: The "Concentric Rings" Model
docs.text:
Ring 1 — Same-origin content        (fully trusted)
Ring 2 — Trusted third-party embed  (sandbox with specific tokens)
Ring 3 — Untrusted third-party      (sandbox="", separate origin)
Ring 4 — User-submitted content     (sandbox="", separate origin, sanitized)

Every embed belongs to exactly one ring. Misclassification is the root cause of most embedding vulnerabilities.

docs.title: The "Contract" Model
docs.text:
Every embed is a contract between you and the browser:

You promise The browser enforces Only load from listed origins CSP frame-src Do not frame this page elsewhere CSP frame-ancestors Deny powerful features to the frame allow="" Do not share credentials with the frame credentialless, sandbox without same-origin

Break the contract, and the browser blocks the load — visible as a CSP violation in DevTools.

docs.title: The "Blast Radius" Model
docs.text: Think about what happens if the embedded content is malicious. Then choose the smallest ring that still lets the feature work.

docs.title: Concept 1: Same-Origin Policy (SOP)
docs.text:
The foundation. Origin = scheme + host + port.

https://app.example.com:443
https://app.example.com:443   ← same origin
http://app.example.com:443    ← different (scheme)
https://api.example.com:443   ← different (host)
https://app.example.com:8443  ← different (port)

Scripts cannot read data from a different origin. Embedded content that shares your origin has full access to your cookies, storage, and DOM.

docs.title: Concept 2: Opaque Origin
docs.text:
sandbox without allow-same-origin gives the frame a unique opaque origin ("null"). It cannot access cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB, or same-origin endpoints.

This is why sandbox="" is the strongest iframe isolation that still allows content to render.

docs.title: Concept 3: The sandbox Attribute
docs.text:
Full token table:

Token Grants (empty) No privileges allow-scripts JS execution allow-forms Form submission allow-same-origin Same-origin access (nullifies isolation) allow-popups window.open, target="_blank" allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox Popups inherit no sandbox allow-top-navigation Navigate top-level page allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation Same, only after user gesture allow-modals alert, confirm, prompt allow-downloads File downloads allow-presentation Presentation API allow-pointer-lock Pointer Lock API allow-orientation-lock Screen Orientation Lock allow-storage-access-by-user-activation Storage Access API

Golden rule: allow-scripts + allow-same-origin = no sandbox. The frame can access its own origin and rewrite its own sandbox restrictions.

docs.title: Concept 4: CSP frame-ancestors
docs.text:
Controls who can embed your page:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted.example.com

Overrides X-Frame-Options when both are present.

docs.title: Concept 5: X-Frame-Options (Legacy)
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options: DENY
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM https://trusted.example.com   (deprecated)

Only two values are reliable: DENY, SAMEORIGIN. ALLOW-FROM is deprecated and ignored by most browsers. Keep XFO alongside CSP for legacy clients.

docs.title: Concept 6: CSP object-src
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy: object-src 'none'

Blocks <object>, <embed>, and legacy <applet>. Best default for nearly every site.

docs.title: Concept 7: CSP frame-src
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-src https://youtube.com https://player.vimeo.com

Whitelists who can be framed by you. Distinct from frame-ancestors (who can frame you).

docs.title: Concept 8: Canvas Tainting (Origin-Clean Flag)
docs.text:
A canvas is origin-clean initially. Drawing cross-origin content without CORS approval sets it to false, permanently blocking getImageData(), toDataURL(), toBlob().

ctx.drawImage(crossOriginImg, 0, 0);
canvas.toDataURL();  // SecurityError: tainted canvas

The flag is irreversible — once tainted, always tainted.

docs.title: Concept 9: SVG as Executable Content
docs.text:
SVG can contain:

  • <script> (JS)
  • <foreignObject> (arbitrary HTML)
  • Event handlers (onload, onclick, onerror)
  • External resource references (<image href>, <use href>)

Execution by context:

Method Scripts run? Inline <svg> ✅ In parent context <img src=".svg"> ❌ Blocked <object data=".svg"> ⚠️ Browser-dependent <iframe src=".svg"> ✅ In iframe context CSS background ❌ Blocked Direct navigation ✅ Full power

The Strela Stealer campaign (2024) and CERT.at's 2025–2026 advisories confirm SVG is now a mainstream malware and phishing vector.

docs.title: Concept 10: crossorigin Attribute
docs.text:
<img src="https://cdn.example.com/pic.png" crossorigin="anonymous">

Required for: canvas pixel reads, cross-origin mask-image, CORS-controlled fonts, <script type="module" crossorigin>.

docs.title: Concept 11: Permissions Policy (allow)
docs.text:
<iframe src="..." allow="camera 'none'; microphone 'none'; geolocation 'none'">

Grants or denies powerful browser features to the frame. Default is deny for sensitive features, but specifying is defense-in-depth.

docs.title: Concept 12: credentialless
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://third-party.com" credentialless></iframe>

Loads the frame in an ephemeral context with no cookies, no client certs, no HTTP auth. Ideal for untrusted embeds where state isn't needed.

docs.title: Concept 13: COOP / COEP
docs.text:
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
  • COOP — isolates the browsing context from window.opener.
  • COEP — requires explicit CORS for every cross-origin subresource.

Together they enable cross-origin isolation — required for SharedArrayBuffer and high-resolution timers, and a strong Spectre mitigation.

docs.title: Concept 14: referrerpolicy
docs.text:
<iframe src="..." referrerpolicy="no-referrer">

Prevents leaking your URL (and query strings) to third-party embeds.

docs.title: Concept 15: require-trusted-types-for 'script'
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script'

Blocks innerHTML = "string", eval, and other string-based DOM sinks. Forces developers to use Trusted Types — eliminates the largest DOM-XSS class.

docs.title: Concept 16: Subresource Integrity (SRI)
docs.text:
<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"
        integrity="sha384-..."
        crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

Pins the exact bytes of a script or stylesheet. If the CDN is compromised, the browser refuses to execute the changed file.

docs.title: Concept 17: Mixed Content
docs.text: An https:// page loading http:// iframes, scripts, or images is blocked by modern browsers. Every embed must be served over HTTPS.

docs.title: Concept 18: iframe loading="lazy"
docs.text: Defers offscreen iframes. Reduces attack surface exposure time and improves performance.

docs.title: Concept 19: Sanitization of SVG and HTML
docs.text:
Use DOMPurify with explicit SVG profile:

DOMPurify.sanitize(dirty, {
    USE_PROFILES: { svg: true, svgFilters: true },
    FORBID_TAGS: ['script', 'foreignObject'],
    FORBID_ATTR: ['onload', 'onclick', 'onerror']
});

docs.title: Concept 20: Defense in Depth
docs.text: No single mechanism is sufficient. Stack them.

docs.title: Sandbox Enforcement Pipeline
docs.text:
<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> parsed
          │
          ▼
New browsing context created
          │
          ▼
Sandbox flag bits set:
  ┌─────────────┬────────┐
  │ Scripts     │  ON    │
  │ Forms       │  OFF   │
  │ Same-origin │  OFF   │
  │ Popups      │  OFF   │
  │ Top-nav     │  OFF   │
  │ Plugins     │  OFF   │
  │ Modals      │  OFF   │
  └─────────────┴────────┘
          │
          ▼
Document loaded from network
          │
          ▼
Every capability check consults sandbox flags
          │
          ▼
Violations silently fail (or log to console)

docs.title: CSP Enforcement Pipeline
docs.text:
Response arrives with CSP header
          │
          ▼
CSP parsed, directives stored on document
          │
          ▼
Any resource load / API use evaluated:
   loadScript() → script-src
   loadIframe() → frame-src
   loadObject() → object-src
   navigate   → form-action / navigate-to
          │
          ├── Allowed → proceed
          └── Blocked → CSP violation + report-to

docs.title: Clickjacking Defense Flow
docs.text:
Attacker page tries: <iframe src="https://bank.example.com">
          │
          ▼
Browser fetches bank.example.com
          │
          ▼
Bank's response headers checked:
   X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
   CSP: frame-ancestors 'self'
          │
          ▼
Current embedder origin ≠ 'self' → BLOCKED
          │
          ▼
Attacker sees blank iframe; attack fails

docs.title: Canvas Tainting Flow
docs.text:
canvas created → origin-clean = true
          │
          ▼
ctx.drawImage(src)
          │
          ├── same-origin or CORS-approved → stays clean
          └── cross-origin without CORS  → origin-clean = false
          │
          ▼
ctx.getImageData() / toDataURL()
          │
          ├── clean  → returns pixels
          └── tainted → throws SecurityError

docs.title: Sandbox Flags Are Bitmasks
docs.text:
Each allow-* token maps to a bit. The HTML parser sets them before the frame's document is created. Every privileged operation queries this mask.

0x0001 ScriptsAllowed
0x0002 FormsAllowed
0x0004 SameOriginAllowed
0x0008 PopupsAllowed
0x0010 TopNavigationAllowed
0x0020 ModalsAllowed
0x0040 PluginsAllowed
0x0080 DownloadsAllowed
...

Zero mask (bare sandbox) = no privileges.

docs.title: Origin Representation
docs.text:
Origins are internally triples: (scheme, host, port). Opaque origins are represented as the literal string "null" and compare unequal to every other origin — including other "null" origins.

frame.contentWindow.origin === 'null'   // opaque origin

This is why two separately sandboxed iframes cannot talk via same-origin APIs.

docs.title: CSP Storage & Inheritance
docs.text: CSP is stored per-document. Child documents inherit none of the parent's CSP — each response carries its own. This is why you must set CSP on every response, not just the top page.

docs.title: Canvas Origin-Clean Flag
docs.text: Maintained in the rendering engine. Any drawImage, putImageData, or font-drawing call that pulls a cross-origin resource flips the flag. There is no API to reset it — the only remedy is to create a new canvas.

docs.title: SVG Script Execution Context
docs.text: The SVG parser executes <script> only when the SVG is the document (navigated directly, framed, or inline). When rendered via <img>, the SVG lives in a static, script-disabled mode.

docs.title: MessageChannel & postMessage Boundaries
docs.text:
sandbox frames can still postMessage to parents. Always validate event.origin and event.source:

window.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
    if (e.origin !== 'https://trusted.example.com') return;
    // ...
});

Failing to check origin is a classic data-leak bug.

docs.title: Decision Workflow for Any Embed
docs.text:
Need to embed content?
          │
          ▼
Same origin as your app?
  ├── Yes → Trust, but still consider CSP frame-src
  └── No  → Continue
          │
          ▼
Is it a known, audited third party (YouTube, Stripe, Vimeo)?
  ├── Yes → sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin …" + allow=""
  └── No  → Continue
          │
          ▼
Is it user-supplied?
  ├── Yes → separate origin + sandbox="" + sanitize any HTML/SVG
  └── No  → Continue
          │
          ▼
Is it needed at all?  → If not, don't embed.
          │
          ▼
Apply: sandbox, allow, credentialless, referrerpolicy, loading=lazy
          │
          ▼
Add CSP frame-src / object-src / frame-ancestors
          │
          ▼
Test with DevTools + CSP Evaluator + securityheaders.com

docs.title: Runtime Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Browser parses iframe tag
2. Applies sandbox flags
3. Sends request (with/without credentials)
4. Receives response, parses CSP
5. Creates child document in new context
6. PostMessage channel available
7. On unload: context destroyed, storage cleared (if opaque origin)

docs.title: Example 1: Baseline Secure Iframe for Untrusted Content
docs.text:
<iframe
    src="https://untrusted.example.com/widget"
    sandbox=""
    allow="camera 'none'; microphone 'none'; geolocation 'none'"
    credentialless
    referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
    loading="lazy"
    width="400" height="300"
    title="Untrusted widget">
</iframe>

Code Breakdown:

  • sandbox="" — full isolation.
  • allow="... 'none'" — explicitly denies sensitive features.
  • credentialless — no cookies or auth sent.
  • referrerpolicy="no-referrer" — URL not leaked.
  • loading="lazy" — deferred.
  • title — accessibility.

docs.title: Example 2: Trusted Video Embed (YouTube Privacy Mode)
docs.text:
<iframe
    src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
    sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-presentation"
    allow="fullscreen; picture-in-picture; encrypted-media"
    loading="lazy"
    width="560" height="315"
    title="Product demo video">
</iframe>

Code Breakdown:

  • youtube-nocookie.com — YouTube's privacy mode; no tracking cookies until play.
  • sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-presentation" — safe here because YouTube is audited.
  • allow="encrypted-media" — required for DRM.
  • title — what is being embedded.

docs.title: Example 3: Site-Wide Clickjacking Defense (Node/Express)
docs.text:
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    res.setHeader('Content-Security-Policy', [
        "default-src 'self'",
        "frame-src https://www.youtube-nocookie.com https://js.stripe.com",
        "object-src 'none'",
        "frame-ancestors 'self'",
        "base-uri 'self'",
        "form-action 'self'",
        "require-trusted-types-for 'script'"
    ].join('; '));
    res.setHeader('X-Frame-Options', 'SAMEORIGIN');
    res.setHeader('Referrer-Policy', 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin');
    res.setHeader('Permissions-Policy', 'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()');
    next();
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Single middleware applies all security headers globally.
  • CSP uses frame-src to permit only specific embeds.
  • object-src 'none' kills <object>/<embed>.
  • frame-ancestors 'self' blocks external framing.
  • require-trusted-types-for blocks string-based DOM sinks.
  • X-Frame-Options is a legacy fallback.
  • Permissions-Policy denies powerful features by default.

docs.title: Example 4: Canvas with Cross-Origin Image
docs.text:
async function loadAndRead(url) {
    const img = new Image();
    img.crossOrigin = 'anonymous';
    img.src = url;
    await img.decode();

    const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    canvas.width = img.naturalWidth;
    canvas.height = img.naturalHeight;
    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });
    ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);

    try {
        return ctx.getImageData(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
    } catch (e) {
        console.error('Canvas tainted:', e);
        return null;
    }
}

Code Breakdown:

  • crossOrigin = 'anonymous' — asks the server for CORS approval.
  • If the server permits, origin-clean remains true.
  • If not, getImageData() throws SecurityError; we return null gracefully.

docs.title: Example 5: Sanitizing User SVG Before Inline Embedding
docs.text:
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';

const sanitized = DOMPurify.sanitize(userSuppliedSVG, {
    USE_PROFILES: { svg: true, svgFilters: true, html: false },
    FORBID_TAGS: ['script', 'foreignObject', 'iframe', 'use'],
    FORBID_ATTR: ['onload', 'onclick', 'onerror', 'onmouseover', 'href'],
    ALLOW_DATA_ATTR: false
});

document.getElementById('preview').innerHTML = sanitized;

Code Breakdown:

  • USE_PROFILES: { svg: true } — enables SVG-specific sanitization rules.
  • FORBID_TAGS — bans the top script/redirect vectors.
  • FORBID_ATTR — removes event handlers and href (which can point to javascript:).
  • ALLOW_DATA_ATTR: false — reduces smuggled-data risk.

docs.title: Example 6: postMessage with Origin Verification
docs.text:
window.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
    if (event.origin !== 'https://trusted.example.com') {
        console.warn('Ignored message from untrusted origin:', event.origin);
        return;
    }
    // handle event.data
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Never trust message events by default.
  • The origin check is mandatory; source can additionally be checked.
  • Fail closed — return on mismatch.

docs.title: Example 7: Complete Secure Embedding Template
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="
        default-src 'self';
        frame-src https://www.youtube-nocookie.com;
        object-src 'none';
        frame-ancestors 'self';
        base-uri 'self';
        form-action 'self';
        require-trusted-types-for 'script';">
    <title>Embedding Demo</title>
</head>
<body>
    <iframe
        src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/abc123"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-presentation"
        allow="fullscreen; picture-in-picture; encrypted-media"
        referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
        loading="lazy"
        width="560" height="315"
        title="Product demo video">
    </iframe>
</body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • Meta CSP sets policy at the top of the document, restricting frame-src.
  • The iframe uses minimal sandbox tokens required by the player.
  • allow="" grants only needed features.
  • referrerpolicy prevents URL leakage.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Configuration Third-party ad iframe sandbox="allow-scripts", credentialless, CSP frame-src Payment iframe (Stripe, Adyen) sandbox="allow-forms allow-scripts allow-same-origin" (trusted) YouTube video youtube-nocookie.com + sandbox + allow="fullscreen" User-generated HTML preview iframe srcdoc + sandbox="" User-uploaded SVG Load via <img> OR sanitize with DOMPurify before inline Cross-origin canvas crossorigin="anonymous" OAuth / SSO iframe sandbox with minimal tokens + allow-storage-access-by-user-activation Analytics sandbox sandbox="allow-scripts", credentialless

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Default to the strongest sandbox. Why: You can always add tokens, but you cannot remove them at runtime.
  2. Never pair allow-scripts with allow-same-origin for untrusted content. Why: The frame can remove its own sandbox and reach same-origin resources.
  3. Serve untrusted content from a separate origin. Why: Origin isolation is the strongest boundary. Sandbox tokens are defense-in-depth, not a substitute.
  4. Set object-src 'none' unless you have a specific need. Why: <object>/<embed> can run plugins and legacy content.
  5. Use frame-ancestors as primary clickjacking defense; keep X-Frame-Options for legacy. Why: Modern browsers honor frame-ancestors; old ones honor XFO.
  6. Load user SVG via <img> whenever possible. Why: Scripts do not execute in image context.
  7. Sanitize any inline SVG. Why: SVG can contain <script>, <foreignObject>, and event handlers.
  8. Always check event.origin on postMessage. Why: Any window can send you messages.
  9. Use crossorigin="anonymous" for cross-origin canvas images. Why: Without CORS, the canvas is tainted and unreadable.
  10. Add referrerpolicy="no-referrer" to untrusted iframes. Why: Prevents leaking your URL, including query strings with tokens.
  11. Use credentialless when cookies aren't needed. Why: Avoids cross-site cookie exposure and tracking.
  12. Restrict features via allow. Why: Camera, mic, and geolocation are powerful.
  13. Add loading="lazy" to iframes below the fold. Why: Reduces attack window and improves CWV.
  14. Enforce require-trusted-types-for 'script'. Why: Eliminates the largest class of DOM-XSS.
  15. Use SRI for third-party scripts. Why: Protects against CDN compromise.
  16. Serve everything over HTTPS. Why: Mixed content is blocked, HTTP is MITM-able.
  17. Set COOP and COEP for isolated browsing contexts. Why: Enables Spectre mitigations and cross-origin isolation.
  18. Monitor CSP violations with report-to. Why: Silent blocks look like broken pages; reports reveal attacks.
  19. Re-audit embeds after dependency updates. Why: Third parties change; policies must follow.
  20. Log and alert on unexpected CSP violations. Why: Violations may indicate a live attack.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" on Untrusted Content
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://untrusted.com/widget"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: The frame can access same-origin resources and run scripts. Because it shares an origin, it can call iframe.removeAttribute('sandbox') from the parent... and if it can reach the parent origin, it can strip its own restrictions.

✅ Correct:

<iframe src="https://untrusted.com/widget" sandbox="allow-scripts"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Clickjacking Defense
docs.text:
# No CSP, no X-Frame-Options

Why it's wrong: Anyone can embed your login page in a transparent iframe and steal clicks.

✅ Correct:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Inline User SVG Without Sanitization
docs.text:
document.getElementById('preview').innerHTML = userSVG;

Why it's wrong: userSVG can contain <script>alert(document.cookie)</script> or <foreignObject> with HTML.

✅ Correct:

document.getElementById('preview').innerHTML =
    DOMPurify.sanitize(userSVG, { USE_PROFILES: { svg: true } });

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No CORS on Cross-Origin Canvas Image
docs.text:
img.src = 'https://cdn.example.com/photo.png';
ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);
ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 10, 10);  // SecurityError

Why it's wrong: The image taints the canvas.

✅ Correct:

img.crossOrigin = 'anonymous';

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Trusting postMessage Without Origin Check
docs.text:
window.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
    doSomethingWith(e.data);  // ❌ anyone can send this
});

Why it's wrong: Every window (including attacker frames) can send messages. Without an origin check, this is an injection point.

✅ Correct:

window.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
    if (e.origin !== 'https://trusted.example.com') return;
    doSomethingWith(e.data);
});

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on X-Frame-Options Alone
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

Why it's wrong: Modern spec prefers frame-ancestors; some browsers ignore XFO if CSP is present without it.

✅ Correct: Set both.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No title on Iframe
docs.text:
<iframe src="..."></iframe>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers can't identify the frame; WCAG failure.

✅ Correct:

<iframe src="..." title="Payment form"></iframe>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: <embed> for Arbitrary Content
docs.text:
<embed src="https://untrusted.com/content" type="text/html">

Why it's wrong: No fallback, no sandbox, plugin-based execution historically.

✅ Correct: Use <iframe sandbox="..."> with a CSP frame-src entry.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing charset and Correct Content-Type
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Mismatched charset can enable character-set based XSS (e.g., UTF-7 tricks in legacy browsers).

✅ Correct:

Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Escaping Reflected Input into Titles or Headers
docs.text:
<title>Search: <?= $_GET['q'] ?></title>

Why it's wrong: Unescaped HTML can inject tags.

✅ Correct: Escape server-side before output.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Sandbox and CSP — negligible runtime cost; parsed once per response.
  • Lazy iframes — loading="lazy" avoids loading below-the-fold embeds.
  • credentialless — skips cookie handshake; small latency win.
  • Separate origin — adds DNS + TLS handshake; mitigate with <link rel="preconnect">.
  • crossorigin — triggers preflight in some cases; negligible for images.
  • SVG sanitization — CPU cost; cache sanitized output when input is repetitive.
  • Too many iframes — each has memory + separate JS realm; limit count.
  • Large SVG with filters — can spike CPU; sanitize + optimize with SVGO.
  • COEP — may cause subresources to fail if CORS isn't set; plan accordingly.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Preconnect to trusted embed origins.
  2. Lazy-load iframes below the fold.
  3. Serve sanitized user SVG from cache when possible.
  4. Avoid stacking sandboxed frames — each costs a document.
  5. Use willReadFrequently: true on canvases you read often.
  6. Use decoding="async" on large <img> elements.

docs.title: Iframe — Threat Matrix
docs.text: Threat Mitigation XSS in frame sandbox without same-origin Clickjacking of your page frame-ancestors, XFO Data leak from frame sandbox without allow-same-origin, credentialless Top-level redirect Omit allow-top-navigation Popup abuse Omit allow-popups Sensitive API access allow="camera 'none'; ..." Referrer leak referrerpolicy="no-referrer"

docs.title: Canvas — Threat Matrix
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Pixel theft from cross-origin images origin-clean flag CORS bypass via redirects Server-side CORS discipline Use-after-free / RCE bugs Browser patching (CVE-2026-13821 etc.) Timing side channel (Spectre) COOP + COEP cross-origin isolation

docs.title: SVG — Threat Matrix
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Script execution Load via <img>; sanitize inline Phishing forms via <foreignObject> Strip tag; sanitize External resource tracking Remove <image href>, <use href> DoS via complex filters SVGO + size limits Redirect via <a> Strip or sanitize

docs.title: Object / Embed — Threat Matrix
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Plugin RCE (legacy) CSP object-src 'none' Flash/PDF plugin abuse Block via CSP + browser policy Data leak via plugin Prefer <iframe>/<img> alternatives

docs.title: CSP Reporting Setup
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    frame-src https://trusted.example.com;
    object-src 'none';
    frame-ancestors 'self';
    report-to csp-endpoint

Reporting-Endpoints: csp-endpoint="https://reports.example.com/csp"

Reports reveal attempted violations — invaluable for detecting live attacks.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools → Console — CSP violations appear here with directive and blocked URL.
  • DevTools → Network → Response Headers — verify CSP, XFO, COOP, COEP are present.
  • DevTools → Application → Frames — inspect sandbox attributes per frame.
  • document.querySelector('iframe').sandbox — read sandbox tokens live.
  • iframe.contentWindow.origin — confirm it's "null" for opaque origins.
  • Test canvas taint: call ctx.getImageData() from console — if it throws, canvas is tainted.
  • Security headers scanners — securityheaders.com, Mozilla Observatory.
  • CSP Evaluator (Google) — grade your policy, spot unsafe-inline mistakes.
  • Report-URI collectors — verify reporting works with a test violation.
  • Cross-browser test — Chrome, Firefox, Safari differ in SVG-in-<object> execution.
  • view-source: — confirm the actual <iframe> attributes match what you wrote.
  • chrome://net-internals/#events — trace iframe load, CSP blocks, and CORS failures.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• sandbox — on any iframe whose content you did not fully write.
  • CSP frame-ancestors — on every page you serve.
  • object-src 'none' — default for all sites.
  • frame-src — whenever you allow iframes.
  • require-trusted-types-for 'script' — for any nontrivial app.
  • crossorigin — for canvas reads, mask-image, module scripts.
  • DOMPurify — for any user-supplied HTML/SVG.
  • credentialless — for third-party widgets that don't need state.
  • COOP + COEP — when you need cross-origin isolation.
  • SRI — for third-party scripts and stylesheets.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not apply sandbox to same-origin content you fully control — it will break functionality.
  • Do not use X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM — deprecated.
  • Do not use frame-ancestors 'none' on pages you intend to embed.
  • Do not combine allow-scripts and allow-same-origin for untrusted content.
  • Do not rely on sandbox alone if the frame shares your origin — origin sharing nullifies the boundary.
  • Do not use 'unsafe-inline' in CSP — it defeats the point.
  • Do not assume object-src 'none' covers all plugins — verify with COEP.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Same-Origin Policy
  • Opaque Origin
  • Content Security Policy
  • Clickjacking
  • Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
  • DOM Clobbering
  • Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Sandbox
  • Canvas Tainting / Origin-Clean Flag
  • SVG Sanitization
  • DOMPurify
  • X-Frame-Options
  • frame-ancestors
  • Permissions Policy
  • COOP / COEP
  • Trusted Types
  • Subresource Integrity
  • Mixed Content
  • credentialless
  • Referrer Policy
  • postMessage origin validation

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" is equivalent to no sandbox for same-origin content.
  • SVG phishing rose sharply in 2024–2026; CERT.at issued multiple advisories.
  • Canvas tainting is irreversible — you must create a new canvas to escape it.
  • frame-ancestors overrides X-Frame-Options in every modern browser.
  • Chrome patched multiple canvas same-origin bypasses in 2026: CVE-2026-11081, CVE-2026-7977, CVE-2026-78908, and an RCE-class CVE-2026-13821.
  • credentialless iframes send zero cookies — an underused privacy primitive.
  • Trusted Types eliminates the entire innerHTML = string XSS class.
  • SRI was introduced in 2016 and is still not used on most third-party script tags.
  • Opaque origins compare unequal even to each other — null !== null in origin terms.
  • CSP Level 3 blocks plugin content in <object>/<embed> unless explicitly allowed.
  • DOMPurify is maintained by Cure53 and is the de facto standard for HTML/SVG sanitization.
  • Google's CSP Evaluator will flag 'unsafe-inline' and missing object-src immediately.
  • COEP: require-corp can break third-party images that don't send CORP/CORS — plan migrations carefully.
  • Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) is the natural companion to mixed-content blocking.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Embedded content is untrusted by default. Treat every embed as foreign code until proven otherwise.
  • sandbox is the primary iframe isolation mechanism. Use minimal tokens; never pair allow-scripts with allow-same-origin for untrusted content.
  • frame-ancestors (CSP) is the modern clickjacking defense. X-Frame-Options is a legacy fallback only.
  • object-src 'none' should be the default. <object> and <embed> are rarely needed and often risky.
  • SVG is executable. Load user SVG via <img>; sanitize inline SVG with DOMPurify.
  • Canvas tainting prevents pixel theft. Use crossorigin="anonymous" for legitimate cross-origin reads.
  • credentialless + referrerpolicy reduce privacy leakage. Use both on untrusted embeds.
  • Defense in depth is mandatory. Origin isolation, sandbox, CSP, headers, sanitization, and monitoring work together.
  • Escape reflected input server-side. Titles, headers, and messages are injection surfaces.
  • Monitor CSP reports. Violations are the visible edge of live attacks.
  • Trusted Types and SRI close the two largest remaining gaps — DOM-XSS and CDN compromise.
  • Every layer assumes the previous one failed. That is the design philosophy of web security.

docs.title: Title
docs.text:
Got it — locked in. Here's the plan:

  • We're in the Metadata section (the top-level one in the outline).
  • We go concept by concept, each one as its own full handbook chapter in the exact same 20-section format we used for Security.
  • Order (from your outline): Title → Meta Tags → Open Graph → Twitter Cards → Favicons → Manifest → Theme Color → SEO Metadata.

Starting with the first concept: <title>.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <title> element is a metadata element placed inside <head> that declares the human-readable name of the HTML document. It is one of the few elements in HTML that is required by the specification — every conforming HTML document must contain exactly one <title> inside <head>.

<head>
    <title>Dashboard — Acme Analytics</title>
</head>

It is not the same as the title global attribute (which provides advisory tooltip text on any element). The <title> element names the document; the title attribute names an element.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <title> element serves multiple consumers simultaneously:

  • Browser UI — displayed in the tab, window title bar, and task switcher.
  • Bookmarks & history — the default label when a user saves or revisits the page.
  • Search engines — the clickable headline in search results (SERPs).
  • Screen readers — the first thing announced when a page loads or a tab is focused.
  • Social & chat previews — fallback when Open Graph or Twitter Card tags are absent.
  • Assistive tech & OS — used by AT to announce the current document to the user.
  • Automation — used by headless browsers, crawlers, and testing tools to identify pages.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
<html>
├── <head>
│   ├── <meta charset>
│   ├── <title>          ← document identity
│   ├── <meta name="description">
│   ├── <meta property="og:title">
│   └── ...
└── <body>
    └── <h1>              ← in-page heading (different concern)

The <title> is the document-level identifier, not to be confused with the <h1> (which is the top-level heading within the visible content). A well-formed page has both — and they often, but not always, match.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: A web page without a title is anonymous. Browsers, users, and machines all need a compact way to identify and distinguish one document from another — especially in a world where a single browser window can host dozens of tabs and a single search engine indexes billions of pages.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text:
Before <title> was formalized:

Limitation Consequence No document identity Tabs and bookmarks showed URLs No user-facing label Screen readers announced nothing meaningful No indexable headline Search engines guessed from content No window/task label OS task switchers were unusable No share preview Chat and social links looked broken

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text: <title> was part of HTML from its earliest drafts (circa 1993). Its introduction solved a fundamental identity problem: every document needs a name. HTML 4 made it required; the HTML Living Standard continues to require it — the <title> element is not optional in conforming documents.

docs.title: Smallest Useful Example
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Home — Acme Corp</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Welcome to Acme Corp</h1>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• <!DOCTYPE html> — declares HTML5, ensuring standards mode.
  • <head> — the metadata container; <title> belongs here.
  • <title>Home — Acme Corp</title> — the document's name. The em dash separates page name from site name, a widely used convention.
  • <h1> — the visible in-page heading, distinct from the document title.

docs.title: Allowed Content
docs.text:
<title> accepts only text — no child elements, no HTML.

<!-- Valid -->
<title>Sign in — Example</title>

<!-- INVALID: cannot contain elements -->
<title><strong>Sign in</strong> — Example</title>
  • Special characters must be escaped (&, <, >).
  • Whitespace is collapsed by the browser.
  • Unicode is fully supported, but be aware of encoding.

docs.title: The title Global Attribute (Different Thing)
docs.text:
<abbr title="Cascading Style Sheets">CSS</abbr>
<button title="Close the panel">✕</button>

This title attribute is an advisory tooltip — separate from the <title> element. Do not confuse them.

docs.title: The "Name on the Envelope" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the HTML document as a letter:

  • The <title> is the name written on the envelope — the first thing anyone sees.
  • The <h1> is the greeting inside — you only see it once you open it.
  • The <meta description> is the back-of-envelope summary.
  • The og:title is the name written on the social media version of the envelope.

docs.title: The "Busy Receptionist" Mental Model
docs.text:
The <title> is the name a busy receptionist calls out. It must be:

  • Distinct — so users can tell two things apart.
  • Concise — because there are 40 tabs open.
  • Informative — because the user may have forgotten what they opened.

docs.title: The "Priority Stack" Mental Model
docs.text:
Different consumers consume the title differently:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Search engine result  → <title>             │
│ Social share preview   → og:title, fallback │
│ Browser tab            → <title>            │
│ Screen reader          → <title>            │
│ Bookmark               → <title>            │
│ Chat unfurl (Slack)    → og:title or <title>│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Concept 1: Required, Singular, and Text-Only
docs.text:
• Required: every HTML document must have one.
  • Singular: exactly one <title> per document.
  • Text-only: no elements may nest inside.
  • Location: must be inside <head>.

docs.title: Concept 2: Title vs Heading (<h1>)
docs.text:
Aspect <title> <h1> Location <head> <body> Visible in page No Yes Visible in tab Yes No Count per page Exactly 1 Typically 1 SEO role SERP headline Content structure AT announcement Page load On navigation to heading

They are complementary. Do not duplicate blindly — but they may be similar.

docs.title: Concept 3: Title vs og:title vs twitter:title
docs.text:
• <title> — governs the browser tab, bookmark, and (fallback) search.
  • og:title — governs social preview on Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, etc.
  • twitter:title — governs the Twitter/X card (often falls back to og:title).

For best results, keep them consistent but not identical — social titles often work best without the site suffix.

docs.title: Concept 4: Front-Loading
docs.text:
Search engines and users scan the first ~50–60 characters. Put the distinguishing part first, then a separator, then the site name.

Blog Post Title — Site Name      ✅
Site Name — Blog Post Title      ⚠️

docs.title: Concept 5: Length Guidelines
docs.text:
Context Recommended Length Browser tab 30–50 characters Search results (SERP) 50–60 characters (before truncation) Social (og:title) 60–70 characters

Beyond these, browsers and search engines will truncate with an ellipsis.

docs.title: Concept 6: Separators
docs.text:
Common patterns:

  • Page — Site (em dash, most common)
  • Page | Site (pipe)
  • Page · Site (middle dot)
  • Page - Site (hyphen, works but less elegant)

Pick one convention and apply it everywhere.

docs.title: Concept 7: Whitespace and Entity Handling
docs.text:
• Runs of whitespace collapse to a single space.
  • Leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed.
  • & renders as &, etc.
<title>  Foo   &   Bar  </title>
<!-- Renders as: Foo & Bar -->

docs.title: Concept 8: document.title (JavaScript)
docs.text:
The title is exposed as a writable property:

console.log(document.title);        // read
document.title = 'New name — Site'; // write (updates tab instantly)

Essential for single-page applications (SPAs) that update content without a full page load.

docs.title: Concept 9: SPA Title Management
docs.text:
In SPAs, <title> in the static HTML is almost always wrong after navigation. You must update it on every route change:

function setTitle(pageName) {
    document.title = `${pageName} — Acme`;
}

Framework routers (React Router, Vue Router, Angular Router) all have title-management hooks.

docs.title: Concept 10: Missing Title Behavior
docs.text:
If <title> is absent:

  • Browser shows the URL or file path in the tab.
  • Screen readers have nothing meaningful to announce.
  • Search engines infer a title from content (usually the <h1> or first text).
  • Validators report an error.

This is a real user-facing failure, not a cosmetic one.

docs.title: Concept 11: Title in Browser History
docs.text: The title at the moment of navigation is stored in history entries. If your SPA updates the title after navigation, the entry may briefly show the old title.

docs.title: Concept 12: Title in Bookmarks
docs.text: When a user bookmarks the page, the current <title> value is used as the default label. Users can edit it, but a good default is essential.

docs.title: Concept 13: Unicode and Encoding
docs.text: The title is rendered in the document's character encoding. If the <meta charset> is missing or mismatched, characters in the title may display as mojibake (garbled text).

docs.title: Concept 14: <title> in SVG
docs.text:
SVG documents also have their own <title> inside the SVG namespace — used for accessible naming of the SVG graphic, not the browser tab.

<svg>
    <title>Bar chart of Q1 revenue</title>
    ...
</svg>

docs.title: Concept 15: HTML Fragments and srcdoc
docs.text: When an iframe uses srcdoc, its inline HTML may also include a <title> — that title is used for the iframe's own document context.

docs.title: Concept 16: Screen Reader Announcement Order
docs.text:
Typical SR announcement on page load:

"Document: Sign in — Acme, browser window, edit field..."

The <title> is the first identifier announced. A missing or generic title is disorienting.

docs.title: Concept 17: The Accessibility Angle
docs.text: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.2 (Page Titled) requires that every page have a title that describes its topic or purpose. This is Level A — the most basic conformance level.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Title Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters <title> inside <head>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Text content is collected (elements are not allowed).
    │
    ▼
3.  Whitespace is collapsed; entities are decoded.
    │
    ▼
4.  Title is stored on the Document object.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser updates the tab/window title.
    │
    ▼
6.  Screen readers are notified.
    │
    ▼
7.  History entry is labeled.
    │
    ▼
8.  Crawlers and social scrapers read it.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: SPA Title Update
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a route link.
    │
    ▼
2.  Router intercepts, prevents full navigation.
    │
    ▼
3.  Router updates the view.
    │
    ▼
4.  Router (or useEffect) updates document.title.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser tab reflects new title.
    │
    ▼
6.  History entry is updated.

docs.title: The Document Title Slot
docs.text:
Each Document object has exactly one title slot. Setting document.title writes to it. The <title> element's text content is what initializes this slot during parsing.

Document
 ├── title (string)             ← what the browser uses
 ├── head
 │    └── <title>              ← where it comes from initially
 └── body

docs.title: Text Content Extraction
docs.text:
When parsing <title>, the parser:

  1. Enters RCDATA state (character data with entity decoding).
  2. Collects everything as text until </title>.
  3. Decodes character references.
  4. Collapses whitespace.
  5. Sets the document title.

Because it's RCDATA, tags are treated as literal text — but entities still decode.

docs.title: Title Storage and Propagation
docs.text:
• Stored once in the document.
  • Propagated to: browser UI (tab, window), session history, accessibility tree, and any snapshotting subsystem (e.g., screenshots, headless tools).

docs.title: Interaction with <base> and Document URL
docs.text: The title and URL are separate. Some browsers, when the title is empty, fall back to the URL. Some crawlers do likewise.

docs.title: Static Page Lifecycle
docs.text:
Author writes <title>
    │
    ▼
Deployed
    │
    ▼
User requests page
    │
    ▼
Browser parses <title>
    │
    ▼
Tab shows title
    │
    ▼
User bookmarks / shares / finds in search

docs.title: Dynamic (SPA) Lifecycle
docs.text:
Initial load: static <title>
    │
    ▼
Router detects change
    │
    ▼
Router updates view
    │
    ▼
Router updates document.title
    │
    ▼
Tab and history reflect new title

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Blog Page
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>How SVG Embedding Works — Dev Notes</title>
</head>
<body>
    <article>
        <h1>How SVG Embedding Works</h1>
        <p>...</p>
    </article>
</body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • <title> puts the distinguishing part (article title) first, then the site name.
  • Em dash — is the preferred separator.
  • The <h1> echoes the title's subject but not the site suffix.

docs.title: Example 2: SPA with Dynamic Titles
docs.text:
// React example
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useLocation } from 'react-router-dom';

function TitleManager() {
    const location = useLocation();

    useEffect(() => {
        const pageTitles = {
            '/': 'Home — Acme',
            '/dashboard': 'Dashboard — Acme',
            '/settings': 'Settings — Acme'
        };
        document.title = pageTitles[location.pathname] ?? 'Acme';
    }, [location]);

    return null;
}

export default TitleManager;

Code Breakdown:

  • Runs on every route change.
  • Maps pathname to a descriptive title.
  • Falls back to the site name if no mapping exists.
  • Keeps tab, history, and screen reader announcements correct.

docs.title: Example 3: Production E-Commerce Title
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41 — Men's Running Shoes | SportStore</title>

    <!-- Social overrides -->
    <meta property="og:title" content="Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41 — Men's Running Shoes">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41 — Men's Running Shoes">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • Product name first — the differentiating part.
  • Category added as context.
  • Site name at the end after a pipe.
  • og:title and twitter:title drop the site suffix so social previews remain clean.

docs.title: Example 4: Accessible Page Title for a Form
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>Sign in — Acme</title>
</head>

Screen reader announces: "Sign in — Acme, page loaded." The user knows exactly where they landed.

docs.title: Example 5: Document Title in an SVG
docs.text:
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100" role="img" aria-labelledby="svg-title">
    <title id="svg-title">Bar chart: Q1 revenue by region</title>
    <rect .../>
</svg>

Code Breakdown:

  • Inside the SVG namespace, <title> names the graphic to assistive tech.
  • This is separate from the HTML document's <title>.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Title Pattern Blog post Post Title — Site Name E-commerce product Product — Category \| Shop Documentation Page Name — Project Docs Dashboard app Dashboard — Acme (dynamic per route) Landing page Product Tagline — Brand Auth page Sign in — Site Error page 404 Not Found — Site Search results "query" — Site Search

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always include a <title>. Why: required by spec, WCAG 2.4.2, and essential for user orientation.
  2. Make each page's title unique. Why: duplicates cause confusion in tabs, bookmarks, and search results.
  3. Front-load the unique part. Why: browsers and SERPs truncate from the end.
  4. Use one separator consistently. Why: a single convention makes the site feel coherent and improves scanability.
  5. Keep it under 60 characters when possible. Why: avoids truncation in SERPs and tabs.
  6. Update document.title on SPA route changes. Why: static titles mislead users and search engines.
  7. Match the title to the page's purpose, not just the site. Why: WCAG 2.4.2 requires topic/purpose, not brand alone.
  8. Use em dash or pipe — not hyphen. Why: em dash is the typographic standard; pipe reads more "webby"; hyphen looks like a mistake.
  9. Avoid keyword stuffing. Why: search engines penalize it; users find it noisy.
  10. Escape &, <, > when needed. Why: prevents parse errors and garbled titles.
  11. Match <title> and <h1> in subject, not always in string. Why: the title carries the site name; the <h1> typically doesn't.
  12. Set og:title and twitter:title alongside. Why: social previews override <title> with these when present.
  13. Test with a screen reader. Why: an ambiguous title is a real accessibility failure.
  14. Consider internationalization. Why: translated pages need translated titles — not just body content.
  15. Avoid generic titles like "Home" or "Page". Why: they tell users and crawlers nothing.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing <title>
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
</head>

Why it's wrong: Violates HTML spec and WCAG 2.4.2. Users see the URL; screen readers announce nothing useful; SEO suffers.

✅ Correct:

<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Home — Acme</title>
</head>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate Titles Site-Wide
docs.text:
<!-- Every page -->
<title>Acme Corporation</title>

Why it's wrong: All tabs, bookmarks, and search results look identical. Users can't distinguish or return to a page reliably.

✅ Correct:

<title>Pricing — Acme</title>
<title>About Us — Acme</title>
<title>Contact — Acme</title>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Site Name First
docs.text:
<title>Acme — Pricing</title>

Why it's wrong: In a tab or SERP, the unique part ("Pricing") is truncated off the end. Users see a wall of identical tabs.

✅ Correct:

<title>Pricing — Acme</title>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: SPA Never Updates Title
docs.text:
// No title management at all
function App() {
    return <Router>...</Router>;
}

Why it's wrong: Every route shows the same tab title; history and screen reader announcements are wrong.

✅ Correct: Add a title-updating hook on route change (see Example 2).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: HTML Inside <title>
docs.text:
<title><strong>Pricing</strong> — Acme</title>

Why it's wrong: <title> accepts only text; tags will be treated as literal text or dropped.

✅ Correct:

<title>Pricing — Acme</title>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Keyword Stuffing
docs.text:
<title>cheap shoes, buy shoes, shoes online, discount shoes, shoes sale</title>

Why it's wrong: Search engines demote it; users see spam.

✅ Correct:

<title>Men's Running Shoes — Free Shipping | ShoeStore</title>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Leaving "Untitled Document" or "New Tab"
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: This is a template default, not a title. It signals low quality to users and crawlers.

✅ Correct: Replace with a descriptive title before deployment.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on og:title for the Tab
docs.text:
<title>Acme</title>
<meta property="og:title" content="Pricing — Acme">

Why it's wrong: Social scrapers use og:title, but browsers, screen readers, and search engines use <title>. The two serve different surfaces.

✅ Correct: Set both with aligned values.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Negligible runtime cost — the title is a short string.
  • Encoding matters — a mismatched <meta charset> can garble titles at render time.
  • SSR vs CSR — server-rendered titles appear immediately; client-rendered titles may lag briefly.
  • Crawler timing — Googlebot renders JS and reads the post-render title. Still, provide a sensible static default for no-JS and social scrapers.
  • Streaming HTML — deliver <title> early in <head> so tabs update quickly.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Place <title> as early in <head> as practical (after <meta charset>).
  2. For SPAs, update title synchronously with route change — not in a delayed effect.
  3. Keep titles short to reduce HTML size (minor but free).
  4. Serve correct Content-Type and charset to avoid re-parse.

docs.title: Tabnabbing (Tab-Napping)
docs.text:
A malicious page can navigate a background tab and change its title to impersonate a trusted site — a "tabnabbing" attack. Modern browsers mitigate this by not allowing background tabs to change their title without user interaction, and by prompting when a page changes favicon+title in a suspicious pattern.

Defense: Users should verify the URL, not the tab title. Developers should ensure sensitive pages don't rely on title alone for identity.

docs.title: Title Spoofing in Search Results
docs.text:
Attackers may craft titles to look like a different brand ("PayPal — Login"). This is a phishing vector enabled by search result rendering.

Defense: Report to search engines; monitor brand misuse; use rel="canonical" and og:site_name correctly.

docs.title: Reflected Content in Titles
docs.text:
If a title is generated from user input (e.g., a search query), the input must be escaped to prevent injection.

<!-- DANGEROUS if query is unescaped -->
<title>Results for <%= query %></title>

✅ Correct — escape on the server:

<title>Results for <escaped-query> — Site</title>

docs.title: CSP and Title
docs.text:
CSP does not restrict <title> content, but reflected content must still be escaped. Trusted Types help prevent DOM-based injection when writing document.title from untrusted sources.

// With Trusted Types enforced, direct innerHTML-style writes are blocked
document.title = untrustedUserInput; // plain string is fine

Note: document.title accepts plain strings and does not parse HTML — it's inherently XSS-safe. The risk lies in server-side templating.

docs.title: Sensitive Information in Titles
docs.text: Do not leak PII or secrets in titles. Titles appear in browser history, sync, and screen recordings.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Check the tab. The title is right there — no DevTools needed for a sanity check.
  • Elements panel — inspect <head> to verify a single <title> exists.
  • document.title in console — read and write it live.
  • Search snippet previews — Google Search Console shows how your title appears in SERPs.
  • Social debuggers — Facebook Sharing Debugger, LinkedIn Post Inspector, Twitter Card Validator.
  • Accessibility Inspector (Firefox) or Chrome's Accessibility panel — confirms what AT will announce.
  • Lighthouse — flags missing or non-descriptive titles under SEO.
  • view-source: — verify the raw HTML title, not just what the runtime has.
  • SPA check — navigate between routes and watch the tab.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Always — every HTML document should have exactly one <title>.
  • For SPAs — update on every route change.
  • For SVG — add an inner <title> for accessible naming.
  • For iframe srcdoc — include a <title> inside the inline document.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Never skip it. There is no correct scenario for a missing document title.
  • Do not add multiple <title> elements. Only the first is used; the rest are ignored or flagged.
  • Do not confuse with the title attribute. They solve different problems.
  • Do not put markup inside <title>. Text only.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <h1> — in-page top-level heading
  • <meta name="description"> — SERP snippet text
  • <meta property="og:title"> — social title override
  • <meta name="twitter:title"> — Twitter card title
  • <meta name="robots"> — indexing control
  • document.title — JS accessor
  • Session history
  • WCAG 2.4.2 (Page Titled)
  • Tabnabbing
  • Search snippet (SERP)

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <title> element is one of the oldest in HTML — it predates HTML 2.0.
  • Google may rewrite your SERP title if it thinks a better one can be derived from the page.
  • Firefox was the first browser to add meaningful tabnabbing protection (2010).
  • A single em dash vs. pipe separator can measurably affect SERP click-through in A/B tests.
  • document.title is one of the few DOM APIs that accepts a plain string with no parsing — it is inherently XSS-safe.
  • Screen readers typically announce the title before the user interacts with anything.
  • Some assistive tech caches the title at document load — updating it after load may not re-announce.
  • The <title> element's content is parsed in RCDATA mode — entities decode, tags do not.
  • WCAG 2.4.2 (Page Titled) is Level A — the most basic requirement.
  • iOS Safari shows a condensed title in the tab bar; short titles work best.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• <title> is the document's name — required, singular, text-only, and lives in <head>.
  • It serves browsers, users, search engines, screen readers, and social platforms simultaneously.
  • Front-load the unique part; keep it under ~60 characters.
  • Use one separator convention consistently (em dash, pipe, or middle dot).
  • In SPAs, update document.title on every route change.
  • Set og:title and twitter:title alongside to control social previews.
  • Escape any user input that flows into a title on the server.
  • Watch for tabnabbing and title spoofing as security issues.
  • WCAG 2.4.2 requires a descriptive title — this is not optional.
  • Debug with the tab, the Elements panel, GSC, social debuggers, and Lighthouse.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A meta tag is an HTML element placed inside the <head> section of a document that provides machine-readable metadata about the page — information that is not displayed to the user but is consumed by browsers, search engines, social platforms, and AI tools.

<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <meta name="description" content="A guide to HTML meta tags.">
</head>

The <meta> element is a void element — it has no closing tag and no content. All information is carried by its attributes.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Meta tags serve multiple consumers simultaneously:

  • Browsers — viewport configuration, character encoding, theme color, referrer policy.
  • Search engines — description snippets, robots directives, canonical hints.
  • Social platforms — Open Graph and Twitter Card previews.
  • AI tools — structured signals that help AI systems interpret and cite content. The same meta tag hygiene that helps you rank in Google also improves visibility in AI-powered features like Google AI Overviews, since AI parsers rely on structured signals to interpret pages.
  • Accessibility tools — language, viewport, and color-scheme information.
  • Mobile operating systems — home screen icons, app-like display, status bar style.

Meta tags are invisible to users but shape how a page appears in search results, social previews, browser UI, and mobile experiences. They operate entirely behind the scenes, living in the <head> of the source code, instrumental in explaining content and structure to machines.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
<html>
├── <head>
│   ├── <meta charset>            ← character encoding (required)
│   ├── <title>                   ← document name (required)
│   ├── <meta name="viewport">    ← mobile viewport (required)
│   ├── <meta name="description"> ← SERP snippet
│   ├── <meta name="robots">      ← indexing directives
│   ├── <meta name="theme-color"> ← browser UI color
│   ├── <meta property="og:*">    ← social preview
│   └── <meta http-equiv="*">     ← HTTP-equivalent pragmas
│
└── <body>
    └── Visible content

Meta tags are not the same as <title>, <link>, <script>, or <style> — those are separate elements that also live in <head>. The <meta> element exists specifically for metadata that other elements cannot express.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A web page is a document designed for humans, but it is also consumed by machines. Without a standardized way to declare metadata, machines would have to infer everything from visible content:

  • How should the page be rendered on mobile?
  • What character encoding does it use?
  • Should search engines index it?
  • What should the search result snippet say?
  • What image and title should appear when shared on social media?

Inferring all of this is unreliable. A page about "Apple" could be the fruit or the company. A product page's best SERP description might not be its first paragraph. Metadata must be declared, not guessed.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No viewport tag Mobile browsers rendered desktop layouts scaled down to unreadable sizes No charset declaration Non-ASCII characters displayed as mojibake No description Search engines guessed snippets from page text — often poorly No robots control Private pages could be indexed accidentally No social preview Shared links showed bare URLs No theme color Browser UI clashed with site design

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <meta> element has existed since HTML 2.0 (1995). Originally used for simple name-value pairs like author and keywords, it evolved:

  • HTML 4.01 — added http-equiv for pragma directives (cache control, content type, refresh).
  • HTML5 (2008–2014) — standardized <meta charset>, added <meta name="viewport">, formalized standard metadata names.
  • Open Graph (2010) — Facebook introduced property="og:*" meta tags using RDFa syntax.
  • HTML Living Standard — continues to add new standard metadata names (theme-color, color-scheme, referrer).

Each addition was a response to a real problem. Meta tags exist because machines need explicit instructions.

docs.title: The Two Attribute Patterns
docs.text:
Every <meta> element uses one of two attribute patterns:

Pattern 1: name + content — named metadata.

<meta name="description" content="A guide to HTML meta tags.">

Pattern 2: http-equiv + content — HTTP-header-equivalent pragmas.

<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'">

Exception: charset — a standalone attribute.

<meta charset="UTF-8">

The WHATWG HTML specification defines that all meta tags except charset must contain either an http-equiv or name attribute, and both types require a content attribute to define the metadata value.

docs.title: The Smallest Useful <head>
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Page Title — Site Name</title>
</head>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• <meta charset="UTF-8"> — declares the character encoding. Must appear within the first 1024 bytes of the document. Prevents mojibake.
  • <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> — tells mobile browsers to use the device's actual width and set the initial zoom to 1:1. Without this, mobile phones render the site as a tiny desktop page.
  • <title> — the document name, displayed in tabs and search results.

docs.title: A Fully Commented Production Example
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Required: character encoding -->
    <meta charset="UTF-8">

    <!-- Required: mobile viewport configuration -->
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <!-- SEO: search result snippet (150–155 characters) -->
    <meta name="description" content="Learn how HTML meta tags shape search previews, social sharing, and browser behavior. Complete guide with examples.">

    <!-- SEO: indexing directives -->
    <meta name="robots" content="index, follow, max-image-preview:large">

    <!-- Canonical URL (in <link>, not <meta>) -->
    <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/page">

    <!-- Browser UI: address bar color (light and dark) -->
    <meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" content="#ffffff">
    <meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" content="#1a1a1a">

    <!-- Browser UI: preferred color scheme -->
    <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">

    <!-- Referrer policy: control Referer header -->
    <meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin-when-cross-origin">

    <!-- Social: Open Graph -->
    <meta property="og:title" content="Page Title">
    <meta property="og:description" content="Description for social sharing.">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/preview.jpg">
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/page">
    <meta property="og:type" content="article">

    <!-- Social: Twitter Card -->
    <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="Page Title">
    <meta name="twitter:description" content="Description for Twitter.">
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/twitter.jpg">
</head>

docs.title: The "Product Packaging" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of meta tags as the packaging of your web page:

  • <title> — the product name on the front of the box.
  • <meta name="description"> — the back-of-box blurb that sells the product.
  • <meta name="robots"> — a "do not display on shelves" sticker.
  • <meta property="og:*"> — a separate display box for the social media aisle.
  • <meta name="viewport"> — instructions for how to fit the box on a mobile shelf.
  • <meta name="theme-color"> — the color of the shelf edge that matches the brand.

If your packaging is off, even a great product struggles to sell.

docs.title: The "Two Audiences" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every meta tag speaks to one of two audiences:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              <head>                          │
│                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐ │
│  │   SEARCH ENGINES    │  │   BROWSERS    │ │
│  │                     │  │               │ │
│  │  description        │  │  charset      │ │
│  │  robots             │  │  viewport     │ │
│  │  canonical          │  │  theme-color  │ │
│  │  og:*               │  │  referrer     │ │
│  │  twitter:*          │  │  color-scheme │ │
│  └─────────────────────┘  └───────────────┘ │
│                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐                     │
│  │   SOCIAL PLATFORMS  │                     │
│  │                     │                     │
│  │  og:title           │                     │
│  │  og:image           │                     │
│  │  og:description     │                     │
│  │  twitter:card       │                     │
│  └─────────────────────┘                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A tag that speaks to the wrong audience is wasted. Know which machine consumes which tag.

docs.title: The "Priority Stack" Mental Model
docs.text:
Not all meta tags are equally important. From most to least critical:

Tier 1 (required):   charset, viewport
Tier 2 (SEO direct): description, robots
Tier 3 (social):     og:title, og:image, og:description
Tier 4 (UX):         theme-color, color-scheme
Tier 5 (legacy):     keywords, author, generator

docs.title: Concept 1: The Three Attribute Forms
docs.text:
Every <meta> element uses one of three forms:

Form Example Purpose charset <meta charset="UTF-8"> Character encoding name + content <meta name="description" content="..."> Named metadata http-equiv + content <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="30"> HTTP-equivalent pragma

docs.title: Concept 2: <meta charset>
docs.text:
Declares the character encoding. HTML5 standardized this from the older http-equiv="Content-Type" form.

<meta charset="UTF-8">
  • Must appear in the first 1024 bytes of the document.
  • UTF-8 is the only valid value for HTML per the specification.
  • Without it, browsers guess encoding — often incorrectly — causing mojibake.

docs.title: Concept 3: <meta name="viewport">
docs.text:
Controls mobile rendering:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Key directives:

Directive Effect width=device-width Match the device's CSS pixel width initial-scale=1 Set initial zoom to 1:1 maximum-scale=5 Cap zoom (avoid 1 — accessibility issue) user-scalable=yes Allow pinch-zoom (should always be yes) viewport-fit=cover Extend into the notch area on modern phones interactive-widget=resizes-content Resize layout when the on-screen keyboard opens (Android Chrome)

Accessibility warning: Never set user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1. This blocks pinch-zoom and violates WCAG 1.4.4.

docs.title: Concept 4: <meta name="description">
docs.text:
Provides a short summary used by search engines for SERP snippets:

<meta name="description" content="Learn how HTML meta tags shape search previews and social sharing.">
  • Google measures snippet length in pixels, not characters. Aim for 150–155 characters and front-load the most important information in the first 110.
  • Descriptions do not directly affect rankings but strongly affect click-through rate (CTR).
  • Unique descriptions per page are essential — duplicates cause poor user experience.

docs.title: Concept 5: <meta name="robots">
docs.text:
Controls indexing and crawling:

<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">

Key directives:

Directive Effect index / noindex Allow or forbid indexing follow / nofollow Allow or forbid following links noarchive Prevent cached copy nosnippet Prevent text snippet max-image-preview:large Allow large image previews in SERPs max-snippet:-1 Allow unlimited snippet length

Can target specific bots: <meta name="googlebot" content="noindex">.

docs.title: Concept 6: <meta name="theme-color">
docs.text:
Sets the browser UI color (address bar, status bar):

<meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" content="#ffffff">
<meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" content="#1a1a1a">

The media attribute forks identity, allowing light and dark variants to coexist. Browsers on Android Chrome, iOS Safari, and desktop Chrome support this.

docs.title: Concept 7: <meta name="color-scheme">
docs.text:
Declares which color schemes the page supports:

<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">

Tells the browser the page can adapt. Affects default UI rendering (form controls, scrollbars) before CSS loads.

docs.title: Concept 8: <meta name="referrer">
docs.text:
Controls the HTTP Referer header:

<meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin-when-cross-origin">

Key values:
