Value Behavior no-referrer Send no referrer origin Send only the origin no-referrer-when-downgrade Send full URL to same-or-higher security; none to lower (default) origin-when-cross-origin Full URL same-origin; origin only cross-origin same-origin Full URL same-origin; no referrer cross-origin strict-origin Origin only, none when downgrading HTTPS→HTTP strict-origin-when-cross-origin Full URL same-origin; origin cross-origin; none on downgrade

Dynamic insertion of <meta name="referrer"> (via document.write() or appendChild()) makes referrer behavior unpredictable. If multiple conflicting policies are defined, no-referrer wins.

docs.title: Concept 9: <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">
docs.text:
Delivers a CSP policy via meta tag:

<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'">

Important limitation: CSP via <meta> does not support frame-ancestors, report-uri, or sandbox directives. Prefer HTTP headers for full CSP. The meta tag is a fallback when header control is unavailable.

docs.title: Concept 10: <meta name="keywords">
docs.text:
Largely obsolete. Search engines (especially Google) have ignored it since the early 2000s due to widespread abuse. Still supported by some niche engines and internal search systems.

<meta name="keywords" content="html, meta tags, seo">

Do not rely on it for SEO.

docs.title: Concept 11: <meta name="author"> and <meta name="generator">
docs.text:
<meta name="author" content="Jane Developer">
<meta name="generator" content="Eleventy v3.0">

Informational only. Not used for ranking. Useful for source auditing.

docs.title: Concept 12: <meta http-equiv="refresh">
docs.text:
Redirects or reloads:

<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="5; url=https://example.com/new-page">

Avoid for redirects. Use HTTP 301/302. The refresh tag is bad for accessibility and SEO.

docs.title: Concept 13: <meta name="application-name">
docs.text:
<meta name="application-name" content="Acme Dashboard">

Identifies the web application. Different from <title>, which may contain page-specific info. Simple web pages should not define this.

docs.title: Concept 14: <meta name="format-detection">
docs.text:
Controls automatic detection of phone numbers and other formats:

<meta name="format-detection" content="telephone=no">

Prevents iOS Safari from turning number sequences into tappable phone links. Useful when numbers are not phone numbers (e.g., product codes, dates).

docs.title: Concept 15: <meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable">
docs.text:
Deprecated. Used to enable full-screen mode for iOS home screen web apps:

<!-- Deprecated -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">

<!-- Modern replacement -->
<meta name="mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">

Use the web app manifest instead for PWA configuration.

docs.title: Concept 16: Open Graph (property="og:*")
docs.text:
Uses RDFa syntax (property instead of name) for social sharing:

<meta property="og:title" content="Page Title">
<meta property="og:description" content="Social description.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/image.jpg">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/page">
<meta property="og:type" content="article">

Consumed by Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord, and many others. Falls back to <title> and <meta name="description"> if absent — but explicit values give better control.

docs.title: Concept 17: Twitter Cards (name="twitter:*")
docs.text:
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="Page Title">
<meta name="twitter:description" content="Twitter description.">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/twitter.jpg">

Twitter/X falls back to og:* tags when twitter:* are absent.

docs.title: Concept 18: No Duplicate Meta Tags
docs.text: The HTML spec states: "There must not be more than one meta element with its name attribute set to an ASCII case-insensitive match for description per document." Duplicate meta tags are ignored or cause unpredictable behavior. Each metadata name should appear once.

docs.title: Concept 19: Meta Tags and AI Search
docs.text: AI-powered search features (Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, etc.) rely on structured signals to interpret and cite content. Proper meta tag hygiene — accurate descriptions, correct robots directives, structured data — improves visibility in AI search results, not just traditional SERPs.

docs.title: Concept 20: Meta Tags Decay Over Time
docs.text: Meta tags are not a one-time setup. Content changes, pages get deleted, URLs change. A full meta tag audit should run at least quarterly, or after any major site migration or CMS update.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Meta Tag Parsing
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters <meta> in <head>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Determines which attribute form:
    │   ├── charset → sets encoding immediately
    │   ├── name + content → stores as named metadata
    │   └── http-equiv + content → stores as pragma directive
    │
    ▼
3.  Metadata stored on the Document object.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser applies relevant metadata:
    │   ├── charset → decode remaining bytes
    │   ├── viewport → configure mobile layout
    │   ├── theme-color → style browser UI
    │   └── referrer → set request policy
    │
    ▼
5.  Search engine crawlers later read stored metadata.
    │
    ▼
6.  Social scrapers read og:* and twitter:* tags.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Social Preview Generation
docs.text:
1.  User pastes URL into a social platform.
    │
    ▼
2.  Platform fetches the HTML.
    │
    ▼
3.  Scraper extracts:
    │   ├── og:title → fallback: <title>
    │   ├── og:description → fallback: meta description
    │   ├── og:image → fallback: first large image
    │   └── og:url → canonical URL
    │
    ▼
4.  Preview card rendered in the post composer.

docs.title: The Document Metadata Registry
docs.text:
Browsers maintain an internal registry of metadata values parsed from <meta> elements. Each name maps to a single value. If a duplicate name appears, the behavior is:

  • Some browsers keep the first occurrence.
  • Some keep the last.
  • The spec discourages duplicates.
Document
 ├── encoding: "UTF-8"
 ├── viewport: { width: "device-width", initialScale: 1 }
 ├── themeColor: "#ffffff"
 ├── colorScheme: "light dark"
 ├── referrer: "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
 ├── metadataRegistry:
 │    ├── "description" → "..."
 │    ├── "robots" → "index, follow"
 │    └── ...
 └── httpEquivRegistry:
      ├── "Content-Security-Policy" → "..."
      └── ...

docs.title: Charset Detection Algorithm
docs.text:
The browser uses a prescan algorithm to find the charset before full parsing:

  1. Scan the first 1024 bytes.
  2. Look for <meta charset="...">.
  3. Look for <meta http-equiv="Content-Type" content="...; charset=...">.
  4. Look for BOM (byte order mark).
  5. Fall back to HTTP Content-Type header.
  6. Fall back to locale default.

This is why <meta charset> must appear early in the document.

docs.title: Viewport and the Visual Viewport API
docs.text:
The width and initial-scale directives from <meta name="viewport"> configure the layout viewport — the CSS coordinate space the page is laid out in. The user can pinch-zoom to change the visual viewport, which is exposed via the Visual Viewport API.

Layout viewport:  device-width (e.g., 390px on iPhone)
Visual viewport:  what the user is currently zoomed into

docs.title: CSP via Meta vs Header
docs.text:
Feature HTTP Header <meta> Tag default-src, script-src, etc. ✅ ✅ frame-ancestors ✅ ❌ Not supported report-uri / report-to ✅ ❌ Not supported sandbox ✅ ❌ Not supported Parsed before any resources ✅ ❌ (after <head> parse)

For full CSP, use HTTP headers. The meta tag is a fallback only.

docs.title: Theme Color Resolution
docs.text:
When multiple <meta name="theme-color"> tags are present, the media attribute is evaluated:

<meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" content="#fff">
<meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" content="#1a1a1a">

The browser picks the first tag whose media query matches the current environment.

docs.title: Static Page Lifecycle
docs.text:
Author writes meta tags in <head>
    │
    ▼
Deployed to server
    │
    ▼
User requests page
    │
    ▼
Browser prescans first 1024 bytes for charset
    │
    ▼
Full parse: all meta tags registered
    │
    ▼
Metadata applied (viewport, theme, referrer)
    │
    ▼
Page renders with correct configuration
    │
    ▼
Search crawler later reads meta tags for indexing
    │
    ▼
Social scraper later reads og:* for previews

docs.title: Meta Tag Audit Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Inventory all meta tags across the site.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check for missing required tags:
    │   ├── charset?
    │   ├── viewport?
    │   └── description?
    │
    ▼
3.  Check for duplicates.
    │
    ▼
4.  Verify descriptions are unique and within length limits.
    │
    ▼
5.  Verify robots directives are correct.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test social previews with platform debuggers.
    │
    ▼
7.  Repeat quarterly or after migrations.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal Production <head>
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Page Title — Site Name</title>
    <meta name="description" content="A concise description of this page for search engines.">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • charset — required; declares UTF-8 encoding.
  • viewport — required for mobile; sets device width and 1:1 zoom.
  • <title> — required; document name.
  • description — recommended; SERP snippet.

docs.title: Example 2: Blog Post with Full Metadata
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>How Meta Tags Work — Dev Notes</title>
    <meta name="description" content="A complete guide to HTML meta tags: viewport, description, robots, Open Graph, and theme color. Learn which tags matter and which to ignore.">

    <meta name="robots" content="index, follow, max-image-preview:large">
    <link rel="canonical" href="https://devnotes.example.com/meta-tags">

    <meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" content="#ffffff">
    <meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" content="#1a1a1a">
    <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">

    <meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin-when-cross-origin">

    <meta property="og:title" content="How Meta Tags Work">
    <meta property="og:description" content="A complete guide to HTML meta tags.">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://devnotes.example.com/preview.png">
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://devnotes.example.com/meta-tags">
    <meta property="og:type" content="article">

    <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="How Meta Tags Work">
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://devnotes.example.com/twitter.png">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • description front-loads the value proposition in the first 110 characters.
  • robots uses max-image-preview:large for rich SERP results.
  • theme-color has light and dark variants with media queries.
  • referrer uses the modern strict policy.
  • og:* and twitter:* provide social preview data.

docs.title: Example 3: E-Commerce Product Page
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41 — Men's Running Shoes | SportStore</title>
    <meta name="description" content="Buy the Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41 men's running shoes. Responsive cushioning, breathable mesh. Free shipping over $75.">

    <meta name="robots" content="index, follow, max-image-preview:large">
    <link rel="canonical" href="https://sportstore.example.com/nike-pegasus-41">

    <meta property="og:title" content="Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41 — Men's Running Shoes">
    <meta property="og:description" content="Responsive cushioning, breathable mesh. Free shipping over $75.">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://sportstore.example.com/img/pegasus-41.jpg">
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://sportstore.example.com/nike-pegasus-41">
    <meta property="og:type" content="product">
    <meta property="product:price:amount" content="139.99">
    <meta property="product:price:currency" content="USD">

    <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • Product name first in title, site name last.
  • Description includes price anchor and shipping incentive.
  • og:type="product" enables product-specific social rendering.
  • product:* tags enable price display in some social previews.

docs.title: Example 4: SPA with Dynamic Meta Tags
docs.text:
// React example: update meta tags on route change
import { useEffect } from 'react';

function useMetaTags({ title, description, image }) {
    useEffect(() => {
        document.title = title;

        setMeta('description', description);
        setMeta('og:title', title, 'property');
        setMeta('og:description', description, 'property');
        setMeta('og:image', image, 'property');
    }, [title, description, image]);
}

function setMeta(nameOrProperty, content, attr = 'name') {
    let el = document.querySelector(`meta[${attr}="${nameOrProperty}"]`);
    if (!el) {
        el = document.createElement('meta');
        el.setAttribute(attr, nameOrProperty);
        document.head.appendChild(el);
    }
    el.setAttribute('content', content);
}

Code Breakdown:

  • SPAs must update meta tags on every route change.
  • setMeta upserts a meta tag — creates if missing, updates if present.
  • Handles both name (standard) and property (Open Graph) attributes.

docs.title: Example 5: CSP via Meta Tag (Fallback)
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
          content="default-src 'self';
                   script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com;
                   style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
                   img-src 'self' data: https:;
                   object-src 'none';
                   base-uri 'self';
                   form-action 'self'">
    <title>Secure Page</title>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • default-src 'self' — baseline: only same-origin.
  • script-src — allows self and a specific CDN.
  • img-src data: — permits inline data URIs.
  • object-src 'none' — blocks <object>/<embed>.
  • Limitation: frame-ancestors cannot be set via meta — must use HTTP header.

docs.title: Example 6: Mobile-Optimized Meta Tags
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover, interactive-widget=resizes-content">

    <meta name="format-detection" content="telephone=no">
    <meta name="mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">

    <meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" content="#ffffff">
    <meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" content="#1a1a1a">
    <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • viewport-fit=cover — extends content into the notch/rounded corners area.
  • interactive-widget=resizes-content — resizes layout viewport when the on-screen keyboard opens (Android Chrome).
  • format-detection telephone=no — prevents iOS from auto-linking numbers.
  • mobile-web-app-capable — modern replacement for the deprecated apple-mobile-web-app-capable.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Required Meta Tags Any HTML page charset, viewport, <title> Blog / article + description, robots, og:* E-commerce product + og:type=product, product:* Documentation site + description, robots SPA / PWA + theme-color, color-scheme, dynamic updates Social sharing page + og:title, og:image, twitter:card Security-sensitive app + CSP via http-equiv Mobile web app + format-detection, mobile-web-app-capable No-index page (staging) + robots="noindex, nofollow"

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always include <meta charset="UTF-8"> as the first meta tag. Why: ensures correct encoding before any text is parsed.
  2. Always include <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">. Why: without it, mobile browsers render a desktop page scaled down, which is unreadable and fails Lighthouse.
  3. Write a unique <meta name="description"> for every page. Why: duplicates cause poor user experience and reduce click-through rates.
  4. Keep descriptions between 150–155 characters. Why: Google measures snippets in pixels; this range fits the standard SERP snippet.
  5. Front-load the most important information in the first 110 characters. Why: mobile SERPs truncate earlier.
  6. Use robots directives intentionally. Why: accidental indexing of staging or private pages is a common and damaging mistake.
  7. Add max-image-preview:large to robots. Why: enables large image previews in SERPs, improving CTR.
  8. Set theme-color for both light and dark schemes using media. Why: matches browser UI to your design in both modes.
  9. Declare color-scheme to tell the browser your page supports dark mode. Why: ensures form controls and scrollbars render correctly before CSS loads.
  10. Use referrer policy to control Referer leakage. Why: URLs may contain sensitive query parameters.
  11. Prefer HTTP headers for CSP; use <meta> only as fallback. Why: frame-ancestors, report-uri, and sandbox are not supported in meta.
  12. Never set user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1 in viewport. Why: blocks pinch-zoom, violating WCAG 1.4.4.
  13. Do not rely on keywords for SEO. Why: Google has ignored it since the early 2000s.
  14. Do not use <meta http-equiv="refresh"> for redirects. Why: use HTTP 301/302 instead — better for SEO and accessibility.
  15. Test social previews with platform debuggers. Why: og:image failures are invisible until you share the link.
  16. Audit meta tags quarterly or after migrations. Why: meta tags decay as content changes.
  17. Update meta tags dynamically in SPAs. Why: static <head> tags become stale and wrong on every route change.
  18. Escape user input in meta content. Why: reflected content in description or og:title is an injection surface.
  19. Keep meta tag count reasonable. Why: excessive tags add bytes without value; every tag should serve a purpose.
  20. Verify with Lighthouse and social debuggers after deployment. Why: automated audits catch missing or malformed tags.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing <meta charset>
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>Page</title>
</head>

Why it's wrong: The browser must guess encoding. Non-ASCII characters may display as mojibake. This is a fundamental correctness issue.

✅ Correct:

<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Page</title>
</head>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing <meta name="viewport">
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Page</title>
</head>

Why it's wrong: Mobile browsers render a desktop-width page scaled down. Text is unreadable; Lighthouse reports a mobile-friendliness failure.

✅ Correct:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate Meta Tags
docs.text:
<meta name="description" content="First description">
<meta name="description" content="Second description">

Why it's wrong: The spec forbids duplicate name values. Behavior is unpredictable across browsers.

✅ Correct: One description tag per page.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing or Duplicate Descriptions
docs.text:
<!-- All pages share the same description -->
<meta name="description" content="Welcome to Acme Corporation.">

Why it's wrong: Duplicate descriptions across pages cause poor SERP diversity and reduce trust.

✅ Correct: Unique, page-specific descriptions.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Blocking Zoom
docs.text:
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, user-scalable=no, maximum-scale=1">

Why it's wrong: Prevents pinch-zoom — an accessibility failure that violates WCAG 1.4.4.

✅ Correct:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using keywords for SEO
docs.text:
<meta name="keywords" content="html, meta, tags, seo, web, development">

Why it's wrong: Google has ignored this tag for over two decades.

✅ Correct: Focus on description, title, and content quality.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: CSP via Meta Without Realizing Its Limits
docs.text:
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="frame-ancestors 'self'">

Why it's wrong: frame-ancestors is not supported in meta-delivered CSP. The directive is silently ignored.

✅ Correct: Set frame-ancestors via HTTP header.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Social Preview Tags
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>Page</title>
</head>

Why it's wrong: Shared links show bare URLs with no image or description.

✅ Correct: Add at minimum og:title, og:description, og:image.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Stale Meta Tags in SPAs
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>My App</title>
    <meta name="description" content="Home page description">
</head>

Why it's wrong: After navigating to /settings, the tab still says "My App" and the description is wrong.

✅ Correct: Update meta tags on every route change (see Example 4).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Reflected Input in Meta Content Without Escaping
docs.text:
<meta name="description" content="<?= $_GET['q'] ?>">

Why it's wrong: Unescaped user input can inject HTML or break the attribute.

✅ Correct: Escape server-side before output.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Meta tags are tiny — a full <head> typically adds 1–3 KB uncompressed.
  • Gzip/Brotli compresses meta tags extremely well (repetitive XML-like text).
  • Prescan for charset — browsers scan the first 1024 bytes; keep <meta charset> early.
  • Too many meta tags — diminishing returns; keep it focused.
  • Dynamic insertion in SPAs — DOM writes are cheap but should be batched.
  • http-equiv="refresh" — causes full page reload; avoid for performance and UX.
  • CSP via meta — parsed after <head> begins; HTTP header CSP applies earlier.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Place charset first in <head>.
  2. Keep descriptions under 160 characters.
  3. Avoid unused meta tags.
  4. Use HTTP headers for CSP when possible.
  5. Batch SPA meta updates in a single effect or lifecycle hook.

docs.title: Reflected Content Injection
docs.text:
If meta tag content is generated from user input (search queries, page params), it must be escaped:

<!-- DANGEROUS -->
<meta name="description" content="Search results for <?= query ?>">

<!-- SAFE (escaped server-side) -->
<meta name="description" content="Search results for <escaped-query>">

Meta tags do not execute scripts, but unescaped input can break out of the attribute and inject HTML.

docs.title: CSP Delivery
docs.text:
Meta-delivered CSP works for most directives but cannot set:

  • frame-ancestors (clickjacking defense)
  • report-uri / report-to (violation reporting)
  • sandbox (full sandboxing)

Use HTTP headers for complete CSP.

docs.title: Referrer Policy and Sensitive URLs
docs.text: URLs with tokens or session IDs in query strings can leak via the Referer header. Set referrer policy to strict-origin-when-cross-origin or no-referrer.

docs.title: Social Scraper Security
docs.text:
Social platforms scrape og:image URLs. Ensure those URLs are:

  • On a trusted origin.
  • Not behind authentication.
  • Not user-controlled (SSRF risk).

docs.title: Trusted Types and Meta
docs.text: Trusted Types (require-trusted-types-for 'script') prevents string-based DOM injection. If dynamically inserting meta tags, use Trusted Types APIs.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• View source — confirm meta tags are present in the raw HTML, not just in the runtime DOM.
  • DevTools → Elements — inspect <head> and verify each meta tag.
  • DevTools → Network — check the Content-Type header for charset.
  • Lighthouse — audits for missing viewport, description, and other SEO basics.
  • Facebook Sharing Debugger — preview how og:* tags render.
  • Twitter Card Validator — preview Twitter card rendering.
  • LinkedIn Post Inspector — preview LinkedIn sharing.
  • Google Search Console — see how Google reads your description and robots directives.
  • CSP Evaluator (Google) — grade meta-delivered CSP.
  • document.querySelectorAll('meta') — list all meta tags in console.
  • Test in device emulation mode — verify viewport behavior.
  • navigator.userAgent + viewport — confirm mobile layout.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• charset — always.
  • viewport — always.
  • description — every indexable page.
  • robots — whenever you need indexing control.
  • theme-color — for branded browser UI.
  • color-scheme — when supporting dark mode.
  • referrer — when URLs may contain sensitive data.
  • og:* — every page intended for social sharing.
  • twitter:* — when Twitter/X previews matter.
  • CSP via http-equiv — only when HTTP headers are unavailable.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• keywords — not for SEO.
  • http-equiv="refresh" — not for redirects; use HTTP status codes.
  • apple-mobile-web-app-capable — deprecated; use mobile-web-app-capable or manifest.
  • Duplicate name values — never.
  • user-scalable=no — never (accessibility).
  • Meta-delivered CSP for frame-ancestors — not supported.
  • Meta tags for sensitive data — never put secrets in meta content.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <title> — document name element
  • <link rel="canonical"> — canonical URL
  • <link rel="manifest"> — web app manifest
  • Open Graph protocol
  • Twitter Cards
  • Content Security Policy
  • Referrer Policy
  • Viewport and Visual Viewport API
  • Character Encoding
  • Robots Exclusion Protocol
  • Structured Data (JSON-LD)
  • SEO Metadata

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Google rewrites roughly 76% of title tags it analyzes — but a well-optimized title still matters because Google's rewrite often preserves key phrases.
  • <meta charset> must appear in the first 1024 bytes — the browser prescans before full parsing.
  • Meta descriptions do not affect rankings but strongly affect click-through rate.
  • og:* tags use property (RDFa), not name — a common source of confusion.
  • Twitter/X falls back to og:* when twitter:* tags are absent.
  • interactive-widget=resizes-content fixes Android Chrome's keyboard overlay behavior, matching iOS.
  • theme-color can have media queries for light/dark variants — a relatively recent addition.
  • CSP via meta cannot set frame-ancestors — a critical limitation often missed.
  • Dynamic insertion of <meta name="referrer"> makes behavior unpredictable; multiple policies resolve to no-referrer.
  • Meta tags decay — audit quarterly or after migrations.
  • AI search tools rely on meta tags for structured signals, citation, and previews.
  • The format-detection meta tag can stop iOS from auto-linking phone numbers.
  • viewport-fit=cover is required for full-bleed layouts on notched devices.
  • The <meta> element is a void element — it has no closing tag and no content.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Meta tags are machine-readable metadata in <head> — invisible to users but consumed by browsers, search engines, social platforms, and AI tools.
  • Three attribute forms: charset, name+content, http-equiv+content.
  • Required tags: charset, viewport, <title>.
  • SEO-critical tags: description (CTR), robots (indexing), <link rel="canonical">.
  • Social tags: og:* for most platforms, twitter:* for X/Twitter.
  • Browser UI tags: theme-color, color-scheme, referrer.
  • CSP via meta works for most directives but not frame-ancestors, report-uri, or sandbox.
  • Avoid: keywords for SEO, http-equiv="refresh" for redirects, user-scalable=no, duplicate name values.
  • SPAs must update meta tags dynamically on every route change.
  • Audit quarterly — meta tags decay as content changes.
  • Test with Lighthouse, social debuggers, and Google Search Console.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Open Graph (OG) is a protocol created by Facebook in 2010 that uses <meta> tags to describe a web page as a rich object — with a title, description, image, URL, and type — so that social platforms, messaging apps, and search engines can generate preview cards when the link is shared.

<meta property="og:title" content="How SVG Embedding Works">
<meta property="og:description" content="A complete guide to embedding SVG in HTML.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/preview.png">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/svg-guide">
<meta property="og:type" content="article">

Open Graph tags use the property attribute (RDFa syntax) — not name — which is part of the original protocol specification.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Open Graph tags exist to solve a specific problem: social platforms cannot read your mind. Without explicit metadata, a platform sharing your link must guess:

  • What title to show.
  • What description to display.
  • What image to use.
  • What type of content the page represents.

Those guesses are often wrong. Open Graph gives you direct control over the preview card that millions of users see when your link is shared on Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord, WhatsApp, and most other platforms.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
<html>
├── <head>
│   ├── <title>                    ← browser tab / SEO headline
│   ├── <meta name="description">  ← SERP snippet
│   ├── <meta property="og:title">       ← social preview title
│   ├── <meta property="og:description"> ← social preview summary
│   ├── <meta property="og:image">       ← social preview image
│   ├── <meta property="og:url">         ← canonical share URL
│   ├── <meta property="og:type">        ← content type
│   ├── <meta property="og:site_name">   ← site name shown in card
│   └── ...
└── <body>

Open Graph is not the same as Twitter Cards — those are a separate set of tags. However, X (Twitter) checks for twitter:* tags first and falls back to og:* tags when they are absent.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before Open Graph, sharing a link on social media produced unpredictable results:

  • The platform grabbed the first image on the page — often a logo, an ad, or a sidebar graphic.
  • The description was pulled from the first paragraph — which might be a cookie notice.
  • The title was taken verbatim from <title> — which was written for SEO, not social sharing.

The result was ugly, inconsistent, and unprofessional previews that undersold the content and reduced click-through rates.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No standard for social metadata Every platform guessed differently No image control Wrong or missing preview images No description control Irrelevant or missing text No type declaration Platforms couldn't distinguish article from product from video No canonical URL Share equity was split across URL variants

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text: Facebook introduced Open Graph in 2010 to solve its own preview problem, but it quickly became the industry default. Today, Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord, WhatsApp, and dozens of other platforms all read Open Graph tags to build link previews. If you only add one type of social metadata to your site, Open Graph is the one to add — it covers the widest range of platforms.

docs.title: The Four Required Properties
docs.text:
Every Open Graph page should have at minimum:

<meta property="og:title" content="Stripe Checkout Guide">
<meta property="og:description" content="Learn how to integrate Stripe Checkout with Next.js 16.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og-image.png">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/blog/stripe-checkout-guide">
<meta property="og:type" content="article">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Tag Purpose Notes og:title Preview headline Can differ from <title> — write for the feed, not the SERP og:description Preview summary 150 characters or fewer; front-load the key point og:image Preview image 1200 × 630px (1.91:1 ratio) is the standard og:url Canonical URL Always use the canonical URL to protect share equity og:type Content type Default is website; use article for posts

docs.title: Fully Commented Production Example
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Required: character encoding -->
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <!-- Standard SEO -->
    <title>How Meta Tags Work — Dev Notes</title>
    <meta name="description" content="A complete guide to HTML meta tags.">

    <!-- Open Graph — the social preview layer -->
    <meta property="og:title" content="How Meta Tags Work">
    <meta property="og:description" content="A complete guide to HTML meta tags: viewport, description, robots, Open Graph, and theme color.">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://devnotes.example.com/preview.png">
    <meta property="og:image:width" content="1200">
    <meta property="og:image:height" content="630">
    <meta property="og:image:alt" content="Illustration of HTML meta tags in a document head">
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://devnotes.example.com/meta-tags">
    <meta property="og:type" content="article">
    <meta property="og:site_name" content="Dev Notes">

    <!-- Article-specific structured properties -->
    <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-01-15T08:00:00Z">
    <meta property="article:author" content="Jane Developer">
</head>

docs.title: The "Business Card" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of your web page as a business, and Open Graph tags as the business card it hands out when someone shares its link:

  • og:title — the name on the card.
  • og:description — the tagline.
  • og:image — the logo.
  • og:url — the address.
  • og:type — the industry.

A bad business card doesn't just look unprofessional — it loses the customer.

docs.title: The "Two Audiences" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every page has two audiences for its metadata:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              <head>                          │
│                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐ │
│  │   SEARCH ENGINES    │  │ SOCIAL PLATFORMS│ │
│  │                     │  │               │ │
│  │  <title>            │  │  og:title     │ │
│  │  meta description   │  │  og:description│ │
│  │  robots             │  │  og:image     │ │
│  │  canonical          │  │  og:url       │ │
│  └─────────────────────┘  └───────────────┘ │
│                                              │
│  These serve DIFFERENT purposes.            │
│  Do NOT copy-paste between them.            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A title written for Google may be too long or too formal for a Facebook feed. A description written for a SERP may be too keyword-heavy for a social preview. Write for the context — the share context is different from the search context.

docs.title: The "Fallback Chain" Mental Model
docs.text:
When a platform builds a preview, it reads tags in a priority order:

1. twitter:* tags        (if the platform is X/Twitter)
2. og:* tags             (universal fallback)
3. <title>               (last resort for title)
4. meta description      (last resort for description)
5. First large image     (last resort for image)

The further down the chain, the worse the preview. Open Graph puts you near the top.

docs.title: Concept 1: og:title
docs.text: The headline displayed in the social preview card. This can and often should differ from your page title. Write it for a reader scrolling through a feed — shorter, more direct, and optimized for the share context. If left blank, platforms fall back to <title>.

docs.title: Concept 2: og:description
docs.text: The summary text below the headline. Most platforms truncate around 150–160 characters, so front-load the key point. This is not the same as your meta description, though they can overlap.

docs.title: Concept 3: og:image
docs.text: The preview image — the most impactful field. A strong image dramatically increases engagement. Recommended dimensions: 1200 × 630px (1.91:1 ratio). Minimum 600 × 315px. Keep important text centered (edges may crop). File size under 1MB, ideally under 300KB. Use absolute URLs including the full domain.

docs.title: Concept 4: og:url
docs.text: The canonical URL of the page. Always use the canonical URL — this protects share equity and keeps attribution clean across campaigns and environments. If this is missing or wrong, social platforms may treat different URL variants as separate objects, splitting likes and shares.

docs.title: Concept 5: og:type
docs.text: Declares the type of content. Default is website, which is correct for the vast majority of pages. Other valid types include article, video.movie, product, and others defined in the protocol. For product pages, og:type=product enables product-specific rendering and can be paired with product:price:amount and product:price:currency.

docs.title: Concept 6: og:site_name
docs.text: The name of the site the content belongs to. Displayed discreetly in the preview card, usually above or below the title. Helps with brand attribution when the title alone doesn't make the source clear.

docs.title: Concept 7: og:image:width and og:image:height
docs.text: Declare the dimensions of the Open Graph image. This helps platforms allocate the correct space before the image loads and can prevent layout shifts in the preview card.

docs.title: Concept 8: og:image:alt
docs.text: Alt text for the preview image. Improves accessibility and helps platforms that display alt text when an image fails to load.

docs.title: Concept 9: Structured Properties
docs.text:
Open Graph supports structured properties beyond the four required tags. For article type:

<meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-01-15T08:00:00Z">
<meta property="article:author" content="Jane Developer">
<meta property="article:section" content="Technology">
<meta property="article:tag" content="HTML">

For product type:

<meta property="product:price:amount" content="139.99">
<meta property="product:price:currency" content="USD">

These enable richer preview rendering on supporting platforms.

docs.title: Concept 10: RDFa Syntax — property Not name
docs.text: Open Graph uses RDFa syntax. The attribute is property, not name. This is part of the original protocol specification, not a typo. Mixing them up is one of the most common implementation errors.

docs.title: Concept 11: Fallback to Twitter Cards
docs.text: X (Twitter) checks for twitter:* tags first and falls back to og:* tags when they are absent. However, relying on the fallback means you cannot explicitly control twitter:card, so providing Twitter Card tags is still recommended.

docs.title: Concept 12: Caching by Social Platforms
docs.text: Social platforms cache Open Graph data aggressively. If you change your OG tags, the platform may still show the old preview. To force a refresh, use the platform's debugger tool (Facebook Sharing Debugger, LinkedIn Post Inspector, etc.) and click "Scrape Again".

docs.title: Concept 13: JavaScript-Rendered Content
docs.text: Most social media crawlers — including Facebook's and Twitter's — do not execute JavaScript. They read the static HTML source only. If your OG tags are injected by client-side JavaScript, the crawler will never see them. For SPAs, you must deliver OG tags from the server, via SSR, SSG, or a prerendering service.

docs.title: Concept 14: Absolute URLs Required
docs.text: og:image and og:url must be absolute URLs including the protocol and domain. Relative paths silently fail — the image simply won't appear in the preview.

docs.title: Concept 15: Image Format
docs.text: Prefer JPEG for the bytes the unfurler receives. PNG is acceptable for simple graphics with few colors. Avoid GIFs and WebP for OG images — some platforms still don't decode them reliably.

docs.title: Concept 16: No Duplicate OG Tags
docs.text: The presence of multiple sets of OG tags is a common mistake that causes platforms to pick unpredictably. There should be exactly one set of Open Graph tags per page.

docs.title: Concept 17: OG vs Schema.org
docs.text: Google now combines Schema.org structured data and Open Graph data to choose which thumbnail to display in search results. This means both should be present and consistent for best visibility.

docs.title: Concept 18: Dynamic OG Images
docs.text: For pages with unique content (blog posts, products, user profiles), consider generating dynamic OG images on the server — using tools like Satori + Resvg or Cloudflare Workers. This ensures every shared link has a unique, relevant preview image.

docs.title: Concept 19: SPA Rendering Strategies
docs.text:
For single-page applications, social crawlers won't execute JavaScript. Options for serving correct OG tags:

  1. SSR / SSG — render HTML on the server with correct tags.
  2. Prerendering — generate static HTML snapshots per route.
  3. Edge injection — use Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Functions to inject tags based on User-Agent.
  4. Static generation per route — convert SPA routes to static HTML files.

docs.title: Concept 20: OG and AI Search
docs.text: AI-powered search features and assistants increasingly rely on structured metadata to interpret and cite content. Well-formed Open Graph tags — combined with Schema.org and clean meta tags — improve visibility in AI-generated summaries and citations.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Social Preview Generation
docs.text:
1.  User pastes a URL into a social platform.
    │
    ▼
2.  Platform's crawler fetches the HTML source.
    │
    ▼
3.  Crawler reads the <head> section.
    │
    ▼
4.  Crawler extracts:
    │   ├── og:title       → preview title
    │   ├── og:description → preview description
    │   ├── og:image       → preview image
    │   ├── og:url         → canonical URL
    │   └── og:type        → content type
    │
    ▼
5.  If og:* tags are missing, crawler falls back to:
    │   ├── <title>
    │   ├── meta description
    │   └── first large image
    │
    ▼
6.  Platform renders the preview card in the feed.
    │
    ▼
7.  Preview is cached for future shares.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: OG Image Loading
docs.text:
1.  Crawler finds og:image tag.
    │
    ▼
2.  Crawler requests the image URL.
    │
    ▼
3.  If URL is relative → fails silently.
    │
    ▼
4.  If image is too small → may be ignored.
    │
    ▼
5.  If image is too large → may be cropped.
    │
    ▼
6.  Image rendered in the preview card.

docs.title: RDFa and the og: Namespace
docs.text:
Open Graph is built on RDFa (Resource Description Framework in Attributes). Each OG tag is a triple: subject → predicate → object.

  • Subject: the page itself.
  • Predicate: the property name (e.g., og:title).
  • Object: the content value.

The og: prefix maps to http://opengraphprotocol.org/schema/. When you write <meta property="og:title" content="Hello">, you are asserting that the page's Open Graph title is "Hello".

docs.title: Required vs Optional Properties
docs.text:
The protocol defines four required properties:

Property Required Purpose og:title ✅ The object's title og:type ✅ The object's type og:image ✅ The object's image URL og:url ✅ The object's canonical URL

Additional properties like og:description, og:site_name, og:image:width, og:image:height, and og:image:alt are optional but recommended.

docs.title: Structured Properties and Object Types
docs.text:
The protocol defines approximately 40 object types, including article, book, profile, video.movie, product, and website. Each type has its own structured properties:

article
├── article:published_time
├── article:modified_time
├── article:author
├── article:section
└── article:tag

product
├── product:price:amount
├── product:price:currency
└── product:availability

docs.title: How Platforms Consume OG Data
docs.text:
Each platform has its own crawler and rendering logic:

Platform Crawler Fallback Behavior Facebook facebookexternalhit Reads og:* only; falls back to and meta description</td> </tr> <tr> <td>LinkedIn</td> <td><code>LinkedInBot</code></td> <td>Reads og:*; may use Schema.org</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Slack</td> <td><code>Slackbot</code></td> <td>Reads og:*; falls back to <title></td> </tr> <tr> <td>Discord</td> <td><code>Discordbot</code></td> <td>Reads og:*; requires og:image</td> </tr> <tr> <td>X (Twitter)</td> <td><code>Twitterbot</code></td> <td>Reads twitter:<em> first, then og:</em></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h3 id="caching-architecture">Caching Architecture</h3> <p>Platforms cache OG data to avoid re-fetching on every share. The cache is keyed by URL. When you update OG tags:</p> <ol> <li>The platform still serves the cached preview.</li> <li>You must use the platform's debugger to force a re-scrape.</li> <li>The new data is cached after re-scrape.</li> </ol> <p>This is why <strong>testing before sharing</strong> is critical.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="8-lifecycle-workflow">8. Lifecycle / Workflow</h2> <h3 id="static-page-lifecycle">Static Page Lifecycle</h3> <div class="language-text highlight"><pre><span></span><code>Author writes OG tags in <head> │ ▼ Deployed to server │ ▼ User shares the URL │ ▼ Social platform crawler fetches the HTML │ ▼ Crawler extracts og:* tags │ ▼ Preview card rendered and cached │ ▼ Subsequent shares use cached preview │ ▼ OG tags change → cache must be invalidated via debugger </code></pre></div> <h3 id="og-tag-audit-lifecycle">OG Tag Audit Lifecycle</h3> <div class="language-text highlight"><pre><span></span><code>1. Best Practices</h2> <ol> <li><strong>Always include the four required OG tags.</strong> Why: without them, platforms guess — often badly.</li> <li><strong>Write <code>og:title</code> for the share <code>og:image</code> and <code>og:url</code>.</strong> Why: relative paths silently fail.</li> <li><strong>Include <code>og:image:width</code> and <code>og:image:height</code>.</strong> Why: helps <code>og:type</code> correctly.</strong> Why: <code>website</code> for most pages, <code>article</code> for posts, <code>product</code> for products.</li> <li><strong>Use <code>og:url</code> as the canonical URL.</strong> Why: protects share equity and prevents duplicate objects.</li> <li><strong>Add Twitter Card tags alongside OG tags.</strong> Why: X falls back to OG, but <code>twitter:card</code> cannot be controlled via fallback.</li> <li><strong>Serve OG tags in the static HTML.</strong> Why: social crawlers don't execute JavaScript.</li> <li><strong>Test with <li><strong>Audit OG tags quarterly or after migrations.</strong> Why: content changes, URLs change, tags decay.</li> <li><strong>Combine OG with Schema.org structured data.</strong> Why: Google now This dramatically reduces engagement.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>:</p> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:image"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"https://example.com/preview.png"</span><span class="p">></span> </code></pre></div> <h3 id="mistake-relative-image-url">❌ Mistake: Relative Image URL</h3> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:image"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"/images/preview.png"</span><span class="p">></span> </code></pre></div> <p><strong>Why it's wrong</strong>: Relative URLs silently fail — the image won't appear.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>:</p> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:image"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"https://example.com/images/preview.png"</span><span class="p">></span> </code></pre></div> <h3 id="mistake-image-too-small">❌ Mistake: Image Too Small</h3> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:image"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"https://example.com/logo.png"</span><span class="p">></span> <span class="cm"><!-- 369×333 --></span> </code></pre></div> <p><strong>Why it's wrong</strong>: The recommended size is 1200×630. Smaller images may be ignored or render poorly.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>: Use a 1200×630px image.</p> <h3 id="mistake-client-side-og-injection">❌ Mistake: Client-Side OG Injection</h3> <div class="language-javascript highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// SPAs often do this — it doesn't work for crawlers</span> <span class="nb">document</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">querySelector</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s1">'meta[property="og:image"]'</span><span class="p">).</span><span class="nx">setAttribute</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s1">'content'</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nx">url</span><span class="p">);</span> </code></pre></div> <p><strong>Why it's wrong</strong>: Social crawlers don't execute JavaScript. They see the static HTML, which still has the old or missing tags.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>: Serve OG tags from the server via SSR, SSG, or edge injection.</p> <h3 id="mistake-using-name-instead-of-property">❌ Mistake: Using <code>name</code> Instead of <code>property</code></h3> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">name</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:title"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"My Page"</span><span class="p">></span> </code></pre></div> <p><strong>Why it's wrong</strong>: Open Graph uses <code>property</code>, not <code>name</code>. This tag is ignored.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>:</p> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:title"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"My Page"</span><span class="p">></span> </code></pre></div> <h3 id="mistake-duplicate-og-tags">❌ Mistake: Duplicate OG Tags</h3> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:title"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"Title A"</span><span class="p">></span> <span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:title"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"Title B"</span><span class="p">></span> </code></pre></div> <p><strong>Why it's wrong</strong>: Multiple sets cause platforms to pick unpredictably.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>: One set of OG tags per page.</p> <h3 id="mistake-not-testing-after-changes">❌ Mistake: Not Testing After Changes</h3> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="cm"><!-- Changed og:image but didn't clear platform cache --></span> </code></pre></div> <p><strong>Why it's wrong</strong>: Platforms cache OG data aggressively. The old preview persists until re-scraped.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>: Use the platform's debugger to force a re-scrape.</p> <h3 id="mistake-same-og-image-for-every-page">❌ Mistake: Same OG Image for Every Page</h3> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="cm"><!-- Every page uses the site logo --></span> <span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:image"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"https://example.com/logo.png"</span><span class="p">></span> </code></pre></div> <p><strong>Why it's wrong</strong>: Unique images drive engagement. A generic logo makes every share look identical.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>: Generate or select unique images per page.</p> <h3 id="mistake-ignoring-ogtype">❌ Mistake: Ignoring <code>og:type</code></h3> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="cm"><!-- No og:type --></span> </code></pre></div> <p><strong>Why it's wrong</strong>: Platforms default to <code>website</code>, missing opportunities for type-specific rendering.</p> <p><strong>✅ Correct</strong>: Set <code>og:type=article</code> for posts, <code>product</code> for products, etc.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="13-performance-considerations">13. Performance Considerations</h2> <ul> <li><strong>OG tags add minimal bytes</strong> — typically under 1 KB uncompressed.</li> <li><strong>OG images are fetched by crawlers</strong>, not by the user's browser — no impact on page load.</li> <li><strong>Large OG images</strong> slow crawler fetching and may be rejected by platforms.</li> <li><strong>Dynamic OG image generation</strong> adds server CPU cost; cache generated images.</li> <li><strong>Prerendering for SPAs</strong> adds infrastructure cost but is necessary for correct social previews.</li> <li><strong>Edge injection</strong> adds minimal latency and is the most efficient SPA solution.</li> </ul> <h3 id="performance-tips">Performance Tips</h3> <ol> <li>Keep OG images under 300 KB.</li> <li>Host OG images on a CDN.</li> <li>Cache dynamically generated OG images.</li> <li>Use JPEG for photographic images.</li> <li>Declare <code>og:image:width</code> and <code>og:image:height</code> to prevent layout shift.</li> </ol> <hr /> <h2 id="14-security-considerations">14. Security Considerations</h2> <h3 id="reflected-content-injection">Reflected Content Injection</h3> <p>If OG tag content is generated from user input (e.g., search queries, page parameters), escape it server-side:</p> <div class="language-html highlight"><pre><span></span><code><span class="cm"><!-- DANGEROUS --></span> <span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:title"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"<?= $_GET['title'] ?>"</span><span class="p">></span> <span class="cm"><!-- SAFE --></span> <span class="p"><</span><span class="nt">meta</span> <span class="na">property</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"og:title"</span> <span class="na">content</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">"<?= htmlspecialchars($_GET['title']) ?>"</span><span class="p">></span> </code></pre></div> <h3 id="ssrf-via-ogimage">SSRF via <code>og:image</code></h3> <p>Social platforms fetch <code>og:image</code> URLs. If your site allows users to set OG images to arbitrary URLs, attackers could use your site as a proxy for SSRF attacks. Validate and whitelist image URLs.</p> <h3 id="xss-via-og-tags">XSS via OG Tags</h3> <p>OG tags are meta tags — they don't execute scripts. But unescaped content can break out of the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML. Always escape.</p> <h3 id="privacy-leakage">Privacy Leakage</h3> <p>OG tags reveal information about your page to any platform that crawls it. Do not put sensitive data, internal URLs, or PII in OG tags.</p> <h3 id="og-image-security">OG Image Security</h3> <p>Serve OG images from a trusted origin. Do not serve user-uploaded images directly as OG images without validation — they could contain malicious payloads or be used for tracking.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="15-debugging-tips">15. Debugging Tips</h2> <ul> <li><strong>Facebook Sharing Debugger</strong> — <code>developers.facebook.com/tools/debug/</code> — preview and force re-scrape.</li> <li><strong>LinkedIn Post Inspector</strong> — <code>linkedin.com/post-inspector/</code> — preview LinkedIn rendering.</li> <li><strong>X Card Validator</strong> — <code>cards-dev.twitter.com/validator</code> — preview X/Twitter cards.</li> <li><strong>Discord</strong> — paste the link in a Discord channel to preview.</li> <li><strong>Slack</strong> — paste the link in a Slack channel to preview.</li> <li><strong>View source</strong> — confirm OG tags are in the static HTML, not just runtime DOM.</li> <li><strong>Curl the page</strong> — <code>curl -s https://example.com | grep og:</code> to see what crawlers see.</li> <li><strong>Prerender.io</strong> — diagnose SPA rendering issues.</li> <li><strong>OpenGraph.xyz</strong> — third-party preview tool.</li> <li><strong>Meta Tags</strong> — <code>metatags.io</code> — multi-platform preview.</li> <li><strong>Test with a fresh URL</strong> — platforms cache by URL; append a query string to bypass cache during testing.</li> </ul> <hr /> <h2 id="16-when-to-use">16. When to Use</h2> <ul> <li><strong>Any page intended for social sharing</strong> — blog posts, products, landing pages.</li> <li><strong>Any page that will be linked in messaging apps</strong> — WhatsApp, Slack, Discord.</li> <li><strong>Any SPA route</strong> — via server-side injection.</li> <li><strong>Any e-commerce product page</strong> — with <code>og:type=product</code>.</li> <li><strong>Any content with a unique image</strong> — to control the preview.</li> </ul> <hr /> <h2 id="17-when-not-to-use">17. When Not to Use</h2> <ul> <li><strong>Private or internal pages</strong> — no need, and may leak information.</li> <li><strong>Pages behind authentication</strong> — crawlers can't access them anyway.</li> <li><strong>Pages with no sharing value</strong> — login pages, error pages, settings.</li> <li><strong>As a replacement for SEO meta tags</strong> — they serve different audiences.</li> </ul> <hr /> <h2 id="18-related-concepts">18. Related Concepts</h2> <ul> <li><code><title></code> — document name element</li> <li><code><meta name="description"></code> — SERP snippet</li> <li>Twitter Cards — X/Twitter-specific preview tags</li> <li>Schema.org — structured data vocabulary</li> <li>JSON-LD — JSON-based structured data</li> <li>RDFa — the syntax Open Graph is built on</li> <li><code>og:type</code> — content type declaration</li> <li>Facebook Sharing Debugger</li> <li>Social crawlers</li> </ul> <hr /> <h2 id="19-did-you-know">19. Did You Know?</h2> <ul> <li><strong>Open Graph was created by Facebook in 2010</strong> and became the industry default for social previews.</li> <li><strong>X (Twitter) falls back to Open Graph tags</strong> when <code>twitter:*</code> tags are absent — but you lose control over <code>twitter:card</code>.</li> <li><strong>Social crawlers do not execute JavaScript</strong> — client-side OG injection never works.</li> <li><strong>The recommended OG image size is 1200 × 630px</strong> (1.91:1 ratio).</li> <li><strong>OG tags use <code>property</code>, not <code>name</code></strong> — a common source of confusion.</li> <li><strong>Google combines Schema.org and Open Graph</strong> data to choose search thumbnails.</li> <li><strong>Platforms cache OG data aggressively</strong> — fixes require debugger re-scraping.</li> <li><strong>The protocol defines ~40 object types</strong>, from <code>article</code> to <code>video.movie</code>.</li> <li><strong>Relative image URLs silently fail</strong> — always use absolute URLs.</li> <li><strong>Dynamic OG images</strong> are generated server-side for unique content — tools include Satori and Cloudflare Workers.</li> <li><strong>Edge injection</strong> (Lambda@Edge, CloudFront Functions) is the most efficient SPA OG solution.</li> <li><strong>Posts with images receive 150% more engagement</strong> than text-only posts.</li> </ul> <hr /> <h2 id="20-summary">20. Summary</h2> <ul> <li><strong>Open Graph is a protocol</strong> created by Facebook in 2010 to control how links appear when shared on social platforms.</li> <li><strong>Four required properties</strong>: <code>og:title</code>, <code>og:type</code>, <code>og:image</code>, <code>og:url</code>.</li> <li><strong>Key best practices</strong>: 1200×630px images, absolute URLs, unique content, write for the share context.</li> <li><strong>X falls back to OG</strong> when <code>twitter:*</code> tags are absent — but providing Twitter Card tags is still recommended.</li> <li><strong>Social crawlers don't execute JavaScript</strong> — SPAs must serve OG tags from the server.</li> <li><strong>Platforms cache OG data</strong> — use debuggers to force re-scrapes.</li> <li><strong>Common mistakes</strong>: missing images, relative URLs, client-side injection, using <code>name</code> instead of <code>property</code>.</li> <li><strong>Test with real platform debuggers</strong> before sharing.</li> <li><strong>OG tags work alongside</strong> <code><title></code>, meta description, and Schema.org structured data.</li> <li><strong>OG tags are essential infrastructure</strong> for any page intended to be shared.</li> </ul> <hr />

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Twitter Cards are a metadata protocol created by Twitter (now X) that allows you to attach rich media previews — images, video, audio, and app download links — to Tweets that contain links to your website. When someone shares your URL on X, the platform's crawler reads twitter:* meta tags in the page's <head> and assembles a visual preview card.

<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="How Meta Tags Work">
<meta name="twitter:description" content="A complete guide to HTML meta tags.">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/preview.png">
<meta name="twitter:site" content="@devnotes">

Twitter Cards use the name attribute (not property), unlike Open Graph. They are a separate protocol from Open Graph, though X will fall back to og:* tags when twitter:* tags are absent.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Twitter Cards exist to make shared links visually compelling and clickable. Without them, a shared URL appears as plain text. With them, X generates a rich preview containing a title, description, and image — turning a bare link into a visual teaser that drives engagement. The protocol also supports specialized card types for mobile apps and embedded media players.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
<html>
├── <head>
│   ├── <title>                         ← browser tab / SEO
│   ├── <meta property="og:*">          ← universal social fallback
│   ├── <meta name="twitter:card">      ← card layout selection
│   ├── <meta name="twitter:title">     ← card headline
│   ├── <meta name="twitter:description">← card summary
│   ├── <meta name="twitter:image">     ← card image
│   ├── <meta name="twitter:site">      ← site handle attribution
│   └── <meta name="twitter:creator">   ← author handle attribution
└── <body>

Twitter Cards are not the same as Open Graph tags — those were created by Facebook and are consumed by a wider range of platforms. Twitter Cards are X-specific, though they add capabilities that Open Graph lacks, such as player cards and app cards.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Before Twitter Cards, sharing a link on Twitter produced a bare URL. Users had no visual preview, no context, and no reason to click. The platform needed a way for publishers to control the preview — the image, headline, and description that appeared beneath the tweet.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No preview Links appeared as plain text No image control No visual hook in the timeline No media embedding Video and audio couldn't play inline No app links Mobile apps had no direct download path from tweets No attribution Publishers couldn't link the card to their handle

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Twitter introduced Cards in 2012 to solve its own preview problem. The protocol was designed to be declarative — add a few meta tags, and X generates the card automatically. Over time, the card types expanded to cover:

  • Summary Card — title, description, and small thumbnail.
  • Summary Card with Large Image — full-width image above the text (the most widely used).
  • App Card — direct download links for mobile apps.
  • Player Card — inline video or audio playback, requiring X approval.

Today, most sites only need Summary or Summary with Large Image. The App and Player cards are niche.

docs.title: The Four Essential Tags
docs.text:
Every Twitter Card requires at minimum:

<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="How SVG Embedding Works">
<meta name="twitter:description" content="A complete guide to embedding SVG in HTML.">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/svg-preview.png">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Tag Purpose Notes twitter:card Selects the card layout summary or summary_large_image twitter:title Card headline Max ~70 characters twitter:description Card summary Max ~200 characters; truncates around 120–140 twitter:image Card image Absolute URL required; relative paths fail

docs.title: Fully Commented Production Example
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <!-- Standard SEO -->
    <title>How SVG Embedding Works — Dev Notes</title>
    <meta name="description" content="A complete guide to embedding SVG in HTML.">

    <!-- Open Graph (universal fallback) -->
    <meta property="og:title" content="How SVG Embedding Works">
    <meta property="og:description" content="A complete guide to embedding SVG in HTML.">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://devnotes.example.com/og/svg-embedding.png">
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://devnotes.example.com/svg-embedding">
    <meta property="og:type" content="article">

    <!-- Twitter Card (X-specific control) -->
    <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
    <meta name="twitter:site" content="@devnotes">
    <meta name="twitter:creator" content="@janedev">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="How SVG Embedding Works">
    <meta name="twitter:description" content="A complete guide to embedding SVG in HTML: inline, img, object, iframe, and sprites.">
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://devnotes.example.com/og/svg-embedding.png">
    <meta name="twitter:image:alt" content="Diagram of SVG embedding methods">
</head>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• twitter:card — selects summary_large_image for maximum visual impact.
  • twitter:site — adds your site's handle as attribution below the card.
  • twitter:creator — attributes the content to the author's handle.
  • twitter:title and twitter:description — control the card text independently of Open Graph.
  • twitter:image — absolute URL to a 1200×675px image (X's recommended size, slightly different from OG's 1200×630).
  • twitter:image:alt — accessibility text for the image.

docs.title: The "Two Protocals, One Preview" Mental Model
docs.text:
X reads social metadata in a priority order:

1. twitter:* tags        ← X-specific control
2. og:* tags             ← universal fallback
3. <title> + meta desc   ← last resort

If you set only Open Graph tags, X will still generate a preview — but you lose explicit control over the card layout, image dimensions, and handle attribution. If you set both, X uses the twitter:* tags first and falls back to og:* for any missing fields.

docs.title: The "Card Type as Layout" Mental Model
docs.text:
The twitter:card tag is a layout selector, not a description of your content. It tells X which template to use:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  twitter:card = "summary"                    │
│  ┌────┐                                     │
│  │img │  Title                              │
│  └────┘  Description...                     │
│                                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  twitter:card = "summary_large_image"        │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │            Full-width image           │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  Title                                       │
│  Description...                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Concept 1: twitter:card
docs.text: The only required tag. Selects the card layout. Valid values: summary, summary_large_image, app, player.

docs.title: Concept 2: twitter:title
docs.text: The card headline. Maximum ~70 characters. Falls back to og:title, then <title>.

docs.title: Concept 3: twitter:description
docs.text: The card summary. Truncates around 120–140 characters on most clients. Falls back to og:description, then meta description.

docs.title: Concept 4: twitter:image
docs.text: The card image. Must be an absolute URL — relative paths silently fail. For summary_large_image, X recommends 1200 × 675px (slightly different from Open Graph's 1200 × 630). Minimum size: 300 × 157px.

docs.title: Concept 5: twitter:site
docs.text: The X handle of the site owner or publisher (e.g., @devnotes). Displayed as attribution below the card. Optional but recommended.

docs.title: Concept 6: twitter:creator
docs.text: The X handle of the content author (e.g., @janedev). Used for attribution when different from the site handle.

docs.title: Concept 7: twitter:image:alt
docs.text: Alt text for the card image. Improves accessibility. Also supported by Open Graph as og:image:alt.

docs.title: Concept 8: The Four Card Types
docs.text:
Card Type Layout Use Case summary Small thumbnail left, text right Blog posts, documentation, articles summary_large_image Full-width image above text Landing pages, product pages, visual content app Mobile app download card App landing pages player Inline video/audio player Media sites (requires X approval)

Most sites only need summary or summary_large_image.

docs.title: Concept 9: Fallback to Open Graph
docs.text: X checks for twitter:* tags first. If twitter:title is absent, it falls back to og:title. If twitter:image is absent, it falls back to og:image. This means a well-configured Open Graph setup will produce a functional — but less controlled — Twitter Card.

docs.title: Concept 10: Absolute URLs Required
docs.text: twitter:image must be an absolute URL including the protocol and domain. Relative paths like /images/preview.png are ignored.

docs.title: Concept 11: Image Size Requirements
docs.text: For summary_large_image, the recommended size is 1200 × 675px. Minimum 300 × 157px. For summary, the thumbnail is square, minimum 144 × 144px. Images below the minimum may be ignored entirely.

docs.title: Concept 12: Caching by X
docs.text: X caches Twitter Card data aggressively. If you change your tags, the old preview may persist for days. Use the Card Validator to force a re-scrape.

docs.title: Concept 13: JavaScript-Rendered Content
docs.text: X's crawler (Twitterbot) does not execute JavaScript. It reads the static HTML source only. For SPAs, you must deliver Twitter Card tags from the server.

docs.title: Concept 14: robots.txt and Twitterbot
docs.text: If your robots.txt blocks Twitterbot, X cannot read your meta tags and will not generate a card.

docs.title: Concept 15: No Duplicate Tags
docs.text: Multiple sets of twitter:* tags cause unpredictable behavior. Each tag should appear once.

docs.title: Concept 16: Player Card Approval
docs.text: The player card type requires approval from X before it will render. The app card type does not require approval.

docs.title: Concept 17: Dynamic Cards for SPAs
docs.text: For single-page applications, Twitter Card tags must be injected server-side. Options include SSR, SSG, prerendering, or edge injection based on User-Agent.

docs.title: Concept 18: Twitter Cards and AI Search
docs.text: AI-powered search features and assistants increasingly read structured metadata. Well-formed Twitter Cards — alongside Open Graph and Schema.org — improve how content is interpreted and cited in AI-generated summaries.

docs.title: Concept 19: Card Validator
docs.text: X provides a Card Validator tool (cards-dev.twitter.com/validator) that previews how your card will render and reports errors. Use it before sharing.

docs.title: Concept 20: Deprecation of Legacy Card Types
docs.text: While app and player cards still exist, most modern sites only need summary or summary_large_image. The Player Card is rarely used outside of media publishers.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Twitter Card Generation
docs.text:
1.  User pastes a URL into a Tweet.
    │
    ▼
2.  X's crawler (Twitterbot) fetches the HTML source.
    │
    ▼
3.  Crawler reads the <head> section.
    │
    ▼
4.  Crawler extracts:
    │   ├── twitter:card       → layout selection
    │   ├── twitter:title      → card headline
    │   ├── twitter:description → card summary
    │   ├── twitter:image      → card image
    │   └── twitter:site       → handle attribution
    │
    ▼
5.  If twitter:* tags are missing, fall back to og:* tags.
    │
    ▼
6.  Card rendered in the Tweet.
    │
    ▼
7.  Card cached for future Tweets.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Card Validation Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Deploy page with Twitter Card tags.
    │
    ▼
2.  Open Card Validator (cards-dev.twitter.com/validator).
    │
    ▼
3.  Enter your URL.
    │
    ▼
4.  Validator fetches the page and renders a preview.
    │
    ▼
5.  Check for errors:
    │   ├── Missing required tags?
    │   ├── Image too small?
    │   ├── Relative image URL?
    │   └── Robots.txt blocking?
    │
    ▼
6.  Fix issues, redeploy, re-validate.

docs.title: The twitter: Namespace
docs.text:
Twitter Cards use a twitter: prefix in the name attribute — not a formal namespace like RDFa. Each tag is a simple name-value pair:

name="twitter:card"     content="summary_large_image"
name="twitter:title"    content="Page Title"
name="twitter:image"    content="https://..."

docs.title: Required vs Optional Tags
docs.text: Tag Required Falls Back To twitter:card ✅ Nothing (must be set) twitter:title Recommended og:title, <title> twitter:description Recommended og:description, meta desc twitter:image Recommended og:image twitter:site Optional Nothing twitter:creator Optional Nothing

docs.title: Card Type Rendering
docs.text:
X's renderer selects a template based on twitter:card:

Card Type Template Image Position summary Compact Left thumbnail summary_large_image Full-width Above text app App download App icon + store links player Media player Inline iframe

docs.title: Caching Architecture
docs.text:
X caches card data by URL. When you update tags:

  1. The old preview persists.
  2. You must use the Card Validator to force a re-scrape.
  3. The new data is cached after re-scrape.

docs.title: The Fallback Chain
docs.text:
twitter:title    → og:title    → <title>
twitter:desc     → og:desc     → meta description
twitter:image    → og:image    → first large image
twitter:card     → (required, no fallback)

This is why setting Open Graph tags first and Twitter-specific tags second is the recommended approach.

docs.title: Static Page Lifecycle
docs.text:
Author writes twitter:* tags in <head>
    │
    ▼
Deployed to server
    │
    ▼
User shares the URL on X
    │
    ▼
Twitterbot fetches the HTML
    │
    ▼
Crawler extracts twitter:* tags
    │
    ▼
Card rendered in the Tweet
    │
    ▼
Card cached
    │
    ▼
Tags change → cache must be cleared via Card Validator

docs.title: Card Audit Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Inventory all twitter:* tags across the site.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check for missing twitter:card tag.
    │
    ▼
3.  Verify image dimensions (1200×675 for large image).
    │
    ▼
4.  Verify image URLs are absolute.
    │
    ▼
5.  Check robots.txt allows Twitterbot.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test with Card Validator.
    │
    ▼
7.  Repeat after content or URL changes.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Blog Post
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>How Meta Tags Work — Dev Notes</title>
    <meta name="description" content="A complete guide to HTML meta tags.">

    <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
    <meta name="twitter:site" content="@devnotes">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="How Meta Tags Work">
    <meta name="twitter:description" content="A complete guide to HTML meta tags: viewport, description, robots, Open Graph, and theme color.">
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://devnotes.example.com/preview.png">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • twitter:card — summary_large_image for a full-width image.
  • twitter:site — handle attribution below the card.
  • twitter:title — drops the "— Dev Notes" suffix for the feed context.
  • twitter:image — absolute URL to a 1200×675px image.

docs.title: Example 2: Complete Production Head with Open Graph and Twitter Cards
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>How SVG Embedding Works — Dev Notes</title>
    <meta name="description" content="Learn how HTML meta tags shape search previews and social sharing.">

    <link rel="canonical" href="https://devnotes.example.com/svg-embedding">

    <!-- Open Graph -->
    <meta property="og:title" content="How SVG Embedding Works">
    <meta property="og:description" content="A complete guide to embedding SVG in HTML: inline, img, object, iframe, and sprites.">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://devnotes.example.com/og/svg-embedding.png">
    <meta property="og:image:width" content="1200">
    <meta property="og:image:height" content="630">
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://devnotes.example.com/svg-embedding">
    <meta property="og:type" content="article">
    <meta property="og:site_name" content="Dev Notes">

    <!-- Twitter Card -->
    <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
    <meta name="twitter:site" content="@devnotes">
    <meta name="twitter:creator" content="@janedev">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="How SVG Embedding Works">
    <meta name="twitter:description" content="A complete guide to embedding SVG in HTML.">
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://devnotes.example.com/og/svg-embedding.png">
    <meta name="twitter:image:alt" content="Diagram of SVG embedding methods">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • Open Graph provides the universal fallback for LinkedIn, Slack, Discord, iMessage, and WhatsApp.
  • Twitter Card tags provide X-specific control over layout and handle attribution.
  • twitter:image uses the same image as og:image — a common and efficient practice.
  • twitter:image:alt improves accessibility.

docs.title: Example 3: SPA with Server-Side Twitter Card Injection
docs.text:
// Express middleware: inject Twitter Card tags for social crawlers
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    const ua = req.headers['user-agent'] || '';
    const isTwitterBot = /Twitterbot/i.test(ua);
    const isSocialCrawler = /facebookexternalhit|Twitterbot|LinkedInBot|Slackbot|Discordbot/i.test(ua);

    if (isSocialCrawler) {
        const page = getPageData(req.path);
        const html = `
            <!DOCTYPE html>
            <html>
            <head>
                <meta charset="UTF-8">
                <title>${page.title}</title>
