                <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
                <meta name="twitter:title" content="${page.title}">
                <meta name="twitter:description" content="${page.description}">
                <meta name="twitter:image" content="${page.image}">
                <meta name="twitter:site" content="@yourapp">
                <meta property="og:title" content="${page.title}">
                <meta property="og:image" content="${page.image}">
            </head>
            <body></body>
            </html>
        `;
        return res.send(html);
    }

    next(); // normal SPA for real users
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Detects social crawlers by User-Agent.
  • Serves static HTML with correct Twitter Card tags.
  • Real users get the normal SPA.
  • This is the edge injection pattern for SPAs.

docs.title: Example 4: Player Card (Media Publishers)
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta name="twitter:card" content="player">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="Live Demo — Product Walkthrough">
    <meta name="twitter:description" content="Watch the full product demo.">
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/video-thumbnail.png">
    <meta name="twitter:player" content="https://example.com/embed/video123">
    <meta name="twitter:player:width" content="1280">
    <meta name="twitter:player:height" content="720">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • twitter:card="player" — embeds a video or audio player in the timeline.
  • twitter:player — the URL of the embeddable player.
  • Width and height declare the player dimensions.
  • Requires X approval before the card will render.

docs.title: Example 5: App Card (Mobile App Landing Page)
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta name="twitter:card" content="app">
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="Acme App — Available on iOS and Android">
    <meta name="twitter:description" content="The fastest way to manage your projects.">
    <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/app-icon.png">
    <meta name="twitter:app:id:iphone" content="123456789">
    <meta name="twitter:app:id:googleplay" content="com.acme.app">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • twitter:card="app" — displays a card with app store links.
  • twitter:app:id:iphone — Apple App Store ID.
  • twitter:app:id:googleplay — Google Play package name.
  • Does not require X approval.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Card Type Required Tags Blog / article summary_large_image card, title, description, image, site Documentation summary card, title, description, image Landing page summary_large_image card, title, description, image Product page summary_large_image card, title, description, image Mobile app app card, title, description, app:id:* Media site player card, title, player, player:width, player:height

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always include twitter:card. Why: it is the only required tag; without it, no card is generated.
  2. Use summary_large_image for visual content. Why: it drives significantly more engagement than a small thumbnail.
  3. Use summary for text-heavy content. Why: documentation and blog posts read better with a compact layout.
  4. Use 1200 × 675px images for large image cards. Why: this is X's recommended size, slightly different from Open Graph's 1200 × 630.
  5. Use absolute URLs for twitter:image. Why: relative paths silently fail.
  6. Add twitter:site and twitter:creator. Why: handle attribution increases brand visibility and author recognition.
  7. Add twitter:image:alt. Why: improves accessibility for screen reader users.
  8. Set Open Graph tags first, then Twitter Card tags. Why: Open Graph covers all other platforms; Twitter tags add X-specific control.
  9. Serve Twitter Card tags in static HTML. Why: Twitterbot does not execute JavaScript.
  10. Do not block Twitterbot in robots.txt. Why: X cannot read your tags if the crawler is blocked.
  11. Test with the Card Validator before sharing. Why: caching means fixes are not visible until re-scraped.
  12. Do not duplicate twitter:* tags. Why: multiple sets cause unpredictable behavior.
  13. Keep twitter:title under 70 characters. Why: longer titles truncate.
  14. Keep twitter:description under 200 characters. Why: most clients truncate around 120–140.
  15. Use the same image for og:image and twitter:image when possible. Why: reduces asset management overhead.
  16. Audit card tags quarterly or after migrations. Why: content changes and tags decay.
  17. Escape user input in Twitter Card content. Why: reflected content is an injection surface.
  18. Verify with real share tests on X. Why: previews may differ from the validator.
  19. Consider dynamic cards for SPAs. Why: static tags become stale on route changes.
  20. Monitor for card errors in X's developer console. Why: broken cards reduce engagement.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing twitter:card
docs.text:
<meta name="twitter:title" content="My Page">
<!-- No twitter:card -->

Why it's wrong: twitter:card is the only required tag. Without it, X may not generate a card at all.

✅ Correct:

<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relative Image URL
docs.text:
<meta name="twitter:image" content="/images/preview.png">

Why it's wrong: Relative URLs silently fail. The image won't appear.

✅ Correct:

<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/images/preview.png">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Image Too Small
docs.text:
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/logo.png"> <!-- 100×100 -->

Why it's wrong: For summary_large_image, the minimum is 300 × 157px. Smaller images may be ignored.

✅ Correct: Use a 1200 × 675px image.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Client-Side Tag Injection
docs.text:
// SPAs often do this — it doesn't work for Twitterbot
document.querySelector('meta[name="twitter:image"]').setAttribute('content', url);

Why it's wrong: Twitterbot does not execute JavaScript. It sees the static HTML, which still has the old or missing tags.

✅ Correct: Serve Twitter Card tags from the server via SSR, SSG, or edge injection.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using property Instead of name
docs.text:
<meta property="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">

Why it's wrong: Twitter Cards use name, not property. This tag is ignored.

✅ Correct:

<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate Twitter Card Tags
docs.text:
<meta name="twitter:title" content="Title A">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="Title B">

Why it's wrong: Multiple sets cause X to pick unpredictably.

✅ Correct: One set of Twitter Card tags per page.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Blocking Twitterbot in robots.txt
docs.text:
User-agent: Twitterbot
Disallow: /

Why it's wrong: X cannot read your meta tags and will not generate a card.

✅ Correct: Allow Twitterbot, or at least don't block it.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing After Changes
docs.text:
<!-- Changed twitter:image but didn't clear X's cache -->

Why it's wrong: X caches card data aggressively. The old preview persists until re-scraped.

✅ Correct: Use the Card Validator to force a re-scrape.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Open Graph Fallback Without Checking
docs.text:
<!-- Only og tags, no twitter tags -->

Why it's wrong: X will fall back to og:*, but the layout and image dimensions may not be ideal for X's rendering.

✅ Correct: Set both OG and Twitter Card tags.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Twitter Card tags add minimal bytes — under 1 KB uncompressed.
  • Card images are fetched by Twitterbot, not by the user's browser — no impact on page load.
  • Large card images slow crawler fetching and may be rejected.
  • Dynamic card generation adds server CPU cost; cache generated images.
  • Prerendering for SPAs adds infrastructure cost but ensures correct previews.
  • Edge injection adds minimal latency and is the most efficient SPA solution.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep card images under 300 KB.
  2. Host card images on a CDN.
  3. Cache dynamically generated card images.
  4. Use JPEG for photographic images.
  5. Declare twitter:image:alt to improve accessibility without performance cost.

docs.title: Reflected Content Injection
docs.text:
If Twitter Card content is generated from user input, escape it server-side:

<!-- DANGEROUS -->
<meta name="twitter:title" content="<?= $_GET['title'] ?>">

<!-- SAFE -->
<meta name="twitter:title" content="<?= htmlspecialchars($_GET['title']) ?>">

docs.title: SSRF via twitter:image
docs.text: X fetches twitter:image URLs. If your site allows users to set card images to arbitrary URLs, attackers could use your site as a proxy for SSRF attacks. Validate and whitelist image URLs.

docs.title: XSS via Twitter Card Tags
docs.text: Twitter Card tags are meta tags — they don't execute scripts. But unescaped content can break out of the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML. Always escape.

docs.title: Privacy Leakage
docs.text: Twitter Card tags reveal information about your page to X's crawler. Do not put sensitive data, internal URLs, or PII in card tags.

docs.title: Card Image Security
docs.text: Serve card images from a trusted origin. Do not serve user-uploaded images directly as card images without validation.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• X Card Validator — cards-dev.twitter.com/validator — preview and force re-scrape.
  • View source — confirm Twitter Card tags are in the static HTML.
  • Curl the page — curl -s https://example.com | grep twitter: to see what crawlers see.
  • Check robots.txt — ensure Twitterbot is not blocked.
  • Test with a fresh URL — append a query string to bypass X's cache during testing.
  • Browser DevTools — inspect <head> to verify tags are present.
  • OpenGraph.xyz — third-party preview tool that supports Twitter Cards.
  • Meta Tags — metatags.io — multi-platform preview.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Any page intended for sharing on X — blog posts, articles, landing pages.
  • Any page with visual content — use summary_large_image.
  • Any page with a unique image — to control the preview.
  • Any SPA route — via server-side injection.
  • Mobile app landing pages — use app card.
  • Media publishers — use player card (with approval).

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Private or internal pages — no need, and may leak information.
  • Pages behind authentication — crawlers can't access them.
  • Pages with no sharing value — login pages, error pages, settings.
  • As a replacement for Open Graph — Twitter Cards are X-specific; Open Graph covers all other platforms.
  • Player Card without approval — it will not render.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Open Graph — universal social metadata protocol
  • <title> — document name element
  • <meta name="description"> — SERP snippet
  • Schema.org — structured data vocabulary
  • JSON-LD — JSON-based structured data
  • X Card Validator
  • Twitterbot
  • Social crawlers
  • Fallback chain (twitter → og → title)

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Twitter Cards were introduced in 2012 as Twitter's answer to Facebook's Open Graph.
  • twitter:card is the only required tag — everything else has a fallback.
  • X falls back to Open Graph tags when twitter:* tags are absent.
  • Twitterbot does not execute JavaScript — client-side tag injection never works.
  • The recommended image size for summary_large_image is 1200 × 675px, slightly different from Open Graph's 1200 × 630.
  • Relative image URLs silently fail — always use absolute URLs.
  • X caches card data aggressively — fixes require Card Validator re-scraping.
  • Blocking Twitterbot in robots.txt prevents card generation.
  • Player Cards require X approval — they are not available by default.
  • App Cards do not require approval — they are available to all sites.
  • The Card Validator is the fastest way to debug card rendering.
  • Open Graph + Twitter Cards together is the recommended setup — OG for universal coverage, Twitter for X-specific control.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Twitter Cards are X-specific metadata that generate rich link previews.
  • The only required tag is twitter:card — everything else has a fallback.
  • Four card types exist: summary, summary_large_image, app, player.
  • Most sites only need summary or summary_large_image.
  • X falls back to Open Graph when twitter:* tags are absent — but you lose control over layout and image dimensions.
  • Image requirements: 1200 × 675px for large image cards; absolute URLs required.
  • Twitterbot does not execute JavaScript — SPAs must serve tags from the server.
  • X caches card data — use the Card Validator to force a re-scrape.
  • Do not block Twitterbot in robots.txt.
  • Set Open Graph first, then Twitter Cards — OG covers all other platforms, Twitter adds X-specific control.
  • Escape user input in card tag content.
  • Test with the Card Validator before sharing.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A favicon (short for "favorites icon") is a small icon associated with a website or web page. It is displayed by browsers in the tab bar, bookmarks menu, browser history, and address bar, and by mobile operating systems on home screens and in app switchers. Favicons are declared in HTML via <link> elements with rel="icon", rel="apple-touch-icon", or through a web app manifest.

<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">
<link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
<link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Favicons serve several purposes simultaneously:

  • Brand recognition — a visual anchor in a tab bar crowded with dozens of open pages.
  • Quick identification — users scan tabs by icon, not text.
  • Bookmark identity — the icon appears alongside the page name in bookmark lists.
  • Mobile home screen — when a site is added to the home screen, the favicon becomes the app icon.
  • PWA installation — installable web apps use manifest icons for the app drawer and splash screen.
  • Professionalism — a missing favicon results in a generic browser icon, which signals neglect.

A well-designed favicon is a tiny brand ambassador that appears in more places than almost any other asset on your site.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
<html>
├── <head>
│   ├── <title>                         ← document name
│   ├── <link rel="icon">               ← browser tab / bookmark icon
│   ├── <link rel="apple-touch-icon">   ← iOS home screen icon
│   ├── <link rel="manifest">           ← PWA icon configuration
│   └── ...
└── <body>

Favicons are declared via <link> elements — not <meta> tags. The rel attribute tells the browser what kind of icon is being linked. The browser then selects the most appropriate icon based on context (tab, bookmark, home screen) and device capabilities (screen density, color scheme).

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: A browser with 40 open tabs is an undifferentiated wall of text. Without icons, users cannot quickly locate the tab they need. Bookmarks without icons are equally difficult to scan. And on mobile devices, a website added to the home screen needs a proper icon — a text-only shortcut is unusable.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No icon in tabs Every tab looks identical No icon in bookmarks Hard to scan bookmark lists No home screen icon Mobile shortcuts showed a screenshot or generic icon No PWA icons Installed apps looked unfinished Single-format icons Blurry on high-DPI screens

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Favicons were introduced by Internet Explorer 5 in 1999 as a way to brand bookmarks. The original format was favicon.ico placed at the site root. Over the decades, the system evolved:

  • 2000s — favicon.ico at the root became a convention.
  • 2010 — Apple introduced apple-touch-icon for iOS home screens.
  • 2015+ — Web app manifest standardized PWA icons.
  • 2020s — SVG favicons gained broad support, offering resolution independence and dark-mode adaptation.

Today, a modern favicon setup requires a small set of files — not the 20-file monsters that older guides recommended. The platforms have consolidated their requirements, and the modern set is lean.

docs.title: The Minimal Modern Setup
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">
    <link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
    <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
    <link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">

    <title>Page Title — Site Name</title>
</head>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Tag Purpose Notes rel="icon" href="favicon.ico" sizes="any" Legacy fallback Contains 16, 32, and 48px entries; browsers pick the frame they need rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" Modern primary icon Sharp at any size; supports dark mode; ignored by Safari < 16.4 rel="apple-touch-icon" iOS home screen 180×180px PNG; fully opaque (no transparency) rel="manifest" PWA configuration References 192px and 512px PNG icons

docs.title: The Five Files a Modern Site Needs
docs.text: File Size Purpose favicon.ico Multi-size (16/32/48) Legacy fallback; also used for PDFs and non-HTML documents icon.svg Vector Modern browsers; sharp at any density; dark-mode adaptable apple-touch-icon.png 180×180 iOS home screen; opaque, no transparency icon-192.png 192×192 Android home screen; PWA install prompt icon-512.png 512×512 PWA splash screen; high-resolution displays

docs.title: The Web App Manifest
docs.text:
{
    "icons": [
        { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
        { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" },
        { "src": "/icon-mask.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "maskable" }
    ]
}

Code Breakdown:

  • 192x192 — used for the Android home screen launcher and install prompt.
  • 512x512 — used for the splash screen and high-resolution displays.
  • purpose: "maskable" — tells Android the image has built-in padding and can be cropped to any shape.

docs.title: The "Five Files, Four Jobs" Mental Model
docs.text:
A modern favicon setup is five files doing four jobs:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Job                    File                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Legacy fallback        favicon.ico                  │
│  Modern browsers        icon.svg                     │
│  iOS home screen        apple-touch-icon.png (180)   │
│  Android home screen    icon-192.png                 │
│  PWA install/splash     icon-512.png                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The SVG is the source of truth — design it once, export the raster fallbacks from it.

docs.title: The "Priority Chain" Mental Model
docs.text:
When a browser needs an icon, it evaluates available <link> elements:

1. SVG favicon        ← if supported (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari 16.4+)
2. PNG favicon        ← if SVG not supported
3. favicon.ico        ← if no PNG declared
4. /favicon.ico       ← if nothing declared (legacy convention)
5. Generic icon       ← if no file exists

The further down the chain, the worse the result. A complete setup puts you at the top.

docs.title: The "Maskable Safe Zone" Mental Model
docs.text:
Android reshapes every installed icon to match the device — circle, squircle, rounded square. A maskable icon must keep its important content inside a safe circle with a radius of 40% of the image width.

┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                     │
│         ┌─────────────────┐         │
│         │   Safe Zone     │         │
│         │   (40% radius)  │         │
│         │  ┌───────────┐  │         │
│         │  │   LOGO    │  │         │
│         │  └───────────┘  │         │
│         │                 │         │
│         └─────────────────┘         │
│                                     │
│  Outer 10% may be cropped away      │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

Design the artwork with padding so it survives any crop.

docs.title: Concept 1: favicon.ico — The Legacy Fallback
docs.text:
The oldest and most durable favicon format. A single ICO file can contain multiple images at different sizes (16×16, 32×32, 48×48), and the browser selects the frame it needs. Even very old browsers know to request favicon.ico from the site root.

Still useful for: PDFs and non-HTML documents where the browser cannot read HTML <link> tags.

docs.title: Concept 2: SVG Favicon — The Modern Primary
docs.text:
An SVG favicon is a vector — it stays sharp at any size and can adapt to dark mode via CSS media queries. Supported by Chrome 80+, Edge 80+, Firefox 41+, Opera 44+, Samsung Internet 13+, and Safari 26+. Safari versions before 16.4 do not support SVG favicons and will fall back to the PNG or ICO.

<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon.svg">

docs.title: Concept 3: Apple Touch Icon — One Size Only
docs.text:
iOS home screens use a single 180×180px PNG. Older tutorials list 57, 60, 72, 76, 114, 120, 144, and 152px variants — these describe devices Apple consolidated years ago. Ship only the 180px file.

Two rules: ship a full square (the device applies its own rounded corner mask), and keep the art fully opaque (no transparency; iOS adds a black background otherwise).

docs.title: Concept 4: Manifest Icons — 192 and 512
docs.text:
Android and desktop Chrome read icons from the web app manifest. Two sizes are required:

  • 192×192 — home screen launcher, install prompt.
  • 512×512 — splash screen, high-resolution displays.

docs.title: Concept 5: Maskable Icons
docs.text:
Since Android 8, the system reshapes every installed icon. A maskable icon is an opaque image with built-in padding, designed to survive any crop. Keep the important content inside a safe circle with a radius of 40% of the width. The outer 10% on each side may be cropped away.

{ "src": "/icon-mask.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "maskable" }

docs.title: Concept 6: sizes Attribute
docs.text:
The sizes attribute declares the dimensions of the linked icon:

<link rel="icon" href="favicon.ico" sizes="any">
<link rel="icon" href="icon-32.png" type="image/png" sizes="32x32">
<link rel="icon" href="icon-16.png" type="image/png" sizes="16x16">
  • sizes="any" — used for scalable formats (SVG) or multi-size ICO files.
  • sizes="32x32" — declares a specific pixel size.
  • Multiple sizes: sizes="16x16 32x32 48x48".

docs.title: Concept 7: The type Attribute
docs.text:
The type attribute tells the browser the MIME type of the icon:

<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/icon.svg">
<link rel="icon" type="image/png" sizes="32x32" href="/favicon-32.png">

This allows browsers to skip unsupported formats without wasting a download.

docs.title: Concept 8: Dark Mode SVG Favicons
docs.text:
SVG favicons can adapt to light and dark color schemes:

<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon-dark.svg" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon-light.svg" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)">

The media attribute forks the icon based on the user's OS preference.

docs.title: Concept 9: rel="shortcut icon" — Deprecated
docs.text:
<link rel="shortcut icon" href="/favicon.ico">

The shortcut keyword is deprecated. Use rel="icon" instead. Modern browsers ignore shortcut.

docs.title: Concept 10: rel="apple-touch-icon-precomposed" — Deprecated
docs.text: The -precomposed variant was used before iOS 7 to prevent automatic corner rounding. Modern iOS rounds corners automatically. Do not use -precomposed.

docs.title: Concept 11: Favicon Caching
docs.text:
Browsers cache favicons aggressively. Changes may not appear for days. To force a refresh, clear the browser cache or open the page in a private window. For production, version the favicon URL:

<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico?v=2">

docs.title: Concept 12: Favicon Discovery for Non-HTML Documents
docs.text: When visiting a PDF or other non-HTML document, the browser cannot read HTML <link> tags. It falls back to requesting /favicon.ico from the site root. This is the one concrete reason to keep a favicon.ico file.

docs.title: Concept 13: PWA Installability
docs.text:
A site becomes installable when it has:

  • A web app manifest with name, start_url, and icons.
  • A 192px and 512px PNG icon.
  • A maskable icon for Android.
  • Served over HTTPS.

docs.title: Concept 14: The Safe Zone for Maskable Icons
docs.text: The maskable safe zone is a circle with radius = 40% of the image width, centered. The outer 10% on each side may be cropped. Design with padding.

docs.title: Concept 15: No More Twenty-File Setups
docs.text:
The modern favicon set is five files:

File Format favicon.ico ICO (16/32/48 multi-size) icon.svg SVG apple-touch-icon.png PNG 180×180 icon-192.png PNG 192×192 icon-512.png PNG 512×512

The old piles of 20+ files are no longer needed.

docs.title: Concept 16: SVG Favicon Content Security
docs.text: An SVG favicon is loaded in the browser's UI context. It cannot contain scripts — the browser strips them. Still, sanitize any user-supplied SVG used as a favicon.

docs.title: Concept 17: Favicon and Search Results
docs.text: Google displays a favicon next to search results. A well-formed favicon improves brand recognition in SERPs. Google's requirements: a square icon, at least 48×48px, in a supported format.

docs.title: Concept 18: Favicon and Browser UI
docs.text:
Browsers use the favicon in multiple UI surfaces:

  • Tab — small icon next to the page title.
  • Bookmarks — icon in the bookmark list.
  • History — icon in the history view.
  • Address bar — icon next to the URL.
  • Taskbar (PWA) — icon for installed apps.

docs.title: Concept 19: Creating the Art
docs.text:
Design the art once as a 512×512px square. From that, generate:

  • The SVG (or design as SVG and export).
  • The ICO (16/32/48 multi-size).
  • The 180px Apple touch icon.
  • The 192px and 512px manifest PNGs.
  • The maskable variant with padding.

Tools: RealFaviconGenerator, Favicon.io, Univik ICO Converter, ImageMagick.

docs.title: Concept 20: Favicon and AI Search
docs.text: AI-powered search features and assistants increasingly read structured metadata. A well-formed favicon — alongside Open Graph and Schema.org — improves brand visibility in AI-generated summaries.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Favicon Selection
docs.text:
1.  Browser parses <head>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Finds all <link rel="icon"> elements.
    │
    ▼
3.  Filters by format support:
    │   ├── SVG? → use if supported (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari 16.4+)
    │   ├── PNG? → use if SVG not supported
    │   └── ICO? → fallback
    │
    ▼
4.  Filters by context:
    │   ├── Tab → small icon (16 or 32px)
    │   ├── Bookmark → larger icon (32 or 48px)
    │   └── Home screen → apple-touch-icon (180px)
    │
    ▼
5.  Picks the most appropriate icon.
    │
    ▼
6.  Renders it in the UI.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: PWA Icon Selection
docs.text:
1.  User taps "Add to Home Screen".
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser reads the web app manifest.
    │
    ▼
3.  Finds the icons array.
    │
    ▼
4.  Selects:
    │   ├── 192px → home screen launcher
    │   ├── 512px → splash screen
    │   └── maskable → Android adaptive icon
    │
    ▼
5.  Icon installed on the home screen.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Maskable Icon Cropping
docs.text:
1.  Android reads the maskable icon.
    │
    ▼
2.  Applies the device's shape mask:
    │   ├── Circle
    │   ├── Squircle
    │   ├── Rounded square
    │   └── ...
    │
    ▼
3.  Crops the image to the mask.
    │
    ▼
4.  The safe zone (40% radius) is preserved.
    │
    ▼
5.  Icon rendered on the home screen.

docs.title: The <link rel="icon"> Element
docs.text:
The <link> element with rel="icon" is a link type defined in the HTML spec. It tells the browser: "This URL points to an icon for this document."

<link rel="icon" href="..." type="..." sizes="...">
  • rel — the relationship: icon.
  • href — the URL of the icon file.
  • type — the MIME type (optional but recommended).
  • sizes — the icon dimensions (optional but recommended).

docs.title: Multiple Icons and Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
When multiple icons are declared, the browser uses the type, sizes, and media attributes to select the most appropriate one. If no attributes are present, the browser may choose arbitrarily.

The WHATWG spec defines a sizes parsing algorithm:

  • The keyword must contain exactly one x.
  • Width and height strings must be valid non-negative integers.
  • The sizes attribute must not represent sizes not actually available in the linked resource.

docs.title: The sizes="any" Keyword
docs.text: sizes="any" indicates a scalable icon — an SVG or a multi-size ICO. The browser knows it can render this icon at any size.

docs.title: SVG Favicon Rendering
docs.text:
SVG favicons are rendered by the browser's SVG engine — the same engine that renders inline SVG. They support:

  • Vector scaling — sharp at any density.
  • CSS media queries — prefers-color-scheme for dark mode.
  • No scripts — browsers strip <script> from favicon SVG.

docs.title: The ICO Container Format
docs.text:
The ICO format is a container that can hold multiple images at different sizes. The browser downloads the entire file, then selects the frame it needs.

favicon.ico
├── 16×16 frame
├── 32×32 frame
└── 48×48 frame

Downside: the entire file must be downloaded before any frame can be used.

docs.title: The Web App Manifest Icons Array
docs.text:
{
    "icons": [
        { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
        { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" },
        { "src": "/icon-mask.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "maskable" }
    ]
}

The purpose field determines how the icon is treated:

Purpose Behavior any (default) Drawn as supplied maskable Cropped to device shape monochrome Used for notification badges

Do not combine any maskable on one file — a maskable icon has padding, which looks small when drawn as a plain icon.

docs.title: Caching Architecture
docs.text:
Browsers cache favicons by URL. The cache is persistent and aggressive. To invalidate:

  • Clear the browser cache.
  • Use a private window.
  • Version the URL (?v=2).

docs.title: Static Site Lifecycle
docs.text:
Designer creates the art (512×512px source)
    │
    ▼
Generate the five files:
    ├── favicon.ico
    ├── icon.svg
    ├── apple-touch-icon.png
    ├── icon-192.png
    └── icon-512.png
    │
    ▼
Deploy to server
    │
    ▼
Add <link> tags to <head>
    │
    ▼
Browser requests and caches icons
    │
    ▼
Icons appear in tabs, bookmarks, home screen

docs.title: Favicon Audit Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Inventory all icon files.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check for missing files:
    │   ├── favicon.ico?
    │   ├── icon.svg?
    │   ├── apple-touch-icon.png?
    │   ├── icon-192.png?
    │   └── icon-512.png?
    │
    ▼
3.  Verify sizes and formats.
    │
    ▼
4.  Verify maskable icon has padding.
    │
    ▼
5.  Test in multiple browsers:
    │   ├── Chrome (SVG support)
    │   ├── Firefox (SVG support)
    │   ├── Safari (PNG/ICO fallback)
    │   └── Mobile (iOS and Android)
    │
    ▼
6.  Repeat quarterly or after rebranding.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal Favicon Setup
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">
    <link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
    <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
    <link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">

    <title>Home — Acme</title>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • favicon.ico — legacy fallback for all browsers and non-HTML documents.
  • icon.svg — modern primary icon for supported browsers.
  • apple-touch-icon.png — 180×180 iOS home screen icon.
  • site.webmanifest — PWA configuration with 192 and 512 icons.

docs.title: Example 2: Complete Production Head
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>Dashboard — Acme</title>
    <meta name="description" content="Acme analytics dashboard.">

    <!-- Favicon set -->
    <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">
    <link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
    <link rel="icon" href="/icon-32.png" type="image/png" sizes="32x32">
    <link rel="icon" href="/icon-16.png" type="image/png" sizes="16x16">
    <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
    <link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">

    <!-- Theme color (matches favicon background) -->
    <meta name="theme-color" content="#3498db">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • favicon.ico with sizes="any" — legacy fallback.
  • icon.svg with type="image/svg+xml" — modern primary.
  • icon-32.png and icon-16.png — PNG fallbacks for browsers that support PNG but not SVG.
  • apple-touch-icon — 180px iOS home screen icon.
  • manifest — PWA configuration.
  • theme-color — matches the icon background.

docs.title: Example 3: SVG Favicon with Dark Mode
docs.text:
<!-- Light mode -->
<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon-light.svg" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)">

<!-- Dark mode -->
<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon-dark.svg" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">

Code Breakdown:

  • Two SVG files — one for light mode, one for dark mode.
  • The media attribute forks the icon based on the user's OS preference.
  • In Chrome on Windows, the dark theme icon appears only when the OS theme is set to dark.

docs.title: Example 4: Web App Manifest with Maskable Icon
docs.text:
{
    "name": "Acme Dashboard",
    "short_name": "Acme",
    "start_url": "/",
    "display": "standalone",
    "background_color": "#ffffff",
    "theme_color": "#3498db",
    "icons": [
        {
            "src": "/icon-192.png",
            "sizes": "192x192",
            "type": "image/png"
        },
        {
            "src": "/icon-512.png",
            "sizes": "512x512",
            "type": "image/png"
        },
        {
            "src": "/icon-mask.png",
            "sizes": "512x512",
            "type": "image/png",
            "purpose": "maskable"
        }
    ]
}

Code Breakdown:

  • 192x192 — Android home screen launcher.
  • 512x512 — PWA splash screen.
  • maskable — Android adaptive icon; padded to survive any crop.
  • theme_color — matches the browser UI color.

docs.title: Example 5: Dynamic Favicon with JavaScript
docs.text:
// Change favicon dynamically (e.g., for notifications)
function setFavicon(url) {
    let link = document.querySelector('link[rel="icon"]');
    if (!link) {
        link = document.createElement('link');
        link.rel = 'icon';
        document.head.appendChild(link);
    }
    link.href = url;
}

// Show a notification badge
setFavicon('/favicon-notification.svg');

// Reset to default
setFavicon('/favicon.svg');

Code Breakdown:

  • Finds the existing favicon link or creates one.
  • Updates the href to swap the icon.
  • Useful for notification badges and dynamic states.

docs.title: Example 6: Generating Favicons from a Source Image
docs.text:
# Using ImageMagick to generate favicon set from a 512×512 source
convert source.png -resize 16x16 favicon-16.png
convert source.png -resize 32x32 favicon-32.png
convert source.png -resize 48x48 favicon-48.png
convert favicon-16.png favicon-32.png favicon-48.png favicon.ico

# Apple touch icon (180×180, opaque)
convert source.png -resize 180x180 -background white -alpha remove -alpha off apple-touch-icon.png

# Manifest PNGs
convert source.png -resize 192x192 icon-192.png
convert source.png -resize 512x512 icon-512.png

Code Breakdown:

  • convert — ImageMagick command-line tool.
  • -resize — scales the source image.
  • -background white -alpha remove -alpha off — flattens transparency for the Apple touch icon.
  • favicon.ico — combines multiple PNGs into one ICO container.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Required Files Notes Basic website favicon.ico, icon.svg Covers tabs and bookmarks PWA + icon-192.png, icon-512.png, manifest Installable on Android and desktop Chrome iOS home screen + apple-touch-icon.png (180px) Fully opaque Android home screen + maskable icon Padded safe zone Dark mode support + dark SVG variant Media query fork Non-HTML documents favicon.ico at root Browsers fall back to /favicon.ico E-commerce Full set Brand recognition in SERPs

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Design the art once as a 512×512px square. Why: everything else can be generated from it.
  2. Ship five files: ICO, SVG, Apple 180, manifest 192, manifest 512. Why: this is the modern minimal set.
  3. Use sizes="any" on the ICO link. Why: indicates a multi-size container.
  4. Use type="image/svg+xml" on the SVG link. Why: lets unsupported browsers skip the download.
  5. Keep the Apple touch icon fully opaque. Why: iOS adds a black background to transparent PNGs.
  6. Ship a maskable icon with padding. Why: Android crops installed icons to device-specific shapes.
  7. Keep maskable content inside the 40% radius safe circle. Why: the outer 10% may be cropped.
  8. Provide dark mode SVG variants when applicable. Why: a dark icon on a dark tab is invisible.
  9. Version the favicon URL after changes. Why: browsers cache aggressively; ?v=2 forces a refresh.
  10. Test in Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and mobile. Why: SVG support varies; Safari requires PNG/ICO fallback.
  11. Do not use rel="shortcut icon". Why: deprecated; use rel="icon".
  12. Do not use apple-touch-icon-precomposed. Why: deprecated since iOS 7.
  13. Do not combine any maskable on one file. Why: a maskable icon has padding, which looks wrong as a plain icon.
  14. Do not ship 20+ files. Why: modern browsers have consolidated requirements.
  15. Do not use transparent PNGs for the Apple touch icon. Why: iOS fills transparency with black.
  16. Keep favicon designs simple. Why: 16×16px is tiny; subtle details turn to noise.
  17. Use high contrast. Why: tab bars are small and often on varied backgrounds.
  18. Audit icons after rebranding. Why: old icons persist in caches and bookmarks.
  19. Serve icons over HTTPS. Why: mixed content is blocked.
  20. Test with Lighthouse and browser DevTools. Why: catches missing or malformed icons.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Favicon at All
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>Page</title>
</head>

Why it's wrong: The browser shows a generic icon. The tab looks unfinished.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Only favicon.ico, No SVG
docs.text:
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">

Why it's wrong: Modern browsers support SVG, which is sharper at any density. The ICO is a raster fallback.

✅ Correct: Add icon.svg.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Transparent Apple Touch Icon
docs.text:
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png"> <!-- transparent -->

Why it's wrong: iOS adds a black background to transparent PNGs.

✅ Correct: Flatten transparency to white or the brand background color.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Maskable Icon
docs.text:
{
    "icons": [
        { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" }
    ]
}

Why it's wrong: Android crops the icon to a shape, possibly clipping the logo.

✅ Correct: Add a maskable icon with padding.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: purpose: "any maskable" on One File
docs.text:
{ "src": "/icon.png", "purpose": "any maskable" }

Why it's wrong: A maskable icon has padding; drawn as a plain icon, it looks small and lost.

✅ Correct: Ship two files — one any, one maskable.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relative Apple Touch Icon URL
docs.text:
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="apple-touch-icon.png">

Why it's wrong: While relative URLs work in <link> tags, it is safer to use absolute paths.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing in Safari
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Safari does not support SVG favicons before 16.4. Without a PNG or ICO fallback, the favicon is missing.

✅ Correct: Always include favicon.ico and PNG fallbacks.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Favicon Not Refreshing After Change
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Browsers cache favicons aggressively.

✅ Correct: Version the URL (?v=2) or clear the cache.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Favicon files are tiny — the full set is typically under 50 KB.
  • SVG is the smallest — often under 1 KB gzipped.
  • ICO files are larger — the multi-size container increases download size.
  • SVG favicons are rendered once and cached by the browser.
  • Manifest icons are loaded on demand — only when installing a PWA.
  • Apple touch icon is loaded on demand — only when adding to home screen.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use SVG as the primary favicon — smallest and sharpest.
  2. Keep the ICO file minimal (16/32/48).
  3. Compress PNGs with tools like ImageOptim or Squoosh.
  4. Serve icons with long cache headers.
  5. Version the URL only when the icon changes.

docs.title: SVG Script Stripping
docs.text: Browsers strip <script> from SVG favicons. An SVG favicon cannot execute JavaScript. However, sanitize any user-supplied SVG used as a favicon.

docs.title: Favicon as a Tracking Vector
docs.text: A favicon request can be used to track users. Browsers now cache favicons per-site, and privacy-focused browsers may block or partition favicon requests.

docs.title: PWA Icon Security
docs.text: Manifest icons are loaded by the browser when installing a PWA. Serve them from a trusted origin. Do not serve user-uploaded images directly as PWA icons.

docs.title: Favicon and CSP
docs.text:
Favicon requests are governed by img-src in CSP. If your CSP blocks img-src, favicons may not load.

Content-Security-Policy: img-src 'self' data: https:

docs.title: Favicon and XSS
docs.text: Favicon content is not parsed as HTML. However, dynamically updating a favicon from untrusted input could lead to issues. Validate any dynamic favicon URLs.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools → Application → Manifest — inspect the manifest and icons.
  • DevTools → Application → Icons — see which icon the browser selected.
  • View source — confirm <link> tags are in the <head>.
  • Hard-reload — bypass cache with Ctrl+Shift+R (or Cmd+Shift+R).
  • Private window — test without cache interference.
  • Check the tab — the favicon is visible there.
  • Check the Network panel — verify favicon requests and response codes.
  • RealFaviconGenerator — validates your setup and generates files.
  • Favicon.io — quick favicon generation.
  • Univik ICO Converter — builds the favicon set from one image.
  • Lighthouse — flags missing or malformed favicons.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every website — a favicon is expected.
  • PWAs — manifest icons are required for installability.
  • iOS home screen shortcuts — apple-touch-icon is required.
  • Dark mode sites — SVG dark mode variant.
  • Brand-heavy sites — favicon reinforces brand recognition.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Local development — not necessary, but harmless.
  • Pages that should not be bookmarked — favicons are automatic; there is no opt-out.
  • Non-HTML documents — favicon.ico at root is the only option.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• <link> element
  • rel attribute
  • Web App Manifest
  • PWA (Progressive Web App)
  • apple-touch-icon
  • SVG
  • ICO format
  • sizes attribute
  • purpose attribute (maskable)
  • Theme Color
  • Open Graph
  • Twitter Cards

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Favicons were introduced by Internet Explorer 5 in 1999 — they are older than most modern web standards.
  • A modern site needs only five icon files — not the 20+ file sets from older guides.
  • SVG favicons are supported by Chrome 80+, Edge 80+, Firefox 41+, Opera 44+, Samsung Internet 13+, and Safari 26+.
  • Safari versions before 16.4 do not support SVG favicons — a PNG or ICO fallback is essential.
  • The Apple touch icon only needs one size: 180×180px — the 57, 76, 114, and 152px variants describe devices Apple consolidated years ago.
  • Maskable icons must keep content inside a 40% radius safe circle — the outer 10% may be cropped.
  • purpose: "any maskable" on one file is a mistake — maskable icons have padding and look wrong when drawn plain.
  • The entire ICO file must be downloaded before any frame can be used — PNGs are more efficient.
  • favicon.ico is still useful for PDFs — browsers cannot read HTML <link> tags from non-HTML documents.
  • Browsers cache favicons aggressively — versioning the URL forces a refresh.
  • rel="shortcut icon" is deprecated — use rel="icon".
  • apple-touch-icon-precomposed is deprecated — iOS rounds corners automatically now.
  • Google displays a favicon in search results — a square icon at least 48×48px.
  • RealFaviconGenerator is the industry-standard tool for generating the full set.
  • The Evil Martians guide to favicons popularized the minimal five-file approach.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A favicon is a small icon displayed in tabs, bookmarks, and home screens.
  • The modern set is five files: favicon.ico, icon.svg, apple-touch-icon.png (180px), icon-192.png, icon-512.png.
  • SVG is the modern primary — sharp at any density, dark-mode adaptable; unsupported by Safari before 16.4.
  • Apple touch icon is one size: 180×180px, fully opaque.
  • Manifest icons: 192px (home screen) and 512px (splash screen).
  • Maskable icons survive Android's shape cropping — keep content inside a 40% radius safe circle.
  • favicon.ico remains useful for legacy browsers and non-HTML documents.
  • Browsers cache favicons aggressively — version the URL after changes.
  • Do not use deprecated shortcut icon or apple-touch-icon-precomposed.
  • Test in Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and mobile — support varies.
  • Design simple, high-contrast art — 16×16px is tiny.
  • Audit icons after rebranding — old icons persist in caches.
  • Favicons are tiny brand ambassadors — they appear in more places than almost any other asset.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Web App Manifest is a JSON file that provides metadata about a web application — its name, icons, display mode, theme colors, start URL, and capabilities — in a standardized format that browsers and operating systems can read to install and launch the app like a native application.

{
    "name": "Acme Dashboard",
    "short_name": "Acme",
    "start_url": "/",
    "display": "standalone",
    "background_color": "#ffffff",
    "theme_color": "#3498db",
    "icons": [
        { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
        { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
    ]
}

The manifest is declared in HTML via a <link> element:

<link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">

Unlike <meta> tags, which are limited to simple name-value pairs, the manifest is a structured JSON document capable of expressing complex application configuration.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The manifest serves several essential purposes:

  • Installability — makes a web app installable to the home screen or desktop. The web app manifest is the key file that powers installation. It's required, along with HTTPS, for a site to be installable.
  • App identity — defines the name, icons, and colors that represent the app on the device.
  • Launch behavior — controls how the app launches (fullscreen, standalone, minimal-ui, browser).
  • OS integration — enables features like shortcuts, share targets, protocol handlers, and file handlers.
  • Splash screen — defines the background color and icon shown while the app loads.
  • Theming — sets the window color and background to match the app's design.

It is the single source of truth for a Progressive Web App's identity and behavior.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
<html>
├── <head>
│   ├── <title>                         ← document name
│   ├── <link rel="manifest">           ← PWA configuration
│   ├── <link rel="icon">               ← favicon
│   ├── <meta name="theme-color">       ← browser UI color
│   └── ...
└── <body>

site.webmanifest  ← separate JSON file
├── name, short_name
├── icons[]
├── start_url, scope
├── display, display_override
├── theme_color, background_color
├── shortcuts[]
├── share_target
├── protocol_handlers[]
├── file_handlers[]
├── screenshots[]
└── categories[]

The manifest is a separate file, not embedded in HTML. It is linked from the HTML, served with the MIME type application/manifest+json (or application/json), and read by the browser during page load.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A website is a collection of pages. An app is a first-class citizen of an operating system. Before the manifest, there was no standard way to tell a browser: "This website should be treated as an app." There was no way to declare:

  • What icon should appear on the home screen.
  • How the app should launch (fullscreen or with browser chrome).
  • What color the splash screen should be.
  • What shortcuts the app supports.

Without this metadata, a "web app" was just a website — bookmarkable at best, but not installable, not launchable, not integrated with the operating system.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No install mechanism Users could only bookmark, not install No icon declaration Home screen shortcuts showed a screenshot No display mode Installed apps always showed browser chrome No splash screen Launching a web app showed a white flash No OS integration No shortcuts, no share targets, no file handling No app identity No way to distinguish one web app from another

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The manifest was introduced as part of the Progressive Web App movement (circa 2015). Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari all support it to varying degrees. The W3C maintains the specification, and the WHATWG has adopted it into the web platform.

The manifest solves a fundamental identity problem: a web app needs to be more than a collection of HTML pages. It needs an identity, a launch behavior, and OS integration. The manifest provides all of this in a single JSON file.

docs.title: The Minimal Manifest
docs.text:
{
    "name": "Acme Dashboard",
    "short_name": "Acme",
    "start_url": "/",
    "display": "standalone",
    "background_color": "#ffffff",
    "theme_color": "#3498db",
    "icons": [
        { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
        { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
    ]
}

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Member Purpose Required? name Full application name Yes (or short_name) short_name Short name for home screen Yes (or name) start_url URL launched when app starts Yes display Launch mode (standalone, fullscreen, minimal-ui, browser) Yes background_color Splash screen background color Recommended theme_color Browser UI / window color Recommended icons App icons (192px and 512px required) Yes

docs.title: The HTML Declaration
docs.text: <link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• rel="manifest" — declares the manifest relationship.
  • href — points to the JSON file.
  • The file is typically named manifest.json, site.webmanifest, or app.webmanifest.
  • It should be served from the same origin as the page, and same-origin with start_url to reduce spoofing risk.

docs.title: Fully Commented Production Example
docs.text:
{
    "name": "Acme Analytics Dashboard",
    "short_name": "Acme",
    "description": "Real-time analytics for your business.",
    "start_url": "/dashboard",
    "scope": "/",
    "display": "standalone",
    "display_override": ["window-controls-overlay", "minimal-ui"],
    "orientation": "any",
    "background_color": "#ffffff",
    "theme_color": "#3498db",
    "categories": ["business", "productivity"],
    "lang": "en-US",
    "dir": "ltr",
    "icons": [
        {
            "src": "/icons/icon-192.png",
            "sizes": "192x192",
            "type": "image/png",
            "purpose": "any"
        },
        {
            "src": "/icons/icon-512.png",
            "sizes": "512x512",
            "type": "image/png",
            "purpose": "any"
        },
        {
            "src": "/icons/icon-mask.png",
            "sizes": "512x512",
            "type": "image/png",
            "purpose": "maskable"
        }
    ],
    "shortcuts": [
        {
            "name": "New Report",
            "short_name": "Report",
            "url": "/reports/new",
            "icons": [{ "src": "/icons/report-96.png", "sizes": "96x96" }]
        }
    ],
    "screenshots": [
        {
            "src": "/screenshots/dashboard.png",
            "sizes": "1280x720",
            "type": "image/png",
            "label": "Dashboard overview"
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: The "App Passport" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the manifest as the passport of your web app:

  • Name and short_name — the name on the passport.
  • Icons — the photo.
  • start_url — the home address.
  • display — the permissions (what the app can do).
  • theme_color — the nationality (brand color).

Without a passport, the app cannot cross borders — it cannot be installed, launched, or integrated with the OS.

docs.title: The "Two Worlds" Mental Model
docs.text:
A web app lives in two worlds:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              BROWSER WORLD                   │
│                                              │
│  <title>          → tab title                │
│  favicon          → tab icon                 │
│  meta theme-color → address bar color        │
│                                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              OS WORLD                        │
│                                              │
│  manifest name    → app name on home screen  │
│  manifest icons   → home screen icon         │
│  manifest display → window chrome behavior   │
│  manifest theme   → window title bar color   │
│                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The browser world is governed by HTML. The OS world is governed by the manifest. Both are needed.

docs.title: The "Fallback Chain" Mental Model
docs.text:
Display modes follow a well-defined fallback chain:

fullscreen → standalone → minimal-ui → browser

If a browser does not support a given mode, it falls back to the next in the chain. The display_override property allows you to specify a custom chain that is evaluated before the display property.

docs.title: Concept 1: name and short_name
docs.text:
"name": "Acme Analytics Dashboard",
"short_name": "Acme"
  • name — the full application name. Used in install prompts and app stores.
  • short_name — a shorter version for home screen labels where space is limited.
  • At least one is required for installability.

docs.title: Concept 2: icons
docs.text:
The icons array defines the app's visual identity. A minimum of two icons is required for installability: 192×192 and 512×512 PNG.

"icons": [
    { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icon-mask.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "maskable" }
]

docs.title: Concept 3: purpose — any vs maskable
docs.text:
• any — the icon is drawn as supplied.
  • maskable — the icon is designed with padding so Android can crop it to any shape without clipping the logo.

Do not combine any maskable on a single file — a maskable icon has padding, which looks small when drawn as a plain icon.

docs.title: Concept 4: start_url
docs.text:
"start_url": "/dashboard"

The URL the app launches to when opened from the home screen. Must be within the scope.

docs.title: Concept 5: scope
docs.text:
"scope": "/"

Defines the set of URLs considered part of the application. Pages within scope provide an app-like interface. Pages outside scope open in the browser.

docs.title: Concept 6: display
docs.text:
"display": "standalone"

Controls the launch mode:

Mode Behavior fullscreen Full screen, no browser UI standalone Own window, no browser chrome minimal-ui Minimal navigation controls browser Standard browser experience

Fallback chain: fullscreen → standalone → minimal-ui → browser.

docs.title: Concept 7: display_override
docs.text:
"display_override": ["window-controls-overlay", "minimal-ui"]

Evaluated before display. Allows new display modes to be introduced without breaking backward compatibility.

docs.title: Concept 8: theme_color and background_color
docs.text:
"theme_color": "#3498db",
"background_color": "#ffffff"
  • theme_color — the color of the window title bar, address bar, and other OS UI elements.
  • background_color — the splash screen background while the app loads.

docs.title: Concept 9: shortcuts
docs.text:
"shortcuts": [
    {
        "name": "New Report",
        "url": "/reports/new",
        "icons": [{ "src": "/icons/report-96.png", "sizes": "96x96" }]
    }
]

Provides quick access to key tasks via a context menu on the app icon. On macOS Sonoma, shortcuts appear in the File menu and Dock context menu.

docs.title: Concept 10: share_target
docs.text:
"share_target": {
    "action": "/share",
    "method": "POST",
    "enctype": "multipart/form-data",
    "params": {
        "title": "title",
        "text": "text",
        "url": "url",
        "files": [{ "name": "file", "accept": ["image/*"] }]
    }
}

Registers the app as a share target for the OS share sheet. Android supports Web Share Target; iOS Safari does not support it and requires a Shortcut instead.

docs.title: Concept 11: protocol_handlers
docs.text:
"protocol_handlers": [
    { "protocol": "mailto", "url": "/newEmail?to=%s" }
]

Allows the web app to handle URL protocols like mailto:, web+jngl, etc. Requires user permission and is validated against the app's scope.

docs.title: Concept 12: file_handlers
docs.text:
"file_handlers": [
    {
        "action": "/openFile",
        "accept": {
            "image/*": [".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".webp", ".svg"]
        }
    }
]

Declares file types the app can open from the OS file manager. The File Handling API requires the action property and an accept object mapping MIME types to extensions.

docs.title: Concept 13: screenshots
docs.text:
"screenshots": [
    {
        "src": "/screenshots/dashboard.png",
        "sizes": "1280x720",
        "type": "image/png",
        "label": "Dashboard overview"
    }
]

Showcases the app's interface in app stores and enriched install prompts. Screenshots and description are used in Chrome's rich install UI.

docs.title: Concept 14: categories
docs.text:
"categories": ["business", "productivity"]

Hints to app catalogs about the app's category. No standard list of values exists, but the W3C maintains a known list.

docs.title: Concept 15: id
docs.text:
"id": "/dashboard"

A unique identifier for the app. Allows browsers to distinguish between different applications and to update installed apps correctly. Must be same-origin with start_url.

docs.title: Concept 16: lang and dir
docs.text:
"lang": "en-US",
"dir": "ltr"

Declares the language and text direction of the manifest's text content. Supports ltr, rtl, and auto.

docs.title: Concept 17: orientation
docs.text:
"orientation": "portrait-primary"

Locks the app's screen orientation when launched. Common values: any, portrait, landscape, portrait-primary, landscape-primary.

docs.title: Concept 18: prefer_related_applications
docs.text:
"prefer_related_applications": false

If true, the browser prefers to install a native app instead of the web app. Must be false or omitted for installability.

docs.title: Concept 19: Installability Criteria
docs.text:
For a PWA to be installable, the manifest must include:

  • name or short_name
  • icons with 192px and 512px PNG
  • start_url
  • display set to fullscreen, standalone, or minimal-ui
  • prefer_related_applications not set to true

Additionally, the site must be served over HTTPS, and a service worker must be registered (Chrome on Android currently requires this).

docs.title: Concept 20: Manifest Update Process
docs.text: As of Chrome 144, the update process for installable web apps with a manifest has been streamlined to be more predictable, deterministic, and efficient.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Manifest Parsing
docs.text:
1.  Browser parses <link rel="manifest" href="...">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Fetches the JSON file over HTTP.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parses the JSON.
    │
    ▼
4.  Validates required members:
    │   ├── name or short_name?
    │   ├── icons with 192 and 512?
    │   ├── start_url?
    │   └── display?
    │
    ▼
5.  Registers the app as installable (if criteria met).
    │
    ▼
6.  Stores manifest data for:
    │   ├── Install prompt
    │   ├── Home screen icon
    │   └── Launch behavior

docs.title: Step-by-Step: PWA Installation
docs.text:
1.  User taps "Add to Home Screen" or install prompt.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser reads the manifest.
    │
    ▼
3.  Selects:
    │   ├── Icon for home screen (192px or maskable)
    │   ├── Splash screen image (512px)
    │   └── Start URL
    │
    ▼
4.  App installed to home screen.
    │
    ▼
5.  User taps icon → app launches to start_url.
    │
    ▼
6.  Display mode applied (standalone, fullscreen, etc.).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Display Mode Fallback
docs.text:
1.  Manifest requests "fullscreen".
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser checks support:
    │   ├── Supports fullscreen? → use fullscreen.
    │   └── Not supported? → fall back to "standalone".
    │
    ▼
3.  If standalone not supported → fall back to "minimal-ui".
    │
    ▼
4.  If minimal-ui not supported → fall back to "browser".

docs.title: The Manifest Data Model
docs.text:
The manifest is a JSON object. The spec defines a WebAppManifest dictionary with dozens of members. Browsers parse it into an internal representation.

WebAppManifest
├── name: string
├── short_name: string
├── description: string
├── icons: ImageResource[]
├── screenshots: ImageResource[]
├── start_url: URL
├── scope: URL
├── display: DisplayMode
├── display_override: DisplayMode[]
├── orientation: Orientation
├── theme_color: Color
├── background_color: Color
├── shortcuts: ShortcutItem[]
├── share_target: ShareTarget
├── protocol_handlers: ProtocolHandler[]
├── file_handlers: FileHandler[]
├── categories: string[]
├── lang: string
├── dir: TextDirection
├── id: URL
└── prefer_related_applications: boolean

docs.title: Display Mode Fallback Algorithm
docs.text:
The browser evaluates display modes in this order:

  1. If display_override is present, iterate through its values.
  2. Use the first supported mode.
  3. If none are supported, evaluate the display member.
  4. If display is not supported, use the fallback chain: fullscreen → standalone → minimal-ui → browser

This allows developers to request cutting-edge modes (like window-controls-overlay) without breaking older browsers.

docs.title: Icon Selection Algorithm
docs.text:
When selecting an icon for the home screen:

  1. Filter by purpose (any or maskable).
  2. Filter by sizes (192px for home screen, 512px for splash).
  3. Filter by type (PNG preferred).
  4. Pick the best match.

If a maskable icon is available, Android uses it for adaptive icon rendering. If not, it uses the any icon and applies a generic mask.

docs.title: The theme_color and background_color Pipeline
docs.text:
theme_color
    │
    ▼
Applied to:
  ├── Window title bar
  ├── Address bar (if browser mode)
  ├── Status bar (mobile)
  └── Task switcher

background_color
    │
    ▼
Applied to:
  ├── Splash screen background
  └── Initial paint before CSS loads

docs.title: The Service Worker Requirement
docs.text: Chrome on Android currently requires a registered service worker for installability. The manifest alone is necessary but not sufficient. This is a Chrome-specific policy; other browsers may have different requirements.

docs.title: Static Site Lifecycle
docs.text:
Author writes manifest.json
    │
    ▼
Deployed to server
    │
    ▼
Linked from HTML with <link rel="manifest">
    │
    ▼
Browser fetches manifest on page load
    │
    ▼
Validates installability criteria
    │
    ▼
Shows install prompt (if eligible)
    │
    ▼
User installs app
    │
    ▼
Icon added to home screen
    │
    ▼
App launches to start_url with configured display mode

docs.title: Manifest Update Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Developer deploys new manifest.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser fetches manifest on next page load.
    │
    ▼
3.  Compares with stored manifest.
    │
    ▼
4.  If changed:
    │   ├── Updates icon (may require re-install)
    │   ├── Updates theme/background color
    │   └── Updates shortcuts
    │
    ▼
5.  Chrome 144+ streamlines this process for predictability.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal PWA Manifest
docs.text:
{
    "name": "Acme Dashboard",
    "short_name": "Acme",
    "start_url": "/",
    "display": "standalone",
    "background_color": "#ffffff",
    "theme_color": "#3498db",
    "icons": [
        { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
        { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
    ]
}

Code Breakdown:

  • name — full app name for install prompts.
  • short_name — compact name for home screen.
  • start_url — launches to /.
  • display: "standalone" — opens in its own window without browser chrome.
  • theme_color — colors the window title bar.
  • background_color — colors the splash screen.
  • Two icons — 192px for home screen, 512px for splash.

docs.title: Example 2: Complete Production Manifest
docs.text:
{
    "id": "/app",
    "name": "Acme Analytics Dashboard",
    "short_name": "Acme",
    "description": "Real-time analytics for your business.",
    "start_url": "/dashboard",
    "scope": "/app/",
    "display": "standalone",
    "display_override": ["window-controls-overlay", "minimal-ui"],
    "orientation": "any",
    "background_color": "#ffffff",
    "theme_color": "#3498db",
    "categories": ["business", "productivity"],
    "lang": "en-US",
    "dir": "ltr",
    "icons": [
        {
            "src": "/icons/icon-192.png",
            "sizes": "192x192",
            "type": "image/png",
            "purpose": "any"
        },
        {
            "src": "/icons/icon-512.png",
            "sizes": "512x512",
            "type": "image/png",
            "purpose": "any"
        },
        {
            "src": "/icons/icon-mask.png",
            "sizes": "512x512",
            "type": "image/png",
            "purpose": "maskable"
        }
    ],
    "shortcuts": [
        {
            "name": "New Report",
            "short_name": "Report",
            "url": "/reports/new",
            "icons": [{ "src": "/icons/report-96.png", "sizes": "96x96" }]
        },
        {
            "name": "Settings",
            "url": "/settings"
        }
    ],
    "share_target": {
        "action": "/share",
        "method": "POST",
        "enctype": "multipart/form-data",
        "params": {
            "title": "title",
            "text": "text",
            "url": "url"
        }
    },
    "screenshots": [
        {
            "src": "/screenshots/dashboard.png",
            "sizes": "1280x720",
            "type": "image/png",
            "label": "Dashboard overview"
        }
    ],
    "prefer_related_applications": false
}

Code Breakdown:

  • id — unique app identifier, same-origin with start_url.
  • scope: "/app/" — the app's navigation scope.
  • display_override — tries window-controls-overlay first, then minimal-ui.
  • purpose: "maskable" — adaptive Android icon with padding.
  • shortcuts — right-click menu items on the app icon.
  • share_target — receives shared content from the OS.
  • screenshots — showcases the app in install prompts.
  • prefer_related_applications: false — allows web app installation.

docs.title: Example 3: HTML Declaration
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>Acme Dashboard</title>
    <meta name="description" content="Real-time analytics for your business.">

    <link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">
    <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">
    <link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
    <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">

    <meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" content="#ffffff">
    <meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" content="#1a1a1a">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • rel="manifest" — links the manifest file.
  • rel="icon" — favicon declarations.
  • apple-touch-icon — iOS home screen icon (not part of the manifest).
  • theme-color — browser UI color (complements theme_color in the manifest).

docs.title: Example 4: File Handlers
docs.text:
"file_handlers": [
    {
        "action": "/openFile",
        "accept": {
            "image/*": [".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".webp", ".svg"],
            "text/markdown": [".md", ".markdown"]
        }
    }
]

Code Breakdown:

  • action — the URL that handles the file.
  • accept — maps MIME types to file extensions.
  • The File Handling API allows the app to open files from the OS file manager.

docs.title: Example 5: Protocol Handlers
docs.text:
"protocol_handlers": [
    {
        "protocol": "mailto",
        "url": "/newEmail?to=%s"
    },
    {
        "protocol": "web+jngl",
        "url": "/lookup?type=%s"
    }
]

Code Breakdown:

  • protocol — the URL scheme to handle.
  • url — the URL template with %s placeholder for the protocol value.
  • Requires user permission and is validated against the app's scope.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Required Manifest Members Basic PWA name, short_name, start_url, display, icons (192, 512), theme_color, background_color Installable on Android + maskable icon, service worker Installable on iOS + apple-touch-icon in HTML Share target + share_target Protocol handler + protocol_handlers File handler + file_handlers App shortcuts + shortcuts Rich install UI + screenshots, description Desktop PWA + display_override for window controls overlay

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always include both name and short_name. Why: name is used in install prompts; short_name is used on the home screen where space is limited.
  2. Provide 192px and 512px PNG icons. Why: these are the minimum sizes required for installability.
  3. Provide a maskable icon. Why: Android crops installed icons to device-specific shapes; a maskable icon survives any crop.
  4. Keep maskable content inside the 40% radius safe circle. Why: the outer 10% may be cropped.
  5. Set theme_color to match your brand. Why: colors the window title bar and OS UI.
  6. Set background_color to match your splash screen. Why: prevents a white flash during launch.
  7. Use display: "standalone" for most apps. Why: provides an app-like experience without browser chrome.
  8. Use display_override for cutting-edge display modes. Why: allows new modes like window-controls-overlay without breaking older browsers.
  9. Set scope to define the app's navigation boundary. Why: pages within scope provide an app-like interface; pages outside open in the browser.
  10. Use id for stable app identity. Why: allows browsers to update installed apps correctly across URL changes.
  11. Add shortcuts for common tasks. Why: improves user experience with direct access to key features.
  12. Serve the manifest with application/manifest+json. Why: this is the correct MIME type; some browsers may not parse it otherwise.
  13. Serve the manifest from the same origin as start_url. Why: reduces spoofing risk and is required for some features.
  14. Test installability with Chrome DevTools. Why: the Application → Manifest panel shows parsed values and installability status.
  15. Audit manifest after rebranding. Why: old icons and colors persist in installed apps until the manifest is updated and the app is re-installed.
  16. Use screenshots and description for rich install UI. Why: Chrome displays these in the enriched install prompt.
  17. Do not combine any maskable on one icon file. Why: a maskable icon has padding; drawn as a plain icon, it looks small.
  18. Keep the manifest file small and focused. Why: it is fetched on every page load; unnecessary bloat adds latency.
  19. Version the manifest URL after major changes. Why: browsers cache the manifest; versioning forces a refresh.
  20. Verify with Lighthouse and real device testing. Why: catches missing or malformed members.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing 192px or 512px Icon
docs.text:
"icons": [
    { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
]

Why it's wrong: Installability requires both 192px and 512px icons. Without the 192px icon, the app is not installable.

✅ Correct:

"icons": [
    { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
]

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No display Member
docs.text:
{
    "name": "My App",
    "icons": [...]
}

Why it's wrong: display is required for installability. Without it, the app may launch in browser mode.

✅ Correct:

"display": "standalone"

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: prefer_related_applications: true
docs.text:
"prefer_related_applications": true

Why it's wrong: This tells the browser to prefer a native app over the web app, making the web app non-installable.

✅ Correct:

"prefer_related_applications": false

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relative start_url Outside Scope
docs.text:
"start_url": "/dashboard",
"scope": "/app/"

Why it's wrong: start_url must be within scope. If it is outside, the manifest is invalid.

✅ Correct:

"start_url": "/app/dashboard",
"scope": "/app/"

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Transparent Maskable Icon
docs.text:
{ "src": "/icon-mask.png", "sizes": "512x512", "purpose": "maskable" }

Why it's wrong: A maskable icon with transparency may show the background color through, making the icon look broken.

✅ Correct: Flatten transparency to a solid background color.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No theme_color
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The window title bar will use the browser's default color, clashing with the app's design.

✅ Correct: Set theme_color to match the brand.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Blocking the Manifest with robots.txt
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The browser cannot fetch the manifest, and the app is not installable.

✅ Correct: Allow the manifest path in robots.txt.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Serving Manifest with Wrong MIME Type
docs.text:
Content-Type: text/plain

Why it's wrong: Some browsers require application/manifest+json to parse the manifest.

✅ Correct:

Content-Type: application/manifest+json

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Service Worker
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Chrome on Android requires a registered service worker for installability.

✅ Correct: Register a service worker.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• The manifest is fetched on every page load — keep it small and cacheable.
  • Large icons are only fetched on demand — during installation or home screen rendering.
  • Screenshots are fetched for the rich install UI — lazy-loaded by the browser.
  • Manifest parsing is negligible — JSON parsing is fast.
  • Service worker adds a separate file and registration cost but is required for installability.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep the manifest under 10 KB.
  2. Serve with long cache headers.
  3. Compress PNG icons with tools like ImageOptim.
  4. Use WebP for screenshots where supported.
  5. Version the manifest URL after changes.

docs.title: Same-Origin Requirement
docs.text: The manifest must be same-origin with start_url to reduce spoofing risk. CDN-served manifest URLs are not initially supported.

docs.title: scope and Navigation
docs.text: The scope member defines the navigation boundary. Pages outside scope open in the browser, not the app. This prevents a malicious app from capturing navigation to unrelated pages.

docs.title: Protocol Handler Security
docs.text: Protocol handlers require user permission and are validated against the app's scope. Privileged schemes (http, https) are rejected.

docs.title: File Handler Security
docs.text: File handlers can only accept file types the user explicitly opens. The app cannot silently access files.

docs.title: Share Target Security
docs.text: Share targets receive data from the OS share sheet. Validate and sanitize all received data on the server.

docs.title: Manifest and CSP
docs.text:
The manifest fetch is not governed by CSP connect-src — it is a document-level resource. However, manifest-src in CSP can restrict which manifests are allowed.

Content-Security-Policy: manifest-src 'self'

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• DevTools → Application → Manifest — inspect parsed manifest values and installability status.
  • DevTools → Application → Service Workers — verify the service worker is registered.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — audit PWA installability.
  • chrome://web-app-internals — inspect installed web apps and their manifests.
  • Chrome DevTools → Console — errors for malformed manifest JSON appear here.
  • beforeinstallprompt event — listen for this event in the console to test install eligibility.
  • navigator.getInstalledRelatedApps() — check if the app is already installed.
  • View source — confirm <link rel="manifest"> is in the <head>.
  • Curl the manifest — curl -s https://example.com/manifest.json | jq to validate JSON.
  • Real device testing — install on iOS and Android to verify home screen icons and launch behavior.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Any Progressive Web App — the manifest is required for installability.
  • Any site with a home screen presence — controls the icon and launch behavior.
  • Any app that needs OS integration — shortcuts, share targets, file handlers.
  • Any app with a brand identity — controls theme colors and icons.
  • Any app intended for app stores — the manifest is the identity document.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Simple content sites — a manifest is not necessary if the site is not an app.
  • Pages that should never be installed — no manifest means no install prompt.
  • Legacy browsers — the manifest is ignored by very old browsers, but this is not a reason to omit it.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Progressive Web App (PWA)
  • Service Worker
  • Favicon
  • Theme Color
  • Web Share Target API
  • File Handling API
  • Protocol Handling API
  • App Shortcuts
  • Install Prompt
  • beforeinstallprompt event
  • display-mode media query
  • apple-touch-icon
  • theme-color meta tag

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The manifest is a JSON file — not HTML, not XML. It is fetched separately from the page.
  • Installability requires both 192px and 512px icons — a common oversight.
  • display_override is evaluated before display — it allows new display modes without breaking older browsers.
