  • Presentational roles (role="presentation") are stripped.
  • Hidden elements (display: none) are excluded.
  • CSS-generated content (::before) may not appear.

docs.title: Accessible Name Computation
docs.text:
The accessible name is what a screen reader announces. The algorithm follows this priority:

  1. aria-labelledby (references other elements)
  2. aria-label (direct string)
  3. Native label (<label>, alt, <caption>)
  4. Text content (for buttons, links)
  5. title attribute (last resort)

docs.title: Role Mapping
docs.text:
Each HTML element maps to an ARIA role:

HTML Element Implicit ARIA Role <button> button <a href> link <h1>–<h6> heading <nav> navigation <main> main <input type="text"> textbox <input type="checkbox"> checkbox <ul> list

docs.title: Focus Order
docs.text: Focus order follows DOM order. CSS order, flex-direction: row-reverse, and absolute positioning can create a mismatch between visual and DOM order — a common accessibility failure.

docs.title: Accessibility Integration Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Design phase:
    │   ├── Color contrast checked
    │   ├── Touch target sizes verified
    │   └── Keyboard flow mapped
    │
    ▼
2.  Development phase:
    │   ├── Semantic HTML first
    │   ├── ARIA only where needed
    │   └── Focus management implemented
    │
    ▼
3.  Automated testing (CI):
    │   ├── axe-core in Playwright/Cypress
    │   └── Lighthouse audits
    │
    ▼
4.  Manual testing:
    │   ├── Keyboard-only walkthrough
    │   ├── Screen reader testing (NVDA, VoiceOver)
    │   └── Zoom to 200%
    │
    ▼
5.  Audit:
    │   ├── Full WCAG 2.2 AA audit
    │   └── Accessibility statement published
    │
    ▼
6.  Monitor and iterate.

docs.title: Example 1: Accessible Button
docs.text:
<!-- Native button: keyboard-operable, focusable, announced as button -->
<button type="button" onclick="save()">
    Save changes
</button>

<!-- Icon-only button: aria-label provides accessible name -->
<button type="button" aria-label="Close dialog" onclick="close()">
    <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16">
        <use href="#icon-close"/>
    </svg>
</button>

Code Breakdown:

  • Native <button> — keyboard-accessible by default; Enter and Space activate it.
  • aria-label="Close dialog" — provides the accessible name for an icon-only button.
  • aria-hidden="true" on the SVG — prevents the icon from being announced.

docs.title: Example 2: Accessible Form
docs.text:
<form>
    <div>
        <label for="email">Email address</label>
        <input id="email" type="email" required
               aria-describedby="email-hint email-error">
        <span id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</span>
        <span id="email-error" role="alert"></span>
    </div>
    <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

Code Breakdown:

  • <label for="email"> — programmatically associates the label with the input.
  • aria-describedby — links hint text and error message to the input.
  • role="alert" — ensures error messages are announced immediately when populated.

docs.title: Example 3: Accessible Modal Focus Management
docs.text:
function openModal(modal, trigger) {
    const previouslyFocused = document.activeElement;

    modal.hidden = false;
    modal.querySelector('button, [href], input, select, textarea')
        .focus();

    // Trap focus inside modal
    modal.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
        if (e.key === 'Escape') closeModal(modal, previouslyFocused);
    });
}

function closeModal(modal, returnFocusTo) {
    modal.hidden = true;
    returnFocusTo?.focus();
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Saves the previously focused element.
  • Moves focus into the modal when opened.
  • Returns focus to the trigger when closed.
  • Escape key closes the modal.

docs.title: Example 4: Skip Navigation Link
docs.text:
<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

<style>
    .skip-link {
        position: absolute;
        top: -40px;
        left: 0;
        background: #000;
        color: #fff;
        padding: 8px;
        z-index: 100;
    }
    .skip-link:focus {
        top: 0;
    }
</style>

<main id="main-content">
    <!-- page content -->
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • The skip link is visually hidden until focused.
  • On focus, it becomes visible at the top of the page.
  • Allows keyboard users to bypass repeated navigation.

docs.title: Example 5: Accessible Data Table
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Q1 2026 Revenue by Region</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Region</th>
            <th scope="col">Revenue</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">North America</th>
            <td>$2.1M</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">Europe</th>
            <td>$1.4M</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

Code Breakdown:

  • <caption> — provides an accessible name for the table.
  • scope="col" — identifies column headers.
  • scope="row" — identifies row headers.
  • Screen readers announce "Region: North America, Revenue: $2.1M" when navigating cells.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Accessibility Approach E-commerce checkout Keyboard-navigable forms, error prevention, accessible authentication Banking portal Screen reader compatibility, keyboard navigation, secure focus management Government services WCAG 2.2 AA, accessibility statement, plain language Media site Captions, transcripts, audio descriptions SaaS dashboard Accessible data tables, charts with text alternatives Mobile app Touch targets 24×24px minimum, screen reader support Documentation Semantic headings, keyboard-navigable code blocks

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Start with semantic HTML. Why: native elements carry built-in roles, states, and keyboard behavior.
  2. Use ARIA only when native HTML cannot express the semantics. Why: pages with ARIA average more errors than pages without.
  3. Test with real screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack). Why: automated tools catch only 30–50% of issues.
  4. Ensure all interactive controls are keyboard-operable. Why: keyboard access is the foundation of accessibility.
  5. Make focus visible at all times. Why: WCAG 2.2 requires focus appearance (2.4.13).
  6. Maintain 4.5:1 contrast for text, 3:1 for UI components. Why: low vision affects millions of users.
  7. Provide text alternatives for all non-text content. Why: screen reader users need alt text.
  8. Use aria-label for icon-only buttons. Why: without it, the button has no accessible name.
  9. Associate labels with form controls. Why: screen readers need programmatic association.
  10. Announce dynamic content changes. Why: screen reader users need to know when content updates.
  11. Manage focus on route changes and modals. Why: keyboard users lose context otherwise.
  12. Provide skip navigation links. Why: keyboard users can bypass repeated navigation.
  13. Use lang on the <html> element. Why: screen readers select the correct voice.
  14. Support text resize up to 200% without loss of content. Why: low-vision users depend on zoom.
  15. Avoid maximum-scale=1 and user-scalable=no. Why: blocks pinch-zoom, violating WCAG 1.4.4.
  16. Use role="alert" for error messages. Why: ensures immediate announcement.
  17. Integrate axe-core into CI/CD. Why: catches regressions before deployment.
  18. Publish an accessibility statement. Why: EAA requires it for relevant services.
  19. Train designers and developers on accessibility. Why: prevention is cheaper than remediation.
  20. Audit against WCAG 2.2 AA. Why: it is the legal target in every modern regulation.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div> for Buttons
docs.text:
<div class="btn" onclick="submit()">Submit</div>

Why it's wrong: Not focusable, not keyboard-operable, not announced as a button.

✅ Correct:

<button type="button" onclick="submit()">Submit</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Alt Text
docs.text:
<img src="chart.png">

Why it's wrong: Screen readers announce the filename, which is meaningless.

✅ Correct:

<img src="chart.png" alt="Q1 revenue: $4.2M, up 18% from Q4">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Removing Focus Outlines
docs.text:
*:focus { outline: none; }

Why it's wrong: Keyboard users cannot see where they are.

✅ Correct:

*:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #3498db; }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Color Alone to Convey Information
docs.text:
<span style="color: red;">Error</span>

Why it's wrong: Color-blind users cannot perceive the error.

✅ Correct:

<span role="alert">Error: Please enter a valid email.</span>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: user-scalable=no in Viewport
docs.text:
<meta name="viewport" content="user-scalable=no">

Why it's wrong: Blocks pinch-zoom, violating WCAG 1.4.4.

✅ Correct:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: role="button" Without Keyboard Handler
docs.text:
<div role="button" onclick="save()">Save</div>

Why it's wrong: ARIA declares semantics but does not add keyboard behavior.

✅ Correct: Use <button> or add tabindex="0" and keyboard handlers.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Form Labels
docs.text:
<input type="text" placeholder="Email">

Why it's wrong: Placeholder is not a label; screen readers may not announce it.

✅ Correct:

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Accessibility Statement
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The EAA requires it for relevant services.

✅ Correct: Publish and maintain an accessibility statement.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Semantic HTML is faster than JavaScript-rendered alternatives.
  • Native elements have no runtime overhead; custom ARIA widgets require JavaScript.
  • Focus management is cheap; a single .focus() call.
  • Screen reader compatibility does not affect page load.
  • Automated testing adds seconds to CI pipelines but prevents regressions.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Prefer native HTML over ARIA-heavy custom widgets.
  2. Use content-visibility: auto for long lists.
  3. Keep focusable elements in DOM order.
  4. Test with throttled CPU to simulate assistive technology overhead.

docs.title: Accessibility Overlays Are Not a Fix
docs.text: Third-party "accessibility overlay" widgets claim to make sites accessible automatically. They do not. They cannot fix missing semantics, keyboard traps, or poor contrast. Overlays have been sued for failing to provide actual accessibility.

docs.title: Screen Reader Data Leakage
docs.text: Screen readers read everything in the accessibility tree — including content hidden visually but not from the accessibility tree. Use aria-hidden="true" to exclude decorative or sensitive content.

docs.title: ARIA and XSS
docs.text: aria-label values are not parsed as HTML — they are safe. However, dynamically injecting ARIA content from untrusted input could expose data.

docs.title: Accessibility Statements and Legal Risk
docs.text: An inaccurate accessibility statement can increase legal risk. Statements must be truthful and maintained.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Accessibility panel — inspect the accessibility tree for any element.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — automated accessibility audit.
  • axe DevTools extension — in-browser accessibility testing.
  • WAVE extension — visual accessibility evaluation.
  • tab through the page — verify focus order and visibility.
  • Screen reader testing — NVDA (Windows), VoiceOver (macOS/iOS), TalkBack (Android).
  • document.activeElement — inspect the currently focused element in console.
  • getComputedStyle(el).outline — verify focus styles.
  • Contrast checkers — WebAIM Contrast Checker, Stark plugin.
  • HTML validator — validator.w3.org — valid HTML is more likely accessible.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every website — accessibility is a baseline requirement.
  • Every form — labels, error messages, keyboard access.
  • Every interactive widget — modals, dropdowns, tabs, carousels.
  • Every image — alt text or aria-hidden.
  • Every page — semantic landmarks, heading hierarchy.
  • Every product serving EU users — EAA compliance since June 2025.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Accessibility overlays — they do not work; fix the source code instead.
  • ARIA when native HTML suffices — it adds errors.
  • role="presentation" on interactive elements — removes semantics.
  • tabindex values greater than 0 — disrupts natural focus order.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• WCAG 2.2
  • WCAG 3.0
  • POUR principles
  • ARIA (WAI-ARIA)
  • Semantic HTML
  • Keyboard navigation
  • Focus management
  • Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack)
  • Accessibility tree
  • Color contrast
  • Alt text
  • Skip navigation
  • Accessibility statement
  • European Accessibility Act
  • ADA Title II
  • Section 508
  • axe-core
  • Lighthouse

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• WCAG 2.2 has 86 success criteria across three conformance levels.
  • WCAG 2.2 added 9 criteria and removed 1 (4.1.1 Parsing).
  • Pages with ARIA average 59.1 detectable errors versus 42 without ARIA, per the 2026 WebAIM Million report.
  • Automated tools catch only 30–50% of accessibility issues.
  • The European Accessibility Act took full effect on 28 June 2025.
  • DOJ extended ADA Title II deadlines in April 2026: large entities to April 2027, small entities to April 2028.
  • WCAG 3.0 is a working draft — not enforceable. It introduces Bronze-Silver-Gold scoring instead of A/AA/AAA.
  • ARIA does not add behavior — it only changes how assistive technology perceives an element.
  • Native HTML elements are the most reliable accessibility primitive.
  • Focus must be visible at all times — WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.4.13.
  • Target size minimum is 24×24 CSS pixels — WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.5.8.
  • Dragging movements must have a non-drag alternative — WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.5.7.
  • Redundant entry must be avoided — WCAG 2.2 criterion 3.3.7.
  • The EAA requires accessibility statements for relevant services.
  • The DGCCRF (France) began inspections of e-commerce sites for EAA compliance in December 2025.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Web accessibility ensures all people can perceive, operate, understand, and interact with digital content.
  • POUR is the framework: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.
  • WCAG 2.2 is the current standard with 86 success criteria across A, AA, and AAA levels.
  • AA is the legal bar — the EAA, ADA Title II, and Section 508 all resolve to WCAG 2.2 AA.
  • The European Accessibility Act took effect June 2025, requiring accessible e-commerce, banking, transport, and digital products.
  • ADA Title II deadlines extended: April 2027 (large entities), April 2028 (small entities).
  • WCAG 3.0 is a working draft with Bronze-Silver-Gold scoring; nothing is enforceable yet.
  • Semantic HTML is the foundation — native elements carry built-in accessibility.
  • ARIA is a supplement, not a replacement — incorrect ARIA is worse than no ARIA.
  • Test with real assistive technology — automated tools catch only 30–50% of issues.
  • Keyboard navigation, focus management, and contrast are core requirements.
  • Accessibility overlays do not work — fix the source code.
  • Accessibility benefits everyone — the curb cut effect.
  • Every site should audit against WCAG 2.2 AA and publish an accessibility statement.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Semantic HTML is the practice of using HTML elements that describe the meaning and purpose of their content — not just its appearance. A <nav> element means "this is navigation." A <button> means "this is an interactive control." A <article> means "this is a self-contained piece of content."

<!-- Semantic -->
<nav aria-label="Main">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

<!-- Non-semantic (div soup) -->
<div class="nav">
    <div class="nav-item"><a href="/">Home</a></div>
    <div class="nav-item"><a href="/about">About</a></div>
</div>

The two examples may look identical visually. But the first tells the browser, the search engine, and the screen reader exactly what the content is. The second tells them nothing.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Semantic HTML serves several essential purposes:

  • Accessibility — screen readers use element roles and landmarks to navigate. <nav> becomes a jump target; <button> becomes an operable control.
  • SEO — search engines weight semantic structure. A <main> with an <h1> communicates hierarchy; a <div> soup does not.
  • Maintainability — semantic markup is self-documenting. A new developer can understand the structure without reading CSS classes.
  • Machine readability — AI systems, browser extensions, reader modes, and translation tools all rely on semantics to interpret content.
  • Keyboard navigation — native elements carry built-in keyboard behavior. <button> responds to Enter and Space; a <div onclick> does not.
  • Default browser behavior — native elements work with browser features: form validation, autofill, password managers, reader mode, find-in-page, and printing.
  • Robustness — semantic HTML degrades gracefully. When CSS or JavaScript fails, the content remains usable.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Semantic HTML is the foundation layer of accessibility. Everything else — ARIA, focus management, keyboard navigation, screen reader compatibility — is built on top of it.

Accessibility Stack
│
├── Semantic HTML        ← foundation (native elements, landmarks, headings)
├── ARIA                 ← supplement (roles, states, properties)
├── CSS                  ← contrast, focus styles, layout
├── JavaScript           ← focus management, dynamic content
└── Testing              ← screen readers, automated tools

If the foundation is wrong, no amount of ARIA or JavaScript can fix it reliably.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTML has always had semantic elements. But in the mid-2000s, developers stopped using them. They used <div> for everything, styling it with CSS classes to look like navigation, headers, articles, and footers. This produced what became known as "div soup" — markup that renders correctly but conveys nothing about meaning.

<!-- Div soup: looks right, means nothing -->
<div class="header">
    <div class="nav">
        <div class="nav-link"><a href="/">Home</a></div>
    </div>
</div>
<div class="content">
    <div class="post">
        <div class="post-title">How SVG Works</div>
        <div class="post-body">...</div>
    </div>
</div>
<div class="footer">...</div>

To a screen reader, this is a flat list of text. To a search engine, it is unstructured content. To a reader mode, it is an undifferentiated block.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No landmarks Screen reader users cannot jump to navigation or main content No heading hierarchy No way to navigate by headings No native controls Keyboard access requires manual JavaScript No form semantics Autofill and validation do not work No SEO signals Search engines cannot weight structure No reader mode Reader modes cannot extract the article

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
HTML5 (2008–2014) introduced a set of sectioning and semantic elements to solve the div-soup problem:

  • <header>, <footer>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <figure>, <figcaption>, <time>, <mark>, <details>, <summary>.

These elements had existed conceptually since HTML 4 (<div id="header">), but HTML5 formalized them as first-class elements with defined roles, landmarks, and accessibility mappings.

The goal: give meaning to structure so that browsers, assistive technology, search engines, and future tools can understand the page without parsing CSS classes.

docs.title: The Semantic Document Skeleton
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Semantic HTML Demo — Dev Notes</title>
</head>
<body>
    <a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

    <header>
        <h1>Dev Notes</h1>
        <nav aria-label="Main">
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
                <li><a href="/blog">Blog</a></li>
                <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
    </header>

    <main id="main-content">
        <article>
            <header>
                <h2>How SVG Embedding Works</h2>
                <p>
                    Published <time datetime="2026-01-15">January 15, 2026</time>
                    by <span rel="author">Jane Developer</span>
                </p>
            </header>
            <section>
                <h3>Inline SVG</h3>
                <p>...</p>
            </section>
            <section>
                <h3>Image SVG</h3>
                <p>...</p>
            </section>
            <footer>
                <p>Filed under: <a href="/tags/svg">SVG</a></p>
            </footer>
        </article>

        <aside aria-label="Related posts">
            <h2>Related</h2>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/css-cascade">The CSS Cascade</a></li>
            </ul>
        </aside>
    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 Dev Notes</p>
    </footer>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element Meaning Accessibility Role <header> Introductory content banner (when top-level) <nav> Navigation links navigation landmark <main> Primary content main landmark <article> Self-contained content article role <section> Thematic grouping region (when labelled) <aside> Complementary content complementary landmark <footer> Closing content contentinfo (when top-level) <h1>–<h6> Heading hierarchy heading role with level <time> Date/time Semantic date <figure>/<figcaption> Figure with caption figure role

docs.title: The Heading Hierarchy
docs.text:
<h1>Page Title</h1>

<h2>Section A</h2>
<h3>Subsection A.1</h3>
<h3>Subsection A.2</h3>

<h2>Section B</h2>
<h3>Subsection B.1</h3>

Rules:

  • One <h1> per page (recommended, not required).
  • Never skip levels (<h1> → <h3> is a failure).
  • Headings must reflect content structure, not visual size.
  • Use CSS to style headings differently — do not choose an <h4> because it "looks right."

docs.title: Native Interactive Elements
docs.text:
<!-- Buttons: keyboard-operable, announced as "button" -->
<button type="button">Save</button>

<!-- Links: navigate to a URL, announced as "link" -->
<a href="/about">About</a>

<!-- Inputs: associated with labels, participate in forms -->
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" required>

<!-- Details/summary: native disclosure widget -->
<details>
    <summary>Show more</summary>
    <p>Hidden content</p>
</details>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• <button> — Enter/Space activates; announced as button. Never use <div onclick> for a button.
  • <a href> — navigates; announced as link. Never use <a> without href as a button.
  • <input> + <label> — autofill, validation, password managers, and screen reader association all work automatically.
  • <details>/<summary> — native disclosure widget; no JavaScript required.

docs.title: The "Meaning vs Appearance" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every HTML element answers two questions:

<div>          → What does it look like? (nothing)
<span>         → What does it look like? (nothing)
<nav>          → What is it? (navigation)
<button>       → What is it? (control)
<article>      → What is it? (content)

Semantic HTML answers "what is it?", not "what does it look like?". Styling is CSS's job.

docs.title: The "Screen Reader Roadmap" Mental Model
docs.text:
A screen reader user navigates by structure, not by visuals. Semantic HTML provides the roadmap:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  <header>           ← landmark: banner       │
│    <nav>            ← landmark: navigation   │
│  <main>             ← landmark: main         │
│    <h1>             ← heading level 1        │
│    <article>        ← content block          │
│      <h2>           ← heading level 2        │
│      <section>      ← region                 │
│        <h3>         ← heading level 3        │
│  <aside>            ← landmark: complementary│
│  <footer>           ← landmark: contentinfo  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Keyboard shortcuts in NVDA/JAWS: - H — next heading - K — next link - B — next button - F — next form field - D — next landmark - 1–6 — heading levels

Without semantics, none of these work.

docs.title: The "Layered Meaning" Mental Model
docs.text:
Semantic HTML provides meaning at multiple levels:

Layer 1: Document structure   → <html>, <head>, <body>
Layer 2: Landmarks            → <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <footer>
Layer 3: Content grouping     → <article>, <section>, <figure>
Layer 4: Headings             → <h1>–<h6>
Layer 5: Text meaning         → <em>, <strong>, <mark>, <time>, <abbr>
Layer 6: Interaction          → <button>, <a>, <input>, <select>, <textarea>

Each layer adds a dimension of meaning. The more layers present, the richer the accessibility tree.

docs.title: The "ARIA as Duct Tape" Mental Model
docs.text:
ARIA is duct tape for when HTML fails. It patches gaps:

<!-- Native HTML: no duct tape needed -->
<button>Save</button>

<!-- ARIA duct tape: adds role but not behavior -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0" onclick="save()" onkeydown="...">
    Save
</div>

The second example requires manual keyboard handling, manual focus styles, manual disabled states. Native HTML gives all of this for free.

Rule 1 of ARIA: if a native HTML element provides the semantics and behavior you need, use it. Use ARIA only when native HTML cannot express the semantics.

docs.title: Concept 1: Landmarks
docs.text:
Landmarks are page regions that screen readers can jump to directly. Modern HTML provides them via native elements:

Element Implicit Landmark Role Count Per Page <header> (top-level) banner 1 <nav> navigation Multiple <main> main 1 <aside> complementary Multiple <footer> (top-level) contentinfo 1 <section> (with aria-label) region Multiple <form> (with aria-label) form Multiple

Rule: one <main> per page; one <header> and <footer> at the top level (nested headers/footers inside <article> and <section> do not create landmarks).

docs.title: Concept 2: The Heading Hierarchy
docs.text:
Headings create a navigable outline. Screen readers announce level (h1, h2) and allow jumping between them. Skip heading levels = broken structure.

<!-- Correct -->
<h1>Page title</h1>
<h2>Section</h2>
<h3>Subsection</h3>

<!-- Wrong: skipped level -->
<h1>Page title</h1>
<h3>Section</h3>

Never use headings for styling. Use CSS classes for that.

docs.title: Concept 3: <article> vs <section> vs <div>
docs.text:
Element Use When <article> Content that could stand alone (blog post, product card, comment) <section> A thematic grouping with a heading <div> A generic container for styling; no semantic meaning

Test for <article>: would this content make sense in an RSS feed on its own? If yes, it is an <article>.

Test for <section>: does it have a heading? If not, use <div>.

docs.title: Concept 4: <header> and <footer>
docs.text:
These are context-dependent:

  • At the top level of <body> — they become banner and contentinfo landmarks.
  • Inside <article> or <section> — they are just semantic grouping; no landmark.
<body>
    <header>...</header>    <!-- banner landmark -->
    <main>
        <article>
            <header>...</header>  <!-- NOT a landmark; article header -->
            <footer>...</footer>  <!-- NOT a landmark; article footer -->
        </article>
    </main>
    <footer>...</footer>    <!-- contentinfo landmark -->
</body>

docs.title: Concept 5: Native Interactive Elements
docs.text:
The single most impactful accessibility decision: use <button> for buttons, <a> for links, and <input>/<select>/<textarea> for forms.

Need Element Why Trigger an action <button> Keyboard-operable, announced as button Navigate to a URL <a href> Announced as link, right-click, middle-click Text input <input type="text"> Autofill, validation, form association Toggle <input type="checkbox"> Announced as checkbox, Space toggles Select from list <select> Native dropdown, keyboard-navigable Disclosure <details>/<summary> Native expand/collapse

docs.title: Concept 6: Text-Level Semantics
docs.text:
Inline elements carry meaning:

Element Meaning <em> Stress emphasis (changes meaning) <strong> Importance (seriousness) <mark> Highlighted/relevant <abbr> Abbreviation; use title for expansion <time> Date/time; use datetime for machine-readable format <code> Code fragment <kbd> User input <samp> Sample output <var> Variable <cite> Title of a work <blockquote> Extended quotation <q> Short inline quotation

docs.title: Concept 7: Landmark Labelling
docs.text:
When a landmark type appears multiple times, label it with aria-label:

<nav aria-label="Main">
    <ul>...</ul>
</nav>

<nav aria-label="Footer">
    <ul>...</ul>
</nav>

Screen readers announce "Main navigation" and "Footer navigation."

docs.title: Concept 8: The <main> Element
docs.text:
<main> wraps the primary content of the page. There should be only one <main> per page, and it should not include repeated content (headers, navigation, footers).

<header>...</header>
<main>
    <h1>Page title</h1>
    <p>Content...</p>
</main>
<footer>...</footer>

docs.title: Concept 9: <figure> and <figcaption>
docs.text:
<figure>
    <img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart of Q1 revenue">
    <figcaption>Figure 1: Q1 2026 revenue by region.</figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption> is announced as the figure's caption. The <figure> is announced as a figure. Screen readers can associate them.

docs.title: Concept 10: <time> with datetime
docs.text:
<time datetime="2026-01-15T08:00:00Z">January 15, 2026</time>

The datetime attribute provides a machine-readable date. Search engines, AI systems, and calendar tools can parse it.

docs.title: Concept 11: <details> and <summary> for Disclosure
docs.text:
<details>
    <summary>Shipping information</summary>
    <p>Free shipping on orders over $75.</p>
</details>

Native disclosure widget. No JavaScript needed. Keyboard-accessible, announced correctly.

docs.title: Concept 12: Semantic HTML and Reader Mode
docs.text: Reader modes in Safari, Firefox, and Chrome extract the "main article" from the page. They rely on semantic elements. A page built with <article>, <h1>, and <p> is reader-mode friendly. A <div> soup is not.

docs.title: Concept 13: Semantic HTML and Find-in-Page
docs.text: Browsers' find-in-page works on text nodes. But structured content — headings, list items, table cells — is easier to navigate. Some browsers support "find in heading" extensions that rely on semantics.

docs.title: Concept 14: Semantic HTML and SEO
docs.text:
Search engines use semantic structure to weight content:

  • <h1> is the page's primary topic.
  • <main> contains the primary content.
  • <article> signals standalone content.
  • <time> provides freshness signals.
  • <nav> and <footer> are deprioritized.

A <div> with class="heading-1" has no such weight.

docs.title: Concept 15: Semantic HTML and AI Systems
docs.text: AI answer engines (AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity) parse HTML structure to extract content. Clean semantic markup — headings, paragraphs, lists, tables — improves extraction and citation accuracy. Div soup produces weaker signals.

docs.title: Concept 16: Semantic HTML and CSS
docs.text:
Semantic markup and CSS are orthogonal. Semantic HTML describes what something is; CSS decides how it looks.

<!-- Bad: chooses element based on appearance -->
<h4>Latest News</h4>

<!-- Good: chooses element based on meaning, styles with CSS -->
<h2 class="visually-small">Latest News</h2>

docs.title: Concept 17: Browser Default Behaviors
docs.text:
Native elements come with browser behaviors that div-based equivalents do not have:

  • <button> responds to keyboard, prevents form submission by default (with type="button"), and integrates with assistive technology.
  • <input> participates in forms, autofill, password managers, and validation.
  • <details> toggles open/closed without JavaScript.
  • <a href> supports right-click, middle-click, and browser URL preview.

docs.title: Concept 18: Semantic HTML and Internationalization
docs.text:
Semantic HTML supports language and direction:

<html lang="en">
<p lang="fr">Bonjour</p>
<p dir="rtl" lang="ar">مرحبا</p>

Screen readers switch voices based on lang. Layout direction is determined by dir.

docs.title: Concept 19: The <search> Element
docs.text:
The <search> element (new in HTML) wraps search functionality:

<search>
    <form action="/search">
        <label for="q">Search</label>
        <input id="q" type="search" name="q">
        <button type="submit">Go</button>
    </form>
</search>

Browser support is still expanding, but it provides a semantic landmark for search.

docs.title: Concept 20: <dialog> for Modals
docs.text:
<dialog id="confirm">
    <form method="dialog">
        <h2>Confirm deletion</h2>
        <p>This cannot be undone.</p>
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<button onclick="document.getElementById('confirm').showModal()">
    Delete
</button>

The native <dialog> element provides focus trapping, Escape handling, and modal semantics — all without JavaScript frameworks.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Semantic Element to Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
1.  HTML is parsed.
    │
    ▼
2.  Each element gets:
    │   ├── Role (from element name)
    │   ├── Name (from content or aria-label)
    │   ├── State (from attributes like disabled, checked)
    │   └── Level (for headings)
    │
    ▼
3.  Accessibility tree is built.
    │
    ▼
4.  Landmarks are registered:
    │   banner, navigation, main, complementary, contentinfo
    │
    ▼
5.  Headings form a navigable tree.
    │
    ▼
6.  Screen reader exposes:
    │   ├── Landmark navigation (D key)
    │   ├── Heading navigation (H key, 1-6 keys)
    │   ├── Link navigation (K key)
    │   └── Form field navigation (F key)

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Keyboard Navigation in a Form
docs.text:
1.  User tabs into form.
    │
    ▼
2.  Focus moves to <input> (native, focusable).
    │
    ▼
3.  Screen reader announces:
    │   "Email address, edit, required"
    │   (from <label> and required attribute)
    │
    ▼
4.  User types.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser validates email format on blur.
    │
    ▼
6.  User tabs to <button type="submit">.
    │
    ▼
7.  Pressing Enter submits the form (native behavior).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Landmark Navigation
docs.text:
Screen reader shortcut: D → next landmark

1.  banner       (header)
2.  navigation   (nav)
3.  main         (main)
4.  complementary (aside)
5.  contentinfo  (footer)

Without semantic elements, these landmarks do not exist.

docs.title: Element-to-Role Mapping
docs.text:
The HTML Accessibility API Mappings specification defines how each element maps to an ARIA role:

Element ARIA Role <article> article <aside> complementary <button> button <footer> (top-level) contentinfo <header> (top-level) banner <h1>–<h6> heading (level 1–6) <main> main <nav> navigation <ol>, <ul> list <li> listitem <table> table <form> (labelled) form <section> (labelled) region

docs.title: The Landmark Calculation Algorithm
docs.text:
Not every <header> is a banner. The rule:

  • A <header> is banner only if it is not a descendant of <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section>.
  • A <footer> is contentinfo only if it is not a descendant of those elements.
  • A <section> is region only if it has an accessible name (via aria-label or aria-labelledby).

docs.title: Native Behavior vs ARIA
docs.text:
Native elements provide both semantics and behavior. ARIA provides only semantics:

<button>              → role + keyboard + focus + disabled + click
<div role="button">   → role only (needs JS for keyboard, focus, disabled)

<input type="email">  → role + validation + autofill + keyboard
<div role="textbox">  → role only (needs JS for everything)

This is why Rule 1 of ARIA exists.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree vs the DOM
docs.text:
The DOM is the browser's internal representation. The accessibility tree is a parallel tree optimized for assistive technology:

  • aria-hidden="true" removes elements from the accessibility tree but not the DOM.
  • display: none removes from both.
  • role="presentation" removes semantics but keeps the element.
  • CSS-generated content (::before) may not appear in the accessibility tree.

docs.title: Authoring Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Outline content structure:
    │   ├── Header
    │   ├── Navigation
    │   ├── Main content
    │   │   ├── Articles
    │   │   ├── Sections
    │   │   └── Figures
    │   ├── Aside
    │   └── Footer
    │
    ▼
2.  Choose elements by meaning, not appearance.
    │
    ▼
3.  Write content with native elements.
    │
    ▼
4.  Add ARIA only where native HTML cannot express semantics.
    │
    ▼
5.  Style with CSS.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test with keyboard and screen reader.

docs.title: Audit Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Inspect the DOM for semantic elements.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check heading hierarchy (no skipped levels).
    │
    ▼
3.  Check landmarks (one main, labelled navs).
    │
    ▼
4.  Check interactive controls (native elements?).
    │
    ▼
5.  Test with screen reader landmark navigation.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test with keyboard only (Tab through everything).
    │
    ▼
7.  Fix, re-test, repeat.

docs.title: Example 1: Accessible Blog Post
docs.text:
<article>
    <header>
        <h1>How SVG Embedding Works</h1>
        <p>
            Published <time datetime="2026-01-15T08:00:00Z">January 15, 2026</time>
            by <span rel="author">Jane Developer</span>
        </p>
    </header>

    <p>SVG can be embedded in seven different ways...</p>

    <section>
        <h2>Inline SVG</h2>
        <p>The most flexible method...</p>
    </section>

    <section>
        <h2>Image SVG</h2>
        <p>The most cacheable method...</p>
    </section>

    <figure>
        <img src="methods.png" alt="Diagram comparing seven SVG embedding methods">
        <figcaption>Figure 1: SVG embedding methods.</figcaption>
    </figure>

    <footer>
        <p>Filed under: <a href="/tags/svg">SVG</a>, <a href="/tags/html">HTML</a></p>
    </footer>
</article>

Code Breakdown:

  • <article> — self-contained; could be syndicated on its own.
  • <header> — article header (not a banner landmark).
  • <h1> — the page's primary heading.
  • <time> with datetime — machine-readable date.
  • <section> — thematic groupings with headings.
  • <figure> + <figcaption> — image with caption.
  • <footer> — article footer (not contentinfo landmark).

docs.title: Example 2: Accessible Site Header
docs.text:
<header>
    <a href="/" aria-label="Acme homepage">
        <img src="logo.svg" alt="Acme" width="100" height="30">
    </a>

    <nav aria-label="Main">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
            <li><a href="/pricing">Pricing</a></li>
            <li><a href="/docs">Docs</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>

    <nav aria-label="Account">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/login">Sign in</a></li>
            <li><a href="/signup">Sign up</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

Code Breakdown:

  • <header> at top level → banner landmark.
  • Two <nav> elements, distinguished by aria-label — both announced as distinct landmarks.
  • Logo link uses aria-label to provide accessible name.

docs.title: Example 3: Accessible Form
docs.text:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
    <fieldset>
        <legend>Newsletter preferences</legend>

        <div>
            <label for="email">Email address</label>
            <input id="email" type="email" name="email" required
                   autocomplete="email"
                   aria-describedby="email-hint">
            <span id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</span>
        </div>

        <div>
            <label for="frequency">Frequency</label>
            <select id="frequency" name="frequency">
                <option value="daily">Daily</option>
                <option value="weekly" selected>Weekly</option>
                <option value="monthly">Monthly</option>
            </select>
        </div>

        <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
    </fieldset>
</form>

Code Breakdown:

  • <fieldset> + <legend> — groups related controls with a name.
  • <label for="..."> — programmatically associates labels with inputs.
  • autocomplete="email" — enables browser autofill.
  • aria-describedby — links hint text to input.
  • <select> — native dropdown, keyboard-navigable.

docs.title: Example 4: Accessible Data Table
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Q1 2026 Revenue by Region</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Region</th>
            <th scope="col">Revenue</th>
            <th scope="col">Growth</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">North America</th>
            <td>$2.1M</td>
            <td>+18%</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">Europe</th>
            <td>$1.4M</td>
            <td>+12%</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

Code Breakdown:

  • <caption> — accessible table name.
  • <thead> / <tbody> — structural grouping.
  • scope="col" — identifies column headers.
  • scope="row" — identifies row headers.
  • Screen readers announce "Region: Europe, Revenue: $1.4M, Growth: +12%" when navigating cells.

docs.title: Example 5: Native Dialog
docs.text:
<dialog id="confirm-delete">
    <form method="dialog">
        <h2>Confirm deletion</h2>
        <p>This action cannot be undone.</p>
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<button onclick="document.getElementById('confirm-delete').showModal()">
    Delete account
</button>

Code Breakdown:

  • <dialog> — native modal; traps focus automatically.
  • showModal() — opens as a modal with backdrop.
  • method="dialog" — form submission closes the dialog; button value is returned.
  • Escape key closes the dialog natively.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Semantic Approach Blog post <article> + <header> + <h1> + <section> + <footer> Product page <article> + <h1> + <section> for specs + <figure> for images Site header <header> + <nav aria-label> + logo <a> Navigation <nav> + <ul> + <li> + <a> Sidebar <aside aria-label="Related"> Footer <footer> + <nav aria-label="Footer"> Form <form> + <fieldset> + <label> + <input> + <button> Modal <dialog> + showModal() Disclosure <details> + <summary> Image with caption <figure> + <img> + <figcaption> Breadcrumbs <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> + <ol> Pagination <nav aria-label="Pagination"> + <ul>

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Choose elements by meaning, not appearance. Why: semantics describe what content is, CSS describes how it looks.
  2. Use <button> for actions, <a> for navigation. Why: native keyboard behavior and correct announcements.
  3. Never use <a> without href as a button. Why: it has no keyboard behavior and is not announced as a link.
  4. Never use <div> or <span> for interactive controls without ARIA and keyboard handlers. Why: they are invisible to assistive technology by default.
  5. Maintain a logical heading hierarchy. Why: screen readers navigate by headings.
  6. Never skip heading levels. Why: it breaks the document outline.
  7. Use only one <main> per page. Why: it is the primary content landmark.
  8. Label repeated landmarks with aria-label. Why: multiple navs need distinct names.
  9. Use <article> for self-contained content. Why: it enables syndication and content extraction.
  10. Use <section> only when it has a heading. Why: unlabelled sections are just <div>s.
  11. Use <figure> and <figcaption> for images with captions. Why: screen readers announce the caption association.
  12. Use <time> with datetime for dates. Why: machine-readable; used by search and AI systems.
  13. Use <label> for every form control. Why: programmatic association is required for accessibility.
  14. Use <fieldset> and <legend> for grouped controls. Why: they provide context.
  15. Use <details> and <summary> for disclosure. Why: native, keyboard-accessible, no JavaScript needed.
  16. Use <dialog> for modals. Why: native focus trapping and Escape handling.
  17. Prefer native HTML over ARIA. Why: native elements have behavior; ARIA only has semantics.
  18. Add lang to <html> and inline language changes. Why: screen readers switch voices.
  19. Test with a screen reader. Why: semantics only matter if they translate to announcements.
  20. Test with keyboard only. Why: native behavior is the accessibility baseline.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div> for Buttons
docs.text:
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

Why it's wrong: Not focusable, not keyboard-operable, not announced as a button.

✅ Correct:

<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <a> Without href as a Button
docs.text:
<a onclick="save()">Save</a>

Why it's wrong: No href means no keyboard focus, no role, no correct announcement.

✅ Correct:

<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <h1> Elements
docs.text:
<h1>Page Title</h1>
<article>
    <h1>Article Title</h1>
</article>

Why it's wrong: Multiple top-level headings confuse the document outline.

✅ Correct:

<h1>Page Title</h1>
<article>
    <h2>Article Title</h2>
</article>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Skipping Heading Levels
docs.text:
<h1>Page Title</h1>
<h4>Section</h4>

Why it's wrong: Breaks the outline; screen reader users lose hierarchy.

✅ Correct:

<h1>Page Title</h1>
<h2>Section</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Headings for Styling
docs.text:
<h4>Latest News</h4>  <!-- chosen because it "looks right" -->

Why it's wrong: Heading level is semantic, not visual.

✅ Correct:

<h2 class="small-heading">Latest News</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <main> Elements
docs.text:
<main>Home content</main>
<main>Sidebar content</main>

Why it's wrong: Only one <main> landmark per page.

✅ Correct:

<main>
    <section>Home content</section>
    <aside>Sidebar content</aside>
</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: <section> Without a Heading
docs.text:
<section>
    <p>Some content</p>
</section>

Why it's wrong: An unlabelled <section> has no accessible name; it is not a landmark.

✅ Correct:

<section>
    <h2>Section Title</h2>
    <p>Some content</p>
</section>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <div> for Paragraphs
docs.text:
<div class="paragraph">Some text.</div>

Why it's wrong: Loses paragraph semantics; reader modes and screen readers treat it as a generic container.

✅ Correct:

<p>Some text.</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No lang Attribute
docs.text:
<html>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers cannot select the correct voice.

✅ Correct:

<html lang="en">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unlabelled Multiple Navs
docs.text:
<nav>...</nav>
<nav>...</nav>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers announce both as "navigation"; the user cannot distinguish them.

✅ Correct:

<nav aria-label="Main">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Account">...</nav>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Semantic elements have no runtime cost — they are parsed the same as <div>.
  • Native elements are faster than ARIA-heavy alternatives — the browser handles keyboard and focus natively.
  • Reader mode extraction works better with semantic content.
  • Search engine parsing is more efficient with clear structure.
  • No JavaScript required for <details>, <dialog>, <button>, and form controls.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Prefer native elements over JavaScript-heavy custom widgets.
  2. Use <details> for accordions instead of JavaScript.
  3. Use <dialog> for modals instead of third-party libraries.
  4. Use semantic landmarks so reader mode extracts the article directly.

docs.title: Semantic HTML Does Not Introduce Security Issues
docs.text: Semantic elements are parsed by the HTML parser — no new attack surface. They do not execute scripts.

docs.title: ARIA and DOM Injection
docs.text: Dynamically setting aria-label from untrusted input could expose data. Escape or validate any ARIA values generated from user input.

docs.title: Form Semantics and Autofill
docs.text: autocomplete attributes on form fields can expose sensitive values if misconfigured (e.g., autocomplete="cc-number" on an unrelated field). Use correct autocomplete values.

docs.title: <dialog> and Focus
docs.text: The <dialog> element traps focus when opened modally. Ensure that closing it returns focus to the trigger.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect any element's role, name, and state.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility tree — see the full accessibility tree.
  • Firefox DevTools → Accessibility — visualizes landmarks and heading hierarchy.
  • axe DevTools extension — flags missing headings, unlabelled landmarks, and div-button patterns.
  • Lighthouse — audits for semantic structure and missing alt text.
  • Screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver) — verify landmarks and heading navigation work.
  • Keyboard-only walkthrough — Tab through the page; verify focus reaches all controls.
  • HTML validator — validator.w3.org — catches invalid nesting.
  • View source — confirm semantic elements are present in static HTML, not injected by JavaScript after load.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Always. Semantic HTML is the default. Every page benefits from it.
  • Every interactive control — buttons, links, inputs.
  • Every content block — articles, sections, figures.
  • Every form — labels, fieldsets, legends.
  • Every image — alt text or aria-hidden.
  • Every page — landmarks and heading hierarchy.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Never skip semantics for the sake of custom styling. Style with CSS; keep the semantics.
  • Do not use <article> for everything. Not every block is self-contained.
  • Do not add <section> just for styling. Use <div> if there is no heading and no thematic grouping.
  • Do not use headings for visual sizing.
  • Do not use ARIA to paper over bad HTML. Fix the HTML.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• ARIA (WAI-ARIA)
  • Accessibility tree
  • Landmarks

  • Keyboard navigation
  • Focus management
  • Screen readers
  • WCAG 2.2 (POUR)
  • Reader mode
  • HTML Accessibility API Mappings
  • <dialog> element
  • <details> element
  • <search> element
  • lang and dir attributes
  • Autocomplete attributes

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• HTML5 introduced 8 new semantic elements in 2008: <article>, <aside>, <figure>, <figcaption>, <footer>, <header>, <nav>, <section>.
  • The <main> element is only one per page — using more than one is invalid.
  • A <header> is only a banner landmark when it is not nested inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section>.
  • A <section> needs an accessible name to become a region landmark. Without one, it is just a container.
  • Screen reader users navigate by landmarks (D), headings (H), links (K), and form fields (F).
  • The <dialog> element provides native focus trapping — no JavaScript library needed.
  • The <details> element is a native disclosure widget — no JavaScript needed for expand/collapse.
  • The <search> element is new in HTML and provides a semantic landmark for search.
  • Rule 1 of ARIA is "don't use ARIA if native HTML can do it."
  • Pages with ARIA average 59.1 detectable errors — versus 42 on pages without ARIA (WebAIM Million 2026).
  • Reader modes in Safari, Firefox, and Chrome rely on semantic elements to extract articles.
  • AI answer engines parse semantic structure to extract and cite content accurately.
  • The <time> element's datetime attribute provides a machine-readable date — used by search engines and AI systems.
  • Search engines weight <h1> and <main> more heavily than div-based equivalents.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Semantic HTML uses elements that describe meaning, not appearance.
  • It is the foundation of accessibility — everything else builds on it.
  • Landmarks (header, nav, main, aside, footer) let screen reader users jump between regions.
  • Heading hierarchy (h1–h6) creates a navigable outline.
  • Native interactive elements (button, a, input, select, details, dialog) provide keyboard behavior and correct announcements for free.
  • Rule 1 of ARIA: use native HTML whenever it suffices.
  • Semantic HTML benefits everyone — accessibility, SEO, AI, maintainability, robustness.
  • Common mistakes: <div> buttons, skipped heading levels, multiple <h1>, unlabelled navs, missing lang.
  • Test with keyboard only, screen reader, and automated tools.
  • Choose elements by meaning — style with CSS.
  • Semantic HTML is the default — every page benefits from it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a W3C specification that adds semantic roles, states, and properties to HTML elements — enabling assistive technologies like screen readers to interpret dynamic web content and custom user interface controls.

<!-- Native HTML: no ARIA needed -->
<button>Save</button>

<!-- ARIA: adds semantics to a div, but not behavior -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0" aria-pressed="false">Save</div>

The two examples may look identical. But the first is a real button — focusable, keyboard-operable, announced correctly. The second is a <div> with ARIA duct tape — it tells the screen reader it is a button, but without JavaScript it does not behave like one.

ARIA is a specification, not a library or a framework. It defines attributes you can add to HTML elements. It does not add functionality. It only changes how assistive technologies perceive an element.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ARIA serves three specific areas that native HTML does not fully cover:

  • Structural landmarks — indicating the main structural areas of a page (though HTML5 now covers most of this natively).
  • Custom widget roles — defining the roles and properties of UI elements that HTML does not natively express (tabs, sliders, comboboxes, trees, grids).
  • Dynamic content announcement — providing a method for communicating alerts, page changes, and dynamically updated information to assistive technology.

ARIA exists to bridge gaps between what HTML can express and what modern web applications need to express.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Accessibility Stack
│
├── Semantic HTML        ← foundation (native elements, landmarks, headings)
├── ARIA                 ← supplement (roles, states, properties)
├── CSS                  ← contrast, focus styles, layout
├── JavaScript           ← focus management, dynamic state updates
└── Testing              ← screen readers, automated tools

ARIA is not a replacement for semantic HTML. It complements it. When native HTML elements carry the correct semantics — <button>, <nav>, <header>, <input> — those elements provide the most reliably accessible experience. ARIA is for situations where native elements cannot express the required widget behavior, or where dynamic content changes need to be communicated.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
In the mid-2000s, web applications became dynamic. AJAX, JavaScript-rendered interfaces, and custom widgets — tabs, sliders, date pickers, autocomplete comboboxes — proliferated. But HTML had no way to express these complex widgets semantically.

A screen reader sees a <div> with a click handler and announces nothing useful. It sees a <span> that opens a dropdown and has no idea it is a control. It sees a list of <li> elements styled as tabs and cannot distinguish the active tab from the inactive ones.

ARIA was created to solve this: give developers a vocabulary to describe custom widgets to assistive technology.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No widget roles Custom controls announced as generic text No state communication "Expanded/collapsed," "selected," "checked" unknown No live region support Dynamic content changes not announced No relationship attributes Labels, descriptions, and controls not connected No landmark roles No way to skip between page regions

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
ARIA was proposed by Richard Schwerdtfeger at IBM in 2006 and became a W3C Recommendation in 2014. The first version (ARIA 1.0) defined the core vocabulary. ARIA 1.1 added new roles and properties. ARIA 1.2 is the current version, adding refinements for comboboxes, feeds, and other widgets.

The goal: make dynamic web applications perceivable to assistive technology without requiring screen readers to reverse-engineer custom widgets from DOM structure.

docs.title: The Three Types of ARIA Declarations
docs.text:
ARIA defines three categories of attributes:

Category What It Declares Examples Roles What an element is role="button", role="tablist", role="slider" States Dynamic condition aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-checked Properties Supplemental description aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-controls

docs.title: The Minimal ARIA Example
docs.text:
<!-- A custom toggle button (ARIA adds semantics, JS adds behavior) -->
<button
    type="button"
    aria-pressed="false"
    onclick="this.setAttribute('aria-pressed',
             this.getAttribute('aria-pressed') === 'false' ? 'true' : 'false')">
    Mute
</button>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• aria-pressed="false" — declares the toggle state. Screen readers announce "not pressed."
  • The JavaScript updates aria-pressed on click. Without this update, the attribute is a lie — the screen reader announces a state that does not match reality.
  • This is a native <button> with ARIA state — the best of both worlds. Behavior comes from HTML; state communication comes from ARIA.

docs.title: Fully Commented Production Example
docs.text:
<!-- Tabs widget: ARIA declares roles, states, and relationships -->
<div class="tabs">
    <!-- Tab list: declares the container as a tab list -->
    <div role="tablist" aria-label="Settings">
        <!-- Tab: declares role, state, and controls relationship -->
        <button role="tab"
                id="tab-general"
                aria-selected="true"
                aria-controls="panel-general"
                tabindex="0">
            General
        </button>
        <button role="tab"
                id="tab-security"
                aria-selected="false"
                aria-controls="panel-security"
                tabindex="-1">
            Security
        </button>
    </div>

    <!-- Tab panel: declares role and labelledby relationship -->
    <div role="tabpanel"
         id="panel-general"
         aria-labelledby="tab-general"
         tabindex="0">
        <h2>General settings</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </div>

    <div role="tabpanel"
         id="panel-security"
         aria-labelledby="tab-security"
         tabindex="0"
         hidden>
        <h2>Security settings</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </div>
</div>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose role="tablist" Declares the container as a tab list role="tab" Declares each control as a tab aria-selected Indicates which tab is active aria-controls Links the tab to its panel role="tabpanel" Declares each content area as a tab panel aria-labelledby Links the panel back to its tab tabindex Manages keyboard focus within the tab list (roving tabindex pattern)

docs.title: The "Duct Tape" Mental Model
docs.text:
ARIA is duct tape for HTML. It patches gaps where native HTML cannot express what a widget is.

<!-- Native HTML: no duct tape needed -->
<button>Save</button>

<!-- ARIA duct tape: adds role but not behavior -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0" onclick="save()" onkeydown="...">
    Save
</div>

The second example requires manual keyboard handling, manual focus styles, manual disabled states. Native HTML gives all of this for free. The best ARIA is no ARIA — because native HTML already provides both semantics and behavior.

docs.title: The "Three Layers" Mental Model
docs.text:
ARIA operates at three layers:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ROLE       → what is it?                    │
│  role="tab"                                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  STATE      → what condition is it in?       │
│  aria-selected="true"                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  PROPERTY   → what else describes it?        │
│  aria-controls="panel-1"                     │
│  aria-label="Settings"                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A complete ARIA widget needs all three layers. A role without state is incomplete. A state without a relationship property leaves the user lost.

docs.title: The "Five Rules" Mental Model
docs.text:
The W3C defines five rules of ARIA use:

Rule 1: Don't use ARIA if native HTML can do it.
Rule 2: Don't change native semantics unless absolutely necessary.
Rule 3: All interactive ARIA controls must be keyboard operable.
Rule 4: Never use role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" on focusable elements.
Rule 5: All interactive elements must have an accessible name.

These rules are not suggestions — they are the foundation of correct ARIA implementation. Violating them produces the errors that make ARIA harmful.

docs.title: The "ARIA Paradox" Mental Model
docs.text:
The 2026 WebAIM Million report found that pages using ARIA averaged 59.1 detectable accessibility errors, compared to 42 on pages without ARIA.

This is the ARIA paradox: more ARIA does not mean more accessibility. It often means more errors.

Why?

  • Developers add ARIA to fix a scan result, then close the ticket without adding the JavaScript behavior the ARIA requires.
  • aria-expanded="false" is added to a dropdown but never updated when the dropdown opens. The screen reader announces it as permanently closed — worse than no ARIA at all.
  • ARIA roles are added to elements that already have native roles, causing conflicting announcements.
  • aria-hidden="true" is added to interactive elements, making them invisible to screen readers.

docs.title: Concept 1: ARIA Does Not Add Behavior
docs.text:
The single most important fact about ARIA: it changes only how assistive technologies perceive an element. It does not add functionality or keyboard behavior.

<!-- A div with role="button" tells a screen reader it's a button -->
<!-- But without JavaScript, it won't respond to Enter or Space -->
<div role="button">Save</div>

A native <button> is focusable, keyboard-operable, and announced correctly — all by default. A <div role="button"> requires tabindex="0", onkeydown handlers for Enter and Space, and focus styles. And even then, it may not behave identically across browsers and screen readers.

docs.title: Concept 2: The Five Rules of ARIA
docs.text:
Rule Meaning Rule 1 Prefer native HTML elements that already have the required semantics and behavior Rule 2 Do not override native element semantics unless absolutely necessary Rule 3 All interactive ARIA controls must be keyboard operable Rule 4 Never use role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" on focusable elements Rule 5 All interactive elements must have an accessible name

Rule 1 is the most important: if native HTML can do it, use native HTML.

docs.title: Concept 3: Roles
docs.text:
Roles declare what an element is. There are six categories of roles:

Category Examples Purpose Landmark banner, navigation, main, complementary, contentinfo Page structure (HTML5 covers most) Widget button, checkbox, tab, slider, combobox Interactive controls Document structure article, heading, list, table Content organization (HTML5 covers most) Window dialog, alertdialog Modal windows Live region alert, status, log Dynamic content Abstract widget, input, select Never use directly

Never use abstract roles. They are for the specification's internal taxonomy, not for developers.

docs.title: Concept 4: States
docs.text:
States describe the current condition of a widget. They change at runtime.

State Applies To Meaning aria-expanded Combobox, menu, disclosure Open or closed aria-selected Tab, option, grid cell Selected or not aria-checked Checkbox, radio, switch Checked, unchecked, mixed aria-pressed Toggle button Pressed or not aria-disabled Any widget Disabled aria-hidden Any element Hidden from assistive technology aria-busy Live region Content is updating aria-current Link, step Current item in a set

States must be updated dynamically. A static aria-expanded="false" that never changes is worse than no attribute at all.

docs.title: Concept 5: Properties
docs.text:
Properties provide supplemental descriptive information that does not change frequently.

Property Purpose aria-label Direct string label aria-labelledby Reference to another element for label aria-describedby Reference to longer description aria-controls Relationship to controlled element aria-owns Relationship to owned elements aria-live Politeness level for live region aria-atomic Whether to announce entire region aria-relevant What changes to announce aria-haspopup Whether element opens a popup aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax Slider/range values

docs.title: Concept 6: The Accessible Name Computation
docs.text:
The accessible name is what a screen reader announces. The computation follows this priority:

1. aria-labelledby    → references other elements
2. aria-label         → direct string
3. Native label       → <label>, alt, <caption>
4. Text content       → for buttons, links
5. title attribute    → last resort

If aria-labelledby is present, it overrides aria-label and all other sources.

docs.title: Concept 7: Live Regions
docs.text:
Live regions announce dynamic content changes to screen readers without moving focus.

Attribute Politeness Use Case aria-live="polite" Waits for user idle Status updates, chat messages aria-live="assertive" Interrupts immediately Alerts, errors role="alert" Implicit assertive Error messages, urgent warnings role="status" Implicit polite General status updates role="log" Implicit polite Chat logs, activity feeds 
<div role="alert" id="error-message"></div>

<script>
    document.getElementById('error-message').textContent =
        'Please enter a valid email address.';
    // Screen reader announces immediately
</script>

docs.title: Concept 8: aria-hidden — Use With Caution
docs.text:
aria-hidden="true" removes an element from the accessibility tree. It is useful for:

  • Decorative icons inside buttons that already have aria-label.
  • Off-screen content that should not be announced.

It is dangerous when applied to interactive elements. aria-hidden="true" on a focusable button makes it invisible to screen readers but still reachable by keyboard — a keyboard trap. This is the most common and severe ARIA implementation error and automated testing catches only 30–40% of such cases.

docs.title: Concept 9: aria-label vs aria-labelledby
docs.text:
<!-- aria-label: direct string -->
<button aria-label="Close dialog">✕</button>

<!-- aria-labelledby: references visible text -->
<h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm deletion</h2>
<div role="dialog" aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
    ...
</div>

Prefer aria-labelledby when visible text exists — it keeps the label and visible text synchronized. Use aria-label only when no visible label exists.

docs.title: Concept 10: Redundant Roles
docs.text:
Adding a role that an element already has natively is redundant and potentially harmful.

<!-- Redundant: button already has role="button" -->
<button role="button">OK</button>

<!-- Redundant: nav already has role="navigation" -->
<nav role="navigation">...</nav>

<!-- Redundant: main already has role="main" -->
<main role="main">...</main>

These are unnecessary. The native roles already provide the correct semantics. Adding a redundant role can cause conflicting announcements in some screen readers.

docs.title: Concept 11: ARIA and Keyboard Navigation
docs.text:
Rule 3: all interactive ARIA controls must be keyboard operable. ARIA declares semantics, but it does not add keyboard functionality.

If you build a custom widget with ARIA roles, you must also implement:

  • tabindex management (roving tabindex for composite widgets).
  • Keyboard event handlers for Enter, Space, Arrow keys, Home, End, Escape.
  • Focus management when the widget opens, closes, or updates.

docs.title: Concept 12: Focus Management in SPAs
docs.text:
Focus management is the most common source of accessibility regressions in single-page applications. When a route changes, focus must be moved deliberately.

// After route change, move focus to the main heading
function onRouteChange() {
    const heading = document.querySelector('main h1');
    heading.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
    heading.focus();
}

docs.title: Concept 13: aria-current
docs.text:
Indicates the current item within a set — useful for navigation.

<nav aria-label="Main">
    <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
</nav>

Screen readers announce "Home, current page."

docs.title: Concept 14: aria-describedby for Hints and Errors
docs.text:
<label for="password">Password</label>
<input id="password" type="password"
       aria-describedby="password-hint password-error">
<span id="password-hint">Must be at least 8 characters.</span>
<span id="password-error" role="alert"></span>

Screen readers announce the hint after the label, and the error when populated.

docs.title: Concept 15: Testing with Real Assistive Technology
docs.text:
Browser simulators do not reliably reflect actual screen reader behavior. Testing with real screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack) is essential.

Automated tools catch only 30–50% of accessibility issues. Manual testing with assistive technology catches the rest.

docs.title: Concept 16: ARIA and Framework Components
docs.text:
UI frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) often generate ARIA-heavy markup. This can be helpful — or harmful. Always verify:

  • Are roles correct for the widget type?
  • Are states updated dynamically?
  • Is keyboard behavior implemented?
  • Is the accessible name correct?

Many frameworks ship components with incorrect ARIA. Do not assume framework ARIA is correct.

docs.title: Concept 17: ARIA and LLM-Generated Code
docs.text: LLM-generated code often over-relies on ARIA where native semantic HTML would be more appropriate. The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) is a useful reference, but its patterns are not gospel. Favor semantic HTML first; use ARIA only where required.

docs.title: Concept 18: The role Attribute and Fallback
docs.text:
If a browser or assistive technology does not support a role, it falls back to the default role of the element.

<div role="slider">  <!-- If slider role unsupported, falls back to generic -->

This is why native elements are more reliable — they have well-established default roles.

docs.title: Concept 19: ARIA Version
docs.text: ARIA 1.2 is the current version. It added refinements for comboboxes, feeds, and other widgets. ARIA 1.3 is in development.

docs.title: Concept 20: The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)
docs.text:
The W3C maintains the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) — a collection of design patterns and examples for building accessible widgets. It includes keyboard interaction patterns, ARIA usage, and example implementations.

The APG is a valuable reference, but it is not the specification. Some patterns are complex and may not be necessary for every project.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: ARIA in the Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
1.  HTML is parsed.
    │
    ▼
2.  Native roles are assigned from element names.
    │
    ▼
3.  ARIA attributes are read:
    │   ├── role → overrides native role (if valid)
    │   ├── aria-* → sets states and properties
    │   └── aria-hidden → removes from tree
    │
    ▼
4.  Accessibility tree is built:
    │   ├── Role (from element or ARIA)
    │   ├── Name (from aria-labelledby, aria-label, etc.)
    │   ├── State (from aria-expanded, aria-selected, etc.)
    │   └── Properties (from aria-controls, aria-describedby, etc.)
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader reads the tree.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Live Region Announcement
docs.text:
1.  Live region exists in the DOM.
    │
    ▼
2.  Content changes (via JavaScript).
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser detects change in live region.
    │
    ▼
4.  Accessibility API fires an event.
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader announces the new content.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Toggle Button State Update
docs.text:
1.  User clicks the toggle button.
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript updates aria-pressed:
    │   btn.setAttribute('aria-pressed',
    │       btn.getAttribute('aria-pressed') === 'false' ? 'true' : 'false');
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser detects ARIA state change.
    │
    ▼
4.  Accessibility API fires state change event.
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader announces "pressed" or "not pressed."

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree and ARIA
docs.text:
The accessibility tree is a parallel representation of the DOM, optimized for assistive technology. ARIA modifies this tree:

  • role changes the node's role in the tree.
  • aria-* attributes add states and properties.
  • aria-hidden="true" removes the node and its subtree.
  • role="presentation" removes the node's semantics but keeps its children.

docs.title: Role Precedence
docs.text:
When both a native role and an ARIA role are present:

  1. ARIA role overrides the native role.
  2. If the ARIA role is invalid, the native role is used.
  3. If the ARIA role is abstract, behavior is undefined.

This is why redundant roles are harmful — they can conflict with native semantics.

docs.title: State and Property Processing
docs.text:
States and properties are read by the browser and exposed via the platform accessibility API:

  • Windows: IAccessible2, UIA
  • macOS: NSAccessibility
  • Linux: ATK/AT-SPI

Screen readers query these APIs to build their announcements.

docs.title: ARIA and the DOM
docs.text: ARIA attributes do not affect DOM structure, CSS rendering, or JavaScript behavior. They are metadata only — read by the accessibility API, invisible to the user.

docs.title: The aria-labelledby Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Find all elements referenced by ID in aria-labelledby.
  2. Concatenate their text content.
  3. Use the result as the accessible name.

If multiple IDs are referenced, the names are concatenated in order.

docs.title: ARIA Implementation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Can native HTML express this widget?
    │   ├── Yes → Use native HTML. No ARIA needed.
    │   └── No  → Continue.
    │
    ▼
2.  Choose the correct ARIA role from the specification.
    │
    ▼
3.  Add required states (aria-expanded, aria-selected, etc.).
    │
    ▼
4.  Add relationship properties (aria-controls, aria-labelledby, etc.).
    │
    ▼
5.  Implement keyboard behavior (Enter, Space, arrows, Escape).
    │
    ▼
6.  Implement focus management (roving tabindex, focus trapping).
    │
    ▼
7.  Update ARIA states dynamically in JavaScript.
    │
    ▼
8.  Test with keyboard only.
    │
    ▼
9.  Test with real screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver).
    │
    ▼
10. Fix, re-test, repeat.

docs.title: ARIA Audit Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Inspect all ARIA attributes in the DOM.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check for redundant roles.
    │
    ▼
3.  Check for static states (aria-expanded that never changes).
    │
    ▼
4.  Check for aria-hidden on focusable elements.
    │
    ▼
5.  Check for missing accessible names.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test keyboard navigation.
    │
    ▼
7.  Test with screen reader.
    │
    ▼
8.  Fix, re-test, repeat.

docs.title: Example 1: Toggle Button
docs.text:
<button type="button"
        aria-pressed="false"
        onclick="this.setAttribute('aria-pressed',
                 this.getAttribute('aria-pressed') === 'false' ? 'true' : 'false')">
    Mute
</button>

Code Breakdown:

  • Native <button> — keyboard-operable, focusable.
  • aria-pressed — declares the toggle state.
  • JavaScript updates the state on click.
  • Screen reader announces "Mute, toggle button, not pressed" → "Mute, toggle button, pressed."

docs.title: Example 2: Accessible Tabs
docs.text:
<div role="tablist" aria-label="Account settings">
    <button role="tab" id="tab-profile" aria-selected="true"
            aria-controls="panel-profile" tabindex="0">
        Profile
    </button>
    <button role="tab" id="tab-billing" aria-selected="false"
            aria-controls="panel-billing" tabindex="-1">
        Billing
    </button>
</div>

<div role="tabpanel" id="panel-profile"
     aria-labelledby="tab-profile" tabindex="0">
    <h2>Profile settings</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</div>

<div role="tabpanel" id="panel-billing"
     aria-labelledby="tab-billing" tabindex="0" hidden>
    <h2>Billing settings</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</div>

Code Breakdown:

  • role="tablist" — declares the tab container.
  • role="tab" — declares each tab.
  • aria-selected — indicates the active tab.
  • aria-controls — links tab to panel.
  • role="tabpanel" and aria-labelledby — links panel back to tab.
  • tabindex — roving tabindex: only the active tab is in the tab order.

docs.title: Example 3: Live Region for Form Errors
docs.text:
<form>
    <label for="email">Email address</label>
    <input id="email" type="email" required
           aria-describedby="email-error">
    <span id="email-error" role="alert"></span>

    <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

<script>
    document.querySelector('form').addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
        const email = document.getElementById('email');
        const error = document.getElementById('email-error');
        if (!email.validity.valid) {
            e.preventDefault();
            error.textContent = 'Please enter a valid email address.';
        }
    });
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • role="alert" — implicitly aria-live="assertive" and aria-atomic="true".
  • When textContent is set, the screen reader announces immediately.
  • aria-describedby links the error to the input.

docs.title: Example 4: Accessible Modal
docs.text:
<div role="dialog"
     aria-modal="true"
     aria-labelledby="dialog-title"
     id="confirm-dialog">
    <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm deletion</h2>
    <p>This action cannot be undone.</p>
    <button onclick="closeDialog()">Cancel</button>
    <button onclick="confirmDelete()">Delete</button>
</div>

Code Breakdown:

  • role="dialog" — declares the modal.
  • aria-modal="true" — tells assistive technology the rest of the page is inert.
  • aria-labelledby — links to the dialog title.

docs.title: Example 5: Live Region for Status Updates
docs.text:
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" id="status-message"></div>

<script>
    function updateStatus(message) {
        document.getElementById('status-message').textContent = message;
    }
    updateStatus('Settings saved successfully.');
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • role="status" — implicitly aria-live="polite".
  • aria-live="polite" — waits for the user to be idle before announcing.
  • Screen reader announces "Settings saved successfully" without interrupting.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
