docs.text: Use Case ARIA Approach Toggle button aria-pressed Tabs role="tablist", role="tab", role="tabpanel", aria-selected, aria-controls Accordion aria-expanded, aria-controls Modal dialog role="dialog", aria-modal="true", aria-labelledby Live region role="alert", role="status", aria-live Combobox role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-controls Slider role="slider", aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax Tree role="tree", role="treeitem", aria-expanded Navigation aria-current="page" Progress bar role="progressbar", aria-valuenow

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use native HTML first. Why: native elements have behavior; ARIA only has semantics.
  2. Use ARIA only when native HTML cannot express the required semantics. Why: pages with ARIA average more errors than pages without.
  3. Never override native semantics with redundant roles. Why: it confuses assistive technology.
  4. Ensure all interactive ARIA controls are keyboard operable. Why: ARIA does not add keyboard behavior.
  5. Update ARIA states dynamically. Why: a static aria-expanded="false" is worse than no attribute.
  6. Never use aria-hidden="true" on focusable elements. Why: it creates a keyboard trap.
  7. Provide accessible names for all interactive elements. Why: screen readers need a name to announce.
  8. Prefer aria-labelledby over aria-label when visible text exists. Why: keeps label and visible text synchronized.
  9. Use role="alert" for urgent messages. Why: it interrupts immediately.
  10. Use role="status" for non-urgent updates. Why: it waits for user idle.
  11. Test with real screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver). Why: browser simulators do not reflect actual behavior.
  12. Test with keyboard only. Why: ARIA widgets must be keyboard-operable.
  13. Use the APG as a reference, not gospel. Why: its patterns are complex and may not suit every project.
  14. Do not use abstract roles. Why: they are for the specification's internal taxonomy.
  15. Verify framework-generated ARIA. Why: frameworks often ship incorrect ARIA.
  16. Use aria-current for navigation. Why: it identifies the current item in a set.
  17. Use aria-describedby for hints and errors. Why: it links supplemental information to inputs.
  18. Manage focus in SPAs and modals. Why: focus management is the most common regression source.
  19. Keep ARIA simple. Why: complex ARIA is more likely to be wrong.
  20. Audit ARIA regularly. Why: ARIA decays as content and behavior change.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: aria-hidden="true" on Focusable Elements
docs.text:
<button aria-hidden="true">Save</button>

Why it's wrong: The button is invisible to screen readers but still reachable by keyboard — a keyboard trap.

✅ Correct:

<button>Save</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Static aria-expanded
docs.text:
<button aria-expanded="false">Menu</button>
<!-- Never updated when menu opens -->

Why it's wrong: The screen reader announces the menu as permanently closed — worse than no ARIA at all.

✅ Correct:

<button aria-expanded="false" id="menu-btn">Menu</button>
<script>
    btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const expanded = btn.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
        btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', !expanded);
    });
</script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Redundant Roles
docs.text:
<button role="button">OK</button>
<nav role="navigation">...</nav>

Why it's wrong: The native roles already provide the correct semantics.

✅ Correct:

<button>OK</button>
<nav>...</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: aria-label on Non-Interactive Elements
docs.text:
<p aria-label="Important paragraph">Some text.</p>

Why it's wrong: aria-label on static text is often ignored by screen readers and can cause confusion.

✅ Correct: Use visible text or aria-describedby if needed.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Accessible Name on Icon Button
docs.text:
<button>
    <svg>...</svg>
</button>

Why it's wrong: The button has no accessible name; screen readers announce nothing useful.

✅ Correct:

<button aria-label="Close dialog">
    <svg aria-hidden="true">...</svg>
</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using role="button" Without Keyboard Handler
docs.text:
<div role="button" onclick="save()">Save</div>

Why it's wrong: ARIA declares semantics but does not add keyboard behavior.

✅ Correct: Use <button> or add tabindex="0" and keyboard handlers.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Misspelled ARIA Attribute
docs.text:
<button arialabel="Close">X</button>

Why it's wrong: arialabel is not a valid attribute; the button has no accessible name.

✅ Correct:

<button aria-label="Close">X</button>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• ARIA attributes have no rendering cost — they are metadata only.
  • Live regions have minimal overhead — content updates trigger accessibility events.
  • Complex ARIA widgets may add JavaScript overhead for state management.
  • Focus management is cheap — a single .focus() call.
  • Automated testing catches some ARIA errors but adds CI time.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Prefer native HTML over ARIA-heavy custom widgets.
  2. Keep live regions minimal.
  3. Update ARIA states only when they change.
  4. Use roving tabindex for composite widgets rather than managing tabindex on every child.

docs.title: ARIA and DOM Injection
docs.text: Dynamically setting aria-label from untrusted input could expose data. Escape or validate any ARIA values generated from user input.

docs.title: aria-hidden and Content Leakage
docs.text: aria-hidden="true" removes elements from the accessibility tree but not the DOM. Sensitive content hidden this way is still in the DOM and accessible via DevTools.

docs.title: Live Region Abuse
docs.text: Rapidly updating live regions can overwhelm screen reader users. Use aria-live="polite" for non-urgent updates and avoid spamming.

docs.title: Framework ARIA and Supply Chain
docs.text: Framework components with incorrect ARIA can introduce accessibility vulnerabilities. Audit third-party components.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect any element's role, name, and state.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility tree — see the full accessibility tree with ARIA applied.
  • Firefox DevTools → Accessibility — visualizes ARIA roles and landmarks.
  • axe DevTools extension — flags ARIA errors and misuse.
  • Lighthouse — audits for ARIA issues.
  • Screen reader testing — NVDA (Windows), VoiceOver (macOS/iOS), TalkBack (Android).
  • getComputedAccessibleNode() — experimental API for checking accessible name and role.
  • element.ariaExpanded — DOM property for reading ARIA state.
  • document.querySelectorAll('[role]') — list all roles on the page.
  • document.querySelectorAll('[aria-hidden="true"]') — find hidden elements.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• When native HTML cannot express the widget semantics — tabs, sliders, comboboxes, trees, grids.
  • When dynamic content needs to be announced — live regions, alerts, status updates.
  • When relationships need to be communicated — aria-controls, aria-describedby, aria-labelledby.
  • When states need to be communicated — aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed.
  • When native HTML has gaps — but only after verifying native HTML cannot do it.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• When native HTML can do it. Use <button>, <nav>, <input>, <dialog>, <details>.
  • When ARIA would be redundant. Do not add role="button" to <button>.
  • When you cannot implement the required behavior. A role without keyboard behavior is worse than no ARIA.
  • When you cannot test with real assistive technology. Untested ARIA is risky ARIA.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Semantic HTML
  • Accessibility tree
  • WAI-ARIA specification
  • ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)
  • Accessible name computation
  • Live regions
  • Focus management
  • Keyboard navigation
  • Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack)
  • WCAG 2.2
  • Roles, states, and properties
  • aria-hidden
  • aria-label / aria-labelledby
  • aria-expanded
  • role="alert" / role="status"

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Pages using ARIA averaged 59.1 detectable errors versus 42 on pages without ARIA, per the 2026 WebAIM Million report.
  • In 2025, WebAIM detected over 105 million ARIA attributes across the top million home pages — averaging 106 per page.
  • 35% of ARIA menus introduced new accessibility barriers because of missing required interactions or roles.
  • ARIA does not add behavior — it only changes how assistive technologies perceive an element.
  • The first rule of ARIA is "don't use ARIA if native HTML can do it."
  • aria-hidden="true" on interactive elements is the most common and severe ARIA implementation error.
  • aria-labelledby overrides aria-label in the accessible name computation.
  • A static aria-expanded that never updates is worse than no ARIA at all.
  • ARIA was proposed in 2006 and became a W3C Recommendation in 2014.
  • ARIA 1.2 is the current version — ARIA 1.3 is in development.
  • Browser simulators do not reliably reflect actual screen reader behavior.
  • Automated tools catch only 30–50% of accessibility issues.
  • LLM-generated code often over-relies on ARIA where native semantic HTML would be more appropriate.
  • The best ARIA is no ARIA — because native HTML already provides both semantics and behavior.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• ARIA adds semantic roles, states, and properties to HTML elements for assistive technology.
  • It does not add behavior — it only changes how assistive technologies perceive an element.
  • Rule 1: prefer native HTML — use ARIA only when native HTML cannot express the required semantics.
  • The five rules of ARIA govern correct implementation: native first, no redundant roles, keyboard operable, no aria-hidden on focusable elements, accessible names.
  • Pages with ARIA average 59.1 errors versus 42 on pages without ARIA.
  • States must be updated dynamically — static ARIA is worse than no ARIA.
  • Live regions announce dynamic content — role="alert" for urgent, role="status" for polite.
  • aria-labelledby overrides aria-label in the accessible name computation.
  • Never use aria-hidden="true" on focusable elements — it creates keyboard traps.
  • Test with real screen readers — browser simulators are unreliable.
  • The APG is a reference, not gospel — patterns are complex and may not suit every project.
  • The best ARIA is no ARIA — native HTML provides both semantics and behavior.
  • Audit ARIA regularly — ARIA decays as content and behavior change.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Landmark roles are a set of eight ARIA roles that identify the major structural regions of a web page — header, navigation, main content, complementary content, footer, search, form, and generic region. They allow assistive technology users to jump directly to any major section of a page without tabbing through every element in between.

<header>...</header>       <!-- banner landmark -->
<nav>...</nav>             <!-- navigation landmark -->
<main>...</main>           <!-- main landmark -->
<aside>...</aside>         <!-- complementary landmark -->
<footer>...</footer>       <!-- contentinfo landmark -->

In modern HTML, each landmark is produced by a native semantic element. ARIA landmark roles exist for cases where native elements cannot be used — but in most cases today, the correct approach is to use the native element and let the browser generate the landmark automatically.

The eight landmark roles are:

Role Native HTML Purpose banner <header> (top-level) Site-wide header navigation <nav> Navigation links main <main> Primary content complementary <aside> Supporting content contentinfo <footer> (top-level) Site-wide footer form <form> (labelled) Form region region <section> (labelled) Named generic region search <search> Search functionality

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Landmarks serve several essential purposes:

  • Fast navigation — screen reader users jump between regions with a single keystroke (D key in NVDA/JAWS, rotor in VoiceOver).
  • Context awareness — users know immediately which region they are in.
  • Reduced cognitive load — no need to tab through every link in the navigation to reach the main content.
  • Consistent structure — landmarks create a predictable page skeleton across a site.
  • Skip navigation — landmarks are the primary mechanism for bypassing repeated content.
  • SEO benefits — search engines understand the page hierarchy more clearly.

A landmark is the difference between a screen reader user navigating a page in 3 seconds versus 30 seconds.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Page Structure
│
├── <header>           → banner landmark
│   └── <nav>          → navigation landmark
│
├── <main>             → main landmark
│   ├── <article>      → (content, not a landmark)
│   ├── <section aria-label>  → region landmark
│   └── <form aria-label>     → form landmark
│
├── <aside>            → complementary landmark
│
├── <search>           → search landmark
│
└── <footer>           → contentinfo landmark

Landmarks are the top-level skeleton of the page. They are not for every grouping — only for the major structural regions that a user would want to jump to.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A screen reader user cannot scan a page visually. They cannot glance at the top and see "there's a nav bar, a sidebar, a main article, and a footer." Instead, they must navigate linearly — through every link, every paragraph, every form field.

On a page with 40 navigation links, reaching the main content requires 40 Tab presses. Without landmarks, the navigation is a wall of links with no escape.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No structural markers Screen reader users had to tab through everything No skip mechanism Navigation could not be bypassed No context announcement Users did not know which region they were in No consistent skeleton Every page required new orientation

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
ARIA 1.0 (2014) introduced landmark roles to give screen readers a way to identify structural regions. HTML5 elements — <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <footer> — were added around the same time, and the HTML Accessibility API Mappings specification defined that these native elements produce landmark roles automatically.

Landmarks exist because screen reader users need a structural map of the page — not a linear stream of content. They are the screen reader equivalent of a visual layout.

docs.title: The Native HTML Approach (Recommended)
docs.text:
<body>
    <a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

    <header>
        <nav aria-label="Main">
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
                <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
    </header>

    <main id="main-content">
        <h1>Welcome</h1>
        <p>Page content.</p>
    </main>

    <aside aria-label="Related articles">
        <h2>Related</h2>
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/post-1">Post 1</a></li>
        </ul>
    </aside>

    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 Acme</p>
    </footer>
</body>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element Landmark Role Notes <header> (top-level) banner Only when not nested in <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, <section> <nav aria-label="Main"> navigation Labelled because there may be multiple navs <main id="main-content"> main Only one per page; the skip link target <aside aria-label="Related articles"> complementary Optional label improves clarity <footer> (top-level) contentinfo Only when not nested

docs.title: The ARIA Approach (When Native HTML Cannot Be Used)
docs.text:
<!-- Only use when a native element is impossible (rare) -->
<div role="banner">
    <div role="navigation" aria-label="Main">
        <a href="/">Home</a>
    </div>
</div>

<div role="main">
    <h1>Page content</h1>
</div>

<div role="contentinfo">
    <p>© 2026 Acme</p>
</div>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• role="banner" — declares a top-level header region.
  • role="navigation" — declares a navigation region; aria-label distinguishes it.
  • role="main" — declares the primary content region.
  • role="contentinfo" — declares a top-level footer region.

Rule: Use native HTML whenever possible. ARIA roles are a fallback, not a first choice.

docs.title: The <search> Element
docs.text:
<search>
    <form action="/search">
        <label for="q">Search</label>
        <input id="q" type="search" name="q">
        <button type="submit">Go</button>
    </form>
</search>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• <search> — new HTML element; produces a search landmark.
  • Browser support is expanding; use role="search" on a <form> as a fallback if wider support is needed.

docs.title: The "Building Directory" Mental Model
docs.text:
Imagine walking into a large office building. At the entrance, there is a directory listing every floor and department:

Floor 1: Reception (header)
Floor 2: Main offices (main)
Floor 3: Conference rooms (aside)
Floor 4: Human resources (nav)
Floor 5: Mail room (footer)

Landmarks are the same: they tell a screen reader user "here are the regions of this page, and here's how to jump to each one."

docs.title: The "Landmark vs Content" Mental Model
docs.text:
Landmarks are not for every grouping. They are for top-level structural regions:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  <header>           ← landmark: banner       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  <nav>              ← landmark: navigation   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                              │
│  <main>             ← landmark: main         │
│    <article>        ← NOT a landmark         │
│    <section>        ← NOT a landmark (unless labelled)
│    <form>           ← NOT a landmark (unless labelled)
│                                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  <aside>            ← landmark: complementary│
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  <footer>           ← landmark: contentinfo  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Not everything needs to be a landmark. Only the regions a user would want to jump to.

docs.title: The "Landmark Rules" Mental Model
docs.text:
Three strict rules govern landmarks:

Rule 1: Only one <main> per page.
Rule 2: Only one top-level <header> and <footer> per page.
Rule 3: Nested <header> and <footer> (inside article/section) are NOT landmarks.

Violating these breaks the landmark model and confuses screen reader users.

docs.title: The "Landmark Labelling" Mental Model
docs.text:
When a landmark type appears multiple times, it must be labelled:

<nav>                     → "navigation"
<nav aria-label="Main">   → "Main navigation"
<nav aria-label="Footer"> → "Footer navigation"

Without labels, screen readers announce both as "navigation" — the user cannot distinguish them.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Eight Landmark Roles
docs.text:
There are exactly eight ARIA landmark roles:

Role HTML Equivalent Count Per Page banner <header> (top-level) 1 complementary <aside> Multiple contentinfo <footer> (top-level) 1 form <form> (labelled) Multiple main <main> 1 navigation <nav> Multiple region <section> (labelled) Multiple search <search> 1

No other ARIA role is a landmark.

docs.title: Concept 2: Native Elements Produce Landmarks Automatically
docs.text:
Modern browsers map native HTML elements to landmark roles via the HTML Accessibility API Mappings specification:

<header> (top-level) → role="banner"
<nav>                → role="navigation"
<main>               → role="main"
<aside>              → role="complementary"
<footer> (top-level) → role="contentinfo"
<form> (labelled)    → role="form"
<section> (labelled) → role="region"
<search>             → role="search"

This is why redundant ARIA is harmful: adding role="navigation" to <nav> produces a redundant, sometimes conflicting, role.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Top-Level Rule for <header> and <footer>
docs.text:
A <header> or <footer> becomes a landmark only when it is top-level — meaning it is not nested inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section>.

<body>
    <header>              <!-- banner landmark ✅ -->
    <main>
        <article>
            <header>...</header>  <!-- NOT a landmark ✅ (correct) -->
        </article>
    </main>
    <footer>              <!-- contentinfo landmark ✅ -->
</body>

This allows pages to have nested <header> and <footer> elements inside articles and sections without creating duplicate landmarks.

docs.title: Concept 4: The One-Main Rule
docs.text:
<main> must appear exactly once per page. Using more than one is invalid and breaks the landmark model.

<!-- Wrong: two main elements -->
<main>Home content</main>
<main>Sidebar content</main>

<!-- Correct: one main, sidebar is aside -->
<main>
    <section>Home content</section>
    <aside>Sidebar content</aside>
</main>

docs.title: Concept 5: Labelling Landmarks
docs.text:
When a landmark type appears more than once, it must be labelled with aria-label or aria-labelledby:

<nav aria-label="Main">
    <ul>...</ul>
</nav>

<nav aria-label="Footer">
    <ul>...</ul>
</nav>

Screen readers announce "Main navigation" and "Footer navigation." Without labels, both are announced as "navigation" — the user cannot tell them apart.

docs.title: Concept 6: The region Role
docs.text:
role="region" (or <section> with an accessible name) is a generic landmark for any named content region. It is useful for creating jump targets that no other landmark covers.

<section aria-labelledby="news-heading">
    <h2 id="news-heading">Latest News</h2>
    <ul>...</ul>
</section>

Screen readers announce this as a landmark named "Latest News."

Important: A <section> without an accessible name does NOT become a landmark. It is just a <div>.

docs.title: Concept 7: The form Role
docs.text:
role="form" (or <form> with an accessible name) creates a landmark for a form region.

<form aria-labelledby="search-heading">
    <h2 id="search-heading">Search</h2>
    <label for="q">Query</label>
    <input id="q" type="search" name="q">
</form>

Important: A <form> without an accessible name does NOT become a landmark.

docs.title: Concept 8: The search Role
docs.text:
role="search" (or the new <search> element) identifies a region containing search functionality.

<search>
    <form action="/search">
        <label for="q">Search</label>
        <input id="q" type="search" name="q">
        <button type="submit">Go</button>
    </form>
</search>

<search> is the modern element; role="search" on a <form> or <div> is the ARIA fallback.

docs.title: Concept 9: Screen Reader Landmark Navigation
docs.text:
Each major screen reader supports landmark navigation:

Screen Reader Landmark Key NVDA (Windows) D (next landmark) JAWS (Windows) ; or R VoiceOver (macOS) Control+Option+U → Landmarks rotor VoiceOver (iOS) Rotor → Landmarks TalkBack (Android) Swipe up then down → Landmarks

docs.title: Concept 10: Skip Links and Landmarks
docs.text:
The classic "skip to main content" link is the original landmark navigation technique. When landmarks are present, screen reader users can skip the skip link and use landmark navigation directly. But skip links remain useful for keyboard-only users who do not use a screen reader.

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>
...
<main id="main-content">...</main>

docs.title: Concept 11: Landmarks in the Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
Landmarks appear as nodes in the accessibility tree. Screen readers query the tree for landmark roles and expose them as jump targets.

Accessibility Tree
├── banner
│   └── navigation (Main)
├── main
│   ├── heading (h1)
│   └── region (Latest News)
├── complementary (Related articles)
└── contentinfo

docs.title: Concept 12: Landmarks and <article>
docs.text:
<article> is not a landmark. It is a content grouping element, not a structural region. Screen readers do not expose articles as landmarks.

However, <article> has its own navigation pattern (A key in NVDA) and can be reached via the article rotor in VoiceOver.

docs.title: Concept 13: Landmarks and <div>
docs.text:
A <div> has no landmark role. It is invisible to assistive technology unless ARIA is added.

<!-- No landmark -->
<div class="sidebar">...</div>

<!-- Complementary landmark -->
<aside class="sidebar">...</aside>

<!-- ARIA fallback (only if <aside> cannot be used) -->
<div class="sidebar" role="complementary">...</div>

docs.title: Concept 14: Landmarks and CSS
docs.text:
Landmarks can be styled like any other element:

nav { background: #f5f5f5; padding: 1rem; }
main { max-width: 800px; margin: 0 auto; }
aside { float: right; width: 300px; }

The landmark role does not affect styling. It only affects the accessibility tree.

docs.title: Concept 15: The <search> Element Support
docs.text: The <search> element was added to HTML in 2023. It is supported in modern browsers (Chrome 118+, Firefox 118+, Safari 17+). For older browsers, use role="search" on a <form> or <div>.

docs.title: Concept 16: Nested Landmarks
docs.text:
A landmark can contain another landmark of a different type:

<main>
    <section aria-label="Newsletter">
        <form aria-label="Subscribe">
            ...
        </form>
    </section>
</main>

This produces a main landmark containing a region landmark containing a form landmark.

docs.title: Concept 17: Landmarks and HTML Outlines
docs.text: Before HTML5, the "HTML outline algorithm" was supposed to compute a document structure from headings and sectioning elements. It was never implemented in browsers. Landmarks are the practical, browser-supported version of document structure.

docs.title: Concept 18: Landmarks and Reader Mode
docs.text: Reader modes in Safari, Firefox, and Chrome use landmarks to identify the "main article" of the page. A <main> landmark helps reader mode extract the right content.

docs.title: Concept 19: Landmarks and AI Systems
docs.text: AI answer engines parse page structure to extract content. Landmarks — especially <main> and <article> — help AI systems identify the primary content and exclude navigation, sidebars, and footers.

docs.title: Concept 20: Landmarks vs Headings
docs.text:
Landmarks and headings are complementary navigation mechanisms:

Mechanism Purpose Key Landmarks Jump between page regions D (NVDA) Headings Jump between content sections H (NVDA) Links Jump between link targets K (NVDA) Form fields Jump between form controls F (NVDA)

Both are needed. Landmarks give the macro structure; headings give the micro structure.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Landmark Detection
docs.text:
1.  Browser parses HTML.
    │
    ▼
2.  For each element, checks if it produces a landmark role:
    │   ├── <header> top-level? → banner
    │   ├── <nav>? → navigation
    │   ├── <main>? → main
    │   ├── <aside>? → complementary
    │   ├── <footer> top-level? → contentinfo
    │   ├── <form> with name? → form
    │   ├── <section> with name? → region
    │   └── <search>? → search
    │
    ▼
3.  Adds landmark nodes to accessibility tree.
    │
    ▼
4.  Exposes landmarks via platform API.
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader registers landmarks as jump targets.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Landmark Navigation
docs.text:
1.  Screen reader user presses D.
    │
    ▼
2.  Screen reader queries accessibility tree for next landmark.
    │
    ▼
3.  Focus/reading cursor moves to the landmark.
    │
    ▼
4.  Screen reader announces:
    │   "Navigation landmark, Main"
    │
    ▼
5.  User presses D again to reach the next landmark.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Skip Link Activation
docs.text:
1.  User tabs to the skip link (first focusable element).
    │
    ▼
2.  Skip link becomes visible.
    │
    ▼
3.  User presses Enter.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser scrolls to #main-content and moves focus there.
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader announces the main region.

docs.title: The Accessibility API Mappings
docs.text:
The HTML-AAM specification defines how each HTML element maps to a landmark role:

HTML Element Landmark Role Condition <header> banner Not nested in article/aside/main/nav/section <nav> navigation Always <main> main Always <aside> complementary Always <footer> contentinfo Not nested in article/aside/main/nav/section <form> form Only if it has an accessible name <section> region Only if it has an accessible name <search> search Always

docs.title: The "Nested Header/Footer" Algorithm
docs.text:
The rule is precise: a <header> is a banner if and only if its nearest ancestor sectioning content is the <body>. Otherwise, it is a generic header role, not a landmark.

<body>
    <header>              → banner ✅
    <main>
        <header>          → generic header (not landmark)
    </main>
    <article>
        <header>          → generic header (not landmark)
    </article>
</body>

The same rule applies to <footer>.

docs.title: Accessible Name Computation for Landmarks
docs.text:
A landmark's accessible name comes from:

  1. aria-labelledby
  2. aria-label
  3. Native labels (for <form>, <section>)

For <section> to become a region, it needs an accessible name from one of these sources. For <form> to become a form landmark, it needs an accessible name.

docs.title: Landmark Order in the Accessibility Tree
docs.text: Landmarks are exposed in DOM order. Screen reader landmark navigation follows the DOM, not the visual order (which may differ due to CSS order).

docs.title: Authoring Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Plan the page structure:
    │   ├── What regions does the page have?
    │   ├── Which are repeated across the site?
    │   └── Which are unique to this page?
    │
    ▼
2.  Choose native elements:
    │   ├── header → <header>
    │   ├── nav → <nav>
    │   ├── main → <main>
    │   ├── sidebar → <aside>
    │   └── footer → <footer>
    │
    ▼
3.  Label repeated landmarks with aria-label.
    │
    ▼
4.  Add skip link to <main>.
    │
    ▼
5.  Style with CSS.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test with screen reader landmark navigation.

docs.title: Landmark Audit Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Check for exactly one <main>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check for exactly one top-level <header> and <footer>.
    │
    ▼
3.  Check for labelled <nav> elements when multiple exist.
    │
    ▼
4.  Check that <section> elements used as landmarks have names.
    │
    ▼
5.  Check that skip link target exists and is focusable.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test with NVDA (D key), VoiceOver (rotor), JAWS.
    │
    ▼
7.  Fix, re-test, repeat.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Landmark Structure
docs.text:
<body>
    <a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

    <header>
        <nav aria-label="Main">
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
                <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
    </header>

    <main id="main-content">
        <h1>Welcome</h1>
        <p>Page content.</p>
    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 Acme</p>
    </footer>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • Skip link lets keyboard users bypass the header and nav.
  • <header> top-level → banner landmark.
  • <nav aria-label="Main"> → navigation landmark named "Main."
  • <main id="main-content"> → main landmark; skip link target.
  • <footer> top-level → contentinfo landmark.

docs.title: Example 2: Multi-Navigation Page
docs.text:
<header>
    <nav aria-label="Main">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>

    <nav aria-label="Account">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/login">Sign in</a></li>
            <li><a href="/cart">Cart</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</header>

<main>
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
</main>

<footer>
    <nav aria-label="Footer">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/privacy">Privacy</a></li>
            <li><a href="/terms">Terms</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>
</footer>

Code Breakdown:

  • Three navs on the page, each distinguished by aria-label.
  • Screen readers announce "Main navigation," "Account navigation," and "Footer navigation."
  • Without labels, all three would be announced as just "navigation."

docs.title: Example 3: Article with Nested Header/Footer
docs.text:
<main>
    <article>
        <header>
            <h1>How SVG Embedding Works</h1>
            <p>Published <time datetime="2026-01-15">January 15, 2026</time></p>
        </header>

        <p>SVG can be embedded in seven different ways...</p>

        <footer>
            <p>Filed under: <a href="/tags/svg">SVG</a></p>
        </footer>
    </article>
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • <article> is NOT a landmark — it is a content grouping.
  • The nested <header> and <footer> inside <article> are NOT landmarks — they are article-level structure.
  • Only the top-level <header> and <footer> in <body> create landmarks.

docs.title: Example 4: Section with Accessible Name (Region Landmark)
docs.text:
<main>
    <h1>Dashboard</h1>

    <section aria-labelledby="sales-heading">
        <h2 id="sales-heading">Sales</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>

    <section aria-labelledby="inventory-heading">
        <h2 id="inventory-heading">Inventory</h2>
        <p>...</p>
    </section>
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • Each <section> has an accessible name via aria-labelledby.
  • Each becomes a region landmark.
  • Screen readers announce "Sales region" and "Inventory region."
  • Without the labels, the sections would not be landmarks — just containers.

docs.title: Example 5: Search Landmark
docs.text:
<header>
    <search>
        <form action="/search" method="get">
            <label for="q">Search</label>
            <input id="q" type="search" name="q" placeholder="Search products...">
            <button type="submit">Go</button>
        </form>
    </search>
</header>

Code Breakdown:

  • <search> produces a search landmark.
  • Screen readers can jump directly to the search region.
  • The <form> inside does not need role="search" when wrapped in <search>.
  • For older browsers, use <form role="search"> as a fallback.

docs.title: Example 6: Skip Link with Focus Styles
docs.text:
<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

<style>
    .skip-link {
        position: absolute;
        left: -9999px;
        top: 0;
        background: #000;
        color: #fff;
        padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
        z-index: 100;
    }
    .skip-link:focus {
        left: 0;
    }
</style>

<main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">
    <h1>Page content</h1>
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • Skip link is off-screen until focused.
  • On focus, it appears at the top-left.
  • tabindex="-1" on <main> makes it programmatically focusable, so :focus works when the skip link is activated.
  • Screen reader announces "Main region" after skip.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Landmark Approach Site header <header> (top-level) Primary navigation <nav aria-label="Main"> Secondary navigation <nav aria-label="Account"> Footer navigation <nav aria-label="Footer"> Main content <main id="main-content"> Sidebar <aside aria-label="Related"> Site footer <footer> (top-level) Search bar <search> or <form role="search"> Newsletter form <form aria-label="Newsletter"> Dashboard widgets <section aria-labelledby="..."> Article header <header> (nested, not a landmark) Article footer <footer> (nested, not a landmark)

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use native HTML elements to produce landmarks. Why: browsers handle the mapping automatically; no ARIA needed.
  2. Use only one <main> per page. Why: it is the primary content landmark; multiple mains break the model.
  3. Use only one top-level <header> and <footer> per page. Why: multiple banners or contentinfo confuse assistive technology.
  4. Label repeated landmarks with aria-label. Why: without labels, screen readers cannot distinguish multiple navs.
  5. Use aria-labelledby when a visible heading exists. Why: keeps the label and visible text synchronized.
  6. Give <section> elements an accessible name to make them region landmarks. Why: unlabelled sections are not landmarks.
  7. Give <form> elements an accessible name to make them form landmarks. Why: unlabelled forms are not landmarks.
  8. Add a skip link to <main>. Why: benefits keyboard-only users who do not use a screen reader.
  9. Make the skip link target focusable. Why: some browsers require tabindex="-1" for the :focus state to apply.
  10. Test with real screen reader landmark navigation. Why: the D key in NVDA, rotor in VoiceOver — the only way to confirm landmarks work.
  11. Do not add redundant ARIA roles. Why: <nav role="navigation"> is redundant and can conflict.
  12. Do not use ARIA landmarks when native elements work. Why: native elements are more reliable.
  13. Do not nest landmarks of the same type. Why: a <nav> inside a <nav> creates nested navigation landmarks that confuse users.
  14. Do not use <aside> for critical content. Why: aside is complementary; the content should be non-essential to the main flow.
  15. Do not style landmarks so they appear in different visual order than DOM order. Why: landmark order follows DOM order; visual mismatch confuses users.
  16. Test on mobile screen readers (TalkBack, VoiceOver iOS). Why: landmark navigation differs on mobile.
  17. Use <search> with a fallback for older browsers. Why: <search> is new; older browsers need role="search".
  18. Consider reader mode. Why: <main> helps reader mode extract the article.
  19. Document the landmark structure for your site. Why: consistency across pages is essential.
  20. Audit landmarks after any template change. Why: templates affect every page.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <main> Elements
docs.text:
<main>Page content</main>
<main>Sidebar content</main>

Why it's wrong: Only one <main> landmark is allowed per page.

✅ Correct:

<main>
    <section>Page content</section>
    <aside>Sidebar content</aside>
</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unlabelled Multiple Navs
docs.text:
<nav>...</nav>
<nav>...</nav>

Why it's wrong: Both announced as "navigation"; the user cannot distinguish them.

✅ Correct:

<nav aria-label="Main">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Footer">...</nav>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: role="banner" on Nested Header
docs.text:
<article>
    <header role="banner">...</header>  <!-- wrong -->
</article>

Why it's wrong: A nested <header> should not be a banner landmark; only one top-level banner is allowed.

✅ Correct:

<article>
    <header>...</header>  <!-- automatically not a landmark -->
</article>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: <section> Without Accessible Name
docs.text:
<section>
    <p>Some content</p>
</section>

Why it's wrong: An unlabelled <section> is not a landmark; it does not appear in the landmark navigation.

✅ Correct:

<section aria-labelledby="section-heading">
    <h2 id="section-heading">Section Title</h2>
    <p>Some content</p>
</section>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Redundant Role on Native Element
docs.text:
<nav role="navigation">...</nav>
<main role="main">...</main>

Why it's wrong: Native elements already produce the correct landmark roles; adding redundant ARIA can conflict.

✅ Correct:

<nav>...</nav>
<main>...</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Skip Link
docs.text:
<header>...</header>
<nav>...</nav>
<main>...</main>

Why it's wrong: Keyboard-only users must tab through every navigation link to reach the content.

✅ Correct:

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>
<main id="main-content">...</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Skip Link Target Not Focusable
docs.text:
<a href="#main-content">Skip</a>
<main id="main-content">...</main>

Why it's wrong: Some browsers do not move focus to a <main> without tabindex="-1".

✅ Correct:

<main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">...</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Landmarks in Visual Order Different from DOM Order
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Landmark navigation follows DOM order; visual mismatch confuses users.

✅ Correct: Keep DOM order and visual order aligned.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nested Same-Type Landmarks
docs.text:
<nav>
    <nav>...</nav>  <!-- nested navigation landmark -->
</nav>

Why it's wrong: Nested navigation landmarks confuse screen reader users.

✅ Correct: Use a single <nav> or flatten the structure.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Landmarks have no rendering cost — they are accessibility metadata.
  • No JavaScript required — native landmarks work without scripting.
  • Reader mode benefits — <main> helps extract the article.
  • Search engines — landmarks improve content identification.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Prefer native elements over ARIA landmarks.
  2. Keep DOM order aligned with visual order.
  3. Avoid nesting same-type landmarks.
  4. Use landmarks consistently across pages.

docs.title: Landmarks Do Not Introduce Security Issues
docs.text: Landmark roles are metadata. They do not execute scripts or expose data.

docs.title: Skip Link Focus Hijacking
docs.text: A malicious skip link could theoretically move focus to an unexpected element. Ensure skip links point to legitimate targets.

docs.title: Landmarks and Screen Reader Content Leakage
docs.text: Landmarks expose the structure of the page to assistive technology. Do not put sensitive content in landmark regions with names that would leak information.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect an element's landmark role.
  • Firefox DevTools → Accessibility — visualizes landmarks on the page.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — flags missing main landmark.
  • NVDA (Windows) → D key — cycle through landmarks.
  • VoiceOver (macOS) → Control+Option+U → Landmarks rotor — cycle through landmarks.
  • JAWS (Windows) → semicolon — landmark navigation.
  • TalkBack (Android) — swipe to landmark navigation.
  • axe DevTools — flags unlabelled landmarks and multiple mains.
  • document.querySelectorAll('main') — verify only one main exists.
  • document.querySelectorAll('nav') — list navs and check labels.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every page — at least one <main> landmark.
  • Every site with navigation — <nav> landmarks.
  • Every site with a header — top-level <header>.
  • Every site with a footer — top-level <footer>.
  • Any page with a sidebar — <aside> landmark.
  • Any page with search — <search> or role="search".
  • Any page with a form region — labelled <form>.
  • Any repeated named content region — labelled <section> as region.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use role="banner" on nested <header> elements.
  • Do not use role="contentinfo" on nested <footer> elements.
  • Do not add redundant ARIA roles to native elements.
  • Do not use <aside> for essential content.
  • Do not create unlabelled <section> landmarks.
  • Do not nest landmarks of the same type.
  • Do not use landmarks as a substitute for headings.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Semantic HTML
  • ARIA
  • Accessibility tree
  • Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack)
  • Skip navigation
  • Heading hierarchy
  • <main> element
  • <nav> element
  • <header> element
  • <footer> element
  • <aside> element
  • <section> element
  • <form> element
  • <search> element
  • HTML Accessibility API Mappings

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• There are exactly eight landmark roles in ARIA.
  • <main> must appear only once per page — using more is invalid.
  • A <header> is only a banner landmark when it is not nested inside <article>, <aside>, <main>, <nav>, or <section>.
  • A <section> needs an accessible name to become a region landmark.
  • A <form> needs an accessible name to become a form landmark.
  • The D key in NVDA cycles through landmarks.
  • The rotor in VoiceOver lists all landmarks on the page.
  • Skip links remain useful for keyboard-only users who do not use screen readers.
  • The <search> element was added to HTML in 2023 — supported in Chrome 118+, Firefox 118+, Safari 17+.
  • Landmarks are the practical version of the long-abandoned HTML outline algorithm.
  • Reader modes in Safari, Firefox, and Chrome use <main> to extract the article.
  • AI answer engines use landmarks to identify primary content.
  • Redundant ARIA roles on native elements can cause conflicting announcements.
  • The best landmarks are invisible — they work through native HTML elements, not ARIA.
  • Landmark navigation is 10× faster than tabbing through every link.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Landmark roles identify the major structural regions of a page for assistive technology.
  • There are eight landmark roles: banner, navigation, main, complementary, contentinfo, form, region, search.
  • Native HTML elements produce landmarks automatically — no ARIA needed in most cases.
  • Only one <main> per page; only one top-level <header> and <footer>.
  • Nested <header> and <footer> inside articles/sections are NOT landmarks.
  • Label repeated landmarks with aria-label or aria-labelledby.
  • <section> and <form> need accessible names to become landmarks.
  • Screen reader users navigate landmarks with the D key (NVDA), rotor (VoiceOver), or semicolon (JAWS).
  • Skip links remain useful for keyboard-only users.
  • Redundant ARIA roles are harmful — native elements already provide the correct roles.
  • Test with real screen readers — automated tools cannot verify landmark navigation works.
  • Landmarks are the skeleton of accessible page structure — invisible but essential.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Keyboard navigation is the practice of ensuring that every interactive element, control, and piece of content on a web page can be reached and operated using only a keyboard — without requiring a mouse, trackpad, or touchscreen. It is the foundational interaction model of web accessibility, and the primary way screen reader users, motor-impaired users, and power users interact with the web.

<!-- Native button: keyboard-operable by default -->
<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

<!-- Custom div: keyboard-inoperable without JavaScript -->
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

The first is operable with Tab (focus), Enter and Space (activate). The second does nothing when focused — assuming it can be focused at all.

Keyboard navigation is governed by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1 (Keyboard), which requires that all functionality be operable through a keyboard interface. It is a Level A requirement — the most basic conformance level.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Keyboard navigation serves several essential purposes:

  • Motor accessibility — users with motor impairments who cannot use a mouse rely entirely on the keyboard.
  • Screen reader compatibility — screen readers are keyboard-driven; if content is not keyboard-accessible, it is invisible to screen reader users.
  • Power user efficiency — developers, data entry professionals, and power users navigate faster with keyboard shortcuts.
  • Switch device support — users operating a switch device emit keyboard events; keyboard navigation is their only path.
  • Voice control — voice control systems often emit keyboard events to activate controls.
  • Situational limitations — a user with a broken arm, a cramped tray table on a plane, or a missing mouse driver.
  • Legal compliance — WCAG 2.2, ADA, Section 508, and the European Accessibility Act all require keyboard accessibility.

Keyboard navigation is not a feature — it is a baseline requirement of the web platform.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Accessibility Stack
│
├── Semantic HTML        ← native elements are keyboard-accessible by default
├── ARIA                 ← declares semantics; does NOT add keyboard behavior
├── Keyboard Navigation  ← reach and operate everything with a keyboard
├── Focus Management     ← move focus deliberately on dynamic changes
├── Screen Reader        ← keyboard-driven assistive technology
└── Testing              ← keyboard-only walkthrough, screen reader testing

Keyboard navigation is the interaction layer of accessibility. Semantic HTML provides the structure; keyboard navigation provides the operation; focus management ensures the user never gets lost.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The web was designed for mouse interaction. Native HTML elements — links, buttons, form controls — were keyboard-accessible from the beginning, but as web applications grew more complex, developers built custom widgets using <div> and <span> with JavaScript click handlers. These custom widgets looked and behaved like native controls when used with a mouse — but they were completely inoperable by keyboard.

A screen reader user would tab through the page and encounter nothing. A motor-impaired user could not activate the control at all. A keyboard-only user was locked out.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence <div onclick> widgets No keyboard focus, no keyboard activation No focus indicators Keyboard users could not see where they were No focus management Focus lost on dynamic content changes Keyboard traps Users could enter a component but not leave No skip links Keyboard users tabbed through every navigation link Inconsistent tab order tabindex values greater than 0 disrupted natural order

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
WCAG 1.0 (1999) established keyboard accessibility as a requirement. WCAG 2.0 (2008) formalized it in Success Criterion 2.1.1. WCAG 2.2 (2023) added new requirements for focus appearance (2.4.13) and focus not obscured (2.4.11), addressing gaps that had existed for decades.

The HTML inert attribute (baseline in all browsers since April 2023) simplified focus trapping in modals — replacing the 50-line JavaScript focus-trap pattern that had been the standard for years. The :focus-visible pseudo-class (native in all major browsers since 2020–2021) resolved the long-standing tension between designers who stripped focus outlines and keyboard users who needed them.

Keyboard navigation exists because the keyboard is the universal input device. Every assistive technology — screen readers, switch devices, voice control — emits keyboard events. If your page works with a keyboard, it works with almost everything.

docs.title: The Minimal Keyboard-Accessible Page
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Keyboard Navigation Demo</title>
    <style>
        /* WCAG 2.2: focus must be visible */
        :focus-visible {
            outline: 3px solid #3498db;
            outline-offset: 2px;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

    <nav aria-label="Main">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>

    <main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">
        <h1>Page content</h1>
        <button type="button">Click me</button>
        <a href="/next">Next page</a>
    </main>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element / Attribute Purpose :focus-visible Shows focus outline only for keyboard navigation — WCAG 2.2 requirement Skip link Lets keyboard users bypass repeated navigation <nav> Native landmark; keyboard users can jump to it <main tabindex="-1"> Programmatically focusable; target of the skip link <button> Native keyboard-operable control <a href> Native keyboard-operable link

docs.title: The tabindex Attribute
docs.text:
The tabindex attribute controls whether an element is focusable and where it sits in the tab order:

Value Behavior tabindex="0" Element is focusable and joins the natural tab order (DOM order) tabindex="-1" Element is focusable programmatically (via .focus()) but not by Tab tabindex="1"+ Element is focusable and placed before all tabindex="0" elements (avoid)

Best practice: Use tabindex="0" only on custom interactive elements that cannot be replaced by native HTML. Use tabindex="-1" for programmatic focus targets (skip link destinations, modal containers, route-change focus targets). Never use positive tabindex values — they disrupt the natural tab order and create unpredictable navigation.

docs.title: The :focus-visible Pseudo-Class
docs.text:
/* Wrong: removes focus indicator for everyone */
*:focus { outline: none; }

/* Correct: shows focus indicator only for keyboard navigation */
:focus-visible {
    outline: 3px solid #3498db;
    outline-offset: 2px;
}

:focus-visible is now supported in all major browsers — Chrome 86+, Firefox 85+, Safari 15.4+. No polyfill is needed in 2025/2026 codebases. The browser uses heuristics to determine whether the focus event was triggered by keyboard navigation (show ring) or pointer interaction (usually suppress it).

docs.title: Roving Tabindex
docs.text:
For composite widgets (tabs, toolbars, menus, radio groups), the roving tabindex pattern makes the entire widget a single tab stop:

<div role="tablist" aria-label="Settings">
    <button role="tab" tabindex="0" aria-selected="true"
            aria-controls="panel-1" id="tab-1">General</button>
    <button role="tab" tabindex="-1" aria-selected="false"
            aria-controls="panel-2" id="tab-2">Security</button>
    <button role="tab" tabindex="-1" aria-selected="false"
            aria-controls="panel-3" id="tab-3">Advanced</button>
</div>

Code Breakdown:

  • Exactly one tab has tabindex="0" — the currently selected tab.
  • All other tabs have tabindex="-1" — they are reachable via arrow keys, not Tab.
  • ArrowRight/ArrowLeft moves focus between tabs and updates tabindex.
  • Tab moves focus out of the tab list entirely.

This pattern is the standard for tabs, toolbars, menus, and radio groups. It reduces tab stops and matches native platform behavior.

docs.title: The inert Attribute
docs.text:
The inert attribute makes an element and all its descendants non-focusable and non-interactive:

<dialog open>
    <h2>Confirm deletion</h2>
    <button>Cancel</button>
    <button>Delete</button>
</dialog>

<main inert>
    <!-- Background content is now non-interactive -->
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • inert on <main> removes the background from the tab order.
  • Focus cannot reach any element inside an inert container.
  • inert is baseline in all browsers since April 2023.
  • Replaces the old 50-line JavaScript focus-trap pattern.

docs.title: The enterkeyhint Attribute
docs.text:
<input type="text" enterkeyhint="next" placeholder="First name">
<input type="text" enterkeyhint="done" placeholder="Last name">
<input type="search" enterkeyhint="search">

Code Breakdown:

  • enterkeyhint="next" — the on-screen keyboard shows "Next" instead of "Enter."
  • enterkeyhint="done" — shows "Done."
  • enterkeyhint="search" — shows a search icon.
  • Valid values: enter, done, go, next, previous, search, send.
  • Improves mobile accessibility by telling users what the Enter key will do.

docs.title: The "Tab Order as a Path" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of keyboard navigation as a path through the page. The Tab key moves forward; Shift+Tab moves backward. Every interactive element is a stop on the path.

Start
  │
  ▼
[Skip link] → [Nav link 1] → [Nav link 2] → [Main button] → [Main link]
  │
  ▼
End

The path should follow the visual reading order — top to bottom, left to right (or right to left for RTL languages). A path that jumps around the page is disorienting.

docs.title: The "Focus as a Spotlight" Mental Model
docs.text:
Focus is the spotlight that tells the user where they are. The :focus-visible outline is the visible beam of that spotlight. Without it, the user is navigating in the dark.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ┌─────────────┐                             │
│  │ [Button]    │ ← focus is here             │
│  └─────────────┘   (outline visible)         │
│                                              │
│  [Link]   [Button]                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The spotlight must always be visible (WCAG 2.4.7), not obscured by other elements (WCAG 2.4.11), and apparent enough to be seen (WCAG 2.4.13).

docs.title: The "Three Keyboard Operations" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every keyboard interaction falls into three categories:

1. NAVIGATION   → move focus (Tab, Shift+Tab, Arrow keys)
2. ACTIVATION   → trigger an action (Enter, Space)
3. DISMISSAL    → close or escape (Escape)

Every interactive control must support all three that apply. A button supports Navigation and Activation. A modal supports Navigation, Activation, and Dismissal.

docs.title: The "Native vs Custom" Mental Model
docs.text:
Native HTML elements:
  ✅ Focusable by default
  ✅ Keyboard-operable by default
  ✅ Announced correctly by default
  ✅ No JavaScript required

Custom <div>/<span> widgets:
  ❌ Not focusable by default
  ❌ Not keyboard-operable by default
  ❌ Not announced by default
  ⚠️ Requires tabindex + JS + ARIA + testing

The gap between native and custom is the entire reason the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide exists. Every custom widget you build requires manual implementation of all four characteristics.

docs.title: The "Focus Management" Mental Model
docs.text:
Static pages have a simple tab order. Dynamic pages — SPAs, modals, dropdowns, live regions — require deliberate focus management:

Trigger event → Where should focus go?
    │
    ├── Modal opens → focus moves INTO the modal
    ├── Modal closes → focus returns to the trigger
    ├── Route changes → focus moves to the new page's <h1>
    ├── Content deleted → focus moves to a logical next element
    └── Error occurs → focus moves to the error message

Without focus management, the user is stranded — focus stays on a removed element or a stale link.

docs.title: Concept 1: WCAG 2.1.1 — Keyboard (Level A)
docs.text: The foundational requirement: all functionality must be operable through a keyboard interface. This does not mean the keyboard must be the only input — it means the keyboard must be sufficient. Mouse and touch can be additional, but the keyboard cannot be optional.

docs.title: Concept 2: WCAG 2.1.2 — No Keyboard Trap (Level A)
docs.text:
If focus can move into a component, it must be able to move out using standard keys (Tab, Shift+Tab, arrow keys, Escape). A keyboard trap occurs when a user enters a widget and cannot leave without a mouse.

Exception: Modal dialogs and popovers may restrict focus to the dialog, provided the user knows how to exit (typically Escape). This does not violate 2.1.2 because the user can "untrap" focus.

docs.title: Concept 3: WCAG 2.4.7 — Focus Visible (Level AA)
docs.text: Any keyboard-operable user interface must have a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible. This is a Level AA requirement — the legal bar.

docs.title: Concept 4: WCAG 2.4.11 — Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA)
docs.text: When navigating with a keyboard, the focused element must not be entirely hidden by other content — such as a sticky header, footer, or cookie banner.

docs.title: Concept 5: WCAG 2.4.13 — Focus Appearance (Level AA)
docs.text:
WCAG 2.2 added specific numeric minimums for focus indicators:

  • Area: The focus indicator must have an area of at least 2 CSS pixels thick on the perimeter of the element.
  • Contrast: The focus indicator must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors.
  • Not obscured: Must meet 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured).

This is a new requirement in WCAG 2.2 that many existing sites fail.

docs.title: Concept 6: Tab Order Follows DOM Order
docs.text:
The natural tab order follows DOM order, not visual order. CSS order, flex-direction: row-reverse, and absolute positioning can create a mismatch between visual and DOM order — a common and serious accessibility failure.

Rule: Keep DOM order aligned with visual order. Do not use CSS to reorder interactive elements.

docs.title: Concept 7: tabindex="0" vs tabindex="-1"
docs.text: Value Focusable by Tab? Focusable programmatically? Use Case tabindex="0" ✅ ✅ Custom interactive elements tabindex="-1" ❌ ✅ Skip link targets, modal containers, route-change focus targets No tabindex Depends on element Depends on element Native elements are focusable by default tabindex="1"+ ✅ (before everything) ✅ Never use

docs.title: Concept 8: The Roving Tabindex Pattern
docs.text:
For composite widgets (tabs, toolbars, menus, radio groups, grids), the roving tabindex pattern makes the widget a single tab stop. Exactly one child has tabindex="0"; all others have tabindex="-1". Arrow keys move focus between children and update the tabindex values.

Benefits: - Fewer tab stops — the user can bypass the entire widget with one Tab press. - Matches native platform behavior for grouped controls. - Reduces cognitive load.

docs.title: Concept 9: aria-activedescendant vs Roving Tabindex
docs.text:
Two patterns manage focus in composite widgets:

Pattern How It Works When to Use Roving tabindex Focus moves to each child element Non-virtualized collections, small widget counts aria-activedescendant Focus stays on the container; aria-activedescendant points to the active child Virtualized lists, large datasets, comboboxes

Roving tabindex is the default for non-virtualized collections.

docs.title: Concept 10: Focus Trapping with inert
docs.text:
The inert attribute makes an element and all its descendants non-focusable and non-interactive. Apply it to the background content when a modal is open.

function openModal(modal) {
    document.querySelector('main').inert = true;
    modal.showModal();
}

function closeModal(modal) {
    document.querySelector('main').inert = false;
    modal.close();
}

inert replaces the old JavaScript focus-trap pattern and handles edge cases natively — iframes, Shadow DOM, dynamically added content.

docs.title: Concept 11: <dialog> and Focus
docs.text:
The native <dialog> element with showModal() traps focus natively. You do not need to implement a JavaScript focus trap. The W3C APA Working Group concluded that the native dialog's behavior — allowing users to tab to the browser chrome — is correct and beneficial.

Important: Focus-trapping advice for <dialog> is deprecated. Use native <dialog> or inert instead.

docs.title: Concept 12: Skip Navigation Links
docs.text:
A skip link is the first focusable element on the page. It allows keyboard users to bypass repeated navigation and jump directly to the main content.

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>
<main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">...</main>

The target must have tabindex="-1" so it is programmatically focusable. Without it, some browsers do not move focus.

docs.title: Concept 13: SPA Route Change Focus Management
docs.text:
Single-page applications break the browser's automatic focus reset on navigation. Without manual focus management, focus stays on the clicked link — which may no longer exist — and screen readers do not announce the new page.

The three mandatory SPA fixes: 1. Update document.title on every route change. 2. Move focus to the new page's <h1> or <main> (with tabindex="-1"). 3. Announce the route change via an ARIA live region.

Focus must go to the <h1> or <main> — not document.body, which is invisible to screen readers and does not announce the new page context.

docs.title: Concept 14: Focus Restoration
docs.text:
When a modal, dropdown, or overlay closes, focus must return to the element that triggered it. Without this, focus is lost — often returning to the top of the page or to document.body.

function openModal(trigger) {
    const returnFocusTo = trigger;
    // ... open modal
}

function closeModal() {
    returnFocusTo.focus();
}

docs.title: Concept 15: :focus-visible — The Modern Focus Indicator
docs.text:
The :focus pseudo-class fires on both keyboard and mouse focus. The :focus-visible pseudo-class fires only when the browser determines the focus was keyboard-triggered (or otherwise benefits from a visible indicator).

Rules: - Never use *:focus { outline: none; }. - Style :focus-visible with a prominent indicator. - Optionally style :focus with a lighter indicator for pointer interactions.

docs.title: Concept 16: The inert Attribute vs aria-hidden
docs.text:
Attribute Removes from Tab Order? Removes from Accessibility Tree? Handles Click Events? inert ✅ ✅ ✅ aria-hidden="true" ❌ ✅ ❌

inert is the correct tool for making background content non-interactive during a modal. aria-hidden="true" alone does not remove elements from the tab order — it creates a keyboard trap.

docs.title: Concept 17: Focus and CSS visibility
docs.text:
Elements with visibility: hidden are not focusable. Elements with display: none are also not focusable. Elements with opacity: 0 are focusable — a common source of invisible focus.

/* Not focusable */
.hidden { display: none; }
.invisible { visibility: hidden; }

/* Still focusable — dangerous */
.transparent { opacity: 0; }

docs.title: Concept 18: enterkeyhint for Mobile Keyboards
docs.text: On mobile devices, the on-screen keyboard's "Enter" key label can be customized with enterkeyhint. This improves accessibility by telling users what the Enter key will do: "Next," "Done," "Search," "Go," etc..

docs.title: Concept 19: Focus Order and RTL Languages
docs.text: For right-to-left languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Farsi), the tab order should follow the visual reading order — right to left. This is determined by the dir attribute and DOM order, not by CSS.

docs.title: Concept 20: Testing with Keyboard Only
docs.text: The only reliable way to verify keyboard accessibility is to put away the mouse and navigate the entire page with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrow keys, and Escape. Automated tools catch some issues — but only 30–50% of accessibility problems are detectable by automation. Keyboard-only testing catches what automation misses.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Tab Order Construction
docs.text:
1.  Browser parses HTML.
    │
    ▼
2.  Identifies all focusable elements:
    │   ├── <a href> (with href)
    │   ├── <button> (not disabled)
    │   ├── <input> (not disabled, not type="hidden")
    │   ├── <select> (not disabled)
    │   ├── <textarea> (not disabled)
    │   ├── <details> > <summary>
    │   ├── <iframe>
    │   └── [tabindex] (any element with tabindex)
    │
    ▼
3.  Builds tab order:
    │   ├── Positive tabindex values (in order) — first
    │   ├── tabindex="0" and native focusable elements (DOM order)
    │   └── Excluded: tabindex="-1", inert, hidden
    │
    ▼
4.  Tab moves focus to the next element in order.
    │
    ▼
5.  Focus indicator appears via :focus-visible.
    │
    ▼
6.  Enter/Space activates the focused element.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Modal Focus Management with inert
docs.text:
1.  User activates the modal trigger.
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript saves the trigger element for later.
    │
    ▼
3.  Background content receives the inert attribute.
    │
    ▼
4.  Modal opens (showModal() on <dialog>).
    │
    ▼
5.  Focus moves to the modal (native behavior).
    │
    ▼
6.  User navigates within modal via Tab.
    │
    ▼
7.  User presses Escape or clicks Cancel.
    │
    ▼
8.  Modal closes; inert removed from background.
    │
    ▼
9.  Focus returns to the trigger element.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: SPA Route Change Focus Management
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a route link.
    │
    ▼
2.  Router intercepts; no full page reload.
    │
    ▼
3.  View updates in the DOM.
    │
    ▼
4.  After render:
    │   ├── document.title = new page title
    │   ├── focus moves to <main> or <h1>
    │   └── live region announces "Navigated to [title]"
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader announces the new page.
    │
    ▼
6.  Keyboard user is at the top of the new content.

docs.title: The Focus Model
docs.text:
The browser maintains a single document.activeElement — the element with focus. Tab moves focus through the tab order. Only one element has focus at a time.

document.activeElement; // returns the currently focused element

docs.title: The Tab Order Algorithm
docs.text:
The browser builds the tab order by:

  1. Collecting all elements with positive tabindex values, sorted numerically.
  2. Collecting all elements with tabindex="0" and natively focusable elements, in DOM order.
  3. Excluding elements that are disabled, inert, hidden, or inside an inert container.
  4. Excluding elements with tabindex="-1" from the Tab sequence.

docs.title: Native Focusability
docs.text:
Not all elements are focusable by default:

Element Focusable? <a href> ✅ <a> without href ❌ <button> ✅ <input type="hidden"> ❌ <input> (other types) ✅ <select> ✅ <textarea> ✅ <div> ❌ <span> ❌ <h1>–<h6> ❌ <details> ✅ <summary> ✅

docs.title: The :focus-visible Heuristic
docs.text:
Browsers implement the :focus-visible heuristic using their own logic:

  • A <button> clicked with a mouse typically does not match :focus-visible — the user can already see what they clicked.
  • A text <input> clicked with a mouse does match :focus-visible — focusing a text field signals the user is about to type.
  • Any focus reached via Tab, Shift+Tab, or arrow-key navigation reliably matches :focus-visible.

docs.title: The inert Attribute Mechanics
docs.text:
inert is a boolean attribute that makes an element and all its descendants non-focusable, non-clickable, and hidden from assistive technology. It handles:

  • Tab order exclusion
  • Click event suppression
  • Accessibility tree removal
  • Focus prevention
  • Shadow DOM descendants

docs.title: Static Page Keyboard Navigation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  User presses Tab.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser moves focus to the first focusable element.
    │
    ▼
3.  :focus-visible styles apply.
    │
    ▼
4.  Screen reader announces the element.
    │
    ▼
5.  User presses Tab again to advance.
    │
    ▼
6.  User presses Enter or Space to activate.
    │
    ▼
7.  Action fires.

docs.title: Dynamic Content Focus Management Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Content changes (modal opens, route changes, item deleted).
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript determines the new focus target:
    │   ├── Modal → focus inside modal
    │   ├── Route change → focus to <main> or <h1>
    │   ├── Item deleted → focus to logical next item
    │   └── Error → focus to error message
    │
    ▼
3.  JavaScript calls .focus() on the target.
    │
    ▼
4.  (Optional) aria-live announces the change.
    │
    ▼
5.  User continues navigating from the new focus position.

docs.title: Focus Restoration Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  User activates a modal trigger.
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript saves document.activeElement (the trigger).
    │
    ▼
3.  Modal opens; focus moves inside.
    │
    ▼
4.  User closes the modal.
    │
    ▼
5.  Focus returns to the saved trigger element.
    │
    ▼
6.  User continues from where they left off.

docs.title: Example 1: Skip Link with Focus Styles
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <style>
        .skip-link {
            position: absolute;
            left: -9999px;
            top: 0;
            background: #000;
            color: #fff;
            padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
            z-index: 100;
        }
        .skip-link:focus {
            left: 0;
        }
        :focus-visible {
            outline: 3px solid #3498db;
            outline-offset: 2px;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

    <nav aria-label="Main">
        <ul>
            <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
            <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
        </ul>
    </nav>

    <main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">
        <h1>Welcome</h1>
        <p>Page content.</p>
    </main>
</body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • Skip link is off-screen until focused.
  • :focus-visible provides a visible outline for keyboard users.
  • <main tabindex="-1"> is the skip link target and is programmatically focusable.
  • The skip link is the first focusable element on the page.

docs.title: Example 2: Accessible Tabs with Roving Tabindex
docs.text:
<div role="tablist" aria-label="Account settings">
    <button role="tab" id="tab-profile" aria-selected="true"
            aria-controls="panel-profile" tabindex="0">Profile</button>
    <button role="tab" id="tab-billing" aria-selected="false"
            aria-controls="panel-billing" tabindex="-1">Billing</button>
    <button role="tab" id="tab-security" aria-selected="false"
            aria-controls="panel-security" tabindex="-1">Security</button>
</div>

<div role="tabpanel" id="panel-profile"
     aria-labelledby="tab-profile" tabindex="0">
    <h2>Profile settings</h2>
    <p>...</p>
</div>

const tablist = document.querySelector('[role="tablist"]');
const tabs = [...tablist.querySelectorAll('[role="tab"]')];

tablist.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
    const currentIndex = tabs.indexOf(document.activeElement);
    let newIndex;

    if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') {
        newIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % tabs.length;
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft') {
        newIndex = (currentIndex - 1 + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
    } else if (e.key === 'Home') {
        newIndex = 0;
    } else if (e.key === 'End') {
        newIndex = tabs.length - 1;
    } else {
        return;
    }

    e.preventDefault();
    tabs[newIndex].focus();
    // Update aria-selected and tabindex
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Only the selected tab has tabindex="0" — the widget is a single tab stop.
  • Arrow keys move focus between tabs.
  • Home and End jump to the first and last tabs.
  • Tab moves focus out of the tab list entirely.
  • Roving tabindex is the standard pattern for tabs, toolbars, menus, and radio groups.

docs.title: Example 3: Modal with inert Focus Management
docs.text:
<dialog id="confirm-dialog">
    <form method="dialog">
        <h2>Confirm deletion</h2>
        <p>This action cannot be undone.</p>
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<main id="app-content">
    <h1>Dashboard</h1>
    <button id="delete-btn">Delete account</button>
</main>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('confirm-dialog');
    const main = document.getElementById('app-content');
    let returnFocusTo = null;

    document.getElementById('delete-btn').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
        returnFocusTo = e.currentTarget;
        main.inert = true;
        dialog.showModal();
    });

    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        main.inert = false;
        returnFocusTo?.focus();
    });
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • inert on <main> removes the background from the tab order.
  • dialog.showModal() opens the dialog with native focus management.
  • No JavaScript focus trap is needed — <dialog> handles it natively.
  • On close, inert is removed and focus returns to the trigger.

docs.title: Example 4: SPA Route Change Focus Management
docs.text:
// React example
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useLocation } from 'react-router-dom';

function RouteAnnouncer() {
    const location = useLocation();

    useEffect(() => {
        const pageTitle = getPageTitle(location.pathname);

        // 1. Update document title
        document.title = pageTitle;

        // 2. Move focus to main content
        const main = document.querySelector('main');
        if (main) {
            main.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
            main.focus();

            // Remove tabindex after blur so it doesn't appear in tab order
            main.addEventListener('blur', () => {
                main.removeAttribute('tabindex');
            }, { once: true });
        }

        // 3. Announce route change to screen readers
        const announcer = document.getElementById('route-announcer');
        if (announcer) {
            announcer.textContent = `Navigated to ${pageTitle}`;
        }
    }, [location]);

    return null;
}

// Place in the app shell:
// <div id="route-announcer" role="status" aria-live="polite"
//      style="position:absolute;width:1px;height:1px;overflow:hidden;">
// </div>

Code Breakdown:

  • Updates document.title on every route change.
  • Moves focus to <main> with tabindex="-1".
  • Removes tabindex after blur so it does not appear in normal tab order.
  • Live region announces "Navigated to [title]" for screen readers.
  • This is the three mandatory SPA fixes.

docs.title: Example 5: Custom Button with Keyboard Support
docs.text:
<div role="button" tabindex="0" id="custom-btn">
    Save changes
</div>

<script>
    const btn = document.getElementById('custom-btn');

    btn.addEventListener('click', save);
    btn.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
        if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') {
            e.preventDefault();
            save();
        }
    });

    function save() {
        console.log('Saved');
    }
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • role="button" — declares the element as a button.
  • tabindex="0" — makes it focusable via Tab.
  • keydown handler — responds to Enter and Space.
  • e.preventDefault() on Space — prevents page scroll.
  • This is the ARIA pattern — but native <button> is always better. This example is for cases where native HTML cannot be used.

docs.title: Example 6: enterkeyhint for Mobile Forms
docs.text:
<form>
    <label for="first">First name</label>
    <input id="first" type="text" enterkeyhint="next">

    <label for="last">Last name</label>
    <input id="last" type="text" enterkeyhint="next">

    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input id="email" type="email" enterkeyhint="done">

    <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

Code Breakdown:

  • enterkeyhint="next" — the on-screen keyboard shows "Next."
  • enterkeyhint="done" — shows "Done" on the last field.
  • Improves mobile accessibility by telling users what the Enter key will do.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Keyboard Pattern Navigation links Native <a href>; tab order Buttons Native <button>; Enter and Space Form fields Native <input>, <select>, <textarea>; labels Tabs Roving tabindex; arrow keys; Home/End Accordion Enter/Space to toggle; aria-expanded Modal dialog <dialog> or inert; Escape to close Dropdown menu Enter/Space to open; arrow keys to navigate; Escape to close Combobox Arrow keys; Enter to select; Escape to close Slider Arrow keys to adjust; Home/End for min/max Tree view Arrow keys; Right/Left to expand/collapse SPA route change Focus to <main> or <h1>; announce via live region Skip link First focusable element; targets <main tabindex="-1"> Focus restoration Save trigger; return focus on close

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use native HTML elements whenever possible. Why: native elements are keyboard-accessible by default.
  2. Never use *:focus { outline: none; }. Why: it removes focus indicators for everyone, violating WCAG 2.4.7.
  3. Style :focus-visible with a prominent indicator. Why: it shows focus only for keyboard navigation — the modern standard.
  4. Use outline-offset to separate the indicator from the element. Why: improves visibility against varied backgrounds.
  5. Ensure focus indicator meets WCAG 2.2 numeric requirements. Why: 2px thick, 3:1 contrast.
  6. Keep DOM order aligned with visual order. Why: tab order follows DOM, not CSS layout.
  7. Never use positive tabindex values. Why: they disrupt the natural tab order.
  8. Use tabindex="-1" for programmatic focus targets. Why: skip link destinations, modals, route-change targets.
