  9. Use roving tabindex for composite widgets. Why: reduces tab stops and matches native behavior.
  10. Use inert instead of JavaScript focus traps. Why: native, handles edge cases, simpler.
  11. Use native <dialog> for modals. Why: native focus management; no focus trap needed.
  12. Add a skip link as the first focusable element. Why: lets keyboard users bypass navigation.
  13. Make the skip link target focusable with tabindex="-1". Why: ensures focus moves correctly.
  14. Manage focus on every route change in SPAs. Why: SPAs break automatic focus reset.
  15. Move focus to <h1> or <main> on route change. Why: not document.body — screen readers need a meaningful target.
  16. Return focus to the trigger when closing modals. Why: without it, focus is lost.
  17. Ensure focus is not obscured by sticky headers or footers. Why: WCAG 2.2 requires it.
  18. Test with keyboard only. Why: automated tools catch only 30–50% of issues.
  19. Test with a screen reader. Why: keyboard navigation and screen reader behavior are linked.
  20. Use enterkeyhint on mobile form fields. Why: tells users what the Enter key will do.
  21. Handle nested modals carefully. Why: focus management becomes complex with stacked dialogs.
  22. Document keyboard shortcuts. Why: users need to discover them.
  23. Avoid autofocus on page load. Why: it can disorient screen reader users.
  24. Use visibility: hidden or display: none — not opacity: 0 — to hide focusable elements. Why: opacity: 0 elements remain focusable.
  25. Audit keyboard navigation after every significant UI change. Why: custom widgets frequently break keyboard accessibility.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: *:focus { outline: none; }
docs.text:
*:focus { outline: none; }

Why it's wrong: Removes focus indicators for keyboard users — a WCAG 2.4.7 failure and a legal liability under ADA/Section 508.

✅ Correct:

:focus-visible {
    outline: 3px solid #3498db;
    outline-offset: 2px;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: <div> for Buttons Without Keyboard Support
docs.text:
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

Why it's wrong: Not focusable, not keyboard-operable, not announced as a button.

✅ Correct:

<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Keyboard Trap
docs.text:
<div id="widget">
    <!-- Focus can enter but not leave -->
</div>

Why it's wrong: Violates WCAG 2.1.2 (Level A). Users cannot escape without a mouse.

✅ Correct: Ensure Tab, Shift+Tab, or Escape moves focus out of the widget.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: aria-hidden="true" on Focusable Element
docs.text:
<button aria-hidden="true">Save</button>

Why it's wrong: The button is invisible to screen readers but still reachable by keyboard — a keyboard trap.

✅ Correct:

<button>Save</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Positive tabindex
docs.text:
<input tabindex="1">
<input tabindex="2">
<button tabindex="3">

Why it's wrong: Positive tabindex values place elements before all tabindex="0" and native elements — disrupting natural order.

✅ Correct: Use DOM order.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: opacity: 0 for Hidden Focusable Elements
docs.text:
.hidden { opacity: 0; }

Why it's wrong: The element is still focusable — invisible focus.

✅ Correct:

.hidden { display: none; }
/* or */
.hidden { visibility: hidden; }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Skip Link
docs.text:
<header>
    <nav>
        <!-- 40 navigation links -->
    </nav>
</header>
<main>Content</main>

Why it's wrong: Keyboard users must tab through every navigation link to reach content.

✅ Correct:

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>
<main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">Content</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: SPA Route Change Without Focus Management
docs.text:
// Route changes but focus stays on the clicked link

Why it's wrong: Focus remains on a link that may no longer be visible; screen readers do not announce the new page.

✅ Correct: Move focus to <main> or <h1> on every route change.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Modal Without Focus Management
docs.text:
<div class="modal">...</div>
<!-- No focus management; background remains interactive -->

Why it's wrong: Keyboard users can tab into the background — the modal is not a modal.

✅ Correct: Use <dialog> with showModal() or apply inert to the background.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Focus Lost After Modal Close
docs.text:
function closeModal() {
    modal.hidden = true;
    // Focus is lost — returns to <body>
}

Why it's wrong: The user loses their place in the page.

✅ Correct:

function closeModal() {
    modal.hidden = true;
    returnFocusTo.focus();
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Focus Obscured by Sticky Header
docs.text:
.sticky-header {
    position: sticky;
    top: 0;
    height: 80px;
}

Why it's wrong: Focused elements may be hidden behind the sticky header — violates WCAG 2.4.11.

✅ Correct: Add scroll-margin-top to focusable elements or use :target styles to offset the header.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No :focus-visible Styling
docs.text:
<!-- Browser default focus ring is removed by CSS reset -->

Why it's wrong: Without explicit :focus-visible styling, keyboard users may have no visible indicator.

✅ Correct: Always style :focus-visible explicitly.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Native keyboard navigation has no runtime cost — the browser handles it natively.
  • Roving tabindex requires minimal JavaScript — only for updating tabindex and aria-selected.
  • inert is a native browser feature — no JavaScript focus-trap overhead.
  • :focus-visible is a CSS pseudo-class — no performance impact.
  • SPA route focus management adds a single .focus() call per navigation — negligible.
  • Live region announcements are processed by the browser's accessibility API — minimal overhead.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use native HTML elements — no JavaScript needed for keyboard behavior.
  2. Use inert instead of JavaScript focus traps.
  3. Use <dialog> instead of custom modal implementations.
  4. Batch focus management updates — one .focus() call per interaction.
  5. Avoid using setTimeout for focus management — use requestAnimationFrame or framework lifecycle hooks.

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts and XSS
docs.text: Custom keyboard shortcuts implemented via keydown listeners can be exploited if they trigger navigation or DOM manipulation based on untrusted input. Validate all keyboard-triggered actions.

docs.title: Focus Hijacking
docs.text: Malicious scripts can move focus unexpectedly — a technique used in clickjacking and UI redressing attacks. Modern browsers restrict programmatic focus to elements that are already visible or have been interacted with.

docs.title: inert and Content Leakage
docs.text: inert removes elements from the accessibility tree and tab order but does not remove them from the DOM. Sensitive content hidden with inert is still visible in DevTools.

docs.title: Modal Focus Trapping and Escape
docs.text: Ensure that modal focus trapping cannot be exploited to prevent users from leaving the page. The Escape key must always close the modal, and browser chrome must remain accessible — the W3C APA Working Group explicitly confirmed that tabbing to the browser chrome from a dialog is correct behavior.

docs.title: Autofocus Abuse
docs.text: autofocus on page load can disorient screen reader users and can be abused by malicious pages. Use it sparingly and only on pages where it is expected (e.g., login forms).

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Put away the mouse. Tab through the entire page. This is the only reliable test.
  • Check tab order — does focus move in a logical order? Does it follow visual order?
  • Check focus visibility — can you always see where focus is?
  • Check for keyboard traps — can you always Tab or Escape out?
  • Check skip link — is it the first focusable element? Does it work?
  • Check modals — does focus move in? Does it return on close?
  • Check SPAs — does focus move on route change?
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect focusable elements.
  • document.activeElement — check the currently focused element in console.
  • document.querySelectorAll('[tabindex]') — list all elements with tabindex.
  • document.querySelectorAll('*:focus') — not directly queryable, but :focus-visible can be tested.
  • axe DevTools extension — flags keyboard traps, missing focus styles, and tabindex misuse.
  • Lighthouse — audits for keyboard accessibility.
  • Screen reader testing — NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack — keyboard-driven.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every interactive element — buttons, links, form controls, custom widgets.
  • Every page — skip link, logical tab order, visible focus.
  • Every modal — focus trapping with inert or <dialog>.
  • Every SPA route change — focus management and announcement.
  • Every composite widget — roving tabindex or aria-activedescendant.
  • Every dynamic content change — focus management or live region.
  • Every form — enterkeyhint on mobile fields.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use positive tabindex values. Use DOM order.
  • Do not use *:focus { outline: none; }. Style :focus-visible instead.
  • Do not use aria-hidden="true" on focusable elements. Use inert or remove from tab order.
  • Do not use opacity: 0 to hide focusable elements. Use display: none or visibility: hidden.
  • Do not implement a JavaScript focus trap for <dialog>. It is deprecated advice.
  • Do not move focus to document.body on SPA route change. Move to <h1> or <main>.
  • Do not autofocus on page load unless the page is a search or login form.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A)
  • WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A)
  • WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA)
  • WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Level AA)
  • WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (Level AA)
  • tabindex attribute
  • Roving tabindex
  • aria-activedescendant
  • inert attribute
  • <dialog> element
  • :focus-visible pseudo-class
  • Skip navigation
  • Focus management
  • Focus restoration
  • SPA route change focus
  • enterkeyhint attribute
  • Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack)
  • Semantic HTML
  • ARIA
  • Keyboard trap

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• :focus-visible is supported in all major browsers — Chrome 86+, Firefox 85+, Safari 15.4+ — no polyfill needed in 2025/2026 codebases.
  • The inert attribute is baseline in all browsers since April 2023 — it replaces the 50-line JavaScript focus-trap pattern.
  • Focus-trapping advice for <dialog> is deprecated — the native dialog handles focus natively, and the W3C APA Working Group confirmed that tabbing to the browser chrome is correct behavior.
  • WCAG 2.2 added numeric minimums for focus indicators — 2px thick, 3:1 contrast — that many existing sites fail.
  • Chrome fixed its skip-link bug in 2023 — the correct pattern now requires tabindex="-1" on the target.
  • element.focus({ focusVisible: true }) lets you force the focus ring programmatically — solving a long-standing UX bug as of 2025.
  • Positive tabindex values are an anti-pattern — they place elements before all native focusable elements.
  • Roving tabindex makes a composite widget a single tab stop — exactly one child has tabindex="0"; all others have tabindex="-1".
  • aria-activedescendant is preferred for virtualized lists — roving tabindex for non-virtualized collections.
  • SPAs break all three automatic browser behaviors — focus reset, title announcement, and scroll reset. All three must be fixed manually.
  • Focus must go to <h1> or <main> on route change — not document.body, which is invisible to screen readers.
  • inert handles iframes and Shadow DOM — which JavaScript focus traps often miss.
  • opacity: 0 elements are still focusable — a common source of invisible focus.
  • WCAG 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap) is Level A — the most basic conformance level.
  • Keyboard traps can end a screen reader session — they are among the most severe accessibility failures.
  • enterkeyhint tells mobile users what the Enter key will do — "next," "done," "search," "go".
  • One in seven people worldwide has a disability — keyboard accessibility benefits everyone.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Keyboard navigation ensures every interactive element can be reached and operated with a keyboard alone.
  • WCAG 2.1.1 (Keyboard) is Level A — the foundational requirement.
  • WCAG 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap) is Level A — focus must always be able to leave a component.
  • WCAG 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) is Level AA — focus indicators must be visible.
  • WCAG 2.4.11 and 2.4.13 are new in WCAG 2.2 — focus must not be obscured and must meet numeric minimums.
  • :focus-visible is the modern focus indicator — shows only for keyboard navigation; supported in all major browsers; no polyfill needed.
  • Native HTML elements are keyboard-accessible by default — use <button>, <a href>, <input>, <select>, <textarea>, <dialog>, <details>.
  • tabindex="0" makes custom elements focusable; tabindex="-1" makes them programmatically focusable only; never use positive values.
  • Roving tabindex makes composite widgets a single tab stop — exactly one child has tabindex="0".
  • The inert attribute replaces JavaScript focus traps — baseline since April 2023.
  • <dialog> with showModal() handles focus natively — focus-trapping advice for dialog is deprecated.
  • Skip links let keyboard users bypass navigation — target must have tabindex="-1".
  • SPAs must manage focus on every route change — update title, move focus to <h1> or <main>, announce via live region.
  • Focus restoration is required when modals close — return focus to the trigger.
  • Test with keyboard only — automated tools catch only 30–50% of issues.
  • Keyboard navigation is the universal input model — it works with screen readers, switch devices, voice control, and power users.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Focus management is the practice of deliberately controlling where keyboard focus goes as the user interacts with a web page — including after modals open and close, after route changes in single-page applications, after content is dynamically added or removed, and after validation errors occur.

// Focus management: move focus to a newly loaded content region
const heading = document.querySelector('main h2');
heading.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
heading.focus();

Focus management is not about making focus visible (that is :focus-visible styling) and it is not about making elements focusable (that is tabindex and native HTML). It is about the decision of where focus should be at each moment in the interaction lifecycle — and executing that decision reliably.

It is the most common source of accessibility regressions in dynamic interfaces, and the single most important practice for making single-page applications, modals, and interactive widgets usable by keyboard and screen reader users.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Focus management serves several essential purposes:

  • Continuity of attention — the user always knows where they are, because focus is deliberately placed.
  • Screen reader context — screen readers announce the element with focus; moving focus tells the user what changed.
  • Keyboard efficiency — focus lands on the content the user needs next, not at the top of the page.
  • Regression prevention — SPAs break the browser's automatic focus reset; focus management restores it.
  • Modal integrity — modals must prevent focus from reaching background content.
  • Error recovery — after a validation failure, focus should move to the first invalid field.
  • Legal compliance — WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order) and 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap) are Level A requirements.

Without focus management, a screen reader user clicks a link in an SPA, hears nothing, and has no idea the page changed. A keyboard user opens a modal, closes it, and is returned to the top of the page — losing their place entirely.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Accessibility Stack
│
├── Semantic HTML        ← native elements are focusable and keyboard-operable
├── ARIA                 ← declares roles, states, properties
├── Keyboard Navigation  ← reach and operate everything with a keyboard
├── Focus Management     ← move focus deliberately on dynamic changes
├── :focus-visible       ← make focus visible for keyboard users
└── Testing              ← keyboard-only walkthrough, screen reader testing

Keyboard navigation is the input layer. Focus management is the state layer. :focus-visible is the output layer. All three are needed.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Traditional page loads reset focus automatically. When a browser navigates to a new page, it moves focus to the top of the document, announces the new page title, and resets scroll position. The user always starts in a predictable place.

Single-page applications break all three of these automatic behaviors. When React Router, Vue Router, or Angular Router navigates, the browser does not reload — it swaps the DOM content in place. Focus stays on the clicked link (which may no longer exist). The document title does not change. The screen reader announces nothing. The user is stranded in the old context while the visual content has changed.

The same problem occurs with modals, dropdowns, and dynamic content. Without deliberate focus management, the accessibility tree and the user's attention drift out of sync.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No focus reset in SPAs Focus stays on a stale link; screen readers announce nothing No focus trapping in modals Keyboard users tab into background content No focus restoration Closing a modal sends focus to <body> — the user loses their place No focus on error Screen readers do not announce validation errors No focus on new content Dynamically added content is never reached by keyboard No inert attribute JavaScript focus traps had to manage every edge case manually

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Focus management is not a new feature — it has been a WCAG requirement since WCAG 1.0. But three recent platform changes made it dramatically simpler:

  • The inert attribute (baseline in all browsers since April 2023) replaced the 50-line JavaScript focus-trap pattern. Applying inert to background content removes it from the tab order, the accessibility tree, and click handling — all natively, handling iframes and Shadow DOM edge cases that JavaScript traps often miss.
  • The native <dialog> element (landed in major browsers in March 2022) provides focus trapping, Escape handling, and modal semantics without JavaScript. The W3C APA Working Group explicitly concluded that the dialog's behavior of allowing focus to tab to browser chrome is correct and beneficial — focus-trapping advice for <dialog> is now deprecated.
  • element.focus({ focusVisible: true }) (as of 2025) allows developers to force the focus ring programmatically — solving a long-standing UX bug where .focus() did not trigger :focus-visible.

docs.title: The Core API: element.focus()
docs.text:
// Move focus to an element
element.focus();

// Move focus and show the focus ring programmatically
element.focus({ focusVisible: true });

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• .focus() — moves focus to the element. The element must be focusable (native focusable element or tabindex set).
  • { focusVisible: true } — forces the focus indicator to show, even if the focus was not triggered by a keyboard event. This is useful after programmatic focus changes.

docs.title: The tabindex Attribute for Focus Management
docs.text:
<!-- tabindex="-1" makes an element programmatically focusable -->
<!-- but removes it from the Tab order -->
<main tabindex="-1">...</main>
<h1 tabindex="-1">...</h1>
<div tabindex="-1" id="error-message">...</div>

Code Breakdown:

  • tabindex="-1" — the element is focusable via .focus() but not reachable via Tab.
  • This is the standard pattern for skip link targets, modal containers, route-change focus targets, and error messages.
  • Remove the tabindex after blur so it does not remain a permanent focus target.

docs.title: The inert Attribute
docs.text:
<main inert>
    <!-- Background content is non-focusable and non-interactive -->
</main>

<dialog id="my-dialog">...</dialog>

const dialog = document.getElementById('my-dialog');
const main = document.querySelector('main');

// Open modal
main.inert = true;
dialog.showModal();

// Close modal
dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
    main.inert = false;
    returnFocusTo.focus();
});

Code Breakdown:

  • inert — makes the element and all descendants non-focusable, non-clickable, and hidden from assistive technology.
  • inert handles iframes, Shadow DOM, and dynamically added content natively — edge cases JavaScript focus traps often miss.
  • inert is a boolean attribute; setting main.inert = true adds it.

docs.title: The Native <dialog> Element
docs.text:
<dialog id="confirm">
    <form method="dialog">
        <h2>Confirm deletion</h2>
        <p>This action cannot be undone.</p>
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<button id="open-btn">Delete account</button>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('confirm');
    const openBtn = document.getElementById('open-btn');

    openBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        dialog.showModal();
        // Focus moves into the dialog automatically
    });

    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        // Return focus to the trigger
        openBtn.focus();
    });
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • showModal() — opens the dialog as a modal, moves focus into it automatically, and makes the background inert.
  • dialog.close() — closes the dialog. The close event fires.
  • The W3C APA Working Group confirmed that the native dialog's behavior — allowing focus to tab to the browser chrome — is correct and beneficial. Do not implement a JavaScript focus trap for <dialog>.

docs.title: The enterkeyhint Attribute
docs.text:
<input type="text" enterkeyhint="next" placeholder="First name">
<input type="text" enterkeyhint="done" placeholder="Last name">
<input type="search" enterkeyhint="search">

Code Breakdown:

  • enterkeyhint="next" — the on-screen keyboard shows "Next" instead of "Enter."
  • enterkeyhint="done" — shows "Done."
  • enterkeyhint="search" — shows a search icon.
  • Improves mobile accessibility by telling users what the Enter key will do.

docs.title: The "Three Mandatory SPA Fixes" Mental Model
docs.text:
Single-page applications break three automatic browser behaviors. All three must be fixed manually:

Traditional page load:
  ✅ Focus resets to top
  ✅ Title is announced to screen readers
  ✅ Scroll resets to top

SPA route change:
  ❌ Focus stays on the clicked link (which may not exist)
  ❌ Title does not change
  ❌ Screen reader announces nothing

The three mandatory fixes:
  1. document.title = newPageTitle
  2. focus to <main> or <h1> (with tabindex="-1")
  3. announce via ARIA live region

The "Three Mandatory SPA Fixes" pattern is the single most important focus management practice for modern web applications.

docs.title: The "Focus Decision Tree" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every dynamic change requires a decision about where focus should go:

What changed?
    │
    ├── Modal opened
    │   └── Focus moves INTO the modal
    │
    ├── Modal closed
    │   └── Focus returns to the TRIGGER
    │
    ├── Route changed (SPA)
    │   └── Focus moves to <main> or <h1>
    │
    ├── Content added dynamically
    │   └── Focus moves to the new content (or announce via live region)
    │
    ├── Content removed
    │   └── Focus moves to the next logical element
    │
    └── Validation error
        └── Focus moves to the first invalid field

Every dynamic change has a correct focus destination. The decision tree makes it explicit.

docs.title: The "Inert vs Tabindex vs aria-hidden" Mental Model
docs.text:
Three tools, three different behaviors:

Tool Removes from Tab Order? Removes from AT Tree? Handles Click Events? inert ✅ ✅ ✅ tabindex="-1" ✅ ❌ ❌ aria-hidden="true" ❌ ✅ ❌

inert is the correct tool for making background content non-interactive during a modal. aria-hidden="true" alone does not remove elements from the tab order — it creates a keyboard trap.

docs.title: The "Don't Trap Focus on <dialog>" Mental Model
docs.text:
The old advice: "Trap focus inside the modal." The new advice: "Don't trap focus on <dialog>."

Old pattern (custom modal):
  - Implement JavaScript focus trap
  - Listen for Tab/Shift+Tab
  - Manually loop focus
  - Handle edge cases (iframes, Shadow DOM)
  - 50+ lines of code

New pattern (native <dialog>):
  - dialog.showModal()
  - Background becomes inert automatically
  - Focus moves into dialog automatically
  - Tab to browser chrome is allowed (correct behavior)
  - 0 lines of focus-trap code

The W3C APA Working Group concluded that allowing keyboard users to tab to browser chrome — open a new tab, check something, come back — is beneficial, not a bug.

docs.title: Concept 1: WCAG 2.4.3 — Focus Order (Level A)
docs.text: The foundational requirement: focus must move in an order that preserves meaning and operability. The order must be logical — typically following the visual reading order (top to bottom, left to right).

docs.title: Concept 2: WCAG 2.1.2 — No Keyboard Trap (Level A)
docs.text: If focus can move into a component, it must be able to move out. A keyboard trap occurs when the user cannot leave a widget without a mouse. Focus management must always provide an exit.

docs.title: Concept 3: WCAG 2.4.7 — Focus Visible (Level AA)
docs.text: Any keyboard-operable interface must have a mode of operation where the focus indicator is visible. The :focus-visible pseudo-class is the modern standard.

docs.title: Concept 4: WCAG 2.4.11 — Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA)
docs.text: When a UI component receives keyboard focus, the component must not be entirely hidden due to author-created content. Sticky headers, sticky footers, and cookie banners commonly obscure focused elements. The AA criterion allows partial obscuring, but the component must be at least partially visible. For best visibility, none of the component should be obscured — this preferred outcome is covered by the AAA criterion Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced).

docs.title: Concept 5: WCAG 2.4.13 — Focus Appearance (Level AAA)
docs.text:
WCAG 2.2 added numeric minimums for focus indicators. When the keyboard focus indicator is visible, an area of the indicator must:

  • Be at least as large as the area of a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter of the unfocused component.
  • Have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in focused and unfocused states.

This is a Level AAA criterion, but it is a best practice to meet it at AA.

docs.title: Concept 6: document.title Update on Route Change
docs.text: Screen readers announce the document title when the page loads. SPAs must update document.title on every route change so the new page context is announced.

docs.title: Concept 7: Focus Target — <main> or <h1>
docs.text: On SPA route change, focus should move to the <main> element or the new page's <h1>. Not document.body — which is invisible to screen readers and does not announce the new page context. The target needs tabindex="-1" to be programmatically focusable.

docs.title: Concept 8: ARIA Live Region Announcement
docs.text:
After moving focus on route change, announce the change via an ARIA live region. The live region should be visually hidden but present in the DOM.

<div id="route-announcer"
     role="status"
     aria-live="polite"
     aria-atomic="true"
     style="position:absolute;width:1px;height:1px;overflow:hidden;clip:rect(0,0,0,0);">
</div>

docs.title: Concept 9: Focus Restoration
docs.text:
When a modal, dropdown, or overlay closes, focus must return to the element that triggered it. Without this, focus is lost — often returning to document.body or the top of the page.

function openModal(trigger) {
    returnFocusTo = trigger;
    modal.showModal();
}

function closeModal() {
    modal.close();
    returnFocusTo?.focus();
}

docs.title: Concept 10: The inert Attribute for Background Content
docs.text: When a modal is open, background content should receive the inert attribute. This prevents focus from reaching background elements and removes them from the accessibility tree. inert is baseline in all browsers since April 2023.

docs.title: Concept 11: Native <dialog> Focus Behavior
docs.text:
The <dialog> element with showModal():

  • Moves focus into the dialog automatically (honoring autofocus).
  • Makes the background inert.
  • Allows Escape to close the dialog.
  • Allows Tab to reach browser chrome (this is correct behavior).

Do not implement a JavaScript focus trap for <dialog> — it is deprecated advice.

docs.title: Concept 12: Roving Tabindex
docs.text: For composite widgets (tabs, toolbars, menus, radio groups), roving tabindex makes the entire widget a single tab stop. Exactly one child has tabindex="0"; all others have tabindex="-1". Arrow keys move focus between children and update the tabindex values.

docs.title: Concept 13: aria-activedescendant for Virtualized Lists
docs.text: For virtualized lists, comboboxes, and large datasets where DOM nodes are not always present, aria-activedescendant keeps focus on the container and points to the active child by ID.

docs.title: Concept 14: element.focus({ focusVisible: true })
docs.text: As of 2025, calling element.focus() does not trigger :focus-visible. The focusVisible: true option forces the focus ring to show, solving a long-standing UX bug. Use it after programmatic focus changes.

docs.title: Concept 15: scroll-margin-top for Sticky Headers
docs.text:
Focused elements may be obscured by sticky headers. scroll-margin-top tells the browser to scroll the element into view with additional offset:

:focus {
    scroll-margin-top: 80px; /* height of sticky header */
}

docs.title: Concept 16: Focus Management in SPAs — Framework Patterns
docs.text:
Every major framework has a focus management pattern:

Framework Approach React useEffect on route change; move focus to <main> Vue router.afterEach(); move focus to <main> Angular Router events; move focus to <main> Svelte afterNavigate(); move focus to <main>

docs.title: Concept 17: Focus on Error
docs.text:
After form validation fails, focus should move to the first invalid field. This ensures the screen reader announces the error and the user can correct it immediately.

form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    const firstInvalid = form.querySelector(':invalid');
    if (firstInvalid) {
        e.preventDefault();
        firstInvalid.focus();
        firstInvalid.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
    }
});

docs.title: Concept 18: Focus on New Content
docs.text: When content is dynamically added (e.g., a new item appears in a list), focus should move to the new content or an announcement should be made via a live region.

docs.title: Concept 19: Focus After Deletion
docs.text: When content is removed, focus should move to the next logical element — the next item in the list, or the list container.

docs.title: Concept 20: Testing Focus Management
docs.text: Focus management can only be tested manually. Put away the mouse, tab through the page, open modals, close them, navigate routes, submit forms with errors — and verify that focus is always in the right place.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Modal Focus Management
docs.text:
1.  User activates the modal trigger.
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript saves document.activeElement (the trigger).
    │
    ▼
3.  Background content receives the inert attribute.
    │
    ▼
4.  dialog.showModal() is called.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser automatically moves focus into the dialog.
    │
    ▼
6.  User navigates within the dialog via Tab.
    │
    ▼
7.  User presses Escape or clicks a button.
    │
    ▼
8.  dialog.close() is called; the close event fires.
    │
    ▼
9.  inert is removed from the background.
    │
    ▼
10. Focus returns to the trigger element.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: SPA Route Change Focus Management
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a route link.
    │
    ▼
2.  Router intercepts; no full page reload.
    │
    ▼
3.  View updates in the DOM.
    │
    ▼
4.  After render:
    │   ├── document.title = new page title
    │   ├── focus moves to <main> or <h1> (tabindex="-1")
    │   └── live region announces "Navigated to [title]"
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader announces the new page.
    │
    ▼
6.  Keyboard user is at the top of the new content.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Focus Restoration on Close
docs.text:
1.  User activates a modal trigger.
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript saves the trigger element.
    │
    ▼
3.  Modal opens; focus moves inside.
    │
    ▼
4.  User closes the modal.
    │
    ▼
5.  Focus returns to the saved trigger element.
    │
    ▼
6.  User continues from where they left off.

docs.title: The Document Active Element
docs.text:
The browser maintains a single document.activeElement — the element with focus. Only one element has focus at a time.

document.activeElement; // returns the currently focused element

docs.title: The Focus Target Algorithm
docs.text:
When .focus() is called:

  1. The browser checks if the element is focusable.
  2. If focusable, it moves focus to the element.
  3. :focus styles apply.
  4. :focus-visible applies if the focus was keyboard-triggered or focusVisible: true was specified.
  5. The accessibility API fires a focus event.
  6. Screen reader announces the element.

docs.title: The inert Attribute Mechanics
docs.text:
inert is a boolean attribute that makes an element and all its descendants:

  • Non-focusable (removed from tab order).
  • Non-clickable (click events suppressed).
  • Hidden from assistive technology (removed from accessibility tree).
  • Not reachable via document.activeElement.

inert handles iframes, Shadow DOM, and dynamically added content natively.

docs.title: The Native <dialog> Focus Algorithm
docs.text:
When showModal() is called:

  1. The dialog is displayed as a modal.
  2. The background content becomes inert.
  3. Focus moves to the first focusable element inside the dialog (or the element with autofocus).
  4. Tab cycles through the dialog's focusable elements.
  5. After the last element, Tab moves to the browser chrome (address bar, etc.) — this is correct behavior.
  6. Escape closes the dialog.

docs.title: The :focus-visible Heuristic
docs.text:
Browsers implement :focus-visible using their own heuristics:

  • A <button> clicked with a mouse typically does not match :focus-visible.
  • A text <input> clicked with a mouse does match :focus-visible.
  • Any focus reached via Tab, Shift+Tab, or arrow-key navigation reliably matches :focus-visible.
  • element.focus({ focusVisible: true }) forces :focus-visible.

docs.title: Modal Lifecycle
docs.text:
Trigger clicked → save trigger → inert background → showModal()
    │
    ▼
Focus moves into modal → user interacts → user closes
    │
    ▼
close event fires → remove inert → restore focus to trigger

docs.title: SPA Route Change Lifecycle
docs.text:
Route link clicked → router intercepts → view updates
    │
    ▼
After render:
  1. document.title = newPageTitle
  2. focus to <main> or <h1>
  3. live region announces
    │
    ▼
User continues from new content

docs.title: Form Error Lifecycle
docs.text:
Form submitted → validation fails
    │
    ▼
Focus moves to first invalid field
    │
    ▼
Screen reader announces error
    │
    ▼
User corrects the field

docs.title: Example 1: SPA Route Change Focus (React)
docs.text:
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useLocation } from 'react-router-dom';

function RouteAnnouncer() {
    const location = useLocation();

    useEffect(() => {
        // 1. Update document title
        const pageTitle = getPageTitle(location.pathname);
        document.title = pageTitle;

        // 2. Move focus to main content
        const main = document.querySelector('main');
        if (main) {
            main.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
            main.focus();

            // Remove tabindex after blur so it doesn't appear in tab order
            main.addEventListener('blur', () => {
                main.removeAttribute('tabindex');
            }, { once: true });
        }

        // 3. Announce route change
        const announcer = document.getElementById('route-announcer');
        if (announcer) {
            announcer.textContent = `Navigated to ${pageTitle}`;
        }
    }, [location]);

    return null;
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Updates document.title on every route change.
  • Moves focus to <main> with tabindex="-1".
  • Removes tabindex after blur so it does not appear in normal tab order.
  • Live region announces "Navigated to [title]" for screen readers.
  • This is the three mandatory SPA fixes.

docs.title: Example 2: Modal with Focus Restoration
docs.text:
<dialog id="confirm">
    <form method="dialog">
        <h2>Confirm deletion</h2>
        <p>This action cannot be undone.</p>
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<button id="delete-btn">Delete account</button>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('confirm');
    const deleteBtn = document.getElementById('delete-btn');

    deleteBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        dialog.showModal();
        // Focus moves into the dialog automatically
    });

    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        // Return focus to the trigger
        deleteBtn.focus();
    });
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • showModal() opens the dialog with native focus management.
  • No JavaScript focus trap is needed — <dialog> handles it natively.
  • On close, focus returns to the trigger.

docs.title: Example 3: Custom Modal with inert
docs.text:
<div id="custom-modal" role="dialog" aria-modal="true"
     aria-labelledby="modal-title" hidden>
    <h2 id="modal-title">Confirm deletion</h2>
    <p>This action cannot be undone.</p>
    <button id="cancel-btn">Cancel</button>
    <button id="confirm-btn">Delete</button>
</div>

<main id="app-content">
    <h1>Dashboard</h1>
    <button id="open-modal">Delete account</button>
</main>

<script>
    const modal = document.getElementById('custom-modal');
    const main = document.getElementById('app-content');
    const openBtn = document.getElementById('open-modal');
    let returnFocusTo = null;

    openBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        returnFocusTo = openBtn;
        main.inert = true;
        modal.hidden = false;
        modal.querySelector('button').focus();
    });

    document.getElementById('cancel-btn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        modal.hidden = true;
        main.inert = false;
        returnFocusTo?.focus();
    });
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • inert on <main> removes the background from the tab order.
  • Focus moves to the first button in the modal.
  • On close, inert is removed and focus returns to the trigger.
  • This is the pattern for custom modals when <dialog> cannot be used.

docs.title: Example 4: Form Error Focus
docs.text:
const form = document.querySelector('form');

form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    const firstInvalid = form.querySelector(':invalid');
    if (firstInvalid) {
        e.preventDefault();
        firstInvalid.focus();
        firstInvalid.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');

        // Announce error
        const error = document.getElementById(firstInvalid.getAttribute('aria-describedby'));
        if (error) {
            error.textContent = firstInvalid.validationMessage;
        }
    }
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Finds the first invalid field.
  • Prevents submission.
  • Moves focus to the first invalid field.
  • Sets aria-invalid="true".
  • Populates the error message.

docs.title: Example 5: focus({ focusVisible: true }) for Programmatic Focus
docs.text:
// After route change, move focus and show the focus ring
const main = document.querySelector('main');
main.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
main.focus({ focusVisible: true });

Code Breakdown:

  • focusVisible: true forces the focus ring to show.
  • Without it, .focus() may not trigger :focus-visible.
  • This is the modern solution to the "invisible focus after programmatic focus" bug.

docs.title: Example 6: scroll-margin-top for Sticky Headers
docs.text:
:focus {
    scroll-margin-top: 80px; /* height of sticky header */
}

Code Breakdown:

  • When a focused element is scrolled into view, scroll-margin-top adds offset.
  • Prevents the sticky header from obscuring the focused element.
  • Meets WCAG 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured).

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Focus Management Pattern SPA route change Update title, focus <main> or <h1>, announce Modal open Focus into modal (or showModal()) Modal close Focus returns to trigger Dropdown open Focus into dropdown or use aria-activedescendant Form error Focus first invalid field Content deleted Focus next logical element Content added Focus new content or announce via live region Tabs Roving tabindex; arrow keys move focus Skip link Focus <main tabindex="-1"> Accordion Focus stays on header; aria-expanded updates Carousel Focus moves to slide controls Toast notification Do not move focus; use live region

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Decide where focus goes for every DOM change. Why: dynamic content is the most common source of focus regressions.
  2. Update document.title on every SPA route change. Why: screen readers announce the title on navigation.
  3. Move focus to <main> or <h1> on route change. Why: not document.body — screen readers need a meaningful target.
  4. Use tabindex="-1" on focus targets. Why: makes them programmatically focusable without adding them to the tab order.
  5. Remove tabindex after blur. Why: prevents the element from remaining a permanent tab stop.
  6. Use element.focus({ focusVisible: true }). Why: forces the focus ring to show after programmatic focus.
  7. Return focus to the trigger when closing modals. Why: without it, focus is lost.
  8. Use inert for background content when a modal is open. Why: native, handles edge cases, simpler than JavaScript.
  9. Use native <dialog> with showModal(). Why: native focus management; no JavaScript trap needed.
  10. Do not trap focus on <dialog>. Why: the native behavior of allowing tab to browser chrome is correct.
  11. Use scroll-margin-top for sticky headers. Why: prevents focused elements from being obscured.
  12. Focus the first invalid field on form error. Why: ensures the error is announced and correctable.
  13. Use ARIA live regions for non-focus-moving announcements. Why: not every change should move focus.
  14. Do not move focus on first page load. Why: disorients screen reader users who expect the page to start at the top.
  15. Use roving tabindex for composite widgets. Why: reduces tab stops and matches native behavior.
  16. Test with keyboard only. Why: focus management can only be verified manually.
  17. Test with a screen reader. Why: focus management and screen reader behavior are linked.
  18. Document focus management decisions. Why: consistency across a team prevents regressions.
  19. Audit focus management after every significant UI change. Why: custom widgets frequently break focus.
  20. Use framework-specific focus management patterns. Why: React, Vue, Angular, and Svelte have established patterns.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: SPA Route Change Without Focus Management
docs.text:
// Router navigates; no focus management

Why it's wrong: Focus stays on the clicked link (which may no longer exist); screen readers announce nothing; the user is stranded.

✅ Correct:

// After route change:
document.title = newTitle;
main.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
main.focus({ focusVisible: true });
announcer.textContent = `Navigated to ${newTitle}`;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Focus Lost After Modal Close
docs.text:
function closeModal() {
    modal.hidden = true;
    // Focus is lost — returns to <body>
}

Why it's wrong: The user loses their place in the page.

✅ Correct:

function closeModal() {
    modal.hidden = true;
    returnFocusTo?.focus();
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Moving Focus to document.body
docs.text:
document.body.focus(); // Does nothing useful

Why it's wrong: document.body is invisible to screen readers and does not announce the new page context.

✅ Correct:

main.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
main.focus();

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: JavaScript Focus Trap on <dialog>
docs.text:
// Old advice: implement a focus trap on <dialog>
dialog.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
    if (e.key === 'Tab') {
        // ... trap logic
    }
});

Why it's wrong: Focus-trapping advice for <dialog> is deprecated. The native behavior of allowing tab to browser chrome is correct and beneficial.

✅ Correct: Use dialog.showModal() without a JavaScript focus trap.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: aria-hidden="true" on Background Content
docs.text:
<main aria-hidden="true">
    <!-- Background content -->
</main>

Why it's wrong: aria-hidden removes elements from the accessibility tree but does not remove them from the tab order — creating a keyboard trap.

✅ Correct:

<main inert>
    <!-- Background content -->
</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Moving Focus on First Page Load
docs.text:
window.addEventListener('load', () => {
    main.focus();
});

Why it's wrong: Disorients screen reader users who expect the page to start at the top.

✅ Correct: Only move focus on subsequent navigation.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Focus Indicator After Programmatic Focus
docs.text:
main.focus(); // Focus moves but no visible ring

Why it's wrong: The user cannot see where focus is.

✅ Correct:

main.focus({ focusVisible: true });

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Focused Element Obscured by Sticky Header
docs.text:
.sticky-header {
    position: sticky;
    top: 0;
    height: 80px;
}

Why it's wrong: Focused elements may be hidden behind the sticky header — violates WCAG 2.4.11.

✅ Correct:

:focus {
    scroll-margin-top: 80px;
}

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Focus management has negligible performance cost — a single .focus() call.
  • inert is a native browser feature — no JavaScript focus-trap overhead.
  • <dialog> is a native element — no JavaScript modal overhead.
  • Live region announcements are processed by the browser's accessibility API — minimal overhead.
  • SPA route focus management adds one .focus() call per navigation.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use native <dialog> and inert — no JavaScript focus-trap overhead.
  2. Batch focus management updates — one .focus() call per interaction.
  3. Use requestAnimationFrame for focus after DOM updates.
  4. Avoid setTimeout for focus management.

docs.title: Focus Hijacking
docs.text: Malicious scripts can move focus unexpectedly — a technique used in clickjacking and UI redressing attacks. Modern browsers restrict programmatic focus to elements that are already visible or have been interacted with.

docs.title: inert and Content Leakage
docs.text: inert removes elements from the accessibility tree and tab order but does not remove them from the DOM. Sensitive content hidden with inert is still visible in DevTools.

docs.title: Modal Focus and Escape
docs.text: Ensure that modal focus management cannot prevent users from leaving the page. The Escape key must always close the modal, and browser chrome must remain accessible.

docs.title: Autofocus Abuse
docs.text: autofocus on page load can disorient screen reader users and can be abused by malicious pages. Use it sparingly and only on pages where it is expected.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Put away the mouse. Tab through the page. This is the only reliable test.
  • Check document.activeElement — log it after every interaction.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect focusable elements.
  • document.querySelectorAll('[tabindex]') — list all elements with tabindex.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — audits for focus management issues.
  • axe DevTools extension — flags focus management problems.
  • Screen reader testing — NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack.
  • Test modal open/close — verify focus moves in and returns.
  • Test SPA route changes — verify title, focus, and announcement.
  • Test form errors — verify focus moves to the first invalid field.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every SPA route change — update title, move focus, announce.
  • Every modal — focus in, focus out.
  • Every dynamic content change — decide where focus goes.
  • Every form error — focus first invalid field.
  • Every content deletion — focus next logical element.
  • Every composite widget — roving tabindex or aria-activedescendant.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not move focus on first page load. Let the browser reset to the top.
  • Do not move focus for toast notifications. Use a live region instead.
  • Do not move focus on hover. Focus is a keyboard concept.
  • Do not use a JavaScript focus trap on <dialog>. It is deprecated.
  • Do not use aria-hidden="true" instead of inert. It creates keyboard traps.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)
  • WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A)
  • WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA)
  • WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Level AA)
  • WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (Level AAA)
  • element.focus()
  • element.focus({ focusVisible: true })
  • tabindex attribute
  • inert attribute
  • <dialog> element
  • aria-activedescendant
  • Roving tabindex
  • scroll-margin-top
  • SPA route change focus
  • Focus restoration
  • ARIA live regions
  • Screen readers

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Focus management is the most common source of accessibility regressions in dynamic web applications.
  • The three mandatory SPA fixes are: update document.title, move focus to <main> or <h1>, and announce via live region.
  • document.body is invisible to screen readers — never move focus there.
  • The inert attribute is baseline in all browsers since April 2023 — it replaces the 50-line JavaScript focus-trap pattern.
  • Focus-trapping advice for <dialog> is deprecated — the W3C APA Working Group confirmed that tabbing to browser chrome is correct.
  • element.focus({ focusVisible: true }) forces the focus ring to show — solving a long-standing UX bug as of 2025.
  • WCAG 2.2 added numeric minimums for focus indicators — 2px thick, 3:1 contrast.
  • Sticky headers and cookie banners commonly obscure focused elements — scroll-margin-top fixes this.
  • A modal without focus management is not a modal — it is a dialog box that happens to be positioned in the center.
  • ARIA live regions announce changes without moving focus — ideal for toast notifications.
  • Focus must return to the trigger when a modal closes — without it, the user loses their place.
  • aria-hidden="true" does not remove elements from the tab order — it creates a keyboard trap.
  • tabindex="-1" makes an element programmatically focusable without adding it to the tab order.
  • Roving tabindex makes a composite widget a single tab stop — arrow keys move between children.
  • Focus management can only be tested manually — automated tools catch only 30–50% of issues.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Focus management is the deliberate control of where keyboard focus goes as the user interacts with a dynamic page.
  • It is the most common source of accessibility regressions in SPAs, modals, and interactive widgets.
  • The three mandatory SPA fixes: update document.title, move focus to <main> or <h1>, announce via live region.
  • Focus targets need tabindex="-1" to be programmatically focusable without entering the tab order.
  • element.focus({ focusVisible: true }) forces the focus ring to show.
  • Modal focus management: focus into the modal on open; return to the trigger on close.
  • Use inert for background content when a modal is open — native, handles edge cases.
  • Use native <dialog> with showModal() — no JavaScript focus trap needed.
  • Do not trap focus on <dialog> — the native behavior of allowing tab to browser chrome is correct.
  • Focus the first invalid field on form error.
  • Use scroll-margin-top for sticky headers — prevents focused elements from being obscured.
  • Use ARIA live regions for non-focus-moving announcements.
  • Test with keyboard only and with a screen reader — focus management can only be verified manually.
  • Focus management is the difference between a dynamic interface that works for everyone and one that only works for mouse users.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A screen reader is assistive technology that converts the visual interface of a web page — its text, structure, roles, states, and dynamic updates — into speech output or Braille. It allows blind and low-vision users to perceive, navigate, and interact with digital content by listening rather than looking.

<!-- A button with an accessible name -->
<button type="button" aria-label="Close dialog">✕</button>

<!-- Screen reader announces: "Close dialog, button" -->

A screen reader does not read the visual pixels on the screen. It reads the accessibility tree — a structured representation of the page that the browser builds from your HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and ARIA. If your markup is wrong, the screen reader has nothing meaningful to say.

There are four dominant screen readers:

Screen reader Platform Cost Market share (desktop) NVDA Windows Free, open source 37.7% JAWS Windows Commercial (~$90/year or ~$1,000 perpetual) 40.5% VoiceOver macOS, iOS, iPadOS, visionOS Built-in 9.7% desktop; ~70.6% mobile TalkBack Android Built-in ~34.7% of mobile users

Nearly three-quarters of screen reader users run more than one screen reader. 91.3% use a screen reader on a mobile device.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Screen readers serve several essential purposes:

  • Independence — blind and low-vision users can browse, shop, bank, work, and communicate without sighted assistance.
  • Structural navigation — screen readers navigate by headings, landmarks, links, form fields, buttons, and tables — not linearly like a sighted reader scanning a page.
  • Dynamic content announcement — live regions, alerts, and status messages are announced as they change.
  • Form interaction — labels, instructions, error messages, and validation feedback are announced at the correct moment.
  • Context awareness — the screen reader announces role, name, state, and value for every focused element.
  • Legal compliance — WCAG, ADA, Section 508, and the European Accessibility Act all require compatibility with screen readers.

Screen readers are the primary assistive technology for blind users, and testing with them is the only way to verify that your site actually works for the people who depend on them.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Accessibility Stack
│
├── Semantic HTML        ← provides roles, names, states to the accessibility tree
├── ARIA                 ← supplements native semantics for custom widgets
├── Keyboard Navigation  ← screen readers are keyboard-driven
├── Focus Management     ← screen reader follows focus
├── Screen Reader        ← converts the accessibility tree to speech/Braille
└── Testing              ← manual testing with real screen readers

A screen reader depends on everything beneath it in the stack. If semantic HTML is missing, ARIA is wrong, or keyboard navigation is broken, the screen reader experience fails.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: A visual user perceives a page in a single glance — layout, hierarchy, navigation, content, and interactive controls are all apparent simultaneously. A blind user cannot do this. Without a screen reader, the web is a wall of inaccessible content.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No text-to-speech Blind users could not access digital content No structural navigation Users had to read linearly, line by line No dynamic content announcement Page changes happened silently No accessible names Buttons and links announced as "button" or "link" with no label No landmark navigation No way to jump between page regions No form label association Inputs announced as "edit" with no purpose

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Screen readers evolved from early text-to-speech systems in the 1980s and 1990s. JAWS (Job Access With Speech) was released in 1995 by Freedom Scientific. NVDA (NonVisual Desktop Access) was released in 2006 as a free, open-source alternative. Apple integrated VoiceOver into macOS in 2005 and iOS in 2009. Google released TalkBack for Android in 2009.

Each screen reader was created to solve the same problem: give blind users access to the graphical interface through audio. As the web evolved from static documents to dynamic applications, screen readers added support for ARIA, live regions, and complex widgets.

Screen readers exist because the visual interface is inherently inaccessible to blind users. They are the bridge between the visual web and non-visual perception.

docs.title: The Screen Reader's Input: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
A screen reader reads the accessibility tree, not the DOM or the visual pixels. Every element has a role, a name, and a state:

<button type="button" aria-label="Close dialog" disabled>
    ✕
</button>
Property Value Source Role button Native <button> element Name "Close dialog" aria-label State disabled disabled attribute

Screen reader announcement: "Close dialog, button, dimmed" (NVDA) or "Close dialog, button, unavailable" (VoiceOver).

docs.title: The Accessible Name Computation
docs.text:
When multiple naming sources exist, the browser follows a priority order:

1. aria-labelledby    → references other elements by ID
2. aria-label         → direct string
3. Native label       → <label>, alt, <caption>, <legend>
4. Text content       → for buttons, links, headings
5. title attribute    → last resort

If aria-labelledby is present, it overrides all other sources. Accessible names are "flat" strings — they contain no structure or language change information.

docs.title: Common Screen Reader Commands
docs.text: Task NVDA (Windows) JAWS (Windows) VoiceOver (macOS) VoiceOver (iOS) Start/stop Ctrl+Alt+N — Cmd+F5 Triple-click side button Stop speech Ctrl Ctrl Control Two-finger tap Read all NVDA+Down Insert+Down VO+A Two-finger swipe up Next heading H H VO+Cmd+H Rotor → Headings Next link K K VO+Cmd+L Rotor → Links Next form field F F VO+Cmd+J Rotor → Form Controls Next landmark D ; (semicolon) VO+U → Landmarks Rotor → Landmarks Next button B B VO+Cmd+B Rotor → Buttons List headings — Insert+F6 VO+U → Headings Rotor → Headings List links — Insert+F7 VO+U → Links Rotor → Links List landmarks — Insert+Ctrl+R VO+U → Landmarks Rotor → Landmarks Read page title NVDA+T Insert+T VO+Shift+M —

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• NVDA uses the NVDA modifier key (Insert, Numpad 0, or Caps Lock).
  • JAWS uses the Insert key as its modifier.
  • VoiceOver uses VO (Control+Option) on macOS; on iOS, gestures replace keyboard commands.
  • Quick navigation keys (H, K, B, F, D) work in browse mode — the mode where the screen reader reads the page content. They do not work in focus mode (where you are typing in a form field).

docs.title: VoiceOver iOS Gestures
docs.text: Gesture Action Swipe right Next item Swipe left Previous item Double-tap Activate the focused item Two-finger tap Pause/resume speech Two-finger swipe up Read all from the top Two-finger rotate Change rotor setting Three-finger swipe Scroll

docs.title: TalkBack Android Gestures
docs.text: Gesture Action Swipe right Next item Swipe left Previous item Double-tap Activate the focused item Swipe down then right Read from next item Swipe up then down Change reading granularity

docs.title: The "Accessibility Tree" Mental Model
docs.text:
A screen reader does not read the DOM. It reads the accessibility tree — a parallel tree that the browser builds from your markup:

DOM Tree                          Accessibility Tree
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
<div class="header">         →    banner
  <div class="nav">          →      navigation "Main"
    <a href="/">Home</a>     →        link "Home"
<main>                       →    main
  <h1>Welcome</h1>           →      heading level 1 "Welcome"
  <img src="chart.png">      →      image "Bar chart of Q1 revenue"
  <button>Save</button>      →      button "Save"
<footer>                     →    contentinfo

Every element in the accessibility tree has a role, a name, and a state. The screen reader announces these three properties when focus lands on the element.

docs.title: The "Screen Reader vs. Browser" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  YOUR HTML / CSS / JS                        │
│  └── parsed by browser                       │
│       └── accessibility tree built           │
│            └── exposed via platform API      │
│                 └── screen reader reads it   │
│                      └── speech / Braille    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

You write HTML. The browser builds the accessibility tree. The screen reader reads the tree. The user hears speech. Every layer in this stack must be correct.

docs.title: The "Two Modes" Mental Model
docs.text:
Screen readers operate in two modes:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BROWSE MODE (or virtual cursor mode)        │
│  → Arrow keys move through content           │
│  → Quick nav keys (H, K, B, F, D) work      │
│  → Screen reader controls the cursor         │
│  → Used for reading and navigating content   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  FOCUS MODE (or forms mode)                  │
│  → Keyboard input goes to the web page       │
│  → Arrow keys move the text cursor           │
│  → Typing works normally                     │
│  → Used for filling out forms                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The screen reader switches between modes automatically when you Tab into a form field. This is why form fields must have proper labels — in focus mode, the screen reader announces the label only once.

docs.title: The "Screen Reader ≠ Visual Reader" Mental Model
docs.text:
A sighted user scans a page visually. A screen reader user navigates structurally:

Sighted user:        Screen reader user:
"Let me look at the  → "Let me list the headings."
 top of the page."      (Insert+F6 in JAWS)
                       → "Let me jump to the main landmark."
                         (D in NVDA)
                       → "Let me list the links."
                         (Insert+F7 in JAWS)

Screen reader users do not read pages linearly. They navigate by structure — headings, landmarks, links, and form fields. This is why semantic HTML and proper heading hierarchy are so important.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Four Major Screen Readers
docs.text:
Screen reader Platform Engine Cost NVDA Windows NonVisual Desktop Access (NV Access) Free, open source JAWS Windows Job Access With Speech (Freedom Scientific) Commercial VoiceOver macOS, iOS, iPadOS, visionOS Apple Built-in TalkBack Android Google Built-in

Each has its own keyboard shortcuts, gestures, and quirks. Testing with multiple screen readers is recommended — but testing with one is far better than testing with none.

docs.title: Concept 2: Market Share and Testing Priorities
docs.text:
Based on the WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #10 (2024):

  • JAWS: 40.5% primary desktop use
  • NVDA: 37.7% primary desktop use
  • VoiceOver: 9.7% primary desktop use; 70.6% mobile use
  • TalkBack: ~34.7% of mobile screen reader users

Recommended testing combinations (ranked by user impact):

  1. JAWS + Chrome (Windows) — 24.7% of users; the #1 combination by market share
  2. NVDA + Chrome (Windows) — 21.3% of users; free, catches most code issues
  3. VoiceOver + Safari (macOS) — 7.0% desktop users
  4. VoiceOver + Safari (iOS) — the dominant mobile screen reader
  5. TalkBack + Chrome (Android) — 34.7% of mobile users

docs.title: Concept 3: Browse Mode vs. Focus Mode
docs.text:
Screen readers have two modes:

  • Browse mode (NVDA, JAWS) or virtual cursor mode: the screen reader controls the cursor. Arrow keys move through the accessibility tree. Quick nav keys (H, K, B, F, D) work.
  • Focus mode (NVDA, JAWS) or forms mode: the web page controls the cursor. Keyboard input goes to the focused element. Typing works normally.

The screen reader switches automatically when focus enters a form field. In focus mode, the screen reader announces the label once, then stays silent while you type.

docs.title: Concept 4: Quick Navigation Keys
docs.text:
In browse mode, single-letter keys navigate by element type:

Key Function NVDA JAWS H Next heading ✅ ✅ 1–6 Next heading of specific level ✅ ✅ Shift+H Previous heading ✅ ✅ K Next link ✅ ✅ B Next button ✅ ✅ F Next form field ✅ ✅ D Next landmark ✅ — ; Next landmark — ✅ T Next table ✅ ✅ L Next list ✅ ✅

docs.title: Concept 5: Landmark Navigation
docs.text:
Screen readers can jump directly to landmark regions:

  • NVDA: Press D to cycle through landmarks.
  • JAWS: Press ; (semicolon) or Insert+Ctrl+R to list regions.
  • VoiceOver: Rotor → Landmarks.
  • TalkBack: Swipe to landmarks via the reading menu.

docs.title: Concept 6: Heading Navigation
docs.text:
Headings are the primary navigation mechanism for screen reader users. 76.6% of screen reader users have blindness as their primary disability, and headings are how they skim content — the same way sighted users scan visually.

  • NVDA: H for next heading; 1–6 for heading levels.
  • JAWS: Insert+F6 to list all headings; H for next heading.
  • VoiceOver: Rotor → Headings.

docs.title: Concept 7: Form Label Announcement
docs.text:
In focus mode, the screen reader announces the label when focus enters a form field. If the label is missing or not programmatically associated, the screen reader announces something meaningless like "edit" or "input" with no context.

<!-- Correct: label is associated -->
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email" required>
<!-- Announces: "Email address, edit, required" -->

<!-- Wrong: placeholder is not a label -->
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">
<!-- Announces: "edit" — no label -->

docs.title: Concept 8: Live Region Announcements
docs.text:
Live regions announce dynamic content changes without moving focus.

Attribute Politeness Use Case aria-live="polite" Waits for user idle Status updates, chat messages aria-live="assertive" Interrupts immediately Alerts, errors role="alert" Implicit assertive Error messages role="status" Implicit polite General status updates

docs.title: Concept 9: Accessible Name Computation
docs.text:
The accessible name is what the screen reader announces for an element. It is computed from multiple sources in priority order:

  1. aria-labelledby — references other elements by ID
  2. aria-label — direct string
  3. Native label — <label>, alt, <caption>
  4. Text content — for buttons, links
  5. title attribute — last resort

docs.title: Concept 10: Reading Order vs. Visual Order
docs.text: Screen readers follow DOM order, not visual order. CSS order, flex-direction: row-reverse, and absolute positioning can create a mismatch between visual and DOM order — a common and serious accessibility failure.

docs.title: Concept 11: Screen Reader Testing Is Manual
docs.text: Automated tools like axe-core and Lighthouse catch only 30–40% of accessibility issues. Screen reader testing is manual — a human listens to the output and determines whether it makes sense. Reading order, announcement clarity, and interaction flow cannot be automated.

docs.title: Concept 12: Testing with Real Screen Readers
docs.text: Browser simulators do not reliably reflect actual screen reader behavior. Testing with real screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack) is essential.

docs.title: Concept 13: NVDA — Free and Powerful
docs.text:
NVDA is free, open-source, and the most widely used screen reader among developers for testing. It supports:

  • Browse mode and focus mode
  • Quick navigation keys
  • Object navigation
  • Touch gestures
  • Braille output

docs.title: Concept 14: JAWS — The Enterprise Standard
docs.text:
JAWS is the commercial market leader, widely used in enterprise and education. It includes:

  • Page Explorer (AI-powered page summarization)
  • AI Labeler (automatic graphic description)
  • Cloud settings sync
  • HID Braille support

docs.title: Concept 15: VoiceOver — Apple's Built-in Screen Reader
docs.text:
VoiceOver is built into every Mac, iPhone, and iPad. It uses:

  • macOS: VO keys (Control+Option) + arrow keys
  • iOS: Gestures (swipe, double-tap, two-finger rotor)
  • Rotor: A circular menu for changing navigation method

docs.title: Concept 16: TalkBack — Android's Screen Reader
docs.text:
TalkBack is Google's built-in Android screen reader. It supports:

  • Swipe navigation
  • Reading menu
  • Braille display support
  • Customizable gestures

docs.title: Concept 17: Accessible Name Is "Flat"
docs.text: Accessible names are "flat" strings — they contain no structure or language change information. If you have a phrase in a different language inside a button, the screen reader will not switch pronunciation rules unless the language attribute is on the element itself.

docs.title: Concept 18: The lang Attribute Matters
docs.text:
Screen readers use the lang attribute to select the correct voice and pronunciation rules:

<html lang="en">
<p lang="fr">Bonjour</p>

Without lang, the screen reader may mispronounce content — reading French words with English pronunciation rules.

docs.title: Concept 19: Screen Reader Testing Checklist
docs.text:
A basic screen reader test covers five areas:

  1. Headings — are they announced with correct level and text?
  2. Links — are they announced with meaningful text?
  3. Forms — are labels announced before inputs?
  4. Images — are alt texts announced?
  5. Modals — does focus move in and return correctly?

docs.title: Concept 20: Screen Reader Testing in CI/CD
docs.text: Automated accessibility testing (axe-core, Lighthouse) can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines. But screen reader testing remains manual. Some teams use @axe-core/playwright or jest-axe to catch regressions — but these do not replace manual screen reader testing.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Screen Reader Announcement
docs.text:
1.  User navigates to an element.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser exposes the element via the accessibility API:
    │   ├── Role (button, link, heading, etc.)
    │   ├── Name (from aria-label, label, text content)
    │   ├── State (expanded, checked, disabled)
    │   └── Description (from aria-describedby)
    │
    ▼
3.  Screen reader queries the accessibility API.
    │
    ▼
4.  Screen reader builds the announcement:
    │   ├── Name first ("Email address")
    │   ├── Role second ("edit")
    │   ├── State third ("required")
    │   └── Description last
    │
    ▼
5.  Speech synthesizer speaks the announcement.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Form Label Announcement
docs.text:
1.  User tabs into an <input>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Screen reader queries the accessibility API for the input's name.
    │
    ▼
3.  Accessibility API returns the name from the associated <label>.
    │
    ▼
4.  Screen reader announces: "Email address, edit, required."
    │
    ▼
5.  User types — screen reader stays silent.
    │
    ▼
6.  User tabs out — screen reader announces the next element.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Live Region Announcement
docs.text:
1.  Live region exists in the DOM (role="alert", aria-live).
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript updates the content of the live region.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser detects the change.
    │
    ▼
4.  Accessibility API fires a live region event.
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader announces the new content.

docs.title: The Accessibility API
docs.text:
Each operating system exposes accessibility APIs that screen readers query:

Platform API Windows IAccessible2, UIA (UI Automation) macOS NSAccessibility Linux ATK/AT-SPI Android AccessibilityNodeInfo iOS UIAccessibility

The browser translates the accessibility tree into these platform APIs. The screen reader queries the platform API.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree vs. the DOM
docs.text:
The DOM is the browser's internal representation of the page. The accessibility tree is a parallel representation optimized for assistive technology:

  • aria-hidden="true" removes elements from the accessibility tree but not the DOM.
  • display: none removes from both.
  • role="presentation" removes semantics but keeps the element.
  • CSS-generated content (::before) may not appear in the accessibility tree.

docs.title: Browse Mode vs. Focus Mode (Under the Hood)
docs.text:
Browse mode:

  • The screen reader controls the cursor.
  • The screen reader intercepts keyboard input.
  • Quick navigation keys work.
  • Arrow keys move through the accessibility tree.

Focus mode:

  • The web page controls the cursor.
  • Keyboard input goes to the focused element.
  • Quick navigation keys do not work.
  • Typing works normally.

The screen reader switches modes automatically based on the element's role. Form fields trigger focus mode; everything else triggers browse mode.

docs.title: The Accessible Name Computation Algorithm
docs.text:
The algorithm is defined in the W3C Accessible Name and Description Computation specification. It follows this priority:

  1. aria-labelledby — resolve IDs, concatenate text
  2. aria-label — use the string directly
  3. Native labeling — <label for>, alt, <caption>, <legend>
  4. Text content — for buttons, links, headings
  5. title attribute — last resort

docs.title: Screen Reader and Braille
docs.text: Screen readers can output to Braille displays in addition to speech. Braille output is more precise for reading code, math, and structured content. JAWS 2026 and NVDA 2026 support HID Braille — a standardized command set across Braille displays.

docs.title: Screen Reader Testing Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Choose the screen reader(s) to test.
    │   ├── Primary: NVDA or JAWS (Windows)
    │   ├── Secondary: VoiceOver (macOS/iOS)
    │   └── Tertiary: TalkBack (Android)
    │
    ▼
2.  Launch the screen reader.
    │
    ▼
3.  Navigate to the test page.
    │
    ▼
4.  Test page structure:
    │   ├── Page title announced correctly?
    │   ├── Headings in logical order?
    │   ├── Landmarks present and labelled?
    │   └── Reading order matches visual order?
    │
    ▼
5.  Test form fields:
    │   ├── Labels announced before inputs?
    │   ├── Required state announced?
    │   └── Error messages announced?
    │
    ▼
6.  Test interactive elements:
    │   ├── Buttons announced with names?
    │   ├── Links announced with meaningful text?
    │   └── Custom widgets announced correctly?
    │
    ▼
7.  Test dynamic content:
    │   ├── Live regions announced?
    │   ├── Modals trap focus correctly?
    │   └── Route changes announced?
    │
    ▼
8.  Document findings and fix issues.

docs.title: Screen Reader Testing Checklist
docs.text:
Structure:
  [ ] Page title announced correctly
  [ ] Headings in logical order (H1 → H2 → H3, no skips)
  [ ] Landmarks present and labelled
  [ ] Reading order matches visual order
  [ ] Language set on <html>

Links:
  [ ] Links announced with meaningful text
  [ ] Links list (Insert+F7) shows all links
  [ ] Link purpose clear from text alone

Forms:
  [ ] Labels announced before inputs
  [ ] Required state announced
  [ ] Error messages announced and associated
  [ ] Fieldset/legend for grouped controls

Images:
  [ ] Meaningful images have alt text
  [ ] Decorative images skipped (alt="")

Interactive:
  [ ] Buttons announced with names
  [ ] Custom widgets have roles and states
  [ ] Modals trap focus correctly
  [ ] Dropdowns/accordions work with keyboard

Dynamic:
  [ ] Live regions announce updates
  [ ] Route changes announced (SPA)
  [ ] Loading states announced

docs.title: Example 1: Accessible Form with Label
docs.text:
<form>
    <label for="email">Email address</label>
    <input id="email" type="email" required
           aria-describedby="email-hint email-error">
    <span id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</span>
    <span id="email-error" role="alert"></span>

    <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

Screen reader announcement (when tabbing into the field): "Email address, edit, required, We'll never share your email."

Code Breakdown:

  • <label for="email"> — programmatically associates the label with the input.
  • aria-describedby — links hint text and error message to the input.
  • role="alert" — announces error messages immediately when populated.

docs.title: Example 2: Accessible Data Table
docs.text:
<table>
    <caption>Q1 2026 Revenue by Region</caption>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Region</th>
            <th scope="col">Revenue</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">North America</th>
            <td>$2.1M</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">Europe</th>
            <td>$1.4M</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

Screen reader announcement (navigating to the cell with $1.4M): "Europe, Revenue, $1.4M."

Code Breakdown:

  • <caption> — provides an accessible name for the table.
  • scope="col" — identifies column headers.
  • scope="row" — identifies row headers.
  • The screen reader associates the cell with its headers.

docs.title: Example 3: Live Region for Status Updates
docs.text:
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" id="status-message"></div>

<script>
    document.getElementById('status-message').textContent =
        'Settings saved successfully.';
</script>

Screen reader announcement: "Settings saved successfully" (after the user is idle).

Code Breakdown:

  • role="status" — implicitly aria-live="polite".
  • aria-live="polite" — waits for the user to be idle before announcing.
  • The announcement does not interrupt the user's current activity.

docs.title: Example 4: Accessible Modal
docs.text:
<dialog id="confirm-dialog">
    <form method="dialog">
        <h2>Confirm deletion</h2>
        <p>This action cannot be undone.</p>
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<button id="delete-btn">Delete account</button>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('confirm-dialog');
    const deleteBtn = document.getElementById('delete-btn');

    deleteBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        dialog.showModal();
    });

    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        deleteBtn.focus();
    });
</script>

Screen reader behavior:

  • On open: focus moves into the dialog; the <h2> is announced.
  • While open: focus is trapped; background is inert.
  • On close: focus returns to the trigger.

Code Breakdown:

  • dialog.showModal() — native modal with focus management.
  • No JavaScript focus trap needed — <dialog> handles it.
  • On close, focus returns to the trigger.

docs.title: Example 5: Screen Reader Testing with NVDA
docs.text:
## NVDA Test Checklist

### Setup
- [ ] Download NVDA from nvaccess.org
- [ ] Install and launch with Ctrl+Alt+N
- [ ] Open Chrome or Firefox
- [ ] Navigate to test page

### Structure
- [ ] Press NVDA+T — page title announced correctly
