- [ ] Press H — headings cycle through in order
- [ ] Press D — landmarks cycle through
- [ ] Press NVDA+Down — content reads in logical order

### Forms
- [ ] Press F — form fields cycle through
- [ ] Tab into each field — label announced
- [ ] Submit invalid form — error announced via role="alert"

### Links
- [ ] Press K — links cycle through
- [ ] Press NVDA+F7 — links list opens (if available)
- [ ] Verify all links have meaningful text

### Interactive
- [ ] Press B — buttons cycle through
- [ ] Activate buttons with Enter/Space
- [ ] Open modal — focus moves in
- [ ] Close modal — focus returns to trigger

Code Breakdown:

  • This checklist covers the five core areas: structure, forms, links, interactive, and dynamic.
  • Each check maps to a WCAG 2.2 success criterion.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Screen Reader(s) What to Test E-commerce checkout NVDA + Chrome, JAWS + Chrome Form labels, error messages, focus management Blog / documentation NVDA, VoiceOver Heading hierarchy, reading order, link text Government services JAWS + Chrome, NVDA Landmarks, form accessibility, plain language SaaS dashboard NVDA, VoiceOver Data tables, custom widgets, live regions Mobile banking VoiceOver (iOS), TalkBack Touch targets, gestures, form fields Media site VoiceOver, NVDA Video player controls, captions, transcripts SPA application NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver Route change announcements, focus management

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Test with at least two screen readers. Why: different screen readers have different behaviors; testing with one catches only some issues.
  2. Prioritize NVDA and VoiceOver for development. Why: NVDA is free; VoiceOver is built-in; together they cover most code issues.
  3. Test with keyboard only first. Why: screen readers are keyboard-driven; if keyboard navigation fails, screen reader testing will too.
  4. Test page structure first. Why: headings and landmarks are the primary navigation mechanism.
  5. Test form labels and error messages. Why: form accessibility is the most common source of screen reader barriers.
  6. Test dynamic content announcements. Why: live regions are invisible to automated tools.
  7. Test modal focus management. Why: focus trapping is essential for modal accessibility.
  8. Test with real content, not lorem ipsum. Why: meaningful content reveals real issues.
  9. Document screen reader version and browser. Why: screen reader behavior varies by version and pairing.
  10. Test on mobile with VoiceOver and TalkBack. Why: 91.3% of screen reader users also use a mobile device.
  11. Use lang on <html>. Why: screen readers select the correct voice.
  12. Use semantic HTML first. Why: native elements are the most reliably announced.
  13. Provide accessible names for all interactive elements. Why: a button with no name is announced as "button" — useless.
  14. Use aria-describedby for hints and errors. Why: links supplemental information to inputs.
  15. Use role="alert" for urgent messages. Why: announces immediately without moving focus.
  16. Use role="status" for polite updates. Why: waits for user idle.
  17. Never use aria-hidden="true" on focusable elements. Why: creates a keyboard trap.
  18. Test reading order. Why: DOM order determines screen reader order; visual order does not matter.
  19. Test with a screen reader after every significant UI change. Why: regressions are common.
  20. Combine automated testing with manual screen reader testing. Why: automated tools catch only 30–40% of issues.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Form Labels
docs.text:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

Why it's wrong: Screen reader announces "edit" with no label. Placeholder is not a label.

✅ Correct:

<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Alt Text
docs.text:
<img src="chart.png">

Why it's wrong: Screen reader announces the filename, which is meaningless.

✅ Correct:

<img src="chart.png" alt="Q1 revenue: $4.2M, up 18% from Q4">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: aria-hidden="true" on Focusable Element
docs.text:
<button aria-hidden="true">Save</button>

Why it's wrong: The button is invisible to screen readers but still reachable by keyboard — a keyboard trap.

✅ Correct:

<button>Save</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using a <div> as a Button
docs.text:
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

Why it's wrong: Not focusable, not keyboard-operable, not announced as a button.

✅ Correct:

<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No lang Attribute
docs.text:
<html>

Why it's wrong: Screen readers cannot select the correct voice.

✅ Correct:

<html lang="en">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Skipping Heading Levels
docs.text:
<h1>Page Title</h1>
<h4>Section</h4>

Why it's wrong: Breaks the document outline; screen reader heading navigation becomes confusing.

✅ Correct:

<h1>Page Title</h1>
<h2>Section</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Vague Link Text
docs.text:
<a href="/article">Read more</a>

Why it's wrong: In a list of links, "Read more" appears dozens of times with no context.

✅ Correct:

<a href="/article">Read more about SVG embedding</a>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Testing with Only One Screen Reader
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Different screen readers behave differently; one screen reader may pass while another fails.

✅ Correct: Test with at least two screen readers (e.g., NVDA and VoiceOver).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Automated Tools
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Automated tools catch only 30–40% of issues. Reading order, announcement clarity, and interaction flow require manual testing.

✅ Correct: Combine automated testing with manual screen reader testing.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Screen reader testing does not affect page performance.
  • Accessibility tree construction adds minimal overhead — the browser builds it as it parses the DOM.
  • Live region announcements are processed by the accessibility API — no user-facing performance impact.
  • ARIA attributes are metadata — no rendering cost.
  • Large DOM may slow accessibility tree construction — but this is rare.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use semantic HTML — no JavaScript overhead for accessibility.
  2. Use native <dialog> instead of custom modal libraries.
  3. Keep the accessibility tree accurate — remove unnecessary ARIA.
  4. Test with screen readers on slower devices to simulate real user conditions.

docs.title: Screen Reader Content Leakage
docs.text: Screen readers read everything in the accessibility tree — including content hidden visually but not from the accessibility tree. Use aria-hidden="true" to exclude decorative or sensitive content.

docs.title: aria-label Injection
docs.text: If aria-label is generated from untrusted input, escape it. ARIA values are not parsed as HTML, but unescaped content can break the attribute.

docs.title: Live Region Abuse
docs.text: Rapidly updating live regions can overwhelm screen reader users. Use aria-live="polite" for non-urgent updates and avoid spamming.

docs.title: Focus Hijacking
docs.text: Malicious scripts can move focus unexpectedly — a technique used in clickjacking. Modern browsers restrict programmatic focus to elements that are already visible or have been interacted with.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect any element's role, name, and state.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility tree — see the full accessibility tree.
  • Firefox DevTools → Accessibility — visualizes landmarks and heading hierarchy.
  • axe DevTools extension — flags missing labels, contrast issues, and ARIA misuse.
  • Lighthouse — audits for accessibility issues.
  • NVDA — free screen reader; use NVDA+T for title, H for headings, D for landmarks.
  • JAWS — use Insert+F6 for headings list, Insert+F7 for links list, Insert+Ctrl+R for regions.
  • VoiceOver — Cmd+F5 to toggle; VO+U for rotor.
  • TalkBack — enable in Settings → Accessibility → TalkBack.
  • document.activeElement — check the currently focused element in console.
  • document.querySelectorAll('[aria-hidden="true"]') — find hidden elements.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every web application — screen reader compatibility is a baseline requirement.
  • Every form — labels, error messages, and instructions must be announced.
  • Every interactive widget — modals, dropdowns, tabs, carousels.
  • Every dynamic content update — live regions for announcements.
  • Every SPA route change — title update, focus management, announcement.
  • Every e-commerce checkout — form accessibility is critical.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use screen readers as a substitute for semantic HTML. Fix the markup; don't patch with ARIA.
  • Do not rely on automated tools alone. Screen reader testing is manual.
  • Do not test with only one screen reader. Different screen readers catch different issues.
  • Do not assume framework ARIA is correct. Verify framework-generated markup with a screen reader.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Accessibility tree
  • Accessible name computation

  • Keyboard navigation

  • Live regions
  • Landmark roles
  • Heading hierarchy
  • WCAG 2.2 (POUR)
  • NVDA
  • JAWS
  • VoiceOver
  • TalkBack
  • Braille displays
  • lang attribute
  • aria-label / aria-labelledby
  • role="alert" / role="status"

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• JAWS leads primary desktop screen reader use at 40.5%, with NVDA close behind at 37.7% and VoiceOver at 9.7%.
  • 91.3% of screen reader users also use a mobile screen reader — VoiceOver holds 70.6% of mobile use.
  • 76.6% of screen reader users report blindness as their primary disability.
  • Nearly three-quarters of users run more than one screen reader.
  • Automated tools catch only 30–40% of accessibility issues — the rest require manual screen reader testing.
  • NVDA 2026.2 added a built-in Magnifier feature with zoom levels, color filters, and spotlight mode.
  • JAWS 2026 added Page Explorer for AI-powered page summarization and an AI Labeler for graphic descriptions.
  • VoiceOver on iOS 26 added Image Explorer — AI-generated detailed descriptions of images, documents, and receipts.
  • TalkBack 17 improved live region announcements and added customizable braille display commands.
  • Accessible names are "flat" strings — they contain no structure or language change information.
  • The lang attribute is essential for screen readers to select the correct voice and pronunciation rules.
  • Screen readers follow DOM order, not visual order — CSS order can break the reading order.
  • Browse mode and focus mode are the two modes of screen reader operation.
  • Quick navigation keys (H, K, B, F, D) work only in browse mode.
  • The <dialog> element provides native focus management — no JavaScript focus trap needed.
  • Testing with a screen reader is the only way to verify that your site actually works for blind users.
  • In 2026, 95.9% of the top 1,000,000 home pages had WCAG failures — averaging 56.1 errors each.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A screen reader converts the accessibility tree to speech or Braille — it does not read pixels.
  • The four dominant screen readers are NVDA (Windows, free), JAWS (Windows, commercial), VoiceOver (Apple, built-in), and TalkBack (Android, built-in).
  • Market share: JAWS 40.5%, NVDA 37.7%, VoiceOver 9.7% desktop; VoiceOver 70.6% mobile.
  • Test with at least two screen readers — NVDA + VoiceOver covers most code issues.
  • Screen reader testing is manual — automated tools catch only 30–40% of issues.
  • Test page structure first: headings, landmarks, reading order.
  • Test forms: labels, required state, error messages.
  • Test dynamic content: live regions, modals, route changes.
  • Accessible name computation follows a priority order: aria-labelledby → aria-label → native label → text content → title.
  • lang on <html> tells the screen reader which voice to use.
  • Browse mode vs. focus mode — quick nav keys work in browse mode; typing works in focus mode.
  • NVDA 2026, JAWS 2026, VoiceOver 2026, and TalkBack 17 each added AI-powered features.
  • Screen reader testing is the only way to verify that your site works for blind users.
  • 95.9% of top home pages fail WCAG — the web is still largely inaccessible to screen reader users.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Accessible forms are HTML forms designed and built so that every user — regardless of disability, assistive technology, or input method — can perceive the form's purpose, understand what is required, enter data accurately, recover from errors, and submit successfully.

<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
    <fieldset>
        <legend>Newsletter preferences</legend>

        <label for="email">Email address</label>
        <input id="email" type="email" name="email" required
               autocomplete="email"
               aria-describedby="email-hint">
        <span id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</span>

        <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
    </fieldset>
</form>

A form can be visually perfect and still be entirely unusable by a screen reader user, a keyboard-only user, or a voice control user. Accessibility is not about appearance — it is about whether the form's structure, labels, states, errors, and feedback are programmatically available to assistive technology.

Forms are where accessibility failures become conversion failures. An inaccessible form costs money. Every barrier — a missing label, an unannounced error, an unreachable button — is a lost submission.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Accessible forms serve several essential purposes:

  • Label association — every input is programmatically linked to its label so screen readers announce the purpose.
  • Keyboard operability — every field and button is reachable via Tab and operable via standard keys.
  • Error communication — errors are announced, associated with their fields, and never color-only.
  • Instruction delivery — hints, formats, and constraints are available to screen readers before the user types.
  • State communication — required, disabled, invalid, and filled states are announced.
  • Autofill support — autocomplete attributes enable browser and password manager automation.
  • Grouping semantics — related controls are grouped with <fieldset> and <legend>.
  • Legal compliance — WCAG 2.2, ADA Title II, Section 508, and the European Accessibility Act all require accessible forms.

A form is the most common place where a user with a disability will abandon a task. Making it accessible is both a legal obligation and a conversion optimization.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Accessibility Stack
│
├── Semantic HTML        ← <label>, <input>, <fieldset>, <button>
├── ARIA                 ← aria-describedby, aria-invalid, role="alert"
├── Keyboard Navigation  ← Tab order, Enter/Space activation
├── Focus Management     ← focus moves to first invalid field on error
├── Screen Reader        ← announces labels, states, errors
└── Testing              ← keyboard-only + screen reader walkthrough

Forms sit at the intersection of every accessibility concern: semantics, labels, keyboard, focus, announcements, and error recovery. They are the ultimate integration test for accessibility.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A visual user sees a form: the label sits above the input, an asterisk marks the required field, an error message appears in red below the field, and a "Next" button sits at the bottom. All of this is apparent in a glance.

A screen reader user hears none of this automatically. Without programmatic association, the screen reader announces "edit" with no label. Without required, it does not say the field is required. Without aria-describedby, it does not announce the hint. Without aria-invalid, it does not announce the error. Without proper focus management, it does not even move to the error.

The visual form is a design; the accessible form is a programmatic contract. Without the contract, the form is a series of anonymous input boxes.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Placeholder as only label Screen reader announces "edit" with no context No required attribute User does not know the field is mandatory until submission Color-only error indication Color-blind users cannot perceive the error Unassociated error messages Screen reader does not announce the error No fieldset/legend Radio groups and checkboxes announced without group context Positive tabindex Tab order disrupted outline: none on focus Keyboard users cannot see focus No autocomplete Browser autofill does not work Custom dropdown from <div> Keyboard-inoperable; screen reader cannot identify it

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
WCAG 1.0 (1999) required form labels. WCAG 2.0 (2008) formalized criteria for labels, error identification, and error suggestion. WCAG 2.1 (2018) added criteria for redundant entry and accessible authentication. WCAG 2.2 (2023) added four new criteria that directly affect forms:

  • 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (Level A) — do not ask the user for the same information twice in the same process.
  • 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA) — do not require cognitive function tests (puzzles, memorization) for authentication.
  • 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (Level AAA) — no cognitive test even with alternative assistance.
  • 3.2.6 Consistent Help (Level A) — help mechanisms must appear in the same relative location across pages.

These additions reflect a shift: accessibility is not just about screen readers. It is about cognitive load, memory, and authentication too.

docs.title: The Minimal Accessible Form
docs.text:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
    <label for="email">Email address</label>
    <input id="email" type="email" name="email" required>
    <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element / Attribute Purpose <form action> Submission target <form method="post"> HTTP method <label for="email"> Programmatically associates label with input <input id="email"> The id matches the for on the label type="email" Enables email-specific keyboard and validation required Announces field as required <button type="submit"> Native submit; keyboard-operable

docs.title: The Complete Production Form
docs.text:
<form action="/signup" method="post" novalidate>
    <fieldset>
        <legend>Account details</legend>

        <div class="field">
            <label for="name">Full name</label>
            <input id="name"
                   name="name"
                   type="text"
                   required
                   autocomplete="name"
                   aria-describedby="name-hint">
            <span id="name-hint" class="hint">As it appears on your ID.</span>
            <span id="name-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>
        </div>

        <div class="field">
            <label for="email">Email address</label>
            <input id="email"
                   name="email"
                   type="email"
                   required
                   autocomplete="email"
                   aria-describedby="email-hint">
            <span id="email-hint" class="hint">We'll never share your email.</span>
            <span id="email-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>
        </div>

        <div class="field">
            <label for="password">Password</label>
            <input id="password"
                   name="password"
                   type="password"
                   required
                   minlength="8"
                   autocomplete="new-password"
                   aria-describedby="password-hint">
            <span id="password-hint" class="hint">
                At least 8 characters, including a number.
            </span>
            <span id="password-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>
        </div>
    </fieldset>

    <fieldset>
        <legend>Contact preference</legend>

        <div class="radio-group" role="radiogroup" aria-labelledby="contact-legend">
            <input type="radio" id="contact-email" name="contact" value="email" checked>
            <label for="contact-email">Email</label>

            <input type="radio" id="contact-phone" name="contact" value="phone">
            <label for="contact-phone">Phone</label>

            <input type="radio" id="contact-sms" name="contact" value="sms">
            <label for="contact-sms">SMS</label>
        </div>
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element / Attribute Purpose <fieldset> + <legend> Groups related controls; screen reader announces the group name <label for> Associated label; the first thing announced when focus lands autocomplete Enables autofill and password managers aria-describedby Links hint and error text to the input role="alert" Announces error text as soon as it is populated type="radio" + <label for> Each radio has its own label role="radiogroup" Explicit grouping for radios (though <fieldset> handles this natively) novalidate Disables browser validation so you can implement accessible custom messages

docs.title: The Accessible Name and Description Pipeline
docs.text:
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email"
       aria-describedby="email-hint email-error">
<span id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</span>
<span id="email-error" role="alert"></span>

When focus lands on the input, the screen reader announces:

"Email address, edit, required, We'll never share your email."
  • Name comes from <label>.
  • Role comes from <input type="email"> (mapped to textbox).
  • State comes from required.
  • Description comes from aria-describedby (concatenated in order).

When the error span is populated, role="alert" fires an immediate announcement.

docs.title: The "Contract" Mental Model
docs.text:
A visual form is a design. An accessible form is a contract between your markup and assistive technology:

Your markup promises:          The screen reader says:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
<label for="email">       →    "Email address"
<input required>          →    "required"
aria-describedby="hint"   →    "We'll never share your email"
aria-invalid="true"       →    "invalid entry"
role="alert"              →    "*announces error immediately*"

Every visual cue the sighted user sees must have a programmatic counterpart the screen reader can announce. If the visual cue exists without the counterpart, the contract is broken.

docs.title: The "Five Layers of Form Accessibility" Mental Model
docs.text:
Layer 1: Labels        →  Every control has an accessible name.
Layer 2: Grouping      →  Related controls are grouped (fieldset/legend).
Layer 3: State         →  Required, disabled, invalid announced.
Layer 4: Instructions  →  Hints and constraints announced before typing.
Layer 5: Errors        →  Errors announced, associated, and recoverable.

A form that passes layers 1 and 2 but fails layer 5 leaves users stranded after an error. All five layers are required.

docs.title: The "Focus Order = Reading Order" Mental Model
docs.text:
Tab order should follow the visual reading order:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Full name       [____________]              │
│  Email           [____________]              │
│  Password        [____________]              │
│  Contact: ( ) Email ( ) Phone ( ) SMS        │
│                                              │
│  [Create account]                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The tab order follows the DOM order. If your CSS reorders the fields visually (flex-direction: row-reverse, order: -1), the tab order no longer matches — and screen reader users are lost.

docs.title: The "Error Recovery Loop" Mental Model
docs.text:
User submits form
    │
    ▼
Validation fails
    │
    ▼
Identify all invalid fields
    │
    ▼
Mark each with aria-invalid="true"
    │
    ▼
Populate error messages (role="alert")
    │
    ▼
Move focus to FIRST invalid field
    │
    ▼
Screen reader announces the error
    │
    ▼
User fixes the field
    │
    ▼
Clear aria-invalid and error
    │
    ▼
Loop until submission succeeds

Every step in the loop is a place where accessibility can break. The error recovery loop is the most complex and failure-prone part of form accessibility.

docs.title: The "Never Color Alone" Mental Model
docs.text:
Color is never the sole indicator of anything:

❌ Wrong:        Red border indicates error.
                 Red asterisk indicates required.

✅ Correct:      Red border + error icon + error text + aria-invalid.
                 Red asterisk + "required" text + required attribute.

Color-blind users, screen reader users, and users in bright sunlight all need non-color indicators.

docs.title: Concept 1: WCAG 2.2 Form Criteria
docs.text:
The most relevant success criteria for forms:

Criterion Level Requirement 1.3.1 Info and Relationships A Structure is programmatically determinable 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose AA autocomplete matches the purpose 2.1.1 Keyboard A All functionality keyboard-operable 2.4.3 Focus Order A Focus order is logical 2.4.6 Headings and Labels AA Labels and headings describe purpose 2.4.7 Focus Visible AA Focus indicator visible 3.2.2 On Input A Input does not cause unexpected context change 3.3.1 Error Identification A Errors are identified in text 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions A Labels or instructions provided 3.3.3 Error Suggestion AA Suggested correction provided 3.3.4 Error Prevention AA Reversible for legal/financial data 3.3.7 Redundant Entry A Do not ask for the same info twice 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) AA No cognitive function test 3.2.6 Consistent Help A Help mechanisms in consistent location

docs.title: Concept 2: Label Association
docs.text:
Every form control must have a programmatically associated label. There are two ways:

<!-- Method 1: for/id (preferred) -->
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email">

<!-- Method 2: wrapping (also valid) -->
<label>
    Email address
    <input type="email">
</label>

Never use placeholder as the only label. Placeholders disappear when the user types and have poor contrast. They are not announced as labels by most screen readers.

docs.title: Concept 3: fieldset and legend
docs.text:
Group related controls with <fieldset> and <legend>:

<fieldset>
    <legend>Shipping address</legend>
    <label for="street">Street</label>
    <input id="street" autocomplete="street-address">
    <label for="city">City</label>
    <input id="city" autocomplete="address-level2">
</fieldset>

The screen reader announces the legend when entering the group, then each field within.

docs.title: Concept 4: Required Fields
docs.text:
Required fields must be indicated both visually and programmatically:

<label for="email">
    Email address
    <span aria-hidden="true">*</span>
    <span class="visually-hidden">(required)</span>
</label>
<input id="email" type="email" required>
  • required on the input — programmatic indication.
  • Visible asterisk — visual indication.
  • aria-hidden="true" — prevents the asterisk from being announced.
  • .visually-hidden text — provides a non-symbolic indicator for screen readers.
  • A legend at the top of the form should explain what * means.

docs.title: Concept 5: Error Identification
docs.text:
Every error must be:

  1. Identified in text (not color alone).
  2. Associated with the field that caused it.
  3. Announced when it occurs or when the user returns to the field.
<input id="email" type="email" required
       aria-describedby="email-error"
       aria-invalid="true">
<span id="email-error" role="alert">
    Please enter a valid email address, e.g. name@example.com.
</span>

docs.title: Concept 6: aria-invalid
docs.text: aria-invalid="true" tells the screen reader the field has an invalid entry. Without it, the error is visually apparent but not programmatically announced.

docs.title: Concept 7: role="alert" vs aria-live
docs.text: role="alert" is implicitly aria-live="assertive" and aria-atomic="true". Use it for error messages and urgent updates. For non-urgent updates, use role="status" or aria-live="polite".

docs.title: Concept 8: autocomplete Attribute
docs.text:
The autocomplete attribute enables browser autofill and password managers:

Value Purpose name Full name email Email address tel Phone number street-address Street address postal-code Postal code cc-number Credit card number current-password Existing password new-password New password one-time-code OTP / 2FA code

For WCAG 2.2 criterion 1.3.5 (AA), autocomplete must match the input's actual purpose.

docs.title: Concept 9: inputmode Attribute
docs.text:
inputmode controls the on-screen keyboard type on mobile:

<input type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]*">

Values: text, decimal, numeric, tel, email, url, search, none.

docs.title: Concept 10: enterkeyhint Attribute
docs.text:
<input type="text" enterkeyhint="next">
<input type="email" enterkeyhint="done">
<input type="search" enterkeyhint="search">

Values: enter, done, go, next, previous, search, send.

docs.title: Concept 11: Grouping Radios and Checkboxes
docs.text:
Radio buttons that belong to the same question must share a name attribute:

<fieldset>
    <legend>Contact preference</legend>

    <input type="radio" id="contact-email" name="contact" value="email" checked>
    <label for="contact-email">Email</label>

    <input type="radio" id="contact-phone" name="contact" value="phone">
    <label for="contact-phone">Phone</label>
</fieldset>

Screen readers announce "Contact preference, group" then each option.

docs.title: Concept 12: Redundant Entry (WCAG 3.3.7)
docs.text:
Do not ask for the same information twice in the same process:

<!-- Wrong: ask for email in step 1 and step 3 -->
<label for="email1">Email (step 1)</label>
<label for="email2">Email (step 3)</label>

<!-- Correct: pre-fill from step 1, allow edit -->
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" value="pre-filled@example.com">

Exception: re-entering a password for verification is allowed. Mark the second entry as "Confirm password."

docs.title: Concept 13: Accessible Authentication (WCAG 3.3.8)
docs.text:
Do not require a cognitive function test for authentication:

  • No puzzles (CAPTCHA, image selection).
  • No memorization (transcription of a code).
  • No reliance on remembering complex passwords.

Acceptable alternatives: password managers, email links, biometrics, WebAuthn / passkeys, magic links, OTP autofill via autocomplete="one-time-code".

docs.title: Concept 14: Consistent Help (WCAG 3.2.6)
docs.text: If the page provides help mechanisms (contact info, chat, FAQ link), they must appear in the same relative order across pages. This helps users with cognitive disabilities find help predictably.

docs.title: Concept 15: Error Prevention (WCAG 3.3.4)
docs.text:
For legal, financial, or data-deletion submissions, the form must be reversible, checked, or confirmed:

  • Reversible: submission can be undone.
  • Checked: input is validated for errors before submission.
  • Confirmed: user reviews and confirms before final submission.

A "confirm before delete" modal is the classic pattern.

docs.title: Concept 16: Focus Order in Forms
docs.text: Tab order follows DOM order. If CSS reorders fields visually, the tab order breaks. Never use tabindex values greater than 0 to control form order — use DOM order.

docs.title: Concept 17: Focus on First Invalid Field
docs.text:
After form validation fails, focus must move to the first invalid field:

const firstInvalid = form.querySelector(':invalid');
firstInvalid?.focus();

This ensures the error is announced and the user can correct it immediately.

docs.title: Concept 18: novalidate for Custom Messages
docs.text: Browsers have built-in validation, but their messages are inconsistent across browsers and may not be accessible. Use novalidate and implement custom accessible error messages.

docs.title: Concept 19: Password Managers and Accessibility
docs.text: Password managers are accessibility tools. Users with cognitive disabilities, motor impairments, or memory conditions depend on them. Do not block paste, autofill, or password manager interaction.

docs.title: Concept 20: Mobile Form Accessibility
docs.text:
Mobile forms have specific accessibility concerns:

  • inputmode selects the correct on-screen keyboard.
  • enterkeyhint tells the user what Enter will do.
  • Touch targets must be at least 24×24 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.5.8).
  • autocomplete="one-time-code" enables OTP autofill.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Form Field Announcement
docs.text:
1.  User presses Tab.
    │
    ▼
2.  Focus moves to the next focusable element.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser queries the accessibility tree for the element.
    │
    ▼
4.  Accessibility API returns:
    │   ├── Role: "textbox"
    │   ├── Name: "Email address" (from <label>)
    │   ├── State: "required" (from required attribute)
    │   └── Description: "We'll never share your email"
    │
    ▼
5.  Screen reader announces:
    │   "Email address, edit, required, We'll never share your email."
    │
    ▼
6.  User types.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Form Error Recovery
docs.text:
1.  User clicks Submit.
    │
    ▼
2.  Form is validated (custom JS with novalidate).
    │
    ▼
3.  Invalid fields identified.
    │
    ▼
4.  For each invalid field:
    │   ├── Set aria-invalid="true"
    │   ├── Populate error span with text
    │   └── role="alert" fires announcement
    │
    ▼
5.  Focus moves to the first invalid field.
    │
    ▼
6.  Screen reader announces:
    │   "Email address, edit, required, invalid entry,
    │    Please enter a valid email address."
    │
    ▼
7.  User corrects the field.
    │
    ▼
8.  On blur or input:
    │   ├── Clear aria-invalid
    │   └── Clear error span
    │
    ▼
9.  User submits again.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Autofill Interaction
docs.text:
1.  Page loads.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser detects autocomplete attributes.
    │
    ▼
3.  Password manager offers to fill the form.
    │
    ▼
4.  User accepts.
    │
    ▼
5.  Fields are populated.
    │
    ▼
6.  Screen reader announces new values if focused.

docs.title: The Label Association Algorithm
docs.text:
When a screen reader queries the name of an input, the browser follows this priority:

  1. aria-labelledby — reference to other element(s)
  2. aria-label — direct string
  3. <label for="..."> — associated label
  4. <label> wrapping — ancestor label
  5. title attribute — last resort
  6. Placeholder (in some cases) — not reliable

If no label is found, the screen reader announces a generic role with no name.

docs.title: The Fieldset/Legend Algorithm
docs.text:
When focus enters a control inside a <fieldset>:

  1. The browser walks up the DOM to find the nearest <fieldset>.
  2. It reads the <legend> and associates it with the control.
  3. The screen reader announces: "[Legend text], group, [field label], edit."

docs.title: The Error Announcement Mechanism
docs.text:
Two ways errors are announced:

Via role="alert": When the error span's text content is set or changed, the accessibility API fires an alert event. The screen reader interrupts and announces the text.

Via aria-describedby: When focus lands on the input, the screen reader concatenates the accessible description from all referenced elements and announces it as part of the field's description.

Both together provide the most robust experience: the error is announced immediately on update and re-announced when the user returns to the field.

docs.title: The autocomplete Token Parsing
docs.text:
The browser parses autocomplete tokens and exposes them to the browser's autofill system. autocomplete="email" tells the browser to fill the field with the user's saved email address. autocomplete="new-password" tells the password manager to offer to generate a new password.

The tokens are also exposed to the accessibility tree, where they map to aria-* properties such as aria-autocomplete.

docs.title: Focus Order vs. DOM Order
docs.text:
The browser builds the tab order from DOM order, excluding:

  • Elements with tabindex="-1"
  • Disabled elements
  • Hidden elements (display: none, visibility: hidden)
  • Elements inside inert containers

CSS order, flex-direction, and absolute positioning do not affect tab order — they only affect visual layout. This is why DOM order must match visual order.

docs.title: Accessible Form Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Design the form:
    │   ├── Identify all fields
    │   ├── Determine which are required
    │   ├── Plan the error messages
    │   └── Plan the autocomplete values
    │
    ▼
2.  Write the markup:
    │   ├── <form> with action and method
    │   ├── <fieldset> + <legend> for groups
    │   ├── <label> for every input
    │   ├── required, autocomplete, inputmode, enterkeyhint
    │   └── <button type="submit">
    │
    ▼
3.  Implement validation:
    │   ├── novalidate on the form
    │   ├── Custom validation on submit
    │   ├── Set aria-invalid="true" on invalid fields
    │   ├── Populate error spans with role="alert"
    │   └── Focus first invalid field
    │
    ▼
4.  Test with keyboard only:
    │   ├── Tab through every field
    │   ├── Verify focus is visible
    │   ├── Submit with errors — verify focus moves
    │   └── Correct errors — verify they clear
    │
    ▼
5.  Test with a screen reader:
    │   ├── Labels announced before inputs
    │   ├── Required state announced
    │   ├── Hints announced
    │   ├── Errors announced
    │   └── Group context announced
    │
    ▼
6.  Test with zoom and high contrast.
    │
    ▼
7.  Test on mobile with VoiceOver/TalkBack.

docs.title: Error Recovery Lifecycle
docs.text:
Submit → Validate → Identify errors → Mark invalid
    │
    ▼
Populate errors → Focus first invalid → Announce
    │
    ▼
User corrects → Clear error → Loop until success

docs.title: Example 1: Login Form
docs.text:
<form action="/login" method="post" novalidate>
    <h1>Sign in</h1>

    <div class="field">
        <label for="email">Email address</label>
        <input id="email"
               name="email"
               type="email"
               required
               autocomplete="email"
               aria-describedby="email-error">
        <span id="email-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>
    </div>

    <div class="field">
        <label for="password">Password</label>
        <input id="password"
               name="password"
               type="password"
               required
               autocomplete="current-password"
               aria-describedby="password-error">
        <span id="password-error" class="error" role="alert"></span>
    </div>

    <button type="submit">Sign in</button>
</form>

Code Breakdown:

  • autocomplete="email" — enables autofill for email.
  • autocomplete="current-password" — enables password manager autofill.
  • role="alert" on error spans — announces errors immediately.
  • Native <button type="submit"> — keyboard-operable.

docs.title: Example 2: Registration Form with Fieldsets
docs.text:
<form action="/register" method="post" novalidate>
    <fieldset>
        <legend>Account details</legend>

        <div class="field">
            <label for="name">Full name</label>
            <input id="name" name="name" type="text" required
                   autocomplete="name">
        </div>

        <div class="field">
            <label for="email">Email address</label>
            <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required
                   autocomplete="email"
                   aria-describedby="email-hint">
            <span id="email-hint" class="hint">
                We'll send a verification link.
            </span>
        </div>

        <div class="field">
            <label for="password">Password</label>
            <input id="password" name="password" type="password" required
                   minlength="8"
                   autocomplete="new-password"
                   aria-describedby="password-hint">
            <span id="password-hint" class="hint">
                At least 8 characters, including a number.
            </span>
        </div>
    </fieldset>

    <fieldset>
        <legend>Contact preference</legend>

        <input type="radio" id="contact-email" name="contact" value="email" checked>
        <label for="contact-email">Email</label>

        <input type="radio" id="contact-phone" name="contact" value="phone">
        <label for="contact-phone">Phone</label>

        <input type="radio" id="contact-sms" name="contact" value="sms">
        <label for="contact-sms">SMS</label>
    </fieldset>

    <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

Code Breakdown:

  • Two <fieldset> groups: "Account details" and "Contact preference."
  • Each input has autocomplete for autofill.
  • minlength="8" enforces password length.
  • Radio buttons share name="contact" — they are mutually exclusive.
  • Each radio has its own <label for>.

docs.title: Example 3: Custom Error Handling
docs.text:
const form = document.querySelector('form');

form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();

    const fields = form.querySelectorAll('input, select, textarea');
    let firstInvalid = null;

    fields.forEach((field) => {
        const errorId = field.getAttribute('aria-describedby')?.split(' ')
            .find((id) => id.endsWith('-error'));
        const errorEl = errorId ? document.getElementById(errorId) : null;

        // Clear previous state
        field.removeAttribute('aria-invalid');
        if (errorEl) errorEl.textContent = '';

        // Validate
        if (!field.checkValidity()) {
            field.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
            if (errorEl) errorEl.textContent = getErrorMessage(field);
            if (!firstInvalid) firstInvalid = field;
        }
    });

    if (firstInvalid) {
        firstInvalid.focus();
    } else {
        form.submit();
    }
});

function getErrorMessage(field) {
    if (field.validity.valueMissing) {
        return `${field.labels[0].textContent} is required.`;
    }
    if (field.validity.typeMismatch) {
        return `Please enter a valid ${field.type}.`;
    }
    if (field.validity.tooShort) {
        return `Please enter at least ${field.minLength} characters.`;
    }
    return 'Please check this field.';
}

Code Breakdown:

  • preventDefault — prevents native submission until validation passes.
  • checkValidity — uses the browser's built-in validation.
  • aria-invalid="true" — marks the field as invalid for the screen reader.
  • role="alert" (on error elements in the HTML) — announces the error text.
  • Focus moves to the first invalid field after all errors are populated.

docs.title: Example 4: Error Prevention — Confirmation Modal
docs.text:
<form action="/delete-account" method="post" id="delete-form">
    <button type="button" id="delete-btn">Delete account</button>
</form>

<dialog id="confirm-dialog">
    <form method="dialog">
        <h2>Confirm deletion</h2>
        <p>This will permanently delete your account. This cannot be undone.</p>
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm" id="confirm-delete">Delete</button>
    </form>
</dialog>

<script>
    const dialog = document.getElementById('confirm-dialog');
    const deleteBtn = document.getElementById('delete-btn');

    deleteBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
        dialog.showModal();
    });

    document.getElementById('confirm-delete').addEventListener('click', () => {
        document.getElementById('delete-form').submit();
    });

    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        deleteBtn.focus();
    });
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • WCAG 3.3.4 (Error Prevention) — irreversible action is confirmed before submission.
  • <dialog> — native modal with focus management.
  • Focus returns to the trigger when the dialog closes.

docs.title: Example 5: Accessible OTP Input
docs.text:
<label for="otp">Verification code</label>
<input id="otp"
       name="otp"
       type="text"
       inputmode="numeric"
       autocomplete="one-time-code"
       pattern="[0-9]{6}"
       maxlength="6"
       required
       aria-describedby="otp-hint">
<span id="otp-hint">Enter the 6-digit code we sent to your phone.</span>

Code Breakdown:

  • autocomplete="one-time-code" — enables iOS and Android OTP autofill.
  • inputmode="numeric" — shows numeric keyboard on mobile.
  • pattern="[0-9]{6}" — validates the format.
  • aria-describedby — announces the hint before the user types.

docs.title: Example 6: Accessible Date Input
docs.text:
<label for="birthdate">Date of birth</label>
<input id="birthdate"
       name="birthdate"
       type="date"
       autocomplete="bday"
       required
       aria-describedby="birthdate-hint">
<span id="birthdate-hint">Format: YYYY-MM-DD.</span>

Code Breakdown:

  • type="date" — native date picker, keyboard-accessible.
  • autocomplete="bday" — enables autofill.
  • aria-describedby — announces the format hint.

docs.title: Example 7: Password with Show/Hide Toggle
docs.text:
<div class="field">
    <label for="password">Password</label>
    <input id="password" type="password" autocomplete="new-password" required>
    <button type="button"
            aria-pressed="false"
            aria-controls="password"
            onclick="togglePassword(this)">
        Show password
    </button>
</div>

<script>
    function togglePassword(btn) {
        const input = document.getElementById('password');
        const showing = btn.getAttribute('aria-pressed') === 'true';
        btn.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(!showing));
        btn.textContent = showing ? 'Show password' : 'Hide password';
        input.type = showing ? 'password' : 'text';
    }
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • aria-pressed — announces the toggle state.
  • aria-controls — associates the button with the input.
  • Native <button> — keyboard-operable.
  • The button label changes to reflect the current state.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Required Practices Login form autocomplete="email", autocomplete="current-password" Registration form autocomplete="new-password", minlength, hints Checkout form autocomplete for name, address, cc-number, cc-exp Contact form <label>, <textarea>, error handling Search form role="search", type="search", enterkeyhint="search" Survey <fieldset>/<legend>, radio groups File upload <label for="file">, accept attribute Date/time input type="date", autocomplete="bday" OTP input inputmode="numeric", autocomplete="one-time-code" Multi-step form Save state, avoid redundant entry (WCAG 3.3.7)

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Associate a label with every form control. Why: without a label, the screen reader announces a generic role with no purpose.
  2. Never use placeholder as a label. Why: it disappears on typing and has poor contrast.
  3. Use fieldset and legend for grouped controls. Why: screen readers announce group context.
  4. Indicate required fields both visually and programmatically. Why: color or asterisk alone is insufficient.
  5. Provide hints via aria-describedby. Why: hints are announced before the user types.
  6. Use autocomplete for every field with a known purpose. Why: enables autofill for all users, including those with disabilities.
  7. Use inputmode and enterkeyhint on mobile. Why: shows the correct keyboard and enter-key label.
  8. Validate on submit, then focus the first invalid field. Why: ensures the error is announced.
  9. Mark invalid fields with aria-invalid="true". Why: tells the screen reader the entry is invalid.
  10. Announce error messages with role="alert". Why: interrupts and announces errors immediately.
  11. Never rely on color alone to indicate errors or required fields. Why: color-blind users cannot perceive color-only indicators.
  12. Use novalidate and implement custom accessible error messages. Why: browser-native messages vary by browser and may not be accessible.
  13. Avoid positive tabindex values. Why: disrupts natural tab order.
  14. Keep DOM order aligned with visual order. Why: tab order follows DOM order.
  15. Use native form elements. Why: native <input>, <select>, <textarea>, <button> are keyboard-operable and announced correctly.
  16. Enable password managers and autofill. Why: they are accessibility tools for cognitive and motor disabilities.
  17. Support paste in password fields. Why: blocking paste blocks password managers.
  18. Do not require cognitive function tests for authentication (WCAG 3.3.8). Why: puzzles and memorization exclude users with cognitive disabilities.
  19. Avoid redundant entry (WCAG 3.3.7). Why: re-asking for the same information increases cognitive load.
  20. Provide error prevention for legal/financial submissions (WCAG 3.3.4). Why: irreversible actions require confirmation.
  21. Test with keyboard only. Why: keyboard accessibility is the foundation.
  22. Test with a screen reader. Why: forms are the most common source of screen reader barriers.
  23. Test on mobile. Why: mobile has different keyboard, autofill, and gesture behavior.
  24. Ensure touch targets are at least 24×24 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.5.8). Why: small touch targets are inaccessible.
  25. Audit forms quarterly or after any change. Why: form accessibility decays as fields change.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placeholder as Label
docs.text:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

Why it's wrong: Placeholder is not a label. Screen reader announces "edit" with no context.

✅ Correct:

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No required Attribute
docs.text:
<label for="email">Email *</label>
<input id="email" type="email">

Why it's wrong: The asterisk is visual-only; screen readers do not announce it.

✅ Correct:

<label for="email">
    Email
    <span aria-hidden="true">*</span>
    <span class="visually-hidden">(required)</span>
</label>
<input id="email" type="email" required>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Color-Only Error Indication
docs.text:
<input style="border-color: red">

Why it's wrong: Color-blind users cannot perceive the error.

✅ Correct:

<input aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="email-error">
<span id="email-error" role="alert">
    Please enter a valid email address.
</span>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unassociated Error Message
docs.text:
<input type="email">
<p class="error">Invalid email</p>

Why it's wrong: The error is not programmatically associated with the input; the screen reader does not announce it.

✅ Correct:

<input type="email" aria-describedby="email-error" aria-invalid="true">
<span id="email-error" role="alert">Invalid email</span>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Positive tabindex
docs.text:
<input tabindex="1">
<input tabindex="2">
<button tabindex="3">

Why it's wrong: Positive tabindex values override DOM order and disrupt natural tab flow.

✅ Correct: Use DOM order; remove tabindex.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing fieldset/legend on Radio Groups
docs.text:
<input type="radio" name="contact" value="email"> Email
<input type="radio" name="contact" value="phone"> Phone

Why it's wrong: Screen reader does not announce the group context. The user hears "Email, radio button" with no question.

✅ Correct:

<fieldset>
    <legend>Contact preference</legend>
    <input type="radio" id="c-email" name="contact" value="email">
    <label for="c-email">Email</label>
    <input type="radio" id="c-phone" name="contact" value="phone">
    <label for="c-phone">Phone</label>
</fieldset>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Blocking Paste in Password Fields
docs.text:
<input type="password" onpaste="return false">

Why it's wrong: Blocks password managers — a critical accessibility tool.

✅ Correct: Allow paste.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: CAPTCHA with No Accessible Alternative
docs.text:
<div class="captcha">
    <img src="puzzle.png">
    <input placeholder="Enter the code">
</div>

Why it's wrong: Violates WCAG 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication). Users with cognitive or visual disabilities cannot complete it.

✅ Correct: Use WebAuthn, magic links, or an accessible CAPTCHA with audio and screen reader support.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Focus Management on Error
docs.text:
// Validation fails but focus stays on the submit button

Why it's wrong: The user does not know which field failed. Screen readers do not announce the error.

✅ Correct:

firstInvalid.focus();

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Re-Asking for the Same Information
docs.text:
<!-- Step 1: Email -->
<!-- Step 3: Confirm your email again -->

Why it's wrong: Violates WCAG 3.3.7 (Redundant Entry).

✅ Correct: Pre-fill the email from step 1; allow editing.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Form accessibility has no runtime cost — labels and ARIA attributes are metadata.
  • Custom validation adds JavaScript but is necessary for accessible error messages.
  • autocomplete improves conversion and reduces typing.
  • inputmode improves mobile keyboard usability.
  • Native <dialog> has no JavaScript focus-trap overhead.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use native validation (checkValidity) rather than writing your own from scratch.
  2. Avoid excessive JavaScript on every input event — use blur and submit.
  3. Use native <dialog> for confirmations — no JavaScript focus trap needed.
  4. Keep forms small — fewer fields, less cognitive load, better conversion.

docs.title: Password Managers Are Accessibility Tools
docs.text: Blocking password managers (autocomplete="off", onpaste="return false") excludes users with cognitive and motor disabilities. Modern guidance from NIST and the UK NCSC recommends allowing password managers.

docs.title: Autofill and PII
docs.text: autocomplete values expose the expected data type to the browser. This is safe if the values are correct. Misconfigured values (e.g., autocomplete="cc-number" on a non-payment field) can cause incorrect autofill.

docs.title: CAPTCHA and Accessibility
docs.text: Inaccessible CAPTCHAs are both an accessibility barrier and a security theater. Prefer WebAuthn, magic links, and rate limiting over CAPTCHAs.

docs.title: Error Message Information Leakage
docs.text: Avoid revealing internal validation rules that could aid attackers (e.g., "password must contain..."). Provide minimum guidance rather than a full rule list.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text: Forms that change state (POST) must be protected with CSRF tokens. Accessibility and CSRF are orthogonal — but both are required.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Keyboard only: Tab through every field. Verify labels are announced and focus is visible.
  • Screen reader: Test with NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, or TalkBack.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane: Inspect the accessible name and description for any input.
  • element.labels: Returns an array of associated labels for an input.
  • form.checkValidity(): Returns true if all fields are valid.
  • field.validity: Inspect validation state.
  • document.activeElement: Check which field currently has focus.
  • axe DevTools: Flags missing labels and ARIA misuse.
  • Lighthouse: Audits for missing form labels.
  • WAVE: Visualizes label associations.
  • Mobile testing: Test with VoiceOver (iOS) and TalkBack (Android).
  • Zoom to 200%: Verify form remains usable.
  • High contrast mode: Verify form controls remain visible.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every form on every website — accessibility is a baseline requirement.
  • Every input, select, textarea, button — labels and states are required.
  • Every error message — must be announced.
  • Every group of controls — fieldset/legend.
  • Every authentication flow — accessible authentication.
  • Every multi-step form — avoid redundant entry.
  • Every form on a mobile device — inputmode and enterkeyhint.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use ARIA to replace native form elements. Native is more reliable.
  • Do not use <div> for buttons or inputs. Use native controls.
  • Do not use placeholder as a label.
  • Do not rely on color alone.
  • Do not block password managers or paste.
  • Do not require CAPTCHA with no accessible alternative.
  • Do not use positive tabindex.
  • Do not use aria-invalid without an associated error message.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• WCAG 2.2 (1.3.1, 1.3.5, 3.3.1–3.3.9, 2.5.8, 3.2.6)
  • <label> element
  • <input> element
  • <select> element
  • <textarea> element
  • <fieldset> and <legend>
  • <button> element
  • autocomplete attribute
  • inputmode attribute
  • enterkeyhint attribute
  • aria-describedby
  • aria-invalid
  • aria-required
  • role="alert"
  • role="status"
  • Native <dialog>
  • Form validation
  • Error recovery
  • Password managers
  • WebAuthn / passkeys
  • Redundant Entry (WCAG 3.3.7)
  • Accessible Authentication (WCAG 3.3.8)
  • Consistent Help (WCAG 3.2.6)

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Forms are the #1 source of accessibility barriers on the web — missing labels, unannounced errors, and inaccessible widgets.
  • WCAG 2.2 added four new form-related criteria: Redundant Entry, Accessible Authentication (Minimum and Enhanced), and Consistent Help.
  • autocomplete is an accessibility feature — it enables password managers and autofill for users with cognitive and motor disabilities.
  • Blocking paste in password fields blocks password managers — a WCAG violation and a security anti-pattern.
  • Placeholder text is not a label — it disappears on typing and is often not announced.
  • role="alert" is implicitly aria-live="assertive" — it interrupts the screen reader.
  • aria-invalid="true" is the correct way to mark invalid fields for screen readers.
  • Focus must move to the first invalid field after validation fails — otherwise the error is not announced.
  • autocomplete="one-time-code" enables OTP autofill on iOS and Android.
  • inputmode="numeric" shows a numeric keyboard on mobile — critical for OTP and PIN inputs.
  • CAPTCHAs are an accessibility barrier — WCAG 3.3.8 requires accessible authentication.
  • The <dialog> element provides native focus management — no JavaScript focus trap needed.
  • Touch targets must be at least 24×24 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.5.8) — smaller targets are inaccessible on mobile.
  • The "show password" toggle should use aria-pressed — so screen readers announce the toggle state.
  • Redundant entry (WCAG 3.3.7) is a Level A requirement — do not ask for the same information twice in the same process.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Accessible forms are a programmatic contract between your markup and assistive technology.
  • Every input needs a label — <label for> or wrapping <label>.
  • Group related controls with <fieldset> and <legend>.
  • Indicate required fields both visually and programmatically — required attribute + non-color indicator.
  • Provide hints with aria-describedby — announced before the user types.
  • Use autocomplete for every field with a known purpose — enables autofill and password managers.
  • Use inputmode and enterkeyhint on mobile — correct keyboard and Enter key.
  • Mark invalid fields with aria-invalid="true" and announce errors with role="alert".
  • Focus the first invalid field on validation failure.
  • Never rely on color alone.
  • Avoid positive tabindex; keep DOM order aligned with visual order.
  • Use native form elements — <input>, <select>, <textarea>, <button>, <dialog>.
  • Support password managers and paste — they are accessibility tools.
  • Meet WCAG 2.2 form criteria: 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication, 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.4 Error Prevention.
  • Test with keyboard only, screen reader, and mobile.
  • Forms are the most common place accessibility failures become conversion failures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Accessibility testing is the systematic process of evaluating a web page, application, or digital product against established accessibility standards — primarily WCAG 2.2 Level AA — using a combination of automated tools, manual inspection, and assistive technology testing. Its purpose is to identify barriers that prevent people with disabilities from perceiving, operating, understanding, and interacting with digital content.

<!-- What automated tools catch -->
<img src="chart.png">                     <!-- missing alt -->
<button style="color:#aaa;background:#fff">  <!-- contrast 2.3:1 -->

<!-- What only manual testing catches -->
<a href="/article">Read more</a>          <!-- vague link text -->
<div tabindex="0">Custom widget</div>     <!-- no role, no keyboard handler -->

The first example produces automated violations. The second produces zero automated violations but is completely inaccessible to screen reader and keyboard users. This is the central truth of accessibility testing: automation finds the obvious; humans find the important.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Accessibility testing serves several essential purposes:

  • Barrier identification — discovers what prevents users with disabilities from completing tasks.
  • Legal compliance — demonstrates conformance with WCAG 2.2 AA, the standard referenced by the ADA, Section 508, and the European Accessibility Act.
  • Regression prevention — catches accessibility breaks before they reach production.
  • User experience — improves the experience for all users, not just those with disabilities.
  • Risk reduction — identifies issues before lawsuits, fines, or enforcement actions.
  • Continuous improvement — establishes a baseline and measures progress over time.

Accessibility testing is not a one-time audit. It is a continuous practice integrated into design, development, and release cycles.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Accessibility Testing
│
├── Automated testing      ← axe-core, Lighthouse, WAVE (30–40% of issues)
├── Manual testing         ← keyboard navigation, focus, reading order (~42%)
├── Assistive technology   ← NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack
├── Mobile testing         ← VoiceOver iOS, TalkBack Android
├── CI/CD integration      ← axe-core in Playwright/Cypress
└── Real user testing      ← users with disabilities

Testing spans the entire development lifecycle — from design review to post-release monitoring.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The 2026 WebAIM Million report found that 95.9% of the top one million home pages have automatically detectable WCAG failures, averaging 56.1 errors per page — a 10.1% increase from 2025, reversing years of gradual improvement. And since automated tools catch only 30–40% of real accessibility issues, the true failure rate is significantly higher.

Without systematic testing, these barriers remain invisible to the teams that build them. Developers use mice, see the screen, and navigate visually. They never encounter the barriers that screen reader users, keyboard-only users, and low-vision users face daily.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No testing at all Accessibility treated as an afterthought Automated-only testing 60–70% of issues missed entirely No screen reader testing Announcement quality and reading order never verified No keyboard-only testing Focus traps and tab order issues ship undetected No mobile testing Touch target, gesture, and VoiceOver issues missed Testing only before launch Regressions introduced by every subsequent change No CI integration Issues caught too late, remediation expensive

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Accessibility testing evolved alongside accessibility standards. WCAG 1.0 (1999) introduced testable checkpoints. WCAG 2.0 (2008) made them technology-agnostic and testable. WCAG 2.2 (2023) added new criteria that require new testing methods.

The testing tooling evolved in parallel:

  • 2010s — WAVE and basic automated scanners.
  • 2015 — Deque released axe-core, the first engine with zero false positives on automated checks.
  • 2018 — Lighthouse integrated axe-core for accessibility audits.
  • 2020s — CI/CD integration became standard; accessibility testing shifted left into development.
  • 2025–2026 — The European Accessibility Act made testing a legal requirement for EU-facing digital products. France's DGCCRF began inspections in December 2025. The Dutch ACM moved toward active enforcement in mid-2026. In June 2026, a French court ordered Carrefour to make its site and app accessible within six months, with €500 per day penalties for delay.

Accessibility testing exists because you cannot fix what you cannot see. Testing makes barriers visible before they reach users, regulators, and courts.

docs.title: The Three-Layer Testing Strategy
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LAYER 1: AUTOMATED (30–40%)                 │
│  axe-core, Lighthouse, WAVE                  │
│  Runs in CI/CD, catches structural issues    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYER 2: MANUAL (~42% irreducible)          │
│  Keyboard navigation, focus, reading order   │
│  Human judgement required                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYER 3: ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY               │
│  NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack            │
│  Real screen reader testing                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Layer 1: Automated Testing with axe-core
docs.text:
// Playwright + axe-core integration
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('homepage has no accessibility violations', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://example.com');

    const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
        .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa'])
        .analyze();

    expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
});

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• @axe-core/playwright — integrates axe-core into Playwright tests.
  • .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa']) — restricts to WCAG 2.2 A and AA criteria.
  • .analyze() — runs the scan and returns violations, incomplete items, and passes.
  • expect(results.violations).toEqual([]) — fails the test if any violations exist.

docs.title: Layer 2: Manual Keyboard Testing
docs.text:
## Keyboard Navigation Test Protocol

### Setup
- [ ] Put away the mouse
- [ ] Open the page in Chrome or Firefox

### Test Steps
1. **Tab forward** — press `Tab` repeatedly
   - [ ] Every interactive element receives focus
   - [ ] Focus order follows visual order
   - [ ] Focus indicator is visible on every element

2. **Tab backward** — press `Shift+Tab`
   - [ ] Reverse order is correct

3. **Activate** — press `Enter` and `Space`
   - [ ] Buttons activate
   - [ ] Links navigate
   - [ ] Form controls respond

4. **Escape** — press `Escape`
   - [ ] Modals close
   - [ ] Dropdowns dismiss

5. **Arrow keys** — within composite widgets
   - [ ] Tabs navigate
   - [ ] Menus navigate
   - [ ] Radio groups navigate

### Verify
- [ ] No keyboard traps (can always Tab out)
- [ ] Focus not obscured by sticky headers
- [ ] Skip link works

docs.title: Layer 3: Screen Reader Testing
docs.text:
## NVDA Test Protocol (Windows)

### Setup
- [ ] Download NVDA from nvaccess.org
- [ ] Launch with Ctrl+Alt+N
- [ ] Open Chrome or Firefox

### Structure
- [ ] NVDA+T — page title announced correctly
- [ ] H — headings cycle in logical order
- [ ] D — landmarks cycle through
- [ ] NVDA+Down — content reads in logical order

### Forms
- [ ] F — form fields cycle through
- [ ] Tab into each field — label announced
- [ ] Submit invalid form — error announced via role="alert"

### Interactive
- [ ] B — buttons cycle through with names
- [ ] Open modal — focus moves in
- [ ] Close modal — focus returns to trigger

docs.title: WCAG 2.2 AA Testing Checklist
docs.text:
Fifty-five success criteria separate a site from WCAG 2.2 AA compliance — 31 at Level A and 24 at Level AA. The following table maps criteria to testing method:

Criterion Level Automated Manual AT 1.1.1 Non-text Content A ✅ Partial ✅ ✅ 1.3.1 Info and Relationships A ✅ Partial ✅ ✅ 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) AA ✅ — — 1.4.4 Resize Text AA — ✅ — 2.1.1 Keyboard A — ✅ ✅ 2.4.3 Focus Order A — ✅ — 2.4.7 Focus Visible AA — ✅ — 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured AA — ✅ — 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA ✅ Partial ✅ — 3.3.1 Error Identification A — ✅ ✅ 3.3.7 Redundant Entry A — ✅ — 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication AA — ✅ —

docs.title: The "Iceberg" Mental Model
docs.text:
Automated testing sees only the tip of the iceberg:

                    ▲
                   ╱ ╲          ← Automated catches this
                  ╱   ╲            (30–40% of issues)
                 ╱─────╲
                ╱       ╲
               ╱         ╲      ← Manual testing required
              ╱           ╲        (60–70% of issues)
             ╱             ╲
            ╱───────────────╲
           ╱                 ╲
          ╱                   ╲
         ╱─────────────────────╲

The visible tip: missing alt text, insufficient contrast, missing form labels. The submerged mass: reading order, focus management, error announcement, keyboard traps, announcement quality, cognitive load.

docs.title: The "Four Testing Layers" Mental Model
docs.text:
Layer 1: LINT (at keystroke)
  └── ESLint a11y plugins, TypeScript types
  └── Catches: missing alt in JSX, invalid ARIA

Layer 2: AUTOMATED (CI/CD)
  └── axe-core, Pa11y, Lighthouse
  └── Catches: contrast, labels, ARIA validity

Layer 3: MANUAL (pre-merge)
  └── Keyboard, focus, reading order, zoom
  └── Catches: tab order, focus traps, reading order

Layer 4: ASSISTIVE TECH (pre-release)
  └── NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack
  └── Catches: announcement quality, interaction flow

Each layer catches what the layer above cannot. Skipping a layer leaves gaps.

docs.title: The "Tool Selection" Mental Model
docs.text: Need Tool Why CI/CD pipeline axe-core, Pa11y Free, accurate, scriptable Developer education WAVE Visual overlay, intuitive Quick health check Lighthouse Built into Chrome, fast Guided manual review axe DevTools IGT Semi-automated checks for incomplete items Screen reader testing NVDA Free, widely used Enterprise coverage JAWS Market leader Mobile testing VoiceOver, TalkBack Built into devices

docs.title: The "Cost of Late Discovery" Mental Model
docs.text:
Design phase:      $1 to fix
Development:       $10 to fix
QA:                $100 to fix
Production:        $1,000 to fix
Litigation:        $100,000+ to fix

Accessibility issues found in design cost almost nothing to fix. Issues found in production cost 1,000× more. Testing must happen early and continuously.

docs.title: Concept 1: Automated Tools Catch 30–40%
docs.text:
The 2026 consensus: automated engines catch roughly 30–40% of WCAG AA failures. Deque claims ~57% with axe-core plus Intelligent Guided Tests. But ~42% of WCAG 2.2 AA criteria cannot be automated at all, and a further ~45% require human judgement to interpret.

Implication: Automated testing alone can never achieve compliance. It is the floor, not the ceiling.

docs.title: Concept 2: axe-core — The Industry Standard
docs.text: axe-core is the open-source engine that powers Lighthouse, axe DevTools, and most CI integrations. It has zero false positives on automated checks. It runs on WCAG 2.0/2.1/2.2 A and AA criteria.

docs.title: Concept 3: Lighthouse — Fast Health Check, Not Compliance Signal
docs.text: Lighthouse uses axe-core under the hood but only ships a subset of its rules — around 50–60 audits as of early 2026. It is useful for a quick "is this page in the ballpark" check but is not a compliance signal.

docs.title: Concept 4: WAVE — Visual Feedback for Education
docs.text: WAVE (WebAIM) places icons directly on the rendered page, showing issues in context. It has a higher false-positive rate than axe-core and is not appropriate for CI, but it is excellent for developer education and stakeholder walkthroughs.

docs.title: Concept 5: Lint as the Floor
docs.text: ESLint accessibility plugins (eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, eslint-plugin-vue-a11y) catch issues at keystroke — missing alt in JSX, invalid ARIA attributes, click handlers on non-interactive elements. Lint is the floor, not the ceiling.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Irreducible Manual 42%
docs.text: Roughly 42% of WCAG 2.2 AA criteria cannot be automated. These include: keyboard operability, focus order, focus visibility, reading order, error recovery, redundant entry, and accessible authentication.

docs.title: Concept 7: Keyboard Navigation Testing
docs.text:
The keyboard pass is the single highest-value manual test:

  • Tab / Shift+Tab — forward and backward through all interactive elements.
  • Enter / Space — activate buttons and links.
  • Arrow keys — within widgets (menus, tabs, listbox, autocomplete).
  • Escape — close modals, dropdowns, dismiss popovers.

Verify: coverage (every mouse action has a keyboard equivalent), order (tab follows visual layout), visible indicator (every focusable element has visible focus), and not obscured (sticky headers do not hide focused elements).

docs.title: Concept 8: Screen Reader Market Share (2026)
docs.text:
Based on the WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #10 (2024, still the most recent data):

Screen reader Desktop primary Mobile primary JAWS 40.5% — NVDA 37.7% — VoiceOver 9.7% ~70.6% TalkBack — ~34.7%

Testing priority: NVDA + Chrome (free, 21.3% of users), JAWS + Chrome (24.7%, #1 combination), VoiceOver + Safari (mobile dominance).

docs.title: Concept 9: Testing Matrix
docs.text: Priority Screen reader Browser OS 1 JAWS Chrome Windows 2 NVDA Chrome Windows 3 VoiceOver Safari macOS 4 VoiceOver Safari iOS 5 TalkBack Chrome Android

docs.title: Concept 10: Mobile Accessibility Testing
docs.text: Mobile testing is not optional: 91.3% of screen reader users also use a mobile device. Mobile-specific checks: touch target size (44×44pt iOS, 48×48dp Android), gestures, dynamic type, and reduced motion.

docs.title: Concept 11: The Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Design → Lint → Automated → Manual → AT → Mobile → Release
  │        │        │          │       │       │        │
  │        │        │          │       │       │        └── Monitor
  │        │        │          │       │       └── VoiceOver/TalkBack
  │        │        │          │       └── NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver
  │        │        │          └── Keyboard, focus, zoom, contrast
  │        │        └── axe-core in CI/CD
  │        └── ESLint a11y plugins
  └── Color contrast, touch targets, semantic structure

docs.title: Concept 12: CI/CD Integration
docs.text: Automated accessibility checks should run in CI/CD on every pull request. Use @axe-core/playwright, jest-axe, or pa11y to gate merges. This prevents regressions from reaching production.

docs.title: Concept 13: Real User Testing
docs.text: The most valuable testing is with real users with disabilities. Automated tools, manual checklists, and screen reader testing all catch issues — but real users reveal usability problems that no checklist anticipates.

docs.title: Concept 14: Testing Is Continuous
docs.text: Accessibility decays. Every new feature, every CMS update, every design change can introduce barriers. Testing must be continuous, not a one-time audit.

docs.title: Concept 15: The European Accessibility Act Enforcement (2026)
docs.text:
Since June 2025, the EAA requires accessible e-commerce, banking, transport, and digital products in the EU. Enforcement accelerated in 2026:

  • Netherlands: Dutch ACM moving toward active enforcement mid-2026.
  • France: Carrefour ordered by court in June 2026 to fix its site within six months, with €500/day penalties.
  • Italy: Implementing Decree with transitional arrangements until 2030.

Testing is no longer optional — it is a legal requirement.

docs.title: Concept 16: WCAG 2.2 Testing Checklist
docs.text: 55 criteria (31 A + 24 AA) must be verified. The checklist should be a workflow, not a scorecard: scan first, fix templates, automate what can be automated, manually verify the rest.

docs.title: Concept 17: axe DevTools Intelligent Guided Tests
docs.text: axe DevTools browser extension offers Intelligent Guided Tests (IGT) — semi-automated checks for incomplete items like color-meaning use, link-purpose, and focus-order. Deque demonstrates ~80% issue coverage when combining the engine with guided manual review.

docs.title: Concept 18: Testing the New WCAG 2.2 Criteria
docs.text:
WCAG 2.2 added criteria that require new testing methods:

  • 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured — keyboard sweep to verify focus is not hidden by sticky elements.
  • 2.5.7 Dragging Movements — verify non-drag alternative exists.
  • 2.5.8 Target Size — verify 24×24 CSS pixel minimum.
  • 3.3.7 Redundant Entry — verify no duplicate data requests.
  • 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication — verify no cognitive function tests.

docs.title: Concept 19: Testing Zoom and Reflow
docs.text: WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text) and 1.4.10 (Reflow) require testing at 200% zoom and 320 CSS pixel viewport. Automated tools do not test zoom and reflow — manual inspection is required.

docs.title: Concept 20: Accessibility Statements
docs.text: The EAA requires organizations to publish accessibility statements describing compliance status, known issues, and contact information. Testing provides the data for these statements.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Automated Testing in CI/CD
docs.text:
1.  Developer pushes code.
    │
    ▼
2.  CI pipeline runs:
    │   ├── ESLint a11y plugins (lint)
    │   ├── axe-core via Playwright (automated)
    │   └── Lighthouse CI (health check)
    │
    ▼
3.  Violations reported in PR.
    │
    ▼
4.  Developer fixes violations.
    │
    ▼
5.  Merge blocked until violations resolved.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Manual Keyboard Testing
docs.text:
1.  Put away the mouse.
    │
    ▼
2.  Press Tab repeatedly.
    │
    ▼
3.  Verify:
    │   ├── Every interactive element receives focus
    │   ├── Focus order follows visual order
    │   └── Focus indicator is visible
    │
    ▼
4.  Press Enter/Space to activate.
    │
    ▼
5.  Press Escape to dismiss.
    │
    ▼
6.  Verify no keyboard traps.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Screen Reader Testing
docs.text:
1.  Launch NVDA (Windows) or VoiceOver (macOS/iOS).
    │
    ▼
2.  Navigate to the page.
    │
    ▼
3.  Test structure:
    │   ├── Page title announced correctly
    │   ├── Headings cycle in logical order
    │   └── Landmarks present and labelled
    │
    ▼
4.  Test forms:
    │   ├── Labels announced before inputs
    │   ├── Required state announced
    │   └── Errors announced
    │
    ▼
5.  Test dynamic content:
    │   ├── Live regions announce updates
    │   ├── Modals trap focus correctly
    │   └── Route changes announced
    │
    ▼
6.  Document findings.

docs.title: How axe-core Works
docs.text:
axe-core injects into the page and walks the DOM. For each node, it:

  1. Determines the element's role and accessible name.
  2. Checks against rule definitions (e.g., image-alt, color-contrast).
  3. Returns violations, incomplete items, passes, and inapplicable rules.

The engine is rules-based, not AI-based. It can only check what is programmatically determinable.

docs.title: Why Automated Tools Have Limits
docs.text:
Automated tools cannot determine:
