  • Whether alt text is meaningful or just present.
  • Whether link text is descriptive in context.
  • Whether reading order is logical.
  • Whether focus order makes sense.
  • Whether error messages are helpful.
  • Whether content is understandable.

These require human judgement.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree and Testing
docs.text: Screen readers read the accessibility tree, not the DOM. Testing tools inspect the DOM and the accessibility tree. Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane shows the computed accessible name, role, and state for any element.

docs.title: Lighthouse vs axe-core
docs.text:
Lighthouse uses axe-core but:

  • Ships only ~50–60 of axe-core's ~100+ rules.
  • Weights results by user impact.
  • Reports a score (0–100), which can be misleading.

Use Lighthouse for a quick check. Use axe-core directly for compliance.

docs.title: CI/CD Integration Architecture
docs.text:
Developer push → CI pipeline
                    │
                    ├── Install Playwright + axe-core
                    ├── Start dev server
                    ├── Run tests against all routes
                    ├── Collect violations
                    └── Fail build if violations > 0

docs.title: The Full Testing Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  DESIGN PHASE
    │   ├── Color contrast checked
    │   ├── Touch target sizes verified
    │   └── Keyboard flow mapped
    │
    ▼
2.  DEVELOPMENT PHASE
    │   ├── ESLint a11y plugins (lint)
    │   ├── axe-core in unit tests
    │   └── Manual keyboard testing
    │
    ▼
3.  PRE-MERGE (CI)
    │   ├── axe-core via Playwright
    │   ├── Lighthouse CI
    │   └── Pa11y on key templates
    │
    ▼
4.  PRE-RELEASE
    │   ├── Screen reader testing (NVDA, VoiceOver)
    │   ├── Zoom and reflow testing
    │   └── Mobile testing (VoiceOver iOS, TalkBack)
    │
    ▼
5.  POST-RELEASE
    │   ├── Monitor CSP violations
    │   ├── Monitor accessibility dashboards
    │   └── Schedule quarterly audits

docs.title: Tool Selection Workflow
docs.text:
Need a quick check?
  → Lighthouse (built into Chrome)

Need CI gating?
  → axe-core (Playwright/Cypress)

Need visual feedback for stakeholders?
  → WAVE

Need guided manual review?
  → axe DevTools IGT

Need screen reader testing?
  → NVDA (free), JAWS (enterprise), VoiceOver (Apple)

docs.title: Example 1: Playwright + axe-core CI Test
docs.text:
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

const routes = ['/', '/about', '/products', '/contact'];

for (const route of routes) {
    test(`${route} has no accessibility violations`, async ({ page }) => {
        await page.goto(route);

        const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
            .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa'])
            .analyze();

        expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
    });
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Iterates over all routes.
  • .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa']) — restricts to WCAG 2.2 A and AA criteria.
  • expect(results.violations).toEqual([]) — fails the test if any violations exist.
  • This runs in CI on every pull request.

docs.title: Example 2: Keyboard Testing Protocol
docs.text:
## Keyboard Test — Checkout Flow

### Coverage
- [ ] Can I complete the entire purchase with keyboard only?
- [ ] Can I reach every form field?
- [ ] Can I activate every button?
- [ ] Can I dismiss every modal?

### Order
- [ ] Tab follows visual order (top → bottom, left → right)
- [ ] No positive tabindex values
- [ ] DOM order matches visual order

### Focus Visibility
- [ ] Focus indicator visible on every focusable element
- [ ] Focus indicator meets 2px + 3:1 contrast

### Not Obscured
- [ ] Sticky header does not hide focused element
- [ ] Cookie banner does not cover focused element
- [ ] scroll-margin-top applied where needed

### Traps
- [ ] Can always Tab out of any widget
- [ ] Escape closes modals and dropdowns

Code Breakdown:

  • Covers the four keyboard testing dimensions: coverage, order, visibility, and traps.
  • Each checkbox maps to a WCAG 2.2 success criterion.

docs.title: Example 3: NVDA Screen Reader Test
docs.text:
## NVDA Test — Registration Form

### Structure
- [ ] NVDA+T — page title announced
- [ ] H — headings in logical order
- [ ] D — landmarks present

### Form
- [ ] F — form fields cycle through
- [ ] Tab into email — "Email address, edit, required" announced
- [ ] Submit empty — error announced via role="alert"
- [ ] Focus moves to first invalid field

### Interactive
- [ ] B — buttons announced with names
- [ ] Open modal — focus moves in
- [ ] Close modal — focus returns to trigger

Code Breakdown:

  • Covers structure, form, and interactive testing.
  • Each check maps to a WCAG 2.2 success criterion.

docs.title: Example 4: Lighthouse CI Configuration
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/lighthouse.yml
name: Lighthouse CI
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  lighthouse:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: treosh/lighthouse-ci-action@v12
        with:
          urls: |
            https://example.com/
            https://example.com/about
          budgetPath: ./lighthouse-budget.json
          uploadArtifacts: true

Code Breakdown:

  • Runs Lighthouse on every pull request.
  • budgetPath — enforces performance and accessibility budgets.
  • uploadArtifacts — stores results for review.

docs.title: Example 5: WAVE for Stakeholder Education
docs.text:
## WAVE Walkthrough for Designers

1. Install WAVE extension (Chrome/Firefox)
2. Navigate to the page
3. Click WAVE icon
4. Review:
   - [ ] Red icons = errors
   - [ ] Yellow icons = alerts
   - [ ] Green icons = features
   - [ ] Contrast errors highlighted on page

5. Discuss findings with the team

Code Breakdown:

  • WAVE's visual overlay makes issues tangible for non-engineers.
  • Not appropriate for CI — use axe-core for that.

docs.title: Example 6: Mobile VoiceOver Test
docs.text:
## VoiceOver iOS Test — Checkout

### Setup
- [ ] Settings → Accessibility → VoiceOver → On
- [ ] Open Safari

### Navigation
- [ ] Swipe right — moves through elements
- [ ] Double-tap — activates focused element
- [ ] Two-finger swipe up — reads all
- [ ] Rotor — switch to Headings

### Touch Targets
- [ ] All buttons ≥ 44×44pt
- [ ] No adjacent targets closer than 8pt

### Forms
- [ ] Labels announced before inputs
- [ ] Correct keyboard type (numeric for OTP)
- [ ] Error announced

Code Breakdown:

  • Covers mobile-specific concerns: gestures, touch targets, and on-screen keyboard.
  • Maps to WCAG 2.5.8 (Target Size) and platform guidelines.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Primary Tool Secondary Tool CI/CD regression prevention axe-core (Playwright) Pa11y Developer education WAVE axe DevTools Quick health check Lighthouse WAVE Pre-release audit NVDA + JAWS + VoiceOver axe DevTools IGT Mobile app testing VoiceOver iOS, TalkBack Manual gestures Design review Contrast checkers Touch target rulers Enterprise compliance JAWS + Chrome axe-core + manual Legal/EAA compliance Full WCAG 2.2 AA audit Real user testing

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Start testing in design, not development. Why: issues caught in design cost 1,000× less to fix.
  2. Integrate axe-core into CI/CD. Why: prevents regressions from reaching production.
  3. Use ESLint a11y plugins. Why: catches issues at keystroke, before CI.
  4. Test with keyboard only. Why: keyboard accessibility is the foundation of all accessibility.
  5. Test with at least one screen reader. Why: automated tools cannot verify announcement quality.
  6. Test with NVDA and VoiceOver at minimum. Why: NVDA is free; VoiceOver covers Apple platforms.
  7. Test on mobile. Why: 91.3% of screen reader users also use mobile.
  8. Test zoom to 200%. Why: WCAG 1.4.4 requires it; automated tools do not test zoom.
  9. Test reflow at 320 CSS pixels. Why: WCAG 1.4.10 requires it.
  10. Use axe-core directly, not just Lighthouse. Why: Lighthouse ships only a subset of axe rules.
  11. Combine automated and manual testing. Why: automated catches 30–40%; manual catches the rest.
  12. Document testing protocols. Why: consistency across team members.
  13. Test after every significant UI change. Why: accessibility regressions are common.
  14. Use real content, not lorem ipsum. Why: meaningful content reveals real issues.
  15. Involve users with disabilities. Why: they find issues no checklist anticipates.
  16. Audit quarterly. Why: accessibility decays as content and code change.
  17. Publish an accessibility statement. Why: EAA requires it; testing provides the data.
  18. Track violations over time. Why: measure progress and identify regression patterns.
  19. Train the team. Why: accessibility is everyone's responsibility.
  20. Use the WCAG 2.2 checklist as a workflow, not a scorecard. Why: it is a process, not a grade.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Automated-Only Testing
docs.text:
// CI passes, but no screen reader testing

Why it's wrong: Automated tools catch only 30–40% of issues. The site may be unusable with a screen reader despite passing CI.

✅ Correct: Combine automated, manual, and screen reader testing.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Keyboard Testing
docs.text:
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

Why it's wrong: Automated tools do not catch keyboard inoperability. The button works with a mouse but not a keyboard.

✅ Correct: Test keyboard navigation on every release.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Testing Only at the End
docs.text:
<!-- Accessibility audit scheduled two weeks before launch -->

Why it's wrong: Issues found late are expensive to fix and may delay launch.

✅ Correct: Test continuously from design through release.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Lighthouse Score
docs.text:
<!-- Lighthouse score 100, but no manual testing -->

Why it's wrong: Lighthouse uses a subset of axe-core rules and weights them by impact. A perfect score does not mean compliance.

✅ Correct: Use Lighthouse for a quick check; use axe-core and manual testing for compliance.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Testing Only on Desktop
docs.text:
<!-- Desktop testing only -->

Why it's wrong: 91.3% of screen reader users also use mobile. Mobile has unique concerns: touch targets, gestures, VoiceOver/TalkBack.

✅ Correct: Test on iOS and Android with VoiceOver and TalkBack.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No CI Integration
docs.text:
<!-- Accessibility tested manually once per quarter -->

Why it's wrong: Regressions reach production between audits.

✅ Correct: Integrate axe-core into CI/CD.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring WCAG 2.2 New Criteria
docs.text:
<!-- Testing only WCAG 2.1 criteria -->

Why it's wrong: WCAG 2.2 added criteria that many existing sites fail: Focus Not Obscured, Focus Appearance, Dragging Movements, Target Size, Redundant Entry, Accessible Authentication.

✅ Correct: Test against WCAG 2.2 AA.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Accessibility Statement
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The EAA requires it for relevant services.

✅ Correct: Publish and maintain an accessibility statement.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• axe-core adds minimal overhead — typically under 100ms per page.
  • Lighthouse audits take 10–30 seconds per page — run in CI, not on every commit.
  • Screen reader testing is manual — no performance impact on the page.
  • CI integration adds seconds to pipeline — but prevents regressions.
  • Large DOM may slow automated scanning — but this is rare.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Run axe-core on key templates, not every page.
  2. Use Lighthouse CI on pull requests, not every push.
  3. Cache npm dependencies for CI.
  4. Run automated tests in parallel with other CI jobs.

docs.title: Accessibility Overlays Are Not a Fix
docs.text: Third-party overlay widgets claim to make sites accessible automatically. They do not. They cannot fix missing semantics, keyboard traps, or poor contrast. Overlays have been sued for failing to provide actual accessibility.

docs.title: Testing Tools and Data
docs.text: Automated testing tools run in the browser. Do not test on production with sensitive data unless the tool is vetted. Use staging environments.

docs.title: Screen Reader Testing and Authentication
docs.text: Screen reader testing often requires logging in. Ensure test accounts are set up with appropriate security.

docs.title: CI/CD Access
docs.text: Accessibility testing tools in CI/CD may need network access to staging environments. Secure credentials and limit scope.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect accessible name, role, and state.
  • axe DevTools extension — run scans directly in the browser.
  • WAVE extension — visual overlay of issues.
  • Lighthouse — built into Chrome DevTools.
  • document.activeElement — check which element has focus.
  • element.labels — verify label association.
  • form.checkValidity() — check form validation state.
  • NVDA — NVDA+T for title, H for headings, D for landmarks.
  • VoiceOver — VO+U for rotor.
  • prefers-reduced-motion — test in DevTools → Rendering.
  • Zoom to 200% — test in browser zoom.
  • Mobile emulation — Chrome DevTools device toolbar.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every project — accessibility testing is a baseline requirement.
  • Every release — test before shipping.
  • Every new component — test in isolation.
  • Every form — labels, errors, keyboard.
  • Every interactive widget — modals, dropdowns, tabs.
  • Every EU-facing product — EAA compliance since June 2025.
  • Every government service — Section 508, ADA Title II.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not rely on automated testing alone. It catches only 30–40%.
  • Do not use overlays as a substitute. They do not work.
  • Do not skip manual keyboard testing. Automated tools cannot verify tab order.
  • Do not skip screen reader testing. Automated tools cannot verify announcement quality.
  • Do not test only at the end. Test continuously.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• 95.9% of the top one million home pages have automatically detectable WCAG failures, averaging 56.1 errors per page — a 10.1% increase from 2025.
  • Automated tools catch only 30–40% of WCAG AA failures.
  • ~42% of WCAG 2.2 AA criteria cannot be automated at all.
  • axe-core has zero false positives on automated checks.
  • Lighthouse ships only ~50–60 of axe-core's ~100+ rules — it is a health check, not a compliance signal.
  • Deque claims ~80% issue coverage when combining axe-core with Intelligent Guided Tests.
  • JAWS leads desktop screen reader use at 40.5%, with NVDA at 37.7% and VoiceOver at 9.7%.
  • VoiceOver dominates mobile screen reader use at ~70.6%.
  • 91.3% of screen reader users also use a mobile device.
  • The European Accessibility Act took effect June 2025 — enforcement accelerated in 2026.
  • A French court ordered Carrefour in June 2026 to make its site accessible within six months, with €500/day penalties.
  • The Dutch ACM moved toward active enforcement in mid-2026.
  • WCAG 2.2 added 9 criteria and removed 1 — the new criteria require new testing methods.
  • Testing at 200% zoom and 320px reflow is required by WCAG but not tested by automated tools.
  • The 2026 WebAIM Million found the first increase in errors after years of gradual improvement.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Accessibility testing is the systematic evaluation of digital products against WCAG 2.2 AA using automated tools, manual inspection, and assistive technology.
  • 95.9% of top home pages fail WCAG — averaging 56.1 errors per page, up 10.1% from 2025.
  • Automated tools catch only 30–40% of issues; ~42% of criteria cannot be automated at all.
  • Three-layer strategy: automated (axe-core, Lighthouse, WAVE), manual (keyboard, focus, zoom), assistive technology (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack).
  • axe-core is the industry standard — zero false positives, powers Lighthouse and CI integrations.
  • Lighthouse is a quick check, not a compliance signal — it ships only a subset of axe-core rules.
  • Keyboard testing is the highest-value manual test — coverage, order, visibility, no traps.
  • Screen reader testing is mandatory — test with NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver.
  • Mobile testing is not optional — 91.3% of screen reader users also use mobile.
  • WCAG 2.2 added 9 new criteria requiring new testing methods.
  • The EAA is enforced — fines and court orders began in 2026.
  • Integrate axe-core into CI/CD to prevent regressions.
  • Test continuously — from design through release and beyond.
  • Use real users with disabilities — they find what no tool can.
  • Accessibility testing is both a legal obligation and a competitive advantage.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Semantic structure is the practice of using HTML elements according to their meaning and purpose — not their visual appearance — to create a document outline that machines and humans can both understand. It is the deliberate organization of a page's content into a logical hierarchy using headings (<h1>–<h6>), sectioning elements (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <footer>), and text-level semantics (<strong>, <em>, <time>, <cite>).

<main>
    <article>
        <header>
            <h1>How SVG Embedding Works</h1>
            <p>Published <time datetime="2026-01-15">January 15, 2026</time></p>
        </header>

        <section>
            <h2>Inline SVG</h2>
            <p>The most flexible method...</p>
            <h3>Advantages</h3>
            <p>Full CSS and JavaScript access...</p>
        </section>

        <section>
            <h2>Image SVG</h2>
            <p>The most cacheable method...</p>
        </section>
    </article>
</main>

The visual result may be identical to a page built entirely from <div> elements. But the semantic version tells search engines, AI systems, screen readers, and future developers exactly what the content is — not just how it looks.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Semantic structure serves several essential purposes:

  • Search engine comprehension — search engines use semantic structure to identify content hierarchies, relationships between sections, and the relevance of each block of information.
  • AI visibility — AI answer engines (AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity) parse semantic markup to extract, summarize, and cite content accurately.
  • Accessibility — screen readers navigate by headings and landmarks; semantic structure is the foundation of the accessibility tree.
  • Featured snippet eligibility — clear heading hierarchy and standalone content units improve the chance of securing featured snippets.
  • Crawl efficiency — semantic markup helps search engines rapidly index content and identify the core content of a page.
  • Maintainability — semantic markup is self-documenting; developers can understand the structure without reading CSS classes.
  • Robustness — semantic HTML degrades gracefully. When CSS or JavaScript fails, the content remains usable and its structure remains understandable.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
SEO Stack
│
├── Semantic Structure    ← the outline that machines and humans understand
├── Heading Hierarchy     ← the navigable tree within the structure
├── Metadata              ← title, description, canonical, robots
├── Structured Data       ← JSON-LD, Schema.org
├── Canonical URLs        ← consolidation of duplicate content
└── Content Quality       ← E-E-A-T, depth, originality

Semantic structure is the foundation layer of SEO. Every other SEO signal — metadata, structured data, canonical URLs — is built on top of a well-structured document.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Search engines and AI systems cannot "see" a page the way a human does. They cannot glance at a layout and instantly understand "this is the article, that is the sidebar, this is navigation." They must infer structure from markup.

When a page is built entirely from <div> and <span> elements, there is no structure to infer. The page is what Jono Alderson calls "div soup" — markup that renders correctly but conveys nothing about meaning. Google must then render the page, execute JavaScript, and analyze visual layout to guess what the content is. This is expensive, slow, and unreliable.

Semantic HTML solves this by making the structure explicit in the markup. A <main> element says "this is the primary content." An <article> says "this is a self-contained piece of content." An <h1> says "this is the page's main topic." A <nav> says "this is navigation."

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Div soup No structure to infer; search engines must render and guess No heading hierarchy Content topics unclear; poor snippet eligibility No landmarks No way to identify main content vs. navigation vs. footer No article/sectioning Content relationships invisible to machines JavaScript-dependent Content invisible until rendered; slow indexing

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
HTML has always had semantic elements. But in the mid-2000s, WYSIWYG editors and later JavaScript frameworks encouraged developers to use <div> for everything — treating HTML as a layout engine rather than a markup language.

HTML5 (2008–2014) introduced a set of sectioning and semantic elements to reverse this trend: <header>, <footer>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <figure>, <figcaption>, <time>, <mark>, <details>, <summary>. These elements had existed conceptually since HTML 4 (<div id="header">), but HTML5 formalized them as first-class elements with defined roles and accessibility mappings.

The goal: give meaning to structure so that browsers, assistive technology, search engines, and AI systems can understand the page without parsing CSS classes or executing JavaScript.

docs.title: The Semantic Document Skeleton
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>How SVG Embedding Works — Dev Notes</title>
</head>
<body>
    <header>
        <h1>Dev Notes</h1>
        <nav aria-label="Main">
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
                <li><a href="/blog">Blog</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
    </header>

    <main>
        <article>
            <header>
                <h1>How SVG Embedding Works</h1>
                <p>Published <time datetime="2026-01-15">January 15, 2026</time></p>
            </header>

            <section>
                <h2>Inline SVG</h2>
                <p>Inline SVG gives full CSS and JavaScript access...</p>

                <h3>Advantages</h3>
                <ul>
                    <li>Styleable via CSS</li>
                    <li>Scriptable via JavaScript</li>
                    <li>Inherits <code>currentColor</code></li>
                </ul>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>Image SVG</h2>
                <p>Image SVG is cacheable but sandboxed...</p>
            </section>
        </article>

        <aside aria-label="Related posts">
            <h2>Related</h2>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/css-cascade">The CSS Cascade</a></li>
            </ul>
        </aside>
    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 Dev Notes</p>
    </footer>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element Meaning SEO Role <header> (top-level) Introductory content Identifies site header; not part of main content <nav> Navigation links Identifies navigation; deprioritized for content ranking <main> Primary content Critical: identifies the core content of the page <article> Self-contained content Identifies standalone content; eligible for rich results <section> Thematic grouping Groups related content with a heading <aside> Complementary content Identifies sidebar content; not part of main content <footer> (top-level) Closing content Identifies site footer <h1>–<h6> Heading hierarchy Critical: signals topic and subtopic structure <time> Date/time Provides machine-readable date for freshness signals

docs.title: The Heading Hierarchy
docs.text:
<h1>Page Title</h1>

<h2>Section A</h2>
<h3>Subsection A.1</h3>
<h3>Subsection A.2</h3>

<h2>Section B</h2>
<h3>Subsection B.1</h3>

Rules:

  • One <h1> per page (recommended, not strictly required by Google, but best practice).
  • Never skip levels (<h1> → <h3> is a failure).
  • Headings must reflect content structure, not visual size.
  • Use CSS to style headings differently — do not choose an <h4> because it "looks right."

docs.title: The Text-Level Semantics
docs.text:
<p>This is <strong>important</strong> and this is <em>emphasized</em>.</p>
<p>Published <time datetime="2026-01-15">January 15, 2026</time> by <cite>Jane Developer</cite>.</p>
<p>The <abbr title="Cascading Style Sheets">CSS</abbr> cascade is fundamental.</p>
Element Meaning <strong> Importance (seriousness) <em> Stress emphasis (changes meaning) <time> Date/time with machine-readable datetime <cite> Title of a work <abbr> Abbreviation with expansion

docs.title: The "Outline" Mental Model
docs.text:
A semantic page is an outline — a hierarchical tree of topics and subtopics:

H1: How SVG Embedding Works
├── H2: Inline SVG
│   ├── H3: Advantages
│   └── H3: Use Cases
├── H2: Image SVG
│   ├── H3: Advantages
│   └── H3: Limitations
└── H2: Sprites
    └── H3: Implementation

Search engines, AI systems, and screen readers all read this outline. A well-structured outline is easy to navigate, easy to summarize, and easy to cite. A flat outline (<h1> followed by twenty <h2> elements with no <h3> nesting) is harder to interpret.

docs.title: The "Standalone Content Unit" (SCU) Mental Model
docs.text:
An H2 should be a standalone content unit — a self-contained section that directly answers a question or addresses a topic. Immediately after the H2, provide a direct one- or two-sentence answer. This snippet-style response feeds Google's extraction algorithms and satisfies skimming readers.

H2: How Does H2 Tag Optimisation Improve CTR?
Answer: H2 tags improve CTR by making content scannable,
matching long-tail queries, and enabling featured snippet extraction.
[Expand with context, examples, and internal links]

docs.title: The "Two Audiences" Mental Model
docs.text:
Semantic structure serves two audiences simultaneously:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              SEMANTIC HTML                   │
│                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐ │
│  │   MACHINES          │  │   HUMANS      │ │
│  │                     │  │               │ │
│  │  Search engines     │  │  Screen       │ │
│  │  AI answer engines  │  │  readers      │ │
│  │  Crawlers           │  │  Readers      │ │
│  │  Indexers           │  │  Developers   │ │
│  └─────────────────────┘  └───────────────┘ │
│                                              │
│  Same markup. Different consumers.          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The same <h2> that helps Google understand the page's subtopic also helps a screen reader user jump to that section. The same <article> that signals standalone content to a search engine also tells a reader mode where the article begins and ends.

docs.title: The "Google Doesn't Need Perfect Order" Mental Model
docs.text:
Google's Gary Illyes clarified that while semantic heading order is recommended, Google does not strictly require hierarchical ordering for SEO. The SEO Starter Guide says: "Having headings in semantic order is fantastic for screen readers, but from Google Search perspective, it doesn't matter if you're using them out of order."

However: Correct hierarchy is still best practice because it improves accessibility, AI comprehension, and content maintainability. Google's leniency is not a license for sloppy markup.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Document Outline
docs.text: The document outline is the hierarchical tree formed by headings and sectioning elements. It is the primary structure that search engines and AI systems use to understand a page.

docs.title: Concept 2: The <main> Element
docs.text: <main> wraps the primary content of the page. There should be only one <main> per page. It should not include repeated content (headers, navigation, footers). Search engines use <main> to identify the core content of the page.

docs.title: Concept 3: The <article> Element
docs.text: <article> wraps self-contained content — content that could stand alone in an RSS feed, a syndicated context, or a search result. Blog posts, product cards, comments, and forum posts are articles. Google may use <article> to identify content eligible for rich results.

docs.title: Concept 4: The <section> Element
docs.text: <section> wraps a thematic grouping of content with a heading. A <section> without a heading is not a section — it is a <div>. Use <section> to group related content within an article or main.

docs.title: Concept 5: Heading Hierarchy
docs.text:
Headings form a tree. <h1> is the root; <h2> elements are its children; <h3> elements are grandchildren. Skipping levels breaks the tree.

Google's position: Semantic order is recommended but not strictly required. However, correct hierarchy improves accessibility and AI comprehension.

docs.title: Concept 6: The One H1 Rule
docs.text:
Use one <h1> per page. The <h1> should match or closely align with the page's primary keyword. Multiple <h1> elements confuse the outline and dilute topical focus.

Exception: In HTML5, multiple <h1> elements were theoretically allowed inside sectioning elements (the "HTML5 outline algorithm"), but this was never implemented by browsers and is not recommended.

docs.title: Concept 7: H2 as Question-Led Sections
docs.text: Frame H2s as questions or clear outcomes your audience actively searches for. "How Does H2 Tag Optimisation Improve CTR?" is better than "Benefits of H2s." Question-led headings match long-tail queries and improve featured snippet eligibility.

docs.title: Concept 8: H3 for Detail and Steps
docs.text: H3s zoom in on specifics: steps, checklists, definitions, or mini-case studies. They let scanners glean key points without reading whole paragraphs. Each H3 should be descriptive and self-contained.

docs.title: Concept 9: Semantic HTML for AI Visibility
docs.text: AI answer engines rely on clear structural cues to decide which page earns a citation. Semantic markup — headings, paragraphs, lists, tables — improves extraction and citation accuracy. Div soup produces weaker signals.

docs.title: Concept 10: Semantic HTML for Featured Snippets
docs.text: Featured snippets are extracted from content with clear structure. A direct answer immediately following a question-led H2 is the ideal snippet format. Semantic markup influences eligibility for featured snippets and AI Overviews.

docs.title: Concept 11: The "Div Soup" Anti-Pattern
docs.text: Using <div> for everything — navigation, headers, articles, sections — creates markup that renders correctly but conveys nothing. It requires search engines to render and guess, which is slow and unreliable.

docs.title: Concept 12: Semantic HTML and Reader Mode
docs.text: Reader modes in Safari, Firefox, and Chrome extract the "main article" from the page. They rely on semantic elements. A page built with <article>, <h1>, and <p> is reader-mode friendly. A <div> soup is not.

docs.title: Concept 13: The Role of Landmarks
docs.text: Landmarks (banner, navigation, main, complementary, contentinfo) identify major structural regions. They are produced natively by <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, and <footer>. Landmarks help screen readers jump between regions and help search engines identify the primary content.

docs.title: Concept 14: Semantic HTML and Crawl Efficiency
docs.text: Semantic markup helps search engines rapidly index content and process the page more efficiently. A well-structured page requires less rendering and less inference.

docs.title: Concept 15: Heading Tags Are Not for Styling
docs.text: Heading levels are semantic, not visual. Never choose an <h4> because it "looks right." Choose the heading level that reflects the content's position in the outline, then style it with CSS.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Flat Outline Anti-Pattern
docs.text: A page with one <h1> and twenty <h2> elements with no <h3> nesting is a flat outline. It conveys topics but not subtopics. Search engines and AI systems have difficulty identifying the relationships between sections.

docs.title: Concept 17: Semantic HTML and Content Extraction
docs.text: Google's rendering process is expensive and slow. News publishers and time-sensitive content benefit enormously from raw HTML that is already structured — allowing Google to extract the article content without full rendering.

docs.title: Concept 18: The lang Attribute
docs.text:
<html lang="en">

The lang attribute tells search engines and screen readers the language of the content. It supports correct indexing, correct pronunciation, and international targeting.

docs.title: Concept 19: Semantic HTML and Structured Data
docs.text: Semantic HTML and structured data (JSON-LD) work together. Semantic HTML provides the document structure; structured data provides the entity-level metadata. Both are needed for full SEO and AI visibility.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Testing Mindset
docs.text:
Semantic structure should be tested by:

  • Outline tools — browser extensions that render the heading tree.
  • Screen reader — verify heading and landmark navigation works.
  • Lighthouse — audits for missing <main>, heading hierarchy, and semantic elements.
  • HTML validator — catches invalid nesting.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Search Engine Parsing of Semantic Structure
docs.text:
1.  Crawler fetches the HTML.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser builds the DOM.
    │
    ▼
3.  Semantic elements identified:
    │   ├── <main> → primary content
    │   ├── <article> → standalone content
    │   ├── <nav> → navigation (deprioritized)
    │   └── <aside> → complementary (deprioritized)
    │
    ▼
4.  Heading tree constructed:
    │   ├── H1 → page topic
    │   ├── H2 → subtopics
    │   └── H3 → sub-subtopics
    │
    ▼
5.  Content relevance scored by position in outline.
    │
    ▼
6.  Page indexed with semantic structure preserved.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: AI Answer Engine Extraction
docs.text:
1.  AI engine retrieves candidate pages.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parses semantic structure:
    │   ├── <main> content extracted
    │   ├── Heading tree analyzed
    │   └── Direct answers under H2s identified
    │
    ▼
3.  Generates answer with citations.
    │
    ▼
4.  Citation links to canonical URL.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Screen Reader Navigation
docs.text:
1.  Screen reader user presses H.
    │
    ▼
2.  Screen reader queries the accessibility tree for headings.
    │
    ▼
3.  Focus moves to the next heading.
    │
    ▼
4.  Screen reader announces:
    │   "Heading level 2, Inline SVG"
    │
    ▼
5.  User presses H again to continue.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree and Semantic Structure
docs.text:
The browser builds an accessibility tree from the DOM. Semantic elements produce specific roles:

HTML Element Accessibility Role <main> main landmark <article> article <section> region (if labelled) <nav> navigation landmark <aside> complementary landmark <header> (top-level) banner landmark <footer> (top-level) contentinfo landmark <h1>–<h6> heading (with level)

docs.title: The Document Outline Algorithm
docs.text: The HTML specification defines an outline algorithm that computes the document structure from headings and sectioning elements. It was never implemented by browsers. However, search engines and screen readers implement their own versions of this algorithm to build navigation trees.

docs.title: The Heading Tree
docs.text:
The heading tree is a hierarchical representation of the page's topics:

H1: How SVG Embedding Works
├── H2: Inline SVG
│   ├── H3: Advantages
│   └── H3: Use Cases
├── H2: Image SVG
│   ├── H3: Advantages
│   └── H3: Limitations

Search engines weight content by its depth in this tree. H2 content is weighted more heavily than H3 content.

docs.title: Semantic Elements and Content Extraction
docs.text:
Search engines and reader modes use semantic elements to extract content:

  • <main> and <article> identify primary content.
  • <nav>, <aside>, and <footer> are excluded from content extraction.
  • <section> provides thematic boundaries.
  • <figure> and <figcaption> associate images with captions.

docs.title: The Role of role and ARIA
docs.text: Semantic HTML provides roles natively. ARIA roles are for custom widgets where native HTML cannot express the required semantics. Native semantic HTML is always preferred — it is more reliable and requires no additional testing.

docs.title: Authoring Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Outline content structure:
    │   ├── What is the page's main topic? (H1)
    │   ├── What are the main sections? (H2)
    │   └── What are the subsections? (H3)
    │
    ▼
2.  Choose elements by meaning:
    │   ├── <main> for primary content
    │   ├── <article> for standalone content
    │   ├── <section> for thematic groupings
    │   └── <nav>, <aside>, <header>, <footer> for structural regions
    │
    ▼
3.  Write content with proper nesting.
    │
    ▼
4.  Validate the outline:
    │   ├── One H1?
    │   ├── No skipped levels?
    │   └── Every section has a heading?
    │
    ▼
5.  Style with CSS.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test with screen reader and outline tool.

docs.title: Audit Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Run an outline tool (browser extension).
    │
    ▼
2.  Verify one H1 per page.
    │
    ▼
3.  Verify no skipped heading levels.
    │
    ▼
4.  Verify every <section> has a heading.
    │
    ▼
5.  Verify <main> exists and contains primary content.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test with screen reader heading navigation.
    │
    ▼
7.  Fix, re-test, repeat.

docs.title: Example 1: Blog Post with Full Semantic Structure
docs.text:
<main>
    <article>
        <header>
            <h1>How SVG Embedding Works</h1>
            <p>
                Published <time datetime="2026-01-15">January 15, 2026</time>
                by <span rel="author">Jane Developer</span>
            </p>
        </header>

        <section>
            <h2>Inline SVG</h2>
            <p>Inline SVG is the most flexible method...</p>

            <h3>Advantages</h3>
            <ul>
                <li>Full CSS and JavaScript access</li>
                <li>Inherits <code>currentColor</code></li>
                <li>Interactive and accessible</li>
            </ul>
        </section>

        <section>
            <h2>Image SVG</h2>
            <p>Image SVG is the most cacheable method...</p>

            <h3>Advantages</h3>
            <ul>
                <li>Cacheable across pages</li>
                <li>Simple markup</li>
            </ul>

            <h3>Limitations</h3>
            <ul>
                <li>No CSS or JavaScript access</li>
                <li>No <code>currentColor</code> inheritance</li>
            </ul>
        </section>
    </article>
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • <main> wraps the primary content.
  • <article> identifies the blog post as standalone content.
  • <header> inside <article> provides article metadata.
  • <h1> is the article title.
  • <h2> elements are main sections; <h3> elements are subsections.
  • <time> provides a machine-readable date.

docs.title: Example 2: E-Commerce Product Page
docs.text:
<main>
    <article>
        <h1>Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41</h1>

        <section>
            <h2>Description</h2>
            <p>Responsive cushioning, breathable mesh...</p>
        </section>

        <section>
            <h2>Specifications</h2>
            <dl>
                <dt>Weight</dt>
                <dd>10.1 oz</dd>
                <dt>Drop</dt>
                <dd>10mm</dd>
            </dl>
        </section>

        <section>
            <h2>Reviews</h2>
            <h3>Customer Ratings</h3>
            <p>4.5 out of 5 stars...</p>
        </section>
    </article>
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • <article> identifies the product as a standalone content unit.
  • <h1> is the product name — the page's primary topic.
  • <section> groups related content: description, specifications, reviews.
  • <dl> provides semantic definition lists for specifications.

docs.title: Example 3: Documentation Page
docs.text:
<main>
    <article>
        <h1>CSS Grid Layout</h1>

        <nav aria-label="Table of contents">
            <h2>On this page</h2>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="#basics">Basics</a></li>
                <li><a href="#tracks">Tracks</a></li>
                <li><a href="#areas">Areas</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>

        <section id="basics">
            <h2>Basics</h2>
            <p>CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system...</p>
        </section>

        <section id="tracks">
            <h2>Tracks</h2>
            <p>Grid tracks are the rows and columns...</p>

            <h3>Defining Tracks</h3>
            <p>Use <code>grid-template-columns</code> and <code>grid-template-rows</code>...</p>
        </section>
    </article>
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • Table of contents uses <nav> with aria-label.
  • Each section has an <h2> that matches the table of contents link.
  • <h3> provides deeper structure within the tracks section.

docs.title: Example 4: Homepage with Landmarks
docs.text:
<body>
    <header>
        <a href="/" aria-label="Acme homepage">
            <img src="logo.svg" alt="Acme">
        </a>
        <nav aria-label="Main">
            <ul>
                <li><a href="/products">Products</a></li>
                <li><a href="/pricing">Pricing</a></li>
            </ul>
        </nav>
    </header>

    <main>
        <h1>Analytics for modern teams</h1>
        <p>Real-time insights without the complexity.</p>

        <section aria-labelledby="features-heading">
            <h2 id="features-heading">Features</h2>
            <ul>
                <li>Real-time dashboards</li>
                <li>Custom reports</li>
            </ul>
        </section>
    </main>

    <aside aria-label="Testimonials">
        <h2>What customers say</h2>
        <blockquote>
            <p>Acme transformed our analytics.</p>
            <cite>— Jane CTO</cite>
        </blockquote>
    </aside>

    <footer>
        <p>© 2026 Acme</p>
    </footer>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • <header> top-level → banner landmark.
  • <nav aria-label="Main"> → navigation landmark.
  • <main> → main landmark; contains primary content.
  • <aside aria-label="Testimonials"> → complementary landmark.
  • <footer> top-level → contentinfo landmark.
  • Each section has a heading for navigation.

docs.title: Example 5: The Standalone Content Unit Pattern
docs.text:
<section>
    <h2>How Does H2 Tag Optimisation Improve CTR?</h2>
    <p>
        H2 tags improve CTR by making content scannable, matching
        long-tail queries, and enabling featured snippet extraction.
    </p>
    <p>
        When a user scans a page, headings act as signposts...
    </p>
</section>

Code Breakdown:

  • H2 is framed as a question.
  • The first sentence is a direct, standalone answer (40–60 words).
  • The following paragraph expands with context.
  • This pattern feeds Google's extraction algorithms and satisfies skimming readers.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Semantic Approach Blog post <article> + <header> + <h1> + <section> + <footer> Product page <article> + <h1> + <section> for specs, reviews Documentation <article> + <nav> for TOC + <section> per topic Homepage <main> + <section> + <aside> + landmarks Landing page <main> + <section> per feature + <h2> per section News article <article> + <h1> + <time> + <section> FAQ page <section> per question + <h2> per question Recipe <article> + <h2> for ingredients, instructions

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use one <h1> per page. Why: the H1 is the page's primary topic; multiple H1s dilute topical focus.
  2. Never skip heading levels. Why: skipped levels break the document outline and confuse assistive technology.
  3. Use <main> for primary content. Why: search engines use <main> to identify the core content of the page.
  4. Use <article> for standalone content. Why: identifies content eligible for rich results and syndication.
  5. Use <section> only when it has a heading. Why: an unlabelled section is just a <div>.
  6. Frame H2s as questions or clear outcomes. Why: question-led headings match long-tail queries and improve snippet eligibility.
  7. Place a direct answer immediately after each H2. Why: feeds Google's extraction algorithms and satisfies skimming readers.
  8. Use H3s for detail, steps, and micro-answers. Why: H3s let scanners glean key points without reading whole paragraphs.
  9. Use semantic text-level elements. Why: <strong>, <em>, <time>, <cite>, <abbr> convey meaning that <b> and <i> do not.
  10. Use landmarks for structural regions. Why: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <footer> produce landmarks that aid navigation.
  11. Use <time> with datetime for dates. Why: provides machine-readable freshness signals.
  12. Set lang on <html>. Why: tells search engines and screen readers the language of the content.
  13. Keep DOM order aligned with visual order. Why: screen readers and search engines follow DOM order, not CSS order.
  14. Avoid div soup. Why: <div> conveys no meaning; semantic elements do.
  15. Do not use headings for styling. Why: heading levels are semantic, not visual.
  16. Validate your HTML. Why: invalid nesting breaks the outline and confuses parsers.
  17. Test with an outline tool. Why: visualizes the heading tree and reveals structural issues.
  18. Test with a screen reader. Why: heading and landmark navigation are the primary navigation methods for screen reader users.
  19. Combine semantic HTML with structured data. Why: semantic HTML provides document structure; structured data provides entity metadata.
  20. Audit semantic structure after template changes. Why: template changes affect every page.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple <h1> Elements
docs.text:
<h1>Page Title</h1>
<article>
    <h1>Article Title</h1>
</article>

Why it's wrong: Multiple top-level headings confuse the document outline and dilute topical focus.

✅ Correct:

<h1>Page Title</h1>
<article>
    <h2>Article Title</h2>
</article>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Skipping Heading Levels
docs.text:
<h1>Page Title</h1>
<h4>Section</h4>

Why it's wrong: Breaks the outline; screen reader users lose hierarchy.

✅ Correct:

<h1>Page Title</h1>
<h2>Section</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Div Soup
docs.text:
<div class="header">
    <div class="nav">...</div>
</div>
<div class="content">
    <div class="post">...</div>
</div>

Why it's wrong: No structure to infer; search engines must render and guess.

✅ Correct:

<header>
    <nav>...</nav>
</header>
<main>
    <article>...</article>
</main>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: <section> Without a Heading
docs.text:
<section>
    <p>Some content</p>
</section>

Why it's wrong: An unlabelled <section> is not a landmark; it conveys no structure.

✅ Correct:

<section>
    <h2>Section Title</h2>
    <p>Some content</p>
</section>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Heading Levels Chosen for Visual Size
docs.text:
<h4>Latest News</h4>  <!-- chosen because it "looks right" -->

Why it's wrong: Heading level is semantic, not visual.

✅ Correct:

<h2 class="small-heading">Latest News</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No <main> Element
docs.text:
<body>
    <header>...</header>
    <div class="content">...</div>
    <footer>...</footer>
</body>

Why it's wrong: Search engines cannot identify the primary content.

✅ Correct:

<body>
    <header>...</header>
    <main>...</main>
    <footer>...</footer>
</body>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Vague H2 Text
docs.text:
<h2>Benefits</h2>

Why it's wrong: Does not match a query or provide a standalone answer.

✅ Correct:

<h2>How Does H2 Tag Optimisation Improve CTR?</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Keyword Stuffing in Headings
docs.text:
<h2>SEO, SEO tools, SEO services, best SEO</h2>

Why it's wrong: Degrades readability and can reduce ranking potential.

✅ Correct:

<h2>How to Choose the Right SEO Tool for Your Team</h2>

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Semantic elements have no runtime cost — they are parsed the same as <div>.
  • Semantic HTML improves crawl efficiency — search engines require less rendering and inference.
  • Reader mode extraction works better with semantic content.
  • Raw HTML structured semantically allows Google to extract content without full rendering.
  • No JavaScript required for semantic structure.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use semantic HTML — no JavaScript overhead for structure.
  2. Keep the DOM shallow — avoid unnecessary <div> nesting.
  3. Place primary content in <main> — helps reader mode and content extraction.
  4. Use <time> with datetime for freshness signals.

docs.title: Semantic HTML Does Not Introduce Security Issues
docs.text: Semantic elements are parsed by the HTML parser — no new attack surface. They do not execute scripts.

docs.title: Content Injection and Outline Manipulation
docs.text: If content is generated from user input, escape it. Unescaped input can break the outline or inject malicious markup.

docs.title: AI Systems and Misleading Structure
docs.text: Search engines and AI systems trust semantic structure. Do not use semantic elements to mislead — marking navigation as <article> or ads as <main> may be treated as spam.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Outline tools — browser extensions that render the heading tree (e.g., HTML5 Outliner).
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect roles and landmarks.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — audits for missing <main> and heading hierarchy.
  • Firefox DevTools → Accessibility — visualizes landmarks and heading hierarchy.
  • W3C Validator — catches invalid nesting and structural issues.
  • Screen reader — NVDA H key, VoiceOver rotor → Headings.
  • document.querySelectorAll('h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6') — list all headings in DOM order.
  • document.querySelectorAll('main') — verify only one main exists.
  • Reader mode — test in Safari, Firefox, or Chrome.
  • View source — confirm semantic elements are in the static HTML, not injected by JavaScript after load.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every page — semantic structure is the foundation of SEO and accessibility.
  • Every article — <article>, <h1>, <section>.
  • Every navigation — <nav>.
  • Every primary content region — <main>.
  • Every heading — correct level and hierarchy.
  • Every date — <time>.
  • Every emphasis — <strong>, <em>.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use <article> for everything. Not every block is self-contained.
  • Do not add <section> just for styling. Use <div> if there is no heading and no thematic grouping.
  • Do not use headings for visual sizing.
  • Do not use multiple <h1> elements.
  • Do not skip heading levels.
  • Do not use <div> for navigation, headers, articles, or footers.

docs.text:
