docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Canonical tags are hints, not commands — Google treats them as one signal among approximately 40.
  • Self-referencing canonicals are best practice in 2026 — even on pages with no duplicates.
  • A self-referencing canonical on every indexable page is recommended by Google Search Central.
  • 301 redirects are the strongest canonical signal — they are directives, not hints.
  • Sitemap inclusion is the weakest canonical signal — but it stacks with other methods.
  • Canonical chains dilute signals — keep to one jump.
  • Canonical targets must return 200 OK — not 404s or redirects.
  • JavaScript-injected canonicals fail when AI systems fetch static HTML.
  • Google's July 10, 2026 update clarified that canonical fixes can take up to two weeks to register.
  • Pages split out faster if the content difference is clear and significant.
  • The Preferred Domain setting was retired in March 2019.
  • The URL Parameters tool was retired in April 2022.
  • Any SEO article recommending these tools is out of date.
  • Google uses approximately 40 different signals to determine canonical URLs.
  • Canonicalization is becoming even more important for AI search — AI systems ingest multiple versions of pages when generating answers.
  • Your canonical URLs are becoming your citation IDs for AI systems.
  • 847 variations of a single category page — all indexed, all competing, none ranking — is a real-world example of canonical chaos.
  • Infinite URL traps from faceted navigation can create millions of worthless URLs.
  • One e-commerce client had 50 variations of the same product page scattered across parameter combinations.
  • Pagination should self-canonicalize — do not canonicalize pages 2+ to page 1.
  • Localized versions should self-canonicalize — use hreflang, not canonicals, to indicate relationships.
  • noindex and canonical are not interchangeable — noindex blocks the page from Search entirely.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A canonical URL is the preferred, authoritative URL for a piece of content when it is accessible at multiple URLs.
  • Canonical tags are hints, not directives — Google treats them as one signal among approximately 40.
  • Use rel="canonical" in the <head> for HTML pages; use the HTTP Link header for non-HTML files.
  • Include a self-referencing canonical on every indexable page — even pages with no duplicates.
  • Align all canonical signals — canonical tags, sitemaps, internal links, and redirects should all point to the same URL.
  • Use 301 redirects when content has truly moved — use canonical tags when both URLs must remain accessible.
  • Handle URL parameters with a strategy — content-changing, tracking, sorting/filtering, and pagination each need different treatment.
  • Pick one canonical filter state for faceted navigation — prevent infinite URL traps.
  • Keep canonical chains to one jump — chains dilute signals.
  • Server-render canonical tags — JavaScript-injected canonicals fail when crawlers or AI systems fetch static HTML.
  • Canonical targets must return 200 OK — not 404s or redirects.
  • Do not use noindex or robots.txt for canonicalization — use rel="canonical".
  • Canonical fixes can take up to two weeks to register — Google may hold pages in a duplicate cluster.
  • Canonical URLs are the source-of-truth ID for each content entity — they consolidate ranking signals, reduce index bloat, and improve AI retrieval.
  • In 2026, canonicalization is a mission-critical element of technical SEO — not a checkbox.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Robots — in the SEO context — refers to the mechanisms by which a site owner communicates crawling and indexing instructions to search engine and AI crawlers. There are three primary mechanisms:

  • robots.txt — a plain text file at the root of the domain that controls crawling (which URLs bots may access).
  • robots meta tag — an HTML meta tag that controls indexing and content presentation on a per-page basis.
  • X-Robots-Tag — an HTTP response header that controls indexing and presentation, equivalent to the meta tag but available for non-HTML resources (PDFs, images, video).
<!-- robots meta tag: do not index this page -->
<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">

# robots.txt: block all crawlers from /admin/
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/

# X-Robots-Tag: do not index this PDF
X-Robots-Tag: noindex

These three mechanisms are complementary, not interchangeable. robots.txt controls whether a crawler is allowed to fetch a URL. The robots meta tag and X-Robots-Tag control whether a fetched URL is indexed and shown. A page blocked in robots.txt can still be indexed if it is linked externally — just without a snippet. A page with noindex can be crawled but will not be indexed.

Robots.txt, the Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP), is the implementation of the Robots Exclusion Standard, formally standardized as RFC 9309 in 2022. Since 2022, the landscape has shifted dramatically: robots.txt is no longer just about search engines — it is now the primary mechanism for governing AI crawler access. A 2026-ready robots.txt covers four jobs: hide sensitive paths, trim crawl waste, declare the sitemap, and govern AI crawler access (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Robots directives serve several essential purposes:

  • Crawl control — prevents crawlers from wasting resources on low-value URLs (admin panels, checkout flows, internal search results).
  • Indexing control — prevents specific pages from appearing in search results (staging environments, private pages, duplicate content).
  • Snippet control — controls whether a text snippet appears in search results (nosnippet, max-snippet).
  • Image preview control — controls whether large image previews appear (max-image-preview).
  • AI crawler governance — controls whether AI training crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended) and retrieval crawlers (OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot) can access content.
  • Crawl budget optimization — ensures crawlers spend their time on pages that matter.
  • Security posture — prevents crawling of sensitive paths, though it is not a security tool.
  • Compliance — robots.txt and noindex are the standard mechanisms for excluding pages from search, as required by privacy and data-protection practices.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
SEO Stack
│
├── Semantic Structure    ← document outline (headings, landmarks)
├── Heading Hierarchy     ← navigable tree within the structure
├── Metadata              ← title, description, canonical, robots
├── Structured Data       ← entity-level metadata (JSON-LD, Schema.org)
└── Content Quality       ← E-E-A-T, depth, originality

Robots directives sit inside the crawl and index control layer — they are the first gatekeepers in the SEO pipeline. A crawler must pass robots.txt to access a URL, and it must pass the robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag to be indexed. Every other SEO signal — content quality, backlinks, structured data — is meaningless if the page is blocked at this layer.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A search engine crawler is a finite resource. It cannot crawl every URL on the internet. It has a crawl budget — a finite number of URLs it will fetch from a given site within a given time period. If a site allows crawlers to access every URL — including admin panels, checkout flows, internal search results, session-ID-decorated URLs, and infinite faceted navigation — the crawler wastes its budget on low-value pages and never reaches the pages that matter.

Similarly, a site may have pages that should not appear in search results: staging environments, private user data, duplicate content, or pages that exist for technical reasons but have no search value. Without a mechanism to exclude these pages, they compete with the pages that should rank.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No crawl control Crawlers waste budget on low-value URLs No indexing control Staging and private pages indexed accidentally No snippet control Full text content scraped into SERPs No image preview control Large images shown without context No AI crawler governance AI companies train on content without permission noindex in robots.txt Unsupported directive; Google deprecated it in 2019

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP) — better known as robots.txt — has been around since 1994 and was officially adopted as an IETF standard in 2022 (RFC 9309).

The robots meta tag was introduced in the late 1990s as a page-level mechanism for indexing control. The X-Robots-Tag HTTP header followed as an equivalent for non-HTML resources.

In 2019, Google deprecated the unsupported noindex directive in robots.txt — a directive that had been used by some site owners but was never officially supported. Since September 1, 2019, the noindex directive in robots.txt no longer works; site owners must use the robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag instead.

The most significant evolution has been the rise of AI crawlers. Since 2022, Google introduced Google-Extended (control over AI training usage), OpenAI introduced GPTBot (training crawler) and OAI-SearchBot (retrieval crawler), Anthropic introduced ClaudeBot, and Perplexity introduced PerplexityBot. In 2026, the most common reason to edit a robots.txt file is to control AI crawler access.

docs.title: The robots.txt File
docs.text:
A robots.txt file is a plain text file placed at the root of the domain. It must be UTF-8 or ASCII encoded. The file uses simple directives:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /checkout/
Allow: /

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Directive Purpose User-agent Specifies the crawler the rules apply to. * means all crawlers Disallow Tells the crawler which paths it cannot access Allow Tells the crawler which paths it can access (overrides Disallow) Sitemap Declares the location of the XML sitemap Crawl-delay Non-standard — requests a delay between requests (not supported by Google)

docs.title: The robots Meta Tag
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">
</head>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Directive Purpose index / noindex Allow or forbid indexing follow / nofollow Allow or forbid following links noarchive Prevent cached copy nosnippet Prevent text snippet in SERPs max-snippet: [number] Limit snippet length (-1 for unlimited) max-image-preview: [size] Control image preview size (none, standard, large) max-video-preview: [number] Limit video preview length notranslate Prevent translation in search results noimageindex Prevent images on the page from being indexed unavailable_after: [date] Remove from index after a specified date

docs.title: The X-Robots-Tag HTTP Header
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Robots-Tag: noindex

For non-HTML resources (PDFs, images, video):

X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow

With a user-agent specification:

X-Robots-Tag: googlebot: noindex
X-Robots-Tag: otherbot: noindex, nofollow

docs.title: The AI Crawler Template (2026)
docs.text:
# Allow AI search crawlers (retrieval)
User-agent: GPTBot
Allow: /blog/
Disallow: /premium/

User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Allow: /

User-agent: ClaudeBot
Allow: /blog/
Disallow: /premium/

User-agent: PerplexityBot
Allow: /

# Block training-only crawlers
User-agent: CCBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: Bytespider
Disallow: /

# Block Google AI training (does not affect Search)
User-agent: Google-Extended
Disallow: /

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• GPTBot — OpenAI training crawler. Blocking removes content from future model training but does not affect current ChatGPT browsing.
  • OAI-SearchBot — OpenAI retrieval crawler for ChatGPT search citations. Blocking this costs you traffic.
  • ClaudeBot — Anthropic training crawler. Same tradeoff as GPTBot.
  • PerplexityBot — Perplexity retrieval crawler. Perplexity links aggressively, so this crawler has high traffic-per-crawl value.
  • CCBot — Common Crawl. Feeds training at many organizations; blocking removes content from academic and research use.
  • Bytespider — ByteDance. Widely reported as aggressive on crawl rate and inconsistent about honoring robots.txt.
  • Google-Extended — A permission token, not a crawler. It fetches nothing; it controls whether content Googlebot already crawled may be used for Gemini training and grounding. Disallowing it has no effect on Google Search rankings or inclusion in the Search index.

docs.title: The "Two Doors" Mental Model
docs.text:
Crawling and indexing are two separate doors:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              THE TWO DOORS                   │
│                                              │
│  Door 1: robots.txt      → Can the crawler  │
│    (Crawl control)         ACCESS the page? │
│                                              │
│  Door 2: robots meta tag → Can the crawler  │
│    (Index control)         INDEX the page?  │
│                                              │
│  A page blocked at Door 1 can still be       │
│  indexed if linked externally — just without │
│  a snippet.                                   │
│                                              │
│  A page with noindex at Door 2 can be        │
│  crawled but will not be indexed.            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The most common mistake in robots management is confusing Disallow with noindex. A Disallowed URL can still appear in search results if it is linked from external sites — just without a snippet. To fully exclude a page from search, use a noindex meta tag or an HTTP 401/403 response.

docs.title: The "Training vs. Retrieval" Mental Model (AI Crawlers)
docs.text:
The single most important distinction in 2026 AI crawler governance:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         TRAINING CRAWLERS                    │
│  Purpose: Collect content for training       │
│  future models.                              │
│                                              │
│  Blocking cost: LOW — no traffic today.     │
│  Examples: GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│         RETRIEVAL CRAWLERS                   │
│  Purpose: Build search indexes for AI        │
│  answers and citations.                      │
│                                              │
│  Blocking cost: HIGH — you disappear from   │
│  the answers that send traffic.              │
│  Examples: OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│         USER-INITIATED FETCHERS              │
│  Purpose: Fetch a page on behalf of a        │
│  specific user asking a specific question.   │
│                                              │
│  Blocking cost: HIGHEST — a human is        │
│  waiting on the response.                    │
│  Examples: ChatGPT-User, Claude-User         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Blocking a training crawler such as GPTBot costs you nothing in traffic today. Blocking a retrieval crawler such as OAI-SearchBot removes you from the answers that produce the referrals you can actually measure. Same file, opposite consequences.

docs.title: The "Robots.txt Is Not a Security Tool" Mental Model
docs.text: robots.txt is a visibility control mechanism, not a security tool. Most major crawlers respect Disallow rules, but some scrapers, spoofed bots, and user-triggered AI tools may ignore them. Do not use robots.txt to hide sensitive paths — that advertises them. Use authentication, authorization, and noindex instead.

docs.title: The "Cache Window" Mental Model
docs.text: Google caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours. When you change your robots.txt file, Google may not see the change immediately. To refresh the cache faster, use the Request a Recrawl function in the Search Console robots.txt report. John Mueller strongly advises against dynamically modifying robots.txt multiple times per day — it is not effective because Google caches the file for approximately 24 hours.

docs.title: Concept 1: robots.txt — Crawling Control
docs.text: robots.txt is a plain text file at the root of the domain that tells crawlers which URLs they may access. It implements the Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP), standardized as RFC 9309 in 2022. It controls crawling, not indexing.

docs.title: Concept 2: The robots Meta Tag — Indexing Control
docs.text: The robots meta tag is placed in the <head> of an HTML page and controls whether the page is indexed and presented in search results. Google confirmed in March 2026 that it also processes robots meta tags in the <body> section.

docs.title: Concept 3: X-Robots-Tag — Indexing Control for Non-HTML Files
docs.text: The X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header is the equivalent of the robots meta tag for non-HTML resources — PDFs, images, video. It supports all the same directives as the meta tag.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Disallow vs. Noindex Distinction
docs.text:
Directive Controls Where Effect Disallow Crawling robots.txt Prevents fetching; URL can still be indexed if linked externally noindex Indexing robots meta tag / X-Robots-Tag Prevents indexing; page can still be crawled

To fully exclude a page from search, use noindex — not Disallow.

docs.title: Concept 5: The noindex in robots.txt Deprecation
docs.text: Google officially dropped support for the noindex directive in robots.txt on September 1, 2019. If you have rules like Noindex: in your robots.txt file, they no longer work. Use the robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag instead.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Crawl-Delay Directive
docs.text: Crawl-delay is a non-standard extension to robots.txt that requests a delay between crawler requests. It is not part of RFC 9309. Google does not support it. Applebot typically ignores it. Some crawlers (including Anthropic) support it where appropriate. Best practice: avoid relying on crawl-delay; use Search Console's crawl rate settings or CDN rate limiting instead.

docs.title: Concept 7: Wildcards in robots.txt
docs.text:
Google supports two wildcards:

  • * — matches any sequence of characters.
  • $ — marks the end of a URL.
# Block any URL containing "?sort="
Disallow: /*?sort=

# Block all .xls files
Disallow: /*.xls$

# Block only /page, not /page1 or /page/subpage
Disallow: /page$

docs.title: Concept 8: The File Size Limit
docs.text: Crawlers must parse at least 500 KiB (512,000 bytes) of a robots.txt file per RFC 9309. Search engines may stop processing robots.txt midway through if the file is larger than 500 KiB, leading to incorrect crawling.

docs.title: Concept 9: The 24-Hour Cache
docs.text: Google caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours. Changes are not picked up immediately. Use the Request a Recrawl function in Search Console to refresh the cache faster.

docs.title: Concept 10: The Google-Extended Token
docs.text: Google-Extended is a permission token, not a crawler. It controls whether content that Googlebot already crawled may be used for Gemini training and grounding. Disallowing it has no effect on Google Search rankings or your inclusion in the Search index. This is the single most common misconception in AI crawler governance.

docs.title: Concept 11: Training Crawlers
docs.text:
Training crawlers collect content for training future AI models:

  • GPTBot (OpenAI) — training data.
  • ClaudeBot (Anthropic) — training data.
  • CCBot (Common Crawl) — nonprofit archive feeding training at many organizations.
  • Bytespider (ByteDance) — widely reported as aggressive and inconsistent about honoring robots.txt.

Blocking training crawlers is cheap — it costs nothing in traffic today.

docs.title: Concept 12: Retrieval Crawlers
docs.text:
Retrieval crawlers build search indexes for AI answers and citations:

  • OAI-SearchBot (OpenAI) — builds the index behind ChatGPT search results.
  • PerplexityBot (Perplexity) — indexes pages for Perplexity answers.

Blocking retrieval crawlers costs you traffic — you disappear from the answers that send referrals.

docs.title: Concept 13: User-Initiated Fetchers
docs.text:
User-initiated fetchers fire when a person asks an AI assistant something that requires visiting a page right now:

  • ChatGPT-User (OpenAI).
  • Claude-User (Anthropic).

These are the highest-intent requests — a human is waiting on the response. Blocking them means the model answers from stale memory or says it cannot read the page, in front of a person who was actively evaluating you.

docs.title: Concept 14: The "More Restrictive Directive Wins" Rule
docs.text: When multiple robots meta tags or directives conflict, the more restrictive directive wins. noindex always overrides index.

docs.title: Concept 15: The robots Meta Tag in the Body
docs.text: Google updated its documentation in March 2026 to clarify that it does not enforce placement of robots meta tags in the <head> — it will respect robots meta tags in the <body> section as well. This is not a specification change; it is a clarification of existing behavior. The recommended placement remains the <head>.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Sitemap Directive
docs.text: The Sitemap directive declares the location of an XML sitemap. It helps crawlers discover the sitemap faster. It should be placed at the end of the robots.txt file.

docs.title: Concept 17: The User-Agent Matching
docs.text: A crawler uses the group matching its token (case-insensitive) and falls back to the group addressed to the asterisk wildcard. If neither matches, nothing is restricted.

docs.title: Concept 18: The Allow Directive
docs.text:
The Allow directive (introduced in 2012) gives site owners granular control. It can override Disallow for specific paths:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /private/
Allow: /private/public-file.html

This keeps certain files accessible while protecting others.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Request a Recrawl Function
docs.text: Search Console's robots.txt report includes a Request a Recrawl function that refreshes Google's cached version of robots.txt faster than the 24-hour automatic cycle.

docs.title: Concept 20: The "Not a Security Tool" Caveat
docs.text: robots.txt is a visibility control mechanism, not a security tool. It does not protect data. Do not list sensitive paths — that advertises them. Use authentication, authorization, and noindex instead.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Crawler Respects robots.txt
docs.text:
1.  Crawler wants to fetch a URL.
    │
    ▼
2.  Crawler fetches /robots.txt from the domain root.
    │
    ▼
3.  Crawler checks its User-Agent against the groups in robots.txt.
    │
    ▼
4.  Crawler checks the Disallow/Allow rules for the URL.
    │
    ▼
5.  If allowed → crawler fetches the URL.
    If disallowed → crawler skips the URL.
    │
    ▼
6.  Crawler caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Crawler Respects noindex
docs.text:
1.  Crawler fetches a URL (allowed by robots.txt).
    │
    ▼
2.  Crawler parses the HTML <head>.
    │
    ▼
3.  Crawler finds <meta name="robots" content="noindex">.
    │
    ▼
4.  Crawler does NOT index the page.
    │
    ▼
5.  Page may still be crawled for link discovery.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Google Processes robots Meta Tag in the Body
docs.text:
1.  Googlebot fetches a page.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser processes the <head>.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser continues into the <body>.
    │
    ▼
4.  If a <meta name="robots"> tag is found in the <body>:
    │   └── Google still processes it.
    │
    ▼
5.  The directive is applied.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: AI Crawler Governance Decision
docs.text:
1.  Do you want AI training on your content?
    │   ├── Yes → Allow GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot.
    │   └── No  → Disallow GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot.
    │
    ▼
2.  Do you want to appear in AI search results?
    │   ├── Yes → Allow OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot.
    │   └── No  → Disallow OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot.
    │
    ▼
3.  Do you want AI assistants to fetch your page on demand?
    │   ├── Yes → Allow ChatGPT-User, Claude-User.
    │   └── No  → Disallow ChatGPT-User, Claude-User.
    │
    ▼
4.  Do you want Google AI training on your content?
    │   ├── Yes → Allow Google-Extended.
    │   └── No  → Disallow Google-Extended (does not affect Search).

docs.title: The Robots Exclusion Protocol (RFC 9309)
docs.text:
RFC 9309 defines the syntax and semantics of robots.txt. Key requirements:

  • The file must be at the root of the domain (/robots.txt).
  • The file must be UTF-8 encoded (ASCII subset).
  • The file size must not exceed 500 KiB.
  • The User-agent, Disallow, and Allow directives are the core directives.
  • Sitemap is an extension (not part of the core REP but widely supported).
  • Crawl-delay is a non-standard extension, not part of RFC 9309.

docs.title: The Meta Tag Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
HTML parsed
    │
    ▼
<meta name="robots"> found
    │
    ▼
Content parsed: "noindex, nofollow"
    │
    ▼
Directives extracted
    │
    ▼
Applied to the URL:
  ├── noindex → exclude from index
  └── nofollow → do not follow links

docs.title: The X-Robots-Tag Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
HTTP response received
    │
    ▼
X-Robots-Tag header found
    │
    ▼
Header value parsed
    │
    ▼
Directives applied to the URL

docs.title: The AI Crawler Taxonomy
docs.text:
AI CRAWLERS
├── Training Crawlers
│   ├── GPTBot (OpenAI)
│   ├── ClaudeBot (Anthropic)
│   ├── CCBot (Common Crawl)
│   └── Bytespider (ByteDance)
│
├── Retrieval/Search Crawlers
│   ├── OAI-SearchBot (OpenAI)
│   └── PerplexityBot (Perplexity)
│
├── User-Initiated Fetchers
│   ├── ChatGPT-User (OpenAI)
│   └── Claude-User (Anthropic)
│
└── Permission Tokens
    └── Google-Extended (controls Gemini training)

docs.title: The robots.txt Cache Architecture
docs.text: Google caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours. The cache is refreshed automatically during the crawling process. The Request a Recrawl function in Search Console can force a faster refresh.

docs.title: robots.txt Implementation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Identify URLs to block:
    │   ├── Admin panels
    │   ├── Checkout flows
    │   ├── Internal search results
    │   ├── Session-ID URLs
    │   └── Infinite faceted navigation
    │
    ▼
2.  Write robots.txt with:
    │   ├── User-agent groups
    │   ├── Disallow/Allow rules
    │   └── Sitemap directive
    │
    ▼
3.  Upload to the domain root.
    │
    ▼
4.  Validate with Search Console robots.txt report.
    │
    ▼
5.  Monitor for crawl errors.

docs.title: noindex Implementation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Identify pages to exclude from index:
    │   ├── Staging environments
    │   ├── Private pages
    │   └── Duplicate content
    │
    ▼
2.  Add <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> to the <head>.
    │
    ▼
3.  For non-HTML files, add X-Robots-Tag: noindex header.
    │
    ▼
4.  Validate with the URL Inspection tool.
    │
    ▼
5.  Monitor index coverage in Search Console.

docs.title: AI Crawler Governance Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Decide your AI content policy:
    │   ├── Allow training?
    │   ├── Allow retrieval?
    │   └── Allow user-initiated fetches?
    │
    ▼
2.  Configure robots.txt:
    │   ├── User-agent: GPTBot
    │   ├── User-agent: ClaudeBot
    │   ├── User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
    │   ├── User-agent: PerplexityBot
    │   └── User-agent: Google-Extended
    │
    ▼
3.  Monitor AI crawler traffic in server logs.
    │
    ▼
4.  Adjust policy based on traffic and citation data.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic robots.txt
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /checkout/
Disallow: /cart/
Disallow: /search?
Allow: /

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

Code Breakdown:

  • Blocks sensitive paths from all crawlers.
  • Allow: / ensures the rest of the site is crawlable (functionally equivalent to no Disallow at all, but explicit).
  • Declares the sitemap location.

docs.title: Example 2: noindex Meta Tag
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • noindex — do not index this page.
  • nofollow — do not follow links on this page.
  • Use on staging environments and private pages.

docs.title: Example 3: X-Robots-Tag for a PDF
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/pdf
X-Robots-Tag: noindex

Code Breakdown:

  • The PDF will not be indexed.
  • The X-Robots-Tag header is the only way to control indexing of non-HTML files.

docs.title: Example 4: Blocking a Specific Image from Google Images
docs.text:
User-agent: Googlebot-Image
Disallow: /images/dogs.jpg

Code Breakdown:

  • Blocks a single image from Google Images.
  • Google cannot index images and videos without crawling them.

docs.title: Example 5: Blocking All .xls Files
docs.text:
User-agent: Googlebot
Disallow: /*.xls$

Code Breakdown:

  • * matches any sequence of characters.
  • $ marks the end of the URL.
  • Blocks all URLs ending in .xls.

docs.title: Example 6: Blocking Query Parameter Variants
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /*?sort=
Disallow: /*?sessionid=
Disallow: /*?utm_

Code Breakdown:

  • Blocks URLs containing ?sort=, ?sessionid=, or ?utm_.
  • Prevents parameter-decorated duplicates from wasting crawl budget.

docs.title: Example 7: AI Crawler Governance
docs.text:
# Allow AI search crawlers
User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Allow: /

User-agent: PerplexityBot
Allow: /

User-agent: ChatGPT-User
Allow: /

User-agent: Claude-User
Allow: /

# Block training crawlers
User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: ClaudeBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: CCBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: Bytespider
Disallow: /

# Block Google AI training (does not affect Search)
User-agent: Google-Extended
Disallow: /

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

Code Breakdown:

  • Allows retrieval crawlers and user-initiated fetchers.
  • Blocks training crawlers.
  • Blocks Google AI training without affecting Search.

docs.title: Example 8: noindex with max-snippet and max-image-preview
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta name="robots" content="index, follow, max-snippet:-1, max-image-preview:large, max-video-preview:-1">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • index, follow — allow indexing and link following.
  • max-snippet:-1 — no limit on snippet length.
  • max-image-preview:large — allow large image previews.
  • max-video-preview:-1 — no limit on video preview length.

docs.title: Example 9: Blocking Entire Site During Development
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /

Code Breakdown:

  • Blocks all crawlers from the entire site.
  • Use on staging environments.
  • Remember: URLs may still be indexed if linked externally — use noindex for full exclusion.

docs.title: Example 10: Allowing a Single Crawler
docs.text:
User-agent: Googlebot-News
Allow: /

User-agent: *
Disallow: /

Code Breakdown:

  • Only Googlebot-News may crawl the site.
  • All other crawlers are blocked.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Directive Mechanism Block admin panel from crawlers Disallow: /admin/ robots.txt Exclude staging site from index noindex, nofollow Meta tag Exclude PDF from index noindex X-Robots-Tag Prevent snippet in SERPs nosnippet Meta tag Allow large image previews max-image-preview:large Meta tag Block AI training crawlers User-agent: GPTBot robots.txt Allow AI retrieval crawlers User-agent: OAI-SearchBot robots.txt Block query parameter variants Disallow: /*?sort= robots.txt Block file type Disallow: /*.pdf$ robots.txt Declare sitemap Sitemap: robots.txt

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use noindex — not Disallow — to exclude a page from search. Why: Disallow prevents crawling but the URL can still be indexed if linked externally; noindex prevents indexing.
  2. Place the robots meta tag in the <head>. Why: this is the recommended and most reliable placement, even though Google also processes it in the <body>.
  3. Use X-Robots-Tag for non-HTML files. Why: PDFs, images, and video cannot contain <meta> tags.
  4. Keep robots.txt simple and focused. Why: it's generally best to keep things simple.
  5. Do not use robots.txt to hide sensitive paths. Why: robots.txt is public; listing sensitive paths advertises them.
  6. Avoid using crawl-delay for major search engines. Why: it's not supported consistently across major crawlers and is not part of RFC 9309.
  7. Keep robots.txt under 500 KiB. Why: crawlers may stop processing larger files.
  8. Remember Google caches robots.txt for 24 hours. Why: changes are not immediate; use Request a Recrawl for priority changes.
  9. Allow CSS and JavaScript files to be crawled. Why: blocking them hurts rendering and prevents Google from understanding the page.
  10. Use Allow to override Disallow for specific paths. Why: gives granular control without blocking entire directories.
  11. Declare your sitemap in robots.txt. Why: helps crawlers discover it faster.
  12. Do not block OAI-SearchBot or PerplexityBot if you want AI search citations. Why: these are retrieval crawlers; blocking them costs you traffic.
  13. Blocking training crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot) is cheap. Why: it costs nothing in traffic today.
  14. Remember Google-Extended does not affect Search. Why: it controls Gemini training only; disallowing it has no effect on Google Search rankings or index inclusion.
  15. Do not rely on robots.txt as a security tool. Why: only cooperative bots follow it; scrapers and spoofed bots may ignore it.
  16. Validate robots.txt with Search Console. Why: catches syntax errors and unintended blocks.
  17. Monitor index coverage in Search Console. Why: ensures noindex pages are excluded and indexable pages are included.
  18. Use the URL Inspection tool to verify page-level directives. Why: shows Google-selected canonical, robots directives, and indexing status.
  19. Keep robots.txt directives case-consistent. Why: URLs in directives are case-sensitive.
  20. Document your AI crawler policy. Why: consistency across a team prevents accidental blocking of retrieval crawlers.
  21. Use the Sitemap directive at the end of robots.txt. Why: keeps the file organized and ensures crawlers find it.
  22. Test robots.txt changes in a staging environment. Why: one incorrect rule can block major sections of your site from search engines and AI bots.
  23. Audit robots.txt quarterly. Why: crawler landscape changes; AI crawlers emerge; business rules change.
  24. Do not block Googlebot-Image if you want images indexed. Why: Google cannot index images without crawling them.
  25. Use max-image-preview:large for rich thumbnails. Why: enables large image previews in SERPs.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Disallow to Exclude a Page from Search
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /private-page/

Why it's wrong: A Disallowed URL can still be indexed if linked externally — just without a snippet. The page is still in search results.

✅ Correct:

<meta name="robots" content="noindex">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using noindex in robots.txt
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Noindex: /page/

Why it's wrong: Google deprecated the noindex directive in robots.txt on September 1, 2019. It no longer works.

✅ Correct:

<meta name="robots" content="noindex">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Blocking CSS and JavaScript
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /css/
Disallow: /js/

Why it's wrong: Blocking CSS and JavaScript hurts rendering and prevents Google from understanding the page.

✅ Correct: Allow CSS and JavaScript to be crawled.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Blocking AI Retrieval Crawlers
docs.text:
User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Disallow: /

Why it's wrong: OAI-SearchBot powers ChatGPT search citations. Blocking it removes you from AI answers that send traffic.

✅ Correct: Allow OAI-SearchBot if you want AI search visibility.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Thinking Google-Extended Affects Search
docs.text:
User-agent: Google-Extended
Disallow: /

Why it's wrong: Google-Extended is a permission token for Gemini training. It has no effect on Google Search rankings or index inclusion.

✅ Correct: Understand the difference; use Google-Extended for AI training control only.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using crawl-delay for Google
docs.text:
User-agent: Googlebot
Crawl-delay: 10

Why it's wrong: Google does not support crawl-delay.

✅ Correct: Use Search Console's crawl rate settings or CDN rate limiting.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Robots.txt File Over 500 KiB
docs.text:
# 600 KiB robots.txt file

Why it's wrong: Crawlers may stop processing robots.txt midway through if the file is larger than 500 KiB.

✅ Correct: Keep robots.txt under 500 KiB.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Blocking the Entire Site on Production
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /

Why it's wrong: Blocks all crawlers from the entire site — a catastrophic SEO failure if deployed to production.

✅ Correct: Only use Disallow: / on staging environments.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Listing Sensitive Paths in robots.txt
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /secret-admin-panel/

Why it's wrong: robots.txt is public; listing sensitive paths advertises them.

✅ Correct: Use authentication and authorization to protect sensitive paths.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Conflicting Directives
docs.text:
<meta name="robots" content="noindex">
<meta name="robots" content="index">

Why it's wrong: The more restrictive directive wins — noindex overrides index. But conflicting directives cause confusion.

✅ Correct: Use one clear directive per page.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• robots.txt is fetched once per crawl session — negligible overhead.
  • robots.txt is cached for 24 hours — no repeated fetches.
  • The robots meta tag adds minimal bytes — a single line of HTML.
  • X-Robots-Tag adds a single HTTP header — negligible overhead.
  • Blocking CSS/JS hurts rendering performance — allow them to be crawled.
  • Blocking crawl-heavy paths improves crawl efficiency — saves crawl budget.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep robots.txt small and focused.
  2. Block low-value paths to save crawl budget.
  3. Allow CSS and JavaScript for proper rendering.
  4. Use X-Robots-Tag for non-HTML files — no page size increase.

docs.title: robots.txt Is Not a Security Tool
docs.text: robots.txt is a visibility control mechanism, not a security tool. Most major crawlers respect Disallow rules, but some scrapers, spoofed bots, and user-triggered AI tools may ignore them. Do not use robots.txt to hide sensitive paths — that advertises them. Use authentication, authorization, and noindex instead.

docs.title: noindex Is Not a Security Tool
docs.text: noindex prevents pages from appearing in search results but does not protect data. A page with noindex is still accessible to anyone who knows the URL.

docs.title: AI Crawler Governance Is a Policy Decision
docs.text: Blocking AI training crawlers is a policy decision. Blocking retrieval crawlers costs you traffic. Understand the tradeoff before configuring your robots.txt.

docs.title: Do Not Block Security-Related Crawlers
docs.text: Some crawlers are used for security scanning (e.g., Google Safe Browsing). Blocking them may prevent security checks.

docs.title: Robots.txt and Data Leakage
docs.text: If your robots.txt file lists sensitive paths, it leaks information about your site structure. Use it as a crawl control mechanism, not a security mechanism.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Google Search Console → robots.txt report — validates robots.txt syntax and shows crawled vs. blocked URLs.
  • Google Search Console → URL Inspection tool — shows Google-selected canonical, robots directives, and indexing status.
  • Google Search Console → Page Indexing report — shows "Excluded by 'noindex' tag" and "Blocked by robots.txt" statuses.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements — inspect the robots meta tag.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network — inspect the X-Robots-Tag response header.
  • curl -s https://example.com/robots.txt — fetch the robots.txt file.
  • curl -I https://example.com/page — check response headers for X-Robots-Tag.
  • view-source: — confirm the robots meta tag is in the static HTML.
  • Screaming Frog — crawls your site and reports robots.txt and meta robots issues.
  • Sitebulb — visualizes robots.txt and indexing directives across the site.
  • Test with the Rich Results Test — validates that the page is indexable.
  • Use the Request a Recrawl function — refreshes Google's cached robots.txt faster.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• robots.txt — for crawl control: block low-value paths, declare sitemaps, govern AI crawlers.
  • robots meta tag — for index control: exclude pages from search, control snippets and previews.
  • X-Robots-Tag — for non-HTML files: PDFs, images, video.
  • noindex — for pages that should not appear in search results.
  • Disallow — for paths that should not be crawled.
  • Sitemap — to declare the sitemap location.
  • AI crawler directives — to govern AI training and retrieval access.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use robots.txt to hide sensitive paths. Use authentication.
  • Do not use Disallow to exclude a page from search. Use noindex.
  • Do not use noindex in robots.txt. It is deprecated since 2019.
  • Do not block CSS or JavaScript. It hurts rendering.
  • Do not use crawl-delay for Google. It is not supported.
  • Do not block OAI-SearchBot or PerplexityBot if you want AI citations.
  • Do not use Disallow: / on production. Use it only on staging.
  • Do not rely on robots.txt for security. It is a visibility control mechanism.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP)
  • RFC 9309
  • robots.txt
  • robots meta tag
  • X-Robots-Tag
  • noindex
  • nofollow
  • nosnippet
  • max-snippet
  • max-image-preview
  • max-video-preview

  • notranslate
  • noimageindex
  • unavailable_after
  • Sitemap directive

  • GPTBot
  • ClaudeBot
  • OAI-SearchBot
  • PerplexityBot
  • CCBot
  • Bytespider
  • Google-Extended
  • ChatGPT-User
  • Claude-User
  • AI crawler governance
