docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Robots.txt has been around since 1994 but was only officially adopted as an IETF standard in 2022 (RFC 9309).
  • Google deprecated the noindex directive in robots.txt on September 1, 2019.
  • Google caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours.
  • The crawl-delay directive is not part of RFC 9309 and is not supported by Google.
  • Crawlers must parse at least 500 KiB of a robots.txt file.
  • Google confirmed in March 2026 that it processes robots meta tags in the <body>.
  • Google-Extended is a permission token, not a crawler — it controls Gemini training but has no effect on Google Search.
  • Blocking a training crawler costs nothing in traffic today — blocking a retrieval crawler costs you citations and referrals.
  • OAI-SearchBot builds the index behind ChatGPT search results — blocking it removes you from AI citations.
  • ChatGPT-User is a user-initiated fetcher — a human is waiting on the response.
  • PerplexityBot has unusually high traffic-per-crawl value because Perplexity links aggressively.
  • CCBot feeds training at a very large number of organizations — blocking it removes you from academic and research use.
  • Bytespider is widely reported as aggressive and inconsistent about honoring robots.txt.
  • A Disallowed URL can still be indexed if linked externally — just without a snippet.
  • The Allow directive was introduced in 2012 to give site owners granular control.
  • In 2026, the most common reason to edit robots.txt is to control AI crawler access.
  • A 2026-ready robots.txt covers four jobs: hide sensitive paths, trim crawl waste, declare the sitemap, and govern AI crawler access.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Robots directives control crawling and indexing through three mechanisms: robots.txt, the robots meta tag, and the X-Robots-Tag.
  • robots.txt controls crawling — which URLs bots may access. It is a plain text file at the domain root, standardized as RFC 9309.
  • The robots meta tag controls indexing — whether a page is indexed and shown in search results. Place it in the <head>; Google also processes it in the <body>.
  • X-Robots-Tag controls indexing for non-HTML files — PDFs, images, video.
  • The most common mistake is confusing Disallow with noindex. A Disallowed URL can still be indexed if linked externally; a noindex page can be crawled but will not be indexed.
  • Google deprecated noindex in robots.txt on September 1, 2019. Use the meta tag or X-Robots-Tag instead.
  • crawl-delay is not part of RFC 9309 and is not supported by Google.
  • Keep robots.txt under 500 KiB. Crawlers may stop processing larger files.
  • Google caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours. Use Request a Recrawl for priority changes.
  • In 2026, robots.txt is the primary mechanism for AI crawler governance.
  • Training crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot) collect content for model training — blocking them is cheap.
  • Retrieval crawlers (OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot) build search indexes for AI answers — blocking them costs you traffic.
  • User-initiated fetchers (ChatGPT-User, Claude-User) fire when a human is waiting on a response — blocking them is the highest cost.
  • Google-Extended is a permission token, not a crawler — disallowing it has no effect on Google Search.
  • robots.txt is not a security tool. Use authentication and authorization to protect sensitive data.
  • Validate robots.txt with Search Console, monitor index coverage, and audit quarterly.
  • A 2026-ready robots.txt covers four jobs: hide sensitive paths, trim crawl waste, declare the sitemap, and govern AI crawler access.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A sitemap is a structured file that lists a website's URLs, helping search engines and AI crawlers discover and index its content. There are three primary forms:

  • XML sitemap — a machine-readable file, typically sitemap.xml, listing URLs with optional metadata (<lastmod>, <changefreq>, <priority>). Designed for search engines.
  • HTML sitemap — a human-readable page listing links to the site's main pages. Designed for users.
  • Specialized XML sitemaps — extensions to the standard XML sitemap for images, video, news, and hreflang annotations.
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/blog/xml-sitemap-guide/</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-06-10</lastmod>
    </url>
</urlset>

A sitemap is a discovery aid, not a ranking factor. It does not boost rankings, it does not guarantee indexing, and it does not override your site's actual link structure. Google's own documentation is blunt: "Using a sitemap doesn't guarantee that all the items in your sitemap will be crawled and indexed."

But for large sites, new sites, sites with weak internal linking, and fast-changing sites, it is essential infrastructure. It is the difference between Google finding your content in hours versus weeks — or not at all.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Sitemaps serve several essential purposes:

  • Discovery acceleration — tells crawlers exactly which URLs exist, without relying on link-following.
  • Crawl budget optimization — focuses crawler attention on canonical, indexable URLs by excluding low-value pages.
  • Indexing control — ensures only pages you want indexed are included.
  • Change notification — <lastmod> tells Google what changed since the last crawl, triggering recrawls.
  • Search Console reporting — enables filtering indexing status by sitemap, revealing which segments have problems.
  • Specialized content coverage — image, video, and news sitemaps ensure rich media content is discoverable.
  • AI crawler guidance — AI systems use sitemaps to discover content for retrieval and citation.
  • Bing and IndexNow integration — sitemaps feed Bing's index, which powers ChatGPT Search and Microsoft Copilot.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
SEO Stack
│
├── Semantic Structure    ← document outline (headings, landmarks)
├── Heading Hierarchy     ← navigable tree within the structure
├── Metadata              ← title, description, canonical, robots
├── Structured Data       ← entity-level metadata (JSON-LD, Schema.org)
├── Sitemap               ← URL inventory and discovery layer
└── Content Quality       ← E-E-A-T, depth, originality

Sitemaps sit in the crawl and discovery layer, alongside robots.txt. robots.txt controls what crawlers may access; the sitemap tells crawlers what exists. Together they form the crawl governance mechanism for the entire site.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Search engine crawlers discover content by following links. If Page A links to Page B, the crawler will eventually find Page B. But in real life, websites are messy:

  • Some pages don't have many internal links.
  • Some pages are buried deep in navigation.
  • Some pages are brand new.
  • Some pages are generated dynamically.
  • And sometimes the site structure is fine, but Google just doesn't bother crawling everything quickly.

Without a sitemap, crawlers waste time "stumbling across" pages. With a sitemap, you hand the crawler a direct list of URLs you want indexed. This doesn't guarantee rankings, but it absolutely helps with indexing and discovery.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No URL inventory Crawlers relied entirely on link discovery No change notification Google had no way to know which pages were updated No crawl prioritization Crawl budget wasted on low-value URLs No special media discovery Images, videos, and news buried in pages No Search Console reporting No way to filter indexing status by content type No sitemap index Large sites exceeded file size limits

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The sitemaps.org protocol was established in 2005 by Google, Yahoo, and Microsoft as a unified standard for URL discovery. The protocol defined the XML format, the 50,000 URL / 50 MB limits, and the sitemap index mechanism for larger sites.

Since then, the protocol has expanded with extensions for images (2007), video (2007), news (2008), and hreflang annotations. Each extension adds specialized metadata that helps crawlers understand rich media content.

The most significant recent evolution is the retirement of the sitemap ping endpoint. Google retired the old www.google.com/ping?sitemap= endpoint in June 2023. The endpoint was deprecated due to its ineffectiveness and association with spam. Automatic sitemap re-pings from plugins no longer do anything on Google's side. Search Console submission is now the only supported mechanism for Google.

For Bing, the game changed with IndexNow (2021), a free protocol that lets sites instantly notify Bing (and Yandex, Seznam, and Naver) whenever a URL is added, updated, or deleted. IndexNow replaces the older ping-endpoint pattern and is dramatically faster than waiting for Bing to re-crawl your sitemap.

Sitemaps exist because search engines need a map of your site. Without one, they guess. With one, they know.

docs.title: The Minimal Valid Sitemap
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/blog/xml-sitemap-guide/</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-06-10</lastmod>
    </url>
</urlset>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
Element Purpose Required? <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> XML declaration ✅ Always required <urlset> Wraps all URL entries ✅ Always required xmlns Sitemaps.org namespace ✅ Always required <url> A single URL entry ✅ Always required <loc> The URL itself ✅ Always required <lastmod> Last modification date (ISO 8601) ⚠️ Recommended

Notice what's missing: no <priority>, no <changefreq>. Google ignores both entirely — this is confirmed, not speculation. Gary Illyes said it plainly, and Google's own sitemap documentation now states: "Google ignores priority and changefreq values."

docs.title: The Protocol Limits
docs.text:
Limit Value Max URLs per sitemap file 50,000 Max file size (uncompressed) 50 MB Max sitemaps in a sitemap index 50,000 Encoding UTF-8 Compression Gzip allowed (.xml.gz)

Past 50,000 URLs (or 50 MB), you split into multiple sitemap files and point a sitemap index at them.

docs.title: The Sitemap Index
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<sitemapindex xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
    <sitemap>
        <loc>https://example.com/sitemap-posts.xml</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-06-12</lastmod>
    </sitemap>
    <sitemap>
        <loc>https://example.com/sitemap-pages.xml</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-05-30</lastmod>
    </sitemap>
</sitemapindex>

Code Breakdown:

  • <sitemapindex> — wraps all child sitemap entries.
  • <sitemap> — a single child sitemap entry.
  • <loc> — the URL of the child sitemap.
  • <lastmod> — the last modification date of the child sitemap.

An index can list up to 50,000 sitemaps, so the practical ceiling is 2.5 billion URLs. You'll run out of crawl budget long before you run out of protocol.

docs.title: The Image Sitemap Extension
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"
        xmlns:image="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-image/1.1">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/sample1.html</loc>
        <image:image>
            <image:loc>https://example.com/image.jpg</image:loc>
        </image:image>
        <image:image>
            <image:loc>https://example.com/photo.jpg</image:loc>
        </image:image>
    </url>
</urlset>

Code Breakdown:

  • xmlns:image — declares the image sitemap namespace.
  • <image:image> — encloses all information about a single image.
  • <image:loc> — the URL of the image.
  • Each <url> tag can contain up to 1,000 <image:image> tags.

Note: <image:caption>, <image:geo_location>, <image:title>, and <image:license> were deprecated and removed from Google's documentation. Do not use them.

docs.title: The Video Sitemap Extension
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"
        xmlns:video="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-video/1.1">
    <url>
        <loc>https://www.example.com/videos/some_video_landing_page.html</loc>
        <video:video>
            <video:thumbnail_loc>https://www.example.com/thumbs/123.jpg</video:thumbnail_loc>
            <video:title>Grilling steaks for summer</video:title>
            <video:description>Alkis shows you how to get perfectly done steaks every time</video:description>
            <video:content_loc>http://streamserver.example.com/video123.mp4</video:content_loc>
            <video:player_loc>https://www.example.com/videoplayer.php?video=123</video:player_loc>
            <video:duration>600</video:duration>
        </video:video>
    </url>
</urlset>

Code Breakdown:

  • xmlns:video — declares the video sitemap namespace.
  • <video:video> — encloses all information about a single video.
  • <video:thumbnail_loc> — the thumbnail image URL.
  • <video:title> — the video title.
  • <video:description> — the video description.
  • <video:content_loc> — the video file URL (must be accessible to Googlebot, no streaming protocols).
  • <video:player_loc> — the embed player URL.
  • <video:duration> — duration in seconds.

Critical rule: Do not list videos that are unrelated to the content of the host page. All files referenced must be accessible to Googlebot — no robots.txt blocks, no login requirements, no firewalls.

docs.title: The News Sitemap Extension
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"
        xmlns:news="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-news/0.9">
    <url>
        <loc>http://www.example.org/business/article55.html</loc>
        <news:news>
            <news:publication>
                <news:name>The Example Times</news:name>
                <news:language>en</news:language>
            </news:publication>
            <news:publication_date>2008-12-23</news:publication_date>
            <news:title>Companies A, B in Merger Talks</news:title>
        </news:news>
    </url>
</urlset>

Code Breakdown:

  • xmlns:news — declares the news sitemap namespace.
  • <news:news> — encloses news-specific metadata.
  • <news:publication> — the publication entity.
  • <news:name> — the publication name.
  • <news:language> — the publication language (ISO 639-1 code).
  • <news:publication_date> — publication date.
  • <news:title> — the article title.

Critical rule: News sitemaps should include only articles published within the last two days. After a URL is more than two days old, remove it from the news sitemap or remove the <news:news> metadata. A single sitemap can contain up to 1,000 <news:news> tags.

docs.title: The "Hand-Delivered Map" Mental Model
docs.text:
A sitemap is a map you hand to a crawler. Without it, the crawler has to explore your site like a tourist with no map — following links, getting lost in dead ends, and missing the interesting places. With it, the crawler knows exactly where to go.

Without sitemap:
  Crawler → link → link → link → ... (eventually finds content)

With sitemap:
  Crawler → sitemap.xml → [list of URLs] → crawl each URL directly

The sitemap doesn't guarantee the crawler will visit every URL. But it removes the guesswork.

docs.title: The "Discovery Aid, Not Ranking Factor" Mental Model
docs.text:
A sitemap is a discovery aid, not a ranking factor. This distinction is critical:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WHAT A SITEMAP DOES                         │
│  ├── Helps crawlers discover URLs            │
│  ├── Signals what changed (via lastmod)      │
│  ├── Focuses crawl budget on canonical URLs  │
│  └── Enables Search Console segmentation     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WHAT A SITEMAP DOES NOT DO                  │
│  ├── Boost rankings                          │
│  ├── Guarantee indexing                      │
│  ├── Override link structure                 │
│  └── Compensate for poor content quality    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The sitemap tells Google "these URLs exist." It does not tell Google "these URLs are good." Ranking is a separate system driven by content quality, backlinks, Core Web Vitals, and E-E-A-T.

docs.title: The "Segmentation Is Non-Optional" Mental Model
docs.text:
In 2026, the era of one massive sitemap.xml is over. Segmentation is non-optional:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  OLD APPROACH (2015)                         │
│  sitemap.xml                                 │
│  └── 50,000 URLs, all types mixed together   │
│                                              │
│  → Search Console shows one giant error count│
│  → No isolation of problems by content type  │
│  → Slow processing for large files           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  NEW APPROACH (2026)                         │
│  sitemap-index.xml                           │
│  ├── sitemap-products.xml                    │
│  ├── sitemap-blog.xml                        │
│  ├── sitemap-categories.xml                  │
│  ├── sitemap-images.xml                      │
│  └── sitemap-videos.xml                      │
│                                              │
│  → Isolate coverage issues per segment       │
│  → Faster processing per file                │
│  → Real e-commerce client: index rate        │
│     jumped from 87% to 98% after segmenting  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

One e-commerce site saw product index rates jump from 87% to 98% after segmenting into five sitemaps. Average time to index dropped from 6 days to 1.4 days. Organic traffic increased by 156%.

docs.title: The "lastmod Is the Only Field That Matters" Mental Model
docs.text:
Of the three optional metadata fields — <lastmod>, <priority>, and <changefreq> — only <lastmod> carries weight. Google and Bing officially ignore the other two:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FIELD          │ GOOGLE IN 2026            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  <loc>          │ ✅ Required. The URL.     │
│  <lastmod>      │ ✅ Used as recrawl signal │
│  <priority>     │ ❌ Ignored                │
│  <changefreq>   │ ❌ Ignored                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

But <lastmod> only works if it is honest. If every URL claims it changed today, every day, Google learns your dates are noise and stops reading them for your whole site. One dishonest field poisons the rest.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Sitemaps.org Protocol
docs.text: The sitemaps.org protocol defines the XML format, the 50,000 URL / 50 MB limits, and the sitemap index mechanism. It is maintained by Google, Microsoft, and Yahoo.

docs.title: Concept 2: The 50,000 URL / 50 MB Limits
docs.text: A single sitemap can list up to 50,000 URLs and must stay under 50 MB uncompressed. (The older 10 MB cap was raised to 50 MB in 2016; articles referencing the 10 MB limit are out of date.)

docs.title: Concept 3: The Sitemap Index
docs.text: Past 50,000 URLs, you split into multiple sitemap files and point a sitemap index at them. An index can list up to 50,000 sitemaps — a practical ceiling of 2.5 billion URLs.

docs.title: Concept 4: Only Canonical, Indexable URLs
docs.text: Every URL in your sitemap should be canonical, indexable, and return a 200 status code. Exclude redirects, 404s, noindex pages, and parameter-decorated duplicates. Including a noindex page in your sitemap sends Google mixed messages — "please index this" and "don't index this" simultaneously.

docs.title: Concept 5: <lastmod> — The Only Field That Works
docs.text: Google uses <lastmod> for recrawl scheduling. When you declare "this URL has changed since your last crawl," Google concentrates a finite crawl budget on pages that actually moved. But that only holds if your declaration is trustworthy.

docs.title: Concept 6: <priority> and <changefreq> — Ignored
docs.text: Google and Bing officially state they ignore these two tags. Yandex is among the few engines that documents using priority as a crawl-prioritization hint. Including them doesn't hurt, but it bloats the file and signals that whoever built the generator hasn't read the docs since 2010.

docs.title: Concept 7: The Sitemap Ping Retirement
docs.text: Google retired the old sitemap ping endpoint in June 2023. Automatic sitemap re-pings from plugins no longer do anything on Google's side. Submit sitemaps in Google Search Console under Indexing → Sitemaps instead.

docs.title: Concept 8: IndexNow for Bing and Beyond
docs.text: Microsoft launched IndexNow in October 2021 as a free protocol that lets sites instantly notify Bing (and Yandex, Seznam.cz, and Naver) whenever a URL is added, updated, or deleted. IndexNow replaces the older ping-endpoint pattern and is dramatically faster than waiting for Bing to re-crawl your sitemap. Most major CMSes support it through plugins (Yoast, Rank Math, AIOSEO all include IndexNow integration).

docs.title: Concept 9: Sitemap Segmentation
docs.text: Instead of one massive sitemap.xml, split by content type, business value, and update frequency. One e-commerce client saw product page index rates jump from 87% to 98% after segmenting into five sitemaps. Segmentation also lets you isolate coverage issues per segment in Search Console.

docs.title: Concept 10: The Sub-Sitemap Size Sweet Spot
docs.text: Keep each sub-sitemap under 10,000–20,000 URLs for optimal processing speed — well below the protocol limit of 50,000. Smaller files process faster and reveal problems more clearly.

docs.title: Concept 11: Dynamic vs. Static Sitemaps
docs.text: A static sitemap doesn't change unless manually updated. A dynamic sitemap updates automatically when you publish, delete, or change content. For most modern websites — blogs, ecommerce stores, SaaS sites — a dynamic sitemap is the better choice. One missed update and search engines might not discover your newest content quickly.

docs.title: Concept 12: The Image Sitemap Extension
docs.text: Image sitemaps tell Google about images it might not otherwise find — especially images loaded via JavaScript. Each <url> tag can contain up to 1,000 <image:image> tags. The <image:caption>, <image:geo_location>, <image:title>, and <image:license> tags were deprecated and removed from Google's documentation.

docs.title: Concept 13: The Video Sitemap Extension
docs.text: Video sitemaps provide metadata (thumbnail, title, description, duration, player location) that helps Google understand and index video content. All files referenced must be accessible to Googlebot — no robots.txt blocks, no login requirements, no streaming protocols. Do not list videos unrelated to the host page.

docs.title: Concept 14: The News Sitemap Extension
docs.text: News sitemaps are for Google News publishers. They include only articles published within the last two days and must include <news:publication>, <news:publication_date>, and <news:title>. A single sitemap can contain up to 1,000 <news:news> tags.

docs.title: Concept 15: The lastmod Trust Problem
docs.text: The most common sitemap bug: every build updates every page's lastmod to "today." Passing new Date() straight into sitemap generation is the classic version. Nothing changed, yet every page declares itself updated. Let that run long enough and Google stops trusting your lastmod declarations altogether. Build lastmod around actual change detection — not the publish date, not the build date.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Sitemap URL Location
docs.text: Host the sitemap at https://example.com/sitemap.xml with a 200 response, UTF-8 encoding, and application/xml content type. Reference it in robots.txt and submit it to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

docs.title: Concept 17: The robots.txt Sitemap Directive
docs.text: Declare your sitemap in robots.txt with the Sitemap: directive. This helps crawlers discover it faster without relying on Search Console submission alone.

docs.title: Concept 18: The Search Console Reporting Benefit
docs.text: Once you submit a sitemap, the Search Console Pages report can filter indexing status by sitemap. That's how you find out 40% of your blog posts are sitting in "Crawled — currently not indexed" instead of guessing. This is one of the most underrated benefits of sitemap segmentation.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Sitemap Index Consolidation
docs.text: Don't scatter dozens of standalone XML files across the site. Point one master sitemap index file at every sub-sitemap you need, reference it in robots.txt, and submit the index URL to Bing Webmaster Tools. RSS feeds should list only your most recent content, not your full archive.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Sitemap Is a Hint
docs.text: Google's own documentation: "Using a sitemap doesn't guarantee that all the items in your sitemap will be crawled and indexed." A sitemap is a hint, and Google treats every part of it as a hint. It helps discovery. It does not boost rankings.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How a Crawler Uses a Sitemap
docs.text:
1.  Crawler discovers the sitemap:
    │   ├── Via robots.txt Sitemap directive
    │   ├── Via Search Console submission
    │   └── Via Bing Webmaster Tools submission
    │
    ▼
2.  Crawler fetches the sitemap XML.
    │
    ▼
3.  Crawler parses the URL list.
    │
    ▼
4.  Crawler checks each URL against robots.txt.
    │
    ▼
5.  Crawler fetches each allowed URL.
    │
    ▼
6.  Crawler uses <lastmod> to prioritize recrawls.
    │
    ▼
7.  Crawler ignores <priority> and <changefreq>.
    │
    ▼
8.  Crawler indexes pages that pass indexing rules.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Sitemap Segmentation Strategy
docs.text:
1.  Identify content types:
    │   ├── Products
    │   ├── Blog posts
    │   ├── Categories
    │   ├── Images
    │   └── Videos
    │
    ▼
2.  Create a sub-sitemap for each type.
    │
    ▼
3.  Keep each sub-sitemap under 10,000–20,000 URLs.
    │
    ▼
4.  Create a sitemap index pointing to all sub-sitemaps.
    │
    ▼
5.  Reference the index in robots.txt.
    │
    ▼
6.  Submit the index to Search Console.
    │
    ▼
7.  Monitor indexing status per segment.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: IndexNow Submission
docs.text:
1.  Generate an IndexNow API key.
    │
    ▼
2.  Host the key file at the site root.
    │
    ▼
3.  On content publish/update/delete:
    │   └── Send HTTP request to https://api.indexnow.org/indexnow
    │       with the URL(s) to notify.
    │
    ▼
4.  Bing, Yandex, Seznam, and Naver are notified.
    │
    ▼
5.  Crawlers prioritize the new/updated URLs.

docs.title: The Sitemaps XML Schema
docs.text:
The sitemaps.org schema defines the structure of a sitemap:

urlset
├── url (1..50,000)
│   ├── loc (1)
│   ├── lastmod (0..1)
│   ├── changefreq (0..1)  ← ignored by Google
│   ├── priority (0..1)    ← ignored by Google
│   └── [extension elements]

Each <url> element represents a single URL. The <loc> element is required; all others are optional. Extension elements (image, video, news) are namespaced and nested within <url>.

docs.title: The Sitemap Index Schema
docs.text:
sitemapindex
├── sitemap (1..50,000)
│   ├── loc (1)
│   └── lastmod (0..1)

Each <sitemap> element represents a single child sitemap. The <loc> element is required; <lastmod> is optional.

docs.title: The Namespace System
docs.text:
Each sitemap extension uses a separate XML namespace:

Extension Namespace Core sitemap http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9 Image http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-image/1.1 Video http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-video/1.1 News http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-news/0.9 hreflang http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml

Namespaces allow extensions to coexist with the core schema without conflict.

docs.title: The lastmod Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
Sitemap fetched
    │
    ▼
<lastmod> extracted for each URL
    │
    ▼
Date validated (ISO 8601)
    │
    ▼
Compared against last crawl date
    │
    ▼
If lastmod > last crawl:
    └── URL queued for recrawl
    │
    ▼
If lastmod is consistently inaccurate:
    └── Google stops trusting the signal

docs.title: The IndexNow Architecture
docs.text:
Content published/updated/deleted
    │
    ▼
CMS/plugin triggers IndexNow API call
    │
    ▼
POST https://api.indexnow.org/indexnow
    {
      "host": "example.com",
      "key": "your-key",
      "urlList": ["https://example.com/new-page"]
    }
    │
    ▼
IndexNow distributes the notification to:
    ├── Bing
    ├── Yandex
    ├── Seznam.cz
    └── Naver
    │
    ▼
Crawlers prioritize the new/updated URLs

docs.title: Sitemap Implementation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Generate the sitemap:
    │   ├── CMS plugin (Yoast, Rank Math, AIOSEO)
    │   ├── Static site generator plugin
    │   └── Custom script
    │
    ▼
2.  Validate the sitemap:
    │   ├── XML well-formedness
    │   ├── Namespace correctness
    │   └── URL format (absolute, 200 status)
    │
    ▼
3.  Deploy the sitemap to the domain root.
    │
    ▼
4.  Reference in robots.txt.
    │
    ▼
5.  Submit to Google Search Console.
    │
    ▼
6.  Submit to Bing Webmaster Tools.
    │
    ▼
7.  Configure IndexNow for real-time updates.
    │
    ▼
8.  Monitor Search Console for indexing status.

docs.title: Sitemap Maintenance Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  After every content publish/update/delete:
    │   └── Sitemap regenerates automatically (dynamic sitemaps)
    │
    ▼
2.  Weekly:
    │   ├── Check Search Console sitemap status
    │   └── Check for "Submitted URL not found" errors
    │
    ▼
3.  Monthly:
    │   ├── Audit for stale URLs
    │   ├── Audit for noindex URLs
    │   └── Audit for redirects in sitemap
    │
    ▼
4.  Quarterly:
    │   ├── Review segmentation strategy
    │   └── Check for new content types to add

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal Valid Sitemap
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/blog/xml-sitemap-guide/</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-06-10</lastmod>
    </url>
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/blog/svg-embedding/</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-01-20</lastmod>
    </url>
</urlset>

Code Breakdown:

  • Only <loc> and <lastmod> — the two fields Google actually reads.
  • No <priority>, no <changefreq>.
  • Absolute URLs with https://.
  • lastmod in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD).

docs.title: Example 2: Sitemap Index with Segmentation
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<sitemapindex xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
    <sitemap>
        <loc>https://example.com/sitemap-products.xml</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-06-12</lastmod>
    </sitemap>
    <sitemap>
        <loc>https://example.com/sitemap-blog.xml</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-06-10</lastmod>
    </sitemap>
    <sitemap>
        <loc>https://example.com/sitemap-categories.xml</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-05-30</lastmod>
    </sitemap>
    <sitemap>
        <loc>https://example.com/sitemap-images.xml</loc>
        <lastmod>2026-06-01</lastmod>
    </sitemap>
</sitemapindex>

Code Breakdown:

  • One index file pointing to four segmented sitemaps.
  • Each segment represents a content type.
  • Submit the index to Search Console; Google follows the child sitemaps.
  • Isolate coverage issues per segment in Search Console.

docs.title: Example 3: Image Sitemap
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"
        xmlns:image="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-image/1.1">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/blog/svg-embedding/</loc>
        <image:image>
            <image:loc>https://example.com/images/svg-methods.png</image:loc>
        </image:image>
        <image:image>
            <image:loc>https://example.com/images/svg-comparison.png</image:loc>
        </image:image>
    </url>
</urlset>

Code Breakdown:

  • xmlns:image — declares the image sitemap namespace.
  • Two <image:image> entries nested in one <url>.
  • Each <image:loc> points to an image URL.
  • Image URLs may be on a different domain (e.g., CDN) if verified in Search Console.

docs.title: Example 4: Video Sitemap
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"
        xmlns:video="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-video/1.1">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/videos/svg-tutorial/</loc>
        <video:video>
            <video:thumbnail_loc>https://example.com/thumbs/svg-tutorial.jpg</video:thumbnail_loc>
            <video:title>SVG Embedding Tutorial</video:title>
            <video:description>A complete guide to embedding SVG in HTML.</video:description>
            <video:content_loc>https://example.com/videos/svg-tutorial.mp4</video:content_loc>
            <video:duration>600</video:duration>
        </video:video>
    </url>
</urlset>

Code Breakdown:

  • xmlns:video — declares the video sitemap namespace.
  • <video:thumbnail_loc> — the thumbnail image.
  • <video:title> — the video title.
  • <video:description> — the video description.
  • <video:content_loc> — the video file URL (must be accessible to Googlebot).
  • <video:duration> — duration in seconds.

docs.title: Example 5: News Sitemap
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"
        xmlns:news="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-news/0.9">
    <url>
        <loc>https://example.com/news/svg-embedding-update/</loc>
        <news:news>
            <news:publication>
                <news:name>Dev Notes</news:name>
                <news:language>en</news:language>
            </news:publication>
            <news:publication_date>2026-06-10</news:publication_date>
            <news:title>SVG Embedding Update: New Methods</news:title>
        </news:news>
    </url>
</urlset>

Code Breakdown:

  • xmlns:news — declares the news sitemap namespace.
  • <news:publication> — the publication entity.
  • <news:name> — the publication name.
  • <news:language> — the publication language (ISO 639-1).
  • <news:publication_date> — publication date.
  • <news:title> — the article title.
  • Only include articles published within the last two days.

docs.title: Example 6: robots.txt with Sitemap Directive
docs.text:
User-agent: *
Allow: /
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /checkout/

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap-index.xml

Code Breakdown:

  • Sitemap: directive declares the sitemap index location.
  • Place at the end of the robots.txt file.
  • Helps crawlers discover the sitemap without Search Console submission.

docs.title: Example 7: IndexNow API Call
docs.text:
// After publishing a new page, notify IndexNow
async function notifyIndexNow(url) {
    const response = await fetch('https://api.indexnow.org/indexnow', {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            host: 'example.com',
            key: 'your-indexnow-key',
            urlList: [url]
        })
    });
    return response.ok;
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Sends a POST request to the IndexNow API.
  • host — your domain.
  • key — your IndexNow API key (hosted at https://example.com/your-indexnow-key.txt).
  • urlList — an array of URLs to notify.
  • Bing, Yandex, Seznam, and Naver are notified simultaneously.

docs.title: Example 8: Sitemap Validation Script
docs.text:
// Validate sitemap URLs return 200 and are canonical
const sitemapUrls = await fetchSitemap('https://example.com/sitemap.xml');

for (const url of sitemapUrls) {
    const response = await fetch(url, { method: 'HEAD' });
    if (response.status !== 200) {
        console.error(`${url} returns ${response.status}`);
    }

    const html = await fetch(url).then(r => r.text());
    const canonical = html.match(/<link rel="canonical" href="([^"]+)"/)?.[1];
    if (canonical !== url) {
        console.error(`${url} canonical mismatch: ${canonical}`);
    }
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Fetches the sitemap and extracts URLs.
  • Checks each URL for a 200 status code.
  • Checks each URL's canonical tag matches the sitemap URL.
  • Run in CI/CD to catch sitemap regressions.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Sitemap Type Strategy Blog Standard XML Dynamic generation; <lastmod> on update E-commerce Segmented XML Products, categories, images in separate files News site News sitemap Only articles from last 2 days Video site Video sitemap Thumbnail, title, description, duration Image-heavy site Image sitemap <image:loc> for each image Large site (>50k URLs) Sitemap index Split by content type New site Standard XML Submit to Search Console for discovery Bing/Copilot visibility IndexNow Real-time URL notification

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Include only canonical, indexable URLs that return 200. Why: dead URLs waste crawl budget and send mixed signals.
  2. Use <lastmod> — and keep it honest. Why: it's the only metadata field Google reads; dishonest dates poison the signal.
  3. Drop <priority> and <changefreq>. Why: Google and Bing officially ignore both.
  4. Segment your sitemap by content type. Why: isolates coverage issues and speeds processing.
  5. Keep sub-sitemaps under 10,000–20,000 URLs. Why: optimal processing speed, well below the 50,000 limit.
  6. Use a sitemap index for sites over 50,000 URLs. Why: the protocol limit; the index allows up to 2.5 billion URLs.
  7. Reference the sitemap in robots.txt. Why: helps crawlers discover it faster.
  8. Submit to Google Search Console. Why: the only supported submission mechanism for Google.
  9. Submit to Bing Webmaster Tools. Why: Bing powers ChatGPT Search and Copilot.
  10. Configure IndexNow for real-time updates. Why: dramatically faster than waiting for a recrawl.
  11. Keep the sitemap dynamic. Why: static sitemaps go stale the moment you create them.
  12. Set lastmod from your database's updated_at timestamp. Why: not the build date, not the publish date — the actual content change date.
  13. Use ISO 8601 format for dates. Why: 2026-06-10 or 2026-06-10T14:30:00+00:00 — both valid.
  14. Host the sitemap at the domain root. Why: https://example.com/sitemap.xml with UTF-8 and application/xml.
  15. Keep the uncompressed file under 50 MB. Why: the protocol limit; gzip compression is allowed.
  16. Use absolute URLs. Why: relative URLs may not resolve correctly.
  17. Exclude noindex pages. Why: including them sends mixed signals to crawlers.
  18. Exclude redirects and 404s. Why: they waste crawl budget.
  19. Exclude parameter-decorated duplicates. Why: they split signals and waste crawl budget.
  20. Update the sitemap when you publish, move, or remove pages. Why: crawlers detect changes faster.
  21. Audit the sitemap weekly for broken entries. Why: stale URLs accumulate over time.
  22. Use the sitemap segmentation for Search Console reporting. Why: isolate indexing problems by content type.
  23. Don't scatter dozens of standalone XML files. Why: consolidate into one sitemap index.
  24. Use image and video sitemaps for visual content. Why: captures traffic from Google Images and video search.
  25. Audit the sitemap quarterly. Why: content changes, URLs change, priorities change.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Every Build Updates Every lastmod
docs.text:
// Wrong: stamps today's date on every URL
<lastmod>${new Date().toISOString().split('T')[0]}</lastmod>

Why it's wrong: Nothing changed, yet every page declares itself updated. Google learns your dates are noise and stops trusting them entirely.

✅ Correct:

// Correct: uses the actual content modification date
<lastmod>${page.updatedAt}</lastmod>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Including noindex Pages in the Sitemap
docs.text:
<url>
    <loc>https://example.com/private/</loc>
    <!-- noindex meta tag on the page -->
</url>

Why it's wrong: Sends mixed signals — "please index this" and "don't index this" simultaneously.

✅ Correct: Exclude noindex pages from the sitemap.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using <priority> and <changefreq>
docs.text:
<priority>0.8</priority>
<changefreq>daily</changefreq>

Why it's wrong: Google and Bing officially ignore both. They bloat the file and signal outdated knowledge.

✅ Correct: Drop both fields.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Exceeding 50,000 URLs in One File
docs.text:
<!-- 80,000 URLs in a single sitemap -->

Why it's wrong: Violates the protocol limit; the file may not be processed.

✅ Correct: Split into multiple files with a sitemap index.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Exceeding 50 MB Uncompressed
docs.text:
<!-- 60 MB sitemap file -->

Why it's wrong: Violates the protocol limit; the file may be rejected.

✅ Correct: Gzip the file or split into smaller files.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Relative URLs
docs.text:
<loc>/blog/post/</loc>

Why it's wrong: Relative URLs may not resolve correctly.

✅ Correct:

<loc>https://example.com/blog/post/</loc>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on the Sitemap Ping Endpoint
docs.text:
// Wrong: ping endpoint retired June 2023
fetch('https://www.google.com/ping?sitemap=https://example.com/sitemap.xml');

Why it's wrong: Google retired the endpoint in June 2023. It returns a 404 error.

✅ Correct: Submit via Search Console; use IndexNow for Bing.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Static Sitemap That Never Updates
docs.text:
<!-- sitemap.xml generated once, never regenerated -->

Why it's wrong: New pages are never discovered; deleted pages remain in the sitemap.

✅ Correct: Use a dynamic sitemap that regenerates automatically.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Sitemap at All
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Crawlers rely entirely on link discovery; new or buried content may take weeks to be found.

✅ Correct: Generate a sitemap and submit it.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Submitting to Search Console
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Without submission, Google may not discover the sitemap quickly; no Search Console reporting.

✅ Correct: Submit the sitemap index in Search Console under Indexing → Sitemaps.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Sitemaps add minimal bytes — typically a few KB per 1,000 URLs.
  • Gzip compression reduces file size by 70–90%.
  • Segmented sitemaps process faster — smaller files, quicker parsing.
  • Dynamic generation adds server cost but ensures freshness.
  • IndexNow is a single HTTP request — negligible overhead.
  • Search Console reporting is free and requires no performance trade-off.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Gzip large sitemaps (.xml.gz).
  2. Keep sub-sitemaps under 20,000 URLs.
  3. Use a CDN for sitemap delivery.
  4. Regenerate dynamically on content change, not on a schedule.
  5. Use IndexNow for real-time notifications instead of relying on recrawl cycles.

docs.title: Sitemaps Reveal Site Structure
docs.text: A sitemap is a public file listing your URLs. It reveals your site structure to anyone who reads it. Do not include URLs that you do not want public.

docs.title: Do Not Include Sensitive URLs
docs.text: Never include admin panels, private pages, or URLs with sensitive parameters in a sitemap. Use authentication and authorization to protect sensitive paths — not robots.txt or sitemap exclusion.

docs.title: The Sitemap Ping Spam Problem
docs.text: The old sitemap ping endpoint was deprecated due to its ineffectiveness and association with spam. Do not use it.

docs.title: IndexNow Key Security
docs.text: Your IndexNow API key is hosted at a public URL (https://example.com/your-key.txt). Anyone can see it. This is by design — the key identifies your site, not your identity. Do not use a sensitive string as your key.

docs.title: Sitemap XML Injection
docs.text: If your sitemap is generated from user input, escape it. XML injection can break the sitemap or inject malicious URLs.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Google Search Console → Sitemaps — shows submission status, discovered URLs, and errors.
  • Google Search Console → Page Indexing — filter by sitemap to see indexing status per segment.
  • Bing Webmaster Tools → Sitemaps — shows Bing's crawl status.
  • Validate XML — use an XML validator to check well-formedness.
  • Check the sitemap URL — curl -I https://example.com/sitemap.xml should return 200 and application/xml.
  • Check for stale URLs — audit for 404s and redirects in the sitemap.
  • Check for noindex URLs — audit for pages that should be excluded.
  • Check lastmod accuracy — compare sitemap dates to actual content update dates.
  • Screaming Frog — crawls your site and compares against the sitemap.
  • Sitebulb — visualizes sitemap coverage and indexing status.
  • Semrush Site Audit — checks sitemap format and reachability.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every site — a sitemap costs nothing and helps discovery.
  • Large sites — hundreds or thousands of pages where some get buried.
  • New sites — few external links pointing in.
  • Sites with weak internal linking — pages not reachable from navigation.
  • Fast-changing sites — blogs, news, e-commerce where <lastmod> tells Google what changed.
  • Sites with rich media — image, video, and news sitemaps for specialized content.
  • Sites wanting Bing/Copilot visibility — IndexNow for real-time notifications.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use <priority> or <changefreq>. Google ignores both.
  • Do not include noindex pages. It sends mixed signals.
  • Do not include redirects or 404s. They waste crawl budget.
  • Do not use relative URLs. Use absolute URLs.
  • Do not rely on the sitemap ping endpoint. It was retired in June 2023.
  • Do not exceed 50,000 URLs or 50 MB per file. Use a sitemap index.
  • Do not include sensitive URLs. Sitemaps are public.
  • Do not use a static sitemap that never updates. Use dynamic generation.
