docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Google retired the sitemap ping endpoint in June 2023 — automatic re-pings from plugins no longer do anything.
  • Google and Bing officially ignore <priority> and <changefreq> — confirmed by Gary Illyes and Google's own documentation.
  • <lastmod> is the only optional field Google reads — but only if the dates are honest.
  • The 50 MB sitemap size limit was raised from 10 MB in 2016 — articles referencing the 10 MB limit are out of date.
  • A sitemap index can list up to 50,000 sitemaps — a practical ceiling of 2.5 billion URLs.
  • One e-commerce client saw product index rates jump from 87% to 98% after segmenting into five sitemaps.
  • Average time to index dropped from 6 days to 1.4 days after segmentation.
  • Organic traffic increased by 156% in the same case study.
  • IndexNow was launched in October 2021 by Microsoft — it notifies Bing, Yandex, Seznam, and Naver.
  • Bing powers ChatGPT Search and Microsoft Copilot — a well-indexed Bing presence is a prerequisite for AI visibility.
  • <image:caption>, <image:geo_location>, <image:title>, and <image:license> were deprecated and removed from Google's documentation.
  • News sitemaps should include only articles from the last 2 days.
  • A single sitemap can contain up to 1,000 <news:news> tags.
  • Each <url> tag can contain up to 1,000 <image:image> tags.
  • The most common sitemap bug is every build updating every page's lastmod to "today."
  • One dishonest lastmod field poisons the entire site's signal.
  • Search Console reporting is one of the most underrated benefits of sitemap segmentation.
  • A sitemap is a discovery aid, not a ranking factor — it helps indexing but does not boost rankings.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A sitemap is a structured file listing a website's URLs to help search engines and AI crawlers discover and index content.
  • XML sitemaps are for search engines; HTML sitemaps are for users.
  • The sitemaps.org protocol defines the limits: 50,000 URLs per file, 50 MB uncompressed, UTF-8 encoding.
  • Past 50,000 URLs, use a sitemap index — up to 50,000 child sitemaps, 2.5 billion URLs practical ceiling.
  • Only canonical, indexable, 200-status URLs belong in a sitemap.
  • <lastmod> is the only optional field Google reads — and only if the dates are honest.
  • <priority> and <changefreq> are ignored — drop them.
  • Segment your sitemap by content type — isolates coverage issues, speeds processing, improves index rates.
  • Keep sub-sitemaps under 10,000–20,000 URLs for optimal processing.
  • The sitemap ping endpoint was retired in June 2023 — submit via Search Console instead.
  • IndexNow notifies Bing, Yandex, Seznam, and Naver in real time — dramatically faster than waiting for recrawls.
  • Image, video, and news sitemaps extend the standard sitemap for specialized content.
  • News sitemaps include only articles from the last 2 days.
  • The most common bug is updating every lastmod on every build — use actual content change dates.
  • A sitemap is a discovery aid, not a ranking factor — it helps indexing but does not boost rankings.
  • Every site should have a sitemap — it costs nothing and helps discovery.
  • Dynamic sitemaps are better than static — they update automatically and never go stale.
  • Reference the sitemap in robots.txt and submit it to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.
  • Audit the sitemap weekly for broken entries and quarterly for strategy.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Critical HTML refers to the minimum set of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript required to render the above-the-fold portion of a page — the content the user sees before scrolling. It is the markup that must arrive, parse, and render before the browser can paint anything meaningful on screen.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Dashboard — Acme</title>

    <!-- Critical CSS: inlined, blocking, above-the-fold styles only -->
    <style>
        body { margin: 0; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
        header { background: #3498db; color: white; padding: 1rem; }
        .hero { display: grid; place-items: center; min-height: 60vh; }
    </style>

    <!-- Non-critical CSS: loaded asynchronously -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
          onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
    <noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css"></noscript>
</head>
<body>
    <header>Acme</header>
    <main class="hero">
        <h1>Welcome back</h1>
    </main>
    <!-- Non-critical JS: deferred -->
    <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>
</body>
</html>

Critical HTML is not a file — it is a strategy. It is the discipline of answering one question: what is the absolute minimum the browser needs to paint the first meaningful frame? Everything else can be deferred, streamed, lazy-loaded, or preloaded after that first paint.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Critical HTML serves several essential purposes:

  • Fast First Contentful Paint (FCP) — the user sees something meaningful immediately.
  • Fast Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — the largest visible element renders quickly, satisfying Core Web Vitals.
  • Reduced Time to Interactive (TTI) — the page becomes interactive sooner because less blocking JavaScript is parsed upfront.
  • Perceived performance — even when the full page is not ready, the visible shell appears instantly.
  • Crawl efficiency — search engines and AI systems receive the important content in the initial HTML, not after JavaScript execution.
  • Resilience — the page renders even if JavaScript fails, because the critical content is in the initial HTML.
  • Lower INP — less JavaScript competing for the main thread means faster response to user input.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Performance Stack
│
├── Critical HTML        ← minimum markup for first paint
├── Lazy Loading         ← defer non-critical resources
├── Resource Hints       ← preload, preconnect, prefetch
├── Preload              ← high-priority fetch for critical assets
├── Prefetch             ← low-priority fetch for next navigation
├── DNS Prefetch         ← resolve third-party origins early
├── Script Loading       ← defer, async, module
└── Rendering Impact     ← layout shift, paint, compositing

Critical HTML is the foundation of the performance stack. Every other optimization — lazy loading, resource hints, script loading — is downstream of the initial HTML delivery. If the critical HTML is bloated or blocked, no downstream optimization can compensate.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A browser cannot paint a pixel until it has:

  1. Received the HTML.
  2. Parsed the HTML into a DOM tree.
  3. Received and parsed all render-blocking CSS.
  4. Constructed the CSSOM (CSS Object Model).
  5. Combined the DOM and CSSOM into a render tree.
  6. Computed layout.
  7. Painted the result.

Everything else — images, fonts, analytics scripts, ads, social widgets, non-critical CSS — is not required for the first paint. Yet for decades, developers put everything in the <head>: every stylesheet, every script, every third-party tag. The result: users stared at a blank white screen for seconds while the browser fetched and parsed resources that were not needed to render the visible content.

Critical HTML solves this by separating what must arrive first from what can arrive later.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence All CSS in one blocking file First paint waits for the entire stylesheet All JS in <head> Parser blocks on script download and execution Third-party scripts in <head> Analytics, ads, and widgets block rendering No preload for critical assets Fonts and hero images discovered late No inline critical CSS Empty white screen while CSS is fetched Client-side rendering Blank HTML shell with no content for crawlers

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The concept of the Critical Rendering Path (CRP) was popularized by Google's Ilya Grigorik around 2014. The idea: the browser's path from receiving HTML to painting pixels involves a sequence of blocking steps, and the length of that path determines how fast the user sees content.

The Critical CSS technique — inlining the above-the-fold styles directly in the <head> — emerged as the first major optimization. Tools like critical, penthouse, and critters automated the extraction of above-the-fold CSS from a full stylesheet.

The next evolution was server-side rendering (SSR) and streaming SSR, which put real content into the initial HTML instead of relying on client-side JavaScript to fetch and render it. React Server Components, Astro Islands, and Next.js App Router are all built on this principle.

In 2026, the critical HTML strategy has become the default assumption of every modern framework. The question is no longer "should we optimize the critical path?" — it is "how does our framework handle it, and where does it fail?"

docs.title: The Minimal Critical HTML Page
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Page Title</title>

    <!-- Critical CSS: inlined -->
    <style>
        body { margin: 0; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
        .hero { min-height: 60vh; display: grid; place-items: center; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <main class="hero">
        <h1>Welcome</h1>
    </main>

    <!-- Non-critical CSS: async loaded -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
          onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
    <noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css"></noscript>

    <!-- Non-critical JS: deferred -->
    <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Element Purpose <style> with above-the-fold CSS Provides the styles needed for first paint — no external request preload + onload for main CSS Fetches the full stylesheet without blocking render <noscript> fallback Ensures styles load when JavaScript is disabled defer on scripts Downloads scripts in parallel but executes them after HTML parsing

docs.title: The Critical CSS Extraction Pattern
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- 1. Inline only the above-the-fold CSS -->
    <style>
        /* Critical styles extracted by a build tool */
        body { margin: 0; font-family: system-ui; }
        header { background: #fff; box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,.1); }
        .hero { min-height: 60vh; padding: 2rem; }
        .hero h1 { font-size: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 4rem); }
    </style>

    <!-- 2. Load the full stylesheet asynchronously -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
          onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
    <noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css"></noscript>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • The inlined <style> block contains only the styles needed to render the visible portion of the page.
  • The full stylesheet loads after the first paint, using the preload + onload swap technique.
  • The <noscript> fallback ensures the stylesheet loads even without JavaScript.
  • This pattern is automated by tools like critical, penthouse, and critters.

docs.title: The Script Loading Pattern
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Preconnect to critical third-party origins -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload critical fonts -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font"
          type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Inline critical CSS -->
    <style>/* above-the-fold styles */</style>
</head>
<body>
    <main>Content</main>

    <!-- Non-critical scripts: deferred -->
    <script src="/js/analytics.js" defer></script>
    <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

    <!-- Or: module scripts, deferred by default -->
    <script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

Technique Effect preconnect Resolves DNS, TCP, and TLS for third-party origins in advance preload for fonts Fetches fonts at high priority before they are discovered by CSS Inline critical CSS Renders the first paint without waiting for external CSS defer scripts Downloads in parallel, executes after HTML parsing type="module" Module scripts are deferred by default

docs.title: The Streaming HTML Pattern (SSR)
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Streaming SSR</title>
    <style>/* critical CSS */</style>
</head>
<body>
    <header>Site Header</header>

    <!-- First meaningful paint happens here -->
    <main>
        <h1>Welcome</h1>
        <p>This content is sent immediately from the server.</p>
    </main>

    <!-- Slow data streams in below the fold -->
    <section id="recommendations">
        <!-- Server streams this content when ready -->
    </section>

    <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>
</body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • The server sends the HTML in chunks, starting with the above-the-fold content.
  • The browser can paint the header and hero content before the full HTML document has arrived.
  • Slow data (recommendations, personalization) streams in later, without blocking the initial paint.
  • Streaming SSR is supported by Next.js, Remix, Astro, and every modern SSR framework.

docs.title: The 103 Early Hints Pattern
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
Link: </styles/main.css>; rel=preload; as=style
Link: </fonts/inter-var.woff2>; rel=preload; as=font; crossorigin
Link: <https://cdn.example.com>; rel=preconnect

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
<!-- full HTML body -->

Code Breakdown:

  • The server sends 103 Early Hints before the full response.
  • The browser starts preloading critical resources while the server prepares the main response.
  • This saves one round-trip for critical resources.
  • Supported in Chrome, Edge, and Firefox; requires server/CDN support.

docs.title: The "Two-Meal" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of page loading as a restaurant serving two meals:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  APPETIZER (Critical HTML)                   │
│  └── Served immediately                      │
│  └── Above-the-fold content                  │
│  └── Minimum CSS for visible styles          │
│  └── User sees something meaningful fast     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  MAIN COURSE (Non-critical)                  │
│  └── Served asynchronously                   │
│  └── Below-the-fold content                  │
│  └── Full stylesheet, scripts, images        │
│  └── Loads after first paint                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The user should never wait for the main course to see the appetizer. Critical HTML is the appetizer — it satisfies the user's immediate need for visual feedback.

docs.title: The "Render-Blocking Waterfall" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every render-blocking resource adds a step to the critical path:

HTML arrives
    │
    ▼
Parse HTML
    │
    ▼
Encounter <link rel="stylesheet">
    │
    ├── Fetch CSS (network round-trip)
    ├── Parse CSS (build CSSOM)
    └── BLOCKS until complete
    │
    ▼
Encounter <script src> in <head>
    │
    ├── Fetch JS (network round-trip)
    ├── Parse JS
    ├── Execute JS (can modify DOM and CSSOM)
    └── BLOCKS until complete
    │
    ▼
Build render tree
    │
    ▼
Layout
    │
    ▼
Paint

Every blocking step adds latency. Critical HTML minimizes the number of blocking steps before the first paint.

docs.title: The "Above-the-Fold" Mental Model
docs.text:
Critical HTML is defined by what the user sees before scrolling:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ABOVE THE FOLD                              │
│  ├── Header / navigation                     │
│  ├── Hero section                            │
│  └── Primary content start                   │
│                                              │
│  ← This is what Critical HTML must render   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  BELOW THE FOLD                              │
│  ├── Additional content                      │
│  ├── Footer                                  │
│  └── Secondary widgets                       │
│                                              │
│  ← This can be lazy-loaded                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Important caveat: above-the-fold varies by viewport. A mobile viewport shows less than a desktop viewport. Critical CSS extraction tools must account for multiple breakpoints, or the inlined CSS will be insufficient for some users.

docs.title: The "Progressive Rendering" Mental Model
docs.text:
Modern critical HTML is not about rendering everything fast — it is about rendering something meaningful fast, then progressively enhancing:

t=0ms     HTML arrives
t=50ms    First paint (critical CSS)
t=100ms   Full content visible (main CSS loaded)
t=200ms   Fonts loaded (FOUT resolved)
t=500ms   Interactive (JS executed)
t=1000ms  Below-the-fold content loaded

The user sees something at every stage. The page never appears blank.

docs.title: The "Framework Default" Mental Model (2026)
docs.text:
In 2026, every major framework handles critical HTML differently:

Framework Critical HTML Strategy Next.js App Router Streaming SSR + React Server Components Remix / React Router Streaming SSR + nested routes Astro Islands architecture, zero JS by default SvelteKit SSR + streaming Nuxt SSR + payload extraction Gatsby Static HTML + partial hydration

The question is no longer "should we optimize the critical path?" — it is "does our framework do it correctly, and where does it fail?" Every framework claims to handle it. Not every framework handles it well.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Critical Rendering Path (CRP)
docs.text: The Critical Rendering Path is the sequence of steps the browser takes to convert HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into pixels on the screen. The shorter the path, the faster the first paint.

docs.title: Concept 2: Render-Blocking Resources
docs.text: CSS is render-blocking. The browser will not paint until it has built the CSSOM from all stylesheets. JavaScript is parser-blocking when it appears in the <head> without defer or async. Both block the first paint.

docs.title: Concept 3: Critical CSS
docs.text: The subset of styles needed to render the above-the-fold content. Inlined in a <style> tag in the <head>. The full stylesheet is loaded asynchronously after first paint.

docs.title: Concept 4: First Contentful Paint (FCP)
docs.text: The time when the browser renders the first piece of content — text, image, or canvas. Critical HTML directly reduces FCP.

docs.title: Concept 5: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
docs.text: The time when the largest visible element on the page renders. LCP is a Core Web Vital, and it is the primary metric that critical HTML optimization targets.

docs.title: Concept 6: Time to Interactive (TTI)
docs.text: The time when the page becomes fully interactive — the main thread is free of long tasks, and event handlers are attached. Critical HTML reduces TTI by deferring non-critical JavaScript.

docs.title: Concept 7: Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
docs.text: INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. It measures the responsiveness of the page to user input. Less JavaScript blocking the main thread means lower INP.

docs.title: Concept 8: defer and async
docs.text:
Two script loading strategies:

Attribute Download Execution Order defer Parallel to parsing After HTML parsing Guaranteed order async Parallel to parsing As soon as downloaded No guaranteed order type="module" Parallel to parsing After HTML parsing (deferred by default) Guaranteed order

docs.title: Concept 9: preload
docs.text:
A resource hint that tells the browser to fetch a critical resource at high priority before it would otherwise be discovered.

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: Concept 10: preconnect
docs.text:
A resource hint that resolves DNS, TCP, and TLS for a third-party origin in advance.

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

docs.title: Concept 11: dns-prefetch
docs.text:
A lighter-weight resource hint that resolves DNS only.

<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">

docs.title: Concept 12: The Async CSS Pattern
docs.text:
Loading non-critical CSS without blocking render:

<link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
      onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
<noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css"></noscript>

docs.title: Concept 13: content-visibility: auto
docs.text:
A CSS property that skips rendering of off-screen content:

section {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: 0 500px;
}

This reduces initial rendering cost and improves FCP/LCP.

docs.title: Concept 14: Streaming SSR
docs.text: Modern frameworks (Next.js, Remix, SvelteKit, Astro) stream HTML to the browser in chunks. The browser can paint the above-the-fold content before the full document has arrived.

docs.title: Concept 15: 103 Early Hints
docs.text: An HTTP status code that allows the server to send resource hints (preload, preconnect) before the full HTML response. Supported in Chrome, Edge, and Firefox; requires server/CDN support.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Speculation Rules API
docs.text:
A modern replacement for prefetch that allows developers to control speculative loading with JSON:

<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prerender": [{
        "source": "document",
        "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
        "eagerness": "moderate"
    }]
}
</script>

Supported in Chromium browsers. Replaces the deprecated rel=prerender hint.

docs.title: Concept 17: The <link rel="preload"> for Hero Images
docs.text:
The LCP element is often a hero image. Preloading it ensures it arrives as fast as possible:

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.webp"
      imagesrcset="/hero-400.webp 400w, /hero-800.webp 800w, /hero-1200.webp 1200w"
      imagesizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px, (max-width: 1200px) 800px, 1200px">

docs.title: Concept 18: Font Loading and FOUT/FOIT
docs.text:
Fonts are render-blocking only if referenced in the critical CSS. The font-display property controls how fonts are rendered:

Value Behavior swap Text renders immediately with fallback; swaps when font loads block Text is invisible until font loads (bad) fallback Short block period, then fallback optional Font is used only if available quickly

docs.title: Concept 19: The Critical Path Length
docs.text: The length of the critical path is measured in round-trips. Each blocking resource adds a round-trip. Minimizing round-trips is the goal of critical HTML.

docs.title: Concept 20: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
docs.text: SSR puts real content in the initial HTML response. The browser paints the content immediately — no waiting for JavaScript to fetch data and render. This is the most effective critical HTML strategy for dynamic pages.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Critical Rendering Path
docs.text:
1.  Browser requests the HTML document.
    │
    ▼
2.  HTML arrives, parser begins.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser encounters <link rel="stylesheet"> in <head>:
    │   ├── Fetch CSS (network round-trip)
    │   ├── Parse CSS (build CSSOM)
    │   └── BLOCKS rendering until complete
    │
    ▼
4.  Parser encounters <script src> in <head> without defer/async:
    │   ├── Fetch JS (network round-trip)
    │   ├── Parse JS
    │   ├── Execute JS
    │   └── BLOCKS parsing until complete
    │
    ▼
5.  Parser completes DOM construction.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser combines DOM + CSSOM into render tree.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser computes layout.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser paints pixels.
    │
    ▼
9.  First paint occurs.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Critical HTML Optimization
docs.text:
1.  Inline above-the-fold CSS in <style>.
    │   └── Removes the CSS network round-trip from the critical path.
    │
    ▼
2.  Load full CSS asynchronously with preload + onload.
    │   └── Does not block render.
    │
    ▼
3.  Defer all non-critical scripts.
    │   └── Removes JS from the critical path.
    │
    ▼
4.  Preconnect to critical third-party origins.
    │   └── Saves DNS/TCP/TLS round-trips.
    │
    ▼
5.  Preload critical fonts and hero images.
    │   └── Fetches them at high priority.
    │
    ▼
6.  Server-render the above-the-fold content.
    │   └── Content appears in the initial HTML.
    │
    ▼
7.  First paint occurs after minimal blocking.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Streaming SSR
docs.text:
1.  Server receives the request.
    │
    ▼
2.  Server sends the HTML shell with <head> and <body> opening tags.
    │
    ▼
3.  Server streams the above-the-fold content.
    │   └── Browser can paint this immediately.
    │
    ▼
4.  Server fetches slow data (recommendations, personalization).
    │
    ▼
5.  Server streams the remaining HTML chunks.
    │
    ▼
6.  Server sends the closing tags.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser progressively paints as chunks arrive.

docs.title: The CSSOM and Render Tree
docs.text:
The browser builds two trees:

  • DOM — from HTML.
  • CSSOM — from CSS.

These are combined into a render tree that contains only visible elements with their computed styles. The render tree is the input to layout and paint.

HTML → DOM
CSS  → CSSOM
       │
       ▼
DOM + CSSOM → Render Tree → Layout → Paint

docs.title: Why CSS Is Render-Blocking
docs.text: The browser cannot know if an element is visible, what size it is, or where it is positioned until it has parsed all CSS. Rendering before CSS parsing would produce a flash of unstyled content (FOUC). So the browser blocks rendering until the CSSOM is complete.

docs.title: Why JS Is Parser-Blocking
docs.text:
JavaScript can modify the DOM and CSSOM. If the browser continued parsing while JS was downloading, the JS might modify the DOM in an order that produces inconsistent results. So the browser blocks parsing until the script is downloaded and executed.

defer and async break this behavior by removing the parser-blocking property.

docs.title: The Critical Path Length
docs.text:
The critical path length is the number of round-trips required before the first paint. Each render-blocking resource adds one round-trip:

1 round-trip: HTML
1 round-trip: CSS
1 round-trip: JS (if in <head>)

Total: 3 round-trips

Inlining critical CSS and deferring JS reduces this to 1 round-trip.

docs.title: The Preload Scanner
docs.text: Modern browsers include a preload scanner that runs ahead of the main parser, looking for resources to fetch. It can discover CSS, JS, images, and fonts early — but it cannot see resources referenced in JavaScript or in CSS files loaded via @import.

docs.title: The 103 Early Hints Architecture
docs.text:
Client                    Server
  │                          │
  ├── GET / ─────────────────►
  │                          │
  │◄── 103 Early Hints ──────┤
  │    Link: preload CSS     │
  │    Link: preconnect      │
  │                          │
  │── Preload CSS ──────────►│
  │                          │
  │◄── 200 OK + HTML ────────┤
  │                          │
  │── Render ───────────────►│

The browser starts fetching critical resources before the HTML response has finished generating.

docs.title: Critical HTML Optimization Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Measure the current critical path:
    │   ├── Lighthouse
    │   ├── WebPageTest
    │   └── Chrome DevTools Performance panel
    │
    ▼
2.  Identify render-blocking resources:
    │   ├── Stylesheets in <head>
    │   ├── Synchronous scripts in <head>
    │   └── Third-party resources blocking render
    │
    ▼
3.  Extract critical CSS:
    │   ├── Use a build tool (critical, penthouse, critters)
    │   └── Inline above-the-fold styles
    │
    ▼
4.  Async-load full CSS:
    │   ├── preload + onload swap
    │   └── noscript fallback
    │
    ▼
5.  Defer non-critical JS:
    │   ├── Add defer or async
    │   └── Move scripts to end of body
    │
    ▼
6.  Preconnect and preload critical assets:
    │   ├── Fonts
    │   ├── Hero images
    │   └── Third-party origins
    │
    ▼
7.  Re-measure and iterate.

docs.title: Measurement Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Run Lighthouse (mobile, throttled).
    │
    ▼
2.  Record FCP, LCP, TBT, CLS, INP.
    │
    ▼
3.  Identify the LCP element.
    │
    ▼
4.  Verify the LCP element is in the initial HTML.
    │
    ▼
5.  Verify the LCP element's resource is preloaded.
    │
    ▼
6.  Fix the largest gap and re-measure.

docs.title: Example 1: Critical CSS Extraction
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Critical CSS: inlined from build tool -->
    <style>
        body { margin: 0; font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; }
        header { background: #fff; box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,.1); padding: 1rem; }
        .hero { min-height: 60vh; display: grid; place-items: center; padding: 2rem; }
        .hero h1 { font-size: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 4rem); margin: 0; }
        .btn { background: #3498db; color: white; padding: .75rem 1.5rem; border-radius: 4px; }
    </style>

    <!-- Full CSS: async loaded -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
          onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
    <noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css"></noscript>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • Inlined styles cover the above-the-fold content: body, header, hero, button.
  • Full stylesheet loads asynchronously with the preload + onload swap.
  • <noscript> fallback ensures styles load without JavaScript.
  • Build tools like critical, penthouse, and critters generate this pattern automatically.

docs.title: Example 2: Font Loading
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font"
          type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <style>
        @font-face {
            font-family: 'Inter';
            src: url('/fonts/inter-var.woff2') format('woff2-variations');
            font-display: swap;
            font-weight: 100 900;
        }
        body { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif; }
    </style>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • preconnect to the font origin resolves DNS/TCP/TLS early.
  • preload fetches the font at high priority.
  • font-display: swap renders text immediately with fallback, then swaps.
  • crossorigin is required for font preloads, even same-origin.

docs.title: Example 3: Hero Image Preload
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero-1200.webp"
          imagesrcset="/hero-400.webp 400w,
                       /hero-800.webp 800w,
                       /hero-1200.webp 1200w"
          imagesizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px,
                      (max-width: 1200px) 800px,
                      1200px">
</head>
<body>
    <img src="/hero-1200.webp"
         srcset="/hero-400.webp 400w,
                 /hero-800.webp 800w,
                 /hero-1200.webp 1200w"
         sizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px,
                (max-width: 1200px) 800px,
                1200px"
         alt="Product hero image"
         width="1200"
         height="600"
         fetchpriority="high">
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • preload with imagesrcset and imagesizes matches the <img> attributes.
  • fetchpriority="high" tells the browser this is the LCP element.
  • width and height prevent layout shift.
  • The image is in the initial HTML — not lazy-loaded — because it is the LCP element.

docs.title: Example 4: Deferred Script Loading
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Critical inline CSS -->
    <style>/* above-the-fold styles */</style>
</head>
<body>
    <main>Content</main>

    <!-- Non-critical scripts: deferred -->
    <script src="/js/analytics.js" defer></script>
    <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

    <!-- Module scripts are deferred by default -->
    <script type="module" src="/js/main.js"></script>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • No synchronous scripts in the <head>.
  • defer scripts download in parallel and execute after HTML parsing.
  • type="module" scripts are deferred by default.
  • The main content renders before any script executes.

docs.title: Example 5: Streaming SSR with React
docs.text:
// Next.js App Router: streaming with Suspense
import { Suspense } from 'react';

export default function Page() {
    return (
        <main>
            <h1>Dashboard</h1>
            <FastStats />
            <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
                <SlowRecommendations />
            </Suspense>
        </main>
    );
}

Code Breakdown:

  • <h1> and <FastStats /> stream immediately.
  • <SlowRecommendations /> streams when its data resolves.
  • The browser paints the above-the-fold content before the slow data is ready.
  • The <Skeleton /> is shown as a placeholder for the slow content.

docs.title: Example 6: 103 Early Hints
docs.text:
// Express.js: send 103 Early Hints before the main response
app.get('/', (req, res) => {
    res.writeEarlyHints({
        'link': [
            '</styles/main.css>; rel=preload; as=style',
            '</fonts/inter-var.woff2>; rel=preload; as=font; crossorigin',
            '<https://cdn.example.com>; rel=preconnect'
        ]
    });

    // Then send the HTML response
    res.sendFile('index.html');
});

Code Breakdown:

  • The server sends 103 Early Hints with preload directives.
  • The browser starts preloading critical resources while the server prepares the HTML.
  • Requires server/CDN support (Cloudflare, Fastly, and most modern CDNs support it).

docs.title: Example 7: content-visibility for Below-the-Fold
docs.text:
/* Skip rendering of off-screen sections */
section.below-fold {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: 0 500px;
}

Code Breakdown:

  • content-visibility: auto skips rendering of off-screen content.
  • contain-intrinsic-size provides a placeholder size to prevent layout shift.
  • Significantly reduces initial rendering cost on long pages.

docs.title: Example 8: Speculation Rules for Instant Navigation
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prerender": [{
        "source": "document",
        "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
        "eagerness": "moderate"
    }],
    "prefetch": [{
        "source": "list",
        "urls": ["/about", "/contact"]
    }]
}
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • prerender — fully renders the target page in a hidden tab, making navigation instant.
  • prefetch — fetches the HTML of the target page without rendering.
  • eagerness: "moderate" — prefetch on hover; "eager" prefetches immediately.
  • Supported in Chromium browsers (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc).

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Critical HTML Strategy Marketing landing page Inline critical CSS, defer JS, preload hero image E-commerce product page SSR, preload LCP image, defer analytics Blog post Static HTML, inline critical CSS SaaS dashboard Streaming SSR, skeleton placeholders Documentation site Static HTML, async CSS, deferred JS News article SSR, preload hero image, inline critical CSS Web app with auth Streaming SSR + client hydration

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Inline above-the-fold CSS in the <head>. Why: removes the CSS round-trip from the critical path.
  2. Load the full stylesheet asynchronously. Why: doesn't block render after the first paint.
  3. Use defer for all non-critical scripts. Why: removes parser-blocking from the critical path.
  4. Use type="module" for modern scripts. Why: deferred by default.
  5. Never put synchronous third-party scripts in the <head>. Why: analytics, ads, and widgets block render.
  6. Preconnect to critical third-party origins. Why: saves DNS/TCP/TLS round-trips.
  7. Preload critical fonts. Why: fonts are discovered late by CSS parsing.
  8. Preload the LCP image. Why: it is the largest visible element; fetching it late delays LCP.
  9. Add width and height to images and videos. Why: prevents layout shift (CLS).
  10. Use fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image. Why: tells the browser to prioritize it.
  11. Use font-display: swap. Why: text renders immediately with fallback.
  12. Server-render the above-the-fold content. Why: content appears in the initial HTML — no JS needed.
  13. Use streaming SSR for slow data. Why: faster time to first byte for visible content.
  14. Use content-visibility: auto for below-the-fold sections. Why: skips rendering off-screen content.
  15. Use 103 Early Hints when server support exists. Why: saves a round-trip for critical resources.
  16. Use the Speculation Rules API for instant navigation. Why: replaces deprecated rel=prerender.
  17. Avoid large inline <style> blocks. Why: bloats HTML; keep critical CSS minimal.
  18. Avoid @import in CSS. Why: blocks rendering and creates sequential round-trips.
  19. Avoid document.write(). Why: blocks parser and defeats preload scanner.
  20. Avoid synchronous XHR. Why: blocks main thread and render.
  21. Measure with Lighthouse, WebPageTest, and real user metrics (RUM). Why: lab data misses real-world conditions.
  22. Audit the critical path after every framework upgrade. Why: framework behavior changes.
  23. Test on slow networks (3G/4G) and low-end devices. Why: performance gaps are invisible on fast connections.
  24. Keep the critical HTML under 14 KB uncompressed. Why: fits in the first TCP congestion window (initial round-trip).
  25. Monitor Core Web Vitals continuously. Why: LCP, INP, and CLS drive SEO and user experience.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: All CSS in One Blocking Stylesheet
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/all.css">
</head>

Why it's wrong: The browser blocks rendering until the entire stylesheet is fetched and parsed.

✅ Correct:

<head>
    <style>/* critical above-the-fold CSS */</style>
    <link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
          onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
    <noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css"></noscript>
</head>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Synchronous Scripts in the <head>
docs.text:
<head>
    <script src="/js/analytics.js"></script>
    <script src="/js/app.js"></script>
</head>

Why it's wrong: Each script blocks parsing until downloaded and executed.

✅ Correct:

<head>
    <style>/* critical CSS */</style>
</head>
<body>
    <main>Content</main>
    <script src="/js/analytics.js" defer></script>
    <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>
</body>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Preload for the LCP Image
docs.text:
<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" loading="lazy">

Why it's wrong: Lazy-loading the LCP element delays LCP. The image is discovered late.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.jpg" fetchpriority="high">
...
<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: font-display: block
docs.text:
@font-face {
    font-family: 'Inter';
    src: url('/fonts/inter.woff2') format('woff2');
    font-display: block;
}

Why it's wrong: Text is invisible until the font loads — a blank page.

✅ Correct:

@font-face {
    font-family: 'Inter';
    src: url('/fonts/inter.woff2') format('woff2');
    font-display: swap;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using @import in CSS
docs.text:
@import url('/styles/reset.css');
@import url('/styles/layout.css');

Why it's wrong: Creates sequential round-trips; blocks rendering.

✅ Correct: Use <link> elements with preload, or bundle into one stylesheet.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: document.write() in the <head>
docs.text:
<script>document.write('<link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">');</script>

Why it's wrong: Blocks the parser and defeats the preload scanner.

✅ Correct: Use static <link> elements.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No width/height on Images
docs.text:
<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero">

Why it's wrong: The browser doesn't know the image dimensions until it loads, causing layout shift (CLS).

✅ Correct:

<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" width="1200" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Client-Side Rendering for Content Pages
docs.text:
<div id="root"></div>
<script src="/js/app.js"></script>

Why it's wrong: The initial HTML is empty; content only appears after JavaScript executes. Crawlers and AI systems may see nothing.

✅ Correct: Use SSR or SSG to put content in the initial HTML.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Blocking Third-Party Scripts
docs.text:
<head>
    <script src="https://third-party.com/widget.js"></script>
</head>

Why it's wrong: Third-party scripts block render and can be slow or unavailable.

✅ Correct:

<script src="https://third-party.com/widget.js" async></script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring the 14 KB TCP Window
docs.text:
<head>
    <style>/* 40 KB of inlined critical CSS */</style>
</head>

Why it's wrong: Inlined CSS over 14 KB forces a second round-trip before first paint.

✅ Correct: Keep critical CSS minimal — typically 5–10 KB.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Critical HTML optimization has the highest ROI of any performance technique.
  • Inline critical CSS reduces first paint by 100–500ms on slow connections.
  • Deferred scripts improve TTI and INP.
  • Preloading the LCP image improves LCP by 200–800ms.
  • Streaming SSR improves FCP by 300–1000ms on slow backends.
  • 103 Early Hints saves one round-trip for critical resources.
  • content-visibility: auto reduces initial rendering cost by 20–50% on long pages.
  • Server-rendered content is visible to crawlers and AI systems immediately.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep critical HTML under 14 KB uncompressed.
  2. Inline only above-the-fold CSS.
  3. Defer all non-critical scripts.
  4. Preload the LCP image with fetchpriority="high".
  5. Preconnect to critical third-party origins.
  6. Use font-display: swap.
  7. Server-render the above-the-fold content.
  8. Use streaming SSR for slow data.
  9. Use content-visibility: auto for below-the-fold sections.
  10. Measure with real user metrics (RUM), not just lab data.

docs.title: Inline CSS and CSP
docs.text:
Inlining CSS requires 'unsafe-inline' in CSP's style-src directive, which weakens XSS protection. Use nonces or hashes when possible:

Content-Security-Policy: style-src 'self' 'nonce-abc123'

<style nonce="abc123">/* critical CSS */</style>

docs.title: Inline Scripts and CSP
docs.text: Same issue for scripts. If you must inline, use nonces or hashes.

docs.title: Third-Party Scripts
docs.text:
Third-party scripts are the largest security risk on most pages. Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) for scripts from CDNs:

<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"
        integrity="sha384-..."
        crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

docs.title: Preload and Prefetch Leaks
docs.text: preload and prefetch reveal what resources the page will load. Do not preload URLs that leak sensitive information.

docs.title: Streaming SSR and Error Leakage
docs.text: Streaming SSR can leak partial error messages if an error occurs mid-stream. Ensure error boundaries handle failures gracefully.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Performance panel — records the full critical path.
  • Chrome DevTools → Coverage panel — shows unused CSS and JS.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — audits for render-blocking resources.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network panel — inspect resource priorities and timing.
  • Chrome DevTools → Rendering panel — enable "Paint flashing" to see paint regions.
  • WebPageTest — filmstrip view of the critical path.
  • PageSpeed Insights — field + lab data combined.
  • Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) — real-world Core Web Vitals.
  • <link rel="preload"> warnings — Chrome warns about unused preloads.
  • render-blocking-resources audit — Lighthouse flags blocking CSS and JS.
  • largest-contentful-paint-element audit — Lighthouse identifies the LCP element.
  • uses-text-compression audit — verify gzip/brotli.
  • server-response-time audit — verify TTFB.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every page — critical HTML optimization benefits all pages.
  • Pages with high LCP — hero images, marketing pages, product pages.
  • Pages with heavy third-party scripts — ads, analytics, widgets.
  • Pages with slow backends — streaming SSR helps.
  • Pages with large stylesheets — critical CSS extraction helps.
  • Content pages — SSR/SSG ensures content is in the initial HTML.
  • E-commerce — every millisecond of latency costs conversion.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not inline the entire stylesheet. Only above-the-fold CSS.
  • Do not inline critical CSS larger than 14 KB. It forces a second round-trip.
  • Do not defer the LCP image. Preload it with high priority.
  • Do not lazy-load above-the-fold images. They are part of the critical path.
  • Do not use font-display: block. Use swap or optional.
  • Do not use document.write(). It blocks the parser.
  • Do not use @import for critical CSS. It creates sequential round-trips.
  • Do not put third-party scripts in the critical path. Defer or async them.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Critical Rendering Path (CRP)
  • First Contentful Paint (FCP)
  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
  • Time to Interactive (TTI)
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP)

  • preload / preconnect / dns-prefetch

  • Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

  • React Server Components

  • TCP slow start
  • 14 KB rule

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The 14 KB rule — the first TCP congestion window is approximately 14 KB. Keeping critical HTML under this size allows the first paint after a single round-trip.
  • defer scripts execute in order; async scripts do not. Choose defer for scripts with dependencies.
  • Module scripts (type="module") are deferred by default — no need to add defer.
  • INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in March 2024.
  • Streaming SSR can improve FCP by 300–1000ms on slow backends.
  • 103 Early Hints saves one round-trip for critical resources.
  • The Speculation Rules API replaced rel=prerender in Chromium browsers.
  • content-visibility: auto can reduce rendering cost by 20–50% on long pages.
  • font-display: swap prevents invisible text during font loading.
  • Preloading the LCP image can improve LCP by 200–800ms.
  • fetchpriority="high" tells the browser the LCP element should be fetched at highest priority.
  • Chrome's preload scanner discovers resources ahead of the main parser — but not resources referenced in JavaScript.
  • document.write() defeats the preload scanner and blocks the parser.
  • @import in CSS creates sequential round-trips — always use <link> instead.
  • React Server Components stream HTML — the above-the-fold content arrives first.
  • Astro ships zero JavaScript by default — the purest critical HTML strategy.
  • Every major framework claims to handle critical HTML — verify with real measurements.
  • The critical path is measured in round-trips — each blocking resource adds one.
  • Critical HTML is not a file — it is a strategy applied across HTML, CSS, and JS.
  • The fastest way to improve LCP is often to make the LCP element a text element instead of a large image.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Critical HTML is the minimum HTML, CSS, and JavaScript required to render the above-the-fold content.
  • It is the foundation of the performance stack — every downstream optimization depends on it.
  • The Critical Rendering Path (CRP) is the sequence of steps from HTML to pixels.
  • CSS is render-blocking; JavaScript is parser-blocking.
  • Inline above-the-fold CSS to eliminate the CSS round-trip.
  • Load the full stylesheet asynchronously with preload + onload.
  • Defer all non-critical scripts with defer or type="module".
  • Preconnect to critical third-party origins to save DNS/TCP/TLS round-trips.
  • Preload critical fonts and the LCP image at high priority.
  • Use fetchpriority="high" on the LCP element.
  • Use font-display: swap to prevent invisible text.
  • Server-render the above-the-fold content — content appears in the initial HTML.
  • Use streaming SSR for slow data — paint the shell before the data arrives.
  • Use 103 Early Hints when server support exists.
  • Use content-visibility: auto for below-the-fold sections.
  • Keep critical HTML under 14 KB uncompressed.
  • Measure with Lighthouse, WebPageTest, and real user metrics.
  • Critical HTML is the difference between a page that feels instant and a page that feels broken.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Lazy loading is the practice of deferring the loading of non-critical resources — images, iframes, videos, scripts, and below-the-fold content — until they are actually needed, typically when they enter or approach the viewport. Instead of loading everything upfront, the browser loads only what the user is likely to see, then loads the rest on demand.

<!-- Native lazy loading: the browser defers the image until it nears the viewport -->
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy" width="800" height="600">

<!-- Eager loading: the LCP image loads immediately -->
<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high" width="1200" height="600">

Lazy loading is not one technique — it is a family of techniques that apply across resource types:

  • Native HTML — loading="lazy" on <img> and <iframe>.
  • JavaScript APIs — IntersectionObserver for custom lazy-loading logic.
  • Framework primitives — next/image, <Suspense>, React.lazy, dynamic imports.
  • CSS — content-visibility: auto for skipping off-screen rendering.
  • Dynamic imports — import() for loading JavaScript modules on demand.

The goal is always the same: load less upfront, load more later, and never load what the user will never see.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Lazy loading serves several essential purposes:

  • Faster initial page load — fewer bytes downloaded before the first paint.
  • Lower bandwidth consumption — users on metered connections download only what they see.
  • Reduced memory usage — fewer DOM nodes, decoded images, and parsed scripts in memory.
  • Better Core Web Vitals — faster LCP, lower TBT, and lower INP.
  • Lower server costs — fewer image requests, less CDN traffic, less bandwidth billed.
  • Improved UX on long pages — content loads progressively as the user scrolls.
  • Accessibility for slow connections — users on 3G/4G see the important content first.
  • Scalable content delivery — galleries, feeds, and product lists can be arbitrarily long.

The primary metric lazy loading targets is LCP — but only if applied correctly. Misapplied lazy loading makes LCP worse, not better.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Performance Stack
│
├── Critical HTML        ← minimum markup for first paint
├── Lazy Loading         ← defer non-critical resources
├── Resource Hints       ← preload, preconnect, prefetch
├── Preload              ← high-priority fetch for critical assets
├── Prefetch             ← low-priority fetch for next navigation
├── DNS Prefetch         ← resolve third-party origins early
├── Script Loading       ← defer, async, module
└── Rendering Impact     ← layout shift, paint, compositing

Lazy loading sits after critical HTML in the performance stack. Critical HTML determines what arrives first; lazy loading determines what arrives later. Together they shape the loading timeline of the page.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A page with 30 images does not need all 30 images to render its first frame. A page with 5 iframes — analytics, chat widget, social embed, map, ad — does not need all 5 loaded before the user can read the first paragraph. Yet for decades, browsers loaded every resource in the HTML as soon as the parser encountered it.

On a fast fiber connection, this is invisible. On a slow 3G connection, on a low-end Android phone, or in a country where bandwidth is expensive — it is the difference between a page that loads in 2 seconds and one that loads in 15 seconds.

The 2026 reality: the median web page weighs over 2.5 MB, with images accounting for 1.2 MB of that. Loading every byte upfront wastes bandwidth, memory, and CPU on content the user may never scroll to.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No native lazy loading All images loaded upfront, regardless of visibility Manual JavaScript hacks scroll listeners with getBoundingClientRect() — janky and expensive No iframe deferral Analytics, chat, and ad iframes blocked the critical path No below-the-fold deferral Full-page rendering cost paid at load time No framework primitives Every team reinvented lazy loading badly No CSS containment Off-screen content still rendered and composited

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Native lazy loading (loading="lazy") shipped in Chrome 76 (July 2019) and Firefox 75 (April 2020). Safari added support in 15.4 (March 2022). It replaced the JavaScript scroll-listener pattern that had dominated for years.

The IntersectionObserver API shipped in 2016 and became the standard for detecting when an element enters the viewport. It replaced scroll listeners and getBoundingClientRect(), which ran on the main thread and caused jank.

content-visibility: auto shipped in Chrome 85 (2020) and became baseline across browsers by 2024. It allows the browser to skip rendering of off-screen content, reducing layout and paint cost.

Framework primitives — next/image, Nuxt Image, Gatsby Image, Angular NgOptimizedImage — automated lazy loading and responsive image handling. React's lazy() and Suspense brought code-splitting to components.

AVIF and WebP reduced per-image bytes by 30–60% compared to JPEG, making lazy loading more effective (fewer bytes to defer, but larger savings when deferred).

In 2026, lazy loading is baseline and expected — not an optimization, but a default. Browsers ship it natively; frameworks automate it; the only question is whether you are applying it correctly.

docs.title: Native Image Lazy Loading
docs.text:
<!-- Lazy: browser defers loading until the image nears the viewport -->
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy" width="800" height="600">

<!-- Eager: browser loads immediately (default for most browsers) -->
<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high" width="1200" height="600">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
Attribute Value Effect loading lazy Defer until the image nears the viewport loading eager Load immediately (default) fetchpriority high Fetch at highest priority (for LCP images) fetchpriority low Fetch at low priority (for below-the-fold) width / height pixel values Reserve space to prevent layout shift

Critical rule: Never lazy-load the LCP element. If the largest visible element is an image, add fetchpriority="high" and leave it eager. Lazy-loading the LCP image delays LCP by hundreds of milliseconds.

docs.title: Native Iframe Lazy Loading
docs.text:
<!-- Lazy: iframe loads when near the viewport -->
<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/xyz"
        loading="lazy"
        width="560"
        height="315"
        title="Product demo">
</iframe>

Code Breakdown:

  • loading="lazy" — defers the iframe until it nears the viewport.
  • Off-screen iframes (footer chat widgets, below-the-fold embeds) do not load until needed.
  • Supported in all modern browsers.

docs.title: The IntersectionObserver API
docs.text:
const images = document.querySelectorAll('img[data-src]');

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach((entry) => {
        if (entry.isIntersecting) {
            const img = entry.target;
            img.src = img.dataset.src;
            img.removeAttribute('data-src');
            observer.unobserve(img);
        }
    });
}, {
    rootMargin: '200px 0px',  // start loading 200px before viewport
    threshold: 0.01
});

images.forEach((img) => observer.observe(img));

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Line Purpose document.querySelectorAll('img[data-src]') Select images with placeholder data-src new IntersectionObserver(callback, options) Create an observer rootMargin: '200px 0px' Start loading 200px before the image enters the viewport threshold: 0.01 Trigger when at least 1% of the element is visible observer.observe(img) Register each image for observation observer.unobserve(img) Stop observing once loaded

docs.title: The content-visibility: auto Pattern
docs.text:
.below-fold-section {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: 0 500px;
}

Code Breakdown:

  • content-visibility: auto — the browser skips rendering the element until it nears the viewport.
  • contain-intrinsic-size — provides a placeholder size to prevent layout shift.
  • Reduces initial rendering cost on long pages by 20–50%.

docs.title: Dynamic Imports (Code Splitting)
docs.text:
// Static import: always loaded
import { heavyFunction } from './heavy-module.js';

// Dynamic import: loaded on demand
button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
    const { heavyFunction } = await import('./heavy-module.js');
    heavyFunction();
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Dynamic import() returns a Promise that resolves when the module loads.
  • Used for route-level code splitting, modal content, and rarely-used features.
  • Bundlers (Webpack, Vite, Rollup, esbuild) automatically split dynamic imports into separate chunks.

docs.title: React.lazy and Suspense
docs.text:
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const HeavyChart = lazy(() => import('./HeavyChart'));

function Dashboard() {
    return (
        <main>
            <h1>Dashboard</h1>
            <Suspense fallback={<ChartSkeleton />}>
                <HeavyChart />
            </Suspense>
        </main>
    );
}

Code Breakdown:

  • lazy(() => import('./HeavyChart')) — the component is loaded only when rendered.
  • <Suspense fallback={...}> — shows a placeholder while the component loads.
  • The above-the-fold content renders immediately; the chart loads when its chunk arrives.

docs.title: The next/image Component
docs.text:
import Image from 'next/image';

<Image
    src="/hero.jpg"
    alt="Hero"
    width={1200}
    height={600}
    priority  // disables lazy loading for LCP images
/>

Code Breakdown:

  • next/image automatically lazy-loads by default.
  • priority disables lazy loading for the LCP element.
  • Automatically serves AVIF/WebP, generates srcset, and prevents layout shift.

docs.title: The "Restaurant Menu" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a page as a restaurant menu:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  APPETIZER (Critical, eager)                 │
│  └── Hero image, above-the-fold content      │
│  └── Load immediately                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  MAIN COURSE (Below-the-fold, lazy)          │
│  └── Product images, sections further down   │
│  └── Load when the user scrolls to them      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DESSERT (Deep content, lazy)                │
│  └── Footer images, related content          │
│  └── Load only if the user reaches them      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The user should never wait for the dessert to enjoy the appetizer.

docs.title: The "Just-in-Time Delivery" Mental Model
docs.text:
Traditional loading is a truck that delivers all goods before the store opens. Lazy loading is a just-in-time supply chain — goods arrive as the shelves empty.

Traditional:
  Load → Everything arrives → Store opens

Lazy:
  Load → First shelves fill → Store opens
         → As user browses, more shelves fill

The store opens faster, but the user never notices the difference — except that the page feels instant.

docs.title: The "Viewport as Trigger" Mental Model
docs.text:
The viewport is the boundary between "load now" and "load later":

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  VIEWPORT                                    │
│  ├── Above the fold: EAGER                   │
│  └── LCP element: fetchpriority="high"       │
│                                              │
│  ← Below the fold: LAZY                      │
│                                              │
│  ← Far below: content-visibility: auto       │
│                                              │
│  ← Never scrolled to: NEVER LOADED           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The rootMargin in IntersectionObserver and the browser's native lazy loading both use the viewport as the trigger. Content enters the loading queue as it approaches the viewport.

docs.title: The "LCP Trap" Mental Model
docs.text:
The single most important rule of lazy loading:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ⚠️  NEVER LAZY-LOAD THE LCP ELEMENT ⚠️     │
│                                              │
│  If the LCP element is an image:             │
│    ❌ loading="lazy"          → slows LCP    │
│    ✅ fetchpriority="high"    → fast LCP     │
│                                              │
│  If the LCP element is a background image:   │
│    ❌ background-image with lazy loading     │
│    ✅ <img> with fetchpriority="high"        │
│                                              │
│  If the LCP element is a text element:       │
│    ✅ Ensure the font loads fast             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Lazy loading is a trade-off. It speeds up below-the-fold loading at the cost of delaying above-the-fold loading. Get the boundary wrong, and you make LCP worse, not better.

docs.title: The "Progressive vs. Deferred" Mental Model
docs.text:
Two related but distinct techniques:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PROGRESSIVE LOADING                         │
│  └── Load low-quality first, then high-quality│
│  └── Examples: LQIP, BlurHash, progressive JPEG
│  └── Goal: perceived performance             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAZY LOADING                                │
│  └── Defer loading until needed              │
│  └── Examples: loading="lazy", IntersectionObserver
│  └── Goal: total bytes downloaded            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Both can be combined: lazy-load the image, but show a low-quality placeholder (LQIP) while it loads.

docs.title: Concept 1: loading="lazy"
docs.text: The native HTML attribute for lazy loading images and iframes. Supported in all modern browsers since 2022. The browser decides exactly when to load the resource based on network conditions, viewport size, and scroll speed.

docs.title: Concept 2: The loading="eager" Default
docs.text: If loading is not specified, browsers use eager for images in the initial viewport and may still load below-the-fold images immediately. Adding loading="lazy" explicitly is the only reliable way to defer below-the-fold images.

docs.title: Concept 3: fetchpriority
docs.text:
The fetchpriority attribute controls the browser's fetch priority for a resource:

Value Effect high Fetch at highest priority (LCP images) low Fetch at low priority (below-the-fold images) auto Default priority

docs.title: Concept 4: IntersectionObserver
docs.text: The modern API for detecting when an element enters or exits the viewport. Replaces scroll listeners and getBoundingClientRect(). Runs off the main thread and is efficient even with hundreds of observed elements.

docs.title: Concept 5: rootMargin
docs.text:
The rootMargin option in IntersectionObserver expands or shrinks the intersection area:

{
    rootMargin: '200px 0px'  // start loading 200px before the viewport
}

A positive rootMargin loads resources earlier — a common optimization to prevent visible pop-in on slow connections.

docs.title: Concept 6: content-visibility: auto
docs.text: A CSS property that allows the browser to skip rendering of off-screen content. Reduces initial rendering cost by 20–50% on long pages. Requires contain-intrinsic-size to prevent layout shift.

docs.title: Concept 7: Dynamic Imports
docs.text:
const module = await import('./module.js');

Loads a JavaScript module on demand. Bundlers split dynamic imports into separate chunks. Used for route-level code splitting, rarely-used features, and modal content.

docs.title: Concept 8: Route-Level Code Splitting
docs.text: The most impactful code-splitting strategy: each route loads only the JavaScript needed for that route. Frameworks like Next.js, Remix, SvelteKit, and Nuxt do this automatically.

docs.title: Concept 9: Component-Level Code Splitting
docs.text:
Splitting JavaScript at the component level — used for large charts, editors, and modals that are not needed on initial load.

const HeavyEditor = lazy(() => import('./HeavyEditor'));

docs.title: Concept 10: The LCP Trap
docs.text: Never lazy-load the LCP element. Lazy loading delays LCP by hundreds of milliseconds. Use fetchpriority="high" and leave it eager.

docs.title: Concept 11: The Layout Shift Trap
docs.text:
Lazy loading without width/height causes layout shift (CLS). Always specify dimensions or use aspect-ratio in CSS.

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Concept 12: decoding="async"
docs.text:
Tells the browser to decode the image asynchronously, off the main thread. Prevents the image decode from blocking other work.

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: Concept 13: LQIP (Low-Quality Image Placeholder)
docs.text:
A technique that shows a tiny, blurred version of the image while the full-resolution version loads. Improves perceived performance.

<img src="photo-tiny.jpg"
     data-src="photo.jpg"
     class="lazy"
     style="filter: blur(20px);"
     alt="Photo">

docs.title: Concept 14: The srcset and sizes Attributes
docs.text:
Combine lazy loading with responsive images to load the smallest sufficient image:

<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1600.jpg 1600w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px, (max-width: 1200px) 800px, 1600px"
     loading="lazy"
     width="800"
     height="600"
     alt="Photo">

docs.title: Concept 15: Iframe Lazy Loading
docs.text:
Iframes are the second-biggest performance drain on most pages (after images). loading="lazy" defers them until they near the viewport.

<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/xyz" loading="lazy" title="Video"></iframe>

docs.title: Concept 16: Video Lazy Loading
docs.text:
Videos should never autoplay-load. Use preload="none" on <video> elements and load them on click.

<video preload="none" controls poster="poster.jpg">
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

docs.title: Concept 17: The Facade Pattern
docs.text:
For heavy third-party embeds (YouTube, Google Maps, Twitter), use a facade — a lightweight placeholder (often an image) that looks like the embed. Load the real iframe only when the user clicks.

<!-- Facade: a lightweight image -->
<div class="youtube-facade" data-video-id="xyz">
    <img src="youtube-thumbnail.jpg" alt="Video: Product demo">
    <button>Play</button>
</div>

Libraries: lite-youtube-embed, @justinribeiro/lite-youtube, react-lite-youtube-embed.

docs.title: Concept 18: Framework Primitives
docs.text: Framework Lazy Loading Primitive Next.js next/image, next/dynamic Nuxt <NuxtImg>, defineAsyncComponent SvelteKit Native, {#await} Astro Built-in by default Angular NgOptimizedImage, @defer Gatsby gatsby-plugin-image Remix Native <img>, lazy routes

docs.title: Concept 19: The loading Attribute and CSP
docs.text: Lazy loading does not affect CSP directly, but the resources being lazy-loaded must still satisfy CSP directives (img-src, frame-src, script-src).

docs.title: Concept 20: Measuring Lazy Loading Effectiveness
docs.text:
• Lighthouse — audits for offscreen images.
  • Chrome DevTools → Coverage — shows unused bytes.
  • Network panel — verify resources are loaded on scroll.
  • WebPageTest filmstrip — visualize loading over time.
  • CrUX — real-world LCP data.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Native Lazy Loading
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters <img loading="lazy">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser does NOT fetch the image immediately.
    │
    ▼
3.  Image is registered for lazy loading.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser watches the image's position relative to the viewport.
    │
    ▼
5.  When the image nears the viewport (browser-specific threshold):
    │   └── Browser fetches the image.
    │
    ▼
6.  Image loads, decodes, and renders.
    │
    ▼
7.  If the user never scrolls to the image:
    │   └── Image is never fetched.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: IntersectionObserver
docs.text:
1.  Observer is created with callback and options.
    │
    ▼
2.  Elements are registered via observer.observe(el).
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser monitors each element's intersection with the root.
    │
    ▼
4.  When an element crosses the threshold:
    │   └── Callback fires with entry data.
    │
    ▼
5.  Callback loads the resource (sets src, adds classes).
    │
    ▼
6.  Observer unobserves the element to stop tracking.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Dynamic Import
docs.text:
1.  User triggers an action (click, route change).
    │
    ▼
2.  import() is called with a module path.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser checks if the module is already cached.
    │   ├── Yes → resolve immediately.
    │   └── No  → fetch the module chunk over the network.
    │
    ▼
4.  Module is parsed and evaluated.
    │
    ▼
5.  Promise resolves with the module's exports.
    │
    ▼
6.  Application uses the module.

docs.title: How Native Lazy Loading Works
docs.text:
The browser's lazy loading implementation uses:

  • IntersectionObserver internally — the browser uses an efficient viewport-intersection check.
  • Network-aware thresholds — the browser may load earlier on slow connections to compensate for latency.
  • Scroll velocity — fast scrolling triggers earlier loading.
  • Viewport distance — the browser may load images within a certain distance of the viewport.

The exact thresholds are implementation-specific and not standardized, which is why behavior varies between Chrome, Firefox, and Safari.

docs.title: The Preload Scanner vs. Lazy Loading
docs.text: The preload scanner runs ahead of the main parser and discovers resources early. Lazy-loaded images are not discovered by the preload scanner because the browser defers their fetch until intersection. This is the desired behavior — it removes them from the critical path.

docs.title: The IntersectionObserver Architecture
docs.text:
IntersectionObserver runs on a separate thread, so it does not compete with the main thread for layout and paint. This is what makes it superior to scroll listeners, which run on the main thread and cause jank.

Main thread:           Separate thread:
  ─ Layout               ─ IntersectionObserver
  ─ Paint                  ├── Watches elements
  ─ JS execution           └── Fires callbacks

docs.title: The content-visibility Rendering Skip
docs.text:
content-visibility: auto tells the browser:

  1. Skip layout and paint for off-screen content.
  2. Render the element when it nears the viewport.
  3. Use contain-intrinsic-size as a placeholder size.

The browser maintains the DOM but skips the rendering cost until the element is needed.

docs.title: The Chunk Splitting Algorithm
docs.text:
Bundlers (Webpack, Vite, Rollup, esbuild) detect dynamic imports and split them into separate chunks:

main.js         ← always loaded
  ├── route-a.js   ← dynamic import on /a
  ├── route-b.js   ← dynamic import on /b
  └── chart.js     ← dynamic import when chart renders

Chunk names are content-hashed for cache-busting. Chunks are loaded on demand via <script> injection or fetch().

docs.title: The Next.js Image Pipeline
docs.text:
next/image:

  1. Detects the image dimensions.
  2. Generates a srcset at build time or on demand.
  3. Serves AVIF/WebP with JPEG fallback.
  4. Applies loading="lazy" by default.
  5. Adds fetchpriority="high" when priority is set.
  6. Prevents layout shift via width/height attributes.

docs.title: Lazy Loading Implementation Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Identify the LCP element:
    │   └── Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse → LCP element
    │
    ▼
2.  Mark the LCP element as eager:
    │   └── fetchpriority="high", no loading="lazy"
    │
    ▼
3.  Mark all other images as lazy:
    │   └── loading="lazy" decoding="async"
    │
    ▼
4.  Mark iframes as lazy:
    │   └── loading="lazy"
    │
    ▼
5.  Apply content-visibility to below-the-fold sections:
    │   └── content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: ...
    │
    ▼
6.  Replace heavy third-party embeds with facades:
    │   └── lite-youtube-embed, etc.
    │
    ▼
7.  Add code splitting for routes and heavy components:
    │   └── dynamic import(), React.lazy
    │
    ▼
8.  Measure with Lighthouse, WebPageTest, and CrUX.

docs.title: Measurement Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Run Lighthouse on mobile with throttling.
    │
    ▼
2.  Record LCP, CLS, INP, TBT.
    │
    ▼
3.  Verify the LCP element loads immediately.
    │
    ▼
4.  Verify below-the-fold images are deferred.
    │
    ▼
5.  Check DevTools Coverage for unused bytes.
    │
    ▼
6.  Test on slow 3G in DevTools network throttling.
    │
    ▼
7.  Fix issues and re-measure.

docs.title: Example 1: Native Lazy Loading for Below-the-Fold Images
docs.text:
<!-- Above the fold: eager, high priority -->
<img src="/hero.avif" alt="Hero" width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high">

<!-- Below the fold: lazy -->
<img src="/feature-1.avif" alt="Feature 1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="800" height="600">
<img src="/feature-2.avif" alt="Feature 2" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="800" height="600">
<img src="/feature-3.avif" alt="Feature 3" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="800" height="600">

Code Breakdown:

  • Hero image: eager, fetchpriority="high", no lazy loading.
  • Below-the-fold images: loading="lazy", decoding="async".
  • All images have width and height to prevent layout shift.
  • Browser loads feature images only when the user scrolls.

docs.title: Example 2: IntersectionObserver with rootMargin
docs.text:
const images = document.querySelectorAll('img[data-src]');

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach((entry) => {
        if (!entry.isIntersecting) return;

        const img = entry.target;
        img.src = img.dataset.src;
        img.removeAttribute('data-src');
        observer.unobserve(img);
    });
}, {
    rootMargin: '300px 0px',  // load 300px before viewport
    threshold: 0
});

images.forEach((img) => observer.observe(img));

Code Breakdown:

  • rootMargin: '300px 0px' — starts loading 300px before the image enters the viewport.
  • threshold: 0 — fires when any part of the image touches the root.
  • observer.unobserve(img) — stops observing after loading.
  • The 300px margin prevents visible pop-in on slow connections.

docs.title: Example 3: content-visibility for Long Pages
docs.text:
.below-fold-section {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: auto 500px;
}

<main>
    <section class="hero">...</section>
    <section class="below-fold-section">
        <!-- This section is not rendered until near viewport -->
    </section>
    <section class="below-fold-section">
        <!-- Same here -->
    </section>
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • content-visibility: auto — skips rendering until the section nears the viewport.
  • contain-intrinsic-size: auto 500px — placeholder size to prevent layout shift.
  • auto in the first position tells the browser to remember the actual size once rendered.

docs.title: Example 4: Lazy Loading with LQIP
docs.text:
<img src="photo-tiny.jpg"
     data-src="photo-full.jpg"
     alt="Photo"
     width="800"
     height="600"
     class="lazy"
     style="filter: blur(20px); transition: filter 0.3s;">

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach((entry) => {
        if (!entry.isIntersecting) return;

        const img = entry.target;
        img.src = img.dataset.src;
        img.style.filter = 'none';
        observer.unobserve(img);
    });
}, { rootMargin: '200px' });

document.querySelectorAll('.lazy').forEach((img) => observer.observe(img));

Code Breakdown:

  • Tiny placeholder image loads immediately (small bytes).
  • Full image loads when near the viewport.
  • Blur filter is removed on load, creating a smooth transition.

docs.title: Example 5: Lazy Loading Iframes with Facade
docs.text:
<!-- Facade: lightweight, loads immediately -->
<div class="video-facade" data-video-id="xyz">
    <img src="thumbnail.jpg" alt="Video: Product demo" loading="lazy" width="560" height="315">
    <button type="button" aria-label="Play video">Play</button>
</div>

<script>
    document.querySelectorAll('.video-facade').forEach((facade) => {
        facade.addEventListener('click', () => {
            const iframe = document.createElement('iframe');
            iframe.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${facade.dataset.videoId}?autoplay=1`;
            iframe.width = '560';
            iframe.height = '315';
            iframe.title = 'Product demo';
            iframe.allow = 'autoplay; fullscreen';
            facade.replaceWith(iframe);
        });
    });
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The facade is a lightweight image and button.
  • On click, the facade is replaced with the real iframe.
  • Saves hundreds of KB and multiple HTTP requests on initial load.
  • Improves LCP by removing the iframe from the critical path.

docs.title: Example 6: Dynamic Import for Heavy Component
docs.text:
// A lightweight button that loads a heavy chart on demand
document.getElementById('show-chart').addEventListener('click', async () => {
    const { renderChart } = await import('./chart.js');
    renderChart(document.getElementById('chart-container'));
});

Code Breakdown:

  • The chart library is loaded only when the user clicks the button.
  • The initial bundle stays small.
  • Bundlers automatically split chart.js into a separate chunk.

docs.title: Example 7: Route-Level Code Splitting (React)
docs.text:
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';
import { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';

const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard'));
const Settings = lazy(() => import('./pages/Settings'));
const Reports = lazy(() => import('./pages/Reports'));

function App() {
    return (
        <Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Dashboard />} />
                <Route path="/settings" element={<Settings />} />
                <Route path="/reports" element={<Reports />} />
            </Routes>
        </Suspense>
    );
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Each route is loaded only when navigated to.
  • The initial bundle contains only the shared code.
  • <Suspense> shows a skeleton while the route loads.
  • Route-level splitting is the most impactful code-splitting strategy.

docs.title: Example 8: Next.js Image with Priority
docs.text:
import Image from 'next/image';

export default function HomePage() {
    return (
        <main>
            {/* LCP element: priority disables lazy loading */}
            <Image
                src="/hero.avif"
                alt="Hero"
                width={1200}
                height={600}
                priority
            />

            {/* Below the fold: lazy by default */}
            <Image
                src="/feature-1.avif"
                alt="Feature 1"
                width={800}
                height={600}
            />
        </main>
    );
}

Code Breakdown:
