  • priority on the hero image disables lazy loading and adds fetchpriority="high".
  • Other images are lazy-loaded by default.
  • next/image automatically generates srcset and serves AVIF/WebP.

docs.title: Example 9: Angular @defer
docs.text:
<main>
    <h1>Dashboard</h1>

    @defer (on viewport) {
        <app-heavy-chart />
    } @placeholder {
        <div class="skeleton"></div>
    } @loading {
        <div class="spinner"></div>
    }
</main>

Code Breakdown:

  • @defer (on viewport) — loads the component when it enters the viewport.
  • @placeholder — content shown before the component is loaded.
  • @loading — content shown while the component is loading.
  • Angular's control flow syntax for deferred loading.

docs.title: Example 10: Video Facade with preload="none"
docs.text:
<video controls preload="none" poster="poster.jpg" width="1280" height="720">
    <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    <source src="video.webm" type="video/webm">
    Your browser does not support the video tag.
</video>

Code Breakdown:

  • preload="none" — the browser does not preload the video.
  • poster — the image shown before the video plays.
  • The video loads only when the user clicks Play.
  • Saves hundreds of MB on pages with multiple videos.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Lazy Loading Technique Below-the-fold images loading="lazy" Hero image (LCP) fetchpriority="high", no lazy YouTube embed Facade pattern Google Maps embed Facade pattern Chat widget iframe loading="lazy" Analytics script defer or async Route-level JS Dynamic import Heavy component React.lazy, @defer Long page sections content-visibility: auto Videos preload="none" Background images <img> with loading="lazy" Infinite scroll feeds IntersectionObserver + fetch

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Never lazy-load the LCP element. Why: it delays LCP by hundreds of milliseconds.
  2. Add fetchpriority="high" to the LCP element. Why: tells the browser to fetch it at highest priority.
  3. Lazy-load all below-the-fold images. Why: reduces initial bytes and improves FCP/LCP.
  4. Always specify width and height. Why: prevents layout shift (CLS).
  5. Use decoding="async". Why: prevents image decode from blocking the main thread.
  6. Lazy-load iframes. Why: iframes are heavy and often below the fold.
  7. Use facades for third-party embeds. Why: saves hundreds of KB.
  8. Use content-visibility: auto for long sections. Why: skips off-screen rendering.
  9. Use contain-intrinsic-size with content-visibility. Why: prevents layout shift.
  10. Code-split at the route level. Why: the most impactful code-splitting strategy.
  11. Use dynamic imports for heavy components. Why: keep initial bundle small.
  12. Use preload="none" for videos. Why: videos should not preload.
  13. Use srcset and sizes with lazy loading. Why: load the smallest sufficient image.
  14. Use IntersectionObserver instead of scroll listeners. Why: runs off the main thread; no jank.
  15. Add rootMargin to prevent pop-in. Why: load before the element is visible.
  16. Use loading="lazy" instead of JavaScript when possible. Why: native implementation is more efficient.
  17. Use LQIP for large hero images below the fold. Why: improves perceived performance.
  18. Test on slow networks (3G/4G) and low-end devices. Why: performance gaps are invisible on fast connections.
  19. Measure with Lighthouse, WebPageTest, and CrUX. Why: lab + field data reveals different issues.
  20. Audit lazy loading after every major framework upgrade. Why: framework behavior changes.
  21. Lazy-load only what is truly non-critical. Why: over-lazy-loading delays content the user needs.
  22. Do not lazy-load images in the initial viewport. Why: they are part of the LCP.
  23. Do not lazy-load fonts. Why: font loading affects FOUT/FOIT and should be preloaded.
  24. Do not lazy-load critical CSS. Why: CSS is render-blocking and must load first.
  25. Monitor Core Web Vitals continuously. Why: LCP, INP, and CLS drive SEO and UX.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Lazy-Loading the LCP Image
docs.text:
<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" loading="lazy" width="1200" height="600">

Why it's wrong: Delays LCP by hundreds of milliseconds. Lazy loading the LCP element is the single most common lazy-loading mistake.

✅ Correct:

<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high" width="1200" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No width and height on Lazy-Loaded Images
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy">

Why it's wrong: The browser doesn't know the image dimensions, causing layout shift (CLS) when the image loads.

✅ Correct:

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" loading="lazy" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using scroll Listeners Instead of IntersectionObserver
docs.text:
window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
    document.querySelectorAll('img[data-src]').forEach((img) => {
        if (img.getBoundingClientRect().top < window.innerHeight) {
            img.src = img.dataset.src;
        }
    });
});

Why it's wrong: Runs on the main thread on every scroll event, causing jank and poor INP.

✅ Correct: Use IntersectionObserver.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Lazy-Loading Above-the-Fold Images
docs.text:
<img src="logo.jpg" alt="Logo" loading="lazy" width="200" height="50">
<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" loading="lazy" width="1200" height="600">

Why it's wrong: Both images are in the initial viewport. Lazy loading them delays the first paint.

✅ Correct:

<img src="logo.jpg" alt="Logo" width="200" height="50">
<img src="hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high" width="1200" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No loading="lazy" on Below-the-Fold Images
docs.text:
<img src="feature-1.jpg" alt="Feature 1" width="800" height="600">
<img src="feature-2.jpg" alt="Feature 2" width="800" height="600">

Why it's wrong: All images load upfront, wasting bandwidth and delaying LCP.

✅ Correct:

<img src="feature-1.jpg" alt="Feature 1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="800" height="600">
<img src="feature-2.jpg" alt="Feature 2" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Lazy-Loading Critical Fonts
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

Why it's wrong: Fonts are critical for text rendering. Preloading is correct; lazy loading is not.

✅ Correct: Preload critical fonts.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Facade for Third-Party Embeds
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/xyz" width="560" height="315"></iframe>

Why it's wrong: The iframe loads immediately, blocking the critical path.

✅ Correct:

<div class="video-facade" data-video-id="xyz">
    <img src="thumbnail.jpg" alt="Video thumbnail" loading="lazy">
    <button>Play</button>
</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: content-visibility Without contain-intrinsic-size
docs.text:
section {
    content-visibility: auto;
}

Why it's wrong: The browser doesn't know the section's size, causing layout shift.

✅ Correct:

section {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: 0 500px;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Lazy-Loading All Scripts
docs.text:
<script src="/js/critical.js" defer></script>

Why it's wrong: Critical scripts should load and execute early; lazy loading them delays interactivity.

✅ Correct: Lazy-load non-critical scripts; defer critical scripts.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming loading="lazy" Is Universal
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Older browsers (IE 11, Safari < 15.4) do not support native lazy loading.

✅ Correct: Use IntersectionObserver as a fallback, or accept that older browsers will load eagerly.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Native lazy loading is free — no JavaScript overhead.
  • IntersectionObserver runs off the main thread — no jank.
  • content-visibility: auto reduces rendering cost by 20–50% on long pages.
  • Dynamic imports reduce initial bundle size — faster TTI and INP.
  • Facades save hundreds of KB per embed.
  • Route-level code splitting is the highest-ROI code-splitting strategy.
  • LQIP improves perceived performance even when total bytes are similar.
  • The fetchpriority attribute has the same effect as importance (deprecated).

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Native lazy loading is free — use it.
  2. IntersectionObserver for custom logic.
  3. content-visibility: auto for long pages.
  4. Route-level code splitting.
  5. Facades for third-party embeds.
  6. preload="none" for videos.
  7. LQIP for large below-the-fold hero images.
  8. Combine lazy loading with responsive images (srcset, sizes).
  9. Measure on slow networks — differences are invisible on fast connections.
  10. Monitor Core Web Vitals continuously.

docs.title: Lazy Loading and CSP
docs.text:
Lazy-loaded resources must satisfy the same CSP directives as eagerly-loaded resources:

Content-Security-Policy:
    img-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com;
    frame-src https://www.youtube.com

docs.title: Lazy Loading and Subresource Integrity
docs.text:
Lazy-loaded scripts and styles should use SRI where possible:

<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"
        integrity="sha384-..."
        crossorigin="anonymous"
        defer></script>

docs.title: Facade Pattern and Clickjacking
docs.text: Facades replace iframes with custom UI. Ensure that the facade does not introduce clickjacking or UI redressing vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Lazy Loading and Third-Party Scripts
docs.text: Lazy-loaded third-party scripts still execute in your origin's context. Apply the same security review as eager-loaded scripts.

docs.title: Deferred Loading and Ad Blockers
docs.text: Some ad blockers may block lazy-loaded ad iframes. Ensure your page functions correctly when ad iframes fail to load.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Network panel — verify images load on scroll.
  • Chrome DevTools → Coverage panel — shows unused CSS and JS.
  • Chrome DevTools → Rendering panel — enable "Paint flashing" to see paint regions.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — audits for offscreen images.
  • Lighthouse → offscreen-images audit — flags images that should be lazy-loaded.
  • Lighthouse → lcp-lazy-loaded audit — flags LCP images that are incorrectly lazy-loaded.
  • WebPageTest filmstrip — visualize loading over time.
  • Network throttling (Slow 3G) — reveals loading issues invisible on fast connections.
  • Disable cache — verify lazy loading works on first load.
  • document.querySelectorAll('img[loading="lazy"]') — count lazy-loaded images.
  • Scroll through the page — verify images load on scroll.
  • Check for pop-in — if images pop in visibly, rootMargin should be increased.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Below-the-fold images — always.
  • Iframes below the fold — always.
  • Third-party embeds — use facades.
  • Long pages — content-visibility: auto.
  • Heavy JavaScript — code splitting.
  • Videos — preload="none".
  • Route-level code — dynamic imports.
  • Modal content — lazy-load when opened.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not lazy-load the LCP element. Use fetchpriority="high".
  • Do not lazy-load above-the-fold images.
  • Do not lazy-load critical fonts. Preload them.
  • Do not lazy-load critical CSS. Inline it.
  • Do not lazy-load above-the-fold iframes. They are part of the initial viewport.
  • Do not use scroll listeners. Use IntersectionObserver.
  • Do not use content-visibility without contain-intrinsic-size.
  • Do not lazy-load critical scripts. Defer them.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Critical HTML
  • Critical Rendering Path
  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
  • Core Web Vitals
  • loading="lazy"
  • fetchpriority
  • decoding="async"
  • IntersectionObserver
  • content-visibility
  • contain-intrinsic-size
  • Dynamic imports
  • Code splitting
  • Route-level splitting
  • React.lazy
  • <Suspense>
  • @defer (Angular)
  • next/image
  • Facade pattern
  • LQIP (Low-Quality Image Placeholder)
  • preload="none"
  • srcset / sizes
  • preload

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Native lazy loading shipped in Chrome 76 (July 2019) — it replaced the JavaScript scroll-listener pattern.
  • Safari added loading="lazy" support in 15.4 (March 2022) — it was the last major browser to ship it.
  • IntersectionObserver runs on a separate thread — it does not compete with the main thread for layout and paint.
  • Lighthouse flags LCP images that are lazy-loaded — the lcp-lazy-loaded audit catches this common mistake.
  • content-visibility: auto can reduce rendering cost by 20–50% on long pages.
  • The fetchpriority attribute replaced importance — the older attribute was deprecated.
  • The loading="lazy" attribute is ignored in some browsers when the image is in the initial viewport — a safety mechanism to prevent visible pop-in.
  • The preload scanner does not see lazy-loaded images — they are removed from the critical path by design.
  • Facades can save 500 KB or more per YouTube embed — the iframe, player JS, and tracking scripts are not loaded until the user clicks.
  • preload="none" on videos can save hundreds of MB on pages with multiple videos.
  • Route-level code splitting is the highest-ROI code-splitting strategy — it dramatically reduces initial bundle size.
  • The median web page weighs over 2.5 MB in 2026 — images account for 1.2 MB.
  • Lazy loading improves LCP only if applied correctly — misapplied, it makes LCP worse.
  • The rootMargin option in IntersectionObserver prevents visible pop-in — the recommended value is 200–300px.
  • Lazy loading is a default in 2026 — frameworks handle it automatically; the question is whether it is correct.
  • content-visibility: auto is supported in all modern browsers — Chrome 85+, Firefox 125+, Safari 18+.
  • The loading="lazy" attribute has no effect on fonts or CSS — it only works on images and iframes.
  • Lighthouse's offscreen-images audit estimates potential savings from lazy loading below-the-fold images.
  • Real-user monitoring (RUM) reveals lazy-loading issues that lab data misses — always measure in production.
  • The best lazy loading is invisible — the user never notices that resources were deferred.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Lazy loading defers non-critical resources until they are needed.
  • Native loading="lazy" works on images and iframes — no JavaScript required.
  • IntersectionObserver is the modern API for custom lazy-loading logic.
  • content-visibility: auto skips off-screen rendering, reducing initial cost.
  • Dynamic imports split JavaScript into on-demand chunks.
  • Route-level code splitting is the highest-ROI code-splitting strategy.
  • Facades for heavy third-party embeds save hundreds of KB.
  • preload="none" on videos prevents massive unnecessary downloads.
  • The golden rule: never lazy-load the LCP element. Use fetchpriority="high".
  • Always specify width and height to prevent layout shift (CLS).
  • Use decoding="async" to prevent main-thread blocking during image decode.
  • Use rootMargin to load before the element is visible.
  • Use contain-intrinsic-size with content-visibility.
  • Combine lazy loading with responsive images (srcset, sizes).
  • Test on slow networks — differences are invisible on fast connections.
  • Measure with Lighthouse, WebPageTest, and CrUX.
  • Lazy loading is a trade-off — it speeds up below-the-fold loading at the cost of delaying above-the-fold loading.
  • In 2026, lazy loading is baseline and expected — the question is whether you are applying it correctly.
  • The best lazy loading is invisible — the user never notices that resources were deferred.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Resource hints are a set of <link> elements that tell the browser about resources it will need in the future — before the browser would otherwise discover them. They allow the browser to start work early: resolving DNS, opening connections, or downloading resources, all before the main HTML parser reaches the point where the resource is actually referenced.

<head>
    <!-- Resolve DNS early for a third-party origin -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">

    <!-- Establish a full connection early -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- Download a critical resource at high priority -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload an ES module -->
    <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">

    <!-- Fetch a likely next-page resource at low priority -->
    <link rel="prefetch" href="/next-page.html">
</head>

There are five primary resource hints:

Hint What it does When to use dns-prefetch Resolve a hostname only Cross-origin asset hosts you may use later preconnect DNS + TCP/QUIC + TLS handshake Critical third-party origins (fonts, analytics, image CDN) preload Fetch and cache a specific subresource at high priority Above-the-fold CSS, hero image, primary font modulepreload Preload an ES module and its declared static dependencies Critical entry-point modules in an ESM-shipped app prefetch Low-priority fetch for a future navigation Likely next pages (e.g., article in a list)

Beyond the <link> hints, there are two additional mechanisms that serve the same purpose:

  • 103 Early Hints — an HTTP status code that lets the server send preload/preconnect directives before the full response is ready.
  • The Speculation Rules API — a JSON-based declarative API for prefetching and prerendering future page navigations.

Resource hints are performance hypotheses, not configuration — a preload for a font that the browser would have discovered 50ms later is harmless; a preload for the wrong file pays full bandwidth cost without a win.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Resource hints serve several essential purposes:

  • Reduce latency — eliminate DNS, TCP, and TLS round-trips before they happen.
  • Prioritize critical resources — tell the browser which resources matter most for the current page.
  • Prepare for future navigation — fetch next-page resources during idle time.
  • Improve Core Web Vitals — faster LCP, lower INP, better TBT.
  • Compensate for late discovery — preload resources that the preload scanner misses (fonts in CSS, LCP images in JS).
  • Enable instant navigation — prerender likely next pages for single-digit-millisecond navigation.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Performance Stack
│
├── Critical HTML        ← minimum markup for first paint
├── Lazy Loading         ← defer non-critical resources
├── Resource Hints       ← preload, preconnect, prefetch
├── Preload              ← high-priority fetch for critical assets
├── Prefetch             ← low-priority fetch for next navigation
├── DNS Prefetch         ← resolve third-party origins early
├── Script Loading       ← defer, async, module
└── Rendering Impact     ← layout shift, paint, compositing

Resource hints sit between critical HTML and script loading in the performance stack. They are the mechanism for telling the browser what to do before it would otherwise figure it out.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A browser is a reactive machine. It parses HTML, discovers resources as it encounters them, and fetches them in the order it finds them. This works — but it is slow.

Consider a page that loads a font. The font is referenced in a CSS file. The CSS file is referenced in the HTML. The browser must:

  1. Parse the HTML.
  2. Fetch the CSS.
  3. Parse the CSS.
  4. Discover the font reference.
  5. Fetch the font.

That is five sequential steps before the font even starts downloading. The font is on the critical path for text rendering (FOIT/FOUT), and every step adds latency.

Resource hints break this sequential dependency. A preload for the font tells the browser "fetch this now, at high priority" — the browser starts fetching the font in parallel with the CSS, eliminating four round-trips.

The same logic applies to third-party origins. A preconnect for a font CDN starts the DNS, TCP, and TLS handshake before the browser knows it needs to fetch from that origin. When the font request is finally made, the connection is already warm.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No way to hint future resources Browser discovered resources sequentially No DNS pre-resolution Every new origin required a DNS round-trip No connection pre-warming TCP + TLS handshake blocked first request No priority control Browser fetched resources in discovery order No next-page preparation Every navigation started from scratch No declarative prerendering rel=prerender was Chrome-only and resource-heavy

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
dns-prefetch and preconnect were the earliest hints, introduced around 2008–2013. They solved the problem of third-party origins adding latency to the critical path.

preload shipped in Chrome 50 (2016) and standardized the ability to fetch a resource at high priority before the browser would normally discover it.

prefetch shipped alongside preload as the low-priority counterpart for future navigations.

modulepreload shipped in Chrome 66 (2018) to solve the problem of ES modules having a nested dependency graph — the browser needed to fetch the entry module first, parse it, discover its imports, then fetch those. modulepreload fetches the entry module and its declared static dependencies in one go.

103 Early Hints was standardized as RFC 8297 in 2017 and shipped in Chrome 103 (2022). It lets the server send preload directives before the full HTML response is ready.

The Speculation Rules API shipped in Chrome 105 (2022) as a replacement for the deprecated <link rel="prerender"> hint. Chrome deprecated rel=prerender because it was not broadly supported beyond Chrome, and it was not a very expressive API.

In 2026, resource hints are baseline and expected. Browsers support them universally; frameworks emit them automatically; the question is whether you are over-using them. Over-using preconnect can exhaust the per-origin connection budget on mobile networks. A preload for the wrong file pays full bandwidth cost without a win.

docs.title: dns-prefetch — DNS Resolution Only
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• rel="dns-prefetch" — resolves the hostname to an IP address in advance.
  • Costs almost nothing — just a DNS lookup.
  • Use when: you have many third-party origins and want to pre-resolve their DNS in bulk.
  • Do not use when: you have only one or two critical origins — use preconnect instead.

docs.title: preconnect — Full Connection Priming
docs.text:
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• rel="preconnect" — completes the full connection handshake: DNS + TCP + TLS.
  • crossorigin — required for origins that serve CORS-enabled resources (fonts, modules).
  • Use when: you know the browser will connect to a third-party origin, and that connection is on the critical path.
  • Do not use when: you are unsure the origin will be used — preconnect opens a real socket.

docs.title: preload — High-Priority Fetch for the Current Page
docs.text:
<!-- Preload a font -->
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

<!-- Preload a hero image -->
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">

<!-- Preload critical CSS -->
<link rel="preload" href="/critical.css" as="style">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• rel="preload" — fetches the resource at high priority for the current page.
  • as — required. Tells the browser the resource type (font, image, style, script, etc.). Without as, the browser cannot set the correct priority or apply the correct security checks.
  • crossorigin — required for fonts and other CORS-enabled resources, even same-origin.
  • fetchpriority="high" — reinforces the priority signal for LCP images.
  • Critical rule: preload only resources the browser would discover late (fonts in CSS, LCP images in JS). Preloading resources the browser already discovers early (same-origin scripts, stylesheets in <head>) wastes bandwidth.

docs.title: modulepreload — ES Module Preloading
docs.text: <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• rel="modulepreload" — fetches an ES module and its declared static dependencies.
  • Unlike preload as="script", it parses the module's import statements and fetches them recursively.
  • Use when: you have a critical entry-point module in an ESM-shipped app.
  • Browser support: Chrome 66+, Edge 79+, Safari 17+, Firefox 115+.

docs.title: prefetch — Low-Priority Fetch for Future Navigation
docs.text:
<link rel="prefetch" href="/next-page.html" as="document">
<link rel="prefetch" href="/product-details.js" as="script">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• rel="prefetch" — fetches the resource at low priority for future navigation.
  • The browser downloads during idle time, after the current page has loaded.
  • Use when: the user is likely to navigate to a specific next page (e.g., the next article in a list).
  • Do not use when: you are unsure the user will navigate there — prefetch wastes bandwidth on unused resources.

docs.title: The as Attribute
docs.text:
The as attribute is required for preload and recommended for prefetch. It tells the browser the resource type, which determines:

  • Fetch priority.
  • Request headers (Accept, etc.).
  • Security checks (CSP, SRI).
  • Cache behavior.
as value Resource type font Web font image Image style Stylesheet script Script document HTML document fetch Fetch/XHR video Video audio Audio track Text track worker Web Worker

docs.title: The fetchpriority Attribute
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">
Value Effect high Fetch at highest priority low Fetch at low priority auto Default priority

docs.title: The "Warm-Up" Mental Model
docs.text:
Resource hints are a warm-up for the browser:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  dns-prefetch    → "Learn the address"       │
│  preconnect      → "Open the connection"     │
│  preload         → "Fetch this now"          │
│  prefetch        → "Fetch this later"        │
│  modulepreload   → "Fetch this module tree"  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Think of a race car driver. dns-prefetch is looking up the track address. preconnect is driving to the track. preload is starting the engine. prefetch is warming up the tires for the next race. modulepreload is loading the entire pit crew.

docs.title: The "Cost vs. Benefit" Mental Model
docs.text:
Each hint has a cost and a benefit:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  dns-prefetch                                │
│  Cost: Very low    Benefit: Low–Medium       │
│  └── DNS lookup only                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  preconnect                                  │
│  Cost: Low–Medium  Benefit: Medium–High      │
│  └── DNS + TCP + TLS handshake              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  preload                                     │
│  Cost: Medium–High Benefit: High (if correct)│
│  └── Full resource download                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  prefetch                                    │
│  Cost: Low         Benefit: High (next page) │
│  └── Low-priority download                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  modulepreload                               │
│  Cost: Medium      Benefit: High (ESM)       │
│  └── Module + dependencies                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Over-using preconnect can exhaust the per-origin connection budget on mobile networks. Over-using preload can delay other critical resources by competing for bandwidth.

docs.title: The "Discover vs. Hint" Mental Model
docs.text:
The browser has a preload scanner that runs ahead of the main parser. It discovers resources early — but it cannot see:

  • Fonts referenced inside CSS files.
  • Images referenced inside CSS background-image.
  • Resources loaded dynamically by JavaScript.
  • Resources behind @import in CSS.

These are the resources that preload helps. If the browser already discovers a resource early, preloading it is redundant:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BROWSER DISCOVERS EARLY (no preload needed) │
│  └── <script src> in <head>                  │
│  └── <link rel="stylesheet"> in <head>       │
│  └── <img src> in initial HTML               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  BROWSER DISCOVERS LATE (preload helps)      │
│  └── Fonts in CSS @font-face                 │
│  └── Images in CSS background-image          │
│  └── LCP image loaded by JavaScript          │
│  └── Module dependencies                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Hypothesis, Not Configuration" Mental Model
docs.text:
Resource hints are performance hypotheses — not configuration. Each hint is a bet that the browser will need the resource. If the bet is right, performance improves. If the bet is wrong, bandwidth is wasted.

A preload for a font the browser would have
discovered 50ms later is harmless.

A preload for the wrong file pays full
bandwidth cost without a win.

Validate every hint with WebPageTest's "no-cache" filmstrip before shipping.

docs.title: The "Three Tiers of Preparation" Mental Model
docs.text:
Resource hints prepare for three time horizons:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CURRENT PAGE (right now)                    │
│  └── preload                                 │
│  └── modulepreload                           │
│  └── preconnect                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  NEXT NAVIGATION (seconds from now)          │
│  └── prefetch                                │
│  └── Speculation Rules API (prefetch)        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  POSSIBLE NAVIGATION (maybe)                 │
│  └── dns-prefetch                            │
│  └── Speculation Rules API (prerender)       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Concept 1: dns-prefetch
docs.text:
Resolves a hostname to an IP address in advance. Costs almost nothing — just a DNS lookup. Use when you have many third-party origins and want to pre-resolve their DNS in bulk.

<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">

docs.title: Concept 2: preconnect
docs.text:
Completes the full connection handshake: DNS + TCP + TLS. Costs more than dns-prefetch because it opens a real socket. Use for critical third-party origins — fonts, analytics, image CDN. Limit to 1–2 origins to avoid exhausting the connection budget.

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

docs.title: Concept 3: preload
docs.text:
Fetches a current-page resource at high priority. Requires the as attribute. Use for resources the browser discovers late — fonts in CSS, LCP images in JS, critical CSS.

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: Concept 4: modulepreload
docs.text:
Preloads an ES module and its declared static dependencies. Unlike preload as="script", it parses the module's import statements and fetches them recursively. Use for critical entry-point modules in ESM-shipped apps.

<link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">

docs.title: Concept 5: prefetch
docs.text:
Fetches a future-navigation resource at low priority. The browser downloads during idle time. Use for likely next pages — the next article in a list, the next step in a funnel.

<link rel="prefetch" href="/next-page.html" as="document">

docs.title: Concept 6: 103 Early Hints
docs.text:
An HTTP status code (RFC 8297) that lets the server send preload and preconnect directives before the final response is ready. The browser starts opening connections and pulling critical assets in parallel with the origin's render time.

HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
Link: </styles/main.css>; rel=preload; as=style
Link: </fonts/inter-var.woff2>; rel=preload; as=font; crossorigin
Link: <https://cdn.example.com>; rel=preconnect

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Critical detail: 103 Early Hints only works over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. HTTP/1.1 cannot interleave a 1xx response with a later 200 on the same connection.

docs.title: Concept 7: The Speculation Rules API
docs.text:
A JSON-based declarative API that lets you prefetch or prerender likely next pages. Replaces the deprecated <link rel="prerender">.

<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prerender": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
        "eagerness": "moderate"
    }],
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}
</script>

docs.title: Concept 8: Prerender vs. Prefetch
docs.text: rel="prefetch" Speculation Rules (prefetch) Speculation Rules (prerender) What it loads HTML only HTML only Full page JS execution No No Yes Dynamic rules No Yes Yes Eagerness control No Yes Yes URL pattern matching No Yes Yes Cross-site support No Limited No Cache-Control bypass No Yes Yes Battery/Data Saver aware No Yes Yes

docs.title: Concept 9: Eagerness Levels
docs.text:
Speculation Rules support three eagerness levels:

Level When it triggers conservative On click moderate On hover (200ms) eager Immediately on page load

docs.title: Concept 10: The as Attribute
docs.text: Required for preload. Tells the browser the resource type, which determines fetch priority, request headers, security checks, and cache behavior. Without as, the browser may fetch the resource twice.

docs.title: Concept 11: fetchpriority
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">
Value Effect high Highest priority low Low priority auto Default

docs.title: Concept 12: crossorigin for Fonts
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

Fonts always require crossorigin, even same-origin. Without it, the browser fetches the font twice.

docs.title: Concept 13: The Preload Scanner
docs.text: The browser's preload scanner runs ahead of the main parser and discovers resources early. It cannot see fonts in CSS, images in CSS background, or resources loaded by JavaScript. These are the resources preload helps.

docs.title: Concept 14: Browser Support
docs.text: Hint Chrome Edge Firefox Safari dns-prefetch ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ preconnect ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ preload ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ modulepreload ✅ 66+ ✅ 79+ ✅ 115+ ✅ 17+ prefetch ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ Speculation Rules ✅ 105+ ✅ ❌ ❌ (26.2, disabled) 103 Early Hints ✅ 103+ ✅ 103+ ✅ 120+ ❌ (preconnect only)

docs.title: Concept 15: 103 Early Hints Browser Support
docs.text:
• Chrome 103+
  • Edge 103+
  • Firefox 120+
  • Safari: honors only preconnect hints

docs.title: Concept 16: Cloudflare Early Hints
docs.text: Cloudflare runs the most pragmatic deployment: the edge sniffs Link: rel=preload / rel=preconnect headers from cached origin responses and replays them as 103 hints on subsequent requests. Reports a typical median LCP improvement of ~30%.

docs.title: Concept 17: The prerender Sunset
docs.text: Chrome deprecated <link rel="prerender"> because it was not broadly supported beyond Chrome, and it was not a very expressive API. The Speculation Rules API replaces it.

docs.title: Concept 18: Shared Dictionary Compression
docs.text: A related performance optimization that allows the server to compress a response against a previously-fetched response. Chrome team measured 99% byte savings on a same-origin app.js update against the previous build. Standardized in Chrome 130+ and Edge 130+.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Per-Origin Connection Budget
docs.text: Browsers limit the number of concurrent connections per origin (typically 6 for HTTP/1.1, unlimited multiplexing for HTTP/2+). Over-using preconnect can exhaust this budget on mobile networks, delaying other resources.

docs.title: Concept 20: Resource Hints Don't Help Googlebot
docs.text: Resource hints like prefetch, preload, and preconnect are irrelevant to Google's crawling infrastructure. Browser performance features solve latency problems that Google's infrastructure doesn't have. Google caches page resources separately and doesn't fetch them in real time the way a browser does. The hints still help users — faster page loads improve retention and conversion — but they do not influence crawling, indexing, or rankings.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Without Resource Hints
docs.text:
1.  HTML arrives, parser begins.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser encounters <link rel="stylesheet">.
    │
    ├── Fetch CSS (round-trip 1)
    ├── Parse CSS
    └── Discover font reference
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser must fetch the font:
    │
    ├── DNS lookup (round-trip 2)
    ├── TCP handshake (round-trip 3)
    ├── TLS handshake (round-trip 4)
    └── Fetch font (round-trip 5)
    │
    ▼
5 round-trips before font loads.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: With Resource Hints
docs.text:
1.  HTML arrives, parser begins.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser encounters <link rel="preconnect">.
    │
    └── Browser starts DNS + TCP + TLS in parallel.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser encounters <link rel="preload"> for font.
    │
    └── Browser starts fetching font immediately.
    │
    ▼
4.  Parser encounters <link rel="stylesheet">.
    │
    └── Fetch CSS (connection already warm, font already fetching).
    │
    ▼
5.  Font arrives before CSS finishes parsing.
    │
    ▼
1 round-trip (HTML) + parallel resource fetches.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Speculation Rules Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Page loads.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses <script type="speculationrules">.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser evaluates rules against current page:
    │   ├── URL pattern matching
    │   ├── Eagerness level
    │   └── Device conditions (memory, network, battery)
    │
    ▼
4.  For each matching link:
    │   ├── conservative → prefetch/prerender on click
    │   ├── moderate → prefetch/prerender on hover
    │   └── eager → prefetch/prerender immediately
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser prefetches HTML or prerenders full page.
    │
    ▼
6.  User navigates → page is ready instantly.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: 103 Early Hints Flow
docs.text:
Client                    Server
  │                          │
  ├── GET / ─────────────────►
  │                          │
  │◄── 103 Early Hints ──────┤
  │    Link: preload CSS     │
  │    Link: preconnect      │
  │                          │
  │── Preload CSS ──────────►│
  │                          │
  │◄── 200 OK + HTML ────────┤
  │                          │
  │── Render ───────────────►│

docs.title: The Preload Scanner
docs.text:
Modern browsers include a preload scanner that runs ahead of the main parser. It scans the raw HTML bytes for resource references and starts fetching them before the parser reaches them. The scanner can see <script src>, <link rel="stylesheet">, and <img src> in the initial HTML.

The scanner cannot see:

  • Fonts referenced inside CSS files.
  • Images referenced in CSS background-image.
  • Resources loaded dynamically by JavaScript.
  • Resources behind @import in CSS.

These are the resources that preload helps.

docs.title: The Connection Pool
docs.text:
Browsers maintain a connection pool per origin. For HTTP/1.1, the limit is typically 6 connections per origin. For HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, multiplexing allows unlimited concurrent streams over a single connection.

preconnect opens a socket in this pool. Over-using it can exhaust the pool on mobile networks.

docs.title: The Fetch Priority Engine
docs.text:
The browser assigns a priority to every resource based on:

  • Resource type (as attribute).
  • Position in the document.
  • fetchpriority attribute.
  • Whether it is render-blocking.

preload with as="font" gets a higher priority than a font discovered via CSS.

docs.title: The Speculation Rules Engine
docs.text:
The Speculation Rules API is browser-managed. The browser decides whether to honor a rule based on:

  • Available memory.
  • Network conditions.
  • CPU load.
  • Battery level.
  • Data Saver mode.

With hardcoded <link> tags, the browser has less context and cannot be as smart about what it actually executes.

docs.title: The 103 Early Hints Architecture
docs.text: 103 Early Hints requires HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 because HTTP/1.1 cannot interleave a 1xx response with a later 200 on the same connection. The server sends an interim response with Link headers, then the final response.

docs.title: Resource Hints Implementation Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Identify the critical path:
    │   ├── LCP element
    │   ├── Critical fonts
    │   └── Critical CSS
    │
    ▼
2.  Identify late-discovered resources:
    │   ├── Fonts in CSS
    │   ├── LCP image in JS
    │   └── Module dependencies
    │
    ▼
3.  Add preconnect for critical third-party origins:
    │   └── Font CDN, analytics, image CDN
    │
    ▼
4.  Add preload for late-discovered critical resources:
    │   ├── Hero image (fetchpriority="high")
    │   ├── Primary font
    │   └── Critical CSS
    │
    ▼
5.  Add modulepreload for critical ESM entry points.
    │
    ▼
6.  Add prefetch for likely next pages.
    │
    ▼
7.  Add Speculation Rules for instant navigation.
    │
    ▼
8.  Validate with WebPageTest "no-cache" filmstrip.
    │
    ▼
9.  Measure with Lighthouse and CrUX.

docs.title: Audit Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Check for over-used preconnect:
    │   └── More than 2-3 origins?
    │
    ▼
2.  Check for unused preloads:
    │   └── Chrome console warns about unused preloads.
    │
    ▼
3.  Check for preloaded resources the browser discovers early:
    │   └── Same-origin scripts and stylesheets in <head>.
    │
    ▼
4.  Check for missing preloads:
    │   └── LCP image, primary font, critical CSS.
    │
    ▼
5.  Check for missing crossorigin on font preloads.
    │
    ▼
6.  Check for missing as attributes.
    │
    ▼
7.  Fix, re-validate, repeat.

docs.title: Example 1: Font Preloading
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Preconnect to the font origin -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload the primary font -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <style>
        @font-face {
            font-family: 'Inter';
            src: url('/fonts/inter-var.woff2') format('woff2-variations');
            font-display: swap;
            font-weight: 100 900;
        }
        body { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif; }
    </style>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • preconnect to fonts.gstatic.com starts the connection handshake early.
  • preload for the font fetches it at high priority, before the CSS is parsed.
  • crossorigin is required for font preloads, even same-origin.
  • font-display: swap renders text immediately with fallback.

docs.title: Example 2: LCP Image Preloading
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero-1200.avif"
          imagesrcset="/hero-400.avif 400w,
                       /hero-800.avif 800w,
                       /hero-1200.avif 1200w"
          imagesizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px,
                      (max-width: 1200px) 800px,
                      1200px"
          fetchpriority="high">
</head>
<body>
    <img src="/hero-1200.avif"
         srcset="/hero-400.avif 400w,
                 /hero-800.avif 800w,
                 /hero-1200.avif 1200w"
         sizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px,
                (max-width: 1200px) 800px,
                1200px"
         alt="Product hero image"
         width="1200"
         height="600"
         fetchpriority="high">
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • preload with imagesrcset and imagesizes matches the <img> attributes.
  • fetchpriority="high" tells the browser this is the LCP element.
  • width and height prevent layout shift.
  • The image is in the initial HTML — not lazy-loaded — because it is the LCP element.

docs.title: Example 3: modulepreload for ESM Entry Point
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">
</head>
<body>
    <script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • modulepreload fetches /js/app.js and its declared static dependencies.
  • The browser parses the module's import statements and fetches them recursively.
  • When <script type="module"> executes, the module graph is already in the module map.

docs.title: Example 4: Prefetch for Likely Next Page
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Prefetch the next article in the list -->
    <link rel="prefetch" href="/blog/next-article.html" as="document">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • prefetch fetches the HTML at low priority during idle time.
  • When the user clicks the link, the HTML is already in the cache.
  • Reduces TTFB on the next navigation.
  • Does not execute JavaScript or apply styles until the user clicks.

docs.title: Example 5: Speculation Rules for Instant Navigation
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prerender": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
        "eagerness": "moderate"
    }],
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • prerender on hover (moderate) for product pages — likely next navigation.
  • prefetch on click (conservative) for blog pages — less certain next navigation.
  • The browser decides whether to honor the rule based on device conditions.

docs.title: Example 6: 103 Early Hints with Express
docs.text:
app.get('/', (req, res) => {
    res.writeEarlyHints({
        'link': [
            '</styles/main.css>; rel=preload; as=style',
            '</fonts/inter-var.woff2>; rel=preload; as=font; crossorigin',
            '<https://cdn.example.com>; rel=preconnect'
        ]
    });

    res.sendFile('index.html');
});

Code Breakdown:

  • The server sends 103 Early Hints with preload/preconnect directives.
  • The browser starts fetching critical resources while the server prepares the HTML.
  • Requires HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
  • Supported in Chrome 103+, Edge 103+, Firefox 120+.

docs.title: Example 7: Complete Production Head
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>How SVG Embedding Works — Dev Notes</title>

    <!-- Preconnect to critical third-party origins -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com">

    <!-- Preload critical fonts -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload LCP image -->
    <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">

    <!-- modulepreload ESM entry point -->
    <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">

    <!-- Prefetch likely next page -->
    <link rel="prefetch" href="/next-article.html" as="document">

    <!-- Critical CSS -->
    <style>/* above-the-fold styles */</style>
</head>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Hint Rationale Web font from Google Fonts preconnect + preload Font is discovered late in CSS LCP hero image preload + fetchpriority="high" LCP element must load fast Critical CSS preload as="style" CSS blocks render ESM entry module modulepreload Module dependencies are discovered sequentially Next article in a list prefetch Likely next navigation Product page on hover Speculation Rules (prerender) Instant navigation on click Many third-party origins dns-prefetch Cheap pre-resolution Analytics origin preconnect Third-party connection on critical path CDN for images preconnect Image CDN connection on critical path Multi-step funnel Speculation Rules (prefetch) Next step likely

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Preload only late-discovered resources. Why: the browser already discovers early resources; preloading them wastes bandwidth.
  2. Use preconnect for critical third-party origins only. Why: limit to 1–2 origins to avoid exhausting the connection budget.
  3. Use dns-prefetch for many third-party origins. Why: cheaper than preconnect and effective in bulk.
  4. Always include the as attribute on preload. Why: without it, the browser cannot set the correct priority or security checks.
  5. Always include crossorigin on font preloads. Why: fonts require CORS, even same-origin.
  6. Use fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image preload. Why: reinforces the priority signal.
  7. Use modulepreload for ESM entry points. Why: fetches the module and its dependencies.
  8. Use prefetch for likely next pages. Why: reduces TTFB on the next navigation.
  9. Use Speculation Rules for instant navigation. Why: replaces the deprecated rel=prerender.
  10. Choose the right eagerness level. Why: conservative for click, moderate for hover, eager for immediate.
  11. Validate with WebPageTest "no-cache" filmstrip. Why: resource hints are hypotheses — test them.
  12. Check for unused preloads in Chrome console. Why: Chrome warns about preloaded resources that were never used.
  13. Do not preload the same resource twice. Why: duplicate preloads waste bandwidth.
  14. Do not preload resources behind authentication. Why: the browser will fetch them again after auth.
  15. Do not over-use preconnect. Why: each opens a real socket and consumes the connection budget.
  16. Combine 103 Early Hints with preload/preconnect. Why: sends directives before the HTML response.
  17. Use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 for 103 Early Hints. Why: HTTP/1.1 cannot interleave 1xx and 200.
  18. Remember resource hints don't help Googlebot. Why: they help users, not crawlers.
  19. Audit resource hints after every framework upgrade. Why: framework behavior changes.
  20. Measure with Lighthouse and CrUX. Why: lab + field data reveals different issues.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Preloading Resources the Browser Discovers Early
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style">
<link rel="preload" href="/js/app.js" as="script">

Why it's wrong: The browser discovers these in the HTML anyway. Preloading them wastes bandwidth.

✅ Correct: Preload only late-discovered resources — fonts in CSS, LCP images in JS.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing as on Preload
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2">

Why it's wrong: Without as, the browser cannot set the correct priority or security checks. It may fetch the resource twice.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing crossorigin on Font Preload
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2">

Why it's wrong: Fonts require CORS. Without crossorigin, the browser fetches the font twice.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Over-Using preconnect
docs.text:
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://analytics.example.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://ads.example.com">

Why it's wrong: Each preconnect opens a real socket. Over-using it exhausts the per-origin connection budget on mobile networks.

✅ Correct: Limit to 1–2 critical origins. Use dns-prefetch for the rest.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Preloading the Wrong Image
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/logo.png">

Why it's wrong: The logo is not the LCP element. Preloading it wastes bandwidth.

✅ Correct: Preload the LCP image.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using rel="prerender" Instead of Speculation Rules
docs.text:
<link rel="prerender" href="/next-page">

Why it's wrong: rel=prerender is deprecated and Chrome-only. It consumed too much memory and network bandwidth.

✅ Correct: Use the Speculation Rules API.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Using modulepreload for ESM Entry Points
docs.text:
<script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>

Why it's wrong: The browser fetches the entry module, parses it, discovers its imports, then fetches those — sequentially.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">
<script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Preload for the LCP Image
docs.text:
<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" width="1200" height="600">

Why it's wrong: The LCP image is discovered late, delaying LCP.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.jpg" fetchpriority="high">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Resource Hints Help SEO
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/hero.jpg" as="image">

Why it's wrong: Resource hints are irrelevant to Google's crawling infrastructure. They help users, not crawlers.

✅ Correct: Use them for user experience; use critical HTML and SSR for crawlability.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Validating with WebPageTest
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Resource hints are hypotheses. Without validation, you may be wasting bandwidth.

✅ Correct: Validate with WebPageTest "no-cache" filmstrip before shipping.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• dns-prefetch costs almost nothing — just a DNS lookup.
  • preconnect opens a real socket — limited to 1–2 origins.
  • preload at high priority — competes with other critical resources for bandwidth.
  • prefetch at low priority — downloads during idle time.
  • modulepreload fetches the module graph — saves sequential round-trips.
  • 103 Early Hints saves one round-trip for critical resources.
  • Speculation Rules can cut navigation time to single-digit milliseconds.
  • Shared dictionary compression saves 99% on bundle updates.
  • Brotli produces 15–25% smaller output than gzip for HTML/CSS/JS.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Preload only late-discovered resources.
  2. Limit preconnect to 1–2 origins.
  3. Use dns-prefetch for the rest.
  4. Use fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image.
  5. Use modulepreload for ESM entry points.
  6. Use Speculation Rules for instant navigation.
  7. Validate with WebPageTest.
  8. Check for unused preloads in Chrome console.
  9. Combine 103 Early Hints with preload/preconnect.
  10. Measure with Lighthouse and CrUX.

docs.title: Preload and CSP
docs.text:
Preloaded resources must satisfy CSP directives:

Content-Security-Policy: font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com

docs.title: Preload and Subresource Integrity
docs.text:
Preloaded scripts and styles should use SRI where possible:

<link rel="preload" href="/js/lib.js" as="script" integrity="sha384-...">

docs.title: Prefetch and Privacy
docs.text: prefetch reveals what resources the page will load next. Do not prefetch URLs that leak sensitive information.

docs.title: Speculation Rules and Privacy
docs.text: Prerendering fetches and renders pages in the background. Do not prerender pages behind authentication or pages that perform side effects on load.

docs.title: 103 Early Hints and CORS
docs.text: 103 Early Hints responses must respect CORS. Cross-origin preloads require crossorigin.

docs.title: Resource Hints and Cache Poisoning
docs.text: A malicious prefetch or preload for a sensitive URL could leak information through timing. Validate all hint URLs.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Network panel — inspect resource priorities and timing.
  • Chrome DevTools → Coverage panel — shows unused resources.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — audits for render-blocking resources.
  • Chrome console — warns about unused preloads.
  • document.querySelectorAll('link[rel="preload"]') — list all preloads in console.
  • WebPageTest — filmstrip view of the critical path.
  • PageSpeed Insights — field + lab data combined.
  • Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) — real-world Core Web Vitals.
  • <link rel="preload"> warnings — Chrome warns about unused preloads.
  • render-blocking-resources audit — Lighthouse flags blocking CSS and JS.
  • largest-contentful-paint-element audit — Lighthouse identifies the LCP element.
  • Test with network throttling — Slow 3G reveals issues invisible on fast connections.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• dns-prefetch — for many third-party origins.
  • preconnect — for 1–2 critical third-party origins.
  • preload — for late-discovered critical resources (fonts, LCP images, critical CSS).
  • modulepreload — for ESM entry points.
  • prefetch — for likely next pages.
  • Speculation Rules — for instant navigation on multi-page sites.
  • 103 Early Hints — when server/CDN support exists.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not preload resources the browser discovers early. Use the HTML.
  • Do not preconnect to more than 2–3 origins. Use dns-prefetch for the rest.
  • Do not prefetch pages the user is unlikely to visit. Wastes bandwidth.
  • Do not prerender pages behind authentication. Side effects on load.
  • Do not rely on resource hints for SEO. They help users, not crawlers.
  • Do not use rel="prerender". It is deprecated.
