docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Resource hints don't help Googlebot — Gary Illyes confirmed they are irrelevant to Google's crawling infrastructure.
  • preconnect opens a real socket — over-using it exhausts the per-origin connection budget on mobile networks.
  • Fonts require crossorigin on preload, even same-origin — without it, the browser fetches the font twice.
  • as is required for preload — without it, the browser may fetch the resource twice.
  • modulepreload fetches the module graph — unlike preload as="script", it resolves imports recursively.
  • 103 Early Hints only works over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 — HTTP/1.1 cannot interleave 1xx and 200 responses.
  • Cloudflare's Early Hints deployment reports ~30% median LCP improvement.
  • The Speculation Rules API replaced rel="prerender" — Chrome deprecated the old hint because it was Chrome-only and not expressive.
  • Speculation Rules support conservative, moderate, and eager eagerness levels.
  • Prerender rules execute JavaScript — prefetch rules do not.
  • Shared dictionary compression saves 99% on bundle updates — Chrome team measured this on a same-origin app.js update.
  • Brotli produces 15–25% smaller output than gzip for HTML/CSS/JS.
  • Zstandard matches gzip on ratio while compressing meaningfully faster.
  • Safari does not support prefetch — only Chrome, Edge, and Firefox do.
  • Safari honors only preconnect hints in 103 Early Hints responses.
  • modulepreload is supported in Chrome 66+, Edge 79+, Firefox 115+, Safari 17+.
  • The preload scanner cannot see fonts in CSS or images in CSS background — these are the resources preload helps.
  • Resource hints are performance hypotheses, not configuration — validate with WebPageTest.
  • The fastest one-line win in many stacks is enabling brotli_static and shipping pre-compressed .br artifacts.
  • Resource hints are a warm-up for the browser — they eliminate latency before it happens.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Resource hints tell the browser about future resources before it discovers them.
  • Five primary hints: dns-prefetch, preconnect, preload, modulepreload, prefetch.
  • dns-prefetch resolves a hostname only — cheap, use in bulk for many origins.
  • preconnect completes DNS + TCP + TLS — limit to 1–2 critical origins.
  • preload fetches a current-page resource at high priority — requires as.
  • modulepreload preloads an ES module and its dependencies.
  • prefetch fetches a future-navigation resource at low priority.
  • 103 Early Hints lets the server send preload/preconnect before the full response.
  • The Speculation Rules API enables prefetch and prerender for instant navigation.
  • Resource hints don't help Googlebot — they help users.
  • Preload only late-discovered resources — the browser discovers early resources.
  • Always include as on preload — it determines priority and security checks.
  • Always include crossorigin on font preloads — fonts require CORS.
  • Use fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image preload.
  • Validate with WebPageTest "no-cache" filmstrip — resource hints are hypotheses.
  • Over-using preconnect exhausts the connection budget.
  • Combine 103 Early Hints with preload/preconnect when server support exists.
  • Use Speculation Rules for instant navigation on multi-page sites.
  • Resource hints are baseline and expected in 2026 — the question is whether you are applying them correctly.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Preload is a resource hint that tells the browser to fetch a specific resource at high priority for the current page, before the browser would otherwise discover it during normal HTML parsing. It is declared with a <link rel="preload"> element in the <head>.

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

The preload hint exists to solve a specific problem: late discovery. The browser's preload scanner reads raw HTML bytes and fetches resources early — but it cannot see resources that are:

  • Referenced inside CSS files (fonts, background images).
  • Referenced inside JavaScript (dynamically inserted elements).
  • Hidden behind CSS @import chains.
  • Referenced in attributes that the scanner does not scan.

preload closes this gap. It tells the browser "this resource is needed on this page, and you will discover it late — fetch it now."

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Preload serves several essential purposes:

  • Eliminate late-discovery latency — fonts in CSS, LCP images in JavaScript, above-the-fold background images.
  • Prioritize critical resources — moves a resource from the back of the fetch queue to the front.
  • Accelerate LCP — preloading the LCP image reduces LCP by hundreds of milliseconds.
  • Eliminate font swap delay — preloading the primary font reduces FOUT/FOIT.
  • Reduce render-blocking cost — preloading critical CSS lets it arrive before the HTML parser needs it.
  • Improve TTI and INP — preloading critical scripts shortens the time to interactivity.

Preload is a performance hypothesis — a bet that the resource will be needed. If the bet is wrong, the browser pays the full bandwidth cost of fetching the resource, may issue a console warning, and may delay other critical resources by competing for bandwidth.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Resource Hints
│
├── dns-prefetch     ← resolve hostname only
├── preconnect       ← DNS + TCP + TLS handshake
├── preload          ← fetch a current-page resource at high priority
├── modulepreload    ← fetch an ES module graph at high priority
└── prefetch         ← fetch a next-navigation resource at low priority

Preload is the middle tier of resource hints: more aggressive than preconnect, less speculative than prefetch. It is the hint that solves the greatest number of real-world performance problems, and the hint that most often gets misused.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The browser's preload scanner runs ahead of the main HTML parser, fetching resources it can see in the raw bytes of the HTML: <script src>, <link rel="stylesheet">, <img src>, and <link rel="preload"> itself.

What it cannot see:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WHAT THE PRELOAD SCANNER CAN SEE            │
│  ├── <script src>                            │
│  ├── <link rel="stylesheet">                 │
│  ├── <img src>                               │
│  ├── <link rel="preload">                    │
│  └── <video>, <audio>, <source>              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WHAT THE PRELOAD SCANNER CANNOT SEE         │
│  ├── @font-face inside CSS                   │
│  ├── background-image inside CSS             │
│  ├── <img src> inserted by JavaScript        │
│  ├── <script src> inserted by JavaScript     │
│  └── @import chains inside CSS               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A font referenced inside a CSS file is discovered only after the CSS file has been downloaded and parsed. The font request starts several hundred milliseconds after it could have. preload starts it now.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Fonts hidden inside CSS Fonts discovered after CSS parse — huge delay LCP images set via JS LCP image discovered after JS execution Critical CSS behind @import Sequential round-trips for stylesheets No priority override Browser fetched resources in DOM order No way to hint background images Above-the-fold hero backgrounds discovered late No declarative script priority Scripts fetched at default priority

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
<link rel="preload"> shipped in Chrome 50 (April 2016) and was standardized in the HTML Living Standard. Before it, developers hacked around the problem with:

  • Invisible <img> elements — fetching a font by referencing it in a zero-sized <img> tag (doesn't work for fonts, but was tried).
  • <object> tags — fetching a resource by embedding it.
  • XHR/fetch in inline scripts — fetching resources manually, bypassing the cache.
  • CSS @font-face on a hidden element — a hack to force a font fetch.

All of these were fragile, non-standard, and easy to break. preload made it declarative: one line in the <head>.

The spec has since evolved:

  • fetchpriority attribute (2023) — explicit priority control.
  • imagesrcset and imagesizes on preload (2021) — preload responsive images correctly.
  • Interaction with 103 Early Hints (2022) — server-sent preload directives.
  • Automatic preloading of LCP images (Chrome, 2024) — Chrome fetches the LCP image at highest priority even without an explicit preload hint, further reducing the need in some cases.

In 2026, preload is baseline and universally supported — and increasingly automatic. Chrome's LCP image auto-preloading means developers can often skip the manual hint for the hero image. But for fonts, critical CSS, and JS-discovered images, preload remains essential.

docs.title: The Minimal Preload
docs.text: <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose Required? rel="preload" Declares the hint ✅ href The URL to preload ✅ as The resource type (font, image, style, script, fetch, track, video, audio, document) ✅ type The MIME type — allows the browser to skip unsupported formats Recommended crossorigin CORS mode — required for fonts and cross-origin resources Required for fonts media A media query — the browser skips the preload if the query does not match Optional fetchpriority Priority override (high, low, auto) Optional

docs.title: The as Attribute — Required
docs.text:
The as attribute is required for preload. It tells the browser:

  • What kind of resource this is.
  • What Accept header to send.
  • What CSP directives to check against.
  • What priority to assign.
  • What cache partition to use.

Without as, the browser:

  • Sets a very low priority.
  • Sets the wrong Accept header.
  • May fetch the resource twice (once without as, once with).

Valid as values:

Value Resource type Notes font Web font Always requires crossorigin image Image Supports imagesrcset and imagesizes style Stylesheet — script JavaScript — fetch Fetch/XHR/WebSocket — document HTML document — video Video file — audio Audio file — track Text track — worker Web Worker —

docs.title: The crossorigin Attribute — Required for Fonts
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

Fonts are always fetched in CORS mode, even same-origin. If the preload lacks crossorigin, the browser:

  1. Fetches the font without CORS (no credentials).
  2. Fetches the font again with CORS when the CSS references it.

The result is a double fetch — the preload is wasted.

Use:

  • crossorigin (or crossorigin="anonymous") — for CORS requests without credentials.
  • crossorigin="use-credentials" — for CORS requests with credentials (rarely needed for fonts).

docs.title: Preloading a Responsive Image
docs.text:
<link rel="preload"
      as="image"
      href="/hero-1200.avif"
      imagesrcset="/hero-400.avif 400w,
                   /hero-800.avif 800w,
                   /hero-1200.avif 1200w"
      imagesizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px,
                  (max-width: 1200px) 800px,
                  1200px"
      fetchpriority="high">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• imagesrcset — the same srcset you would use on the <img> element.
  • imagesizes — the same sizes you would use on the <img> element.
  • fetchpriority="high" — reinforces the priority for the LCP element.
  • The href on the preload is a fallback for browsers that do not support imagesrcset.

docs.title: The Media Query Conditional
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/hero-desktop.avif" as="image" media="(min-width: 768px)">
<link rel="preload" href="/hero-mobile.avif" as="image" media="(max-width: 767px)">

Code Breakdown:

  • media — the browser skips the preload if the media query does not match the current environment.
  • Prevents preloading a desktop hero image on mobile devices.
  • When media matches, the resource is preloaded; when it doesn't, the preload is ignored entirely (no download).

docs.title: The Full Production Head
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>How SVG Embedding Works — Dev Notes</title>

    <!-- Preconnect to font CDN -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload primary font -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload LCP image (with responsive srcset) -->
    <link rel="preload"
          as="image"
          href="/hero-1200.avif"
          imagesrcset="/hero-400.avif 400w, /hero-800.avif 800w, /hero-1200.avif 1200w"
          imagesizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px, (max-width: 1200px) 800px, 1200px"
          fetchpriority="high">

    <!-- Critical CSS: inlined -->
    <style>/* above-the-fold styles */</style>

    <!-- Full CSS: async loaded -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
          onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
    <noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css"></noscript>
</head>

docs.title: The Preload + Async CSS Pattern
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
      onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
<noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css"></noscript>

Code Breakdown:

  • rel="preload" — fetches the stylesheet at high priority, but does not apply it.
  • onload="this.rel='stylesheet'" — swaps the relation to stylesheet after the fetch completes, applying the styles.
  • this.onload=null — prevents the handler from firing again if rel changes.
  • <noscript> fallback — applies the stylesheet for users without JavaScript.

Important caveat: This pattern was popularized in 2016–2019 but is no longer recommended in 2026. Modern browsers (Chrome 90+, Firefox 118+, Safari 17+) handle async CSS better with <link rel="stylesheet" media="print" onload="this.media='all'"> or, better, by inlining critical CSS and loading the full stylesheet normally. The preload-as-CSS pattern has measurable downsides: it bypasses the browser's render-blocking heuristic, which can cause FOUC on slow connections.

docs.title: The Preload + onload for Scripts
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/js/app.js" as="script">
<script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The preload fetches the script early.
  • The <script> tag executes it after the preload completes.
  • Rarely needed — the preload scanner already discovers <script src> in the initial HTML. Use preload for scripts only when they are referenced by other scripts or by CSS.

docs.title: The "Hands Raised Before the Question" Mental Model
docs.text:
The browser is a student taking an exam. The preload scanner is the student reading ahead. A preload hint is the student raising their hand before the teacher asks the question — announcing what they need before the teacher would naturally get to it.

Without preload:
  Teacher: "...and what font does this page use?"
  Student: (looks at CSS) "Inter."
  Teacher: "Go get it."
  [Round-trip]

With preload:
  Student: (raises hand) "I'll need Inter."
  Teacher: "Go get it now."
  [Round-trip starts earlier]

The end result is the same resource. The difference is when the fetch starts.

docs.title: The "Fetch vs. Apply" Mental Model
docs.text:
The most misunderstood aspect of preload: it fetches a resource, but it does not apply it.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  <link rel="preload">                        │
│  └── Fetches the resource                    │
│  └── Stores it in the cache                  │
│  └── Does NOT apply it                       │
│                                              │
│  When the actual <link rel="stylesheet">     │
│  or <script> tag needs the resource:         │
│  └── Browser retrieves it from cache         │
│  └── No second network request               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is why the as attribute matters: the browser must know what kind of resource this is so it can apply the correct security checks, priority, and cache partitioning.

docs.title: The "Late Discovery" Mental Model
docs.text:
Preload solves a specific problem: resources that the preload scanner cannot see.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE LATE-DISCOVERY CHAIN                    │
│                                              │
│  HTML → <link rel="stylesheet"> → CSS       │
│                    │                         │
│                    ▼                         │
│          @font-face { src: url(font) }       │
│                    │                         │
│                    ▼                         │
│              Font fetched                    │
│                                              │
│  Total sequential round-trips: 3             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WITH PRELOAD                                │
│                                              │
│  HTML → <link rel="preload" href="font">     │
│                    │                         │
│                    ▼                         │
│              Font fetched (parallel)         │
│                                              │
│  Total sequential round-trips: 1             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The savings come from parallelism — starting the font fetch at the same time as the CSS fetch, rather than waiting for it.

docs.title: The "Hypothesis, Not Directive" Mental Model
docs.text:
Preload is a hypothesis: "I think this resource will be needed soon."

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  GOOD HYPOTHESIS (Preload helps)             │
│  └── Font that the page definitely uses      │
│  └── LCP image visible in the initial viewport│
│  └── Critical CSS for above-the-fold content │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  BAD HYPOTHESIS (Preload wastes bandwidth)   │
│  └── Font for a page that changes font       │
│  └── Image below the fold                    │
│  └── Script not needed on this page          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every wrong preload is a wasted fetch. And on slow connections, a wasted preload competes with legitimate resources, delaying them.

docs.title: The "Discovery vs. Priority" Mental Model
docs.text:
Preload solves two related but distinct problems:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DISCOVERY PROBLEM                           │
│  The browser does not know it needs the      │
│  resource until too late.                    │
│  → Solved by: preload (fetch it now)         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  PRIORITY PROBLEM                            │
│  The browser knows it needs the resource     │
│  but fetches it at the wrong priority.       │
│  → Solved by: fetchpriority                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  COMBINED                                    │
│  Font hidden in CSS:                         │
│  → preload (discovery)                       │
│  → as="font" (priority)                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The as attribute solves both problems: it tells the browser to fetch the resource early and at the correct priority.

docs.title: Concept 1: The rel="preload" Link Element
docs.text: The declarative syntax for preload. Placed in the <head>. Supports href, as, type, crossorigin, media, fetchpriority, imagesrcset, and imagesizes.

docs.title: Concept 2: The as Attribute
docs.text: Required. Specifies the resource type. Without it, the browser may fetch the resource twice, may issue a console warning, and always uses the wrong priority.

docs.title: Concept 3: The crossorigin Attribute for Fonts
docs.text: Fonts always require crossorigin on preload, even same-origin. Without it, the browser fetches the font twice.

docs.title: Concept 4: The type Attribute
docs.text:
The type attribute lets the browser skip the preload if it does not support the format:

<link rel="preload" href="/font.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

If the browser does not support WOFF2, the preload is skipped — saving bandwidth.

docs.title: Concept 5: The media Attribute
docs.text:
The media attribute lets the browser conditionally skip the preload:

<link rel="preload" href="/hero-desktop.avif" as="image" media="(min-width: 768px)">

If the media query does not match, the preload is skipped entirely.

docs.title: Concept 6: The imagesrcset and imagesizes Attributes
docs.text: Preloading responsive images correctly requires imagesrcset and imagesizes — the same values as the corresponding <img> element.

docs.title: Concept 7: The fetchpriority Attribute
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">
Value Effect high Highest priority low Low priority auto Default

docs.title: Concept 8: The LCP Image Auto-Preload (2024+)
docs.text: Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers now automatically preload the LCP image at high priority, even without an explicit <link rel="preload">. This reduces the need for manual preloading of the LCP image on some sites — but the behavior is browser-specific. Manual preload is still recommended for cross-browser consistency.

docs.title: Concept 9: The Preload + onload CSS Pattern
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style"
      onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">

This pattern fetches the stylesheet at high priority and applies it after fetch. No longer recommended in 2026 — modern browsers handle this better, and the pattern can cause FOUC.

docs.title: Concept 10: Preload and 103 Early Hints
docs.text: The server can send preload directives in a 103 Early Hints response, before the full HTML is ready. The browser starts fetching critical resources while the server prepares the main response.

docs.title: Concept 11: Preload vs. Prefetch
docs.text: Preload Prefetch Priority High Low Target Current page Future navigation Trigger Immediately During idle time Cache Current navigation cache Next navigation cache

docs.title: Concept 12: Preload vs. Preconnect
docs.text: Preload Preconnect What it fetches A specific resource A connection to an origin Cost Full resource download DNS + TCP + TLS Use case Font, LCP image, critical CSS Third-party origin

docs.title: Concept 13: The Double-Fetch Trap
docs.text:
If you preload a resource with the wrong as value, the browser fetches it twice:

  • Once with the preload's as value.
  • Once with the actual resource's as value.

This is the most common preload mistake.

docs.title: Concept 14: The Unused Preload Warning
docs.text:
Chrome warns in the console when a preloaded resource is not used within 3 seconds:

The resource <URL> was preloaded using link preload but not used
within a few seconds from the window's load event.

Unused preloads waste bandwidth and should be removed.

docs.title: Concept 15: The Preload Cache Partition
docs.text: Preloaded resources are cached in the current navigation cache. They are available for the current page but not for cross-origin subresources (unless CORS is used).

docs.title: Concept 16: Preload and CSP
docs.text:
Preloaded resources must satisfy CSP directives:

Content-Security-Policy: font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com

docs.title: Concept 17: Preload and Subresource Integrity
docs.text:
Preloaded scripts and styles can use SRI:

<link rel="preload" href="/js/lib.js" as="script" integrity="sha384-...">

docs.title: Concept 18: Preload and content-visibility
docs.text: Preloading resources for content that is not rendered (because of content-visibility: auto) wastes bandwidth. Only preload resources that will be rendered.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Preload Cache
docs.text: Preloaded resources are cached. When the actual <link> or <script> tag references the resource, the browser retrieves it from cache — no second network request.

docs.title: Concept 20: Debugging Preload
docs.text: Chrome DevTools shows preload issues in the console, the Network panel, and the Coverage panel. Use all three when debugging.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Without Preload
docs.text:
1.  HTML arrives, parser begins.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser encounters <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">.
    │   └── Fetch CSS (round-trip 1)
    │
    ▼
3.  CSS arrives, parser parses it.
    │
    ▼
4.  Parser encounters @font-face { src: url(/fonts/inter.woff2) }.
    │   └── Fetch font (round-trip 2)
    │
    ▼
5.  Font arrives, text renders.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: With Preload
docs.text:
1.  HTML arrives, parser begins.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser encounters <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" crossorigin>.
    │   └── Fetch font (round-trip 1, parallel)
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser encounters <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">.
    │   └── Fetch CSS (round-trip 1, parallel)
    │
    ▼
4.  CSS arrives, parser parses it.
    │
    ▼
5.  Parser encounters @font-face { src: url(/fonts/inter.woff2) }.
    │   └── Font is already in cache (no round-trip)
    │
    ▼
6.  Text renders with the font already available.

Round-trips: 1 instead of 2.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Preload Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Browser parses <link rel="preload">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser determines the resource type from `as`.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser checks CSP against the resource type.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser starts fetching the resource at high priority.
    │
    ▼
5.  Resource is stored in the preload cache.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser parses the actual <link rel="stylesheet"> or <script>.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser retrieves the resource from the preload cache.
    │
    ▼
8.  Resource is applied (stylesheet applied, script executed).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Preload + 103 Early Hints
docs.text:
Client                    Server
  │                          │
  ├── GET / ─────────────────►
  │                          │
  │◄── 103 Early Hints ──────┤
  │    Link: preload font    │
  │    Link: preload hero    │
  │                          │
  │── Preload font ─────────►│
  │── Preload hero ─────────►│
  │                          │
  │◄── 200 OK + HTML ────────┤
  │                          │
  │── Render ───────────────►│

docs.title: The Preload Cache
docs.text:
Preloaded resources are stored in a preload cache — a separate cache from the HTTP cache. When the actual resource is requested (via <link>, <script>, <img>), the browser checks the preload cache first.

Preload requested  →  Preload cache  →  HTTP cache  →  Network
Actual requested   →  Preload cache  →  HTTP cache  →  Network

The preload cache is per-document and per-navigation. It is not shared across navigations.

docs.title: The Fetch Priority Engine
docs.text:
The browser assigns a priority to every resource based on:

  • Resource type (as attribute).
  • Position in the document.
  • fetchpriority attribute.
  • Whether it is render-blocking.
  • Whether it is LCP-related.

Preload with as="font" gets a higher priority than a font discovered via CSS.

docs.title: The CSP Check
docs.text:
The browser validates every preload against the page's CSP. If the CSP blocks the resource type, the preload is ignored.

Preload found
    │
    ▼
CSP check: does `as` value match a CSP directive?
    ├── Yes → proceed
    └── No  → block preload

docs.title: The Double-Fetch Protection
docs.text:
Modern browsers detect preload/actual mismatches and warn in the console:

The resource <URL> was preloaded using link preload but not used
within a few seconds from the window's load event.

The double-fetch happens when:

  • as is missing.
  • as is wrong (e.g., as="fetch" for a stylesheet).
  • crossorigin is missing for fonts.
  • type is missing (font preload without type may double-fetch on some browsers).

docs.title: The 103 Early Hints Parser
docs.text: When the browser receives a 103 Early Hints response, it extracts the Link headers and processes them as if they were <link> elements in the HTML. The parser does not wait for the final response to start fetching.

docs.title: Preload Implementation Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Identify late-discovered resources:
    │   ├── Fonts referenced in CSS
    │   ├── LCP images referenced in JS
    │   └── Above-the-fold background images in CSS
    │
    ▼
2.  Add preload for each resource:
    │   ├── Font: as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin
    │   ├── Image: as="image" fetchpriority="high" (with imagesrcset)
    │   └── CSS: as="style" (rare in 2026)
    │
    ▼
3.  Add preconnect for the font CDN.
    │
    ▼
4.  Validate:
    │   ├── Chrome console warnings for unused preloads
    │   ├── Network panel to verify resource loads once
    │   └── Coverage panel to check for unused bytes
    │
    ▼
5.  Measure LCP, FCP, TTI.

docs.title: Audit Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Check for preloaded resources that are not used:
    │   └── Chrome console warnings
    │
    ▼
2.  Check for double-fetched resources:
    │   └── Network panel — two requests for the same URL
    │
    ▼
3.  Check for missing `as`:
    │   └── Preload without `as` fetches at low priority
    │
    ▼
4.  Check for missing `crossorigin` on font preloads:
    │   └── Font double-fetched
    │
    ▼
5.  Check for preloaded resources the browser discovers early:
    │   └── Same-origin scripts and stylesheets in <head>
    │
    ▼
6.  Remove unused preloads.

docs.title: Example 1: Preloading a Font
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <style>
        @font-face {
            font-family: 'Inter';
            src: url('/fonts/inter-var.woff2') format('woff2-variations');
            font-display: swap;
            font-weight: 100 900;
        }
        body { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif; }
    </style>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • preconnect to fonts.gstatic.com starts the connection handshake early.
  • preload fetches the font at high priority.
  • crossorigin is required for font preloads.
  • type="font/woff2" lets the browser skip the preload if WOFF2 is unsupported.
  • font-display: swap renders text immediately with fallback.

docs.title: Example 2: Preloading the LCP Image
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="preload"
          as="image"
          href="/hero-1200.avif"
          imagesrcset="/hero-400.avif 400w, /hero-800.avif 800w, /hero-1200.avif 1200w"
          imagesizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px, (max-width: 1200px) 800px, 1200px"
          fetchpriority="high">
</head>
<body>
    <img src="/hero-1200.avif"
         srcset="/hero-400.avif 400w, /hero-800.avif 800w, /hero-1200.avif 1200w"
         sizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px, (max-width: 1200px) 800px, 1200px"
         alt="Product hero image"
         width="1200"
         height="600"
         fetchpriority="high">
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • preload with imagesrcset and imagesizes matches the <img> attributes.
  • fetchpriority="high" reinforces the LCP priority.
  • width and height prevent layout shift.

docs.title: Example 3: Preloading Critical CSS
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Preload the stylesheet at high priority -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/styles/critical.css" as="style">

    <!-- Then reference it as a stylesheet (browser uses the preloaded copy) -->
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/critical.css">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • preload fetches the stylesheet at high priority.
  • The <link rel="stylesheet"> references the same URL — the browser uses the preloaded copy.
  • The stylesheet is still render-blocking (via the <link rel="stylesheet">), but the fetch starts earlier.

Note: For critical CSS, inlining is generally better than preloading in 2026. Preloading a stylesheet does not change its render-blocking behavior; it just fetches it faster.

docs.title: Example 4: Conditional Preload with Media Query
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="preload" href="/hero-desktop.avif" as="image" media="(min-width: 768px)" fetchpriority="high">
    <link rel="preload" href="/hero-mobile.avif" as="image" media="(max-width: 767px)" fetchpriority="high">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • Desktop and mobile hero images are preloaded conditionally.
  • Only the matching media query triggers the preload.
  • Saves bandwidth by not fetching both.

docs.title: Example 5: Preload with the Wrong as (Anti-Pattern)
docs.text:
<!-- WRONG: as="script" for a font -->
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="script">

Why it's wrong: The browser sets the wrong Accept header, the wrong priority, and may fetch the font twice.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: Example 6: Preload a Web Worker
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/js/worker.js" as="worker">

const worker = new Worker('/js/worker.js');

Code Breakdown:

  • The worker script is fetched at high priority.
  • When new Worker() is called, the script is already cached.

docs.title: Example 7: Preload with 103 Early Hints
docs.text:
// Express.js: send 103 Early Hints before the HTML response
app.get('/', (req, res) => {
    res.writeEarlyHints({
        'link': [
            '</fonts/inter-var.woff2>; rel=preload; as=font; type=font/woff2; crossorigin',
            '</hero-1200.avif>; rel=preload; as=image; fetchpriority=high'
        ]
    });

    res.sendFile('index.html');
});

Code Breakdown:

  • The server sends 103 Early Hints with preload directives.
  • The browser starts fetching critical resources while the server prepares the HTML.
  • Requires HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
  • Supported in Chrome 103+, Edge 103+, Firefox 120+.

docs.title: Example 8: Complete Preload Audit Script
docs.text:
// In DevTools console: audit preload usage
const preloads = [...document.querySelectorAll('link[rel="preload"]')];

console.table(preloads.map(link => ({
    href: link.href,
    as: link.as,
    type: link.type,
    crossorigin: link.crossOrigin,
    media: link.media
})));

// Check for missing `as` (common mistake)
const missingAs = preloads.filter(l => !l.as);
if (missingAs.length) {
    console.warn('Preloads missing `as`:', missingAs.map(l => l.href));
}

// Check for font preloads missing `crossorigin`
const fontNoCors = preloads.filter(l => l.as === 'font' && !l.crossOrigin);
if (fontNoCors.length) {
    console.error('Font preloads missing crossorigin:', fontNoCors.map(l => l.href));
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Lists all preloads with their attributes.
  • Warns about preloads missing as.
  • Errors about font preloads missing crossorigin.
  • Run in DevTools to catch common preload mistakes.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Preload Attributes Web font from CDN as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin LCP hero image as="image" fetchpriority="high" with imagesrcset Responsive LCP image as="image" with imagesrcset and imagesizes Conditional LCP image as="image" media="..." Above-the-fold background as="image" Critical CSS as="style" (rarely needed) Web Worker as="worker" Video poster as="image" Fetch/XHR data as="fetch" crossorigin Font subset as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Preload only resources the browser discovers late. Why: the browser already discovers early resources.
  2. Always include the as attribute. Why: without it, the browser fetches at low priority and may double-fetch.
  3. Always include crossorigin on font preloads. Why: fonts require CORS, even same-origin.
  4. Always include type on font preloads. Why: lets the browser skip the preload if the format is unsupported.
  5. Use fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image preload. Why: reinforces the LCP priority.
  6. Use imagesrcset and imagesizes for responsive LCP images. Why: preload the correct responsive variant.
  7. Use media for conditional preloads. Why: prevents preloading resources for the wrong device.
  8. Use preconnect before preload for third-party origins. Why: connection must be open before the fetch.
  9. Audit for unused preloads. Why: Chrome warns in the console; unused preloads waste bandwidth.
  10. Audit for double-fetched resources. Why: Network panel shows two requests for the same URL.
  11. Do not preload resources you are not sure about. Why: wrong preloads waste bandwidth.
  12. Do not preload resources the browser discovers early. Why: same-origin scripts and stylesheets in <head> are already discovered.
  13. Do not preload more than 2–3 resources per page. Why: too many preloads compete for bandwidth.
  14. Do not preload lazy-loaded images. Why: they are deferred by design.
  15. Do not preload resources behind authentication. Why: the browser refetches them after auth.
  16. Use 103 Early Hints for server-sent preloads. Why: fetches critical resources before the HTML response.
  17. Combine preload with preconnect for third-party fonts. Why: connection + resource fetch in parallel.
  18. Test on slow networks. Why: differences are invisible on fast connections.
  19. Measure LCP, FCP, and TTI. Why: preload's impact is measured in these metrics.
  20. Audit preload after every framework upgrade. Why: framework behavior changes.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing as Attribute
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2">

Why it's wrong: Without as, the browser sets a low priority, the wrong Accept header, and may fetch the resource twice.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing crossorigin on Font Preload
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2">

Why it's wrong: Fonts require CORS. Without crossorigin, the browser fetches the font twice.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Wrong as Value
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/font.woff2" as="script">

Why it's wrong: The browser sets the wrong priority and may fetch the resource twice.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" href="/font.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Preloading Resources the Browser Discovers Early
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css">

Why it's wrong: The browser discovers the stylesheet in the HTML anyway. The preload is wasted bandwidth.

✅ Correct: Preload only late-discovered resources (fonts, LCP images in JS).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Preloading Lazy-Loaded Images
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/below-fold.jpg">
<img src="/below-fold.jpg" loading="lazy" alt="Below fold">

Why it's wrong: The image is lazy-loaded by design. Preloading defeats the purpose.

✅ Correct: Preload only above-the-fold LCP images.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Too Many Preloads
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/font-1.woff2" as="font" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/font-2.woff2" as="font" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/font-3.woff2" as="font" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/font-4.woff2" as="font" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/hero.avif" as="image">
<link rel="preload" href="/logo.svg" as="image">
<link rel="preload" href="/icon.svg" as="image">

Why it's wrong: Too many preloads compete for bandwidth, delaying critical resources.

✅ Correct: Preload only the 1–3 most critical resources.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Preloading Images Without imagesrcset
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.jpg">

Why it's wrong: Mobile devices download the desktop-sized image. On responsive images, preloading without imagesrcset defeats the purpose.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero-1200.avif"
      imagesrcset="/hero-400.avif 400w, /hero-800.avif 800w, /hero-1200.avif 1200w"
      imagesizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px, (max-width: 1200px) 800px, 1200px">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Preloading Without preconnect
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com/s/inter.woff2" as="font" crossorigin>

Why it's wrong: The preload fetches the resource, but the connection to fonts.gstatic.com is not pre-established.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com/s/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Preloading Resources Behind Authentication
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/dashboard/data.json" as="fetch" crossorigin>

Why it's wrong: The preload may be blocked by authentication; the browser refetches after auth.

✅ Correct: Do not preload authenticated resources; preload public assets.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using the Preload + onload CSS Pattern
docs.text:
<link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style" onload="this.rel='stylesheet'">

Why it's wrong: This pattern bypasses the browser's render-blocking heuristic, causing FOUC on slow connections. It is no longer recommended in 2026.

✅ Correct: Inline critical CSS and load the full stylesheet normally.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Preload reduces LCP by 200–800ms for late-discovered LCP images.
  • Preload reduces font swap delay by 100–500ms.
  • Preload for the wrong resource wastes bandwidth and delays legitimate resources.
  • Too many preloads compete for bandwidth — limit to 1–3.
  • Preload + 103 Early Hints saves one round-trip.
  • Chrome's automatic LCP image preload (2024+) reduces the need for manual hints — but cross-browser consistency still requires manual preload.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Preload only late-discovered critical resources.
  2. Limit to 1–3 preloads per page.
  3. Combine preconnect + preload for third-party fonts.
  4. Use fetchpriority="high" on LCP image preload.
  5. Use imagesrcset for responsive image preload.
  6. Combine with 103 Early Hints.
  7. Validate with WebPageTest.
  8. Measure with Lighthouse and CrUX.

docs.title: Preload and CSP
docs.text:
Preloaded resources must satisfy CSP directives:

Content-Security-Policy: font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com

If the CSP blocks a resource type, the preload is ignored.

docs.title: Preload and Subresource Integrity
docs.text:
Preloaded scripts and styles can use SRI:

<link rel="preload" href="/js/lib.js" as="script" integrity="sha384-...">

docs.title: Preload and CORS
docs.text: Cross-origin preloads require crossorigin. Without it, the browser may fetch the resource without CORS headers, which could leak information or cause double fetches.

docs.title: Preload and Privacy
docs.text: Preloading a resource reveals intent — the page will fetch that resource. Do not preload URLs that leak sensitive information (session tokens, user IDs).

docs.title: Preload and 103 Early Hints
docs.text: 103 Early Hints responses must respect CORS. Cross-origin preloads require crossorigin.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Network panel — inspect the preload and the actual resource request. Verify a single fetch.
  • Chrome DevTools → Console — Chrome warns about unused preloads and double-fetched resources.
  • Chrome DevTools → Coverage panel — shows unused resources.
  • document.querySelectorAll('link[rel="preload"]') — list all preloads.
  • performance.getEntriesByType('resource') — inspect resource timing.
  • Lighthouse — audits for render-blocking resources.
  • WebPageTest — filmstrip view of resource loading.
  • PageSpeed Insights — field + lab data combined.
  • CrUX — real-world Core Web Vitals.
  • Look for was preloaded but not used in console — remove unused preloads.
  • Look for two network requests for the same URL — indicates as or crossorigin mismatch.
  • <link rel="preload"> with integrity failing — indicates SRI mismatch.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Late-discovered critical resources — fonts in CSS, LCP images in JS.
  • Critical fonts — preload the primary font.
  • LCP images — preload the hero image (or let Chrome auto-preload).
  • Critical CSS — preload only when the fetch starts late (rare).
  • Web Workers — preload worker scripts.
  • Video posters — preload the above-the-fold video poster.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not preload resources the browser discovers early. Same-origin scripts and stylesheets in <head>.
  • Do not preload lazy-loaded resources. They are deferred by design.
  • Do not preload more than 1–3 resources per page.
  • Do not preload behind authentication.
  • Do not use the preload + onload CSS pattern in 2026.
  • Do not preload without as.
  • Do not preload fonts without crossorigin.
  • Do not preload resources you are not sure about.
