docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Preload shipped in Chrome 50 (April 2016) — it replaced a generation of hacks for early resource fetching.
  • The as attribute is required — without it, the browser fetches at low priority and may double-fetch.
  • Fonts always require crossorigin on preload, even same-origin.
  • Chrome warns about unused preloads within 3 seconds of the load event.
  • Chrome's automatic LCP image preload (2024+) reduces the need for manual LCP preloads — but cross-browser consistency still requires manual hints.
  • The preload + onload CSS pattern is no longer recommended in 2026 — it can cause FOUC.
  • Preload reduces LCP by 200–800ms for late-discovered LCP images.
  • Preload can reduce font swap delay by 100–500ms.
  • The type attribute lets the browser skip unsupported formats — no bandwidth wasted.
  • The media attribute lets the browser skip preloads for non-matching environments.
  • imagesrcset and imagesizes on preload prevent mobile devices from downloading desktop-sized images.
  • Preload works with 103 Early Hints — the server can send preload directives before the HTML response.
  • Preload is a hypothesis — wrong preloads waste bandwidth and delay legitimate resources.
  • Chrome's preload cache is per-navigation — not shared across navigations.
  • The preload scanner cannot see fonts in CSS — this is the canonical use case for preload.
  • Preload does not change render-blocking behavior — a preloaded stylesheet is still render-blocking.
  • The fastest path to reducing LCP is often to preload the LCP element — but Chrome's auto-preload may already do this.
  • Too many preloads compete for bandwidth — limit to 1–3 per page.
  • Preload is universally supported — Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari all support it.
  • Preload is baseline in 2026 — the question is whether you are applying it correctly.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Preload is a resource hint that fetches a specific resource at high priority for the current page.
  • It solves late-discovery latency — fonts in CSS, LCP images in JavaScript.
  • The as attribute is required — without it, the browser fetches at low priority and may double-fetch.
  • crossorigin is required for fonts — even same-origin.
  • Use fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image preload.
  • Use imagesrcset and imagesizes for responsive image preloads.
  • Use media for conditional preloads.
  • Combine preconnect + preload for third-party fonts.
  • Combine with 103 Early Hints for server-sent preloads.
  • Preload only late-discovered resources — the browser discovers early resources.
  • Do not preload more than 1–3 resources per page.
  • Do not preload lazy-loaded resources.
  • Do not preload resources behind authentication.
  • Chrome warns about unused preloads — audit and remove them.
  • Chrome's automatic LCP image preload (2024+) reduces the need for manual hints — but cross-browser consistency still requires manual preload.
  • Preload is a hypothesis — wrong preloads waste bandwidth.
  • Preload reduces LCP by 200–800ms for late-discovered LCP images.
  • Preload is baseline and universally supported in 2026.
  • Validate every preload with WebPageTest and the Chrome console before shipping.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Prefetch is a resource hint that tells the browser to fetch a resource at low priority for a future navigation — typically the next page the user is likely to visit. It is declared with a <link rel="prefetch"> element or via the Speculation Rules API. The browser downloads the resource during idle time, after the current page has finished loading, and stores it in the HTTP cache. When the user navigates to the prefetched page, the resource is already available — reducing latency and improving perceived performance.

<!-- Classic link-based prefetch -->
<link rel="prefetch" href="/next-article.html" as="document">
<link rel="prefetch" href="/js/product-details.js" as="script">

<!-- Speculation Rules API (modern replacement) -->
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}
</script>

Prefetch is the low-priority, future-focused member of the resource hints family. It answers the question: "What will the user need next?" — and prepares it in the background.

Unlike preload (which targets the current page at high priority) and preconnect (which only opens connections), prefetch fetches actual resources for a future navigation at the lowest priority, during idle time, without blocking anything on the current page.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Prefetch serves several essential purposes:

  • Reduce next-navigation latency — the next page's resources are already cached.
  • Improve perceived performance — navigation feels instant.
  • Prepare likely pages during idle time — uses bandwidth that would otherwise be wasted.
  • Enable instant navigation — combined with prerender, prefetch can deliver sub-100ms navigation.
  • Reduce TTFB on the next page — the HTML is already in the cache.
  • Reduce LCP on the next page — critical resources are already in the cache.
  • Increase conversion on multi-step flows — checkout, onboarding, and signup funnels.

Prefetch is a speculative bet on the user's next action. If the bet is right, navigation feels instant. If the bet is wrong, bandwidth is wasted, and — in the worst case — the user's data plan is consumed for content they never see.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Resource Hints
│
├── dns-prefetch     ← resolve hostname only
├── preconnect       ← DNS + TCP + TLS handshake
├── preload          ← fetch current-page resource at high priority
├── modulepreload    ← fetch ES module graph at high priority
└── prefetch         ← fetch future-navigation resource at low priority

Prefetch is the forward-looking tier of resource hints. It is the only hint that explicitly targets a future navigation rather than the current page.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Every navigation has a cost. When a user clicks a link, the browser starts from scratch:

  1. DNS lookup for the new origin (if cross-origin).
  2. TCP handshake.
  3. TLS handshake.
  4. HTTP request for the HTML document.
  5. HTML parse.
  6. Discovery and fetching of subresources (CSS, JS, images, fonts).
  7. Parse, execute, render.

Even on a fast connection, this takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. On a slow connection, it can take 10+ seconds.

Prefetch closes this gap by doing most of the work before the user clicks. The result: navigation feels instant, because the browser has already downloaded the HTML, JS, CSS, and images for the next page.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No way to pre-fetch next page Every navigation started from scratch No way to prefetch subresources Next page's JS/CSS fetched after navigation No idle-time fetching Bandwidth unused after current page loaded No declarative API Hacks used new Image() and XHR No priority control Prefetch requests competed with current page No pattern matching Every link had to be prefetched manually

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
<link rel="prefetch"> was introduced in the HTML Living Standard as a resource hint around 2014–2016. Before it, developers used several hacks:

  • new Image().src = url — preload images via a hidden <img> element.
  • <link rel="dns-prefetch"> — only resolved DNS.
  • XMLHttpRequest or fetch — fetched resources manually, bypassing the cache.

All of these were fragile and did not integrate with the browser's cache or priority system.

The Speculation Rules API shipped in Chrome 105 (September 2022) as a replacement for the deprecated <link rel="prerender"> hint. Chrome deprecated rel=prerender because it was not broadly supported beyond Chrome, and it was not a very expressive API. The Speculation Rules API brought:

  • URL pattern matching — prefetch/prerender any page matching a pattern.
  • Eagerness levels — conservative, moderate, eager.
  • Battery/data-aware decisions — the browser skips speculation if the device is in Data Saver mode or on low battery.
  • Declarative JSON syntax — no JavaScript required.

In 2026, prefetch is baseline in Chrome, Edge, and Firefox — but not supported in Safari. The Speculation Rules API is Chrome/Edge-only as of mid-2026, with Safari 26.2 shipping it behind a flag.

Critical caveat: prefetching pages that the user does not visit wastes bandwidth. On metered connections, this can be a real cost. Modern browsers mitigate this with network-aware and battery-aware heuristics — especially in Speculation Rules.

docs.title: The Classic Link-Based Prefetch
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Prefetch an HTML document -->
    <link rel="prefetch" href="/next-article.html" as="document">

    <!-- Prefetch a script -->
    <link rel="prefetch" href="/js/product-details.js" as="script">

    <!-- Prefetch an image -->
    <link rel="prefetch" href="/images/next-slide.avif" as="image">

    <!-- Prefetch a stylesheet -->
    <link rel="prefetch" href="/styles/next-page.css" as="style">
</head>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose rel="prefetch" Declares the hint href The URL to prefetch as The resource type — recommended but not required crossorigin CORS mode for cross-origin prefetches media Media query condition for the prefetch type MIME type hint

docs.title: The as Attribute — Recommended but Not Required
docs.text:
Unlike preload, prefetch does not require the as attribute. But including it helps:

  • Sets the correct Accept header.
  • Sets the correct security checks (CSP, SRI).
  • Sets the correct priority (still low, but correctly categorized).
  • Ensures the resource is stored in the correct cache partition.

Without as, the browser may fetch the resource twice (once with the prefetch, once with the actual navigation).

docs.title: The Speculation Rules API — Modern Replacement
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}
</script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Property Purpose prefetch Array of prefetch rules where Conditions for which URLs to prefetch href_matches URL pattern (supports * wildcards) eagerness When to trigger the prefetch

docs.title: The Eagerness Levels
docs.text: Level Trigger Use Case conservative On click Lower confidence in user intent moderate On hover (200ms) Higher confidence in user intent eager Immediately on page load Very high confidence in user intent

docs.title: The where Clause
docs.text:
The where clause supports multiple matching strategies:

// Match by URL pattern
"where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" }

// Match by CSS selector
"where": { "selector_matches": ".prefetch-link" }

// Match by multiple patterns
"where": {
    "and": [
        { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        { "not": { "href_matches": "/blog/private/*" } }
    ]
}

docs.title: The urls Clause
docs.text:
For explicitly listing URLs:

<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prefetch": [{
        "urls": ["/about", "/contact", "/pricing"],
        "eagerness": "eager"
    }]
}
</script>

docs.title: The Full Production Head
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>How SVG Embedding Works — Dev Notes</title>

    <!-- Preconnect to third-party origins -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload critical fonts -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload LCP image -->
    <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">

    <!-- Speculation Rules: prefetch/prerender likely next pages -->
    <script type="speculationrules">
    {
        "prerender": [{
            "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
            "eagerness": "moderate"
        }],
        "prefetch": [{
            "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
            "eagerness": "conservative"
        }]
    }
    </script>
</head>

docs.title: Prefetch vs. Prerender
docs.text:
Prefetch Prerender What it fetches HTML + subresources Full page (including JS execution) JS execution No Yes Memory cost Low High CPU cost Low High Network cost Medium High Eagerness default conservative conservative Best for Blog posts, docs E-commerce, forms, dashboards

Prefetch downloads resources. Prerender downloads and renders the page in a hidden tab, making navigation feel truly instant.

docs.title: The "Speculative Bet" Mental Model
docs.text:
Prefetch is a bet on the user's next action:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE BET                                     │
│                                              │
│  You bet: "The user will click this link."    │
│  Cost: Bandwidth to download the resource.    │
│  Reward: Instant navigation if correct.       │
│                                              │
│  If correct:  User experiences zero-latency   │
│  If wrong:    Bandwidth is wasted.            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The math is simple: if the probability of navigation × the benefit of instant navigation > the cost of the wasted bandwidth, prefetch is worth it. For a "next article" link in a blog list, the probability is high and the bandwidth is low. For a "terms of service" link, both are wrong.

docs.title: The "Idle-Time Opportunism" Mental Model
docs.text:
Prefetch happens during idle time:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PAGE LOAD TIMELINE                          │
│                                              │
│  t=0ms      Navigation starts                │
│  t=500ms    Above-the-fold content painted   │
│  t=1500ms   Page fully loaded                │
│  t=2000ms   Network idle                     │
│             │                                │
│             ▼                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  PREFETCH WINDOW                     │   │
│  │  Browser fetches likely next pages   │   │
│  │  at low priority                     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                              │
│  t=5000ms   User clicks next article         │
│             → Instant navigation             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Prefetch uses bandwidth that would otherwise be idle. On a fast connection, the user never notices. On a slow connection, the browser may skip prefetch entirely.

docs.title: The "Data Saver Awareness" Mental Model (2026)
docs.text:
Modern browsers are data-saver aware:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BROWSER PREFETCH HEURISTICS (2026)          │
│                                              │
│  ✅ Prefetch if:                             │
│  ├── Device on Wi-Fi                         │
│  ├── Battery > 20%                           │
│  ├── Network is not metered                  │
│  ├── Memory is available                     │
│  └── Page is not in a background tab         │
│                                              │
│  ❌ Skip prefetch if:                        │
│  ├── Data Saver mode is on                   │
│  ├── Battery < 20% and not charging          │
│  ├── Network is 2G                           │
│  ├── Device memory is low                    │
│  └── User has visited recently               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Speculation Rules API is browser-managed — the browser decides whether to honor a rule based on these conditions. With hardcoded <link rel="prefetch"> tags, the browser has less context and cannot be as smart.

docs.title: The "Three Horizons" Mental Model
docs.text:
Resource hints prepare for three time horizons:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HORIZON 1: RIGHT NOW (current page)         │
│  ├── preload                                 │
│  ├── modulepreload                           │
│  └── preconnect                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  HORIZON 2: SECONDS FROM NOW (next nav)      │
│  ├── prefetch                                │
│  └── Speculation Rules (prefetch)            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  HORIZON 3: MAYBE (possible nav)             │
│  ├── dns-prefetch                            │
│  └── Speculation Rules (prerender)           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Prefetch is Horizon 2: the next navigation, in seconds.

docs.title: The "Prefetch Doesn't Replace Preload" Mental Model
docs.text:
Prefetch and preload serve different pages:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PRELOAD                                     │
│  └── For the CURRENT page                    │
│  └── High priority                           │
│  └── Fetches at document parse               │
│                                              │
│  PREFETCH                                    │
│  └── For the NEXT page                       │
│  └── Low priority                            │
│  └── Fetches during idle time                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Using prefetch for a resource the current page needs is a mistake — it fetches at low priority and delays rendering. Using preload for a resource the next page needs is also a mistake — it wastes high-priority bandwidth.

docs.title: Concept 1: The <link rel="prefetch"> Element
docs.text: The classic declarative syntax for prefetch. Supported in Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. Not supported in Safari — Safari ignores rel="prefetch" entirely.

docs.title: Concept 2: The Speculation Rules API
docs.text: The modern replacement for rel="prefetch" and rel="prerender". JSON-based. Supports pattern matching, eagerness levels, and browser-managed heuristics. Chrome/Edge only as of mid-2026. Safari 26.2 ships it behind a flag.

docs.title: Concept 3: The as Attribute
docs.text: Recommended for prefetch, though not required. Sets the correct Accept header, security checks, priority, and cache partition. Without as, the browser may fetch the resource twice.

docs.title: Concept 4: The crossorigin Attribute
docs.text: Required for cross-origin prefetches that need CORS. Same-origin prefetches do not need crossorigin.

docs.title: Concept 5: The media Attribute
docs.text:
Conditionally skips the prefetch based on a media query:

<link rel="prefetch" href="/mobile-page.html" media="(max-width: 767px)">

docs.title: Concept 6: The type Attribute
docs.text: A MIME type hint that lets the browser skip the prefetch if the format is unsupported.

docs.title: Concept 7: Eagerness Levels
docs.text:
Speculation Rules support three eagerness levels:

Level Trigger conservative On click moderate On hover (200ms) eager Immediately

docs.title: Concept 8: URL Pattern Matching
docs.text:
The where clause supports URL patterns via href_matches:

"where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" }

The * wildcard matches any sequence of characters. The pattern is matched against the URL path, not the full URL.

docs.title: Concept 9: CSS Selector Matching
docs.text:
The where clause also supports CSS selectors:

"where": { "selector_matches": ".prefetch-link" }

Only links matching the selector are prefetched.

docs.title: Concept 10: The and and not Operators
docs.text:
Rules can be combined:

"where": {
    "and": [
        { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        { "not": { "href_matches": "/blog/private/*" } }
    ]
}

docs.title: Concept 11: Prefetch vs. Prerender
docs.text: Prefetch Prerender HTML ✅ ✅ Subresources ✅ ✅ JS execution ❌ ✅ Memory cost Low High Navigation speed ~50–200ms ~0–50ms

docs.title: Concept 12: The Prerender Replacement
docs.text: The Speculation Rules API replaces the deprecated <link rel="prerender">. Chrome deprecated rel=prerender because it was not broadly supported beyond Chrome and was not expressive.

docs.title: Concept 13: The Cross-Origin Prefetch Limitation
docs.text: Cross-origin prefetching has limited support in the Speculation Rules API. Chrome's initial implementation only supports same-origin prefetching. Cross-origin prefetch via <link rel="prefetch"> is supported but may be blocked by CORS.

docs.title: Concept 14: Cache Behavior
docs.text: Prefetched resources are stored in the HTTP cache. Unlike preload, which uses a separate preload cache, prefetch uses the standard HTTP cache. This means prefetched resources are available across navigations — but also that they are subject to the same cache eviction rules as any other resource.

docs.title: Concept 15: Cache-Control Interaction
docs.text: The Speculation Rules API can bypass cache-control directives in some cases. This is important for pages that must not be cached.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Prefetch Priority
docs.text: Prefetched resources are fetched at the lowest priority. They do not compete with current-page resources. If the network is busy, prefetches are deferred.

docs.title: Concept 17: The Idle Time Trigger
docs.text: Prefetch happens after the current page has finished loading — during network idle. On slow connections, the browser may skip prefetch entirely.

docs.title: Concept 18: The Data Saver Interaction
docs.text: In Data Saver mode, browsers do not prefetch. This is a user-controlled setting that saves bandwidth on metered connections.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Battery Saver Interaction
docs.text: On low battery, browsers may skip prefetch. This is a device-controlled heuristic.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Prefetch Failure Mode
docs.text: If the user navigates to a page that was not prefetched, no harm done — the browser fetches normally. If the user navigates to a page that was prefetched but the resource is stale, the browser may fetch it again. Prefetch is a best-effort optimization, not a guarantee.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Link-Based Prefetch
docs.text:
1.  HTML parsed, <link rel="prefetch"> discovered.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser registers the prefetch.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser waits for the current page to finish loading.
    │
    ▼
4.  Network goes idle.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser fetches the prefetched resource at low priority.
    │
    ▼
6.  Resource stored in HTTP cache.
    │
    ▼
7.  User navigates to the prefetched page.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser retrieves the resource from cache.
    │
    ▼
9.  Navigation completes faster.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Speculation Rules Prefetch
docs.text:
1.  Page loads.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses <script type="speculationrules">.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser evaluates the rules:
    │   ├── URL pattern matching
    │   ├── Eagerness level
    │   └── Device conditions (memory, network, battery)
    │
    ▼
4.  For each matching link:
    │   ├── conservative → prefetch on click
    │   ├── moderate → prefetch on hover
    │   └── eager → prefetch immediately
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser prefetches the HTML (and subresources).
    │
    ▼
6.  User navigates → browser uses the prefetched resources.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Prefetch + Navigation
docs.text:
User clicks a link
    │
    ▼
Browser checks the HTTP cache
    │
    ├── Cache hit → navigation is instant
    └── Cache miss → normal navigation
    │
    ▼
Page renders

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Prerender Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Browser evaluates prerender rule.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser opens a hidden tab.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser navigates the hidden tab to the target URL.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser fetches HTML, CSS, JS, images, fonts.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser executes JavaScript.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser renders the page in the background.
    │
    ▼
7.  User clicks the link → browser swaps in the prerendered tab.
    │
    ▼
8.  Navigation appears instant.

docs.title: The HTTP Cache
docs.text:
Prefetched resources are stored in the HTTP cache, not a separate prefetch cache. This is different from preload, which uses a dedicated preload cache.

Implication: Prefetched resources are subject to the same cache eviction rules as any other resource. If the cache is full, prefetched resources may be evicted before the user navigates.

docs.title: The Speculation Rules Engine
docs.text:
The Speculation Rules API is browser-managed. The browser:

  1. Parses the JSON rules.
  2. Evaluates the where clause against all links on the page.
  3. Checks device conditions (memory, network, battery, Data Saver).
  4. Decides whether to prefetch or prerender.
  5. Manages the prefetch/prerender lifecycle.

The browser can cancel a prefetch or prerender if conditions change (e.g., user goes offline, battery drops).

docs.title: The Prerender Process
docs.text:
Prerendering is complex:

  1. The browser creates a hidden browsing context — a separate tab.
  2. The hidden tab runs its own JavaScript.
  3. The hidden tab may fire analytics events, make network requests, or perform side effects.
  4. When the user navigates, the browser swaps in the prerendered tab.

Critical issue: prerendering can trigger side effects — analytics hits, ad impressions, form submissions — that should not fire until the user actually sees the page. Modern implementations use the Page Lifecycle API (prerenderingchange event) so pages can detect prerendering and defer side effects.

docs.title: The prerenderingchange Event
docs.text:
document.addEventListener('prerenderingchange', () => {
    if (document.prerendering === false) {
        // The page is now visible to the user
        startAnalytics();
    }
});

docs.title: The Data Saver Architecture
docs.text:
Chrome's Data Saver mode:

  • Detects the user's network type.
  • Disables prefetch and prerender if the network is metered.
  • Disables prefetch on 2G connections.

docs.title: The Cross-Origin Restriction
docs.text:
For cross-origin prefetch, the Speculation Rules API:

  • Only supports same-origin in the initial implementation.
  • Cross-origin prefetch requires explicit Link headers or CORS.
  • Cross-origin prerender is not supported.

docs.title: The Prefetch Cache Behavior
docs.text: Prefetched resources are cached with the same cache headers as normal fetches. The browser respects Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified.

docs.title: The Speculation-Rules HTTP Header
docs.text:
Servers can deliver Speculation Rules via an HTTP header:

Speculation-Rules: "/speculation-rules.json"

This lets the server manage speculation rules without embedding them in the HTML.

docs.title: Prefetch Implementation Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Identify likely next pages:
    │   ├── Next article in a list
    │   ├── Next step in a funnel
    │   ├── Product from a category page
    │   └── Docs page from a TOC
    │
    ▼
2.  Choose the mechanism:
    │   ├── Classic <link rel="prefetch"> for simple cases
    │   └── Speculation Rules API for pattern-based
    │
    ▼
3.  Configure the rules:
    │   ├── URL patterns
    │   ├── Eagerness levels
    │   └── Include/exclude conditions
    │
    ▼
4.  Handle page lifecycle:
    │   └── Use prerenderingchange event for side effects
    │
    ▼
5.  Validate:
    │   ├── Chrome DevTools → Application → Speculative Loads
    │   ├── Network panel to see prefetch requests
    │   └── Real user metrics (RUM) for navigation timing
    │
    ▼
6.  Measure and iterate.

docs.title: Prerender Safety Checklist
docs.text:
1.  Does the page fire analytics on load?
    │   └── Use prerenderingchange to defer.
    │
    ▼
2.  Does the page make third-party requests?
    │   └── Ensure they are deferred.
    │
    ▼
3.  Does the page read cookies or auth state?
    │   └── Handle prerendering gracefully.
    │
    ▼
4.  Does the page have side effects on load?
    │   └── Defer until prerenderingchange.
    │
    ▼
5.  Does the page require user interaction?
    │   └── Prefetch, don't prerender.

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Link-Based Prefetch
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="prefetch" href="/next-article.html" as="document">
</head>

<article>
    <h1>Current Article</h1>
    <p>...</p>
    <a href="/next-article.html">Read the next article</a>
</article>

Code Breakdown:

  • The prefetch declares the next article as a likely navigation.
  • The browser fetches it during idle time at low priority.
  • When the user clicks, the HTML is already in the cache.

docs.title: Example 2: Speculation Rules — Blog Prefetch
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • where: { href_matches: "/blog/*" } — matches all blog URLs.
  • eagerness: "conservative" — prefetches on click.
  • Browser decides whether to honor the rule based on device conditions.

docs.title: Example 3: Speculation Rules — E-Commerce Prerender
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prerender": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
        "eagerness": "moderate"
    }]
}
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • where: { href_matches: "/product/*" } — matches all product pages.
  • eagerness: "moderate" — prerenders on hover (200ms).
  • When the user hovers over a product link, the browser prerenders it.
  • Navigation is instant.

docs.title: Example 4: Combining Prefetch and Prerender
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prerender": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
        "eagerness": "moderate"
    }],
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • Product pages are prerendered on hover — high-value, likely navigation.
  • Blog pages are prefetched on click — lower-value, less certain navigation.
  • The browser decides whether to honor each rule.

docs.title: Example 5: Excluding Pages with not
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": {
            "and": [
                { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
                { "not": { "href_matches": "/blog/private/*" } }
            ]
        },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • Prefetch all blog pages except private ones.
  • The and operator combines conditions.
  • The not operator excludes matches.

docs.title: Example 6: Explicit URL List
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prefetch": [{
        "urls": ["/about", "/contact", "/pricing"],
        "eagerness": "eager"
    }]
}
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • Explicitly lists the URLs to prefetch.
  • eagerness: "eager" — prefetches immediately.
  • Use for a small set of high-confidence pages.

docs.title: Example 7: Handling Prerendering Side Effects
docs.text:
// Defer analytics until the page is actually visible
document.addEventListener('prerenderingchange', () => {
    if (document.prerendering === false) {
        startAnalytics();
        startAds();
    }
});

// Check the current prerendering state
if (document.prerendering) {
    // Page is being prerendered — do not fire side effects
} else {
    // Page is visible to the user
}

Code Breakdown:

  • prerenderingchange fires when the page transitions from prerendering to visible.
  • Check document.prerendering to know the current state.
  • Defer side effects (analytics, ads) until the page is visible.

docs.title: Example 8: Server-Delivered Speculation Rules
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Speculation-Rules: "/speculation-rules.json"

{
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}

Code Breakdown:

  • The Speculation-Rules HTTP header points to a JSON file.
  • The server can manage rules without embedding them in the HTML.
  • Useful for dynamically adjusting rules based on user behavior.

docs.title: Example 9: Complete Prefetch + Prerender Configuration
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Acme Store — Running Shoes</title>

    <!-- Preconnect to third-party origins -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload critical fonts -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload LCP image -->
    <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">

    <!-- Speculation Rules -->
    <script type="speculationrules">
    {
        "prerender": [{
            "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
            "eagerness": "moderate"
        }],
        "prefetch": [{
            "where": { "href_matches": "/category/*" },
            "eagerness": "conservative"
        }]
    }
    </script>
</head>
<body>
    <main>
        <h1>Running Shoes</h1>
        <a href="/product/nike-pegasus-41">Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41</a>
        <a href="/category/trail">Trail running shoes</a>
    </main>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Strategy Eagerness Blog article list Prefetch next article conservative E-commerce category Prerender product pages moderate Docs site Prefetch TOC links conservative Multi-step funnel Prefetch next step moderate Search results Prefetch top result moderate Landing page Prefetch CTA target moderate Paginated content Prefetch next page conservative Mobile nav Prefetch tab targets conservative

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Prefetch the most likely next navigation. Why: high hit rate means high ROI.
  2. Use conservative eagerness for lower-confidence links. Why: avoids wasted bandwidth.
  3. Use moderate eagerness for hover-based prefetch. Why: hover is a strong signal of intent.
  4. Use eager sparingly. Why: fetches immediately on page load — wastes bandwidth if wrong.
  5. Exclude private or authenticated pages from prefetch. Why: they may leak information or fail.
  6. Handle prerendering side effects. Why: analytics, ads, and forms should not fire during prerendering.
  7. Use the prerenderingchange event. Why: defers side effects until the page is visible.
  8. Use where clauses to target patterns, not individual URLs. Why: scales to any number of links.
  9. Use the not operator to exclude sensitive URLs. Why: prevents accidental prefetching.
  10. Prefetch same-origin resources. Why: cross-origin prefetch is limited.
  11. Test on real devices. Why: browser heuristics vary by device.
  12. Monitor prefetch hit rate. Why: low hit rate means wasted bandwidth.
  13. Combine with preload and preconnect. Why: resource hints work together.
  14. Do not prefetch resources the user is unlikely to need.
  15. Do not prerender pages with side effects. Why: analytics and ads may fire incorrectly.
  16. Do not prefetch authenticated pages. Why: credentials may not be available.
  17. Do not prefetch on metered connections. Why: browsers skip it, but validate.
  18. Do not rely on prefetch for SEO. Why: it is a user experience optimization, not a crawlability one.
  19. Audit prefetch rules after every major site change. Why: URL patterns change.
  20. Measure with RUM, not just lab data. Why: prefetch impact is only visible in real user navigation times.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Prefetch for the Current Page
docs.text:
<link rel="prefetch" href="/styles/main.css" as="style">

Why it's wrong: Prefetch is for the next page. The current page needs preload.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preload" href="/styles/main.css" as="style">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Prefetching Too Many Pages
docs.text:
<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/*" },
        "eagerness": "eager"
    }]
}
</script>

Why it's wrong: Fetches every link on the page at page load — massive bandwidth waste.

✅ Correct:

<script type="speculationrules">
{
    "prefetch": [{
        "where": { "href_matches": "/blog/*" },
        "eagerness": "conservative"
    }]
}
</script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Prerender Side-Effect Handling
docs.text:
// Analytics fires on load — even during prerendering
analytics.track('pageview');

Why it's wrong: Prerendered pages fire analytics before the user sees them, inflating pageview counts.

✅ Correct:

document.addEventListener('prerenderingchange', () => {
    if (!document.prerendering) {
        analytics.track('pageview');
    }
});

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Prerendering Forms or Checkout Pages
docs.text:
"prerender": [{ "where": { "href_matches": "/checkout/*" } }]

Why it's wrong: Checkout pages may have side effects (reserved inventory, session creation). Prerendering them can cause data issues.

✅ Correct: Prerender browse-only pages; prefetch (or nothing) for action pages.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Prefetching Authenticated Pages
docs.text:
<link rel="prefetch" href="/dashboard" as="document">

Why it's wrong: The prefetch may not include the user's credentials; the browser refetches after auth.

✅ Correct: Prefetch public pages only.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using rel="prerender"
docs.text:
<link rel="prerender" href="/next-page">

Why it's wrong: rel=prerender is deprecated and Chrome-only.

✅ Correct: Use the Speculation Rules API.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Data Saver
docs.text:
<link rel="prefetch" href="/next-page.html" as="document">

Why it's wrong: On Data Saver mode, this wastes the user's data.

✅ Correct: The Speculation Rules API automatically respects Data Saver. If using <link rel="prefetch">, accept that the browser may still honor it — and validate on metered connections.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Prefetching on Slow Connections
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Prefetch on 2G delays the current page.

✅ Correct: The Speculation Rules API skips prefetch on slow connections automatically.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing Prefetch
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Prefetch rules may not match the intended links; the hit rate may be zero.

✅ Correct: Test with Chrome DevTools → Application → Speculative Loads, and monitor RUM.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Prefetch improves next-navigation speed by 100–500ms.
  • Prefetch consumes bandwidth even if the user doesn't navigate.
  • Prerender consumes more memory and CPU than prefetch.
  • Prefetch has zero impact on the current page's load time — it happens during idle time.
  • Prefetch may delay subresources if the network is congested.
  • Speculation Rules are browser-managed — the browser skips them when conditions are poor.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Prefetch only high-confidence next pages.
  2. Use conservative or moderate eagerness.
  3. Combine with preconnect for cross-origin targets.
  4. Do not prerender on metered connections.
  5. Test on slow connections and low-end devices.
  6. Monitor prefetch hit rate.
  7. Use RUM to measure navigation timing.
  8. Audit prefetch rules after URL structure changes.

docs.title: Prefetch and Privacy
docs.text: Prefetch reveals what the user is likely to visit next. On shared or monitored networks, this can leak information.

docs.title: Prefetch and Cross-Site Tracking
docs.text: Cross-origin prefetch can be used for tracking. Modern browsers mitigate this with cache partitioning — prefetched resources are cached per-origin.

docs.title: Prerender and Side Effects
docs.text: Prerendering executes JavaScript, which may fire analytics, ads, or forms. Use the prerenderingchange event to defer side effects.

docs.title: Prefetch and Authentication
docs.text: Prefetching authenticated pages can leak session tokens or cause unintended actions. Do not prefetch authenticated pages.

docs.title: Speculation Rules and CSP
docs.text:
Speculation Rules are subject to CSP. Add script-src directives to allow them:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'

Or use nonces:

<script type="speculationrules" nonce="abc123">...</script>

docs.title: Prefetch and Cache Poisoning
docs.text: Prefetched resources are stored in the HTTP cache. An attacker with control over a prefetch URL could poison the cache. Validate prefetch URLs.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Application → Speculative Loads — shows prefetch and prerender activity.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network panel — filter by prefetch to see prefetched requests.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network → Priority column — verify prefetches are low priority.
  • Chrome DevTools → Application → Cache Storage — inspect the HTTP cache.
  • document.prerendering — check if the page is being prerendered.
  • prerenderingchange event — verify side effect deferral.
  • performance.getEntriesByType('navigation') — inspect navigation timing.
  • RUM data — measure real user navigation times.
  • Lighthouse — audits for prefetch usage.
  • WebPageTest — visualize prefetch activity.
  • Chrome flags — chrome://flags/#prerender2 to enable/disable prerendering.
  • Chrome DevTools → Performance panel — see prefetch activity in the timeline.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Likely next navigation — next article, next product.
  • Multi-step funnels — checkout, onboarding.
  • Documentation TOCs — prefetch pages the user is likely to visit.
  • Search results — prefetch the top result.
  • Paginated content — prefetch the next page.
  • High-value pages — where instant navigation improves conversion.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not prefetch resources the current page needs. Use preload.
  • Do not prefetch authenticated pages. Session tokens may not be available.
  • Do not prefetch on metered connections. Browsers handle this, but validate.
  • Do not prerender pages with side effects. Use the prerenderingchange event.
  • Do not use rel="prerender". Use the Speculation Rules API.
  • Do not prefetch every link on the page. Use targeted patterns.
  • Do not rely on prefetch for SEO. It's a user-experience optimization.
