docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• <link rel="prefetch"> is not supported in Safari — Safari ignores the hint.
  • The Speculation Rules API shipped in Chrome 105 (September 2022) as a replacement for rel=prerender.
  • Chrome deprecated <link rel="prerender"> because it was Chrome-only and not expressive.
  • Prefetch happens during idle time, after the current page has finished loading.
  • Prefetched resources are stored in the HTTP cache — not a separate prefetch cache.
  • The Speculation Rules API is browser-managed — the browser decides whether to honor a rule based on memory, network, and battery conditions.
  • Data Saver mode disables prefetch — a user-controlled setting for metered connections.
  • Prerender executes JavaScript — which may fire analytics before the user sees the page.
  • The prerenderingchange event fires when a prerendered page becomes visible.
  • document.prerendering is true while the page is being prerendered.
  • Chrome's cross-origin prefetch support is limited — same-origin is the primary use case.
  • Prefetch improves next-navigation speed by 100–500ms.
  • Prerender makes navigation appear instant — but consumes more memory and CPU.
  • Speculation Rules can bypass cache-control directives — important for pages that must not be cached.
  • The Speculation-Rules HTTP header lets servers deliver rules without embedding them in HTML.
  • Safari 26.2 ships Speculation Rules behind a flag.
  • Edge supports Speculation Rules — it is Chromium-based.
  • Firefox supports <link rel="prefetch"> but not the Speculation Rules API as of mid-2026.
  • The where clause supports and, not, and or operators for complex rule logic.
  • Prefetch is a speculative bet — a wrong bet wastes bandwidth; a right bet feels instant.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Prefetch is a resource hint that fetches a resource at low priority for a future navigation.
  • It happens during idle time — after the current page has loaded.
  • The <link rel="prefetch"> element is the classic syntax — supported in Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, not Safari.
  • The Speculation Rules API is the modern replacement — supports pattern matching, eagerness levels, and browser-managed heuristics.
  • Eagerness levels: conservative (click), moderate (hover), eager (immediate).
  • Prefetch vs. prerender: prefetch downloads resources; prerender also executes JavaScript and renders the page.
  • Prefetched resources are stored in the HTTP cache — not a separate cache.
  • Prerendering requires side-effect handling — use the prerenderingchange event.
  • Do not prefetch authenticated pages.
  • Do not prerender pages with side effects.
  • Prefetch only high-confidence next pages.
  • Combine with preconnect and preload for a complete resource hints strategy.
  • Browsers are data-saver and battery-aware — prefetch is skipped in poor conditions.
  • Measure with RUM, not just lab data.
  • Prefetch improves next-navigation speed by 100–500ms.
  • Prerender makes navigation appear instant.
  • Prefetch is a speculative bet — validate the hit rate, adjust the rules, and iterate.
  • Prefetch is baseline in 2026 — the question is whether you are applying it correctly.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
DNS prefetch is a resource hint that tells the browser to resolve a hostname to an IP address in advance — before the browser would otherwise need to make a request to that host. It is declared with a <link rel="dns-prefetch"> element in the <head>.

<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">

DNS prefetch is the lightest resource hint in the family. It performs only the DNS lookup step of the connection handshake — no TCP, no TLS, no resource fetch. The cost is negligible; the benefit is a head start on the DNS resolution that every cross-origin request requires.

When a browser contacts a new origin for the first time, it must:

  1. DNS lookup — resolve the hostname (fonts.googleapis.com) to an IP address.
  2. TCP handshake — open a connection to that IP.
  3. TLS handshake — negotiate encryption.
  4. HTTP request — send the actual request.

DNS prefetch performs step 1 only — but that step is often the slowest and most variable. DNS lookups typically take 20–120ms on a fast connection, and can exceed 500ms on slow mobile networks. Resolving the hostname in advance removes that latency from the critical path.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
DNS prefetch serves several essential purposes:

  • Eliminate DNS latency — the DNS lookup is already complete when the resource is needed.
  • Pre-resolve many origins cheaply — unlike preconnect, there is no socket cost, so you can pre-resolve dozens of hosts.
  • Improve third-party performance — analytics, fonts, CDNs, and ad networks all benefit.
  • Complement preconnect — use dns-prefetch as a fallback for browsers that do not support preconnect.
  • Reduce TTFB for cross-origin resources — the DNS step is removed from the request chain.
  • Prepare for future navigation — resolve origins for likely next pages.

DNS prefetch is a low-cost, high-value optimization. It is the cheapest resource hint by a wide margin, and the one with the fewest downsides. Unlike preload, it never double-fetches. Unlike preconnect, it never exhausts the connection budget.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Resource Hints
│
├── dns-prefetch     ← resolve hostname only (cheapest)
├── preconnect       ← DNS + TCP + TLS handshake
├── preload          ← fetch current-page resource at high priority
├── modulepreload    ← fetch ES module graph at high priority
└── prefetch         ← fetch future-navigation resource at low priority

DNS prefetch is the lightest tier of resource hints. It sits below preconnect in cost, and below preload in aggressiveness.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Every time a browser contacts a new origin, it must perform a DNS lookup — translating the human-readable hostname into the numeric IP address the network actually uses. That lookup is not free.

User visits example.com
    │
    ▼
Browser needs to fetch a font from fonts.gstatic.com
    │
    ▼
DNS lookup for fonts.gstatic.com
    │
    ├── Query the OS resolver
    ├── Query the configured DNS server
    ├── Query the root nameservers
    ├── Query the TLD nameservers
    ├── Query the authoritative nameservers
    └── Return the IP address
    │
    ▼
TCP + TLS handshake
    │
    ▼
Font fetched

On a fast connection, the DNS lookup takes 20–120ms. On a slow mobile connection, it can take 500ms or more. And because DNS lookups block the entire request chain, every millisecond spent resolving is a millisecond the user waits.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence DNS resolved on demand Every new origin added 20–500ms of latency No way to pre-resolve Each origin resolved at the moment of first request No declarative API Hacks used new Image() and hidden <link> tags No control over DNS caching Browsers cached aggressively but only after first lookup No bulk resolution Each hostname required its own separate lookup

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch"> was introduced by Chromium in 2009 and later standardized in the HTML Living Standard as part of the resource hints family.

Before it, developers used several hacks:

  • new Image().src = "//third-party.com/favicon.ico" — triggered a DNS lookup as a side effect.
  • <link rel="preconnect"> — worked but was heavier and less widely supported at the time.
  • Inline scripts — no clean declarative mechanism.

DNS prefetch was designed to be cheap and safe:

  • It only resolves the hostname — no socket, no TLS, no fetch.
  • It can be applied to dozens of origins without exhausting the connection budget.
  • It costs almost nothing in terms of network and CPU.
  • It has no meaningful downside on fast connections.

In 2026, DNS prefetch is universally supported — Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, and Opera all support it. It is the safest resource hint to add, and the most commonly recommended for sites with many third-party origins.

docs.title: The Minimal DNS Prefetch
docs.text: <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose Required? rel="dns-prefetch" Declares the hint ✅ href The origin or hostname to resolve ✅ crossorigin CORS mode — rarely needed for DNS prefetch Optional

docs.title: Multiple DNS Prefetches
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Font providers -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">

    <!-- Analytics -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.googletagmanager.com">

    <!-- CDN -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://images.example.com">

    <!-- Third-party widgets -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://widgets.example.com">
</head>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• dns-prefetch — the browser resolves the hostname to an IP address in advance.
  • You can add many DNS prefetches — there is no practical limit.
  • Each costs almost nothing: no socket, no TLS, no fetch.

docs.title: The Protocol-Relative Form
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="//fonts.gstatic.com">

Code Breakdown:

  • Protocol-relative URLs (//) work but are legacy.
  • In 2026, always use https:// for clarity.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch + Preconnect Together
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Preconnect for critical origins -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- DNS prefetch as fallback for browsers that don't support preconnect -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">

    <!-- DNS prefetch for non-critical origins -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • preconnect for the most critical origin — resolves DNS, TCP, and TLS.
  • dns-prefetch for the same origin as a fallback — some older browsers support only dns-prefetch.
  • dns-prefetch for less critical origins — cheap bulk resolution.

docs.title: The HTML Standard Syntax
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">

The href can be either:

  • A full origin — https://cdn.example.com
  • A protocol-relative URL — //cdn.example.com
  • A bare hostname — cdn.example.com (browsers resolve the hostname only)

docs.title: The Complete Production Head
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>How SVG Embedding Works — Dev Notes</title>

    <!-- DNS prefetch for all third-party origins -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.googletagmanager.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://widgets.example.com">

    <!-- Preconnect for the most critical origins -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload critical fonts -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload LCP image -->
    <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">

    <!-- Critical CSS -->
    <style>/* above-the-fold styles */</style>
</head>

docs.title: The DNS Prefetch vs. Preconnect Decision Matrix
docs.text: Scenario Use Critical third-party origin (fonts, ad CDN) preconnect + dns-prefetch fallback Many third-party origins (analytics, widgets) dns-prefetch for all Origin might be used later in the session dns-prefetch Origin with many subdomains dns-prefetch each subdomain Origin used only for the current page preconnect (if critical) Origin used across many pages dns-prefetch

docs.title: The "Phone Book" Mental Model
docs.text:
A DNS lookup is like looking up a phone number in a phone book. dns-prefetch is looking up the number in advance, before you need to make the call.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WITHOUT DNS PREFETCH                        │
│                                              │
│  Need to call "Pizza Palace"                 │
│  → Find the phone book                       │
│  → Look up "Pizza Palace"                    │
│  → Find the number                           │
│  → Dial the number                           │
│  → Pizza arrives                             │
│                                              │
│  Time: 30 seconds (lookup) + 20 minutes      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WITH DNS PREFETCH                           │
│                                              │
│  Look up "Pizza Palace" now (while idle)     │
│  → Number is ready                           │
│                                              │
│  Later: need to call "Pizza Palace"          │
│  → Dial the number                           │
│  → Pizza arrives                             │
│                                              │
│  Time: 20 minutes (lookup already done)      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The lookup is not the slow part — but it happens while the user is waiting, so it adds up.

docs.title: The "Bulk Resolution" Mental Model
docs.text:
DNS prefetch is the cheapest resource hint. You can use it in bulk:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DNS PREFETCH                                │
│  Cost: ~1ms per lookup                       │
│  Use for: 5, 10, 20+ origins                 │
│                                              │
│  PRECONNECT                                  │
│  Cost: ~50–100ms per origin (real socket)    │
│  Use for: 1–2 origins                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

DNS prefetch is cheap enough that you can add it for every third-party origin without worrying about the connection budget.

docs.title: The "First Visit vs. Repeat Visit" Mental Model
docs.text:
DNS lookups only happen on first contact. After the first lookup, the browser caches the resolved IP address for the DNS TTL (typically 5 minutes to 24 hours).

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FIRST VISIT                                 │
│  └── DNS lookup happens                      │
│  └── dns-prefetch saves 20–500ms             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  SUBSEQUENT VISITS                           │
│  └── DNS is already cached                   │
│  └── dns-prefetch provides no benefit        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

DNS prefetch has the highest ROI on first visits — new users, first-page loads, cold caches. Returning users benefit less.

docs.title: The "Chained Latency" Mental Model
docs.text:
DNS prefetch saves the first step in a chained sequence:

Without dns-prefetch:
  DNS (100ms) → TCP (30ms) → TLS (60ms) → Request (200ms)
  Total: 390ms

With preconnect:
  DNS + TCP + TLS (190ms) → Request (200ms)
  Total: 390ms

With dns-prefetch + preconnect:
  DNS already done → TCP (30ms) → TLS (60ms) → Request (200ms)
  Total: 290ms

With only dns-prefetch:
  DNS already done → TCP (30ms) → TLS (60ms) → Request (200ms)
  Total: 290ms

Wait — that's the same as preconnect? Let's clarify:

  • dns-prefetch only resolves DNS.
  • preconnect resolves DNS and opens TCP and TLS.
  • dns-prefetch + preconnect is redundant — preconnect already includes the DNS step.
  • dns-prefetch is used alone for non-critical origins, and as a fallback for browsers that do not support preconnect.

docs.title: The "Silent Optimization" Mental Model
docs.text:
DNS prefetch has no visible downside:

  • No bandwidth cost.
  • No socket cost.
  • No priority competition.
  • No unused-preload warnings.
  • No double-fetch risk.

It is a silent, background optimization that improves performance without any risk. This is why it is often the first resource hint developers add.

docs.title: Concept 1: The DNS Lookup
docs.text: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves human-readable hostnames to IP addresses. Every cross-origin request requires a DNS lookup — unless the hostname is already cached.

docs.title: Concept 2: DNS Latency
docs.text: DNS lookups typically take 20–120ms on fast connections and 500ms+ on slow mobile connections. This latency is on the critical path for any cross-origin resource.

docs.title: Concept 3: DNS Caching
docs.text: After the first lookup, the browser caches the resolved IP address for the DNS TTL. Subsequent requests to the same origin skip the DNS step.

docs.title: Concept 4: The rel="dns-prefetch" Element
docs.text: The declarative syntax for DNS prefetch. Placed in the <head>. Takes href and optional crossorigin.

docs.title: Concept 5: Bulk Resolution
docs.text: DNS prefetch is cheap enough to apply to every third-party origin. There is no connection budget concern.

docs.title: Concept 6: DNS Prefetch vs. Preconnect
docs.text: dns-prefetch preconnect DNS ✅ ✅ TCP ❌ ✅ TLS ❌ ✅ Cost Very low Low–medium Bulk use ✅ ❌

docs.title: Concept 7: DNS Prefetch as Preconnect Fallback
docs.text: For browsers that support preconnect, the browser ignores dns-prefetch if the origin is already preconnected. For browsers that do not support preconnect (very old browsers), the dns-prefetch still resolves the hostname.

docs.title: Concept 8: The Connection Budget
docs.text: Browsers limit the number of concurrent connections per origin (typically 6 for HTTP/1.1, unlimited for HTTP/2+). preconnect consumes a connection; dns-prefetch does not.

docs.title: Concept 9: The DNS TTL
docs.text: DNS records have a TTL (time to live) that determines how long the browser caches the resolved IP. Common TTLs: 300 seconds (5 minutes) to 86400 seconds (24 hours).

docs.title: Concept 10: Browser Support
docs.text: dns-prefetch is supported in all modern browsers — Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, and Opera. It is the most widely supported resource hint.

docs.title: Concept 11: DNS Prefetch vs. Preload
docs.text: dns-prefetch preload What it does Resolve hostname Fetch resource Priority None High Cost Very low Full resource Target Any origin Current page

docs.title: Concept 12: Cross-Origin Only
docs.text: DNS prefetch is only useful for cross-origin origins. Same-origin resources do not require a DNS lookup — the browser already knows the IP.

docs.title: Concept 13: Subdomain Resolution
docs.text: Each subdomain (cdn1.example.com, cdn2.example.com) is a separate hostname and requires a separate DNS prefetch.

docs.title: Concept 14: DNS Prefetch for Future Navigation
docs.text:
DNS prefetch can resolve origins for likely next pages:

<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://checkout.example.com">

Even if the current page does not use the origin, the browser resolves it for a future navigation.

docs.title: Concept 15: The DNS Prefetch Rendering Hint
docs.text: Chromium browsers internally treat dns-prefetch as a lower-priority hint than preconnect. The browser may skip the DNS prefetch if the connection budget is exhausted or the network is congested.

docs.title: Concept 16: DNS Prefetch and the Preload Scanner
docs.text: The preload scanner discovers dns-prefetch hints in the raw HTML bytes and starts the DNS resolution immediately, often before the main parser reaches the element.

docs.title: Concept 17: DNS Prefetch and Privacy
docs.text: DNS prefetch reveals which origins the page will use. On shared or monitored networks, this can leak information.

docs.title: Concept 18: DNS Prefetch and CSP
docs.text: DNS prefetch is not directly affected by CSP, but the origins it resolves must satisfy the relevant CSP directives (font-src, script-src, etc.) if the resources are later loaded.

docs.title: Concept 19: DNS Prefetch and Secure DNS
docs.text: Modern browsers increasingly use DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) and DNS-over-TLS (DoT), which resolve hostnames over encrypted channels. dns-prefetch works the same way regardless of the DNS transport.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Cost-Benefit of DNS Prefetch
docs.text: Cost Benefit 1 DNS query 20–500ms saved on first request ~1ms CPU No socket, no TLS, no fetch No bandwidth No cache pollution No connection budget Safe to use in bulk

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Without DNS Prefetch
docs.text:
1.  HTML parsed, browser discovers a font from fonts.gstatic.com.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser needs to fetch the font.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser checks the DNS cache.
    │   └── Miss (first visit)
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser performs a DNS lookup.
    │   ├── Query the OS resolver
    │   ├── Query the DNS server
    │   └── Return the IP address (20–500ms)
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser opens TCP connection.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser performs TLS handshake.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser sends the HTTP request.
    │
    ▼
8.  Font arrives (Total: 300–700ms).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: With DNS Prefetch
docs.text:
1.  HTML parsed, browser discovers <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser starts DNS resolution for fonts.gstatic.com in the background.
    │
    ▼
3.  HTML parsed, browser discovers a font from fonts.gstatic.com.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser needs to fetch the font.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser checks the DNS cache.
    │   └── Hit (DNS prefetch already resolved it)
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser opens TCP connection.
    │
    ▼
7.  Browser performs TLS handshake.
    │
    ▼
8.  Browser sends the HTTP request.
    │
    ▼
9.  Font arrives (Total: 200–400ms).

DNS lookup is removed from the critical path.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: DNS Prefetch + Preconnect
docs.text:
1.  HTML parsed, browser discovers <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser starts DNS + TCP + TLS handshake in the background.
    │
    ▼
3.  HTML parsed, browser discovers a font from fonts.gstatic.com.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser needs to fetch the font.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser uses the pre-connected socket.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser sends the HTTP request immediately.
    │
    ▼
7.  Font arrives (Total: 100–300ms).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: DNS Prefetch Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Browser parses <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser checks its DNS cache.
    │   ├── Hit → done
    │   └── Miss → continue
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser enqueues a DNS resolution.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser resolves the hostname to an IP address.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser stores the result in the DNS cache.
    │
    ▼
6.  When the resource is needed, the DNS is already resolved.

docs.title: The DNS Resolver
docs.text:
The browser's DNS resolver performs the lookup. It:

  1. Checks the OS resolver cache.
  2. Checks the browser's internal DNS cache.
  3. Queries the configured DNS server (which may use DoH, DoT, or plain DNS).
  4. Follows the DNS hierarchy if necessary (root → TLD → authoritative).
  5. Returns the resolved IP address.
  6. Caches the result for the TTL.

docs.title: The DNS Cache
docs.text: The browser maintains an internal DNS cache separate from the OS resolver cache. The cache is keyed by hostname and stores the IP address for the TTL duration.

docs.title: The Preload Scanner
docs.text: The preload scanner parses the raw HTML bytes and discovers dns-prefetch hints before the main parser reaches them. The DNS resolution starts early.

docs.title: The Network Priority Engine
docs.text: dns-prefetch hints are assigned a very low priority. They do not compete with current-page resources. If the network is busy, DNS prefetch may be deferred.

docs.title: The Connection Budget
docs.text: dns-prefetch does not consume a connection slot. It only performs the DNS resolution step. The connection budget is only consumed by preconnect or an actual request.

docs.title: The DNS TTL
docs.text:
DNS records have a TTL that determines cache lifetime. Common values:

TTL Meaning 60 1 minute — very short 300 5 minutes — common for CDNs 3600 1 hour — typical 86400 24 hours — long

The browser caches the result for the full TTL. If the DNS record changes, the browser may not see the change until the TTL expires.

docs.title: DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH)
docs.text: Modern browsers increasingly use DNS-over-HTTPS to resolve hostnames over encrypted channels. DoH adds a small latency (one extra HTTP round-trip to the DoH server) but improves privacy. dns-prefetch works with DoH transparently.

docs.title: DNS-over-TLS (DoT)
docs.text: Similar to DoH but uses a dedicated port. dns-prefetch works with DoT transparently.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch Implementation Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Identify third-party origins:
    │   ├── Font providers
    │   ├── Analytics
    │   ├── CDNs
    │   ├── Widgets
    │   └── Ad networks
    │
    ▼
2.  Add dns-prefetch for every origin:
    │   └── <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://...">
    │
    ▼
3.  Add preconnect for the 1–2 most critical origins:
    │   └── <link rel="preconnect" href="https://...">
    │
    ▼
4.  Validate:
    │   ├── Network panel to see DNS resolution
    │   ├── Chrome DevTools → Network → Timing tab
    │   └── WebPageTest for first-visit performance
    │
    ▼
5.  Measure and iterate.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch Audit Workflow
docs.text:
1.  List all third-party origins on the page.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check which have dns-prefetch declared.
    │
    ▼
3.  Check for redundant dns-prefetch + preconnect pairs.
    │
    ▼
4.  Check for origins that no longer exist.
    │
    ▼
5.  Add missing dns-prefetch hints.
    │
    ▼
6.  Remove unused ones.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic DNS Prefetch
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • Each dns-prefetch resolves the hostname to an IP address in advance.
  • Cost is negligible.
  • Benefit is 20–500ms saved on the first request to each origin.

docs.title: Example 2: DNS Prefetch + Preconnect
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Preconnect for the most critical origin -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- DNS prefetch as fallback and for less critical origins -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • preconnect for fonts.gstatic.com — the font origin is critical.
  • dns-prefetch for the same origin as a fallback — some older browsers support only dns-prefetch.
  • dns-prefetch for other origins — cheap bulk resolution.

docs.title: Example 3: DNS Prefetch for Likely Next Navigation
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Current page uses example.com -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://example.com">

    <!-- User is likely to click through to checkout -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://checkout.example.com">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • The current page might not use checkout.example.com.
  • But the user is likely to navigate there.
  • DNS prefetch resolves the hostname in advance.

docs.title: Example 4: Bulk DNS Prefetch for Many Origins
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- Fonts -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">

    <!-- Analytics -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.googletagmanager.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://connect.facebook.net">

    <!-- CDNs -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://images.example.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://static.example.com">

    <!-- Widgets -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://widgets.example.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://support.example.com">

    <!-- Ads -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://ads.example.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://tracking.example.com">
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • 12 DNS prefetches, all cheap.
  • No connection budget concern.
  • Ideal for pages with many third-party origins.

docs.title: Example 5: Adding DNS Prefetch to an Existing Site
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>Acme Store — Running Shoes</title>

    <!-- Existing setup -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- New: dns-prefetch for all third-party origins -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://widgets.example.com">
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Page content -->
</body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • The preconnect and preload hints were already in place.
  • DNS prefetch is added for the remaining origins.
  • Order: preconnect first (most critical), then dns-prefetch for the rest.

docs.title: Example 6: DNS Prefetch with Media Query
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://mobile-cdn.example.com" media="(max-width: 767px)">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://desktop-cdn.example.com" media="(min-width: 768px)">

Code Breakdown:

  • Conditional DNS prefetch based on viewport.
  • The browser only resolves the matching origin.
  • Useful for device-specific CDNs.

docs.title: Example 7: DNS Prefetch for Third-Party Scripts
docs.text:
<head>
    <!-- DNS prefetch for third-party scripts -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://unpkg.com">
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Scripts loaded later -->
    <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/lib@1.2.3/dist/lib.min.js" defer></script>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • DNS prefetch resolves the CDN hostnames early.
  • The script is loaded later (deferred).
  • When the script loads, the DNS is already resolved.

docs.title: Example 8: Complete Production Head
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Acme Dashboard</title>

    <!-- Preconnect for the most critical origin -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- DNS prefetch for the same origin (fallback) and others -->
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://www.google-analytics.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">
    <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://widgets.example.com">

    <!-- Preload critical fonts -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload LCP image -->
    <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">

    <!-- Critical CSS -->
    <style>/* above-the-fold styles */</style>
</head>
<body>
    <main>Content</main>

    <!-- Non-critical scripts -->
    <script src="/js/analytics.js" defer></script>
    <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Example 9: Auditing DNS Prefetch in DevTools
docs.text:
// In DevTools console: list all DNS prefetches
const prefetches = [...document.querySelectorAll('link[rel="dns-prefetch"]')];

console.table(prefetches.map(link => ({
    href: link.href,
    media: link.media
})));

Code Breakdown:

  • Lists all DNS prefetch hints on the page.
  • Useful for auditing after a template change.

docs.title: Example 10: Removing Stale DNS Prefetches
docs.text:
<!-- Before: stale origins no longer used -->
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://old-cdn.example.com">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://deprecated-widget.example.com">

<!-- After: remove them -->

Why it matters: Every DNS prefetch is a DNS query. Stale hints waste queries on origins the page no longer uses.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case DNS Prefetch Target Google Fonts fonts.googleapis.com, fonts.gstatic.com Google Analytics www.google-analytics.com, www.googletagmanager.com Facebook Pixel connect.facebook.net CDN assets cdn.example.com Image CDN images.example.com Static assets static.example.com Third-party widgets widgets.example.com Support chat support.example.com Ad networks ads.example.com Video CDN video.example.com E-commerce checkout checkout.example.com

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Add dns-prefetch for every third-party origin. Why: cheap, safe, and effective.
  2. Use preconnect for the 1–2 most critical origins. Why: opens a full connection, but costs more.
  3. Add dns-prefetch as a fallback alongside preconnect. Why: supports browsers that do not support preconnect.
  4. Add dns-prefetch for likely next-navigation origins. Why: prepares for future navigation.
  5. Keep DNS prefetch hints up to date. Why: stale origins waste DNS queries.
  6. Do not add dns-prefetch for same-origin resources. Why: no DNS lookup is needed.
  7. Do not add dns-prefetch for origins you never use. Why: wasted DNS query.
  8. Use dns-prefetch for subdomains separately. Why: each subdomain is a separate hostname.
  9. Combine with preconnect for maximum benefit. Why: DNS prefetch as fallback, preconnect for critical.
  10. Validate with WebPageTest's first-view test. Why: DNS prefetch only helps on cold caches.
  11. Monitor DNS resolution in the Network panel. Why: confirms DNS prefetch is working.
  12. Consider the privacy implications. Why: DNS prefetch reveals origins to the network.
  13. Audit DNS prefetch quarterly. Why: third-party origins change.
  14. Test on slow networks. Why: DNS latency is highest on mobile.
  15. Combine with preload for critical resources. Why: DNS prefetch + preload = full pipeline priming.
  16. Use DNS prefetch for third-party scripts. Why: CDN DNS resolution is often slow.
  17. Do not use DNS prefetch as a substitute for preconnect. Why: they solve different problems.
  18. Do not overthink DNS prefetch. Why: it is cheap and safe — add it liberally.
  19. Document your DNS prefetch strategy. Why: consistency across a team prevents drift.
  20. Measure with real user metrics (RUM). Why: DNS latency varies by network and region.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: DNS Prefetch for Same-Origin Resources
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://example.com">

Why it's wrong: Same-origin resources do not require a DNS lookup — the browser already knows the IP.

✅ Correct: Only use DNS prefetch for cross-origin hosts.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: DNS Prefetch Without Preconnect for Critical Origins
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">

Why it's wrong: DNS prefetch only resolves the hostname. The critical font origin should also be preconnected.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Stale DNS Prefetch Hints
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://old-cdn.example.com">

Why it's wrong: The origin is no longer used — the DNS query is wasted.

✅ Correct: Remove stale hints during audits.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Subdomain Prefetches
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://example.com">

Why it's wrong: cdn.example.com is a separate hostname and needs its own DNS prefetch.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://images.example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on DNS Prefetch Alone for Critical Resources
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
<!-- No preconnect, no preload -->

Why it's wrong: DNS prefetch only resolves the hostname. For critical resources, use preconnect and preload.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No DNS Prefetch at All
docs.text:
<head>
    <title>Page</title>
</head>

Why it's wrong: Every third-party origin adds DNS latency to the critical path.

✅ Correct: Add DNS prefetch for every third-party origin.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: DNS Prefetch on HTTPS with Mixed Content
docs.text:
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="http://cdn.example.com">

Why it's wrong: DNS prefetch over HTTP is a mixed-content risk.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: DNS Prefetch Without Validation
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Hints may be malformed or point to non-existent origins.

✅ Correct: Validate with WebPageTest and DevTools Network panel.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• DNS prefetch saves 20–500ms per origin on the first request.
  • DNS prefetch has no bandwidth cost — just the DNS query.
  • DNS prefetch has no connection budget cost — no socket opened.
  • DNS prefetch is highest-ROI on first visits — cold caches.
  • DNS prefetch is lowest-ROI on repeat visits — DNS already cached.
  • Bulk DNS prefetch is safe — no practical limit.
  • DNS prefetch complements preconnect — different steps of the same pipeline.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Add DNS prefetch for every third-party origin.
  2. Combine with preconnect for critical origins.
  3. Validate on first-visit tests.
  4. Test on mobile networks with high DNS latency.
  5. Audit for stale hints.
  6. Use RUM to measure DNS impact.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch and Privacy
docs.text: DNS prefetch reveals which origins the page will use. On shared or monitored networks, this can leak information — including the existence of third-party services the user did not know were in use.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch and CSP
docs.text: DNS prefetch is not directly affected by CSP. But the origins it resolves must satisfy the relevant CSP directives if the resources are later loaded.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch and Mixed Content
docs.text: DNS prefetch over HTTP is a mixed-content risk. Always use https:// in the href.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch and DNS-over-HTTPS
docs.text: Modern browsers use DoH to resolve hostnames over encrypted channels. DNS prefetch works the same way but with improved privacy.

docs.title: DNS Prefetch and Cache Poisoning
docs.text: DNS prefetch is not directly vulnerable to cache poisoning, but the resolved IP address could be malicious if the DNS resolver is compromised. Browser DNS caches have protections against this.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Network panel — DNS resolution time appears in the Timing tab.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network → Timing tab — shows "DNS Lookup" time.
  • WebPageTest — shows DNS timing in the waterfall.
  • performance.getEntriesByType('resource') — resource timing includes DNS time.
  • document.querySelectorAll('link[rel="dns-prefetch"]') — list all DNS prefetches.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network → filter by Domain — see DNS lookups.
  • chrome://net-internals/#dns — inspect the browser DNS cache.
  • Test on first visit — DNS prefetch has no benefit on repeat visits.
  • Use Private Browsing — clears the DNS cache for testing.
  • Check for stale hints — audit the DNS prefetch list.
  • Look for dns-prefetch errors in console — malformed hints may warn.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every third-party origin — always.
  • Many third-party origins — use DNS prefetch for all.
  • Critical third-party origins — use preconnect + dns-prefetch fallback.
  • Subdomains — each subdomain needs its own DNS prefetch.
  • Likely next-navigation origins — pre-resolve for future navigation.
  • Third-party scripts — pre-resolve CDN hostnames.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use DNS prefetch for same-origin resources. No DNS lookup needed.
  • Do not use DNS prefetch for origins you never use. Wastes DNS queries.
  • Do not use DNS prefetch over HTTP. Use HTTPS.
  • Do not rely on DNS prefetch alone for critical resources. Combine with preconnect and preload.
  • Do not forget to audit stale hints.

docs.text:
