docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• DNS prefetch was introduced by Chromium in 2009 — it is one of the oldest resource hints.
  • DNS prefetch only resolves the hostname — no TCP, no TLS, no fetch.
  • DNS lookups take 20–120ms on fast connections and 500ms+ on slow mobile networks.
  • DNS prefetch is supported in all modern browsers — Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera.
  • DNS prefetch has the highest ROI on first visits — subsequent visits use the DNS cache.
  • The DNS TTL determines cache lifetime — common values are 5 minutes to 24 hours.
  • Each subdomain requires a separate DNS prefetch — cdn1.example.com and cdn2.example.com are separate.
  • DNS prefetch does not consume the connection budget — it opens no socket.
  • You can safely add dozens of DNS prefetch hints — the cost is negligible.
  • DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) is increasingly used by browsers — DNS prefetch works transparently with it.
  • DNS prefetch is often the first resource hint developers add — it is the safest.
  • Chrome's preload scanner discovers DNS prefetch hints early — resolution starts immediately.
  • The connection budget is typically 6 per origin for HTTP/1.1 — unlimited for HTTP/2+.
  • DNS prefetch and preconnect are complementary — DNS prefetch is a fallback and for non-critical origins.
  • Stale DNS prefetch hints waste DNS queries — audit them quarterly.
  • DNS prefetch can leak information on shared networks — the origins the page uses are visible.
  • The fastest DNS lookup is the one you never make — DNS prefetch eliminates the lookup from the critical path.
  • DNS prefetch is the cheapest resource hint in the family — cost is a single DNS query.
  • DNS prefetch is the most widely supported resource hint — no browser-specific quirks.
  • In 2026, DNS prefetch is baseline and expected — the question is whether you have added it for every third-party origin.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• DNS prefetch resolves a hostname to an IP address in advance — before the browser needs to make a request.
  • It is declared with <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://..."> in the <head>.
  • It performs only the DNS lookup — no TCP, no TLS, no fetch.
  • Cost is negligible — a single DNS query.
  • Benefit is 20–500ms saved on the first request to each origin.
  • Use it for every third-party origin — analytics, fonts, CDNs, widgets, ad networks.
  • Combine with preconnect for critical origins — DNS prefetch as a fallback for older browsers.
  • DNS prefetch does not consume the connection budget — safe to use in bulk.
  • Each subdomain needs its own DNS prefetch.
  • Same-origin resources do not need DNS prefetch.
  • DNS prefetch has the highest ROI on first visits — cold caches.
  • DNS prefetch has no bandwidth cost — just the DNS query.
  • DNS prefetch works with DNS-over-HTTPS — encrypted DNS is transparent.
  • Audit DNS prefetch hints quarterly — remove stale origins.
  • DNS prefetch is the cheapest and safest resource hint — the one with the fewest downsides.
  • In 2026, DNS prefetch is baseline and expected — the question is whether you have added it for every third-party origin.
  • The best DNS lookup is the one already done.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Script loading is the practice of controlling how, when, and in what order JavaScript files are fetched, parsed, and executed by the browser. It is the set of techniques — async, defer, type="module", nomodule, dynamic imports, and preload hints — that determine whether a script blocks HTML parsing, delays rendering, or runs independently.

<!-- Blocking: parser stops until the script is downloaded and executed -->
<script src="/js/critical.js"></script>

<!-- Deferred: downloads in parallel, executes after HTML parsing -->
<script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

<!-- Async: downloads in parallel, executes as soon as it is ready -->
<script src="/js/analytics.js" async></script>

<!-- Module: deferred by default, executes in module scope -->
<script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>

The default <script src="..."> is parser-blocking — the browser stops parsing the HTML, downloads the script, executes it, and only then continues parsing. That single line of HTML can delay the first paint by hundreds of milliseconds or more, especially on slow connections.

Choosing the right loading strategy is not a micro-optimization. It is the single most impactful JavaScript performance decision you make on most pages.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Script loading serves several essential purposes:

  • Unblock HTML parsing — defer and async prevent scripts from blocking the parser.
  • Control execution order — defer preserves document order; async does not.
  • Enable code splitting — dynamic imports load JavaScript on demand.
  • Improve Core Web Vitals — faster LCP, lower TBT, better INP.
  • Isolate scope — module scripts run in strict mode with their own scope.
  • Optimize third-party scripts — analytics and widgets should never block rendering.
  • Support modern and legacy browsers — nomodule provides fallback for legacy.
  • Reduce main-thread contention — fewer blocking scripts means faster time to interactive.

The primary metric script loading targets is Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — but it also directly affects LCP and TBT. Every blocking script delays the moment the page becomes usable.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Performance Stack
│
├── Critical HTML        ← minimum markup for first paint
├── Lazy Loading         ← defer non-critical resources
├── Resource Hints       ← preload, preconnect, prefetch
├── Preload              ← high-priority fetch for critical assets
├── Prefetch             ← low-priority fetch for next navigation
├── DNS Prefetch         ← resolve third-party origins early
├── Script Loading       ← defer, async, module
└── Rendering Impact     ← layout shift, paint, compositing

Script loading sits near the bottom of the performance stack. It is the layer where JavaScript either unblocks the page or holds it hostage. Every other optimization above it — critical HTML, lazy loading, resource hints — is undermined by a single blocking script in the wrong place.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The <script> element is the most consequential tag in HTML. By default, when the parser encounters a <script src="..."> element, it:

  1. Stops parsing HTML.
  2. Fetches the script — network round-trip.
  3. Parses the JavaScript.
  4. Executes the JavaScript.
  5. Resumes parsing HTML.

This is called parser-blocking. It exists because JavaScript can modify the DOM — it can call document.write(), insert elements, change styles. The browser cannot continue parsing safely without knowing what the script does.

The problem: this behavior is catastrophically bad for performance. Every blocking script adds a network round-trip and a main-thread execution to the critical path. A page with 10 blocking scripts in the <head> can delay the first paint by 2–5 seconds on a slow connection.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Synchronous scripts block parsing First paint delayed by every script No ordering control Scripts executed in document order, blocking each other No async/defer attributes No way to load scripts without blocking No module system Global namespace pollution No code splitting Every script loaded on every page No dynamic loading All scripts upfront, regardless of need

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
async and defer shipped in Internet Explorer 4 (1997) as IE-only attributes. They were standardized in HTML5 (2008–2014) and are now universally supported. They solve the parser-blocking problem:

  • async — download in parallel, execute as soon as ready.
  • defer — download in parallel, execute after parsing, in document order.

ES modules (type="module") shipped in Chrome 61 (2017). They introduced:

  • Native module system — import and export.
  • Strict mode by default.
  • Module scope (no global pollution).
  • Deferred by default (no blocking).
  • Automatic dependency resolution.

nomodule shipped alongside modules as a fallback mechanism — a script with nomodule is ignored by module-supporting browsers and executed only by legacy browsers.

Dynamic import() shipped in Chrome 63 (2017) and became the foundation of code splitting in modern bundlers.

fetchpriority shipped in Chrome 102 (2022) as a way to control the fetch priority of scripts.

In 2026, script loading is fully specified — every major browser supports every technique. The question is not whether the tools exist, but whether you are using them correctly.

docs.title: The Default — Parser-Blocking Script
docs.text: <script src="/js/app.js"></script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• The parser stops when it reaches this element.
  • The browser fetches the script.
  • The browser parses and executes the script.
  • The parser resumes.
  • Blocking: Yes — HTML parsing and rendering are both blocked.

docs.title: defer — Deferred Execution
docs.text: <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Property Value Download Parallel to HTML parsing Execution After HTML parsing, before DOMContentLoaded Order Guaranteed — scripts execute in document order Blocking No — HTML parsing continues Use for Most application scripts

docs.title: async — Asynchronous Execution
docs.text: <script src="/js/analytics.js" async></script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Property Value Download Parallel to HTML parsing Execution As soon as downloaded — may interrupt parsing Order Not guaranteed — scripts execute in download order Blocking Partial — execution still blocks the parser Use for Independent third-party scripts

docs.title: type="module" — ES Modules
docs.text: <script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Property Value Download Parallel to HTML parsing Execution After HTML parsing (like defer) Order Guaranteed — modules execute in document order Scope Module scope (not global) Strict mode Always on Blocking No

docs.title: nomodule — Legacy Fallback
docs.text:
<script type="module" src="/js/app.mjs"></script>
<script nomodule src="/js/app.legacy.js"></script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• type="module" — executed by modern browsers.
  • nomodule — executed only by browsers that do not support modules.
  • Modern browsers ignore the nomodule script entirely.
  • Legacy browsers ignore the type="module" script entirely.
  • Only one of the two scripts ever executes.

docs.title: async + defer Together
docs.text: <script src="/js/app.js" async defer></script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• If the browser supports async, it uses async.
  • If the browser supports only defer, it uses defer.
  • Legacy fallback pattern — largely unnecessary in 2026.
  • In modern browsers, this behaves exactly like async.

docs.title: Dynamic Import — Code Splitting
docs.text:
// Static import: loaded upfront
import { heavyFunction } from './heavy-module.js';

// Dynamic import: loaded on demand
button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
    const { heavyFunction } = await import('./heavy-module.js');
    heavyFunction();
});

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• import() returns a Promise that resolves when the module loads.
  • Bundlers (Webpack, Vite, Rollup, esbuild) split dynamic imports into separate chunks.
  • Loads on demand — reduces initial bundle size.

docs.title: The <script type="importmap"> Element
docs.text:
<script type="importmap">
{
    "imports": {
        "lodash": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/lodash-es@4.17.21/lodash.js",
        "app/": "/js/"
    }
}
</script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• importmap — maps bare module specifiers to URLs.
  • Enables import 'lodash' in browsers without bundling.
  • Must appear before any module script.
  • Supported in Chrome 89+, Edge 89+, Safari 16.4+, Firefox 108+.

docs.title: The Preload + Module Pattern
docs.text:
<link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">
<script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• modulepreload — fetches the module and its dependencies.
  • When the <script type="module"> executes, the module graph is already in the module map.
  • Eliminates the sequential dependency resolution problem.

docs.title: The fetchpriority Attribute
docs.text:
<script src="/js/critical.js" defer fetchpriority="high"></script>
<script src="/js/analytics.js" async fetchpriority="low"></script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Value Effect high Fetch at highest priority low Fetch at low priority auto Default priority

docs.title: The Complete Production Head
docs.text:
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

    <title>Dashboard — Acme</title>

    <!-- Preconnect to third-party origins -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

    <!-- Preload critical fonts -->
    <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

    <!-- Critical CSS: inlined -->
    <style>/* above-the-fold styles */</style>

    <!-- Modulepreload critical entry point -->
    <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">

    <!-- Deferred application script -->
    <script src="/js/app.js" type="module"></script>
</head>
<body>
    <main>Content</main>

    <!-- Non-critical third-party scripts -->
    <script src="https://www.google-analytics.com/analytics.js" async></script>
</body>

docs.title: The "Assembly Line" Mental Model
docs.text:
The HTML parser is an assembly line. A <script> element is a stop sign on the line:

WITHOUT async/defer:
  HTML ──► <script> ──► STOP ──► Fetch ──► Execute ──► Resume ──► HTML

WITH defer:
  HTML ─────────────────────────────────────► Continue
       └── Fetch in parallel ──► Execute after parsing

WITH async:
  HTML ─────────────► Continue (with possible pause)
       └── Fetch in parallel ──► Execute as soon as ready

async and defer remove the stop sign. The line keeps moving.

docs.title: The "Three Ways to Load a Script" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BLOCKING (default)                          │
│  └── Parser stops                            │
│  └── Fetch + execute                         │
│  └── Parser resumes                          │
│  └── Order: guaranteed                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DEFER                                       │
│  └── Fetch in parallel                       │
│  └── Execute after parsing                   │
│  └── Order: guaranteed                       │
│  └── Best for most scripts                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ASYNC                                       │
│  └── Fetch in parallel                       │
│  └── Execute as soon as ready                │
│  └── Order: not guaranteed                   │
│  └── Best for independent third-party scripts│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Order Dependency" Mental Model
docs.text:
The key question for choosing between defer and async:

Does the script depend on another script,
or does another script depend on it?

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  YES → use defer                    │
  │  └── Order is preserved             │
  │                                     │
  │  NO → use async                     │
  │  └── Order does not matter          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

If script B calls a function defined in script A, both must be defer (or both blocking). If script B is independent (analytics, ads, chat widgets), use async.

docs.title: The "Main Thread" Mental Model
docs.text:
Script loading is about the main thread:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MAIN THREAD                                 │
│  ├── HTML parsing                            │
│  ├── CSS parsing                             │
│  ├── JavaScript execution                    │
│  ├── Layout                                  │
│  ├── Paint                                   │
│  └── Event handling                          │
│                                              │
│  Only one thing runs at a time.              │
│  A blocking script stops everything else.    │
│  A deferred script waits its turn.           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

JavaScript execution blocks the main thread. The goal of script loading is to minimize how long the main thread is blocked — especially before the first paint.

docs.title: The "Execution Timeline" Mental Model
docs.text:
BLOCKING SCRIPT:
  t=0    HTML parse starts
  t=50   <script> encountered → STOP
  t=250  Script downloaded
  t=300  Script executed
  t=300  HTML parse resumes
  t=500  First paint
  FCP = 500ms

DEFER SCRIPT:
  t=0    HTML parse starts
  t=50   <script defer> encountered → continue parsing
  t=50   Fetch starts in parallel
  t=200  HTML parse complete
  t=250  Script downloaded
  t=300  Script executed (after parsing)
  t=350  DOMContentLoaded
  FCP = 200ms (before script execution)

ASYNC SCRIPT:
  t=0    HTML parse starts
  t=50   <script async> encountered → continue parsing
  t=50   Fetch starts in parallel
  t=200  Script downloaded → execute immediately
  t=200  HTML parsing paused during execution
  t=250  HTML parse resumes
  FCP = 250ms

Deferred scripts do not delay the first paint. Blocking scripts do.

docs.title: Concept 1: Parser-Blocking Scripts
docs.text: The default <script src="..."> behavior. The parser stops, fetches the script, executes it, then resumes. Every blocking script adds latency to the critical path.

docs.title: Concept 2: defer
docs.text: Downloads in parallel, executes after HTML parsing, in document order. The right choice for most application scripts.

docs.title: Concept 3: async
docs.text: Downloads in parallel, executes as soon as downloaded, without order guarantee. The right choice for independent third-party scripts.

docs.title: Concept 4: type="module"
docs.text: ES modules. Deferred by default, strict mode, module scope. The modern standard for application code.

docs.title: Concept 5: nomodule
docs.text: A fallback attribute. Scripts with nomodule execute only in browsers that do not support ES modules.

docs.title: Concept 6: Dynamic import()
docs.text: Loads a module on demand. The foundation of code splitting.

docs.title: Concept 7: importmap
docs.text: Maps bare module specifiers to URLs. Enables import 'lodash' without bundling.

docs.title: Concept 8: modulepreload
docs.text: Preloads an ES module and its dependency graph.

docs.title: Concept 9: The fetchpriority Attribute
docs.text: Controls the fetch priority of a script.

docs.title: Concept 10: The Order Guarantee
docs.text:
• Blocking: order guaranteed (execution in document order).
  • defer: order guaranteed (execution in document order).
  • async: order not guaranteed (execution in download order).
  • type="module": order guaranteed (execution in document order, like defer).

docs.title: Concept 11: DOMContentLoaded
docs.text: The event fired when the HTML document has been completely parsed, and all deferred scripts have executed. async scripts may or may not have executed.

docs.title: Concept 12: Code Splitting
docs.text: The practice of splitting JavaScript into multiple chunks loaded on demand. Route-level splitting is the highest-ROI strategy.

docs.title: Concept 13: Route-Level Code Splitting
docs.text: Each route loads only the JavaScript needed for that route. Frameworks like Next.js, Remix, SvelteKit, and Nuxt do this automatically.

docs.title: Concept 14: Component-Level Code Splitting
docs.text: Splitting JavaScript at the component level. Used for large charts, editors, and modals.

docs.title: Concept 15: The modulepreload + type="module" Combination
docs.text: modulepreload fetches the module and its dependencies; type="module" executes it after parsing. Together, they eliminate the sequential module resolution problem.

docs.title: Concept 16: Third-Party Script Strategy
docs.text: Third-party scripts (analytics, ads, chat widgets) should always use async. They are independent, and they should never block the parser.

docs.title: Concept 17: The defer + async Fallback
docs.text:
<script src="..." async defer></script>

Modern browsers use async; legacy browsers use defer. Rarely needed in 2026.

docs.title: Concept 18: The Script Execution Order
docs.text:
1. Blocking scripts (in document order)
2. Deferred scripts (in document order)
3. Module scripts (in document order, like defer)
4. Async scripts (as soon as downloaded)
5. DOMContentLoaded fires
6. Async scripts may still be executing

docs.title: Concept 19: The Main Thread Budget
docs.text: The main thread should be idle during the first paint. Any JavaScript execution delays the first paint and the LCP. Minimize what runs before the first render.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Script Loading Decision Tree
docs.text:
Does the script need to run before the page can render?
├── Yes → inline it or use a blocking script in <head>
└── No → Is it a third-party script?
         ├── Yes → async
         └── No → Is it part of the app?
                  ├── Yes → type="module" or defer
                  └── No → dynamic import()

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Blocking Script
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters <script src="/js/app.js">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser stops.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser fetches /js/app.js.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser parses and executes the script.
    │
    ▼
5.  Parser resumes.
    │
    ▼
6.  First paint may be delayed.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Deferred Script
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters <script src="/js/app.js" defer>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser starts fetching the script in parallel.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser continues.
    │
    ▼
4.  Parser completes HTML parsing.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser executes deferred scripts in document order.
    │
    ▼
6.  DOMContentLoaded fires.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Async Script
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters <script src="/js/analytics.js" async>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser starts fetching the script in parallel.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser continues.
    │
    ▼
4.  Script downloads and executes immediately.
    │
    ├── If parser is still active, it pauses briefly.
    │
    ▼
5.  Parser continues.
    │
    ▼
6.  Async script may execute before or after DOMContentLoaded.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Module Script
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters <script type="module" src="/js/app.js">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser starts fetching the module in parallel.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser continues.
    │
    ▼
4.  Parser completes HTML parsing.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser resolves the module graph:
    │   ├── Fetch each import
    │   └── Fetch their imports recursively
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser executes modules in document order.
    │
    ▼
7.  DOMContentLoaded fires.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Dynamic Import
docs.text:
1.  User clicks a button.
    │
    ▼
2.  import('./heavy-module.js') is called.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser checks if the module is cached.
    │   ├── Yes → resolve immediately.
    │   └── No  → fetch the module chunk.
    │
    ▼
4.  Module parsed and evaluated.
    │
    ▼
5.  Promise resolves with the module exports.
    │
    ▼
6.  Application uses the module.

docs.title: The HTML Parser and JavaScript
docs.text:
The HTML parser is a single-pass, streaming parser. It reads bytes, builds DOM nodes, and emits events. When it encounters a <script> element, it must stop because:

  • JavaScript can modify the DOM (document.write, appendChild, etc.).
  • JavaScript can change the document structure.
  • JavaScript can throw errors that affect the rest of the page.

The parser cannot continue safely without executing the script first.

docs.title: defer and async Implementation
docs.text:
The browser tracks scripts in two queues:

  • Deferred queue — scripts execute after parsing, in document order.
  • Async queue — scripts execute as soon as they are downloaded.

When a defer script finishes downloading, the browser adds it to the deferred queue. When parsing completes, the browser drains the queue in order.

When an async script finishes downloading, the browser executes it immediately. If the parser is still active, the parser pauses briefly.

docs.title: The Module Graph Resolution
docs.text:
ES modules have a static dependency graph. When the browser loads a module, it:

  1. Parses the module source.
  2. Extracts all import statements.
  3. Fetches each imported module.
  4. Recursively resolves their imports.
  5. Topologically sorts the graph.
  6. Executes in dependency order.

This sequential resolution is why modulepreload matters: it fetches the entire graph in parallel, eliminating the sequential round-trips.

docs.title: The importmap Resolution
docs.text:
The import map is parsed before any module script. It maps bare specifiers to URLs:

import 'lodash'
       │
       ▼
importmap lookup: 'lodash' → 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/lodash-es@4.17.21/lodash.js'
       │
       ▼
Fetch the resolved URL

The import map must appear before any module script. Multiple import maps are merged, with the last one winning for conflicting keys.

docs.title: The Script Execution Environment
docs.text: Type Scope Strict mode this at top level Classic Global No window type="module" Module Yes undefined Dynamic import() Module Yes undefined

docs.title: The Main Thread Budget
docs.text:
The main thread is shared by:

  • HTML parsing.
  • CSS parsing.
  • JavaScript execution.
  • Layout.
  • Paint.
  • Event handling.

Any long-running JavaScript task blocks everything else. The Interaction to Next Paint (INP) metric measures how often this happens.

docs.title: The fetchpriority Engine
docs.text:
The browser assigns a priority to every script based on:

  • Position in the document.
  • async / defer.
  • fetchpriority attribute.
  • Whether it is render-blocking.

A deferred script with fetchpriority="high" is fetched at higher priority than one without.

docs.title: Script Loading Decision Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Does the script need to run before the first paint?
    │
    ├── YES → Inline it or use a blocking script in <head>
    │
    └── NO → Continue
         │
         ▼
2.  Is it a third-party script?
    │
    ├── YES → Use async
    │
    └── NO → Continue
         │
         ▼
3.  Is it a modern ES module?
    │
    ├── YES → Use type="module" + modulepreload
    │
    └── NO → Use defer

docs.title: Implementation Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Audit existing scripts:
    │   ├── Blocking scripts in <head>
    │   ├── Third-party scripts
    │   └── Module dependencies
    │
    ▼
2.  Move non-critical scripts to defer:
    │   └── Add defer attribute
    │
    ▼
3.  Move third-party scripts to async:
    │   └── Add async attribute
    │
    ▼
4.  Convert application code to modules:
    │   └── type="module"
    │
    ▼
5.  Add modulepreload for entry points:
    │   └── <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">
    │
    ▼
6.  Split code at route level:
    │   └── dynamic import() per route
    │
    ▼
7.  Measure with Lighthouse, WebPageTest, CrUX.

docs.title: Example 1: Deferred Application Script
docs.text:
<head>
    <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • defer — downloads in parallel, executes after parsing.
  • Preserves order with other deferred scripts.
  • Does not block the first paint.

docs.title: Example 2: Async Third-Party Script
docs.text:
<script src="https://www.google-analytics.com/analytics.js" async></script>

Code Breakdown:

  • async — downloads in parallel, executes as soon as ready.
  • Independent — no ordering dependency.
  • Does not block the parser (except briefly during execution).

docs.title: Example 3: Module Script with Preload
docs.text:
<head>
    <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">
    <script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • modulepreload fetches /js/app.js and its dependencies.
  • type="module" executes after parsing.
  • The module graph is already in the module map when execution begins.

docs.title: Example 4: Nomodule Fallback
docs.text:
<script type="module" src="/js/app.mjs"></script>
<script nomodule src="/js/app.legacy.js"></script>

Code Breakdown:

  • Modern browsers execute /js/app.mjs.
  • Legacy browsers (no module support) execute /js/app.legacy.js.
  • Only one runs.

docs.title: Example 5: Dynamic Import for Heavy Component
docs.text:
document.getElementById('show-chart').addEventListener('click', async () => {
    const { renderChart } = await import('./chart.js');
    renderChart(document.getElementById('chart-container'));
});

Code Breakdown:

  • chart.js is loaded only when the button is clicked.
  • Bundlers split chart.js into a separate chunk.
  • Initial bundle stays small.

docs.title: Example 6: Route-Level Code Splitting (React)
docs.text:
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';
import { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';

const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard'));
const Settings = lazy(() => import('./pages/Settings'));

function App() {
    return (
        <Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>
            <Routes>
                <Route path="/" element={<Dashboard />} />
                <Route path="/settings" element={<Settings />} />
            </Routes>
        </Suspense>
    );
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Each route is loaded only when navigated to.
  • The initial bundle contains only shared code.
  • <Suspense> shows a skeleton while the route loads.

docs.title: Example 7: Import Map
docs.text:
<script type="importmap">
{
    "imports": {
        "lodash": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/lodash-es@4.17.21/lodash.js",
        "preact": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/preact@10.19.0/dist/preact.module.js",
        "app/": "/js/"
    }
}
</script>

<script type="module">
    import { debounce } from 'lodash';
    import { render } from 'preact';
    import { init } from 'app/init.js';
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • importmap maps bare specifiers to URLs.
  • import 'lodash' resolves to the CDN URL.
  • import 'app/init.js' resolves to /js/init.js.
  • Must appear before any module script.

docs.title: Example 8: Inline Critical JavaScript
docs.text:
<head>
    <script>
        // Inline critical script — runs immediately, blocks parser briefly
        document.documentElement.classList.add('js-enabled');
    </script>
</head>

Code Breakdown:

  • Inline scripts execute immediately when parsed.
  • Used for critical rendering decisions (e.g., .js-enabled class).
  • Keep inline scripts tiny — they block the parser.
  • Use nonces or hashes for CSP.

docs.title: Example 9: Complete Production Script Strategy
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Acme Dashboard</title>

    <!-- Inline critical script -->
    <script>document.documentElement.classList.add('js-enabled');</script>

    <!-- Preload critical CSS -->
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css">

    <!-- Modulepreload the entry point -->
    <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">
</head>
<body>
    <main id="app">Loading...</main>

    <!-- Deferred application script (module) -->
    <script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>

    <!-- Async third-party scripts -->
    <script src="https://www.google-analytics.com/analytics.js" async></script>
    <script src="https://widgets.example.com/chat.js" async></script>
</body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • Inline critical script — runs immediately.
  • Modulepreload — fetches the entry point and its dependencies.
  • Deferred module script — executes after parsing.
  • Async third-party scripts — independent, non-blocking.

docs.title: Example 10: Script Loading Audit
docs.text:
// In DevTools console: list all scripts and their loading strategy
const scripts = [...document.querySelectorAll('script[src]')];

console.table(scripts.map(s => ({
    src: s.src,
    async: s.async,
    defer: s.defer,
    type: s.type,
    module: s.type === 'module',
    nomodule: s.noModule
})));

Code Breakdown:

  • Lists all external scripts with their attributes.
  • Useful for auditing after a template change.
  • Identify blocking scripts that should be deferred.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Loading Strategy Application entry point type="module" + modulepreload Critical rendering script Inline blocking (small) Analytics async Ad scripts async Chat widget async Framework bundle type="module" Route-level code Dynamic import() Heavy component Dynamic import() Polyfills nomodule Third-party widgets async

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Never put synchronous scripts in the <head> unless absolutely necessary. Why: blocking scripts delay the first paint.
  2. Use defer for application scripts. Why: downloads in parallel, executes after parsing, preserves order.
  3. Use async for independent third-party scripts. Why: no ordering dependency; does not block the parser.
  4. Use type="module" for modern application code. Why: deferred by default, module scope, strict mode.
  5. Use modulepreload for the module entry point. Why: fetches the module graph in parallel.
  6. Use nomodule for legacy fallback. Why: modern and legacy browsers each load the right script.
  7. Split code at the route level. Why: the highest-ROI code-splitting strategy.
  8. Use dynamic import() for heavy components. Why: keep the initial bundle small.
  9. Use importmap when not using a bundler. Why: enables bare specifier imports in the browser.
  10. Add fetchpriority="high" to critical scripts. Why: tells the browser to fetch them first.
  11. Add fetchpriority="low" to non-critical scripts. Why: tells the browser to fetch them last.
  12. Inline tiny critical scripts. Why: avoids a network round-trip for a few bytes.
  13. Use async for all third-party scripts. Why: they should never block the parser.
  14. Test on slow networks. Why: differences are invisible on fast connections.
  15. Measure INP, LCP, and TBT. Why: script loading directly affects these metrics.
  16. Audit script loading after every framework upgrade. Why: framework behavior changes.
  17. Avoid document.write(). Why: blocks the parser and defeats the preload scanner.
  18. Avoid synchronous XHR. Why: blocks the main thread and the parser.
  19. Use nonces or hashes for inline scripts. Why: required for strict CSP.
  20. Monitor third-party script performance. Why: third-party scripts are the largest source of performance regressions.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Synchronous Scripts in <head>
docs.text:
<head>
    <script src="/js/analytics.js"></script>
    <script src="/js/app.js"></script>
</head>

Why it's wrong: Each script blocks parsing. The first paint is delayed by every script's download and execution.

✅ Correct:

<head>
    <link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">
</head>
<body>
    <main>Content</main>
    <script src="/js/analytics.js" async></script>
    <script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>
</body>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using async for Dependent Scripts
docs.text:
<script src="/js/jquery.js" async></script>
<script src="/js/plugin.js" async></script>

Why it's wrong: plugin.js depends on jquery.js, but async does not guarantee execution order. plugin.js may run before jquery.js is loaded.

✅ Correct:

<script src="/js/jquery.js" defer></script>
<script src="/js/plugin.js" defer></script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using defer for Third-Party Scripts
docs.text:
<script src="https://www.google-analytics.com/analytics.js" defer></script>

Why it's wrong: defer preserves order and executes after parsing. For independent third-party scripts, async is more efficient.

✅ Correct:

<script src="https://www.google-analytics.com/analytics.js" async></script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No modulepreload
docs.text:
<script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>

Why it's wrong: The browser fetches the entry module, parses it, discovers its imports, then fetches those — sequentially.

✅ Correct:

<link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/app.js">
<script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Loading All Routes Upfront
docs.text:
import Dashboard from './pages/Dashboard';
import Settings from './pages/Settings';
import Reports from './pages/Reports';
import Admin from './pages/Admin';

Why it's wrong: Every route's code is in the initial bundle, even though the user visits only one.

✅ Correct:

const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard'));
const Settings = lazy(() => import('./pages/Settings'));

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: document.write()
docs.text:
<script>document.write('<script src="/js/app.js"><\/script>');</script>

Why it's wrong: Blocks the parser and defeats the preload scanner.

✅ Correct: Use static <script> elements.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No fetchpriority on Critical Scripts
docs.text:
<script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

Why it's wrong: The browser fetches at default priority.

✅ Correct:

<script src="/js/app.js" defer fetchpriority="high"></script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Inline Scripts Without CSP Nonce
docs.text:
<script>console.log('critical');</script>

Why it's wrong: A strict CSP (script-src 'self') blocks inline scripts.

✅ Correct:

<script nonce="abc123">console.log('critical');</script>

With the CSP header:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'nonce-abc123'

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Loading Polyfills for Modern Browsers
docs.text:
<script src="/js/polyfills.js"></script>
<script src="/js/app.js"></script>

Why it's wrong: Modern browsers do not need most polyfills; loading them wastes bandwidth.

✅ Correct:

<script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>
<script nomodule src="/js/app.legacy.js"></script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Third-Party Script Impact
docs.text:
<script src="https://widgets.example.com/heavy.js" async></script>

Why it's wrong: Third-party scripts are often the largest source of performance regressions. async prevents parser-blocking, but execution still blocks the main thread.

✅ Correct: Audit third-party scripts; load them asynchronously and defer their initialization.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Blocking scripts delay the first paint by the full download + parse + execute time.
  • defer scripts do not delay the first paint — they execute after parsing.
  • async scripts may delay the first paint if they execute before the first paint.
  • Module scripts are deferred by default — they do not block parsing.
  • Dynamic imports reduce initial bundle size — faster TTI and INP.
  • Route-level code splitting is the highest-ROI strategy.
  • Third-party scripts are the largest source of performance regressions.
  • The main thread is shared — long-running scripts block layout, paint, and event handling.
  • INP is directly affected by script execution time.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use defer for application scripts.
  2. Use async for third-party scripts.
  3. Use type="module" for modern code.
  4. Use modulepreload for entry points.
  5. Split code at the route level.
  6. Use dynamic import() for heavy components.
  7. Add fetchpriority to critical and non-critical scripts.
  8. Audit third-party scripts regularly.
  9. Measure with Lighthouse, WebPageTest, and CrUX.
  10. Test on slow networks and low-end devices.

docs.title: CSP and Script Loading
docs.text:
Strict CSP directives block certain script loading patterns:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'nonce-abc123'
  • Inline scripts require nonces or hashes.
  • eval() and new Function() require 'unsafe-eval'.
  • External scripts must match script-src.

docs.title: Subresource Integrity (SRI)
docs.text:
External scripts should use SRI:

<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"
        integrity="sha384-..."
        crossorigin="anonymous"
        defer></script>

docs.title: Third-Party Scripts and Supply Chain Risk
docs.text:
Third-party scripts execute in your origin's context. A compromised third-party script can:

  • Steal user data.
  • Redirect users.
  • Mine cryptocurrency.
  • Inject ads.

Audit third-party scripts; use SRI where possible; consider self-hosting.

docs.title: importmap and CSP
docs.text:
importmap is subject to CSP. Add script-src directives to allow it:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'

Or use nonces:

<script type="importmap" nonce="abc123">...</script>

docs.title: Dynamic Import and CSP
docs.text: Dynamic import() is subject to CSP. The imported module must match script-src.

docs.title: document.write() and XSS
docs.text: document.write() is a common XSS vector. Do not use it.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Network panel — inspect script priorities and timing.
  • Chrome DevTools → Performance panel — see script execution in the timeline.
  • Chrome DevTools → Coverage panel — shows unused JavaScript.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — audits for render-blocking scripts.
  • render-blocking-resources audit — flags blocking scripts.
  • unused-javascript audit — flags unused code.
  • document.querySelectorAll('script[src]') — list all scripts.
  • performance.getEntriesByType('resource') — inspect script timing.
  • WebPageTest — filmstrip view of script loading.
  • PageSpeed Insights — field + lab data combined.
  • CrUX — real-world Core Web Vitals.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements — inspect script attributes.
  • document.currentScript — the currently executing script.
  • DOMContentLoaded event — fires after deferred scripts execute.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• defer — for application scripts and scripts with dependencies.
  • async — for independent third-party scripts.
  • type="module" — for modern application code.
  • nomodule — for legacy fallback.
  • Dynamic import() — for heavy components and route-level code splitting.
  • modulepreload — for the module entry point.
  • importmap — when not using a bundler.
  • Inline scripts — for tiny critical scripts.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use blocking scripts in <head> unless they are truly critical.
  • Do not use async for dependent scripts. Use defer.
  • Do not use defer for third-party scripts. Use async.
  • Do not load all routes upfront. Use code splitting.
  • Do not use document.write(). It blocks the parser.
  • Do not use synchronous XHR. It blocks the main thread.
  • Do not load polyfills for modern browsers. Use nomodule.
  • Do not ignore third-party script impact. Audit regularly.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
  • Total Blocking Time (TBT)
  • Core Web Vitals

  • async

  • nomodule
