docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Composite-only animations are 5–10× cheaper than layout animations.
  • transform and opacity are the only two universally compositor-only properties.
  • will-change promotes an element to its own compositing layer — but uses GPU memory.
  • Layer explosion — too many promoted layers — can cause jank, not prevent it.
  • Layout thrashing can block the main thread for hundreds of milliseconds.
  • content-visibility: auto can reduce rendering cost by 20–50% on long pages.
  • The frame budget is 16.7ms for 60fps and 8.3ms for 120fps.
  • Long tasks over 50ms are flagged by the browser as performance problems.
  • INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in March 2024.
  • CLS target is < 0.1.
  • INP target is < 200ms.
  • requestAnimationFrame batches visual updates to the next frame.
  • scheduler.yield() is the modern API for yielding to the browser (Chrome 129+).
  • aspect-ratio reserves space without needing explicit dimensions.
  • The View Transitions API provides native page transitions on the compositor thread.
  • contain: paint clips paint to the element's bounds.
  • contain: layout isolates the element's layout from its surroundings.
  • Paint flashing highlights painted regions in green.
  • Layer borders outline compositing layers in orange.
  • Chrome DevTools → Layers panel shows the 3D layer tree.
  • The Layout Instability API reports layout shifts programmatically.
  • performance.getEntriesByType('layout-shift') returns all recorded shifts.
  • The browser's compositor thread handles transform, opacity, and scroll animations.
  • Rendering impact is the last mile of performance — everything above it is undermined by jank.
  • The fastest animation is the one the compositor does alone.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Rendering impact is the cost a page imposes on the browser's rendering pipeline.
  • The pipeline: DOM → CSSOM → Render Tree → Layout → Paint → Composite.
  • Layout is the most expensive — recomputes geometry.
  • Paint is medium — fills in pixels.
  • Composite is cheapest — assembles layers.
  • Animate only transform and opacity — they run on the compositor thread.
  • Never animate width, height, top, left, margin, or padding — they trigger layout.
  • Use will-change sparingly — promote only what animates.
  • Use contain to isolate subtrees from the rest of the page.
  • Use content-visibility: auto to skip off-screen rendering.
  • Always specify width and height on images — prevents CLS.
  • Reserve space for ads and embeds — prevents CLS.
  • Batch DOM reads and writes — prevents layout thrashing.
  • Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates.
  • Break long tasks with scheduler.yield().
  • Measure with Lighthouse, Performance panel, and RUM.
  • Test on low-end devices — rendering gaps are invisible on fast hardware.
  • CLS target: < 0.1. INP target: < 200ms.
  • Rendering impact directly affects Core Web Vitals — CLS, INP, and the smoothness of every interaction.
  • The fastest animation is the one the compositor does alone.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Tokenization is the first stage of HTML parsing — the process by which the browser converts a stream of raw characters into a sequence of discrete, meaningful tokens. Each token represents a structural unit of HTML: a start tag, an end tag, an attribute, a comment, a character, or a doctype declaration.

<p class="intro">Hello</p>

The tokenizer processes this string and produces:

StartTag(p)
  Attribute(name="class", value="intro")
EndTag(p)
Character("Hello")

Tokenization is the bridge between bytes on the wire and the tree structure the browser builds next. It is a state machine — a set of rules that define, for every character, which state the tokenizer is in and what it should do next.

The HTML tokenizer is defined in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard. It is not a regex, not a parser, and not a library — it is a precisely specified algorithm with over 80 states, each defining behavior for every possible input character.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Tokenization serves several essential purposes:

  • Translate bytes into structure — converts flat text into semantic units.
  • Handle error recovery — browsers must parse malformed HTML, not reject it.
  • Enable streaming parsing — tokens are emitted as bytes arrive, not after the full document is downloaded.
  • Support incremental rendering — the parser can build the DOM before the document is complete.
  • Enable the preload scanner — a lightweight tokenizer discovers resources before the full parser runs.
  • Ensure deterministic behavior — every browser parses the same input the same way.
  • Prevent XSS via malformed input — error handling rules are security-relevant.

Tokenization is the first and most fundamental stage of browser parsing. Everything the browser does with HTML — DOM construction, CSS application, accessibility tree, layout — depends on the tokenizer producing a correct stream of tokens.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Browser Parsing Pipeline
│
├── Bytes          ← raw bytes from the network
├── Characters     ← decoded via charset
├── Tokenization   ← characters → tokens (THIS CHAPTER)
├── Tree Construction ← tokens → DOM nodes
├── DOM            ← the document object model
├── Script Blocking ← JavaScript pauses parsing
└── Rendering Pipeline ← DOM + CSSOM → pixels

Tokenization is the second stage of the parsing pipeline, after character decoding and before tree construction. It is the layer where the browser first understands what the bytes mean.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTML is a loosely specified format. Unlike JSON or XML, HTML tolerates malformed input. A missing closing tag, an unquoted attribute, a stray < character — all must be handled gracefully. The browser cannot simply reject a page because a developer forgot a </p>.

But handling malformed input requires rules. What happens when the tokenizer encounters < followed by a space? What about <div class=foo bar>? What about <script> containing </script> inside a string literal? These cases must be specified precisely so every browser produces the same result.

Tokenization exists to define those rules — a state machine that determines, for every possible input character, what token to emit and what state to transition to.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No formal tokenizer spec Browsers parsed HTML differently No error recovery Malformed HTML broke parsing No streaming Full document needed before parsing No preload scanner Resources discovered late No deterministic behavior Same HTML → different DOM in different browsers

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The HTML tokenizer was formalized in the HTML5 specification (2008–2014) to end the era of browser-specific parsing. Before HTML5, different browsers handled malformed HTML differently — a page might work in IE but break in Firefox.

The HTML5 tokenizer defined:

  • 80+ states — each with precise rules for every character.
  • Error recovery — malformed input is handled gracefully, not rejected.
  • Streaming — tokens are emitted as bytes arrive.
  • Deterministic behavior — same input → same output in every browser.

The tokenizer is also the basis for the preload scanner — a lightweight version that runs ahead of the main parser to discover resources early.

In 2026, the HTML tokenizer is fully specified and universally implemented. Every modern browser follows the WHATWG HTML Living Standard. The question is not "does it work?" but "how does it work under the hood?"

docs.title: The Token Types
docs.text:
The HTML tokenizer produces these token types:

Token Example Meaning DOCTYPE <!DOCTYPE html> Document type declaration StartTag <div> Opening tag EndTag </div> Closing tag Comment <!-- ... --> Comment Character a, B, 1, ! Text character EOF — End of file

docs.title: A Simple Tokenization Example
docs.text:
<p class="intro">Hello, world!</p>

Tokens produced:

1. StartTag(p)
     Attribute(name="class", value="intro")
2. Character("H")
3. Character("e")
4. Character("l")
5. Character("l")
6. Character("o")
7. Character(",")
8. Character(" ")
9. Character("w")
10. Character("o")
11. Character("r")
12. Character("l")
13. Character("d")
14. Character("!")
15. EndTag(p)
16. EOF

Note: Characters are grouped for efficiency in practice, but the specification emits them individually.

docs.title: The State Machine
docs.text:
The tokenizer is a state machine. It is always in exactly one state at a time. The current character determines the next state and the action.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Data state                                  │
│  ├── See `<` → Tag open state                │
│  ├── See `&` → Character reference state     │
│  ├── See `\0` → Parse error; emit character  │
│  └── See any other character → emit character│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The Data State — The Default
docs.text:
The tokenizer starts in the Data state. It emits every character until it encounters one of the special characters:

  • < — transitions to the Tag open state.
  • & — transitions to the Character reference state.
  • \0 — parse error; the null character is emitted as-is.

docs.title: The Tag Open State
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Tag open state                              │
│  ├── See `!` → Markup declaration open state │
│  ├── See `/` → End tag open state            │
│  ├── See ASCII letter → Tag name state       │
│  └── See anything else → Parse error;        │
│      emit `<` and reconsume in Data state    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The Tag Name State
docs.text:
The tokenizer collects the tag name, character by character, until it encounters:

  • Tab, LF, FF, space → Before attribute name state.
  • / → Self-closing start tag state.
  • > → Data state (emit the tag).
  • Uppercase ASCII letter → lowercase it and continue.

docs.title: The Attribute Name State
docs.text: Collects the attribute name. Handles quoted and unquoted values. Terminates on =, whitespace, /, or >.

docs.title: The Attribute Value State
docs.text: Collects the attribute value. Handles double-quoted, single-quoted, and unquoted values. Supports character references (&, A, etc.).

docs.title: The Comment State
docs.text: Collects comment text until --> is encountered.

docs.title: A Realistic Example with Attributes
docs.text:
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank" data-id=42>Link</a>

Tokens produced:

1. StartTag(a)
     Attribute(name="href", value="https://example.com")
     Attribute(name="target", value="_blank")
     Attribute(name="data-id", value="42")
2. Character("L")
3. Character("i")
4. Character("n")
5. Character("k")
6. EndTag(a)

docs.title: The RCDATA and RAWTEXT States
docs.text:
Two special states for elements with special content rules:

  • RCDATA — used inside <title> and <textarea>. Character references are decoded, but tags are not parsed.
  • RAWTEXT — used inside <script>, <style>, <xmp>, <iframe>, <noembed>, and <noframes>. Neither tags nor character references are parsed — the content is passed through as raw text until the closing tag is found.
<title>Hello & Goodbye</title>

Produces a Character("Hello & Goodbye") token — the & is decoded.

<script>if (a < b) {}</script>

Produces a Character("if (a < b) {}") token — the < is not decoded. Script content is passed through raw.

docs.title: The "Telegraph Operator" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the tokenizer as a telegraph operator receiving a stream of dots and dashes:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INPUT: dots and dashes                      │
│  └── .... . .-.. .-.. ---                   │
│                                              │
│  OPERATOR (state machine)                    │
│  ├── Recognizes patterns                     │
│  ├── Groups them into letters                │
│  └── Emits letters                           │
│                                              │
│  OUTPUT: H E L L O                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The tokenizer reads characters one at a time, recognizes patterns, and emits tokens.

docs.title: The "State Machine" Mental Model
docs.text:
The tokenizer is always in exactly one state. Every character determines:

1. What action to take (emit token, append to buffer, error)
2. What state to transition to next

Data ──'<'──► TagOpen ──'a'──► TagName ──' '──► BeforeAttrName
  ▲              │              │              │
  │              │              │              │
  └──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
       (on '>' — emit tag, return to Data)

Every path through the state machine is deterministic. The same input always produces the same output.

docs.title: The "Streaming Parser" Mental Model
docs.text:
The tokenizer is a streaming parser. It does not wait for the full document to arrive.

Bytes arrive from network:
  ────[<div>Hel]────[lo</div>]────[<p>...]────►
       │              │              │
       ▼              ▼              ▼
  Tokenizer emits tokens as bytes arrive:
  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │ <div>        │  │ "llo"    │  │ <p>      │
  │ "Hel"        │  │ </div>   │  │ ...      │
  └──────────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘

This is why the browser can render pages before the full HTML is downloaded.

docs.title: The "The Tokenizer Is Not the Parser" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TOKENIZER                                   │
│  └── Converts characters → tokens            │
│  └── Knows nothing about the DOM             │
│  └── Knows nothing about nesting             │
│  └── Stateless about document structure      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  TREE CONSTRUCTION (Parser)                  │
│  └── Consumes tokens → DOM nodes             │
│  └── Knows about nesting, implicit tags      │
│  └── Knows about the HTML specification      │
│  └── Maintains the parse stack               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The tokenizer emits tokens without understanding structure. The parser (tree construction) builds the DOM from the token stream. They are two separate stages with different responsibilities.

docs.title: The "Error Recovery" Mental Model
docs.text:
HTML is not XML. Malformed input is not rejected — it is corrected.

Input: <p class=foo bar>
Tokenizer sees:
  ├── `<` → Tag open
  ├── `p` → Tag name: "p"
  ├── ` ` → Before attribute name
  ├── `class` → Attribute name: "class"
  ├── `=` → Before attribute value
  ├── `foo` → Attribute value: "foo"
  ├── ` ` → Before attribute name (unquoted value ended)
  ├── `bar` → Attribute name: "bar"
  └── `>` → Emit tag

The unquoted foo ended at whitespace — a parse error, but the tokenizer recovers and produces a valid token.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Tokenizer State Machine
docs.text: The HTML tokenizer is a state machine with over 80 states. Each state defines behavior for every possible input character.

docs.title: Concept 2: The Data State
docs.text: The default state. Emits characters until it sees <, &, or \0.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Tag Open State
docs.text: Transitioned to when the Data state sees <. Determines whether the token is a start tag, end tag, or markup declaration.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Tag Name State
docs.text: Collects the tag name. Lowercases ASCII letters.

docs.title: Concept 5: The Attribute States
docs.text: Handle attribute names and values. Support double-quoted, single-quoted, and unquoted values.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Comment States
docs.text: Handle <!-- ... --> and its malformed variants (<!-->, <!--->, etc.).

docs.title: Concept 7: The DOCTYPE States
docs.text: Handle <!DOCTYPE ...>. The DOCTYPE affects the document's rendering mode (quirks, limited quirks, no-quirks).

docs.title: Concept 8: The RCDATA State
docs.text: Used inside <title> and <textarea>. Character references are decoded; tags are not parsed.

docs.title: Concept 9: The RAWTEXT State
docs.text: Used inside <script>, <style>, and similar elements. Neither tags nor character references are parsed. Content is passed through as raw text.

docs.title: Concept 10: The Script Data States
docs.text: A set of special states for <script> content. Handle the <!--, <script>, and </script> sequences specially to avoid breaking script content.

docs.title: Concept 11: The Character Reference States
docs.text: Handle &, A, A, and named character references. Decode to the corresponding character.

docs.title: Concept 12: The Parse Error
docs.text: A state where the input is malformed. The tokenizer recovers rather than rejecting. Parse errors are logged in DevTools but do not break the page.

docs.title: Concept 13: The Emission of Character Tokens
docs.text: The tokenizer emits one Character token per character in the specification. In practice, browsers batch them for efficiency.

docs.title: Concept 14: The EOF Token
docs.text: Emitted at the end of the input. Signals the parser to close remaining open elements.

docs.title: Concept 15: The Preload Scanner
docs.text: A lightweight version of the tokenizer that runs ahead of the main parser. It scans the raw bytes for <script>, <link>, <img>, and other resource references and starts fetching them immediately.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Reconsume Rule
docs.text: When a state determines that a character does not belong, it can reconsume the character in the previous state. This is how the tokenizer handles transitions without losing input.

docs.title: Concept 17: The Insertion Mode
docs.text: The tree constructor maintains an insertion mode — a state machine of its own — that determines how tokens are converted to DOM nodes. The insertion mode is not the same as the tokenizer state.

docs.title: Concept 18: The Stack of Open Elements
docs.text: The tree constructor maintains a stack of open elements — the element nesting context. The tokenizer does not know about this stack.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Active Formatting Elements List
docs.text: A list of formatting elements (<b>, <i>, <a>) that are active at the current point. The tree constructor maintains this list.

docs.title: Concept 20: The "Parse Error" Is Not a Rejection
docs.text: A parse error in HTML is a recoverable event. The tokenizer and parser continue, applying the specified recovery rules. Pages with hundreds of parse errors may still render correctly.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Tokenizing <p>Hello</p>
docs.text:
Input: <p>Hello</p>

1.  State: Data
    ├── See `<` → transition to Tag open state
    │
2.  State: Tag open
    ├── See `p` → emit nothing; append to tag name buffer; transition to Tag name state
    │
3.  State: Tag name
    ├── See `>` → emit StartTag(p); transition to Data state
    │
4.  State: Data
    ├── See `H` → emit Character("H")
    ├── See `e` → emit Character("e")
    ├── See `l` → emit Character("l")
    ├── See `l` → emit Character("l")
    ├── See `o` → emit Character("o")
    │
5.  State: Data
    ├── See `<` → transition to Tag open state
    │
6.  State: Tag open
    ├── See `/` → transition to End tag open state
    │
7.  State: End tag open
    ├── See `p` → transition to Tag name state
    │
8.  State: Tag name
    ├── See `>` → emit EndTag(p); transition to Data state
    │
9.  State: Data
    └── EOF → emit EOF token

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Tokenizing an Attribute
docs.text:
Input: <a href="x">y</a>

1.  State: Data → `<` → Tag open
2.  State: Tag open → `a` → Tag name
3.  State: Tag name → ` ` → Before attribute name
4.  State: Before attribute name → `h` → Attribute name
5.  State: Attribute name → `ref` collected → `=` → Before attribute value
6.  State: Before attribute value → `"` → Attribute value (double-quoted)
7.  State: Attribute value (double-quoted) → `x` → append to value buffer
8.  State: Attribute value (double-quoted) → `"` → After attribute value (quoted)
9.  State: After attribute value (quoted) → `>` → emit StartTag(a) with href="x"
10. State: Data → `y` → emit Character("y")
11. State: Data → `<` → Tag open
12. State: Tag open → `/` → End tag open
13. State: End tag open → `a` → Tag name
14. State: Tag name → `>` → emit EndTag(a)
15. State: Data → EOF → emit EOF

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Preload Scanner
docs.text:
1.  Main parser starts parsing the HTML.
    │
    ▼
2.  Preload scanner runs ahead, scanning raw bytes.
    │
    ▼
3.  Scanner finds <script src="app.js">.
    │   └── Starts fetching app.js immediately.
    │
    ▼
4.  Scanner finds <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">.
    │   └── Starts fetching style.css immediately.
    │
    ▼
5.  Main parser reaches these elements later.
    │   └── Resources are already in flight or cached.
    │
    ▼
6.  First paint is faster.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: RCDATA vs RAWTEXT
docs.text:
Input: <title>Hello & Goodbye</title>
       └─── RCDATA state

1.  Tokenizer sees <title> → transitions to RCDATA state.
2.  RCDATA state: emits Character("Hello ").
3.  RCDATA state: sees `&` → decodes → emits Character("&").
4.  RCDATA state: emits Character(" Goodbye").
5.  RCDATA state: sees `</title>` → emits EndTag(title).
6.  Returns to Data state.

Output: Character("Hello & Goodbye")

Input: <script>if (a < b) {}</script>
       └─── RAWTEXT state

1.  Tokenizer sees <script> → transitions to Script data state.
2.  Script data state: passes through all characters verbatim.
   └── No character references decoded.
   └── No tags parsed (except </script>).
3.  Script data state: sees `</script>` → emits EndTag(script).
4.  Returns to Data state.

Output: Character("if (a < b) {}")

docs.title: The State Machine Specification
docs.text:
The HTML tokenizer is specified as a state machine with a precise algorithm:

For each state:
  For each character class:
    ├── Action: emit token, append to buffer, error
    └── Next state: transition to

There are over 80 states, each with rules for every possible character.

docs.title: The Input Stream
docs.text:
The tokenizer consumes an input stream of Unicode characters. The stream is produced by:

  1. Fetching bytes over the network.
  2. Decoding bytes using the declared or detected character encoding (UTF-8, ISO-8859-1, etc.).
  3. Normalizing newlines (CR, CRLF → LF).

docs.title: The Token Emission
docs.text:
The tokenizer maintains buffers:

  • Tag name buffer — accumulates the tag name.
  • Attribute name buffer — accumulates the current attribute name.
  • Attribute value buffer — accumulates the current attribute value.
  • Comment buffer — accumulates comment text.

When a token is complete, it is emitted to the tree constructor.

docs.title: The Character Token Batching
docs.text: The specification emits one Character token per character. In practice, browsers batch adjacent characters into a single Character token for efficiency. This is an optimization, not a specification change.

docs.title: The Reconsume Mechanism
docs.text:
Many states use the reconsume rule: if a character does not belong in the current state, the tokenizer transitions to a new state without consuming the character, and the new state re-examines it.

Example:
  State: Attribute value (unquoted)
  See `>` → transition to Data state; reconsume `>` 
  State: Data
  See `>` → emit Character(">")

The reconsume rule is what makes the state machine work correctly without losing input.

docs.title: The Parse Error Reporting
docs.text:
Parse errors are reported to the browser's DevTools console. They do not stop parsing. Common parse errors:

  • Unquoted attribute value containing =.
  • Missing DOCTYPE.
  • Duplicate attribute name.
  • Unclosed comment.

docs.title: The Script Data Escaped States
docs.text:
The <script> element has its own tokenizer states — the Script data states — that handle:

  • <!-- sequences inside the script.
  • <script> sequences inside the script (rare, but possible in string literals).
  • </script> sequences inside the script (to detect the actual closing tag).

This is why you cannot write </script> inside a JavaScript string without escaping it — the tokenizer will treat it as the end of the script element.

<script>
    // ❌ This breaks the script
    const str = "</script>";
</script>

<script>
    // ✅ This works
    const str = "<\/script>";
</script>

docs.title: The Preload Scanner Architecture
docs.text:
The preload scanner is a speculative tokenizer that runs on the raw bytes of the HTML, in parallel with the main parser. It:

  • Scans for <script src>, <link rel="stylesheet">, <img src>, etc.
  • Starts fetching resources immediately.
  • Does not wait for the main parser to reach the element.

The scanner is less precise than the main tokenizer — it uses heuristics to find resource references. But it is dramatically faster and runs off the main thread.

docs.title: The Tree Construction Interface
docs.text:
The tokenizer calls into the tree constructor with each emitted token:

Tokenizer emits StartTag(p)
    │
    ▼
Tree constructor:
  ├── Determines the insertion mode
  ├── Checks the stack of open elements
  ├── Creates a DOM node
  └── Appends to the DOM tree

The tokenizer does not know about the DOM. It only produces tokens.

docs.title: Tokenization Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Bytes arrive from the network.
    │
    ▼
2.  Bytes decoded to characters (charset).
    │
    ▼
3.  Tokenizer consumes characters one at a time.
    │
    ▼
4.  State machine transitions based on characters.
    │
    ▼
5.  Tokens emitted to the tree constructor.
    │
    ▼
6.  Tree constructor builds the DOM.
    │
    ▼
7.  Repeat until EOF.
    │
    ▼
8.  EOF token emitted.

docs.title: The Streaming Lifecycle
docs.text:
Bytes: ────[<!DOCTYPE html><html>]────[<head>...]────[<body>...]────►
        │                          │              │
        ▼                          ▼              ▼
Tokens: DOCTYPE, StartTag(html)   StartTag(head) StartTag(body)
        │                          │              │
        ▼                          ▼              ▼
DOM:    <html>                     <head>         <body>

The DOM is built incrementally as bytes arrive. The user may see content before the full document is downloaded.

docs.title: Example 1: Tokenizing a Simple Document
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Test</title></head>
<body><p>Hello</p></body>
</html>

Tokens emitted (in order):

1. DOCTYPE(html)
2. StartTag(html)
3. StartTag(head)
4. StartTag(title)
5. Character("T"), Character("e"), Character("s"), Character("t")
6. EndTag(title)
7. EndTag(head)
8. StartTag(body)
9. StartTag(p)
10. Character("H"), Character("e"), Character("l"), Character("l"), Character("o")
11. EndTag(p)
12. EndTag(body)
13. EndTag(html)
14. EOF

docs.title: Example 2: Self-Closing Tag
docs.text:
<br/>

Tokens emitted:

StartTag(br) with self-closing flag

Note: In HTML (not XHTML), the / is optional. <br> and <br/> produce the same token. The self-closing flag is ignored for non-void elements.

docs.title: Example 3: Unquoted Attributes
docs.text:
<div id=main class=container>

Tokens emitted:

StartTag(div)
  Attribute(name="id", value="main")
  Attribute(name="class", value="container")

Note: Unquoted attributes are valid in HTML but not in XHTML.

docs.title: Example 4: Boolean Attributes
docs.text:
<input disabled required>

Tokens emitted:

StartTag(input)
  Attribute(name="disabled", value="")
  Attribute(name="required", value="")

Note: Boolean attributes have an empty string value.

docs.title: Example 5: Entity Decoding
docs.text:
<p>Hello & Goodbye <3</p>

Tokens emitted:

StartTag(p)
Character("H"), Character("e"), Character("l"), Character("l"), Character("o"),
Character(" "), Character("&"), Character(" "),
Character("G"), Character("o"), Character("o"), Character("d"), Character("b"),
Character("y"), Character("e"), Character(" "),
Character("<"), Character("3")
EndTag(p)

The & decoded to & and < decoded to <.

docs.title: Example 6: Comments
docs.text:
<!-- This is a comment -->

Token emitted:

Comment(" This is a comment ")

docs.title: Example 7: Malformed HTML with Recovery
docs.text:
<p>Hello<p>World

Tokens emitted:

StartTag(p)
Character("H"), ..., Character("o")
StartTag(p)
Character("W"), ..., Character("d")
EOF

Note: The tokenizer emits both <p> start tags. The tree constructor recognizes that a <p> cannot contain another <p> and implicitly closes the first one. This is a tree construction behavior, not a tokenizer behavior.

docs.title: Example 8: Script Content
docs.text:
<script>
  const x = 1 < 2;
  const y = 3 > 2;
</script>

Tokens emitted:

StartTag(script)
Character(" \n  const x = 1 < 2;\n  const y = 3 > 2;\n")
EndTag(script)

Note: Inside <script>, the tokenizer does not parse <, >, or &. It passes content through raw until it sees </script>.

docs.title: Example 9: The </script> Trap
docs.text:
<script>
  const s = "</script>";
</script>

Tokens emitted:

StartTag(script)
Character(" \n  const s = \"")
EndTag(script)         ← the tokenizer sees </script> and ends the element
Character("\";\n")     ← the rest is text, not script
StartTag(script)       ← the second <script> is parsed separately
EndTag(script)

The fix:

<script>
  const s = "<\/script>";
</script>

docs.title: Example 10: Character Reference in Attribute
docs.text:
<a href="?a=1&b=2">Link</a>

Tokens emitted:

StartTag(a)
  Attribute(name="href", value="?a=1&b=2")   ← & decoded
Character("L"), ..., Character("k")
EndTag(a)

docs.title: Example 11: The Preload Scanner in Action
docs.text:
<head>
  <script src="/app.js"></script>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
</head>

Main parser timeline:

t=0ms    Parser starts
t=10ms   Parser reaches <head>
t=20ms   Parser reaches <script src="/app.js">
         └── If preload scanner already fetched app.js, execute it.
t=25ms   Parser reaches <link rel="stylesheet">
         └── If preload scanner already fetched style.css, apply it.

Preload scanner timeline:

t=5ms    Scanner discovers <script src="/app.js"> → starts fetch
t=8ms    Scanner discovers <link rel="stylesheet"> → starts fetch

The preload scanner starts fetches before the main parser reaches the element.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Tokenizer Behavior Parsing HTML Data → Tag open → Tag name → Data Parsing attributes Tag name → Before attr name → Attr name → Attr value → Data Parsing comments Markup declaration open → Comment → Data Parsing DOCTYPE Markup declaration open → DOCTYPE → Data Parsing script content Script data states Parsing style content RAWTEXT state Parsing title content RCDATA state Parsing textarea content RCDATA state Decoding entities Character reference states Preload scanning Lightweight tokenizer

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Validate your HTML. Why: parse errors indicate malformed markup that may behave unexpectedly.
  2. Always include a DOCTYPE. Why: the DOCTYPE determines the document's rendering mode.
  3. Quote attribute values. Why: unquoted values are valid but error-prone.
  4. Use lowercase tag names. Why: the tokenizer lowercases them anyway.
  5. Escape & as & in content. Why: ambiguous ampersands may be parsed unexpectedly.
  6. Escape < as < in content. Why: an unescaped < starts a tag.
  7. Escape </script> in script content as <\/script>. Why: the tokenizer ends the script element at the first </script>.
  8. Use <!-- --> for comments. Why: malformed comments may be parsed unexpectedly.
  9. Do not rely on malformed HTML. Why: recovery behavior is specified but not guaranteed in every detail.
  10. Use the W3C Validator. Why: catches parse errors before deployment.
  11. Test with view-source: and DevTools. Why: confirms the tokenizer sees what you intend.
  12. Understand the preload scanner. Why: it affects resource discovery and loading.
  13. Avoid document.write(). Why: it interrupts the tokenizer and defeats the preload scanner.
  14. Do not use < in attribute values without escaping. Why: it may be parsed as a new tag.
  15. Understand the difference between RCDATA and RAWTEXT. Why: it affects how content is parsed.
  16. Do not put <!-- inside a script without understanding the script data states. Why: it changes the tokenizer's behavior.
  17. Test on multiple browsers. Why: even though the spec is deterministic, edge cases may differ.
  18. Audit HTML after template changes. Why: template systems may introduce malformed markup.
  19. Use modern HTML5 syntax. Why: the tokenizer is designed for HTML5, not XHTML.
  20. Understand that the tokenizer does not build the DOM. Why: it emits tokens; the tree constructor builds the tree.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: </script> Inside a JavaScript String
docs.text:
<script>
  const s = "</script>";
</script>

Why it's wrong: The tokenizer sees </script> and ends the script element, breaking the JavaScript.

✅ Correct:

<script>
  const s = "<\/script>";
</script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unescaped < in Content
docs.text:
<p>1 < 2</p>

Why it's wrong: The tokenizer sees < and starts a tag.

✅ Correct:

<p>1 < 2</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unescaped & in Content
docs.text:
<p>Tom & Jerry</p>

Why it's wrong: The tokenizer sees & and starts a character reference — ambiguous.

✅ Correct:

<p>Tom & Jerry</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing DOCTYPE
docs.text:
<html>
<head><title>Test</title></head>
</html>

Why it's wrong: Without a DOCTYPE, the browser enters quirks mode — different layout and CSS behavior.

✅ Correct:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
...

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unquoted Attribute with Special Characters
docs.text:
<div class=foo bar>

Why it's wrong: The unquoted value foo ends at the space, and bar becomes a separate attribute. The tokenizer recovers, but the result may not match intent.

✅ Correct:

<div class="foo bar">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unclosed Comment
docs.text:
<!-- This is a comment

Why it's wrong: The tokenizer treats the rest of the document as comment content.

✅ Correct:

<!-- This is a comment -->

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: document.write() in the Middle of Parsing
docs.text:
<script>document.write('<div>Injected</div>');</script>

Why it's wrong: document.write() interrupts the tokenizer and forces the parser to re-parse injected content. It defeats the preload scanner.

✅ Correct: Use DOM APIs to insert content.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Parse Error Recovery
docs.text:
<p>Hello<p>World

Why it's wrong: The tokenizer handles this, but the tree constructor's recovery behavior may not match your intent.

✅ Correct:

<p>Hello</p>
<p>World</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using XHTML Syntax in HTML
docs.text:
<div />

Why it's wrong: In HTML, <div/> is a start tag with a self-closing flag — but the flag is ignored for non-void elements. The <div> is not closed.

✅ Correct:

<div></div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming the Tokenizer Knows Structure
docs.text:
<p>Hello<div>World</div></p>

Why it's wrong: The tokenizer emits the tokens as specified. The tree constructor is what recognizes that a <p> cannot contain a <div> and closes the <p>.

✅ Correct: Understand the separation between tokenization and tree construction.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Tokenization is fast — it is a single-pass state machine.
  • Streaming tokenization — the tokenizer emits tokens as bytes arrive; it does not wait for the full document.
  • Character token batching — browsers batch adjacent characters for efficiency.
  • The preload scanner — runs off the main thread and starts resource fetches early.
  • Memory — the tokenizer uses small buffers; memory usage is minimal.
  • Large documents — tokenization scales linearly with document size.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep HTML small — less to tokenize.
  2. Avoid malformed HTML — parse errors add overhead.
  3. Do not use document.write() — it interrupts streaming.
  4. Understand the preload scanner — it affects resource loading.
  5. Minify HTML — removes whitespace and comments.
  6. Avoid excessive comments — comments are tokens.

docs.title: XSS via Malformed Input
docs.text:
Attackers can craft malformed HTML that the tokenizer parses unexpectedly. Examples:

  • Nested <script> tags.
  • Unclosed comments that swallow legitimate content.
  • Attribute injection via unquoted values.

Defense: Sanitize user input; escape <, >, &, ", '.

docs.title: The </script> Escape
docs.text:
The </script> sequence terminates the script element even if it appears inside a JavaScript string. This can be exploited to inject scripts.

Defense: Escape </script> as <\/script> in generated JavaScript.

docs.title: The Preload Scanner and CSP
docs.text:
The preload scanner respects CSP. Resources that violate CSP are not fetched by the scanner.

Defense: Set CSP directives on all responses.

docs.title: RCDATA and RAWTEXT Injection
docs.text:
Content inside RCDATA and RAWTEXT elements is not parsed as HTML. But content inside <title> or <textarea> can still be exploited if it is later extracted and inserted into the DOM unsafely.

Defense: Escape content when moving it between contexts.

docs.title: The DOCTYPE and Quirks Mode
docs.text:
Missing or malformed DOCTYPEs trigger quirks mode, which may enable legacy CSS and JavaScript behaviors with security implications.

Defense: Always include <!DOCTYPE html>.

docs.title: Attribute Value Injection
docs.text:
Unquoted attribute values are terminated by whitespace — an attacker can inject additional attributes.

Defense: Always quote attribute values; sanitize user input.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements — inspect the DOM produced by the tree constructor.
  • Chrome DevTools → View Source — see the raw HTML.
  • W3C Validator — validator.w3.org — catches parse errors.
  • view-source: — view the raw HTML before parsing.
  • Chrome DevTools → Console — parse errors may be logged.
  • HTML5 Validator — html5.validator.nu — validates against the WHATWG spec.
  • Test with curl and inspect the raw HTML — verifies what the tokenizer sees.
  • Use document.documentElement.outerHTML — see the DOM after parsing.
  • Test with <template> — inspect parsed content without rendering it.
  • Use DOMParser — parse HTML strings programmatically.
  • Test on multiple browsers — verify consistent behavior.
  • Check for parse errors — Chrome DevTools → Sources → check the parser error console.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Understanding HTML parsing — tokenization is the first stage.
  • Debugging malformed HTML — the tokenizer reveals parse errors.
  • Optimizing resource loading — the preload scanner depends on tokenization.
  • Security review — understanding the tokenizer is essential for XSS prevention.
  • Building HTML parsers — tokenization is the first step.
  • Sanitizing HTML — sanitizers must model the tokenizer's behavior.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not rely on the tokenizer to build the DOM. Tree construction is a separate stage.
  • Do not assume recovery behavior is ideal. Recovery is specified but not always intuitive.
  • Do not use malformed HTML. Always validate.
  • Do not ignore the </script> trap. It breaks scripts.
  • Do not assume the preload scanner is perfect. It uses heuristics.
