docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The HTML tokenizer has over 80 states — each with precise rules for every character.
  • The tokenizer is a state machine — the current character determines the next state and action.
  • The tokenizer emits one Character token per character in the specification, but browsers batch them for efficiency.
  • The tokenizer does not know about the DOM. It only emits tokens; the tree constructor builds the tree.
  • The preload scanner is a lightweight tokenizer that runs ahead of the main parser.
  • <script> content is not parsed as HTML — the tokenizer uses special script data states.
  • </script> inside a JavaScript string ends the script element — the most famous tokenizer trap.
  • <title> and <textarea> use RCDATA state — character references are decoded, but tags are not parsed.
  • <style> and <script> use RAWTEXT-like states — neither tags nor character references are parsed.
  • The DOCTYPE determines the document's rendering mode — quirks, limited quirks, or no-quirks.
  • Missing DOCTYPE triggers quirks mode — different layout and CSS behavior.
  • Parse errors are recoverable — the tokenizer and parser continue.
  • The reconsume rule lets the state machine transition without losing input.
  • <div/> in HTML is not self-closing — the self-closing flag is ignored for non-void elements.
  • <br> and <br/> produce the same token — the / is optional.
  • Unquoted attributes are valid in HTML — but terminated by whitespace.
  • Boolean attributes have an empty value — <input disabled> produces Attribute(name="disabled", value="").
  • Character references (&, A) are decoded by the tokenizer — except inside RAWTEXT elements.
  • The tree constructor maintains an insertion mode — a state machine of its own.
  • The stack of open elements tracks the current nesting context — the tokenizer does not.
  • The active formatting elements list tracks <b>, <i>, <a> — the tree constructor maintains it.
  • Tokenization is fast — it is a single-pass state machine.
  • Streaming tokenization — the browser renders pages before the full HTML is downloaded.
  • The tokenizer is fully specified — every browser produces the same tokens for the same input.
  • HTML is not XML — malformed input is corrected, not rejected.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Tokenization is the first stage of HTML parsing — converting characters into tokens.
  • It is a state machine with over 80 states.
  • It emits tokens — DOCTYPE, StartTag, EndTag, Comment, Character, EOF.
  • The Data state is the default — emits characters until it sees <, &, or \0.
  • The Tag open state determines whether the token is a start tag, end tag, or markup declaration.
  • The Attribute states handle attribute names and values.
  • RCDATA — used in <title> and <textarea> — decodes character references but not tags.
  • RAWTEXT — used in <script> and <style> — passes content through raw.
  • The tokenizer does not build the DOM — the tree constructor does.
  • The preload scanner is a lightweight tokenizer that runs ahead of the main parser.
  • Parse errors are recoverable — the tokenizer and parser continue.
  • </script> inside a JavaScript string breaks the script — the most famous tokenizer trap.
  • Always include a DOCTYPE — it determines the document's rendering mode.
  • Always escape <, >, &, ", ' in content and attributes.
  • Always quote attribute values — unquoted values are error-prone.
  • Understand the separation between tokenization and tree construction — they are different stages.
  • The tokenizer is fully specified and universally implemented — every browser follows the WHATWG HTML Living Standard.
  • Tokenization is fast, streaming, and deterministic — it is the foundation of the browser's parsing pipeline.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Tree construction is the second stage of HTML parsing — the process by which the browser converts the stream of tokens emitted by the tokenizer into a Document Object Model (DOM) tree. It is the stage where individual tokens become structured, nested DOM nodes with parent-child relationships, attributes, and text content.

Tokenizer output:          Tree constructor output:

StartTag(html)             html
StartTag(head)             ├── head
StartTag(title)            │   └── title
Character("Test")          │       └── "Test"
EndTag(title)              └── body
EndTag(head)                   └── p
StartTag(body)                     └── "Hello"
StartTag(p)
Character("Hello")
EndTag(p)
EndTag(body)
EndTag(html)

The tokenizer produces a flat sequence of tokens. The tree constructor gives them structure — deciding which elements nest inside which, which tags are implicitly closed, which missing tags must be inserted, and how malformed markup should be recovered.

Tree construction is the stage where the browser interprets the token stream according to the HTML specification. It is where <p>Hello<p>World becomes two sibling paragraphs, where a missing </li> is silently closed, and where a <table> inside a <p> breaks the paragraph.

This stage is formally called the tree construction stage in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard. It operates on top of the tokenizer, consuming tokens one at a time and building the DOM incrementally.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Tree construction serves several essential purposes:

  • Build the DOM — the in-memory representation of the document.
  • Determine structure — nesting, parent-child relationships, sibling order.
  • Handle implicit tags — insert missing <html>, <head>, <body>, and <tbody> elements.
  • Enforce content models — a <p> cannot contain a <div>; the parser auto-closes.
  • Recover from malformed markup — mismatched tags, unclosed elements, stray end tags.
  • Support incremental rendering — the tree is built and rendered as tokens arrive.
  • Enable script interaction — JavaScript sees the partially built DOM as it grows.
  • Preserve accessibility — the DOM is the source of the accessibility tree.

Tree construction is the heart of HTML parsing. The tokenizer produces raw material; the tree constructor decides what it means.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Browser Parsing Pipeline
│
├── Bytes              ← raw bytes from the network
├── Characters         ← decoded via charset
├── Tokenization       ← characters → tokens
├── Tree Construction  ← tokens → DOM nodes (THIS CHAPTER)
├── DOM                ← the document object model
├── Script Blocking    ← JavaScript pauses parsing
└── Rendering Pipeline ← DOM + CSSOM → pixels

Tree construction sits between tokenization and the DOM. It consumes tokens and produces the DOM tree that every subsequent stage depends on.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The tokenizer produces a flat sequence of tokens. It has no concept of nesting, no understanding of which elements can contain which others, and no ability to recover from mismatched tags. A <div> token is just a <div> token — the tokenizer does not know that it opens a container that must eventually be closed.

Real HTML is messy. Developers forget closing tags, nest elements incorrectly, and write markup that cannot be parsed by simple rules:

<p>Hello<div>World</div>

This is malformed. The <div> cannot be inside a <p> — the HTML content model forbids it. But the browser cannot reject the page. It must recover by implicitly closing the <p> before the <div>:

<p>Hello</p><div>World</div>

Tree construction exists to apply these rules — to interpret the token stream according to the HTML specification, insert implicit elements, auto-close misnested tags, and build a well-formed DOM tree even from malformed input.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No tree construction spec Browsers built different DOMs from the same HTML No implicit tag insertion Missing <body> broke rendering No auto-closing Mismatched tags broke the document structure No content model enforcement Invalid nesting produced broken DOM No fragment parsing No way to parse HTML snippets No template element support Client-side templating was impossible

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Before HTML5, browsers had different tree construction algorithms. A page that rendered correctly in Internet Explorer might break in Firefox. The HTML5 specification (2008–2014) formalized the tree construction algorithm with:

  • Insertion modes — a state machine that determines how tokens are handled.
  • The stack of open elements — tracks the current nesting context.
  • The list of active formatting elements — tracks <b>, <i>, <a> across auto-closing.
  • Implicit tag insertion — inserts <html>, <head>, <body> automatically.
  • Auto-closing rules — closes <p>, <li>, <option>, <td>, etc. automatically.
  • Adoption agency algorithm — handles misnested formatting elements.

The goal: every browser produces the same DOM from the same input. This is critical for interoperability, security, and the web's fundamental contract that a URL renders consistently everywhere.

In 2026, tree construction is fully specified and universally implemented. The algorithm is mature, well-tested, and the same across every browser engine.

docs.title: The Tree Construction Algorithm
docs.text:
Tree construction is a state machine over insertion modes — not to be confused with the tokenizer's states:

Insertion Mode Purpose initial Before DOCTYPE before html Before <html> before head Before <head> in head Inside <head> after head After </head> in body Inside <body> text Inside <script>, <style>, <title>, <textarea> in table Inside <table> in table text Text inside a table in caption Inside <caption> in column group Inside <colgroup> in table body Inside <tbody>, <thead>, <tfoot> in row Inside <tr> in cell Inside <td>, <th> in select Inside <select> in template Inside <template> after body After </body> after after body After </html> in frameset Inside <frameset> after frameset After </frameset> after after frameset After the frameset

docs.title: The Core Data Structures
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STACK OF OPEN ELEMENTS                      │
│  └── The current nesting context             │
│  └── [html, body, div, p]                    │
│  └── The last element is the "current node"  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LIST OF ACTIVE FORMATTING ELEMENTS          │
│  └── Tracks <b>, <i>, <a>, <em>, <strong>   │
│  └── Used by the adoption agency algorithm  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  INSERTION MODE                              │
│  └── The current parsing context             │
│  └── Determines how tokens are handled      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  HEAD ELEMENT POINTER                        │
│  └── Points to the <head> element            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  FORM ELEMENT POINTER                        │
│  └── Points to the current <form> element    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• Stack of open elements — the nesting context. The last element is the "current node" where new content is inserted.
  • List of active formatting elements — tracks inline formatting across implicit closes.
  • Insertion mode — the current parsing context (in body, in table, etc.).
  • Head element pointer — points to <head> for reference.
  • Form element pointer — points to the current <form> for reference.

docs.title: A Simple Example
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Test</title></head>
<body><p>Hello</p></body>
</html>

Tree construction trace:

1.  DOCTYPE(html) → set quirks mode = no-quirks; switch to "before html"
2.  StartTag(html) → create <html>; push to stack; switch to "before head"
3.  StartTag(head) → create <head>; push to stack; switch to "in head"
4.  StartTag(title) → create <title>; push; switch to "text"
5.  Character("Test") → insert text into <title>
6.  EndTag(title) → pop <title>; switch to "in head"
7.  EndTag(head) → pop <head>; switch to "after head"
8.  StartTag(body) → create <body>; push; switch to "in body"
9.  StartTag(p) → create <p>; push
10. Character("Hello") → insert text into <p>
11. EndTag(p) → pop <p>
12. EndTag(body) → switch to "after body"
13. EndTag(html) → switch to "after after body"
14. EOF → stop parsing

DOM produced:

html
├── head
│   └── title
│       └── "Test"
└── body
    └── p
        └── "Hello"

docs.title: The Token Insertion Point
docs.text:
Every token is inserted at the current node — the last element on the stack of open elements.

// Pseudo-code for tree construction
function insertToken(token) {
    const current = stack[stack.length - 1]; // current node
    current.appendChild(createNode(token));
}

docs.title: The Implicit Tag Insertion
docs.text:
The tree constructor inserts missing elements automatically:

<!-- Input -->
<p>Hello</p>

<!-- Implicitly becomes -->
<html>
<head></head>
<body>
<p>Hello</p>
</body>
</html>

Even without <html>, <head>, or <body> tags, the browser builds a full document tree.

docs.title: The Auto-Closing Rules
docs.text:
Certain elements auto-close when a conflicting start tag appears:

Element Auto-closes when... <p> A block-level element starts (<div>, <p>, <h1>, etc.) <li> Another <li> starts <dt> / <dd> Another <dt> or <dd> starts <option> Another <option> or <optgroup> starts <td> / <th> Another <td>, <th>, or <tr> starts <tr> Another <tr> starts <thead> / <tbody> / <tfoot> A conflicting table section starts

docs.title: The Adoption Agency Algorithm
docs.text:
The adoption agency algorithm handles misnested formatting elements like:

<p>1<b>2<i>3</b>4</i>5</p>

The algorithm produces:

<p>1<b>2<i>3</i></b><i>4</i>5</p>

It reconstructs the formatting elements to produce a well-formed tree. This is one of the most complex parts of the HTML specification.

docs.title: The "Building a House" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of tree construction as building a house from a list of materials:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TOKENS (materials list)                     │
│  ├── StartTag(html)  → "foundation"          │
│  ├── StartTag(body)  → "living room"         │
│  ├── StartTag(p)     → "furniture"           │
│  ├── Character(...)  → "decorations"         │
│  └── EndTag(p)       → "furniture placed"    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TREE CONSTRUCTOR (builder)                  │
│  ├── Stack of open elements (rooms being built)│
│  ├── Insertion mode (current floor plan)     │
│  └── Active formatting (ongoing decorations) │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DOM TREE (finished house)                   │
│  ├── html (foundation)                       │
│  ├── body (structure)                        │
│  └── p (rooms and furniture)                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Stack of Open Elements" Mental Model
docs.text:
The stack of open elements is the nesting context — a running list of elements that have been opened but not yet closed.

Input: <div><p><span>Hello</span></p></div>

Stack evolution:
  1. StartTag(div)   → [html, body, div]
  2. StartTag(p)     → [html, body, div, p]
  3. StartTag(span)  → [html, body, div, p, span]
  4. Character("Hello") → insert into span
  5. EndTag(span)    → [html, body, div, p]
  6. EndTag(p)       → [html, body, div]
  7. EndTag(div)     → [html, body]

The last element in the stack is the current node — where new content is inserted.

docs.title: The "Insertion Mode" Mental Model
docs.text:
The insertion mode is like a context switch. Different parts of the document have different rules:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IN BODY                                     │
│  └── Normal HTML content                     │
│  └── Most elements handled here              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  IN TABLE                                    │
│  └── Table-specific rules                    │
│  └── Implicit <tbody> insertion              │
│  └── Text is foster-parented                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  IN SELECT                                   │
│  └── Only <option> and <optgroup> allowed    │
│  └── Other elements are ignored              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The insertion mode is determined by the current context — not by a single element, but by the overall nesting.

docs.title: The "Everything Is Recoverable" Mental Model
docs.text:
Tree construction never fails. Every input produces a DOM tree, no matter how malformed.

<!-- Input -->
<div><p>Hello</div>

<!-- Output: DOM tree -->
<div>
  <p>Hello</p>
</div>

The <p> is auto-closed when </div> is encountered. The DOM is well-formed even though the input was not.

docs.title: The "Incremental" Mental Model
docs.text:
Tree construction is incremental. The DOM grows as tokens arrive:

t=0ms   StartTag(html) → <html> added to DOM
t=5ms   StartTag(head) → <head> added
t=10ms  StartTag(title) → <title> added
t=15ms  Character("Test") → text added to <title>
...
t=100ms EndTag(html) → parsing complete

The user can see and interact with the page before parsing finishes.

docs.title: Concept 1: The DOM Tree
docs.text: The Document Object Model — a tree of nodes representing the document. The tree constructor builds this incrementally.

docs.title: Concept 2: The Stack of Open Elements
docs.text: A stack tracking the current nesting context. The last element is the "current node" where new content is inserted.

docs.title: Concept 3: The List of Active Formatting Elements
docs.text: A list of active inline formatting elements (<b>, <i>, <a>, etc.). Used by the adoption agency algorithm.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Insertion Mode
docs.text: A state machine determining how tokens are handled in the current context. There are over 20 insertion modes.

docs.title: Concept 5: The "In Body" Insertion Mode
docs.text: The default mode for most content. Handles the vast majority of elements.

docs.title: Concept 6: The "In Head" Insertion Mode
docs.text: Handles <title>, <meta>, <link>, <script>, <style>, <base>.

docs.title: Concept 7: The "In Table" Insertion Mode
docs.text: Handles table content. Implicitly inserts <tbody> when <tr> appears without a section.

docs.title: Concept 8: The "In Select" Insertion Mode
docs.text: Handles <select> content. Only <option> and <optgroup> are allowed.

docs.title: Concept 9: Implicit Tag Insertion
docs.text: The parser inserts missing elements — <html>, <head>, <body>, <tbody> — automatically.

docs.title: Concept 10: Auto-Closing
docs.text:
Certain elements auto-close when a conflicting element starts:

  • <p> closes on a block-level element.
  • <li> closes on another <li>.
  • <td> closes on another <td> or <tr>.
  • <option> closes on another <option>.

docs.title: Concept 11: The Adoption Agency Algorithm
docs.text: Handles misnested formatting elements. Reconstructs the tree to be well-formed.

docs.title: Concept 12: Foster Parenting
docs.text:
Text and elements that appear directly inside <table> but are not allowed there are foster-parented — moved before the table.

<!-- Input -->
<table>text<tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>

<!-- Output -->
text
<table><tbody><tr><td>cell</td></tr></tbody></table>

docs.title: Concept 13: The "Reconstruct the Active Formatting Elements" Step
docs.text: Before inserting a character or start tag, the parser may reconstruct the active formatting elements — re-adding <b>, <i>, etc. that were auto-closed.

docs.title: Concept 14: The Content Model
docs.text: The HTML specification defines which elements can contain which others. The tree constructor enforces these rules.

docs.title: Concept 15: The "Anything Else" Rule
docs.text: Each insertion mode has an "anything else" clause that handles unhandled tokens — usually by inserting them into the current node.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Implied End Tags
docs.text:
Certain elements are implied to be closed when another element starts:

<!-- Input -->
<ul><li>Item 1<li>Item 2</ul>

<!-- Output -->
<ul>
  <li>Item 1</li>
  <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: Concept 17: The DOCTYPE and Quirks Mode
docs.text: The DOCTYPE determines the document's rendering mode: no-quirks, limited-quirks, or quirks. Quirks mode changes CSS and JavaScript behavior for legacy compatibility.

docs.title: Concept 18: The <template> Element
docs.text: The <template> element has its own content document fragment. Its content is not rendered but is available for JavaScript to clone.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Fragment Parsing Algorithm
docs.text: The same tree construction algorithm is used to parse HTML fragments — snippets of markup injected via innerHTML.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Preload Scanner and Tree Construction
docs.text: The preload scanner runs in parallel with tree construction. It discovers resources early while the tree constructor builds the DOM.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Tree Construction for a Simple Document
docs.text:
Input tokens:
  1. DOCTYPE(html)
  2. StartTag(html)
  3. StartTag(head)
  4. StartTag(title)
  5. Character("Test")
  6. EndTag(title)
  7. EndTag(head)
  8. StartTag(body)
  9. StartTag(p)
  10. Character("Hello")
  11. EndTag(p)
  12. EndTag(body)
  13. EndTag(html)
  14. EOF

Tree construction trace:

1.  DOCTYPE(html)
    ├── Insertion mode: initial
    ├── Set quirks mode = no-quirks
    └── Switch to "before html"

2.  StartTag(html)
    ├── Insertion mode: before html
    ├── Create <html> element
    ├── Push to stack: [html]
    └── Switch to "before head"

3.  StartTag(head)
    ├── Insertion mode: before head
    ├── Create <head> element
    ├── Push to stack: [html, head]
    └── Switch to "in head"

4.  StartTag(title)
    ├── Insertion mode: in head
    ├── Create <title> element
    ├── Push to stack: [html, head, title]
    └── Switch to "text"

5.  Character("Test")
    ├── Insertion mode: text
    └── Insert text into <title>

6.  EndTag(title)
    ├── Insertion mode: text
    ├── Pop <title>
    ├── Stack: [html, head]
    └── Switch to "in head"

7.  EndTag(head)
    ├── Insertion mode: in head
    ├── Pop <head>
    ├── Stack: [html]
    └── Switch to "after head"

8.  StartTag(body)
    ├── Insertion mode: after head
    ├── Create <body> element
    ├── Push to stack: [html, body]
    └── Switch to "in body"

9.  StartTag(p)
    ├── Insertion mode: in body
    ├── Create <p> element
    ├── Push to stack: [html, body, p]
    └── Stay in "in body"

10. Character("Hello")
    ├── Insertion mode: in body
    └── Insert text into <p>

11. EndTag(p)
    ├── Insertion mode: in body
    ├── Pop <p>
    ├── Stack: [html, body]
    └── Stay in "in body"

12. EndTag(body)
    ├── Insertion mode: in body
    └── Switch to "after body"

13. EndTag(html)
    ├── Insertion mode: after body
    └── Switch to "after after body"

14. EOF
    └── Stop parsing

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Implicit Tag Insertion
docs.text:
Input: <p>Hello</p>

1.  No DOCTYPE → quirks mode = quirks
2.  Insertion mode: initial → before html
3.  StartTag(p)
    ├── Before html: no <html> yet
    ├── Create <html> implicitly
    ├── Switch to "before head"
    ├── Create <head> implicitly
    ├── Switch to "after head"
    ├── Create <body> implicitly
    ├── Switch to "in body"
    └── Create <p>
4.  Character("Hello") → insert into <p>
5.  EndTag(p) → pop <p>
6.  EOF → stop

DOM:
  html
  ├── head (empty)
  └── body
      └── p
          └── "Hello"

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Auto-Closing <p>
docs.text:
Input: <p>Hello<div>World</div>

1.  StartTag(p) → create <p>; stack: [html, body, p]
2.  Character("Hello") → insert into <p>
3.  StartTag(div)
    ├── Insertion mode: in body
    ├── <p> is on the stack
    ├── A <div> cannot be inside a <p>
    ├── Auto-close <p> (pop from stack)
    ├── Stack: [html, body]
    ├── Create <div>; stack: [html, body, div]
    └── Switch to "in body"
4.  Character("World") → insert into <div>
5.  EndTag(div) → pop <div>
6.  EOF

DOM:
  body
  ├── p
  │   └── "Hello"
  └── div
      └── "World"

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Foster Parenting
docs.text:
Input: <table>text<tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>

1.  StartTag(table) → create <table>; switch to "in table"
2.  Character("text")
    ├── In table mode: text is not allowed directly in <table>
    ├── Foster-parent: insert text before <table>
    └── "text" becomes a sibling before <table>
3.  StartTag(tr)
    ├── In table mode: <tr> requires a table section
    ├── Implicitly create <tbody>; push to stack
    └── Create <tr>
4.  StartTag(td) → create <td>
5.  Character("cell") → insert into <td>
6.  EndTag(td) → pop <td>
7.  EndTag(tr) → pop <tr>; pop <tbody>
8.  EndTag(table) → pop <table>

DOM:
  body
  ├── "text"
  └── table
      └── tbody
          └── tr
              └── td
                  └── "cell"

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Adoption Agency Algorithm
docs.text:
Input: <p>1<b>2<i>3</b>4</i>5</p>

1.  StartTag(p) → create <p>
2.  Character("1") → insert into <p>
3.  StartTag(b) → create <b>; add to active formatting list
4.  Character("2") → insert into <b>
5.  StartTag(i) → create <i>; add to active formatting list
6.  Character("3") → insert into <i>
7.  EndTag(b)
    ├── <b> is not the current node (<i> is)
    ├── Invoke adoption agency algorithm
    ├── Find the formatting element <b> in the list
    ├── The <b> is on the stack, but <i> is above it
    ├── Clone <i>, put it after <b>
    ├── The algorithm rearranges
    └── Result: <b><i>3</i></b><i>4</i>5</p>
8.  Character("4") → insert into the cloned <i>
9.  EndTag(i) → pop <i>
10. EndTag(p) → pop <p>

DOM:
  p
  ├── "1"
  ├── b
  │   ├── "2"
  │   └── i
  │       └── "3"
  ├── i
  │   └── "4"
  └── "5"

The adoption agency algorithm is complex but produces a well-formed tree from misnested input.

docs.title: The Insertion Mode State Machine
docs.text:
The tree constructor's insertion mode is a state machine similar to the tokenizer's states. Each insertion mode defines handling for every token type.

Insertion Mode: "in body"
  ├── Character → insert text
  ├── StartTag(p) → insert <p>
  ├── StartTag(div) → close open <p>; insert <div>
  ├── StartTag(table) → insert <table>; switch to "in table"
  ├── StartTag(select) → insert <select>; switch to "in select"
  ├── EndTag(body) → switch to "after body"
  └── Anything else → insert into current node

docs.title: The Stack of Open Elements
docs.text:
The stack is the core data structure. It tracks the current nesting context.

Initial stack (after implicit <html>, <head>, <body>):
  [html, body]

StartTag(div):
  [html, body, div]

StartTag(p):
  [html, body, div, p]

EndTag(p):
  [html, body, div]

StartTag(span):
  [html, body, div, span]

EndTag(div):     ← implicit
  ├── <span> is above <div>
  ├── <div> is on the stack but not current
  ├── Auto-close <span> first (pop)
  ├── Then close <div> (pop)
  └── [html, body]

docs.title: The List of Active Formatting Elements
docs.text:
Formatting elements are tracked separately because they can be reconstructed:

StartTag(b):
  Active formatting list: [b]

StartTag(i):
  Active formatting list: [b, i]

EndTag(b):     ← misnested
  ├── Adoption agency algorithm runs
  ├── b is removed from the list
  └── Active formatting list: [i]

StartTag(em):
  Active formatting list: [i, em]

docs.title: The Reconstruct Active Formatting Elements Step
docs.text:
Before inserting any character or start tag, the parser checks if the active formatting elements are on the stack. If not, they are reconstructed (cloned and re-added).

Stack: [html, body, p]
Active formatting: [b, i]

Character("Hello"):
  ├── Are <b> and <i> on the stack? No.
  ├── Reconstruct: clone <b> and <i>
  ├── Stack: [html, body, p, b, i]
  └── Insert "Hello" into <i>

docs.title: The Foster Parenting Mechanism
docs.text:
When text or elements appear in <table> where they do not belong, the parser foster parents them — moves them before the table.

<table>
  "text"        ← foster-parented
  <tr>...</tr>
</table>

Result:
"text"           ← before <table>
<table>
  <tbody>
    <tr>...</tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: The Fragment Parsing Algorithm
docs.text:
innerHTML uses the same tree construction algorithm but with a context element. The context determines the insertion mode and the stack.

const div = document.createElement('div');
div.innerHTML = '<p>Hello</p>';
// Uses the same tree construction, but with div as context

docs.title: The <template> Content Document
docs.text: <template> elements have a content document fragment that is not rendered. When the parser sees <template>, it switches to a "in template" insertion mode and builds the content in a separate tree.

docs.title: The Script Blocking Behavior
docs.text:
When the tree constructor encounters a <script> element:

  1. It creates the <script> node.
  2. It switches to the "text" insertion mode.
  3. It pauses parsing until the script is fetched and executed.
  4. It resumes parsing.

This is why scripts block the parser — tree construction cannot continue until the script is done.

docs.title: The Preload Scanner and Tree Construction
docs.text:
The preload scanner runs concurrently with tree construction. It scans the raw bytes for resource references and starts fetching them while the tree constructor builds the DOM.

Main thread:
  Tree construction (building DOM)

Separate thread (or ahead-of-parser):
  Preload scanner (discovering resources)

docs.title: Tree Construction Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Tokens arrive from the tokenizer.
    │
    ▼
2.  Determine the current insertion mode.
    │
    ▼
3.  Process the token according to the insertion mode:
    │   ├── Insert a new element
    │   ├── Insert a character
    │   ├── Auto-close elements
    │   ├── Insert implicit elements
    │   ├── Foster-parent
    │   └── Run the adoption agency algorithm
    │
    ▼
4.  Update the stack of open elements.
    │
    ▼
5.  Update the active formatting elements.
    │
    ▼
6.  Transition to a new insertion mode if needed.
    │
    ▼
7.  Repeat for the next token.
    │
    ▼
8.  EOF token → finalize the DOM.

docs.title: The Streaming Lifecycle
docs.text:
Bytes arrive: <!DOCTYPE html><html><head>...
    │
    ▼
Tokens emitted: DOCTYPE, StartTag(html), StartTag(head), ...
    │
    ▼
Tree constructor builds DOM incrementally:
  t=0ms   html added
  t=5ms   head added
  t=10ms  title added
  t=15ms  text added
  ...
    │
    ▼
DOM available for rendering and scripting incrementally.

docs.title: The Script Blocking Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Tree constructor encounters <script>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Pauses parsing.
    │
    ▼
3.  Script fetched (if external).
    │
    ▼
4.  Script executed.
    │
    ▼
5.  Parsing resumes.

docs.title: Example 1: Implicit Tag Insertion
docs.text:
<!-- Input (no html, head, or body tags) -->
<h1>Hello</h1>

<!-- Output DOM -->
<html>
  <head></head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello</h1>
  </body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • The parser inserts <html>, <head>, and <body> implicitly.
  • The <h1> is placed inside the implicit <body>.
  • The DOM is well-formed even though the input was minimal.

docs.title: Example 2: Auto-Closing <p>
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<p>First<div>Second</div>

<!-- Output DOM -->
<body>
  <p>First</p>
  <div>Second</div>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • <div> is a block-level element and cannot be inside <p>.
  • The parser auto-closes <p> before inserting <div>.
  • The DOM is valid.

docs.title: Example 3: Auto-Closing <li>
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<ul>
  <li>Item 1
  <li>Item 2
</ul>

<!-- Output DOM -->
<ul>
  <li>Item 1</li>
  <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

Code Breakdown:

  • The second <li> auto-closes the first <li>.
  • No explicit </li> needed.

docs.title: Example 4: Table with Implicit <tbody>
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<table>
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

<!-- Output DOM -->
<table>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Cell</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Code Breakdown:

  • The parser inserts <tbody> implicitly.
  • This is why DevTools shows <tbody> even when not written.
  • The DOM is valid HTML.

docs.title: Example 5: Foster Parenting
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<table>
  text
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

<!-- Output DOM -->
<body>
  "text"
  <table>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • Text is not allowed directly inside <table>.
  • The parser foster-parents the text — moves it before the table.
  • This is why stray text near a table appears above the table.

docs.title: Example 6: Misnested Formatting
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<p>1<b>2<i>3</b>4</i>5</p>

<!-- Output DOM -->
<p>
  1
  <b>
    2
    <i>3</i>
  </b>
  <i>4</i>
  5
</p>

Code Breakdown:

  • The <b> and <i> are misnested.
  • The adoption agency algorithm reconstructs the tree.
  • The final DOM is well-formed.

docs.title: Example 7: Mismatched End Tag
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<div>
  <p>Hello
</div>

<!-- Output DOM -->
<div>
  <p>Hello</p>
</div>

Code Breakdown:

  • The </div> triggers auto-closing of <p>.
  • The DOM is well-formed.

docs.title: Example 8: Stray End Tag
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<p>Hello</p>
</div>

<!-- Output DOM -->
<body>
  <p>Hello</p>
  <!-- stray </div> ignored -->
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • A stray </div> is ignored if there is no <div> on the stack.
  • The tokenizer emits the token, but the tree constructor ignores it.

docs.title: Example 9: Script Blocking
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<h1>Before</h1>
<script>
  // This runs before <h1>After</h1> is parsed
  document.write('<p>During</p>');
</script>
<h1>After</h1>

Output:

Before
During (from document.write)
After

Code Breakdown:

  • The parser pauses at <script>.
  • The script executes.
  • document.write() inserts content into the document.
  • The parser resumes and parses <h1>After</h1>.

docs.title: Example 10: DOM Inspection
docs.text:
// Inspect the tree construction result
console.log(document.documentElement.outerHTML);

// Check for implicit elements
console.log(document.querySelector('tbody')); // often exists even if not written
console.log(document.querySelector('body'));  // always exists

// Check the stack of open elements — not directly accessible
// But the DOM reflects the tree construction result

Code Breakdown:

  • The DOM is the result of tree construction.
  • Implicit elements are visible in the DOM.
  • document.documentElement is the <html> element.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Tree Construction Behavior Basic document Insert <html>, <head>, <body> implicitly Lists Auto-close <li> on next <li> Tables Insert <tbody> implicitly Paragraphs Auto-close <p> on block elements Forms Track current <form> with pointer Modals <dialog> handled as a block element Templates Content stored in a document fragment Scripts Parsing pauses during script execution innerHTML Uses the same algorithm with a context element

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Write well-formed HTML. Why: the parser recovers, but the result may not match intent.
  2. Always include a DOCTYPE. Why: determines the rendering mode (quirks vs no-quirks).
  3. Close all elements explicitly. Why: auto-closing is convenient but error-prone.
  4. Do not nest block elements inside <p>. Why: the parser auto-closes the <p>.
  5. Understand the implicit <tbody>. Why: it appears in the DOM even if not written.
  6. Use the W3C Validator. Why: catches malformed markup before deployment.
  7. Test with view-source:. Why: confirms what the parser sees.
  8. Use DevTools → Elements to inspect the DOM. Why: the DOM is the parser's output.
  9. Avoid document.write(). Why: it interrupts parsing and causes re-parsing.
  10. Do not rely on parse error recovery. Why: recovery is specified but may not match intent.
  11. Understand foster parenting. Why: text near tables may move unexpectedly.
  12. Use valid HTML5. Why: the parser is optimized for HTML5, not legacy HTML.
  13. Test with multiple browsers. Why: edge cases may differ despite the spec.
  14. Use <template> for client-side templating. Why: content is not rendered until cloned.
  15. Understand the adoption agency algorithm. Why: misnested formatting is surprisingly common.
  16. Use innerHTML cautiously. Why: it uses the same parser with a context element.
  17. Avoid dynamic HTML generation without sanitization. Why: malformed input can introduce XSS.
  18. Use DOM APIs for structure. Why: createElement bypasses the parser.
  19. Verify the DOM in CI/CD. Why: template changes may introduce parse errors.
  20. Audit tree construction after framework upgrades. Why: framework output may change.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on <div> Inside <p>
docs.text:
<p>Hello<div>World</div></p>

Why it's wrong: The parser auto-closes <p> before <div>, producing:

<p>Hello</p>
<div>World</div>
<p></p>

✅ Correct: Do not nest block elements inside <p>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing <tbody> in Table Markup
docs.text:
<table>
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

Why it's wrong: The browser inserts <tbody> implicitly. Your CSS selectors like table > tr will not match.

✅ Correct:

<table>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Stray Text Inside <table>
docs.text:
<table>
  Some text
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

Why it's wrong: The text is foster-parented — moved before the table.

✅ Correct: Put text inside a <td> or <caption>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unclosed <li>
docs.text:
<ul>
  <li>Item 1
  <li>Item 2
</ul>

Why it's wrong: The parser auto-closes the first <li>, but this is not explicit.

✅ Correct:

<ul>
  <li>Item 1</li>
  <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing DOCTYPE
docs.text:
<html>...</html>

Why it's wrong: The browser enters quirks mode — different layout and CSS behavior.

✅ Correct:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>...</html>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using document.write() After Load
docs.text:
window.addEventListener('load', () => {
  document.write('<p>Hello</p>');
});

Why it's wrong: document.write() after load replaces the entire document.

✅ Correct:

document.body.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', '<p>Hello</p>');

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming innerHTML Preserves Structure
docs.text:
el.innerHTML = '<tr><td>Cell</td></tr>';

Why it's wrong: Depends on the context element. If el is a <div>, the <tr> may be stripped.

✅ Correct: Use a table-aware context or create elements programmatically.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Misnested Formatting
docs.text:
<p>1<b>2<i>3</b>4</i>5</p>

Why it's wrong: The adoption agency algorithm produces a specific result, but it may not match intent.

✅ Correct: Write well-nested markup.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Every Browser Produces the Same DOM
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Although the spec is deterministic, edge cases and browser bugs exist.

✅ Correct: Test on multiple browsers for edge cases.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Tree construction is fast — linear in the number of tokens.
  • Streaming construction — the DOM is built incrementally as tokens arrive.
  • Script blocking — scripts pause the parser; minimize blocking scripts.
  • Large documents — tree construction scales linearly with document size.
  • Malformed HTML — parse error recovery adds slight overhead.
  • Foster parenting — moves nodes; slightly more expensive than normal insertion.
  • The adoption agency algorithm — complex but rarely invoked.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep HTML well-formed — less recovery overhead.
  2. Avoid blocking scripts.
  3. Use streaming SSR — content appears incrementally.
  4. Minify HTML — fewer tokens to process.
  5. Avoid excessive DOM depth.
  6. Test with large documents.

docs.title: XSS via Malformed HTML
docs.text:
The parser's recovery behavior can be exploited. Attackers craft input that the parser interprets unexpectedly.

Defense: Sanitize user input; escape <, >, &, ", '.

docs.title: Mutation XSS (mXSS)
docs.text:
A class of XSS where sanitized HTML is re-parsed by the browser and produces a different (malicious) tree. This happens because the browser's parser handles malformed input differently than the sanitizer.

Defense: Use DOMPurify; test sanitized output with the actual browser parser.

docs.title: document.write() and XSS
docs.text:
document.write() with untrusted input is a classic XSS vector.

Defense: Never pass untrusted input to document.write().

docs.title: The <template> Element
docs.text:
Content inside <template> is not rendered but is parsed. Malicious content can be extracted and used.

Defense: Sanitize template content.

docs.title: Foster Parenting and CSP
docs.text:
Foster-parented content may escape CSP checks in some cases.

Defense: Understand foster parenting; test with CSP.

docs.title: The Adoption Agency and Sanitizers
docs.text:
The adoption agency algorithm is often exploited in mXSS attacks because sanitizers do not model it correctly.

Defense: Use a sanitizer that models the browser's tree construction algorithm.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements — inspect the DOM tree.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Properties — inspect element properties.
  • document.documentElement.outerHTML — view the entire DOM as HTML.
  • document.body.innerHTML — view the body as HTML.
  • element.children — inspect child elements.
  • element.parentNode — inspect parent.
  • W3C Validator — validator.w3.org.
  • HTML5 Validator — html5.validator.nu.
  • view-source: — compare raw HTML with parsed DOM.
  • DevTools → Console — parse errors may be logged.
  • DOMParser — parse HTML strings and inspect the result.
  • innerHTML with a context — test fragment parsing.
  • Test with document.implementation.createHTMLDocument() — parse HTML in a sandbox.
  • Look for unexpected <tbody> — confirms implicit insertion.
  • Look for moved text near tables — confirms foster parenting.
  • Look for auto-closed <p> — confirms content model enforcement.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every HTML document — tree construction is always running.
  • Sanitizing HTML — understanding the algorithm is essential.
  • Building HTML parsers — the tree construction algorithm is the reference.
  • Debugging unexpected DOM — the algorithm explains the structure.
  • Testing mXSS — understanding the algorithm is required.
  • Implementing innerHTML — the fragment algorithm is used.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not rely on tree construction to fix your HTML. Write well-formed HTML.
  • Do not assume recovery is ideal. Recovery is specified but may surprise.
  • Do not use document.write(). Use DOM APIs.
  • Do not assume innerHTML preserves all markup. Depends on context.
  • Do not assume all browsers behave identically. Test edge cases.
