docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Tree construction is a state machine over insertion modes — over 20 modes.
  • The stack of open elements tracks the nesting context — the last element is the "current node."
  • The list of active formatting elements tracks <b>, <i>, <a> across auto-closing.
  • The adoption agency algorithm handles misnested formatting — one of the most complex parts of the spec.
  • Foster parenting moves text out of <table> — text directly inside a table is moved before it.
  • <tbody> is inserted implicitly — even when not written, it appears in the DOM.
  • <html>, <head>, and <body> are inserted implicitly — a full document tree is always produced.
  • <p> auto-closes on block-level elements — a <div> cannot be inside a <p>.
  • <li> auto-closes on another <li> — no explicit closing tag needed.
  • The DOCTYPE determines the rendering mode — quirks, limited-quirks, or no-quirks.
  • Scripts block parsing — tree construction pauses during script execution.
  • document.write() interrupts parsing — it forces the parser to re-parse injected content.
  • innerHTML uses the same algorithm — with a context element for fragment parsing.
  • The <template> element has its own content document — content is parsed but not rendered.
  • Mutation XSS (mXSS) exploits parser re-parsing — sanitizers must model the browser's tree construction.
  • The preload scanner runs concurrently — discovering resources while the tree constructor builds.
  • Every browser produces the same DOM — the algorithm is fully specified.
  • Tree construction never fails — every input produces a DOM tree.
  • The DOM is built incrementally — content appears as tokens arrive.
  • The tree constructor's output is the input to the accessibility tree — a correct DOM is essential for accessibility.
  • The tree constructor's output is the input to layout and paint — a correct DOM is essential for rendering.
  • Tree construction is the heart of HTML parsing — it turns a stream of tokens into a structured document.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Tree construction converts tokens into a DOM tree — the second stage of HTML parsing.
  • It is a state machine over insertion modes — over 20 modes.
  • The stack of open elements tracks the nesting context — the last element is the current node.
  • The list of active formatting elements tracks inline formatting across auto-closing.
  • Implicit tag insertion inserts <html>, <head>, <body>, and <tbody>.
  • Auto-closing closes <p> on block elements, <li> on another <li>, <td> on another <td>.
  • The adoption agency algorithm handles misnested formatting elements.
  • Foster parenting moves text out of tables.
  • The DOCTYPE determines the rendering mode — quirks, limited-quirks, or no-quirks.
  • Scripts block parsing — tree construction pauses during script execution.
  • innerHTML uses the same algorithm with a context element.
  • The <template> element has its own content document.
  • Mutation XSS exploits parser re-parsing — sanitizers must model the algorithm.
  • The preload scanner runs concurrently — discovering resources while the tree constructor builds.
  • Every browser produces the same DOM — the algorithm is fully specified.
  • Tree construction never fails — every input produces a DOM tree.
  • The DOM is built incrementally — content appears as tokens arrive.
  • Write well-formed HTML — recovery is specified but may surprise.
  • Test with DevTools and the W3C Validator.
  • Tree construction is the heart of HTML parsing — it turns a stream of tokens into a structured document.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
DOM creation is the process by which the browser constructs the Document Object Model — a live, in-memory, tree-structured representation of the HTML document — from the token stream produced by the tokenizer and structured by the tree constructor. It is the stage where abstract tokens become real JavaScript objects with properties, methods, and event handlers that scripts can read and modify.

// The DOM is a tree of objects
document.documentElement;                    // <html> element
document.body;                               // <body> element
document.querySelector('h1');                // <h1> element
document.querySelector('h1').textContent;    // "Hello"
document.querySelector('h1').parentNode;     // <body>

The DOM is not a string of HTML. It is not a serialization. It is a live object graph — every element, attribute, and text node is a JavaScript object with a class, a prototype chain, and a set of interfaces defined by the DOM specification.

When the browser finishes parsing <p>Hello</p>, the resulting DOM contains:

  • An HTMLParagraphElement object.
  • A Text node with the value "Hello".
  • A parent-child relationship between them.
  • A prototype chain connecting the element to HTMLElement, Element, Node, and EventTarget.

DOM creation is the moment HTML becomes programmable.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
DOM creation serves several essential purposes:

  • Programmable representation — JavaScript can read and modify the page.
  • Source of truth for rendering — layout and paint read from the DOM.
  • Source of truth for accessibility — the accessibility tree is derived from the DOM.
  • Live updates — changes to the DOM are reflected immediately on screen.
  • Event handling — the DOM is the event dispatch target.
  • CSS matching — the DOM is the structure that CSS selectors match against.
  • Serialization — the DOM can be serialized back to HTML.
  • State preservation — the DOM holds form state, scroll position, and focus.

The DOM is the single source of truth for the rendered page. Every other system — layout, paint, accessibility, scripting — reads from the DOM.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Browser Parsing Pipeline
│
├── Bytes              ← raw bytes from the network
├── Characters         ← decoded via charset
├── Tokenization       ← characters → tokens
├── Tree Construction  ← tokens → DOM nodes
├── DOM Creation       ← DOM nodes → live JavaScript objects (THIS CHAPTER)
├── DOM                ← the document object model
├── Script Blocking    ← JavaScript pauses parsing
└── Rendering Pipeline ← DOM + CSSOM → pixels

DOM creation is the culmination of the parsing pipeline. It is where tokens stop being text and become the objects that JavaScript can manipulate.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The tokenizer produces tokens. The tree constructor builds a tree structure. But a tree of what? The tokens are just data — they have no behavior, no methods, no JavaScript representation.

A web page is not static. JavaScript must be able to:

  • Read the content of an element.
  • Change the text of a node.
  • Add or remove children.
  • Attach event listeners.
  • Read and write attributes.
  • Traverse the tree.

For this to work, every node in the tree must be a JavaScript object with a defined interface — properties to read, methods to call, events to dispatch. The DOM is that object graph.

DOM creation exists to turn the parsed tree into a live object graph — a data structure that scripts, layout, and accessibility can all use.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No object model Scripts had no way to read the page No live updates Changing the page required full reload No event handling No interactive behavior No standard interface Every browser exposed a different API No prototype chain No shared methods, no consistency No accessibility exposure Assistive technology had no data source

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The DOM was originally specified in 1998 by the W3C as "DOM Level 1." It defined:

  • A tree of nodes — every element, attribute, and text is a node.
  • Interfaces — Node, Element, Document, HTMLElement.
  • Methods — getElementById, appendChild, removeChild.

Successive DOM levels added:

  • DOM Level 2 (2000) — events, CSS, traversal, ranges.
  • DOM Level 3 (2004) — XPath, load and save, validation.
  • DOM Level 4 / WHATWG DOM (2015–present) — the current living standard. Adds querySelector, classList, dataset, MutationObserver, Shadow DOM, Custom Elements.

The modern DOM is specified by the WHATWG as a living standard. It defines the interfaces, the prototype chain, and the behavior of every DOM node in every modern browser.

In 2026, the DOM is fully specified and universally implemented. Every browser exposes the same interfaces, with minor browser-specific extensions.

docs.title: The DOM Node Types
docs.text:
The DOM defines 12 node types, each with a numeric code:

Type Code Interface Example Element 1 Element <div> Attribute 2 Attr class="intro" (deprecated) Text 3 Text "Hello" CDATASection 4 CDATASection (XML only) EntityReference 5 EntityReference (deprecated) Entity 6 Entity (deprecated) ProcessingInstruction 7 ProcessingInstruction (XML only) Comment 8 Comment <!-- comment --> Document 9 Document the document itself DocumentType 10 DocumentType <!DOCTYPE html> DocumentFragment 11 DocumentFragment a detached subtree Notation 12 Notation (deprecated)

docs.title: The Core Interface Hierarchy
docs.text:
EventTarget
    │
    ▼
Node
    ├── Element
    │   ├── HTMLElement
    │   │   ├── HTMLDivElement
    │   │   ├── HTMLParagraphElement
    │   │   ├── HTMLButtonElement
    │   │   └── ...
    │   ├── SVGElement
    │   └── MathMLElement
    ├── Text
    │   └── CDATASection
    ├── Comment
    ├── Document
    │   └── HTMLDocument
    ├── DocumentFragment
    ├── DocumentType
    └── Attr

docs.title: The Prototype Chain
docs.text:
Every DOM node inherits from a chain of prototypes:

const p = document.querySelector('p');

p instanceof HTMLParagraphElement; // true
p instanceof HTMLElement;          // true
p instanceof Element;              // true
p instanceof Node;                 // true
p instanceof EventTarget;          // true
p instanceof Object;               // true

Each link in the chain adds methods and properties.

docs.title: The Node Interface — The Foundation
docs.text:
Every node exposes:

Property/Method Purpose nodeType Numeric type (1 for Element, 3 for Text) nodeName Name ("P" for <p>, "#text" for text) nodeValue Value (text content for Text nodes) parentNode The parent node childNodes A NodeList of children firstChild / lastChild First and last child nextSibling / previousSibling Siblings appendChild(node) Add a child removeChild(node) Remove a child replaceChild(new, old) Replace a child cloneNode(deep) Clone a node contains(node) Check if a node is a descendant isEqualNode(node) Deep equality check

docs.title: The Element Interface — The HTML-Specific Layer
docs.text:
Elements add:

Property/Method Purpose tagName Uppercase tag name ("P") id The id attribute className The class attribute (string) classList The class attribute (DOMTokenList) attributes A NamedNodeMap of attributes getAttribute(name) Read an attribute setAttribute(name, value) Write an attribute removeAttribute(name) Remove an attribute hasAttribute(name) Check attribute existence querySelector(selector) Find a descendant querySelectorAll(selector) Find all descendants getBoundingClientRect() Get geometry innerHTML / outerHTML Get/set HTML textContent / innerText Get/set text insertAdjacentHTML(position, html) Insert HTML at a position closest(selector) Find the nearest ancestor matching a selector matches(selector) Check if the element matches a selector

docs.title: The HTMLElement Interface — HTML-Specific Properties
docs.text:
HTML elements add:

Property Purpose dataset The data-* attributes style The inline style declaration hidden The hidden attribute tabIndex The tabindex attribute title The title attribute lang The lang attribute dir The dir attribute offsetHeight, offsetWidth Rendered dimensions clientHeight, clientWidth Content dimensions scrollHeight, scrollWidth Scrollable dimensions focus(), blur() Focus management click() Programmatic click

docs.title: Specialized Element Interfaces
docs.text:
Each HTML element type has a specialized interface:

HTMLAnchorElement     // <a>
HTMLButtonElement     // <button>
HTMLFormElement       // <form>
HTMLInputElement      // <input>
HTMLImageElement      // <img>
HTMLSelectElement     // <select>
HTMLTableElement      // <table>
HTMLTemplateElement   // <template>
HTMLDialogElement     // <dialog>
HTMLVideoElement      // <video>

Each adds element-specific properties:

const input = document.querySelector('input');
input.value;          // input value
input.checked;        // checkbox/radio state
input.type;           // input type
input.disabled;       // disabled state
input.validity;       // validation state

docs.title: The Document Interface
docs.text:
The Document is the root of the tree:

Property/Method Purpose documentElement The <html> element head The <head> element body The <body> element title The document title URL The document URL domain The document domain cookie Cookies (with limitations) getElementById(id) Find by ID getElementsByClassName(cls) Find by class getElementsByTagName(tag) Find by tag querySelector(selector) Find first match querySelectorAll(selector) Find all matches createElement(tag) Create an element createTextNode(text) Create a text node createDocumentFragment() Create a fragment createComment(text) Create a comment importNode(node, deep) Import from another document adoptNode(node) Adopt from another document

docs.title: The Text Interface
docs.text:
Text nodes have minimal interface:

Property/Method Purpose data The text content length The length wholeText The concatenated text splitText(offset) Split the text node

docs.title: The DocumentFragment Interface
docs.text:
A lightweight, detached container:

const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();

for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `Item ${i}`;
    fragment.appendChild(li);
}

// One DOM mutation instead of 1000
document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(fragment);

docs.title: The DOM Creation Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose document.createElement(tag) Create an element document.createTextNode(text) Create a text node document.createComment(text) Create a comment document.createDocumentFragment() Create a fragment element.cloneNode(deep) Clone a node element.innerHTML = html Parse HTML into the element element.insertAdjacentHTML(pos, html) Insert parsed HTML DOMParser.parseFromString(html, type) Parse a full document

docs.title: A Complete Example
docs.text:
// Create a list programmatically
const list = document.createElement('ul');
list.className = 'items';

const items = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry'];

for (const item of items) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = item;
    li.dataset.fruit = item.toLowerCase();
    list.appendChild(li);
}

document.body.appendChild(list);

// The DOM now contains:
// <ul class="items">
//   <li data-fruit="apple">Apple</li>
//   <li data-fruit="banana">Banana</li>
//   <li data-fruit="cherry">Cherry</li>
// </ul>

docs.title: The "Object Graph" Mental Model
docs.text:
The DOM is not a string — it is a live object graph:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  document                                    │
│  └── documentElement (HTMLHtmlElement)       │
│      ├── head (HTMLHeadElement)              │
│      │   └── title (HTMLTitleElement)        │
│      │       └── "Page Title" (Text)         │
│      └── body (HTMLBodyElement)              │
│          ├── h1 (HTMLHeadingElement)         │
│          │   └── "Hello" (Text)              │
│          └── p (HTMLParagraphElement)        │
│              └── "World" (Text)              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every node is an object. Every relationship is a live reference. Changing a node updates the tree. The tree updates the screen.

docs.title: The "Live vs. Static" Mental Model
docs.text:
The DOM is live:

const p = document.querySelector('p');

// p is a reference to the actual element in the tree
p.textContent = 'Changed';

// The screen updates immediately
// Other references to the same element see the change

This is different from a static snapshot. The DOM is the actual state of the page.

docs.title: The "Prototype Chain" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every node inherits from a chain of prototypes:

Node.prototype
  └── Element.prototype
      └── HTMLElement.prototype
          └── HTMLParagraphElement.prototype
              └── p (the instance)

Methods are shared. All paragraphs share the same methods. All elements share the same Node methods.

docs.title: The "Source of Truth" Mental Model
docs.text:
The DOM is the source of truth for:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DOM                                         │
│  ├── Layout reads the DOM                    │
│  ├── Paint reads the DOM                     │
│  ├── Accessibility reads the DOM             │
│  ├── JavaScript reads/writes the DOM         │
│  ├── CSS matches selectors against the DOM   │
│  └── Events dispatch through the DOM         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every other system is downstream of the DOM.

docs.title: The "Live Updates" Mental Model
docs.text:
Changing the DOM triggers a cascade:

1.  JavaScript changes the DOM.
    │
    ▼
2.  Layout is invalidated.
    │
    ▼
3.  Paint is invalidated.
    │
    ▼
4.  Composite is invalidated.
    │
    ▼
5.  The browser re-renders on the next frame.

This is why DOM mutations are expensive if not batched.

docs.title: The "Accessibility Tree" Mental Model
docs.text:
The accessibility tree is derived from the DOM:

DOM                              Accessibility Tree
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
<div role="button">        →    button
  "Click me"               →      name: "Click me"

Changing the DOM changes the accessibility tree. This is why correct DOM structure is essential for accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 1: The DOM as a Live Tree
docs.text: The DOM is a live, in-memory tree of JavaScript objects. Every node is an object with methods and properties.

docs.title: Concept 2: Node Types
docs.text: The DOM defines 12 node types. The most common are Element (1), Text (3), Comment (8), Document (9), DocumentType (10), and DocumentFragment (11).

docs.title: Concept 3: The Prototype Chain
docs.text: Every node inherits from EventTarget → Node → Element → HTMLElement → specialized interface.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Document Interface
docs.text: The Document is the root of the tree. It provides methods for creating nodes, querying the tree, and accessing document-level properties.

docs.title: Concept 5: The Element Interface
docs.text: Elements are the most common node type. They provide attribute access, query methods, and geometry methods.

docs.title: Concept 6: The HTMLElement Interface
docs.text: HTML elements add HTML-specific properties like dataset, style, hidden, and tabIndex.

docs.title: Concept 7: Specialized Element Interfaces
docs.text: Each HTML element type has its own interface. <a> becomes HTMLAnchorElement, <input> becomes HTMLInputElement.

docs.title: Concept 8: The Text Interface
docs.text: Text nodes hold character data. They are the leaves of the tree.

docs.title: Concept 9: The DocumentFragment Interface
docs.text: A lightweight, detached container. Used to batch DOM mutations.

docs.title: Concept 10: The innerHTML Property
docs.text: Parses HTML and inserts it into the element. Uses the tree construction algorithm. Security risk if used with untrusted input.

docs.title: Concept 11: The textContent Property
docs.text: Gets or sets the text content of an element. Does not parse HTML. Safe for untrusted input.

docs.title: Concept 12: The classList API
docs.text: A DOMTokenList for managing classes. add(), remove(), toggle(), contains().

docs.title: Concept 13: The dataset API
docs.text: Access to data-* attributes as an object. element.dataset.foo maps to data-foo.

docs.title: Concept 14: The style Property
docs.text: Inline style manipulation. element.style.color = 'red'. Writes to the style attribute.

docs.title: Concept 15: The MutationObserver API
docs.text:
Observes DOM mutations asynchronously:

const observer = new MutationObserver((mutations) => {
    for (const m of mutations) {
        console.log(m.type, m.target);
    }
});

observer.observe(element, {
    childList: true,
    attributes: true,
    subtree: true,
    characterData: true
});

docs.title: Concept 16: The Shadow DOM
docs.text: Encapsulated DOM subtrees attached to elements. Provides style and structure isolation.

docs.title: Concept 17: The Custom Elements API
docs.text: User-defined element types with their own lifecycle callbacks.

docs.title: Concept 18: The Template Element
docs.text: Content stored in a document fragment. Cloned via template.content.cloneNode(true).

docs.title: Concept 19: The DocumentFragment Batching
docs.text: Appending a fragment appends all its children in one operation. Reduces layout and paint invalidations.

docs.title: Concept 20: The DOM Serialization
docs.text: The DOM can be serialized back to HTML via outerHTML or innerHTML. This is used for caching, testing, and server-side rendering.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: DOM Creation for a Simple Element
docs.text:
Token stream:
  1. StartTag(div) with class="box"
  2. Character("Hello")
  3. EndTag(div)

DOM creation:
  1. Tree constructor creates an HTMLDivElement.
     ├── Set className = "box"
     └── Append to current parent (e.g., body)

  2. Tree constructor creates a Text node with data "Hello".
     └── Append to the div

  3. EndTag(div) → pop the div from the stack

docs.title: Step-by-Step: DOM Creation with Methods
docs.text:
// Create an element
const div = document.createElement('div');
// div is an HTMLDivElement
// div is not yet in the tree

// Set attributes
div.className = 'box';
div.id = 'main';

// Create a text node
const text = document.createTextNode('Hello');

// Append the text to the div
div.appendChild(text);

// Append the div to the body
document.body.appendChild(div);
// div is now in the tree and rendered

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Prototype Chain
docs.text:
document.createElement('div')
    │
    ▼
New HTMLDivElement object created
    │
    ▼
Prototype chain set:
  HTMLDivElement.prototype
    └── HTMLElement.prototype
        └── Element.prototype
            └── Node.prototype
                └── EventTarget.prototype
                    └── Object.prototype
    │
    ▼
Object returned to JavaScript

docs.title: Step-by-Step: DOM Mutations and Rendering
docs.text:
1.  JavaScript modifies the DOM.
    │
    ▼
2.  The browser marks the DOM as dirty.
    │
    ▼
3.  At the next frame boundary:
    │   ├── Style recalculation
    │   ├── Layout
    │   ├── Paint
    │   └── Composite
    │
    ▼
4.  The screen updates.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: innerHTML
docs.text:
1.  JavaScript sets element.innerHTML = '<p>Hello</p>'.
    │
    ▼
2.  The browser runs the tree construction algorithm
    │   on the string, with the element as context.
    │
    ▼
3.  The resulting nodes are inserted as children
    │   of the element.
    │
    ▼
4.  The element's previous children are removed.

docs.title: The DOM Tree in Memory
docs.text:
The DOM is stored as a linked tree of C++ objects in the browser engine. Each node has:

  • A type (Element, Text, etc.).
  • A parent pointer.
  • A list of children.
  • Attributes (for elements).
  • Data (for text nodes).

The JavaScript objects are wrappers around the underlying C++ objects. Accessing a property calls into the engine; modifying a property updates the C++ object and marks the DOM as dirty.

docs.title: The Wrapper Objects
docs.text:
When you call document.querySelector('p'), the browser:

  1. Finds the matching C++ node.
  2. Creates or retrieves a JavaScript wrapper object.
  3. Returns the wrapper.

If the same node is queried twice, the same wrapper is returned (cached per node).

docs.title: The Prototype Chain in Memory
docs.text:
The prototype chain is built from interface prototypes:

Node.prototype
  ├── appendChild
  ├── removeChild
  ├── cloneNode
  └── ...

Element.prototype (inherits from Node.prototype)
  ├── getAttribute
  ├── setAttribute
  ├── querySelector
  └── ...

HTMLElement.prototype (inherits from Element.prototype)
  ├── dataset
  ├── style
  ├── hidden
  └── ...

Each element wrapper's prototype is set to the appropriate specialized prototype.

docs.title: The Live NodeList vs. Static NodeList
docs.text:
• getElementsByTagName, getElementsByClassName, childNodes — return live NodeLists. They update automatically when the DOM changes.
  • querySelectorAll — returns a static NodeList. It does not update.
const live = document.getElementsByTagName('p');    // live
const static = document.querySelectorAll('p');      // static

document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('p'));

console.log(live.length);   // 2 (updated)
console.log(static.length); // 1 (not updated)

docs.title: The DOM Mutation Pipeline
docs.text:
JavaScript modifies DOM
    │
    ▼
MutationObserver queue (microtask)
    │
    ▼
Style recalculation
    │
    ▼
Layout
    │
    ▼
Paint
    │
    ▼
Composite

Mutations are batched. The browser does not re-render on every change.

docs.title: The Shadow DOM Architecture
docs.text:
Shadow DOM creates a separate tree attached to a host element:

<my-element>                 ← host
  #shadow-root (open)
    <style>...</style>
    <button>Click</button>
  </my-element>

The shadow tree is encapsulated. Styles inside do not leak out. Selectors outside do not reach in. The shadow root is accessible via element.shadowRoot.

docs.title: The Custom Elements Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Element is created (document.createElement)
    └── constructor() called

2.  Element is inserted into the DOM
    └── connectedCallback() called

3.  Element is removed from the DOM
    └── disconnectedCallback() called

4.  An attribute changes
    └── attributeChangedCallback() called

5.  Element is moved to a new document
    └── adoptedCallback() called

docs.title: The MutationObserver Internals
docs.text:
MutationObserver records mutations in a queue and delivers them as microtasks — after the current JavaScript task, before rendering.

JavaScript task
    │
    ▼
Mutation recorded (queued)
    │
    ▼
JavaScript task ends
    │
    ▼
Microtask queue: MutationObserver callbacks
    │
    ▼
Rendering: style, layout, paint

docs.title: DOM Creation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Tree constructor emits a token.
    │
    ▼
2.  The engine creates a C++ node.
    │
    ▼
3.  A JavaScript wrapper is created (lazily).
    │
    ▼
4.  The node is linked into the tree.
    │
    ▼
5.  The node is exposed to JavaScript.
    │
    ▼
6.  The DOM is marked as dirty.
    │
    ▼
7.  The browser re-renders on the next frame.

docs.title: Custom Element Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  document.createElement('my-element')
    │
    ▼
2.  constructor() called
    │
    ▼
3.  Element is configured
    │
    ▼
4.  Element is appended to the DOM
    │
    ▼
5.  connectedCallback() called
    │
    ▼
6.  Attribute changes → attributeChangedCallback()
    │
    ▼
7.  Element is removed → disconnectedCallback()

docs.title: The MutationObserver Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Observer is created with a callback.
    │
    ▼
2.  observer.observe(target, options)
    │
    ▼
3.  DOM mutations occur.
    │
    ▼
4.  Mutations are recorded in a queue.
    │
    ▼
5.  Microtask fires: callback called with mutations.
    │
    ▼
6.  observer.disconnect() stops observation.

docs.title: Example 1: Creating Elements
docs.text:
// Create a div
const div = document.createElement('div');
div.className = 'card';
div.id = 'card-1';
div.textContent = 'Hello, world!';

// Append to the body
document.body.appendChild(div);

// The DOM now contains:
// <div class="card" id="card-1">Hello, world!</div>

Code Breakdown:

  • createElement('div') — creates an HTMLDivElement.
  • .className — sets the class attribute.
  • .id — sets the id attribute.
  • .textContent — sets the text content.
  • .appendChild() — inserts the element into the tree.

docs.title: Example 2: DocumentFragment Batching
docs.text:
const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();

for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `Item ${i}`;
    fragment.appendChild(li);
}

document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(fragment);

Code Breakdown:

  • createDocumentFragment() — creates a lightweight container.
  • 1000 <li> elements are appended to the fragment.
  • The fragment is appended to the <ul> — a single DOM mutation.
  • Much faster than appending each <li> individually.

docs.title: Example 3: innerHTML vs textContent
docs.text:
// ❌ Dangerous: parses HTML, can execute scripts
element.innerHTML = userInput;

// ✅ Safe: treats input as text
element.textContent = userInput;

Code Breakdown:

  • innerHTML — parses the string as HTML, inserts nodes. XSS risk.
  • textContent — treats the string as text. Safe.

docs.title: Example 4: The classList API
docs.text:
const el = document.querySelector('.card');

el.classList.add('active');
el.classList.remove('inactive');
el.classList.toggle('highlighted');
el.classList.contains('active'); // true

// Multiple classes
el.classList.add('a', 'b', 'c');

Code Breakdown:

  • classList is a DOMTokenList.
  • add(), remove(), toggle(), contains() are the primary methods.
  • More ergonomic than manipulating className as a string.

docs.title: Example 5: The dataset API
docs.text:
<div id="user" data-id="42" data-role="admin"></div>

const user = document.getElementById('user');

console.log(user.dataset.id);   // "42"
console.log(user.dataset.role); // "admin"

user.dataset.status = 'active';
// Sets data-status="active" on the element

Code Breakdown:

  • dataset maps data-* attributes to camelCase properties.
  • data-id → dataset.id
  • data-user-name → dataset.userName

docs.title: Example 6: The MutationObserver API
docs.text:
const target = document.querySelector('#messages');

const observer = new MutationObserver((mutations) => {
    for (const mutation of mutations) {
        if (mutation.type === 'childList') {
            for (const node of mutation.addedNodes) {
                console.log('Added:', node);
            }
        }
    }
});

observer.observe(target, {
    childList: true,
    subtree: true,
    attributes: true
});

// Later:
observer.disconnect();

Code Breakdown:

  • MutationObserver watches for DOM changes.
  • childList: true — observes child additions/removals.
  • subtree: true — observes descendants.
  • attributes: true — observes attribute changes.
  • disconnect() — stops observation.

docs.title: Example 7: Creating a Custom Element
docs.text:
class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
    }

    connectedCallback() {
        this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
            <style>
                .card { border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 1rem; }
            </style>
            <div class="card">
                <h2>${this.getAttribute('name')}</h2>
                <p>${this.getAttribute('email')}</p>
            </div>
        `;
    }
}

customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);

<user-card name="Jane" email="jane@example.com"></user-card>

Code Breakdown:

  • class UserCard extends HTMLElement — defines the custom element.
  • attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }) — creates a shadow root.
  • connectedCallback() — runs when the element is inserted.
  • customElements.define() — registers the element.

docs.title: Example 8: Using a <template>
docs.text:
<template id="card-template">
    <div class="card">
        <h2 class="title"></h2>
        <p class="body"></p>
    </div>
</template>

const template = document.getElementById('card-template');
const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);

clone.querySelector('.title').textContent = 'Title';
clone.querySelector('.body').textContent = 'Body';

document.body.appendChild(clone);

Code Breakdown:

  • <template> content is not rendered.
  • template.content is a DocumentFragment.
  • cloneNode(true) clones the content deeply.
  • The clone is inserted into the DOM.

docs.title: Example 9: Serializing the DOM
docs.text:
// Get the HTML of an element
console.log(element.outerHTML);

// Get the HTML of the children
console.log(element.innerHTML);

// Get the text content
console.log(element.textContent);

// Serialize the whole document
console.log(document.documentElement.outerHTML);

Code Breakdown:

  • outerHTML — the element and its content.
  • innerHTML — the content only.
  • textContent — the text content only.

docs.title: Example 10: The DocumentFragment for Performance
docs.text:
// ❌ Slow: 1000 reflows
for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `Item ${i}`;
    document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(li);
}

// ✅ Fast: 1 reflow
const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();
for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `Item ${i}`;
    fragment.appendChild(li);
}
document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(fragment);

Code Breakdown:

  • The first version appends each <li> individually — 1000 layout invalidations.
  • The second version batches into a fragment — 1 layout invalidation.
  • The fragment approach is dramatically faster.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case DOM API Create an element document.createElement() Create text document.createTextNode() Batch DOM changes document.createDocumentFragment() Find elements querySelector, querySelectorAll, getElementById Modify attributes setAttribute, getAttribute, classList, dataset Modify content textContent, innerHTML, innerText Insert HTML insertAdjacentHTML, innerHTML Observe mutations MutationObserver Encapsulate styles Shadow DOM Define elements Custom Elements Clone nodes cloneNode, template.content.cloneNode Serialize outerHTML, innerHTML

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use textContent for untrusted input. Why: innerHTML parses HTML and can execute scripts.
  2. Batch DOM changes with DocumentFragment. Why: minimizes layout invalidation.
  3. Use classList instead of className. Why: safer and more ergonomic.
  4. Use dataset instead of getAttribute('data-*'). Why: cleaner API.
  5. Cache DOM queries. Why: querySelector is not free.
  6. Use querySelectorAll for static lists. Why: live NodeLists update unexpectedly.
  7. Detach elements before heavy modifications. Why: prevents unnecessary reflow.
  8. Use template for reusable markup. Why: parsed once, cloned many times.
  9. Use Shadow DOM for encapsulation. Why: isolates styles and structure.
  10. Use Custom Elements for reusable components. Why: native component model.
  11. Use MutationObserver for DOM watching. Why: replaces deprecated MutationEvents.
  12. Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates. Why: batched to the next frame.
  13. Avoid innerHTML in loops. Why: each assignment re-parses HTML.
  14. Avoid document.write(). Why: it blocks parsing and destroys the DOM.
  15. Use getBoundingClientRect sparingly. Why: it forces layout.
  16. Batch layout reads and writes. Why: prevents forced synchronous layout.
  17. Use element.cloneNode(true) for deep clones. Why: true clones descendants.
  18. Remember that NodeLists are live. Why: unexpected mutations cause bugs.
  19. Prefer querySelectorAll for consistent behavior. Why: static NodeLists are predictable.
  20. Clean up observers and listeners. Why: prevents memory leaks.
  21. Use requestIdleCallback for non-critical DOM work. Why: runs during idle time.
  22. Use scheduler.postTask for prioritized work. Why: modern scheduling API.
  23. Test DOM APIs in all target browsers. Why: minor differences exist.
  24. Use TypeScript for DOM-heavy code. Why: type safety reduces bugs.
  25. Audit the DOM after framework upgrades. Why: framework output may change.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using innerHTML with Untrusted Input
docs.text:
element.innerHTML = userInput;

Why it's wrong: XSS vulnerability. User input is parsed as HTML and can execute scripts.

✅ Correct:

element.textContent = userInput;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Appending Elements in a Loop
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `Item ${i}`;
    document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(li);
}

Why it's wrong: 1000 layout invalidations — slow.

✅ Correct:

const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();
for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `Item ${i}`;
    fragment.appendChild(li);
}
document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(fragment);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Live NodeLists
docs.text:
const items = document.getElementsByTagName('li');
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    items[i].remove(); // items is live — length changes
}

Why it's wrong: The live NodeList updates, causing the loop to skip elements.

✅ Correct:

const items = document.querySelectorAll('li');
for (const item of items) {
    item.remove();
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using className for Multi-Class Manipulation
docs.text:
element.className = element.className + ' active';

Why it's wrong: String manipulation is error-prone (duplicates, whitespace).

✅ Correct:

element.classList.add('active');

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Querying the DOM Repeatedly
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    document.querySelector('.item').textContent = i;
}

Why it's wrong: querySelector is called 100 times.

✅ Correct:

const item = document.querySelector('.item');
for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    item.textContent = i;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Modifying the DOM During Iteration
docs.text:
const items = document.querySelectorAll('li');
items.forEach(item => {
    item.remove(); // Modifying during iteration
});

Why it's wrong: Can cause unexpected behavior with live collections or re-entrant code.

✅ Correct:

const items = document.querySelectorAll('li');
for (const item of items) {
    item.remove();
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Cleaning Up Observers
docs.text:
const observer = new MutationObserver(callback);
observer.observe(element, { childList: true });
// Never disconnect

Why it's wrong: Memory leak — the observer holds a reference to the element.

✅ Correct:

const observer = new MutationObserver(callback);
observer.observe(element, { childList: true });
// Later:
observer.disconnect();

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using document.write()
docs.text:
document.write('<p>Hello</p>');

Why it's wrong: Blocks parsing, destroys the existing DOM if called after load.

✅ Correct:

document.body.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', '<p>Hello</p>');

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming querySelectorAll Returns an Array
docs.text:
const items = document.querySelectorAll('li');
items.map(item => item.textContent); // Error: map is not a function

Why it's wrong: querySelectorAll returns a NodeList, not an Array.

✅ Correct:

const items = [...document.querySelectorAll('li')];
items.map(item => item.textContent);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Reading Layout Properties in a Loop
docs.text:
for (const el of elements) {
    el.style.width = el.offsetWidth + 10 + 'px'; // Forces layout
}

Why it's wrong: Forces a synchronous layout on every iteration (layout thrashing).

✅ Correct:

const widths = elements.map(el => el.offsetWidth);
elements.forEach((el, i) => {
    el.style.width = widths[i] + 10 + 'px';
});

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• DOM operations are expensive. Batch them.
  • DocumentFragment reduces reflows. One mutation instead of N.
  • innerHTML is fast but re-parses HTML. Use textContent when possible.
  • querySelector is not free. Cache results.
  • Live NodeLists update automatically. Use querySelectorAll for static lists.
  • MutationObserver is async. Batches mutations into microtasks.
  • Shadow DOM isolates styles. Reduces style recalculation scope.
  • Custom Elements have lifecycle overhead. Use sparingly.
  • Reading layout properties forces layout. Batch reads and writes.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use DocumentFragment for batch inserts.
  2. Cache DOM queries.
  3. Use querySelectorAll for static lists.
  4. Avoid innerHTML in loops.
  5. Batch layout reads and writes.
  6. Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates.
  7. Use requestIdleCallback for non-critical work.
  8. Use scheduler.postTask for prioritized work.
  9. Detach elements before heavy modifications.
  10. Clean up observers and listeners.

docs.title: XSS via innerHTML
docs.text:
innerHTML parses strings as HTML and can execute scripts. Never use it with untrusted input.

Defense: Use textContent for untrusted input; sanitize with DOMPurify if HTML is required.

docs.title: DOM Clobbering
docs.text:
A DOM clobbering attack exploits the fact that named elements (id, name) become properties on the window object and on forms.

<img name="location">
<script>
    console.log(location); // The <img>, not the window.location
</script>

Defense: Avoid global name collisions; use window.location explicitly.

docs.title: Mutation XSS (mXSS)
docs.text:
A class of XSS where sanitized HTML is re-parsed and produces a different (malicious) tree.

Defense: Use DOMPurify; test sanitized output with the browser parser.

docs.title: document.write() and XSS
docs.text:
document.write() with untrusted input is a classic XSS vector.

Defense: Never pass untrusted input to document.write().

docs.title: Shadow DOM and CSP
docs.text: Shadow DOM content is subject to CSP. Ensure policies cover shadow roots.

docs.title: Custom Elements and XSS
docs.text:
Custom element content is inserted via innerHTML in connectedCallback — a common XSS vector.

Defense: Sanitize or use textContent for user-provided data.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Modifying HTMLElement.prototype or other DOM prototypes can introduce vulnerabilities.

Defense: Do not modify DOM prototypes in application code.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements — inspect the DOM tree.
  • Chrome DevTools → Console — access document, $0 (selected element).
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Properties — inspect element properties.
  • document.documentElement.outerHTML — view the entire DOM as HTML.
  • $0 — the currently selected element in DevTools.
  • $$('selector') — shorthand for querySelectorAll.
  • $('selector') — shorthand for querySelector.
  • copy($0.outerHTML) — copy the selected element's HTML.
  • console.dir(element) — inspect element properties.
  • getEventListeners(element) — see event listeners (DevTools only).
  • monitorEvents(element) — log events on an element (DevTools only).
  • document.querySelectorAll('*').length — count all elements.
  • document.querySelectorAll(':not(*)') — never matches; sanity check.
  • new MutationObserver(...) — observe DOM changes.
  • element.getBoundingClientRect() — get geometry.
  • Performance panel — profile DOM operations.
  • Layers panel — inspect compositing layers.
  • Accessibility panel — inspect the accessibility tree derived from the DOM.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every interactive web page — the DOM is the API for the page.
  • Dynamic content — add, remove, modify elements.
  • Form manipulation — read and write values.
  • Event handling — attach listeners.
  • Custom components — Custom Elements and Shadow DOM.
  • Data binding — frameworks read and write the DOM.
  • Testing — DOM inspection and manipulation.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use innerHTML with untrusted input. Use textContent.
  • Do not use document.write(). Use DOM APIs.
  • Do not modify DOM prototypes. Use composition.
  • Do not query the DOM in a loop. Cache results.
  • Do not append elements one by one. Batch with a fragment.
  • Do not read layout in a loop. Batch reads and writes.
  • Do not assume querySelectorAll returns an array. Convert with spread.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The DOM defines 12 node types — Element, Text, Comment, Document, DocumentFragment, DocumentType, and more.
  • Every DOM node is a JavaScript object with a prototype chain.
  • The prototype chain is: EventTarget → Node → Element → HTMLElement → specialized interface.
  • querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList — getElementsByTagName returns a live NodeList.
  • innerHTML re-parses HTML — textContent treats the string as text.
  • DocumentFragment batches DOM mutations — one reflow instead of N.
  • MutationObserver is the modern replacement for MutationEvents — async, batched, microtask-delivered.
  • Shadow DOM isolates styles and structure — no CSS leakage in or out.
  • Custom Elements have five lifecycle callbacks — constructor, connected, disconnected, attributeChanged, adopted.
  • The <template> element stores content in a DocumentFragment — parsed but not rendered.
  • DOM clobbering exploits named elements — <img name="location"> shadows window.location.
  • Mutation XSS (mXSS) exploits parser re-parsing — sanitizers must model the browser's parser.
  • document.write() is deprecated — it blocks parsing and destroys the DOM after load.
  • Reading layout properties forces layout — batch reads and writes.
  • Live NodeLists update automatically — can cause unexpected behavior in loops.
  • classList is a DOMTokenList — add, remove, toggle, contains.
  • dataset maps data-* attributes to camelCase properties — data-user-name → dataset.userName.
  • The DOM is the source of truth for layout, paint, and accessibility — every other system reads from it.
  • The accessibility tree is derived from the DOM — correct DOM structure is essential for accessibility.
  • The DOM is a live, in-memory tree — changes are reflected immediately on screen.
  • DOM operations are expensive — batch them for performance.
  • The DOM is fully specified by the WHATWG — every modern browser implements the same interfaces.
  • The DOM is the programmatic interface to the page — every interactive web app depends on it.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• DOM creation is the process of building the live, in-memory object tree from the parsed token stream.
  • Every node is a JavaScript object with a prototype chain.
  • The prototype chain is: EventTarget → Node → Element → HTMLElement → specialized interface.
  • Node types: Element, Text, Comment, Document, DocumentFragment, DocumentType.
  • The Document interface provides methods for creating, querying, and modifying the tree.
  • The Element interface provides attribute access, query methods, and geometry methods.
  • The HTMLElement interface adds HTML-specific properties: dataset, style, hidden.
  • Specialized interfaces exist for each HTML element type.
  • createElement, createTextNode, createDocumentFragment are the primary creation methods.
  • innerHTML parses HTML — XSS risk with untrusted input.
  • textContent treats input as text — safe.
  • classList and dataset are the modern APIs for classes and data attributes.
  • DocumentFragment batches DOM mutations — one reflow instead of N.
  • MutationObserver observes DOM changes asynchronously.
  • Shadow DOM encapsulates styles and structure.
  • Custom Elements define reusable components with lifecycle callbacks.
  • The <template> element stores content in a DocumentFragment.
  • The DOM is the source of truth for layout, paint, and accessibility.
  • DOM operations are expensive — batch them for performance.
  • The DOM is fully specified by the WHATWG — every modern browser implements the same interfaces.
  • The DOM is the programmatic interface to the page — every interactive web app depends on it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Error recovery is the set of rules and behaviors that govern how the HTML parser — both the tokenizer and the tree constructor — handles malformed, invalid, or unexpected input. Unlike XML, JSON, or most programming languages, HTML does not reject malformed input. It recovers from it, producing a well-formed DOM tree from even the most broken markup.

<p>Hello<div>World</div>

This is invalid HTML — a <div> cannot be inside a <p>. But the browser does not throw an error, refuse to render, or show a warning to the user. It recovers by implicitly closing the <p>:

<p>Hello</p><div>World</div>

Error recovery is the specification's answer to a fundamental reality: the web is full of broken HTML. If browsers rejected malformed markup, most of the web would not render. Error recovery ensures that every input — no matter how malformed — produces a valid DOM tree, deterministically, in every browser.

The HTML specification defines error recovery through:

  • Parse errors — violations of the specification that do not stop parsing.
  • Recovery rules — specific behaviors the parser must follow when a parse error occurs.
  • Insertion mode handling — each mode defines how unexpected tokens are handled.
  • The adoption agency algorithm — the complex recovery for misnested formatting elements.
  • Foster parenting — the recovery for content misplaced inside tables.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Error recovery serves several essential purposes:

  • Interoperability — every browser produces the same DOM from the same malformed input.
  • Resilience — pages render despite developer mistakes.
  • Backward compatibility — legacy HTML from the 1990s still renders correctly.
  • Security — deterministic parsing prevents parser-differential attacks.
  • User experience — users never see a "parse error" page.
  • Standards compliance — the specification defines exactly what to do.
  • Browser engine consistency — Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge all produce identical trees.
  • Testability — the specification is precise enough to test.

Error recovery is the safety net of the web platform. It is the reason the web is resilient, interoperable, and enduring.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Browser Parsing Pipeline
│
├── Bytes              ← raw bytes from the network
├── Characters         ← decoded via charset
├── Tokenization       ← characters → tokens (error recovery here)
├── Tree Construction  ← tokens → DOM nodes (error recovery here)
├── DOM Creation       ← DOM nodes → live JavaScript objects
├── Error Recovery     ← the rules that keep parsing alive (THIS CHAPTER)
└── Rendering Pipeline ← DOM + CSSOM → pixels

Error recovery is not a separate stage — it is a property of the tokenizer and tree constructor. Every state and every insertion mode defines its own recovery behavior.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTML is not XML. XML parsers reject malformed documents. A single unclosed tag, a single mismatched bracket, and the XML parser stops with a fatal error. This works for machine-generated data, where strict validation is desirable.

The web is different. HTML is written by:

  • Humans — who make mistakes.
  • CMSs — which generate markup with bugs.
  • Frameworks — which may produce non-standard output.
  • Legacy systems — which use pre-HTML5 constructs.
  • Email templates — which use table-based layouts and proprietary attributes.
  • Ad networks — which inject markup into third-party pages.

If the browser rejected malformed HTML, most of the web would not render. The web's design principle is the opposite: be liberal in what you accept, conservative in what you send (Postel's Law).

Error recovery is the mechanism that makes this principle work.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No formal recovery rules Browsers handled malformed HTML differently No parse error reporting Developers could not find issues No deterministic behavior Same HTML → different DOM in different browsers No spec for edge cases Cross-browser bugs were common No recovery for new elements Legacy elements broke in new browsers No recovery for attributes Malformed attributes were dropped

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Before HTML5, browsers had different error recovery behavior. A page that rendered correctly in Internet Explorer might break in Firefox, and vice versa. The HTML5 specification (2008–2014) formalized error recovery by:

  1. Defining parse errors precisely — every specification violation is a parse error.
  2. Specifying recovery behavior for every parse error.
  3. Requiring deterministic behavior — same input → same output.

The result: in every modern browser, the same malformed HTML produces the exact same DOM tree. This is critical for:

  • Interoperability — websites work consistently.
  • Security — parser-differential attacks are prevented.
  • Testing — a test suite can verify recovery behavior.
  • Developer experience — developers can predict what the parser will do.

The specification's error recovery rules were derived from the actual behavior of browsers in the wild. The spec authors studied how IE, Firefox, Safari, and Chrome handled malformed HTML and codified the most common behavior.

In 2026, error recovery is fully specified and universally implemented. The WHATWG HTML Living Standard is the definitive reference. Every modern browser follows it precisely.

docs.title: The Parse Error
docs.text:
A parse error is a violation of the HTML specification that does not stop parsing. Parse errors are:

  • Silent — the user does not see them.
  • Recoverable — parsing continues.
  • Logged — in DevTools, parse errors may appear in the console.
  • Testable — the specification defines precisely what triggers each parse error.

Examples of parse errors:

<p>Hello<div>World</div>       <!-- block element inside <p> -->
<ul><li>Item<li>Item</ul>       <!-- unclosed <li> -->
<div class=foo bar>             <!-- unquoted attribute with space -->
<script>const s = "</script>";  <!-- </script> inside string -->
<!-- unclosed comment              <!-- unclosed comment -->

Each of these triggers a parse error, but the parser recovers.

docs.title: The Recovery Categories
docs.text:
Error recovery falls into several categories:

Category Example Recovery Implicit tag insertion No <html> Insert <html>, <head>, <body> Auto-closing <p>Hello<div> Close <p>, start <div> Ignoring stray tokens </div> with no <div> Ignore the token Foster parenting Text inside <table> Move text before the table Adoption agency Misnested <b>/<i> Reconstruct the tree Attribute recovery Unquoted value with space End the value at whitespace Duplicate attribute <div class="a" class="b"> Ignore the duplicate Invalid character in tag name <1div> Treat as text

docs.title: The Implicit Tag Insertion
docs.text:
The parser inserts missing structural elements:

<!-- Input -->
<h1>Hello</h1>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<html>
<head></head>
<body>
<h1>Hello</h1>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: The Auto-Closing Rules
docs.text:
Certain elements auto-close when a conflicting element appears:

<!-- Input -->
<p>First<p>Second

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<p>First</p>
<p>Second</p>

<!-- Input -->
<ul>
  <li>Item 1
  <li>Item 2
</ul>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<ul>
  <li>Item 1</li>
  <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: Stray End Tags
docs.text:
Stray end tags are ignored:

<!-- Input -->
<p>Hello</p>
</div>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<p>Hello</p>
<!-- The </div> is ignored -->

docs.title: Foster Parenting
docs.text:
Text inside <table> is foster-parented:

<!-- Input -->
<table>
  Some text
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<body>
  "Some text"
  <table>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</body>

docs.title: The Adoption Agency Algorithm
docs.text:
Misnested formatting elements are reconstructed:

<!-- Input -->
<p>1<b>2<i>3</b>4</i>5</p>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<p>
  1
  <b>2<i>3</i></b>
  <i>4</i>
  5
</p>

docs.title: Attribute Recovery
docs.text:
Malformed attributes are handled:

<!-- Input: unquoted value with space -->
<div class=foo bar>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<div class="foo" bar=""></div>

<!-- Input: duplicate attribute -->
<div class="a" class="b">

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<div class="a"></div>  <!-- the second is ignored -->

docs.title: The </script> Trap
docs.text:
The most famous error recovery case:

<!-- Input -->
<script>
  const s = "</script>";
</script>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<script>const s = "</script>       <!-- script ends at </script> -->
<p>";                               <!-- the rest is text -->
</script>

The recovery: the tokenizer sees </script> and ends the script element. The remainder becomes text.

The fix: escape the sequence:

<script>
  const s = "<\/script>";
</script>

docs.title: The "Postel's Law" Mental Model
docs.text:
"Be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you accept."

The web is built on this principle:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  YOU (the sender)                            │
│  └── Should write well-formed HTML            │
│  └── Should validate before deploying         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  THE BROWSER (the receiver)                   │
│  └── Accepts anything                        │
│  └── Recovers from malformed input            │
│  └── Produces a deterministic DOM             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Error recovery is the browser's side of Postel's Law.

docs.title: The "Never Fail" Mental Model
docs.text:
The HTML parser never fails. Every input produces a DOM tree.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INPUT                                       │
│  └── Any bytes                                │
│  └── Any characters                           │
│  └── Any malformed markup                     │
│                                              │
│  OUTPUT                                      │
│  └── A valid DOM tree                        │
│  └── Deterministic across browsers            │
│  └── No fatal errors                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is not a bug — it is a design feature. The web must render, no matter what.

docs.title: The "Parse Error ≠ Rejection" Mental Model
docs.text:
A parse error is not a fatal error. It is a recoverable event:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PARSE ERROR                                 │
│  ├── Recorded in the spec                     │
│  ├── May be logged in DevTools               │
│  ├── Triggers a recovery rule                │
│  └── Parsing continues                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  FATAL ERROR (XML)                           │
│  ├── Parsing stops                           │
│  ├── Document rejected                       │
│  └── User sees an error page                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

HTML is not XML. HTML does not reject.

docs.title: The "Deterministic Recovery" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every browser produces the exact same DOM from the same input:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INPUT: <p>Hello<div>World</div>             │
│                                              │
│  Chrome:  <p>Hello</p><div>World</div>       │
│  Firefox: <p>Hello</p><div>World</div>       │
│  Safari:  <p>Hello</p><div>World</div>       │
│  Edge:    <p>Hello</p><div>World</div>       │
│                                              │
│  ALL IDENTICAL                                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is the result of the specification. The spec does not just say "recover" — it says exactly how.

docs.title: The "Recovery Categories" Mental Model
docs.text:
Error recovery falls into distinct categories:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IMPLICIT INSERTION                          │
│  └── Add missing structural elements          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  AUTO-CLOSING                                │
│  └── Close elements when a conflict appears   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  IGNORING                                    │
│  └── Drop stray or invalid tokens             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  REPOSITIONING                               │
│  └── Move content to the correct location     │
│  └── Foster parenting                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  RECONSTRUCTION                              │
│  └── Rebuild misnested formatting             │
│  └── Adoption agency algorithm                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Each category applies to different parse errors.

docs.title: The "Silent Failures" Mental Model
docs.text:
Error recovery is silent. The user does not see a warning. The page does not break. But the DOM may not match the developer's intent.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DEVELOPER INTENT                            │
│  └── <p>Hello<div>World</div>                │
│      Wanted: <p>Hello<div>World</div></p>    │
│                                              │
│  ACTUAL DOM                                  │
│  └── <p>Hello</p><div>World</div>            │
│                                              │
│  Silent difference — no error shown to user. │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is why validation is essential. The browser will not tell you that your HTML is wrong.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Parse Error
docs.text: A violation of the HTML specification that does not stop parsing. Parse errors are logged but not fatal.

docs.title: Concept 2: Implicit Tag Insertion
docs.text: The parser inserts missing <html>, <head>, <body>, and <tbody> elements automatically.

docs.title: Concept 3: Auto-Closing
docs.text: Certain elements close automatically when a conflicting element starts: <p>, <li>, <dt>, <dd>, <option>, <td>, <th>, <tr>.

docs.title: Concept 4: Stray Token Ignoring
docs.text: Unexpected end tags or invalid characters are ignored.

docs.title: Concept 5: Foster Parenting
docs.text: Content that appears directly inside <table> but is not allowed there is moved before the table.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Adoption Agency Algorithm
docs.text: The complex recovery for misnested formatting elements (<b>, <i>, <a>, etc.).

docs.title: Concept 7: Attribute Recovery
docs.text:
Malformed attributes are handled:

  • Unquoted values end at whitespace.
  • Duplicate attributes — the first wins.
  • Invalid characters in names — parse error.
  • Missing values — empty string.

docs.title: Concept 8: Character Reference Recovery
docs.text:
Malformed character references are handled:

  • &amp without ; — treated as text.
  • &#x; without digits — treated as text.
  • Named entities with typos — treated as text.

docs.title: Concept 9: The </script> Trap
docs.text: The </script> sequence ends the script element even inside a JavaScript string. Recovery: the remaining content becomes text.

docs.title: Concept 10: The DOCTYPE Recovery
docs.text: A missing or malformed DOCTYPE triggers quirks mode. The parser inserts a default DOCTYPE.

docs.title: Concept 11: The Table Recovery
docs.text:
Tables have extensive recovery:

  • Implicit <tbody> insertion.
  • Foster parenting for stray content.
  • Auto-closing of <td>, <th>, <tr>.
  • Handling of <table> inside <table>.

docs.title: Concept 12: The Select Recovery
docs.text: <select> only allows <option> and <optgroup>. Other elements are ignored or handled specially.

docs.title: Concept 13: The Template Recovery
docs.text: <template> content is parsed in a separate document fragment. Recovery applies within the fragment.

docs.title: Concept 14: The Fragment Parsing Recovery
docs.text: innerHTML uses the same recovery rules, with the context element determining the insertion mode.

docs.title: Concept 15: The Foreign Content Recovery
docs.text: SVG and MathML content is parsed with different rules. Recovery is defined for the transition between HTML and foreign content.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Character Encoding Recovery
docs.text: If the encoding is invalid or unsupported, the parser falls back to a default (usually UTF-8 or windows-1252).

docs.title: Concept 17: The Null Character Recovery
docs.text: Null characters (\0) are handled specially — usually replaced with U+FFFD (replacement character).

docs.title: Concept 18: The EOF Recovery
docs.text: At EOF, the parser closes all open elements and finalizes the DOM. If parsing was interrupted (e.g., by a script), EOF may trigger additional recovery.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Script Error Recovery
docs.text: If a script fails to load or execute, the parser continues. The error is reported but does not stop parsing.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Validation vs Recovery Distinction
docs.text: Validation tools (W3C Validator) report parse errors. The browser recovers from them. Validation catches issues before deployment; recovery ensures the page renders regardless.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Auto-Closing <p>
docs.text:
Input: <p>Hello<div>World</div>

1.  StartTag(p) → create <p>; stack: [html, body, p]
2.  Character("Hello") → insert into <p>
3.  StartTag(div)
    ├── Insertion mode: in body
    ├── <p> is on the stack
    ├── <div> cannot be inside <p>
    ├── Parse error: "unexpected start tag div in <p>"
    ├── Recovery: auto-close <p> (pop from stack)
    ├── Stack: [html, body]
    ├── Create <div>; stack: [html, body, div]
    └── Continue parsing
4.  Character("World") → insert into <div>
5.  EndTag(div) → pop <div>
6.  EOF

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Foster Parenting
docs.text:
Input: <table>text<tr><td>Cell</td></tr></table>

1.  StartTag(table) → create <table>; switch to "in table"
2.  Character("text")
    ├── In table mode: text is not allowed
    ├── Parse error: "text in table"
    ├── Recovery: foster parent the text
    ├── Insert "text" before <table>
    └── Continue
3.  StartTag(tr)
    ├── In table mode: <tr> requires a table section
    ├── Parse error: "tr without tbody"
    ├── Recovery: insert <tbody> implicitly
    ├── Create <tbody>; create <tr>
    └── Continue
4.  StartTag(td) → create <td>
5.  Character("Cell") → insert into <td>
6.  EndTag(td) → pop <td>
7.  EndTag(tr) → pop <tr>; pop <tbody>
8.  EndTag(table) → pop <table>

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Stray End Tag
docs.text:
Input: <p>Hello</p></div>

1.  StartTag(p) → create <p>
2.  Character("Hello") → insert into <p>
3.  EndTag(p) → pop <p>
4.  EndTag(div)
    ├── Insertion mode: in body
    ├── No <div> on the stack
    ├── Parse error: "stray end tag div"
    ├── Recovery: ignore the token
    └── Continue
5.  EOF

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Adoption Agency Algorithm
docs.text:
Input: <p>1<b>2<i>3</b>4</i>5</p>

1.  StartTag(p) → create <p>
2.  Character("1") → insert into <p>
3.  StartTag(b) → create <b>; add to active formatting
4.  Character("2") → insert into <b>
5.  StartTag(i) → create <i>; add to active formatting
6.  Character("3") → insert into <i>
7.  EndTag(b)
    ├── <b> is not the current node (<i> is)
    ├── Parse error: "misnested <b>"
    ├── Recovery: run the adoption agency algorithm
    ├── 1. Find <b> in the active formatting list
    ├── 2. Find <b> in the stack of open elements
    ├── 3. <b> is in the stack, but <i> is above it
    ├── 4. Clone <i>, put it after <b>
    ├── 5. The algorithm rearranges
    └── Result: <b><i>3</i></b><i>4</i>5</p>
8.  Character("4") → insert into the cloned <i>
9.  EndTag(i) → pop <i>
10. EndTag(p) → pop <p>

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Attribute Recovery
docs.text:
Input: <div class=foo bar>

1.  State: Tag name → "div"
2.  State: Before attribute name → "class"
3.  State: Attribute name → "class"
4.  State: Before attribute value → "="
5.  State: Attribute value (unquoted) → "foo"
    ├── See space → end the unquoted value
    ├── Parse error: "unexpected space in unquoted attribute"
    ├── Recovery: attribute value is "foo"
    └── Continue
6.  State: Before attribute name → "bar"
7.  State: Attribute name → "bar"
8.  State: After attribute name → ">"
    ├── Parse error: "attribute without value"
    ├── Recovery: value is empty
    └── Emit

docs.title: The Parse Error Reporting
docs.text:
Parse errors are reported to the browser's DevTools console. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all log parse errors. The error messages vary slightly but reference the specification's parse error names.

DevTools Console:
  [Deprecation] Unexpected start tag "div" in <p>
  [Deprecation] Stray end tag "div"
  [Deprecation] Text inside <table>

docs.title: The Recovery Rule Dispatch
docs.text:
Each parse error triggers a recovery rule defined in the specification. The rule is dispatched based on the current insertion mode and the token type.

Token: StartTag(div)
Insertion mode: in body
  ├── Is <div> allowed here?
  ├── Check the stack of open elements
  ├── Check the content model
  └── If conflict → auto-close, then insert

docs.title: The Foster Parenting Algorithm
docs.text:
Foster parenting is complex:

  1. Find the last <table> on the stack.
  2. Determine the foster parent — the element before the table.
  3. Insert the misplaced content before the table.
  4. If the content is a character token, group adjacent characters.

docs.title: The Adoption Agency Algorithm — Step by Step
docs.text:
The adoption agency algorithm is one of the most complex parts of the specification:

Input: <p>1<b>2<i>3</b>4</i>5</p>
EndTag(b) encountered:

1.  Find the "formatting element" — <b>.
2.  Find it in the active formatting list.
3.  Find it in the stack of open elements.
4.  If not found in either → ignore the end tag.
5.  If found but not on the stack:
    ├── Remove from the active formatting list
    └── Ignore the end tag.
6.  If found on the stack but not in scope:
    ├── Parse error
    └── Ignore the end tag.
7.  Otherwise:
    ├── Create a new element for the formatting element.
    ├── Move the children.
    ├── Reparent the cloned element.
    └── Continue.
8.  The algorithm may need to clone multiple elements.

The result is a well-formed tree with the formatting elements reconstructed.

docs.title: The Insertion Mode Handling
docs.text:
Each insertion mode defines behavior for every token type. Unexpected tokens trigger parse errors and recovery rules.

Insertion Mode: "in table"
  ├── Character (non-whitespace)
  │   └── Parse error; foster parent
  ├── StartTag(tr)
  │   └── If no <tbody>, insert implicitly
  ├── StartTag(td)
  │   └── If no <tr>, insert implicitly
  ├── EndTag(table)
  │   └── Pop table; switch to "in body"
  └── Anything else
      └── Parse error; foster parent

docs.title: The Fragment Parsing Context
docs.text:
innerHTML uses a different context:

// Context: div
div.innerHTML = '<tr><td>Cell</td></tr>';
// Result: the <tr> and <td> are stripped — they cannot be inside <div>

The context element determines the insertion mode and the stack.

docs.title: The Character Encoding Recovery
docs.text:
If the declared encoding is invalid, the parser falls back:

1.  Check for BOM.
2.  Check <meta charset>.
3.  Check HTTP Content-Type header.
4.  Fall back to UTF-8 (modern) or windows-1252 (legacy).

docs.title: The Null Character Handling
docs.text:
Null characters (\0) are handled specially:

  • In normal content: replaced with U+FFFD.
  • In script content: preserved (for JavaScript strings).
  • In comments: preserved.

docs.title: Error Recovery Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Tokenizer encounters invalid input.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parse error is recorded.
    │
    ▼
3.  Recovery rule is dispatched.
    │
    ▼
4.  Tokenizer or tree constructor applies the recovery.
    │
    ▼
5.  Parsing continues.
    │
    ▼
6.  Error may be logged in DevTools.
    │
    ▼
7.  DOM is produced.

docs.title: Recovery Rule Dispatch Lifecycle
docs.text:
Token arrives at the tree constructor
    │
    ▼
Check the current insertion mode
    │
    ▼
Is the token valid for this mode?
    │
    ├── YES → Process normally
    │
    └── NO → Parse error
              │
              ▼
         Apply recovery rule
              │
              ▼
         Continue parsing

docs.title: The Validation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Developer writes HTML.
    │
    ▼
2.  Run W3C Validator.
    │
    ▼
3.  Validator reports parse errors.
    │
    ▼
4.  Developer fixes errors.
    │
    ▼
5.  Deploy.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser parses without recovery.

Validation catches errors before they reach the browser. Recovery ensures the page still works if validation is skipped.

docs.title: Example 1: Missing <html>, <head>, <body>
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<p>Hello</p>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<html>
  <head></head>
  <body>
    <p>Hello</p>
  </body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • The parser inserts <html>, <head>, and <body> implicitly.
  • The DOM is well-formed even though the input was minimal.
  • This is why DevTools always shows a full document tree.

docs.title: Example 2: Block Element Inside <p>
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<p>Hello<div>World</div>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<body>
  <p>Hello</p>
  <div>World</div>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • <div> cannot be inside <p>.
  • The parser auto-closes <p> before inserting <div>.
  • This is a common source of CSS selector bugs.

docs.title: Example 3: Unclosed <li>
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<ul>
  <li>Item 1
  <li>Item 2
</ul>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<ul>
  <li>Item 1</li>
  <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

Code Breakdown:

  • The second <li> auto-closes the first.
  • The DOM is well-formed.
  • This is valid HTML5 — </li> is optional in some cases.

docs.title: Example 4: Implicit <tbody>
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<table>
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<table>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Code Breakdown:

  • The parser inserts <tbody> implicitly.
  • CSS selectors like table > tr do not match — use table > tbody > tr.

docs.title: Example 5: Foster Parenting
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<table>
  Some text
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<body>
  "Some text"
  <table>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</body>

Code Breakdown:

  • Text directly inside <table> is foster-parented.
  • The text moves before the table.
  • This can cause unexpected visual results.

docs.title: Example 6: Misnested Formatting
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<p>1<b>2<i>3</b>4</i>5</p>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<p>
  1
  <b>2<i>3</i></b>
  <i>4</i>
  5
</p>

Code Breakdown:

  • The adoption agency algorithm reconstructs the tree.
  • The result is well-formed but may not match developer intent.

docs.title: Example 7: The </script> Trap
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<script>
  const s = "</script>";
</script>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<script>const s = "</script>
<p>";</p>

Code Breakdown:

  • The tokenizer sees </script> and ends the script element.
  • The rest becomes text.
  • Fix: escape as <\/script>.

docs.title: Example 8: Duplicate Attribute
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<div class="a" class="b">

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<div class="a"></div>

Code Breakdown:

  • The second class attribute is ignored.
  • The first value wins.
  • A parse error is logged.

docs.title: Example 9: Stray End Tag
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<p>Hello</p>
</div>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<p>Hello</p>
<!-- The </div> is ignored -->

Code Breakdown:

  • No <div> on the stack.
  • The end tag is ignored.
  • A parse error is logged.

docs.title: Example 10: Character Reference Recovery
docs.text:
<!-- Input -->
<p>Tom & Jerry</p>

<!-- Recovered DOM -->
<p>Tom & Jerry</p>

Code Breakdown:

  • The parser sees & and attempts to parse a character reference.
  • & Jerry is not a valid reference.
  • The parser treats it as text (with a parse error).
  • In practice, this often works, but & is the correct form.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Recovery Behavior Missing structural tags Implicit insertion Block element in <p> Auto-close <p> Unclosed list items Auto-close <li> Table rows without <tbody> Implicit <tbody> Text inside <table> Foster parenting Misnested formatting Adoption agency algorithm Duplicate attributes First wins Stray end tags Ignored Malformed character references Treated as text </script> in string Script ends; rest is text Missing DOCTYPE Quirks mode Invalid encoding Fallback to UTF-8

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Validate your HTML. Why: the browser will not tell you about errors.
  2. Always include a DOCTYPE. Why: prevents quirks mode.
  3. Close all tags explicitly. Why: auto-closing may not match intent.
  4. Do not nest block elements inside <p>. Why: the parser auto-closes.
  5. Always include <tbody> in tables. Why: the parser inserts it anyway — be explicit.
  6. Escape <, >, &, ", '. Why: prevents parse errors.
  7. Escape </script> in script content. Why: prevents the script from breaking.
  8. Quote all attribute values. Why: unquoted values are error-prone.
  9. Do not duplicate attributes. Why: the first wins; the second is ignored.
  10. Use the W3C Validator in CI/CD. Why: catches errors before deployment.
  11. Test with view-source:. Why: confirms what the parser sees.
  12. Use DevTools to inspect the DOM. Why: the DOM is the parser's output.
  13. Understand the adoption agency algorithm. Why: misnested formatting is common.
  14. Understand foster parenting. Why: text near tables may move unexpectedly.
  15. Do not rely on recovery. Why: recovery is specified but may not match intent.
  16. Use modern HTML5 syntax. Why: the parser is optimized for HTML5.
  17. Sanitize user input. Why: malformed input can introduce XSS.
  18. Use DOMPurify for HTML sanitization. Why: it models the browser's parser.
  19. Test mXSS scenarios. Why: mutation XSS exploits parser re-parsing.
  20. Audit recovery after framework upgrades. Why: framework output may change.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Auto-Closing
docs.text:
<p>Hello<div>World</div>

Why it's wrong: The parser auto-closes <p> — the DOM may not match intent.

✅ Correct:

<p>Hello</p>
<div>World</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing <tbody> in Table
docs.text:
<table>
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

Why it's wrong: The parser inserts <tbody> — CSS selectors like table > tr fail.

✅ Correct:

<table>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: </script> Inside a String
docs.text:
<script>
  const s = "</script>";
</script>

Why it's wrong: The script ends at </script>; the rest becomes text.

✅ Correct:

<script>
  const s = "<\/script>";
</script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unescaped &
docs.text:
<p>Tom & Jerry</p>

Why it's wrong: The parser attempts to parse a character reference — may produce a parse error.

✅ Correct:

<p>Tom & Jerry</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unescaped <
docs.text:
<p>1 < 2</p>

Why it's wrong: The parser sees < and starts a tag.

✅ Correct:

<p>1 < 2</p>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Stray End Tag
docs.text:
<p>Hello</p>
</div>

Why it's wrong: The </div> is ignored — a parse error.

✅ Correct: Remove the stray tag.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate Attribute
docs.text:
<div class="a" class="b">

Why it's wrong: The second class is ignored — a parse error.

✅ Correct:

<div class="a b">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Text Inside <table>
docs.text:
<table>
  Some text
  <tr><td>Cell</td></tr>
</table>

Why it's wrong: The text is foster-parented — moved before the table.

✅ Correct: Put text inside a <td> or <caption>.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming the Parser Will Report Errors
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Parse errors are silent — the user sees a normal page.

✅ Correct: Use validation tools (W3C Validator, Lighthouse) to find errors.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using innerHTML with Untrusted Input
docs.text:
element.innerHTML = userInput;
