Why it's wrong: innerHTML parses HTML and can execute scripts — XSS.

✅ Correct:

element.textContent = userInput;

Or, if HTML is required:

element.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(userInput);

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Recovery is fast — the parser handles malformed input efficiently.
  • Parse errors add slight overhead — logging and rule dispatch.
  • Malformed HTML may produce unexpected DOM — additional layout/paint work.
  • Large documents with many parse errors — slightly slower parsing.
  • Validation catches errors before they reach the browser — no runtime cost.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Write well-formed HTML — less recovery work.
  2. Validate before deployment.
  3. Minimize malformed input.
  4. Use streaming SSR — content appears incrementally.
  5. Test with large documents.

docs.title: Mutation XSS (mXSS)
docs.text:
A class of XSS where sanitized HTML is re-parsed by the browser and produces a different (malicious) tree. The sanitizer and the browser disagree about how to parse the input.

Defense: Use DOMPurify; test sanitized output with the browser parser.

docs.title: Parser Differentials
docs.text: If different browsers parsed malformed HTML differently, attackers could exploit the difference. Error recovery eliminates this by ensuring deterministic parsing.

docs.title: The </script> Trap
docs.text:
Attackers can inject content that ends a script element prematurely, breaking out into HTML context.

Defense: Escape </script> as <\/script> in generated JavaScript.

docs.title: document.write() and XSS
docs.text:
document.write() with untrusted input is a classic XSS vector.

Defense: Never pass untrusted input to document.write().

docs.title: DOM Clobbering
docs.text:
Named elements can shadow global variables and properties.

<img name="location">
<script>
  console.log(location); // The <img>, not window.location
</script>

Defense: Avoid global name collisions; use explicit references.

docs.title: The innerHTML Attack Surface
docs.text:
innerHTML parses HTML and can execute scripts embedded in event handlers, <script> tags, and JavaScript URLs.

Defense: Use textContent for untrusted input; sanitize with DOMPurify for HTML.

docs.title: Error Recovery and Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Error recovery is not affected by CSP. But malformed input that survives parsing may still be blocked by CSP at execution time.

Defense: Set strict CSP directives on all responses.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Console — parse errors may be logged.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements — inspect the actual DOM.
  • W3C Validator — validator.w3.org — catches parse errors.
  • HTML5 Validator — html5.validator.nu.
  • view-source: — view the raw HTML.
  • document.documentElement.outerHTML — see the recovered DOM.
  • DOMParser — parse HTML strings and inspect the result.
  • document.implementation.createHTMLDocument() — parse in a sandbox.
  • Look for unexpected <tbody> — confirms implicit insertion.
  • Look for moved text near tables — confirms foster parenting.
  • Look for auto-closed <p> — confirms content model enforcement.
  • Look for ignored stray tags — confirms error recovery.
  • Test with innerHTML on different context elements — confirms fragment parsing.
  • Use console.dir(element) — inspect element properties.
  • Compare browser output — verify deterministic behavior.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Understanding the browser — error recovery is always running.
  • Debugging unexpected DOM — the recovery rules explain the structure.
  • Security testing — mXSS exploits recovery behavior.
  • Sanitizer development — models the browser's recovery.
  • Parser development — the specification is the reference.
  • Testing cross-browser behavior — verify deterministic parsing.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not rely on error recovery. Write well-formed HTML.
  • Do not skip validation. The browser will not report errors.
  • Do not use malformed HTML intentionally. It may not match intent.
  • Do not assume recovery produces the same DOM in every browser. Test edge cases.
  • Do not use innerHTML with untrusted input.
  • Do not use document.write().
  • Do not ignore parse errors. Fix them.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Browser Parsing
  • Tokenization
  • Tree Construction
  • DOM Creation
  • Parsing Algorithm
  • Script Blocking
  • Rendering Pipeline
  • HTML Living Standard
  • WHATWG
  • Parse error
  • Implicit tag insertion
  • Auto-closing
  • Foster parenting
  • Adoption agency algorithm
  • Content model
  • Quirks mode
  • DOCTYPE
  • Mutation XSS (mXSS)
  • DOMPurify
  • DOM clobbering
  • Parser differentials

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• HTML never fails to parse. Every input produces a DOM tree.
  • Parse errors are silent. The user never sees a warning.
  • The HTML5 specification defines every parse error and its recovery.
  • All modern browsers produce the same DOM from the same malformed HTML.
  • The adoption agency algorithm is one of the most complex parts of the specification.
  • Foster parenting moves text out of tables.
  • <tbody> is inserted implicitly — even when not written.
  • <html>, <head>, <body> are inserted implicitly.
  • <p> auto-closes on block-level elements.
  • <li> auto-closes on another <li>.
  • </script> inside a string ends the script element — the most famous recovery trap.
  • Duplicate attributes — the first wins.
  • Stray end tags are ignored.
  • Malformed character references are treated as text.
  • Mutation XSS (mXSS) exploits parser re-parsing — sanitizers must model the browser's parser.
  • DOM clobbering exploits named elements — <img name="location"> shadows window.location.
  • The specification was derived from real browser behavior — the spec authors studied how browsers handled malformed HTML.
  • Error recovery is the reason the web is resilient — most of the web would not render without it.
  • Validation catches errors before they reach the browser — the W3C Validator is the standard tool.
  • The browser will not tell you your HTML is wrong — validation is essential.
  • Postel's Law: "Be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you accept."
  • Error recovery is deterministic — same input → same DOM in every browser.
  • The web is built on error recovery — it is the foundation of interoperability.
  • Error recovery is silent but not invisible — DevTools and validators reveal the errors.
  • The best error recovery is the one you never need — write well-formed HTML.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Error recovery is the set of rules for handling malformed HTML.
  • HTML never fails to parse — every input produces a DOM tree.
  • Parse errors are silent — the user does not see them.
  • Recovery categories: implicit insertion, auto-closing, ignoring, foster parenting, adoption agency.
  • Implicit insertion adds missing <html>, <head>, <body>, <tbody>.
  • Auto-closing closes <p>, <li>, <td>, <tr> when conflicting elements appear.
  • Stray end tags are ignored.
  • Foster parenting moves text out of tables.
  • The adoption agency algorithm reconstructs misnested formatting elements.
  • Attribute recovery: unquoted values end at whitespace; duplicate attributes — first wins.
  • The </script> trap ends the script element even inside a string.
  • All modern browsers produce the same DOM from the same input.
  • Mutation XSS (mXSS) exploits parser re-parsing — use DOMPurify.
  • DOM clobbering exploits named elements — avoid global name collisions.
  • The W3C Validator catches parse errors before deployment.
  • DevTools reveals the actual DOM produced by recovery.
  • Postel's Law: "Be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you accept."
  • Error recovery is deterministic — same input → same DOM everywhere.
  • The best error recovery is the one you never need — write well-formed HTML.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The <template> element is an HTML element that holds markup which is parsed but not rendered. Its content is stored in a separate DocumentFragment — not in the main DOM tree — and remains inert until cloned and inserted by JavaScript. It is a declarative mechanism for defining HTML fragments that can be instantiated repeatedly at runtime.

<template id="card-template">
    <article class="card">
        <h2 class="card-title"></h2>
        <p class="card-body"></p>
    </article>
</template>

<script>
    const template = document.getElementById('card-template');
    const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);

    clone.querySelector('.card-title').textContent = 'Hello';
    clone.querySelector('.card-body').textContent = 'World';

    document.body.appendChild(clone);
</script>

The template's content is not displayed when the page loads. It is not in the DOM. It is not in the accessibility tree. It is not laid out or painted. It is a blueprint — a pattern that JavaScript can stamp out as many times as needed.

Templates are the foundation of Web Components. They are how custom elements define their shadow DOM structure, how slots receive content, and how reusable components encapsulate their markup.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The <template> element serves several essential purposes:

  • Deferred parsing — HTML is parsed once but rendered only when instantiated.
  • Reusable markup — define a pattern once, clone it many times.
  • Client-side templating — generate dynamic content without string concatenation.
  • Web Components — the markup foundation for custom elements.
  • Performance — parsed once, cloned cheaply.
  • Security — inert content does not execute scripts or load resources.
  • Declarative structure — markup is written in HTML, not built in JavaScript.
  • Encapsulation — templates combine with Shadow DOM for style isolation.

A template is a blueprint, not a rendered element. It is the difference between "write markup once" and "generate markup N times."

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Web Components
│
├── Templates           ← reusable markup (THIS CHAPTER)
├── Slots               ← content projection
├── Shadow DOM          ← style and structure encapsulation
├── Custom Elements     ← reusable component definitions
└── Declarative Shadow DOM ← server-rendered shadow DOM

The <template> element is the first building block of Web Components. It provides the markup that custom elements instantiate, that slots project into, and that Shadow DOM encapsulates.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Before <template>, developers had several bad options for holding reusable markup:

  • Strings in JavaScript — fragile, no syntax highlighting, no HTML parsing.
  • Hidden <div> elements — parsed and rendered (wasted work), could leak styles, could be affected by CSS.
  • <script type="text/template"> — a hack that abused the script element to hide markup.
  • innerHTML with string concatenation — XSS risks, poor performance, no parsing until runtime.

None of these were designed for the job. Each had significant drawbacks:

<!-- Old approach: hidden div -->
<div id="template" style="display: none;">
    <article class="card">
        <h2 class="card-title"></h2>
    </article>
</div>

<!-- Problem: parsed, laid out (then hidden), part of the DOM, affected by CSS -->

// Old approach: string concatenation
const html = `<article class="card"><h2>${title}</h2></article>`;
container.innerHTML = html;

// Problem: XSS risks, parsing overhead, no static analysis

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No native template element No declarative way to hold reusable markup Hidden divs were rendered Wasted parsing, layout, and paint Hidden divs were in the DOM CSS selectors matched them, accessibility tools saw them String concatenation XSS risks, poor performance No inert content Scripts in hidden markup could execute No encapsulation Templates leaked styles and structure into the page

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <template> element was introduced as part of the Web Components specification, which was proposed in 2011 and standardized in the HTML Living Standard. It was designed to solve the exact problem of holding reusable markup without the drawbacks of hidden divs or string concatenation.

The template element was originally called <template> in the Web Components working group and was adopted into the HTML specification. It shipped in Chrome 26 (2013), Firefox 22 (2013), Safari 8 (2014), and Edge 13 (2015).

The key innovation: the template's content is parsed but stored in a separate DocumentFragment — not in the main DOM tree. This means:

  • The content is parsed (valid HTML, accessible via template.content).
  • The content is inert (scripts do not run, images do not load).
  • The content is not rendered (no layout, no paint).
  • The content is not in the accessibility tree.
  • The content is not matched by CSS selectors targeting the main tree.

The template element is the only HTML element with these properties. It is a unique primitive in the web platform.

In 2026, the <template> element is baseline and universally supported. It is the foundation of Web Components and is used in every modern framework — React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, Lit, and many others — either directly or through their templating systems.

docs.title: The Minimal Template
docs.text:
<template id="my-template">
    <p>Hello, world!</p>
</template>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• <template> — the template element.
  • id="my-template" — a standard id attribute for JavaScript access.
  • <p>Hello, world!</p> — the template's content.

docs.title: Accessing the Content
docs.text:
const template = document.getElementById('my-template');

// The content is a DocumentFragment
console.log(template.content); // #document-fragment
console.log(template.content.querySelector('p').textContent); // "Hello, world!"

// The content is NOT a child of the template element
console.log(template.children.length); // 0 — children are empty!
console.log(template.childNodes.length); // 0 — childNodes are empty!

Critical detail: template.children and template.childNodes are empty. The content lives in template.content, a DocumentFragment. This is the most commonly misunderstood aspect of the template element.

docs.title: Cloning the Content
docs.text:
const template = document.getElementById('my-template');

// Clone the content (deep clone)
const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);

// Insert the clone into the DOM
document.body.appendChild(clone);

// The clone is now part of the DOM and rendered

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• template.content — the DocumentFragment holding the template's content.
  • .cloneNode(true) — deep clone of all descendants.
  • document.body.appendChild(clone) — inserts the clone into the DOM.

docs.title: The Two-Step Pattern
docs.text:
Every use of a template follows the same two-step pattern:

1.  Clone the template content:
    └── const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);

2.  Insert the clone into the DOM:
    └── container.appendChild(clone);

Between the two steps, you can modify the clone — set text, attributes, event listeners — before it is rendered.

docs.title: A Complete Example
docs.text:
<ul id="fruit-list"></ul>

<template id="fruit-template">
    <li class="fruit">
        <span class="fruit-name"></span>
        <span class="fruit-color"></span>
    </li>
</template>

<script>
    const fruits = [
        { name: 'Apple', color: 'Red' },
        { name: 'Banana', color: 'Yellow' },
        { name: 'Cherry', color: 'Dark red' }
    ];

    const template = document.getElementById('fruit-template');
    const list = document.getElementById('fruit-list');
    const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();

    for (const fruit of fruits) {
        const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
        clone.querySelector('.fruit-name').textContent = fruit.name;
        clone.querySelector('.fruit-color').textContent = fruit.color;
        fragment.appendChild(clone);
    }

    list.appendChild(fragment);
</script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• template.content.cloneNode(true) — clones the template content.
  • clone.querySelector(...) — finds elements within the clone.
  • fragment.appendChild(clone) — batches the clones into a DocumentFragment.
  • list.appendChild(fragment) — inserts the fragment in one DOM operation.

docs.title: The shadowrootmode Attribute (Declarative Shadow DOM)
docs.text:
<template shadowrootmode="open">
    <style>
        p { color: blue; }
    </style>
    <p>This is in a shadow root</p>
</template>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• shadowrootmode="open" — declares the template as a shadow root.
  • The content becomes the shadow DOM of the template's parent element.
  • Supported in Chrome 90+, Edge 90+, Safari 16.4+, Firefox 123+.
  • This is Declarative Shadow DOM — covered in detail in a later chapter.

docs.title: The shadowrootdelegatesfocus Attribute
docs.text:
<template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootdelegatesfocus>
    <input type="text">
</template>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• shadowrootdelegatesfocus — enables focus delegation to the first focusable element in the shadow root.
  • Useful for form controls and custom inputs.

docs.title: The shadowrootclonable Attribute
docs.text:
<template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootclonable>
    <p>Clonable shadow root</p>
</template>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• shadowrootclonable — allows the shadow root to be cloned via cloneNode().
  • Added in 2024 for use cases that require cloning shadow roots.

docs.title: The shadowrootserializable Attribute
docs.text:
<template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootserializable>
    <p>Serializable shadow root</p>
</template>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• shadowrootserializable — allows the shadow root to be serialized via getHTML().
  • Added in 2024 for server-side rendering and serialization.

docs.title: The "Blueprint" Mental Model
docs.text:
A template is a blueprint, not a rendered element:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TEMPLATE (blueprint)                        │
│  └── Parsed but not rendered                 │
│  └── Stored in a DocumentFragment            │
│  └── Inert                                    │
│  └── Not in the DOM                           │
│                                              │
│  CLONE (instance)                            │
│  └── Created via cloneNode(true)             │
│  └── Inserted into the DOM                    │
│  └── Rendered and interactive                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A blueprint is not a building. A template is not a rendered element. It is the source from which instances are created.

docs.title: The "Two-Tree" Mental Model
docs.text:
The template element creates two trees:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MAIN DOM TREE                                │
│  └── The document body                        │
│  └── Rendered, interactive, accessible        │
│                                              │
│  TEMPLATE CONTENT TREE                        │
│  └── template.content (DocumentFragment)      │
│  └── Parsed but not rendered                  │
│  └── Inert                                    │
│  └── Not in the accessibility tree            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The template's content is a separate tree from the main DOM. It is parsed, but it lives in a DocumentFragment, not in the document.

docs.title: The "Children Are Empty" Mental Model
docs.text:
The most counterintuitive aspect of the template element:

const template = document.querySelector('template');

template.children.length;    // 0
template.childNodes.length;  // 0
template.innerHTML;          // "" (empty!)

template.content.children.length;    // 1 (the actual content)
template.content.childNodes.length;  // 1

The template element has no children in the normal sense. Its content is in a separate DocumentFragment. This is why template.innerHTML returns an empty string — the content is not in the template element itself.

docs.title: The "Inert Content" Mental Model
docs.text:
The template's content is inert. Nothing in it executes or loads until cloned and inserted:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INSIDE A TEMPLATE                           │
│  ├── Scripts do not run                       │
│  ├── Images do not load                       │
│  ├── Styles do not apply                      │
│  ├── Videos do not preload                    │
│  ├── Iframes do not load                      │
│  └── Event handlers do not attach             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  AFTER CLONING AND INSERTION                  │
│  ├── Scripts run                              │
│  ├── Images load                              │
│  ├── Styles apply                             │
│  ├── Videos preload                           │
│  ├── Iframes load                             │
│  └── Event handlers attach                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is why templates are safe — you can put anything inside, and nothing will happen until you clone it.

docs.title: The "Parse Once, Clone Many" Mental Model
docs.text:
The template's content is parsed once when the page loads. Cloning is cheap — it copies the parsed tree, not the HTML string:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WITHOUT TEMPLATE                            │
│  └── innerHTML = '...'                       │
│  └── Parses the HTML string on every use      │
│  └── Repeats parsing for each instance        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WITH TEMPLATE                               │
│  └── Parsed once at page load                 │
│  └── cloneNode(true) copies the parsed tree  │
│  └── Cheap for each instance                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Templates are dramatically faster than string concatenation for repeated markup.

docs.title: The "Foundation of Web Components" Mental Model
docs.text:
The template element is the first building block of Web Components:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TEMPLATE                                    │
│  └── Holds the markup                         │
│                                              │
│  SLOT                                        │
│  └── Projects content into the markup         │
│                                              │
│  SHADOW DOM                                  │
│  └── Encapsulates the markup                  │
│                                              │
│  CUSTOM ELEMENTS                             │
│  └── Instantiates the markup                  │
│                                              │
│  DECLARATIVE SHADOW DOM                      │
│  └── Server-renders the shadow root           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every Web Component starts with a template.

docs.title: Concept 1: The <template> Element
docs.text: An HTML element whose content is parsed but not rendered. It is stored in a DocumentFragment accessible via template.content.

docs.title: Concept 2: The content Property
docs.text: A read-only DocumentFragment containing the template's parsed content. This is where the template's markup actually lives.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Empty Children
docs.text: The template element's children, childNodes, and innerHTML are empty. The content is not in the template element itself.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Inert Content
docs.text: Template content is inert — scripts do not run, images do not load, styles do not apply, iframes do not load. Nothing happens until the content is cloned and inserted.

docs.title: Concept 5: The cloneNode(true) Pattern
docs.text:
Templates are instantiated by deep-cloning the content:

const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);

docs.title: Concept 6: The DocumentFragment
docs.text: The template's content is a DocumentFragment — a lightweight, detached container. It can hold nodes but is not itself rendered.

docs.title: Concept 7: The Two-Step Pattern
docs.text:
Every template use follows two steps: clone, then insert.

const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
container.appendChild(clone);

docs.title: Concept 8: The id Attribute
docs.text: Templates typically have an id for JavaScript access. The id is the standard mechanism for finding the template.

docs.title: Concept 9: Nested Templates
docs.text:
Templates can contain other templates. This is useful for recursive structures.

<template id="tree-node">
    <li>
        <span></span>
        <ul></ul>
    </li>
</template>

docs.title: Concept 10: Templates in Shadow DOM
docs.text:
Templates are commonly used with Shadow DOM to define the shadow root's initial content:

const template = document.getElementById('my-template');
const shadowRoot = element.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
shadowRoot.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));

docs.title: Concept 11: Templates and Slots
docs.text:
Templates can include <slot> elements for content projection:

<template id="card-template">
    <div class="card">
        <slot name="title"></slot>
        <slot name="body"></slot>
    </div>
</template>

docs.title: Concept 12: Declarative Shadow DOM
docs.text:
The shadowrootmode attribute turns a template into a declarative shadow root:

<template shadowrootmode="open">
    <p>Shadow content</p>
</template>

docs.title: Concept 13: The shadowrootdelegatesfocus Attribute
docs.text: Enables focus delegation to the first focusable element in the shadow root.

docs.title: Concept 14: The shadowrootclonable Attribute
docs.text: Allows the shadow root to be cloned via cloneNode().

docs.title: Concept 15: The shadowrootserializable Attribute
docs.text: Allows the shadow root to be serialized via getHTML().

docs.title: Concept 16: Templates vs. Hidden Elements
docs.text:
Templates differ from hidden elements:

Template Hidden element Rendered No Yes (then hidden) In DOM No Yes In accessibility tree No No Scripts run No Yes Images load No Yes CSS matches No Yes

docs.title: Concept 17: Templates vs. String Concatenation
docs.text:
Templates are faster than string concatenation for repeated markup:

// Slow: parses HTML string on every use
for (const item of items) {
    container.innerHTML += `<li>${item}</li>`;
}

// Fast: parsed once, cloned cheaply
for (const item of items) {
    const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
    clone.querySelector('li').textContent = item;
    fragment.appendChild(clone);
}
container.appendChild(fragment);

docs.title: Concept 18: The template.content Mutation
docs.text:
The template content is a live DocumentFragment. Changes to it affect subsequent clones:

template.content.querySelector('p').textContent = 'Changed';
// All future clones will have "Changed"

docs.title: Concept 19: Templates and Frameworks
docs.text:
Most frameworks use templates internally:

  • Lit uses html tagged templates.
  • Vue uses <template> in single-file components.
  • Angular uses <ng-template>.
  • Svelte compiles templates to JavaScript.
  • React uses JSX (not <template>).

docs.title: Concept 20: Templates and Server-Side Rendering
docs.text: Templates are client-side constructs. For server-side rendering, use Declarative Shadow DOM (shadowrootmode) or server-rendered HTML.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Parsing a Template
docs.text:
1.  Tokenizer encounters <template>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Tree constructor creates an HTMLTemplateElement.
    │
    ▼
3.  Tree constructor switches to a special mode.
    │   └── Content is parsed into a DocumentFragment.
    │
    ▼
4.  All content between <template> and </template> is
    │   parsed into the template's content fragment.
    │
    ▼
5.  The template element is inserted into the DOM,
    │   but the content fragment is not.
    │
    ▼
6.  Parsing continues after </template>.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Cloning and Inserting
docs.text:
1.  JavaScript accesses the template.
    │
    ▼
2.  template.content.cloneNode(true) creates a deep clone
    │   of the DocumentFragment.
    │
    ▼
3.  The clone is a new DocumentFragment.
    │   └── Not yet in the DOM.
    │
    ▼
4.  JavaScript modifies the clone (set text, attributes, etc.).
    │
    ▼
5.  container.appendChild(clone) inserts the clone's children
    │   into the container.
    │
    ▼
6.  The clone is now part of the DOM and rendered.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Declarative Shadow DOM
docs.text:
1.  Tokenizer encounters <template shadowrootmode="open">.
    │
    ▼
2.  Tree constructor recognizes the shadowrootmode attribute.
    │
    ▼
3.  Tree constructor creates a shadow root on the parent element.
    │
    ▼
4.  Content is parsed directly into the shadow root.
    │
    ▼
5.  The template element is removed from the DOM.
    │
    ▼
6.  The shadow root is now attached to the parent element.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Inert Content
docs.text:
1.  Template content is parsed.
    │
    ▼
2.  Scripts are NOT executed.
    │   └── <script> elements are parsed but not run.
    │
    ▼
3.  Images are NOT loaded.
    │   └── <img> elements are parsed but no network request.
    │
    ▼
4.  Styles are NOT applied.
    │   └── <style> elements are parsed but not applied.
    │
    ▼
5.  Iframes are NOT loaded.
    │   └── <iframe> elements are parsed but no network request.
    │
    ▼
6.  Everything remains inert until cloned and inserted.

docs.title: The HTMLTemplateElement Interface
docs.text:
The template element is represented by the HTMLTemplateElement interface:

interface HTMLTemplateElement extends HTMLElement {
    readonly content: DocumentFragment;
    shadowRootMode: string;
    shadowRootDelegatesFocus: boolean;
    shadowRootClonable: boolean;
    shadowRootSerializable: boolean;
}

docs.title: The content Property
docs.text:
The content property is a read-only DocumentFragment. It is not a child of the template element — it is a separate tree.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HTMLTemplateElement                         │
│  ├── children: [] (empty)                    │
│  ├── childNodes: [] (empty)                  │
│  ├── innerHTML: "" (empty)                   │
│  └── content: DocumentFragment               │
│      └── The actual parsed content            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Template Contents Owner Document"
docs.text: The template's content fragment belongs to a separate owner document — the "template contents owner document." This is why the content is inert: it is not part of the main document, and the parser treats it as a separate context.

docs.title: The Parsing Mode Switch
docs.text:
When the tree constructor encounters <template>:

  1. It creates an HTMLTemplateElement.
  2. It inserts the template element into the current node.
  3. It switches the stack of open elements to include a "template insertion mode" marker.
  4. It parses the content into the template's content fragment.
  5. When </template> is encountered, the template is popped.

docs.title: The shadowrootmode Processing
docs.text:
When the parser sees <template shadowrootmode="open">:

  1. It checks if the parent element is a valid shadow host.
  2. It attaches a shadow root to the parent element.
  3. It parses the content directly into the shadow root.
  4. It removes the template element from the DOM.

This is Declarative Shadow DOM — the only way to create a shadow root from HTML.

docs.title: The Clone Algorithm
docs.text:
template.content.cloneNode(true):

  1. Creates a new DocumentFragment.
  2. Deep-clones each child node.
  3. Returns the new fragment.
  4. The clone's owner document is the current document — not the template's owner document.

docs.title: The DocumentFragment Optimization
docs.text:
DocumentFragment is optimized for batch DOM operations:

Appending a fragment:
  └── All children are moved to the target in one operation.
  └── One DOM mutation.
  └── One style recalculation.
  └── One layout.

docs.title: The innerHTML on Templates
docs.text:
template.innerHTML returns an empty string because the content is not in the template element. To get the HTML of the content, use:

template.innerHTML;              // "" (empty)
template.content.firstElementChild.outerHTML; // the actual HTML

docs.title: The outerHTML on Templates
docs.text:
template.outerHTML returns the template element without its content:

template.outerHTML; // "<template id="my-template"></template>"

This is a common surprise.

docs.title: Template Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Parsing: template content is parsed into a DocumentFragment.
    │
    ▼
2.  Ready: the template is available in the DOM.
    │   └── Content is inert.
    │
    ▼
3.  Cloning: cloneNode(true) creates an instance.
    │
    ▼
4.  Modification: the clone is customized.
    │
    ▼
5.  Insertion: the clone is added to the DOM.
    │
    ▼
6.  Rendering: the clone is rendered.
    │
    ▼
7.  Interaction: the clone is now live.

docs.title: Declarative Shadow DOM Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  HTML parsed.
    │
    ▼
2.  <template shadowrootmode> encountered.
    │
    ▼
3.  Shadow root created on the parent.
    │
    ▼
4.  Content parsed into the shadow root.
    │
    ▼
5.  Template removed from the DOM.
    │
    ▼
6.  Shadow root is live and rendered.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Template Instantiation
docs.text:
<template id="greeting-template">
    <p class="greeting">Hello!</p>
</template>

<div id="container"></div>

<script>
    const template = document.getElementById('greeting-template');
    const container = document.getElementById('container');

    const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
    clone.querySelector('.greeting').textContent = 'Hello, Alice!';
    container.appendChild(clone);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The template holds a <p class="greeting">.
  • The clone is created with cloneNode(true).
  • The text is customized before insertion.
  • The clone is appended to the container.

docs.title: Example 2: Repeating a Template
docs.text:
<ul id="list"></ul>

<template id="item-template">
    <li class="item">
        <span class="name"></span>
        <span class="price"></span>
    </li>
</template>

<script>
    const items = [
        { name: 'Apple', price: '$1.00' },
        { name: 'Banana', price: '$0.50' },
        { name: 'Cherry', price: '$3.00' }
    ];

    const template = document.getElementById('item-template');
    const list = document.getElementById('list');
    const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();

    for (const item of items) {
        const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
        clone.querySelector('.name').textContent = item.name;
        clone.querySelector('.price').textContent = item.price;
        fragment.appendChild(clone);
    }

    list.appendChild(fragment);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • Each item is a clone of the template.
  • Text is customized per clone.
  • Clones are batched into a DocumentFragment.
  • One DOM operation for all items.

docs.title: Example 3: Template with Nested Template
docs.text:
<template id="tree-template">
    <li class="node">
        <span class="label"></span>
        <ul class="children"></ul>
    </li>
</template>

<script>
    const template = document.getElementById('tree-template');

    function renderNode(node) {
        const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
        clone.querySelector('.label').textContent = node.label;

        if (node.children) {
            const childrenList = clone.querySelector('.children');
            for (const child of node.children) {
                childrenList.appendChild(renderNode(child));
            }
        }

        return clone;
    }

    const tree = {
        label: 'Root',
        children: [
            { label: 'Child 1' },
            { label: 'Child 2', children: [{ label: 'Grandchild' }] }
        ]
    };

    document.getElementById('tree').appendChild(renderNode(tree));
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The template is recursive — it contains a .children list.
  • renderNode clones the template and recursively renders children.
  • The result is a nested tree structure.

docs.title: Example 4: Template with Event Listeners
docs.text:
<template id="button-template">
    <button class="action">Click me</button>
</template>

<div id="container"></div>

<script>
    const template = document.getElementById('button-template');
    const container = document.getElementById('container');

    const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
    const button = clone.querySelector('.action');

    button.addEventListener('click', () => {
        console.log('Clicked!');
    });

    container.appendChild(clone);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The clone is created.
  • Event listeners are attached before insertion.
  • The clone is appended to the container.
  • The listener is now active.

docs.title: Example 5: Template for a Custom Element
docs.text:
<template id="user-card-template">
    <style>
        .card {
            border: 1px solid #ccc;
            padding: 1rem;
            border-radius: 8px;
        }
        .name { font-weight: bold; }
    </style>
    <div class="card">
        <div class="name"></div>
        <div class="email"></div>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
        constructor() {
            super();
            this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        }

        connectedCallback() {
            const template = document.getElementById('user-card-template');
            const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);

            clone.querySelector('.name').textContent = this.getAttribute('name');
            clone.querySelector('.email').textContent = this.getAttribute('email');

            this.shadowRoot.appendChild(clone);
        }
    }

    customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);
</script>

<user-card name="Alice" email="alice@example.com"></user-card>

Code Breakdown:

  • The template contains both styles and markup.
  • The custom element clones the template into its shadow root.
  • The <style> is encapsulated in the shadow root.

docs.title: Example 6: Template with Slots
docs.text:
<template id="card-template">
    <div class="card">
        <header><slot name="title"></slot></header>
        <main><slot name="body"></slot></main>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    class Card extends HTMLElement {
        constructor() {
            super();
            const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
            const template = document.getElementById('card-template');
            shadow.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
        }
    }
    customElements.define('card-component', Card);
</script>

<card-component>
    <h2 slot="title">My Card</h2>
    <p slot="body">Card content goes here.</p>
</card-component>

Code Breakdown:

  • The template defines named slots.
  • The custom element clones the template into its shadow root.
  • The slot content is projected from the light DOM.

docs.title: Example 7: Declarative Shadow DOM
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <style>
            p { color: blue; }
        </style>
        <p>Shadow DOM content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

<script>
    class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
        connectedCallback() {
            console.log('Shadow root:', this.shadowRoot);
        }
    }
    customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The <template shadowrootmode="open"> declares a shadow root.
  • The content becomes the shadow DOM of <my-element>.
  • The template is removed from the DOM.
  • The custom element can access its shadow root.

docs.title: Example 8: Template with DocumentFragment Batching
docs.text:
<ul id="list"></ul>

<template id="item-template">
    <li class="item"></li>
</template>

<script>
    const template = document.getElementById('item-template');
    const list = document.getElementById('list');
    const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();

    for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
        const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
        clone.querySelector('.item').textContent = `Item ${i}`;
        fragment.appendChild(clone);
    }

    list.appendChild(fragment);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • 1000 clones are created.
  • Each is appended to a DocumentFragment.
  • The fragment is appended to the list in one DOM operation.
  • This is dramatically faster than 1000 individual appends.

docs.title: Example 9: Template with Conditional Content
docs.text:
<template id="user-template">
    <div class="user">
        <span class="name"></span>
        <span class="admin-badge" hidden>Admin</span>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    const template = document.getElementById('user-template');
    const users = [
        { name: 'Alice', isAdmin: true },
        { name: 'Bob', isAdmin: false }
    ];

    const container = document.getElementById('users');
    const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();

    for (const user of users) {
        const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
        clone.querySelector('.name').textContent = user.name;

        if (user.isAdmin) {
            clone.querySelector('.admin-badge').hidden = false;
        }

        fragment.appendChild(clone);
    }

    container.appendChild(fragment);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The template includes a hidden badge.
  • The clone's badge is shown conditionally.
  • The hidden attribute is manipulated per clone.

docs.title: Example 10: Template as a Source for Cloning
docs.text:
<template id="modal-template">
    <div class="modal" role="dialog" aria-modal="true">
        <h2 class="modal-title"></h2>
        <div class="modal-body"></div>
        <button class="modal-close" aria-label="Close">✕</button>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    class Modal {
        constructor(title, body) {
            const template = document.getElementById('modal-template');
            this.element = template.content.cloneNode(true).firstElementChild;

            this.element.querySelector('.modal-title').textContent = title;
            this.element.querySelector('.modal-body').textContent = body;

            this.element.querySelector('.modal-close').addEventListener('click', () => {
                this.close();
            });
        }

        open() {
            document.body.appendChild(this.element);
        }

        close() {
            this.element.remove();
        }
    }

    const modal = new Modal('Confirm', 'Are you sure?');
    modal.open();
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The template defines a modal's structure.
  • The Modal class clones the template.
  • The clone is customized and inserted.
  • The modal can be opened and closed repeatedly.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Description Repeating list items Clone a template for each item Table rows Clone a template for each row Cards Clone a template for each card Modals Clone a template for each modal Form fields Clone a template for repeated fields Web Components Define shadow DOM structure Custom Elements Instantiate component markup Tree structures Recursive template cloning Nested lists Recursive templates Client-side templating Replace string concatenation

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use templates instead of string concatenation. Why: parsed once, cloned cheaply.
  2. Use template.content.cloneNode(true). Why: the content property is the actual content.
  3. Batch clones with a DocumentFragment. Why: one DOM operation for many clones.
  4. Customize the clone before insertion. Why: avoids unnecessary DOM mutations.
  5. Attach event listeners to the clone before insertion. Why: avoids re-querying after insertion.
  6. Use id for template identification. Why: standard way to find templates.
  7. Keep templates focused. Why: small templates are easier to maintain.
  8. Use templates with Shadow DOM. Why: encapsulates styles and structure.
  9. Use templates with slots. Why: enables content projection.
  10. Use shadowrootmode for declarative shadow DOM. Why: server-renderable.
  11. Remember that template.children is empty. Why: content is in template.content.
  12. Remember that template.innerHTML is empty. Why: content is not in the template.
  13. Do not put scripts in templates. Why: they do not run until cloned and inserted.
  14. Do not put external resources in templates. Why: they do not load until cloned and inserted.
  15. Use <template> for reusable markup. Why: declarative, parsed once.
  16. Use <div hidden> for hidden content. Why: different use case — hidden content is rendered but hidden.
  17. Nest templates for recursive structures. Why: enables tree rendering.
  18. Cache template references. Why: getElementById is not free.
  19. Test templates in all target browsers. Why: shadowrootmode support varies.
  20. Use Declarative Shadow DOM for SSR. Why: server-rendered shadow DOM.
  21. Clean up clones when no longer needed. Why: prevents memory leaks.
  22. Use DocumentFragment for cloning batching. Why: performance.
  23. Use templates in frameworks when supported. Why: native primitive.
  24. Audit template usage after framework upgrades. Why: framework output may change.
  25. Document template patterns. Why: consistency across the team.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using template.innerHTML
docs.text:
template.innerHTML; // "" (empty!)

Why it's wrong: The content is not in the template element — it is in template.content.

✅ Correct:

template.content.querySelector('p').textContent;
// or
template.content.firstElementChild.outerHTML;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using template.children
docs.text:
template.children.length; // 0

Why it's wrong: The template element has no children — the content is in template.content.

✅ Correct:

template.content.children.length; // the actual count

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Appending the Template Directly
docs.text:
container.appendChild(template);

Why it's wrong: Appends the template element itself, not its content.

✅ Correct:

container.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Clone
docs.text:
container.appendChild(template.content);

Why it's wrong: Moves the content out of the template — subsequent uses find nothing.

✅ Correct:

container.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: String Concatenation Instead of Templates
docs.text:
for (const item of items) {
    container.innerHTML += `<li>${item}</li>`;
}

Why it's wrong: Re-parses HTML on every iteration — slow and error-prone.

✅ Correct:

for (const item of items) {
    const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
    clone.querySelector('li').textContent = item;
    fragment.appendChild(clone);
}
container.appendChild(fragment);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No DocumentFragment Batching
docs.text:
for (const item of items) {
    container.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
}

Why it's wrong: Each append is a separate DOM mutation.

✅ Correct:

const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();
for (const item of items) {
    fragment.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
}
container.appendChild(fragment);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Scripts Inside Templates
docs.text:
<template>
    <script>console.log('Hello');</script>
</template>

Why it's wrong: Scripts in templates do not run until cloned and inserted. This may surprise.

✅ Correct: Understand that scripts run on insertion, not on parse.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Images Inside Templates
docs.text:
<template>
    <img src="large-image.jpg">
</template>

Why it's wrong: Images in templates do not load until cloned and inserted.

✅ Correct: This is actually a feature — it defers loading.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming shadowrootmode Is Universally Supported
docs.text:
<template shadowrootmode="open">
    <p>Shadow content</p>
</template>

Why it's wrong: shadowrootmode requires Chrome 90+, Edge 90+, Safari 16.4+, Firefox 123+.

✅ Correct: Test in target browsers; provide a polyfill if needed.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Caching Template References
docs.text:
for (const item of items) {
    const template = document.getElementById('item-template');
    // ...
}

Why it's wrong: getElementById is called on every iteration.

✅ Correct:

const template = document.getElementById('item-template');
for (const item of items) {
    // ...
}

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Templates are parsed once — cheap to clone.
  • Cloning is fast — copies the parsed tree, not the HTML string.
  • DocumentFragment batching — one DOM mutation for many clones.
  • Inert content — no scripts run, no images load until cloned.
  • innerHTML is slower — re-parses the HTML string on every use.
  • Template cloning is faster than string concatenation for repeated markup.
  • cloneNode(true) deep clones — shallow clones are cheaper but rarely useful.
  • DocumentFragment avoids reflows — the fragment is not rendered until appended.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Parse once, clone many.
  2. Batch with DocumentFragment.
  3. Customize before insertion.
  4. Cache template references.
  5. Use templates instead of string concatenation.
  6. Avoid modifying the template content directly.
  7. Use shallow clones when possible.
  8. Test with large numbers of clones.

docs.title: Inert Content Is Safe
docs.text: Template content is inert — scripts do not run, images do not load. This makes templates safe to hold untrusted markup until it is cloned.

docs.title: Cloning Does Not Sanitize
docs.text:
Cloning a template does not sanitize its content. If the template contains malicious markup, the clone will too.

Defense: Sanitize content before inserting it into a template.

docs.title: innerHTML on Template Content
docs.text:
Setting template.content.innerHTML = userInput parses HTML. This is an XSS risk if the input is untrusted.

Defense: Use textContent or sanitize with DOMPurify.

docs.title: Declarative Shadow DOM and CSP
docs.text: Declarative Shadow DOM is subject to CSP. Ensure policies cover shadow roots.

docs.title: shadowrootclonable and shadowrootserializable
docs.text: These attributes allow cloning and serializing shadow roots — verify they do not expose sensitive content.

docs.title: Template Injection
docs.text:
If a template's content is generated from user input without escaping, attackers can inject markup.

Defense: Escape user input; use textContent for text content.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements — templates appear in the DOM, but their content does not.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Properties — inspect template.content.
  • $0.content — the selected template's content.
  • $0.content.children — the template's actual children.
  • $0.innerHTML — returns empty (surprise).
  • $0.outerHTML — returns the template element without content.
  • Chrome DevTools → Console — inspect templates directly.
  • document.querySelectorAll('template') — list all templates.
  • template.content.cloneNode(true) — test cloning in console.
  • Chrome DevTools → Layers — verify declarative shadow roots.
  • element.shadowRoot — access a shadow root created by shadowrootmode.
  • getHTML() — serialize a shadow root with shadowrootserializable.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Repeating markup — lists, cards, rows, items.
  • Web Components — define shadow DOM structure.
  • Custom Elements — instantiate component markup.
  • Client-side templating — replace string concatenation.
  • Dynamic content — generate markup on demand.
  • Recursive structures — trees, nested lists.
  • Deferred parsing — parse once, clone many.
  • Declarative Shadow DOM — server-render shadow roots.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use templates for single-use markup. Just write it directly.
  • Do not use templates for hidden content. Use <div hidden>.
  • Do not use templates for string concatenation. Templates are for DOM cloning.
  • Do not put scripts in templates expecting them to run. They run on insertion.
  • Do not use template.innerHTML. Use template.content.
  • Do not use templates without cloning. Always clone before insertion.
  • Do not assume shadowrootmode is universally supported. Test target browsers.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <template> element was added to HTML5 as part of the Web Components specification.
  • Template content is stored in a DocumentFragment — not in the template element itself.
  • template.children is empty — the content is in template.content.
  • template.innerHTML returns an empty string — the content is not in the template.
  • Template content is inert — scripts do not run, images do not load, styles do not apply.
  • Templates are parsed once, cloned many times — faster than string concatenation.
  • cloneNode(true) deep clones — false shallow clones.
  • DocumentFragment batches DOM mutations — one operation for many clones.
  • Declarative Shadow DOM uses <template shadowrootmode="open">.
  • shadowrootdelegatesfocus enables focus delegation.
  • shadowrootclonable allows cloning the shadow root.
  • shadowrootserializable allows serializing the shadow root.
  • Declarative Shadow DOM is supported in Chrome 90+, Edge 90+, Safari 16.4+, Firefox 123+.
  • Most frameworks use templates internally — Lit, Vue, Angular, Svelte.
  • React uses JSX, not <template> — but the concept is similar.
  • Templates are safe to hold untrusted markup — content is inert.
  • Cloning a template does not sanitize content — sanitize before inserting.
  • <template> is not the same as <div hidden> — hidden elements are rendered (then hidden).
  • <template> is not the same as <script type="text/template"> — the script hack is obsolete.
  • Templates are the foundation of Web Components — every component starts with a template.
  • The template element is a unique primitive — no other element has inert content.
  • Templates are ideal for repeated markup — performance and maintainability.
  • The template element is baseline and universally supported — Chrome 26+, Firefox 22+, Safari 8+, Edge 13+.
  • The template element is the declarative way to define reusable markup — no JavaScript required to parse.
  • The best template is the one you never have to modify — write once, clone many.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The <template> element holds markup that is parsed but not rendered.
  • The content lives in template.content — a DocumentFragment.
  • template.children and template.innerHTML are empty — the content is not in the template element.
  • Template content is inert — scripts do not run, images do not load.
  • Instantiate templates with template.content.cloneNode(true).
  • Modify the clone before inserting it into the DOM.
  • Batch clones with a DocumentFragment — one DOM operation for many.
  • Templates are faster than string concatenation — parsed once, cloned cheaply.
  • Templates are the foundation of Web Components.
  • Declarative Shadow DOM uses <template shadowrootmode="open">.
  • shadowrootdelegatesfocus, shadowrootclonable, and shadowrootserializable extend declarative shadow DOM.
  • Templates work with slots for content projection.
  • Templates are supported in all modern browsers.
  • Templates are used in most frameworks — Lit, Vue, Angular, Svelte.
  • Do not use template.innerHTML — use template.content.
  • Do not forget to clone — always clone before insertion.
  • Do not put scripts in templates expecting them to run — they run on insertion.
  • Do not use templates for hidden content — use <div hidden>.
  • Templates are the declarative way to define reusable markup.
  • The best template is the one you never have to modify — write once, clone many.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A slot is a placeholder inside a shadow tree that marks where content from the light DOM (the element's actual children) should be projected. It is declared with the <slot> element and enables content projection — the mechanism that lets a Web Component accept and render markup provided by the consumer.

<!-- Component definition (shadow tree) -->
<template id="card-template">
    <div class="card">
        <header class="card-header">
            <slot name="title">Default title</slot>
        </header>
        <main class="card-body">
            <slot>Default body content</slot>
        </main>
    </div>
</template>

<!-- Component usage (light DOM) -->
<my-card>
    <h2 slot="title">Hello</h2>
    <p>This is the body.</p>
</my-card>

The <slot name="title"> in the shadow tree receives the <h2 slot="title"> from the light DOM. The unnamed <slot> receives the <p> — the default slot. The rendered output combines shadow markup with light DOM content.

Slots are the content projection mechanism of Web Components. They answer a fundamental question: how does a custom element let users inject their own content into a predefined structure?

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Slots serve several essential purposes:

  • Content projection — the core mechanism for composing Web Components.
  • Composition over inheritance — build complex components from simpler ones.
  • Reusability — a single component template can render arbitrary content.
  • Encapsulation with flexibility — shadow DOM encapsulates styles while slots allow content injection.
  • Declarative API — consumers provide content via standard HTML, not JavaScript props.
  • Accessibility preservation — projected content retains its native semantics.
  • Framework parity — the same concept exists as "children" in React, "slots" in Vue, "content" in Angular.

Slots are how Web Components become composable rather than monolithic. They are the difference between "use this exact component" and "use this component with your own content inside."

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Web Components
│
├── Templates           ← reusable markup
├── Slots               ← content projection (THIS CHAPTER)
├── Shadow DOM          ← style and structure encapsulation
├── Custom Elements     ← reusable component definitions
└── Declarative Shadow DOM ← server-rendered shadow DOM

Slots sit between templates and Shadow DOM. Templates define the shadow structure; Shadow DOM encapsulates it; slots project light DOM content into that structure.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A Web Component with Shadow DOM encapsulates its markup and styles. But encapsulation alone is not enough. Consider a <user-card> component:

class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).innerHTML = `
            <div class="card">
                <h2>User Name</h2>
                <p>User bio here.</p>
            </div>
        `;
    }
}

This component hardcodes its content. A consumer cannot provide their own name or bio. To change the content, they would need to:

  • Modify the component's source code.
  • Pass data via attributes or properties and hope the component renders it.
  • Abandon Shadow DOM encapsulation entirely.

None of these are satisfactory. The component is closed — it does not accept content from its consumers.

Slots solve this. They mark places in the shadow tree where light DOM content should appear:

<my-card>
    <h2 slot="title">Alice</h2>
    <p>Alice is a software engineer.</p>
</my-card>

The component projects the consumer's content into the correct places. It is open — it accepts content.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No content projection Components were monolithic Hardcoded content Consumers could not customize Attribute-only API Complex content was impossible No style encapsulation Component styles leaked to projected content No encapsulation Projected content could not be encapsulated No composition model Components could not nest cleanly

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The <slot> element was introduced as part of the Shadow DOM specification (2014–2016). It was designed to solve the composition problem in Web Components.

Before slots, developers used several workarounds:

  • innerHTML passthrough — copy the element's innerHTML into the shadow tree (breaks encapsulation).
  • Template attributes — serialize content into attributes (limited, insecure).
  • No Shadow DOM — accept style leakage in exchange for content flexibility.

Slots formalized content projection as a first-class primitive. They shipped alongside Shadow DOM in Chrome 53 (2016), Firefox 63 (2018), Safari 10 (2016), and Edge 79 (2020).

In 2026, slots are baseline and universally supported. They are the standard mechanism for content projection in Web Components, used by Lit, FAST, Stencil, and every major Web Component library.

docs.title: The Minimal Slot
docs.text:
<!-- Component definition -->
<template id="my-component">
    <div class="wrapper">
        <slot></slot>
    </div>
</template>

<!-- Component usage -->
<my-component>
    <p>This content is projected into the slot.</p>
</my-component>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• <slot> — the placeholder inside the shadow tree.
  • The <p> from the light DOM is projected into the slot.
  • The rendered output combines <div class="wrapper"> from the shadow with <p> from the light DOM.

docs.title: Named Slots
docs.text:
<!-- Component definition -->
<template id="card-template">
    <div class="card">
        <header><slot name="title"></slot></header>
        <main><slot name="body"></slot></main>
        <footer><slot name="footer"></slot></footer>
    </div>
</template>

<!-- Component usage -->
<my-card>
    <h2 slot="title">Card Title</h2>
    <p slot="body">Card body content.</p>
    <small slot="footer">Footer note.</small>
</my-card>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• <slot name="title"> — receives content with slot="title".
  • <slot name="body"> — receives content with slot="body".
  • <slot name="footer"> — receives content with slot="footer".
  • The slot attribute on the light DOM elements matches the name on the slot.

docs.title: The Default Slot
docs.text:
<template id="card-template">
    <div class="card">
        <slot name="title"></slot>
        <slot></slot>  <!-- default slot -->
    </div>
</template>

<my-card>
    <h2 slot="title">Card Title</h2>
    <p>This goes into the default slot.</p>
    <p>So does this.</p>
</my-card>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• The unnamed <slot> is the default slot.
  • Any light DOM content without a slot attribute goes into the default slot.
  • Multiple elements can be projected into the same slot.

docs.title: Fallback Content
docs.text:
<template id="card-template">
    <div class="card">
        <slot name="title">Untitled</slot>
        <slot>No content provided.</slot>
    </div>
</template>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• Content inside <slot> is fallback content.
  • It is rendered only when no matching light DOM content is provided.
  • Fallback content is optional.

docs.title: Multiple Slots in a Component
docs.text:
<template id="user-card-template">
    <div class="user-card">
        <slot name="avatar"></slot>
        <div class="info">
            <slot name="name"></slot>
            <slot name="email"></slot>
        </div>
        <slot name="actions"></slot>
    </div>
</template>

<user-card>
    <img slot="avatar" src="alice.jpg" alt="Alice">
    <span slot="name">Alice</span>
    <span slot="email">alice@example.com</span>
    <button slot="actions">Follow</button>
</user-card>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• Four named slots: avatar, name, email, actions.
  • Each slot receives the corresponding light DOM element.
  • Content is projected into the correct position.

docs.title: The slot Attribute
docs.text:
<!-- The slot attribute on the light DOM element matches the name -->
<h2 slot="title">Title</h2>

<!-- Corresponding slot in the shadow tree -->
<slot name="title"></slot>

docs.title: The assignedSlot Property
docs.text:
// On a light DOM element, assignedSlot returns the slot it is assigned to
const h2 = document.querySelector('h2[slot="title"]');
console.log(h2.assignedSlot); // <slot name="title">

docs.title: The slotAssignment Property
docs.text:
// On a shadow root, slotAssignment controls how slots are assigned
shadowRoot.slotAssignment; // "named" (default) or "manual"

docs.title: The slotchange Event
docs.text:
const slot = shadowRoot.querySelector('slot');
slot.addEventListener('slotchange', (event) => {
    console.log('Slot content changed:', slot.assignedNodes());
});

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• slotchange fires when the slot's assigned nodes change.
  • Fires on initial assignment and when content is added/removed.
  • Used to react to projected content changes.

docs.title: The Imperative Slot API
docs.text:
// assign() and assignNodes() let you control slot assignment manually
slot.assign(element1, element2);

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• slot.assign(...) — imperatively assigns nodes to a slot.
  • Requires slotAssignment: "manual".
  • Useful for advanced projection scenarios.

docs.title: The ::slotted() CSS Pseudo-Element
docs.text:
/* Styles slotted content from within the shadow tree */
::slotted(h2) {
    color: blue;
    font-size: 1.5rem;
}

::slotted(p) {
    margin: 0;
}

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• ::slotted() — styles light DOM content from within the shadow tree.
  • Only top-level slotted elements can be styled — descendants cannot.
  • Styles do not leak into slotted content — only the top-level element is targeted.

docs.title: The "Content Projection" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of slots as windows in the shadow tree through which light DOM content is visible:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SHADOW DOM (component's internal structure) │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │  <div class="card">                     ││
│  │    <header>                             ││
│  │      <slot name="title">  ←── window    ││
│  │    </header>                            ││
│  │    <main>                               ││
│  │      <slot>               ←── window    ││
│  │    </main>                              ││
│  │  </div>                                 ││
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    ▲
                    │ projects
                    │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LIGHT DOM (consumer's content)              │
│  <h2 slot="title">Title</h2>  ───┐          │
│  <p>Body content.</p>  ──────────┘          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Slots are the windows. Light DOM content shows through them.

docs.title: The "Theater Seating" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of slots as reserved seating:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THEATER (shadow tree)                       │
│                                              │
│  Row A: [slot name="title"]  ← reserved     │
│  Row B: [slot name="body"]   ← reserved     │
│  Row C: [slot]               ← general      │
│                                              │
│  Attendees (light DOM content)              │
│  ├── <h2 slot="title"> → Row A              │
│  ├── <p slot="body">   → Row B              │
│  └── <p>              → Row C               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Named slots are reserved seats. The default slot is general admission.

docs.title: The "Named vs Unnamed" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NAMED SLOTS                                 │
│  └── <slot name="title">                     │
│  └── Receives content with slot="title"      │
│  └── Multiple named slots per component      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DEFAULT SLOT (unnamed)                      │
│  └── <slot>                                  │
│  └── Receives content with no slot attribute │
│  └── Only one default slot per shadow tree   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every shadow tree can have multiple named slots but only one default slot.

docs.title: The "Encapsulation with Openings" Mental Model
docs.text:
Shadow DOM provides full encapsulation — styles do not leak in, structure does not leak out. But encapsulation without openings is a monolith. Slots are the openings:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SHADOW DOM                                  │
│  ├── Styles: encapsulated                    │
│  ├── Structure: encapsulated                 │
│  └── Slots: the only openings                │
│                                              │
│  Light DOM content enters through slots.    │
│  Nothing else crosses the boundary.         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Slots are the API of a component — the only way for consumers to inject content.

docs.title: The "Declarative API" Mental Model
docs.text:
Slots provide a declarative API for component composition:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ATTRIBUTE API (alternative)                 │
│  <my-card title="Hello" body="World">        │
│  └── Works for simple strings                │
│  └── Cannot accept complex markup            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  SLOT API (preferred)                        │
│  <my-card>                                   │
│    <h2 slot="title">Hello</h2>               │
│    <p slot="body">World</p>                  │
│  </my-card>                                  │
│  └── Accepts any markup                      │
│  └── Declarative                              │
│  └── Native HTML syntax                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Slots let consumers use native HTML to provide content. No JavaScript needed on the consumer's side.

docs.title: The "Fallback Content" Mental Model
docs.text:
A slot can provide fallback content that renders when no light DOM content is supplied:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  <slot name="title">Untitled</slot>          │
│                                              │
│  If consumer provides <h2 slot="title">      │
│    → "Untitled" is replaced by the <h2>     │
│                                              │
│  If consumer provides nothing                │
│    → "Untitled" is rendered                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Fallback content is the default value for a slot.

docs.title: Concept 1: The <slot> Element
docs.text: A placeholder in the shadow tree that marks where light DOM content should be projected.

docs.title: Concept 2: Named Slots
docs.text:
Slots with a name attribute receive content with a matching slot attribute.

<slot name="title">    ← receives <h2 slot="title">

docs.title: Concept 3: The Default Slot
docs.text: An unnamed <slot> receives all light DOM content without a slot attribute.

docs.title: Concept 4: Fallback Content
docs.text: Content inside <slot> that renders when no matching light DOM content is provided.

docs.title: Concept 5: The slot Attribute
docs.text: The attribute on light DOM elements that assigns them to a named slot.

docs.title: Concept 6: The assignedSlot Property
docs.text: A property on light DOM elements that returns the slot they are assigned to.

docs.title: Concept 7: The assignedNodes() Method
docs.text:
A method on slots that returns the nodes projected into the slot.

slot.assignedNodes(); // the projected nodes
slot.assignedNodes({ flatten: true }); // includes fallback content

docs.title: Concept 8: The assignedElements() Method
docs.text:
A method on slots that returns only the element nodes projected into the slot.

slot.assignedElements(); // element nodes only

docs.title: Concept 9: The slotchange Event
docs.text: An event that fires when a slot's assigned nodes change — on initial assignment and on content changes.

docs.title: Concept 10: The ::slotted() Pseudo-Element
docs.text: A CSS pseudo-element that styles slotted content from within the shadow tree. Only top-level slotted elements can be styled.

docs.title: Concept 11: Fallback Content vs. Assigned Content
docs.text:
• Assigned content — light DOM content projected into the slot.
  • Fallback content — the slot's own children, shown only when no assigned content.

docs.title: Concept 12: Multiple Elements in One Slot
docs.text: Multiple light DOM elements can be assigned to the same slot. They are rendered in DOM order.

docs.title: Concept 13: Nested Slots
docs.text:
A slotted element can contain its own shadow DOM with its own slots.

<outer-component>
    <inner-component slot="content">
        <p slot="inner">Nested content</p>
    </inner-component>
</outer-component>

docs.title: Concept 14: Imperative Slot Assignment
docs.text: The slotAssignment: "manual" option allows imperative slot assignment via slot.assign().

docs.title: Concept 15: The slot Attribute Restriction
docs.text: The slot attribute is only meaningful for direct children of the shadow host. Nested descendants are not assigned.

docs.title: Concept 16: Shadow DOM Encapsulation
docs.text: Slots do not break encapsulation. The slotted content is still in the light DOM; the shadow tree only renders it.

docs.title: Concept 17: Style Encapsulation
docs.text: Shadow styles do not apply to slotted content. To style slotted content, use ::slotted().

docs.title: Concept 18: Style Inheritance
docs.text: CSS properties (like color, font-family) inherit through the shadow boundary into slotted content. Only non-inherited properties are encapsulated.

docs.title: Concept 19: Accessibility and Slots
docs.text: Slotted content retains its native semantics. The accessibility tree sees the projected content in its rendered position.

docs.title: Concept 20: Slot Fallback Content Is Optional
docs.text: Fallback content is optional. A slot without fallback content renders nothing when no content is assigned.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Content Projection
docs.text:
1.  Consumer writes:
    <my-card>
        <h2 slot="title">Hello</h2>
        <p>World</p>
    </my-card>
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses the light DOM.
    │   └── <h2> and <p> are children of <my-card>.
    │
    ▼
3.  Custom element's connectedCallback runs.
    │   └── attachShadow() creates a shadow root.
    │
    ▼
4.  Template is cloned into the shadow root.
    │   └── Shadow tree has <slot name="title"> and default <slot>.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser performs slot assignment.
    │   └── <h2 slot="title"> → slot[name="title"]
    │   └── <p> → default slot
    │
    ▼
6.  Rendered output:
    │   └── Shadow tree structure with projected content.
    │
    ▼
7.  Accessibility tree reflects the rendered output.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Slot Assignment Algorithm
docs.text:
1.  For each slot in the shadow tree:
    │
    ▼
2.  Find light DOM children of the host with a matching slot attribute:
    │   ├── Named slot: match slot="name"
    │   └── Default slot: match no slot attribute
    │
    ▼
3.  Assign the matched elements to the slot.
    │
    ▼
4.  If no elements are assigned:
    │   └── Render the slot's fallback content.
    │
    ▼
5.  The slot's assigned nodes are rendered in the slot's position.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The slotchange Event
docs.text:
1.  Slot is created.
    │
    ▼
2.  Content is assigned to the slot.
    │
    ▼
3.  slotchange event fires (initial assignment).
    │
    ▼
4.  Consumer adds/removes content.
    │
    ▼
5.  slotchange event fires again.
    │
    ▼
6.  Listener can react to the change.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: ::slotted() Style Application
docs.text:
1.  Shadow styles include ::slotted(h2) { color: blue; }.
    │
    ▼
2.  Consumer provides <h2 slot="title">.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser assigns <h2> to slot[name="title"].
    │
    ▼
4.  Shadow styles apply to the top-level slotted element.
    │
    ▼
5.  The <h2> renders in blue.

docs.title: The Slot Assignment Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SHADOW HOST (e.g., <my-card>)              │
│  ├── Light DOM children (the "flattened tree" source) │
│  │   ├── <h2 slot="title">                  │
│  │   └── <p>                                │
│  └── Shadow root                             │
│      └── Shadow tree                         │
│          ├── <slot name="title">             │
│          └── <slot>                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The flattened tree is the combination of the shadow tree and the projected light DOM content. It is what is rendered.

docs.title: The Flattened Tree
docs.text:
Shadow tree + Light DOM → Flattened tree → Rendering

The flattened tree is computed at render time. It is not a persistent data structure — it is a view.

docs.title: The Slot Assignment Algorithm
docs.text:
For each slot in the shadow tree:

  1. If slotAssignment is "named" (default):
  2. Find the slot's name.
  3. Find all light DOM children of the host with a matching slot attribute (or no attribute for the default slot).
  4. Assign those elements to the slot.
  5. If slotAssignment is "manual":
  6. Slots are assigned imperatively via slot.assign().
  7. slotchange fires on assignment changes.

docs.title: The assignedNodes() and assignedElements() Methods
docs.text:
• slot.assignedNodes() — returns all assigned nodes (elements + text).
  • slot.assignedElements() — returns only elements.
  • slot.assignedNodes({ flatten: true }) — includes fallback content when no nodes are assigned.

docs.title: The ::slotted() Selector Implementation
docs.text:
::slotted() is a pseudo-element that targets top-level slotted elements. It is:

  • One level deep — it does not match descendants of slotted elements.
  • Shadow-scoped — it does not apply to elements outside the shadow tree.
  • Specificity-aware — it participates in the cascade with the shadow tree's styles.

docs.title: The slot Attribute and Direct Children
docs.text:
Only direct children of the shadow host are assigned to slots. Grandchildren are not:

<my-card>
    <div>
        <h2 slot="title">Nested</h2>  <!-- NOT assigned -->
    </div>
</my-card>

The <h2> is a grandchild, not a direct child. It is not projected.

docs.title: The slotAssignment Modes
docs.text:
Mode Behavior "named" Default. Slots assigned by name matching. "manual" Slots assigned via slot.assign().

Manual assignment is used for advanced scenarios where the component wants full control over which content goes where.

docs.title: The slotchange Event Timing
docs.text:
slotchange fires:

  • After the shadow root is created and initial content is assigned.
  • After any change to the assigned nodes (added/removed).
  • After slot.assign() is called in manual mode.

The event is asynchronous — it fires at the end of the current microtask, allowing batched changes.

docs.title: The Style Encapsulation Exception
docs.text:
While styles are encapsulated, inherited properties cross the shadow boundary:

  • color, font-family, font-size, line-height — inherit.
  • background-color, border — do not inherit.

This is why slotted content often inherits text styling from the host but not box styling.

docs.title: Slot Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Shadow root is created.
    │
    ▼
2.  Shadow tree is populated with templates.
    │
    ▼
3.  Slots are created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Slot assignment algorithm runs.
    │
    ▼
5.  Assigned content is projected.
    │
    ▼
6.  slotchange event fires.
    │
    ▼
7.  Consumer modifies content.
    │
    ▼
