8.  slotchange event fires again.

docs.title: Component Lifecycle with Slots
docs.text:
1.  Custom element constructed.
    │
    ▼
2.  connectedCallback runs.
    │
    ▼
3.  attachShadow() creates the shadow root.
    │
    ▼
4.  Template content is cloned into the shadow root.
    │
    ▼
5.  Slots are assigned.
    │
    ▼
6.  slotchange fires.
    │
    ▼
7.  Component may react (e.g., apply styles, attach listeners).

docs.title: The slotchange Event Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Shadow root created.
    │
    ▼
2.  Initial slot assignment → slotchange fires.
    │
    ▼
3.  Consumer adds a slotted element → slotchange fires.
    │
    ▼
4.  Consumer removes a slotted element → slotchange fires.
    │
    ▼
5.  Component is removed → no more slotchange.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Slot
docs.text:
<template id="wrapper-template">
    <div class="wrapper">
        <slot></slot>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    class Wrapper extends HTMLElement {
        constructor() {
            super();
            const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
            const template = document.getElementById('wrapper-template');
            shadow.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
        }
    }
    customElements.define('x-wrapper', Wrapper);
</script>

<x-wrapper>
    <p>Hello from the light DOM!</p>
</x-wrapper>

Code Breakdown:

  • The template has one default slot.
  • The <p> is projected into the slot.
  • The <div class="wrapper"> wraps the projected content.

docs.title: Example 2: Named Slots
docs.text:
<template id="card-template">
    <div class="card">
        <header class="card-header">
            <slot name="title">Untitled</slot>
        </header>
        <main class="card-body">
            <slot>No content.</slot>
        </main>
        <footer class="card-footer">
            <slot name="footer"></slot>
        </footer>
    </div>
</template>

<my-card>
    <h2 slot="title">Card Title</h2>
    <p>Card body content.</p>
    <small slot="footer">Footer note.</small>
</my-card>

Code Breakdown:

  • Three slots: title, default, footer.
  • Each light DOM element is assigned to the correct slot.
  • Fallback content shows when no element is provided.

docs.title: Example 3: Slotted Styling
docs.text:
<template id="card-template">
    <style>
        .card {
            border: 1px solid #ccc;
            border-radius: 8px;
            padding: 1rem;
        }
        ::slotted(h2) {
            margin-top: 0;
            color: #2c3e50;
        }
        ::slotted(p) {
            margin-bottom: 0;
        }
    </style>
    <div class="card">
        <slot name="title"></slot>
        <slot></slot>
    </div>
</template>

Code Breakdown:

  • ::slotted(h2) styles the top-level <h2> slotted into the component.
  • ::slotted(p) styles the top-level <p>.
  • Only the top-level slotted element is styled — descendants are not.

docs.title: Example 4: Slot Change Detection
docs.text:
class LazyLoader extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        shadow.innerHTML = `<slot></slot>`;

        const slot = shadow.querySelector('slot');
        slot.addEventListener('slotchange', () => {
            const nodes = slot.assignedElements();
            console.log('Slotted content:', nodes);
            // React to slotted content
        });
    }
}
customElements.define('lazy-loader', LazyLoader);

Code Breakdown:

  • slotchange fires when slot content changes.
  • slot.assignedElements() returns the slotted elements.
  • The component can react to the slotted content.

docs.title: Example 5: Nested Slots
docs.text:
<!-- Outer component -->
<template id="outer-template">
    <div class="outer">
        <slot name="content"></slot>
    </div>
</template>

<!-- Inner component -->
<template id="inner-template">
    <div class="inner">
        <slot name="title"></slot>
        <slot></slot>
    </div>
</template>

<!-- Usage -->
<outer-component>
    <inner-component slot="content">
        <h3 slot="title">Nested Title</h3>
        <p>Nested body content.</p>
    </inner-component>
</outer-component>

Code Breakdown:

  • <inner-component slot="content"> is slotted into the outer's content slot.
  • Within inner-component, its own slots receive <h3 slot="title"> and <p>.
  • Slots can nest arbitrarily.

docs.title: Example 6: Slot Fallback Content
docs.text:
<template id="avatar-template">
    <style>
        .avatar {
            width: 40px;
            height: 40px;
            border-radius: 50%;
            background: #ccc;
            display: inline-block;
            overflow: hidden;
        }
        .avatar img {
            width: 100%;
            height: 100%;
            object-fit: cover;
        }
    </style>
    <div class="avatar">
        <slot>
            <!-- Fallback: an icon -->
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor">
                <circle cx="12" cy="8" r="4"></circle>
                <path d="M12 14c-4 0-8 2-8 6v2h16v-2c0-4-4-6-8-6z"></path>
            </svg>
        </slot>
    </div>
</template>

<!-- With content -->
<user-avatar>
    <img src="alice.jpg" alt="Alice">
</user-avatar>

<!-- Without content → fallback icon shows -->
<user-avatar></user-avatar>

Code Breakdown:

  • The fallback content is an SVG icon.
  • When the consumer provides an image, the SVG is not rendered.
  • When no image is provided, the SVG renders.

docs.title: Example 7: Multiple Elements in One Slot
docs.text:
<template id="actions-template">
    <div class="actions">
        <slot name="actions"></slot>
    </div>
</template>

<my-actions>
    <button slot="actions">Save</button>
    <button slot="actions">Cancel</button>
    <button slot="actions">Delete</button>
</my-actions>

Code Breakdown:

  • All three buttons have slot="actions".
  • All are assigned to the actions slot.
  • They render in DOM order.

docs.title: Example 8: The assignedNodes() API
docs.text:
const component = document.querySelector('my-card');
const slot = component.shadowRoot.querySelector('slot[name="title"]');

// Get all assigned nodes
console.log(slot.assignedNodes());

// Get only elements
console.log(slot.assignedElements());

// Include fallback content
console.log(slot.assignedNodes({ flatten: true }));

Code Breakdown:

  • assignedNodes() — all assigned nodes (elements + text).
  • assignedElements() — only elements.
  • { flatten: true } — includes fallback content.

docs.title: Example 9: ::slotted() with Descendants
docs.text:
<template id="article-template">
    <style>
        /* Only the top-level slotted element can be styled */
        ::slotted(article) {
            border: 1px solid #ccc;
            padding: 1rem;
        }

        /* This does NOT work — descendants of slotted content cannot be styled */
        ::slotted(article h2) {
            color: red; /* Invalid */
        }

        /* To style descendants, use inherited properties */
        ::slotted(article) {
            color: #333; /* Inherits into descendants */
        }
    </style>
    <slot></slot>
</template>

Code Breakdown:

  • ::slotted(article) styles the top-level slotted <article>.
  • ::slotted(article h2) is invalid — descendant selectors are not allowed.
  • Only inherited properties (color, font-family) propagate into descendants.

docs.title: Example 10: Complete Card Component with Slots
docs.text:
<template id="product-card-template">
    <style>
        .card {
            display: grid;
            grid-template-areas:
                "image info"
                "actions actions";
            grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr;
            gap: 1rem;
            border: 1px solid #e0e0e0;
            border-radius: 8px;
            padding: 1rem;
            font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
        }
        .image { grid-area: image; }
        .info { grid-area: info; }
        .actions {
            grid-area: actions;
            display: flex;
            gap: 0.5rem;
        }
        ::slotted(img) {
            width: 120px;
            height: 120px;
            object-fit: cover;
            border-radius: 4px;
        }
        ::slotted(h3) {
            margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0;
            color: #333;
        }
        ::slotted(.price) {
            font-weight: bold;
            color: #2c7a2c;
        }
    </style>
    <div class="card">
        <div class="image"><slot name="image"></slot></div>
        <div class="info">
            <slot name="title"></slot>
            <slot name="price"></slot>
            <slot></slot>
        </div>
        <div class="actions"><slot name="actions"></slot></div>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    class ProductCard extends HTMLElement {
        constructor() {
            super();
            const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
            const template = document.getElementById('product-card-template');
            shadow.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
        }
    }
    customElements.define('product-card', ProductCard);
</script>

<product-card>
    <img slot="image" src="product.jpg" alt="Product">
    <h3 slot="title">Awesome Product</h3>
    <span slot="price" class="price">$29.99</span>
    <p>This product is amazing.</p>
    <button slot="actions">Buy</button>
    <button slot="actions">Details</button>
</product-card>

Code Breakdown:

  • Four named slots: image, title, price, actions, plus the default slot.
  • Each slot receives the corresponding light DOM element.
  • ::slotted() styles the top-level slotted elements.
  • The component provides a complete layout with flexible content.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Slot Pattern Card component title, body, footer slots Layout component Default slot for content Tabs tab and panel slots Modals title, body, actions slots Tooltips Default slot for content Accordions header and content slots Lists Default slot for items Dropdowns trigger and menu slots Navigation Default slot for links Data tables header and row slots Avatars Default slot for image Buttons Default slot for text

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use named slots for structured content. Why: clearer API for consumers.
  2. Use the default slot for simple content. Why: simpler for single-content components.
  3. Provide fallback content. Why: renders when no content is provided.
  4. Style slotted content with ::slotted(). Why: shadow styles do not apply to slotted content otherwise.
  5. Only style top-level slotted elements. Why: ::slotted() does not match descendants.
  6. Use inherited properties for deep styling. Why: color and font-family inherit into descendants.
  7. Listen to slotchange to react to content. Why: slotted content may change dynamically.
  8. Use assignedElements() to get slotted elements. Why: filters out text nodes.
  9. Remember that only direct children are slotted. Why: grandchildren are not assigned.
  10. Use slotAssignment: "manual" only when needed. Why: named assignment is the default.
  11. Test slots with dynamic content. Why: slotted content may change at runtime.
  12. Document the slot API. Why: consumers need to know the slot names.
  13. Use consistent slot naming. Why: predictability aids adoption.
  14. Avoid hardcoded content in shadow trees. Why: use slots for flexibility.
  15. Combine slots with Custom Elements. Why: the full Web Components API.
  16. Test on multiple browsers. Why: minor differences in slotchange timing exist.
  17. Use ::slotted() with specific selectors. Why: broad selectors may cause unintended styling.
  18. Consider accessibility. Why: slotted content retains its semantics.
  19. Do not rely on slot order for behavior. Why: order is DOM-based, not slot-based.
  20. Use slots for composition, not for state. Why: slots are for structure.
  21. Document slot fallback behavior. Why: consumers need to know what happens when no content is provided.
  22. Test slotted content with screen readers. Why: verify the accessibility tree is correct.
  23. Use slots with Declarative Shadow DOM. Why: server-rendered shadow DOM uses the same model.
  24. Cache slot references. Why: querying shadow roots is not free.
  25. Audit slots after component changes. Why: API changes affect consumers.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Styling Slotted Content Without ::slotted()
docs.text:
/* Shadow style — does NOT apply to slotted content */
h2 {
    color: blue;
}

Why it's wrong: Shadow styles are encapsulated. They do not apply to slotted content.

✅ Correct:

::slotted(h2) {
    color: blue;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Descendant Selectors in ::slotted()
docs.text:
::slotted(article h2) {
    color: red; /* Invalid */
}

Why it's wrong: ::slotted() only matches top-level slotted elements. Descendant selectors are not allowed.

✅ Correct:

::slotted(article) {
    color: #333; /* Inherits into descendants */
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Expecting Grandchildren to Be Slotted
docs.text:
<my-card>
    <div>
        <h2 slot="title">Title</h2>  <!-- NOT slotted -->
    </div>
</my-card>

Why it's wrong: Only direct children of the shadow host are assigned to slots.

✅ Correct:

<my-card>
    <h2 slot="title">Title</h2>  <!-- Direct child — slotted -->
</my-card>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Providing Fallback Content
docs.text:
<slot name="title"></slot>

Why it's wrong: When no content is provided, the slot renders nothing.

✅ Correct:

<slot name="title">Untitled</slot>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using the Wrong Slot Name
docs.text:
<!-- Component definition -->
<slot name="heading"></slot>

<!-- Consumer -->
<h2 slot="title">Title</h2>  <!-- Wrong name -->

Why it's wrong: The slot names do not match. The content is not projected.

✅ Correct:

<h2 slot="heading">Title</h2>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Slot Order
docs.text:
<slot name="first"></slot>
<slot name="second"></slot>

Why it's wrong: Consumers may provide content in any order. Slot order is determined by the shadow tree, not by the consumer's markup.

✅ Correct: Do not rely on slot order for behavior — use named slots with a clear contract.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting slotchange Fires Asynchronously
docs.text:
slot.addEventListener('slotchange', () => {
    // This runs at the end of the microtask, not immediately
});

Why it's wrong: If you need synchronous access, you may be surprised.

✅ Correct: Understand the async nature of slotchange.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mutating Slotted Content Directly
docs.text:
slot.assignedElements().forEach(el => el.remove());

Why it's wrong: Removes the consumer's content — they own it, not the component.

✅ Correct: Do not remove consumer content. Use slotchange to react, not to mutate.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using assignedNodes() When assignedElements() Is Better
docs.text:
const nodes = slot.assignedNodes();
// nodes may include text nodes

Why it's wrong: Text nodes may be present (whitespace). Use assignedElements() for elements only.

✅ Correct:

const elements = slot.assignedElements();

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing Slots with Dynamic Content
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Consumers may add/remove content at runtime. slotchange handles this, but it must be tested.

✅ Correct: Test with dynamic content insertion and removal.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Slot assignment is fast — linear in the number of slotted elements.
  • slotchange fires asynchronously — batched at the microtask level.
  • ::slotted() selectors are efficient — only match top-level slotted elements.
  • Shadow DOM styles are scoped — style recalculation is faster.
  • Slots do not clone content — they project it. No duplication.
  • Slotted content retains its identity — no wrapper elements.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use slots instead of cloning content into the shadow tree.
  2. Minimize slotchange listeners.
  3. Cache slot references.
  4. Use assignedElements() over assignedNodes().
  5. Batch DOM changes.

docs.title: Slotted Content Is Trusted
docs.text: Slotted content comes from the consumer. The component cannot sanitize it — the consumer is responsible.

docs.title: Slot Injection
docs.text: If a component injects consumer content into innerHTML, XSS is possible. Use textContent or sanitize.

docs.title: Shadow DOM Isolation
docs.text: Shadow DOM does not prevent XSS. Scripts inside slotted content still run in the document context.

docs.title: Slots and CSP
docs.text: Slots do not affect CSP. Slotted scripts are still subject to CSP.

docs.title: Slot Names and DOM Clobbering
docs.text: Slot names should not conflict with global identifiers. Use clear, specific names.

docs.title: ::slotted() and CSS Injection
docs.text: ::slotted() is safe — it does not allow arbitrary CSS injection.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements — inspect shadow trees and slots.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Shadow tree — expand the shadow root.
  • $0.shadowRoot — the shadow root of the selected element.
  • $0.shadowRoot.querySelector('slot') — the slots in the shadow tree.
  • $0.shadowRoot.querySelector('slot').assignedElements() — the slotted elements.
  • $0.assignedSlot — the slot the element is assigned to.
  • slot.assignedNodes() — all assigned nodes.
  • slot.assignedElements() — elements only.
  • slotchange event — inspect slotted content changes.
  • DevTools → Accessibility — inspect the accessibility tree with slotted content.
  • getComputedStyle(slottedElement) — inspect styles applied via ::slotted().
  • Test with dynamic content — add/remove slotted content at runtime.
  • Test with no content — verify fallback content renders.
  • Test with extra content — verify unassigned content is handled.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Composable components — cards, modals, tabs, layouts.
  • Content projection — accept content from consumers.
  • Fallback content — provide defaults.
  • Declarative APIs — let consumers use HTML.
  • Layout components — wrappers, containers.
  • Web Components — every component with consumer content.
  • Design systems — flexible, composable components.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use slots for state. Use properties or attributes.
  • Do not use slots for simple strings. Use attributes or properties.
  • Do not use slots for events. Use custom events.
  • Do not use slots when content is fixed. Hardcode markup instead.
  • Do not use slots to sanitize content. Slotted content is the consumer's responsibility.
  • Do not rely on slot order for behavior. Use named slots.
  • Do not style descendants of slotted content directly. Use ::slotted() on top-level elements or inherited properties.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Web Components
  • Shadow DOM
  • Custom Elements
  • Templates
  • Declarative Shadow DOM
  • <slot> element
  • slot attribute
  • Named slots
  • Default slot
  • Fallback content
  • assignedSlot
  • assignedNodes()
  • assignedElements()
  • slotchange event
  • ::slotted() pseudo-element
  • slotAssignment
  • attachShadow()
  • Shadow root
  • Flattened tree
  • Light DOM
  • Shadow tree

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• The <slot> element is unique to Shadow DOM — it has no meaning outside a shadow tree.
  • Slots project content, they do not copy it — the light DOM content is not duplicated.
  • ::slotted() only matches top-level slotted elements — descendant selectors are invalid.
  • ::slotted() was the first pseudo-element designed for Shadow DOM.
  • Slots can have fallback content — rendered when no content is provided.
  • Only direct children of the shadow host are slotted — grandchildren are not.
  • slotchange fires asynchronously — batched at the microtask level.
  • assignedNodes({ flatten: true }) includes fallback content — useful for inspection.
  • Inherited CSS properties cross the shadow boundary — color, font-family inherit into slotted content.
  • Non-inherited properties are encapsulated — background, border do not leak.
  • Slots are used by every major Web Component library — Lit, FAST, Stencil, and more.
  • The same concept exists in frameworks — React's children, Vue's slots, Angular's ng-content.
  • The slot attribute is only meaningful on direct children — nested descendants are not slotted.
  • Manual slot assignment was added in 2021 — slotAssignment: "manual" with slot.assign().
  • Slots preserve accessibility semantics — slotted content retains its native role.
  • Slots do not break encapsulation — the shadow tree remains encapsulated.
  • Slots are the API of a Web Component — the primary way consumers provide content.
  • Slots are a native HTML feature — no framework required.
  • Slots are baseline and universally supported — Chrome 53+, Firefox 63+, Safari 10+, Edge 79+.
  • The best slot API is the one consumers never have to think about — clear names, sensible fallbacks, minimal ceremony.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Slots are placeholders in a shadow tree that mark where light DOM content should be projected.
  • They enable content projection — the core mechanism for composing Web Components.
  • Named slots receive content with a matching slot attribute.
  • The default slot (unnamed) receives all light DOM content without a slot attribute.
  • Fallback content renders when no matching content is provided.
  • Only direct children of the shadow host are slotted.
  • slotchange fires when a slot's assigned nodes change.
  • assignedNodes() and assignedElements() return the projected content.
  • ::slotted() styles top-level slotted elements from within the shadow tree.
  • Inherited CSS properties (color, font-family) cross the shadow boundary; non-inherited properties do not.
  • Slots do not clone content — they project it.
  • Slots preserve accessibility semantics — projected content retains its native role.
  • Slots do not break encapsulation — the shadow tree remains encapsulated.
  • Manual slot assignment is available via slotAssignment: "manual" and slot.assign().
  • Slots are the API of a Web Component — the primary way consumers provide content.
  • Slots are supported in all modern browsers.
  • Use named slots for structured content; use the default slot for simple content.
  • Always provide fallback content.
  • Style slotted content with ::slotted().
  • The best slot API is the one consumers never have to think about.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The rendering pipeline is the sequence of stages the browser executes to convert the DOM tree (structure) and the CSSOM tree (style) into pixels on the screen. It is the mechanical process that transforms an abstract document model into a visible, painted interface.

<p class="intro">Hello</p>

.intro { color: blue; font-size: 16px; }

Given these two inputs, the browser must:

  1. Parse the HTML → DOM.
  2. Parse the CSS → CSSOM.
  3. Combine them → Render Tree.
  4. Compute geometry → Layout.
  5. Fill in pixels → Paint.
  6. Assemble layers → Composite.
  7. Display → Screen.

Each stage is deterministic, incremental, and interdependent. The output of one stage is the input to the next. Breaking any stage breaks the chain.

The rendering pipeline is the physical layer of the browser — the place where abstract data becomes a visual interface. It is separate from but dependent on the parsing pipeline (bytes → DOM) and the scripting layer (JavaScript execution).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The rendering pipeline serves several essential purposes:

  • Visual output — converts the document model into pixels.
  • Layout computation — determines the position and size of every visible element.
  • Paint ordering — determines the drawing order for overlapping elements.
  • Layer composition — assembles independent layers on the GPU.
  • Style application — matches CSS rules to DOM nodes and computes final styles.
  • Incremental rendering — renders partial content as parsing proceeds.
  • Frame production — produces a new frame up to 60 times per second.
  • Visual consistency — ensures the same document renders identically everywhere.

The rendering pipeline is the last mile of the browser. Every byte downloaded, every token parsed, every DOM node created, every style computed — all of it exists to feed the rendering pipeline.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Browser Architecture
│
├── Networking          ← fetch bytes
├── Parsing Pipeline    ← bytes → DOM
│   ├── Tokenization
│   ├── Tree Construction
│   ├── DOM Creation
│   └── Error Recovery
├── Scripting Layer     ← JavaScript execution
├── Rendering Pipeline  ← DOM + CSSOM → pixels (THIS CHAPTER)
│   ├── Style
│   ├── Layout
│   ├── Paint
│   └── Composite
└── Display             ← GPU → screen

The rendering pipeline sits after parsing and scripting. It is the stage where the abstract model becomes the visual interface.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A DOM tree is not a picture. It is a data structure — nodes, attributes, and relationships. A CSSOM tree is not a picture either. It is a set of rules — selectors, properties, and values. Neither is visible to the user.

To display a web page, the browser must:

  • Match styles to elements.
  • Compute final styles for every element.
  • Determine geometry — position, size, margin, padding, border.
  • Determine what to draw — background, text, borders, shadows.
  • Determine draw order — what overlaps what.
  • Rasterize — convert vectors and text to pixels.
  • Composite — assemble layers into the final image.
  • Present — send the image to the display.

The rendering pipeline exists to perform these operations in a well-defined, deterministic sequence so that every browser produces the same visual output from the same inputs.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No formal pipeline Browsers rendered differently No incremental rendering Pages waited for full download No layer separation Every change re-rendered everything No GPU acceleration Slow animations, high CPU No compositor thread Main thread blocked during scroll No style scoping Style recalc was global

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The rendering pipeline evolved over three decades:

  • 1990s — simple layout and paint on a single thread.
  • 2000s — incremental rendering, reflow optimization, CSSOM.
  • 2010s — GPU-accelerated compositing, layer separation, compositor thread.
  • 2020s — Paint Holding, Content-visibility, View Transitions, Scroll-driven animations.

The modern pipeline is multi-threaded, GPU-accelerated, and incremental. It can render partial content, optimize layer composition, and animate at 60fps on the compositor thread.

The pipeline is specified across multiple standards:

  • CSS — the styling language.
  • CSSOM — the CSS Object Model.
  • HTML — the DOM structure.
  • WHATWG DOM — the DOM API.
  • CSS Containment — the isolation API.
  • Compositing — the layer model.

In 2026, the rendering pipeline is fully specified and consistently implemented across all major browser engines (Blink, Gecko, WebKit). The details vary by engine, but the stages are the same.

docs.title: Stage 1: DOM
docs.text:
The DOM is produced by the parsing pipeline.

HTML → Tokenizer → Tree Constructor → DOM

docs.title: Stage 2: CSSOM
docs.text:
The CSSOM is produced by parsing CSS:

CSS → Tokenizer → Parser → CSSOM

Each CSS rule becomes a CSSOM rule with a selector and a set of declarations.

docs.title: Stage 3: Render Tree
docs.text:
The render tree is the combination of DOM and CSSOM:

DOM + CSSOM → Render Tree

The render tree contains only visible elements:

  • Elements with display: none are excluded.
  • Elements with visibility: hidden are included (they take up space).
  • Pseudo-elements (::before, ::after) are included.

docs.title: Stage 4: Layout
docs.text:
Layout computes geometry for every node in the render tree:

Render Tree → Layout Tree

Each node gets:

  • Position — x, y coordinates.
  • Size — width, height.
  • Margins, padding, border — box model.
  • Relationship to siblings — flow, float, flex, grid.

docs.title: Stage 5: Paint
docs.text:
Paint generates draw commands for each region:

Layout Tree → Display Lists

Each node gets one or more draw commands:

  • Draw background.
  • Draw border.
  • Draw text.
  • Draw image.
  • Draw shadow.

docs.title: Stage 6: Composite
docs.text:
Composite assembles layers into the final image:

Display Lists → Layers → Composite → Final Image

Layers are composited on the GPU, often on a separate thread.

docs.title: Stage 7: Display
docs.text:
The final image is sent to the display:

Final Image → GPU → Display

docs.title: The Rendering Waterfall
docs.text:
For a single frame, the pipeline runs in this order:

1.  JavaScript (if any)
2.  Style recalculation
3.  Layout
4.  Paint
5.  Composite
6.  Display

Each stage must complete before the next can begin. The frame budget (16.7ms for 60fps) includes all stages.

docs.title: A Complete Example
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui; }
        .box {
            width: 200px;
            height: 100px;
            background: #3498db;
            color: white;
            padding: 20px;
            border-radius: 8px;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <div class="box">Hello</div>
</body>
</html>

Pipeline trace:

1. DOM:
   html → head → style
                → body → div.box → "Hello"

2. CSSOM:
   body { font-family: system-ui }
   .box { width: 200px; ... }

3. Render Tree:
   html
   └── body
       └── div.box
           └── "Hello"

4. Layout:
   body: 0, 0, viewport-size
   div.box: 0, 0, 240×140 (200+40 padding, 100+40 padding)
   text: inside box

5. Paint:
   Draw body background
   Draw div.box background (#3498db)
   Draw div.box border-radius
   Draw "Hello" text (white)

6. Composite:
   Single layer (no transform/opacity)
   Composite to screen

7. Display:
   Rendered to screen.

docs.title: The "Two Trees" Mental Model
docs.text:
The rendering pipeline combines two independent trees:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DOM TREE                                    │
│  └── Structure: what elements exist          │
│  └── Relationships: parent-child, siblings   │
│  └── Attributes: id, class, src, href        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CSSOM TREE                                  │
│  └── Styles: how elements look               │
│  └── Selectors: which elements match          │
│  └── Rules: property-value pairs              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  RENDER TREE                                 │
│  └── DOM nodes + computed styles             │
│  └── Only visible elements                   │
│  └── The input to layout and paint           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The DOM answers "what exists?" The CSSOM answers "how does it look?" The render tree combines both.

docs.title: The "Three-Layer" Mental Model
docs.text:
The rendering pipeline produces three layers of output:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STYLE LAYER                                 │
│  └── Computed styles for every element       │
│  └── color, font, background, dimensions     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  GEOMETRY LAYER                              │
│  └── Position and size for every element     │
│  └── x, y, width, height, margin, padding    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  PAINT LAYER                                 │
│  └── Draw commands for every region          │
│  └── Backgrounds, borders, text, images      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Each layer is the output of a stage and the input to the next.

docs.title: The "Frame Budget" Mental Model
docs.text:
The pipeline runs once per frame:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  60 FPS = 16.7ms per frame                   │
│  120 FPS = 8.3ms per frame                   │
│                                              │
│  Frame budget:                              │
│  ├── JavaScript:  ~5ms                       │
│  ├── Style:       ~1ms                       │
│  ├── Layout:      ~3ms                       │
│  ├── Paint:       ~3ms                       │
│  ├── Composite:   ~2ms                       │
│  └── Total:       ~16.7ms                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Exceeding the budget causes dropped frames and visible jank.

docs.title: The "Incremental Rendering" Mental Model
docs.text:
The pipeline is incremental:

Bytes arrive:
  <html><head>...
    │
    ▼
DOM starts building
    │
    ▼
First layout of partial content
    │
    ▼
First paint of partial content
    │
    ▼
User sees something
    │
    ▼
More bytes arrive → more DOM → more layout → more paint

The page renders progressively as parsing proceeds. It does not wait for the full document.

docs.title: The "Style Recalc vs Layout vs Paint" Mental Model
docs.text:
Different changes trigger different stages:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STYLE CHANGE ONLY                           │
│  └── color, background-color                 │
│  └── Pipeline: Style → Paint → Composite     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYOUT CHANGE                               │
│  └── width, height, top, left                │
│  └── Pipeline: Style → Layout → Paint → Composite │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  COMPOSITE CHANGE ONLY                       │
│  └── transform, opacity                      │
│  └── Pipeline: Composite only                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The goal: make changes that touch only the composite stage — the cheapest.

docs.title: Concept 1: The DOM
docs.text: The Document Object Model — the structure of the page. Produced by the parsing pipeline.

docs.title: Concept 2: The CSSOM
docs.text: The CSS Object Model — the styles of the page. Produced by parsing CSS.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Render Tree
docs.text: The combination of the DOM and CSSOM. Contains only visible elements with computed styles.

docs.title: Concept 4: Layout
docs.text: The computation of geometry — position, size, and relationships.

docs.title: Concept 5: Paint
docs.text: The generation of draw commands — backgrounds, borders, text, images.

docs.title: Concept 6: Composite
docs.text: The assembly of layers into the final image, usually on the GPU.

docs.title: Concept 7: Display
docs.text: The presentation of the final image on the screen.

docs.title: Concept 8: The Frame Budget
docs.text: The time available per frame: 16.7ms for 60fps, 8.3ms for 120fps.

docs.title: Concept 9: The Render Tree Excludes display: none
docs.text: Elements with display: none are excluded from the render tree. Elements with visibility: hidden are included.

docs.title: Concept 10: The CSSOM Is Built From Stylesheets
docs.text: Stylesheets are parsed into CSSOM rules. External stylesheets block rendering until parsed.

docs.title: Concept 11: Style Recalculation
docs.text: Matching CSS rules to DOM nodes. Triggered by DOM changes or stylesheet changes.

docs.title: Concept 12: Layout Invalidation
docs.text: Marking layout as dirty when geometry changes. Triggers a full or partial re-layout.

docs.title: Concept 13: Paint Invalidation
docs.text: Marking paint as dirty when visual properties change. Triggers a re-paint of affected regions.

docs.title: Concept 14: Compositing Layers
docs.text: Independent layers of the page. Promoted via transform, opacity, will-change, position: fixed, etc.

docs.title: Concept 15: The Compositor Thread
docs.text: A separate thread that handles compositing, transform, and opacity animations. Keeps animation smooth even when the main thread is busy.

docs.title: Concept 16: The Main Thread
docs.text: Where parsing, styling, layout, paint, and JavaScript run. The bottleneck for most rendering.

docs.title: Concept 17: Paint Holding
docs.text: A Chromium optimization that delays the first paint until enough content is ready. Prevents showing an empty page.

docs.title: Concept 18: Content-Visibility
docs.text: A CSS property that skips rendering of off-screen content. Reduces initial rendering cost.

docs.title: Concept 19: Containment
docs.text: CSS contain isolates a subtree from the rest of the layout. Improves rendering performance.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Accessibility Tree
docs.text: A parallel tree derived from the DOM and render tree. Consumed by assistive technology.

docs.title: Concept 21: The Visual Viewport vs Layout Viewport
docs.text:
• Layout viewport — the CSS coordinate space.
  • Visual viewport — what the user sees (affected by zoom).

docs.title: Concept 22: The GPU
docs.text: The Graphics Processing Unit. Accelerates compositing, transforms, and filters.

docs.title: Concept 23: Rasterization
docs.text: The conversion of vectors and text to pixels. Performed by the GPU or CPU.

docs.title: Concept 24: The Display List
docs.text: A list of draw commands produced by paint. Consumed by the compositor.

docs.title: Concept 25: The Layer Tree
docs.text: The hierarchy of compositing layers. The input to the GPU compositor.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Full Pipeline for a Static Page
docs.text:
1.  HTML arrives.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parsing pipeline produces the DOM.
    │
    ▼
3.  CSS is parsed into the CSSOM.
    │
    ▼
4.  DOM + CSSOM → Render Tree.
    │   └── Only visible elements.
    │   └── Computed styles for each.
    │
    ▼
5.  Layout computes geometry.
    │   └── Position and size for each node.
    │
    ▼
6.  Paint generates draw commands.
    │   └── Backgrounds, text, borders, images.
    │
    ▼
7.  Composite assembles layers.
    │   └── Layer tree → GPU → final image.
    │
    ▼
8.  Display presents the image.
    │
    ▼
9.  User sees the page.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Style Recalculation
docs.text:
1.  A DOM change occurs (class added).
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser marks elements for style recalc.
    │
    ▼
3.  For each affected element:
    │   ├── Match CSS selectors.
    │   ├── Compute the cascade.
    │   ├── Resolve inheritance.
    │   └── Compute the final style.
    │
    ▼
4.  If styles affecting layout changed → layout invalidation.
    │
    ▼
5.  If styles affecting paint changed → paint invalidation.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Layout
docs.text:
1.  Layout is triggered by a geometry change.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser walks the render tree.
    │
    ▼
3.  For each node:
    │   ├── Compute position (x, y).
    │   ├── Compute size (width, height).
    │   ├── Apply box model.
    │   └── Determine relationship to siblings.
    │
    ▼
4.  Layout produces the layout tree.
    │
    ▼
5.  Paint uses the layout tree as input.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Paint
docs.text:
1.  Paint is triggered.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser walks the layout tree.
    │
    ▼
3.  For each node:
    │   ├── Generate draw commands.
    │   ├── Background.
    │   ├── Border.
    │   ├── Text.
    │   ├── Image.
    │   └── Shadow.
    │
    ▼
4.  Draw commands are sorted by stacking order.
    │
    ▼
5.  Display lists are produced.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Composite
docs.text:
1.  Paint produces display lists.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser assigns display lists to layers.
    │
    ▼
3.  Layers are rasterized (GPU or CPU).
    │
    ▼
4.  Layer tree is built.
    │
    ▼
5.  GPU composites layers into the final image.
    │
    ▼
6.  Image is presented to the display.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: An Animation Frame
docs.text:
1.  requestAnimationFrame callbacks fire.
    │
    ▼
2.  JavaScript updates the DOM.
    │
    ▼
3.  Style recalculation.
    │
    ▼
4.  Layout (if needed).
    │
    ▼
5.  Paint (if needed).
    │
    ▼
6.  Composite.
    │
    ▼
7.  Display.
    │
    ▼
8.  Next frame scheduled.

docs.title: The Render Tree Construction
docs.text:
DOM + CSSOM → Render Tree

For each DOM node:
  ├── Compute the final style.
  ├── If display: none → skip.
  ├── Create a render object.
  ├── Attach to parent render object.
  └── Recurse into children.

The render tree is also called the layout tree or frame tree in different engines.

docs.title: The Style Computation Algorithm
docs.text:
For each element, the browser:

  1. Collects matching rules — all CSS selectors that match.
  2. Sorts by specificity — cascade order.
  3. Applies inheritance — inherited properties from parent.
  4. Resolves computed values — relative units to absolute.
  5. Stores the computed style — the final set of properties.

docs.title: The Layout Algorithm
docs.text:
Layout is a tree traversal:

  1. Block layout — determines widths and heights for block elements.
  2. Inline layout — determines line breaks and text flow.
  3. Flex layout — distributes space along a main axis.
  4. Grid layout — places items in a two-dimensional grid.
  5. Positioned layout — handles absolute and fixed positioning.

Layout is incremental — the browser only re-layouts what changed.

docs.title: The Paint Algorithm
docs.text:
Paint generates display lists:

  1. Background phase — backgrounds, borders.
  2. Float phase — floats.
  3. Foreground phase — text, images, inline content.
  4. Outline phase — outlines.

Display lists are sorted by stacking context (z-index, position).

docs.title: The Compositing Algorithm
docs.text:
Compositing assembles layers:

  1. Layer promotion — elements with transform, opacity, will-change get their own layer.
  2. Rasterization — layers are converted to textures (GPU or CPU).
  3. Composition — textures are assembled on the GPU.
  4. Presentation — the final image is sent to the display.

docs.title: The Compositor Thread
docs.text:
The compositor thread runs separately from the main thread:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MAIN THREAD                                 │
│  ├── Parsing                                 │
│  ├── JavaScript                              │
│  ├── Style                                   │
│  ├── Layout                                  │
│  └── Paint                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  COMPOSITOR THREAD                           │
│  ├── Layer compositing                       │
│  ├── Transform animations                    │
│  ├── Opacity animations                      │
│  └── Scroll                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Transform and opacity animations run entirely on the compositor thread — smooth even when the main thread is busy.

docs.title: The Paint Holding Optimization
docs.text: Chromium's Paint Holding delays the first paint by up to 500ms to allow enough content to render. This prevents the user from seeing an empty page.

docs.title: The Content-Visibility Optimization
docs.text: content-visibility: auto tells the browser to skip rendering of off-screen content. The browser calculates an estimated size using contain-intrinsic-size.

docs.title: The CSS Containment Optimization
docs.text: contain: layout paint isolates a subtree from the rest of the document. Changes inside the subtree do not affect the rest of the page.

docs.title: The View Transitions API
docs.text: The View Transitions API captures a snapshot of the old page and the new page, and animates between them on the compositor thread.

docs.title: The Rendering Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Parsing completes (or is incremental).
    │
    ▼
2.  DOM is built.
    │
    ▼
3.  CSSOM is built.
    │
    ▼
4.  Render Tree is built.
    │
    ▼
5.  Layout is computed.
    │
    ▼
6.  Paint generates display lists.
    │
    ▼
7.  Composite assembles layers.
    │
    ▼
8.  Display presents the image.
    │
    ▼
9.  On any change → invalidate → re-run affected stages.

docs.title: The Style Recalc Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  DOM or CSSOM change.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser marks affected elements.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser recomputes styles.
    │
    ▼
4.  If layout-affecting properties changed → layout invalidation.
    │
    ▼
5.  If paint-affecting properties changed → paint invalidation.

docs.title: The Layout Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Layout invalidation.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser marks the layout root.
    │
    ▼
3.  Layout traversal from the root.
    │
    ▼
4.  New layout tree.
    │
    ▼
5.  Paint uses the new layout.

docs.title: The Paint Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Paint invalidation.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser identifies affected regions.
    │
    ▼
3.  New display lists for those regions.
    │
    ▼
4.  Compositor uses the new display lists.

docs.title: The Composite Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Paint produces display lists.
    │
    ▼
2.  Layer assignment.
    │
    ▼
3.  Rasterization.
    │
    ▼
4.  GPU composition.
    │
    ▼
5.  Display.

docs.title: Example 1: Rendering a Simple Box
docs.text:
<div class="box">Hello</div>

<style>
    .box {
        width: 200px;
        height: 100px;
        background: #3498db;
        color: white;
        padding: 20px;
    }
</style>

Pipeline:

DOM:        div.box → "Hello"
CSSOM:      .box { width, height, background, color, padding }
Render Tree: div.box (200×100 content + 20px padding = 240×140)
Layout:     position, size computed
Paint:      background, text drawn
Composite:  single layer
Display:    pixels on screen

docs.title: Example 2: Style Recalc Only
docs.text:
element.style.color = 'red';

Pipeline:

Style:     recompute color for element
Paint:     re-draw text with new color
Composite: unchanged (same layer)

Layout is not triggered because color does not affect geometry.

docs.title: Example 3: Layout Trigger
docs.text:
element.style.width = '300px';

Pipeline:

Style:     recompute width
Layout:    re-layout the element and its siblings
Paint:     re-draw affected regions
Composite: unchanged

Layout is triggered because width affects geometry.

docs.title: Example 4: Composite-Only Animation
docs.text:
element.style.transform = 'translateX(100px)';

Pipeline:

Composite: transform applied on compositor thread

No style recalc, no layout, no paint. The cheapest animation.

docs.title: Example 5: content-visibility Optimization
docs.text:
.below-fold-section {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: 0 500px;
}

Pipeline:

Initial render: skip rendering of the section
On scroll: render when it nears the viewport

Reduces initial rendering cost by 20–50%.

docs.title: Example 6: contain Optimization
docs.text:
.widget {
    contain: layout paint;
}

Pipeline:

Changes inside the widget:
  └── Do not trigger layout on the rest of the page.

Isolates the subtree from the rest of the document.

docs.title: Example 7: Transform Animation on the Compositor Thread
docs.text:
.card {
    transition: transform 200ms ease;
}
.card:hover {
    transform: translateY(-8px);
}

Pipeline:

1.  User hovers → style change → transform: translateY(-8px)
2.  The browser recognizes the change is composite-only.
3.  The animation runs on the compositor thread.
4.  No main-thread work after the initial setup.
5.  Smooth 60fps.

docs.title: Example 8: The Layout Thrashing Example
docs.text:
// ❌ Layout thrashing
for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    const width = element.offsetWidth; // forces layout
    element.style.width = width + 10 + 'px'; // invalidates layout
}

Pipeline:

1.  Read offsetWidth → forces synchronous layout
2.  Write style.width → invalidates layout
3.  Read offsetWidth → forces synchronous layout AGAIN
4.  Repeat 100 times → 100 layouts

✅ Batched version:

const width = element.offsetWidth; // one layout
for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    element.style.width = width + i * 10 + 'px';
}

docs.title: Example 9: Declarative Shadow DOM Rendering
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <style>
            p { color: blue; }
        </style>
        <p>Shadow content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

Pipeline:

1.  Parser creates the shadow root during HTML parsing.
2.  Shadow tree is built.
3.  Render tree includes the shadow tree.
4.  Layout and paint use the flattened tree.

docs.title: Example 10: View Transitions
docs.text:
document.startViewTransition(() => {
    // Update the DOM
    updateContent();
});

Pipeline:

1.  Old page snapshot captured.
2.  DOM updated.
3.  New page snapshot captured.
4.  Transition animates between snapshots on the compositor thread.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Pipeline Stages Affected Text change Style, Paint, Composite Background color change Style, Paint, Composite Width/height change Style, Layout, Paint, Composite Transform change Composite only Opacity change Composite only Scroll Composite Zoom Layout, Paint, Composite Resize Layout, Paint, Composite Font load Style, Layout, Paint Image load Layout, Paint (if dimensions not reserved)

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Understand which stages your change triggers. Why: different changes have different costs.
  2. Use transform and opacity for animations. Why: composite-only, cheapest.
  3. Avoid animating layout properties. Why: triggers layout on every frame.
  4. Reserve space for images and ads. Why: prevents layout shifts.
  5. Use content-visibility: auto for long pages. Why: skips off-screen rendering.
  6. Use contain for self-contained widgets. Why: isolates subtrees.
  7. Batch DOM reads and writes. Why: prevents forced synchronous layout.
  8. Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates. Why: batches to the next frame.
  9. Avoid large display lists. Why: paint is proportional to the number of commands.
  10. Minimize layer count. Why: too many layers waste memory.
  11. Use will-change sparingly. Why: only promote what animates.
  12. Test with the Performance panel. Why: identifies pipeline bottlenecks.
  13. Profile with Paint Flashing. Why: shows what is being painted.
  14. Use Layer Borders to inspect compositing. Why: identifies unnecessary layers.
  15. Monitor Core Web Vitals. Why: LCP, INP, and CLS measure pipeline performance.
  16. Test on low-end devices. Why: pipeline cost is most visible there.
  17. Consider the frame budget. Why: 16.7ms per frame at 60fps.
  18. Prefer CSS animations over JavaScript. Why: many run on the compositor thread.
  19. Use content-visibility and contain together. Why: complementary optimizations.
  20. Audit rendering after significant UI changes. Why: regressions are common.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Animating Layout Properties
docs.text:
.box:hover {
    width: 300px;
}

Why it's wrong: Triggers layout on every frame.

✅ Correct:

.box:hover {
    transform: scale(1.1);
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Reading Layout in a Loop
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    el.style.width = el.offsetWidth + 10 + 'px';
}

Why it's wrong: Forces synchronous layout on every iteration.

✅ Correct:

const width = el.offsetWidth;
for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    el.style.width = width + i * 10 + 'px';
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Reserving Space for Images
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo">

Why it's wrong: Layout shift when the image loads.

✅ Correct:

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo" width="800" height="600">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Over-Promoting Layers
docs.text:
.card {
    will-change: transform;
    transform: translateZ(0);
    backface-visibility: hidden;
}

Why it's wrong: Every card gets its own layer — GPU memory exhaustion.

✅ Correct: Promote only what animates.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No content-visibility on Long Pages
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The browser lays out and paints off-screen content.

✅ Correct:

section {
    content-visibility: auto;
    contain-intrinsic-size: 0 500px;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using top/left for Animation
docs.text:
.ball {
    transition: top 200ms;
}
.ball:hover {
    top: -10px;
}

Why it's wrong: top triggers layout.

✅ Correct:

.ball {
    transition: transform 200ms;
}
.ball:hover {
    transform: translateY(-10px);
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing on Slow Devices
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Pipeline jank is invisible on fast hardware.

✅ Correct: Test on low-end devices with CPU throttling.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring the Frame Budget
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Long tasks drop frames.

✅ Correct: Break long tasks; yield to the browser.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using box-shadow on Animated Elements
docs.text:
.card:hover {
    transition: box-shadow 200ms;
    box-shadow: 0 10px 30px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3);
}

Why it's wrong: box-shadow triggers paint on every frame.

✅ Correct: Animate a pseudo-element's opacity instead.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Excessive DOM Depth
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Deep trees are slower to layout and paint.

✅ Correct: Keep the DOM shallow.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Layout is the most expensive stage.
  • Paint is medium.
  • Composite is cheapest.
  • Transform and opacity animations are 5–10× cheaper than layout animations.
  • content-visibility: auto reduces rendering cost by 20–50%.
  • contain isolates subtrees.
  • Layer promotion costs GPU memory.
  • Paint is proportional to the number of draw commands.
  • Layout is proportional to the number of nodes.
  • The frame budget is 16.7ms at 60fps.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Animate transform and opacity.
  2. Use content-visibility for long pages.
  3. Use contain for widgets.
  4. Batch DOM reads and writes.
  5. Reserve space for images and ads.
  6. Limit layer promotion.
  7. Keep the DOM shallow.
  8. Test on low-end devices.
  9. Profile with the Performance panel.
  10. Monitor Core Web Vitals.

docs.title: Rendering and CSP
docs.text: CSP does not directly affect rendering. But inline styles used in animations require 'unsafe-inline' in style-src unless nonces or hashes are used.

docs.title: Rendering and Timing Side Channels
docs.text: Rendering timing can leak information. Modern browsers mitigate with high-resolution timer restrictions and cross-origin isolation.

docs.title: Rendering and Layout Leaks
docs.text: Ad and widget iframes can read the parent page's layout in some cases. Use contain to isolate them.

docs.title: View Transitions and Snapshots
docs.text: The View Transitions API captures page snapshots. Ensure sensitive data is not exposed during the transition.

docs.title: Layer Promotion and Memory
docs.text: Promoting layers uses GPU memory. Adversarial content can exhaust GPU memory by promoting many layers.

docs.title: Content-Visibility and Accessibility
docs.text: content-visibility: auto skips rendering but the content is still in the accessibility tree. Ensure it remains accessible.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Performance panel — record and profile the pipeline.
  • Chrome DevTools → Rendering panel — enable Paint Flashing, Layer Borders, FPS Meter.
  • Chrome DevTools → Layers panel — inspect compositing layers.
  • Chrome DevTools → Coverage panel — unused CSS and JS.
  • Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse — audits for rendering performance.
  • Performance panel → Main thread — see style, layout, paint.
  • Performance panel → Frames — see the frame-by-frame pipeline.
  • performance.getEntriesByType('paint') — FCP, LCP timing.
  • PerformanceObserver — observe paint and layout shifts.
  • WebPageTest — filmstrip view of rendering.
  • PageSpeed Insights — field + lab data.
  • CrUX — real-world Core Web Vitals.
  • Paint Flashing — green flashes show painted regions.
  • Layer Borders — orange borders show compositing layers.
  • FPS Meter — real-time frame rate.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Understanding browser behavior — the pipeline is always running.
  • Optimizing animations — choose the right properties.
  • Debugging performance — identify the bottleneck stage.
  • Reducing CLS — reserve space for dynamic content.
  • Optimizing INP — minimize long tasks.
  • Optimizing LCP — prioritize the LCP element.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not animate layout properties. Use transform.
  • Do not read layout in a loop. Batch reads.
  • Do not over-promote layers. Limit will-change.
  • Do not ignore the frame budget. Break long tasks.
  • Do not skip testing on slow devices.
  • Do not assume the pipeline is free. It costs CPU and GPU.
