docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Browsers use Shadow DOM internally for built-in elements — <video>, <input>, <details>.
  • closed mode is not a security boundary — DevTools can still access it.
  • Inherited properties cross the shadow boundary — color, font-family, line-height.
  • Non-inherited properties are encapsulated — background, border, padding.
  • Event retargeting preserves encapsulation — external listeners see the host, not internal elements.
  • composed: true allows an event to cross the shadow boundary.
  • ::part() is the controlled API for external styling — the component chooses what to expose.
  • ::slotted() only matches top-level slotted elements — descendant selectors are invalid.
  • Declarative Shadow DOM shipped in Chrome 90+, Safari 16.4+, Firefox 123+.
  • Shadow DOM was proposed in 2011 as part of the Web Components specification.
  • Firefox was the last major browser to ship Shadow DOM v1 — in Firefox 63 (2018).
  • Shadow DOM v0 and v1 had different APIs — v0 was deprecated.
  • The :host selector has a specificity of (0, 1, 0) — one pseudo-class.
  • delegatesFocus was added in 2020 — for focus delegation.
  • slotAssignment: "manual" was added in 2021 — for imperative slot assignment.
  • Shadow DOM is used by every major Web Component library — Lit, FAST, Stencil.
  • The accessibility tree is derived from the flattened tree — shadow content is accessible.
  • Form-associated custom elements use ElementInternals to participate in form submission.
  • Shadow DOM does not hide content from SEO — search engines may not index shadow content.
  • The best use of Shadow DOM is where encapsulation is essential — not everywhere.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Shadow DOM is a browser API for encapsulating a DOM subtree attached to a host element.
  • It provides style encapsulation, structure encapsulation, and event encapsulation.
  • The shadow tree is separate from the main document — page styles do not leak in; shadow styles do not leak out.
  • Inherited properties cross the boundary — color, font-family, line-height.
  • mode: 'open' exposes the shadow root via element.shadowRoot; mode: 'closed' hides it.
  • closed mode is not a security boundary.
  • :host, :host(), and :host-context() style the host from within the shadow tree.
  • ::part() exposes internal elements for external styling.
  • ::slotted() styles top-level slotted content from within the shadow tree.
  • Events bubble out of the shadow tree with retargeting — the target becomes the host.
  • composed: true allows events to cross the shadow boundary.
  • Slots project light DOM content into the shadow tree.
  • The flattened tree combines shadow and light DOM — what is rendered.
  • Accessibility reflects the flattened tree — shadow content is accessible.
  • Declarative Shadow DOM (shadowrootmode) enables server-rendered shadow roots.
  • Shadow DOM is the foundation of Web Components — combined with templates, slots, and custom elements.
  • Shadow DOM is supported in all modern browsers.
  • Use Shadow DOM where encapsulation is needed — not everywhere.
  • The best Shadow DOM is invisible to the consumer — it just works.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Custom Elements is a browser API that lets developers define their own HTML elements — complete with a tag name, a JavaScript class, lifecycle callbacks, and (optionally) a shadow root. A custom element is a first-class HTML element: it participates in parsing, styling, DOM APIs, form submission, and accessibility just like a built-in element.

class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        shadow.innerHTML = `
            <style>
                .card { border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 1rem; }
            </style>
            <div class="card">
                <h2>${this.getAttribute('name')}</h2>
                <p>${this.getAttribute('email')}</p>
            </div>
        `;
    }
}

customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);

<user-card name="Alice" email="alice@example.com"></user-card>

The browser parses <user-card> like any other element. But behind the tag, UserCard is a JavaScript class with a constructor, lifecycle callbacks, and its own encapsulated shadow tree. Custom Elements are the definition mechanism of Web Components — they bind templates, slots, and shadow DOM into a reusable, declarative tag.

Custom Elements are not a framework. They are a platform primitive — the ability to extend HTML with new elements natively, without JavaScript libraries, build tools, or compilers.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Custom Elements serve several essential purposes:

  • New HTML elements — define tags that did not exist.
  • Reusable components — encapsulate behavior and presentation.
  • Declarative API — consumers use HTML, not JavaScript configuration.
  • Encapsulation — combine with Shadow DOM for style and structure isolation.
  • Lifecycle callbacks — react to connection, disconnection, and attribute changes.
  • Form participation — act as form controls via ElementInternals.
  • Accessibility — participate in the accessibility tree naturally.
  • Framework interoperability — work alongside React, Vue, Angular, Svelte.

Custom Elements are the tag layer of Web Components. Templates define the markup; slots project content; Shadow DOM encapsulates; custom elements define the tag.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Web Components
│
├── Templates              ← reusable markup
├── Slots                  ← content projection
├── Shadow DOM             ← style and structure encapsulation
├── Custom Elements        ← reusable component definitions (THIS CHAPTER)
└── Declarative Shadow DOM ← server-rendered shadow roots

Custom Elements sit at the top of the Web Components stack — they bind the other primitives to a tag.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTML has a fixed set of elements. Developers can use <div>, <span>, <button>, and the rest of the standard vocabulary, but they cannot invent new elements. The browser does not know what a <user-card> or <data-chart> is. It treats them as unknown elements — semantically meaningless, indistinguishable from a <div> in the accessibility tree.

Before Custom Elements, developers used several workarounds:

  • class attributes with framework components — React.Component, Vue.component, etc. Framework-specific, not native.
  • Directives — Angular's ng-*, Vue's v-*. Not native elements.
  • Web Components polyfills — attempted to emulate custom elements but with performance and compatibility costs.
  • No encapsulation — every component shared the global namespace.
  • No lifecycle — no standard way to react to connection, disconnection, or attribute changes.

The platform needed a way to extend HTML with new elements that behaved natively — parsed by the HTML parser, styled by CSS, manipulated by DOM APIs, and exposed to accessibility tools.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Fixed HTML vocabulary No new elements Framework-specific components Not portable across frameworks No encapsulation Global namespace collisions No lifecycle callbacks No standard way to react to DOM changes No native upgrade Components initialized inconsistently No form participation Custom controls could not submit No accessibility integration Custom elements were invisible to assistive technology

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The Custom Elements specification was proposed as part of the Web Components initiative in 2011 by Google. It was designed to bring extensibility to HTML — the ability to define new elements natively.

The specification went through two versions:

  • Custom Elements v0 (2013) — an early version shipped in Chrome, with a different API (document.registerElement()).
  • Custom Elements v1 (2016) — the standardized version with the modern API (customElements.define()).

The v1 API became the standard and shipped in Chrome 54 (2016), Firefox 63 (2018), Safari 10.1 (2017), and Edge 79 (2020).

The specification defines:

  • The customElements registry — a global registry of custom element definitions.
  • The customElements.define() method — registers a custom element.
  • The HTMLElement base class — custom elements extend it.
  • Lifecycle callbacks — connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback, attributeChangedCallback, adoptedCallback.
  • The element upgrade process — how the browser upgrades unknown elements to custom elements.
  • Autonomous vs. customized built-in elements — two flavors of custom elements.

Custom Elements are inspired by similar mechanisms in other platforms:

  • XBL (XUL) — Mozilla's XML Binding Language.
  • Flex/Flash — custom components.
  • HTML's own extensibility — the dream of <my-widget> since the 1990s.

In 2026, Custom Elements are baseline and universally supported. They power every major Web Component library — Lit, FAST, Stencil, Polymer — and are used by Google, Adobe, Microsoft, Salesforce, and thousands of production applications.

docs.title: The Minimal Custom Element
docs.text:
class HelloWorld extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        this.textContent = 'Hello, world!';
    }
}

customElements.define('hello-world', HelloWorld);

<hello-world></hello-world>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• class HelloWorld extends HTMLElement — the custom element class.
  • connectedCallback() — runs when the element is inserted into the DOM.
  • this.textContent = 'Hello, world!' — sets the element's text.
  • customElements.define('hello-world', HelloWorld) — registers the custom element.

docs.title: The Two Flavors
docs.text:
// Autonomous custom element: extends HTMLElement
class MyButton extends HTMLElement { }
customElements.define('my-button', MyButton);

// Customized built-in element: extends a specific built-in element
class FancyButton extends HTMLButtonElement { }
customElements.define('fancy-button', FancyButton, { extends: 'button' });

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
Flavor Extends Tag usage Autonomous HTMLElement <my-button> Customized built-in HTMLButtonElement <button is="fancy-button">

Note: Safari does not support customized built-in elements as of 2026. Autonomous elements are the recommended approach.

docs.title: The Naming Rules
docs.text:
Custom element names must:

  • Start with a lowercase letter.
  • Contain a hyphen (-).
  • Be unique across the page.
  • Not conflict with reserved names.
// ✅ Valid names
'my-element'
'user-card'
'x-component'
'data-chart'

// ❌ Invalid names
'myElement'         // no hyphen
'MY-ELEMENT'        // uppercase
'annotation-xml'    // reserved
'color-profile'     // reserved
'font-face'         // reserved

The hyphen requirement exists to prevent collisions with future HTML elements.

docs.title: The customElements Registry
docs.text:
// The global registry
console.log(customElements); // CustomElementRegistry

// Define a custom element
customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);

// Check if a name is defined
console.log(customElements.get('my-element')); // MyElement
console.log(customElements.get('nonexistent')); // undefined

// Get all definitions (not a standard API; use window.customElements)
customElements.whenDefined('my-element').then(() => {
    console.log('my-element is ready');
});

docs.title: The whenDefined() Method
docs.text:
customElements.whenDefined('my-element').then(() => {
    // The element is defined
});

Returns a Promise that resolves when the custom element is defined. Useful for coordinating initialization.

docs.title: The upgrade() Method
docs.text:
customElements.upgrade(element);

Forces the upgrade of a custom element. Used when elements are created in a different document or need manual upgrading.

docs.title: The Lifecycle Callbacks
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        // Called when the element is created
    }

    connectedCallback() {
        // Called when the element is added to the DOM
    }

    disconnectedCallback() {
        // Called when the element is removed from the DOM
    }

    adoptedCallback() {
        // Called when the element is moved to a new document
    }

    static get observedAttributes() {
        return ['name', 'email'];
    }

    attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
        // Called when an observed attribute changes
    }
}

docs.title: A Complete Example with Shadow DOM
docs.text:
<template id="user-card-template">
    <style>
        .card {
            border: 1px solid #ccc;
            border-radius: 8px;
            padding: 1rem;
            font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
        }
        .name { font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25rem; }
        .email { color: #666; }
    </style>
    <div class="card">
        <div class="name"><slot name="name"></slot></div>
        <div class="email"><slot name="email"></slot></div>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
        constructor() {
            super();
            const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
            const template = document.getElementById('user-card-template');
            shadow.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
        }
    }
    customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);
</script>

<user-card>
    <span slot="name">Alice</span>
    <span slot="email">alice@example.com</span>
</user-card>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• The class extends HTMLElement.
  • The constructor calls super() and attachShadow().
  • The template is cloned into the shadow root.
  • The element is registered with customElements.define().

docs.title: Reactive Attributes
docs.text:
class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
    static get observedAttributes() {
        return ['name', 'email'];
    }

    attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
        if (oldValue === newValue) return;

        if (name === 'name') {
            this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.name').textContent = newValue;
        }
        if (name === 'email') {
            this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.email').textContent = newValue;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• observedAttributes — a static getter returning the attributes to observe.
  • attributeChangedCallback — called when an observed attribute changes.
  • Updates the shadow DOM in response to attribute changes.

docs.title: Form-Associated Custom Elements
docs.text:
class MyInput extends HTMLElement {
    static formAssociated = true;

    constructor() {
        super();
        this._internals = this.attachInternals();
        const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        shadow.innerHTML = `<input type="text">`;

        const input = shadow.querySelector('input');
        input.addEventListener('input', () => {
            this._internals.setFormValue(input.value);
        });
    }

    get value() {
        return this._internals.value;
    }

    set value(v) {
        this.shadowRoot.querySelector('input').value = v;
        this._internals.setFormValue(v);
    }
}

customElements.define('my-input', MyInput);

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• static formAssociated = true — declares the element as form-associated.
  • attachInternals() — returns an ElementInternals object.
  • setFormValue() — sets the value submitted with the form.
  • The element participates in form submission.

docs.title: The ElementInternals API
docs.text:
this._internals = this.attachInternals();

this._internals.setFormValue(value);
this._internals.setValidity(flags, message, anchor);
this._internals.reportValidity();
this._internals.checkValidity();
this._internals.form;          // the associated form
this._internals.labels;        // the associated labels
this._internals.willValidate;  // whether the element will validate
this._internals.validity;      // the validity state

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• setFormValue — sets the value submitted with the form.
  • setValidity — sets the validity state.
  • reportValidity — shows the validation message.
  • form — the associated form.
  • labels — the labels associated with the element.
  • validity — the current validity state.

docs.title: The "Tag Definition" Mental Model
docs.text:
A custom element is a tag definition — a tag name bound to a JavaScript class:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TAG NAME: "user-card"                       │
│  CLASS: UserCard                             │
│                                              │
│  When the browser sees <user-card>:          │
│  └── Instantiate UserCard                    │
│  └── Run constructor                         │
│  └── Run connectedCallback                   │
│  └── Render the shadow tree                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The browser treats <user-card> exactly like <div> or <button>. It is a first-class element.

docs.title: The "Upgrade" Mental Model
docs.text:
The browser may encounter a custom element before it is defined:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. HTML PARSED                              │
│     └── <user-card> is an unknown element     │
│                                              │
│  2. SCRIPT LOADS                             │
│     └── customElements.define() is called    │
│                                              │
│  3. UPGRADE                                  │
│     └── The browser "upgrades" all existing  │
│         <user-card> elements                 │
│     └── Constructor runs                    │
│     └── connectedCallback runs              │
│                                              │
│  4. FUTURE ELEMENTS                          │
│     └── New <user-card> elements are         │
│         upgraded immediately                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is why custom elements work regardless of script load order — the browser upgrades unknown elements when the definition arrives.

docs.title: The "Two Flavors" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AUTONOMOUS CUSTOM ELEMENTS                  │
│  └── Extend HTMLElement                      │
│  └── Use <my-element>                        │
│  └── Fully custom behavior                   │
│  └── Supported everywhere                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CUSTOMIZED BUILT-IN ELEMENTS                │
│  └── Extend HTMLButtonElement, etc.          │
│  └── Use <button is="my-button">             │
│  └── Inherit built-in behavior               │
│  └── Not supported in Safari                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Autonomous elements are the recommended approach.

docs.title: The "Lifecycle" Mental Model
docs.text:
Custom elements have five lifecycle events:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. constructor()                            │
│     └── Element is created                   │
│     └── Do: attachShadow, setup state         │
│     └── Don't: inspect attributes, children  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  2. connectedCallback()                      │
│     └── Element is added to the DOM          │
│     └── Do: fetch data, attach listeners      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  3. disconnectedCallback()                   │
│     └── Element is removed from the DOM      │
│     └── Do: cleanup, detach listeners         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  4. attributeChangedCallback()                │
│     └── Observed attribute changes           │
│     └── Do: react to the change              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  5. adoptedCallback()                         │
│     └── Element moves to a new document       │
│     └── Rare; used for cross-document moves   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Declarative API" Mental Model
docs.text:
Custom elements let consumers use native HTML:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FRAMEWORK COMPONENT (React)                 │
│  <UserCard name="Alice" email="..." />        │
│  └── JSX — needs a compiler                  │
│  └── Framework-specific                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CUSTOM ELEMENT                              │
│  <user-card name="Alice" email="...">         │
│     <span slot="name">Alice</span>            │
│  </user-card>                                 │
│  └── Native HTML                              │
│  └── No compiler needed                       │
│  └── Works with any framework                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Custom elements are framework-agnostic — they work everywhere HTML works.

docs.title: The "Registry" Mental Model
docs.text:
The customElements registry is a global map of tag names to classes:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  customElements REGISTRY                     │
│  └── 'user-card' → UserCard class            │
│  └── 'data-chart' → DataChart class          │
│  └── 'my-button' → MyButton class            │
│                                              │
│  Once a name is defined, it cannot be        │
│  redefined.                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Once you call customElements.define('user-card', ...), the name is bound forever. You cannot redefine it.

docs.title: Concept 1: The customElements Registry
docs.text: The global registry of custom element definitions. Accessed via window.customElements.

docs.title: Concept 2: customElements.define()
docs.text: Registers a custom element. Takes a tag name and a class.

docs.title: Concept 3: The HTMLElement Base Class
docs.text: Custom elements extend HTMLElement (or a built-in element for customized built-ins).

docs.title: Concept 4: Autonomous Custom Elements
docs.text: Extend HTMLElement. Use <my-element>.

docs.title: Concept 5: Customized Built-in Elements
docs.text: Extend a specific built-in element. Use <button is="my-button">. Not supported in Safari.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Naming Rules
docs.text: Custom element names must start with a lowercase letter, contain a hyphen, and not conflict with reserved names.

docs.title: Concept 7: The Five Lifecycle Callbacks
docs.text:
• constructor — element created.
  • connectedCallback — element added to the DOM.
  • disconnectedCallback — element removed from the DOM.
  • attributeChangedCallback — observed attribute changed.
  • adoptedCallback — element moved to a new document.

docs.title: Concept 8: The observedAttributes Static Getter
docs.text: Returns an array of attribute names to observe. attributeChangedCallback fires for these attributes.

docs.title: Concept 9: The Upgrade Process
docs.text: The browser upgrades unknown elements to custom elements when the definition arrives.

docs.title: Concept 10: customElements.whenDefined()
docs.text: Returns a Promise that resolves when a custom element is defined.

docs.title: Concept 11: customElements.upgrade()
docs.text: Forces the upgrade of a custom element.

docs.title: Concept 12: Shadow DOM Integration
docs.text: Custom elements commonly use attachShadow() to create an encapsulated shadow tree.

docs.title: Concept 13: Template Integration
docs.text: Custom elements commonly clone a <template> into their shadow root.

docs.title: Concept 14: Slot Integration
docs.text: Custom elements can include <slot> elements for content projection.

docs.title: Concept 15: Form-Associated Custom Elements
docs.text: Custom elements with static formAssociated = true participate in form submission via ElementInternals.

docs.title: Concept 16: The attachInternals() Method
docs.text: Returns an ElementInternals object for form participation, ARIA, and accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 17: The ElementInternals API
docs.text:
Provides methods and properties for form participation and accessibility:

  • setFormValue(value) — sets the value.
  • setValidity(flags, message, anchor) — sets validity.
  • form — the associated form.
  • labels — the labels.
  • validity — the validity state.

docs.title: Concept 18: Accessibility with Custom Elements
docs.text: Custom elements participate in the accessibility tree. Use role, aria-*, and ElementInternals for semantics.

docs.title: Concept 19: The constructor Restrictions
docs.text:
• Must call super() first.
  • Must not inspect attributes or children.
  • Must not attach child nodes (except shadow root).
  • Must not change the host's own attributes.

docs.title: Concept 20: The is Attribute
docs.text:
Customized built-in elements use the is attribute:

<button is="my-button">Click</button>

docs.title: Concept 21: The Custom Element Registry Names
docs.text: Once defined, a name cannot be redefined. Attempting to redefine throws an error.

docs.title: Concept 22: The customElements.getName() Method
docs.text: Returns the tag name for a constructor. Added in 2023.

docs.title: Concept 23: The ElementInternals ARIA Methods
docs.text:
ElementInternals also provides ARIA methods for accessibility:

this._internals.role = 'button';
this._internals.ariaLabel = 'Click me';

docs.title: Concept 24: Custom Elements vs. Framework Components
docs.text: Custom Elements Framework Components Standard HTML/DOM Framework-specific Parsing Native Compiler required Interop Works with any framework Framework-locked Accessibility Native Framework-dependent Encapsulation Shadow DOM Framework-dependent Lifecycle Standard callbacks Framework-specific

docs.title: Concept 25: The Custom Element Lifecycle Order
docs.text:
1.  constructor
2.  attributeChangedCallback (for initial attributes)
3.  connectedCallback
4.  attributeChangedCallback (for subsequent changes)
5.  disconnectedCallback
6.  adoptedCallback (if moved to a new document)

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Defining a Custom Element
docs.text:
1.  JavaScript class extends HTMLElement.
    │
    ▼
2.  customElements.define('my-element', MyElement) is called.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser validates the name (must contain a hyphen).
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser stores the mapping in the registry.
    │
    ▼
5.  Browser upgrades any existing <my-element> elements.
    │
    ▼
6.  Future <my-element> elements are upgraded immediately.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Upgrade Process
docs.text:
1.  HTML parser encounters <user-card>.
    │
    ▼
2.  The element is not defined yet.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser creates an HTMLElement (unknown element).
    │
    ▼
4.  Element is inserted into the DOM.
    │
    ▼
5.  Script loads; customElements.define() is called.
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser upgrades all <user-card> elements:
    │   ├── Change the prototype from HTMLElement to UserCard
    │   ├── Run constructor
    │   ├── Run attributeChangedCallback for initial attributes
    │   └── Run connectedCallback
    │
    ▼
7.  Future elements upgrade on creation.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Constructor
docs.text:
1.  Element created (document.createElement or parser).
    │
    ▼
2.  Constructor called.
    │
    ▼
3.  super() must be called first.
    │
    ▼
4.  attachShadow() may be called.
    │
    ▼
5.  Shadow tree may be populated.
    │
    ▼
6.  Event listeners may be attached (to the shadow tree).
    │
    ▼
7.  Do NOT inspect attributes or children yet.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The connectedCallback
docs.text:
1.  Element is inserted into the DOM.
    │
    ▼
2.  connectedCallback is called.
    │
    ▼
3.  Attributes are now available.
    │
    ▼
4.  Children are now available.
    │
    ▼
5.  Element can fetch data, attach listeners, etc.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Form Participation
docs.text:
1.  Class declares static formAssociated = true.
    │
    ▼
2.  constructor calls attachInternals().
    │
    ▼
3.  Element is inside a <form>.
    │
    ▼
4.  Form submission triggers setFormValue().
    │
    ▼
5.  Value is submitted with the form.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Attribute Observation
docs.text:
1.  Class declares observedAttributes.
    │
    ▼
2.  Element is created.
    │
    ▼
3.  attributeChangedCallback fires for each initial attribute.
    │
    ▼
4.  Subsequent attribute changes fire attributeChangedCallback.
    │
    ▼
5.  Element updates its shadow tree in response.

docs.title: The Custom Element Registry
docs.text:
The customElements registry is a global map of tag names to classes:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  customElements REGISTRY                     │
│  └── Map<string, CustomElementConstructor>   │
│      ├── 'user-card' → UserCard              │
│      ├── 'data-chart' → DataChart            │
│      └── 'my-button' → MyButton              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Once a name is defined, it cannot be redefined. Attempting to redefine throws a NotSupportedError.

docs.title: The Element Upgrade Algorithm
docs.text:
When an element is created:

  1. Browser checks if the tag name is in the registry.
  2. If yes:
  3. Change the element's prototype to the custom class.
  4. Run constructor.
  5. Run attributeChangedCallback for initial attributes.
  6. If connected, run connectedCallback.
  7. If no:
  8. The element remains an unknown HTMLElement.
  9. It will be upgraded later when defined.

docs.title: The Prototype Chain
docs.text:
Custom elements have a prototype chain:

Object.prototype
  └── EventTarget.prototype
      └── Node.prototype
          └── Element.prototype
              └── HTMLElement.prototype
                  └── MyElement.prototype
                      └── myElement (instance)

docs.title: The Form-Associated Lifecycle
docs.text:
Form-associated custom elements have additional callbacks:

  • formAssociatedCallback(form) — called when the element is associated with a form.
  • formDisabledCallback(disabled) — called when the element is disabled.
  • formResetCallback() — called when the form is reset.
  • formStateRestoreCallback(state, mode) — called when the form state is restored.

docs.title: The ElementInternals API
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ElementInternals                            │
│  ├── setFormValue(value, state)              │
│  ├── setValidity(flags, message, anchor)     │
│  ├── form → HTMLFormElement                  │
│  ├── labels → NodeList                       │
│  ├── validity → ValidityState                │
│  ├── willValidate → boolean                  │
│  ├── checkValidity() → boolean               │
│  ├── reportValidity() → boolean              │
│  ├── role → string                           │
│  └── ariaLabel → string                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The Custom Element Name Validation
docs.text:
The browser validates names during define():

  • Must start with a lowercase letter.
  • Must contain a hyphen.
  • Must not be in the reserved list.
  • Must not already be defined.

docs.title: The Reserved Names
docs.text:
The following names are reserved and cannot be used:

  • annotation-xml
  • color-profile
  • font-face
  • font-face-src
  • font-face-uri
  • font-face-format
  • font-face-name
  • missing-glyph

docs.title: The Custom Element Lifecycle Order
docs.text:
1.  constructor
2.  attributeChangedCallback (initial attributes)
3.  connectedCallback
4.  attributeChangedCallback (subsequent changes)
5.  formAssociatedCallback (for form-associated elements)
6.  disconnectedCallback
7.  adoptedCallback (if moved to a new document)

docs.title: The ::part() and ::slotted() Integration
docs.text:
Custom elements expose internal elements via part and receive content via slot:

<my-button>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <button part="button"><slot></slot></button>
    </template>
</my-button>

docs.title: Custom Element Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Element is created (document.createElement or parser).
    │
    ▼
2.  constructor runs.
    │
    ▼
3.  attributeChangedCallback fires for initial attributes.
    │
    ▼
4.  Element is inserted into the DOM.
    │
    ▼
5.  connectedCallback runs.
    │
    ▼
6.  Attribute changes fire attributeChangedCallback.
    │
    ▼
7.  Element is removed from the DOM.
    │
    ▼
8.  disconnectedCallback runs.
    │
    ▼
9.  Element is moved to a new document (rare).
    │
    ▼
10. adoptedCallback runs.

docs.title: The Full Lifecycle with Form Association
docs.text:
1.  constructor
2.  attributeChangedCallback (initial)
3.  connectedCallback
4.  formAssociatedCallback (if in a form)
5.  attributeChangedCallback (changes)
6.  formDisabledCallback (if disabled)
7.  formResetCallback (if form reset)
8.  disconnectedCallback
9.  adoptedCallback (if applicable)

docs.title: The Upgrade Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Page loads.
    │
    ▼
2.  HTML parser encounters <my-element>.
    │
    ▼
3.  Unknown element created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Script loads.
    │
    ▼
5.  customElements.define('my-element', MyElement).
    │
    ▼
6.  Browser upgrades all <my-element> elements.
    │
    ▼
7.  Constructor, attributeChangedCallback, connectedCallback run.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Custom Element
docs.text:
class HelloWorld extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        this.textContent = 'Hello, world!';
    }
}

customElements.define('hello-world', HelloWorld);

<hello-world></hello-world>

Code Breakdown:

  • The class extends HTMLElement.
  • connectedCallback sets the text content.
  • The element is registered with customElements.define().

docs.title: Example 2: Custom Element with Shadow DOM
docs.text:
class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        shadow.innerHTML = `
            <style>
                .card {
                    border: 1px solid #ccc;
                    border-radius: 8px;
                    padding: 1rem;
                    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
                }
                .name { font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25rem; }
                .email { color: #666; }
            </style>
            <div class="card">
                <div class="name">${this.getAttribute('name') || ''}</div>
                <div class="email">${this.getAttribute('email') || ''}</div>
            </div>
        `;
    }
}

customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);

<user-card name="Alice" email="alice@example.com"></user-card>

Code Breakdown:

  • The constructor calls attachShadow().
  • The shadow tree is populated with styles and markup.
  • Attributes are read in the constructor (safe here since they are known).

docs.title: Example 3: Reactive Attributes
docs.text:
class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
    static get observedAttributes() {
        return ['name', 'email'];
    }

    constructor() {
        super();
        const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        shadow.innerHTML = `
            <style>
                .name { font-weight: bold; }
                .email { color: #666; }
            </style>
            <div class="name"></div>
            <div class="email"></div>
        `;
    }

    attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
        if (oldValue === newValue) return;

        if (name === 'name') {
            this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.name').textContent = newValue;
        }
        if (name === 'email') {
            this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.email').textContent = newValue;
        }
    }
}

customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);

// Usage:
const card = document.createElement('user-card');
card.setAttribute('name', 'Alice');    // triggers attributeChangedCallback
card.setAttribute('email', 'alice@example.com'); // triggers attributeChangedCallback
document.body.appendChild(card);

Code Breakdown:

  • observedAttributes declares which attributes to watch.
  • attributeChangedCallback reacts to changes.
  • The shadow tree is updated in response.

docs.title: Example 4: Custom Element with Template and Slots
docs.text:
<template id="card-template">
    <style>
        .card {
            border: 1px solid #ccc;
            border-radius: 8px;
            padding: 1rem;
        }
        ::slotted(h2) {
            margin-top: 0;
        }
    </style>
    <div class="card">
        <slot name="title"></slot>
        <slot></slot>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    class Card extends HTMLElement {
        constructor() {
            super();
            const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
            const template = document.getElementById('card-template');
            shadow.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
        }
    }
    customElements.define('my-card', Card);
</script>

<my-card>
    <h2 slot="title">Card Title</h2>
    <p>Card body content.</p>
</my-card>

Code Breakdown:

  • The template contains a shadow tree with slots.
  • The custom element clones the template into the shadow root.
  • Slots project the consumer's content.

docs.title: Example 5: Lifecycle Logging
docs.text:
class LifecycleDemo extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        console.log('constructor');
    }

    connectedCallback() {
        console.log('connectedCallback');
    }

    disconnectedCallback() {
        console.log('disconnectedCallback');
    }

    adoptedCallback() {
        console.log('adoptedCallback');
    }

    static get observedAttributes() {
        return ['name'];
    }

    attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
        console.log(`attributeChangedCallback: ${name} = ${newValue}`);
    }
}

customElements.define('lifecycle-demo', LifecycleDemo);

// Usage:
const el = document.createElement('lifecycle-demo');
// Logs: constructor
el.setAttribute('name', 'Alice');
// Logs: attributeChangedCallback: name = Alice
document.body.appendChild(el);
// Logs: connectedCallback
el.setAttribute('name', 'Bob');
// Logs: attributeChangedCallback: name = Bob
el.remove();
// Logs: disconnectedCallback

Code Breakdown:

  • Each lifecycle callback logs to the console.
  • The order is constructor → attributeChangedCallback → connectedCallback → disconnectedCallback.

docs.title: Example 6: Form-Associated Custom Element
docs.text:
class MyInput extends HTMLElement {
    static formAssociated = true;

    constructor() {
        super();
        this._internals = this.attachInternals();
        const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        shadow.innerHTML = `
            <style>
                input {
                    padding: 0.5rem;
                    border: 1px solid #ccc;
                    border-radius: 4px;
                }
            </style>
            <input type="text" part="input">
        `;

        shadow.querySelector('input').addEventListener('input', (event) => {
            this._internals.setFormValue(event.target.value);
        });
    }

    get value() {
        return this.shadowRoot.querySelector('input').value;
    }

    set value(v) {
        this.shadowRoot.querySelector('input').value = v;
        this._internals.setFormValue(v);
    }

    formResetCallback() {
        this.value = '';
    }
}

customElements.define('my-input', MyInput);

<form>
    <my-input name="username"></my-input>
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

Code Breakdown:

  • static formAssociated = true — declares the element as form-associated.
  • attachInternals() — creates the ElementInternals object.
  • setFormValue() — sets the value submitted with the form.
  • formResetCallback() — clears the value when the form is reset.

docs.title: Example 7: Custom Element with Accessibility
docs.text:
class MyToggle extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this._internals = this.attachInternals();
        this._internals.role = 'switch';
        this._internals.ariaChecked = 'false';

        const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        shadow.innerHTML = `
            <style>
                .track {
                    width: 40px;
                    height: 20px;
                    background: #ccc;
                    border-radius: 10px;
                    cursor: pointer;
                    position: relative;
                    transition: background 0.2s;
                }
                .track[aria-checked="true"] {
                    background: #3498db;
                }
                .thumb {
                    width: 16px;
                    height: 16px;
                    background: white;
                    border-radius: 50%;
                    position: absolute;
                    top: 2px;
                    left: 2px;
                    transition: left 0.2s;
                }
                .track[aria-checked="true"] .thumb {
                    left: 22px;
                }
            </style>
            <div class="track" role="switch" aria-checked="false" tabindex="0">
                <div class="thumb"></div>
            </div>
        `;

        const track = shadow.querySelector('.track');
        track.addEventListener('click', () => this.toggle());
        track.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
            if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') {
                e.preventDefault();
                this.toggle();
            }
        });
    }

    toggle() {
        const current = this._internals.ariaChecked === 'true';
        this._internals.ariaChecked = String(!current);
        this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.track').setAttribute('aria-checked', String(!current));
    }
}

customElements.define('my-toggle', MyToggle);

Code Breakdown:

  • ElementInternals is used for ARIA.
  • role = 'switch' declares the semantic role.
  • ariaChecked reflects the toggle state.
  • Keyboard support is added manually.

docs.title: Example 8: Custom Element with Data Fetching
docs.text:
class DataChart extends HTMLElement {
    static get observedAttributes() {
        return ['src'];
    }

    constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
            <style>
                .chart {
                    width: 100%;
                    height: 200px;
                    border: 1px solid #ccc;
                }
            </style>
            <div class="chart">Loading...</div>
        `;
    }

    async connectedCallback() {
        await this.loadData();
    }

    async attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
        if (name === 'src' && oldValue !== newValue) {
            await this.loadData();
        }
    }

    async loadData() {
        const src = this.getAttribute('src');
        if (!src) return;

        try {
            const response = await fetch(src);
            const data = await response.json();
            this.render(data);
        } catch (error) {
            this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.chart').textContent = 'Error loading data';
        }
    }

    render(data) {
        // Render the chart
        this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.chart').textContent = JSON.stringify(data);
    }
}

customElements.define('data-chart', DataChart);

Code Breakdown:

  • observedAttributes includes src.
  • connectedCallback loads data.
  • attributeChangedCallback reloads when src changes.
  • Data is fetched asynchronously.

docs.title: Example 9: Custom Element with CSS Custom Properties
docs.text:
class StyledButton extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
            <style>
                button {
                    background: var(--button-bg, #3498db);
                    color: var(--button-color, white);
                    padding: var(--button-padding, 0.5rem 1rem);
                    border: none;
                    border-radius: 4px;
                    cursor: pointer;
                    font: inherit;
                }
                button:hover {
                    filter: brightness(0.9);
                }
            </style>
            <button><slot></slot></button>
        `;
    }
}

customElements.define('styled-button', StyledButton);

<style>
    styled-button {
        --button-bg: #e74c3c;
        --button-color: white;
    }
</style>

<styled-button>Click me</styled-button>

Code Breakdown:

  • CSS custom properties cross the shadow boundary.
  • Consumers can theme the component via custom properties.
  • var(--name, fallback) provides defaults.

docs.title: Example 10: Complete Custom Element with Everything
docs.text:
<template id="product-card-template">
    <style>
        :host {
            display: block;
            font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
        }
        .card {
            display: grid;

        }
        .card:hover {

        .image {

            object-fit: cover;
            border-radius: 4px;
        }
        .name {
            font-weight: bold;

        }
        .price {
            color: #2c7a2c;
            font-weight: bold;
        }
        ::slotted(img) {
            width: 100px;
            height: 100px;
            object-fit: cover;
            border-radius: 4px;
        }
    </style>
    <div class="card" part="card">
        <div><slot name="image"></slot></div>
        <div>
            <slot name="name"></slot>
            <slot name="price"></slot>
            <slot></slot>
        </div>
    </div>
</template>

<script>
    class ProductCard extends HTMLElement {
        static get observedAttributes() {
            return ['featured'];
        }

        constructor() {
            super();
            const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
            const template = document.getElementById('product-card-template');
            shadow.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
        }

        connectedCallback() {
            this.setAttribute('role', 'article');
        }

        attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
            if (name === 'featured' && newValue !== null) {
                this.setAttribute('part', 'card featured');
            }
        }
    }

    customElements.define('product-card', ProductCard);
</script>

<product-card featured>
    <img slot="image" src="product.jpg" alt="Product">
    <h3 slot="name">Awesome Product</h3>
    <span slot="price">$29.99</span>
    <p>This product is amazing.</p>
</product-card>

Code Breakdown:

  • Complete component with template, shadow DOM, slots, observed attributes, and lifecycle.
  • part exposes internals for external styling.
  • CSS custom properties could be added for theming.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Description Design system components Buttons, cards, modals, inputs Web apps Custom widgets and controls Third-party widgets Embeddable components Micro-frontends Isolated sub-applications Form controls Form-associated custom elements Data visualization Charts and graphs Video players Custom controls Rich text editors Encapsulated editing UI Component libraries Lit, FAST, Stencil, Polymer Progressive enhancement Enhance native elements

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use autonomous custom elements. Why: they work in all browsers, including Safari.
  2. Name elements with a hyphen. Why: required by the specification.
  3. Use lowercase names. Why: required by the specification.
  4. Call super() first in the constructor. Why: required by the specification.
  5. Do not inspect attributes or children in the constructor. Why: they may not be available yet.
  6. Use connectedCallback for DOM-dependent initialization. Why: attributes and children are available.
  7. Use disconnectedCallback for cleanup. Why: prevents memory leaks.
  8. Use observedAttributes for reactive attributes. Why: standard way to react to changes.
  9. Attach event listeners in connectedCallback. Why: element may be disconnected and reconnected.
  10. Remove event listeners in disconnectedCallback. Why: prevents memory leaks.
  11. Use attachShadow() in the constructor. Why: shadow root should exist before connectedCallback.
  12. Use templates for shadow tree content. Why: declarative, parse-once.
  13. Use ElementInternals for form participation. Why: standard way to participate in forms.
  14. Use ElementInternals for ARIA. Why: standard way to set ARIA on custom elements.
  15. Use CSS custom properties for theming. Why: they cross the shadow boundary.
  16. Expose parts via part for external styling. Why: controlled customization.
  17. Test with assistive technology. Why: verify the accessibility tree.
  18. Handle the upgrade case. Why: elements may exist before the definition loads.
  19. Use customElements.whenDefined() for coordination. Why: ensures the element is ready.
  20. Avoid redefining custom elements. Why: names can only be defined once.
  21. Test on all target browsers. Why: customized built-in elements are not supported in Safari.
  22. Document the public API. Why: attributes, slots, parts, and events.
  23. Use semantic HTML inside the shadow tree. Why: accessibility and default styles.
  24. Consider lazy loading. Why: only load component scripts when needed.
  25. Audit components after framework upgrades. Why: integration may change.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing the Hyphen in the Name
docs.text:
customElements.define('myelement', MyElement); // ❌ Error

Why it's wrong: Custom element names must contain a hyphen.

✅ Correct:

customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Inspecting Attributes in the Constructor
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        console.log(this.getAttribute('name')); // ❌ May be null
    }
}

Why it's wrong: Attributes may not be available in the constructor.

✅ Correct:

class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        console.log(this.getAttribute('name')); // ✅ Available
    }
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Calling super() First
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }); // ❌ Error
        super();
    }
}

Why it's wrong: super() must be called before this.

✅ Correct:

class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
    }
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Redefining a Custom Element
docs.text:
customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);
customElements.define('my-element', AnotherElement); // ❌ Error

Why it's wrong: Names can only be defined once.

✅ Correct: Use a different name or check before defining.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Attaching Event Listeners Without Cleanup
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        window.addEventListener('resize', this.handleResize);
    }
    // No cleanup
}

Why it's wrong: Memory leak if the element is removed.

✅ Correct:

class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        window.addEventListener('resize', this.handleResize);
    }
    disconnectedCallback() {
        window.removeEventListener('resize', this.handleResize);
    }
    handleResize = () => { /* ... */ }
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Customized Built-in Elements in Safari
docs.text:
customElements.define('fancy-button', FancyButton, { extends: 'button' });

<button is="fancy-button">Click</button>

Why it's wrong: Safari does not support customized built-in elements.

✅ Correct: Use autonomous custom elements.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Handling Missing Attributes
docs.text:
class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = `<h2>${this.getAttribute('name')}</h2>`;
        // "null" if attribute is missing
    }
}

Why it's wrong: getAttribute returns null if the attribute is missing.

✅ Correct:

this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = `<h2>${this.getAttribute('name') ?? ''}</h2>`;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Shadow DOM
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        this.innerHTML = '<p>Hello</p>'; // Overwrites consumer content
    }
}

Why it's wrong: Overwrites consumer content; no encapsulation.

✅ Correct: Use shadow DOM and slots.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Registering the Element
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    // ...
}
// Missing: customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);

Why it's wrong: The element is not registered.

✅ Correct:

customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Accessing Shadow DOM Before It Exists
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
        this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.foo'); // null if no shadow root
    }
}

Why it's wrong: shadowRoot is null if attachShadow was not called.

✅ Correct: Call attachShadow in the constructor.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using innerHTML with User Input
docs.text:
this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = `<p>${userInput}</p>`;

Why it's wrong: XSS vulnerability.

✅ Correct: Use textContent for user input.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Custom elements add minimal overhead — the browser handles upgrade natively.
  • Shadow DOM styles are scoped — style matching is faster.
  • Templates are parsed once — cloning is cheap.
  • Lifecycle callbacks are cheap — avoid heavy work in connectedCallback.
  • Attribute observation is efficient — only observed attributes trigger callbacks.
  • Form-associated custom elements add minimal overhead.
  • Custom element definitions are loaded once.
  • Too many custom element instances — each has its own shadow root.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use templates for shadow tree content.
  2. Minimize work in connectedCallback.
  3. Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates.
  4. Debounce attribute change reactions.
  5. Cache shadow root references.
  6. Lazy-load custom element definitions.
  7. Avoid re-rendering the entire shadow tree.
  8. Use CSS containment.

docs.title: XSS in Custom Elements
docs.text: Custom elements are subject to the same XSS risks as any DOM code. Use textContent for user input; sanitize HTML with DOMPurify.

docs.title: Attribute Injection
docs.text: Attributes are parsed as strings. Do not pass untrusted content through attributes expecting it to be safe.

docs.title: Shadow DOM Is Not a Security Boundary
docs.text: Shadow DOM provides encapsulation, not security. Scripts inside the shadow tree run in the document context.

docs.title: Form Participation and CSRF
docs.text: Form-associated custom elements submit values with the form. Ensure CSRF protection is applied.

docs.title: Custom Element Names and DOM Clobbering
docs.text: Custom element names should not conflict with global identifiers. Use unique, specific names.

docs.title: ElementInternals and Accessibility
docs.text: Use ElementInternals for ARIA to ensure the element is exposed correctly to assistive technology.

docs.title: Deprecation and Versioning
docs.text: Once a custom element is defined, it cannot be redefined. Plan the API carefully.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements — inspect custom elements and their shadow roots.
  • Chrome DevTools → Console — test custom elements.
  • customElements.get('my-element') — check if an element is defined.
  • customElements.whenDefined('my-element') — wait for definition.
  • document.createElement('my-element') — create a custom element.
  • $0.shadowRoot — inspect the shadow root.
  • DevTools → Elements → Properties — inspect custom element properties.
  • DevTools → Console → console.dir($0) — inspect all properties.
  • Test lifecycle callbacks — add logging to each.
  • Test upgrade — create the element before defining it.
  • Test with document.createElement — different from parsing.
  • Test with frameworks — verify framework integration.
  • Test on multiple browsers — customized built-ins differ.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Reusable components — buttons, cards, modals.
  • Design systems — consistent, encapsulated components.
  • Framework interoperability — components that work anywhere.
  • Form controls — custom inputs with validation.
  • Third-party widgets — embeddable components.
  • Micro-frontends — isolated sub-applications.
  • Progressive enhancement — enhance native elements.
  • Web applications — modular, encapsulated UI.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use custom elements for one-off markup. Use plain HTML.
  • Do not use custom elements without a hyphen in the name. Invalid.
  • Do not inspect attributes in the constructor. Use connectedCallback.
  • Do not forget to call super() first. Required.
  • Do not redefine custom elements. Names can only be defined once.
  • Do not rely on customized built-in elements. Not supported in Safari.
  • Do not use shadow DOM as a security boundary. It is not one.
  • Do not put heavy work in connectedCallback. It blocks the main thread.
