docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Custom Elements v1 shipped in 2016 — the modern API (customElements.define()).
  • Custom Elements v0 had a different API — document.registerElement().
  • Custom element names must contain a hyphen — to prevent collisions with future HTML elements.
  • The hyphen rule dates back to the original specification — it ensures forward compatibility.
  • Safari was the last major browser to ship Custom Elements v1 — in Safari 10.1 (2017).
  • Safari does not support customized built-in elements — as of 2026.
  • Form-associated custom elements shipped in 2020 — attachInternals(), setFormValue().
  • ElementInternals can set ARIA roles and properties — for custom element accessibility.
  • The upgrade process handles elements created before the definition — the browser upgrades them.
  • customElements.whenDefined() returns a Promise — for coordinating initialization.
  • customElements.upgrade() forces an upgrade — used for elements in other documents.
  • Custom elements are the definition mechanism of Web Components — they bind everything else to a tag.
  • Lit, FAST, Stencil, and Polymer all use custom elements.
  • React, Vue, and Angular all support custom elements — with some caveats.
  • The is attribute is used for customized built-in elements.
  • The constructor must call super() first — a JavaScript requirement.
  • The constructor must not inspect attributes — they may not be available.
  • connectedCallback may be called multiple times — if the element is reconnected.
  • disconnectedCallback is where you clean up — remove listeners, cancel fetches.
  • Attribute names are case-insensitive in HTML — but the observed names must match.
  • The observed attributes list is static — declared once on the class.
  • Custom elements are baseline and universally supported — Chrome 54+, Firefox 63+, Safari 10.1+, Edge 79+.
  • The best custom element is the one that feels like a native element — no leaks, no surprises.
  • Custom elements are the native way to extend HTML — the platform's answer to framework components.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Custom Elements is the browser API for defining new HTML elements.
  • A custom element is a JavaScript class extending HTMLElement.
  • Register with customElements.define('my-element', MyElement).
  • Names must contain a hyphen and start with a lowercase letter.
  • Two flavors: autonomous (<my-element>) and customized built-in (<button is="my-button">).
  • Safari does not support customized built-in elements.
  • Five lifecycle callbacks: constructor, connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback, attributeChangedCallback, adoptedCallback.
  • observedAttributes declares which attributes trigger attributeChangedCallback.
  • The browser upgrades unknown elements when the definition loads.
  • Custom elements combine with templates, slots, and Shadow DOM.
  • Form-associated custom elements use ElementInternals to participate in forms.
  • ElementInternals also provides ARIA methods for accessibility.
  • CSS custom properties cross the shadow boundary for theming.
  • part and ::part() expose internals for external styling.
  • Custom elements are framework-agnostic — they work everywhere HTML works.
  • Custom elements are baseline and universally supported.
  • Use autonomous elements — Safari does not support customized built-ins.
  • Call super() first in the constructor.
  • Do not inspect attributes in the constructor — use connectedCallback.
  • Clean up in disconnectedCallback — remove listeners, cancel fetches.
  • Use templates and Shadow DOM for encapsulation.
  • Use slots for content projection.
  • Use ElementInternals for form participation and ARIA.
  • The best custom element is the one that feels like a native element — no leaks, no surprises.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM is the ability to define a shadow root directly in HTML — without JavaScript — by placing a <template> element with the shadowrootmode attribute as a child of the host element. The browser parses the template's content into a shadow root on the parent during HTML parsing, producing a fully-formed shadow tree before any script runs.

<my-card>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <style>
            .card {
                border: 1px solid #ccc;
                border-radius: 8px;
                padding: 1rem;
            }
        </style>
        <div class="card">
            <h2>Hello</h2>
            <p>This is inside a shadow root.</p>
        </div>
    </template>
</my-card>

Before Declarative Shadow DOM, creating a shadow root required JavaScript:

class MyCard extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).innerHTML = '...';
    }
}

With Declarative Shadow DOM, the shadow root exists immediately after parsing — no script, no flash of unstyled content (FOUC), no hydration delay. It is server-renderable, streaming-friendly, and progressive-enhancement-compatible.

Declarative Shadow DOM is the server-side rendering (SSR) story for Web Components — the missing piece that makes Web Components viable for content sites, e-commerce, and any page where JavaScript cannot be assumed.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM serves several essential purposes:

  • Server-side rendering (SSR) — shadow trees can be rendered on the server.
  • No FOUC — styles apply before the first paint.
  • Faster first paint — the shadow root is present immediately.
  • Progressive enhancement — components work without JavaScript.
  • Streaming-friendly — content can be streamed progressively.
  • SEO — shadow content is present in the initial HTML.
  • Accessibility — the accessibility tree is built correctly on load.
  • Hydration — custom elements upgrade into existing shadow roots.
  • Framework support — Lit SSR, Next.js, Astro, Remix, and others.

Declarative Shadow DOM is the rendering primitive that makes Web Components production-ready for server-driven applications.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Web Components
│
├── Templates              ← reusable markup
├── Slots                  ← content projection
├── Shadow DOM             ← style and structure encapsulation
├── Custom Elements        ← reusable component definitions
└── Declarative Shadow DOM ← server-rendered shadow roots (THIS CHAPTER)

Declarative Shadow DOM is the bridge between server-side rendering and client-side encapsulation. It lets the shadow tree exist in the HTML — and the custom element upgrade into it later.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Shadow DOM has one major limitation in a server-rendered world: it can only be created by JavaScript.

Before Declarative Shadow DOM, a Web Component's shadow root existed only after:

  1. The HTML was parsed.
  2. The JavaScript loaded.
  3. The custom element was defined.
  4. The element was upgraded.
  5. attachShadow() was called.
  6. The shadow tree was populated.

This produced a cascade of problems:

  • Flash of unstyled content (FOUC) — content rendered before the shadow root existed.
  • Slow first paint — first paint waited for JavaScript.
  • SEO concerns — shadow content was invisible to crawlers without JS execution.
  • No SSR — server-rendered HTML could not include shadow roots.
  • Progressive enhancement failure — components did not work without JavaScript.
  • Hydration mismatch — client-created shadow roots were not in the initial HTML.

For static sites, blogs, e-commerce, and any content-driven application, this was a fundamental blocker for adopting Web Components.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Shadow DOM required JavaScript No SSR FOUC on component load Visual jank First paint delayed Poor Core Web Vitals Shadow content invisible to crawlers SEO concerns No progressive enhancement Required JavaScript No streaming support Whole document needed Hydration mismatch Client-rendered content only

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM was proposed as a solution to the SSR problem. It was designed to let shadow roots be declared in HTML — parsed by the browser during normal HTML parsing — so that:

  • Shadow trees exist immediately.
  • Styles apply before first paint.
  • No JavaScript is required for initial render.
  • Crawlers see the shadow content.
  • Custom elements upgrade into existing shadow roots.

The specification shipped in stages:

  • Chrome 90 (April 2021) — the shadowroot attribute (later renamed).
  • Chrome 111 (March 2023) — the shadowrootmode attribute (final syntax).
  • Safari 16.4 (March 2023) — support for shadowrootmode.
  • Firefox 123 (February 2024) — support for shadowrootmode.

Additional attributes were added in 2024:

  • shadowrootdelegatesfocus — focus delegation.
  • shadowrootclonable — shadow root cloning.
  • shadowrootserializable — shadow root serialization.

In 2026, Declarative Shadow DOM is baseline and supported in all modern browsers. It is the standard mechanism for server-rendering Web Components and is used by Lit SSR, Astro, Next.js, Remix, and every modern framework that supports Web Components.

docs.title: The Minimal Declarative Shadow Root
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <p>Shadow content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Part Purpose <template shadowrootmode="open"> Declares a declarative shadow root The template's content Becomes the shadow tree The parent element Becomes the shadow host The template element Is removed after parsing

docs.title: The Two Modes
docs.text:
<!-- Open mode: accessible via element.shadowRoot -->
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <p>Open shadow root</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

<!-- Closed mode: not accessible via element.shadowRoot -->
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="closed">
        <p>Closed shadow root</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Mode element.shadowRoot Behavior open Returns the shadow root Accessible closed Returns null Hidden

docs.title: With Styles and Slots
docs.text:
<my-card>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <style>
            .card {
                border: 1px solid #ccc;
                border-radius: 8px;
                padding: 1rem;
                font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
            }
            .header {
                font-weight: bold;
                margin-bottom: 0.5rem;
            }
            ::slotted(h2) {
                margin: 0;
                color: #333;
            }
        </style>
        <div class="card">
            <div class="header">
                <slot name="title">Untitled</slot>
            </div>
            <div class="body">
                <slot>No content.</slot>
            </div>
        </div>
    </template>

    <h2 slot="title">Hello</h2>
    <p>This is the body.</p>
</my-card>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• The template's content becomes the shadow tree.
  • <slot> elements project light DOM content.
  • Styles are encapsulated in the shadow tree.
  • Light DOM children (outside the template) are the slotted content.

docs.title: The Full Attribute Set
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open"
              shadowrootdelegatesfocus
              shadowrootclonable
              shadowrootserializable>
        <p>Shadow content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Attribute Purpose shadowrootmode="open" Creates an open shadow root shadowrootmode="closed" Creates a closed shadow root shadowrootdelegatesfocus Host focus goes to the first focusable element shadowrootclonable Shadow root can be cloned via cloneNode() shadowrootserializable Shadow root can be serialized via getHTML()

docs.title: The shadowrootdelegatesfocus Attribute
docs.text:
<my-input>
    <template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootdelegatesfocus>
        <style>
            :host {
                display: inline-block;
                border: 1px solid #ccc;
                padding: 0.25rem;
                border-radius: 4px;
            }
            input {
                border: none;
                outline: none;
                font: inherit;
            }
        </style>
        <input type="text" placeholder="Type here">
    </template>
</my-input>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• shadowrootdelegatesfocus — when the host is focused, the first focusable element in the shadow root receives focus.
  • Useful for wrapping form controls.

docs.title: The shadowrootclonable Attribute
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootclonable>
        <p>Clonable shadow root</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

<script>
    const el = document.querySelector('my-element');
    const clone = el.cloneNode(true);
    console.log(clone.shadowRoot); // the cloned shadow root
</script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• shadowrootclonable — allows the shadow root to be cloned via cloneNode().
  • Without it, cloneNode() on the host does not clone the shadow root.

docs.title: The shadowrootserializable Attribute
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootserializable>
        <p>Serializable shadow root</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

<script>
    const el = document.querySelector('my-element');
    console.log(el.getHTML({ serializableShadowRoots: true }));
    // Includes the shadow root HTML
</script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• shadowrootserializable — allows the shadow root to be serialized via getHTML().
  • Enables server-side serialization and content extraction.

docs.title: The Custom Element Upgrade
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <p>Shadow content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

<script>
    class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
        connectedCallback() {
            console.log('Shadow root:', this.shadowRoot);
            // The shadow root already exists — no attachShadow needed
        }
    }
    customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);
</script>

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• The custom element does not call attachShadow().
  • The shadow root already exists from the declarative markup.
  • connectedCallback finds it via this.shadowRoot.

docs.title: The attachShadow() Error
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }); // ❌ Error if declarative shadow root exists
    }
}

Error: NotSupportedError: Shadow root cannot be created on a host which already hosts a shadow tree.

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
If the element has a declarative shadow root, calling attachShadow() throws. The component must check whether a shadow root already exists:

if (!this.shadowRoot) {
    this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
}

docs.title: The "SSR for Shadow DOM" Mental Model
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM is SSR for shadow roots:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CLIENT-ONLY SHADOW DOM (before DSD)         │
│  └── HTML parsed                             │
│  └── JavaScript loads                        │
│  └── Custom element defined                  │
│  └── attachShadow() called                   │
│  └── Shadow tree populated                   │
│  └── FOUC during this gap                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DECLARATIVE SHADOW DOM (with DSD)           │
│  └── HTML parsed                             │
│  └── Shadow tree created during parsing      │
│  └── Styles apply immediately                │
│  └── First paint is correct                  │
│  └── Custom element upgrades into it later   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Declarative Shadow DOM eliminates the client-side shadow DOM gap.

docs.title: The "Parsed, Not Executed" Mental Model
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM is parsed, not executed:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  <template shadowrootmode="open">            │
│  └── Parsed by the HTML parser               │
│  └── Recognized as a shadow root declaration │
│  └── Content becomes the shadow tree         │
│  └── Template element is removed             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

No JavaScript runs. No attachShadow() call. The shadow root is a parsing-time construct.

docs.title: The "The Template Is Consumed" Mental Model
docs.text:
Unlike normal <template> elements, a declarative shadow DOM template is consumed:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NORMAL <template>                           │
│  └── Stays in the DOM                        │
│  └── Content accessible via template.content │
│  └── Used for cloning                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  <template shadowrootmode="open">            │
│  └── Removed from the DOM                    │
│  └── Content becomes the shadow tree         │
│  └── The template element does not persist   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The declarative shadow DOM template is consumed by the parser. It is not a reusable template.

docs.title: The "Progressive Enhancement" Mental Model
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM enables progressive enhancement:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WITHOUT JAVASCRIPT                          │
│  └── Shadow tree is present                  │
│  └── Styles apply                            │
│  └── Content renders                         │
│  └── Slotted content projects                │
│  └── The page works                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WITH JAVASCRIPT                             │
│  └── Custom element upgrades                 │
│  └── Lifecycle callbacks run                 │
│  └── Interactivity is added                  │
│  └── The component is enhanced               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The component works without JavaScript and enhances with it.

docs.title: The "Hydration" Mental Model
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM is the hydration model for Web Components:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. SERVER RENDERS                           │
│  └── <my-element>                            │
│      <template shadowrootmode="open">        │
│        ...shadow content...                  │
│      </template>                             │
│      ...slotted content...                   │
│  └── Sent as HTML                            │
│                                              │
│  2. BROWSER PARSES                           │
│  └── Shadow root is created                  │
│  └── Content is rendered                     │
│  └── Styles apply                            │
│  └── No JavaScript required                  │
│                                              │
│  3. JAVASCRIPT LOADS                         │
│  └── Custom element is defined               │
│  └── Existing elements upgrade               │
│  └── Event listeners attach                  │
│  └── The component becomes interactive       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

There is no "hydration mismatch" because the shadow tree was never client-created.

docs.title: The "Streaming" Mental Model
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM is streaming-friendly:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STREAMED HTML                               │
│                                              │
│  <header>...</header>                        │
│  ─── flushed ───                             │
│  <my-card>                                   │
│    <template shadowrootmode="open">          │
│      ...shadow content...                    │
│    </template>                               │
│    ...slotted content...                     │
│  </my-card>                                  │
│  ─── flushed ───                             │
│  <footer>...</footer>                        │
│  ─── flushed ───                             │
│                                              │
│  Browser renders as chunks arrive.          │
│  Shadow roots exist as soon as parsed.      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

No need to wait for the full document — shadow roots render as they stream.

docs.title: The "Framework Interop" Mental Model
docs.text:
Declarative Shadow DOM works with any framework:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SERVER FRAMEWORKS                           │
│  ├── Next.js — RSC + DSD                     │
│  ├── Astro — partial hydration + DSD         │
│  ├── Remix — streaming + DSD                 │
│  ├── SvelteKit — SSR + DSD                   │
│  └── Lit SSR — first-class DSD               │
│                                              │
│  CLIENT FRAMEWORKS                           │
│  ├── React — web components + DSD            │
│  ├── Vue — web components + DSD              │
│  └── Angular — web components + DSD          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Declarative Shadow DOM is framework-agnostic — it is a platform primitive.

docs.title: Concept 1: The shadowrootmode Attribute
docs.text: Declares the shadow root mode: "open" or "closed". Required for declarative shadow DOM.

docs.title: Concept 2: The <template> Requirement
docs.text: The declarative shadow DOM must be a <template> element with shadowrootmode. No other element works.

docs.title: Concept 3: The Parent Element Is the Host
docs.text: The template's parent element becomes the shadow host.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Template Is Consumed
docs.text: After parsing, the template element is removed. The content lives in the shadow root.

docs.title: Concept 5: The Shadow Root Exists Immediately
docs.text: The shadow root is created during HTML parsing — before any script runs.

docs.title: Concept 6: No attachShadow() Call
docs.text: Custom elements must not call attachShadow() if a declarative shadow root exists.

docs.title: Concept 7: The Upgrade
docs.text: Custom elements upgrade into existing shadow roots. this.shadowRoot returns the declarative shadow root.

docs.title: Concept 8: shadowrootdelegatesfocus
docs.text: Delegates focus to the first focusable element in the shadow tree.

docs.title: Concept 9: shadowrootclonable
docs.text: Allows the shadow root to be cloned via cloneNode().

docs.title: Concept 10: shadowrootserializable
docs.text: Allows the shadow root to be serialized via getHTML().

docs.title: Concept 11: Streaming Support
docs.text: Declarative shadow roots can be streamed progressively.

docs.title: Concept 12: SSR Integration
docs.text: Server frameworks can generate declarative shadow DOM for web components.

docs.title: Concept 13: No FOUC
docs.text: Styles apply before first paint — no flash of unstyled content.

docs.title: Concept 14: SEO Benefits
docs.text: Shadow content is present in the initial HTML, visible to crawlers.

docs.title: Concept 15: Accessibility Benefits
docs.text: The accessibility tree is built correctly on load.

docs.title: Concept 16: Progressive Enhancement
docs.text: Components work without JavaScript and enhance with it.

docs.title: Concept 17: Hydration
docs.text: No hydration mismatch — the shadow tree was never client-created.

docs.title: Concept 18: Framework Support
docs.text: Lit SSR, Next.js, Astro, Remix, SvelteKit all support DSD.

docs.title: Concept 19: The Polyfill
docs.text: @webcomponents/template-shadowroot polyfills DSD for older browsers.

docs.title: Concept 20: The attachShadow() Guard
docs.text: Custom elements must check whether a shadow root exists before calling attachShadow().

docs.title: Concept 21: The shadowrootmode Values
docs.text: Only "open" and "closed" are valid.

docs.title: Concept 22: The closed Mode
docs.text: Closed mode is not a security boundary — DevTools can still access it.

docs.title: Concept 23: The Template Content Is a Shadow Tree
docs.text: The template's content becomes the shadow tree, not a document fragment.

docs.title: Concept 24: The Template Is Not Clonable
docs.text: Unlike normal templates, declarative shadow DOM templates cannot be cloned after parsing.

docs.title: Concept 25: The Upgrade Triggers
docs.text: The upgrade happens when: - The element is created after the definition. - The definition loads after the element exists.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Parsing a Declarative Shadow Root
docs.text:
1.  HTML parser encounters <my-element>.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser encounters <template shadowrootmode="open">.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser recognizes the shadowrootmode attribute.
    │
    ▼
4.  Parser creates a shadow root on <my-element>.
    │
    ▼
5.  Parser parses the template's content directly into the shadow root.
    │
    ▼
6.  Parser removes the template element from the DOM.
    │
    ▼
7.  Parser continues with any remaining light DOM content.
    │
    ▼
8.  Shadow root is live and rendered.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Custom Element Upgrade
docs.text:
1.  HTML is parsed; declarative shadow root exists.
    │
    ▼
2.  Custom element definition loads.
    │
    ▼
3.  customElements.define('my-element', MyElement) is called.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser upgrades existing <my-element> elements:
    │   ├── Changes prototype
    │   ├── Runs constructor
    │   ├── Runs attributeChangedCallback
    │   └── Runs connectedCallback
    │
    ▼
5.  The element finds its shadow root already exists.
    │
    ▼
6.  The component skips attachShadow().
    │
    ▼
7.  The component attaches listeners, fetches data, etc.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Full Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Server renders HTML with declarative shadow DOM.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser parses HTML.
    │
    ▼
3.  Shadow root is created during parsing.
    │
    ▼
4.  First paint with correct styles.
    │
    ▼
5.  JavaScript loads.
    │
    ▼
6.  Custom element is defined.
    │
    ▼
7.  Element upgrades.
    │
    ▼
8.  connectedCallback runs.
    │
    ▼
9.  Event listeners attach.
    │
    ▼
10. Component is interactive.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The getHTML() Method
docs.text:
const html = element.getHTML({ serializableShadowRoots: true });

1.  Called on an element.
    │
    ▼
2.  Walks the element's subtree.
    │
    ▼
3.  If the element has a serializable shadow root:
    │   └── Serializes the shadow root's content.
    │
    ▼
4.  Returns the HTML with shadow content embedded.

docs.title: The Parser's Shadow Root Creation
docs.text:
When the parser encounters <template shadowrootmode="open">:

  1. It checks if the parent element is a valid shadow host.
  2. It creates a shadow root on the parent.
  3. It switches to a shadow tree parsing mode.
  4. It parses the template's content into the shadow root.
  5. It does not create a <template> element in the tree.
  6. It removes the template from the DOM.

docs.title: The shadowrootmode Handling
docs.text:
The shadowrootmode attribute is a parser directive:

  • It is read during parsing.
  • It determines the mode of the shadow root.
  • It is not reflected to the DOM as a property.

docs.title: The Attribute Set
docs.text: Attribute Effect shadowrootmode "open" or "closed" shadowrootdelegatesfocus Focus delegation shadowrootclonable Shadow root cloning shadowrootserializable Shadow root serialization

docs.title: The Parser Algorithm
docs.text:
The full algorithm:

  1. Parser encounters <template> with shadowrootmode.
  2. Validate the parent element is a shadow host (any element can be a shadow host).
  3. Validate that no shadow root already exists on the parent.
  4. Create a shadow root on the parent with the given mode.
  5. Set the shadow root's flags (delegates focus, clonable, serializable).
  6. Parse the template's content into the shadow root.
  7. Remove the template element from the DOM.

docs.title: The attachShadow() Error
docs.text:
If attachShadow() is called on a host with a declarative shadow root:

NotSupportedError: Shadow root cannot be created on a host which already hosts a shadow tree.

The custom element must check:

if (!this.shadowRoot) {
    this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
}

docs.title: The Upgrade Algorithm
docs.text:
When a custom element is defined:

  1. For each element matching the tag name:
  2. Change the prototype from HTMLElement to the custom class.
  3. Run constructor.
  4. Run attributeChangedCallback for initial attributes.
  5. Run connectedCallback if the element is connected.

If a declarative shadow root exists:

  • this.shadowRoot returns it.
  • constructor must not call attachShadow().

docs.title: The getHTML() Serialization
docs.text:
The getHTML() method (added in 2024) serializes an element's subtree, including:

  • Light DOM children.
  • Serializable shadow roots (if serializableShadowRoots: true).
element.getHTML({ serializableShadowRoots: true });

docs.title: The Polyfill
docs.text:
@webcomponents/template-shadowroot polyfills DSD for older browsers:

<script type="module">
    import { polyfill } from '@webcomponents/template-shadowroot';
    polyfill();
</script>

The polyfill:

  1. Finds all <template shadowrootmode> elements.
  2. Creates shadow roots on their parents.
  3. Moves the content into the shadow roots.
  4. Removes the templates.

docs.title: The Polyfill's Timing
docs.text: The polyfill must run before custom elements upgrade — otherwise, the element may not find the shadow root.

docs.title: The declarativeShadowRoot Property
docs.text:
The property shadowRoot on the host returns the declarative shadow root:

element.shadowRoot; // the shadow root

docs.title: The Shadow Root Mode Is Immutable
docs.text: Once created, the shadow root mode cannot be changed.

docs.title: The Declarative Shadow DOM Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Server renders HTML with declarative shadow DOM.
    │
    ▼
2.  HTML is sent to the browser.
    │
    ▼
3.  Browser parses HTML.
    │
    ▼
4.  Shadow root is created during parsing.
    │
    ▼
5.  Content is parsed into the shadow root.
    │
    ▼
6.  Template is removed from the DOM.
    │
    ▼
7.  First paint with correct styles.
    │
    ▼
8.  JavaScript loads.
    │
    ▼
9.  Custom element is defined.
    │
    ▼
10. Element upgrades into the shadow root.
    │
    ▼
11. connectedCallback runs.
    │
    ▼
12. Event listeners attach.
    │
    ▼
13. Component is interactive.

docs.title: The Server-Side Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Server renders the component.
    │
    ▼
2.  Server generates the declarative shadow DOM.
    │
    ▼
3.  Server sends the HTML.
    │
    ▼
4.  Browser parses and renders immediately.

docs.title: The Client-Side Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Client framework hydrates.
    │
    ▼
2.  Custom element upgrades.
    │
    ▼
3.  Event listeners attach.
    │
    ▼
4.  Component is interactive.

docs.title: The Polyfill Workflow
docs.text:
1.  HTML loaded.
    │
    ▼
2.  Polyfill script runs.
    │
    ▼
3.  Polyfill finds templates.
    │
    ▼
4.  Polyfill creates shadow roots.
    │
    ▼
5.  Polyfill removes templates.
    │
    ▼
6.  Custom elements upgrade.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Declarative Shadow Root
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <style>
            :host {
                display: block;
                padding: 1rem;
                border: 1px solid #ccc;
                border-radius: 8px;
            }
        </style>
        <p>Shadow content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

Code Breakdown:

  • The <template shadowrootmode="open"> creates a shadow root on <my-element>.
  • The content becomes the shadow tree.
  • Styles are encapsulated.

docs.title: Example 2: SSR with a Custom Element
docs.text:
<my-card>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <style>
            .card {
                border: 1px solid #ccc;
                border-radius: 8px;
                padding: 1rem;
            }
        </style>
        <div class="card">
            <h2><slot name="title"></slot></h2>
            <slot></slot>
        </div>
    </template>

    <h2 slot="title">Hello</h2>
    <p>World</p>
</my-card>

<script>
    class MyCard extends HTMLElement {
        connectedCallback() {
            // The shadow root already exists
            console.log(this.shadowRoot);
        }
    }
    customElements.define('my-card', MyCard);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The server renders the declarative shadow root.
  • The custom element upgrades into it.
  • No FOUC.

docs.title: Example 3: Focus Delegation
docs.text:
<my-input>
    <template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootdelegatesfocus>
        <style>
            :host {
                display: inline-block;
                border: 1px solid #ccc;
                padding: 0.25rem;
                border-radius: 4px;
            }
            input {
                border: none;
                outline: none;
                font: inherit;
            }
        </style>
        <input type="text" placeholder="Type here">
    </template>
</my-input>

Code Breakdown:

  • shadowrootdelegatesfocus — when the host is focused, the input receives focus.
  • Useful for wrapping form controls.

docs.title: Example 4: Clonable Shadow Root
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootclonable>
        <p>Clonable content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

<script>
    const el = document.querySelector('my-element');
    const clone = el.cloneNode(true);
    console.log(clone.shadowRoot.innerHTML); // "<p>Clonable content</p>"
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • shadowrootclonable — the shadow root is cloned via cloneNode().
  • Without it, the clone would not have a shadow root.

docs.title: Example 5: Serializable Shadow Root
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootserializable>
        <p>Serializable content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

<script>
    const el = document.querySelector('my-element');
    console.log(el.getHTML({ serializableShadowRoots: true }));
    // "<my-element><template shadowrootmode=open>...</template></my-element>"
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • shadowrootserializable — the shadow root is serialized via getHTML().
  • Enables server-side serialization.

docs.title: Example 6: Lit SSR with Declarative Shadow DOM
docs.text:
import { LitElement, html } from 'lit';
import { render } from '@lit-labs/ssr';

class MyCard extends LitElement {
    static properties = { name: { type: String } };

    render() {
        return html`
            <style>
                .card { border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 1rem; }
            </style>
            <div class="card">
                <h2>${this.name}</h2>
                <slot></slot>
            </div>
        `;
    }
}

customElements.define('my-card', MyCard);

// Server
const result = render(html`<my-card name="Alice">Content</my-card>`);
// Produces declarative shadow DOM markup

Code Breakdown:

  • Lit SSR generates declarative shadow DOM.
  • The server sends the rendered HTML.
  • The client hydrates.

docs.title: Example 7: Astro Component with DSD
docs.text:
---
// MyCard.astro
const { name } = Astro.props;
---

<my-card>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <style>
            .card { border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 1rem; }
        </style>
        <div class="card">
            <h2>{name}</h2>
            <slot></slot>
        </div>
    </template>
    <slot />
</my-card>

Code Breakdown:

  • Astro renders the declarative shadow DOM at build time.
  • The client hydrates the custom element.
  • Zero JavaScript for the initial render.

docs.title: Example 8: Polyfill for Older Browsers
docs.text:
<script type="module">
    import { polyfill } from '@webcomponents/template-shadowroot';
    polyfill();
</script>

<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <p>Shadow content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

<script type="module">
    class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
        connectedCallback() {
            console.log(this.shadowRoot);
        }
    }
    customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The polyfill creates shadow roots for browsers without native DSD support.
  • It runs before the custom element definition.

docs.title: Example 9: Streaming SSR
docs.text:
// Express-style streaming
res.write('<html><body>');
res.write('<my-card>');
res.write('<template shadowrootmode="open">');
res.write('<style>.card { border: 1px solid #ccc; }</style>');
res.write('<div class="card">');
res.write('<slot></slot>');
res.write('</div>');
res.write('</template>');
res.write('<p>Card content</p>');
res.write('</my-card>');
res.write('</body></html>');
res.end();

Code Breakdown:

  • The server streams the declarative shadow DOM.
  • The browser parses and renders each chunk as it arrives.
  • No need to wait for the full document.

docs.title: Example 10: Complete Custom Element with DSD and Hydration
docs.text:
<my-counter>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <style>
            .counter {
                display: flex;
                align-items: center;
                gap: 1rem;
                font-family: system-ui;
            }
            button {
                padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
                border: 1px solid #ccc;
                border-radius: 4px;
                cursor: pointer;
                font: inherit;
            }
            .value { font-size: 1.5rem; font-weight: bold; }
        </style>
        <div class="counter">
            <button class="decrement">-</button>
            <span class="value">0</span>
            <button class="increment">+</button>
        </div>
    </template>
</my-counter>

<script>
    class MyCounter extends HTMLElement {
        constructor() {
            super();
            // Do NOT call attachShadow — it already exists
        }

        connectedCallback() {
            // Shadow root exists from the declarative markup
            this._value = 0;
            this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.decrement')
                .addEventListener('click', () => this.decrement());
            this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.increment')
                .addEventListener('click', () => this.increment());
        }

        increment() {
            this._value++;
            this.updateValue();
        }

        decrement() {
            this._value--;
            this.updateValue();
        }

        updateValue() {
            this.shadowRoot.querySelector('.value').textContent = this._value;
        }
    }

    customElements.define('my-counter', MyCounter);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The declarative shadow root provides the initial HTML.
  • The custom element upgrades into it.
  • Event listeners attach in connectedCallback.
  • The component is interactive after JavaScript loads.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Why DSD Helps Server-rendered apps SSR for Web Components Static sites Pre-rendered shadow DOM E-commerce Product cards rendered on server Blogs Content visible to crawlers Design systems Components work without JS Progressive enhancement Graceful degradation Streaming SSR Progressive rendering Micro-frontends Isolated server-rendered components Documentation SSR for component docs PWAs Fast first paint

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use shadowrootmode="open" by default. Why: closed offers no security benefit.
  2. Do not call attachShadow() in the constructor if a declarative shadow root exists. Why: it throws an error.
  3. Check this.shadowRoot before calling attachShadow(). Why: supports both DSD and client-only rendering.
  4. Use shadowrootdelegatesfocus for form controls. Why: better UX.
  5. Use shadowrootclonable when cloning is needed. Why: enables shadow root cloning.
  6. Use shadowrootserializable for SSR. Why: enables serialization.
  7. Render declarative shadow DOM on the server. Why: no FOUC, faster first paint.
  8. Stream declarative shadow DOM. Why: progressive rendering.
  9. Use the polyfill for older browsers. Why: shadowrootmode support varies.
  10. Load the polyfill before custom elements. Why: it must create shadow roots before upgrade.
  11. Do not rely on closed mode for security. Why: it is not a security boundary.
  12. Test with SSR frameworks. Why: Lit SSR, Astro, Next.js have different behavior.
  13. Test the upgrade path. Why: verify the element finds its shadow root.
  14. Test without JavaScript. Why: progressive enhancement.
  15. Test accessibility. Why: verify the accessibility tree is correct.
  16. Test with screen readers. Why: verify announcements.
  17. Test with SEO tools. Why: verify crawlers see the content.
  18. Avoid inline scripts in DSD content. Why: they run when cloned (rare).
  19. Keep the shadow tree small. Why: it is part of the initial HTML.
  20. Document the component's DSD support. Why: consumers need to know.
  21. Use framework-specific SSR tools. Why: they generate correct DSD.
  22. Audit DSD after framework upgrades. Why: SSR output may change.
  23. Test streaming. Why: verify chunks render correctly.
  24. Test with shadowrootclonable and shadowrootserializable. Why: verify they work as expected.
  25. Consider the total HTML size. Why: DSD increases HTML payload.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Calling attachShadow() in the Constructor
docs.text:
class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }); // ❌ Error if DSD exists
    }
}

Why it's wrong: Throws NotSupportedError if a declarative shadow root exists.

✅ Correct:

class MyElement extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
        super();
        if (!this.shadowRoot) {
            this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
        }
    }
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing shadowrootmode
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template>
        <p>Not a shadow root</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

Why it's wrong: Without shadowrootmode, the template is a normal template — not a shadow root.

✅ Correct:

<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">
        <p>Shadow content</p>
    </template>
</my-element>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using DSD Without the Polyfill
docs.text:
<my-element>
    <template shadowrootmode="open">...</template>
</my-element>

Why it's wrong: Older browsers do not support shadowrootmode.

✅ Correct: Include the polyfill.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Loading the Polyfill After Custom Elements
docs.text:
<script type="module">
    class MyElement extends HTMLElement { }
    customElements.define('my-element', MyElement);
</script>
<script type="module">
    import { polyfill } from '@webcomponents/template-shadowroot';
    polyfill();
</script>

Why it's wrong: The custom element upgrades before the shadow root exists.

✅ Correct: Load the polyfill first.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using closed Mode for Security
docs.text:
<template shadowrootmode="closed">
    <p>Secret content</p>
</template>

Why it's wrong: closed is not a security boundary — DevTools can access it.

✅ Correct: Use open unless you have a specific reason.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing Without JavaScript
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: DSD is designed for progressive enhancement. If the component requires JavaScript, you lose the benefit.

✅ Correct: Test the page with JavaScript disabled.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing the Upgrade
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The upgrade path may fail silently.

✅ Correct: Test with the custom element definition loaded after the HTML.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring HTML Size
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: DSD increases the initial HTML payload significantly.

✅ Correct: Measure the HTML size and consider lazy loading.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using DSD for Components That Don't Need It
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: DSD adds complexity. Simple components may not need it.

✅ Correct: Use DSD for SSR-critical components.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Include DSD in the Server Response
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The client-only fallback requires JavaScript, defeating the purpose.

✅ Correct: Ensure the server renders the DSD.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• DSD eliminates FOUC — no flash of unstyled content.
  • DSD improves first paint — content renders immediately.
  • DSD increases HTML size — the shadow tree is in the initial HTML.
  • DSD is streaming-friendly — chunks render progressively.
  • DSD reduces JavaScript payload — less client-side rendering.
  • DSD avoids hydration mismatch — the shadow tree exists before JavaScript.
  • DSD improves LCP — the LCP element may be inside a shadow tree.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Stream DSD for large pages.
  2. Keep shadow trees small.
  3. Lazy-load non-critical components.
  4. Use shadowrootserializable for caching.
  5. Measure the HTML payload.
  6. Test with slow networks.
  7. Test with low-end devices.
  8. Monitor Core Web Vitals.

docs.title: closed Mode Is Not a Security Boundary
docs.text: As with client-side shadow DOM, closed mode hides the shadow root but does not prevent access.

docs.title: XSS in DSD
docs.text:
DSD content is parsed HTML. If it contains user input without escaping, XSS is possible.

Defense: Sanitize user input before including it in DSD.

docs.title: CSP and DSD
docs.text: DSD is subject to CSP. Inline styles and scripts are still blocked by strict CSP unless nonces or hashes are used.

docs.title: SSR and Injection
docs.text:
If the server generates DSD from user input, escape it.

Defense: Use a templating engine with auto-escaping.

docs.title: DSD and Trusted Types
docs.text: Trusted Types may be required for DSD generation if the server uses innerHTML-style APIs.

docs.title: Hydration and Security
docs.text: Do not put sensitive data in DSD that should only be available to authenticated users.

docs.title: shadowrootserializable and Data Leakage
docs.text: shadowrootserializable allows shadow root serialization. Ensure the shadow tree does not contain sensitive data.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements — DSD shadow roots appear in the tree.
  • Chrome DevTools → Elements → Shadow root — expand the shadow tree.
  • $0.shadowRoot — inspect the shadow root.
  • $0.shadowRoot.innerHTML — inspect the shadow tree's HTML.
  • Check the raw HTML — view-source: shows the DSD markup.
  • Check the DOM — the template element is removed from the DOM.
  • document.querySelectorAll('template[shadowrootmode]') — should return empty (templates are consumed).
  • customElements.whenDefined('my-element') — wait for definition.
  • Check the upgrade — verify the element upgraded.
  • Test with JavaScript disabled — verify DSD renders.
  • Test with a slow connection — verify streaming.
  • Test accessibility — DevTools → Accessibility panel.
  • Test with screen readers.
  • Test SEO — Google Search Console, Rich Results Test.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Server-rendered apps — SSR for Web Components.
  • Static sites — pre-rendered shadow DOM.
  • Content sites — blogs, docs, marketing.
  • E-commerce — product cards on the server.
  • Progressive enhancement — components without JS.
  • Streaming SSR — progressive rendering.
  • SEO-critical pages — shadow content visible to crawlers.
  • Design systems — SSR components.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use DSD for client-only components. Use attachShadow().
  • Do not use DSD if the component is not server-rendered. It adds no benefit.
  • Do not use DSD without the polyfill for older browsers.
  • Do not use DSD for tiny components. The HTML cost may not be worth it.
  • Do not use DSD for data that changes frequently. Use client-side rendering.
  • Do not use closed mode for security.
  • Do not forget to test the upgrade.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Declarative Shadow DOM was originally called shadowroot — renamed to shadowrootmode in Chrome 111.
  • Chrome 90 shipped the first version — April 2021.
  • Chrome 111 standardized the syntax — March 2023.
  • Safari 16.4 shipped support — March 2023.
  • Firefox 123 shipped support — February 2024.
  • shadowrootdelegatesfocus, shadowrootclonable, and shadowrootserializable were added in 2024.
  • DSD eliminates FOUC — no flash of unstyled content.
  • DSD is parsed, not executed — no JavaScript needed.
  • The template element is consumed — it is removed from the DOM.
  • The shadow root exists before any script runs.
  • The custom element upgrades into the existing shadow root.
  • attachShadow() throws if a declarative shadow root exists.
  • DSD is framework-agnostic — works with any server framework.
  • Lit SSR generates DSD — first-class support.
  • Astro uses DSD for Web Components — partial hydration.
  • Next.js supports DSD in React Server Components.
  • DSD works with streaming SSR — progressive rendering.
  • The polyfill @webcomponents/template-shadowroot supports older browsers.
  • DSD improves LCP — content is in the initial HTML.
  • DSD is the SSR story for Web Components — the missing piece for production adoption.
  • DSD makes Web Components viable for content sites — blogs, e-commerce, marketing.
  • DSD is progressive enhancement for components — works without JavaScript.
  • DSD is baseline and supported in all modern browsers.
  • The best DSD is invisible to the consumer — they just write HTML.
  • DSD is the future of Web Components on the server — no framework required.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Declarative Shadow DOM lets shadow roots be defined in HTML — no JavaScript required.
  • The syntax is <template shadowrootmode="open"> as a child of the host.
  • The template is consumed by the parser — it is removed from the DOM.
  • The shadow root exists immediately — before any script runs.
  • The custom element upgrades into the existing shadow root.
  • attachShadow() throws if a declarative shadow root exists.
  • Check this.shadowRoot before calling attachShadow().
  • shadowrootmode="open" or "closed" — the mode of the shadow root.
  • shadowrootdelegatesfocus — focus delegation.
  • shadowrootclonable — shadow root cloning.
  • shadowrootserializable — shadow root serialization.
  • DSD eliminates FOUC — styles apply before first paint.
  • DSD is streaming-friendly — progressive rendering.
  • DSD improves LCP — the LCP element may be in a shadow tree.
  • DSD is SEO-friendly — shadow content is in the initial HTML.
  • DSD is progressive enhancement — works without JavaScript.
  • DSD is the SSR story for Web Components.
  • Lit SSR, Astro, Next.js, Remix, and SvelteKit support DSD.
  • The @webcomponents/template-shadowroot polyfill supports older browsers.
  • DSD is baseline and supported in all modern browsers.
  • DSD is the future of Web Components on the server — no framework required.
  • The best DSD is invisible to the consumer — they just write HTML.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The HTML Validator is a tool that checks an HTML document against a formal specification — typically the WHATWG HTML Living Standard or a W3C Recommendation — and reports any deviations as errors, warnings, or info messages. It is the mechanism by which developers verify that their markup conforms to the standard before deploying it.

<!-- Valid -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Valid Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <p>Hello, world!</p>
</body>
</html>

<!-- Invalid: missing DOCTYPE, unclosed <p>, unknown element -->
<html>
<head>
    <title>Invalid Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <p>Hello, world!
    <foo>Unknown element</foo>
</body>

The validator is the first line of defense against malformed HTML. It catches the errors that the browser silently recovers from — missing DOCTYPEs, unclosed tags, invalid nesting, deprecated attributes, unknown elements, and more.

The most widely used validator is the W3C Nu HTML Checker (also called the W3C Markup Validation Service), available at validator.w3.org and validator.nu. It is the reference implementation of HTML validation, maintained by the W3C and used by millions of developers, CI/CD pipelines, and content management systems.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
HTML Validator serves several essential purposes:

  • Standards compliance — verifies markup against the HTML specification.
  • Error detection — catches issues browsers silently recover from.
  • Cross-browser consistency — valid HTML behaves the same in every browser.
  • Accessibility improvement — many validation errors are also accessibility failures.
  • SEO benefits — valid markup is easier for search engines to parse.
  • Maintainability — valid HTML is easier to debug and modify.
  • Security — validation catches some XSS-enabling patterns.
  • Automation — integrates into CI/CD pipelines for continuous verification.

The validator is the first tool a developer should run after writing HTML. It is fast, free, and catches errors before they reach production.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Validation
│
├── HTML Validator         ← markup correctness (THIS CHAPTER)
├── Common Errors          ← frequent validation errors
├── Accessibility Validation ← automated a11y checks
├── Browser Compatibility  ← cross-browser testing
└── Debugging HTML         ← tools and techniques

The HTML Validator is the foundation of the validation stack. Every other validation tool — accessibility checkers, browser compatibility testers, performance audits — builds on valid HTML.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTML is forgiving. Browsers never reject a page — they recover from every error, no matter how severe. A missing closing tag, an unquoted attribute, an unknown element — the browser handles it silently, produces a DOM tree, and renders the page.

This is a feature of the web. But it is also a trap. Because browsers never complain:

  • Developers do not know their HTML is broken.
  • Errors accumulate silently over time.
  • Bugs appear in production with no obvious cause.
  • Cross-browser behavior diverges on edge cases.
  • Accessibility tools cannot interpret malformed markup.
  • Search engines struggle with ambiguous structure.
  • Security issues hide in malformed patterns.

The HTML Validator exists to surface these errors — to tell the developer what the browser silently recovers from. It is the compiler error that the browser refuses to show you.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No validation tooling Developers had no feedback Browsers recovered silently Errors accumulated unnoticed Cross-browser bugs Same HTML rendered differently Accessibility failures Malformed markup broke assistive tech SEO issues Search engines struggled with malformed structure Security vulnerabilities Malformed patterns enabled XSS Manual validation Error-prone and time-consuming

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The W3C Markup Validation Service launched in December 1997 as one of the W3C's earliest tools. It was designed to solve a growing problem in the early web: pages were written in wildly inconsistent ways, and there was no way to check whether they conformed to the HTML specifications.

The validator initially checked against HTML 3.2 and later HTML 4.01. When HTML5 was proposed, the validator was updated to support the new standard, and in 2014, the Nu HTML Checker was introduced as a modern replacement. The Nu validator is now the primary validation service, with the older validator used for HTML4 and XHTML.

The validator has evolved with the web:

  • 1997 — W3C Markup Validation Service launches.
  • 2008 — HTML5 support added.
  • 2014 — Nu HTML Checker released.
  • 2016+ — Validator integrates with the WHATWG HTML Living Standard.
  • 2020s — CI/CD integrations, API access, and editor plugins.

In 2026, the W3C Nu HTML Checker is the reference implementation of HTML validation. It is used by:

  • W3C — validator.w3.org.
  • Google — for indexing and quality signals.
  • Mozilla — Firefox tooling.
  • Editors — VS Code, Sublime, Atom plugins.
  • CI/CD — GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins.
  • CMSs — WordPress, Drupal, Joomla.
  • Frameworks — server-side rendering checks.

docs.title: The W3C Validator UI
docs.text:
The simplest way to validate HTML is the online service:

1.  Visit validator.w3.org
2.  Enter a URL, upload a file, or paste HTML
3.  Click "Check"
4.  Review the results

docs.title: The Results Format
docs.text:
The validator returns a report:

Error: Element "foo" not allowed as child of element "body" in this context.
  → Line 8, Column 5
  → <foo>Unknown element</foo>

Each message includes:

  • Severity — Error, Warning, or Info.
  • Description — what is wrong.
  • Location — line and column.
  • Source — the offending markup.

docs.title: The Validator API
docs.text:
The Nu validator can be used programmatically:

curl -H "Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8" \
     --data-binary @index.html \
     "https://validator.w3.org/nu/?out=json"

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• -H "Content-Type: ..." — declares the content type.
  • --data-binary @index.html — sends the file.
  • ?out=json — requests JSON output.
  • The response contains the validation messages.

docs.title: The JSON Output
docs.text:
{
    "messages": [
        {
            "type": "error",
            "lastLine": 8,
            "lastColumn": 30,
            "message": "Element \"foo\" not allowed as child of element \"body\" in this context."
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text: Field Meaning type error, info, or warning lastLine The line number lastColumn The column number message The human-readable description

docs.title: Common Validation Commands
docs.text:
# Validate a local file
curl -H "Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8" \
     --data-binary @index.html \
     "https://validator.w3.org/nu/?out=json"

# Validate a URL
curl "https://validator.w3.org/nu/?doc=https://example.com&out=json"

# Validate with a specific parser
curl -H "Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8" \
     --data-binary @index.html \
     "https://validator.w3.org/nu/?out=json&parser=html5"

docs.title: The out Parameter
docs.text: Value Output format json JSON xml XML gnu GNU error format text Plain text

docs.title: The parser Parameter
docs.text: Value Standard html5 HTML5 / HTML Living Standard html4 HTML 4.01 xhtml XHTML 1.0 / 1.1 xml XML

docs.title: The showsource Parameter
docs.text:
?showsource=yes

Includes the source in the output.

docs.title: The level Parameter
docs.text:
?level=error
?level=warning

Restricts output to specific severities.

docs.title: A GitHub Actions Example
docs.text:
name: HTML Validation
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Validate HTML
        uses: Cyb3r-Jak3/html5validator-action@v7
        with:
          root: public/
          format: text

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• Cyb3r-Jak3/html5validator-action — a GitHub Action for HTML validation.
  • root: public/ — the directory to validate.
  • format: text — the output format.

docs.title: A VS Code Extension Example
docs.text:
1.  Install "HTMLHint" or "vscode-html-validate"
2.  Open an HTML file
3.  Errors appear inline
4.  The Problems panel lists all issues

docs.title: The Validator's Error Messages
docs.text:
Common message types:

Message Meaning Element X not allowed as child of element Y Invalid nesting End tag X seen, but there were open elements Unclosed tags Duplicate attribute X Attribute repeated Attribute X not allowed on element Y Invalid attribute Element X is obsolete Deprecated element The document is not mappable to XML Unquoted attributes Bad value X for attribute Y Invalid attribute value An img element must have an alt attribute Missing accessibility The first child of a <ul> should be <li> Structural issue The document has no document element Missing <html> Start tag seen without seeing a doctype first Missing DOCTYPE

docs.title: The "Compiler Error" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the HTML Validator as a compiler for HTML:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  COMPILER (C++, Rust, Go)                    │
│  └── Rejects invalid code                    │
│  └── Reports errors with line numbers        │
│  └── Refuses to run if errors exist          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  HTML VALIDATOR                              │
│  └── Reports invalid HTML                    │
│  └── Reports errors with line numbers        │
│  └── Does NOT refuse to render               │
│  └── The browser still renders it            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The validator is like a compiler — but the browser is like an interpreter that never refuses to run. You need the validator to see the errors.

docs.title: The "Silent Recovery" Mental Model
docs.text:
The browser silently recovers from every error. The validator shouts about every error:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BROWSER                                     │
│  └── Sees <p>Hello<div>World</div>            │
│  └── Silently closes <p>                     │
│  └── Renders the page                        │
│  └── Says nothing                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  VALIDATOR                                   │
│  └── Sees <p>Hello<div>World</div>            │
│  └── Reports: "Element <div> not allowed      │
│       as child of <p>. Line 5, Column 10."    │
│  └── Says everything                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The validator reveals what the browser hides.

docs.title: The "Three Severities" Mental Model
docs.text:
The validator produces three severities:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ERROR                                       │
│  └── Violates the specification              │
│  └── Must be fixed for validity              │
│  └── Example: <div> inside <p>               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WARNING                                     │
│  └── Suspicious or potentially problematic   │
│  └── Should be reviewed                      │
│  └── Example: <script> with no src           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  INFO                                        │
│  └── Informational, not a problem            │
│  └── Example: The document uses HTML5         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Errors are the most important. Warnings are advisory. Info is contextual.

docs.title: The "Validation vs. Recovery" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  VALIDATION                                  │
│  └── Static analysis of source               │
│  └── Checks against the specification        │
│  └── Reports all deviations                  │
│  └── Does not consider runtime behavior      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  RECOVERY                                    │
│  └── Runtime behavior of the browser         │
│  └── Handles malformed input                 │
│  └── Produces a DOM tree regardless          │
│  └── Hides errors from the developer         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Validation catches errors before recovery is needed.

docs.title: The "Contract" Mental Model
docs.text:
Valid HTML is a contract:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  YOU PROMISE                                 │
│  └── To write conforming HTML                 │
│                                              │
│  THE BROWSER PROMISES                        │
│  └── To render it consistently                │
│  └── In every browser                         │
│  └── With predictable behavior                │
│  └── To assistive technology correctly        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When you break the contract, the browser still renders — but the behavior is no longer guaranteed.

docs.title: The "Prerequisite for Everything" Mental Model
docs.text:
Validation is a prerequisite for other quality checks:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  VALIDATION                                  │
│  └── Markup is correct                       │
│                                              │
│  ACCESSIBILITY                               │
│  └── Screen readers can interpret it         │
│                                              │
│  SEO                                          │
│  └── Search engines can parse it             │
│                                              │
│  PERFORMANCE                                 │
│  └── The parser is efficient                  │
│                                              │
│  SECURITY                                    │
│  └── Malformed patterns are absent            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Without valid HTML, every other quality check is harder.

docs.text: Informational messages. Not problems.

docs.text: The Nu validator can be used programmatically via HTTP.

docs.text: A structured format for validation results.

docs.text: Includes the source in the output.

docs.text: Filters by severity.

docs.title: Concept 12: Local Validation
docs.text:
The Nu validator can be run locally:

java -jar vnu.jar index.html

docs.title: Concept 13: CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
The validator can be integrated into pipelines:

  • GitHub Actions
  • GitLab CI
  • Jenkins
  • Travis CI
  • CircleCI

docs.title: Concept 14: Editor Integration
docs.text: Plugins for VS Code, Sublime, Atom, and others.

docs.title: Concept 15: Common Errors
docs.text:
The most frequent validation errors:

  • Missing DOCTYPE.
  • Unclosed elements.
  • Invalid nesting.
  • Duplicate attributes.
  • Unknown elements.
  • Invalid attribute values.
  • Missing alt attributes.

docs.title: Concept 16: Deprecated Elements
docs.text:
Elements no longer in the HTML standard:

  • <center>, <font>, <marquee>, <blink>, <frame>, <frameset>, <big>, <strike>, <tt>, <applet>, <acronym>.

docs.title: Concept 17: Obsolete Attributes
docs.text:
Attributes no longer valid:

  • align, bgcolor, border, cellpadding, cellspacing, valign, width, height (on some elements).

docs.title: Concept 18: The is Attribute
docs.text: Customized built-in elements use the is attribute. The validator understands custom element naming.

docs.title: Concept 19: HTML5 vs. XHTML
docs.text: HTML5 is the current standard. XHTML is legacy. The validator supports both.

docs.title: Concept 20: The Validator's Limits
docs.text:
The validator cannot check:

  • Runtime behavior.
  • JavaScript-generated DOM.
  • CSS validity (see CSS Validator).
  • Accessibility (see accessibility checkers).
  • Security (see security scanners).

docs.title: Concept 21: The Firefox Extension
docs.text: Firefox has a built-in validator in the DevTools.

docs.title: Concept 22: The Chrome Extension
docs.text: Chrome has validation extensions available.

docs.title: Concept 23: The Bookmarklet
docs.text: The W3C provides a bookmarklet for validating the current page.

docs.title: Concept 24: The Offline Validator
docs.text:
The Nu validator can be run offline:

java -jar vnu.jar --skip-non-html --format json index.html

docs.title: Concept 25: The Validator's Error Messages
docs.text:
Each message includes:

  • Severity.
  • Description.
  • Line and column.
  • The offending markup.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Validating a URL
docs.text:
1.  User enters a URL at validator.w3.org.
    │
    ▼
2.  The validator fetches the URL.
    │
    ▼
3.  The HTML is parsed using the Nu parser.
    │
    ▼
4.  Each token is checked against the specification.
    │
    ▼
5.  Errors, warnings, and info messages are collected.
    │
    ▼
6.  The report is generated.
    │
    ▼
7.  The user reviews the report.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Validating a File
docs.text:
1.  User uploads a file.
    │
    ▼
2.  The file is read.
    │
    ▼
3.  The Nu parser processes the HTML.
    │
    ▼
4.  Errors are collected.
    │
    ▼
5.  The report is generated.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Validation Algorithm
docs.text:
1.  Check for DOCTYPE.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parse the document element.
    │
    ▼
3.  For each element:
    │   ├── Is the tag name valid?
    │   ├── Is the element allowed here?
    │   ├── Are the attributes valid?
    │   ├── Are the attribute values valid?
    │   └── Is the nesting correct?
    │
    ▼
4.  For each attribute:
    │   ├── Is the attribute allowed on this element?
    │   ├── Is the value valid?
    │   └── Is it a duplicate?
    │
    ▼
5.  Report all issues.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The CI/CD Flow
docs.text:
1.  Developer pushes code.
    │
    ▼
2.  CI pipeline runs.
    │
    ▼
3.  HTML validation action runs.
    │
    ▼
4.  The validator checks HTML files.
    │
    ▼
5.  Errors are reported.
    │
    ▼
6.  Build fails if errors exist.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Editor Flow
docs.text:
1.  Developer opens an HTML file.
    │
    ▼
2.  The editor's validator runs.
    │
    ▼
3.  Errors are underlined inline.
    │
    ▼
4.  The Problems panel lists all issues.
    │
    ▼
5.  Developer fixes errors.

docs.title: The Nu HTML Checker
docs.text:
The Nu HTML Checker is built on validator.nu — a Java-based validator that implements the WHATWG HTML Living Standard.

Its architecture:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INPUT (HTML, URL, or file)                  │
│                    │                         │
│                    ▼                         │
│  PARSER (Nu parser)                          │
│  └── Tokenizes and parses HTML                │
│                    │                         │
│                    ▼                         │
│  VALIDATOR ENGINE                            │
│  └── Checks tokens against the spec           │
│  └── Runs the checker pipeline                │
│                    │                         │
│                    ▼                         │
│  MESSAGE COLLECTOR                           │
│  └── Collects errors, warnings, info          │
│                    │                         │
│                    ▼                         │
│  REPORTER (JSON, XML, text, gnu)             │
│  └── Formats the output                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The Checker Pipeline
docs.text:
The validator runs a series of checkers on the parsed document:

  • DOCTYPE checker — verifies the DOCTYPE.
  • Content model checker — verifies nesting.
  • Attribute checker — verifies attributes.
  • Value checker — verifies attribute values.
  • ARIA checker — verifies ARIA attributes.
  • Microdata checker — verifies microdata.
  • RDFa checker — verifies RDFa.
  • Link checker — verifies links (optional).

docs.title: The Nu Parser
docs.text: The Nu parser is a streaming HTML parser that produces an event stream. It is used by the validator to check the document as it is parsed.

docs.title: The Validation Rules
docs.text: The validator's rules are derived from the WHATWG HTML Living Standard. Each rule corresponds to a requirement in the spec.

docs.title: The Error Message Format
docs.text:
Each error message includes:

  • Type — error, warning, or info.
  • Line and column — the location.
  • Message — a human-readable description.
  • Extract — the offending markup.

docs.title: The Validator's API
docs.text:
The Nu validator exposes a REST API:

POST /nu/
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>...

The response is a JSON object with the validation messages.

docs.title: The Validator's Cache
docs.text: The validator caches results for URLs. Repeated validations of the same URL return the cached result.

docs.title: The Validator's Rate Limiting
docs.text: The public validator has rate limits. For heavy use, run the validator locally.
