docs.title: Example 1: Valid HTML
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Valid Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello, world!</h1>
    <p>This is valid HTML.</p>
</body>
</html>

Validation result:

The document validates according to the specified schema(s).

Code Breakdown:

  • DOCTYPE is present.
  • lang attribute on <html>.
  • Charset declared.
  • All tags closed.
  • Valid nesting.

docs.title: Example 2: Missing DOCTYPE
docs.text:
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <title>Missing DOCTYPE</title>
</head>
<body>
    <p>Hello</p>
</body>
</html>

Validation result:

Error: Start tag seen without seeing a doctype first.
Expected "<!DOCTYPE html>".
  → Line 1, Column 1

Code Breakdown:

  • The DOCTYPE is missing.
  • Browsers enter quirks mode.
  • Fix: add <!DOCTYPE html> at the top.

docs.title: Example 3: Invalid Nesting
docs.text:
<p>Hello
    <div>World</div>
</p>

Validation result:

Error: Element "div" not allowed as child of element "p" in this context.
  → Line 2, Column 5

Code Breakdown:

  • <div> cannot be inside <p>.
  • The browser auto-closes <p>.
  • Fix: use <span> or restructure.

docs.title: Example 4: Unclosed Elements
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
    <li>Item 2
</ul>

Validation result:

Error: End tag "li" implied, but there were open elements.
  → Line 3, Column 5

Code Breakdown:

  • The <li> elements are implicitly closed.
  • Fix: add explicit </li> tags.

docs.title: Example 5: Duplicate Attributes
docs.text:
<div class="foo" class="bar">Content</div>

Validation result:

Error: Duplicate attribute "class".
  → Line 1, Column 22

Code Breakdown:

  • class appears twice.
  • Only the first wins.
  • Fix: combine into one attribute.

docs.title: Example 6: Missing alt Attribute
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg">

Validation result:

Error: An "img" element must have an "alt" attribute, except under certain conditions.
  → Line 1, Column 1

Code Breakdown:

  • The alt attribute is missing.
  • Accessibility issue.
  • Fix: add alt="..." (or alt="" for decorative images).

docs.title: Example 7: Unknown Element
docs.text:
<my-custom-element>Content</my-custom-element>

Validation result:

Info: Element "my-custom-element" is not a known element. This is not an error.
  → Line 1, Column 1

Code Breakdown:

  • Custom elements are valid if they follow the naming rules.
  • The validator reports as info, not error.

docs.title: Example 8: Obsolete Element
docs.text:
<center>Centered text</center>

Validation result:

Error: Element "center" is obsolete. Use CSS instead.
  → Line 1, Column 1

Code Breakdown:

  • <center> is deprecated.
  • Fix: use CSS text-align: center.

docs.title: Example 9: Invalid Attribute Value
docs.text:
<input type="invalid-type">

Validation result:

Error: Bad value "invalid-type" for attribute "type" on element "input".
  → Line 1, Column 1

Code Breakdown:

  • The value is not a valid input type.
  • Fix: use a valid type (text, email, password, etc.).

docs.title: Example 10: GitHub Actions Workflow
docs.text:
name: Validate HTML
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  html-validation:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: HTML5 Validator
        uses: Cyb3r-Jak3/html5validator-action@v7.2.0
        with:
          root: public/
          format: text
          blacklist: "legacy-page.html"

Code Breakdown:

  • Runs on every push and pull request.
  • Validates all HTML files in public/.
  • Excludes legacy-page.html.
  • Fails the build on errors.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Approach Manual validation validator.w3.org Programmatic validation Nu API (JSON output) Local validation vnu.jar CI/CD validation GitHub Actions, GitLab CI Editor validation VS Code, Sublime plugins Pre-deploy checks Build scripts CMS integration WordPress, Drupal plugins Framework integration Next.js, Astro build steps Accessibility preprocessing Validation before a11y audits SEO preprocessing Validation before SEO audits

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Validate after every significant change. Why: catches errors early.
  2. Integrate validation into CI/CD. Why: prevents errors from reaching production.
  3. Use the JSON API for automation. Why: structured output is easier to process.
  4. Run the validator locally for heavy use. Why: the public API has rate limits.
  5. Fix all errors before warnings. Why: errors break the specification.
  6. Review warnings carefully. Why: they may indicate subtle issues.
  7. Do not ignore info messages. Why: they may indicate custom elements or other valid patterns.
  8. Use editor plugins for immediate feedback. Why: faster than manual validation.
  9. Validate both source and rendered HTML. Why: JavaScript may introduce errors.
  10. Validate on multiple devices and browsers. Why: some errors only appear in specific environments.
  11. Combine validation with accessibility checks. Why: many validation errors are accessibility issues.
  12. Combine validation with SEO audits. Why: valid HTML is easier for search engines.
  13. Keep a baseline of validation errors. Why: new errors are easier to spot.
  14. Document known validation exceptions. Why: some errors may be intentional.
  15. Update validation rules periodically. Why: the specification evolves.
  16. Use the Nu validator, not the legacy W3C validator. Why: the Nu validator supports HTML5.
  17. Test on the WHATWG spec. Why: it is the current standard.
  18. Use the validator's API for testing. Why: enables automated tests.
  19. Validate before deploying. Why: catches errors before users see them.
  20. Validate after CMS updates. Why: CMS changes may introduce errors.
  21. Validate after framework upgrades. Why: framework output may change.
  22. Keep HTML small enough to validate quickly. Why: validation time is proportional to size.
  23. Do not use validation as a substitute for testing. Why: validation is static; testing is dynamic.
  24. Combine validation with screen reader testing. Why: validation is not sufficient for accessibility.
  25. Use validation as a signal, not a goal. Why: valid HTML is a means, not an end.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing DOCTYPE
docs.text:
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
</html>

Why it's wrong: Triggers quirks mode.

✅ Correct:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
...

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Block Elements in <p>
docs.text:
<p>Hello<div>World</div></p>

Why it's wrong: <div> is not allowed inside <p>.

✅ Correct:

<p>Hello</p>
<div>World</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unclosed Elements
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
    <li>Item 2
</ul>

Why it's wrong: The <li> elements are implicitly closed.

✅ Correct:

<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate Attributes
docs.text:
<div class="foo" class="bar">

Why it's wrong: Duplicate attributes are invalid.

✅ Correct:

<div class="foo bar">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing alt Attribute
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg">

Why it's wrong: Accessibility failure and validation error.

✅ Correct:

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Description">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Obsolete Elements
docs.text:
<center>Centered</center>

Why it's wrong: <center> is obsolete.

✅ Correct:

<div style="text-align: center;">Centered</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Validation Errors
docs.text:
<!-- Browser renders it, so it must be fine -->

Why it's wrong: The browser silently recovers, but the behavior may not be what you intend.

✅ Correct: Fix all errors.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Validating Only the Source
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: JavaScript-generated HTML may introduce errors.

✅ Correct: Validate both source and rendered HTML.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Only the Legacy Validator
docs.text:
# Uses the old W3C validator

Why it's wrong: The legacy validator does not support HTML5.

✅ Correct: Use the Nu HTML Checker.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Validating After CMS Changes
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: CMS updates may introduce errors.

✅ Correct: Validate after every significant change.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Validation is fast — typically under a second for a page.
  • The public API has rate limits — run locally for heavy use.
  • Large documents take longer — proportional to size.
  • Streaming validation — the Nu parser is streaming.
  • CI/CD validation adds seconds — negligible compared to other checks.
  • Editor validation is instant — inline feedback.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Run validation in CI/CD, not on every keystroke.
  2. Use editor plugins for immediate feedback.
  3. Cache validation results.
  4. Run the validator locally for large sites.
  5. Use the JSON API for batch processing.

docs.title: Validation as Defense
docs.text:
Validation catches some XSS-enabling patterns:

  • Unescaped < in content.
  • Unquoted attribute values with special characters.
  • Attribute injection.

docs.title: Validation Is Not a Security Tool
docs.text:
Validation does not catch:

  • XSS via JavaScript.
  • CSRF.
  • SQL injection.
  • Server-side vulnerabilities.

Defense: Use security scanners in addition to validation.

docs.title: Validation and CSP
docs.text: CSP and validation are complementary. CSP enforces runtime security; validation enforces static correctness.

docs.title: Trusting the Validation Server
docs.text:
The public validator is a third party. Do not submit sensitive HTML to it.

Defense: Run the validator locally for sensitive content.

docs.title: Validation and SSR
docs.text: Server-rendered HTML should be validated before deployment.

docs.title: Validation and DSD
docs.text: Declarative Shadow DOM is validated by the Nu validator. Ensure the syntax is correct.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• validator.w3.org — the primary UI.
  • Nu API — for programmatic use.
  • Editor plugins — inline feedback.
  • GitHub Actions — CI/CD integration.
  • JSON output — structured results.
  • Line and column numbers — locate errors quickly.
  • The showsource parameter — include source in output.
  • The level parameter — filter by severity.
  • The parser parameter — choose the standard.
  • Local vnu.jar — for offline validation.
  • Compare before/after — track error changes.
  • Validate rendered HTML — use the DevTools' "Copy outerHTML".
  • Validate against multiple standards — HTML5, XHTML, etc.
  • Test on multiple browsers — some errors only appear in specific engines.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every HTML document — always validate.
  • Every pull request — CI/CD integration.
  • Every CMS change — after template updates.
  • Every framework upgrade — framework output may change.
  • Every accessibility audit — validation is the first step.
  • Every SEO audit — valid HTML is easier to parse.
  • Every content deployment — verify before publishing.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not use validation as a substitute for testing. Testing is dynamic.
  • Do not use validation as a substitute for accessibility testing. Validation is not sufficient.
  • Do not use validation as a substitute for security scanning. Validation is not a security tool.
  • Do not ignore validation errors. They matter.
  • Do not submit sensitive HTML to the public validator.
  • Do not validate only the source, ignoring rendered HTML.
  • Do not expect valid HTML to be perfect. Valid HTML is a floor, not a ceiling.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Common errors in HTML validation are the recurring mistakes that appear across millions of web pages — the violations of the HTML specification that developers make most frequently. They are the errors that validation tools like the W3C Nu HTML Checker report most often, the errors that browsers silently recover from, and the errors that break accessibility, SEO, and cross-browser consistency.

<!-- Missing DOCTYPE -->
<html>
<head>
    <title>Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Block element inside <p> -->
    <p>Hello<div>World</div></p>

    <!-- Missing alt attribute -->
    <img src="photo.jpg">

    <!-- Unclosed elements -->
    <ul>
        <li>Item 1
        <li>Item 2
    </ul>
</body>
</html>

This page renders in every browser. But it contains four distinct validation errors, each of which represents a class of mistake that appears on millions of websites:

  1. Missing DOCTYPE — triggers quirks mode.
  2. Block element inside <p> — invalid content model.
  3. Missing alt attribute — accessibility failure.
  4. Unclosed <li> elements — implicit closing relies on browser recovery.

Common errors are not exotic edge cases. They are the bread-and-butter mistakes that developers make every day — the ones that show up in code reviews, CMS templates, and framework output. Understanding them is the first step toward writing valid HTML consistently.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Understanding common errors serves several essential purposes:

  • Faster debugging — recognizing known patterns speeds up fixing.
  • Prevention — knowing the errors prevents making them.
  • Pattern recognition — the same errors appear in every codebase.
  • Accessibility improvement — many common errors are a11y failures.
  • Cross-browser consistency — fixing errors ensures identical rendering.
  • SEO benefits — valid HTML is easier for search engines to parse.
  • Code review efficiency — reviewers spot common errors faster.
  • Template auditing — CMS templates often contain these errors.

Common errors are the vocabulary of HTML quality. Learning them is how developers move from "it works in my browser" to "it works correctly everywhere."

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Validation
│
├── HTML Validator         ← markup correctness
├── Common Errors          ← frequent validation errors (THIS CHAPTER)
├── Accessibility Validation ← automated a11y checks
├── Browser Compatibility  ← cross-browser testing
└── Debugging HTML         ← tools and techniques

Common Errors is the practical companion to the HTML Validator. The validator tells you what is wrong; common errors help you understand why it is wrong and how to fix it.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The HTML specification is large. It defines hundreds of elements, thousands of attributes, and intricate content models that determine which elements can contain which others. No developer memorizes all of it. The result is a predictable set of errors that appear repeatedly across the web:

  • Structural errors — missing DOCTYPE, incorrect nesting.
  • Content model errors — block elements in inline contexts.
  • Attribute errors — missing, duplicated, invalid values.
  • Accessibility errors — missing alt text, missing labels.
  • Deprecated patterns — using obsolete elements.
  • Template errors — errors introduced by CMS systems.

These errors are predictable — they appear in the same forms across thousands of sites. They are also fixable — each has a known cause and a known solution.

Understanding common errors is how developers move from reacting to validation reports to anticipating and preventing them.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No catalog of common errors Developers fixed the same mistakes repeatedly No pattern recognition Every error was a surprise No prevention guidance Errors accumulated over time No template auditing CMS output was never validated No code review patterns Reviewers missed known error types No training material New developers repeated the same mistakes

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
The catalog of common HTML errors has emerged from decades of web development. It is documented across:

  • W3C validation statistics — the most frequent errors reported by validator.w3.org.
  • Accessibility audits — the most frequent a11y failures.
  • SEO audits — the most frequent markup issues.
  • Browser bug reports — the errors that caused cross-browser issues.
  • Framework documentation — the errors frameworks commonly produce.
  • CMS documentation — the errors CMS templates commonly contain.

The most frequently cited source is the W3C's own validation statistics, which show that a small number of errors account for the vast majority of validation failures. The WebAIM Million report provides similar data for accessibility errors.

In 2026, common HTML errors are well-documented and well-understood. The challenge is not knowing them — it is applying that knowledge consistently across every project.

docs.title: The Most Common Errors
docs.text:
The following are the most frequently reported HTML validation errors across the web:

Rank Error Frequency 1 Missing alt attribute on <img> Very high 2 Missing DOCTYPE High 3 Block element inside <p> High 4 Unclosed elements (<li>, <p>, <td>) High 5 Duplicate attributes Medium 6 Obsolete elements (<center>, <font>) Medium 7 Invalid nesting (<div> in <span>) Medium 8 Missing form labels High 9 Invalid attribute values Medium 10 Unknown/typo'd elements Low

docs.title: Error 1: Missing alt Attribute
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: img must have alt -->
<img src="photo.jpg">

Validation message:

Error: An "img" element must have an "alt" attribute, except under certain conditions.

✅ Fix:

<!-- Meaningful image -->
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A golden retriever playing in the park">

<!-- Decorative image -->
<img src="decoration.png" alt="">

docs.title: Error 2: Missing DOCTYPE
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: no DOCTYPE -->
<html lang="en">
...

Validation message:

Error: Start tag seen without seeing a doctype first. Expected "<!DOCTYPE html>".

✅ Fix:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
...

docs.title: Error 3: Block Element Inside <p>
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: <div> not allowed inside <p> -->
<p>Hello<div>World</div></p>

Validation message:

Error: Element "div" not allowed as child of element "p" in this context.

✅ Fix:

<p>Hello</p>
<div>World</div>

docs.title: Error 4: Unclosed Elements
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: <li> implicitly closed -->
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
    <li>Item 2
</ul>

Validation message:

Error: End tag "li" implied, but there were open elements.

✅ Fix:

<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: Error 5: Duplicate Attributes
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: class specified twice -->
<div class="foo" class="bar">Content</div>

Validation message:

Error: Duplicate attribute "class".

✅ Fix:

<div class="foo bar">Content</div>

docs.title: Error 6: Obsolete Elements
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: <center> is obsolete -->
<center>Centered text</center>

Validation message:

Error: Element "center" is obsolete. Use CSS instead.

✅ Fix:

<div style="text-align: center;">Centered text</div>

docs.title: Error 7: Invalid Nesting
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: <div> not allowed inside <span> -->
<span>Hello<div>World</div></span>

Validation message:

Error: Element "div" not allowed as child of element "span" in this context.

✅ Fix:

<span>Hello</span>
<div>World</div>

docs.title: Error 8: Missing Form Labels
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: form control has no label -->
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

Validation message:

Warning: The "for" attribute of the "label" element must refer to a form control.

✅ Fix:

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: Error 9: Invalid Attribute Values
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: type="invalid" is not a valid input type -->
<input type="invalid">

Validation message:

Error: Bad value "invalid" for attribute "type" on element "input".

✅ Fix:

<input type="email">

docs.title: Error 10: Unknown/Typos
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Error: <dvi> is a typo for <div> -->
<dvi>Content</dvi>

Validation message:

Info: Element "dvi" is not a known element.

✅ Fix:

<div>Content</div>

docs.title: The Error Categories
docs.text:
Common errors fall into distinct categories:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STRUCTURAL                                  │
│  ├── Missing DOCTYPE                          │
│  ├── Unclosed elements                        │
│  └── Incorrect nesting                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CONTENT MODEL                               │
│  ├── Block elements in <p>                    │
│  ├── <div> in <span>                          │
│  └── Invalid parent-child relationships       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ATTRIBUTE                                   │
│  ├── Missing required attributes              │
│  ├── Duplicate attributes                     │
│  └── Invalid attribute values                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ACCESSIBILITY                               │
│  ├── Missing alt attributes                   │
│  ├── Missing form labels                      │
│  └── Missing ARIA labels                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DEPRECATED                                  │
│  ├── Obsolete elements                        │
│  ├── Obsolete attributes                      │
│  └── Legacy patterns                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Same Mistakes Everywhere" Mental Model
docs.text:
Common errors are predictable:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SITE A                                      │
│  ├── Missing alt on 20 images                │
│  ├── Missing DOCTYPE                          │
│  └── Unclosed <li>                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  SITE B                                      │
│  ├── Missing alt on 15 images                │
│  ├── Missing DOCTYPE                          │
│  └── Unclosed <li>                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  SITE C                                      │
│  ├── Missing alt on 30 images                │
│  ├── Missing DOCTYPE                          │
│  └── Unclosed <li>                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The same mistakes appear everywhere. Learning them once means recognizing them forever.

docs.title: The "Error Class" Mental Model
docs.text:
Each common error is a class of mistake, not a single instance:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ERROR CLASS: Missing alt                     │
│  └── Instance 1: <img src="a.jpg">           │
│  └── Instance 2: <img src="b.jpg">           │
│  └── Instance 3: <img src="c.jpg">           │
│  └── ... hundreds more                       │
│                                              │
│  Fix the class, not just the instances.     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Fixing a class of error is more valuable than fixing individual instances. A template fix eliminates hundreds of errors at once.

docs.title: The "Cause" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every common error has a cause:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MISSING alt                                 │
│  └── Cause: Developer forgot                │
│  └── Cause: CMS didn't require it           │
│  └── Cause: Framework ignored it            │
│  └── Cause: Image is decorative             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  MISSING DOCTYPE                             │
│  └── Cause: Template omitted it             │
│  └── Cause: Developer copied from old HTML  │
│  └── Cause: CMS stripped it                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Fixing the cause prevents the error from recurring.

docs.title: The "Silent Recovery" Mental Model
docs.text:
Browsers silently recover from these errors. The user never sees a problem. Only the validator reports them:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DEVELOPER WRITES                            │
│  <p>Hello<div>World</div></p>                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  BROWSER SILENTLY FIXES                      │
│  <p>Hello</p><div>World</div><p></p>         │
│  └── Renders fine                            │
│  └── Says nothing                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  VALIDATOR REPORTS                           │
│  Error: Element "div" not allowed as         │
│  child of element "p".                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The error is invisible unless you look for it.

docs.title: The "Template Propagation" Mental Model
docs.text:
Most common errors come from templates, not individual pages:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HEADER TEMPLATE                             │
│  └── Error: missing alt on logo              │
│                                              │
│  This error appears on every page:           │
│  ├── Homepage                                │
│  ├── About page                              │
│  ├── Products page                           │
│  └── ... thousands more                      │
│                                              │
│  Fix the template → fix thousands of pages.  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Fixing templates is the highest-leverage way to fix common errors.

docs.title: The "Priority" Mental Model
docs.text:
Not all errors are equally important:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CRITICAL (fix immediately)                  │
│  ├── Missing form labels                     │
│  ├── Missing alt on meaningful images        │
│  └── Missing DOCTYPE                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  IMPORTANT (fix soon)                        │
│  ├── Invalid nesting                         │
│  ├── Unclosed elements                       │
│  └── Duplicate attributes                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LOW PRIORITY (fix when possible)            │
│  ├── Obsolete elements                       │
│  └── Redundant attributes                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Critical errors affect accessibility and rendering. Low-priority errors are cosmetic.

docs.title: Concept 1: Missing alt Attribute
docs.text: The most common validation error. Every <img> must have an alt attribute — meaningful text for informative images, empty for decorative images.

docs.title: Concept 2: Missing DOCTYPE
docs.text: The DOCTYPE is required. Without it, browsers enter quirks mode, changing layout and CSS behavior.

docs.title: Concept 3: Block Elements Inside <p>
docs.text: <p> can only contain phrasing content. Block elements (<div>, <h1>, <ul>, etc.) are not allowed. The browser auto-closes the <p>.

docs.title: Concept 4: Unclosed Elements
docs.text: Elements like <li>, <p>, <td>, <tr>, <option> can be implicitly closed. But explicit closing is required for validity.

docs.title: Concept 5: Duplicate Attributes
docs.text: Duplicate attributes are invalid. Only the first is used.

docs.title: Concept 6: Obsolete Elements
docs.text:
Elements removed from the specification:

  • <center>, <font>, <big>, <strike>, <tt>, <marquee>, <blink>, <frame>, <frameset>, <applet>, <acronym>, <dir>, <isindex>, <menu> (as list), <noembed>, <plaintext>, <rb>, <rtc>, <xmp>.

docs.title: Concept 7: Obsolete Attributes
docs.text:
Attributes removed from the specification:

  • align, bgcolor, border, cellpadding, cellspacing, valign, width, height (on some elements), name (on some elements), language, version, hspace, vspace, alink, link, text, vlink, nowrap, noshade, compact.

docs.title: Concept 8: Invalid Nesting
docs.text:
Some elements cannot be nested inside others:

  • <div> cannot be inside <p>.
  • <div> cannot be inside <span>.
  • <li> cannot be outside <ul>, <ol>, or <menu>.
  • <td> cannot be outside <tr>.
  • <tr> cannot be outside <table>, <thead>, <tbody>, or <tfoot>.

docs.title: Concept 9: Missing Form Labels
docs.text: Every form control must have a label. Missing labels are a validation warning and an accessibility failure.

docs.title: Concept 10: Invalid Attribute Values
docs.text:
Attribute values must match the specification:

  • type on <input> must be a valid type.
  • rel on <link> and <a> must be valid.
  • target must be _self, _blank, _parent, _top, or a valid name.
  • lang must be a valid language tag.

docs.title: Concept 11: Unknown Elements
docs.text:
Typos or non-standard elements:

  • <dvi> instead of <div>.
  • <spam> instead of <span>.
  • <dev> instead of <div>.

docs.title: Concept 12: Missing <html> lang Attribute
docs.text: The <html> element should have a lang attribute for accessibility.

docs.title: Concept 13: Missing <meta charset>
docs.text: The character encoding should be declared.

docs.title: Concept 14: Missing <title>
docs.text: Every document must have a <title>.

docs.title: Concept 15: Missing <meta name="viewport">
docs.text: The viewport meta tag is required for responsive design.

docs.title: Concept 16: Invalid role Values
docs.text: ARIA role attributes must be valid values.

docs.title: Concept 17: Invalid ARIA Attributes
docs.text: ARIA attributes must be valid and correctly applied.

docs.title: Concept 18: Redundant ARIA
docs.text: Redundant roles (e.g., role="button" on <button>) are warnings.

docs.title: Concept 19: Missing Heading Structure
docs.text: Headings should follow a logical hierarchy.

docs.title: Concept 20: Invalid Table Structure
docs.text:
Tables must follow the correct structure:

  • <table> contains <caption>, <colgroup>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, <tr>.
  • <tr> contains <td> or <th>.
  • <td> and <th> cannot be directly inside <table>.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How Errors Accumulate
docs.text:
1.  Developer writes HTML.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser renders it (silently recovering).
    │
    ▼
3.  Developer sees no problem.
    │
    ▼
4.  Errors are copied into templates.
    │
    ▼
5.  Templates are used across many pages.
    │
    ▼
6.  Errors multiply.
    │
    ▼
7.  Validation reveals hundreds of errors.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Fixing a Class of Errors
docs.text:
1.  Run the validator.
    │
    ▼
2.  Identify the most common error.
    │
    ▼
3.  Find the template or component causing it.
    │
    ▼
4.  Fix the template.
    │
    ▼
5.  Re-generate the pages.
    │
    ▼
6.  Re-validate.
    │
    ▼
7.  Hundreds of errors are fixed at once.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Preventing Common Errors
docs.text:
1.  Learn the common error patterns.
    │
    ▼
2.  Add validation to CI/CD.
    │
    ▼
3.  Add editor plugins.
    │
    ▼
4.  Add code review checklists.
    │
    ▼
5.  Fix templates.
    │
    ▼
6.  Monitor for new errors.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Debugging an Error
docs.text:
1.  Validator reports an error.
    │
    ▼
2.  Read the message.
    │
    ▼
3.  Find the line and column.
    │
    ▼
4.  Understand the cause.
    │
    ▼
5.  Apply the fix.
    │
    ▼
6.  Re-validate.

docs.title: The Validator's Error Detection
docs.text:
The Nu validator checks each element against the specification:

For each element:
  ├── Is the tag name known?
  ├── Is the element allowed here?
  ├── Are required attributes present?
  ├── Are attribute values valid?
  ├── Is nesting correct?
  └── Are ARIA attributes valid?

docs.title: The Content Model
docs.text:
Each element has a content model — what it can contain:

Element Content model <p> Phrasing content <div> Flow content <span> Phrasing content <ul> <li> or script-supporting <table> <caption>, <colgroup>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, <tr> <tr> <td> or <th>

docs.title: The Error Classification
docs.text:
The validator classifies errors by type:

  • Content model violation — invalid nesting.
  • Attribute error — missing, duplicate, or invalid attribute.
  • Value error — invalid attribute value.
  • Obsolete element — removed from the spec.
  • Obsolete attribute — removed from the spec.
  • Unknown element — not in the spec.
  • ARIA error — invalid ARIA usage.

docs.title: The Error Message Format
docs.text:
Each error message includes:

  • Type — error, warning, info.
  • Location — line and column.
  • Description — human-readable explanation.
  • Extract — the offending markup.

docs.title: The Most Common Error Patterns
docs.text:
The most common patterns, by category:

Structural: - Missing DOCTYPE. - Missing <html> lang. - Missing <meta charset>. - Unclosed <p>, <li>, <td>. - Incorrect nesting.

Content model: - <div> in <p>. - <div> in <span>. - <ul> without <li>. - <table> without <tr>. - <tr> without <td>.

Attribute: - Missing alt. - Duplicate class. - Invalid type. - Invalid rel. - Invalid target.

Deprecated: - <center>. - <font>. - <marquee>. - align attribute.

Accessibility: - Missing alt. - Missing form labels. - Missing ARIA labels. - Invalid ARIA.

docs.title: The Error Accumulation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Developer writes HTML with errors.
    │
    ▼
2.  Browser renders it fine.
    │
    ▼
3.  Developer copies the pattern.
    │
    ▼
4.  Errors spread across the codebase.
    │
    ▼
5.  Errors spread across templates.
    │
    ▼
6.  Errors spread across pages.
    │
    ▼
7.  Validation reveals hundreds of errors.

docs.title: The Error Fixing Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Run the validator.
    │
    ▼
2.  Identify the top errors.
    │
    ▼
3.  Find the template causing them.
    │
    ▼
4.  Fix the template.
    │
    ▼
5.  Re-generate the pages.
    │
    ▼
6.  Re-validate.
    │
    ▼
7.  Repeat for the next error class.

docs.title: The Error Prevention Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Learn the common errors.
    │
    ▼
2.  Add validation to CI/CD.
    │
    ▼
3.  Add editor plugins.
    │
    ▼
4.  Add code review checklists.
    │
    ▼
5.  Monitor for regressions.

docs.title: Example 1: The Alt Attribute
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Missing alt -->
<img src="logo.png">

<!-- ❌ alt with placeholder -->
<img src="logo.png" alt="logo">

<!-- ✅ Meaningful alt -->
<img src="logo.png" alt="Acme Corporation">

<!-- ✅ Decorative image -->
<img src="decoration.png" alt="">

<!-- ✅ Functional image (button) -->
<button>
    <img src="search.svg" alt="Search">
</button>

Code Breakdown:

  • Missing alt is the most common validation error.
  • Meaningful alt describes the image.
  • Empty alt marks the image as decorative.
  • Functional alt describes the action.

docs.title: Example 2: The DOCTYPE
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Missing DOCTYPE -->
<html lang="en">
<head>...</head>
</html>

<!-- ✅ Correct DOCTYPE -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>...</head>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • DOCTYPE must be the first thing in the document.
  • <!DOCTYPE html> triggers standards mode.
  • Missing DOCTYPE triggers quirks mode.

docs.title: Example 3: Block Elements in <p>
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Invalid: <div> in <p> -->
<p>Hello<div>World</div></p>

<!-- ✅ Correct: separate elements -->
<p>Hello</p>
<div>World</div>

<!-- ✅ Alternative: <span> instead of <div> -->
<p>Hello<span>World</span></p>

Code Breakdown:

  • <p> can only contain phrasing content.
  • Block elements are not allowed.
  • The browser auto-closes <p> before <div>.

docs.title: Example 4: Unclosed Elements
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Unclosed <li> -->
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
    <li>Item 2
</ul>

<!-- ✅ Explicitly closed -->
<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

<!-- ❌ Unclosed <td> -->
<table>
    <tr>
        <td>Cell 1
        <td>Cell 2
    </tr>
</table>

<!-- ✅ Explicitly closed -->
<table>
    <tr>
        <td>Cell 1</td>
        <td>Cell 2</td>
    </tr>
</table>

Code Breakdown:

  • Browsers auto-close <li>, <td>, <tr>, <p>, <option>.
  • Explicit closing is required for validity.

docs.title: Example 5: Duplicate Attributes
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Duplicate class -->
<div class="foo" class="bar">Content</div>

<!-- ❌ Duplicate id -->
<div id="a" id="b">Content</div>

<!-- ✅ Combined -->
<div class="foo bar">Content</div>
<div id="a">Content</div>

Code Breakdown:

  • Duplicate attributes are invalid.
  • Only the first is used.
  • Combine class values with a space.

docs.title: Example 6: Obsolete Elements
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Obsolete elements -->
<center>Centered</center>
<font color="red">Red text</font>
<marquee>Scrolling text</marquee>
<big>Big text</big>
<strike>Struck through</strike>
<tt>Monospace</tt>

<!-- ✅ Modern equivalents -->
<div style="text-align: center;">Centered</div>
<span style="color: red;">Red text</span>
<div style="overflow: hidden;">...</div>
<span style="font-size: larger;">Big text</span>
<s>Struck through</s>
<code>Monospace</code>

Code Breakdown:

  • Obsolete elements are removed from the spec.
  • Use CSS and modern semantic elements instead.

docs.title: Example 7: Invalid Nesting
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ <div> inside <span> -->
<span>Hello<div>World</div></span>

<!-- ❌ <li> outside <ul> -->
<li>Item</li>

<!-- ❌ <td> outside <tr> -->
<td>Cell</td>

<!-- ✅ Correct nesting -->
<span>Hello</span>
<div>World</div>

<ul>
    <li>Item</li>
</ul>

<table>
    <tr>
        <td>Cell</td>
    </tr>
</table>

Code Breakdown:

  • Elements have specific content models.
  • Invalid nesting triggers validation errors.
  • The browser recovers, but the result may not match intent.

docs.title: Example 8: Missing Form Labels
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Missing label -->
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

<!-- ✅ Label with for/id -->
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

<!-- ✅ Wrapping label -->
<label>
    Email
    <input type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
</label>

<!-- ✅ ARIA label for icon-only inputs -->
<input type="search" aria-label="Search">

Code Breakdown:

  • Every form control must have a label.
  • placeholder is not a label.
  • Use <label for>, wrapping <label>, or aria-label.

docs.title: Example 9: Invalid Attribute Values
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Invalid input type -->
<input type="invalid">

<!-- ❌ Invalid rel -->
<link rel="invalid" href="style.css">

<!-- ❌ Invalid target -->
<a href="/" target="invalid">Link</a>

<!-- ✅ Valid values -->
<input type="email">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
<a href="/" target="_blank">Link</a>

Code Breakdown:

  • Attribute values must match the specification.
  • type on <input> has a defined set of values.
  • rel on <link> and <a> has defined values.
  • target must be _self, _blank, _parent, _top, or a valid name.

docs.title: Example 10: Invalid Table Structure
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Invalid table structure -->
<table>
    <td>Cell 1</td>
    <td>Cell 2</td>
</table>

<!-- ✅ Correct table structure -->
<table>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Header 1</th>
            <th>Header 2</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>Cell 1</td>
            <td>Cell 2</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

Code Breakdown:

  • <td> cannot be directly inside <table>.
  • <td> must be inside <tr>.
  • <tr> must be inside <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, or <table>.

docs.title: Example 11: Common Template Error
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Blog post template with errors -->
<article>
    <h1><?= $title ?></h1>
    <img src="<?= $image ?>">
    <p><?= $content ?> <div class="share">Share</div></p>
</article>

<!-- ✅ Fixed template -->
<article>
    <h1><?= htmlspecialchars($title) ?></h1>
    <img src="<?= htmlspecialchars($image) ?>" alt="<?= htmlspecialchars($title) ?>">
    <p><?= htmlspecialchars($content) ?></p>
    <div class="share">Share</div>
</article>

Code Breakdown:

  • Template errors propagate to every page using the template.
  • Fix the template to fix thousands of pages at once.
  • Escape user data to prevent XSS.

docs.title: Example 12: Validation Report
docs.text:
Error: An "img" element must have an "alt" attribute, except under certain conditions.
From line 42, column 5; to line 42, column 30
<img src="photo.jpg">↩

Error: Start tag seen without seeing a doctype first.
From line 1, column 1; to line 1, column 6
<html>↩

Error: Element "div" not allowed as child of element "p" in this context.
From line 55, column 5; to line 55, column 10
<div>World</div>↩

Warning: The "for" attribute of the "label" element must refer to a form control.
From line 72, column 3; to line 72, column 25
<label for="missing">...</label>

Code Breakdown:

  • Each error includes type, description, and location.
  • Fix errors from the top of the report.
  • Re-validate after fixing.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Common Error Blog posts Missing alt on images E-commerce Unclosed <li>, <td> CMS templates Missing DOCTYPE Framework output Duplicate attributes Legacy sites Obsolete elements Contact forms Missing form labels Landing pages Block elements in <p> Newsletter emails Invalid nesting Documentation Missing lang attribute Single-page apps Client-rendered content not validated

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Validate after every change. Why: catches errors early.
  2. Fix errors by category. Why: fixing a class eliminates many instances.
  3. Fix templates, not just pages. Why: highest leverage.
  4. Integrate validation into CI/CD. Why: prevents new errors.
  5. Use editor plugins. Why: immediate feedback.
  6. Learn the common errors. Why: recognition prevents repetition.
  7. Add alt to every image. Why: accessibility and validity.
  8. Always include DOCTYPE. Why: prevents quirks mode.
  9. Close all elements explicitly. Why: avoids relying on recovery.
  10. Keep block elements out of <p>. Why: invalid nesting.
  11. Avoid obsolete elements. Why: they are removed from the spec.
  12. Quote all attribute values. Why: unquoted values are error-prone.
  13. Use <label> for every form control. Why: accessibility and validity.
  14. Validate attribute values. Why: invalid values trigger errors.
  15. Follow the content model. Why: correct nesting is essential.
  16. Test in multiple browsers. Why: recovery behavior varies.
  17. Document known exceptions. Why: some errors may be intentional.
  18. Audit CMS templates. Why: templates propagate errors.
  19. Audit framework output. Why: frameworks may generate invalid HTML.
  20. Review validation reports regularly. Why: new errors appear over time.
  21. Use a checklist in code review. Why: catches common errors.
  22. Train the team. Why: shared knowledge prevents errors.
  23. Fix the cause, not just the symptom. Why: prevents recurrence.
  24. Keep a baseline. Why: new errors are easier to spot.
  25. Celebrate error-free pages. Why: reinforces good practices.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Validation Errors
docs.text:
<!-- Browser renders it, so it's fine -->

Why it's wrong: The browser silently recovers; the error remains.

✅ Correct: Fix the error.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Fixing Only the Instances
docs.text:
<!-- Fixing each page individually -->

Why it's wrong: The template still produces the error.

✅ Correct: Fix the template.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Alt on Images
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg">

Why it's wrong: Accessibility failure and validation error.

✅ Correct:

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Description">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Placeholder as Label
docs.text:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">

Why it's wrong: Placeholder is not a label.

✅ Correct:

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unclosed Elements
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
    <li>Item 2
</ul>

Why it's wrong: Implicit closing relies on browser recovery.

✅ Correct:

<ul>
    <li>Item 1</li>
    <li>Item 2</li>
</ul>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Block Elements in <p>
docs.text:
<p>Hello<div>World</div></p>

Why it's wrong: Invalid content model.

✅ Correct:

<p>Hello</p>
<div>World</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Obsolete Elements
docs.text:
<center>Centered</center>

Why it's wrong: <center> is obsolete.

✅ Correct:

<div style="text-align: center;">Centered</div>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate Attributes
docs.text:
<div class="foo" class="bar">

Why it's wrong: Only the first is used.

✅ Correct:

<div class="foo bar">

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing DOCTYPE
docs.text:
<html>
...

Why it's wrong: Triggers quirks mode.

✅ Correct:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
...

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Validating Rendered HTML
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: JavaScript-generated HTML may have errors.

✅ Correct: Validate both source and rendered HTML.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Trusting the Browser's Rendering
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The browser hides errors.

✅ Correct: Validate explicitly.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Validation is fast — under a second for typical pages.
  • Fixing templates has high leverage — one fix, many pages.
  • Common errors are easy to fix — they are well-understood.
  • Prevention is cheaper than fixing — integrate validation early.
  • CI/CD validation adds seconds — negligible cost.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Validate in CI/CD, not on every keystroke.
  2. Fix templates to reduce total error count.
  3. Use editor plugins for immediate feedback.
  4. Cache validation results.
  5. Monitor for new errors.

docs.title: XSS via Unescaped Output
docs.text:
Common errors in templates often involve unescaped user input:

<!-- ❌ XSS risk -->
<p><?= $userInput ?></p>

<!-- ✅ Escaped -->
<p><?= htmlspecialchars($userInput) ?></p>

Defense: Always escape user input.

docs.title: Attribute Injection
docs.text:
Unquoted attributes are vulnerable to injection:

<!-- ❌ Vulnerable -->
<div class=<?= $userClass ?>>

<!-- ✅ Safe -->
<div class="<?= htmlspecialchars($userClass) ?>">

Defense: Quote all attribute values; escape user input.

docs.title: innerHTML and XSS
docs.text:
Using innerHTML with untrusted content is a common XSS vector.

Defense: Use textContent; sanitize with DOMPurify for HTML.

docs.title: Missing rel="noopener"
docs.text:
Using target="_blank" without rel="noopener" is a security issue (tabnabbing).

Defense: Add rel="noopener" to external links with target="_blank".

docs.title: Obsolete Elements and Security
docs.text:
Some obsolete elements (like <applet>, <frame>) have security implications.

Defense: Remove obsolete elements.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• validator.w3.org — run validation.
  • Editor plugins — inline feedback.
  • GitHub Actions — CI/CD validation.
  • JSON output — for automation.
  • Line and column numbers — locate errors.
  • Fix from the top — errors cascade.
  • Fix by category — fix similar errors together.
  • Fix templates — highest leverage.
  • Validate the rendered HTML — use DevTools.
  • Compare before/after — track error reductions.
  • Use the showsource parameter — see the offending markup.
  • Use the level parameter — filter by severity.
  • Test on multiple browsers — recovery varies.
  • Test with view-source: — see the raw HTML.
  • Test with JavaScript disabled — see the no-JS case.
  • Check the DOM — after JavaScript runs.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every HTML document — always validate.
  • Every template — fix errors at the source.
  • Every pull request — CI/CD integration.
  • Every framework upgrade — output may change.
  • Every CMS update — templates may change.
  • Every code review — check for common errors.
  • Every accessibility audit — validation is the first step.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not ignore errors because the browser renders. Silent recovery hides problems.
  • Do not fix instances only — fix templates. Templates propagate errors.
  • Do not assume validation is sufficient. It is not a substitute for testing.
  • Do not skip validation because it's tedious. Automation handles it.
  • Do not trust framework output. Validate it.
  • Do not trust CMS output. Validate it.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Missing alt is the most common HTML validation error — reported on millions of pages.
  • Missing DOCTYPE triggers quirks mode — different layout and CSS behavior.
  • Block elements inside <p> — the browser auto-closes the <p>.
  • Unclosed <li> elements — browsers implicitly close them.
  • Duplicate attributes — only the first is used.
  • Obsolete elements — removed from the HTML specification.
  • <center>, <font>, <marquee> are obsolete — use CSS instead.
  • <big>, <strike>, <tt> are obsolete — use semantic elements.
  • Missing form labels are a validation warning — and an accessibility failure.
  • Placeholder is not a label — a common mistake.
  • Unescaped user input in templates — an XSS risk.
  • target="_blank" without rel="noopener" — a security issue.
  • The WebAIM Million reports missing alt as the most common a11y error.
  • Templates propagate errors — fixing them fixes thousands of pages.
  • Fixing a class of errors — more valuable than fixing individual instances.
  • Validation catches errors the browser hides — silent recovery is a trap.
  • The validator reports line and column numbers — for quick fixes.
  • Most common errors are well-understood — they have known fixes.
  • Validation is fast and free — no excuse to skip it.
  • The best validation is the one you never have to think about — integrated into your workflow.
  • Fix errors early — before they propagate.
  • Fix errors by category — efficiently eliminate entire error types.
  • Validate the rendered HTML — JavaScript-generated HTML may have errors.
  • The browser never tells you your HTML is broken — the validator does.
  • Common errors are the vocabulary of HTML quality — learn them once, recognize them forever.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Common errors are the recurring validation mistakes that appear across millions of pages.
  • Missing alt attribute — the most common error.
  • Missing DOCTYPE — triggers quirks mode.
  • Block elements inside <p> — invalid content model.
  • Unclosed elements — <li>, <td>, <p> rely on browser recovery.
  • Duplicate attributes — only the first is used.
  • Obsolete elements — <center>, <font>, <marquee>, etc.
  • Invalid nesting — <div> in <span>, <li> outside <ul>.
  • Missing form labels — accessibility and validation failure.
  • Invalid attribute values — type, rel, target, etc.
  • Unknown elements — typos like <dvi>.
  • Fix errors by category — eliminates many instances at once.
  • Fix templates, not just pages — highest leverage.
  • Integrate validation into CI/CD — prevents new errors.
  • Use editor plugins — immediate feedback.
  • Learn the common errors — recognition prevents repetition.
  • Escape user input — XSS prevention.
  • Validate rendered HTML — JavaScript may introduce errors.
  • The browser hides errors — the validator reveals them.
  • Common errors are the vocabulary of HTML quality.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Accessibility validation is the systematic process of evaluating a web page or application against accessibility standards — primarily WCAG 2.2 Level AA — using a combination of automated tools, manual inspection, and assistive technology testing. Its purpose is to identify barriers that prevent people with disabilities from perceiving, operating, understanding, and interacting with digital content.

<!-- What automated tools catch -->
<img src="chart.png">                        <!-- missing alt -->
<button style="color:#aaa;background:#fff">  <!-- contrast 2.3:1 -->

<!-- What only manual testing catches -->
<a href="/article">Read more</a>             <!-- vague link text -->
<div tabindex="0">Custom widget</div>        <!-- no role, no keyboard handler -->

The first example produces automated violations. The second produces zero automated violations but is completely inaccessible to screen reader and keyboard users. This is the central truth of accessibility validation: automation finds the obvious; humans find the important.

Accessibility validation is governed by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1 (Keyboard) at minimum, and by the full POUR framework (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) for comprehensive coverage. It is not a single tool or a single pass — it is a layered discipline.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Accessibility validation serves several essential purposes:

  • Barrier identification — discovers what prevents users with disabilities from completing tasks.
  • Legal compliance — demonstrates conformance with WCAG 2.2 AA, the standard referenced by the ADA, Section 508, and the European Accessibility Act.
  • Regression prevention — catches accessibility breaks before they reach production.
  • User experience — improves the experience for all users, not just those with disabilities.
  • Risk reduction — identifies issues before lawsuits, fines, or enforcement actions.
  • Continuous improvement — establishes a baseline and measures progress over time.

The 2026 WebAIM Million report found that 95.9% of the top one million home pages have automatically detectable WCAG failures, averaging 56.1 errors per page — a 10.1% increase from 2025, reversing years of gradual improvement. With automated tools catching only 30–40% of real accessibility issues, the true failure rate is significantly higher.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Validation
│
├── HTML Validator          ← markup correctness
├── Common Errors           ← frequent validation errors
├── Accessibility Validation ← automated + manual a11y checks (THIS CHAPTER)
├── Browser Compatibility   ← cross-browser testing
└── Debugging HTML          ← tools and techniques

Accessibility Validation is the second layer of the validation stack. HTML Validator ensures the markup is correct; accessibility validation ensures the page actually works for users with disabilities.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
An accessible web page cannot be tested by looking at it. A developer with perfect vision, full motor control, and standard hearing can use almost any page. The barriers are invisible to them.

But for a screen reader user, a keyboard-only user, a low-vision user, or a user with a cognitive disability, the page may be entirely unusable. And those barriers are invisible to sighted, mouse-using developers.

<!-- Looks fine to a sighted developer -->
<div class="button" onclick="save()">Save</div>

<!-- But: not focusable, not keyboard-operable, not announced as a button -->

Accessibility validation exists to reveal the invisible — to surface the barriers that users with disabilities encounter but developers never see.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No testing at all Accessibility treated as an afterthought Automated-only testing 60–70% of issues missed entirely No screen reader testing Announcement quality and reading order never verified No keyboard-only testing Focus traps and tab order issues shipped undetected No mobile testing Touch target, gesture, and VoiceOver issues missed Testing only before launch Regressions introduced by every subsequent change No CI integration Issues caught too late, remediation expensive

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Accessibility validation evolved alongside accessibility standards:

  • 1999 — WCAG 1.0 published; automated checkers began emerging.
  • 2008 — WCAG 2.0 introduced testable criteria.
  • 2015 — Deque released axe-core, the first engine with zero false positives on automated checks.
  • 2018 — Lighthouse integrated axe-core for accessibility audits.
  • 2020s — CI/CD integration became standard; accessibility shifted left.
  • 2025–2026 — The European Accessibility Act made testing a legal requirement for EU-facing digital products. France's DGCCRF began inspections in December 2025. The Dutch ACM moved toward active enforcement in mid-2026. In June 2026, a French court ordered Carrefour to make its site and app accessible within six months, with €500 per day penalties for delay.

Accessibility validation exists because you cannot fix what you cannot see. Testing makes barriers visible before they reach users, regulators, and courts.

docs.title: The Three-Layer Testing Strategy
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LAYER 1: AUTOMATED (30–40%)                 │
│  axe-core, Lighthouse, WAVE, Pa11y           │
│  Runs in CI/CD, catches structural issues    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYER 2: MANUAL (~42% irreducible)          │
│  Keyboard navigation, focus, reading order   │
│  Human judgement required                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYER 3: ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY               │
│  NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack            │
│  Real screen reader testing                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Layer 1: Automated Testing with axe-core
docs.text:
// Playwright + axe-core integration
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('homepage has no accessibility violations', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://example.com');

    const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
        .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa'])
        .analyze();

    expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
});

docs.title: Code Breakdown
docs.text:
• @axe-core/playwright — integrates axe-core into Playwright tests.
  • .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa']) — restricts to WCAG 2.2 A and AA criteria.
  • .analyze() — runs the scan and returns violations, incomplete items, and passes.
  • expect(results.violations).toEqual([]) — fails the test if any violations exist.

docs.title: Layer 2: Manual Keyboard Testing
docs.text:
## Keyboard Navigation Test Protocol

### Setup
- [ ] Put away the mouse
- [ ] Open the page in Chrome or Firefox

### Test Steps
1. **Tab forward** — press `Tab` repeatedly
   - [ ] Every interactive element receives focus
   - [ ] Focus order follows visual order
   - [ ] Focus indicator is visible on every element

2. **Tab backward** — press `Shift+Tab`
   - [ ] Reverse order is correct

3. **Activate** — press `Enter` and `Space`
   - [ ] Buttons activate
   - [ ] Links navigate
   - [ ] Form controls respond

4. **Escape** — press `Escape`
   - [ ] Modals close
   - [ ] Dropdowns dismiss

5. **Arrow keys** — within composite widgets
   - [ ] Tabs navigate
   - [ ] Menus navigate
   - [ ] Radio groups navigate

### Verify
- [ ] No keyboard traps (can always Tab out)
- [ ] Focus not obscured by sticky headers
- [ ] Skip link works

docs.title: Layer 3: Screen Reader Testing
docs.text:
## NVDA Test Protocol (Windows)

### Setup
- [ ] Download NVDA from nvaccess.org
- [ ] Launch with Ctrl+Alt+N
- [ ] Open Chrome or Firefox

### Structure
- [ ] NVDA+T — page title announced correctly
- [ ] H — headings cycle in logical order
- [ ] D — landmarks cycle through
- [ ] NVDA+Down — content reads in logical order

### Forms
- [ ] F — form fields cycle through
- [ ] Tab into each field — label announced
- [ ] Submit invalid form — error announced via role="alert"

### Interactive
- [ ] B — buttons cycle through with names
- [ ] Open modal — focus moves in
- [ ] Close modal — focus returns to trigger

docs.text: Tool Type Best For axe-core Engine CI/CD integration Lighthouse Browser tool Quick health check WAVE Browser extension Visual feedback Pa11y CLI tool CI/CD integration axe DevTools Browser extension Developer education IBM Equal Access Engine + extension Comprehensive ruleset

docs.text:
55 criteria (31 A + 24 AA) must be verified:

docs.title: The axe-core Browser Extension
docs.text:
1.  Install axe DevTools extension
2.  Open DevTools → axe DevTools tab
3.  Click "Scan ALL of my page"
4.  Review violations, incomplete items, and passes
5.  Fix violations and re-scan

docs.text:
1.  Open Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse tab
2.  Select "Accessibility"
3.  Click "Analyze page load"
4.  Review the score and the issues

docs.text:

2.  Click the WAVE icon in the toolbar
3.  View the overlaid icons on the page

docs.title: The Pa11y CLI
docs.text:
# Install
npm install -g pa11y

# Run
pa11y https://example.com

# With WCAG 2.2 AA
pa11y --standard WCAG2AA https://example.com

# JSON output
pa11y --reporter json https://example.com > report.json

docs.title: The jest-axe Integration
docs.text:
import { axe, toHaveNoViolations } from 'jest-axe';

expect.extend(toHaveNoViolations);

test('component is accessible', async () => {
    const { container } = render(<MyComponent />);
    const results = await axe(container);
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
});

docs.title: The "Iceberg" Mental Model
docs.text:
Automated testing sees only the tip of the iceberg:

                    ▲
                   ╱ ╲          ← Automated catches this
                  ╱   ╲            (30–40% of issues)
                 ╱─────╲
                ╱       ╲
               ╱         ╲      ← Manual testing required
              ╱           ╲        (60–70% of issues)
             ╱             ╲
            ╱───────────────╲
           ╱                 ╲
          ╱                   ╲
         ╱─────────────────────╲

The visible tip: missing alt text, insufficient contrast, missing form labels. The submerged mass: reading order, focus management, error announcement, keyboard traps, announcement quality, cognitive load.

docs.title: The "Four Testing Layers" Mental Model
docs.text:
Layer 1: LINT (at keystroke)
  └── ESLint a11y plugins, TypeScript types
  └── Catches: missing alt in JSX, invalid ARIA

Layer 2: AUTOMATED (CI/CD)
  └── axe-core, Pa11y, Lighthouse
  └── Catches: contrast, labels, ARIA validity

Layer 3: MANUAL (pre-merge)
  └── Keyboard, focus, reading order, zoom
  └── Catches: tab order, focus traps, reading order

Layer 4: ASSISTIVE TECH (pre-release)
  └── NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack
  └── Catches: announcement quality, interaction flow

Each layer catches what the layer above cannot. Skipping a layer leaves gaps.

docs.title: The "Tool Selection" Mental Model
docs.text: Need Tool Why CI/CD pipeline axe-core, Pa11y Free, accurate, scriptable Developer education WAVE Visual overlay, intuitive Quick health check Lighthouse Built into Chrome, fast Guided manual review axe DevTools IGT Semi-automated checks for incomplete items Screen reader testing NVDA Free, widely used Enterprise coverage JAWS Market leader Mobile testing VoiceOver, TalkBack Built into devices

docs.title: The "Real Users" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AUTOMATED TOOLS                             │
│  └── Catch: missing alt, contrast, labels    │
│  └── Miss: reading order, focus, semantics   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  MANUAL TESTING                              │
│  └── Catch: keyboard navigation, zoom        │
│  └── Miss: announcement quality              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  SCREEN READER TESTING                       │
│  └── Catch: announcement clarity, flow       │
│  └── Miss: edge cases in real usage          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  REAL USERS WITH DISABILITIES                │
│  └── Catch: everything above, and more       │
│  └── The gold standard                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The most valuable testing is with real users with disabilities. No tool or checklist catches what real users encounter.

docs.title: The "Cost of Late Discovery" Mental Model
docs.text:
Design phase:      $1 to fix
Development:       $10 to fix
QA:                $100 to fix
Production:        $1,000 to fix
Litigation:        $100,000+ to fix

Accessibility issues found in design cost almost nothing. Issues found in production cost 1,000× more. Testing must happen early and continuously.

docs.title: Concept 1: Automated Tools Catch 30–40%
docs.text: The 2026 consensus: automated engines catch roughly 30–40% of WCAG AA failures. Deque claims ~57% with axe-core plus Intelligent Guided Tests. But ~42% of WCAG 2.2 AA criteria cannot be automated at all, and a further ~45% require human judgement to interpret.

docs.title: Concept 2: axe-core — The Industry Standard
docs.text: axe-core is the open-source engine that powers Lighthouse, axe DevTools, and most CI integrations. It has zero false positives on automated checks. It runs on WCAG 2.0/2.1/2.2 A and AA criteria.

docs.title: Concept 3: Lighthouse — Fast Health Check, Not Compliance Signal
docs.text: Lighthouse uses axe-core under the hood but only ships a subset of its rules — around 50–60 audits as of early 2026. It is useful for a quick "is this page in the ballpark" check but is not a compliance signal.

docs.title: Concept 4: WAVE — Visual Feedback for Education
docs.text: WAVE (WebAIM) places icons directly on the rendered page, showing issues in context. It has a higher false-positive rate than axe-core and is not appropriate for CI, but it is excellent for developer education and stakeholder walkthroughs.

docs.title: Concept 5: Lint as the Floor
docs.text: ESLint accessibility plugins (eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, eslint-plugin-vue-a11y) catch issues at keystroke — missing alt in JSX, invalid ARIA attributes, click handlers on non-interactive elements. Lint is the floor, not the ceiling.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Irreducible Manual 42%
docs.text: Roughly 42% of WCAG 2.2 AA criteria cannot be automated. These include: keyboard operability, focus order, focus visibility, reading order, error recovery, redundant entry, and accessible authentication.

docs.title: Concept 7: Keyboard Navigation Testing
docs.text:
The keyboard pass is the single highest-value manual test:

  • Tab / Shift+Tab — forward and backward through all interactive elements.
  • Enter / Space — activate buttons and links.
  • Arrow keys — within widgets (menus, tabs, listbox, autocomplete).
  • Escape — close modals, dropdowns, dismiss popovers.

Verify: coverage (every mouse action has a keyboard equivalent), order (tab follows visual layout), visible indicator (every focusable element has visible focus), and not obscured (sticky headers do not hide focused elements).

docs.title: Concept 8: Screen Reader Market Share (2026)
docs.text:
Based on the WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #10 (2024, still the most recent data):

Screen reader Desktop primary Mobile primary JAWS 40.5% — NVDA 37.7% — VoiceOver 9.7% ~70.6% TalkBack — ~34.7%

Testing priority: NVDA + Chrome (free, 21.3% of users), JAWS + Chrome (24.7%, #1 combination), VoiceOver + Safari (mobile dominance).

docs.title: Concept 9: Testing Matrix
docs.text: Priority Screen reader Browser OS 1 JAWS Chrome Windows 2 NVDA Chrome Windows 3 VoiceOver Safari macOS 4 VoiceOver Safari iOS 5 TalkBack Chrome Android

docs.title: Concept 10: Mobile Accessibility Testing
docs.text: Mobile testing is not optional: 91.3% of screen reader users also use a mobile device. Mobile-specific checks: touch target size (44×44pt iOS, 48×48dp Android), gestures, dynamic type, and reduced motion.

docs.title: Concept 11: The Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Design → Lint → Automated → Manual → AT → Mobile → Release
  │        │        │          │       │       │        │
  │        │        │          │       │       │        └── Monitor
  │        │        │          │       │       └── VoiceOver/TalkBack
  │        │        │          │       └── NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver
  │        │        │          └── Keyboard, focus, zoom, contrast
  │        │        └── axe-core in CI/CD
  │        └── ESLint a11y plugins
  └── Color contrast, touch targets, semantic structure

docs.title: Concept 12: CI/CD Integration
docs.text: Automated accessibility checks should run in CI/CD on every pull request. Use @axe-core/playwright, jest-axe, or pa11y to gate merges. This prevents regressions from reaching production.

docs.title: Concept 13: Real User Testing
docs.text: The most valuable testing is with real users with disabilities. Automated tools, manual checklists, and screen reader testing all catch issues — but real users reveal usability problems that no checklist anticipates.

docs.title: Concept 14: Testing Is Continuous
docs.text: Accessibility decays. Every new feature, every CMS update, every design change can introduce barriers. Testing must be continuous, not a one-time audit.

docs.title: Concept 15: The European Accessibility Act Enforcement (2026)
docs.text:
Since June 2025, the EAA requires accessible e-commerce, banking, transport, and digital products in the EU. Enforcement accelerated in 2026:

  • Netherlands: Dutch ACM moving toward active enforcement mid-2026.
  • France: Carrefour ordered by court in June 2026 to fix its site within six months, with €500/day penalties.
  • Italy: Implementing Decree with transitional arrangements until 2030.

Testing is no longer optional — it is a legal requirement.

docs.title: Concept 16: WCAG 2.2 Testing Checklist
docs.text: 55 criteria (31 A + 24 AA) must be verified. The checklist should be a workflow, not a scorecard: scan first, fix templates, automate what can be automated, manually verify the rest.

docs.title: Concept 17: axe DevTools Intelligent Guided Tests
docs.text: axe DevTools browser extension offers Intelligent Guided Tests (IGT) — semi-automated checks for incomplete items like color-meaning use, link-purpose, and focus-order. Deque demonstrates ~80% issue coverage when combining the engine with guided manual review.

docs.title: Concept 18: Testing the New WCAG 2.2 Criteria
docs.text:
WCAG 2.2 added criteria that require new testing methods:

  • 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured — keyboard sweep to verify focus is not hidden by sticky elements.
  • 2.5.7 Dragging Movements — verify non-drag alternative exists.
  • 2.5.8 Target Size — verify 24×24 CSS pixel minimum.
  • 3.3.7 Redundant Entry — verify no duplicate data requests.
  • 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication — verify no cognitive function tests.

docs.title: Concept 19: Testing Zoom and Reflow
docs.text: WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text) and 1.4.10 (Reflow) require testing at 200% zoom and 320 CSS pixel viewport. Automated tools do not test zoom and reflow — manual inspection is required.

docs.title: Concept 20: Accessibility Statements
docs.text: The EAA requires organizations to publish accessibility statements describing compliance status, known issues, and contact information. Testing provides the data for these statements.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Automated Testing in CI/CD
docs.text:
1.  Developer pushes code.
    │
    ▼
2.  CI pipeline runs:
    │   ├── ESLint a11y plugins (lint)
    │   ├── axe-core via Playwright (automated)
    │   └── Lighthouse CI (health check)
    │
    ▼
3.  Violations reported in PR.
    │
    ▼
4.  Developer fixes violations.
    │
    ▼
5.  Merge blocked until violations resolved.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Manual Keyboard Testing
docs.text:
1.  Put away the mouse.
    │
    ▼
2.  Press Tab repeatedly.
    │
    ▼
3.  Verify:
    │   ├── Every interactive element receives focus
    │   ├── Focus order follows visual order
    │   └── Focus indicator is visible
    │
    ▼
4.  Press Enter/Space to activate.
    │
    ▼
5.  Press Escape to dismiss.
    │
    ▼
6.  Verify no keyboard traps.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Screen Reader Testing
docs.text:
1.  Launch NVDA (Windows) or VoiceOver (macOS/iOS).
    │
    ▼
2.  Navigate to the page.
    │
    ▼
3.  Test structure:
    │   ├── Page title announced correctly
    │   ├── Headings cycle in logical order
    │   └── Landmarks present and labelled
    │
    ▼
4.  Test forms:
    │   ├── Labels announced before inputs
    │   ├── Required state announced
    │   └── Errors announced
    │
    ▼
5.  Test dynamic content:
    │   ├── Live regions announce updates
    │   ├── Modals trap focus correctly
    │   └── Route changes announced
    │
    ▼
6.  Document findings.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The axe-core Scan
docs.text:
1.  Run the scan.
    │
    ▼
2.  Results categorized:
    │   ├── Violations — definite failures
    │   ├── Incomplete — need manual review
    │   ├── Passes — verified
    │   └── Inapplicable — not relevant
    │
    ▼
3.  Fix violations.
    │
    ▼
4.  Review incomplete items manually.
    │
    ▼
5.  Re-scan to verify.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: A Lighthouse Audit
docs.text:
1.  Open Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse.
    │
    ▼
2.  Select "Accessibility".
    │
    ▼
3.  Run the audit.
    │
    ▼
4.  Review the score and the failing audits.
    │
    ▼
5.  Fix and re-run.

docs.title: How axe-core Works
docs.text:
axe-core injects into the page and walks the DOM. For each node, it:

  1. Determines the element's role and accessible name.
  2. Checks against rule definitions (e.g., image-alt, color-contrast).
  3. Returns violations, incomplete items, passes, and inapplicable rules.

The engine is rules-based, not AI-based. It can only check what is programmatically determinable.

docs.title: Why Automated Tools Have Limits
docs.text:
Automated tools cannot determine:

  • Whether alt text is meaningful or just present.
  • Whether link text is descriptive in context.
  • Whether reading order is logical.
  • Whether focus order makes sense.
  • Whether error messages are helpful.
  • Whether content is understandable.

These require human judgement.

docs.title: The Accessibility Tree and Testing
docs.text: Screen readers read the accessibility tree, not the DOM. Testing tools inspect the DOM and the accessibility tree. Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane shows the computed accessible name, role, and state for any element.

docs.title: Lighthouse vs axe-core
docs.text:
Lighthouse uses axe-core but:

  • Ships only ~50–60 of axe-core's ~100+ rules.
  • Weights results by user impact.
  • Reports a score (0–100), which can be misleading.

Use Lighthouse for a quick check. Use axe-core directly for compliance.

docs.title: CI/CD Integration Architecture
docs.text:
Developer push → CI pipeline
                    │
                    ├── Install Playwright + axe-core
                    ├── Start dev server
                    ├── Run tests against all routes
                    ├── Collect violations
                    └── Fail build if violations > 0

docs.title: The axe DevTools IGT Architecture
docs.text:
Intelligent Guided Tests (IGT) are a hybrid approach:

  • The engine runs automated checks.
  • For incomplete items, it guides the developer through manual verification.
  • The developer answers questions about the content.
  • The tool combines the results.

This achieves ~80% coverage vs. ~57% for automated-only.

docs.title: The WebAIM Million Data
docs.text:
The WebAIM Million is an annual automated accessibility analysis of the top 1,000,000 home pages. It provides:

  • The percentage of pages with WCAG failures.
  • The average number of errors per page.
  • The most common error types.
  • Trends over time.

The 2026 report: 95.9% of pages have WCAG failures, averaging 56.1 errors per page — a 10.1% increase from 2025.

docs.title: The Full Testing Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  DESIGN PHASE
    │   ├── Color contrast checked
    │   ├── Touch target sizes verified
    │   └── Keyboard flow mapped
    │
    ▼
2.  DEVELOPMENT PHASE
    │   ├── ESLint a11y plugins (lint)
    │   ├── axe-core in unit tests
    │   └── Manual keyboard testing
    │
    ▼
3.  PRE-MERGE (CI)
    │   ├── axe-core via Playwright
    │   ├── Lighthouse CI
    │   └── Pa11y on key templates
    │
    ▼
4.  PRE-RELEASE
    │   ├── Screen reader testing (NVDA, VoiceOver)
    │   ├── Zoom and reflow testing
    │   └── Mobile testing (VoiceOver iOS, TalkBack)
    │
    ▼
5.  POST-RELEASE
    │   ├── Monitor CSP violations
    │   ├── Monitor accessibility dashboards
    │   └── Schedule quarterly audits

docs.title: Tool Selection Workflow
docs.text:
Need a quick check?
  → Lighthouse (built into Chrome)

Need CI gating?
  → axe-core (Playwright/Cypress)

Need visual feedback for stakeholders?

Need guided manual review?

Need screen reader testing?

2.  Run automated scans on all pages.

3.  Categorize issues.
    │
    ▼
4.  Fix high-impact issues first.
