docs.title: Example 1: Playwright + axe-core CI Test
docs.text:
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

const routes = ['/', '/about', '/products', '/contact'];

for (const route of routes) {
    test(`${route} has no accessibility violations`, async ({ page }) => {
        await page.goto(route);

        const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
            .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa'])
            .analyze();

        expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
    });
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Iterates over all routes.
  • .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa']) — restricts to WCAG 2.2 A and AA criteria.
  • expect(results.violations).toEqual([]) — fails the test if any violations exist.
  • This runs in CI on every pull request.

docs.title: Example 2: Keyboard Testing Protocol
docs.text:
## Keyboard Test — Checkout Flow

### Coverage
- [ ] Can I complete the entire purchase with keyboard only?
- [ ] Can I reach every form field?
- [ ] Can I activate every button?
- [ ] Can I dismiss every modal?

### Order
- [ ] Tab follows visual order (top → bottom, left → right)
- [ ] No positive tabindex values
- [ ] DOM order matches visual order

### Focus Visibility
- [ ] Focus indicator visible on every focusable element
- [ ] Focus indicator meets 2px + 3:1 contrast

### Not Obscured
- [ ] Sticky header does not hide focused element
- [ ] Cookie banner does not cover focused element
- [ ] scroll-margin-top applied where needed

### Traps
- [ ] Can always Tab out of any widget
- [ ] Escape closes modals and dropdowns

Code Breakdown:

  • Covers the four keyboard testing dimensions: coverage, order, visibility, and traps.
  • Each checkbox maps to a WCAG 2.2 success criterion.

docs.title: Example 3: NVDA Screen Reader Test
docs.text:
## NVDA Test — Registration Form

### Structure
- [ ] NVDA+T — page title announced
- [ ] H — headings in logical order
- [ ] D — landmarks present

### Form
- [ ] F — form fields cycle through
- [ ] Tab into email — "Email address, edit, required" announced
- [ ] Submit empty — error announced via role="alert"
- [ ] Focus moves to first invalid field

### Interactive
- [ ] B — buttons announced with names
- [ ] Open modal — focus moves in
- [ ] Close modal — focus returns to trigger

Code Breakdown:

  • Covers structure, form, and interactive testing.
  • Each check maps to a WCAG 2.2 success criterion.

docs.title: Example 4: Lighthouse CI Configuration
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/lighthouse.yml
name: Lighthouse CI
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  lighthouse:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: treosh/lighthouse-ci-action@v12
        with:
          urls: |
            https://example.com/
            https://example.com/about
          budgetPath: ./lighthouse-budget.json
          uploadArtifacts: true

Code Breakdown:

  • Runs Lighthouse on every pull request.
  • budgetPath — enforces performance and accessibility budgets.
  • uploadArtifacts — stores results for review.

docs.title: Example 5: WAVE for Stakeholder Education
docs.text:
## WAVE Walkthrough for Designers

1. Install WAVE extension (Chrome/Firefox)
2. Navigate to the page
3. Click WAVE icon
4. Review:
   - [ ] Red icons = errors
   - [ ] Yellow icons = alerts
   - [ ] Green icons = features
   - [ ] Contrast errors highlighted on page

5. Discuss findings with the team

Code Breakdown:

  • WAVE's visual overlay makes issues tangible for non-engineers.
  • Not appropriate for CI — use axe-core for that.

docs.title: Example 6: Mobile VoiceOver Test
docs.text:
## VoiceOver iOS Test — Checkout

### Setup
- [ ] Settings → Accessibility → VoiceOver → On
- [ ] Open Safari

### Navigation
- [ ] Swipe right — moves through elements
- [ ] Double-tap — activates focused element
- [ ] Two-finger swipe up — reads all
- [ ] Rotor — switch to Headings

### Touch Targets
- [ ] All buttons ≥ 44×44pt
- [ ] No adjacent targets closer than 8pt

### Forms
- [ ] Labels announced before inputs
- [ ] Correct keyboard type (numeric for OTP)
- [ ] Error announced

Code Breakdown:

  • Covers mobile-specific concerns: gestures, touch targets, and on-screen keyboard.
  • Maps to WCAG 2.5.8 (Target Size) and platform guidelines.

docs.title: Example 7: jest-axe Unit Test
docs.text:
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';
import { axe, toHaveNoViolations } from 'jest-axe';
import MyButton from './MyButton';

expect.extend(toHaveNoViolations);

describe('MyButton', () => {
    it('has no accessibility violations', async () => {
        const { container } = render(<MyButton>Click me</MyButton>);
        const results = await axe(container);
        expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
    });

    it('renders an accessible button', () => {
        const { getByRole } = render(<MyButton>Click me</MyButton>);
        expect(getByRole('button', { name: 'Click me' })).toBeInTheDocument();
    });
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Tests the component in isolation.
  • axe(container) runs the automated scan.
  • toHaveNoViolations() — custom matcher for jest-axe.
  • The second test verifies the accessible name.

docs.title: Example 8: Pa11y CI Configuration
docs.text:
{
    "defaults": {
        "standard": "WCAG2AA",
        "timeout": 30000,
        "wait": 1000,
        "chromeLaunchConfig": {
            "args": ["--no-sandbox"]
        }
    },
    "urls": [
        "https://example.com/",
        "https://example.com/about",
        "https://example.com/products"
    ]
}

pa11y-ci --config .pa11yci.json

Code Breakdown:

  • standard: "WCAG2AA" — targets WCAG 2.2 AA.
  • urls — the pages to test.
  • pa11y-ci — the CI-friendly wrapper around Pa11y.

docs.title: Example 9: Testing WCAG 2.2 Focus Not Obscured
docs.text:
/* Potential violation: sticky header obscures focused elements */
.sticky-header {
    position: sticky;
    top: 0;
    height: 80px;
}

/* Fix: add scroll-margin-top to focusable elements */
:focus {
    scroll-margin-top: 80px;
}

Test protocol:

## Focus Not Obscured Test (WCAG 2.4.11)

1. Put away the mouse
2. Tab through the page
3. For each focused element:
   - [ ] Is the focused element fully visible?
   - [ ] Is any part obscured by a sticky header?
   - [ ] Is any part obscured by a cookie banner?
4. If obscured → add `scroll-margin-top`

Code Breakdown:

  • WCAG 2.2 added 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured).
  • Automated tools cannot test this — manual verification is required.
  • scroll-margin-top is the standard fix.

docs.title: Example 10: The Complete Accessibility Test Suite
docs.text:
// accessibility.spec.js
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test.describe('Accessibility', () => {
    test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
        await page.goto('/');
    });

    test('automated WCAG 2.2 AA scan', async ({ page }) => {
        const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
            .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa'])
            .analyze();
        expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
    });

    test('page has a single h1', async ({ page }) => {
        const h1Count = await page.locator('h1').count();
        expect(h1Count).toBe(1);
    });

    test('all images have alt text', async ({ page }) => {
        const images = await page.locator('img').all();
        for (const img of images) {
            const alt = await img.getAttribute('alt');
            expect(alt).not.toBeNull();
        }
    });

    test('all form inputs have labels', async ({ page }) => {
        const inputs = await page.locator('input:not([type="hidden"])').all();
        for (const input of inputs) {
            const id = await input.getAttribute('id');
            const ariaLabel = await input.getAttribute('aria-label');
            const label = id ? await page.locator(`label[for="${id}"]`).count() : 0;
            expect(label > 0 || ariaLabel).toBeTruthy();
        }
    });

    test('keyboard navigation reaches the main content', async ({ page }) => {
        await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
        const focused = await page.evaluate(() => document.activeElement?.textContent);
        expect(focused).toContain('Skip to');
    });
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Combines automated scanning with targeted structural tests.
  • Runs in CI on every pull request.
  • Catches regressions before they reach production.

docs.text: Use Case Primary Tool Secondary Tool CI/CD regression prevention axe-core (Playwright) Pa11y Developer education WAVE axe DevTools Quick health check Lighthouse WAVE Pre-release audit NVDA + JAWS + VoiceOver axe DevTools IGT Mobile app testing VoiceOver iOS, TalkBack Manual gestures Design review Contrast checkers Touch target rulers Enterprise compliance JAWS + Chrome axe-core + manual Legal/EAA compliance Full WCAG 2.2 AA audit Real user testing Component library testing jest-axe Storybook a11y addon Design system auditing axe-core + manual Accessibility statements

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Start testing in design, not development. Why: issues caught in design cost 1,000× less to fix.
  2. Integrate axe-core into CI/CD. Why: prevents regressions from reaching production.
  3. Use ESLint a11y plugins. Why: catches issues at keystroke, before CI.
  4. Test with keyboard only. Why: keyboard accessibility is the foundation of all accessibility.
  5. Test with at least one screen reader. Why: automated tools cannot verify announcement quality.
  6. Test with NVDA and VoiceOver at minimum. Why: NVDA is free; VoiceOver covers Apple platforms.
  7. Test on mobile. Why: 91.3% of screen reader users also use mobile.
  8. Test zoom to 200%. Why: WCAG 1.4.4 requires it; automated tools do not test zoom.
  9. Test reflow at 320 CSS pixels. Why: WCAG 1.4.10 requires it.
  10. Use axe-core directly, not just Lighthouse. Why: Lighthouse ships only a subset of axe rules.
  11. Combine automated and manual testing. Why: automated catches 30–40%; manual catches the rest.
  12. Document testing protocols. Why: consistency across team members.
  13. Test after every significant UI change. Why: accessibility regressions are common.
  14. Use real content, not lorem ipsum. Why: meaningful content reveals real issues.
  15. Involve users with disabilities. Why: they find issues no checklist anticipates.
  16. Audit quarterly. Why: accessibility decays as content and code change.
  17. Publish an accessibility statement. Why: EAA requires it; testing provides the data.
  18. Track violations over time. Why: measure progress and identify regression patterns.
  19. Train the team. Why: accessibility is everyone's responsibility.
  20. Use the WCAG 2.2 checklist as a workflow, not a scorecard. Why: it is a process, not a grade.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Automated-Only Testing
docs.text:
// CI passes, but no screen reader testing

Why it's wrong: Automated tools catch only 30–40% of issues. The site may be unusable with a screen reader despite passing CI.

✅ Correct: Combine automated, manual, and screen reader testing.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Keyboard Testing
docs.text:
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

Why it's wrong: Automated tools do not catch keyboard inoperability. The button works with a mouse but not a keyboard.

✅ Correct: Test keyboard navigation on every release.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Testing Only at the End
docs.text:
<!-- Accessibility audit scheduled two weeks before launch -->

Why it's wrong: Issues found late are expensive to fix and may delay launch.

✅ Correct: Test continuously from design through release.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Relying on Lighthouse Score
docs.text:
<!-- Lighthouse score 100, but no manual testing -->

Why it's wrong: Lighthouse uses a subset of axe-core rules and weights them by impact. A perfect score does not mean compliance.

✅ Correct: Use Lighthouse for a quick check; use axe-core and manual testing for compliance.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Testing Only on Desktop
docs.text:
<!-- Desktop testing only -->

Why it's wrong: 91.3% of screen reader users also use mobile. Mobile has unique concerns: touch targets, gestures, VoiceOver/TalkBack.

✅ Correct: Test on iOS and Android with VoiceOver and TalkBack.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No CI Integration
docs.text:
<!-- Accessibility tested manually once per quarter -->

Why it's wrong: Regressions reach production between audits.

✅ Correct: Integrate axe-core into CI/CD.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring WCAG 2.2 New Criteria
docs.text:
<!-- Testing only WCAG 2.1 criteria -->

Why it's wrong: WCAG 2.2 added criteria that many existing sites fail: Focus Not Obscured, Focus Appearance, Dragging Movements, Target Size, Redundant Entry, Accessible Authentication.

✅ Correct: Test against WCAG 2.2 AA.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Accessibility Statement
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The EAA requires it for relevant services.

✅ Correct: Publish and maintain an accessibility statement.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Automated Tools Catch Everything
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Automated tools catch only 30–40%. The rest requires manual testing.

✅ Correct: Use a layered testing strategy.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Testing with Lorem Ipsum
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Real content reveals real issues (unclear link text, missing context, complex tables).

✅ Correct: Test with real, representative content.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• axe-core adds minimal overhead — typically under 100ms per page.
  • Lighthouse audits take 10–30 seconds per page — run in CI, not on every commit.
  • Screen reader testing is manual — no performance impact on the page.
  • CI integration adds seconds to pipeline — but prevents regressions.
  • Large DOM may slow automated scanning — but this is rare.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Run axe-core on key templates, not every page.
  2. Use Lighthouse CI on pull requests, not every push.
  3. Cache npm dependencies for CI.
  4. Run automated tests in parallel with other CI jobs.
  5. Use jest-axe for component-level testing — faster than full-page scans.

docs.title: Accessibility Overlays Are Not a Fix
docs.text: Third-party overlay widgets claim to make sites accessible automatically. They do not. They cannot fix missing semantics, keyboard traps, or poor contrast. Overlays have been sued for failing to provide actual accessibility. They can also introduce security risks — they often load third-party JavaScript.

docs.title: Testing Tools and Data
docs.text: Automated testing tools run in the browser. Do not test on production with sensitive data unless the tool is vetted. Use staging environments.

docs.title: Screen Reader Testing and Authentication
docs.text: Screen reader testing often requires logging in. Ensure test accounts are set up with appropriate security.

docs.title: CI/CD Access
docs.text: Accessibility testing tools in CI/CD may need network access to staging environments. Secure credentials and limit scope.

docs.title: Accessibility Statements and Legal Risk
docs.text: An inaccurate accessibility statement can increase legal risk. Statements must be truthful and maintained.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane — inspect accessible name, role, and state.
  • axe DevTools extension — run scans directly in the browser.
  • WAVE extension — visual overlay of issues.
  • Lighthouse — built into Chrome DevTools.
  • document.activeElement — check which element has focus.
  • element.labels — verify label association.
  • form.checkValidity() — check form validation state.
  • NVDA — NVDA+T for title, H for headings, D for landmarks.
  • VoiceOver — VO+U for rotor.
  • prefers-reduced-motion — test in DevTools → Rendering.
  • Zoom to 200% — test in browser zoom.
  • Mobile emulation — Chrome DevTools device toolbar.
  • axe-core console — axe.run() in the console.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every project — accessibility testing is a baseline requirement.
  • Every release — test before shipping.
  • Every new component — test in isolation.
  • Every form — labels, errors, keyboard.
  • Every interactive widget — modals, dropdowns, tabs.
  • Every EU-facing product — EAA compliance since June 2025.
  • Every government service — Section 508, ADA Title II.
  • Every design system — consistent accessible components.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not rely on automated testing alone. It catches only 30–40%.
  • Do not use overlays as a substitute. They do not work.
  • Do not skip manual keyboard testing. Automated tools cannot verify tab order.
  • Do not skip screen reader testing. Automated tools cannot verify announcement quality.
  • Do not test only at the end. Test continuously.
  • Do not use lorem ipsum for testing. Use real content.
  • Do not trust a perfect Lighthouse score. It is not compliance.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• 95.9% of the top one million home pages have automatically detectable WCAG failures, averaging 56.1 errors per page — a 10.1% increase from 2025.
  • Automated tools catch only 30–40% of WCAG AA failures.
  • ~42% of WCAG 2.2 AA criteria cannot be automated at all.
  • axe-core has zero false positives on automated checks.
  • Lighthouse ships only ~50–60 of axe-core's ~100+ rules — it is a health check, not a compliance signal.
  • Deque claims ~80% issue coverage when combining axe-core with Intelligent Guided Tests.
  • JAWS leads desktop screen reader use at 40.5%, with NVDA at 37.7% and VoiceOver at 9.7%.
  • VoiceOver dominates mobile screen reader use at ~70.6%.
  • 91.3% of screen reader users also use a mobile device.
  • The European Accessibility Act took effect June 2025 — enforcement accelerated in 2026.
  • A French court ordered Carrefour in June 2026 to make its site accessible within six months, with €500/day penalties.
  • The Dutch ACM moved toward active enforcement in mid-2026.
  • WCAG 2.2 added 9 criteria and removed 1 — the new criteria require new testing methods.
  • Testing at 200% zoom and 320px reflow is required by WCAG but not tested by automated tools.
  • The 2026 WebAIM Million found the first increase in errors after years of gradual improvement.
  • Missing alt text is the most common WCAG failure — reported on 55.5% of home pages.
  • Low contrast text is the second most common failure — reported on 79.1% of home pages.
  • Empty links are the third most common failure — reported on 45.4% of home pages.
  • Missing form labels are the fourth most common failure — reported on 48.2% of home pages.
  • The average home page has 56.1 accessibility errors — up from 51 in 2025.
  • Accessibility overlays have been sued for failing to provide actual accessibility.
  • Real user testing is the gold standard — it catches what no tool or checklist anticipates.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Accessibility validation is the systematic evaluation of digital products against WCAG 2.2 AA.
  • 95.9% of top home pages fail WCAG — averaging 56.1 errors per page, up 10.1% from 2025.
  • Automated tools catch only 30–40% of issues; ~42% of criteria cannot be automated at all.
  • Three-layer strategy: automated (axe-core, Lighthouse, WAVE, Pa11y), manual (keyboard, focus, zoom), assistive technology (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack).
  • axe-core is the industry standard — zero false positives, powers Lighthouse and CI integrations.
  • Lighthouse is a quick check, not a compliance signal — it ships only a subset of axe-core rules.
  • Keyboard testing is the highest-value manual test — coverage, order, visibility, no traps.
  • Screen reader testing is mandatory — test with NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver.
  • Mobile testing is not optional — 91.3% of screen reader users also use mobile.
  • WCAG 2.2 added 9 new criteria requiring new testing methods.
  • The EAA is enforced — fines and court orders began in 2026.
  • Integrate axe-core into CI/CD to prevent regressions.
  • Test continuously — from design through release and beyond.
  • Use real users with disabilities — they find what no tool can.
  • Accessibility testing is both a legal obligation and a competitive advantage.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Browser compatibility is the practice of building web pages and applications that function correctly — structurally, visually, and behaviorally — across all browsers and devices that a target audience uses. It is the discipline of understanding what works where, what degrades gracefully, and what requires a fallback.

<!-- Works everywhere: progressive enhancement -->
<button type="button">Save</button>

<!-- Works in modern browsers; older browsers ignore unknown attributes -->
<input type="text" autocomplete="off" inputmode="numeric" enterkeyhint="done">

<!-- Feature-detected enhancement -->
<script>
    if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) {
        // Use IntersectionObserver
    } else {
        // Fallback to scroll listener
    }
</script>

Browser compatibility is not about supporting every browser ever made. It is about deliberately choosing which browsers to support, understanding the feature landscape for those browsers, and implementing the right fallbacks where needed.

The question is no longer "does this work in IE?" — Internet Explorer was officially retired on June 15, 2022 [9†L40-L42]. The question in 2026 is: "What is Baseline for this feature, and does my target audience fall within Baseline?"

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Browser compatibility serves several essential purposes:

  • Universal access — users on any browser can access content.
  • Consistent experience — the page works predictably across engines.
  • Progressive enhancement — modern features enhance; core functionality works everywhere.
  • Graceful degradation — older browsers get a functional fallback.
  • Cost management — supporting too many browsers is expensive.
  • Legal compliance — some regulations require compatibility with specific browsers.
  • Performance — modern browsers get optimized experiences.
  • Future-proofing — the site works in browsers that do not exist yet.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Validation
│
├── HTML Validator          ← markup correctness
├── Common Errors           ← frequent validation errors
├── Accessibility Validation ← automated a11y checks
├── Browser Compatibility   ← cross-browser testing (THIS CHAPTER)
└── Debugging HTML          ← tools and techniques

Browser Compatibility is the final validation layer. Valid HTML, accessible markup, and error-free pages all mean nothing if the page does not work in the user's browser.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The web is not a single platform. It is a collection of engines — Blink (Chrome, Edge, Opera, Brave), Gecko (Firefox), WebKit (Safari, iOS browsers) — each with its own implementation of the standards. When a new feature ships in Chrome, it may take months or years to reach Safari. When Safari implements a feature differently, code that works in one browser breaks in another.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BLINK (Chrome, Edge, Opera, Brave)          │
│  └── Largest market share                    │
│  └── Fastest feature adoption                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  GECKO (Firefox)                             │
│  └── Independent implementation              │
│  └── Strong standards focus                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WEBKIT (Safari, iOS browsers)               │
│  └── iOS requires WebKit for all browsers    │
│  └── Slower feature adoption historically    │
│  └── Unique iOS-specific constraints         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A developer writing code in Chrome cannot assume it works in Safari. A feature that is "widely supported" may have subtle implementation differences. Cross-browser compatibility exists to manage these differences deliberately.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No feature support data Developers guessed what worked No market share data Hard to prioritize which browsers to support No baseline standard Every feature required manual research Vendor prefixes -webkit-, -moz-, -ms- everywhere No polyfill ecosystem Every feature required custom fallback code No testing infrastructure Real-device testing was manual and slow IE legacy Years of hacks for a single browser

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Browser compatibility has been a concern since the first browser wars of the 1990s. But the modern approach was shaped by:

  • 2006 — jQuery launched, abstracting away browser differences.
  • 2008 — Can I Use launched, providing feature support data.
  • 2015 — Autoprefixer automated vendor prefixing.
  • 2019 — Babel and @babel/preset-env made transpilation standard.
  • 2023 — Baseline launched, providing a unified compatibility standard.
  • 2024–2026 — Baseline adopted by GitLab, MDN, and major frameworks.

Baseline, maintained by the W3C WebDX Community Group, defines two tiers:

Tier Meaning Adoption Baseline Newly available Interoperable across Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari 13.9% of users Baseline Widely available Interoperable for 30+ months 98.0% of users

A feature that is Baseline Newly available works in all current browsers but may not work in older versions. A feature that is Baseline Widely available has been stable for at least 30 months and is safe to use without fallbacks in most production environments.

In 2026, browser compatibility is not about checking every feature manually. It is about knowing the Baseline status of each feature and choosing a support target for your audience.

docs.title: The Baseline Standard
docs.text:
The Web Platform Baseline is the 2026 standard for browser compatibility. It answers one question: "Does this feature work in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari?"

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BASELINE NEWLY AVAILABLE                    │
│  └── Works in all current browsers           │
│  └── May not work in older versions          │
│  └── 13.9% of users                          │
│  └── Example: View Transitions               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  BASELINE WIDELY AVAILABLE                   │
│  └── Works in all browsers for 30+ months    │
│  └── Safe to use without fallbacks           │
│  └── 98.0% of users                          │
│  └── Example: CSS Grid, Flexbox, Container Queries │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Checking Baseline Status
docs.text:
On MDN:

Every MDN feature page includes a Baseline badge:

✅ Baseline Widely available
⚠️ Baseline Newly available
❌ Limited availability

On Can I Use:

Can I Use provides detailed support tables for every feature, browser, and version.

On webstatus.dev:

The Web Platform Status dashboard shows Baseline status for every feature.

docs.title: The Recommended Support Target (2026)
docs.text:
For most organizations in 2026, the recommended support target is:

Browser Support target Google Chrome Latest 2 versions Microsoft Edge Latest 2 versions Mozilla Firefox Latest 2 versions Apple Safari (macOS) Latest 2 versions Safari on iOS Current & previous major iOS version Chrome on Android Current version Samsung Internet Recommended for Android-heavy audiences

This mirrors guidance from Google and aligns with MDN Baseline Compatibility.

docs.title: Feature Detection
docs.text:
// Check if a feature exists
if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) {
    // Use IntersectionObserver
} else {
    // Fallback
}

// Check if a CSS property is supported
if (CSS.supports('display', 'grid')) {
    // Use Grid
}

// Check if an API is available
if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
    navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js');
}

docs.title: CSS Feature Queries
docs.text:
/* Apply styles only if the feature is supported */
@supports (display: grid) {
    .layout {
        display: grid;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
    }
}

@supports not (display: grid) {
    .layout {
        display: flex;
        flex-wrap: wrap;
    }
}

docs.title: Progressive Enhancement
docs.text:
<!-- Base: works everywhere -->
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input id="email" type="email" name="email" required>
    <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

<!-- Enhanced: better UX in modern browsers -->
<script>
    if ('fetch' in window && 'FormData' in window) {
        form.addEventListener('submit', async (e) => {
            e.preventDefault();
            const response = await fetch('/subscribe', {
                method: 'POST',
                body: new FormData(form)
            });
            // Handle response
        });
    }
</script>

docs.title: The GitLab Baseline Adoption
docs.text: GitLab adopted the Web Platform Baseline "Widely available" browser set as their frontend support target, replacing market-share-based queries.

docs.title: The "Three Engines" Mental Model
docs.text:
In 2026, there are three major browser engines:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BLINK                                       │
│  ├── Chrome (desktop, Android)               │
│  ├── Edge                                    │
│  ├── Opera                                   │
│  ├── Brave                                   │
│  ├── Vivaldi                                 │
│  └── Arc                                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  GECKO                                       │
│  └── Firefox (desktop, Android)              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WEBKIT                                      │
│  ├── Safari (macOS, iOS)                     │
│  └── All iOS browsers (required)             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

If a feature works in all three engines, it is Baseline. If it works in only one or two, it is limited availability.

docs.title: The "Baseline Decision" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IS THE FEATURE BASELINE?                    │
│                                              │
│  YES → Use it. No fallback needed.           │
│                                              │
│  NO → Is it critical to functionality?       │
│       │                                      │
│       ├── YES → Use a polyfill or fallback   │
│       │                                      │
│       └── NO  → Progressive enhancement      │
│                  (use where supported)        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Baseline standard gives a clear answer to the compatibility question.

docs.title: The "Progressive Enhancement" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LAYER 1: CORE FUNCTIONALITY                 │
│  └── Works in every browser                  │
│  └── HTML, basic CSS, basic JS               │
│  └── Always present                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYER 2: ENHANCED EXPERIENCE                │
│  └── Works in modern browsers                │
│  └── CSS Grid, Flexbox, modern APIs          │
│  └── Applied via @supports or feature detection │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYER 3: OPTIONAL EXTRAS                    │
│  └── Works in cutting-edge browsers          │
│  └── View Transitions, Anchor Positioning    │
│  └── Bonus for users who have them           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Build for Layer 1. Enhance for Layer 2. Experiment with Layer 3.

docs.title: The "Market Share vs. Baseline" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MARKET SHARE (2026)                         │
│  ├── Chrome: ~65%                            │
│  ├── Safari: ~18%                            │
│  ├── Edge: ~5%                               │
│  ├── Firefox: ~3%                            │
│  └── Others: ~9%                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  BASELINE (2026)                             │
│  ├── Newly available: 13.9% of users         │
│  └── Widely available: 98.0% of users        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Market share tells you who is using which browser. Baseline tells you whether a feature works in all browsers. You need both to make good decisions.

docs.title: The "Fallback Strategy" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FEATURE IS BASELINE                         │
│  └── No fallback needed                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  FEATURE IS NOT BASELINE                     │
│  └── Option 1: Polyfill                      │
│  └── Option 2: @supports fallback            │
│  └── Option 3: Feature detection             │
│  └── Option 4: Ignore (progressive enhancement)│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Not every non-Baseline feature needs a fallback. Some features are enhancements — if they do not work, the page still functions.

docs.title: The "Choosing a Support Target" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  QUESTION: Which browsers must work?         │
│                                              │
│  ANSWER: Depends on your audience.           │
│                                              │
│  Consumer site → Latest 2 versions           │
│  Enterprise → Latest 2 + older ESR           │
│  Government → Specific compliance list        │
│  Global → Baseline Widely available          │
│  Cutting-edge → Baseline Newly available     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

There is no universal answer. The support target is a business decision, not a technical one.

docs.title: Concept 1: Baseline
docs.text: The Web Platform Baseline defines whether a feature is interoperable across Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari. Maintained by the W3C WebDX Community Group.

docs.title: Concept 2: Baseline Newly Available
docs.text: The feature works in all current browsers. 13.9% of users have a browser that supports the full Baseline Newly available set.

docs.title: Concept 3: Baseline Widely Available
docs.text: The feature has been interoperable for 30+ months. 98.0% of users have a browser that supports the full Baseline Widely available set.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Three Engines
docs.text: Blink (Chrome, Edge), Gecko (Firefox), WebKit (Safari). A feature is Baseline if it works in all three.

docs.title: Concept 5: Market Share
docs.text: Google Chrome dominates with ~65% global share. Safari is second at ~18%. Edge and Firefox are smaller.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Recommended Support Target
docs.text: Latest 2 versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari; current and previous iOS version; current Chrome for Android.

docs.title: Concept 7: Feature Detection
docs.text: Checking at runtime whether a feature exists before using it. 'IntersectionObserver' in window, CSS.supports().

docs.title: Concept 8: CSS @supports
docs.text: A CSS feature query that applies styles only if the browser supports a given property-value pair.

docs.title: Concept 9: Polyfills
docs.text: JavaScript code that implements a feature in browsers that do not support it natively. Polyfills should be loaded conditionally.

docs.title: Concept 10: Transpilation
docs.text: Converting modern JavaScript (ES2020+) to older syntax (ES5) using tools like Babel.

docs.title: Concept 11: Autoprefixer
docs.text: A tool that adds vendor prefixes to CSS based on the target browsers.

docs.title: Concept 12: browserslist
docs.text: A configuration format for specifying target browsers, used by Babel, Autoprefixer, and other tools.

docs.title: Concept 13: Can I Use
docs.text: The primary database of browser feature support.

docs.title: Concept 14: MDN Baseline Badges
docs.text: MDN shows Baseline status for every feature page.

docs.title: Concept 15: Web Platform Status
docs.text: The webstatus.dev dashboard shows Baseline status for every feature.

docs.title: Concept 16: Internet Explorer Is Retired
docs.text: IE 11 was officially retired on June 15, 2022. It is no longer a supported browser.

docs.title: Concept 17: Edge (EdgeHTML) Is Retired
docs.text: The original EdgeHTML engine was replaced by Chromium in Edge 79 (2020).

docs.title: Concept 18: Safari on iOS
docs.text: All browsers on iOS must use WebKit. This means Chrome on iOS is effectively Safari.

docs.title: Concept 19: Container Queries
docs.text: Container Queries became Baseline Widely available on August 14, 2025.

docs.title: Concept 20: Subgrid
docs.text: Subgrid became Baseline Widely available in June 2026.

docs.title: Concept 21: Temporal API
docs.text: Firefox 139 shipped Temporal unflagged in May 2025. Chrome 144 and Edge 144 shipped Temporal in 2026. Safari's support was still pending as of mid-2026.

docs.title: Concept 22: WebGPU
docs.text: WebGPU's Baseline availability was blocked since January 2026 by Firefox, with an 8-month gap.

docs.title: Concept 23: Feature Queries in CSS
docs.text: @supports allows conditional CSS based on feature support. Example: @supports (grid-template-columns: subgrid) { ... }.

docs.title: Concept 24: Polyfill Caveats
docs.text: The perfect polyfill is hard to find. Most have caveats, performance impacts, or maintenance risks. Understand the polyfill before using it.

docs.title: Concept 25: Baseline Year
docs.text: Instead of targeting "Widely available," you can target a specific Baseline year (e.g., 2023, 2024). This allows you to use features from that year and later without fallbacks.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Determining Browser Support
docs.text:
1.  Identify the feature you want to use.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check its Baseline status:
    │   ├── MDN feature page
    │   ├── Can I Use
    │   └── webstatus.dev
    │
    ▼
3.  Is it Baseline Widely available?
    │   ├── YES → Use it. No fallback needed.
    │   └── NO  → Continue.
    │
    ▼
4.  Is it Baseline Newly available?
    │   ├── YES → Use it. Consider fallback for older versions.
    │   └── NO  → Continue.
    │
    ▼
5.  Is there a polyfill?
    │   ├── YES → Evaluate the polyfill.
    │   └── NO  → Use progressive enhancement or fallback.
    │
    ▼
6.  Implement the feature with the chosen strategy.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Feature Detection
docs.text:
// Check for a JavaScript API
if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) {
    // Use IntersectionObserver
} else {
    // Fallback: load polyfill or use alternative
}

// Check for a CSS feature
if (CSS.supports('display', 'grid')) {
    // Use Grid
} else {
    // Use Flexbox
}

// Check for a DOM API
if ('attachShadow' in Element.prototype) {
    // Use Shadow DOM
} else {
    // Fallback
}

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The @supports Workflow
docs.text:
/* Base styles: work everywhere */
.layout {
    display: flex;
    flex-wrap: wrap;
    gap: 1rem;
}

/* Enhanced: works in browsers that support Grid */
@supports (display: grid) {
    .layout {
        display: grid;

    }

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Polyfill Workflow
docs.text:
<!-- Load polyfill only if needed -->
<script>
    if (!('IntersectionObserver' in window)) {
        document.write('<script src="/polyfills/intersection-observer.js"><\/script>');
    }
</script>

<!-- Or using dynamic import -->
<script type="module">
    if (!('IntersectionObserver' in window)) {
        await import('/polyfills/intersection-observer.js');
    }
</script>

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Transpilation Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Write modern JavaScript (ES2020+).
    │
    ▼
2.  Configure Babel with @babel/preset-env.
    │
    ▼
3.  Specify target browsers (via browserslist).
    │
    ▼
4.  Babel transpiles to compatible syntax.
    │
    ▼
5.  Deploy the transpiled code.
    │
    ▼
6.  Modern browsers get optimized code (via module/nomodule).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Baseline Adoption Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Choose a Baseline target:
    │   ├── Widely available (98% of users)
    │   ├── Newly available (13.9% of users)
    │   └── A specific year (e.g., 2024 = 85.4% of users)
    │
    ▼
2.  Configure browserslist to match.
    │
    ▼
3.  Configure Babel/Autoprefixer.
    │
    ▼
4.  Use features that are Baseline for your target.
    │
    ▼
5.  Test in the target browsers.

docs.title: The Baseline Algorithm
docs.text:
Baseline is determined by the W3C WebDX Community Group:

  1. A feature is proposed.
  2. Browser vendors implement it.
  3. When Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari all ship it, it becomes Baseline Newly available.
  4. After 30 months of stable support, it becomes Baseline Widely available.

The 30-month window ensures that users on older browser versions are not left behind.

docs.title: The Market Share Data
docs.text:
Global browser market share (2026):

Browser Share Chrome ~65% Safari ~18% Edge ~5% Firefox ~3% Samsung Internet ~3% Other ~6%

On Windows, Chrome accounts for 69.3%, Edge 18.5%, Firefox 6.6%, Opera 2.7%, Brave 1.6%.

docs.text: Engine Browsers Market Share Blink Chrome, Edge, Opera, Brave, Vivaldi, Arc ~73% WebKit Safari (macOS, iOS) ~18% Gecko Firefox ~3%

docs.title: The Polyfill Architecture
docs.text:
Polyfills typically:

  1. Detect whether the feature is missing.
  2. Provide a JavaScript implementation.
  3. Patch the global scope (e.g., window.IntersectionObserver).

Polyfills are loaded conditionally — only when the feature is missing.

docs.title: The Transpilation Architecture
docs.text:
Source code (ES2020+)
    │
    ▼
Babel (@babel/preset-env)
    │
    ▼
Target browsers (browserslist)
    │
    ▼
Transpiled code (ES5+)
    │
    ▼
Bundle (Webpack, Vite, Rollup)

docs.text:
CSS source
    │
    ▼
Autoprefixer
    │
    ▼
Target browsers (browserslist)
    │
    ▼
CSS with vendor prefixes

docs.title: The CSS @supports Architecture
docs.text:
@supports is a conditional group rule in CSS:

@supports (condition) {
    /* Applied only if condition is true */
}

The condition can be:

  • A property-value pair: (display: grid).
  • A conjunction: (display: grid) and (gap: 1rem).
  • A disjunction: (display: grid) or (display: flex).
  • A negation: not (display: grid).

1.  DEFINE THE TARGET

docs.title: Example 1: Checking Baseline on MDN
docs.text:
1.  Visit developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_grid_layout
2.  Look for the Baseline badge:
    ✅ Baseline Widely available
3.  The feature is safe to use.

Code Breakdown:

  • MDN shows Baseline status for every feature.
  • ✅ Widely available — safe to use.
  • ⚠️ Newly available — use with caution.
  • ❌ Limited availability — use with fallback.

docs.title: Example 2: The @supports Fallback
docs.text:
/* Base: Flexbox (works everywhere) */
.card-grid {
    display: flex;
    flex-wrap: wrap;
    gap: 1rem;
}

.card {
    flex: 1 1 300px;
}

/* Enhanced: CSS Grid (Baseline Widely available) */
@supports (display: grid) {
    .card-grid {
        display: grid;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr));
    }
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Base styles work in every browser.
  • @supports applies Grid styles only where supported.
  • Grid is Baseline Widely available, so the fallback is rarely used.

docs.title: Example 3: Feature Detection with Fallback
docs.text:
// Check for IntersectionObserver
if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) {
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
        entries.forEach((entry) => {
            if (entry.isIntersecting) {
                entry.target.classList.add('visible');
            }
        });
    });

    document.querySelectorAll('.animate').forEach((el) => {
        observer.observe(el);
    });
} else {
    // Fallback: show everything
    document.querySelectorAll('.animate').forEach((el) => {
        el.classList.add('visible');
    });
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Modern browsers get the animation.
  • Older browsers get the fallback.
  • No polyfill required.

docs.title: Example 4: Polyfill with Dynamic Import
docs.text:
<script type="module">
    // Check for a feature and load the polyfill only if needed
    if (!('IntersectionObserver' in window)) {
        await import('/polyfills/intersection-observer.js');
    }

    // Now the feature is available
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(/* ... */);
</script>

Code Breakdown:

  • The polyfill is loaded only when needed.
  • import() is dynamic — modern browsers only.
  • The polyfill patches the missing feature.

last 2 Safari versions

iOS >= 15

  • corejs: 3 uses the CoreJS 3 polyfill set.

docs.title: Example 7: Testing with Playwright

// playwright.config.js
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
    projects: [
        { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
        { name: 'firefox', use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] } },
        { name: 'webkit', use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] } },
        { name: 'mobile-chrome', use: { ...devices['Pixel 7'] } },
        { name: 'mobile-safari', use: { ...devices['iPhone 15'] } }
    ]
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Tests run across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.
  • Mobile viewports are included.
  • The same test suite runs in all browsers.

docs.title: Example 8: Testing with BrowserStack
docs.text:
// Using the browser-compatibility-tester package
import { testOn } from '@intentsolutionsio/browser-compatibility-tester';

await testOn({
    provider: 'browserstack',
    browsers: ['chrome', 'firefox', 'safari', 'edge'],
    devices: ['desktop', 'mobile'],
    url: 'https://example.com'
});

Code Breakdown:

  • Connects to BrowserStack's real-device cloud.
  • Tests across all major browsers and devices.
  • Provides screenshots and compatibility reports.

docs.title: Example 9: Baseline Alert in CI
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/baseline.yml
name: Baseline Check
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  baseline:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm install
      - run: npx baseline-check --target widely-available

Code Breakdown:

  • Checks that all features used are Baseline Widely available.
  • Fails the build if a non-Baseline feature is used.
  • Prevents compatibility regressions.

docs.title: Example 10: The Complete Browser Compatibility Strategy
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Compatible Page</title>

    <!-- Base styles: work everywhere -->
    <style>
        .layout { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; }
    </style>

    <!-- Enhanced styles: Baseline Widely available -->
    <style>
        @supports (display: grid) {
            .layout {
                display: grid;
                grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
            }
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <main class="layout">
        <article>Content</article>
    </main>

    <!-- Feature-detected enhancement -->
    <script>
        if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) {
            // Enhanced behavior
        } else {
            // Fallback behavior
        }
    </script>

    <!-- Modern JavaScript with fallback -->
    <script type="module" src="/js/app.js"></script>
    <script nomodule src="/js/app.legacy.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

Code Breakdown:

  • Base styles work everywhere.
  • Enhanced styles applied via @supports.
  • Feature detection for JavaScript enhancements.
  • Module/nomodule for modern vs. legacy JavaScript.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Strategy Consumer website Support latest 2 versions of major browsers Enterprise app Support latest 2 versions + older ESR Government site Support specific compliance list Global audience Target Baseline Widely available Cutting-edge app Target Baseline Newly available Mobile-first Prioritize iOS Safari and Chrome Android Legacy system Evaluate case-by-case; often not supported Component library Target Baseline Widely available Design system Target Baseline Widely available E-commerce Support all browsers that generate revenue

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Adopt Baseline as your compatibility standard. Why: it is the 2026 industry standard.
  2. Choose a support target based on your audience. Why: there is no universal answer.
  3. Use feature detection over browser sniffing. Why: browser sniffing is unreliable.
  4. Use @supports for CSS fallbacks. Why: clean, declarative, native.
  5. Use browserslist for tooling configuration. Why: single source of truth.
  6. Use @babel/preset-env for transpilation. Why: automatic target-based transforms.
  7. Use Autoprefixer for vendor prefixes. Why: no more manual prefixes.
  8. Load polyfills conditionally. Why: do not ship polyfills to browsers that do not need them.
  9. Test across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. Why: the three engines cover all browsers.
  10. Test on real devices for mobile. Why: emulators do not catch all issues.
  11. Use Playwright for local cross-browser testing. Why: fast, free, reliable.
  12. Use BrowserStack or Sauce Labs for cloud testing. Why: real devices and OS combinations.
  13. Monitor browser analytics. Why: know which browsers your users actually use.
  14. Set Baseline alerts in CI. Why: prevent compatibility regressions.
  15. Use progressive enhancement. Why: core functionality works everywhere.
  16. Use graceful degradation where progressive enhancement is not possible. Why: fallbacks for older browsers.
  17. Do not use browser-specific hacks. Why: they are fragile and hard to maintain.
  18. Do not support Internet Explorer. Why: it was retired in June 2022.
  19. Do not support EdgeHTML. Why: it was replaced by Chromium in 2020.
  20. Do not assume Chrome behavior applies to Safari. Why: WebKit has unique constraints.
  21. Do not ship polyfills for Baseline Widely available features. Why: they are unnecessary.
  22. Evaluate polyfills carefully. Why: most have caveats, performance impacts, or maintenance risks.
  23. Test accessibility across browsers. Why: engine differences affect a11y.
  24. Keep your target browsers up to date. Why: the landscape changes annually.
  25. Document your browser support policy. Why: consistency across the team.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Supporting Internet Explorer
docs.text:
// IE-specific hacks
if (navigator.userAgent.indexOf('MSIE') !== -1) { ... }

Why it's wrong: IE 11 was retired on June 15, 2022. No modern site should support it.

✅ Correct: Remove IE support from your browserslist and code.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Browser Sniffing
docs.text:
if (navigator.userAgent.indexOf('Safari') !== -1) {
    // Safari-specific code
}

Why it's wrong: User agent strings are unreliable and easily spoofed.

✅ Correct: Use feature detection.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Chrome = Safari
docs.text:
/* Works in Chrome, not in Safari */
.example { position: sticky; }

Why it's wrong: Safari has unique implementation differences.

✅ Correct: Test in both and use @supports.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Shipping Polyfills to Everyone
docs.text:
<script src="/polyfills/all.js"></script>

Why it's wrong: Wastes bandwidth on browsers that do not need it.

✅ Correct: Load polyfills conditionally.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing in Firefox
docs.text:
// Only tested in Chrome

Why it's wrong: Gecko has different behavior for some APIs.

✅ Correct: Test in all three engines.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing on Real iOS Devices
docs.text:
// Tested only in Chrome DevTools

Why it's wrong: iOS Safari has unique constraints (no beforeunload, limited requestAnimationFrame, etc.).

✅ Correct: Test on real iOS devices or BrowserStack.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Non-Baseline Features Without Fallback
docs.text:
/* Not Baseline yet */
.view-transition { view-transition-name: card; }

Why it's wrong: Browsers without support see a broken layout.

✅ Correct: Use @supports or progressive enhancement.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No Browser Support Policy
docs.text:
<!-- No documented target browsers -->

Why it's wrong: Inconsistent decisions across the team.

✅ Correct: Document the support target in .browserslistrc.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Manual Vendor Prefixes
docs.text:
.example {
    -webkit-transform: translateX(10px);
    -moz-transform: translateX(10px);
    -ms-transform: translateX(10px);
    transform: translateX(10px);
}

Why it's wrong: Error-prone and unnecessary.

✅ Correct: Use Autoprefixer.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Monitoring Browser Analytics
docs.text:
<!-- No idea which browsers users use -->

Why it's wrong: The support target may not match the actual audience.

✅ Correct: Review analytics quarterly.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Transpiled code is larger — ES5 output is larger than ES2020 input.
  • Polyfills add weight — load them conditionally.
  • Feature detection is cheap — a simple in check.
  • @supports is parsed once — negligible cost.
  • Multiple browser builds — module/nomodule doubles the build output.
  • Cloud testing is slower than local — use Playwright for fast feedback.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use module/nomodule to avoid shipping modern code to older browsers.
  2. Load polyfills conditionally with dynamic import.
  3. Use Babel with useBuiltIns: "usage" for automatic polyfill injection.
  4. Prefer feature detection over polyfills where possible.
  5. Test on low-end devices in target browsers.
  6. Monitor Core Web Vitals by browser.

docs.title: Polyfill Supply Chain Risk
docs.text:
Polyfills are third-party JavaScript. A compromised polyfill can inject malicious code.

Defense: Use well-maintained polyfills; pin versions; use SRI where possible.

docs.title: Browser-Specific Security Bugs
docs.text:
Different engines have different security bugs. A feature that is safe in Chrome may be vulnerable in Safari.

Defense: Test security-critical features in all target browsers.

docs.title: CSP and Polyfills
docs.text:
Polyfills may use eval() or new Function(), which require 'unsafe-eval' in CSP.

Defense: Use polyfills that do not require 'unsafe-eval'.

docs.title: Autoprefixer and Security
docs.text: Autoprefixer only adds CSS properties. It does not introduce security risks.

docs.title: Feature Detection and Security
docs.text: Feature detection is safe — it only checks for the presence of APIs.

docs.title: User Agent Sniffing and Security
docs.text: User agent strings are spoofable. Do not use them for security decisions.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Can I Use — caniuse.com — feature support data.
  • MDN Baseline — Baseline badges on feature pages.
  • webstatus.dev — Baseline status dashboard.
  • Chrome DevTools → Rendering panel — emulate features.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network panel — check polyfill loading.
  • CSS.supports() — check CSS feature support in console.
  • 'feature' in window — check JavaScript API support.
  • Playwright — local cross-browser testing.
  • BrowserStack / Sauce Labs — cloud real-device testing.
  • LambdaTest — another cloud testing option.
  • TestGrid — cross-browser testing tool.
  • browserslist CLI — npx browserslist to see the resolved target.
  • npx browserslist --coverage — coverage percentage for the target.
  • Baseline alerts — basewatch.dev for feature notifications.
  • Lighthouse — Baseline Features audit now available.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Every web project — browser compatibility is always relevant.
  • Every public-facing site — support the browsers users actually use.
  • Every component library — target Baseline for maximum reuse.
  • Every design system — consistent behavior across browsers.
  • Every e-commerce site — every browser is a potential customer.
  • Every government site — compliance requirements often specify browsers.
  • Every enterprise app — balance modern features with required support.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not support Internet Explorer. It was retired in June 2022.
  • Do not support EdgeHTML. It was replaced by Chromium in 2020.
  • Do not use browser sniffing. Use feature detection.
  • Do not ship polyfills for Baseline Widely available features.
  • Do not assume Chrome behavior applies to all browsers.
  • Do not skip testing in Firefox or Safari.
  • Do not skip mobile testing.
  • Do not use vendor prefixes manually.
  • Do not target "all browsers." It is neither feasible nor necessary.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Baseline launched in 2023 — the first unified browser compatibility standard.
  • Baseline Widely available covers 98.0% of users — safe for production.
  • Baseline Newly available covers 13.9% of users — works in current browsers only.
  • GitLab adopted Baseline Widely available as their frontend support target.
  • Google Chrome dominates with ~65% market share — but Safari has ~18%.
  • There are only three major browser engines — Blink, Gecko, WebKit.
  • All iOS browsers must use WebKit — Chrome on iOS is Safari under the hood.
  • Internet Explorer 11 was retired on June 15, 2022.
  • EdgeHTML was replaced by Chromium in Edge 79 (2020).
  • The recommended support target is the latest 2 versions of major browsers.
  • Container Queries became Baseline Widely available in August 2025.
  • Subgrid became Baseline Widely available in June 2026.
  • WebGPU's Baseline availability was blocked by Firefox in January 2026.
  • Temporal API was shipped in Firefox 139, Chrome 144, and Edge 144.
  • The perfect polyfill is hard to find — most have caveats.
  • Baseline alerts are available on webstatus.dev.
  • The Baseline Features audit is now available in Lighthouse.
  • Cross-browser testing market is growing — $1.5B in 2024 to $5.2B projected by 2033.
  • Playwright supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit — all three engines.
  • BrowserStack offers 3,000+ browser/OS combinations.
  • Sauce Labs provides live cross-browser testing on real devices.
  • LambdaTest offers 2,000+ real browsers and OS combinations.
  • Baseline eliminates the "does it work in Safari?" question — the answer is in the badge.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Browser compatibility is the practice of building pages that work across all target browsers.
  • Baseline is the 2026 standard — maintained by the W3C WebDX Community Group.
  • Baseline Newly available — works in all current browsers (13.9% of users).
  • Baseline Widely available — stable for 30+ months (98.0% of users).
  • The recommended support target is the latest 2 versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari.
  • There are only three major engines — Blink, Gecko, WebKit.
  • Internet Explorer is retired — June 15, 2022.
  • Feature detection is preferred over browser sniffing.
  • @supports provides CSS feature queries.
  • Polyfills should be loaded conditionally.
  • Transpilation with Babel converts modern JS to compatible syntax.
  • Autoprefixer adds vendor prefixes automatically.
  • browserslist is the single source of truth for target browsers.
  • Can I Use, MDN Baseline, and webstatus.dev provide feature support data.
  • Playwright, BrowserStack, and Sauce Labs are the primary testing tools.
  • Progressive enhancement ensures core functionality works everywhere.
  • Graceful degradation provides fallbacks for older browsers.
  • Baseline alerts prevent compatibility regressions.
  • Document your browser support policy in .browserslistrc.
  • Test across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit — the three engines cover all browsers.
  • Test on real iOS devices — emulators do not catch all issues.
  • Monitor browser analytics to validate your support target.
  • Baseline eliminates the guesswork — the badge tells you what works.
  • The best browser compatibility strategy is deliberate, documented, and tested.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Debugging HTML is the systematic practice of diagnosing, isolating, and fixing problems in HTML — structural errors, missing content, broken layout, unexpected rendering, accessibility failures, and performance issues — using browser DevTools, validators, linters, and systematic inspection techniques.

<!-- The source shows this -->
<div class="card">
    <h2>Title</h2>
    <p>Content</p>
</div>

<!-- But the DOM shows this -->
<div class="card">
    <h2>Title</h2>
    <p>Content</p>
    <!-- Something unexpected appeared here -->
</div>

The browser never tells you something is wrong. It renders whatever it can and moves on. Debugging HTML is the discipline of comparing what you wrote to what the browser actually built — and correcting the difference.

Debugging is not a single tool. It is a workflow: inspect, isolate, hypothesize, test, and fix. It spans every layer of the browser stack — parsing, DOM construction, CSSOM, rendering, accessibility, and performance.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Debugging HTML serves several essential purposes:

  • Identify broken markup — find errors that browsers silently recover from.
  • Diagnose unexpected DOM — understand why the DOM differs from the source.
  • Isolate CSS issues — trace style bugs to their source.
  • Fix accessibility problems — identify missing labels, roles, and focus management.
  • Resolve cross-browser issues — compare behavior across engines.
  • Improve performance — identify layout thrashing, paint issues, and blocking resources.
  • Understand framework output — see what the framework actually rendered.
  • Reproduce and fix bugs — from a symptom to a root cause.

Debugging is the bridge between writing code and shipping it.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Validation
│
├── HTML Validator           ← markup correctness
├── Common Errors            ← frequent validation errors
├── Accessibility Validation ← automated a11y checks
├── Browser Compatibility    ← cross-browser testing
└── Debugging HTML           ← tools and techniques (THIS CHAPTER)

Debugging HTML is the practical application of every other validation layer. When a validator reports an error, debugging is how you find and fix it. When an accessibility test fails, debugging is how you understand why. When a page breaks in Safari, debugging is how you reproduce it.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
HTML does not fail loudly. A missing closing tag, an incorrectly nested element, or an invalid attribute does not produce an error page. The browser recovers silently. The page renders. The bug hides.

Consider the following HTML:

<p>Hello
<div>World</div>

The source looks fine. But the browser auto-closes the <p> and produces:

<p>Hello</p>
<div>World</div>

The visual result may be different from what the developer intended — but the developer will not see the difference unless they compare the source to the DOM.

Debugging exists because the browser hides the errors you need to see.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No browser dev tools Debugging required alert() and console.log No DOM inspection Developers could not see the rendered tree No computed styles CSS bugs were traced manually No network panel Resource loading was opaque No accessibility tree A11y issues were invisible No performance profiling Rendering issues were mysteries No source maps Minified code was unreadable

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Debugging tools evolved with the web:

  • 1990s — view-source: was the only way to see HTML.
  • 2001 — Mozilla's DOM Inspector shipped with Netscape 6.
  • 2006 — Firebug launched for Firefox, the first modern debugging tool.
  • 2008 — Google Chrome launched with built-in DevTools.
  • 2010s — DevTools panels expanded: Elements, Network, Performance, Accessibility.
  • 2020s — AI-assisted debugging, Baseline integration, and improved visual tools.

In 2026, browser DevTools are full IDEs for the web. They inspect the DOM, CSS, network, performance, accessibility, memory, and more. They support mobile emulation, device simulation, and remote debugging. The question is not whether the tools exist — it is whether developers know how to use them.

docs.title: Opening DevTools
docs.text: Browser Shortcut Chrome / Edge F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I (Windows/Linux) Chrome / Edge Cmd+Option+I (macOS) Firefox F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I Safari Enable Develop menu → Cmd+Option+I Safari iOS Settings → Safari → Advanced → Web Inspector

docs.title: The DevTools Panels
docs.text: Panel Purpose Elements Inspect the DOM, styles, and layout Console Execute JavaScript, view errors Sources Debug JavaScript, set breakpoints Network Inspect requests, timings, and headers Performance Profile rendering, scripting, and paint Memory Inspect memory usage Application Inspect storage, service workers, manifests Lighthouse Run audits Security Inspect certificate and mixed content Accessibility (side panel) Inspect the accessibility tree

docs.title: The Elements Panel
docs.text:
The Elements panel is the primary tool for HTML debugging:

1.  Right-click an element → "Inspect"
2.  The element is highlighted in the Elements panel
3.  The Styles pane shows applied CSS rules
4.  The Computed pane shows final computed values
5.  The Layout pane shows box model, grid, flexbox
6.  The Accessibility pane shows role, name, and state

docs.title: The Console Panel
docs.text:
// Log the entire DOM
console.log(document.documentElement.outerHTML);

// Inspect a specific element
console.log(document.querySelector('.card'));

// Log as a table
console.table([...document.querySelectorAll('a')]);

// Inspect all elements matching a selector
console.log(document.querySelectorAll('.card'));

// Inspect the selected element in the Elements panel
$0;             // the selected element
$0.outerHTML;   // its HTML
$0.classList;   // its class list
$1;             // the previously selected element

docs.title: The $ and $$ Shortcuts
docs.text:
// $ = document.querySelector
$('.card');              // first .card element

// $$ = document.querySelectorAll (returns an array)
$$('.card');             // all .card elements

// $_ = the last evaluated result in the Console
$_;                      // the previous result

docs.title: The Copy Function
docs.text:
// Copy the selected element's HTML to the clipboard
copy($0.outerHTML);

// Copy the selected element's styles
copy(getComputedStyle($0).cssText);

// Copy all elements matching a selector
copy([...document.querySelectorAll('a')].map(a => a.href).join('\n'));

docs.title: The Break on Attribute
docs.text:
1.  Right-click an element → "Break on" → "attribute modifications"
2.  DevTools pauses when the element's attributes change
3.  Inspect the call stack to find the code that modified it

docs.title: The monitorEvents() Function
docs.text:
// Log all events fired by the selected element
monitorEvents($0);

// Log only specific events
monitorEvents($0, ['click', 'keydown']);

// Stop monitoring
unmonitorEvents($0);

docs.title: The getEventListeners() Function
docs.text:
// List all event listeners on the selected element
getEventListeners($0);

// List listeners on window
getEventListeners(window);

docs.title: The debug() Function
docs.text:
// Break when the function is called
debug(myFunction);

// Stop debugging
undebug(myFunction);

docs.title: The inspect() Function
docs.text:
// Inspect an object in the Elements panel (if it is an element)
inspect(document.querySelector('.card'));

// Inspect a JavaScript object in the Console
inspect(window.someObject);

docs.title: The Source Panel
docs.text:
1.  Open DevTools → Sources
2.  Find the HTML file in the file tree
3.  Set breakpoints on JavaScript
4.  Use the console to inspect state
5.  Use "Pretty print" ({}) to format minified code

docs.title: The Network Panel
docs.text:
1.  Open DevTools → Network
2.  Reload the page
3.  Filter by type (HTML, CSS, JS, Img)
4.  Click a request to inspect headers, timing, and response
5.  Use "Preserve log" to keep requests across navigations

docs.title: The Performance Panel
docs.text:
1.  Open DevTools → Performance
2.  Click the record button
3.  Interact with the page
4.  Stop recording
5.  Inspect the flame chart, frame rate, and main thread

docs.title: The "Source vs. DOM" Mental Model
docs.text:
The source is what you wrote. The DOM is what the browser built. They are often different:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SOURCE (view-source:)                       │
│  └── The raw HTML bytes you sent             │
│  └── Includes your mistakes                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DOM (Elements panel)                        │
│  └── The parsed tree after recovery          │
│  └── Includes implicit elements              │
│  └── Includes JavaScript modifications       │
│  └── Includes browser-inserted elements      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Always inspect the DOM, not just the source. The DOM is what the browser actually renders.

docs.title: The "Inspect Layer by Layer" Mental Model
docs.text:
Debugging HTML means inspecting each layer of the browser stack:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HTML       → Elements panel → DOM tree      │
│  CSS        → Styles pane → applied rules    │
│  Layout     → Layout pane → box model        │
│  JavaScript → Console → errors, state        │
│  Network    → Network panel → requests       │
│  Rendering  → Performance panel → pipeline   │
│  A11y       → Accessibility pane → tree      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Each layer has its own tool. Debugging means knowing which layer to inspect.

docs.title: The "Bisect the Problem" Mental Model
docs.text:
When you do not know where the bug is, bisect:

1.  Does it happen in the source? → Check view-source.
2.  Does it happen in the DOM? → Check Elements panel.
3.  Does it happen with JS disabled? → Disable JS.
4.  Does it happen with CSS disabled? → Disable CSS.
5.  Does it happen in another browser? → Test cross-browser.
6.  Does it happen on another page? → Compare.

Each test narrows the problem.

docs.title: The "Hypothesis and Test" Mental Model
docs.text:
Debugging is the scientific method:

1.  Observe the symptom.
2.  Form a hypothesis.
3.  Design a test.
4.  Run the test.
5.  Analyze the result.
6.  Refine the hypothesis.
7.  Repeat until fixed.

Every DevTools interaction is a test. Every observation refines the hypothesis.

docs.title: The "Reading the DOM" Mental Model
docs.text:
The Elements panel shows the rendered DOM, not the source. Reading the DOM means:

  • Understanding the structure — what elements exist.
  • Understanding the nesting — what contains what.
  • Understanding the attributes — what each element has.
  • Understanding the computed styles — how it renders.
  • Understanding the accessibility tree — how it is announced.

The DOM is the source of truth for rendering.

docs.title: The "Console Is the Fastest Tool" Mental Model
docs.text:
Many debugging tasks are faster in the Console than in the Elements panel:

// Instead of scrolling through the tree
document.querySelectorAll('.card').length;

// Instead of manually inspecting styles
getComputedStyle(document.querySelector('.card')).color;

// Instead of looking at each element
[...document.querySelectorAll('img:not([alt])')];

The Console is the fastest way to answer many questions.

docs.title: The DevTools Protocol
docs.text:
DevTools communicates with the browser via the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). The protocol exposes:

  • DOM domain — inspect and manipulate the DOM.
  • CSS domain — inspect and manipulate styles.
  • Network domain — inspect requests.
  • Runtime domain — execute JavaScript.
  • Debugger domain — set breakpoints.
  • Performance domain — profile rendering.

The DevTools UI is a client of this protocol.

docs.title: The Elements Panel Architecture
docs.text: The Elements panel queries the DOM via CDP. It renders the tree, applies syntax highlighting, and shows styles.

docs.title: The Console Architecture
docs.text: The Console is a JavaScript REPL. It executes expressions in the page's context. It also shows errors, warnings, and logs.

docs.title: The Network Panel Architecture
docs.text:
The Network panel intercepts all HTTP requests via CDP. It captures:

  • Request and response headers.
  • Timing information.
  • Response bodies.
  • Priority and protocol.

docs.title: The Performance Panel Architecture
docs.text:
The Performance panel uses CDP to capture:

  • Screenshots.
  • Frame timing.
  • JavaScript call stacks.
  • Layout and paint events.
  • User interactions.

docs.title: The Sources Panel Architecture
docs.text:
The Sources panel uses CDP to:

  • Load source files.
  • Set breakpoints.
  • Step through execution.
  • Inspect scope and call stack.

docs.title: The Accessibility Panel Architecture
docs.text:
The Accessibility panel uses CDP to:

  • Query the accessibility tree.
  • Compute roles and names.
  • Show the relationship to the DOM.

docs.title: The Rendering Panel Architecture
docs.text:
The Rendering panel uses CDP to enable:

  • Paint Flashing.
  • Layer Borders.
  • Frame Rendering Stats.
  • Emulate CSS Media.
  • Emulate Vision Deficiencies.

docs.title: The Coverage Panel Architecture
docs.text:
The Coverage panel uses CDP to record:

  • Which CSS rules were used.
  • Which JavaScript functions were executed.
  • Unused bytes.

docs.title: The Debugging Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  OBSERVE
    │   ├── What is the symptom?
    │   ├── Where does it appear?
    │   └── When does it occur?
    │
    ▼
2.  INSPECT
    │   ├── Open DevTools.
    │   ├── Select the element.
    │   ├── Check the DOM.
    │   └── Check the styles.
    │
    ▼
3.  HYPOTHESIZE
    │   ├── What could cause this?
    │   ├── Is it HTML? CSS? JS? Network?
    │   └── Is it browser-specific?
    │
    ▼
4.  TEST
    │   ├── Disable JS.
    │   ├── Disable CSS.
    │   ├── Test in another browser.
    │   └── Toggle rules.
    │
    ▼
5.  ISOLATE
    │   ├── Reduce to a minimal reproduction.
    │   ├── Comment out code.
    │   └── Test hypotheses.
    │
    ▼
6.  FIX
    │   ├── Apply the fix.
    │   ├── Verify the symptom is gone.
    │   └── Verify nothing else broke.
    │
    ▼
7.  PREVENT
    │   ├── Add a test.
    │   ├── Add a lint rule.
    │   └── Document the fix.

docs.title: Example 1: Comparing Source to DOM
docs.text:
<!-- Source: view-source: -->
<p>Hello<div>World</div>

<!-- DOM: Elements panel -->
<p>Hello</p>
<div>World</div>

Debugging:

1.  Open DevTools → Elements.
2.  Find the <p> element.
3.  Notice it is closed before the <div>.
4.  The browser auto-closed the <p>.
5.  Fix: add </p> explicitly.

docs.title: Example 2: Finding Unclosed Elements
docs.text:
<ul>
    <li>Item 1
    <li>Item 2
</ul>

Debugging:

1.  Inspect the <ul>.
2.  The DOM shows:
    <ul>
        <li>Item 1</li>
        <li>Item 2</li>
    </ul>
3.  The browser implicitly closed the <li> tags.
4.  Fix: add explicit </li> tags.

docs.title: Example 3: Debugging CSS Specificity
docs.text:
.card { color: blue; }
#main .card { color: red; }

Debugging:

1.  Select .card in the Elements panel.
2.  Open the Styles pane.
3.  See both rules.
4.  The #main .card rule is winning (higher specificity).
5.  The .card rule is struck through.
6.  Fix: increase specificity or use a different selector.

docs.title: Example 4: Debugging Layout Shift
docs.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Photo">

Debugging:

1.  Open DevTools → Performance.
2.  Enable "Layout Shifts" in the Rendering panel.
3.  Reload the page.
4.  Purple rectangles highlight shifting elements.
5.  The image is shifting because dimensions are missing.
6.  Fix: add width and height attributes.

docs.title: Example 5: Debugging Missing Accessibility Name
docs.text:
<button>
    <svg>...</svg>
</button>

Debugging:

1.  Select the button.
2.  Open the Accessibility pane.
3.  The "Name" field is empty.
4.  Fix: add aria-label="Close" to the button.
5.  Re-check: the name is now "Close".

docs.title: Example 6: Debugging Event Listeners
docs.text:
// Find all event listeners on the selected element
getEventListeners($0);

// Output:
// { click: [{ listener: ..., useCapture: false }] }

Debugging:

1.  Select an element.
2.  Run getEventListeners($0) in the Console.
3.  See all listeners.
4.  Identify unexpected listeners.
5.  Find the source in the Sources panel.

docs.title: Example 7: Debugging with Break on Attribute
docs.text:
1.  Right-click an element.
2.  Select "Break on" → "attribute modifications".
3.  Interact with the page.
4.  DevTools pauses when the attribute changes.
5.  Inspect the call stack.
6.  Find the code that modified the attribute.

docs.title: Example 8: Debugging Network Requests
docs.text:
1.  Open DevTools → Network.
2.  Reload the page.
3.  Filter by "Img".
4.  A request shows 404.
5.  Click the request.
6.  Inspect the URL.
7.  Fix the path in the HTML.

docs.title: Example 9: Debugging with monitorEvents
docs.text:
// Log all click events on the selected element
monitorEvents($0, 'click');

// Interact with the element
// Console logs: click { target: ..., ... }

Debugging:

1.  Select the element.
2.  Run monitorEvents($0, 'click').
3.  Click the element.
4.  See the event details in the Console.
5.  Verify the event is firing.

docs.title: Example 10: Complete Debugging Session
docs.text:
<!-- Source -->
<div class="card">
    <h2>Title</h2>
    <img src="image.jpg">
    <p>Content</p>
</div>

<!-- DOM (after parsing) -->
<div class="card">
    <h2>Title</h2>
    <img src="image.jpg">
    <p>Content</p>
</div>

Debugging steps:

1.  Inspect the .card element.
2.  Check the DOM structure — it looks correct.
3.  Check the Styles pane — verify styles.
4.  Check the Computed pane — verify dimensions.
5.  Check the Accessibility pane — the <img> has no alt.
6.  Check the Network panel — the image returns 404.
7.  Fix the alt attribute.
8.  Fix the image path.
9.  Re-verify in all panels.
