docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always inspect the DOM, not just the source. Why: the DOM is what the browser renders.
  2. Use $0 to reference the selected element. Why: fast access in the Console.
  3. Use $ and $$ for quick queries. Why: shorter than document.querySelector.
  4. Use copy($0.outerHTML) to copy the DOM. Why: faster than manual selection.
  5. Use monitorEvents() to debug events. Why: see what fires.
  6. Use getEventListeners() to find listeners. Why: discover hidden listeners.
  7. Use "Break on" to find attribute changes. Why: pause when the DOM changes.
  8. Use "Preserve log" in the Network panel. Why: see requests across navigations.
  9. Use "Disable cache" during development. Why: avoid stale resources.
  10. Use the Coverage panel to find unused code. Why: reduce bundle size.
  11. Use the Rendering panel for visual debugging. Why: Paint Flashing, Layer Borders.
  12. Use the Accessibility pane to verify names. Why: catch a11y issues early.
  13. Use the Performance panel for rendering issues. Why: find the bottleneck.
  14. Use device emulation for mobile. Why: test responsive layouts.
  15. Use the Sources panel for JavaScript debugging. Why: set breakpoints and step through.
  16. Read errors in the Console carefully. Why: they often point to the root cause.
  17. Fix the cause, not the symptom. Why: prevent recurrence.
  18. Add tests after fixing bugs. Why: prevent regressions.
  19. Document complex debugging findings. Why: help future developers.
  20. Use debug() to break on function calls. Why: find when a function is called.
  21. Use inspect() to open objects. Why: view data structures.
  22. Use "Pretty print" for minified code. Why: make it readable.
  23. Use source maps for transpiled code. Why: debug the original source.
  24. Compare behavior across browsers. Why: catch engine-specific issues.
  25. Close DevTools when measuring performance. Why: DevTools adds overhead.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Debugging the Source Instead of the DOM
docs.text:
<!-- Source looks fine, but the DOM is different -->

Why it's wrong: The browser modifies the DOM during parsing and JavaScript execution.

✅ Correct: Always inspect the DOM in the Elements panel.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Console Errors
docs.text:
// Errors appear in the Console but are ignored

Why it's wrong: Errors are the fastest path to the root cause.

✅ Correct: Read and fix all Console errors.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Using the Correct Panel
docs.text:
// Trying to debug CSS in the Console

Why it's wrong: Each type of problem has a dedicated panel.

✅ Correct: Use the Elements panel for CSS, Network panel for requests, etc.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Debugging with Cached Resources
docs.text:
// Stale resources cause confusion

Why it's wrong: The browser may serve old versions.

✅ Correct: Enable "Disable cache" in DevTools.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing Cross-Browser
docs.text:
// Works in Chrome, breaks in Safari

Why it's wrong: Engines differ.

✅ Correct: Test in all target browsers.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Debugging Without a Hypothesis
docs.text:
// Randomly toggling things

Why it's wrong: Inefficient and confusing.

✅ Correct: Form a hypothesis, then test it.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Reproducing the Bug
docs.text:
// "It works on my machine"

Why it's wrong: Without a reproduction, the bug cannot be fixed reliably.

✅ Correct: Reduce to a minimal reproduction.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Fixing the Symptom, Not the Cause
docs.text:
/* Adding !important to force the style */
.card { color: red !important; }

Why it's wrong: The symptom is fixed, but the cause remains.

✅ Correct: Find and fix the specificity issue.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Checking the Accessibility Tree
docs.text:
// Missing alt, missing labels

Why it's wrong: Accessibility issues are invisible without inspection.

✅ Correct: Use the Accessibility pane to verify.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Measuring Performance with DevTools Open
docs.text:
// DevTools adds overhead

Why it's wrong: Measurements are skewed.

✅ Correct: Close DevTools when measuring real-world performance.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• DevTools adds overhead — close it when measuring performance.
  • The Performance panel is heavy — recording sessions is resource-intensive.
  • The Coverage panel is slow — use it selectively.
  • The Network panel logs everything — large sites may slow it down.
  • Emulation is approximate — real devices perform differently.
  • Source maps add overhead — only enable them during debugging.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Close DevTools when measuring real-world performance.
  2. Use the Performance panel to find bottlenecks.
  3. Use the Coverage panel to find unused code.
  4. Use the Rendering panel for visual debugging.
  5. Test on real devices for accurate measurements.
  6. Use device emulation for responsive layouts.
  7. Use "Disable cache" during development.

docs.title: DevTools and Sensitive Data
docs.text: DevTools shows everything — including sensitive data in the DOM, network responses, and storage. Do not debug on production with real user data.

docs.title: Console and XSS
docs.text:
Running untrusted code in the Console can execute XSS in your own session.

Defense: Only run code you trust.

docs.title: copy() and Sensitive Data
docs.text:
copy() sends data to the clipboard, which can be read by other applications.

Defense: Do not copy sensitive data.

docs.title: Emulation and Security
docs.text: Device emulation does not change security behavior. Do not assume emulated browsers are secure.

docs.title: Service Worker Debugging
docs.text: Service workers can intercept requests. Debug them in the Application panel.

docs.title: CSP and DevTools
docs.text: DevTools can bypass CSP in some cases. Do not rely on DevTools to test CSP compliance.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• view-source: — see the raw HTML.
  • Elements panel — inspect the DOM.
  • Styles pane — inspect CSS rules.
  • Computed pane — inspect final values.
  • Layout pane — inspect box model, grid, flexbox.
  • Accessibility pane — inspect the accessibility tree.
  • Console — run JavaScript, see errors.
  • $0 — the selected element.
  • $ / $$ — query shortcuts.
  • copy($0.outerHTML) — copy the DOM.
  • monitorEvents($0) — log events.
  • getEventListeners($0) — list listeners.
  • debug(fn) — break on function calls.
  • inspect(obj) — inspect an object.
  • "Break on" — pause on attribute changes.
  • "Preserve log" — keep network requests across navigations.
  • "Disable cache" — avoid stale resources.
  • Device toolbar — emulate mobile.
  • Rendering panel — Paint Flashing, Layer Borders, Layout Shifts.
  • Coverage panel — find unused code.
  • Performance panel — profile rendering.
  • Sources panel — debug JavaScript.
  • Network panel — inspect requests.
  • Application panel — inspect storage, service workers.
  • Lighthouse — run audits.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Whenever something looks wrong — debugging is the tool.
  • Before deploying — verify the DOM is correct.
  • After changing templates — verify the output.
  • After framework upgrades — verify the rendered DOM.
  • When performance degrades — profile with Performance panel.
  • When accessibility fails — inspect the accessibility tree.
  • When cross-browser issues appear — compare behavior.
  • When bugs are reported — reproduce and fix.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Do not debug on production with real user data. Use staging.
  • Do not leave DevTools open while measuring performance. It adds overhead.
  • Do not rely on DevTools to test CSP compliance. Use a real browser session.
  • Do not copy sensitive data to the clipboard.
  • Do not run untrusted code in the Console.
  • Do not assume emulation matches real devices. Test on real hardware.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Firebug was the first modern web debugging tool — launched in 2006 for Firefox.
  • Chrome DevTools shipped with Chrome in 2008 — it is now the most widely used.
  • The $0 variable refers to the currently selected element in the Elements panel.
  • $ is document.querySelector and $$ is document.querySelectorAll — but $$ returns an array.
  • copy($0.outerHTML) copies the DOM to the clipboard.
  • monitorEvents() logs all events on an element.
  • getEventListeners() lists all event listeners.
  • debug() sets a breakpoint on a function.
  • inspect() opens an object in the appropriate panel.
  • "Break on" pauses when an element's attributes change.
  • "Preserve log" keeps network requests across navigations.
  • "Disable cache" prevents stale resources.
  • Paint Flashing highlights painted regions in green.
  • Layer Borders highlights compositing layers in orange.
  • Layout Shifts highlights shifting elements in purple.
  • The Coverage panel shows unused CSS and JavaScript.
  • The Performance panel profiles rendering, scripting, and paint.
  • The Accessibility pane shows the computed role and name.
  • The Sources panel debugs JavaScript with breakpoints.
  • The Network panel inspects requests, headers, and timing.
  • The Application panel inspects storage, service workers, and manifests.
  • The Rendering panel emulates prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion, and more.
  • view-source: shows the raw HTML, before parsing.
  • The DOM is not the source — the DOM is what the browser built.
  • DevTools adds overhead — close it when measuring performance.
  • The Chrome DevTools Protocol powers DevTools — and can be used programmatically.
  • Safari's Web Inspector is enabled via the Develop menu.
  • Firefox Developer Tools include a Grid Inspector and Accessibility panel.
  • The Console is the fastest debugging tool — use it liberally.
  • The best debugging is systematic — observe, inspect, hypothesize, test, isolate, fix, prevent.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Debugging HTML is the systematic practice of diagnosing, isolating, and fixing problems.
  • The DOM is not the source — always inspect the DOM, not just view-source:.
  • The Elements panel shows the DOM, styles, layout, and accessibility.
  • The Styles pane shows applied CSS rules with source and line numbers.
  • The Computed pane shows final computed values.
  • The Layout pane shows box model, grid, and flexbox.
  • The Accessibility pane shows the computed role, name, and state.
  • The Console executes JavaScript and shows errors.
  • $0 is the selected element; $ and $$ are query shortcuts.
  • copy(), monitorEvents(), getEventListeners(), debug(), inspect() are essential Console functions.
  • "Break on" pauses on attribute changes.
  • "Preserve log" keeps network requests across navigations.
  • "Disable cache" prevents stale resources.
  • The Network panel inspects requests, headers, and timing.
  • The Performance panel profiles rendering, scripting, and paint.
  • The Sources panel debugs JavaScript with breakpoints.
  • The Coverage panel finds unused CSS and JavaScript.
  • The Rendering panel provides Paint Flashing, Layer Borders, and Layout Shifts.
  • The Application panel inspects storage, service workers, and manifests.
  • Device emulation tests responsive layouts.
  • Test cross-browser — engines differ.
  • Form a hypothesis before testing.
  • Reproduce the bug before fixing it.
  • Fix the cause, not the symptom.
  • Add tests after fixing bugs to prevent regressions.
  • Close DevTools when measuring performance.
  • The best debugging is systematic — observe, inspect, hypothesize, test, isolate, fix, prevent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The JavaScript ecosystem is the interconnected collection of engines, runtimes, package managers, frameworks, libraries, build tools, standards bodies, and communities that surround the JavaScript language. It is what transforms JavaScript from a language spec into a practical platform for building everything from a single-page website to a distributed backend.

// What "the ecosystem" looks like in one file
import React from "react";                    // framework
import { z } from "zod";                      // library
import { defineConfig } from "vite";          // build tool
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest"; // test runner

export const UserSchema = z.object({
    name: z.string(),
    age: z.number().int().positive(),
});

No single company owns it. No single registry contains all of it. It is distributed, pluralistic, and fast-moving — and that is both its greatest strength and its greatest source of complexity.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The ecosystem exists to solve the problems that the language itself deliberately does not:

  • Running code — engines and runtimes execute JavaScript outside a browser.
  • Sharing code — registries and package managers distribute libraries.
  • Building apps — frameworks provide structure, routing, and state.
  • Shipping code — bundlers, transpilers, and minifiers prepare artifacts for production.
  • Ensuring quality — linters, formatters, type checkers, and test runners.
  • Coordinating change — standards bodies (TC39, WHATWG, W3C) evolve the platform.
  • Fostering community — conferences, RFCs, blogs, and open-source governance.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A language alone cannot build software. Developers need:

  • A place to publish and consume reusable code.
  • Tools that transform, combine, and optimize source.
  • Libraries for common tasks (HTTP, dates, UI, validation).
  • Frameworks that impose structure on large applications.
  • Test runners to verify behavior.
  • Type systems to catch errors early.
  • Standards processes to evolve the language without breaking the web.

None of this is part of ECMAScript. It had to be built — and because no central authority governs it, it was built by many people, in parallel, sometimes competing, sometimes cooperating.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text:
Era Limitation Pre-2009 JS mostly confined to browsers; no server runtime Pre-npm (2010) No standard package manager; manual script tags Pre-ES modules No standard module system; globals + IIFEs Pre-Babel (2014) You could only use features the browser supported Pre-bundlers Every <script> was a global; load order mattered Pre-TypeScript (2012) No static types for large codebases

Each limitation created a need; each need spawned tools; those tools often became the de facto standard for a period before being superseded.

docs.title: Why It Grew This Way
docs.text:
• Open source culture — most of the ecosystem is MIT-licensed and volunteer-driven.
  • Low barrier to publish — npm publish is one command.
  • Fast iteration — no committee approval needed to ship a library.
  • Browser diversity — polyfills and transpilers bridged the gaps.
  • Node.js (2009) — unlocked server-side JS and a huge npm registry.
  • Modularity — small packages compose into larger systems.
  • Network effects — the more packages exist, the more useful the registry becomes.

The result is the largest package ecosystem in the world — npm alone hosts millions of packages.

docs.title: A Typical Modern Project
docs.text:
# Create a project
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-app

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Add a library
npm install zod

# Add a dev tool
npm install -D eslint prettier vitest

# Run dev server
npm run dev

# Build for production
npm run build

# Run tests
npm test

docs.title: Package Manifest (package.json)
docs.text:
{
    "name": "my-app",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "type": "module",
    "scripts": {
        "dev": "vite",
        "build": "tsc && vite build",
        "test": "vitest"
    },
    "dependencies": {
        "react": "^18.3.0",
        "zod": "^3.23.0"
    },
    "devDependencies": {
        "typescript": "^5.4.0",
        "vite": "^5.2.0",
        "vitest": "^1.5.0"
    }
}

docs.title: Importing from the Ecosystem
docs.text:
// Runtime dependencies
import express from "express";           // web framework (Node)
import axios from "axios";               // HTTP client
import dayjs from "dayjs";               // date library

// Dev-time tools (used in config, not shipped)
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import ts from "typescript";

docs.title: Running Anywhere
docs.text:
# In the browser
<script type="module" src="/src/main.js"></script>

# In Node.js
node server.js

# In Deno
deno run --allow-net server.ts

# In Bun
bun run server.ts

docs.title: A Minimal App Using Three Ecosystem Pieces
docs.text:
// server.js — Express (framework) + Zod (validation)
import express from "express";
import { z } from "zod";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const UserSchema = z.object({
    name: z.string().min(1),
    email: z.string().email(),
});

app.post("/users", (req, res) => {
    const result = UserSchema.safeParse(req.body);
    if (!result.success) return res.status(400).json(result.error);
    res.status(201).json({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), ...result.data });
});

app.listen(3000);

Breakdown:

  • Express — a server framework.
  • Zod — a runtime validation library.
  • crypto.randomUUID — a host API (Node).
  • This is a small slice of the ecosystem working together.

docs.title: The "City" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of the ecosystem as a city:

  • Standards bodies — the government (slow, deliberative).
  • Engines — the infrastructure (roads, power).
  • Runtimes — the districts (browser, server, edge).
  • Registries — the marketplaces (npm, JSR).
  • Frameworks — the architecture firms.
  • Libraries — the shops and services.
  • Tooling — the utilities (water, trash, transit).
  • Community — the citizens.

You can live your whole career in one neighborhood and never visit the others — but the city as a whole is what makes each neighborhood viable.

docs.title: The "Layered Stack" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Applications (your code)           │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Frameworks (React, Next, Express)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Libraries (zod, axios, dayjs)      │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Tooling (Vite, Babel, ESLint)      │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Package Managers (npm, pnpm, bun)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Runtimes (Browser, Node, Deno)     │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Engines (V8, JSC, SpiderMonkey)    │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Language (ECMAScript)              │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

Each layer depends on the ones below. Replacements happen layer by layer — you can swap Vite for webpack without touching React.

docs.title: The "Darwinian Marketplace" Mental Model
docs.text:
Thousands of packages compete for attention. Survival is decided by developers, not committees:

  • Popularity → adoption → maintenance → more popularity.
  • Unmaintained packages get forked or replaced.
  • Better DX (developer experience) often wins over raw performance.

This is why the ecosystem changes fast — and why "best practice" has a shelf life.

docs.title: The "Standards vs. Innovation" Mental Model
docs.text:
• Standards move slowly and prioritize stability.
  • The ecosystem moves fast and prioritizes novelty.
  • Innovation that succeeds is often standardized later (e.g., fetch, promises, modules).

docs.title: Concept 1: Standards Bodies
docs.text:
Body Scope TC39 Evolves ECMAScript (the language) WHATWG Living standards: HTML, DOM, Fetch, Streams, URL W3C Accessibility, CSS, some APIs ECMA International Publishes ECMA-262 (the spec) IETF HTTP, TLS, and network protocols

TC39 proposals go through stages 0–4; Stage 4 means "shipped in the next spec version."

docs.title: Concept 2: Engines
docs.text:
Engine Vendor Used By V8 Google Chrome, Edge, Node.js, Deno, Bun SpiderMonkey Mozilla Firefox JavaScriptCore Apple Safari, Bun (partially) Hermes Meta React Native QuickJS Independent Embedded, low-memory

Engines implement the language. They are not the browser, not Node.

docs.title: Concept 3: Runtimes
docs.text:
Runtime Host Use Case Browser Window, DOM Web pages and apps Node.js Process, fs, net Servers, CLI, tooling Deno Permissions, std Modern servers, secure scripts Bun Fast startup All-in-one toolchain Cloudflare Workers V8 isolates Edge compute Electron / Tauri Native shell Desktop apps

Runtimes provide host APIs — the objects the language itself does not define.

docs.title: Concept 4: Package Registries
docs.text:
Registry Notes npm Largest; default for Node and browsers JSR Modern, TS-first, from the Deno team GitHub Packages Integrated with GitHub Verdaccio Self-hosted Artifactory / Nexus Enterprise

Registries store package metadata and tarballs. npm dominates.

docs.title: Concept 5: Package Managers
docs.text:
Manager Characteristics npm Bundled with Node; ubiquitous yarn Introduced lockfiles + workspaces; classic and berry pnpm Hard-linked store; disk-efficient bun Extremely fast; built into Bun runtime

A lockfile (package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml) pins exact versions for reproducible installs.

docs.title: Concept 6: Semantic Versioning (SemVer)
docs.text:
1  .  2  .  3
│     │     └── patch — bug fix, no API change
│     └──────── minor — backward-compatible addition
└────────────── major — breaking change

Ranges:

  • ^1.2.3 — compatible with 1.x.x (default in npm install).
  • ~1.2.3 — compatible with 1.2.x.
  • 1.2.3 — exact.
  • * — any (avoid).

docs.title: Concept 7: Frameworks vs. Libraries
docs.text:
Library Framework Control You call it It calls you (inversion of control) Structure Minimal Opinionated Examples zod, axios, dayjs React, Angular, Next.js

The line blurs. React calls itself a "library" but behaves like a framework in practice.

docs.title: Concept 8: Transpilers
docs.text:
• Babel — converts modern JS (and JSX, TS) to older JS.
  • SWC — Rust-based, much faster.
  • TypeScript Compiler (tsc) — types + emit.
  • esbuild — Go-based bundler + transpiler.

Transpilers exist because browsers lag the spec and teams want new syntax today.

docs.title: Concept 9: Bundlers
docs.text:
Combine many modules into fewer files for the browser.

Bundler Notes webpack Long-standing, powerful, complex Rollup Library-focused, tree-shaking pioneer esbuild Extremely fast, Go-based Vite Dev server + Rollup prod build; standard in 2024+ Parcel Zero-config Turbopack / Rspack Rust-based next-gen

docs.title: Concept 10: Linters and Formatters
docs.text:
• ESLint — static analysis; catches bugs and style issues.
  • Prettier — opinionated code formatter.
  • Biome — Rust-based linter + formatter (ESLint + Prettier replacement).
  • oxlint — Rust-based linter.

Together they enforce consistency and correctness before code runs.

docs.title: Concept 11: Test Runners
docs.text: Tool Purpose Jest All-in-one test framework (historical default) Vitest Vite-native; fast; Jest-compatible API Mocha Minimal, flexible Playwright End-to-end browser testing Cypress End-to-end, in-browser Testing Library DOM-focused testing utilities

docs.title: Concept 12: Type Systems
docs.text:
• TypeScript — Microsoft; industry standard.
  • Flow — Meta; historically used with React; declining.
  • JSDoc — type annotations in comments; supported by TS.

TypeScript is now the default for new large projects.

docs.title: Concept 13: Monorepos
docs.text:
A monorepo hosts multiple packages in one repository. Tools:

  • npm workspaces, yarn workspaces, pnpm workspaces
  • Nx, Turborepo, Rush, Lerna

Benefits: shared tooling, atomic changes, consistent versioning.

docs.title: Concept 14: Module Systems
docs.text:
System Syntax Runtime CommonJS require / module.exports Node (legacy) ESM import / export Browsers, Node (modern) AMD define Legacy (RequireJS) UMD Wrapper Libraries targeting both

ESM is the future. CommonJS persists in older Node code.

docs.title: Concept 15: Runtimes and Package Managers Are Not the Same
docs.text:
• Node is a runtime. npm is a package manager.
  • Bun is both a runtime and a package manager.
  • Deno is a runtime with its own registry (JSR) but can consume npm.

docs.title: Concept 16: Distribution Formats
docs.text:
Packages ship in multiple targets:

  • ESM — for modern bundlers and browsers.
  • CJS — for older Node.
  • UMD — for <script> tags.
  • Types (.d.ts) — for TypeScript consumers.

Modern packages declare exports in package.json to route consumers to the right file.

docs.title: Concept 17: The Web Platform APIs
docs.text:
Browsers expose a large, standardized API surface that is not ECMAScript:

  • DOM, Fetch, Streams, WebSocket, Storage, History
  • Service Workers, Web Workers, Web Components
  • WebGL, WebGPU, Canvas
  • IndexedDB, CacheStorage, Crypto

These are hosted by the browser runtime; Node and Deno implement many of them, too.

docs.title: Concept 18: Governance Models
docs.text:
• Benevolent dictator — one maintainer decides (e.g., Vue, Svelte).
  • Foundation — OpenJS, Linux Foundation, Apache (e.g., Node.js, Express).
  • Corporate — Meta (React), Google (Angular), Microsoft (TypeScript).
  • Community RFC — Rust-style (Deno, Remix).
  • Working group — TC39, WHATWG.

Governance affects longevity, licensing, and direction.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Installing a Dependency
docs.text:
1.  npm install zod
    │
    ▼
2.  npm resolves the latest matching version from the registry.
    │
    ▼
3.  Downloads the tarball to a cache.
    │
    ▼
4.  Extracts to node_modules/zod.
    │
    ▼
5.  Installs zod's transitive dependencies (recursively).
    │
    ▼
6.  Records exact versions in package-lock.json.
    │
    ▼
7.  Adds "zod": "^3.x.x" to package.json dependencies.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Building a Modern App
docs.text:
1.  Source code (JS/TS/JSX/Vue/Svelte)
    │
    ▼
2.  Dev server (Vite) serves modules over HTTP with HMR
    │
    ▼
3.  Production build:
    │   - Transpile (esbuild/SWC/Babel)
    │   - Bundle (Rollup/webpack/esbuild)
    │   - Tree-shake unused exports
    │   - Minify + mangle names
    │   - Generate source maps
    │
    ▼
4.  Emit static assets to dist/
    │
    ▼
5.  Deploy to CDN / server / edge.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Running a Node Project
docs.text:
1.  git clone
    │
    ▼
2.  npm install (or pnpm/yarn/bun install)
    │
    ▼
3.  Read package.json scripts.
    │
    ▼
4.  npm run dev → starts server / watcher
    │
    ▼
5.  Edit code → restart or hot-reload
    │
    ▼
6.  npm test → runs test runner
    │
    ▼
7.  npm run build → produces dist/

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Publishing a Package
docs.text:
1.  Write code + README + LICENSE.
    │
    ▼
2.  Set name, version, main/exports, types in package.json.
    │
    ▼
3.  npm login
    │
    ▼
4.  npm publish (or npm publish --access public)
    │
    ▼
5.  Registry stores the tarball; consumers can install.
    │
    ▼
6.  Updates require version bumps (SemVer).

docs.title: Dependency Graphs
docs.text:
A project's dependencies form a directed acyclic graph (DAG):

your-app
├── react
│   ├── loose-envify
│   └── scheduler
├── zod
└── axios
    ├── follow-redirects
    └── form-data

Flat installs (npm 3+) hoist dependencies to the top level where possible; pnpm uses a content-addressable store with symlinks.

docs.title: Lockfiles
docs.text:
Lockfiles capture:

  • Every dependency (direct + transitive).
  • Exact resolved versions.
  • Integrity hashes (SHA-512).
  • Registry URLs.

Without a lockfile, npm install may resolve different versions over time.

docs.title: Package Resolution (node_modules)
docs.text:
node_modules/
├── react/
├── zod/
├── axios/
│   └── node_modules/
│       └── follow-redirects/
└── ...

Node resolves require("x") by walking up node_modules directories. ESM resolution is similar but stricter.

docs.title: The exports Field
docs.text:
Modern packages declare entry points:

{
    "exports": {
        ".": {
            "import": "./dist/index.mjs",
            "require": "./dist/index.cjs",
            "types": "./dist/index.d.ts"
        },
        "./package.json": "./package.json"
    }
}

This routes consumers by module system and tooling.

docs.title: Tree-Shaking
docs.text:
Bundlers analyze static imports to drop unused exports:

import { add } from "./math.js"; // only `add` is bundled

CommonJS require is harder to tree-shake — a reason ESM won.

docs.title: Toolchain Pipeline
docs.text:
Source → TS/Babel/SWC → Bundler → Minifier → Assets
         (transpile)   (bundle)   (minify)

Each step is configurable and swappable. Vite collapses several steps into one DX.

docs.title: The npm Registry Protocol
docs.text:
Clients speak HTTP to registry.npmjs.org:

  • GET /package-name — metadata.
  • GET /package-name/-/package-name-1.2.3.tgz — tarball.
  • PUT — publish (auth required).

Caches, mirrors, and proxies (Verdaccio, Artifactory) sit in front.

docs.title: Project Lifecycle
docs.text:
Idea
  │
  ▼
Scaffold (create-vite, create-next-app, degit)
  │
  ▼
Add dependencies (npm install)
  │
  ▼
Develop (dev server, HMR)
  │
  ▼
Lint + format (ESLint, Prettier)
  │
  ▼
Type-check (tsc --noEmit)
  │
  ▼
Test (Vitest, Jest, Playwright)
  │
  ▼
Build (Vite, webpack)
  │
  ▼
Deploy (Vercel, Netlify, S3+CloudFront, Fly.io)
  │
  ▼
Monitor (Sentry, Datadog, OpenTelemetry)
  │
  ▼
Maintain (deps updates, security patches)

docs.title: Dependency Lifecycle
docs.text:
Discovery → Evaluation → Adoption → Locking → Updates → Retirement
  • Discovery — npm search, GitHub, community.
  • Evaluation — activity, download count, license, security, size.
  • Adoption — add to package.json.
  • Locking — commit lockfile.
  • Updates — Dependabot, Renovate.
  • Retirement — replace or fork when unmaintained.

docs.title: Community Lifecycle
docs.text:
Proposal → RFC → Early adopters → Growth → Peak → Consolidation → Standardization

Some tools standardize (e.g., ESM). Others fade. The churn rate in the JS ecosystem is famously high.

docs.title: Example 1: Full-Stack App with Next.js
docs.text:
npx create-next-app@latest my-app --typescript --eslint --app
cd my-app && npm run dev

// app/page.tsx
export default async function Page() {
    const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/data", { cache: "no-store" });
    const data = await res.json();
    return <main><h1>{data.title}</h1></main>;
}

Breakdown:

  • create-next-app — scaffolding CLI.
  • Next.js bundles React, routing, SSR, and build tooling.
  • TypeScript and ESLint wired by default.

docs.title: Example 2: Node Server with Express + Zod
docs.text:
import express from "express";
import { z } from "zod";
import helmet from "helmet";
import morgan from "morgan";

const app = express();
app.use(helmet());
app.use(morgan("dev"));
app.use(express.json());

const Query = z.object({ q: z.string().min(1).max(100) });

app.get("/search", (req, res) => {
    const parsed = Query.safeParse(req.query);
    if (!parsed.success) return res.status(400).json({ error: parsed.error.flatten() });
    res.json({ results: [] });
});

app.listen(3000, () => console.log("http://localhost:3000"));

Breakdown:

  • express — web framework.
  • zod — validation.
  • helmet — security headers.
  • morgan — logging.
  • Every piece is a separate ecosystem package.

docs.title: Example 3: Library with Dual ESM/CJS Output
docs.text:
{
    "name": "my-lib",
    "version": "0.1.0",
    "type": "module",
    "main": "./dist/index.cjs",
    "module": "./dist/index.mjs",
    "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
    "exports": {
        ".": {
            "import": "./dist/index.mjs",
            "require": "./dist/index.cjs",
            "types": "./dist/index.d.ts"
        }
    },
    "files": ["dist"],
    "scripts": {
        "build": "tsup src/index.ts --format esm,cjs --dts"
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • tsup — bundler for libraries (esbuild + Rollup).
  • exports routes consumers.
  • files limits what gets published.

docs.title: Example 4: Monorepo with pnpm Workspaces
docs.text:
my-monorepo/
├── pnpm-workspace.yaml
├── package.json
└── packages/
    ├── ui/
    │   └── package.json
    ├── utils/
    │   └── package.json
    └── web/
        └── package.json

# pnpm-workspace.yaml
packages:
    - "packages/*"

Breakdown:

  • Single lockfile for all packages.
  • Cross-package imports via workspace names.
  • Faster installs via hard-linked store.

docs.title: Example 5: Testing Stack
docs.text:
// user.test.ts — Vitest
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { createUser } from "./user";

describe("createUser", () => {
    it("creates a user with a name", () => {
        const u = createUser({ name: "Ada" });
        expect(u.name).toBe("Ada");
    });
});

// e2e — Playwright
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("homepage loads", async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto("http://localhost:3000");
    await expect(page.getByRole("heading")).toContainText("Welcome");
});

Breakdown:

  • Vitest for unit tests (fast, Vite-native).
  • Playwright for end-to-end browser tests.
  • Both are ecosystem packages, not language features.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Need Ecosystem Solution Web framework React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Qwik Full-stack framework Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Remix, Astro Server framework Express, Fastify, Koa, Hono, NestJS HTTP client fetch (built-in), axios, ky Validation zod, yup, valibot, joi, ajv Date/time date-fns, dayjs, luxon, Temporal (spec) State management Redux, Zustand, Jotai, Pinia Data fetching TanStack Query, SWR Forms React Hook Form, Formik UI components MUI, Chakra, Radix, shadcn/ui CSS-in-JS styled-components, Emotion, vanilla-extract Testing Vitest, Jest, Playwright, Cypress Linting ESLint, Biome, oxlint Formatting Prettier, Biome, dprint Bundling Vite, webpack, esbuild, Rollup, Turbopack Type checking TypeScript Monorepo Nx, Turborepo, pnpm workspaces Deployment Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, Fly.io Observability Sentry, Datadog, OpenTelemetry

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Commit your lockfile. Why: reproducible installs across machines.
  2. Pin Node/runtime version. Why: .nvmrc, engines, or .tool-versions.
  3. Prefer ESM for new packages. Why: static analysis, tree-shaking, future-proof.
  4. Use TypeScript for non-trivial projects. Why: catches bugs before runtime.
  5. Audit dependencies regularly. Why: supply-chain risk is real.
  6. Prefer fewer, well-maintained dependencies. Why: every dep is a liability.
  7. Vendor critical paths. Why: avoid breakage when a package disappears.
  8. Automate dependency updates. Why: Renovate/Dependabot keep you current.
  9. Define exports, types, and files in published packages. Why: correct resolution + smaller tarballs.
  10. Follow SemVer. Why: consumers rely on it for ranges.
  11. Write a README, LICENSE, and CHANGELOG. Why: adoption depends on clarity.
  12. Use the same tooling across a team. Why: consistency beats novelty.
  13. Prefer standards-aligned APIs (fetch, crypto, URL). Why: portability across runtimes.
  14. Measure before optimizing the toolchain. Why: dev velocity matters more than theoretical speed.
  15. Pin or lock production dependencies. Why: avoid surprise breakage.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Committing node_modules
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Bloats the repo; installs should be reproducible via lockfile.

✅ Correct: Commit package.json + lockfile; add node_modules/ to .gitignore.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Deleting the Lockfile
docs.text:
"It fixes version conflicts."

Why it's wrong: Removes reproducibility; different machines install different versions.

✅ Correct: Fix conflicts in the lockfile; never delete without reason.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Chasing Every New Tool
docs.text:
"We rewrote our build in the framework released last week."

Why it's wrong: Churn erodes productivity; teams relearn tooling instead of shipping.

✅ Correct: Adopt after maturity, ecosystem, and migration cost are assessed.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using latest for Everything
docs.text:
{ "dependencies": { "react": "latest" } }

Why it's wrong: latest resolves to whatever the maintainer published; breakage is silent.

✅ Correct: Use ^ or exact versions with a lockfile.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Trusting npm install some-package Blindly
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Typosquats and malicious packages exist; postinstall scripts can run arbitrary code.

✅ Correct: Verify maintainers, download counts, repo, and code before adoption.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Peer Dependencies
docs.text:
npm WARN peer dependency react@^18 not satisfied

Why it's wrong: Runtime errors, version mismatch, subtle bugs.

✅ Correct: Align peers; use overrides or resolutions deliberately.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Bundling Dev Dependencies
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Larger bundles, leaking internal tooling.

✅ Correct: Use devDependencies for build/test/lint tooling.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Overreliance on Transpilation
docs.text:
"We target ES5 for 'safety'."

Why it's wrong: Larger bundles, slower runtime, and modern engines don't benefit.

✅ Correct: Target the environments you actually support (browserslist).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Adding a Framework for a Static Page
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Complexity, bundle size, and maintenance for zero benefit.

✅ Correct: Use plain HTML/CSS/JS or a static-site generator.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Confusing Registry and Runtime
docs.text:
"npm runs my JavaScript."

Why it's wrong: npm only distributes code; the runtime executes it.

✅ Correct: Distinguish engines, runtimes, registries, and package managers.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Install time — npm vs pnpm vs yarn vs bun varies widely; pnpm and bun are typically fastest.
  • Cold start — edge runtimes (Workers, Deno Deploy) minimize cold starts with isolates.
  • Bundle size — smaller bundles parse and execute faster.
  • Transpilation cost — Babel is slower; SWC and esbuild are 10–100× faster.
  • Type checking cost — tsc is slow on large projects; tsc --noEmit in CI, and swc/esbuild in dev.
  • Dev server latency — Vite's native ESM dev server beats bundle-everything webpack for HMR.
  • Dependency depth — deep transitive trees slow install and increase risk.
  • Duplicate packages — multiple versions of the same dep bloat bundles.
  • Tree-shaking efficacy — depends on ESM and how libraries are authored.
  • Node startup — large CLIs can take seconds; --enable-source-maps slows further.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use a fast package manager (pnpm, bun).
  2. Prefer esbuild/SWC over Babel in dev.
  3. Keep bundles small with tree-shaking + code splitting.
  4. Use browserslist to avoid unnecessary transpilation.
  5. Pre-warm caches in CI (actions/cache).
  6. Split dev vs prod builds.
  7. Avoid mega-frameworks for small sites.
  8. Lazy-load heavy dependencies with dynamic import().
  9. Deduplicate via overrides / resolutions.
  10. Measure with real user metrics (RUM), not just lab tests.

docs.title: Supply-Chain Attacks
docs.text:
• Typosquatting — express vs expresss.
  • Malicious packages — steal env vars, crypto wallets, tokens.
  • Postinstall scripts — arbitrary code execution during npm install.
  • Dependency confusion — public packages shadow internal ones.
  • Protestware / sabotage — maintainers deliberately breaking packages.

Defenses: lockfiles, npm audit, npm ci, Snyk/Dependabot, allowlists, SRI in browsers, --ignore-scripts where feasible, artifact signing (npm provenance, Sigstore).

docs.title: Vulnerable Transitive Dependencies
docs.text:
A single vulnerable transitive dep (e.g., old lodash, minimist) can compromise a whole app.

Defenses: audit tools, version pinning, frequent updates, minimal dependency surface.

docs.title: Leaking Secrets in Published Packages
docs.text:
Publishing npm publish sends whatever is in the tarball — including .env if not excluded.

Defenses: files field, .npmignore, npm pack --dry-run before publish.

docs.title: CDN and Third-Party Scripts
docs.text:
Loading scripts from third-party CDNs means trusting those CDNs. A compromise is a compromise of your site.

Defenses: Subresource Integrity (SRI), self-hosting critical scripts, CSP.

docs.title: eval in Dependencies
docs.text:
Some libraries use eval or new Function, which is blocked by strict CSP.

Defenses: audit dependencies; prefer CSP-compatible libraries.

docs.title: Risky Dev Tools
docs.text:
Dev servers (Vite, webpack-dev-server) have had RCE vulnerabilities when exposed to the public internet.

Defenses: bind to localhost; never expose dev servers.

docs.title: License Compliance
docs.text:
Every dependency carries a license; some (GPL) impose obligations on distribution.

Defenses: license scanners (FOSSA, license-checker), allowlists in CI.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Read the stack trace — all of it. Transitive frames reveal the culprit.
  • node --trace-warnings — surface deprecation warnings.
  • npm ls <pkg> — see who pulled in a dependency.
  • npm why <pkg> — explain why a version is installed.
  • npm outdated — see stale packages.
  • npm audit --production — security holes in shipped deps.
  • npm pack --dry-run — preview what a publish will include.
  • node --inspect-brk — debug in Chrome DevTools.
  • NODE_OPTIONS=--enable-source-maps — readable stack traces.
  • Vite --debug, webpack --stats=detailed — verbose build logs.
  • Bundle analyzers — vite-bundle-visualizer, webpack-bundle-analyzer, source-map-explorer.
  • publint and arethetypeswrong — validate published package correctness.
  • bundlephobia — inspect package size before adopting.
  • CI matrix logs — reproduce issues across Node versions.

docs.title: 16. When to Use (This Ecosystem)
docs.text:
• Building any modern web application. The ecosystem is where the tooling lives.
  • Publishing reusable code. npm and JSR are the standard distribution channels.
  • Working in a team. Shared tooling enforces consistency.
  • Targeting browsers, Node, edge, desktop, or mobile. Each has a mature ecosystem path.
  • Needing a specific capability fast. There is almost always a package for it.
  • Serving large teams and codebases. TypeScript, monorepos, and CI tooling pay off.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Tiny static sites. Ship hand-written HTML/CSS/JS.
  • Embedded systems with constrained memory. A runtime is too heavy.
  • Regulated environments that forbid third-party code. Vendor or rewrite.
  • When the toolchain outweighs the app. A 3KB page shouldn't need 200MB of node_modules.
  • Very long-lived systems where dependency churn is expensive. Consider minimal-dep stacks.
  • When team skills don't match the ecosystem. The wrong tool for the team is the wrong tool.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• ECMAScript — the language standard
  • JavaScript Engines — V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore
  • Runtime Environments — browser, Node, Deno, Bun
  • ECMAScript Modules — the module system
  • CommonJS — the legacy Node module system
  • Package Managers — npm, yarn, pnpm, bun
  • TypeScript — the dominant typed superset
  • Bundlers — Vite, webpack, esbuild, Rollup
  • Transpilers — Babel, SWC
  • Linters — ESLint, Biome
  • TC39 — standards committee
  • WHATWG — living web standards
  • SemVer — versioning scheme
  • Supply chain security — npm provenance, Sigstore
  • WebAssembly — binary companion in the web stack

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• npm hosts over 2 million packages — the largest registry in any language.
  • The average modern web app pulls in hundreds of transitive dependencies.
  • Left-pad, an 11-line package, was unpublished in 2016 and broke builds worldwide, prompting npm to change its unpublish policy.
  • event-stream (2018) was a widely used package whose maintainer handed it to a stranger who injected a crypto-stealing payload — a canonical supply-chain attack.
  • colors and faker were sabotaged in 2022 by their own maintainer, breaking thousands of builds.
  • Vite was created by Evan You (also the creator of Vue) and became the default dev tool for new projects within two years.
  • pnpm uses a content-addressable store with hard links, so a single copy of each version lives on disk.
  • Bun ships a runtime, package manager, bundler, and test runner in one binary.
  • Deno was created by Ryan Dahl, the creator of Node.js, to fix what he considered Node's design mistakes.
  • JSR is a modern registry that natively serves TypeScript.
  • The exports field in package.json replaced several legacy fields (main, module, browser).
  • TC39 proposals go through five stages (0–4); most never reach Stage 4.
  • The npm registry serves tens of billions of downloads per week.
  • Renovate and Dependabot automate dependency updates in most modern repos.
  • Some companies run private registries (Verdaccio, Artifactory) to control supply chains.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• The JavaScript ecosystem is everything around the language: standards, engines, runtimes, registries, package managers, frameworks, libraries, tooling, and community.
  • It exists because a language alone cannot build and ship software.
  • Layered: standards → engines → runtimes → package managers → tooling → libraries → frameworks → apps.
  • Distributed and pluralistic — no single owner; evolution is market-driven.
  • Standards bodies (TC39, WHATWG, W3C) evolve the platform slowly and safely.
  • Package managers (npm, yarn, pnpm, bun) distribute code; lockfiles ensure reproducibility.
  • Bundlers, transpilers, linters, formatters, and type checkers shape the build pipeline.
  • Frameworks and libraries provide structure and capabilities.
  • SemVer governs version contracts; ranges and lockfiles balance flexibility with stability.
  • Supply chain security is a first-class concern: typosquats, malicious postinstalls, transitive vulns.
  • Performance is measured across install, build, bundle size, and runtime.
  • Churn is high — adopt tools deliberately, not reflexively.
  • The ecosystem is the platform most developers actually work in.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
ECMAScript is the standardized specification that defines the JavaScript language. It is published by Ecma International as the ECMA-262 standard and describes the syntax, types, semantics, built-in objects, and execution model of the language — but not the browser APIs, Node.js APIs, or any host environment.

// This is ECMAScript:
const x = 10;
const double = (n) => n * 2;
const arr = [1, 2, 3].map(double);

// This is NOT ECMAScript (it's a host API):
document.getElementById("app");
process.argv;
fetch("/api");

The relationship is precise: ECMAScript is the language spec; JavaScript is the language as implemented in engines, plus whatever host APIs the environment provides.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ECMAScript exists to solve a fundamental coordination problem: how do you evolve a programming language used by billions of devices without breaking the web? The spec provides:

  • A single source of truth for what the language is.
  • A compatibility contract so engines agree on behavior.
  • A predictable evolution process (TC39 proposals, annual releases).
  • A test suite (Test262) to verify conformance.
  • A legal and technical separation between the language and its implementations.

Without ECMAScript, each browser vendor would invent its own dialect — and the web would fragment.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   JavaScript (the language)            │
│                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              ECMAScript (ECMA-262)                │  │
│  │  Syntax · Types · Semantics · Built-ins · APIs   │  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                        │
│  ┌────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Host APIs         │  │  Host APIs               │  │
│  │  (Browser: DOM,    │  │  (Node: fs, net,         │  │
│  │   Fetch, Storage)  │  │   process)               │  │
│  └────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • ECMAScript — the language core.
  • Host environments — provide the platform-specific APIs.
  • Engines — implement ECMAScript (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore).
  • Runtimes — combine an engine with host APIs (browsers, Node.js, Deno, Bun).

Other ECMAScript standards exist alongside ECMA-262:

Standard Scope ECMA-262 The language itself ECMA-402 Internationalization API (Intl) ECMA-419 Embedded systems API ECMA TR/114 Runtime keys

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
In 1995, Netscape shipped JavaScript and Microsoft shipped JScript. They were almost compatible — but not quite. Each added features the other lacked. Developers had to write branching code or pick a side. The web was heading toward dialect fragmentation — the same problem that had plagued BASIC, SQL, and other standards-optional languages.

A language used by every browser, on every OS, by every device must have a single definition. Without it:

  • Code written for one browser breaks in another.
  • Features can't be added safely.
  • Engines can't be held accountable.
  • Documentation and education become incoherent.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence No standard Browser-specific dialects (document.all, ActiveX, etc.) No evolution process Features added ad hoc, inconsistently No conformance suite Engines shipped partial or buggy implementations No versioning "JavaScript 1.5" meant different things to different vendors No legal clarity "JavaScript" trademarked by Sun/Oracle; spec needed a neutral name

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
Netscape submitted the language to ECMA International in November 1996. The first edition of ECMA-262 was published in June 1997. The name "ECMAScript" was a compromise — "JavaScript" was trademarked by Sun Microsystems (later Oracle), so a neutral name was needed for the standard.

Since then, ECMAScript has gone through 17 editions (as of 2026), evolving from a small scripting language into a full-featured, multi-paradigm programming language used across browsers, servers, mobile, desktop, and embedded systems.

docs.title: What ECMAScript Defines
docs.text:
// Values and types
const n = 42;               // Number
const s = "hello";          // String
const b = true;             // Boolean
const u = undefined;        // Undefined
const nul = null;           // Null
const sym = Symbol("id");   // Symbol
const big = 9007199254740993n; // BigInt

// Objects and arrays
const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 };
const arr = [1, 2, 3];

// Functions
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
const mul = (a, b) => a * b;

// Classes
class Point {
    constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    distance() { return Math.hypot(this.x, this.y); }
}

// Control flow
if (n > 10) { /* ... */ }
for (const item of arr) { /* ... */ }
try { /* ... */ } catch (e) { /* ... */ }

// Async
async function fetchData() {
    const res = await fetch("/api"); // fetch is a host API, not ECMAScript
    return res.json();
}

// Modules
export const VERSION = "1.0";
import { VERSION } from "./config.js";

docs.title: What ECMAScript Does Not Define
docs.text:
// ❌ Not in ECMAScript:
document.querySelector("div");   // DOM (WHATWG)
window.localStorage;             // Storage (WHATWG)
setTimeout(() => {}, 1000);      // Timers (WHATWG / Node)
fetch("/api");                   // Fetch (WHATWG)
process.env;                     // Node.js
Deno.readFileSync("file");       // Deno
Bun.file("file");                // Bun
console.log("hi");               // Console (WHATWG / Node) — technically a host API

The line is often blurry in practice, but it matters: ECMAScript describes the language; everything else is the host.

docs.title: A Conforming ECMAScript Program
docs.text:
// Runs in any conforming ECMAScript host with no host APIs:
function fibonacci(n) {
    let [a, b] = [0, 1];
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) [a, b] = [b, a + b];
    return a;
}

const result = fibonacci(10); // 55

This program uses only language features — no DOM, no Node, no browser APIs.

docs.title: The "Spec vs. Implementation" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│         ECMAScript Spec              │  ← the blueprint
│  (ECMA-262, written in prose +      │
│   formal grammar + algorithms)      │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────┘
               │  implemented by
               ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Engines                      │  ← the buildings
│  V8 · SpiderMonkey · JavaScriptCore │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────┘
               │  embedded in
               ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Runtimes                     │  ← the cities
│  Chrome · Firefox · Safari · Node   │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘

The spec is normative — it defines what must happen. Engines are conformant to varying degrees. Test262 verifies conformance.

docs.title: The "Constitution" Mental Model
docs.text:
ECMAScript is like a constitution:

  • It defines the rules (grammar, semantics).
  • It is amended over time (annual editions).
  • Amendments go through a formal process (TC39 stages).
  • Courts (engines) interpret and apply it.
  • Citizens (developers) live under it — often without reading it.

docs.title: The "Annual Train" Mental Model
docs.text:
Since 2015, ECMAScript releases on a predictable annual cadence:

Proposal → Stage 0 → Stage 1 → Stage 2 → Stage 3 → Stage 4 → Next Edition

Features that reach Stage 4 by the cutoff are included in that year's edition. This replaced the old "big bang" releases (ES6 took six years) with a steady train of smaller, safer changes.

docs.title: Concept 1: ECMA-262 Is the Language Spec
docs.text:
ECMA-262 defines:

  • Grammar — what valid programs look like.
  • Types — Undefined, Null, Boolean, String, Symbol, Number, BigInt, Object.
  • Semantics — what each construct does.
  • Built-in objects — Object, Array, Map, Set, Promise, Math, JSON, Reflect, Proxy, etc.
  • Execution model — realms, agents, jobs, the event loop contract.

It does not define:

  • The DOM.
  • console.
  • Timers.
  • Networking.
  • File systems.
  • Rendering.

docs.title: Concept 2: Editions and Versions
docs.text:
Edition Year Common Name Highlights 1 1997 ES1 Initial standard 2 1998 ES2 Editorial 3 1999 ES3 Regex, try/catch, switch 5 2009 ES5 Strict mode, JSON, getters/setters 6 2015 ES2015 / ES6 let/const, classes, modules, promises, arrows 7 2016 ES2016 **, Array.prototype.includes 8 2017 ES2017 async/await, Object.entries 9 2018 ES2018 Rest/spread for objects, async iteration 10 2019 ES2019 flat, flatMap, Object.fromEntries 11 2020 ES2020 Optional chaining, nullish coalescing, BigInt 12 2021 ES2021 replaceAll, Promise.any, logical assignment 13 2022 ES2022 Top-level await, .at(), class fields 14 2023 ES2023 toSorted, toReversed, findLast 15 2024 ES2024 Object.groupBy, Map.groupBy, Promise.withResolvers 16 2025 ES2025 Iterator helpers, Set methods, JSON modules, regex modifiers 17 2026 ES2026 Temporal, Map.getOrInsert, Array.fromAsync, Error.isError

Note: Edition 4 was abandoned (too ambitious); edition 5 came after a long gap.

docs.title: Concept 3: TC39 — The Standards Committee
docs.text:
TC39 (Technical Committee 39) is the ECMA committee that evolves ECMAScript. Members include representatives from browser vendors (Google, Mozilla, Apple, Microsoft), tooling companies, and invited experts.

TC39 operates by consensus — no single vendor can force a feature through.

docs.title: Concept 4: The TC39 Proposal Process
docs.text:
Stage 0 → Stage 1 → Stage 2 → Stage 3 → Stage 4 → Included in next edition
Stage Name Meaning 0 Strawperson An idea submitted to TC39 1 Proposal A champion is identified; problem is well-defined 2 Draft Spec text is written; syntax and semantics are precise 2.7 — Spec text is complete; implementations underway 3 Candidate Spec is complete; implementations and feedback begin 4 Finished Two+ implementations ship; Test262 tests pass; included in spec

Features at Stage 4 are guaranteed to be in the next annual edition.

docs.title: Concept 5: Test262
docs.text: Test262 is the official ECMAScript conformance test suite. Engines must pass it to claim conformance. It contains tens of thousands of tests covering every part of the spec.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Annual Release Cadence
docs.text:
Since ES2015:

  • February 1 — TC39 meeting; features that reached Stage 4 by this date are candidates.
  • March — Final Stage 4 approval.
  • June — Ecma General Assembly approves the new edition.
  • Publication — ECMA-262 year edition is published.

This cadence makes the language predictable — developers know when to expect new features and can plan upgrades.

docs.title: Concept 7: Backward Compatibility
docs.text:
ECMAScript is strictly backward-compatible. No feature has ever been removed. This is why:

  • var still exists despite let/const.
  • == still coerces despite ===.
  • typeof null === "object" is still a bug.
  • with is deprecated but not deleted.

The web cannot break — old pages must keep working forever.

docs.title: Concept 8: Strict Mode
docs.text:
"use strict";

Introduced in ES5, strict mode:

  • Turns silent errors into exceptions.
  • Forbids with, implicit globals, and octal literals.
  • Makes this undefined in plain function calls.
  • Is default in modules and classes.

docs.title: Concept 9: ECMA-402 (Internationalization)
docs.text:
ECMA-402 standardizes the Intl object:

new Intl.DateTimeFormat("de-DE").format(new Date());
new Intl.NumberFormat("ja-JP", { style: "currency", currency: "JPY" }).format(1000);

It is a separate standard from ECMA-262 but part of the ECMAScript family.

docs.title: Concept 10: The Relationship with TypeScript
docs.text:
TypeScript is a superset of ECMAScript. It adds:

  • Static types.
  • Interfaces, generics, enums.
  • Decorators, namespaces.

Then it compiles to ECMAScript. The TypeScript team tracks ECMAScript editions closely and adds support for new features as they reach Stage 3/4.

docs.title: Concept 11: Feature Detection over Version Detection
docs.text:
You cannot reliably detect "ES2020 support" in a browser. Instead:

if (typeof BigInt !== "undefined") { /* ... */ }
if (typeof Array.prototype.at === "function") { /* ... */ }

Feature detection is the correct approach.

docs.title: Concept 12: Polyfills and Transpilation
docs.text:
• Polyfills — implement missing APIs at runtime.
  • Transpilers (Babel, SWC) — rewrite newer syntax into older syntax.

Both are bridges between the spec and the engines that lag behind it.

docs.title: Concept 13: The ecma262 Repository
docs.text: The ECMAScript spec lives at tc39.es/ecma262 and is maintained in a GitHub repository. You can read the spec, file issues, and follow discussions.

docs.title: Concept 14: The Relationship with WHATWG
docs.text: WHATWG maintains the "living standards" for HTML, DOM, Fetch, Streams, and many other web APIs. These are not ECMAScript, but they are part of the JavaScript platform.

docs.title: Concept 15: Current Status (2026)
docs.text:
As of 2026:

  • ECMAScript 2026 (17th edition) was approved on June 30, 2026, and published in June 2026 as ECMA-262 17th edition .
  • ECMAScript 2025 (16th edition) was published in June 2025 as ECMA-262 16th edition .
  • Temporal API reached Stage 4 in March 2026 and is part of ES2026 .
  • Explicit Resource Management (using / await using) reached Stage 4 in 2025 and is part of ES2026 .
  • Iterator Sequencing (Iterator.concat) reached Stage 4 in November 2025 .

docs.title: Concept 16: Key Features by Recent Edition
docs.text:
ES2025 added:

  • Iterator Helpers — .map(), .filter(), .take(), .drop() on iterators.
  • New Set methods — .union(), .intersection(), .difference().
  • JSON modules — import data from "./data.json" with { type: "json" }.
  • RegExp modifiers — inline flags like (?i:...).
  • Promise.try() — streamline promise chains.
  • Float16Array — a new typed array.
  • RegExp /v flag — upgrade to the /u flag.
  • RegExp.escape() — escape strings for regex use.

ES2026 added:

  • Temporal API — modern, immutable date/time handling with time zones and calendars.
  • Map.prototype.getOrInsert() / getOrInsertComputed() — upsert semantics for maps .
  • Array.fromAsync() — collect async iterables into arrays .
  • Error.isError() — reliably identify error objects .
  • Math.sumPrecise() — accurate summation of floating-point numbers .
  • Iterator.concat() — lazily sequence iterators .
  • Uint8Array base64/hex methods — encode/decode binary data .
  • JSON.rawJSON() — fine control over JSON.stringify output .
  • JSON.parse reviver context — access the matched segment of JSON source .
  • Explicit Resource Management — using and await using for automatic cleanup .

docs.title: Concept 17: The Edition Numbering
docs.text:
ECMAScript editions are numbered sequentially (1st, 2nd, 3rd, ..., 17th). The year name (ES2026) is the colloquial name. The edition number is the formal name in the spec.

  • Edition 17 = ES2026 = ECMA-262 17th edition.

docs.title: Concept 18: The engines Field and Conformance
docs.text:
Engines report conformance via:

  • Test262 pass rates.
  • Baseline (web-platform-tests) status.
  • Can I Use and MDN compatibility tables.

No engine is 100% conformant at all times — the spec evolves faster than any implementation can perfectly track.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: From Proposal to Standard
docs.text:
1.  Idea posted to TC39 (Stage 0)
    │
    ▼
2.  Champion presents; TC39 accepts (Stage 1)
    │
    ▼
3.  Spec text drafted; syntax + semantics precise (Stage 2)
    │
    ▼
4.  Spec text complete; implementations begin (Stage 2.7 / 3)
    │
    ▼
5.  Two+ independent implementations ship
    │
    ▼
6.  Test262 tests pass
    │
    ▼
7.  TC39 consensus to advance (Stage 4)
    │
    ▼
8.  Included in next ECMAScript edition

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How an Edition Is Published
docs.text:
1.  All Stage 4 features by Feb 1 are candidates.
    │
    ▼
2.  March TC39 meeting finalizes the feature set.
    │
    ▼
3.  Spec editors integrate all features into ECMA-262.
    │
    ▼
4.  Test262 updated.
    │
    ▼
5.  Ecma General Assembly approves (June).
    │
    ▼
6.  ECMA-262 Nth edition published.
    │
    ▼
7.  Engines update; Baseline status assigned.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How Engines Implement the Spec
docs.text:
1.  Read the spec text for a feature.
    │
    ▼
2.  Implement parser / lexer changes.
    │
    ▼
3.  Implement runtime semantics.
    │
    ▼
4.  Add Test262 tests (and write new ones).
    │
    ▼
5.  Ship behind a flag.
    │
    ▼
6.  Ship unflagged.
    │
    ▼
7.  Report conformance.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How a Developer Uses a New Feature
docs.text:
1.  Check Stage 4 status on the TC39 proposals repo.
    │
    ▼
2.  Check MDN / Can I Use for engine support.
    │
    ▼
3.  Option A: Use a transpiler (Babel, SWC) to target older engines.
    │
    ▼
4.  Option B: Feature-detect at runtime and provide a fallback.
    │
    ▼
5.  Option C: Wait for Baseline support.
    │
    ▼
6.  Ship.

docs.title: The Spec's Structure
docs.text:
ECMA-262 is organized into:

  • Clauses — numbered sections.
  • Algorithms — numbered steps with abstract operations.
  • Grammar — BNF-style syntax rules.
  • Internal slots and methods — [[Prototype]], [[Get]], etc.

Example algorithm (simplified):

Array.prototype.map ( callbackfn [ , thisArg ] )
1. Let O be ? ToObject(this value).
2. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(O).
3. If IsCallable(callbackfn) is false, throw a TypeError.
4. Let A be ? ArraySpeciesCreate(O, len).
5. Let k be 0.
6. Repeat, while k < len:
   a. Let Pk be ! ToString(𝔽(k)).
   b. Let kPresent be ? HasProperty(O, Pk).
   c. If kPresent is true:
      i. Let kValue be ? Get(O, Pk).
      ii. Let mappedValue be ? Call(callbackfn, thisArg, « kValue, 𝔽(k), O »).
      iii. Perform ? CreateDataPropertyOrThrow(A, Pk, mappedValue).
   d. Set k to k + 1.
7. Return A.

This is normative — engines must follow it.

docs.title: Realms, Agents, and Jobs
docs.text:
• Realm — a global environment (global object, global scope, built-ins). Each iframe has its own realm.
  • Agent — a thread of execution with its own call stack and job queues.
  • Job — a unit of asynchronous work (e.g., a promise reaction).

These concepts define how execution proceeds across contexts.

docs.title: The Execution Model
docs.text:
┌──────────────┐
│  Call Stack  │
└──────┬───────┘
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│  Job Queue   │  ← promise jobs, host jobs
└──────┬───────┘
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│  Event Loop  │  ← host-defined
└──────────────┘

The spec defines the job queue semantics; the event loop is host-defined (WHATWG for browsers, Node for Node.js).

docs.title: Intrinsics and the Global Object
docs.text:
Every realm has a set of intrinsic objects:

  • %Object%, %Array%, %Function%, %Promise%, %Map%, %Set%, %Math%, %JSON%, %Reflect%, %Proxy%, etc.

These are the built-ins available to all code in that realm.

docs.title: The [[Prototype]] Chain
docs.text:
Object.prototype
    ▲
    │
Array.prototype
    ▲
    │
[]

The spec defines prototype chains and property lookup precisely.

docs.title: Test262
docs.text:
The conformance suite lives at github.com/tc39/test262. Each test is a small JavaScript file with metadata:

/*---
description: Array.prototype.at returns the last element
features: [Array.prototype.at]
---*/
assert.sameValue([1, 2, 3].at(-1), 3);

Engines run Test262 in CI.

docs.title: The Proposal Lifecycle
docs.text:
Idea
  │
  ▼
Stage 0: Strawperson
  │
  ▼
Stage 1: Proposal (champion + problem statement)
  │
  ▼
Stage 2: Draft (spec text + syntax)
  │
  ▼
Stage 2.7: Complete spec text
  │
  ▼
Stage 3: Candidate (implementations + feedback)
  │
  ▼
Stage 4: Finished (two implementations + Test262)
  │
  ▼
Included in next edition
  │
  ▼
Engines ship unflagged
  │
  ▼
Baseline status assigned

docs.title: The Developer Lifecycle
docs.text:
Feature announced (Stage 3 or 4)
  │
  ▼
Decide: use now, transpile, or wait?
  │
  ▼
Transpile with Babel/SWC (if needed)
  │
  ▼
Feature-detect at runtime
  │
  ▼
Ship
  │
  ▼
Later: remove polyfill/transpile when Baseline

docs.title: The Edition Lifecycle
docs.text:
Feb 1: Stage 4 cutoff for the year
  │
  ▼
March: TC39 finalizes feature set
  │
  ▼
April–May: Spec editors integrate
  │
  ▼
June: Ecma General Assembly approves
  │
  ▼
June–July: ECMA-262 published
  │
  ▼
Rest of year: Engines update
  │
  ▼
Next Feb: Cutoff for next edition

docs.title: Example 1: Using ES2026's Array.fromAsync()
docs.text:
async function* fetchAllPages(url) {
    while (url) {
        const res = await fetch(url);
        const page = await res.json();
        yield* page.items;
        url = page.next;
    }
}

const allItems = await Array.fromAsync(fetchAllPages("/api/items"));
console.log(allItems.length);

Code Breakdown:

  • Array.fromAsync collects an async iterable into an array .
  • Equivalent to for await...push, but concise.
  • Part of ECMAScript 2026 .

docs.title: Example 2: Using ES2026's Map.getOrInsert()
docs.text:
const employeesByDept = new Map();

for await (const employee of employeeStream) {
    employeesByDept
        .getOrInsertComputed(employee.department, () => [])
        .push(employee);
}

Code Breakdown:

  • getOrInsertComputed lazily creates the default value .
  • Replaces the has/set/get boilerplate.
  • Part of ECMAScript 2026 .

docs.title: Example 3: Using ES2026's Error.isError()
docs.text:
try {
    riskyOperation();
} catch (err) {
    if (Error.isError(err)) {
        console.error("Real error:", err.message);
    } else {
        console.warn("Non-error thrown:", err);
    }
}

Code Breakdown:

  • Error.isError() reliably identifies real error objects .
  • Handles the fact that JavaScript allows throwing anything.

docs.title: Example 4: Using ES2026's Temporal API
docs.text:
const now = Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO("America/New_York");
const meeting = now.add({ hours: 2 });
console.log(meeting.toString());

const birthday = Temporal.PlainDate.from("1990-05-15");
const age = birthday.until(Temporal.Now.plainDateISO()).years;
console.log(`Age: ${age}`);

Code Breakdown:

  • Temporal replaces the broken Date object .
  • Immutable, time-zone-aware, calendar-aware.
  • Part of ECMAScript 2026.

docs.title: Example 5: Using ES2025's Iterator Helpers
docs.text:
function* naturals() {
    let i = 0;
    while (true) yield i++;
}

const firstFiveEvens = naturals()
    .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)
    .take(5)
    .toArray();

console.log(firstFiveEvens); // [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

Code Breakdown:

  • Iterator Helpers add .map(), .filter(), .take(), .drop(), .toArray() to iterators.
  • Part of ECMAScript 2025 .

docs.title: Example 6: Using ES2025's Set Methods
docs.text:
const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
const b = new Set([3, 4, 5]);

console.log(a.union(b));        // Set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
console.log(a.intersection(b)); // Set {3}
console.log(a.difference(b));   // Set {1, 2}

Code Breakdown:

  • Native set operations, no library needed .
  • Part of ECMAScript 2025.

docs.title: Example 7: Using ES2026's JSON.rawJSON()
docs.text:
const bigNumber = JSON.rawJSON("9007199254740993");
const json = JSON.stringify({ id: bigNumber });
console.log(json); // {"id":9007199254740993}

Code Breakdown:

  • Preserves integers larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER .
  • Avoids precision loss during serialization.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Need ECMAScript Feature Modern date/time Temporal (ES2026) Resource cleanup using / await using (ES2026) Async array collection Array.fromAsync() (ES2026) Error detection Error.isError() (ES2026) Map upserts Map.getOrInsert() (ES2026) Iterator composition Iterator.concat() (ES2026) Base64/hex encoding Uint8Array methods (ES2026) Set operations Set.prototype.union() etc. (ES2025) Iterator chaining Iterator Helpers (ES2025) JSON modules import ... with { type: "json" } (ES2025) RegExp modifiers Inline flags (ES2025) Async iteration for await...of (ES2018) Optional chaining ?. (ES2020) Nullish coalescing ?? (ES2020) Top-level await ESM (ES2022)

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Know which edition introduced a feature. Why: determines engine support and transpilation needs.
  2. Check Stage 4 status before relying on a feature. Why: Stage 3 features can change.
  3. Use feature detection, not version detection. Why: engines ship features at different times.
  4. Prefer Baseline-supported features for production. Why: guaranteed cross-browser support.
  5. Transpile only what you need. Why: smaller bundles, faster builds.
  6. Follow TC39 proposals. Why: plan for upcoming features.
  7. Read the spec when behavior is surprising. Why: the spec is normative.
  8. Use Test262 to verify engine conformance. Why: catches differences early.
  9. Update TypeScript with new editions. Why: target and lib should match your runtime.
  10. Avoid polyfilling what engines already support. Why: wasted bytes.
  11. Understand backward compatibility. Why: old features never disappear — but new ones might not be everywhere.
  12. Use Intl (ECMA-402) for internationalization. Why: it's the standardized path.
  13. Follow the annual release cadence. Why: plan upgrades around June approvals.
  14. Prefer ECMAScript built-ins over libraries when available. Why: smaller dependencies.
  15. Document the ECMAScript baseline for your project. Why: teams need a shared target.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Confusing ECMAScript with JavaScript
docs.text:
"ECMAScript added fetch."

Why it's wrong: fetch is a WHATWG API, not ECMAScript. ECMAScript does not define networking.

✅ Correct: Distinguish the language spec (ECMA-262) from host APIs (WHATWG, Node).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming "ES6" Means All Modern JavaScript
docs.text:
"We target ES6."

Why it's wrong: ES6 (2015) is a decade old. ES2026 has added many features since.

✅ Correct: Specify the minimum edition and the target engines.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Stage 3 Features in Production Without a Plan
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Stage 3 features can change before Stage 4.

✅ Correct: Use Stage 3 features behind a flag or with a transpiler, and track the proposal.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Version Detection
docs.text:
if (navigator.userAgent.includes("Chrome/120")) { /* ... */ }

Why it's wrong: Fragile, unreliable, and doesn't reflect the actual feature set.

✅ Correct:

if (typeof Array.prototype.at === "function") { /* ... */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming "Latest Spec = Latest Browser"
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Engines lag the spec, and browsers lag engines.

✅ Correct: Check MDN / Can I Use / Baseline for actual support.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Edition Numbering
docs.text:
"ES2025 is the 15th edition."

Why it's wrong: ES2025 is the 16th edition; ES2026 is the 17th.

✅ Correct: Know the edition numbers: ES2015 = 6th, ES2020 = 11th, ES2025 = 16th, ES2026 = 17th.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Thinking the Spec Defines the DOM
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The DOM is a WHATWG living standard, not ECMAScript.

✅ Correct: ECMAScript defines the language; WHATWG defines the DOM and other web APIs.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Skipping Intl (ECMA-402)
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Hand-rolled date/number formatting is error-prone and locale-insensitive.

✅ Correct: Use Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.NumberFormat, Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, etc.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming All Engines Implement the Same Edition
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore ship features on different schedules.

✅ Correct: Use feature detection and Baseline.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Never Reading the Spec
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Surprising behaviors (coercion, prototype chains, async ordering) are explained precisely in the spec.

✅ Correct: Read tc39.es/ecma262 when behavior matters.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Spec conformance is not performance. Engines optimize beyond what the spec requires.
  • Newer features are often faster. Array.fromAsync can be faster than manual loops; Math.sumPrecise is optimized.
  • Temporal is designed to be efficient compared to the legacy Date.
  • Iterator Helpers avoid intermediate arrays — lazy evaluation saves memory.
  • Set methods are optimized in engines versus userland polyfills.
  • Transpilation overhead — transpiled code can be slower than native.
  • Polyfill cost — large polyfills add parse and runtime cost.
  • JIT deoptimization — using rarely-seen syntax can deopt hot functions.
  • Spec-compliant edge cases can be slower than non-compliant shortcuts.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Prefer native implementations over polyfills when available.
  2. Use Array.fromAsync over manual for await loops when collecting.
  3. Use Map.getOrInsert to avoid repeated has/get/set.
  4. Use Iterator Helpers instead of building intermediate arrays.
  5. Use Math.sumPrecise for numerically sensitive summation.
  6. Use Temporal for complex date math — it's faster and safer than hand-rolled.
  7. Avoid transpiling features your target engines already support.
  8. Check Baseline status before adding polyfills.
  9. Benchmark in the engines you ship to.
  10. Track engine conformance for performance improvements.

docs.title: Spec Compliance and Security
docs.text: Engines that deviate from the spec can introduce security bugs. Test262 and web-platform-tests help catch these.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
ECMAScript's prototype chain is powerful and dangerous. Malicious input can modify Object.prototype:

Object.assign({}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}'));

Defenses: validate keys, use Object.create(null), freeze prototypes.

docs.title: eval and Function
docs.text:
eval and the Function constructor execute arbitrary strings as code.

Defenses: never evaluate untrusted input; CSP can block eval.

docs.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS)
docs.text:
Complex regexes can cause catastrophic backtracking.

Defenses: use safe-regex tools, limit input length, prefer linear-time patterns.

docs.title: Temporal and Time-Zone Data
docs.text:
Temporal depends on the IANA time zone database, which updates periodically.

Defenses: keep runtimes updated; don't hard-code time zone data.

docs.title: JSON Parsing
docs.text:
JSON.parse is safe by design — it does not execute code. But JSON.parse on untrusted input can still produce large objects that exhaust memory.

Defenses: limit input size; use streaming parsers for large payloads.

docs.title: Supply-Chain Risk in Polyfills
docs.text:
Polyfills are packages. They can be compromised like any other dependency.

Defenses: audit polyfills; prefer official core-js and polyfill-library; use SRI.

docs.title: Spec Ambiguity
docs.text:
Some spec corners are subtle; different engines may interpret edge cases differently. This is rare but real.

Defenses: test on multiple engines; report spec bugs to TC39.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Read the spec. tc39.es/ecma262 is searchable and precise.
  • Check MDN for practical documentation and browser support.
  • Check Can I Use for feature support tables.
  • Check Baseline for "newly available" / "widely available" status.
  • Use Test262 to verify engine behavior.
  • Use node --version and process.versions.v8 to know your runtime.
  • Use npx browserslist to see which browsers your build targets.
  • Use Babel's REPL to see transpiled output.
  • Use console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyNames(globalThis)) to list available globals.
  • Use feature detection to verify runtime support:
console.log(typeof Array.fromAsync); // "function" if supported
console.log(typeof Temporal);        // "object" if supported
  • Track TC39 proposals at github.com/tc39/proposals.
  • Follow ecmascript.news for weekly updates.

docs.title: 16. When to Use (ECMAScript Features)
docs.text:
• Whenever a native feature exists — prefer it over a library.
  • When the feature is at Stage 4 — it's guaranteed in the next edition.
  • When Baseline support covers your targets — safe for production.
  • When transpilation is acceptable — for Stage 3 / newly Stage 4 features.
  • For new projects — target the latest edition you can support.
  • For libraries — target a conservative Baseline to maximize reach.
  • For internal tools — target the latest edition your runtime supports.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Stage 0–2 features in production. Too unstable.
  • Stage 3 features without a fallback. May change.
  • Features your runtime doesn't support unless transpiled.
  • Features that add more complexity than they remove.
  • New features just because they exist — evaluate the trade-off.
  • Polyfills for features already in your Baseline.
  • Temporal in environments with outdated time-zone data.
  • eval and Function for dynamic code — security and performance risks.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• JavaScript — the language as implemented
  • ECMA-262 — the language specification
  • ECMA-402 — internationalization API
  • ECMA-419 — embedded systems API
  • TC39 — the standards committee
  • Test262 — conformance test suite
  • Stage 4 proposals — finished features
  • Baseline — cross-browser support standard
  • TypeScript — typed superset of ECMAScript
  • Transpilers — Babel, SWC
  • Polyfills — core-js, polyfill-library
