  • WHATWG — living standards for web APIs
  • W3C — accessibility, CSS, some APIs
  • IETF — HTTP, TLS, URLs
  • Intl — internationalization
  • Temporal — modern date/time API
  • Iterator Helpers — chainable iterator methods

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• ECMAScript was named after Ecma International, not the other way around.
  • Edition 4 was abandoned — it was too ambitious and nearly killed the standard.
  • ES6 took six years (2009–2015); the annual cadence was introduced to prevent that.
  • The typeof null === "object" bug is preserved for backward compatibility and will never be fixed.
  • NaN !== NaN is the only value not equal to itself — defined by IEEE-754.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 — floating-point arithmetic, not a spec bug.
  • Test262 has over 50,000 tests and runs in every major engine's CI.
  • TC39 operates by consensus — any member can block a proposal.
  • Stage 2.7 was added in 2023 to bridge Stage 2 and Stage 3.
  • Temporal replaces the Date object, which has been criticized for decades.
  • Explicit Resource Management (using) was inspired by C# and Python's with.
  • Iterator Helpers bring functional programming to lazy sequences.
  • Array.fromAsync was requested by developers for years before reaching Stage 4.
  • Math.sumPrecise solves a real numerical-analysis problem.
  • Error.isError() addresses the fact that you can throw 42.
  • ECMAScript 2026 is the 17th edition, approved on June 30, 2026 .
  • ECMAScript 2025 is the 16th edition, published in June 2025 .
  • JSON modules (ES2025) let you import JSON natively.
  • RegExp /v flag (ES2025) is a superset of /u for Unicode sets.
  • Promise.try() (ES2025) simplifies promise chain error handling.
  • Float16Array (ES2025) is useful for ML and graphics workloads.
  • The spec is written in prose + algorithms, not code — engines translate it.
  • You can read the spec for free at tc39.es/ecma262.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• ECMAScript is the standardized specification of JavaScript, published as ECMA-262.
  • It defines the language: syntax, types, semantics, built-ins, and execution model.
  • It does not define host APIs — DOM, Fetch, fs, timers are separate standards.
  • TC39 evolves the language through a five-stage proposal process (0–4).
  • Since ES2015, releases are annual and named by year (ES2026, ES2025, etc.).
  • Stage 4 means a feature is finished and will be in the next edition.
  • Test262 is the official conformance test suite.
  • Backward compatibility is absolute — no feature is ever removed.
  • ECMA-402 covers internationalization (Intl); ECMA-419 covers embedded systems.
  • ES2025 added Iterator Helpers, Set methods, JSON modules, RegExp modifiers, Promise.try, and Float16Array.
  • ES2026 (17th edition, approved June 30, 2026) adds Temporal, Map.getOrInsert, Array.fromAsync, Error.isError, Math.sumPrecise, Iterator.concat, Uint8Array base64/hex, JSON.rawJSON, and Explicit Resource Management.
  • Feature detection beats version detection.
  • Baseline is the cross-browser support standard.
  • Read the spec at tc39.es/ecma262; follow proposals at github.com/tc39/proposals.
  • ECMAScript is the blueprint; JavaScript is the building.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A JavaScript engine is the program that parses, compiles, and executes JavaScript code. It is the component that turns your source text into machine instructions your CPU can run. Every runtime that executes JavaScript — browsers, Node.js, Deno, Bun — contains a JavaScript engine.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Runtime (Browser, Node, Deno)       │
│                                                 │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │         JavaScript Engine                 │  │
│  │  (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore,       │  │
│  │   Hermes, QuickJS)                        │  │
│  │                                           │  │
│  │  Parser → Interpreter → JIT Compilers     │  │
│  │  Garbage Collector                        │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                 │
│  Host APIs (DOM, fs, fetch, crypto, …)          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The engine implements ECMAScript. The runtime wraps the engine and adds host APIs.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
JavaScript engines exist to solve a fundamental tension: JavaScript is dynamically typed, yet it must run fast. The engine must:

  • Parse source text into an abstract syntax tree (AST).
  • Interpret or compile that AST into executable form.
  • Optimize hot code paths using runtime feedback.
  • Manage memory automatically via garbage collection.
  • Bridge JavaScript to the host environment (DOM, filesystem, network).

Without engines, JavaScript would be a specification with no execution. They are the implementation layer between the ECMAScript standard and the machines that run it.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
ECMAScript Spec (ECMA-262)
        │
        │ implemented by
        ▼
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              JavaScript Engines                   │
│                                                   │
│  V8 · SpiderMonkey · JavaScriptCore · Hermes      │
└───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                        │ embedded in
                        ▼
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Runtimes                             │
│                                                   │
│  Chrome · Firefox · Safari · Node.js · Deno · Bun │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Layer Examples Spec ECMA-262 Engines V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore, Hermes Runtimes Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Node.js, Deno, Bun Host APIs DOM, Fetch, fs, process, crypto

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
JavaScript is dynamically typed. A variable can hold a number now and a string later. Property lookups are late-bound. Functions are first-class values. This flexibility makes JavaScript easy to write — and hard to run fast.

A naive interpreter would be too slow for modern applications. A traditional ahead-of-time (AOT) compiler cannot work because types are unknown until runtime. The engine must observe how code actually behaves and speculate about what will happen next.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Early interpreters (1995–2008) 10–100× slower than native code No JIT Every operation required dispatch through a switch statement No type feedback Could not optimize property access Stop-the-world GC Long pauses froze the UI Single-tier compilation Either fast startup or fast steady-state — not both

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced
docs.text:
JavaScript engines were not designed once — they evolved in response to pressure. As web applications grew more complex (Gmail, Google Maps, Figma), the performance gap between JavaScript and native code became unacceptable. Vendors responded with:

  • Trace-based JITs (early Firefox, 2008) — record hot paths, compile them to machine code.
  • Method-based JITs (V8, 2008) — compile entire functions.
  • Multi-tier pipelines (V8, 2016+) — interpret first, optimize later.
  • New engines for new platforms (Hermes, 2019) — optimize for mobile startup, not peak throughput.

Each generation solved a limitation of the previous one. The result is the modern engine: a layered, speculative, garbage-collected runtime that runs JavaScript near native speed.

docs.title: You Don't "Use" an Engine Directly
docs.text:
Engines are not invoked by developers. They are embedded in runtimes:

# Node.js embeds V8
node script.js

# Chrome embeds V8
google-chrome https://example.com

# Firefox embeds SpiderMonkey
firefox https://example.com

# Bun embeds JavaScriptCore
bun run script.ts

docs.title: Detecting the Engine
docs.text:
// V8 (Chrome, Edge, Node, Deno)
console.log(typeof globalThis.chrome !== "undefined"); // Chrome
console.log(typeof process?.versions?.v8 !== "undefined"); // Node

// SpiderMonkey (Firefox)
console.log(typeof globalThis.window !== "undefined" &&
            typeof globalThis.chrome === "undefined"); // Firefox heuristic

// JavaScriptCore (Safari, Bun)
console.log(typeof Bun !== "undefined"); // Bun

There is no standardized API for engine detection. Feature detection is preferred.

docs.title: Engine-Specific Debugging Hooks
docs.text:
// V8 — heap snapshot
// (via Chrome DevTools Memory panel)

// Node.js — expose GC
node --expose-gc -e "global.gc(); console.log('GC ran')"

// V8 — trace deoptimizations
// node --trace-deopt script.js

docs.title: Compiler Flags (Node.js / V8)
docs.text:
node --max-old-space-size=4096 script.js    # heap size
node --jitless script.js                    # disable JIT (for testing)
node --trace-opt script.js                  # log optimizations
node --trace-deopt script.js                # log deoptimizations
node --prof script.js                       # CPU profiling

These flags expose the engine's internals for debugging and tuning.

docs.title: The "Translator" Mental Model
docs.text:
A JavaScript engine is like a simultaneous interpreter at the UN:

  • It hears the source language (JavaScript).
  • It translates on the fly into the audience's language (machine code).
  • It gets faster at common phrases (JIT optimization).
  • It occasionally stumbles on an unfamiliar word and must backtrack (deoptimization).
  • It cleans up after itself (garbage collection).

docs.title: The "Tiered Pipeline" Mental Model
docs.text:
Modern engines are pipelines, not single compilers:

Source Code
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Parser    │  → AST
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  Ignition   │  → bytecode + type feedback (interpreter)
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  Sparkplug  │  → baseline machine code (fast, unoptimized)
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Maglev    │  → mid-tier optimized code
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  TurboFan   │  → top-tier speculative optimizing compiler
└─────────────┘

Each tier trades compile time for runtime speed. Code starts in the interpreter and tiers up as it gets hotter.

docs.title: The "Speculation + Bailout" Mental Model
docs.text:
Optimizing JITs assume that code will behave the same way it did before:

function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

add(1, 2);       // observed: both numbers
add(3, 4);       // observed: both numbers
add(5, 6);       // JIT speculates: "a and b are always numbers"
add("x", "y");   // speculation fails → deoptimize back to interpreter

The engine emits guards that check assumptions. If a guard fails, the engine deoptimizes — reconstructs the interpreter state and resumes. Incorrect speculation never produces wrong results, only slower execution.

docs.title: The "Hidden Class" Mental Model
docs.text:
Objects in JavaScript are dynamic bags of properties. Engines make property access fast by assigning each object shape a hidden class (also called a Map in V8):

const a = { x: 1, y: 2 };  // hidden class H1: {x, y}
const b = { x: 1, y: 2 };  // same hidden class H1
const c = { x: 1 };         // different hidden class H2: {x}
c.y = 2;                    // new hidden class H3: {x, y}

Property access becomes a fixed-offset memory load instead of a hash lookup. Changing object shape invalidates the hidden class and triggers deoptimization.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Engine Landscape (2026)
docs.text: Engine Vendor Used By Notable For V8 Google Chrome, Edge, Node.js, Deno Fastest peak performance; most widely deployed SpiderMonkey Mozilla Firefox First JIT; strong spec conformance JavaScriptCore Apple Safari, Bun Four-tier JIT; powering Bun Hermes Meta React Native (default since 0.84) Optimized for mobile startup and memory QuickJS Independent Embedded, low-memory Small, embeddable, no JIT

docs.title: Concept 2: V8 — The Dominant Engine
docs.text:
V8 powers Chrome, Edge, Node.js, and Deno. Its architecture (as of 2026) includes:

  • Ignition — bytecode interpreter.
  • Sparkplug — baseline JIT compiler.
  • Maglev — mid-tier optimizing JIT (introduced 2023, shipped stable 2024).
  • TurboFan — top-tier speculative optimizing JIT.
  • Turboshaft — the new IR that replaced TurboFan's "Sea of Nodes" as of 2025.
  • Orinoco — concurrent, generational garbage collector.

V8's four-tier pipeline:

Tier Compilation Speed Execution Speed Trigger Ignition Instant Slow (~100× native) Always Sparkplug ~10μs/function Moderate ~8 calls Maglev ~100μs/function Fast ~500 calls TurboFan ~1ms/function Near-native ~6000 calls

Maglev exists to fill the gap between Sparkplug and TurboFan. TurboFan alone was too slow to tier up to, leaving a performance gap that real workloads kept falling into. Maglev compiles hot functions in a few milliseconds while delivering most of TurboFan's peak performance.

Turboshaft replaced the Sea of Nodes IR in 2025. The old design was elegant on paper but became a decade-long tax on the V8 team's productivity — implicit control flow was hard for humans to reason about, scheduling was fragile, and onboarding was brutal. The V8 team published a blog post titled "Land ahoy: leaving the Sea of Nodes" in March 2025.

docs.title: Concept 3: SpiderMonkey — Mozilla's Engine
docs.text:
SpiderMonkey powers Firefox. As of 2026:

  • asm.js optimizations were disabled by default in Firefox 148 and the code will be removed entirely in a future release. The replacement is WebAssembly, whose implementation in SpiderMonkey is "far more advanced than the asm.js compiler".
  • SpiderMonkey often implements new ECMAScript proposals first — it has a reputation for early adoption.
  • It supports the full range of modern ECMAScript features: nullish coalescing (??), optional chaining (?.), public static class fields, numeric separators (1_000_000), String.replaceAll(), Promise.allSettled(), and Intl APIs.

docs.title: Concept 4: JavaScriptCore — Apple's Engine
docs.text:
JavaScriptCore (JSC) powers Safari and Bun. Key facts:

  • Temporal API implementation has been in progress since at least November 2021. Temporal reached Stage 4 on March 11, 2026, and is part of ECMAScript 2026.
  • Bun uses JavaScriptCore and has been experimenting with shared-memory threads inside JSC as of June 2026.
  • JSC's architecture is a four-tier pipeline: LLInt (low-level interpreter) → Baseline JIT → DFG (Data Flow Graph) → FTL (Faster Than Light).

docs.title: Concept 5: Hermes — Meta's Mobile Engine
docs.text:
Hermes is optimized for React Native. As of React Native 0.84 (February 2026), Hermes V1 is the default JavaScript engine on both iOS and Android.

Hermes compiles JavaScript to bytecode ahead of time (AOT), which:

  • Improves app startup time.
  • Reduces memory usage.
  • Decreases app size compared to JavaScriptCore.

Hermes V1 brings "significant improvements to both the compiler and VM" with "measurably better JavaScript performance". No migration is required for apps already using Hermes.

docs.title: Concept 6: The Four-Tier Pipeline
docs.text:
Modern engines use multiple compilation tiers to balance startup latency against steady-state speed:

┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐
│  Ignition   │ ──▶ │  Sparkplug  │ ──▶ │   Maglev    │ ──▶ │  TurboFan   │
│ (interpreter)│     │ (baseline)  │     │ (mid-tier)  │     │ (top-tier)  │
└─────────────┘     └─────────────┘     └─────────────┘     └─────────────┘
      instant            ~10μs              ~100μs              ~1ms
      slow               moderate           fast                near-native

This is the classic "compilation time vs. steady-state speed" tradeoff that every JIT faces. JavaScriptCore has Baseline/DFG/FTL; HotSpot (Java) has C1/C2; V8 has Sparkplug/Maglev/TurboFan.

docs.title: Concept 7: Speculative Optimization
docs.text:
Every optimizing JIT does speculation:

  1. Observe — collect type feedback during interpretation.
  2. Assume — the function will be called the same way next time.
  3. Emit — machine code with guards that check assumptions.
  4. Bail out — if a guard fails, deoptimize back to a lower tier.

Example:

function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

add(1, 2);   // feedback: both numbers
add(3, 4);   // feedback: both numbers
// JIT compiles: assumes both are numbers, emits fast integer add
add("a", "b"); // guard fails → deoptimize → interpreter handles strings

docs.title: Concept 8: Hidden Classes (Maps)
docs.text:
V8's hidden classes (called Maps) transform dynamic property access into fixed-offset memory loads:

const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };
// Hidden class: {name, age} → offsets [0, 1]

user.email = "ada@example.com";
// New hidden class: {name, age, email} → offsets [0, 1, 2]

Objects with the same shape share a hidden class. Property access becomes a single map check + direct load. Changing shape (adding/deleting properties) triggers a hidden class transition and may deoptimize hot code.

docs.title: Concept 9: Inline Caches (ICs)
docs.text:
Inline Caches track which object shapes appear at each property access site:

  • Monomorphic (1 shape) — fastest; single map check + direct load.
  • Polymorphic (2–4 shapes) — linear chain of checks.
  • Megamorphic (>4 shapes) — optimization abandoned for that site.

docs.title: Concept 10: Garbage Collection
docs.text:
Engines reclaim memory automatically. V8's Orinoco GC uses:

  • Generational hypothesis — most objects die young.
  • Parallel young-generation collection — multiple threads.
  • Concurrent old-generation marking — runs alongside JavaScript.
  • Sub-millisecond pause times in typical workloads.

docs.title: Concept 11: The Feedback Vector
docs.text: Type feedback is stored in a FeedbackVector separate from code, enabling safe speculation. When speculation fails, the engine reconstructs the interpreter frame and resumes in Ignition.

docs.title: Concept 12: JIT Bugs Are Security Bugs
docs.text:
"JIT bugs are essentially 2nd order vulnerabilities."

A type confusion in a JIT compiler can lead to arbitrary code execution. CVE-2026-85046 is an example: a type confusion in V8's inline Array.prototype.sort (Maglev/TurboFan) with CVSS 8.8.

docs.title: Concept 13: Engine Conformance
docs.text: Engines must pass Test262, the official ECMAScript conformance test suite. No engine is 100% conformant at all times — the spec evolves faster than any implementation can perfectly track.

docs.title: Concept 14: Engine-Agnostic Code
docs.text:
Write code that runs everywhere:

// ✅ Good — works in all engines
const result = arr.map(x => x * 2);

// ❌ Bad — engine-specific
const result = new Intl.Segmenter().segment(str); // check support first

Feature detection is the correct approach:

if (typeof Array.prototype.at === "function") { /* ... */ }

docs.title: Step-by-Step: From Source to Execution
docs.text:
1.  Source code (JavaScript text)
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser → AST (Abstract Syntax Tree)
    │
    ▼
3.  Bytecode generator → Ignition bytecode
    │
    ▼
4.  Ignition interprets bytecode, collecting type feedback
    │
    ▼
5.  Function becomes hot → Sparkplug compiles to baseline machine code
    │
    ▼
6.  Function gets hotter → Maglev compiles mid-tier optimized code
    │
    ▼
7.  Function is very hot and type-stable → TurboFan compiles near-native code
    │
    ▼
8.  If speculation fails → deoptimize back to Ignition
    │
    ▼
9.  Orinoco GC reclaims unreachable memory

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How Maglev Decides to Optimize
docs.text:
1.  Function is called repeatedly.
    │
    ▼
2.  Ignition accumulates type feedback in FeedbackVector.
    │
    ▼
3.  Call count exceeds Maglev threshold (~500 calls).
    │
    ▼
4.  Maglev builds SSA/CFG IR from bytecode + feedback.
    │
    ▼
5.  Speculative guards are inserted for observed types.
    │
    ▼
6.  Machine code is emitted (~100μs/function).
    │
    ▼
7.  Code runs fast; if a guard fails, deoptimize to Ignition.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How Hidden Classes Enable Fast Property Access
docs.text:
1.  Object literal { x: 1, y: 2 } is created.
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine assigns hidden class H1 with property offsets.
    │
    ▼
3.  obj.x → check map == H1 → load offset 0 → fast.
    │
    ▼
4.  obj.z = 3 → hidden class transition to H2.
    │
    ▼
5.  Existing optimized code for H1 deoptimizes.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: How GC Works (V8 Orinoco)
docs.text:
1.  Young generation (nursery) fills up.
    │
    ▼
2.  Minor GC: parallel scavenge — live objects promoted.
    │
    ▼
3.  Old generation fills up.
    │
    ▼
4.  Major GC: concurrent mark → parallel sweep.
    │
    ▼
5.  Pauses kept sub-millisecond via concurrent marking.

docs.title: V8's Pipeline (2026)
docs.text:
Source
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Parser    │ → AST
└─────────────┘
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  Ignition   │ → bytecode + FeedbackVector
└─────────────┘
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  Sparkplug  │ → baseline machine code
└─────────────┘
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Maglev    │ → mid-tier SSA/CFG optimized code
└─────────────┘
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  TurboFan   │ → top-tier speculative optimizing compiler
│ (Turboshaft │
│  IR)        │
└─────────────┘
  │
  ▼
Machine Code

docs.title: Turboshaft: The New IR
docs.text:
As of 2025, TurboFan uses Turboshaft instead of the old Sea of Nodes IR. The Sea of Nodes represented the program as a "sea" of operation nodes connected only by data and effect dependencies, with control flow largely implicit. In practice, this was:

  • Hard for humans — implicit control flow made debugging miscompilations difficult.
  • Fragile — scheduling the "sea" back into linear machine code produced hard-to-reproduce crashes.
  • Brutal for onboarding — new compiler engineers struggled to reason about the IR.

Turboshaft is a more conventional CFG-based IR that is easier to work with and compile quickly.

docs.title: JavaScriptCore's Pipeline
docs.text:
Source
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│    LLInt    │ → low-level interpreter
└─────────────┘
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│ Baseline JIT│ → baseline machine code
└─────────────┘
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│    DFG      │ → Data Flow Graph optimizer
└─────────────┘
  │
  ▼
┌─────────────┐
│    FTL      │ → Faster Than Light (top-tier)
└─────────────┘

docs.title: SpiderMonkey's Architecture
docs.text:
SpiderMonkey has:

  • Baseline Interpreter
  • Baseline Compiler (JIT)
  • IonMonkey (optimizing JIT)
  • Warp (IonBuilder replacement)

Its asm.js optimizations were disabled in Firefox 148.

docs.title: Hermes' Architecture
docs.text: Hermes differs fundamentally: it compiles JavaScript to bytecode ahead of time, then executes that bytecode in a register-based VM. No JIT by default — the focus is on startup time and memory, not peak throughput.

docs.title: The Orinoco GC
docs.text:
V8's garbage collector:

  • Generational — young (nursery) and old generations.
  • Parallel — multiple threads for scavenging.
  • Concurrent — marking and sweeping overlap with JavaScript execution.
  • Sub-millisecond pauses in typical workloads.

docs.title: Engine Execution Lifecycle
docs.text:
Parse
  │
  ▼
Bytecode generation
  │
  ▼
Interpret (Ignition)
  │
  ▼
Collect type feedback
  │
  ▼
Tier up (Sparkplug → Maglev → TurboFan)
  │
  ▼
Run optimized code
  │
  ▼
Deoptimize if speculation fails
  │
  ▼
Re-optimize with new feedback
  │
  ▼
GC reclaims memory

docs.text:
New ECMAScript proposal (Stage 3/4)
  │
  ▼
Engine team implements parser/semantics
  │
  ▼
Add Test262 tests
  │
  ▼
Ship behind a flag
  │
  ▼
Ship unflagged
  │
  ▼
Report conformance
  │
  ▼
Optimize JIT support

docs.title: Choosing an Engine (2026)
docs.text:
Web browser → V8 (Chrome/Edge), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JSC (Safari)
Server/CLI  → V8 (Node.js, Deno), JSC (Bun)
Mobile app  → Hermes (React Native), JSC (iOS)
Embedded    → QuickJS

docs.title: Example 1: Observing Tier-Up in Node.js
docs.text:
node --trace-opt --trace-deopt script.js

function hot(x) { return x * 2; }

for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) hot(i);

Output (abbreviated):

[optimizing: hot / ...] (Maglev)
[optimizing: hot / ...] (TurboFan)

Breakdown:

  • The function tiers up from Ignition → Maglev → TurboFan.
  • Flags expose the engine's internal decisions.

docs.title: Example 2: Deoptimization Triggered by Type Change
docs.text:
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) add(i, i); // optimized for numbers
add("hello", "world"); // deoptimize

Breakdown:

  • Adding strings after numbers violates the JIT's speculation.
  • The function deoptimizes back to Ignition.

docs.title: Example 3: Hidden Class Impact
docs.text:
// ✅ Monomorphic — same shape
function createUser(name, age) {
    return { name, age };
}

// ❌ Polymorphic — different shapes
function createUser(name, age, email) {
    const user = { name, age };
    if (email) user.email = email; // shape change
    return user;
}

Breakdown:

  • Objects with stable shapes optimize better.
  • Avoid adding properties after creation.

docs.title: Example 4: Inspecting JSC in Bun
docs.text:
bun --smol run script.ts   # small memory mode
bun --hot run server.ts    # hot reload

Breakdown:

  • Bun uses JavaScriptCore, not V8.
  • Engine-specific flags control memory and reload behavior.

docs.title: Example 5: Hermes Bytecode Compilation
docs.text:
# React Native compiles to Hermes bytecode
npx react-native bundle --platform android --dev false \
    --entry-file index.js --bundle-output bundle.js
hermesc -emit-binary -out bundle.hbc bundle.js

Breakdown:

  • Hermes compiles JavaScript to bytecode ahead of time.
  • The bytecode runs on the device's Hermes VM.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Engine Why Chrome/Edge extension V8 Chrome/Edge use V8 Firefox extension SpiderMonkey Firefox uses SpiderMonkey Safari extension JavaScriptCore Safari uses JSC Node.js server V8 Node embeds V8 Deno server V8 Deno embeds V8 Bun server JavaScriptCore Bun embeds JSC React Native app Hermes Default since RN 0.84 Embedded/IoT QuickJS Small footprint, no JIT Serverless (Cloudflare) V8 isolates Workers use V8 Serverless (Deno Deploy) V8 Deno Deploy uses V8

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Write engine-agnostic code. Why: your code runs in V8, JSC, SpiderMonkey, and Hermes.
  2. Keep object shapes stable. Why: hidden class transitions deoptimize hot code.
  3. Initialize all properties in the constructor. Why: avoids hidden class transitions.
  4. Avoid delete on hot objects. Why: it destroys hidden class optimizations.
  5. Prefer monomorphic call sites. Why: single-shape ICs are fastest.
  6. Don't block the event loop. Why: long synchronous work prevents GC and rendering.
  7. Use const and let. Why: engines optimize block-scoped variables better.
  8. Avoid arguments in hot functions. Why: it prevents some optimizations.
  9. Don't use eval or new Function. Why: they disable optimizations and enable XSS.
  10. Keep functions small and focused. Why: easier for JITs to optimize.
  11. Test on multiple engines. Why: V8, JSC, and SpiderMonkey behave differently at the margins.
  12. Track engine release notes. Why: new optimizations and regressions ship constantly.
  13. Use --trace-opt and --trace-deopt when debugging performance. Why: reveals JIT behavior.
  14. Profile before optimizing. Why: intuition about hot paths is often wrong.
  15. Keep runtimes updated. Why: JIT and GC improvements ship with each release.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming All Engines Behave Identically
docs.text:
"It works in Chrome, so it works everywhere."

Why it's wrong: V8, JSC, and SpiderMonkey have different optimization strategies, GC behaviors, and edge-case handling.

✅ Correct: Test on all target engines. Use feature detection.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Changing Object Shape After Creation
docs.text:
const user = {};
user.name = "Ada";  // hidden class transition
user.age = 36;      // another transition

Why it's wrong: Each addition creates a new hidden class; optimized code deoptimizes.

✅ Correct:

const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using delete on Hot Objects
docs.text:
delete user.email;

Why it's wrong: delete destroys hidden class optimizations and forces dictionary mode.

✅ Correct: Set to null or create a new object without the property.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Megamorphic Property Access
docs.text:
function getValue(obj) { return obj.value; }
getValue({ value: 1 });
getValue({ value: 2, extra: 3 });
getValue({ value: 3, other: 4 });
// ... many different shapes → megamorphic → slow

Why it's wrong: After 4+ shapes, the IC abandons optimization.

✅ Correct: Keep object shapes consistent.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Hermes Works Like V8
docs.text:
"We'll just use V8 performance techniques on React Native."

Why it's wrong: Hermes is a bytecode VM without a JIT. It optimizes for startup and memory, not peak throughput.

✅ Correct: Profile with Hermes-specific tools; understand its AOT model.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Engine-Specific Security Advisories
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: JIT bugs are exploitable. CVE-2026-85046 was a V8 type confusion with CVSS 8.8.

✅ Correct: Keep runtimes updated; track security advisories.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Over-Optimizing for the JIT
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Premature micro-optimization based on JIT assumptions often backfires.

✅ Correct: Write clear code; profile; optimize only measured hot spots.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using with or eval
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Disables optimizations and creates security holes.

✅ Correct: Avoid them entirely.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming SpiderMonkey Has asm.js
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: asm.js optimizations were disabled in Firefox 148 (2026) and will be removed.

✅ Correct: Use WebAssembly for performance-critical code.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Testing on Safari
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: JavaScriptCore has different optimization thresholds and bug profiles.

✅ Correct: Test on Safari (or use Playwright/WebKit).

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Tier-up thresholds determine when code gets optimized. V8: Sparkplug ~8 calls, Maglev ~500, TurboFan ~6000.
  • Compilation cost vs. steady-state speed — TurboFan pays off on hot loops but wastes time on short-lived functions.
  • Hidden class stability — monomorphic code is fastest.
  • Inline cache states — monomorphic > polymorphic > megamorphic.
  • GC pauses — Orinoco keeps them sub-millisecond in typical workloads.
  • Hermes trades peak performance for startup speed — better for mobile apps.
  • JSC powers Bun — benchmarks show Bun handling ~59,000 Express requests/second on Linux x64 vs ~25,000 for Deno and ~19,000 for Node.js.
  • Deoptimization is expensive — avoid type instability in hot paths.
  • Memory layout matters — object shape and property order affect cache locality.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep object shapes stable across call sites.
  2. Initialize all properties at construction time.
  3. Avoid delete on hot objects.
  4. Prefer monomorphic functions.
  5. Use --trace-opt/--trace-deopt to find deoptimizations.
  6. Profile with engine-specific tools (Chrome DevTools for V8, Web Inspector for JSC).
  7. Keep functions small and predictable.
  8. Avoid arguments in hot functions.
  9. Use Map for dynamic key collections, not objects.
  10. Batch DOM reads and writes to avoid layout thrashing.

docs.title: JIT Bugs Are Security Bugs
docs.text:
JIT compilers are attack surface. A type confusion in the JIT can lead to arbitrary code execution. V8 CVEs are regularly exploited in the wild.

Defenses: keep engines updated; subscribe to security advisories.

docs.title: CVE-2026-85046 — V8 Type Confusion
docs.text:
A type confusion in V8's inline Array.prototype.sort (Maglev/TurboFan) with CVSS 8.8. Exploited via JIT training with polymorphic element-kind feedback (2000 iterations).

Defense: update Chrome to 152.0.7977.82 or later.

docs.title: JavaScriptCore Use-After-Free
docs.text:
ZDI-26-610: JavaScriptCore B3 ReduceStrength Phase Use-After-Free Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (August 2026).

Defense: update Safari/WebKit.

docs.title: JavaScriptCore WebAssembly Memory Bug
docs.text:
CVE-2026-20664: stale pointer handling with non-shared resizable WebAssembly memory in JavaScriptCore after memory growth.

Defense: update WebKit.

docs.title: Speculative Execution Attacks
docs.text:
JIT-compiled code can be vulnerable to Spectre-class attacks if not properly mitigated.

Defense: engines implement mitigations; keep them updated.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Engines that allow __proto__ modification can enable prototype pollution.

Defense: validate input; use Object.create(null) for dictionaries.

docs.title: Hermes and Mobile Security
docs.text:
Hermes' bytecode is not encrypted; sensitive logic can be reverse-engineered from .hbc files.

Defense: avoid shipping secrets in JavaScript; use native modules for sensitive logic.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• node --trace-opt script.js — log optimizations.
  • node --trace-deopt script.js — log deoptimizations.
  • node --prof script.js — CPU profiling.
  • node --expose-gc — manually trigger GC.
  • Chrome DevTools Performance panel — flame charts for V8.
  • Chrome DevTools Memory panel — heap snapshots.
  • Safari Web Inspector — JavaScriptCore profiling.
  • Firefox Profiler — SpiderMonkey profiling.
  • --jitless — disable JIT to test pure interpreter behavior.
  • --max-old-space-size — control heap size.
  • Hermes debugger — React Native debugging via Chrome DevTools.
  • hermesc -dump-bytecode — inspect Hermes bytecode.
  • bun --smol — small memory mode for JSC.
  • Bundle analyzers — V8, JSC, and SpiderMonkey all have engine-specific tools.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• V8 — for Chrome, Edge, Node.js, Deno, Cloudflare Workers.
  • SpiderMonkey — for Firefox and Gecko-based environments.
  • JavaScriptCore — for Safari, Bun, and Apple platforms.
  • Hermes — for React Native (default since 0.84).
  • QuickJS — for embedded systems with tight memory constraints.
  • Multiple engines — when you need cross-browser compatibility.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Don't assume V8 behavior in Safari — JSC has different thresholds.
  • Don't use Hermes for peak-throughput servers — it's optimized for startup.
  • Don't use QuickJS for CPU-heavy workloads — no JIT.
  • Don't use asm.js on SpiderMonkey — disabled in Firefox 148.
  • Don't optimize for JIT quirks — write clear code first.
  • Don't ignore engine updates — security patches ship constantly.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• ECMAScript — the specification engines implement
  • Runtime Environments — browsers, Node.js, Deno, Bun
  • JIT Compilation — just-in-time compilation
  • Garbage Collection — Orinoco, generational GC
  • Hidden Classes / Maps — V8's object shape optimization
  • Inline Caches — property access optimization
  • Speculative Optimization — type feedback and deoptimization
  • Turboshaft — V8's new IR (2025)
  • Maglev — V8's mid-tier JIT (2023)
  • Hermes V1 — React Native's default engine (2026)
  • Test262 — conformance test suite
  • WebAssembly — binary companion to JavaScript

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• V8 was named after the V8 engine — eight cylinders, high performance.
  • SpiderMonkey was the first JavaScript engine, created by Brendan Eich in 1995.
  • JavaScriptCore is also known as SquirrelFish (its interpreter) and Nitro (Safari's marketing name).
  • Hermes compiles JavaScript to bytecode ahead of time, unlike V8's runtime compilation.
  • V8's Maglev was introduced in 2023 and shipped stable in 2024 to fill the gap between Sparkplug and TurboFan.
  • V8 left the Sea of Nodes in 2025 — the biggest change to its optimizing compiler in a decade.
  • SpiderMonkey disabled asm.js in Firefox 148 (2026); WebAssembly replaced it.
  • JavaScriptCore has been implementing Temporal since at least November 2021.
  • Hermes V1 became the default React Native engine in RN 0.84 (February 2026).
  • Bun uses JavaScriptCore — and is testing shared-memory threads inside JSC.
  • V8's tier-up thresholds: Sparkplug ~8 calls, Maglev ~500, TurboFan ~6000.
  • Hidden classes turn property access into a single map check + direct load.
  • Orinoco keeps GC pauses sub-millisecond in typical workloads.
  • JIT bugs are 2nd order vulnerabilities — type confusion can lead to RCE.
  • CVE-2026-85046 was a V8 type confusion in Array.prototype.sort with CVSS 8.8.
  • QuickJS has no JIT — it's designed for embedded systems.
  • Engine conformance is verified by Test262, with over 50,000 tests.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A JavaScript engine parses, compiles, and executes JavaScript.
  • Engines implement ECMAScript; runtimes embed engines and add host APIs.
  • The four major engines in 2026: V8 (Chrome, Edge, Node, Deno), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari, Bun), Hermes (React Native).
  • V8's pipeline: Ignition → Sparkplug → Maglev → TurboFan (Turboshaft IR).
  • Maglev fills the gap between baseline and top-tier optimization.
  • Turboshaft replaced the Sea of Nodes IR in 2025.
  • SpiderMonkey disabled asm.js in Firefox 148; WebAssembly replaced it.
  • JavaScriptCore powers Bun and has been implementing Temporal since 2021.
  • Hermes V1 is the default React Native engine as of RN 0.84 (2026).
  • Hidden classes, inline caches, and speculative optimization make dynamic JavaScript fast.
  • Deoptimization is the safety net — incorrect speculation never produces wrong results.
  • Orinoco provides sub-millisecond GC pauses.
  • JIT bugs are security bugs — keep engines updated.
  • Write engine-agnostic code; test on all target engines.
  • Profile before optimizing; use --trace-opt and --trace-deopt.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A JavaScript runtime environment is the complete system that executes JavaScript code. It consists of three layers: a JavaScript engine (the core that parses and runs the language), a set of host APIs (the platform-specific interfaces the engine exposes), and the event loop (the concurrency model that orchestrates asynchronous work). The engine is the same everywhere — V8 in Chrome and Node.js, JavaScriptCore in Safari and Bun — but the host APIs and event loop differ profoundly.

// Same language, different runtimes:

// Browser runtime:
document.querySelector("#app");       // DOM API
localStorage.setItem("key", "val");   // Storage API
window.fetch("/api");                 // Fetch API

// Node.js runtime:
const fs = require("node:fs");        // File system API
process.env.NODE_ENV;                 // Process API
fs.readFileSync("./data.json");       // Synchronous I/O

// Deno runtime:
const file = await Deno.readTextFile("./data.json"); // Deno API
Deno.env.get("HOME");                 // Environment API

// Bun runtime:
const server = Bun.serve({ fetch: () => new Response("hi") }); // Bun API
Bun.file("./data.json");              // Bun file API

The runtime is what turns ECMAScript — a specification — into a working program that can read files, make network requests, and interact with users.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Runtime environments exist because ECMAScript deliberately says nothing about I/O. The spec defines the language; it does not define how to read a file, open a network connection, or render a button. Runtimes bridge that gap:

  • Browsers provide the DOM, CSSOM, Fetch, Storage, and the rendering pipeline.
  • Node.js provides the filesystem, process, network, and CommonJS/ESM module systems.
  • Deno provides a permissioned, web-standard-first runtime with TypeScript support.
  • Bun provides an all-in-one toolchain with a built-in package manager, bundler, and test runner.
  • Edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, Vercel Edge) provide lightweight, globally distributed execution with restricted APIs.

Without runtimes, JavaScript would be a language that could compute but not do anything. The runtime is what makes JavaScript a platform.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
ECMAScript defines how to compute, not how to communicate. A language that can add numbers but cannot read a file, open a socket, or draw a pixel is a calculator, not a platform. The web needed a language that could:

  • React to user input in real time.
  • Fetch data from servers without reloading the page.
  • Run on servers, not just in browsers.
  • Execute in constrained environments (mobile, edge, embedded).

Each of these requires host APIs — and each host has different capabilities, security models, and constraints.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation 1995–2008 JavaScript confined to browsers; no server-side runtime Pre-Node (2009) No standard server API; no package registry Pre-Deno (2018) Node's security model was opt-in and incomplete Pre-Bun (2022) Toolchains were assembled from many separate tools Pre-Edge (2018+) Serverless functions were slow and cold-start heavy

docs.title: Why Different Runtimes Exist
docs.text:
Runtimes were not designed by committee — they were built to solve specific problems:

  • Browsers needed to execute untrusted code safely while rendering UI.
  • Node.js (2009) needed to bring JavaScript to the server with I/O and a package ecosystem.
  • Deno (2018) was created by Ryan Dahl to fix what he saw as Node's design mistakes: insecure by default, awkward module system, no TypeScript support.
  • Bun (2022) was created to offer a single, fast toolchain — runtime, package manager, bundler, and test runner in one.
  • Edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, Vercel Edge) were created to run code close to users with minimal cold starts.

Each runtime solves a different problem. Choosing a runtime means choosing which problems matter most.

docs.title: Browser Runtime
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Browser Runtime</title></head>
<body>
    <div id="app"></div>
    <script type="module">
        // DOM API
        const app = document.querySelector("#app");
        app.textContent = "Hello from the browser";

        // Fetch API
        const res = await fetch("/api/data");
        const data = await res.json();
        app.textContent = data.message;

        // Storage API
        localStorage.setItem("lastVisit", Date.now().toString());
    </script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Node.js Runtime
docs.text:
// server.js — Node.js (ESM)
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import process from "node:process";

const server = createServer(async (req, res) => {
    if (req.url === "/") {
        const html = await readFile("./index.html", "utf8");
        res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "text/html" });
        res.end(html);
    } else {
        res.writeHead(404);
        res.end("Not found");
    }
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
    console.log(`Server running on port ${process.env.PORT ?? 3000}`);
});

docs.title: Deno Runtime
docs.text:
// server.ts — Deno (TypeScript directly)
const server = Deno.serve({ port: 3000 }, async (req) => {
    if (req.url.endsWith("/")) {
        const html = await Deno.readTextFile("./index.html");
        return new Response(html, {
            headers: { "Content-Type": "text/html" },
        });
    }
    return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
});

docs.title: Bun Runtime
docs.text:
// server.ts — Bun (TypeScript directly)
const server = Bun.serve({
    port: 3000,
    async fetch(req) {
        if (new URL(req.url).pathname === "/") {
            return new Response(Bun.file("./index.html"), {
                headers: { "Content-Type": "text/html" },
            });
        }
        return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
    },
});

docs.title: Edge Runtime (Cloudflare Workers)
docs.text:
// worker.js — Cloudflare Workers
export default {
    async fetch(request, env, ctx) {
        const url = new URL(request.url);
        if (url.pathname === "/") {
            return new Response("Hello from the edge", {
                headers: { "Content-Type": "text/plain" },
            });
        }
        return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
    },
};

docs.title: WinterCG-Compliant Runtime (LLRT)
docs.text:
// handler.mjs — LLRT (Low Latency Runtime)
export const handler = async (event, context) => {
    return {
        statusCode: 200,
        body: JSON.stringify({ message: "Hello from LLRT" }),
    };
};

docs.title: The "Runtime Spectrum" Mental Model
docs.text:
Full-featured ←──────────────────────────────→ Minimal

Browsers  Node.js  Deno  Bun   Edge   LLRT   QuickJS
  │        │        │     │      │      │       │
  DOM      fs       Deno  Bun    Fetch  Fetch   Core
  Fetch    net      APIs  APIs   KV     only    only
  Storage  process        SQLite
  Canvas   crypto         Test
  WebGL    Streams        Bundler

The more features a runtime provides, the heavier it is. Edge runtimes trade features for cold start speed and global distribution.

docs.title: The "Security Model" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Browser:          Sandboxed by origin                │
│  Node.js:          Full access, opt-in permissions    │
│  Deno:             Deny by default, explicit grants   │
│  Bun:              Full access, opt-in permissions    │
│  Edge:             Restricted APIs, no filesystem     │
│  LLRT:             Minimal API surface                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The security model determines how much damage a compromised dependency can do.

docs.title: The "Deployment Target" Mental Model
docs.text:
Local dev  →  Node.js, Deno, Bun
Server     →  Node.js, Deno, Bun
Edge       →  Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, Vercel Edge
Mobile     →  Hermes (React Native), JavaScriptCore (iOS)
Embedded   →  QuickJS, JerryScript
Serverless →  AWS Lambda (Node), LLRT, Cloudflare Workers

Each target has a recommended runtime based on its constraints.

docs.title: Concept 1: Browser Runtimes
docs.text:
Browsers are the original JavaScript runtime. They provide:

  • DOM — the document object model.
  • CSSOM — the stylesheet object model.
  • Fetch API — HTTP requests.
  • Storage APIs — localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB.
  • Web Workers — background threads.
  • Canvas / WebGL / WebGPU — graphics.
  • Event Loop — the WHATWG-defined task/microtask model.

Browsers are sandboxed by origin: scripts from example.com cannot read data from bank.com.

docs.title: Concept 2: Node.js — The Incumbent
docs.text:
Node.js (2009) brought JavaScript to the server. As of 2026:

  • Current LTS: Node.js 24.x ("Krypton").
  • Latest: Node.js 26.x.
  • Built-in test runner — no Jest required for basic testing.
  • Native ESM support alongside CommonJS.
  • Built-in watch mode — node --watch.
  • Permission model — still maturing, opt-in.
  • Temporal API — Node.js 26 ships with Temporal enabled by default.
  • V8 14.6 — the engine powering Node.js 26.
  • Streams iter API — new node:stream/iter implementation.
  • util.throttle() and util.debounce() — new utilities.

Node's strengths: ecosystem depth, everywhere-supported hosting, native module compatibility. Its weakness: TypeScript still requires a build step or loader, and the toolchain is assembled rather than provided.

docs.title: Concept 3: Deno — Secure by Default
docs.text:
Deno (2018) was created by Ryan Dahl to fix Node's design mistakes. As of 2026:

  • Deno 2.9 — current release.
  • Temporal API stabilized in Deno 2.7 (no --unstable-temporal flag needed).
  • Windows on ARM — official builds.
  • npm overrides in package.json.
  • Deno Desktop — build native desktop apps from web tech.
  • CSS module imports.
  • import defer — deferred imports.
  • 3.66× faster cold npm installs.
  • Node.js 26 compatibility.
  • Deny-by-default permissions — the runtime refuses filesystem, network, and environment access unless explicitly granted.
  • TypeScript runs directly — no build step.

Deno's strengths: security model, web-standard APIs, TypeScript-first. Its weakness: smaller ecosystem than Node.

docs.title: Concept 4: Bun — The All-in-One Toolchain
docs.text:
Bun (2022) is an all-in-one runtime, package manager, bundler, and test runner. As of 2026:

  • Bun 1.4 — the first release written in Rust instead of Zig.
  • 50% faster startup on Linux.
  • 35% less memory for HTTP servers.
  • 5× lower idle CPU usage.
  • Node.js 26 compatibility — 1,517 additional Node.js compatibility tests passing.
  • Bun.serve supports HTTP/2.
  • Bun.Image, Bun.WebView, Bun.markdown, Bun.cron(), Bun.Terminal — new APIs.
  • bun install is faster for packages using node-gyp.
  • bun audit fix, bun dedupe, bun prune — dependency management.
  • Uses JavaScriptCore — not V8.

Bun's strengths: developer iteration speed, single toolchain, fast installs. Its weakness: smaller ecosystem, newer than Node.

docs.title: Concept 5: Edge Runtimes
docs.text:
Edge runtimes run code close to users on globally distributed infrastructure. They are optimized for cold start speed and low latency.

Edge Runtime Engine Notes Cloudflare Workers V8 (workerd) Node.js compatibility enabled by default since August 2026 Deno Deploy V8 Generally available since February 2026; supports Deno.cron() Vercel Edge V8 Deprecated in Next.js; use Node.js runtime instead

Edge runtimes do not support all Node.js APIs. They are a subset designed for web-standard compatibility.

docs.title: Concept 6: The WinterCG / WinterTC Standardization
docs.text:
WinterCG (Web-interoperable Runtimes Community Group) was a W3C community group working to define a common API surface for server-side JavaScript runtimes. In 2025, it transitioned to WinterTC — an Ecma International Technical Committee — to formalize the standardization process.

The goal: ensure that code written for one runtime (Deno, Cloudflare Workers) can run on another with minimal changes.

docs.title: Concept 7: Lightweight Runtimes
docs.text:
LLRT (Low Latency Runtime) — AWS's experimental runtime built in Rust using QuickJS. Designed for fast cold starts in serverless. No JIT, so it can be slower than Node for CPU-heavy work, but ~10× faster cold starts.

WinterJS — a JavaScript Service Workers server written in Rust using SpiderMonkey. Compliant with the WinterCG specification.

QuickJS — a small, embeddable engine with no JIT, used in LLRT and other constrained environments.

docs.title: Concept 8: The Event Loop Across Runtimes
docs.text:
The event loop is host-defined:

Runtime Event Loop Model Browser WHATWG: macrotasks + microtasks + rendering Node.js libuv: timers, I/O, check, close callbacks Deno Tokio: async Rust runtime Bun JavaScriptCore + Bun's own event loop

The microtask queue (promises) is drained before the next macrotask in all runtimes. But timing and ordering of I/O callbacks differ.

docs.title: Concept 9: Module Systems Across Runtimes
docs.text:
Runtime CommonJS ESM TypeScript Browser ❌ ✅ Via bundler Node.js ✅ ✅ Via build step or loader Deno Via npm compat ✅ ✅ directly Bun ✅ ✅ ✅ directly

ESM is the future, but CommonJS persists in Node's ecosystem.

docs.title: Concept 10: Package Management Across Runtimes
docs.text:
Runtime Package Manager Registry Node.js npm, yarn, pnpm npm Deno Built-in, npm specifiers npm, JSR Bun Built-in (bun install) npm Edge Via bundler npm

JSR (JavaScript Registry) is a modern, TypeScript-first registry from the Deno team.

docs.title: Concept 11: Permissions Models
docs.text:
Runtime Default Permission Model Browser Sandboxed by origin Same-origin policy Node.js Full access Opt-in --permission flag Deno Deny by default Explicit --allow-read, --allow-net, etc. Bun Full access Opt-in permissions Edge Restricted APIs No filesystem access

Deno's deny-by-default model is the strictest.

docs.title: Concept 12: Deployment Targets
docs.text: Target Recommended Runtime Chrome extension V8 (browser) Firefox extension SpiderMonkey (browser) Safari extension JavaScriptCore (browser) Node.js server Node.js Deno server Deno Bun server Bun Cloudflare Workers workerd (V8) Deno Deploy Deno Vercel Functions Node.js (recommended) AWS Lambda Node.js or LLRT React Native Hermes Embedded QuickJS

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Runtime Initialization (Node.js)
docs.text:
1.  `node script.js` invoked.
    │
    ▼
2.  V8 engine initialized.
    │
    ▼
3.  Node.js bootstraps its host APIs (fs, net, process).
    │
    ▼
4.  libuv event loop starts.
    │
    ▼
5.  script.js is parsed, compiled, and executed.
    │
    ▼
6.  Top-level code runs to completion.
    │
    ▼
7.  Event loop waits for I/O, timers, and callbacks.
    │
    ▼
8.  Process exits when no more work is pending.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Runtime Initialization (Deno)
docs.text:
1.  `deno run --allow-net server.ts` invoked.
    │
    ▼
2.  V8 engine initialized.
    │
    ▼
3.  Deno's permission system checks granted permissions.
    │
    ▼
4.  TypeScript is transpiled (no separate build step).
    │
    ▼
5.  Tokio async runtime starts.
    │
    ▼
6.  Code executes with access only to granted APIs.
    │
    ▼
7.  Event loop processes async work.
    │
    ▼
8.  Process exits when work completes.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Edge Runtime Execution
docs.text:
1.  Request arrives at edge location.
    │
    ▼
2.  V8 isolate is spun up (cold start or warm).
    │
    ▼
3.  Worker script executes.
    │
    ▼
4.  Fetch handler processes request.
    │
    ▼
5.  Response returned to user.
    │
    ▼
6.  Isolate is kept warm or evicted.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Event Loop (Browser vs Node)
docs.text:
Browser:                          Node.js:
┌─────────────┐                   ┌─────────────┐
│ Macrotask   │                   │ Timers      │
│ (script,    │                   │             │
│  setTimeout,│                   │ I/O         │
│  UI events) │                   │             │
└──────┬──────┘                   └──────┬──────┘
       │                                │
       ▼                                ▼
┌─────────────┐                   ┌─────────────┐
│ Microtask   │                   │ Check       │
│ (promises,  │                   │ (setImmediate)│
│  queueMicro)│                   │             │
└──────┬──────┘                   └──────┬──────┘
       │                                │
       ▼                                ▼
┌─────────────┐                   ┌─────────────┐
│ Rendering   │                   │ Close       │
│ (if needed) │                   │ callbacks   │
└─────────────┘                   └─────────────┘

Both drain microtasks before the next macrotask, but the macrotask categories differ.

docs.title: Example 1: Same Server, Four Runtimes
docs.text:
Node.js:

import { createServer } from "node:http";

createServer((req, res) => {
    res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    res.end(JSON.stringify({ runtime: "node", version: process.version }));
}).listen(3000);

Deno:

Deno.serve({ port: 3000 }, () =>
    Response.json({ runtime: "deno", version: Deno.version.deno })
);

Bun:

Bun.serve({
    port: 3000,
    fetch: () => Response.json({ runtime: "bun", version: Bun.version }),
});

Cloudflare Workers:

export default {
    fetch: () => Response.json({ runtime: "workers", version: "2026" }),
};

All four run the same language — but with different APIs and deployment models.

docs.title: Example 2: Permission Model in Deno
docs.text:
# ❌ Fails — no read permission
deno run server.ts

# ✅ Succeeds — read and net permissions granted
deno run --allow-read --allow-net server.ts

# ✅ Succeeds — specific domains only
deno run --allow-net=api.example.com server.ts

Breakdown:

  • Deno denies by default.
  • Permissions are granted per-resource.
  • This prevents compromised dependencies from exfiltrating data.

docs.title: Example 3: Edge Function with Caching
docs.text:
// Cloudflare Worker with KV caching
export default {
    async fetch(request, env, ctx) {
        const cacheKey = new URL(request.url).pathname;

        // Check KV cache
        const cached = await env.MY_KV.get(cacheKey);
        if (cached) {
            return new Response(cached, {
                headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "X-Cache": "HIT" },
            });
        }

        // Fetch from origin
        const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com${cacheKey}`);
        const data = await res.json();

        // Store in KV
        ctx.waitUntil(env.MY_KV.put(cacheKey, JSON.stringify(data), {
            expirationTtl: 3600,
        }));

        return Response.json(data, { headers: { "X-Cache": "MISS" } });
    },
};

Breakdown:

  • env.MY_KV — Cloudflare KV namespace.
  • ctx.waitUntil — extends the worker's lifetime for async work.
  • Edge caching reduces latency and origin load.

docs.title: Example 4: LLRT for Serverless
docs.text:
// lambda.mjs — LLRT handler
export const handler = async (event) => {
    const { name = "World" } = event;

    return {
        statusCode: 200,
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            message: `Hello, ${name}!`,
            runtime: "LLRT",
        }),
    };
};

Breakdown:

  • LLRT uses QuickJS — no JIT.
  • Cold starts are ~10× faster than Node.
  • Best for I/O-bound, low-compute serverless functions.

docs.title: Example 5: WinterJS Service Worker
docs.text:
// winterjs-worker.js
addEventListener("fetch", (event) => {
    event.respondWith(
        new Response("Hello from WinterJS", {
            headers: { "Content-Type": "text/plain" },
        })
    );
});

Breakdown:

  • WinterJS runs Service Workers scripts on the server.
  • Powered by SpiderMonkey (Firefox's engine).
  • Compliant with the WinterCG specification.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Runtime Best For Browser Web apps, extensions, PWAs Node.js Servers, CLIs, tooling, native modules Deno Security-sensitive apps, TypeScript-first projects Bun Fast local dev, all-in-one toolchain, performance Cloudflare Workers Global edge APIs, low-latency functions Deno Deploy Edge functions, full-stack apps, cron jobs Vercel Edge Deprecated — use Node.js runtime LLRT Serverless, cold-start-sensitive functions WinterJS Service Workers on the server Hermes React Native mobile apps QuickJS Embedded, IoT, constrained environments

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Choose the runtime based on constraints, not hype. Why: each runtime has trade-offs.
  2. Use feature detection, not runtime detection. Why: code should be portable where possible.
  3. Prefer web-standard APIs (fetch, URL, crypto). Why: portability across runtimes.
  4. Isolate runtime-specific code behind adapters. Why: makes migration possible.
  5. Understand the security model before deploying. Why: Deno denies by default; Node grants freely.
  6. Keep dependencies minimal. Why: every dependency is a potential supply-chain risk.
  7. Use lockfiles. Why: reproducible installs across machines and runtimes.
  8. Test on the runtime you deploy to. Why: V8 and JavaScriptCore differ in edge cases.
  9. Monitor cold starts. Why: edge and serverless runtimes are sensitive to startup latency.
  10. Use the built-in tools where possible. Why: Bun and Deno ship test runners, bundlers, and formatters.
  11. Don't assume Node.js APIs exist everywhere. Why: edge runtimes are a subset.
  12. Use node: prefix for Node built-ins. Why: explicit, future-proof, works in ESM.
  13. Update runtimes regularly. Why: security patches and performance improvements ship frequently.
  14. Profile with runtime-specific tools. Why: Chrome DevTools for V8, Web Inspector for JSC.
  15. Document your runtime choice. Why: teams need to know why they chose Node vs Deno vs Bun.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Node.js APIs Work on the Edge
docs.text:
// ❌ Fails on Cloudflare Workers
import fs from "node:fs";
const data = fs.readFileSync("./data.json");

Why it's wrong: Edge runtimes have no filesystem access.

✅ Correct: Use KV storage or fetch data from an origin.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using process.env in Edge Runtimes
docs.text:
// ❌ Fails on Cloudflare Workers
const key = process.env.API_KEY;

Why it's wrong: process is not available in edge runtimes.

✅ Correct: Use env bindings:

export default {
    async fetch(request, env) {
        const key = env.API_KEY;
    },
};

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Deno's Permission Model
docs.text:
# ❌ Fails
deno run server.ts

# ✅ Correct
deno run --allow-net server.ts

Why it's wrong: Deno denies by default — this is a feature, not a bug.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Bun Is Node
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Bun uses JavaScriptCore, not V8. Some Node APIs are missing or behave differently.

✅ Correct: Test your code on Bun before deploying.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using require in ESM-Only Runtimes
docs.text:
// ❌ Fails in browsers and Deno
const fs = require("fs");

Why it's wrong: ESM uses import, not require.

✅ Correct:

import fs from "node:fs";

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Runtime-Specific Event Loop Behavior
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: setTimeout(0) and setImmediate ordering differs between Node and browsers.

✅ Correct: Understand the event loop of your target runtime.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming All Runtimes Support TypeScript Natively
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Node.js requires a build step or loader; browsers don't support TypeScript at all.

✅ Correct: Use Deno or Bun for native TypeScript, or transpile for Node and browsers.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Overlooking Cold Start Costs
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Serverless and edge functions pay a cold start penalty. Node.js cold starts are slower than LLRT or Cloudflare Workers.

✅ Correct: Choose a runtime optimized for your cold-start requirements.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using eval in Edge Runtimes
docs.text:
// ❌ Blocked in Edge Runtime
eval("console.log('hi')");

Why it's wrong: Edge runtimes disable eval and new Function for security.

✅ Correct: Avoid dynamic code execution entirely.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting That Edge Runtimes Are Subsets
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: The Edge Runtime is a subset of Node.js APIs, not a superset.

✅ Correct: Check compatibility before deploying.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Cold start — LLRT (~10× faster than Node), Cloudflare Workers (< 5ms), Node.js (~100ms+).
  • Throughput — Bun and Deno often outperform Node.js in synthetic benchmarks, but real workloads vary.
  • Memory — Bun 1.4 reduced idle memory by up to 35%.
  • Startup time — Bun 1.4 is 50% faster on Linux.
  • Concurrency — Node's libuv vs Deno's Tokio vs Bun's JavaScriptCore event loop.
  • JIT warmup — V8 and JavaScriptCore have different warmup profiles.
  • GC pauses — Orinoco (V8) vs JSC's GC vs QuickJS (no JIT, no GC tuning).
  • Network I/O — Bun's Bun.serve is highly optimized for HTTP.
  • Package install — Bun's install is up to 29% faster than npm on Node 26.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Benchmark on your workload, not synthetic benchmarks.
  2. Use Bun for fast local development iteration.
  3. Use Node.js for ecosystem maturity and native modules.
  4. Use Deno for security-sensitive applications.
  5. Use LLRT for cold-start-sensitive serverless functions.
  6. Use edge runtimes for globally distributed, low-latency APIs.
  7. Profile with runtime-specific tools.
  8. Keep dependencies minimal to reduce startup cost.
  9. Use streaming APIs for large payloads.
  10. Monitor real-user metrics (RUM), not just lab tests.

docs.title: Deno's Permission Model
docs.text:
Deno denies by default. A script cannot read files, access the network, or read environment variables without explicit permission.

deno run --allow-read=./data --allow-net=api.example.com server.ts

This is the strictest security model among major runtimes.

docs.title: Node.js Permission Model
docs.text:
Node.js has an opt-in permission model:

node --permission --allow-fs-read=./data server.js

Still maturing, but available since Node 20.

docs.title: Supply-Chain Risk Across Runtimes
docs.text:
All runtimes that use npm packages are vulnerable to supply-chain attacks. The 2025–2026 npm supply-chain attacks affected multiple ecosystems.

Defenses: lockfiles, npm audit, provenance, allowlists, minimal dependencies.

docs.title: Edge Runtime Security
docs.text: Edge runtimes disable eval and new Function. They also have no filesystem access. This makes them inherently safer for running untrusted code.

docs.title: Sandboxing
docs.text:
For running untrusted JavaScript, consider:

  • Deno's permission model.
  • isolated-vm (Node.js).
  • quickjs-emscripten (WASM-based QuickJS).
  • Edge runtime isolates.

docs.title: Runtime-Specific CVEs
docs.text:
• V8: CVE-2026-85046 (type confusion in Array.prototype.sort, CVSS 8.8).
  • JavaScriptCore: ZDI-26-610 (use-after-free in B3 ReduceStrength).
  • JavaScriptCore: CVE-2026-20664 (WebAssembly memory bug).

Keep runtimes updated.

docs.title: Secrets Management
docs.text:
• Node.js: process.env or a secrets manager.
  • Deno: Deno.env.get() with --allow-env.
  • Cloudflare Workers: env bindings.
  • Bun: Bun.env.

Never hard-code secrets in code.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Node.js: node --inspect-brk → Chrome DevTools.
  • Deno: deno run --inspect-brk → Chrome DevTools.
  • Bun: bun --inspect → Chrome DevTools.
  • Cloudflare Workers: wrangler dev → local debugging.
  • Deno Deploy: deno deploy --dry-run → local preview.
  • LLRT: Use standard Node.js debugging tools where compatible.
  • Runtime versions: node --version, deno --version, bun --version.
  • Engine versions: process.versions.v8 (Node), Deno.version.v8 (Deno).
  • --trace-opt / --trace-deopt: V8 optimization logging.
  • --prof: V8 CPU profiling.
  • bun --smol: Small memory mode.
  • deno lint: Built-in linter.
  • deno fmt: Built-in formatter.
  • bun test: Built-in test runner.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Browser — any web page or web app.
  • Node.js — servers, CLIs, native modules, long-term maintenance.
  • Deno — security-sensitive applications, TypeScript-first projects, modern web-standard APIs.
  • Bun — fast local development, all-in-one toolchain, performance-critical HTTP servers.
  • Cloudflare Workers — globally distributed APIs, low-latency edge functions.
  • Deno Deploy — edge functions, full-stack apps, cron jobs.
  • LLRT — cold-start-sensitive serverless functions.
  • Hermes — React Native mobile apps.
  • QuickJS — embedded, IoT, constrained environments.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Node.js — when you need strict security by default (use Deno).
  • Deno — when you need deep ecosystem compatibility (use Node).
  • Bun — when you need maximum ecosystem maturity (use Node).
  • Edge runtimes — when you need full Node.js API access.
  • LLRT — when you need JIT performance (use Node or Bun).
  • Hermes — when you need peak throughput (use V8).
  • QuickJS — when you need JIT performance.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• JavaScript Engines — V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore, Hermes
  • ECMAScript — the language specification
  • Event Loop — concurrency model
  • WinterCG / WinterTC — runtime standardization
  • Node.js — server-side runtime
  • Deno — secure runtime
  • Bun — all-in-one toolchain
  • Cloudflare Workers — edge runtime
  • Deno Deploy — edge platform
  • LLRT — low-latency runtime
  • WinterJS — SpiderMonkey-based runtime
  • QuickJS — embedded engine
  • JSR — JavaScript Registry
  • npm — Node package manager

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Node.js was created by Ryan Dahl in 2009 and is now maintained by the OpenJS Foundation.
  • Deno was also created by Ryan Dahl — to fix what he considered Node's design mistakes.
  • Bun was rewritten in Rust as of version 1.4 (2026) — it was previously written in Zig.
  • Bun 1.4 reduced idle CPU usage by 5× and memory by 35%.
  • Deno 2.7 stabilized the Temporal API — no --unstable-temporal flag needed.
  • Deno Deploy became generally available in February 2026.
  • Cloudflare Workers enabled Node.js compatibility by default in August 2026.
  • Vercel deprecated the Edge Runtime in Next.js — Node.js is now the recommended runtime.
  • LLRT uses QuickJS, which is less than 1 MB in size.
  • WinterJS uses SpiderMonkey — the same engine as Firefox.
  • WinterCG became WinterTC — an Ecma International Technical Committee.
  • Node.js 26 ships with Temporal API enabled by default.
  • Bun uses JavaScriptCore — the same engine as Safari.
  • Deno uses V8 — the same engine as Chrome.
  • Hermes is the default React Native engine as of RN 0.84.
  • The Edge Runtime is a subset of Node.js APIs, not a superset.
  • Deno denies all permissions by default — you must opt in.
  • Node.js grants all permissions by default — you must opt out.
  • Bun ships a package manager, bundler, and test runner in one binary.
  • LLRT achieves ~10× faster cold starts than Node.js.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A runtime environment combines an engine, host APIs, and an event loop.
  • Browsers provide the DOM, Fetch, Storage, and the rendering pipeline.
  • Node.js (2009) is the incumbent: deep ecosystem, native modules, everywhere-supported.
  • Deno (2018) is secure by default: deny-by-default permissions, TypeScript-first, web-standard APIs.
  • Bun (2022) is an all-in-one toolchain: runtime, package manager, bundler, and test runner in one.
  • Edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy) run code close to users with minimal cold starts.
  • WinterCG / WinterTC standardizes the API surface across server-side runtimes.
  • LLRT and WinterJS are lightweight runtimes for serverless and edge.
  • Hermes is optimized for React Native mobile apps.
  • QuickJS is a small, embeddable engine for constrained environments.
  • Security models differ: browsers are sandboxed by origin; Node grants all by default; Deno denies all by default.
  • Performance differs: Bun is fast; LLRT has fast cold starts; Node has mature ecosystem.
  • Choose based on constraints: ecosystem, security, performance, deployment target.
  • Write portable code using web-standard APIs where possible.
  • Test on the runtime you deploy to — engines and host APIs differ.
  • The runtime is the platform — it determines what your JavaScript can actually do.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Writing your first script is the act of creating, running, and observing a minimal JavaScript program. It is the moment the language stops being an abstraction and becomes something that executes on a machine — printing a message, responding to a click, reading a file, or serving a response.

// The smallest useful script:
console.log("Hello, world");

There is no single "correct" first script. The right one depends on where you are running it — a browser, Node.js, Deno, or Bun. But the core experience is identical: write text → execute → see output.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A first script exists to establish the feedback loop:

  • Write — type code into a file or console.
  • Run — hand the code to a runtime.
  • Observe — see what happened.
  • Iterate — change, run again.

This loop is the foundation of all programming. Everything else — syntax, libraries, frameworks, deployment — is built on top of it. A developer who has a working feedback loop can learn anything; a developer without one is stuck.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Learning JavaScript
├── Introduction
│   ├── What is JavaScript?          ✅ done
│   ├── JavaScript Ecosystem          ✅ done
│   ├── ECMAScript                   ✅ done
│   ├── JavaScript Engines           ✅ done
│   ├── Runtime Environments         ✅ done
│   └── Writing Your First Script    ← you are here
│
└── Language Fundamentals
    ├── Variables
    ├── Data Types
    └── ...

This is the last concept in the Introduction section. After this, you move into the language itself.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Reading about JavaScript is not the same as writing it. The gap between understanding syntax and making something happen is bridged only by actually running code. A first script exists to cross that gap as quickly as possible — ideally in under 60 seconds.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Barrier Consequence No runtime installed Can't run anything Complex setup Beginners abandon before first success Unclear where to write code Confusion about files, editors, terminals No visible output "I ran it and nothing happened" Wrong runtime Code works in one environment, fails in another

docs.title: Why It Was Introduced (as a Concept)
docs.text:
The "first script" is not a language feature — it is a pedagogical necessity. Every language community has its version of "Hello, world" because it solves a universal problem: proving the toolchain works before teaching the language. In JavaScript, the first script is uniquely accessible because:

  • Browsers are already installed — zero setup required.
  • The console is a REPL — instant feedback.
  • Node, Deno, and Bun are one install away — for server-side work.
  • The same language runs everywhere — skills transfer across environments.

docs.title: Option A: Browser Console (Zero Setup)
docs.text:
Step 1: Open any browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari).

Step 2: Press F12 (or Cmd + Option + J on Mac) to open Developer Tools.

Step 3: Click the Console tab.

Step 4: Type:

console.log("Hello, world");

Step 5: Press Enter. You will see:

Hello, world

You just ran JavaScript. No installation, no downloads, no configuration.

docs.title: Option B: Browser with an HTML File
docs.text:
Create index.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>My First Script</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1 id="greeting">Loading…</h1>
    <button id="btn">Click me</button>

    <!-- defer: downloads in parallel, executes after HTML parsing, preserves order -->
    <script defer src="app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

Create app.js:

console.log("Script loaded");

document.getElementById("greeting").textContent = "Hello from JavaScript!";

document.getElementById("btn").addEventListener("click", () => {
    alert("Button clicked!");
});

Open index.html in a browser. You will see the greeting change and the button work.

Why defer? Without defer or async, the browser blocks HTML parsing while downloading and executing the script. defer downloads in parallel, executes after parsing completes, and preserves execution order — the safest choice for scripts that depend on the DOM or other scripts. async downloads in parallel but executes as soon as ready, with no order guarantee — use it for independent scripts like analytics.

docs.title: Option C: Node.js (Server-Side)
docs.text:
Step 1: Install Node.js from nodejs.org or via a version manager.

Step 2: Verify:

node --version
# v26.x.x (or v24.x.x LTS)

Step 3: Create hello.js:

console.log("Hello from Node.js");

const name = process.argv[2] ?? "world";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);

Step 4: Run:

node hello.js
# Hello from Node.js
# Hello, world!

node hello.js Ada
# Hello from Node.js
# Hello, Ada!

Step 5 (Node 26+): Run TypeScript directly — no build step required:

// hello.ts
const name: string = process.argv[2] ?? "world";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);

node hello.ts
# Node 26 strips TypeScript types natively

Node.js 26 made native TypeScript type-stripping stable — the experimental warning is gone, and running .ts files works by default. The ts-node, tsx, and nodemon toolchain collapses into the runtime itself.

docs.title: Option D: Deno (Secure by Default)
docs.text:
Step 1: Install Deno:

# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://deno.land/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://deno.land/install.ps1 | iex

Step 2: Verify:

deno --version
# deno 2.9.x

Step 3: Create hello.ts:

interface User {
    name: string;
    balance: number;
}

function getBalance(user: User): string {
    return `Balance: $${user.balance.toFixed(2)}`;
}

console.log(getBalance({ name: "Alice", balance: 42 }));

Step 4: Run:

deno run hello.ts
# Balance: $42.00

Deno natively supports TypeScript, JSX, and modern ECMAScript with zero configuration. It denies all permissions by default — a script cannot read files, access the network, or read environment variables unless explicitly granted.

docs.title: Option E: Bun (All-in-One Toolchain)
docs.text:
Step 1: Install Bun:

# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash

# Windows (PowerShell)
powershell -c "irm bun.sh/install.ps1 | iex"

Step 2: Verify:

bun --version
# 1.4.x

Step 3: Create hello.ts:

const name: string = Bun.argv[2] ?? "world";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);

Step 4: Run:

bun run hello.ts
# Hello, world!

Bun 1.4 (August 2026) is the first production release running fully on the Rust rewrite — it reduces idle CPU usage by 5×, reduces memory usage by up to 35%, and starts 50% faster on Linux. It passes +1,517 additional Node.js compatibility tests, making it a drop-in replacement for much of the ecosystem.

docs.title: The "Feedback Loop" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────┐
│   WRITE     │  ← type code
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│    RUN      │  ← hand to runtime
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   OBSERVE   │  ← see output
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   ITERATE   │  ← change and repeat
└─────────────┘

Every programming skill is built on this loop. The faster the loop, the faster you learn. The browser console has the fastest loop (seconds); a full build pipeline has the slowest (minutes).

docs.title: The "Where Does It Run?" Mental Model
docs.text:
Your code
    │
    ├── Browser    →  DOM, Fetch, Storage
    ├── Node.js    →  fs, process, net
    ├── Deno       →  Deno APIs, permissions
    └── Bun        →  Bun APIs, Node compat

The same JavaScript runs everywhere, but what it can do depends on the runtime. A first script should be written for the runtime you are actually using.

docs.title: The "Script vs. Module" Mental Model
docs.text:
<script>                    <script type="module">
   Classic script               ES module
   Global scope                 Module scope
   No import/export             import/export
   Sloppy mode by default       Strict mode by default
   `this` = window              `this` = undefined

Modern code should use modules (type="module" in browsers, "type": "module" in package.json for Node). ES modules are the standard.

docs.title: The "Toolchain Collapse" Mental Model
docs.text:
2020 toolchain:             2026 toolchain:
─────────────────           ────────────────
ts-node / tsx               node file.ts
nodemon                     node --watch
Jest / Mocha                node --test
Babel / SWC                 node (native)
npm install everything      node (built-in)

Node.js 26 has collapsed much of the external toolchain into the runtime itself. Deno and Bun go further — they ship linters, formatters, test runners, and bundlers built in.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Three Ways to Run JavaScript
docs.text: Method Setup Best For Browser console None Instant experiments HTML + <script> Text editor Web pages Node/Deno/Bun One install Server, CLI, tooling

docs.title: Concept 2: The Console Is a REPL
docs.text:
A REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) executes each line immediately. The browser console and node (without a file) are REPLs:

> 1 + 1
2
> const x = 10
undefined
> x * 2
20

REPLs are for experimentation, not for building programs.

docs.title: Concept 3: console.log Is Not ECMAScript
