docs.text: console is a host API — it is not part of the ECMAScript specification. It exists in browsers, Node.js, Deno, and Bun, but it is provided by the runtime, not the language.

docs.title: Concept 4: Script Placement Matters
docs.text:
<!-- ❌ Blocks parsing; DOM may not exist yet -->
<script src="app.js"></script>

<!-- ✅ Downloads in parallel; runs after parsing; order preserved -->
<script defer src="app.js"></script>

<!-- ✅ Downloads in parallel; runs ASAP; no order guarantee -->
<script async src="app.js"></script>

<!-- ✅ Modern: module semantics; deferred by default -->
<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>

When in doubt, use defer — it provides most of the performance benefit with none of the order risk.

docs.title: Concept 5: Classic Scripts vs. Modules
docs.text:
// Classic script (no type="module")
var x = 10;             // global
console.log(window.x);  // 10

// ES module (type="module")
const x = 10;           // module-scoped
console.log(window.x);  // undefined

Modules are strict mode by default, have module scope, and support import/export. They are the modern standard.

docs.title: Concept 6: Top-Level Await
docs.text:
In ES modules, you can use await at the top level:

// app.js — type="module"
const res = await fetch("/api/data");
const data = await res.json();
console.log(data);

This is not allowed in classic scripts. Top-level await is part of ECMAScript 2022.

docs.title: Concept 7: The First Script Should Be Observable
docs.text:
A script that produces no output teaches nothing. Always log, render, alert, or throw:

console.log("Script started");
console.log("Script finished");

docs.title: Concept 8: Errors Are Information
docs.text:
console.log(undefinedVariable);
// ReferenceError: undefinedVariable is not defined

Errors are not failures — they are the runtime telling you what went wrong. Read the error message, the stack trace, and the line number.

docs.title: Concept 9: Node.js 26 Runs TypeScript Natively
docs.text:
node file.ts

Type-stripping removes type annotations and runs the remaining JavaScript. It does not transpile enums, namespaces, or decorator emit — use --experimental-transform-types or a real compiler for those. It also does not rewrite module systems — a .ts file still obeys package.json "type".

docs.title: Concept 10: Deno Runs TypeScript Natively, Secure by Default
docs.text:
deno run hello.ts

Deno denies all permissions by default. A script that needs to read a file must be granted --allow-read; one that needs the network must be granted --allow-net.

docs.title: Concept 11: Bun Runs TypeScript Natively, Fast
docs.text:
bun run hello.ts

Bun 1.4 is 50% faster to start on Linux and uses 35% less memory than previous versions. It is a drop-in replacement for Node.js in many cases, passing 97%+ of Node's own test suite for node:http, node:fs, node:stream, and others.

docs.title: Concept 12: require(esm) Is Stable in Node.js
docs.text:
// CommonJS file
const esmModule = require("./esm-module.js"); // works in Node 26

Node.js now allows synchronously requiring ESM (without top-level await). This does not work if the target uses top-level await — fall back to import().

docs.title: Concept 13: The Browser Console Is a Sandbox
docs.text: Code in the browser console runs in the page's origin. It can access the DOM, but not the filesystem or the network beyond what the page is allowed.

docs.title: Concept 14: The Terminal Is Not the Console
docs.text: The browser console is a JavaScript REPL. The terminal is a shell. They are different tools. node starts a JavaScript REPL in the terminal; console.log writes to the terminal when running Node.

docs.title: Concept 15: A First Script Should Be Minimal
docs.text:
console.log("Hello, world");

This is enough. It proves:

  • The runtime is installed.
  • The file is found.
  • The syntax is valid.
  • Output is visible.

Do not start with frameworks, build tools, or package managers.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Browser Console Execution
docs.text:
1.  You type `console.log("Hello")` and press Enter.
    │
    ▼
2.  The browser's engine parses the expression.
    │
    ▼
3.  `console` is resolved from the host environment.
    │
    ▼
4.  `log` is called with the string argument.
    │
    ▼
5.  The console panel renders "Hello".

docs.title: Step-by-Step: HTML <script> Execution
docs.text:
1.  Browser requests index.html.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser encounters <script defer src="app.js">.
    │
    ▼
3.  Script downloads in parallel (parsing continues).
    │
    ▼
4.  HTML parsing completes.
    │
    ▼
5.  Script executes (DOM is ready).
    │
    ▼
6.  DOMContentLoaded fires.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Node.js Execution
docs.text:
1.  `node hello.js` invoked.
    │
    ▼
2.  V8 parses hello.js.
    │
    ▼
3.  Bytecode is generated.
    │
    ▼
4.  Top-level code executes.
    │
    ▼
5.  console.log writes to stdout.
    │
    ▼
6.  Process exits when no work remains.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Deno Execution
docs.text:
1.  `deno run hello.ts` invoked.
    │
    ▼
2.  TypeScript is stripped/transpiled (no build step).
    │
    ▼
3.  Permission system checks granted permissions.
    │
    ▼
4.  V8 executes the JavaScript.
    │
    ▼
5.  Output is written.
    │
    ▼
6.  Process exits.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Bun Execution
docs.text:
1.  `bun run hello.ts` invoked.
    │
    ▼
2.  Bun's runtime (Rust) initializes JavaScriptCore.
    │
    ▼
3.  TypeScript is stripped.
    │
    ▼
4.  JavaScriptCore executes the code.
    │
    ▼
5.  Output is written.
    │
    ▼
6.  Process exits (fast).

docs.title: What Happens When You Press Enter in the Console
docs.text:
Input: console.log("Hello")
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Parser    │ → AST
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  Ignition   │ → bytecode
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────┐
│  Execution  │
│  ├── resolve `console` (host API)
│  ├── resolve `log` (method)
│  ├── coerce argument to string
│  └── call host function
└─────────────┘
    │
    ▼
Output: "Hello"

docs.title: What Happens When Node.js Runs a File
What Happens in the Browser with defer
docs.text:
HTML parsing
    │
    ├── <script defer src="app.js">
    │       │
    │       ├── download starts (parallel)
    │       └── parsing continues
    │
    ▼
Parsing complete
    │
    ▼
Deferred scripts execute in order
    │
    ▼
DOMContentLoaded fires

docs.title: What Happens in the Browser with async
docs.text:
HTML parsing
    │
    ├── <script async src="a.js">
    │       │
    │       ├── download starts (parallel)
    │       └── parsing continues
    │
    ▼
a.js finishes downloading
    │
    ▼
a.js executes immediately (parsing may still be ongoing)

async scripts can execute before the DOM is fully parsed.

docs.title: First Script Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Choose a runtime (browser, Node, Deno, Bun).
    │
    ▼
2.  Install the runtime (if needed).
    │
    ▼
3.  Create a file (or open the console).
    │
    ▼
4.  Write console.log("Hello").
    │
    ▼
5.  Run the script.
    │
    ▼
6.  Observe output.
    │
    ▼
7.  Change the code.
    │
    ▼
8.  Run again.
    │
    ▼
9.  Repeat.

docs.title: Development Environment Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Install a code editor (VS Code recommended).
    │
    ▼
2.  Install extensions:
    │   - ESLint (catches errors)
    │   - Prettier (formats code)
    │   - Live Server (auto-reload)
    └── JavaScript snippets
    │
    ▼
3.  Create a project folder.
    │
    ▼
4.  Add index.html + app.js.
    │
    ▼
5.  Open with Live Server.
    │
    ▼
6.  Edit code → auto-reload → observe.

VS Code is the most popular editor for JavaScript — it is free, cross-platform, and has an enormous extension ecosystem.

docs.title: Example 1: Browser Console — 60 Seconds
docs.text:
console.log("Hello, world");

Output:

Hello, world

docs.title: Example 2: Browser Console — Interactive
docs.text:
const name = prompt("What is your name?");
alert(`Hello, ${name}!`);

Breakdown:

  • prompt and alert are host APIs (browser only).
  • This demonstrates variables, template literals, and browser functions.

docs.title: Example 3: HTML + External Script
docs.text:
index.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>My First Script</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1 id="greeting">Loading…</h1>
    <button id="btn">Click me</button>
    <script defer src="app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

app.js:

console.log("Script loaded");

document.getElementById("greeting").textContent = "Hello from JavaScript!";

document.getElementById("btn").addEventListener("click", () => {
    alert("Button clicked!");
});

Breakdown:

  • defer ensures the DOM is ready before the script runs.
  • textContent is safe — no HTML parsing.
  • addEventListener wires user input to behavior.

docs.title: Example 4: Node.js — Script with Arguments
docs.text:
// hello.js
const name = process.argv[2] ?? "world";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);

node hello.js
# Hello, world!

node hello.js Ada
# Hello, Ada!

Breakdown:

  • process.argv holds CLI arguments.
  • ?? (nullish coalescing) provides a default only when the value is null or undefined.

docs.title: Example 5: Node.js 26 — TypeScript Directly
docs.text:
// hello.ts
function greet(name: string): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

const name: string = process.argv[2] ?? "world";
console.log(greet(name));

node hello.ts
# Hello, world!

Breakdown:

  • Node 26 strips TypeScript types natively.
  • No ts-node, tsx, or build step required.

docs.title: Example 6: Deno — Secure by Default
docs.text:
// server.ts
Deno.serve({ port: 3000 }, (req) => {
    return new Response("Hello from Deno!", {
        headers: { "Content-Type": "text/plain" },
    });
});

deno run --allow-net server.ts
# Listening on http://localhost:3000/

Breakdown:

  • Without --allow-net, the script fails — Deno denies network access by default.
  • Deno.serve is a modern, web-standard HTTP server.

docs.title: Example 7: Bun — Fast Server
docs.text:
// server.ts
Bun.serve({
    port: 3000,
    fetch: () => new Response("Hello from Bun!"),
});

bun run server.ts
# Listening on http://localhost:3000/

Breakdown:

  • Bun.serve is a high-performance HTTP server.
  • Bun 1.4 starts 50% faster on Linux.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Goal First Script Verify runtime works console.log("Hello") Learn variables const x = 10; console.log(x); Learn functions function add(a, b) { return a + b; } Learn DOM document.body.style.background = "red"; Learn async fetch("/api").then(r => r.json()).then(console.log); Learn CLI args console.log(process.argv) Learn file I/O fs.readFile("file.txt", "utf8", console.log) Learn HTTP server http.createServer(...).listen(3000) Learn TypeScript node hello.ts (Node 26)

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Start with the console. Why: fastest feedback, zero setup.
  2. Use defer for scripts that need the DOM. Why: downloads in parallel, runs after parsing, preserves order.
  3. Use async only for independent scripts. Why: execution order is not guaranteed.
  4. Use type="module" for modern code. Why: strict mode, module scope, import/export.
  5. Use const by default, let when reassigning. Why: prevents accidental mutation.
  6. Never use var. Why: function-scoped, hoisting bugs.
  7. Use template literals. Why: cleaner than string concatenation.
  8. Use optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??). Why: safe defaults without clobbering 0, "", or false.
  9. Prefer node --watch over nodemon. Why: built into Node.js.
  10. Prefer node --test over Jest for basic suites. Why: built into Node.js.
  11. Use node file.ts instead of ts-node. Why: native type-stripping in Node 26.
  12. Use Deno's permission model deliberately. Why: deny-by-default prevents supply-chain attacks.
  13. Keep the first script minimal. Why: proves the toolchain works before adding complexity.
  14. Always produce observable output. Why: a silent script teaches nothing.
  15. Read errors carefully. Why: the runtime tells you exactly what went wrong.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting defer or async
docs.text:
<script src="app.js"></script>

Why it's wrong: Blocks HTML parsing; the DOM may not exist when the script runs.

✅ Correct:

<script defer src="app.js"></script>

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using async When Order Matters
docs.text:
<script async src="a.js"></script>
<script async src="b.js"></script>
<!-- b.js may run before a.js -->

Why it's wrong: async scripts execute as soon as they download — order is not preserved.

✅ Correct: Use defer when order matters.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Querying the DOM Before It Exists
docs.text:
// ❌ In <head> without defer
document.getElementById("app").textContent = "Hello";
// TypeError: Cannot set properties of null

✅ Correct: Use defer, place the script at the end of <body>, or wait for DOMContentLoaded.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming console Is ECMAScript
docs.text:
// ❌ Not guaranteed in every ECMAScript host
console.log("Hello");

Why it's wrong: console is a host API, not part of the language spec.

✅ Correct: In browsers, Node, Deno, and Bun, console exists — but it is not a language feature.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using var in New Code
docs.text:
var x = 10;

Why it's wrong: Function-scoped, hoisted, allows redeclaration.

✅ Correct:

const x = 10;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using || for Defaults When 0 Is Valid
docs.text:
// ❌ If config.timeout is 0, it becomes 5000
const timeout = config.timeout || 5000;

Why it's wrong: || treats 0, "", and false as falsy.

✅ Correct:

const timeout = config.timeout ?? 5000;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Running TypeScript with ts-node
docs.text:
npx ts-node hello.ts

Why it's wrong: Node 26 runs .ts files natively — ts-node is unnecessary.

✅ Correct:

node hello.ts

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting Deno Permissions
docs.text:
deno run server.ts
# error: Requires net access

Why it's wrong: Deno denies by default.

✅ Correct:

deno run --allow-net server.ts

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Node.js 18/20 Are Still Supported
docs.text:
node --version
# v18.0.0 — end of life

Why it's wrong: Node 18 and 20 are end of life.

✅ Correct: Use Node 24 LTS (production) or Node 26 (current).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mixing require and import
docs.text:
// ❌ Mixing in the same module
const fs = require("fs");
import path from "path";

Why it's wrong: Do not mix CommonJS and ESM in the same module.

✅ Correct: Use ESM exclusively in new code.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• defer vs async vs blocking — the choice affects page load time.
  • Browser console — instant, no build step.
  • Node.js startup — ~100ms+ depending on module count.
  • Deno startup — V8 + Tokio; TypeScript transpilation adds overhead.
  • Bun startup — 50% faster on Linux after 1.4.
  • Type-stripping — Node 26's native type-stripping is faster than ts-node.
  • Module count — more imports means slower startup.
  • Console output — console.log is fast; console.dir with depth is slower.
  • Live Server auto-reload — reloads the page on save; may be slower than HMR.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use defer for non-critical scripts.
  2. Use type="module" — deferred by default.
  3. Keep the first script minimal to isolate problems.
  4. Use Bun for fast local iteration.
  5. Use node --watch instead of polling with nodemon.
  6. Avoid importing large libraries in the first script.
  7. Profile with runtime-specific tools.

docs.title: Browser Console Is a Sandbox
docs.text: The browser console runs in the page's origin. It can access the DOM but not the filesystem.

docs.title: Node.js Is Not Sandboxed
docs.text:
Node.js scripts run with full system access by default. A compromised dependency can read files, open network connections, and exfiltrate data.

Defense: Use --permission (opt-in), or use Deno for untrusted code.

docs.title: Deno Denies by Default
docs.text:
deno run --allow-net=api.example.com server.ts

Deno's permission model prevents supply-chain attacks by default.

docs.title: Bun Grants Full Access
docs.text: Bun grants full access like Node.js. Use permissions explicitly if available.

docs.title: eval and new Function in First Scripts
docs.text: Avoid them entirely — they are security risks and disable optimizations.

docs.title: Secrets in Scripts
docs.text: Never hard-code API keys in client-side scripts. They are visible to anyone who opens DevTools.

docs.title: Supply-Chain Risk
docs.text: Every package you install is code you run. Keep dependencies minimal in your first script — ideally zero.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Browser console: F12 → Console tab.
  • console.log: The universal debugging tool.
  • console.table: Display arrays/objects as tables.
  • console.error: Red error output.
  • debugger;: Pause execution in DevTools.
  • Node.js: node --inspect-brk hello.js → Chrome DevTools.
  • Deno: deno run --inspect-brk hello.ts → Chrome DevTools.
  • Bun: bun --inspect hello.ts → Chrome DevTools.
  • Read stack traces: They tell you exactly where the error occurred.
  • Check the Elements panel: Verify the DOM state.
  • Check the Network panel: Verify script loading.
  • Check the Sources panel: Verify the script is what you think it is.
  • VS Code: Use the built-in debugger (Run and Debug panel).
  • Live Server: Auto-reloads the browser on save.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• Browser console — for instant experiments and learning.
  • HTML + <script defer> — for web pages.
  • HTML + <script type="module"> — for modern web apps.
  • Node.js — for servers, CLIs, and tooling.
  • Deno — for security-sensitive projects and TypeScript-first work.
  • Bun — for fast development and all-in-one tooling.
  • node file.ts — for running TypeScript without a build step (Node 26+).

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Browser console — for anything you want to keep or share.
  • Inline <script> without defer — for scripts that need the DOM.
  • async for dependent scripts — order is not guaranteed.
  • var — use const or let.
  • ts-node / tsx — use node file.ts in Node 26+.
  • nodemon — use node --watch.
  • Jest for simple tests — use node --test.
  • Framework for a first script — start with plain JavaScript.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Runtime Environments — where scripts run
  • ECMAScript — the language specification
  • JavaScript Engines — V8, JavaScriptCore, SpiderMonkey
  • Browser APIs — DOM, Fetch, Storage
  • Node.js APIs — fs, process, net
  • Deno APIs — Deno.serve, Deno.readTextFile
  • Bun APIs — Bun.serve, Bun.file
  • ES Modules — import/export
  • defer and async — script loading strategies
  • TypeScript — typed superset of JavaScript
  • REPL — Read-Eval-Print Loop
  • Live Server — auto-reloading development server
  • VS Code — the most popular JavaScript editor

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• You can run JavaScript in the browser console without installing anything — just press F12.
  • The defer attribute has been supported in browsers since July 2015 — it is Baseline Widely Available.
  • Node.js 26 made native TypeScript type-stripping stable — ts-node is no longer required for basic scripts.
  • require(esm) is stable in Node.js — you can synchronously require ESM modules (without top-level await).
  • Deno denies all permissions by default — this is a feature, not a bug.
  • Bun 1.4 was rewritten in Rust — it is 50% faster to start on Linux and uses 35% less memory.
  • Bun 1.4 passes +1,517 additional Node.js compatibility tests.
  • The even/odd release model ends with Node 26 — from Node 27 on, every major becomes LTS.
  • VS Code is the most popular JavaScript editor — free, cross-platform, with a huge extension ecosystem.
  • Live Server auto-reloads the browser when you save a file — instant feedback.
  • The browser console is a REPL — Read-Eval-Print Loop.
  • console is not ECMAScript — it is a host API provided by the runtime.
  • Top-level await works only in ES modules — not in classic scripts.
  • defer preserves order; async does not.
  • Deno ships with a linter, formatter, test runner, and bundler built in.
  • Bun ships with a package manager, bundler, and test runner built in.
  • node --watch replaces nodemon — no external dependency.
  • node --test replaces Jest for basic suites — built into Node.js.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A first script establishes the feedback loop: write → run → observe → iterate.
  • The browser console is the fastest way to start — zero setup, instant feedback.
  • HTML + <script defer> is the standard for web pages — downloads in parallel, executes after parsing, preserves order.
  • async is for independent scripts — no order guarantee.
  • type="module" enables strict mode, module scope, and import/export.
  • Node.js 26 runs TypeScript natively — node file.ts works without ts-node.
  • Deno runs TypeScript natively and denies all permissions by default.
  • Bun 1.4 runs TypeScript natively and is 50% faster to start on Linux.
  • Use const by default, let when reassigning, and never var.
  • Use template literals, optional chaining (?.), and nullish coalescing (??).
  • Errors are information — read them carefully.
  • Keep the first script minimal — console.log("Hello, world") is enough.
  • Use modern tooling: node --watch, node --test, node file.ts.
  • Choose the runtime that matches your target: browser, Node, Deno, or Bun.
  • The first script is not about the code — it is about proving the toolchain works.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A variable is a named binding that associates an identifier with a value in memory. JavaScript provides several ways to declare variables, each with different scoping, hoisting, and reassignment rules:

var legacy = "function-scoped";
let mutable = "block-scoped, reassignable";
const constant = "block-scoped, not reassignable";
using resource = acquireResource(); // ES2026: auto-disposed at block exit
await using asyncResource = acquireAsync(); // ES2026: async disposal

Variables are the fundamental storage mechanism of any program. Every value your code produces — a user's name, a computed total, a DOM element — is held in a variable somewhere.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Variables exist to solve the most basic problem in programming: how do you give a name to a value so you can refer to it later? Without variables, every computation would have to be used immediately and then discarded. Variables allow programs to:

  • Store intermediate results.
  • Reuse values across statements.
  • Name concepts for readability.
  • Scope data to prevent conflicts.
  • Manage resources with automatic cleanup.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Language Fundamentals
├── Variables             ← you are here
├── Data Types
├── Operators
├── Expressions
├── Statements
├── Type Conversion
├── Equality
└── Strict Mode

Variables are the first concept in Language Fundamentals because everything else depends on them. Types describe what variables hold; operators act on them; statements control the flow around them.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A programming language that cannot remember values is useless. Every computation would be isolated — you could add two numbers, but you could not store the result, compare it later, or pass it to another function. Variables solve the memory problem: they give programs a way to name and retrieve values.

But variables also create a second problem: if every variable is global, every program becomes a collision waiting to happen. Two libraries both declaring count would silently overwrite each other.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES5 Only var — function-scoped, hoisted, confusing var pitfalls Redeclaration allowed; accidental globals; capture bugs in loops No block scope if and for blocks leaked variables to the enclosing function No constants Nothing prevented reassignment No resource management Manual cleanup in finally blocks

docs.title: Why Modern Declarations Exist
docs.text:
ES2015 (ES6) introduced let and const to fix var's problems:

  • let — block-scoped, no redeclaration, no accidental globals.
  • const — block-scoped, reassignment forbidden, must be initialized.

ES2026 introduced using and await using — variables whose resources are automatically disposed when the block exits.

The goal across all of these is the same: make the common case safe, and make the unsafe case explicit.

docs.title: The Five Declaration Keywords (2026)
docs.text:
// var — function-scoped, hoisted with undefined, redeclarable
var old = "legacy";

// let — block-scoped, hoisted but TDZ, reassignable
let mutable = "can change";
mutable = "changed";

// const — block-scoped, hoisted but TDZ, not reassignable
const fixed = "cannot change";
// fixed = "error"; // TypeError

// using — block-scoped, auto-disposed at block exit (ES2026)
using file = openFile("data.txt");
// file is disposed synchronously when the block exits

// await using — async disposal (ES2026)
await using conn = await openConnection();
// conn is disposed asynchronously when the block exits

docs.title: Declaration vs. Assignment
docs.text:
let x;          // declaration (x is undefined)
x = 10;         // assignment
let y = 20;     // declaration + initialization

const z = 30;   // const must be initialized at declaration
// const w;     // ❌ SyntaxError: Missing initializer

docs.title: Multiple Declarations
docs.text:
let a = 1, b = 2, c = 3;        // comma-separated
const x = 10, y = 20;           // multiple constants

// Destructuring
const [first, second] = [1, 2];
const { name, age } = user;

docs.title: Naming Rules
docs.text:
// ✅ Valid
let userName;
let _private;
let $dollar;
let 名 = "unicode";  // Unicode letters allowed

// ❌ Invalid
// let 1stPlace;     // cannot start with digit
// let my-var;       // hyphen not allowed
// let class;        // reserved word

docs.title: Template Literals with Variables
docs.text:
const name = "Ada";
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!`;

docs.title: The "Labeled Box" Mental Model
docs.text:
A variable is a labeled box that holds a value:

┌─────────────┐
│   name      │  ← label (identifier)
│  "Ada"      │  ← value
└─────────────┘

const means the label cannot be moved to a different box — but the contents of the box can still change if the value is an object.

docs.title: The "Scope Ladder" Mental Model
docs.text:
Variables live in scopes, and scopes nest:

┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Global scope                          │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Function scope                    │ │
│  │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ │
│  │  │  Block scope ({ })             │ │ │
│  │  │  let, const, using             │ │ │
│  │  └───────────────────────────────┘ │ │
│  │  var lives here (function scope)   │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘
  • var climbs to the function level.
  • let, const, using stay at the block level.

docs.title: The "Temporal Dead Zone" Mental Model
docs.text:
let and const are hoisted but not initialized. The period between entering the scope and reaching the declaration is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) — accessing the variable there throws a ReferenceError.

{
    // TDZ starts here
    // console.log(x); // ❌ ReferenceError
    let x = 10;        // TDZ ends here
    console.log(x);    // 10
}

var has no TDZ — it is hoisted and initialized to undefined.

docs.title: The "Resource Lifetime" Mental Model
docs.text:
using ties a resource's lifetime to a block:

{
    using file = openFile("data.txt");
    // use file
} // ← file is automatically closed here

This is the JavaScript equivalent of C#'s using and Python's with — deterministic cleanup without manual finally blocks.

docs.title: Concept 1: var — Function-Scoped, Hoisted, Legacy
docs.text:
function example() {
    if (true) {
        var x = 10;
    }
    console.log(x); // 10 — var leaks out of the block
}

var characteristics:

  • Function-scoped — ignores block boundaries.
  • Hoisted and initialized to undefined — accessible before declaration.
  • Redeclarable — var x = 1; var x = 2; is legal.
  • Attaches to globalThis in script mode (not module mode).

var is legacy. It exists for backward compatibility. Do not use it in new code.

docs.title: Concept 2: let — Block-Scoped, Reassignable
docs.text:
let count = 0;
count = 1; // ✅ reassignment allowed

{
    let blockScoped = "inside";
}
// blockScoped is not accessible here

let characteristics:

  • Block-scoped — { }, if, for, while, switch all create scope.
  • Hoisted but TDZ — no access before declaration.
  • Not redeclarable in the same scope.
  • Does not attach to globalThis.

docs.title: Concept 3: const — Block-Scoped, Not Reassignable
docs.text:
const PI = 3.14159;
// PI = 3; // ❌ TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

const characteristics:

  • Block-scoped — same as let.
  • Hoisted but TDZ — same as let.
  • Must be initialized at declaration.
  • Cannot be reassigned — but objects are still mutable:
const user = { name: "Ada" };
user.name = "Grace"; // ✅ allowed — mutating the object
// user = {};         // ❌ TypeError — reassigning the binding

const does not freeze objects. It freezes the binding, not the value.

docs.title: Concept 4: using — Deterministic Resource Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text:
{
    using file = openFile("data.txt");
    // use file
} // file[Symbol.dispose]() is called automatically

using characteristics:

  • Block-scoped — like const.
  • Auto-disposed at block exit via Symbol.dispose.
  • Synchronous disposal.
  • Part of ECMAScript 2026.

docs.title: Concept 5: await using — Async Resource Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text:
{
    await using conn = await openConnection();
    // use conn
} // await conn[Symbol.asyncDispose]() is called

await using characteristics:

  • Block-scoped — like const.
  • Auto-disposed asynchronously at block exit via Symbol.asyncDispose.
  • Requires await — only valid in async contexts.
  • Part of ECMAScript 2026.

docs.title: Concept 6: Hoisting
docs.text:
Hoisting is the behavior where declarations are lifted to the top of their scope during the memory-creation phase, before code executes.

Keyword Hoisted? Initialized to TDZ? var Yes undefined No let Yes Uninitialized Yes const Yes Uninitialized Yes using Yes Uninitialized Yes function Yes Function body No

docs.title: Concept 7: The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
docs.text:
The TDZ is the period from entering a scope until the let/const/using declaration is executed.

{
    // TDZ for name starts
    console.log(name); // ❌ ReferenceError: Cannot access 'name' before initialization
    let name = "Ada";
    // TDZ ends
}

The TDZ exists to catch bugs — accessing a variable before it is declared is almost always a mistake.

docs.title: Concept 8: Block Scope
docs.text:
Blocks are created by:

  • { } — explicit blocks.
  • if, else — conditionals.
  • for, while, do...while — loops.
  • switch — cases.
  • try, catch, finally — error handling.
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    // `i` is scoped to each iteration
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// Output: 0, 1, 2 (not 3, 3, 3)

var in the same loop prints 3, 3, 3 — the classic var capture bug.

docs.title: Concept 9: Function Scope
docs.text:
Functions create a new scope. Variables declared inside a function are not accessible outside:

function greet() {
    let message = "Hello";
    console.log(message);
}
greet();
// console.log(message); // ❌ ReferenceError

Parameters are also function-scoped.

docs.title: Concept 10: Global Scope
docs.text:
Variables declared at the top level (outside any function or block) are global:

  • In script mode, var and function declarations attach to globalThis.
  • In module mode, top-level declarations are module-scoped, not global.
  • let and const never attach to globalThis.

docs.title: Concept 11: Module Scope (ES Modules)
docs.text:
ES modules have module scope — top-level declarations are shared within the module but not exposed globally:

// module.js
const secret = "not global";
export const shared = "exported";

// app.js
import { shared } from "./module.js";
// console.log(secret); // ❌ ReferenceError

Module scope is strict mode by default.

docs.title: Concept 12: Re-declaration Rules
docs.text:
Declaration Redeclare var? Redeclare let? Redeclare const? var x ✅ allowed ❌ SyntaxError ❌ SyntaxError let x ❌ SyntaxError ❌ SyntaxError ❌ SyntaxError const x ❌ SyntaxError ❌ SyntaxError ❌ SyntaxError

var is the only keyword that allows redeclaration in the same scope.

docs.title: Concept 13: Accidental Globals
docs.text:
function f() {
    x = 10; // ❌ creates a global in sloppy mode
}

In strict mode (modules, classes, "use strict"), this throws a ReferenceError. Always declare variables explicitly.

docs.title: Concept 14: const Is Not Immutability
docs.text:
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
arr.push(4);      // ✅ allowed — mutating the array
// arr = [5, 6];  // ❌ TypeError — reassigning the binding

For true immutability, use Object.freeze():

const frozen = Object.freeze({ a: 1 });
frozen.a = 2; // silently fails in sloppy mode, throws in strict mode

docs.title: Concept 15: using and Symbol.dispose
docs.text:
using works with any object that implements Symbol.dispose:

class Resource {
    [Symbol.dispose]() {
        console.log("Resource disposed");
    }
}

{
    using r = new Resource();
} // logs "Resource disposed"

await using uses Symbol.asyncDispose instead.

docs.title: Concept 16: Variable Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• camelCase — variables and functions (userName, getData).
  • PascalCase — classes and constructors (User, HttpClient).
  • UPPER_SNAKE_CASE — true constants (MAX_RETRIES, API_URL).
  • Descriptive names — usersByRegion beats data.
  • Avoid abbreviations — button beats btn in most contexts.

docs.title: Concept 17: ES2026 Global Declaration Behavior
docs.text: Per ES2026 §16.1.7, top-level var and function declarations in script mode should bind on the global object even when a built-in property with the same name exists. This is a subtle edge case that affects engines, not typical application code.

docs.title: Concept 18: Best Practice — const by Default
docs.text:
The modern consensus is:

const name = "Ada";        // default
let count = 0;             // only when reassigning
// var — never in new code

Use const unless you know the binding will be reassigned. This prevents accidental mutation and signals intent.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Variable Lifecycle
docs.text:
1.  Engine enters a scope.
    │
    ▼
2.  Memory creation phase:
    │   - var → allocated, initialized to undefined
    │   - let/const/using → allocated, uninitialized (TDZ)
    │   - function → allocated with full body
    │
    ▼
3.  Code execution phase:
    │   - var assignment → value written
    │   - let/const declaration → TDZ ends, value written
    │   - using → resource acquired, registered for disposal
    │
    ▼
4.  Block exit:
    │   - using → Symbol.dispose() called
    │   - await using → Symbol.asyncDispose() awaited
    │
    ▼
5.  Scope exits; bindings become unreachable.
    │
    ▼
6.  Garbage collector reclaims memory.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: let in a for Loop
docs.text:
1.  Loop starts; new block scope per iteration.
    │
    ▼
2.  `let i = 0` creates a binding in iteration 1 scope.
    │
    ▼
3.  Body executes; `i` is captured by closures.
    │
    ▼
4.  Iteration ends; `i` value is copied to next iteration scope.
    │
    ▼
5.  Repeat for each iteration.
    │
    ▼
6.  Each closure sees its own `i`.

This is why let fixes the classic var loop bug.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: using Disposal
docs.text:
1.  `using r = acquire()` executes.
    │
    ▼
2.  `acquire()` returns an object with `[Symbol.dispose]`.
    │
    ▼
3.  The object is registered with the block's disposal list.
    │
    ▼
4.  Block body executes.
    │
    ▼
5.  Block exits (normally or via throw).
    │
    ▼
6.  `Symbol.dispose()` is called.
    │
    ▼
7.  Scope exits.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: TDZ Enforcement
docs.text:
1.  Scope entered.
    │
    ▼
2.  `let x` binding created in memory (uninitialized).
    │
    ▼
3.  Any access to `x` before declaration → ReferenceError.
    │
    ▼
4.  Declaration statement executed → `x` initialized.
    │
    ▼
5.  Subsequent accesses → normal.

docs.title: The Scope Chain
docs.text:
Every execution context has a scope chain:

Global Execution Context
    │
    └── Function Execution Context
            │
            └── Block Execution Context
                    │
                    └── Variable lookup walks up the chain

Variable resolution: local scope → outer scope → global scope.

docs.title: Declarative vs. Object Environment Records
docs.text:
The spec distinguishes:

  • Declarative Environment Record — let, const, using, class (stored in a declarative record).
  • Object Environment Record — var, function (stored on the global object in script mode).

This is why var attaches to globalThis but let does not.

docs.title: The TDZ in the Spec
docs.text: The TDZ is enforced via uninitialized bindings. When a let binding is created in the environment record, its value is set to a special uninitialized marker. Accessing it throws ReferenceError.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
Execution Context
├── Variable Environment (var, function)
│   └── x: undefined
│
├── Lexical Environment (let, const, using)
│   └── y: <uninitialized>  ← TDZ
│
└── this binding

docs.title: Disposal Registry
docs.text: using adds the object to a disposal list attached to the block. On block exit, the list is iterated in reverse order (last-in, first-out) — like a stack.

docs.title: Garbage Collection
docs.text: Variables are roots for garbage collection. When a binding goes out of scope and is not captured by a closure, the value becomes unreachable and is reclaimed.

docs.title: Declaration Lifecycle
docs.text: Declare → Initialize → Access → Reassign (if let) → Scope exit → GC

docs.title: const Lifecycle
docs.text:
Declare + Initialize → Access → Mutate object (allowed) → Scope exit → GC
                     ↘ Reassign → TypeError

docs.title: using Lifecycle
docs.text: Declare → Initialize → Use → Block exit → Dispose → GC

docs.title: Variable Scope Workflow
docs.text:
Enter function
    │
    ├── var hoisted to function top
    ├── let/const in TDZ
    │
    ▼
Execute code
    │
    ├── var accessible (undefined until assigned)
    ├── let/const accessible after declaration
    │
    ▼
Exit function
    │
    └── All bindings out of scope

docs.title: Development Lifecycle
docs.text:
Write variable declaration
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint: prefer-const, no-var)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript)
    │
    ▼
Run
    │
    ▼
Debug (TDZ errors, ReferenceErrors)

ESLint rules like prefer-const and no-var enforce modern declarations automatically.

docs.title: Example 1: const by Default
docs.text:
const API_URL = "https://api.example.com";
const users = await fetchUsers(API_URL);
const activeUsers = users.filter(u => u.active);
console.log(`Active: ${activeUsers.length}`);

Breakdown:

  • API_URL is a true constant.
  • users and activeUsers are not reassigned — const is correct.
  • Only use let when the binding changes.

docs.title: Example 2: let When Reassignment Is Needed
docs.text:
let retries = 0;
const MAX_RETRIES = 3;

while (retries < MAX_RETRIES) {
    try {
        await fetchData();
        break;
    } catch (err) {
        retries++;
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • retries changes → let.
  • MAX_RETRIES never changes → const.

docs.title: Example 3: Block Scope Prevents Leaks
docs.text:
{
    const secret = "hidden";
    console.log(secret); // "hidden"
}
// console.log(secret); // ❌ ReferenceError

docs.title: Example 4: let in Loops (The Fix)
docs.text:
// ❌ var — all callbacks log 3
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}

// ✅ let — each callback logs its own i
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// Output: 0, 1, 2

Breakdown:

  • var creates one function-scoped i shared by all closures.
  • let creates a new i per iteration — each closure captures its own.

docs.title: Example 5: TDZ in Practice
docs.text:
function example() {
    console.log(typeof x); // ❌ ReferenceError (TDZ)
    let x = 10;
}

Breakdown:

  • typeof does not protect against TDZ for let/const.
  • var would return "undefined" here.

docs.title: Example 6: const Object Mutation
docs.text:
const config = { debug: false };
config.debug = true;        // ✅ allowed — mutating the object
// config = {};             // ❌ TypeError — reassigning the binding

const frozen = Object.freeze({ debug: false });
frozen.debug = true;        // silently fails in sloppy mode
console.log(frozen.debug);  // false

docs.title: Example 7: using for Resource Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text:
class FileHandle {
    #fd;
    constructor(path) {
        this.#fd = openSync(path, "r");
    }
    [Symbol.dispose]() {
        closeSync(this.#fd);
        console.log("File closed");
    }
}

{
    using file = new FileHandle("data.txt");
    // read from file
} // logs "File closed" automatically

Breakdown:

  • using guarantees disposal even if an exception is thrown.
  • No manual try/finally required.

docs.title: Example 8: await using for Async Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text:
class Connection {
    async close() { /* ... */ }
    async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() { await this.close(); }
}

{
    await using conn = await openConnection();
    await conn.query("SELECT 1");
} // await conn[Symbol.asyncDispose]() called automatically

Breakdown:

  • await using handles async disposal.
  • Only valid inside async functions or modules.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Declaration Configuration constant const Loop counter let Accumulator let Object/array reference const Function parameter (implicit) File handle using (ES2026) Database connection await using (ES2026) Module-level export const + export Temporary computation const Flag that changes let

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use const by default. Why: prevents accidental reassignment; signals intent.
  2. Use let only when reassigning. Why: makes mutation explicit.
  3. Never use var in new code. Why: function-scoped, hoisting bugs, redeclaration allowed.
  4. Always initialize const. Why: required by the language.
  5. Avoid global variables. Why: collision risk, hard debugging, memory leaks.
  6. Use meaningful names. Why: usersByRegion beats data.
  7. Use camelCase for variables. Why: JavaScript convention.
  8. Avoid abbreviations. Why: clarity at review time.
  9. Use using for resources that need cleanup. Why: deterministic disposal (ES2026).
  10. Use await using for async resources. Why: async cleanup without manual finally.
  11. Enable strict mode (modules do this by default). Why: catches accidental globals.
  12. Lint with no-var and prefer-const. Why: enforces modern declarations automatically.
  13. Don't use const for values that change. Why: use let instead.
  14. Understand TDZ. Why: accessing let/const before declaration throws.
  15. Document why a variable is let. Why: mutation should be intentional.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using var in New Code
docs.text:
var count = 0;

Why it's wrong: Function-scoped, hoisted with undefined, redeclarable.

✅ Correct:

let count = 0;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Initialize const
docs.text:
const x; // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

const x = 10;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Confusing const with Immutability
docs.text:
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
arr.push(4); // ✅ allowed — const does not freeze

✅ Correct: Use Object.freeze() for immutability.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Accessing let Before Declaration
docs.text:
console.log(x); // ❌ ReferenceError (TDZ)
let x = 10;

✅ Correct: Declare before use.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: var Loop Capture Bug
docs.text:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 3, 3, 3
}

✅ Correct: Use let.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Accidental Globals
docs.text:
function f() {
    x = 10; // ❌ creates global in sloppy mode
}

✅ Correct: Always declare. Use strict mode (modules).

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Redeclaring with let
docs.text:
let x = 1;
let x = 2; // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct: Use different names or reassign.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using let When const Works
docs.text:
let name = "Ada"; // never reassigned

✅ Correct:

const name = "Ada";

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring using for Resources
docs.text:
const file = openFile("data.txt");
// ... manual cleanup in finally

✅ Correct (ES2026):

using file = openFile("data.txt");
// auto-disposed

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming typeof Protects Against TDZ
docs.text:
console.log(typeof x); // ❌ ReferenceError for let
let x = 10;

✅ Correct: Do not access before declaration.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• const vs let — negligible performance difference; engines optimize both.
  • var vs let — let is generally optimized equally well.
  • TDZ checks — minimal runtime cost; engines inline the checks.
  • Block scope — creates a new lexical environment; tiny overhead, usually optimized away.
  • using — adds a disposal registry; overhead is proportional to the number of using declarations.
  • Closure capture — capturing let in loops creates per-iteration environments; V8 optimizes this well.
  • Global variables — slower property lookup on globalThis than local bindings.
  • Garbage collection — variables that go out of scope become unreachable; GC reclaims them.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use const and let — they optimize as well as var.
  2. Avoid globals — local bindings are faster.
  3. Keep scopes small — fewer bindings to track.
  4. Use using for resources — avoids leaking handles.
  5. Don't micro-optimize declaration choice — readability wins.
  6. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt if needed.

docs.title: TDZ as a Safety Feature
docs.text: The TDZ prevents access to uninitialized variables, reducing the risk of using undefined in ways that cause security bugs.

docs.title: var and Global Pollution
docs.text: var at the top level of a script attaches to globalThis — a vector for prototype pollution and cross-script interference. Modules avoid this.

docs.title: Accidental Globals
docs.text: In sloppy mode, assigning to an undeclared variable creates a global. In strict mode (modules, classes), it throws — preventing silent global pollution.

docs.title: using and Resource Leaks
docs.text: using guarantees disposal even on exceptions, preventing file handle leaks, connection leaks, and similar resource exhaustion attacks.

docs.title: const and Defensive Programming
docs.text: const prevents binding reassignment — an attacker cannot redirect a constant to a malicious object. (It does not prevent mutation — use Object.freeze() for that.)

docs.title: Scope Isolation
docs.text: Module scope isolates variables from the global object — a security boundary that prevents one script from tampering with another's bindings.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization — TDZ violation; declare before use.
  • ReferenceError: x is not defined — undeclared variable; check spelling and scope.
  • TypeError: Assignment to constant variable — attempted reassignment of const.
  • SyntaxError: Identifier 'x' has already been declared — redeclaration.
  • console.log(typeof x) — can detect var hoisting but not let TDZ.
  • ESLint no-var — flags var usage.
  • ESLint prefer-const — suggests const when let is not reassigned.
  • Chrome DevTools Scope panel — inspect variable values at each scope.
  • debugger; — pause and inspect scope chain.
  • Node.js --inspect-brk — step through variable initialization.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Declaration When to Use const Default — value is not reassigned let Value is reassigned using Resource needs synchronous cleanup (ES2026) await using Resource needs async cleanup (ES2026) var Never in new code; legacy maintenance only

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• var — never in new code.
  • let — when const works.
  • const — when reassignment is needed.
  • using — when no cleanup is required.
  • Globals — when module or block scope suffices.
  • eval-created variables — never; security and performance risk.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Data Types — what variables hold
  • Scope — where variables are accessible
  • Hoisting — how declarations are lifted
  • Temporal Dead Zone — the uninitialized period
  • Closures — variables captured by functions
  • Strict Mode — prevents accidental globals
  • ES Modules — module scope
  • Symbol.dispose — the disposal protocol (ES2026)
  • Symbol.asyncDispose — the async disposal protocol (ES2026)
  • Destructuring — extracting values into variables
  • Garbage Collection — memory reclamation

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• let and const were introduced in ES2015 — a decade before the current spec.
  • let is not a reserved word in ES5 — it was a "future reserved word."
  • const in ES2015 is block-scoped — unlike const in older engines (which was function-scoped).
  • The TDZ has no runtime cost in optimized code — engines inline the checks.
  • var attaches to globalThis in script mode; let and const never do.
  • using and await using are part of ECMAScript 2026.
  • using disposes in reverse order — last declared, first disposed.
  • const does not freeze objects — it freezes the binding only.
  • Object.freeze() is shallow — nested objects are still mutable.
  • ESLint's prefer-const rule can automatically fix let → const.
  • TypeScript 5.0+ enforces const type parameters — related but distinct.
  • let in a for...of loop creates a new binding per iteration.
  • var is the only declaration that allows redeclaration.
  • Module scope is strict mode — accidental globals throw.
  • globalThis is the standardized name for the global object (ES2020).
  • ES2026 §16.1.7 clarifies var/function shadowing of built-in globals in script mode.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Variables are named bindings that hold values.
  • Five declaration keywords in 2026: var, let, const, using, await using.
  • var is legacy — function-scoped, hoisted with undefined, redeclarable.
  • let — block-scoped, TDZ, reassignable.
  • const — block-scoped, TDZ, not reassignable, must be initialized.
  • using (ES2026) — auto-disposed at block exit via Symbol.dispose.
  • await using (ES2026) — async disposal via Symbol.asyncDispose.
  • Hoisting lifts declarations; var initializes to undefined, let/const stay in the TDZ.
  • Block scope is created by { }, if, for, while, switch.
  • Function scope is the enclosing function.
  • Module scope is the ES module — strict mode by default.
  • Use const by default; let only when reassigning; never var in new code.
  • const does not freeze objects — use Object.freeze() for immutability.
  • using guarantees cleanup even on exceptions.
  • TDZ catches bugs — accessing let/const before declaration throws.
  • ESLint rules (no-var, prefer-const) enforce modern declarations.
  • Variables are the foundation of every JavaScript program.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A data type is a classification that specifies which kind of value a variable can hold and what operations can be performed on it. JavaScript is a dynamically typed language — types are associated with values, not with variables. A single variable can hold a number now and a string later without any type declaration.

let value = 42;          // number
value = "hello";         // now a string
value = true;            // now a boolean
value = { a: 1 };        // now an object

The ECMAScript 2026 specification defines eight language types:

Type Category typeof Result Undefined Primitive "undefined" Null Primitive "object" (historical bug) Boolean Primitive "boolean" String Primitive "string" Symbol Primitive "symbol" Number Numeric "number" BigInt Numeric "bigint" Object Structural "object"

Of these, seven are primitive (Undefined, Null, Boolean, String, Symbol, Number, BigInt) and one is structural (Object).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Data types exist to solve a fundamental problem: how does a program know what operations are valid on a value? You can add two numbers, but you cannot add a number to an object without first defining what "addition" means. Types give the engine enough information to:

  • Allocate the right amount of memory.
  • Select the right operation (e.g., numeric addition vs. string concatenation).
  • Coerce values when types don't match.
  • Optimize code paths based on observed type feedback.
  • Prevent certain operations at runtime (e.g., mixing BigInt and Number).

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Language Fundamentals
├── Variables             ✅ done
├── Data Types            ← you are here
├── Operators
├── Expressions
├── Statements
├── Type Conversion
├── Equality
└── Strict Mode

Data types sit directly after variables because a variable is only meaningful once you know what it can hold. The next concept — Operators — describes what you can do with those values.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
JavaScript was designed for the web, where flexibility matters more than safety. A form input arrives as a string; a calculation needs a number; a checkbox gives a boolean. Forcing developers to declare types would have made JavaScript harder to learn and slower to write. Instead, JavaScript chose dynamic typing — types are inferred from values at runtime.

But dynamic typing creates a second problem: what happens when types don't match? JavaScript's answer is weak typing — it allows implicit type conversion (coercion) instead of throwing type errors.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES5 No Symbol, no BigInt, limited numeric range Number only Integers above 2⁵³ - 1 lost precision No symbols No way to create truly unique property keys No BigInt Cryptography and large-integer math required libraries Date only No immutable, time-zone-aware date types

docs.title: Why Each Type Was Introduced
docs.text:
• Undefined — indicates a variable has been declared but not assigned.
  • Null — represents an intentional absence of value.
  • Boolean — logical true/false; drives control flow.
  • String — text; immutable sequences of UTF-16 code units.
  • Symbol — unique, immutable identifiers (ES2015).
  • Number — IEEE 754 double-precision floating point; the only numeric type until ES2020.
  • BigInt — arbitrary-precision integers (ES2020).
  • Object — collections of properties; the structural type.
  • Temporal — immutable date/time types (ES2026, Stage 4).

docs.title: Primitive Types at a Glance
docs.text:
// Undefined — declared but not assigned
let notAssigned;
console.log(notAssigned); // undefined

// Null — intentional absence
const empty = null;

// Boolean — logical values
const isActive = true;
const isDeleted = false;

// String — text (immutable)
const greeting = "Hello";
const template = `Hello, ${name}`;
const unicode = "😀"; // surrogate pair

// Symbol — unique identifier
const id = Symbol("id");
const shared = Symbol.for("app.id"); // global registry

// Number — IEEE 754 double-precision
const integer = 42;
const float = 3.14;
const hex = 0xFF;
const binary = 0b1010;
const octal = 0o755;
const infinity = Infinity;
const notANumber = NaN;

// BigInt — arbitrary precision
const big = 9007199254740991n;
const bigFromString = BigInt("9007199254740993");

// Object — collections of properties
const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
const fn = () => {};
const date = new Date();
const regex = /pattern/;

docs.title: Checking Types with typeof
docs.text:
typeof undefined;     // "undefined"
typeof null;          // "object" (historical bug)
typeof true;          // "boolean"
typeof "hello";       // "string"
typeof Symbol("id");  // "symbol"
typeof 42;            // "number"
typeof 42n;           // "bigint"
typeof {};            // "object"
typeof [];            // "object" (arrays are objects)
typeof function(){};  // "function" (special case)

typeof null returns "object" because the original JavaScript implementation used a type tag where null was represented as the null pointer (0x00), which was indistinguishable from the object tag.

docs.title: typeof Edge Cases
docs.text:
typeof NaN;           // "number" (NaN is a number type)
typeof Infinity;      // "number"
typeof /regex/;       // "object"
typeof new Date();    // "object"
typeof BigInt(42);    // "bigint"

docs.title: Detecting Types Beyond typeof
docs.text:
// Arrays
Array.isArray([]);                    // true

// Plain objects
Object.prototype.toString.call({});   // "[object Object]"
Object.prototype.toString.call([]);   // "[object Array]"
Object.prototype.toString.call(null);// "[object Null]"

// Null
value === null;                       // only reliable check

// NaN
Number.isNaN(NaN);                    // true (not global isNaN)

// Integers
Number.isInteger(42);                 // true
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53 - 1);    // true

docs.title: Temporal Types (ES2026)
docs.text:
// Immutable, time-zone-aware date/time types
const instant = Temporal.Instant.from("2026-06-30T12:00:00Z");
const zoned = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-06-30T12:00[America/New_York]");
const plainDate = Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-06-30");
const plainTime = Temporal.PlainTime.from("14:30:00");
const duration = Temporal.Duration.from({ hours: 2, minutes: 30 });

// All Temporal operations return new values — never mutate
const tomorrow = plainDate.add({ days: 1 });
console.log(plainDate.toString()); // still "2026-06-30"

Temporal reached Stage 4 in March 2026 and is part of ECMAScript 2026. Firefox 139 shipped it first (May 2025), followed by Chrome 144 (January 2026).

docs.title: The "Two Families" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   All Values                        │
│                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐  │
│  │   Primitives         │  │   Objects            │  │
│  │   (7 types)          │  │   (1 type)           │  │
│  │                      │  │                      │  │
│  │  • Undefined         │  │  • Plain objects     │  │
│  │  • Null              │  │  • Arrays            │  │
│  │  • Boolean           │  │  • Functions         │  │
│  │  • String            │  │  • Dates             │  │
│  │  • Symbol            │  │  • RegExp            │  │
│  │  • Number            │  │  • Maps, Sets        │  │
│  │  • BigInt            │  │  • TypedArrays       │  │
│  │                      │  │                      │  │
│  │  Immutable           │  │  Mutable             │  │
│  │  Passed by value     │  │  Passed by reference │  │
│  └─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Primitives are immutable and compared by value. Objects are mutable and compared by reference.

docs.title: The "Type Tag" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every value carries an internal type tag that the engine uses to decide what operations are valid:

42          → Number tag
"hello"     → String tag
true        → Boolean tag
{}          → Object tag
null        → Null tag (but typeof bug reports Object)
undefined   → Undefined tag

The typeof operator reads this tag — except for null, which is special-cased incorrectly due to a 1995 implementation detail.

docs.title: The "Box" vs. "Reference" Mental Model
docs.text:
Primitive:                    Object:
┌─────────┐                   ┌─────────┐
│  x = 42 │                   │ x = ────┼──→ ┌─────────────┐
└─────────┘                   └─────────┘    │ { a: 1 }    │
                                             └─────────────┘
Copying x copies 42.          Copying x copies the reference.
Both boxes are independent.   Both boxes point to the SAME object.

This is why mutating an object through one reference is visible through another.

docs.title: The "Numeric Duality" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Number                    BigInt                │
│  ├── 64-bit IEEE 754       ├── Arbitrary precision│
│  ├── Fractions allowed     ├── Integers only     │
│  ├── Max safe: 2⁵³ - 1    ├── No practical limit │
│  ├── 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3      ├── Exact arithmetic   │
│  └── Cannot mix with BigInt└── Cannot mix with Number│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

You must explicitly convert between Number and BigInt — the engine will not coerce them.

docs.title: Concept 1: Primitive vs. Object
docs.text: Aspect Primitive Object Mutability Immutable Mutable Comparison By value By reference Assignment Copies value Copies reference Methods Via wrapper objects Direct typeof Specific type "object" Examples 42, "hi", true, null {}, [], function(){}

docs.title: Concept 2: Undefined vs. Null
docs.text:
Aspect undefined null Meaning Not assigned Intentionally empty Default Automatic for unassigned variables Must be explicitly set typeof "undefined" "object" (bug) Loose equality undefined == null → true Same Strict equality undefined === null → false Same

null is a keyword (reserved word); undefined is a property of the global object.

docs.title: Concept 3: Boolean and Falsy Values
docs.text:
Every value in JavaScript is implicitly either truthy or falsy. There are exactly eight falsy values:

false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN

Everything else is truthy — including "0", [], {}, and function(){}.

docs.title: Concept 4: String Immutability
docs.text:
Strings are immutable — you cannot change a character in place:

let str = "hello";
str[0] = "H";       // silently fails
console.log(str);   // still "hello"

str = "H" + str.slice(1); // create a new string
console.log(str);   // "Hello"

All string methods return new strings; the original is unchanged.

docs.title: Concept 5: Number — IEEE 754 Double-Precision
docs.text:
JavaScript's Number type is a 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point value:

  • Precision: ~17 decimal digits.
  • Max safe integer: 2⁵³ - 1 (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER).
  • Max value: ~1.8 × 10³⁰⁸; beyond that → Infinity.
  • No integer type: 37 is a floating-point value, not an integer.
  • Special values: NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, -0.
0.1 + 0.2;               // 0.30000000000000004
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;  // 9007199254740991
Number.isInteger(37);    // true
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53); // false

docs.title: Concept 6: BigInt — Arbitrary Precision
docs.text:
BigInt represents integers of arbitrary size:

const big = 9007199254740993n;
const alsoBig = BigInt("9007199254740993");
big + 1n; // 9007199254740994n
// big + 1; // ❌ TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types

BigInt rules:

  • Created with the n suffix or BigInt().
  • Cannot be mixed with Number in arithmetic — convert explicitly.
  • Cannot be used with Math methods.
  • typeof returns "bigint".
  • 0n is falsy; 1n is truthy.

docs.title: Concept 7: Symbol — Unique Identifiers
docs.text:
Symbol creates a unique, immutable value, often used as an object property key that cannot collide with string keys:

const id = Symbol("id");
const id2 = Symbol("id");
id === id2; // false — every symbol is unique

const obj = { [id]: "secret" };
obj[id]; // "secret"

Well-known symbols customize language behavior: Symbol.iterator, Symbol.asyncIterator, Symbol.hasInstance, Symbol.toPrimitive, Symbol.dispose, Symbol.asyncDispose, etc..

docs.title: Concept 8: Object — The Structural Type
docs.text:
Object is the only non-primitive type. It is a collection of properties (key-value pairs). Almost everything non-primitive is an object:

  • Plain objects {}
  • Arrays []
  • Functions function(){}
  • Dates new Date()
  • Regular expressions /pattern/
  • Maps, Sets, WeakMaps, WeakSets
  • TypedArrays and ArrayBuffers
  • Promises, Errors, etc.

Object.prototype is the root of the prototype chain — its prototype is always null and cannot be changed.

docs.title: Concept 9: Wrapper Objects
docs.text:
Every primitive except null and undefined has a wrapper object:

Primitive Wrapper String String Number Number Boolean Boolean Symbol Symbol BigInt BigInt

When you access a property on a primitive, JavaScript temporarily wraps it:

"hello".toUpperCase(); // "HELLO" — string wrapped in String object
(42).toFixed(2);       // "42.00"
true.toString();       // "true"

docs.title: Concept 10: Type Coercion (Weak Typing)
docs.text:
JavaScript implicitly converts types in many operations:

"5" + 3;   // "53" (number → string)
"5" - 3;   // 2 (string → number)
true + 1;  // 2 (boolean → number)
[] + [];   // "" (arrays → strings)
{} + [];   // 0 or "[object Object]" depending on context

Explicit conversion is safer:

Number("5");    // 5
String(42);     // "42"
Boolean(0);     // false
parseInt("5px"); // 5
parseFloat("3.14"); // 3.14

docs.title: Concept 11: Falsy Values (Complete List)
docs.text:
false        — the boolean false
0            — positive zero
-0           — negative zero
0n           — BigInt zero
""           — empty string
null         — null
undefined    — undefined
NaN          — not a number

Everything else is truthy, including "0", "false", [], {}, and function(){}.

docs.title: Concept 12: NaN — Not a Number
docs.text:
NaN === NaN;           // false — the only value not equal to itself
Number.isNaN(NaN);     // true — reliable check
isNaN("hello");        // true — coerces, unreliable
Number.isNaN("hello"); // false — does not coerce

NaN is a Number type value. typeof NaN returns "number".

docs.title: Concept 13: Temporal Types (ES2026)
docs.text:
Temporal introduces a namespace of immutable date/time types:

Type Represents Temporal.Instant Exact moment in time Temporal.ZonedDateTime Time-zone-aware date/time Temporal.PlainDate Calendar date (no time zone) Temporal.PlainTime Wall-clock time Temporal.PlainDateTime Date + time (no time zone) Temporal.Duration Difference between two points

All operations return new values — no mutation. First-class IANA time-zone and calendar support.

docs.title: Concept 14: Records and Tuples (Stage 2, Abandoned)
docs.text: The Records and Tuples proposal aimed to add deeply immutable value types compared by content rather than identity. As of August 2026, the proposal was abandoned.

docs.title: Concept 15: ES2026 — New Type-Related Methods
docs.text:
ECMAScript 2026 added several type-related utilities:

  • Error.isError() — reliably identify error objects.
  • Math.sumPrecise() — sum numbers minimizing precision loss.
  • Uint8Array base64/hex methods — convert binary data to/from strings.
  • JSON.rawJSON() — control JSON.stringify output for primitives.
  • Map.getOrInsert() / getOrInsertComputed() — default values during retrieval.
  • Array.fromAsync() — construct arrays from async iterables.
  • Iterator.concat() — sequence iterators.
  • Explicit Resource Management — using / await using for deterministic cleanup.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Type Determination at Runtime
docs.text:
1.  Value is created (literal, function return, etc.).
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine assigns an internal type tag.
    │
    ▼
3.  `typeof` reads the tag and maps to a string.
    │
    ▼
4.  Operations check the tag before proceeding.
    │
    ▼
5.  If tags mismatch, coercion or TypeError occurs.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Primitive vs. Object Assignment
docs.text:
Primitive:
1.  let a = 42;
2.  Engine stores 42 directly in a's slot.
3.  let b = a;
4.  Engine copies 42 into b's slot.
5.  a and b are independent.

Object:
1.  const a = { x: 1 };
2.  Engine stores a reference to the object.
3.  const b = a;
4.  Engine copies the reference.
5.  a and b point to the SAME object.
6.  Mutating a.x changes b.x.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Coercion in +
docs.text:
1.  Operator `+` encounters operands of different types.
    │
    ▼
2.  If either operand is a string → string concatenation.
    │
    ▼
3.  Otherwise → ToPrimitive on both operands.
    │
    ▼
4.  If either result is a string → concatenation.
    │
    ▼
5.  Otherwise → numeric addition.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: BigInt and Number Separation
docs.text:
1.  BigInt and Number have separate type tags.
    │
    ▼
2.  Arithmetic operators check if both operands share a type.
    │
    ▼
3.  Mixed BigInt/Number → TypeError.
    │
    ▼
4.  Explicit conversion required: BigInt(42) or Number(42n).

docs.title: The Type Tag
docs.text:
Engines store a type tag with every value. V8 uses a compressed representation:

SMI (small integer)  → immediate value
HeapNumber           → pointer to heap object
String               → pointer to heap object
Object               → pointer to heap object
undefined / null / true / false → special immediates

Small integers (SMIs) are stored inline — no heap allocation. Larger numbers become HeapNumber objects.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
Stack (primitives)          Heap (objects)
┌─────────────┐            ┌─────────────────┐
│ x = 42      │            │ { name: "Ada" } │
│ y = "hi"    │            │ { items: [...] }│
│ z = true    │            │ function f(){}  │
└─────────────┘            └─────────────────┘

Primitives live on the stack (or inline in objects); objects live on the heap.

docs.title: String Representation
docs.text:
V8 represents strings in multiple ways:

  • SeqString — sequential UTF-16 code units.
  • ConsString — concatenation of two strings (lazy).
  • SlicedString — a view into another string.
  • ThinString — a reference to another string's content.

This enables efficient concatenation and slicing without immediate copying.

docs.title: Number Representation
docs.text:
SMI (31-bit on 32-bit, 32-bit on 64-bit) → immediate
HeapNumber (64-bit double) → heap-allocated

Arithmetic on SMIs is fast; results that exceed SMI range are boxed as HeapNumber.

docs.title: BigInt Representation
docs.text: BigInt is stored as an array of digits (usually 30-bit or 64-bit chunks) with a sign. Arithmetic is implemented in software, not hardware — slower than Number for small values.

docs.title: Symbol Representation
docs.text:
Symbols are unique heap objects. Internally, each symbol has:

  • A description (optional string).
  • A unique identity — no two symbols are equal unless they are the same object.
  • Well-known symbols are pre-created and shared across realms.

docs.title: Prototype Chain
docs.text:
Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] slot. Property lookup walks the chain:

obj → Object.prototype → null
arr → Array.prototype → Object.prototype → null
fn → Function.prototype → Object.prototype → null

Object.prototype is the only object whose prototype is null and cannot be changed.

docs.title: Primitive Lifecycle
docs.text: Literal created → Stored on stack (or inline) → Copied by value → GC (if heap-allocated)

docs.title: Object Lifecycle
docs.text: Object created → Stored on heap → Reference copied → Mutated → Unreachable → GC

docs.title: Type Coercion Workflow
docs.text:
Operation encounters mismatched types
    │
    ▼
Engine applies ToPrimitive / ToNumber / ToString
    │
    ├── Explicit conversion? → Use Number(), String(), Boolean()
    │
    └── Implicit coercion? → Follow operator rules
            │
            ├── `+` with string → concatenation
            ├── `-`, `*`, `/` → numeric conversion
            ├── `==` → complex coercion rules
            └── `if`, `&&`, `||` → boolean conversion

docs.title: Temporal Type Lifecycle (ES2026)
docs.text:
Create Temporal object (immutable)
    │
    ▼
Perform operations → returns NEW Temporal object
    │
    ▼
Original remains unchanged
    │
    ▼
All Temporal values are immutable and compared by value

docs.title: Example 1: Detecting Types Reliably
docs.text:
function getType(value) {
    if (value === null) return "null";
    if (Array.isArray(value)) return "array";
    return typeof value;
}

console.log(getType(null));       // "null"
console.log(getType([]));         // "array"
console.log(getType(42));         // "number"
console.log(getType("hi"));       // "string"
console.log(getType(Symbol()));   // "symbol"
console.log(getType(42n));        // "bigint"

docs.title: Example 2: Safe Numeric Handling
docs.text:
// ❌ Unsafe — precision loss
const unsafe = 9007199254740993; // loses precision
console.log(unsafe); // 9007199254740992

// ✅ Safe — BigInt
const safe = 9007199254740993n;
console.log(safe); // 9007199254740993n

// ✅ Safe — Number.isSafeInteger
const check = Number.isSafeInteger(9007199254740993);
console.log(check); // false — use BigInt

docs.title: Example 3: Falsy Value Pitfalls
docs.text:
// ❌ `0` is falsy — this silently fails
function setVolume(vol) {
    if (!vol) vol = 50; // 0 becomes 50!
    return vol;
}

// ✅ Use `??` to only default on null/undefined
function setVolume(vol) {
    return vol ?? 50;
}
setVolume(0);   // 0
setVolume(null); // 50

docs.title: Example 4: String Immutability in Practice
docs.text:
const original = "hello";
const upper = original.toUpperCase();

console.log(original); // "hello" — unchanged
console.log(upper);    // "HELLO" — new string

// ✅ Correct way to "modify" a string
let mutable = "hello";
mutable = mutable[0].toUpperCase() + mutable.slice(1);
console.log(mutable); // "Hello"

docs.title: Example 5: Symbol as Unique Key
docs.text:
const USER_ID = Symbol("userId");
const ADMIN_ID = Symbol("userId"); // different symbol

const users = {
    [USER_ID]: "user-123",
    [ADMIN_ID]: "admin-456",
};

console.log(users[USER_ID]);   // "user-123"
console.log(users[ADMIN_ID]);  // "admin-456"

docs.title: Example 6: Temporal Instead of Date (ES2026)
docs.text:
// ❌ Legacy Date — mutable, confusing
function addOneWeek(myDate) {
    myDate.setDate(myDate.getDate() + 7); // mutates!
    return myDate;
}

// ✅ Temporal — immutable, predictable
function addOneWeek(date) {
    return date.add({ days: 7 }); // returns new value
}

const today = Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-06-30");
const nextWeek = addOneWeek(today);
console.log(today.toString());    // "2026-06-30" — unchanged
console.log(nextWeek.toString()); // "2026-07-07"

docs.title: Example 7: using for Resource Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text:
class DatabaseConnection {
    [Symbol.dispose]() {
        console.log("Connection closed");
    }
}

{
    using conn = new DatabaseConnection();
    // use conn
} // logs "Connection closed" automatically

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Need Type Text String Whole numbers Number (or BigInt for large) Fractions Number Large integers BigInt True/false Boolean Absence (intentional) Null Absence (uninitialized) Undefined Unique keys Symbol Collections Object (or Map/Set) Dates Temporal (ES2026) Binary data TypedArray Asynchronous results Promise

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use const by default, let when reassigning. Why: prevents accidental type changes.
  2. Prefer === over ==. Why: avoids coercion surprises.
  3. Use Number.isNaN() not global isNaN(). Why: global isNaN coerces.
  4. Use Number.isInteger() for integer checks. Why: typeof only says "number".
  5. Use BigInt for values above 2⁵³ - 1. Why: Number loses precision.
  6. Do not mix BigInt and Number in arithmetic. Why: throws TypeError.
  7. Use null for intentional absence, undefined for uninitialized. Why: conveys intent.
  8. Use Symbol for private-ish keys. Why: avoids name collisions.
  9. Remember strings are immutable. Why: all methods return new strings.
  10. Use Temporal instead of Date (ES2026). Why: immutable, time-zone-aware.
  11. Use Array.isArray() to detect arrays. Why: typeof [] is "object".
  12. Use Object.prototype.toString.call() for precise type detection. Why: handles edge cases.
  13. Avoid new for primitives. Why: new String("x") creates an object, not a primitive.
  14. Use explicit conversion over implicit coercion. Why: clearer, predictable.
  15. Enable TypeScript for type safety. Why: catches type errors at compile time.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: typeof null === "object"
docs.text:
if (typeof value === "object") { /* ... */ } // also matches null!

✅ Correct:

if (value !== null && typeof value === "object") { /* ... */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using typeof for Arrays
docs.text:
typeof []; // "object"

✅ Correct:

Array.isArray([]); // true

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: NaN === NaN
docs.text:
NaN === NaN; // false

✅ Correct:

Number.isNaN(NaN); // true

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mixing BigInt and Number
docs.text:
1n + 1; // ❌ TypeError

✅ Correct:

1n + BigInt(1); // 2n
Number(1n) + 1; // 2

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Treating "0" as Falsy
docs.text:
if ("0") { /* runs! "0" is truthy */ }

✅ Correct: Only "" is falsy among strings.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mutating Strings
docs.text:
let str = "hello";
str[0] = "H"; // silently fails

✅ Correct:

str = "H" + str.slice(1);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Confusing const with Immutability
docs.text:
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
arr.push(4); // ✅ allowed — const does not freeze

✅ Correct: Use Object.freeze() for immutability.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using new for Primitives
docs.text:
typeof new String("hi"); // "object" — not "string"

✅ Correct:

typeof "hi"; // "string"

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming undefined Is a Reserved Word
docs.text:
// In non-global scope, this is legal (but terrible):
function f(undefined) { /* ... */ }

✅ Correct: Never use undefined as an identifier.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using == with null
docs.text:
null == undefined; // true
null == 0;         // false

✅ Correct: Use === null or === undefined explicitly.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• SMIs (Small Integers) — fastest numeric representation; stored inline.
  • HeapNumber — boxed doubles; slower than SMIs.
  • BigInt — software arithmetic; slower than Number for small values.
  • String concatenation — V8 uses ConsString for lazy concatenation.
  • String comparison — may require flattening ConsString.
  • Symbol — unique heap objects; fast as property keys.
  • Type stability — monomorphic types optimize best.
  • Coercion — implicit coercion has runtime cost; explicit conversion is clearer and often faster.
  • typeof — very fast; reads the internal type tag.
  • Object creation — objects with stable shapes optimize best.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use Number for small integers; BigInt only when needed.
  2. Keep types stable in hot loops.
  3. Avoid implicit coercion in performance-critical code.
  4. Use Temporal for date math — it's optimized and immutable.
  5. Prefer Map over objects for dynamic key collections.
  6. Avoid delete on hot objects — destroys hidden classes.
  7. Use Array.isArray() — faster than instanceof.
  8. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Malicious input can modify Object.prototype, affecting every object:

Object.assign({}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}'));

Defense: validate keys, use Object.create(null), freeze prototypes.

docs.title: typeof and Security
docs.text: Do not rely on typeof for security decisions. A value that passes typeof x === "string" can still contain malicious content.

docs.title: Symbol and Property Privacy
docs.text: Symbols are not private — they can be discovered via Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(). Use #private fields or WeakMap for true privacy.

docs.title: Coercion Attacks
docs.text:
Implicit coercion can be exploited:

// Attacker controls `input`
if (input == 1) { /* bypassed with "1" or [1] */ }

Defense: always use ===.
