        case "mon":
        case "tue":
        case "wed":
        case "thu":
        case "fri":
            return "weekday";
        default:
            return "invalid";
    }
}

docs.title: Example 3: for...of with break and continue
docs.text:
for (const item of items) {
    if (!item.active) continue;
    if (item.critical) break;
    process(item);
}

docs.title: Example 4: Labelled Loops
docs.text:
search: for (let i = 0; i < grid.length; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < grid[i].length; j++) {
        if (grid[i][j] === target) {
            console.log(`Found at ${i},${j}`);
            break search;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Example 5: try/catch/finally
docs.text:
function readConfig(path) {
    let file;
    try {
        file = openFile(path);
        return JSON.parse(file.read());
    } catch (err) {
        console.error("Failed to read config:", err);
        return null;
    } finally {
        file?.close();
    }
}

docs.title: Example 6: Resource Management with using (ES2026)
docs.text:
function processData(path) {
    using file = openFile(path);
    const data = file.read();
    return JSON.parse(data);
    // file is disposed automatically — even on parse error
}

docs.title: Example 7: for await...of (ES2018)
docs.text:
async function* streamPages(url) {
    while (url) {
        const res = await fetch(url);
        const page = await res.json();
        yield* page.items;
        url = page.next;
    }
}

const allItems = [];
for await (const item of streamPages("/api/items")) {
    allItems.push(item);
}

docs.title: Example 8: Pattern Matching (Stage 3, Proposed)
docs.text:
function describe(value) {
    return value match {
        0 => "zero",
        n when n > 0 => `positive: ${n}`,
        n when n < 0 => `negative: ${n}`,
        _ => "unknown",
    };
}

Pattern matching is Stage 3 — not yet standard. It provides a cleaner alternative to complex if/else and switch chains.

docs.title: Example 9: ASI Pitfall
docs.text:
// ❌ ASI inserts semicolon after `return`
function f() {
    return
        { value: 10 };
}
console.log(f()); // undefined

// ✅ Correct
function f() {
    return { value: 10 };
}
console.log(f()); // { value: 10 }

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Statement Use Case let / const Variable declaration using / await using Resource cleanup (ES2026) if / else Simple branching switch Multi-way branching for Counter-based loops for...of Iterable values for await...of Async iterables (ES2018) while / do...while Condition-based loops break / continue Loop control return Function exit throw Exception signaling try / catch / finally Error handling label Nested loop control debugger Interactive debugging

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use const by default, let when reassigning. Why: prevents accidental mutation.
  2. Always use braces with if/for/while. Why: prevents dangling-else and scope bugs.
  3. Always use break in switch cases. Why: prevents unintentional fall-through.
  4. Use for...of over for...in for arrays. Why: for...in iterates keys and inherited properties.
  5. Use for await...of for async iterables. Why: native async iteration (ES2018).
  6. Use using for resources needing cleanup. Why: deterministic disposal even on exceptions (ES2026).
  7. Use labels sparingly. Why: they can make code harder to follow.
  8. Always use semicolons. Why: avoids ASI pitfalls.
  9. Never use return with a newline before the value. Why: ASI inserts a semicolon, returning undefined.
  10. Use try/catch for recoverable errors only. Why: not all errors should be caught.
  11. Use finally for cleanup that must always run. Why: guaranteed execution.
  12. Prefer pattern matching when it reaches Stage 4. Why: declarative and concise (currently Stage 3).
  13. Use debugger instead of console.log for complex debugging. Why: interactive inspection.
  14. Lint with no-fallthrough, no-unreachable, no-constant-condition. Why: catches statement mistakes.
  15. Keep statements small and focused. Why: readability and testability.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing break in switch
docs.text:
switch (x) {
    case 1:
        console.log("one");
    case 2:
        console.log("two"); // runs for x === 1 too!
}

✅ Correct:

switch (x) {
    case 1:
        console.log("one");
        break;
    case 2:
        console.log("two");
        break;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: return with Newline
docs.text:
function f() {
    return
        { value: 10 }; // ASI inserts semicolon → returns undefined
}

✅ Correct:

function f() {
    return { value: 10 };
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: for...in on Arrays
docs.text:
for (const i in arr) { console.log(arr[i]); } // iterates inherited properties too

✅ Correct:

for (const value of arr) { console.log(value); }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Braces
docs.text:
if (x > 5)
    console.log("big");
    console.log("always"); // NOT part of the if!

✅ Correct:

if (x > 5) {
    console.log("big");
    console.log("always");
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: continue in switch
docs.text:
switch (x) {
    case 1:
        continue; // ❌ SyntaxError outside loop
}

✅ Correct: Use break in switch.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting await in for await...of
docs.text:
for (const x of asyncIterable) {} // ❌ not async

✅ Correct:

for await (const x of asyncIterable) {}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using using Outside a Block
docs.text:
using file = openFile("a.txt"); // at top level — disposes at module exit

Why it's wrong: Top-level using disposes at module exit, not immediately.

✅ Correct: Use using inside a block for deterministic disposal.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Pattern Matching Is Standard
docs.text:
Pattern matching is Stage 3 — not standard.

✅ Correct: Use with a transpiler and track the proposal.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unreachable Code After return
docs.text:
function f() {
    return 1;
    console.log("never"); // unreachable
}

✅ Correct: Remove unreachable code.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Constant Conditions
docs.text:
if (false) { /* never runs */ }

✅ Correct: Remove dead code.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Loop overhead — for loops are generally fastest; for...of has iterator overhead.
  • for...in — slowest; iterates inherited properties.
  • switch — optimized by engines; can be faster than if/else chains for many cases.
  • try/catch — deoptimizes functions in some engines; avoid in hot paths.
  • using — adds disposal registry; overhead proportional to resource count.
  • for await...of — async overhead per iteration; use for I/O, not CPU-bound loops.
  • ASI — parser-level; no runtime cost.
  • Labels — no runtime cost; purely syntactic.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use for for counter-based loops in hot paths.
  2. Use for...of for readability — optimize later if needed.
  3. Avoid try/catch in hot loops.
  4. Use switch for multi-way branching.
  5. Keep loop bodies small.
  6. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.

docs.title: eval and Function
docs.text: Never evaluate untrusted strings as statements. Use JSON.parse for data.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution in for...in
docs.text:
for...in iterates inherited properties — including polluted ones.

Defense: Use Object.hasOwn() or for...of with Object.keys().

docs.title: try/catch and Error Masking
docs.text:
Catching all errors can hide security-relevant failures.

Defense: Catch specific errors; re-throw unexpected ones.

docs.title: using and Resource Exhaustion
docs.text: using guarantees disposal — preventing file handle and connection leaks.

docs.title: Label Injection
docs.text: Labels are syntactic — no injection risk.

docs.title: ASI and Security
docs.text:
ASI can cause unexpected parsing — a potential source of bugs with security implications.

Defense: Always use semicolons.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• debugger; — pause in DevTools.
  • console.log — print values.
  • console.trace — print stack trace.
  • ESLint no-fallthrough — flags missing break.
  • ESLint no-unreachable — flags dead code.
  • ESLint no-constant-condition — flags always-true/false conditions.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on statements.
  • Node.js --inspect-brk — debug statements in Node.
  • try/catch with console.error — log exceptions.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Statement When to Use let / const Always — default declarations using / await using Resources needing cleanup (ES2026) if / else Simple branching switch Multi-way branching with === for Known iteration count for...of Iterable values for await...of Async iterables (ES2018) while Unknown iteration count do...while At-least-once execution break / continue Loop control try / catch / finally Error handling label Nested loop control (sparingly) debugger Interactive debugging

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• var — never in new code.
  • for...in on arrays — use for...of.
  • switch without break — unless fall-through is intentional.
  • try/catch for control flow — use conditionals.
  • Labels — when simpler structure suffices.
  • debugger in production — remove before deploy.
  • Pattern matching in production — Stage 3; may change.
  • using at top level — disposes at module exit, not immediately.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Expressions — values that statements act upon
  • Declarations — let, const, using
  • Control Flow — if, switch, loops
  • Jumps — break, continue, return, throw
  • Exceptions — try/catch/finally
  • Resource Management — using/await using (ES2026)
  • Pattern Matching — Stage 3 proposal
  • ASI — Automatic Semicolon Insertion
  • Completion Records — how the engine tracks control flow
  • Directives — "use strict"

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• ECMAScript 2026 was approved on June 30, 2026 as the 17th edition.
  • using and await using are part of ES2026 and reached Stage 4.
  • for await...of has been Baseline Widely Available since January 2020.
  • Labels cannot be used with goto — JavaScript has no goto statement.
  • ASI can change the meaning of code when the next line begins with (, [, `, +, -, or a regex.
  • switch uses strict equality (===) for comparison.
  • Pattern matching is Stage 3 — it may change before Stage 4.
  • try/catch can deoptimize functions in V8.
  • for...in iterates inherited enumerable properties — not just own properties.
  • using disposes in reverse order — last declared, first disposed.
  • debugger has no effect when DevTools is closed.
  • ES2026 also added Array.fromAsync, Error.isError, Math.sumPrecise, and Map.getOrInsert.
  • Babel transforms using into try/catch/finally patterns.
  • for await...of falls back to [Symbol.iterator]() if [Symbol.asyncIterator]() is absent.
  • Statements are the action layer — expressions are the value layer.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A statement expresses an action; an expression produces a value.
  • Declaration statements — let, const, var, using, await using, function, class.
  • Conditional statements — if/else, switch.
  • Iteration statements — for, for...in, for...of, for await...of, while, do...while.
  • Jump statements — break, continue, return, throw.
  • Exception handling — try/catch/finally.
  • Labelled statements — break label;, continue label; — no goto.
  • Resource management — using / await using (ES2026) with Symbol.dispose / Symbol.asyncDispose.
  • for await...of — async iteration (ES2018).
  • Pattern matching — Stage 3 proposal, cleaner than switch.
  • ASI — automatic semicolon insertion; always use semicolons to avoid pitfalls.
  • Best practices — const by default, braces always, break in switch, for...of over for...in.
  • ES2026 added using, await using, Array.fromAsync, Error.isError, Math.sumPrecise, and more.
  • Statements are the control layer — they decide what happens, when, and in what order.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Type conversion (also called type casting or type coercion) is the process of changing a value from one data type to another. JavaScript performs type conversion in two ways: explicitly (when you call conversion functions like Number() or String()) and implicitly (when the engine automatically converts values during operations like comparison, arithmetic, or concatenation).

// Explicit conversion — you ask for it
const num = Number("42");        // "42" → 42
const str = String(42);          // 42 → "42"
const bool = Boolean(0);         // 0 → false

// Implicit conversion — the engine does it
const result = "5" + 3;          // 3 → "3" → "53"
const comparison = "5" == 5;     // "5" → 5 → true
const truthy = !!"hello";        // "hello" → true

JavaScript is a weakly typed and dynamically typed language. Weak typing means it performs implicit coercion rather than throwing type errors. Dynamic typing means types are associated with values, not variables — a single variable can hold different types over its lifetime.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Type conversion exists to solve the problem of mismatched types in operations. A form input arrives as a string; a calculation needs a number. A comparison needs both operands to be the same type. Without conversion, every operation would require manual type checking and explicit conversion by the developer.

JavaScript's approach — automatic coercion — makes the language more forgiving but also more surprising. The purpose of understanding type conversion is not to embrace coercion everywhere, but to know when it happens, why it happens, and how to control it.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Language Fundamentals
├── Variables             ✅ done
├── Data Types            ✅ done
├── Operators             ✅ done
├── Expressions           ✅ done
├── Statements            ✅ done
├── Type Conversion       ← you are here
├── Equality
└── Strict Mode

Type conversion sits between Statements and Equality because equality (== vs ===) is the most common context where conversion rules matter. Understanding conversion first makes the equality chapter much clearer.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
JavaScript was designed for the web, where data arrives as strings. Form inputs, URL parameters, and HTML attributes are all strings. But calculations, comparisons, and logic require numbers, booleans, and objects. A language that refused to convert types would force developers to manually convert everything — tedious, error-prone, and verbose.

JavaScript chose automatic coercion to make the language more forgiving. But this created a second problem: coercion rules are complex, asymmetric, and sometimes surprising. The goal of understanding type conversion is to know the rules so you can predict behavior and write code that is both concise and correct.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES5 No Number.isNaN() — global isNaN coerces unpredictably No Object.is() No reliable way to compare NaN or +0/-0 No BigInt Large numbers lost precision; no separate numeric type No Number.parseInt Global parseInt existed but no namespaced version No JSON.rawJSON No control over JSON.stringify output for primitives

docs.title: Why New Conversion Features Were Introduced
docs.text:
• Number.isNaN() (ES2015) — reliable NaN check without coercion.
  • Object.is() (ES2015) — SameValue comparison for NaN and -0.
  • BigInt (ES2020) — arbitrary-precision integers with explicit conversion.
  • Number.parseInt, Number.parseFloat (ES2015) — namespaced, non-coercing versions.
  • Math.sumPrecise() (ES2026) — high-precision summation minimizing floating-point error.
  • Uint8Array base64/hex methods (ES2026) — direct conversion between binary and string encodings.
  • JSON.rawJSON() (ES2026) — fine control over JSON.stringify output for primitive values.
  • JSON.parse reviver context (ES2026) — access the matched segment of JSON source to recover exact values.

Each new feature solves a specific conversion problem: either making an implicit conversion explicit, or providing a safer alternative to a coercing method.

docs.title: Explicit Conversion — The Three Primitives
docs.text:
// To Number
Number("42");         // 42
Number("");           // 0
Number("  42  ");     // 42 (whitespace trimmed)
Number("42px");       // NaN (not a valid number)
Number(true);         // 1
Number(false);        // 0
Number(null);         // 0
Number(undefined);    // NaN
Number([]);           // 0
Number([5]);          // 5
Number([1, 2]);       // NaN

// To String
String(42);           // "42"
String(true);         // "true"
String(null);         // "null"
String(undefined);    // "undefined"
String([1, 2, 3]);    // "1,2,3"
String({ a: 1 });     // "[object Object]"

// To Boolean
Boolean(0);           // false
Boolean("");          // false
Boolean(null);        // false
Boolean(undefined);   // false
Boolean(NaN);         // false
Boolean("0");         // true (non-empty string)
Boolean([]);          // true (objects are truthy)
Boolean({});          // true

docs.title: Parsing Strings to Numbers
docs.text:
parseInt("42");         // 42
parseInt("42px");       // 42 (stops at first non-digit)
parseInt("ff", 16);     // 255 (explicit radix)
parseInt("");           // NaN
parseFloat("3.14");     // 3.14
parseFloat("3.14abc");  // 3.14
parseFloat("abc");      // NaN

Number.parseInt("42");  // 42 (namespaced, ES2015)
Number.parseFloat("3.14"); // 3.14

Always pass a radix to parseInt — otherwise, strings starting with 0 may be parsed as octal (legacy behavior), and 0x strings are parsed as hex.

docs.title: Conversion with Unary Operators
docs.text:
+"42";       // 42 (unary plus — same as Number())
-"42";       // -42
+true;       // 1
+false;      // 0
+null;       // 0
+undefined;  // NaN
+"";         // 0
+" 42 ";     // 42
+"42px";     // NaN

!!"hello";   // true (double negation — same as Boolean())
!!0;         // false
!![];        // true

docs.title: Implicit Conversion — Where It Happens
docs.text:
// `+` operator — string concatenation takes priority
"5" + 3;       // "53" (number → string)
3 + "5";       // "35"
true + "5";    // "true5"
1 + 2 + "3";   // "33" (1+2=3, then 3+"3"="33")
"1" + 2 + 3;   // "123"

// Other arithmetic operators — numeric conversion
"5" - 3;       // 2 (string → number)
"5" * 3;       // 15
"5" / 2;       // 2.5
"5" % 2;       // 1
"5" ** 2;      // 25

// Comparison operators — numeric or string comparison
"5" > 3;       // true (string → number)
"a" > "b";     // false (lexicographic)
"10" > "9";    // false (lexicographic — "1" < "9")

// Loose equality — complex coercion rules
"5" == 5;      // true
0 == false;    // true
"" == false;   // true
null == undefined; // true
null == 0;     // false
NaN == NaN;    // false

docs.title: Conversion via Symbol.toPrimitive
docs.text:
Objects can customize their conversion behavior:

const obj = {
    [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) {
        if (hint === "number") return 42;
        if (hint === "string") return "hello";
        return true; // "default" hint
    },
};

+obj;        // 42 (hint: "number")
`${obj}`;    // "hello" (hint: "string")
obj + "";    // "true" (hint: "default")

Symbol.toPrimitive is called with a hint of "number", "string", or "default". If absent, JavaScript falls back to valueOf() and toString().

docs.title: ES2026 Conversion Additions
docs.text:
// Math.sumPrecise — high-precision summation
Math.sumPrecise([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]); // 0.6 (not 0.6000000000000001)

// Uint8Array base64/hex conversion
const bytes = new Uint8Array([72, 101, 108, 108, 111]);
bytes.toBase64();                // "SGVsbG8="
Uint8Array.fromBase64("SGVsbG8="); // Uint8Array [72, 101, 108, 108, 111]
bytes.toHex();                   // "48656c6c6f"
Uint8Array.fromHex("48656c6c6f"); // Uint8Array [72, 101, 108, 108, 111]

// JSON.rawJSON — preserve exact primitive values
const bigNumber = JSON.rawJSON("9007199254740993");
JSON.stringify({ id: bigNumber }); // {"id":9007199254740993}

docs.title: The "Conversion Triangle" Mental Model
docs.text:
Every value can be converted to Number, String, or Boolean:

┌─────────────┐
│   Number    │
│             │
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐       ┌─────────────┐
│   String    │◄─────►│   Boolean   │
│             │       │             │
└─────────────┘       └─────────────┘
  • To Number — via Number(), unary +, parseInt(), parseFloat().
  • To String — via String(), template literals, + with a string.
  • To Boolean — via Boolean(), !!, logical operators, conditionals.

docs.title: The "Falsy Eight" Mental Model
docs.text:
There are exactly eight falsy values:

false        — boolean false
0            — positive zero
-0           — negative zero
0n           — BigInt zero (ES2020)
""           — empty string
null         — null
undefined    — undefined
NaN          — not a number

Everything else is truthy — including "0", "false", [], {}, and function(){}.

docs.title: The "ToPrimitive Pipeline" Mental Model
docs.text:
When an object needs to become a primitive, JavaScript follows a pipeline:

Object → [Symbol.toPrimitive]? → Yes → Call it → Primitive
                    │
                    ▼ No
              → [hint === "string"]? → toString() then valueOf()
                    │
                    ▼ No
              → valueOf() then toString()

The hint determines the order:

Hint Context Preferred Order "number" Arithmetic, comparison valueOf() → toString() "string" Template literals, String() toString() → valueOf() "default" +, == valueOf() → toString()

docs.title: The "Asymmetric Conversion" Mental Model
docs.text:
Conversion is not symmetric:

"5" + 3   → "53"    (number → string)
"5" - 3   → 2       (string → number)

+ prefers strings; other arithmetic operators prefer numbers. This is one of the most common sources of confusion.

docs.title: Concept 1: Explicit vs. Implicit Conversion
docs.text: Aspect Explicit Implicit Control Developer Engine Visibility Visible in code Invisible Predictability High Low Recommended Yes Only when intentional Examples Number(), String() "5" + 3, "5" == 5

docs.title: Concept 2: The Abstract Operations
docs.text:
The ECMAScript spec defines conversion via abstract operations:

Operation Purpose ToPrimitive Convert object to primitive ToBoolean Convert to boolean ToNumber Convert to number ToNumeric Convert to number or BigInt ToString Convert to string ToObject Convert primitive to object ToPropertyKey Convert to string or symbol ToInt32 Convert to 32-bit signed integer ToUint32 Convert to 32-bit unsigned integer ToBigInt Convert to BigInt

These operations are normative — engines must follow them.

docs.title: Concept 3: ToBoolean — The Simplest Conversion
docs.text:
ToBoolean never throws and never coerces objects:

Input Type Result Undefined false Null false Boolean Input value Number false if +0, -0, or NaN; otherwise true String false if empty; otherwise true Symbol true BigInt false if 0n; otherwise true Object true

There are exactly eight falsy values — everything else is truthy.

docs.title: Concept 4: ToNumber — String to Number Rules
docs.text:
String Number "" 0 " 42 " 42 (whitespace trimmed) "42" 42 "42.5" 42.5 "0x1F" 31 (hex) "0b101" 5 (binary) "0o17" 15 (octal) "42px" NaN "hello" NaN "Infinity" Infinity "-Infinity" -Infinity

Number() is strict — it requires the entire string to be a valid number. parseInt() and parseFloat() are lenient — they parse as much as they can.

docs.title: Concept 5: ToString — Number to String Rules
docs.text:
Number String 42 "42" 3.14 "3.14" 0 "0" -0 "0" NaN "NaN" Infinity "Infinity" 1e21 "1e+21" 1e-7 "1e-7"

Numbers use the shortest representation that round-trips exactly.

docs.title: Concept 6: The + Operator — Concatenation vs. Addition
docs.text:
The + operator has two modes:

  1. String concatenation — if either operand is a string (after ToPrimitive).
  2. Numeric addition — if both operands are numbers (after ToPrimitive).
1 + 2;          // 3 (both numbers)
1 + "2";        // "12" (string wins)
"1" + 2;        // "12"
1 + 2 + "3";    // "33" (left to right)
"1" + 2 + 3;    // "123"

docs.title: Concept 7: The == Operator — Loose Equality
docs.text:
== performs complex coercion:

  • null == undefined → true
  • null == 0 → false
  • "5" == 5 → true (string → number)
  • 0 == false → true (boolean → number)
  • "" == false → true (both → number: 0 == 0)
  • NaN == NaN → false
  • Objects compared to primitives → ToPrimitive then compare

Always use === unless you specifically need null/undefined coalescing.

docs.title: Concept 8: Symbol.toPrimitive — Custom Conversion
docs.text:
Objects can override conversion by implementing Symbol.toPrimitive:

const obj = {
    [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) {
        if (hint === "number") return 42;
        if (hint === "string") return "hello";
        return true;
    },
};

The hint is "number", "string", or "default". This is the only way to fully control object-to-primitive conversion.

docs.title: Concept 9: valueOf() and toString() — The Fallback
docs.text:
If Symbol.toPrimitive is absent, JavaScript uses valueOf() and toString():

  • "number" hint — valueOf() first, then toString().
  • "string" hint — toString() first, then valueOf().
  • "default" hint — valueOf() first, then toString().

Most objects inherit Object.prototype.valueOf() (returns the object itself) and Object.prototype.toString() (returns "[object Object]").

docs.title: Concept 10: Parsing vs. Conversion
docs.text: Number() parseInt() parseFloat() Strictness Strict Lenient Lenient Whitespace Trimmed Ignored Ignored Trailing chars Error → NaN Stops parsing Stops parsing Radix Auto (0x, 0b, 0o) Must specify N/A Empty string 0 NaN NaN

docs.title: Concept 11: BigInt Conversion
docs.text:
BigInt(42);         // 42n
BigInt("42");       // 42n
BigInt(true);       // 1n
// BigInt(42.5);    // ❌ RangeError — no fractions
// BigInt(null);    // ❌ TypeError
// BigInt(undefined); // ❌ TypeError

Number(42n);        // 42
// 42n + 1;        // ❌ TypeError — cannot mix BigInt and Number
42n + 1n;           // 43n

BigInt and Number cannot be mixed in arithmetic — explicit conversion is required.

docs.title: Concept 12: ES2026 Conversion Additions
docs.text:
• Math.sumPrecise() — sums numbers minimizing floating-point error.
  • Uint8Array.toBase64() / fromBase64() — binary ↔ base64 string.
  • Uint8Array.toHex() / fromHex() — binary ↔ hex string.
  • JSON.rawJSON() — preserve exact primitive values in JSON.stringify.
  • JSON.parse reviver context — access the matched segment of JSON source.

docs.title: Concept 13: Object.is() — SameValue Comparison
docs.text:
Object.is(NaN, NaN);   // true (unlike ===)
Object.is(0, -0);      // false (unlike ===)
Object.is(42, 42);     // true
Object.is("a", "a");   // true

Object.is() is the SameValue algorithm — it does not coerce and treats NaN and -0 specially.

docs.title: Concept 14: Conversion in switch
docs.text:
switch uses strict equality (===) for case matching — no coercion.

switch ("5") {
    case 5: console.log("number"); break;   // ❌ not matched
    case "5": console.log("string"); break; // ✅ matched
}

docs.title: Concept 15: Conversion in Array.prototype.sort
docs.text:
sort() converts elements to strings by default:

[10, 2, 1].sort(); // [1, 10, 2] — lexicographic, not numeric
[10, 2, 1].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 10] — numeric

docs.title: Concept 16: Conversion in Template Literals
docs.text:
Template literals convert interpolated values to strings:

const x = 42;
`${x}`; // "42"
`${null}`; // "null"
`${undefined}`; // "undefined"
`${[1, 2]}`; // "1,2"
`${{ a: 1 }}`; // "[object Object]"

docs.title: Concept 17: Conversion in JSON.stringify
docs.text:
JSON.stringify converts values to JSON-compatible types:

JSON.stringify({ a: undefined });    // "{}"
JSON.stringify({ a: function() {} }); // "{}"
JSON.stringify({ a: NaN });          // '{"a":null}'
JSON.stringify({ a: Infinity });     // '{"a":null}'
JSON.stringify({ a: 42n });          // TypeError

docs.title: Concept 18: Conversion in JSON.parse
docs.text:
JSON.parse converts JSON values to JavaScript types:

JSON.parse("42");        // 42 (number)
JSON.parse('"42"');      // "42" (string)
JSON.parse("true");      // true (boolean)
JSON.parse("null");      // null
JSON.parse('{"a":1}');   // { a: 1 }

ES2026 adds a reviver context parameter to access the matched segment of JSON source, useful for recovering exact values from numbers that lose precision.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: ToPrimitive Pipeline
docs.text:
1.  Object needs to become a primitive.
    │
    ▼
2.  Does it have Symbol.toPrimitive?
    │   ├── Yes → call it with hint → return result
    │   └── No → continue
    │
    ▼
3.  Determine hint:
    │   - "number" (arithmetic, comparison)
    │   - "string" (template literals, String())
    │   - "default" (+, ==)
    │
    ▼
4.  For "string" hint:
    │   - try toString() → if primitive, return
    │   - try valueOf() → if primitive, return
    │
    ▼
5.  For "number" or "default" hint:
    │   - try valueOf() → if primitive, return
    │   - try toString() → if primitive, return
    │
    ▼
6.  If neither works → TypeError

docs.title: Step-by-Step: ToNumber for Strings
docs.text:
1.  String is trimmed of leading/trailing whitespace.
    │
    ▼
2.  If empty → 0.
    │
    ▼
3.  If starts with "0x", "0b", "0o" → parse as hex/binary/octal.
    │
    ▼
4.  If "Infinity" or "-Infinity" → Infinity.
    │
    ▼
5.  If valid numeric string → parse as decimal.
    │
    ▼
6.  Otherwise → NaN.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: ToBoolean for Objects
docs.text:
1.  Object is always truthy.
    │
    ▼
2.  No coercion occurs.
    │
    ▼
3.  Result is true.

This is why [] and {} are truthy even though they "look empty."

docs.title: Step-by-Step: + Operator Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  Evaluate left operand.
    │
    ▼
2.  Evaluate right operand.
    │
    ▼
3.  Apply ToPrimitive to both.
    │
    ▼
4.  If either result is a string → string concatenation.
    │
    ▼
5.  Otherwise → numeric addition.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: == Loose Equality
docs.text:
1.  If both operands are same type → strict comparison.
    │
    ▼
2.  If one is null and other is undefined → true.
    │
    ▼
3.  If one is number and other is string → string → number.
    │
    ▼
4.  If one is boolean → boolean → number.
    │
    ▼
5.  If one is object and other is primitive → object → primitive.
    │
    ▼
6.  Otherwise → false.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: ES2026 Math.sumPrecise
docs.text:
1.  Iterable of numbers is consumed.
    │
    ▼
2.  Numbers are summed using a high-precision algorithm.
    │
    ▼
3.  Floating-point errors are minimized.
    │
    ▼
4.  Result is returned as a single Number.

docs.title: The Abstract Operations in ECMA-262
docs.text:
The spec defines conversion in Section 7.1:

7.1.1  ToPrimitive ( input [, preferredType ] )
7.1.2  ToBoolean ( argument )
7.1.3  ToNumeric ( value )
7.1.4  ToNumber ( argument )
7.1.5  ToIntegerOrInfinity ( argument )
7.1.6  ToInt32 ( argument )
7.1.7  ToUint32 ( argument )
7.1.13 ToBigInt ( argument )
7.1.17 ToString ( argument )
7.1.18 ToObject ( argument )
7.1.19 ToPropertyKey ( argument )

These are normative — engines must follow them exactly.

docs.title: ToPrimitive in Detail
docs.text:
ToPrimitive(input, preferredType):
1.  If input is not an Object → return input.
2.  Let exoticToPrim = GetMethod(input, @@toPrimitive).
3.  If exoticToPrim is not undefined:
    a.  Let hint be preferredType (or "default").
    b.  Let result = Call(exoticToPrim, input, « hint »).
    c.  If result is not an Object → return result.
    d.  Throw TypeError.
4.  If preferredType is not present → hint = "default".
5.  Return OrdinaryToPrimitive(input, hint).

docs.title: OrdinaryToPrimitive
docs.text:
OrdinaryToPrimitive(O, hint):
1.  If hint is "string":
    a.  methodNames = « "toString", "valueOf" ».
2.  Else:
    a.  methodNames = « "valueOf", "toString" ».
3.  For each name in methodNames:
    a.  Let method = Get(O, name).
    b.  If IsCallable(method):
        i.   Let result = Call(method, O).
        ii.  If result is not an Object → return result.
4.  Throw TypeError.

docs.title: The hint Values
docs.text: Hint When Used "number" Arithmetic operators (-, *, /, %, **), relational comparison "string" String(), template literals, alert() "default" +, ==, !=

docs.title: Conversion in the Engine
docs.text:
V8 optimizes conversion with type feedback:

function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
add(1, 2);   // feedback: both numbers → fast integer add
add("a", "b"); // guard fails → deoptimize → string concat

Each call site records the types it has seen. The JIT compiles speculative code based on that feedback. If a new type appears, the guard fails and the function deoptimizes.

docs.title: Memory and Performance
docs.text:
• SMIs (small integers) convert inline — fast.
  • HeapNumbers convert with boxing — slower.
  • String parsing — Number() uses a fast path for simple numeric strings.
  • parseInt() — slower than Number() because it scans character by character.
  • Symbol.toPrimitive — function call overhead.

docs.title: Conversion Lifecycle
docs.text: Value → Determine target type → Apply conversion rules → Result

docs.title: Explicit Conversion Workflow
docs.text:
Developer calls Number(x) → ToNumber algorithm → Result
Developer calls String(x) → ToString algorithm → Result
Developer calls Boolean(x) → ToBoolean algorithm → Result

docs.title: Implicit Conversion Workflow
docs.text:
Operation encounters mismatched types
    │
    ▼
Engine determines required conversion
    │
    ▼
Applies ToPrimitive / ToNumber / ToString / ToBoolean
    │
    ▼
Operation proceeds with converted values

docs.title: ToPrimitive Workflow
docs.text:
Object → Symbol.toPrimitive? → Yes → Call with hint → Primitive
                    │
                    ▼ No
              Hint determines order
                    │
                    ▼
              toString() / valueOf()
                    │
                    ▼
              Primitive or TypeError

docs.title: ES2026 Conversion Workflow
docs.text:
Uint8Array → toBase64() → string
Uint8Array → toHex() → string
Uint8Array.fromBase64(string) → Uint8Array
Uint8Array.fromHex(string) → Uint8Array

JSON.stringify({ id: JSON.rawJSON("...") }) → exact primitive
JSON.parse(source, reviver) → reviver receives context

docs.title: Example 1: Explicit Conversion — The Safe Path
docs.text:
const input = "42";
const num = Number(input);        // 42
const str = String(num);          // "42"
const bool = Boolean(input);      // true

console.log(typeof num, typeof str, typeof bool);
// "number" "string" "boolean"

Breakdown:

  • Number() is strict — it returns NaN for invalid strings.
  • String() never throws.
  • Boolean() follows the falsy-eight rule.

docs.title: Example 2: Implicit Conversion — String Concatenation
docs.text:
const a = 1 + 2 + "3";    // "33"
const b = "1" + 2 + 3;    // "123"

console.log(a); // "33"
console.log(b); // "123"

Breakdown:

  • Left to right: 1 + 2 = 3, then 3 + "3" = "33".
  • "1" + 2 = "12", then "12" + 3 = "123".

docs.title: Example 3: Implicit Conversion — Numeric
docs.text:
const a = "5" - 3;        // 2
const b = "5" * 3;        // 15
const c = "5" / 2;        // 2.5
const d = "5" % 2;        // 1

console.log(a, b, c, d); // 2 15 2.5 1

Breakdown:

  • All arithmetic operators except + convert strings to numbers.

docs.title: Example 4: Loose vs. Strict Equality
docs.text:
console.log("5" == 5);    // true
console.log("5" === 5);   // false
console.log(null == undefined); // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false
console.log(NaN == NaN);  // false
console.log(NaN === NaN); // false
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN)); // true

Breakdown:

  • == coerces; === does not.
  • Object.is() treats NaN as equal to itself.

docs.title: Example 5: Symbol.toPrimitive — Custom Conversion
docs.text:
class Temperature {
    constructor(celsius) {
        this.celsius = celsius;
    }

    [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) {
        if (hint === "number") return this.celsius;
        if (hint === "string") return `${this.celsius}°C`;
        return this.celsius;
    }
}

const temp = new Temperature(25);

console.log(+temp);        // 25
console.log(`${temp}`);    // "25°C"
console.log(temp + 5);     // 30

Breakdown:

  • Symbol.toPrimitive controls conversion for all hints.
  • Without it, temp + 5 would produce "[object Object]5".

docs.title: Example 6: parseInt vs. Number
docs.text:
console.log(parseInt("42px"));    // 42
console.log(Number("42px"));      // NaN
console.log(parseInt(""));        // NaN
console.log(Number(""));          // 0
console.log(parseInt("ff", 16));  // 255
console.log(Number("0xff"));      // 255

Breakdown:

  • parseInt is lenient; Number is strict.
  • Always pass a radix to parseInt.

docs.title: Example 7: Math.sumPrecise (ES2026)
docs.text:
const sum = 0.1 + 0.2;           // 0.30000000000000004
const precise = Math.sumPrecise([0.1, 0.2]); // 0.3

console.log(sum);     // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(precise); // 0.3

Breakdown:

  • Math.sumPrecise minimizes floating-point error.
  • Part of ES2026.

docs.title: Example 8: Uint8Array Base64/Hex (ES2026)
docs.text:
const bytes = new Uint8Array([72, 101, 108, 108, 111]); // "Hello"

console.log(bytes.toBase64());  // "SGVsbG8="
console.log(bytes.toHex());     // "48656c6c6f"

const decoded = Uint8Array.fromBase64("SGVsbG8=");
console.log(decoded); // Uint8Array [72, 101, 108, 108, 111]

Breakdown:

  • Direct conversion between binary and string encodings.
  • Part of ES2026.

docs.title: Example 9: JSON.rawJSON (ES2026)
docs.text:
const bigNumber = JSON.rawJSON("9007199254740993");
const json = JSON.stringify({ id: bigNumber });
console.log(json); // {"id":9007199254740993}

Breakdown:

  • Preserves integers larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.
  • Part of ES2026.

docs.title: Example 10: Conversion in sort
docs.text:
const nums = [10, 2, 1];
console.log(nums.sort());              // [1, 10, 2] — lexicographic!
console.log(nums.sort((a, b) => a - b)); // [1, 2, 10] — numeric

Breakdown:

  • Default sort() converts to strings.
  • Always provide a comparator for numbers.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Conversion Use Case Number(x) Parse numeric input String(x) Convert for display Boolean(x) Coerce for conditions parseInt(x, 10) Parse integers from strings parseFloat(x) Parse decimals from strings +x Quick numeric conversion !!x Quick boolean conversion `${x}` Quick string conversion Symbol.toPrimitive Custom object conversion Object.is() SameValue comparison Math.sumPrecise() High-precision summation (ES2026) Uint8Array.toBase64() Binary → base64 (ES2026) JSON.rawJSON() Exact JSON primitives (ES2026)

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Default to explicit conversion in production code. Why: makes type changes visible and intentional.
  2. Use Number(), String(), Boolean() over shorthand (+x, !!x, `${x}). Why: clarity over cleverness.
  3. Always use === and !==. Why: avoids coercion surprises.
  4. Use Number.isNaN() not global isNaN(). Why: global isNaN coerces.
  5. Always pass a radix to parseInt(). Why: avoids legacy octal and hex parsing.
  6. Use Number() for strict parsing, parseInt() for lenient parsing. Why: different tools for different jobs.
  7. Convert at system boundaries (API, input, storage). Why: keep internal data in the right types.
  8. Use Symbol.toPrimitive for custom object conversion. Why: full control over all hints.
  9. Use Object.is() for SameValue comparison. Why: handles NaN and -0 correctly.
  10. Provide a comparator to Array.prototype.sort(). Why: default converts to strings.
  11. Use Math.sumPrecise() for floating-point summation. Why: minimizes precision loss (ES2026).
  12. Use Uint8Array base64/hex methods for binary data. Why: native, efficient (ES2026).
  13. Use JSON.rawJSON() when exact primitive preservation matters. Why: avoids precision loss (ES2026).
  14. Enable ESLint eqeqeq and no-implicit-coercion. Why: enforces safe conversion practices.
  15. Understand the falsy eight. Why: predicts conditional behavior.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using == Instead of ===
docs.text:
0 == "";    // true
0 == false; // true
"" == false; // true

✅ Correct:

0 === "";    // false
0 === false; // false
"" === false; // false

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting parseInt Radix
docs.text:
parseInt("08"); // 8 in modern engines, but legacy risk

✅ Correct:

parseInt("08", 10); // 8

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Number("") Is NaN
docs.text:
Number(""); // 0, not NaN

✅ Correct: Use parseInt("") for NaN, or check for empty strings first.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using || for Numeric Defaults
docs.text:
const count = userCount || 10; // 0 becomes 10

✅ Correct:

const count = userCount ?? 10; // only null/undefined become 10

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: sort() Without Comparator
docs.text:
[10, 2, 1].sort(); // [1, 10, 2] — wrong!

✅ Correct:

[10, 2, 1].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 10]

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mixing BigInt and Number
docs.text:
1n + 1; // ❌ TypeError

✅ Correct:

1n + 1n; // 2n
Number(1n) + 1; // 2

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming typeof null Is "null"
docs.text:
typeof null; // "object" — historical bug

✅ Correct: value === null.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Global isNaN
docs.text:
isNaN("hello"); // true — coerces

✅ Correct:

Number.isNaN("hello"); // false — does not coerce

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using + for Conversion Ambiguously
docs.text:
+"42"; // 42 — but could be string concatenation if not careful

✅ Correct: Use Number("42") for clarity.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting Template Literal Conversion
docs.text:
`${[1, 2]}`; // "1,2"
`${{ a: 1 }}`; // "[object Object]"

✅ Correct: Use JSON.stringify() for objects.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Number() vs parseInt() — Number() is faster for strict parsing.
  • Unary + vs Number() — similar performance; Number() is clearer.
  • String() vs template literals — template literals are slightly slower.
  • Symbol.toPrimitive — adds function call overhead per conversion.
  • String concatenation — ConsString lazy evaluation; flattening costs.
  • Math.sumPrecise() — slower than + but accurate for floating-point.
  • JSON.parse — fast for valid JSON; reviver adds overhead.
  • sort() comparator — required for numeric sort; adds function call cost.
  • Type stability — keep types stable in hot loops for JIT optimization.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Convert once at boundaries, not in hot loops.
  2. Use Number() for strict numeric parsing.
  3. Keep operand types stable in arithmetic.
  4. Use Math.sumPrecise() only when precision matters.
  5. Use Uint8Array base64/hex methods for binary data.
  6. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.

docs.title: Coercion Attacks
docs.text:
if (input == 1) { /* bypassed with "1" or [1] */ }

Defense: Always use ===.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Malicious input can modify Object.prototype, affecting all objects.

Defense: Validate keys, use Object.create(null), freeze prototypes.

docs.title: eval and Implicit Conversion
docs.text: Never pass untrusted strings to eval() or new Function().

docs.title: parseInt and Radix
docs.text:
Omitting the radix can lead to unexpected parsing (octal in legacy engines).

Defense: Always pass 10 for decimal.

docs.title: Symbol.toPrimitive Abuse
docs.text: Objects can override conversion to return unexpected values. Never trust objects from untrusted sources without validation.

docs.title: JSON Parsing
docs.text:
JSON.parse is safe by design — it does not execute code. But parsing large payloads can exhaust memory.

Defense: Limit input size.

docs.title: BigInt and Denial of Service
docs.text:
Huge BigInt operations can block the event loop.

Defense: Validate input size; avoid BigInt arithmetic on untrusted values.

docs.title: Uint8Array Base64/Hex
docs.text: These methods are safe, but ensure you validate decoded data before use.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.log(typeof x, x) — log both type and value.
  • Number.isNaN() — reliable NaN check.
  • Object.is() — SameValue comparison.
  • Object.prototype.toString.call() — precise type detection.
  • Chrome DevTools Console — type-aware autocomplete.
  • debugger; — pause and inspect values.
  • ESLint eqeqeq — flags ==.
  • ESLint no-implicit-coercion — flags !!x, +x, etc.
  • TypeScript — catches type errors at compile time.
  • Break expressions into variables — easier to inspect.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Conversion When to Use Number() Strict numeric parsing parseInt() Lenient integer parsing parseFloat() Lenient decimal parsing String() Explicit string conversion Boolean() Explicit boolean conversion Symbol.toPrimitive Custom object conversion Object.is() SameValue comparison Math.sumPrecise() High-precision summation (ES2026) Uint8Array base64/hex Binary ↔ string (ES2026) JSON.rawJSON() Exact JSON primitives (ES2026)

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• == — never; use ===.
  • || for defaults — when 0, "", false are valid.
  • Global isNaN() — use Number.isNaN().
  • parseInt() without radix — always pass 10.
  • Implicit coercion in production — prefer explicit conversion.
  • eval() for conversion — never.
  • new Number() / new String() — creates objects, not primitives.
  • Mixing BigInt and Number — explicit conversion required.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Data Types — what values are being converted
  • Operators — where conversion happens
  • Equality — == vs ===
  • Expressions — how conversion fits into evaluation
  • Strict Mode — catches some conversion errors
  • Symbol.toPrimitive — custom conversion
  • Object.is() — SameValue comparison
  • Math.sumPrecise() — ES2026 precision
  • Uint8Array base64/hex — ES2026 binary conversion
  • JSON.rawJSON() — ES2026 JSON precision
  • TypeScript — static typing to avoid conversion bugs

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• There are exactly eight falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN.
  • Number("") returns 0 — but parseInt("") returns NaN.
  • typeof null === "object" is a bug from 1995 that will never be fixed.
  • NaN !== NaN — the only value not equal to itself.
  • Object.is(NaN, NaN) returns true — unlike ===.
  • [10, 2, 1].sort() returns [1, 10, 2] — lexicographic, not numeric.
  • "5" + 3 is "53" — but "5" - 3 is 2.
  • Symbol.toPrimitive was introduced in ES2015.
  • ES2026 added Math.sumPrecise() for high-precision summation.
  • ES2026 added Uint8Array.toBase64() and toHex() for binary conversion.
  • ES2026 added JSON.rawJSON() for exact JSON primitives.
  • The hint in Symbol.toPrimitive is "number", "string", or "default".
  • parseInt without a radix was a common source of bugs in legacy engines.
  • + is the only arithmetic operator that prefers string concatenation.
  • switch uses === — no coercion occurs.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Type conversion changes a value from one type to another.
  • Explicit conversion uses Number(), String(), Boolean(), parseInt(), parseFloat().
  • Implicit conversion (coercion) happens automatically in operations.
  • ToPrimitive is the core algorithm for object-to-primitive conversion.
  • Symbol.toPrimitive lets objects customize conversion with hints.
  • There are exactly eight falsy values — everything else is truthy.
  • + prefers strings; other arithmetic operators prefer numbers.
  • == coerces; === does not — always use ===.
  • Number() is strict; parseInt() and parseFloat() are lenient.
  • Always pass a radix to parseInt().
  • Object.is() handles NaN and -0 correctly.
  • ES2026 added Math.sumPrecise(), Uint8Array base64/hex, and JSON.rawJSON().
  • Convert at boundaries — keep internal data in the right types.
  • Use explicit conversion in production — it is visible and predictable.
  • Type conversion is the bridge between JavaScript's dynamic nature and the type-specific operations you need.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Equality in JavaScript is the determination of whether two values are considered the same. The language provides three distinct comparison operations — each using a different definition of "same":

// Strict equality (===)
1 === 1;              // true
"1" === 1;            // false — different types
NaN === NaN;          // false — IEEE 754 rule
-0 === +0;            // true — signed zero ignored

// Loose equality (==)
"1" == 1;             // true — string coerced to number
null == undefined;    // true — special case
0 == false;           // true — boolean coerced to number

// SameValue (Object.is)
Object.is(NaN, NaN);  // true — unlike ===
Object.is(-0, +0);    // false — unlike ===
Object.is("1", 1);    // false — no coercion

Under the hood, these correspond to four equality algorithms defined in the ECMAScript specification:

Algorithm Operator / Method Coercion? NaN equal? -0 = +0? IsLooselyEqual == Yes No Yes IsStrictlyEqual === No No Yes SameValue Object.is() No Yes No SameValueZero Built-ins (Map, Set, includes) No Yes Yes

The choice of operation depends entirely on what kind of comparison you need. The distinction between them is purely about how primitives are handled — none of them compares object structure, and for non-primitive objects that are structurally identical but distinct in memory, all four return false .

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Equality exists to answer a fundamental question in every program: "Is this value the same as that one?" Every conditional, every loop termination check, every lookup in a collection depends on some definition of equality. JavaScript gives you three — each optimized for a different use case:

  • === — the default. Strict, predictable, almost always correct.
  • == — loose equality. Performs type coercion; occasionally useful for null/undefined checks.
  • Object.is() — SameValue. Needed for NaN comparison and signed-zero distinction.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Language Fundamentals
├── Variables             ✅ done
├── Data Types            ✅ done
├── Operators             ✅ done
├── Expressions           ✅ done
├── Statements            ✅ done
├── Type Conversion       ✅ done
├── Equality              ← you are here
└── Strict Mode

Equality sits after Type Conversion because loose equality is type conversion applied to comparison. Understanding coercion first makes the equality rules predictable rather than surprising.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A programming language must decide what it means for two values to be equal. This sounds trivial until you consider:

  • Should "1" equal 1? The string and the number represent the same idea but have different types.
  • Should NaN equal NaN? IEEE 754 says no — NaN is the result of an undefined operation, so two NaNs are not necessarily the same result.
  • Should -0 equal +0? Mathematically they are the same number, but they carry different sign information.
  • Should { a: 1 } equal { a: 1 }? They have the same structure but are different objects in memory.

Every language answers these differently. JavaScript's answer is to provide multiple equality algorithms and let the developer choose.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES2015 No Object.is() — no way to compare NaN or distinguish -0 == only Coercion surprises were the only option for loose comparison No SameValueZero in spec Built-in behavior was inconsistent across engines No ES2020 BigInt Equality across numeric types was simpler but less precise

docs.title: Why Object.is() Was Introduced
docs.text:
Before ES2015, there was no standard way to:

  • Check if two values are both NaN.
  • Distinguish -0 from +0.

The Object.is() method was added in ES2015 to provide the SameValue algorithm — a stricter comparison that treats NaN as equal to itself and -0 as different from +0 .

docs.title: Why SameValueZero Exists
docs.text: The spec also defines SameValueZero — used internally by Map, Set, Array.prototype.includes, and other built-ins. It differs from SameValue only in that it treats +0 and -0 as equal . This is the algorithm that makes new Set([NaN, NaN]) contain only one element.

docs.title: Strict Equality (===)
docs.text:
// Same type — compare values
1 === 1;              // true
"hello" === "hello";  // true
true === true;        // true

// Different types — always false
1 === "1";            // false
null === undefined;   // false
true === 1;           // false

// Special numeric cases
NaN === NaN;          // false (IEEE 754)
-0 === +0;            // true (signed zero ignored)
Infinity === Infinity; // true

docs.title: Loose Equality (==)
docs.text:
// Same type — behaves like ===
1 == 1;               // true

// Different types — coercion occurs
1 == "1";             // true (string → number)
0 == false;           // true (boolean → number)
"" == false;          // true (both → number: 0 == 0)
null == undefined;    // true (special case)
null == 0;            // false (null only equals undefined)
NaN == NaN;           // false

// Objects
[] == false;          // true (both → number: 0 == 0)
[] == 0;              // true
[1] == 1;             // true
[1, 2] == "1,2";      // true
{} == "[object Object]"; // true

docs.title: SameValue (Object.is())
docs.text:
Object.is(1, 1);              // true
Object.is("1", 1);            // false
Object.is(NaN, NaN);          // true
Object.is(-0, +0);            // false
Object.is(null, null);        // true
Object.is(undefined, undefined); // true
Object.is({}, {});            // false (distinct objects)

docs.title: SameValueZero (Built-In Usage)
docs.text:
// Map uses SameValueZero for keys
const map = new Map();
map.set(NaN, "value");
map.get(NaN); // "value" — NaN keys work

// Set uses SameValueZero
new Set([NaN, NaN]).size; // 1

// Array.prototype.includes uses SameValueZero
[NaN].includes(NaN);      // true
[NaN].indexOf(NaN);       // -1 (indexOf uses ===)

docs.title: Negation Operators
docs.text:
1 !== 2;    // true (strict inequality)
1 != 2;     // true (loose inequality)
1 !== "1";  // true (different types)
1 != "1";   // false (coerced, so equal)

docs.title: ES2026 and Equality
docs.text:
ES2026 does not introduce new equality operators. However, it adds features that interact with equality:

// Object.is is recommended for memoization and diffing
Object.is(prevState, nextState); // ES2026 best practice

// Error.isError — reliable error detection
Error.isError(new Error()); // true
Error.isError({ message: "fake" }); // false

// Map.getOrInsert — upsert with SameValueZero key matching
map.getOrInsert(key, defaultValue);

docs.title: The "Four Lenses" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of equality as looking at two values through four different lenses:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Equality Lenses                          │
│                                                             │
│  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐                  │
│  │  IsLooselyEqual │  │  IsStrictlyEqual│                  │
│  │  (==)           │  │  (===)          │                  │
│  │                 │  │                 │                  │
│  │  Coerces types  │  │  No coercion    │                  │
│  │  NaN ≠ NaN      │  │  NaN ≠ NaN      │                  │
│  │  -0 = +0        │  │  -0 = +0        │                  │
│  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘                  │
│                                                             │
│  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐                  │
│  │  SameValue      │  │  SameValueZero  │                  │
│  │  (Object.is)    │  │  (Built-ins)    │                  │
│  │                 │  │                 │                  │
│  │  No coercion    │  │  No coercion    │                  │
│  │  NaN = NaN      │  │  NaN = NaN      │                  │
│  │  -0 ≠ +0        │  │  -0 = +0        │                  │
│  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SameValueZero is the "middle ground" — it differs from Strict Equality only in treating NaN as equal to itself, and differs from SameValue only in treating -0 and +0 as equal.

docs.title: The "Same Value, Different Question" Mental Model
docs.text:
The four algorithms answer different questions:

Algorithm Question It Answers === "Are these the same value, ignoring signed zero, and treating NaN as unequal?" == "Are these equal after coercing types?" Object.is() "Are these the exact same value, including NaN and signed zero?" SameValueZero "Are these the same value for collection lookup, treating NaN as equal and signed zero as equal?"

docs.title: The "Coercion Ladder" Mental Model
docs.text:
== follows a specific coercion order:

1. Same type? → Use ===
2. null vs undefined? → true
3. Number vs String? → String → Number
4. Boolean? → Boolean → Number
5. Object vs Primitive? → ToPrimitive(Object)
6. Otherwise → false

docs.title: The "IEEE 754 vs. JavaScript" Mental Model
docs.text:
NaN and -0 are inherited from IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic:

  • NaN is the result of undefined operations (0/0, Math.sqrt(-1)).
  • -0 is a signed zero that preserves direction information.

JavaScript's === follows IEEE 754 for NaN (not equal to itself) but deviates for -0 (treats it as equal to +0) . Object.is() restores the IEEE 754 view for both.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Four Equality Algorithms
docs.text: Algorithm Spec Name Used By Coercion NaN Equal -0 = +0 Loose IsLooselyEqual == Yes No Yes Strict IsStrictlyEqual === No No Yes SameValue SameValue Object.is() No Yes No SameValueZero SameValueZero Map, Set, includes, indexOf (partially) No Yes Yes

docs.title: Concept 2: Strict Equality (===) — The Default
docs.text:
Strict equality compares two values without type coercion:

  • If the types differ → false.
  • If both are NaN → false.
  • If one is +0 and the other -0 → true.
  • Otherwise, compare values directly.
"0" === 0;     // false
null === undefined; // false
NaN === NaN;   // false
-0 === +0;     // true

Strict equality is almost always the correct comparison to use .

docs.title: Concept 3: Loose Equality (==) — Coercion Rules
docs.text:
== performs type coercion before comparing:

Comparison Result Reason null == undefined true Special case null == 0 false null only equals undefined "5" == 5 true String → Number 0 == false true Boolean → Number "" == false true Both → Number: 0 == 0 [] == false true Both → Number: 0 == 0 [1] == 1 true Array → String → Number NaN == NaN false IEEE 754

docs.title: Concept 4: SameValue (Object.is()) — The Strictest
docs.text:
Object.is() uses the SameValue algorithm:

  • No type coercion.
  • NaN is equal to NaN.
  • -0 is not equal to +0.
  • Objects are compared by reference.
Object.is(NaN, NaN);   // true
Object.is(-0, +0);     // false
Object.is(0, -0);      // false
Object.is({}, {});     // false

docs.title: Concept 5: SameValueZero — The Built-In Standard
docs.text:
SameValueZero is used by:

  • Map keys
  • Set values
  • Array.prototype.includes
  • TypedArray.prototype.includes
  • String.prototype.includes (indirectly)

It treats NaN as equal to itself and +0/-0 as equal .

new Map([[NaN, "a"]]).get(NaN); // "a"
new Set([NaN, NaN]).size;       // 1
[NaN].includes(NaN);            // true
[NaN].indexOf(NaN);             // -1 (indexOf uses ===)

docs.title: Concept 6: Object Comparison Is Always by Reference
docs.text:
None of the equality algorithms compare object structure.

{} === {};              // false
[] === [];              // false
Object.is({}, {});      // false
new Date(0) === new Date(0); // false

For deep equality, you need a library or custom function.

docs.title: Concept 7: NaN Is Never Equal to Itself with === or ==
docs.text:
NaN === NaN;  // false
NaN == NaN;   // false

This follows IEEE 754. To check for NaN, use:

Number.isNaN(value);  // reliable, no coercion
Object.is(value, NaN); // also reliable

docs.title: Concept 8: -0 and +0 Are Equal with === and ==
docs.text:
-0 === +0;  // true
-0 == +0;   // true

But Object.is() distinguishes them:

Object.is(-0, +0); // false

docs.title: Concept 9: null and undefined — Loose Equality Special Case
docs.text:
null == undefined;   // true
null === undefined;  // false

null does not equal 0, "", or false:

null == 0;     // false
null == "";    // false
null == false; // false

docs.title: Concept 10: BigInt Equality
docs.text:
1n === 1n;    // true
1n == 1;      // true (coercion)
1n === 1;     // false (different types)
0n == false;  // true (both → number: 0 == 0)
0n === false; // false

BigInt can be loosely compared to Number, but strict comparison requires same type.

docs.title: Concept 11: Object.is() and === Differences
docs.text: Value Pair === Object.is() NaN, NaN false true -0, +0 true false 0, -0 true false Everything else Same Same

docs.title: Concept 12: When to Use Each
docs.text: Need Use Default comparison === null/undefined check == null (loose) NaN comparison Object.is() or Number.isNaN() Signed zero distinction Object.is() Collection keys SameValueZero (built-in) Deep object equality Custom or library

docs.title: Concept 13: ES2026 Equality-Related Features
docs.text:
• Object.is() is recommended for memoization and diffing in modern code .
  • Error.isError() provides reliable error detection.
  • Map.getOrInsert() uses SameValueZero for key matching.
  • Math.sumPrecise() does not change equality but improves numeric precision.

docs.title: Concept 14: ESLint and Equality
docs.text: The ESLint rule eqeqeq enforces === and !== — it is considered good practice to use type-safe equality operators .

docs.title: Concept 15: isNaN() vs Number.isNaN() vs Object.is()
docs.text:
isNaN("hello");          // true (coerces — unreliable)
Number.isNaN("hello");   // false (no coercion — reliable)
Object.is("hello", NaN); // false (no coercion — reliable)

docs.title: Concept 16: Equality in switch
docs.text:
switch uses strict equality (===) for case matching:

switch ("5") {
    case 5: console.log("number"); break;   // ❌ not matched
    case "5": console.log("string"); break; // ✅ matched
}

docs.title: Concept 17: Equality in Array.prototype.sort
docs.text:
The default sort() converts elements to strings and compares lexicographically — not the same as === comparison:

[10, 2, 1].sort(); // [1, 10, 2] — lexicographic
[10, 2, 1].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 10] — numeric

docs.title: Concept 18: Equality and Set/Map
docs.text:
new Set([1, "1", 1]).size;   // 2 (1 and "1" are distinct)
new Set([NaN, NaN]).size;    // 1 (SameValueZero)
new Set([-0, +0]).size;      // 1 (SameValueZero)

docs.title: Step-by-Step: === Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  If Type(x) ≠ Type(y) → return false.
    │
    ▼
2.  If both are Undefined → return true.
3.  If both are Null → return true.
4.  If both are Boolean → compare values.
5.  If both are String → compare code units.
6.  If both are Number:
    │   - If either is NaN → return false.
    │   - If same value → return true.
    │   - If +0 and -0 → return true.
7.  If both are BigInt → compare values.
8.  If both are Symbol → compare identity.
9.  If both are Object → compare references.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: == Evaluation (IsLooselyEqual)
docs.text:
1.  If Type(x) = Type(y) → return IsStrictlyEqual(x, y).
    │
    ▼
2.  If x is null and y is undefined → return true.
3.  If x is undefined and y is null → return true.
4.  If x is Number and y is String → return x == ToNumber(y).
5.  If x is String and y is Number → return ToNumber(x) == y.
6.  If x is BigInt and y is String → String → BigInt.
7.  If x is String and y is BigInt → String → BigInt.
8.  If x is Boolean → return ToNumber(x) == y.
9.  If y is Boolean → return x == ToNumber(y).
10. If x is Number/String/BigInt/Symbol and y is Object → ToPrimitive(y).
11. If x is Object and y is Number/String/BigInt/Symbol → ToPrimitive(x).
12. If x is BigInt and y is Number → compare if mathematical values equal.
13. If x is Number and y is BigInt → compare if mathematical values equal.
14. Otherwise → return false.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Object.is() Evaluation (SameValue)
docs.text:
1.  If Type(x) ≠ Type(y) → return false.
    │
    ▼
2.  If both are Undefined → return true.
3.  If both are Null → return true.
4.  If both are Boolean → compare values.
5.  If both are String → compare code units.
6.  If both are Symbol → compare identity.
7.  If both are Number:
    │   - If both are NaN → return true.
    │   - If both are +0 → return true.
    │   - If both are -0 → return true.
    │   - If both are non-zero, not NaN, and same value → return true.
    │   - Otherwise → return false.
8.  If both are BigInt → compare values.
9.  If both are Object → compare references.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: SameValueZero
docs.text:
Identical to SameValue except:

If both are Number and one is +0 and the other is -0 → return true.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Object.is() in Practice
docs.text:
// Memoization example
function memoize(fn) {
    let lastArgs = null;
    let lastResult;
    return (...args) => {
        if (lastArgs && args.length === lastArgs.length &&
            args.every((arg, i) => Object.is(arg, lastArgs[i]))) {
            return lastResult;
        }
        lastArgs = args;
        lastResult = fn(...args);
        return lastResult;
    };
}

Object.is() correctly handles NaN arguments and distinguishes -0 from +0 — important for numerical memoization.

docs.title: The Abstract Operations in ECMA-262
docs.text:
The spec defines equality in Section 7.2:

Operation Spec Section Operator/Method IsLooselyEqual 7.2.12 == IsStrictlyEqual 7.2.13 === SameValue 7.2.10 Object.is() SameValueZero 7.2.11 Built-ins

docs.title: SameValue vs. SameValueZero
docs.text:
From the spec:

SameValueZero differs from SameValue only in its treatment of +0 and -0 .

  • SameValue: +0 and -0 are different.
  • SameValueZero: +0 and -0 are the same.

docs.title: Object.is() Is Not ===
docs.text:
Object.is() is not equivalent to ===. The only differences are in their treatment of signed zeros and NaN values :

  • === treats -0 and +0 as equal but NaN as unequal.
  • Object.is() treats -0 and +0 as unequal but NaN as equal.

docs.title: How V8 Optimizes Equality
docs.text:
V8 compiles === and == into specialized bytecode based on type feedback:

function compare(a, b) { return a === b; }
compare(1, 2);   // feedback: number, number → fast integer compare
compare("a", "b"); // guard fails → deoptimize → string compare

Each comparison site records the types it has seen. The JIT emits speculative machine code with guards. If a guard fails, the function deoptimizes.

docs.title: SameValueZero in Built-Ins
docs.text:
Map, Set, and Array.prototype.includes use SameValueZero internally. This is why NaN keys work in Map and why [NaN].includes(NaN) is true while [NaN].indexOf(NaN) is -1:

  • includes uses SameValueZero.
  • indexOf uses Strict Equality.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of NaN
docs.text: NaN is defined as not equal to itself by IEEE 754. The spec preserves this for == and === but reverses it for SameValue and SameValueZero.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of -0
docs.text: -0 and +0 are the same mathematical value but different IEEE 754 representations. The spec treats them as equal for == and === but different for SameValue.

docs.title: Equality Evaluation Lifecycle
docs.text: Values → Select algorithm → Apply type rules → Compare → Boolean result

docs.title: Loose Equality Workflow
docs.text:
Values → Same type? → Yes → IsStrictlyEqual
              │
              ▼ No
         Special cases? → null/undefined → true
              │
              ▼
         Coerce → Compare → Result

docs.title: Strict Equality Workflow
docs.text:
Values → Same type? → No → false
              │
              ▼ Yes
         Compare values → Result

docs.title: SameValue Workflow
docs.text:
Values → Same type? → No → false
              │
              ▼ Yes
         NaN? → true
         -0/+0? → false
         Compare → Result

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write comparison → ESLint eqeqeq → TypeScript → Run → Debug

ESLint's eqeqeq rule enforces === and !==, catching accidental loose comparisons at lint time .

docs.title: Example 1: Strict Equality Is the Default
docs.text:
const a = 1;
const b = "1";

console.log(a === b); // false
console.log(a == b);  // true (coercion)

Breakdown:

  • === returns false because types differ.
  • == returns true because "1" is coerced to 1.

docs.title: Example 2: NaN Comparison
docs.text:
const result = 0 / 0;

console.log(result === result);          // false
console.log(Object.is(result, NaN));     // true
console.log(Number.isNaN(result));       // true

Breakdown:

  • NaN is never equal to itself with ===.
  • Object.is() and Number.isNaN() are reliable.

docs.title: Example 3: Signed Zero
docs.text:
console.log(-0 === +0);               // true
console.log(Object.is(-0, +0));       // false
console.log(1 / -0);                  // -Infinity
console.log(1 / +0);                  // Infinity

Breakdown:

  • === ignores sign of zero.
  • Object.is() distinguishes them.

docs.title: Example 4: null vs undefined
docs.text:
console.log(null == undefined);   // true
console.log(null === undefined);  // false
console.log(null == 0);           // false
console.log(undefined == 0);      // false

Breakdown:

  • null and undefined are loosely equal.
  • Neither equals 0 loosely.

docs.title: Example 5: Object Comparison
docs.text:
const obj1 = { a: 1 };
const obj2 = { a: 1 };

console.log(obj1 === obj2);           // false
console.log(Object.is(obj1, obj2));   // false
console.log(obj1 === obj1);           // true

Breakdown:

  • Objects are compared by reference.
  • Deep equality requires a library.

docs.title: Example 6: Map and Set with SameValueZero
docs.text:
const map = new Map();
map.set(NaN, "value");
console.log(map.get(NaN)); // "value"

const set = new Set([NaN, NaN, -0, +0]);
console.log(set.size); // 2 (NaN and 0)

Breakdown:

  • Map and Set use SameValueZero.
  • NaN works as a key.
  • -0 and +0 are treated as the same value.

docs.title: Example 7: Array.prototype.includes vs indexOf
docs.text:
const arr = [NaN, 1, 2];

console.log(arr.includes(NaN)); // true
console.log(arr.indexOf(NaN));  // -1

Breakdown:

  • includes uses SameValueZero → NaN is found.
  • indexOf uses Strict Equality → NaN is not found.

docs.title: Example 8: BigInt Equality
docs.text:
console.log(1n === 1n); // true
console.log(1n == 1);   // true
console.log(1n === 1);  // false
console.log(0n == false); // true

Breakdown:

  • BigInt can be loosely compared to Number.
  • Strict comparison requires same type.

docs.title: Example 9: Object.is() for Memoization
docs.text:
function memoize(fn) {
    const cache = new Map();
    return (...args) => {
        const key = args.map(a => Object.is(a, NaN) ? "NaN" : a).join("|");
        if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);
        const result = fn(...args);
        cache.set(key, result);
        return result;
    };
}

Breakdown:

  • Object.is() correctly identifies NaN.
  • Ensures NaN arguments don't break memoization.

docs.title: Example 10: eqeqeq ESLint Rule
docs.text:
{
    "rules": {
        "eqeqeq": ["error", "always"]
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • Enforces === and !==.
  • Prevents accidental loose comparisons.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Need Operator / Method Default comparison === null/undefined check == null NaN comparison Object.is() or Number.isNaN() Signed zero distinction Object.is() Collection keys Map, Set (SameValueZero) Array membership includes (SameValueZero) Deep object equality Library or custom Memoization Object.is() Switch cases ===

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use === and !== by default. Why: avoids coercion surprises; predictable.
  2. Use == null only for null/undefined checks. Why: the one legitimate loose equality use case.
  3. Use Object.is() for NaN and signed-zero comparison. Why: only way to distinguish them.
  4. Use Number.isNaN() for NaN detection. Why: reliable, no coercion.
  5. Enable ESLint eqeqeq. Why: enforces type-safe equality automatically.
  6. Avoid == except for null/undefined. Why: coercion rules are complex.
  7. Use includes over indexOf for NaN. Why: includes uses SameValueZero.
  8. Understand that objects compare by reference. Why: {a:1} === {a:1} is false.
  9. Use libraries for deep equality. Why: JavaScript has no built-in deep comparison.
  10. Be aware of -0 and NaN in numeric code. Why: === cannot distinguish them.
  11. Use Object.is() in memoization and diffing. Why: handles edge cases correctly (ES2026 best practice).
  12. Keep comparisons simple. Why: complex expressions are hard to debug.
  13. Use TypeScript to catch type mismatches. Why: prevents unintended comparisons.
  14. Document intentional loose equality. Why: == usage should be justified.
  15. Test edge cases: NaN, -0, null, undefined. Why: equality bugs hide there.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using == Instead of ===
docs.text:
0 == "";    // true
0 == false; // true
"" == false; // true

✅ Correct:

0 === "";    // false
0 === false; // false
"" === false; // false

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: NaN === NaN for NaN Check
docs.text:
if (value === NaN) { /* never runs */ }

✅ Correct:

if (Number.isNaN(value)) { /* ... */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Comparing Objects by Value
docs.text:
if ({ a: 1 } === { a: 1 }) { /* never runs */ }

✅ Correct: Use a deep equality library.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting -0 vs +0
docs.text:
if (value === 0) { /* matches -0 too */ }

✅ Correct:

if (Object.is(value, 0)) { /* only +0 */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: indexOf for NaN
docs.text:
[NaN].indexOf(NaN); // -1

✅ Correct:

[NaN].includes(NaN); // true

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming null == 0
docs.text:
null == 0; // false

✅ Correct: null only loosely equals undefined.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Object.is() When === Works
docs.text:
Object.is(1, 1); // true — but === is clearer

✅ Correct: Use === unless NaN or -0 matters.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting switch Uses ===
docs.text:
switch ("5") {
    case 5: /* not matched */ break;
}

✅ Correct: Use the same type in case.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Understanding SameValueZero
docs.text:
new Map([[NaN, 1]]).get(NaN); // 1 — works because SameValueZero

✅ Correct: Understand that Map and Set use SameValueZero.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: ESLint eqeqeq Disabled
docs.text: ✅ Correct: Enable eqeqeq to catch loose equality mistakes automatically.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• === is fastest — no coercion, direct comparison.
  • == is slower — coercion adds overhead.
  • Object.is() — similar to ===; slight function call overhead.
  • Type stability — keep compared types consistent for JIT optimization.
  • Map/Set lookups — O(1) average with SameValueZero.
  • includes vs indexOf — includes is optimized for SameValueZero.
  • Deep equality — library-dependent; avoid in hot paths.
  • String comparison — can be expensive for long strings.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use === in hot loops.
  2. Avoid == in performance-critical code.
  3. Keep comparison types stable.
  4. Use Map/Set for lookups.
  5. Use includes over indexOf for correctness and speed.
  6. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.

docs.title: Coercion Attacks
docs.text:
if (input == 1) { /* bypassed with "1" or [1] */ }

Defense: Always use ===.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Objects with manipulated prototypes can affect equality checks.

Defense: Validate input; use Object.create(null).

docs.title: NaN and DoS
docs.text:
Comparing with NaN can lead to unexpected logic branches.

Defense: Use Number.isNaN() explicitly.

docs.title: Signed Zero
docs.text:
Security-sensitive numeric code may care about -0 vs +0.

Defense: Use Object.is() when sign matters.

docs.title: Object Reference Comparison
docs.text:
Comparing objects by reference can lead to security bugs if identity is assumed.

Defense: Use deep equality for untrusted data.

docs.title: Map/Set Key Collisions
docs.text:
SameValueZero treats -0 and +0 as the same key.

Defense: Be aware of this when keys are numeric.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.log(a === b, a, b) — log comparison and both values.
  • Number.isNaN(value) — reliable NaN check.
  • Object.is(a, b) — SameValue check.
  • Object.prototype.toString.call(value) — precise type detection.
  • ESLint eqeqeq — flags ==.
  • debugger; — inspect values during comparison.
  • Chrome DevTools Console — type-aware autocomplete.
  • TypeScript — catches type mismatches.
  • Break comparisons into variables — easier to inspect.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Operator / Method When to Use === Default — almost always == null null/undefined check Object.is() NaN or signed-zero comparison Number.isNaN() NaN detection includes Array membership with NaN Map/Set Collection with SameValueZero

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• == — never, except == null.
  • === for NaN — use Number.isNaN().
  • === for signed zero — use Object.is().
  • indexOf for NaN — use includes.
  • Object comparison with any operator — use deep equality.
  • Object.is() when === suffices — prefer === for clarity.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Type Conversion — coercion rules that drive ==
  • Data Types — what is being compared
  • Operators — comparison operators
  • Strict Mode — catches some equality errors
  • Object.is() — SameValue algorithm
  • Number.isNaN() — reliable NaN check
  • SameValueZero — built-in collection equality
  • Map — uses SameValueZero
  • Set — uses SameValueZero
  • Array.prototype.includes — uses SameValueZero
  • ESLint eqeqeq — enforces strict equality

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• JavaScript has four equality algorithms, not three — SameValueZero is the fourth, used by built-ins .
  • NaN !== NaN is the only value not equal to itself — a direct consequence of IEEE 754.
  • Object.is() was added in ES2015 — before that, there was no standard way to compare NaN or distinguish -0 .
  • Object.is() is not equivalent to === — it differs only on NaN and signed zeros .
  • SameValueZero differs from SameValue only in treating +0 and -0 as equal .
  • Map and Set use SameValueZero, which is why NaN keys work.
  • Array.prototype.includes uses SameValueZero — indexOf uses Strict Equality.
  • null == undefined is true, but null == 0 is false.
  • "1" == 1 is true — string is coerced to number.
  • [] == false is true — both become 0.
  • switch uses === — no coercion occurs.
  • ESLint's eqeqeq rule enforces type-safe equality .
  • ES2026 recommends Object.is() for memoization and diffing .
  • ES2026 added Error.isError() for reliable error detection.
  • Objects always compare by reference — none of the four algorithms does deep comparison.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• JavaScript has four equality algorithms: IsLooselyEqual (==), IsStrictlyEqual (===), SameValue (Object.is()), and SameValueZero (built-ins).
  • === is the default — no coercion, predictable.
  • == performs coercion — only use == null for null/undefined checks.
  • Object.is() handles NaN and signed zeros correctly — use it when those matter.
  • SameValueZero is used by Map, Set, and includes — treats NaN as equal and +0/-0 as equal.
  • NaN !== NaN — use Number.isNaN() for detection.
  • -0 === +0 — use Object.is() to distinguish.
  • Objects compare by reference — no built-in deep equality.
  • null == undefined is true; null == 0 is false.
  • ESLint eqeqeq enforces === and !==.
  • ES2026 recommends Object.is() for memoization and diffing.
  • Use includes over indexOf for NaN.
