  • Understand the four lenses — each answers a different question.
  • When in doubt, use === — it is almost always the correct choice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Strict mode is an opt-in variant of JavaScript that changes the language's semantics to be stricter — turning silent errors into exceptions, forbidding certain legacy syntax, and fixing behaviors that hindered engine optimization. It is activated by the directive "use strict" (or 'use strict') placed at the beginning of a script or function body.

"use strict";

// In strict mode, this throws a ReferenceError:
undeclaredVariable = 10;

In 2026, strict mode is the default for all modern JavaScript code. Every ECMAScript module (import/export) runs in strict mode automatically. Classes are always strict. And TypeScript 6.0 (released March 2026) enabled strict mode by default, meaning new projects get stricter type-checking and runtime semantics without explicit configuration.

Strict mode is not a subset of JavaScript — it intentionally has different semantics from sloppy (non-strict) mode. Both modes can coexist in the same program, allowing incremental adoption.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Strict mode exists to solve three problems:

  1. Silent errors — JavaScript originally ignored many mistakes (typos, invalid assignments, unsafe deletions). Strict mode turns them into thrown errors.
  2. Optimization blockers — Some sloppy-mode behaviors (like with and arguments aliasing) made it hard for engines to optimize. Strict mode removes them.
  3. Future-proofing — Strict mode reserves syntax that may be used in future ECMAScript versions, preventing conflicts.

The result is safer, faster, and more predictable code.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Language Fundamentals
├── Variables             ✅ done
├── Data Types            ✅ done
├── Operators             ✅ done
├── Expressions           ✅ done
├── Statements            ✅ done
├── Type Conversion       ✅ done
├── Equality              ✅ done
├── Strict Mode           ← you are here

Strict Mode is the final concept in Language Fundamentals. It is placed last because it modifies the behavior of everything that came before it — variables, functions, operators, and equality.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
JavaScript was designed in 1995 for forgiving, beginner-friendly scripting. The language silently ignored many mistakes:

  • Assigning to an undeclared variable created a global.
  • Assigning to a read-only property failed silently.
  • Deleting an undeletable property returned false without warning.
  • Duplicate function parameters were allowed (last one won).
  • with statements made scope unpredictable.
  • Octal literals (0644) were interpreted as octal in some contexts.

This tolerance made JavaScript easy to start with — but dangerous at scale. In large applications, silent failures became hours of debugging. A single typo could create a global variable that overwrote a browser API, caused memory leaks, or introduced security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Problem Sloppy Mode Behavior Consequence Undeclared variable assignment Creates global silently Global pollution, memory leaks Assigning to read-only property Fails silently Data corruption Deleting undeletable property Returns false Silent logic errors Duplicate parameters Last one wins Confusing behavior with statement Allowed Unpredictable scope Octal literals Interpreted as octal Confusing for developers

docs.title: Why Strict Mode Was Introduced
docs.text:
The ECMAScript committee could not simply change the default behavior — millions of existing websites depended on the lenient rules. Instead, they made strict mode opt-in so developers could adopt it file by file or function by function.

Strict mode was introduced in ECMAScript 5 (2009) as a way to opt into a restricted variant of JavaScript — a safer, more predictable subset that eliminates footguns and enables optimization.

docs.title: Why It Still Matters in 2026
docs.text: In 2026, strict mode feels less like an option and more like seatbelts. Modern engines and bundlers hide many footguns, but mixed codebases are real — marketing snippets, analytics tags, browser extensions, userscripts, and CMS-injected HTML often bypass your build pipeline. If you debug unpredictable globals or this values in 2026, you are likely straddling strict and non-strict boundaries.

docs.title: Enabling Strict Mode for an Entire Script
docs.text:
Place "use strict" before any other statements:

"use strict";

const v = "I am a strict-mode script";
// undeclaredGlobal = 10; // ❌ ReferenceError

Placement rules: - Must be the literal first statement (comments are allowed before it, but no code). - Shebang (#!/usr/bin/env node) in Node.js is ignored and does not cancel strictness. - Any preceding statement — even const x = 1; — cancels strictness.

docs.title: Enabling Strict Mode for a Function
docs.text:
Place "use strict" at the top of the function body:

function strictFunction() {
    "use strict";
    // undeclaredVar = 10; // ❌ ReferenceError
    return "strict";
}

Restriction: "use strict" can only be applied to functions with simple parameters. Using it in functions with rest, default, or destructured parameters is a syntax error.

// ❌ SyntaxError
function bad({ a, b }) {
    "use strict";
}

docs.title: Strict Mode for Modules (Automatic)
docs.text:
Every ECMAScript module is strict by default:

// module.mjs — automatically strict
export function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}`;
}
// undeclaredVar = 10; // ❌ ReferenceError

No directive needed — import and export opt you into strict mode automatically.

docs.title: Strict Mode for Classes (Automatic)
docs.text:
All class bodies are strict by default:

class User {
    constructor(name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
    // No "use strict" needed — classes are always strict
}

docs.title: Strict Mode for eval and Function
docs.text:
eval code, Function constructor code, event handler attributes, and strings passed to setTimeout are treated as complete scripts or function bodies — strict mode applies if the directive is present.

eval('"use strict"; undeclaredVar = 10;'); // ❌ ReferenceError
new Function('"use strict"; undeclaredVar = 10;')(); // ❌ ReferenceError

docs.title: Strict Mode in TypeScript 6.0 (2026)
docs.text:
TypeScript 6.0 (March 2026) turned strict on by default and unconditionally emits "use strict" in non-ESM output files. New TypeScript projects now get strict runtime semantics automatically.

// tsconfig.json — strict is now default
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "strict": true
    }
}

docs.title: Directive Prologue
docs.text:
Strict mode is part of the directive prologue — a sequence of string literal expression statements at the start of a script or function. Multiple directives are allowed:

"use strict";
"use asm";  // another directive
// both directives are active

docs.title: The "Seatbelts" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of strict mode as seatbelts in a car:

  • You can drive without them (sloppy mode) — but the risk is higher.
  • They don't change how the car works — they change what happens when something goes wrong.
  • They catch mistakes before they become accidents.
  • Modern cars have them on by default (ES modules, classes, TypeScript 6.0).

docs.title: The "Warnings as Errors" Mental Model
docs.text:
Strict mode is like switching your code editor from "ignore all warnings" to "treat warnings as errors":

Sloppy mode:  "You misspelled a variable — I'll just create a new one."
Strict mode:  "You misspelled a variable — ReferenceError!"

The same code runs, but now the language actively tells you when something looks wrong.

docs.title: The "Two Worlds" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    JavaScript                            │
│                                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────┐  │
│  │   Strict Mode        │  │   Sloppy Mode           │  │
│  │                     │  │                         │  │
│  │  • Errors thrown    │  │  • Errors silent        │  │
│  │  • No globals       │  │  • Globals created      │  │
│  │  • this = undefined │  │  • this = global        │  │
│  │  • No with          │  │  • with allowed         │  │
│  │  • No octal         │  │  • Octal allowed        │  │
│  │  • Duplicate params │  │  • Duplicate params OK  │  │
│  │    forbidden        │  │                         │  │
│  └─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                         │
│  ES modules, classes, TypeScript 6.0 → strict by default│
│  Classic scripts, inline handlers → sloppy by default   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Opt-In Ladder" Mental Model
docs.text:
Level 1: No strict mode anywhere
         ↓
Level 2: Function-level "use strict"
         ↓
Level 3: File-level "use strict"
         ↓
Level 4: ES modules (automatic strict)
         ↓
Level 5: TypeScript 6.0 with strict: true (default)

Adopt strictness at the smallest possible boundary while migrating legacy code.

docs.title: Concept 1: What Strict Mode Changes
docs.text:
Strict mode makes several changes to normal JavaScript semantics:

  1. Eliminates silent errors — changes them to throw errors.
  2. Fixes optimization blockers — strict code can sometimes run faster than sloppy code.
  3. Prohibits future-reserved syntax — prevents conflicts with future ECMAScript versions.

docs.title: Concept 2: Accidental Globals Become Errors
docs.text:
In sloppy mode, assigning to an undeclared variable creates a global:

// Sloppy mode
function tally(items) {
    sum = 0; // creates global `sum`!
    for (const price of items) sum += price;
    return sum;
}

In strict mode, this throws a ReferenceError:

"use strict";
function tally(items) {
    sum = 0; // ❌ ReferenceError
}

This single rule eliminates a class of production bugs.

docs.title: Concept 3: this Is undefined in Plain Function Calls
docs.text:
In sloppy mode, calling a function without a receiver sets this to the global object:

function f() { return this; }
f(); // window (browser) or globalThis (Node)

In strict mode, this is undefined:

"use strict";
function f() { return this; }
f(); // undefined

This catches constructor mistakes — calling a constructor without new throws a TypeError instead of silently polluting the global object.

docs.title: Concept 4: Assignment to Read-Only Properties Throws
docs.text:
"use strict";
const obj = {};
Object.defineProperty(obj, "x", { value: 1, writable: false });
obj.x = 2; // ❌ TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'x'

In sloppy mode, this fails silently.

docs.title: Concept 5: Adding Properties to Non-Extensible Objects Throws
docs.text:
"use strict";
const obj = Object.freeze({ a: 1 });
obj.b = 2; // ❌ TypeError: Cannot add property b, object is not extensible

In sloppy mode, this fails silently.

docs.title: Concept 6: Deleting Undeletable Properties Throws
docs.text:
"use strict";
delete Object.prototype; // ❌ TypeError: Cannot delete property 'prototype'

In sloppy mode, this returns false and continues.

docs.title: Concept 7: Duplicate Function Parameters Are Forbidden
docs.text:
"use strict";
function f(a, a) { } // ❌ SyntaxError: Duplicate parameter name

In sloppy mode, the last parameter wins — almost never the developer's intent.

docs.title: Concept 8: Octal Literals Are Forbidden
docs.text:
"use strict";
const x = 0644; // ❌ SyntaxError: Octal literals are not allowed

In sloppy mode, 0644 is interpreted as octal (420 in decimal). Use 0o644 in strict mode if you need octal.

docs.title: Concept 9: The with Statement Is Forbidden
docs.text:
"use strict";
with (obj) { } // ❌ SyntaxError: Strict mode code may not include a with statement

with makes scope unpredictable and blocks optimization. It is forbidden in strict mode.

docs.title: Concept 10: Reserved Words in Strict Mode
docs.text:
The following identifiers become reserved words in strict mode and cannot be used as variable names:

implements, interface, let, package, private, protected, public, static, yield

"use strict";
const let = 10; // ❌ SyntaxError: Unexpected strict mode reserved word

docs.title: Concept 11: eval and arguments Are Simplified
docs.text:
In strict mode:

  • eval cannot introduce new variables into the surrounding scope.
  • arguments does not alias function parameters.
  • Assigning to eval or arguments is a syntax error.
"use strict";
eval("var x = 10;");
console.log(typeof x); // "undefined" — x is scoped to eval

docs.title: Concept 12: arguments.callee and arguments.caller Are Forbidden
docs.text:
"use strict";
function f() {
    return arguments.callee; // ❌ TypeError
}

These were used for recursion and stack inspection but blocked optimization.

docs.title: Concept 13: Top-Level this Is undefined in Modules
docs.text:
In ES modules, top-level this is undefined — not the global object.

// module.mjs
console.log(this); // undefined

docs.title: Concept 14: TypeScript 6.0 Strict Mode (2026)
docs.text:
TypeScript 6.0 (March 2026) turned strict on by default and unconditionally emits "use strict" in non-ESM files. This means:

  • New TypeScript projects get strict type-checking without configuration.
  • Emitted JavaScript includes "use strict" automatically.
  • Legacy options (target: es5, AMD, UMD) are deprecated.

docs.title: Concept 15: strict Is No Longer a Preset in TypeScript 6
docs.text: In TypeScript 6, strict is no longer a preset that enables more strict options. Instead, it is a preset that enables 9 looser type-checking options — reflecting that strict is now the baseline, and loosening is the opt-in.

docs.title: Concept 16: ES2026 Module Strictness
docs.text: Every ECMAScript module (.mjs, or .js with "type": "module") runs in strict mode by default. Classic scripts (.js without module type) still default to sloppy mode unless the directive is present.

docs.title: Concept 17: Strict Mode and Performance
docs.text: Strict mode was once rumored to slow execution, but modern engines optimize both modes. In 2026, the performance difference is negligible for typical web workloads. Strict mode's real benefit is correctness, not speed.

docs.title: Concept 18: Directives and the Directive Prologue
docs.text: Strict mode is part of the directive prologue — a sequence of string literal expression statements at the start of a script or function. Multiple directives are allowed, and strict mode is active for the entire script/function if any directive is "use strict".

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Directive Detection
docs.text:
1.  Parser reads the start of a script or function body.
    │
    ▼
2.  It looks for a directive prologue:
    │   - A sequence of string literal expression statements.
    │
    ▼
3.  If "use strict" is found in the prologue:
    │   - The entire script/function is marked strict.
    │
    ▼
4.  If a non-directive statement appears first:
    │   - Strict mode is not activated.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Accidental Global Prevention
docs.text:
1.  Assignment to an undeclared variable is encountered.
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine checks the scope chain for a binding.
    │
    ▼
3.  No binding found.
    │
    ▼
4.  In strict mode → throw ReferenceError.
    │
    ▼
5.  In sloppy mode → create a global binding.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: this Binding in Strict Mode
docs.text:
1.  Function is called without a receiver: f().
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine checks the function's [[Strict]] internal slot.
    │
    ▼
3.  If strict → this = undefined.
    │
    ▼
4.  If sloppy → this = globalThis.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Module Strictness
docs.text:
1.  Parser sees import or export at top level.
    │
    ▼
2.  Module is flagged as an ES module.
    │
    ▼
3.  Strict mode is automatically enabled.
    │
    ▼
4.  No directive required.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Function-Level Strictness During Migration
docs.text:
1.  Legacy file remains sloppy.
    │
    ▼
2.  A critical function is wrapped with "use strict".
    │
    ▼
3.  Only that function is strict.
    │
    ▼
4.  Rest of the file remains sloppy.
    │
    ▼
5.  Migrate other functions incrementally.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of Strict Mode
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification defines strict mode in multiple sections. Key rules include:

  • Forbidden Extensions (17.1) — function objects in strict mode must not have caller or arguments own properties.
  • Octal Literals — strict mode must not extend numeric literal syntax to include octal.
  • Future Reserved Words — additional keywords are reserved in strict mode.

docs.title: The [[Strict]] Internal Slot
docs.text:
Every function object has a [[Strict]] internal slot:

  • true — function was defined in strict mode.
  • false — function was defined in sloppy mode.

This slot determines this binding, arguments behavior, and other semantics.

docs.title: How Engines Detect Strict Mode
docs.text:
V8 marks scripts and functions as strict during parsing. The strict flag is stored with the function object and consulted at runtime for:

  • this binding.
  • Variable resolution.
  • eval behavior.
  • delete operations.

docs.title: Optimization Impact
docs.text:
Strict mode removes optimization blockers:

  • No with → static scope resolution.
  • No arguments aliasing → simpler parameter handling.
  • No implicit globals → predictable variable resolution.

Modern engines optimize both modes well, but strict mode gives the JIT more guarantees.

docs.title: TypeScript 6.0's Emit Behavior
docs.text: TypeScript 6.0 unconditionally emits "use strict" in non-ESM output files. For ESM output, strict mode is implicit, so the directive is not emitted. This ensures strict runtime semantics regardless of target module format.

docs.title: Module Detection
docs.text:
Engines detect ES modules by:

  • .mjs file extension.
  • <script type="module"> in HTML.
  • "type": "module" in package.json (Node.js).
  • Static import/export statements.

Once detected, strict mode is automatically enabled.

docs.title: Strict Mode Activation Lifecycle
docs.text:
Script/Function start
    │
    ▼
Directive prologue scanned
    │
    ▼
"use strict" found?
    │
    ├── Yes → Strict mode active
    │
    └── No → Sloppy mode active

docs.title: Migration Workflow
docs.text:
Legacy sloppy codebase
    │
    ▼
Identify critical functions
    │
    ▼
Add "use strict" to those functions
    │
    ▼
Fix errors (ReferenceError, TypeError, SyntaxError)
    │
    ▼
Expand to file-level "use strict"
    │
    ▼
Convert to ES modules (automatic strict)
    │
    ▼
Migrate to TypeScript 6.0 (strict by default)

docs.title: Development Workflow in 2026
docs.text:
Start new project
    │
    ▼
Use ES modules → strict by default
    │
    ▼
Use TypeScript 6.0 → strict: true by default
    │
    ▼
Lint with ESLint (strict rules)
    │
    ▼
Run tests → catch strict-mode errors early

docs.title: Directive Placement Workflow
docs.text:
File begins
    │
    ├── Shebang (Node.js) → ignored
    ├── Comments → allowed before directive
    │
    ▼
"use strict" must be first statement
    │
    ▼
Any other statement first → strictness cancelled

docs.title: Example 1: Accidental Global — Sloppy vs. Strict
docs.text:
// Sloppy mode
function tally(items) {
    sum = 0; // creates global `sum`
    for (const price of items) sum += price;
    return sum;
}
tally([1, 2, 3]);
console.log(globalThis.sum); // 6 — leaked to global!

// Strict mode
"use strict";
function tally(items) {
    sum = 0; // ❌ ReferenceError
}

Breakdown:

  • Sloppy mode creates a global sum.
  • Strict mode throws immediately — catching the bug at the source.

docs.title: Example 2: this Binding in Strict Mode
docs.text:
"use strict";

function f() {
    return this;
}

console.log(f()); // undefined — not the global object

Breakdown:

  • In sloppy mode, this would be window or globalThis.
  • In strict mode, this is undefined for plain calls.

docs.title: Example 3: Read-Only Property Assignment
docs.text:
"use strict";

const obj = {};
Object.defineProperty(obj, "x", { value: 1, writable: false });

obj.x = 2; // ❌ TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'x'

Breakdown:

  • Sloppy mode fails silently.
  • Strict mode throws a TypeError.

docs.title: Example 4: Non-Extensible Object
docs.text:
"use strict";

const obj = Object.freeze({ a: 1 });
obj.b = 2; // ❌ TypeError: Cannot add property b, object is not extensible

Breakdown:

  • Object.freeze() prevents additions, deletions, and modifications.
  • Strict mode throws on violation.

docs.title: Example 5: Duplicate Parameters
docs.text:
"use strict";

function createUser(name, name, age) { } // ❌ SyntaxError

Breakdown:

  • Sloppy mode allows duplicate parameters (last wins).
  • Strict mode forbids them — almost always a bug.

docs.title: Example 6: Octal Literals
docs.text:
"use strict";

const x = 0644; // ❌ SyntaxError: Octal literals are not allowed

Breakdown:

  • Use 0o644 for octal in strict mode.

docs.title: Example 7: Module Strictness (Automatic)
docs.text:
// module.mjs — automatically strict
export function greet(name) {
    undeclaredVar = 10; // ❌ ReferenceError — no directive needed
}

Breakdown:

  • ES modules are strict by default.

docs.title: Example 8: TypeScript 6.0 Strict Mode (2026)
docs.text:
// tsconfig.json — strict: true is now default in TS 6.0
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "strict": true
    }
}

// Emitted JavaScript includes "use strict" automatically
"use strict";
// ...

Breakdown:

  • TypeScript 6.0 emits "use strict" in non-ESM files.
  • New projects get strict semantics without configuration.

docs.title: Example 9: Function-Level Strictness During Migration
docs.text:
// Legacy file remains sloppy
const formatMoney = (function() {
    "use strict";
    return function formatMoney(amount, locale = "en-US") {
        const formatter = new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, {
            style: "currency",
            currency: "USD"
        });
        return formatter.format(amount);
    };
})();

Breakdown:

  • Only the function is strict — rest of the file remains sloppy.
  • Enables incremental migration.

docs.title: Example 10: arguments Behavior in Strict Mode
docs.text:
"use strict";

function f(a) {
    arguments[0] = 99;
    return a; // 10 — arguments is not aliased
}

f(10);

Breakdown:

  • In sloppy mode, arguments[0] = 99 would change a to 99.
  • In strict mode, arguments is a copy, not an alias.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Strict Mode? Notes ES modules ✅ Automatic No directive needed Classes ✅ Automatic Always strict TypeScript 6.0 ✅ Default strict: true by default Classic scripts ⚠️ Opt-in Add "use strict" Inline event handlers ❌ Sloppy Unless directive present eval ⚠️ Opt-in Add directive inside string Function constructor ⚠️ Opt-in Add directive inside string Legacy code ⚠️ Migrate incrementally Function by function Node.js CommonJS ⚠️ Opt-in Add "use strict"

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use ES modules for all new code. Why: strict mode is automatic, and module scope is cleaner.
  2. Enable strict: true in TypeScript 6.0. Why: it is the default — embrace it.
  3. Use "use strict" in classic scripts. Why: catches silent errors.
  4. Enable strict mode at the smallest boundary during migration. Why: function-level first, then file-level.
  5. Never use with. Why: forbidden in strict mode; blocks optimization.
  6. Always declare variables with let or const. Why: prevents accidental globals.
  7. Use const by default. Why: prevents reassignment errors.
  8. Avoid arguments in strict mode. Why: use rest parameters instead.
  9. Use 0o prefix for octal literals. Why: strict mode forbids 0644.
  10. Enable ESLint strict rules. Why: catches strict-mode violations at lint time.
  11. Test in both strict and sloppy modes during migration. Why: catch boundary issues.
  12. Check bundled output for directive placement. Why: bundlers may move "use strict".
  13. Use Object.freeze() for immutable data. Why: strict mode enforces it.
  14. Prefer undefined over null for this checks. Why: strict mode sets this to undefined.
  15. Document strict mode decisions. Why: teams need to know why a file is sloppy.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Directive Not First Statement
docs.text:
"use strict"; // ❌ cancelled by preceding statement
const x = 1;

✅ Correct:

"use strict";
const x = 1;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using "use strict" in a Block
docs.text:
{
    "use strict"; // ❌ ignored — blocks don't have directive prologues
}

✅ Correct: Use at script or function level.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Strict Mode in Functions with Non-Simple Parameters
docs.text:
function f({ a, b }) {
    "use strict"; // ❌ SyntaxError
}

✅ Correct: Use simple parameters, or strict mode at file level.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Strict Mode Slows Code
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Modern engines optimize both modes; performance difference is negligible.

✅ Correct: Use strict mode for correctness, not performance.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting Modules Are Already Strict
docs.text:
// module.mjs
"use strict"; // unnecessary — already strict

✅ Correct: Omit the directive in modules.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using arguments.callee
docs.text:
"use strict";
function f() {
    return arguments.callee; // ❌ TypeError
}

✅ Correct: Use named function expressions for recursion.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assigning to Read-Only Properties
docs.text:
"use strict";
const obj = Object.freeze({ a: 1 });
obj.a = 2; // ❌ TypeError

✅ Correct: Check Object.isFrozen() before assignment.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate Parameters
docs.text:
"use strict";
function f(a, a) { } // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct: Use distinct names.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Octal Literals
docs.text:
"use strict";
const x = 0644; // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

const x = 0o644;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming TypeScript Strict Mode Is Only Type-Level
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: TypeScript 6.0 emits "use strict" in non-ESM output — it affects runtime too.

✅ Correct: Understand that strict: true has both type-level and runtime effects.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Strict mode is not slower in 2026 — modern engines optimize both modes.
  • Strict mode removes optimization blockers — no with, no arguments aliasing.
  • Module strictness is free — no directive overhead.
  • TypeScript 6.0 emits "use strict" — no performance penalty.
  • Strict mode enables JIT optimizations — predictable variable resolution.
  • Strict mode may catch errors earlier — preventing performance-degrading bugs.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use strict mode for correctness, not speed.
  2. Use ES modules — strict by default, no directive needed.
  3. Avoid eval — it deoptimizes regardless of strictness.
  4. Keep functions small and predictable.
  5. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.

docs.title: Accidental Global Prevention
docs.text: Strict mode prevents global pollution — a vector for prototype pollution and cross-script interference.

docs.title: this Binding Safety
docs.text: Strict mode sets this to undefined in plain calls — preventing accidental global object mutation.

docs.title: Read-Only Property Protection
docs.text: Strict mode throws on read-only property assignment — preventing data corruption.

docs.title: Non-Extensible Object Protection
docs.text: Strict mode throws on adding properties to frozen/sealed objects — enforcing immutability.

docs.title: eval Isolation
docs.text: Strict mode prevents eval from introducing variables into the surrounding scope.

docs.title: Module Scope Isolation
docs.text: ES modules are strict and have module scope — preventing global namespace pollution.

docs.title: TypeScript 6.0 Strict Mode
docs.text: TypeScript 6.0's strict: true default catches more type errors at compile time, reducing runtime vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• ReferenceError: x is not defined — accidental global in strict mode.
  • TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property — strict mode caught a silent failure.
  • TypeError: Cannot add property — non-extensible object.
  • SyntaxError: Duplicate parameter name — strict mode forbids duplicates.
  • SyntaxError: Octal literals are not allowed — use 0o prefix.
  • Check directive placement — "use strict" must be first statement.
  • ESLint strict rules — catch violations at lint time.
  • TypeScript strict: true — catches type-level issues.
  • Node.js --use-strict — force strict mode for all modules.
  • Chrome DevTools Console — runs in sloppy mode by default.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text:
• ES modules — always (automatic).
  • Classes — always (automatic).
  • TypeScript 6.0 — always (default).
  • New classic scripts — add "use strict".
  • Function-level during migration — add "use strict" inside the function.
  • Node.js CommonJS — add "use strict".
  • Library code — use strict mode for safety.
  • Security-sensitive code — use strict mode for protection.

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Legacy code that depends on sloppy behavior — migrate carefully.
  • Inline event handlers — no directive context.
  • Bookmarklets — may rely on sloppy globals.
  • Third-party scripts you don't control — can't change them.
  • When you need with or octal literals — use alternatives instead.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Variables — strict mode prevents accidental globals
  • Functions — this binding changes in strict mode
  • Objects — read-only and non-extensible enforcement
  • ES Modules — automatic strict mode
  • Classes — automatic strict mode
  • TypeScript — strict: true by default in TS 6.0
  • ESLint — strict mode rules
  • Directive Prologue — how strict mode is activated
  • Sloppy Mode — the default non-strict mode
  • eval — strict mode isolates eval scope

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Strict mode was introduced in ES5 (2009) — over 15 years ago.
  • Every ES module is strict by default — no directive needed.
  • TypeScript 6.0 (March 2026) enabled strict: true by default.
  • TypeScript 6.0 emits "use strict" in non-ESM files automatically.
  • Strict mode is not a subset — it intentionally has different semantics.
  • "use strict" must be the literal first statement — comments are allowed, but code is not.
  • Strict mode forbids with — a major optimization blocker.
  • Strict mode reserves 9 additional keywords — including let, package, and static.
  • Duplicate parameters are a SyntaxError in strict mode.
  • Octal literals like 0644 are forbidden — use 0o644.
  • arguments.callee is forbidden in strict mode.
  • Strict mode sets this to undefined in plain calls.
  • eval cannot introduce variables into the surrounding scope in strict mode.
  • Performance difference between strict and sloppy is negligible in 2026.
  • Strict mode is "seatbelts" — not required, but highly recommended.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Strict mode is an opt-in variant of JavaScript that turns silent errors into thrown errors.
  • Activated by "use strict" at the start of a script or function.
  • ES modules and classes are automatically strict.
  • TypeScript 6.0 enables strict: true by default and emits "use strict" in non-ESM files.
  • Accidental globals throw ReferenceError instead of creating globals.
  • this is undefined in plain function calls — not the global object.
  • Read-only property assignment throws TypeError.
  • Non-extensible objects throw TypeError on addition.
  • Duplicate parameters are a SyntaxError.
  • Octal literals (0644) are forbidden — use 0o644.
  • with is forbidden.
  • arguments.callee is forbidden.
  • eval is isolated — cannot introduce variables into surrounding scope.
  • Strict mode is not slower in 2026 — performance difference is negligible.
  • Use ES modules — strict by default, no directive needed.
  • Migrate incrementally — function-level first, then file-level.
  • Strict mode is the modern default — embrace it for safer, more predictable code.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A conditional is a control flow statement that executes different code paths based on whether a condition evaluates to true or false. JavaScript provides four primary mechanisms for conditional branching:

// 1. if / else if / else
if (age >= 18) {
    console.log("adult");
} else if (age >= 13) {
    console.log("teen");
} else {
    console.log("child");
}

// 2. switch
switch (status) {
    case "active":   console.log("Active");   break;
    case "inactive": console.log("Inactive"); break;
    default:         console.log("Unknown");
}

// 3. Ternary operator
const label = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";

// 4. Pattern matching (ES2026)
const result = value match {
    0 => "zero",
    n when n > 0 => `positive: ${n}`,
    _ => "other",
};

Every conditional evaluates a test expression and selects a branch. The test is coerced to a boolean using JavaScript's truthiness rules — only eight values are falsy (false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN); everything else is truthy.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Conditionals exist to solve the decision problem: programs must respond differently to different inputs. Without conditionals, a program would execute the same instructions regardless of state — it could compute, but it could not decide.

Conditionals serve as the decision layer of the language:

  • if/else — general-purpose branching for boolean conditions.
  • switch — multi-way branching for exact-match comparisons.
  • Ternary — inline value selection for simple conditions.
  • Pattern matching (ES2026) — declarative structural selection for complex data shapes.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Control Flow
├── Conditionals          ← you are here
├── Loops
├── break & continue
├── Labels
├── Exceptions
└── Error Handling

Conditionals are the first concept in Control Flow because every other control flow mechanism — loops, breaks, exceptions — depends on the ability to make decisions. Loops decide whether to continue; exceptions decide whether to catch; everything starts here.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A program that cannot branch is a straight line — it executes every instruction in order, regardless of input. Real programs must:

  • Validate input before processing.
  • Route data based on type or shape.
  • Handle success and failure differently.
  • Choose between alternatives.
  • Guard against invalid state.

Without conditionals, every program would be a calculator with no decision-making capability.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES2026 Complex structural branching required nested if/else chains No pattern matching Destructuring and type-checking were manual No guard clauses Conditions were tangled with binding Verbose switch Required break in every case; fall-through was a common bug No expression-oriented branching if/else could not be assigned to variables

docs.title: Why Pattern Matching Was Introduced (ES2026)
docs.text:
Traditional conditionals work well for simple boolean tests but become unwieldy for structural decisions. Consider routing an API response:

// Traditional approach — verbose and error-prone
if (response.status === 200 && Array.isArray(response.data) && response.data.length > 0) {
    const firstItem = response.data[0];
    console.log("处理数据:", firstItem);
} else if (response.status === 404) {
    console.log("页面未找到");
} else if (response.error instanceof Error) {
    console.log("捕获到错误:", response.error.message);
} else {
    console.log("未知状态");
}

This code mixes business logic with type checking and structural validation. Miss one null check and it crashes at runtime.

Pattern matching (ES2026) solves this by letting you express structural conditions declaratively:

// ES2026 pattern matching
const result = response match {
    { status: 200, data: [firstItem, ...rest] } => process(firstItem),
    { status: 404 } => "Not found",
    { error: err when err instanceof Error } => `Error: ${err.message}`,
    _ => "Unknown state",
};

Pattern matching is Stage 4 and part of ECMAScript 2026, supported in Chrome 130+, Firefox 140+, and Node.js 24+. It is the most significant addition to JavaScript's control flow since switch.

docs.title: if Statement
docs.text:
if (condition) {
    // runs when condition is truthy
}

docs.title: if...else Statement
docs.text:
if (condition) {
    // runs when condition is truthy
} else {
    // runs when condition is falsy
}

docs.title: if...else if...else Chain
docs.text:
if (score >= 90) {
    grade = "A";
} else if (score >= 80) {
    grade = "B";
} else if (score >= 70) {
    grade = "C";
} else {
    grade = "F";
}

JavaScript has no elseif keyword — else if is an else branch containing a single if statement.

docs.title: switch Statement
docs.text:
switch (expression) {
    case value1:
        // runs when expression === value1
        break;
    case value2:
        // runs when expression === value2
        break;
    default:
        // runs when no case matches
}

switch uses strict equality (===) for case matching — no coercion occurs.

docs.title: Grouped Cases
docs.text:
switch (day) {
    case "sat":
    case "sun":
        return "weekend";
    default:
        return "weekday";
}

docs.title: Ternary Operator
docs.text:
const label = condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse;

// Nested (use sparingly)
const access = isAdmin ? "full" : isEditor ? "edit" : "read";

The ternary operator is the only JavaScript operator that takes three operands.

docs.title: Pattern Matching (ES2026)
docs.text:
const result = value match {
    0 => "zero",
    n when n > 0 => `positive: ${n}`,
    n when n < 0 => `negative: ${n}`,
    _ => "unknown",
};

Core features:

  • Structural matching — destructure objects and arrays while validating types.
  • Guard clauses — when conditions filter matches.
  • Expression property — match is an expression; assign results directly.
  • Fallback — _ or default handles unmatched values.

docs.title: Pattern Matching with Destructuring
docs.text:
const result = user match {
    { role: "admin", age } when age >= 18 => grantAccess(user),
    { role: "admin" } => "Admin but underage",
    { name: String } => `Hello, ${name}`,
    _ => "Unknown user",
};

docs.title: Pattern Matching with Type Guards
docs.text:
const output = input match {
    String => input.trim(),
    Number => Math.abs(input),
    _ => "Unsupported type",
};

docs.title: Truthiness in Conditionals
docs.text:
if (value) { /* runs when value is truthy */ }
if (!value) { /* runs when value is falsy */ }
if (value ?? fallback) { /* nullish coalescing */ }
if (value?.property) { /* optional chaining */ }

docs.title: The "Fork in the Road" Mental Model
docs.text:
A conditional is a fork in the execution path:

            [condition?]
                 │
        ┌────────┴────────┐
       Yes               No
        │                 │
   [if branch]      [else branch]
        │                 │
        └────────┬────────┘
                 │
            [continue]

The condition determines which path execution takes. Only one branch runs.

docs.title: The "Multiple Choice" Mental Model
docs.text:
switch and pattern matching are like multiple-choice questions:

switch (x) {
    case A: → answer A
    case B: → answer B
    case C: → answer C
    default: → fallback
}

The expression is evaluated once, then compared against each case. Only the matching case runs (unless fall-through occurs).

docs.title: The "Expression vs. Statement" Mental Model
docs.text:
Mechanism Type Can Be Assigned? if/else Statement No switch Statement No Ternary Expression Yes Pattern matching Expression Yes

This is why const x = if (cond) { 1 } else { 2 }; is a syntax error — if is a statement, not an expression. The ternary operator and pattern matching solve this by being expressions that produce values.

docs.title: The "Declarative vs. Imperative" Mental Model
docs.text:
• if/else — imperative: "check this, then check that, then do this."
  • switch — semi-declarative: "compare against these cases."
  • Pattern matching — fully declarative: "describe the shape of the data you want."

Pattern matching represents JavaScript's evolution from procedural to declarative control flow.

docs.title: Concept 1: if — The Fundamental Conditional
docs.text:
if (condition) statement;
if (condition) statement1; else statement2;

The condition is any expression — it is coerced to boolean via truthiness. Braces { } are optional for single statements but strongly recommended for clarity and safety.

docs.title: Concept 2: else if — Chained Conditions
docs.text:
if (a) { /* ... */ }
else if (b) { /* ... */ }
else if (c) { /* ... */ }
else { /* ... */ }

Conditions are checked in order — the first truthy condition wins. Remaining branches are skipped.

docs.title: Concept 3: switch — Multi-Way Exact Match
docs.text:
switch (expression) {
    case value1: /* ... */ break;
    case value2: /* ... */ break;
    default: /* ... */
}
  • Expression evaluated once.
  • Each case compared using strict equality (===).
  • break prevents fall-through.
  • default handles unmatched values.

docs.title: Concept 4: Fall-Through in switch
docs.text:
Without break, execution falls through to the next case:

switch (x) {
    case 1:
        console.log("one");
    case 2:
        console.log("two"); // runs for x === 1 too!
        break;
}

Fall-through is occasionally intentional (grouped cases) but is usually a bug.

docs.title: Concept 5: The Ternary Operator — Inline Selection
docs.text:
const result = condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse;

The ternary is an expression — it produces a value. It is the only three-operand operator in JavaScript. Use it for simple, readable conditions. Avoid nesting.

docs.title: Concept 6: Pattern Matching — ES2026's Structural Selector
docs.text:
const result = value match {
    pattern1 => expression1,
    pattern2 when guard => expression2,
    _ => fallback,
};

Pattern matching combines structural destructuring, type checking, and guard conditions into a single declarative expression. It is supported in Chrome 130+, Firefox 140+, and Node.js 24+.

docs.title: Concept 7: Guard Clauses (when)
docs.text:
const result = value match {
    n when n > 0 => "positive",
    n when n < 0 => "negative",
    _ => "zero",
};

Guards filter matches with additional conditions — like case but with arbitrary expressions.

docs.title: Concept 8: Type Patterns in Pattern Matching
docs.text:
const output = input match {
    String => input.trim(),
    Number => Math.abs(input),
    Boolean => !input,
    _ => "Unsupported",
};

Type patterns match by type without explicit typeof checks.

docs.title: Concept 9: Destructuring Patterns
docs.text:
const result = response match {
    { status: 200, data: [first, ...rest] } => process(first),
    { status: 404 } => "Not found",
    { error: Error } => "Error occurred",
    _ => "Unknown",
};

Patterns can destructure nested objects and arrays while validating structure.

docs.title: Concept 10: Truthiness and Falsiness
docs.text:
Only eight values are falsy:

false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN

Everything else is truthy — including "0", [], {}, and function(){}.

docs.title: Concept 11: Strict Equality in Conditionals
docs.text:
switch uses === — no coercion. This is a feature, not a limitation:

switch ("5") {
    case 5: console.log("number"); break;   // ❌ not matched
    case "5": console.log("string"); break; // ✅ matched
}

docs.title: Concept 12: Early Return Pattern
docs.text:
Instead of deep if/else nesting, use early returns:

function getAccess(user) {
    if (!user) return "none";
    if (user.role === "admin") return "full";
    if (user.role === "editor") return "edit";
    return "read";
}

This flattens the logic and eliminates the else branch.

docs.title: Concept 13: Ternary vs. if/else
docs.text: Aspect if/else Ternary Type Statement Expression Can be assigned No Yes Readability Better for complex logic Better for simple selections Nesting Allowed but discouraged Allowed but discouraged

docs.title: Concept 14: Pattern Matching vs. switch
docs.text: Aspect switch Pattern matching Type Statement Expression Comparison === on single value Structural patterns Guards Not supported when clauses Destructuring Not supported Supported Fall-through Requires break No fall-through

docs.title: Concept 15: ES2026 Pattern Matching Adoption
docs.text: Pattern matching is natively implemented by JavaScript engines (V8, SpiderMonkey). Engines can apply branch prediction optimizations that hand-written if/else chains cannot. For older environments, Babel plugins are available.

docs.title: Concept 16: The default Case
docs.text:
Both switch and pattern matching support fallbacks:

// switch
switch (x) {
    case 1: return "one";
    default: return "other";
}

// pattern matching
const result = x match {
    1 => "one",
    _ => "other",
};

Always include a default/fallback case.

docs.title: Concept 17: Conditionals in Expressions
docs.text:
Only ternary and pattern matching are expressions:

// ✅ Expression — can be assigned
const label = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";

// ✅ Expression — can be assigned (ES2026)
const result = value match { 0 => "zero", _ => "other" };

// ❌ Statement — cannot be assigned
const x = if (true) { 1 } else { 2 }; // SyntaxError

docs.title: Concept 18: ESLint Rules for Conditionals
docs.text: Rule Purpose eqeqeq Enforce === and !== no-else-return Flag unnecessary else after return no-fallthrough Flag missing break in switch no-lonely-if Flag else { if } that should be else if no-unneeded-ternary Flag x ? true : false curly Enforce braces

docs.title: Step-by-Step: if Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  Condition expression is evaluated.
    │
    ▼
2.  Result is coerced to boolean via ToBoolean.
    │
    ▼
3.  If truthy → execute consequent block.
    │
    ▼
4.  If falsy and else exists → execute alternate block.
    │
    ▼
5.  Continue to next statement.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: switch Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  Discriminant expression is evaluated once.
    │
    ▼
2.  Each case value is compared using === (strict equality).
    │
    ▼
3.  First matching case is entered.
    │
    ▼
4.  Execution continues until break or end of switch.
    │
    ▼
5.  If no match and default exists → default runs.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Ternary Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  Condition is evaluated.
    │
    ▼
2.  Coerced to boolean.
    │
    ▼
3.  If truthy → evaluate and return the true-expression.
    │
    ▼
4.  If falsy → evaluate and return the false-expression.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Pattern Matching Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  Target value is evaluated.
    │
    ▼
2.  Each pattern is tested in order.
    │
    ▼
3.  If pattern matches and guard (when) passes:
    │   - The corresponding expression is evaluated.
    │   - Result is returned.
    │
    ▼
4.  If no pattern matches → fallback (_) is used.
    │
    ▼
5.  If no fallback → undefined is returned.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Fall-Through in switch
docs.text:
1.  Matching case is entered.
    │
    ▼
2.  Statements execute.
    │
    ▼
3.  If break is encountered → exit switch.
    │
    ▼
4.  If no break → continue to next case's statements.
    │
    ▼
5.  Repeat until break or end of switch.

docs.title: Bytecode Compilation
docs.text:
V8 compiles if/else into conditional jumps in Ignition bytecode:

evaluate condition
jump-if-false → else_block
  [consequent bytecode]
  jump → end
else_block:
  [alternate bytecode]
end:

switch compiles into a jump table when cases are dense integers, or a sequence of comparisons when cases are sparse.

docs.title: Pattern Matching in the Engine
docs.text: Pattern matching is natively implemented by the engine. V8 applies branch prediction optimizations — the engine can optimize the match structure based on observed data shapes. This makes native pattern matching faster than hand-written if/else chains for complex structural decisions.

docs.title: Type Feedback and JIT
docs.text:
Each conditional site records type feedback:

function check(x) {
    return x > 10 ? "big" : "small";
}
check(5);   // feedback: number
check(15);  // feedback: number → JIT optimizes for numbers
check("5"); // guard fails → deoptimize

The JIT compiles speculative code based on observed types. Type changes trigger deoptimization.

docs.title: Truthiness in the Engine
docs.text:
V8 implements ToBoolean as a fast check:

  • false, null, undefined, 0, -0, NaN, "" → false
  • Everything else → true

This is a single instruction in optimized code.

docs.title: switch Performance
docs.text:
Engines optimize switch based on case density:

  • Dense integer cases → jump table (O(1)).
  • Sparse cases → sequential comparison (O(n)).
  • String cases → hash-based lookup.

docs.title: ES2026 Pattern Matching Performance
docs.text: Pattern matching is natively implemented — engines can apply optimizations not available to userland code, including branch prediction and structural caching.

docs.title: Conditional Execution Lifecycle
docs.text: Evaluate condition → Coerce to boolean → Select branch → Execute → Continue

docs.title: switch Lifecycle
docs.text: Evaluate discriminant → Compare cases → Enter matching case → Execute until break → Exit

docs.title: Pattern Matching Lifecycle
docs.text: Evaluate target → Test patterns → Evaluate guards → Select match → Evaluate expression → Return value

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write conditional → Lint (ESLint) → Type-check (TypeScript) → Run → Debug

ESLint rules like no-fallthrough, eqeqeq, and no-else-return catch conditional mistakes at lint time.

docs.title: Migration to Pattern Matching Workflow
docs.text:
Identify complex if/else chains
    │
    ▼
Identify structural patterns
    │
    ▼
Rewrite as match expression
    │
    ▼
Test in modern engines
    │
    ▼
Transpile for older environments

docs.title: Example 1: Basic if/else if/else
docs.text:
function getGrade(score) {
    if (score >= 90) return "A";
    if (score >= 80) return "B";
    if (score >= 70) return "C";
    if (score >= 60) return "D";
    return "F";
}

Breakdown:

  • Early returns eliminate the need for else.
  • Each condition is checked in order.

docs.title: Example 2: switch with Grouped Cases
docs.text:
function getDayType(day) {
    switch (day) {
        case "sat":
        case "sun":
            return "weekend";
        case "mon":
        case "tue":
        case "wed":
        case "thu":
        case "fri":
            return "weekday";
        default:
            return "invalid";
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • Grouped cases share the same code path.
  • default handles unmatched values.

docs.title: Example 3: Ternary Operator
docs.text:
const access = isAdmin ? "full" : isEditor ? "edit" : "read";

Breakdown:

  • Nested ternaries work but should be used sparingly.
  • For complex logic, use if/else or pattern matching.

docs.title: Example 4: Early Return Pattern
docs.text:
function processOrder(order) {
    if (!order) return null;
    if (!order.items?.length) return "empty";
    if (order.status === "cancelled") return "cancelled";

    return "processed";
}

Breakdown:

  • Flattens logic — no nested else.
  • Each condition is a guard clause.

docs.title: Example 5: Pattern Matching with Destructuring (ES2026)
docs.text:
function handleResponse(response) {
    return response match {
        { status: 200, data: [first, ...rest] } => first,
        { status: 404 } => "Not found",
        { status: 500 } => "Server error",
        _ => "Unknown",
    };
}

Breakdown:

  • Destructures data and extracts first.
  • Guards by status value.
  • _ handles unmatched shapes.

docs.title: Example 6: Pattern Matching with Type Guards (ES2026)
docs.text:
function normalize(input) {
    return input match {
        String => input.trim(),
        Number => Math.abs(input),
        Boolean => !input,
        _ => "Unsupported",
    };
}

Breakdown:

  • Type patterns match by type.
  • _ handles the fallback.

docs.title: Example 7: Pattern Matching with when Guards (ES2026)
docs.text:
function classify(n) {
    return n match {
        x when x > 0 => "positive",
        x when x < 0 => "negative",
        _ => "zero",
    };
}

Breakdown:

  • when adds arbitrary conditions.
  • Cleaner than if/else chains.

docs.title: Example 8: switch Fall-Through (Intentional)
docs.text:
switch (level) {
    case 3:
        unlockFeatureC();
        // fall through
    case 2:
        unlockFeatureB();
        // fall through
    case 1:
        unlockFeatureA();
        break;
    default:
        console.log("Unknown level");
}

Breakdown:

  • Fall-through is intentional — documented with comments.
  • Without comments, this would be a bug.

docs.title: Example 9: Ternary vs. if/else
docs.text:
// ✅ Ternary — simple selection
const label = count === 0 ? "empty" : "filled";

// ❌ Ternary — too complex, use if/else
const result = a > 0 ? b > 0 ? "both" : "a only" : b > 0 ? "b only" : "neither";

Breakdown:

  • Ternary is best for simple, readable selections.
  • Nested ternaries become unreadable quickly.

docs.title: Example 10: ESLint no-else-return
docs.text:
// ❌ Unnecessary else
function f(x) {
    if (x > 0) {
        return "positive";
    } else {
        return "non-positive";
    }
}

// ✅ Correct
function f(x) {
    if (x > 0) return "positive";
    return "non-positive";
}

Breakdown:

  • ESLint's no-else-return rule flags unnecessary else after return.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Best Mechanism Simple boolean test if Two-way selection if/else or ternary Multiple exact matches switch Value selection inline Ternary Complex structural data Pattern matching (ES2026) Type-based dispatch Pattern matching (ES2026) Guard clauses Early return Nested conditions Pattern matching or early returns Fallback handling default / _

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use === and !== in conditions. Why: avoids coercion surprises (Pluralsight lab explicitly teaches this).
  2. Always use braces { } with if/else. Why: prevents dangling-else and scope bugs.
  3. Always include default in switch. Why: handles unmatched values explicitly.
  4. Always include break in switch cases. Why: prevents unintentional fall-through.
  5. Use early returns to flatten logic. Why: eliminates deep else nesting.
  6. Use pattern matching for complex structural decisions. Why: declarative and more readable than nested if/else (ES2026).
  7. Avoid nested ternaries. Why: they become unreadable quickly.
  8. Use switch for exact-match multi-way branching. Why: clearer than long if/else chains.
  9. Document intentional fall-through. Why: future readers won't mistake it for a bug.
  10. Use ?? instead of || for defaults. Why: respects 0, "", false.
  11. Use ?. for safe property access. Why: prevents TypeError on null/undefined.
  12. Enable ESLint conditional rules. Why: no-fallthrough, eqeqeq, no-else-return catch common bugs.
  13. Prefer pattern matching when it reaches Stage 4. Why: it is now ES2026 — use it for structural decisions.
  14. Keep conditions small and readable. Why: complex conditions are hard to debug.
  15. Use guard clauses at the top of functions. Why: handles edge cases first, then the happy path.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using == Instead of ===
docs.text:
if (input == 1) { /* bypassed with "1" or [1] */ }

✅ Correct:

if (input === 1) { /* type-safe */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing break in switch
docs.text:
switch (x) {
    case 1: console.log("one");
    case 2: console.log("two"); // runs for x === 1 too!
}

✅ Correct:

switch (x) {
    case 1: console.log("one"); break;
    case 2: console.log("two"); break;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No default Case
docs.text:
switch (status) {
    case "active": return true;
    case "inactive": return false;
    // no default — what if status is something else?
}

✅ Correct:

switch (status) {
    case "active": return true;
    case "inactive": return false;
    default: return false;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nested Ternaries
docs.text:
const result = a ? b ? c ? "yes" : "no" : "maybe" : "unknown";

✅ Correct: Use if/else or pattern matching.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Braces
docs.text:
if (x > 5)
    console.log("big");
    console.log("always"); // NOT part of the if!

✅ Correct:

if (x > 5) {
    console.log("big");
    console.log("always");
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unnecessary else After return
docs.text:
function f(x) {
    if (x > 0) {
        return "positive";
    } else {
        return "non-positive";
    }
}

✅ Correct:

function f(x) {
    if (x > 0) return "positive";
    return "non-positive";
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using if Where Ternary Works
docs.text:
let label;
if (age >= 18) {
    label = "adult";
} else {
    label = "minor";
}

✅ Correct:

const label = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Pattern Matching Is Not Available
docs.text:
// "Pattern matching is too new to use."

✅ Correct: It is ES2026 — supported in Chrome 130+, Firefox 140+, and Node.js 24+.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting when Guards in Pattern Matching
docs.text:
const result = value match {
    n => "number", // matches everything, including non-numbers!
};

✅ Correct:

const result = value match {
    n when typeof n === "number" => "number",
    _ => "other",
};

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Deeply Nested if/else
docs.text:
if (a) {
    if (b) {
        if (c) {
            // ...
        }
    }
}

✅ Correct: Use early returns or pattern matching.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• === is faster than == — no coercion overhead.
  • switch with dense integer cases — engines generate jump tables (O(1)).
  • switch with sparse cases — sequential comparison (O(n)).
  • Pattern matching — natively optimized with branch prediction (ES2026).
  • Ternary — same performance as if/else when simple.
  • Early returns — no performance difference; improves readability.
  • if/else chains — O(n) for n conditions.
  • Pattern matching with guards — guard evaluation adds cost proportional to guard complexity.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use === over == in conditions.
  2. Use switch for dense exact-match cases.
  3. Use pattern matching for complex structural decisions (ES2026).
  4. Keep conditions simple — complex conditions are harder to optimize.
  5. Avoid deeply nested if/else — use early returns.
  6. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt if needed.

docs.title: Coercion Attacks
docs.text:
if (input == 1) { /* bypassed with "1" or [1] */ }

Defense: Always use ===.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
switch and if conditions can be manipulated if input objects have polluted prototypes.

Defense: Validate input; use Object.create(null).

docs.title: Pattern Matching and Untrusted Data
docs.text:
Pattern matching executes guard clauses — if guards call user-controlled functions, they can be exploited.

Defense: Ensure guards are trusted functions.

docs.title: Fall-Through Bugs
docs.text:
Unintentional fall-through can lead to logic errors with security implications.

Defense: Always use break; document intentional fall-through.

docs.title: Ternary and Readability
docs.text:
Complex ternaries can hide bugs that lead to security vulnerabilities.

Defense: Use if/else for complex logic.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.log in each branch — verify which branch executes.
  • debugger; — pause and inspect condition values.
  • ESLint no-fallthrough — flags missing break.
  • ESLint eqeqeq — flags ==.
  • ESLint no-else-return — flags unnecessary else.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on conditions.
  • switch fall-through visualization — use comments to document.
  • Pattern matching testing — test each pattern and guard independently.
  • TypeScript — catches type mismatches in conditions.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Mechanism When to Use if Simple boolean test if/else Two-way branching if/else if/else Multiple boolean conditions switch Exact-match multi-way branching Ternary Simple inline value selection Pattern matching (ES2026) Complex structural decisions Early returns Flattening nested logic

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• switch for boolean conditions — use if/else.
  • Ternary for complex logic — use if/else.
  • Deeply nested if/else — use early returns or pattern matching.
  • Pattern matching for simple boolean tests — use if/else.
  • switch without default — always include fallback.
  • switch without break — unless fall-through is intentional and documented.
  • == in any condition — use ===.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Loops — repeat decisions
  • break & continue — loop control
  • Exceptions — error-based branching
  • Expressions — values that conditions evaluate
  • Statements — control flow structure
  • Truthiness — boolean coercion rules
  • Strict Equality — === vs ==
  • Pattern Matching — ES2026 structural selection
  • ESLint — conditional rules
  • TypeScript — type-safe conditions

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• JavaScript has no elseif keyword — else if is just else containing an if.
  • Pattern matching reached Stage 4 in ES2026 — it is now standard.
  • Pattern matching is supported in Chrome 130+, Firefox 140+, and Node.js 24+.
  • switch uses === — no type coercion occurs.
  • switch fall-through is a feature, not a bug — but it must be intentional.
  • The ternary operator is the only three-operand operator in JavaScript.
  • if/else cannot be assigned to variables — they are statements, not expressions.
  • Pattern matching is natively optimized by engines for branch prediction.
  • Early returns are a widely recommended alternative to nested if/else.
  • ESLint no-else-return flags unnecessary else after return.
  • Only eight values are falsy — everything else is truthy.
  • switch with dense integer cases generates jump tables for O(1) lookup.
  • Pattern matching supports when guards — arbitrary conditions on matched patterns.
  • Babel plugins can transpile pattern matching for older environments.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Conditionals control which code runs based on boolean tests.
  • if/else if/else — general-purpose branching.
  • switch — multi-way exact-match branching using ===.
  • Ternary — inline value selection; the only three-operand operator.
  • Pattern matching (ES2026) — declarative structural selection with destructuring and guards.
  • Always use === and !== in conditions.
  • Always use braces with if/else.
  • Always include default in switch.
  • Always include break in switch cases (unless fall-through is intentional).
  • Use early returns to flatten nested logic.
  • Use pattern matching for complex structural decisions.
  • Avoid nested ternaries — they hurt readability.
  • ESLint rules (eqeqeq, no-fallthrough, no-else-return) catch common mistakes.
  • Pattern matching is ES2026 — supported in Chrome 130+, Firefox 140+, Node.js 24+.
  • Conditionals are the decision layer — everything in control flow depends on them.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A loop is a control flow statement that repeats a block of code while a condition holds or until a collection is exhausted. JavaScript provides six looping constructs, each designed for a different iteration need:

// 1. for — counter-based iteration
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { console.log(i); }

// 2. for...of — iterate values of iterables (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets)
for (const value of [10, 20, 30]) { console.log(value); }

// 3. for...in — iterate enumerable property keys of objects
for (const key in { a: 1, b: 2 }) { console.log(key); }

// 4. for await...of — iterate async iterables (ES2018)
for await (const chunk of asyncStream) { console.log(chunk); }

// 5. while — repeat while condition is truthy
let n = 0;
while (n < 3) { n++; }

// 6. do...while — repeat at least once, then while condition is truthy
let m = 0;
do { m++; } while (m < 3);

Every loop evaluates a continuation condition on each iteration and decides whether to run the loop body again. When the condition fails (or the iterable is exhausted), execution resumes after the loop.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Loops exist to solve the repetition problem: programs must process collections, repeat calculations, poll for state changes, and walk data structures. Without loops, every element of a list would require a separate statement — unmaintainable and impossible when the collection size is unknown at author time.

Loops serve as the repetition layer of the language:

  • for — precise control over initialization, condition, and update.
  • for...of — value-oriented iteration over iterable collections.
  • for...in — key-oriented iteration over object properties.
  • for await...of — async iteration over streams and async generators.
  • while — condition-driven repetition with an unknown iteration count.
  • do...while — guarantees at least one execution before testing.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Control Flow
├── Conditionals          ✅ done
├── Loops                 ← you are here
├── break & continue
├── Labels
├── Exceptions
└── Error Handling

Loops sit directly after Conditionals because every loop is a conditional at its core — the loop condition is a boolean test evaluated repeatedly. The next concept, break & continue, describes how to alter loop execution from within.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A program that cannot repeat must unroll every iteration manually:

// Without loops — brittle and unscalable
process(items[0]);
process(items[1]);
process(items[2]);
// What if items has 10,000 elements?

Loops solve this by letting the program iterate over data structures of any size without knowing the size in advance. They also enable polling (waiting for state to change), accumulation (summing values), and generation (producing sequences).

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES2015 No for...of — iteration required for or forEach No async iteration Streaming data required manual callback chains No Array.fromAsync Collecting async iterables required manual for await accumulation No iterator helpers Lazy functional chains required intermediate arrays forEach cannot break Early termination required for or for...of

docs.title: Why New Loop Features Were Introduced
docs.text:
• for...of (ES2015) — uniform iteration over any iterable (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, generators).
  • for await...of (ES2018) — native async iteration over streams, async generators, and any async iterable.
  • Array.fromAsync (ES2026) — collects an async iterable into an array in a single call, replacing verbose for await...of accumulation.
  • Iterator Helpers (ES2025) — lazy .map(), .filter(), .take(), .drop() chains on iterators, avoiding intermediate arrays.

Each new feature solves a specific limitation. for...of unified iteration. for await...of brought that unification to async code. Array.fromAsync filled the gap between async iteration and array construction.

docs.title: for — Counter-Based Loop
docs.text:
for (initialization; condition; update) {
    // body
}

// Example
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
}

// Multiple declarations (comma operator)
for (let i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i++, j--) {
    console.log(i, j);
}

// Omitted parts (all three are optional)
let k = 0;
for (; k < 3;) {
    k++;
}

All three clauses — initialization, condition, update — are optional. Omitting the condition creates an infinite loop (for (;;)).

docs.title: for...of — Value Iteration
docs.text:
for (const value of iterable) {
    // body
}

// Array
for (const n of [10, 20, 30]) { console.log(n); }

// String
for (const char of "abc") { console.log(char); } // "a", "b", "c"

// Map — [key, value] pairs
for (const [key, value] of new Map([["a", 1]])) {
    console.log(key, value);
}

// Set — values
for (const value of new Set([1, 2, 3])) { console.log(value); }

// Generator
function* range(n) { for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) yield i; }
for (const i of range(3)) { console.log(i); }

for...of works on anything implementing Symbol.iterator — arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, generators, typed arrays, and more.

docs.title: for...in — Key Iteration
docs.text:
for (const key in object) {
    // body
}

const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };
for (const key in user) {
    console.log(key, user[key]); // "name" "Ada", "age" 36
}

for...in iterates enumerable property keys — including inherited properties from the prototype chain.

docs.title: for await...of — Async Iteration
docs.text:
for await (const value of asyncIterable) {
    // body
}

// Async generator
async function* fetchPages() {
    yield await fetch("/page/1");
    yield await fetch("/page/2");
}

for await (const page of fetchPages()) {
    console.log(page);
}

// Sync iterables work too — each value is awaited
for await (const value of [Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve(2)]) {
    console.log(value); // 1, 2
}

for await...of first calls [Symbol.asyncIterator](); if absent, it falls back to [Symbol.iterator]() and awaits each result. It can only be used inside async functions or ES modules.

docs.title: while — Condition-First Loop
docs.text:
while (condition) {
    // body
}

let n = 0;
while (n < 3) {
    console.log(n); // 0, 1, 2
    n++;
}

The condition is checked before each iteration. If it is falsy initially, the body never runs.

docs.title: do...while — Body-First Loop
docs.text:
do {
    // body
} while (condition);

let m = 0;
do {
    console.log(m); // 0, 1, 2
    m++;
} while (m < 3);

The body runs at least once, then the condition is checked. The trailing ; after the condition is required.

docs.title: Array.fromAsync (ES2026)
docs.text:
const allItems = await Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable);

Array.fromAsync collects an async iterable into an array in a single call, replacing verbose for await...of accumulation. It reached Stage 4 in ES2026 and is supported in Chrome 130+, Firefox 140+, and Node.js 24+.

docs.title: Iterator Helpers (ES2025)
docs.text:
const firstFiveEvens = Array(100000000)
    .keys()
    .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)
    .take(5)
    .toArray(); // [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

Iterator helpers add lazy .map(), .filter(), .take(), .drop(), and .toArray() to iterators — no intermediate arrays created.

docs.title: The "Loop as a Machine" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a loop as a machine with four parts:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Loop                    │
│                                         │
│  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    │
│  │ Initialize  │───▶│   Test      │    │
│  └─────────────┘    └──────┬──────┘    │
│                            │            │
│                     true   │   false    │
│                            ▼            │
│                     ┌─────────────┐     │
│                     │   Body      │     │
│                     └──────┬──────┘     │
│                            │            │
│                            ▼            │
│                     ┌─────────────┐     │
│                     │   Update    │     │
│                     └──────┬──────┘     │
│                            │            │
│                            └────────────┘
│                                         │
│  Exit ──────────────────────────────────┘
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Initialize — set up the loop variable.
  • Test — check the condition.
  • Body — execute the loop body.
  • Update — modify the loop variable.

while and do...while omit the initialize and update clauses (they are done manually inside the body).

docs.title: The "Three Questions" Mental Model
docs.text:
Choosing a loop comes down to three questions:

Question Answer Loop Do I know the collection? Yes — I want values for...of Do I know the collection? Yes — I want keys for...in Do I know the collection? Yes — I want index control for Do I know the collection? Yes — it's async for await...of Do I know the collection? No — condition-driven while Do I know the collection? No — must run at least once do...while

docs.title: The "Iterator Protocol" Mental Model
docs.text:
for...of and for await...of are built on the iterator protocol:

Iterable → [Symbol.iterator]() → Iterator → .next() → { value, done }

When you write for (const x of arr), JavaScript:

  1. Calls arr[Symbol.iterator]().
  2. Calls .next() repeatedly.
  3. Assigns value to x.
  4. Stops when done is true.

for await...of uses [Symbol.asyncIterator]() with the same protocol, but each .next() returns a Promise.

docs.title: Concept 1: The Six Loop Types
docs.text: Loop Iterates Over Best For for Counter Precise index control for...of Iterable values Arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, generators for...in Enumerable keys Object property names for await...of Async iterable values Streams, async generators, Promises while Condition Unknown iteration count do...while Condition (body-first) At-least-once execution

docs.title: Concept 2: for — The Most Flexible Loop
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    console.log(arr[i]);
}
  • All three clauses are optional.
  • Condition is evaluated before each iteration.
  • Update runs after the body.
  • Use when you need the index or non-standard iteration.

docs.title: Concept 3: for...of — The Modern Default
docs.text:
for (const value of iterable) {
    // ...
}
  • Works on any object implementing Symbol.iterator.
  • Gives you values, not keys.
  • Cannot be used on plain objects (they are not iterable by default).
  • Preferred over for...in for arrays — for...in iterates inherited properties.

docs.title: Concept 4: for...in — Keys, Not Values
docs.text:
for (const key in obj) {
    if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) {
        console.log(key, obj[key]);
    }
}
  • Iterates enumerable property keys, including inherited ones.
  • Order is not guaranteed for all keys.
  • Always guard with Object.hasOwn() when iterating own properties.
  • Do not use for...in on arrays — it iterates indices as strings and includes inherited properties.

docs.title: Concept 5: for await...of — Async Iteration (ES2018)
docs.text:
for await (const chunk of asyncStream) {
    process(chunk);
}
  • Works on async iterables ([Symbol.asyncIterator]()).
  • Falls back to sync iterables ([Symbol.iterator]()) and awaits each value.
  • Only usable inside async functions or ES modules.
  • The only way to iterate async iterables natively alongside async generators.

docs.title: Concept 6: while — Condition-First
docs.text:
while (condition) {
    // body
}
  • Condition checked before each iteration.
  • Zero iterations if condition is initially falsy.
  • Use when the iteration count is unknown.

docs.title: Concept 7: do...while — Body-First
docs.text:
do {
    // body
} while (condition);
  • Body runs at least once.
  • Condition checked after each iteration.
  • Trailing ; is required.
  • Use when the body must run before testing.

docs.title: Concept 8: Infinite Loops
docs.text:
for (;;) { }        // infinite
while (true) { }    // infinite
do { } while (true); // infinite

Infinite loops are intentional when paired with break:

while (true) {
    const input = getInput();
    if (input === "quit") break;
    process(input);
}

docs.title: Concept 9: Loop Scope
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// Output: 0, 1, 2 — each iteration has its own `i`

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// Output: 3, 3, 3 — `var` is function-scoped

let creates a new binding per iteration; var uses one function-scoped binding.

docs.title: Concept 10: for...of vs. for...in
docs.text:
Aspect for...of for...in Iterates Values Keys Works on Iterables Objects Arrays ✅ Values ❌ Indices (as strings) Inherited props No Yes Order Guaranteed Not guaranteed Use case Arrays, strings, Maps, Sets Object keys

Rule of thumb: Use for...of for arrays; use for...in for object keys (with Object.hasOwn()).

docs.title: Concept 11: Array.fromAsync (ES2026)
docs.text:
const allItems = await Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable);
  • Collects an async iterable into an array in one call.
  • Replaces for await...of + push accumulation.
  • Reached Stage 4 in ES2026; supported in Chrome 130+, Firefox 140+, Node.js 24+.

docs.title: Concept 12: Iterator Helpers (ES2025)
docs.text:
const result = iter
    .map(x => x * 2)
    .filter(x => x > 10)
    .take(5)
    .toArray();
  • Lazy — no intermediate arrays.
  • Available on all iterators, not just arrays.
  • .map(), .filter(), .take(), .drop(), .flatMap(), .reduce(), .toArray(), .forEach(), .some(), .every(), .find().

docs.title: Concept 13: The Iterator Protocol
docs.text:
const iter = arr[Symbol.iterator]();
iter.next(); // { value: 1, done: false }
iter.next(); // { value: 2, done: false }
iter.next(); // { value: undefined, done: true }

for...of consumes this protocol automatically. Any object implementing [Symbol.iterator]() is iterable.

docs.title: Concept 14: The Async Iterator Protocol
docs.text:
const asyncIter = stream[Symbol.asyncIterator]();
await asyncIter.next(); // { value: chunk, done: false }

for await...of consumes this protocol. Any object implementing [Symbol.asyncIterator]() is async iterable.

docs.title: Concept 15: Caching Array Length
docs.text:
// ❌ Re-evaluates arr.length every iteration
for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) { }

// ✅ Caches length
for (let i = 0, len = arr.length; i < len; i++) { }

Modern engines optimize arr.length well, but caching is still a valid pattern for very large arrays or when the array may change.

docs.title: Concept 16: Reverse Loops
docs.text:
for (let i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    process(arr[i]);
}

Reverse iteration is sometimes faster because the comparison to 0 is cheaper, and it is safe when removing elements during iteration.

docs.title: Concept 17: ES2026 Loop-Related Features
docs.text:
• Array.fromAsync — collect async iterables into arrays.
  • Iterator Helpers — lazy chains on iterators (ES2025).
  • Map.getOrInsert() — upsert during iteration without extra lookups.
  • Iterator.concat() — lazily sequence multiple iterators.

docs.title: Concept 18: forEach vs. for...of
docs.text:
Aspect forEach for...of Type Method Statement Break/continue ❌ Not possible ✅ Possible Async/await ❌ Not compatible ✅ Compatible Early exit ❌ Throws or returns ✅ break Return value undefined N/A

Use for...of when you need to break, continue, or await.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: for Loop Execution
docs.text:
1.  Initialization runs once.
    │
    ▼
2.  Condition is evaluated.
    │   ├── Falsy → exit loop.
    │   └── Truthy → continue.
    │
    ▼
3.  Body executes.
    │
    ▼
4.  Update runs.
    │
    ▼
5.  Repeat from step 2.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: for...of Execution
docs.text:
1.  Get the iterable's [Symbol.iterator]() method.
    │
    ▼
2.  Call it to get an iterator.
    │
    ▼
3.  Call iterator.next().
    │   ├── done: true → exit loop.
    │   └── done: false → assign value to loop variable.
    │
    ▼
4.  Execute body.
    │
    ▼
5.  Repeat from step 3.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: for await...of Execution
docs.text:
1.  Get the iterable's [Symbol.asyncIterator]() method.
    │   ├── Present → use it.
    │   └── Absent → fall back to [Symbol.iterator]().
    │
    ▼
2.  Call next() and await the result.
    │   ├── done: true → exit loop.
    │   └── done: false → assign value.
    │
    ▼
3.  Execute body.
    │
    ▼
4.  Repeat from step 2.
