docs.title: Step-by-Step: while Execution
docs.text:
1.  Condition is evaluated.
    │   ├── Falsy → exit loop.
    │   └── Truthy → continue.
    │
    ▼
2.  Body executes.
    │
    ▼
3.  Repeat from step 1.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: do...while Execution
docs.text:
1.  Body executes (unconditionally).
    │
    ▼
2.  Condition is evaluated.
    │   ├── Falsy → exit loop.
    │   └── Truthy → continue.
    │
    ▼
3.  Repeat from step 1.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Array.fromAsync (ES2026)
docs.text:
1.  Get the async iterable.
    │
    ▼
2.  Create an empty array.
    │
    ▼
3.  For each value from the async iterator:
    │   - await the value.
    │   - push it into the array.
    │
    ▼
4.  Return the array.

docs.title: Bytecode Compilation
docs.text:
V8 compiles for loops into bytecode with conditional jumps and increment operations:

initialization
loop_start:
  evaluate condition
  jump-if-false → loop_end
  body bytecode
  update
  jump → loop_start
loop_end:

while and do...while compile similarly, with the condition check repositioned.

docs.title: Iterator Protocol in the Engine
docs.text:
for...of is compiled to a sequence of abstract operations:

1.  GetIterator(iterable)
2.  Repeat:
    a.  IteratorStep(iteratorRecord)
    b.  If done → exit
    c.  Assign value to loop variable
    d.  Execute body
3.  IteratorClose (on break/return/throw)

IteratorClose ensures the iterator's return() method is called when the loop exits early — this is how for...of cleans up resources in generators.

docs.title: Async Iterator Protocol
docs.text: for await...of uses AsyncIteratorClose — the async equivalent of IteratorClose. It awaits the return() method if the loop exits early.

docs.title: Type Feedback and JIT
docs.text:
V8 records type feedback at loop sites:

function sum(arr) {
    let total = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
        total += arr[i];
    }
    return total;
}
sum([1, 2, 3]); // feedback: array of numbers

The JIT compiles speculative optimized code for the observed types. If the array type changes, the function deoptimizes.

docs.title: Loop Optimization in V8
docs.text:
V8 applies several optimizations:

  • Loop-invariant code motion — hoists calculations out of the loop.
  • Loop unrolling — duplicates the body to reduce overhead.
  • Induction variable analysis — simplifies counter arithmetic.
  • Bounds check elimination — removes redundant array bounds checks.

docs.title: Memory and GC
docs.text: Loops that allocate objects in each iteration create GC pressure. Reusing objects or pre-allocating arrays reduces GC pauses.

docs.title: for...in and Prototype Chain
docs.text:
for...in walks the entire prototype chain, collecting enumerable properties. This is why inherited properties appear:

const parent = { a: 1 };
const child = Object.create(parent);
child.b = 2;

for (const key in child) {
    console.log(key); // "b", "a" — includes inherited "a"
}

docs.title: Array.fromAsync Implementation
docs.text: Array.fromAsync uses the async iterator protocol internally, awaiting each value and pushing it into a new array. It is natively optimized by engines.

docs.title: Loop Execution Lifecycle
docs.text: Initialize → Test → Body → Update → Test → ... → Exit

docs.title: for...of Lifecycle
docs.text: Get Iterator → next() → Body → next() → ... → done → IteratorClose → Exit

docs.title: for await...of Lifecycle
docs.text: Get Async Iterator → await next() → Body → await next() → ... → done → AsyncIteratorClose → Exit

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Choose loop type → Write loop → Lint (ESLint) → Type-check → Run → Debug

ESLint rules like no-unused-vars, for-direction, and guard-for-in catch common loop mistakes.

docs.title: Performance Optimization Workflow
docs.text:
Identify hot loop
    │
    ▼
Cache array length
    │
    ▼
Avoid function calls inside loop
    │
    ▼
Use break/continue strategically
    │
    ▼
Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt
    │
    ▼
Measure again

docs.title: Example 1: Basic for Loop
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    console.log(i);
}
// 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

docs.title: Example 2: for...of with Array
docs.text:
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
for (const fruit of fruits) {
    console.log(fruit);
}
// "apple", "banana", "cherry"

docs.title: Example 3: for...in with Object.hasOwn()
docs.text:
const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };

for (const key in user) {
    if (Object.hasOwn(user, key)) {
        console.log(`${key}: ${user[key]}`);
    }
}
// "name: Ada", "age: 36"

docs.title: Example 4: for await...of with Async Generator
docs.text:
async function* fetchPages() {
    yield await fetch("/page/1").then(r => r.json());
    yield await fetch("/page/2").then(r => r.json());
}

for await (const page of fetchPages()) {
    console.log(page);
}

docs.title: Example 5: Array.fromAsync (ES2026)
docs.text:
const allItems = await Array.fromAsync(asyncGenerator());

Breakdown:

  • Collects all async values into an array.
  • Replaces for await...of + push.
  • ES2026, supported in Chrome 130+, Firefox 140+, Node.js 24+.

docs.title: Example 6: while with Unknown Iteration Count
docs.text:
let input;
while ((input = getInput()) !== "quit") {
    process(input);
}

docs.title: Example 7: do...while for At-Least-Once
docs.text:
let attempts = 0;
do {
    attempts++;
    const success = tryConnect();
} while (!success && attempts < 3);

docs.title: Example 8: Iterator Helpers (ES2025)
docs.text:
const result = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    .values()
    .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)
    .map(n => n * 10)
    .toArray();
// [20, 40]

docs.title: Example 9: Labeled Loop with break
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (i === 1 && j === 1) break outer;
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}

docs.title: Example 10: Caching Array Length
docs.text:
const arr = new Array(1000000).fill(0);
for (let i = 0, len = arr.length; i < len; i++) {
    // process arr[i]
}

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Loop Iterate array values for...of Iterate array with index for Iterate object keys for...in + Object.hasOwn() Iterate Map/Set for...of Iterate async stream for await...of Collect async iterable Array.fromAsync (ES2026) Unknown iteration count while At-least-once execution do...while Lazy functional chain Iterator Helpers (ES2025) Early termination for...of + break

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use for...of for arrays by default. Why: it iterates values, not keys, and respects iterator protocol.
  2. Never use for...in on arrays. Why: it iterates indices as strings and includes inherited properties.
  3. Guard for...in with Object.hasOwn(). Why: avoids inherited properties.
  4. Cache array length in hot loops. Why: avoids repeated property lookups.
  5. Use for await...of for async iteration. Why: native async iteration (ES2018).
  6. Use Array.fromAsync to collect async iterables. Why: concise and native (ES2026).
  7. Use do...while only when at-least-once execution is required. Why: otherwise while is clearer.
  8. Avoid forEach when you need break or await. Why: forEach cannot break and is not async-aware.
  9. Keep loop bodies small. Why: easier to read and optimize.
  10. Use break and continue strategically. Why: reduces nested conditionals.
  11. Avoid function calls inside hot loops. Why: function call overhead adds up.
  12. Use reverse loops when removing elements. Why: avoids index shifting bugs.
  13. Use iterator helpers for lazy chains. Why: no intermediate arrays (ES2025).
  14. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt. Why: reveals JIT behavior.
  15. Write clean code first, optimize later. Why: premature optimization is the root of all evil.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: for...in on Arrays
docs.text:
for (const i in arr) { console.log(arr[i]); } // iterates inherited properties too

✅ Correct:

for (const value of arr) { console.log(value); }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mutating Array During for...of
docs.text:
for (const item of arr) {
    arr.push(item); // infinite loop!
}

✅ Correct: Iterate a copy or use a for loop with a fixed length.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: forEach with await
docs.text:
[1, 2, 3].forEach(async (n) => {
    await process(n); // does not wait — forEach ignores the promise
});

✅ Correct:

for (const n of [1, 2, 3]) {
    await process(n);
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing break in switch Inside a Loop
docs.text:
for (const x of items) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1: console.log("one"); // falls through!
    }
}

✅ Correct: Add break or return.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Infinite while Loop
docs.text:
let i = 0;
while (i < 3) {
    console.log(i); // i is never incremented!
}

✅ Correct:

let i = 0;
while (i < 3) {
    console.log(i);
    i++;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: var in Loops with Closures
docs.text:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 3, 3, 3
}

✅ Correct:

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 0, 1, 2
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: for...of on Plain Objects
docs.text:
for (const x of { a: 1 }) { } // TypeError: not iterable

✅ Correct:

for (const key of Object.keys({ a: 1 })) { }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting await in for await...of
docs.text:
for (const x of asyncIterable) { } // ❌ not async

✅ Correct:

for await (const x of asyncIterable) { }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No default in switch Inside Loop
docs.text:
switch (x) {
    case 1: return "one";
    // no default — unmatched values silently ignored
}

✅ Correct: Always include default.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: do...while Without Trailing Semicolon
docs.text:
do { } while (true) // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

do { } while (true);

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• for loops — fastest for counter-based iteration.
  • for...of — slight iterator overhead; optimized in modern engines.
  • for...in — slowest; walks prototype chain.
  • while / do...while — same performance as for.
  • Iterator Helpers — lazy; avoid intermediate arrays.
  • Array.fromAsync — native; faster than manual for await accumulation.
  • Caching array length — minor gain in modern engines, but valid.
  • Reverse loops — sometimes faster due to simpler comparison.
  • Function calls inside loops — extra overhead; hoist if possible.
  • Object allocation in loops — GC pressure; reuse objects.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use for for simple iterations.
  2. Use for...of for readability — optimize later if needed.
  3. Cache array length in very large loops.
  4. Avoid for...in on arrays.
  5. Use iterator helpers for lazy chains.
  6. Move invariant calculations outside the loop.
  7. Avoid function calls in hot loops.
  8. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution in for...in
docs.text:
for...in iterates inherited properties — including polluted ones.

Defense: Use Object.hasOwn() or for...of with Object.keys().

docs.title: Infinite Loops as DoS
docs.text:
An infinite loop can block the event loop and hang the application.

Defense: Always ensure loop conditions terminate; add iteration limits.

docs.title: for await...of and Resource Leaks
docs.text:
If a loop exits early, the async iterator's return() is called for cleanup.

Defense: Rely on the protocol; avoid manual iteration without finally.

docs.title: Mutation During Iteration
docs.text:
Mutating an array during for...of can cause infinite loops or skipped elements.

Defense: Iterate a copy or use a fixed-length for loop.

docs.title: Iterator Helpers and Untrusted Data
docs.text:
Lazy chains consume iterators incrementally — ensure source iterators are trusted.

Defense: Validate input before iterating.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.log inside loop — verify iteration count and values.
  • debugger; — pause inside the loop body.
  • for...of with console.log — verify iterator behavior.
  • ESLint guard-for-in — flags unguarded for...in.
  • ESLint for-direction — flags incorrect loop direction.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints inside loops.
  • Node.js --inspect-brk — step through loops.
  • --trace-opt / --trace-deopt — JIT optimization logging.
  • Performance panel — identify slow loops.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Loop When to Use for Index control, simple counter for...of Arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, generators for...in Object keys (with Object.hasOwn()) for await...of Async iterables (ES2018) while Unknown iteration count do...while At-least-once execution Array.fromAsync Collect async iterable (ES2026) Iterator Helpers Lazy functional chains (ES2025)

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• for...in on arrays — use for...of.
  • forEach when you need break — use for...of.
  • forEach with async/await — use for...of.
  • while when for...of works — prefer the more declarative option.
  • do...while when zero iterations are valid — use while.
  • Infinite loops without break — ensure termination.
  • Loops for simple array transformations — use .map(), .filter(), .reduce().
  • Manual iteration when iterator helpers work — use them (ES2025).

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Conditionals — loop conditions are boolean tests
  • break & continue — alter loop execution
  • Labels — target nested loops
  • Iterators — the protocol behind for...of
  • Generators — create custom iterables
  • Async Iterators — the protocol behind for await...of
  • Async Generators — create custom async iterables
  • Iterator Helpers — lazy chains (ES2025)
  • Array.fromAsync — collect async iterable (ES2026)
  • Array.prototype.forEach — array-specific iteration
  • ESLint guard-for-in — enforce safe for...in

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• for...of was introduced in ES2015 — before that, iteration required for or forEach.
  • for await...of was introduced in ES2018 — it brought async iteration to the language.
  • Array.fromAsync is part of ES2026 — it replaces verbose for await...of accumulation.
  • Iterator Helpers became Baseline widely available in 2025 — .map(), .filter(), .take() on any iterator.
  • for...in walks the prototype chain — it includes inherited enumerable properties.
  • for...of calls IteratorClose — it cleans up generators on early exit.
  • do...while is the only loop that guarantees at least one execution.
  • for (;;) is a valid infinite loop — all three clauses are optional.
  • let creates a new binding per iteration — var does not.
  • forEach cannot break — use for...of for early termination.
  • forEach ignores promises — async/await requires for...of.
  • V8 unrolls hot loops — loop unrolling reduces overhead.
  • Reverse loops are sometimes faster — comparison to 0 is cheaper.
  • ESLint guard-for-in enforces Object.hasOwn().
  • Loops are the repetition layer — everything from data processing to polling depends on them.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Six loop types: for, for...of, for...in, for await...of, while, do...while.
  • for — counter-based; full control over init, condition, and update.
  • for...of — value iteration over any iterable (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, generators).
  • for...in — key iteration over objects; always guard with Object.hasOwn().
  • for await...of — async iteration over async iterables (ES2018).
  • while — condition-first; zero or more iterations.
  • do...while — body-first; at least one iteration.
  • Array.fromAsync — collect async iterable into an array (ES2026).
  • Iterator Helpers — lazy .map(), .filter(), .take() on iterators (ES2025).
  • for...of is preferred over for...in for arrays.
  • forEach cannot break or await — use for...of when needed.
  • let creates per-iteration bindings — var does not.
  • Cache array length in hot loops.
  • Avoid for...in on arrays.
  • Use break and continue strategically.
  • Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.
  • Loops are the repetition layer — everything in control flow builds on them.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
break and continue are jump statements that alter the normal flow of loops and switch statements. They are the primary tools for early termination and iteration skipping within repetitive code.

// break — exits the loop immediately
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i === 3) break;
    console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2
}

// continue — skips to the next iteration
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i === 3) continue;
    console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
}

Both statements can optionally accept a label to target an outer loop or block:

outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j === 1) continue outer; // skip to next i
        if (i === 2) break outer;    // exit both loops
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}

break terminates the current loop or switch statement and transfers control to the statement following it. continue terminates the current iteration and resumes the loop with the next iteration — in a while or do...while loop, it jumps back to the condition; in a for loop, it jumps to the update expression; in a for...in, for...of, or for await...of loop, it jumps to the next iteration.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
break and continue exist to solve the early exit problem: loops often need to stop before their natural termination condition, or skip processing for specific elements. Without these statements, every early exit would require a flag variable — a boolean that is checked on every iteration, cluttering the loop and slowing execution.

// Without break — flag variable
let found = false;
for (const item of items) {
    if (!found) {
        if (item.id === targetId) {
            found = true;
            result = item;
        }
    }
}

// With break — direct and clear
for (const item of items) {
    if (item.id === targetId) {
        result = item;
        break;
    }
}

They serve as the loop control layer of the language:

  • break — exit a loop or switch entirely.
  • continue — skip the rest of the current iteration.
  • Labels — target outer loops from nested ones.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Control Flow
├── Conditionals          ✅ done
├── Loops                 ✅ done
├── break & continue      ← you are here
├── Labels
├── Exceptions
└── Error Handling

break and continue sit directly after Loops because they only make sense inside loops — they are the tools that modify loop execution from within. The next concept, Labels, extends their power to nested loops.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Loops execute until their condition fails. But real programs often need to stop early:

  • Found the item you were searching for — no need to continue.
  • Detected an error — abort the loop.
  • Encountered a null value — skip this iteration.
  • Reached a sufficient result — stop processing.

Without break and continue, every early exit requires a flag variable that is tested on every iteration — verbose, error-prone, and slower because the loop continues running even after the useful work is done.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation No break Loops could only exit via condition failure No continue Skipping required nested if blocks around the entire body No labels Nested loop exits required flag variables forEach limitation forEach cannot break or continue — a major gap

docs.title: Why break and continue Were Introduced
docs.text:
break was part of the original JavaScript (1995). It solved the need for early loop termination and switch case termination. continue was also in the original language, providing a way to skip iterations without wrapping the body in conditionals.

Labels were added to extend break and continue to nested loops — allowing a break inside an inner loop to exit an outer loop directly, without flag variables.

docs.title: Why forEach Cannot Break
docs.text: Array.prototype.forEach was introduced in ES5 as a functional iteration method. It calls a callback for each element — but the callback cannot break or continue the outer loop because it is a function, not a loop body. break and continue are loop statements, not function statements. This is a fundamental design limitation of forEach, and the primary reason for...of is preferred when early termination is needed.

docs.title: break — Unlabeled
docs.text:
break;

Exits the innermost loop or switch statement.

// In a for loop
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i === 3) break;
    console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2
}

// In a while loop
let i = 0;
while (i < 10) {
    if (i === 3) break;
    console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2
    i++;
}

// In a switch
switch (value) {
    case 1:
        console.log("one");
        break;
    case 2:
        console.log("two");
        break;
}

docs.title: break — Labeled
docs.text:
break label;

Exits the statement identified by label. The break statement must be nested within the labeled statement.

outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (i === 1 && j === 1) break outer;
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}
// 0 0
// 0 1
// 0 2
// 1 0

docs.title: continue — Unlabeled
docs.text:
continue;

Skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds to the next.

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    if (i === 2) continue;
    console.log(i); // 0, 1, 3, 4
}

docs.title: continue — Labeled
docs.text:
continue label;

Continues the loop identified by label. The continue statement must be nested within the labeled loop, and the label must refer to a looping statement (not a plain block).

outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j === 1) continue outer;
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}
// 0 0
// 1 0
// 2 0

docs.title: Labeled Blocks with break
docs.text:
Labels can be attached to any statement, not just loops. break can exit a labeled block:

outerBlock: {
    innerBlock: {
        console.log("1");
        break outerBlock; // exits both blocks
        console.log("never runs");
    }
    console.log("never runs");
}

docs.title: continue Cannot Target Blocks
docs.text:
continue can only target looping statements. It cannot be used with a plain block label:

block: {
    continue block; // ❌ SyntaxError
}

docs.title: Loop-Specific Behavior of continue
docs.text:
The behavior of continue depends on the loop type:

Loop continue Jumps To while The condition do...while The condition for The update expression for...in Next property key for...of Next value for await...of Next async value

docs.title: The "Emergency Exit" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of break and continue as doors in a building:

  • break — the emergency exit. You leave the building immediately, abandoning whatever you were doing. No more iterations. No more code in the loop. You are outside.
  • continue — the skip button. You finish the current room and move directly to the next one. The building continues operating. You just didn't finish this particular room.
Loop body:
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│                                 │
│  [statement]                    │
│  [statement]                    │
│  ─── continue ───▶ next iteration
│                                 │
│  [statement]                    │
│  [statement]                    │
│  ─── break ───▶ exit loop       │
│                                 │
│  [statement]                    │
│                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Flag Variable Replacement" Mental Model
docs.text:
Before break and continue, loops used flag variables:

Without break:                    With break:
┌─────────────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────┐
│ let found = false;  │          │ for (const x of xs) │
│ for (const x of xs) │          │   if (match(x)) {   │
│   if (!found) {     │          │     result = x;     │
│     if (match(x)) { │          │     break;          │
│       found = true; │          │   }                 │
│       result = x;   │          │ }                   │
│     }               │          │                     │
│   }                 │          │ Clean. Direct.      │
│ }                   │          │                     │
│                     │          │                     │
│ Every iteration     │          │ Exits immediately.  │
│ checks `!found`.    │          │                     │
└─────────────────────┘          └─────────────────────┘

break and continue eliminate the flag variable — simpler code, faster execution.

docs.title: The "Nested Loop Problem" Mental Model
docs.text:
In nested loops, unlabeled break and continue only affect the innermost loop:

outer: for (i) {
    inner: for (j) {
        break;        → exits inner only
        continue;     → continues inner only
    }
}

To affect an outer loop, you need a label:

outer: for (i) {
    inner: for (j) {
        break outer;     → exits both
        continue outer;  → continues outer
    }
}

Labels are the bridge between inner and outer loops.

docs.title: The "forEach Trap" Mental Model
docs.text:
for...of:                          forEach:
┌─────────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────────┐
│ for (const x of xs)│           │ xs.forEach(x => {   │
│   if (skip(x))     │           │   if (skip(x)) {    │
│     continue;      │           │     // can't continue│
│   if (stop(x))     │           │   }                 │
│     break;         │           │   if (stop(x)) {    │
│   process(x);      │           │     // can't break  │
│ }                  │           │   }                 │
│                    │           │   process(x);       │
│ ✅ break/continue  │           │ });                 │
│                    │           │                     │
│                    │           │ ❌ No break/continue│
└─────────────────────┘           └─────────────────────┘

This is why for...of is preferred when early termination is needed.

docs.title: Concept 1: break Terminates, continue Skips
docs.text: Statement Effect break Exits the loop or switch immediately continue Skips the rest of the current iteration; proceeds to the next

docs.title: Concept 2: Both Work in All Loop Types
docs.text:
break and continue work in:

  • for
  • while
  • do...while
  • for...in
  • for...of
  • for await...of

docs.title: Concept 3: break Also Works in switch
docs.text:
break is the standard way to prevent fall-through in switch cases:

switch (x) {
    case 1:
        console.log("one");
        break; // prevents fall-through to case 2
    case 2:
        console.log("two");
        break;
}

docs.title: Concept 4: Labels Target Outer Statements
docs.text:
A label is an identifier prefixed to a statement:

label: statement;

break label exits the labeled statement. continue label continues the labeled loop.

docs.title: Concept 5: Label Scope
docs.text:
A label is available only within the labeled statement. It cannot be referenced from outside:

outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    // `outer` is available here
}
// `outer` is NOT available here

docs.title: Concept 6: continue Requires a Loop
docs.text:
continue label requires the label to be attached to a looping statement:

// ❌ SyntaxError — block is not a loop
block: {
    continue block;
}

// ✅ Valid — label is on a loop
loop: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    continue loop;
}

docs.title: Concept 7: break Works with Any Labeled Statement
docs.text:
break label can target any labeled statement — including blocks:

outerBlock: {
    console.log("1");
    break outerBlock;
    console.log("never runs");
}

docs.title: Concept 8: Nested Labels
docs.text:
A statement can have multiple labels:

outer: inner: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    break outer; // both labels are equivalent
}

All labels on the same statement are functionally equivalent.

docs.title: Concept 9: break and continue Cannot Be Used at Top Level
docs.text:
A break or continue statement — with or without a label — cannot be used at the top level of a script, module, function body, or static initialization block, even if the function is contained within a loop.

// ❌ SyntaxError
break;

// ❌ SyntaxError
continue;

function f() {
    break; // ❌ SyntaxError
}

docs.title: Concept 10: forEach Cannot Use break or continue
docs.text:
Array.prototype.forEach takes a callback function. break and continue are loop statements — they cannot appear inside a callback because the callback is not a loop body.

[1, 2, 3].forEach(x => {
    if (x === 2) break; // ❌ SyntaxError
});

Solution: Use for...of when early termination is needed.

docs.title: Concept 11: Iterator Protocol Cleanup
docs.text:
When break exits a for...of loop early, JavaScript calls the iterator's return() method to perform cleanup — this is called IteratorClose. This is how generators clean up resources when a loop exits early.

function* gen() {
    try {
        yield 1;
        yield 2;
        yield 3;
    } finally {
        console.log("cleanup");
    }
}

for (const x of gen()) {
    if (x === 2) break; // triggers finally → "cleanup"
}

docs.title: Concept 12: break in switch Inside a Loop
docs.text:
When a switch is inside a loop, break inside the switch exits the switch, not the loop:

for (const x of items) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1:
            console.log("one");
            break; // exits switch, not loop
        case 2:
            return; // exits function
    }
    // continues loop after switch
}

To exit the loop from inside the switch, use a label:

loop: for (const x of items) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1:
            break loop; // exits the loop
    }
}

docs.title: Concept 13: continue in switch Inside a Loop
docs.text:
continue inside a switch inside a loop continues the loop — not the switch:

for (const x of items) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1:
            continue; // skips to next loop iteration
    }
}

docs.title: Concept 14: Labels and break vs. continue Semantics
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j === 1) continue outer; // skip to next i
        if (i === 2) break outer;    // exit outer loop
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}
  • continue outer — skips the rest of the inner loop and the rest of the current outer iteration, then proceeds to the next outer iteration.
  • break outer — exits the outer loop entirely.

docs.title: Concept 15: break and continue in try/finally
docs.text:
break and continue inside a try block still execute the finally block:

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    try {
        if (i === 2) break;
        if (i === 1) continue;
        console.log(i);
    } finally {
        console.log("finally", i);
    }
}

Output:

0
finally 0
finally 1
finally 2

docs.title: Concept 16: ESLint Rules for break and continue
docs.text:
Rule Purpose no-unsafe-finally Disallow break/continue in finally blocks no-unreachable Flag code after break/continue no-extra-label Flag unnecessary labels no-labels Disallow labels entirely no-continue Disallow continue no-restricted-syntax Restrict break/continue patterns

The no-unsafe-finally rule is particularly important — using break or continue in a finally block overwrites control flow from try and catch, which is considered unexpected behavior.

docs.title: Concept 17: break and continue Are Performance-Neutral
docs.text: break and continue compile to conditional jumps in bytecode — the same primitive used by if and loop conditions. They do not add overhead; they remove overhead by exiting loops early.

docs.title: Concept 18: ES2026 and Loop Control
docs.text:
ES2026 does not introduce new break or continue syntax. However, it adds features that reduce the need for manual loop control:

  • Array.fromAsync — collects async iterables without manual for await...of loops.
  • Iterator Helpers (ES2025) — .take(n) replaces break after n iterations.
  • Iterator.concat() — sequences iterators without nested loops.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: break Execution
docs.text:
1.  `break` statement is encountered.
    │
    ▼
2.  If unlabeled:
    │   - Find the innermost enclosing loop or switch.
    │   - Exit that statement.
    │
    ▼
3.  If labeled:
    │   - Find the statement with the matching label.
    │   - Verify `break` is nested within it.
    │   - Exit that statement.
    │
    ▼
4.  If the loop is a for...of or for await...of:
    │   - Call iterator.return() for cleanup (IteratorClose).
    │
    ▼
5.  Resume execution after the terminated statement.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: continue Execution
docs.text:
1.  `continue` statement is encountered.
    │
    ▼
2.  If unlabeled:
    │   - Find the innermost enclosing loop.
    │   - Skip to the next iteration.
    │
    ▼
3.  If labeled:
    │   - Find the loop with the matching label.
    │   - Verify `continue` is nested within it.
    │   - Skip to the next iteration of that loop.
    │
    ▼
4.  Jump target depends on loop type:
    │   - while / do...while → condition
    │   - for → update expression
    │   - for...in / for...of / for await...of → next iteration
    │
    ▼
5.  Continue executing the loop.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Labeled break in Nested Loops
docs.text:
1.  outer: for (i) { ... inner: for (j) { ... break outer; ... } }
    │
    ▼
2.  `break outer` is encountered inside inner loop.
    │
    ▼
3.  Engine searches for label `outer`.
    │
    ▼
4.  Finds `outer` attached to the outer for loop.
    │
    ▼
5.  Exits the outer loop entirely.
    │
    ▼
6.  Resumes after the outer loop.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: IteratorClose on break
docs.text:
1.  for (const x of generator) { if (x === 2) break; }
    │
    ▼
2.  `break` exits the loop.
    │
    ▼
3.  Engine calls iterator.return().
    │
    ▼
4.  Generator's finally block executes.
    │
    ▼
5.  Resource cleanup completes.
    │
    ▼
6.  Execution resumes after the loop.

docs.title: Bytecode Compilation
docs.text:
V8 compiles break and continue into unconditional jumps in Ignition bytecode:

for loop:
  initialization
loop_start:
  condition
  jump-if-false → loop_end
  body
  if (condition) → jump loop_start  // continue
  jump loop_end                    // break
  update
  jump loop_start
loop_end:

Both statements are single-jump instructions — they do not add runtime overhead.

docs.title: Completion Records
docs.text:
In the ECMAScript spec, break and continue produce Completion Records:

break → { [[Type]]: break, [[Target]]: label }
continue → { [[Type]]: continue, [[Target]]: label }

These records propagate up through the loop's evaluation until the loop handles them.

docs.title: LoopContinues Abstract Operation
docs.text: The spec defines LoopContinues(completion, labelSet) — an abstract operation that determines whether a loop should continue based on a completion record. This is the mechanism behind break and continue in for...of and for await...of loops.

docs.title: IteratorClose on break
docs.text: When break exits a for...of loop, the spec's IteratorClose abstract operation is invoked. It calls the iterator's return() method if present, ensuring generators and other iterables clean up resources.

docs.title: Labels in the Parser
docs.text:
Labels are resolved during parsing. The parser maintains a label set — a stack of active labels. When a break or continue with a label is encountered, the parser verifies:

  1. The label exists in the current scope.
  2. The label is attached to an appropriate statement (loop for continue, any statement for break).
  3. The break/continue is nested within the labeled statement.

If any check fails, a syntax error is thrown.

docs.title: finally Interaction
docs.text:
break and continue inside a try block trigger the finally block before completing:

try {
    break;  // finally runs first, then break completes
} finally {
    cleanup();
}

This is why ESLint's no-unsafe-finally rule warns against break/continue in finally — they overwrite pending control flow from try/catch.

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text: The JIT compilers (Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFan) treat break and continue as branch instructions. They are optimized as part of the loop's control flow graph. There is no performance penalty for using them.

docs.title: break Execution Lifecycle
docs.text: Encountered → Find target → Exit statement → (IteratorClose) → Resume after

docs.title: continue Execution Lifecycle
docs.text: Encountered → Find target loop → Skip to next iteration → Resume loop

docs.title: Labeled break Lifecycle
docs.text: Encountered → Resolve label → Verify nesting → Exit labeled statement → Resume after

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write loop → Add break/continue → Lint (ESLint) → Run → Debug

ESLint rules like no-unreachable and no-unsafe-finally catch common break/continue mistakes.

docs.title: Loop Control Decision Workflow
docs.text:
Need to exit loop early?
    │
    ├── Yes → Use break
    │
    └── No → Need to skip current iteration?
              │
              ├── Yes → Use continue
              │
              └── No → Normal loop

docs.title: Example 1: Basic break
docs.text:
const items = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
const target = 3;

for (const item of items) {
    if (item === target) {
        console.log("Found:", item);
        break;
    }
    console.log("Checking:", item);
}
// Checking: 1
// Checking: 2
// Found: 3

Breakdown:

  • Loop exits as soon as item === 3.
  • Remaining elements (4, 5) are not processed.

docs.title: Example 2: Basic continue
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i % 2 === 0) continue; // skip even numbers
    console.log(i); // 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
}

Breakdown:

  • continue skips the rest of the iteration for even numbers.
  • Only odd numbers are printed.

docs.title: Example 3: break in switch
docs.text:
function getDayType(day) {
    switch (day) {
        case "sat":
        case "sun":
            return "weekend";
        case "mon":
        case "tue":
        case "wed":
        case "thu":
        case "fri":
            return "weekday";
        default:
            return "invalid";
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • return exits the function — break is not needed.
  • In non-returning switch, break prevents fall-through.

docs.title: Example 4: Labeled break in Nested Loops
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (i === 1 && j === 1) break outer;
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}
// 0 0
// 0 1
// 0 2
// 1 0

Breakdown:

  • break outer exits both loops.
  • Without the label, only the inner loop would exit.

docs.title: Example 5: Labeled continue in Nested Loops
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j === 1) continue outer;
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}
// 0 0
// 1 0
// 2 0

Breakdown:

  • continue outer skips to the next outer iteration.
  • The inner loop is abandoned for the current outer iteration.

docs.title: Example 6: break in a for...of with Iterator Cleanup
docs.text:
function* gen() {
    try {
        yield 1;
        yield 2;
        yield 3;
    } finally {
        console.log("cleanup");
    }
}

for (const x of gen()) {
    if (x === 2) break;
    console.log(x); // 1
}
// cleanup (from finally)

Breakdown:

  • break triggers IteratorClose, which runs the generator's finally block.
  • Resource cleanup is guaranteed.

docs.title: Example 7: break in switch Inside a Loop
docs.text:
for (const x of [1, 2, 3]) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1:
            console.log("one");
            break; // exits switch only
        case 2:
            console.log("two");
            break;
        case 3:
            console.log("three");
            break;
    }
}
// one, two, three

Breakdown:

  • break exits the switch, not the loop.
  • To exit the loop, use a label.

docs.title: Example 8: break in try/finally
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    try {
        if (i === 2) break;
        console.log("try", i);
    } finally {
        console.log("finally", i);
    }
}

Output:

try 0
finally 0
try 1
finally 1
finally 2

Breakdown:

  • break triggers finally before exiting.
  • The finally block runs for iteration i = 2.

docs.title: Example 9: continue with for...of
docs.text:
const users = [
    { name: "Ada", active: true },
    { name: "Grace", active: false },
    { name: "Alan", active: true },
];

for (const user of users) {
    if (!user.active) continue;
    console.log("Active:", user.name);
}
// Active: Ada
// Active: Alan

docs.title: Example 10: forEach Cannot break
docs.text:
// ❌ SyntaxError
[1, 2, 3].forEach(x => {
    if (x === 2) break;
});

// ✅ Correct — use for...of
for (const x of [1, 2, 3]) {
    if (x === 2) break;
    console.log(x); // 1
}

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Statement Stop searching after finding target break Exit loop on error break Skip invalid elements continue Exit nested loops break label Skip outer loop iteration continue label Prevent switch fall-through break Exit a labeled block break label Process only valid items continue Early return from search break + return

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use break for early termination. Why: eliminates flag variables and speeds up loops.
  2. Use continue to skip iterations. Why: flattens nested conditionals.
  3. Use labels sparingly. Why: labels can make code harder to follow; prefer extracting functions.
  4. Prefer for...of over forEach when you need break or continue. Why: forEach cannot break.
  5. Document intentional switch fall-through. Why: missing break is usually a bug.
  6. Always include break in switch cases unless fall-through is intentional. Why: prevents accidental fall-through.
  7. Never use break or continue in finally blocks. Why: overwrites control flow from try/catch (ESLint no-unsafe-finally).
  8. Use return instead of break when the loop is the last statement in a function. Why: simpler control flow.
  9. Keep labels close to their usage. Why: distant labels are hard to trace.
  10. Avoid deeply nested loops with labels. Why: consider extracting the inner loop into a function.
  11. Use break in switch inside loops carefully. Why: break exits the switch, not the loop — use a label to exit the loop.
  12. Use IteratorClose awareness with generators. Why: break triggers cleanup in for...of.
  13. Enable ESLint no-unreachable. Why: flags code after break/continue.
  14. Prefer some() or find() over loops with break. Why: more declarative and expressive.
  15. Test edge cases: first iteration, last iteration, no match. Why: break/continue bugs often hide at boundaries.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using break in forEach
docs.text:
[1, 2, 3].forEach(x => {
    if (x === 2) break; // ❌ SyntaxError
});

✅ Correct:

for (const x of [1, 2, 3]) {
    if (x === 2) break;
    console.log(x);
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting break in switch
docs.text:
switch (x) {
    case 1:
        console.log("one");
    case 2:
        console.log("two"); // runs for x === 1 too!
}

✅ Correct:

switch (x) {
    case 1:
        console.log("one");
        break;
    case 2:
        console.log("two");
        break;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: break in switch Inside a Loop
docs.text:
for (const x of items) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1:
            break; // exits switch, not loop
    }
    // continues looping
}

✅ Correct:

loop: for (const x of items) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1:
            break loop; // exits the loop
    }
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: continue Targeting a Block
docs.text:
block: {
    continue block; // ❌ SyntaxError
}

✅ Correct: continue requires a loop label.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: break at Top Level
docs.text:
break; // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct: break must be inside a loop or switch.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unreachable Code After break
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    break;
    console.log(i); // unreachable
}

✅ Correct: Remove unreachable code.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: break in finally
docs.text:
try {
    // ...
} finally {
    break; // ❌ no-unsafe-finally
}

✅ Correct: Never use break/continue in finally.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Overusing Labels
docs.text:
outer: for (...) {
    inner: for (...) {
        loop: for (...) {
            if (x) continue outer;
        }
    }
}

✅ Correct: Extract inner loops into functions.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Confusing break and continue
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    if (i === 2) break; // exits loop, not skip
    console.log(i); // 0, 1
}

✅ Correct: Use continue to skip, break to exit.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming break Works in map/filter
docs.text:
[1, 2, 3].map(x => {
    if (x === 2) break; // ❌ SyntaxError
    return x * 2;
});

✅ Correct: Use for...of when early exit is needed.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• break and continue are free — they compile to jumps with no runtime overhead.
  • Early exit saves work — break skips remaining iterations.
  • continue skips work — avoids processing unwanted elements.
  • Flag variables are slower — they require a check on every iteration.
  • Labeled break is as fast as unlabeled — resolved at parse time.
  • IteratorClose adds overhead — but only on early exit from for...of.
  • finally blocks add overhead — break inside try triggers finally before exiting.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use break to exit loops as soon as possible.
  2. Use continue to skip expensive processing for unwanted elements.
  3. Prefer for...of with break over forEach with flags.
  4. Avoid break inside try/finally in hot loops — the finally overhead adds up.
  5. Labels are free — do not avoid them for performance reasons.

docs.title: Infinite Loop Prevention
docs.text:
break is the primary mechanism for exiting intentional infinite loops:

while (true) {
    const input = getInput();
    if (input === "quit") break;
    process(input);
}

Without break, this loop would run forever.

docs.title: Iterator Cleanup and Resource Leaks
docs.text: break from a for...of loop triggers IteratorClose, which calls the iterator's return() method. This prevents resource leaks in generators, file handles, and database connections.

docs.title: break in finally — Security Risk
docs.text: Using break or continue in a finally block can overwrite control flow from try and catch, leading to unexpected behavior that may have security implications. ESLint's no-unsafe-finally rule flags this.

docs.title: Loop Bound Enforcement
docs.text:
break can enforce maximum iteration limits, preventing denial-of-service (DoS) via unbounded loops:

let count = 0;
for (const item of untrustedInput) {
    if (++count > MAX_ITERATIONS) break;
    process(item);
}

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.log before break/continue — verify when they trigger.
  • debugger; — pause inside the loop body.
  • ESLint no-unreachable — flags code after break/continue.
  • ESLint no-unsafe-finally — flags break/continue in finally.
  • ESLint no-extra-label — flags unnecessary labels.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on break/continue.
  • Loop iteration counter — add a counter to verify loop exits correctly.
  • Label verification — check that labels are attached to the correct statement.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Statement When to Use break Exit loop early — found target, error, or sufficient result continue Skip current iteration — invalid item, filter condition break label Exit nested loops continue label Skip outer loop iteration break in switch Prevent fall-through break label in switch inside loop Exit the loop from the switch

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• forEach — cannot use break/continue; use for...of.
  • finally blocks — avoid break/continue; use no-unsafe-finally.
  • Top-level code — syntax error outside loops.
  • Simple transformations — use .map(), .filter(), .find() instead.
  • When some() or find() works — more declarative.
  • Labels when functions would be clearer — extract the inner loop.
  • Unnecessary break in switch with return — return is cleaner.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Loops — break and continue only work inside loops
  • Labels — target outer loops
  • Conditionals — break/continue are often inside if blocks
  • switch — break prevents fall-through
  • for...of — break triggers IteratorClose
  • Generators — finally runs on break
  • forEach — cannot use break/continue
  • some / find — declarative alternatives
  • ESLint no-unsafe-finally — flags dangerous usage
  • ESLint no-unreachable — flags dead code

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• break and continue were in the original JavaScript (1995).
  • break works in switch — it is not limited to loops.
  • continue only works in loops — it cannot target a block.
  • Labels are the only "goto" in JavaScript — JavaScript has no goto statement.
  • break from a for...of loop triggers IteratorClose — generators clean up resources.
  • break in a finally block is flagged by ESLint — it overwrites control flow.
  • forEach cannot break — this is a fundamental limitation.
  • break inside a switch inside a loop exits the switch — not the loop.
  • Labels can be attached to any statement — not just loops.
  • Multiple labels on one statement are equivalent — outer: inner: for....
  • break and continue compile to jumps — no runtime overhead.
  • continue in a for loop jumps to the update expression — not the condition.
  • continue in a while loop jumps to the condition.
  • break and continue cannot be used at top level — syntax error.
  • LoopContinues is the spec abstract operation behind loop control.
  • ES2026 does not add new break/continue syntax — they remain as they were.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• break exits the innermost loop or switch immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds to the next.
  • Labels target outer loops: break label; and continue label;.
  • break works with any labeled statement — including blocks.
  • continue requires a loop label — it cannot target a block.
  • break and continue work in all loop types — for, while, do...while, for...in, for...of, for await...of.
  • break prevents switch fall-through.
  • break inside a switch inside a loop exits the switch — use a label to exit the loop.
  • forEach cannot use break or continue — use for...of.
  • break from for...of triggers IteratorClose — generators clean up.
  • break and continue in finally are unsafe — ESLint no-unsafe-finally.
  • break and continue compile to jumps — no runtime overhead.
  • Use labels sparingly — extract functions when possible.
  • Prefer some() / find() over loops with break for declarative searches.
  • break and continue are the loop control layer — they make loops terminate early and skip unwanted work.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A labeled statement is any JavaScript statement prefixed with an identifier followed by a colon. The label gives a name to the statement, which can then be referenced by break or continue statements nested within it.

label: statement;

outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    inner: for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (i === 1 && j === 1) break outer;
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}
// Output:
// 0 0
// 0 1
// 0 2
// 1 0

A label is an identifier — any valid JavaScript identifier that is not a reserved word — and the statement it prefixes can be any statement, not just a loop. However, continue can only reference labels attached to looping statements, while break can reference any labeled statement.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Labels exist to solve the nested loop exit problem. Without labels, a break inside an inner loop only exits the inner loop. Exiting an outer loop requires either:

  • A flag variable checked on every iteration.
  • Refactoring the loops into separate functions.
  • return from the enclosing function (only works if the loop is the last thing the function does).

Labels provide a direct, built-in mechanism for this problem:

// Without labels — flag variable
let found = false;
for (let i = 0; i < 3 && !found; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3 && !found; j++) {
        if (grid[i][j] === target) {
            found = true;
            result = { i, j };
        }
    }
}

// With labels — direct
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (grid[i][j] === target) {
            result = { i, j };
            break outer;
        }
    }
}

Labels serve as the loop targeting layer of the language — the bridge that lets an inner statement control an outer loop.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Control Flow
├── Conditionals          ✅ done
├── Loops                 ✅ done
├── break & continue      ✅ done
├── Labels                ← you are here
├── Exceptions
└── Error Handling

Labels sit directly after break & continue because labels extend what break and continue can target. They are inseparable from those statements — a label without break or continue is dead code.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Nested loops are common in programming — searching a 2D grid, validating a matrix, walking a tree, matching patterns. But break and continue only affect the innermost loop. To control an outer loop from an inner one, developers needed a way to name the outer loop so an inner statement could reference it.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation No labels Nested loop exits required flag variables Flag variables Checked on every iteration; verbose and error-prone forEach limitation forEach cannot break at all, let alone target outer loops No goto JavaScript never had goto — labels are the closest alternative

docs.title: Why Labels Were Introduced
docs.text:
Labels were part of the original JavaScript (1995). They solved the nested loop problem by allowing a statement to be named and referenced from within. The design was deliberately limited:

  • Labels can only be used with break and continue.
  • There is no goto — you cannot jump to an arbitrary label from anywhere.
  • A label is only in scope within the statement it prefixes.
  • continue can only target looping statements; break can target any labeled statement.

This limited design was intentional. By the mid-1990s, goto had become widely discouraged — Dijkstra's famous 1968 letter "Go To Statement Considered Harmful" had shaped programming language design for a generation. JavaScript's labels are a watered-down version of goto — enough to solve the nested loop problem, but not enough to create spaghetti code.

docs.title: Why Labels Are Discouraged in Modern JavaScript
docs.text:
Despite solving a real problem, labels carry a readability cost. They make control flow harder to trace — a reader must jump between the label and the break/continue that references it. Modern JavaScript offers better alternatives:

  • return from a function — usually the cleanest solution.
  • .some() / .find() — declarative search with early exit.
  • .flatMap() / .filter() — restructure the problem.
  • Extracting inner loops into functions — encapsulate the logic.

ESLint's no-labels rule disallows labels entirely, and the JavaScript coding standards at James Madison University explicitly advise: "Avoid the continue statement, but if necessary, use a labeled continue statement." The general consensus in 2026 is: use labels only when nothing else works.

docs.title: Basic Label Syntax
docs.text:
label: statement;
  • label — any valid JavaScript identifier that is not a reserved word.
  • statement — any JavaScript statement.

docs.title: Labeled Loop with break
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (i === 1 && j === 1) break outer;
        console.log(`i = ${i}, j = ${j}`);
    }
}
// Output:
// "i = 0, j = 0"
// "i = 0, j = 1"
// "i = 0, j = 2"
// "i = 1, j = 0"

When break outer is encountered, the outer loop terminates entirely, and execution continues after the labeled statement.

docs.title: Labeled Loop with continue
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j === 1) continue outer;
        console.log(`i = ${i}, j = ${j}`);
    }
}
// Output:
// "i = 0, j = 0"
// "i = 1, j = 0"
// "i = 2, j = 0"

When continue outer is encountered, the outer loop proceeds to its next iteration — the inner loop is abandoned for the current outer iteration.

docs.title: Labeled Block with break
docs.text:
Labels can be attached to any statement, not just loops. A labeled block with break acts as an early exit from the block:

outerBlock: {
    console.log("1");
    innerBlock: {
        console.log("2");
        break outerBlock; // exits both blocks
        console.log("never runs");
    }
    console.log("never runs");
}
// Output:
// "1"
// "2"

break outerBlock terminates the labeled block entirely, and execution continues after it. This pattern is occasionally used to simulate a multi-level early return within a function without using a function.

docs.title: continue Requires a Loop
docs.text:
continue can only target looping statements — for, while, do...while, for...in, for...of, for await...of:

// ✅ Valid — label is on a loop
loop: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    continue loop;
}

// ❌ SyntaxError — label is on a block, not a loop
block: {
    continue block;
}

docs.title: Multiple Labels on One Statement
docs.text:
A statement can have multiple labels:

outer: inner: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    break outer; // both labels are equivalent
}

All labels on the same statement are functionally equivalent — break outer and break inner behave identically.

docs.title: Labeled Function Declaration (Deprecated)
docs.text:
// ❌ DEPRECATED — do not use
label: function f() {}

The labeled function declaration syntax is deprecated and should not be used, even in non-strict code. In strict mode, it is a syntax error.

docs.title: ASI Pitfall with Labels
docs.text:
// ❌ This is NOT a labeled statement
let x = 1;
foo: bar(); // `foo` is a label for `bar()`

Labels are parsed at statement boundaries. A line like foo: bar(); creates a label foo on the expression statement bar(). This is rarely intentional.

docs.title: The "Named Door" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a label as a named door on a room:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Building                 │
│                                         │
│  ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐     │
│  │  Room A      │   │  Room B      │     │
│  │  (outer loop)│   │  (inner loop)│     │
│  │              │   │              │     │
│  │  ┌────────┐  │   │  ┌────────┐  │     │
│  │  │ Door:  │  │   │  │ Door:  │  │     │
│  │  │ outer  │◄─┼───┼──│ inner  │  │     │
│  │  └────────┘  │   │  └────────┘  │     │
│  └─────────────┘   └─────────────┘     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • break outer — open the outer door and leave the building (exit outer loop).
  • continue outer — open the outer door and go to the next iteration of the outer loop.
  • Without labels — you can only use the inner door (exit the inner loop).

docs.title: The "Flag Variable Replacement" Mental Model
docs.text:
Labels replace flag variables for nested loops:

Without labels:                        With labels:
┌─────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ let found = false;          │       │ outer: for (i) {            │
│ for (i; i < n && !found; i++)│       │   for (j; j < n; j++) {    │
│   for (j; j < n && !found; j++)│     │     if (match) {           │
│     if (match) {            │       │       result = x;          │
│       found = true;         │       │       break outer;         │
│       result = x;           │       │     }                      │
│     }                       │       │   }                        │
│ }                           │       │ }                          │
│                             │       │                            │
│ Flag checked every iteration│       │ Direct exit. Clean.        │
└─────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "No goto" Mental Model
docs.text:
Labels are not goto. The limitations are deliberate:

What labels CAN do:                What labels CANNOT do:
─────────────────────              ─────────────────────
✅ Exit a labeled statement         ❌ Jump to an arbitrary label
✅ Continue a labeled loop         ❌ Jump backward to earlier code
✅ Target from nested code          ❌ Jump into a labeled statement
✅ Work with break/continue         ❌ Work with any other statement

Labels only allow forward jumps out of a statement — never backward, never into a statement. This prevents the most dangerous uses of goto while still solving the nested loop problem.

docs.title: The "Scope of a Label" Mental Model
docs.text:
A label is in scope only within the statement it prefixes:

outer: for (i) {
    // `outer` is in scope here
    // `outer` can be referenced by break/continue
}
// `outer` is OUT of scope here — cannot be referenced

Think of a label as a local variable available only inside its own statement.

docs.title: Concept 1: Labels Name Statements
docs.text:
label: statement;

A label is an identifier followed by a colon, prefixed to any statement. The label gives the statement a name.

docs.title: Concept 2: Labels Are Only Used with break and continue
docs.text:
JavaScript has no goto. Labels can only be referenced by break or continue statements nested within the labeled statement.

outer: for (...) {
    break outer;    // ✅ valid
    continue outer; // ✅ valid
    // goto outer; // ❌ no goto in JavaScript
}

docs.title: Concept 3: break label Exits Any Labeled Statement
docs.text:
break can target any labeled statement — loop, block, switch, if, or even a plain expression statement.

block: {
    console.log("1");
    break block;
    console.log("never runs");
}

docs.title: Concept 4: continue label Requires a Looping Statement
docs.text:
continue can only target labels attached to looping statements:

  • for
  • while
  • do...while
  • for...in
  • for...of
  • for await...of
// ❌ SyntaxError
block: {
    continue block;
}

docs.title: Concept 5: Label Scope Is Limited to the Labeled Statement
docs.text:
A label is available only within the statement it prefixes. It cannot be referenced from outside.

outer: for (...) {
    // `outer` is available here
}
// `outer` is NOT available here

docs.title: Concept 6: Multiple Labels on One Statement
docs.text:
A statement can have multiple labels, all functionally equivalent:

outer: inner: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    break outer; // same as break inner
}

docs.title: Concept 7: Labels and Nested Loops
docs.text:
Labels solve the nested loop exit problem:

outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (i === 1 && j === 1) break outer;
        console.log(i, j);
    }
}

Without break outer, only the inner loop would exit.

docs.title: Concept 8: Labels and continue Semantics
docs.text:
• continue outer — skips the rest of the inner loop and the rest of the current outer iteration, then proceeds to the next outer iteration.
  • continue inner — skips the rest of the current inner iteration only.

docs.title: Concept 9: Labels and break Semantics
docs.text:
• break outer — exits the outer loop entirely.
  • break inner — exits the inner loop only.

docs.title: Concept 10: Labeled Function Declaration Is Deprecated
docs.text:
// ❌ DEPRECATED
label: function f() {}

The labeled function declaration syntax is deprecated and should not be used, even in non-strict code. In strict mode, it is a syntax error.

docs.title: Concept 11: Labels Are Rarely Used in Modern JavaScript
docs.text:
JavaScript coding standards and ESLint rules discourage labels:

  • ESLint no-labels — disallows labels entirely.
  • JMU coding standards — "Avoid the continue statement, but if necessary, use a labeled continue statement."
  • MDN — "Labels are not very commonly used in JavaScript since they make programs harder to read and understand."

docs.title: Concept 12: Alternatives to Labels
docs.text: Alternative When to Use return Exit from a function .some() Search with early exit .find() Find first match .findIndex() Find index of first match Extracted function Encapsulate nested loop throw Exceptional early exit

docs.title: Concept 13: Array.prototype.forEach Cannot Use Labels
docs.text:
forEach takes a callback function — break and continue cannot be used inside it, with or without labels:

[1, 2, 3].forEach(x => {
    // break outer; // ❌ SyntaxError
});

Use for...of when early termination is needed.

docs.title: Concept 14: Labels and switch
docs.text:
Labels can be attached to switch statements:

mySwitch: switch (value) {
    case 1:
        break mySwitch; // exits the switch
}

break mySwitch exits the switch — same as unlabeled break inside a switch.

docs.title: Concept 15: Labels and try/finally
docs.text:
break label and continue label inside a try block still execute the finally block:

outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
        if (i === 1) break outer;
        console.log(i);
    } finally {
        console.log("finally", i);
    }
}
// Output:
// 0
// finally 0
// finally 1

docs.title: Concept 16: ESLint no-labels Rule
docs.text:
ESLint's no-labels rule disallows labeled statements. It warns whenever:

  • A labeled statement is encountered.
  • break or continue is used with a label.

The rule has options:

Option Default Meaning allowLoop false If true, ignores labels on loop statements allowSwitch false If true, ignores labels on switch statements

docs.title: Concept 17: ES2026 and Labels
docs.text: ES2026 does not introduce new label syntax or features. Labels remain as they have been since 1995 — a limited, rarely-used mechanism for nested loop control. The ES2026 spec (Section 14.13) covers labeled statements, including early errors for invalid labeled continue targets and labeled identifier forms accepted in non-strict code.

docs.title: Concept 18: Labels and continue in for...of
docs.text:
outer: for (const row of grid) {
    for (const cell of row) {
        if (cell === null) continue outer;
        process(cell);
    }
}

continue outer skips to the next row when a null cell is found.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Label Resolution
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters `identifier: statement`.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parser adds `identifier` to the label set.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser parses the labeled statement.
    │
    ▼
4.  Within the statement, `break identifier` and `continue identifier`
    │   are resolved against the label set.
    │
    ▼
5.  After the statement, `identifier` is removed from the label set.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: break label Execution
docs.text:
1.  `break label` is encountered inside a labeled statement.
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine searches for the matching label.
    │
    ▼
3.  If found and `break` is nested within it:
    │   - Terminate the labeled statement.
    │
    ▼
4.  If the labeled statement is a loop with an iterator:
    │   - Call iterator.return() for cleanup (IteratorClose).
    │
    ▼
5.  Resume execution after the labeled statement.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: continue label Execution
docs.text:
1.  `continue label` is encountered inside a labeled loop.
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine searches for the matching loop label.
    │
    ▼
3.  If found and the label is on a loop:
    │   - Skip to the next iteration of that loop.
    │
    ▼
4.  If the label is not on a loop:
    │   - SyntaxError.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Label Scope
docs.text:
1.  Parser enters a labeled statement.
    │
    ▼
2.  Label is added to the active label set.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parser processes the statement body.
    │   - `break label` and `continue label` are valid here.
    │
    ▼
4.  Parser exits the labeled statement.
    │
    ▼
5.  Label is removed from the active label set.
    │   - `break label` outside is a SyntaxError.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Nested Labels
docs.text:
outer: inner: for (i) {
    // Both `outer` and `inner` are in scope here.
    // break outer and break inner are equivalent.
}

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of Labels
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification covers labeled statements in Section 14.13 (Labelled Statements). Key points:

  • A LabelledStatement is an identifier followed by : and a statement.
  • IsLabelledFunction — static semantics determine whether a labeled statement contains a function declaration.
  • Early errors — the spec defines when labeled continue targets are invalid.
  • Labeled identifier forms — the spec accepts certain labeled identifier forms in non-strict code.

docs.title: Completion Records and Labels
docs.text:
break and continue with labels produce Completion Records:

break outer → { [[Type]]: break, [[Target]]: "outer" }
continue outer → { [[Type]]: continue, [[Target]]: "outer" }

The [[Target]] field stores the label identifier. Loop evaluation checks this target to decide whether to handle the completion.

docs.title: Label Resolution in the Parser
docs.text:
Labels are resolved during parsing, not at runtime. The parser maintains a label set — a stack of active labels. When a break or continue with a label is encountered:

  1. The parser checks that the label exists in the current label set.
  2. For continue, the parser checks that the label is attached to a looping statement.
  3. The parser checks that the break/continue is nested within the labeled statement.

If any check fails, a SyntaxError is thrown before the code ever runs.

docs.title: Runtime Semantics
docs.text: At runtime, labels have no representation in the bytecode. A break label compiles to an unconditional jump to the end of the labeled statement. A continue label compiles to a jump to the loop's update/condition. There is zero runtime overhead for using labels.

docs.title: Optimization in the JIT
docs.text: The JIT compilers (Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFan) treat labeled break/continue as control flow edges in the loop's control flow graph. They are optimized like any other branch.

docs.title: Labeled Function Declarations
docs.text: Labeled function declarations are deprecated in the spec. In strict mode, they are a syntax error. Engines may still support them in sloppy mode for backward compatibility, but they should never be used in new code.

docs.title: IteratorClose with Labeled Break
docs.text: When break label exits a for...of loop with a label, IteratorClose is invoked — the iterator's return() method is called to clean up resources. This works identically to unlabeled break.

docs.title: Label Lifecycle
docs.text: Parsed → Added to label set → Statement body parsed → Label removed from set

docs.title: Labeled break Lifecycle
docs.text: Encountered → Resolve label → Verify nesting → Exit labeled statement → (IteratorClose) → Resume after

docs.title: Labeled continue Lifecycle
docs.text: Encountered → Resolve loop label → Verify loop target → Skip to next iteration → Resume loop

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write nested loops
    │
    ▼
Need to exit outer loop from inner loop?
    │
    ├── Yes → Consider alternatives first:
    │        - return from function
    │        - .some() / .find()
    │        - Extract inner loop
    │        - throw
    │
    ▼
If none work → Use label + break/continue
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint no-labels) → Review → Document why

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Labeled break
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (i === 1 && j === 1) break outer;
        console.log(`i = ${i}, j = ${j}`);
    }
}
// Output:
// "i = 0, j = 0"
// "i = 0, j = 1"
// "i = 0, j = 2"
// "i = 1, j = 0"

Breakdown:

  • break outer exits both loops.
  • Execution resumes after the labeled statement.

docs.title: Example 2: Basic Labeled continue
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j === 1) continue outer;
        console.log(`i = ${i}, j = ${j}`);
    }
}
// Output:
// "i = 0, j = 0"
// "i = 1, j = 0"
// "i = 2, j = 0"

Breakdown:

  • continue outer skips to the next outer iteration.
  • The inner loop is abandoned for the current outer iteration.

docs.title: Example 3: Labeled Block with break
docs.text:
function process(data) {
    validation: {
        if (!data) {
            console.log("No data");
            break validation;
        }
        if (!data.id) {
            console.log("No ID");
            break validation;
        }
        if (!data.name) {
            console.log("No name");
            break validation;
        }
        console.log("All valid");
    }
    console.log("Done");
}

Breakdown:

  • Labeled block acts as a multi-level early return.
  • break validation exits the block and continues after it.

docs.title: Example 4: Search in a 2D Grid
docs.text:
function findInGrid(grid, target) {
    let result = null;

    search: for (let row = 0; row < grid.length; row++) {
        for (let col = 0; col < grid[row].length; col++) {
            if (grid[row][col] === target) {
                result = { row, col };
                break search;
            }
        }
    }

    return result;
}

Breakdown:

  • break search exits both loops when the target is found.
  • Cleaner than a flag variable.

docs.title: Example 5: Labeled continue in a for...of Loop
docs.text:
const grid = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, null, 6],
    [7, 8, 9],
];

outer: for (const row of grid) {
    for (const cell of row) {
        if (cell === null) continue outer;
        console.log(cell);
    }
}
// Output:
// 1, 2, 3
// (row 2 skipped)
// 7, 8, 9

Breakdown:

  • continue outer skips to the next row when a null cell is found.

docs.title: Example 6: Multiple Labels
docs.text:
outer: inner: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    break outer; // both labels are equivalent
}

docs.title: Example 7: Labels vs. return
docs.text:
// With labels
function findWithLabel(grid, target) {
    search: for (let i = 0; i < grid.length; i++) {
        for (let j = 0; j < grid[i].length; j++) {
            if (grid[i][j] === target) {
                return { i, j };
            }
        }
    }
    return null;
}

// Same function — no labels needed
function findWithoutLabel(grid, target) {
    for (let i = 0; i < grid.length; i++) {
        for (let j = 0; j < grid[i].length; j++) {
            if (grid[i][j] === target) {
                return { i, j };
            }
        }
    }
    return null;
}

Breakdown:

  • When the loop is the last thing the function does, return is cleaner than a label.
  • Labels are only needed when more code follows the loops.

docs.title: Example 8: Labels vs. .find()
docs.text:
// With labels
function findWithLabel(rows, predicate) {
    outer: for (const row of rows) {
        for (const cell of row) {
            if (predicate(cell)) break outer;
        }
    }
}

// Without labels — using .some()
function findWithSome(rows, predicate) {
    rows.some(row => row.some(predicate));
}

Breakdown:

  • .some() provides early exit without labels.
  • More declarative, but returns a boolean, not the value.

docs.title: Example 9: Labeled break in a while Loop
docs.text:
outer: while (true) {
    const input = prompt("Enter a number (or 'quit'):");
    if (input === "quit") break outer;

    let n = Number(input);
    while (isNaN(n)) {
        const retry = prompt("Invalid — enter a number:");
        if (retry === "quit") break outer;
        n = Number(retry);
    }
    console.log("You entered:", n);
}

Breakdown:

  • break outer exits the outer while loop from within the inner loop.

docs.title: Example 10: ESLint no-labels Rule
docs.text:
{
    "rules": {
        "no-labels": ["error", { "allowLoop": true }]
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • no-labels disallows all labels.
  • allowLoop: true permits labels on loop statements only.
  • allowSwitch: true permits labels on switch statements only.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Label Pattern Search 2D grid break search after finding target Validate multi-field object Labeled block with break Skip invalid rows continue outer Exit nested loops on error break outer Simulate multi-level return Labeled block with break Target outer loop from inner break outer / continue outer

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Avoid labels when return works. Why: return is clearer and achieves the same result.
  2. Prefer .some() / .find() for searches. Why: declarative, no labels needed.
  3. Extract inner loops into functions. Why: encapsulates logic, eliminates labels.
  4. Use labels only when no cleaner alternative exists. Why: labels reduce readability.
  5. Keep labels close to their usage. Why: distant labels are hard to trace.
  6. Use meaningful label names. Why: outer beats lbl1.
  7. Never use labeled function declarations. Why: deprecated; syntax error in strict mode.
  8. Remember continue requires a loop label. Why: blocks cannot be continued.
  9. Enable ESLint no-labels for new projects. Why: enforces label-free code.
  10. If using labels, document why. Why: future readers need context.
  11. Don't nest more than two loops. Why: deep nesting is a design smell.
  12. Consider restructuring data. Why: a flat array may eliminate nested loops entirely.
  13. Use break label for early exit, not continue label. Why: break is more predictable.
  14. Test label behavior at boundary conditions. Why: labels can hide bugs at loop edges.
  15. Know the alternatives before reaching for labels. Why: labels are a last resort.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: continue Targeting a Block
docs.text:
block: {
    continue block; // ❌ SyntaxError
}

✅ Correct: continue requires a loop label.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Labeled Function Declaration
docs.text:
label: function f() {} // ❌ Deprecated; SyntaxError in strict mode

✅ Correct: Never use labeled function declarations.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Unnecessary Labels
docs.text:
outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    break outer; // unnecessary — the loop breaks anyway
}

✅ Correct: Remove unnecessary labels.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Label Out of Scope
docs.text:
outer: for (...) { }
break outer; // ❌ SyntaxError — label out of scope

✅ Correct: Labels must be used within the labeled statement.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting continue Requires a Loop
docs.text:
myLabel: if (condition) {
    continue myLabel; // ❌ SyntaxError — `if` is not a loop
}

✅ Correct: continue only works with loop labels.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Labels Instead of return
docs.text:
function find(grid) {
    search: for (let i = 0; i < grid.length; i++) {
        for (let j = 0; j < grid[i].length; j++) {
            if (grid[i][j]) break search;
        }
    }
    return result; // more code after
}

✅ Correct: If nothing follows the loops, use return.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Nested Labels on Same Statement Thinking They Differ
docs.text:
outer: inner: for (...) {
    break inner; // same as break outer — both exit the loop
}

✅ Correct: Multiple labels on the same statement are equivalent.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Labels in forEach
docs.text:
[1, 2, 3].forEach(x => {
    outer: for (...) { } // ❌ cannot break/continue the forEach
});

✅ Correct: Use for...of when labels and early exit are needed.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: break in switch Inside a Loop Without a Label
docs.text:
for (const x of items) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1: break; // exits switch, not loop
    }
}

✅ Correct: Use break loop with a label to exit the loop.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: ASI with Labels
docs.text:
let x = 1;
foo: bar(); // `foo` is a label — rarely intended

✅ Correct: Understand that foo: is a label, not part of the expression.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
