• Labels have zero runtime cost — they are resolved at parse time and compile to jumps.
  • break label is as fast as unlabeled break — no additional overhead.
  • Labels can be faster than flag variables — no per-iteration flag check.
  • return is ~25% faster than labels for breaking nested loops in some benchmarks.
  • Labels are ~1% faster in HPC/science workloads — negligible difference.
  • Labels do not affect JIT optimization — they are control flow edges like any other branch.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Labels are free — do not avoid them for performance reasons.
  2. Use return when it works — slightly faster and cleaner.
  3. Avoid flag variables — labels are faster and cleaner.
  4. Profile only if labels are in a hot path.

docs.title: Labels Are Not goto
docs.text: Labels cannot jump arbitrarily — they can only exit labeled statements via break or continue. This prevents the most dangerous goto-style control flow.

docs.title: Iterator Cleanup with Labeled Break
docs.text: break label from a for...of loop triggers IteratorClose — resources are cleaned up. This prevents resource leaks in generators and async iterators.

docs.title: finally Interaction
docs.text: break label and continue label inside try blocks still execute finally. This is safe but can be surprising — ESLint's no-unsafe-finally rule flags break/continue in finally blocks.

docs.title: Labeled Statements and Security
docs.text: Labels themselves have no security implications. They are a parse-time construct with no runtime representation.

docs.title: Loop Bound Enforcement
docs.text: Labels can enforce maximum iteration limits in nested loops, preventing denial-of-service (DoS) via unbounded iteration.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.log at the label and break — verify label targeting.
  • debugger; — pause inside labeled loops.
  • ESLint no-labels — flags label usage.
  • ESLint no-extra-label — flags unnecessary labels.
  • ESLint no-unreachable — flags code after break label.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints at label and break.
  • Check label scope — labels only work within the labeled statement.
  • Verify continue target — only loop labels can be continued.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Scenario Use Label? Exit nested loops when more code follows ✅ Yes Skip to next outer iteration ✅ Yes Search in 2D data with early exit ⚠️ Prefer .some() / .find() Exit from a function ❌ Use return Simulate multi-level return ⚠️ Prefer labeled block or restructure Simple single loop ❌ No label needed forEach iteration ❌ Cannot use labels

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• When return works — cleaner.
  • When .some() / .find() works — declarative.
  • When the inner loop can be extracted into a function — encapsulated.
  • When a flag variable is clear enough — labels are not always better.
  • In new projects with ESLint no-labels — follow the rule.
  • When labels make code harder to understand — readability wins.
  • In forEach callbacks — impossible.
  • With labeled function declarations — deprecated.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• break & continue — labels only work with these statements
  • Loops — labels are most commonly attached to loops
  • Conditionals — labels can be attached to if statements
  • switch — labels can be attached to switch statements
  • for...of — labeled break triggers IteratorClose
  • return — the primary alternative to labels
  • .some() — declarative early-exit alternative
  • .find() — declarative search alternative
  • ESLint no-labels — rule that disallows labels
  • goto — what JavaScript deliberately does not have

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Labels have been in JavaScript since 1995 — they predate ES5.
  • JavaScript has no goto — labels are the closest alternative.
  • Labels are a watered-down goto — they only allow forward jumps out of statements.
  • Labels are Baseline Widely available — supported across browsers since July 2015.
  • Labeled function declarations are deprecated — and a syntax error in strict mode.
  • A statement can have multiple labels — all are functionally equivalent.
  • Labels are resolved at parse time — they have zero runtime cost.
  • continue can only target loop labels — break can target any labeled statement.
  • Labels are in scope only within the labeled statement — they cannot be referenced outside.
  • ESLint's no-labels rule disallows labels entirely — with options to allow loops or switches.
  • MDN advises against labels — "they make programs harder to read and understand."
  • Labels can replace flag variables — cleaner and faster.
  • return is ~25% faster than labels for breaking nested loops in some benchmarks.
  • Labels compile to unconditional jumps — same as break and continue.
  • ES2026 added early errors for invalid labeled continue targets — stricter parsing.
  • Labels are a last resort — prefer return, .some(), .find(), or extracted functions.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A labeled statement is an identifier followed by a colon, prefixed to any statement.
  • Labels are referenced by break label and continue label.
  • break label exits any labeled statement.
  • continue label only works with looping statements.
  • Labels solve the nested loop exit problem — replacing flag variables.
  • JavaScript has no goto — labels are the limited alternative.
  • Labels are in scope only within the labeled statement.
  • A statement can have multiple labels — all equivalent.
  • Labeled function declarations are deprecated — syntax error in strict mode.
  • ESLint no-labels disallows labels; allowLoop and allowSwitch options permit limited use.
  • Alternatives: return, .some(), .find(), extracted functions, throw.
  • Labels have zero runtime cost — resolved at parse time.
  • break label triggers IteratorClose in for...of loops.
  • finally blocks execute before labeled break/continue complete.
  • Use labels sparingly — only when no cleaner alternative exists.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An exception is a signal that an unexpected or exceptional condition has occurred during program execution, interrupting the normal flow of control. JavaScript provides a built-in mechanism for throwing, propagating, and catching exceptions through the throw statement and the try...catch...finally construct.

try {
    riskyOperation();
} catch (error) {
    console.error("Something went wrong:", error.message);
} finally {
    cleanup();
}

Exceptions in JavaScript are values — you can throw any expression, not just Error objects. In practice, however, you should always throw Error objects (or instances of Error subclasses), because code that catches the error may expect standard properties like message, name, and stack to be present.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Exceptions exist to solve the error propagation problem: when something goes wrong deep in a call stack, the code that can handle the error is often many frames away. Without exceptions, every function would need to return a status code, and every caller would need to check it — verbose, error-prone, and easy to forget.

Exceptions serve as the error signaling layer of the language:

  • throw — signal that an exceptional condition has occurred.
  • try — mark a block of code that may throw.
  • catch — handle the exception if one occurs.
  • finally — guarantee cleanup regardless of outcome.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Control Flow
├── Conditionals          ✅ done
├── Loops                 ✅ done
├── break & continue      ✅ done
├── Labels                ✅ done
├── Exceptions            ← you are here
└── Error Handling

Exceptions sit after Labels because they are the final control flow mechanism — the one that handles the unpredictable. The next concept, Error Handling, describes the strategies and patterns for using exceptions effectively.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A program that cannot signal failure must encode failure in return values. Every function that can fail must return either a value or an error code, and every caller must check which one it got. In a deep call stack, this means every frame must handle every possible error from below — even if it cannot do anything useful with it.

// Without exceptions — error codes everywhere
function readConfig(path) {
    const result = readFile(path);
    if (result.error) return { error: result.error };
    const parsed = parseJSON(result.data);
    if (parsed.error) return { error: parsed.error };
    return { value: parsed.value };
}

Exceptions solve this by separating the detection of an error from its handling. A function deep in the stack can throw; a function high in the stack can catch. Everything in between is bypassed automatically.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES3 No try/catch — errors were handled via return codes No finally Cleanup required duplication in every code path No Error subclassing All errors were generic catch without binding Required a named binding even when unused (ES2019 fixed this) No cause Chained errors required custom properties (ES2022 fixed this)

docs.title: Why New Error Features Were Introduced
docs.text:
• try/catch (ES3, 1999) — brought structured exception handling to JavaScript.
  • finally (ES3) — guaranteed cleanup regardless of whether an exception was thrown.
  • Error subclassing (ES6, 2015) — enabled custom error types with class extends Error.
  • Optional catch binding (ES2019) — catch {} without a parameter when the error is unused.
  • Error.cause (ES2022) — chain errors to preserve the original cause.
  • Error.isError() (ES2026) — reliably identify error objects across realms, replacing unreliable instanceof Error checks.

Each feature solved a specific gap in error handling expressiveness.

docs.title: The throw Statement
docs.text:
throw expression;

The throw statement stops execution of the current function and passes control to the first catch block in the call stack. If no catch exists, the program terminates.

throw new Error("Something went wrong");
throw new TypeError("Expected a string");
throw new RangeError("Value out of range");
throw new ValidationError("Invalid input", { field: "email" });

You can throw any expression, but you should throw Error objects:

throw "a string";       // ❌ works, but no stack trace
throw 42;               // ❌ works, but no message
throw new Error("ok");  // ✅ always throw Error objects

docs.title: The try...catch Statement
docs.text:
try {
    // code that may throw
} catch (error) {
    // handle the error
}

The try block executes first. If it throws, the catch block executes with the thrown value bound to error. If no exception is thrown, catch is skipped.

docs.title: The try...catch...finally Statement
docs.text:
try {
    // code that may throw
} catch (error) {
    // handle the error
} finally {
    // always runs, regardless of outcome
}

The finally block always executes before control leaves the construct — whether an exception was thrown, caught, or not thrown at all. It runs even if the try or catch block contains a return, break, or continue.

docs.title: try...finally (Without catch)
docs.text:
try {
    // code that may throw
} finally {
    // cleanup — the exception propagates after finally runs
}

A try block can have finally without catch. The exception propagates up the stack after finally completes.

docs.title: Optional Catch Binding (ES2019)
docs.text:
try {
    risky();
} catch {
    console.error("Something went wrong");
    // error object is not available
}

When you don't need the error object, you can omit the binding entirely.

docs.title: The Error Constructor
docs.text:
new Error("message");
new Error("message", { cause: originalError }); // ES2022

The cause option chains errors — preserving the original error that led to the current one.

docs.title: Error.isError() (ES2026)
docs.text:
Error.isError(new Error());        // true
Error.isError({ message: "fake" }); // false
Error.isError("error");            // false

Error.isError() is a static method that determines whether a value is a genuine Error object. It performs a branded check for a private field initialized by the Error() constructor — the same mechanism used by Array.isArray().

It is more reliable than instanceof Error because it:

  • Rejects values that are not real Error instances, even if they have Error.prototype in their prototype chain (instanceof would accept them).
  • Accepts Error objects created in another realm (e.g., an iframe) — instanceof Error returns false for these because the Error constructor identity differs between realms.

Error.isError() also returns true for DOMException instances, because DOMException behaves like Error for the purposes of this check.

docs.title: The "Bubble" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of an exception as a bubble rising through water:

Call Stack:
┌─────────────────────┐
│  functionC()        │  ← throws
│    ↑                │
│  functionB()        │  ← no catch — bubble passes through
│    ↑                │
│  functionA()        │  ← no catch — bubble passes through
│    ↑                │
│  main()             │  ← catch — bubble stops here
└─────────────────────┘

When a function throws, the exception bubbles up the call stack, bypassing every frame that does not have a try/catch. The first catch it encounters handles it. If it reaches the top without being caught, the program crashes.

docs.title: The "Fire Alarm" Mental Model
docs.text:
Exceptions are like fire alarms:

  • throw — pull the alarm. You don't handle the fire yourself; you signal that something is wrong.
  • try — the building where the alarm might go off.
  • catch — the fire department. They respond to the alarm.
  • finally — the evacuation procedure. It happens regardless of whether there was a fire.

docs.title: The "Separation of Concerns" Mental Model
docs.text:
Exceptions separate detection from handling:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│            Deep in the stack            │
│                                         │
│  "Something is wrong here."             │
│         ↓                               │
│      throw new Error(...)               │
│                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           High in the stack             │
│                                         │
│  "I know how to handle this."           │
│         ↓                               │
│      try { ... } catch (e) { ... }      │
│                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

The code that detects an error is often not the code that handles it. Exceptions let each function do what it is best at.

docs.title: The "Stack Unwinding" Mental Model
docs.text:
When an exception is thrown, JavaScript unwinds the call stack — it discards frames from the throw point back to the catch point. This means:

  • Local variables in discarded frames are destroyed.
  • finally blocks in discarded frames run before the frame is destroyed.
  • The stack property of the Error object records where the exception was thrown.

docs.title: Concept 1: throw Stops Execution
docs.text:
When throw executes, the current function stops immediately. Statements after throw do not run. Control passes to the nearest catch in the call stack.

function f() {
    console.log("before");
    throw new Error("stop");
    console.log("never runs"); // unreachable
}

docs.title: Concept 2: catch Binds the Thrown Value
docs.text:
try {
    throw new TypeError("bad type");
} catch (error) {
    console.log(error.name);    // "TypeError"
    console.log(error.message); // "bad type"
}

The catch parameter receives whatever was thrown — not necessarily an Error object.

docs.title: Concept 3: finally Always Runs
docs.text:
The finally block executes before control leaves the try construct, regardless of:

  • Whether an exception was thrown.
  • Whether an exception was caught.
  • Whether return, break, or continue was used.
function f() {
    try {
        return "from try";
    } finally {
        console.log("finally runs");
    }
}
f(); // logs "finally runs", returns "from try"

docs.title: Concept 4: try Can Have catch, finally, or Both
docs.text: Construct Valid? try { } catch { } ✅ try { } finally { } ✅ try { } catch { } finally { } ✅ try { } alone ❌ SyntaxError

docs.title: Concept 5: Exceptions Propagate Up the Call Stack
docs.text:
function a() { b(); }
function b() { c(); }
function c() { throw new Error("deep"); }

try {
    a();
} catch (e) {
    console.log(e.message); // "deep"
}

The exception thrown in c() propagates through b() and a() — neither of which has a catch — and is caught in the outer try.

docs.title: Concept 6: Built-in Error Types
docs.text:
JavaScript provides several built-in error constructors:

Error Type When It Occurs Error Generic base error TypeError Value is not of expected type RangeError Value is outside valid range ReferenceError Undeclared variable used SyntaxError Invalid syntax (usually at parse time) URIError Invalid URI handling EvalError Rare — eval() misuse AggregateError Multiple errors wrapped together (ES2021)

docs.title: Concept 7: Custom Error Classes
docs.text:
class ValidationError extends Error {
    constructor(message, field) {
        super(message);
        this.name = "ValidationError";
        this.field = field;
    }
}

Custom error classes extend Error and add domain-specific properties. They should set this.name explicitly for better stack traces.

docs.title: Concept 8: Error.cause (ES2022)
docs.text:
try {
    parseConfig(data);
} catch (err) {
    throw new Error("Failed to load config", { cause: err });
}

The cause option preserves the original error, creating a chain of causation.

docs.title: Concept 9: AggregateError (ES2021)
docs.text:
throw new AggregateError([err1, err2], "Multiple operations failed");

AggregateError wraps multiple errors into one — useful for Promise.any() and batch operations.

docs.title: Concept 10: Error.isError() (ES2026)
docs.text:
Error.isError(new Error());        // true
Error.isError(new TypeError());    // true
Error.isError({ message: "x" });   // false
Error.isError("error");            // false

Error.isError() is the reliable way to check if a value is an error object. It replaces instanceof Error, which fails across realms and produces false positives for objects with Error.prototype in their chain.

docs.title: Concept 11: Optional Catch Binding (ES2019)
docs.text:
try {
    JSON.parse(input);
} catch {
    console.error("Invalid JSON");
}

When the error object is not needed, the binding can be omitted.

docs.title: Concept 12: finally Overrides try and catch Returns
docs.text:
If finally contains a return statement, it overrides any return from try or catch:

function f() {
    try {
        return "try";
    } finally {
        return "finally"; // overrides "try"
    }
}
f(); // "finally"

This is almost always a mistake. Never use return in a finally block.

docs.title: Concept 13: Exceptions and Async Code
docs.text:
Exceptions in async functions become rejected promises:

async function f() {
    throw new Error("async error");
}
f().catch(e => console.log(e.message)); // "async error"

try...catch works inside async functions:

async function f() {
    try {
        await risky();
    } catch (e) {
        console.error(e);
    }
}

docs.title: Concept 14: Uncaught Exceptions
docs.text: If an exception is not caught by any catch, it propagates to the top of the call stack and the program terminates. In browsers, the window.onerror / unhandledrejection events fire. In Node.js, the uncaughtException / unhandledRejection events fire.

docs.title: Concept 15: The stack Property
docs.text:
Error objects have a stack property that records the call stack at the point of the error:

const err = new Error("test");
console.log(err.stack);
// Error: test
//     at <anonymous>:1:13

docs.title: Concept 16: finally and Resource Cleanup
docs.text:
finally is the pre-ES2026 way to guarantee cleanup:

let file;
try {
    file = openFile("data.txt");
    process(file);
} finally {
    file?.close();
}

ES2026's using declaration replaces this pattern:

{
    using file = openFile("data.txt");
    process(file);
} // file closed automatically

docs.title: Concept 17: Throwing in Callbacks
docs.text:
Exceptions thrown in asynchronous callbacks are not catchable by the outer try:

try {
    setTimeout(() => {
        throw new Error("async"); // NOT caught here
    }, 0);
} catch (e) {
    console.log("never runs");
}

The exception propagates to the global handler instead.

docs.title: Concept 18: Exceptions Are Expensive
docs.text: Throwing and catching exceptions has performance cost — the engine must capture the stack trace, unwind the stack, and create the error object. Do not use exceptions for normal control flow.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: throw Execution
docs.text:
1.  `throw expression` is encountered.
    │
    ▼
2.  Expression is evaluated to produce the thrown value.
    │
    ▼
3.  Execution of the current function stops immediately.
    │
    ▼
4.  Control passes to the nearest enclosing try...catch.
    │
    ▼
5.  If none exists in the call stack → program terminates.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: try...catch Execution
docs.text:
1.  `try` block begins execution.
    │
    ▼
2.  If no exception is thrown:
    │   - `try` completes normally.
    │   - `catch` is skipped.
    │   - `finally` runs (if present).
    │
    ▼
3.  If an exception is thrown:
    │   - `try` block execution stops.
    │   - `catch` block executes with the thrown value bound to its parameter.
    │   - `finally` runs (if present).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: finally Execution
docs.text:
1.  try block completes (normally or via exception).
    │
    ▼
2.  catch block completes (if it ran).
    │
    ▼
3.  finally block ALWAYS executes.
    │
    ▼
4.  If finally has a return/throw, it overrides the pending completion.
    │
    ▼
5.  Control resumes after the try statement.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Error.isError() (ES2026)
docs.text:
1.  Error.isError(value) is called.
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine performs a branded check for a private field.
    │
    ▼
3.  If the private field is present → true.
    │
    ▼
4.  If not → false.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Exception Propagation in Async Code
docs.text:
1.  Async function throws.
    │
    ▼
2.  The exception is captured.
    │
    ▼
3.  The returned promise is rejected with the error.
    │
    ▼
4.  Caller's .catch() or try/catch around await handles it.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of Exceptions
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification covers exceptions in Section 14.15 (try Statement) and Section 14.14 (throw Statement). Key concepts:

  • Completion Records — every statement returns a completion record with a [[Type]] of normal, break, continue, return, or throw.
  • ThrowCompletion — the completion record produced by throw.
  • UpdateEmpty — ensures thrown values are propagated correctly.

docs.title: The [[ErrorData]] Internal Slot
docs.text: Error objects have an internal slot called [[ErrorData]]. The Error.isError() method checks for this slot via a branded check — the same mechanism used by Array.isArray().

docs.title: Stack Trace Capture
docs.text: When an Error object is created, V8 captures the current call stack and stores it in the stack property. This is the most expensive part of throwing an exception — capturing the stack involves walking every frame.

docs.title: Stack Unwinding
docs.text:
When an exception propagates, V8 unwinds the call stack — discarding frames from the throw point back to the catch point. For each frame, it:

  1. Runs any finally blocks.
  2. Destroys local variables.
  3. Moves to the previous frame.

docs.title: finally and Completion Records
docs.text: finally blocks are implemented via Completion records. The try block produces a completion record. The finally block runs. If finally produces a completion record of type normal, the original completion is preserved. If finally produces return, throw, break, or continue, it overrides the original.

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text:
• try blocks do not deoptimize by themselves in modern V8.
  • throw and catch are expensive — stack capture, object allocation, and unwinding.
  • finally blocks add overhead to every exit path from the try.
  • Engines optimize by not capturing stack traces unless the error is actually used.

docs.title: Error.isError() Implementation
docs.text: Error.isError() is implemented as a branded check — it inspects the internal [[ErrorData]] slot directly, bypassing the prototype chain entirely. This makes it fast, reliable, and immune to prototype pollution.

docs.title: Exception Lifecycle
docs.text:
Thrown → Propagates up stack → Caught → Handled → Execution resumes after catch
                                      │
                                      └── Not caught → Program terminates

docs.title: try...catch...finally Lifecycle
docs.text:
try block → (exception?) → catch block → finally block → after try
     │                                        │
     └── (no exception) ──────────────────────┘

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write code → Identify failure points → Add try/catch → Add finally for cleanup
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint no-unused-vars, no-unsafe-finally)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript strict)
    │
    ▼
Run tests → Catch unhandled exceptions

docs.title: Error Recovery Workflow
docs.text:
Exception thrown
    │
    ▼
Catch at appropriate level
    │
    ├── Recoverable? → Handle and continue
    │
    ├── Not recoverable? → Log and rethrow
    │
    └── Unknown? → Let propagate

docs.title: Example 1: Basic try...catch
docs.text:
try {
    const data = JSON.parse('{"invalid": }');
} catch (error) {
    console.error("Parse failed:", error.message);
}

Breakdown:

  • JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError for invalid JSON.
  • catch handles the error gracefully.

docs.title: Example 2: try...finally for Cleanup
docs.text:
function readFile(path) {
    let file;
    try {
        file = openFile(path);
        return file.read();
    } finally {
        file?.close();
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • finally guarantees the file is closed even if read() throws.
  • file?.close() handles the case where openFile itself failed.

docs.title: Example 3: Custom Error Class
docs.text:
class ValidationError extends Error {
    constructor(message, field) {
        super(message);
        this.name = "ValidationError";
        this.field = field;
    }
}

function validateEmail(email) {
    if (!email.includes("@")) {
        throw new ValidationError("Invalid email", "email");
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • ValidationError extends Error.
  • this.name is set explicitly for better stack traces.
  • field stores domain-specific data.

docs.title: Example 4: Error.cause (ES2022)
docs.text:
try {
    const config = JSON.parse(rawConfig);
} catch (err) {
    throw new Error("Failed to load configuration", { cause: err });
}

Breakdown:

  • The original SyntaxError is preserved as error.cause.
  • The new error adds context without losing the original.

docs.title: Example 5: Error.isError() (ES2026)
docs.text:
try {
    riskyOperation();
} catch (err) {
    if (Error.isError(err)) {
        console.error("Real error:", err.message);
    } else {
        console.warn("Non-error thrown:", err);
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • Error.isError() reliably identifies real error objects.
  • Handles the fact that JavaScript allows throwing anything.

docs.title: Example 6: AggregateError
docs.text:
const results = await Promise.allSettled([
    fetch("/a"),
    fetch("/b"),
    fetch("/c"),
]);

const errors = results
    .filter(r => r.status === "rejected")
    .map(r => r.reason);

if (errors.length > 0) {
    throw new AggregateError(errors, "Some requests failed");
}

Breakdown:

  • AggregateError wraps multiple errors into one.
  • Useful for batch operations.

docs.title: Example 7: Async Error Handling
docs.text:
async function loadUser(id) {
    try {
        const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return await res.json();
    } catch (err) {
        console.error("Failed to load user:", err);
        throw err; // rethrow — caller decides what to do
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • try/catch works inside async functions.
  • throw err rethrows — preserving the error for the caller.

docs.title: Example 8: Optional Catch Binding (ES2019)
docs.text:
try {
    JSON.parse(input);
} catch {
    console.error("Invalid JSON");
}

Breakdown:

  • No binding needed when the error object is not used.

docs.title: Example 9: using for Resource Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text:
{
    using file = openFile("data.txt");
    const data = file.read();
} // file closed automatically — even if read() throws

Breakdown:

  • using replaces try/finally for resource cleanup.
  • Disposal happens in reverse order.

docs.title: Example 10: Uncaught Exception Handler (Node.js)
docs.text:
process.on("uncaughtException", (err) => {
    console.error("Uncaught exception:", err);
    process.exit(1);
});

process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => {
    console.error("Unhandled rejection:", reason);
    process.exit(1);
});

Breakdown:

  • Global handlers for exceptions that escape all catch blocks.
  • Should log and exit — not swallow.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Approach Validate user input Throw ValidationError Parse JSON try/catch around JSON.parse Network requests try/catch around fetch File operations try/finally or using (ES2026) Batch operations AggregateError Chain errors Error.cause (ES2022) Cross-realm error detection Error.isError() (ES2026) Async errors try/catch inside async functions Global handling uncaughtException / unhandledRejection

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always throw Error objects. Why: standard properties (message, stack) are expected by catch blocks.
  2. Use Error.isError() instead of instanceof Error. Why: reliable across realms (ES2026).
  3. Use Error.cause to chain errors. Why: preserves the original cause (ES2022).
  4. Use custom error classes for domain errors. Why: enables specific handling.
  5. Always set this.name in custom errors. Why: better stack traces.
  6. Use finally for cleanup. Why: guarantees execution.
  7. Never use return in finally. Why: overrides try/catch returns.
  8. Use using instead of try/finally for resource cleanup. Why: cleaner, less error-prone (ES2026).
  9. Never swallow errors silently. Why: hides bugs and security issues.
  10. Rethrow if you cannot handle. Why: lets the caller decide.
  11. Keep try blocks focused. Why: avoid catching unrelated errors.
  12. Do not use exceptions for normal control flow. Why: expensive — stack capture and unwinding.
  13. Handle async errors with try/catch or .catch(). Why: async functions reject promises.
  14. Use optional catch binding when the error is unused. Why: cleaner code (ES2019).
  15. Log errors with context. Why: bare console.error(e) loses information.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Throwing Strings Instead of Errors
docs.text:
throw "Something went wrong"; // ❌ no stack trace

✅ Correct:

throw new Error("Something went wrong");

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using instanceof Error Across Realms
docs.text:
if (err instanceof Error) { /* fails for errors from iframes */ }

✅ Correct:

if (Error.isError(err)) { /* works across realms */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Swallowing Errors
docs.text:
try { risky(); } catch (e) { } // ❌ silent failure

✅ Correct:

try { risky(); } catch (e) { console.error(e); throw e; }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: return in finally
docs.text:
try { return "try"; } finally { return "finally"; } // overrides

✅ Correct: Never use return in finally.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Catching Too Much
docs.text:
try {
    validateInput();
    saveToDatabase();
    sendEmail();
} catch (e) {
    console.error("Something failed"); // which one?
}

✅ Correct: Keep try blocks focused on one operation.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming catch Catches Async Errors
docs.text:
try {
    setTimeout(() => { throw new Error("async"); }, 0);
} catch (e) { /* never runs */ }

✅ Correct: Handle async errors in the callback or use promises.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing name in Custom Errors
docs.text:
class MyError extends Error {} // name is "Error"

✅ Correct:

class MyError extends Error {
    constructor(msg) { super(msg); this.name = "MyError"; }
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using finally Without catch for Recovery
docs.text:
try { risky(); } finally { cleanup(); } // exception still propagates

✅ Correct: Use catch if you want to handle the error.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Throwing Non-Errors in Libraries
docs.text:
throw { code: 404 }; // ❌ no message, no stack

✅ Correct:

const err = new Error("Not found");
err.code = 404;
throw err;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Handling Unhandled Rejections
docs.text:
fetch("/api").then(r => r.json()); // no catch

✅ Correct:

fetch("/api").then(r => r.json()).catch(console.error);

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• throw is expensive — capturing the stack trace is the most costly part.
  • catch is cheap — binding the error is a simple assignment.
  • try blocks do not deoptimize — modern V8 optimizes them.
  • finally adds overhead — every exit path from try runs finally.
  • Stack capture can be deferred — V8 captures the stack only when error.stack is accessed.
  • Do not use exceptions for flow control — a throw/catch pair is orders of magnitude slower than an if check.
  • Error.isError() is fast — it performs a branded check, not a prototype walk.
  • AggregateError has overhead — wrapping many errors creates many objects.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use exceptions for exceptional conditions, not normal control flow.
  2. Prefer return values or Result-style objects for expected failures.
  3. Avoid throwing in hot loops.
  4. Keep try blocks small — the overhead is proportional to the block size.
  5. Use Error.isError() — it's faster than instanceof across realms.
  6. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt if exceptions appear in hot paths.

docs.title: Information Leakage via Stack Traces
docs.text:
Stack traces can leak internal file paths, function names, and library versions.

Defense: Sanitize error messages before returning them to users; log full traces server-side only.

docs.title: Uncaught Exceptions as DoS
docs.text:
An uncaught exception can crash the process — a denial-of-service vector.

Defense: Handle exceptions at trust boundaries; use per-request error boundaries.

docs.title: Error Objects as Attack Surface
docs.text:
Error objects may contain user-controlled data in their messages.

Defense: Sanitize error messages; never render them as HTML.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution and Error Detection
docs.text:
instanceof Error can be fooled by objects with Error.prototype in their chain.

Defense: Use Error.isError() — it performs a branded check, immune to prototype pollution.

docs.title: Rethrowing Sensitive Errors
docs.text:
Rethrowing an error with cause can leak the original error's details.

Defense: Create new errors for user-facing messages; log the cause internally.

docs.title: uncaughtException Handler Abuse
docs.text:
A global uncaughtException handler that swallows errors leaves the process in an unknown state.

Defense: Log, clean up, and exit the process.

docs.title: AggregateError and Sensitive Data
docs.text:
AggregateError may wrap errors containing sensitive data.

Defense: Sanitize before aggregating; never expose raw aggregates to users.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.error(e) — log the full error object.
  • console.trace() — print a stack trace at the current point.
  • debugger; — pause inside catch blocks.
  • Error.captureStackTrace() — Node.js — capture custom stack traces.
  • Error.isError() — reliably identify error objects (ES2026).
  • process.on("uncaughtException") — Node.js global handler.
  • window.onerror — browser global handler.
  • unhandledrejection — browser/Node.js promise rejection handler.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on throw.
  • ESLint no-unused-vars — flags unused catch bindings.
  • ESLint no-unsafe-finally — flags return/break/continue in finally.
  • TypeScript useUnknownInCatchVariables — strict catch variable typing.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Scenario Use Validate input throw new ValidationError(...) Handle I/O failures try/catch Guarantee cleanup finally or using (ES2026) Chain errors Error.cause (ES2022) Detect error objects Error.isError() (ES2026) Aggregate multiple errors AggregateError Handle async errors try/catch in async functions Global error handling uncaughtException / unhandledRejection

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For normal control flow — use conditionals.
  • For expected validation failures — return error objects instead.
  • In hot loops — exceptions are expensive.
  • To swallow errors — always handle or rethrow.
  • return in finally — overrides try/catch.
  • instanceof Error across realms — use Error.isError().
  • Throwing non-Error values — always throw Error objects.
  • Catching exceptions you cannot handle — let them propagate.

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• try/catch was introduced in ES3 (1999) — JavaScript had structured exception handling from its early days.
  • finally guarantees execution — even if try or catch contains return.
  • Error.isError() is part of ES2026 — it replaces unreliable instanceof Error checks.
  • Error.isError() returns true for DOMException — because DOMException behaves like Error.
  • Error.cause was added in ES2022 — chaining errors preserves the original cause.
  • Optional catch binding was added in ES2019 — catch {} without a parameter.
  • AggregateError was added in ES2021 — it wraps multiple errors into one.
  • throw must be followed by an expression — ASI can break throw across lines.
  • finally with return overrides try and catch — almost always a bug.
  • Uncaught exceptions terminate the program — unless a global handler exists.
  • Exceptions thrown in async callbacks are not catchable by outer try.
  • Error.isError() performs a branded check — the same mechanism as Array.isArray().
  • Stack traces are captured lazily — V8 captures the stack only when error.stack is accessed.
  • Exceptions are expensive — do not use them for normal control flow.
  • using declarations (ES2026) replace try/finally for resource cleanup.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Exceptions signal unexpected conditions and interrupt normal control flow.
  • throw stops execution and passes control to the nearest catch.
  • try...catch handles exceptions; finally guarantees cleanup.
  • Always throw Error objects — they have message, stack, and standard properties.
  • Error.isError() (ES2026) is the reliable way to identify error objects.
  • Error.cause (ES2022) chains errors to preserve the original cause.
  • Custom error classes extend Error and add domain-specific data.
  • AggregateError (ES2021) wraps multiple errors into one.
  • Optional catch binding (ES2019) — catch {} when the error is unused.
  • finally always runs — but never use return in it.
  • Exceptions propagate up the call stack until caught or the program terminates.
  • Async exceptions become rejected promises; use try/catch with await.
  • Uncaught exceptions crash the program — handle at trust boundaries.
  • Exceptions are expensive — use them for exceptional conditions, not control flow.
  • using (ES2026) replaces try/finally for deterministic resource cleanup.
  • Error.isError() replaces instanceof Error — it works across realms and resists prototype pollution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Error handling is the practice of anticipating, detecting, and responding to failures in a program so that it can continue operating, degrade gracefully, or terminate cleanly. In JavaScript, error handling spans several mechanisms — the try/catch/finally construct, promise rejection handling, global handlers, custom error types, and the newer using declaration for deterministic resource cleanup (ES2026).

// Synchronous error handling
try {
    const data = JSON.parse(input);
} catch (error) {
    logger.error("Parse failed", { error, input });
    throw new AppError("INVALID_JSON", 400);
}

// Asynchronous error handling
try {
    const res = await fetch("/api/users");
    if (!res.ok) throw new AppError("HTTP_ERROR", res.status);
} catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof AppError && error.statusCode === 404) {
        return [];
    }
    throw error;
}

// Deterministic resource cleanup (ES2026)
{
    using connection = await db.connect();
    await connection.query("SELECT 1");
} // connection[Symbol.asyncDispose]() called automatically

Error handling is not a single feature — it is a strategy that combines language constructs, error taxonomy, logging, and recovery patterns. It is the final concept in Control Flow because it is the mechanism that deals with everything control flow cannot predict.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Error handling exists to solve the failure problem: programs fail. Networks drop, files disappear, inputs are malformed, servers return errors. A program that cannot handle failure is a program that crashes. Error handling provides:

  • Detection — identify when something has gone wrong.
  • Isolation — prevent one failure from cascading into others.
  • Recovery — allow the program to continue or degrade gracefully.
  • Diagnosis — capture enough information to debug the failure later.
  • Cleanup — release resources regardless of outcome.

Error handling is what separates toy programs from production systems. A program that only works when everything succeeds is not a program — it is a demo.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Control Flow
├── Conditionals          ✅ done
├── Loops                 ✅ done
├── break & continue      ✅ done
├── Labels                ✅ done
├── Exceptions            ✅ done
├── Error Handling        ← you are here
│
Language Fundamentals
├── Functions
├── Objects
└── ...

This is the last concept in the Control Flow section. Everything that follows — Functions, Objects, Modules, Async — builds on the error handling patterns established here. The next section is Functions.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Every non-trivial program encounters failures. But handling failure poorly is worse than not handling it at all. A program that swallows errors silently hides bugs. A program that crashes on every error is unusable. A program that leaks internal details in error messages is a security risk.

The problem is not "how do I catch an error?" — JavaScript provides try/catch for that. The problem is "what do I do with the error once I catch it?" That is the question error handling answers.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation No structured errors Errors were strings — no type, no stack, no metadata No async error handling Callbacks had no standard error propagation No custom errors All errors were generic Error objects No cause Chained errors required manual property copying No Error.isError() instanceof Error failed across realms No resource cleanup try/finally was the only option — verbose and error-prone

docs.title: Why Error Handling Evolved
docs.text:
Error handling in JavaScript has evolved from basic exception catching to a layered strategy:

  • ES3 (1999) — try/catch/finally brought structured exceptions.
  • ES6 (2015) — class extends Error enabled custom error types.
  • ES2019 — optional catch binding removed noise.
  • ES2021 — AggregateError wrapped multiple errors.
  • ES2022 — Error.cause chained errors.
  • ES2026 — Error.isError() and using declarations for reliable detection and deterministic cleanup.

Each addition solved a specific weakness in the previous generation's approach. The result is a layered defense — not a single mechanism, but a set of tools that work together.

docs.title: The Modern Consensus (2026)
docs.text:
By 2026, the industry has converged on several principles:

  1. Structured errors — use custom error classes with codes and metadata, not raw Error objects.
  2. Structured logging — log errors as queryable JSON, not console.error(err).
  3. Centralized handling — use middleware, error boundaries, and global handlers.
  4. Boundary catching — catch at trust boundaries, not everywhere.
  5. Graceful degradation — fail one component, not the whole system.
  6. Resource safety — use using for deterministic cleanup (ES2026).
  7. Reliable detection — use Error.isError() instead of instanceof (ES2026).

docs.title: The try/catch/finally Construct
docs.text:
try {
    // code that may throw
} catch (error) {
    // handle the error
} finally {
    // always runs — cleanup
}

docs.title: Throwing Errors
docs.text:
throw new Error("Something went wrong");
throw new TypeError("Expected a string");
throw new RangeError("Value out of range");
throw new AppError("USER_NOT_FOUND", 404, { userId });

Always throw Error objects — they have message, stack, and standard properties. Throwing strings or plain objects loses this information.

docs.title: Custom Error Classes
docs.text:
class AppError extends Error {
    constructor(message, code, statusCode = 500, context = {}) {
        super(message);
        this.name = "AppError";
        this.code = code;
        this.statusCode = statusCode;
        this.context = context;
        Error.captureStackTrace?.(this, this.constructor);
    }
}

Custom errors add domain-specific metadata — error codes, HTTP status codes, field names — enabling precise handling.

docs.title: Error Chaining with cause (ES2022)
docs.text:
try {
    const config = JSON.parse(rawConfig);
} catch (err) {
    throw new AppError("Failed to load configuration", "CONFIG_ERROR", 500, {
        cause: err,
    });
}

The cause option preserves the original error, creating a chain of causation that aids debugging.

docs.title: Error.isError() (ES2026)
docs.text:
try {
    riskyOperation();
} catch (err) {
    if (Error.isError(err)) {
        logger.error("Real error", { message: err.message, stack: err.stack });
    } else {
        logger.warn("Non-error thrown", { value: String(err) });
    }
}

Error.isError() is a static method that reliably identifies Error objects. It replaces instanceof Error, which fails across realms (iframes, workers) and returns false positives for objects with Error.prototype in their chain.

docs.title: Optional Catch Binding (ES2019)
docs.text:
try {
    JSON.parse(input);
} catch {
    showError("Invalid JSON");
}

When the error object is not needed, omit the binding.

docs.title: Promise Error Handling
docs.text:
// .catch()
fetch("/api")
    .then(res => res.json())
    .catch(err => logger.error("Fetch failed", { err }));

// async/await with try/catch
async function loadData() {
    try {
        const res = await fetch("/api");
        if (!res.ok) throw new AppError("HTTP_ERROR", res.status);
        return await res.json();
    } catch (err) {
        logger.error("Load failed", { err });
        throw err;
    }
}

docs.title: Global Handlers
docs.text:
// Browser
window.addEventListener("error", (event) => {
    reportToTelemetry({ type: "sync", error: event.error });
});

window.addEventListener("unhandledrejection", (event) => {
    reportToTelemetry({ type: "async", reason: String(event.reason) });
});

// Node.js
process.on("uncaughtException", (err) => {
    logger.fatal("Uncaught exception", { err });
    process.exit(1);
});

process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => {
    logger.fatal("Unhandled rejection", { reason });
    process.exit(1);
});

docs.title: Deterministic Cleanup with using (ES2026)
docs.text:
{
    using file = openFile("data.txt");
    const data = file.read();
} // file[Symbol.dispose]() called automatically — even if read() throws

{
    await using conn = await db.connect();
    await conn.query("SELECT 1");
} // await conn[Symbol.asyncDispose]() called automatically

using and await using guarantee resource cleanup when the block exits — normally or via exception. This replaces verbose try/finally patterns.

docs.title: AggregateError (ES2021)
docs.text:
const errors = results
    .filter(r => r.status === "rejected")
    .map(r => r.reason);

if (errors.length > 0) {
    throw new AggregateError(errors, "Multiple operations failed");
}

AggregateError wraps multiple errors into one — useful for batch operations and Promise.any().

docs.title: The "Boundary Layer" Mental Model
docs.text:
Error handling is most effective when organized as boundaries:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   Application                       │
│                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐          │
│  │   HTTP Layer    │  │   Data Layer    │          │
│  │   (Express)     │  │   (Database)    │          │
│  │                 │  │                 │          │
│  │  try/catch      │  │  try/catch      │          │
│  │  → AppError     │  │  → AppError     │          │
│  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘          │
│                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │           Global Handler                     │   │
│  │  uncaughtException / unhandledRejection     │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Each boundary catches, translates, and rethrows errors in the vocabulary of that layer. The HTTP layer translates database errors into HTTP responses. The global handler catches anything that escapes.

docs.title: The "Error Taxonomy" Mental Model
docs.text:
Not all errors are the same. Classify them:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   Error Types                        │
│                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Operational        │  │  Programmer          │  │
│  │  (expected)          │  │  (bug)              │  │
│  │                      │  │                      │  │
│  │  • Network timeout  │  │  • TypeError         │  │
│  │  • Validation fail  │  │  • ReferenceError    │  │
│  │  • 404 Not found    │  │  • Logic bugs        │  │
│  │                      │  │                      │  │
│  │  → Handle gracefully│  │  → Fix the code      │  │
│  │  → Retry             │  │  → Log and crash     │  │
│  │  → Degrade           │  │  → Alert developer   │  │
│  └─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Operational errors are expected — handle them. Programmer errors are bugs — fix the code, don't swallow the error.

docs.title: The "Layered Defense" Mental Model
docs.text:
Layer 1: Local try/catch       → handle what you can
Layer 2: Boundary translation  → translate to layer vocabulary
Layer 3: Centralized middleware→ consistent API responses
Layer 4: Global handlers       → last resort — log and exit

Each layer has a specific job. No single layer handles everything.

docs.title: The "Resource Lifetime" Mental Model
docs.text:
using ties a resource's lifetime to a block:

{
    using file = openFile("data.txt");
    // use file
} // file disposed automatically — even on exception

This is the JavaScript equivalent of C#'s using and Python's with. It replaces the try/finally pattern with deterministic, automatic disposal.

docs.title: Concept 1: Operational vs. Programmer Errors
docs.text:
Type Example Handling Operational Network timeout, 404, validation failure Handle, retry, degrade gracefully Programmer TypeError, ReferenceError, logic bugs Fix the code; don't swallow

Operational errors are expected — they are part of normal operation. Programmer errors are bugs — they should be fixed, not handled.

docs.title: Concept 2: Error Boundaries
docs.text:
An error boundary is a layer that catches errors from below and translates them into a form suitable for above:

  • HTTP boundary — catches database errors, returns HTTP status codes.
  • UI boundary — React Error Boundary catches rendering errors.
  • Module boundary — catches errors from a subsystem and translates them.

docs.title: Concept 3: Structured Errors
docs.text:
Structured errors carry metadata:

class AppError extends Error {
    constructor(message, code, statusCode, context) {
        super(message);
        this.code = code;
        this.statusCode = statusCode;
        this.context = context;
    }
}

This enables machine-readable handling — the caller can switch on error.code instead of string-matching the message.

docs.title: Concept 4: Structured Logging
docs.text:
Replace console.error(err) with structured logging:

logger.error("Failed to fetch users", {
    error: err.message,
    stack: err.stack,
    endpoint: "/api/users",
    component: "UsersList",
});

Structured logs are queryable JSON — the difference between debugging in seconds vs hours.

docs.title: Concept 5: Error Chaining with cause (ES2022)
docs.text:
try {
    parseConfig(data);
} catch (err) {
    throw new AppError("Config load failed", "CONFIG_ERROR", 500, { cause: err });
}

The cause preserves the original error, creating a chain of causation that aids debugging.

docs.title: Concept 6: Error.isError() (ES2026)
docs.text:
Error.isError(new Error());        // true
Error.isError({ message: "fake" }); // false
Error.isError("error");            // false

Error.isError() performs a branded check for the internal [[ErrorData]] slot. It is:

  • Reliable across realms — works for errors from iframes and workers.
  • Resistant to prototype pollution — objects with Error.prototype in their chain return false.
  • A replacement for instanceof Error — which fails in both cases.

docs.title: Concept 7: Optional Catch Binding (ES2019)
docs.text:
try {
    JSON.parse(input);
} catch {
    console.error("Invalid JSON");
}

When the error object is unused, omit the binding.

docs.title: Concept 8: AggregateError (ES2021)
docs.text:
throw new AggregateError([err1, err2], "Multiple failures");

Wraps multiple errors into one — useful for batch operations and Promise.any().

docs.title: Concept 9: Unhandled Rejections
docs.text:
In Node.js 15+, unhandled promise rejections crash the process by default. In browsers, they fire the unhandledrejection event.

Best practice: Always attach .catch() to promise chains, or use try/catch with await.

docs.title: Concept 10: Global Handlers
docs.text:
// Node.js — last resort: log and exit
process.on("uncaughtException", (err) => {
    logger.fatal("Uncaught exception", { err });
    process.exit(1);
});

Global handlers are not a recovery mechanism — they are for logging and graceful shutdown. After an uncaught exception, the process is in an unknown state.

docs.title: Concept 11: Retry with Exponential Backoff
docs.text:
async function withRetry(fn, maxAttempts = 3) {
    for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
        try {
            return await fn();
        } catch (err) {
            if (attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
            await sleep(2 ** attempt * 100);
        }
    }
}

Retry transient failures — network timeouts, rate limits, temporary unavailability. Do not retry permanent failures — 400 Bad Request, validation errors.

docs.title: Concept 12: using for Deterministic Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text:
{
    using file = openFile("data.txt");
    // use file
} // file[Symbol.dispose]() called automatically

using guarantees disposal even if an exception occurs. It replaces try/finally for resource cleanup.

docs.title: Concept 13: Error Suppression and Masking
docs.text:
Never swallow errors silently:

try { risky(); } catch (e) { } // ❌ hides bugs

If you cannot handle an error, rethrow it or log it. Silent failure is a security risk — it masks attacks and leaves the system in an unknown state.

docs.title: Concept 14: finally and Cleanup
docs.text:
finally runs regardless of outcome — but it is verbose:

let file;
try {
    file = openFile("data.txt");
    process(file);
} finally {
    file?.close();
}

ES2026's using replaces this pattern with automatic disposal.

docs.title: Concept 15: Error Handling in React
docs.text:
React has Error Boundaries — components that catch errors in their child tree:

class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
    state = { hasError: false };
    static getDerivedStateFromError() { return { hasError: true }; }
    render() {
        if (this.state.hasError) return <div>Section failed to load</div>;
        return this.props.children;
    }
}

Place boundaries at multiple levels — one crash should not kill the entire UI.

docs.title: Concept 16: Error Handling in Express
docs.text:
Express 5 automatically forwards async handler rejections to error middleware:

app.get("/users/:id", async (req, res, next) => {
    try {
        const user = await getUser(req.params.id);
        res.json(user);
    } catch (err) {
        next(err); // forward to error middleware
    }
});

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
    if (err instanceof AppError) {
        return res.status(err.statusCode).json({ code: err.code, message: err.message });
    }
    res.status(500).json({ code: "INTERNAL_ERROR", message: "Unexpected error" });
});

In Express 4, async rejections bypass error middleware unless wrapped.

docs.title: Concept 17: Error Handling in Server Actions
docs.text:
Server Actions should return structured error state — never throw uncaught:

return { ok: false, fieldErrors: { email: "Invalid" }, formError: null };

Validation errors render inline with role="alert" and aria-invalid.

docs.title: Concept 18: ES2026 Error Handling Features
docs.text:
• Error.isError() — reliable error detection across realms.
  • using / await using — deterministic resource cleanup.
  • AggregateError — already in ES2021, but now widely adopted.
  • Error.cause — already in ES2022, but now standard practice.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Error Propagation
docs.text:
1.  Error is thrown at some point in the call stack.
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine unwinds the stack, running finally blocks.
    │
    ▼
3.  First try...catch in the stack catches the error.
    │
    ▼
4.  If no catch exists → global handler fires.
    │
    ▼
5.  If no global handler → program terminates.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Promise Rejection Handling
docs.text:
1.  Async function throws or promise rejects.
    │
    ▼
2.  The rejection propagates through the promise chain.
    │
    ▼
3.  First .catch() or try/catch around await handles it.
    │
    ▼
4.  If no handler → unhandledRejection fires.
    │
    ▼
5.  In Node.js 15+ → process crashes by default.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Error Boundary Translation
docs.text:
1.  Database query fails with a low-level error.
    │
    ▼
2.  Data layer catches and translates to AppError.
    │
    ▼
3.  HTTP layer catches AppError and maps to status code.
    │
    ▼
4.  Client receives structured JSON error response.
    │
    ▼
5.  Client-side error handler displays user-friendly message.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: using Disposal (ES2026)
docs.text:
1.  using resource = acquire() executes.
    │
    ▼
2.  Resource is registered with the block's disposal stack.
    │
    ▼
3.  Block body executes.
    │
    ▼
4.  Block exits — normally or via exception.
    │
    ▼
5.  Resources are disposed in reverse order.
    │
    ▼
6.  Symbol.dispose() or Symbol.asyncDispose() is called.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Retry with Exponential Backoff
docs.text:
1.  Attempt 1 → fail
    │
    ▼
2.  Wait 100ms
    │
    ▼
3.  Attempt 2 → fail
    │
    ▼
4.  Wait 200ms
    │
    ▼
5.  Attempt 3 → succeed
    │
    ▼
6.  Return result

docs.title: Completion Records
docs.text:
In the ECMAScript spec, every statement returns a Completion Record:

{ [[Type]]: normal | break | continue | return | throw,
  [[Value]]: any,
  [[Target]]: label }

throw produces a ThrowCompletion. try/catch checks the completion type.

docs.title: The [[ErrorData]] Internal Slot
docs.text: Error objects have an internal slot called [[ErrorData]]. Error.isError() performs a branded check for this slot — the same mechanism used by Array.isArray().

docs.title: Stack Trace Capture
docs.text: When an Error object is created, V8 captures the current call stack. This is the most expensive part of throwing. V8 captures the stack lazily — only when error.stack is accessed.

docs.title: Error Boundaries in Frameworks
docs.text:
• React — componentDidCatch and getDerivedStateFromError.
  • Express — error middleware (app.use((err, req, res, next) => {})).
  • Next.js — error.tsx per route segment.

docs.title: using Implementation
docs.text: using is implemented via DisposableStack and AsyncDisposableStack — internal data structures that track resources and dispose them in reverse order. Babel transforms using into try/catch/finally with _usingCtx helpers.

docs.title: Global Handler Implementation
docs.text:
• Browser — window.onerror / window.addEventListener("error").
  • Node.js — process.on("uncaughtException") and process.on("unhandledRejection").
  • Web Workers — self.onerror / self.addEventListener("error").

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text:
• try blocks do not deoptimize in modern V8.
  • throw is expensive — stack capture, object allocation, unwinding.
  • finally adds overhead — every exit path runs finally.
  • Error.isError() is fast — branded check, no prototype walk.

docs.title: Error Handling Lifecycle
docs.text: Detect → Throw/Reject → Propagate → Catch at boundary → Translate → Log → Respond → Recover

docs.title: Production Error Handling Workflow
docs.text:
1.  Anticipate failure points (I/O, network, parsing, validation)
    │
    ▼
2.  Throw structured errors (AppError with code, status, context)
    │
    ▼
3.  Catch at trust boundaries (HTTP, DB, UI)
    │
    ▼
4.  Log structured data (error, code, stack, context)
    │
    ▼
5.  Translate to layer-specific response
    │
    ▼
6.  Global handler as last resort (log and exit)

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write code → Identify failure points → Add try/catch → Add finally/using
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint no-unused-vars, no-unsafe-finally)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript strict, useUnknownInCatchVariables)
    │
    ▼
Run tests → Verify error paths
    │
    ▼
Monitor production → Alert on error rates

docs.title: Error Recovery Workflow
docs.text:
Error thrown
    │
    ▼
Catch at appropriate boundary
    │
    ├── Recoverable? → Retry, fallback, degrade
    │
    ├── Not recoverable? → Log, translate, respond
    │
    └── Unknown? → Log, rethrow, global handler

docs.title: Example 1: Structured Error Class
docs.text:
class AppError extends Error {
    constructor(message, code, statusCode = 500, context = {}) {
        super(message);
        this.name = "AppError";
        this.code = code;
        this.statusCode = statusCode;
        this.context = context;
        Error.captureStackTrace?.(this, this.constructor);
    }
}

throw new AppError("User not found", "USER_NOT_FOUND", 404, { userId: 42 });

Breakdown:

  • code — machine-readable error code.
  • statusCode — HTTP status code.
  • context — additional debugging data.
  • Error.captureStackTrace — cleaner stack traces (Node.js).

docs.title: Example 2: Structured Logging
docs.text:
try {
    const res = await fetch("/api/users");
    if (!res.ok) throw new AppError("Users API failed", "HTTP_ERROR", res.status);
    const data = await res.json();
} catch (err) {
    logger.error("Failed to fetch users", {
        error: err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err),
        stack: err instanceof Error ? err.stack : undefined,
        endpoint: "/api/users",
        component: "UsersList",
    });
    throw err;
}

Breakdown:

  • Structured JSON logging — queryable, searchable.
  • Error.isError() could replace instanceof for reliability.

docs.title: Example 3: Centralized Express Error Handling
docs.text:
app.get("/users/:id", async (req, res, next) => {
    try {
        const user = await getUser(req.params.id);
        res.json(user);
    } catch (err) {
        next(err);
    }
});

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
    if (err instanceof AppError) {
        return res.status(err.statusCode).json({
            error: { code: err.code, message: err.message },
        });
    }
    logger.error("Unhandled error", { err });
    res.status(500).json({
        error: { code: "INTERNAL_ERROR", message: "Unexpected error" },
    });
});

Breakdown:

  • next(err) forwards to error middleware.
  • Express 5 forwards async rejections automatically.
  • Centralized error response format.

docs.title: Example 4: React Error Boundary
docs.text:
class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
    state = { hasError: false };

    static getDerivedStateFromError() {
        return { hasError: true };
    }

    componentDidCatch(error, info) {
        logger.error("React error boundary caught", { error, info });
    }

    render() {
        if (this.state.hasError) {
            return <div role="alert">Section failed to load</div>;
        }
        return this.props.children;
    }
}

<ErrorBoundary level="section">
    <RevenueChart />
</ErrorBoundary>
<ErrorBoundary level="section">
    <RecentOrders />
</ErrorBoundary>

Breakdown:

  • Multiple boundaries — one crash doesn't kill the page.
  • componentDidCatch logs structured data.
  • role="alert" announces the failure to assistive tech.

docs.title: Example 5: Retry with Exponential Backoff
docs.text:
async function withRetry(fn, maxAttempts = 3) {
    for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
        try {
            return await fn();
        } catch (err) {
            if (attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
            const delay = 2 ** attempt * 100;
            await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
        }
    }
}

const result = await withRetry(() => paymentProvider.charge(amount));

Breakdown:

  • Retries on failure.
  • Exponential backoff — 200ms, 400ms, 800ms.
  • Throws on final attempt.

docs.title: Example 6: using for Database Connection (ES2026)
docs.text:
async function getUser(id) {
    {
        await using conn = await db.connect();
        const result = await conn.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id]);
        return result.rows[0];
    } // conn[Symbol.asyncDispose]() called automatically
}

Breakdown:

  • await using guarantees connection cleanup.
  • Even if query throws, the connection is disposed.

docs.title: Example 7: Error Chaining with cause (ES2022)
docs.text:
try {
    const config = await loadConfig();
} catch (err) {
    throw new AppError("Failed to initialize app", "INIT_ERROR", 500, {
        cause: err,
    });
}

Breakdown:

  • The original error is preserved as error.cause.
  • The new error adds context without losing the original.

docs.title: Example 8: Error.isError() (ES2026)
docs.text:
try {
    riskyOperation();
} catch (err) {
    if (Error.isError(err)) {
        logger.error("Real error", { message: err.message, stack: err.stack });
    } else {
        logger.warn("Non-error thrown", { value: String(err) });
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • Error.isError() reliably identifies Error objects.
  • Handles the fact that JavaScript allows throwing anything.

docs.title: Example 9: Global Handlers (Node.js)
docs.text:
process.on("uncaughtException", (err) => {
    logger.fatal("Uncaught exception", { err });
    process.exit(1);
});

process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => {
    logger.fatal("Unhandled rejection", { reason });
    process.exit(1);
});

Breakdown:

  • Global handlers are last resort — log and exit.
  • Do not attempt to continue after an uncaught exception.

docs.title: Example 10: Fire-and-Forget Async Calls
docs.text:
// ❌ Dangerous — unhandled rejection
sendNotification(userId);

// ✅ Safe — explicit .catch()
sendNotification(userId).catch(err => {
    logger.error("Notification failed", { err, userId });
});

Breakdown:

  • Fire-and-forget async calls need explicit .catch().
  • Otherwise, an unhandled rejection crashes the process.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Strategy API request fails try/catch + retry with backoff Database query fails Translate to AppError, return 500 Validation fails Return structured field errors File operation fails using for automatic cleanup (ES2026) Promise rejection .catch() or try/catch with await React component crash Error Boundary Express route failure Error middleware Server Action failure Return { ok: false, fieldErrors, formError } Uncaught exception Global handler — log and exit Error detection Error.isError() (ES2026)

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use structured errors with codes and metadata. Why: enables machine-readable handling.
  2. Use Error.isError() instead of instanceof Error. Why: reliable across realms (ES2026).
  3. Use Error.cause to chain errors. Why: preserves the original cause (ES2022).
  4. Log structured data, not console.error(err). Why: queryable JSON is debuggable.
  5. Catch at boundaries, not everywhere. Why: avoids swallowing errors.
  6. Always rethrow if you cannot handle. Why: lets the caller decide.
  7. Never swallow errors silently. Why: hides bugs and security issues.
  8. Use using for resource cleanup. Why: deterministic, exception-safe (ES2026).
  9. Use exponential backoff for retries. Why: avoids overwhelming failing services.
  10. Attach .catch() to fire-and-forget promises. Why: prevents process crashes.
  11. Use global handlers for logging and graceful shutdown. Why: last resort — not recovery.
  12. Place Error Boundaries at multiple levels in React. Why: one crash doesn't kill the page.
  13. Centralize Express error handling in middleware. Why: consistent responses.
  14. Keep try blocks focused. Why: precise error handling.
  15. Enable TypeScript useUnknownInCatchVariables. Why: forces type-safe error handling.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Swallowing Errors
docs.text:
try { risky(); } catch (e) { } // ❌ silent failure

✅ Correct:

try { risky(); } catch (e) { logger.error(e); throw e; }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using instanceof Error Across Realms
docs.text:
if (err instanceof Error) { /* fails for errors from iframes */ }

✅ Correct:

if (Error.isError(err)) { /* works across realms */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: console.error(err) for Production
docs.text:
catch (err) { console.error(err); } // ❌ unstructured

✅ Correct:

catch (err) {
    logger.error("Operation failed", { error: err.message, stack: err.stack, context });
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: No .catch() on Fire-and-Forget Promises
docs.text:
sendNotification(userId); // ❌ unhandled rejection

✅ Correct:

sendNotification(userId).catch(err => logger.error("Notification failed", { err }));

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: return in finally
docs.text:
try { return "try"; } finally { return "finally"; } // overrides

✅ Correct: Never use return in finally.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Throwing Strings
docs.text:
throw "Something went wrong"; // ❌ no stack trace

✅ Correct:

throw new AppError("Something went wrong", "GENERIC_ERROR");

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Catching Too Much
docs.text:
try {
    validateInput();
    saveToDatabase();
    sendEmail();
} catch (e) {
    console.error("Something failed"); // which one?
}

✅ Correct: Keep try blocks focused.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Missing Global Handlers
docs.text:
// No uncaughtException handler

✅ Correct:

process.on("uncaughtException", (err) => { logger.fatal(err); process.exit(1); });

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using uncaughtException to Continue
docs.text:
process.on("uncaughtException", () => { /* ignore and continue */ });

✅ Correct: Log and exit — the process is in an unknown state.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Express 4 Forwards Async Errors
docs.text:
app.get("/", async (req, res) => { throw new Error(); }); // Express 4: not caught

✅ Correct: Use try/catch + next(err) in Express 4; Express 5 forwards automatically.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• throw is expensive — stack capture, object allocation, unwinding.
  • try blocks do not deoptimize — modern V8 optimizes them.
  • finally adds overhead — every exit path runs finally.
  • using adds disposal registry overhead — proportional to resource count.
  • Error.isError() is fast — branded check, no prototype walk.
  • Structured logging has overhead — batch or sample in high-throughput systems.
  • Retries increase latency — use only for transient failures.
  • Global handlers add minimal overhead — they fire only on uncaught errors.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use exceptions for exceptional conditions, not control flow.
  2. Keep try blocks focused — the overhead is proportional to block size.
  3. Use Error.isError() — faster than instanceof across realms.
  4. Batch structured logging in high-throughput paths.
  5. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt if exceptions appear in hot paths.

docs.title: Information Disclosure via Stack Traces
docs.text:
Stack traces leak file paths, framework versions, and internal function names.

Defense: Log full detail internally; return generic messages externally. Keep source maps off public paths.

docs.title: Broken Flows Leave Unsafe State
docs.text:
An uncaught exception mid-sequence can leave the system half-committed — a deduction with no audit record.

Defense: Wrap security-sensitive flows so failures roll back rather than stopping mid-sequence.

docs.title: Uncaught Errors Mask Attacks
docs.text:
A malicious payload that triggers an exception you swallow silently loses the signal.

Defense: Log all errors — even handled ones. Never suppress error signals.

docs.title: Unhandled Rejections Crash the Process
docs.text:
In Node.js 15+, unhandled rejections crash the process by default.

Defense: Always attach .catch() or use try/catch with await.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution and Error Detection
docs.text:
instanceof Error can be fooled by objects with Error.prototype in their chain.

Defense: Use Error.isError() — branded check, immune to prototype pollution.

docs.title: Sensitive Data in Error Messages
docs.text:
Error messages may contain user data, SQL fragments, or connection strings.

Defense: Sanitize error messages before returning them to users.

docs.title: Denial of Service via Uncaught Exceptions
docs.text:
An uncaught exception can crash the process — a DoS vector.

Defense: Per-request error boundaries; global handlers for graceful shutdown.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Structured logging — log errors as JSON with context.
  • Error.captureStackTrace() — Node.js — cleaner stack traces.
  • Error.isError() — reliably identify error objects (ES2026).
  • debugger; — pause inside catch blocks.
  • console.trace() — print a stack trace at the current point.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on throw and catch.
  • Node.js --inspect-brk — step through error handling.
  • ESLint no-unused-vars — flags unused catch bindings.
  • ESLint no-unsafe-finally — flags return/break/continue in finally.
  • TypeScript useUnknownInCatchVariables — forces type-safe error handling.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Scenario Approach I/O operations try/catch Resource cleanup using / await using (ES2026) Async operations try/catch with await Fire-and-forget async .catch() Error detection Error.isError() (ES2026) Error chaining Error.cause (ES2022) Batch errors AggregateError (ES2021) Global handling uncaughtException / unhandledRejection React UI Error Boundaries Express routes Error middleware

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• For normal control flow — use conditionals.
  • For expected validation failures — return error objects.
  • In hot loops — exceptions are expensive.
  • To swallow errors — always handle or rethrow.
  • return in finally — overrides try/catch.
  • instanceof Error across realms — use Error.isError().
  • uncaughtException to continue — log and exit.
  • console.error(err) in production — use structured logging.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Exceptions — the mechanism behind error handling
  • Error Types — built-in and custom errors
  • try/catch/finally — the exception handling construct
  • throw — signaling exceptions
  • Custom Errors — extending Error
  • Error.cause — chaining errors (ES2022)
  • Error.isError() — reliable error detection (ES2026)
  • AggregateError — wrapping multiple errors (ES2021)
  • using — resource cleanup (ES2026)
  • Uncaught exceptions — global handlers
  • Promises — async error handling
  • React Error Boundaries — UI error handling

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Unhandled rejections crash the process in Node.js 15+ by default.
  • Error.isError() is part of ES2026 — it replaces unreliable instanceof Error checks.
  • Error.cause was added in ES2022 — chaining errors preserves the original cause.
  • using declarations are part of ES2026 — they replace try/finally for cleanup.
  • AggregateError was added in ES2021 — it wraps multiple errors.
  • try blocks do not deoptimize in modern V8.
  • Stack traces are captured lazily — V8 captures the stack only when error.stack is accessed.
  • Express 5 forwards async errors automatically — Express 4 does not.
  • React Error Boundaries catch errors in child components — but not in event handlers.
  • Fire-and-forget promises need .catch() — otherwise they crash the process.
  • Global handlers are for logging and exit — not for recovery.
  • Structured logging is the difference between debugging in seconds vs hours.
  • Error.isError() works across realms — instanceof Error fails for iframe errors.
  • using disposes in reverse order — last declared, first disposed.
  • Server Actions should return structured error state — never throw uncaught.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Error handling is a layered strategy — not a single mechanism.
  • Classify errors: operational (handle) vs. programmer (fix the code).
  • Use structured errors with codes, status codes, and context.
  • Use Error.isError() (ES2026) instead of instanceof Error.
  • Use Error.cause (ES2022) to chain errors.
  • Use using (ES2026) for deterministic resource cleanup.
  • Use structured logging — queryable JSON, not console.error.
  • Catch at boundaries — HTTP, DB, UI — not everywhere.
  • Never swallow errors silently — log and rethrow.
  • Always attach .catch() to fire-and-forget promises.
  • Use global handlers for logging and graceful shutdown — not recovery.
  • Use retry with exponential backoff for transient failures.
  • Place Error Boundaries at multiple levels in React.
  • Centralize Express error handling in middleware.
  • Keep try blocks focused — precise error handling.
  • Enable TypeScript useUnknownInCatchVariables.
  • Error handling is what makes production systems resilient — it is not optional.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function declaration is a statement that creates a named function and binds it to an identifier in the current scope. It is the most traditional and widely recognized way to define a reusable block of code in JavaScript.

function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

A function declaration consists of four parts:

  1. The function keyword.
  2. The function name (an identifier).
