docs.text: Arrow functions inherit super from the enclosing method. They cannot be used as constructors, so super() is not available inside them — but super.method() works if the enclosing method is a class method.

docs.title: Concept 6: Cannot Be Generators
docs.text: There is no =>* syntax. Arrow functions cannot contain yield and cannot be generator functions. Use function* for generators.

docs.title: Concept 7: Implicit Return
docs.text:
When the body is a single expression without braces, the expression's value is returned automatically:

const double = x => x * 2; // implicit return

When the body uses braces, an explicit return is required:

const double = x => { return x * 2; }; // explicit return

docs.title: Concept 8: Object Literal Parentheses
docs.text:
Returning an object literal requires parentheses to distinguish it from a block body:

const toObject = value => ({ result: value });

Without parentheses, { result: value } is parsed as a block with a label, and the function returns undefined.

docs.title: Concept 9: .call(), .apply(), and .bind() Have No Effect on this
docs.text:
Because arrow functions have lexical this, methods like .call(), .apply(), and .bind() cannot change this:

const arrow = () => this;
arrow.call({ name: "Ada" }); // `this` is still the enclosing scope

For functions that need dynamic this, use a regular function.

docs.title: Concept 10: Function Name Inference
docs.text:
When assigned to a variable, arrow functions infer their name from the variable:

const greet = () => "Hello";
console.log(greet.name); // "greet"

This improves stack traces and debugging.

docs.title: Concept 11: Arrow Functions in Modules Capture Module this
docs.text: In ES modules, top-level this is undefined. Arrow functions in modules capture this undefined value — they do not see globalThis.

docs.title: Concept 12: ES2026 Spec Clarification
docs.text: Per ES2026 §10.2.1.1 OrdinaryCallBindThis, if F.[[ThisMode]] is lexical, the engine does nothing — arrow functions inherit this lexically. This is the normative confirmation of arrow function this behavior.

docs.title: Concept 13: Performance — No Runtime Difference
docs.text:
V8 developer jmrk confirmed: "Arrow functions are (mostly) just 'syntactic sugar' for conventional function declarations. There is no performance difference".

The "arrow functions are faster" claim is a misconception. Arrow functions and regular functions perform identically in optimized code.

docs.title: Concept 14: No prototype Property — Security Benefit
docs.text: Because arrow functions have no prototype property, they are immune to prototype chain traversal attacks that exploit regular function prototypes.

docs.title: Concept 15: ESLint prefer-arrow-callback
docs.text:
ESLint's prefer-arrow-callback rule requires arrow functions for callbacks where they would produce identical behavior:

// ❌ Flagged
foo(function(a) { return a; });
foo(function() { return this.a; }.bind(this));

// ✅ Correct
foo(a => a);
foo(() => this.a);

docs.title: Concept 16: ESLint arrow-body-style
docs.text:
ESLint's arrow-body-style rule enforces consistent brace usage:

Option Meaning "always" Require braces "as-needed" (default) No braces where they can be omitted "never" No braces — constrain to expression bodies

docs.title: Concept 17: When to Use Arrow Functions — Decision Table
docs.text: Situation Use Arrow? Use Regular? Why Array callback (map, filter, reduce) ✅ Yes Okay Concise; this not needed Promise .then() callback ✅ Yes Okay Lexical this usually desired setTimeout / setInterval callback ✅ Yes With caution Preserves outer this Object method ❌ No ✅ Yes Method needs this = object Prototype method ❌ No ✅ Yes Method needs this = instance Constructor function ❌ No ✅ Yes Arrows cannot be used with new Event handler needing this ❌ No ✅ Yes this should be the DOM element Event handler using event.target ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Access via parameter, not this Generator function ❌ No ✅ Yes No =>* syntax Nested helper needing outer this ✅ Yes No Lexical this is the point

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Arrow Function Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters `=>` in expression position.
    │
    ▼
2.  ArrowFunction node is created in the AST with:
    │   - [[ThisMode]] = lexical
    │   - No [[Construct]] method
    │   - No own prototype property
    │
    ▼
3.  When execution reaches the expression:
    │   - A new function object is created.
    │   - Its [[Environment]] is set to the current lexical environment.
    │   - It captures `this` from the enclosing scope.
    │
    ▼
4.  The function is assigned, passed, or returned.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Lexical this Resolution
docs.text:
1.  Arrow function is called.
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine checks F.[[ThisMode]].
    │
    ▼
3.  If [[ThisMode]] is lexical → do nothing (ES2026 §10.2.1.1).
    │
    ▼
4.  `this` resolves to the enclosing scope's `this`.
    │
    ▼
5.  `.call()`, `.apply()`, `.bind()` have no effect.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Implicit Return
docs.text:
1.  Arrow function body is an expression (no braces).
    │
    ▼
2.  Expression is evaluated.
    │
    ▼
3.  Result is returned automatically.
    │
    ▼
4.  No `return` keyword needed.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Object Literal Return
docs.text:
1.  `x => ({ result: x })` is parsed.
    │
    ▼
2.  Parentheses make the braces an expression, not a block.
    │
    ▼
3.  Object literal is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  Object is returned automatically.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: No arguments Object
docs.text:
1.  Arrow function accesses `arguments`.
    │
    ▼
2.  Engine searches the scope chain.
    │
    ▼
3.  If enclosing regular function exists → inherit its `arguments`.
    │
    ▼
4.  If not → ReferenceError.
    │
    ▼
5.  Use rest parameters (`...args`) instead.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of Arrow Functions
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification covers arrow functions in Section 15.3 (Arrow Function Definitions). Key points:

  • ArrowFunction is a grammar production for expression position.
  • InstantiateArrowFunctionExpression — the abstract operation that creates the function object.
  • [[ThisMode]] — set to lexical for arrow functions.
  • No [[Construct]] — arrow functions are not constructors.
  • No prototype property — arrow functions lack it entirely.

docs.title: OrdinaryCallBindThis (ES2026 §10.2.1.1)
docs.text:
The spec defines how this is bound when a function is called:

OrdinaryCallBindThis(F, calleeContext, thisArgument):
1.  Let thisMode be F.[[ThisMode]].
2.  If thisMode is lexical → return (do nothing).
3.  If thisMode is strict → thisValue = thisArgument.
4.  Else → thisValue = globalThis.
5.  ...

For arrow functions, [[ThisMode]] is lexical, so step 2 returns immediately — no this binding occurs. The arrow function uses the this of its enclosing environment.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
Arrow Function Object:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [[Call]]           → bytecode      │
│  [[Environment]]    → outer scope   │
│  [[FormalParameters]] → [a, b]      │
│  [[FunctionBody]]   → AST           │
│  [[ThisMode]]       → lexical       │
│  name               → "" or inferred│
│  length             → param count   │
│  ❌ NO prototype property           │
│  ❌ NO [[Construct]] method         │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Function Name Inference
docs.text:
When assigned to a variable, arrow functions infer their name:

const greet = () => {};
console.log(greet.name); // "greet"

This is defined in the spec's Function Name Inference algorithm.

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text:
• No performance difference — V8 optimizes arrow and regular functions identically.
  • Class field arrows — create a new function per instance, which has memory implications.
  • Arrow functions in hot loops — avoid creating functions in loops; move them outside.

docs.title: No prototype Property
docs.text: Arrow functions do not have a prototype property. This is why they cannot be used as constructors — the new operator requires a prototype property to set up the instance chain.

docs.title: Arrow Function Lifecycle
docs.text: Parsed → Function object created at runtime → `this` captured lexically → Called → Executed → GC

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write callback or utility
    │
    ▼
Need dynamic `this`?
    │
    ├── Yes → Use regular function or method shorthand
    │
    └── No → Use arrow function
              │
              ▼
         Lint (ESLint prefer-arrow-callback, arrow-body-style)
              │
              ▼
         Type-check (TypeScript)
              │
              ▼
         Run / Test

docs.title: Choosing Between Arrow and Regular Workflow
docs.text:
Need `this` from call site?     → Regular function
Need `arguments`?                → Regular function
Need `new`?                      → Regular function / class
Need `yield`?                    → Regular generator
Object method?                   → Method shorthand
Prototype method?                → Regular function
Callback?                        → Arrow function ✅
Array method?                    → Arrow function ✅
Short utility?                   → Arrow function ✅
Nested helper needing outer this? → Arrow function ✅

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Arrow Function
docs.text:
const greet = (name) => `Hello, ${name}!`;
console.log(greet("Ada")); // "Hello, Ada!"

Breakdown:

  • Single parameter — parentheses optional.
  • Implicit return — no braces, no return.

docs.title: Example 2: Lexical this in Class
docs.text:
class Timer {
    constructor() {
        this.seconds = 0;
    }
    start() {
        setInterval(() => {
            this.seconds++;
            console.log(this.seconds);
        }, 1000);
    }
}

new Timer().start();
// 1, 2, 3, ... — `this` is the Timer instance

Breakdown:

  • Arrow function captures this from start().
  • Without arrow function, this would be the global object.

docs.title: Example 3: Array Methods with Arrow Functions
docs.text:
const users = [
    { name: "Ada", age: 36 },
    { name: "Grace", age: 45 },
    { name: "Alan", age: 41 },
];

const names = users.map(u => u.name);
const adults = users.filter(u => u.age >= 40);
const totalAge = users.reduce((sum, u) => sum + u.age, 0);

docs.title: Example 4: Returning Object Literals
docs.text:
const createUser = (name, age) => ({ name, age });
console.log(createUser("Ada", 36)); // { name: "Ada", age: 36 }

Breakdown:

  • Parentheses around { name, age } make it an object literal.
  • Without parentheses, it would be parsed as a block body.

docs.title: Example 5: Currying
docs.text:
const add = a => b => a + b;
const add5 = add(5);
console.log(add5(3)); // 8

Breakdown:

  • Arrow function returning an arrow function.
  • Enables partial application.

docs.title: Example 6: Async Arrow Function
docs.text:
const loadUser = async (id) => {
    try {
        const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return await res.json();
    } catch (err) {
        console.error("Failed:", err);
        throw err;
    }
};

docs.title: Example 7: IIAFE — Immediately Invoked Arrow Function
docs.text:
(() => {
    const privateVar = "secret";
    console.log(privateVar);
})();

docs.title: Example 8: Class Field Arrow Function
docs.text:
class Button {
    constructor(label) {
        this.label = label;
    }
    handleClick = () => {
        console.log(`Clicked: ${this.label}`);
    };
}

const btn = new Button("Submit");
btn.handleClick(); // "Clicked: Submit"

Breakdown:

  • Arrow function in class field binds this to the instance.
  • Each instance gets its own function — memory trade-off.

docs.title: Example 9: What NOT to Do — Object Method
docs.text:
// ❌ Arrow function as object method
const user = {
    name: "Ada",
    greet: () => `Hello, ${this.name}`,
};
console.log(user.greet()); // "Hello, undefined"

// ✅ Correct — method shorthand
const user = {
    name: "Ada",
    greet() { return `Hello, ${this.name}`; },
};
console.log(user.greet()); // "Hello, Ada"

docs.title: Example 10: What NOT to Do — Constructor
docs.text:
// ❌ Arrow function as constructor
const Person = (name) => { this.name = name; };
new Person("Ada"); // ❌ TypeError

// ✅ Correct — class
class Person {
    constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
}
new Person("Ada"); // works

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Arrow Function? Array methods (map, filter, reduce) ✅ Yes Promise callbacks (.then(), .catch()) ✅ Yes setTimeout / setInterval ✅ Yes Event handlers using event.target ✅ Yes Nested helpers needing outer this ✅ Yes Currying / partial application ✅ Yes Functional composition ✅ Yes Object methods ❌ No Prototype methods ❌ No Constructors ❌ No Generator functions ❌ No Event handlers needing this = element ❌ No

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use arrow functions for callbacks and array methods. Why: concise syntax and lexical this.
  2. Use method shorthand for object methods. Why: arrow functions break this.
  3. Use regular functions for constructors. Why: arrows cannot be used with new.
  4. Use rest parameters instead of arguments. Why: arrows have no arguments.
  5. Wrap object literals in parentheses when returning them. Why: avoids block-body parsing.
  6. Name your arrow functions when debugging matters. Why: improves stack traces.
  7. Avoid creating arrow functions in loops. Why: each iteration creates a new function.
  8. Use async arrow functions for async callbacks. Why: concise and lexical this.
  9. Enable ESLint prefer-arrow-callback. Why: enforces arrow functions for callbacks.
  10. Enable ESLint arrow-body-style. Why: enforces consistent brace usage.
  11. Use arrow functions for nested helpers. Why: eliminates self/bind hacks.
  12. Do not use arrow functions as object methods. Why: this will not be the object.
  13. Do not use arrow functions as prototype methods. Why: same this issue.
  14. Do not use arrow functions as event handlers needing this. Why: use event.target instead.
  15. Prefer arrow functions in class fields for event handlers. Why: binds this to the instance.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Arrow Function as Object Method
docs.text:
const user = {
    name: "Ada",
    greet: () => `Hello, ${this.name}`, // ❌ `this` is not user
};

✅ Correct:

const user = {
    name: "Ada",
    greet() { return `Hello, ${this.name}`; },
};

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Arrow Function as Constructor
docs.text:
const Person = (name) => { this.name = name; };
new Person("Ada"); // ❌ TypeError

✅ Correct:

class Person {
    constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting Parentheses for Object Return
docs.text:
const bad = () => { result: 42 }; // ❌ returns undefined

✅ Correct:

const good = () => ({ result: 42 });

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using arguments in Arrow Function
docs.text:
const f = () => arguments; // ❌ ReferenceError

✅ Correct:

const f = (...args) => args;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using .call() to Change this
docs.text:
const arrow = () => this;
arrow.call({ name: "Ada" }); // `this` unchanged

✅ Correct: Use a regular function when dynamic this is needed.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Arrow Function as Generator
docs.text:
const gen = *() => { yield 1; }; // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

function* gen() { yield 1; }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Arrow Function in Event Handler Needing this
docs.text:
button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log(this); // ❌ not the button
});

✅ Correct:

button.addEventListener("click", function() {
    console.log(this); // ✅ the button
});
// Or use event.target:
button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
    console.log(event.target); // ✅
});

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Creating Arrow Functions in Loops
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    arr.push(() => i); // creates 1000 functions
}

✅ Correct: Move function creation outside the loop when possible.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Arrow Functions Are Faster
docs.text:
// Arrow functions are NOT faster — no performance difference

✅ Correct: Choose based on semantics, not performance.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Arrow Functions for Prototype Methods
docs.text:
Array.prototype.first = () => this[0]; // ❌ `this` is not the array

✅ Correct:

Array.prototype.first = function() { return this[0]; };

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• No performance difference — V8 developer confirms arrow functions are "mostly syntactic sugar".
  • Class field arrows — create a new function per instance; memory trade-off.
  • Arrow functions in loops — each iteration creates a new function object; avoid in hot paths.
  • No prototype property — slightly less memory per function object.
  • JIT optimization — arrow functions optimize identically to regular functions.
  • this resolution — lexical this is resolved at creation time; no per-call binding cost.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Choose based on semantics, not performance.
  2. Avoid creating arrow functions inside loops.
  3. Use method shorthand for object methods — no per-instance function creation.
  4. Use class field arrows for event handlers when binding is needed.
  5. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt if needed.

docs.title: No prototype Property — Prototype Pollution Immunity
docs.text:
Arrow functions have no prototype property, making them immune to prototype chain traversal attacks that exploit regular function prototypes:

When a Cloud Function handler is declared using the function keyword and its validator is a plain object or arrow function, ... Use arrow functions instead of the function keyword for Cloud Function handlers. Arrow functions do not have a prototype property and are not affected by this vulnerability.

docs.title: Lexical this and Security
docs.text: Arrow functions capture this lexically — they cannot be tricked into binding to an attacker-controlled object via .call(), .apply(), or .bind(). This makes them safer for callbacks where this should be predictable.

docs.title: CSP Compatibility
docs.text: Arrow functions are compatible with strict Content Security Policy — they do not require eval or new Function.

docs.title: Async Arrow Functions and Unhandled Rejections
docs.text:
An async arrow function that throws an unhandled rejection can crash the process in Node.js.

Defense: Always attach .catch() or use try/catch inside the async arrow function.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Name your arrow functions — inferred names improve stack traces.
  • Use debugger; — pause inside arrow function bodies.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on arrow functions.
  • console.log(f) — displays the function source.
  • Check f.name — returns the inferred or explicit name.
  • ESLint prefer-arrow-callback — flags callbacks that should be arrows.
  • ESLint arrow-body-style — enforces consistent brace usage.
  • TypeScript — catches type errors at compile time.
  • Avoid deep nesting of arrow functions — harder to debug.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Scenario Use Arrow Function? Array callbacks ✅ Yes Promise callbacks ✅ Yes setTimeout / setInterval ✅ Yes Event handlers using event.target ✅ Yes Nested helpers needing outer this ✅ Yes Currying / partial application ✅ Yes Functional composition ✅ Yes Short utility functions ✅ Yes Class field event handlers ✅ Yes

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Object methods — this will not be the object.
  • Prototype methods — same this issue.
  • Constructors — arrows cannot be used with new.
  • Generators — no =>* syntax.
  • Event handlers needing this = element — use regular function or event.target.
  • Functions needing arguments — use rest parameters.
  • Functions needing dynamic this — use regular function.
  • Hot loops — avoid creating functions per iteration.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Function Declarations — the statement form
  • Function Expressions — the value form
  • Lexical this — the defining feature of arrow functions
  • arguments — not available in arrow functions
  • Constructors — arrow functions cannot be constructors
  • Generators — arrow functions cannot be generators
  • ESLint prefer-arrow-callback — enforces arrows for callbacks
  • ESLint arrow-body-style — enforces brace consistency
  • ES2026 §10.2.1.1 — lexical this binding
  • Currying — enabled by arrow functions
  • Functional Composition — cleaner with arrow syntax

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Arrow functions were introduced in ES2015 (ES6) — along with let/const, classes, and promises.
  • They are Baseline Widely available — supported since September 2016.
  • No performance difference — V8 developer confirms they are "mostly syntactic sugar".
  • They have no prototype property — making them immune to prototype chain traversal attacks.
  • They cannot be generators — there is no =>* syntax.
  • They cannot be constructors — calling with new throws a TypeError.
  • They have no arguments object — use rest parameters instead.
  • Lexical this is confirmed in ES2026 §10.2.1.1 — if [[ThisMode]] is lexical, the engine does nothing.
  • In modules, arrow functions capture undefined as this — not globalThis.
  • The object literal parentheses rule is the most common beginner mistake.
  • ESLint prefer-arrow-callback enforces arrows for callbacks.
  • ESLint arrow-body-style enforces consistent brace usage.
  • Arrow functions are the backbone of functional patterns — currying, composition, pipelines.
  • ES2026 did not add new arrow function syntax — the feature set is mature.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• An arrow function is a compact function expression using =>.
  • Lexical this — inherits from enclosing scope; .call(), .apply(), .bind() have no effect.
  • No arguments object — use rest parameters (...args).
  • No prototype property — cannot be used as constructors; immune to prototype traversal.
  • No yield — cannot be generators.
  • No new.target or super of their own.
  • Implicit return — single-expression bodies return automatically.
  • Object literal return — wrap in parentheses: x => ({ result: x }).
  • Use arrows for: callbacks, array methods, promises, nested helpers, currying.
  • Do NOT use arrows for: object methods, prototype methods, constructors, generators, event handlers needing this.
  • No performance difference — choose based on semantics, not speed.
  • ESLint prefer-arrow-callback enforces arrows for callbacks.
  • ESLint arrow-body-style enforces brace consistency.
  • ES2026 §10.2.1.1 confirms lexical this behavior.
  • Arrow functions are the foundation of modern functional JavaScript.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A parameter is a named variable declared in a function's definition that receives a value when the function is called. Parameters are the inputs to a function — the mechanism by which data flows from the caller into the function body. They are listed inside the parentheses of the function signature, separated by commas.

function greet(name, greeting) {
    return `${greeting}, ${name}!`;
}

greet("Ada", "Hello"); // "Hello, Ada!"

In JavaScript, parameters behave as local variables within the function body. All the usual variable rules apply: they are scoped to the function, they can be reassigned (unless declared in a context that forbids it), and they shadow outer variables with the same name.

JavaScript provides three special parameter syntaxes beyond simple named parameters:

// 1. Default parameters — fallback values
function greet(name = "world") { /* ... */ }

// 2. Rest parameters — collect remaining arguments into an array
function sum(...numbers) { /* ... */ }

// 3. Destructured parameters — extract values from objects/arrays
function createUser({ name, age }) { /* ... */ }

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Parameters exist to solve the data input problem: a function without parameters is a closed box that always does the same thing. Parameters make functions reusable and configurable — the same logic can operate on different data each time it is called.

Parameters serve as the interface layer between a function and its callers:

  • Simple parameters — named inputs for straightforward functions.
  • Default parameters — optional inputs with fallback values.
  • Rest parameters — variadic inputs collected into an array.
  • Destructured parameters — structured inputs extracted from objects or arrays.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Functions
├── Function Declarations       ✅ done
├── Function Expressions        ✅ done
├── Arrow Functions             ✅ done
├── Parameters                  ← you are here
├── Rest Parameters
├── Default Parameters
├── Closures
├── Higher-Order Functions
└── Pure Functions

Parameters sit after Arrow Functions because all function forms share the same parameter syntax. Arrow functions support every parameter feature that regular functions do — with one restriction: parentheses are always required when using default, rest, or destructured parameters. The next concept, Rest Parameters, dives deep into the ... syntax.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A function that cannot receive input must either:

  • Hardcode its values — making it useless for general use.
  • Reach outside its scope to access global variables — creating hidden dependencies and brittle code.
// ❌ Hardcoded — always calculates the same thing
function calculateBill() {
    const total = 100 * 1.15; // hardcoded bill and tax rate
    return total;
}

// ❌ Reaches outside — depends on global variables
let bill = 100;
const taxRate = 0.15;
function calculateBill() {
    return bill * (1 + taxRate); // reads global state
}

Parameters solve both problems by making the function's inputs explicit:

// ✅ Parameters — explicit inputs, reusable
function calculateBill(billAmount, taxRate) {
    return billAmount * (1 + taxRate);
}

calculateBill(100, 0.15); // 115
calculateBill(200, 0.08); // 216

The function now declares what it needs. Callers provide the data. The function is self-contained and testable.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES2015 No default parameter values — required manual || checks No rest parameters Variadic functions required the arguments object No destructured parameters Extracting object properties required manual assignment arguments object limitations Not a real array; unavailable in arrow functions No parameter documentation Function signatures did not reveal optional parameters

docs.title: Why Special Parameter Syntaxes Were Introduced
docs.text:
ES2015 (ES6) introduced three major parameter features:

  1. Default parameters — initialize parameters with fallback values when no argument or undefined is provided.
  2. Rest parameters — collect an indefinite number of arguments into a real array.
  3. Destructured parameters — extract values from objects and arrays directly in the parameter list.

These features replaced the older workarounds:

Old Workaround Modern Replacement param = param || default param = default arguments object ...rest parameter Manual property extraction { prop } destructuring

docs.title: Why Parameters Still Matter in 2026
docs.text: In 2026, parameter syntaxes are Baseline Widely available — supported across all modern browsers since 2016. ES2026 does not introduce new parameter syntax; the feature set is mature. However, the ES2026 spec clarifies the behavior of mapped arguments objects in non-strict mode: the binding exists only in non-strict functions with simple parameter lists, and the mapping behavior is controlled by the parameter-list shape.

docs.title: Simple Parameters
docs.text:
function add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

add(2, 3); // 5

Simple parameters are named identifiers. They are the default form and require no special syntax.

docs.title: Default Parameters
docs.text:
function greet(name = "world") {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

greet();            // "Hello, world!" — no argument provided
greet("Ada");       // "Hello, Ada!" — argument provided
greet(undefined);   // "Hello, world!" — undefined triggers default
greet(null);        // "Hello, null!" — null does NOT trigger default

Default parameters are applied in exactly two situations: no parameter provided, or undefined explicitly provided. Passing null does not trigger the default.

Default values can be any expression, including function calls:

function createId(prefix = "user", timestamp = Date.now()) {
    return `${prefix}_${timestamp}`;
}

Default parameters can reference earlier parameters:

function createRange(start, end = start + 10) {
    return [start, end];
}

createRange(5);    // [5, 15]
createRange(5, 20); // [5, 20]

docs.title: Rest Parameters
docs.text:
function sum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
}

sum(1, 2, 3);       // 6
sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5); // 15

The rest parameter must be the last parameter and there can be only one per function. Trailing commas after the rest parameter are not allowed.

Rest parameters work with leading named parameters:

function log(level, ...messages) {
    console.log(`[${level}]`, ...messages);
}

log("INFO", "Server started", "Port 3000");
// [INFO] Server started Port 3000

Rest parameters can be destructured:

function ignoreFirst(...[, b, c]) {
    return b + c;
}

ignoreFirst(1, 2, 3); // 5

docs.title: Destructured Parameters
docs.text:
Object destructuring:

function createUser({ name, age, role = "viewer" }) {
    return { name, age, role };
}

createUser({ name: "Ada", age: 36 }); // { name: "Ada", age: 36, role: "viewer" }

Array destructuring:

function getFirstThree([first, second, third]) {
    return [first, second, third];
}

getFirstThree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]); // [1, 2, 3]

Renaming destructured properties:

function display({ name: userName, age: userAge }) {
    return `${userName} is ${userAge}`;
}

display({ name: "Ada", age: 36 }); // "Ada is 36"

Nested destructuring:

function processOrder({ customer: { name }, items: [first, ...rest] }) {
    return { name, firstItem: first, otherCount: rest.length };
}

docs.title: Default Values with Destructuring
docs.text:
function createConfig({ debug = false, timeout = 5000, retries = 3 } = {}) {
    return { debug, timeout, retries };
}

createConfig();                  // { debug: false, timeout: 5000, retries: 3 }
createConfig({ debug: true });  // { debug: true, timeout: 5000, retries: 3 }

The = {} default is essential when destructuring — without it, calling the function with no arguments throws a TypeError because it tries to destructure undefined.

docs.title: arguments Object (Legacy)
docs.text:
function legacy() {
    console.log(arguments); // [1, 2, 3] — array-like, not a real array
}

legacy(1, 2, 3);

The arguments object is not a real array and is not available in arrow functions. Use rest parameters instead.

docs.title: Parameter length Property
docs.text:
function f(a, b, c = 1, ...rest) {}
console.log(f.length); // 2 — parameters before the first default or rest

The length property counts parameters before the first default or rest parameter.

docs.title: The "Fill in the Blanks" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a function as a form with blanks:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  calculateBill( ______, ______ )        │
│                 │       │               │
│            billAmount  taxRate          │
│                                         │
│  When you call the function, you fill   │
│  in the blanks with arguments.          │
│                                         │
│  calculateBill( 100, 0.15 )             │
│                  │      │               │
│                  └──────┴── arguments   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Parameters are the blanks; arguments are what you write in them.

docs.title: The "Default Parameter Trigger" Mental Model
docs.text:
Default parameters trigger in exactly two cases:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           Default Parameter Trigger          │
│                                             │
│  ✅ No argument provided     → use default  │
│  ✅ undefined provided       → use default  │
│                                             │
│  ❌ null provided            → use null     │
│  ❌ 0 provided               → use 0        │
│  ❌ "" provided              → use ""       │
│  ❌ false provided           → use false    │
│  ❌ NaN provided             → use NaN      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is why ?? (nullish coalescing) is often a better choice than || for defaults — it respects 0, "", and false.

docs.title: Concept 1: Parameters Are Local Bindings
docs.text:
Parameters behave as local variables in the function body. They are scoped to the function and shadow any outer variables with the same name.

const name = "outer";

function greet(name) {
    return `Hello, ${name}`; // shadows outer `name`
}

greet("Ada"); // "Hello, Ada"

docs.title: Concept 2: Arguments Are Passed by Value
docs.text:
JavaScript always passes arguments by value — but for objects, the "value" is a reference to the object.

function modify(obj) {
    obj.name = "changed"; // mutates the object
}

function reassign(obj) {
    obj = { name: "new" }; // reassigns local binding — no effect outside
}

const user = { name: "Ada" };
modify(user);    // user.name is now "changed"
reassign(user);  // user is still the same object

docs.title: Concept 3: Missing Arguments Are undefined
docs.text:
JavaScript does no parameter checking. Missing arguments are undefined.

function add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

add(1); // NaN — b is undefined

docs.title: Concept 4: Extra Arguments Are Ignored (Unless Rest)
docs.text:
Extra arguments are ignored unless captured by a rest parameter or the arguments object.

function f(a) { return a; }
f(1, 2, 3); // 1 — extra arguments ignored

docs.title: Concept 5: Default Parameters (ES2015)
docs.text:
function greet(name = "world") { /* ... */ }

Default parameters provide fallback values when no argument or undefined is passed.

docs.title: Concept 6: Rest Parameters (ES2015)
docs.text:
function sum(...numbers) { /* ... */ }

Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into a real array. They must be last and only one per function.

docs.title: Concept 7: Destructured Parameters (ES2015)
docs.text:
function createUser({ name, age }) { /* ... */ }

Destructured parameters extract values from objects or arrays directly in the function signature. They are especially common in React props, API handlers, and configuration objects.

docs.title: Concept 8: arguments Object vs. Rest Parameters
docs.text:
Aspect arguments Rest Parameters Type Array-like Real array Methods ❌ No map, filter ✅ Full array methods Arrow functions ❌ Not available ✅ Available Count All arguments Remaining arguments Status Legacy Modern

The arguments object is not a real array and lacks array methods. Rest parameters are real arrays and should be preferred.

docs.title: Concept 9: Parameter length Property
docs.text:
The length property of a function counts parameters before the first default or rest parameter.

function f(a, b, c = 1, ...rest) {}
console.log(f.length); // 2

docs.title: Concept 10: Default Parameters Can Reference Earlier Parameters
docs.text:
function createRange(start, end = start + 10) {
    return [start, end];
}

Default expressions are evaluated left to right, so earlier parameters are available.

docs.title: Concept 11: Destructuring Requires a Default Object
docs.text:
function f({ a, b } = {}) { /* ... */ }

Without = {}, calling f() throws TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'a' of 'undefined'.

docs.title: Concept 12: ES2026 Spec — Mapped arguments Objects
docs.text: Per ES2026 §10.2.11 / §10.4.4.6 / §10.4.4.7, the arguments object binding exists only in non-strict functions with simple parameter lists. The mapping behavior — whether arguments[0] stays in sync with the first parameter — is controlled by the parameter-list shape. Functions with default, rest, or destructured parameters create unmapped arguments objects.

docs.title: Concept 13: Arrow Functions and Parameters
docs.text:
Arrow functions support all parameter syntaxes — default, rest, and destructured — but parentheses are always required when using them.

const add = (a, b) => a + b;                    // simple
const greet = (name = "world") => `Hi, ${name}`; // default
const sum = (...nums) => nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b); // rest
const f = ({ a, b }) => a + b;                  // destructured

docs.title: Concept 14: TypeScript Parameter Features
docs.text:
TypeScript adds type annotations, optional parameters (?), and readonly parameters:

function greet(name: string, age?: number): string { /* ... */ }

TypeScript also supports parameter properties in constructors — a shorthand for declaring and assigning class fields.

docs.title: Concept 15: Default Parameters vs. || Defaults
docs.text: Aspect || Default Default Parameter Triggers on Any falsy value Only undefined 0 respected ❌ No ✅ Yes "" respected ❌ No ✅ Yes false respected ❌ No ✅ Yes Readability Lower Higher

docs.title: Concept 16: ESLint Rules for Parameters
docs.text: Rule Purpose default-param-last Enforce default parameters last no-dupe-args Disallow duplicate parameter names max-params Limit number of parameters prefer-rest-params Prefer rest over arguments

docs.title: Concept 17: Parameter Destructuring in React
docs.text:
function UserCard({ name, avatar, role = "user" }) {
    return <div>{name} — {role}</div>;
}

Destructured parameters are the standard pattern for React component props.

docs.title: Concept 18: Performance — Parameters Are Free
docs.text: Parameter binding is extremely fast — parameters are allocated on the stack or in registers. There is no meaningful performance difference between simple parameters, default parameters, or rest parameters in optimized code.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Parameter Binding
docs.text:
1.  Function is called with arguments.
    │
    ▼
2.  New execution context is created.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parameters are bound in the function's local scope:
    │   - Simple: bound to corresponding argument (or undefined)
    │   - Default: bound to argument, or default if undefined
    │   - Rest: bound to array of remaining arguments
    │   - Destructured: pattern is matched against argument
    │
    ▼
4.  Function body executes.
    │
    ▼
5.  Execution context is destroyed.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Default Parameter Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  Function is called.
    │
    ▼
2.  For each parameter with a default:
    │   - If argument is undefined → evaluate default expression.
    │   - Else → use the argument.
    │
    ▼
3.  Default expressions are evaluated left to right.
    │
    ▼
4.  Earlier parameters are available to later defaults.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Rest Parameter Collection
docs.text:
1.  Function is called with arguments.
    │
    ▼
2.  Named parameters before the rest are bound first.
    │
    ▼
3.  All remaining arguments are collected into an array.
    │
    ▼
4.  The rest parameter is bound to that array.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Destructured Parameter Binding
docs.text:
1.  Object argument is passed.
    │
    ▼
2.  Destructuring pattern is applied.
    │
    ▼
3.  Each property is extracted and bound to a local variable.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default values are applied for missing properties.
    │
    ▼
5.  If the argument is undefined and `= {}` is present → use empty object.
    │
    ▼
6.  If the argument is undefined and no `= {}` → TypeError.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: arguments Object Creation
docs.text:
1.  Non-strict function with simple parameters is called.
    │
    ▼
2.  `arguments` object is created.
    │
    ▼
3.  It is **mapped** — `arguments[i]` stays in sync with parameter `i`.
    │
    ▼
4.  For functions with default/rest/destructured params → **unmapped**.
    │
    ▼
5.  Arrow functions → no `arguments` at all.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of Parameters
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification covers parameter lists in Section 15.1 (Parameter Lists). Key subclauses:

Clause Title 15.1.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors 15.1.2 Static Semantics: ContainsExpression 15.1.3 Static Semantics: ExpectedArgumentCount 15.1.4 Static Semantics: BoundNames 15.1.5 Static Semantics: IsSimpleParameterList 15.1.6 Runtime Semantics: IteratorBindingInitialization

docs.title: ExpectedArgumentCount
docs.text: The spec defines ExpectedArgumentCount — the number of parameters before the first default or rest parameter. This is exposed as the function's length property.

docs.title: IsSimpleParameterList
docs.text:
A parameter list is simple if it contains only simple identifiers. It is not simple if it contains default, rest, or destructured parameters. This distinction affects:

  • Whether the arguments object is mapped or unmapped.
  • Whether "use strict" can be applied inside the function.

docs.title: IteratorBindingInitialization
docs.text: For destructured parameters, the engine uses IteratorBindingInitialization — an abstract operation that iterates over the pattern and binds each extracted value to a local variable.

docs.title: Mapped vs. Unmapped arguments
docs.text:
Per ES2026 §10.2.11 / §10.4.4.6 / §10.4.4.7:

  • Mapped — arguments[i] and parameter i are aliases. Changing one changes the other.
  • Unmapped — arguments[i] is a copy. Changing one does not affect the other.

Only non-strict functions with simple parameter lists create mapped arguments objects. Functions with default, rest, or destructured parameters create unmapped arguments objects.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
Function Execution Context:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Parameter Environment              │
│                                     │
│  a: 10        ← simple parameter    │
│  b: "hello"   ← simple parameter    │
│  c: [1,2,3]   ← rest parameter      │
│  {name, age}  ← destructured        │
│                                     │
│  arguments: [10, "hello", 1, 2, 3]  │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text:
• Parameter binding is free — parameters are allocated on the stack or in registers.
  • Default parameter evaluation — costs the same as a conditional check.
  • Rest parameter allocation — creates an array; minor cost.
  • Destructuring — property extraction; optimized by the JIT.

docs.title: Parameter Lifecycle
docs.text: Function defined → Parameters declared → Function called → Arguments bound → Body executes → Context destroyed

docs.title: Default Parameter Lifecycle
docs.text: Function called → Check if argument is undefined → Evaluate default if needed → Bind parameter

docs.title: Rest Parameter Lifecycle
docs.text: Function called → Bind named parameters → Collect remaining arguments into array → Bind rest parameter

docs.title: Destructured Parameter Lifecycle
docs.text: Function called → Check if argument is undefined → Apply `= {}` if needed → Match pattern → Bind extracted values

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write function signature
    │
    ▼
Choose parameter style:
    ├── Simple → named params
    ├── Optional → default params
    ├── Variadic → rest params
    └── Structured → destructured params
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint default-param-last, max-params, prefer-rest-params)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript)
    │
    ▼
Run / Test

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Parameters
docs.text:
function add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

console.log(add(2, 3)); // 5

docs.title: Example 2: Default Parameters
docs.text:
function createUser(name, role = "viewer", active = true) {
    return { name, role, active };
}

console.log(createUser("Ada"));
// { name: "Ada", role: "viewer", active: true }

Breakdown:

  • role and active have defaults.
  • Calling with just name uses defaults.

docs.title: Example 3: Default Parameters with null
docs.text:
function greet(name = "world") {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

console.log(greet());          // "Hello, world!"
console.log(greet(undefined)); // "Hello, world!"
console.log(greet(null));      // "Hello, null!"

Breakdown:

  • null does not trigger the default.

docs.title: Example 4: Rest Parameters
docs.text:
function sum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
}

console.log(sum(1, 2, 3));       // 6
console.log(sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)); // 15

docs.title: Example 5: Rest with Leading Named Parameters
docs.text:
function log(level, ...messages) {
    console.log(`[${level}]`, ...messages);
}

log("INFO", "Server started", "Port 3000");
// [INFO] Server started Port 3000

docs.title: Example 6: Destructured Parameters
docs.text:
function createUser({ name, age, role = "viewer" }) {
    return { name, age, role };
}

console.log(createUser({ name: "Ada", age: 36 }));
// { name: "Ada", age: 36, role: "viewer" }

docs.title: Example 7: Destructured Parameters with Default Object
docs.text:
function createConfig({ debug = false, timeout = 5000 } = {}) {
    return { debug, timeout };
}

console.log(createConfig());                 // { debug: false, timeout: 5000 }
console.log(createConfig({ debug: true })); // { debug: true, timeout: 5000 }

Breakdown:

  • = {} is essential — without it, createConfig() throws.

docs.title: Example 8: Nested Destructuring
docs.text:
function processOrder({ customer: { name }, items: [first, ...rest] }) {
    return { name, firstItem: first, otherCount: rest.length };
}

console.log(processOrder({
    customer: { name: "Ada" },
    items: ["book", "pen", "lamp"],
}));
// { name: "Ada", firstItem: "book", otherCount: 2 }

docs.title: Example 9: Arrow Function Parameters
docs.text:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const greet = (name = "world") => `Hello, ${name}!`;
const sum = (...nums) => nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
const f = ({ a, b }) => a + b;

Breakdown:

  • Arrow functions support all parameter syntaxes.

docs.title: Example 10: arguments vs. Rest Parameters
docs.text:
// ❌ Legacy — arguments is not a real array
function oldSum() {
    return Array.from(arguments).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

// ✅ Modern — rest parameter is a real array
function newSum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Parameter Style Simple function Simple parameters Optional configuration Default parameters Variadic function Rest parameters Configuration object Destructured parameters React props Destructured parameters API request options Destructured parameters with defaults Math utilities Rest parameters Event handlers Simple or destructured React components Destructured props CLI argument parsing Rest parameters

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use default parameters instead of || for defaults. Why: respects 0, "", and false.
  2. Use rest parameters instead of arguments. Why: real arrays, available in arrow functions.
  3. Use destructured parameters for configuration objects. Why: self-documenting, concise.
  4. Always provide = {} when destructuring. Why: prevents TypeError on no-argument calls.
  5. Place default parameters last. Why: earlier defaults make length unpredictable.
  6. Keep parameter lists short. Why: more than 3-4 params suggests a configuration object.
  7. Name parameters meaningfully. Why: billAmount beats b.
  8. Use null only when you mean "explicitly no value". Why: null does not trigger defaults.
  9. Document default values. Why: callers need to know what happens when they omit arguments.
  10. Use JSDoc or TypeScript for parameter types. Why: type safety and documentation.
  11. Enable ESLint default-param-last. Why: enforces default parameter placement.
  12. Enable ESLint prefer-rest-params. Why: discourages arguments.
  13. Avoid mutating parameter objects. Why: side effects on caller data are surprising.
  14. Use object destructuring for more than 3 parameters. Why: callers can use named arguments.
  15. Prefer arrow functions for callbacks with parameters. Why: concise and lexical this.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using || for Defaults
docs.text:
function setVolume(vol) {
    vol = vol || 50; // ❌ 0 becomes 50
    return vol;
}
setVolume(0); // 50 — wrong!

✅ Correct:

function setVolume(vol = 50) {
    return vol;
}
setVolume(0); // 0

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting = {} in Destructured Parameters
docs.text:
function f({ a, b }) {}
f(); // ❌ TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'a' of 'undefined'

✅ Correct:

function f({ a, b } = {}) {}
f(); // ✅ works

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Rest Parameter Not Last
docs.text:
function f(...rest, last) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

function f(first, ...rest) {}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Rest Parameters
docs.text:
function f(...a, ...b) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct: Only one rest parameter.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Trailing Comma After Rest
docs.text:
function f(...rest,) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

function f(...rest) {}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using arguments in Arrow Functions
docs.text:
const f = () => arguments; // ❌ ReferenceError

✅ Correct:

const f = (...args) => args;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Expecting Default to Trigger on null
docs.text:
function f(x = 10) { return x; }
f(null); // null — not 10

✅ Correct: Use x ?? 10 inside the body if null should trigger the default.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Duplicate Parameter Names
docs.text:
function f(a, a) {} // ❌ SyntaxError in strict mode

✅ Correct: Use distinct names.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mutating Parameter Objects
docs.text:
function addItem(cart, item) {
    cart.push(item); // ❌ mutates caller's array
}

✅ Correct:

function addItem(cart, item) {
    return [...cart, item]; // returns a new array
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Destructuring a Primitive
docs.text:
function f({ length }) {}
f("hello"); // ✅ works — strings have length
f(42); // ✅ works — number wrapped, length undefined
f(null); // ❌ TypeError

✅ Correct: Always provide = {} or validate input.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Parameter binding is free — stack/register allocation.
  • Default parameter evaluation — costs the same as a conditional check.
  • Rest parameter allocation — creates an array; minor cost.
  • Destructuring — property extraction; optimized by the JIT.
  • arguments object — creates a mapped array-like object; more expensive than rest.
  • Too many parameters — JIT may deoptimize; keep lists short.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use rest parameters instead of arguments — faster and cleaner.
  2. Avoid creating functions with many parameters — use configuration objects.
  3. Keep destructuring shallow when possible.
  4. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt if needed.

docs.title: Parameter Injection
docs.text:
Untrusted input passed as arguments can lead to injection attacks if not validated.

Defense: Validate all parameters at trust boundaries.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution via Destructuring
docs.text:
Destructuring __proto__ from untrusted objects can pollute the prototype chain.

Defense: Validate input; use Object.create(null) for dictionaries.

docs.title: Default Parameter Side Effects
docs.text:
Default expressions can call functions with side effects.

Defense: Keep default expressions pure.

docs.title: Rest Parameter Exhaustion
docs.text:
A rest parameter can collect an unbounded number of arguments — a potential DoS vector.

Defense: Limit input size at boundaries.

docs.title: arguments Object and Strict Mode
docs.text:
In strict mode, arguments does not alias parameters — this prevents some classes of bugs.

Defense: Use strict mode (or ES modules, which are strict by default).

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Check f.length — number of parameters before defaults/rest.
  • console.log(arguments) — inspect the legacy arguments object.
  • console.log([...args]) — inspect rest parameters as a real array.
  • debugger; — pause inside the function.
  • ESLint default-param-last — flags misplaced defaults.
  • ESLint prefer-rest-params — flags arguments usage.
  • TypeScript — catches type mismatches at compile time.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Parameter Style When to Use Simple Required inputs Default Optional inputs with fallbacks Rest Variadic functions Destructured Configuration objects, React props arguments Legacy code only — prefer rest

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• || for defaults — use default parameters instead.
  • arguments in new code — use rest parameters.
  • Too many simple parameters — use a configuration object.
  • Destructuring without = {} — always provide the default object.
  • Rest parameter not last — syntax error.
  • Duplicate parameter names — syntax error in strict mode.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Rest Parameters — the ... syntax for variadic functions
  • Default Parameters — fallback values
  • Destructuring — extracting values from objects/arrays
  • Function Declarations — function syntax
  • Function Expressions — function values
  • Arrow Functions — parameter syntax in arrow functions
  • arguments Object — legacy alternative to rest parameters
  • Closures — parameters captured by closures
  • Higher-Order Functions — functions that take/return functions
  • TypeScript — type annotations for parameters

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Default parameters were introduced in ES2015 (ES6) — along with rest and destructured parameters.
  • Default parameters trigger only on undefined — not on null.
  • Rest parameters must be last — and only one per function.
  • Destructured parameters are the standard for React props — function UserCard({ name }) {}.
  • arguments is not a real array — it lacks map, filter, and forEach.
  • Arrow functions have no arguments — use rest parameters.
  • ES2026 §10.2.11 clarifies mapped arguments — only non-strict simple parameter lists create mapped objects.
  • Function length counts parameters before defaults/rest — function f(a, b, c = 1) {}.length is 2.
  • Default parameters can reference earlier parameters — function f(a, b = a + 1) {}.
  • = {} is required for destructured parameters — without it, no-argument calls throw.
  • The arguments object was the original way to access all arguments — before rest parameters.
  • ES2026 does not add new parameter syntax — the feature set is mature.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• Parameters are named inputs declared in a function's signature.
  • Four parameter styles: simple, default, rest, destructured.
  • Default parameters — fallback values; trigger only on undefined.
  • Rest parameters — collect remaining arguments into a real array; must be last.
  • Destructured parameters — extract values from objects/arrays directly in the signature.
  • Always provide = {} with destructured parameters.
  • Use ?? not || when 0, "", or false are valid values.
  • Use rest instead of arguments — real arrays, arrow function compatible.
  • arguments is legacy — unmapped in ES2026 for default/rest/destructured params.
  • Function length counts parameters before defaults/rest.
  • ESLint rules — default-param-last, prefer-rest-params, max-params.
  • TypeScript adds type annotations and optional parameters.
  • ES2026 does not change parameter syntax — the features are mature.
  • Parameters are the interface between function and caller — master them for clean, reusable code.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A rest parameter is a special parameter syntax that allows a function to accept an indefinite number of arguments and collect them into a real array. It is denoted by three dots (...) followed by an identifier, placed as the last parameter in a function's signature.

function sum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
}

sum(1, 2, 3);       // 6
sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5); // 15

The rest parameter collects all remaining arguments — those not already bound to named parameters — into a standard JavaScript Array. Unlike the legacy arguments object, the rest parameter is a true array instance, meaning all array methods (map, filter, reduce, sort, forEach, pop, etc.) can be applied directly to it without conversion.

Rest parameters work identically in function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions — they are fully supported across all function forms.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Rest parameters exist to solve the variadic function problem: functions that need to accept an arbitrary number of arguments. Before ES2015, this required the arguments object — an array-like object that lacked array methods, was unavailable in arrow functions, and had confusing aliasing behavior in non-strict mode.

Rest parameters serve as the modern variadic input mechanism of the language:

  • Variadic utilities — functions like sum, average, log, and format that accept any number of values.
  • Framework APIs — React hooks, Vue composition functions, and middleware that accept variable arguments.
  • Event aggregation — collecting callbacks, listeners, or handlers.
  • Argument forwarding — passing through arguments to other functions.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Functions
├── Function Declarations       ✅ done
├── Function Expressions        ✅ done
├── Arrow Functions             ✅ done
├── Parameters                  ✅ done
├── Rest Parameters             ← you are here
├── Default Parameters
├── Closures
├── Higher-Order Functions
└── Pure Functions

Rest parameters sit directly after Parameters because they are a specialized parameter syntax. The next concept, Default Parameters, describes how parameters receive fallback values — and rest parameters cannot have defaults, which makes the two concepts complementary.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
JavaScript functions have no arity checking — you can call any function with any number of arguments. The language needed a way to capture those extra arguments in a useful form. Before ES2015, the only option was the arguments object.

The arguments object had serious limitations:

// ❌ arguments is not a real array
function sum() {
    return arguments.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // TypeError!
}

// ❌ arguments is not available in arrow functions
const sum = () => arguments; // ReferenceError

// ❌ arguments aliases parameters in non-strict mode
function f(a) {
    arguments[0] = 99;
    console.log(a); // 99 — unexpected!
}

The arguments object is an array-like object — it has a length property and indexed elements, but it does not have map, filter, reduce, forEach, or any other Array.prototype methods. To use array methods, you had to convert it:

// The old way — verbose conversion
function sum() {
    const args = Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments);
    return args.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES2015 No rest parameters — arguments was the only option arguments not an array Required Array.prototype.slice.call() conversion arguments unavailable in arrows Arrow functions could not capture variadic args arguments aliasing Non-strict functions had mapped arguments — confusing No destructuring Could not extract specific positions from variadic args Performance overhead Converting arguments to an array was costly

docs.title: Why Rest Parameters Were Introduced
docs.text:
Rest parameters were introduced in ES2015 (ES6) as part of a broader language overhaul. They solved the arguments problem by:

  1. Creating a real array — all array methods work directly.
  2. Working in arrow functions — unlike arguments.
  3. Eliminating aliasing — the rest parameter is always a copy, never mapped to named parameters.
  4. Supporting destructuring — you can extract specific positions from the collected array.
  5. Improving performance — creating an array is faster than the arguments object machinery.

The design was deliberately restrictive: only one rest parameter per function, it must be last, it cannot have a default value, and trailing commas are not allowed. These restrictions keep the syntax unambiguous and the semantics predictable.

docs.title: Why Rest Parameters Still Matter in 2026
docs.text:
In 2026, rest parameters are Baseline Widely available — supported across all modern browsers since July 2015 (though implementation rolled out through 2016). They are the preferred modern approach for variadic functions, having replaced the arguments object in virtually all new code.

ES2026 does not introduce new rest parameter syntax — the feature set is mature. However, the ES2026 spec continues to define rest parameters in Section 15.1 (Parameter Lists), specifically through the IsSimpleParameterList and ExpectedArgumentCount static semantics.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
function name(param0, ...restParam) {
    // restParam is an array of remaining arguments
}

The rest parameter is three dots followed by an identifier, placed as the last parameter in the signature.

docs.title: Minimal Rest Parameter
docs.text:
function collect(...items) {
    return items;
}

collect();           // []
collect(1);          // [1]
collect(1, 2, 3);    // [1, 2, 3]

docs.title: Rest with Leading Named Parameters
docs.text:
function log(level, ...messages) {
    console.log(`[${level}]`, ...messages);
}

log("INFO", "Server started", "Port 3000");
// [INFO] Server started Port 3000

The first argument binds to level; all remaining arguments bind to messages.

docs.title: Rest in Arrow Functions
docs.text:
const sum = (...numbers) => numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
const log = (level, ...messages) => console.log(level, ...messages);

Rest parameters work identically in arrow functions — no arguments workaround needed.

docs.title: Rest in Function Expressions
docs.text:
const multiply = function(factor, ...values) {
    return values.map(v => v * factor);
};

multiply(2, 1, 2, 3); // [2, 4, 6]

docs.title: Rest with No Arguments
docs.text:
function empty(...args) {
    return args.length;
}

empty(); // 0

The rest parameter is an empty array when no arguments are provided — never undefined.

docs.title: Destructured Rest Parameters
docs.text:
function firstTwo(...[first, second]) {
    return { first, second };
}

firstTwo(1, 2, 3); // { first: 1, second: 2 }
firstTwo(1);       // { first: 1, second: undefined }

Rest parameters can be destructured to extract specific positions from the collected array.

docs.title: Rest with Spread (Forwarding)
docs.text:
function forward(...args) {
    return otherFunction(...args); // spread back out
}

Rest and spread are complementary — rest collects, spread distributes.

docs.title: Async Function with Rest
docs.text:
async function fetchAll(...urls) {
    const responses = await Promise.all(urls.map(url => fetch(url)));
    return responses;
}

docs.title: Generator Function with Rest
docs.text:
function* yieldAll(...values) {
    yield* values;
}

docs.title: Syntax Restrictions
docs.text:
// ❌ Rest parameter must be last
function bad(...rest, last) {}

// ❌ Only one rest parameter allowed
function bad(...a, ...b) {}

// ❌ No trailing comma after rest
function bad(...rest,) {}

// ❌ Rest parameter cannot have a default value
function bad(...rest = []) {}

docs.title: The "Collector" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a rest parameter as a collector — it gathers all remaining arguments into a container:

Function call: sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐
              │  ...numbers     │
              │                 │
              │  [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]│  ← Real array
              └─────────────────┘

The rest parameter is the destination for arguments that do not have a named parameter.

docs.title: The "Rest vs. Spread" Mental Model
docs.text:
Rest and spread use the same syntax (...) but do opposite things:

Rest (collect):                     Spread (distribute):
┌─────────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────────┐
│  ...args            │            │  ...arr             │
│                     │            │                     │
│  Gathers multiple   │            │  Spreads one        │
│  values into ONE    │            │  collection into    │
│  array              │            │  MULTIPLE values    │
│                     │            │                     │
│  Function params    │            │  Function calls,    │
│                     │            │  array literals,    │
│                     │            │  object literals    │
└─────────────────────┘            └─────────────────────┘

Rest is about receiving; spread is about sending.

docs.title: The "Arguments Object vs. Rest Parameter" Mental Model
The "Last Parameter Rule" Mental Model
docs.text:
The rest parameter must be last because it collects everything that remains:

function f(a, b, ...rest) {}

Call: f(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

     a = 1
     b = 2
     rest = [3, 4, 5]  ← everything after a and b

There is no room for another parameter after rest — it has consumed all remaining arguments.

docs.title: Concept 1: Rest Parameters Are Real Arrays
docs.text:
Unlike the arguments object, rest parameters are true Array instances. All array methods work directly:

function sortAndSum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

This eliminates the need for Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments) conversions.

docs.title: Concept 2: Rest Parameter Must Be Last
docs.text:
function f(...rest, last) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

The rest parameter collects remaining arguments — it cannot be followed by another parameter.

docs.title: Concept 3: Only One Rest Parameter Per Function
docs.text:
function f(...a, ...b) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

There can be only one rest parameter per function signature.

docs.title: Concept 4: No Trailing Comma After Rest
docs.text:
function f(...rest,) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

The rest parameter cannot be followed by a trailing comma.

docs.title: Concept 5: Rest Parameters Cannot Have Default Values
docs.text:
function f(...rest = []) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

Rest parameters cannot have default values. They are always arrays (empty if no arguments).

docs.title: Concept 6: Rest Parameters Work in Arrow Functions
docs.text:
const sum = (...numbers) => numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);

Unlike arguments, rest parameters are fully available in arrow functions.

docs.title: Concept 7: Rest Parameters Can Be Destructured
docs.text:
function f(...[a, b, c]) {
    return a + b + c;
}

f(1, 2, 3); // 6
f(1, 2, 3, 4); // 6 — fourth argument ignored
f(1); // NaN — b and c are undefined

Destructuring allows extracting specific positions from the collected array.

docs.title: Concept 8: Rest Parameters and Function length
docs.text:
The length property of a function does not count the rest parameter:

function f(a, b, ...rest) {}
console.log(f.length); // 2 — rest is not counted

This is defined by the spec's ExpectedArgumentCount static semantics.

docs.title: Concept 9: Rest Parameters and arguments
docs.text:
When a function has a rest parameter, the arguments object is not mapped to the parameters:

function f(a, ...rest) {
    arguments[0] = 99;
    console.log(a); // unchanged — arguments is unmapped
}

Per ES2026 §10.2.11 / §10.4.4.6 / §10.4.4.7, functions with rest parameters create unmapped arguments objects.

docs.title: Concept 10: Rest Parameters Are Not Counted in Function.length
docs.text:
function f(a, b, c, ...rest) {}
f.length; // 3

Only parameters before the rest parameter are counted.

docs.title: Concept 11: Rest Parameters Replace arguments for Variadic Functions
docs.text:
// Old way
function sum() {
    return Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments)
        .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

// Modern way
function sum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

ESLint's prefer-rest-params rule enforces this preference.

docs.title: Concept 12: Rest Parameters and Spread Are Complementary
docs.text:
function forward(...args) {
    return target(...args);
}

Rest collects arguments into an array; spread distributes them back out.

docs.title: Concept 13: Rest Parameters in Class Methods
docs.text:
class Calculator {
    add(...numbers) {
        return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    }
}

Rest parameters work in class methods, including constructors.

docs.title: Concept 14: Rest Parameters in Object Methods
docs.text:
const obj = {
    sum(...numbers) {
        return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    },
};

docs.title: Concept 15: ES2026 Spec — IsSimpleParameterList
docs.text:
Per ES2026 §15.1.3, a parameter list is simple if it contains only simple identifiers. A parameter list with a rest parameter is not simple. This distinction affects:

  • Whether the arguments object is mapped or unmapped.
  • Whether "use strict" can be applied inside the function.

docs.title: Concept 16: Performance — Rest Parameters Are Faster Than arguments
docs.text:
Benchmarks show that using ...args is significantly faster than Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments). One test showed:

Running this under node took ~480ms for the old arguments version and about ~110ms for the new ...args version. Running with --trace-gc produced 1010 vs 95 reported scavenges.

The performance difference comes from V8's ability to avoid allocating the arguments object when rest parameters are used.

docs.title: Concept 17: ESLint Rules for Rest Parameters
docs.text: Rule Purpose prefer-rest-params Prefer rest over arguments no-useless-rename Disallow redundant renaming in destructuring

docs.title: Concept 18: Rest Parameters in Modern Frameworks
docs.text:
// React hook
function useLogger(...messages) {
    useEffect(() => console.log(...messages), messages);
}

// Express middleware
app.use((req, res, ...next) => { /* ... */ });

Rest parameters are widely used in React, Vue, Express, and most modern npm packages.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Rest Parameter Binding
docs.text:
1.  Function is called with arguments.
    │
    ▼
2.  New execution context is created.
    │
    ▼
3.  Named parameters before the rest are bound first.
    │
    ▼
4.  All remaining arguments are collected into a new Array.
    │
    ▼
5.  The rest parameter is bound to that array.
    │
    ▼
6.  Function body executes.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Rest Parameter with Destructuring
docs.text:
1.  Function is called with arguments.
    │
    ▼
2.  All arguments are collected into an array.
    │
    ▼
3.  Destructuring pattern is applied to the array.
    │
    ▼
4.  Each extracted value is bound to a local variable.
    │
    ▼
5.  Remaining values are discarded (if not captured).

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Rest vs. arguments
docs.text:
Rest:                                arguments:
1.  Function called.                 1.  Function called.
2.  Remaining args → new Array.      2.  arguments object created.
3.  Array has all methods.           3.  Array-like, no array methods.
4.  Available in arrows.             4.  Not available in arrows.
5.  Never mapped.                    5.  Mapped in non-strict simple lists.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Performance Optimization in V8
docs.text:
1.  Function with rest parameter is called.
    │
    ▼
2.  V8 checks if the rest array is actually needed.
    │
    ▼
3.  If the function just forwards to another function (spread),
    │   V8 can avoid allocating the array entirely.
    │
    ▼
4.  The JSCallForwardVarargs operator passes parameters directly.
    │
    ▼
5.  No allocation, no deconstruction — maximum performance.

V8's TurboFan compiler includes an optimization to avoid allocating rest parameters when they are immediately spread into another call. This is implemented via the JSCallForwardVarargs operator.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of Rest Parameters
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification covers rest parameters in Section 15.1 (Parameter Lists). Key subclauses:

Clause Title 15.1.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors 15.1.2 Static Semantics: ContainsExpression 15.1.3 Static Semantics: IsSimpleParameterList 15.1.4 Static Semantics: HasInitializer 15.1.5 Static Semantics: ExpectedArgumentCount 15.1.6 Runtime Semantics: IteratorBindingInitialization

docs.title: IsSimpleParameterList (ES2026 §15.1.3)
docs.text:
A parameter list is simple if it contains only simple identifiers. It is not simple if it contains:

  • Default parameters
  • Rest parameters
  • Destructured parameters

Functions with non-simple parameter lists create unmapped arguments objects.

docs.title: ExpectedArgumentCount (ES2026 §15.1.5)
docs.text:
This static semantic determines the function's length property — the number of parameters before the first default or rest parameter.

function f(a, b, c = 1, ...rest) {}
f.length; // 2 — a and b

docs.title: Mapped vs. Unmapped arguments (ES2026 §10.2.11 / §10.4.4.6 / §10.4.4.7)
docs.text:
• Mapped — arguments[i] and parameter i are aliases. Only in non-strict functions with simple parameter lists.
  • Unmapped — arguments[i] is a copy. Functions with rest parameters create unmapped objects.

docs.title: IteratorBindingInitialization
docs.text: For destructured rest parameters, the engine uses IteratorBindingInitialization — an abstract operation that iterates over the pattern and binds each extracted value.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
Function Execution Context:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Parameter Environment              │
│                                     │
│  a: 1         ← named parameter     │
│  b: 2         ← named parameter     │
│  rest: [3, 4, 5]  ← real Array      │
│                                     │
│  arguments: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]         │
│    (unmapped — because of rest)     │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: V8 Optimization: JSCallForwardVarargs
docs.text:
V8's TurboFan compiler has a special optimization for the pattern:

function forward(...args) {
    return target(...args);
}

Instead of allocating an array for args and then spreading it back out, V8 uses the JSCallForwardVarargs operator to pass the incoming parameters directly. This avoids both allocation and deconstruction.

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text:
• Rest parameter binding — allocates a new array; fast but not free.
  • Forwarding optimization — V8 can eliminate the allocation entirely for spread calls.
  • Rest is faster than arguments — benchmarks show ~4x improvement and 10x fewer GC scavenges.

docs.title: Rest Parameter Lifecycle
docs.text: Function defined → Rest parameter declared → Function called → Remaining args collected into array → Bound → Body executes

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Need to accept variadic arguments?
    │
    ▼
Use rest parameter: function f(...args) {}
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint prefer-rest-params)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript: ...args: T[])
    │
    ▼
Run / Test

docs.title: Choosing Between Rest and arguments Workflow
docs.text:
Need to capture extra arguments?
    │
    ├── Yes → Use rest parameter (...args)
    │
    └── No → Use named parameters
              │
              ▼
         Need ALL arguments (including named)?
              │
              ├── Yes → Use arguments (legacy, rare)
              │
              └── No → Use rest parameter

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Sum Function
docs.text:
function sum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
}

console.log(sum(1, 2, 3));       // 6
console.log(sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)); // 15
console.log(sum());              // 0

Breakdown:

  • numbers is a real array.
  • reduce works directly on it.

docs.title: Example 2: Rest with Leading Named Parameters
docs.text:
function formatMessage(prefix, ...parts) {
    return `[${prefix}] ${parts.join(" ")}`;
}

console.log(formatMessage("INFO", "User", "logged", "in"));
// [INFO] User logged in

docs.title: Example 3: Rest in Arrow Function
docs.text:
const average = (...numbers) => {
    if (numbers.length === 0) return 0;
    return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / numbers.length;
};

console.log(average(10, 20, 30)); // 20

docs.title: Example 4: Rest with Destructuring
docs.text:
function extractFirst(...[first, ...rest]) {
    return { first, rest };
}

console.log(extractFirst(1, 2, 3, 4));
// { first: 1, rest: [2, 3, 4] }

docs.title: Example 5: Forwarding with Spread
docs.text:
function forward(...args) {
    return console.log(...args);
}

forward("a", "b", "c"); // logs: a b c

docs.title: Example 6: Rest vs. arguments
docs.text:
// ❌ Old way — arguments is not a real array
function oldSum() {
    return Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments)
        .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

// ✅ Modern way — rest is a real array
function newSum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

docs.title: Example 7: Async Function with Rest
docs.text:
async function fetchAll(...urls) {
    const responses = await Promise.all(urls.map(url => fetch(url)));
    return Promise.all(responses.map(r => r.json()));
}

const [users, posts] = await fetchAll("/api/users", "/api/posts");

docs.title: Example 8: Class Method with Rest
docs.text:
class EventEmitter {
    emit(event, ...args) {
        this.listeners[event]?.forEach(fn => fn(...args));
    }
}

docs.title: Example 9: Rest in Object Method
docs.text:
const logger = {
    log(level, ...messages) {
        console[level](...messages);
    },
};

logger.log("warn", "Deprecated", "API", "usage");

docs.title: Example 10: Rest Parameter length
docs.text:
function f(a, b, ...rest) {}
console.log(f.length); // 2 — rest not counted

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Use Rest Parameter? Sum/average utilities ✅ Yes Logging functions ✅ Yes Event emitters ✅ Yes Argument forwarding ✅ Yes React hooks ✅ Yes Express middleware ✅ Yes Batch async operations ✅ Yes Variadic math functions ✅ Yes Collecting callbacks ✅ Yes Configuration objects ⚠️ Prefer destructured parameters

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Prefer rest parameters over arguments. Why: real arrays, arrow function compatible, faster.
  2. Place the rest parameter last. Why: it collects all remaining arguments — required by syntax.
  3. Use destructuring with rest for specific positions. Why: cleaner than index access.
  4. Name rest parameters meaningfully. Why: numbers beats args when the type is known.
  5. Use rest parameters for variadic utilities. Why: natural fit for functions with unknown arity.
  6. Use spread to forward rest parameters. Why: rest and spread are complementary.
  7. Enable ESLint prefer-rest-params. Why: enforces rest over arguments.
  8. Avoid arguments in new code. Why: legacy, limited, and slower.
  9. Keep rest parameters as the only variadic mechanism. Why: consistency and readability.
  10. Use TypeScript's ...args: T[] for type safety. Why: ensures type correctness.
  11. Do not use rest parameters for fixed-arity functions. Why: named parameters are clearer.
  12. Understand Function.length behavior. Why: rest parameters are not counted.
  13. Use rest with async functions for batch operations. Why: Promise.all + rest is a powerful pattern.
  14. Consider performance in hot paths. Why: rest parameter allocation is fast but not free.
  15. Document variadic functions clearly. Why: callers need to know the expected argument shape.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Rest Parameter Not Last
docs.text:
function f(...rest, last) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

function f(first, ...rest) {}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Multiple Rest Parameters
docs.text:
function f(...a, ...b) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct: Only one rest parameter.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Trailing Comma After Rest
docs.text:
function f(...rest,) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

function f(...rest) {}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Default Value on Rest Parameter
docs.text:
