function f(...rest = []) {} // ❌ SyntaxError

✅ Correct:

function f(...rest) {} // rest is always an array

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using arguments Instead of Rest
docs.text:
function sum() {
    return arguments.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // ❌ TypeError
}

✅ Correct:

function sum(...numbers) {
    return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Expecting arguments to Be Mapped with Rest
docs.text:
function f(a, ...rest) {
    arguments[0] = 99;
    console.log(a); // unchanged — unmapped
}

✅ Correct: Understand that rest parameters create unmapped arguments.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Rest for Fixed-Arity Functions
docs.text:
function add(...numbers) { // ❌ less clear than (a, b)
    return numbers[0] + numbers[1];
}

✅ Correct:

function add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting Rest Is an Array
docs.text:
function f(...rest) {
    return rest.length; // ✅ correct — rest is an array
    // return rest.length; // ✅ also correct
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using ... in Object Setters
docs.text:
const obj = {
    set value(...args) {} // ❌ SyntaxError — rest not allowed in setters
};

✅ Correct: Use a regular method instead.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Rest Works Everywhere
docs.text:
// ❌ Rest parameters cannot be used in object literal setters
const obj = {
    set x(...args) {}
};

✅ Correct: Use rest in functions, methods, and constructors — not in setters.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Rest parameter allocation — creates a new array; fast but not free.
  • Forwarding optimization — V8 can eliminate allocation for spread-forwarding patterns.
  • Rest is faster than arguments — ~4x improvement and ~10x fewer GC scavenges in benchmarks.
  • Rest in hot loops — avoid creating variadic functions in loops.
  • Destructured rest — additional destructuring cost; minor.
  • Function.length — rest parameters are not counted; no performance impact.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use rest parameters instead of arguments — faster and cleaner.
  2. Use spread-forwarding patterns — V8 optimizes them.
  3. Avoid creating variadic functions in hot loops.
  4. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt if needed.

docs.title: Rest Parameters and arguments Obfuscation
docs.text:
Rest parameters are an ordinary binding ... Do rest parameters and spread at call sites survive protection? Yes. Rest parameters still produced real arrays, spread at the call site still delivered the right values including a mixed spread of two arrays, and spreading a string or a Set into a call was unchanged.

Rest parameters are not affected by obfuscation — they behave consistently in minified and obfuscated code.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution via Rest
docs.text: Rest parameters create plain arrays — they do not carry prototype pollution risk beyond what normal array operations introduce.

docs.title: Function Constructor and Rest Parameters
docs.text:
The value must correspond to a valid JavaScript parameter (any of plain identifier, rest parameter, or destructured parameter, optionally with a default), or a list of such strings separated with commas.

The Function constructor accepts rest parameters — but like all Function constructor usage, it is an injection sink and should never be used with untrusted input.

docs.title: Rest Parameters in CSP Contexts
docs.text: Rest parameters are compatible with strict Content Security Policy — they do not require eval or new Function.

docs.title: Argument Exhaustion
docs.text:
A rest parameter can collect an unbounded number of arguments — a potential denial-of-service vector if input size is not limited.

Defense: Limit input size at trust boundaries.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.log(args) — inspect the rest array.
  • console.log(args.length) — verify argument count.
  • console.log(Array.isArray(args)) — confirms rest is a real array.
  • debugger; — pause inside the function.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on variadic functions.
  • ESLint prefer-rest-params — flags arguments usage.
  • TypeScript — catches type mismatches in rest parameters.
  • f.length — verify parameter count (rest not counted).

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Scenario Use Rest Parameter? Variadic utilities (sum, average, log) ✅ Yes Argument forwarding ✅ Yes Event emitter emit ✅ Yes React hooks ✅ Yes Express middleware ✅ Yes Batch async operations ✅ Yes Collecting callbacks ✅ Yes Fixed-arity functions ❌ No Configuration objects ⚠️ Prefer destructured parameters

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Fixed-arity functions — named parameters are clearer.
  • Configuration objects — use destructured parameters.
  • Object literal setters — rest is not allowed.
  • When arguments is needed for all arguments — rare; use arguments (legacy).
  • In performance-critical loops — rest allocates an array per call.
  • When the function arity is known — named parameters document intent.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Parameters — the general parameter concept
  • Default Parameters — fallback values (rest cannot have defaults)
  • Destructuring — extracting values from arrays/objects
  • Spread Operator — the complementary distribution syntax
  • arguments Object — the legacy variadic mechanism
  • Function length — does not count rest parameters
  • ESLint prefer-rest-params — enforces rest over arguments
  • ES2026 §15.1 — Parameter Lists spec section
  • IsSimpleParameterList — spec static semantic
  • ExpectedArgumentCount — spec static semantic
  • TypeScript — ...args: T[] type syntax

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Rest parameters were introduced in ES2015 (ES6) — part of the same release as let/const, classes, and promises.
  • They are Baseline Widely available — supported across all browsers since July 2015.
  • Rest parameters are real arrays — unlike the arguments object.
  • They work in arrow functions — arguments does not.
  • Only one rest parameter per function — and it must be last.
  • Rest parameters cannot have defaults — they are always arrays.
  • Destructured rest parameters allow extracting specific positions.
  • Function.length does not count rest parameters — only parameters before the first default or rest.
  • V8 optimizes spread-forwarding patterns — no allocation when ...args is immediately spread.
  • Rest is ~4x faster than arguments — benchmarks show 480ms vs 110ms and 10x fewer GC scavenges.
  • ES2026 §15.1 defines rest parameters through IsSimpleParameterList and ExpectedArgumentCount.
  • Rest parameters create unmapped arguments — per ES2026 §10.2.11.
  • Rest parameters survive obfuscation — they still produce real arrays.
  • React hooks use rest parameters extensively — useEffect, useCallback, and custom hooks.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A rest parameter (...args) collects remaining arguments into a real array.
  • It must be the last parameter and there can be only one per function.
  • No trailing comma, no default value — syntax restrictions.
  • Real array — all array methods work directly.
  • Works in arrow functions — unlike arguments.
  • Never mapped — unlike arguments in non-strict simple lists.
  • Destructurable — extract specific positions from the collected array.
  • Not counted in Function.length — ExpectedArgumentCount excludes it.
  • Faster than arguments — ~4x improvement in benchmarks.
  • V8 optimizes spread-forwarding — no allocation when immediately spread.
  • Replaces arguments in modern code — ESLint prefer-rest-params.
  • ES2026 §15.1 defines the spec behavior.
  • Use for variadic functions — sum, log, forward, emit.
  • Do not use for fixed arity — named parameters are clearer.
  • Rest parameters are the modern variadic input mechanism for JavaScript.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A default parameter is a parameter in a function signature that is initialized with a fallback value if no argument or undefined is passed when the function is called. The default value is specified using the assignment operator (=) directly in the parameter list.

function greet(name = "world") {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

greet();          // "Hello, world!"
greet("Ada");     // "Hello, Ada!"
greet(undefined); // "Hello, world!" — undefined triggers the default
greet(null);      // "Hello, null!" — null does NOT trigger the default

Default parameters are evaluated at call time — a new default value is created each time the function is called without an argument, unlike Python's behavior where defaults are evaluated once at definition time. They work with any expression, including function calls, object literals, and references to earlier parameters.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Default parameters exist to solve the optional argument problem: functions often need to accept arguments that are optional, with sensible fallback values. Before ES2015, developers had to check for undefined inside the function body or use the || operator — both approaches were verbose and error-prone.

// ❌ Pre-ES2015 — verbose and buggy
function greet(name) {
    name = name || "world"; // 0, "", false become "world"!
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

// ✅ ES2015+ — clean and correct
function greet(name = "world") {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

Default parameters serve as the declarative fallback layer of function signatures:

  • Self-documenting — the function signature shows which parameters are optional and what their defaults are.
  • Clean — no body-level checks.
  • Correct — respects 0, "", and false (unlike || defaults).
  • Flexible — default values can be any expression, including function calls.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Functions
├── Function Declarations       ✅ done
├── Function Expressions        ✅ done
├── Arrow Functions             ✅ done
├── Parameters                  ✅ done
├── Rest Parameters             ✅ done
├── Default Parameters          ← you are here
├── Closures
├── Higher-Order Functions
└── Pure Functions

Default parameters sit after Rest Parameters because they are the second special parameter syntax. The next concept, Closures, describes how functions capture their lexical environment — and default parameters interact with closures when they reference outer variables.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
JavaScript functions have no arity checking. Missing arguments are undefined, and operations on undefined produce surprising results:

function multiply(a, b) {
    return a * b;
}

multiply(5); // NaN — b is undefined

Before ES2015, developers had to handle this inside the function body:

// ❌ Verbose
function multiply(a, b) {
    if (b === undefined) b = 1;
    return a * b;
}

// ❌ Buggy — 0, "", false become 1
function multiply(a, b) {
    b = b || 1;
    return a * b;
}

The || approach fails for falsy values. multiply(5, 0) returns 5, not 0 — because 0 is falsy and triggers the fallback.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-ES2015 No default parameter syntax — required body-level checks || defaults Failed for 0, "", false if (x === undefined) Verbose and repetitive No parameter documentation Signatures did not reveal optional parameters No default for destructured params Destructuring required separate defaults

docs.title: Why Default Parameters Were Introduced
docs.text:
Default parameters were introduced in ES2015 (ES6) as part of a broader language overhaul. They solved the optional argument problem by making the fallback value part of the signature rather than part of the body.

The design goals, as stated in the original TC39 proposal, were:

Goal: convenience and readability. Non-goal: subtle expressiveness. Guiding principle: defaults should be fully understandable without inspecting the function body.

The feature was designed to be obvious from the signature alone — a developer should not need to read the function body to know what happens when an argument is omitted.

docs.title: Why Default Parameters Still Matter in 2026
docs.text: Default parameters are Baseline Widely available — supported across all modern browsers since September 2016. ES2026 does not introduce new default parameter syntax; the feature set is mature. However, the ES2026 spec continues to define default parameters in Section 15.1 (Parameter Lists) through the HasInitializer and ExpectedArgumentCount static semantics.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
function name(param = defaultValue) {
    // body
}

docs.title: Minimal Default Parameter
docs.text:
function greet(name = "world") {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

greet();          // "Hello, world!"
greet("Ada");     // "Hello, Ada!"

docs.title: Multiple Default Parameters
docs.text:
function createUser(name, role = "viewer", active = true) {
    return { name, role, active };
}

createUser("Ada");
// { name: "Ada", role: "viewer", active: true }

createUser("Ada", "admin");
// { name: "Ada", role: "admin", active: true }

docs.title: Default Parameters with Destructuring
docs.text:
function createConfig({ debug = false, timeout = 5000 } = {}) {
    return { debug, timeout };
}

createConfig();                // { debug: false, timeout: 5000 }
createConfig({ debug: true }); // { debug: true, timeout: 5000 }

The = {} default is essential — without it, calling createConfig() throws TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'debug' of 'undefined'.

docs.title: Default Parameters in Arrow Functions
docs.text:
const greet = (name = "world") => `Hello, ${name}!`;
const add = (a, b = 10) => a + b;

add(5);    // 15
add(5, 20); // 25

docs.title: Default Parameters Referencing Earlier Parameters
docs.text:
function createRange(start, end = start + 10) {
    return [start, end];
}

createRange(5);    // [5, 15]
createRange(5, 20); // [5, 20]

Default expressions are evaluated left to right — earlier parameters are available to later defaults.

docs.title: Default Parameters with Function Calls
docs.text:
function createId(prefix = "user", timestamp = Date.now()) {
    return `${prefix}_${timestamp}`;
}

createId(); // "user_1727884800000"

Default expressions are evaluated at call time — a new Date.now() value is produced each call.

docs.title: Default Parameters with null
docs.text:
function greet(name = "world") {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

greet(null); // "Hello, null!" — null does NOT trigger the default

Default parameters trigger only on undefined — not on null, 0, "", or false.

docs.title: Default Parameters in Class Methods
docs.text:
class Calculator {
    add(a, b = 0) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

docs.title: Default Parameters in Object Methods
docs.text:
const logger = {
    log(message, level = "info") {
        console[level](message);
    },
};

docs.title: TypeScript Default Parameters
docs.text:
function greet(name: string = "world"): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

TypeScript supports default parameters with type annotations. Parameters with defaults are considered optional — no ? needed.

docs.title: The "Fallback Value" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a default parameter as a fallback value that is used when the caller does not provide one:

Function call: greet(          )
                    │
                    ▼
              No argument?
                    │
                    ├── Yes → Use default: "world"
                    │
                    └── No → Use provided argument

docs.title: The "Default Trigger" Mental Model
docs.text:
Default parameters trigger in exactly two cases:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Default Parameter Trigger            │
│                                             │
│  ✅ No argument provided     → use default  │
│  ✅ undefined provided       → use default  │
│                                             │
│  ❌ null provided            → use null     │
│  ❌ 0 provided               → use 0        │
│  ❌ "" provided              → use ""       │
│  ❌ false provided           → use false    │
│  ❌ NaN provided             → use NaN      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Signature as Documentation" Mental Model
docs.text:
Default parameters make the function signature self-documenting:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  function createUser(                       │
│      name,              ← required          │
│      role = "viewer",   ← optional, default │
│      active = true      ← optional, default │
│  )                                          │
│                                             │
│  The signature alone tells you:             │
│  - name is required                         │
│  - role defaults to "viewer"                │
│  - active defaults to true                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Call-Time Evaluation" Mental Model
docs.text:
Default expressions are evaluated at call time, not at definition time:

Definition time:                    Call time:
┌─────────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────────┐
│ function f(x = new  │            │ f() → x = new       │
│   Date()) {}        │            │   Date()  ← new     │
│                     │            │   object each call  │
│ No Date created.    │            │                     │
└─────────────────────┘            └─────────────────────┘

This differs from Python, where defaults are evaluated once at definition time — a common source of bugs with mutable defaults.

docs.title: The "|| vs. Default Parameter" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  || Default              Default Parameter  │
│                                             │
│  Triggers on:            Triggers on:       │
│  • undefined             • undefined        │
│  • null                                     │
│  • 0                                        │
│  • ""                                       │
│  • false                                    │
│  • NaN                                      │
│                                             │
│  ❌ Loses 0, "", false  ✅ Respects all     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Concept 1: Default Parameters Trigger Only on undefined
docs.text:
function f(x = 10) { return x; }

f();          // 10
f(undefined); // 10
f(null);      // null
f(0);         // 0
f("");        // ""
f(false);     // false

null does not trigger the default — use ?? inside the body if null should also fall back:

function f(x) {
    x = x ?? 10; // handles both null and undefined
}

docs.title: Concept 2: Default Expressions Are Evaluated at Call Time
docs.text:
function f(x = Date.now()) { return x; }

f(); // timestamp 1
f(); // timestamp 2 — different each call

Unlike Python, a new value is created each call.

docs.title: Concept 3: Earlier Parameters Are Available to Later Defaults
docs.text:
function f(a, b = a * 2) {
    return [a, b];
}

f(5);    // [5, 10]
f(5, 20); // [5, 20]

Default expressions are evaluated left to right.

docs.title: Concept 4: Default Parameters Can Be Any Expression
docs.text:
function f(x = 1 + 2) { return x; }
function f(x = "hello".toUpperCase()) { return x; }
function f(x = [1, 2, 3]) { return x; }
function f(x = { a: 1 }) { return x; }
function f(x = () => "hi") { return x; }

docs.title: Concept 5: Default Parameters Create a Separate Scope
docs.text:
Default parameter expressions exist in their own scope — separate from the function body. This means they cannot access variables declared in the body:

function f(a = b) {
    let b = 10; // ❌ ReferenceError — b is not available in the parameter scope
}

docs.title: Concept 6: Default Parameters with Destructuring
docs.text:
function createUser({ name, role = "viewer" } = {}) {
    return { name, role };
}

createUser();                    // { name: undefined, role: "viewer" }
createUser({ name: "Ada" });     // { name: "Ada", role: "viewer" }

The = {} default prevents TypeError when no argument is passed.

docs.title: Concept 7: Default Parameters and Function length
docs.text:
The length property counts parameters before the first default or rest parameter:

function f(a, b, c = 1) {}
console.log(f.length); // 2

docs.title: Concept 8: Default Parameters and arguments
docs.text:
Functions with default parameters create unmapped arguments objects — arguments[0] does not alias the first parameter:

function f(a = 1) {
    arguments[0] = 99;
    console.log(a); // unchanged — arguments is unmapped
}

Per ES2026 §10.2.11 / §10.4.4.6 / §10.4.4.7, functions with default parameters create unmapped arguments objects — the parameter-list shape controls the mapping behavior.

docs.title: Concept 9: Default Parameters and "use strict"
docs.text:
A function with default parameters cannot contain "use strict" in its body:

function f(a = 1) {
    "use strict"; // ❌ SyntaxError
}

This is because a directive prologue cannot appear in a function with non-simple parameters.

docs.title: Concept 10: Default Parameters Replace || and if Checks
docs.text:
// ❌ Old way — buggy for falsy values
function f(x) {
    x = x || 10;
    return x;
}

// ✅ Modern way
function f(x = 10) {
    return x;
}

docs.title: Concept 11: Default Parameters and TypeScript
docs.text:
TypeScript supports default parameters with type annotations:

function greet(name: string = "world"): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

Parameters with defaults are automatically optional — no ? needed.

docs.title: Concept 12: ES2026 Spec — HasInitializer
docs.text:
The spec's HasInitializer static semantic determines whether a parameter has a default value. This affects:

  • Whether the parameter list is simple (IsSimpleParameterList).
  • Whether the arguments object is mapped or unmapped.
  • Whether the function's length property includes the parameter.

docs.title: Concept 13: ES2026 Spec — ExpectedArgumentCount
docs.text: The ExpectedArgumentCount static semantic counts parameters before the first default or rest parameter. This is exposed as the function's length property.

docs.title: Concept 14: Default Parameters and Side Effects
docs.text:
Default expressions should not have side effects — they make reasoning about the function harder:

// ❌ Confusing side effect
let count = 0;
function f(x = count++) { return x; }

Best practice: Keep default expressions pure.

docs.title: Concept 15: Default Parameters with Mutable Objects
docs.text:
Avoid using mutable objects as default values — they can lead to shared state issues:

// ❌ Shared array across calls
function f(arr = []) {
    arr.push(1); // each call gets the SAME array
    return arr;
}

// ✅ Fresh array each call
function f(arr = []) {
    return arr; // new array each call — defaults are call-time evaluated
}

In JavaScript, defaults are evaluated at call time, so arr = [] creates a new array each call — this is safe. The warning applies more to languages with definition-time evaluation.

docs.title: Concept 16: ESLint Rules for Default Parameters
docs.text: Rule Purpose default-param-last Enforce default parameters last no-unused-vars Flag unused parameters prefer-rest-params Prefer rest over arguments

docs.title: Concept 17: Default Parameters in React
docs.text:
Default parameters are the standard pattern for React component props:

function UserCard({ name, role = "user", active = true }) {
    return <div>{name} — {role}</div>;
}

docs.title: Concept 18: Performance — No Significant Overhead
docs.text: Default parameters are initialized only when needed — there is no performance hit when the argument is provided. The default expression is only evaluated if the argument is undefined.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Default Parameter Evaluation
docs.text:
1.  Function is called with arguments.
    │
    ▼
2.  New execution context is created.
    │
    ▼
3.  For each parameter with a default:
    │   - If argument is undefined → evaluate default expression.
    │   - Else → use the argument.
    │
    ▼
4.  Default expressions are evaluated left to right.
    │
    ▼
5.  Earlier parameters are available to later defaults.
    │
    ▼
6.  Function body executes.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Default Expression Scope
docs.text:
1.  Function is called.
    │
    ▼
2.  A new parameter scope is created.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parameters are bound in this scope (uninitialized).
    │
    ▼
4.  Default expressions are evaluated in this scope.
    │
    ▼
5.  The parameter scope is popped before the function body runs.
    │
    ▼
6.  Function body executes in a separate scope.

This is why defaults cannot access body variables — the body scope does not exist yet when defaults are evaluated.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Default vs. ||
docs.text:
Default parameter:                  || default:
1.  Argument === undefined?         1.  Argument is falsy?
2.  Yes → use default.              2.  Yes → use default.
3.  No → use argument.              3.  No → use argument.
    │                                    │
    ▼                                    ▼
0 → 0                               0 → default (❌ wrong)
"" → ""                             "" → default (❌ wrong)
false → false                       false → default (❌ wrong)

docs.title: Step-by-Step: HasInitializer Static Semantic
docs.text:
1.  Parser encounters parameter with `=`.
    │
    ▼
2.  HasInitializer returns true.
    │
    ▼
3.  Parameter list is marked non-simple.
    │
    ▼
4.  arguments object becomes unmapped.
    │
    ▼
5.  Parameter is excluded from Function.length.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of Default Parameters
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification covers default parameters in Section 15.1 (Parameter Lists). Key subclauses:

Clause Title 15.1.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors 15.1.2 Static Semantics: ContainsExpression 15.1.3 Static Semantics: IsSimpleParameterList 15.1.4 Static Semantics: HasInitializer 15.1.5 Static Semantics: ExpectedArgumentCount 15.1.6 Runtime Semantics: IteratorBindingInitialization

docs.title: HasInitializer (ES2026 §15.1.4)
docs.text:
The HasInitializer static semantic determines whether a parameter has a default value. This is used by:

  • IsSimpleParameterList — a parameter list with any default is not simple.
  • ExpectedArgumentCount — default parameters are excluded from length.
  • arguments mapping — non-simple parameter lists create unmapped arguments.

docs.title: IsSimpleParameterList (ES2026 §15.1.3)
docs.text:
A parameter list is simple if it contains only simple identifiers. It is not simple if it contains:

  • Default parameters
  • Rest parameters
  • Destructured parameters

Functions with non-simple parameter lists:

  • Create unmapped arguments objects.
  • Cannot contain "use strict" in their body.

docs.title: ExpectedArgumentCount (ES2026 §15.1.5)
docs.text:
This static semantic determines the function's length property — the number of parameters before the first default or rest parameter.

function f(a, b, c = 1, ...rest) {}
f.length; // 2 — a and b

docs.title: Mapped vs. Unmapped arguments (ES2026 §10.2.11 / §10.4.4.6 / §10.4.4.7)
docs.text:
• Mapped — arguments[i] and parameter i are aliases. Only in non-strict functions with simple parameter lists.
  • Unmapped — arguments[i] is a copy. Functions with default parameters create unmapped objects.

docs.title: The Parameter Scope
docs.text:
Default parameter expressions run in a separate scope from the function body. This scope:

  • Contains the parameter bindings.
  • Does not contain body variables.
  • Is popped before the body executes.

This is why defaults cannot reference body variables.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
Function Execution Context:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Parameter Scope                    │
│                                     │
│  a: 10                              │
│  b: 20 (default: a * 2 = 20)       │
│                                     │
│  arguments: [10, undefined]         │
│    (unmapped — because of default)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Body Scope                         │
│                                     │
│  (body variables)                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text:
• Default initialization is conditional — only runs when argument is undefined.
  • No performance hit when argument is provided.
  • Default expressions are evaluated at call time — dynamic values created each call.
  • V8 optimizes default parameters — same as regular parameter binding.

docs.title: Default Parameter Lifecycle
docs.text:
Function defined → Default parameter declared → Function called
    → Check if argument is undefined → Evaluate default if needed
    → Bind parameter → Body executes

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write function signature
    │
    ▼
Need optional parameter?
    │
    ├── Yes → Use default parameter: param = defaultValue
    │
    └── No → Use simple parameter
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint default-param-last)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript)
    │
    ▼
Run / Test

docs.title: Choosing Default Style Workflow
docs.text:
Need fallback for undefined only?
    │
    ├── Yes → Default parameter: param = value
    │
    └── No → Need fallback for all falsy values?
              │
              ├── Yes → Use || in body
              │
              └── No → Need fallback for null too?
                        │
                        ├── Yes → Use ?? in body
                        │
                        └── No → Default parameter

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Default Parameter
docs.text:
function greet(name = "world") {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

console.log(greet());          // "Hello, world!"
console.log(greet("Ada"));     // "Hello, Ada!"
console.log(greet(undefined)); // "Hello, world!"
console.log(greet(null));      // "Hello, null!"

Breakdown:

  • null does not trigger the default.
  • Only undefined (or no argument) triggers the default.

docs.title: Example 2: Multiple Defaults
docs.text:
function createUser(name, role = "viewer", active = true) {
    return { name, role, active };
}

console.log(createUser("Ada"));
// { name: "Ada", role: "viewer", active: true }

docs.title: Example 3: Default Referencing Earlier Parameter
docs.text:
function createRange(start, end = start + 10) {
    return [start, end];
}

console.log(createRange(5));    // [5, 15]
console.log(createRange(5, 20)); // [5, 20]

docs.title: Example 4: Default with Destructuring
docs.text:
function createConfig({ debug = false, timeout = 5000 } = {}) {
    return { debug, timeout };
}

console.log(createConfig());                 // { debug: false, timeout: 5000 }
console.log(createConfig({ debug: true })); // { debug: true, timeout: 5000 }

docs.title: Example 5: Arrow Function with Default
docs.text:
const greet = (name = "world") => `Hello, ${name}!`;
const add = (a, b = 10) => a + b;

console.log(add(5));    // 15
console.log(add(5, 20)); // 25

docs.title: Example 6: Default vs. ||
docs.text:
// ❌ Buggy — 0 becomes 10
function bad(x) {
    x = x || 10;
    return x;
}

// ✅ Correct — 0 stays 0
function good(x = 10) {
    return x;
}

console.log(bad(0));  // 10 — wrong!
console.log(good(0)); // 0 — correct

docs.title: Example 7: Default with Function Call
docs.text:
function createId(prefix = "user", timestamp = Date.now()) {
    return `${prefix}_${timestamp}`;
}

console.log(createId()); // "user_1727884800000"

Breakdown:

  • Date.now() is evaluated at call time.
  • A new timestamp each call.

docs.title: Example 8: Default and arguments
docs.text:
function f(a = 1) {
    arguments[0] = 99;
    console.log(a); // unchanged — unmapped
}

f(); // a is still 1

docs.title: Example 9: TypeScript Default Parameter
docs.text:
function greet(name: string = "world"): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

Breakdown:

  • Default parameter with type annotation.
  • No ? needed — parameters with defaults are optional.

docs.title: Example 10: React Component with Default Props
docs.text:
function UserCard({ name, role = "user", active = true }) {
    return (
        <div className={active ? "active" : "inactive"}>
            {name} — {role}
        </div>
    );
}

<UserCard name="Ada" />
// Renders: Ada — user (active)

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Default Value Optional configuration config = {} Pagination defaults page = 1, limit = 20 Retry defaults maxAttempts = 3 Timeout defaults timeout = 5000 Logging level level = "info" React props role = "user" API parameters format = "json" Sorting direction direction = "asc" Locale defaults locale = "en-US" Currency defaults currency = "USD"

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use default parameters instead of || for defaults. Why: respects 0, "", and false.
  2. Place default parameters last. Why: parameters after a default cannot be omitted without passing undefined.
  3. Keep default expressions simple and pure. Why: side effects make reasoning harder.
  4. Always provide = {} with destructured parameters. Why: prevents TypeError on no-argument calls.
  5. Use null only when you mean "explicitly no value". Why: null does not trigger defaults.
  6. Document default values. Why: callers need to know what happens when they omit arguments.
  7. Use TypeScript for type-safe defaults. Why: catches type mismatches at compile time.
  8. Enable ESLint default-param-last. Why: enforces default parameter placement.
  9. Avoid using mutable objects as defaults. Why: can lead to shared state confusion.
  10. Use default parameters for React props. Why: standard pattern, clean and readable.
  11. Do not reference body variables in defaults. Why: they are not available in the parameter scope.
  12. Use ?? when null should also trigger the fallback. Why: default parameters only trigger on undefined.
  13. Keep parameter lists short. Why: more than 3-4 params suggests a configuration object.
  14. Prefer destructuring with defaults for configuration objects. Why: self-documenting and flexible.
  15. Test default behavior at boundaries. Why: undefined, null, 0, "", and false are common edge cases.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using || for Defaults
docs.text:
function setVolume(vol) {
    vol = vol || 50; // ❌ 0 becomes 50
    return vol;
}
setVolume(0); // 50 — wrong!

✅ Correct:

function setVolume(vol = 50) {
    return vol;
}
setVolume(0); // 0

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Expecting Default to Trigger on null
docs.text:
function f(x = 10) { return x; }
f(null); // null — not 10

✅ Correct: Use x ?? 10 inside the body if null should fall back.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Default Parameter Before Required Parameter
docs.text:
function f(a = 1, b) { } // ❌ b cannot be provided without passing a

✅ Correct:

function f(b, a = 1) { }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting = {} in Destructured Parameters
docs.text:
function f({ a, b }) {}
f(); // ❌ TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'a' of 'undefined'

✅ Correct:

function f({ a, b } = {}) {}
f(); // ✅ works

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Referencing Body Variables in Defaults
docs.text:
function f(a = b) {
    let b = 10; // ❌ ReferenceError
}

✅ Correct: Defaults can only reference earlier parameters and outer-scope variables.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Side Effects in Defaults
docs.text:
let count = 0;
function f(x = count++) { return x; } // ❌ confusing side effect

✅ Correct: Keep default expressions pure.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Default Parameter in the Middle
docs.text:
function f(a = 1, b, c = 3) { } // ❌ b must be passed explicitly

✅ Correct: Place all defaults at the end.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: "use strict" with Default Parameters
docs.text:
function f(a = 1) {
    "use strict"; // ❌ SyntaxError
}

✅ Correct: Use strict mode at the script or module level.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming length Includes Defaults
docs.text:
function f(a, b = 1, c = 2) {}
f.length; // 1 — not 3

✅ Correct: Understand that length stops at the first default.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mutating Default Objects
docs.text:
function f(arr = []) {
    arr.push(1); // safe in JS — new array each call
    return arr;
}

Why it's generally safe: JavaScript evaluates defaults at call time, so [] creates a new array each call. However, shared state issues can arise if the default is a reference to an outer object:

const shared = [];
function f(arr = shared) { /* ... */ } // ❌ shared state

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• No performance hit when arguments are provided.
  • Default evaluation is conditional — only runs when argument is undefined.
  • Default expressions are evaluated at call time — dynamic values created each call.
  • Destructuring with defaults — additional cost per call; minor.
  • Complex default expressions — function calls in defaults add overhead.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Keep default expressions simple — avoid function calls when possible.
  2. Use default parameters instead of || — same or better performance.
  3. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt if defaults are in hot paths.
  4. Avoid complex default expressions in hot functions.

docs.title: Default Values and Injection
docs.text:
Untrusted input passed as arguments can lead to injection attacks if not validated. Default values do not sanitize input — they only provide fallbacks.

Defense: Validate all parameters at trust boundaries.

docs.title: Side Effects in Defaults
docs.text:
Default expressions with side effects can cause unexpected behavior.

Defense: Keep default expressions pure.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Destructuring with defaults does not introduce additional prototype pollution risk beyond normal destructuring.

Defense: Validate input; use Object.create(null) for dictionaries.

docs.title: Default Parameters and CSP
docs.text: Default parameters are compatible with strict Content Security Policy — they do not require eval or new Function.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Check f.length — number of parameters before defaults/rest.
  • console.log(f) — displays the function source including defaults.
  • debugger; — pause inside the function.
  • ESLint default-param-last — flags misplaced defaults.
  • TypeScript — catches type mismatches at compile time.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on functions with defaults.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Scenario Use Default Parameter? Optional argument with fallback ✅ Yes Configuration object ✅ Yes (with destructuring) React props ✅ Yes API parameters ✅ Yes Pagination defaults ✅ Yes Timeout/retry defaults ✅ Yes Fallback for all falsy values ❌ Use \|\| Fallback for null too ❌ Use ??

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• When fallback should apply to null — use ??.
  • When fallback should apply to all falsy values — use ||.
  • Before required parameters — default parameters should come last.
  • With side effects — keep defaults pure.
  • When the parameter is required — do not provide a default.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Parameters — the general parameter concept
  • Rest Parameters — variadic parameter syntax
  • Destructuring — extracting values from objects/arrays
  • || Operator — falsy-based defaults (legacy)
  • ?? Operator — nullish coalescing (modern)
  • Function length — does not count default parameters
  • arguments Object — unmapped with default parameters
  • ESLint default-param-last — enforces default placement
  • TypeScript — type-safe default parameters
  • ES2026 §15.1 — Parameter Lists spec section
  • HasInitializer — spec static semantic
  • ExpectedArgumentCount — spec static semantic

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Default parameters were introduced in ES2015 (ES6) — along with let/const, classes, and promises.
  • They are Baseline Widely available — supported across all browsers since September 2016.
  • They trigger only on undefined — not on null, 0, "", or false.
  • Default expressions are evaluated at call time — unlike Python, a new value each call.
  • They can reference earlier parameters — function f(a, b = a * 2) {}.
  • They create a separate scope — defaults cannot access body variables.
  • Function.length does not count default parameters — it stops at the first default.
  • Functions with defaults create unmapped arguments — per ES2026 §10.2.11.
  • "use strict" cannot appear in a function with defaults — syntax error.
  • The spec's HasInitializer static semantic determines whether a parameter has a default.
  • The spec's ExpectedArgumentCount determines the function's length property.
  • React props use default parameters extensively — function UserCard({ role = "user" }) {}.
  • TypeScript default parameters are automatically optional — no ? needed.
  • Default parameters have no performance penalty when arguments are provided.
  • Avoid side effects in defaults — they make code harder to reason about.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A default parameter (param = value) provides a fallback when no argument or undefined is passed.
  • Triggers only on undefined — not on null, 0, "", or false.
  • Evaluated at call time — a new value each call (unlike Python).
  • Can reference earlier parameters — evaluated left to right.
  • Creates a separate scope — cannot access body variables.
  • Works with destructuring — function f({ a = 1 } = {}) {}.
  • = {} is required with destructured parameters to avoid TypeError.
  • Function.length does not count defaults — stops at the first default.
  • Functions with defaults create unmapped arguments — ES2026 §10.2.11.
  • "use strict" cannot appear in a function with defaults — syntax error.
  • No performance penalty when arguments are provided.
  • Use default parameters over || — respects 0, "", false.
  • Use ?? when null should also fall back.
  • Place defaults last — before required parameters is a mistake.
  • Keep defaults pure — avoid side effects.
  • ESLint default-param-last enforces placement.
  • TypeScript adds type annotations to default parameters.
  • ES2026 does not change default parameter syntax — the feature is mature.
  • Default parameters are the declarative fallback mechanism for function signatures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A closure is the combination of a function and the lexical environment in which it was declared. It is the mechanism by which a function "remembers" the variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished executing.

function outer() {
    const secret = "hidden";
    return function inner() {
        console.log(secret); // inner remembers `secret`
    };
}

const fn = outer(); // outer() has finished executing
fn(); // "hidden" — secret is still alive

When outer() returns, its execution context is destroyed. But inner still has access to secret because it was created inside outer's lexical scope. The closure is the backpack that inner carries — it holds references to the variables it needs from its birthplace.

In the ECMAScript specification, closures are implemented through the [[Environment]] internal slot on every function object. This slot holds a reference to the lexical environment where the function was created. When the function is called, its [[Environment]] becomes the outer environment of the new execution context.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Closures exist to solve the state persistence problem: functions are normally stateless — they take input, produce output, and forget everything. But real programs need functions that remember things:

  • Counters — increment a value across calls.
  • Private state — encapsulate data that cannot be accessed from outside.
  • Event handlers — remember the context they were created in.
  • Factory functions — produce functions with pre-configured behavior.
  • Memoization — cache results between calls.
  • Currying — partially apply arguments across multiple calls.

Closures are not a feature that was added to JavaScript — they are an emergent property of lexical scoping. Every function in JavaScript is a closure if it references variables from an outer scope.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Functions
├── Function Declarations       ✅ done
├── Function Expressions        ✅ done
├── Arrow Functions             ✅ done
├── Parameters                  ✅ done
├── Rest Parameters             ✅ done
├── Default Parameters          ✅ done
├── Closures                    ← you are here
├── Higher-Order Functions
└── Pure Functions

Closures sit after all the parameter concepts because they depend on function creation and lexical scoping — both of which are established by the preceding concepts. The next concept, Higher-Order Functions, builds directly on closures — a higher-order function is often just a function that returns a closure.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A programming language with lexical scoping automatically creates closures. But why did JavaScript choose lexical scoping in the first place?

The alternative is dynamic scoping — where a function's variable references are resolved based on the call stack rather than the lexical structure of the code. Dynamic scoping makes it impossible to reason about what a function will do without tracing every possible call path. It also makes closures impossible — a function cannot "capture" anything if its variables depend on where it is called rather than where it is defined.

Lexical scoping was chosen because it is predictable, analyzable, and enables closures. A function's behavior is determined entirely by its source code — not by who calls it or when.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation Pre-closures No way to persist state between function calls without globals No private state All data was either local (lost after return) or global (shared) var in loops All closures shared the same binding — the classic loop bug No module pattern Encapsulation required global objects and naming conventions No memoization Caching required global objects No WeakRef/WeakMap Closures could not hold weak references to objects

docs.title: Why Closures Matter
docs.text:
Closures are not just a language feature — they are the foundation of JavaScript's programming model:

  • React Hooks — useState, useEffect, and useCallback are all closures.
  • Event handlers — every addEventListener callback is a closure.
  • Module patterns — private state and public APIs.
  • Functional programming — currying, composition, partial application.
  • Async patterns — debouncing, throttling, and memoization.

As one analysis put it: "If you understand closures deeply, entire categories of bugs simply disappear" .

docs.title: Why ES2026 Matters for Closures
docs.text:
ES2026 does not introduce new closure syntax. But it does clarify the spec's CreatePerIterationEnvironment abstract operation — the mechanism that gives each iteration of a for loop with let/const its own binding . This is the spec-level explanation for why let fixes the classic var loop closure bug.

The ES2026 spec (17th edition, approved June 30, 2026) also continues to define the Environment Record and Abstract Closure specification types , which are the formal foundations of lexical scoping and closures.

docs.title: The Canonical Closure Example
docs.text:
function outer() {
    const message = "Hello from the closure";
    return function inner() {
        console.log(message);
    };
}

const fn = outer();
fn(); // "Hello from the closure"

The inner function references message from the outer scope. When outer() returns, message would normally be garbage-collected. But because inner still references it, it stays alive.

docs.title: Counter with Private State
docs.text:
function createCounter() {
    let count = 0;
    return {
        increment() { return ++count; },
        decrement() { return --count; },
        getCount() { return count; },
    };
}

const counter = createCounter();
counter.increment(); // 1
counter.increment(); // 2
counter.decrement(); // 1
counter.getCount();  // 1
// counter.count;    // undefined — private!

count is not accessible from outside the returned object — only through the methods that close over it.

docs.title: The Classic Loop Bug (and Fix)
docs.text:
// ❌ var — all closures share the same binding
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// Output: 3, 3, 3

// ✅ let — each iteration gets its own binding
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// Output: 0, 1, 2

The ES2026 spec's CreatePerIterationEnvironment (Section 14.7.4.4) is the mechanism that creates a new lexical environment per iteration for let/const loops . Each closure captures its own binding cell.

docs.title: Factory Function
docs.text:
function createMultiplier(factor) {
    return function(number) {
        return number * factor;
    };
}

const double = createMultiplier(2);
const triple = createMultiplier(3);

double(5);  // 10
triple(5);  // 15

Each returned function captures its own factor.

docs.title: Memoization with Closure Cache
docs.text:
function memoize(fn) {
    const cache = new Map();
    return function(...args) {
        const key = JSON.stringify(args);
        if (cache.has(key)) {
            return cache.get(key);
        }
        const result = fn.apply(this, args);
        cache.set(key, result);
        return result;
    };
}

const slowSquare = memoize((n) => {
    console.log("computing...");
    return n * n;
});

slowSquare(5); // "computing..." then 25
slowSquare(5); // 25 (from cache, no "computing...")

The cache is private to the returned function — inaccessible from outside.

docs.title: Debounce with Closure State
docs.text:
function debounce(fn, delay) {
    let timeout;
    return function(...args) {
        clearTimeout(timeout);
        timeout = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), delay);
    };
}

The timeout variable persists between calls — it is captured by the closure.

docs.title: Module Pattern (Pre-ES6)
docs.text:
const Module = (function() {
    let privateVar = 0;

    function privateMethod() {
        privateVar++;
    }

    return {
        publicMethod() {
            privateMethod();
            return privateVar;
        },
    };
})();

Module.publicMethod(); // 1
Module.privateVar;     // undefined

docs.title: IIFE for Scope Isolation
docs.text:
(function() {
    const privateData = "secret";
    console.log(privateData); // "secret"
})();
// privateData is not accessible here

docs.title: Closures in Arrow Functions
docs.text:
const createGreeter = (greeting) => (name) => `${greeting}, ${name}!`;

const sayHello = createGreeter("Hello");
sayHello("Ada"); // "Hello, Ada!"

Arrow functions close over their lexical scope just like regular functions.

docs.title: WeakMap for Private Object State
docs.text:
const privateData = new WeakMap();

class User {
    constructor(name) {
        privateData.set(this, { name });
    }
    getName() {
        return privateData.get(this).name;
    }
}

WeakMap keys are weakly held — when the User instance is garbage-collected, the entry is automatically removed.

docs.title: using for Closure Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text:
function createResource() {
    let resource = acquire();
    return {
        [Symbol.dispose]() {
            resource.release();
        },
    };
}

{
    using res = createResource();
    // use res
} // res[Symbol.dispose]() called automatically

ES2026's using declarations guarantee cleanup even if exceptions occur .

docs.title: The "Backpack" Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of a closure as a function wearing a backpack:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Function Object                 │
│                                             │
│  ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Code       │   │  Backpack            │ │
│  │  (what it   │   │  (what it carries)   │ │
│  │   does)     │   │                      │ │
│  │             │   │  • secret            │ │
│  │             │   │  • count             │ │
│  │             │   │  • cache             │ │
│  └─────────────┘   └─────────────────────┘ │
│                                             │
│  The backpack holds references to the       │
│  variables from the function's birthplace.  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The backpack is the [[Environment]] slot — a reference to the lexical environment where the function was created .

docs.title: The "Lexical Scope vs. Execution Context" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Lexical Scope                                       │
│                                                     │
│  • Defined at WRITE time                            │
│  • Based on where functions are written in code     │
│  • NEVER changes                                    │
│  • Determines what a closure can access             │
│                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Execution Context                          │   │
│  │                                             │   │
│  │  • Created at RUN time                      │   │
│  │  • Determines what is currently executing   │   │
│  │  • Comes and goes                           │   │
│  │                                             │   │
│  │  Closures use LEXICAL scope — not           │   │
│  │  execution order.                           │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is why moving code around can break logic even if it "looks the same" .

docs.title: The "Closure Decides What to Keep" Mental Model
docs.text:
Closures are intelligent — they only keep variables that are actually used inside the inner function:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Outer function:                             │
│                                             │
│  const used = "kept";                       │
│  const unused = "discarded";                │
│  const global = "not in closure";           │
│                                             │
│  return function() {                        │
│      console.log(used); // ← only `used`    │
│  };                                         │
│                                             │
│  Result:                                    │
│  • `used` → in the closure                  │
│  • `unused` → NOT in the closure            │
│  • `global` → accessible directly           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

As one analysis put it: "Variables used inside the function are kept 'inside,' variables in outer scopes that aren't used aren't included, and global variables are accessible directly" .

docs.title: The "Memory Backpack" Mental Model
docs.text:
Anything referenced by a closure cannot be garbage-collected :

Closure alive → Backpack alive → Everything in backpack alive

This is the source of both the power and the danger of closures.

docs.title: Concept 1: Lexical Scoping
docs.text:
Closures exist because JavaScript uses lexical scoping — a function can access variables from the place where it was written, not where it is called.

const x = "global";

function a() {
    const x = "inside a";
    return function b() {
        return x; // looks UP the scope chain from where b was written
    };
}

const fn = a();
fn(); // "inside a" — not "global"

docs.title: Concept 2: The [[Environment]] Slot
docs.text: Every function object has an internal [[Environment]] slot that references the lexical environment where the function was created. When the function is called, this environment becomes the outer scope of the new execution context.

docs.title: Concept 3: Closures Capture Variables, Not Values
docs.text:
Closures capture references to variables — not copies of their values:

let status = "idle";

async function run() {
    await delay(1000);
    console.log(status); // "done" — not "idle"
}

status = "done";
run();

If you need the value at creation time, capture it explicitly:

const currentStatus = status;
async function run() {
    await delay(1000);
    console.log(currentStatus); // "idle"
}

docs.title: Concept 4: Per-Iteration Environments (ES2026 §14.7.4.4)
docs.text:
The CreatePerIterationEnvironment abstract operation creates a new lexical environment for each iteration of a for loop with let/const . Each closure captures its own binding cell.

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 0, 1, 2
}

With var, there is one shared binding — all closures see the final value.

docs.title: Concept 5: Closures and Garbage Collection
docs.text: Anything referenced by a closure cannot be garbage-collected. The closure holds a reference to its outer scope, preventing GC of enclosed variables .

docs.title: Concept 6: Private State
docs.text:
Closures enable true private state — variables that cannot be accessed or modified from outside:

function createAccount(initialBalance) {
    let balance = initialBalance;

    return {
        deposit(amount) { balance += amount; },
        withdraw(amount) { balance -= amount; },
        getBalance() { return balance; },
    };
}

balance is inaccessible except through the returned methods.

docs.title: Concept 7: Factory Functions
docs.text:
A factory function is a function that creates and returns another function, using closures to pre-configure behavior:

function createLogger(prefix) {
    return (message) => console.log(`[${prefix}] ${message}`);
}

const info = createLogger("INFO");
const error = createLogger("ERROR");

info("Server started");   // [INFO] Server started
error("Connection failed"); // [ERROR] Connection failed

docs.title: Concept 8: Memoization
docs.text:
Closures are the simplest way to build a cache that persists between function calls:

function memoize(fn) {
    const cache = new Map();
    return function(...args) {
        const key = JSON.stringify(args);
        return cache.has(key) ? cache.get(key) : cache.set(key, fn(...args)).get(key);
    };
}

docs.title: Concept 9: Stale Closures
docs.text:
A stale closure occurs when a closure captures a variable that has since been updated, but the closure still sees the old value:

function Counter() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    useEffect(() => {
        setInterval(() => {
            console.log(count); // always logs 0 — stale closure!
        }, 1000);
    }, []); // empty deps — effect runs once
}

Fix: Use a functional update or include the variable in the dependency array .

docs.title: Concept 10: Closures and this
docs.text:
Arrow functions capture this lexically — they close over the this of the enclosing scope. Regular functions have their own this binding.

class Timer {
    constructor() {
        this.seconds = 0;
    }
    start() {
        setInterval(() => {
            this.seconds++; // arrow — `this` is the Timer instance
        }, 1000);
    }
}

docs.title: Concept 11: Memory Leaks from Closures
docs.text:
Closures can cause memory leaks when they unintentionally keep large objects alive:

// ❌ The entire array stays in memory
function create() {
    const bigData = new Array(1_000_000).fill("*");
    return () => bigData.length;
}

// ✅ Only the length is captured
function create() {
    const bigData = new Array(1_000_000).fill("*");
    const length = bigData.length;
    return () => length;
}

docs.title: Concept 12: WeakMap for Private Object State
docs.text: WeakMap allows closures to hold weak references to objects — when the object is garbage-collected, the entry is automatically removed .

docs.title: Concept 13: using for Deterministic Cleanup (ES2026)
docs.text: ES2026's using declaration ties resource lifetime to a block — the resource is disposed automatically when the block exits . This replaces try/finally for cleanup.

docs.title: Concept 14: React Hooks Are Closures
docs.text: useState, useEffect, useCallback, and useMemo are all closure-based primitives. The "stale closure" problem in React is the same problem as in vanilla JavaScript .

docs.title: Concept 15: Closures and the Event Loop
docs.text:
Closures capture variables by reference. When combined with asynchronous code, this can lead to surprising behavior:

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 3, 3, 3 — shared binding
}

docs.title: Concept 16: Closures in Loops with let
docs.text: The ES2026 spec's CreatePerIterationEnvironment guarantees that each iteration of a let/const loop gets a new binding — so each closure captures its own value .

docs.title: Concept 17: Closures and Module Scope
docs.text: In ES modules, top-level variables are module-scoped — not global. Functions in a module close over the module scope, creating a natural closure-based module pattern.

docs.title: Concept 18: Performance of Closures
docs.text: Closures are fast — modern V8 engines optimize them aggressively. The main performance concern is memory retention — closures keep their entire outer scope alive in some engines .

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Closure Creation
docs.text:
1.  Function `outer` is called.
    │
    ▼
2.  A new execution context is created for `outer`.
    │
    ▼
3.  A new LexicalEnvironment is created for `outer`.
    │
    ▼
4.  `inner` function is created inside `outer`.
    │
    ▼
5.  `inner.[[Environment]]` is set to `outer`'s LexicalEnvironment.
    │
    ▼
6.  `outer` returns `inner`.
    │
    ▼
7.  `outer`'s execution context is destroyed — but its LexicalEnvironment
    │   is NOT garbage-collected because `inner.[[Environment]]` references it.
    │
    ▼
8.  `inner` is called.
    │
    ▼
9.  A new execution context is created for `inner`.
    │
    ▼
10. `inner`'s outer environment is `inner.[[Environment]]` — the captured
    │   environment from `outer`.
    │
    ▼
11. Variable lookup for `secret` walks up the scope chain and finds it.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Per-Iteration Environment
docs.text:
1.  `for (let i = 0; ...)` — let binding is created.
    │
    ▼
2.  Before each iteration, CreatePerIterationEnvironment is called.
    │
    ▼
3.  A new LexicalEnvironment is created.
    │
    ▼
4.  The previous iteration's `i` value is copied into the new environment.
    │
    ▼
5.  The loop body executes with the new environment.
    │
    ▼
6.  Closures created in the body capture THIS iteration's environment.
    │
    ▼
7.  After the loop, each closure has its own `i`.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Variable Capture
docs.text:
1.  Inner function references `x`.
    │
    ▼
2.  At function creation, JavaScript analyzes which outer variables are used.
    │
    ▼
3.  Only the used variables are included in the closure.
    │
    ▼
4.  Unused variables are NOT captured.
    │
    ▼
5.  Global variables are NOT captured — accessible directly.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Closure and Garbage Collection
docs.text:
1.  Closure is created — holds reference to outer scope.
    │
    ▼
2.  Outer function returns — execution context destroyed.
    │
    ▼
3.  GC scans for reachable objects.
    │
    ▼
4.  Closure is still reachable (stored in variable).
    │
    ▼
5.  Closure's [[Environment]] is reachable.
    │
    ▼
6.  All variables in that environment are reachable.
    │
    ▼
7.  GC does NOT collect them.
    │
    ▼
8.  When closure becomes unreachable → environment becomes unreachable → GC collects.

docs.title: The Spec's Treatment of Closures
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification defines closures through several interconnected concepts:

Spec Section Concept 6.2.7 The Environment Record Specification Type 6.2.8 The Abstract Closure Specification Type 9.1 Environment Records 10.2 Ordinary Function Objects 14.7.4.4 CreatePerIterationEnvironment

docs.title: The [[Environment]] Slot
docs.text: Every function object has an internal [[Environment]] slot that references the LexicalEnvironment where the function was created. When the function is called, this environment becomes the outer environment of the new execution context.

docs.title: The Scope Chain
docs.text:
Variable lookup walks the scope chain — a linked list of environments:

Current Environment → Outer Environment → Outer Environment → ... → Global

Closures keep the chain alive by holding a reference to their birth environment.

docs.title: CreatePerIterationEnvironment (ES2026 §14.7.4.4)
docs.text:
The ES2026 spec defines CreatePerIterationEnvironment as:

The abstract operation CreatePerIterationEnvironment with argument perIterationBindings is performed as follows: 1. If perIterationBindings has any elements, then a. Let lastIterationEnv be the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment. b. Let outer be lastIterationEnv.[[OuterEnv]]. ... 2. Return undefined .

This operation creates a new environment per iteration for let/const loops — each closure captures its own binding cell .

docs.title: Mapped vs. Unmapped Environments
docs.text: Functions with simple parameter lists create mapped environments where parameters and arguments are aliased. Functions with default, rest, or destructured parameters create unmapped environments.

docs.title: V8 Optimization: Context Allocation
docs.text:
V8 optimizes closures by:

  1. Context allocation — only variables actually captured are stored in the context.
  2. Context chain — the [[Environment]] chain is optimized to avoid unnecessary allocation.
  3. Escape analysis — V8 can determine when a closure does not escape and stack-allocate its context.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
Closure Object:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [[Call]]           → bytecode      │
│  [[Environment]]    → ──────────────┼──▶ LexicalEnvironment
│  [[FormalParameters]] → [a, b]      │       │
│  [[FunctionBody]]   → AST           │       │
│  name               → "inner"       │       ▼
└─────────────────────────────────────┘   Environment Record
                                              │
                                              ├── secret: "hidden"
                                              ├── count: 0
                                              └── ...

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text:
• Closures are fast — V8 optimizes them aggressively.
  • Context allocation — small cost per closure creation.
  • Escape analysis — V8 can stack-allocate non-escaping closures.
  • Memory retention — closures keep their entire environment alive in some engines.

docs.title: Closure Lifecycle
docs.text:
Function created → [[Environment]] set → Outer function returns
    → Environment kept alive by closure → Closure called → Environment accessed
    → Closure released → Environment eligible for GC

docs.title: Memory Lifecycle
docs.text:
Closure created → Environment referenced → Variables kept alive
    → Closure invoked → Variables read/written
    → Closure released → Environment unreferenced → GC collects

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write function that returns function
    │
    ▼
Inner function references outer variables
    │
    ▼
Closure is created automatically
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint no-loop-func, prefer-const)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript)
    │
    ▼
Run / Test
    │
    ▼
Debug with Chrome DevTools [[Scopes]] panel

docs.title: Memory Leak Debugging Workflow
docs.text:
Suspect memory leak
    │
    ▼
Open Chrome DevTools → Memory tab
    │
    ▼
Take heap snapshot
    │
    ▼
Perform suspected action several times
    │
    ▼
Take another snapshot
    │
    ▼
Compare — look for retaining paths
    │
    ▼
Check [[Scopes]] in DevTools to see what closure captures
    │
    ▼
Null out large references or restructure

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Closure
docs.text:
function outer() {
    const message = "Hello";
    return function inner() {
        return message;
    };
}

const fn = outer();
console.log(fn()); // "Hello"

docs.title: Example 2: Counter with Private State
docs.text:
function createCounter() {
    let count = 0;
    return {
        increment: () => ++count,
        decrement: () => --count,
        getCount: () => count,
    };
}

const counter = createCounter();
console.log(counter.increment()); // 1
console.log(counter.increment()); // 2
console.log(counter.getCount());  // 2
// counter.count → undefined

docs.title: Example 3: Loop Closure Bug and Fix
docs.text:
// ❌ var — all closures share `i`
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// 3, 3, 3

// ✅ let — each iteration has its own `i`
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
// 0, 1, 2

docs.title: Example 4: Memoization
docs.text:
function memoize(fn) {
    const cache = new Map();
    return function(...args) {
        const key = JSON.stringify(args);
        if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);
        const result = fn.apply(this, args);
        cache.set(key, result);
        return result;
    };
}

const fib = memoize((n) => n <= 1 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2));
console.log(fib(40)); // fast — cached

docs.title: Example 5: Debounce
docs.text:
function debounce(fn, delay) {
    let timeoutId;
    return function(...args) {
        clearTimeout(timeoutId);
        timeoutId = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), delay);
    };
}

const search = debounce((query) => {
    console.log("Searching:", query);
}, 300);

search("a");
search("ab");
search("abc"); // only "abc" is logged after 300ms

docs.title: Example 6: Module Pattern
docs.text:
const BankAccount = (function() {
    let balance = 0;

    return {
        deposit(amount) {
            if (amount > 0) balance += amount;
        },
        withdraw(amount) {
            if (amount > 0 && amount <= balance) balance -= amount;
        },
        getBalance() {
            return balance;
        },
    };
})();

BankAccount.deposit(100);
BankAccount.withdraw(30);
console.log(BankAccount.getBalance()); // 70
// BankAccount.balance → undefined

docs.title: Example 7: Factory Function
docs.text:
function createValidator(rules) {
    return (value) => {
        const errors = [];
        for (const [rule, message] of Object.entries(rules)) {
            if (!rule(value)) errors.push(message);
        }
        return errors;
    };
}

const validateEmail = createValidator({
    [(v) => v.includes("@")]: "Must contain @",
    [(v) => v.length > 5]: "Must be longer than 5 characters",
});

console.log(validateEmail("test")); // ["Must contain @", "Must be longer..."]

docs.title: Example 8: Stale Closure Fix
docs.text:
// ❌ Stale closure
function Counter() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    useEffect(() => {
        const id = setInterval(() => {
            console.log(count); // always 0
        }, 1000);
        return () => clearInterval(id);
    }, []);
}

// ✅ Functional update
function Counter() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    useEffect(() => {
        const id = setInterval(() => {
            setCount(prev => {
                console.log(prev); // latest value
                return prev;
            });
        }, 1000);
        return () => clearInterval(id);
    }, []);
}

docs.title: Example 9: Memory Leak Fix
docs.text:
// ❌ Entire array stays in memory
function createProcessor() {
    const hugeData = loadHugeData(); // 300MB
    const map = buildMap(hugeData);
    return function(id) {
        return map[id];
    };
}

// ✅ Only `map` is captured
function createProcessor() {
    const map = (() => {
        const hugeData = loadHugeData();
        return buildMap(hugeData);
    })();
    return function(id) {
        return map[id];
    };
}

docs.title: Example 10: WeakMap Private State
docs.text:
const privateData = new WeakMap();

class User {
    constructor(name, age) {
        privateData.set(this, { name, age });
    }
    getName() {
        return privateData.get(this).name;
    }
}

const user = new User("Ada", 36);
console.log(user.getName()); // "Ada"
// user.name → undefined
// When `user` is GC'd, WeakMap entry is automatically removed

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Closure Pattern Counter Private state + methods Factory function Pre-configured behavior Memoization Cache between calls Debounce/Throttle Timer state persistence Event handlers Context capture Module pattern Private/public API Currying Partial application React Hooks State and effects Iterators Stateful iteration Async patterns Capturing loop variables

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Close over only what you need. Why: avoid retaining large objects .
  2. Null out large references when done. Why: allow garbage collection.
  3. Always clean up event listeners. Why: prevent leaks from long-lived closures .
  4. Use let/const in loops, never var. Why: per-iteration bindings prevent the classic bug.
  5. Capture values explicitly in async code. Why: closures capture references, not values.
  6. Use WeakMap for object-keyed private state. Why: allows GC when objects are no longer needed.
  7. Keep lexical scopes small. Why: smaller scopes mean smaller closures .
  8. Use using for resource cleanup (ES2026). Why: deterministic disposal.
  9. Be aware of stale closures in React. Why: use functional updates or dependency arrays.
  10. Use Chrome DevTools [[Scopes]] to inspect closures. Why: see exactly what is captured .
  11. Prefer const for captured variables. Why: prevents accidental mutation.
  12. Avoid creating closures in hot loops. Why: per-iteration context allocation.
  13. Use memoization with LRU eviction. Why: prevent unbounded cache growth .
  14. Understand the CreatePerIterationEnvironment mechanism. Why: explains let loop behavior (ES2026 §14.7.4.4).
  15. Test memory behavior with heap snapshots. Why: closures are the most common source of leaks.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: var in Loops with Closures
docs.text:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 3, 3, 3
}

✅ Correct:

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 0, 1, 2
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Closures Capture Values
docs.text:
let status = "idle";
async function run() {
    await delay(1000);
    console.log(status); // "done" — not "idle"
}
status = "done";
run();

✅ Correct:

const currentStatus = status;
async function run() {
    await delay(1000);
    console.log(currentStatus); // "idle"
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Memory Leak from Large Object
docs.text:
function create() {
    const bigData = new Array(1_000_000).fill("*");
    return () => bigData.length; // entire array stays in memory
}

✅ Correct:

function create() {
    const bigData = new Array(1_000_000).fill("*");
    const length = bigData.length;
    return () => length; // only length is captured
}

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Stale Closure in React
docs.text:
useEffect(() => {
    setInterval(() => console.log(count), 1000); // always 0
}, []);

✅ Correct:

useEffect(() => {
    setInterval(() => setCount(prev => { console.log(prev); return prev; }), 1000);
}, []);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Forgetting to Remove Event Listeners
docs.text:
window.addEventListener("resize", this.onResize); // never removed

✅ Correct:

window.addEventListener("resize", this.onResize);
// later: window.removeEventListener("resize", this.onResize);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Closures Capture the Entire Scope
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Closures capture only the variables they use — not the entire scope .

✅ Correct: Understand that JavaScript intelligently determines which variables to keep.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using Closures for Fixed-Arity Functions
docs.text:
function add() {
    return function(a, b) { return a + b; };
}

✅ Correct: Use closures for state persistence, not for every function.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Not Using WeakMap for Object Private State
docs.text:
const privateData = {}; // strong reference — never GC'd

✅ Correct:

const privateData = new WeakMap(); // weak reference — GC'd with object

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Global Variables Are in the Closure
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Global variables are not included in closures — they are accessible directly .

✅ Correct: Only variables from the enclosing function scope are captured.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Closures in Hot Loops
docs.text:
for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    arr.push(() => i); // 10,000 closures — each with its own environment
}

✅ Correct: Move function creation outside the loop when possible.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Closure creation — small cost per closure; V8 optimizes heavily.
  • Context allocation — only captured variables are stored.
  • Escape analysis — V8 can stack-allocate non-escaping closures.
  • Memory retention — closures keep their environment alive.
  • Per-iteration environments — let creates a new environment per iteration .
  • Closures in hot loops — avoid creating functions per iteration.
  • WeakMap — allows GC of object keys.
  • using — deterministic cleanup (ES2026).

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Close over only what you need — smaller closures are cheaper.
  2. Avoid creating closures in hot loops.
  3. Use let/const — V8 optimizes them well.
  4. Use WeakMap for object-keyed caches.
  5. Null out large references when done.
  6. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.
  7. Use Chrome DevTools Memory panel to find leaks.

docs.title: Closure-Based Encapsulation
docs.text: Closures provide true private state — variables captured by a closure cannot be accessed from outside. This is a security benefit for sensitive data.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution and Closures
docs.text: Closures do not expose their captured variables to prototype pollution — they are isolated in the lexical environment.

docs.title: Memory Exhaustion
docs.text:
Closures that capture large objects can cause memory exhaustion — a denial-of-service vector if unbounded.

Defense: Limit closure scope; null out large references.

docs.title: Stale Closures and Security
docs.text:
Stale closures in security-sensitive code can lead to logic bugs — e.g., a permission check that uses an outdated role.

Defense: Capture values explicitly; use functional updates.

docs.title: eval and Closures
docs.text:
eval can access and modify closure variables — a security risk if eval is used with untrusted input.

Defense: Never use eval with untrusted input; use strict CSP.

docs.title: WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry
docs.text: WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry allow observing garbage collection — but their timing is non-deterministic and should not be relied on for security-critical cleanup .

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• Chrome DevTools [[Scopes]] — inspect exactly what a closure captures .
  • Heap snapshots — take before/after snapshots to find leaks .
  • %DebugTrackRetainingPath(object) — V8 native syntax to trace what is retaining an object .
  • console.dir(fn) — inspect function properties.
  • ESLint no-loop-func — flags closures in loops.
  • ESLint prefer-const — enforces const for captured variables.
  • debugger; — pause inside closures.
  • Memory panel — monitor heap growth over time.
  • Performance monitor — watch GC activity.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Scenario Use Closure? Private state ✅ Yes Factory functions ✅ Yes Memoization ✅ Yes Debounce/Throttle ✅ Yes Event handlers ✅ Yes Module pattern ✅ Yes Currying ✅ Yes React hooks ✅ Yes Simple transformations ❌ Use pure functions Fixed-arity utilities ❌ No closure needed

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• Simple transformations — use pure functions instead.
  • When globals suffice — but prefer closures for encapsulation.
  • Hot loops — avoid creating closures per iteration.
  • Large object capture — null out references when done.
