  • Security-critical timing — don't rely on WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry.
  • When a class is clearer — use classes for object-oriented designs.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• Lexical Scoping — the foundation of closures
  • Scope Chain — how variable lookup works
  • [[Environment]] — the internal slot that holds the closure's scope
  • CreatePerIterationEnvironment — ES2026 §14.7.4.4
  • Higher-Order Functions — functions that take/return functions
  • Pure Functions — functions without side effects
  • Currying — partial application via closures
  • Memoization — caching via closures
  • WeakMap — weak references for private state
  • WeakRef — weak references to objects
  • FinalizationRegistry — cleanup callbacks
  • using — resource cleanup (ES2026)
  • React Hooks — closure-based state management
  • Garbage Collection — how closures affect memory

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• Every function in JavaScript is a closure — if it references variables from an outer scope.
  • Closures are not a feature — they are an emergent property of lexical scoping.
  • The [[Environment]] slot is the spec-level mechanism behind closures.
  • CreatePerIterationEnvironment (ES2026 §14.7.4.4) creates a new binding per let/const loop iteration .
  • V8 optimizes closures — only used variables are captured .
  • Global variables are never included in closures — they are accessible directly .
  • Closures capture references, not values — this is why async loops with var fail.
  • WeakMap is the modern way to attach private state to objects .
  • React Hooks are closures — useState, useEffect, and useCallback all depend on closure semantics.
  • The "stale closure" problem is one of the most common React bugs .
  • Closures cause memory leaks when they capture large objects unnecessarily .
  • Chrome DevTools [[Scopes]] shows exactly what a closure captures .
  • ES2026's using provides deterministic cleanup for closure-held resources .
  • %DebugTrackRetainingPath() is a V8 native syntax for tracing closure retention .
  • Closures are the backbone of JavaScript — from modules to hooks to functional programming.

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A closure is a function that remembers its lexical scope.
  • Lexical scoping — functions access variables from where they were written, not where they are called.
  • [[Environment]] — the internal slot that holds a closure's captured scope.
  • Closures capture references, not values — this is why async loops with var fail.
  • CreatePerIterationEnvironment (ES2026 §14.7.4.4) — per-iteration bindings for let/const loops.
  • Closures enable private state — variables inaccessible from outside.
  • Closures enable factories, memoization, debounce, and currying.
  • Closures can cause memory leaks — they keep their entire captured scope alive in some engines.
  • Close over only what you need — null out large references when done.
  • Use WeakMap for object-keyed private state.
  • Use let/const in loops — never var with closures.
  • Stale closures — use functional updates or dependency arrays in React.
  • React Hooks are closures — understanding closures is essential for React.
  • ES2026's using provides deterministic cleanup for closure-held resources.
  • Chrome DevTools [[Scopes]] — inspect exactly what a closure captures.
  • ESLint no-loop-func — flags closures in loops.
  • Closures are the foundation of JavaScript's programming model — from modules to hooks to functional patterns.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A higher-order function (HOF) is a function that does at least one of the following:

  • Takes one or more functions as arguments (these functions are called callbacks).
  • Returns a function as its result.

That is the complete definition. There is no special syntax — higher-order functions emerge naturally from JavaScript's treatment of functions as first-class values .

// Takes a function as an argument (callback)
[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2);           // [2, 4, 6]

// Returns a function
function createMultiplier(factor) {
    return n => n * factor;
}
const double = createMultiplier(2);
double(5); // 10

// Both — takes a function AND returns a function
function compose(f, g) {
    return x => f(g(x));
}

Higher-order functions are the core abstraction mechanism of functional programming in JavaScript. If you have used map(), filter(), reduce(), setTimeout(), or addEventListener(), you have already been working with higher-order functions — they are the built-in HOFs that ship with every JavaScript environment .

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Higher-order functions exist to solve the repetition problem at a higher level: not repetition of values, but repetition of patterns. Instead of writing the same loop structure, the same validation logic, or the same error-handling wrapper over and over, you extract the pattern into a HOF and pass in the varying behavior as a callback.

They serve as the abstraction layer of JavaScript:

  • Data transformation — map, filter, reduce abstract over iteration.
  • Behavior composition — compose, pipe, curry abstract over function combination.
  • Cross-cutting concerns — logging, timing, retry, and caching wrappers.
  • Configuration — factory functions that produce pre-configured behavior.
  • Event handling — callbacks registered with event systems.

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Functions
├── Function Declarations       ✅ done
├── Function Expressions        ✅ done
├── Arrow Functions             ✅ done
├── Parameters                  ✅ done
├── Rest Parameters             ✅ done
├── Default Parameters          ✅ done
├── Closures                    ✅ done
├── Higher-Order Functions      ← you are here
└── Pure Functions

Higher-Order Functions sit directly after Closures because closures are the mechanism that makes HOFs powerful. Without closures, a function could not return another function that remembers its configuration. The next concept, Pure Functions, describes the functional-programming principle that HOFs most commonly enable.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Every program repeats patterns. A loop that transforms every element. A validation that checks every input. A function call that needs logging before and after. Without higher-order functions, each repetition of a pattern requires copying the structure and changing only the details:

// ❌ Without HOFs — the pattern is duplicated
const doubled = [];
for (const n of numbers) doubled.push(n * 2);

const tripled = [];
for (const n of numbers) tripled.push(n * 3);

const squared = [];
for (const n of numbers) squared.push(n * n);

Three functions, three loops, one pattern. The pattern (iterate, transform, collect) is repeated every time.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation No first-class functions Functions could not be passed as values Manual loops only Every transformation required a hand-written for loop No callbacks Event handling and async required global state No function factories Configuration could not be pre-baked into behavior No composition Multi-step transformations required nested calls No currying Partial application was impossible

docs.title: Why Higher-Order Functions Matter
docs.text:
JavaScript was designed from the beginning with functions as first-class values. This single design decision made higher-order functions not just possible, but fundamental to the language:

  • Array methods — map, filter, reduce, forEach, some, every, find, flatMap are all HOFs.
  • Asynchronous patterns — setTimeout, setInterval, addEventListener, .then(), .catch() all take callbacks.
  • React — hooks (useState, useEffect) and Higher-Order Components are HOF patterns.
  • Express — middleware is a chain of HOFs: app.use((req, res, next) => {}).
  • Functional programming — currying, composition, and partial application are built on HOFs.

docs.title: The 2026 Landscape
docs.text:
In 2026, higher-order functions are Baseline Widely available and remain the primary abstraction tool in JavaScript. However, the landscape has shifted in one important area: JavaScript decorators (Stage 3, shipped in Chrome January 2025) now provide a cleaner syntax for class methods where HOFs were previously used as wrappers. The consensus in 2026 is clear:

Decorators are class-only. For wrapping bare functions, higher-order functions remain the tool. For class methods, decorators are cleaner — they move the wiring to the call site, eliminate manual rebinding, and give you context.name for free .

So the answer in 2026 is not "decorators or HOFs" — it is decorators for class methods, HOFs for everything else.

docs.title: Higher-Order Function That Takes a Callback
docs.text:
function repeat(times, action) {
    for (let i = 0; i < times; i++) {
        action(i);
    }
}

repeat(3, (i) => console.log(`Iteration ${i + 1}`));
// Iteration 1
// Iteration 2
// Iteration 3

docs.title: Higher-Order Function That Returns a Function
docs.text:
function createMultiplier(factor) {
    return function(number) {
        return number * factor;
    };
}

const double = createMultiplier(2);
const triple = createMultiplier(3);

double(5); // 10
triple(5); // 15

docs.title: Higher-Order Function That Does Both
docs.text:
function compose(f, g) {
    return function(x) {
        return f(g(x));
    };
}

const addOne = x => x + 1;
const double = x => x * 2;
const doubleThenAddOne = compose(addOne, double);

doubleThenAddOne(5); // 11 — double(5) = 10, addOne(10) = 11

docs.title: Built-In Higher-Order Functions
docs.text:
// Array.map — transform each element
[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6]

// Array.filter — select elements
[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2 === 0); // [2, 4]

// Array.reduce — accumulate to a single value
[1, 2, 3].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // 6

// Array.forEach — side effects per element
[1, 2, 3].forEach(n => console.log(n));

// Array.some / Array.every — boolean aggregation
[1, 2, 3].some(n => n > 2);  // true
[1, 2, 3].every(n => n > 0); // true

// Array.find — first match
[1, 2, 3].find(n => n > 1); // 2

// Array.flatMap — map then flatten
[1, 2].flatMap(n => [n, n * 2]); // [1, 2, 2, 4]

// Timers and events
setTimeout(() => console.log("later"), 1000);
button.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("clicked"));

// Promises
fetch("/api").then(res => res.json()).catch(err => console.error(err));

docs.title: Function Factory
docs.text:
function createRangeValidator(min, max) {
    return function(value) {
        return value >= min && value <= max;
    };
}

const isValidAge = createRangeValidator(18, 120);
isValidAge(25); // true
isValidAge(15); // false

This is the function factory pattern — a HOF that produces specialized functions. As one 2026 lab puts it: "You'll write createRangeValidator, a higher-order function that accepts min and max parameters and returns a new function. That returned function is a closure: it remembers the bounds from its outer scope and uses them every time it validates a value" .

docs.title: Currying with HOFs
docs.text:
// Uncurried
function add(a, b, c) {
    return a + b + c;
}

// Curried
function curriedAdd(a) {
    return function(b) {
        return function(c) {
            return a + b + c;
        };
    };
}

curriedAdd(1)(2)(3); // 6

// Arrow function currying
const add = a => b => c => a + b + c;

Currying transforms a function with multiple arguments into a chain of single-argument functions. Arguments are accumulated across calls through closures rather than passed together in one invocation, allowing execution to remain deferred until the full input set is available .

docs.title: Partial Application
docs.text:
function partial(fn, ...fixedArgs) {
    return function(...remainingArgs) {
        return fn(...fixedArgs, ...remainingArgs);
    };
}

const add = (a, b, c) => a + b + c;
const add5 = partial(add, 5);
add5(2, 3); // 10

docs.title: Function Composition
docs.text:
// compose — right to left
const compose = (...fns) => x => fns.reduceRight((acc, fn) => fn(acc), x);

// pipe — left to right
const pipe = (...fns) => x => fns.reduce((acc, fn) => fn(acc), x);

const process = pipe(
    x => x * 2,
    x => x + 1,
    x => x.toString()
);

process(5); // "11"

docs.title: Decorator Pattern (HOF-Based)
docs.text:
function withLogging(fn) {
    return function(...args) {
        console.log(`Calling ${fn.name} with`, args);
        const result = fn.apply(this, args);
        console.log(`${fn.name} returned`, result);
        return result;
    };
}

const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const loggedAdd = withLogging(add);
loggedAdd(2, 3);
// "Calling add with [2, 3]"
// "add returned 5"

This decorator pattern — a HOF that wraps a function to add behavior — is the foundation of logging, timing, retry, and caching wrappers in JavaScript .

docs.title: ES2026 Additions Relevant to HOFs
docs.text:
ES2026 adds several methods that work naturally with higher-order functions:

  • Array.fromAsync — the async twin of Array.from, collecting async iterables into arrays.
  • Map.getOrInsert() / getOrInsertComputed() — upsert semantics that eliminate boilerplate key-existence checks.
  • Iterator.concat() — lazily sequence multiple iterators.
  • Math.sumPrecise() — accurate floating-point summation, useful in reduce chains.

These don't change HOF syntax, but they expand the built-in HOF surface available to developers .

docs.title: The "Manager vs. Worker" Mental Model
docs.text:
A higher-order function is a manager; the callback is a worker:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Higher-Order Function           │
│              (Manager)                       │
│                                             │
│  "I control WHEN and HOW the worker runs.   │
│   I decide how many times, with what data,  │
│   and what to do with the results."         │
│                                             │
│              ┌─────────────────────┐        │
│              │  Callback (Worker)  │        │
│              │                     │        │
│              │  "I do the actual   │        │
│              │   work. I don't     │        │
│              │   control the flow."│        │
│              └─────────────────────┘        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

map is the manager — it controls iteration. The callback is the worker — it transforms one element. The manager doesn't know what the transformation is; the worker doesn't know about the loop.

docs.title: The "Assembly Line" Mental Model
docs.text:
HOFs compose like stations on an assembly line:

Input → [filter] → [map] → [reduce] → Output
        │          │        │
        │          │        └── Accumulate to single value
        │          └── Transform each element
        └── Select elements

Each station is a HOF. The data flows through, transformed at each step. This is the pipe/compose pattern — and it is the essence of declarative data processing.

docs.title: The "Function Factory" Mental Model
docs.text:
A HOF that returns a function is a factory:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           createMultiplier(2)                │
│                                             │
│  Input: factor = 2                          │
│                                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Returns: function(number) {        │    │
│  │      return number * 2;  ← captured │    │
│  │  }                                  │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                             │
│  The returned function "remembers" factor   │
│  through closure.                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every function returned by a HOF is a specialized worker with its configuration pre-baked.

docs.title: The "Abstraction Levels" Mental Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Level 3: Composition                        │
│  pipe(validate, transform, save)             │
│                                              │
│  Level 2: Higher-Order Functions             │
│  map, filter, reduce, curry, compose         │
│                                              │
│  Level 1: First-Class Functions              │
│  Functions can be assigned and passed        │
│                                              │
│  Level 0: The Language                       │
│  Syntax, types, control flow                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

You cannot have HOFs without first-class functions. You cannot have composition without HOFs. Each level builds on the one below.

docs.title: The "Declarative vs. Imperative" Mental Model
docs.text:
Imperative (how):                  Declarative (what):
┌─────────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────────┐
│ const result = [];  │           │ const result =      │
│ for (const n of     │           │   numbers           │
│   numbers) {        │           │     .filter(n =>    │
│   if (n % 2 === 0)  │           │       n % 2 === 0)  │
│     result.push(    │           │     .map(n =>       │
│       n * 2);       │           │       n * 2);       │
│ }                   │           │                     │
│                     │           │                     │
│ "Do this, then      │           │ "Give me the even   │
│  that, then that."  │           │  numbers, doubled." │
└─────────────────────┘           └─────────────────────┘

HOFs let you say what you want, not how to compute it.

docs.title: Concept 1: First-Class Functions
docs.text:
Higher-order functions are only possible because JavaScript treats functions as first-class values — they can be:

  • Assigned to variables.
  • Passed as arguments.
  • Returned from functions.
  • Stored in data structures.
const fn = x => x * 2;        // assigned
[1, 2, 3].map(fn);             // passed
function make() { return fn; } // returned
const ops = { double: fn };    // stored

docs.title: Concept 2: Callbacks
docs.text:
A callback is a function passed to another function to be called later. The function that accepts the callback is the higher-order function.

function repeat(n, callback) {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) callback(i);
}

Callbacks are the most common form of HOF usage.

docs.title: Concept 3: Function Factories
docs.text:
A function factory is a HOF that returns a new function, pre-configured with captured values:

function createLogger(prefix) {
    return (message) => console.log(`[${prefix}] ${message}`);
}

const info = createLogger("INFO");
const error = createLogger("ERROR");

Factories are the return-function form of HOFs.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Built-In HOFs
docs.text:
JavaScript ships with a rich set of built-in higher-order functions:

HOF Purpose Returns map Transform each element New array filter Select elements New array reduce Accumulate to single value Any forEach Side effects per element undefined some Any element matches? Boolean every All elements match? Boolean find First match Element or undefined findIndex Index of first match Number flatMap Map then flatten New array sort Order elements Mutated array setTimeout Delayed execution Timer ID addEventListener Event handling — .then() / .catch() Promise chaining Promise

docs.title: Concept 5: Currying
docs.text:
Currying transforms a function with multiple arguments into a chain of single-argument functions:

const add = a => b => c => a + b + c;
add(1)(2)(3); // 6

Arguments are accumulated across calls through closures rather than passed together in one invocation .

docs.title: Concept 6: Partial Application
docs.text:
Partial application fixes some arguments of a function, producing a new function that accepts the rest:

function partial(fn, ...fixed) {
    return (...rest) => fn(...fixed, ...rest);
}

Currying is a special case of partial application — one argument at a time.

docs.title: Concept 7: Function Composition
docs.text:
Composition combines multiple functions into one, where the output of each becomes the input of the next:

const compose = (...fns) => x => fns.reduceRight((acc, fn) => fn(acc), x);
const pipe = (...fns) => x => fns.reduce((acc, fn) => fn(acc), x);
  • compose — right to left (mathematical convention).
  • pipe — left to right (Unix pipeline convention).

docs.title: Concept 8: The Decorator Pattern
docs.text:
A decorator is a HOF that wraps a function to add behavior without modifying the original:

const withTiming = (fn) => (...args) => {
    const start = performance.now();
    const result = fn(...args);
    console.log(`${fn.name}: ${performance.now() - start}ms`);
    return result;
};

Common decorators: logging, timing, retry, caching, authentication, rate limiting.

docs.title: Concept 9: HOFs and Closures
docs.text:
Higher-order functions return closures. When a HOF returns a function, that function captures the HOF's variables:

function createCounter() {
    let count = 0;            // captured by the returned function
    return () => ++count;
}

Without closures, returned functions could not remember their configuration.

docs.title: Concept 10: Async HOFs
docs.text:
Higher-order functions work with async code:

// async callback
await Promise.all(urls.map(async (url) => {
    const res = await fetch(url);
    return res.json();
}));

// HOF that returns an async function
function withRetry(fn, maxAttempts = 3) {
    return async (...args) => {
        for (let i = 1; i <= maxAttempts; i++) {
            try { return await fn(...args); }
            catch (err) { if (i === maxAttempts) throw err; }
        }
    };
}

docs.title: Concept 11: some and every Are Short-Circuiting HOFs
docs.text:
Unlike filter().length > 0, some and every can stop as soon as the answer is known:

// ❌ Iterates the entire array
if (arr.filter(x => x > 10).length > 0) { }

// ✅ Stops at the first match
if (arr.some(x => x > 10)) { }

This is a significant performance win for large arrays .

docs.title: Concept 12: reduce Can Replace map + filter
docs.text:
For large datasets, chaining map and filter creates intermediate arrays. A single reduce avoids them:

// ❌ Creates two intermediate arrays
const result = numbers
    .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)
    .map(n => n * 2);

// ✅ Single pass, no intermediates
const result = numbers.reduce((acc, n) => {
    if (n % 2 === 0) acc.push(n * 2);
    return acc;
}, []);

docs.title: Concept 13: Higher-Order Components (React)
docs.text:
In React, a Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component:

function withAuth(Component) {
    return function AuthenticatedComponent(props) {
        const user = useAuth();
        if (!user) return <Login />;
        return <Component {...props} user={user} />;
    };
}

HOCs are the React manifestation of the HOF pattern.

docs.title: Concept 14: Decorators vs. HOFs (2026)
docs.text:
JavaScript decorators (Stage 3, shipped in Chrome January 2025) provide a cleaner syntax for class methods where HOF wrappers were previously used:

// HOF wrapper (still valid for bare functions)
const withLogging = (fn) => (...args) => {
    console.log(`→ ${fn.name}`, args);
    return fn(...args);
};

// Decorator (cleaner for class methods)
function log(originalMethod, context) {
    return function (...args) {
        console.log(`→ ${String(context.name)}`, args);
        return originalMethod.call(this, ...args);
    };
}

class UserService {
    @log
    fetchUser(id) { /* ... */ }
}

The key 2026 guidance: decorators are class-only. For bare functions, HOFs remain the tool .

docs.title: Concept 15: HOFs and Immutability
docs.text:
HOFs like map, filter, and reduce do not mutate the original array — they return new arrays. This makes them the foundation of immutable data transformation:

const original = [1, 2, 3];
const doubled = original.map(n => n * 2);
console.log(original); // [1, 2, 3] — unchanged

docs.title: Concept 16: Performance — Function Call Overhead
docs.text: Higher-order functions introduce function call overhead. In V8, JIT techniques inline higher-order calls and specialize them based on runtime types, achieving up to 2–5× speedups for functional workloads over interpreted execution . However, for hot paths, curried style is ergonomics, not a zero-cost abstraction — prefer uncurried functions when performance matters .

docs.title: Concept 17: HOFs and this
docs.text:
When passing methods as callbacks, this may be lost:

// ❌ `this` is undefined inside handleClick
button.addEventListener("click", this.handleClick);

// ✅ Bind or use arrow function
button.addEventListener("click", this.handleClick.bind(this));
button.addEventListener("click", () => this.handleClick());

In 2026, most code uses arrow functions which do not bind this — if your callback relies on this, you need explicit binding .

docs.title: Concept 18: ES2026 HOF-Relevant Additions
docs.text:
ES2026 adds methods that complement HOF patterns:

  • Array.fromAsync — collect async iterables into arrays.
  • Map.getOrInsert() — upsert during iteration without extra lookups.
  • Iterator.concat() — sequence multiple iterators lazily.
  • Math.sumPrecise() — accurate summation, useful in reduce.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: HOF with Callback
docs.text:
1.  HOF is called with a callback argument.
    │
    ▼
2.  HOF's execution context is created.
    │
    ▼
3.  The callback is bound as a local parameter.
    │
    ▼
4.  HOF executes its logic (e.g., iterates over an array).
    │
    ▼
5.  For each element, HOF invokes the callback.
    │
    ▼
6.  Callback's return value is used by the HOF.
    │
    ▼
7.  HOF returns its result.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: HOF Returning a Function
docs.text:
1.  HOF is called with configuration arguments.
    │
    ▼
2.  HOF's execution context is created.
    │
    ▼
3.  A new function is created inside the HOF.
    │
    ▼
4.  The new function's [[Environment]] captures the HOF's scope.
    │
    ▼
5.  HOF returns the new function.
    │
    ▼
6.  HOF's execution context is destroyed — but the environment
    │   is kept alive by the returned function's [[Environment]].
    │
    ▼
7.  When the returned function is called, it accesses
    │   the captured configuration variables.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: map Internals (Simplified)
docs.text:
1.  Create a new empty array.
    │
    ▼
2.  For each index i in the source array:
    │   - Call the callback with (element, i, sourceArray).
    │   - Push the callback's return value to the new array.
    │
    ▼
3.  Return the new array.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: compose Evaluation
docs.text:
compose(f, g)(x)
    │
    ▼
1.  compose is called with f and g.
    │
    ▼
2.  Returns a function that calls f(g(x)).
    │
    ▼
3.  When called with x:
    │   a. g(x) is evaluated first.
    │   b. f is called with the result.
    │
    ▼
4.  The final result is returned.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Currying Execution
docs.text:
curriedAdd(1)(2)(3)
    │
    ▼
1.  curriedAdd(1) returns a function that captures a = 1.
    │
    ▼
2.  That function is called with (2) — returns a function
    │   that captures b = 2.
    │
    ▼
3.  That function is called with (3) — now a, b, c are all
    │   available; the original logic executes.
    │
    ▼
4.  Returns 6.

docs.title: First-Class Functions in the Spec
docs.text:
Functions are objects in ECMAScript. They have a [[Call]] internal method and can be:

  • Assigned to bindings.
  • Passed as arguments.
  • Returned as values.
  • Stored in properties.

This is what makes HOFs possible — the language has no special "HOF" feature; HOFs are a consequence of first-class functions.

docs.title: The [[Environment]] Slot
docs.text:
When a HOF returns a function, that function's [[Environment]] slot captures the HOF's lexical environment. This is how returned functions remember their configuration:

createMultiplier(2)
    │
    ▼
Returns function(number) { return number * 2; }
    │
    ▼
The returned function's [[Environment]] → createMultiplier's scope
    │
    ▼
`factor` is still alive in that scope

docs.title: V8 Optimizations for HOFs
docs.text:
V8's TurboFan compiler applies several optimizations to HOFs:

  1. Inlining — small callbacks are inlined at the call site.
  2. Specialization — the JIT specializes based on observed callback types.
  3. Escape analysis — if a returned function does not escape, it can be stack-allocated.
  4. Feedback vectors — type feedback drives speculative optimization.

V8 achieves up to 2–5× speedups for functional workloads over interpreted execution .

docs.title: Why Curried Functions Are Not Free
docs.text:
A curried function requires one function call per argument:

curriedAdd(1)(2)(3)  // 3 function calls
add(1, 2, 3)         // 1 function call

Each call creates a new execution context and a new closure. For hot paths, the uncurried version is strictly cheaper unless everything gets inlined and optimized away. As one Stack Overflow answer puts it: "curried style in JS is ergonomics, not a zero-cost abstraction" .

docs.title: The Call Stack and HOFs
docs.text: Each callback invocation pushes a new frame onto the call stack. Deeply nested HOF chains (compose with many functions, recursive reduce) can exhaust the stack.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
HOF Returned Function:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [[Call]]           → bytecode      │
│  [[Environment]]    → ──────────────┼──▶ HOF's scope
│  [[FormalParameters]] → [number]    │       │
│  [[FunctionBody]]   → AST           │       ▼
│  name               → ""            │   Environment Record
└─────────────────────────────────────┘       │
                                              ├── factor: 2
                                              └── ...

docs.title: Performance in the JIT
docs.text:
• Inlining — V8 inlines small callbacks.
  • Monomorphic call sites — same callback type at a site → optimized.
  • Polymorphic/megamorphic sites — different callback types → deoptimization.
  • Closure allocation — each returned function allocates a context.

docs.title: HOF with Callback Lifecycle
docs.text:
HOF called → Callback bound → HOF iterates → Callback invoked per element
    → Results collected → HOF returns → Callback released

docs.title: Function Factory Lifecycle
docs.text:
Factory called → Configuration captured → New function created
    → New function returned → Factory context destroyed
    → Returned function holds environment → Called → Uses captured config

docs.title: Composition Lifecycle
docs.text:
compose(f, g, h) called → Returns composed function
    → Composed function called with x
    → h(x) → g(result) → f(result) → Final result

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write repetitive pattern
    │
    ▼
Identify the varying behavior
    │
    ▼
Extract the pattern into a HOF
    │
    ▼
Pass the varying behavior as a callback
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint prefer-arrow-callback, no-loop-func)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript)
    │
    ▼
Run / Test

docs.title: Choosing the Right HOF Workflow
docs.text:
Need to transform every element?     → map
Need to select some elements?        → filter
Need a single value from elements?   → reduce
Need side effects per element?       → forEach
Need a boolean from elements?        → some / every
Need the first match?                → find
Need to flatten after mapping?       → flatMap
Need to pre-configure behavior?      → factory function
Need to combine functions?           → compose / pipe
Need one argument at a time?         → curry
Need to add behavior to a function?  → decorator HOF
Need to add behavior to a class method? → decorator (2026)

docs.title: Example 1: Custom map
docs.text:
function map(array, transform) {
    const result = [];
    for (const item of array) {
        result.push(transform(item));
    }
    return result;
}

map([1, 2, 3], n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6]

Breakdown:

  • map is the HOF — it controls iteration.
  • transform is the callback — it does the work.

docs.title: Example 2: Custom filter
docs.text:
function filter(array, predicate) {
    const result = [];
    for (const item of array) {
        if (predicate(item)) result.push(item);
    }
    return result;
}

filter([1, 2, 3, 4], n => n % 2 === 0); // [2, 4]

docs.title: Example 3: Function Factory
docs.text:
function createRangeValidator(min, max) {
    return function(value) {
        return value >= min && value <= max;
    };
}

const isValidPrice = createRangeValidator(0.01, 9999.99);
const isValidAge = createRangeValidator(18, 120);

isValidPrice(50);  // true
isValidAge(15);    // false

Breakdown:

  • createRangeValidator is the factory.
  • Each returned validator captures its own min and max.

docs.title: Example 4: Currying
docs.text:
const curry = (fn) => {
    return function curried(...args) {
        if (args.length >= fn.length) {
            return fn(...args);
        }
        return (...next) => curried(...args, ...next);
    };
};

const add = (a, b, c) => a + b + c;
const curriedAdd = curry(add);

curriedAdd(1)(2)(3); // 6
curriedAdd(1, 2)(3); // 6
curriedAdd(1)(2, 3); // 6

docs.title: Example 5: Composition with pipe
docs.text:
const pipe = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduce((acc, fn) => fn(acc), x);

const processUser = pipe(
    user => ({ ...user, name: user.name.trim() }),
    user => ({ ...user, name: user.name.toUpperCase() }),
    user => ({ ...user, active: true })
);

processUser({ name: "  ada  ", age: 36 });
// { name: "ADA", age: 36, active: true }

docs.title: Example 6: Logging Decorator
docs.text:
const withLogging = (fn) => (...args) => {
    console.log(`Calling ${fn.name} with`, args);
    const result = fn(...args);
    console.log(`${fn.name} returned`, result);
    return result;
};

const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const loggedAdd = withLogging(add);
loggedAdd(2, 3);
// "Calling add with [2, 3]"
// "add returned 5"

docs.title: Example 7: Retry Decorator
docs.text:
function withRetry(fn, maxAttempts = 3) {
    return async (...args) => {
        for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
            try {
                return await fn(...args);
            } catch (err) {
                if (attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
                await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 2 ** attempt * 100));
            }
        }
    };
}

const fetchWithRetry = withRetry(fetch);
await fetchWithRetry("/api/data");

docs.title: Example 8: some vs. filter
docs.text:
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

// ❌ Iterates the entire array
const hasLarge = numbers.filter(n => n > 4).length > 0;

// ✅ Stops at the first match
const hasLarge = numbers.some(n => n > 4);

Breakdown:

  • some short-circuits — it stops as soon as the predicate returns true.
  • For large arrays, this is a significant performance win .

docs.title: Example 9: Single reduce Instead of Chained map + filter
docs.text:
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

// ❌ Two passes, two intermediate arrays
const result = numbers
    .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)
    .map(n => n * 2);

// ✅ One pass, no intermediates
const result = numbers.reduce((acc, n) => {
    if (n % 2 === 0) acc.push(n * 2);
    return acc;
}, []);

docs.title: Example 10: HOF with Async Callback
docs.text:
async function processUrls(urls) {
    return Promise.all(urls.map(async (url) => {
        const res = await fetch(url);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return res.json();
    }));
}

Breakdown:

  • map is the HOF.
  • The async arrow function is the callback.
  • Promise.all collects the results.

docs.title: Example 11: React Higher-Order Component
docs.text:
function withAuth(Component) {
    return function AuthenticatedComponent(props) {
        const { user } = useAuth();
        if (!user) return <Login />;
        return <Component {...props} user={user} />;
    };
}

const ProtectedDashboard = withAuth(Dashboard);

docs.title: Example 12: Decorator for Class Methods (2026)
docs.text:
function log(originalMethod, context) {
    return function (...args) {
        console.log(`→ ${String(context.name)}`, args);
        const result = originalMethod.call(this, ...args);
        console.log(`← ${String(context.name)}`, result);
        return result;
    };
}

class UserService {
    @log
    fetchUser(id) {
        return { id, name: "Ada" };
    }
}

Breakdown:

  • Decorators are the cleaner 2026 alternative for class methods .
  • For bare functions, HOFs remain the tool.

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario HOF Pattern Transform array elements map Select array elements filter Accumulate to single value reduce Side effects per element forEach Boolean aggregation some / every Find first match find / findIndex Flatten after mapping flatMap Pre-configure behavior Factory function Combine functions compose / pipe Partial application curry / partial Add logging/timing Decorator HOF Add retry logic Decorator HOF Cache results Memoization HOF Event handling addEventListener Async iteration map + Promise.all React component enhancement Higher-Order Component

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use named callbacks for testability. Why: named functions are easier to test and debug.
  2. Use some / every instead of filter().length. Why: they short-circuit and are faster .
  3. Use a single reduce instead of chained map + filter for large data. Why: avoids intermediate arrays.
  4. Keep callbacks pure when possible. Why: pure callbacks are easier to reason about and test.
  5. Use arrow functions for simple callbacks. Why: concise and lexical this.
  6. Bind or arrow-wrap methods passed as callbacks. Why: prevents this loss .
  7. Use function factories for reusable configuration. Why: eliminates duplication .
  8. Use compose / pipe for multi-step transformations. Why: declarative and readable.
  9. Use currying for partial application. Why: creates specialized functions from general ones.
  10. Use decorator HOFs for cross-cutting concerns. Why: logging, timing, retry, and caching without modifying the original.
  11. Use decorators for class methods in 2026. Why: cleaner syntax, no manual rebinding .
  12. Prefer uncurried functions in hot paths. Why: currying is ergonomics, not zero-cost .
  13. Avoid creating HOFs in hot loops. Why: each iteration creates a new closure.
  14. Document the callback contract. Why: callers need to know the expected signature.
  15. Use TypeScript generics for type-safe HOFs. Why: catches type errors at compile time.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Calling the Callback Instead of Passing It
docs.text:
[1, 2, 3].map(double()); // ❌ double() is called immediately

✅ Correct:

[1, 2, 3].map(double); // ✅ pass the function reference

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Losing this in Callbacks
docs.text:
button.addEventListener("click", this.handleClick); // ❌ `this` is undefined

✅ Correct:

button.addEventListener("click", this.handleClick.bind(this));
button.addEventListener("click", () => this.handleClick());

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using filter().length for Existence Checks
docs.text:
if (arr.filter(x => x > 10).length > 0) { } // ❌ iterates entire array

✅ Correct:

if (arr.some(x => x > 10)) { } // ✅ short-circuits

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Chaining map + filter on Large Arrays
docs.text:
const result = hugeArray.filter(pred).map(transform); // ❌ two passes

✅ Correct:

const result = hugeArray.reduce((acc, x) => {
    if (pred(x)) acc.push(transform(x));
    return acc;
}, []);

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Mutating the Source Array in a Callback
docs.text:
arr.map((item, i) => { arr[i] = item * 2; return item; }); // ❌ mutates source

✅ Correct:

const doubled = arr.map(item => item * 2); // ✅ returns new array

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming forEach Returns a Value
docs.text:
const result = [1, 2, 3].forEach(n => n * 2); // ❌ result is undefined

✅ Correct:

const result = [1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2); // ✅ map returns a new array

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Currying in Hot Paths
docs.text:
// ❌ 3 function calls per invocation
const add = a => b => c => a + b + c;

✅ Correct:

// ✅ 1 function call — use currying for ergonomics, not hot paths
const add = (a, b, c) => a + b + c;

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Ignoring Async Errors in HOF Callbacks
docs.text:
urls.map(async (url) => { await fetch(url); }); // ❌ unhandled rejections

✅ Correct:

await Promise.all(urls.map(async (url) => {
    try { await fetch(url); }
    catch (err) { console.error(err); }
}));

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Using HOFs for Fixed-Arity Logic
docs.text:
[1, 2, 3].forEach(n => { if (n === 2) return; process(n); });

✅ Correct: Use a for...of loop when you need break or continue.

docs.title: ❌ Mistake: Assuming Decorators Replace All HOFs
docs.text:
Why it's wrong: Decorators are class-only — they cannot wrap bare functions .

✅ Correct: Use decorators for class methods, HOFs for everything else.

docs.title: 13. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Function call overhead — each callback invocation pushes a stack frame.
  • JIT inlining — V8 inlines small callbacks at monomorphic call sites.
  • 2–5× speedup — V8 achieves this for functional workloads over interpreted execution .
  • Currying overhead — one function call per argument; not free .
  • Intermediate arrays — chained map + filter creates extra arrays.
  • Short-circuiting — some and every stop early .
  • Closure allocation — each returned function allocates a context.
  • Megamorphic call sites — different callback types at the same site cause deoptimization.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use some/every instead of filter().length.
  2. Use a single reduce instead of chained map + filter.
  3. Keep callbacks monomorphic — same type at the same call site.
  4. Avoid currying in hot paths.
  5. Avoid creating HOFs in hot loops.
  6. Profile with --trace-opt / --trace-deopt.

docs.title: Callback Injection
docs.text:
Untrusted input should never be used as a callback function. If user input is passed to eval or new Function to create a callback, it is an injection sink.

Defense: Never construct callbacks from untrusted input.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution via HOFs
docs.text:
HOFs that iterate over object properties can be affected by prototype pollution.

Defense: Use Object.hasOwn() or Object.keys() to iterate own properties only.

docs.title: ReDoS in Callbacks
docs.text:
Regular expressions used inside HOF callbacks can cause catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS).

Defense: Use safe-regex tools; limit input length.

docs.title: Unbounded Callback Chains
docs.text:
Chaining many HOFs (e.g., deep compose) can cause stack overflow — a potential DoS vector.

Defense: Limit composition depth; use iterative approaches for unbounded chains.

docs.title: Memory Exhaustion
docs.text:
HOFs that accumulate results (e.g., map on a huge array) can exhaust memory.

Defense: Use lazy iterators or reduce with early termination.

docs.title: this Binding Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Losing this in a callback can lead to unexpected behavior — e.g., a logging function that writes to the wrong object.

Defense: Bind or arrow-wrap methods passed as callbacks.

docs.title: 15. Debugging Tips
docs.text:
• console.log inside the callback — verify it is called with expected arguments.
  • Named callbacks — easier to find in stack traces.
  • debugger; — pause inside the callback.
  • Chrome DevTools Sources panel — set breakpoints on callback invocations.
  • console.trace() — see the call stack from inside a callback.
  • ESLint no-loop-func — flags closures in loops.
  • TypeScript — catches callback signature mismatches.
  • Check fn.name — verify the right function is passed.

docs.title: 16. When to Use
docs.text: Scenario Use HOF? Array transformation ✅ Yes (map) Array filtering ✅ Yes (filter) Array aggregation ✅ Yes (reduce) Short-circuit existence check ✅ Yes (some/every) Pre-configured behavior ✅ Yes (factory) Function composition ✅ Yes (compose/pipe) Partial application ✅ Yes (curry) Cross-cutting concerns ✅ Yes (decorator HOF) Class method enhancement ⚠️ Prefer decorators (2026) Fixed-arity logic with break ❌ Use for...of Hot-path numeric computation ❌ Use uncurried functions

docs.title: 17. When Not to Use
docs.text:
• When break or continue is needed — use for...of.
  • When the callback is called immediately — pass the function reference, not the call.
  • When the pattern is used once — a HOF adds indirection without reuse.
  • In hot paths where currying adds overhead — use uncurried functions.
  • When a class method is the target — decorators are cleaner in 2026.
  • When the abstraction obscures intent — readability wins.
  • When the callback has side effects on the source array — use a pure transformation.

docs.title: 18. Related Concepts
docs.text:
• First-Class Functions — the foundation of HOFs
  • Closures — the mechanism that makes returned functions remember
  • Pure Functions — the functional principle HOFs enable
  • Callbacks — the function passed to a HOF
  • Array Methods — map, filter, reduce, forEach, some, every
  • Currying — transforming multi-arg functions into chains
  • Partial Application — fixing some arguments
  • Function Composition — compose and pipe
  • Decorator Pattern — wrapping functions to add behavior
  • JavaScript Decorators — the 2026 class-method alternative
  • Higher-Order Components — React's HOF pattern
  • Memoization — caching via HOF
  • Retry Pattern — async HOF for resilience
  • ES2026 Map.getOrInsert — upsert for iteration
  • ES2026 Array.fromAsync — async iteration collection

docs.title: 19. Did You Know?
docs.text:
• map, filter, and reduce are all higher-order functions — they take callbacks.
  • setTimeout and addEventListener are higher-order functions — they take callbacks .
  • Higher-order functions are not a special syntax — they emerge from first-class functions.
  • Currying is named after Haskell Curry — the mathematician and logician.
  • compose is right-to-left; pipe is left-to-right — both are HOFs.
  • V8 achieves 2–5× speedups for functional workloads over interpreted execution .
  • some and every short-circuit — filter().length does not .
  • Currying is not free — one function call per argument .
  • JavaScript decorators shipped in Chrome January 2025 — they are class-only .
  • For bare functions, HOFs remain the tool in 2026 — don't wait for function decorators .
  • Higher-Order Components (HOCs) are React's HOF pattern.
  • React hooks are closures, not HOFs — but they compose like HOFs.
  • A single reduce can replace map + filter — avoiding intermediate arrays.
  • ES2026 adds Array.fromAsync and Map.getOrInsert — new built-in HOF-compatible methods.
  • The "Manager vs. Worker" analogy is a common way to explain HOFs .

docs.title: 20. Summary
docs.text:
• A higher-order function is a function that takes a function as an argument, returns a function, or both.
  • HOFs are possible because JavaScript treats functions as first-class values.
  • Callbacks are functions passed to HOFs — the most common form.
  • Function factories are HOFs that return pre-configured functions.
  • Built-in HOFs: map, filter, reduce, forEach, some, every, find, flatMap, setTimeout, addEventListener.
  • Currying transforms multi-arg functions into chains of single-arg functions.
  • Partial application fixes some arguments of a function.
  • Composition (compose/pipe) combines functions into pipelines.
  • Decorator HOFs wrap functions to add logging, timing, retry, or caching.
  • Decorators (2026) are class-only — use HOFs for bare functions.
  • some/every short-circuit — prefer them over filter().length.
  • A single reduce avoids intermediate arrays from chained map + filter.
  • Currying is ergonomics, not zero-cost — prefer uncurried in hot paths.
  • V8 inlines and specializes HOF callbacks for performance.
  • Bind or arrow-wrap methods passed as callbacks to preserve this.
  • HOFs are the core abstraction mechanism of functional JavaScript.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A pure function is a function that satisfies two fundamental properties:

  1. Deterministic — Given the same input arguments, it always returns the same output.
  2. No observable side effects — It does not modify any state outside its own scope, and it does not depend on any external mutable state.
// ✅ Pure — deterministic, no side effects
function add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

// ✅ Pure — returns a new object, does not mutate the input
function formatUser(user) {
    return {
        displayName: `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`,
        initials: `${user.firstName[0]}${user.lastName[0]}`,
    };
}

A pure function is a mathematical function in the truest sense. It is a mapping from inputs to outputs with no other effects. The same input always produces the same output — no exceptions, no surprises.

In the ECMAScript specification, there is no pure keyword. Purity is a convention and a discipline, not a language feature. It emerges from how you write the function, not from any syntax. The language does not enforce purity — the developer does.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Pure functions exist to solve the predictability problem in software. Impure functions — those that depend on external state or cause side effects — are the source of the most insidious bugs in JavaScript. A function that reads from a global variable, mutates its arguments, or calls Math.random() cannot be reasoned about in isolation. Its behavior depends on when it is called and what the state of the world is at that moment.

Pure functions eliminate this class of bug entirely:

  • Deterministic — the output depends only on the input.
  • Testable — no mocking, no setup, no teardown. Just input → output.
  • Composable — pure functions can be freely combined without worrying about hidden dependencies.
  • Cacheable — since the same input always produces the same output, results can be memoized.
  • Parallelizable — pure functions have no shared state, so they can run concurrently without race conditions.
  • Referentially transparent — any call to a pure function can be replaced by its return value without changing the program's behavior.

As one 2026 guide puts it: "Pure functions are stable, consistent, and predictable. Given the same parameters, pure functions will always return the same result".

docs.title: Where It Fits
docs.text:
Functions
├── Function Declarations       ✅ done
├── Function Expressions        ✅ done
├── Arrow Functions             ✅ done
├── Parameters                  ✅ done
├── Rest Parameters             ✅ done
├── Default Parameters          ✅ done
├── Closures                    ✅ done
├── Higher-Order Functions      ✅ done
├── Pure Functions              ← you are here

Pure Functions are the final concept in the Functions section. They sit at the end because they represent the culmination of functional programming principles — the ideal that higher-order functions, closures, and immutability all point toward. The next section is Objects.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Every non-trivial program needs to change state. It reads user input, fetches data, writes to the DOM, updates a database, and logs messages. These are side effects — interactions with the world outside the function. Without them, a program could compute but not do anything.

But side effects are dangerous. A function that modifies a global variable can break another function that depends on that variable. A function that mutates its argument can corrupt the caller's data. A function that reads Date.now() returns different results on every call, making it impossible to test deterministically.

The problem is not side effects themselves — they are necessary. The problem is side effects that are hidden inside functions that pretend to be pure. When a function's signature says (a, b) => a + b but the body also writes to localStorage, the caller has no way to know. The function is lying about what it does.

docs.title: Previous Limitations
docs.text: Era Limitation No pure function concept All functions could have hidden side effects No immutability Arrays and objects were mutated in place No functional programming State was modified everywhere No memoization Caching required global objects No referential transparency Functions could not be replaced by their values No test isolation Every test required mocking external state

docs.title: Why Pure Functions Matter
docs.text:
Pure functions are the foundation of functional programming in JavaScript. They are what make the following possible:

  • React — React assumes every component is a pure function. "By strictly only writing your components as pure functions, you can avoid an entire class of baffling bugs and unpredictable behavior as your codebase grows".
  • Redux — Redux reducers must be pure functions. "The reducer does not perform side effects... does not call non-pure functions (like Date.now or Math.random)... does not mutate its arguments".
  • Memoization — caching only works for pure functions. Impure functions produce different results for the same input.
  • Testing — pure functions are trivial to test. No mocking, no setup, no teardown. Just given A → expect B.

As the Syncfusion guide states: "Pure functions are readable because of independent behavior. Moreover, they are straightforward to debug".

docs.title: The 2026 Consensus
docs.text:
In 2026, the consensus is clear: pure functions are the default for business logic; side effects should be pushed to the edges of the application. As one modern JavaScript guide puts it: "Copy instead of mutating. Keep transforms pure, push I/O to the edge".

This does not mean every function must be pure. It means that the core of your application should be pure, and the impure shell that interacts with the outside world should be as thin as possible.

docs.title: Pure Function — Deterministic, No Side Effects
docs.text:
// ✅ Pure — same input, same output, no side effects
function add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

function formatName(first, last) {
    return `${first} ${last}`;
}

function filterEvens(numbers) {
    return numbers.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);
}

docs.title: Impure Function — External State
docs.text:
// ❌ Impure — depends on external variable
let counter = 0;

function increment() {
    return ++counter; // modifies external state
}

// ❌ Impure — non-deterministic
function randomPick(arr) {
    return arr[Math.floor(Math.random() * arr.length)];
}

// ❌ Impure — side effect (I/O)
function saveUser(user) {
    localStorage.setItem("user", JSON.stringify(user));
}

docs.title: Impure Function — Mutating Arguments
docs.text:
// ❌ Impure — mutates the input array
function addItem(cart, item) {
    cart.push(item);
    return cart;
}

// ✅ Pure — returns a new array
function addItem(cart, item) {
    return [...cart, item];
}

// ❌ Impure — mutates the input object
function setActive(user) {
    user.active = true;
    return user;
}

// ✅ Pure — returns a new object
function setActive(user) {
    return { ...user, active: true };
}

docs.title: Pure Function — Non-Mutating Array Operations
docs.text:
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

const withSix = [...nums, 6];           // append
const withZero = [0, ...nums];          // prepend
const withoutThree = nums.filter(n => n !== 3); // remove by value
const withoutSecond = nums.toSpliced(1, 1);     // remove by index (ES2023)
const updated = nums.with(2, 99);       // replace at index (ES2023)
const sorted = nums.toSorted((a, b) => b - a);  // sort (ES2023)
const reversed = nums.toReversed();     // reverse (ES2023)

ES2023 added toSorted, toReversed, with, and toSpliced — non-mutating versions of the classic array methods.

docs.title: Pure Function — Non-Mutating Object Updates
docs.text:
const user = { name: "Alice", age: 30, address: { city: "NYC" } };

const older = { ...user, age: 31 };                          // update property
const withZip = { ...user, address: { ...user.address, zip: "10001" } }; // nested update
const { age, ...userWithoutAge } = user;                     // remove property
const clone = structuredClone(user);                         // deep clone

docs.title: Purifying Impure Functions — Dependency Injection
docs.text:
// ❌ Impure — depends on Date.now()
function isExpired(token) {
    return token.expiresAt < Date.now();
}

// ✅ Pure — time is injected
function isExpired(token, now) {
    return token.expiresAt < now;
}
isExpired(token, Date.now()); // caller provides the time

// ❌ Impure — depends on Math.random()
function shuffle(array) {
    return array.toSorted(() => Math.random() - 0.5);
}

// ✅ Pure — randomness is injected
function shuffle(array, random = Math.random) {
    return array.toSorted(() => random() - 0.5);
}

This dependency injection pattern purifies the function by making its dependencies explicit.

docs.title: Pure Function with Closure — Capturing Constants
docs.text:
// ✅ Pure — `PI` is a constant, never changes
const PI = 3.14159;
const circleArea = (radius) => PI * radius * radius;

A closure over a constant is still pure — the captured variable never changes. A closure over a mutable variable is impure.

docs.title: Pure Function with Destructuring
docs.text:
// ✅ Pure — destructures input, returns new object
function processOrder({ items, taxRate = 0.1 }) {
    const subtotal = items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0);
    return {
        subtotal,
        tax: subtotal * taxRate,
        total: subtotal * (1 + taxRate),
    };
}

docs.title: Pure Function with Rest Parameters
docs.text:
// ✅ Pure — collects args, returns new array
function sortNumbers(...numbers) {
    return [...numbers].sort((a, b) => a - b);
}

docs.title: The "Mathematical Function" Mental Model
docs.text:
A pure function is a mathematical function. Think of y = 2x:

x = 2  →  y = 4     (always)
x = 3  →  y = 6     (always)
x = 3  →  y = 6     (still — not 9, not -1, not 2.5)

There is no hidden state. There is no time dependency. There is no randomness. The output is completely determined by the input.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           Pure Function                      │
│                                             │
│  Input ──────▶ [ f(x) ] ──────▶ Output      │
│                                             │
│  No external reads                          │
│  No external writes                         │
│  No randomness                              │
│  No time dependency                         │
│                                             │
│  Same input → Same output, always.          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The "Reference Transparency" Mental Model
docs.text:
Referential transparency means you can replace a function call with its return value without changing the program:

const result = add(2, 3); // add(2, 3) can be replaced with 5
// The program behaves identically whether you call add(2, 3) or write 5

This is the defining property of pure functions. If you can substitute the function call with the value it returns and nothing breaks, the function is pure.

docs.title: The "Boundary" Mental Model
docs.text:
Pure functions live in the core; impure functions live at the boundaries:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Application                        │
│                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │           Impure Boundary                    │   │
│  │  (I/O, network, DOM, database, time, random) │   │
│  │                                             │   │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐    │   │
│  │  │         Pure Core                    │    │   │
│  │  │                                     │    │   │
│  │  │  Business logic, calculations,       │    │   │
│  │  │  transformations, validation         │    │   │
│  │  │                                     │    │   │
│  │  │  ✅ Deterministic                    │    │   │
│  │  │  ✅ No side effects                  │    │   │
│  │  │  ✅ Referentially transparent        │    │   │
│  │  │  ✅ Testable without mocks           │    │   │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────┘    │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Push side effects to the edges. Keep the core pure.

docs.title: The "Testability" Mental Model
docs.text:
Pure functions are trivial to test. Impure functions require mocking, setup, and teardown:

Pure Function Test:                 Impure Function Test:
┌─────────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────────┐
│ expect(add(2, 3))   │            │ jest.mock("fs")     │
│   .toBe(5);         │            │ jest.mock("crypto") │
│                     │            │ jest.mock("Date")   │
│ Done.               │            │                     │
│                     │            │ const result =      │
│ No mocks.           │            │   processFile(...); │
│ No setup.           │            │                     │
│ No teardown.        │            │ expect(result)...   │
│                     │            │                     │
│                     │            │ Done.               │
│                     │            │ (if the mocks work) │
└─────────────────────┘            └─────────────────────┘

As one source puts it: "The code's definitely easier to test. We don't need to mock anything".

docs.title: The "Immutable Data" Mental Model
docs.text:
Pure functions require immutable data. You cannot mutate inputs — you must return new values:

❌ Mutation:                        ✅ Non-Mutation:
┌─────────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────────┐
│ arr.push(item)      │            │ [...arr, item]      │
│                     │            │                     │
│ Same array,         │            │ New array,          │
│ modified.           │            │ original untouched. │
│                     │            │                     │
│ Caller's data is    │            │ Caller's data is    │
│ changed.            │            │ safe.               │
└─────────────────────┘            └─────────────────────┘

docs.title: Concept 1: Determinism
docs.text:
A pure function is deterministic — the same input always produces the same output. There is no randomness, no time dependency, and no external state that can change the result.

// ✅ Deterministic
function square(n) { return n * n; }

// ❌ Non-deterministic
function randomInRange(min, max) {
    return Math.random() * (max - min) + min;
}

docs.title: Concept 2: No Side Effects
docs.text:
A side effect is any observable interaction with the world outside the function. Pure functions have none of the following:

  • Modifying a global or static variable.
  • Modifying any of the arguments passed to the function.
  • Making HTTP calls or database queries.
  • Writing to disk, localStorage, or the DOM.
  • Logging to the console.
  • Calling Date.now(), Math.random(), or any non-deterministic function.
  • Throwing exceptions (in the strictest definition).

docs.title: Concept 3: Referential Transparency
docs.text:
A function is referentially transparent if any call to it can be replaced by its return value without changing the program.

// Pure — referentially transparent
const area = circleArea(5); // can be replaced with 78.539...

docs.title: Concept 4: Immutability
docs.text:
Pure functions do not mutate their inputs. Instead, they return new values. This is the foundation of immutable data management.

// ✅ Pure — returns a new array
const doubled = numbers.map(n => n * 2);

// ❌ Impure — mutates the input
numbers.forEach((n, i) => { numbers[i] = n * 2; });

docs.title: Concept 5: Dependency Injection for Purity
docs.text:
Impure dependencies — time, randomness, I/O — can be injected as parameters, making the function pure:

// ❌ Impure — depends on Date.now()
function isExpired(token) { return token.expiresAt < Date.now(); }

// ✅ Pure — time is injected
function isExpired(token, now) { return token.expiresAt < now; }

This is the dependency injection pattern for purifying impure functions.

docs.title: Concept 6: Pure Functions Enable Memoization
docs.text:
Because pure functions are deterministic, their results can be cached:

function memoize(fn) {
    const cache = new Map();
    return (...args) => {
        const key = JSON.stringify(args);
        if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);
        const result = fn(...args);
        cache.set(key, result);
        return result;
    };
}

Memoization only works for pure functions — impure functions produce different results for the same input.

docs.title: Concept 7: Pure Functions Enable Testing Without Mocks
docs.text:
Pure functions can be tested with just given → expect:

test("add returns the sum of two numbers", () => {
    expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5);
});

No mocking. No setup. No teardown.

docs.title: Concept 8: Pure Functions Enable Composition
docs.text:
Because pure functions have no hidden state, they compose freely:

const process = pipe(
    validateInput,
    normalizeData,
    transformData,
    formatOutput
);

Each step is independent. Each can be tested in isolation.

docs.title: Concept 9: Pure Functions and React
docs.text: React assumes every component is a pure function. "Same inputs, same output. Given the same inputs, a pure function should always return the same result". This is why React can efficiently re-render components — if the props haven't changed, the component's output hasn't changed.

docs.title: Concept 10: Pure Functions and Redux
docs.text: Redux reducers must be pure functions. "Does not perform side effects... does not call non-pure functions... does not mutate its arguments". This is what enables Redux DevTools' time-travel debugging — replaying the same actions produces the same state.

docs.title: Concept 11: Pure Functions and ES2023 Non-Mutating Array Methods
docs.text:
ES2023 added toSorted, toReversed, with, and toSpliced — non-mutating versions of sort, reverse, and index-based operations. These are the pure alternatives to their mutating counterparts.

Mutating Non-Mutating (ES2023) arr.sort() arr.toSorted() arr.reverse() arr.toReversed() arr[2] = x arr.with(2, x) arr.splice() arr.toSpliced()

docs.title: Concept 12: Pure Functions and structuredClone
docs.text:
For deep cloning without mutation, structuredClone() is the modern standard:

const clone = structuredClone(obj); // handles circular refs, preserves types

docs.title: Concept 13: Purity Is a Spectrum
docs.text: Not every function must be pure. The goal is to maximize purity in the core and isolate impurity at the edges. As one source notes: "Pure functions are great, but realistically they represent the limit to which our code should attempt to reach and not what most of our code should look like".

docs.title: Concept 14: Pure Functions and Asynchronous Code
docs.text:
Asynchronous functions are usually impure because they involve I/O — which is a side effect. However, the logic inside an async function can be pure:

// Impure shell — handles I/O
async function fetchAndProcess(url) {
    const response = await fetch(url);
    const data = await response.json();
    return processData(data); // pure core
}

// Pure core — deterministic logic
function processData(data) {
    return data.filter(item => item.active).map(item => item.name);
}

docs.title: Concept 15: ESLint Rules for Pure Functions
docs.text: Rule Purpose no-param-reassign Prevent mutation of function parameters functional/prefer-readonly-type Enforce readonly types (TypeScript) functional/no-let Prefer const over let functional/immutable-data Prevent mutating operations

docs.title: Concept 16: Pure Functions in TypeScript
docs.text:
TypeScript can enforce purity through readonly types:

function processItems(items: readonly Item[]): readonly Item[] {
    return items.filter(item => item.active);
}

readonly prevents mutation at compile time.

docs.title: Concept 17: Pure Functions and the V8 JIT
docs.text: V8's TurboFan compiler can inline pure functions aggressively. A function is easier to optimize when it is pure, small, and stable. Pure functions have a higher chance of inlining because they have no observable side effects that would prevent optimization.

docs.title: Concept 18: The 2026 Reality — Pragmatic Purity
docs.text: In 2026, the consensus is pragmatic purity: pure functions for business logic, impure functions at the boundaries. As one modern guide puts it: "Keep transforms pure, push I/O to the edge". The goal is not 100% purity — the goal is predictability where it matters.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Evaluating Purity
docs.text:
1.  Examine the function body.
    │
    ▼
2.  Does it read any external mutable state?
    │   - Global variables → impure
    │   - Closure over mutable variable → impure
    │   - Module-level mutable variable → impure
    │
    ▼
3.  Does it write any external state?
    │   - Modifies global → impure
    │   - Modifies argument → impure
    │   - I/O (console, DOM, network) → impure
    │   - Calls Date.now() or Math.random() → impure
    │
    ▼
4.  Does the same input always produce the same output?
    │   - If no → impure
    │   - If yes → pure

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Purifying an Impure Function
docs.text:
1.  Identify the impurity:
    │   - External state read
    │   - External state write
    │   - Non-deterministic dependency
    │
    ▼
2.  Make the dependency explicit:
    │   - Inject as parameter
    │   - Return a new value instead of mutating
    │
    ▼
3.  Verify purity:
    │   - Same input → same output
    │   - No side effects

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Testing a Pure Function
docs.text:
1.  Define input and expected output.
    │
    ▼
2.  Call the function with the input.
    │
    ▼
3.  Assert the output matches.
    │
    ▼
4.  Call again with the same input.
    │
    ▼
5.  Assert the output is identical.
    │
    ▼
6.  No mocks, no setup, no teardown.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Memoizing a Pure Function
docs.text:
1.  Create a cache (Map or object).
    │
    ▼
2.  When the function is called:
    │   - Compute a key from the arguments.
    │   - Check if the key is in the cache.
    │   - If yes → return cached value.
    │   - If no → compute, store, return.

docs.title: Purity in the ECMAScript Specification
docs.text:
The ECMAScript specification does not define "pure functions." There is no [[Pure]] internal slot, no pure keyword, and no purity enforcement. Purity is a convention, not a language feature.

However, the spec does define concepts that relate to purity:

  • [[Call]] — the internal method that executes a function.
  • [[Environment]] — the slot that holds a closure's captured scope.
  • Completion Records — how functions return values or throw exceptions.

None of these enforce purity. Purity is entirely the developer's responsibility.

docs.title: How V8 Optimizes Pure Functions
docs.text:
V8's TurboFan compiler can inline pure functions more aggressively than impure ones. A pure function has a higher chance of inlining because:

  1. No observable side effects — the compiler can reorder and eliminate calls without changing behavior.
  2. Deterministic — the compiler can constant-fold repeated calls.
  3. Small and stable — pure functions tend to be small and have stable type feedback.

V8 inlines functions that are pure, small, and stable — meeting these criteria maximizes the chance of optimization.

docs.title: The /*#__PURE__*/ Annotation
docs.text:
Bundlers like Rollup and webpack recognize the /*#__PURE__*/ comment annotation. A function call marked with this annotation is treated as pure — if its result is not used, the call can be dropped during tree-shaking:

const result = /*#__PURE__*/ expensiveCalculation();
// If `result` is unused, the entire call can be removed.

docs.title: Memory Layout of Pure Functions
docs.text:
Pure functions do not retain any external state — their memory footprint is limited to their parameters and local variables:

Pure Function:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [[Call]]           → bytecode      │
│  [[Environment]]    → outer scope   │
│                     (read-only)     │
│  [[FormalParameters]] → [a, b]      │
│  [[FunctionBody]]   → AST           │
│                                     │
│  No mutable state retained.         │
│  No side effects.                   │
│  Safe to inline, cache, or eliminate│
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The Cost of Impurity
docs.text:
Impure functions retain references to external state, which:

  1. Prevents garbage collection of captured variables.
  2. Prevents JIT inlining and constant folding.
  3. Prevents memoization (results change).
  4. Prevents safe parallelization.

docs.title: Pure Function Lifecycle
docs.text:
Written → Verified pure → Tested without mocks → Composed with other pure functions
    → Called → Returns deterministic output → No state changed

docs.title: Purification Workflow
docs.text:
Identify impure function
    │
    ▼
Identify impurity sources:
    ├── External state read → inject as parameter
    ├── External state write → return new value
    ├── Non-determinism → inject dependency
    └── I/O → isolate at boundary
    │
    ▼
Rewrite function
    │
    ▼
Verify purity (same input → same output)
    │
    ▼
Test without mocks

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Write business logic
    │
    ▼
Keep it pure:
    ├── No external reads
    ├── No external writes
    ├── No mutation
    └── Inject dependencies
    │
    ▼
Push I/O to the edges:
    ├── Fetch in the boundary layer
    ├── Pass data into pure core
    └── Write results at the boundary
    │
    ▼
Lint (ESLint no-param-reassign)
    │
    ▼
Type-check (TypeScript readonly)
    │
    ▼
Test (no mocks needed)

docs.title: Testing Workflow for Pure Functions
docs.text:
Define input
    │
    ▼
Call pure function
    │
    ▼
Assert output
    │
    ▼
Call again with same input
    │
    ▼
Assert identical output
    │
    ▼
Done — no mocks, no setup, no teardown

docs.title: Example 1: Pure Addition
docs.text:
function add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

console.log(add(2, 3)); // 5
console.log(add(2, 3)); // 5 — always

docs.title: Example 2: Impure Counter
docs.text:
let count = 0;

function increment() {
    return ++count;
}

console.log(increment()); // 1
console.log(increment()); // 2 — different output!

docs.title: Example 3: Pure vs. Impure Array Update
docs.text:
// ❌ Impure — mutates the input
function addItemImpure(cart, item) {
    cart.push(item);
    return cart;
}

// ✅ Pure — returns a new array
function addItemPure(cart, item) {
    return [...cart, item];
}

const cart = ["apple"];
addItemPure(cart, "banana");
console.log(cart); // ["apple"] — unchanged

docs.title: Example 4: Pure vs. Impure Object Update
docs.text:
// ❌ Impure — mutates the input
function activateImpure(user) {
    user.active = true;
    return user;
}

// ✅ Pure — returns a new object
function activatePure(user) {
    return { ...user, active: true };
}

const user = { name: "Ada", active: false };
activatePure(user);
console.log(user.active); // false — unchanged

docs.title: Example 5: Purifying with Dependency Injection
docs.text:
// ❌ Impure — depends on Date.now()
function isExpiredImpure(token) {
    return token.expiresAt < Date.now();
}

// ✅ Pure — time is injected
function isExpiredPure(token, now) {
    return token.expiresAt < now;
}

console.log(isExpiredPure({ expiresAt: 1000 }, 2000)); // true

docs.title: Example 6: Memoization
docs.text:
function memoize(fn) {
    const cache = new Map();
    return function(...args) {
        const key = JSON.stringify(args);
        if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);
        const result = fn(...args);
        cache.set(key, result);
        return result;
    };
}

const fibonacci = memoize(function fib(n) {
    return n <= 1 ? n : fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);
});

console.log(fibonacci(40)); // fast — cached

docs.title: Example 7: Pure Function Composition
docs.text:
const pipe = (...fns) => x => fns.reduce((acc, fn) => fn(acc), x);

const processUser = pipe(
    user => ({ ...user, name: user.name.trim() }),
    user => ({ ...user, name: user.name.toUpperCase() }),
    user => ({ ...user, active: true })
);

console.log(processUser({ name: "  ada  " }));
// { name: "ADA", active: true }

docs.title: Example 8: Testing a Pure Function
docs.text:
// Pure function
function calculateDiscount(price, discountRate) {
    return price * (1 - discountRate);
}

// Test — no mocks needed
test("calculateDiscount applies the discount rate", () => {
    expect(calculateDiscount(100, 0.1)).toBe(90);
    expect(calculateDiscount(100, 0.1)).toBe(90); // same input, same output
});

docs.title: Example 9: React Pure Component
docs.text:
function UserCard({ name, role }) {
    return (
        <div className="user-card">
            <h3>{name}</h3>
            <p>{role}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

// Same props → same JSX. Always.

docs.title: Example 10: Redux Pure Reducer
docs.text:
function todosReducer(state = [], action) {
    switch (action.type) {
        case "ADD_TODO":
            return [...state, action.payload]; // new array
        case "REMOVE_TODO":
            return state.filter(todo => todo.id !== action.payload); // new array
        default:
            return state;
    }
}

// Same state + action → same new state. Always.

docs.title: Example 11: ES2023 Non-Mutating Array Methods
docs.text:
const numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5];

// ❌ Mutating
// numbers.sort(); // original array changed

// ✅ Non-mutating (ES2023)
const sorted = numbers.toSorted((a, b) => a - b);
const reversed = numbers.toReversed();
const replaced = numbers.with(2, 99);

console.log(numbers); // [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] — unchanged

docs.title: Example 12: Structured Clone for Deep Copy
docs.text:
const original = { a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } };
const copy = structuredClone(original);

copy.nested.b = 99;
console.log(original.nested.b); // 2 — unchanged

docs.title: 10. Common Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Pure Function? Business calculations ✅ Yes Data transformation ✅ Yes Validation logic ✅ Yes Formatting (dates, numbers, text) ✅ Yes Reducers (Redux) ✅ Yes (required) React components ✅ Yes (expected) Array methods (map, filter, reduce) ✅ Yes HTTP requests ❌ No — side effect DOM manipulation ❌ No — side effect Logging ❌ No — side effect Random number generation ❌ No — non-deterministic Reading Date.now() ❌ No — non-deterministic Writing to localStorage ❌ No — side effect

docs.title: 11. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Default to pure functions for business logic. Why: predictable, testable, composable.
  2. Push side effects to the edges of the application. Why: keep the core pure.
  3. Use const by default. Why: prevents accidental mutation.
  4. Use spread syntax ([...arr], {...obj}) instead of mutation. Why: returns new values.
  5. Use ES2023 non-mutating array methods (toSorted, toReversed, with, toSpliced). Why: pure alternatives to mutating methods.
  6. Inject dependencies (time, randomness, I/O) as parameters. Why: purifies impure functions.
  7. Use readonly in TypeScript for input arrays and objects. Why: compile-time enforcement of purity.
  8. Use structuredClone() for deep copies. Why: avoids mutation of nested objects.
  9. Test pure functions without mocks. Why: given → expect is enough.
  10. Memoize expensive pure functions. Why: deterministic results can be cached.
  11. Use the /*#__PURE__*/ annotation for bundler tree-shaking. Why: allows dead code elimination.
  12. Keep pure functions small and focused. Why: easier to test and optimize.
